## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of all the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority and force in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in what places of their works they did so. The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one weighs the neatness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient form of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical scholarship. The Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition, comprising 1,200 volumes, is sold for 1,000 francs; the Greek-Latin edition, comprising 800 volumes, for 1,300 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the year of the Lord 1085

## Pope Saint Gregory VII of Rome

[Col. 0009]

## Prolegomena

### Eulogy from the Roman Martyrology

At Salerno, the burial of blessed Gregory VII, the most zealous champion and defender of the liberty of the Church.

### Legend from the Roman Breviary

[Col. 0009A]

### Lesson IV

Pope Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, was born at Soana in Etruria. Eminent above all for learning, holiness, and every kind of virtue, he wonderfully enlightened the whole Church of God.

When, as a little child still ignorant of letters, he was playing at the feet of a craftsman carving wood, he is said nevertheless to have accidentally formed from the discarded chips those letters of the Davidic oracle, “He shall rule from sea to sea,” with divine Providence guiding the boy’s hand. By this it was signified that the most extensive authority in the world would belong to him.

He then went to Rome and was brought up under the protection of Saint Peter. As a young man, deeply grieving over the liberty of the Church, oppressed by laymen, and over the corrupted morals of ecclesiastics, he put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Cluny, where at that time the observance of a stricter life under the Rule of Saint [Col. 0009B] Benedict was flourishing most strongly. He served the divine majesty with such ardor of devotion that he was elected prior by the holy fathers of that monastery.

But since divine providence was arranging greater things through him for the salvation of many, Hildebrand was brought out of Cluny and first elected abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls; afterward he was made a cardinal of the Roman Church. Under the supreme pontiffs Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II, he discharged important offices and legations. Blessed Peter Damian called him a man of the most holy and purest counsel.

Sent by Pope Victor II as a legate *a latere* [Col. 0009C] to Gaul, at Lyons he compelled a bishop infected with the plague of simony to confess his crime by a miracle; at the Council of Tours he forced Berengar to abjure his heresy a second time; and by his own strength he also suppressed the schism of Cadalus.

### Lesson V

After the death of Alexander II, he was elected supreme pontiff, unwilling and grieving, by the unanimous consent of all, on the tenth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0010A] May—that is, 22 April—in the year of Christ 1073. He shone like the sun in the house of God. Powerful in deed and word, he devoted himself with such zeal to restoring ecclesiastical discipline, propagating the faith, restoring the liberty of the Church, and uprooting errors and corruptions, that from the age of the Apostles no pontiff is said to have endured greater labors and hardships for the Church of God, or to have fought more fiercely for her liberty.

He purged several provinces of the stain of simony. Against the impious efforts of the emperor Henry he remained in every respect a courageous athlete, fearless, and did not hesitate to set himself as a wall before the house of Israel. He deprived that same Henry, who had fallen into the depths of evil, of the communion of the faithful [Col. 0010B] and of his kingdom, and freed the subject peoples from the oath of fidelity they had given him.

### Lesson VI

While he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, devout men saw a dove descend from heaven, settle upon his right shoulder, and, with outstretched wings, cover his head. This signified that, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he was guided in the government of the Church, not by calculations of human prudence.

When Rome was being hard-pressed by a severe siege from the army of the wicked Henry, he extinguished a fire kindled by the enemies by the sign of the cross. At last rescued from his hands by Robert Guiscard, the Norman duke, he withdrew to Cassino and from there hastened to Salerno to dedicate the church of the Apostle Saint Matthew.

When on one occasion he had addressed the people in that city, he fell [Col. 0010C] ill, exhausted by sufferings, and foresaw that he would die of the illness. The last words of the dying Gregory were: “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.”

Countless are the things that this truly holy man, avenger of crimes and most zealous defender of the Church [Col. 0011A], either courageously endured or wisely established after convoking many synods in the city. Thus, after completing twelve years in the pontificate, he departed to heaven in the year of salvation 1085, distinguished by many miracles both during his life and after his death [Col. 0012A]. His sacred body was honorably buried in the cathedral basilica at Salerno.

# Acts of Saint Gregory VII

*(In Bolland, May, volume V, day 25, page 568.)*

[Col. 0011]

## Preliminary commentary

### § I. The deceased’s praisers and defenders; the Life written by Paul of Bernried; three pontifical Acts

[Col. 0011B]

The most holy and generous Roman pontiff Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, died on 25 May 1085. He governed the whole Church for twelve years, one month, and four days—that is, reckoned from 22 April 1073, as is plainly established by the decree of election to be presented below.

Those have been mistaken who wish him to have been elected only on the 25th of that month, taking the occasion for their error from catalogues in which the death of his predecessor, who died three days before that election, is confused with his burial.

During his life he suffered many persecutions, and after his death he continued to suffer calumnies. Yet there were not lacking very zealous defenders of his innocence, courage, and justice in defending the Church of God [Col. 0011C]. Among them may be counted Cardinal Caesar Baronius and Jacob Gretser.

Baronius did so in his *Ecclesiastical Annals*, in which he traces his deeds year by year from writers who were chiefly contemporaries, from the councils held under him, and from his Register of Letters, divided into eleven books.

Gretser did so in volume 2 of Cardinal Bellarmine’s *Defense of the Controversies*, defending him against various sectarians of the period, especially in book 4, chapter 13, and afterward in a notable *Apology*, in which he adduces fifty witnesses who present in their writings the deeds of this Saint Gregory and defend him against his adversaries.

[Col. 0011D]

2. The first of these is Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, who died in the year immediately following the death of the holy pontiff. Against Guibert the antipope, and in defense of Gregory the legitimate pontiff, he wrote a book.

The second witness is the domestic priest and penitentiary who wrote the Life of that Saint Anselm; we illustrated this Life on his feast day, 18 March.

Next come the Vatican Acts cited by Baronius under the year 1073, and the public Acts of the election, which are presented below.

Then are cited the ancient historians or chroniclers, among whom is Lambert of Hersfeld, *On the Deeds of the Germans*, though his account extends only to the year 1077 and the fourth year of Saint Gregory’s pontificate; then Paul Langius in the *Chronicle of Citiz*, with testimonies drawn from the Magdeburg Annals and the Thuringian Chronicles; also Marianus Scotus and his continuator Dodechin, and Stephen, bishop of Halberstadt, produced by Dodechin, who pursued Gregory’s cause with the greatest vigor against King Henry.

Next comes Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, whose Acts we published on 21 April; then Berthold of Constance and Paul of Bernried, about whom we shall speak shortly; Domnizo the priest, in his two books of verse on the Life of Countess Matilda; Leo of Ostia, in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, carried down to the year 1086; Bruno in the *History of the Saxon War*; Saint Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg, and Saint Gebhard, bishop of Constance, together with those who wrote their Lives, which we shall publish in due time, on 16 June and 27 [Col. 0012C] August.

Finally, omitting others, there is Bernald, priest of Constance, whose little works were published from a Regensburg manuscript by the aforementioned Gretser and deal almost entirely with defending the deeds of Saint Gregory—especially his *Apology* and his Letters in defense of the decrees of Saint Gregory. Christian Lupus also learnedly expounded these among the decrees and canons of the general and provincial synods, in an entire book or fifth part.

To all these the highly praised Gretser added the Life, election, and deeds of Gregory VII, drawn from book four of Onuphrius Panvinius’s *On the Various Elections of the Supreme Pontiff* and from the Bavarian Library. All these may be consulted in the edition published at Ingolstadt in 1609. There he published the following year [Col. 0012D] an *Apology for Cardinal Baronius*, in which several chapters concern the controversy raised in the case of Saint Gregory, as the curious reader will find there.

Francis d’Enghien, a Dominican and licentiate in sacred theology, also deserves to be read. He recently published a book entitled *The Authority of the Apostolic See Vindicated for Pope Gregory VII against Natalis Alexander, Doctor of Theology of the Same Order*, among the selected chapters of Ecclesiastical History, century II, part 3. In dealing with Gregory, he forgot his profession so completely that, for this reason alone, he may have deserved the extremely severe censure by which all his books were struck by Pope Innocent XI.

3. Omitting all others, we present here first [Col. 0013A] the Life of Saint Gregory written by Paul of Bernried.

Paul had been a canon of the Church of Regensburg. But after being driven into exile by Henry IV, he received the habit of the Order of Regular Canons in the recently founded monastery of Bernried. Around the year 1120 he was ordained a priest by Ulrich, bishop of Passau, who governed that church from 1091 until 1124. Seven years after that bishop’s death, Paul completed this Life, around the year 1131.

Gretser, who published it together with his *Apology for Cardinal Baronius*, believes that “when Paul was at Rome, he was a familiar of Pope Callistus II,” who occupied the see from 4 February 1119 until 12 December 1124 and confirmed the foundation of the monastery of Bernried in 1122. On that occasion Paul may have gone to Rome [Col. 0013B]. In section 11 below he reports that “Pope Callistus was accustomed to relate that a bishop elected by simony had been unable to recite ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.’”

Likewise, in section 16 he says that “John, formerly chamberlain of Pope Alexander II, was accustomed to relate” that through the prayers of Saint Alexander a burning fever had been driven away. Here and there he inserts various miracles performed during Gregory’s lifetime. But in section 104 he reserves for those who are nearer to them the miracles “performed by heaven at his tomb, or which the more devout Romans say are performed.”

Nevertheless, at the end, in section 114, he adds “an appended account of two miracles performed by heaven at Salerno.” From this we infer the author’s great diligence in reporting everything accurately [Col. 0013C]. Anyone may likewise infer it who examines the annotations we add and compares them with the other authors, as well as with Gregory’s letters and the synods held at that time.

Everything agrees completely, especially where the discussion concerns the Simoniacs and the Nicolaitans, that is, fornicator-clerics. Blessed Peter Damian also frequently calls those men Nicolaitans whose deeds Christ says in chapter 2 of Saint John’s Apocalypse that he hates. Concerning them, the letter of Saint Ignatius to the Trallians—though interpolated by later writers—contains these words: “Flee the most filthy Nicolaitans, falsely so called, lovers of lust and wicked slanderers.”

4. In these Acts, moreover, the Preface is missing, although the opening words imply that it was present. Paul also omitted what took place in the condemnation of Berengar carried out by Saint Gregory, and he explains more briefly the events worthy of report and knowledge during the Roman siege, repeatedly renewed by Henry.

Furthermore, since the author intended to compose a history, not a chronicle, he did not take care to preserve the order of time scrupulously, nor did he explain what he did in the celebrated synods during each year of his pontificate.

I therefore judged it appropriate to append three pontifical Acts. The first we shall gather from Berthold of Constance, who, as stated below in section 18, was ordained a priest in 1084, on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle, by Otho, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, afterward himself supreme pontiff under the name Urban II. This was five months before Saint Gregory’s death. Berthold himself recorded the individual events of his time and appended them to the Chronicle of Hermann the Lame as far as the year 1100.

At the same time, and with no less certain, if not more certain, knowledge, were written the Acts that Cencius the chamberlain—whom Ciacconius believes to be the same man who was made pope in 1216 and took the name Honorius III—reported in the *Book of Censuses of the Roman Church*, preserved in a very large volume in the secret Vatican Archive.

Our fathers, John Francis Vannius and Conrad Janning, obtained a copy of it through the favor of D. Saraiga, keeper of that archive, and compared it with the text previously transcribed from a codex of the Vatican Library.

This codex, often praised by Baronius and beginning the deeds of the pontiffs with Leo IX, was “arranged and caused to be written,” as its title states, “from various registers and books of the Apostolic Chamber by Brother Nicholas, Cardinal of Aragon.” It therefore falls between the year 1352, when he was created cardinal, and 1362, when he died.

He was a distinguished glory of the Order of Preachers, known to Ciacconius and his interpolators under the name Nicholas Rosselli. He was called “of Aragon” from his homeland, and because, while provincial of Aragon, he was promoted to the purple at the urging of King Peter, to whom he was especially dear.

Finally, we have decided to transcribe a third set of Acts, in many respects fuller and more precise, and not much more recent—or perhaps even older—than the second, from our manuscript of the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, carried down to Martin V.

For the greater part, these Acts are taken from the Register of Letters, which contains summaries of nearly all the synods Gregory celebrated at Rome. Baronius first extracted these summaries from the Register; Binius received them from Baronius and included them in the body of the councils.

Perhaps someone will later undertake to trace and collect in greater detail, from the letters of this Saint Gregory themselves—of which the Register contains more than three hundred and fifty—the individual deeds of this holy pontiff. This would be like what John the Deacon once did from the letters of Saint Gregory the Great, which our Henschenius illustrated on 12 March; or, rather, like the Acts of Saint Leo, equally the Great, collected and arranged from his letters by the most learned Paschasius Quesnel. For us there is presently no leisure for such a task.

Natalis Alexander did something of this kind in century 11, part 1, where he deserved better of Gregory than elsewhere. Our Cornelius Hazart also did so in German in his *Triumph of the Roman Pontiffs*, in which, as a perpetual hammer of heretics in Belgium, he refuted with lucid arguments their monstrous calumnies concerning this and the other pontiffs.

5. Let this paragraph concerning the writers who collected, defended, and praised Gregory’s Acts conclude with the notable letter of William, abbot of the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz, after Warinus. It has already been published in the first volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, but deserves to be reprinted here because it more clearly explains the hopes that all good men conceived when they heard the news of such an election.

It reads as follows:

“W. the sinner to the venerable and universal Lord Pope G., an expression of devoted prayer and an act of humble service.

“Although the wisdom of God governs all things made through it with wondrous arrangement and unshakable order, it never consults human affairs more advantageously than when, choosing a man [or: one man] from the people, it sets him over his own people as their head, so that in his life and conduct the lower people may behold what they ought to strive toward.

“Whoever is not envious sees that the Lord has granted this benefit to our times, since he has made you, long trained in ecclesiastical disciplines, now the occupant of that Chair from which all the lights of virtue are spread throughout the world, and toward which all things converge like lines in a circle toward that central point which geometers call the center.

“Such, as we have been told, was the agreement of the whole people in your election, that no one at all in so great a multitude appeared to dissent. And from where, I ask, could such unanimity and harmony have arisen, except from the prompting of that Spirit by whose ancient inspiration the primitive people of believers are described as having one heart and one soul?

6. “Thanks therefore to God, most excellent Father; thanks to God, who so favored your election that the Church did not fall into schism.

“Whoever now opposes your priesthood, whatever merit or learning he may appear to possess, does not aspire to that heavenly building, because through the fault of pride and discord he deprives himself of the peace of all the members.

“We trust that no one will dare do this except one who, mindful of his wretched conscience, fears that the weight of your sentence hangs over him.

“Hence that devil of Vercelli and his accomplices are striving to prevent your confirmation in the See, the wretch fearing that, through the zeal with which you customarily burn against the enemies of the Church, his crimes, his disgrace, and his shame may now be condemned.

“Yet you please all good men all the more because you displease the wicked; for it is no small or insignificant testimony of uprightness to have displeased the children of iniquity.”

Thus wrote Abbot William, vividly depicting the Vercellian Gregory, unworthy of that name, chancellor of the Emperor Henry in Italy. He had already been excommunicated by Pope Nicholas, in the year 1061, together with the bishops of Milan, Turin, Novara, Brescia, and Lodi, because two years earlier they had held an assembly at Fontaneto at which they had decided by common agreement that clerics might have wives.

Nevertheless, at Henry’s command he approved Gregory’s election, more with his pen than in his heart, as is clear even from this letter, which William continues as follows:

“Now therefore gird your sword upon your thigh, most powerful one—the sword, I say, which the Prophet declares must not be withheld from blood, and which the Lord mercifully promises will devour flesh.

“You surely see the Amalekites and Midianites in the Israelite camp, together with all the other plagues, conspiring at once. Great vigilance, profound counsel, and constant effort are needed if so many monsters and beasts are to be either slaughtered or subdued.

“Therefore let no fear of anyone and no threat of anyone delay you from this spiritual conflict and holy contest. As that Gideon did, when you go forth to battle, do not fear the breaking of the pitchers.

“Behold, placed on high and set upon a watchtower, you are observed by the eyes and faces of all. Everyone desires to hear great things about you, gathering from the past what you will now do in the greater office, since formerly, placed in the lesser, you served with no little glory.

“But foolish am I to presume to admonish you and to try to impel one who is already running, since with wondrous fervor you are undertaking greater things than our weakness imagines; and, flying over all things below like an eagle, you strive to fix your gaze upon the very radiance of the sun.”

## § II. The translation of the body and the cult of Blessed Gregory VII

[Col. 0016B]

7. Marcus Antonius Marsilius Columna, proclaimed archbishop of Salerno in 1574, besides the other works of episcopal care by which he made the fourteen years of his prelacy memorable to posterity, composed a book on the life, deeds, and translation of the blessed Apostle and Evangelist Matthew.

We have not yet seen the book itself, but know it from the elegant description of his metropolitan church which Ferdinand Ughelli extracted from it and prefixed to the catalogue of the archbishops of Salerno in volume 7 of *Sacred Italy*.

After describing the tribune, or apse, of the church, Marsilius speaks as follows:

“The corner made on the right at the lower end of the church has been made truly illustrious by the splendid chapel of mosaic work which John of Procida of Salerno erected and endowed; by the magnificent urns of several prelates; and especially by the marble tomb in which Robert Guiscard placed the body of Gregory VII, that supreme and most excellent pontiff whom he had received as a fugitive guest, in order to withdraw him from the treachery of Henry IV and the Romans.

“We ourselves this year, which is nearly the five-hundredth from his burial, saw with our own eyes and touched with our own hands his relics, wholly undamaged and clothed in pontifical garments. We restored the place itself, almost collapsed through age, and, in honor of the most holy and noble pontiff [Col. 0016D], whose honor had almost been hidden, erected this monument”—the monument that may still be seen on a marble tablet and is also quoted by Louis Jacob in the *Pontifical Library*—“to Gregory VII of Soana, Supreme and Best Pontiff, most zealous defender and steadfast champion of ecclesiastical liberty:

“‘While he was vigorously defending the authority of the Roman pontiff against the treachery of Henry, he died a holy death at Salerno in the year of the Lord 1085, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

“‘M. Antonius Columna Marsilius, Bolognese, archbishop of Salerno, having found the body of that pontiff, after approximately five hundred years, clothed in sacred vestments and almost intact, erected this monument so that the tomb of so great a pontiff might no longer lack remembrance, under Gregory XIII of Bologna, on the day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord 1577.’”

[Col. 0017A]

8. Robert Guiscard, founder of the Norman duchies in Calabria and Sicily, later the kingdom, died in July of the same year as Gregory, or at least the following year. His son Roger succeeded him and survived until 1101.

The erection of the marble tomb might perhaps more properly be attributed to Roger. For Orderic Vitalis, a twelfth-century writer of ecclesiastical history, seems to indicate in book 8 that the Saint was first buried elsewhere. He speaks as follows:

“The body of the deceased pope was buried in the Confession of the blessed Apostle Bartholomew, where divine power displayed an abundance of miracles for the merits of those who sought them in faith. Lepers asked for the water with which his body had been washed; after obtaining it, they washed themselves in faith and, with God’s help, were immediately cleansed.”

This perhaps occurred when the body was transferred from the place of its first burial to the Confession itself, to the place where, nearly two hundred years after Gregory’s death, John Procida—famous author of the Sicilian Vespers—found his tomb.

I do not know what other reason that chapel could have had for being built so magnificently on the very site of the tomb, apart from a special affection for the pontiff buried there, based on the popular belief in his holiness and miracles—although the chapel itself was dedicated to Saint Michael the Archangel, not to Gregory.

Nor is it irrelevant to establishing his ancient cult that Pope Anastasius IV, not many more than sixty years after Gregory, when decorating with paintings the apse and altar of the Oratory of Saint Nicholas in the City—as I have shown in a bronze plate in the appendix to the first part of my *Chronico-historical Attempt concerning the Roman Pontiffs*—had Gregory VII painted, together with the other saints and the Mother of God, with the title “Saint” and a halo drawn around his head.

But since these matters were either entirely unknown or uncertain to Marsilius, he prudently refrained from using such a title and considered that he ought to await the judgment of the Roman See.

I do not know whether, or in what way, that judgment was declared to him. I see only this: after six years had passed from the discovery mentioned above and Marsilius had died, Gregory XIII, while arranging in 1584 for the Roman Martyrology also to be corrected by learned men along with the corrected Calendar, and for it to be printed corrected and enlarged in many places—the copy of which is in our possession—allowed Gregory VII to be inserted after Saint Boniface IV with this eulogy:

“At Salerno, the burial of blessed Gregory VII, pope, who, succeeding Alexander II, vindicated ecclesiastical liberty in his time from the pride of princes and defended it manfully by pontifical authority.”

In a new edition of the same Martyrology, soon enlarged by the annotations of Cardinal Caesar Baronius and approved by Sixtus V, this was written instead:

“At Salerno, the burial of blessed Gregory VII, pope, the most zealous champion and defender of ecclesiastical liberty.”

This wording has remained to the present.

9. From this point the feast of Blessed Gregory began to be celebrated by the canons of Salerno, who were deeply indebted to the memory of that holy pontiff because he had honored them with the cardinalitial title and granted them the privilege of using a red mantle and Damascene mitre, a privilege later confirmed by Lucius III.

Meanwhile the sacred body remained either in the monument where Archbishop Marsilius had found it, or, after being removed from there, was kept in the sacristy until the Roman pontiff should consent to its burial beneath an altar.

The author of the most recent marble monument, which was under the sculptor’s hand in 1685, asserts that this first took place in 1595; this will bring the present paragraph to a close.

At that time the Roman pontiff was Clement VIII, whose rescript I would wish to produce. The archbishop of Salerno was Marius Bolognini. If he carried out the aforesaid translation, he may also have separated the sacred head from the rest of the body, to be enclosed in a silver head and placed upon a costly statue made of gilded bronze and adorned with gems and stones.

This took place on 4 May, the day on which the Church of Salerno thereafter undertook to celebrate the aforesaid translation annually. On that day, and also on 25 May, it was customary to carry the said head from the sacristy to that altar in a solemn procession, with a great display of lights and a gathering of the people.

Some, however, make Archbishop Marsilius himself the author of this translation. He is said to have died in 1582, and therefore the translation would have preceded the aforementioned edition of the Gregorian Martyrology by two years.

Yet two editions of the Martyrology had also preceded that one, although Baronius did not take care to tell us their dates. Either or both of them could have been enlarged with the name of Gregory VII before Marsilius carried out the translation—if indeed he was the one who carried it out.

10. By these stages the cult of Blessed Gregory VII gradually advanced and was finally raised to the celebration of a Double Office specifically devoted to him, under John Bellarmine, the successor of Bolognini.

From him a Brief was obtained and ordered to be printed for the knowledge and use of all the clergy of Salerno in 1610. To receive a copy of it, together with several other relevant instructions, in notarized form and under notarized authentication, the Reverend Lord Nicolaus Lavianus, rector of our Salernitan College in 1685, took care to provide it.

It is as follows:

[Col. 0018D]

## Paul V, pope, for perpetual remembrance

“Although we undeservedly exercise on earth the place of our Lord Jesus Christ, who rewards his servants with eternal glory in heaven, we are altogether bound, by the duty of the office entrusted to us, to ensure that the honor and veneration of those servants of Christ also be advanced on earth. Therefore we willingly grant the requests of the faithful that concern a particular cult directed toward them, insofar as we discern in the Lord that this is expedient.

“Indeed, it has recently been represented to us, in the name of Brother John, archbishop of Salerno, and of our beloved sons the dean and chapter of the church, as well as the entire clergy of the city of Salerno, that, because of the particular devotion they bear toward Blessed Gregory, Pope VII, whose unworthy successor divine providence has willed us to be, they desire, with a particular rite, on his feast day and on the day sacred to his translation, to recite concerning the same Blessed Gregory the most sacred Mass and the other divine Offices in the form that follows.”

### Double Office to be recited annually by the chapter and clergy of the city of Salerno on the feast day and on the day of the translation of Blessed Gregory VII

Everything is taken from the Common of a Confessor Pontiff, except for what is supplied as proper.

### Prayer

“O God, who exalted Blessed Gregory, your Confessor and Pontiff, with the glory of your saints: mercifully grant that we, who are weighed down by the burden of our sins, may be lifted up by his prayers before you. Through the Lord,” etc.

Let there be a commemoration of Saint Urban, pope and martyr, at First Vespers and at Lauds, whenever he occurs [Col. 0019B], and at Matins, Lesson IX.

Likewise, at Second Vespers, of Saint Eleutherius, pope and martyr.

11. At Matins, in the first Nocturn, the lessons are taken from the beginning of the Second Epistle of Blessed Peter the Apostle, as found in the Roman Breviary for the Friday within the Octave of the Ascension. In the second Nocturn:

**LESSON IV.** Gregory VII, Pope, born at Soana in Etruria, exceptionally distinguished in learning, holiness, and every kind of virtue, wondrously enlightened the whole Church of God; and he was granted, in an admirable manner, to foreshadow the supreme dignity of His priesthood on earth—He who is “admirable in His saints.” For, when still a little child, he is said to have been playing at the feet of a craftsman shaping wood, already ignorant of letters; yet from the discarded [Col. 0019C] scraps he is said by divine providence to have fashioned the words of David’s oracle, “He shall rule from sea to sea.” From early youth he cultivated his mind at Rome in honorable disciplines and was brought up in the household of Saint Peter, worthy of such a nurturer and foster-son: so that, since by God’s favor he was one day to receive that household’s highest authority, having been educated in the bosom of the Apostle himself, he might be more fully imbued with those apostolic virtues that he afterward displayed in exercising the supreme pontificate. But thou, O Lord, etc.

12. **LESSON V.** As a young man, grieving intensely over the liberty of the Church, oppressed by laymen, and over the corrupted morals of ecclesiastics, he put on the monastic habit at the Monastery of Cluny, where at that time the observance of a more austere life under the Rule of Saint Benedict was flourishing most vigorously. He served the Divine Majesty there with such ardor of piety that he was elected prior by the holy Fathers of that monastery. Soon afterward, Pope Saint Leo IX brought him to Rome, since a shining and burning lamp ought not to remain hidden in the narrow confines of the cloister but, by God’s command, was to be placed upon the Church’s highest summit; he was ordained Subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church and became so dear to Saint Leo and his successors that they undertook nothing without his counsel. Sent by Pope Victor II as a legate *a latere* to Gaul, he divinely convicted a bishop publicly infected with the taint of simony, since he could not be convicted by human means. When the bishop was ordered to pronounce aloud, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” he readily pronounced the names of the two divine Persons, but was utterly unable to utter the name of the third, [Col. 0020A] whose gift—the episcopate—he had purchased with money. But thou, O Lord.

13. **LESSON VI.** Finally, created Cardinal Archdeacon by Pope Nicholas II and likewise Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church by Alexander II, he merited to succeed the latter in the supreme pontificate. Raised to the summit of so great an honor, he became already a model for the flock; and what he taught in word he also demonstrated by example. A strong athlete in every respect, he did not fear to set himself as a wall for the house of Israel. He deprived Henry IV, King of Germany, hostile to the Church, of the communion of the faithful and of his kingdom, and freed the subject peoples from the faith they had pledged to him. Later, when he was being hard-pressed at Rome by a severe siege from the army of the wicked king, he extinguished a fire kindled by the enemy by the sign of the Cross; [Col. 0020B] and he was illustrious through other miracles as well, both during his life and after his death. From the age of the Apostles, no pontiff is said to have endured greater labors and hardships for the Church of God, or to have fought more fiercely for her freedom. Innumerable are the things that he either courageously endured or wisely decreed in many synods convened in the City. At last rescued from the hands of Henry by Robert Guiscard, Duke of the Normans, he came to Salerno and there, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, after having presided over the Church for twelve years, one month, and three days, and after creating numerous cardinals and bishops at Rome and elsewhere, he departed to the Lord on a Sunday. His sacred body was honorably buried in the cathedral basilica of Salerno. [Col. 0020C] But thou, O Lord, etc.

In the third Nocturn, the lessons are taken from a homily of Pope Saint Leo on the Gospel, “Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi,” which the Roman Breviary contains for 22 February, the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch.

14. The Mass is said according to that assigned in the Roman Missal for 11 April, the feast of Saint Leo, Pope, except for the Collects.

**FIRST COLLECT.** “O God, who [ . . . ] Blessed Gregory, etc.,” as above.

**SECRET.** “May the annual solemnity of Gregory, thy Confessor and Pontiff, we beseech thee, O Lord, render us [to thee] acceptable; so that through these dutiful offices of reconciliation, blessed recompense may accompany him and win for us the gifts of thy grace. Through our Lord.

**POST-COMMUNION.** Grant, we beseech thee, O Lord, that the faithful people may always rejoice in the veneration of thy Confessor and Pontiff, Blessed Gregory, and be protected by his perpetual [Col. 0020D] intercession. Through our Lord, etc.

15. “And since both John, Archbishop, and the aforementioned Dean, Chapter, and Clergy caused us humbly to be petitioned that, in our Apostolic kindness, we might deign to provide them with the appropriate permission in the matters aforesaid; we, greatly commending their laudable desire in the Lord, and absolving each of them by this document—and declaring them to be absolved—for the sole purpose of obtaining the effects herein contained, from any excommunications, suspensions, interdicts, and other ecclesiastical sentences, censures, and penalties, imposed by law or by human authority for whatever occasion or cause, if they are in any way bound by them; yielding to such petitions, with the counsel of our venerable brethren, the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, prefects of the sacred rites, whom we commissioned to examine and carefully discuss the matter, we grant and bestow by the authority of the Apostolic See, by these presents, perpetual permission and faculty [Col. 0021A] to the same Archbishop of Salerno, and to the Dean and Chapter of the Church, and to the Clergy of the City of Salerno, both those now existing and those who shall exist in the future, freely and lawfully to recite each year, under the double rite, the aforesaid Office with the Mass from the Common of One Pontiff, together with the Collects and the proper lessons of the second Nocturn, on the feast days both of Blessed Gregory himself and of his Translation.

“Notwithstanding Apostolic constitutions and ordinances, as well as statutes and customs of the aforesaid Church, even those strengthened by Apostolic confirmation under oath or by any other force, and all other contrary provisions whatsoever. [Col. 0021B]

“Given at Rome, at Saint Mark’s, under the Fisherman’s Ring, on 18 July 1609, in the fifth year of our pontificate.” S. Cobellutius.

16. “John Beltranus de Guevara, by the mercy of God and the grace of the Apostolic See Archbishop of Salerno, Royal Counsellor, and at present General Visitor in the Kingdom of Naples on behalf of His Sacred Royal Majesty: among the other heavenly and almost innumerable treasures with which it has pleased divine kindness to enrich and illuminate the Church of Salerno, the sacred and venerable body of Saint Gregory VII must certainly be counted not in the last place. [Col. 0021C] After so many labors, so many hardships and persecutions, endured with the greatest courage and steadfastness for the Church of God, he at last—by the disposition of divine Providence—fell asleep in the Lord in the city of Salerno; so that the Church which he had gladdened for a time in his mortal body by his venerable presence, he might also illuminate forever by his precious death, having been summoned to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

“We, although unworthy, placed in charge of the Church of Salerno, when visiting places dedicated to the Divine Majesty carefully examined the monument of the aforesaid glorious Pontiff in our own cathedral basilica, and could not bear with an untroubled mind that he should lack the honor and veneration due to the heavenly ones. We therefore judged that a diploma must be diligently obtained from the Apostolic See, [Col. 0021D] so that suitable honor might be shown to the holy Pontiff by all, and so that the city of Salerno might daily merit more and more the clemency of God, aided by the intercession of so distinguished a Confessor and Pontiff, especially pleasing to God.

“Nor do we think that we should pass over in silence that consideration which no antiquity and no forgetfulness among you ought ever to erase: namely, that since the Chapter of Salerno received great honors from the same Blessed Pontiff—as our predecessor of blessed memory, Marsilius, recorded in writing—you ought to devote yourselves eagerly and with every effort to the worship and veneration of him who deserved so well of you. [Col. 0022A]

“Therefore, desiring at this time to execute piously and faithfully the diploma recently obtained from the Apostolic See, by the authority with which we are invested we command and enjoin our beloved sons in Christ, the Chapter and Clergy of our city of Salerno, that each year, in accordance with the tenor of the aforesaid diploma, both on 25 May, when the Nativity of Saint Gregory the Pope is celebrated, and on 4 May, when the feast of his Translation is celebrated, they shall henceforth be bound to sing or recite, under the double rite, the proper Mass and Office printed by our command for the honor of that glorious Pontiff.

“But if anyone should disdain to obey this constitution of ours, which shall remain perpetually valid, let him know that he has bound himself by the chain of a grave fault before the dread tribunal of Almighty God.

“Given at Salerno, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, 1610.”

[Col. 0022B]

17. Not content with this, Beltraminius had an excellent marble statue sculpted, which still exists today, and had it placed in the chapel, employing the hand of a skilled sculptor. I do not know whether it may even preserve a true likeness of the living Gregory, such as could have been preserved at Salerno. Certainly such a likeness would deserve to be represented here in an engraving, rather than the invention of I. B. de Cavalleriis, who portrayed Gregory and his immediate predecessors and successors with shaven beards, contrary to the custom of that age, as may be learned from the Anastasian panel of Saint Nicholas in the City, which, as I have mentioned above, was displayed elsewhere.

When Beltraminius was transferred to the Church of Pacensis in Spain, Cardinal Lucius Sanseverinus succeeded him in 1612. [Col. 0022C] In the third year of his archiepiscopate, he too gave evidence of his devotion toward Blessed Gregory in the following inscription, placed beneath Marsilius’s older panel on another marble tablet:

“I, Lucius Sanseverinus, Archbishop of Salerno, consecrated this altar in honor of Blessed Gregory VII, Pope; and I enclosed his sacred body within it. To those present, I granted one year [of indulgence]; thereafter, on the anniversary day of the consecration, I granted, in accordance with the custom of the Church, forty days of true indulgence to those who piously visit it. In the year of Our Lord 1614, on 4 May.”

This must have been the new altar that occasioned the repetition of the Translation. It was wisely appointed for the same day as the earlier one, so that there would be no need to multiply the feasts.

On the same occasion, one might suppose that the arm had been obtained from the people of Soana, if the instructions [Col. 0022D] sent to me did not say that the Cardinal of Soana, enrolled in the Sacred College at the creation of Paul V and moved by pious affection toward his fellow-citizen Pontiff, while residing at Salerno during the vacancy of the see, obtained from Paul V a Papal Brief addressed to the Chapter of Salerno. By it the Canons were ordered, for the consolation of the city of Soana and the honor of Blessed Gregory himself, to bestow some distinguished relic of him.

This Brief, together with letters of recommendation from the Grand Duke of Tuscany and others from the Cardinal himself, was presented to the Chapter by two envoys of the people of Soana. It is said to have persuaded the Chapter to give them the right arm, and a notarial instrument concerning the matter is said to have been drawn up and preserved in the cathedral archive. [Col. 0023A]

Since these events are said to have occurred while the See of Salerno was vacant and Paul V was seated on the papal throne, they must have taken place after Beltraminius had departed for Spain and before Lucius had succeeded him—that is, in 1612. But I have been unable to learn from the new Ciacconius of Oldoini which cardinal at that time had Soana as his homeland, since he names no such person among the sixty whom Paul created. I therefore wish that I could see the instrument itself and seek from it the solution of this doubt.

18. What the subsequent history of the chapel so often mentioned was can be read there afterward in marble, in the following words, composed and inscribed by Don Fabritius Pintus:

“This chapel, once dedicated to the divine Michael the Archangel, invincible leader, by the valiant soldier John de Procida, a Salernitan patrician and ornament of his homeland, received beneath its altar in the year 1595 the sacred bones of the Blessed Gregory—not the Great, but the More-than-Great Pontiff—when they were translated there; [Col. 0023B] so that the dead man might lie under the protection of the Archangel who, while alive at Rome, made himself secure in the fortress of Saint Angelo against the schismatic Emperor Henry, and so that the relics of the champion of ecclesiastical liberty might have as their defender the one through whom heaven itself recognizes that it has been freed from spirits rebelling against God.

“At last, through the munificence of the Most Eminent Cardinal Fabritius Sabellus, the rights of the chapel having been bestowed upon the Most Reverend Chapter of Salerno, the Canons succeeded the author of the Sicilian Vespers as its possessors. Adorned by that Pontiff with both the name and insignia of the Cardinals, they shall sing forever the glories of Gregory VII—not the glorious victory won from the Gauls by John.”

Thus far Pintus. [Col. 0023C] If these words were understood to mean that, until the Translation mentioned above, Gregory’s body had lain somewhere other than in this chapel itself, they would not sufficiently accord with the most highly praised and entirely certain testimony of Marsilius. They must therefore be accepted without such a restriction.

I am also surprised that no mention is made here of the recently deceased Archbishop Gregory Carafa, through whose memorable munificence the same chapel, as I am informed, now shines, adorned on every side with new paintings and golden splendor. Those paintings chiefly represent the Pontiff’s honorable reception into the City, together with Duke Robert, who came to his aid (so the text reads), amid the festive acclamations of the faithful people reverently venerating the Vicar of Christ.

## § III. On the Monastic Life of Saint Gregory VII and the Period during Which He Served as Prior of Cluny

[Col. 0023D]

19. The lessons mentioned above are not free from their own errors concerning this subject. For they assert that Gregory received the habit at Cluny and seem to say that he was elected prior there before he was enrolled among the Roman clergy. We think neither statement can stand as true; therefore the matter deserves to be examined here more carefully.

Paul, the author of the Life, describing the beginnings of this holy Pontiff, asserts in no. 6 that “in childhood he was entrusted by his parents to his uncle, the Abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary on the Aventine Hill, for instruction in the liberal arts and the formation of moral discipline … Having entered adolescence, he proceeded to France, there to subdue the wantonness of the flesh through the hardship of travel [Col. 0024A] and the application of learning. After several years he was to return to Rome, but he spent some time at the court of Henry III … After this, having returned to Rome and applying himself earnestly to the pursuit of perfection, he resolved to enter the regions of Germany and Gaul. When he had reached Acquapendente,” he was prevented from proceeding farther by a triple vision, “and so was recalled for the consolation of the Roman Church … He was ordained Subdeacon by Pope Leo IX and was placed over the monastery of Saint Paul, which had been pitifully desolate.”

When you read this, you see that he was made an abbot; but you will rightly doubt whether he was a Regular, or a Secular or Commendatory abbot, since you find nothing in what precedes by which you can understand that he was truly a monk. Yet Paul explicitly calls him a monk, and he was in an excellent position to know this, when he says: [Col. 0024B]

“In those days”—that is, at Worms in the year 1047, when Leo was designated Pontiff in the presence of the Emperor—“there was a certain Roman monk, a young man of noble character, Hildebrand by name, of distinguished intelligence and holy religion.” “Accordingly, Blessed Bishop Bruno”—later called Leo—“called him to himself and asked him to return to Rome together.”

20. Hildebrand, therefore, was a monk, and indeed a Roman monk—that is, surely, of the same monastery in which he had been educated as a boy. He crossed into France as a monk and conducted himself as such at the court of the Emperor Henry. Consequently, the authors of monastic calendars, Dorganius, Menardus, and Bucelinus, rightly enrolled him among their own.

This is especially so since Otto of Freising says that he “administered the obedience of the priorship of Cluny” [Col. 0024C] when Leo was designated Pontiff. But if it is true, there is uncertainty about when this could have occurred, since he crossed the Alps with Gregory VI only in 1046, and was still an adolescent when Bruno encountered him at Worms two years later.

What? Could those venerable Fathers, in the great old age of their abbot Saint Odilo—who died at the end of 1048—have appointed as their prior a foreign adolescent who had spent only a few months among them, and then sent him to the imperial court? Yet the aforementioned Paul writes that he spent some time at the court and several years in France before returning to Rome.

The knot is difficult, but it seems capable of being untied [Col. 0024D] by taking the term “adolescent” somewhat more broadly and distinguishing two journeys by Hildebrand across the Alps. Born around the year 1020, he may afterward, in the sixteenth year of his age, in the year of Christ 1036, when the Roman Church was being shaken by the foulest storms under the tyranny rather than the pontificate of Benedict IX, have gone to Cluny while still a novice.

Perhaps he did so at the advice of his uncle, lest his tender years be corrupted by the extremely depraved customs then prevailing in the city of Rome—where almost the entire clergy was either simoniacal or concubinous, or stained by both vices—and lest the first sparks of piety, once kindled, be smothered by so evil an example.

He may therefore have spent six or seven years there under the excellent discipline of Saint Odilo, until, already sufficiently known and approved, he was permitted to return to Rome in order to introduce Cluniac discipline [Col. 0025A] into his uncle’s monastery. Before this, however, he may have made his way to the imperial court on some occasion, and finally have come to Rome around the twenty-fourth year of his age, in the year of Christ 1044.

When he found everything in a worse condition than before, with two men simultaneously exercising the papacy—namely the Benedict IX whom I have mentioned and Silvester III, recently elected by the Romans against him—he may once again have abandoned that Babylonian confusion and withdrawn to Gaul or Germany. But he was recalled from his journey by the visions mentioned above and enrolled in the Roman clergy by Gregory VI, who at about the same time had persuaded both false pontiffs to withdraw from the position they had wrongly invaded, thereby earning the right to be raised to it himself by free election.

21. Certainly Hildebrand himself, later Gregory VII, protested in the Roman Council, saying: “You know that I did not willingly approach the sacred Order, and that against my will I crossed the mountains with my lord Pope Gregory.” By these words he indicates clearly enough [Col. 0025B] that, before departing from Rome for the second and more widely known time, he had been taken from the monastery to serve Gregory VI and given to the clergy of the Roman Church.

How he crossed the Alps again with Gregory must here be explained briefly. Gregory VI had been ordained Pontiff in the Church’s very present emergency and from a just fear that Benedict, changing his mind, might withdraw his resignation. He had not first obtained the consent of King Henry, by this name the third King of Germany and the second Emperor. [Col. 0025C]

Since he gave good men the greatest hope of reforming the Church, but evil men cause for fear, those who knew themselves to possess the dignities of the Churches through simony or to defile them through fornication easily turned Henry’s mind. He was distressed that he had been passed over, and they persuaded him to come to Italy in order to remove so great a scandal in a legitimate synod of bishops, since the Roman Church was already said to have three pontiffs simultaneously.

Gregory VI was not displeased by this, having no doubt that he would easily prove his cause to the King and be confirmed in the papacy. But he was far deceived in his expectation. For when the Synod of Sutri was convened, he himself was accused of having given money to Benedict and therefore of being incapable of obtaining the papacy.

Struck by this unexpected development, and seeing that the bishops were inclined, at the King’s wish, toward his condemnation and deposition, Gregory voluntarily resigned and placed himself at their discretion. Others, however, maintain with more than ordinary likelihood that in the act of which he was accused he did not commit simony, but merely warded off an injury from the Church; that he had not purchased the dignity from Benedict, but had obtained it by merit from the Roman clergy. Hence Saint Peter Damian praises him, and Rudolf Glaber, Otto of Freising, and others acknowledge that the reform of the ecclesiastical order began with him.

On this understanding, just as it was an honor to John Gratian—for that was his earlier name—to have redeemed the Church from the servitude to which she had been unjustly enslaved and to have removed the schism by which she was afflicted; [Col. 0026A] so it must also be counted to his credit that, seeing his promotion displeasing to the Prince and to the synod of bishops, although they were poorly informed about the case, he preferred to resign rather than dissolve the peace he himself had established by trying to retain his position. [Col. 0025D]

22. Throughout this whole matter, the judgment of Hildebrand, although he was still a young man, must be valued most highly. Later, when he was older, he confirmed and approved it by the support of his supreme authority, showing how steadfast he had been even in youth.

Thus writes the aforementioned Otto:

“They say that Hildebrand followed this Gratian as he crossed the Alps. [Col. 0026B] Later, when he became supreme Pontiff, he wished to be called Gregory VII out of affection for him, because Gratian had been removed from the Catalogue of Pontiffs; and, as you find in Lucan,

> ‘The victorious cause pleased the gods, but the defeated cause pleased Cato,’

so this cause, in which the judgment of the Prince and the bishops prevailed, always displeased that Hildebrand, who was always most steadfast in ecclesiastical rigor.”

Our manuscript, speaking of the aforesaid Gratian, says that after his abdication he was led into the Cisalpine regions—that is, by the Emperor, who in this way removed the opportunity for renewed disturbances from those whom he understood not to approve the act entirely.

If no error is concealed here, it must be said that Gratian and Hildebrand withdrew to one of the Lombard monasteries, perhaps Saint Saviour’s near Pavia, since about sixty years earlier it had been reformed according to the pattern of Cluniac observance by Saint Maiolus and was everywhere celebrated for the reputation of its stricter discipline. [Col. 0026C]

They could not, however, have remained there for a long time, because the Emperor, departing from Italy, was unwilling to leave Gratian on this side of the Alps.

23. Where, then, did Hildebrand take him? “In Gaul,” says Baronius under the year 1049, “he set out with Gregory VI and stayed among the Cluniacs, in whose midst he knew that monastic observance flourished, living as a monk among monks.” I add: “and a long-known guest, exceedingly dear to all according to the merit of his extraordinary virtue and wisdom.”

When Gregory’s favor and authority were added to these prerogatives of Hildebrand, even though Gregory had already been deposed, and when Gregory’s merit among the Cluniac monks was immense, it would not have been surprising if Saint Odilo had appointed Hildebrand prior, so that, with the vigor of youth—for he had by then reached the age of twenty-seven—he might sustain Odilo’s old age and provide Gregory with what was necessary, exercising greater authority. [Col. 0026D]

Meanwhile, at Rome it happened that not only Clement, who had been substituted for Gregory, but also Damasus died—both being the second of their names—and that everything was thrown into confusion by Benedict, who was attempting to return once more to the Apostolic See. Consequently, the Romans thought it best to send a legation to ask the King himself to designate whom he wished them to elect as Pontiff.

When news of this matter reached Cluny, I believe that Hildebrand went out to the King, to whom he had long been dear, in the hope that he might persuade him to restore Gregory. Hildebrand did not believe that Gregory had been removed from office without some injustice, and he knew that Gregory burned with the same zeal for reforming the Church that animated himself. [Col. 0027A]

But God had ordained a different outcome for this journey, because through that opportunity Hildebrand came to the notice of the new Pontiff, designated at the end of the year 1047. The Pontiff, finding in Hildebrand a man no less acquainted with than hostile to the vices and corruptions of the city of Rome, believed that he could be of the greatest use to him in counsel and assistance if he could persuade him to come with him.

24. Otto of Freising relates the matter somewhat differently, as though the newly designated Pontiff, traveling through Gaul on his way to Rome and passing through Cluny, had found Hildebrand there as prior. He adds that Hildebrand, “approaching him, full of zeal for God, firmly rebuked him for what he had begun, saying that it was unlawful for a Supreme Pontiff to enter violently upon the governance of the Church through the agency of a layman. But if he wished to trust his counsels, he promised that he would bring about both that the imperial majesty should not be irritated against him and that the liberty of the Church should be renewed in a canonical election. [Col. 0027B]

“Moved by this, he laid aside the purple at his admonition, assumed the habit of a pilgrim, and, taking Hildebrand with him, set out on his journey. When they had come as far as the City, Bruno, soon called Leo, was elected Supreme Pontiff by the clergy and people on Hildebrand’s advice.”

The Life of Leo says nothing about the assumed purple; and concerning the pilgrim’s habit, it says that he assumed it after celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Tulli. Nevertheless, I would not for that reason reject the whole account of so ancient an author, who wrote not merely a century after the event, provided that he allows us to excuse and correct a slight error in place and to believe that what he says happened at Cluny actually happened at Worms. [Col. 0027C]

In the Roman synod cited above, “Gregory VII” declares that he “went unwillingly across the mountains with his lord Pope Gregory VI and returned even more unwillingly with his lord Pope Leo to the particular church” of the Roman clergy.

I believe that he consented to return on no other condition than that Leo, following this counsel of his, should decide to enter Rome as a private man and seek the free consent of the clergy for his election, although this may perhaps not have been entirely necessary if the Romans themselves had transferred to the Emperor, by a compromise, the authority to choose the Pontiff, as some think, contrary to Baronius’s view.

Our manuscript of the Lives of the Pontiffs, speaking of Leo, says: “This man, elected Pontiff by God, came to the Roman City, taking with him Hildebrand, who had gone with Pope Gregory to those regions … and he did everything on the journey and in this city according to the counsel of that same Hildebrand.” [Col. 0027D]

25. Someone might perhaps ask here with what confidence Hildebrand, who had spent only a year and a half at the Roman court with Gregory and had then been absent for another year and a half, could promise Leo such effective assistance in obtaining the consent of the Roman clergy and people, much less actually provide it.

If I may venture a conjecture, I would say that Hildebrand made this promise not from confidence in his own authority, which he knew must be slight at Rome, but in the authority of others—namely, that of Saint Odilo, his abbot, and of his master, Laurence, [Col. 0028A] Archbishop of Amalfi. He knew that both of them were then at Rome and that, because of their outstanding holiness, they possessed the greatest authority and favor there.

We know both facts from the Life of Saint Odilo. When Odilo died at Silviniacum in Gaul, on the last day of the year 1048 toward evening, not yet a full year had passed since he had returned from Rome. Laurence, however, as the same Life records, had been a source of the greatest comfort to Odilo during the five months of his illness there. He was a man who, in the testimony of Saint Peter Damian, “was learned and bilingual (*biglossus*; the printed reading is *bigiossus*), knew Greek and Latin, and, what is far more excellent, possessed the brilliance of a praiseworthy life.” He died at Rome during the Lent immediately following Saint Odilo’s death.

In another and older Life by Liziardus, the same Laurence is called “a man in every respect most holy, most eloquent in the Scriptures of both languages, and the intimate companion of this Father; their hearts were joined by the spirit of indivisible love.” [Col. 0028B]

If you ask where and when Hildebrand had Laurence as his master, learn the most certain truth from the utterly mendacious Benno. Benno accuses Gregory VI of having “always kept Laurence, who was living at Rome, in his household, in his archpresbytery of Saint John before the Latin Gate.” There can be no doubt that Laurence was also in the Lateran patriarchate when Gregory was Pontiff and had Hildebrand as his household cleric or secretary.

We would not know that Hildebrand had been Laurence’s disciple if the same Benno, driven by satanic fury against him, had not taught us this, when—according to Baronius’s testimony, for I do not deign to consult Benno himself—he declaims against Laurence as “a remarkable magician, an accomplice of Benedict IX in every evil, a teacher and prince of misdeeds, who also practiced divination publicly and openly professed magic and other forbidden arts of that kind at Rome for all who wished to learn them; from him Hildebrand, his disciple, learned those same magical arts, condemned by divine and human laws.” [Col. 0028C]

Hildebrand, therefore, hoping that the assistance of these two men and perhaps of other outstanding persons then living at Rome would by no means be lacking to him in securing a matter of such importance, could promise Leo what he did with confidence in the best outcome.

Whether, when they arrived at Rome, they still found Saint Odilo there is uncertain to me; but they certainly must have found Laurence. [Col. 0028D]

26. As a further defense of Otto of Freising for wrongly attributing to Cluny what had happened at Worms, this consideration also helps: there can be no doubt that Leo and Hildebrand, traveling by way of Lorraine and Burgundy, turned aside to Cluny.

For the most convenient route to Lyons runs along the Saône. Midway along it, on the right bank, lies the city of Chalon, and Cluny is two leagues west of there. Leo could have been drawn there both by the celebrated holiness of the place and by the opportunity to converse with the former Pontiff Gregory, from whom he could receive the most timely counsels. Hildebrand himself, however, must have been drawn there by the necessity of resigning the priorship and arranging the condition of the monastery, since Abbot Odilo had not yet returned from Italy. [Col. 0029A]

No one explains in which year of Leo’s pontificate Hildebrand was placed in charge of governing and reforming the monastery of Saint Paul. Paul of Bernried reports a vision shown to Hildebrand himself concerning this matter in no. 8. Our manuscript describes another, similar vision shown to Leo in these words:

“Afterward, Leo entrusted the church of Saint Paul to Hildebrand to govern, because of a certain vision that he had seen: namely, because in the aforesaid vision he saw Blessed Peter cheerful, while he perceived Blessed Paul to be sad and troubled toward him.”

## § IV. How This Saint Was Recently Enrolled in the Vallumbrosan Order

27. After comparing testimonies from authors everywhere, I could establish about the monastic life of Gregory VII only what I have set out above, whether as fact or conjecture, until a few years ago, when our friend Tiberius Petraccius [Col. 0029B]—then Procurator General of his Vallumbrosan Order and now Abbot of Saint Michael of Pistoia—obtained from the Sacred Congregation of Rites a decree signed on 21 January 1693.

By this decree, certain holy men of that order were ordered to be entered in the Roman Martyrology, and it expressly added to the eulogy of our Gregory quoted above that he was “of the Order of Vallombrosa.”

Later, on 4 March of the same year, another decree was issued at the petition of the same procurator. It approved and granted proper lessons for those same saints, and specifically for “Saint Gregory, Pope VII,” where it says that, “being estranged from the world and desiring to serve God alone, he professed the monastic life and built in his homeland a monastery of Saint Benedict according to the Vallumbrosan institute, which he had embraced long before.”

Ambrosius Locatellus, the father and most diligent investigator of Vallumbrosan history, mentioned Gregory VII with praise a hundred years ago, as a man especially devoted to his order. In particular, in chapter 63, he relates in Italian the same matter that is expressed in Latin in the Life soon to be cited, concerning the events at the Roman synod under Alexander II. At that synod, most of the prelates, and even Saint Peter Damian himself, opposed the monks sent by Saint John to accuse Peter, Bishop of Florence, of simony.

The account is expressed in these words:

“Meanwhile, a certain outstanding and most excellent man rose in the council, another Gamaliel, as it were, named Hildebrand: a monk, archdeacon of the Roman Church, and cardinal. He had previously been prior of the monastery of Cluny of the Order of Saint Benedict, and afterward, following the death of Alexander II, was endowed with the Apostolic dignity.

“And because it pleased him to become a defender of Christ’s cause, he afterward became the Vicar of that same Christ—that is, Pope—and was called Gregory VII. While he was a cardinal, he listened prudently to this controversy and wisely weighed the authority of the canons. He nobly proved himself the monks’ helper and defender in every respect; he defended them not by proceeding step by step through argument, but openly and with the greatest courage, against everyone’s opinion.”

28. But neither this author, nor Locatellus, who had the earlier writers of his own order before his eyes, stated anywhere—whether here or elsewhere, where the subject required it—that Hildebrand had been a monk of the Vallumbrosan Order. Only in chapter 67 do I find the same Locatellus relating how Hildebrand, coming to Florence with the aforementioned Pope Alexander to settle the dispute between the monks and the bishop around the year 1063, proposed to test St. John Gualbert’s patience, in order to discover whether his sanctity was genuine or feigned. He prepared words apparently intended as an insult:

> “Yet all these words—as he himself later related—slipped from his memory as soon as he came into the presence of the saint. The cardinal, taking this silence, so unusual for him, otherwise an eloquent man, as a miracle,”

says Locatellus,

> “regarded it as a sign of God, confirming the man’s holiness; and from then on he loved him as a brother, and from that hour wished to be counted among the sons of our Vallumbrosan religion.”

Even if all this were proved true, however, the name of spiritual sonship—which devout believers of every condition and sex cause themselves to be enrolled in certain religious orders under—extends so broadly, even to laymen and married people, that this reason alone scarcely seems sufficient to assign a saint to one particular order as its own. For thus one and the same person could be claimed by many orders, providing an occasion for foolish disputes, as the parties contended over which had the greater right to him. Examples are at hand, but there is no need to produce them now. I say only that, if Petraccius had no other foundation for his claim than Locatellus’s testimony, he possessed an altogether weak foundation.

But before I demonstrate this, a certain letter of Hildebrand, already pope, written after the founder’s death, must be presented. It runs as follows:

29. “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, monks, and religious laymen who imitate the discipline of John Gualbert, of holy memory, their abbot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Although we did not see John, of venerable memory, your father, with bodily eyes, nevertheless, because the purity of his faith shone forth wondrously throughout Tuscany, we loved him with great affection. Although we do not doubt that you earnestly strive to imitate his holy way of life, so that the vigor of your uprightness may watch more diligently and burn more fervently to uproot the weeds from the Lord’s field, we offer you the words of a fatherly exhortation.

“Therefore, beloved, following his life insofar as your ability permits, and proving yourselves truly his sons and heirs by a similar way of life, act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Let your minds meditate daily upon the teachings of the Holy Scriptures, by which the arguments of heretics are destroyed and the faith of the holy Church defended against the members of the devil; and let your minds rise with the freedom customary to them amid the confusion of the wicked.

“Those who place their trust in you and intend to follow the way of your religious life, receive, after the manner of your aforesaid Father, and instruct them by holy exhortations in whatever seems to pertain to their salvation; so that the surrounding peoples, observing the holy works not only of yourselves but also of those who follow you, may glorify your Father who is in heaven.

“As for us, we desire to show to you, as long as our spirits govern our limbs, the same love that we formerly bestowed upon your Father and upon you. Indeed, we shall cherish you thereafter with all the greater charity, the more fervent we find you to be in divine affairs. In these matters, with God’s help, we shall provide you not only spiritual but also, if necessary, temporal assistance.

“Pray, therefore, to almighty God that he may grant us the strength and resources by which we may bear the unbearable burden of the government we have undertaken and restore the holy Church to the condition of her ancient religion.

“Farewell.”

30. St. John Gualbert died on 12 July, in the same year—1073—in which Gregory had become pope, a few days after his episcopal, or pontifical, consecration, which, as we shall show below, took place on 30 June. Thus this was one of Gregory’s first letters, written when he was already a bishop.

This information was supplied to us by the Life of the holy Founder, which we possess through the kindness of the most illustrious Francesco Redi, from an excellent manuscript copy of the Abbey of Ripoli near Florence, preserved at Florence by the Most Reverend Abbot Ascanio Tamburini. The author of that Life speaks of himself in the Prologue as follows:

> “At the request of the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Bartholomew, abbot of the monastery of St. Bartholomew at Fossato, of the Vallumbrosan Order and of the diocese of Genoa, I, Lord Andrew of St. Ambrose, a native citizen of Genoa and humble prior of the monastery of St. Matthew in the diocese of Genoa, of the Order of St. Benedict—last and least among so many disciples of the blessed John who have written his deeds, virtues, and miracles—will undertake, in the name of the Lord, to construct one work from the writings of those disciples and also from other deeds of the same blessed John, taken from the archives of the major monastery of Vallombrosa and delivered to me at Florence in September of the year of the Lord 1419, as well as from other deeds preserved in the chests of the said monastery of St. Bartholomew at Fossato. …

“But so that I may remove any occasion for doubt, I have stated above, and state again, for each individual matter that I describe, from which authors these things became known to me. For they come from the writings of his disciples, whose names are these: Lord Acto, who was bishop of Pistoia, and Lord Andrew, who was abbot of the monastery of St. Fidelis at Strumi, of the same Order of Vallombrosa.”

31. We dealt with the blessed Andrew just mentioned on 10 March, and in no. 13 we lamented that his distinguished work on the life of St. John could at present be found nowhere. Yet just as the Life of St. Ariald the Martyr, written by the same man and to be published by us on 28 June, has fortunately emerged into the light of this age, so we hope that the other work too will come forth from somewhere out of darkness before July reaches our hands.

This Andrew was flourishing while the holy Founder was still alive, and in the year 1060 was a faithful assistant to the blessed Ariald the Martyr among the Milanese in combating the Simoniacs. St. Acto, as we have already seen on his feast day, 22 May, died in 1155 and was born around 1070. He therefore could in no way be numbered among the disciples of the living saint. Rather, he received his information from them, and specifically from the blessed Theuzo, one of the earliest men said to have prolonged his life until 1095 and to have committed certain matters concerning the life of the holy Father to writing.

This Theuzo, however, according to the words cited from an old Italian translation of the year 1250 preserved in the Vallumbrosan archive, does not name Hildebrand but Cardinal Gregory as the person to whom the event related above happened. If St. Acto identifies Hildebrand with him, supposing that by anticipation he was called Gregory, he did so on the basis of his own conjecture, and a very insecure one at that, since Pope Gregory declares that he had never “seen the saint with bodily eyes.”

Alphonsus Ciacconius, in his *Lives of the Pontiffs and Cardinals*, together with Victorellus, Ughellus, and Oldoinus, his revisers and enlargers, for the year 1063, in which this meeting with St. John is supposed to have occurred, presents no Cardinal Gregory to us. But since it is certain that many men were omitted by them in that middle period, because they had not obtained knowledge of them—as the very abundance of the supplements repeatedly added proves—there is nothing to prevent us from thinking that under Pope Alexander II there really was among the cardinals some Gregory not otherwise known to us. A century later, St. Acto, failing to distinguish him, may have wrongly supposed that Hildebrand the Cardinal was the Gregory called by that name in the papacy.

32. Recognizing the manifest contradiction between the statements of Acto and Locatellus and Gregory’s own assertion, Didacus de Franchis, abbot of Ripoli, in his *History of St. John Gualbert*, published in Italian in twelve books around the year 1638, elsewhere absolves himself by carefully marking in both margins the passages and words of the authors. But in the eleventh book, when treating the argument just cited, he places in the outer margin the Italian words of Theuzo, where he mentions Gregory, and in the other margin the Latin words of the *Proper Lessons* published in 1624, in which the name Hildebrand is expressed. He omits everything from which one might understand that the man who had deliberately prepared the rebuke really came into the saint’s presence.

This author imagines that, while the cardinal was privately recalling the words prepared beforehand, their memory slipped from him; afterward, however, he was frustrated in his request for an audience because the saint at that time allowed himself to be seen by no one, conducting everything through messengers and letters. For the circumstances in question, when such difficult business ought to have been conducted personally, this seems incredible, since none of the ancient authorities asserts it.

Then, resuming the Latin words of St. Acto that I mentioned above, the author writes in the margin of page 429, at the place cited:

> “Thereafter such love was established between the two as is accustomed to exist between dearest friends and brothers born of the same womb.”

33.
