You have here the source of the spiritual sonship, first invented gratuitously by Locatellus, accepted still more gratuitously by Petraccius, and introduced into the *Lessons of the Martyrology* and of the morning Office, as though Hildebrand had “long before embraced the Vallumbrosan institution.”

But how long before? Hear the *Lessons* again:

> “Having professed the monastic life, he built in his native land a monastery of St. Benedict according to the Vallumbrosan institution, which he had long before embraced; then, having gone to Gaul, he remained in the monastery of Cluny.”

Thus, according to this account, Hildebrand embraced the Vallumbrosan institution at Rome, while still entirely a young man and almost a boy, before the year 1046—if he ever embraced it at all.

Yet in that century the Vallumbrosan institution had no monastery at Rome. The monastery it now possesses under the title of St. Praxedes first became Vallumbrosan around the year 1170, if Onuphrius Panvinius correctly calculated the period of four hundred years in his booklet on the principal churches of the City, published around 1570.

Regarding the monastery at Sovana—which no prudent person will believe was founded by so young a man—the highly praised Didacus de Franchis, in book 8, page 254, refers to the acquisition, toward the end of John’s life, of a suburban place called Calvello, then inhabited by a few hermits. There the aforesaid abbey was gradually built and was finally transferred within the city in 1496, the hermits being brought there as well.

When Didacus mentions this place, he does not forget to note that “Sovana is the homeland of the famous monk Hildebrand.” He also adds that it was the tradition of the inhabitants—for he says that the documents perished in a fire around 1550—that St. John himself once honored the place with his presence. And are we to believe that, if he had detected even the faintest trace of it, he would have said nothing about Hildebrand the founder?

34. In general, however, as regards numbering Pope Gregory VII among the Vallumbrosan saints, the aforesaid Didacus, in book 9, page 293, assigns no other reason than:

> “obedience and gratitude, because he canonized St. John Gualbert and gave the Order its first Cardinal, St. Peter Igneus. It is precisely in the same manner that the Vallumbrosan Order preserves an honored memory of Pope Victor II, similar to that which it retains of its own blessed members—not as an act of worship for holiness, but out of obedience and gratitude, because he was the first to strengthen the newly born Congregation with Apostolic Privileges.

> “But,” he says, “some outsiders, insufficiently acquainted with this pious and honorable custom, rashly turn it into a reproach against us, attributing it to an immoderate desire to increase the number of illustrious persons among us.”

May the soul of the author—at once most candid and most discerning—rest well. Without prejudice to the truth, he knew how to explain the intention of the Order, which calls Gregory and Victor its own, in such a way that he neither allows it, through ignorance, to be extended further, nor imposes upon others an obligation to assign the title of the Vallumbrosan Order to those whom they prefer to call without such a title, because they know that these men were not bound to the Order by the bond of its customary profession. For among the common people the title would be understood according to its more obvious and stricter meaning, creating a danger of ambiguity.

Meanwhile, through Didacus’s sincere confession, we understand not only in what sense Petraccius sought to have the words cited above inserted into the *Martyrology* and recited in the *Lessons*, and in what sense the Sacred Congregation of Rites approved them; we also have an easy and convenient way to explain the countless difficulties repeatedly brought against us, and repeatedly to be brought against us, by those who are distressed that, adhering to the more common meaning of words as they are used among the people, we do not present under the title of their Order all the saints whom their predecessors judged assignable to it for whatever reason, and whom the Church permits—rather than commands—to be privately attributed to each Order in that Order’s own Offices.

If neither our most friendly Petraccius nor the Vallumbrosan monks—whose generous hospitality we gratefully acknowledge that we enjoyed, and whose remarkable kindness assisted us—will be displeased with me because I have explained their mind here, I hope that all other religious will likewise excuse us whenever we discuss certain saints without the title of their Order, although they themselves, either by ancient custom or by a more recent concession of the Sacred Congregation, recite the Office as though those saints belonged to them, when that title is less certain and established in our judgment.

Since, however, we cannot expect everyone to exercise the moderation with which we trust that the Vallumbrosan Fathers will read these words, it will be appropriate at times to keep silent about the reasons for such an omission, and no one should wish to compel us to state them against our will. Otherwise, after we have stated them, we may too late regret our ill-advised insistence and wish that the question had never been raised against us.

I should add one thing: after these pages had already been sent to the press, a letter arrived from Lord Placidus Poltri, a Vallumbrosan, promising, I know not what new proof. I shall gladly examine it in the Appendix to be published after volume 7 and shall follow it as far as I can. Accordingly, let what has been said thus far be accepted without prejudice to a judgment that may perhaps one day be established more soundly than has yet been done.

§ V. The Genealogical Pedigree of the Saint and His Episcopal Ordination

35. In the preceding paragraph, the Most Reverend Abbot Petraccius, often mentioned by me, sought to serve both his Order and St. Gregory well. Having explained the sense in which he connected Gregory with that Order through additions made to the *Martyrology of the Roman Church* and to the Breviary of his Congregation—with Cardinal Bona favoring him in all these matters and enabling him to overcome great difficulties, since the Sacred Congregation of Rites had entrusted the matter to Bona’s judgment—he also exerted every power of his intellect and diligence to show that the saints who had been granted new Offices at his insistence were of the most illustrious lineage, and that they were connected with one another not so much by similarity in spiritual progress as by bodily descent.

After searching widely through the recesses of the archives, he wove their genealogical pedigree. He urgently begged me to insert it in this place, wishing to test the judgment of the Florentine nobility in our work, while he prepared for publication his own treatise, in which, by producing tables of ancient documents, the truth of each individual degree would be demonstrated with respect to the bonds of affinity and the succession of blood relationships.

The day of 25 May was not as near to the press as Petraccius supposed when he wrote this, for the printing of the first volume had only just begun ten years earlier. Yet before we reached this point there was ample time for him to publish his treatise in the meantime. Since he has not done so, and since learned men in Florence to whom I communicated the proposed scheme replied that the author seemed to promise more than he could solidly prove, I do not think it advisable to give it a place in our work or to incur the expense of engraving a genealogical tree resting perhaps upon insufficiently firm roots.

36. Nevertheless, allow me briefly to indicate the sequence of the genealogy proposed by Petraccius. He presumes that the Aldobrandeschi family, noble in Etruria but now extinct in name because its male line failed, while its women married into the Orsini and Sforza families, descended from the Carolingian lineage of the Frankish kings. In that same house, he says, the name Hildebrand was frequent, and from it, in the century when surnames began to become established among noble families, the surname “Aldobrandeschi” arose.

For the year 948 he produces a certain Hildebrand, son of Theuzo, who, being both Count of Sovana and Marquis of Tuscany, fathered Willa, the mother of St. John Gualbert, founder of the Vallumbrosans, and Bonizo, in 979 Count of Pitigliano and Sovana, the father of Pope St. Gregory VII. Thus, according to him, the two saints—the abbot and the pontiff—were cousins.

From this same Bonizo Petraccius further makes Desiderius descend, Count of Sovana, from whom Peter Igneus, Cardinal of the Vallumbrosan Order, was born; he died on 8 February 1078. He also makes Aldobranda descend from Bonizo, the mother of St. Bernard, bishop of Parma and cardinal of the same Order, who died on 4 December 1133.

So runs his account.

In another part of the same scheme, he traces St. Gualbert’s paternal lineage from a certain Count Schiava of the Val di Pescia, descended from the Lombard kings. He traces St. Bernard’s lineage from the Uberti family, which Ricordanus and others believe to have sprung from the ancient Romans, although its more recent name was taken from a certain Uberto, the first to bear that name, who lived in the tenth century.

Let the advocates of these very ancient origins provide their proof. Petraccius is obliged to produce documents by which the descent of Saints John Gualbert and Gregory VII from the Counts of Sovana, and their close kinship, may be proved.

Whatever may be the case concerning the holy Abbot, whose noble birth is beyond dispute, I fear that Petraccius had no other basis for tracing the Pope to the Aldobrandeschi than that they trace their own lineage to the Hildebrands, Counts of Sovana; that Gregory is said to have been born at Sovana; and that he received the name Hildebrand at baptism. But it is not unusual for names familiar among princes to become common among their subjects, however ignoble, either out of regard for their lords or for some other reason.

37. Cardinal Baronius, in the year 1073, no. 15, when about to treat of Hildebrand, already elected pontiff, after saying that “some relate that he was from Sovana, others from Siena”—a view easily reconciled with the author of the *Sienese Annals*, who understands Sovana to be included within the territory of Siena—asserts that he was “born in a humble station,” the son of a craftsman. He says that we know this was thrown against him by his adversaries as an insult, although in this respect he would deserve greater praise, since the more evident signs of a true apostolate would shine forth in him, if the Apostle says:

> “For consider your calling, brothers: not many are powerful, not many are noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are, so that no flesh might glory in his presence” (1 Corinthians 1:26–28).

Thus speaks the Apostle, while human pride rejects with excessive arrogance that title of birth by which God wished his Son, having become man, to be honored as the son of a craftsman.

They add this about the craftsman’s son: when, as a boy, he played at his father’s feet while his father was shaping wood, he supposedly formed by chance, from the discarded shavings, the letters whose combination expressed the Davidic oracle, although he did not know his letters:

> “He shall rule from sea to sea” (Psalm 72:8).

This was to signify that, with divine Providence guiding the boy’s hand, he would one day possess the greatest authority in the world.

So Baronius relates it, but he names no author, either in the text or in the margin. The same story is told in the lessons of the Proper Office in a form that does not support his lowly origin. They say that it happened “when, as a little boy ignorant of letters, he played at the feet of a craftsman shaping wood,” not “at the feet of his father, the craftsman.”

Indeed, the claim of a far from ordinary nobility is favored by the fact that in our manuscripts of the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, “Rusticus, nephew of Gregory,” said to have been “Prefect of the Seven Halls,” is reported to have held the same place, like a fortified house, against the Emperor Henry, who besieged it and battered it with engines. Such an office does not seem to have been entrusted to a common man.

I say nothing here of the “uncle who was abbot of the monastery of St. Mary on the Aventine,” mentioned in Life no. 5. Although distinguished birth has always been a matter of no small consideration even in the conferral of monastic offices, it is nevertheless less unusual for those offices to be attained by men born in the lowest station when character, merit, or learning supplies the distinction that their stock did not provide.

38. From Gregory’s first birth on earth I pass to his second and holier birth in the Chair, which, according to custom and established practice, he undoubtedly celebrated annually with greater solemnity. It may nevertheless be disputed on what day he celebrated it, since Lambert of Hersfeld, a writer of that very period, in the year 1073—in which Gregory was elected pontiff—on the day stated in the decree, 10 Kalends of May, says that, while awaiting the king’s consent, he was first ordained “the following year, on the Purification of St. Mary.”

But the *Pontifical Acts* preserved by Cencius Camerarius assert:

> “As soon as the king learned the truth of the election, he gave his assent and sent Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the kingdom of Italy, to the City, so that by royal authority he might confirm the election itself and strive to be present at Gregory’s consecration. This was done without delay. For within the octave of Pentecost Hildebrand was ordained priest, and on the feast of the Apostles he was consecrated Roman Pontiff.”

Pentecost in that year, in which Easter fell on 31 March and the Dominical Letter was F, was celebrated on 14 May. The feast of the Apostles therefore fell on a Saturday.

It might seem that this day was chosen especially for the election of that holy pontiff, since otherwise the consecration of pontiffs usually took place on Sundays, because he remembered that the Prince of the Apostles, Peter, “from infancy had nourished him beneath his wings with a singular affection and cherished him in the lap of his clemency,” as he had earlier written to the princes of Saxony.

Yet that the Sunday customarily expected was the one on which the special commemoration of St. Paul was to be observed, as though the feast of the Apostles’ Nativity were in some way continued, is suggested by his twelfth letter in the *Register*. In it “Gregory, elected Roman Pontiff,” wrote to William, bishop of Pavia, “greeting in the Lord Jesus Christ,” on the very day of 3 Kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction.

That the consecration took place no later than 30 June is proved by the following letter. It is dated 2 Kalends of July, likewise in the eleventh indiction, and Gregory is no longer described as “elected Roman Pontiff,” but, with the customary change of style, as “Bishop, servant of the servants of God,” addressing Manasses, archbishop of Reims, with greeting and apostolic blessing.

39. This pontiff did not observe the practice that we see Pope Clement III begin and Pope Celestine III consistently maintain a hundred years later: namely, numbering the years of his pontificate in the subscriptions to his letters, at least in the *Register*. Nor are there surviving examples in which the scribes or chancellors of the Holy Roman Church, subscribing in fuller form, added that or any other chronological indication.

Therefore we cannot prove from such evidence that Gregory was accustomed to reckon the beginning of his pontifical years from 30 June. Nevertheless, we may believe that in this matter too he followed the custom of his predecessors, and thus that only eleven years, ten months, and twenty-six days should be assigned to his pontificate, which began when he became a bishop.

In this way we calculate the periods of all the preceding pontiffs in our treatise on the chronology of the Roman pontiffs, now finally published. At the same time we observe the Sunday as the day anciently prescribed for ordinations. By these two rules we hope to resolve countless difficulties in ecclesiastical history, which repeatedly disturb and entangle the Baronian chronology concerning the pontiffs, because it observes neither rule.

40. The aforementioned Otto of Hersfeld seems to propose, not without some probability, a sufficiently suitable reason for the delay of the ordination when he writes that, after Gregory’s election had become known, and “since he was most fervent in the zeal of God, the bishops of Gaul immediately began to be deeply troubled, lest a man of vehement character and sharp faith toward God should at some time examine them more strictly for their negligence. Therefore, having attacked the king with united counsel, they begged him to declare invalid the election that had been made without his command, asserting that unless he hastened to forestall the man’s attack, this evil would redound upon no one more than upon the king himself.

“Immediately the king sent Count Eberhard from his side. He was to meet the Roman nobles and ask them why, contrary to the custom of their ancestors and without consulting the king, they had ordained the pontiff of the Roman Church; and, if he did not provide an adequate answer, he was to order him to renounce the dignity unlawfully received.

“When he came to Rome, he was kindly received by the aforesaid man. After he had explained the king’s commands, Gregory replied that, with God as his witness, he had never sought the summit of this honor through ambition; that he had been elected by the Romans and that the burden of ecclesiastical government had been forcibly imposed upon him. Nevertheless, he could in no way be compelled to allow himself to be ordained until he learned through a reliable embassy that both the king and the princes of the Teutonic kingdom had consented to his election. For this reason he had delayed his ordination and would certainly continue to delay it until a messenger arriving from there made the king’s will known to him.

“When this was reported to the king, he gladly accepted the explanation and, with the happiest approval, ordered that Gregory be ordained.”

41. I do not know how far from or near to Rome the king then was, and therefore I cannot determine whether, during those ten weeks that elapsed between the Election and the Ordination, messengers could have traveled back and forth as often as necessary for Gregory to have waited until, after the return of the aforesaid count, he received new messages from the king.

But I do not see that this was necessary. For the highly praised *Acts* from the Vatican Archive state that “on the following day” after the Election, Gregory, “considering anxiously within himself the grave danger into which he had been brought, began to burn with excessive grief. But when he found no excuse for abandoning the papacy, he promptly sent messengers to King Henry, through whom he both disclosed the election that had been made over him and earnestly begged him not to give his consent; for, if he did not do so, he was certain that he would in no way tolerate his more serious and manifest excesses with impunity.”

I therefore think that matters unfolded as follows. The fame of the Election—and of the Ordination that had followed or was shortly to follow it—preceded Gregory’s messengers, as commonly happens. The Roman people seemed unwilling to tolerate any delay, as may sufficiently be understood from Gregory’s reply to the count. The count was therefore sent while the Gallican bishops—who at that time perhaps were present at the king’s court from Burgundy and Lorraine—were representing the neglect of royal authority as certain.

After the count had departed, the messengers arrived with letters disproving the aforesaid report. Consequently, without awaiting the count’s return, an order was sent to the bishop of Vercelli that he should arrange to be present at the pontifical ordination. He did so without delay and arrived in Rome in the tenth week after the Election—perhaps sooner than the count could have returned to the king.

In this way, even if the king had been in the innermost parts of Germany, everything reported on both sides could have taken place. Where Lambert obtained the date of the Purification, I do not know. That he was mistaken is proved by certain documents; that is sufficient.

[Col. 0039]

## The Life of St. Gregory VII, by Paul of Bernried, Regular Canon

### Chapter One. The Name Hildebrand and the Fiery Miracles Shown Concerning Him. Events up to the Year 1052

Thus Gregory VII, upon whom the spirit of the first Gregory truly rested, was German by nation. His father was named Bonicus.

[Note: Our manuscript gives the father’s name more correctly, writing *Bonizo*. Here it should at least have been written *Bonizus* or *Bonitus*, not *Bonicus*.]

He himself received the name Hildebrand at baptism, not without a great foreshadowing of things to come.

The name Hildebrand,

[Note: According to differing dialects, this name is written in various ways: Hiltebrant, Hildebrand, Heldebrant, and—even for the sake of smoother pronunciation—Hellebrand. The last form, because it can be interpreted in different ways, gave Gregory’s enemies and slanderers an opportunity, as is said below in no. 4. It was understood as “infernal brand,” although *helle* signifies not only hell as a noun, descending from *Hellen*, but also “bright” as an adjective. Our author, omitting the etymology of the first part and dwelling on the second, derived from *branden*, “to burn” or “to blaze,” and rendered it as “burning.” But *Brand* means burning, conflagration, or firebrand. *Hilt* or *Held* means “hero”; thus Hildebrand means “the burning of heroes” or “heroic ardor.” In ancient usage it is scarcely distinguished from Childebrand, just as Childebert is not distinguished from Hildebert. There is nevertheless a difference in meaning, insofar as *childe* among the ancient Franks and Saxons, and even today among the English, signifies a child, son, and so forth. Italians generally pronounce the name without aspiration, as Ildebrando; later usage transformed it into Aldobrando. Furthermore, what is said immediately afterward, concerning Elijah, on the occasion of the fiery ardor signified by the name, is taken from apocryphal writings and could more properly be referred to Elijah’s feast on 20 July.]

in the native vernacular of the Teutonic language, signifies “burning,” namely, the burning of an earthly desire of the sort that the Psalmist asks to be divinely bestowed upon him when he says in Psalm 25:

> “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart …”

The name was aptly given at baptism, since John the Baptist says in Mark 1:

> “I indeed baptize you in water for repentance; but he who comes after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry: he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

Of this fire the Savior himself says in Luke 12:

> “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?”

Since, therefore, this man was destined by fiery speech to drive the burning arrows of the enemy away from the house of God, it was not inappropriate that he should bear, in his name, the fire that he would display through the most ardent testimony of charity and truth.

2. We still possess firmer indications of divine fervor in him. From these we once compared him with the prophet Elijah, when perhaps we were reading Isidore’s account of the birth and death of the prophets. There, if memory does not deceive me, the head of the newly born Elijah is said to have been illumined by a globe of fire, plainly to foreshadow the ardor of divine zeal with which he was eventually to be inflamed against the transgressions of the worst kings and the seductions of false prophets.

In a similar way, sparks of fire were seen to leap from the clothing of the little Gregory, or Hildebrand, undoubtedly to foreshadow the fervor of holy zeal with which he too was to be kindled against the most grievous insolence of Henry’s madness and against the intolerable excesses of priestly incontinence.

This vision of the sparks, which was shown repeatedly, is said first to have been noted by St. Majolus, father of the monastery of Cluny,

[Note: We give the Life of Majolus on 11 May, where we show that he died in the year 994. Yet in 1048 Hildebrand was still an adolescent. Therefore what is attributed here to St. Majolus must have been said under one of his disciples or successors, St. Odilo.]

who applied to it the words of the blessed John the Baptist:

> “This child will be great before the Lord.”

Finally, so that we may mention without interruption all the visions of fire that we have learned concerning him, a flame was also seen at one time to proceed from his head, making the likeness to Elijah still more exact, if we were supported by a corresponding agreement of ages. Yet just as that prodigy of prophetic rebuke occurred in infancy, so this display of apostolic scrutiny occurred in mature age.

### 3.

There was also in this a certain resemblance to Elijah: despised by a particular slanderer, he was terribly avenged by heavenly fire. For when he was archdeacon under his predecessor Alexander, a poor man, suffering intolerable injustice because his inheritance had been taken from him by a most wicked and dangerously powerful man, brought his mournful complaint to the Roman Pontiff. But the Pontiff feared that, on this account, he too might suffer harm from an irreverent and shameless person, and hesitated to support mercy with a just sentence. The just Hildebrand, confident as a lion, first tried to rouse and encourage the Pontiff to exact vengeance; but when he could not at all free him from his faintheartedness, he asked that this act of mercy and truth be entrusted to him. Having immediately received it, he pronounced a sentence of anathema against the plunderer. But the man, either lacking fear or ashamed to appear afraid of so great a judgment, on the third day afterward was boasting among his fellow soldiers of his customary mounted service, exulting or taunting as usual. Suddenly struck by a thunderbolt, he was plunged, like the hardened Pharaoh, into a lake of burning fire.

### 4.

Meanwhile he saw that famous dream, a prophecy of pontifical excellence and power: namely, that fire came forth from his mouth and set the whole world ablaze—without doubt that fire which the Lord Jesus Christ sent upon the earth and wished to be kindled intensely. But the impious did not interpret it thus, nor did those who maliciously opposed him experience it thus. For because they blasphemed the Holy Spirit, and called him, through his servant, reproving sin, a brand from Hell, by the just vengeance of God they became bound by an unforgivable offense, fell into perpetual misery because of their wicked designation, and—marvelously—the thing that was salutary to the devout became deadly to the impious.

Here follows a miracle glorious not only through the examples of Elijah but also through those of the righteous Abel, the most wise Solomon, and other Fathers, into whose offerings the grace of the Holy Spirit descended under the appearance of fire. For when, by the Lord’s authority, he had been raised to the watchtower of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and, as their sound went forth into all the earth and their words were spread to the ends of the world, he stirred up against himself the most severe persecution from the modern Nero, namely King Henry IV, whose crimes and wicked deeds found every preaching of the truth as intolerable as a consuming fire. Compelled therefore by necessity to flee from city to city, he sought for a time the protection of the most Christian Countess Matilda.

When his place was made peaceful with her, and his dwelling was in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of divine contemplation—the wheel of time came around, and the day approached that was especially devoted to pontifical offices, commonly called the Lord’s Supper. To celebrate it, he therefore went to the abbey called Nonantula, glorious through the patronage of his holy predecessors Sylvester and Adrian.

[Note: Nonantula was founded on the borders of the Modenese and Bolognese territories by Saint Anselm, its first abbot, who enriched it with the relics of Saint Sylvester, as stated in the Life of Saint Anselm on 3 March. It is also shown in the Pontifical Chronology that the body of Pope Adrian—not I, but III—is kept there.]

There, as he was engaged in the sacred ministries and had nearly completed the sanctification of the chrism, heaven suddenly kindled the blessed liquid with a visible form of fire; and he was glorified by a sign of divine acceptance, in keeping with the ancient Fathers.

### 5.

[Note: Berthold of Constance mentions the following history under the year 1082.]

But it now seems appropriate to end the miracles involving fire with the marvelous extinguishing of fire. In the Chronicles of venerable men it is reported that the following occurred on this occasion. When the aforementioned Henry had besieged the walls of the city of Rome with a hostile force, he set fire at one place so that, while the people turned from defending the fortifications to avert the dangers of the conflagration, he might enter without opposition. But Gregory, exceedingly strong in the faith of Christ, recognizing this trick, made the sign of the Cross, and immediately extinguished the fire, as though he had poured forth an inundation of the Tiber. He then ordered the people to return to the defense of the fortifications.

### 6.

Let us now return to the recollection of his boyhood. His parents entrusted him to his uncle, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, on the Aventine Hill, for the cultivation of liberal learning and the formation of moral discipline. In a short time he displayed conspicuous flowers of both kinds of nourishment.

When he had entered adolescence, he went to France, there to subdue the wantonness of the flesh through the hardships of travel and the application required by study. After several years, while returning from there to Rome, by God’s hidden preparation he spent some time at the court of Henry III, so that, since he was destined to be raised to the summit of the priesthood, his progress might be made visible to all from the lofty watchtower of the kingdom. Hence the Emperor himself used to say that he had never heard a man preach the Word of God with such confidence. The most distinguished bishops too, who were concerned for the welfare of the state, marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth.

### 7.

After this, when he had returned to Rome and was earnestly pursuing perfection, striving to double the talents of understanding and action divinely entrusted to him, he found his sluggish countrymen hostile and proved the saying of truth: “No prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke 4).

Therefore, wishing to spare envy and seek a greater fruit of charity, he decided to enter the regions of Germany and Gaul. When he had come to Aqua-pendens, Saint Peter appeared to him in a vision—Peter who was already arranging his ascent to his own Chair—and forbade him to proceed farther.

[Note: Aqua-pendens was a town in the Papal States, in the territory of Orvieto.]

But he, thinking the apparition deceptive, did not turn back from his proposed journey. The following night he passed over a similar vision as well. Then, on the third night, the apostolic figure confronted him with the greatest terror and threatened that he would pay dearly if he did not return. Thus it called him back for the consolation of the Roman Church.

### 8.

In those days, after the death of Damasus II, Leo IX succeeded him.

[Note: Damasus II was created on 17 July 1048 and, having occupied the See for twenty-three days, died, as is believed, by poison.]

[Note: We gave the Life of Saint Leo IX on 19 April. The year at that time was 1084.]

Leo venerated and embraced the prudence and holiness of this praiseworthy man from the depths of his heart and accepted his counsel in everything. Their harmony produced abundant fruit in the Lord’s field after the thorns had been uprooted.

Meanwhile, having been ordained subdeacon by that same Pope, he was placed over the monastery of Saint Paul, which had been pitifully desolate, after first being strengthened by the following vision. Saint Paul appeared to him standing in his basilica. Holding cow dung openly in his hands, he lifted it from the floor and threw it outside. When the onlooker stood by idly, the Apostle rebuked him for not helping and ordered him to seize and remove the dung openly, just as he himself was doing.

For Campanian brigands were plundering the provisions, and observance of holiness and the Rule had fallen into such a state of languor that herds of cattle freely entering defiled the house of prayer, while women who supplied what was needed in the refectory brought disgrace upon the reputation of the very few monks who remained. After therefore eliminating all impurity and recovering an adequate supply of provisions, he gathered an honorable multitude of monks living under the Rule. Through their religious observance and discipline, this place flourishes venerably to the present day.

### 9.

Finally, he began to have such singular confidence in the aid of their prayers that, whenever he was not delivered from adversities, it became for him the clearest sign that some offense among them was obstructing him. Once this had been corrected through his immediate examination, their prayer brought his deliverance forward in its customary course (Galatians 6).

Truly a blessed Father, and blessed sons, among whom ignorance and impunity could not delay the punishment of sin, but in the example of Joshua, exposed and chastised in a spirit of gentleness according to the Apostle’s command!

Nevertheless, if any persons, whatever their profession, dared to commit greater offenses at Saint Paul’s—especially offenses involving uncleanness or sacrilege—they soon perished at the hands of the Destroyer, as a testimony to apostolic reverence. For just as, in the time of the first Gregory, Saint Andrew the Apostle is said to have acted as the avenger of his sanctuary, so in the days of Hildebrand, the same Gregory VII, Saint Paul the Apostle shone forth as the avenger of his holy place, with each Apostle assisting his servant.

## CHAPTER II. Miracles and Deeds before the Papacy

### 10.

Meanwhile the spiritual farmer, namely Pope Saint Leo IX, observing and greatly admiring the abundant fruit of this branch—for he himself remained in Christ and Christ in him—enlarged Christ’s dwelling in him by conferring the Levitical Order; and, so that he might bear more fruit, appointed him archdeacon of the Roman Church.

[Note: When Victor II succeeded Saint Leo IX, having been created on 13 April 1055, Hildebrand himself testifies that he was sent into Gaul, in his account to Desiderius, Abbot of Monte Cassino and later Pope Victor II, in Book 3 of the Dialogues, and to Peter Damian in Opusculum 19, chapter 6. In those accounts the following history is told, but he is called a subdeacon. Below, however, Berthold, number 1, and Archbishop Grutmund of Aversa, Book 3 of On the Truth of Christ’s Body in the Eucharist, call him an archdeacon.]

After this he was sent into the regions of Gaul. There he discharged the office entrusted to him as a substitute for the Apostle so faithfully that he could rightly say with the Apostle: “Thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, indeed, an odor of death unto death; to others, an odor of life unto life” (2 Corinthians 2).

### 11.

Lyon, the principal see of Gaul, received the first fragrance of this odor through a synodal investigation. For, as Pope Callixtus used to relate, on the first day of the Council a certain pseudo-bishop was accused of having ascended to the pontifical dignity through simony. But because the proof could not be brought to completion, it was postponed until the following day.

Meanwhile, what was the man who was conscious of his guilt to do? Where could he turn? He dared not attempt to soften the mind of the judge, harder than diamond, with any gift, knowing that by this he would provoke rather than appease one who loved the truth with the greatest ardor. Therefore, having given money, he sealed the mouths of both accusers and witnesses. Then, emboldened by his insolent sense of security, he insulted the judge on the following day, saying: “Where are those who accused me? No one has condemned me.”

At this, the zealous servant of God sighed deeply and, with a contemptuous gesture, indicated that his heart was a frying pan for those who had been corrupted. He said to the corruptor: “Do you believe, O bishop, that the Holy Spirit is of one substance and one divinity with the Father and the Son?”

When he answered, “I believe,” Hildebrand said: “Say, ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’”

When he had confidently begun this verse, which the Fathers of Nicaea had introduced in hymnody to commend faith in the Holy Trinity, and which Saint Jerome had recommended to Pope Damasus as the response to the individual Psalms:

“Glory be to the Father and to the Son,”

he could not at all name the Holy Spirit. Ordered to try a second time, he failed at “the Son.” Permitted to repeat it a third time, he fell silent at “the Father.” At last, falling at the feet of the papal legate, he confessed that he was a Simonist.

As soon as he had been deposed from the episcopate, he rang out in a clear voice: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” Through these signs of divine knowledge, some of the pseudo-bishops are said to have been moved to repentance, to have revealed their evil consciences by spontaneous confession, and to have justly relinquished dignities unjustly acquired.

[Note: We discussed this response, commended by Saint Jerome, in the annotations to the prefatory letters attributed to both men, before the old Catalogues of the ancient Pontiffs, published before volume I of the April collection, part IV.]

### 12.

The same venerable archdeacon held a synod attended by Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.

[Note: We gave the various Acts of Saint Hugh on 29 April.]

At it he deposed a certain bishop by judicial procedure. Then the two men departed together and, coming to a certain river, crossed it. The archdeacon went ahead of the abbot.

After crossing the river, he turned around, looked back, and said: “Why did you think such things about me?”

The abbot replied: “Are you God, who claim to know the thoughts of men?”

“I am not God,” he said, “but nevertheless I heard what you were turning over in your mind. For you said in your heart that I had deposed that bishop more for the sake of boasting than out of zeal for God.”

Struck by the knowledge of his conscience, the abbot said: “I ask you, by the love of God, to tell me how you were able to perceive this.”

“Because,” he replied, “I looked back at you as you came through the riverbed; and, as though a thread [were] stretched from your mouth to my ears, I perceived from this what you were thinking.”

### 13.

On the following day, when the archdeacon and the aforesaid abbot of Cluny had entered a church, the abbot’s chamberlain, standing at prayer, secretly brought out some coins from his purse and counted them from hand to hand to distribute for expenses.

Interrupting his prayer with a shout, the archdeacon said: “Get out, devil!” and forced him to leave the church.

Then the abbot said: “You are acting inhumanely, since you do not even allow us to complete our prayer.”

“Ask your monk about the prayer,” he replied, “and you will be able to discover why I did this.”

The abbot therefore questioned him and found that he had been counting money. The archdeacon then added: “I too saw the most hideous spirit pretending to do this same thing in front of him.”

### 14.

On the same journey they came to a certain city suffering from a great mortality. There he saw an angel of God standing with a sword, ready to kill.

Therefore, when they went according to custom to a place of prayer, he asked the abbot to shorten the prayer and leave the city as quickly as possible; otherwise, all would perish.

The abbot obeyed his words and quickly returned to the lodging. Behold, he found two traveling companions struck down by sudden death. When they had departed from the place of pestilence with the utmost haste, the abbot, now free to inquire, asked the venerable Levite what he had seen that had made him order such haste. He heard what has just been related.

### 15.

Meanwhile, as he was traveling to Rome, he heard that after the death of Pope Stephen a certain Benedict had been installed in the Apostolic See by wicked and importunate men, contrary to the Canons. He therefore hastened his journey.

[Note: He died in 1054. Saint Leo IX was substituted for him in the following year by Victor II; after Victor died in 1057, Stephen IX succeeded him and died after approximately eight months. According to Leo of Ostia, Book 2 of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, chapter 100, Stephen ordered that no one should be elected Pope after his death unless Hildebrand were present.]

Having gathered a synod of bishops in Tuscany, Hildebrand condemned Benedict by the judgment of the Holy Spirit. Gerard, the venerable bishop of Florence, elected by the common agreement of the good, he enthroned in the Apostolic See and named Nicholas II.

[Note: Nicholas II occupied the See from January 1059 until approximately June 1061, when Alexander II succeeded him. Malmesbury, Book 3 of On the Deeds of the Kings of the English, page 107 of the Frankfurt edition, says that Hildebrand was appointed by Alexander to head the Apostolic Chancery.]

After Nicholas died two years later, Alexander II succeeded him.

### 16.

The chamberlain of this Alexander, named John, used to relate a miracle of divine healing performed upon himself through the venerable Hildebrand, who was still an archdeacon.

When this John was being tormented at Tusculum by an excessively severe fever, he sent a messenger and earnestly begged the blessed man not to be reluctant to come to him. Without delay, because he recognized the messenger as a bearer of good news, he did not refuse to come.

John, filled with immense joy at his arrival, entrusted all his affairs to him and humbly implored him to pray to the common Lord on his behalf and to urge religious men to do the same.

Then the man of God, moved by domestic affection from the depths of his heart, dismissed everyone and devoted himself for a very long time to prayer, with tears and without the sound of words. When the prayer was complete, he called the countess with whom John was staying and urged her to prepare food for the sick man—namely, a chicken.

She resisted because she knew that his stomach had been so weakened by his long illness that he had even recoiled from taking food during the preceding several weeks. The man of God replied: “Let it be for now. For you should know that it will not be prepared so quickly as he himself will desire it.”

The event proved this true. After he had eaten sufficiently, John fell asleep, overcome by drowsiness, and without delay recovered from that most serious illness.

### 17.

Again the blessed man was sent by the Lord Pope to direct the Churches. Among the many good works he performed, he had rescued a certain bishop, accused by false charges, from the slanders of malicious men, guided by the Spirit of truth.

When he returned to Rome, he entered the Basilica of the Apostle Peter for the sake of prayer and thanksgiving. He had a customary place of retreat: he would prostrate himself in prayer before the icon of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which stood inside the same basilica, and pour out his heart in tears.

When on this occasion he had approached to do the same according to his custom, he saw—marvelous to relate—the image itself shedding tears, as though expressing its own sorrow over some affliction suffered by her beloved.

Filled with wonder and ecstasy, after remaining fixed in amazement for some time, he abundantly answered tears with tears. When his supplication was complete, he returned to the Lateran Palace to visit the Lord Pope.

The Pope had just received a report of the false rumor: namely, that Hildebrand had justified the aforementioned bishop in exchange for gifts. He made it plainly understood what the likeness of shared grief in the sacred image had signified. But when Hildebrand began to explain the matter with the wisdom that shone upon his face, all his adversaries who were present grew ashamed. In accordance with Saint Jerome, the false rumor was quickly crushed and the biting tongue quickly pierced, since his life commended him by both word and example.

Afterward, when he returned to the image according to his usual custom, the miracle was reversed: he saw it smile at him as at a triumphant victor.

### 18.

Lest these miracles, although involving saints, nevertheless involving insensible things, appear incredible, we wish to provide support for belief from the more credible writings of orthodox Fathers, borrowing several examples that we do not consider ineffective against this kind of disbelief.

Thus it is read in the Acts of the Seventh Ecumenical Council, assembled under the authority of Pope Adrian I:

[Note: These matters are found in the Spiritual Meadow, or Book 10 of the Lives of the Fathers, by John Moschus, chapter 180.]

“Dionysius, priest of the Church of Ascalon, told us about Abbot John the anchorite, saying:

“Because this man was great in the present generation, and because of the miracle that God wrought concerning him in the state pleasing to God, he related the following:

“‘An old man sat in a cave in the region of Socho, nearly nine miles from Jerusalem.

[Note: In the same place the distance is given as approximately twenty miles. Scripture names Socho in various places and relates events that took place between it and Azekah. It lies toward the southeast, in the direction of Egypt.]

“‘The old man had in the cave an image of our holy and undefiled Lady, Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, holding the Lord Christ in her arms.

“‘Whenever he wished to go somewhere—whether to distant deserts, to Jerusalem to adore the Holy Cross and the holy places, to pray on Mount Sinai, or to visit martyrs who were many leagues distant from Jerusalem—for the old man was exceedingly fond of the martyrs, going sometimes to Saint John at Ephesus, sometimes to Saint Theodore at Euchaita, sometimes to Saint Thecla at Seleucia, or to Saint Sergius at Araphani—

[Note: Euchaita has been incorrectly printed. Consult what we said about Saint Theodore in his Life on 7 February.]

[Note: More properly Saraphas, as will be said in the Life of Saints Theodore and Bacchus on 7 October. Consult Baronius’s notes for that day.]

“‘—he would prepare a candle and light it, as was his custom. Standing in prayer that his journey might be directed, he would say to the Lady, looking toward her image:

“‘“Holy Lady, Mother of God, since I have a long road to travel, extending over many days, take care of your candle and keep it unextinguished according to my intention; for I will go with your help as my companion.”

“‘After saying this to the image, he would depart. When he had completed the journey he had undertaken, he would return, having sometimes remained away for one month, sometimes for two or three, and sometimes for five or six. He would then find the candle properly arranged and burning, just as he had left it when departing on his journey. He never saw it at any time extinguished of itself, neither when rising from sleep nor when returning from the desert to the cave.’”

### 19.

Likewise, from the same Acts, from the Life of Saint Theodore the Archimandrite:

[Note: From Act 4 it is clear that this was Saint Theodore, Abbot of Siceon. We gave his very distinguished Acts on 22 April, six from the Latin translation alone, prepared by Lipomanus. Since this miracle is absent from that translation, it appears that Lipomanus himself did not possess the complete Greek text, which for that reason we desire all the more to be discovered.]

“When he was about twelve years old, a mortality caused by a bubo broke out in that village, so that he too fell ill almost to death. They carried him to the oratory of Saint John the Baptist, which stood beside the village, and laid him at the entrance to the altar.

“Above him, in the recess of the Cross, stood an image of the Savior Jesus Christ. While he was being tormented by the pain of the bubo, drops of dew suddenly fell upon him from the image. Immediately, by the grace of God, he recovered from the pain, became well, and went home.”

Since these examples are sufficient to establish belief, let us return to the order of our narrative.

### 20.

The venerable Hildebrand therefore saw a vision foreshadowing the apostolic compassion that he was soon to receive. Simon Magus appeared to him, dancing and exulting in a ship; and Hildebrand himself seemed to leap upon him and, wrestling with him, bring him under his feet and bind him with unbreakable bonds.

Few people are unaware of what this signifies concerning the renewal of the Church. Before this blessed man’s apostolate, Simon Magus had played his sacrilegious game of buying and selling ecclesiastical dignities far and wide through his followers—freely and shamelessly purchasing and selling them. How he was overthrown and bound by this athlete of God, we shall relate in its proper place.

At about the same time, some Pisans were spending the night in the Basilica of Saint Peter for the sake of prayer. Behold, they saw the very Prince of the Apostles walking in that same house of his with this predestined heir, and ordering him to gather into a sack, which could be seen lying nearby, the dung of various animals that appeared to be scattered there, place it upon his back, and carry it outside.

It is readily apparent that this dung signified the lusts and filth of various men, especially the Nicolaitans and their patron, the fourth Henry. But how it was carried away and removed, we shall demonstrate in due time, with God’s inspiration.

## CHAPTER III. His Election to the Papacy and the Vision of the Dove that Followed; Illnesses Divinely Inflicted upon and Removed from Gregory; the Healing of the Sick

### 21.

Now let us present the legitimate order of his election after the death of Pope Alexander, just as his electors recorded it:

“In the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 183 of his most merciful Incarnation, in the eleventh indiction and the eleventh lunar cycle, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Monday, the day of the burial of the Lord Alexander II, Pope of good memory:

“Lest the Apostolic See should long mourn, deprived of its own Pastor, we, the Cardinals, Clerics, Acolytes, Subdeacons, Deacons, and Priests of the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, gathered in the Basilica of Saint Peter in Chains, with venerable bishops present; with abbots, clerics, and monks giving their consent; and with great crowds of both sexes and of various ranks acclaiming, have elected for ourselves as Pastor and Supreme Pontiff a religious man, endowed with the prudence of twofold knowledge, an outstanding lover of equity and justice, strong in adversity, temperate in prosperity, and, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, adorned with good morals: chaste, modest, sober, pure, hospitable, ruling his household well; nobly educated and instructed from childhood in the bosom of this Mother Church; and, by the merit of his life, raised to the honor of archdeacon to the present day—namely, Hildebrand the Archdeacon.

“We wish and approve that from now and forever he both be and be called Pope Gregory and Apostolicus.

“Does this please you?”

“It pleases us.”

“Do you want him?”

“We want him.”

“Do you praise him?”

“We praise him.”

“Enacted at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction.”

### 22.

Gregory himself immediately sent the following letters concerning his election.

“Gregory, elected Roman Pontiff, to Desiderius, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino, greetings in Christ Jesus.

“Lord Pope Alexander has died. His death has fallen upon me and, shaking all my inward parts, has utterly disturbed me. For at his death the Roman people, contrary to custom, remained so quiet and surrendered the reins of deliberation into our hands that it plainly appeared to have happened through God’s mercy.

“Therefore, having taken counsel, we resolved that after a three-day fast, after litanies and the prayers of many, seasoned with almsgiving, and supported by divine aid, we should determine what seemed best concerning the election of the Roman Pontiff.

“But suddenly, when our aforesaid Lord Pope was being committed to burial in the Church of the Savior, a great tumult and roaring of the people arose, and they rose up against me like madmen, so that I can say with the Prophet: ‘I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me’; ‘I have labored crying, my throat has become hoarse’; and: ‘Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me.’

“But because I am lying in bed, greatly exhausted, and cannot dictate sufficiently, I shall refrain from recounting my anguish.

“I therefore beg you, by the almighty Lord, to urge and invite the suffragan brothers and sons whom you nourish in Christ to pray to God for me, in true charity, so that the prayer that ought to have freed me from danger may at least protect me now that I am in danger.

“You yourself must not fail to come to us as quickly as possible. You know how much the Roman Church needs you and how much confidence it places in your prudence.

“Greet on our behalf the Lady Agnes, the Empress, and the venerable Rainaldus, Bishop of Como.

[Note: Agnes, Empress and mother of Henry IV, governed the kingdom peacefully while her son was still a child after her husband’s death. Later, seeing that her son’s mind had been turned away from her by the jealousy of the princes, she withdrew to Italy. As Leo of Ostia says in Book 3, chapter 32 of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, she stayed at Monte Cassino for almost half a year; Gregory therefore greets her as being there at that time.]

[Note: Rainaldus appears to have been in exile at Monte Cassino at that time. Saint Gregory consoles him in Letter 20 of Book 1, written the following year, in which he mentions the said Empress Agnes. He also wrote him a letter in Book 6, in the second indiction, in the year 1079.]

“Now faithfully beg them in our place to show how much affection they have had toward us.

“Given at Rome, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction.”

### 23.

“Gregory, elected Roman Pontiff, to Gottifredus, Duke, greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: Gottifredus, or Godefridus, surnamed the Bearded or the Elder, Duke of Lorraine and Tuscany, had two wives: first Doda, by whom he fathered Godefridus the Hunchback and Blessed Ida, widow and Countess of Boulogne, whose Life we gave on 13 April. He later married, in 1054, Beatrice, widow of Boniface, Marquis of Tuscany. Before him she had borne Boniface Matilda, Marchioness or Countess.]

“We are pleased by your joy, which we have learned from your letters that you feel over our promotion—not because any delight in our cause produces this in you, but because we do not doubt that it has flowed from the source of sincere affection and a faithful mind.

“For our promotion, which supplies you and the other faithful with a pious opinion of us and with joy, generates in us the bitterness of inward grief and the anguish of excessive anxiety. We see how great a concern surrounds us; we feel how heavily the burden of the office we have undertaken weighs upon us. Beneath it, while the consciousness of our weakness trembles, our soul desires in Christ the repose of release more than life amid such dangers.

“Indeed, consideration of the office entrusted to us troubles us so greatly that, unless some confidence in the prayers of spiritual people sustained us after God, our mind would collapse beneath the immensity of our cares.

“For through the agency of sins, almost the whole world has been placed in the power of the Evil One, so that all—and especially those who are prelates in the Church—strive rather to disturb it than to defend or honor it with faithful devotion. While they gape after their own profits or the desires for present glory, they oppose themselves like enemies to everything belonging to the religion and justice of God.

“This is all the more grievous to us, since we have undertaken the governance of the universal Church amid such difficulty and can neither administer it properly nor safely abandon it.

“Nevertheless, because we know that, by God’s gift, the virtue of faith and constancy resides in you, and because we place in you all the confidence that is fitting in a dearly beloved son of Saint Peter, we do not wish you in any way to doubt our equally steadfast affection for you and our most ready goodwill toward your honors.

“Concerning the king, you can fully know our mind and desire. Insofar as we understand in the Lord, we believe that no one should be preferred to us as more concerned for his present and future glory or as desiring it more abundantly.

“It is also our will that, as soon as the opportunity is offered, we should approach him through our messengers with paternal affection and admonition concerning those matters which we judge to pertain to the advancement of the Church and the honor of his royal dignity.

“If he listens to us, we shall rejoice in his salvation no less than in our own. He will then most certainly be able to gain salvation for himself if, in maintaining justice, he acquiesces in our admonitions and counsels.

“But if—which we do not desire—he returns hatred to us for affection and, by disregarding God’s justice, renders contempt to almighty God in return for the great honor conferred upon him, the threat that says, ‘Cursed is the man who withholds his sword from blood,’ will not, by God’s providence, come upon us.

“For it is not permitted us to set aside the law of God for the personal favor of anyone, or to depart from the path of righteousness for human approval, as the Apostle says: ‘If I wished to please men, I would not be a servant of God.’

“Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh indiction.”

### 24.

After this, once he had been confirmed by pontifical blessing, the heavenly Father showed, after the example of the Gospel, how acceptable he was to him, since he revealed to little ones the mysteries that he had hidden from the wise and prudent.

Two peasants, moved by a curiosity that was not unreasonable, learned of the new Pontiff’s arrival in the Lateran diocese. Urging one another on, they hurried to the church to see him. When they arrived, they found him celebrating the solemnities of Mass beside the altar.

They watched him attentively and carefully noted all his bodily movements and gestures. But one of them, as though carried away in ecstasy, saw a dove descend from heaven and sit upon Gregory’s right shoulder. With its wings spread out, it covered his head.

When the Canon had been completed, the dove stretched out its neck and, as it appeared to the peasant, inserted its beak into the chalice. Then, withdrawing it, it immediately returned to the place from which it had come.

The peasant, astonished at the new miracle, soon came back to himself and returned home.

[Note: Leo of Ostia relates that something similar later happened to the same Gregory at Monte Cassino, in Book 3, chapter 54 of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino.]

25. On the following night three men appeared to him, of dignified bearing and splendid appearance. One of them, with his garment girded up and a becoming gray head of hair, presented the figure of Peter to him, as he was accustomed to see it in paintings. Another, splendid in countenance and tall in stature, inspired the beholder with both wonder and fear. He did not inquire very carefully what sort of man the third was.

Accordingly, hesitating for a long time over who the more approachable of these three might be, he finally addressed the gray-haired man and asked who the other, greater one was, or by what name he was known. Receiving the answer that he was called Sol, he was further rebuked as follows: “Why did you not announce to Gregory what you saw yesterday?” Terrified, he declared that he had seen nothing. “Have you forgotten,” he said, “that yesterday, during the solemn celebration of Mass, you saw a dove resting upon his shoulder?” He then unfolded the whole vision to him just as he had seen it.

Next he ordered him to go to Gregory as quickly as possible, because Gregory was to pass through that place on the same day, and to recount the vision to him in due order. When morning came, the peasant was uncertain what to do; and, considering within himself whether the vision might be an illusion, he approached a religious man of the same place and told him what he had seen. He received this counsel: he should earnestly beseech the Lord that, if this vision had come from Him, He would deign to reveal it to him a second and a third time. The peasant devoutly did so.

[Col. 0052C] On the second night, therefore, he was likewise admonished, and he persisted still more earnestly in prayer. On the third night, when the same men presented themselves more terrifyingly than usual, one of them ordered him, if he wished to prolong his life for any length of time, not to hesitate to announce to the Apostolic Lord what he had been commanded. He added: “If, when he was near, you did not at all obey our commands, you will have to go farther after him and labor.”

But the peasant, desiring to elicit something still more certain from them, said: “I am indeed a peasant and unlearned. What sign will be given me, so that I may be believed by such a person?” One of them, who habitually spoke for the others, said: “You will say this to Gregory, which he himself also recognizes as true: that, when he approached the altar, he deserved to obtain from the almighty Lord what he had considered that very day.”

[Col. 0052D] The peasant reached Gregory and asked for a private audience with him. He faithfully explained what had been the cause of his journey and labor. Gregory, however, smiling kindly and recognizing the sign beforehand, permitted the peasant—the messenger of so great an embassy—to return home with the Apostolic blessing.

26. At another time [Note: Namely, in the following year, 1074. He fell ill, and indicates that he had recovered from the illness in a letter to Beatrice and her daughter Matilda, letter 9 of book 2, written on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November. In it he laments that he had emerged from a dangerous illness and had been preserved for the care of the Church, which was almost shipwrecking.], when he was confined by a very serious bodily illness, one of his nieces had come to visit him and was asking how he was faring. Then, in order to lighten his niece’s anxiety about his illness, he held her jewels in his hand and asked whether she wished to marry.

Afterward, when he had recovered his health and was occupied with his customary duties, he was unable—neither by recalling past evils, nor by hoping for future goods, nor by desire, nor, in short, by any means—to reach the point of bringing forth even a single little tear. For a long time, therefore, he reflected with sorrowful heart on what he had done, by what offense he had wronged God, and finally by what fault he had lost the gift of compunction that had been granted him. At length, having moderated his grief, he adopted the following counsel: he asked religious men to implore the Lord together with him through fasting and prayers, so that He might deign to reveal for what offense the gift he had formerly possessed had been taken away from him.

This was carried out with fitting devotion. When two weeks of vigils, fasting, and [Col. 0053B] bodily discipline had been completed, the gracious and swift hearer granted him the desire of his heart. For the Blessed Mother of God appeared in a vision to a certain innocent and simple man and commanded him, saying: “Go and tell Gregory that, although I had chosen him for the choir”—there is no doubt that this means the choir of virgins—“he himself, on the contrary, acted otherwise than he ought.”

Moved by this new pronouncement, Gregory began to hesitate even more, and he prayed more earnestly that God’s mercy might show him more clearly what it meant. Again the most holy Virgin Mary, Mother of the Lord, appeared in sleep to the same man as before and said: “You will say this to Gregory: he handled his niece’s jewels contrary to the strictness of our institution; for that reason he lost the grace that he had. But now, because he has done penance for his sin, he will receive back the gift of tears.”

Here we are reminded of that saying: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7).

27. During a certain summer, which is very hostile to human bodies at Rome, while the same man of God was burning with severe fevers throughout an entire week, the Blessed Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, appeared to him. To show her indignation, she struck his belly with the back of her hand and departed.

Afterward he was so weakened during the following week that those awaiting his death could scarcely perceive him breathing. When that week had ended, the Blessed Mother of God came to him again, at about the sixth hour of the day, and asked him how he was and whether he thought that he had yet suffered enough. He replied to her: “Most merciful Lady, as it seems to you.”

Then, gently passing her hand over him as though anointing his body, she vanished from his sight. Soon afterward he asked for his garments, as though he were about to go to church. Those present thought, because of his extreme weakness, that his mind was not sound. But he affirmed that he was suffering no harm, compelled them to dress him, and had them lead him to the church. Once this had been done, he recovered his health so completely that on the following day he even celebrated publicly the solemn Mass in the church of the Savior.

[Col. 0054A] 28. Meanwhile, how much obedience ought to be shown to so great a man was divinely revealed to Hermann, at that time a Cardinal but afterward bishop of the Church of Brescia [Note: Hermann, also called Arimannus or Armanus, was elected Bishop of Brescia in 1096 through the favor of the Countess Matilda.].

For when he had been invited by Gregory to dinner one day but had not come, a terrifying apparition appeared to him the following night and severely rebuked him, saying: “Why, wretched man, have you imitated the disobedience of Dathan and Abiron by disregarding Gregory’s invitation to dinner, just as they proudly rejected Moses’ summons to the assembly? Have you forgotten how many thousands upon thousands have been plunged into hell because of the disobedience of the first-created man? Hurry, therefore, to make satisfaction, if you wish to escape the condemnation due to rebels.”

Accordingly, as soon as an opportunity was given, he fell at the feet of the most merciful Pope; and without delay he obtained pardon through his tearful supplication.

29. Now I wish briefly to set down two miracles of holiness divinely performed through the Blessed Gregory, lest, as we enter the denser forest of history, they perhaps slip from our memory.

At a certain time, when he was washing his sacred hands as usual, the water of the washing itself became like milk and immediately freed a certain sick man from his illness when he took it as a remedy in faith that he would recover his health.

Likewise, while he was staying in the retinue of the glorious Matilda and avoiding the fury of the persecution of which we shall speak more fully later, the venerable Ubald, Bishop of Mantua [Note: Ubald, also called Ubaldo, was made Bishop of Mantua in 1082, but was expelled by King Henry and lived in exile with Saint Gregory.], informed him one day that his cook, weighed down by a severe illness, could not rise from his bed.

But Gregory, having no replacement for this necessary office, moved the mountain of illness through faith comparable to a mustard seed, and the cook grew strong through the grace of restored health. At the very hour when the cook heard the command, he arose and prepared what was necessary.

CHAPTER IV. The Decretal Letters of Gregory against the Simoniacs and Fornicators

30. The time now demands that we set down several Decretal Letters of the blessed Bishop, sent against the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans to Gaul and Germany [Note: This letter is preserved as inserted into the First Council held at Rome under Saint Gregory in 1074, in the Apologeticus, chapter 1]; and afterward, as we promised, offer some conjecture about what that sack filled with excrement, which we mentioned above as having been seen by the Pisans, might signify.

For the announcement of the regular judgment, shaking and restraining the disgrace of the aforesaid heretics and of those who favored them, may not unreasonably be compared to a sack containing excrement. The holy man, in a certain sense, carried this sack while, by sending letters, he patiently awaited for a long time the conversion of those whom he had censured; but he carried it away when, because of their persistence in error, he separated them from the Church by synodal decision.

The first of these Letters that comes before us is addressed to Otto, Bishop of Constance, and reads as follows:

31. “Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Otto, Bishop of Constance: greetings and Apostolic blessing. The urgency of your messengers …” See below among the letters of Saint Gregory.

32. But how the aforementioned Bishop resisted—or rather, insulted—the salutary decrees is disclosed by the following Letter:

“Gregory, servant of the servants of God, [Note: Otto supported the party of King Henry; for this reason he was excommunicated, sent into exile in 1074, and died two years later while still under excommunication. He was buried at Basel. So says the Chronicle of Constance edited by Pictorius.] to Otto, Bishop of Constance: greetings and Apostolic blessing. It has been reported to Us …” See among the letters.

33. Here he commands the clergy and people not to obey the disobedient Bishop:

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the greater and lesser Clerics and Laity residing in the Bishopric of Constance, who love the Christian law: greetings and Apostolic blessing. We have sent to our brother, your Bishop Otto …” See among the letters of Saint Gregory.

34. To the Laity, for carrying out the foregoing decrees:

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rudolph, Duke of Swabia, and Berthold, Duke of Carinthia: greetings and Apostolic blessing [Note: This is Letter 45 of book 2]. We know that your prudence weighs with discerning mind the pitiable desolation of the Christian religion …” See among the letters.

35. Likewise to the Laity concerning the same decrees:

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ and most noble Count Adalbert and his wife: greetings and Apostolic blessing. We give thanks to God …” See above.

36. That no one should obey Bishops who despise or neglect the aforesaid statutes:

“Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all Clerics and Laity established in the kingdom of the Teutons: greetings and Apostolic blessing. We have heard that certain Bishops residing among you …” See above.

37. These Letters were followed by a general Synod presided over by Gregory himself. At it, as its acts report, a sentence of anathema was pronounced against all the Simoniac and Nicolaitan heretics who, hardened in the sect of their error, knowingly disobeyed the definitions of the holy Fathers and their Decretal statutes, and, with the obstinacy of apostates, deliberately and willingly resisted them.

Behold the sack full of excrement (Ezek. 1:9), carried until then by arguing, pleading, and reproving with all patience and instruction; but from that time carried out by the just vengeance of divine zeal, according to the order that the Lord Himself showed through the Prophet Ezekiel to those who would execute His vengeance, saying: “Begin at my sanctuary.”

For the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah had multiplied exceedingly even up to the pontificate of Gregory (Isa. 1:9), in this respect: the aforementioned heretics and their supporters, unrestrained by an excessive freedom to sin, proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not conceal it. Therefore, unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed of incorruption, we would have been like Sodom and would have resembled Gomorrah.

38. Stirred by this reputation for righteousness, the clerics of Babenberg [Note: Letter 84 of book 1 was written to Hermann of Bamberg, in which Gregory admonished him. But because Hermann withdrew from the judgment of the Apostolic See, invaded the church by simony, and squandered its goods, Gregory excommunicated him and deprived him of priestly office, as he writes to the people of Bamberg, to Siegfried, Archbishop of Mainz, and to King Henry. These are Letters 1, 2, and 3 of book 3. Fruschius says that he eventually entered the monastery of Schwarzach in Eastern Francia, that is, Franconia.] brought to Gregory’s ears the Simoniac induction of their pseudo-bishop, named Hermann.

But he, having gathered no small sum of money and an abundance of precious metal and clothing, hoped that Apostolic severity could be softened by gifts. Approaching Rome, he entreated the venerable Hermann, Bishop of the Church of Metz and Legate of the Apostolic See [Note: Saint Gregory had entrusted Hermann, Bishop of Metz, with his responsibilities in the case of the Bishop of Bamberg, as is said in the cited Letter 84 of book 1. He also wrote to him in Letter 53 of book 1; Letters 2 and 21 of book 2; Letter 5 of book 6; and Letter 21 of book 8. In them he entrusted various matters to him and indicated the authority of the Apostolic See in excommunicating King Henry.], who happened at that time to be traveling in the same company, to go ahead of him to the Lord Pope and intercede for him.

When Hermann had attempted this and had indicated that there was substantial material for human appeasement, the just man, who was accustomed to shake his hands free of every gift, replied from his chamber, inflamed by the Holy Spirit: “Tell him that, if he wishes to obtain any communion with the faithful, he must return to his own regions and undertake, by penance, the strict yoke of the monastic rule. For, may God be merciful to me, even if he were to fill this house for me with gold and silver, he would never, with my consent, exercise the episcopal office.”

Thus this Simoniac too was removed from the priesthood.

CHAPTER V. The Conspiracy against the Life of Saint Gregory: His Capture and Liberation

39. We must by no means pass over in silence how the strongest athlete of God overcame, for the Lord’s name, the deceits, temptations, dangers, slanders, mockeries, captures, and imprisonments of his enemies; and finally, with the Lord’s help and support and with the intercession of the Apostles accompanying him, how he overcame kings, tyrants, dukes, princes, and captors and devourers of human souls; moreover, wolves—namely, ministers of Antichrist—Archbishops, Bishops, and other ecclesiastical invaders.

This should serve as an example both to those now living and to those who will come after, so that the people of the holy Church may learn that our age once fell under so great and such a Pastor. For it seems improper and unfitting to consign this Father’s labor to oblivion, when even the memory of profane events is preserved among secular people as an example of courage.

If this example is entrusted to tenacious memory, it becomes an adornment of the holy Church, an ornament of Christ’s faithful, and a loss to profane heresies. For from this the beginnings of the struggle of the righteous again took their first principles; from this, ecclesiastical victory and, in a certain sense, an inheritance of perpetual happiness were propagated through the Son.

40. There was, then, in the City a certain man, a son of perdition, the most criminal and wicked of all men, whose memory itself seems to stain the air. Perjury, deceit, lust, treachery, murders, schemes, whisperings, conspiracies, frauds, deceptions, and secret gatherings had been his delights; and he believed that everything capable of opposing virtue was permitted to him in every respect.

He was the father of thieves and companion of perjurers, the shield of the deceitful and the spear of the adulterer, the helmet of murderers and the shield of treachery, the covering of schemes, the guardian of whispering, the anxiety of conspiracy, the disguise of fraud, the laughter of deception, and the hiding place of evil agreement. Every heretic and every criminal hastened to take refuge with him. His wing concealed scandals, and beneath his shadow Leviathan himself, that twisting serpent, rested sweetly and pleasantly.

To increase this great traffic, he had built many towers in the City. Setting aside enmity both toward God and toward man, he strove to carry out whatever the instigator of wickedness—that is, the devil—had placed before the eyes of his perverse mind. His words were smooth and sweet, but in the end they were darts and wormwood.

For his own destruction, he killed a certain fellow godfather. Before the matter was fully known, he broke into the man’s house and destroyed it as well. After committing so great a crime, he withdrew into the tower that he had built while his father Stephen was still Prefect of the City.

[Note: In the Manuscript Deeds of the Pontiffs, carried down to Pope Martin V, he is called Cencius, son of Stephen; Bertoldo calls him Cincius. Here the name seems to have been concealed in silence out of consideration for the family and for Cincius, the Prefect of the City, a most holy man, as will appear below.]

Incensed to avenge this crime, the man of God, while Pope Alexander was still alive, bound him with the bonds of a curse and anathema. To increase his own disgrace, he went with certain men whom he had attached to himself—namely, Nicholas and Bertram—to the son of perdition, King Henry.
