After sharing in a plan of great impiety, he received as a guest Cadalous of Parma [Note: Cadalous, Bishop of Parma, was established as a pseudo-pope after a new schism had been formed, taking the name Honorius II, on 28 October 1061.], a heretic brought to Rome.

[Col. 0058A] He engaged in many battles in the City on Cadalous’s behalf. All the Simoniac heretics gave him whatever assistance they could and intended through him to bring shame upon the holy Church.

But when that heresiarch finally died [Note: In the same place, no. 39, Nicholas of Aragon says: “Cadalous too, after a few days, by divine judgment suffered a most evil death.”], this man, now confounded, promised to make an agreement with the Lord Pope and to swear allegiance. He did so; but what faith could there be in one to whom truth had never adhered?

Because of the power of the Supreme Priest, he stood like a bound robber; yet he did not cease to conceive in his mind whatever deceits he could. Whenever the venerable Father Gregory exhorted him to withdraw his foot from such things, the hellish heir daily stirred his heart toward worse. Thus it came about that in the very tower which he had built of extraordinary size above the bridge of Saint Peter, he stationed hired assassins who plundered every person entering or leaving, taking whatever goods were being carried.

40*. For this reason the Prefect of the City, a man named Cincius [Note: Cinthius, whom Saint Peter Damian praises in book 8, letters 1 and 2.], prudent indeed and dear to God and men—who cultivated justice in all things, serving God not as a layman but as a faithful monk—captured him one day and handed over so great a robber to the squalor of prison, as he deserved.

At length, through the intervention of certain Roman nobles, with the clemency of the Lord Pope permitting it, after oaths had been made over the body of Saint Peter concerning his improvement, hostages had been given, and the tower on which he relied had been surrendered, he was released.

Then, after battering rams and engines and iron hammers had been brought, the tower was utterly overthrown. Thus the City enjoyed some respite, and the faction of the wicked, shaken by great fear, fell silent.

But what could the wretched man do? As long as he was able, he approached the wicked, though they were far away, both personally and through his messengers. He himself traveled through Apulia and Lucania, visiting Duke Guiscard and the other excommunicates [Note: Robert Guiscard, Duke of the Normans, was excommunicated by Saint Gregory in 1074, but, obedient to the Church, was absolved in 1080, as Baronius explains at greater length under those years.]. He arranged with them a suitable time and a plan for capturing and killing the Lord Pope.

He sent his son to Guibert, the heretical Archbishop of Ravenna [Note: Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna and later Antipope, was always hostile to Saint Gregory, supported his adversaries, and was excommunicated.], to arrange the same pact. He also sent letters of deceit to the King, promising to bring the same Father before the royal presence.

After such schemes had been arranged, he rested for a time, evidently awaiting an opportunity to capture Gregory and hand him over to the people of the wicked to be killed.

But the almighty Lord, who, by being captured, freed the world and captured the devil, advanced the condition of the Church through the capture and blood of this Father. He not only prevented the son of iniquity from harming His servant, but also deprived him of his possessions.

41. When almost a year had passed, the time came for the ministers of the devil. As the feast of the Lord’s Nativity approached, he began to urge his conspirators, with whom he had sworn the conspiracy, to assemble ready in mind for so great a crime and to prepare their courage. He promised them unspeakable rewards, future liberty, and limitless profit, imitating in every respect his brother and master, the devil, who promised that through the Lord’s death alone the whole world would belong to him.

But, as it is written, while he captures, he is captured; while he begins to plunder, he becomes the plunder; and while he seeks unlawful things that he did not yet possess, he loses what he had acquired and retained.

Thus this man also, being that one’s minister, if he had perceived in his heart that he was about to be stripped of such possessions, might perhaps by some means have withdrawn his hand from the commission of so great a crime, out of love for his property more than for God. But because his own wickedness had blinded him, and he went about burdened with it, he attempted to bring the matter to completion, not fearing—or rather, placing second—the danger to his soul. A second Judas, he laid hands upon his Lord and the Lord’s Christ.

On the day of so great a feast, the Pontiff went, as was customary, to the church of Blessed Mary, which, because of the merits of so many devotions, is called the Major, to perform the service of the Vigils, accompanied by a small number of Clerics and Laity.

For it had always been the custom of the City, at the splendor of so great a solemnity, for everyone to flock to that same church and spend the entire night awake, intent upon hymns and praises. But by the Lord’s arrangement, to prevent so great a church from being drenched in the blood of so great a Pastor, the people were prevented from gathering then, so that the ministers of the devil might be able to accomplish what their destructive desire had wickedly conceived.

On the very day of the Vigils, the sky had poured forth such a flood of waters that it seemed to everyone that the deluge of ancient times was about to return. Scarcely anyone could leave the threshold of his house, or enter the hut of a neighbor close by if necessity required it, let alone reach a church situated so far away. The elements of the world were, in a certain sense, proclaiming the future crime and foreshadowing an unheard-of deed.

[Col. 0059D] 42. But why say more? The night arrives in which the son of darkness attacks the minister of light.

Scouts were sent out, and they came to other investigators; for the conspirator had enlisted a certain group from among the inhabitants of the neighborhood beside that same church. They observed everything and sent word to that criminal of what they had discovered.

Then he hastily brought up his legion, armed with breastplates. He positioned it so that, once victory had been achieved—whether by the Pope’s death or by triumphantly carrying him away alive—each man could mount whatever horse he might have, lest anyone attempt to rise against them.

At last they reached the church. The glorious Pope, placed at the manger, was chanting the first Mass of the night, as religious observance prescribes. Both he and his Clergy had received the Lord’s Body; the others who were present were still receiving the same Sacraments when suddenly a great shout and great howling thundered forth without warning and filled the church.

They then searched the church on every side, striking with drawn swords those whom they could reach, and gathered at the place of the manger where the illustrious Pope was seated. After striking several people there and breaking through the little doors, they entered with savage hands the small corner of the manger of the eternal King and His Mother.

Then they laid hands upon him and seized him. One of them drew his sword and wished to cut off his head, but, because the Lord willed otherwise, he could not. They nevertheless struck him on the forehead, wounded him severely, and dragged him away from the unfinished Mass with violent hands, beating and striking him.

But he, like an innocent and gentle lamb, raised his eyes to heaven and gave them no answer. He did not protest or resist, nor did he ask them to show him mercy in any respect.

At length they stripped him of the Pallium and the Chasuble—or Dalmatic—and Tunic with the Shirt, leaving him only the amice and stole. Then, like a thief being dragged away, they placed him behind the back of one of the sacrilegious men.

The man who had struck his forehead with the sword was seized by a demon and rolled about for a long time, foaming, before the atrium of that same church; and his horse, which had fled, was never found again.

43. The report of so great an evil quickly shook the whole City. Who could ever recount such weeping and such funeral lamentations? Just as the City had been accustomed to rejoice more greatly than other cities at the Nativity of our Lord, so now, shaken by the event, it proclaimed that no small sorrow had come upon it.

Heaven and earth alike were terrified by this deed, and the hearts of all were prepared to avenge so great a crime. Then was fulfilled what had been spoken through the Prophet: “Your feast days shall be turned into lamentation and mourning, and your joy into weeping” (Tob. 2).

And this: “She wept bitterly in the night, and her tears were upon her cheeks; there was none to comfort her among all her dear ones” (Lam. 1).

Then the holy Church of God said: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night?” (Jer. 9).

And this: “Hear, I beseech you, all peoples, and behold my sorrow.”

Then every husband took up lamentation, and the women who sat upon the marriage bed mourned. The entire Clergy, after the Pastor had been struck, ran here and there, and as they left they stripped almost all the altars.

Nothing was done anywhere in the churches on that day in the divine Office except what had been stated beforehand. Yet the elements, which had been disturbed until that moment, were seen to have become calm, lest they hinder the people who were zealous for the Lord’s zeal.

The earth, absorbing almost all the water that it had endured in the excessive flood, once again showed itself, in a certain sense, dry, so that all might avenge the deed.

Throughout the entire night, while trumpets and horns sounded and soldiers searched every entrance lest he be carried outside the City by any device, no trace was found anywhere. Since the matter was uncertain and everyone was ignorant whether he was alive or dead, the people gathered in the Capitol. Then some men reported that he was being held captive in a certain tower, and the news became known.

At this, all peoples raised their voices to the stars.

44. But as soon as daylight had been restored to the earth, innumerable people, encouraging one another, came to the house of the Antichrist. Battle was joined, but at the first encounter the hostile party took flight, and the entire faction shut itself inside the same tower.

The tower was then surrounded on every side, fire was set to it, and, after engines and battering rams had been brought, the wall was breached. Everything enclosed there became plunder for the people of the Lord.

No one avoided personal danger; forgetting himself, each fought as best he could.

A certain man, together with a noble matron, followed Father Gregory, and for some time they gave him comfort. The man, afflicted by the weariness of the assault and by the cold of the winter night, warmed Gregory with skins that he brought and placed his feet in his lap.

The matron, for her part, lamenting as she did so, soothed our Father’s wound, weakened by the excessive flow of rosy blood, with the application of her remedy. She cried out against all those enemies of God, murderers and sacrilegious men, becoming another Mary.

For just as that woman, weeping for her sins, had bathed the Lord’s feet with her tears, so this one, bearing the crimes of all, washed that great Pastor with her tears.

She had kissed the feet of the Lord and Savior, so that, after they had been washed, she might eventually reach His head. But this woman, clean through her first baptism and then scorched by the ardor of her heart, kissed the head and breast of the servant of God and Lord and drenched them with tears.

O memorable breast! O praiseworthy heart of a most devout woman! How great a fire of charity had then taken hold of you, when before your eyes you saw the minister of the eternal King handled wickedly and wounded by the hands of evil men, and when you did not withhold from Satan’s ministers, from your modest mouth and purified holy kisses—those with which you had kissed the feet, hands, and head of so great a Father—reproaches worthy of them and darts of curses!

It is truly credible that you wished to lay down your soul for the Father’s life, and that you would rather undergo unimaginable torments than see your lord captured and so badly treated.

The noble heroine fought with all her strength and, as a sharer in everyone’s immeasurable reward, was accumulating as much for herself.

45. But in proportion to the courage of the former woman’s faith was the verbal treachery of the other woman. Just as, long ago, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, the maidservant who kept the door had terrified Peter, so this woman disturbed his Vicar with biting insults.

She had been the sister of that traitor and therefore did not fear to curse so great a Father. Another man, the minister and henchman of the same traitor, held a drawn sword and blasphemously asserted that he would cut off the head of so great a man on that very day.

The Lord’s swiftest judgment did not delay the vengeance for this impiety. A spear hurled from outside severed the artery of his dreadful voice in the throat and struck him down to the earth, dying and twitching. Thus it sent him to Tartarus.

46. But the traitor, now seeing that the tower was about to be captured and that the danger of death threatened him, was forced to fall at the feet of the most blessed Pope and say:

“You have always taught mercy, Father; by teaching, you have perfected it. You convert those who err and strengthen those who have been converted in the faith. Receive me, who am erring and turning away from iniquities; strengthen me once converted, lest the depth of despair swallow me.

“I have sinned, I have erred, I have betrayed, I have killed, I have committed sacrilege. I violated the bedchamber of the King’s Mother and with violent hands [Note: The Lord’s manger, from which Saint Gregory had been dragged away, is meant.] violated the hut and little private chamber of the Son of God. I dragged you, Father and my Lord, like a parricide, through perjuries and sacrileges, with polluted hands, from that bosom.

“Receive me, free me, protect me; show mercy; give remedy, counsel, and assistance. Impose a penalty; assign the penance of imprisonment, exile, and flight from my homeland. Appease, as is customary, the people whom divine judgment, most justly aroused against me, has stirred up.

“Receive me, polluted as I am, with your holy hands, and grant me, repentant, a period of respite on this day. I see in my heart the gallows rightly prepared for me; I behold the punishment I deserve. Therefore, with my body prostrate and my heart humbled, I surrender myself to your power.”

Then the most merciful Pope, as was his nature, addressed the suppliant:

“I see you bound by the gall of bitterness, and the eyes of your mind covered by dark squalor. They were unable to recognize the light of true light, although we had labored so long on your behalf.

“You yourself know how many religious men I sent to admonish you and with how many most patient admonitions I personally urged you. You not only did not heed them, but also rushed into worse things. Nevertheless, the door of life is still open to you, provided only that you turn in your heart.”

At once he fell to the ground, confessed that he was truly guilty and wretched, and promised without delay to carry out everything imposed upon him.

At length the very gentle man, moved by his customary compassion, replied:

“Whatever injury you inflicted upon me personally, I forgive you as a father. But what you committed against God and His Mother, the Apostles, and the whole Church must be expiated. I decree, therefore, that you first travel to Jerusalem; and afterward, if you return from there alive, present yourself to us, to be dealt with by our hands and counsel, so that at least in some manner you may be able to regain the grace of almighty God.

“And just as you have until now been an example of ruin to all the children of the Church, so henceforth become an example of conversion.”

He most willingly promised that he would carry out all these things, as he appeared to have been commanded. Thus he earned release on that day.

47. At last, the pious Pope, standing upright at the window, signaled with outstretched hands to the raging crowd that they should keep calm, and that some of the leading men should climb the tower. But certain men, supposing that he was urging them on to the undertaking they had begun, climbed the tower with the greatest force. And thus he was brought out, [Col. 0063A] while all the crowds wept for joy and cried out from devotion; for he was seen to be entirely spattered with an immense quantity of blood, and therefore, struck with overwhelming horror, they raised their voices to the heavens. After the victory had been won, all of them, together with Pope Gregory, assembled with no little joy at the church of the Mother of God, from which he himself had been dragged during the night. Then the common Father completed at that very hour the Mass which, because the ministers of the devil had obstructed him, he had been unable to finish during the night; and he gave the grace of the Lord’s blessing to those returning after so great a victory.

48. Then, after tasting only a little food, they gathered together again to search more thoroughly for all those who had joined themselves to God’s enemy. When they found them, they took away all their possessions and delivered them to destruction, [Col. 0063B] leaving nothing at all except the persons who had secured the protection of flight. But while the people were giving thanks to God at the aforesaid church for the liberation of their Shepherd, that wicked Judas fled with his wife, sons, and brothers, and, abandoning his possessions in this way, escaped naked. Whatever might once have belonged to him by right, the people who came afterward sold off; the towers and houses were overturned, while the estates were incorporated under the title of the fisc. But the son of perdition and minister of Antichrist, condemned before the foundation of the world, after his escape not only failed entirely to fulfill anything he had promised; he also, joined to certain profane men like himself, did not shrink, for as long as he lived, from giving counsel of wickedness against his liberator. [Col. 0063C]

## CHAPTER VI. The perversity of Henry IV, repeatedly returning to his vomit, against the rights of the Church

49. With these matters prefaced, let us turn to what was done with King Henry; and, by demonstrating the innocence of Pope Gregory, let us indicate, as far as we can, the evils that he had received in return for his good deeds, both to those now living and to those who will follow. For we believe that there will be some who, partly through ignorance of what occurred and partly through ignorance of the authorities of the holy Fathers and of the Decretals, will not fear to criticize and defame the common Father, to the peril of their own salvation, and—something altogether wicked and beyond measure in the sight of God—to heap curses upon him. If, however, moved by divine inspiration, they were doing this more from a desire to know the truth than from the impulse of proud insolence, they would believe men of truth, approved and religious, when questioned.

For they have countless bishops distinguished by religion; and, to name a few out of many, Gerald of Ostia [Note: Gerald, or Gerard, of Regensburg, a bishop of Ostia who had been a prior of Cluny, is said by Ciaconius to have been created Cardinal in the eighth place in the year 1072. In 1074 he was sent as legate to Henry IV. The letters of St. Gregory to him are letters 6 and 16 of Book I.], who, on account of the merit of his life, was taken from the Gallic regions by the Apostolic See and earned the seventh throne among the Cardinal Bishops. He was sent by the Apostolic See to investigate the case of that same king, and, in order to confirm the testimony delivered by his own mouth, he endured many labors, dangers, bonds, and imprisonments for the truth itself.

They have the Bishop of Praeneste [Note: Hubertus, below Humbertus, Bishop of Praeneste, was created Cardinal together with the aforementioned Gerald and sent to Henry IV.], who was sent from the city of Rome to undertake the same labor. There is also Peter of Albano [Note: Blessed Peter Igneus, a Vallombrosan monk and disciple of St. John Gualbert, was created Cardinal Bishop of Albano by St. Gregory in 1074 and died a holy death on 8 January. What is said here, however, occurred in the time of Alexander II, in the case of Peter the Simoniac, Bishop of Florence; it is also recorded in the Life of St. John Gualbert.], who, to confirm the testimony of truth against the Simoniacs, passed unharmed through a huge pyre with bare feet, as is found written in the Register of Pope Alexander II.

There are also several men from the regions beyond the Alps: Udo of Trier [Note: Udo is discussed below; Hermann has been discussed above. The Life of St. Altmann is to be given on 8 August. To this man there is also Letter 10 of Book IX.], Hermann of Metz, Altmann of Passau or Lorch, Adelbero of Würzburg [Note: Adelbero resisted the schismatics most steadfastly together with St. Altmann and was repeatedly driven into exile. He died in 1090 at the monastery of Lambach, founded by his parents.], and Hugh of Die [Note: John Columbus describes, over eight pages in his Bishops of Die, the deeds and legations throughout Gaul entrusted to Hugh, Bishop of Die in the Dauphiné, by St. Gregory. Seven letters of St. Gregory to him are also extant.], at whose election such a great light is said to have descended from heaven that it overcame the day, and that all who were present did not doubt that the Holy Spirit had come.

Let men of the other orders also be summoned to satisfy the unbelieving: namely, the abbot of Cluny [Note: This is St. Hugh the Abbot, whose Life we gave on 29 April; he is discussed above in numbers 12, 13, and 14. Five letters of St. Gregory to him are extant.], the father of that same king in baptism; and Bernard of Marseille [Note: Bernard, Abbot of St. Victor of Marseille, was appointed in 1066 and died in 1080. Together with Bernard of Padua, he was sent by St. Gregory as legate to the princes of the Empire and to Spain because of the dispute involving Berengar, Count of Barcelona. Letters of the former to the latter and to the monks of Marseille are extant. In one of these, Book VI, Letter 15, he urges them to bear the absence of their abbot with equanimity; in the other, Book VII, Letter 8, he grieves over the death of that same abbot.], who, because of his most ardent zeal for the faith, became a confessor twice and endured exiles and fetters for the Lord; Rapoto [Note: Rapoto seems to have been the Count Palatine whose death is reported by the Chronicler of Ursperg under the year 1099.], who, because of the nobility of his blood and the uprightness of his character, is said to have been sought by the people as king; Adelbert and Odalscalchus [Note: Adelbert, or Albert, was a count to whom, and to whose wife, Letter 11 of Book II is extant. Odalscalchus likewise seems to have been a Count of the Empire. These three are discussed near the end of Letter 10 of Book III.]. To these men responsibility had been entrusted both by the king and by the pope. [Col. 0065A]

50. And, so that no sex may be passed over, let us also come to honorable women, wealthy both in religion and in the power of secular affairs: namely, Queen Agnes, the mother of that most wicked king, and truly a queen, who, having laid aside her royal diadem and abandoning this present age, adhered unremittingly to the footsteps of God, his Mother, and his Apostles Peter and Paul; and, moreover, Beatrice and her most noble daughter Matilda. Although, while governing Italy, they exercised the worldly office of dukes’ authority—having in truth become like Deborah, who, judging Israel, scattered Jabin and all his forces into the torrent of Kishon—they often crushed the wicked into confusion.

These women were mediators between the Lord Pope and the king, and they ardently desired to arrange and consolidate the condition of the kingdom. To refuse to accept the testimonies of all these people, and of other worthy persons of every condition, is nothing other than to merit the wrath of God and to undergo the sentence of perpetual damnation.

Having recalled these matters to demonstrate the innocence of so great a Father, let us join to our little book the frauds and plots of that king, and at times also his insults against St. Peter, so that we may not allow those who wish to know to lie in the ignorance of dark error; and let us pursue what we have begun with all our strength.

51. When Henry III had died [Note: On 5 October 1056 at Bodsfeld, near the Hercynian Forest.], that Henry, the fourth king of the name, succeeded him by hereditary right, with the permission of the Roman Pontiff Victor, who was then present at the dying man’s side—he was, of course, still a boy. But, as Solomon attests when he says, “Woe to you, land whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning,” he perpetrated every crime that could exist, to the destruction of himself and of the entire kingdom.

Blind in heart and wanton, he did not fear the Father; but although all were bearing witness to his boyhood and imperfect age, the Roman Pontiffs tolerated his wantonness, thinking that he would reach manhood, when he could correct himself. They did not attend to what is written: “He who spares the rod hates his son.” Thus vice is nourished; and while a tender branch is not pruned or torn out, once it reaches maturity it can scarcely be cut off by hand or iron.

In this way, climbing into the chariot of his elders, that man strove with all his strength to place the entire Church beneath his proud heel and offer her up to be trampled, vile as a maidservant. The Roman Church, however, could not endure this crime, for she is the head and teacher of all religion, and it is her proper task, above all others, to correct the powerful of this age and strengthen those who are wavering, as the Lord himself commanded the Apostle Peter: “And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

She therefore began to address him in letters, to admonish him, and to preach to him. But his neck, unable to bear the yoke of Christ and hardened by the freedom of his own will, fled by turning this way and that. Turning over new counsels in a new breast, he awaited an opportune time when he might subject the Roman Church to himself like the others; and afterward, as became clear in reality, he was driven toward this with all the strength he possessed.

For when Pope Nicholas II had died and the blessed Alexander had been quietly brought in, seized by the madness of his mind, he did not fear to raise the heretic Cadalus, the ill-named Bishop of Parma, to the papacy, having conferred investiture upon him by his own hand. But when everyone withdrew from him, opposed by God, he could not bring what he had decided to completion. The books of that Father Alexander testify how many paternal letters he received at that time [Note: Especially Book II, Letters 30 and 31; Book III, Letters 3, 7, and 10.].

52. After Father Gregory, by the will of the Lord, had been compelled to succeed him, although he had fled and resisted, he visited him with paternal admonition, as was fitting: [Col. 0066B] praying and asking him, for love of the King of all things, for the salvation of his own position, and for the remedy of his soul, to withdraw his foot from the actions from which so great a son and member of the holy Church ought to abstain; and to acknowledge above himself the King of Kings as an overseer, who, knowing the counsels of hearts and the hidden things of darkness, repays each person according to his works.

He also asked him to dismiss his most wicked counselors, who loved themselves more than they loved him; for he indicated that to consent to the counsels of such men was nothing other than to acquire death, overturn the kingdom, and wish to become a subject of ridicule to all nations.

At this the king himself was moved for a little while and sent a suppliant letter [Note: These letters are extant in Baronius under the year 1073, no. 49.], promising amendment—though later it became clear that the letters were deceitful. When the letter had been brought, the entire Church rejoiced, hoping that Priesthood and Kingdom, joined together by the grace of God, would cleanse everything filthy that was scattered throughout it.

Then, by common counsel, it was decided that, for so great a cause and one so worthy of God, his mother Agnes Augusta, together with the venerable Bishops of Ostia and Praeneste, sent from the side of the Lord Pope, should approach the king with the Apostolic letters, so that, having understood such a great promise, he might wish to put a definite end to the evil that had hitherto been committed.

The king himself received her honorably together with the aforesaid Apostolic messengers; and, returning to his senses, as was just, he made satisfaction in all things to God and St. Peter. Whatever the legates imposed upon him, he promised to bear with the greatest humility at their hands; henceforth to guard himself; to drive far from him all Simoniacs, wicked counselors, and excommunicated persons; and to leave the Church of God to be ordered and arranged according to canonical institution through the counsel of the Pope.

After these and other matters had been settled, they returned to the Apostolic See.

53. The king, too, returned to the same wallows in which he had been accustomed to wallow, believing, of course, more in his own flattering will and wicked counselors than in sound religion. To correct this, his mother Augusta was again sent from the Roman See. After spending some time with him, she laid bare to him the whole affection of the holy Mother Church toward him.

He received the seed of the word in the field of his heart; but, according to the Gospel parable, while his mother was sowing, some fell beside the road, where it was both trampled under human feet and snatched away by birds; some fell among thorns and, choked by what sprang up, could not bear fruit; and some was cast upon the hardness of a stony heart and, scorched by the heat of the sun, could not take root.

By human feet, anyone sensible can understand the counsels of the wicked men whom he employed; by the birds, the suggestions of unclean spirits; by the thorns, riches and royal pleasures; and by the rock, hardness of heart. [Col. 0067B]

While the queen delayed, the Pope again sent his letters, so that she might persist in the word and in the liberation of her son. He asked the king himself to guard himself in the way stated in the letters formerly sent to him [Note: This is Letter 85 of Book I.] and demonstrated by the promise and pledge given into the hands of the legates; above all, to restrain his spirit from the Simoniacal heresy in which he was laboring; and to cast far away the excommunicated counselors whom the Apostolic See and the Synod had justly condemned for his salvation and for the condition of his kingdom, lest he fall under the same curse.

When the queen returned to Rome, she declared that her son had been inclined toward the justice and honor of God. Not long afterward, when he was wavering, flattering and suitable letters were sent to him twice [Note: These are Letters 30 and 31 of Book I.].

54. At that time the Saxons, because they saw themselves treated by him with excessive cruelty, unanimously conspired not to have him as their king any longer. Then, compelled to do so, he sent a suppliant letter to the Apostolic, begging him to receive him as one commended to his prayers, so that by his merits the right hand of the most high King might rescue him from the terrible and fearful judgment that was already impending; and he promised again and again never again to do anything concerning the churches of God that the holy Canons could reproach.

Moved by his prayers, the Pope sent letters and messengers to those same Saxons. Digging around the roots of that king, he sent the baskets of his preaching, waiting, of course, to gather large figs from the tree. But from the place where he ought to have drawn a fullness of good moisture, he afterward withered and dried up; and the vine that had been expected to bear rich clusters produced poor and meager wild grapes; and the crop, adorned with beautiful leaves, produced at harvest-time nothing other than the darnel of an unspeakable mixture. [Col. 0067D]

He did indeed warn the king to suspend himself from arms for the time being, until he received messengers from the Saxon regions. But the king, refusing to heed the Father’s letters and admonitions, entered Saxon territory, where, because the sins of men demanded it, much human blood was shed on both sides.

Yet victory was given into the king’s hands by the just judgment of God [Note: The Hersfeld monk describes this war at length in his Historical Chronicle of Germany, beginning on page 744 of volume I of the Illustrious Writers of Germany, printed at Basel in 1574. Bruno the monk likewise wrote On the Saxon War, in volume I of Freher’s German Historical Writers.]. For this he ought to have been humbled beneath the hands of the Lord; but, like a man made fiery and inflated by the spirit of arrogance, he swelled up against him. For everything that he had previously promised through his mother, through the bishops, through the clergy, through public messengers, and through private ones, he afterward, because he felt secure, rendered void.

Indeed, the churches which he had placed under oath in the hands of the Lord Pope so that they might be corrected, he not only failed to relinquish; he also, contrary to the decretal institutions of the Fathers, handed them over under investiture to certain adulterers and Simoniacs.

Among these was Gotefridus [Note: St. Gregory, in Letter 15 of Book I to all the faithful of Christ in Lombardy, announces that he had excommunicated Gotefredus because he had occupied the Church of Milan by Simony.], whom, although excommunicated for invading the Church of Milan, he invested in that same adulterous invasion; and Altonus [Note: Altonus, called Atho by Ughellus, was a cleric of the Ambrosian College, elected in 1076. Ughellus may be consulted concerning him and the disturbance of the Church of Milan in his Archbishops of Milan, column 156.], whom the better part of the clergy and people had chosen as their lord and archbishop, while the Pope was staying there.

He also gave the Church of Fermo and that of Spoleto [Note: St. Gregory, Letter 15 of Book III, to King Henry: “Contrary to the statutes of the Apostolic See, you have handed over the Churches of Fermo and Spoleto . . . to certain persons entirely unknown even to us.” Grifforanus received the See of Fermo; a certain Teuton by nationality received that of Spoleto. St. Gregory excommunicated both and deposed them from their Sees. Consult Ughellus under the respective bishops, volumes I and II of Sacred Italy.] . . . . . .

## CHAPTER VII. The Synod celebrated at Rome by Gregory against the assembly held at Mainz by the followers of Henry

55. When these matters had been reported to the Apostolic See, Pope Gregory was greatly troubled. Meanwhile he began to be agitated by many anxieties, because he saw that everything he had hoped would lead to peace was being turned into its opposite. At last he disclosed to certain persons and honorable men some matters that had been secretly conveyed to him by certain legates, so that they might weigh what ought to be decided concerning them.

When such great promises—or rather, such great pretenses—had been examined, everyone began to wonder. Yet, so that the Roman See might not appear to be acting unjustly or precipitately, it was decided that sharper letters should be written to the king, in which he would fully understand that the Roman Shepherd could not abandon justice through fear or affection.

He wrote to Beatrice and her daughter Matilda, who at that time governed all Italy above others; to the king himself; to the invader of Milan; and to all the suffragans.

56. Then the king, seized by deep grief and fear, rushing here and there with a frenzied mind, summoned all his wicked counselors. Certain seducers were brought forward before the eyes of his perverse mind, and they proposed many things by which the human mind is accustomed to be deceived: the honor of the kingdom handed down by the Father; free will; boundless wealth; an abundance and strength of soldiers; bishops, dukes, tyrants, and princes bound by loyalty; the necks of the proud crushed beneath his yoke; and, moreover, the profit from the churches handed over into his hands—and many other things that, as we have said, entice secular minds.

Among them was the Archbishop of Mainz and the suffragans who lived under him. [Note: He was to appear at Rome for the Synod on the Monday of the second week of Lent, to answer the charges that would be brought against him; otherwise, he was to know that, without any delay, on that same day he would be cut off from the body of the holy Church by Apostolic anathema. Thus Lambert under the year 1076. By contrast, the pseudo-synod of Worms, mentioned shortly afterward, was summoned for the Sunday of Septuagesima.]

When such an assembly had been held, they decreed that an imperial edict should order all the bishops residing in his kingdom, with couriers sent everywhere, to appear before him [Note: This was Siegfried, who presided over the Church of Mainz from 1059 to 1084. Serarius gives a very extensive account of his deeds in Book V of his Mainz Affairs, from page 742 to page 788. His name is expressed below, when he passed over to the party of King Rudolf.], and that, when all had been gathered, they should subscribe to the anathema which the heretical Archbishop of Mainz was composing against the Vicar of Blessed Peter, indeed against his Lord and Apostle.

If any of them, moved by some reverence, wished to withdraw, he was to be deprived of all his possessions and dignity and, as one liable to royal majesty, suffer a capital sentence.

Meanwhile, while legates were being sent in every direction [Note: “Hugh, surnamed the White,” says Lambert, who has similar material. Domnizo likewise sings in Book I of his Life of Matilda:

“Here then came Hugh, the false one, who is called the White;

Here the priest of the Roman city offers many things;

Three times condemned, because by payment he restored

The buyers of Christ’s temples, and joined to them

Against the Pope, pretending evil, he gladdened

The hearts of the wicked, of the king and his allies alike.”], a certain Hugh came from the city, formerly a Cardinal but then the leading figure among the heretical bishops. He had already been condemned three times by the Apostolic See because he had presumed to reconcile certain Simoniacs.

Presenting, in forged letters, the persons of archbishops and bishops, he arrived praising everything they had contrived against the Lord Pope. He also produced other letters, headed in the names of all the Cardinals, the Senate, and the people, by which certain proclamations supposedly delivered to the royal presence were represented. These included a demand for a new pontiff and the rejection of the lawful Shepherd.

He added many hostile acts that he claimed to suffer from the Normans, from the surrounding counts, and even from those traitors who remained in the city. When the king saw these things, he rejoiced greatly and received the desired encouragement for arranging his undertaking.

The devilish pontiffs were then brought forward, and they pronounced an anathema against the Lord Pope—indeed against themselves. [Note: Domnizo continues in the same way:

“That very bold Archbishop of Mainz,

He did not fear Christ when he cursed the Pope;

All subscribe: they curse themselves even more.”]

Messengers and letters were also sent from the king’s side to Lombardy and the March. It was decided that they should subscribe to the anathema once it had been enacted. Thus, when all had gathered at Pavia by the king’s command—and, as the matter revealed, more from their own malevolence and hatred—they subscribed to the anathema.

For, to display the full accumulation of their evil will, they placed the sacred Gospels before them and confirmed by oath that they would in no way henceforth recognize Gregory as Pope or show him obedience. They then sent messengers and compelled others to do the same.

57. The king himself wrote letters to Rome, dishonorable through every kind of insult and filled with falsehood, ordering the Lord Pope to rise from his See and abandon the Church. He called him a perjurer, an invader, and a diminisher of royal dignity, especially of the Simoniacs laboring in Lombardy.

They also decided that the letters and words should not be delivered until the Synod that had been convened in the Roman Church could hear the matter fully; and this was done. For while the Pope was holding the Synod, a certain cleric of Parma did not shrink from presenting himself with those same letters as an insult to the Lord Apostolic, nor did he fear to utter those blasphemies in the face of the entire Church and assembly.

At the same time, as a sign of that wickedness and a confirmation of what was to come, a portent arose in the city near the Church of Blessed Peter, and it had thrown everyone’s hearts into profound astonishment. No one could fittingly or appropriately assign or express any interpretation concerning it.

For a hen laid an egg wonderfully decorated by the work of heaven, [Col. 0070C] in which two marvelous signs were marked: the likeness of a serpent and of a shield, darkened by overwhelming horror. The serpent, which had raised itself from the same eggshell in a triple winding, attempted to lift its head upward toward the top of the egg; but it had extended its tail toward the darkened part of it. As it reached toward the egg’s upper surface, however, it was struck by some blow and bent its head backward as far as its belly.

Its scales—not painted, but placed outside the order of the shell—could be detected and handled by hand like any other material object. [Note: By “scales,” Gretserus understands a scaly skin; for in German Schuppen means “scales.”]

While all the bishops and the others seated in the Synod were observing and marveling at these things, that messenger of Antichrist arrived. [Col. 0070D]

58. After the hymn had been completed, the Pope had taken his seat in order to deliver words of exhortation to everyone. [Col. 0070D] That precursor of Antichrist, showing no honor to God and loving earthly power more than heavenly authority, addressed the same Pope as follows:

“My lord the King, and all the bishops from beyond the Alps and from Italy, command and order you to abandon from now on the See of Blessed Peter and the Roman Church, which you have invaded. For it is not right to ascend to so great an honor without their command and an imperial gift.”

Then he turned to the Roman clergy and said:

“You are told, brothers, to present yourselves before the royal presence for the coming solemnity of Pentecost, there to receive from the hands of the king a Pope and Father; for this man is recognized to be not a pope but a ravening wolf.”

At his words, Bishop John of Porto, a distinguished man in integrity of character and religion, immediately sprang to his feet and shouted in a great voice: “Let him be seized.” [Note: John succeeded another John around the year 1066 and adhered most faithfully to St. Gregory, so that neither the emperor’s threats nor his power could turn him aside. He is praised by Peter of Ostia in Book IV, chapter 2, of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, and by others.]

Then the Prefect, rushing forward with the judges, soldiers, and Roman nobles, wished to kill that utter impostor before the presence of the Lord Pope, drawing their swords in the very Church of the Savior. He would have done so if the pious Father had not thrown his whole body over him, while everyone was crying out for his death. [Col. 0071B]

59. At last, when silence had scarcely been obtained, the Lord Pope said:

“Do not, my sons, disturb the peace of the holy Church of our Lord God by turning it into some sedition. For, according to the sequence of the divine Scriptures (II Tim. III), perilous times must come, in which people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud, arrogant, and disobedient to their parents. Thus the patience of the children of God may make the demonstration of our faith much more precious than gold tested by fire.

“The divine word cries out to us, saying: ‘It is necessary that scandals come; but woe to that man through whom the scandal comes’ (Matt. XVIII). And again, to show the character proper to us and how we ought to conduct ourselves toward our enemies, it is added: ‘Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves. Therefore be wise as serpents and simple as doves’ (Luke and Matthew X).

“Now, although the precursor of Antichrist has risen up against the Church, nevertheless we, taught for many ages by both the Lord and the holy Fathers, should proceed along the former paths bearing the gift of a twofold knowledge. Just as the pious Fathers joined the wisdom of the serpent to the simplicity of the dove and drove away heretics who employed serpent-like cunning, [Col. 0071D] so let us retain the gentleness of the bird without gall and not abandon the prudence of the serpent. [Note: This passage concerning serpentine prudence and dove-like simplicity, mutilated in the manuscripts and extremely confused even with the supplement of the Bollandist editor, has been restored here on the basis of this conjecture, while the text has been brought more faithfully into conformity with Matthew’s words (10:16). (Patrologia editor.)]

“To bear both qualities in the mind is not a fault but a secret of worthy discernment. For we ought not to pursue anyone with hatred, but we ought to tolerate those who wish through imprudence or foolishness to violate the law of the Lord.

“Behold, the acceptable time is here; behold, again the Lord walks spiritually among human beings, crying out and saying: ‘Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself’ (Matt. XVI), and the rest.” [Col. 0072A]

60. “Therefore we must follow the Lord calling us to the way of life, if we desire to gather the fruit of eternal inheritance. ‘Through many tribulations,’ as our Teacher taught us, ‘we must enter the kingdom of God’ (Acts XIV).

“It is enough that until now we have lived in the peace of the Church. But now it is fitting that the long-dried harvest of the saints be watered again with blood, so that its fruit, long withered by age, may be renewed by the fresh dew and return to its former beauty.

“We see the devil’s battle leaping into the open field, formerly covered by dark squalor. Therefore it is fitting now to confront it, as Christ’s recruits carry trained hands into battle, so that the faith of Christ—which, through the devil’s infection, is seen to have been scattered and abandoned across almost the whole world—may be restored everywhere, while the Lord God fights through us.

“To the detriment of their own salvation, we see secular men fighting daily, gaining nothing other than hell. Therefore let us, for whom Christ must be life and to die for his love gain; for whom eternal happiness is prepared as a reward after this wretched and imaginary life—let us not, by yielding to the enemy, draw back our foot from the laws of God and from our orthodox faith.

“At least let the Lord’s voice move us, the voice that says: ‘Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his majesty, and that of the Father and of the holy angels’ (Luke IX). [Col. 0072C]

“It ought to seem terrible to us if at that time, before so great a tribunal, we receive through our negligence a sentence of dreadful shame—though the Judge of all wishes to reward others for their labors (Num. VIII). For this reason eternal Wisdom wished us to be watchmen of his house, so that, when he himself later comes as its inhabitant, he may have a clean house through our diligence.

“The priests of the Lord urge us to undertake this distinguished work when, at the proper age, those growing old after their fiftieth year are commanded to become guardians of the vessels of the Lord. For, as Blessed Gregory says, the vessels are our hearts, by which we carry everything that we think.

“That hearts are also the temple of the living God is attested by the sacred writings (I Cor. III). They must therefore be cleansed and adorned with that much greater diligence, by how much more pure than the rest of the world we recognize their inhabitant to be.

“For it is written: ‘The pure inhabitant seeks a pure house’ (I Cor. XV). And again: ‘Awake, you righteous, and do not sin’ (ibid.). And again: ‘Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me’ (Rev. III).

“We see now, brothers, if we try attentively to examine our hearts, that our Creator is knocking and admonishing us to open to him, to close the door to the devil, and to resist with all our strength his satellites and accomplices, ready, according to the Apostle (II Cor. X), to avenge every disobedience.

“Nor should we fear even if they are able to prevail against us, since it is for this reason that power is handed over to them by the just Judge: that they may become the furnace of our testing, soon to be consumed into ash and embers, while we, as vessels that have been tested, are to be taken up perpetually into the service of the Lord.

“We hope and do not doubt that no tribulation, persecution, sword, bonds, prisons, exiles, present or future hardships will be able to separate us from the charity that is in Christ Jesus and from his holy laws.

“For it is better to die for the laws of the Lord than to betray the rights of the Church by turning one’s back on those who would persuade men against and destroy those laws; for plainly not to oppose such men is to deny the faith of Christ.”

61. We see before our eyes and in our hands the sign of the ancient serpent, which almighty God has shown you for this reason: to make you cautious and watchful, and to indicate what we ought to do against the son of pride who exalts himself against this holy Catholic Church. Holy Scripture denotes the Faith and the figure of the holy Church by the name “egg”; and no believer doubts that within it the wicked are mingled with the good until the end of the world. Although they strive for a time to hide themselves by frauds and deceptions, they cannot always remain concealed, once the Lord reveals them; so that, when they come into the open and burst forth, the fraud that had been hidden may appear to all, and the holy Church of God may draw the sword of vengeance against those now recognized.

This king, whose likeness God wished me to have demonstrated and recognized through the image of a serpent, has until now, fearing, hidden like a serpent in the darkness of night, by his deceitful words and messengers. But now, leaping out, he has sufficiently revealed what he carried in his heart, to his condemnation for the outrage he had everywhere committed against the Churches of God. Now, as you see, he has begun to raise his head against the foundation of our faith, as it is written: “They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth.” Of him the Apostle John says: “And a mouth was given to him speaking great things and blasphemies” (Apoc. XIII). And again: “And his tail [the dragon’s] dragged a third of the stars” (Apoc. XVIII).

The wretch has not heeded what Truth itself said to our Master and Prince of the Church: “Upon this rock, he said, I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18). Now therefore, brothers, it is fitting to draw the sword of vengeance and strike down the enemy of God and of the Church by binding him, so that the struck head—which is known to have been raised against the foundation of the Faith and of all the Churches—may fall; so that, just as it was said to him at the beginning of his pride, he may crawl upon his breast and belly.

“Do not fear,” says the Lord, “little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke XII, 32). You have endured enough up to this point, and you have admonished him rightly and suitably; now let him recognize that he has had a seared conscience.

62. When these and several other matters had been brought to a conclusion, the holy and great Synod said:

“Let your censure, most holy Father—you whom divine clemency brought forth to govern the age of our time—pronounce against this blasphemer, invader, tyrant, and deserter a sentence that will crush him and provide future ages with a warning against transgression. For it is right to obey and comply with your commands, as far as we are able, nor do we wish to hold our lives more precious to ourselves. Indeed, if necessary, we shall gladly embrace death, lest we appear to abandon the footsteps of our fathers. Why should we not give for the holy laws of our God that which is being taken from us against our will? Draw the sword; execute judgment, so that every righteous person may rejoice when he sees vengeance and wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.”

At last, with everyone acclaiming, it was determined that both the aforementioned king and all his supporters should be deprived of royal honor and bound by the bonds of anathema.

### CHAPTER VIII. King Henry Is Excommunicated. Letters of Saint Gregory Concerning This Matter, and Examples of the Vengeance That Soon Followed.

63. Having therefore gained confidence, the lord Pope, with the consent and judgment of the entire Synod, pronounced anathema against him in these terms:

“Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, incline, I beg you, your loving ears toward us, and hear me, your servant, whom you nourished from infancy and have preserved to this day from the hands of the wicked, who hate and have hated me because of my loyalty to you. You are my witness, as are my Lady, the Mother of God, and blessed Paul, your brother among all the saints, that your holy Roman Church drew me, unwilling, to its helm; and I did not regard it as an act of robbery to ascend your See. Rather, I preferred to end my life in pilgrimage than to seize your place, through worldly ambition and secular ingenuity, for the sake of worldly glory.

“Therefore, by your grace and not through my own works, I believe that it has pleased and still pleases you that the Christian people specially entrusted to you should specially obey me, in your place entrusted to me. And by your grace power has been given to me by God to bind and loose in heaven and on earth.

“Trusting, therefore, in this power, for the honor and defense of your Church, in the name of almighty God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, through your power and authority, I deny to Henry, king, son of the Emperor Henry, who has risen against your Church with unheard-of pride, the government of the whole Kingdom of the Teutons and of Italy; and I absolve all Christians from the bond of the oath that they have sworn or may swear to him. I forbid anyone to serve him as king. For it is right that he who seeks to diminish the honor of your Church should himself lose the honor that he appears to possess.

“And because, as a Christian, he has scorned to obey and has not returned to the Lord whom he abandoned, by associating with the excommunicated and committing many iniquities, and by despising—as you are my witness—the admonitions that I sent him for his salvation; and because, attempting to split your Church, he has separated himself from it, I bind him in your place with the bond of anathema. And I bind him so confidently in reliance upon you that the nations may know and acknowledge that you are Peter, and that upon your rock the Son of the living God built his Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

64. After this he sent letters to various persons, setting forth the same anathema and its causes. We have taken care to insert two of them in the present work.

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who desire to be numbered among the sheep whom Christ entrusted to blessed Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“You have heard, dearest brothers, of the new and unheard-of presumption; you have heard the criminal chatter and audacity of the schismatics who blaspheme the Lord’s name in the person of blessed Peter; you have heard of the pride inflicted upon the holy Apostolic See as an injury and insult—such as your fathers neither saw nor ever heard, and such as the sequence of Scripture never teaches to have arisen among pagans or heretics. Even if some example of this evil had ever preceded it, after the faith of Christ had been founded and propagated, all the faithful would nevertheless have had to mourn and lament such contempt and trampling underfoot of Apostolic, indeed divine, authority.

“Therefore, if you believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were handed over to blessed Peter by our Lord God Jesus Christ, and if you desire that through his hands the entrance to the joys of eternal life should be opened to you, you must consider how deeply you ought now to grieve over the insult inflicted upon him. For unless here, where your faith and hearts are tested through the dangers of temptations, you become companions in suffering, you are undoubtedly unworthy to share in future consolation and, as children of the kingdom, to receive the heavenly crown and glory (II Cor. I).

“We therefore ask your charity to strive earnestly to implore divine mercy, so that either it may turn the hearts of the wicked to repentance, or, by restraining their criminal designs, it may show how foolish and senseless are those who attempt to overthrow the rock founded by Christ and violate divine privileges. But how and for what reasons blessed Peter bound the king with the bond of anathema, you may learn fully from the document enclosed with this one.”

[Note: I believe this little document to have been either the sentence of excommunication placed above or a copy of what is read in the following letter.]

[Col. 0075D] 65–68. “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops, dukes, counts, and other faithful persons in the Kingdom of the Teutons who defend the Christian faith: greeting and apostolic blessing. We have heard that some among you doubt the excommunication that we pronounced against the king,” etc. See among the letters of Saint Gregory.

69. Therefore, after the king’s excommunication and deposition, by the Lord’s grace going before them, many nobles and commoners turned to God with all their hearts and abandoned the aforementioned king. Even those who had previously conspired against the Apostolic See, some through royal blandishments and others through terrors and threats, subsequently converted and wrote in favor of the anathema rightly pronounced against the king. They sent suppliant messengers to the Apostolic See, asking that a penance be imposed (*epitimium*) [Greek: ἐπιτίμιον, a fine, penalty, or punishment; but perhaps *epithemium*, from τίθημι, “I place,” here signifies an imposition]. The disciple of mercy, not seeking to be satiated with the punishments of the guilty, opened to them the bosom of the holy Church; and, so that they might be strengthened in the faith of the Lord, he sent them letters of consolation.

Some bishops, mourning so great a crime, came barefoot to the Apostolic See and remained there until the lord Pope, moved by compassion, opened toward them the hand of mercy and the inner recesses of his pity.

70. Meanwhile the Lord performed a great miracle before the eyes of the king and of everyone, and when it became known, many abandoned him. For after the day of the excommunication, on the solemnity of Easter, he did not shrink from coming to the Church—which had been divinely closed against him—with royal pomp and a procession of magnificent multitude.

At the king’s command, therefore, a certain bishop—if he may be called one, or rather a heretic and Simoniac—prepared himself to celebrate the Mass.

[Note: William of Utrecht obstinately defended the king’s cause against what was good and just. Out of partisan zeal, on almost all solemn days, during the celebration of Mass, he declaimed many things against the Roman Pontiff with raging mouth, calling him a perjurer, adulterer, and pseudo-apostle, etc. Thus report Lambert of Hersfeld and the previously cited Bruno, as well as A. Langius in his *Chronicle of Titz*. “When the king,” he says, “was at Utrecht, and the king’s excommunication, pronounced by the Roman Pontiff, had been presented … the bishop, preaching to the people during Mass, mockingly announced that the king had been excommunicated.”]

At last, after the Gospel had been read, the same bishop climbed the pulpit, intending, according to custom, to deliver a popular sermon. But after saying little about the Gospel passage, he immediately burst forth, with blind heart and deranged mind, into blasphemy against Pope Gregory—blasphemy that, because of its excessive horror, I have preferred to pass over in silence.

It is difficult for the integrity of those whose conscience is sound to escape the bite of detractors’ tongues, or for one to whom justice is a friend to evade the insults of the wicked. Nevertheless, if one considers the vengeance that immediately followed, it becomes clear what that same blasphemy was in the eyes of the Lord.

For, before the joy of Easter had ended, the sky suddenly thundered with a crash, and fire appeared to descend from heaven. It suddenly consumed that entire church and all the houses prepared for the king’s reception, and changed the joy of the profane into mourning. The blasphemous bishop, struck suddenly, was killed by divine vengeance.

[Note: Lambert and the monk of Hersfeld relate the matter as follows: “Suddenly, seized by a most grievous illness … he cried out before all who were present with miserable wailing: ‘By the just judgment of God I have lost both the present life and the eternal one, because I gave my efforts with the greatest exertion to everything the king wickedly intended, and, in hope of his favor, knowingly and deliberately inflicted grave insults upon the Roman Pontiff, a most holy man and one endowed with apostolic virtues, though he was innocent.’ According to their report, he died uttering these words, without Communion and without any satisfaction.”]

But before he completely breathed out his life, he was compelled to tell the ministers prepared for his death what they were. “I see myself,” he said, “bound with fiery ropes and dragged from this life by dreadful pulling figures. Yet go and tell the king to correct the outrage that he has committed against God, blessed Peter, and his Vicar, lest he follow me, who am going before him, to the regions of hell.”

[Note: Langius explains it thus: “I send this message to the king: he, I, and all who favor his iniquity have been condemned forever … Behold, demons surround my bed, so that as soon as I expire they may seize me. Therefore, when I have been led out of the body, I ask you and all the faithful not to trouble yourselves by making supplications for me.” He died in despair and lay unburied for a long time, until word was sent to Rome. After counsel had been sought there, lest the people be corrupted by the stench, he was buried by apostolic command without the customary commendations. Thus Langius, from the chronicles of the Magdeburg Church.]

Having said this, he expired. Warned by this example, we exhort and beseech everyone who reads these writings to avoid the tongues of detractors, if he prefers to share Gregory’s company in the resurrection of life rather than suffer punishment with the detractors.

At this point the no less terrible condemnation of the Bishop of Speyer returns to mind.

[Note: Henry, Bishop of Speyer, had been brought up from childhood with King Henry and had been promoted by him to that See. After he had squandered the treasures of the Church with childish frivolity and distributed estates to soldiers as benefices … he suddenly felt a small pustule growing on his neck. As it swelled, he died before midnight. Thus Lambert, and Bruschius in the earlier account.]

He was struck suddenly, as though by some invisible weapon, at the same hour and on the same day—that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of March—and began to fall ill at Speyer at the very hour when our Pope Gregory began to discuss his case in the Roman Synod. He likewise expired miserably on the third day, that is, the fourth day before the Kalends of March, experiencing an effect no less powerful than that of the sentence by which the Apostle Peter condemned Ananias and Sapphira.

### CHAPTER IX. Henry’s Feigned Repentance. The Assembly of the Princes at Ulm. Gregory’s Embassy to Them.

71. The princes had long awaited the aforesaid king’s conversion in vain, and they saw the condition of the Kingdom becoming more dangerously disturbed each day, indeed already completely deprived of a head. At last, armed with zeal for God, they met with the legates of the Apostolic See and earnestly entreated him to heed their counsel and come to his senses; otherwise, they declared, they would no longer communicate with or obey him.

[Note: They met at Oppenheim, then an imperial city, later mortgaged to the Palatine of the Rhine, between Mainz and Worms. This occurred in 1077; or, as others hold, they met at Tribur, opposite Oppenheim, formerly a celebrated city but now a lowly village that still retains its name.]

Under this pressure, he promised—though, as later became evident, only hypocritically—that he would obey in every respect both the counsel of the princes and the commands of the Apostolic Lord. Their counsel was that the Apostolic Lord should come to a general conference at Augsburg on the approaching Purification of Saint Mary, so that his case might there be lawfully determined in the hearing of the entire Kingdom.

The princes likewise sent an embassy and humbly asked the lord Pope to come on the appointed day. They found him most ready to undertake the journey, as his letters reproduced below attest. But contrary to his promise and to the counsel of the princes, the king sought through his legates to extort from the Apostolic Lord a promise that he would not come to Augsburg, but would permit him to come to him at Rome. His intention was that he might deceive the Pope all the more easily because fewer princes of the Kingdom—who had already suffered his cunning many times—would be present to examine his case.

The Pope therefore did not yield to his wishes. Instead, as the princes had requested, he resolved to come on the appointed day and sent the following letters to the princes of the Kingdom concerning the arrangement of his journey.

72. “Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and also the greater and lesser persons established in the Kingdom of the Teutons: greeting and apostolic blessing. We, unworthy and useless servants of the Prince of the Apostles,” etc. See below among the letters.

73. “Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, marquises, and all who defend and observe the Christian faith and the faith and teaching of blessed Peter: greeting and the blessing of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, together with absolution from all sins. I, whatever sort of priest I may be, servant of the Prince of the Apostles,” etc. See below among the letters.

74. Meanwhile, distrustful of his own case and therefore avoiding a hearing before this Kingdom, the king secretly entered Italy with the excommunicated, contrary to the Pope’s command and the counsel of the princes. He met the Apostolic Lord, who was traveling toward Augsburg for the appointed day, at Canossa before the Purification of Saint Mary.

There he remained for three days before the castle gate, having laid aside all royal adornment and miserably dressed, barefoot and clothed in woolen garments. He did not cease, with much weeping, to implore the aid and consolation of Apostolic mercy until he moved all who were present, and all to whom the report reached, to such pity and compassionate mercy that they interceded for him with many prayers and tears. Everyone marveled at the unusual harshness of the lord Pope; some even loudly declared that what appeared in him was not the gravity of Apostolic serenity but the cruelty of tyrannical severity.

At length the Pope was overcome by his earnest contrition and by the great supplication of all who were there. He released him from the bond of anathema and received him into the grace of communion and the bosom of holy Mother Church. He accepted from him securities, whose confirmation he also received through the hands of the Abbot of Cluny, the noble countesses Matilda and Adelaide, and the other princes, bishops, and laymen whom he judged useful for this matter, in these terms.

[Note: Adelaida, also called Adelasia or Adalais, daughter of Olric, the magnificent Marquis of Susa, married in 1014 Humbert the Saxon, Marquis of Susa and Count of Savoy and Maurienne. Because of the many benefits she conferred upon the Apostolic See, she was called “daughter of Saint Peter.” She died in 1080, as Pignonius indicates in *Augusta Taurinorum*.]

75. “I, Henry, king, shall, within the period that the lord Pope establishes, either do justice according to his judgment or establish concord according to his counsel concerning the murmuring and dissension that the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and other princes of the Kingdom of the Teutons, and those who follow them in the same cause of dissension, now have against me—unless some definite impediment should stand in the way of me or of him. When that period has elapsed, I shall be prepared to carry this out.

“Likewise, if the same lord Pope Gregory should wish to go beyond the mountains or to other regions, he shall be secure, on my part and on the part of those whom I can compel, from every injury to his life or limbs and from capture, both he himself and those who are in his escort or company, whether going there, remaining there, or returning from there. Nor shall he have any other impediment from my consent that would be contrary to his honor; and if anyone harms him, I shall assist him in good faith, according to my ability.”

76. After he had been received into communion—but with the question of the Kingdom postponed—the king departed, released by the Apostolic Lord. He paid little attention to what he had promised him under oath at his reconciliation, and did not hesitate to return to his customary wickedness and to assent to the counsels of his Simoniacs against the Pope.

For all the Simoniacs and their associates, to whose tyranny he had subjected holy Mother Church and by whose faction he had previously attempted to deprive the Apostolic See of its authority—these men, I say, all returned to him after his reconciliation. Instead of fear, they received from him boldness for the iniquity they had committed. Indeed, they found in him an opportunity to conspire against the Apostolic Lord.

He himself and his accomplices had hastened to receive communion for this reason: according to the law of the Teutons, they did not doubt that they would be deprived of estates and benefices if they remained under excommunication for a full year. Only one month of that period remained when they returned to reconciliation.

They therefore sought communion not in order to correct themselves, but to restore to themselves the many who had long been separated from them by the anathema. Thus they could oppress the holy Church with their customary tyranny all the more boldly and cruelly, the more numerous their allies became. For immediately after the reconciliation, as has been said, they did not hesitate to return to their former mire and to support the Simoniacs, as men like themselves, against the Apostolic See.

77. Not long afterward, however, the king cunningly sought from the Apostolic Lord the concession of the Kingdom, under the pretext of communion. He sent an embassy and humbly begged him either to permit him to be crowned once, at Saint John’s in Monza, by the bishops of Pavia and Milan, according to the custom of earlier kings, or, if he did not wish this to be done by such bishops, since they were excommunicated, at least to grant any bishop the privilege of carrying it out by Apostolic authority. He especially desired to be crowned so that he might appear also to have received the Kingdom in communion from the Roman Pontiff.

[Note: Our manuscript adds: “Acted on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction.”]

But the Pope, having already sufficiently experienced his cunning, refused in every way to comply with his wishes. He carefully reflected that he had deposed him from the Kingdom for many crimes, and especially for the disobedience and contumacy inflicted upon the Apostolic See; and that he had made all who had sworn allegiance to him free from his dominion. For this reason, he could in no way place him, any more than another, over the princes as king—since they were free men—without their election.

Moreover, the whole Kingdom had accused him of so many and such great injuries and acts of treachery that he first had to be cleared of them, if this could in any way be done, and only then could he lawfully be crowned with the consent of the entire Kingdom.

The king therefore, on this occasion too, did not usurp the royal insignia at Monza, while pretending obedience.

[Note: Monza is ten miles from Milan. There the emperors were also accustomed to receive the iron crown.]

Nevertheless, not long afterward he did not fear to resume them contrary to the lord Pope’s ban and to usurp the government of the Kingdom, which had been placed under interdict.

78. Meanwhile the period that the king, before the legates of the Apostolic See and with the princes of the Kingdom, had fixed for Augsburg on the Purification of Saint Mary was passing. The Pope had already begun his journey there and would already have arrived, if the same king, entering Italy contrary to the common decree of all, had not deterred those who were to escort the Apostolic Lord from providing him with an escort.

That was the appointed place where, before the Apostolic Lord and in the hearing of the entire Kingdom, he could be canonically cleared of the charges brought against him, if he were innocent, and, once lawfully cleared, be restored to the Kingdom with everyone’s consent. He despised coming there; indeed, distrustful of his own case, he did not dare to come. He deceitfully forestalled the Pope in Lombardy to prevent him from coming there.

79. When the princes of the Kingdom realized that the king had evaded the period established by general decree, and that on this occasion too they had been deceived by his customary treachery; and when they learned from the most reliable report that his cunning had not ceased even during or after his reconciliation, they immediately assembled in Swabia at Ulm and deliberated that they would no longer permit themselves to be mocked by him—or rather to be endangered by his former cunning—but would provide for their safety by electing a legitimate prince.

At the same assembly at Ulm, they scheduled a more general conference at Forchheim for the fourth day before the Ides of March, for the election of a new king.

[Note: Forchheim was a very strongly fortified town belonging to the Bishop of Bamberg, between Bamberg and Nuremberg.]

They also sent an embassy to request that the counsel and assistance of the Apostolic Lord come to them. When the Pope heard this, he sent legates to the assembly to ask the princes to postpone the arrangement of the Kingdom until his arrival, if they hoped this could be done without danger. He certainly did not command them to do so definitively, lest he could rightly be held responsible if the condition of the Kingdom suffered some danger from the delay.

On the day after the legates’ departure, Count Manegold, a great lover of truth, arrived. Through his report the Pope learned that a new king was to be appointed, and he sent another legate—Gregory, a deacon of the Roman Church—to the princes of the Kingdom. The legate was to compel them by Apostolic authority to await the Pope’s arrival, but first to ascertain whether the king, who was still staying in Lombardy, would, when summoned by the legate, provide a security permitting the lord Pope to cross into the Teutonic lands so that his case might be determined.

If the king refused to grant this, the Pope commanded the legate to return to him and not to suspend the princes, even for any period of delay, from providing for the needs of the Kingdom.

When assigning this embassy to the same legate, the Pope said among other things that he had demanded such a security almost as an indication of what was to come: the granting of the security, he said, would foreshadow that the king could be restored to the Kingdom, whereas the denial of the security would signify, by divine indication, that this could not happen.

80. While the Pope was speaking these words, three fingers of his right hand suddenly appeared bloody as far as the middle joints. Thinking that they had been stained by blood flowing from his nostrils, he began to wipe them, but could not remove the bloody marks.

For this reason he and the other wise men who witnessed the miracle did not doubt that these signs portended something great. At that time the aforementioned Count Manegold and the venerable priest Erkinbert were present, together with many others, in the town of Canossa at the beginning of the Fast, which that year fell on the Kalends of March.

[Note: This is confirmed by the Easter date, which was then celebrated on 16 April, with lunar cycle 14, solar cycle 22, and dominical letter A.]

After receiving the embassy, the legate immediately hastened to the king with the aforesaid count. But the king scorned to provide the security that the Pope had requested. The legate therefore did not delay in returning to the Apostolic Lord.

The count, however, hurried to attend the forthcoming conference at Forchheim, where the earlier legates had already arrived. They had been sent by the Apostolic Lord only one day before the aforementioned count departed.

These were the legates: Bernard, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church; and another Bernard, a religious abbot from Marseille, father of nearly six hundred monks.
