He also brought with him an outstanding scholar named Christian, later bishop of Aversa, whose excellent work against Berengar of Tours is extant.

[Note: Rather, his name was Wismund or Guitmund. He was also a Gaul and had been a monk of Lofred in Normandy. His works are extant in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Consult Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.]

81. It does not seem inappropriate at this point to pause briefly in the course of the narrative and explain what a faithful follower and propagator of Apostolic teaching our Gregory found in the repeatedly mentioned Count Manegold.

He was born from the noble and religious lineage of blessed Udalric, Bishop of Augsburg.

[Note: Saint Udalric is commemorated on 4 July; this matter may be investigated then. In the meantime, consult the genealogy that Velferus added at the end of the *Life* in the Augsburg edition of 1595.]

He was educated with exactness in every observance of the Christian religion by his most learned brother, Hermann—called “the Lame.” As a virgin he took a virgin as his wife. By her he had two sons, whom he brought up in such strict discipline until young manhood that, leading one of them to a similar single marriage, he left him as his heir; while the other, killed in celibacy, he miraculously recognized through the spirit, even though he was far away and separated from the place of the killing by a great distance. He both grieved and rejoiced: he wept because of the bitterness of the unexpected death, and rejoiced because of the preservation of the young man’s uncontaminated chastity.

What especially kept his children chaste was that their truthful father threatened to disinherit them if they were discovered to have defiled themselves with women outside legitimate union.

This most Christian man loved blessed Pope Gregory with extraordinary affection because of his righteous teachings, and often visited him on account of the similarity of their character. On one occasion, while he was in Rome, he fell into such a serious illness that those present despaired of his life. When the sad report reached the lord Pope, Gregory came to him quickly, broke a little bread into a cup, poured pure wine over it, and gave it to the sick man as a blessing.

As soon as the man tasted it, he received not only the pleasure of eating but also the strength to rise from his bed in full health.

When he returned home, he diligently disseminated the Apostolic statutes everywhere, especially those concerning the avoidance of the offices of incontinent priests, and tolerated no such abominations among the clergy and churches specially subject to him.

The wife of a certain priest under his authority, angered by the separation from her husband, threatened before her intimates that she would cause the count to suffer the same distress that she herself endured through separation from her spouse. She spoke, and—alas!—with God permitting it, she committed so wicked a crime against the count’s wife.

For she offered her delightful foods infected with poison and deceived her, suspecting no evil, by feigned kindness.

The devout count, widowed while still in the strength of life, could not be persuaded by any exhortations from his family to enter a second marriage. He said that it seemed shameful and horrifying to him to appear before Christ’s tribunal on the day of judgment with two wives.

Through his devoted obedience to our Pope Gregory he progressed so far that, before his end—which he reached as an old man full of days—he shone with certain signs of virtue and was honored by the gift of prophecy, as became clear in the case of his son’s killing.

[Note: It is strange that he is nowhere found listed among the saints of Augsburg, nor have I been able to read anything about the place of his burial or the day of his death.]

82. The memory of the precious death of blessed Cinthius, prefect of the City of Rome, may appropriately be joined to this count of blessed memory. We briefly described his virtues above.

For our Lord Jesus Christ crowned him with martyrdom because of the faith he repeatedly displayed—and which will repeatedly be mentioned—that he had shown toward Pope Gregory. The Lord also immediately glorified his tomb with twenty miracles, counted and approved in the Synod.

[Note: If only those miracles still existed together with the decree of beatification, so that the day of his cult could be restored to this man, who deserves to be honored among the martyrs—or at least so that it might be known where he was buried.]

For, because he possessed zeal for the Lord and displayed faith according to the holy form of Apostolic teaching, he was killed by the agents of Henry’s persecution.

### CHAPTER X. The Conference at Forchheim, the Election of Rudolph as King, and the Revolt Stirred Up by the Simoniacs and Concubinaries.

83. When the assembly had therefore been held at Forchheim, the aforementioned legates brought forward the Apostolic letters:

“The lord Pope has been scarcely pleased by the king’s promise, since the adversaries of the Church have received more boldness than fear from the king’s presence. For this reason,” they said, “he asks that, if they judge it possible to do so without danger, they postpone the election of the new king, of which he has heard, until his arrival.”

When the embassy had been completed, the archbishops, bishops, dukes, marquises, counts both great and small, showing due reverence to the legates, rose one by one from their seats. They began to lament to the legates how many insults and dangers they had already suffered from King Henry, or how many they had no doubt they would yet suffer. They said that they had barely escaped his snares even amid the kisses of peace, so that they could no longer place any trust in his oath.

They added that they had tolerated him for so long after his deposition not because they expected his correction—for that was entirely hopeless—but to remove an opportunity for slanderers, who might perhaps complain that his correction had been prevented if he were not awaited for so long. The entire day was spent in complaints of this kind, and they could not even enumerate half of the injuries inflicted upon them.

## 84.

On the following day, however, they again assembled at the Legates’ lodgings and consulted them about relieving their difficulty, suggesting that an extremely dangerous and irrevocable schism would arise throughout the entire Kingdom unless, at that same assembly, they hastened to forestall it by forming a confederation around the elevation of some new head, as they had resolved.

The Legates, mindful of the purpose of their mission, replied to this quite briefly: it seemed best to them if, in accordance with their embassy, they could safely defer the establishment of a king until the arrival of the Lord Pope. But, they said, the preservation of the Kingdom lay not so much in their counsel as in the judgment of the Princes, who held the commonwealth in their hands and knew best the loss or advantage of the entire Kingdom. Therefore the Princes of the Kingdom, uncertain about the Pope’s arrival but entirely certain that great dissension and danger would result if they delayed, obtained permission from the Legates and assembled with the Archbishop of Mainz. They carefully discussed among themselves what ought to be done, considering that they were not being compelled by the Apostolic representative to any delay, but that the matter had been left to their judgment, and that if delay proved harmful, no one but themselves would thereafter be held responsible.

Moreover, they were not bound to render any submission to King Henry; indeed, if they rendered him any submission thereafter, they would be condemned for violating the Apostolic ban. For, before anathematizing him, the Pope, in the name of almighty God, Saint Peter, and himself, had placed the Kingdom under interdict; he had absolved all Christians from the oath they had sworn or would swear to Henry; and he had forbidden anyone to serve him as king. Later, through a false promise of correction, Henry recovered communion from the Pope alone, not the Kingdom.

## 85.

After the Princes of the Kingdom had examined these matters with the greatest care, they recognized that they had been completely emancipated from King Henry’s authority, as stated above, and that they were no more bound to him by any oath of fidelity or submission than he was bound to them. Thus, as free men, they raised Duke Rudolf of Swabia—who had long resisted in vain and had vainly asked for even a single hour’s delay in order to deliberate—to royal dignity: a man truly outstanding in humility and suitable for royal honor in age and character. They subjected themselves to him by the required oath of fidelity.

He, considering the Kingdom entrusted to him not as his own possession but according to the disposition made for him, rejected every hereditary right to it and absolutely denied that he would adopt such a claim even for his son. He most justly declared that it lay within the Princes’ discretion, after his death, to elect freely neither his son nor anyone else, unless they found him worthy of that summit by age and moral seriousness.

Archbishops Mainz and Magdeburg, together with their suffragans, in the presence of the Legates of the Apostolic See and the Princes of the Kingdom, consecrated this lawfully elected Rudolf with royal anointing. He was elected by the Archbishops, Bishops, Dukes, and greater and lesser Counts at the assembly at Forchheim, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1077, the fourth year of the venerable Pope Gregory VII’s pontificate under that name, in the fifteenth indiction, on the Ides of March. On the twelfth day afterward he was consecrated at Mainz, that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, when the middle of Lent occurred.

On the day of the aforesaid election, the snow and ice began to thaw—snow and ice which that year had covered the land of the Germans and Lombardy from the feast of All Saints until that day. Certain wise men interpreted this as follows: God had indicated to the world his approval in the election of the lawful Prince, by driving away the unaccustomed cold and restoring milder weather. This was especially evident since no one disliked this elevation except those alone who did not doubt that, under a lawful Prince, they would have to renounce the Simoniac heresy and other crimes—those who, under the previous King, who not merely permitted but cooperated in their conduct, had not ceased to defile the holy Church.

Certainly, no cleric, monk, or layman disliked the elevation of this Prince except one who feared that he himself would have to be corrected under his authority; except one who feared that the holy Church would be ordered according to the canonical decrees; except one who did not doubt that his wealth would be diminished once the commerce of Simony was shut down.

## 86.

No one can justly charge King Rudolf and his Princes with perjury, although they had long ago sworn an oath of fidelity to the deposed King. That oath was to be observed only so long as he presided over the Kingdom. But after all Christians had been released from that oath by the Pope, once Henry had been deposed and anathematized, no more submission was owed to him on account of that oath than subjects obey a Bishop after he has been deposed, even if communion with him has been retained.

No one will deny that the Roman Pontiff can depose kings from their kingdoms if he does not judge the decrees of the most holy Pope Gregory worthy of condemnation. For that Apostolic man, to whom the Holy Spirit dictated in his ear what should be decreed, established irrefragably, while seated in the Apostolic See, that kings should fall from their dignities and be deprived of participation in the Lord’s Body and Blood if they presumed to despise the commands of the Apostolic See.

For if the See of Blessed Peter releases and judges heavenly and spiritual matters, how much more earthly and secular ones, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels, how much more worldly matters?” Thus, by the authority of Pope Stephen, Hilderic, King of the Franks, was deposed for his indolence; and after he had been deposed, shorn, and sent to a monastery, Pepin was installed in the Kingdom.

Furthermore, free men had made Henry their king on the condition that he would justly judge his electors and endeavor to govern them with royal foresight. He afterward did not cease to violate and despise this agreement, oppressing innocent people with tyrannical cruelty and compelling everyone he could to resist the Christian religion.

Therefore, even without a judgment of the Apostolic See, the Princes could rightly reject him as king, since he had despised fulfilling the agreement he had promised them in exchange for his election. Once it was not fulfilled, he could not be king. For no one can be king who strives not to govern his subjects but to lead them into error.

What more need be said? Is not every soldier bound to his lord by an oath of fidelity on the condition that the lord also does not deny him what the lord owes the soldier? If, then, the lord refuses to render the soldier what is owed, may the soldier not freely refuse thereafter to have him as lord? Most freely, I say. Nor will anyone justly accuse such a soldier of infidelity or perjury, since he has fulfilled everything he promised: he served his lord, that is, for as long as the lord did for him what a lord owed his soldier.

## 87.

Therefore, once Rudolf had been raised to the kingship, he immediately informed the Apostolic representative of his elevation by sending an embassy and promised him the required obedience in ecclesiastical administration. He showed himself much more ready to obey the Apostolic See than his predecessor had been.

Indeed, on the very day of his consecration, in obedience to the Lord Pope’s ban, he refused to accept the office of a certain Simoniac Deacon who, already dressed in sacred vestments, came forward before the King to read at Mass. Consequently, Archbishop Siegfried of Mainz removed him from the altar ministry and appointed another in his place.

This aroused the greatest hatred against the King among the Simoniacs and incontinent ministers of the altar. By obeying the Apostolic ban at the very moment of his elevation, he showed through the rejection of the aforementioned Subdeacon that he rejected the offices of such men. For they had no doubt that, under so lawful a Prince, they would either have to relinquish their offices or renounce their concubines and their churches acquired through Simony.

Therefore, on that very day of the royal consecration, after the meal, the clergy of that city incited their fellow citizens—raging with wine and madness—against their Bishop, the King, and the other Princes. A certain boy from the city, whether moved by his own will or persuaded by someone, we do not know, attempted furtively to cut away part of the Archbishop’s precious vestment from a certain soldier. The soldier immediately seized him. When the city’s official heard of this, he took the boy into custody, then released him and allowed him to depart freely, without any revolt having yet been stirred up.

But when the clergy heard this report, although they knew that the boy had already been released, they did not hesitate to ring the bells, and to rouse—or rather, compel—the citizens to revolt by gestures and shameful exhortations. The King, however, after finishing his meal, went down from the palace to the church and began to hear Vespers.

Meanwhile the enraged populace, thirsting for the blood of the King and the others, attempted to break into the church and palace. But the King’s soldiers restrained them, although they were unarmed, for during the days of Lent it was customary to proceed without weapons; and whatever weapons they had left in their lodgings throughout the city, they could not retrieve because of the citizens’ revolt.

When Vespers had ended, the King returned from the church to the palace with the Archbishop and the other Princes. He saw that the furious people did not intend to desist from their undertaking, but were conspiring in a mad revolt to profane that Sunday in Lent, the church cemetery, and even their own mother church, and thus, with many sacrileges, to bring about the death of the King, the Bishops, and all their own people, though none of them had suffered any injury at their hands. He therefore girded on his sword and resolved to restrain their madness.

But his Princes did not permit him to proceed contrary to royal custom. At his command, they borrowed weapons wherever they could find them, first entering the church to pray to God, then singing aloud, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*), and finally leaping out of the church through the gate that was under the heaviest attack. Although they were very few, they immediately put the enormous multitude of their enemies to flight, so thoroughly that some of them, expecting to die, even threw themselves into the Rhine, although the royal soldiers pursued them only a short distance beyond the church cemetery.

## CHAPTER XI. Gregory Sends Legates to Germany to Remove the Schism in the Empire by Arbitration.

## 88.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1078, in the first indiction, when both kings—namely Henry and Rudolf—were seeking assistance from the Apostolic See, Pope Gregory VII, presiding over a general Synod, decreed:

“Since it is observed that the disturbance of the Kingdom daily redounds to the greatest danger and detriment of the holy Church, it pleases us to labor with all our strength so that suitable envoys, distinguished both by religion and by knowledge, may be sent from the side of the Apostolic See to those regions. They shall summon all religious people and lovers of justice residing in the lands of the German Kingdom, both clerics and laymen, and men suitable for this undertaking. With these men, with the grace of the Lord going before them, they shall either justly establish an end and peace, or, after learning the truth, be able to discover fully which side justice favors more, so that the unjust party may desist and the justice supported by Apostolic authority may obtain strength and the force of authority.

“Yet because we are not unaware that certain men, gathered together by diabolical inspiration, inflamed by the torches of their tyranny and enslaved to the greed of disgraceful profit, desire discord rather than peace and wish to see it produced, we decree that no person of any power whatsoever—whether King, Archbishop, Bishop, Duke, Margrave, Count, or Knight—shall attempt, through presumption or reckless daring, fraud or deceit, or any disturbance, to resist or oppose our Legates, lest they establish justice and an end to the conflict.

“Whoever, however, with reckless daring—which we do not desire—becomes a violator of this constitution of ours and attempts to obstruct the aforesaid Legates as they go to establish this peace, we bind him with the bond of anathema. By Apostolic power we bind him not only in spirit but also in body and in every prosperity of this life, and we take victory from him in arms, so that at least he may be confounded and crushed by a twofold confusion and contrition.”

“Enacted at Rome in the Church of the Lord Savior, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the first indiction.”

## 89.

[Note: This is Letter 15 of Book 5.]

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the Apostolic blessing to the Archbishops, Bishops, clerics, Dukes, Margraves, Counts, and all greater and lesser persons established in the German Kingdom, except those held under canonical excommunication.

“We wish it to be known to you, dearest brothers, that at the Synod which we recently celebrated at Rome…” etc. See among the letters of Saint Gregory below.

## 90.

[Note: Udo presided over the Church of Trier from the year 1068 until the year 1077. Brower relates his deeds in Book XII of the *Annals of Trier*, where he teaches that Udo defected from the schism of Henry IV and recalled other schismatic Bishops to sounder counsels.]

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the Apostolic blessing to Udo, Archbishop of Trier…”

[Note: This is Letter 16 of Book V. Letters 81 of Book I and 10 of Book II were also addressed to him, as well as Letter 12 of Book III, addressed jointly to Udo, Theodoric of Verdun, and Hermann of Metz, and finally seven others in Book V addressed to him and his suffragans.]

“How great our concern and how great our sadness are over the disturbance—or rather, the division—of your once most renowned and powerful kingdom…” etc. See the passage cited above.

## 91.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1078, in the sixth year of the pontificate of the Lord Pope Gregory VII, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the second indiction, a Synod was convened at Rome in the Church of Saint Savior. There the legates of Henry and Rudolf swore, each on behalf of his own lord, that they would obstruct by no deceit the conference to be held in the German Kingdom by the Legates of the Apostolic See.

## 92.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1079, in the month of February, in the second indiction, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the Lord Pope Gregory VII, the Legates of King Rudolf lodged a complaint against Henry: sparing neither place nor person, he was crushing and trampling the transalpine region; he showed due honor or reverence to no one; and priests, as well as Bishops and Archbishops, were being seized and reduced to bondage like worthless slaves, with some already being slaughtered.

Many members of the Council therefore decreed that the Apostolic sword ought to be unsheathed against his tyranny. But Apostolic gentleness postponed this, also considering what Gregory wrote to Bishops Peter of Albano and Altmann of Passau concerning the same matter. Among other things, he said:

“Thus present yourselves equally to both parties and, as far as lies within you, with the help of divine grace, keep yourselves free from every blemish of suspicion, so that you may always uphold justice and in no way favor either party, according to the model you have from us. For, after the judgment of this great matter was committed to the hands of Blessed Peter, you are witnesses that we seek nothing else except to proceed along the path of justice. We have bent the sincerity of Apostolic discernment toward no party; we have yielded to no promises or threats; nor do we trust, with God protecting us, that we shall ever act otherwise.”

[Note: The matter of Blessed Peter the Fiery and Saint Altmann was treated above.]

## 93.

The legates of King Henry, who were present when the aforesaid complaint was brought against him, swore according to the following formula:

“The legates of my lord King Henry will come to you within the period before the Ascension of the Lord, except in the case of legitimate *sonni*—that is, death, serious illness, or captivity without deceit—and they will safely conduct the legates of the Roman See there and back. The lord King will obey them in all things according to their justice and judgment, and he will observe all these matters without deceit, except insofar as anything remains outstanding by your command. This we swear at the command of our lord King Henry.”

[Note: In our manuscript, “except *matrice vi*” [an uncertain reading]. *Sonna*, *Sunnis*, or *Sunnia* is found in Cange’s *Glossary*, meaning a cause alleged by someone to prevent him from appearing to have his case heard according to law. That most learned man offers much concerning the uncertain etymology of this word, which may be read in his work.]

Likewise, the legates of King Rudolf swore as follows:

“If, at your command, a conference is arranged in the German regions, at the place and time determined by you, before your presence or that of your Legates, our lord King Rudolf will either come himself or send his Bishops and faithful men. He will be prepared to submit to the judgment which the holy Roman Church decrees concerning the case of the Kingdom, and by no evil device will he obstruct the assembly arranged by you or by your Legates.

“After he sees your duly authorized envoy concerning the establishment and confirmation of peace in the Kingdom, he will endeavor to ensure that your embassy may bring about peace and concord in the Kingdom. All these things shall be observed except insofar as anything remains outstanding by your permission, or because of a legitimate impediment, namely death, serious illness, or captivity without deceit.”

## 94.

After this, an edict of Apostolic benevolence was issued once more. We include it here in full so that both the wise and the foolish may understand clearly that our Gregory was a prince in that blessedness of which the Lord says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

[Note: It is also found in Bruno’s *On the Saxon War*, volume I of Freher’s collection, p. 147.]

“Gregory, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the Apostolic blessing to all Archbishops and Bishops residing in the German and Saxon Kingdoms, and also to all greater and lesser persons who are not excommunicated and are willing to obey.

“Since the quarrel and dissension that has existed among you for so long…” etc. See among the letters below.

## CHAPTER XII. After the Deposition of Henry and the Election of Rudolf Had Been Promulgated, Gregory Dies Piously.

## 95.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1080, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the third indiction, the Pope himself celebrated a Synod at Rome. Archbishops and Bishops from various cities attended, together with an innumerable multitude of Abbots and clerics and laymen of various orders.

The Legates of King Rudolf and of the Princes of the German Kingdom also arrived and brought forward the following complaint concerning Henry’s tyranny:

“We, as the envoys of our lord King Rudolf and of his Princes, complain before God and Saint Peter, before Your Paternity and this entire most holy Council, that Henry, whom you deposed from the Kingdom by Apostolic authority, has tyrannically invaded that same Kingdom in defiance of your interdict and has devastated everything around him with sword, plunder, and fire.

“By impious cruelty he expelled Archbishops and Bishops from their bishoprics and distributed their bishoprics as benefices to his supporters. Through his tyranny, the Archbishop of Magdeburg, Weinharius, of blessed memory, was killed. Adalbert, Bishop of Worms, is still being tortured by him in captivity, contrary to the command of the Apostolic See. Many thousands of men have been killed by his faction; very many churches have been burned and utterly destroyed after their relics were removed.

“There are innumerable crimes which this same Henry has perpetrated against our Princes because they refused to obey him as king in opposition to the decree of the Apostolic See. The conference which you decreed should take place in order to investigate justice and establish peace has failed through Henry’s fault and that of his supporters.

“Therefore we humbly implore your clemency: render to us—or rather, to the holy Church of God—the justice decreed against this sacrilegious invader of churches.”

[Note: Weinharius, or Wernerus, also called Wecel, was killed by Henry IV in 1078, on 7 August, near the river Unstrut, while defending the party of the Roman Pontiff. Thus Strenesdorf reports in his *Primate of Magdeburg*, following manuscript annals. But in our manuscript annals of the Anonymous Saxon, he is said to have been killed in flight by common people.]

[Note: Adalbert, restored after a long exile, died in the year 1108, on 6 July. Thus Bruschius. His restoration under the succeeding Pope is discussed below.]

Stirred by these and similar complaints, the spirit of the man of God perceived that the day was approaching which the Blessed Mother of God had designated to him in a vision for pronouncing sentence of condemnation against that adversary of the Church, and concerning which she had commanded and warned him not to delay any longer. With profound sorrow and groaning he brought forth his sentence; and while the Council listened and lent its support, he finally burst into these words.

## 96.

[Note: These words are found in the Acts of the Roman Council.]

“Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and you, blessed Paul, Teacher of the nations, please deign to incline your ears toward me and graciously hear me, because you are disciples and lovers of truth. Help me to speak the truth to you, with every falsehood removed, for you utterly detest falsehood, so that my brothers may more readily heed me and know and understand that, trusting in you, after the Lord and his mother, ever-Virgin Mary, I resist the wicked and unjust, while I offer assistance to your faithful.

“You know that I did not willingly enter the sacred Order, and that against my will I crossed the mountains with the Lord Pope Gregory.

[Note: This was Gregory VI, whose journey is related by Baronius under the year 1047.]

“But still more unwillingly, with my lord Pope Leo, I returned to your special Church, in which I served you as best I could. Then, very unwillingly, with great sorrow, groaning, and lamentation, I was placed, most unworthy, upon your throne.

“I say this because I did not choose you; rather, you chose me and placed upon me the exceedingly heavy burden of your Church. And because you commanded me to climb a high mountain, to cry out, and to proclaim to the people of God their crimes and to the children of the Church their sins, the members of the devil began to rise against me and dared to lay hands upon me even unto bloodshed.

“Kings of the earth stood forth, and Princes gathered together; secular and ecclesiastical persons, courtiers and commoners, gathered as one against the Lord and against you, his anointed ones, saying: ‘Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us.’ They attempted in many ways to rise against me, so as to overwhelm me completely either by death or exile.

## 97.

“Among them, Henry in particular—whom they call king, the son of Emperor Henry—raised his heel against your Church. Conspiring with many men from beyond the Alps and from Italy, he strove to subject it to himself by overthrowing me.

“Your authority resisted his pride, and your power destroyed it. Confounded and humbled, he came to me in Lombardy and sought absolution from the excommunication under which he lay. Seeing him humbled, and after receiving many promises from him concerning the correction of his life, I restored communion to him alone. I did not, however, restore him to the Kingdom, from which I had deposed him at the Roman Synod; nor did I command that the fidelity of the men who had sworn or were about to swear to him—men whom I had all absolved at that same Synod—be preserved for him.

“I withheld these things in order to render justice or establish peace between him and the transalpine Bishops and Princes who, at the command of your Church, had resisted him, just as Henry himself had promised me by oath through two Bishops.

“But when the aforesaid transalpine Bishops and Princes heard that he was not keeping what he had promised me, they became, as it were, desperate concerning him and, without my counsel, with you as witnesses, chose Duke Rudolf as their king. King Rudolf, having promptly sent a messenger to me, informed me that he had been compelled to take up the government of the Kingdom, but that he was ready to obey me in every way.

“And so that this might be believed more firmly, from that time onward he always sent me the same message, adding that he would confirm what he promised by giving my son as a hostage and the son of his faithful Berthold.

“Meanwhile Henry began to beg me to assist him against the aforementioned Rudolf. I replied that I would gladly do so after hearing the case of both parties, so that I might know which side justice favored more. But he, believing that he could overcome Rudolf by his own strength, disregarded my response.

“When he perceived that he could not act as he had hoped, two Bishops—Theodoric of Verdun and Bernard of Osnabrück—came to Rome from among his supporters.

[Note: Theodoric governed the Church of Verdun from the year 1047 to 1090.]

[Note: Bernard governed the Church of Osnabrück from 1068 to 1086. Cratepolus praises him highly.]

“At the Synod, on Henry’s behalf, they asked me to render him justice, and Rudolf’s envoys approved that this should be done. At last, with God’s inspiration, as I believe, I decreed at that same Synod that a conference should be held in the transalpine regions, so that either peace might be established there or it might be discovered which side justice favored more.

“For, as you, my fathers and lords, are my witnesses, until today I have resolved to assist no party except the one whom justice favored more. And because I thought that the more unjust party would refuse a conference in which justice would maintain its place, I excommunicated and bound with the chain of anathema every person—whether King, Duke, Bishop, or any other man—who by any device obstructed the conference so that it could not take place.

## 98.

“But the aforementioned Henry and his supporters, fearing no danger from disobedience—which is the crime of idolatry—incurred excommunication by obstructing the conference and bound themselves with the chain of anathema. He also delivered a great multitude of Christians to death, caused churches to be scattered, and gave almost the entire German Kingdom over to desolation.

“Therefore, trusting in the judgment and mercy of God and in that of his most merciful mother, ever-Virgin Mary, and supported by your authority, I subject the aforementioned Henry, whom they call king, and all his supporters to excommunication and bind them with the chain of anathema. Again, in the name of almighty God and on your behalf, I place the German Kingdom and Italy under interdict against him; I remove from him every royal dignity and power; and I forbid any Christian to obey him as king.

“I absolve all who have sworn or will swear to him concerning dominion over the Kingdom from the obligation of their oath. But let Henry himself and his supporters obtain no strength and no victory in any battle throughout their lives.

“Yet, so that Rudolf may rule and defend the German Kingdom, whom the Germans have chosen as their king, I give, bestow, and grant him, on your behalf, to your fidelity. To all who faithfully adhere to him, trusting in your support, I grant absolution from all sins and a true blessing in this life and in the life to come.

“For just as Henry, on account of his pride, disobedience, and falsehood, is justly cast down from the dignity of the Kingdom, so power and dignity over the Kingdom are granted to Rudolf for his humility, obedience, and truth.”

## 99.

“Act now, I beg you, most holy Fathers and Princes, so that the whole world may understand and know that if you can bind and loose in heaven, you can also, according to each person’s merits, take away and grant on earth empires, kingdoms, duchies, principalities, marches, counties, and the possessions of all men.

“You have frequently taken Patriarchates, Primacies, Archbishoprics, and Bishoprics from wicked and unworthy men and given them to religious men. If you judge spiritual matters, what should be believed concerning what you can do with secular matters?

“Let kings and all the Princes of this world now learn how great you are and what you can do, and let them fear to make light of the command of your Church. Exercise your judgment against the aforementioned Henry so promptly that all may know he will fall and be confounded not by chance but by your power—if only for repentance, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

“Enacted at Rome, on the Nones of March, in the third indiction.”

## 100.

Thus the wretched Henry, handed over to Satan and to the rabid fury of demons, climbed higher and higher toward the summit of wickedness. Desiring to depose the lawful Pope, he raised up, like a new Nebuchadnezzar, a golden statue for the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans in the city of Rome, which Peter and John call Babylon: namely, Guibert, Bishop of Ravenna, who had long before been condemned by a synodal sentence by our Gregory on account of incest and his other crimes.

[Note: Guibert, appointed Archbishop by King Henry in 1072, was excommunicated in 1078 at the Sixth Roman Council, attended by nearly one hundred Bishops and others, and again in 1080 at the Seventh Roman Council.]

A most severe persecution having been stirred up against the man of God, he withdrew to Salerno. There, most effectively cleansed by the wormwood of heavenly medicine through bodily illnesses, he deserved to be gladdened by a sweet response of divine consolation: namely, that these purifications would benefit and suffice for him forever, and that he need fear no chastisement after death.

Finally, as a sign of everlasting health, he regained temporal bodily well-being; and, something that may seem highly glorious, around the Kalends of January he began to foresee that the dissolution of his body would occur around the Kalends of June. When these approached and he began the struggle of his final suffering, Bishops and Cardinals stood beside him, declaring him blessed on account of the labors of his holy life and teaching. He replied:

“My most beloved brothers, I attach no importance to any of my labors. I trust in this one thing alone: that I have always loved justice and hated iniquity.”

Again, when they lamented their anxiety over his condition after his departure, the pious Father raised his eyes toward heaven and extended his hands in that direction, as if in ascension:

“Thither I shall ascend,” he said, “and, with fervent prayers, I shall commend you to God, if he is propitious.”

## 101.

Furthermore, when he was asked, amid such great disturbance among the faithful, to designate a successor for himself and for the Church as an avenger against the aforementioned adulterer, he gave three choices: Desiderius, Cardinal and Abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino; and the most reverend Bishops Otto of Ostia and Hugh of Lyon.

But because Otto had not yet returned from the regions of Germany and Gaul, where he had carried out an Apostolic legation and, in the Pope’s presence and with his support, had consecrated the venerable Gebhard as ruler of the Church of Constance, and had prudently arranged several other matters pertaining to the stability of the Church,

[Note: For six years there had been great disturbance at Constance because King Henry had sent his chaplains Rupert, and afterward Berthold, to govern the bishopric. Since the clergy did not accept them, Gebhard was appointed.]

[Note: Otto was later made Pope in the year 1088 and was called Urban II.]

while Hugh was also far away, inspecting the affairs of his own governance, he advised that the nearby Desiderius be elected. Although Desiderius would live only a very short time, he was nevertheless to be called a victor not without a typological prefiguration.

For during the four months allotted to his days, the Lord granted a famous victory to the defenders of the Apostolic See over its adversaries. Through that victory, the Bishop of Würzburg, Adalbero, a man remarkable in age, honorable in appearance and conduct, also recovered his See, which had long been held by invaders. He returned with the venerable fellow Bishops mentioned above, Gebhard of Constance and Hermann of Metz, who themselves had lost their Sees on account of their fidelity to our Gregory.

The holy Father had foretold Desiderius that he would not be present at Gregory’s passing, although he had visited him because of his illness and would remain with him to the end and celebrate the holy funeral rites with the other faithful. This had left Desiderius greatly astonished and saddened.

While he remained perplexed about what obstacle might arise, news suddenly reached him that the Normans had surrounded a certain castle subject to his monastery. Compelled by the necessity of coming to the aid of his people, he obtained permission to depart. Thus, although unwilling, he gave the prophecy an opportunity to be fulfilled.

### 102

Meanwhile, when blessed Pope Gregory was asked whether he wished to grant any dispensation concerning those whom he had excommunicated, he replied:

> “Moreover, I absolve and bless the so-called King Henry and Guibert, the invader of the Apostolic See, and all those leading persons who, whether by counsel or by assistance, favor their wickedness or impiety—whoever unhesitatingly believes that I possess this special power in the place of the Apostles Peter and Paul.”

In addition, after admonishing them about many matters, he gave them this command:

> “In the name of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, I command you to acknowledge no one as Roman Pontiff unless he has been canonically elected and elected and ordained with the authority of the holy Fathers.”

When he was lying at the point of death, his final words were:

> “I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.”

In response, a certain venerable bishop is said to have answered:

> “You cannot, Lord, die in exile, since in the place of Christ and his Apostles you have received from God the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

Thus the spirit of the seventh Gregory, filled with sevenfold grace, had reproved the world and its princes concerning sin, justice, and judgment. Taking up the heavenly way in the strength of the heavenly food he had recently received, and deservedly carried aloft, as if by a fiery chariot, like Elijah, [Note: [Col. 0095D] Of Saint Urban I, pope and martyr, whose Acts we have already given.] he greatly increased the joy in heavenly glory of his predecessor Urban, whose feast occurred on that day, and of all the blessed who rejoice with Christ. On earth, however, by his departure he struck the pilgrim Church with no small grief.

His body was committed to burial near blessed Matthew the Evangelist; concerning the recent discovery of whose remains he had joyfully written a letter a few years earlier.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] This is Letter 8 of Book VIII, addressed to Alphanus, Bishop of Salerno.]

## CHAPTER XIII. Examples of those who obeyed or disobeyed Gregory’s decrees and were divinely approved or disapproved

### 103

Next, it seems appropriate to introduce his principal follower and heir in virtue, blessed Anselm, Bishop of the Church of Lucca,

[Note: [Col. 0096D] We gave the Life of Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca, on 18 March.]

who above all things always devoted himself to imitating Gregory in every respect, to such a degree that he absolutely refused to differ from him in anything. Whatever was found in Anselm, moreover, he always attributed to Gregory’s merits. Gregory was like a fountain; Anselm flowed like a stream and irrigated what was dry. Gregory, like the head, governed the whole body; Anselm, like an industrious hand, performed whatever was assigned to him. Gregory, like the sun, illuminated everything; Anselm, like a ray of light, made each thing manifest.

Long ago, when Elijah was about to depart from the company of mortals, he left his mantle to Elisha, the instrument of prophetic office. Likewise, when Gregory was about to depart from this mortal life, he transmitted to Anselm the insignia of pontifical power—namely, the mitre from his own head. God cooperated in this so that, just as Elisha inherited the prerogative of prophecy through Elijah’s mantle, so Anselm might obtain priestly eminence through the mitre.

Indeed, the resemblance went so far that, just as Elisha had demonstrated through Elijah’s mantle the signs of his virtues, so Anselm displayed certain great works through Gregory’s mitre. To mention one especially well known rather than offer many examples, the reverend Ubaldus, prelate of the Mantuan Church,

[Note: [Col. 0096D] Udaldus was made bishop in 1082 and was driven from his see by King Henry.]

had for many years suffered severely from splenetic disease and was ulcerated throughout his body, especially in the legs, so that he could scarcely stand in any manner and could scarcely lie down or sit. He had also spent much money on physicians without receiving any benefit. When the same mitre was placed upon him where the pain had become most severe, he was restored to his former health.

Let us extract a few passages from Anselm’s book on the exposition of the Psalms and show more clearly how devoutly he felt toward the sanctity of his master Gregory. Thus he speaks in his exposition of the second Psalm:

> “The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

The kings of the earth—members, that is, of the one who reigns over all the sons of pride—not only came but stood by, and with their army besieged the Roman Church. The princes of the priests gathered together in conspiracy against holy Peter and against his Vicar Gregory; indeed, against the very one who said, “Whoever touches you touches me; whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10). They crucify the Son of God again.

For it is certain that our head suffers in his members and is weakened in his members, just as he himself said to blessed Peter: “I am going again to Rome to be crucified.” Do not the princes of the priests seem to you once again to gather a council in Pilate’s house in order to hand Christ over to death, when Henry has prepared so many false witnesses against the supreme Pontiff and all cry out, “He is worthy of death”?

Is not Barabbas chosen again and Christ condemned to death under Pilate, when Guibert of Ravenna is chosen and Pope Gregory rejected? Thus they seek to preserve the robber who is condemned by the law, and they condemn the just man through whom all are saved.

Does Pilate not seem once again to have washed his hands and said, “I am clean from the blood of this man; I find no cause in him,” when Henry, after feigning repentance, worshiped the supreme Pontiff and then said to his false bishops, “Judge him according to your law”?

Furthermore:

> “Let us break their bonds,” and so forth.

“Let us oppress the just man,” they say, “because he is opposed to our works. For if we let him remain thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.”

Again:

> “If Pope Gregory lives, he will send preachers of the truth against us. They will examine our life and deeds, rescue Christ’s sheep from our hands, and the just will plunder our spoils and leave the Church to those who will make it fruitful.”

As for the sanctity of this expositor, we have partly discerned it from reading the accounts of his holy deeds and partly learned it from the reports of religious brothers who testified that they had come from afar, summoned by revelation to his tomb, and had immediately been freed from serious and long-standing illnesses.

### 104

Now we think it worthwhile to demonstrate briefly how God’s favor or anger commended, among our people—that is, in the German regions—the decrees of our Gregory against the avarice and lust of the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. In this way, the righteous may become more vigilant in avoiding the sin of forbidden communion, while the workers of iniquity, filled with greater fear, may strive with the utmost efforts of repentance to escape the punishment of their transgression.

We reserve for those who are nearer at hand the heavenly events that occurred—or are said to have occurred—at his tomb among the more devout Romans, since they know more readily the persons among whom these things either occurred or are occurring.

To set down first an example against the first plague in the Church, that of Simon Magus: the most reverend Father Willelmus of the monastery of Hirsau,

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Willelmus died in 1091, on 5 July. He is greatly praised by Berthold of Constance and by Trithemius in the Hirsau Chronicle.]

whose piety is also reverently approved by the writings of our Gregory, received among the many who sought his special medicine a certain priest stained by the leprosy of Simoniacal depravity, intending to heal him with the antidote of humility.

But alas! Because of the force of the monks’ persistence—for their worst custom is to pay little or no attention to the sacred Canons—he did not restrain the man from the unlawful sacrifice of the immaculate Lamb. As a result, the Savior himself terrified him with a dreadful vision when, after the beginning of the Mass of the Catechumens, he was sitting in his own stall.

Overcome by sleep, he saw the Savior with torn clothing and an appearance like that of a leper. When he was astonished and wondered whom he was seeing and why such an apparition had appeared, the Savior said:

> “You treated me in this way. Although you knew that you were a Simoniac, you nevertheless presumed to approach to consecrate the sacraments of my Body and Blood.”

Meanwhile, when the hour for rising to the reading of the Gospel was approaching, many of the brothers signaled that he should be awakened. But the aforesaid abbot, considering the matter more deeply, refused, lest the revelation, if there was one, be interrupted. He perceived that such profound sleep at that time and place was not without significance.

Accordingly, the Mass of the Sacraments was reached. Then, necessarily awakened for the purpose of celebrating the mystery, the priest revealed his weakness and inability. He immediately accepted a substitute for that Mass and from then on completely ceased exercising the priestly office.

### 105

From here we must present examples effective against the Nicolaitans and those who associate with them. The virgin Herluca, of blessed memory, to whom visions and revelations of the Lord were familiar, together with the infirmities of the Apostle,

[Note: [Col. 0097D] We gave the Lives of Saint Wicterpus, bishop, and blessed Herluca, virgin, on 18 April. The latter was written by the same Paul of Bernried; in section 22 he recalls this story, which he had described in that Life.]

faithfully related to us that on one occasion, while she was sitting alone in her cell, she suddenly saw the Lord Jesus enter, accompanied by blessed Wicterpus, formerly prelate of the Church of Augsburg. After remaining silent for a little while, he stood there and displayed only his wounds, streaming with blood.

When she shuddered with fear at the unfamiliar vision, the bishop addressed her:

> “Do you shrink, sister, from the bloody appearance of the Savior?”

She replied:

> “Yes, Lord.”

He said:

> “Do you wish not to see him in this manner again?”

She answered:

> “I do.”

He said:

> “Then from now on do not hear the Masses of the priest Richard, who does not wish to preserve the chastity required by so great an office.”

That was the name of the priest who unworthily presided over the church near which the virgin, devoted to God, lived. From that time onward, after he had been publicly refuted by divine visitation, she encouraged the people by her example to do the same.

### 106

The following vision also seems worthy of remembrance. The monk Adalbert, beloved by God and human beings and of blessed memory, had himself suffered insults and terrors from the adversaries of our Gregory because of his obedience to Gregory’s decrees. He related that the same Herluca had seen a vision concerning a certain Nicolaitan who, serving carnal desires, had polluted the church located in a place called Rota.

[Note: [Col. 0098D] This vision is repeated in the same work, section 24.]

Those regions lay on the boundary between the Norici and the Alamanni, whom the river Lech separates. The dwelling places of the venerable old man and of the blessed virgin were not far apart, and they loved one another deeply in Christ because they recognized in each other an outstanding grace of God.

Thus the beloved man related the story of the beloved woman. One day blessed Herluca was sitting, as usual, among her fellow virgins and widows, diligently occupied with her customary handiwork. Suddenly, as she looked out through the window, she began to lament and cry out grievously:

> “Woe, woe! It would have been better for that man if he had never been born.”

A certain noble woman named Hadewiga, greatly astonished, asked her what she had seen and why she was so agitated.

Herluca replied:

> “That unhappy priest from Rota has died, and his soul is being carried to hell by the angels of Satan. I saw them passing by in triumph, while the soul accompanied them with wailing.”

When Hadewiga wished this not to be true, Herluca said:

> “Let someone be sent to discover the truth.”

The messenger who was sent found the household mourning and learned at that very hour that the priest had died, just as the blessed virgin had seen his soul carried away by evil spirits.

### 107

Meanwhile, divine vengeance also raged terribly against the wives or concubines of the Nicolaitans. Some of them, handed over to a depraved mind, committed themselves to the flames. Others went to bed healthy and were found dead in the morning, without any preceding sign of illness. As for others, after their souls had been torn away, evil spirits seized their bodies and placed them in their own hiding places, depriving them of human burial.

Moreover, God’s anger manifested itself on several occasions against incestuous celebrants of the Mass. When they were on the point of communicating, a violent whirlwind suddenly rushed in, overturned the chalice, and spilled the Blood, while it miraculously snatched away the holy Bread beyond human discovery.

We have not investigated sufficiently what kind of priest that was who once dared to put on the chasuble of our often-mentioned and ever-to-be-mentioned Gregory, which had been given to him as a pledge, in order to celebrate Mass during the time of Pope Gelasius II.

[Note: [Col. 0099B] Gelasius II, elected in 1118, held office for only one year.]

But we learned this for certain from the report of the Romans: he immediately became scabrous and escaped only through worthy fruits of repentance.

### 108

How great a grace of God followed those who obeyed the Gregorian institution is shown by the “Quadrangular Religion,” begun in these regions through the venerable blessing of our Gregory’s Apostolic authority and happily multiplied.

[Note: [Col. 0099C] This is confirmed by Letter 24 of his Book VII, to the said Abbot Wilhelm of Hirsau, in which he approves his undertaking the care of the monastery of Saint Salvator. Trithemius says of Wilhelm: “For he is the one who strove to reform our Order in nearly all the provinces of the Teutonic kingdom.” It is called the Quadrangular Religion because it is an order constituted from four groups, namely two ranks of each sex. For more, see the Trithemius already cited.]

It consisted of tonsured servants of Christ and of brothers who served them faithfully,

[Note: [Col. 0099C] That is, lay brothers, whom Trithemius says Willelmus either instituted or restored after they had fallen into disuse. Whereas the clerics shaved their beards, these men grew theirs for the sake of distinction. A certain German poetaster, in the first volume of the German Writers, in a satire against Henry V in the Laurisheim Chronicle, ridicules them as follows:

> “Now listen more attentively to those who are bearded.”

They are therefore laymen associated with the “Millet-eaters”—for this is apparently what the jester called the monks of Hirsau because they commonly ate bread made from millet.

He says:

> “There are laymen associated with the Millet-eaters,  
> whom the laughter of the people has given this name to bear,  
> because, with long beards combed down to their chests,  
> they are deformed . . . with stern faces and heads closely shorn.”

Their hair was cut carefully and to a fixed length—that is, it was not long, though it was not shaved to the skin, as with those whom our Paul calls “the Tonsured” in relation to their office and whom the same poetaster mocks as having only a thin line of short hair encircling the head like a crown:

> “With great tonsures and great cowls,  
> their heads shaved, their sleeves reaching to the ground.”

As for the notable virtue of both groups in the monasteries praised above, Berthold is more worthy of being heard. In his Chronicle under the year 1083 he describes it as follows:

> “At that time, in the kingdom of the Teutons, three monasteries with their dependent cells, established according to regular discipline, flourished splendidly: the monastery of Saint Blasius in the Black Forest; Saint Aurelius, which is called Hirsau; and Saint Salvator, which is called Schaffhausen—that is, ‘house of ships.’
>
> “In that period a remarkable multitude of noble and prudent men fled to these monasteries within a short time. They laid aside their weapons and resolved to pursue evangelical perfection under regular discipline, in such numbers that the buildings of the monasteries had necessarily to be enlarged, since otherwise they would not have had room to live there.
>
> “In these monasteries even the external offices are administered not by secular persons but by religious brothers. The nobler they had been in the world, the more eagerly they desire to occupy themselves with despised duties, so that those who had once been counts and margraves in the world now regard it as the greatest delight to serve their brothers in the kitchen and bakery, and to pasture their pigs in the fields. There, indeed, the swineherds and oxherds are, apart from their clothing, the same men as the monks.
>
> “All burn with such ardor of charity that each wishes not so much his own advancement as that of another. They labor so wonderfully in showing hospitality that they seem to think they have lost whatever they have not distributed to Christ’s poor and to guests.”]

the virgins continually enclosed in singular devotion, and likewise the virgins who guarded their entrances and exits with regular discipline.

The four principal rulers of this quadrangle or quadriga were the outstanding renewer of canonical life, Altmann, Bishop of Passau; Odalric, Prior of Cluny, of blessed memory;

[Note: [Col. 0100D] In the Life of blessed Herluca, section 42, he is called Udalricus, provost of a Cluniac foundation among the Swabians.]

and the venerable Fathers Willelmus of Hirsau and Sigefridus of the cell of Saint Salvator.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] In the village of Schaffhausen and in the diocese of Constance, as is said in Gregory’s cited Letter 24 of Book VII.]

### 109

Since we have just mentioned Cluny, we wish, as a reminder to those who preside over monasteries, to recall two visions that occurred there to our Gregory, so that those who have thus far advanced through his word and example may henceforth advance no less through contemplation of these visions.

When he was still an Apostolic Legate, Gregory once came to Cluny and sat beside the abbot presiding over the chapter of the brothers,

[Note: [Col. 0100D] This was Saint Hugh, the abbot. The same event is related in his Life by Abbot Raynald, on 29 April, page 649, no. 4, and in another Life on page 656, no. 3.]

he was lifted in spirit and began to see Jesus standing in the midst: at one moment gently inclining toward the abbot when he judged rightly, and at another turning away indignantly when the abbot happened to be insufficiently attentive to right conduct. After the chapter had ended, Gregory secretly reported this to the Father, thereby urging him to exercise considerable caution thereafter.

On another occasion, after Gregory had been forewarned by divine revelation and had ordered, by apostolic authority, that all who there proved to be murderers, adulterers, or criminals in any way should cease from service at the altar according to the decrees of the Canons, the same men immediately confessed their offenses in fear. The aforesaid abbot related that he had seen them in a dream, as though beheaded by an angel.

### 110

At the end of the book it is pleasant to commemorate a pair bound by complete devotion and drenched in the blood of martyrdom: namely, Burchard, Bishop of Halberstadt, and Theodomar, Bishop of Salzburg, most effective defenders of Gregorian teaching.

Burchard, closely akin in blood and religion to the most reverend archbishops Anno of Cologne and Werenharius of Magdeburg, had long endured the extremely heavy burden of Henry’s persecution with praiseworthy steadfastness. At last, as the day of heavenly recompense approached, he saw in a night vision blessed Blaise, martyr and bishop, standing beside him and promising him a share in the glory of blessed martyrdom.

Thus, when he had been hemmed in at Goslar by the terrifying encirclement of the furious schismatic crowd and had been mortally wounded,

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Berthold Fista records under the year 1088: “In Saxony, Burchard, Bishop of Halberstadt, of pious memory and most steadfast in the cause of Saint Peter, alas, was killed . . . . . He departed to the Lord on 6 April,” as we then said among the matters passed over and deferred to this day, if perhaps we might learn something about his ecclesiastical veneration.]

he admonished those present with remarkable cheerfulness for as long as he survived, urging them both to beware the contagion of heretics and to remain obedient to the Catholic Pontiff. Finally, while speaking words of holy exhortation and prayer, he gave up his spirit. He was buried in the Memorial of the Apostles Peter and Paul, which he himself had built from the foundations and dedicated.

### 111

[Note: Theodomar—also called Diethmar, or rather Thiemo—was the twenty-ninth archbishop of Salzburg, or Juvavum. He was made archbishop around 1088. Having gone with Duke Welf to assist the Christians who were restoring the Christian cause in Palestine after the recovery of Jerusalem, he fell into the hands of the Saracens and was martyred by them in 1101, on 28 September, when his Acts will be discussed. They are extant in volume IV of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings* and in the *Salzburg Metropolis* of Hundius, edited by Gewold, page 58 and following.]

Theodomar, distinguished by the excellence of his nature and by every practice of humility and honesty, had been harassed by the frequent need to flee from the Guibertines and Henricians and was finally worn down by a long captivity. After seeing that he could not bear fruit within his own territories, he resolved to cross over to Jerusalem. On the journey he was intercepted by pagans and, for his unconquerable confession of the name of Christ, was cut limb from limb. Thus, as a glorious victor, he entered the heavenly Jerusalem.

He had ordained the bishop who ordained us, namely the most reverend Udalric, Bishop of Lauriacum or Passau

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Udalric, Saint Altmann’s successor in 1091, is said to have died in that metropolitan see in 1124.]

and legate of the Apostolic See. Seven years before this,

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Therefore the author wrote this around the year 1131.]

after many struggles lawfully fought in defense of Gregorian teaching—the standard according to which he had been elected and promoted—Udalric fell asleep in the Lord at the age of one hundred and five, leaving, alas, no one like him among all the prelates of Germany.

For we see no one so well ordered in character, so honorable in appearance, so modest in dress, so venerable in authority, always possessing speech seasoned with the salt of grace and ready with suitable answers on every side, and possessing other distinctions that we have preferred to conceal rather than stir up vain envy among those unable to equal him.

Nevertheless, with the permission of all, we think this may be said: nothing was more pleasing than his severity, and nothing was more severe than his pleasantness. He restrained the virtue of remarkable abstinence with such great cheerfulness that it gave off no scent whatsoever of ostentation.

### 112

A certain consecrated virgin, his special pupil,

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Gretserus thinks that blessed Hertuca is meant. I would rather understand another woman, still living when this was written and therefore not named; otherwise the author would not later have failed, in the Life of Herluca, to mention her mother and maternal aunts, women of such remarkable sanctity.]

saw heavenly visions and received gifts that were not irrelevant to commending Gregorian obedience and therefore must not be passed over in silence.

She had loved a certain priest because he had lived chastely and had received Holy Orders from so legitimate a pontiff, namely Odalric. In the divine offices, even in the very tone of his voice, he had attained a pleasing likeness to her own charity.

It therefore happened that on one occasion she seemed to see him celebrating the sacred mysteries, with the right hand of the divine majesty appearing above and making the canonical signs together with him. But after the holy prelate’s death, when God, in response to sins, had set the darkness of ignorance in place and the night of insolence had come, all the beasts of the forest passed through it, and the whelps of lions roared as they sought from God their food—that is, the evil spirits.

What is grievous to say is that they corrupted this priest, hitherto blameless, with the bite of lust. This was made known to the aforementioned virgin in the following way: she again saw him engaged in the sacred mysteries, with the Lord’s right hand still appearing, but hanging down as though weakened and accomplishing absolutely nothing.

These things were shown to the virgin by divine revelation.

### 113

On several occasions, when in accordance with the Gregorian prohibition she physically avoided the ministry of incontinent priests, she nevertheless directed her faith and prayer toward those to whom she could not offer her bodily presence. Through the Savior’s wondrous generosity, she began to taste in her mouth the same sweetness which, when she occasionally received communion from Catholics in reality, she rejoiced to have experienced through the manifest reception of the sacraments.

The prelate Odalric, of blessed memory, loved this virgin above the other virgins no more on account of her good character than because of the honorable widowhood of her holy mother and the praiseworthy virginity of her maternal aunts, all of whom instructed her especially well.

Concerning her mother, whose name was Helisaea, it should briefly be added that, excelling in many virtues and in the spirit of prophecy through her ardent obedience to our Gregory, she prepared a suitable solitude when the moment of her departure from this world was at hand. She then migrated to Christ under the glorious protection of those gracious spirits who visited her.

The sisters who had gone away returned immediately and found her, like Paul the first hermit, with her hands extended toward the Lord in the posture of a suppliant. Through this, the merciful Creator wished to show in the deceased woman how devotedly she had supplicated him while she lived.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] The same Gretserus believed that this was not the mother of the virgin but the mother of the bishop himself; we think he was mistaken.]

### 114

As we write these things, an account has perhaps been brought to us of two miracles performed at Salerno from heaven, one occurring as soon as blessed Gregory had *recensisset* there [the verb is uncertain in the supplied text].

When he first began to preach in that place, a certain peasant standing nearby began to say inwardly, with malicious intent:

> “Behold the author of wars and seditions! After stirring up the whole world, he has come to disturb this city as well.”

While he was thinking these things and even wished to speak them aloud, he was distressed to discover that he had become mute. When necessity compelled him to approach the man of God, he fell at his feet and made known by whatever signs he could that he had sinned and repented. Gregory pitied him and blessed him, and the man recovered his speech, intending to give thanks to almighty God and to his servant.

After Gregory had died and been buried, thieves secretly entered during the night, wishing to open the tomb for the sake of the pontifical garments. But a wind of such violence blew against them that all the lamps burning in the crypt of blessed Matthew were extinguished. The thieves themselves fell into madness and lay there until they became a spectacle to the clergy and the people.

[Col. 0103]

# PONTIFICAL ACTS

## I. FROM THE CHRONICLE OF BERTHOLD OF CONSTANCE

### CHAPTER ONE. The Acts of Saint Gregory up to the Year 1083

[Col. 0103B]

In the year 1056, Pope Victor, having sent Hildebrand—then archdeacon but later Apostolic Pontiff—convened a general synod at Tours. At it, Berengar, a canon of the Church of Angers, from whom the Beringarian heresy takes its name, was examined synodally and in person concerning that heresy.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Blessed Lanfranc mentions this synod in Book IV of his work against Berengar, as does Guitmund in Book III; Guitmund also says that Gregory was then archdeacon.]

Since Berengar could not defend himself, he anathematized and abjured his heresy before everyone, according to the formula prescribed by the holy and universal Synod of Ephesus.

### 2

In the year 1061, Anselm, Bishop of Lucca, was ordained pope and called Alexander.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] At the councils held at Rome in the years 1063 and 1065.]

He vigorously destroyed the Simoniacal heresy and, under pain of excommunication, prohibited ministers of the altar from having intercourse with their wives, in accordance with the statutes of the Canons. He also prohibited laypeople, under ban, from attending the services of incontinent clerics. Thus he restrained clerical incontinence with considerable prudence.

The principal author of this constitution was Hildebrand, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, who was especially hostile to heretics.

### 3

In the year 1073, Pope Alexander died at Rome. In his place, the venerable Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was sought by the common counsel of all to be made pope.

When he heard this, the archdeacon, judging himself unequal to so great an honor—or rather burden—asked for time to reply. He then escaped by flight and remained hidden for several days at Saint Peter ad Vincula.

At last he was scarcely found and was forcibly brought to the Apostolic See. He was ordained as the one hundred and fifty-ninth pope on 25 April and took the name Gregory VII. Through his prudence, the incontinence of priests was restrained not only in Italy but also in the Teutonic regions. What his predecessor had prohibited in Italy, Gregory strove to prohibit throughout the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0104B]

### 4

In the year 1074, legates of the Apostolic See came to the King in Alemannia to correct the King’s conduct. The King entrusted himself to their hands by promising correction and firmly promised his assistance to the Apostolic Lord in deposing the Simoniacs.

All the King’s counselors likewise promised under oath before the same legates that they would restore all the property of the Churches that they had unjustly acquired. They had purchased these possessions from Simoniacs and, by their counsel, assisted men unworthy of ecclesiastical dignity in obtaining them.

With these matters arranged, the legates of the Apostolic See returned.

### 5

In the year 1075, Hermann, Bishop of Bamberg, was accused by his clergy of the Simoniacal heresy and was deposed by the Pope. Rudbert was appointed in his place.

[Col. 0104C]

During the first week of Lent, Pope Gregory convened a synod at Rome. There he examined the case of the Bishop of Speyer, who was a Simoniac. On the very day when his case was being examined at Rome—that is, 24 February—he fell ill at Speyer. Then, on 26 February, he died miserably, at the same time receiving from Pope Gregory the sentence of his condemnation that had been defined at the Roman Synod.

At the same synod Pope Gregory decreed that clerics who had obtained any grade or office of Holy Orders by payment should no longer minister in the Church; that no one should retain a church acquired by payment; and that henceforth no one should be permitted to sell or buy a church.

He further decreed that all who made themselves blameworthy through incontinence should cease from clerical office. He also decreed that the people should in no way accept the services of clerics whom they perceived to despise the aforementioned Apostolic institutions.

### 6

In the year 1076, King Henry did not cease defiling the holy Church through the Simoniacal heresy—investing bishoprics, abbeys, and other such offices for payment, and, among his other crimes, associating with excommunicated persons.

A certain Roman citizen named Cincius seized Pope Gregory while he was celebrating the solemn Masses on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. One of Cincius’s soldiers intended to kill the Pope after he had been captured. But when the soldier brandished his sword above the Pope’s head, he was overcome by great terror, collapsed, and could not complete the blow.

Cincius led the captured Pope to his own tower. The Romans soon afterward utterly demolished that tower, and the Pope was wisely rescued. He also scarcely managed to secure the life of his captor from the Romans.

Since the King, although repeatedly warned by the Pope long beforehand, refused to correct himself, and since the Pope achieved nothing by admonishing him, Gregory finally sent him word that he would excommunicate him at the next Roman Synod unless he repented. This message reached the King during the Octave of the Nativity of the Lord.

Accordingly, after a council had been held at Worms during Septuagesima and another in Lombardy at Piacenza, the King forced everyone he could to swear that he would not render obedience to the aforesaid Pope. He then sent a delegation to the Roman Synod, which was celebrated during the following Lent, and insolently ordered the Apostolic Pontiff to descend from the Apostolic See.

His envoys, however, were treated most shamefully at the synod and escaped from the Romans only with the Pope’s assistance. When the synod judged the matter, it deprived the King of the loyalty of his subjects, his kingdom, and communion, and released from their oath all who had sworn allegiance to him as king.

It deprived all the bishops who had willingly supported the King against the Pope of office and communion. To the others, who had taken part in the conspiracy against their will, it granted a delay until the feast of Saint Peter. [lacuna]

[Col. 0105C]

Bishop Willelmus of Utrecht, who had uttered many insults against the Apostolic Pontiff, was punished with sudden death after Easter, without ecclesiastical communion.

By now almost all the princes of the kingdom had separated themselves from Henry’s communion. Therefore, in October, the princes of the kingdom convened a council at Oppenheim, which was attended by a delegation of the Apostolic See.

There Henry most firmly promised that on the coming Purification of Saint Mary he would appear before the Lord Pope at Augsburg. Indeed, he himself, together with the princes of the kingdom, had invited the Apostolic Lord to come there.

7. In the year 1077, King Henry, mistrusting his own cause and therefore evading a general judgment, secretly entered Italy contrary to the Pope’s command and the counsels of the princes [Col. 0105D]. He encountered the Apostolicus at Canossa before the Purification of Saint Mary, as the latter was proceeding to Augsburg on the appointed day. There, through an appearance of unheard-of humiliation, Henry barely extorted from him, insofar as he could, not the concession of the kingdom but only of communion; yet he first gave an oath that he would submit to the Pope’s judgment concerning the crimes charged against him and would consent to inflict no injury on the Pope or on any of his faithful, whether going or returning.

He observed this oath for not even fifteen days, having captured the venerable bishops Gerald of Ostia and Anselm of Lucca [Col. 0106A]. Therefore the Pope, sending legates, declared to the princes of the kingdom that he had accomplished little by receiving Henry into communion, since Henry was then favoring Simoniacs and excommunicated persons no less than before. After hearing this, the princes of the kingdom, at a general assembly held at Forchheim on the third day before the Ides of March, raised the distinguished Duke Rudolph to be king; on the seventh day before the Kalends of April—when the middle of Lent fell that year—they crowned him.

The immense snow that had covered the whole land for so long that year at last began to melt at the election of the new king. On the day of Rudolph’s consecration, a great riot arose at Mainz through the instigation of Simoniacal clerics, so that the rioters even wanted to break into the palace and kill the most devout clerics and monks [Col. 0106B]. But the right hand of God protected the soldiers of the new prince, although they were unarmed, so effectively that they lost not even one of their own; among the adversaries, however, more than a hundred were killed, some by the sword and some by water. For these homicides the legates of the Apostolic See imposed the following penance: each man was either to fast for forty days or to feed forty poor people once, while nevertheless they were not to avoid ecclesiastical communion as homicides.

8. After his consecration, King Rudolph withdrew into Swabia and brought the kingdom under his control. Meanwhile Henry was staying in Lombardy. Cincius, a Roman citizen, came to Pavia with him, bringing the captured venerable bishop of Como, Reginald, since he wished to be rewarded by Henry for having now captured this bishop in Henry’s service and, in the preceding year, the Apostolicus. But there, overtaken by sudden death, he received the reward he had not feared to deserve through so many sacrileges.

When Henry heard of Rudolph’s advancement, he sought the Pope’s aid against him, although he allowed the aforesaid Bishop of Ostia still to be held captive. The Pope therefore replied that he could not satisfy Henry’s appeal so long as Saint Peter was being held bound in his legate. His supplication thus frustrated, Henry turned his mind toward tyranny. He now planned to obtain the kingdom not by justice but by violence.

King Rudolph, meanwhile, celebrated a most glorious Easter at Augsburg with the legates of the Apostolic See. One of them, the most devout Abbot Bernard, was sent to Rome; but he was captured and plundered by Count Ulrich of Lenzburg, Henry’s accomplice, and remained in captivity for nearly half a year. The Abbot of Cluny finally wrested him from Henry’s hands . . . .

The bishop of Vercelli [Col. 0105D; note: Gregory, made bishop of Vercelli in 1046, at times sane and at times deranged, died on the very Kalends of May.
