Consult Ughelli and Francesco Agostino ab Ecclesia, *On the Bishops of the Piedmontese Region*], chancellor of the deposed king, summoned a general assembly at Runcalia around the Kalends of May, intending, if he could somehow do so, to depose Pope Gregory. But by that same appointed time he miserably laid down both life and episcopate, alas, without ecclesiastical communion—the very things with which he had presumptuously resolved to depose the Pope [Col. 0107A].

Not long after this death, the prefect of the city of Rome, an indefatigable soldier of Saint Peter against the schismatics, was cruelly killed by a certain supporter of Henry [Col. 0107D: Paul, no. 40, calls him Cincius; Peter Damian calls him Cinthius]. At his body, as we learned from the report of faithful men, more than twenty miracles occurred within a short time.

Bishop Imbrico of Augsburg [Col. 0107D: Imbrico was made bishop of Augsburg by Henry IV in 1064 and died on 3 August 1077; he is sufficiently praised by Bruschius], who at the preceding Easter had sworn fealty to King Rudolph, joined Henry when he arrived, caring nothing for his perjury. One day, while celebrating Mass before Henry, he miserably imposed this condition upon himself: if his lord Henry should unjustly usurp the kingdom, receiving the sacred Oblation would become a judgment against him [Col. 0107B]. After this rash reception, during the brief time he survived until his death, he never rose from his bed in good health. For around the Kalends of July he died without ecclesiastical communion.

Likewise Sigehard [Col. 0108D: Sigheardus, called Sigiardus or Singifredus by Ughelli, a German, governed from 1068 to 1077], patriarch of Aquileia, came armed to aid Henry against the Apostolicus’s ban. He was driven into madness at Regensburg and was overtaken by sudden death on the very journey. Thus he was carried home, dead in body and soul, not without the funerals of some of his men.

9. In the name of Saint Peter, the Pope commanded both kings to make a truce with each other and not to obstruct his arrival in the German lands to settle the dispute [Col. 0107C], but to provide him with the necessary counsel and aid for that journey. He also commanded his legates, who were still staying in the German lands, to excommunicate whichever of the two kings failed to obey the aforesaid legation, and to confirm the obedient king in the kingdom in the name of Saint Peter. This was done not long afterward, namely at Goslar on the day after the feast of Saint Martin: Henry was again excommunicated for disobedience, while Rudolph was raised to the kingdom for his obedience.

For Henry did not deign even to receive the Pope’s legation, nor did he turn his mind toward arranging a truce, but toward the cruelty of tyranny.

10. In the year 1078, Henry again complained to the Apostolic See about his condemnation, which he called unjust. Therefore Pope Gregory, having held a council in March [Col. 0107D]—at which council certain persons were excepted from Henry’s excommunication, temporarily at least, namely wives, children, servants, and others who associated with the excommunicated not knowingly, or at least not willingly—again sent suitable legates to settle the kingdom’s case justly at a general assembly. By synodal sentence he condemned all who might prevent the assembly from taking place.

Rudolph very willingly wished this to occur [Col. 0108A]. Henry, however, did not cease to obstruct it by every means available. For, contrary to the Apostolicus’s command, he gathered a very large multitude of wicked men and prepared an expedition into Saxony. King Rudolph met him at Struva with an army, routed him, and won the field of victory on the seventh day before the Ides of August. Yet on Rudolph’s side the venerable Wecel, bishop of Magdeburg, fell [Col. 0108D: Wecel, mentioned in the earlier Life of Werinharius, chapter 12, note 91], and the bishop of Worms was captured [Col. 0108D: Adelbertus, discussed in the same place]. An innumerable multitude fell on both sides, though more—and more distinguished men—fell on Henry’s side.

At another council held at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, the legates of both kings, although not with equal sincerity, swore in the synod that their lords would not prevent an assembly from being held to settle the kingdom’s case. Therefore on that occasion the Pope could not judge between them, although he knew very well which side justice favored [Col. 0108B].

At this synod Berengar, canon of Angers, was formally admonished to repent of his heresy, and a delay was granted him until the next synod.

11. In the year 1070, Pope Gregory convened a synod at Rome in February. There Berengar, convicted for the third time, abjured and anathematized his heresy. At the same synod Henry, patriarch of Aquileia, swore to the Pope that henceforth he would communicate with no one whom he knew to have been excommunicated by the Pope.

At this synod the Pope deposed priests who thereafter fell into fornication, without hope of restoration [Col. 0108C] . . . . The legates of King Rudolph protested against Henry, because he did not cease to throw the whole kingdom into confusion and trample upon the holy Church.

The Pope therefore again sent his legates to the German lands to settle the kingdom’s case, namely the venerable Peter, bishop of Albano . . . . Udalric, bishop of Padua, was sent on the legation with him.

Before they departed, Henry’s legate made the Pope’s legates secure by oath concerning their safe conduct and their lord’s obedience. Rudolph’s legate likewise swore in the synod concerning his lord’s obedience. When the legates of the Apostolic See reached the German land, they established beyond doubt Rudolph’s obedience and Henry’s disobedience; when they returned, they also declared this openly to the Pope.

12. In the year 1080, Pope Gregory convened a synod at Rome in March. The legates of the aforesaid Apostolic See returned to it from the German lands and reported to the Apostolicus Rudolph’s complete obedience and Henry’s disobedience. Therefore, at the end of the synod, he deposed Henry, anathematized him together with all his supporters, and confirmed Rudolph in the royal dignity by Apostolic authority [Col. 0109A].

His rival, therefore, having gathered a multitude of schismatics and excommunicated persons, renounced the legitimate Pope at Brixen. He chose Guibert of Ravenna, formerly a bishop but already deposed irrecoverably and anathematized by Pope Gregory for three years, not as Pope but as a heresiarch. Then, after holding an assembly at Mainz, he caused that same election to be confirmed by everyone whom he could persuade.

By the middle of October, Henry was again preparing an expedition into Saxony when he was put to flight by Rudolph’s soldiers after a day’s march, although in that very engagement King Rudolph, of pious memory, fell.

At this time Henry so greatly disturbed Italy that no one could safely go to the thresholds of the Apostles without first swearing that he would not go to Pope Gregory [Col. 0109B].

13. In the year 1081, after King Rudolph’s death, Henry came to Verona at Easter. From there he set out to invade Rome with his Guibert—not an Apostolicus but an apostate, since he had repeatedly perjured himself toward the Apostolicus and had been anathematized—but soon returned.

At the same time the princes of the German kingdom—archbishops, bishops, dukes, margraves, and counts—held an assembly and elected the nobleman Hermann as their king.

14. In the year 1082, Henry set out for Italy with his apostate Guibert, intending once again to invade Rome, after summoning a multitude of schismatics [Col. 0109C]. He remained there throughout that summer and labored almost in vain, because the Romans did not allow him to enter even this time.

He also tried, through a certain traitor, to set fire to the house of Saint Peter, but by God’s mercy and protection he could not do so. His plan was to burst suddenly through the gates if the Romans, abandoning the fortifications, should rush to extinguish the fire; but the Apostolicus countered this stratagem. For when he first saw the fire, he sent all the Roman soldiers to defend the controls and defenses, while he alone, relying on the confidence of Saint Peter, made the sign of the Cross against the fire and prevented it from advancing farther.

Henry therefore captured the venerable bishop of Sutri [Col. 0109D: Berthold himself calls him Bonizo elsewhere. Ughelli says in volume II of *Italia sacra* that he flourished in 1078 and, after various harsh exiles, was chosen by the Catholic Insubrians as bishop of the city of Piacenza. Finally captured by heretics, deprived of both eyes, and mutilated in his other limbs through exquisite tortures, he gained the noble palm of martyrdom in 1089] and several others. Leaving his apostate Guibert in the city of Tivoli to harass the Romans, he himself returned to Lombardy [Col. 0109D].

## CHAPTER II. Events of the Last Two Years. Death and Burial

15. In the year 1083, Henry again advanced with a multitude of schismatics and excommunicated persons before Pentecost, intending to attack Rome [Col. 0110A]. Thus he enthroned Guibert of Ravenna—perjured, deposed, and anathematized—at Saint Peter’s, not through the bishops of Ostia, Albano, and Porto [Col. 0109D: These were Otto, later Pope Urban II; Blessed Peter Igneus; and John, made bishop of Porto in 1066, always most faithful to the supreme pontiffs and the chief promoter of Urban II, as Leo of Ostia testifies in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Chronicle of Cassino], who possess the privilege of consecrating the Pope, but through the bishops of Modena and Rimini [Col. 0110D: These were Herbert of Modena, created in 1054 and deceased in 1094, and Obizzo, elected in 1071], who had already been deposed and anathematized for many years.

Immediately afterward he made a certain hillock near Saint Peter’s, called Palatiolum, into a fortress, and stationed many soldiers there to attack the Romans. These soldiers completely prevented him from entering the districts of the city across the Tiber.

Many Romans, however, had agreed to this, some induced by money and others deceived by many promises; all alike had already been worn out by the three-year siege. What more need be said? [Col. 0110B] Almost all the Romans, except the Prince of Salerno, approved the proposal that Pope Gregory should convene a synod at Rome in the middle of November, whose decrees concerning the kingdom’s case neither Henry nor the Romans—indeed, no one at all—would be permitted to violate.

Henry also swore an oath guaranteeing the safety of those going to and returning from that synod. Therefore the Pope summoned all devout bishops and abbots to the synod by letter.

When Henry had returned to Lombardy, sudden death struck almost all his soldiers whom he had left in the fortress near Saint Peter’s. Among them Udalric of Goscezehim, the author of this schism and instigator of the conspiracy, died, alas, without ecclesiastical communion.

Of the four hundred soldiers left to guard that fortress, scarcely thirty escaped, as they say, having been spared by the sword of Saint Peter; the Romans completely leveled the fortress to the ground.

Henry therefore set out for the aforesaid synod, having meanwhile sent his Ravennate to Ravenna. The legates of the German princes were also supposed to go there, but Henry captured them on the road near Forum Cassii around the feast of Saint Martin [Col. 0110D: Forum Cassii was once an episcopal city and is now a village in the Patrimony of Saint Peter, seven miles south of Viterbo], although he had promised by oath security to all who were traveling to that synod. Consequently the Romans began to murmur greatly against Henry.

They were most devout monks and clerics, whom he caused to be tortured in captivity. With them he also held captive the venerable Otto, bishop of Ostia, who had been sent to Henry by the Apostolic See [Col. 0110D]. Many bishops and abbots from Francia nevertheless reached that synod.

But Henry specifically prevented the better bishops, those more necessary to the Apostolicus, from reaching the synod: Hugh of Lyon, Anselm of Lucca, and Reginald of Como [Col. 0110D: These are discussed in the earlier Life, numbers 101, 103, and 122; see our notes there].

The Lord Pope nevertheless celebrated the synod solemnly for three days. He was scarcely persuaded by the synod not to anathematize Henry again personally; he nevertheless excommunicated all who in any way hindered anyone coming to Saint Peter and the Pope.

16. But now the appointed time arrived at which the Romans, without the Pope’s knowledge, had sworn to Henry that they would either cause Pope Gregory to crown him or, after expelling Gregory, elect another whom they themselves would choose.

Although this oath had been made during the preceding summer, it remained almost completely hidden from all the Pope’s intimates until the appointed time. When that time arrived, the Romans disclosed the oath to the Pope, saying that they had sworn not that the Pope should crown Henry with the solemn royal anointing, but simply that he should give him a crown.

The Pope therefore agreed to their wishes so that he might release them from the oath: he would give Henry the crown if Henry wished to receive it with justice, but otherwise with a curse [Col. 0111B]. They therefore sent word to Henry that he should come to receive the crown with justice if he wished; otherwise he should receive it from the castle of Sant’Angelo by means of a rod lowered to him by the Pope.

When Henry refused both alternatives, they sent him another legate, saying that they had sworn and were not bound by that oath. Thus they adhered to the Lord Pope’s counsel and aid much more firmly than before.

Henry, however, labored more insistently to draw them over to his side, now threatening and now promising. He remained around Rome for a long time and devoted himself to this matter.

For seven years now the entire Roman empire had suffered from civil war and the excessive division of schism. Some favored the Apostolicus and others Henry, and on this account both sides were miserably devastating the whole kingdom through plunder, sword, and fire.

Very few Catholic bishops remained on the Apostolicus’s side. They had been driven from their own sees and were not allowed to care for their flocks. Therefore almost all the devout, whether clerics or laymen, withdrew into the hiding places of monasteries to escape such evils. They did not wish to witness the devastation of the holy Church, since they could offer it no assistance; for they considered it better at least to save themselves by hiding than to perish with others while laboring uselessly on their behalf.

17. In the year 1084, Henry wintered in Roman territory [Col. 0111D] and there awaited the arrival of his Guibert of Ravenna, so that Guibert might crown him at Saint Peter’s, since Henry could not bend Pope Gregory to this purpose and Gregory was unwilling to crown him unless he had been legitimately reconciled.

At this time the emperor of Constantinople sent a large sum of money to Henry, formerly king, so that Henry might attack in war Robert Guiscard [Col. 0111D: Robert Guiscard was reconciled to the Pope in 1080], duke of Calabria and Apulia, a sworn soldier of the Lord Pope, in revenge for that same king [Col. 0112A] . . . .

But Henry spent the money he received not on an expedition against Robert, as he had promised by oath, but on winning over the Roman populace. With its assistance, on the Thursday before Palm Sunday, he entered the Lateran palace with his Ravennate, Guibert.

The Roman nobles, with very few exceptions, remained with Pope Gregory. They gave him forty hostages, while the Pope withdrew into the castle of Sant’Angelo and secured control of all the bridges over the Tiber and the stronger Roman fortifications.

On the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, Henry received from his Ravennate heresiarch a crown not of glory but of disgrace . . . .

For Guibert himself had been archbishop of Ravenna and had sworn complete obedience to the Roman Pontiff [Col. 0112B], but at no time faithfully carried it out. Not long afterward, despising his oath, he rose up in singular contumacy against the Apostolic See. Therefore, after the canonical delays had been observed, he was irrecoverably deposed and anathematized by the Apostolic See and by the bishops of the whole Church in a Roman synod—not once and not in a single synod, but in every synod held at Rome over six years . . . .

Therefore it is not doubted that Henry, crowned by this same man, inherited his condemnation; and likewise all who usurped as though received from the aforesaid heresiarch anything that ought to have been received from the Lord Pope.

Henry was staying in the Lateran palace with his Ravennate and was not allowed by the Pope’s faithful to cross the city to Saint Peter’s [Col. 0112C]. During that very Easter week he attacked the faithful. In the engagement he lost nearly forty men, dead or wounded, for the rest fled; on the side of the Lord Pope not a single man fell.

18. Robert Guiscard, duke of the Normans, invaded Rome with an armed force after the Kalends of May in the service of Saint Peter. Having driven Henry away, he completely stripped the whole city, which had rebelled against Pope Gregory, and consumed most of it with fire [Col. 0111D: Leo of Ostia gives this account of the cause of the fire in book III, chapter 53: “At the advice,” he says, “of Cincius, consul of the Romans, he set fire to the city. The Romans, struck by the unexpected event and intent on extinguishing the fire, while they were occupied in this task, the Duke immediately hastened with his army to the fortress of Sant’Angelo, drew the Pontiff out from there, and without delay departed from Rome. He led Pope Gregory as far as this monastery and supported the Apostolicus until his death, together with the bishops and cardinals who had followed him”]. This occurred because the Romans wounded one of Robert’s soldiers.

Afterward, having received hostages from the Romans and placed them in the castle of Sant’Angelo, which they call the house of Theodoric, Robert returned to recover Saint Peter’s territory and soon recovered many fortresses and cities for the Lord Pope [Col. 0112D].

Henry, unable to resist Robert, returned to the German lands with considerable haste . . . .

The Lord Pope, having convened a synod, again promulgated a sentence of anathema against the heresiarch Guibert, Henry, and all their supporters. He had also done this some time earlier at Rome on the preceding feast of Saint John the Baptist, while Henry was still there.

The legates of the Apostolic See—Peter, bishop of Albano, in Francia, and Otto, bishop of Ostia, in the German lands—proclaimed this sentence everywhere [Col. 0113A].

While staying in Alemannia, the bishop of Ostia also ordained a Catholic pastor for the holy Church of Constance, which had long been widowed: Gebehard, son of Duke Berthold. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of January he consecrated him bishop; on the preceding day, that is, on the feast of Saint Thomas, he had made him a priest together with other clerics. Among these he ordained the author of these chronicles to the priesthood in the same solemnity and granted him, by Apostolic authority, the power to receive penitents . . . .

19. In the year 1085, almighty God, unwilling to let his servant Pope Gregory labor any longer and wishing instead to reward him worthily for his labors, called him from the prison-house of this life. After suffering serious bodily illness for some time, but remaining utterly steadfast in defending justice until death, he closed his final day at Salerno.

All the devout of both sexes, and especially the poor, grieved at his death. For he was a most fervent teacher of the Catholic religion and a most vigorous defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He certainly did not wish the ecclesiastical order to lie subject to the hands of laymen; rather, by the holiness of its morals and the dignity of its order, he wished it to stand above them.

This will be evident to anyone who carefully reads the Register of that Apostolicus. After he had lawfully contended for twelve years and one month in governing the Apostolic See—indeed, the whole Church—he was finally taken from this light in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. There is no doubt that he received the *βραβεῖον*—the prize or reward—of the heavenly calling. He was buried at Salerno in the church of Saint Matthew, which he himself dedicated in that same year.

## II. FROM THE MANUSCRIPT CENSUS-BOOK OF CINCIUS THE CHAMBERLAIN, LATER HONORIUS III, COLLATIONED WITH THE MANUSCRIPT OF CARDINAL NICHOLAS OF ARAGON

[Col. 0113C: Nicholas Rosellus, taken from the Order of Preachers and called “of Aragon” because, being from Tarragona, he remained almost continually at the court of Peter, king of Aragon. He places this title before the work: “Concerning Pope Gregory VII, who began in the year of the Lord 1703, during the reign of the Emperor Henry III of this name.”]

[Col. 0113]

## CHAPTER ONE. The Election of Gregory; the Machinations of Cincius the Roman and Guibert of Ravenna Punished; Henry’s Insolence in Proceeding toward the Deposition of the Pontiff Chastised

[Col. 0113B]

1. Gregory VII, a Tuscan by nation and from Suana by homeland, from the town of Ronaco [Col. 0113B: Nicholas has “Ronaco”; our manuscript has “Raonaco.” It must have been an insignificant town in the diocese of Suana, whose name today is not even found on topographical maps. This provides no small prejudice against the nobility attributed to him from the Petilian and Suanan counts [Col. 0114C], though it does not decisively exclude it. Below we shall cite from our manuscript something that, conversely, might affirm it], son of Bonitus, sat for twelve years, one month, and four days.

After Pope Alexander died and was honorably buried in the Lateran church, while the archdeacon Hildebrand was still occupied with his funeral rites, suddenly a great gathering of the Roman clergy and people formed in that very church, shouting and saying, “Blessed Peter has chosen Hildebrand the archdeacon.”

When the archdeacon heard this, he was terrified and, as though beside himself, ran to the pulpit, wishing to calm the very people who were roaring and turn them away from their purpose [Col. 0114C: Nicholas has “frequently”]. But when Cardinal Hugh Candidus realized beyond doubt that everyone’s votes had converged upon the same archdeacon, he hurried to the people and addressed them in these words:

“Behold, dearest brothers, you know and recognize beyond doubt that from the days of Blessed Pope Leo this archdeacon, as a prudent and proven man, has greatly exalted this holy Roman Church and delivered this city from impending dangers. Therefore, since we cannot find anyone more suitable for the governance of the Church and the defense of the City, we, the bishops and cardinals, in the name of the Lord, unanimously elect him for ourselves and for you as the pastor and bishop of your souls.”

Immediately, as the whole people and clergy acclaimed him [Col. 0114C: Here ‘immediately’ must be restricted to the people’s acclamation alone, if it is true that he remained hidden for several days, as Berthold relates], Saint Peter chose Lord Gregory as Pope. He was clothed in a red cloak, as is customary, and adorned with the papal mitre [Col. 0114C: Elsewhere I knew that the purple was immediately placed upon the elected man; concerning the mitre, see it described in the *Acts of Saint Peter Celestine*, written by Cardinal of Saint George, book III, volume 165]. Against his will and in grief, he was enthroned in the chair of Saint Peter.

2. The next day, considering anxiously within himself how grave a danger he had entered, he began to burn with distress and grieve exceedingly. But when he found no other excuse for relinquishing the papacy, he quickly sent messengers to King Henry. Through them he disclosed to Henry that he had been elected and earnestly begged him not to give his assent. If Henry did not do so, it would be certain to him that Gregory would by no means leave Henry’s graver and manifest offenses unpunished.

When the king learned the truth of the election, he gave his assent to it. He immediately sent Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the Italian kingdom, to the City, so that by royal authority he might confirm the election and take part in Gregory’s consecration.

This was done without delay. For Gregory was ordained priest within the octave of Pentecost and consecrated Roman Pontiff on the feast of the Apostles.

Having thus received the fullness of Apostolic dignity, he kindly and fatherly admonished the same king to show himself a devoted and subject son to his mother, the holy Roman Church, and to cease entirely from selling bishoprics and churches. To pursue this pious work effectively, he endeavored to send Henry’s mother, Agnes the empress [Col. 0115C: Concerning her, a Saxon manuscript chronicle extending almost to the end of the twelfth century says: “In the year of the Lord 1609, Agnes the empress, mother of King H., afflicted with weariness, or rather pierced by God, laid down the duchy of Bavaria; and, utterly despising the governance of the kingdom for Christ’s sake, she withdrew to Rome. There, serving God with remarkable humility through worthy fruits of penance, she departed in the Lord after some years,” namely in 1077, as is clear from her epitaph in Baronius. From the labor of this legation undertaken for the Apostolic See, understand how devoted she was to it. The event itself is assigned to the year 1074], together with Gerard, bishop of Ostia; Hubert, bishop of Praeneste; and R., bishop of Como [Col. 0115D: Of the Church of Como, which became extinct before the end of the thirteenth century, Ughelli in volume VI of *Italia sacra* could name scarcely six bishops. Here you have one to add to them for the year 1074. I think R. was Roger, Robert, Roland, or something similar; it was easy to supply from other names the deficiency caused by Cincius’s practice of writing names only by their initial letter].

Having undertaken the same pontiff’s legation, they crossed into Bavaria and together approached the king. The king received the legates affectionately and treated them with due honor. For many days he listened meekly and patiently to words of holy admonition concerning his correction. Yet he scarcely removed from his companionship and association five of his familiar nobles, who had been excommunicated by Pope Alexander.

He did not permit the legates to celebrate a synod in that region, alleging that through Bishop Leimar of Bremen [Col. 0115D: Albert of Stade calls him “Leimar of Bavaria” and says that Albert succeeded him in 1077, occupied the see for thirty years, and died in 1101, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, after which Humbert succeeded him. We later read that his excommunication was confirmed at a synod held at Rome in 1075] the Roman Pontiff’s powers had been granted to the archbishop of Mainz in Germany, as contained in the ancient privileges of his church.

The legates of the Apostolic See replied to him as follows:

“Concerning the office of legation, Venerable Brother, you must be certain that neither canonical authority nor ecclesiastical custom provides that it should extend beyond the death of the one who granted it. Moreover, as is contained in a certain chapter of Pope Leo I [Col. 0116A; 0116C: I have not yet found this chapter], the Roman Pontiff entrusts his powers to bishops in such a way that they are called to share his solicitude, not the fullness of his power.”

But, to bring this controversy briefly to an end, when the synod had been disrupted by this stratagem and the same bishop of Bremen had been suspended from priestly office for disobedience and rebellion, the legates, honored by the king with generous gifts, returned safely to the Roman City with his favor and gracious reply.

### 3.

After a few days had passed, Hermann, Bishop of Bamberg, who had come to Rome to receive the pallium, was convicted of simony in the presence of Pope Gregory and incurred deposition from his episcopal and priestly office; another was appointed in his place by the mandate of that same Pontiff. The same thing was done with the Bishop of Constance.

[Note: We have given the bull by which Leo IX granted the pallium to Hartwig of Bamberg, out of consideration for Clement II and Saint Henry the Emperor, who lie buried there, in the *Pontifical Chronology*, where we discuss this Clement; yet, in the Appendix to Leo himself, we admit that it is not altogether genuine. The truth of the event, however, is confirmed by this passage of Cencius.]

[Note: Otto was the bishop concerned here. The *Chronicle of Constance*, published by Pistorious under the year 1070, reports that when Henry ordered him to be ordained he said: “The chapter of Constance did not want a suitable prelate; so let them take this fool Otto as bishop.”]

Meanwhile, Pope Gregory of Rome, suspecting nothing evil concerning King Henry, summoned a general council, at which Guibert of Ravenna sat together with a vast multitude of bishops from various provinces. Moreover, the distinguished Countess Matilda, Marquis Azzo, and Gisulf, Prince of Salerno, were not absent from that council. Among the other acts of the council, the Normans and Robert Guiscard were excommunicated.

[Note: Nicholas passed over Marquis Azzo, who seems to have been present on account of his incestuous marriage with Matilda—not the famous Countess named here, who at that time had Godefrey, Duke of Lorraine, as her husband, although she never shared his bed, but the sister of William, Bishop of Pavia, who was related to Azzo in the fourth degree.]

When the council had been dissolved and the others who had been summoned had returned to their own places, Guibert of Ravenna remained behind with Pope Gregory deceitfully, since he was already aspiring to the papacy. And since it is commonly characteristic of each person to wish to associate with himself others like himself, he sought to make all the criminals and enemies of the Pontiff whom he found in Rome favorable to himself and bound by oath, through gifts or promises. Among them he won over that most wicked man Cencius, son of the Prefect Stephen, whom we mentioned above, as a friend and secretary, and with him wickedly took up arms against his own Father.

[Note: From this it also appears that the *Acts of the preceding Alexander* were written by the same author.]

Among the other evils which he had committed with impunity, Cencius had built a lofty tower above the bridge of Saint Peter and continually extorted from passers-by a new toll.

[Note: Nicholas has *pedagium*; concerning both words, see Du Cange.]

This man, hateful to God and human beings, on the most sacred night of the Nativity of the Lord, sacrilegiously seized Lord Gregory the Pope, the Vicar of Christ, while he was celebrating the solemn Mass, from the altar of the holy Mother of God called “at the Manger”; and with his accomplices he dared to carry him away by force to the aforementioned tower.

At this, the whole Roman populace, enraged at the attack upon its Pontiff, burned fiercely with anger and on that same night strictly besieged him in the same tower. At dawn the Romans utterly destroyed the tower and would have slaughtered the sacrilegious man with terrible violence, had not the blessed Pontiff, a good disciple of the good Master, rescued him from the danger of death.

After this, intending to celebrate with his brothers and the other faithful of the Church the customary banquet, he returned to the Lateran palace. On the second day after Easter, however, the Roman people condemned Cencius, together with all his accomplices, with the forfeiture of his property, and permanently excluded him from the city of Rome.

### 4.

After this, the aforementioned Guibert deceitfully asked Lord Gregory for permission to return to Ravenna, so that he might more conveniently harm the man whom he fraudulently pretended to love. For when he reached Ravenna, setting aside the oath which he had sworn at his consecration to Pope Alexander and his successors, he conspired with Theobald of Milan and other stiff-necked bishops of Lombardy, and secretly fomented sedition against his own Pastor.

As a result, the expedition which the Pontiff had raised from Lombardy through Duke Godefrey, his wife the illustrious Countess Matilda, and other nobles, against the Normans and the other enemies of the Church, was disrupted and broken up to the detriment of the Church.

Through Hugh Candidus he also did everything he could to incite King Henry and Robert Guiscard against that same Pontiff, like an apostate man full of every kind of deceit and wickedness, who had already shown no shame at returning a second time to apostasy.

At the same time, around the middle of Lent, Lord Gregory held a council. Since the aforementioned Guibert had contemptuously refused to come when summoned, the council suspended him from episcopal office as a perjurer. It also permanently separated that same Hugh Candidus from the Church, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Avoid a heretical man after the first and second admonition” (Titus 3:10).

But while these things were happening in Italy, the Saxons rebelled vigorously against King Henry, specifically because he was striving to impose an unbearable burden upon them. Accordingly, the King entered Saxony unexpectedly with a strong force and a great multitude. Since he attacked them unprepared, he won a victory, though an exceedingly bloody one.

For, as prudent men said, five thousand men on the King’s side fell in that battle. Nevertheless, because he was unable to subjugate those same Saxons, the King returned to Franconia.

[Note: Here *Francia* is repeatedly used for Franconia, taking the name in a broader sense so as also to include the neighboring region.]

Immediately, after summoning a vast multitude of bishops, he did not give thanks to God for the victory he had gained. Instead, his heart was lifted up, and, exalting himself excessively above himself, he rushed into such boldness and madness that, at the counsel of the wicked, he dared to depose his Father, Pope Gregory, who had held the Apostolic See peacefully for three years, and did everything in his power to drive him from the Church.

[Note: Nicholas less correctly has “for the victors.”]

He also firmly decreed and established that no bishop, abbot, duke, or other person of rank should thereafter obey Gregory in any way as Pope.

### 5.

In order to carry out this pernicious decision effectively, he sent to Rome a certain Roland of Parma, a detestable cleric, and other execrable men, with letters of his own, so that they might pursue the matter energetically and fearlessly.

Having accepted this wicked embassy, they proceeded as far as the City. When they came to the Pontiff, who was then seated in council, they first presented the King’s letters and then, through Roland himself, spoke with excessive arrogance and insolence in these words:

“Our lord King Henry has sent us, on the advice of his bishops and princes, to make publicly known to you and vigorously pursue those things which he has recently judged concerning the state of the Church and irrevocably decreed. Therefore we command—and, by the authority of the King, commanding, we order—you, Gregory, to descend from the Apostolic See without delay, and henceforth, as you value your life, to have nothing whatsoever to do with the papacy.

“We likewise enjoin upon you bishops and cardinals to hasten to receive a Pontiff in the presence of that same King.”

When these blasphemies had been heard, the whole council blazed with such vehement anger against that reviler of the Pontiff that, had the pious gentleness of the blessed Pope Gregory not intervened, the Church’s faithful would have killed him with stones.

On the following day, letters from the bishops beyond the Alps were brought to the Pontiff. In them they confessed that they had erred and sinned grievously; they also requested pardon and firmly promised that thereafter they would observe complete obedience to him.

When the tumult had scarcely been calmed, the synodal proceedings continued peacefully. But when the time had come to conclude the council, the Pontiff, after taking more beneficial counsel with one hundred and ten bishops, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against that same King, who had attempted to divide the unity of the Church, and ordered that the sentence be firmly maintained until he had rendered appropriate satisfaction.

No one should judge this either reprehensible or unprecedented, since it in no way differed from the decrees of the holy Fathers, and since the same thing is found to have been done by several Roman Pontiffs even for lesser causes.

### 6.

[Note: In the first session about 360 are named, nor can any more be found thereafter. That synod was held in 451; Anatolius, subscribing to the case of the condemned Dioscorus, states that he had proved disobedient to all the rules of the holy Fathers and, though canonically summoned a third time, had refused to comply.]

Thus, in the Council of Chalcedon, with six hundred bishops present, we read the following concerning Dioscorus of Alexandria:

“Since, in his prior excess, he had greatly surpassed wickedness—for he had presumed to dictate a sentence of excommunication against the most holy Pope Leo—Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, said: ‘Dioscorus is not to be condemned on account of the faith, but because he excommunicated the Lord Archbishop Leo.’”

Is there any indication there that an inquiry was made whether Dioscorus had been excommunicated justly or unjustly? Certainly not. It was because, although he was inferior, he had attempted to assail his superior with every kind of insult.

Likewise, in the Eighth Council, among other things, we read:

“We have decreed that no worldly potentate at all should dishonor any of those who preside over the patriarchal sees or expel them from their own throne, but that they should be judged worthy of every honor and reverence—especially the most holy Pope of elder Rome. Nor should anyone compose or contrive accusations and words against the Roman Pontiff, as though he were a slanderer of certain crimes, as Photius recently and Dioscorus long ago did.

“But whoever should use such boastfulness and boldness that, following the example of Photius and Dioscorus, he should raise, in writing or without writing, any insults against the First See of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, shall receive the same and equal condemnation as they did.”

[Note: In the Council of Chalcedon of 870, Act 10, Canon 13, it reads as follows: “If anyone should be carried away by such boldness as Photius and Dioscorus, and should dare to utter, in writing or without writing, certain ravings against the Chair of Peter, the Coryphaeus of the Apostles, let him undergo the same sentence of condemnation as they did.” I do not know where the rest of the material cited here, whether the following or the preceding passages, may be found.]

“But if anyone, enjoying or possessing some power from God, should attempt to expel the aforementioned Pope of the Apostolic Chair, or any other of the patriarchs, let him be anathema.”

Moreover, it is most well known and beyond dispute that many Roman Pontiffs, even for lesser causes, not only excommunicated certain emperors and kings but also deposed them from their kingdoms and appointed others in their places.

Indeed, Pope Innocent excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius, son of the great Theodosius, because he had taken part in the deposition of John Chrysostom, which Theophilus of Alexandria, together with the other Eastern patriarchs and with the agreement of the other bishops but without the consent of the Roman Pontiff, had decreed. Innocent also annulled their deposition. When the most merciful Emperor learned what had happened, he did not rebel but humbly asked for and obtained pardon.

Pope Constantine excommunicated the Emperor Justinian, son of Constantine, because he had not received his legates with due honor. Later, the Emperor prostrated himself at the Pope’s feet in the streets of Constantinople, together with his crown, and sought pardon until he obtained it.

[Note: Nicholas is correct here. In Cencius’s book it is incorrectly written “Justinus, son of Constantine,” although there was no such person, much less one living in the time of Pope Constantine. We know that in the year 710 Justinian Rhinotmetus summoned Constantine from Rome to Constantinople and received him with the humility described here. Baronius thinks that the reason for this summons was none other than to bring to an end the controversy over the canons added to the Fifth and Sixth Councils.]

Pope Anastasius excommunicated the Emperor Anastasius, who, after speaking arrogantly about the Pope, was struck by lightning and died in the very palace.

[Note: This was Anastasius II. He did indeed write a letter of admonition to the Emperor Anastasius; see Baronius under the year 497. But the Pope who excommunicated him was Symmachus, as can be found in the same Baronius under the year 502, no. 29.]

Gregory III not only excommunicated the Emperor Leo but also deprived him of his kingdom.

[Note: Gregory III bound Leo the Isaurian and all the Iconoclasts with an anathema, says Zonaras, and halted the taxes which until that time had been paid from Italy to the Empire. He did this after entering into an alliance with the Franks, as may be seen in Baronius under the year 726, no. 24, abandoning obedience to the Emperor because of his perverse opinion.

Thus, when Otto of Freising says, “I read and reread the deeds of the Roman kings and emperors, and nowhere do I find any of them, before this man—Henry—either excommunicated by the Roman Pontiff or deprived of his kingdom,” he shows that he is speaking of those who ruled in the West, not of the Greek emperors, several of whom were certainly struck with anathema on account of heresy.]

Pope Stephen deposed Charles, the brother of King Pepin, from the kingdom and substituted Pepin in his place.

[Note: Nicholas knew that Charles, or rather Carloman, the brother of Pepin, had become a monk at Monte Cassino long before Pope Stephen existed. He substituted the name of Pope Zacharias here and the name of King Childeric, intending, I believe, that Chilperic, the last of the Merovingian kings, should be understood; some say that Zacharias consented to his deposition.

As for Carloman, we know from Anastasius the Librarian that, although he was already a monk and had been sent into Francia by Aistulf, King of the Lombards, to his brother in order to turn him away from giving assistance to the Pope—and was earnestly pursuing this mission, having been badly persuaded—King Pepin and Pope Stephen, by common agreement, placed him in a monastery there in Francia, in accordance with his vow to live a monastic life. This may have given Cencius an opportunity to hallucinate, as though he had read there of some deposition of Carloman carried out by the King.]

Pope Nicholas likewise excommunicated two emperors at one and the same time: namely, Michael of the East, because he had expelled Ignatius, Bishop of Constantinople, from his see without a judgment of the Pope; and Lothair of the West, because of his relationship with Waldrada, his concubine.

[Note: Here Lothair the King—whence the kingdom of Lothair, later called Lorraine—is confused with his relative, the Emperor Lothair. Excommunication was often threatened against the former and was personally pronounced against Waldrada; nevertheless, he avoided it through feigned repentance. Similarly, Pope Nicholas went no further than threats against Michael Balbus. Nicholas died in the year 867.]

The blessed Ambrose also—not a Roman but a Milanese Pontiff—excommunicated Maximus the Tyrant and the Emperor Theodosius, both driven from the Church; this is beyond doubt.

Who, then, unless he is bereft of reason, is unaware that royal power is subject to the pontiffs? And who would believe himself exempt from subjection to the Roman Pontiff except one who, because of his sins, has not deserved to be numbered among Christ’s sheep?

But let us now continue the sequence of events which we began.

## CHAPTER II  
### Henry’s Obstinacy, the Election of Rudolf, and Gregory’s Unsuccessful Efforts for Peace

### 7.

Meanwhile, when news of the King’s ban resounded in the ears of the people, the whole Roman world, terrified by extraordinary fear, was shaken to no small degree. For the Italian prelates and the bishops of the Teutonic kingdom divided themselves into factions over so great a disagreement. At Guibert’s instigation, the contumacious bishops of Lombardy gathered together at Pavia after Easter. There, imitating Photius and Dioscorus, they dared, under diabolical inspiration, to excommunicate the Lord Pope of elder Rome with sacrilegious lips.

When the princes of the kingdom took note of this act, they began to doubt considerably whether they ought to disregard the excommunication or reverently observe it, especially since their law contained the provision that, if someone were not absolved from the bond of excommunication within a year and a day, he would lose every honor of rank.

Accordingly, prudent bishops gave them the following answer for their consolation: according to the statutes and examples of the holy Fathers, the Roman Pontiff can in no way be judged or excommunicated by anyone.

Therefore, since they could find nothing better suited to the malice of the present time, those princes, together with the Dukes Rudolf, Welf, and Theoderic, and other leading men of the kingdom, confirmed by oath that, if the King were willing to accept their counsel, they would effectively employ their efforts so that Pope Gregory might come beyond the mountains and absolve him from the bond of excommunication.

After this, the King himself swore with his own lips that, upon the arrival of the Pontiff, he would obey his command without any evil design. The princes then swore again in these terms: if the King kept what he had sworn, they would proceed with him in force to the city of Rome; and, having received the dignity of the imperial crown from Lord Pope Gregory, they would descend with an army into Apulia and Calabria against the Normans, who were then hostile to the Apostolic See, and, after expelling the Normans, restore that land to blessed Peter and the Roman Church.

But if the King refused to do this, from that moment they were no longer to regard him either as King or as Lord.

When these matters had been duly completed and confirmed by oath, they sent the Archbishop of Trier to Rome, so that he might make known to the bishops and cardinals what they had established concerning the pacification of the disagreement between Church and Empire, and for this purpose safely escort the Roman Pontiff as far as the city of Augsburg.

But, because the Archbishop himself was deceitfully captured at Piacenza through the King’s veiled stratagem and was later released only with difficulty, we omit writing about it because of the length of the history.

[Note: Udo—called Ado by some—was Archbishop of Trier from 1067 to 1078. Browerus mentions this embassy in the *Annals of Trier* under the year 1077, no. 57, but was unaware of the injury inflicted upon Udo on that occasion.]

### 8.

When the venerable Pope Gregory heard the embassy of so many princes, although the harshest winter was approaching, he undertook the difficulty of the journey with that same Archbishop, lest the great good hoped for from peace should be lost through his negligence, and proceeded as far as Vercelli.

While he suspected nothing sinister concerning the King’s promise, news suddenly rang out that the King himself had already crossed the Alps at the swiftest possible pace and was hastening toward the Pontiff in a hostile manner.

When the Bishop of Vercelli learned of this unexpected deed, although he was regarded as the King’s chancellor, he nevertheless faithfully disclosed the truth of the matter to the Pontiff.

When the Pontiff heard and verified this, he immediately turned the reins and hastened without delay to the safest castle of the Countess Matilda, that most devoted daughter of blessed Peter, called Canossa, and took refuge there in safety with his brothers.

The King, conscious of the perjury he had committed, learned that his guilt had unquestionably been made public. He laid aside his ferocity and, like a cunning fox, put on dove-like simplicity. He did not cease following the Pontiff as far as the castle itself, so that he might merit absolution. There he stood for several days upon snow and ice with bare feet and earnestly begged for the grace of absolution.

After many disputes and various counsels, after satisfaction had been made and the grace of absolution granted, the same Pontiff, during the solemn celebration of Mass, handed the King the Host of Christ and said:

“If you approach with a good heart and intend to observe what you profess with your mouth, may this sacred Body be for you, as it was for the Apostles, unto salvation. Otherwise, you will receive it unworthily, as Judas did, and without doubt you will eat judgment unto yourself.”

He immediately received him to the kiss of peace and, after Mass, ate with him in fatherly charity. He also had those who had come with the King and were excommunicated absolved, and dismissed them all in peace.

### 9.

When the cycle of the present year had run its course, although the King appeared outwardly devoted and obedient to the Pontiff, in heart and deed—as the outcome of events later showed—he was opposed to him and remained constantly active in plotting against him.

At night he spoke familiarly with Guibert and with the Roman Cencius, that most wicked man whom we mentioned above, and with other enemies of the Church, and he gave his support to their wicked counsels.

But when he saw that Pope Gregory could in no way be dislodged from the fortress of Canossa, he went to Pavia to remain there, where he found that same Cencius dead by a most wretched death. Guibert and the other excommunicated men celebrated his execrable funeral with pomp and lamentation.

At the same time, while King Henry was staying in the regions of Italy, the princes of the kingdom gathered together at Forchheim and unanimously elected for themselves Rudolf, an outstanding duke, as king—a man of great counsel, frequently tested in arms, and exceedingly distinguished.

When King Henry heard this, he was greatly disturbed and burned fiercely with anger. Nevertheless, as a crafty and shrewd man, he earnestly entreated Lord Pope Gregory through his messengers, suavely and humbly, to subject that same Rudolf to excommunication at once.

After taking counsel, the Pontiff replied that he would gladly do this if Rudolf, summoned by him, refused to give an account of his action. For it did not seem just or reasonable that he should be punished with the sword of excommunication before he had been summoned to appear.

Because of this reply, Henry conceived the greatest indignation against the Pontiff. But since very serious affairs pressed upon him, he set this matter aside and hastened with a strong force into Franconia and Bavaria against Rudolf. Rudolf, for his part, confident in the justice of his cause, advanced with the greatest eagerness toward the armed conflict.

What more is there to say? A horrible battle was fought fiercely on both sides, and many thousands of men were slain here and there; but it is not known with certainty which of them prevailed.

### 10.

After this, Lord Gregory returned honorably to the city of Rome. He immediately summoned a council, at which envoys of both kings were present. The Pontiff strictly commanded them that the kings themselves should not dare to fight before the arrival of their legates, but that the bishops of both parties should find a suitable place where each side could safely present its case before those legates.

Although this statement pleased the envoys themselves, it was disrupted through the interference of the enemy of the human race; and, because their sins demanded it, the same kings again fought one another horribly, in a battle where a very great multitude of brave men fell.

When this reached the ears of the supreme Pontiff, he lamented deeply over so great a slaughter. Yet, out of pious devotion, he was unwilling to abandon an undertaking which had already begun, and therefore summoned the council again for the following Lent.

The envoys of both parties came to it and swore with their own lips that the conference established by the Apostolic See had in no way been disrupted through the fault of the kings themselves.

Accordingly, after deliberation, the Pontiff resolved to send to those regions the venerable bishops Peter of Albano and Odalric of Padua, together with the Patriarch of Aquileia, in order to suppress the evil of so great a disagreement.

[Note: This was Saint Peter Igneus, of the Order of Vallombrosa, created Cardinal-Bishop of Albano in the year 1074.]

[Note: Ughellus calls him Uldaric. He governed the church of Padua until the year 1090 and had been made bishop not long before this embassy.]

[Note: Henry, appointed after the wretched death of the schismatic Siegfried, in this same year 1077, is called Sigehard by others. Ughellus does not distinguish Siegfried from Sigehard.]

He instructed them to prohibit the same kings from engaging in battle and, after summoning a council, to order bishops and religious men to come into their presence.

Having received this mandate, they crossed over to the King in Bavaria and presented to him the counsel and will of his Father, the Pontiff. But they were entirely unable to bring him to permit a council to be held in his kingdom unless they first bound King Rudolf, without citation, confession, or conviction, with the bond of excommunication.

Because the legates did not dare to do this, they grieved that their labor was to remain fruitless and returned to the city with the matter unfinished.

Again, the same kings fought one another fiercely, and many thousands of men, especially Bohemians, were slain.

Meanwhile, the venerable Pontiff, having received envoys from Robert Guiscard, the distinguished Duke of the Normans, set out toward Apulia after the octave of Pentecost and held a conference with him at Aquino.

After receiving from him appropriate satisfaction, he first absolved him from the bond of excommunication and then received his fidelity and homage. Afterwards, having received him as a special knight of blessed Peter, he invested him, by the banner of the Apostolic See, with the duchy of all Apulia and Calabria.

## CHAPTER III  
### The Promotion of Guibert the Antipope, Henry’s Flight from the City, and Gregory’s Death

### 11.

At the same time, King Henry, lifted up in great pride, sent the aforementioned Leimar of Bremen and Hermann, Bishop of Bamberg, stiff-necked men, to the city of Rome. Through them he issued an extremely insolent command to Pope Gregory, as though he possessed authority over him, that he should not delay in any way in excommunicating Rudolf, who opposed him.

If he did not do so, he himself would acquire a pope for himself who would restrain the insolence of his enemy by ecclesiastical censure.

[Note: Cencius: “the papacy.”]

The venerable Pope, who was prepared to shed his own blood for justice, looked not to the insolent words of the proud King but to the commands of the eternal Judge. He absolutely refused to anathematize the aforesaid Rudolf, who claimed a just cause, as he ought not to do.

But because that same King had been repeatedly admonished and did not repent of his excesses, and because he had not allowed the legates of the Apostolic See to hold a council in the land under his rule, the Pontiff subjected him once more to excommunication as a disobedient and rebellious man.

When these things had been carried out, the legates returned indignantly to the King’s presence, and, as men hateful to God, stirred his mind even more urgently toward worse things.

When the King realized that, by sentence of the Roman Pontiff, he had been separated from the fellowship of the faithful, he became sad. But since different people offered him different counsel, he was placed in anxious uncertainty and did not know what he should choose above all.

At last, when the judgment of the perverse prelates and impious princes had prevailed, he resolved to hold a general assembly at Brixia.

Many seditious and infamous bishops therefore gathered at that place, together with a multitude of clerics and princes, so that they might arrange or decree something harmful to Lord Pope Gregory and establish discord between the Roman Church and the Empire for future times.

After communicating their execrable and detestable plan, with the consent of the King himself they elected Guibert of Ravenna as Roman Pontiff—or rather, as Antipope—a man manifestly perjured and full of every kind of wickedness and deceit.

And since it often happens that sin becomes the punishment of sin, from the root of pride he proceeded to perjury, from perjury to disobedience, from disobedience he fell into excommunication, and from excommunication he arrived at idolatry.

As we have said, King Henry prostrated himself upon the ground and worshiped this man. He is also said to have sworn, at the urging of Dionysius, Bishop of Piacenza, that he would receive from him the imperial crown.

What more is there to say? Thus, because their sins demanded it, all who were present were blinded in mind. Instead of looking toward heaven, they all bowed down together—alas, shame and grief!—to kiss his feet.

When these matters had been completed, the King, having fallen into open heresy, returned to his own lands during the Octave of the Apostles. Guibert, however, the heresiarch, adorned with the papal insignia, entered Italy pompously with his accomplices.

### 12.

At the same time, that same King, with the greatest power and a strong force, entered Saxony insolently in order to engage in battle with King Rudolf. Rudolf met him powerfully from the opposite direction. When a most atrocious engagement had taken place on both sides, Henry shamefully turned his back and, pursued fiercely by the enemy for a long distance, already despairing of his life, withdrew into a certain fortress, where he hid for seven days.

Rudolf, however, as a very brave and renowned man, tested in the practice of arms, did not flee at all but fell as victor and triumphator, because his own men, not recognizing him, had mortally wounded him.

[Note: Others report Rudolf’s death very differently. Some maintain that he was pierced by the imperial standard-bearer—whom they believe to have been Godefrey of Bouillon—and that another man who came upon him cut off his right hand. Concerning the hand, Abbot of Ursperg and the author of the *Life of Henry* both explicitly speak in such a way as to say that this was vengeance for his failure to keep faith with Henry. The Ursperg author even says that Rudolf himself acknowledged this at his death. Since these accounts were written by Henry’s partisans, one may rightly doubt whether they deserve belief; likewise, the accounts written against him by defenders of the better side are by no means certain in every respect.]

When his companions had searched for him for a long time, he was finally found lying above the slaughter and corpses of his enemies, amid the greatest lamentation.

When his death was reported to Henry, who was hiding and considering flight, he immediately raised his horn on high and began to speak insolently against Lord Pope Gregory, uttering insults and threats, believing that his detestable deeds had pleased the Lord because of Rudolf’s death.

After these events, a few days later, Henry’s son fought with the army of the illustrious Countess Matilda. Since, as commonly happens, the outcome of war is uncertain, he won the victory.

Provoked by these successes, he suddenly entered Italy. After Easter, coming to Rome with the idol he had set up, he pitched his camp around Pentecost in Nero’s meadow.

But who among so many prudent men could fail to marvel at the open madness and shameless folly of the King and the heresiarch Guibert? Although they had lost the eyes of their minds, they had not lost their bodily sight. Did they not see how honorably the Romans received and venerated that beast whom they were leading?

Instead of praises they offered insults; instead of songs, howlings; instead of candles, spears; instead of gatherings of clerics, armed men.

To summarize much in a few words: after the devastation of the fields and the many massacres of their fellow citizens, after the various disasters and miseries which the Romans endured because they had refused to receive the Pseudo-Pope, the King, deprived of the hope and desire he had conceived and confounded in his shame, returned to Lombardy with his idol, while Lord Pope Gregory remained undaunted in the Apostolic See.

13. In the second year he returned to the City by way of the Duchy of Spoleto and besieged Rome itself with great hostility throughout the entire Lenten season. When the Paschal season arrived, in order to avoid the summer heat, he dispersed his army among the surrounding cities and himself hastened to return to Lombardy with a few men [Col. 0126C]. He left Guibert at Tibur and placed him in command of his army. Guibert, setting aside his priesthood, spent the oppressive summer ravaging the fields and crops of the Romans and inflicted other evils upon those same Romans in a hostile manner, like a man of blood.

Thus, in the third year also, the same King returned to besiege Rome. But when he learned that he was certainly regarded as excommunicated by the Abbot of Cluny and by other religious men who feared God, he resorted to cunning arguments, so that he might more effectively circumvent their simplicity.

[Note: [Col. 0126D] St. Lugo of Cluny was the abbot referred to here. We have shown, in § 2 before the Acts of St. Hugh, 29 April, how Henry, pretending repentance, sought his favor through suppliant letters, especially when he began to experience opposition from his son. At that time he was in Italy and visited the monastery of Monte Cassino, as Baronius reports under the year 1083, no. 16.]

Accordingly, after the capture of the Bishop of Ostia and many others, whom he ordered to be released, he gave a firm guarantee of safety to all who wished to visit Rome and publicly confirmed it by oath. Moreover, in order to secure completely the favor and goodwill of the people, he declared in public that he wished to receive from Pope Gregory the dignity of the imperial crown.

When the Roman people and the religious men heard this, they were all greatly rejoiced [Col. 0127A]. They approached the Pontiff’s feet with tears and earnestly implored him to take pity on their almost ruined homeland and to grieve for it with fatherly clemency.

The Pontiff, who, in order to defend justice and ecclesiastical liberty, was fully prepared to suffer death if a reasonable cause required it, replied firmly in these words:

“I have often experienced the King’s evasions and cunning. But if he wishes to make satisfaction to God and the Church for those matters in which he has manifestly sinned, I shall gladly absolve him and place the imperial crown upon him with a blessing. Otherwise, I neither ought nor can hear you in this matter in any way.”

14. When the King, with his conscience reproaching him, refused to do this, and the people for several days vehemently pressed the Pontiff to receive the King without satisfaction [Col. 0127B], while the Pontiff remained completely unmoved by their blind entreaties, the King gradually began to purchase the people’s favor with money and intimidation.

As soon as the Pontiff clearly recognized this, and having entirely lost confidence in the people’s steadfastness, he withdrew with his brothers to the fortress of Crescentius. Since the King had undoubtedly drawn the Roman people to his will, he forcibly intruded Guibert into the Apostolic See.

But since he could obtain no bishop or cardinal from the Roman Church, he had him execrably “blessed,” according to the custom of the Roman Pontiffs, by the pseudo-bishops of Bologna, Modena, and Cervia [Col. 0127D]. On the feast of Easter he shamelessly received from that same Hubert the crown of the Empire. Shortly afterward he led all the Romans to besiege the fortress of Crescentius.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] It was anciently the Mausoleum of Hadrian, then began to be called St. Angelo under Gregory I, and, after fortifications were added, the Castle. In 985 it long retained the name of Crescentius Numentanus, who later strengthened it with new works, and apparently still bore it in this period. Ospergensis calls it the Castle of Crescentius, commonly called the House of Theodoric.]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] These were Sigefridus of Bologna and Heribertus of Modena. The name of the bishop of Cervia is unknown, since the succession of its bishops fails from the year 1069, when a certain Bonus is known to have lived; perhaps he survived until this time. Blondus substitutes the bishop of Treviso for the bishop of Cervia; this could have been Accelinus, who presided over that Church in 1082. From these men Guibert received not a consecration but his execration, on Palm Sunday in the year 1084, namely 24 March; for Easter was celebrated on the 31st of that same month.]

The Pontiff, however, as a prudent and provident man, had long endeavored to solicit Robert Guiscard, the distinguished Duke of the Normans, so that he might come powerfully to his aid with a strong hand against the violence inflicted upon him. He heard that Robert was coming magnificently for his liberation with a very great army.

When King Henry learned this truth, he was terrified. He immediately returned to the church of St. Peter, destroyed the Capitoline house and the Leonine City, bade farewell to the Romans, and fled with the same Guibert, not without great shame.

On the following day, before the King had reached Siena, the aforementioned Duke Robert, like a most powerful lion, violently entered Rome. He captured it with a strong hand in one and the same day—not over three years, as King Henry had done [Col. 0127D]—and, with the merits of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul supporting him, most powerfully liberated the blessed Father and our Lord the Pope from the siege in which he was held.

Having swiftly conquered that venerable city, he possessed it for many days like a glorious victor. He sold many of those treacherous citizens who had lost their Lord and Shepherd; some he mutilated, and some he led captive with him as far as Calabria. But, upon entering the City, he burned the Lateran district as far as the Colosseum with iron and fire.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] The Colosseum, called the Amphitheater by Niccolò, was already known by the name “Coliseum,” which remains in use today, and it bore that name when Anastasius the Librarian wrote. They hold that this was the enormous amphitheater built by Vespasian and Titus beside the Sacred Way, at the place that had borne a name since Nero’s time because of the monstrous colossus, 120 feet high, which Nero had erected for himself.]

After these events, the Duke returned to his own lands and left his father, Pope Gregory, seated in the Lateran palace with his brother bishops and cardinals [Col. 0128B], peacefully conducting, as his office required, the business of the Church arising from the various regions of the world.

15. Here he delivered the church of Blessed Peter from the unlawful occupation of sixty mansionarii, who were forcibly holding all its oratories or chapels and ministries, except the high altar, and were diverting to their own uses all the offerings of those who came to pray.

They were Roman citizens, married men or concubinarians, with shaven beards and wearing mitres. They deceived those who came to pray, especially the multitude of Lombard peasants, claiming that they were cardinal priests. After receiving their offerings, they shamelessly and wickedly granted them indulgence and remission of sins.

Taking the occasion of guarding the church, they would rise in the silence of the dead of night and commit, with impunity, many murders, robberies, various acts of sexual violence, and diverse acts of brigandage within and around that same church. As we have said, the Blessed Pontiff removed them from that church, not without great difficulty, and entrusted and handed over its guardianship to upright clerics and priests.

This truly blessed Pontiff, blessed three and four times over, after remaining for a long time in the City, descended into Apulia. When the aforementioned Duke Robert Guiscard met him, he entered the renowned city of Salerno in glory.

There, while he was giving admonitions concerning salvation to the crowd gathered around him, he suddenly fell onto a bed of illness and, shortly afterward, happily closed his final day in a blessed confession. Over his body, honorably buried in the basilica of Blessed Matthew [Col. 0128D], God in his wonder deigned to perform many miracles.

## III. From Our Manuscript on the Lives of the Pontiffs, Continued up to Martin V

[Col. 0129]

## CHAPTER ONE. Events during the First Five Years of This Pontificate

[Note: [Col. 0129C] A decree of election is prefixed, in the same words as in the Life, no. 21, with this sole variation: there it simply says that the election took place on the day of the burial of Lord Alexander; here, on the third day of the burial. Since it was easier for something to disappear from the original text through the carelessness of copyists than for something to be added, this does not seem a detail to be omitted without reason. I suspect, however, that the original read: “on the third day after his death and on the day of his burial.”]

[Col. 0129A]

This illustrious and beneficent Pontiff, in the third year of his pontificate, on the Night of the Nativity of the Lord, at St. Mary Major at the Crèche, was seized by a certain Cencio son of Stephen while celebrating Mass, at the breaking of the Lord’s Body upon the altar, and was brought to the house of the said Cencio. This house stood in a place called the Parrione.

[Note: [Col. 0129C] Our copy reads Parriam, but it abounds in such errors, having been transcribed with greater elegance than accuracy. Parrione was the name of one of the fourteen districts into which the entire City is divided, and also of the street running from it toward the Bridge of Sant’Angelo. Thus the texts in which it is called the tower at the Bridge of St. Peter can easily be reconciled, since by this route one goes to the Borgo of St. Peter, or the city commonly called the Leonine City.]

But since it was a very solemn day, all the Romans assembled and proceeded to seize the aforementioned house, and they liberated the Lord Pope from so great an outrage.

Once liberated, the Lord Pope returned to the church in which he had been captured, put on the solemn vestments as was customary, and completed the Mass he had begun. Finally, crowned, he returned to the palace with the full praise of the bishops, cardinals, and nobles, and celebrated whatever the customary rites required [Col. 0129B].

Unable to endure so great an outrage, the Romans devastated Cencio’s house together with all its goods and cast it to the ground, against the will of the Lord Pope. But the man who had committed this evil and aforementioned crime escaped from their hands and sought the court of the Teutonic King.

What evil he committed, what falsehoods he fabricated, what discord he created between the Kingdom and the Priesthood, and how, finally, at his instigation, he brought that discord to its conclusion, I shall explain in what follows, as best I can. For now, I shall endeavor to relate, as far as I am able, what the aforementioned Pontiff did during the brief interval in which that man went away, remained absent, and returned [Col. 0130A].

2. In the second year of his pontificate, before this event had occurred, by which the aforementioned malevolent man had obtained an opportunity, the Pope held a council at Rome from the sixth day before the Kalends of March until the second day before the Kalends of that month. In it he separated five members of the household of the King of the Teutons, by whose counsels the churches were being sold, from the thresholds of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Our manuscripts of the Lives of the Pontiffs indeed have “May,” but the Summary of the Acts, copied in the register of the second book or year, has “March,” as Baronius testifies, and rightly so. For this summary, which records the deposition of Dionysius, is contained in Letter 54, issued at Rome on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction. The summary itself is placed immediately after Letter 2, issued at the Synod on the second day before the Kalends of March. Since the following Easter, to which Hermann of Bamberg is cited below, was celebrated on 5 April, it follows that this Synod began approximately on the third day of the first week of Lent, on the feast of St. Matthias. The year of Christ 1074, recorded in the same register, indicates that the Romans were still reckoning their year until the following feast of the Annunciation, according to the usage of the Florentines, as Baronius also noted.]

Thus, if they did not come to Rome from that time until the Kalends of June and make satisfaction, they were to be regarded as excommunicated.

If Philip, King of the Franks, did not provide security to the Pope’s messengers who were going to Gaul concerning satisfaction and correction, he was to be regarded as excommunicated.

He suspended Liemarus, Archbishop of Bremen, from episcopal office because of the disobedience arising from his pride, and barred him from the Body and Blood of the Lord. He suspended Guarnerius of Strasbourg from episcopal and priestly office. He suspended Henry of Speyer. He likewise suspended Hermann of Bamberg if he did not come before Easter to make satisfaction.

In Lombardy also he suspended William of Pavia and Cunibert of Turin. He deposed Dionysius of Piacenza. He excommunicated Robert, Duke of Apulia, already anathematized, and Robert of Loritello, invaders of the possessions of St. Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0130C] Gregory had ordered Rudolf, Bishop of Chalon, by a letter issued at Piperno on the second day before the Nones of December, in the twelfth indiction—nearly three months before this Synod—to admonish Philip, King of France, who had been accused of simony by the clergy of Mâcon.]

3. In the third year, the same Pope held a Synod at Rome in the Basilica of the Savior. In it he suspended Sigefridus, Archbishop of Mainz, who had attempted to sever the bishops and abbots of the Teutonic Kingdom from the holy Roman Church, their special mother, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, from all episcopal office and separated him from communion in the Body and Blood of the Lord—unless, perhaps, the danger of death should overtake him, and only on the condition that, moved to repentance, he should come to his senses. The others who subscribed to his schism by consenting to it he likewise suspended from all episcopal office.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] The fact that this Synod too was held during Lent is suggested by the note of the year 1075, which was still being reckoned until the Annunciation, added by Baronius from the same register, as we believe. In the summaries of the other Synods held under Gregory, I have no doubt that the succession of years was uniformly begun in this way, although Baronius thereafter changed his method and records the years as beginning with the Kalends of January.]

[Note: [Col. 0131D] From the same source I again add what follows.]

He tolerated those who had not consented of their own accord until the feast of St. Peter, out of consideration that, if by that deadline they had not offered suitable satisfaction for their presence, either personally or through their messengers, they would thereafter be deprived of episcopal office.

He suspended from all episcopal office, by the authority of that same blessed Peter, the bishops of Lombardy who, scorning canonical and apostolic authority, had conspired against Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and against the oath sworn to him; and he separated them from communion with the Holy Church.

He excommunicated Berengarius, Bishop of Agde, because he had communicated with the excommunicated Bishop of Narbonne and had performed episcopal functions on his behalf.

He excommunicated Hermann, Bishop of Vienne, justly deposed for simony, perjuries, sacrileges, and apostasy, because he did not cease to trouble the Church of Vienne. He also prohibited divine worship in the Churches of Romans and St. Isidore of Lyons until he had occupied them.

He excommunicated Desiderius and the clergy of the Church of Romans, who had expelled its regular clergy and communicated with excommunicated persons, until they should make satisfaction [Col. 0131C].

He likewise excommunicated the Abbot of St. Giles and the Count of St. Giles because of a female relative; the Count of Forez and Umberto of Beaujeu because of their attacks upon the Church of Lyons; Stephen, the simoniacal and murderous Bishop of Le Puy, who had been excommunicated by his legates; and Pontius of Grenoble, until he should come to his senses.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] A conjunction was missing, and we have supplied it. The passage apparently concerns the Bishop of Le Puy, who at that time was Stephen, and therefore the same man.]

He confirmed what the Bishop of Die had done in the Bishopric of Die concerning tithes, first fruits, and churches, as well as the other measures established during the Apostolic Legation.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The letters of Gregory make frequent mention of the legation entrusted to Hugh of Die throughout Gaul, but all these references are later than this year. It therefore seems that the legation had begun not long before.]

4. He also excommunicated Henry, son of the Emperor Henry, in the same Synod, in the following manner:

“Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, etc.”

[Note: [Col. 0132D] You have already read this same formula in the Life, no. 63; for that reason it is omitted here.]

[Text omitted in the manuscript.]

After the excommunication, certain people repeatedly begged him to make peace with Henry. His response was as follows:

“We wish to have peace with him if he strives to have peace with God. For your fraternity is certainly not ignorant of how long the holy Church has endured the King’s unheard-of depravity and various iniquities—and would that he were a true Christian! [Col. 0132A] And what a gateway to ruin and calamity was opened, with him as its author and the ancient enemy leading the way.
