“Moved by fatherly love and affection for his father and mother, while we were still in the diaconate, we sent him words of the sweetest admonition and made every effort, most earnestly and repeatedly, to recall him through men.”

To those who said that the King could not be excommunicated, he replied:

“When God entrusted his Church three times to Blessed Peter, saying, ‘Feed my sheep,’ did he except kings? When God principally gave Blessed Peter the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, did he except anyone or withdraw anything from his power? For whoever denies that he can be bound by the Church’s bond must consequently deny that he can be absolved by its power. Whoever shamelessly denies this entirely separates himself from Christ” [Col. 0132B].

Now let us say how the aforementioned King, after his excommunication, returned to the obedience of the Lord Pope, and what he did.

5. The King came to the town of Canossa in Lombardy, where the Lord Pope was staying with a few companions. There he remained for three days before the gate of the fortress [lacuna], moving everyone to compassionate mercy [lacuna].

Finally, overcome by the earnestness of his remorse and by the great supplication of all who were present, the Lord Pope received him, after releasing him from the bond of anathema, into the grace of communion and the bosom of Mother Church, having received from him the securities written below [lacuna].

This is the oath of Henry, King of the Teutons:

“I, Henry, King, etc.”

As above in the Life, no. 75.

Done at Canossa on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction [Col. 0132C].

[Note: [Col. 0132D] Thus, in the year 1077. Paulus omitted the date. It is clear that he copied this entire passage word for word from here; therefore, since we do not wish to repeat the same material, we refer the reader there by the marked dots.]

While he remained under excommunication, a certain division arose between King Henry and Rudolf concerning the dignity of kingship. Many loudly claimed that this division had been caused by the Lord Pope. But the aforementioned Pontiff declared that he had in no way offended them [Col. 0132D].

[Note: [Col. 0132D] “Offended,” that is, “incited them to mutual hostility.”]

Indeed, he sent word to both men that they should prepare the way for him, so that he might proceed securely toward defining so great a matter; for he would rather die a thousand times, if possible, than that, because of him, so many thousands of men should be delivered over to death.

6. [Note: [Col. 0132D] The Acts of the Synod in Baronius mark the year 1078, and Book V, Letter 13, shows that it was convened for the first week of the coming Lent, whose Sunday in that year, Easter falling on 8 April, had to fall on 25 February.]

In the fifth year of his pontificate [Col. 0132D], he held a Synod at Rome. Nearly one hundred archbishops and bishops from various cities were present, along with an innumerable multitude of abbots and clerics and laymen of various orders.

By apostolic authority he corrected many things that required correction and confirmed what required confirmation. Among other matters, at the end of the synodal absolution, he suspended Tedaldus, called Archbishop of Milan, and Guibert of Ravenna, who were exalting themselves against the holy Catholic Church with unheard-of arrogance and heresy, from episcopal and priestly office [Col. 0133A]. He also renewed the anathema previously pronounced against them, because they had refused to come when summoned to the Synod.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Our manuscript, having previously noted no. 166 and having been silent about Tedaldus, placed everything in the singular. But the title states that the letter written expressly to Guibert was also directed to all the bishops of Lombardy and others. It is likely that an exemplar was sent expressly to Tedaldus, as head of the bishops of Lombardy, just as Guibert was head of Emilia.]

He deposed Arnulf of Cremona, publicly convicted before the Lord Pope and confessing himself to be a simoniac, from all episcopal office without hope of recovery, and struck him with anathema until he had made fitting satisfaction.

He likewise condemned Roland of Treviso, who, having become a deceitful legate in order to obtain the honor of the episcopate, did not shrink from creating a schism between the Kingdom and the Priesthood [Col. 0133B].

He decreed, by apostolic censure, that Roland should lack episcopal dignity henceforth and forever; he prohibited in every possible way that any of his successors should consent in any manner to his consecration; and he bound him with perpetual anathema, unless he should repent and make worthy satisfaction to God.

He deprived Hugh, Cardinal of the title of St. Clement, who had been condemned for the third time by the Apostolic See because he had become an aspirant to, and associate of, the heresy of Cadolus, Bishop of Parma [Col. 0133B]—having again been appointed legate and joined himself to persons condemned by the Apostolic See, and, having become an apostate and heresiarch for a third time, having caused schisms, divisions, and ruptures in the Church of God while attempting to tear it apart—from all priestly office. Under a perpetual and irrevocable sentence, he removed him both from entry into and honor in the aforementioned Church and from all the churches, until he made satisfaction.

[Text in parentheses preserved separately in the source.]

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The following material, concerning the sending of legates to establish peace, which Paulus gives in no. 90, followed here. Before the conclusion—which states that all this was enacted at Rome in the church of the Lord Savior, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the first indiction—several other decrees are found in Baronius and consequently in the collection of councils; it is sufficient that they can be found there.]

He also renewed the excommunication previously pronounced against Gaufredus, Archbishop of Narbonne, and removed him from episcopal office without any hope of restoration.

After the Council was completed, he sent his messengers, namely Bernard the Deacon and Bernard, Abbot of Marseille [Col. 0133C], together with Udo, Archbishop of Trier, to establish peace with King Henry and Rudolf, whom the Teutons had chosen as their king.

He instructed them to determine carefully which of the two had the greater justice and to hand over the governance of the Kingdom to whichever had justice on his side, because the more just party can place greater trust in God and will certainly be aided by the power of Blessed Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Bernard the Deacon of Pavia had been made a cardinal by Nicholas II, according to Lambert of Hersfeld; some maintain that Gregory himself first promoted him.]

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Gregory had also made this man, the Abbot of St. Victor, a cardinal. Berthold of Constance praises him as a man full of every charity; he died in the year 1079.]

## CHAPTER II. The Many Synods Held by Gregory during the Rest of His Pontificate

7. In the sixth year of Gregory’s pontificate, on 18 November, in the eleventh indiction, Marro, son of Guilleri, a resident of the Duchy of Spoleto, for the redemption of his soul and those of his parents, offered to Blessed Peter and upon his altar everything belonging to him from the castle called Moricida, situated between Murice and Clarignano. He had acquired it by exchange from Liraldus and Hugh, nephews of Hugh son of Ascarius, in the parish of Luzano.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Luigiano lies five Roman miles from Spoleto toward the March; two or three miles from there, according to the topographical map of Umbria, are C. Moro, that is, Castle of Maurus, and Can-Moro, that is, Field of Maurus. These seem relevant here, although the names Murice and Clarignano are no longer found.]

He reserved the usufruct for the days of his own life and for those of his son Brutulus and Brutulus’s sons, if they were male and born of a lawful marriage.

In that same year, on the third day before the Kalends of December, a Synod was held by the same Pontiff. Among other matters, the Emperor of Constantinople was excommunicated.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] Nicephorus Botaneiates, tyrannically claiming the Empire for himself, had captured Michael, together with his wife and son, at Blachernae and confined them in a monastery. Michael, however, adhered to communion with the Roman Church.]

At the same Synod, the legates of Henry and Rudolf each swore on behalf of his lord that they would not impede, by any deceit, the meeting of the legates of the Apostolic See in the Teutonic Kingdom.

Many other matters were also established by him at that Synod, but it would take too long to recount them.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The titles of thirty-three chapters still survive, but only twelve corresponding decrees remain.]

He also renewed the anathema pronounced against Guibert of Ravenna and announced to all the citizens, both great and small, that Guibert was excommunicated and a destroyer of the Church of Ravenna.

8. In the following year, the seventh of the same pontificate, in the month of February, in the second indiction, a Synod was held at Rome in the Basilica of St. Savior, for the honor of God and the edification of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] This was the year 1079, for the preceding Synod belongs to the year 1078.] All the archbishops and religious persons gathered there to celebrate the holy Synod.

When everyone had assembled, a discussion was held concerning the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. At first, some held one view and others another.

The greater part maintained that the bread and wine, through the words of the sacred prayer and the consecration by the priest, with the Holy Spirit invisibly at work, were substantially converted into the Lord’s Body, born of the Virgin, which also hung upon the cross, and into the Blood that was poured from his side by the soldier’s lance. They defended this position in every way by the authorities of the orthodox Fathers, both Greek and Latin.

Certain others, however, struck by excessive blindness, attempted by various quibbles to assert that it was only a figure (and that that substantial body sits at the Father’s right hand), deceiving themselves and others.

But when the matter began to be debated, even before the third day had arrived in the Synod, the opposing party ceased to resist the truth. Indeed, the fire of the Holy Spirit, consuming the chaff and darkening false light by striking it with its brightness, turned the darkness of night into light.

Finally, Berengarius, the teacher of this error, after having taught his impiety for a long time, confessed before the numerous council that he had been in error. He asked and pleaded for pardon, obtained it through apostolic clemency, and swore as follows:

9. “I, Berengarius, believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, through the mystery of the sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, substantially converted into the true, proper, and life-giving flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0135B].

“After the consecration, they are the true Body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, which was offered for the salvation of the world and hung upon the cross, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and the true Blood of Christ, which was poured from his side—not merely through the sign and power of the sacrament, but in the properness of nature and the truth of substance, as this brief statement contains, as I have read, and as you understand.

“Thus I believe, and against this faith I shall teach nothing further. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels of God.”

Then the Lord Pope, by the authority of almighty God and of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, ordered Berengarius never again to presume to dispute with anyone or teach anyone concerning the Body and Blood of the Lord, except for the purpose of restoring to this faith those who had departed from it through his teaching [Col. 0135C].

10. After these pious and successful proceedings, amid many public accusations, the legates of King Rudolf complained against Henry that, sparing neither place nor person, he was crushing and trampling upon the region [possibly “religion”] beyond the Alps; that no one was protected by due order, honor, or reverence; and that, like base slaves, not only priests and clerics but even archbishops and bishops were being captured, bound, and in part slaughtered.

Accordingly, many members of the council decreed that the apostolic sword ought to be drawn against his tyranny. But apostolic gentleness postponed the act.

The legates of King Henry therefore swore the oath found written below:

“The legates of my lord will come to you before the appointed time of the Ascension of the Lord [Col. 0135D], except in the event of a major impediment—that is, death, serious illness, or captivity without deceit. They will safely conduct the legates of the Roman Church there and back; and the Lord King will obey them according to their justice and judgment. All this shall be done without deceit, except insofar as it remains undone by your command. And this I swear at the command of my lord King Henry.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The Ascension of the Lord, in the year in which Easter was celebrated on 24 March, fell on 2 May.]

Likewise, Rudolf’s oath was as follows:

“If, at your command, a meeting is arranged in the Teutonic lands, at the place and time determined by you, before your presence or that of your legates, our lord King Rudolf will either come himself or send his bishops and faithful men. He will be prepared to submit the case of the Kingdom to judgment, and by no evil artifice will he impede the meeting arranged by you or your legates.

“When he sees from there a trustworthy messenger of yours concerning the establishment and confirmation of peace in the Kingdom, he will endeavor to ensure that your legation may proceed toward peace and concord in the Kingdom.

“All these things shall be observed, except insofar as something is prevented by your permission or by a legitimate impediment, namely death, serious illness, or captivity without deceit.”

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Labbeus adds that, in the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, another Council was held. In the presence of four bishops, several cardinals, abbots, and archpriests [Col. 0136D], it was debated whether the goods of the churches could be pledged in order to collect money for resisting Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, who was attempting to invade the Roman See.]

11. In the seventh year of his pontificate, the same Pontiff held a Synod at Rome. Archbishops and bishops from various cities were present, together with an innumerable multitude of abbots, clerics of various orders, and laymen.

At this Synod, strengthening the apostolic constitutions, he corrected many things that required correction and confirmed what required confirmation. Among other matters, at the end of the synodal absolution, he added the following and ordered it to be written for perpetual remembrance by posterity:

“Following the statutes of the holy Fathers, just as in the earlier councils that by God’s mercy we have celebrated we established regulations concerning the ordination of ecclesiastical dignities, so now also, by apostolic authority, we decree and confirm that if anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or abbey from the hand of any layperson, he shall in no way be counted among bishops or abbots, nor shall any hearing be granted to him as bishop or abbot.

“Moreover, we forbid him the grace of St. Peter and entry into the Church until, by repentance, he abandons the position which he holds under the charge both of ambition and of disobedience, which is the crime of idolatry.

“We likewise establish the same concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.

“Furthermore, if any emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, or any secular power or person presumes to grant the investiture of a bishopric or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him understand that he is bound by the bond of the same sentence.

“Moreover, unless he repents and leaves the Church her proper liberty, let him feel the vengeance of divine judgment in this present life, both in his body and in his other possessions, so that at the coming of the Lord his spirit may be saved” [Col. 0136D].

12. Likewise, we confirm and strengthen the sentence of deposition and excommunication, already pronounced in large part, against Theodald, called archbishop of Milan, Guibert of Ravenna, and Roland of Treviso; and we condemn with the same sentence Peter, formerly bishop of Rodon [Ruthenen], but now intruder into the Church of Narbonne. Likewise, if any of the Normans should presume to invade or plunder the lands of Saint Peter—namely, that part of the March of Fermo which has not yet been occupied, the duchy of Spoleto, Campania, the coastal territories, the Sabine territory, and the county of Tivoli, as well as the monastery of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino and the lands belonging to it, and also Benevento—we forbid him the grace of Saint Peter and entry into the church until satisfaction has been made. Nevertheless, if any one of them has a just cause against the inhabitants of these lands, let him first seek justice from us, or from the rectors or ministers appointed there. If justice is denied him, we grant that, in recovering his property, he may take from that land—but not beyond measure or in the manner of brigands, rather as befits a Christian, one who seeks to recover what is his rather than seize what belongs to another, and who fears losing the grace of God and incurring the curse of blessed Peter.

[Note: In our manuscript there followed, from the *Lives of the Pontiffs*, the excommunication of King Henry: “. . . . . . Enacted at Rome on the Nones of March, in the third indiction,” exactly as you find it printed in the *Life*, no. 96 and following. All of this, together with the two chapters omitted here, concerning false repentance and the election of pontiffs, is found printed in Baronius under the year 1080. The fact that the year 1079 is recorded in the *Register* from which it was taken arises from the previously noted method of extending the Florentine year until the Annunciation. Since Easter in the leap year 1080 was celebrated on 12 April, it is also understood that this synod met in the first week of Lent, after the Sunday that fell on 29 February.]

[lacuna]

13. In the eighth year of his pontificate, in a letter to the bishops established throughout the principalities of Apulia and Calabria, among other statements, he denounced the wickedness of King Henry and of Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, “excommunicated in the aforesaid synod.”

[Note: This is Book VIII, Letter 5, dated at Cicanum on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.]

First, he made known the wickedness that Henry had attempted to commit against the lord pope Alexander through Cadalus of Parma; and he announced that God, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, had justly permitted their pride to fall, on account of their crimes, into the pit that they had prepared for others. He designated Guibert, perjurer against the Roman Church and devastator of the Church of Ravenna, as antichrist and heresiarch on account of his most abominable crimes. He notified all the bishops and suffragans of the Church of Ravenna, and all the greater and lesser persons of that city, as well as those throughout the entire March and duchy, that Guibert had been condemned and deposed without hope of restoration. Relying on the aid of this benevolent prelate, just as blessed Peter sent blessed Apollinaris to preach, he likewise—although unworthy, he held Peter’s place—took care to send an archbishop there to win human souls for God and destroy the aforesaid Guibert’s heresy.

[Note: Book VIII, Letter 14, written to all the bishops, abbots, counts, and knights living in the diocese of Ravenna and the Pentapolis, as well as in the March of Fermo and the duchy of Spoleto—namely, to those who love blessed Peter and are not bound by the chains of excommunication. To these alone he gives greeting and apostolic blessing. Dated on the second day before the Ides of December, it commends to them the archbishop of Ravenna, R., whom, after the long and countless occupations of the invaders, the Ravennans had most recently deserved to receive from the Roman Church, just as formerly blessed Peter had sent Apollinaris. Baronius reads “Richard” and calls him a man of great distinction. We may believe no less of him, although nowhere do we find anything performed by him.]

In that same year a synod was held by the same pontiff in the basilica of Saint Saviour at Rome.

[Note: If this synod, like the others, was a Lenten synod—as may reasonably be presumed—it must have been convened after the first Sunday, which fell on 21 February in the year 1081, when Easter was celebrated on 4 April.]

Among other matters, the pope confirmed the sentence of deposition against the archbishops of Arles and Narbonne, and the sentence of excommunication promulgated by the legates of the Apostolic See, those present applauding it. He also excommunicated and anathematized Henry, the so-called king, and all his supporters who had hardened their hearts in the aforesaid excommunication; likewise Ildimund and Lando, the Campanian tyrants, and all their associates. Moreover, he suspended from office certain bishops who, although invited to the council, had come neither themselves nor through representatives acting on their behalf.

14. In the twelfth year of the pontificate of the same lord Gregory, from the Incarnation of the Lord 1084, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, while the same apostolic lord presided, a synod was held for three days in the Lateran basilica. Present were the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of Campania and of the principalities of Calabria and Apulia, together with a few from Gaul; for Henry’s treachery compelled very many to turn back on their journey. He had ordered—or permitted—the bishop of Ostia, returning from an apostolic legation, to be captured contrary to law and to the faith of his oath.

[Note: This was Otho Castillionaeus, later Pope Urban II.]

The persecution of the same Henry prevented three Lenten synods.

[Note: Those of the years 1082, 1083, and 1084.]

He attacked blessed Paul once and blessed Peter twice, and finally, after much blood had been shed, seized the gates and walls—not so much through the courage of his own men as through the negligence of the citizens. For the Roman populace, the more numerous part of the city, exhausted by a two-year war, was suffering from severe hunger. They were not permitted to go even to the neighboring towns or fortresses, while Henry’s sworn adherents were unwilling to come into the city for trade. Many, driven by hunger, had abandoned the city; consequently, those who remained devoted themselves less attentively to the war, and each person absented himself from the watches more carelessly and without fear, as he pleased.

15. Since the occasion has presented itself, it is enough to have touched briefly upon these matters concerning Henry’s tyranny. (Furthermore, in the same synod the Apostolic Lord spoke openly—not with a human but with an angelic voice—about the form of faith and the conduct of Christian religion, and also about the strength and steadfastness of spirit necessary in the present oppression. On the third day he compelled almost the entire assembly to sighs and tears; and thus, after the council had been gladdened by the apostolic blessing, he dismissed it in peace.)

As has been said, Henry came to Rome three times. But one matter must not be passed over in silence: on the last occasion he brought Guibert of Ravenna with him, already condemned and deposed many times, and set the intruder over the lord pope Gregory. But what the devil and the Antichrist did in Rome and throughout all its territory would take too long to recount.

The lord pope shut himself up with a few companions in the fortress of Saint Angelo, since otherwise he could not remain in Rome. The Romans, however, began once more to carry out their evil custom, which they had had from the beginning: they surrounded the fortress on every side with walls, so that no one was permitted either to enter or to leave. The king ascended the Capitol, overthrew all the houses of the Corsini, and began to treat Rome as his own house. Then, besieging the Septem-solia, where Rusticus, the nephew of the aforesaid prelate, was stationed, he made the attempt with many engines of war and overturned very many columns.

[Note: Ciacconius, in the *Life of Gregory IX*, says that it was erected near the Septizonium, in the diaconia of Saint Lucy at the Septisolium. Alexander Donatus considers it to have been what is now called Saint Lucy in Silice, and says that it stood on the Esquiline. It is, however, plausible that “Septisolium” is a popular corruption of “Septizonium.”]

[Note: This prefecture was evidently a military office. From the nobility of the office held by his nephew, one might therefore infer the nobility of Gregory’s own paternal or maternal uncle, in favor of Petracius, who asserts the same.]

A messenger came to him announcing that, unless he withdrew from the siege, he would be expelled by Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, and no one would be able to rescue him from Robert’s hands. For the aforesaid duke was faithful and devoted to blessed Peter and to the aforementioned pontiff, and it was fitting that a son should rescue his father from so great a captivity.

16. The king, after taking counsel with his men, addressed all the Romans as follows:

“Fathers and sons, I entrust to your hands and power the imperial crown and the reins of the kingdom, and I place my life in your care. Since it is worthwhile for me to turn my journey toward Lombardy, I promise you that, if I ever return, I shall surrender myself entirely, together with everything that I have and may acquire, in every possible way.”

But the merciful and compassionate Lord, who knows everyone’s thoughts, did not allow the Church to be harassed by him for long; he never again returned to that city.

Robert Guiscard, approaching Rome in those days to free the lord pope, did not enter at first; but he did not remain outside for long before entering. He gained access through the Flaminian Gate. When the Romans heard that he had entered, they raised a war against him; but they could do nothing to him. Rather, he and his men completely destroyed and almost reduced to nothing that entire district in which the churches of Saint Sylvester and Saint Lawrence in Lucina are situated.

Then he went to the fortress of Saint Angelo, rescued the lord pope from it, and brought him with him to the Lateran. He then began to plunder and strip all the Romans, and—even though it is shameful to report—to dishonor women and burn with fire those districts situated around the Lateran and the Colosseum.

[Note: Here, from Berthold, there ought to have been added an account of how, in Rome on the feast of Saint John the Baptist—namely, 24 June—while Henry was still staying there, Gregory renewed the anathema against him and Guibert. He did so again after the king’s departure, in a synod convened, as we believe, in December; for, as Paul says in no. 100, around the Kalends of January he began to foresee the dissolution of his body. Nevertheless, a synod may also have been held at the beginning of the following Lent, after 9 March, since Easter was to be celebrated on 20 April. Since Berthold so expressly says that the earlier renewal of the anathema was made at Rome, he seems to indicate that this synod was not held there, but elsewhere—for example, at Monte Cassino—before the pontiff was taken to Salerno.]

17. In that same year there was a great famine throughout the whole world, as a result of which many people died; and the sun suffered an eclipse.

[Note: No other historian recorded this eclipse, which is why Calvisius, accustomed in his chronological work to calculating from astronomical principles all the eclipses he had found, lacked the opportunity to determine it more precisely.]

There was an earthquake, and the fortress of Saint Angelo was captured.

[Note: By the rebellious Romans, perhaps after Gregory’s departure or death, when they were supporting Guibert? I suspect so, for Guibert was then residing in Rome.]

The duke of Apulia, taking the lord pope with him, left him at Salerno. There that man, beloved of God, a Catholic and defender of the Church against the arms of heretics, liberator of the poor, and consoler of captives and compassionate guardian of orphans, ended his life and gave back his soul to God on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

[VITA OF SAINT GREGORY VII]

[Col. 0139]

MABILLON’S PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY VII, WRITTEN BY PAUL OF BERNRIED, HIS CONTEMPORARY  
(*Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, Part II of the Sixth Century, p. 403.)

1. That enormous discord between the priesthood and the empire, which erupted under Pope Gregory VII and Emperor Henry IV, gave rise to great controversies. Various authors of histories, both ancient and modern, have written about these matters in different ways, according as they were attached to one side or the other. It is not my intention to reopen questions of this kind, which have no bearing on our purpose and can easily be learned from other authors. It will be enough for us to present the life of this pontiff, which we have taken from Gretser and Bollandus, written shortly after Gregory’s death by Paul of Bernried, an author contemporary with him.

Paul, the author of this Life, was initially a canon of the Church of Regensburg. When Henry IV expelled him from that city because he did not support Henry’s party, he withdrew to the newly founded monastery of Bernried, where, having adopted the institute of the regular canons, he lived for several years. From there he went to Rome and became familiar with the pontiffs. Besides the Life of Gregory, he also composed several other short works, among them the Life of the blessed Herluca, which he himself cites below and which the Bollandists published on 18 April from the edition of Gretser.

2. Several more recent writers state that Gregory came from the highly noble family of the Aldobrandini. To prove this, however, they can scarcely produce anything beyond the similarity of names. Before he was raised to the pontificate, he was called Hildebrand, as everyone knows. Yet everyone can see how frivolous such reasoning is.

Baronius, by contrast, says that Gregory was born in humble circumstances, specifically to a father who was a woodworker. That this could not bring disgrace upon Gregory is demonstrated by the example of our Lord Jesus Christ. Although he was the Word of the Father and the true Son of God, he did not disdain to be born of a poor Virgin and, as was thought, to have a craftsman for his father.

Papebrochius, although he rejects the first opinion, does not accept the second either. In his preliminary remarks to the Bollandist Life of Gregory VII, on 25 May, he thinks it can be proved that Gregory came from a noble family because, in manuscript *Acts of the Pontiffs* which he says are preserved in his possession, one reads that Rusticus, prefect of the Septem-solia—or of the fortified dwelling resembling a citadel which Emperor Henry unsuccessfully attempted to conquer with military engines—was Gregory’s nephew. That office, he says, would certainly not have been entrusted to a commoner.

He confirms the same opinion by the authority of Paul himself, who in Gregory’s Life observes that the same pontiff had an uncle who was abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary on the Aventine. Yet since nothing certain is found in the ancient records by which such controversies might be settled, and since the authorities are by no means in agreement, there is no point in devoting further effort to debating them. Paul expressly says that Gregory was born in Tuscany, although some maintain that this occurred at Siena and others near Soana. Hugh of Flavigny contradicts them in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, where he states in explicit terms that Gregory was born at Rome to Roman citizen parents.

3. Paul reports several omens of Gregory’s future sanctity, but he omits the event said to have occurred when Gregory was still an infant in the workshop of a craftsman whom some, as we have just said, claim to have been his father. Although he did not yet know his letters, he is said to have arranged discarded fragments while playing so that they formed the words of that Davidic prophecy: “He shall rule from sea to sea.”

The canon Theodoric Engelhusius of Hildesheim adds another omen of his future power in his *Lives of the Emperors Descended from the House of Brunswick*. In the Life of Emperor Henry III, surnamed the Black, he relates that Hildebrand—then tutor to Henry’s son—appeared in a dream to the emperor seated at table with the emperor’s own son, possessing horns raised to heaven, with which he hurled the same Henry, the son, into the mud. When the empress interpreted this vision as meaning that Henry’s son would be driven from the imperial throne through Hildebrand, the emperor is said to have cast Hildebrand into chains to be starved to death. Later, however, through his wife’s intervention, he allowed him to depart free, lest by rashly believing dreams he order an innocent man to perish. But these matters are uncertain, like many other things fabricated by more recent writers, and for that reason we have decided to omit them.

4. It is entirely certain that from his earliest childhood Gregory enrolled in the monastic profession, which he both loved throughout the rest of his life and, insofar as the necessity of public affairs allowed, diligently practiced. Orderic Vitalis, a most exact writer of those times, explicitly states in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History* that Gregory was a monk from childhood. He repeats the same statement in Book VII, where he treats Gregory’s history at length. Our manuscript Saxon Chronicler likewise calls him a monk by profession.

As Hugh of Flavigny says in the *Chronicle of Verdun*, “Having adopted a purpose of sanctity, he mastered his youth among those who despised the world, not without great signs of perfection.” Domnizo adds the same in the *Life of Matilda*, where he observes that monks mourned Gregory’s death more than others because Gregory himself had been a monk.

Indeed, in his thirty-second short work, which Peter Damian dedicated to Hildebrand while the latter was still a monk, he always calls him his brother, both in the preface and throughout the work. We omit Theodoric, mentioned above in section 3, as well as Trithemius and other writers of this kind.

Paul himself seems to have indicated the place where Gregory made his monastic profession in section 9, where he writes that from childhood Hildebrand was entrusted to his uncle, the abbot of Saint Mary on the Aventine, to learn both letters and moral discipline. He recalls that this was accomplished by the uncle in a short time.

5. Most writers, especially more recent ones, believe that Gregory lived the monastic life in the celebrated monastery of Cluny, and they assert that he was given the office of prior there. This is stated explicitly by Otto, bishop of Freising, a writer of no small distinction. He relates that Leo IX, designated pope by the emperor and traveling toward Italy, turned aside to Cluny, where Hildebrand was then prior. On Hildebrand’s advice, Leo abandoned the pontifical insignia and proceeded to Rome in the guise of a pilgrim, accompanied by Hildebrand, who induced the Romans to elect Leo, already chosen by the emperor.

Certainly no one can question that Gregory was most favorably disposed toward the Cluniacs. He was also on familiar terms with Saint Hugh, as is clear from Hugh’s Life. It may be inferred from the beginning of the Life that Gregory was instructed in spiritual matters under Saint Maiolus—or rather, since we think Paul’s memory failed him there, under Saint Odilo’s discipline. It says that Saint Maiolus, father of the monastery of Cluny, first noted in Hildebrand the vision of sparks repeatedly shown to him and applied to him the words concerning John the Baptist: “This child shall be great before the Lord.”

The same author observes that, on entering adolescence, Hildebrand went to France to master the wantonness of the flesh through the hardship of pilgrimage and the rigor of study. Perhaps he accomplished this in the monastery of Cluny, then the most celebrated of its time. After returning to Rome, and then being forced into exile with Gregory VI, he undoubtedly returned to Cluny, where he was given the office of prior—if indeed he ever held that dignity.

It can certainly be inferred that he was instructed in monastic disciplines from the fact that, after his return to the City, Leo IX placed him in charge of the monastery of Saint Paul, so that he might restore there the regular discipline that had grown lax. This is the same man who, in that capacity, transferred to the monks of Vendôme the church of Saint Prisca, situated on the Aventine in Rome, on the condition that twelve monks from Vendôme—and never fewer than eight—should always live there according to the rule.

We learn this from letters of Pope Alexander, written in the fifth year of his pontificate, by which he confirmed the agreement made concerning this matter between Hildebrand, archdeacon and steward or rector of the monastery of Saint Paul, and Oderic, abbot of Vendôme.

Papebrochius explains and refutes at length, in paragraph 4, the grounds on which some have recently assigned Gregory to the Vallombrosan order; among learned authors, however, there can be no difficulty concerning this matter. Our Hildebrand must nevertheless be distinguished from another prior or provost of Cluny with the same name, who is praised in the Life of Saint Odo.

How great was our Hildebrand’s devotion to the monastic profession after he had been raised to the pontificate is clear from various letters of his. In them he frequently praises the holiness of monks and, against all who are hostile to them, provides fatherly protection for their peace. His Letter 13 of Book I should be read on this subject, where he restrains Manasses, archbishop of Reims, who was harassing the monks of Saint Remigius. He wrote several letters to Lanfranc on behalf of the monks of England.

He admitted many of them to the college of cardinals. As soon as he was proclaimed pontiff, he wished the abbot of Cassino to be with him. When death was approaching, he designated Hugh of Die, Otto—formerly a canon of Reims and then cardinal bishop of Ostia—and Desiderius of Cassino as the only men worthy to succeed him. The last two became Benedictine pontiffs. Finally, as Orderic Vitalis says in Book IV, he also promoted other monks as reason dictated and honorably placed them in charge of various churches.

6. Gregory was an exceptionally zealous defender of ecclesiastical authority and discipline, both before and after he undertook the pontificate. His chief zeal was directed against priests living in concubinage and against simoniacs; these two vices were then bringing ruin upon the Church, especially in Germany and Lombardy.

When these men, taking advantage of the question of investitures, had drawn Henry, king of the Germans, who was already hostile to the pontiff, over to their side, and Gregory could not tolerate this, they kindled a great fire in the Catholic Church, as some favored the pontiff and others the king.

The pontiff deprived the king of communion and then of his kingdom, as one guilty of many crimes and repeatedly admonished in vain through letters and legates. This so agitated Henry and his followers that Henry himself also attempted to drive the pontiff from his see. Through bishops attached to him, he arranged the election of Guibert of Ravenna against Gregory; Guibert assumed the name Clement III. From this arose the gravest schism, and frequent gatherings of bishops and nobles took place at that time.

7. Gregory’s prudence in imposing excommunication at the Roman council held in 1078 is entirely commendable. To provide peace of conscience for simpler people who were not sufficiently capable of discerning the causes of such disputes, he declared that such persons were not bound by the sentence of excommunication, nor were those who, because of their condition, age, or nature, were unable to avoid the company of excommunicated persons.

Gregory’s words should be quoted from Hugh of Flavigny’s *Chronicle of Verdun* under the year 1078:

“And because, through the demands of our sins, we see many perish daily on account of the cause of excommunication—some overcome by ignorance, some by excessive simplicity, some by fear, and some by extreme necessity—we temper the sentence of the anathema, insofar as we can, opportunely and for a time, overcome by mercy.

“Therefore, by apostolic authority, we remove from the bond of anathema wives, children, male servants, maidservants or slaves, as well as peasants and servants, and all others who are not so closely associated with the court that crimes are perpetrated on their advice; and those who unknowingly associate with excommunicated persons, as well as those who associate with persons who associate with excommunicated persons.

“Furthermore, if any petitioner, pilgrim, or traveler comes into the land of excommunicated persons, where he cannot buy or has no means with which to buy, we grant him permission to receive what he needs from the excommunicated. And if anyone wishes to give something to excommunicated persons—not to support their pride, but out of humanity—we do not forbid it.”

The priest Berthold of Constance gives the same testimony in his *Chronicle* under the year 1078.

Gregory had undoubtedly learned this from the rule of the blessed father Benedict, who once and again forbids those who do not know how great the punishment of excommunication is to be struck by it. Since such a censure ought to be applied only for edification, when it is otherwise administered it frequently becomes an instrument of destruction.

Much excellent legislation concerning the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline and the eradication of vices can be found in the various councils convened by that pontiff. It is not our purpose to describe it here in greater detail; it is readily available in the published collections of councils.

8. The same ardent zeal for reforming the Church and advancing virtue shines forth in most of the letters of that blessed pontiff. Among them are many addressed to various kings and princes throughout the Christian world. In these he urges the good, with praise and congratulations, to undertake still greater things for the benefit of the Church; the vicious he endeavors, through threats and ecclesiastical censures, to recall to better conduct.

He deterred Alfonso, king of Castile, from the incestuous marriage into which he had taken his wife’s kinswoman. He deprived Robert Guiscard, prince of the Normans in Italy, who was devastating the lands of the Church, of communion, and later restored him to ecclesiastical communion after he repented of his deed.

By contrast, he strove by every means within his power to win the best princes to his side. Thus he confirmed to the duke of Bohemia the use of the mitre, already permitted by Alexander II. He wrote more than once to Sweyn, king of the Danes, congratulating him on his very devoted attitude toward the Apostolic See and asking him to send one of his sons to Italy to be a duke, prince, and defender of Christianity. He wrote to the same king’s son, who had succeeded him after his father’s death, inviting him, as an imitator of his father’s virtue, to defend the Churches.

9. He also possessed an immense desire to bring all the Churches back into one harmony of faith. How earnestly he sought the union of the Greek Church with the Roman Church may be learned from his eighteenth letter of Book I, addressed to Michael, emperor of the East.

Indeed, he was planning to travel to the East, as he testified in Letter 30 of Book II to Henry, king of the Romans—not only to reconcile Greeks, Armenians, and other heretics to the Church, but also to rescue Christians who were groaning under Saracen servitude.

10. He desired everyone to seek communion with the Roman Church so strongly that he could scarcely tolerate differences of rite. For this reason he labored so intensely to abolish entirely the Mozarabic rite, which the Churches of Spain had used for several centuries.

His letters on this subject are Letters 63 and 64 of Book I, addressed to Alfonso of Castile and Sancho of Aragon.

On this occasion, common Spanish authors say that the Mozarabic rite was divinely approved by a miracle: when a Mozarabic book and one containing the Roman rite were thrown into the fire, the latter was immediately reduced to ashes, while the former remained unharmed. But no one recorded this before Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, as the most devout Cardinal Bona observes; Rodrigo lived around the middle of the thirteenth century.

Nor is it likely that the Spaniards abandoned this rite at the very time when it had been confirmed by God himself through so evident a miracle. Its use was not abolished in the Churches of Spain to such an extent that, even in Rodrigo’s time, it was not still observed in most monasteries and even in some cathedral churches. Finally it was printed at the command of Cardinal Ximenes, and it is said still to be observed in a chapel of the Church of Toledo and in certain parish churches.

Gregory was inflamed by the same desire when he congratulated King F. of Sweden on having received certain Gallic ministers of the word of God, from whom he had received the rites of the Roman Church. In Letter 11 of Book VIII he urges the king to send some of his clerics or bishops to Rome, so that, after explaining to the Apostolic See the customs of the people and the conditions of the land, they might bring commands back to their homeland by which the entire nation could be instructed.

The same purpose is served by Letter 13 of Book VIII, in which he advises Olaf, king of Norway—as he says he had already written to the king of the Danes—to send some of the younger and more noble men of his kingdom to the Roman court. There, instructed under the wings of the apostles Peter and Paul, they could later return to their homeland and teach the entire region the customs of the Roman Church.

The author of the *Micrologus* reports several regulations concerning ecclesiastical rites instituted by Gregory, which Baronius cites under the year 1085.

11. The most vigilant pontiff restrained Berengar the heretic, who repeatedly returned to his vomit after repeated condemnations. In 1055, under Victor II, when Hildebrand was then a legate of the Apostolic See at the Council of Tours, he had already compelled Berengar to renounce his heresy. After becoming pontiff, he summoned Berengar to Rome and, in two councils, restored him to the Church after he had issued two confessions of faith.

But this matter has been treated in the preface placed before this volume.

12. Here we must not omit his profound devotion in frequent participation in the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist, and his piety toward the most blessed Virgin Mary. He commended these two things to the countess Matilda as two exceedingly firm bulwarks against the enemy of the human race, wishing them to be joined with hatred of sin and humble contrition of heart.

His Letter 47 of Book I should be read on this subject. “Among the other weapons,” he says, “which, with God’s favor, I have supplied to you against the prince of this world, I have pointed out the most important: that you should frequently receive the Lord’s Body; and I have instructed you to entrust yourself entirely to sure trust in the Mother of the Lord.””

He then presents selected testimonies from Saints Ambrose, Gregory, and John Chrysostom, by which those most holy men invited the faithful of their age to frequent the sacraments. Finally, after praising the most blessed Virgin’s clemency toward converted sinners, he concludes:

“Therefore put an end to your willingness to sin, and, prostrate before her, pour out tears from a contrite and humbled heart; you will undoubtedly find her more ready,” and so forth.

13. Lambert of Schaffhausen, a monk, suggests under the year 1077 that Gregory also became famous for miracles before his death. He says that the signs and wonders frequently performed through Gregory’s prayers, together with the most fervent zeal with which he burned for God and the ecclesiastical laws, were sufficient to expose the poisonous slanders of his enemies.

He died at Salerno, where he had taken refuge to avoid Henry’s plots. There is no disagreement among the commonly published authorities concerning the time of his death: all acknowledge that he departed this life in the year 1085, on 25 May. He was buried there in the metropolitan church.

Orderic Vitalis, however, suffered a lapse of memory in Book VIII, where he writes that Gregory died at Benevento and was buried there in the confession of blessed Bartholomew the Apostle. The same author testifies that a wealth of miracles occurred at the tomb of that pontiff. “There,” he says, “through his merits, an abundance of miracles was divinely shown to the faithful who sought them.” He then adds:

“For lepers requested water with which his body had been washed. When they had obtained it, they washed themselves in faith and, with God’s help, were immediately cleansed.”

Most authors, both recent and ancient, pursue his praises at greater length. Gretser, in his defense of Gregory, lists no fewer than fifty of his praisers. Peter Damian calls him a man of the holiest and purest counsel. Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, who succeeded him under the name Victor III, writes in the third book of his *Dialogues* that Gregory illumined the Church of Christ through both words and examples. Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, published a distinguished book in his defense against the antipope Guibert. I omit the others, whose names alone would be difficult to list because of their number. Hugh of Flavigny says in his *Chronicle* that Gregory died as a confessor and martyr; the same work contains many further details about his deeds and death.

14. Yet Gregory’s feast was nowhere celebrated with public worship before the beginning of this century. It was first permitted by Pope Paul V, as is clear from his bull issued in 1609, which Papebrochius reproduces in full in paragraph 2 of his preliminary remarks to the Life of this blessed man. There he also includes the letter of Giovanni Beltramo de Guevara, archbishop of Salerno, who ordered the office of that blessed pontiff to be recited with solemn rite throughout his entire diocese.

Gregory’s memory, however, had already been recorded in the Roman Martyrology, in the year 1584, when it had been corrected by the authority of Gregory XIII. In the new edition prepared under the authority of Sixtus V by Baronius, the same blessed pontiff is praised on 25 May in these words:

“At Salerno, the deposition of blessed Gregory, pope and seventh of that name, the most vigorous champion and defender of ecclesiastical liberty.”

[Col. 0147]

THE LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY VII  
By Paul of Bernried

(See above in the already published *Acts* of this volume, col. 39.)

[Col. 0147]

# On the Deeds of Gregory VII: Against Investitures and Simony, and for the Celibacy of the Clergy

*(Mabillon, Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti, Preface to Part II of the Third Century, p. 41.)*

[Col. 0147C] That Gregory VII was a great man, and that he possessed great spirits in a small body—even if not everyone agreed—was certainly demonstrated sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, by the distinguished deeds that he undertook for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline and accomplished for the most part. If in some matters he seems to have exceeded moderation—for it is difficult always to remain measured in affairs so grave and difficult—the merits of such great achievements should excuse him. These achievements benefited the Christian commonwealth and cannot rightly be condemned by anyone.

For what was more reasonable, or more difficult, than to uproot entirely the abuses of ecclesiastical investitures, strengthened by so long a passage of time and by the authority of so many secular rulers; to eradicate Simony, which was rampant almost everywhere; and to recall the celibacy of the clergy, [Col. 0147D] almost at the point of destruction? Yet this most energetic pontiff accomplished all these things—something that Leo IX and the other Roman pontiffs after him had attempted with almost no success—despite the resistance everywhere of the princes of the age and the opposition, insults, and attacks of adversaries on every side, namely the Nicolaitans and Simoniacs, who inflamed the minds of the princes against him, especially that of the emperor Henry, whose party they supported, so that he might protect them against Gregory and his decrees.

Indeed, that Gregory was by natural temperament inclined more toward leniency than toward excessive fervor is shown both by what he did for the restoration of many bishops (Gregory VII, book V, letter 17) and by the letters that he wrote at the beginning to the emperor Henry (book III, letters 7 and 10, and elsewhere). But the emperor’s obstinacy and inconsistency alike embittered the pontiff’s spirit: his obstinacy in resisting Gregory’s most pious and necessary efforts to reform the clergy; and his inconsistency, since he so often broke the pledges he had given. To these things was added the fact that he confined the pontiff himself in custody at Rome and installed Guibert as antipope in his place.

In such matters, and in others of the same kind, it is impossible always to observe moderation without exceeding it in some respect. But if Gregory’s adversaries assailed him with insults, sufficiently and more than sufficiently vindicated him were the not insignificant writers of that age. It is preferable to refer the reader to them rather than say more about a familiar and slippery subject.

More than a hundred years had already passed since the sacred celibacy of the clergy—until that time unstained, consecrated by the practice of so many centuries and by the chastity and authority of so many great men—had been assailed by certain incontinent and corrupt ministers of the Church, when unworthy pontiffs occupied the Roman See. Matters had reached the point that some priests were not ashamed to take wives publicly.

One of the earliest examples of this is found in a certain priest of the parish of Châlons [Col. 0149B] in Gaul, named Angelricus (Analecta, vol. III, p. 438), who had betrothed a woman before his parishioners. When he was proceeding to take her into his house, good, devout, and faithful men resisted his wicked attempt and accused him before Bishop Mantio. Summoned into the bishop’s presence at the synod held at Châlons on 5 May, he confessed his guilt. The bishop then sent him to Fulco, the metropolitan, uncertain and doubtful what correction and punishment should be imposed upon this new and evil presumption.

What Fulco wrote in reply on this matter is not known. Nevertheless, from Mantio’s letter we understand that this crime was then new and unprecedented. Gradually, however, this abnormal license advanced so far that in the eleventh century it had almost stripped away the disgrace that deserved public infamy.

Nicholas II judged that such a great disgrace to the Church had to be confronted by issuing a decree against clerics living in concubinage. Since this plague was especially prevalent among the Milanese clergy, he sent there Cardinal Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, together with Bishop Anselm of Lucca, so that they might strive to reform it and at the same time remove the stain of Simony that had infected the ministers of that Church.

The clergy assembled at a synod before the legates with such an uproar that they scarcely refrained from laying hands upon them. At last, however, the sedition was calmed by Peter Damian’s speech and prudence, and the clergy swore that henceforth they would live more chastely and purely. Peter Damian recounts all this at length in his letter to Hildebrand, then archdeacon of the Roman Church; there is no doubt that the matter was undertaken at his prompting and on his advice.

But once Hildebrand became supreme pontiff, he advanced everywhere the work that had been begun, in whatever manner, and finally completed it. The immoral clergy raged against him and cast accusations upon his chastity, but their attempt was so futile that, as Lambert of Hersfeld says, “the dignity of his life admitted not even the slightest stain of sinister rumor upon his conduct.” Certainly, even to Bennō, a schismatic cardinal and Gregory’s most bitter enemy, this accusation seemed so monstrous and beyond all belief that, although he invented many charges against Gregory, he never brought this crime against him. We shall say no more about these matters, since they are obvious to everyone.

As for investitures, a long struggle with the emperors was necessary before the rights of both empires, the sacred and the secular, could finally be preserved. After many disputes, in which matters reached the extreme—not without blame on both sides—the issue was at last settled under Callistus II in this way: instead of the ring and staff, which they had been accustomed to give to new bishops, the emperors invested them only by handing over a scepter. This signified that the bishops received temporal rights from the emperor, which he had claimed for himself through investitures, but did not receive spiritual rights, which the pontiffs rightly denied him.

If this method of settling the dispute had been adopted from the beginning, many and very great scandals, wars, and killings would have been avoided. Abbot Goffrid of Vendôme published on this subject a short but learned and substantial treatise, in which he correctly distinguishes the rights of the Church and of the kingdom.

As Gregory lay near death, the cardinals asked his advice. He replied that, if they wanted a man powerful in worldly affairs, they should elect Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who would break the [probably: violent] power of the antipope Wibert; but if they wanted an ecclesiastical and eloquent man, they should accept Odo, bishop of Ostia.

Thus died a man of blessed grace before God, though perhaps of excessive austerity in the eyes of men, says William of Malmesbury (*William, book III, On the Kings of England*).

[Col. 0149]

# The Life, Election, and Deeds of Saint Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiff

By Onuphrius Panvinus  
*(Book IV, On the Various Creations of Roman Pontiffs.)*  
Edited by Gretser, volume II of his works, p. 97, from the Bavarian Library.

## To the Reader

I wish to warn you briefly, Christian reader, that Onuphrius, while following too hastily in the footsteps of Sigebert, the Ursperger, and Aventinus, occasionally departed from the straight path—as commonly happens to those who choose as their guides schismatic writers, such as Sigebert, or writers of unsound faith and doctrine, such as Aventinus, without carefully examining each of the things they report.

But you have the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, whose thread will keep you from ever straying from the truth, in the eleventh volume of his *Annals*. There he treats copiously and faithfully of the life and deeds of Gregory VII from the year 1073 to the year 1085. From that work we have also appended notes to this commentary of Onuphrius.

I believe it happened by divine providence that, while sectarians were advancing in crowds to suppress the name and honor of this pontiff beneath immense heaps of accusations fabricated and piled up against him—some new, some ancient—there arose on the other side men from among the orthodox who opposed their ruinous efforts and rescued the glory of the magnanimous pontiff from the clouds raised by those agents of darkness. We have likewise wished to imitate their zeal on behalf of the excellent pontiff.

Moreover, among the other detractors of Gregory VII there has recently appeared the posthumous book of Witackerus, who in his *Controversy concerning the Supreme Pontiff*, question 6, could not restrain himself from hurling against this pontiff the darts of his own venomous style and pen.

But what sort of darts? Trivial, and therefore blunt; for they were drawn from the quivers of Bennō and Sigebert, one of whom was Gregory’s sworn enemy and the other his most sworn enemy. I laughed when Witackerus called Bennō a learned man. What sort of learned man was he, whose entire commentary is nothing but ignorance and madness; whose style is one continuous barbarism and solecism? Evidently, in the judgment of the sectarians, anyone is learned who pours forth outrageous calumnies against the pope, even if he does so most foolishly and ignorantly—as Bennō did, who possessed so little intelligence that he was unable to slander aptly and cleverly.

The other witnesses cited by Witackerus are of the same sort: the council of Brixen, Aventinus, and the clergy reported by Lambert and Nauclerus. Since they found it difficult to endure Gregory’s placing a restraint upon their fornication, Simony, and other crimes, they persisted in raging against him with insults, as usually happens when someone attempts to take away from another what he desperately lacks.

Witackerus cannot digest the fact that the pope admitted and heard Henry, who was humbly seeking absolution from excommunication, only after three days, when the emperor had laid aside his imperial insignia and stood barefoot while everything was rigid with frost. “What Luciferian pride was this!” Witackerus cries. “Was this a good man? In this matter he certainly surpassed the devil himself in wickedness and pride.”

Not at all, O Calvinist. A persistent disease required sharp medicine; and the sacrilege of schism, committed at such great cost to the empire, had to be expiated by a harsher punishment. Henry’s changeable and inconsistent spirit also had to be tested, to determine whether he was seriously considering better conduct.

To do penance barefoot, laying aside every adornment of the body and wearing garments suited to mourning and sorrow, and to seek the favor and friendship of the one who had been offended, was entirely customary in the ecclesiastical court, and is so also in the civil court.

Hear, Calvinist, what Henry himself did, not toward one but toward many princes of Saxony, when they wished to be restored to Henry’s favor. I shall not use my own words here, but those of the Lutheran Fabricius in book III of his *Origins of Saxony*:

“There was a broad, open plain called Spiraugia. There the king solemnly sat upon his throne, resplendent in gold and purple. The army, arranged for the spectacle, stood around him, leaving an open space through the middle so that the passing Saxon dukes and bishops might be visible to everyone.

“The prelates advanced in mourning attire: Uvezelo of Magdeburg, Bucco of Halberstadt, Bennō of Meissen, and Uvernerus of Merseburg. Among the dukes were Otto of Göttingen, an exile from Bavaria; Magnus, Elector of Saxony; Hermann, his uncle and count of Saxony; Frederick, count palatine of Saxony; Ditericus, count of Katlenburg; and Albert of Thuringia. There were also the counts Rudigerus, Sizzo, Beringarius, Berno, and five others, including Siffridus, though their surnames are not given.

“Large columns of men of noble, free, and distinguished birth followed them. When they came into the king’s sight, they threw themselves at his feet in filthy clothing. He allowed them to lie there until their misery had satisfied his spirit and his countenance.”

This is what the Lutheran Fabricius says about Henry, who, contrary to his pledged word, cast all those suppliant princes into chains and sent them away, carefully guarded, to various provinces, separated from one another. They might perhaps never have escaped if everything had succeeded according to Henry’s wishes.

I ask: who was harsher toward suppliants, Henry or Gregory? Gregory absolved Henry after three days of submission—of whatever quality, but certainly not to be despised if it was sincere; and if it was then sincere, it would have been constant. But Henry imprisoned all those princes who had voluntarily surrendered themselves, solely so that no more Christian blood might be shed, contrary to the agreements, and treated them with complete indignity. If fear of a greater evil had not prevented him, he would have put them to death, especially Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt, whom he hated with the utmost severity.

But now, leaving Witackerus aside, let us hear Onuphrius.

# The Life, Election, Deeds, and Constitutions of Pope Gregory VII Concerning the New Election of the Roman Pontiff

[Col. 0151]

[Col. 0151A] In describing the assembly by which Gregory VII was proclaimed pope, and the regulations that he established concerning the election, it will not be foreign to our purpose to repeat a few things that I said about him in the proclamation of Pope Leo IX and to add other matters, so that it may be understood what sort of man he was before his pontificate and on what occasion he accomplished so many and such great deeds, worthy of remembrance, against the emperor Henry IV for ecclesiastical liberty.

[Col. 0152A] Gregory VII, previously called Hildebrand, was Tuscan by nation, a native of Soana, and born of noble stock. He belonged to the family that was later called Hildebrandine after him, or “of Pitigliano,” of which town he was at one time lord. His father was named Bonitus, an energetic man.

As a young man of outstanding ability, he went to the imperial court, where he made great progress. There, having incurred envy on account of his virtue, he yielded to the fury of many and withdrew into religion. For he professed the monastic life in the monastery of Cluny, then filled with the holiest men, under Abbot Odilo.

Some say [Note: So Baronius, *Annals*, 1073, no. 16] that he was born in the lowest and almost sordid station, was the son of a carpenter, and, while still a boy, went to the imperial court, where he grew up in the court of Emperor Conrad and of his son Henry III.

Some unknown storyteller invents awkward little tales about him. He says that, because he was the son of a carpenter, he arranged twigs in order and, without knowing it, formed these letters, which a literate man standing nearby read as: “I shall rule from sea to sea.” Others say that, guided more by prophetic inspiration than by instruction, he showed that he would become [Col. 0153B] “lord from sea to sea.”

From this the literate man inferred that there was something divine in the boy and advised his father to give him over to letters. Once entrusted to study, he progressed so far that he reached the emperor’s chancery. [Note: On this dream Baronius says nothing; it has the flavor of a fable, as Onuphrius correctly judges.]

There, after the emperor had been warned in a dream about this same clerk of his—for the man seemed to have horns with which he would crush the emperor’s son—the emperor threw him into chains. He was freed from them by the empress Agnes, sought the monastery of Cluny, and there advanced first to the subdiaconate, then to the cardinalate, and finally to become Pope Gregory VII.

But I declare that this was the invention of a most frivolous man and deserves ridicule.

It is nevertheless sufficiently established that Hildebrand went from the imperial court to the monastery of Cluny. There, when he had grown into a man whom everyone judged especially suited to the conduct of affairs and exceptionally discerning and prudent, he was sent to Rome by the same abbot to transact the business of the monastery and congregation of Cluny at the Apostolic See.

For a long time he lived honorably in the monastery of Saints Lawrence and Stephen outside the walls of the City, during the pontificate of Benedict IX [Note: Benedict began his pontificate in 1040]. At that time he enjoyed the closest friendship of John Gratian, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and archpriest of Saint John before the Latin Gate. John later became Roman pontiff after three schismatics had abdicated and was called Gregory VI [Note: Elected in 1044].

Gregory VI greatly loved Hildebrand, who was already a monk, because of his most agreeable character, prudence, and remarkable learning.

When Gregory was deprived of the pontificate by the authority of Emperor Henry III at the council assembled at Sutri [Note: See Baronius, 1046], Hildebrand, mindful of their friendship and of the benefits he had received, followed him all the way to his monastery of Cluny, to which he had been banished by Emperor Henry in order to avoid schism. Not long afterward Gregory himself died there, worn out by grief.

It happened that in the same year the prior of the monastery of Cluny—the second dignity after the abbot—died. Therefore, immediately, with the consent of the abbot and the monks, that office was entrusted to Hildebrand. [Note: Read Baronius, year 1049.]

At that time Bruno, elected Roman pontiff, happened to be passing from Cluny, or through Besançon. Hildebrand secretly met him and, full of zeal for the honor of God, steadfastly reproved him concerning the novelty itself. He declared that it was wholly improper and contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers that the greatest pontiff of the Christian world should be thrust by a lay hand into the governance of the entire Church.

He added that, if Bruno were willing to follow his counsels, he would bring about both that Bruno would not incur the emperor’s displeasure on this account and that ecclesiastical liberty would remain unharmed and preserved through a legitimate and just ordination of the pontiff.

The pious and holy man humbly obeyed his admonitions [Col. 0154B]. He immediately removed his purple garment and the other pontifical vestments, adopted the dress of a pilgrim, and took with him the monk Hildebrand, who had given him such salutary advice. He then set out toward Rome with the Roman legates and other companions, including bishops.

He was received in Rome with the greatest honor. On the day after his arrival, when the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people had assembled in the basilica of Saint Peter, he addressed them in these words, having been instructed by Hildebrand:

“Brothers and friends most dear to me in Christ, having learned of your embassy, I went to the emperor to inquire into his will and intention—not in order to be elected Roman pontiff by him [Note: The emperor has no right in the election of the pontiff], for I know that he possesses no right in such an election [Col. 0154C], but because the matter belongs freely to you.

“I have come here for no other reason than to visit the thresholds of the apostles. Since this Apostolic See has long been vacant of a shepherd, it is no longer fitting that it remain so. Therefore I exhort and admonish all of you to choose for yourselves as soon as possible, without any delay, a suitable shepherd and bishop.”

Immediately, by Hildebrand’s advice, all the cardinal bishops and the other nobles replied: “We want you alone, and no other, and we elect you Roman pontiff.”

Then the archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, according to ancestral custom, cried out: “Saint Peter has chosen Bishop Bruno.”

While the entire clergy and people repeated the same cry, he was immediately seized by everyone and placed upon the pontifical throne. He was consecrated pontiff by the cardinal bishops and crowned with the diadem of the Holy Roman Church in Rome, in the basilica of Saint Peter at the Vatican, with the clergy and people standing by, on the Sunday before the first Sunday of Lent, on the day before the Ides of February in the year of the Lord 1059. He was called Leo IX.

He sat upon the Apostolic See for five years, two months, and eight days.

After he had been consecrated pontiff, Leo created the monk Hildebrand, on whose sound advice all these things had been accomplished, cardinal subdeacon, custodian of the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle, treasurer of the Holy Roman Church, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul outside the walls of the City on the Ostian Way [Col. 0155A]. Later he spent almost the whole period of his pontificate relying upon Hildebrand’s advice and authority in everything.

At Hildebrand’s urging, the blessed pontiff, among the many things he did, also held a synod in which numerous decrees were enacted against married priests and Simoniac bishops.

After Leo’s death, Hildebrand, as legate of the clergy, senate, and Roman people, was sent to the emperor to request a new pontiff from him. When Bishop Gebhard of Eichstätt had been elected by the emperor and called Victor II [Note: See Baronius, years 1054 and 1055], Hildebrand brought him to Rome for consecration.

He also exercised very great influence with Victor, as he had with Leo IX, in all matters. He was a man highly distinguished by his skill in conducting affairs, and to this he added the greatest religious devotion and strictness of life.

After the death of Victor II, Hildebrand, although still only a subdeacon, was considered worthy of the Roman pontificate. But when Pope Stephen IX [Note: X; see Baronius, year 1058] was placed over him and made Roman pontiff, Hildebrand also possessed the greatest authority with him.

Because the stain of Simony was spreading throughout Italy and Gaul [Note: This occurred under Victor II; Baronius, year 1035, no. 15 and following], Stephen sent Hildebrand as legate of the Apostolic See into Gaul with several bishops, so that he might preside in the apostolic capacity over the synod that Stephen had ordered to be assembled at Lyon against the Simoniac prelates.

At that synod Hildebrand’s virtue and religious devotion shone forth most brightly. While all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots were seated in council, a certain learned and eloquent archbishop was accused of having purchased his bishopric.

After corrupting all his accusers by lavish gifts, he returned to the synod on the following day and said with great boldness: “Where are my accusers? Let them rise publicly against me; let them come forward now.”

When everyone remained silent, Hildebrand rose and, turning to him, said: “Do you believe, archbishop, that the Holy Spirit is of the same substance and divinity as the Father and the Son?”

When he answered that he did, Hildebrand said: “Say, ‘Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.’”

When the archbishop began the verse, he readily said, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son,” but he was utterly unable to utter the words concerning the Holy Spirit [Col. 0155D].

When he repeated the attempt many times without success, he realized that he had been convicted by divine judgment. Throwing himself at the legate’s feet, he confessed his error in full.

When, by the judgment of all, he was immediately deprived of the episcopal office, he sang, in a free and fluent voice: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

This event so terrified the remaining Simoniac prelates that seventeen of them confessed that they had been Simoniacs and renounced the bishoprics they had purchased [Col. 0156A].

After the synod had been held and ecclesiastical affairs arranged with great foresight, Hildebrand returned to the City.

Then Pope Stephen IX sent him as legate of the Apostolic See to the emperor and to his adolescent son, Henry IV, after the solemn oath that all the bishops and cardinals had sworn to him—not to elect a Roman pontiff, if he should die, until Hildebrand, who was then being sent to the emperor concerning this matter, had returned [Note: Baronius, year 1058, who reports the matter differently from Leo of Ostia].

When Hildebrand returned after hearing of Stephen IX’s death, he annulled by his authority Benedict X, who had invaded the Apostolic See after Stephen [Note: Baronius, years 1058 and 1059], and Nicholas II was proclaimed supreme pontiff [Col. 0156B].

Mindful of the service he had received—for he attributed to Hildebrand the fact that he was Roman pontiff—Nicholas created him archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church after Mincius. Hildebrand possessed such favor and authority with Nicholas himself that the pontiff never decided anything without consulting him.

After Nicholas’s death, Hildebrand, concerned for ecclesiastical liberty and already aspiring to wrest the election of the Roman pontiff from the hands of the emperors, was the principal force behind the beginning of the Roman Church’s recovery of the liberty that it had long lost in the election of its pontiffs.

He secured the annulment of Cadolus, bishop of Parma, who had been elected by the emperor [Note: Baronius, year 1061], and arranged for Anselm, bishop of Lucca, to be elected at Rome by the free votes of the cardinals. He vigorously defended the cause of Anselm, already elected and consecrated [Col. 0156C].

Through Hildebrand’s efforts it was finally accomplished that Cadolus himself [Note: Called Cadalaus by others], who had twice come to Rome with armed forces to occupy the See of Saint Peter, was twice repulsed by force with the aid of Duke Godfrey and driven from the City. Finally, at the council assembled at Mantua for this reason, the pontificate was taken from him by the judgment of the synod, while the ordination of Pope Alexander II was approved as having been carried out by legitimate votes.

For Alexander II, Hildebrand recovered the patrimony of Saint Peter in Campania, which the Normans had occupied, by summoning Duke Godfrey with his own army and that of Countess Matilda, defeating the Normans, and recovering the territory.

[Note: Baronius, year 1073.] At last, when Alexander died at the Lateran [Col. 0156D], on the day of his death, Hildebrand—who was most learned in sacred letters and, during the time of so many preceding pontiffs, celebrated in the Roman Church for every kind of virtue—was proclaimed supreme pontiff by the votes of all the cardinals, clergy, and Roman people, amid immense joy and with the unanimous and complete agreement of everyone, without awaiting any consent or will of the emperor.

[Note: This was not the true cause of the schism, but Henry’s obstinacy, since at the beginning he approved Gregory’s election.]

From this event a most serious schism later arose, the occasion being that Gregory had been established solely by the election of the Roman clergy, without the emperor’s consent.

Gregory himself, who for a long time—from the deposition of Pope Gregory VI onward—had labored to obtain ecclesiastical liberty, now that he had been elevated to the pontificate considered it disgraceful to abandon what he had begun. For this reason, as well as to eradicate Simony and suppress the incontinence of the clergy, he worked with the greatest zeal.
