Finally, he not only summoned the emperor frequently to synodal hearings for such matters, but also, by issuing decrees, prohibited throughout the Roman world the marriages of clerics from the subdiaconate to the episcopate. Having become a model for the flock, he demonstrated by example what he taught in words; and, as a strong athlete in all things, he did not fear to set himself as a wall for the house of the Lord.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord 1073, after Pope Alexander II had died and been honorably buried in the Lateran Basilica, on the very day of his death and burial—namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of May—while the archdeacon Hildebrand was still occupied with his obsequies [read: funeral rites], a great crowd of the Roman clergy and people suddenly gathered in the church, crying out and saying: “Saint Peter has chosen Hildebrand the archdeacon.”

When the archdeacon himself heard this, he was extremely afraid, fearing the many disadvantages that commonly arise from such tumultuous elections—for he was a most prudent man.

He therefore ran to the pulpit in the middle of the Lateran church, intending to address and calm the people and to advise and exhort them to abandon this innovation. It was contrary both to the canons, which ordered that no new pontiff be elected before the third day after the death of the shepherd, and to the custom then in use, according to which the emperor was consulted in the election of a new Roman pontiff.

But because, amid the uproar and the speed of the enraged people, he could not do this—chiefly because of the urging of Hugo Blancus of Trent, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement and archpriest of the Holy Roman Church [Note: He later defected from Gregory to the schismatics], who, after learning that all the votes were directed toward Hildebrand, abandoned his initial undertaking in order to obstruct the archdeacon’s election and seek the Roman pontificate, which he had greatly desired—Hildebrand was forcibly seized and led to the Title of Saint Peter in Chains, called that of Eudoxia.

There, on that very day, he was proclaimed Roman pontiff in place of Pope Alexander, with the complete agreement of all, by the cardinals, clergy, senate, and Roman people. He was a monk and archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, and the election took place contrary to the custom of that time, without consulting the emperor and without his authority—or that of the bishops and princes of Germany—being interposed or awaited.

He sat upon the Apostolic See while the emperor Caesar Henry IV Augustus was reigning for twelve years, one month, and three days.

It is pleasing to add how he was created and how great his reputation then was in the Roman Church, drawing upon the form of his election recorded in his *Book of the Register*, as follows:

“While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns . . . . The remainder may be seen in the *Register*.”

Then Cardinal Hugh Candidus, priest of the title of Saint Clement, when Gregory himself had been proclaimed pope by the cardinals contrary to Hugh’s opinion, laid aside his hostility and, for a time, assumed a semblance of friendship [Note: Just as no violence is permanent, so nothing feigned lasts long. Accordingly, shortly afterward this Hugh removed his mask].

Since he was archpriest of the Holy Roman Church, he pronounced, on behalf of all the cardinals, a laudatory address honoring Gregory’s creation and seeking his favor, in the customary manner:

“Most noble citizens, none of you has ever doubted that Hildebrand, archdeacon of our Church, a most prudent man and one whose faith and integrity have been tested before all, has from the time of Leo IX adorned it wondrously by his virtues, increased it by his labors, protected it by his zeal and industry, and rescued it from many dangers.

“Therefore, since the Fathers have judged that no one is better suited to govern our city and the Roman Church, I, in the name of all the cardinal bishops, priests, and deacons of the Holy Roman Church, with everyone consenting to the election, proclaim him before us and you as Roman bishop and shepherd of our souls.”

After this, Gregory was immediately seized, dressed according to ancestral custom in a purple garment, crowned with the pontifical diadem, and, although unwilling and resisting, magnificently placed upon the Apostolic See amid the greatest joy and happiness.

For they believed that he alone was able and willing to restore ecclesiastical affairs, to rescue the Roman Church, long enslaved, from the emperor’s hands, and to vindicate and restore it to its former liberty.

After being elected Roman pontiff, Hildebrand wrote, according to ancestral custom, letters to the abbot of Monte Cassino and the archbishop of Ravenna [Note: Onuphrius recites these letters. We have omitted them for the sake of brevity. They are found in volume III of the *Decretal Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, Roman edition, pp. 550–551; in volume III of the new edition of the Councils, Cologne; and in Baronius, volume XI, year 1073]. In them he informed them of the form and manner of his election.

After Hildebrand the archdeacon had been elected Roman pontiff, he judged that the opportune time had come when, now proclaimed supreme pontiff, he could assert the ecclesiastical liberty for which he had labored so intensely as a private individual, both for the Roman Church and for the other churches, and restore everything to its former freedom.

Yet he began to grieve and struggle intensely within himself and to consider into how many grave dangers of schism and other calamities he would cast himself and the Roman Church if he wished to retain the pontificate once assumed. He had been created Roman pontiff contrary to custom and without the consent of the emperor and the princes of Germany.

He remembered the evils, seditions, and schism that had arisen at the election of Alexander II through the emperor and Cadolus [Cadalaus]. He feared the most powerful emperor, the young, bold, and exceedingly fierce Henry IV, whom he believed would not allow the rights of the empire to be lost [Note: But they were not rights].

Moreover, he was troubled because he knew that he was hated by many princes of Germany and by bishops of great renown [Note: But by Simoniacs and men living in concubinage]. For, having often been sent as legate to the imperial court under his predecessors, he had incurred the greatest hostility of the bishops and stirred up their hatred against himself. He was thought to be excessively harsh, severe, and extremely tenacious of ecclesiastical rigor.

He was all the more distressed because he believed that, if the opportunity to restore the Church to its former liberty were removed at that time, no such favorable opportunity could ever arise again. For the emperor was then still a young man and had not yet been fully established in the empire. He was also being harassed in Saxony by the greatest storms of war, which prevented him above all from turning his attention to other matters [Note: See Bruno, *On the Saxon War*].

Many men of the highest rank among the Saxons had defected from him and were plotting the greatest rebellions. Gregory believed that he himself would lack neither courage nor strength to accomplish all these things.

He knew very well, indeed, what a great undertaking he was attempting and how difficult, arduous, and dangerous it was. He also thought that in the future it would be difficult for any Roman pontiff to dare such things, taking the example of his predecessors.

Although he had repeatedly persuaded Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II to undertake these measures, they had never dared to attempt them, fearing the power of the emperor, who possessed everything.

If he himself did not succeed in being confirmed as Roman pontiff, he thought that all would be lost concerning ecclesiastical liberty, for which he yearned with all his strength. He believed that he alone was suited to so great an undertaking.

So that at no time a dispute might arise that the pontiff had been elected and consecrated by insufficiently legitimate votes, and that for this reason he might at some point have to contend with the emperor concerning the pontificate—an outcome he knew the emperor would endure very gravely—because he himself had been proclaimed Roman pontiff without the emperor’s knowledge and contrary to custom and to the privileges of his ancestors, granted by the Apostolic See to emperors [Col. 0159D] [Note: No privileges of this kind exist; those that appear to exist are fictitious]—and so that his ordination might be regarded by everyone as legitimate and never thereafter called into question (for, had that happened, he could have accomplished none of what he had planned), he could never be induced by any means to consent to being consecrated and crowned until he had ascertained the wishes of the emperor and the princes concerning his election [Note: [Col. 0160D] See Baronius, 1073 and 1074].

Immediately after his election, therefore, he wrote to the Imperial Prefect in Italy concerning his elevation. In the same manner, through his legates, he reported to the emperor Henry IV, then in Germany, the cause and circumstances of his election, which had been imposed upon him by the violence of the Romans [Col. 0160A]. He asserted that, although he had been elected because he could not resist the will of the enraged populace, he had nevertheless never wished, nor did he now wish, to be consecrated, and that he would never accept the administration of the pontificate unless the consent of the emperor and of the bishops and princes of Germany were first present. For this reason, as soon as he had been released by the people after his election, he had immediately withdrawn to Albano outside the City, lest he should be compelled, contrary to custom, to receive the office of consecration from that same people.

When he had received the emperor’s letters and an assembly of bishops had been convened, Gregory VII’s election was carefully examined [Note: [Col. 0160D] The king and the princes approve Gregory’s election. See Henry’s Letters, book I, letter 29; Baronius, 1073]. When the emperor learned that it was legitimate and had been carried out by the free votes of all, both the Roman clergy and the people, he and the other princes wished it to be ratified and gave their consent to it.

There were, however, in that assembly many prelates, bishops, and abbots of Germany who, moved by serious scruples, opposed the same election. They knew very well the character of Hildebrand himself, his deeds, his unbending constancy, his most fervent zeal for divine honor, and his tenacious determination to carry out his purpose, over the many preceding years during which he had lived at the imperial court, both as a private person and in public legations of the Holy Roman Church. They feared that a man of vehement intellect and ardent faith toward God might one day subject them to a stricter examination for their negligence and demand a more exact account from them of the flocks entrusted to them [Col. 0160C].

These men, acting by common agreement, approached the Emperor and suggested to him that Hildebrand in particular had to be guarded against. They tried to persuade him by every means not to consent to the election of a man who would become his bitterest enemy in so supreme and exalted an office, but to declare it invalid as having been made without his command. They predicted that, unless he hastened to forestall the man’s assault, the Roman Empire would suffer the greatest loss at his hands and the emperor himself would be embroiled by him in many calamities and misfortunes; indeed, they said that this evil would ultimately rebound upon no one more gravely than upon Caesar himself [Col. 0160D]. They also affirmed as certain what later came to pass: that Gregory would care for nothing more than to wrest the appointment of bishops and abbots from the emperor’s hands and authority and to bring the empire itself wholly to ruin.

After hearing this, the king was somewhat disturbed and ordered Count Eberhard to go from his side and meet with the Roman nobles, asking them why, contrary to the custom of their ancestors and without consulting the king at least, they had elected a pontiff of the Roman Church. If he did not give a satisfactory answer, he was to order the pope to resign the dignity he had illicitly accepted [Col. 0161A].

When Eberhard came to Rome, Pope Gregory received him kindly. After Eberhard had explained the king’s command, Gregory replied, as he had written to the king, that—God as his witness—he had never sought the summit of this honor through ambition. Rather, he had been elected by the Romans, and the necessity of ecclesiastical government had been violently imposed upon him. Nevertheless, he could in no way be compelled to permit himself to be ordained until he had learned by a reliable embassy that both the king and the princes of the Teutonic kingdom had consented to his election. For this reason he had postponed his ordination and would unquestionably continue to postpone it until a trustworthy messenger arriving from there disclosed the king’s will to him.

When this was reported to the king, he gladly accepted the answer, since divine will was thus arranging human affairs: the Roman Empire was destined to be diminished by priestly power and almost reduced to nothing. He therefore decided that the bishops who seemed to be speaking the truth, and who recognized future events as they recognized past ones, were by no means to be heeded. He declared Gregory to be a holy man, most worthy of so great a priesthood, and one who would never forget a benefit received from him. He immediately wrote back with the most joyful assent that Gregory should be consecrated, and sent to the City Gregory, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of the Italian kingdom, so that, by imperial authority, he might ratify the election and be present at Gregory’s consecration.

Thus Gregory, contrary to expectation, obtained what he had desired so greatly—namely, that the emperor should consent to his election—and, judging that nothing should be delayed, had himself ordained a priest at the approaching feast of Pentecost. On the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul he was consecrated Roman pontiff and received the insignia of his coronation.

Having thus been confirmed in the Roman See, so that no further hesitation might seem able to enter anyone’s mind concerning the legitimacy of his elevation—for he had already been elected and consecrated by the cardinals, clergy, senate, and people of Rome, with the consent and approval of the emperor and the princes, and was then regarded as the legitimate, true, and unquestioned pontiff—he soon after his consecration prepared to put into execution what he had long conceived in his mind.

For he was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to attempt to deprive the emperor not only of the election of the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0161D] Because that authority did not belong to him], as Adrian III had once also done, but also of every authority by which he appointed the other prelates, namely bishops and abbots [Note: [Col. 0161D] He did this without any legitimate authority]. If necessary, he intended to excommunicate the emperor should he refuse obedience and to depose him from the empire; those who received prelacies from him were likewise to be struck by the sword of anathema.

But since these were matters of great weight, and he did not expect them to succeed so easily, he decided to begin gradually and little by little. He spent almost the entire first year of his pontificate on such plans, until mid-Lent, the time prescribed by his predecessors for convening a synod [Col. 0162A].

In the year of the Lord 1074, therefore, still the first year of his pontificate, at the appointed time he laid the foundations for recovering ecclesiastical liberty. In mid-Lent he first convened at Rome, in the Lateran basilica called Constantiniana, a general synod of many bishops, abbots, and other prelates. There he issued about thirty chapters [Note: [Col. 0161D] Baronius maintains that these chapters were written and issued at the synod of 1076], or canons, which he called *dictates*. Most of them had previously been little observed and had never been attempted by any of his predecessors [Col. 0162B]; yet they were well suited to laying the firmest foundations for the Church’s status and to attempting everything he had been considering. From them it could be understood what authority the Roman pontiff then possessed. Among them were especially the following chapters:

*(We omit them for the sake of brevity. See below in the Roman council of the year 1076.)*

By these decrees [Note: [Col. 0161D] All these matters are derived from divine law, partly directly and partly indirectly. The pontiff enacted nothing new, but only what had fallen into oblivion among many] he prepared a step and a road for himself toward carrying out everything he had conceived. After these decrees had been laid down and the foundations established in the synod, he first courteously and humanely entreated King Henry by letter not to reject subjection to the holy Roman Church, as a good and Catholic [Col. 0162C] prince, but to show himself a devoted son of that Church.

He urged him entirely to refrain from the Simoniac heresy—that is, from the sale or traffic of bishoprics and abbeys, which he conferred upon those whom he had been bribed to favor—and to restrain himself from the other vices of which he had been denounced and accused before the Apostolic See, both under his predecessor Pope Alexander II and under Gregory after his elevation to the pontificate. Otherwise, he warned, he would use ecclesiastical censures against him and against those who transgressed.

So that all these matters may be understood more accurately, and so that it may be known from where the origin of so many evils and schisms began, I shall relate the custom of those times and trace its beginnings somewhat further back.

[Col. 0162D] At that time there existed a custom, introduced from the time of the emperor Charlemagne, first through the authority of Pope Adrian I [Note: [Col. 0162D] This is not so. Sigebert deceived Onuphrius; Baronius thoroughly refutes him, volume IX, year of Christ 774, no. 10 and following], that when the bishop of some city or abbey, or an abbot, died, the clergy or monks would immediately assemble and send legates to the emperor then reigning. They would bring to him the deceased prelate’s episcopal staff and ring and, in the name of their community, petition him to choose a new bishop.

The emperor would then immediately convene his council and, usually following its advice [Col. 0163A], would select at his discretion, according to the dignity of the place, someone either from those communities or from among his friends, chaplains, other household members, and familiar associates. When the ring and pastoral staff of the deceased prelate had been sent to him, he would bestow them upon the person he had chosen and order him to be consecrated bishop or abbot, having been invested—so it was then said—with that priesthood by his imperial charter, that is, having been granted that dignity, without any further election by the clergy or monks.

This custom was practiced throughout Gaul, Germany, and Italy, which were then regarded as the Latin world.

Following its example, other kings also adopted it, including those of Spain, the Franks, Hungary, and similar realms. This custom was observed not only, as I have said, by all the Churches of the Latin world, but also often and for a long time by the Roman Church in the elections of several of its pontiffs, especially in the elections of John XIII, Gregory V, Sylvester, Clement, Damasus, Victor, Nicholas II, and Leo IX, all of whom, as we saw above, were elected as Roman pontiffs by the decision of the emperors Otto I and Otto III and also Henry III and Henry IV, without the votes of the Roman clergy, and were invested in the Roman papacy by those same emperors through the ring and staff.

William of Tyre, writing about four hundred years ago in book I, chapter 13 of *The Sacred War*, reports this matter as follows [Note: [Col. 0163] Tyre did report this, but he did not approve it; indeed, he expressly disapproved of it and regarded it as a detestable custom]:

“Henry, the Teutonic king and likewise Roman emperor, had endured from Pope Gregory VII a dispute and no small controversy concerning the ring and staff of deceased bishops. For a custom had grown up, especially in the empire, that when prelates of churches died, the ring and pastoral staff were sent to the lord emperor. He would then send one of his household members or chaplains, invested by him, to the vacant church, so that he might perform there the office of shepherd, without awaiting the election of the clergy. Pope Gregory, recognizing that this was done contrary to all propriety and perceiving that ecclesiastical rights were being trampled underfoot by this act, admonished the same emperor once, twice, and three times to desist from so detestable a presumption. When he could not recall him despite these salutary admonitions, he bound him with the bond of anathema. The emperor bore this deed with extreme indignation, and so forth.”

Since all these matters are not unworthy of fuller understanding [Col. 0163D], I shall now briefly retrace them from the beginning and review in concise language what I wrote above in two books.

After the times of the emperor Justinian, when the Goths had finally been driven from Italy—which they had possessed for seventy-seven years—by his generals Belisarius and Narses in an eighteen-year war, Vigilius, who was then Roman pontiff, and the supreme pontiffs who followed him remained for a long time under the authority and protection of the Constantinopolitan Empire in Rome and in that part of Italy which the Lombards were unable to occupy. This continued until the times of Leo the Iconoclast and Pope Gregory II [Col. 0164A].

During that period the Lombards, entering Italy from Pannonia under the younger Justin Augustus, first seized its more important part and then gradually almost all of it, except Rome alone. Rome, as is clear, never came under the power of that people, because the Roman pontiffs, strongly supported by the aid and protection of the Eastern emperors, defended it vigorously against them.

After the Greeks had been driven out or killed by the Lombards, and Ravenna and the Exarchate—the only province remaining under the rule of the Constantinopolitan emperor—had been captured, the Lombards under King Aistulf also longed for Rome. They inflicted many calamities and hardships upon the Romans, who, at the urging of the pontiffs, refused to surrender.

The Roman pontiffs feared the Lombards’ ferocity and barbarism. They also feared that, while the Greek emperors neglected Rome, the Lombards might seize the city, which had become their possession and of which they regarded themselves as masters. At that time, as the majesty of the Roman Empire in the East grew obsolete and gradually declined while the barbarians claimed everything for themselves, the Constantinopolitan emperors fell into heresy and attacked the orthodox faith and the Catholic Roman Church, which refused to agree with them, over the removal of images.

The Roman pontiffs could never be induced to subscribe to the impious decrees for abolishing images. Indeed, they undertook to defend the images against the fury of the Eastern emperors. For these reasons the Roman Church, deprived of the Eastern assistance by which it had until then defended its liberty against the Lombards, began to look toward and turn to the power and strength of the Franks, who at that time were flourishing especially in the West, and to ask their aid against Lombard arrogance [Col. 0164C].

For Stephen II was the first, when he was being oppressed by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, to obtain assistance against the Lombards from Pippin, king of the Franks and father of Charles, later emperor. Pippin came to Italy and splendidly protected the city of Rome and the Apostolic See. After defeating Aistulf in battle and compelling him to accept terms of peace, he kept him in obedience for a long time, as long as he lived. He also gave to the Roman Church, for the first time, the Exarchate of Ravenna, which Aistulf had shortly before taken by force from the Greeks [Col. 0164D].

After Aistulf, king of the Lombards, and Pippin, king of the Franks, had died, Charles ruled the Franks and Desiderius the Lombards. The former inherited devotion toward the Roman Church, while the latter inherited hatred of it.

Desiderius began to harass and attack the Romans so severely under Pope Adrian that the pontiff, being far inferior to the strength of the Lombards and deprived of Eastern assistance, was compelled, following the example of Stephen II, to summon Charles the Great, son of Pippin and king of the Franks, to Italy in aid of the Roman Church. At that time Charles was engaged in the Saxon war.

Obeying the pontiff, Charles came to Italy with a huge army after crossing the Alps [Col. 0165A]. There he defeated Desiderius in battle and shortly afterward captured him, transferring the Lombard kingdom to Frankish jurisdiction.

To show himself grateful to the Roman Church, for whose protection he had obtained so wealthy a kingdom, he divided the Lombard kingdom into three parts. One part—namely, Ticinum, the seat of the Lombard kingdom, together with everything that the Lombards had acquired in Italy in ancient times—he retained for himself.

The second part comprised what the Lombards had shortly before taken in Italy from the Eastern Roman emperors: the Exarchate and part of Umbria and Picenum. This he confirmed to the Roman Church or granted to it anew.

The third part contained that portion of Italy facing toward Sicily, where Benevento was situated, and which is today called the kingdom of Naples. He left this to the duke of Benevento, the sole survivor of the royal Lombard line, and to the Constantinopolitan emperor together with the island of Sicily.

Having arranged these matters, Charles became the first of all princes to increase the Roman Church so greatly both in dignity and in secular territory and wealth [Col. 0165B].

Not unmindful of so many and such great benefits, Pope Adrian, under whom Charles had deserved so magnificently well of the Roman Church, convened in the year of salvation 785 a synod of 153 bishops, abbots, and many other prelates at the Lateran, in the basilica of St. Savior called Constantiniana [Note: [Col. 0165D] Nothing concerning a synod held in this year appears in legitimate and genuine ecclesiastical records. Baronius refutes this entire fiction under the year 774].

At this synod, with the consent of the entire assembly, he granted Charles the right and power to elect and ordain the pontiff of the Apostolic See, although at that time it was customary for the Roman pontiff to be created by the free votes of the Roman clergy and people.

Moreover, Adrian decreed that the bishops, archbishops, and abbots of all the provinces subject to Charles should receive from him investiture in the priestly offices over which they presided, so that unless they were commended and invested by the king, no one could consecrate a bishop or abbot. He marked with anathema all who acted contrary to this decree and proscribed their goods.

Anastasius the Librarian mentions this matter in his ecclesiastical history [Note: [Col. 0165D] Gratian was led into error by Sigebert, whose words he copied verbatim. Sigebert assigns this fictitious synod to the year 773; why does Onuphrius assign it to 785? Anastasius says nothing of this in Adrian’s Life. Nor in his ecclesiastical history, which I read in manuscript, could I find even a trace or vestige of any privilege granted by Adrian I to Charlemagne to elect the Roman pontiff]. Gratian, the collector of canons, noted the passage in distinction 63.

When the emperors who succeeded Charlemagne had sunk into such negligence that they not only refused to defend a privilege of this kind but did not even care for any of the rights of the empire, Pope Adrian III seized the opportunity [Note: [Col. 0165D] Adrian acted rightly and legitimately]. Under the emperor Charles III, in the year of salvation 884, he entirely abolished and annulled what had gradually fallen out of use under earlier pontiffs by convening a synod, establishing that the emperor should not interfere in the election of the pope.

The privilege of Adrian I, taken from the emperor by Adrian III, was restored, renewed, and newly confirmed by Pope Leo VIII to the emperor Otto I, who had deserved exceedingly well of the Roman Church by rescuing it from the hands of the tyrants Berengar and Adalbert and restoring it to the liberty it had lost. This was done in the year of the Lord 962 in a synod convened at the Lateran, following the example of Adrian I, who had granted that privilege to King Charles [Note: [Col. 0165D] Leo was not pope but an antipope. It is surprising that Onuphrius did not notice this. Baronius solidly refutes the fictitious privilege of Leo and clearly demonstrates the error of Gratian in distinction 63, chapter 23] [Col. 0166B].

Afterward, no Roman pontiff openly protested or contradicted this decree of Leo VIII [Note: [Col. 0166D] What need was there to contradict it, since both privileges are fictitious? No emperor, king, or prince possesses the right to elect the Roman pontiff. The first to arrogate this right to himself tyrannically was Theodoric, the Arian king. God soon removed him from the midst of the living as punishment for this deed. See Baronius, volume VII, year 526, no. 22 and following. Justinian later followed him, as did the other Eastern emperors, who at least claimed for themselves the right of confirming the pontiff, and did so only after exacting money—a practice Gregory repeatedly detests and bitterly laments, especially in his commentary on the four penitential psalms. See Baronius, volume VIII, year 590, no. 5 and following. Constantine Pogonatus remitted the money payable for confirmation in the year of Christ 681, while retaining the right of confirmation; yet shortly afterward, namely in 684, he wholly renounced it. See Baronius under that year. We shall discuss below a certain grant made by Nicholas II to Henry], until Gregory VII.

Gregory was the first who, offended by the emperors’ Simony, wholly abolished these two privileges of Adrian I and Leo VIII by decrees issued to the contrary and introduced a new arrangement.

It is sufficiently established that John XIII, who immediately succeeded Leo VIII, Gregory V, and Sylvester II were imposed upon the Apostolic See solely by imperial authority, without the votes of the clergy or Roman people being sought. As for the other Roman pontiffs who lived between John XIII and Sylvester II, although it is not recorded that they were elected by the emperors but rather by the clergy, senate, and people of Rome [Col. 0166C], the reason was that at the time of their elections the emperors were absent from the City and so entangled in major wars in Germany and elsewhere that they could not provide a new pontiff for the Roman See.

Nevertheless, it is certain that whenever the emperors—I mean the three Ottos—were in or near the City, or at least in Italy, and the Roman Church happened then to be without a pastor, they gave it a new supreme pontiff. If, however, at the time of a new election they happened to be far from Italy, it is certain that the Roman pontiffs were elected by the clergy, senate, and people of Rome, but were not consecrated without the emperors’ consent.

These included Benedicts VI and VII, Boniface VII, the usurper of the Apostolic See, who was also driven out, and John XIV, XV, and XVI [Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167D] This John was an antipope]. The last of these, as some writers say, was elected and consecrated without the consent of the emperor Otto III; he was driven from the City and deprived of the priesthood, and Gregory V was substituted in his place.

From Leo VIII until Gregory VII, therefore, no pope ever protested against this privilege, although the emperors did not observe it with complete consistency. But when the emperor Otto III died under Sylvester II around the year of the Lord 1000, his successor Henry II, a most holy man and later numbered among the saints, and after him Conrad II, did not appear to concern themselves with such a privilege.

For after Sylvester II, who died during the reign of Henry II, all the Roman pontiffs up to Clement II were proclaimed without imperial authority [Col. 0167B]. Whether they sought the emperors’ consent before being consecrated, although it seems probable to me, I have never discovered.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] St. Henry did not wish rashly to arrogate to himself what was not owed to him. Conrad the Salian seems to have held the same view.]

This should be believed to have happened both because of the exceptional holiness of Henry II, who wished the election of the Roman pontiff to be free—for in the preceding book III I also reported an ancient document belonging to him—and because of the occupations of Conrad II, who was kept away from the City and engaged in the greatest wars throughout his life.

Nor is it ever recorded that either of these two emperors was in Rome or Italy when the See was vacant. Perhaps, following the example of their three predecessors named Otto, they would have given a Roman pontiff.

[Note: There was no negligence. I ask, why did scarcely anyone invoke the privileges of Adrian and Leo against Gregory VII and others, except Sigebert and Walram in the Treatise on Investitures in Illyricus’s *Catalogue of Witnesses*? Walram wrote this treatise in the year of Christ 1109.]

Moreover, if through their negligence in defending imperial rights the privilege of Leo VIII had perhaps fallen into disuse, then, taking advantage of the opportunity provided by the great schism among three pontiffs, after eight or nine Roman pontiffs had been created by the clergy, senate, and people of Rome without their election [Col. 0167C], Henry III, son of Conrad II [Note: [Col. 0167D] Henry possessed the same right as Theodoric, king of the Goths—that is, none. Read Baronius, year 1046], came into Italy and magnificently vindicated this imperial privilege, as I explained above in the Life of Clement II.

Following the form of the privileges of Adrian I and Leo VIII, he abolished the three pontiffs Benedict VIII, Sylvester III, and John XX, and also deprived Gregory VI. He gave the Roman See a new pontiff, his own chaplain Suideger, a Saxon and then bishop of Bamberg, whom he called Clement II. He compelled the cardinals, clergy, senate, and people of Rome by oath to swear according to his will that they would accept no Roman pontiff unless he had been created by the emperor’s command [Col. 0167D].

As long as he lived, Henry held this most eminent right of the empire with an iron grip [Note: [Col. 0167D] It would have been a pre-eminent right if it had not been an injustice. The author of the *Apology for Henry* knew nothing of this right [Col. 0168D]. At least he did not bring it forward against Catholics, nor did he derive any argument from it in support of his Henry. Nor do the Catholics, who refute all the objections of the schismatics, ever touch upon it]. At his own discretion he designated Clement II, Damasus II, Leo IX, and Victor II as Roman pontiffs [Col. 0168A].

How and in what manner the Roman Church conducted itself in such elections from the election of Clement II until the pontificate of Gregory VII, and the beginnings of the causes that moved Pope Gregory VII to assert ecclesiastical liberty in pontifical elections, I have sufficiently explained above. I shall now relate the events.

From the deposition of Gregory VI onward, Gregory VII was badly disposed toward the emperors [Note: [Col. 0168D] Not improperly, except insofar as they wrongly arrogated another’s right to themselves]. Once he became pontiff, he neglected no opportunity to strip the emperors of their authority to create the Roman pontiff.

The countess Matilda provided a major occasion for this undertaking, since by a certain right he could proceed against the emperor himself. Matilda was that illustrious and throughout Italy most celebrated woman, daughter and heiress of Boniface, the greatest prince in Italy. Fearing the power of the emperor Henry IV [Note: [Col. 0168D] Read Baronius, year 1077, no. 24 and following], she donated to Pope Gregory and the Holy Roman Church several cities in Lombardy, Tuscany, and Liguria that belonged to her by hereditary right.

Here the seed of hatred between the emperor and the pontiff first arose, when the emperor in no way wished to approve that donation as prejudicial to the empire, of which Matilda was a beneficiary; indeed, he attempted to occupy all those territories as having devolved upon him.

The pontiff then found an opportunity: because the emperor was claiming the Church’s rights, Gregory later excommunicated him, when another and far more dangerous cause had also arisen.

For the emperor Henry IV, being involved in many great wars and in need of enormous sums of money, usually bestowed bishoprics and abbeys upon those who offered him the most [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Turks today follow the same practice in Greece and elsewhere, wherever they have Christians under their rule], without considering the quality or condition of the persons. This act could not escape the stain of the Simoniac heresy.

Accordingly, accused before the Apostolic See of this matter and many other crimes, both under Alexander II and under Gregory VII, Henry was often admonished and sharply reproved by Gregory VII. When the pontiff realized that Henry refused to obey him when he was rightly admonished, he began to press him with letters full of threats.

The pope’s naturally hostile disposition toward the emperor was stirred up by several princes of Germany and Saxony who were in rebellion against Henry. Relying also on the assistance of the Normans and on the aid of the countess Matilda, he ventured to undertake many actions against the emperor as soon as he was able [Col. 0168D] [Note: [Col. 0168D] But rightfully, since he was acting for ecclesiastical liberty against the most disgraceful stain of Simony. Read Baronius, 1076].

In the year of the Lord 1075, therefore, judging that the matter must now be settled by deeds rather than words, he sent his legates to the emperor, commanding him to come to Rome on the second Monday of the second week of Lent in the following year, 1076, to give an account of the crimes laid against him. Otherwise, he was to know that on that same day he would be marked with anathema without any delay.

This embassy so greatly disturbed Henry that, after immediately dismissing the legates with serious insult, he began to consider two courses of action. One was to have Gregory secretly captured or killed; the other was, if such an attempt failed, to deprive him of the pontificate.

He therefore secretly arranged through his messengers that on Christmas night, while the pope was celebrating Mass, Gregory should be captured by Cencio, the prefect of the City’s son and Henry’s agent [Note: [Col. 0169D] Cencio; Baronius, year 1075] [Col. 0169B]. This was in fact done. But when Cencio was outlawed by the Roman people, Gregory was freed and eluded the emperor’s impious attempt.

When the emperor saw that his ambush had failed, he turned to force [Note: [Col. 0169D] 1076]. He convened at Worms, on the Sunday of Septuagesima, an assembly of twenty-four bishops and many abbots whom Gregory had previously harassed with various excommunications [Note: [Col. 0169D] But for this very reason, so that persecution might provide understanding].

Taking as his opportunity the fact that Gregory had occupied the Apostolic See without the emperor’s consent, although with the support of the Romans alone [Note: [Col. 0169D] Henry had consented, but being changeable, later turned his consent into dissent], they deprived him of the papacy.

The formula of this deprivation is said to have been as follows:

“Since your entrance has been begun by such great perjuries, and the Church of God is endangered by so great a storm through the abuse of your innovations, and you have dishonored your life by your conduct with so many forms of infamy, we declare that we withdraw the obedience that we never promised you and that we shall not preserve for you hereafter. And since, as you publicly proclaimed, none of us has hitherto been your bishop, you likewise shall henceforth be apostolic for none of us.”

Not only many bishops of Germany and Gaul but also most of those in Italy subscribed to this decree at a gathering held at Pavia by the emperor’s command.

When this hostile decree concerning Pope Gregory, which had been issued at the Lenten council he himself had convened at the Lateran, was brought to the pontiff, he immediately judged that no delay should be permitted. With the sentence of all the bishops and abbots present at the synod, he marked the emperor and all his supporters and adherents with the gravest anathema, deprived him of the empire, and absolved all his subjects from every oath they had sworn to him [Col. 0169D].

As a result, when almost all the secular princes of Germany had defected from him [Note: [Col. 0169D] Rather, the bishops also, who had subscribed to the decree of the conciliabulum, as Sigebert, although a schismatic, testifies under the year 1077], they decided to create another emperor unless Caesar Henry were released from excommunication by the pontiff within a year. They secretly entreated Gregory through their messengers not to release the emperor from it.

Driven by so many threats, Caesar came into Italy after crossing the Alps in the harshest season of the year. At Canossa, where he had found Pope Gregory, after many prayers and a great display of repentance for his past actions, he made peace with him under certain severe conditions, against the will of the princes of Italy, and secured his release from anathema.

In this way he broke the power of the German princes and their inflexible determination against him. This occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth year of Gregory VII’s pontificate, and in the year of salvation 1077.

But after Caesar had been freed from great fear and encouraged by promises from the Italian princes, he again rebelled against Pope Gregory and became his declared enemy [Note: [Col. 0170D] Rather, his treacherous ambusher. Baronius, 1077, no. 36]. He attempted to capture him secretly as he was returning from Canossa to Rome.

When the pope learned that Caesar’s disposition toward him had changed [Col. 0170B], he immediately sent legates to Germany, to the emperor’s enemies, the Saxons and other princes. They were to report the king’s rashness, crimes, and perjuries and urge the princes to create a new king for themselves, abolishing Henry, whom Gregory would afterward anoint emperor.

When the princes of Germany heard the pope’s embassy, they immediately convened an assembly at Forchheim and elected Rudolf, duke of the Swabians, king of the Romans, on the condition that he relinquish the investitures of ecclesiastical offices and not declare his sons his successors as though by hereditary right.

When the emperor Henry heard this, he was inflamed by violent indignation. Having assembled a huge army, he returned to Germany and declared war on the rebellious princes. The war continued with varying fortune for nearly three years [Col. 0170C].

In the year 1080 [Note: [Col. 0170D] See Baronius, year 1080], in the pontificate of Gregory VII, the pontiff, having assembled a council at the Lateran during Lent, with many bishops and abbots present, and with King Henry entangled in the German wars, convinced that he could not possibly escape from the hands of his German enemies, then for the first time openly spewed forth what he had long been planning and had gradually foreshadowed in several earlier decrees [Note: [Col. 0170D] This expression befits a schismatic, not a Catholic.].

For then, for the first time, he issued that constitution by which he attempted to deprive the emperor not only of the authority to appoint the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0170D] He never possessed this by right. Why should it not be permitted to snatch the lamb from the wolf’s jaws?], which his predecessors had possessed for nearly three hundred years, but also of the investiture of all other ecclesiastical offices; and he reduced the entire procedure for appointing bishops and abbots to the form of elections by chapters and monks [Col. 0170D]. An example of this decree follows:

“Following the statutes of the holy Fathers,” etc. It is printed below in the Roman council.

He called all those Simoniacs who received the investiture of any benefice from the hand of a layman. By this decree, without doubt, the emperor Henry and all the Latin and Western kings were attacked [Col. 0171A] [Note: [Col. 0171D] No one was attacked by this decree except Simoniacs and those who had invaded another’s right; and they were demanding that the right be restored to them by the invaders. It is plainly false that all were of this sort.]; thereafter the bishops and the entire clergy of Gaul, Germany, and Italy were also assailed.

Regarding the election of bishops, he defined the matter as follows:

“Whenever, upon the death of the pastor of some church, another is to be canonically substituted for him, the clergy and people, with the visiting bishop who has been sent to that church by the Apostolic See or by its metropolitan presiding, and with every secular ambition, fear, and favor removed, shall elect for themselves, with the consent of the Apostolic See or of their metropolitan, a pastor according to God. But if anyone, corrupted by some vice [Note: [Col. 0171D] What follows is plainly unworthy of a learned man, much less of Onuphrius, who nevertheless seems to be writing this from Henry’s perspective rather than his own. For he reports what Henry’s and the schismatics’ position was concerning Gregory’s decrees.], should presume to act otherwise, he shall lose every benefit of the improperly conducted election and shall henceforth possess no power of election; rather, the entire power of election shall rest with the deliberation of the Apostolic See or of the metropolitan. For if the person to whom the consecration pertains, by not consecrating properly, loses the grace of blessing—as Blessed Leo testifies—then consequently the person who has turned toward a vain election is deprived of the power to elect.”

By these decrees, the majesty and dignity of the Roman Empire were overthrown in two principal respects; and, what was far worse, foundations were laid by which the power of the Roman Empire would be utterly weakened.

I shall speak first of the former matter. At that time there was a custom [Note: [Col. 0171D] This was a very bad and harmful abuse, and it had to be cut away by the sword of excommunication, as Gregory VII did when he abolished this trafficking.] that from nearly every region of the Latin world, almost countless thousands of men of every condition crowded the imperial court. Among them were monks from various communities, teachers, men of letters [Col. 0171C], nobles and commoners, all of whom gathered there in the hope that they might obtain ecclesiastical offices from the emperor, just as is now customary in the Roman Curia. For the emperor not only bestowed all bishoprics and abbeys, as well as all lesser ecclesiastical offices—such as prebends, canonries, provostships, deaneries, and the like [Note: [Col. 0171D] Namely, upon the one who gave more, whether he was suitable or unsuitable, because there was perpetual trafficking at court.]—but, as has already been noted, he also designated the Roman pontiff himself.

If, therefore, Gregory’s decrees were to take effect, it immediately followed that all this majesty of the imperial court would grow obsolete [Note: [Col. 0171D] Could the imperial court not flourish without the sale of ecclesiastical benefices?], once the hope of obtaining ecclesiastical offices from the Caesar had been removed, since those offices would henceforth be conferred by election without any further intervention by the emperor. Nor would it have continued to be possible for the imperial court to be frequented by so many distinguished men of different nations, distinguished by learning and nobility [Col. 0172A].

Another cause, which greatly pressed the emperor and was considered far more important, was this: if the Caesar lost the investitures of prelates—for that was what they called the conferral of office—he would lose the greater, better, and stronger part of his empire and would make the empire a seedbed of the greatest calamities [Note: [Col. 0172D] This entire discussion of investitures seems to have been fabricated and copied from Walram’s treatise on the same subject, found in Illyricus’s catalogue of witnesses; the whole work is built upon privileges that were never granted but were forged and invented.].

For when privileges concerning the investiture of prelates had been granted to the emperors Augustus Charlemagne and Otto I by the Apostolic See, the churches and bishoprics at that time were poor, weak, and without such revenues [Note: [Col. 0172D] This is not universally true, for Charlemagne greatly enriched many churches, and especially the Roman Church, to say nothing of the earlier emperors.]. But after the election of those prelates had become a right of the empire, just as the other secular princes of the empire were, the Caesars, who wished to serve religion well without prejudice to the empire, began to honor bishops and abbots, on account of their religion and as the more important members of the empire, above other lay princes; to dignify them with secular jurisdiction and immense wealth; and to grant to bishoprics castles, towns, cities, marches, duchies, provinces, toll roads, customs duties, taxes, port duties, and many other things that belonged properly to the empire—whether from their own possessions, which belonged to the empire, or from the fiefs of others [Note: [Col. 0172D] Very many things were donated to churches by emperors, even directly, but not everything. Nor did any emperor or prince who loved Catholic piety enrich the Roman Church or other churches with the intention of seizing for himself the right to elect and invest prelates, because this right belongs not to laymen but to the Church.].

For when lay princes died without a legitimate heir, they granted their provinces—which by feudal right belonged to the empire—not to other lay rulers but to bishops. In this way they had made all the bishoprics and abbeys of Italy, Gaul, and Germany, indeed of the entire Latin world, and finally the Roman pontiff himself, from poor men into the richest and most powerful princes, using resources that had previously belonged to the empire, while believing that the imperial rights were thereby diminished in no respect whatever, since they were certain that all those prelates would be appointed by them and would obtain their ecclesiastical offices only by their command and will.

Gregory, therefore, by his decrees was taking half the empire away from the Caesar [Note: [Col. 0172D] False: what Gregory was attempting to take from the Caesar had never belonged to the empire by right, but only through force and illegitimate usurpation.]. For the bishops could in no way be induced to surrender and restore to the emperor what they had obtained from earlier emperors, since they would have to tear it from their own authority—for that was what the Caesar himself was seeking—and the emperor could not compel the bishops to restore to the empire what they had obtained from emperors not as bishops but as members of the empire [Col. 0173A] [Note: [Col. 0173D] Rather, they had obtained those things as bishops.]. Thus, if the appointment of prelates were taken away from the emperor while the prelates retained the benefices and other possessions that had formerly belonged to the empire, half the empire was altogether taken away from the emperor [Note: [Col. 0173D] Nothing whatsoever owed to the empire was taken away, because the bishops remained members of the empire, even though they were not invested by the emperor as bishops.].

Moreover, what most distressed the Caesar was that, if the bishops of Germany and Italy, even when elected and invested by the emperor, could scarcely be kept in office without plotting various and frequent rebellions against him, what would they do thereafter if they were entirely freed and released from the emperor’s power, and if it lay within the power of any church, chapter, or college to elect as head of a very noble and powerful bishopric someone who was the emperor’s most bitter enemy and would subsequently cause the greatest ruin of the empire [Col. 0173B] [Note: [Col. 0173D] This danger can be avoided while preserving the rights of the Church and without any of the trafficking in benefices that prevailed at that time.]?

These, then, were the causes that moved the Caesar and the other lay princes most strongly against the pontiff. For the question then being debated above all was whether the empire should be abolished altogether or established permanently. The Caesar wished to defend the rights of the empire—and indeed those rights in their full extent—while the pope wished to assert the freedom of the Church without regard for the destruction of the empire. He loudly proclaimed that it was unworthy for priests to be created by a lay hand, although this practice had been usurped for nearly three hundred years, from the time of Charlemagne, under sixty or more Roman pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0173D] This is Sigebert’s claim, not the truth.]. The emperor therefore had to strive with all his might to prevent these decrees from standing if he wished the rights of the empire, indeed the empire itself, to remain intact, for he believed that it would unquestionably be scattered by such papal edicts [Col. 0173C] [Note: [Col. 0174D] But wrongly: the empire is not destroyed by preserving the rights of the Church.].

The pontiff also, by these constitutions, immediately made the bishops [Note: [Col. 0174D] Simoniacs who had purchased ecclesiastical benefices.], abbots, and other prelates no less hostile to him than to the emperor himself. They were compelled either to lose their bishoprics and abbeys, or to submit to excommunication, or to receive their bishoprics and abbeys from the hand of the emperor. For what college or chapter would then dare, against such an ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0174D] How ancient indeed!], established and practiced for so many centuries, to appoint a new prelate in place of a deceased bishop or abbot without consulting the most powerful emperor [Col. 0173D]? For both the electors and the elected prelate would not only have failed to obtain what they desired, but would immediately have paid the penalty for their rash attempt to the emperor.

Or what bishop or abbot, even if he could be safely elected by the college of his own church, could or would dare to assume the office contrary to the emperor’s decision, when he would immediately be driven from his see by armed force after another had been substituted by the emperor [Col. 0174A]? It was therefore impossible for anyone who wished to obtain a bishopric or abbey to receive it in any other way than from the emperor, especially in the provinces subject to the empire.

Conversely, if anyone had received an ecclesiastical office from the emperor in this manner, he was immediately branded with excommunication by the Roman bishop. At that time men feared excommunication so greatly that the Roman pontiffs, relying especially upon it, did not doubt that they would ultimately obtain everything they desired. This indeed eventually succeeded according to their wishes, although not without dangers and difficulties. For scarcely could any devotee of theirs remain in one place for a long period, since everyone avoided him like a public plague and believed that, if they dealt with an excommunicated person, they would immediately be swallowed alive by a chasm in the earth [Col. 0174B].

The prelates of the Church were therefore then placed in the greatest straits and calamities and under excessive pressure, so that many preferred to surrender their dignities rather than either incur the emperor’s displeasure by refusing to receive investiture from him, when it could not be done otherwise, or incur excommunication by accepting it, and be mocked by everyone and regarded as impious and criminal.

The Caesar himself, too, and many other princes and prelates, despised the Roman pontiff’s anathema as unjust, unlawful, and contrary to the laws, and persuaded and compelled others to despise it as well. Yet the multitude of the people, and the greater part of the princes—both lay and ecclesiastical—greatly feared the pope’s excommunication, either because they truly felt its force, or out of hatred for the emperor, whom many German princes, especially the Saxons—whom the Caesar himself had worn down by frequent wars as rebels—held in intense hatred.

For such are the dispositions of the German princes [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Germans obey an emperor of their own accord; a tyrant only under compulsion.]: they are unwilling to obey an emperor whom they themselves have elected unless compelled, being most eager to defend their ancestral liberty.

The bishops of Germany and Italy were therefore exceedingly provoked by this decree of the pope. Since the emperor was unwilling in any way to obey it, Pope Gregory, both for this reason and because of the rebellion he had undertaken after obtaining the first peace and absolution, as well as many other crimes of which the Saxons had accused him before the pontiff, again branded the Caesar with the most severe anathema and deprived him of the empire. He confirmed Rudolf, whom some German princes had created as Augustus against Henry in the schism, and absolved everyone from the oath sworn to Henry. He also excommunicated everywhere Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna and the emperor’s principal friend, depriving him of his office [Col. 0175A], together with many other bishops, archbishops, and abbots who defended Henry’s cause.

When all this reached the emperor’s ears, he was greatly afraid. Dreading the pontiff’s boldness [Note: [Col. 0175D] Rather, his magnanimity.], he resolved to forestall the man whom he saw directing all his strength toward forcing him, deprived of the empire, into a religious order [Note: [Col. 0175D] This was not Gregory’s aim. He sought to restore the Church’s right to it, abolish Simony, and overturn the tables of the money-changers. The empire is not overturned when the Church’s right is left intact.], and toward utterly overturning the majesty and rights of the empire. He also knew for certain that the pope himself clung most steadfastly to his enemy Rudolf, and he complained that he had been excommunicated for frivolous reasons, as he called them. He therefore resolved altogether to deprive the pontiff of the papacy and substitute another in his place.

In that same year, 1080, he held two councils in Germany against Pope Gregory. The first was at Mainz at Pentecost, with nineteen bishops; the second, when he came into Italy, was at Brixen [Note: [Col. 0175D] In the Tyrolean territory.], in Noricum, with thirty bishops. All the lay princes who defended the emperor’s cause were also present there, not only from Germany but from Italy as well.

There, by the emperor’s authority, all agreed against Pope Hildebrand. They affirmed that he was a pseudo-monk, the baneful leader of every madness, and especially an invader of the Holy See; they judged that he should be expelled from the Apostolic See, although he had neither been heard nor been present; and, at the emperor’s wish, they elected Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, to be substituted for him.

From this arose the greatest beginning of the dissensions. Both King Henry and all the princes [Col. 0175C] and bishops prostrated themselves on the ground and adored the man who had been elected [Note: [Col. 0175D] Let the sectarians take note of this. Henry and his followers did not deny the authority of the Apostolic See; what they did was out of hatred for Gregory, not for the See or the throne.].

The conclusion of that decree by which the bishops of Henry’s faction at the Council of Brixen deprived Gregory VII of the papacy was as follows [Note: [Col. 0176D] This sentence was taken from the Chronicle of Ursperg; concerning it, see Baronius, 1080, nos. 18 and following]:

“Since it is evident, they say, that he was not elected by God but, through fraud and money, most recklessly thrust forward by himself; since he subverts the ecclesiastical order, disturbs the kingdom of the Christian empire, threatens the Catholic and peaceful king with death in body and soul, defends a perjured king, sows discord among the harmonious, quarrels among the peaceful, scandals among brothers, and disagreement among spouses, and has shaken whatever seemed to stand peacefully among devout people; we, gathered together as one by God’s authority, relying upon the envoys and letters of the nineteen bishops assembled at Mainz on the holy day of the past Pentecost, judge that the same most insolent Hildebrand—who preaches sacrileges and fires, defends perjuries and murders, calls into question the Catholic and Apostolic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, is an ancient disciple of the heretic Berengar, a worshiper of divinations and dreams [Col. 0176A], an obvious necromancer, afflicted by a Pythonic spirit, and therefore deviating from the true faith—is canonically to be deposed and expelled; and, unless he withdraws from that See itself after hearing these charges, he is to be condemned forever. Done on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, Thursday, in the second indiction.”

The Caesar Henry also wrote him this letter:

“Henry, by the grace of God king, etc., to Hildebrand, etc.

“Until now I had expected from you those things that belong to a Father, and I had obeyed you in everything, to the great indignation of our faithful men. In return, I received from you what one ought to expect from him who was the most destructive enemy of our life and kingdom. For when you had first, in your pride, seized the entire hereditary dignity that was owed to me by that Apostolic See [Col. 0176B], you proceeded further and attempted by the worst devices to alienate the kingdom of Italy. Not content with this, you did not hesitate to lay hands upon the most reverend bishops, who are united to us like our sweetest members, and to harass them with the most arrogant injuries and bitterest insults, contrary, as they themselves say, to divine and human law.

“While I concealed all these things with a certain patience, you, thinking this not patience but cowardice, dared to rise against the very head, commanding what you know—namely, to use your own words, that either you should die or that you would take away my life and kingdom, etc.”

When this decree and letter had been delivered to him, Gregory, fearing nothing, took care to strengthen the courage of his followers and persuaded the Saxons, the emperor’s enemies, to remain confident [Col. 0176C] [Note: [Col. 0176D] This was fabricated by schismatics on the basis of a certain letter written by Gregory, concerning which see Baronius, 1090, no. 49 and following. Sigebert inserted it, as he did many other things of this sort, into his Chronology. Onuphrius copied it from there.].

For he confidently asserted that the false king would die in that year, just as had been divinely revealed to him. In fact, he foretold the truth; but his conjecture about the false king deceived him, since he interpreted it according to his own desire as referring to King Henry. For after the Council of Brixen, when the antipope Guibert had come into Italy with the pontifical insignia and was awaiting the emperor’s arrival, by whose armed force he was to be brought to Rome, the emperor went instead to Germany against Rudolf. A battle between the two kings took place on the fourth day before the Ides of October, and King Rudolf, wounded severely, died not long afterward.

After Rudolf had been killed and the affairs of Germany had been settled, Henry, having assembled a great army, came into Italy in order to impose the antipope Guibert by force upon the Apostolic See, after driving out Gregory [Col. 0176D].

Therefore, in the year of the Lord 1081 [Note: [Col. 0176D] Baronius, 1081, no. 13 and following.], after celebrating the Paschal festivals, the emperor Henry came into Italy with an army. Taking the antipope Guibert with him, he reached the city on the eve of Pentecost [Col. 0177A]. The Romans and Pope Gregory resisted him, and he besieged the city for nearly two years, until finally, in the year of the Lord 1083, on the Nones of June, the Romans surrendered and he entered.

When the city had been occupied by Henry partly by force and partly by treachery, Pope Gregory withdrew with his followers into the fortress of Sant’Angelo, which he had strongly fortified. But since no path to reconciliation remained between the emperor and the pontiff, in the following year, 1094, while Gregory was still in the fortress of Sant’Angelo, the emperor, with the agreement of some Roman nobles and cardinals—whom he had drawn to his side partly by force and fear, partly by gifts and promises—had Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, who three years earlier at Brixen had been designated Roman pontiff by the emperor’s authority, inaugurated as antipope on Palm Sunday, giving him the name Clement III [Col. 0177B]. At the following Easter festival, he was crowned emperor and Augustus by him, together with his wife Berta.

Then, turning to attack the fortress of Sant’Angelo, in which Gregory VII remained, and pressing it fiercely, he compelled the pontiff to summon Robert Guiscard with a very large Norman army to his aid. Terrified by Robert’s arrival, the emperor fled from Rome with the antipope.

Robert, entering Rome, brought Gregory out of the fortress and restored him to his See at the Lateran. But when he heard that the emperor, having gathered forces from Tuscany and Lombardy, was returning to Rome with the antipope whom he had driven from the city, and at the same time feared the inconstancy of the Romans, he led the pontiff out of Rome and brought him with him to the strongly fortified city of Salerno, so that he might remain there until peace was granted to the Church [Col. 0177C]. There he stayed throughout the year 1084 and part of the year 1085, until the day of his death, while in the meantime the emperor and the antipope occupied Rome and the entire patrimony of the Church.

After these events, the emperor returned to Germany, leaving the antipope in the city with a large force of soldiers and commending him to the Romans.

Then, in the following year, 1085, Pope Gregory VII—venerable in life, most prudent, Catholic, beloved by God, an indefatigable hammer of heretics, a most skillful restorer and guardian of ecclesiastical law, and worthy of perpetual memory—having spent several months at Salerno, began to be oppressed by the force of a serious illness. Knowing that the time of his departure from this world was approaching [Col. 0177D], three days before his death, when the bishops and cardinals who happened to be present with Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, asked him what order he wished to give concerning the government of the Roman See after his death, he urged them all without hesitation to create a new pontiff in his place. He proposed to them above all Abbot Desiderius as equal to so great an office.

Besides being a cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, Desiderius possessed the highest prudence and outstanding religious character, and enjoyed the singular goodwill and friendship of princes. If they could in no way persuade him to accept the Roman pontificate, Gregory urged them to strive, once he himself had died, to elect either Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, or Otto of Ostia, or Anselm, bishop of Lucca [Col. 0178A].

When these arrangements had been made, and he knew that the time of his death was now very near, he cried out: “I have loved justice, and hated iniquity, and therefore I die in exile.”

After saying these words, and having been fortified by all the ecclesiastical sacraments, the glorious and blessed pontiff returned his soul to heaven on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, a Sunday, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1085. He was buried with the greatest honor in the church of Saint Matthew, which is the cathedral church of Salerno. After his death, the Roman See remained vacant for one year because of the difficulties of the time and circumstances.

When, therefore, the empire in the Roman ruler had been severely struck and severed from the Church, the Roman Church also, deprived of so great a pastor—who among all princes was distinguished for exceptional zeal and authority—felt no small grief [Col. 0178B]. For this pontiff was a most steadfast man, firm in his upright purpose, and one who never departed even by a finger’s breadth, as the saying goes, from the right path, neither through threats nor prayers. A man of ancient character, comparable to those early Roman pontiffs who endured various kinds of suffering for Christ, he was bold, prudent, cautious, and the greatest defender of ecclesiastical liberty.

To him alone both the Latin Church as a whole and especially the Roman Church must give thanks for being free and rescued from the emperor’s hand; for having been enriched with such wealth, resources, and secular jurisdiction; and for being placed over kings, emperors, and all Christian princes. From him, finally—to encompass everything in a single phrase—there proceeded that great and extraordinary condition in which the Roman Church is mistress of all Christians, whereas previously, like a worthless maidservant, she was oppressed not only by emperors but by any prince supported by the resources of the Roman emperor. From him above all came the right of that Roman pontiff, dreadful and venerable throughout every age, to an almost unlimited power [Col. 0178C].

For although earlier Roman pontiffs were honored as the heads of the Christian religion, vicars of Christ, and successors of Peter, their authority did not extend beyond asserting or defending the doctrines of the faith. Otherwise they were subject to the emperors [Note: [Col. 0177D] Not to all, but to some, and that in fact, not by right; through force and tyranny, not through law and equity.]; everything was done at their nod; they were created by them; and the Roman pope did not dare to judge them or decree anything [Col. 0178D] [Note: [Col. 0178D] This is not true.].

Gregory VII was the first of all the Roman pontiffs who, relying on the arms of the Normans and trusting in the resources of Countess Matilda, the most powerful woman in Italy, and inflamed by the discord of the German princes, who were suffering from civil war, after obtaining the supreme pontificate contrary to the custom of his predecessors and disregarding the emperor’s authority and power, dared to excommunicate the Caesar himself—by whom, if he had not been elected, he had at least been confirmed—and even to deprive him of his kingdom and empire. Such a thing had never before been heard of in those centuries.

I attach no importance to the stories circulated about Arcadius, Anastasius, and Leo the Iconoclast [Col. 0179A] [Note: They are not stories. Read Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book II, chapter 19, and book III, chapter 2. See what we said in book II, chapter 19.]. Thus Otto of Freising, a writer of these times, says: “I read and reread the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, and nowhere do I find that before this Henry any of them was excommunicated or deprived of his kingdom by a Roman pontiff,” etc.

As for what a certain cardinal of those times, Benno, a German, wrote against Gregory VII in the emperor’s interest, I have no intention of refuting it now, since the things he accuses this pontiff of doing are partly false, partly ridiculous, and of no importance. Since Benno was both Gregory’s bitterest enemy and, in light of what I have said, altogether unworthy of belief, I consider no credence should be given to him.

My judgment can be confirmed by the writers of those times, both German and Italian, who composed books about this pernicious discord, some deliberately and some incidentally. The principal among them were Paul of Bernried [Note: [Col. 0179D] A monk of the Order of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine.], a priest of Regensburg; Geroch of Reichersberg, bishop [Note: [Col. 0179D] Not a bishop, but a provost.]; Lambert of Schaffhausen, a monk of Hersfeld; and Conrad of Liechtenau—all Germans.

Among the Italians were Leo of Marsica, bishop of Ostia; the unknown author of the Palatine Library, who wrote the Life of this pontiff; and, most recently, Anselm, bishop of Lucca, Gregory’s indefatigable associate. Anselm interpreted the hymns and other writings composed about the sufferings of our Savior as referring to Gregory himself, and confirmed Gregory’s teaching in an elegantly written book. He was a man learned in letters, exceptionally keen in intellect, outstanding in eloquence, and—what is greater than all these things—most celebrated for fear of God and holy conduct, so that he is said to have shone with miracles both during his life and after his death [Col. 0179C].

In a letter to the antipope Guibert, in which he calls him a transgressor and a proud man, Anselm wrote, among other things:

“Therefore, to speak of our blessed Father Gregory, as blessed Cyprian wrote concerning Cornelius: Gregory became bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy—or, to speak more truly, of all of them—by the suffrage of the people who were then present, and by the college of good and ancient priests, when no one had been made bishop before him; when the place of Alexander, that is, the place of Peter, and the rank of the priestly chair were vacant. Once that place had been occupied according to God’s will and Gregory had been ordained with the consent of all of us, whoever now wishes to become bishop must necessarily remain outside. Whoever does not hold the unity of the Church does not possess ecclesiastical ordination. Whoever he may be—even if he boasts greatly of himself and claims much for himself—he is profane, alien, and outside. And since there cannot be a second after the first, whoever has been made after the one who alone ought to exist is no longer second, but no one,” etc.

The same thing was reported by many other writers.

Finally, to bring this matter to an end once and for all: on the occasion of these events, an exceedingly destructive sedition and the most pestilent of all heresies spread throughout the Christian people at this time; and the world, if ever, was then tossed upon the waves of war. The human race was everywhere enveloped in a whirlwind of arms, so that we do not read of the Church ever having suffered more serious dangers and calamities during any schism.

Having dealt with Gregory VII, I shall now explain who Clement III the antipope was and what he did.

## THE ELECTION OF CLEMENT III, THE ANTIPOPE

Clement III, who was created antipope in the schism against Pope Gregory VII by the emperor Henry IV in order to defend the rights of the empire [Col. 0180B] [Note: [Col. 0179D] Rather, to satisfy his own desire and overturn divine right], was an Italian by nationality and a native of Parma. He was born into the highest rank, from the Corrigia family, which at one time held the chief authority in that city. He had previously been called Guibertus.

From an early age he went to the emperor’s court—which, for the purpose of obtaining ecclesiastical offices [Note: [Col. 0179D] The comparison is unequal: in Rome there is a legitimate tribunal, but in the court an illegitimate one, especially since everything there was for sale, and no one but Simon and Gehazi administered justice. Domnizo, concerning Guibert: “Guibert, bishop of the city of Ravenna, was greater than all others, learned, wise, and nobly born. He had been a citizen, or cleric, of Parma; before he was elected, this Gregory had sworn allegiance to Guibert.”] was frequented from the whole world, just as is customary in Rome in our time—in order to try his fortune, when Chunradus, Henry III’s father, held power.

When he had reached manhood, he was regarded as distinguished in talent, eloquence, and prudence, and outstanding in nobility. Little by little he gained the favor of Henry III, who always treated him with great honor. With Henry’s wife Agnes, however, he possessed such influence and authority [Col. 0180C] that he arranged to be made chancellor of the Italian kingdom. She had found him to be a prudent, energetic, and wise man in many difficult affairs.

At that time the entire weight of the empire turned according to his nod and will. In this office, during the schism against Pope Alexander II, he strongly supported Cadolus of Parma, whom Henry III had created as antipope, and, as long as he could, protected him in the pontifical dignity.

Moreover, after Empress Agnes had been removed from the administration of affairs—a responsibility she had exercised for a long time after the death of her husband, Henry III, since her son, the Caesar Henry, was still a child—and after Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, had undertaken by the agreement of the princes to manage imperial affairs on behalf of the boy-king, Guibert was deprived of his office [Col. 0180D]. A certain bishop of Vercelli was substituted for him, since Guibert had incurred the envy of many of the empire’s nobles on account of his virtue.

But when the Caesar Henry, now an adolescent, had escaped the control of his guardians, and had come to know Guibert’s industry and virtue, he received him among his closest friends and advisers; and not long afterward he designated him Archbishop of Ravenna. After the death of Alexander II, Guibert remained in office for some time and obeyed Gregory VII, who had succeeded Alexander. But when Guibert learned that the emperor’s attitude toward him had become alienated, he betrayed the pontiff whom he had obeyed, went over to the emperor, and, inflamed by ambition, vehemently stirred him up against Pope Gregory.

After Gregory had finally been deprived of the pontificate at Brixina by the emperor’s authority, in the year 1084, during the pontificate of that same Gregory VII, Guibert himself, by order of the emperor, was substituted for that pontiff by the bishops who were present at the assembly, on 25 June, the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction; and he was called Clement III. In schism against Gregory VII, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II, he occupied the position for approximately twenty-one years.
