Then, in the year 1084, at Rome, on 22 March, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, on Palm Sunday [Col. 0181B], he was inaugurated by the bishops of Bologna, Modena, and Piacenza, since the cardinals were absent; and at the following Easter he crowned the emperor Henry with his wife, Bertha.

When news was heard of the arrival of Robert Guiscard, duke of the Normans, who was coming to the aid of Gregory VII, then shut up in the fortress of Sant’Angelo, the emperor and the antipope left the city: Guibert went to Lombardy, while the emperor went to Germany. There, in the following year, 1085, after a synod of the bishops of Germany had assembled at Mainz, he ordered the ordination of Clement III and the deposition of Gregory VII to be confirmed. At that time, when first Hermann and then, after Hermann’s death, another man named Egbert had been created king by the Saxons against him, he began to be so deeply entangled in new civil wars that he could no longer devote himself adequately to Italian affairs [Col. 0181C]. When Robert Guiscard, moreover, departed from Rome with Gregory VII, Guibert returned there and, together with the emperor’s prefect, obtained the fortress of Sant’Angelo and nearly all its surrounding places.

Meanwhile, having heard of the death of Gregory VII and of Victor III, who had succeeded him, and having learned that Urban II had been appointed in his place, Guibert then first understood that the hatred of his adversaries toward him would be perpetual and that he would never possess the Roman pontificate peacefully. Therefore, throughout the pontificate of Urban II, he fought with the Hildebrandine faction in varying [Note: Rather, with the orthodox.] combat: sometimes expelled from Rome, sometimes in Rome—according as the support of the Romans and of the emperor was favorable or unfavorable to him. Nevertheless, he held the city for most of Urban II’s pontificate, after Urban himself had been driven from Rome.

[Col. 0181D] When Paschal II had been created pope, Guibert fomented sedition and civil war against him. At last he died in the fortress of Sant’Angelo, which was still under his jurisdiction, and was transferred to the church of Ravenna, where he was buried, in the twenty-first year of his pontificate and in the year of Christ 1101. This Clement was certainly a learned man, endowed with intellect, eloquence, nobility, and every other gift of mind and body, and exceedingly distinguished in the dignity of his person. He might perhaps have pleased God had he not, inflamed by force and ambition, attempted things that were not permitted him. He made poor use both of Rome and of Ravenna at that time. He rose above one living pope, Gregory, although—as he himself said—under compulsion, and survived three successive pontiffs. For a long time he was an exile from both sees, Roman and Ravennate, and, as he often used to say, would have preferred never to have assumed the name of “apostolic.”

After peace had subsequently been made between Henry V and Paschal II, his corpse was removed from the tomb in which it had lain for five years and burned by order of Paschal II; all his acts were declared void in the synod assembled at the Lateran.

A certain author of those times writes of him as follows:

> Guibert, who, after giving his lord, Gregory VII of blessed memory, oaths of loyalty and displaying obedience for seven years, invaded the Apostolic See. He absolved the emperor Henry from observing the oath which he had once sworn to Pope Gregory at Canossa, a town of Lombardy [Col. 0182B]; he drew him to Rome and began to wage war against the Roman Church with him. Those who were on Gregory’s side beyond the mountains, when they learned that the emperor was remaining in Italy, planned to rebel against him. Advancing against them, the emperor fought repeatedly in many battles, with varying outcomes; on both sides there were great slaughters, and many fires and plunderings occurred. At last, leaving troops in Germany to resist them at his own expense and with hired soldiers, he afflicted Rome and all its suburbs with plundering, fires, and slaughter as fiercely as he could. Finally, having placed his own Simon in the Apostolic See more by money than by virtue, he received from him the imperial crown. Since neither the Romans nor his accomplices favored him and his followers, nor opposed them, he launched a most savage persecution. Because of this, almost the entire Roman Empire was laid waste, Christian religion was scattered, and more than twenty thousand people were killed in many places through Guibert’s agency. After expelling Catholic bishops and abbots and other rulers of the churches who excelled in learning and religion, he placed criminal and illiterate men over individual cities, monasteries, and churches. Often replacing one man each year, and more often two, through the detestable commercial transaction of his master Simon, he raged far and wide with the destructive savagery of Nero and Decius against holy places and against Christians who did not favor him—and even against those who did favor him, whenever there was no one to resist him by force of arms.
>
> The same man—who, with greater justice, would have been called a madman pope than Clement—waited in his own town, which is called Argenta, in a lofty tower that had been built there, for the Simoniac angels with whom he might fly and fall into the Stygian marsh. While God in every respect favored Pope Gregory, his legs were broken, since no one rendered him apostolic obedience or reverence except the emperor and his accomplices, or those who, because of avarice, which is the worship of idols, had committed themselves to him under oath, either perpetually or for a time. Many of these, once his treachery had become clear to them, could not bear to be present while he offered the accursed divine sacrifices, knowing that he had succeeded no Roman pontiff [Col. 0183A], but had been added to Pope Gregory as a treacherous, perjured, invading, and Simoniac usurper. The Catholics, however, who defended faith and religion out of zeal for God, adhered to Pope Gregory, who excelled in holiness and religion.

Thus writes Leo, Bishop of Ostia, in Book III, chapter 69, of the *Cassinese History*.

After Clement III’s death, the see remained vacant in his obedience [Col. 0184A] for several days. For, in schism against Pope Paschal II, he had several successors, created in Italy through the efforts of the emperor Henry by his prefects, dukes, and supporters, with an outcome sufficiently unfortunate for the men themselves. The first of them was a certain Albert the Attelamus; then came Theodoric and Maginulf [Note: On all of these Onuphrius treats later.].

[Col. 0183]

## INFORMATION FROM THE COUNCILS OF MANSI

*(Vol. XX, col. 56.)*

[Col. 0183B] Gregory, seventh of that name, previously called Hildebrand, was lawfully created pontiff by unanimous consent in the year of Christ 1073. He was born in Soana in Tuscany, of humble origin, the son of a smith, and was raised under the protection of Saint Peter. As a young man he acquired as his teacher Laurence, Archbishop of Amalfi, whom the unimpeachable witness Peter Damian testifies to have been, not a prince of evildoers, but a prince of the saints of his age.

Besides Laurence, he also had as his teacher John Gratian, archpresbyter and later called Pope Gregory VI. He followed him into Germany after Gratian had abdicated the pontificate, and on that occasion remained among the Cluniacs. He went to Rome with Leo IX, whom he rebuked for assuming the episcopal office while clothed in the pontifical purple and receiving it through a lay hand [Col. 0183C]. By his counsel he ordered that Bruno, later called Leo, be elected, and he was made subdeacon of the Roman Church.

After the death of the aforesaid Leo, he was sent by the Roman clergy to the emperor, asking him that, since the disturbed condition of ecclesiastical affairs did not permit him to do so personally, he should elect the Roman pontiff not in his own name but in the name of the clergy, and should defend the one elected against the invaders.

Sent into Gaul by Victor, whose election he had requested, he miraculously compelled a certain Simoniac archbishop at Lyons to confess his crime. When that man was unable to exalt the Holy Spirit in the hymn of glorification which Hildebrand had commanded him to recite, he confessed with his own mouth that he was polluted by the crime of simony. In the same place he saw Saint Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, with Christ seated beside him and suggesting to him what he should do or say [Col. 0183D].

He also compelled Berengar, archdeacon of the Church of Angers, at the Council of Tours to repeat his renunciation of his heresy and his profession of the Catholic faith. It is therefore entirely false that he defended or followed the Berengarian heresy, as Benno slanderously alleges.

After the death of Stephen IX, when Benedict, tenth of that name, a schismatic pseudopope, had invaded the Apostolic See, Hildebrand was sent to the Empress Agnes, asking her not to refuse her consent to the future election of Gerard, Bishop of Florence, who was called Nicholas II. Having successfully obtained this, he expelled the schismatic through the agency of Duke Godfrey and installed the legitimate pontiff in peaceful possession.

On the best advice of this same man, Alexander II was elected after Nicholas’s death. Cadalous, Bishop of Parma and pseudopontiff, was expelled; the royal ministers and supporters had raised him to the Apostolic Throne against Alexander. Although Hildebrand was small in stature, he was nevertheless admirable to all through the grace of miracles and prophecy.

To the miracle mentioned above he added another, far more remarkable. Though he was at a considerable distance from Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, he knew the thoughts of Hugh’s mind, by which he was saying inwardly to himself:

> “This little man of slight stature and contemptible parentage is swelling with pride and measuring himself against higher things, since so many worldly powers await his nod.”

While praying with that same abbot, Hildebrand saw Christ standing beside him and an angel brandishing a sword, and he foretold a coming mortality.

It is written that, when Peter Damian seemed in a dream to have lost the light of his eyes, Hildebrand interpreted the dream for him and said:

> “It is by no means, as you fear, an indication of approaching death; rather, someone close to you, who is as dear to you as your eye, will be extinguished.”

Peter Damian admits in his letter to Pope Alexander that this truly happened to him through the death of Dominic Loricatus.

He instructed Saint Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, who was complaining that royal authority had been violated in the election of the Roman pontiff, so effectively that, in the synod held for this purpose at Mantua [Col. 0184D], Anno himself joined in and determined that Alexander’s election was just, while Cadalous’s was unjust and illegitimate.

For these reasons, by the judgment of Pope Alexander and of the entire Roman clergy, Hildebrand was considered worthy to be made chancellor of the Roman Church while Alexander was alive and to be substituted for him in the pontificate after his death.

On the very day on which Alexander died—namely, the tenth day before the Kalends of May—he was elected pope by the unanimous consent and signatures of all the cardinals and by the approval of the entire people and clergy. He was unwilling, amid a proclamation of those virtues that are enumerated in the decree of election placed at the beginning of Gregory’s letters [Col. 0185A].

Out of love and reverence for his former teacher, and as an act of gratitude, he wished to be called Gregory. To confirm the legitimacy of that teacher’s see, and to refute the opinion of certain people concerning the illegitimacy of his pontificate—as I said above in the case of Gregory VI—he wished to be called the seventh, thereby indicating that the sixth had been an intermediate, true, and legitimate shepherd of the Apostolic See.

Lambert of Hersfeld calls him a man most learned in sacred letters and, throughout the Church, even during the time of his predecessors, pre-eminent in every kind of virtue. Writing in Germany during those days, Marianus Scotus praises the same Gregory as venerable and recites and commends decrees issued by him.

Although Sigebert favored the Henrician party [Col. 0185B] against the Roman pontiffs and accused Gregory of excessive severity, he nevertheless never dared to say that Gregory had been illegitimately created pontiff.

Otto, Bishop of Freising, a most learned writer, says this about Gregory VII:

> “Having become a model of the flock, he demonstrated by example what he taught by word, and, a strong athlete in every respect, he did not fear to set himself like a wall for the house of Israel.”

Only the Abbot of Ursperg, himself a patron of the schismatics and an adherent of the schismatic Cardinal Benno, cites certain passages from Gregory’s writings. Yet even he did not dare to assert that Gregory’s election had been wholly spurious; he says only this:

> “Since he had ascended this height with no consent of the king and with only the Romans favoring him, there are those who maintain that he was not canonically appointed but tyrannically [Col. 0185C] usurped the papacy for himself; and for this reason he was deposed by certain bishops.”

But how false it is that King Henry’s consent was not obtained is clear from the acts of Gregory’s life. They report that, when Gregory had written to the king asking him not to give his assent to the election by virtue of the privilege granted to him, the king not only did not dissent but confirmed the election by sending an embassy and was present at Gregory’s consecration through a legate. Lambert of Hersfeld makes the same assertion in the passage cited above.

Let the innovators therefore consider how little truth supports those calumnies which the leader of the schismatic cardinals, Benno, brings against the character, election, and faith of this excellent and greatest pontiff. Let them consider under what leader and author they attack the Chair of Peter [Col. 0185D], and how gravely they err when, adhering to one, two, or at most three supporters of the schismatics, they rashly withdraw from the judgment and authority of the thirty-two most approved writers whom the most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine names individually in Book IV, chapter 13, of his controversy *On the Roman Pontiff* in defense of Gregory.

During his pontificate, besides the vigilance which he devoted to carefully supervising nearly all the kings and bishops of the entire world, after that first embassy sent to King Henry, Gregory dispatched Hugh Candidus, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to Spain, so that, after the cities of Spain had been recovered from the Moors, he might demand the rights, tribute, and census customarily paid to the Apostolic See [Col. 0186A].

When the Emperor Michael of Constantinople had congratulated Gregory by letter on his accession to the pontificate, Gregory seized the opportunity to send Dominic, Patriarch of Venice, to him in order to settle the schism.

He sent a fourth embassy to Wratislaus, Duke of Bohemia, so that he might pay the census owed for the duchy of Bohemia, as he had promised God by a vow that he would do after having received from Pope Alexander permission to use the mitre.

He warned Anselm, the bishop-elect, not to receive investiture from King Henry before the king had made satisfaction to the Roman Church concerning his communion with excommunicated persons.

He restrained by a written admonition the Saxons, who had revolted against the king because of his unspeakable crimes and were attempting to elect another king [Col. 0186B].

He sent a fifth embassy into Germany to purge the churches of Germany and Gaul from the stain of simony. After the king had performed the required penance for the alleged crime, he received the legates honorably. But, so that a council might not be held in Germany for this purpose, he opposed it through the persuasion of Liemar, Archbishop of Bremen, as though, for this reason, a synod ought to be convened only by the vicars of the Apostolic See from Bremen or Mainz.

The legates returned to Rome and explained what had happened to the pontiff. When Liemar was summoned a second time to the Apostolic See, he became disobedient, rebellious, and schismatic. Resisting the commands of the legates and of the pontiff himself, he stirred up the king against the pontiff [Col. 0186C], and through his instigation the unfortunate prince’s good intention withered.

But it happened, by God’s singular favor, that when secular princes and the more powerful bishops were conspiring against the Roman Church, God aroused for the defense of that see Agnes, the mother of King Henry; Beatrice; and Matilda, her daughter, still a girl and a virgin, although she had been married to Godfrey.

From this arose, without doubt, the origin of the calumny which the concubinary priests circulated for their own exculpation: that after the divorce between Matilda and Godfrey, the pontiff enjoyed Matilda’s secret embraces. This calumny was refuted and exposed so learnedly and solidly—not only in his own time by Lambert, but also in our age by Baronius from Gregory’s register of letters [Col. 0186D]—and was rescued from its wrappings of lies so completely that thereafter no one except a slanderer and heretic could lend an ear to the false tale.

So that, to the great benefit of the Christian religion, he might not only defeat the Saracens in battle but also unite the Eastern Church, divided from the Western by schism, and restore the Armenians, who had wholly strayed from the Catholic faith, to the path of true faith, he enlisted and gathered more than fifty thousand soldiers.

After Henry had subdued the Saxons, Gregory began to be despised by him, who had grown more insolent after that victory. Then, through the deceit and fraud of Cincio, the Roman prefect, Gregory was attacked, captured, and held in prison because of Guibert, the ancient schismatic and later Bishop of Ravenna, until he was rescued by the tumultuous people [Col. 0187A], who were prepared to avenge so monstrous a crime, and restored to his former freedom.

But when so great a crime had been rendered void through the Roman people’s intervention, Guibert, having received permission from the pope, went to Ravenna, where he contrived a conspiracy of rebellious Lombard bishops.

Henry, freed from fear of the Saxons, scorned to fulfill what he had previously promised to the legates of the Apostolic See, and received and supported those whom the pontiff had excommunicated. Since the pontiff judged that this contempt could no longer be tolerated, he summoned the same king by legates to Rome to give an account at a synod to be assembled during the coming Lent.

The king received the legation, but afterward rejected the legates with great insult to the pontiff. He then convoked the assembly at Worms and arranged for the absent pontiff to be condemned and deposed by a sentence concerning the charges brought against him, and for that sentence to be communicated to him [Col. 0187B].

When the legates had returned to Rome, a synod was held the following day. After they had reported the injuries inflicted upon them and the letters sent by the king had been read, Siegfried of Mainz, William of Utrecht, and Robert of Bamberg were excommunicated together with King Henry.

The pontiff announced the sentence to all his subjects, absolving them from their oath of fidelity. God carried it out against the excommunicated bishops who supported Henry through the intervention of a most evil death.

The Saxons defected from the king and rose against him in battle with a terrifying force. Likewise, the greater princes of Germany, the principal bishops [Col. 0187C], and all the faithful, whom the pontiff had admonished at the request of Hermann, Bishop of Metz, to exhort the king to repentance, convened an assembly at Tribur.

While the question of choosing another king of Germany was being discussed there, Henry begged for peace through legates and promised to reform his conduct. After being rejected several times, he was finally received on this condition: that he dismiss the excommunicated men whom he was supporting, submit to the Roman pontiff, and arrange to be absolved by the Roman pontiff from the bond of excommunication.

The king obeyed and, coming into Italy, obtained absolution from the pontiff. But through the instigation of the schismatic and concubinary bishops, it happened that, scarcely having returned to Germany, he fell back again into his former ways [Col. 0187D]. For he entered into a most shameful new conspiracy against the pontiff with Guibert and certain other rebels.

When the German princes learned of this, they elected Rudolph, Duke of Swabia, as king without consulting Gregory, and had him brought to Mainz and consecrated by Siegfried.

After undertaking war against Rudolph and conducting it successfully, Henry became more haughty and began to despise Gregory. Fearing for himself and his kingdom, he had until then pretended to honor Gregory and to attend upon him.

For this reason Henry was again excommunicated by synodal agreement at Rome and deservedly forfeited the kingdom that had been granted to Rudolph. He, however, having held a council of schismatics at Brixina [Brixen], ordered a sentence of deposition to be issued against Gregory in his absence and Guibert, the author of the schism—who had often been excommunicated and deposed—to be substituted for him in the pontificate.

Meanwhile King Rudolph died, and through his death German affairs were placed in a more secure condition. Henry prepared to enter Italy so that he might depose Pope Gregory, whom he considered his bitterest enemy, from the See of Peter and place his adversary Guibert, the antipope, there.

After he had captured the Leonine City, which he had unsuccessfully attacked and besieged twice, following two years of persecution, he enthroned the perjured, deposed, and anathematized Guibert of Ravenna at Saint Peter’s through the agency of the bishops of Modena and Rimini, who themselves had been deposed and excommunicated many years earlier, and imposed upon him the name Clement III.

He finally conquered Rome itself and its citizens, which he could not overcome by arms, only after a three-year siege, through gold and money. Pope Gregory withdrew with a few nobles into the fortress of Sant’Angelo. Meanwhile, the crown of the empire—which Gregory had solemnly refused, even to the point of bloodshed, to confer upon a schismatic and excommunicated emperor—was placed by Clement the antipope upon the schismatic king, and the pseudopontiff [Col. 0188C] made him a pseudoemperor.

While Henry remained on the Aventine and pursued the siege of the city with tireless determination, Gregory implored assistance from Robert, Duke of the Normans, who had promised it to the Roman Church by oath. Robert immediately gathered fresh forces and hastened into Italy, drove out Henry, and most successfully liberated the pontiff himself. He expelled from the city all the pseudocardinals whom Guibert the pseudopontiff had created, or at least had drawn away from the true pontiff.

After these men had been expelled, Gregory convened a council at Rome, where he again excommunicated the pseudopontiff together with the pseudoemperor Henry. Later he withdrew from the city and came to Cassino; from there he went to Salerno to dedicate the basilica of Saint Matthew [Col. 0188D] the Apostle, and remained there until his death. He died on 24 May in the year of Christ our Redeemer 1085, after having sat twelve years, one month, and three days.

Distinguished after death for holiness and miracles, he was buried within the basilica of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, which he had consecrated to divine worship shortly before his death.

[Col. 0189]

## APOLOGY FOR GREGORY VII AGAINST THE SECTARIANS

Containing certain hitherto unpublished treatises on behalf of the same pontiff by Bernaldus, priest of Constance; authored and edited by Jacob Gretser, theologian of the Society of Jesus.

*(Opp. vol. VI, p. 6.)*

[Col. 0189A] It is altogether incredible and inexplicable how fiercely the modern innovators burn with hatred against the Roman pontiffs, both ancient and recent, and in how many ways they make this hatred known and openly display it—not human hatred, but plainly Tartarean hatred.

Among these methods, the first place is occupied by lies, curses, insults, fabrications, and innumerable inventions, with which they fill and stuff almost all their books. They do so with such immoderation and recklessness that many books issuing from this workshop seem to be nothing other than a single lie and insult woven together by one perpetual and never-interrupted thread.

They do not allow themselves to be restrained by reverence for anything above or below, so as to act more moderately and adopt even for a moment the reflection of a sober-minded person. Although they are convicted of the most evident falsehood and caught in manifest false stories and slanders, they show no sign of shame. Instead, they thrust forward, pile up, chant, repeat, and privately and publicly reiterate their calumnies, even when these are utterly alien to the truth, so as to make the Roman pontiffs hated and detested by everyone, remembering that saying:

> “Fraud or valor, falsehood or truth—who would demand these in an enemy?”

Although scarcely any heretic can be found—especially one who is a preacher of the word and a defender of his sect through written records—who does not excel in this art, Luther nevertheless surpassed them all, as though he had won the prize among all men.

His writings are so crammed with curses against the supreme pontiffs that I can scarcely contain my amazement at how any mortal can place confidence in this most abusive and furious reviler [Col. 0189C]. What do I mean, “place confidence”? They even decide by their vote that he should be granted a place among the prophets and almost among the evangelists and apostles themselves.

I shall not go far afield. Examine even Luther’s final book, *On the Papacy Founded and Established by the Devil*, which he composed and published when he was already close to death and ripe for the Stygian realm. It is nothing other than a continuous frenzy against the pope—neither human nor bestial, but plainly diabolical—so that I have no doubt that the capital enemy of our salvation, the arch-strategist and begetter of all calumniators, was the parent of this book, and that Luther committed everything it contains to paper at the devil’s dictation.

[Col. 0190A] But let these men roar, gnash their teeth, rage, and finally dash their hands, feet, heels, and heads against the rock upon which the Apostolic See was founded. “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Psalm II).

Let them thunder, hurl lightning, and flash; let them tear and lacerate the ministers of the Apostolic See with thousands of curses and most lying fictions. We, together with Saint Augustine, openly and fearlessly repeat to them from Book II, chapter 51, *Against Petilianus*:

> “What has the Chair of the Roman Church done to you, in which Peter sat and in which Anastasius sits today (Paul V)? Or what has the Chair of the Jerusalem Church done, in which James sat and in which John sits today? We are joined to these in Catholic unity, while you have separated yourselves from them by your criminal madness.
>
> “Why do you call it the chair of pestilence, the Apostolic Chair? If it is because of the men whom you think speak the law but do not practice it, did the Lord Jesus Christ, because of the Pharisees about whom he said, ‘For they say and do not do,’ do any injury to the chair in which they sat? Did he not commend the chair of Moses and, while preserving the honor of the chair, rebuke them? For he says: ‘The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore, whatever they tell you, do and observe; but do not do according to their works, for they say and do not do.’
>
> “If you considered these things, you would not blaspheme the Apostolic Chair, with which you do not communicate, because of the men whom you defame. What else is this than not knowing what to say, while nevertheless being unable to do anything but curse?”

Now, even if some men less praiseworthy and commendable in life and conduct had obtained or held the Chair of Peter [Col. 0190C], what follows from that? As Saint Augustine says in Letter 166, concerning evil superiors, he made his people secure so that the chair of saving doctrine would not be abandoned on their account, since even bad men are compelled to speak good things in it.

For what they say is not their own, but belongs to God, who placed the doctrine of truth in the chair of unity. Even if, says the same Saint Augustine in Letter 165, some traitor—meaning an evil man—had slipped into that succession of bishops which extends from Peter himself to Anastasius (Paul V), who now occupies the same chair, it would in no way prejudice the Church or innocent Christians, for the Lord, providing for them, said concerning evil superiors:

> “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

[Col. 0191A] “Remember,” says Saint Augustine in Book II, chapters 47 and 61, *Against Petilianus*, “that the conduct of evil men does not harm the sacraments, so that they either cease altogether to be what they are or become less holy; rather, it harms the evil men themselves, so that the sacraments become for them evidence of condemnation and not an aid to healing.

“Therefore, because of the wicked and criminal Pharisees, the Lord did not command the abandonment of the Chair of Moses, in which he plainly prefigured his own. Although he said that they sat upon the chair of Moses and spoke but did not act, he nevertheless instructed the people to do what they said and not to do what they did, lest the holiness of the chair be abandoned and, on account of evil shepherds, the unity of the flock be divided.

“Especially since, out of so many pontiffs, the sectarians single out only a very few against whom they bring specific crimes and offenses—not from reliable and approved witnesses and authors, but from those whose concern for truth was of the lowest kind. Such are, in our own age, those sectarians who have professed to commend the deeds of the pontiffs in writing. Among them, Balaeus in Latin and Nigrinus in German have fabricated many most mendacious stories about the pontiffs in their works, or have woven into their books stories fabricated by their fellow buffoons, and have transmitted them to posterity—stories as numerous as the stars that shine in the sky on a clear night.

“Driven and scattered by these insults and accusations, light chaff flies and flutters outside the Lord’s threshing floor. Not so those whose feet have been set and firmly planted upon the rock.

“If we were to see these crimes and offenses, even if they were true and present,” says Saint Augustine in Letter 162 to the bishops of the Donatists, “and if, sparing the weeds for the sake of the grain, we tolerated them for the sake of unity, anyone who heard the Holy Scriptures without deafness of heart would say that we deserved not merely no blame but even considerable praise.

“Aaron tolerates the multitude demanding, making, and worshiping an idol. Moses tolerates the many thousands murmuring against God and repeatedly offending his holy name. David tolerates Saul, his persecutor, who abandons heavenly things through criminal conduct and seeks the underworld through magical arts; he avenges the murdered man and calls him ‘the Lord’s anointed’ because of the sacrament of venerable anointing.

“Samuel tolerates the wicked sons of Eli and his own perverse sons; because the people did not wish to tolerate them, it was accused by divine authority and punished by divine severity. Finally, he tolerates the proud people themselves, who despise God.

“Isaiah tolerates those against whom he hurls so many true accusations. Jeremiah tolerates those from whom he suffers so much. Zechariah tolerates the Pharisees and scribes whom Scripture testifies to have existed in that period.

“I know that I have omitted many. Let those who wish read; let those who can read the heavenly utterances read. They will find that all the holy servants and friends of God have always had among their people men whom they tolerated, with whom, while sharing in the sacraments of that time, they were not only not defiled but also bore them commendably, striving, as the Apostle says, ‘to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace’ (Ephesians IV).

“Let them also consider what occurred after the Lord’s coming. We would find many more examples of this tolerance throughout the whole world if everything could have been written down and established as authoritative. Nevertheless, consider these examples that we possess.

“The Lord himself tolerates Judas, his devil, thief, and betrayer; he allows him to receive, among the innocent disciples, what the faithful know to be the price of our redemption. The apostles tolerate pseudo-apostles who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ. Paul, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, associates with them with the greatest tolerance.”

Thus Saint Augustine speaks most beautifully.

If, then, for the sake of unity and concord, so that schism may be avoided, evil sheep ought to be tolerated, how much more ought an evil shepherd to be endured for that same purpose, if such a one should ever arise?

Neither by words and books alone do heretics rage against the Roman pontiffs with the greatest injury and abuse, but also through sculptures, engravings, statues, images, and most disgraceful paintings—some of them such that no decent eye can look upon them without a blush of shame. Indeed, sectarians borrow from pagans, heretics, and schismatics not only perverse opinions and pernicious doctrines, but also the lust for accusing and for mocking both profane and sacred things, especially that which has attacked the Church’s prelates and orders through paintings and images. To demonstrate this, I shall not repeat the old story of the harmful mercenary in the baiting of wild beasts, who, as Tertullian records in the *Apologeticus*, displayed a picture with the inscription: “The god of the Christians, the ass-eared one” (*Deus Christianorum ononychites*). He had ass’s ears, one hoofed foot, carried a book, and wore a toga. For the innovators could say that this deed had redounded to Christ’s own disgrace—as though what they themselves have committed, with almost equal mockery, against Christ’s vicar and servants did not likewise rebound upon Christ’s contempt.

But I shall pass over, as I said, the wickedness of this mercenary, so that from Nicetas, who composed the life of Ignatius, patriarch of Constantinople, I may make clear that these men are the truest and most genuine imitators of Photius and the Photian schismatics, especially Gregory of Syracuse. In order to make the holy Ignatius, the true and legitimate patriarch, hated and detested by all and to drive him from his see, they fabricated countless accusations against him, even composing a book—not without insulting images—made and arranged through the work of Gregory of Syracuse, that outstanding painter and fabricator. Concerning these things the aforesaid Nicetas writes as follows:

But so that all the wickedness perpetrated against that holy man Ignatius might become more manifest, God, “who catches the wise in their craftiness and scatters the counsels of the wicked” (Job 5:13), put into the mind of the emperor Basil the plan that he should send to Photius and command him, without any delay, to send back all the writings he had received when he departed from the patriarchate. Photius, however, affirmed under oath—although falsely—that, because of the haste of his departure, he had received nothing of the kind from there.

While these things were being said by Photius to the prefect of Bahanes, Photius’s servants, with great haste, moved seven sacks full of writings, sealed with leaden seals, to Calamon, a nearby place, in order to conceal them. When the prefect’s servants saw this and took the sacks away from them, they brought them to the emperor. Upon opening them, they found two books, plated on the outside with gold and silver foil and covered with silk, while within they were written in very beautiful and ornate letters. One of them contained seven synodal proceedings against Ignatius which had never existed or been conducted, but had merely been devised in vain by diabolical counsel. At the beginning of each proceeding there were the following pictures, executed by that Gregory of Syracuse, surnamed Asbestas. That good man was skilled in painting—perhaps as an addition to his other evils. Ignatius himself was depicted there.

In the first proceeding he depicted Ignatius being dragged along and beaten. Above his head he wrote: “THE DEVIL.” Have you not recoiled from the excess of this blasphemy? For if he called the head of the household Beelzebul, what ought he to have done to his servants? (Matthew 10:25.)

In the second proceeding he again depicted Ignatius befouled with spittle and dragged with great force. The inscription read: “PRINCE OF SIN.”

In the third proceeding he depicted Ignatius deprived of office, with this inscription: “SON OF INIQUITY.”

In the fourth proceeding likewise he represented the same Ignatius condemned by anathema and exile, and the inscription was: “SIMON MAGUS.”

At the beginning of the fifth proceeding he depicted Ignatius surrounded by bonds and bound, with the inscription: “EXALTING HIMSELF ABOVE EVERYTHING THAT IS CALLED GOD.”

In the sixth proceeding he depicted Ignatius handed over to condemnation. His inscription was: “THE ABOMINATION OF DESOLATION.”

Finally, in the seventh and last proceeding, he depicted Ignatius dragged forward so that his head might be cut off; the inscription read: “ANTICHRIST.”

Do you not see, friendly reader, the forerunners of our sectarians—or rather, their teachers and masters? Just as they once depicted Ignatius, do not the innovators of today likewise depict the prelates of the Catholic Church, especially the supreme pontiff, in a disgraceful and shameful manner? They add to their pictures every sort of most disgraceful jest. Consider, I beg you, that image of the pope which is placed at the front of the book entitled *Apiarium*. Consider also the one placed by Spannenberger, a Lutheran preacher, at the head of the notorious pamphlet to which he gave the title *Wider die bösen Sitten ins Teuffels-Kahrnoffelspihl*—“Against the Evil Customs in the Devil’s Carnival.” Likewise consider the image appearing in the vestibule of the book called *Das Wolffgesang*—“The Wolf’s Song.” In Luther’s Latin and German volumes you will find *Papasellum*, illustrated by the commentaries of Philip. Illyricus, because of his kinship and affinity with it, judged that it should be published again separately and illustrated with new glosses—or rather, calumnies and lies.

What shall I say about Luther’s *Passional*, which appears in volume I of the new German works of Luther collected by Aurifaber? Of the same kind is that *Passion of Christ* in which the pontiff, cardinals, bishops, and monks play the roles of Caiaphas, Annas, Pilate, Herod, the executioners, and the torturers of Christ.

In 1527 the impious Paracelsus published thirty images filled with disgrace and abuse against the Roman pontiff. They appear in the appendix to volume X of Paracelsus’s works. So that he himself would not seem to be the author, he invented the story that he had found them somewhere in ancient monuments or on walls. In this very year, 1608, a certain fanatical sectarian, Johann Rudrauff, brought them out again in his fabricated commentary on the comet of the previous year—a work which one might rightly call a storehouse of every kind of stupidity and madness—and proceeded to adorn them with the vainest explanations.

Johann Wolfius reproduced the same images, together with Paracelsus’s annotations, the marginal notes of Adam Durischius, and the explanations of Johann Adrasderus, “son of the earth,” an ignoble sectarian, in his twelfth *Centenary*. Wolfius had only one concern and aim: whatever disgraceful and insulting matter he had ever read, heard, or received from others against pontiffs, bishops, monks, nuns, and the entire ecclesiastical and religious estate and order, he gathered and bound into a single bundle, so that scorners and buffoons might always have abundant material at hand whenever they wished to sharpen their tongues or pens against the pope and [Col. 0194C] others. And when do they not wish to do so?

Nor does it matter that Paracelsus, Wolfius, and the others of his tribe put forward the name of Joachim the abbot, for no one is unaware that they were so contrived and fashioned that, under the names of others as though under disguises, they might conceal their wickedness and depravity as far as possible. Nor do the thirty prophecies of Joachim the abbot—as Wolfius calls them—differ from these: they were set forth in the twelfth *Centenary of Lies* with insulting images, through the industry of heretics.

Of the same kind is Paracelsus’s *Prognostication*, consisting of thirty-two figures or images. Wolfius, having had it translated from German into Latin by Schram, a preacher of Neuburg, inserted it into the sixteenth *Centenary* of his lies and calumnies. He also included the antitheses of Christ and Antichrist, composed by some unknown sectarian, Simon Rosario, in most abusive verses, together with impious and disgraceful pictures, so that hatred of the pope—whom the fanatical poetaster always calls Antichrist and Pluto—might pass through the eyes themselves more deeply into the minds of readers and spectators.

This also includes the twofold portrait of Pope Julius II, from the years 1512 and 1513, and the double image which Wolfius exhibits under the year of Christ 1580. Wolfius fabricated both of them from the letters of Beza, a witness of supposedly unimpeachable credibility—one who, in order to avoid every suspicion of a recent invention, contrives an antiquity which perhaps does not go beyond our own age; or, if it does, descends from some Wycliffite or Hussite.

Strange to say, whenever our innovators find some sculpture, painting, or engraving, they never turn their eyes back upon themselves and their own people, but immediately rush to the pontiff and those devoted to the pontiff, especially priests and monks, and interpret the whole symbol as referring to them, not to themselves and their own. Such are the images which Wolfius, together with the Lutheran Herbrand, reports and explains in the sixteenth *Centenary* of his lies as having been found—if the innovators are not lying—in the principal church at Strasbourg.

Why should an ass standing at an altar signify a Catholic priest performing the mysteries of the divine sacrifice, and not rather a preacher standing at his own table and preparing the dishes of the Lutheran or Calvinist Supper—especially one who, like an ape of orthodox priests, dresses in prescribed garments and celebrates a German Mass, as is commonly done in certain cities where Lutheranism prevails? You say that it is a sacrificer. I insist that it is a preacher, and I shall prove it when the time for proof comes.

In the same way, I maintain that the ass reading from the book held by the cat is a preacher, whether Lutheran or Calvinist, reading mysteries which are known not to me but to preachers. The image in which a pig and a he-goat carry the funeral bier of a sleeping fox represents no others than these men. The same applies to the image showing a bear carrying a pitcher of holy water, a wolf bearing the cross, and a hare carrying a torch—or, to use ecclesiastical language, presenting us with a candle-bearer. All these things fit preachers most aptly, as could easily be demonstrated if the matter and occasion required it.

The same men are represented to the life by the image which Wolfius—or Lupus, the fabulist whose character corresponds to his name—there placed before the eyes of his readers, taking it from Herbrand. A wolf dressed in a monastic cowl, from whose hood hanging behind his shoulders a goose protrudes, stands in a pulpit. With his forefeet, as though they were hands, he holds a book from which he seems to be reciting something unknown to me but well known to Wolfius, Herbrand, and others familiar with the lupine tongue. Beneath the pulpit sits a little fox, as though lying in ambush. Opposite stand several geese, each holding a rosary in its beak and listening to the preaching Wolf. Beside the geese there also stands, as though a guard, a fool in his customary dress. What an elegant image and delineation of Lutheran and Calvinist preachers! Whoever wishes may add a commentary; he will find abundant material for interpretation.

How well Wolfius would have employed his labor if he had referred these *τυπώματα* and *ἔκτυπα*—“types” and “impressions”—to the people they concern, namely, his own preachers! As it is, what else has he done than openly show that he was burning with an incredible itch to slander? And yet he advertises his volumes under the title *Memorable and Recondite Readings*. Is it a memorable reading to read and heap together whatever anyone from the dregs of the common people has spat out against popes, priests, monks, and nuns? Is it a recondite reading to collect and pile into one heap every infamous sheet that almost any buffoon has ever dragged into the open and released among the people? Truly recondite reading: to unearth the dungheaps, stinking places, sewers, and every kind of filth contained in the writings of such darklings, and diligently to bring it forth and thrust it into the faces and mouths of readers and spectators.

But, leaving aside for a while that monstrous Wolf, or Wolfius, it would be a mere waste of time to speak of the image of the Babylonian harlot sitting upon a beast with seven heads and ten horns and holding a golden cup in her hand. Nothing is more certain among sectarians than that this figure vividly represents the Roman pope. Therefore it is everywhere to be seen, with the kings and emperors of the earth themselves prostrate before it in veneration and adoration. Nor does fear or reverence for a Catholic emperor deter them from this sacrilegious boldness, although they live within the empire; for long ago they wiped every fear from their hearts and every reverence from their faces.

What Luther’s attitude was toward the pope, the cardinals, the bishops, and the entire ecclesiastical order is made clear and manifest on countless other occasions, but especially in that diabolical book against the Papacy mentioned above. There Islebius Furippus rages as follows, according to the translation from German by Matthaeus Judex, a most clamorous and seditious preacher:

“Now then, O Caesar, kings, princes, and nobles, and whoever you are able to seize, seize them. Cursed be the idle and sluggish hand. First, strip the pontiff of Rome, Romagna, Urbino, Bologna, and everything which he holds and possesses under the title of pontiff; for he is a possessor of the worst faith, and acquired everything through lies and frauds.

“But why do I speak of lies and murders? Rather, by his blasphemies and idolatries he has withdrawn and snatched these things from the Roman Empire, subjected them to himself, and, as the reward for his superstition, led innumerable souls to hell, as he himself boasts, *Decretum* 40, chapter ‘If the Pope,’ and elsewhere.

“Next, the magistrates ought to seize the pontiff, the cardinals, and the rest of his order, companions in superstition and impure holiness, and, as blasphemers are accustomed to be punished, draw out and cut off their tongues through the back of their necks, then arrange them in order upon the gallows, precisely as they themselves customarily attach seals to their bulls—although this punishment would be far inferior and milder than their blasphemies and idolatries.

“When these matters had duly been carried out, they could certainly be granted permission to celebrate, among the ravens on the gallows or among the devils in hell, one council—or as many as they wished, at their own discretion.”

In the same book the insane apostate raves as follows:

“If I were in Caesar’s place, I would do this at once: I would drive all those wicked and infamous scoundrels—the pope, the cardinals, and the rest of that sort—bound and girded together as though with a single chain, no farther than three miles away, namely to Ostia. If they were unbound and ungirded, they would scarcely go so far in the direction they did not wish to take.

“There is a certain pool in that place, which the Latins call the Tyrrhenian Sea: a healthful bath against all the plagues, ailments, and diseases of the pontifical unclean holiness, and of all the cardinals and the entire pestilence of the curia. I would place these men in it as gently as possible and wash them vigorously.

“If it happened that they shrank from enduring the water, as the ill-disposed and possessed commonly tremble at water, I would add something from the rock upon which they and their Church are founded; indeed, I would fasten something to those keys by which they are able to loose everything in heaven and on earth, so that they might command the waters to do whatever they wished.

“They ought also to have their pastoral staffs and maces ready, with which they could strike the water such blows that blood would pour from their mouths and nostrils.

“Finally, when they went off with their pastures, in which they might refresh and restore themselves in the bath—namely, all the decrees, decretals, the *Sext*, the Clementines, the extravagants, bulls, indulgences, and buttery, cheesy, and milky letters hanging from their necks, for complete security—I would dare to wager anything that, if they were submerged to the bottom of that bath for half an hour, they would be freed from all their sickness, ailment, and disease.”

Thus Luther.

As Matthaeus Judex, the preacher, says, Luther represented the same opinion a few years before his death in those images printed at Wittenberg and later reprinted at Jena. In them the pontiff and cardinals are hung upon a gallows or cross, while evil demons fly around them, receiving their souls and carrying them into hell. The title inscribed upon the image was: “The Worthy Reward of the Pope’s Satanism and of His Cardinals,” followed by these German verses:

*Wie zeitlich gestrafft solt werden*  
*Bapst und Cardinal auf Erden,*  
*Ihr Lasterung verdienet het,*  
*Wie ihr Recht hie gemalet steht.*

“How pope and cardinal ought to be punished in this world,  
As their blasphemy has deserved,  
As you see their due here portrayed.”

And, if corporal punishment were now to be inflicted upon both cardinals and pope, their blasphemy would truly have deserved that reward which you see depicted here.

This is what the wicked Judex wrote about the sacrilegious Luther. Schlusselfburg likewise repeats it in his book *On the Adiaphorists*, lest the sparks of seditions once kindled should be extinguished.

Nor did Luther merely take care to have painted in colors the punishment which he thought ought to be inflicted upon the pope, cardinals, bishops, and all ecclesiastics. He also wanted many other things, which he had spewed forth in the filthiest and most disgraceful manner against the pope in that book, to be painted. These pictures were so foul, filthy, and detestable that, according to Illyricus himself, in his pamphlet against the Interimists and Adiaphorists, many Lutherans were gravely offended when they saw them, and thought that this entire unspeakable kind of abuse ought to be attributed to Luther, by then delirious from drink or old age. Illyricus, however, being a man of gross judgment, takes a very different view and almost worships these images of Luther, painted in a pigsty and sewer, contrary to his own decree that images should not be worshiped.

In Luther’s *Symposiac Conversations*, under the heading “On Antichrist,” mention is made of an image presented to Luther in which the Roman pope was seen hanging together with Judas from his moneybags and keys. Luther was extraordinarily pleased by this figure and understood it as though it were the just vengeance of the divine power against the pope: the picture declared that the man who had not feared to condemn Luther together with his Gospel was worthy of the noose.

But concerning the verbal insults and abuses, and the pictures by which adversaries most wantonly and disgracefully traduce the Roman pontiffs and strive to expose them to ridicule, we have spoken at great length in the four apologies against Misenus and in our response to the Hunnian theses. We have likewise touched upon many matters in book III of *On the Pontiff*, where the subject was Antichrist; on that occasion we sufficiently chastised and overthrew the sort of curses and lies which sectarians loudly proclaim with puffed-out throats.

Although in our own time heretics attack and rage against the Roman prelates with the greatest fury, they have nevertheless selected certain men from their number and rank whom they might pursue and tear apart with abuse more violently and shamelessly than the rest. Among these the chief appears to be Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, who began his pontificate in the year of our Redemption 1073 and died in 1085, as Cardinal Baronius reckons in volume II of his chronology.

The sectarians scourge this pontiff everywhere with their poisoned mouths, styles, and pens, scarcely allowing him to be a human being, but banishing him far below nature and human society. In doing so they follow as leaders and guides, on the one hand, the itch for lying and for accusing all the Roman pontiffs which is innate in them, and, on the other, Bennon, the pseudo-cardinal, who left to posterity a commentary on Gregory VII filled with lies and ignorance. Illyricus inserted this work, as though it were a most precious gem, into his catalogue of witnesses to Lutheran truth. From it the Centuriators also enriched their eleventh *Centenary* with the addition of many falsehoods and accusations; Wolfius, moreover, splendidly adorned with it the eleventh *Centenary* of his lies.

Reiner Reineccius, likewise a Lutheran or Calvinist heretic, arranged for it to be printed again at Frankfurt in the year of salvation 1581 together with Helmold and Arnold of Lübeck. He claimed that only a few copies of Bennon remained—a supposed great loss to the Christian commonwealth. For it is greatly in the interest of the Christian commonwealth that such patchworks of calumny should endure and survive, so that those who plan to learn and practice the art of slandering and lying may have before them an example—and indeed a perfect one—with which to compare and conform themselves.

Before all these, in the year of the Lord 1535, Orthuinus Gratius published Bennon together with certain other unhealthy writings, which he says he had found in some manuscript codex—I know not which. Bellarmine considers it probable that this book, under Bennon’s name, was fabricated and published by some Lutheran heretic.

Sutlivius cries out: “Orthuinus Gratius refuted Bellarmine’s lie and shamelessness in the *Fasciculus rerum expetendarum et fugiendarum*, in which he published this book, although otherwise he was extremely friendly to the pontiff.” How friendly Gratius was to the Roman pontiff is sufficiently and more than sufficiently indicated by the *Fasciculus*—or rather, by that bundle of calumnies and accusations—which he brought to light with very little benefit to the Church and no honor to himself. How much better he would have acted had he left that codex to be devoured by moths and cockroaches!

Nor is the following argument valid, nor does it weaken Bellarmine’s suspicion: “Orthuinus published Bennon; therefore it was not fabricated by some Lutheran.” For from the year of the Lord 1517 to the year 1535 various works could have been fabricated by Lutherans, and in fact were fabricated. Gratius included in his *Fasciculus* not only materials that preceded Luther but also others contemporary with Luther, as the *Grievances of Germany* presented at the diets of Nuremberg, Adrian VI’s letter to the German princes, Hutten’s declamation against the Donation of Constantine, the constitution for removing abuses, the ordinance for reforming the life of the clergy by Cardinal Laurentius, and other writings of this kind bear witness.

For what Sutlivius says—that things similar to the Bennonian material about Gregory were written by the Urspergensian, Sigebert, and the author of the *Life of Henry*—is a shameless fiction. Although the Urspergensian was not very favorably disposed toward Gregory, and Sigebert even less so, neither of them accused him of those horrible crimes with which Bennon charges him. Indeed, neither did the author of the *Life of Henry*, nor the writer who composed an apology for Henry IV, as I shall point out below in their proper places. Sutlivius also invokes Schaffnaburgensis with brazen impudence: nothing Bennonian appears in him, just as nothing of the kind appears in Helmold, whose testimonies about Gregory VII will shortly be produced.

Although Cardinal Bellarmine, in book VI of *On the Pontiff*, chapter 13, defended our Gregory most fully and learnedly against the accusations of heretics, adducing many and very weighty writers—many of whom lived in the very century in which Gregory ruled the Apostolic See, and some of whom were distinguished not only by learning but also by holiness of life and miracles—who write and testify in a very different way and about very different matters from that fabricator and architect of lies, Bennon, nevertheless few people possess all the authors whom Bellarmine sets against heretical shamelessness on Gregory VII’s behalf. It therefore seemed worthwhile to transcribe their testimonies word for word and place them before the eyes of readers, and afterward briefly refute Bennon’s lies and abuses—if indeed there is any need to refute what collapses of its own accord when so many and such great witnesses have been brought forward and heard. Let the procession, then, begin.

**I. Anselm, bishop of Lucca**

In volume VI of the learned D. Heinrich Canisius’s *Ancient Readings* there are two apologetic books by Anselm on behalf of Gregory VII against Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna and antipope under the name Clement III, whom the emperor Henry III—commonly called Henry IV—had set against Gregory, the legitimate shepherd.

In the first book Anselm thus addresses Guibert, the false pontiff:

“Do not therefore say that we have undertaken the care of the universal Church. For how was the Church entrusted to you, when it is clear that you did not enter through the door, which is Christ, but climbed up from elsewhere like a thief? (John 10:1.) The Apostolic and universal Church had its own shepherd.

“To speak of blessed Gregory, our father, in the words which Cyprian wrote about Cornelius: he was made bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy—or, to speak truly, of all of them—by the support of the people who were then present, and by the fellowship of the ancient priests and good men, when no one before him had been made bishop, while the place of Alexander, the place of Peter, or the rank of the priestly chair was vacant.

“Once that place had been occupied and he had been ordained by the will of God and by the consent of all of us, whoever thereafter wishes to become bishop must remain outside and cannot have ecclesiastical ordination, since he does not preserve the unity of the Church. Whoever he may be, even if he vaunts himself greatly and claims much for himself, he is profane, alien, and outside. Since there cannot be a second after the first, whoever has been made after the one who alone ought to exist is not a second, but no one.”

The abbot of Ursperg cites and recites these words in his *Chronicle*, from a letter which he says Anselm wrote to Guibert. This letter appears to have been different from the two books, as Baronius likewise judges in the appendix to volume XII of the *Annals*. It is not improbable that Anselm alludes to it in the words found at the very beginning of the first book: “I have written a few things to you with great sorrow and sincere affection, so that, recognizing your error, you might return to your senses,” and so forth; “but because your words are iniquity and deceit, and you have not wished to understand in order to do good” (Psalm 35:4), “listen meanwhile,” and so forth.

He likewise addresses Guibert as follows:

“But you have climbed up from elsewhere and have approached without being called by God; do not usurp for yourself the care of so great a government. For, as has already been said: If Gregory was in the Church—and he also remained established in your presence—he could be condemned by no judge. It is therefore clear that you, cut off from the root of the Church, have withered away and possess no power or right.”

Who, then, was this Anselm of Lucca? Was he some nobody from the crossroads, whose testimony could be blown away and scattered at the first hearing? Certainly not. Hear the Urspergensian, who in other respects was more inclined toward the schismatics than toward Gregory VII:

“Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was a man thoroughly learned in letters, extremely sharp in intellect, outstanding in eloquence, and—what is greater than all of these—highly renowned in the fear of God and holy conduct, so much so that he is reported to have been distinguished by miracles both during life and after death.”

The author who committed Anselm’s life to writing says the same concerning him, in Baronius, volume II, under the year of Christ 1086:

“In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1086, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, in the ninth indiction, after seven full years had passed since the excommunication of Henry, formerly king, and after the passing of the most blessed Pope Gregory VII, in the ninth month and on the twenty-third day, the venerable lord and our father Anselm, bishop of Lucca, fell asleep in the Lord on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the city of Mantua, while the most reverend bishop Ubaldo presided and the most noble duchess and marchioness, Lady Matilda, ruled there.”

The same author adds:

“On the third night after the venerable passing of the most holy Father Anselm, a crippled person who had always crawled on one hand and on her hindquarters rather than walked, and who had remained for one year, two months, and half a month in the house of the bishop’s nephew, was made sound and stood upright at the tomb of the aforesaid Father during the first watch of the night. On the following day, around the third hour, as it appeared, a woman blind from birth is said to have been given sight there; we heard at that time that she was a resident of the county of Brescia.”

“For the sake of brevity,” Baronius says, “we omit describing the eighty remarkable miracles performed there by the saint up to the fiftieth day after his death, when that same author was writing.”

Would not so great a man, renowned for doctrine and miracles, have been sufficient by himself to close the impure mouths of Bennon and the other slanderers of Gregory VII, even if no one else had existed to stand for Gregory VII against the lying Bennon?

**II. The author of the Life of Saint Anselm of Lucca**

The author who wrote the *Life of Saint Anselm of Lucca* was contemporary with Gregory and Anselm, and indeed was also Anselm’s disciple:

“He”—Gregory—“sent the mitre from his own head to this man, namely Anselm, as his power to bind and loose, and, I believe, also to perform miracles. For not long afterward, while we all knew what had happened, God performed through that same mitre certain splendid miracles, through Anselm’s counsel and great faith. Among other things, the most reverend lord Ubaldo, namely the bishop of Mantua, who had suffered for many years from a severe splenic illness and whose entire body was ulcerated, especially his legs, so that he could scarcely stand in any manner and scarcely even lie or sit, and who had spent much money on physicians without gaining any benefit—when that same mitre was applied to the place where the pain was greatest, was restored to his former health.”

“Thus such a blessed and great master, Gregory, performed many miracles both while alive and after death. His good disciple Anselm did likewise: master in God, disciple in God and in his most blessed master,” and so forth.

“At the end of his life, as we learned from his religious chaplains, he said: ‘I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile’ (Psalm 118:163). Thus in life and in death, almost as though by testament, he confirmed what master and disciple had taught. Gregory, while still alive, blessed those who obeyed him and, when dying, commended them also. But he utterly rejected the followers of Henry unless, after a great conversion and repentance, they finally returned. Anselm, in our presence, commanded us in the word of the Lord to remain steadfast in the faith and teaching of the most blessed Pope Gregory.”

So writes that author.

Berchtold of Constance also testifies in his *Chronicle* that Saint Anselm, both while alive and after his death, stirred up and strengthened many so that they would not cross over to the camp of the schismatics. Berchtold’s words are these:

“Blessed Anselm, formerly bishop of Lucca, began to shine with innumerable miracles in that very year of his deposition. After the death of the venerable Pope Gregory VII, while still living in the flesh, he greatly encouraged the faithful of Saint Peter against the tyranny of Henry; but after his death, shining with miracles, he encouraged them far more to persevere against that same man. Therefore Henry’s party began day by day to decline, while the Catholics did not cease to advance in fidelity to Saint Peter.”

The same author of the *Life of Saint Anselm* writes:

“Above all, he always made it his endeavor to imitate his most holy master, Pope Gregory, in everything, so that he absolutely refused to differ from him in even the smallest matter. Whatever virtue there was in him, he always attributed to the merits of that man, while recalling the monastic and solitary life, which he frequently lamented having lost,” and so forth.

The same writer of the *Life of Saint Anselm* says:

“When Pope Alexander had died, and the most holy Gregory had been elected Roman pontiff, after long resistance, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and by the unanimous vote of clergy and laity, Anselm too was elected bishop of the Church of Lucca, so that he might follow Gregory in all things; afterward he was consecrated by him.

“Accordingly, when for some time he stayed with that most religious ordainer of his—not once or twice, but repeatedly—he observed a life ineffably wonderful and wonderfully ineffable. For, although people came to him from every region and boundary of the world, he satisfied everyone; true truth and justice never departed from his mouth. First—and this is more astonishing—amid secular affairs he repeatedly transcended his own mind, his spirit made joyful by heavenly contemplation; and if at times he was left alone, he was also gladdened and strengthened by divine revelations. While he ardently desired to follow in this man’s footsteps, he began to forget the world,” and so forth.

### III. The Vatican Acts concerning the deeds of Gregory VII, in Baronius, volume XI, under the year 1073

When Pope Alexander had died and had been honorably buried in the Lateran Church, while the archdeacon Hildebrand was occupied with his funeral rites, suddenly a very great gathering of the Roman clergy and people took place in that very church, shouting and saying: “Saint Peter has chosen Hildebrand the archdeacon.” When he heard this, the archdeacon was exceedingly frightened and, as though carried outside himself, ran to the pulpit, wishing to calm the assembled people and to make them withdraw and desist from their intention. But Cardinal Hugo Candidus, when he had unquestionably recognized that everyone’s votes had converged upon the archdeacon, quickly went ahead and addressed the people in these words:

“Behold, dearest brothers: you know and recognize without doubt that, from the days of blessed Pope Leo, this archdeacon, as a prudent and approved man, has greatly exalted this most holy Roman Church and has freed this city from impending dangers. Therefore, since we cannot find anyone more suitable to govern the Church, we, the cardinal bishops, unanimously choose him for ourselves and for you as pastor and bishop of our souls.”

And immediately, with the whole people and clergy acclaiming, “Saint Peter has chosen Lord Gregory as pope,” he was clothed in a red cloak, as is customary, and adorned with the papal mitre. Unwilling and grieving, he was enthroned in the chair of Saint Peter.

### IV. The official acts of Gregory VII’s election, as they appear in the Register of Gregory’s letters, volume III of the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs, and volume III of the new edition of the councils published at Cologne

“In the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 1073 of his most merciful Incarnation, in the eleventh indiction and eleventh lunar month, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Monday, the day of the burial of Lord Alexander, of blessed memory, the second pope: so that the apostolic see might not mourn for long, deprived of its own shepherd, we, the cardinals, clergy, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests of the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church, gathered in the basilica of Saint Peter at the Chains, with venerable bishops and abbots, clergy and monks present, and with very many crowds of both sexes and of various ranks acclaiming, choose for ourselves as pastor and supreme pontiff a religious man, endowed with the prudence of a twofold learning, a most distinguished lover of equity and justice, strong in adversity, temperate in prosperity, and, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching, adorned with good morals: chaste, modest, sober, pure, hospitable, and ruling his own household well (1 Tim. 3:2). From childhood he was educated and taught with sufficient distinction in the bosom of this mother Church, and on account of the merit of his life he has until today been elevated to the dignity of archdeacon—namely, Hildebrand the archdeacon. From this moment and forever we desire and approve that he both be and be called Pope Gregory and Apostolicus.

“Do you approve?” “We approve.”  
“Do you want him?” “We do.”  
“Do you praise him?” “We praise him.”

“Enacted at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh indiction.”

### V. Lambert of Schaffnaburg, in his Chronicle, under the year 1073

Pope Alexander, also called Anselm, died. The Romans immediately, without consulting the king, elected Hildebrand as his successor, a man exceedingly learned in the sacred writings and, throughout the whole Church, including the time of the preceding pontiffs, renowned above all for every kind of virtue.

Since he was exceptionally fervent in the zeal of God, the bishops of Gaul soon began to be deeply troubled by the fear that a man of such forceful character and such ardent faith toward God might at some time subject them to a stricter examination for their negligence. Therefore they all attacked the king with a common policy and begged him to declare invalid the election that had been made without his command. They asserted that, unless he hastened to forestall the man’s assault, this evil would rebound upon no one more seriously than upon the king himself.

At once the king sent Count Eberhard from his side, so that, after meeting with the Roman nobles, he might ask them why they had appointed a pontiff of the Roman Church without consulting the king and contrary to the custom of their ancestors, and, if he did not provide a suitable answer, order him to renounce the unlawfully acquired dignity.

When Eberhard came to Rome, the aforesaid man received him kindly. After Eberhard had explained the king’s instructions, Hildebrand replied that, with God as his witness, he had never sought the summit of this honor through ambition; rather, he had been elected by the Romans, and the burden of ecclesiastical government had been imposed upon him by force. Nevertheless, he could in no way have been compelled to allow himself to be ordained until he had learned through a reliable embassy that both the king and the princes of the Teutonic kingdom had consented to his election. For this reason he had postponed his ordination and would undoubtedly continue to postpone it until a trustworthy messenger from there informed him of the king’s will.

When this was reported to the king, he readily accepted the explanation and, with the happiest approval, ordered that Hildebrand be ordained. This was done in the following year, on the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary.

The same Lambert, not far from the end of his Chronicle, where he discusses the absolution of Emperor Henry from excommunication, writes:

“After he had thus been absolved from excommunication, the pope celebrated the solemnities of the Mass. When the sacred offering had been made, he summoned the king and the rest of the large crowd that was present to the altar. Holding the Lord’s body in his hand, he said:

“‘I received letters from you and your supporters some time ago, in which you accused me of having occupied the apostolic see through the heresy of simony and of having stained my life with various other crimes, both before and after receiving the episcopate—crimes which, according to the prescriptions of the canons, would bar me from every approach to sacred orders. Although I can certainly refute the charge through the testimony of many suitable witnesses—namely, those who know with complete integrity the whole formation of my life from childhood, and those who were responsible for my promotion to the episcopate—nevertheless, lest I appear to rely upon human rather than divine testimony, and so that I may remove every cause of scandal from everyone by a brief act of satisfaction, behold: may the Lord’s body, which I am about to receive, serve me today as a test of my innocence, so that almighty God may, by his own judgment, either absolve me today from suspicion of the charge brought against me, if I am innocent, or destroy me by sudden death, if I am guilty.’

“Having first spoken these and other terrifying words, as is customary, by which he implored God to be present as the most equitable judge of his cause and the defender of his innocence, he took a portion of the Lord’s body and ate it. After he had consumed it without hesitation, and the people had acclaimed for some time in praise of God and in congratulation upon his innocence, he finally obtained silence and turned to the king:

“‘Do, then, my son, if you please, what you have seen me do. If you know yourself to be innocent, and if your reputation is being attacked by your rivals through false and slanderous accusations, briefly free both the Church of God from scandal and yourself from the uncertainty of a prolonged dispute. Take this remaining portion of the Lord’s body, so that, with your innocence proved before God as witness, every mouth that speaks wickedly against you may be stopped; and so that the princes may thereafter be reconciled to you, with me as your advocate and most vigorous defender in your cause and of your innocence, and your kingdom may be restored.’”

At these unexpected words he was thunderstruck and distressed. He prevaricated, withdrew from the crowd, conferred with his intimates, and anxiously sought their advice about what had to be done and how he might escape the necessity of so dreadful a test.

The same Lambert reports the horrible end of William, bishop of Utrecht, who was pursuing Gregory VII with utter hatred:

“William, bishop of Utrecht, obstinately defended the king’s cause against what was good and just. Out of devotion to the king’s party, on almost every solemn day, during the solemnities of Mass, he declaimed many insults against the Roman pontiff with savage mouth, calling him a perjurer, an adulterer, and a false apostle, and declaring that he had been excommunicated many times both by himself and by the other bishops.

“Shortly after the king had departed from Utrecht, once the Easter holidays were over, William was suddenly seized by a most serious illness. As he was being tormented by the sharpest sufferings of body and soul, he cried out in pitiable lamentation before all who were present that, by the just judgment of God, he had lost both the present life and the eternal one. He confessed that he had offered his services with the utmost zeal to the king in all the wrongs he had undertaken, and that, in the hope of gaining the king’s favor, he had knowingly and deliberately inflicted grave insults upon the most holy Roman pontiff, a man of apostolic virtue, though innocent.

“Thus, they say, he died while making this confession, without communion and without any satisfaction.”

### VI. The Magdeburg Annals likewise report this concerning William, in Paul Lang’s Citiz Chronicle

“In the very place,” they say, “where he had denigrated the Roman pontiff, he himself was seized by ill health, and was held by it until the pitiable end of his life. As the illness grew increasingly worse, while a certain royal official asked him to send a message through him to the king, he said:

“‘I send him this message: he himself, I, and all who favor his iniquity are condemned forever.’

“When the clergy who were present admonished him not to say such things, he replied:

“‘What else am I saying except what I visibly behold to be true? For behold, demons surround my bed in order that, as soon as I expire, they may seize me. Therefore, when I have been taken from the body, I ask you and all the faithful not to trouble yourselves by offering prayers for me.’

“Thus he died in despair and lay unburied for a long time, until word was sent to Rome. After counsel had been sought there, lest the people be corrupted by the stench, he was buried by apostolic command without the customary commendatory rites.”

### VII. Lang adds that this man is the seventh witness for the innocence of Gregory VII

The sectarians will all the more willingly admit him, since toward the nascent Lutheran sect, near the end of his Chronicle, he showed himself more kindly and fairly disposed:

“Thus several other supporters of Henry came to a bad end. Udo, archbishop of Trier, died a sudden death. Burghard, prefect of Meissen, fell from his horse and expired. So too Duke Godfrey, an enemy of Saxony, was struck down and died without confession.
