“Likewise Bishop Eppo, our great supporter and flatterer of Henry, met an evil death. In the previously mentioned chronicles of the Church of Magdeburg this is written word for word:

“‘Eppo, bishop of Citiz, while seated firmly on horseback, was crossing a certain stream near the episcopal residence of Saint Kilian—a stream that anyone on foot could have crossed without danger, where there was no fear whatsoever. When the horse fell, he died and perished in this way, Saint Kilian so arranging it that the man who had violently seized his property and had often unjustly drunk his wine would not seek anything beyond wine by justly drinking his water. And because he remained irreconcilable to us, he departed this life unreconciled to God.’

“These words are read verbatim in the aforementioned Annals of the Church of Magdeburg.”

### VIII. The Thuringian Chronicles, in the same Lang

In the year of the Lord 1073, Hildebrand, a monk by profession and archdeacon of the Roman Church, a Tuscan by birth, was solemnly and canonically elected pope with the consent of all the cardinals. He was the 147th in number and was called Gregory VII. He sat for twelve years, one month, and four days.

Through his prudence, the lack of restraint among priests was curbed not only in Italy itself but also in the Teutonic provinces. As Martin says, after holding a council of 110 bishops, he excommunicated Emperor Henry as though he were a divider of the Roman Church; but eventually he absolved him and afterward excommunicated him again, because Henry had brought about a schism in the Church, his youth and inexperience being involved in the matter.

### IX. Marianus Scotus, book III of his Chronicle

Meanwhile, after Lord Alexander the Apostolic had been taken from this world, Gregory VII, also called Hildebrand, a monk by profession, assumed the apostolic see. After hearing the just complaints and outcries of Catholics against Henry and the enormity of his crimes, he was inflamed by the zeal of God and declared the aforementioned king excommunicated, especially on account of simony.

This pleased Catholic men greatly, but it displeased the Simoniacs and the king’s supporters exceedingly. They said that it had never been heard of for a king to be subjected to excommunication. Thus the greatest division arose in the Church of God: Catholics zealously favoring the Apostolic Lord and obeying his commands, while the schismatics offered heartfelt obedience to Henry and his collaborators.

Among these Catholics was the leader and standard-bearer of justice, beloved by God and human beings, blessed Anno, archbishop of Cologne, whose memory is blessed, together with the most reverend heads of the Churches, Siegfried of Mainz, Wezelin of Magdeburg, Rucher of Halberstadt, and other bishops and abbots, monks and clerics. The princes of all Saxony also agreed with them: Duke Otto, Duke Magnus, Margrave Udo, Count Louis, and countless other military men, both noble and humble.

When the venerable Pope Gregory heard of their faithful devotion and their fervor for justice, and saw the savagery of Henry and his supporters rising against them—as it was also rising against himself—he feared that they might fail amid the tribulations they were suffering at the hands of the wicked. Instead, he wished them to become stronger, indeed more firmly established by the virtue of steadfastness. Therefore, in letters sent to them, he briefly assailed the boldness, verbosity, and pride of the heretics, raised up under Henry as their author and defender, to the injury and dishonor of the holy apostolic see.

For this reason he informed them by letter that he had bound the king with the bond of anathema. Through these letters the Catholics were made more steadfast in resisting the wicked heretics.

The same Marianus, in the same place:

“Thus the venerable bishop Gregory, recognizing the madness of the heretics and also, with truth confirming it, the steadfastness of the Catholics, sent letters to King Rudolf in which he conveyed the apostolic blessing. In them he also universally declared to all the faithful of Christ who professed obedience to blessed Peter and to himself, his vicar, that Henry, on account of his pride, disobedience, and falsehood, had been deprived of the dignity of the kingdom, while King Rudolf, because of his humility, obedience, and truth, had received it by the authority of Saint Peter.”

### X. Dodechin, continuator of Marianus

Pope Urban himself confirmed the writings and statements of the venerable Pope Gregory made against the schismatics. Under the year 1090 he mentions Pope Gregory, of blessed memory.

### XI. Stephen, bishop of Halberstadt

Stephen fought Gregory VII’s cause with the greatest vigor against King Henry in the letter he wrote to Waltram, bishop of the Church of Magdeburg—as the Pistorian edition of Dodechin has it—under the name of Count Louis. Waltram had attempted to draw Louis over to Henry’s side. The letter appears in Dodechin under the year of Christ 1090. Among other things, Stephen writes:

“Hear what is true, not embellished. Hear what is strong, not frivolous. Everyone who sells spiritual dignities is a heretic. But Lord Henry, whom they call king, sells bishoprics and abbeys. Indeed, he sold Constance, Bamberg, Mainz, and several others for money; Regensburg, Augsburg, and Strasbourg for the sword; the abbey of Fulda for adultery; and the bishopric of Münster—for it is impious even to say and hear it—for Sodomitic uncleanness.

“If you wish shamelessly to deny these things, heaven and earth as witnesses, even all the little scholars returning from the oven will conclude: ‘Therefore Lord Henry is a heretic.’ On account of these unspeakable evils he has been excommunicated by the apostolic see, and, because we are Catholics, he will be able to obtain neither the kingdom nor any authority over us.”

The same Stephen further writes:

“As for your condemning Pope Gregory, King Rudolf, and Margrave Egbert to the worst of deaths, while praising your lord because he survives them, it is plainly clear that you are devoid of all spiritual understanding. Is it not more blessed to die well than to live badly? ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake’ (Matt. 5). By this reasoning you would now also consider Nero blessed because he survived the apostles Peter and Paul, Herod because he survived the apostle James, and Pilate because he survived the Lord Jesus Christ. What could be said more insane or more wretched than such an opinion?”

### XII. Saint Anselm of Canterbury

In the preface to his book *On Fermented and Unleavened Bread*, Anselm refuses to offer any greeting of salvation to Waleram, or Walram, bishop of Naumburg, because he followed Henry’s party and had been excommunicated. He writes:

“If I were certain that your Prudence did not favor the successor of Julius Caesar, Nero, and Julian, and the power directed against the successor and vicar of the apostle Peter, I would most gladly greet you, both as a very dear friend and as a reverend bishop. But since you are seeking, according to your ability, to defend the truth against the Greeks who have come to you, we ought to fail no one in whatever way we can. I have therefore sent you the little work that I published against them concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.”

In his eighth letter to Abbot William, the same Anselm also teaches that the sentence of excommunication pronounced against the Henricians, Simoniacs, and incontinent clergy was just, and that such people, as deprived of ecclesiastical communion, ought therefore to be avoided.

Dodechin speaks with great commendation of both letters—namely, the one addressed to Walram, bishop of Naumburg, and the one addressed to Abbot William—in his appendix to Marianus under the year of the Lord 1094.

### XIII. A chronological compilation by an unknown author

In volume I of the *Writers of Germany*, formerly published by the distinguished Dr. Johann Pistorius:

“In the year of the Lord 1076”—the date is erroneous—“Pope Gregory VII of that name was ordained as the 167th from Saint Peter, etc. He was called Hildebrand and was exceedingly learned in the Scriptures, etc. This pope also strictly prohibited, under penalty, omens, divination, incantations, and magical arts.”

### XIV. Godfrey of Viterbo

Pope Gregory himself, intending to eradicate simony and restrain the incontinence of clergy, frequently summoned the emperor to synodal proceedings on these matters. By a decretal edict he prohibited throughout the Roman world, forever, the marriages of clerics from the subdiaconate upward, and established himself as God’s champion and a wall for the house of the Lord.

### XV. *Fasciculus temporum*, or Werner Rolewinck

This Gregory was a holy man and suffered many persecutions for justice. Previously he had been called Hildebrand, prior of Cluny. He was a legate in Gaul and proceeded harshly against the Simoniacs. He also miraculously defeated a certain bishop concerning simony, because that bishop could not resist the Holy Spirit.

After becoming pope, he held a synod in which he proceeded against them with similar zeal and against married priests, removing them from divine office. For the times were exceedingly barren. And because he appeared to uphold the rigor of justice in his customary manner, many rose up against him.

First, Cinthius, the prefect’s son, seized him while he was celebrating his first Mass on the night of the Nativity and placed him in his tower. But the Romans destroyed the tower, freed the pope, and expelled Cinthius from the city.

Then Gregory excommunicated the emperor on account of the schism. The emperor later came to him and, standing barefoot upon the ice for several days, scarcely obtained absolution. But the emperor did not persevere in the humble obedience with which he had begun.

### XVI. Paul of Bernried

### XVII. Gerhoch of Reichersberg

Aventine discusses both of them in book V of his *Annals of Bavaria*:

“I have read many authors, especially Paul of Bernried and Gerhoch, bishop of Reichersberg, Augustinian mystics born in Bavaria. Each published books about this destructive discord; each was a party to the upheaval—Paul at Regensburg, Gerhoch as priest of the principal church at Augsburg. Both devoted themselves to Hildebrand’s cause, etc.

“Even Henry’s friends do not deny that he was infamous for having burned with lust, amorous passions, shamelessness, and adultery, etc. Paul of Bernried, who set forth Gregory’s life in two books, and the other most vigorous defenders of his party, reveal that Gregory, though a most holy man, was rather obstinate.”

I diligently sought these two authors in Bavaria and beyond, partly through my own efforts and partly through those of friends, but I did not find them. Nevertheless, it is certain that Aventine saw and read, and perhaps also plundered, the works of both. In the same fifth book he records the following, apparently concerning William of Utrecht:

“Paul of Bernried relates that a certain bishop, while condemning Hildebrand in a public sermon, was struck by lightning. As he was dying, he said: ‘Bound by a fiery chain, I am being dragged to hell. Go and tell Caesar that he must come to his senses and compensate by his good works for the crime committed against God, blessed Peter, and his vicar, unless he prefers to follow me, who am going before him, into eternal punishments.’

“On that same day—that is, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March at Easter—as Paul likewise relates, the bishop of Speyer, an enemy of Gregory VII, died, having been devoted to destruction by him on the Kalends of March.

“When Gregory entered Salerno as an exile, a certain citizen said: ‘The author of dissension, who has involved the whole world in arms and wars, has come to disturb the peace of this city as well.’ Immediately, after saying these words, he became speechless. He was brought before Gregory, confessed his error, and was restored by Gregory to health.”

### XVIII. Berthold of Constance, in his Chronicle

Provided, however, that he is different from Bernold of Constance, whose new testimonies in favor of Gregory VII we are now bringing to light:

“Pope Alexander died at Rome. In his place the venerable Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was sought by the common counsel of all to be made pope. When he heard this, the archdeacon, considering himself unequal in strength to so great an honor—or rather burden—asked for time to reply. Then, having escaped by flight, he remained hidden for several days at Saint Peter’s at the Chains.

“But at last, scarcely discovered and forcibly brought to the apostolic see, he was ordained Pope 159 on the seventh day before the Kalends of May and was called Gregory VII. Through his prudence the incontinence of priests was restrained not only in Italy but also in the Teutonic regions: namely, what his predecessor had attempted to prohibit in Italy, he himself sought to prohibit throughout the whole Catholic Church.”

The same Berthold, under the year of Christ 1076, writes concerning the same pontiff:

“A certain Roman citizen, Cinthius, seized Pope Gregory on the day of the Nativity of the Lord while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass. One of Cinthius’s soldiers intended to kill him while he was held captive. But when the soldier brandished his sword above Gregory’s head, he was overcome by excessive terror, fell down, and could not complete the blow he had begun.”

The same Berthold records several examples of divine vengeance against the adversaries of Gregory VII and the followers of King Henry. They may appropriately be set down here:

“The bishop of Vercelli, the deposed king’s chancellor, arranged a general meeting with all his followers near the Kalends of May at Rumald, so that, if possible, he might depose Pope Gregory. But by that same date he himself, without ecclesiastical communion, miserably laid down both his life and his episcopate—alas!—at the time when he had presumed wickedly to depose the pope.

“Not long after his death, the prefect of the city of Rome, an indefatigable soldier of Saint Peter against the schismatics, was cruelly killed by a certain supporter of Henry. At his body, within a short time, more than twenty miracles occurred, as we learned from the reports of faithful men.

“Imbrico, bishop of Augsburg, who had sworn fidelity to King Rudolf at the preceding Easter, paid no attention to his perjury but joined Henry when he arrived. One day, while celebrating Mass before him, the wretched man imposed this condition upon himself: that receiving the sacred offering would become a judgment against him if his lord Henry unjustly usurped the kingdom.

“After this rash reception, throughout the brief period that he survived until his death, he never rose healthy from his bed. For he died around the Kalends of July without ecclesiastical communion.

“Likewise, Sigehard, patriarch of Aquileia, came armed to assist Henry against the apostolic ban. At Regensburg he was turned into madness and, on that very journey, was struck down by sudden death. Thus he was carried home dead in body and soul, not without the funerals of some of his companions.”

The same Berthold, under the year 1085, writes:

“But now almighty God, unwilling that his servant Pope Gregory should labor any longer and wishing rather to reward him worthily for his labors, called him from the prison of this life. After having been seriously ill in body for some time, yet remaining most steadfast in the defense of justice until death, he closed his final day at Salerno.

“All the devout of both sexes, and especially the poor, mourned his death. For he was a most fervent instructor in the Catholic religion and a most energetic defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He certainly did not want the ecclesiastical order to be subject to the hands of laymen; rather, he wanted it to surpass them both in holiness of conduct and in the dignity of its order. This cannot be hidden from anyone who carefully reads his register as Apostolicus.

“After he had legitimately struggled for twelve years and one month in the government of the apostolic see—or rather, of the whole Church—he was finally taken from this light in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. There is no doubt that he received the prize of the heavenly calling (*βραβεῖον*, reward), and he was buried at Salerno in the church of Saint Matthew, which he himself dedicated in that same year.

“But Guibert the heresiarch greatly rejoiced at his death, although his party gained little prosperity from it. For after the death of the Apostolic Lord, all the Catholics resisted that heresiarch no less than before and compelled him to retreat from Rome to Ravenna.”

### XIX. Bernard

Bernard, first master of the schools at Constance and later a monk of Corvey in Saxony, wrote an apology for Gregory VII. Berthold of Constance speaks of him in his Chronicle under the year 1088:

“Bernard, master of the schools at Constance, a most learned man and most fervent in the cause of Saint Peter, departed to the Lord in Saxony under the monastic profession.”

The same Berthold, under the year 1091, writes of him:

“Bernard, master of the schools at Constance, also left us many monuments of his intellect and wrote many elegant works in behalf of the Catholics against the schismatics of his time. First, indeed, he wrote to certain friends of his concerning the judgment of Pope Gregory VII upon the schismatics and concerning sacraments usurped outside the Church.

“Afterward he composed a great and splendid book for the venerable Hartung, bishop of Magdeburg, on the same subject, writing in the person of the holy Church. In it he appears prudently to have nullified, by testimonies from the holy Fathers, all the treacherous quibbles of those schismatics.

“Nevertheless, in these writings he is noted to have exceeded the proper measure in some places, driven by excessive zeal—namely, where he discusses the sacraments of the schismatics. For he absolutely denies that sacraments can be effected by them or by those who communicate with them, to such an extent that he holds that those ordained by them should, if they repent, be ordained again.

“Anyone who wishes to know these matters more fully should read with the greatest care a writing addressed to that same Bernard by a certain person concerning this question. Through testimonies from the holy Fathers, it will demonstrate most clearly what the holy Fathers judged should be thought about that question.

“Yet this venerable Bernard, in this matter, just as blessed Cyprian did in his position on rebaptism, did not act obstinately against the Church. Rather, in his excessive zeal against the schismatics, he exceeded the ecclesiastical rule to some degree.”

It is sufficiently clear that Bernard held this view from his letter to Bernold of Constance, which you will find below among Bernold’s minor works, and from Bernold’s first treatise *On the Sacraments of the Excommunicated*. Bernold appears to have composed the latter at the request of Bernard, later a monk of Corvey; more will be said about this below.

### XX. Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg

Berthold writes of him under the year 1088:

“Gebehard, archbishop of Juvavum, of venerable memory, preeminent in the cause of Saint Peter, who was accustomed publicly to refute the schismatics in speech and writing, was taken from this light on the eighteenth day before the Kalends [lacuna]. He left the Catholics in great sorrow.”

### XXI. The author who wrote the Life of Saint Gebehard, in volume VI of *Ancient Readings*

“After several years King Henry was excommunicated in a Roman synod, and the individual bishops, after letters had been sent by Pope Gregory, were warned and even entreated to observe obedience to Saint Peter and his vicar. They were also placed under the ban and bound, under threat of their office, not to communicate with the anathematized king or with his named counselors.

“Whether this new—or at least rare—anathema against a king derived its causes from the sale of bishoprics and abbeys or from some other disgrace, let those who knew and judged these things determine. For us, the sentence of the shepherd is to be feared, whether it is just or unjust.

“For the aforementioned Pope Gregory, of pious memory, like another Elijah, full of the Spirit of God and inflamed with zeal for justice and truth, had slaughtered the priests of Baal—not four hundred, but countless thousands—because, with Peter’s sword, he had cut down all at once either those who had obtained bishoprics, abbeys, provostships, prebends, or churches through simony; or those who had wives while in the priesthood or diaconate; or those who had been ordained by Simoniacs or schismatics.

“Therefore, at their instigation, Emperor Henry, after expelling the aforementioned Pope Gregory, enthroned Guibert, the heresiarch of Ravenna, at Rome.

“You would then have seen the little boat of blessed Peter, as though Jesus were meanwhile sleeping, almost sinking and being shaken by the violence of the storms, while the raging and seething sea either dragged all who preserved truth and faith toward blessed Peter and his vicar into the dreadful waves of death, or cast them into prolonged exile, deprived of homeland, honors, and possessions.

“Truly, exceedingly dangerous times were then approaching. Apart from our champion of Christ, Lord Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg, there could be found in the entire Teutonic kingdom no Catholic bishop except Altmann of Passau, Adalbero of Würzburg, Hermann of Metz, and Meginward of Freising—these five alone.

“At that time, therefore, this lord of ours, the aforementioned archbishop, faithful to the Roman Church and a defender of Catholic truth, stood out. Like another Maccabee, he girded himself with the breastplate of faith and protected the camps of the Church throughout the entire Teutonic kingdom with the sword of his word.”

### XXII. The *Micrologus*, or Guido of Arezzo, chapter 14 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*

“In our time God has appointed over the Roman see such a governor as Pope Gregory, of reverend memory. From childhood he was raised and educated at Rome under ten of his predecessors. He investigated all the apostolic traditions with the greatest diligence and took the greatest care to put what he had investigated into practice.

“Therefore we have decided to imitate this teacher, preeminent in religion and authority—or rather, through him the apostolic tradition itself—in the consecration of the mysteries above all, etc. Pope Gregory, of reverend memory, did this, etc.”

### XXIII. Domnizo the priest

Domnizo described the life of Matilda in verse. In this work there are various praises of Gregory VII and Anselm of Lucca. Baronius transcribes much from his book, throughout volume XI, in the years of Gregory VII’s pontificate.

### XXIV. Leo of Ostia, in the Cassinese Chronicle, book III, chapter 64

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, when Pope Gregory VII, of venerable and ever-to-be-remembered memory, was being severely oppressed by the force of illness at Salerno, three days before his death, at the request of the bishops and cardinals who happened at that time to be present together with Desiderius, he urged them, if they could in any way do so, to make Desiderius pope after his death, etc.”

In the same book III, chapter 55, Leo also relates that a heavenly vision appeared: a snow-white dove rested above Gregory while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass. Since the person who saw the vision hesitated to make it public, he was divinely commanded to disclose it in these words:

“Go quickly and report this very thing to the pope, so that, with the strength of the Holy Spirit, he may steadfastly carry out what he has begun.”

### XXV. Otho of Freising, book VI

“In the following year Alexander, having completed his life and priesthood, died and left the see to his archdeacon Hiltprand, who was called Gregory VII. From this arose a most serious schism, because Gregory had been established by election without the king’s consent.

“He himself, who for a long time had labored in private to obtain the liberty of the Church, now elevated to priestly dignity, considered it unworthy to abandon what he had begun. For this reason, as well as in order to eradicate simony and restrain the incontinence of clergy, he labored exceedingly.

“Finally, he not only summoned the king frequently to answer before synodal tribunals on such matters, but also, by promulgated decrees, restrained throughout the Roman world the marriages of clerics from the subdiaconate upward. Having become a model for the flock, he demonstrated by his example what he taught by his word, and, a strong champion in every respect, he did not fear to establish himself as a wall for the house of the Lord, etc.”

The same Otho: The aforesaid Pope Gregory was expelled from the city by the king, and Guibert, Bishop of Ravenna, was thrust into his place. Gregory, meanwhile, remaining at Salerno and approaching the time of his calling, is said to have uttered: “I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” Since, then, the kingdom in its ruler—severed from the Church—had been grievously struck, the Church too suffered no small grief, deprived of so great a pastor, who among all priests and Roman pontiffs had been distinguished by outstanding zeal and authority.

The same, book VII, chapter 1: “When Pope Gregory, of blessed memory, had died at Salerno,” etc.

[Col. 0213D] XXVI. Bruno, in the *History of the Saxon War*. It appears in volume I of the *Illustrious Writers of Germany*, published by Calvinianus Freherus. This entire History is directed against Henry and the Henricians in defense of Gregory VII and those who supported the cause of Saint Peter. He too enumerates the tragic deaths of certain schismatics, concerning whom something was said above from the Schafnaburg Chronicle and the Chronicle of Città di Castello:

“The patriarch,” says Bruno, “who, as the apostolic legate, had been the chief instigator of Henry’s renunciation and of the institution of a new king, after he had attached himself to the former king as though to a king, was turned back; overtaken by sudden death, because he maintained communion with excommunicated persons, he was taken from this life without communion and without confession.”

But since it did not befit a man of such great dignity to go alone to hell, he had, as we heard, fifty of his own as companions, seized by the same sudden death, so that those whom he had had as partners in iniquity he might not lack as participants in retribution.

Udo, Archbishop of Trier, full of every form of piety, while, being excessively mild and not resisting tyranny, he obeyed Henry more than was fitting, supplied fuel to his flaming fury with the oil of his own consent, and granted permission for churches to be plundered, was found dead the very next morning, so that it might be plainly evident to all that he had died such a death for this reason: because, in the plundering of churches, he had not feared to give his assent.

Concerning Eppo, Bishop of Città di Castello, whom Bruno also mentions here, we have already spoken above: Godefrid, duke and the greatest enemy of Saxony, perished when he was pierced by a savage blade in the more private part of his body, neither cleansed by a final confession nor fortified by holy communion.

Godebald, while lifting the hind foot of his newly shod horse in order to inspect whether the shoe had been properly fitted, was struck in the forehead by that very foot and thus carried away from this life.

Burchard, prefect of Meissen, while he was attacked by the townspeople in one of the cities under his authority, tried to flee after fruitlessly wounding with his spurs the horse on which he was mounted. That horse, which had previously often been praised for its speed, at the very moment when the greatest speed was needed became stationary, as though saying: “I am not permitted to rescue from you now the man who, when it was permitted him, did not wish to correct himself.” He therefore died with great danger to his soul, because he had often given his consent to the perilous counsels of the most savage king.

Luipold, brother of Berthald, the king’s counselor, who was himself also the king’s counselor, was riding one day beside the king and conversing with him about various matters. A hawk, which he carried on his left hand, began to flutter about as though seeking prey. Leaning forward somewhat after the bird, he fell heavily from his horse; and the sword with which he was girded slipped from its sheath, its hilt fixed in the ground, and entered the middle of his chest. He who had often been a partner in, or author of, evil counsel departed from this life without counsel for eternal salvation.

XXVII. Helmold, book I of the *Chronicle of the Slavs*, chapter 28:

“After a few days, the princes of Saxony, released from captivity against the king’s will, returned to their own lands [Col. 0214D] and thereafter never again placed confidence in the king’s promises. Having therefore sent a report, the Saxon princes complained to the most reverend Pope Gregory VII at the apostolic see that the king, a contemner of divine law, was taking away from the Churches of God all freedom of canonical election in the appointment of bishops, forcibly installing whichever bishops he wished. Moreover, they complained that, after the manner of the Nicolaitans, he had made his wife a public prostitute, subjecting her by force to the lust of others, along with many other acts that appeared improper and difficult to hear. For this reason the apostolic lord, moved by zeal for justice, sent legates and summoned the king to a hearing before the apostolic see. He disregarded the second and third summonses; but finally, compelled by the advice of his intimates, who feared that he would justly be deposed from the kingdom, he went to Rome,” etc.

XXVIII. Albert, Abbot of Stade, writes almost the same things in his *Chronicle*. He also writes under the year 1085:

“Pope Hildebrand, also called Gregory, dies at Salerno; Desiderius, Roman cardinal and Abbot of Cassino, a true servant of Christ, is appointed in his place, though greatly unwilling, with the consent of the Normans, of the most powerful woman in Italy, Matilda, and of all who zealously followed that party. Those who seemed more perfect and to be pillars in the house of God adhered to Desiderius just as they had adhered to Gregory; the rest, driven either by fear or by imperial favor, followed Guibert, also called Clement,” etc.

Since he praises Gregory’s successor—whom he well knew to have been especially devoted to Gregory—with such great commendation, he could not have thought ill of Gregory or written from a hostile judgment, since the successor’s cause was precisely the same as that of Gregory, his predecessor.

XXIX. Alphanus, Archbishop of Salerno, in a metrical oration in Baronius, volume XI:

> Protect Gregory, who shines with the honor  
> Of the chief apostolic dignity; you know that he loves Peter.  
> May he, seventh in number among the watchful,  
> Always possess the seven gifts of your Spirit.

XXX. Deusdedit, cardinal priest, in his commentary *On the Privileges of the Roman Church*, in Baronius, volume XI, under the year 1080:

“After he had sworn oaths of fidelity to his lord, Pope Gregory VII of blessed memory, and had exhibited obedience for eight years, he invaded the apostolic throne.” He is speaking of the antipope Guibert.

XXXI. The *Great Belgian Chronicle*, recently published by the most illustrious and praiseworthy man of blessed memory, Joannes Pistorius:

“Gregory VII, Tuscan by nationality,” etc.; “formerly called Hildebrand,” etc.; “afterward a cardinal, he was elected pope by the cardinals on account of his praiseworthy life,” etc.

Further on:

“When Pope Gregory, of blessed memory, had died at Salerno,” etc.

XXXII. William of Tyre, book I of the *Sacred War*, chapter 13, where, speaking of the investitures of bishoprics customarily conferred by Henry, he writes as follows:

“The lord pope, observing that this was being done contrary to all propriety and perceiving that ecclesiastical rights were being trampled underfoot in that act, warned the same emperor once, twice, and three times to desist from so detestable a presumption. When he could not recall him by salutary admonitions, he bound him with the chain of anathema,” etc.

XXXIII. Vincent, in the *Speculum*, book XXV, chapter 44, writes that Gregory became renowned for miracles and for the charism of knowing the secrets of hearts.

XXXIV. Saint Antoninus, part II of the *Summa of History*, title 16, chapter 1, § 21:

“This man, Gregory VII, was religious and God-fearing, a lover of justice and equity, steadfast in adversity and moderate in prosperity. He was also very courageous, an exceedingly zealous defender of the rights of the Church, and one who, apart from God, would have feared nothing in carrying out what pertained to justice.”

XXXV. Blondus, second Decade, book III, where he recounts at length, and with praise of Gregory, the events carried out by him.

XXXVI. Aeneas Sylvius, epitomator of Blondus, in his abridgment of Blondus.

XXXVII. Joannes Villanus, book IV of the *History of Florence*.

XXXVIII. Martinus Polonus, in his *Chronicle*:

“On account of his praiseworthy life he was elected pope by the cardinals,” etc. “He died at Salerno, shining with miracles.”

XXXIX. Sabellicus, *Enneads*, Ennead IX, book III.

XL. Volaterranus, book XXII of the *Anthropology*:

“This man, Gregory VII, endured great hardships beyond all others, because he was a pious man and a most zealous defender of the Christian religion.”

[Col. 0216B] XLI. Trithemius, in the *Hirsau Chronicle*, under the year of the Lord 1073:

“After Pope Alexander’s death, Hildebrand, Abbot of Saint Paul of our order and archdeacon of the Roman Church, succeeded him. He presided for twelve years and was called Gregory, the seventh of that name—a man certainly of great learning and of great piety, prudence, justice, constancy, and religion, who both accomplished many good things in defense of ecclesiastical liberty and endured adversity. He had first been a Cluniac monk; and, having been appointed by Pope Leo IX as archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, he was assigned to the monastery of Saint Paul. In this year, after Alexander, he was created supreme pontiff by unanimous consent.”

XLII. Nauclerus, in his *Chronicle*, Generations 36 and 37.

XLIII. Albert Crantzius, book V of the *Metropolis*, chapter I:

“Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, an Etruscan by nationality, after having done much for the Roman pontiffs, was designated by the Fathers with great and unanimous votes, the clergy and people acclaiming Hildebrand as elected by blessed Peter as his successor. XLIV. Philippus Bergomensis, in the *Supplement to the Chronicles*:

“Pope Gregory VII, an Etruscan by nationality,” etc. “A man certainly most pleasing to God and to human beings, prudent, just, merciful, the patron and father of the poor, orphans, and widows, and also the sole and most zealous defender of the Roman Church against the wickedness of heretics and the power of evil princes attempting to seize ecclesiastical property by force.”

A little farther below, concerning the same pontiff after his capture:

A little later, concerning Matilda:

“Countess Matilda, a most noble, excellent, and illustrious woman, renowned and celebrated everywhere for her virtue and her outstanding achievements.”

He calls that Guibert, who was called Clement, an antipope. A little later he adds:

“This man, the head of all evils, was seized by sudden death and paid the penalty for his crimes.”

XLV. Andreas of Regensburg, in a manuscript *Chronicle* of the Library at Saint Emmeram in Regensburg:

[Col. 0217A] “Gregory VII, a Tuscan by nationality, formerly Hiltprand, Prior of Cluny, was elected pope by the cardinals on account of his praiseworthy life. He had as antipope Wichpert, Archbishop of Ravenna, who was called Clement.”

A little farther below:

“Afterward descending into Apulia, he died at Salerno, shining with miracles.”

Further on he reports the miracle that the legate performed at Lyons concerning the simoniacal Archbishop Eberudunensis, who before his deposition could not say, “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit”; but afterward he said without difficulty, “and to the Holy Spirit.” Gobelinus reports the same story in his *Cosmodrome*, Age VI, chapter 57.

XLVI. Platina, in the *Life of Gregory VII*.

XLVII. Onuphrius, in his book *On the Supreme Pontiffs*, and in his annotations on Platina, where he says that he composed the life of this pontiff in five books.

XLVIII. Sigonius, book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, where he elegantly draws much in praise of this pontiff from older records.

XLIX. Joannes, Archbishop of Lyons, in a letter to Ivo of Chartres—letter 239 among the letters of Ivo:

“Do you accuse Gregory VII, who condemned King Henry for his crimes?”

Let these works of Bernald of Constance, now brought to light for the first time, therefore stand as the fiftieth witness in defense of Gregory VII’s innocence. Since heretics are so diligent in publishing their most mendacious Bennon, the great enemy and accuser of Gregory, it is hardly fitting that orthodox Christians should cease seeking out Gregory’s defenders and advocates.

[Col. 0217C] It should be observed that these works were composed by Bernald on the occasion of the decrees that Pope Gregory had promulgated at various times, under penalty of excommunication, against simoniacs, concubinarians, and married clerics, adding an injunction that no one should attend the Masses of such priests. Many of the authors mentioned above refer to this sanction, which was also included by Gratian in the *Decretum*, distinction 81:

“If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons who lie in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of Saint Peter, entrance into the church until they repent and amend. But if any should prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you dare to hear their office, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: ‘I will curse your blessings, he says’ (Malachi 2). But whoever refuses to obey this most salutary command incurs the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies: ‘To refuse obedience is the sin of divination, and not to submit is like the crime of idolatry’ (1 Samuel 15); and as blessed Gregory affirms: ‘Whoever, while claiming to be a Christian, disdains to obey the apostolic see, incurs the sin of paganism.’”

From this some people—among whom Sigebert in his *Chronicle* was by no means the least—seized an opportunity to construct a charge against Gregory, as though he believed that sacraments could not be validly administered by wicked and excommunicated persons, an error long ago condemned among the ancient heretics, especially the Donatists.

Others, although most devoted to Gregory, nevertheless, not from ill will but evidently carried away by excessive zeal against schismatics, simoniacs, and concubinarians, persisted in defending this very position as consistent with sound and orthodox teaching, and therefore even with the apostolic see itself. One of their number was that Bernard of Corbie, as appears from his letter, which you will find below; we also noted this above from the *Chronicle* of Bertold of Constance.

There were, moreover, not a few who mocked, disparaged, and rejected Gregory’s decrees because they were little pleasing or agreeable to flesh and blood and to the deeply corrupt morals of the clergy. Consequently, wherever they were promulgated, the clerics were almost driven mad and preferred to endure anything rather than have a restraint placed upon their license. Hear Lambert:

“Pope Hildebrand, meeting with the bishops of Italy, had already decreed in frequent synods that, according to the provisions of the ancient canons, priests should not have wives; those who had them should either dismiss them or be deposed; and no one at all should be admitted to the priesthood who did not profess perpetual continence and a celibate life. After this decree had been promulgated throughout Italy, he sent frequent letters to the bishops of Gaul, instructing them also to act similarly in their own churches and to cut off all women permanently by anathema from the companionship of priests.”

[Col. 0218C] “Against this decree the entire faction of the clergy immediately roared with great violence, loudly proclaiming that he was plainly a heretic and a man of deranged doctrine. They said that, having forgotten the Lord’s saying, ‘Not all accept this word; let him accept it who can’ (Matthew 19), and the Apostle’s: ‘If they cannot remain continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn’ (1 Corinthians 7), he was forcing people by violent exaction to live in the manner of angels; and, while denying the customary course of nature, was loosening the reins on fornication and uncleanness. If he continued to confirm his judgment, they would prefer to abandon the priesthood rather than marriage; and then he would see—he to whom human beings were so offensive—from where he would procure angels to govern the peoples through the Church of God.”

Nevertheless, he persisted, and by continual embassies accused all the bishops of sluggishness and negligence. Unless they speedily carried out the task entrusted to them, he threatened that he would proceed against them with apostolic censure.

The Archbishop of Mainz, knowing that this undertaking would not be a small matter—namely, to uproot a custom established over so long a time and to reform a world already grown old back to the beginnings of the nascent Church—acted more moderately with them. At first he gave them a half-year’s delay and an opportunity for deliberation, urging them to do voluntarily what necessarily had to be done and thus to remove from himself and from the Roman pontiff the necessity of issuing some harsher decree against them.

Finally, when a synod had been convened at Erfurt in the month of October, he pressed them more closely, insisting that, with all evasion set aside for the present, they should either renounce marriage or withdraw from the ministry of the sacred altar.

They, on the other hand, brought forward many arguments by which they tried to evade his urgent and pressing demand and to annul his judgment. Since neither arguments nor supplications and entreaties achieved anything against the authority of the apostolic see—by which, he claimed, he had been compelled to impose this requirement against his own will—they went out, as though to deliberate, and formed a plan not to return to the synod but all, without being dismissed, to depart to their homes.

Some even cried out in confused voices that it seemed better to them to return to the synod, drive the bishop from his episcopal chair before he promulgated the execrable judgment against them, and, having punished him with the death he deserved, transmit a notable memorial to posterity, so that none of his successors would thereafter attempt to devise a charge against the priestly name,” etc.

This is what Lambert reports concerning the clergy, who used the same kind of argumentation as Lutheran and Calvinist preachers today use against celibacy.

The king and the courtiers likewise, most unwillingly, allowed the rich and abundant morsels of ecclesiastical property—which they had already seized with greedy jaws—to be taken from them; nor did they wish the ecclesiastical liberty, miserably oppressed by royal power and royal domination, to be restored to its former freedom. Hence arose the common hatred of all orders against Gregory, and from hatred, as usually happens, curses, fabrications, lies, and whatever brilliant bile suggests.

[Col. 0219C] To confront these and similar charges, our Bernald published these studies. In the first [Col. 0220A] treatise and in several letters he demonstrated that the sacraments are validly administered by excommunicated persons. Likewise, he engaged in an epistolary skirmish with Alboin concerning continence. Alboin initially fought in defense of clerical marriages, using almost the same weapons with which heretics today attack continence in general.

Bernald also composed a complete apology for Gregory’s synodal decrees, as an eyewitness to the turbulent and disgraceful things that were then being done by the schismatics in the empire.

Nor did Gregory VII ever forbid the faithful to attend the Masses of concubinarians for the reason that he supposed the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood could not validly be prepared and offered by them. Rather, because the disease had become entrenched and could not be overcome by any easy remedy, it demanded this harsh treatment at that time. [Col. 0220B] Saint Anselm says in his letter to William, Abbot of Hirsau:

“It is wholly unfitting that one should reverently be present where men, obstinately, openly, and shamelessly reeking with lust, serve at the sacred altars while despising the prohibition of God and the saints; indeed, they do not serve, but, so far as they are concerned, pollute them. This is not so that anyone should consider the things they handle contemptible, but so that he should regard the handlers as execrable, and that those who do not reverence the presence of God and the angels may at least, driven away by human detestation, cease to contaminate holy things. Nor is it at all proper that those who, through uncleanness, make themselves strangers to the altar should be companions of those who participate at the altar.”

But before we hear Bernald himself, it will not be out of place to investigate who this Bernald was. Know, then, the following.

[Col. 0219]

## PROEM OF JACOB GRETSER, PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS, TO PAUL OF BERNRIED’S BOOK ON THE DEEDS OF GREGORY VII, SUPREME PONTIFF

(*Works of Jacob Gretser*, volume VI, p. 120.)

[Col. 0219D] To the most reverend and most illustrious prince and lord, Lord John Godfrey, Bishop of the Church of Bamberg, etc., Jacob Gretser.

When last year, most reverend and most illustrious prince, I published the second volume of the *Bellarminian Defense*, in which Christ and his supreme vicar on earth are discussed, I added at the end of the work a special apology for Gregory VII, supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0219D] You will find this above]. I did so because the heretics of our age and the schismatics of the preceding generation hate this one man, above all the other pontiffs, with the greatest malice, tear him apart with countless curses and insults, and aim and discharge all the arrows of their poisoned tongues at him as at their principal target.

If we cut the matter to the quick and examine it more deeply, they do this for no other reason than that Gregory was the most steadfast and undaunted champion and defender of ecclesiastical liberty and discipline. He allowed himself to be led from the right path by no threats and no dangers—of which he endured very many. Along with various other things that offer splendid testimony to his integrity, innocence, and holiness, this above all bears witness to him: that the most learned men of those times and of the years immediately following, celebrated for their renown in virtue, fearlessly joined Gregory’s side in the schism that had arisen. Some of them preferred to lose all their possessions and go into exile rather than lose their faith, reverence, and obedience toward the apostolic see.

Among these the following led the way: Anselm of Lucca, Anselm of Canterbury, Hermann of Metz, Altmann and Ulrich of Passau, Gebhard of Constance, Gebhard and Thiemo of Salzburg, Anno of Cologne, and Burckhard of Halberstadt, all archbishops and bishops; likewise William, Abbot of Hirsau, a man celebrated by everyone for his reputation for religious devotion—to say nothing of others.

Nor were there lacking among the learned those who, by written records, made it known to posterity how diligent and indefatigable a pastor of the Church Gregory VII had been, with what care and vigilance he had governed Christ’s fold, and how falsely and calumniously he was traduced by the sowers of schisms, as though the cause and blame of all disturbances and upheavals had clung, or still clung, to him alone.

Among these apologetic defenders of Gregory VII, two formerly shone in Bavaria under Kings and Emperors Henry IV and Henry V: Paul of Bernried and Geroch of Reichersberg. But, lamentably, their works on behalf of Gregory VII came into being as though they had never been born, buried in long oblivion and darkness. We might perhaps have remained unaware that they had ever existed, had not Aventine, who saw and read them, given an indication in the *Bavarian Annals*. Aventine not only saw them but, it seems, begrudged them to posterity, lest they should possess men to set against Pseudo-Benno in his frenzied accusations against Gregory VII.

However matters may stand, through a kindly providence I finally came upon Paul of Bernried, after seeking him carefully, indeed anxiously, in various libraries. Nor have I entirely abandoned hope concerning Geroch, the companion both of this writer and of the hardships that Paul suffered from the schismatics.

[Col. 0221D] Meanwhile, while Geroch is being sought and rescued from darkness into the light, I have ordered Paul, furnished with annotations, to come forth publicly—and indeed under your patronage, most reverend and most illustrious prince.

It was fitting that, amid this public and solemn joy shared by all good people—some congratulating themselves, some, and indeed especially, the most noble Church and diocese of Bamberg on Your Highness’s elevation to the throne of Saint Otto, and others offering pious prayers for Your Highness’s long safety and for the auspicious administration of your episcopate and principality—I too should openly express the joy conceived in Bavaria and now widely manifested.

When Saint Basil had been elevated to the archbishopric of Caesarea with the common approval and joy of all who loved the orthodox faith, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus sent him a congratulatory letter (letter 24), which he began in this manner:

“After I learned that you had been placed upon the lofty throne, and that even that lamp which had previously shone dimly had been displayed before the eyes of all above the lampstand by the victorious Spirit, I rejoiced, I confess. And why should I not? For I saw that the body of the Church was in poor condition and needed such guidance and assistance.”

Most illustrious bishop, permit me, with Your Highness’s kind indulgence, to speak openly and frankly of what is true. As soon as Fame—otherwise tenacious of both bad and good, and the messenger of both falsehood and truth—brought us news of Your Highness’s election, and brought it with complete truthfulness, the spirit and speech of all the Catholics whom I saw were the same as once those of Nazianzus when Basil was adorned with the episcopal tiara.

Many burst forth with Gregory, the father of Gregory of Nazianzus, into these words (letter 23 among the letters of Nazianzus):

“Others will choose and put forward other men, each according to his own character or advantage, as commonly happens in such matters. But we choose no one; for it is not lawful—we can prefer no one, not now to Basil, but to John Godfrey of Aschaffenburg. For whom among all whom we know shall we find more approved in life, more powerful in speech and learning, and more thoroughly polished on every side in the refinement of virtue?”

Nor does common joy arise without reason when a diligent governor, attentive in every direction, is placed over a Church. For, as the same Gregory says (letter 22):

“The lamp of the body is the eye—not merely the eye that sees and is seen in a bodily manner, but also that which looks spiritually and is spiritually regarded. The bishop, however, is the lamp of the Church. Therefore, just as when the eye is pure and sound the body too is rightly guided, but when it is impure the body is not rightly guided, so likewise, according to the condition in which the bishop of the Church finds himself, it is altogether necessary that the Church share either danger or salvation.”

These words were spoken with complete truth by Gregory of Nazianzus, at once a most holy and most learned bishop.

Since at this time, among my literary and bookish possessions, I found nothing with which to congratulate Your Highness on the dignity you have attained except Paul, I did not hesitate to send him forth as Your Highness’s messenger. For if, three years ago, Your Highness received so kindly the *Preacher Flogged* that I offered you, what may Paul not promise himself? He comes accompanied by a supreme pontiff—and by one so great and so distinguished—and not only by a pontiff but also by a cardinal, the most illustrious and learned Caesar Baronius, whom Your Highness, I have no doubt, holds dear and in high esteem on account of the golden volumes of his *Annals*. With his apologetic, so to speak, sponge I wiped away the Calvinist stains, just as Paul once wiped away the schismatic stains from Gregory VII.

This entire work of mine, whatever it may be, I both willingly and reverently speak and offer to Your Highness, until something more worthy of Your Highness’s dignity and rank should appear. I humbly pray God to preserve for as long as possible, safe and surviving, a most vigilant governor for the Church of Bamberg, a singular patron for our Society, and a benevolent Maecenas for all learned people, always flourishing through heavenly gifts and support.

Ingolstadt, 19 March, in the year of the Redeemer 1610.

# PROLEGOMENA TO THE LIFE OF GREGORY VII, SUPREME PONTIFF

[Col. 0223]

I ask you, friendly Reader, to read this preface before you proceed to read this commentary.

## Who Paul of Bernried Was

[Col. 0223B]

Aventine will explain this to us in book V of the *Bavarian Annals*:

“I have read many men, especially Paul of Bernried and Geroch, prelate of Reichersberg, Augustinian religious born in Bavaria. Both published books concerning this kind of pernicious discord, and both were parties to this disturbance. The former was a priest at Regensburg; the latter, a priest of the principal church at Augsburg; both supported the cause of Hildebrand. For this reason they were driven from their seats and into exile.”

So Aventine.

That Paul was a priest or canon of Regensburg is made clear from chapters 43 and 44 of the *Life of the Virgin Herluca*. It seems that, after being expelled from Regensburg, he embraced the institution of the Canons Regular at Bernried, or Beronica—not before then, although even earlier he occasionally withdrew from Regensburg in order to avoid the persecution of the Henricians, as is clear from the same *History of the Blessed Virgin Herluca*.

The same Aventine, in the same place:

“Paul of Bernried, who encompassed his Life in two books, and the other most zealous champions of his party, report that Gregory, a most holy man, proved rather too obstinate.”

I do not know with what eyes Aventine read the Bernried author. Certainly, in my Paul there is no trace of this accusation or charge of obstinacy. Indeed, Gregory was so far from being obstinate in this matter that whenever King Henry showed even the slightest sign of amendment, Gregory was prepared to receive him again into the favor and communion of the apostolic see.

The Saxons, in fact, were so far from accusing Gregory of obstinacy that they almost charged him with excessive slowness in condemning Henry, in letters sent to him and incorporated by Bruno into his *History of the Saxon War*. And Gregory’s own prayer to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, recited by Paul when he excommunicated Henry for the last time, sufficiently demonstrates how little Gregory acted stubbornly in this affair.

Aventine continues:

“Geroch too—than whom no one defended Hildebrand more vigorously in written books, since he explains the charges brought against the Emperor, which I have read nowhere else—was finally compelled by truth to mark the obstinacy, not to say tyranny, of his own party in these words: ‘The Romans,’ he says, ‘claim divine honor for themselves, refuse to give an account of their actions, and cannot calmly endure being asked: Why do you act in this way?’” etc.

I have not seen Geroch; would that I might see him someday! But from what Aventine himself relates about Geroch, from Aventine’s character, and likewise from what he attributes to Paul of Bernried, it is possible to estimate with what reliability he reported these things about Geroch. I shall believe that Geroch uttered such words when I have read them with my own eyes in Geroch.

The same Aventine:

“Paul of Bernried relates that a certain bishop, while censuring Hildebrand in a sermon before the people, was struck by lightning; and, while he was giving up his soul, said: ‘Bound by a fiery chain, I am dragged to the realms below. Go and tell the Emperor to come to his senses and compensate by his deeds for the crime committed against God, Saint Peter, and his vicar, unless he prefers that eternal punishments follow me as I go before him.’ On that same day, namely at Easter, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, as the same Paul relates, the Bishop of Speyer, hostile to Gregory VII, who had been cursed by that same Gregory on the Kalends of March, died.

“When Gregory, an exile, entered Salerno, a certain citizen had said: ‘The author of dissension, who has enveloped the whole world in arms and wars, has come to disturb the peace of this city as well.’ Immediately after saying these words he became mute. He was led to Gregory, confessed his error, and was restored by him to health.

“Bernried is a college of Augustal priests in Upper Vindelicia, near Lake Wörth, fifteen miles above Munich; there the tomb of Herluca, a consecrated woman, is shown. She lived at that time and, accustomed to participate in nocturnal encounters with beings above and below and in secret conversations, was accustomed to relate that the accursed were tormented by the most burning flame of all.”

All these things, as Aventine records them, are found in the *Life of Gregory* that we are now publishing, as are also the matters he mentions concerning Ruland, a cleric of Parma, and concerning the prodigious egg. The former—Ruland—escaped only through Gregory’s help, as Paul reports. A comparison of Aventine’s narrative with this Life will clearly show that almost everything Aventine writes there was extracted from Paul of Bernried.

I except, however, the calumnies that Aventine repeatedly sprinkles through his history. He either fabricated these from his own head or received them from the unnamed author of an apology for Henry IV. I strongly suspect that Aventine’s following assertion was taken from the same source:

“Gregory VII also distributed among soldiers and men skilled in warfare the ecclesiastical riches by which the poor had hitherto been nourished. Geroch of Reichersberg and Paul of the Hildebrandine party do not deny this; the latter excuses it as a good deed and defends its lawfulness.”

I do not find this excuse or defense in my Paul. Did Aventine possess a Paul who was not more abundant but more compliant—one who would say whatever Aventine himself, hostile to Gregory, wished?

How it may be established that Paul of Bernried is the author of this commentary.

The codex from which the exemplar of this Life was taken did not bear the name of Paul of Bernried. How, then, is it clear that this work ought to be ascribed to Paul? I reply that this is made evident by Aventine, whose codex bore the name of Paul of Bernried written at its head; moreover, everything that Aventine quotes from his Paul is found in our copy, as we said earlier. It makes no difference that in our exemplar the work is not divided into two books. For Aventine testifies that Paul comprised Gregory’s Life in two books, whereas Wolfhard, the collector of Lives—of whom more shortly—who gathered Gregory’s Life together with the others into a single volume, perhaps removed this division, as frequently happens in books of every kind. Indeed, the history that we are now publishing is lengthy and can most conveniently be divided into two books.

## II

Paul of Bernried wrote a Life of the virgin Herluca, a considerable portion of which the Reverend and highly learned Father Charles Stengelius, of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Ulrich in Augsburg, transferred into the Life of Saint Wicterp, bishop of Augsburg; I present that Life in its entirety below. In that little work Paul testifies that he had likewise committed Gregory’s Life to writing, and that what he wrote in Herluca’s Acts concerning a certain heavenly vision granted to Herluca he had already explained in his commentary [Col. 0225C] *On the Deeds of Gregory VII*. Whatever Paul writes in the virgin Herluca’s Life about Christ, who in broad daylight, wounded and dripping with much blood, had made himself visible to her, appears in this Life not far from the end, as we noted there; the same is true of what is related in the Life of the virgin Herluca concerning the death of Adalbert, the priest of Rota. From these facts it is plainly evident that Paul of Bernried was the author of both works.

Paul wrote Gregory VII’s Life in the year of the Lord 1131. This is made clear by the fact that, at the end of this commentary, he speaks as follows of Ulrich, bishop of Passau and successor of Altmann:

> “This man—namely, Thiemo or [Col. 0225D] Theodeman, archbishop of Salzburg—had ordained the ordainer of our humility, namely the most reverend Ulrich, bishop of Lorch or Passau and legate of the Apostolic See, who seven years ago, after many struggles, fell asleep in the Lord in defense of the Gregorian doctrine,” etc.

Ulrich died on the seventh day before the Ides of August in the year 1124, although the *Chronicon Austriacum* places his death in the year 1121. If one counts seven years from that year, one arrives at the year of our Redeemer 1131.

Paul also mentions in this history Callistus II and Gelasius II, Roman pontiffs; Gelasius began his pontificate in 1118, and Callistus in 1119.

[Col. 0226A] Baronnius also records, under the year of salvation 1106, a letter of Paschal II to Ulrich, or Oderic, bishop of Passau, and to Gebhard, bishop of Constance.

Berthold likewise speaks of the same matter in his *Chronicle*, under the year 1092:

> “The bishop of Salzburg, Dimo—Thiemo—came into Bavaria and ordained for the Church of Passau, which had long been widowed, a bishop named Ulrich, provost of the Church of Augsburg; and on Pentecost itself he solemnly consecrated him together with the bishops of Constance and Worms. This gave the Catholics great confidence, so that they might persist in loyalty to Saint Peter and resist the madness of the schismatics with greater perseverance.”

[Col. 0226B] What sort of codex this history was copied from, you will learn more satisfactorily from the words of the most distinguished and learned man, Sebastian Tengnagel, without whose help and labor Paul would still be lying in darkness, decay, and filth, contending with cockroaches and moths, perhaps without any hope of publication. Thus he wrote to me from Vienna:

> “I believe that I have fortunately unearthed your Paul, whom you have long and diligently sought, unless my conjecture deceives me. I possess Lives of the Saints for April, May, and June, contained in a single volume, a large and substantial book, collected by a certain Wolfhard—as is clear from the preface to June—and written on parchment. The manuscript is of quite good quality and was written approximately four hundred [Col. 0226C] years ago. At the end of May a Life of Pope Gregory VII has been added. It begins as follows: ‘Therefore Gregory VII, upon whom the spirit of the first Gregory truly rested, a Tuscan by birth, had Bonicus as his father, and at baptism himself received the name Hildebrand,’ etc. From there it proceeds to his praises and records several miracles. Then, when it comes to Rulandus of Parma, our author relates what Aventine attributes to Paul: that the pious father—that is, Gregory—threw his whole body over Rulandus, so that he would not be cut down, while everyone was shouting that he was dead. This speech of Gregory, which Aventine also touches on briefly, follows. He also adds the story of the hen that laid an egg wonderfully decorated by art. I am therefore led to believe that Aventine both possessed this author and, in some places, secretly extracted from him both words and meaning. As for Aventine’s testimony that this Paul comprised Gregory’s Life in two books, whereas our copy is not divided into books, I think that Paul’s little work was abridged into this epitome by Wolfhard. Be that as it may, the author appears to have lived not long after the Gregorian age. For on the last page, where he records the death of Theodomar, bishop of Juvavum, he adds the following: ‘This man—that is, Theodomar—had ordained the ordainer of our humility, namely the most reverend Ulrich, bishop of Passau, who seven years ago, after many struggles in defense of the Gregorian doctrine, according to whose rule he had been both elected and promoted, fell asleep in the Lord in the hundred and fifth year of his age,’ etc.”

[Col. 0227A] Such were the words of that most learned and gracious man. Yet I am scarcely persuaded by his theory of an epitome. For in this history of ours the deeds of Gregory VII are described so fully—with the exception of the condemnation of Berengar, which Paul passes over—that no one could reasonably desire a fuller account.

In copying this Gregorian history from an old exemplar and comparing it with the autograph, the Reverend Father Georgius Sturnus, a member of our Society and professor of philosophy in the Vienna College, has undertaken an entirely outstanding and fruitful service to the Catholic cause. Accordingly, both the distinguished Tengnagel and he deserve Paul of Bernried’s thanks for his salvation and life; and all true lovers of truth, as well as haters of schismatics and heretics, owe them great gratitude. Would that it had been possible to obtain a second exemplar! For my part, I spared no effort to acquire one. But I have labored in vain—at least until now; yet I do not despair. There will be someone who completes what we have begun, once Geroch too has been brought to light. May it be so, may it be so! For I see no other way to express my desire.

## On the Etymology of the Name Hildebrand

It is worth hearing what investigators of origins have handed down concerning the etymology of the word *Hildebrandus*. Since sectarians constantly have this name in their mouths, and scarcely ever call Pope Gregory VII “Gregory,” but almost always “Hildebrand,” it is necessary to examine whether it is the sort of name that may legitimately be hurled at Gregory as an insult, and whether they have sufficient reason for transforming *Hildebrand* into *Hellebrand*, in imitation of the ancient schismatics.

There is an anonymous author *On the Proper Names of the Germans*, whom some consider to have been Luther. It appears in the first volume of a historical work published at Basel in 1574. This little book was also published separately at Ursel in 1569, expressly under Luther’s name. He writes:

> “*Brynn* or *Brenn*—as the ancient songs of heroes, the *Heldenbuch*, indicate—is a helmet, especially one with a crest or horns. Therefore *Brennus* is ‘the helmeted man,’ and *Brennburg* is either the castle of Duke Brennus or the castle of the Brenni, that is, a stronghold of helmeted and armed men for the protection of the region. And that rather large beetle which, equipped with red horns and shell-colored wings like a helmet, is called in our region a *Husbrenner*. *Hiltebrand* for *Heltbrenn* means ‘the giant and hero of the Brenni,’ as their head and leader, today *Hauptmann über den reisigen Zeug*, commander over the mounted troops. For *Helt* signifies a hero, such as Achilles or Hector. We have said that Luitprand, king of Lombardy, stands for *Lutbrenn*, that is, ‘the helmeted man of the people,’ who protects people with arms; for *Luit*, *Lyt*, or, in Swabian, *Leute*, signifies ‘people’ in the plural.”

Although the change from *Brand* to *Brenn* in this etymology may seem excessively forced, it nevertheless makes clear that for Luther *Hildebrand* was not *Hellebrand*, that is, “a firebrand of hell,” as Lutherans and Calvinists now slanderously claim. Rather, it means “the leader, head, stronghold, and protector of the Brenni,” that is, of helmeted men. And Gregory VII truly was such a Hildebrand. He showed himself a hero, leader, and standard-bearer to that army concerning which the Apostle’s exhortation in Ephesians 6 is found:

> “Stand therefore, with your loins girded with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, etc., and take up the helmet of salvation,” etc.

For how many wars this hero—and, as the Germans call him, *Helde*, from which Luther derives the name *Hiltebrand*—undertook, and how successfully he brought them to an end against both visible and invisible enemies, our Paul, among others, makes abundantly clear. Thus it was only by divine providence that the name *Hiltebrand* first came to him. For such an honorable etymology we have reason to thank Luther, otherwise wholly undeserving of thanks—if, that is, Luther was the author of the little book mentioned above.

[Col. 0228B] The etymology proposed above is not far removed from another offered by the Calvinist Goldast, who, in his notes on the *Paraeneses* of Tyrol, king of the Scots, supposes that those whom the ancients called Celts were called *Cheld*, or, with doubled aspiration, *Hheld*, which for us is now *Held*. Thus *Hildebrand* would mean *Chelte Bren*, that is, “the Celtic Brennus”; and the following names would likewise derive from the same origin: *Hiltebolt*, *Hiltiman*, and *Hiltiwin*. Among women’s names are *Hiltigart*, *Hiltrut*, *Hiltegunt*, *Adilhilt*, and *Reginhilt*. Here again one sees that in the name *Hildebrand* there is nothing infernal or Tartarean, as the heretics allege, but everything heroic, deriving from the Celt or hero and from the helmet.

Aventine writes in his *Nomenclature of Proper Names*:

> “*Helt*: hero. *Hyld*, *Huld*: love. *Hyldeprand*: firebrand of love.”

He gives the same interpretation for *Luitprand*: “firebrand and love of the people.” But for many it is scarcely credible that *prand* or *brand* in such compounds should be understood as “firebrand,” although our Paul too holds this opinion at the very beginning of his history. However that may be, Aventine did not think of seeking the etymology of *Hildebrand* in the Underworld; rather, he derived it from hero or love. The Germans have many proper names of this kind, such as *Huldreich*, *Huldenreich*: “love of the kingdom,” or “rich and full of love.” In common usage, Ulrich; among the ancients, Hilderic; among the Celts, Childeric. *Hyldeprecht*: “worthy of love.” *Hyldebertus*; among the Celts, Childebertus. *Hyldegart*: “garden of love.” You will find very many words of this kind, both men’s and women’s names, in the *Catalogue of Proper Names by Which the Alemanni Were Formerly Called*, volume II of the *Alemannic Writers*.

Among our ancestors *Brand* also meant “sword,” in which sense Italian poets still use the word. What, then, if *Hiltebrand* or *Hildebrand* means “the hero’s sword” or “the sword of love”? The man who, in a little book entitled *Etymologies of Various Names*, devised the following etymology for us seems ridiculous to me:

> “*Hillebrant*, *Hillebrandus*: burning, loving, wooing *Hillam*.”

At least he should have said: “loving *Hilt* or *Hiltam*,” for these are two women’s names, as is clear from the catalogue cited immediately above. So much concerning the name Hildebrand.

That Gregory in Greek is the same as *Vigilius* and *Vigilantius* in Latin is too well known to require lengthy demonstration—although the name *Vigilantius* is now disgraceful and ill-omened because of the heretic Vigilantius. Among the ancient Alemanni, Gregory was called *Vuachar*, *Vuachere*, *Vuachiri*, *Vuacho*, or *Vuahcho*. Moreover, Catholics know with joy that Gregory VII did not bear the name Gregory without reason; schismatics and heretics know it with groaning.

[Col. 0229]

# EXCERPT FROM GRETSER’S DISSERTATION ENTITLED: “CAESAR BARONIUS, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, VINDICATED FROM THE CALUMNIES OF THE CALVINIST *RATIONALIS*, AND IN HIM THE OTHER ROMAN PONTIFFS, INCLUDING GREGORY VII, BY JAMES GRETSER, THEOLOGIAN OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS”  
(*Works of James Gretser*, VI, 224)

## On the Council of Worms against Gregory VII

[Col. 0229B] On this subject, see Baronius, volume XI, under the year of salvation 1076. From Albert of Stade he reports that the Saxon bishops by no means consented to the deposition of Gregory VII. The Calvinist objects: “Albert is not at hand for me, and therefore I cannot decide.” But Albert was at hand for Baronius. Hear Albert’s own words:

> “In the year of the Lord 1076 a council was held at Worms in the presence of King Henry, at which almost all the German bishops, except the Saxons, deposed Pope Gregory.”

The Calvinist attacks Baronius with the utmost fury and, to obtain more abundant material for his assault, invents out of his own brain the claim that Baronius said that Reiner Reineccius was the first person to publish the Life of Henry IV and Bennon’s work on Gregory VII. He demonstrates [Col. 0229C] that this is false. He does well, because he exposes not a falsehood of Baronius but his own: Baronius said that Reineccius was the editor; he did not say that he was the first.

Baronius rejects as spurious Henry’s letter to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, because Anno, the archbishop, had already died the previous year, that is, in 1085, and yet in 1086 he is invited to the synod of Worms. To extricate himself from this difficulty, the Calvinist changes Anno into Hildolphus and says that the letter was addressed by Henry to him. This invention occurred to neither Reineccius, nor Urstisius, nor Reuber, nor anyone else. For all of them published this letter under the name of Anno, not Hildolphus. The Calvinist owes this to his “fertile criticism,” [Col. 0229D] by which, armed with it, he dissolves even knots that cannot be untied.

By the same benefit of his criticism he transforms *Pentecosten*, which appears at the end of Henry’s letter, into *Heptecosten* or *Heptacosten*, a new and unheard-of word in the Latin Church, supposedly meaning *Septuagesima*. If we follow this method of criticism, scarcely any error will be so obvious that one cannot make a medicine for it from the apothecary’s shop of criticism—if this is making medicine, rather than turning everything upside down. The very beginning of the letter sufficiently refutes the Calvinist fiction. For the author praises the person to whom he writes not as someone recently appointed, but as a veteran prince of many merits. This cannot be said of Hildolphus, who was the newest bishop at the time of the council at Worms. For, as Berthold of Constance testifies in his *Chronicle*:

> “Aimo or Anno, the venerable archbishop of Cologne, [Col. 0230C] of wondrous holiness, rested in peace on the eleventh day before the Nones of December in 1075; Hiltolfus, inferior in birth and character, succeeded him.”

The Worms synod began immediately afterward, at Septuagesima in the year 1076.

Baronius says that no one has ever handed down to memory that Henry’s envoys were received by Gregory VII in the manner imagined by the author of this letter. The Calvinist, not without monstrous abuse, thrusts Aventine upon Baronius. This, of course, was all that remained! As though Baronius had pronounced this judgment about ancient writers, rather than about those recent writers infected with heresy. Produce, if you can, an ancient and venerable witness; for we attach no value to this newcomer, whose mouth and style are equally bad. You will not even find this story about the envoys in Bennon.

In the Life of Saint Anselm of Lucca, Gregory VII’s deposition is called “a deed unheard of throughout the ages.” Gregory himself says the same in one of his letters. The Calvinist objects: “Popes have often been deposed by emperors and synods.” He then quotes from his own Illyricus a letter of the bishops of Gaul and Germany “to Anastasius II, Roman pontiff, in which they warn the pope and the Italian bishops to dismiss themselves and not continue exercising tyranny over them.” He also adduces another letter of the bishops of Germany and Belgium to Nicholas I, from the Council of Cologne in 863.

But neither those who are said to have written to Anastasius, nor those who wrote to Nicholas, removed either one or the other from his see or excommunicated him, as the leaders of the council at Worms did. Those bishops were compelled—not merely in some fashion, but by an oath, according to a prescribed formula set out in [Col. 0231B] Bruno’s *On the Saxon War*—to curse and abandon Gregory VII. If we weigh all the circumstances of this pseudo-synod, what was done by those men may rightly be called “a deed unheard of throughout the ages,” for no similar example can be produced. For all the other acts that were at any time committed unlawfully and unjustly against pontiffs, including the deposition of John XII in the Roman pseudo-synod, carry with them less disgrace. John’s depravity of life, by which he had stained himself from sole to crown, could in some measure excuse those who attempted to depose him; but in Gregory VII, a man of wholly blameless life, there was no such circumstance.

But to say something about the letter to Anastasius: no reliable author mentions it. Illyricus copied it into his *Catalogue* from Aventine’s manuscript notes and adversaria, and he did not know where Aventine had obtained it. Am I then to place faith in a letter whose origin and birthplace are unknown? Illyricus also doubts whether it was sent to Anastasius I or Anastasius II. The person who thinks most correctly will believe that it was sent to neither. Our Calvinist, wiser than Aventine, assigns it to Anastasius II in the year 497, although no trace whatsoever of any council held in Gaul is found in the Frankish or other annals. Yet the Calvinist attaches to it the title containing these words: “From the Council.” Tell me, please, what kind of council this is! He also prefixed a title as though the letter came from bishops, although it comes from Illyricus.

Concerning the other letter of Guntharius and Theutgaud, read Baronius, volume X, under the year of Christ 863, no. 18 and following. You will see that our sectarians are worthy of undertaking a cause against the Roman pontiffs with such utterly corrupt patrons and defenders.

[Col. 0231]
