# EXCERPTS FROM THE DISSERTATION ENTITLED: “A TWOFOLD DEFENSE—OR RATHER A FOURFOLD REPLY—AGAINST THE CALVINIST REPLIER, OR RATHER QUADRUPLIER, MELCHIOR GULDINASTUS: THE FIRST PART CAREFULLY EXAMINES AND REFUTES THE CALVINIST REPLY, WHICH DESTROYS THE ANCIENT MAJESTY OF THE HOLY ROMAN ORTHODOX AND CATHOLIC EMPIRE; THE SECOND PRESENTS TO THE READER SEVERAL HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED DOCUMENTS IN DEFENSE OF GREGORY VII AND OTHER ROMAN PONTIFFS”  
By Gretser, theologian of the Society of Jesus; edited by C. V. Sebastian Tengnagel, J.U.D. and prefect of the Imperial Library at Vienna  
(*Works of Gretser*, VI, 299)

## I. On the Oath that Henry IV Swore to Gregory VII

[Col. 0231C] The Calvinist rages most violently here because I called Henry IV “king of Germany”: “for he was king of many other kingdoms as well.” Why do you rave, O Calvinist? Did I thereby deny that Henry’s power extended beyond the borders of Germany? If I call Philip III “king of the Spains,” do I by this designation deprive him of possession of the two Indies, Sicily, Naples, and so many other kingdoms? Do I do him an injury if I name him from his best-known and principal kingdom?

The Calvinist is displeased that Roman emperors call themselves “kings of Germany,” and he says that Maximilian I “was the first to use this title, and that this happened through the imprudence of his counselors.” [Col. 0232C] But, unless I am mistaken, the Calvinist would do an excellent thing if he went to Prague and instructed the most sacred emperor himself and his counselors as to which title ought to be used. They would understand that this is the title to be used:

> “Rudolph, Roman emperor, etc., king of the Franks, Lombards, and Hungarians.”

Do we still hesitate to crown this brother of a thief—the reformer of the whole empire, of the emperor himself, and of his counselors—with roses plucked from Calvin’s dung heap, especially when, in chapter 26 of his *Tartarean Reply*, page 267, he was not ashamed to burst out in these words?

> “Know, moreover, that Gaul and Germany are not kingdoms of the Roman Empire, but free and immediate states, exercising their own right, and no more subject to the Roman emperor, insofar as he is emperor, than Persia, Ethiopia, or Japan.”

I am not concerned with Gaul. As for Germany, I shall believe you when you prove to me, by the testimony of the emperor himself [Col. 0233A] and of the Imperial court, that the emperor writes himself king of Germany by any title other than the title of emperor—that is, because he is emperor.

## II. On the Letter of the Princes of the Empire to Innocent III Concerning the Election of Otto IV as Emperor

This chapter is at once the most verbose and garrulous, the most mendacious, and, if I may put it so, the most irrelevant of all. It neither seeks nor touches nor attacks me; it pursues nothing but Calvinist phantoms and fabrications. Its beginning and end, and everything lying between them, are nothing other than falsehood, abusive railing, absurdity, or utterly empty babble. See an example of its falsehood in this single instance.

[Col. 0233B] He falsely claims that the following inference is mine, or derives from my thinking:

> “The Roman pope has the right to anoint, consecrate, and crown the elected Roman emperor; therefore, without the confirmation of the Roman pope, no one can be a legitimate Roman emperor. Consequently, the person whom the pope does not wish to confirm neither ought nor can be, or be called, emperor.”

This brother of a thief invents and attributes this to me from his own brain. I never drew such an argument from anointing and consecration alone. I was certain that the supreme pontiff possesses greater power over the Roman Empire than the mere consecration and anointing of the elected emperor; and I had demonstrated this from the testimony of kings and emperors themselves, from sacred and secular histories, from ancient letters [Col. 0233C] and charters, and from the common judgment of all. Therefore everything that the stupid Calvinist babbles—or, rather, raves—for nearly eleven folios collapses. Nor will he ever produce an ancient charter from the early emperors, or letters written by the emperors themselves in a later age, in which they name themselves anything other than elected kings or emperors. The present usage is indeed an excellent one: those who speak about them, or address them either in person or by letter, call them emperors without any qualification, and rightly so. Nevertheless, the emperors themselves are not ignorant of what their ancestors and predecessors thought concerning the power of the supreme pontiff over the Roman Empire.

For just as leaves fall in the forests, so titles fall away as time advances, and other titles succeed them, while the right of each remains intact. If certain historians once gave the name “emperor” to kings who had not been crowned, they did so either in a broad sense or used the word “emperor” for a designated and elected emperor, as has often already been said. Nor should the most insane and frenzied Calvinists of this school—*Lugen* in German—be assigned any other place than the catalogue of the most loathsome accusations when they shout that we deny that “an emperor, simply by being elected, acquires full power to administer the affairs of the empire, and ought not to be or to be called either emperor or Augustus.”

Attribute all these things to the teacher of this Calvinist, from whom every slander and piece of malicious deception flows as from its first source. This brawler breathes and pants with that teacher’s spirit and breath; whatever he breathes and pants contains scarcely three words without four or five lies.

[Col. 0233]

# DISSERTATION ON THE OFFICE OF SAINT GREGORY VII

(Dom Guéranger, *Liturgical Institutions*, vol. II, p. 450)

[Col. 0233D] One of the most glorious names in history is, without a doubt, that of the great pontiff Saint Gregory VII. A tardy but brilliant justice has been rendered to this hero of the Church and of humanity, and one may even say that his glory continues to grow every day. In order to help make this providential phenomenon fully evident, we have wished in the present chapter to recount a small part of the outrages suffered by this great man, this admirable saint—not from Protestants and philosophers of the last century, for that would be less instructive, but from several persons who, while claiming still to belong to the Roman Church, did not hesitate to reject as interested the august judgment by which she enrolled this truly apostolic pontiff among the saints and offered him to universal veneration. It is good that certain characteristic facts of an age, capable of displaying certain principles in action, should be impartially recorded and published, lest, when these same facts are lost, the important lessons that can be drawn from them should likewise be lost. And if even today some disfavor were to pursue the person who dares to plead such a cause, we accept it as our duty, unworthy though we are of it, and rise without fear to avenge the man who, together with his august predecessor Saint Gregory I, is and will remain the greatest of the popes whom the Benedictine order has given to the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] We shall dare to say something here about the personal motives that oblige us to defend and honor the memory of Saint Gregory VII. If our readers remember that this great pontiff, a monk of Saint Peter of Cluny, is one of the glories of Benedictine France, and that before ascending the chair of Saint Peter he occupied the abbatial see of the distinguished monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, [Col. 0235C] they will understand the nature of the feelings we must have experienced when, in 1837, summoned—despite our unworthiness—by the sovereign pontiff Gregory XVI, successor of Gregory VII and a son of Saint Benedict, to receive the succession of the abbots of Cluny, we made our solemn profession into the hands of the abbot of Saint Paul, himself likewise the successor of the heroic Hildebrand. May the glorious pontiff, who has become in so particular a way our father, kindle in our weak heart some sparks of his ardent love for the Church of Jesus Christ, and grant us some share in that complete self-abnegation [Col. 0235D] with which he always served her!]

[Col. 0235A] We shall not give here the history of Saint Gregory VII. It is written everywhere: in his admirable letters, preserved in such great number through the care of a providence uniquely attentive to them; in his generous works, which saved the Church and on which she still relies today; and in the accounts, full of admiration and certainly no less disinterested, devoted to him by so many writers whose impartiality is not suspect. Today everyone knows this history. We therefore intend here only to address the liturgical question concerning Saint Gregory VII—that is, the worship accorded to this illustrious pontiff by the Church, and the various incidents that occurred in its establishment and development.

[Col. 0235B] The idea of Gregory VII’s high sanctity was already widespread during his lifetime and only increased after his death. In vain did the schismatics who supported the emperor Henry IV, led by the impetuous Bennon, cardinal archpriest of the antipope Guibert, strive to blacken his memory. In vain, to explain the superiority of his genius, they accused him of having dealings with Satan, claiming that whenever he shook his sleeves, abundant sparks of fire fell from them. In vain they called him a false prophet and accused him of having failed to show sufficient consideration for the emperor. The silence they maintain concerning his morals only attests more forcefully, as Fleury himself observes, to the moral integrity of the holy pope and to the high [Col. 0235C] esteem in which his virtue was held.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXIII, 26.]

In any event, the testimony of the devout men who had known him did not fail in his defense. The courageous Saint Anselm of Lucca, his faithful friend, avenged his memory in the book he directed [Col. 0236A] against the antipope Guibert.

[Note: [Col. 0235D] Roccaberti, *Pontifical Library*, vol. IV.—Margarin de la Bigne, *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, vol. XVIII.]

Saint Peter Damian, who had known him for many years, calls him “a man of most holy and pure counsel.”

[Note: [Col. 0235D] “A man of most holy and pure counsel.” Saint Peter Damian, *Letters*, book I, letter 7.]

Saint Alphanus, archbishop of Salerno, in an ode filled with the most manly poetry, compares him to the holy apostles:

> How much glory has often been bestowed  
> upon those who defend the public cause;  
> we have not thought, Hildebrand,  
> that your knowledge was hidden,  
> and we do not think so now.  
> The sacred and Latin road  
> reports the same thing,  
> and the distinguished summit  
> of the Capitol, the throne  
> that wields imperial power, bears witness to it.
>
> But why should you be troubled or ashamed  
> by that arduous labor and envy,  
> by fraud or deceit?  
> For it harms good men  
> more than sudden pestilence.  
> The hidden poison of envy  
> places its sickness  
> in wretched affairs,  
> and brings death and danger  
> to these and no others.
>
> But it is fitting that you should be envied,  
> not that you should envy.  
> Your skill, which made you uniquely  
> master of the merit  
> possessed by the upright and good,  
> has established this.  
> Every right favors your judgment;  
> without it no one can give me  
> either the reward of my purpose  
> or the reward of favor.
>
> The outstanding vigor of your heart,  
> and your noble life, which pursued  
> the best things, certainly prove  
> the genius of the law  
> whose arts you employ.  
> By them Rome, head of cities,  
> is made more just, and almost  
> the whole world fears those laws;  
> savage barbarism still shines  
> with royal lineage.
>
> Here too, with the fervent sword  
> of Peter, the chief of the apostles,  
> break the strength and assaults  
> of that enemy, so that the ancient yoke  
> may feel the final blow.
>
> What power belongs to an anathema!  
> Whatever Marius previously did,  
> whatever Julius accomplished,  
> with the greatest slaughter of soldiers,  
> you accomplish by a moderate word.  
> What more did Rome owe  
> to the Scipios and the other Quirites  
> than to you, whose efforts  
> found the path by which  
> her power was obtained?
>
> Since they had rightly contributed  
> many benefits to their country,  
> they are prevented from enjoying  
> perpetual peace in the regions  
> of light.  
> But you, endowed with greater merits,  
> are destined for a glorious life  
> everlasting, so that you may be  
> compared with the apostles  
> by your fellow citizens.

(Saint Alphanus’s poems, in Ughelli, *Sacred Italy: Anecdotes*, vol. X, ed. 1722, p. 77.)

The Blessed Victor III, who, after professing the Rule of Saint Benedict like Gregory, became his successor in the chair of Saint Peter, attests that Gregory glorified the Church of Christ by his examples as much as by his virtues.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] “He made it illustrious by words as well as by examples.” Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part II.]

Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; Saint Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg; and another Saint Gebhard, bishop of Constance—all contemporaries—join those whom we have just named in admirable agreement. Thus [Col. 0236B] one would find it difficult to identify a saint whose sanctity is attested by so great a number of contemporary saints.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] See Papebroch, *Acts of the Saints*, May 25.]

It seems that divine wisdom, foreseeing the outrages to which he would be subjected, took pleasure in surrounding his name with the most august testimonies, thus preparing in advance the best of all answers to the blasphemies that would later be uttered.

Let us now consult the contemporary historians of Gregory VII and gather the expressions with which they conclude the account of his labors and tribulations. The first whom we shall cite is Paul, canon of Bernried, who wrote the Life of the holy pope around 1131.

“Thus,” he says, “filled with the sevenfold grace, the spirit of the seventh Gregory, who reproved the world and its princes concerning sin, injustice, and judgment, strengthened by the power of the heavenly food he had just received, embarking upon the heavenly way, and deservedly borne aloft, like Elijah, in a fiery chariot because of his zeal for divine interests, on the very day devoted to the memory of Urban, his predecessor, greatly increased the joy of that holy pontiff and of all the blessed who rejoice with Christ in the glory of heaven; while on earth, by his departure, he left the pilgrim Church overwhelmed in no small sorrow [Note: Thus, filled with the sevenfold grace, the spirit of the seventh Gregory, who reproved the world and its princes concerning sin, injustice, and judgment, embarking upon the heavenly way in the strength of the heavenly food recently received, and deservedly borne aloft, like Elijah, in a fiery chariot because of his divine zeal, greatly increased the joy of Urban, his predecessor, whose feast occurred on that day, and of all the blessed who rejoice with Christ in heavenly glory; but on earth, by his departure, he cast the pilgrim Church into profound sorrow. Paul of Bernried, *Life of Gregory VII*, chap. 12, §102.]”

“Upon Gregory’s death,” says Berthold, likewise a contemporary, in his *Chronicle*, “the faithful of both sexes were plunged into mourning, but especially the poor; for he was the most ardent teacher of the Catholic religion and the most steadfast defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He certainly did not wish the clerical order to remain subject to the hands of laymen, but rather to surpass them both in holiness of conduct and in the dignity of its order [Note: At his death, all religious persons of both sexes, and especially the poor, mourned; for he was the most fervent instructor of the Catholic religion and the most resolute defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He certainly did not wish the ecclesiastical order to be subject to the hands of laymen, but rather to excel them in both holiness of conduct and the dignity of its order. Berthold, *Chronicle*, under the year 1085.]”

“Meanwhile,” says the poet Domnizo, a witness of the event, “deep lamentation arises for the pontiff Gregory, whom the Lord Christ has just carried up to heaven, seven days before the end of May. The monks mourn him, because he is known to have been a monk; the clerics weep for him, and the laymen likewise grieve, those whose pure faith is far removed from the schismatics [Note:

Meanwhile, deep lamentation arises for the pontiff

Gregory, whom the Lord Christ carries to heaven

Seven days before the end of May.

The monks mourn him, because he is known to have been a monk;

The clerics weep for him, and the laymen grieve greatly,

Whose pure faith is far removed from the schismatics.

Domnizo, *Life of Matilda*.]”

Hugh of Flavigny, in his precious *Chronicle*, thus concludes the history of our great pontiff, who had honored him with his friendship: “Thus, as martyr and confessor, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1085, he gave up his soul to the Creator [Note: Thus, giving up his spirit to the Creator, he died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, a martyr and confessor. Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle of Verdun*, in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscripts*, vol. I.]”

Such is the judgment of Gregory’s contemporaries in the various accounts they have left us of his life and deeds. It is clear from this that public veneration could not long delay manifesting itself toward him and preparing the foundations of that immemorial cult which the Apostolic See was later to recognize and ratify.

Moreover, the wonders that had more than once enhanced the greatness of his actions during his life shone forth still at his tomb. Paul of Bernried reports them with all the authority, and also the simplicity, of an eyewitness [Note: *Life of Gregory VII*, chaps. 1, 2, 3, 13.]. Lambert of Schaffnaburg, whose *Chronicle* extends only to Gregory’s fourth year, attests the existence of miraculous events which, he says, served powerfully to confound the enemies of the holy pontiff [Note: The signs and wonders that more frequently occurred through the pope’s prayers, together with his most fervent zeal for God and for ecclesiastical laws, sufficiently fortified him against the poisonous tongues of detractors. Under the year 1077, *Writers of German History*, vol. I.]. Orderic Vital, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, speaks as of an established fact of the healing of several lepers by means of water that had touched Gregory’s body [Note: The lepers asked for water with which his body had been washed; having obtained it, they faithfully washed themselves, and, with God’s assistance, were immediately cleansed. Part II, book VIII, p. 677.]. Finally, on this subject one may consult the brief but illuminating discussion by Benedict XIV in his treatise *On the Canonization of the Saints* [Note: Book I, chap. 41, §10, no. 16.].

[Col. 0238B] But could one believe that Catholic writers were to be found, even in this very century, who took scandal from the trials by which divine justice purified the soul of God’s servant, and whose faltering faith failed to perceive the full significance of those precious adversities which, by saving the holy cause of the Church’s liberty, secured for the dying pontiff the reward and glory of the martyrs? “I have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile!” Gregory said upon his deathbed. But did the Savior himself, who went about doing good and healing every weakness and infirmity, not feel abandoned by his Father to such a degree that he cried: “My God! [Col. 0238C] My God! Why have you forsaken me?” Yet his enemies, witnessing his agony, said while shaking their heads: “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross.” Perhaps they believed that the salvation of the world could be accomplished without the sacrifice of the victim. Those of whom we speak apparently did not know either that ecclesiastical liberty could not be saved without the life and honor of its defender being sacrificed. Gregory had to succumb for the salvation of many; his name therefore had to be cursed, for the disciple is not above his master [Note: Matthew 10:24.].

Let no one say to us any longer: Gregory VII’s cause was not God’s cause, because his bold enterprises did not receive the consecration of success. We shall answer with these words of the great Baronius, which conclude the account of our hero’s sublime death:

“Thus, through endless persecutions, afflictions of every kind, and often even the slaughter of priests, the Church more happily receives peace, ecclesiastical liberty is acquired and consolidated, and the salvation of souls is secured. Thus Christ taught his priests to fight and to conquer; through his sufferings and infirmities strength and courage are supplied to the faithful, and finally, through his death, their life is obtained. Unless I am mistaken, the experience of events up to the present time has shown that it is to Gregory’s labors that we must attribute the recovery of the investitures of the Churches from the hands of princes, the restoration of the free election of the Roman pontiffs, the complete repair of ecclesiastical discipline after its collapse, and the innumerable other benefits secured for the Church [Note: Thus, through unceasing persecutions, hardships of every kind, and often even the slaughter of priests, the Church’s peace is brought about much more fruitfully, ecclesiastical liberty is acquired and confirmed, and the salvation of souls is sought. Thus Christ taught his priests to fight and to conquer; through his sufferings and infirmities, strength and courage were obtained for the faithful, and finally, through his death, life was obtained for them. Unless I lie, these things can now be demonstrated by the experience of events: through Gregory, the investitures of the Churches were wrested from the hands of princes, the free election of the Roman pontiffs was restored, ecclesiastical discipline, which had utterly collapsed, was repaired, and countless other benefits were gained. Under the year 1085, no. 13.]”

Yes, Gregory was defeated according to the flesh; like the Son of Man, he found himself with nowhere to lay his head; he died in humiliation, so much so that men regarded him as one struck by the hand of God [Note: Isaiah 53.]. Yet for him too death, victorious at first, remained buried within its triumph. His name, glory, and merits inspired and sustained, in the arduous defense of ecclesiastical liberties, not only the incomparable Thomas of Canterbury in his struggle against a king of England, but also many illustrious popes who knew how to stand as a rampart for the house of Israel: Paschal II against the Emperor Henry V; Innocent IV against Frederick II; Boniface VIII against Philip the Fair; Gregory XIII, Sixtus V, Gregory XIV, and Clement VIII against Henry of Bourbon; Innocent XI against Louis XIV; Clement XIII against the courts of Madrid, Lisbon, Naples, and Parma; Pius VII against Napoleon; and Gregory XVI against Frederick William.

We have just heard the testimony of the contemporary historians concerning the reputation for holiness that surrounded Gregory VII during his life and after his [Col. 0239D] death. Let us now follow through the centuries the various manifestations of this conviction, which was later to motivate the infallible judgment of the Holy See.

[Col. 0240A] Scarcely sixty years had passed since the day when the glorious champion of the Church died in exile when one of his successors, Anastasius IV, who left behind a venerable memory, placed his image among those of the saints in the mosaic of the Chapel of Saint Nicholas at the Lateran patriarchal palace [Note: Papebroch, *Acta Sanctorum*, May, vol. VI; *Historical Essay on the Roman Pontiffs*, Part I, Appendix, p. 208; Benedict XIV, *On Canonization*, book I, chap. 41.]. Gregory’s body had been buried through the care of Robert Guiscard, or of Roger, his son [Note: Papebroch, ibid.], in a marble tomb and placed in the cathedral of Salerno, already famous for possessing the relics of the apostle and evangelist Saint Matthew. Orderic Vital, the eleventh-century historian whom we cited above, speaks of the crowds of pilgrims at the tomb of the holy pope and of the healings received there [Note: Through his merits, an abundance of miracles was divinely displayed to the faith of those who asked. *Ecclesiastical History*, Part II, book VIII, ibid.]. A chronicle composed at the order of Cencius Savelli, apostolic chamberlain, who became pope in 1226 under the name Honorius III, attests for his own time the continuation of the cult of Saint Gregory VII and the wonders performed through his intercession [Note: At his body, honorably buried in the basilica of Blessed Matthew, God graciously deigned to perform many marvelous miracles. From the manuscript censual book of Cencius, chamberlain, concerning Gregory VII, at the end.]. And when, toward the end of the same century, John of Procida endowed and magnificently decorated the chapel called Saint Michael in the cathedral of Salerno, it is natural to think, with Papebroch, that he intended to manifest his devotion toward the pontiff who rested in that same chapel, where he was the object of the worship of the people drawn there by reports of the wonders performed in it [Note: Papebroch, ibid.].

The body of Saint Gregory VII continued always [Col. 0240C] to be venerated by the inhabitants of Salerno, although this veneration did not spread very far beyond the province of the Kingdom of Naples in which that city is situated. Then, in 1574, Cardinal Marc-Antoine Marsile Colonna took possession of the see formerly occupied by Saint Alphane, the friend of our holy pontiff. Providence intended to use him to increase still further the cult already rendered to God’s servant and to prepare its subsequent development. The prelate opened the tomb and found there the precious remains of the holy pontiff, almost entirely preserved, together with the pontifical vestments in which he had been clothed at his burial. He attests this in an inscription still visible in the cathedral [Col. 0240D] of Salerno, which reads as follows:

“To Gregory VII of Soana, Supreme and Best Pontiff, the most ardent champion and most steadfast defender of ecclesiastical liberty, who, while vigorously defending the authority of the Roman Pontiff against the treachery of Henry, piously died at Salerno in the year of the Lord 1085, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June. Marcus Antonius Colonna Marsilius, Bolognese, Archbishop of Salerno, having found his body, after approximately five hundred years, clothed in sacred vestments and almost intact, [erected this], lest the tomb of so great a Pontiff remain any longer without memorial. Gregory XIII, the Bolognese, being pope. In the year of the Lord 1578, on the day before the Kalends of July [Note: Ciacconius, *Lives and Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 853.]”

The devout cardinal died in 1582 and did not have the consolation of seeing the canonization of the holy pontiff completed. It took place two years later, by the authority of Gregory XIII, who inserted Gregory VII’s name into the Roman Martyrology with this eulogy: “At Salerno, the burial of Blessed Gregory VII, pope, who, succeeding Alexander II, vindicated ecclesiastical liberty in his time from the pride of princes and manfully defended it by pontifical authority.”

This type of canonization, without a prior trial, is distinct from the canonization called formal and is designated by the name “equivalent” or “equipollent.” It occurs when the sovereign pontiff grants public worship to a person already in possession of religious honors rendered by the devotion of the faithful, while the heroism of his virtues and the truth of his miracles are certified by the testimony of trustworthy historians. This canonization has the same authority as formal canonization. Moreover, not only does the cult of nearly all the saints who lived in the Church before the institution of the procedures now [Col. 0241C] in use rest upon a judgment of the same kind, but a great many saints who flourished in the Church after the Apostolic See had reserved canonization cases to itself have nevertheless been entered in the catalogue of the saints only in this equipollent manner. Such are, for example, Saint Romuald, Saint Norbert, Saint Bruno, Saint Peter Nolasco, Saint Raymond Nonnatus, Saint Ferdinand III, Saint John of Matha, Saint Margaret of Scotland, Saint Stephen of Hungary, and others. Ignorance of the rules of the Roman Church alone could therefore have led certain Jansenist and non-Jansenist authors to say that Saint Gregory VII was honored by the Church without having been canonized, since the same ought then to be said of the illustrious saints whom we have just named—a conclusion these authors would doubtless reject.

As for the claim that Gregory XIII intended to direct the effect of this canonization against Henry of Bourbon, who was then pursuing the crown of France, thereby commending the memory of a pontiff who had trampled beneath his feet another Henry, also fourth of that name, it seems unnecessary to resort to this explanation. The translation of Saint Gregory VII’s body by the Archbishop of [Col. 0242A] Salerno, at a time when Gregory XIII was occupied with the edition of the Martyrology, together with the established prior cult, was sufficient to induce that pope finally to define the holiness of the glorious confessor of Salerno.

Sixtus V, Gregory XIII’s successor, made some alteration in the formula consecrated by his predecessor for our holy pope in the Martyrology. He adopted the wording that has remained in the edition of Benedict XIV and those that followed: “At Salerno, the burial of Blessed Gregory VII, pope, the most ardent champion and defender of ecclesiastical liberty.”

Soon afterward, under Clement VIII, in 1595, the body of Saint Gregory VII was removed from the tomb that Cardinal Colonna had prepared for him and placed beneath an [Col. 0242B] altar, still in the same Chapel of Saint Michael. It even appears that it was then, while Mario Bolognini was archbishop, that the head was separated from the rest of the body in order to be enclosed in a special reliquary [Note: Papebroch, ibid.].

Under the pontificate of the same Clement VIII, Baronius published the eleventh volume of his *Annals*, in which he celebrated and vindicated the memory of Saint Gregory VII at once, with his eloquent erudition. A little before him, Bellarmine, in his *Controversies*, and especially in the fourth book, *On the Roman Pontiff*, had likewise had occasion to render this great act of justice. Thus the two most illustrious writers of Catholicism in that age of giants showed themselves concerned with the glory of the holy pontiff; but until then [Col. 0242C] only heretics had risen up to tarnish it.

From the moment when the name of Saint Gregory VII was inserted into the Martyrology, the chapter of the cathedral of Salerno—which the holy pope had formerly showered with privileges, granting its members the red cope and the mitre—was authorized to celebrate his office solemnly. At first, however, it was recited only according to the common rite for confessors who are pontiffs, until, in 1609, at the request of the same chapter and of Archbishop John Beltramini, Paul V, by a brief beginning with the words *Domini Jesu Christi*, granted a proper office, many of whose lessons are found in those published in 1728 by Benedict XIII, of which we shall soon speak.

[Col. 0242D] Archbishop Beltramini had a remarkable statue of the holy pope erected in the cathedral of Salerno at about the same time. After being transferred to another see, he was succeeded by Cardinal Lucius San Severino, no less zealous than he was in guarding the holy deposit entrusted to his Church. He gave solemn proof of this in 1614 by having a new altar constructed for Saint Gregory VII and solemnly placing his body there. This should be counted as the third translation of these precious relics [Note: The first was by Cardinal Marsile Colonna; the second by Mario Bolognini; finally, the one discussed here, carried out by Cardinal San Severino, [Col. 0243D] is attested by an inscription that he had placed in the cathedral of Salerno, in the following terms:

“I, Lucius Sanseverinus, Archbishop of Salerno, consecrated this altar in honor of Blessed Gregory VII, pope, and enclosed his sacred body within it. To those present for one year, and thereafter to those who piously visit it on the anniversary of its consecration, I have, according to the custom of the Church, granted forty days of true indulgence. In the year of the Lord 1614, on the fourth day of May.”]

It was perhaps on this occasion, [Col. 0243A] or at least shortly beforehand [Note: Papebroch, ibid.], that one of the holy pope’s arms was removed in order to be given to the town of Soana in Tuscany, the birthplace of Saint Gregory VII. The town had sent two ambassadors to the chapter of the cathedral of Salerno, carrying letters of recommendation from the grand duke, who added his requests to those of the town.

At about the same time, the learned Jesuit James Gretser, whose immense labors are not sufficiently appreciated today, published a learned apology for the deeds and person of Saint Gregory VII. In this important discussion, he cites no fewer than fifty writers in support of the praises he bestows upon the pontiff, and he victoriously vindicates him against the accusations brought against him [Col. 0243B] both by the schismatics of the eleventh century and by the heretics of the sixteenth.

Toward the middle of the seventeenth century, Alexander VII established the office of Saint Gregory VII in the basilicas of Rome, without yet inserting it into the breviary of the Roman Church [Note: Gretser’s *Works*, vol. VI.]. But this century was to become famous for the attacks directed against the holy pontiff, no longer only by Protestants, but also by jurists and, above all, by Gallican theologians and canonists. We shall merely recall the notorious Edmond Richer, in his book *On Ecclesiastical and Political Power*; Ellies Dupin, in his *Treatise on Ecclesiastical Power*; and Bossuet, in his *Defense of the Declaration of 1682*, a work concerning which the grave and impartial [Col. 0243C] Benedict XIV said:

“It would indeed be difficult to find another work equally opposed to the doctrine received everywhere outside France concerning the infallibility of the sovereign pontiff when defining *ex cathedra*, his superiority over every ecumenical council, and his indirect right—when the chief interest of religion and the Church requires it—over the temporal rights of supreme princes [Note: It is indeed difficult to find another work that is equally opposed to the doctrine universally received outside France concerning the infallibility of the supreme pontiff when defining *ex cathedra*, his superiority over any ecumenical council, and his indirect right, if the chief advantage of religion and the Church requires it, over the temporal rights of supreme rulers. Letter in favor of Cardinal H. Noris, *Apology to the Supreme Spanish Inquisitor*, among the minor works of Benedict XIV, p. 117.]”

Nevertheless, of all the Gallican authors of the seventeenth century who wrote against Saint Gregory VII, the one whose boldness caused the greatest stir, because of the punishment inflicted upon him by the Holy See, was Father Noël Alexandre. He had published the first ten centuries of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 0243D] and had until then deserved the praise of Pope Innocent XI, who occupied the chair of Saint Peter and who [Col. 0244A] had graciously sent him the most flattering testimony of his satisfaction with the erudition and orthodoxy that had thus far guided the work [Note: Touron, *History of the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Dominic*, vol. V, p. 814.]. When he reached the events of the eleventh century, Noël Alexandre devoted two dissertations to bringing out what, in his view, were the faults of a pontiff already placed upon the altars. Innocent XI, the pope who had not yielded before the great king, believed that he had to express vigorously the indignation inspired in him by such conduct on the part of a religious. He issued a decree dated July 13, 1684, condemning the volume that contained these dissertations; and, in order to testify even more forcefully to the displeasure felt by the Holy See, all the writings of the same author were proscribed, [Col. 0244B] with a prohibition against reading, retaining, or printing them under pain of excommunication [Note: Touron, ibid.; Benedict XIV, *On the Canonization of the Saints*, book I, chap. 41; Papebroch, under May 25.]. Thus a pontiff declared venerable by the Congregation of Rites on account of his great virtues showed himself jealous of the honor of his holy predecessor, whose memory was soon to face new outrages while awaiting the honors reserved for it by the nineteenth century.

For the rest, Noël Alexandre did not have to wait long for a refutation of his Gallican theses. A fellow religious, a Dominican like himself, François d’Enghien, soon published a very solid book, in Benedict XIV’s judgment [Note: Benedict XIV, ibid.], entitled *The Authority of the Apostolic See Vindicated on Behalf of Pope Gregory VII, against Natalis Alexander, Doctor of Theology of the Order of Preachers*.

Dom Mabillon, in publishing the *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, likewise had to produce the Life and deeds of our holy pope. The second volume of the sixth Benedictine century appeared in 1701, but the illustrious editor knew how to cross this difficult passage without failing either in prudence or in the fidelity of a Catholic historian.

Meanwhile, Clement XI, at the request of Cardinal Gabrielli, whose conduct had been so firm in the affair of the *Régale*, granted the Cistercian order, in 1705, the privilege of celebrating the office of Saint Gregory VII. Five years later, the same pontiff granted the same favor to the Order of Saint Benedict, at the petition of the procurator general of the Congregation of Monte Cassino. These various grants [Col. 0245A] of the office caused no commotion. But when, by a decree of September 25, 1728, Benedict XIII ordered the feast of Saint Gregory VII to be inserted into the missal and breviary, and enjoined all the Churches of the world to celebrate it, a great storm arose in several European states, particularly in France.

It is doubtless evident that, in establishing this feast and universally promulgating the remarkable legend that was to be read in the office, Rome had a purpose; we do not deny it. But first we shall say that it is a fine spectacle for us, people of this century, to see, at the moment when absurd prejudices were beginning to eclipse all [Col. 0245B] historical truth concerning the Middle Ages, when a false and unintelligent philosophy was trampling underfoot the most salutary teachings of the past—to see, I say, Rome rescue by a courageous act from this universal shipwreck the venerable name of a hero of humanity, in whom the following century was to salute with enthusiasm the avenger of civilization and the guardian of public liberties no less than of ecclesiastical liberties. This was certainly progress, and all the more deserving of praise because the pontiff responsible for it could not fail to know that the authority of the Holy See, already so weakened, would on this very occasion become the object of further attacks.

Secondly, we shall say plainly that Rome did indeed have, by this act, some intention of providing for its honor, outraged by the famous declaration of the assembly of the clergy of 1682 and by all that had followed from it in France on the part of both authorities. King Louis XIV had, it is true, promised to revoke his edict concerning the teaching of the four articles; and as long as he lived, efforts had been made to carry out that undertaking. Together with the bishops’ letter of reparation to the pope, it had been the necessary condition for the canonical institution of prelates appointed for more than ten years to vacant sees. But promises were already no longer being fulfilled. The universities were having theses defended within their walls every day in which Roman doctrines were attacked, apostolic authority confined within arbitrary limits, and the conduct of the holiest popes branded as blind violence and denounced as contrary to natural and divine law. It was time for the great voice of the Apostolic See to be heard, and at least to protest against the ever-growing audacity of those doctors who were always ready to restrict the limits of spiritual power while teaching with such complacency the inadmissibility of royal power. Fortunately, the Church has always possessed in her liturgy a means of repression [Col. 0246A] against rash enterprises undertaken against her doctrine or her honor. What she confesses in universal prayer becomes a rule for her children; and, as we have shown in this history, if some have sought to isolate themselves from the formulas she consecrates, it is because they felt the irrefragable authority with which, in this breviary and in this missal so hateful to them, she imposes her judgments concerning doctrines, persons, and institutions. Benedict XIII therefore intended, by extending the office of Saint Gregory VII to the universal Church, to provide a counterweight to the encroachments of Gallicanism, which were growing daily in danger and importance, especially because of the efforts of a powerful and obstinate sect that increasingly threatened [Col. 0246B] the existence of the Catholic faith within the Kingdom of France. If Rome allowed the memory of the holiest pontiffs of past centuries to remain dishonored any longer, it would give victory to those audacious men who proclaimed from the rooftops that Rome had renewed its ancient transgressions and that Innocent X, Alexander VII, and Clement XI were neither more nor less guilty than Gregory VII, Innocent III, and so many others. Listen instead to one of the sect’s faithful spokesmen:

“At first glance, one grasps the doctrinal connection between the briefs of Innocent XI and Alexander VIII against the assembly of 1682, the ninety-first proposition concerning excommunication, censured by the bull *Unigenitus*, [Col. 0246C] and this legend, contrary to the revealed truths that enjoin upon popes, as upon all other members of society, submission to civil authority [Note: Grégoire, *Historical Essay on the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, p. 98.]”

But it is time to reveal to the reader this monstrous legend that thus placed revealed truths in peril. The pages that follow are doubtless beautiful, full of nobility and eloquent simplicity; yet they are less energetic in their praise of the pontiff than certain pages that may be read every day in the writings of several Protestant historians or publicists. Here is the legend in its entirety:

[Col. 0246D] **For the Feast of Saint Gregory VIII, Pope and Confessor. In the Second Nocturn.**

**Lesson IV.** “Pope Gregory VII, formerly Hildebrand, born at Soana in Etruria, distinguished above all by learning, holiness, and every kind of virtue, wonderfully enlightened the universal Church of God. It is said that, when as a little child he played at the feet of a craftsman shaping wood, still ignorant of letters, he happened by chance to form from the discarded shavings those words of David’s oracle: ‘He shall rule from sea to sea,’ the hand of Providence guiding the boy, thereby signifying that he was destined to possess the most extensive authority in the world. He then went to Rome, where he was brought up under the protection of Saint Peter.

“While still a young man, deeply grieving that the liberty of the Church was oppressed by laymen and that the morals of ecclesiastics had been corrupted, he put on the monastic habit in the monastery of Cluny, where at that time the observance of a more austere life under the Rule of Saint Benedict was flourishing most vigorously. He served the divine majesty with such ardent devotion that he was first elected prior by the holy Fathers of that monastery. But since divine Providence had greater things in store for him, for the salvation of many, Hildebrand was brought out of Cluny, first elected abbot of the monastery of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, and afterward created cardinal of the Roman Church. Under the supreme pontiffs Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II, and Alexander II, he discharged important offices and legations. He was called by Blessed Peter Damian a man of the holiest [Col. 0247B] and purest counsel.

“Sent by Pope Victor II as a legate *a latere* to Gaul, at Lyons he compelled a bishop infected with the Simoniacal taint, by a miracle, to confess his crime. He compelled Berengar at the Council of Tours to abjure his heresy a second time. By his virtue he also suppressed the schism of Cadolaus.”

### Lesson V

“After Alexander II had died, against his will and in sorrow, and by the unanimous consent of all, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [April 22], in the year of Christ 1073, he was elected supreme pontiff. Like the sun, he shone forth in the house of God; for, powerful in deed and speech, he devoted himself with such zeal to restoring ecclesiastical discipline, propagating the faith, restoring the liberty of the Church, and uprooting errors and corruptions [Col. 0247C], that since the age of the apostles no pontiff is said to have endured greater labors and hardships for the Church of God, or to have fought more fiercely for her freedom. He cleansed several provinces of the stain of simony. Against the impious efforts of the emperor Henry he remained in every respect a strong and fearless champion, and did not fear to set himself as a wall for the house of Israel; and he deprived that same Henry, who had fallen into the depths of wickedness, of the communion of the faithful and of his kingdom, while freeing his subjects from the faith they had pledged to him.”

### Lesson VI

“While he was celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, devout men saw a dove descend from heaven, settle upon his right shoulder, and, with extended wings, veil his head [Col. 0247D]. By this it was signified that, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and not by calculations of human prudence, he was guided in the governance of the Church. When he was being hard-pressed at Rome by a severe siege from the army of the wicked Henry, he extinguished a fire set by the enemy with the sign of the cross. At last rescued from his hands by Robert Guiscard, duke of Normandy, he withdrew to Cassino; and from there he hastened to Salerno to dedicate the church of the apostle Saint Matthew. Once, when he had delivered a sermon to the people in that city, he was exhausted by his sufferings and fell ill with a disease of which he foresaw that he would die. The final words of the dying Gregory were: ‘I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.’ Innumerable are the things that he either endured courageously or wisely established in the many synods convened in the City [Rome] [Col. 0248A]—a truly holy man, an avenger of crimes, and the Church’s most vigorous defender. Having thus completed twelve years in the pontificate, he departed to heaven in the year of salvation 1085, renowned for many miracles during his life and after his death; and his sacred body was honorably buried in the cathedral basilica of Salerno.”

The prayer that completes and summarizes the office of Saint Gregory VII in the missal and breviary is composed as follows:

“God, the strength of those who hope in you, who strengthened blessed Gregory, your confessor and pontiff, with steadfast courage for the defense of the Church’s liberty: grant us, through his example and intercession, to overcome courageously everything that opposes us” [Col. 0248B].

Now that we have placed this famous document before the reader, before entering into the account of the events that followed its promulgation, we shall permit ourselves a few reflections on the significance of this papal manifesto.

What follows from the account we have just read of the acts and virtues of an eleventh-century pope? Does it mean that Rome is preparing to swoop down, like an eagle, upon the European states, to dispose arbitrarily of the crowns of the princes who govern them—in a word, to shake the entire world with the thunder of its bolts? We, who live a century after the appearance of this formidable legend, do we find many examples since then of this temporal omnipotence of the medieval pontiffs, exercised by Benedict XIII or his successors? Does it seem to us that the crown of France—a country where the legend was proscribed—has been the object of fewer attacks than the crowns of sovereigns in those states where it was accepted by the clergy? And if, by chance, in our country since that time, kings have suffered death, exile, or humiliation, was it Rome that showed itself so merciless toward them? Let us not lose sight of this point in the various parts of the account that is about to begin. Many people will raise a great outcry, as though royal power were on the point of expiring throughout the whole world solely because of the legend. Their hatred of Rome blinds them; and God has made them a spectacle to our age, which finally knows that Rome does not seek the destruction of monarchs’ power, and seems even to understand that if, in the Catholic ages, she did in fact exercise temporal influence over society, she was then the sole safeguard of the freedom of peoples, as well as the most solid support of authority, whose excesses she restrained [Col. 0248D]. The legend, therefore, is simply the shield under which Rome shelters her honor, compromised by so many sophisms and declamations. By this solemn manifesto, she neutralizes the blind movement that draws certain schools in the footsteps of those heterodox authors who have no concern for the honor of the Roman pontiffs, but have everything to gain if they can make them appear as violators of the divine laws and of the natural order of society [Col. 0249A].

The office of Saint Gregory VII reached France shortly after its publication in Rome, as still happens today when the supreme pontiff imposes new offices. At that time, however, when the use of the Roman liturgy was still almost universal in France, decrees of this kind necessarily concerned both ecclesiastics and the faithful more than they do now. As today, the office was printed on a loose sheet intended to be joined to the breviary, pending its insertion in its proper place in the next edition. The *Nouvelles ecclésiastiques*, the journal of Jansenism, pointed out the bookseller Coignard fils, “at the sign of the Golden Book,” as having had the audacity to keep for sale in Paris the octavo sheet containing the legend [Col. 0249B].

“As soon as this legend appeared,” says the republican Grégoire, “it aroused the horror of all men attached to the Gallican liberties” [Note: [Col. 0249D] *Essay on the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, p. 99.].

Hardly had the Parliament of Paris, the supreme judge in liturgical matters, learned of this seditious manifestation of Roman claims than it assembled and, on July 20, 1729, upon the conclusions of the attorney general Gilbert de Voisins—the same man who, seven years later, was to take under his protection the Paris breviary of Vigier and Mesenguy—issued a decree suppressing the sheet containing the office of Saint Gregory VII and forbidding any public use of it, under penalty of seizure of temporal goods [Col. 0249C]. We shall quote only a few phrases from the attorney general’s requisition; they will suffice to establish the spirit of the kingdom’s highest magistracy on this memorable occasion. The attorney general, barely disguising the hatred with which he and his body were animated against Rome, seeks to make people believe that, by the mere publication of the office of Saint Gregory VII, the French nation is on the eve of shaking off the yoke of its ancient kings. It is true that this happened even before the end of the century in which the honorable magistrate was speaking; but it is highly doubtful that the legend had anything to do with it.

“It was sufficiently well known,” says the attorney general, “that Gregory VII, so famous for his disputes with the emperor Henry, was the one who carried furthest the ambitious claims unheard of in the first centuries of the Church, which caused such long disturbances and kindled such cruel wars in his time [Col. 0249D].

“But, if I may say so,” he adds, “there was no reason to expect that the excess to which he was ultimately led by such dangerous principles would be included in his eulogy and celebrated in an ecclesiastical office. Is it then the masterpiece of his zeal that he undertook to deprive a king of his crown and release his subjects from their oath of loyalty? And can we see without sorrow that, upon a deed so deserving of being buried in oblivion, the titles bestowed upon him—defender of the Church, restorer of her freedom, bulwark of the house of Israel—should be based?

“Why must the traces of an undertaking whose memory time seemed to be weakening reappear today before our very eyes, coming once more to stir up our duty and our zeal? Should we tolerate that, under cover of this alleged supplement to the Roman breviary, there should be placed in the hands of the faithful and in the mouths of the ministers of religion, even in the midst of our holy temples and the solemnity of divine worship, what tends to shake the inviolable and sacred principles of subjects’ attachment to their sovereign?” [Note: [Col. 0249D] We drew some of the documents that we must cite in this chapter from a collection published in 1743 concerning the entire affair. It is entitled *The Devil’s Advocate, or Historical and Critical Memoirs on the Life and Legend of Pope Gregory VII, with Memoirs of the Same Kind on the Bull of Canonization of Vincent de Paul, Founder of the Fathers of the Mission and the Daughters of Charity* (three volumes in duodecimo). The author is Adam, parish priest of Saint-Barthélemy in Paris, a famous appellant. It is noteworthy that the Jansenists pursued Saint Vincent de Paul and Saint Gregory VII with the same hatred—as though better to make distracted minds understand that the same Roman Church which produces Vincent de Pauls for the relief of humanity’s bodily miseries is also the Church that, as needed, produces Gregory VIIs to restore Christian society to its true foundations.]?”

On the twenty-fourth of that same month of July, Daniel-Charles-Gabriel de Caylus, bishop of Auxerre, who had issued in 1726 the new breviary of which we have spoken, faithful to the impulse of the magistracy, displayed his zeal against the legend in a pastoral mandate addressed to the clergy and faithful of his diocese [Col. 0250C]. An appellant against the constitution *Unigenitus*, he had already tested his resistance to the Holy See; he therefore eagerly seized the opportunity to insult that Rome whose yoke he bore only with indignation. Moreover, being as zealous for the absolute and inalienable power of the temporal prince as he was hostile toward apostolic authority, he—like all those of his colleagues from whose mandates we shall quote below—gave the most solemn denial to certain writers of our own time who persist in seeing in the sect of Port-Royal the first manifestation of supposedly liberal ideas.

“It is only with reluctance,” says the prelate, “that we recall here the memory of Gregory VII’s undertakings. It would be desirable that his successors had made known, by their conduct, that they were very far from approving them, and still farther from renewing them . . . . We would thereby be spared the need to take new precautions to oppose them and demonstrate their injustice. We would regard them as a stain that had been erased, and we would take care not to search out in ecclesiastical history deeds that serve only to dishonor their authors and that the holy Church will always disavow” [Col. 0250D] [Note: [Col. 0251D] Admire this profound understanding of the history of medieval institutions!].

“But we cannot remain silent,” continues the bishop of Auxerre; “what we owe to the universal Church, to the Most Christian King, to the State, to the faithful of our diocese, and to ourselves compels us to speak on the occasion of the office of Gregory VII.

“Let us not stop here to observe that Gregory VII’s sanctity is not acknowledged in the Church; that it does not appear that what is observed in the canonization of saints was done for him at Rome; and that the history of his pontificate is difficult to reconcile with the idea of a sanctity formed according to the spirit and rules of the Gospel and worthy of the veneration and public worship of the faithful” [Col. 0251B].

“Let us therefore remain inviolably attached,” the prelate continues, “to the doctrine of holy antiquity, which teaches subjects that no one can dispense them from the fidelity they owe to their legitimate sovereigns, and that there is neither fear nor threat that should prevent them from fulfilling this duty imposed upon them by the law of God; and teaches popes as well as bishops that they do not have the power to give or take away kingdoms, and that, in temporal matters, kings are not subject to them and do not depend upon them, but upon God alone” [Col. 0251C].

Certainly, it is a great advantage for sovereigns not to depend upon either the pope or the bishops; but when the bishop of Auxerre assures them that here below they depend upon God alone, he expresses his desire, no doubt, but not what actually exists. For there is no human being here below who has not encountered, often even face to face, someone superior to him. If today’s kings no longer have to fear the power of the pope—and yet see how many still fear that disarmed Rome! [Col. 0251D]—they have, on the other hand, harsh quarrels and disputes to settle with the peoples, who are surely less just and more self-interested in the matter than the Roman pontiffs would be.

Whatever the case, the bishop of Auxerre ends his mandate by declaring that, in order to fulfill all justice, while giving the king new proofs of his fidelity and zeal for the security of his sacred person and for the tranquility of his kingdom—which might still be exposed to the greatest calamities if the maxims authorized by the office of Pope Gregory VII were to find credence in people’s minds—he forbids all communities and all secular and regular persons of either sex in his diocese, whether claiming exemption or not, who use the Roman breviary or receive the offices of new saints inserted into that breviary, to recite, either publicly or privately, the printed office, and so forth [Col. 0252A].

Thus the pope commands the whole Church to recite the office of Saint Gregory VII, and a bishop is found who forbids his diocesan subjects to submit to this command. Evidently, one of the two is in the wrong; for otherwise, what would become of a society that contained within itself contradictory powers, yet powers that were always legitimate in every circumstance? [Col. 0252B]

The mandate of the bishop of Auxerre was immediately followed by another, published on July 31 by Charles-Joachim Colbert, bishop of Montpellier, so famous for the catechism that bears his name and for his obstinacy in the principles of the appellants. We doubtless remember his zeal in having the new Paris breviary adopted in his diocese, and the chapter’s courageous opposition to that measure. We shall not weary the reader with all the declamations contained in this mandate against Roman claims; we shall extract only the qualifications he applies to an act of the supreme pontiff. The legend of Saint Gregory VII is condemned as “containing seditious doctrine, contrary to the word of God, tending toward schism, derogating from the sovereign authority of kings, and capable of preventing the conversion of infidel and heretical princes” [Col. 0252C] [Note: [Col. 0251D] Nothing is more admirable than the zeal of a heretical bishop for the propagation of the faith among infidels and heretics. Evidently, the pope and his propagandists understand nothing about it.] [Col. 0252D]. He forbids its use under the penalties prescribed by law; orders, under the same penalties, that copies of it be brought to his secretariat; and exhorts his clergy to remain inviolably attached to the doctrine of the four articles of the assembly of 1682.

This was still not enough. On August 16, the mandate published on the same matter by Henri-Charles de Coislin, bishop of Metz, appeared. He was also known for his attachment to the principles of the sect that was then disturbing the Church of France and that had placed its fondest hopes in the doctrines of the declaration of 1682 [Col. 0252D].

After a dark depiction of the calamities that never failed to stain the world with blood whenever a supreme pontiff used spiritual authority to avenge certain great social crimes—a depiction that could be compared, with considerable advantage, to those occasionally encountered in Voltaire’s *Essay on Morals*, with the same understanding of history and the same equity toward the Church—the bishop of Metz adds, with solemn gravity:

“The experience of so many disastrous events, which had taken their origin in Gregory VII’s undertakings, seemed long ago to have halted the course of this conflagration; but a spark has since appeared that could rekindle it, if each of those whom the heavenly Father has placed in charge of his house did not hasten to prevent its spread through the portion of the flock entrusted to him” [Col. 0253A].

Thus it is fully demonstrated that it is the pope who sets the Church on fire, while the gentlemen of Auxerre, Montpellier, and Metz—and later the gentlemen of Verdun, Troyes, Castres, and still others—do everything they can to extinguish it.

“A printed sheet has recently appeared,” again says the bishop of Metz, “to serve as a supplement to the Roman Breviary; and in this sheet, which contains an office devoted to the memory of Gregory VII, the prelates and principal magistrates of the kingdom have perceived what is most capable of inspiring the excesses of ultramontane claims. One reads in the fifth lesson of this office that this pope courageously resisted, and so forth.

“Our knowledge, dearly beloved brethren, of your zeal for the king’s person, of your faithful attachment to the service of His Majesty, and of the obedience you owe to your sovereigns, leaves us no reason to doubt that you were as deeply moved as we were [Col. 0253C] on seeing in these few words a deliberate design to propose to the clergy and the people, as an encomium intended to make the sanctity of a pope credible, what, according to the principles of faith and the lights of reason, ought to serve only for the condemnation of his government. Your piety, doubtless, felt all the more wounded because this astonishing office was made public under the appearance of an authority borrowed from that of the Holy See. But this consideration should not alarm your veneration for that first see of the Church. The holy pontiff whom Providence has placed upon the chair of Saint Peter had no part in the composition, still less in the publication [Col. 0253D], of this artful work. He learned in the school of this chief of the apostles the respect and obedience owed to sovereigns. In this regard, he prefers the instruction and example of Saint Gregory the Great to the conduct and undertakings of Gregory VII. The humility of the servant of the servants of God keeps thoughts of being master of scepters and crowns far from his heart, and his wisdom is too enlightened not to see that so ill-founded a claim can only embitter princes and turn peoples against them.”

It cannot be denied that these lessons given to the head of the Church by a mere bishop ought to have produced a very great effect upon the people to whom the mandate was addressed [Col. 0254A]. As for Benedict XIII himself—whom the bishop of Metz calls a holy pontiff, a judgment that history has at least confirmed—he did not appear very inclined to let people believe that the most important acts of his government were being carried out without his knowledge. We shall soon see the vigorous reply he made to these insolent provocations.

Meanwhile, the prelate declares that, wishing on so important an occasion to give the king proofs of the fidelity he had pledged to him; to the emperor, to His Royal Highness of Lorraine, and to the other sovereigns who possessed some portion of their states within his diocese, proof of the attention he would always give to matters affecting them; and to preserve the souls entrusted to his care [Col. 0254B] from the illusions that the pretext of a misunderstood piety might cause them, he had forbidden and forbade all communities and all persons of either sex in his diocese . . . . . to recite, either publicly or privately, the office of Gregory VII. He likewise forbade all printers, and so forth, to publish the same office. He further ordered that copies of it be returned to the registry of his episcopal chamber—all under the penalties prescribed by law.

Reflections would here be superfluous; we shall therefore continue our account. Encouraged by the zeal of the three prelates, the Parliament of Brittany hastened to follow the example of that of Paris. On August 17, it issued a decree suppressing the legend [Col. 0254C]. The following phrases were noted in the attorney general’s requisition:

“Permit me to remind you, gentlemen, that Gregory VII was the first of all the popes who dared to make his claims over the temporal power of kings explode openly, by arrogating to himself the imaginary right to depose them and release their subjects from the oath of loyalty. A fatal fantasy, which has persisted only too long beyond the mountains among minds for whom ignorance and blind submission almost always take the place of knowledge.

“It is this chimera, against which one cannot be too much on guard in this kingdom, that they now seek to make real by insinuating to the people [Col. 0254D] that it served this pope as a step toward attaining sainthood—an expedient unknown before him. And you will surely view with indignation the fact that these seditious words, ‘Against the emperor Henry,’ and so forth, are placed on the same level as the words of life and peace that came from the mouth of Jesus Christ himself.

“What a combination! And what can one think of this monstrous eulogy, except that those who inserted it into a prayer book believed it would have greater effect and would cause those thunderbolts which popes believe themselves entitled to hurl against monarchs to be respected as permissible? For, it will be said, if it were a crime, or if it exceeded their power, such an action would not have been praised, an action which the ministers of our altars can all too easily abuse in their instructions” [Col. 0255A].

As can be seen, the magistrates—otherwise faithful to their liturgical omnipotence—were no less aware than the bishops of Auxerre, Montpellier, and Metz of the value and authority of a document inserted into the Roman Breviary. It was easy to foresee that the day was not far off when an attempt would be made to break the liturgical bond with Rome in order to free oneself, as we have previously seen, from several things contrary to the maxims of our Gallican Church. Jansenism, doubtless, contributed greatly to the scandals we are recounting; but simple Gallicanism also had its share. This became clear when, on August 21, the mandate of Charles-François d’Hallencourt, bishop of Verdun, appeared [Col. 0255B]. This prelate had adhered to the bull *Unigenitus*, and in the very mandate we are citing he expressly said that obedience to the pope and to the bishops in matters concerning religion is the only sure path to salvation. Let us now hear what the doctrine of 1682 inspired in him concerning the legend:

“No, dearly beloved brethren, whatever the faults of the emperor Henry IV may have been, the pope had no right to take away his crown or to untie the sacred bonds that bound his subjects to his service. This act, in which this pope so unjustly exceeded his power—an act which it may be presumed he expiated through penance [Col. 0255C]—cannot be one of the grounds for his canonization; and if it is regarded merely as a historical fact, it is not in a saint’s legend, nor in the midst of a divine office, that it should be cited.”

Here indeed is the naïveté of certain honest Gallicans, who would be just as far from admitting the consequences of the system in the manner of the Parlements as from sparing ultramontane claims. The bishop of Verdun, more Catholic than the bishop of Montpellier, therefore consents to recognize Gregory VII as a saint; but, in order to account to himself for the value of his canonization, he innocently supposes that this great pope did penance for the deposition of Henry IV. This distinction, however, does not prevent him from ending his mandate with the same prohibition as his three colleagues:

“Lest,” he says, “this legend should mislead some weak minds, and since bishops cannot watch too closely over the safety of kings, in order to bury, as far as lies within our power, this undertaking of Pope Gregory VII in eternal oblivion, by these presents we have forbidden and forbid the recitation, whether publicly or privately, of the office contained in the said sheet, all under the penalties prescribed by law” [Col. 0255D].

After this, no one should have been surprised to hear of a decree of the Parliament of Metz, dated September 1, condemning the legend as the Parlements of Paris and Brittany had condemned it [Col. 0256A]. That of Bordeaux was not long in declaring itself either, by a decree dated the twelfth of the same month; and the attorney general Dudon was even heard to ask the court, in his requisition, to take certain precautions that would provide in future that nothing might slip into books intended for divine service and other books of piety that could injure the rights of the king or disturb the tranquility of the State.

The affair was far from being ended by these scandalous decrees: new disturbances appeared in several places. In Paris, a certain number of parish priests of the city, its suburbs, and the surrounding area presented a petition to Archbishop Vintimille on September 14 [Col. 0256B] and denounced the legend to him. We shall quote nothing from this document, which in substance and wording resembled the mandates and decrees we have cited. The parish priests concluded by asking the archbishop to join his spiritual authority to that of the Parlement, in order to order “what religion, justice, fidelity to the king, and love of the fatherland cannot fail to inspire in the bishop of the kingdom’s capital on such occasions, and in particular to prescribe that the declaration of the clergy of France of 1682 be inviolably maintained and exactly observed in the secular and regular communities and throughout the whole extent of this diocese, in conformity with the laws, so necessary, established by the late king; by such a glorious action he will render an essential service to the Church and to the State” [Col. 0256C].

The archbishop, who perceived that the Jansenists were stirring up all this noise merely to discredit, if possible, the Apostolic See—whose prerogatives were all the more hateful to them because they had experienced their effects—had the prudence to make no public demonstration against the legend, and affected to pass over it in silence in a pastoral instruction that he published on September 29, concerning the religious disputes of the time [Col. 0256D]. The parish priests who had signed the petition we mentioned presented the archbishop with a new memorandum, in which they bitterly complained of the prelate’s severity toward their party and again returned to the matter of the legend. It was then that the archbishop, according to the *Nouvelles ecclésiastiques*, said to them sternly:

“I condemn what was done at Rome, and I am as good a servant of the king as you are; but since the king has had it condemned by his Parlement, it was useless to speak of it. If anyone stirs over this, the official will do his duty, and, if necessary, we shall shorten the proceedings by sending them to the Place de Grève.”

The prelate repeated this twice. The parish priests rose, saying “that they had no intention of causing him distress, but of representing to him the state of their parishes and the scandal caused by the legend, which was in the hands of more than half [Col. 0257A] the priests of the diocese who recite the Roman Breviary” [Note: [Col. 0257C] October 7, 1729.].

While these things were taking place in France, Rome—insulted in what she holds most dear, the honor of the saints whom she invokes, and her own dignity, which, since it is not of this world (*non est de hoc mundo*), must not be sacrificed to human and personal considerations—set about defending herself with the weapons that the King of kings has placed in her hands. Though the mandates we have cited and the decrees of the Parlements, in condemning the legend, had reserved judgment on Benedict XIII’s complicity, claiming that he had been unaware of this attack and that he was too virtuous, too animated by the apostolic spirit of the Church’s first centuries, to have deliberately opposed the French maxims so violently, the holy pontiff took it upon himself to give a solemn denial to these insulting reservations. As early as September 17, an energetic brief was posted in the Holy City, beginning with these words:

“Since it has come to the knowledge of our apostolic office that certain printed sheets in the French language have been circulated among the people, bearing the title: *Mandate of His Lordship the Bishop of Auxerre, forbidding the recitation of the office printed on a loose sheet, which begins with these words: *Die 25 Maii. In Festo sancti Gregorii VII, papae et confessoris* [On 25 May. On the feast of Saint Gregory VII, pope and confessor]. Given at Auxerre, on the twenty-fourth day of July, 1729*; We have chosen several of our venerable brothers, the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, and other doctors of sacred theology, to examine these sheets; and after mature discussion they reported to Us what they thought concerning this matter. Having therefore heard the opinions of the said cardinals and doctors, We declare, by the fullness of apostolic authority, that the injunctions contained in the aforesaid sheets are null, vain, invalid, without effect, unlawful attacks, and wholly lacking in force and significance, both now and forever.

“Nevertheless, for greater caution, and insofar as may be necessary, by this instrument We revoke, cancel, rescind, annul, and wholly deprive them of all force and effect, declaring and ordaining that they shall forever be regarded as revoked, cancelled, rescinded, null, invalid, and abolished. Moreover, by the tenor of these presents, We forbid the reading or retention of the said sheets, whether printed or handwritten, and prohibit their printing, copying, reading, retention, and use by all and each of the Christian faithful, even those worthy of special and individual mention, under penalty of excommunication incurred *ipso facto* by offenders. None of them may be absolved from it except by Us or by the Roman pontiff then in existence, unless at the point of death. We will and command by apostolic authority that those who have these sheets in their possession, as soon as these letters come to their knowledge, deliver and consign them to the ordinaries of the places or to the inquisitors of heretical depravity, who shall take care to deliver them immediately to the flames” [Note: [Col. 0257C]

Pope Benedict XIII, for perpetual remembrance.

When certain leaves printed in the French language came to our attention under the title *Mandate of the Most Reverend Lord Bishop of Auxerre, forbidding the recitation of the office printed on a loose sheet, which begins with these words: “On 25 May, on the feast of Saint Gregory VII, pope and confessor . . . .” Given at Auxerre, 24 July 1729*—we selected several of our venerable brothers, cardinals of the holy Roman Church, and certain masters of sacred theology to examine them [Col. 0257D]. After a careful discussion of those leaves, they reported to Us what they thought about the matter. Having therefore heard the opinions of the aforesaid cardinals and masters of sacred theology, by the fullness of apostolic power, we declare by these presents that the ordinances contained in the aforesaid leaves are null, void, invalid, voided, attempted without authority, and entirely lacking in all force and effect, and that they shall remain so perpetually.

And nevertheless, for greater precaution, and insofar as may be necessary, by the tenor of these presents we revoke, rescind, invalidate, annul, and wholly and entirely deprive them of force and effect; and we wish and order that they always be regarded as revoked, rescinded, invalid, null, void, and abolished, and as wholly and entirely lacking force and effect. Likewise, by the tenor of these presents, we absolutely prohibit all the faithful of Christ, including those worthy of specific and individual mention and designation, from reading or retaining the aforesaid leaves, whether printed or handwritten; and we altogether forbid their printing, copying, reading, retention, and use [Col. 0258C], under penalty of excommunication incurred ipso facto, without any further declaration, by those who contravene this prohibition. None of them may obtain the benefit of absolution from anyone except Us or the Roman pontiff then in office, unless he is at the point of death. We further will and command, by apostolic authority, that whoever has such leaves in his possession must, as soon as these letters have become known to him, deliver and consign them to the local ordinaries or to the inquisitors of heretical depravity; and these officials must immediately arrange for the leaves thus delivered to them to be destroyed by fire [Col. 0258D]. No contrary act or privilege shall stand in the way.

So that these letters might more easily come to everyone’s knowledge, and so that no one might plead ignorance of them, we also will and decree, by the aforesaid authority, that they be published, as is customary, by one of our couriers at the doors of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, of the Apostolic Chancery, and of the general tribunal on Monte Citorio, and in the open square of Campo de’ Fiori in the City; and that copies of them be left affixed there. Thus published, they shall bind and affect all and each of those whom they concern just as if they had been personally notified and formally intimated to each one of them.
