And we decree that exact faith shall everywhere be accorded, both in court and outside it, to transcripts or copies of these present letters—including printed copies signed by the hand of a public notary and authenticated with the seal of a person holding ecclesiastical rank—exactly the same faith that would be accorded to these present letters themselves if they had been produced or shown.

[Col. 0260D] Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, under the Fisherman’s Ring, on 17 September 1729, in the sixth year of our pontificate.]

This was the first sentence of the Apostolic See against the French opposition to the legend of [Col. 0259A] Saint Gregory VII. Rome had shown clearly enough, no doubt, that it had not lightly bestowed this praise upon so illustrious a pontiff, and that it would not retreat from the course it had adopted. Gallicanism, however, had not yet reached the full measure of its audacity in France. On 30 September there appeared a colossal mandate by Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, bishop of Troyes, who joined his colleagues from Auxerre, Montpellier, and Metz and confronted the formidable hazards of a struggle with the Roman Church. This mandate, which was itself a substantial book, had been easy to compose. Its author had simply undertaken to establish the doctrine of the first article of the Declaration of 1682, and for that purpose had thought it sufficient to translate into rather ponderous French [Col. 0259B] several pages that his uncle had devoted to this subject in the still unpublished *Defense of the Declaration of the Clergy of France*. We shall quote only a few lines from this enormous document, filled throughout with brutal insults against the sovereign pontiffs:

“From this simple account, my dear brothers,” said the prelate, “you perceive all the poison with which this sheet is filled; you understand all its danger; you can easily discern the maxims that they would like to instill in you by proposing that, on your feast days, you celebrate actions that ought to have remained buried in eternal oblivion and that can only dishonor their authors; by consecrating through public worship the memory of a bloody tragedy [Col. 0259C]; and by canonizing in the offices of the Church, as though inspired by the Holy Spirit, conduct wholly opposed to the Gospel, to the spirit of Jesus Christ, and to that of the holy Church.”

The bishop of Troyes concluded by forbidding the use of the legend throughout his diocese, in order to give the king new proofs of his attachment to his sacred person, of his zeal for the defense of the rights of his crown and for the preservation of the tranquility of his kingdom, and finally to protect the flock of Jesus Christ from the illusions of false piety.

Rome could not remain unmoved by these new outrages. A second brief, condemning the mandate of the bishop of Metz and composed in the same terms as the one issued [Col. 0259D] against the bishop of Auxerre, was solemnly published and posted throughout Rome on 8 October.

In France, these apostolic acts did not diminish the zeal of Rome’s enemies. The scandal of yet another mandate against the legend erupted noisily. Here are the terms in which Honorat de Quiquerand de Beaujeu, bishop of Castres, spoke of the legend in a pastoral letter of 11 November 1729: “I cannot bring myself here to translate words more suited to scandalizing good Frenchmen than to edifying good Catholics.” We shall not follow him through the course of his commonplace declamations, amid which he seeks to insinuate that purely human motives may have dictated the canonization of Gregory VII. We shall hasten instead to the conclusion, in which the prelate declares that, so far as depended upon him, he wished to prevent the impressions that a false maxim might make upon the minds of all persons who, though very pious, lacked understanding. He therefore forbade the recitation of the new office, whether publicly or privately, ordering that its copies be returned to the registry of his official ecclesiastical court—all under the penalties prescribed by law.

A few weeks later, on 6 December, Rome answered these coarse [Col. 0260B] insults for the third time with a brief that vigorously stigmatized the mandate of the bishop of Montpellier. This brief was soon followed by a fourth, by which Benedict XIII, dated 19 December of the same year, finally inflicted, by his apostolic authority, upon the parliaments of Paris and Bordeaux the punishment they had deserved for their decrees attacking the authority of the Holy See and the honor of a glorious servant of God. In this notable brief, the pope did not merely declare the decrees and injunctions of those parliaments abusive and null in conscience; he also rescinded and annulled them by his own authority, just as, in the very days in which we write these lines, Gregory XVI has just rescinded and annulled all the acts of the regency [Col. 0260C] of Spain that are contrary to the rights and liberty of the Church.

“Since it has come to our ears,” said Benedict XIII, “that several magistrates, officers, and secular ministers have risen up, in edicts, decrees, resolutions, ordinances, mandates, and other regulations and provisions, whatever their name, against the decree recently published by Us extending the office of Saint Gregory VII to the whole Church—an office which, by virtue of the indults of Paul V, Clement X, Alexander VIII, and Clement XI, our predecessors of blessed memory, was already publicly and solemnly celebrated in many churches throughout the Christian world, and which We have made obligatory [Col. 0260D] for all who are bound to the canonical hours, in order to increase the worship of this holy pontiff and confessor, who labored with such tireless courage to restore and renew ecclesiastical discipline and to reform morals—

“Wishing, in accordance with the duty of the pastoral office that divine mercy has entrusted to our lowliness, an office so far above our merits and strength, to defend and preserve without diminution or stain our authority and that of the Church, attacked by the pernicious undertakings of these laymen, and having before our mind the entire sequence of all and each of the things that have occurred [lacuna]; with the counsel of several of our venerable brothers, the cardinals of the holy Roman Church, and by apostolic authority, by the tenor of these presents, We declare the edicts, decrees, resolutions, ordinances, promulgated by magistrates, even supreme magistrates, and all secular officers or ministers of whatever lay power, against our aforesaid decree extending the office of Saint Gregory VII [lacuna], to be null, void, invalid, deprived forever of all force and value, as are also all things that have followed or may follow from them.

“And moreover, for greater security, and insofar as may be necessary, by these presents We revoke, rescind, invalidate, annul, and perpetually abolish them, depriving them of all force and effect; and We wish them always to be held as revoked, rescinded, invalidated, annulled, abolished, and entirely deprived of all force and effect, and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0261B]

Benedict XIII, pope, for perpetual remembrance of the matter.

Since it has come to our ears that certain magistrates, officers, and secular ministers have risen up, through certain edicts, decrees, resolutions of the Senate, precepts, mandates, or other ordinances or provisions of whatever kind and whatever name [Col. 0261C], against the decree recently issued by Us extending to all the faithful of Christ who are bound to the canonical hours the office of Saint Gregory VII, pope—an office which had previously, by virtue of the indults of Paul V, Clement X, Alexander VIII, and Clement XI, Roman pontiffs, our predecessors of blessed memory, been recited everywhere and publicly and solemnly celebrated in many churches of the Christian world, and which was issued to increase the worship of the holy pontiff and confessor who worked strenuously and tirelessly to eradicate errors, restore and renew ecclesiastical discipline, and reform corrupt morals—

“Therefore, wishing, in fulfillment of the duty of the pastoral office that divine favor has entrusted to our humility, though it is far unequal to that office in merits and strength, to protect and preserve our authority and ecclesiastical authority unharmed and unstained from such pernicious undertakings of laymen; and also holding as fully and sufficiently expressed and exactly specified by these presents the whole sequence of all and each of the things done and conducted in the foregoing matters or on their occasion in any manner, as well as anything else requiring specific and individual mention and expression; with the counsel of very many of our venerable brothers, cardinals of the holy Roman Church, by apostolic authority and by the tenor of these presents, We declare that all edicts, decrees, resolutions of the Senate, precepts, mandates, and all other ordinances or provisions, whatever their name, promulgated or to be promulgated in any manner or place by magistrates, even supreme magistrates, or by secular officers and ministers, or by any other lay power or in its name, against the decree extending the office of the same Saint Gregory VII, pope, issued by Us as stated above, as well as all other things done, conducted, or ordered in any manner in the foregoing matters or on their occasion, together with everything that has followed or may at any time follow from them, are entirely and wholly null, void, invalid, presumptuously undertaken in fact, and utterly without force or effect, and shall perpetually remain so [Col. 0262B]. We declare this by apostolic authority and by the tenor of these presents.

“And nevertheless, for greater precaution, and insofar as may be necessary, by this instrument We likewise perpetually revoke, rescind, invalidate, annul, and abolish each and every one of these things [Col. 0262C], wholly and entirely depriving them of force and effect; and We wish them always to be regarded as revoked, rescinded, invalidated, null, void, and abolished, and as wholly and entirely lacking force and effect. Thus, and not otherwise, the foregoing matters must be judged and determined by all ordinary and delegated judges, including the auditors of cases of the Apostolic Palace, and by the cardinals of the aforesaid holy Roman Church, including legates *a latere*, and by all others who exercise or shall exercise whatever preeminence and power; all ability and authority to judge or interpret otherwise being removed from them and from each of them. We decree that anything attempted otherwise in these matters by anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, under any authority, shall be null and void, notwithstanding anything to the contrary.

“So that these same present letters may more easily reach everyone’s knowledge, and so that no one may plead ignorance of them, We will and likewise decree that they be published, as is customary, by one of our couriers at the doors of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, of the Apostolic Chancery, and of the general tribunal on Monte Citorio, and in the open square of Campo de’ Fiori in the City; and that copies of them be left affixed there. Thus published, they shall bind and affect all and each of those whom they concern just as if they had been personally notified and formally intimated to each one of them.

“And We decree that exact faith shall everywhere be accorded, both in court and outside it, to transcripts or copies of these present letters—including printed copies signed by the hand of a public notary and authenticated with the seal of a person holding ecclesiastical rank—exactly the same faith that would be accorded to these present letters themselves if they had been produced or shown.

“Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, under the Fisherman’s Ring, on 19 December 1729, in the sixth year of our pontificate.]”

[Col. 0262A] News of this brief soon reached France and quickly provoked the fury of the agents of Gallicanism. On 23 February 1730, the Parliament of Paris issued a decree against the publication, distribution, and execution of this brief, as well as of those that had been issued against the bishops. The court expressed its indignation through its faithful spokesman, Gilbert de Voisins, who spoke as follows at the beginning of his address:

“After the solemn decree that the court issued, in July last, upon our conclusions, concerning the office of Gregory VII, we had reason to believe that we would have no further duty to fulfill regarding this matter, and that the court of Rome would gradually allow us to lose [Col. 0262B] all memory of it.

“But we painfully recognize how greatly our hopes have been disappointed upon seeing a brief from Rome, now in our hands, of which it may be said that it puts into practice the doctrine disseminated in the office of Gregory VII by rescinding, through pontifical authority, all edicts, decrees, ordinances, and other acts issued on this subject by secular powers, even sovereign powers. [Col. 0263A] This brief undertakes to subject the temporal sovereignty of rulers to the priesthood; it exercises supreme authority over acts bearing the character of their power. It attacks their independence at its foundations and tends to deprive them of the means of defending it.”

Nevertheless, the decree of 22 February 1730, although issued in due form and printed, was not published: the Parliament received an express prohibition to that effect from Cardinal de Fleury. As early as the first days of December 1729, the chancellor had written to the king’s representatives in all the parliaments instructing them not to make any address concerning the liberties of the Gallican Church without first consulting the court. He had even expressly declared to the attorney general of the supreme council of Roussillon that they must proceed cautiously and that the government was not in a position to sustain the matter [Col. 0263B].

This conduct of the government, opposed to the wishes of the magistracy, is easily explained if one recalls the situation of royal power at that time. The maxims that had long prevailed at the court of Versailles certainly did not permit the use of the legend of Saint Gregory VII to be tolerated in the churches of the kingdom. On the other hand, an open clash with Rome would have rallied the Jansenist party, which asked nothing better than to rush against that sacred authority whose preservation the French crown still found useful. The Jansenist pamphlets of the time resounded with the jubilant accents of a party that believed it was on the eve of seeing the hateful condemnation of Quesnel’s Proposition XCI withdrawn through the suppression of the legend [Col. 0263C]. Yet the court needed the bull *Unigenitus* to contain the seditious phalanx of the new Calvinists, while, on the other hand, the four articles of 1682, though vainly revoked by Louis XIV, seemed to it the palladium of royal authority. What it needed, therefore, was neither declamatory mandates nor fanatical decrees, but quite simply a resolution reached amicably by the clergy to suppress the legend without noise.

[Note: [Col. 0263D] The archbishop of Vintimille was too prudent to have placed himself conspicuously at the forefront of this affair. On 6 February 1730, he wrote to the pope asking him to close his eyes to whatever he might regard as the archbishop’s responsibility in the question of the legend, and asking him to consider how much courage it had taken for him not to prohibit it, as others had done, by a mandate. (*Nouvelles ecclésiastiques*, 1 May 1731.) In fact, for the prelates attached to the doctrine of 1682, the situation was very difficult. [Col. 0264D] Their reserve on so delicate an occasion soon exposed them to the Jansenists’ accusation of contradiction.]

That was how the court understood the matter, and that was how it was obediently understood throughout the Church of France, so that until the destruction of the old society in 1789, no secular or religious church had been able to inaugurate the worship of the great pontiff Gregory VII. Let us add a few more features to this deplorable history.

The bishop of Auxerre, still ardent in defense of the twin Gallican and Jansenist causes, and also sensing the false position of the court and the episcopate in their decision to bury the legend without spectacle, agitated desperately to increase the commotion. He submitted a petition to the Parliament of Paris against the brief that had stigmatized his mandate, having first sought the opinion of a council on which no fewer than one hundred lawyers sat. A few days later, on 11 February 1730, he addressed his complaints to the king in a long letter, in which he attempted to stir the monarch’s zeal against the undertakings of the court of Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0264D] As early as the preceding 31 December, the bishop of Montpellier had written a first letter to the king denouncing the danger threatening his person and begging him to have the four articles of 1682 newly declared at the next assembly of the clergy, and to ensure that they thereafter be read every year in the church.]

He nevertheless failed to obtain the spectacle he desired, for on 18 February Cardinal de Fleury wrote the following letter to the king’s representatives, showing that the policy of the moment was to adhere to peace:

“Gentlemen, I have nothing to add to what I am writing to the first president; I also defer to the king’s orders, which the chancellor will communicate to you. In the present circumstances, it is enough that the essential matter—that is, the maxims of the kingdom—be safeguarded; and prudence requires that one not seek to aggravate the illness rather than cure it. Above all, the king wishes no mention to be made of the petition or of the mandate of the bishop of Auxerre. Before publishing it, he ought to have known that it was appropriate for him to learn His Majesty’s intentions on so delicate a matter and to agree upon the manner in which he would express himself. It is even more indecorous for him to have his petition signed [Col. 0264C] by a crowd of lawyers. This procedure has much more the character of a cabal than of genuine zeal.”

Now, the year 1730 was to see the meeting of the general assembly of the clergy, and everyone privately considered how embarrassing the prelates’ situation would then be in this delicate circumstance. Would they rise against the legend? Would they pass over it in complete silence? That was the difficult problem that remained to be solved. In the meantime, whether by chance or design, the assembly opened in Paris on 25 May, the very day of the feast of Saint Gregory VII. On the following 22 June, Cardinal de Fleury appeared before the assembly and took the president’s place. His Eminence, in a speech on the state of ecclesiastical affairs [Col. 0264D], said among other things “that no one was unaware with what artifice and bad faith the innovators sought to spread unjust suspicions against the clergy of France, as though, by declaring itself so solemnly [Col. 0265A] as it had done in favor of the bull *Unigenitus*, it had secretly intended to favor opinions as injurious to the independence of the temporal power of our kings as they were contrary to the ancient maxims that the bishops of France had so consistently defended in every age; and that, although this unworthy accusation bore not even the slightest appearance of plausibility, it nevertheless seemed to him that, in order to deprive their enemies of the last refuge they had imagined for weakening the authority of the judgments pronounced against them, it was a matter of honor for the clergy to explain itself concerning this calumny in such a way as to silence them and expose all their malice [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Minutes of the Proceedings of the Clergy*, volume VII, p. 892].”

[Col. 0265B] The archbishop of Paris, Charles de Vintimille, replied to the cardinal concerning this point in the following terms:

“With regard to our maxims concerning the temporal sovereignty of our kings and the fidelity that we owe them, who has them more at heart and proclaims them with greater zeal than the clergy of France? You know, Monseigneur—and I have had the honor of telling you so privately—what is thought by all those who make up this illustrious assembly, which has resolved not to separate without explaining itself in a manner that will silence an obstinate party which, while failing to recognize the authority of the Church and that of the king, dares to cloak itself in a supposed zeal for these same maxims [Col. 0265C] [Note: [Col. 0266D] *Minutes of the Proceedings of the Clergy*, ibid., p. 894].”

We shall soon see how the assembly escaped from this difficult situation. In the meantime, however, a notable incident compelled it to take a position on the very matter of the legend. The bishop of Auxerre had conceived the idea of addressing a letter to the assembly, admonishing it of its obligation to punish Rome’s scandalous undertaking, and bringing into the affair once again the condemnation of Quesnel’s Proposition XCI. The assembly, having refused to hear the letter read, adopted the following resolutions, which we borrow from its minutes:

“The company unanimously expressed the view that it had just cause to complain of the conduct [Col. 0265D] of the bishop of Auxerre, who thought he ought to stir the assembly’s zeal for maintaining the sacred rights attached to royal authority, as though it deserved to be suspected of lacking such zeal.

“That the conduct of the bishop of Auxerre was all the less appropriate because this prelate took it upon himself to make observations to an assembly that had no need of them and whose sentiments he could not fail to know, while he himself was in open disobedience to the authority of the Church, whose decisions he rejected; and that by this conduct he was refractory to the king’s orders, since the king, as protector of the Church, employed his authority to have its laws carried out.

“That the assembly easily understood that the motive which had led the bishop of Auxerre to write to it was merely to give himself the freedom to rise against the constitution *Unigenitus*; but that the assembly could not regard without indignation the excesses to which he had previously gone against a dogmatic judgment of the universal Church, to which every bishop, like every member of the faithful, must adhere in heart and mind.

“That, moreover, the assembly was rightly scandalized that this prelate claimed there was a connection between the constitution *Unigenitus* and the opinion [Col. 0266B] that attacks the independence of our kings and their crown with respect to temporal matters; finally, that for all these reasons the assembly ought not to permit the reading of the letter that the bishop of Auxerre had addressed to it [Note: [Col. 0266D] *Minutes*, ibid., p. 1062].”

A few days later, the assembly had to consider the letter that the bishop of Montpellier had written to the king on 31 December 1729 concerning the legend, in which he sought to cast suspicion upon the intentions of the prelates who had not thought it appropriate to prohibit the worship of Saint Gregory VII by mandates. Jealous to justify itself against the suspicion of indifference toward His Majesty’s rights, the assembly resolved upon the plan of an address to Louis XV, which was drafted [Col. 0266C] and signed under the date of 11 September. The prelates bitterly complained there of the bishop of Montpellier’s insinuations against their fidelity, and said among other notable things:

“It is through vain declamations and calumnious accusations that the bishop of Montpellier believes he can make people forget his excesses and, under the cover of bitter and misplaced zeal, conceal the errors he proclaims and the scandal he causes in the Church. This artifice is not new; all sectarians have employed it. The enemies of unity make use of it today, and their design is easy to discern. For sixteen years they have occupied themselves with stirring magistrates and peoples against the authority of the [Col. 0266D] constitution and with making those who accepted it contemptible. They seized upon the occasion of the legend of Gregory VII—a legend that no bishop has adopted in your kingdom and whose use has not been and will not be permitted in any of our dioceses. Through malicious and deceptive reflections they believed they could break the union and harmony prevailing between the two powers and, by taking advantage of the divisions they are attempting to provoke, place themselves beyond the reach of both. Through a diversion concerning the disputes they are striving to revive, they wished to obscure the common interest of Church and State, which consists in preserving [Col. 0267A] the unity of the faith and in bringing back or subjecting those who violate it.

“One affects, Sire, to distinguish between the power of Louis XIV and yours. This is an equally injurious insinuation against Your Majesty and your august great-grandfather. Heir to his throne and virtues, having become the love of your peoples from the moment of your birth and having never experienced any opposition, domestic or foreign, what could Your Majesty lack to uphold your rights as he upheld his? Yet, in upholding them, that great king never forgot the wise moderation inspired by religion [Note: [Col. 0267D] *Minutes of the Proceedings of the Clergy*, ibid., p. 1074].”

Here, surely, was something definite. No mandates against the legend of Saint Gregory [Col. 0267B] VII—whom the Gallican Church here simply calls Gregory VII on an occasion precisely concerning the worship accorded to this holy pontiff, thereby protesting against the Martyrology and against the authority that promulgates the Catholic calendar; no individual and impassioned mandates; but a resolution adopted collectively, calmly, and authoritatively by the assembly to suppress this worship and arrest the effect of apostolic commands; to place itself, through flagrant disobedience to the Holy See, in a situation analogous to that of the bishop of Auxerre, whose rebellious spirit had been denounced. Certainly, the assembly’s disobedience to the pope’s orders concerned only a matter of simple discipline; but could it have been believed that the bonds of subordination could long be preserved within the clergy when they were so easily broken with regard to the pontiff who, according to the very doctrine of 1682, issues decrees binding upon all the churches? Rome concealed the insult, but courageously maintained the legend. A century has passed since then, and now an aura of glory surrounds the name of this Gregory VII whom the assembly refused to call a saint; and the public voice acclaims the man whose memory the prelates of 1730 took pride in having banished from their dioceses [Note: [Col. 0267D] And observe that, by condemning merely the memory of Saint Gregory VII to oblivion, the assembly exposed itself to attack by its Jansenist adversaries, who were entitled to reproach it for taking only negative measures against a Roman undertaking against which it nevertheless believed it ought to protest. The Parliament of Paris therefore prepared a decree against the address, and shortly afterward there appeared a vehement pamphlet entitled *The Cause of the State Abandoned by the Clergy of France, or Reflections on the Letter of the Assembly of the Clergy to the King of 11 September 1730*. Quarto, 68 pages.]

Certainly, if God’s patience is all the more imposing because He draws its motive from His eternity, how sublime is that of His noble spouse, our mother, the holy [Col. 0267D] Roman Church, whose passage through time has always avenged the injury done to her!

This deplorable address was signed by fourteen archbishops and bishops of the assembly and by nineteen deputies of the second order. One name alone was missing: that of Jean-César de La Parisière, bishop of Nîmes. This prelate, zealous against Jansenism and honored with the sect’s hatred, was one of those who dared to maintain the Roman breviary in their churches amid the liturgical innovation. In the assembly of 1730, he quickly perceived all that the conduct of his colleagues against the legend of Saint Gregory VII contained that was contrary to the honor of the Apostolic See. Despite all the antipathy he professed toward the person and doctrines of the bishop of Montpellier, he dared refuse to take part in the deliberation held concerning that prelate’s letter to the king, in which the address just discussed was arranged. His isolation with respect to everything that took place in this affair is expressly attested in the minutes of the assembly [Note: [Col. 0268D] p. 1073.]

We do not know how it came about that this [Col. 0268B] prelate, who had refused to share with his colleagues responsibility for the address they presented to Louis XV, assuring him of the fidelity they would maintain toward him even at the expense of the obedience sworn to the Holy See, was nevertheless chosen to draft and deliver the harangue to the king with which the assemblies of the clergy ordinarily concluded. Be that as it may, this courageous and independent harangue dealt exclusively with the ills of the Church. The Bishop of Nîmes eloquently and apostolically denounced the magistrates’ attacks upon ecclesiastical freedom and the insolence of the Jansenist sect, emboldened by such protection; and, recalling the obligation of a Christian king to defend the clergy, he spoke these beautiful words:

[Col. 0268C] “It is for this reason, Sire, that your throne—which, ever since a holy pontiff consecrated it by rescuing the great Clovis from paganism, has never been profaned by error—is such a sure and necessary resource for us, and that the right he gave you to protect us is the most august of all your titles. We come to you to uphold the very work of Jesus Christ, and to preserve for ourselves the freedom of a ministry whose exercise usurpation and violence may indeed obstruct, but which they could never essentially take away from us.

Everything that is merely human may be at the mercy of men; but, as for the deposit of the faith, and our jurisdiction, which necessarily follows from it, this is our treasure, our glory, our obligation: we can never consent to its being taken from us. We are answerable for it to God, to the Church, to the peoples, and to Your Majesty, whose reign is founded upon Catholicity and must always be sustained by the same principles [Note: [Col. 0268D] Proceedings, p. 1220].”

[Col. 0269A] It was the last breath of the ancient freedom that exhaled in these powerful words: “Your Majesty, whose reign is founded upon Catholicity.” Never again did a single word in the acts of the French clergy recall this axiom of the ancient law of Christendom: that a Catholic nation could be governed only by a Catholic prince.

This brief, simple, yet profound expression, which the Bishop of Nîmes had cast into his harangue, was moreover the only allusion it contained to the affair of the legend of Saint Gregory VII; but one could not repudiate with greater delicacy everything that had been done against the heroic pontiff than by recalling, in the very presence of the king, that something still stood above his crown: [Col. 0269B] the interest of Catholicity. Certainly, the harangue would make one forget the address, were one not compelled to see in the harangue the act of a single bishop, and in the address the decision adopted and maintained to the end by the representatives of the clergy of that time: to annihilate the cult of Saint Gregory VII. Now, this took place in 1730; and before the end of that same century, this kingship—which had wished to be incapable of forfeiture—was declared forever abolished. The successor of Louis XV, struck by the vertigo with which God seemed to have afflicted those of his race, after having been led to sanction acts that annihilated the Church, mounted the scaffold, without his loyalty, his virtue, or his repentance being capable of saving the monarchical principles that would remain eclipsed for many years more, [Col. 0269C] while Saint Gregory VII, brought back in triumph, reappears with unprecedented majesty and will henceforth share with Charlemagne the sublime title of founder of European society.

We are eager to bring to an end the shameful account of the outrages that the memory of the incomparable pontiff had to endure in France during the eighteenth century. Let us therefore hasten to say that the Bishop of Montpellier, in his anger against the assembly that had refused to associate itself with his furies, violently attacked his colleague, the Bishop of Nîmes, in a pastoral letter dated November 30, 1730, in which he strove to demonstrate the contradiction—indeed, an evident one—between the prelate’s harangue and the assembly’s address to [Col. 0269D] the king. “In the harangue,” he said, “it is laid down as a maxim that His Majesty’s reign is founded upon Catholicity, and that it must always be sustained by the same principles; from which it is easy to conclude that if a prince had the misfortune to fall into heresy, the pope would have the right to depose him, and the peoples would be released from obeying him!” On the other hand, the Parliament of Paris, roused to indignation, was preparing proceedings against the harangue and had its president make remonstrances to the king concerning the principles injurious to royal majesty that the speaker had professed in it: everything foreshadowed a storm. The peaceful spirit of Cardinal de Fleury once again succeeded in calming it, and the king confined himself to declaring to the Parliament that he was referring the matter to his council. There the matter ended [Note: [Col. 0269D] We do not think we ought to weary the reader with an account of the outcries raised by the Jansenists concerning a painting that Cardinal de Bissy had placed in his cathedral at Meaux. It represented a pope seated upon his throne, clothed in pontifical vestments and handing a globe to a bareheaded and bowed emperor. The pope was Benedict VIII, and the emperor was Saint Henry II, the patron of Cardinal de Bissy. The Bishop of Montpellier, who returns constantly to this subject in his voluminous correspondence, wanted to see in this pope Saint Gregory VII, [Col. 0270D] and in this emperor Henry IV. One could never imagine all the extravagances that this idea led him to utter, and that the party repeated in every possible form. When at last they recognized that these outcries were ridiculous, since nowhere in the whole life of Saint Gregory VII was there any circumstance to which the painting could allude, they retreated into the accusation of bad citizenship against the prelate who dared to place before the people a painting in which royal majesty was thus humbled before a pope.] The waves gradually subsided, but France remained outside Catholicity with regard to the cult of a holy pope. One could then see how far it had travelled since 1682.

[Col. 0270B] If we now investigate what happened in several other regions of Europe concerning the legend, we encounter facts singularly humiliating for us Frenchmen; for it is sad to see the enemies of the Church and even heretics joining with us to annihilate the cult of a saint.

Naples had had the distinction of striking the first blow against the Apostolic See in this deplorable circumstance. The city and its territory then belonged to the emperor, who maintained a viceroy there. This personage, named Count Harrach, having learned that the legend had entered the kingdom, hastened to denounce its publication before the Neapolitan tribunal known as the Collateral Council, where it was naturally treated as an offense; and on March 3, 1729, the viceroy addressed to his sovereign a lengthy report in which, after discussing at length the grave dangers that naturally followed for the imperial crown from the mere fact of the legend, he expressed himself in these terms:

“Of all these great and intolerable prejudices, which arise generally from the publication of the said lessons against the independence of sovereignty, and particularly against Your Majesty’s royal rights as emperor, it seemed naturally to follow that it was the duty of our office, imitating the custom and the address of the Roman court, to prohibit these lessons and order the bishops not to insert them in the breviaries. But having reflected that, notwithstanding this prohibition, the ecclesiastics would have continued to recite them; that the prohibition of an office would have caused scandal to this excessively superstitious people; and that the Roman court, taking advantage of this discontent, would have stirred up other difficulties that would afterward have obliged us to undertake greater commitments, the Collateral Council was of the opinion that the recitation of the lessons should not be prohibited, and that it would even be more expedient to display no resentment, so as not to reveal to simple and ignorant people the hidden poison they contained. It would be sufficient to order that the printers be imprisoned and all the copies suppressed—and this solely on the ground that these lessons had been introduced, reprinted, and sold without my permission and that of the Collateral Council, contrary to the Pragmatic Sanction of this kingdom, all the more so because they had been printed with the permission of the ecclesiastical superiors, although permission to grant such authorization had not been given.”

After the prohibition of the legend of Saint Gregory VII by the Viceroy of Naples came that issued a few days later by the heretical Archbishop of Utrecht, Cornelius John Barchman, in a mandate dated May 12, 1730. In this scandalous document he used the same language that we have observed in the mandates of the bishops of Auxerre, Montpellier, and Troyes. There were the same coarse insults against the head of the Church and the same contempt for her ordinances. “If the law of prayer,” Barchman said, “is to establish the law of faith, the bishops are obliged to watch so as to prevent anything from slipping into the public prayers that might imperceptibly corrupt the law of faith. If the history of the saints is read in the Church so that, by considering the end of the lives of those who announced the word of God to us, we may imitate their faith and follow their examples—which are all the more worthy of imitation insofar as piety appears in them in a more excellent manner—care must be taken to praise nothing in the divine offices that we ought not also to approve and even imitate when the occasion arises.”

The mandate ends with these words: “For these reasons, in order to defend the doctrine of the Catholic Church concerning the distinction between the two [Col. 0271D] powers; in order to preserve, insofar as lies within us, the civil power’s independence from the spiritual power; in order to give Their Lordships the States General, supreme governors of our republic, proofs of the fidelity that we owe them, without in any way weakening the respect that we owe to the Holy Apostolic See, we forbid the recitation of the office of Saint Gregory VII, both publicly in churches and privately, by all those obliged to recite the canonical hours. May the grace of God be with you all. Amen.”

When a prelate who claimed to be Catholic despite the Church indulged in such excesses, there is no longer any reason to be surprised that a Protestant government [Col. 0272A] should not wish to remain behind and should attack with violence the memory of the holy pope. That, therefore, is not what ought to surprise us; what is humiliating is being forced to acknowledge that this Protestant government, in its measures hostile to our faith and to the objects of our veneration, did not show itself more hostile than various powers belonging to the Roman communion. Here is the decree that the States General of the United Provinces had published and posted in every city of the confederation. It is dated September 20, 1730.

“ The States of Holland and West Frisia, to all who shall see these presents, greeting.

Since we have learned that advantage is being taken of our indulgence in tolerating the exercise of the divine service [Col. 0272B] of Roman Catholics, without enforcing in various respects the placards previously issued against that exercise, to the point that the office so called of Pope Gregory VII—settled at Rome by papal authority on September 25, 1728—is being publicly printed in our country of Holland and West Frisia for the use of Roman churches, either separately or with, or at the end of, what is called the Directorium or breviary; although the said office extols as a praiseworthy action this pope’s undertaking in having excommunicated a Roman emperor, deprived that prince of his kingdom, and absolved his subjects from the fidelity they had promised him; and although it cannot be ignored that various powers of the Roman [Col. 0272C] communion regard this undertaking of Gregory VII as so seditious, so contrary to public tranquility, and so dangerous in its consequences that they do not permit its use in their kingdoms and states;

For these reasons, after mature deliberation, we have deemed it appropriate, for the preservation of the common tranquility and for the security of the regency and of the true Reformed religion, to enact and order against the undertakings and machinations of the adherents of the See of Rome, as we hereby enact and order:

First, that no use whatsoever may be made in our country of Holland and West Frisia, whether publicly or privately, of the said office of Pope Gregory VII, under penalty that the Roman Catholic priests who contravene this order shall be punished without any remission as disturbers of the public peace, and that the churches of the Roman religion, chapels, or other assemblies in which use is thereafter made of the said office shall be closed for six months.

Second, that the said office may not be reprinted in our said country, or brought into it from abroad to be distributed or sold there, whether separately or as it is printed at the end of the said Directorium of the Mass and other ceremonies of the Roman Church; and that no mention of the said office may be made in subsequent editions of the said Directorium; all under penalty of a fine of one thousand florins against the person who contravenes this order, half of which shall belong to the officer and the other half to the informer, together with deprivation of the right to trade.

Charging and ordering all officers, judges, and justices of our said country to execute and enforce this present placard and command, and to proceed, and cause proceedings to be taken, without any grace, favor, or concealment against those who contravene it, we desire that it be published and posted wherever necessary. Done at The Hague, September 20, 1730 [Note: [Col. 0273D] Gazette of Holland, October 3, 1730].”

We find, in 1750, a circular issued from the imperial cabinet and addressed to the bishops of the Low Countries, ordering them to remove the office of Saint Gregory VII from the breviary. The clergy of Belgium, already discontented with the Austrian yoke, does not seem to have attached great importance to this prohibition, since, according to Abbé Grégoire [Note: [Col. 0273D] Essay on the Liberties of the Gallican Church, [Col. 0274D] p. 110], the government of Vienna was obliged to renew the proscription of the legend in 1774. It is doubtless unnecessary to observe that Joseph II showed himself implacable against the cult of the fiery Hildebrand; besides, Saint Gregory VII was not the only holy pontiff whom he persecuted in the breviary. An ordinance of the regency of Lower Austria, dated 1787, is cited as suppressing, in the breviary of the regular canons, various passages from the offices of several [Col. 0273C] holy popes, including the following in the fifth lesson for Saint Zachary, on March 15: “Consulted by the Franks, by apostolic authority he transferred that kingdom from Chilperic, a stupid and sluggish man, to Pippin, distinguished for piety and courage” [Consultus a Francis, regnum illud a Chilperico viro stupido et ignavo, ad Pippinum pietate et fortitudine praestantem auctoritate apostolica transtulit]. This office of Saint Zachary is not found in the Roman Breviary properly so called, but simply forms part of the proper offices of the clergy of the city of Rome.

To return to the legend of Saint Gregory VII: it nevertheless finally triumphed in Austria over the ill will of the rulers, though on the condition that it submit to a ridiculous formality imposed by the police. We do not know precisely when this condition was established; but all the Roman breviaries printed in the Austrian states [Col. 0273D] since the beginning of this century that have come into our hands are remarkable for a very curious mutilation. It consists first in suppressing these words, which conclude the fifth lesson: “Against the impious attempts of the Emperor Henry, he remained in every respect a brave and fearless champion, and did not fear to set himself as a wall for the house of Israel; and he deprived that same Henry, who had fallen into the depths of evil, of the communion of the faithful and of his kingdom, and freed the subject peoples from the allegiance they had given him” [Contra Henrici imperatoris impios conatus, fortis per omnia athleta impavidus permansit, seque pro muro domui Israel ponere non timuit, ac eumdem Henricum in profundum malorum prolapsum, fidelium communione, regnoque privavit, atque subditos populos fide ei data liberavit].

[Col. 0274A] Finally, imperial censorship, going beyond all bounds, was not content forever to secure the Caesars’ crown against papal undertakings, thereby guaranteeing the inalienability of the throne against every invasion through the liturgy; this censorship, I say, at the same time decreed imperial impeccability—which has its own merit in this world, and especially in the next. The sixth lesson is therefore retained in its entirety, except for a single word: the adjective iniqui, “iniquitous,” applied to Henry of Germany. Rome and all the Churches that obey its decrees concerning the liturgy read: “when it was being hard pressed at Rome by the grave siege of the army of the iniquitous Henry” [cum ab iniqui Henrici exercitu Romae gravi obsidione premeretur]; in the Austrian states, it is necessary to print and read simply: “when it was being hard pressed at Rome by Henry’s army,” and so forth [Cum ab Henrici exercitu Romae, etc.]. Does this not naturally recall what happened at Milan a few years ago, when a mandate by the cardinal archbishop, on the occasion of the death of Emperor Francis II, was revised by the censors because the prelate had exhorted the faithful to pray for a beloved sovereign who, despite all his virtues, might nevertheless have contracted certain stains of human weakness?

Once again, in the eighteenth century, we see the memory of Saint Gregory VII outraged in a Catholic state, Portugal. It does not appear, however, that the legend was proscribed there; but a man more than rash, António Pereira de Figueiredo, among the numerous writings he published against the rights of the Church and the Holy See, devoted [Col. 0274C] a special dissertation to attacking the person and writings of our great pontiff, under the title *On the Deeds and Writings of Gregory VII* [De gestis et scriptis Gregorii VII]. It was certainly an outrage originating very low down: it came from a man whose attachment to the cause of the Holy See had initially earned him Pombal’s disgrace, and who, having suddenly become the enthusiastic advocate of that minister—one of the most infamous persecutors of the Church—showed himself the ignoble flatterer of as poor a sovereign as Joseph I. No, the apostolic character of Saint Gregory VII had nothing in common with the former Oratorian who applauded the atrocious punishment of Malagrida, and whose venal pen wrote the insipid pamphlets entitled *Parallel between Augustus Caesar and Don [Col. 0274D] Joseph, Magnanimous King of Portugal*, and *The Portuguese Nation’s Vows to the Guardian Angel of the Marquis of Pombal* [Note: [Col. 0274D] Lisbon, 1775]!

The nineteenth century, too, furnished several insults to the memory of the holy pontiff. Without speaking of the blasphemies that more than once issued from the ecclesiastical peers’ bench in the English Parliament against the person of the fiery Hildebrand, there were others whose scene was laid in Catholic countries. Let us begin with Italy.

Until 1810, the office of Saint Gregory VII had continued to be celebrated in the churches of the various [Col. 0275A] dioceses composing the Kingdom of Italy. The excommunication incurred by Napoleon in 1809 made him excessively anxious, and it is generally known how many persecutory measures weighed upon the clergy at that time. But what is less well known is that the great emperor, at the same time as he raised his hand against Pius VII, also dared to defy the majesty of a pontiff who, like Pius VII, had once been besieged and held captive, but had since been and forever would be crowned by him who first drank from the torrent before raising his head [Note: [Col. 0275D] Ps. CIX]. A letter from the Minister of Religious Affairs, Bigot de Préameneu, written in February 1810, ordered the bishops of Italy to imitate the silence of the Gallican Church concerning the name and deeds of Hildebrand. We cannot give the names [Col. 0275B] of the Italian prelates—there were several—who preferred to obey Caesar rather than the Church; but we have in our possession, and preserve as a monument, the autograph letter in which Hyacinth de La Tour, Archbishop of Turin, sends the minister the mandate that he had considered it his duty to issue forbidding the office of Saint Gregory VII, and in which he declares that a copy had been posted in all the sacristies of the churches of his diocese. The letter is dated March 1, 1810.

Hardly had he escaped the violence of the dreaded eagle that was clutching Europe—yet still standing upright in the same place—than the heroic Hildebrand fell prey to those anarchists whose desires are themselves desires for tyranny. In France, the regicide Grégoire, in his *Historical Essay on the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, published in 1818, heaped upon the holy pope and his legend all the blasphemies of the Protestants and Jansenists. In Spain, in March 1822, a proposal was made in the Cortes to suppress part of the office of Gregory VII, “as an attack upon the rights of nations” [Note: [Col. 0275D] *L’Ami de la Religion*, April 13, 1822, vol. XXXI]! Certainly this was a bitter mockery of those courtier-kings and courtier-bishops who had for so long been occupied in persecuting the cult of the holy pontiff and had branded him as guilty of lèse-majesté against royalty! How upright, how pure, therefore, was the policy of this great man; how lofty a conception of public law God had placed within him, if all men of extreme views have agreed to make his name and memory the object of their attacks. Enjoy this glory, holy pontiff: until now no mortal has shared it with you.

One more outrage—and it will be the last. At the beginning of 1828, a new edition of the Roman Breviary appeared in Paris from the bookseller Poussielgue-Rusand. The publisher had thought himself able [Col. 0276A] to insert the office of Saint Gregory VII in it; yet he had placed it only at the end of the volume, not feeling fully reassured by the promise of religious liberty guaranteed to all by the Charter of 1815. A few days after the breviary’s publication, certain newspapers calling themselves liberal, and fraternizing in every respect with the Spanish Cortes of 1822, began to cry out against the ultramontanism overflowing among us, since, as they said, people dared in 1828 to print and offer for sale the legend of Gregory VII. Their outcries were heard, and in Paris, in 1828, the legend of Saint Gregory VII was subjected, by order of the archbishopric, to the mutilations inflicted upon it by Austria in its states, including the charitable suppression [Col. 0276B] of the adjective *iniqui*, so justly assigned by the Church to Henry IV [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Certain newspapers reproach an illustrious prelate with an edition of the Roman Breviary in which there is a legend of Gregory VII; but the accuser does not add that it was not the archbishop who had this edition of the Roman Breviary produced, that he merely authorized the reprinting before it took place, that he neither directed nor supervised the execution of this undertaking, and that, having been informed that a phrase contrary to our principles had slipped into the legend of Gregory VII, he required that a cancel be made at that point; which was done.” *L’Ami de la Religion*, vol. LVI, p. 87, May 31, 1828]. For ten years, several editions of the Roman Breviary have been issued, both at Lyon and at Paris; the office of Saint Gregory VII is read there in its proper place and in its entirety, and the Paris edition of 1828 is gradually being exhausted, retaining to this day the trace of this last weakness, which we could not have concealed without partiality.

Let us hasten to pass over a few difficult years; the hour of rehabilitation has sounded. The God who is admirable in his saints has finally resolved to avenge his servant Gregory. It will no longer be the voice of Leibniz, Jean de Müller, Voigt, and others that resounds; nor even that of Joseph de Maistre, prophet of the past, announcing to Europe [Col. 0276C] that the time has come to worship what it had burned and to burn what it had worshiped. All barriers have fallen; now it is the Church of France that will proclaim Saint Gregory VII the savior of society, the restorer of knowledge, virtue, and justice. The organ of the Church of France in fulfilling this sacred duty will be that pious and learned bishop who was, in intellect as well as in blood, the son of the great Catholic philosopher to whom God granted the ability to probe the primitive legislation of societies and to understand in its full extent the sublime role of the pontiff legislator. Now, it was on March 4, 1838, that at Le Puy Monsignor Louis-Jacques-Maurice de Bonald, now cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0276D] Archbishop of Lyon and Primate of the Gauls, issued this magnificent and courageous pastoral letter on the visible head of the Church. It will remain in the annals of the Church of France as one of the most momentous events witnessed by our century, which has witnessed so many. On that memorable day, from the episcopal pulpit, one heard professed, with no less eloquence than doctrine, faith [Col. 0277A] in the infallibility of the Roman pontiff speaking to the Churches, and the high mission imposed by Providence upon Saint Gregory VII, a mission so worthily fulfilled by his great soul.

“The irruption of the barbarians,” said the prelate, “was only the image of a more dangerous invasion for the Church and the civilized world; it was only the figure of that triple coalition of ignorance, vice, and greed, leagued together to extinguish all light, wither every virtue, and stifle all justice. The Middle Ages saw this abyss widen its jaws in order to swallow society whole. And where would society go to take refuge in its distress? Once more to the feet of the chair of Saint Peter. There it would find its support and its salvation, [Col. 0277B] in a poor monk raised to the sovereign pontificate, but who concealed beneath the coarse garment of the cloister a soul whose elevation was not understood, and would be difficult to understand in our days of speculation and indifference. Hildebrand measured the depth of the wound in the social body. To anyone else, the obstacles to healing it would have appeared insurmountable; for Gregory VII, it was precisely in those obstacles that he drew new courage and rekindled the energy of his character. Armed with unshakable strength and an inflexible rectitude of will, while also yielding to the maxims of his contemporaries and the spirit of his age, he undertook a terrible struggle against his century and all the powers of his century. Knowledge had deserted the sanctuary; he would bring it back. Virtue seemed banished from every heart; he would restore its rights. Justice was trampled underfoot; he would make it triumph. He believed himself sent to oppose a brazen front to vice, whether he found it at the altar or upon the throne. Always inaccessible to fear, always above worldly considerations, Gregory would give no rest to his zeal until he had reformed the palace of the great, the sanctuary of justice, the cloister of the cenobites, and the house of God; until he had rekindled the torch of learning and the heavenly flames of piety; until he had caused this love of justice and hatred of iniquity to pass into the hearts of rulers and priests—virtues which, overflowing in his own soul, poured forth with holy profusion in his writings, his actions, his words, and throughout his entire pontificate. The calumnies, persecutions, and death mattered little to him, provided that he humbled every height and made every knee bend before the eternal laws of justice and truth. In his disputes with the princes of the earth, people wished to see only unjust encroachments; they lodged appeals as from abuse against the holy undertakings of this great pope. What could he do when peoples, crushed beneath the press of their masters’ senseless despotism, came kneeling to demand, as a last support and an extreme remedy for their sufferings, the severe exercise of his jurisdiction and the thunderbolts of his spiritual judgments? What astonishes and almost scandalizes us was, in the eyes of the Middle Ages, merely the exercise of a just right and the necessary fulfillment of a divine mission. Now, what is fighting to establish everywhere the reign of justice, knowledge, and virtue other than fighting to civilize the world? Such were the struggles of Gregory VII, and the source of an immortal glory for him.”

As one reads these calm, episcopal lines, in which the name of this Gregory—whom we have seen pursued with such ferocity in the preceding pages—is blessed with such love, does it not seem to the Catholic reader that he is resting sweetly in a peace that will never again be disturbed? After this mandate, one may say, the battle is won; there are no more Alps; Rome and France are unanimous in celebrating the glory and virtues of Gregory, father of Christendom. Everything is forgotten and renewed; Christ is glorified in his servant. But let us hope that soon Gregory’s praise will no longer resound only in speeches and pastoral instructions; that soon altars will be raised to his glory in this France that he loved and that misunderstood him for too long; that at last the day will come when we shall all sing in Gregory’s honor this beautiful eulogy that Rome and all the other Latin Churches intone in the solemnity [Col. 0278C] of those holy pontiffs who, through their fidelity, deserved to exchange the tiara for the crown of immortality: “While he was supreme pontiff, he feared no earthly thing; but gloriously passed to the heavenly kingdoms” [Dum esset summus pontifex terrena non metuit; sed ad coelestia regna gloriosus migravit].

If we now, according to our custom, proceed to draw the consequences of the facts recorded in the present chapter, they present themselves in such abundance that we would have to devote an entire chapter to gathering them together; but we shall limit ourselves to those that bear directly upon our subject.

The first, which we offer to those of our readers who may not yet understand the full importance of liturgical science, is that nevertheless, as they have been able to see, a single liturgical fact was sufficient to set most of Europe in motion and to occupy the majority of governments in the eighteenth century; so that, in order to recount in the most concise manner the history of a page of the Roman Breviary, we have had to add sixty pages to this already greatly abbreviated history of the liturgy.

In the second place, one may have noticed how carefully divine Providence used the liturgy as the only means remaining to the Holy See of saving the honor of one of its greatest pontiffs, at a time when every other means than the official drafting of his legend would have been powerless to prevent prescription from being acquired against his glory.

In the third place, it has been possible to see how [Col. 0279A] a clergy isolated from Rome, even in matters of secondary importance, always bears the penalty of that isolation through the contradictions into which it plunges, a victim of the false position in which it has placed itself.

Fourthly, it is an instructive spectacle to see secular magistrates quite naturally arrogate to themselves, [Col. 0280A] in matters of the liturgy, the power that they deny to Rome in this respect, while otherwise reasoning correctly about the authority that the insertion of a fact or maxim into the liturgical books of the Roman Church invariably confers upon it.

[Col. 0279]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

*(Philippus Jaffé, Regesta Pontificum Romanorum.)*

[Col. 0279B] In preparing the registers of Gregory VII, I had the good fortune to make use of a most desirable aid: an aid preserved in the oldest Vatican register codex, which is the source of all the extant manuscript codices and editions. For when the distinguished Wilhelm Giesebrecht, some years ago, had access to that excellent codex while enjoying the treasures of the Italian libraries and archives, he carefully transcribed its authentic readings, from which the editions very often depart incorrectly; afterward, in order to enrich my book, he kindly and generously shared them with me. He increased the generosity of his gift still further. When I asked him to investigate for my use the character of the codex and the quality of the script in which it was written, he did not hesitate, with his customary courtesy, to send me the useful and agreeable study printed below.

For my part, I followed the Vatican codex everywhere, as was proper; wherever the editions contained errors in their critical signs, I placed both readings within brackets. Nor did I think that I should omit, lest the reader be deprived of it, the variant reading from the Mutina codex reported by Mansi.

The bulls of Gregory do not provide the names of witnesses. The following sentence is read in them:

**“Your mercies, O Lord, are over all your works”** *(10, 29, 32, 40, 60, 62, 71, 74).*

The hand by which the bulls were written is identified no more than once:

**p. m. Benjamin, notary of the Sacred Palace** (3987).

They were dated by:

[Col. 0279D]

**p. m. Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church** (5, 6, 9, 10, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 29, 32, 36, 37, 40, 54, 61, 62);

**p. m. Peter, chancellor and cardinal** (39);

**p. m. Conon, cardinal priest** (35);

**p. m. John, cardinal deacon of the Roman Church** (38);

**p. m. Benjamin, acting in place of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the Holy Roman Church** (60);

**p. m. Gregory, deacon of the Holy Roman Church** (65).

[Col. 0280B] Giesebrecht’s study, which I mentioned above, was written in the following terms:

> “The Register of Gregory VII that has come down to our time is not identical with that true and genuine register which was once composed by public authority according to the custom then received in the Roman Curia. This is sufficiently shown both by the many letters which one would seek in vain as known from elsewhere, and by the fact that the things which Gregory himself explicitly reports as having been written in it are nowhere found there (Book VII, Letter 16). We are therefore convinced that what is called the Register is nothing other than a collection of letters compiled and published by some unknown writer, in order to serve, to the best of his ability, those curious about historical events and to commend Gregory’s great name to posterity.

> [Col. 0280C] That this collection was composed shortly after the pope’s death and soon became known both in Italy and in Germany is attested by the Roman cardinal Deusdedit in his *Collection of Canons* (Steph. Borgia, *On Temporal Dominion*, Appendix, p. 13 and following) and by Bernold of Constance in his *Chronicle* under the year 1085.

> “The editors unanimously affirm that the work was arranged in eleven books, the tenth of which perished through the injury of time; nor do they appear to doubt that the letters have been placed in their proper locations, with the correct chronological order preserved. Yet, if one examines the work somewhat more carefully, one will easily observe that from the beginning of Book VII almost all the letters lack an indiction, and many even lack the day on which they were issued, whereas in the first seven books the indiction and the day are almost always carefully specified.

> [Col. 0280D] This fact must certainly cause us some hesitation; and when critical method is applied, we shall discover that the letters were by no means written in the order in which they are now read. Rather, they were written at different times, and those now occupying a lower position often belong to much earlier dates than those placed before them. Thus the compiler of the Register neglected, in the final part of the work, the chronological order which he had carefully maintained throughout the preceding seven books. He undoubtedly did so for a serious reason, although we can only conjecture what that reason may have been.

> In my opinion, [Col. 0281A] up to the end of Book VII he used the true and genuine Register of Gregory VII, extracting from it whatever seemed worthy of notice: the pope’s own letters, acts of councils, letters addressed to the pope, notes concerning the ordination of bishops, and so forth. He took care to copy all these into his own book in the same order in which they stood in the Register. Thereafter, however, from the beginning of Book VIII, deprived of this strong aid—whether because the pope’s Register was not composed at all during those most critical years (1080–1085), or because it had been left at Salerno after Gregory’s death—he assembled the letters without order, wherever chance and circumstance happened to offer them to him from different places.

> It therefore appears that, whereas in the earlier part each year of the pontificate corresponded to a separate book, and letters issued in the same year were brought together in the same book, this order was entirely neglected in the latter part.

> “It is also highly doubtful whether the division of the books now presented by the editions possesses the authority of antiquity. Suspicion is already aroused by the fact that Cardinal Deusdedit cites from Book VII—which in our copies contains only twenty-eight letters—Letters 70 and 75, and from Book VIII, although the editions proceed no farther than Letter 23, he cites Letters 29 and 30.

> [Col. 0281B] As regards Book VII, either there is some error in the numbers, or Deusdedit used a copy richer than ours; for the letters he cites are Letters 19 and 24 of that book in our copies. Book VIII must be judged differently. The letters that he cites from it are now found in Book IX, where they are numbered 6 and 7. Hence it seems probable and plausible that in his copy Books VIII and IX were joined together.

> “But if we wish to establish anything certain on this matter, we must turn to the manuscript codices of the Register. They are found quite often in Italian libraries. While travelling through Italy, I examined two in the Vatican Archive at Rome, five in the Vatican Library (Codd. 3797, 4579, 4907, 5638), and one in the Vallicellian Library (Cod. C. 17). At Venice I inspected one in the Library of Saint Mark. John Dominic Mansi praises the Mutina codex and made use of it.

> [Col. 0281C] All these books, however, are of a later age: they were produced no earlier than the sixteenth or seventeenth century, except for the one older codex preserved in the Vatican Archive. It can easily be demonstrated that this codex must be regarded as the source and origin of all the others.

> From it, too, Antonius Caraffa first caused the Register to be printed. All those who afterward undertook a new edition did nothing other than repeat Caraffa’s reading, often very corrupt, literally and without judgment—unless a milder judgment should perhaps be made concerning Hardouin, who corrected some passages reasonably well by conjecture, and concerning Dominic Mansi, who, as I have already stated, used the Mutina codex.

> [Col. 0281D] After Caraffa, no one failed to neglect the most ancient Vatican book, which ought to have been consulted with the greatest care, since no other was more trustworthy. Consequently, all editions of the Register down to the present day have been filled with numerous and serious faults. In these circumstances, every person most skilled in critical method will readily admit that all questions concerning the character and condition of the Register turn entirely upon this very codex and cannot be settled unless it has been carefully examined.

> “It is a small parchment quarto, written in Latin letters of the kind in use toward the end of the eleventh century, and contains 258 folios. In the first quire, after a preface written by a fourteenth-century hand, I found a certain privilege of a monastery near Bantia and documents dated 10 October 1369 concerning John Palaeologus, who had returned to the Roman Church.

> The Register then begins with these words: [Col. 0282B] *In the name of God. Here begins the first book of the Seventh Register of Pope Gregory. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1073, indiction XI, in the reign of our Lord, etc.*

> It was written by different hands, though hands contemporary with one another and so similar that distinguishing them precisely is no small task. Moreover, the same hand that one has already detected in the earlier part of the work often reappears again and again later. The letters now placed first in Book XI were written by a different hand from the preceding letters; and those that follow and bring the Register to an end were again written by a hand entirely different from that one.

> You will find many deletions, alterations, and corrections, so that one could easily be led to the view that the codex belonged to the person who compiled the collection. I would not press that point strongly, however, while again observing that Cardinal Deusdedit may have used a fuller copy.

> As for the division into books, each book has its own title written in red, by the same hands that wrote the letters themselves, through Book VI. It may also be worth noting that the Venetian codex recognizes titles only for these first six books.

> [Col. 0282C] Books VII and VIII in the Vatican codex bear the same titles as in the editions, and those titles are marked in red; but, leaving gaps, a somewhat more recent hand—if I am not mistaken, from the end of the twelfth century—wrote them in.

> Finally, a certain scribe who added his hand long after the book had been completed inserted the following words in ink after Letter 23 of Book VIII, where there was certainly no indication or sign of a new book:

> *From Book VIII of the Register of the same Pope Gregory VII.*

> After the letter to the Flemings (Mansi, *Collection of Councils* XX, p. 370), the same person added a new heading:

> *Here begins Book X*;

> but then corrected it to:

> *XI.*

> When the scribes were compiling the Register, they added neither headings nor numbers to the individual letters. The person who supplied the titles of Books VII and VIII also added headings to the letters through the end of the Register, together with Roman numerals in red through Letter 47 of Book II.

> [Col. 0282D] The scribe who devised the new titles of Books VIII and XI continued the Roman numerals in ink through Letter 9 of Book III. The letters that follow were marked with Arabic numerals only in the fourteenth century, undoubtedly by the same writer who composed the index of the Register.

> For after the Gregorian letters had been carried through to folio 237, an index was added on the remaining fourteenth-century folios. It begins as follows:

> [Col. 0283A] “Here begins the Register of the letters and councils of the lord Gregory VII, most holy and most glorious Roman pontiff, who was elected after the death of the lord Alexander II in the Church of Saint Saviour, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1073.

> “In this book his memory is preserved for only eleven years, according to which this volume has been divided into eleven books, the deeds of each of those years being contained in one book.

> “The first book contains 84 letters. The second contains 76 letters. [Col. 0283B] The third contains 21 letters. The fourth contains 28 letters. The fifth contains 23 letters. The sixth contains 40 letters. The seventh contains 27 letters. The eighth contains 23 letters. The ninth contains 35 letters. The tenth book does not exist, or there is an error in the book and in the division of the books. [Col. 0284A] The eleventh contains two letters.

> “In each book there is a register of the council whose celebration is recorded as having taken place in each of those years. There are also many oaths of princes, certain decrees, and other such matters, which are displayed in the table itself.

> “From what I have so far discussed concerning the Vatican codex, it is manifest, unless I am mistaken, that Gregory’s letters were anciently divided into eight books, not eleven. The first seven books of the true Register corresponded in order to the individual years of the pontificate, while the writer relegated the remaining letters to an eighth book without regard to the years.

> [Col. 0284B] Thus the tenth book is not so much something that perished through the injury of time as something that never truly existed. The original and genuine arrangement of the Register was later altered in the Vatican codex itself by a certain scribe who, having little understanding of the structure of the work, wished all its books to correspond to individual years of the pontificate; for that reason he divided the eighth book into several parts. Most codices and all editions subsequently received this new division of the books from the Vatican codex.”

[Col. 0283]

# FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF SAINT GREGORY VII, ROMAN PONTIFF — REGISTER

[Note: [Col. 0283C] Gregory VII’s Register is preserved in the Vatican Library. Berthold of Constance, who lived at that time, speaks of it in the year 1085, in reference to Gregory VII, as follows: “For he was the most fervent promoter of the Catholic religion and the most energetic defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He certainly did not wish the ecclesiastical order to be subject to the hands of laymen, but wished it to surpass them both in holiness of life and in the dignity of its order. No one who reads his Apostolic Register carefully can fail to understand this.”]

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XX, col. 60.)*

## [NOTE]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1073, indiction XI.

During the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year of his most merciful incarnation 1073, indiction XI and lunar year XI, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, a Monday, the day of the burial of the lord Alexander II, pope of blessed memory, lest the Apostolic See should long mourn, deprived of its own shepherd, we, the cardinals, clerics, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests of the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, assembled in the Basilica of Saint Peter in Chains, with the venerable bishops and abbots present, the clergy and monks consenting, and a great multitude of both sexes and of various orders acclaiming, elect for ourselves as shepherd and supreme pontiff a religious man, endowed with the prudence of twofold knowledge, an outstanding lover of equity and justice, steadfast in adversity, moderate in prosperity, and, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching, adorned with good morals: chaste, modest, sober, pure, hospitable, and ruling his own household well.

[Note: [Col. 0284D] The variants given here were drawn by Father Franciscus Antonius Zacharia, S.J., from the Mutina manuscript codex, which is itself from the sixteenth century but was copied from an older and reliable source, and transmitted to me by him.]

He was nobly brought up and educated from childhood in the bosom of this mother Church and, on account of the merit of his life, had until now been elevated to the dignity of archdeacon—namely, Hildebrand the archdeacon. We wish and approve that from this time forth [*a modo*; variant: *e modo*], unto eternity, he both be and be called Gregory, pope and apostolic pontiff [*approbatis eum?* “Do you approve him?”; *approbamus* “We approve him”].

“Is this your pleasure?” “It is.”

“Do you desire him?” “We desire him.”

“Do you praise him?” “We praise him.”

Done at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

# BOOK ONE OF THE REGISTER

[Col. 0285]

## LETTER ONE — TO ABBOT DESIDERIUS  
*(Year 1073.)*

He announces that he has been unwillingly appointed in the place of the deceased Pope Alexander. He asks him to pray to God for him and to come to him as quickly as possible.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in Christ Jesus to Desiderius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino.

Our lord Pope Alexander has died, and his death has fallen upon me, shaking all my innermost being and utterly disturbing me. At his death, however, the Roman people, contrary to custom, remained so calm and left the reins of deliberation in our hands that it clearly appeared to have happened through God’s mercy.

[Col. 0285B] Therefore, after taking counsel, we decided that, following a three-day fast, the litanies, and the prayers of many people accompanied by almsgiving, we should, supported by divine assistance, determine what seemed best concerning the election of the Roman pontiff.

But suddenly, while the aforesaid lord our pope was being committed to burial in the church of the Savior [Addition: Saint, so everywhere], a great tumult and uproar arose among the people, and they rose against me like madmen, so that with the Prophet I can say:

“I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me. I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Psalm 68);

and:

“Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me” (Psalm 54).

But since I am lying in bed, greatly exhausted, and cannot dictate adequately, I shall refrain from recounting my troubles.

[Col. 0285C] I therefore ask you, by the almighty Lord, to urge the suffragan brothers and sons whom you nurture in Christ to implore God for me, and to invite them, out of true charity, so that the prayer which should have delivered me from falling into danger may at least protect me now that I am placed in danger.

You yourself, moreover, must not fail to come to us as quickly as possible. You know how much the Roman Church needs you and how much confidence it places in your prudence.

Greet the empress Lady Agnes and the venerable Rainaldus, bishop of Como, on our behalf, and faithfully beseech them in our place now to show how much affection they have held for us.
