Issued at Rome, on the eleventh [ninth] day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER TWO — TO GISULF, PRINCE OF SALERNO  
*(Year 1073.)*

The same subject.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in Christ Jesus to Gisulf, prince of Salerno.

Our lord Pope Alexander has died, and his death has fallen upon me. *(Everything as above up to the passage that says:)*

I therefore ask you, by the almighty Lord, to invite the venerable Father Leo and the other religious men living in those regions to implore God for me out of true charity, so that the prayer which should have delivered me from falling into danger may at least protect me now that I am placed in danger.

You yourself, moreover, must not fail to come to us as quickly as possible. You know how much the Roman Church needs you and how much confidence it places in your prudence.

Issued at Rome, on the eleventh [eighth] day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER THREE — TO GUIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA  
*(Year 1073.)*

The same subject; he also asks him to send envoys.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in Christ Jesus to Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna.

We do not doubt that the news has outrun our letter and has informed you, as well as many others, of the death of our lord Pope Alexander. But this is something for which I must greatly grieve: his death has fallen upon me, shaking all my innermost being and utterly disturbing me.

At his death, the Roman people at first, contrary to custom, remained so calm and left the reins of deliberation in our hands that it clearly appeared to have happened through God’s mercy. Therefore, after taking counsel, we decided that, following a three-day fast, the litanies, and the prayers of many people accompanied by almsgiving, we should, supported by divine assistance, determine what seemed best concerning the election of the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0286C] But suddenly, while the aforesaid lord our pope was being committed to burial in the church of Saint Saviour, a great tumult and uproar arose among the people, and they rose against me like madmen, leaving me neither the ability nor the time to speak or deliberate. With violent hands they dragged me into the place of apostolic government, for which I am wholly unequal.

Thus I can rightly say with the Prophet:

“I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me; I have labored crying out; my throat has become hoarse” (Psalm 68).

Finally:

“Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me” (Psalm 54).

But since I am exhausted by many and great cares and cannot dictate adequately, I shall refrain from enumerating my miseries.

[Col. 0286D] I therefore ask you, by the almighty God, to show the charity which you promised to exercise toward the Roman Church, especially at this time, and—as you ought to remember—toward me in particular. The time and the circumstances demand that it be tested now in my case; and, if not on account of my merits, then at least for the love of the apostles, take care to demonstrate it.

Invite and admonish the suffragan bishops and the sons of your Church to implore God for me, so that he may grant me strength to bear the burden imposed upon me against my will and despite my great resistance, and may extend his hand to me. If he does not wish me to remain entirely [perhaps “safely”; Hardouin; likewise the Mutina codex] in harbor, may he at least not abandon me, cast into such deep dangers.

For just as I love you with that sincere charity, so I unquestionably demand from you the same charity and all its duties.

Nor should your affection doubt that we desire to unite the Roman Church and the Church over which, by God’s authority, you preside in such concord, and with all the charity that we can maintain consistently with the common honor of both, that enduring peace and complete affection may always bind us together in our hearts as well.

Therefore, just as we have urged your prudence, know also through our letters that we wish and desire to be able frequently to rejoice together through envoys traveling between us and to enjoy mutual consolation.

Issued at Rome, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER FOUR — TO BEATRICE, DUCHESS, HUGH, ETC.  
*(Year 1073.)*

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings to Beatrice, duchess [duke], Hugh, abbot of Cluny, Manasses, archbishop of Reims, [Addition: Sweyn,] king of the Danes, and the abbot of Marseille.

The letters begin alike, but toward the end they differ individually according to the suitability of the places and persons.

Issued at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER FIVE — TO RAINERIUS, BISHOP OF FLORENCE  
*(Year 1073.)*

He orders that a widow who had married her kinsman be deprived of the gifts and dowry left to her by him.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in Christ Jesus to Rainerius, bishop of Florence.

The bearer of the present letter has made known to our ears that his brother, contrary to divine law and the institution of the holy Fathers, entered the marriage-bed of his kinswoman, although the canons of the Florentine Church had canonically prohibited him from committing this crime.

After he had entered upon the way of all flesh, his kinswoman, that is, the woman he left behind, intends to pass to the bed of another man, together with the gift and dowry which she did not hesitate to accept in violation of both divine and human laws. She ought rather to mourn forever the crime she committed.

[Col. 0287D] Your Fraternity must carefully investigate the line of kinship from the elder members of that place. If you discover such a relationship between the deceased man and the woman who remains alive, then, following the example of other cases, you must use canonical authority to cancel and nullify all the dowry documents, so that she may receive no compensation from the unlawful marriage she contracted by which she could rejoice in the future.

As you love us, let your charity take care to bring the first fruits of our command to completion.

Issued at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER SIX — TO GIRALDUS, BISHOP OF OSTIA, AND RAIMBALDUS, SUBDEACON  
*(Year 1073.)*

He sends a legate to tell them of Alexander’s death and his own election. He advises them to bring the monks and the abbot of Cluny to peace. If the count of Roceio [Rocyo], as he himself had ordered, has not departed for Spain against the pagans, or if other princes wish to depart there against the same enemy, his legate is to proceed there. Finally, he advises them to return as soon as possible.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ to Giraldus, bishop of Ostia, and Raimbaldus, subdeacon, serving as legates in Gaul.

We believe that the report of the death of our lord Pope Alexander, who gave up his spirit to God on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, and the report of our promotion have already reached you. But because we wish you to know everything fully, we have judged it appropriate to send to those regions, in our name, this beloved son, a cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church who was present at both events, so that you may learn through him the exact truth concerning what happened and how it happened.

[Col. 0288C] We earnestly ask your charity to ensure that prayers are diligently offered to God, so that he may transfer Alexander’s soul to the joys of eternal blessedness and extend to us the aid of his mercy for bearing the burden imposed upon us.

Since time and circumstances seemed to require that our confrater, namely Hugh Candidus, be sent to those regions, we wish your prudence to be entirely entreated to strive so to incline and unite Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and the entire congregation of the brothers toward peace and complete affection for this man that, with God’s help, you leave nothing in their minds covered by aversion or the cloud of dissension.

For he too, having abandoned every claim to his own judgment and returning to our heart and our counsels, is now joined to us in the same understanding, will, and zeal. We have also learned that the matters previously imposed upon him while our lord the pope was still alive arose more from the fault of others than from his.

[Col. 0288D] Moreover, you must remember that in letters from our lord Alexander, of blessed memory, and also during our own legation, you were asked and admonished to work, through yourselves and through the aforesaid abbot, to add your support to the case of Count Evulus [Eboli; Mutina: Evoli] of Roceio.

After learning the agreement he made with us concerning the land of Spain, in the written document that we gave him, you were to arrange, together with the abbot’s advice, for suitable persons to be sent there—persons capable of correcting in spiritual matters the error of the Christians who are found there and, if affairs went well, sufficiently fit to pursue the claims of Saint Peter according to the terms of the agreement.

If this has been done, it greatly pleases us. But if it has been postponed for some reason, or if the same agreement has not yet been sought from certain other princes whom we understand intend to go with their forces to the same region independently of Evulus, then we wish Cardinal Hugh to proceed there with your counsel and that of the abbot, and to demand from all of them, on behalf of Saint Peter, a fair agreement and the due payment.

On our behalf, ask the abbot to associate with himself men who will accompany him, so that, with their counsel and assistance, he may confidently undertake that journey and labor, while keeping the legation as his principal concern.

Outside Spain, however, we have never given him permission to undertake any public ecclesiastical business without your consent, for as long as you remain in Gaul.

[Col. 0289A] As for the delay in your return, we are greatly surprised, especially since you have already been urged to return and, while we await your return so anxiously, you have not even indicated the reasons for your delay.

We therefore admonish your affection to return to us as quickly as you can, so that we may learn what you have done and, with God’s help, determine more wisely what should be done hereafter.

In addition to this, we wish the abbot, already so often mentioned, to be specially admonished and earnestly entreated by you in our place, so that now, when there is the greatest need, he may offer through tireless service the charity he has hitherto shown toward us, and may strive to assist our weakness through his prayers and those of his most holy congregation—assisting us all the more strongly because he knows that our weakness is being pressed more heavily beneath the accumulated burden.

Issued at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER SEVEN — TO THE PRINCES OF SPAIN  
*(Year 1073.)*

He states that he granted the count of Roceio, under a certain condition, that part of Spain which he might recover from the hands of the Saracens. He forbids other princes to enter the same region with their forces or to claim any part of that province for themselves unless a fair agreement concerning the payment of Saint Peter’s rights is made. He sends legates concerning this matter.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends perpetual greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ to all princes wishing to depart for the land of Spain.

We believe that you are not unaware that the kingdom of Spain has from ancient times belonged by its own right to Saint Peter, and that, although it has long been occupied by pagans, it nevertheless has not been deprived of its legal status under justice, but belongs equally to no mortal and solely to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0289D] For whatever, by God’s authority, has once justly come into the ownership of the churches cannot, so long as it remains theirs, be separated from their right by the passage of time merely because it has been removed from practical use, unless there is a lawful grant.

Therefore Count Evulus [Evolus] of Roceio, whose reputation among you we believe is by no means obscure, wishing to enter that land in honor of Saint Peter and wrest it from the hands of the pagans, obtained from the Apostolic See this grant: he might possess, under the condition of an agreement made between us on behalf of Saint Peter, that part from which he could expel the pagans by his own efforts and with the assistance of others who joined him.

In this undertaking, whoever among you wishes to attach himself to him is exhorted with every charitable affection to bear such a disposition toward the honor of Saint Peter that he may confidently receive from Evulus both aid in fortifying positions during dangers and the rewards of faithful service.

[Col. 0290A] If, however, some of you prepare to enter the same land independently of him and with forces of your own, in any part of it, you ought to make the cause of your military expedition as just as possible in your hearts, already forming this intention in every vow and firmly resolving in your hearts that, once the land has been captured, you will not inflict upon Saint Peter the same wrongs as those who now occupy it in ignorance of God.

For we wish none of you to be unaware that, unless you determine to acknowledge in that kingdom the fair agreement for payment of Saint Peter’s right, we shall instead oppose you by apostolic authority, forbidding you to proceed there, rather than allow the holy and universal mother Church—suffering the same thing from her sons as from her enemies—to be wounded not only in her property but by the loss of her sons.

[Col. 0290B] For this reason we have sent to those regions this beloved son, Hugh, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church. In his mouth we have placed our counsels and decrees, to be explained to you more fully and openly, and arrangements to be made in our name.

Issued at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER EIGHT — TO UBERTUS, CLERIC, AND ALBERTUS, DEACON  
*(Year 1073.)*

He confirms their legation and urges them to ensure that prayers are offered for him.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ to Ubertus, cleric, and Albertus, deacon.

We believe that, as rumor has announced, you have already received news of the death of Pope Alexander and of how suddenly, and with what violence from the people, we—unworthy and resisting—were carried [perhaps “elevated”; Hardouin and the Mutina codex: “removed”] to the government of the Apostolic See.

But lest the outcome of these events disturb your minds with fear or any uncertainty in the execution of the legation entrusted to you, we have written these brief words to strengthen your charity. Place all your confidence in God and in Saint Peter, whose sons and legates you are; then, supported by apostolic authority, carry out courageously and without hesitation the task for which you were sent, and gird yourselves with faithful constancy to administer justice.

[Col. 0290D] For the matters assigned and entrusted to you by our lord Pope Alexander, of blessed memory, we likewise assign and firmly entrust to you by our present authority. In carrying them out, just as we give you admonitions, so, with God’s help, we shall diligently ensure that the support of apostolic consolation and authority is supplied to you.

For the rest, we admonish you to ask that prayers for me be offered in the venerable places to which you come, so that almighty God—who knows that I never aspired to this honor—may mercifully devote all his resources to my weakness for bearing so heavy a burden, which, out of fear of him, I did not dare refuse when it was imposed.

[Col. 0291A] Issued at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of May, indiction XI.

## LETTER NINE — TO GOTTIFRED, DUKE  
*(Year 1073.)*

He writes that he was pleased that the duke had congratulated him in a letter on his promotion; nevertheless, he indicates that he grieves over the pontifical office he has undertaken, shows his affection toward the duke and the king, and wishes the king to heed his admonitions.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, sends greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ to Gottifred [Gotefred], duke.

We rejoice in your joy, which we have learned from your letter that you feel over our promotion—not because any pleasure in our own cause produces this, but because we do not doubt that it has flowed from the source of sincere affection and a faithful mind. [Col. 0291B] For our promotion, which supplies you and the other faithful with a pious esteem and joy concerning us, generates in us the bitterness of inward sorrow and the anguish of extreme anxiety. We see how great a care surrounds us; we feel how heavily the burden of the office we have undertaken weighs upon us. While the consciousness of our weakness trembles beneath these burdens, our soul in Christ desires rather the repose of release than life amid such dangers.

Indeed, the consideration of the office entrusted to us so troubles us that, unless some confidence in the prayers of spiritual people sustained us after God, our mind would collapse beneath the immensity of its cares. For, because of sins, [Col. 0291C] almost the whole world is placed in the power of the evil one, so that all people—and especially those who have been set over the Church—strive rather to disturb it than to defend or honor it with faithful devotion; and, while they pant after their own profits or the desires of present glory, they oppose themselves like enemies to everything that pertains to the religion and justice of God. This is all the more grievous to us, since we can neither properly administer the government of the universal Church amid such difficulty nor safely abandon it.

Nevertheless, because we know that the virtues of faith and steadfastness have been placed in you by God’s gift, and because we place in you all the confidence that is fitting in a most dear son of Saint Peter, we do not wish you in any way to doubt either our most steadfast affection for you or our most willing disposition toward your honors. [Col. 0291D]

Concerning the king, you can fully know our mind and desire: insofar as we understand in the Lord, we believe that no one can be preferred to us as being more concerned for his present and future glory, or desiring it more abundantly. For it is our will, as soon as a suitable opportunity is offered, to approach him through our messengers concerning those matters which we judge to pertain to the advancement of the Church and the honor of his royal dignity, with paternal affection and admonition. If he listens to us, we shall rejoice no less in his salvation than in our own; and he will most certainly be able to gain that salvation for himself if he follows our admonitions and counsels in maintaining justice. But if—as we do not wish—he returns hatred to us for affection and, by disregarding God's justice, returns not an equal recompense but contempt to almighty God for the great honor bestowed upon him, then, by God’s providence, the threat expressed in the words, “Cursed is the man who restrains his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48), will not come upon us. For it is not permitted to us to put God’s law behind anyone’s personal favor, or to depart from the path of righteousness for human approval, as the Apostle says: “If I were still seeking to please human beings, I would not be a servant of God” (Galatians 1).

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER X. TO GUIDO, COUNT OF IMOLA (1073)

That he should settle the disagreement between the archbishop of Ravenna and the citizens of Imola. And if the archbishop attempts to withdraw them from the authority of the Apostolic See, that he should provide them assistance until the legates depart for that place.

[Col. 0292B]

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, to Guido, count of Imola: greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Certain men of Imola came into our presence and complained to us that our confrater Guibertus [Gibertus, and so throughout], archbishop of Ravenna, was attempting, contrary to the honor of Saint Peter, to whom they had sworn fidelity, to subject them entirely to his own authority and compel them to swear oaths of fidelity to him. This report brought us all the greater astonishment, [Col. 0292C] since the fraternal charity and priestly integrity long observed in him exclude, beyond doubt, grounds for suspicion against him. For we cannot believe that so prudent a man has so forgotten either his nature or the dignity of his position that, having himself promised fidelity by oath to the prince of the apostles, he would, disregarding his own danger, strive through carefully devised oaths to drag others who have done the same into perjury.

Nevertheless, whatever disagreement or cause of trouble may exist between them, we earnestly ask your prudence to strive to settle it and, if you can, to resolve it in firm peace without injury to the honor of Saint Peter. But if, because of certain evil impediments, you cannot accomplish this, and our aforesaid confrater the archbishop, or any other person, persists in forcibly tearing the aforesaid citizens [Col. 0292D] away from fidelity to the Apostolic See by obstinate coercion [perhaps coercition; II], then, just as you desire the support of the apostles to benefit you before almighty God and wish to govern in this life not without an increase of merit, so, at our request and admonition issued by the present authority, do not cease to provide them with the assistance of your protection until our legates come to those parts.

For our part, we ardently desire to have peace with everyone, if this can be done; but we do not refuse, aided by divine power and justice, to oppose the efforts of those who try to extend themselves to the injury of Saint Peter, whose servants we are.

Given at Rome, on the Kalends of June, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XI. TO BEATRICE AND HER DAUGHTER MATHILDA (1073)

[Col. 0293A]

He exhorts them to avoid the Simonians. He recalls certain matters concerning the elected bishop of Lucca. He indicates that he is sending religious men to the king to recall him to the Roman Church.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, to Beatrice and her daughter Mathilda: greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ.

As blessed Gregory says in one of his books explaining the *Morals on Job*: “It has been established before the heavenly Judge how much adversity should strike each person, or prosperity should soothe each person.” Whoever, therefore, whether through hope of the former or fear of the latter, deviates from what is right in a time of temptation shows that he neither hopes in God nor clings to the words of the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0293B]

We say this because neither you nor we—in fact, all who desire to be companions in the adoption as sons of God—should look so much to the circumstances affecting our reputation, namely what may benefit us here or harm us there, as we must carefully consider and strive to hold firmly to the justice of God, which will never lack the end of blessedness. For it is written: “And even if you suffer for the sake of justice, you are blessed” (2 Peter 3).

You know, most beloved daughters of Saint Peter, how openly the bishops of Lombardy have dared to defend and support the Simoniacal heresy: they cursed Gotefredus [Gotifredus], a Simonian who had therefore been excommunicated and condemned, under the appearance of a blessing, [Col. 0293C] and under the shadow of ordination they installed an accursed heretic. Those who until now have secretly hurled stones and arrows against the Lord have now leapt openly into the field of their fury to overturn religion and shake the immovable rock of the holy Roman Church—plainly forerunners of Antichrist and satellites of the ancient enemy.

Let your prudence judge from this how dangerous it is to favor or consent to them. Blessed Gregory says: “What else is it than to deny the faith not to oppose such people with the utmost vigor?” Therefore we exhort and earnestly ask your nobility to strive to avoid and withdraw from their communion, so that you may not offer their factions either counsel or assistance. Nor should any worldly consideration—which is indeed vain, transient, and deceptive—move you in this matter; for, through the mercy of God and of Saint Peter, no stratagem of your enemies will be able to harm you if a clear conscience defends your minds. [Col. 0293D]

Concerning the elected bishop of Lucca, we have discerned [provided] that we have nothing else to say to you except that we have perceived in him such knowledge of the divine writings and such power of discernment that he himself is not ignorant of what is left and what is right. If he inclines to the right, we rejoice greatly; but if, God forbid, to the left, we certainly grieve. Yet we will give no assent to impiety for the sake of any person’s favor or support.

Concerning the king, as you have learned earlier from our letters, [Col. 0294A] this is our will: that we send religious men to him whose admonitions, with God’s inspiration, may recall him to love of the holy Roman Church and of his own mother Church, and instruct and refine him into a worthy form for undertaking the empire. But if—as we do not wish—he refuses to listen to us, nevertheless, with God guarding us, we neither can nor ought to depart from our mother, the Roman Church, which nourished us and has often generated other sons through the blood of her own children. Certainly it is safer for us, in defending the truth for his own salvation, to resist him even to our blood than, by consenting to iniquity in order to fulfill his will, to rush with him—God forbid—toward destruction.

Farewell in Christ, most beloved women, and know that you are joined to us in the depths of our loving heart. [Col. 0294B]

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [July], in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO GUILIELMUS, BISHOP OF PAVIA (1073)

He shows that he has been moved by the bishop’s letter and now thinks well of him; but, in order to retain this opinion of him, he asks him to embrace the statutes of the Roman Church and fight with all his strength against its adversaries.

Gregory, elected Roman pontiff, to Guilielmus, bishop of Pavia: greetings in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Certain things were previously reported to us by a brother about you, [Col. 0294C] from which our mind could not unjustly have been disturbed. But, learning from your letter matters of an entirely different kind, we have been led to a better opinion and hope of joy. We desire both that those reports may have been false and that we may perceive, through the testimony of your deeds, the truth of what your affection promises. You now have an abundant opportunity for this: so that, with doubt removed, we may believe what you urge us to believe about you, and prove that your fraternity is bound to us—or rather to the holy Roman Church—with unimpaired charity.

Let this therefore be an indication to us of how unanimously you are prepared to share our will and to resist with all your strength, for the freedom of the holy Church, those whom we oppose: namely, show that you too will resist with all your power those who strive to overthrow the Catholic faith and the rules of ecclesiastical religion, not merely refusing to consent to them, but supporting with your counsels and assistance that side which, out of reverence for this holy See and due devotion to the faith received, has resolved to oppose them. [Col. 0294D]

Know this beyond doubt: if the Catholic men of Milan give us testimony concerning you that you prudently oppose the excommunicated Gotefredus and the bishops who have incurred the danger of excommunication on his account, and that you faithfully offer consolation to those who are engaged in Christ’s struggle, neither gold nor silver, nor any efforts or services of your fraternity, will be able equally to commend you and your causes to the affection of us and of the whole Roman Church, or bind them to us with an indissoluble care. [Col. 0295A]

For in this way above all you will be able to show yourself a most dear son and faithful co-worker of the holy Roman Church: if, by embracing, firmly holding, and defending her statutes—which do not depart from the path of the holy Fathers—you preserve them. You ought to do this before the other bishops of Lombardy, so that, just as the apostolic and universal Church has exalted the Church which, by God’s will, you are recognized as presiding over with special favor and honor, so, when necessity and the labor of causes demand it, you may sweat more earnestly in the concern of a mother whose lot includes the richer duty of her charity and vicariate administration.

Given at Rome, on the third [fourth] day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XIII. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS (1073)

[Col. 0295B]

That he should no longer harass the monks of Saint Remigius and should arrange for an abbot to be appointed there according to the canonical decrees.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Manasses, archbishop of Rheims: greetings and apostolic blessing.

If you carefully considered the dignity of your position, most beloved brother; the duty of your office; the statutes of the divine laws; and, finally, the reverence and affection that you owe to the holy Roman Church, surely you would not so often allow the requests and admonitions of the Apostolic See to be frustrated in your case—especially since it is a serious fault for you to have provoked or awaited the voice of an admonisher in such a matter. [Col. 0295C]

For whatever responsibilities arise for us from the administration entrusted to us, we cannot neglect without danger to ourselves, much less can we suppose that it is safe for us to confuse them by our will and effort. Your prudence ought to remember how often our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander of venerable memory, and we ourselves, both through letters and through legates, admonished you by requests and exhortations concerning the monastery of Saint Remigius: we urged you not to allow the Apostolic See to be wearied so often by the cries of the brothers under the pressure of necessity; not to appoint to the place of abbot anyone whom the sacred canons opposed; and not, by removing the monastery’s goods from the use of the community, to destroy the place through poverty. Rather, you were to arrange for someone to be regularly appointed to govern the abbey who would lack neither diligence in providing for external matters nor religion or knowledge in spiritual governance. [Col. 0295D]

Although you often promised through your legates that you would do this, you have still not taken care to fulfill it. Instead, as we have learned from the reports of many, day by day you treat that venerable place more harshly and more miserably; and, to say nothing of the losses of temporal goods, you also constrain the religious persons of the brothers through cruel and insulting imprisonment.

Your own skill can therefore judge how serious a fault in you and how great an annoyance to us gnaws at us concerning this matter: the authority of the Apostolic See has not yet been able to benefit, toward peace and tranquility, the place and the brothers whom you ought long ago to have assisted with paternal affection. [Col. 0296A]

Nevertheless, most beloved brother, we have decided to try once more to bend your mind by a gentle appeal. We ask you, and admonish you by apostolic authority on behalf of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and ourselves, that, if you wish henceforth to place hope in our fraternity and affection, you arrange without any delay for a person to be regularly appointed there as abbot who is suitably fitted to that order and office; and that you correct and amend the other matters required by the monastery’s need and justice in such a way that the brothers’ complaint will no longer need to be brought to us.

But if once again you despise, in this matter, the reverence owed to Saint Peter and whatever affection and friendship we have for you, you will undoubtedly—which we say unwillingly—provoke against yourself the severity and anger of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0296B] Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XIV. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY (1073)

That he should accept his letters to the archbishop of Rheims and protect the monks of Saint Remigius.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Let your holiness know that these brothers are monks of the monastery of Saint Remigius. They have remained for a long time at the Apostolic See seeking consolation for their place, which Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, daily dissipates and disorders. [Col. 0296C] At present we could provide them with no more suitable consolation than to send to that same archbishop letters delivered to you together with these men. In them we earnestly ask and admonish him, if he wishes to hope for peace with blessed Peter and the Roman Church, to regulate the aforesaid monastery according to the rule and leave it in peace.

Our concern desires that your charity send these letters to him through a suitable messenger and, at the first opportunity, write back to us whatever he does on their behalf. Meanwhile, we commend these brothers, who have fled from witnessing the desolation of their place, to your kindness, so that you may not be unwilling to care for them until, through God’s mercy, they are able to enjoy the desired peace in their monastery. [Col. 0296D]

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF CHRIST IN LOMBARDY (1073)

He announces that he has excommunicated Gotefredus because he seized the Church of Milan through Simony. He warns them not to consent to him and to defend the faith.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, dwelling among the Lombards: greetings and apostolic blessing.

I want you to know, most beloved brothers—and many of you already know this—that we have been placed in a position in which, whether we wish it or not, we are compelled to announce truth and justice to all peoples, especially Christians. [Col. 0297A] The Lord says: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce their crimes to my people” (Isaiah 58). And elsewhere: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his soul from your hand” (Ezekiel 33). The prophet likewise says: “Cursed is the man who restrains his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48), that is, who restrains the word of preaching from rebuking the carnal.

We have introduced these matters because, among the many evils committed throughout the world, certain ministers of Satan and heralds of Antichrist are also attempting in Lombardy to confuse the Christian faith and provoke God’s anger against themselves. [Col. 0297B] For, as you know, while Guido, the aforesaid archbishop of Milan, was alive, Gotefredus [Gotifredus, and so below] presumed to buy the same Church—a Church once distinguished among all the Churches of Lombardy by religion, freedom, and special [spiritual] glory through the merits of the most glorious virgin and mother of God, Mary, and through the authority of the illustrious teacher Saint Ambrose—as though she were a worthless servant-girl. He attempted to prostitute Christ’s bride to the devil; and, seeking to separate her from the Catholic faith, he endeavored to stain her with the crime of the Simoniacal heresy.

When the holy Roman Church, your mother and the teacher of all Christianity, heard this, she convened a council of many priests from various regions. [Col. 0297C] Supported by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and with the consent of people of various orders, she excommunicated Gotefredus, an enemy of the Catholic faith and Christian law, and pierced him with the dart of anathema together with all who consented to him. This excommunication—even the enemies of the Church cannot deny it—was decreed by the holy Fathers in ancient times, and Catholic men throughout all the holy churches of the entire world affirm and have affirmed it.

Therefore, in the name of God almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, we admonish, exhort, and command you, most beloved brothers, not to consent in any way to the aforesaid heretic Gotefredus. To consent to him in this crime is to deny the faith of Christ. [Col. 0297D] Rather, resist him by whatever means you can, as sons of God, and defend without fail the Christian faith by which you are to be saved.

Let no human arrogance frighten you, for the one who is with us is greater than all and always unconquered. He wishes us to labor for him and, as the Apostle promises, to grant a crown to those who compete lawfully. Our leader is accustomed to crush the many and proud through the few and humble, and to confound all that is strong in the world through what is weak. For so it has pleased, and so it befits, the heavenly and unconquered prince.

May almighty God, who specially entrusted his sheep to blessed Peter and gave him the governance of the whole Church, strengthen you in love for him, so that, absolved from your sins by his authority, [Col. 0298A] you may deserve to suppress the Lord’s enemies and summon their hearts to repentance.

Given at Rome, on the Kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO GIRALDUS, BISHOP OF OSTIA (1073)

He is surprised that Giraldus did not inform him more fully about the synod he had convened. He indicates that he is presently unable to answer the bishops who complained that Giraldus had deposed them, and that he has absolved the bishop of Auch. He orders the bishop of Bigorre to be restored unless he finds other crimes in him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Giraldus, bishop of Ostia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We are surprised and very anxious that, although it has always been customary and highly necessary for a legate of the Apostolic See, whenever he has celebrated a council in distant regions, to return without delay to report everything he has done, [Col. 0298B] your fraternity, after completing the synod at which so many matters arose, has neither returned to us nor sent back the man who is with you, despite consideration of both the necessity and our expectation.

We are certainly pleased that you went to Spain on the affairs of the holy Roman Church. But your prudence ought to have sent to us either the man whom we assigned to you, or someone who had attended the synod and knew how to explain all its proceedings to us reasonably in your place. Then, once everything had been examined, we could have confirmed what was to be confirmed and, if anything seemed to require alteration, changed it with considered judgment. [Col. 0298C]

Although some knowledge of your proceedings has appeared to us in your letters, while you are absent, and while no one is presently here to answer on your behalf with a definite account of what he saw and heard, we are prevented—by the uncertainty of the cases and by regard for preserving your authority—from replying to the many who complain that some were unjustly excommunicated, others irregularly deposed, and others undeservedly placed under interdict. Yet not to reply, or to delay replies for a long time, is attributed to contempt and, because of the prolonged dangers of those under censure, to cruelty.

You have also caused us some anxiety concerning the case of the aforesaid Guilielmus, archbishop of Auch [Ausiensis; in the Mutina manuscript, Auxitensis], for whose restoration you petitioned us. [Col. 0298D] You said that he had been deposed solely because he had knowingly communicated with an excommunicated person, yet that, in his examination concerning the crimes charged against him, apart from admitting that our lord and predecessor Pope Alexander had forgiven him, he had not canonically cleared himself, but had said that he wished to clear himself.

Since we therefore have no small concern about all these matters, we are bound by great difficulty in responding both to you and to the others. Nevertheless, know that, after consulting our brothers, fellow bishops, and cardinals, among other things we have decreed that the aforesaid archbishop of Auch ought not to be subjected to deposition solely because he communicated with an excommunicated person—provided, however, that he can clear himself of the other crimes charged against him in such a way that no suspicion arises against you and no infamy reaches us by common report. [Col. 0299A] Otherwise, reserve the determination of this matter for our hearing.

As for Pontius, the aforesaid bishop of Bigorre, whom you reported to have been deposed for a similar reason, know that he has come to us. But, looking to your honor, we have given no response to his complaints. Nevertheless, since equal laws must be observed in equal cases, we write to your fraternity that, after a careful investigation of the charges brought against him, unless another crime punishable with canonical severity can be found in him by lawful proof [the text prints “if”; Hardouin reads “unless”], he should not be deprived of restoration to his office. For the rest, do not hesitate, when you first find a suitable opportunity, to inform us by letter what we should believe concerning the progress of your wearisome undertaking. [Col. 0299B]

Given at Rome, on the Kalends of June, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XVII. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF BOHEMIA (1073)

He gives thanks because they treated the legates of the Apostolic See kindly; but he complains that they were not generously received by the bishop of Prague. He asks them to exhort the bishop to obey the legates’ admonitions.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia, and his brothers: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because, out of devotion and reverence for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, [Col. 0299C] you received our legates—Bernard and Gregory, who were sent from this holy and Apostolic See to your regions—with the benevolence of due charity, and treat them honorably, as befits your magnificence, we give thanks to almighty God; and in return we offer you our benevolence.

Since, through the negligence of our predecessors and the carelessness of your fathers, who ought to have requested that this be done, apostolic messengers have rarely been sent to your regions, certain of your people, considering this something almost new and failing to heed the Lord’s saying, “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10), hold our legates in contempt. Consequently, by showing them no due reverence, they despise not the legates but the very judgment of truth. [Col. 0299D]

Thus, as is clearer than daylight, they heap up against themselves that judgment of truth to the accumulation of their condemnation, so that, deservedly, while they scandalize the Lord’s little ones, they may slide—unless they repent—into the depth of perdition with millstones hanging from their necks [“having” is lacking].

Your brother Larmir, bishop of Prague [Joramir; in the Mutina manuscript, Jarmirus Pragensis], formerly our friend, has, as we have learned by report, shown himself so rebellious toward our legates Bernard and Gregory that, if the report is true, he seems to have imitated the footsteps of Simon Magus against the prince of the apostles. [Col. 0300A]

Therefore we ask the prudence of your nobility to confer both with our legates and with our aforesaid brother the bishop, and, both personally and on our behalf, to exhort your brother most earnestly to incline his ear in due obedience to the admonitions of our legates. Whatever they suggest to him as just—even if he should think himself seriously burdened by their prejudice—no hearing will be denied him by this Church.

But if he agrees to do neither of these things, we shall confirm the sentence of suspension from his office pronounced against him by our legates [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent in the Mutina manuscript]—and shall unsheathe against him the sword of apostolic indignation, more harshly, namely, even unto destruction [perhaps “extermination”]. Thus it will happen that he, and many others through him, will experience how powerful the authority of this See is. [Col. 0300B]

We are unwillingly compelled to this, and we dare not conceal such presumption. For through the prophet Ezekiel we are driven, under threat of our own destruction, by the words: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, the wicked person will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 33). And elsewhere: “Woe to him who withholds [perhaps ‘the sword’ is missing; the passage is unknown] from the one who sins and persists incorrigibly.”

Act in these and other matters so that the Lord may increase your temporal glory and, through the intercession of the apostles, you may eternally possess an abundance of everlasting blessedness.

Given at Laurentum, on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE EMPEROR MICHAEL (1073)

[Col. 0300C]

He sends Dominicus, patriarch of Venice, to him to discuss with him what he had received from his monks in his name. He shows himself eager to establish peace with the Church of Constantinople.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Michael, emperor of Constantinople: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Certain monks came from your regions, one named Thomas and the other Nicholas. They brought us letters from your Excellency filled with the sweetness of your affection and with no small devotion which you show toward the holy Roman Church. [Col. 0300D] Among other expressions of your nobility, these letters asserted to the same monks that we could believe what they were to report to us orally and privately on your behalf.

But since they did not appear to be persons to whom we could safely entrust our confidence, or through whom we could respond to your greatness concerning such important matters, we decided to send to you our confrater Dominicus, patriarch of Venice, most faithful to the Roman Church and to your empire, [Col. 0301A] so that he may carefully learn from you whether you still persist in the intention which you indicated in your letters and through the more private oral statements of those monks, and whether you wish to bring the words of your embassy to completion.

For our part, we desire not only to renew the ancient harmony, by God’s ordering, between the Roman Church—which, though unworthy, we serve—and her daughter, the Church of Constantinople, but also, if it can be done, to have peace with all human beings, insofar as depends on us. For you know that just as harmony benefited the holy Apostolic See and the empire through our predecessors and yours, so thereafter the cooling of their affection on both sides caused harm.

You can therefore believe without doubt the other matters which we have entrusted to the bearer of this letter to report to you more privately, and through him you may safely inform us of whatever pleases your majesty.

[Col. 0301B] Given at Albano, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the eleventh indiction.

[Note: This constitution is absent from the Mutina manuscript, but in its place it gives the oath of fidelity found below after Letter 21.]

## Constitution Made between Lord Pope Gregory VII and Landulf, Prince of Benevento

This is the constitution which Lord Pope Gregory made with Landulf, prince of Benevento, and which the prince of Benevento himself firmly promised to him in the sacred palace of Benevento, in the first year of his pontificate, on the twelfth day as the month of August was beginning, in the eleventh indiction.

If from that hour onward the prince himself should prove unfaithful to the holy Roman Church and to the pope himself and his successors; or if he should seek in any way to diminish the public affairs of Benevento; or if, without the pope’s permission or without his ordinances [variant: “ordination”], he should make an investiture to anyone of anything belonging to it; or if he should devise any plan with any person, inside or outside the city of Benevento, to make or receive an oath or to create divisions; or if, either personally or through a subordinate, he should in any manner or by any device strive, inside or outside the city of Benevento, to render an evil return or inflict harm upon any of the faithful of the holy Roman Church on account of what they have hitherto done in fidelity to that same holy Roman Church—if he cannot defend himself against this according to the judgment of the apostolic lord when summoned, he shall from the present moment lose his office.

### Subscriptions

I, John, bishop of Porto, recognizing this, have subscribed. [Col. 0301C]

I, John, bishop of Tusculum, was present and subscribed.

I, Ubertus, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Desiderius, priest of the Roman Church, was present and subscribed.

I, Peter, cardinal-priest and librarian of the sacred Roman Church, was present and subscribed. [Col. 0301D]

## LETTER XIX. TO RODULF, DUKE OF SWABIA (1073)

He shows that he does not hate King Henry, but rather desires to make peace with him. He says that, for this to be done suitably, not only he and the emperor but also the emperor’s wife and others should meet together. He asks him to show himself faithful to the Roman Church and to come to the thresholds of the apostles.

[Col. 0302A]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rodulf, duke of Swabia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although the past efforts of your nobility clearly show that you love the honor of the holy Roman Church, the letter you sent us plainly reveals how ardently you now burn with love for it, and how far you surpass the other princes of those regions in the greatness of that love. Among its other words of sweetness, it seemed to advise us of this: that both the empire might be governed more gloriously and the strength of the holy Church more firmly established—namely, that the priesthood and the empire should be joined in harmonious unity [Col. 0302B].

Therefore we wish your nobility to know that we bear no ill will, not only toward King Henry, to whom we are indebted because we elected him king, and because his father, Henry the emperor of praiseworthy memory, treated me with special honor among all the Italians at his court, and because he himself, when dying, commended his son to the Roman Church through the aforesaid Pope Victor of venerable memory; but also that, with God’s help, we wish to hate no Christian person. For the Apostle says: “If I deliver my body so that I may burn, and if I give all my possessions as food to the poor, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. XIII).

But since this harmony [Col. 0302C] between the priesthood and the empire ought to possess nothing feigned, nothing except what is pure, it seems altogether useful to us first to confer with you, with Empress Agnes, with Countess Beatrice, with Rainald, bishop of Como, and with the other God-fearing persons [understand: “I should confer”]. For just as the human body is guided by temporal light through its two eyes, so the body of the Church is shown to be guided and illumined by spiritual light when these two dignities agree in pure religion.

Let us discuss these matters more carefully, so that, once our intention has become well known to you, if you judge our reasons to be just, you may agree with us; but if it should seem to you that something must be added to or subtracted from our reasoning, then, with God’s consent, we shall be ready to yield to your counsels [Col. 0302D]. Therefore we ask your prudence always to strive to increase in fidelity to blessed Peter, and not to be reluctant to come to his threshold, both for the sake of prayer and in consideration of such great usefulness, so that you may make yourself a debtor to blessed Peter in both respects and may rejoice in his intercession both in the present life and in the life to come.

Given at Capua on the Kalends of September, at the beginning of the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO RAINALD, BISHOP OF COMO. (Year 1073.)

He grieves over his calamities. He shows himself prepared to avenge the injuries inflicted upon him. He urges him to come to Rome, both for the purpose of securing peace with Henry and on behalf of the Lombard bishops.

[Col. 0303A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Rainald, bishop of Como.

Having read your Fraternity’s letter concerning the adversity and insult that have befallen you—and indeed us and the whole holy Church as well—we have felt heartfelt compassion for you and have been deeply saddened by heartfelt grief. For if, merely hearing of this from someone unknown to us, or hearing of it concerning a priest, and even [that is, concerning an Egyptian; HARD.], we would have felt grave compassion and would have been compelled by the duty of our office to grieve, what, then, should we feel regarding one whom we have placed as the first member of the holy Roman Church? Whom we cherish as our most beloved brother in the embrace of affection [Col. 0303B]? We open to you the bowels of compassion, the bowels of profound grief, on behalf of our dearest brother.

We have resolved, for your benefit and that of many others, to impose vengeance for this unheard-of crime and punishment for this unprecedented outrage, according to your counsel. For the better you know the character and life of the shedder [possibly, “the one causing the shedding”] of your blood, and of his entire family and homeland, the better you will be able to advise us by what means and with what [possibly, “punishments”] he may most easily be compelled, so that by his example the faithless among you and among the other bishops may be crushed, while good men may rejoice in the hope that the punishment for so great and unheard-of a crime will not be delayed. We wish you, out of obedience, by no means to fail to do this and to write to us about it by the feast of Saint Martin, and to say whether you want us to carry this out publicly or privately [Col. 0303C].

As for what you wrote about the king, receive this answer. You and our most beloved daughter, Empress Agnes, know from long experience that you love him and the holy Roman Church [possibly, “that he loves them”; HARD.], and that we act on its behalf. You therefore know what I think about the king and what I desire concerning him, so that no one [who is] richer than he in worldly goods [could know this] better than you. [Col. 0303D]

[Note: This passage is certainly obscure. In it, evidently, something is missing which, if supplied, would fully express what the author intended; if we attempted to supply it, we could rightly be accused of rashness. This alone appears to us through the darkness: that Gregory here benevolently expressed some kind of wish for the temporal prosperity of King Henry; immediately afterward there follows another wish—which is by no means obscure—for his perfection in virtue and piety. EDIT.]

You know, if perhaps you remember well, how often I have said to both of you that I wished no one to live more religiously than he. I had this thought in mind: if the good character, life, and religion of some private person or prince bring honor and increase to the holy Church, what of the one who is the head of the laity, who is king, and who, with God’s consent, is destined to become emperor at Rome?

I would wish—and with all my heart desire—that he love religion, associate good men with himself out of true love, increase and defend the property of the Churches. God is my witness. We do not hope that he will desire otherwise, unless he avoids the counsels of the wicked as poison and, as has already been reported to us, listens to the good.

Concerning concord between the Roman Church and him, if you wish to arrange something for the benefit of both, understand it as follows. We have heard that Duke Rodulf will enter Lombardy this coming September. Therefore, first of all for the service of the apostles, but secondarily also for this matter, arrange that it should not be burdensome for him and for you to come to Rome. There, together with you and with our most beloved daughter the empress, and also with Beatrice, who has worked much and often on this same matter, we shall be able to speak and deliberate about concord between the Roman Church and the king, so that you may report to the king from our side that everything is secure and peaceful, and that, if he should happen to enter Italy, he may find everything in peace.

I do not object to your speaking with the bishops of Lombardy; but your prudence must take great care not to communicate with them in any other way. What must be decided concerning them we shall determine when you have come to us.

Given at Capua [Rome], on the Kalends of September, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO ANSELM, BISHOP OF LUCCA. (Year 1073.)

[Col. 0304B]

He instructs him not to receive the investiture of the bishopric from Henry.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Anselm, by the grace of God elect bishop of the Lucchese.

Because we have loved and do love your Fraternity with sincere affection, you ought to accept without hesitation what we take care to write to you, whether by word or by letter, concerning the benefit of your life. Since you asked us to make known to you the path on which you should walk, we know of no new or more suitable path than the one we recently indicated to your affection: namely, that you refrain from receiving the investiture of the bishopric from the hand of the king until, having made satisfaction to God concerning communion with the excommunicated and having set matters in good order, he is able to have peace with us [Col. 0304C].

People of the following kind are striving to accomplish this work: certainly our most beloved daughter Empress Agnes, as well as the glorious Beatrice with her daughter Matilda; and also Duke Rodulf of Swabia. We neither can nor ought to disregard their religious counsels. But if completion of the aforesaid work should be delayed for any reason, meanwhile you may remain attached to our intimacy at Rome and share with us either adversity or prosperity.

Given at Capua on the Kalends of September, at the beginning of the twelfth indiction.

## Oath of Fidelity Made by Prince Richard to His Lord, Pope Gregory

[Col. 0304D] I, Richard, by the grace of God and of Saint Peter prince of Capua, from this hour and henceforth shall be faithful to the holy Roman Church and to the apostolic see, and to you, my lord Gregory, universal [venerable] pope.

In counsel or deed by which you might lose life or limb, or be captured in a disastrous captivity, I shall not be involved. The counsel that you entrust to me, and that you forbid me to reveal, I shall not knowingly reveal to your detriment. I shall be an aid to the holy Roman Church and to you [Col. 0305A] in holding, acquiring, and defending the regalia of Saint Peter and his possessions with right faith against all men; and I shall help you to hold the Roman papacy and the land of Saint Peter securely and honorably.

I shall neither seek to invade nor acquire any principality, nor dare to plunder one, without the definite permission of you or of your successors who shall enter upon the honor of Saint Peter, except for that which you grant me or which your successors shall grant. Regarding the revenue from the land of Saint Peter that I hold and shall hold, I shall strive in right faith to ensure that the holy Roman Church receives it annually, as has been established.

I shall also place in your power all the churches that remain under my domination, together with their possessions, and I shall be their defender in fidelity to the holy Roman Church [Col. 0305B]. When I have been admonished by you [as having been admonished by you] or by your successors, I shall swear fidelity to King Henry, while preserving my fidelity to the holy Roman Church.

And if you or your successors should depart this life before me, then, according to the instruction I receive from the better Roman cardinals, clerics, and laymen, I shall assist in having a pope elected and ordained for the honor of Saint Peter. I shall observe all the foregoing faithfully toward the holy Roman Church and toward you; and I shall observe this fidelity toward your successors ordained for the honor of Saint Peter, if they are willing to confirm to me the investiture granted to me by you.

Done at Capua, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO THE CARTHAGINIANS. (Year 1073.)

[Col. 0305C]

He urges them to put aside their enmities and patiently endure the attacks of the Saracens. He complains that they have injured Bishop Cyriacus. He urges them to repent; otherwise he threatens them with excommunication.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the clergy and Christian people of Carthage.

Grace to you and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, his only Son, who in gratuitous mercy was pleased to conform you to the new man through the shedding of his blood; he who was pleased to die and rise once for all, [Col. 0305D] so that he might put you to death in the flesh, but make you alive in the spirit and offer you to God. The rock on which he built gave testimony to this, saying: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Pet. III).

Concerning him the Apostle also says in this way: “He gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Eph. V); and elsewhere the same Apostle says: “Christ became obedient for us unto death” (Phil. II). Be imitators, therefore, of him who, placed upon the cross for your sake, wished to be soiled by spittle, counted among thieves, and wounded for your sins, and thus to bring his end according to the flesh, so that he might cleanse you from sins, making you debtors not to the flesh but to the spirit, which puts the deeds of the flesh to death [Col. 0306A] [possibly, “by the mortification of the flesh”].

For if you are of spiritual life, you will enjoy the inheritance of his kingdom forever as sons, coheirs with Christ and heirs of God. Therefore, moved by fraternal charity, we admonish you to put aside all malice, pretenses, and envies, and all slanders.

But if anything happens to you while you are placed amid the arms of the Saracens, do not be afraid. Rather, whenever you suffer for Christ, rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory you may rejoice and exult. Faithful indeed is the saying: “He who raised Jesus will also raise you” (Rom. VIII), if you have died in the flesh but live through the Spirit of God at his coming, for participation in his glory.

Trusting, therefore, in the hope of ineffable glory and in so faithful a promiser, put your members to death; fix the death of Christ in your hearts; rejoice to suffer all adversities for him, believing with the Apostle that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0306B].

Avoid quarrels and disputes as poison. Disciples of humility, put on humility. Obey as you are bound to him who holds Christ’s place over you. Strive to embrace his counsels and admonitions out of true love, knowing that, when you obey him—and Christ himself, who suffered for you—and receive his preaching and judgments, you receive Christ in every respect. For he says: “Whoever receives you receives me; whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X).

But if you act otherwise, you sin against Christ, despise Christ, and cease to be Christ’s disciples. You resist the Apostle, who says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities” (Rom. XIII). Since the Apostle preached obedience to worldly authorities, how much more to spiritual authorities, who hold Christ’s place among Christians?

I think of these things, dearest sons, groaning; I write them weeping; with the deepest sorrow of heart I send them to you. For it has reached our ears that some of you, irreligiously and against the law of Christ [and] against Christ, accused our venerable brother Cyriacus—your archbishop and teacher, indeed Christ among you—before the Saracens, and so tore him apart with slanderous abuse that he was counted among thieves and beaten naked with blows [Col. 0306C].

An unrighteous example! An example of disgrace to you and to the whole holy Church! Christ is again seized, condemned by false accusers and witnesses, counted among thieves, and beaten with blows. By whom? By those who are said to believe in his incarnation, to venerate his passion, and to embrace the rest of his holy mysteries in faith.

Should we remain silent about these matters? Or should we cry out and correct them with tears? It is written: “Cry out, do not cease” (Isa. LVIII). Elsewhere this command is also given: “Unless you announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. XXXIII).

Therefore I shall cry out from necessity; from necessity I must correct you, lest your blood be required from my hand, lest I be afflicted on account of your sins before the dread Judge, before the just and immutable Judge. Therefore I open to you the bowels of paternal piety, the bowels of mercy [Col. 0307A], partly because the long and dangerous distances of the sea make passage to us difficult for you, and partly because I do not know how to investigate fully the cause of your anger, the cause of your grief and malice, so as to determine a judgment concerning these matters.

I admonish you, and by apostolic authority command you, that just as the stench of your recklessness and of your unheard-of wickedness has disturbed my mind with excessive sadness [“disturbed” in the variant reading], so the fragrant odors of correction and repentance may transform my mind into joy. But if you do not do so, I shall justly strike you with the sword of anathema and send against you the curse of Saint Peter and of ourselves.

Given at Capua, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October [the seventeenth is absent], in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXIII. TO CYRIACUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE. (Year 1073.)

[Col. 0307B]

He praises his steadfastness because he patiently endured the injuries of the Saracens and of wicked Christians, and because, in the presence of King Henry, he refused to conduct ordinations. [Note: This name does not occur in the text of the letter.] He urges him to persevere. He prays to God for the African Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Cyriacus, bishop of Carthage.

Having seen your Fraternity’s letter, we showed fraternal compassion for the troubles inflicted upon you by pagans and by the pseudo-sons of your Church. For we understand that you are wearied by a twofold struggle: you suffer the hidden ambushes of Christians, and through the persecution of the Saracens you are pitifully compelled to lose not only the support of human frailty [Col. 0307C], but faith itself.

For what else is it than a denial of his faith for a priest to obey a worldly power in violating the law of God? But thanks be to God! In the midst of a wicked nation of perverse faith, your steadfastness became known to all like a certain lamp, so that, when presented before the royal hearing, you chose rather to suffer various torments than, at the king’s command, to conduct ordinations contrary to the holy canons.

But how much more precious would the confession of your religion have been if, after the blows you then endured, you had reached even the shedding of your own life by exposing their error and preaching the Christian religion? Although we do not doubt that your Fraternity is devoted to such efforts, and that, for the testimony of truth, you have gone as far as the mutilation of your limbs, so far as concerns you, nevertheless, always urging your devotion toward better things, we exhort you to show yourself always prepared to rejoice in the Lord’s consolation and not to be broken by tribulation.

For many are the tribulations of the righteous, but the Lord will deliver them from them all. By such means the holy Church has grown and is restored. The holy Fathers left us this inheritance: that through many tribulations we enter the kingdom of God. The battle is indeed grave, but the rewards are infinite. For “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0308A].

Although we are absent in body, let us nevertheless be present in spirit and, whenever opportunity permits, devote ourselves to mutual consolation through letters. Let us constantly beseech almighty God to deign at last to look upon the African Church, which has long been afflicted and shaken by the waves of various disturbances, saying with the Psalmist: “Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever. Why do you turn your face away? Why do you forget our poverty and our tribulation?” (Ps. XLIII.)

For our part, showing you in every respect the fraternal compassion that we ought to show, we are sending our letter to your clergy and people, so that, having set aside all hostility, they may venerate you as their spiritual father.

[Col. 0308B] Given at Capua, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, in the eleventh indiction [it should read, as in the others, “twelfth.” So also in the Modena manuscript].

## LETTER XXIV. TO BRUNO, BISHOP OF VERONA. (Year 1073.)

He commends his devotion toward him. He promises him the pallium if he comes to Rome, and declares that he loves the king.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Bruno, bishop of Verona.

Having received your Fraternity’s letter, we clearly understood that you desire us to administer irreproachably the stewardship entrusted to us [Col. 0308C], and that you pour out to us and to the holy Church the prayers of your religion, necessary and most devout before God.

In this matter it is plainly shown with how great a love and devotion you venerate blessed Peter, since, although unworthy, we appear to you to be assigned to the service of his Church and yet are embraced by you with such affection. For whoever loves his lords transfers the love of those lords even to their least servants.

We do not presently repay this love of yours in the matter you requested from us, namely, the grant of the pallium, because the authority of our predecessors has decreed that the pallium may be granted only to a person who is present. Therefore, if your Fraternity comes to us equipped with the privileges of the apostolic see, then, with God’s permission, we shall confer upon you the honor that the Roman pontiffs [Col. 0308D] conferred upon your predecessors.

Just as we desire the other Churches to render the Roman Church the honor due to it, so we desire to preserve each Church’s proper right. At that time we also wish to show your presence how sincerely we love the king’s welfare, and how greatly we desire to watch over his honor both according to God and according to the world—provided that he strives to render to God the honor due to him and wisely imitates the pattern of the holy kings, setting aside childish pursuits.

Given at Capua, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXV. TO HERLEMBALD OF MILAN. (Year 1073.)

[Col. 0309A]

He reports that the Normans persist in their dissension, that King Henry has sent him letters full of humility, and that he has no doubt about the religious devotion of Beatrice and her daughter Matilda. He urges him to act courageously in defense of the Roman Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Herlembald, soldier of Milan.

Let your prudence know that, through God’s mercy, we are healthy and joyful and are staying near Capua, not without great benefit to the holy Church. For the Normans, who were planning to unite for the confusion and danger of the commonwealth and of the holy [Col. 0309B] Church, persist with excessive obstinacy in the disorder in which we found them; they will have peace in no way unless we wish it.

If our judgment approved it as useful to the holy Church, they would already have submitted themselves humbly to us and would have shown the reverence they customarily show. Moreover, know that King Henry has sent us words full of sweetness and obedience, words such as we do not remember either him or his predecessors having sent to the Roman pontiffs.

Some of his leading faithful men also promise us on his behalf that, concerning the affair of the Milanese Church, he will without doubt obey our counsel. How much we can benefit him, and how much, if we withdraw the hand of assistance [Col. 0309C], we can harm him, we hope you will quickly come to understand most clearly, and prove manifestly that God is with us and works with us.

We think there is no reason whatsoever to doubt Countess Beatrice, or her daughter Matilda, in matters belonging to God and to the religion of the holy Church: they are faithful toward us. Therefore, trusting completely in the Lord and in your mother, the Roman Church, act courageously, strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Know that the more heavily the storm of disturbance now rises against you, the more joyfully, with God’s favor, the calm will later smile upon you.

Given at Capua, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXVI. TO THE SAME. (Year 1073.)

[Col. 0309D]

He advises him to deal kindly with the excommunicated who are repenting, concerning whom he had consulted him, and promises that he too will receive them kindly. He urges him not to fear the bishops favoring his enemy, since he hopes the king will entrust his case to his judgment. He advises him to win over the bishop of Vercelli.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Herlembald, soldier of Milan.

As long as you are occupied with the zeal of pious concern in defending the faith and restoring holy religion, we shall not lack the will either to hear your embassies gladly or to assist you abundantly. To your many questions we intend to respond briefly, because we are occupied with other matters [Col. 0310A].

Regarding the associates of that excommunicated man who, after receiving money, wish to return to you; regarding sons whose fathers, or fathers whose sons, adhere to the anathematized Gotefred; and regarding those whose correction you do not wish to carry out without the payment of money—in all these matters, although we admonish you to be merciful, if any wish to attach themselves to your party, we entrust the decision to your prudence, since you know and are able to judge better.

But let all of them who, repenting of their error, desire to come to us for the sake of a remedy know that they will be received kindly and treated mercifully.

Moreover, do not fear greatly the bishops who are trying to support your enemy, since Beatrice and her daughter [Col. 0310B] Matilda, entirely favoring the Roman Church, together with certain great nobles of the kingdom, are working firmly to unite our mind and the king’s. We neither ought nor wish to exercise any hatred against him, unless—God forbid!—he chooses to show himself opposed to divine religion.

They have complete confidence that this king will satisfy our will in other ecclesiastical affairs, and especially that he will give his assent to our disposition concerning your case. Finally, strive by whatever honorable means you can to win over Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, since he professes himself wholly obedient to our command.

For the rest, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, seeking his forgiveness through prayers, almsgiving, and purity of heart, so that he may deign to bring our desire and yours to completion [Col. 0310C].

Given at Capua, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ALBERT, BISHOP-ELECT OF ACQUI. (Year 1073.)

He commends his religious devotion, about which he had once doubted. He urges him to attack the Simoniacs and to assist Herlembald.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Albert, elect of the Church of Acqui.

It reached our ears—and caused us some doubt concerning your religion—that you had taken part in the ordination of that excommunicated man, Gotefred [Col. 0310D]. But after the testimony of those who customarily tell us the truth endeavored, through a faithful report, to excuse you, we not only ceased to doubt you, but also understood that you possess zeal for restoring the honor of your mother, the Milanese Church.

How much your religious devotion pleases us will be proved by clear indications whenever the need of the Roman Church requires your help. Your devotion can make Saint Peter and us his debtors in no matter more than if, armed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, you fight with us against Simon Magus, who has miserably infected the Church of blessed Ambrose with the poison of his venality; and if you extend a helping hand to Herlembald, that most vigorous soldier of Christ, in matters pertaining to the worship of God and to the religion of the holy Church [Col. 0311A].

Your prudence will also commend you no less to the holy apostolic see if it strives to attack that Simoniacal heresy, as it has laudably already begun to do, until it is completely emptied out of its Church, and to recall clerics from a shameful way of life to the purity of chastity.

Let your mind meditate daily on these pursuits of holiness, so that what has become known to us through your reputation may be proved by consideration of your works. Act, therefore, so that the universal mother, the holy Roman Church, may take comfort in you as in a most faithful son, and so that, once the chains of death have been conquered [read: “for those bound by the chains of death”], a hand of liberation may be extended.

[Col. 0311B] Given at Capua, on the third day before the Ides of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (Year 1073.)

Its subject is nearly the same.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to William, bishop of Pavia.
