The letter of your Fraternity sent to us, together with the words of Herlembald of Milan, clearly shows that you wish faithfully to offer the obedience you owe to the holy apostolic see and to obey our exhortations as is fitting.

But there is nothing that we would more readily enjoin upon your Fraternity, nothing that we would more willingly have you do, than to strive through pastoral vigilance to defend your Church and the flock entrusted to you from the heresies that appear to be spreading pestilently in the holy Church [Col. 0311C], and to rise up against them more ardently with every effort and all your strength, fortified by the authority of the holy Fathers, and to recall clerics from a shameful way of life to chastity.

Know also that you will make yourself especially commendable to your mother, the Roman Church, if you extend a helping hand to the aforesaid Herlembald in the works he undertakes at our counsel—or rather, in fear of almighty God—and if, together with him, you fight the war of God against the enemies of the holy Church and resist them courageously.

Let your prudence therefore devote itself vigorously and watchfully to sharing this concern, so that we may prove that what we have received from your promises [Col. 0311D] will be fulfilled through definite execution.

Given at Capua, on the third day before the Ides of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE JUDGES OF SARDINIA. (Year 1073.)

He urges them, following the example of their parents, to show themselves obedient toward the Roman Church; and he says that he has entrusted his envoy with many matters to report to them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Mariano of Torres, Orzocco of Arborea, likewise Orzocco of Cagliari, Constantine of Gallura, judges of Sardinia.

[Col. 0312A] It is known to you and to all who venerate Christ that the Roman Church is the universal mother of all Christians. Although, in view of its office, it ought to watch over the salvation of all peoples, it ought nevertheless to devote a special and, in a certain sense, private concern to you.

But because, through the negligence of our predecessors, that love which existed in ancient times between the Roman Church and your people has grown cold, you have made yourselves strangers to us to such an extent—more than the peoples who are at the ends of the world—that the Christian religion among you has come to the greatest harm.

Therefore it is very necessary for you to think with exceptional diligence about the salvation of your souls, to acknowledge your mother, the Roman Church, as legitimate sons [Col. 0312B], and to show her the devotion that your ancient parents showed her.

It is our desire not only to wish to care for the liberation of your souls, but also to watch more anxiously over the salvation of your homeland. Therefore, if you receive our words with the devotion that is fitting, you will obtain glory and honor in the present life and in the life to come.

But if you act otherwise—which we do not expect—and do not incline your ear to the sound of our exhortation with the obedience that is due, you will be able to attribute any danger that befalls your homeland not to our negligence but to your own fault.

The remaining matters that we are considering concerning your salvation and honor we have entrusted, for the most part, to our confrater Constantine, archbishop of Torres, to report to you. [Col. 0312C] But when our envoy, whom, with God’s consent, we intend to send shortly, comes to you, he will fully make our will known to you and explain more openly what is fitting for your glory and honor.

Given at Capua, on the eleventh day before the Ides of October, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXIX bis. OF HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO POPE GREGORY. (Year 1073.)

He humbly seeks pardon for having invaded ecclesiastical property and sold churches. He asks that, by his authority, Gregory eradicate the stain of Simony from all the Churches, especially the Milanese Church; and he promises that he will obey the pontiff in all things.

[Col. 0312D] To the most vigilant and most desirous lord Pope Gregory, marked by apostolic dignity from heaven, Henry, by the grace of God king of the Romans, offers the most faithful service that is due.

Since kingdom and priesthood, if they are to remain rightly administered in Christ, always need one another’s mutual assistance, it is surely necessary, my lord and most loving father, that they in no way dissent from one another, but rather cling to each other inseparably, joined most closely by the bond of Christ. For only in this way, and not otherwise, are preserved the bond of perfect charity and peace, the harmony of Christian unity, and likewise the well-being of ecclesiastical religion.

But we, who by God’s favor have for some time now been entrusted with the administration of the kingdom, have not rendered to the priesthood, as was right, its legitimate right and honor in all things. Indeed, it was not without cause that we carried the sword as the defender of the power given us by God, yet we have not always drawn it against the guilty with judicial judgment, as justice required. Now, however, having been somewhat pierced by divine mercy and having returned to our senses, we accuse ourselves and confess our former sins before your most indulgent fatherhood, hoping in the Lord that, having been absolved by your apostolic authority, we may deserve to be justified.

Alas, how criminal and wretched we are! Partly through the prompting of flattering youth, partly through the freedom afforded by our own authority and imperial power, and partly through the deceitful deception of those whose seductive counsels [seductiles; variant seductilia, “misleading things”] we followed far too much, we have sinned against heaven and before you, and are now no longer worthy to be called sons of your [Col. 0313B] fatherhood. For not only did we seize ecclesiastical possessions, but we also sold the churches themselves to all sorts of unworthy men, embittered with the gall of simony and entering not through the door but from elsewhere; and we did not defend those churches as we ought to have done.

But now, because we cannot correct the churches by ourselves without your authority, concerning these matters—and likewise concerning all our affairs—we earnestly seek both your counsel and your help, intending to observe your command most diligently in everything. In particular, we ask that the Church of Milan, which through our fault is in error, be canonically corrected by your apostolic severity, and that from there your authoritative judgment proceed to correct the other churches.

Therefore, God willing, we shall not fail you in anything, while humbly asking your fatherhood to be mercifully and cheerfully present to us in all things. Before long you will receive a letter from us by the hands of our most faithful men; through them, with God’s help, you will hear more fully what still remains to be said.

## LETTER XXX. GREGORY TO GEBOARD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG (1073)

He reproves him for not restraining the clergy and urges him to do so. He commends the bearer of the present letter.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Geboard [Gebeard], bishop of Salzburg.

If the affection toward us that, we hope, burns within you [variant: “that we hoped burned within you”], your letter would have reached us before ours reached you, since you have more readily available opportunities to do this through the many who come to the threshold of the apostles than we have through one man traveling from here to you. Nevertheless, although you have not sent us greetings, we offer you the service of greeting and extend to you the sincerity of affection that we customarily show.

But there is a matter for which we think your fraternity deserves to be reproved for negligence: as it has been reported to us, you still appear disobedient regarding the chastity of the clergy and the decrees of the Roman synod, which you attended. In this matter we grieve all the more deeply, wondering at you, the more earnestly we had hoped that you would undertake it.

Therefore we admonish you by apostolic authority to restrain with pastoral severity those of your clergy who conduct themselves disgracefully, and to proclaim and enforce in your Church, with steadfast authority, what the Roman Church has established concerning the uncleanness of the clergy, showing neither favor nor hatred toward anyone.

Furthermore, for the love of Saint Peter, whose threshold the bearer of this letter has sought, let your religious devotion strive to open to him the depths of your compassion, insofar as it seems possible for you to accommodate his weakness without endangering his soul. Thus he will not regret having undertaken the labor of so great a journey, but will rejoice that he has obtained through us, according to his desire, what he sought for so long: the mercy of Saint Peter.

Given at Capua, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXI. TO LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY (1073)

He reproves him for allowing a certain Arfastus [Arfatus, and likewise below] to cause trouble for the abbey of Saint Edmund, contrary to the decrees of his predecessor Alexander. He urges him, in his place, to restrain Arfastus’s audacity and to entreat King William not to show him any favor. If Arfastus refuses obedience, he orders that Arfastus and Abbot Baldwin seek the apostolic see to settle their disputes.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Lanfranc, archbishop of the Cantuarians in England.

We consider it worthy of no small astonishment with what face and with what state of mind you tolerate the said bishop Arfastus mocking the holy Roman Church and despising our predecessor Alexander, of blessed memory, [Col. 0314C] and his decrees. We are fully aware of your prudence: the holy Roman Church has the right given it by God to defend the churches, priests, and consecrations of bishops; and, having received permission from no one, it ought and is able to celebrate its own acts, to have provided—and, with God’s favor, to continue to provide—the firmest defense even in this matter for those who have come to Rome and sought the counsel and assistance of the apostolic see.

By what novel audacity the said bishop Arfastus resists these things, unless perhaps it is because of the words, “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14), we do not know. We are also greatly surprised that your affection remains silent about this matter. Yet because we have no less confidence in you than in ourselves, we confidently beg your fraternity, in our place, to silence Arfastus’s trifles completely and in no way allow the abbey of Saint Edmund to be disturbed contrary to the decree of our predecessor.

For when he had caused that same abbot to be ordained a priest at Rome, he received both the man himself and the monastery over which he presides under the protection of the apostolic see. Therefore we cannot pretend not to notice that his injuries rebound upon us, especially since we perceive that they are inflicted upon him as an insult to our authority.

We therefore also ask your affection to admonish our most dear King William, the only son of the holy Roman Church, by our prayers and in our place concerning these matters, and to urge him not to yield to Arfastus’s empty persuasions. In this respect everyone recognizes that the king’s singular prudence has been diminished and constricted beyond measure.

But if Arfastus [Arfastus] thereafter attempts to resist these commands, order him and Abbot Baldwin, by apostolic authority, to seek the apostolic see for the determination of these matters.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXII. TO ARALD, BISHOP OF CHARTRES (1073)

He instructs him to restore a certain Isimbard to the care of his abbey, after removing another abbot who has intruded, if he finds no other fault in the man who was deprived except that he went to Jerusalem out of devotion.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Arald [Arnald], bishop of Chartres.

The bearer of this letter, Abbot Isimbard of the monastery of Saint Laodomer [Launomar; Audomar, according to the Mutinensis manuscript], coming to the apostolic see, has complained to our ears that he has been deprived of obedience to the aforesaid abbey without any fault intervening, except that, inflamed by divine love, he went to Jerusalem. When he was returning from there, he found a certain abbot named Guido placed over his abbey—so we have heard—who was not endowed with a similar religious character and had not been regularly taken from another [perhaps “from that,” HARD.] monastery.

Therefore let your fraternity undertake a careful and pious investigation both of that man’s removal and of the other’s appointment. If no fault is found in the former except his journey to Jerusalem—which we indeed consider tolerable—and if he is more diligent and religiously capable of governing the brothers, then let him certainly be restored and let the other be deposed.

But if this man too has committed another fault that justly removes him from the administration, while the other is more religiously vigilant than he in the administration and his appointment is found to be legitimate, then let your fraternity send this Isimbard back to us with a letter, and let the other remain in his place.

If, however, the other’s promotion is found to have been defiled by the filth of simony, then let him be removed without delay from the administration of the brothers and let another be regularly appointed in his place. Whatever your religious judgment accomplishes concerning the case of either man, let your fraternity take care to make known to us in a letter.

Given at Argentea [Argentace, and likewise below], on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO THE BROTHERS OF THE MONASTERY OF THE BLESSED MARY (1073)

Because he considered the privilege of his predecessor to be false, he neither wishes to confirm it nor to grant another. He indicates that he had warned the abbot whom they elected, since he did not consider him suitable, to withdraw from the office of abbot; nevertheless, he orders them to obey him for the time being.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the brothers of the monastery of the Blessed Mary, situated in the diocese of Dordonensis.

Brother Benedict, whom your religious community chose as abbot to preside over you after the death of your father Hubert, came into our presence and brought us a certain privilege which we found entitled in the name of our predecessor Alexander, of blessed memory. We discovered by the clearest indications that it was not authentic, namely, from the corruption of its Latin and also from its divergence from canonical authority.

Accordingly, for appropriate reasons, we have presently judged it fitting neither to strengthen the old privilege nor to draw up a new one in our name, since ecclesiastical discipline requires what is just and pious. When the Church of Dordonensis [Dertonensis, and likewise below], to whose parish you belong, has been canonically ordered through the working of heavenly mercy, then, while life endures, with the consent of the bishop of that see, we shall provide for your needs by apostolic authority, supported by a privilege of useful benefit.

But if, because sins demand it, that church has not been canonically ordered, then likewise, by whatever protection we may justly be able to provide [munimine, perhaps read for printed muninime], we shall fully support you.

Although the person of your elected abbot appears to be endowed with honorable morals, he has nevertheless seemed to us weak for the office of abbot, both because of his age and because of bodily infirmity, since he must bear responsibility for everyone. We therefore warned the elected man to withdraw from the office if he should recognize that he is unable to meet the needs of the brothers.

Nevertheless, for as long as he presides, continue steadfastly in the same religious observance in which your deceased father established you, and show him the reverence that is due. We also command by apostolic authority that your fellow monks, living in the cells constructed by that same father of yours, be of one mind with you and reverently obey this abbot of yours.

Because the brevity of a letter does not permit us to make known to your fraternity many things that we have communicated to your brothers, the matters omitted from this letter will be related to you orally by the brothers mentioned above.

Given at Argentea, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO REMEDIUS, BISHOP OF LINCOLN (1073)

He bars a homicide from ministry at the sacred altar; nevertheless, if he has done penance, he grants that he may be supported from the resources of the Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Remedius, bishop of Lincoln in England.

No authority of the holy Fathers permits the bearer of this letter, whom your fraternity’s letter reported to us to be stained by homicide, to minister any longer at the sacred altars. Nor is it proper for us, by giving assent to that constitution—which God forbid!—to contradict the decrees of the canons.

Nevertheless, if your religious judgment perceives that he has presented to God worthy fruit of penance for the crime he committed, let it mercifully provide that he not lack ecclesiastical support, lest, made fainthearted by poverty, he set aside the divine commandments. Although he can in no way ever deserve to receive the priesthood, it is nevertheless fitting that he obtain some benefit from the apostolic see.

Moreover, as you requested, we have judged it fitting to send you the absolution of your sins, supported by the authority of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, whose place, though unworthy, we occupy—provided that, by adhering to good works and mourning the excesses you have committed, you present the dwelling of your body to God as a clean temple, insofar as you are able.

As for what you asked us to command you, so that you might know by what means you could deserve to please us in serving us, this above all we command: that you help us with your prayers, so that together we may deserve to enjoy everlasting joys.

Given at Terracina, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXV. TO RODERIC, BISHOP OF CHALON [ROCLENUS] (1073)

He attacks Philip, king of the Franks, as a seller and destroyer of churches, and wishes him to move the king to permit bishops to be canonically elected.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Roderic [Roclenus], bishop of Chalon.

Among the other rulers of our time who have dissipated the Church of God by selling it through perverse greed, and who have utterly trampled underfoot their Mother—whom, in accordance with the Lord’s commandment, they owed honor and reverence—in servile subjection, we have learned from reliable reports that Philip, king of the Franks, has oppressed the churches of Gaul to such an extent that he appears to have reached the height and culmination of this detestable crime.

We have been all the more distressed by this situation in that kingdom because it is known to be more powerful in prudence, religion, and strength, and much more devoted to the Roman Church. Indeed, both the general concern of our pastoral responsibility and the destruction of those churches had greatly inflamed us, so that we ought to have taken severe action against such bold offenses against holy religion.

But because in days past, through his personal chamberlain Alberic, he firmly promised us that he would correct his life according to the judgment of our authority and put the churches in order, we have meanwhile deferred exercising canonical rigor.

We therefore wish first to test the sincerity of this promise in the Church of Mâcon, which has long been deprived of a shepherd’s governance and has almost been reduced to nothing. Specifically, we want him to allow the archdeacon of Autun, elected by the unanimous consent of clergy and people and, as we have heard, with the king’s own approval, to be placed over the Church, with the bishopric freely granted to him, as is proper.

If he refuses to do this, let him know without doubt that we shall no longer tolerate this ruin of the Church, and that by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we shall restrain his harsh obstinacy in disobedience with canonical severity.

For either the king himself, rejecting the shameful commerce of the heresy of simony, will permit suitable persons to be promoted to sacred governance, or the Franks, unless they prefer to renounce the Christian faith, will be struck by the sword of a general anathema and will refuse to obey him any longer.

We have taken care to make these matters known to you, dearest brother, so that your vigilance may strive to bring them to the attention of the aforesaid king, pressing them upon him by exhortation, entreaty, and every possible means, so that he may permit the aforesaid Church of Mâcon and the other churches to be canonically ordered.

We impose this duty upon you especially because we have learned that your prudence is great and that you enjoy the king’s familiarity. If anything that ought to have been said has been omitted by us, let the sharpness of your intelligence supply it. Therefore labor in this persecution, so that you may deserve both God’s grace and our goodwill.

Given at Piperno, on the second day before the Nones of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO HUMBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS (1073)

He orders that the man elected by him or by his suffragans as bishop of Mâcon be ordained even against the king’s will, and, if he refuses ordination, be compelled to accept it.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons.

The outcry of the clergy of Mâcon has reached us: their Church, now long deprived of a shepherd, is suffering considerable harm. They say that the king of the Franks wishes to obstruct the election made without his consent.

Therefore, because this year he promised through one of his knights, named Albert [perhaps Alberic, as in the preceding letter and likewise in the Mutinensis manuscript], who came to Rome, that he would entirely accept our counsel, we have taken care to send our letter to our brother Roderic [Roclenus], bishop of Chalon, so that, acting as our legate, he may approach the aforesaid king. The king, remembering the promise he made to us, should not merely refrain from obstructing the election of the people of Mâcon, but should give it the approval he ought to give.

But if, persisting in his hardness, he is unwilling either to sympathize with the need of this Church or to obey our exhortation, we command by apostolic authority that your fraternity, neither out of hatred nor out of favor toward anyone, shall fail to strive to ordain as bishop the archdeacon of Autun, Landric, whom they elected, either through yourself or through your suffragans, provided that the authority of the holy Fathers is shown not to oppose this.

If he refuses to accept this order and proves himself inflexible, we wish you, together with his bishop, to apply force to him and, with watchful diligence and pastoral severity, compel him to receive episcopal ordination.

If your fraternity is negligent in this matter, you will undoubtedly incur the displeasure of the apostolic see; and if he comes to us, then, with God’s consent, he will be ordained by us.

Given at Piperno, on the second day before the Nones of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO COUNTESS ALDILASIA (1073)

He recalls her religious devotion and piety toward holy places and exhorts her always to undertake better things. He commends two monasteries to her protection.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Aldilasia [Adelasia], countess.

Although I know that by your spontaneous will you provide assistance to holy places and to their religious inhabitants, I have nevertheless taken care to exhort and admonish you to grow in greater and better things, and to carry out more diligently, at our command and by the authority of blessed Peter, what you have been accustomed to do voluntarily.

For the Lord has granted you both the dignity of honor and the abundance of power for this purpose: that they may be expended in his service and in the service of his people, and that, freely sharing your material goods with them, you may deserve to participate in their spiritual goods.

For this reason we commend to your care and protection the monastery of Fruttuaria and the brothers of that community, so that you may strive to provide them both the assistance of counsel and the support of protection against every affliction inflicted by those who harass them, so that their prayers before God may also bear fruit for the salvation of your soul.

In the same way, we entrust to your vigilance the abbot of the monastery of Clusium and the possessions of that monastery, to be guarded and protected. We have heard that he is laboring under a heavy burden of tribulations.

Nor should anyone’s favor or reward turn you aside from your good intention, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10). We have decided to impress and enjoin these matters upon you briefly, dearest daughter, so as to make you more ready to carry out good works and, as the saying goes, to spur on one who is already running.

Thus, devoted to God and watchful in good deeds and in the protection of God’s servants, may you be able to attain the reward promised by the Lord: “The one who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and the one who receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (ibid.).

Given at Sezze, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF BOHEMIA (1073)

He commends his devotion toward the apostolic see. He confirms what his predecessor Alexander II had granted him as an honor. He urges constancy in his promises. He promises that he himself will decide, within the duke’s territory, whatever the legates cannot determine.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia.

A long interval of time has now passed since your nobility promised the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, an abundant devotion of heart and zeal, and since, among the other rulers, an especially singular and outstanding affection was bound to you by the generous kindness of the apostolic see.

You can sufficiently perceive the proof and indication of this from the goodwill of our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander, who never yielded to your petitions without the concern and labor of himself and the sons of the holy Roman Church. As a sign of intimate affection—a sign not customarily bestowed upon a layperson—he sent you the mitre that you requested.

Nor do we, in our own time, wish, with God’s providence, the grace of such affection to be weakened. Rather, if there is anything in which it may be joined more firmly, together with justice, our concern desires greatly to obtain this from God.

You ought faithfully to consider, both for the sake of your dignity and for your salvation, how constant you are in your vows toward the apostolic see and how persevering in your promises. For it is written: “Vow, and fulfill your vows” (Psalm 75).

As for what those vows are and of what kind, we think your own conscience has sufficiently reminded you. As for the causes and affairs which, in those regions, were brought before the hearing and examination of our legates but, because of the hindrance of sins, could not be determined by a suitable decision, the care of our office compels us, even though no one asks it of us, to bring them, with the Lord’s help, to the conclusion that justice demands.

Moreover, we wish what they themselves have decided there to remain unchanged in the meantime, until the affairs are brought before us, and we command this by apostolic authority.

May almighty God, who is the giver and author of every good, make you such in your vows and actions that, when in the future judgment you come before the heavenly judges, namely Peter and Paul, your conscience may be able to mark and display before their eyes nothing except what is worthy of reward.

Given at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO WOZELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG, AND OTHERS (1073)

He laments that war has arisen between them and King Henry. He orders them to desist from arms until he learns the cause of the dispute through his legates.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Wozelin [Vozelon], archbishop of Magdeburg; Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt; Leton [Toton], margrave; and the other princes of Saxony.

We do not think it hidden or unknown to you with what violence and through what pressure from our brothers I have been compelled to undertake the burden and administration of the universal Church, shaken by many waves of disturbances and almost imperiled as though by a kind of shipwreck. My conscience bears witness to how unequal I judged myself to so great a burden and with what anxiety I longed to avoid the name of apostolic dignity.

But since a person’s way is not in his own hand but in the disposition of the One by whom human steps are directed, it was impossible for me to defend my intended wishes against the divine will. Therefore I must watch and reflect carefully on how, with God’s help, I may proclaim and faithfully administer those things that concern the advancement of ecclesiastical religion and the salvation of the Lord’s flock.

I am compelled to this above all by the fear that, before the heavenly Judge, negligence in the administration entrusted to me may accuse me, and by the duty of love toward the prince of the apostles, who from my infancy nourished me beneath his wings with a singular compassion and cherished me in the lap of his mercy.

Amid the other anxieties of our cares, however, one concern presses most heavily upon us: we have learned that such discord and such hostile actions have arisen between you and Henry, your lord, that as a result many homicides, fires, plundering of churches and of the poor, and the pitiful devastation of the country are taking place, as we hear.

For this reason we have sent to the king, exhorting him and admonishing him on behalf of the apostles Peter and Paul to refrain for the time being from arms and every assault of war, until we send him messengers from the apostolic see who can carefully investigate the causes of so great a disagreement and, with God’s favor, bring it to peace and concord through an equitable settlement.

Likewise, we wish you to understand that we exhort you and admonish you by apostolic authority to quiet every movement on your side and observe these same truces of peace, and not, on any pretext, place an obstacle in the way of the peace that, with God’s help, we must establish.

Since, as you know, lying to us is sacrilege and abandoning justice is shipwreck of the soul, we wish none of you to doubt that, after the truth of this matter has been examined, we shall strive, with God’s providence, to decree whatever appears equitable and to establish it by a firm agreement.

Whichever party we discover to be suffering injuries and the violence of trampled justice, to that party, without doubt, setting aside every fear and consideration of personal favor, we shall grant our favor and the protection of apostolic authority.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XL. TO COUNTESS MATHILDA (1074)

[Col. 0321D] He rejoices in her devotion toward the apostolic see. He urges her to persevere and to come with her mother to visit the thresholds of the blessed apostles.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Mathilda, a maiden of outstanding character.

Because your Serenity’s letter, sent to the apostolic see, testified that your goodness is ready to show the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the same love which Saint Paul, the chosen vessel and Peter’s fellow apostle, earnestly strove to preserve until death for Jesus Christ our Lord, we are filled with immense joy and render to almighty God whatever thanks we can.

But let your prudence know that honorable undertakings and religious beginnings require a more honorable perseverance and, with God’s help, a most devout completion. Therefore, if it should happen that your glorious mother returns to Rome at this time, we earnestly admonish—or rather, we ask—your affection to come with her to visit the apostles, unless some pressing necessity that must not be neglected should detain you.

Furthermore, in the letter that we received in your name on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, we trust that we have already given, through the embassy of our letters, the answer that seemed appropriate to us.

May the mercy of almighty God, which continually surrounds and protects his faithful, graciously deem you worthy of constant protection, and, after the course of this life, prepare your soul for the heavenly kingdom.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XLI. TO ORZOCOR, JUDGE OF CAGLIARI (1074)

[Col. 0322B] He urges him to consult with the other judges of Sardinia concerning the matter he had entrusted to him and to reply within a year with what seemed appropriate to him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Orzocor [Orzocco], judge of Cagliari in the province of Sardinia.

We have received your letter, in which it was stated that you wished to come to us. We therefore are pleased that you should come, and with complete security. Once you have reached our shore, you should know that you need have no doubt that you may travel through the borders of our land both on your journey there and on your return.

Furthermore, we admonish your prudence concerning the matter that, through Archbishop Constantine of Turris, consecrated by us this year at Capua, we entrusted to you: speak with the other judges of Sardinia, and, after firmly sharing counsel among yourselves, promptly make known to us whatever you have decided and whatever is in your heart and mind about it.

For you should know that, unless within this year you give us a definite answer concerning this matter, we shall neither seek your replies any further nor leave the right and honor of Saint Peter unexamined any longer.

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XLII. TO SICARD, ARCHBISHOP OF AQUILEIA (1074)

[Col. 0322D] He calls a council to correct the depraved conduct of rulers and prelates. He urges him to attend on the appointed day together with his suffragans.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Sicard, his brother and fellow bishop of Aquileia.

We do not think your prudence is unaware of the extent to which the Church has everywhere been shaken by waves of disturbances and has almost become shipwrecked and submerged in the calamities of its own desolation.

For the rulers and princes of this world, each seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, trample underfoot every form of reverence and oppress the Church as though she were a worthless servant. They have no fear of bringing her to ruin so long as they can satisfy their desires.

The priests, however, and those who appear to have received the governance of the Church, almost entirely setting aside the law of God and withholding from God and from the sheep entrusted to them the duty of their office, strive through ecclesiastical dignities only for worldly glory. Things that, by a special dispensation, ought to have benefited the interests and salvation of many, they either neglect or disastrously consume in the pomp of pride and excessive expenditure.

Amid all this, the people, directed neither by the moderation of prelates nor by the restraints of commandments along the path of justice—but rather instructed by the example of those who govern in whatever is harmful and contrary to Christian religion—fall headlong and eagerly into almost every form of wickedness. They bear the Christian name not merely without observance of works, [Col. 0323B] but almost without faith.

Therefore, trusting in the mercy of God, we have resolved to assemble a council in the first week of Lent, so that, with divine mercy assisting and with the common counsel of the brothers, we may be able to find some comfort and remedy for so great a danger, lest we see in our time the Church’s ruin and destruction become irreparable.

For this reason we ask your fraternity and admonish you on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to present yourself before us at the aforesaid time, summoning with you, through both our letters and your own, the bishops who are your suffragans. In this way we may gird ourselves all the more safely and firmly for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty and religion, the more abundantly and closely we are surrounded by the counsels of your prudence and by the presence and wise deliberation of our other brothers.

Given at Rome, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XLIII. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF MILAN (1074)

The same subject.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to all the bishops who are suffragans of the Church of Milan, namely those of Brescia, Cremona, Bergamo [Bergomum], Lodi, Novara, Ivrea, Turin, Alba, Asti, Acqui, Tortona [Dertona], [Col. 0323D] and certain others, to some according to their merits.

We do not think it unknown to you that it was established long ago in the Roman Church that every year, for the dignity and benefit of the holy Church, a general council should be held at the apostolic see.

Therefore, considering at this time a very necessary reason for this assembly, we have resolved, with God’s favor, to celebrate a synod at Rome in the first week of Lent. We admonish and command all of you, by apostolic authority, to present yourselves there, so that together with you and with the additional attendance of others of your order, we may conveniently and reverently exercise the proper concern of our office in divine and ecclesiastical matters, with heavenly mercy assisting.

You must also look to this carefully and attentively: whoever, when his lord is hastening into battle, withdraws himself not only recognizes that he has undermined the lord’s favor toward him, but also that he has deservedly forfeited the benefit he received.

Let this example therefore show which of you—or rather, how all of you—are faithful soldiers of Christ. Strive to present yourselves to the divine armies with such ready will and zeal that, after victory has been gained in Christ, you may together be permitted to glory both in the strength of your deeds and in the abundance of your rewards.

Under the same authority and determination we also invite all the abbots of Lombardy to the aforesaid council, and we admonish and command them not to put forward any false excuse in this obedience.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XLIV. TO JERIMOR, BISHOP OF BRAGA (1074)

Restored to the bishop of Prague, who had been suspended, the revenues of his bishopric, so that, setting aside all delay, he might go with the envoys of his adversary-bishop to the threshold of the holy apostles. He mentions that he had written to his brother, the duke, so that he might send the bishop of Moravia and his envoys to Rome.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JEROMIR, bishop of Bragens** [for *Pragensi*, Hardouin, and likewise below]. [Cols. 0324C–0325A]

Although your disobedience and the offense which you committed in contempt of the legates of the holy Roman Church did not merit that your requests should be received while you were absent and not yet prepared to make satisfaction, nevertheless, so that you may not be able for a longer time to defend the delay or occasion of your absence on the grounds of an apostolic severity—though a just one—we have decided to remove the necessity which, as you complained in your letter, presses upon you, and the impediment to your coming to us.

Accordingly, by the authority of this letter we restore to you and grant you permission to retain whatever was forbidden to you by our legates, Bernard and Gregory, apart from the episcopal office. For you excuse yourself by complaining that, having been stripped of the possessions of your church and deprived of the necessities of life, you cannot carry out the obedience required for making satisfaction, as we have said above. We have also notified this to your brother, Duke Wratislaus, admonishing him not to permit anything from the customary tithes and revenues of your church to be denied or withdrawn from you while it is in his power.

Therefore we admonish you and, on behalf of the apostles Peter and Paul and through them with our apostolic authority, command you not to defend your absence any longer by any excuses, but not to fail to visit the threshold of the apostles on Palm Sunday. Know that we have admonished your brother to urge John, bishop of Moravia, likewise to come to us and to send envoys on his behalf such as will enable us, in our examination, to determine the causes of the dissensions.

Meanwhile, we wish and command you not to touch anything belonging to the possessions of the bishopric of Moravia, lest he too avoid appearing before our sight under some excuse concerning harassment. Take care to inform your brother the duke of the aforesaid time appointed for your arrival early enough that he may send the bishop of Moravia and his envoys together with you to the apostolic see.

*Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE XLV. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF BOHEMIA (1074) [Cols. 0325B–0325D]

He orders him to restore the revenues of the bishopric to his brother. He urges him to come to the apostolic see, or at least to send his envoys together with the bishop of Moravia.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WRATISLAUS, duke of the Bohemians, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Your brother Jeromir, bishop of Prague, complains that, having been stripped of the possessions of his church and deprived of the necessities of life, he is unable to come to the apostolic see to give an account of the matters being charged against him. Although his disobedience and evasion have fully deserved this, nevertheless, so that he may not be able to plead this as an excuse for his absence, we wish and command that everything forbidden to him by our legates, Bernard and Gregory, apart from the episcopal office, be restored to him in full, except those matters concerning which John, bishop of Moravia, brings an accusation against him.

In this matter we especially admonish your prudence not to permit anything from the customary tithes or revenues of the church to be denied or withdrawn from him while it is in your power, nor to create any opposition for him by which he might again complain that impediments prevent him from coming to us.

At the time when he himself, as he has been admonished by our letter, ought to visit the apostolic see, we would very much wish you also to be present, if this could be done. But if circumstances or the passage of time prevent it, we strongly admonish your nobility to urge the bishop of Moravia to present himself before us. In addition, send us from among your faithful such envoys as will enable us, after the truth of the matter has been diligently investigated and examined from every side, with the favor of divine clemency, to cut off all the causes of the dissensions and to establish by a definitive judgment whatever shall be equitable.

*Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of February, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE XLVI. TO GUILIELMUS, COUNT OF BURGUNDY (1074) [Cols. 0326A–0326C]

He urges him, together with certain other princes, as he had promised, to come to the aid of the Church, so that, once the Normans have been pacified, he may be able to bring assistance to the people of Constantinople.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GUILIELMUS, count of the Burgundians, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Your prudence should remember with what abundance of affection [the manuscript or print reads *arga affluentia*, evidently corrupt] the Roman Church long ago received your valor, and with what special charity it loved your friendship. For it would not be fitting for it to forget the promise by which you bound yourself to God before the body of the chief of the apostles, Peter, in the presence of our venerable predecessor, Pope Alexander, and of bishops, many abbots, and an innumerable multitude of people from various nations: namely, that whenever it should be necessary, your hand would not be absent from fighting in defense of the possessions of Saint Peter, if indeed you were summoned.

Therefore, mindful of the faithfulness of your nobility, we ask and admonish the prudence of your strength to prepare the valor of your army to come to the aid of the Roman Church, that is, of its liberty [perhaps also “and”]; if necessary, to come here with your army in the service of Saint Peter. We also ask you to urge the Count of Saint-Gilles, the father-in-law of Richard, prince of Capua, and Amedeus, son of Adelleta [Adelicta], as well as all the others whom you know to be faithful to Saint Peter and who likewise promised with hands raised toward heaven.

If you wish to send us some definite reply, give it to us through a messenger who will in every respect make us certain of your intentions. Let that same messenger come through Countess Beatrice, who should see to it that she, together with her daughter and son-in-law, takes pains in this matter.

We are not gathering this multitude of soldiers in order to seek the shedding of Christian blood, but so that the rebels themselves, seeing the expedition and fearing to engage in battle, may more readily submit to justice. We also hope that perhaps another benefit may result from this: namely, that once the Normans have been pacified, we may cross to Constantinople in aid of the Christians, who, grievously afflicted by the repeated attacks of the Saracens, urgently beseech us to extend to them the hand of your [*f.*, *our*, and likewise in Mutina] assistance.

For against those Normans who are rebellious toward us, the soldiers who are with us are sufficient. Be assured, indeed, that Peter and Paul, chiefs of the apostles, will bestow upon you and upon all who are wearied with you in this expedition, as we believe, a double—indeed, manifold—reward.

*Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE XLVII. TO COUNTESS MATILDA (1074) [Cols. 0326D–0328B]

He urges her to receive the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist frequently and to show devotion toward the most blessed Virgin Mary.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, MATILDA, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Only he who searches the secrets of the heart understands how great is my care and how unceasingly concerned I am for you and your salvation; he knows it much better than I myself do. Yet, if you do not neglect to consider the matter carefully, you will perceive, as I think, that I ought to care for you as much as I have detained you through zeal for charity, so that you would not abandon them in order to provide only for the salvation of your own soul. For charity, as I have often said and shall continue to say, following the heavenly trumpet, “does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13).

But since, among the weapons which, with God’s favor, I have given you against the prince of this world, I indicated that the most important was that you should frequently receive the Lord’s body, and commanded you to entrust yourself entirely to the sure protection of the Mother of the Lord, I have explained in this letter what blessed Ambrose thought concerning the reception of the Lord’s body.

For in the fourth book *On the Sacraments*, among other things, he says:

> “If we announce the death of the Lord, we announce the remission of sins. If, whenever the Lord’s blood is poured out, it is poured out for the remission of sins, I ought always to receive it, so that my sins may always be forgiven. Since I always sin, I ought always to have the medicine.”

Again, Ambrose himself, in the fifth book *On the Sacraments*:

> “If it is daily bread, why should you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily; live so that you may daily deserve to receive it. When [*f.*, “He who does not,” from Ambrose, book 5 *On the Sacraments*, no. 25] one deserves to receive it daily, one does not deserve to receive it after a year. Thus holy Job offered sacrifice daily for his sons, lest perhaps they had sinned either in their hearts or in their speech. Therefore you hear that whenever the sacrifice is offered, the death of the Lord, the resurrection of the Lord, and the remission of sins are signified—and you do not receive this daily bread of life? Whoever has a wound seeks medicine. The wound is that we are under sin; the medicine is the heavenly and venerable sacrament.”

Again, Pope Gregory, in Book IV of the *Dialogues*:

> “Therefore we ought to despise the present age with our whole mind, either because we already see that it has passed away, and to offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily victims of his flesh and blood. For this victim alone saves the soul from eternal destruction; through the mystery it restores to us the death of the Only-Begotten. Although, having risen from the dead, he no longer dies and death shall no longer rule over him, nevertheless, living in him immortally and incorruptibly, he is again sacrificed for us in this mystery of the sacred offering. For there his body is received; his flesh suffers for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us, which continually imitates the passion of the Only-Begotten Son for our absolution. For what believer could doubt that at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that what is highest is joined to what is lowest; that earthly things are joined to heavenly things; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?”

Again, John Chrysostom, patriarch, to the newly baptized:

> “See how Christ joined the bride to himself; see with what food of fullness he nourishes you. He himself is the substance and nourishment of our food. For just as a woman, compelled by the nature of her affection, hastens to nourish the child she has borne with the abundance of her milk, so Christ continually nourishes with his blood those whom he himself regenerates.”

For, as the same John writes to the monk Theodore:

> “The mortal condition is slippery by nature: it quickly falls, but is not slowly restored; and just as it falls easily, so it rises swiftly.”

We ought, daughter, to flee to this singular sacrament and desire this singular medicine. I have taken care to write these things, dearest daughter of blessed Peter, so that your faith and confidence in receiving the Lord’s body may increase. Your soul asks such a treasure and such gifts from me, out of love for your father—namely, the prince of heaven—not gold or precious stones, although you may be able to receive far better things from other priests according to your merits.

But concerning the Mother of the Lord, to whom I have principally entrusted you and do entrust you, and to whom I shall never cease entrusting you until we see her, as we desire, what can I say to you? Heaven and earth never cease praising her, although they cannot praise her as she deserves.

Hold this without any doubt: the higher, better, and holier she is than every mother, the more merciful and gentle she is toward converted sinners, both men and women. Therefore put an end to your willingness to sin, and, prostrate before her, pour out tears from a heart contrite and humbled. I promise you without hesitation that you will find her more ready than an earthly mother and gentler in her love for you.

*Given at Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May* [March, and likewise in Mutina], *in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE XLVIII. TO HUBERT, BISHOP OF GENOA (1074) [Cols. 0328C–0329A]

He orders that the wife of a certain Ansaldus, accused of adultery, be admitted to the purgation ordeal, while excommunicating her father and anyone else who should presume to prevent it.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUBERT, bishop of Genoa, and to all the clergy and people of that place, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Having understood your error, we fear greatly for your danger, because we have heard that among you the sacrament of the marriage bond, sanctioned by divine commands and laws, is being defiled by wicked efforts. For it is written concerning the marital bond: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Matthew [sic] 9). And the Truth altogether forbids a man to leave his wife, except perhaps on account of fornication.

We have been informed that a certain Ansaldus, your fellow citizen, was compelled by his father neither to keep his own wife, falsely accused of fornication, nor to accept the judgment of her purgation, which she herself greatly desires in order that the truth may be investigated.

Because this is utterly contrary to divine and human laws, we first admonish you, the bishop, and then all of you, and command by apostolic authority that, if the woman wishes to submit to a lawful examination, she be received with complete tranquility and due expectation, together with the proofs; and, if she appears innocent through the mercy of God, you must not under any circumstances permit her to be separated from her husband.

But if the father of the aforementioned Ansaldus—or indeed any mortal—should presume to obstruct or prohibit these things which we have commanded by divine authority, we admonish your fraternity, bishop, by apostolic authority, that, setting aside every consideration of personal favor, you must not cease to strike the guilty with the sword of anathema and cut them off from the body of the Church. Do not fail to notify us of this as quickly as possible by letter, so that we may impose the final hand.

Moreover, we wish you to strive to present yourself before us as soon as you can.

*Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May* [March, and likewise in Mutina], *in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE XLIX. TO ALL CHRISTIANS (1074) [Cols. 0329B–0329D]

He urges them to bring aid to the people of Constantinople, who were suffering many calamities at the hands of the Saracens.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, greeting and apostolic blessing to all who wish to defend the Christian faith.**

We wish you to know that the bearer of this letter, when he recently returned from the overseas regions, visited the threshold of the apostles and our presence. From him, as from many others, we learned that a pagan people had grown strong against the Christian empire and, with pitiable cruelty, had already devastated and seized by tyrannical violence almost everything as far as the walls of the city of Constantinople, and had killed many thousands of Christians like sheep.

Therefore, if we love God and recognize that we are Christians, we must grieve deeply over the pitiable condition of so great an empire and the great slaughter of Christians. Nor is it enough for our proper concern merely to grieve over this matter: it requires us to lay down our lives for the liberation of our brothers, following the example of our Redeemer and fulfilling the duty of brotherly charity. For just as he laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

Know, therefore, that, trusting in the mercy of God and in the power of his strength, we are acting and preparing in every way so that, with God’s help, we may bring aid to the Christian empire as quickly as possible.

Accordingly, by the faith through which, in Christ, you have been united in adoption as sons of God, we beseech you, and by the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we admonish you: let the wounds and blood of your brothers and the danger of the aforementioned empire move you to worthy compassion, and let your valor, for the name of Christ, willingly undertake the labor of carrying assistance to your brothers.

Whatever divine mercy may inspire in your hearts concerning this matter, take care to report it to us without delay through reliable envoys.

*Given at Rome, on the Kalends of March, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE L. TO BEATRICE AND MATILDA, HER DAUGHTER (1074) [Cols. 0330A–0330D]

He entrusts to them the settlement of the dispute between Dodo, bishop of Roselle, and Count Ugolino.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to BEATRICE and MATILDA, glorious and most beloved daughters in Christ, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Let your nobility not be surprised by what I have written to you concerning the case of Dodo, bishop of Roselle, for it would seem inhuman if I were to disregard the prayers and complaints of Count Ugolino. He has often importuned me to decide justly his case against the bishop of Roselle and to ensure that the same bishop do him justice.

Since I have a singular confidence in you above all the princes of the Roman Empire, I asked that through you the case between them be brought to a definite, just, and peaceful conclusion, so that he who is the just judge may be glorified through your efforts and your piety, at my urging.

For your charity knows, and, as I think, fully understands, that in all your actions I seek the honor of God and your salvation. Therefore I say with the prophet: “Offer the sacrifice of justice, and hope in the Lord” (Psalm 4). And again: “Judge for the orphan, defend the widows; then come and accuse me, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1).

I place helping one’s neighbor out of love for God, assisting the wretched and oppressed, and serving through prayers, fasts, vigils, and many other good works above everything else, because, with the Apostle, I do not hesitate to prefer true charity to all virtues (1 Corinthians 13).

For if this mother of all virtues—which compelled God to come from heaven to earth to bear our misery—did not instruct me, and if there were someone who, in your place, would assist suffering and oppressed churches and serve the universal Church, I would take care to urge you to abandon the world together with all its concerns.

But because you do not cast God away from your court, as many princes do; rather, you invite him to enter it through the sacrifice of justice, we ask you, and admonish you as our dearest daughters, to bring the good work you have begun to its perfect conclusion.

May neither human favor, nor love of money, nor the desire for empty glory obscure your sacrifice. For the one who serves God with this life in view sells a great thing for a paltry price.

By writing so little to you, whom I love with a sincere heart, I reveal that I am burdened with serious concern. For in such matters I do not obtain some substitute to dictate on my behalf, but subject myself to the labor personally, even though my style is rustic. For I know that, if I am loved as I love, you place no mortal above me.

May Almighty God, through the merits of the Supreme Lady and by the authority of blessed Peter and Paul, absolve you from all sins and bring you joyfully to the bosom of your universal mother.

*Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LI. TO ARNOLD, ABBOT OF SAINT-SEVER (1074) [Cols. 0331A–0331B]

He reproves him for not having come when summoned to the synod, confirms the sentence pronounced against him concerning a certain monastery on account of his contumacy, and advises him to come to Rome if he feels himself wronged.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ARNOLD, abbot of Saint-Sever, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We may accuse you of no slight disobedience because, after many complaints had been made against you in the Roman councils, the monastery of the Holy Cross belonging to the church of Saint Mary has still obtained no justice.

Although you appear already for a long time to have avoided the inquiry into the truth of this matter by frivolous excuses, nevertheless, in the present year you were summoned to the synod by our legate, Giraldus [Gerardus], bishop of Ostia, to settle our dispute, and you are said to have shown no reverence to God and Saint Peter. Indeed, despising the authority of the apostolic see, you neither came yourself nor took care to send others who could justly excuse you.

Therefore, because your absence provides the clearest indication of your injustice, it was determined in that synod that the right and possession of the monastery of the Holy Cross should be restored to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary.

Approving this determination, we command you by apostolic authority to permit the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Cross to hold its possession peacefully, as has been established.

But if you are confident that you have justice on your side, strive to come to us by the feast of All Saints, and notify the aforesaid abbot that you will come by the same deadline, so that, after the arguments of both parties have been investigated, we may, with God’s help, impose a definite conclusion upon your case.

*Given at Rome in the synod, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LII. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS (1074) [Cols. 0331C–0332A]

He praises him for appointing a religious abbot over the monastery of Saint Remigius. He authorizes him to administer another abbey if he is able to bear so great a burden; but if he cannot, he orders him to ensure that another abbot is appointed.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to MANASSES, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The Roman Church, long ago embracing your fraternity in the arms of maternal affection, has loved you with a certain special charity and has cherished you with the greatest care. We have supported and approved your advancement to such an extent that we cannot avoid grave danger if you do things that dishonor your order or are unbecoming to your dignity.

Therefore, whenever we have heard things about you that do not accord with your order, we have been overwhelmed with the greatest sorrow, and consequently cannot lightly disregard them.

Among the other complaints about you that have reached our ears, the complaint of the monastery of Saint Remigius severely disturbed and deeply angered our mind against you. But since we have now learned that you have ordered that monastery better than we had heard or hoped, because you placed there a man honorable in conduct and learned in letters, you have refreshed our mind with no small joy.

The abbot is very pleasing to us. If he could bear the burden of governing both abbeys, namely, Metz and Reims, I would praise this on that account, because he is both a religious and a wise man.

Otherwise, if, as he himself admits, the weight of governing both is beyond his strength, we ask your prudence—indeed, we admonish you by apostolic authority—to appoint there, with his counsel and consent, through the election of the community according to the rule of Saint Benedict, a suitable superior, with God’s permission, lest he succumb under excessive strain.

Know with certainty that the honest and regular ordering of that monastery’s governance will be as dear to us as if it were in the monastery of Saint Paul.

*Given at Rome in the synod, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LIII. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF METZ (1074) [Cols. 0332B–0333A]

He testifies to his love for him and asks him to pray to the Lord for him. He reports that Abbot Arnulf wishes to renounce the abbacy of Reims and be content with that of Metz.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HERIMANN [Hermann], bishop of Metz, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We gladly received the letter of your affection, because in it we recognized the abundance of your devotion toward us overflowing.

We wish and ought to show our due care toward everyone, because we have assumed responsibility for all and desire and long for the salvation of all. For although, unworthy in merits, we have accepted the governance of the universal Church and have received the ministry of preaching the Gospel, woe to us if we do not preach the Gospel.

And although we are debtors to all, it is especially fitting and necessary that we show the care of our concern toward those who are members of the household of faith.

Therefore let your fraternity know that our care for you is more earnest and our love for you more ardent, because we await from the prayers of your holiness the gift of a worthy recompense. We have undertaken to carry a heavy burden, and unless we are supported by your prayers and by those of all the faithful of Christendom, we cannot bear it at all.

For this reason we ask that we may deserve to be lifted up by the continual prayers of your holy community. For we ardently require not only the prayers of so holy a community, but also seek and desire those of the whole people.

Moreover, the abbot of Saint Arnulf, a man, as it seems to us, religious and faithful to you, has informed us that he would rather live poor under your rule than be rich and powerful elsewhere. For he wishes, if it seems good to you, to renounce the abbacy of Saint Remigius and be content solely with yours.

For this reason we have sent our letter to the archbishop of Reims, so that, according to God and with the counsel of this man, he may appoint another to govern that abbey, while this man is subject to you alone.

We ask you, therefore, to hold him more dearly for our charity, so that he may feel that coming to us has benefited him.

*Given in the synod, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LIV. TO THE CANONS OF SAINT HILARY (1074) [Cols. 0333A–0333C]

He orders that the custom of the canons of Poitiers be observed on the feast of Saint Hilary and on the feast of All Saints.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of Saint Hilary, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We wish you to know that the canons of Poitiers complained in our synod that you deny and oppose the custom which they ought rightfully to possess in the church of Saint Hilary. Namely, when they come there according to custom in procession on the feast of All Saints and on that of Saint Hilary, if the bishop is present, he himself should celebrate Mass; but if the bishop is absent, the dean or one of the senior canons of the church of Poitiers should perform the service in the bishop’s place.

When this matter was publicly debated before us in council, with Gozelin, archbishop of Bordeaux, defending your case together with certain others, we knew that such a custom was rightly and reasonably observed in the Roman Church at each station and in almost all the churches throughout the world. After the council had judged the matter, we found that they were making a just claim and determined by apostolic authority that they ought to retain the aforesaid usage.

Nevertheless, so that we might satisfy you more fully and remove every occasion for further complaint, we decided that the Poitevin clerics who were present should confirm their claim by oath, since proof always rests upon the one who asserts it. They themselves were entirely ready to do this in the presence of the archbishop of Bordeaux, and the same archbishop, having been admonished by us, declared that he would receive the oath.

Therefore we admonish and command you by apostolic authority, with every dispute between you and the canons of Poitiers brought to an end, to permit them henceforth, without any opposition, to retain their custom and their right, as you know was decreed above by synodal judgment.

*Given at Rome in the synod, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April* [seventeenth, *XVII*], *in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LV. TO THE SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS OF THE CHURCH OF AUCH (1074) [Cols. 0333D–0334A]

He commands them to obey their archbishop, as the legate of the apostolic see had ordered.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishop of Bigorre and the other suffragans of the church of Auch [Aux], greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The legate of the holy Roman Church, namely our confrater Giraldus [Gerardus], bishop of Ostia, admonished you to show due reverence to Guilielmus, your archbishop. But, as that same archbishop reported to us in complaint, afterward neither consideration of the subjection that was owed nor respect for apostolic authority moved you to obedience.

Although this contains no small presumption and condemnable contumacy, nevertheless, for the time being concealing your deeds with apostolic gentleness, we command you and order by apostolic authority that you in no way withhold from him the honor of due subjection.

But if you have anything against him, come together with him into our presence. If you bring forward anything worthy of discussion, then, with God’s help, after careful investigation we shall determine it by a suitable judgment.

*Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LVI. TO ROGER, BISHOP OF CHÂLONS (1074) [Cols. 0334B–0334C]

He commands him to come to Rome before the appointed day, so that his case may be settled.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROGER, called bishop of Châlons.**

King Philip of the Franks, bound to you by no slight affection, has earnestly asked us to absolve you, both by letters and through the words of his envoys. We clearly saw, however, that we could not do this without violating justice, since, according to the rigor of canonical discipline, we recognized that a much more severe judgment ought to be passed against you.

Nevertheless, still suspending the judgment of the punishment you deserve out of apostolic gentleness, we command you by this authority not to fail in any way to present yourself before us from now until the next feast of All Saints, so that, with God’s help, we may bring to a just conclusion the repeatedly renewed complaint of the church of Châlons against you.

We admonish you, moreover, not in the meantime to bring upon yourself still greater danger by contempt of or transgression against the sentence already pronounced.

If you are disobedient to us in these matters, and, excusing yourself by some evasion, do not present yourself before us within the aforesaid deadline, you may no longer doubt your condemnation and irrevocable deposition.

*Given at Rome in the synod, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LVII. TO GUILIELMUS, BISHOP OF PAVIA (1074) [Cols. 0334D–0335A]

He urges him to come to him with Margrave Azo, accused of an incestuous union with the bishop’s sister, so that his case may be investigated.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GUILIELMUS, bishop of Pavia, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have thought it necessary to inform you that Margrave Azo has been accused in the Roman synod of an incestuous union with your sister. For this reason he himself, through the woman’s relatives, promised satisfaction and requested a delay.

Therefore we ask and admonish your fraternity by apostolic authority that, prepared for the service of Saint Peter and instructed so that you may act more effectively, you in no way fail to come to us with that same margrave. Be assured that we shall receive you honorably and send you away honorably.

For although your assistance might not otherwise have been necessary to us, nevertheless, because of this matter you ought to present yourself before us, so that we may investigate carefully the questions that have arisen concerning the aforesaid marriage and, deciding justice by a lawful judgment, with the Lord’s help cut away whatever may appear dangerous and establish what accords with our office and with the salvation of those involved.

*Given at Rome in the synod* [“in the synod” is absent], *on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.*

## EPISTLE LVIII. TO GEUSA, DUKE OF THE HUNGARIANS (1074) [Col. 0335B]

He praises his observance toward the apostolic see and testifies to his affection for him. He writes that he should communicate through Margrave Azo whatever he wishes to make known to him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GEUSA, duke of the Hungarians, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
Having read your letter, we have recognized your praiseworthy profession of devotion, in which we understand that your heart and mind toward reverence for the apostolic see have been inflamed by divine fire. From this, an assured hope of your salvation is revealed, and no small joy has arisen for us: for those who conceive vows of due faith and devotion toward apostolic reverence may by no means fail to expect sure protections and benefits from them. [Col. 0335C]

Therefore we also admonish Your Love that your zeal for the honor of the apostles may always increase, and that, the more you recognize yourself each day as approaching their judgments through the necessary end of your life, the more earnestly you should strive to make them your debtors: so that, through the mercy of God and with their intercession, you may rejoice to attain forgiveness of your sins and the glory of eternal blessedness.

As for our charity, we do not wish you to doubt it in any way. Rather, with our innermost paternal affection poured out upon you, we promise—without any uncertainty—that you have a place with us in which to act and obtain whatever properly pertains to your salvation and honor. And if any of your enemies should wickedly attempt anything against you, he will unquestionably not only be deprived of our hearing, but will feel the indignation of apostolic grace stirred up against him. [Col. 0335D]

If at any time you wish to make known to our ears anything concerning either your own affairs or anything belonging to the service of apostolic reverence, you have the distinguished Margrave Azo, greatly beloved by us among the other princes of Italy, through whom whatever you intend to refer to the apostolic hearing may most suitably be reported and commended to us.

For the rest, may divine clemency protect you from the adversities of this present age and grant you invincible strength and resources to accomplish whatever is pleasing to it.

[Col. 0336A] Given at Rome in synod, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LIX. TO OTTON AND CHUONRAD, BROTHERS (1074)

He warns them not to cause trouble for the Church of Olomouc.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Otton and Chuonrad, brothers of Wratislaus, duke of the Bohemians.

Your nobility ought to remember that you previously received apostolic admonitions concerning the case of the Church of Olomouc: that you should not diminish its justice on any pretext, nor offer any assistance to those troubling it. Now we admonish you and ask you with paternal charity not to act in any way contrary to that Church, but, out of reverence for the holy Roman Church, whose apostolic privileges protect it, to show it love and the zeal of pious devotion, and, insofar as lies within your power, to ensure that its rights and possessions remain inviolate from you and your people.

This is a cause in which you can most suitably gain and secure for yourselves both the glory of divine reward, the sure protection of the apostles, and the fullness of our affection. But if—which we do not wish—you act otherwise, you will undoubtedly be able to corrupt these same things for yourselves and, God forbid, turn them to the contrary.

Given at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LX. TO SIGIFRED, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ (1074)

[Col. 0336C]

He rebukes him because he has presumed to take up for himself a case that had often been brought to the apostolic see, namely the dispute between Jeromir, bishop of Prague, and John, bishop of Moravia.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Sigifred, archbishop of Mainz.

An unworthy report concerning you has reached our ears. We would never have believed it had we not understood from your letter, which you sent us concerning the case of Jeromir, bishop of Prague, and John, bishop of Moravia, that you had conceived the idea of transferring from our judgment to an examination by your own arbitration the matter that they have between them and that has so often been brought before the apostolic hearing.

In this matter, since it is clearly apparent how little your advisers understand or heed the rights of apostolic authority, we invite Your Fraternity to review with us the canonical traditions and decrees of the holy Fathers. There, recognizing anew the arrogance of your presumption, you may likewise discover in yourself the fault of negligence and the rashness of your undertaking.

When John, bishop of Moravia, first wished to defend the rights of the Church over which he presides, he was subjected to many injuries and insults, and even, as we have heard, to scourging; yet he was unable to obtain justice. Nevertheless, your religious office is known to have undertaken no concern and no exertion in investigating the case.
