But after the apostolic see, having received the aforesaid bishop’s complaint, had repeatedly labored through letters and several times through legates to settle the case with a just conclusion and restrain the dispute, only then did your diligence awaken. You judged that the matter should be referred to your own investigations, and, I believe, wished to drag back into the depths of renewed contention and labor a brother who was swimming toward the harbor of justice and peace with the support of the apostolic see.

Although, therefore, on the one hand the negligence of your office and, on the other, the arrogance undertaken against the apostolic see—which accuses you—would rightly oblige us to be moved against you, nevertheless, using apostolic gentleness, we admonish you with calm affection not to presume any longer to undertake matters so disordered and ill-considered. Do not imagine that you—or even any patriarch or primate—possess permission to reconsider apostolic judgments; do not think of attributing or attempting anything against the holy Roman Church, without whose abundant clemency you cannot, as you yourself know, remain even in your own position.

For our part, with God’s help, through the authority of blessed Peter, as has long been decreed in the apostolic see, we shall endeavor to settle the dispute justly between the aforesaid bishops and to decree and confirm for the Church of Moravia those rights that belong to it.

Given at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXI. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF BOHEMIA (1074)

[Col. 0337C]

He urges him to make ever greater progress in observance toward the Roman Church. He explains that he has informed the archbishop of Mainz not to proceed further in the case of the bishop of Prague; therefore he declares that whatever the archbishop has done against him is void.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia.

Since, inflamed by divine fire, you have begun to possess a zeal of devotion toward the holy and apostolic Church, the charity poured out upon you does not permit us to remain silent; rather, through frequent exhortation we admonish you to conceive the ardor of divine service more fervently from day to day. For those vows deserve rewards and glory before God which, through successive stages of good works, strive toward the summit of perfection and continually conceive greater good desires.

Therefore, dearest son in Christ, strive to extend to the perfection of accomplishment the good things that, with God’s inspiration, your mind and devotion have proposed, so that apostolic benevolence, with no sloth weakening it, may always embrace you with greater affection according to your merits.

Concerning the relics and privilege about which you asked us: when your messenger, the church having been completed and perfected, seeks from us counsel regarding its consecration, we shall kindly endeavor to satisfy your wishes.

As for Sigifred, archbishop of Mainz, we severely rebuked him by our letter for the presumption he displayed in the case of Jeromir, bishop of Prague, telling him not to begin occupying himself any further with such negligence [perhaps: rashness] and folly. Nevertheless, if he has done anything against you by a rash judgment, consider it nothing, protected and defended by the prior intervention of apostolic authority until our legation reaches you again; and do not doubt that it will bring danger more to him than to you.

For the rest, rejoice that you are always protected by apostolic blessings.

Given at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXII TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY (1074)

[Col. 0338B]

He wonders why he has not come to visit the apostolic see. He urges him to do so and to arrange for his brothers to offer prayers for him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

Your words are pleasing and sweet to us, but they would delight us far more abundantly if Your Love burned more ardently toward the Roman Church. We discover that the flame of your affection lies in this: we cannot obtain the comfort of your visitation, which we have so often sought.

We do not think this should be attributed to your other occupations, except that we see Your Holiness avoiding labors and, as though through laziness [or: in laziness], evading somewhat weightier affairs by various pretexts. Therefore let Your Religiousness know that, although until now we have endured with astonishment your absence from us, henceforth we cannot bear it without great anxiety and disturbance of mind.

You ought to remember how many and how important affairs we have placed in your hands and in those of our brother Giraldus [Gerard], bishop of Ostia. Because of your absence these matters either perish through neglect or cannot reach a suitable conclusion. For when we sent the aforesaid bishop beyond the mountains in the service of Saint Peter, to the king, we expected you to come.

Therefore, although moved, we admonish Your Love with intimate affection to take care to visit us as soon as possible, since we are placed amid many great anxieties. We carry—for though weak, though beyond the strength of mind and body, we alone nevertheless carry it—in this most serious time an immense burden of affairs, not only spiritual but also worldly; and each day we fear our downfall beneath the impending weight. For we are by no means able to find in this world aids of support [the editor thinks that *nequam*, “wicked,” should be read].

For this reason, by almighty God we beg you to remind your brothers, as we requested from the beginning of our ordination, to pray continually to God for us. Unless we deserve divine assistance through the intercession of them and of other faithful people, we shall not be able to avoid danger to ourselves and, what we fear more, to the Church.

May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, so cause you and those entrusted to you to live in this mortal life that, with God leading, you may reach the true and immortal life.

Given at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXIII. TO SANCHO, KING OF ARAGON (1074)

He commends his observance toward the Roman Church and his efforts to have the Roman office celebrated in his dominions. He refuses to accept the accusation of an absent person and promises to send a messenger after his legate has returned to settle the case.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Sancho, king of Aragon.

We gladly received the letter of Your Nobility, full of sweetness, in which we clearly perceived with what faithfulness you burn toward the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and toward the Roman Church. Even if we had not seen your letters, we had learned this clearly through the legates of the apostolic see.

When you assert that, under your authority, the office of the Roman rite is performed by your zeal and commands, you are recognized as a son of the Roman Church and as possessing with us that concord and friendship which the kings of Spain once had with the Roman pontiffs.

Therefore remain steadfast, hold firm confidence, and complete what you have begun. For we trust in the Lord Jesus Christ that blessed Peter the apostle, whom the Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, established as prince over the kingdoms of the world, and to whom you show yourself faithful, will bring you to the honor of your desire and himself make you victorious over your adversaries.

For when the Lord loves a son, he scourges and chastises him (Hebrews XII). It is better and more advantageous to arrive at prosperity through adversity. He who says to those who laugh, “Woe to you, for you shall weep” (Luke VI), himself declares those who mourn blessed, because they shall be comforted (Matthew V).

At present we have given no answer concerning Solomon, because the sacred canons do not admit an accusation by letter when the accuser is absent. There is also this consideration: our legate, who was in those regions at that time, was absent, and we did not wish to give judgment in the matter without him. When he returns, with God’s favor we shall take counsel and send our messenger to you. After carefully investigating this and the other necessary cases, he will bring each one to the conclusion of a just determination.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXIV. TO ALPHONSO, KING OF CASTILE, AND SANCHO, KING OF ARAGON (1074)

He urges them to receive the Roman office. Through his legates he confirms the excommunication and deposition of a certain Simoniac.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Alphonso [Col. 0340A] and Sancho [Note: [Col. 0339D] Concerning Alphonso and Sancho, kings of Spain: Roderic, archbishop of Toledo, on Spanish affairs], peer kings of Spain (*a paribus*), and to the bishops established in their dominion.

Since the blessed apostle Paul indicates that he visited Spain (Romans XV), and since afterward seven bishops were sent from the city of Rome by the apostles Peter and Paul to instruct the peoples of Spain—bishops who, after destroying idolatry, founded Christianity, planted religion, showed the order and office of divine worship, and dedicated the churches with their blood—your diligence should not be unaware how great a concord Spain had with the Roman city in religion and the order of divine worship. But after the kingdom of Spain had long been polluted by the madness of the Priscillianists, corrupted by the perfidy of the Arians, and separated from the Roman rite, first through the invasions of the Goths and then through the incursions of the Saracens, not only was religion diminished, but worldly resources were also weakened.

Therefore, as beloved sons, I exhort and admonish you that, like good offspring, although after long divisions, you may at last recognize the Roman Church as truly your mother, and find us within her as brothers. Receive the order and office of the Roman Church—not that of Toledo or any other church, but of that Church which was founded by Christ through Peter and Paul upon the firm rock and consecrated with their blood, against which the gates of hell—that is, the tongues of heretics—have never been able to prevail. Hold this order as do the other kingdoms of the West and the North.

Since you do not doubt that you received from her the beginning of your religion, it remains that from her you should also receive the divine office in ecclesiastical order. This is taught by the letter of Pope Innocent addressed to the bishop of Gubbio (Letter 29); it is indicated by the decrees sent by Hormisdas to the bishop of Seville; and it is demonstrated by the councils of Toledo and Braga. Your bishops who recently came to us also promised in writing, according to the constitution of the council, that they would do this, and confirmed it in our hands.

Moreover, just as we have dealt through the legates of the Roman Church with the other excommunications, so we have decreed and confirmed as valid the deposition and excommunication that Bishop Gerard of Ostia, together with Rembaldus [Rambaldus], imposed upon Munio the Simoniac, who had been ordained over Simeon, our venerable brother, bishop of Huesca [Note: [Col. 0340D] Pagius, in the year of Christ 1074, no. 11, advises that “Oscensem” should be read “Ocensem.” For Huesca is distinct from Oca.]—until, coming to his senses, he makes satisfaction concerning the bishopric that he held unlawfully and withdraws from it.

Given at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAGUSA (1074)

He rebukes them because, after imprisoning their bishop, they chose another for themselves. He orders them to release him and sends a legate for this purpose. If the matter cannot be brought to an end through that legate, he orders the bishop and the man whom they elected to come to Rome.

[Col. 0341A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to all the people of Ragusa, if they obey.

It has reached our ears that you seized Vitalis, your bishop, and, after placing him in custody and chains, elected another as your bishop. We believe that no faithful person can doubt how disordered, unjust, criminal, and contrary to divine and human laws this act is.

Therefore we have sent to you our beloved brother Giraldus [Gerard], archbishop of Siponto, so that, acting as our legate in this matter, he may determine the justice of the case. We therefore admonish you and command you by apostolic authority that, after releasing the bishop whom you hold captive, you gather in the presence of the aforesaid archbishop. In order to render canonical justice in this matter, and also in the other ecclesiastical cases among you that require correction, you must show him the same obedience and support that you ought to show in our presence.

But if, because sins obstruct it, the case cannot be examined and settled among you, we wish you to bring into our presence both the bishop whom you have captured and the man whom you irregularly elected, so that, with God’s help, we may judge what is just in the matter and authoritatively establish it.

Otherwise, if you despise our—or rather, the apostolic—admonitions and commands, know that by apostolic authority you are to be expelled and separated from the thresholds of the Church and from all Christian communion.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXVI. TO THE MONKS OF SAINT QUIRICUS, ETC. (1074)

He orders the goods taken from the monastery of Saint Quiricus to be restored to the bishop of Rieti.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to all the monks and laymen of the monastery of Saint Quiricus, to all the Joseppingi, to the sons of Albericus [Alberti, and likewise below], and to the sons of Rapterus.

[Col. 0341D] We wish it to be known to you that we have given the monastery of Saint Quiricus, which belongs by right to the Church of Saint Peter, to our brother Rainerius, our fellow bishop and bishop of Rieti. Therefore we ask—indeed, we command and order—that you assist him in everything and against everyone; that you, the Joseppingi, the sons of Albericus, and the sons of Rapterus, restore to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid bishop the castles that you hold; that you faithfully assist him in these and in all the goods belonging to the aforesaid monastery; and that you cause him no trouble in any way, if you wish to have the favor of Saint Peter and of us.

Otherwise, you will not escape the anger of our displeasure or the bond of excommunication.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXVII. TO GIRALDUS, BISHOP OF SISTERON (1074)

[Col. 0342A]

He orders him to abandon the church of Croscia, which he had invaded, and, if he thinks he has any right in that church, to come to him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Giraldus [Geraldus], bishop of Sisteron, if you obey.

Michael, a priest of the church of Croscia [Ococia], has complained to us that you invaded the aforesaid church—which you do not doubt belongs by right to Saint Peter—plundered its goods, seized its priests and clerics, and compelled them by force, contrary to law and right, to swear an oath.

Since you know that Ananias and Sapphira, because of their own goods which they promised to blessed Peter and did not give, incurred death (Acts V), by what impulse other than a diabolical one did you presume such an invasion? Why did you inflict such an insult? Why did you perpetrate such a sacrilege against the prince of the apostles?

Therefore we command you by apostolic authority, after reading these lines, without any pretext or delay, to release and restore to freedom the aforesaid church of Croscia, which is ours; to set the priests and clerics free; to restore to it everything that you took from there; and to permit them to serve God there in peace and quiet under the jurisdiction of blessed Peter and under our protection.

But if you think you have any right in the aforesaid church, come quickly to us with the aforementioned canons, so that you may receive justice in our presence. If you do not do this, know that you are to be excommunicated by apostolic authority.

Given at Rome on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO FROTERIUS, BISHOP OF NÎMES (1074)

He complains of the injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Saint Giles and its abbot, in contempt of the apostolic see. He orders him to desist.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Froterius, bishop in the province of Nîmes.

We formerly heard that, in the time of our predecessor Alexander, of venerable memory, you acted so unjustly against the monastery of Saint Giles—which that glorious confessor had handed over to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter—that you inflicted injuries upon it to such an extent that you presumed to seize its abbot, consecrated by the Roman pontiff, disregarding the rigor of the canons and despising the privileges derived from the apostolic see.

For this reason we then rightly grieved, and we still grieve, not doubting that insults were inflicted upon the Roman majesty through the abbot. We are likewise displeased that you presume, as though anew, to excommunicate the aforesaid monastery, since the authority of this holy see, in authentic documents granting privileges, testifies that you have no right to do so.

Therefore, commanding, we ask—and asking, we command—that under no pretext, even under the appearance of seeking justice, you presume to disturb the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, whether by excommunicating them or by celebrating Masses.

But if they seem to you to be unjust in any matter, we shall neither lack the will nor the power to render justice to you concerning them. If, however—which God forbid—you should prove neglectful of our exhortation, or rather of our command, [the printed text is defective], then, through the authority given to the apostle Peter, we, his vicars, they are released from the yoke of servitude in order that they may serve God freely.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] The passage seems to require restoration in this form: “But if, which God forbid, you should prove neglectful of our exhortation, or rather command, through the authority given to the apostle Peter, we, his vicars, [you will perceive]; but it will be evident [Col. 0344D] that they are released from the yoke of servitude in order that they may serve God freely.” The word order was improperly altered and a few words are missing. (Ed.)]

Given at Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXIX. TO GUILIELM, COUNT OF DIE (1074)

[Col. 0343B]

He sends back the bishop whom they elected and whom he consecrated, and orders them to obey him, especially in uprooting the Simoniac heresy. He threatens the count with excommunication if he refuses to restore his right to the bishop and his Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Guilielm, count of Die, and to all the faithful and subjects of the Church of Die.

We received your bishop Hugh kindly when he came to us; and because we heard that you had unanimously agreed upon his election, we ordained him as your pastor through episcopal consecration, so that, instructed in spiritual disciplines under his governance, you might, with God’s help, attain the fruit of the faith you have received and eternal glory.

Having therefore fulfilled in him the duty of our ministry, we send him back to you with all charity. We admonish you, by the faith in which you were redeemed and saved through Christ, to receive him with the honor and reverence due to him and to show him obedience and support in everything pertaining to the governance of his episcopate.

We earnestly admonished him, among other things, to rise with all his strength against the Simoniac heresy; not to consecrate the churches of his diocese, nor permit those already consecrated to celebrate divine worship, until they had first been wholly restored from lay hands, as is canonical, to their own right and to his episcopal care.

Therefore, so that no one may oppose him in carrying out our admonitions, we forbid this by apostolic authority under threat of anathema.

But addressing you particularly, aforesaid count, we are greatly surprised that, after you had elected our aforesaid brother bishop through the inspiration of divine clemency, with the consent of everyone else, and had sworn fidelity to him according to custom, you, elated for reasons unknown to me, presumed, while he was present, to stir up an insurrection against him; and that, after he came to the apostolic threshold, you plundered the clerics and citizens of the city and—which is especially wicked—seized a certain cleric.

Although by this great and cruel presumption you have provoked against yourself the judgment of apostolic punishment, nevertheless, at the request of that same bishop, we have so far delayed launching against you the dart of due vengeance.

However, so that this patience of ours may not raise you to audacity or draw us into the guilt of neglected justice, we admonish and command you by apostolic authority, without any delay, to correct with worthy satisfaction whatever you have rashly and unjustly committed against the bishop and the Church entrusted to him, and to presume to trouble him no further by any opposition.

Otherwise, know that our bishop, bound by apostolic command, will separate you as an enemy and opponent of justice from the thresholds of the Church, bound by the chains of anathema. And if he himself—which we do not believe—were to omit this through fear or favor, we nevertheless would not leave unpunished so great a crime of presumption [perhaps: “would leave”]; and the bishop, through negligence of his office, would have to reckon that a serious danger arising from his ministry threatens him.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXX. TO GUILIELM, KING OF THE ENGLISH [Note: [Col. 0344D] Concerning Guilielm, Marianus Scotus and Sigebertus in their chronicles under the year 1066; Guilielm of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, Book I, chapter 1.] (1074)

He commends King Guilielm’s observance toward him and the apostolic see and urges him to defend the churches. He indicates that he and the Church are involved in great disturbances. He advises that a certain privilege of Saint Stephen be upheld. He commends the goods of Saint Peter in England.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Guilielm, king of the English.

We have no doubt, beloved son, that you cling to your holy mother, the Roman Church, from your heart, since you were deeply distressed when you heard of the death of our predecessor, Alexander, of blessed memory, and rejoiced with genuine joy at the news of our promotion. You earnestly and humbly ask in your letters to know our condition. You display the affection of a good son, the affection of a son who loves his mother from the heart.

Therefore, beloved son, fulfill in deeds what you confess with your mouth; effectively carry out what you say, so that you may agree with Truth itself when it cries out, “Whoever loves me will keep my words” (John XIV); and elsewhere, “The proof of love is the showing of a deed.”

These are the words of your mother, among others: Do not cease to labor in every way for justice whenever the occasion requires it. Govern the Churches entrusted to you for defense in such a way that you may prepare remedies for the salvation of your soul and wipe away the stains of your sins; introduce the fragrances of virtues into yourself so that, with the Apostle, you may say, “We are the good odor of Christ” (II Corinthians II).

We advise, admonish, and beg you to place the honor of God and all that belongs to God before yourself and before all worldly things. For this is certainly the one thing whose frequent neglect is accustomed to destroy the powers of your dignity and drive them down to hell.

We impress these things upon you, dearest son, because among kings you alone are the one whom, as stated above, we believe we love more than the others.

As for our condition, which you humbly beg to know, receive it thus: Against our will we have boarded a ship which, through a stormy sea, the violence of winds, the force of whirlwinds, and waves rising as high as the sky, is thrown into uncertainty. Hidden rocks and others appearing from far off in the depths confront it; yet, though with danger, it meets them with all its strength.

The holy Roman Church, over which, though unworthy and unwilling, we preside, is continually and daily shaken by various temptations, by very many persecutions, by the snares and deceitful accusations of hypocrites and heretics; and it is secretly and openly pulled apart in different directions by worldly powers. To oppose all these things and to guard most carefully against these and many other dangers, after God, is especially the concern of our office and care. Day and night we are consumed by it; by these and similar matters we are continually torn apart, although for the time being such things may seem to us to smile upon us through the children of this world.

Yet, thanks be to God, worldly things are compelled to displease us. Thus we live, and, with God’s consent, thus we shall live.

As for the privilege of Saint Stephen about which you wrote, it concerns the salvation of your soul. We therefore advise you to uphold it as valid in the form in which our legates Peter and John Minutus judged that it should canonically be observed.

If, however, something additional seems to you to have been written into the privilege, the more you grant to God and Saint Peter for the sake of blessed Stephen, the greater things you will undoubtedly receive from them in recompense.

Concerning the possessions of Saint Peter that are collected in England, we admonish you to watch over them as you do your own, and we entrust them to your generosity as though they were yours, so that you may find Peter a pious and gracious debtor and may remind him that he ought to assist you in return for the many things you have contributed to him.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Nones of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXI. TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH (1074)

[Col. 0345D]

He commends her humility and charity, urges her to advance in these qualities day by day, and advises her to persuade her husband of those things that chiefly concern the salvation of his soul.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Mathilda, queen of the English.

Having heard the letters of Your Nobility, beloved daughter, we understood that your generosity is devoted to love and humility. From them we gladly received an indication and certain hope of your salvation. We do not think the salvation of one who is recognized as serving humility and love from the heart can be doubted, since the whole law is contained in these.

We expect such gifts and others like them from you—indeed, with the whole desire of our mind we wish to receive them—so that, noble by blood, you may live nobler still through the integrity of holy conduct.

Urge your husband: do not cease to suggest what is useful for his soul. For it is certain that, if an unbelieving husband is saved through a faithful wife, as the Apostle says (I Corinthians VII), then a faithful husband is also increased toward what is better through a faithful wife.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Nones of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXII. TO GOTEFRED, DUKE (1074)

He rebukes him because he did not send soldiers to assist Saint Peter, as he had promised. He urges him to send them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to Gotefred [Gotifred], duke.

If you had remained as steadfast in fidelity to the prince of the apostles as you promised us, and had clung to him from your heart, we would owe you much, as though by agreement and true charity. But because “all have turned aside; together they have become useless,” and, as the Psalmist says, “there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm XIII), you have followed the path of many others and turned aside.

Where is the assistance you promised? Where are the soldiers whom you promised us you would lead for the honor and support of Saint Peter?

But because you have not fulfilled what you promised to blessed Peter, we, although unworthy and called his vicars, remain attached to you by no other promise than that we must counsel you as a Christian.

Remember that your father promised many things to the holy Roman Church. If he had carried them out, we would rejoice with you concerning him in a very different and happier way from what we now feel.

Concerning Sardinia, since the deadline we set has already passed, we send no other instruction than what we said together in person.

Finally, if you wish to remain immovably steadfast in what you promised us—namely, to cling to Saint Peter from your heart—we shall hold you as a dearest son, and you will have us, although unworthy, as a gentle father.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO ISEMBERT, BISHOP OF POITIERS (1074)

[Col. 0346D]

He orders him to give an account in the provincial council before his metropolitan concerning the monastery of Nobiliacum [Obilciacum], which the clerics of Saint Hilary complained was being forcibly held by him; and, if he considers himself wronged, to come to him at Rome.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Isembert, bishop of Poitiers.

The clergy of the congregation of Saint Hilary came [read: *venere*] to us, complaining about you concerning the monastery of Nobiliacum. For they say that it belongs by right to Saint Hilary and is being held by you without any lawful justification. They further testify that your Prudence received the apostolic letters of our predecessor Alexander, but they make clear, by repeated protest, that they have not been able to obtain justice from them. They also assert that an estate called Campaniacum is being unjustly devastated, with your consent, by your brigands. In addition, they state that, according to ancient custom, they went with the sacred relics and their people to the mother church during the Rogation Days, but that your canons, to their humiliation, closed the church doors against them and denied them entry.

If these things have indeed happened, by apostolic authority we command you to appear before the council of the bishops of your province and your metropolitan. After an account has been rendered concerning all these matters and the truth has been fully investigated, you must not fail to provide them with justice accordingly. But if, for any reason, you refuse to do this, or if you recognize that you are being unjustly burdened, come to us on the Feast of All Saints with some of the clergy of Saint Hilary, so that, in our presence, your controversy may be carefully investigated and understood and, with God’s help, may receive its lawful conclusion; and so that both our concern—which keeps watch over many matters—and your dispute may thereafter rest peacefully, brought to an end in these causes.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF BEAUVAIS (1074)

He absolves them from excommunication at the prayers of the bishop whom they had offended. He urges them to obey him and receive penance from him.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Beauvais, if they have repented, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you have done things astonishing and hitherto unheard of, and have perpetrated deeds to be detested and abhorred; because, raging against peoples who do not know God and sharpening inhuman tongues, you presumed against God and your Lord; therefore the holy Roman Church, by the authority of the Fathers and the sanction of the canons, rightly hurled against you the dart of anathema and unsheathed against you the sword of dread punishment, as your great and grievous merits deserved.

But after your son and our brother, your bishop William, moved by paternal compassion, sent us his letter on your behalf at the time of the synod, and after we perceived that he was well disposed toward you and was returning good for evil, we were moved by his prayers and, in our customary compassion, condescended to you. Absolving you by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we immediately arranged to inform you by our letters of the absolution granted to you.

Therefore, by that same authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and by our own, we admonish you henceforth to be subject and obedient to him, as to your bishop and a son of the holy Roman Church. And, if you have not yet done penance for so great a crime, receive it without delay according to the salutary counsel of that same bishop, so that your spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Given at Rome, on the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXV. TO PHILIP I, KING OF THE FRANKS (1074)

[Note: Concerning Philip I, king of the Franks: the continuation of Aimoinus, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, Book V, chapters 48 and 50.]

He urges him to repair the damage inflicted on the church of Beauvais and to imitate his predecessors in defending and enlarging the churches.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Philip, king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

You have informed us by your letters and envoys that you wish to obey blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, devoutly and appropriately, and that you eagerly desire to hear and carry out our admonitions concerning matters belonging to ecclesiastical religion. If this has indeed been fixed in your heart by divine inspiration, we ought to rejoice greatly that Your Eminence, inclined toward divine reverence, considers and understands the matters belonging to royal administration.

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter, we admonish your nobility and entreat you with every affection of charity to strive to appease God. Among the other things that it is your duty to correct, do not fail, in proportion to the greatness of your name and honor, to repair to some degree the injuries inflicted by you upon the church of Beauvais.

For we wish you, together with us, to attend carefully and consider how greatly your predecessors—the most illustrious and renowned kings—were loved by the apostolic see and held in glory and praise throughout nearly the whole world, while their royal majesty was devoted to enlarging and defending the churches and remained free and steadfast in upholding justice. But after such virtue began to grow weak among their successors through the subversion of divine and human laws, the glory, distinction, honor, and power of the whole kingdom were altered along with its perverse customs, and the kingdom’s most noble reputation and condition declined from the summit of their splendor.

The care of the office we have undertaken compels us frequently to impress these and similar matters upon you, even, if necessary, in harsh language. For although it is neither safe nor permitted for us to conceal the word of preaching or keep silent anywhere, nevertheless, the greater the dignity and the more exalted the person, the more earnest ought our care and outcry to be for his correction, as the Lord admonishes us through the prophet, saying: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58), especially since the virtue of Christian rulers ought to be found with us in the camp of that same king, for the protection of Christian soldiery.

Therefore, so that you may be the singular and undivided heir before God and human beings of the nobility and glory of those whose successor you are in the kingdom, we exhort you above all to imitate their virtue and, by pursuing God’s justice with all your strength, to restore and defend the churches as far as you can. Thus may almighty God protect and exalt the government of your kingdom by the right hand of his power here, and grant you the crown of eternal glory in the future reward.

Given at Rome, on the Ides of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO HUMBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS (1074)

He commends the bishop of Mâcon and exhorts him to defend the churches.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, and his suffragan bishops, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are sending to you our brother, the bishop of Mâcon, whom we ordained for certain reasonable causes, with our letters and the apostolic seal, so that he may bring you reliable signs and indications concerning the rank and honor of the priestly office he has undertaken.

Although we do not doubt that you will promptly show him the due affection of brothers, we have nevertheless judged it appropriate to add to his position, and to our recommendation of him to you, something like a privilege, so that your charity toward him may shine more abundantly in proportion as the bond of your fraternity and consideration for apostolic reverence commend him to you as more closely and eminently connected.

Therefore we ask and admonish you in the Lord to receive him with the affection of complete love and worthy congratulations, and to offer him, with every care and effort, whatever counsel and assistance you can for governing the church entrusted to him and for retaining—and, wherever necessary, recovering—its rights.

For the more severely the Church is everywhere shaken in these times by disturbances on account of our sins, the more diligently we must join together our counsels and whatever strength we possess for its defense, so that, with God’s help, we may be able to withstand such dangers, strengthened in the warfare of Christ and in fraternal affairs by mutual support.

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO BEATRICE AND HER DAUGHTER MATILDA (1074)

He praises the humble penance of the bishop of Strasbourg and censures them because they unjustly detained him when he was coming to Rome. He orders them to release him and send him as far as Milan. He declares that he granted the bishop of Piacenza and other bishops of Lombardy, out of necessity, permission only to confirm. He gives an account of certain actions of his that had been criticized.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the duchess Beatrice and her daughter Matilda, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since the Prophet testifies that almighty God, whom we are commanded to imitate, does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (Psalm 50), we who are sinners, even if we do not perceive the contrition of hearts in others sufficiently or completely, ought nevertheless not to disregard what we have learned or count it as though it were nothing.

Guarnerius, bishop of Strasbourg, after he had unworthily treated the dignity of his order through the deeds of his sins, was summoned to correction by our lord of revered memory, Pope Alexander. Alone among all the bishops of the German land—many of whom, having likewise been summoned, were stained not only by carnal crime but also by the pollution of simony—he sought the threshold of the apostles, anticipated the place of judgment in the form of humility, and, fearing the apostolic rod, fell prostrate on his face, announcing and contemplating his sins.

Now, having been corrected by apostolic censure, he has come to have the apostolic clemency pronounced in his case. As we have heard, he demonstrated his remorse and obedience through great exertion, fasting and often traveling on foot, so that our brothers judged and decreed that, considering the circumstances of the times, he ought to be shown mercy. Although we did not grant him the restoration of episcopal office according to his desire, what purpose would it serve at this time to exercise canonical severity against him, when, if he were removed, perhaps no one else would occupy his place except one able to pay a very large sum of money?

For the rest, consider carefully in your hearts how dishonorable what you did to him is for you, how shameful for me, and how insulting to blessed Peter and the apostolic see: in these lands, where the defense of pilgrims ought to be especially secure, unexpected dangers lie hidden, and our will in this matter—although we prohibit it to other rulers—may be accused of appearing to consent because of our familiar affection for you. This is especially so since we commended this same brother to you by our letters with no small confidence.

Therefore we earnestly entreat and admonish your nobility to soothe his injuries as far as you can, to let him depart with every sign of goodwill and open charity, and, as we requested in the letters mentioned above, to provide him safe conduct as far as Lord Erlembald [Erbombald] of Milan. Know that we have instructed him by letter not to undertake anything adverse against you or your people on this account.

As for Dionysius of Piacenza and the other bishops of Lombardy who had come to us, we granted them nothing concerning episcopal office except the confirmation of children, because of necessity. But we hold the reins of the whole matter so firmly in our hand that, whether regarding those who have been corrected and seek pardon or those who are obstinate, there is no reason for despair either of mercy or of punishment.

Because we believe that, out of charity and reverence for the holy Roman Church, you have murmured against us concerning such matters, remembering our lord and father, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, who did not disdain to give an account to disciples murmuring against him, we too willingly render you an account of our actions. In this we have given you no other yet more certain signs of how great is the force of the affection by which we are bound to you.

Nor does it escape us how varied human opinion and judgment concerning us may be: in these same causes and actions, some say that we are credulous, while others say that we are too mild. To such people we see nothing more truthful or more proper to answer than what the Apostle says: “But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day” (1 Corinthians 4). May almighty God, the true examiner of hearts, teach us and you to do his will and place his law in the midst of our hearts.

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF THE BOHEMIANS (1074)

He commends the bishop of Prague, sufficiently cleared of the charges brought against him and restored to his church. He says that he will decide at the next synod the disputes between him and the bishop of Moravia, as well as those being argued between the duke himself and the bishop of Prague.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wratislaus, duke of the Bohemians, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your brother Larmirus [perhaps Jeromirus, as above in Letter 60, and so in Mutina], bishop of Prague, coming to the threshold of the apostles, presented himself before us with the humility that was appropriate. Confessing certain things charged against him, he offered suitable satisfaction for them; other charges he denied and removed himself from them by clearing himself in this manner: namely, that he had not struck John, bishop of Moravia; that he had not ordered that servants of the same bishop be stripped of their hair or that their beards be shaved; and that he had not requested a postponement through his legate as a pretext for evading the synod.

We therefore sent him back to his own see, fully reconciled to our affection and restored to him in its entirety, with our letters and apostolic seal, commending him to your nobility. You should love him with a brotherly heart, after every hatred and hostile rivalry between you has been removed; you should reverently regard in him the episcopal dignity, as is fitting; and whatever belongs by right to the church entrusted to him, or justly pertains to him in any way, you yourself should grant to him, and should compel all who are under your authority to return it to him without opposition.

Concerning the case that has for so long been drawn out between him and the bishop of Moravia because of the latter’s absence, we have decided as follows: at the future synod, both bishops shall either come to us in person or send such messengers that, in their presence and after they have reasonably set forth the case on both sides, we may, with God’s favor, give a clear definition of justice concerning this matter and settle their dispute without any further delay.

We very much wish your envoys also to be present there, so that, representing you, they may assist us in investigating the truth and may serve as witnesses to our decision. In the meantime, we have decided that the bishop of Moravia should hold the land over which the bishops are disputing.

In addition to these matters, your aforementioned brother complains about you, saying that you entirely deprive him of the authority and justice due to him over the provostship and castle of Saint Wenceslaus. Therefore we entreat and admonish Your Excellency with paternal affection: if you recognize that you are inflicting injuries upon him in this matter, then, out of regard for the fear of God—you to whom an account of your deeds will be required at the strict judgment—return, through your unforced goodness, to justice, and allow your brother to have what is his without any opposition.

But if his complaint cannot be settled between you, do not fail, at the appointed time of the aforementioned future synod, to send your envoys to us, even for this matter, so that, after the truth has been investigated and thoroughly understood, we may be able to decide what is just on both sides and, with God’s help, finally join you in brotherly peace and harmony.

Given at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE (1074)

He complains that, since attaining the pontificate, Anno has sent him no letters.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anno [Note: On Anno, Lambert of Hersfeld, *Chronicle* for 1075; Marianus Scotus, *Chronicle* for 1075 and 1077], archbishop of Cologne, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The dignity conferred upon you testifies how greatly the church of Cologne was joined to the Roman Church by serving it in all things. Yet this charity seems to have grown so cold in you that, from the time we undertook the labor of our office, we have received no letters of your visitation except those sent very recently.

We think that such visitation ought to be offered to us more frequently, because, remembering the discipline by which we were nurtured in the church of Cologne during the time of our predecessor, we show that church a special affection among the other churches of the West. As the sons of the Roman Church still testify, during the time of blessed Pope Leo we resisted with all our strength, for the honor of your church, the bishop of Trier—something that the same blessed Leo took seriously.

Since you have not shown our efforts the reciprocal affection that was due, we can rightly accuse you not only of negligence but almost of promoting a quarrel, in accordance with the saying: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12). Although, with God’s help, it would be very easy for us to settle this quarrel by the rod of apostolic correction.

For if we discover that you love the honor of blessed Peter not wholly but only in part, and that you love Cologne rather than Rome, you likewise will not be able to possess us wholly, but only in part. But if love and reverence for your mother, the holy Roman Church, should make you diligent instead of negligent and warm instead of lukewarm, you will undoubtedly obtain, not in part but in full, the favor of our common fisherman and our affection.

Given at Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXX. TO THE PEOPLE OF ANICIUM (1074)

He commands them to obey Stephen, their bishop.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Anicium, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your elected bishop Stephen [our Stephen is probably incorrect] sought the apostolic see with the humility that was required. Giving his hand to ours, he promised that he would obey the Roman Church and thereby recovered its favor, which he had previously appeared to have lost.

Because we have found that he wisely defended your church and through his efforts expelled the simoniacal Stephen and the usurper, we entrusted the governance of your entire bishopric to him, on the condition that, until he returns to us, he is not to exercise episcopal office himself, but is to instruct whichever of the religious bishops of your region he chooses to perform the duties belonging to the episcopal office.

We therefore admonish you by apostolic authority to show him the reverence due to him in all things and faithfully to provide your assistance for the defense of your church. Thus, after every contamination of simoniacal heresy has been expelled from your midst, you may have a lawful bishop and offer pure service to Christ our Lord and to his mother, blessed Mary.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO UDO, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER (1074)

He instructs him, in his place, to rebuke the bishop of Verdun for neglecting the authority of the apostolic see and to admonish him to restore the monastery of Saint Michael to communion. If he claims any right of his own, he is to seek it in an assembly of bishops or before the supreme pontiff. If he neglects to obey, the archbishop himself is to absolve the monastery from the interdict by his own authority and admonish the bishop to come to Rome.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, archbishop of Trier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother Theoderic, bishop of Verdun, as has often been reported to us, has long attempted to bend and compel the inhabitants of a place near a certain monastery of Saint Michael, within his diocese, to certain new customs by his own power and authority. Specifically, he wanted them to visit every year with litanies the greater church—that is, his episcopal see—with everyone assembled together.

When they refused to endure this unfamiliar practice, lest they perhaps give occasion for another [perhaps: “that other”] new exaction, he completely forbade divine worship to be performed there. Although the bishop had already received apostolic letters on this matter, admonishing him to release the place and to exact nothing from it except what was canonical and just, he noted the words—whose full sense has not been preserved—somewhat improperly, but entirely disregarded the intention and meaning of the known directive of his mistress [perhaps: of ours].

Therefore, since even privately speaking we do not have great confidence in his obedience, we admonish your fraternity by apostolic authority to summon, on our behalf and yours, the bishops who are your suffragans—namely Herimann of Metz and Poppo of Toul—assembled with you, and to call the aforesaid bishop to a conference. Inform him that we have not received with an even temper the disregard he has shown for the reverence due to the apostolic see.

We likewise admonish him to restore to the aforesaid place communion in the most holy and divine ministry. If he is confident that he has some right on the basis of justice, he should first grant those same people as much time for peace and quiet as the period during which he violently constrained them; afterward, either in an assembly of religious bishops or in the presence of the Roman pontiff, he should orderly seek whatever he considers to belong to his right.

For we were not placed in authority so that we might treat those entrusted to our care with power rather than justice.

But if he scorns to fulfill the instructions we have arranged to be carried out through you, we charge you, supported by apostolic authority, together with your brothers, to absolve the aforementioned place from every interdict and excommunication. By that same authority, strengthen the priests residing there to celebrate divine worship, and, on behalf of blessed Peter and ourselves, admonish the bishop by apostolic command to come to us and answer for his obstinacy and contempt of us through him [Note: We confess that we do not understand what is meant by “through him” here.]

We have had these letters of ours made known openly for this reason: once shown to the bishop of Verdun as well as to the other bishops, they may provide certainty concerning the administration and authority entrusted to you.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO ALL CHRISTIANS (1074)

He declares excommunicated all who retain the property of the monastery of Augia [the bishop of Constance mentioned below teaches that “Augiensis” should be written] that had been bestowed by Albert the Simoniac.

GREGORY, to all to whom these letters come, and so forth.

Although we recognize that, in accordance with the duty of our office and the universal care that, although unworthy, we have received through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we must diligently watch and labor to repel injuries against all churches and venerable places, nevertheless we are compelled, in a certain twofold manner, to bring the aid and protection of apostolic authority more earnestly to those places which both stand equal with the others in the general body of the members of the holy Roman Church and receive privileges of special patronage above the rest.

Among these places, because the monastery of Augia is joined to this holy and apostolic see by a certain principal and inseparable bond, we grieve greatly over the dispersal of its goods. Therefore we have decided to recall what our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander of revered memory, decreed concerning it and to communicate to all who may receive knowledge of this letter our confirmation of the same judgment.

After our aforementioned lord pope was unable, by any admonitions or threats, to induce Robert the Simoniac and usurper of that monastery either to surrender the abbey or to present himself before the apostolic presence to render an account of his entry, he learned the truth: that, having abandoned another abbey, Robert had sought this one by payment. By synodal judgment he struck him with the dart of anathema unless he repented, placed under the same censure all benefits received from him that belonged to the aforesaid monastery, annulled by apostolic command everything he had arranged, and ordered that these matters be publicly proclaimed by the bishop of Constance and disseminated throughout his diocese.

Thus, through God’s mercy, it came about that he abandoned his insane occupation of the abbey, but not that his supporters, against God and justice, relinquished the monastery’s goods that they had received from him.

Therefore, since that principal and heretical plague has been driven away, and since, by God’s authority, we have consecrated there as abbot our dearest son of Saint Peter, Ecardus, elected from that congregation by his brothers and carefully examined by us, we desire the monastery, after long and many tribulations, now to return to peace and the practice of monastic religion. In the same manner, under the severity and punishment of anathema, we prohibit all who received abbey property as benefices from the oft-mentioned Robert, whether to defend his wickedness or to demonstrate loyalty to him.

For when he, the author and distributor of such arrangements, could not remain in the place to which he had heretically aspired, by what laws or by what right will these people claim for themselves what they acquired by sacrilegious agreement?

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command all faithful Christians who learn of these things not to admit such persons at all to any participation in Christian communion, so long as they possess, with diabolical greed and audacity, the price of their iniquity and death.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO ALPHONSO, KING OF CASTILE (1074)

He commends Bishop Paul, whom he has found to be [the printed reading “stuatosum” is uncertain] devoted toward the apostolic see. He urges the king to restore the ancient see of his bishopric.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Alphonso [Idelphonso], king of Spain, and to the bishops of his kingdom, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish you to know that our brother and bishop Paul, called Monio [Monito], has now come to the threshold of the apostles and to our presence. After rendering an account of the matters concerning which we had summoned him, he was, as was fitting, received into our communion and affection.

He promised that he would celebrate the Roman rite in the divine offices, as did the other Spanish bishops who attended the synod, and that he would observe it as fully as he could. For the rest, because at present we were not able to settle and determine completely all the matters we had with him, we ordered him to return to us again for the future synod, and we received from him a pledge of prompt obedience in this matter.

Therefore, sending him back with our letters, we commend him to your charity, so that you too may love him together with us and remain firmly joined with him and among yourselves by the bond of Christ’s peace. Through him you were united in faith and chosen for a share in the inheritance of God’s glory.

As for you, king, we ask and admonish you as a dearest son, considering and setting before your mind’s eyes the account you will have to render at the strict judgment concerning the administration entrusted to you: strive to adorn the government of your kingdom by upholding equity, and make every effort, with God’s help, to restore and secure for this bishop the ancient see of his bishopric.

May almighty God direct your heart toward everything pleasing to him and make you merit such things in the present life that he may afterward grant you eternal rewards.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF BAMBERG (1074)

He informs him that he has entrusted his own authority to the bishop of Metz in the case of the bishop of Bamberg. He urges him to obey him and to do what is right.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Herimann [Hermann, and so throughout], bishop of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest brother Herimann, bishop of Metz, who stayed with us for several days, pleaded with us earnestly on your behalf and poured out many deep supplications concerning your case. He reported certain things about you that gave rise to no small joy in our heart, since they led us to hope for your correction.

Therefore we have placed in his experience the course of action that seemed to us most suitable for the salvation of your soul and ours and for the benefit of the church over which you preside. We have charged and entrusted him, supported by apostolic authority, to exercise our office in your case, provided that he finds you ready to obey what he presents to you as though from our own mouth.

Because we do not doubt that he has a ready and sufficient will to admonish you well, we write to your fraternity that, among many other things, you must carefully attend to and weigh this: you are approaching the end of your life each day, and you await with certainty the final day, although you do not know how soon it will come.

Therefore, brother, we admonish you with due concern to place before your eyes the dreadful examination and unavoidable judgment of the strict Judge. Hasten to meet his face beforehand through the confession of your conscience and the conduct of your works, so that, in the presence of the divine Presence—before whose eyes all things are naked and open—you may not be weighed down by fear and shame for your faults, but may be made manifest and undaunted by the joyful confidence of receiving recompense for good deeds.

Given on the expedition at Mount Ciminius [Ciminium], on the second day before the Ides of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO AGNES, EMPRESS (1074)

He gives thanks because she is working for the concord of the Church and taking care that King Henry be restored to communion with the Church. He urges her to persevere. He indicates that he is laboring greatly for the Church of Christ and that Beatrice and Matilda are of much assistance to him in this matter.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Agnes, most Christian [Christian] empress, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice and exult in the Lord that the light of your activity has shone all the way to us, and that the fruit of your labor, although not fully gathered according to your wishes, has nevertheless grown—for God’s praise and glory, for our joy, and for your crown of perfect reward. For our hope ought not therefore to be narrowed or humbled if the desire of your holiness has not had the means to fulfill its intention; for God, who bears an integral will, brings everything to completion, since you have not ceased to work as far as you were able.

We know, indeed, that you labor greatly for the peace and concord of the universal Church, and that you desire and seek with tireless concern everything that can bind the priesthood and the empire together with the bond of charity, more than can be expressed. Of these things, the greatest and most closely joined to the unity of love, you have already accomplished: namely, that your son, King Henry, be restored to communion with the Church, and that his kingdom likewise be freed from common peril. For while he was placed outside communion, fear of divine vengeance prevented us from associating with him; whereas those subject to him were daily bound in guilt by his presence, as though by a kind of necessity.

As for the other matters, which are less important, although we do not doubt that your [paupertatem; perhaps pietatem, “piety”] is ready, nevertheless, because of the confidence we have in Christ, we are impelled to urge your glory, as it were, to persist continually in such holy endeavors, out of a desire to reveal your joy. We write to you and make it known with complete certainty that your counsels and your great merits have benefited the aforesaid son of yours, and that your blessedness will yet see with rejoicing how mercifully divine clemency regards him.

When, by God’s mercy, we have seen your presence, we shall plainly explain how and from what source this has become known to us. For the rest, let your Eminence know that in these times we are engaged in no small labor on behalf of the cause of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and that your Beatrice, as well as our common daughter Matilda, labors greatly in our aid day and night, following you and faithfully imitating you, as disciples imitate their lady and teacher.

Through you, therefore—through you, I say—we are often reminded of that new example of ancient joy: those women who once sought the Lord at the tomb. For just as they, before all the disciples, came to the Lord’s sepulcher with a wondrous ardor of charity, so you visit the Church of Christ, placed as though in a tomb of affliction, before many, indeed almost before all the princes of the earth, with devoted love; and, striving with all your strength to raise it again to the condition of its liberty, you summon others to aid the suffering Church, as though instructed by angelic messages.

Therefore you will undoubtedly await the revelation of the heavenly glory and of the eternal life that is in Christ Jesus; and, as companions of those women, you will find the presence of our Savior among the ranks of the angels, enjoying everlasting peace, as he himself testifies [provides; *praestante* in the Mutina manuscript].

As for what you ask us concerning your daughter Matilda, we have received it gladly, praising your holiness because you take such great care for her salvation. She pours out her heart and soul toward you with every desire and feeling of loyalty, seeking your glory as though it were the joy of her own salvation. We gladly pray for her; and although our merits commend our prayers little to God, nevertheless, with the piety of Peter supporting us—for we are his servants—we trust that they are not wholly empty in the sight of the Lord.

Having therefore received your commendation with worthy reverence, we likewise ask you to remember her and us in your prayers, and that we may assist one another before God by our mutual intercessions, so that the charity which here unites us in Christ may, by his provision, produce for us one common seat and joy in the kingdom of our Father.

Given on campaign at Saint Flavian [Fabian], on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [June 15], in the twelfth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] From Gregory VII’s own register, after Epistle 25.] In this first year of his pontificate, Pope Gregory himself appointed and consecrated archbishops and bishops in various places. In the province of Sardinia: James, archbishop of Cagliari, and Constantine, archbishop of Torres; [Col. 0358D] to them he gave the pallium together with privileges. To Bruno, bishop of Verona, he granted the pallium with a privilege, and also to Nacho. He consecrated John, bishop of Sorra. Likewise, in the March of Fermo, Irasmund, bishop of Valva; Teuzo, bishop of Chieti; Leo, bishop of Aquino in Campania; Hugh, bishop of Die in Burgundy; Landeric, likewise bishop of Mâcon in Burgundy; and William, bishop of Massa in the Maritima. He held a synod at Rome, at which, among other things enacted there, he excommunicated and anathematized Robert Guiscard, [Note: [Col. 0357D] Concerning Robert Guiscard, see Leo of Ostia, book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, chapters 15, 44, 52, and 56; Otto of Freising, book I of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick*, chapter 3,] duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, together with all his supporters, until he should repent.

## BOOK TWO OF THE REGISTER

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1074, in the twelfth indiction [Note: [Col. 0359D] Rather, the thirteenth; for, apart from the first epistle—which has been misplaced here—the other epistles that follow belong to the thirteenth indiction].

[Col. 0359]

## EPISTLE I. TO THE BISHOPS AND ABBOTS OF BRITAIN (1074)

[Col. 0359A]

He orders them to come to the synod and to prohibit incestuous unions among their subjects.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops and abbots of Britain: greetings and apostolic blessing.

The responsibility of the office entrusted to us compels us to care for all the Churches and, with vigilant attention, to inquire into and teach them so that they may rightly hold the teachings of the faith and the rules of Sacred Scripture. Since, therefore, we understand that among you the decrees of the holy Fathers and the condition of ecclesiastical religion are neither observed with the diligence nor treated with the zeal that is proper, we invite you, by the obedience that you owe to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and we admonish you by our apostolic authority to assemble without any feigned excuse at the synod which, with God’s help, we have resolved to celebrate at the apostolic see in the second week of Lent.

Thus, with God’s assistance, together with you and with the large number of others of your order whom the order of our administration and of Christian religion requires, we may be able to discover and carry out with discerning zeal what is necessary. For you see that the whole world is already lying in wickedness, and our common mother, the Church, urges us to rise against the ancient enemy all the more ardently because these times display and bring upon us so many weapons and wars of diabolical fraud.

Meanwhile, make this especially your concern: concerning the incestuous union that we ordered by our letters to the people of your land—I mean the bishops—let each of you diligently admonish his subjects in his own diocese by preaching, while personally restraining the lesser offenders with canonical severity for the correction of so great a crime. As for the greater offenders, report to us at the time of the aforesaid council which have been corrected and which remain obstinate, with a reliable account, so that the obedient may be released from guilt through apostolic intervention, while the rebellious may immediately be bound by the chains of anathema through synodal judgment.

Given at Laurentum, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [August 28], in the twelfth indiction [Note: [Col. 0360D] For the thirteenth indiction began only on those Kalends of September, or, according to the older usage, on the twenty-fourth day].

## EPISTLE II TO ISEMBERT, BISHOP OF POITIERS (1074)

[Col. 0359D]

He rebukes him for contempt of the apostolic see and for the injuries inflicted upon the apostolic legates; he orders him to appear before him; meanwhile, he declares excommunicated those through whose ministry he committed these acts.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Isembert, bishop of Poitiers.

[Col. 0360A] When we begin to think about you and your deeds, we can scarcely marvel enough at the utterly immoderate boldness of your presumption. For just as the good strive to ascend toward an increase of good works through faithful desire, so you, having sought out—alas!—an even greater appetite, continually pant to add to the accumulation of iniquity through your efforts at wrongdoing.

Although forbidden by the legates of the apostolic see, you presumed to usurp the episcopal office; you did not blush to incur the crime of disobedience and contempt for apostolic authority. Later, when our legate Amatus, bishop of Oloron [York], and your teacher, namely Gozelin, archbishop of Bordeaux, together with other religious men, had assembled under apostolic obedience for the accomplishment of the divorce between William, count of Poitiers, and his kinswoman, whom he held as his wife—these men, I say, having gathered for a matter so grave and so necessary to Christian religion—you impiously disturbed their assembly through your soldiers.

For after breaking through the monastery’s cloisters and doors and bursting into the gathering, they dishonored the archbishop and our legate with great disgrace; they afflicted the others with threats, insults, blows, and many outrages. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we order you not to fail to present yourself before our presence before the feast of Saint Andrew, to answer for these matters. If you withdraw for any reason, unless perhaps because of a necessary and unavoidable circumstance, know that you will also be deprived of every priestly office and separated from participation in sacred communion.

As for those through whom you carried out so great a crime, both laymen and clerics, we reject them, by apostolic authority, from the body and blood of the Lord and from every divine office until you come to make satisfaction; and we order you, under threat to your rank, to notify all of them of this without delay.

Given at Tivoli, on the fourth day before the Ides of September [September 10], at the beginning of the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE III. TO WILLIAM, COUNT OF POITIERS (1074)

[Col. 0360D]

He commends him for having dismissed his kinswoman, whom he had taken as his wife. He orders him not to permit her to live with him. He informs him that he has summoned Isembert, bishop of Poitiers, to Rome. Finally, he praises his devotion toward the apostolic see.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, count of Poitiers: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We offer praise and thanks to almighty God, who, penetrating the depths of your heart, inclined you toward his love and fear and, overcoming the desire of the flesh, strengthened you in obedience to his commandments. We know indeed that you have abandoned, as justice demanded, what was sweetest to you in the present life, when, out of reverence for Christian religion, you consented to separate from your wife because she is related to you by close blood kinship.

But the more severe the struggle by which you conquered the lust of your heart and the more strictly you humbled yourself before God’s law, the more exalted a glory you should undoubtedly hope has been prepared for you by infinite reward. Therefore our joy also increases greatly, because in this correction of yours a sure hope of your salvation is perceived, and the nobility that has always existed in your house will, by God’s mercy, be preserved. For the nobility of a lineage is greatly corrupted when offspring are not generated from a legitimate marital union.

Your Eminence should be no less surprised that we pressed you so sharply, since the Roman Church, which has always loved your house, you, and your entire lineage with singular and exceptional charity, could not endure seeing you lie in such danger.

As for your desire that she remain at home under your authority until the future synod, although your sister—whom we love as a mother—has appealed to us about this, we dare not consent. We know that the devil, with exceptional cunning, especially suggests to human beings opportunities found in matters that are forbidden. Therefore arrange for her to be entirely removed and distanced from your vicinity, so that your correction and the reverence offered to God may be an example to all, and so that the devil may not, by any cleverness, disturb your salvation.

For the rest, know that unless Isembert, bishop of Poitiers, comes to us before the feast of Saint Andrew to give an account of his presumption, he is deprived of every episcopal and priestly office and of participation itself in sacred communion.

As for your report that you have a ready will to serve blessed Peter, we have received it gladly. But we judged that it would not presently be sufficiently prudent to write you anything definite concerning the expedition, since there is a report that in the regions across the sea the Christians, by God’s mercy, have driven the ferocity of the pagans far away, and we are still awaiting the counsel of divine Providence concerning what we should do hereafter.

Nevertheless, a reward for your good will is stored up for you with God; and, if it should be necessary, we have a firm confidence in your promises, as in those of a beloved brother and son.

Given at Tivoli, on the fourth day before the Ides of September [September 10], in the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE IV. TO GOZELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX (1074)

He urges him to come to Rome, or to send someone who, in the presence of Isembert, bishop of Poitiers, whom the pope has summoned, may accuse him of the injuries that Gozelin has complained in writing he suffered at his hands; and he declares that, unless Isembert comes as ordered, he is excommunicated together with his accomplices in the crime.

[Col. 0362A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gozelin, archbishop of Bordeaux: greetings and apostolic blessing.

As we have understood from your letters, Isembert, bishop of Poitiers, has inflicted great injuries upon almighty God, blessed Peter, and you, his teacher; and he has openly displayed himself to us as an adversary, an opponent of justice, and an enemy of the holy Church.

Now, therefore, since not only our vigilance but yours also is needed for the punishment of his wrongdoing, we strongly admonish your fraternity not to allow any circumstance to make you lukewarm or negligent in this matter. If you learn that he is coming to us, do not yourself, if you can, refuse the labor of making the journey to the threshold of the apostles.

But if your occupations make this too difficult, do not fail to arrange for suitable persons to be sent to us, both on your behalf and on behalf of those who have notified us by letter of the same things concerning the aforesaid bishop as you have. They should be able, in the bishop’s presence, to establish the truth of the matter by an irrefragable assertion.

We do not require this procedure because we doubt that the matters reported to us by you should be handled as described, but so that, preserving the statutes of our Fathers, we may examine everything both reasonably and fully and, with God’s favor, conclude it by an authoritative judgment. For your prudence knows that canonical authority does not approve an accusation by written documents when the persons are absent, nor does it admit cases for examination without first hearing the dispute between the parties.

Therefore, by our letter we have summoned the aforesaid bishop to apostolic judgment under such strict terms that, unless he presents himself before us before the feast of Saint Andrew, he shall be deprived of every episcopal and priestly office and excluded from participation in sacred communion.

If, then, hardened by stubborn defiance, he withdraws from our presence at the appointed time, proclaim the sentence pronounced against him by public preaching, and do not cease in every way to expose the wickedness and shamelessness of the enemy of God. Know also that those whom he himself enlisted for so great a crime, the disturbance of your assembly, both laymen and clerics, have been rejected by apostolic authority from the body and blood of the Lord and from every divine office until they come to make satisfaction.

If the bishop, as he was strictly admonished in our letters, neglects to make these things known to everyone, do not fail to make them public yourself.

Given at Tivoli, on the fourth day before the Ides of September [September 10], in the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE V. TO THE BISHOPS OF THE FRANKS (1074)

He recounts the calamities of the kingdom of France and the king’s unspeakable crimes. He rebukes the bishops for their silence concerning such crimes. He orders them to resist the king; if he refuses to obey, he orders the entire kingdom to be placed under interdict; and if he persists, he orders that an attempt be made to rescue it from his occupation.
