He threatens the bishops with deposition unless they resist him. He further orders that a certain Lanzelin be admonished to release unharmed a pilgrim whom he has captured while returning from Rome.

[Col. 0363A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Manasseh, archbishop of Reims; Richer [Racher], archbishop of Sens; Richard, archbishop of Bourges; Adrald, bishop of Chartres; and the other bishops of France: greetings and apostolic blessing.

A long succession of years has now passed since the kingdom of France, once famous and most powerful, began to decline from its state of glory and, as evil customs increased, to be stripped of most of the insignia of virtue. In these times, however, both the height of its honor and its entire appearance of splendor seem to have collapsed, since, with the laws neglected and all justice trampled underfoot, everything shameful, cruel, pitiable, and intolerable is both done there with impunity and, having acquired license, is now regarded as customary.

Some years ago, after royal power had grown weak among you and injuries were neither prevented nor punished by any law or authority, enemies fought among themselves according to a kind of common law of nations, and each prepared arms and forces according to his strength to avenge his injuries. Although these disturbances generally produced in the country killings, burnings, and other things that accompany war, they were certainly to be deplored, but not so greatly to be wondered at.

Now, however, all are filled with wickedness as though by a kind of pestilential disease, and often commit horrifying and utterly detestable crimes without anyone urging them on. They pay no attention to anything human or divine. They regard perjury, sacrilege, incest, and betraying one another as nothing; and—in a thing found nowhere else on earth—citizens, relatives, and even brothers seize one another out of greed, extort all their goods from them, and make them end their lives in the utmost misery.

They seize pilgrims traveling to and returning from the threshold of the apostles whenever opportunity presents itself, thrust them into prisons, inflict upon them tortures harsher than those of any pagan, and often demand from them more for their ransom than they possess.

Your king—who should be called not a king but a tyrant—is the head and cause of these things, at the devil’s prompting. He has polluted his entire life with disgraceful acts and crimes; and, miserably and unhappily administering the government of the kingdom he assumed, he has not only loosened the people subject to him through an authority too permissive toward crime, but has also incited them, by the examples of his own actions and pursuits, to everything that is unlawful to say or do.

It did not seem enough for him to have earned the wrath of God through the dissolution of Churches, adulteries, most heinous robberies, perjuries, and manifold frauds—for which we have often rebuked him. He also seized an enormous sum of money, in the manner of a brigand, from merchants who had recently gathered at a certain market in France from many regions of the earth—something that, according to reports, had never been done under any previous king. He who ought to have been the defender of laws and justice proved above all to be a plunderer. Clearly, he is acting so that his evils may no longer be confined within the boundaries of the kingdom he occupies, but may, I believe, extend to his own confusion.

Since we must in no way believe that this will escape the judgment of the heavenly Judge, we ask you and, out of true charity, admonish you to beware lest the prophetic curse come upon you, which says: “Cursed is the man who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). This means, as you yourselves understand well, the man who withholds the word of preaching from rebuking carnal people.

For you also, brothers, are implicated in the guilt, because, while you do not resist his most depraved deeds with priestly vigor, you undoubtedly foster his wickedness by consenting to it (Isa. 56). Therefore—and we say this unwillingly and with groaning—we greatly fear that you may receive the sentence not of shepherds but of hirelings: seeing the wolf tearing the Lord’s flock before your eyes, you flee, hiding yourselves in silence like dogs unable to bark.

Indeed, we fear for your danger all the more because we know that you will have no grounds for excusing yourselves at the future judgment, provided we can discover no other causes for your silence than either conscience—if he perpetrates so many evils at your urging, which we do not believe—or negligence, if you care too little about his destruction. You yourselves understand how greatly both must be avoided, especially in the office of administration entrusted to you, since you do not disregard the solicitude required by pastoral care.

For if you think that preventing him from committing offenses is contrary to the law and reverence of the fidelity he has sworn, your opinion is far mistaken. We can establish by every argument that the one who drags another away from the shipwreck of his soul, even against his will, is much more faithful than the one who allows him to perish in the whirlpool of sins through harmful consent.

As for fear, it is pointless to speak of it. If you were united and steadfastly armed for the defense of justice, you would possess such strength that, through faithful correction and without any danger to yourselves, you could turn him away from his accustomed desire to do evil and likewise free your own souls. Even if fear and danger of death threatened, you nevertheless ought not to abandon the freedom of your priestly office.

Therefore we ask you and admonish you by apostolic authority to assemble, take thought for your country, your reputation, [Col. 0364D] and your salvation, and, addressing the king with common counsel and the closest unity of spirit, warn him of his own confusion and of the confusion and danger of his kingdom. Showing him to his face how criminal his deeds and counsels are, strive by every exhortation to bend him, so that he may make restitution for the robbery committed against the merchants mentioned above. Unless it is returned—as you yourselves know—it will produce endless discord and hostility among many.

For the rest, let him correct his offenses; let him abandon the habits of his youth and begin, by upholding justice, to restore the battered dignity and glory of his kingdom. And so that he may be able to restrain others from what is wrong, let him first abandon what is unjust himself.

But if he refuses to listen to you and, casting aside the fear of God, persists in the hardness of his heart against royal dignity and against the salvation of himself and his people, make it known to him as though from our own mouth that he will in no way be able to evade the sword of apostolic punishment any longer.

For this reason, admonished and bound by apostolic authority, imitate your mother, the holy Roman and apostolic Church, with the faith and obedience you owe her; and, completely separating yourselves from his service and communion, forbid the public celebration of every divine office throughout France.

If he does not repent even under this severity, we wish no one to be uncertain or doubtful that, with God’s help, we shall attempt by every means to rescue the kingdom of France from his occupation.

Certainly, if we discover that you are lukewarm in this great and most necessary affair, no longer doubting that he persists in his incorrigibility because he is supported by your confidence, we shall strike you yourselves, as partners and accomplices in his crimes, deprived of episcopal office, with the same weapon of punishment.

God and our own conscience bear witness that we say these things neither moved by prayers nor by anyone’s payment, nor have we conceived them in our minds for such a reason. We are moved only by the inward grief that so noble a kingdom and so countless a number of peoples are perishing through the fault of one utterly depraved man; we can neither conceal this by silence nor ought we to do so.

Remembering, therefore, that divine saying of Wisdom, “He who fears man will soon fall, but he who hopes in the Lord will be lifted up” (Prov. 29), act and conduct yourselves so as to show how free your mind and tongue are. Do not, through fear of a human being, permit the ruin of your weakness; instead, strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, rise up like brave soldiers of Christ to the height of present and future glory.

Furthermore, we greatly ask and admonish your affection to approach Lanzelin, a knight of Beauvais, and, on behalf of blessed Peter and by our apostolic authority, admonish him to release unharmed Folcher of Chartres, our faithful servant, whom he captured while returning from the threshold of the apostles, retaining none of his property.

If he refuses to do this, do not cease to pursue and press him with spiritual and secular arms until you compel him, after releasing the pilgrim of Saint Peter, also to return or renounce whatever he has received or agreed to receive for his ransom.

Given at Tivoli, on the fourth day before the Ides of September [September 10], in the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE VI. TO GEBOARD, BISHOP OF PRAGUE (1074)

He rebukes him for contempt of the authority of the apostolic see, for a false pledge, and for the fraudulent seizure of the property of the bishop of Moravia; he orders the property restored and orders him to come to Rome with the said bishop to settle the case. He rebukes the lies suggested to him against the duke of Bohemia, and finally the excommunication pronounced against the duke’s men without legal judgment.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geboard [perhaps Jerome, as above, Book I, Epistle 44, and Epistle [Col. 0366A] 60; the name is absent in the Mutina manuscript], bishop of Prague, who does not deserve it: greetings and apostolic blessing.

When you came this year to the apostolic see, we received and treated you, exercising apostolic gentleness, much more kindly and mildly than your deeds deserved. But you, following your customary practice of returning evil for good, despising our charity and apostolic authority, dared, contrary to our prohibition, to intrude upon the goods and property concerning which there is a dispute between you and John, bishop of Moravia; and—something that greatly troubles us—you lied that you had done so with our permission.

We remember that we decreed that the bishop of Moravia should retain, in complete peace and quiet until the future synod, the land and other possessions concerning which there was disagreement between you. We expressly indicated this in our letters to your brother, the duke. You promised by placing your hand in ours that you would in no way interfere with this. But although you pressed us greatly to change our decision, you were unable to obtain this from us either by prayers or by payment.

Finally, in your latest complaints—apparently alleging that certain matters concerning your brother, Duke Vratislav, were being fraudulently concluded, although we now understand that you yourself have brought the whole world into discord among many peoples—you asserted that your legal claim was being denied to you concerning a certain castle of Saint Wenceslaus and concerning a provostship. You achieved only this: that in our letter we admonished him that, if he recognized that he had injured you, he should, for our sake—or rather for the love of God—do what was equitable in the matter.

On this pretext, therefore, you both fabricated a lie about us and overturned our decrees. But, I ask, are you not ashamed or afraid that, because of such matters, not only does danger to your rank threaten you, but, through fraternal hatred, even the grace of Christianity that you received no longer remains in you?

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter and by our apostolic authority, we command you to return to the aforesaid bishop of Moravia the castle that you seized so fraudulently, together with all the other property in dispute. For the settlement of the case, as has been established, either come to Rome yourself or send suitable legates. Notify the bishop of Moravia of this in good time, so that he too may be able to prepare himself or his legates for the journey.

Furthermore, as has been reported to us, you do not cease in many ways to disturb the peace that has been established between you and your brother, the duke, especially when you excommunicate his men without canonical fault or legal judgment. This is particularly dangerous for you, because, as blessed Gregory says, “he who binds the innocent corrupts for himself the power of binding and loosing.”

Therefore we admonish you never to presume to brand anyone suddenly or rashly with the sword of anathema, but first to examine each person’s guilt with careful investigation. If anything has arisen between you and the men of your aforesaid brother, deal with him first in a brotherly and friendly way, so that he may compel his men to submit to justice. If he denies you equity, or, through some concealment, permits the rashness of his men—something we do not believe—to grow against you without punishment, do not hesitate to report it to us. With the Lord’s assistance, we shall promptly arrange, through careful admonitions, to resolve the occasion of this complaint.

Given at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [September 22], in the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE VII. TO VRATISLAV, DUKE OF BOHEMIA (1074)

He gives thanks that he sent the tribute and made peace with his brother, the bishop of Prague. He urges him to ensure that the property taken from the bishop of Moravia by the said brother is entirely restored.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Vratislav, duke of the Bohemians: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your messenger reached us and reported the evidence of your great devotion and fidelity; he faithfully presented what you sent to blessed Peter in the name of tribute, namely one hundred marks of silver according to the measure of your weight. We received this gladly. But we embrace your charity much more ardently and affectionately, as though with arms of the heart extended all the way to you, since we perceive that your mind and desire are increasingly inflamed with reverence for the apostolic see.

Blessed Peter, whom you love and to whom you humble the height of your power, will undoubtedly prepare abundant gifts of reward for you and, through his protection, gladden you both in the present age and in the age to come.

For the rest, we thank you because, obeying our admonitions, you made peace with your brother Jerome, bishop of Prague. We treated him, when he was presented to the apostolic see this year, much more mercifully than his guilt deserved. But he, returning an improper favor, dared, as soon as he returned home—as we have learned from an unquestionable report—to intrude upon a certain castle and other property concerning which he is in dispute with John, bishop of Moravia, contrary to our prohibition and to the promise he himself had given into our hands, even lying about us as though we had granted him permission.

What and how we ordered him, reproving him briefly concerning this lie and fraud, you can learn fully from the copy of the letter we sent him that has been transmitted to you.

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter and by our apostolic authority, we ask and command your nobility not to allow him to continue rejoicing in so great a deception. Unless he returns to the bishop of Moravia without delay the castle and the other possessions in dispute, as he himself has been ordered in our letters, drive him out by your authority; and, after restoring everything to the bishop of Moravia, defend him and the property of the Church over which he presides from the injuries and oppression of wicked men, for the love of God and the redemption of your soul.

We send this request to you with the hope and intention that almighty God may defend you and your honors by divine power and, with the support of blessed Peter the apostle, lead you, freed from the bonds of your sins, to eternal joys.

Given at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [September 22], in the thirteenth indiction.

## EPISTLE VIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF MORAVIA (1074)

He consoles him for the injuries suffered at the hands of the bishop of Prague and asserts that he will learn how greatly the pope was moved by this from the messenger and from copies of the letters sent to the duke of Bohemia. He rebukes him for having thought that the pope had lightly changed his decision. He orders him, supported by apostolic authority, to reclaim all the property taken from him by the bishop of Prague.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to John, bishop of Moravia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0368B] Knowing that your charity toward us, brother, is prompt and sincere, we render you due thanks and, with a brother’s heart, have shared in compassion for your labors. For we know by what great deceit the bishop of Prague deceived you; yet, by lying not only to you but also about us, and as though strengthening his rapacity by our concession, he openly proceeded even to insults against us. How gravely we have been moved by this, and what we have decided concerning it, your messenger will be able to tell you here in person; and you yourself can learn it fully from the letters that we sent to the duke and from a copy of the letters that we sent to that same bishop. You indeed acted far too simply in thinking that we would rise against our decrees and change our judgment so lightly: for you had clearly understood that we had assigned to your possession, until the future synod and the examination of your entire disagreement, everything that is in dispute between you and him. Now therefore, commanded and supported by apostolic authority, reclaim without delay the castle and whatever else the aforesaid bishop has taken from you. For we have admonished him and firmly ordered him to return all these things to you without opposition. We have asked the duke that, if the bishop did not obey us, he should drive him from the castle and, after restoring everything to you, defend you, with God’s help, as well as the property of the church over which you preside, for the love of God. Know this with certainty: neither in this matter nor in any other will apostolic care or authority, with God’s providence, be lacking to you for the defense of your justice. May almighty God establish in your priestly vigilance and office a sacrifice pleasing to him, and for you a reward of eternal happiness.

Given at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER IX. TO BEATRICE AND HER DAUGHTER MATILDA. (1074)

He declares his confidence in them. He grieves that he has emerged from a dangerous illness, preserved for the cares of the Church, which is almost shipwrecking. He delays, for just reasons, granting reconciliation to Robert Guiscard, who repeatedly and humbly seeks it. Finally, he says that Margrave Azzo promised to render an account of his marriage, and for this reason he summoned the bishops of Pavia and Modena to Rome.

[Col. 0369A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Beatrice, duchess, and her daughter Matilda: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has not escaped us that various rumors about us are often brought to you, as is the custom of those who envy the affection of friends and their unity. Indeed, if we were willing—as may it never be!—to incline our ears to such things, there are not many in whom we would believe that the feeling of sincere affection toward us was evident. But, avoiding a suspicious mind almost more than anything else, we tell you truly that among all the rulers of the earth we place our confidence nowhere more securely than in your nobility. For your words, your deeds, your devoted zeal, and the outstanding steadfastness of your faith have taught us this.

Nor do we doubt that your true charity toward us shines forth, since through Peter the servant is loved, and Peter in the servant. For the rest, know that, contrary to the expectation of everyone who was with us, we have escaped bodily illness and have now recovered good health. For this reason we think that we ought to grieve rather than rejoice. Our soul was stretching forth, and with all its desire was yearning for that homeland in which he who considers labor and sorrow grants rest and refreshment to the weary. But, having been preserved for our customary labors and endless cares, hour by hour we suffer, as it were, the pains and anxieties of a woman in labor, while we are unable by any means of governance to rescue the Church, almost shipwrecking before our eyes. [Col. 0369C]

For the law and Christian religion have almost everywhere so perished that the Saracens and every kind of pagan hold more firmly to their rites than those who have received the Christian name, [and those for whom, through Christ, an inheritance and the glory of eternal life have been prepared in the kingdom of the Father should observe the commands of the divine law] [Note: [Col. 0369D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Modena manuscript.]. It is therefore less surprising that we desire to flee the afflictions of this life in hope of heavenly consolation, since, placed amid these circumstances, we pay the penalties of each danger simply by recognizing the dangers that flood in upon us.

Furthermore, know that Robert Guiscard often sends suppliant envoys to us and desires to place in our hands such security of loyalty that no one ever ought or could bind himself to any lord by a firmer obligation. But, considering the reasons—by no means uncertain—why this should still be deferred, we await the counsels of heavenly dispensation and apostolic administration. In addition, we have learned that one of you is at this time going across the Alps; but, if it could be done, we greatly desire first to have a conversation with both of you, since we wish to have your counsels, as those of our sisters and daughters of Saint Peter, in our affairs and business.

As for us, be confident that whatever through God we rightly understand and are able to do is open to you in every expression of charity. Know also that you are remembered daily in our prayers and, although we are sinners, earnestly commended to God. Furthermore, you know that Margrave Azzo promised us at the synod and gave his pledge into our hand that, whenever we summoned him, he would come into our presence to render an account of his marriage. For this reason we have summoned him. We have invited by our letters William, bishop of Pavia, and Heribert, bishop of Modena, who know the woman’s relationship, to come to us, so that, having learned the truth of the matter, we may, with God’s help, determine what is just.

Therefore it seems appropriate to us that, through a reliable messenger of your own, you should instruct the aforesaid margrave that he may pass safely through your territory on his journey there and back, lest, because of your fear in this matter, Christian justice suffer harm.

[Col. 0370B] Given at Rome on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER X. TO UDON, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER. (1074)

He entrusts to him and to the bishop of Metz the case that had arisen between the bishop of Toul and one of his clerics. He instructs him to make the cleric safe and to order that everything taken from him be restored; then, after summoning the clerics of Toul, he is to investigate the bishop’s conduct, about which Gregory wishes to be informed before the synod.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, archbishop of Trier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We admonish you, brother, to carry out faithfully, from charity, what we entrust to you, but to do so quickly in accordance with the suitability and necessity of the circumstances and the times, as determined by careful consideration of the cases. In the matter set out below, we wish you to observe both requirements, so that, as we believe, we may recognize you as a faithful and tireless co-worker.

This brother from Toul, as he admits, a cleric who came to us, complained that his lord, namely, as is said, the bishop of Toul, had become angry with him, made him an exile, and stripped him of all his property. He begged that he might find some consolation for such great misery through apostolic mercy. When we carefully inquired why this had happened to him, he reported that he had asked the bishop for a certain church which, according to lawful constitution, was said to belong to the office of custodian that he held.

The bishop, angered by this, not only denied him that church but also entirely prohibited him from exercising the office, under the strictest order of obedience. The cleric replied that he did not owe him the reverence of obedience, since, by selling archdeaconries, church consecrations, and the churches themselves, he had stained himself with the Simoniac heresy; since he was living in public fornication with a certain woman, by whom he had fathered a son and whom, as rumor had it, he had joined to himself through a sacramental marriage and betrothal in the manner of laymen; and since, moreover, some said that he had attained the episcopate through a bargain involving payment.

When the bishop heard these things, as though repenting of manifest offenses and speaking of his correction, both with this man alone and with the other brothers, he was finally inflamed against him by manifest indignation and anger. After the bishop had left the city, his soldiers, knowing their lord’s will, soon afterward denied this cleric every security and threatened him openly within the cloister. When he realized that they were plotting against his life and honor, he secretly departed, so that his absence might moderate the severity of this rage.

The bishop, however, immediately ordered all his property to be plundered and confiscated; and thus, this man complains that he has long been an exile and destitute. Yet these things seem to us disordered and very unjust. For, if they are true, the bishop—or rather the former bishop—ought to have hated and persecuted not this man but his own conscience. If they are false—and would that they were false!—it would nevertheless have been proper for the bishop to correct and chastise him not through soldiers but through the discipline of the canons.

Therefore we wish your fraternity to be admonished and supported by apostolic authority in this matter, so that, having summoned and joined to you our beloved fellow-brother Herimann, venerable bishop of Metz, you may meet with the bishop of Toul and admonish him, by apostolic commands, to receive this cleric into his cloister without any danger to his life and secure from every insult; to restore to him the office of custodian, together with the church he requested, if it justly belongs to it, along with all its other rightful appurtenances and revenues; also his provostship and the office of the schools; and all the property taken from him and the damages inflicted upon him so irrationally.

Then, summoning the clerics of Toul and binding them by true obedience—or rather under threat of anathema—compel them to disclose to you whatever they know about the bishop’s accession and life. After investigating the truth from every side, do not fail to notify us by letter of what we ought to believe concerning the matter, either at the synod or before the synod that we shall celebrate in the first week of Lent.

If the bishop, as we desire, proves innocent of so many and such great crimes, we shall, with God’s prompting, arrange how the cleric, who acted rashly in coming to our tribunal, may be justly corrected. But if the bishop cannot truthfully clear himself of the charges brought against him, it is in no way tolerable to us or to you that a wolf should occupy the place of a shepherd. We have ordered these letters to be openly sealed for this reason: that we might deliver to you more certain authority.

[Col. 0371D] Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XI. TO COUNT ALBERT AND HIS WIFE. (1074)

He praises their faith and religion. He censures the crimes of certain bishops. He urges them to persevere and to maintain the decrees of the Apostolic See concerning Simoniacs and incontinent priests.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Count Albert and his wife: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to God that even laymen and women raise their minds to the Lord, willingly grasp the worship of religion with understanding, and strive to preserve it. For those who have been called and appointed bishops for the winning of souls, and who ought to teach their subjects the way of truth by word and example, have in these times been led astray by the devil. They not only abandon God’s law but do not cease to attack and overthrow it with every effort.

It is therefore less surprising if they do not restrain the lower orders from wrongdoing, since either their ordination was heretical or their life is covered with every impurity and crime. While they neither correct nor heed their own offenses, they also bear the crimes of their subjects, either through negligence or through fear of their own conscience. Concerning such men it is rightly said through the Prophet: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and always bend their back” (Psalm LXVIII).

Therefore, whatever they babble against you—or rather against justice—and whatever they bring against you, as unlearned people, in defense of their wickedness, remain in the purity and steadfastness of your faith. Firmly believe and hold to what you have received from the Apostolic See concerning Simoniac bishops and priests, or those living in fornication.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO THE BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT. (1074)

He praises his observance toward the Roman Church, which he had perceived from the bishop’s grief: the apostolic legates in that kingdom had not been received with the honor that was fitting. He says that he would rather this had happened to the legates than that they, wishing to please human beings more than God, should have violated the authority of the Apostolic See.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishop of Halbisteten [Burchard of Halberstadt]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

You show, brother, that you love the holy Roman Church with sincere affection, since it moves your heart and mind that the legates of the Apostolic See were not received in your kingdom with the honor they ought to have received, nor were they able to accomplish, as necessity required, what Christian religion demanded and still demands.

Yet we much prefer that these things happened to them rather than that they, desiring to please human beings more than God, should have violated, through some pretense, the truth and freedom of the authority represented in them. For if we wished silently to consent to the princes and wealthy men of your land ruling according to their pleasure and trampling upon God’s justice, we could certainly have their friendships, gifts, submission, praise, and magnificent honors.

But because such a course is wholly incompatible with the place in which we stand and the office that we hold, nothing, with Christ himself protecting us, can separate us from the charity of Christ. For us it is safer to die than to abandon his law, or, for the glory of the world, to regard the persons of the impious—if they are powerful—rather than those who, although poor, seek the law of their Creator, love his commandments, and abandon life rather than justice.

Therefore, receiving with due joy the unity of your fraternity, we desire that this flame in your breast may always grow, so that you may advance in the love that you have begun to hold toward the holy and apostolic Church. Be confident, moreover, in our charity—or rather in the protection of blessed Peter and in his apostolic blessing, which is assured.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIII. TO SOLOMON, KING OF THE HUNGARIANS. (1074)

He complains that, although the kingdom of Hungary is the property of Saint Peter by right, Solomon received it as a benefice from the king of the Germans. He urges him, correcting his error, to recognize it as a grant from the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0373B] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Solomon [Note: [Col. 0373D] Concerning Solomon, king of the Hungarians, Lambert, under the year 1074.], king of the Hungarians: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your letter was brought to us late because of the delay of your messenger. Our hand would indeed have received it much more graciously if your rash situation had not so greatly offended blessed Peter. For, as you can learn from the elders of your country, the kingdom of Hungary belongs to the holy Roman Church as its own property. Long ago King Stephen offered and devotedly handed it over to blessed Peter, together with all its rights and power. [Note: [Col. 0373D] On Saint Stephen I, king of the Hungarians: Hermann the Lame, Chronicle, under the year 1038; Bishop Chartuitius, in his Life of him in Surius, vol. IV; Leo of Ostia, book II, ch. 79; and others.]

Moreover, the emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 0374D] Concerning the expedition of Emperor Henry II against the Hungarians, Hermann the Lame under the year 1044.] of pious memory, when he conquered that kingdom in honor of Saint Peter, after defeating the king and achieving victory, sent a lance and crown to the body of blessed Peter and, for the glory of his triumph, sent the insignia of the kingdom there, since he recognized that the primacy of its dignity belonged to him.

Although these things are so, you, in other respects also departing far from royal virtue and conduct, have diminished and alienated, so far as you are concerned, the right and honor of Saint Peter, since, as we have heard, you received his kingdom as a benefice from the king of the Germans.

If this is true, you yourself, if you wish to attend to justice, do not fail to understand how you ought to hope for the grace of blessed Peter or for our goodwill: namely, that you will not possess it, nor will you long reign without apostolic punishment, unless, having corrected your error, you recognize the scepter of the kingdom that you hold as a benefice of apostolic, not royal, majesty. For neither through fear nor affection nor any personal favoritism will we, insofar as we are able with God’s help, leave unexamined the honor due to him whose servants we are.

But if you wish to correct these matters, to order your life as befits a king, and, by God’s mercy, to adorn it, you will undoubtedly be able to possess the love of the holy Roman Church as a beloved son of his mother, and our friendship in Christ, in full measure.

Given at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIV. TO WARNER, BISHOP OF STRASBOURG, AND BURCHARD, BISHOP OF BASEL. (1074)

[Col. 0374A]

He instructs them to assign the guardianship of the monastery of the Holy Cross, founded by Leo IX, to Gerard, his nephew and the elder by birth, in accordance with that pontiff’s constitution, and to exclude Hugh from it.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Warner, bishop of Strasbourg, and Burchard, bishop of Basel: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you know that our lord, Pope Leo of blessed memory, handed over to the holy Roman Church, which he piously and holily governed, the monastery of the Holy Cross, founded in the land of his inheritance and built at his own expense, so that that venerable place might advance more securely and freely in divine service beneath the wings of Saint Peter.

But, as we have learned from a reliable report, his nephews, Hugh namely and Gerard, seeking what is theirs rather than what belongs to God and fearing neither the excommunication of that most holy man, while they contend with one another over the guardianship, plunder the monastery’s goods and make what was established for the support of God’s handmaids into booty for their soldiers through sacrilegious invasions.

Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your fraternity, for the love of and due obedience to Saint Peter, to summon both men to a place suitable for your assembly. Carefully investigating the case on both sides, strive with the greatest diligence to put an end to their dispute, departing in no respect from the constitution and determination set out in the privilege of our aforesaid father, Pope Leo.

For among other provisions, his apostolic sanction decreed there that, among his descendants in the castle of Egeneschen [Engesheim], whoever was the eldest by birth should alone hold responsibility for the guardianship, and that this authority should pass in the same way to all the descendants of his line. In accordance with this ordinance, we think that Gerard should administer the justice and exercise the guardianship, more rightfully than Hugh, because we have learned that he is the elder in age.

If you too discover that this is so, forbid Hugh, on behalf of blessed Peter, by our apostolic authority and also by your episcopal authority, from thereafter interfering in any way with that guardianship, and from attacking the monastery or its goods, whatever their kind, by any injury or opposition. Otherwise, let him know that he will in no way be able to escape the stroke of the apostolic sword and that he will be wholly separated not only from the grace of blessed Peter but also from the communion of the entire Church, judged by the Holy Spirit and excommunicated and condemned by apostolic sentence.

Whatever is done in this matter, take care to report to us as quickly as possible by your letters.

[Col. 0375A] Given at Rome on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO HUMBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS, AND THE OTHERS. (1074)

He instructs them to admonish the clerics of Langres to desist from their injuries and to make satisfaction for the damages inflicted upon the monastery of Pultariensis. If they refuse, they are to bar them from entering the church; if they persist, they are to subject them to excommunication.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Humbert, archbishop of Lyons, and Agino, bishop of Autun, and Rodulf, bishop of Mâcon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Humbert, abbot of Pultariensis, who has long been staying with us because of the needs of his monastery, complains that he has suffered many adversities and disturbances at the hands of the clerics of Langres. Their injury affects us all the more strongly because the cares of apostolic administration through blessed Peter, whose servants we are and to whom that monastery is subject by special and proper right, fall upon us above all others.

But because it would be lengthy to include here each of the abbot’s grounds for complaint, we ask your fraternity and admonish you by apostolic authority to hear from his own mouth the troubles inflicted upon him and the losses suffered by the monastery, and to attend to them carefully. After summoning the clerics named above to make correction and satisfaction, admonish them in our place and by apostolic authority concerning everything of which the abbot complains against them, according to what is just.

If they despise you—or rather blessed Peter and the admonitions administered through us—and, refusing to do justice, persist in the obstinacy of their rashness, do not fail to bar and exclude them from entering the church. But if they are unwilling to repent even under such discipline, and do not make worthy satisfaction to correct the injuries inflicted upon blessed Peter, as violators of his privileges, and the other matters in which they have harmed the abbot and his monastery through unworthy offenses, then, commanded and supported by our apostolic authority, separate them, struck by the sword of anathema, from the body and communion of the entire Church, and condemn them by canonical judgment.

Whatever is done in this matter, notify us without delay by your letters.

[Col. 0375D] Given at Rome on the third day before the Ides of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO RICHER, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (1074)

Concerning men of his diocese by their peers.

Gregory, etc., to Richer, archbishop of Sens: greeting, etc.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Ides of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVII. TO ABBOT SIGEBALD. (1074)

He reproves him for having advised that Alberic be restored to the monastery of Saint Anastasius after another man had been removed, although he later learned that Alberic was notorious for many crimes. He orders either that Alberic restore the monastery or that he come with Sigeobald to Rome to answer in person for the charges brought against him.

[Col. 0376A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sigeobald, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Savior at Perugia: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly surprised that your fraternity, whom we consider religious, did not give us sound advice concerning Alberic, who, as many report, was entangled in many crimes and—what is worse—had also been removed from every ecclesiastical honor under excommunication by the venerable lord Peter of blessed memory and two other bishops. Nevertheless, by our permission, you restored him to the monastery of Saint Anastasius, while, as is reported, you violently and without reason expelled from the honor of the abbacy another man who was better.

When we heard this, it greatly displeased us, and our charity has sent you this letter so that such things may be corrected. Therefore we command you and the aforesaid Alberic to do one of two things: either let him relinquish the monastery that you improperly gave him and restore it to the other man who was unjustly rejected, or come with you to Rome and defend himself in our presence by the truth concerning the crimes of which he is accused.

But if he is unwilling to obey either of these commands, let him know without doubt that he will be excommunicated by the Holy Apostolic See. We strictly command you not to neglect this. For we incur a very great sin together with you if we omit this matter, since it is as many witnesses have reported to us.

[Col. 0376C] Given at Rome on the Ides of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO WILLIAM, COUNT OF POITIERS. (1074)

He instructs him, together with the bishops and nobles of the kingdom of France, to admonish King Philip to desist from disrupting churches and from plundering; otherwise he threatens to excommunicate the king and all who render him obedience.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, count of Poitiers: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although there can be no doubt that the iniquities of Philip, king of the Franks, have come to your knowledge, we nevertheless thought it useful to make known to you how much we grieve over those same iniquities. For, among the other crimes by which he seems to have surpassed not only Christian but also pagan princes, after various destructions of churches which it had been in his power to throw into disorder, he so set aside the dignity of kingship that, inflamed more by greed than compelled by any reason, he plundered the merchants of Italy who had come into your regions.

For this reason, since we have admonished the bishops of France by our letters to address him, we especially admonish you, who love Saint Peter and us sincerely and, as we believe, grieve with us over his dangers, to join with them and with certain of the better and more distinguished nobles of France. Make his iniquities known to him, so that, renouncing the suggestions of fools, adhering to the counsels of good and wise men, and beginning to withdraw his hand from the disruption of churches, he may change his evil conduct after the example of the good kings of France and, without delay, correct the plunderings mentioned above, by which the envoys of Saint Peter are obstructed, captured, and mistreated in many ways.

If he accepts your counsels, we shall treat him with the charity we owe him. Otherwise, if he persists in the perversity of his purposes and, according to the hardness and impenitence of his heart, stores up for himself the wrath of God and of Saint Peter, we, with God’s help and as his wickedness deserves, shall in the Roman synod without doubt exclude from the body and communion of the holy Church both him and anyone who renders him royal honor or obedience. His excommunication shall be confirmed daily upon the altar of Saint Peter.

It is long since we have borne with his iniquities; it is long since, by sparing his youth, we have concealed the injury he has done to the holy Church. But now the perversity of his conduct has made itself so conspicuous that, if he possessed as great health and strength as the pagan emperors employed against the holy martyrs, we would nevertheless not, out of fear, leave so many and such great iniquities of his unpunished.

Given at Rome on the Ides of November, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIX. TO RICHARD, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES. (1074)

He announces that he has entrusted to him and to the archbishop of Tours the dispute between the monastery of Dol and the abbot of Saint-Sulpice, and urges him to settle it.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richard, archbishop of Bourges: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your fraternity knows, the monastery of Dol is recognized as belonging to the right of Saint Peter. If any danger were brought upon it, we ought to come to its aid with special concern. Therefore, because the monastery itself had long ago brought a complaint against the abbot of Saint-Sulpice, we entrusted to our fellow-brother Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, the task of carefully examining, together with you, the dispute between the two monasteries and bringing it, with God’s help, to a lawful conclusion.

Let your fraternity therefore strive to offer our aforesaid fellow-brother such assistance in this matter that it will not be necessary for us to labor in investigating the case.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO RICHER, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (1074)

He instructs him to ensure that Lanzelin, one of his parishioners, who had committed many crimes against the archbishop of Tours, make fitting correction. If Lanzelin refuses, he orders him to exercise canonical censure against him.

[Col. 0378A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richer, archbishop of Sens: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our fellow-brother Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, came to us and reported that he had suffered no small injury from one of your parishioners named Lanzelin. For he asserts that Lanzelin encountered him on the road with armed force, plundered some of his men, wounded others, and—what is more cruel—after his own blood-relative had been killed before his very eyes, dishonored him with many insults.

Therefore we admonish your fraternity to summon the aforesaid Lanzelin and compel him to make fitting correction for so great a crime. Your fraternity ought indeed to have done this even without the admonition of our letters; and, if the report is true, news of punishment rather than of complaint ought to have reached us first, if brotherly charity were vigorous in you.

But if, led by a spirit of pride, he refuses to make satisfaction, do not delay to exercise canonical censure against him.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO THE ABBOT OF BELLILOC. (1074)

[Col. 0378C] He instructs him to obey the archbishop of Tours. If he has any suitable excuse, he is to come to the synod together with the archbishop’s messenger, or send messengers, to answer for his disobedience and the crimes charged against him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot of Belliloc: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our fellow-brother Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, has reported to us that you are unwilling to render him any obedience and that you devote yourself to usury and other crimes with unrestrained license. Therefore we admonish you not to refuse the obedience due to our aforesaid fellow-brother.

But if you know that you can offer some suitable excuse, come with the messenger of our aforesaid fellow-brother to the synod that we shall celebrate in the first week of Lent, or send suitable messengers, so that you may answer both for your disobedience to the archbishop and for the crimes charged against you. For we cannot leave unexamined in you what we rightly censure in laymen and, if the allegation is true, leave it unpunished by a fitting penalty.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO HUGH OF SAINTE-MAURE. (1074)

He instructs him to restore to the archbishop the property of the Church of Tours that he is unjustly retaining, and, if he thinks anything is owed to him, to come with the archbishop’s messenger to Rome for the synod; otherwise he is to be excommunicated.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, soldier of Sainte-Maure.

[Col. 0379A] Our fellow-brother Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, complains that you are unjustly retaining the property of his Church and are unwilling to incline your mind toward doing justice, neither through fear of God nor through reverence for blessed Maurice.

Therefore we admonish you by apostolic authority that, if this is so, you offer the aforesaid fellow-brother fitting satisfaction concerning that property. But if you have discovered that some wrong has been done to you by that archbishop, come with a messenger to our future synod, so that, after the arguments of both sides have been heard, each of you may obtain justice in his complaint.

If you disobey this admonition of ours, you will without doubt be excommunicated at the same synod to which we summon you.

[Col. 0379B] Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXIII. TO ISEMBERT, BISHOP OF POITIERS. (1074)

He confirms the interdict imposed upon him by his legate and excludes him from participation in the sacred rites until the future synod, to which he orders him to come.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Isembert, bishop of Poitiers.

Because, having been interdicted by our legate Gerald, bishop of Ostia, you scorned to obey, violently disrupted the council convened at our command, and were also disobedient to the commands concerning the case of Saint Hilary [f.: our commands; Modena manuscript: also to the commands of the mother], by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul we not only confirm the episcopal office interdict imposed by our legate but also separate you from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until the future synod, which, with God’s assent, we shall celebrate in the first week of Lent—unless, perhaps, the danger of death is imminent and this is preceded by satisfaction confirmed under oath.

We further command, by the same apostolic authority, that at the future council already mentioned you present yourself to us and come prepared to render an account of all these matters and of the other things brought against you. If you do not do so, know that at that synod you are to be deposed without hope of future reconciliation.

Given at Rome on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [XVII], in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXIV. TO GOZELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX, AND WILLIAM, DUKE OF AQUITAINE. (1074)

[Col. 0379D]

He orders that, unless the bishop of Poitiers comes to the synod as Gregory had commanded him, no one is to render him obedience. He entrusts the administration of ecclesiastical affairs to the archbishop of Bordeaux and the administration of justice to Count William.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gozelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, and Guilielmus, duke of Aquitaine: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We wish to make known to you that we have instructed Isembert, bishop of Poitiers [Col. 0380A]—[from the preceding letter: “because he has been interdicted by our legate, Giraldus, bishop of Ostia” (up to the words: “to be deposed without hope of future reconciliation”)]—accordingly. If he is unwilling to comply, we command you by apostolic authority that neither of you shall obey him, nor regard him as bishop.

To you, Gozelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux, we entrust the administration of ecclesiastical affairs; admonish the people and clergy not to obey him. To you, Guilielmus, count, I entrust the administration of justice, and we commit to your hands the conduct of the case of Saint Hilary and the rendering of justice in it.

Given at Rome on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXV. TO ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE. (Year 1074)

[Col. 0380B]

He advises him to decide the case entrusted to him by the apostolic legates between the bishop of Osnabrück and the abbot of Corvey and a certain abbess. If he cannot complete it, he is to urge them to come to the synod; furthermore, he is to impress upon the clergy the necessity of maintaining chastity.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anno, archbishop of Cologne: greetings and apostolic blessing.

As your diligence, dearest brother, can recall, our legates, Ubertus, bishop of Praeneste, and Giraldus, bishop of Ostia, sent to your region, entrusted to your venerable skill the case which was being disputed between Bennon, bishop of Osnabrück [Osburg], and [lacuna] the abbot of Corvey and a certain abbess, after it had been brought before them for settlement. Yet, I do not know because of what obstacle, we are told that the matter still remains undecided. Therefore, dearest brother, we have once again judged it necessary to exhort your charity to hear the aforesaid case carefully and decide it lawfully.

Furthermore, if some circumstance should prevent you from completing this, after they have been shown this letter, admonish them to come to the synod to be held in the first week of the coming Lent, so that the controversy long drawn out between them, every obstacle having been removed, may receive a canonical conclusion.

Moreover, we earnestly admonish your diligence on behalf of blessed Peter, our common Father and lord [Col. 0380D], to ensure through your admonitions that not only in your own diocese but also in all the parishes of your suffragans, priests, deacons, and subdeacons live chastely. For, as your fraternity knows, the other virtues have no value before God without chastity, just as chastity has none without the other virtues. Therefore let your diligence apply itself to this carefully and earnestly, so that, as in your other virtues, you may make Peter, the chief of the apostles, your debtor.

Given at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVI. TO DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF PIACENZA. (Year 1074)

[Col. 0381A]

He states that the abbot has resigned the monastery of Saint Savinus, but that he has entrusted its administration to him until another abbot is elected. He advises him to attend to this matter together with the monks; for this reason he is sending legates, also to settle the controversy existing between him and the abbot of Saint Sepulchre and the people of Piacenza.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We received Rigizon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Savinus [Col. 0381B], whom your diligence sent to our hearing, and we examined him with such thorough investigation that he was rejected by us from the administration of the aforesaid monastery. For far be it from us to attempt to defend ecclesiastical dignities for those who have presumed to seize them for themselves through the intervention of money.

Nevertheless, lest the aforesaid monastery suffer serious loss of its possessions, we entrusted it to the said abbot to guard until an abbot should be solemnly elected there who would be regarded as worthy of God and acceptable to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, without prejudice to the rights of your church. Therefore, dearest brother, let such diligence on your part and that of the brothers together be provided there that it may not appear that we have acted for the monastery’s or the brothers’ detriment rather than for their benefit and advancement [Col. 0381C]. Thus you may receive worthy praise among men and, through this salutary undertaking, find before God forgiveness of sins and perpetual salvation for your soul—something effectively acquired when those who serve God in holy places are piously assisted by the duty of charity.

Furthermore, for this reason we have sent our legates, namely the bearers of this letter, all the way to you: to see to what conclusion the present matter comes, and to hear more attentively the controversy existing between you and the abbot of Saint Sepulchre, the people of Piacenza, or the subdeacon Bonizo [Bonozon], so that they may discern which party’s evasion is attempting to obstruct justice by closing the opportunity for those seeking to bring accusations. May the holy Church of Piacenza, after so many intervals of time and so many great lawsuits, now at last rejoice to receive the peace it has desired and ought to desire through the prudent clemency of your nobility [Col. 0381D], so that, enjoying the quiet due to the aforesaid Church, it may be permitted to serve God.

But may you, having driven away occupations of this kind as unnecessary, be able to delight in the praises and service of our Creator, meditate day and night upon his law, attain true blessedness, and ensure that the wickedness of accusers no longer has any place among us.

Given at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT SAVINUS. (Year 1074)

[Col. 0382A]

That they should elect an abbot canonically and offer prayers to God for themselves and for the condition of the Roman Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the congregation of the monastery of Saint Savinus situated at Piacenza: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We received your abbot Rigizon when he came to our hearing and examined him with such thorough scrutiny that he was rejected by us from the administration of the monastery. Nevertheless, lest the aforesaid monastery suffer serious loss of its possessions, we entrusted it to him until another person should be solemnly elected in the aforesaid monastery who would be found worthy of God and suitable according to the sacred canons [Col. 0382B].

Therefore, by this present letter we exhort you, setting aside every assessment of wicked payment and putting aside the influence of kinship and friendship, to strive to elect for yourselves, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, such a man with whom you may be able to serve God harmoniously and sincerely.

Meanwhile, dearest brothers, we ask you continually to entreat God, whom you faithfully serve, for the restoration of the condition of the holy Roman Church and for its safety, and for me, so that I may be able to care for it.

Given at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO LEMARUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN. (Year 1074)

[Col. 0382C]

He rebukes him because he prevented the apostolic legates from holding a council, as he himself had ordered, and because, although summoned by the same legates to Rome, he scorned to come. Therefore he suspends him from office until he comes to Rome for the synod.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0381] Elsewhere “Liemarus,” as in Lambert in the year 1073 and in other places], to Lemarus, archbishop of Bremen.

Because we have recognized that you are forgetful, indeed ungrateful, for the benefit you received by which the holy Roman Church wished to honor you; because you have also forgotten the promise and canonical obligation by which you canonically bound yourself to be faithful to the holy Roman Church, to love it, and to obey it from your heart—we are not without reason moved to grieve over you, nor without cause are we angry with you, whom we believed to be a faithful son.

Alas, morals have been reversed and times changed! The man whom we thought would be an impregnable wall for the holy Roman Church, over which we preside, though unworthy; whom we believed ought, if necessary, to take up the shield of faith and the sword of Christ; whom, both by virtue of your office and because of the aforesaid obligation, we believed would stand for the holy Roman Church, for us, and also for our successors—we now find to be our enemy and our assailant. Although unjustly, we suffer from you injuries and a disgraceful and unheard-of rejection.

For you vigorously obstructed our legates, Albert [Hubert], bishop of Praeneste [Col. 0383A], and Giraldus, bishop of Ostia, whom we sent to those regions for this purpose: that, having summoned archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious clergy into one assembly, and supported by our authority and acting in our place, they might correct what needed correction and add what needed to be added to religion. Moreover, you prohibited the council from being held. Although summoned by the same men to Rome, you did not come at the appointed time, namely the feast of Saint Andrew [Note: [Col. 0383] See Lambert under the year 1074].

Therefore, to correct these offenses and many others, we command and invite you by apostolic authority to come to the next synod, which, God willing, will be held in the first week of the coming Lent. Moreover, persuaded by the aforesaid offenses, by that same authority we suspend you from every episcopal office until you come to us [Col. 0383B].

Given at Rome on the second day before the Ides of December [perhaps: the Nones], in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXIX. TO SIGEFRID, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. (Year 1074)

He complains that he has been disappointed in the hope and opinion he had formed concerning him. He advises him to come to the synod with his suffragans; or, if he should be prevented, to send messengers who can report both the revenues and the conduct of his suffragans.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sigefrid [Note: [Col. 0383] Concerning Sigefrid, Lambert under the years 1059 and 1072, and frequently elsewhere], archbishop of Mainz: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your fraternity remembers how we loved you with pure affection before the burden of this administration of ours, and how, in view of that same love of ours, you entrusted the counsels of your secrets to us and to a few others. Although for this reason we hoped well of you from that time onward, nevertheless, because you wished to devote the remainder of your life to the monastery of Cluny, we conceived an even greater confidence in your religious character.

Yet, according to the report of certain people, we have learned that you acted otherwise than we had hoped. If we allow this to pass negligently and without investigation, we are shown, not without great danger from our silence, to be offering you too little fraternal love. Therefore, by apostolic authority we admonish your religious devotion to come, if you can, with your suffragans—namely, Otto of Constance, Warner of Strasbourg, Henry of Speyer, Herimann of Bamberg, Imbrico of Augsburg, and Adelbero of Würzburg—to the synod which, God willing, we shall hold in the first week of Lent [Col. 0383D].

But if, God forbid, you are prevented by some illness and cannot come, strive to send us such messengers that we may safely rely upon their counsel and believe their testimony as though you were present. Let your fraternity consider this most carefully, so that neither through entreaties nor through anyone’s favor you fail to investigate with the utmost care the entry into office and conduct of the aforesaid bishops, and to make this known to us through those same messengers of yours [Col. 0384A].

Do not, therefore, be surprised that we have invited more men from your province than from others, since yours is larger than the rest, and there are in it some whose reputation is not praiseworthy.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Nones of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXX. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS. (Year 1074)

He rejoices that he received the apostolic legates kindly, rendered him the service of devoted submission, and is taking care that simony and clerical fornication be eradicated in his kingdom. He advises him to take faithful and prudent counselors into his service, restore its rights to the Church of Milan, and ensure that the bishops summoned to the synod come, sending a legate with them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry [Col. 0384B], king: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although, dearest son, you have not settled the case of the Church of Milan in the manner promised by the sequence and assurance of the letter sent to us, nevertheless, because you showed yourself benevolent and accommodating toward our legates, corrected certain ecclesiastical matters commendably through their intervention, and also sent through them an appropriate greeting and an expression of devoted service to us, we have received this gratefully.

We were also greatly gladdened by what your mother, the empress Agnes of pious memory, steadfastly testified to us, and what the same legate-bishops affirmed: namely, that you wished to eradicate the Simoniac heresy completely from your kingdom and correct with all your strength the long-standing disease of clerical fornication [Col. 0384C].

Our most faithful daughters, the countess Beatrix and her daughter Matilda, also gladdened us greatly by writing to us of your friendship and sincere affection, which we received most gladly. Influenced by their counsel, and also by the persuasion of your most beloved mother, the empress, we were led to write this letter to you.

Therefore, although I am a sinner, I have remembered you and shall remember you during the solemn celebrations of Mass over the tombs of the apostles, humbly beseeching that almighty God establish these good things for you and grant greater ones for the advancement of his Church.

I advise you, most excellent son, and exhort you with sincere charity, to employ as counselors men who love not what is yours but you yourself, and who care for your salvation, not their own profit [Col. 0384D]. If you obey them, you will have as your merciful protector the Lord God, whose cause they commend to you.

Concerning the case of Milan, if you send us religious and prudent men whose reasoning and authority make clear that the decree of the holy Roman Church, twice confirmed by synodal judgment, can or ought to be changed, we shall not find it burdensome to heed their just counsel and incline our mind toward what is more correct. But if it is established that this is impossible, I shall ask and beseech your sublimity, for the love of God and reverence for Saint Peter, freely to restore its right to that Church. Then you may recognize that you rightly possess royal power if you incline the height of your dominion before Christ, the King of kings, to restore and defend his churches, and recall with trembling the words of him who says: “I love those who love me” (Proverbs 8:17), and “I honor those who honor me; but those who despise me shall be treated as ignoble” (1 Samuel 2:30).

Furthermore, let your dignity know that we have sent a letter to Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz, summoning him to the synod which, God willing, we shall hold in the first week of the coming Lent. If it becomes clear that he cannot come, let him send legates to represent him at the council.

Similarly, we command the bishops of Bamberg, Strasbourg, and Speyer to be present and to give an account of their entry into office and their lives [Col. 0385B]. If, as human arrogance often causes, they delay coming, we ask that, through the impulse of your royal power, they be compelled to come. With them we wish legates of such a kind to be sent from your side that they may faithfully inform us both about their arrival and about their lives. Once the truth has been learned from their report, we shall be able with greater certainty to pronounce a clear judgment on matters beyond doubt.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE SAME. (Year 1074)

He testifies to his profound love for him. He asks him to turn his ears away from those who sow discord between him and the pope. He recounts the calamities of Christians who were being oppressed by pagans in the lands beyond the sea; he says that he has urged all Christians to come to their aid and that he is ready to do so himself—both for that purpose and so that the Eastern Church might be united with the Roman Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, glorious king: greetings and apostolic blessing.

If God would grant in some way, through his mercy, that my mind might be open to you, I know without doubt that, by his generous grace, no one could separate you from my love. Nevertheless, I trust in his mercy, because one day it will become clear that I love you with sincere charity.

For the common commandment of all Christians directs me to this; imperial majesty also impels me to it, as does the gentle authority of the apostolic see. For if I do not love you as I ought, I trust in vain in the mercy of God and in the merits of blessed Peter. But because I desire to labor day and night in the vineyard of the Lord, even through many dangers and unto death, I shall always strive, with God’s help, to preserve holy and worthy charity not only toward you, whom God has placed at the summit of affairs, through whom many can either stray from the right path or observe the Christian religion, but also toward the least Christian.

For anyone who attempts to enter the royal wedding without this garment will suffer immense disgrace. Alas, how lamentable! Those who daily plan to sow discord between us do not attend to this with watchful mind. By the nets prepared through diabolical instigation, they seek to capture their own advantages and conceal their own vices; by this madness they provoke against themselves the wrath of God and the sword of Saint Peter [Col. 0386A].

Therefore I warn and exhort you, dearest son: turn your ears away from such men and undoubtedly give a hearing to those who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 13), and who do not place their own honor or profit before justice. By their counsel, may you not lose the glory of this life but confidently acquire the glory that is in Christ Jesus.

Furthermore, I inform your greatness that Christians from the lands beyond the sea—most of whom are being destroyed by pagans in an unheard-of slaughter and killed daily like sheep, so that the Christian people are being reduced to nothing—have humbly sent to me, driven by extreme misery, imploring me to come to the aid of those same brothers of ours by whatever means I could [Col. 0386B], lest, God forbid, the Christian religion perish altogether in our time.

I, deeply afflicted and driven even to the desire for death—for I would rather lay down my life for them than neglecting them rule the whole world according to the desire of the flesh—have sought to urge and impel all Christians to desire, by defending the law of Christ, to lay down their lives for their brothers (John 10) and to display, more clearly than daylight, the nobility of the children of God.

The Italians and those from beyond the Alps received this exhortation willingly, as I believe—indeed, I affirm with complete confidence—through God’s inspiration. More than fifty thousand are now preparing for this purpose: if they can have me as their leader and bishop on the expedition, they intend to rise with armed force against the enemies of God [Col. 0386C] and, under his leadership, reach the Lord’s sepulchre.

Another matter also urges me most strongly toward this undertaking: the Church of Constantinople, dissenting from us concerning the Holy Spirit, awaits [or: seeks] agreement with the apostolic see. Almost all the Armenians have likewise deviated from the Catholic faith, and nearly all the peoples of the East await what the faith of the Apostle Peter will decide amid their differing opinions.

For in our time it is pressing that what the merciful Redeemer graciously chose to reveal and command especially to the chief of the apostles be fulfilled, when he said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22).

And because our fathers, whose footsteps we desire to follow, though unworthy, often visited those regions to strengthen the Catholic faith [Col. 0386D], we too, aided by the prayers of all Christians, if the way is opened under Christ’s leadership—for “the way of man is not in his own hand, and a man’s steps are directed by the Lord” (Psalm 36)—are compelled to cross over there for that same faith and for the defense of Christians.

But because a great undertaking requires great counsel and the assistance of great men, if God permits me to begin this, I ask your counsel and, as you deem appropriate, your aid. For if I go there with God’s favor, after God I leave the Roman Church to you, so that you may guard it as a holy mother and defend its honor.

Send me as soon as you can what you think about these matters and what your wisdom, inspired by God, decides. For if I did not hope in you more than most people do, I would be uttering these words in vain [Col. 0387A]. But since perhaps there is no man whose belief in the sincerity of my love you yet possess without doubt, I entrust this to the Holy Spirit, who can do all things, asking that he reveal to your mind, in his customary manner, what I desire for you and how greatly I love you. May he likewise dispose your mind toward me, so that the desire of the wicked may diminish and that of the good increase.

For these two desires continually keep watch over the two of us, though in different ways, and contend according to the will of him from whom they proceed. May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, through the merits and authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, absolve you from all sins, cause you to walk in the way of his commandments, and lead you to eternal life.

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXII. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS. (Year 1074)

[Col. 0387B]

He accepts the excuse of the archbishop of Rheims, who did not visit the thresholds of the apostles; he says that he will take great delight if the king of France corrects his crimes, but otherwise promises to oppose him in the future; and he commends his legates to him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Manasses, archbishop of Rheims: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you love the holy Roman Church and us, as your duty requires, with such [holy] embraces of affection, and that you burn with such ardor of love for it and for us that we have no hesitation in believing that, if you had full and free opportunity, you would visit the thresholds of the apostles [Col. 0387C].

Now, therefore, receive carefully and diligently, as you ought, the unheard-of evil and detestable crime which Philip, king of France—indeed, a ravening wolf, an unjust tyrant, an enemy of God and of the religion of the holy Church—committed against Italian merchants and those of other provinces, contrary to God and the honor of his kingdom, together with the other matters whose outcries have very frequently reached our ears.

If he corrects these things as justice dictates, we shall undoubtedly rejoice and praise God with thanksgiving, so that your fraternity may know that the lost sheep has been found. But if he acts contrary to this—which we do not desire—we promise that God will undoubtedly be his enemy, and that the holy Roman Church and we, over whom we preside though unworthy, will oppose him with all our strength and by every means [Col. 0387D].

If our legates, as we expect, come to your region to discuss these matters, what you have written to us, and many other things, with you and with your assistance, receive them as representatives of Peter and love them as representatives of us, so that in these matters also you may prove how closely you adhere in love to the chief of the apostles and to us.

Given at Rome on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO CUNIPERT, BISHOP OF TURIN. (Year 1074)

He reproves him because, although summoned, he did not come to the synod and because he caused trouble for the monastery of Saint Michael. He orders him to come to another synod and not to harm the said monastery.

[Col. 0388A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Cunipert [Cunibert], bishop of Turin: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although we ought to inveigh more harshly against your presumption, because, although summoned to the synod which we held around the feast of Saint Andrew, you scorned to come, and because you refused to withdraw the hand of disturbance from the venerable monastery of Saint Michael, neither out of reverence for divine fear nor out of regard for apostolic protection, we nevertheless continue to preserve fraternal affection toward you and await the fruit of your due satisfaction.

Therefore, we again admonish you by apostolic authority to come to the synod which we shall hold in the first week of Lent [Col. 0388B]. We shall retain the abbot of the aforesaid monastery with us until that synod, so that, after hearing the arguments of both sides, both your Church and that monastery may obtain their proper justice.

Meanwhile, we also admonish you not to cause any disturbance to the aforesaid place. But if you disobey this letter of ours, you will compel us to do what the holy Fathers did in such matters and to defend that place by the authority of blessed Peter.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO RAINERIUS. (Year 1074)

He declares invalid everything done by the abbot of Saint Gaudentius. As for what Rainerius himself contracted with him, he postpones its determination until the arrival of his messenger.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainerius, illustrious man: greetings and apostolic blessing.
