Since we have long ago tested your devotion and faith toward blessed Peter, as befits you, and have no doubt that you will receive a reward worthy of your works, we confidently entrust to you his service and justice, hoping that your nobility will not only show itself devoted but will also press others whom it can toward his service.

Since, therefore, we believe that you know, dearest son, how we justly condemned the abbot of Saint Gaudentius [Note: [Col. 0387D] “How” refers to Henry], a wicked man, indeed an invader [Col. 0388D] and heretic, for his wickedness, we now judge that you must be informed that everything perpetrated or alienated by that son of perdition with regard to the Church’s property unlawfully, as by a heretic, must be annulled and utterly voided by canonical and legal authority.

As for what that wicked man entered into with you, namely, ecclesiastical securities, we determine this out of consideration and affection for you: when our messenger comes to you, have with you wise men who fear God and love you. With their counsel, examine the case. When you have found that you cannot retain the property of Saint Gaudentius under such a wicked agreement without danger to your soul and condemnation, strive, for love of Saint Peter and of us, to restore it to the Church as quickly as possible, and also to recover what has been unjustly retained by others [Col. 0389A].

Do not cease to assist our messengers when they come to your region, if you desire to have the favor of Saint Peter and our benefaction.

Given at Rome on the Ides of December, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXV. TO GUILIELMUS, BISHOP OF PAVIA. (Year 1074)

He reproves him because, although summoned, he did not come. He orders him to attend the council, at which he is given an opportunity to defend the marriage of his sister to Azo, whom witnesses affirmed to be her kinsman.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guilielmus [Col. 0389B], bishop of Pavia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although you appear to have acted against us in such a way that we ought not even to have sent you apostolic blessing—namely, because you neither came at the appointed time nor sent a lawful excuse—we nevertheless prefer to be reproved for merciful moderation rather than, by following the rigor of the canons, to avenge your disobedience severely.

Therefore we command you by apostolic authority to come to the synod which, God willing, we shall hold in the first week of Lent, and to answer concerning the case of your sister. Although it is very clear that she had Guido, marquis, as her husband, a kinsman of Azo, marquis, and although it has also been proved before us by oaths and witnesses [Col. 0389C] that your sister and Azo have not yet passed beyond the fourth degree of kinship, we shall nevertheless grant you a hearing at the aforesaid synod. Thus, if you are confident that you have a lawful defense and are able to invalidate before us the testimonies and oaths previously given, their marriage may continue.

Otherwise, if you are then unable to do this, or if you withdraw from the aforesaid synod, we prohibit by apostolic authority that any further question be raised concerning it. Therefore, in the oath by which we bound the aforesaid Azo, we were so careful that, with our permission, if your arguments prove valid, he may take her back and have her as his wife.

[Col. 0389D] Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO COUNTESS MATILDA. (Year 1074)

He orders her to withdraw from Azo’s company; but if she is confident that she can prove that he is not her kinsman, he will hear her case at the next council.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Matilda: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Those who were present at that case can report to you how it was proved before us by witnesses and oaths that you had as your husband a kinsman of Azo, and that you and Azo, marquis, are related within the fourth degree [Col. 0390A].

Therefore, since we have bound Azo, marquis, by an oath not thereafter to have marital relations with you without our permission, we also command you on behalf of blessed Peter to withdraw completely from his company and cohabitation, and to repent of the iniquity committed in such a worthy manner that you may recover God’s grace and avoid the disgrace of so great and shameful an incest.

But if you perhaps think that you are suffering prejudice, and are confident that you can invalidate the testimonies and oaths concerning your kinship, we grant you a hearing at the next Roman synod, where, with God’s help, we shall incline neither to the right nor to the left in carrying out justice, but shall establish what is just.

[Col. 0390B] Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (Year 1074)

He exhorts them to defend the Christians who were being oppressed by unbelievers in the lands beyond the sea.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Saint Peter, especially the transalpine faithful [“especially” is absent], greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you have already learned what our will is and what we have said [or: sent] on behalf of Saint Peter concerning the aid to be given to our brothers who live beyond the sea in the empire of Constantinople. The devil is attempting to turn them away from the Catholic faith by his own action, and through his members he does not cease daily to slaughter them cruelly like sheep [Col. 0390C].

But because he envies good desires, he attempts, if he can, to prevent us from freeing them through the generosity of divine grace and from being crowned by giving our lives for our brothers.

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter, we ask, admonish, and invite you: in the manner that the bearer of this letter will indicate, let some of you come to us—those who wish to defend the Christian faith and serve the heavenly King—so that, with them, God willing, we may prepare the way for all who wish to cross the sea through us in defense of their heavenly nobility and who are not afraid to show that they are sons of God.

Therefore, dearest brothers, be exceedingly strong for battle, for that praise and glory which surpass every desire—you who until now have been strong in fighting for possessions that you cannot retain or possess without pain. For through momentary labor (2 Corinthians 4) you can acquire an eternal reward [Col. 0390D].

May almighty God, who has abridged his entire law into the commandment of charity, grant you to love him with your whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength, so that, loving your neighbors as yourselves, you may deserve, if necessary, to lay down your lives for them.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO COUNT UBERTUS AND THE CLERGY OF FIRMO. (Year 1074)

That they should provide assistance to the archdeacon to whom he had entrusted the administration of the bishopric of Fermo until a suitable pastor could be provided.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ubertus [Col. 0391A], count, and to all the clergy and people of Fermo who remain faithful to Saint Peter: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although many things concerning your archdeacon were reported to us as blameworthy, once he had been placed in our presence and carefully questioned concerning the charges brought against him, we were able to find in him nothing except what appeared to pertain to faithful obedience. Therefore, considering the need of the widowed Church, we entrusted him for the time being with the administration of the entire bishopric, until, through the providential mercy of God, a suitable person might be found to govern the Church and episcopal dignity—both through our solicitude and through the king’s counsel and appropriate provision.

Accordingly, we admonish you and, by apostolic authority, command that you unanimously provide him with your counsel and assistance for carrying these matters out, and that you aid him by every means to recover and properly organize whatever goods of the Church have been dispersed and thrown into confusion. If anyone has wrongfully committed anything against the aforesaid Church, or is attempting to do so, let him strive without delay to make amends and restore it. But if anyone, through some act of recklessness, neglects this, let him know that by apostolic authority he will incur a ban: one hundred pounds if he is wealthy, but, if he is of modest means, the loss of his entire property.

Act, therefore, so that it may be evident that you are freeborn and faithful sons of your mother Church, and so that everything pertaining to her honor and welfare may be vigorously carried out through your efforts under the oversight of the archdeacon. Thus may you deserve the grace of almighty God and the salvation of apostolic blessing. [Col. 0391B–C]

Given at Rome, on the second [XI] day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE DUKE AND PEOPLE OF VENICE. (Year 1074)

He testifies to his affection for them. He urges them to provide what is necessary for preserving life, in keeping with the dignity of the patriarch, who is oppressed by extreme poverty.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Dominico, duke, and to the people of Venice: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe it is known not only to those who have lived with us, but also to many among you, that from our earliest youth we have greatly loved your land and the liberty of this people, and for that reason have endured the hostility of certain princes and noble persons. But after we had assumed, although unworthy, the burden and office of apostolic governance, our affection for you burned all the more fervently, in proportion as the obligation of universal care bound us more anxiously to the administration of your salvation.

For this reason we have sent you a letter, so that we might rouse your nobility to regard the honor and dignity of its ancient rank, lest it lament the loss—God forbid—through prolonged negligence, of an honor which, while it still stands, it does not strive, so far as it can, to honor and preserve. For you know that, above many regions of the earth, divine providence has exalted your land with the dignity of a patriarchate. The eminence of this dignity, by the prerogative of its very name and office, is so restricted and rare that no more than four are found throughout the world.

Yet although this is so, among you this great distinction and the glory of so exalted a priesthood have become so debased through the poverty of temporal resources and the diminution of its power, and have fallen so completely from the proper condition of its honor, that such extreme want seems unable either to become a simple episcopal see or to meet its needs. Hence we perceive that you are ungrateful and forgetful of so great a benefit of divine munificence, fearing that, like degenerate sons, by dissipating the riches and inheritance of your most noble mother—the Church of Grado—you may become more obscure precisely where, after the apostolic see, you were once more illustrious than all the peoples of the West. [Col. 0392A–B]

We indeed remember that Dominicus, the patriarch of blessed memory and predecessor of the present patriarch, wished to abandon this place because of its excessive poverty; and the present patriarch likewise says that he is surrounded by the same necessity. Therefore, as dearly beloved sons, we admonish you not to neglect any longer, mindful of your former nobility and glory, the honor bestowed upon you and the benevolence of the apostolic see toward you. Instead, meet together and deliberate by common counsel how you may sustain the dignity of this leading patriarchate with the veneration due to it and with an increase of temporal resources, and, with God’s help, raise it again to the summit of its exalted status.

Our brother here, the patriarch, has indeed informed us that you, Duke, and many of you have the best possible will concerning this matter. For this reason we begin with greater confidence to exhort your affection to complete this good intention. Whatever you decide and establish among yourselves, report to us as soon as possible by letter or through a reliable messenger. For if, as is proper, you determine something for the glory and nobility both of yourselves and of the aforesaid place and priesthood, we shall rejoice according to your merits; but if some less honorable consideration draws you back, we shall assuredly not allow the name of so great a ministry to become debased among you or to be deprived of the honor due to it. [Col. 0392C–D]

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XL. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (Year 1074)

That they should receive his legates with suitable honor and show them obedience.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Saint Peter to whom the bearers of this letter shall come: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You know that, as wickedness increases and diabolical deceit grows stronger everywhere, the charity of many has now grown cold, and zeal for the whole of religion has almost disappeared from the holy Church. But since it is impossible for us to make our presence felt amid so many and such diverse concerns, we have sent to you beloved sons of the holy Roman Church—namely Gepizo [Geizo, and so everywhere], abbot of Saint Boniface, and Mauro, abbot of Saint Sabbas—through whom our authority may be represented to you and, in our place, those matters pertaining to the welfare of the holy Church may, with God’s help, be diligently carried out.

Therefore, mindful of the divine saying in the Gospel, “Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10), receive them with due veneration and charity, regarding them as representatives not merely of our friendship, but rather of the grace of Saint Peter, whose messengers they are. In everything that either the purpose of their legation or the necessity of their labors may require, provide them with faithful obedience and cooperation.

Moreover, if it should happen that, because of a considered and appropriate need arising from their affairs, they divide and depart separately into different regions, listen to whichever one of them comes to you as you would listen to us, and do not hesitate to show and carry out in him whatever you would owe to our presence. [Col. 0393A–B]

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year of Christ 1075.

## LETTER XLI. TO THE PEOPLE OF FERETRUM AND EUGUBIUM. (Year 1075)

He explains that he has sent legates for the purpose of ensuring that a suitable pastor be elected in their Church. He instructs them to obey the legates.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Feretrum, and to the clergy and people of Eugubium: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Ever since we learned that your Church had been deprived of its pastor, we have been anxious on your behalf with great concern. Although many serious affairs occupy us, our concern that divine mercy provide you with a worthy father remains continually fixed in our heart. We are all the more solicitous for this reason and pour out our prayers to God more attentively because we know that in former times a pastor who was not sufficiently vigilant presided over you.

Therefore we have sent to you these religious sons of the holy Roman Church—namely the abbot of Saint Sabbas and the abbot of Saint Boniface—so that, if perhaps a person suitable for this governance may be found in your Church, they may diligently inquire into the matter and promptly endeavor to present him to us for ordination, commended by your election, as is proper, and approved by canonical decree. But if no such person can be found among you, let them, with every diligence and concern, seek elsewhere someone who can preside over you according to God’s will, and send him to us without delay to receive ordination to the episcopal office.

Therefore, believe and obey them in everything, knowing that in this matter, under God’s protection, they are concerned with nothing except your salvation and the honor of your Church. Moreover, present to their eyes whatever treasure or ornament is held in your Church, so that, through their foresight and recommendation, it may be left in such custody that neither the Church suffers loss nor any suspicion of dishonor falls upon any of you. [Col. 0393C–0394A]

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLII. TO GUIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA. (Year 1075)

He summons him to the synod customarily held in the coming Lent.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You have before your eyes, dearest brother, and can almost touch with your hands, the pitiable disturbance of the holy Church, as well as the senseless and altogether unrestrained presumption of its enemies and attackers, which has continued for so long. Since we who have been chosen for a share in the priestly ministry and in the kingdom of God ought to rise against them and fight with every care and effort, we have resolved, God willing, to celebrate—as has been customary at the apostolic see for several years—a synod in the first week of Lent.

We therefore ask and invite your fraternity, with a special admonition and abundant expression of charity, to come, setting aside all negligence, so that, through the prudent assistance of you and our other brothers, and through both spiritual courage and wisdom, the impious may be restrained from their endeavors and the Christian religion may be strengthened in the liberty and peace in which it was first founded. [Col. 0394B–C]

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLIII. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DIE. (Year 1075)

That he should receive from his subjects what they wish to restore to the Church, and absolve them upon their pledge to come to the synod.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, bishop of Die in Burgundy: greetings and apostolic blessing.

It seems good to us that you receive what the sons of your Church wish to return to you from ecclesiastical property, and absolve them on these terms: that, having given their pledge, some of them promise to come with you to us at Rome—namely, God willing, to the synod that is to be celebrated there—so that they may carry out there whatever we deem right. For we prefer that you occasionally be reproached for piety rather than, through excessive severity, incur the hatred of your Church.

You ought indeed to regard your sons as inexperienced and uneducated, and gradually lead them toward better things, because no one suddenly becomes perfect, and lofty buildings are erected little by little. [Col. 0394D]

Given at Rome, on the Nones of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLIV. TO JUDITH, QUEEN OF THE HUNGARIANS. (Year 1075)

He enumerates several reasons for his sincere affection toward her. He consoles her and urges her to patience. Finally, he asserts that he will gladly attend to everything pertaining to her honor and salvation.

[Col. 0395A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Judith, queen of the Hungarians: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] Concerning Judith, wife of Solomon, king of the Hungarians: Lambert, in the years 1061 and 1063.]

There are many and varied reasons why we love you with the deepest and sincerest affection of the heart. First, because, by undertaking universal governance, we are debtors to all who are in Christ. Then because the most illustrious Emperor Henry, your father, and Agnes, your mother—now no longer an earthly empress but, by God’s mercy, a heavenly Empress Augusta—ever since they came to know me, have treated me honorably, in keeping with their greatness, and with greater charity than the other sons of the holy Roman Church.

Most of all, because now this same mother and lady of yours, setting aside secular concerns and honors, embraces the thresholds of the apostles with complete devotion and veneration. Through her presence, amid the wicked disturbances of this age, we are often granted welcome consolation. Moreover, your distinguished and renowned reputation greatly commends you to us: although still of tender age, among a harsh and unfamiliar people you have adorned the glory of your lineage. For, born into exalted imperial power, you have thus far displayed nothing in your conduct or bearing except imperial dignity.

For these reasons, then—we to whom it is forbidden to deceive anyone—we love you as a true sister; and, if our prayers have any power with God, we trust in God’s goodness that our friendship toward you will not be fruitless. Know also that we greatly grieve over the tribulations and hardships that we have learned you are enduring, and frequently and humbly implore divine mercy for your peace and joy. And whenever place or time provides the opportunity, we very much wish to honor you with temporal assistance as well. [Col. 0395B–C]

But do not let the adversity that now presses upon you frighten you, nor let it depress the spirit of your nobility. If anything sorrowful or burdensome should assail you, conceal it in the expression and bearing of royal steadfastness, and patiently endure the troubles—which God avert—in accordance with the natural strength of your character.

Have firm trust and hope in God our Savior, for he cares for you and never abandons those who hope in him (Judith 13). And the more bitterly he now allows your spirit to be struck by anxieties, the more abundantly he will gladden it through the consolation of his approaching and powerful strength. For he commands nothing without cause and permits nothing without reason; he is the just arbiter and governor of kings, emperors, and all affairs.

Above all, however, we admonish you to act and strive so that the illustrious name of your life and nobility, acquired from your earliest years, may be enlarged and increase day by day. For although integrity of reputation is a crown of the noble and ignoble alike, more than all the riches of the earth, it nevertheless bestows upon each person the greater adornment and glory in proportion as, together with the distinction of lineage, it raises that person higher. The humble are concealed by their humility, but the exalted are revealed by the height innate in them. [Col. 0395D–0396A]

Act, therefore, so that you may show yourself superior in all that the kingdom and empire produce, in proportion as you recognize that all those things are subject to change. But regard your own nature and the imperial seed that is in you as incapable of being changed by any success or adversity.

As for your request that we speak to your mother concerning your affairs, know for certain that we shall gladly inform her, through counsel, of everything pertaining to your honor and salvation, and shall kindly offer apostolic assistance by persuading her that these things be done.

May almighty God, who is the consolation of the sorrowful and the strength of the weak, quickly grant you present joy and bestow true and eternal glory in heavenly happiness. [Col. 0396B]

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLV. TO RODULPH, DUKE OF SWABIA, AND BERTHULPH, DUKE OF CARINTHIA. (Year 1075)

He attacks the bishops who were disobedient in carrying out the decrees of the apostolic see concerning simoniacal and fornicating clerics. He therefore instructs the dukes not to receive any whom they know to be simoniacs or fornicators. He urges Rodulph to spend for pious purposes the money he had received from clerics on account of benefices.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rodulph, duke of Swabia, and Bertulph [Note: [Col. 0396D] Elsewhere Berthold, as in Lambert for the year 1073; and elsewhere Bertaritus], duke of Carinthia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We know that your prudence clearly perceives the pitiable desolation of the Christian religion, which, because of our sins, has now been brought to such an extreme that no living person has seen more wretched times, nor found them recorded in the tradition of the Scriptures since the time of our father, blessed Sylvester.

Yet we are the head and cause of this great evil—we who have been set over the governance of the people and called and appointed as bishops for the winning of souls. For from their positions of authority, as from certain beginnings, come the good or evil of their subjects—they who have undertaken either worldly dignities or spiritual governance. Since they seek nothing except the glory and pleasures of this age, they cannot live without bringing confusion upon themselves and the people. For by pursuing perverse desires in evil deeds, they bind the rights of their authority through guilt and, by their example, loosen the restraints on others’ sinning.

Nor do they transgress through ignorance or lack of foresight. Rather, by presumptuous obstinacy they resist the Holy Spirit, cast aside the divine laws they have learned, and despise the apostolic decrees. The archbishops and bishops of your land know—and this ought to be known to all the faithful—that the sacred canons prohibit those who have been promoted to any rank or office of holy orders through the Simoniacal heresy, that is, through the intervention of a price, from having any further place of ministry in the holy Church. Nor should those who lie in the crime of fornication celebrate Mass or minister at the altar according to the lower orders.

Although the holy and apostolic mother Church has repeatedly admonished, urged, and, by the authority received through Peter, commanded them and the peoples entrusted to them, in councils, through legates and letters, to renew and observe these rules—neglected, as they were, by earlier generations—nevertheless, they have remained disobedient, with very few exceptions. They have made no effort to cut off this utterly detestable custom by any prohibition or punish it with any severity, paying no attention to what is written: “To resist is the sin of divination, and to refuse to obey is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15). [Col. 0396C–0397A]

Since we understand that, while they despise the apostolic—or rather, the commands of the Holy Spirit—and criminally foster the crimes of their subjects, the divine ministries are being handled unworthily and the people deceived, we must in every possible way keep watch against these things, we to whom the care of the Lord’s flock has been entrusted above all others. It seems far better to us to rebuild God’s justice, even through new counsels, than to allow human souls, together with the laws, to perish through neglect.

Therefore we now turn to you and to all whose faith and devotion we trust, asking and admonishing you by apostolic authority that, whatever the bishops may henceforth say or remain silent about, you in no way accept the ministry of those whom you know to have been promoted and ordained through Simony or to be lying in the crime of fornication. Make this same matter known and persuade others of it, under the obligation of obedience, both at the king’s court and throughout the other places and assemblies of the kingdom; and, as far as you can, prevent such men from serving the sacred mysteries, even by force if necessary.

If anyone begins to chatter against you as though this duty did not belong to your office, answer them: “Let them come to us to dispute with us concerning the obedience imposed upon you, without obstructing the salvation of yourselves and the people.”

Since I trust that you, Rodulph, duke and dearly beloved son of Saint Peter, eagerly aspire to the spirit of religion, and since you consulted us, we inform you of whatever seemed to us most perfect for your correction: spend whatever price you remember having received from clerics for arranging their positions in the Church either for the uses of that same Church, if it appears to belong to it, or for the needs of the poor. Thus, with no stain of blame remaining upon you, may you deserve to be enrolled among the chosen citizens of the heavenly kingdom. [Col. 0397B–D]

Given at Rome, on the third [XIII] day before the Ides of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLVI. TO THE ABBOTS GEPITIUS AND MAURO. (Year 1075)

He commands them to arrange for the restoration of the goods of the Church of Pesaro, which its bishop had imprudently alienated, and to settle the dispute between the bishop and the others.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gepitius, abbot of Saint Boniface, and Mauro, abbot of Saint Sabbas, appointed as legates in the Marches: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We command you to meet diligently with those men to whom Michael, bishop of Pesaro, imprudently gave the goods of his Church, and by apostolic authority order them to restore everything to the Church and to the bishop; compel them to do so as appropriate. Moreover, if they are disobedient, strive publicly, on behalf of Saint Peter and ourselves, to place them personally under the ban, and clearly inform them that, if they prove rebellious, they will lose the grace of Saint Peter and our own.

You are also firmly to urge and command the bishops, counts, and all the faithful of Saint Peter to assist the bishop of Pesaro faithfully, with spiritual and secular aid as necessary, in overcoming them. Correct most sharply above all those who, after receiving payment, are still not ashamed to retain the land violently and arrogantly, and restore the Church’s goods by placing them in the bishop’s possession.

You are also to arrange the settlement of every dispute between the bishop and his adversaries for the benefit of the Church of Saint Mary of Pesaro, without allowing negligence or carelessness to intervene. [Col. 0398A–B]

Given at Rome, on the Ides of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLVII. TO RAINERIUS, ETC. (Year 1075)

He announces that he ordered the bishop of Chiusi—who had restored Guido, entangled in many crimes and expelled by his predecessor, Pope Alexander, from a certain provostship—to remove him and substitute another in his place. He orders them not to assist the said Guido in retaining the provostship.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainerius, son of Ugizo [Uguccio, and so elsewhere], and Rainerius, son of Bulgarellus, and also to the wife of Peppo, Lady Willa, and to the sons of Count Ardingo, and to all dwelling in the county of Chiusi, both great and small, faithful to Christ and Saint Peter: greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is well known to you that Guido has incurred perjury in many ways against the Church of Christ and of the martyr and virgin Mustiola; he has also openly persisted in fornication and sustained the crime of adultery, and finally has altogether avoided offering satisfaction. For this reason, he was irrevocably expelled by our predecessor, Lord Alexander of blessed memory, both from the leadership of that Church and, for his contumacious disobedience, was subjected to perpetual anathema should he ever again presume to seek the provostship.

But since our brother Lanfrancus, bishop of Chiusi, relying upon the counsel of certain of his faithful who were wise according to the flesh, attempted to place this same Guido over the Church again canonically, against the authority of the Roman Church and against the unanimous opposition of all its household, both clergy and laity, we subject the bishop to a penance proportionate to his satisfaction, on these terms: he is to publicly excommunicate the aforesaid Guido, remove him from the provostship and from cloistered communion, and substitute another in his place according to God’s will. [Col. 0398C–0399A]

Therefore, dearest sons, if you wish to have God favorable toward you and Saint Peter bring aid to your sins, take every care not to provide the aforesaid sacrilegious Guido with any assistance or counsel against God and our judgment for retaining the provostship, nor to give him any help concerning the possessions of Saint Mustiola. For without doubt, if—which may your nobility be spared—you attempt in any way to assist him, and cause the goods that he gave to his friends for retaining the provostship to remain in their possession, you will share in his excommunication.

But if, as befits Christian men, you strive to restore the Church of God—and, indeed, your mother—to its former condition after his expulsion, you will possess an incorruptible inheritance among God’s saints in the heavenly kingdom, having obtained the remission of sins through the ineffable mercy of God. [Col. 0399B]

Given at Rome, on the Ides of January, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO THE ABBOTS GEPITIUS AND MAURO. (Year 1075)

That they should warn a certain fratricide, who was insisting on marrying another wife before completing his penance, not to do so; instead, he should come to him to hear what concerns his salvation.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gepitius, abbot of Saint Boniface, and Mauro, abbot of Saint Sabbas: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You know that Rainerius, formerly the son of Ugizo, killed his brother at the devil’s instigation. For this reason he has not yet submitted himself to worthy penance, nor repented completely. Forgetful of so great a crime, of the promise concerning ecclesiastical protections that he made when he undertook a feigned penance, and also of Christ’s poor, he has consigned the salvation of his soul to oblivion and is striving to marry another wife.

Therefore we wish your fraternity to be concerned that you meet with him and, in whatever ways you can, warn him gently and sternly, as much as may be necessary and seem appropriate to you, so that he in no way presume to do this. Instead, let him come to us to hear what we have to say to him concerning his salvation.

But if—something we do not wish—he refuses to listen to you and obey us, make him entirely certain that, with God’s help, we shall not neglect to do whatever appears just and canonical. [Col. 0399C–D]

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY. (Year 1075)

He laments his own wretched condition and that of the Church. He therefore asks that prayers for him be poured out to God, and wishes the abbot to exhort all the faithful to restrain the violence of the impious.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Hugh is lacking.]

If it could be done, I would wish you fully to know how great a tribulation afflicts me, how great a labor renewed each day exhausts me, and how greatly its increase disturbs me, so that, in accordance with the tribulations of my heart, fraternal compassion might bend you toward me and you might pour out your heart before the Lord in a flood of tears. Then poor Jesus [read: “to poor Jesus,” H.], through whom all things were made and who governs all things, might extend his hand and, in his customary mercy, deliver the wretched man.

I have often begged him, as he himself enabled me, either to remove me from this present life or to benefit our common mother through me. Yet he has still not rescued me from this great tribulation, nor has my life benefited the aforesaid mother, whose chains he fastened around me, as I had hoped. For immense grief and universal sadness surround me, because the Eastern Church, at the devil’s instigation, has fallen away from the Catholic faith, and through its members that ancient enemy is killing Christians everywhere, so that those whom he kills spiritually as their head may be punished bodily by his members, lest they ever recover their senses through divine grace.

Again, when I turn the attention of my mind to the regions of the West, South, or North, I scarcely find bishops who are canonical either in entry into office or in life, who govern the Christian people out of love for Christ rather than secular ambition. Among all the secular princes, I know none who places God’s honor above his own and justice above profit. As for those among whom I live—Romans, Lombards, and Normans—I rebuke them, as I often tell them, as in some way worse than Jews and pagans. [Col. 0400A–C]

When I return to myself, I find myself so burdened by the weight of my own actions that no hope of salvation remains except in the sole mercy of Christ. For if I did not hope to come to a better life and to serve the welfare of the holy Church, I would in no way remain in Rome, where, as God is my witness, I have now dwelt under compulsion for twenty years. Thus, amid the grief that is renewed in me each day and the hope that, alas, is stretched out too far, battered by a thousand storms, I live somehow while dying.

I await him who bound me with his chains, brought me unwillingly back to Rome, and surrounded me there with a thousand hardships. I frequently say to him: “Hasten; do not delay. Hurry; do not linger. Free me for the love of blessed Mary and Saint Peter.” But since praise is not precious, nor holy prayer quickly effective, on the lips of a sinner whose life is praiseworthy but whose conduct is secular, I beg, implore, and entreat you to ask those who deserve to be heard because of the merits of their lives to intercede with God for me, with that charity and love with which they ought to love the universal mother.

And since we ought to use both hands in place of the right hand to restrain the violence of the impious, and since there is no prince who attends to such matters, we admonish you in fraternal charity to protect the lives of religious men with vigilant zeal, insofar as you can. Warn, ask, and exhort those who love blessed Peter that, if they truly wish to be his sons and soldiers, they should not love secular princes more than him. Those princes scarcely grant miserable and transitory things; but Saint Peter promises blessed and eternal things to all whom he releases from their sins and leads, by the power entrusted to him, into the heavenly homeland.

I wish to know, clearer than daylight, who are truly his faithful, and who love this same heavenly Prince no less for heavenly glory than they love those to whom, for the hope of earthly and miserable things, they subject themselves. [Col. 0400D–0401A]

Given at Rome, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER L. TO SANCHO, KING OF ARAGON. (Year 1075)

He judges it absurd that one born from an illegitimate concubinage should rise to the episcopal rank to which he was being proposed. He says that he had entrusted the matter to the bishop, who wished to resign the episcopate because of illness, so that he might appoint as his coadjutor a person of such a kind who could assume the administration of that bishopric after the bishop’s death.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sancho, king of the Spains: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because we understand that your royal nobility burns with pious devotion and love toward the holy and apostolic see, we desire that you and your kingdom be exalted with fitting honors, and we wish to extend apostolic benevolence toward you and your affairs with sincere charity, not only in our own time but at every time. Moreover, concerning the matter of the bishopric of Aragon, about which you consulted us and indicated that you in some way wished to act, after long and careful consideration, and after discussing it with the sons of the holy Roman Church, we perceived that this would be inappropriate, since we recognized that the canonical decrees stood in our way.

For, as you know, our brother Sancius, bishop of Aragon, came to us, complaining at length about the infirmity of his body and humbly requesting permission from us to abandon the bishopric, since, exhausted and almost consumed by illness, he could no longer govern and guard it for long with suitable competence. And, to obtain this more readily, he informed us about two clerics, announcing that it was your will and his own intention and decision that one of them be elected to the bishopric. When we questioned him about their life and conduct, we learned that in every other respect they were sufficiently good and honorable, except that they had been born of concubines.

Since the venerable canons prohibit anyone of this kind from being advanced to the rank of the priesthood, we judged that it would not be sufficiently prudent to approve them, lest anything contrary to the holy Fathers be left by us as an example and precedent for posterity. For the holy and apostolic see often tolerates many things after careful consideration, but never departs in its decrees and constitutions from the harmony of canonical tradition.

Therefore let your affection know that we have consulted and instructed the bishop as follows: while devoting himself, as far as he can, to the episcopal office in spiritual matters and seeking the assistance of the bishops of his province, he is to appoint in the Church, for the fulfillment of its external and internal responsibilities, a cleric who is prudent enough to undertake such administration and who, if circumstances require it, is suitable to receive the dignity and rank of the episcopal office. If this man remains in the Church for one year or more, and if divine mercy meanwhile restores bodily strength and health to the bishop, then, as is just, the bishop himself is to remain in his place, keeping watch over the Lord’s flock. But if the infirmity and weakness of his body increase, so that he is entirely unable to carry out the administration entrusted to him, then—and only then—provided that his life, morals, and discipline are judged worthy, this is to be reported to the apostolic see by letters from you and from the bishop, as well as under the testimony of the clergy of that Church; and, after deliberate consideration, a certain and salutary response concerning the government of the Church will be given to you, with God’s assent.

We would by no means have spoken so unreservedly about these matters had we not been unable to deny a hearing of fraternal compassion to the bishop when he excused himself and pleaded the impediment caused by his illness. Consider these matters prudently, therefore, beloved son, and assist the bishop as far as you can in observing our instructions, so that you too may deserve to be aided by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in governing the people entrusted to you, and through his merits, freed from the bonds of your sins, may merit to enjoy the glory of eternal blessedness in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

Given at Rome, on the eighth [or ninth] day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LI. TO SUENO, KING OF THE DANES (1075)

[Col. 0402C]

He complains that Sueno has not written to him. He urges him to administer the kingdom rightly. He explains that the envoys sent to him to respond concerning the matters he had requested from Pope Alexander on account of the disturbance in Germany have returned. He therefore asks him to send messengers to Rome and to appoint his son as commander against certain heretics.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to SUENO, king of the Danes, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Note: [Col. 0401] Lambert mentions Sueno, king of the Danes, under the year 1073.]

While we were still in the order of the diaconate, we often received letters and envoys from your affection, through which we understood that your magnificence possessed a ready disposition toward us. But after—although we are unworthy—we reached the position of a higher care and ministry, we discovered that your love had grown cold through your withdrawal from visiting us; and I do not know why we have deserved to be deprived of your letters for so long.

Now, indeed, concern for not only kings and princes but for all Christians weighs upon us all the more heavily, in proportion as, through the universal government entrusted to us, the cause of every person more closely and properly concerns us. Yet because we have understood that the eminence of your nobility surpasses that of the rulers of other kingdoms both in knowledge of letters and in zeal for ecclesiastical exhortation, we direct our writings to you with much greater confidence, judging that we shall more readily win you for God insofar as you are recognized to have advanced further in learning and prudence of conduct.

We therefore ask and admonish you with sincere charity to strive to administer, according to God, the government of the kingdom entrusted to you, and to bear the name of royal excellence with a fitting and harmonious character of virtues, so that you may show that justice—which rules over your subjects through your princely authority—always reigns in your heart.

For you know that the glory and vain delight of this world are fleeting and deceptive. You know that all flesh hastens daily toward its end, and that the necessity of death obeys neither the willing nor the unwilling [perhaps “spares” rather than “obeys”; HARD.]. You know that kings, on equal terms with the poor, will become dust and ashes, and that we shall all come to the strict judgment of the coming examination. This must now be feared and dreaded not only by us who are priests, but also by kings and other princes, all the more anxiously because we shall render an account for ourselves and for our subjects.

Act, therefore, most beloved son, so that you may live and reign in such a way that you may then behold the face of the eternal King and Judge without fear, and, for the glory of your earthly dignity rightly administered, may receive, by God’s gift, the lofty and incomparable crown of the heavenly kingdom.

Furthermore, let it be known to you that we sent envoys to you who were to respond to you and confer with you concerning matters relating to the honor of your kingdom—both the metropolitan see and certain other matters which, during the time of our lord Pope Alexander, you had requested from the apostolic see and had likewise promised in return. But, recognizing that it was then dangerous to do so because of the disturbance in the German lands, they returned to us.

Therefore, if any of these matters lie close to your heart, and if you wish—as we have learned several times through your envoys—to commit yourself and your kingdom with pious devotion to the prince of the apostles and to be strengthened by his authority, strive to send faithful messengers to us without delay. Through them, once we have learned your will in every matter, we may, after deliberate consideration, discern and provide what answer should be given to you and what action should be taken concerning all these matters.

Moreover, if the holy Roman mother Church should need your assistance against the profane and enemies of God, in soldiers and in the material sword, we likewise wish to learn through a reliable embassy from you what hope we may place in you.

There is also, not far from us, a certain extremely wealthy province beside the sea, held by worthless and cowardly heretics. We wish one of your sons to become its commander, prince, and defender of Christianity, if you were to offer him—as a certain bishop of your land has reported to us that you have in mind—to serve in the apostolic court with a considerable number of men who would be his loyal soldiers.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LII. TO LEURALDUS [EURARDUS], A CLERIC OF ORLÉANS (1075)

He rebukes the injuries inflicted on the clerics of Orléans. He orders him to come to Rome with those clerics on a fixed day, in order that their dispute may be heard; meanwhile, he is not to inflict any trouble upon them and is to release the cleric whom he was holding captive. He threatens to confirm the sentence of excommunication imposed upon him by his predecessor if he does not obey.

[Col. 0404A]

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LEURALDUS [EURALDUS; in Mutina, CUNIRARDUS], a cleric of Orléans.**

It is an astonishing and utterly detestable thing that you have so hardened a heart and persist in such savagery that you are unwilling to withdraw your hand from the persecution of the brothers of the Church of Orléans, from whom we have heard that you were separated because of your offenses—neither through fear of divine judgment nor through the vengeance of apostolic correction, which you have already experienced.

For we remember that our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander of venerable memory, in order to restrain the fury and wicked acts of your presumption, hurled against you the dart of anathema and, lest you inflict any further disturbance upon the aforesaid brothers or meddle in the honors and ecclesiastical offices that you had acquired contrary to the rules and authority of the canons, forbade you to do so by apostolic commands. Although we have learned, from the credible report of many brothers, that your audacity has again risen up against these commands, nevertheless, still employing the apostolic gentleness proper to us, we for the moment refrain from wielding the sword of due vengeance [perhaps “drawing it,” HARD.], until we ascertain whether you can be bent to humility by the admonitions already given. We still reserve for you an apostolic hearing and an opportunity of defense in all the matters of which you are accused, provided that your conscience does not hold you back.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you to come into our presence on the next feast of All Saints and, without pretense, to notify the clerics of Orléans who have a case against you, so that they too may be present. Thus, after the causes and occasions of your disagreement have been diligently investigated and ascertained on both sides, we may, with God’s help, settle your lawsuit with an equitable conclusion.

Meanwhile, release the cleric whom you are holding captive, without any loss to his person or property, and do not yourself inflict, nor permit any of your men to inflict, any opposition whatsoever upon the canons of the aforesaid Church.

But if, unsupported by justice, you neither dare nor wish to present yourself before us, and, persisting in your wickedness, presume to inflict further losses or troubles upon the often-mentioned brothers, or fail to strive, as far as you can, to repair and restore the wrongs inflicted, know that the same sentence of excommunication which our aforesaid predecessor pronounced against you has been confirmed by our apostolic authority. And know that not only you, who are the leader and author of such presumption, but also all who have in any way given you counsel, assistance, or consent in the seizure and plundering of the Church’s goods or in the harassment of its clerics, have been condemned by an equal judgment of anathema.

[Col. 0405A]

Given at Rome in the second synod, on the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LIII (1075)

He sets out the agreement concerning the dispute between the bishops of Moravia and Prague over certain properties, an agreement reached by him in a council with the consent of both parties.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God.**

Because we judge that nothing is more suitable or enduring for preserving in memory and clarifying the truth of cases and affairs than written records, we wish it to be made known through our letters not only to those now living but also to those yet to come how the lawsuit and disagreement that had long continued between our fellow bishops—namely John, bishop of Moravia, and Geboard [Hieronymus; elsewhere Gebeard], bishop of Prague—concerning certain tithes and estates was finally settled at the apostolic see by an agreement.

This case, when in the second year of our pontificate it was brought before our hearing and that of the entire council gathered there, while many brothers were seated with us in the basilica of the Savior and the aforesaid bishops had also been summoned and placed before us, was investigated and examined for a long time. It appeared to be so entangled in ambiguity and perplexity that it could not, through the judgments then brought forward, be brought to a sincere investigation of truth and justice.

But, lest their dispute, without the intervention of peace, should continue longer to kindle either fraternal hatred or dangerous partisan zeal on one side or the other, with the advice of our brothers we determined that the case should be settled equitably in this way: everything over which there was contention between them was to be divided equally, and for the time being one was to hold one part and the other the other part, without any disturbance, until they could diligently investigate whether clearer judgments might be found, either in writing or through suitable witnesses.

To prevent either party from being given an endless opportunity to revive the lawsuit, we also fixed a period of ten years for them. Thus, whoever trusted that by definite proofs he could establish his right was to have, within the aforesaid period, the permission and authority to assert and obtain the right of his Church. And if one of them, or both—which we do not wish—should meanwhile die, their successors were to remain in the same agreement and settlement.

For that part concerning which the aforesaid period had elapsed, either in silence or without the proof of truth and justice being produced for which a claim was made, no place, opportunity for protest, or permission to renew the dispute over this matter was thereafter to remain.

In this way, therefore, we reconciled the aforesaid bishops in our presence. They appeared to give their grateful assent to the prescribed settlement [perhaps “they seemed to give their assent,” HARD.], and we dismissed them to their own places with apostolic blessing and fraternal charity. By apostolic authority we command and decree that this agreement remain inviolate and forever unshaken by all.

[Col. 0406A]

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF PIACENZA (1075)

He writes that he deposed Dionysius, their bishop, in a synod and absolved all who had sworn fidelity to him from the bond of their oath. He says that he will see to it that all the faithful assist them in expelling him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the Catholic people of the Church of Piacenza, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

For a long time a complaint concerning the disorder of your Church, beloved sons, has been brought to us, and the destruction of your souls and possessions caused by an unjust shepherd has repeatedly afflicted our paternal heart. We waited for a bad tree to produce good fruit, but the wicked plantation, corrupted at the root and dry throughout, occupies the land, made worse by all our patience. Indeed, it produces a rejected fruit, to the disgrace of the entire Church, for the common destruction and as an example of your ruin.

Although he had formerly been deprived of every office and had been granted only communion with the Church, we had earnestly charged him, with many threats and entreaties, to seek peace with you, returning and restoring what he had taken away. We also gave him, with the [care of the ministry?; perhaps “and care of the ministry,” HARD. whose restitution], the hope of greater benefit if he obeyed our commands. But, God not willing that the sins of his disobedience—which had often offended us—should be covered under the veil of this mercy and that, once covered, they should remain unpunished, he again lied. A man plainly sacrilegious and guilty of many crimes, he disregarded our admonitions.

Therefore, by the unalterable sentence of the holy synod and the irrevocable consent of all the brothers seated around us, we have deposed Dionysius, once called bishop, from every episcopal honor, without any hope whatever of reconciliation, and have decreed that he be denied a hearing forever. And all who swore fidelity to him, lest they act against this decree, we absolve from every bond of their oath.

We shall also take care that all the faithful of Saint Peter assist you in expelling the wolf and ordaining the shepherd who has plundered your possessions and, like a darkened eye, casts the bodies and souls of those who follow him into a pit.

Therefore, citizens of God, take courage, because God is with us. Even if the towered cities of the land of Canaan and the gigantic bodies of the sons of Anak oppose us, our leader Jesus nevertheless enters the promised land fearlessly with a shout. For he himself is the giant who runs the course, who says: “Take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16).

And if any of you should die in defense of justice, may he be freed from all sins through the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LV. TO THE PEOPLE OF LODI (1075)

[Col. 0407A]

He rejoices that they and their bishop are rising up against the Simonian heresy and the fornication of clerics. He urges them to persist and to obey their bishop.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the sons of the Church of Lodi, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We rejoice, beloved, in your pious religious devotion. We have heard that, inflamed by zeal for the divine law against the detestable Simonian heresy and the fornication of priests, you are praiseworthily rising up. We rejoice also concerning our brother and fellow bishop, your shepherd, Lord Opizo, who has shown himself to burn so greatly with the same zeal for piety that he earnestly sought the assistance of this holy see for accomplishing these things.

Therefore we exhort you and admonish you as dearest sons, together with your aforesaid shepherd, our brother, to persist in combating and utterly eradicating these plagues—namely, the Simonian heresy and the fornication of the ministers of the sacred altar—for the honor of almighty God and his holy Church and for the salvation of the whole country.

In rightly and canonically ordering the churches, give him your assistance with all your strength. Indeed, in everything that he intends to do for the honor of God and your salvation, obey him obediently, so that the purity of your holy mother Church may flourish among you—the Church whom Christ joined to himself as a chaste bride, without stain or wrinkle.

Whoever observes these things should confidently hope in the grace of almighty God and should know that he possesses apostolic blessing. But whoever attempts to oppose him in the matters we have mentioned, and does not assist him in everything that belongs to God, should tremble lest he incur the vengeance of divine correction and apostolic curse, in place of the grace and blessing that he does not care to have.

Concerning the administration of the altar situated above the body of blessed Bassianus the confessor, we absolutely command that no one presume to administer there who either entered that same church for a price, or who is a fornicator, or who pursues sordid profit.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0407] Pagius, in the year of Christ 1077, no. 8, proves after others that this is spurious.]

## THE DICTATUS PAPAE

That the Roman Church was founded by the Lord alone.

That the Roman pontiff alone is rightly called universal.

That he alone may depose or reconcile bishops.

That his legate presides over all bishops in a council, even if he is of a lower rank, and may pronounce a sentence of deposition against them.

That he may depose the absent.

That with those whom he has excommunicated, among other things, we must not remain even in the same house.

[Col. 0408A]

That he alone may, when necessity of time requires it, establish new laws, gather new congregations, make an abbey out of a canonical institution, and conversely divide a wealthy bishopric and unite poor ones.

That he alone may use imperial insignia.

That all princes shall kiss the feet of the pope alone.

That his name alone shall be recited in the churches.

That his name is unique in the world.

That he may depose emperors.

That, when necessity compels, he may transfer bishops from one see to another.

That he may ordain a cleric from any church, wherever he wishes.

That one ordained by him may preside over another church, [Col. 0408B] but may not serve in the army, and that he must not receive a higher rank from any bishop.

That no synod may be called general without his command.

That no chapter and no book may be considered canonical without his authority.

That his sentence may be retracted by no one, while he alone may retract the sentences of all.

That he himself ought to be judged by no one.

That no one dare condemn a person who appeals to the apostolic see.

That the greater cases of any church ought to be referred to it.

That the Roman Church has never erred and, as Scripture testifies, will never err.

[Col. 0408C]

That the Roman pontiff, if he has been canonically ordained, is undoubtedly made holy through the merits of blessed Peter, as Saint Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, testifies, with many holy Fathers supporting him, as is contained in the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus.

That by his command and permission subjects may bring accusations.

That he may depose and reconcile bishops without a synodal assembly.

That no one is to be regarded as Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church.

That he may absolve subjects from fidelity to wicked men.

## LETTER LVI. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS (1075)

[Col. 0408D]

He rebukes him for having been negligent in the case of the clerics of Châlons. He declares that the bishop of Châlons must be deposed because of his disobedience, and wishes Manasses to order him to restore the goods seized from the clerics of Châlons. If he refuses to obey, Manasses is commanded to excommunicate him, with the addition that he must appear either before the papal legates or before the pope himself.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to MANASSES, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

If the care of pastoral government made you as solicitous as it ought, the case of the clerics of the Church of Châlons, so often reported to us, would long ago have received a suitable conclusion. But because your negligence and the disobedience of the bishop of the aforesaid city have prolonged the matter until now, it was necessary for us to assist the clerics, who have suffered for so long, and to crush the obstinacy of the disobedient by the force of apostolic authority.

For the aforesaid bishop of Châlons has in many ways scorned to obey our command. First, when summoned, he neglected to come to the synod. Receiving commands directly from our mouth concerning the restoration of the clerics’ benefices, he disdainfully refused to obey. Then, admonished by our letters, he again despised fulfilling what we had commanded.

Therefore, because of such an enormous and reckless disobedience, we have judged that he must be deprived of every episcopal office by apostolic authority, and we have determined that these things be vigorously carried out by you without any delay.

Again we firmly command you to enjoin him, from our part and yours, to restore to the aforesaid clerics, without any excuse, the goods and benefices taken from them, wherever they may wish to remain, together with the restoration and repair of whatever they lost from the revenues of their property, since we command him to do so.

On this occasion, if he refuses to obey this command of ours, let him be kept entirely from the body and blood of the Lord until, through obedience, he learns to submit his neck to the holy Roman Church, against which in his disobedience he has not been ashamed to kick.

But if our legates travel as far as the regions of Gaul by the Kalends of October, he is to arrange to present himself before them prepared to clear himself. [Col. 0409C] Otherwise, he is to present himself before us by the feast of All Saints to clear himself, with every excuse removed.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LVII. TO THE PEOPLE OF FIESOLE (1075)

He rebukes them because, through excessive complaints repeatedly brought against their bishop, they are inflicting losses upon the Church of Fiesole. Therefore he imposes silence upon them, but declares that he will in no way permit the church to be devastated.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Fiesole, both great and small, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We are greatly astonished that, concerning the case of your bishop Irasmundus [Tras­mundus], what is sufficient for the Roman Church is not sufficient for certain of you; that you repeat, through superfluous disputes, a complaint brought to an end by many prolonged investigations—indeed, by divine judgments—and thus consume the very remnants of the Church of Fiesole after its long tribulations.

For even if the bishop were held guilty of everything brought against him, and we were to approve him innocent by divine judgment and human examination, it would nevertheless be fitting for you to preserve your mother, namely the Church of Fiesole, which has not sinned, unharmed, and not to turn the punishment of the sinner into its loss and disgrace.

[Col. 0410A]

It would also have been fitting that, if the pitiable poverty and ruin of your church do not touch you with compassion, shame before the world, and your case—now weakened and altogether held in contempt—should have imposed silence upon you.

Therefore we admonish you that henceforth there be no schisms or contentions among you, but that you think and hold what we think, what is sufficient for us, and what the Roman Church approves. Know that we will in no way permit our church to be devastated under such a pretext of scandal or through the vanities of useless disputation. Rather, as God grants, we shall assist its misery and necessity not only by speaking but also by exercising vengeance against its enemies.

Given at Rome, on the fourth [or third] day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LVIII. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS (1075)

He orders him to compel the bishop of Noyon to restore the village of Bruges, taken from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Utrecht, if this is established as fact; but if he believes that he has some right to it, he is to litigate the case in a synod.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to MANASSES, archbishop of Rheims, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have received in a letter from our fellow bishop William of Utrecht the complaint concerning the Church of Bruges, situated in the bishopric of Noyon. This complaint had previously been laid before our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander, but has not yet received a suitable conclusion.

The bishop of Utrecht asserts that this same Church had been assigned to his see by ancient tradition and had been held absolutely and peacefully for nearly two hundred years for the maintenance of the canons of Utrecht, until Raboth, bishop of Noyon, without any canonical judgment, took it away for himself and—as the legates affirm, which is more serious and altogether unlawful—sold it to another cleric.

Therefore we have judged that you must summon your suffragan, the bishop of Noyon, and rebuke him severely for such great perversity, if the matter is established as true. You must then admonish, indeed even compel, him, following the statutes of the canons, to restore without delay the Church of Utrecht, which he has despoiled after it possessed the property for so long. Afterwards, if he has any legitimate complaint, he is to strive to litigate it by synodal judgment.

But if he neglects to obey our authority or your admonitions, let him be deprived of his episcopal office until he is taught that ecclesiastical cases must be brought to an end not by the magnitude of power but by the judgment of justice.

We therefore wish you to carry out the decision of this matter diligently and energetically, and to notify us as soon as you can by letter of what has been done.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LIX. TO THE MONKS OF ROMANS (1075)

[Col. 0411A]

He receives their abbey under the protection of the Roman Church and confirms the goods already granted to it and those that will be granted. He forbids any canon to be ordained there unless he has professed that he will live according to the rule, and forbids any abbot unless he is regular and elected by regular brothers. He entrusts the consecration of the church to the bishop of Die.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers residing in the abbey situated at Romans on the river Isère, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have received the expressions of your fidelity and devotion that you made known to our ears through your legates. You asked that we grant you the freedom of the Roman Church, which your church has until now possessed from our predecessors. You also wrote—and this greatly rejoices us—that certain among you had begun [perhaps “undertaken,” HARD.] a regular and canonical life, and you announced that you had granted them certain goods of your church, asking us to confirm these things by our authority.

We therefore rejoice with your good intention and wish that you may always advance toward better things. At the request of our son Hugh, bishop of Die, and out of affection for you, we assent to your petitions and grant you the Roman freedom, as you requested.

As for the things that your provost Herimannus and you have given and established for your regular brothers, and included in the letters sent to us—namely, whatever they previously appeared to possess from the goods of the same church, and any of you who wish to join them in regular life, or who has given them anything from his own possessions—we too grant them.

By our authority we decree that, when those who now hold the possessions and administrative offices of the church either convert to the regular life or depart from the world, those possessions and offices, together with lands thereafter given to the aforesaid church, are to belong to the table of the brothers living there according to the rule. No one is henceforth to be made or ordained a canon there unless he has professed that he will live according to the rule.

[Col. 0411D]

By apostolic authority we prohibit you from placing over yourselves a provost, abbot, or minister of any ecclesiastical administration unless the common election of the brothers living according to the rule has chosen him, in accordance with God, from among those of their profession.

And lest anyone presume to violate these salutary statutes established by us, we forbid it by the power of the Holy Spirit and by the authority granted to us by God.

We have entrusted the consecration of your church—which you sought to have reconciled through a legate of the apostolic see—to our aforesaid son, the bishop of Die, who is a son both of the Roman and of the Viennese Church.

Given at Rome, on the seventh [or eighth] day before the Ides of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LX. TO OTTO, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE (1075)

[Col. 0412A]

He orders him to settle the lawsuit between himself and the abbot of Augia. If this cannot be done, both are to come to Rome. Meanwhile, neither is to inflict trouble upon the other.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to OTTO, bishop of Constance, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Just as a complaint has been brought to us from you concerning Ecardus, abbot of the monastery of Augia [“of the rich Augia”], so a complaint has been brought from him concerning you. But because we wish to spare you both the fatigue, we advise and command you to summon mutually agreed friends and wise men who love truth and favor justice more than friendship. At a suitable time and place, meet with them and agree together that your lawsuit be settled by equitable arguments and by some suitable agreement.

But if this cannot be done because of sins, we wish you to know, by the authority presently exercised, that both of you are to come to the threshold of the apostles around the feast of All Saints, so that, with God’s assent, we may examine your case through careful investigation and bring your long-standing disagreement to a just conclusion.

Meanwhile, we command that, with every lawsuit between you brought to silence, a firm and established peace be maintained—as though by the hand of blessed Peter and our own—so that neither party dare provoke or disturb the other by troubles or opposition.

Do not regard it as a small matter to dissolve the rights of peace when so great a mediator has been placed between you. For whoever, in this decree, fails to show reverence and faith toward apostolic authority will, by the impiety of his own presumption, summon faith and judgment against himself and his case.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Ides of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXI. TO DIETWIN, BISHOP OF LIÈGE (1075)

[Col. 0412D]

He rebukes him as a Simonian and urges him to repent, eradicate fornication from the clergy, and refrain from inflicting insults upon the abbot of Saint-Hubert. He also orders him to consecrate a certain church in his diocese, either personally or through the bishop of Metz; and he grants him absolution from his sins.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0411] Dietwin was called bishop of Liège, as in Lambert, under the year 1075], greeting and apostolic blessing.**
We have long since heard, and have learned from the reports of many, that in several matters you have acted in your bishopric against the institutions of the holy Fathers, namely in the sale of ecclesiastical dignities and canonical prebends. We therefore deeply regret this and are greatly astonished, since you accepted so great an honor gratuitously, yet, although you found prudent and religious men, you did not bestow ecclesiastical honors freely; rather, you departed from the example of your predecessor by introducing a new custom. By the rule of justice, therefore, a sentence ought to be pronounced against you for these reasons; but we spare you because of your advanced age and because our most dear brother Herimann, bishop of Metz and son of your Church, has offered many excuses for you before us, attributing whatever you have wrongly arranged in these matters to others whose counsel you followed. [Col. 0413A]

We therefore admonish you by apostolic authority to consider what you have done and to dread the judgment toward which you are hastening; to desist henceforth from such transgressions; and, wherever you can, to strive to correct matters by altering what you have done. We also command you to admonish and restrain all ministers of sacred orders to live chastely and to abandon their concubines entirely. Exterminate the wickedness which, according to the tradition of the Fathers, has arisen in our times through the silence of pastors, lest you be condemned with those who do evil because of your silence, and they themselves incur the danger of eternal death. [Col. 0413B]

It has been reported to us that, on the advice of certain persons, you have inflicted insults upon the abbot of Saint Hubert [Imbert] because of the privilege which he received from us. But we excuse him, since he has done nothing against the interests or honor of your Church. We therefore admonish and ask you to allow him to remain in peace and complete tranquility.

There is also in your diocese a church of the count of Namur [Manucensis; corrected in the source to Namucensis], which you have delayed consecrating until now. We ask you to consecrate it; but if bodily weakness prevents you from doing so, entrust this duty to our most dear son, the bishop of Metz. If you do not agree, write back and explain the just and reasonable cause for which you have left it undone. [Col. 0413C]

And because you appear to be approaching your end, moved by brotherly compassion, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we absolve you from your sins and pray to the Lord for you, that through the intercession of the blessed apostles you may deserve eternal fellowship among the elect.

Given at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXII. TO SICHARD, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA (1075)

He sets forth the decrees issued in the council against clerics who keep concubines and against Simoniacs. He commands him to ensure that they are observed.

[Col. 0413D] **GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sichard, brother and fellow bishop of Aquileia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your Fraternity must not be unaware, nor ought you to ignore the dignity of your order, of the statutes and decrees which we established in the council held during the past Lent, with the assent of our brothers and of the entire assembly, following the authority of the holy Fathers. [Col. 0414A]

For we decreed that if any man belonging to those orders which minister at the sacred altars—namely, a priest or deacon—has a wife or concubine, he must entirely abandon them and perform suitable penance; otherwise he must completely cease ministering at the sacred altars and must no longer enjoy any ecclesiastical benefice, whether newly acquired or already held.

As for those who have been promoted through simony, that is, through the intervention of money, we have decreed by apostolic censure that they be deposed without any hope of restoration.

We therefore admonish you, most beloved brother and fellow bishop—or rather, by apostolic authority we command you—to depose all Simoniacs in your diocese, and to prohibit clerics who fornicate, unless they desist from fornication, from both office and benefice under the condition stated above. Summon your suffragans, either by your letters or in person, and admonish them with the utmost diligence to do the same. [Col. 0414B]

Given at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXIII. TO GEUSA, DUKE OF HUNGARY (1075)

He commends him for his distinguished achievements. He shows that the kingdom of Hungary is subject to no one except the Roman Church, and that his kinsman deservedly lost it, since he had received it from the king of the Teutons. He urges him to care for the churches and to render obedience to the apostolic legates.
