**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geusa, duke of Hungary [Note: Geusa—so in Book I, Letter 58, and below in Letter 70; Lambert, however, calls him Joiades in the years 1073 and 1074. But Bonfinius, in *Rerum Hungaricarum*, decade, Books III and IV, calls him Geisa.], greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0414C] Although through the legates whom you formerly sent to us we dispatched letters to you, which you say you have not yet received, nevertheless, out of the affection of charity with which we admonish all kings and princes as sons, we write to you again, desiring for you, with justice, whatever belongs to honor and glory.

Many good reports about you have reached me, and honorable fame arising from your deeds has come to our ears. For these reasons we love you, and we desire that your reputation may always rise together with the truth of your conduct.

We believe that you should know that the kingdom of Hungary, like the other most noble kingdoms, ought to remain in the condition of its own liberty and be subject to no king of another kingdom, but only to the holy and universal mother, the Roman Church. She does not receive those subject to her as slaves, but welcomes them all as sons. [Col. 0414D]

Because your kinsman obtained dominion over it by usurpation from the king of the Teutons, not from the Roman pontiff, divine judgment, as we believe, prevented him from retaining that dominion [Note: He is speaking of King Solomon, as above in this same book, Letter 13, and below in Letter 70.].

Now that the matter is in your hands, we urge you meanwhile to care for the churches, to devote the greatest zeal to religion, and, when the legates of the holy Roman Church come to you, to show them such obedience that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, you may advance in glory and honor in both lives.

Given at Rome, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXIV. TO IVON, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS (1075)

[Col. 0415A]

He orders him to answer the charges brought against him before his legates and to obey them, or else to come to the apostolic see at the appointed time. Meanwhile, he is to care for the souls entrusted to him.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ivon, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Denis in Paris.

Although the words of Algisus, your monk, have long since presented to the Roman Church an excuse for your coming, and although they have given us some assurance on your behalf, nevertheless we neither can nor ought to allow the growing scandal—which has already been brought to the apostolic see by many persons—to pass without investigation.

Therefore, if it happens that our legates travel to those regions this summer, we command you to explain the case concerning the charge brought against you carefully before them and to obey their decision. [Col. 0415B] If some impediment prevents this, come to us from now until the feast of Saint Andrew to answer the charges.

Meanwhile, we wish you to show yourself energetic and diligent in caring for the souls subject to you, so that, when you come to us, that very devotion to a good way of life may commend both you and those over whom you appear to preside, and may confirm the good reports about you given by Algisus.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXV. TO THE MONKS OF SAINT-DENIS (1075)

[Col. 0415C]

He urges concord and peace while their abbot comes either before the legates or before him to clear himself of simony.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the monks of the monastery of Saint-Denis, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The infamy concerning your abbot Ivon has reached our ears through the reports of many: namely, that he obtained the abbacy by simony, that is, through the intervention of money. Since we neither ought nor can allow such an accusation to pass without investigation, we have commanded him by our letters to present himself before our legates—if they happen to come to those regions this summer—to clear himself of the charges. [Col. 0415D] If, for some intervening reason, the legates do not come, he is to present himself before our hearing between now and the feast of Saint Andrew, to answer the charges.

We therefore admonish your religious community that meanwhile no discord or schism born of the devil’s deception be found among you. You yourselves know that God does not dwell in a division of minds. Rather, with tranquil hearts and the greatest reverence, devote yourselves to the observance of your religion and your order, and obey the aforesaid abbot humbly, lest—God forbid!—through your schism your monastery suffer material loss and you suffer harm to your souls.

Know for certain that we never neglect to watch diligently over the abbacy of Saint-Denis; [Col. 0416A] but, following the Apostle, we wish to act honorably and in an orderly manner. For just as we must greatly fear justifying the guilty, so it is exceedingly dangerous to condemn the innocent.

For the rest, conduct yourselves wisely, dearest sons, remembering us in your prayers.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXVI. TO BURCHARD, BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT (1075)

He commands him, as he had previously done through legates, to root fornication out of the clergy.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Burchard, archbishop of Halberstadt [Helvestensi; perhaps Halberstadiensi or Halberstatensi, and so in Mutina], greetings and apostolic blessing. [Col. 0416B]

We believe that you, dearest brother, are not unaware of the statutes of our predecessors and of the holy apostolic see concerning the chastity of the ecclesiastical orders, statutes which thereafter, through our own efforts, have been promulgated far and wide by letters and legates.

For in the preceding year our brothers and bishops sent to those regions visited you and, in our name, earnestly impressed upon you the duty of carrying out this work. Nevertheless, we have not judged these letters to you on the same subject superfluous, since the Apostle says: “Brothers, for me to write the same things to you is not burdensome, but for you it is necessary” (Philippians 3). [Col. 0416C]

If, having been admonished by the exhortation of our brothers, you immediately applied yourself to this work, these letters will serve, as the saying goes, to urge one who is already running to run more swiftly. But if you have delayed until now, we shall drive away the sleep of sluggishness and rouse you to vigilance with the spur of rebuke.

We fear being condemned for our silence if we are slow to distribute the Lord’s money to our fellow servants, especially to those who are capable of teaching others. For we are pressed by the fear of that curse which is expressed through Solomon: “Cursed is the man who withholds grain from the people” (Proverbs 11). And likewise by what is said through the prophet: “Cursed is the man who keeps his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48), that is, the word of preaching from rebuking the carnal. [Col. 0416D]

Just as these examples urge us to speak, so the many things written everywhere concerning obedience exhort you to receive what we say with brotherly charity. For it is written in Samuel: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams. For to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse assent is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15).

Blessed Gregory, explaining this in the *Moralia* (Book 35, chapter 10), says: “Obedience, therefore, is that without which, although someone may appear faithful, he is proved to be unfaithful.”

Your Fraternity knows that the rules we propose were established by the holy Fathers and are to be observed with all the greater reverence because it is evident that they were promulgated not according to their own will but under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, dearest brother, we earnestly exhort you and command by apostolic authority that you faithfully carry out what our legates have already made known to you and what these letters more fully impress upon you: [Col. 0417A] root the weeds out of the Lord’s field; preserve the grain; kindly support chaste and religious clerics as cooperators in your office; correct the morally unstable and incontinent as a father, or bar the incorrigible from the sacred altars. If they do not heed your exhortations and repent, let even the laity in no way listen to their ministry, so that those whom neither divine fear nor divine love pierces may at least be recalled to sobriety by human shame.

If you pursue these matters vigilantly, you will both escape the guilt of disobedience and obtain from the Lord a manifold and unfailing reward.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXVII. TO ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE (1075)

[Col. 0417B]

He orders him, after holding a council of his bishops, to promulgate and enforce the decrees of the apostolic see concerning the chastity of clerics. He also explains that he confirmed in synod the statutes against Simoniacs.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is well known that the Church of Cologne, among all the Churches of the Teutonic kingdom, has for many years been bound to the holy and apostolic see, which by God’s authority we serve, by such faith, love, and obedience that, through a singular intimacy and grace of charity, she holds a position of distinction before it as a most beloved daughter before her mother. [Col. 0417C]

I am prepared not merely to preserve this praiseworthy practice of goodwill, handed down from our predecessors to us, but also to extend and increase it according to the needs of circumstances and the demands of the times.

Hence, dearest brother, more confidently relying upon your obedience, I exhort and admonish you, and by the authority of our common lord blessed Peter I command you, to devote yourself with all your suffragans to preaching and earnestly inculcating the chastity of clerics, in accordance with the decrees of the Fathers and the authority of the canons. Thus a gracious service may be offered to the bride of Christ, who knows neither stain nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5), by a family made pure and immaculate. [Col. 0417D]

Your Fraternity knows that we have not carved out these commands from our own opinion, but publicly bring forward, as the necessity of our office requires, the sanctions of the ancient Fathers, spoken under the preaching of the Holy Spirit. Otherwise we would incur the danger of sluggish servants if, in silence, we hid the Lord’s money, which he demands back with interest.

Moreover, it has always been clear, and will always remain permitted, to this holy Roman Church to provide new decrees and remedies against newly increasing abuses—decrees and remedies issued by the judgment of reason and authority—which no human being may lawfully reject as invalid.

We are also pressed by fear of that curse which is expressed through Solomon, down to the point stated in the preceding letter (Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book 35, chapter 10): “Obedience, therefore, is that without which, although someone may appear faithful, he is proved to be unfaithful.” [Col. 0418A]

But so that you may pursue more briefly and effectively what we impose upon your affection, we advise you to convene a council with your brothers and fellow bishops. In it, after gathering as large a company of clerics as you can, you shall openly promulgate the canonical laws, the authority of the apostolic see, and your own authority and that of all your fellow bishops. Explain at greater length—as you know, by God’s gift—how great is the virtue of chastity, how necessary it is to the ecclesiastical orders, and how appropriate it is for the attendants of the Bridegroom who is a virgin and of the Virgin who is his bride.

Then declare firmly that it is no longer lawful for them to claim what they have hitherto usurped to their own destruction. For it is altogether more tolerable to cease from office than to impose upon their Savior an incestuous or even burdensome servitude, and thereby heap up for themselves anger and punishment from the very source from which they ought to have earned a reward. [Col. 0418B]

If, while faithfully and firmly carrying out these things, tribulation and persecution should meet you, look to him who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16). Know also without doubt that we, fortified by the shield of blessed Peter, will always be found ready either to repel the enemies, if we can, or to protect you at every hour.

We also wish your Fraternity to know that in synod we confirmed—and the holy Fathers had established it long before—and emphatically prohibited the following concerning the Simoniac heresy: that churches may not be sold in any way, nor may a price be accepted for the laying on of hands.

If anyone has been ordained in this manner, we remove him entirely from the celebration of Mass and the reading of the Gospel, and we earnestly admonish you to observe these provisions carefully.

[Col. 0418C] Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXVIII. TO WEZELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF MAGDEBURG (1075)

Its subject is almost the same.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wezelin [Vencelin], archbishop of Magdeburg, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We read that Joshua, when he succeeded Moses as leader of God’s people and assumed command, exercised his office with such watchful and vigilant obedience that—something rarely written of others—relying upon heavenly power, he commanded even the elements with authority.

He caused the Jordan River to halt its natural course so that the army could cross, [Col. 0418D] and he commanded the sun, hastening toward the west in its revolving motion, to stand still until he had taken vengeance on his enemies, as though he were another Creator. He also brought down and overthrew the walls of Jericho by circling them seven times to the blast of the priests’ trumpets.

You see, dearest brother, what a fervent spirit in divine matters and prompt obedience deserved.

Following the likeness of this deed, we who have undertaken the teaching office of instructing the Christian people must direct our minds vigilantly, lest we allow the walls of the opposing power—raised in rebellion against the true Joshua—to stand or grow stronger through our silence.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we impose upon and command your Fraternity that, in preaching and earnestly inculcating the chastity of clerics, you sound the priestly trumpet more forcefully and insistently (Joshua 6), [Col. 0419A] until you disperse and overthrow the walls of Jericho—that is, the works of rebellion and the pollutions of filthy lust—as [he says] to the prophet [“as the prophet says” (perhaps *dicitur*, “it is said,” is missing, HARD.)]: “Today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jeremiah 1).

We are not setting before you decrees of our own—even though, if necessary, we could lawfully do so—but are renewing the statutes established by the holy Fathers, lest through our silence we incur the sentence against servants who hide the Lord’s money.

Work diligently, therefore; insist in season and out of season, so that the house of God entrusted to you may be purified. Thus you may deserve our thanks for your obedience and, when you receive the reward of your labor, may be joyfully brought into the joy of your Lord.

[Col. 0419B] Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXIX. TO CUNIBERT, BISHOP OF TURIN (1075)

He rebukes him for harassing the monks of Saint Michael. He urges him to make peace with the abbot or to come to the apostolic see on the appointed day for the dispute to be settled; meanwhile, he is to desist from causing trouble, lest he be forced to remove that monastery from his jurisdiction. He also orders him to absolve those whom he had rashly excommunicated.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Cunibert, bishop of Turin, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Dearest brother, out of the reverence which you owe to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and teacher of the universal Church, you ought to have preserved unity and concord with us in the bond of charity and peace, and at least to have helped our labors, so that they might advance and bear fruit, in matters connected with you and conducted with you. [Col. 0419C]

Instead, however—and this is something that we can neither sufficiently wonder at nor grieve over—the outcry of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Michael, or rather the manifold distress which we have heard from the reports of many that they are suffering because of you, gives us clear evidence that you have forgotten our affection, separated yourself from us, and devoted every effort to scattering what we labor to gather.

You must remember how many and how great were the matters which our lord and predecessor, Pope Alexander of blessed memory, and we ourselves discussed with your Fraternity concerning the peace and tranquility of that monastery when you most recently visited the apostolic see and our presence. [Col. 0419D] We wished to prevent the devil, who is always envious of the salvation and peace of God’s servants, from finding some opportunity there to pour in the poison of his wickedness and to tear devoted souls away from the continual practice of prayer and meditation upon divine service.

Although you then promised us most fully that you would either make a suitable peace with the abbot concerning everything or, if that could not be done, bring the matter anew to apostolic judgment without any injury to the monastery, nevertheless, after you departed from us, you have proved, as we have been informed, much harsher and more cruel toward that venerable place than you had been before. You have not spared either words or deeds that would damage it, not only by external force but also by episcopal severity. [Col. 0420A]

We may therefore be deeply angered against you, since we understand that, in contempt of apostolic authority and to the detriment of our own exertions, you are resisting our counsels, admonitions, requests, and the just exercises of our office, so that you are neither able nor willing to tolerate the peace which we desire, with the greatest consideration of justice before God, to provide for God’s servants.

Do you perhaps think that bishops have received such power and license in pastoral government that they may oppress monasteries situated in their dioceses as much as they wish, and, under the pretext of their authority, diminish the zeal for religion by exacting this and that by force and exercising their power?

Or do you not know that the holy Fathers have often separated religious monasteries from the jurisdiction of bishops, and dioceses from the province of a metropolitan see, because of the harassment inflicted by their superiors? [Col. 0420B] Granting them perpetual liberty, they decreed that they should adhere to the apostolic see as principal members to their head.

Examine the privileges of the holy Fathers, and you will find that even archbishops are forbidden to perform their office in many monasteries unless summoned by the abbot, lest monastic quiet be disturbed by the frequent presence and association of secular persons.

Therefore, lest we too be compelled, by the authority and example of those Fathers, to do this concerning the aforesaid monastery of Saint Michael—and lest, while seeking immoderate things, you justly lose what appeared equally to belong to you—we admonish and command you by apostolic authority either to make peace with the abbot through an appropriate agreement and a mutually arranged settlement of the whole case, or, if this cannot be done because of the obstacle of sins, to understand that you have been summoned to the apostolic see on the coming feast of Saint Martin. [Col. 0420C] There, with the present authority of this see, we shall hear the matter, so that, with God’s help, we may settle your dispute and bring it to a just conclusion.

Meanwhile, by that same authority we command you not to harm or disturb, by summoning him to synod, by any interdict, or finally by any kind of exaction whatsoever, either the abbot, the aforesaid monastery, its servants, its properties, or the places and goods belonging to it—whether personally or through anyone of your men.

You have bound by the chain of anathema certain persons among those belonging to that party. Although you did this rashly, nevertheless, out of concern for brotherly charity, we grant you the opportunity and admonish you to absolve them. [Col. 0420D] If you delay in this matter or refuse for any reason to obey us, know that by our apostolic authority they are absolved and free from every bond of your interdict or excommunication.

Act, beloved brother, so that it may not appear that we have written to you even now in vain. Trust our counsels and heed our admonitions. Do not wish to involve us, occupied as we are with many matters, any longer in the labors of this case, nor deny us brotherly and unanimous consent in arranging peace for the aforesaid monastery. Otherwise, if you do not cease resisting us—or rather, blessed Peter—you may be driven into more serious guilt and irreparable loss to yourself [*tuomet*; the printed reading is uncertain], which we do not desire. [Col. 0421A]

For if hereafter you attempt to drag the aforementioned case into error and litigation beyond the terms of this letter, or to inflict any harassment upon the monastery, we, supported by divine and apostolic authority, shall arrange, with God’s help, that this monastery and all its possessions remain in perpetual liberty, so that, after God, it may be subject to the governance or judgment of no one except the holy Roman Church, and may serve God in the purpose of holy religion without being torn apart.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXX. TO GEUSA, DUKE OF HUNGARY (1075)

[Col. 0421B]

He wishes peace to be established between him and King Solomon. He indicates that the right to the kingdom was deservedly transferred from King Solomon to him. He requests his observance toward the apostolic see and asks him to make known by letter whatever he desires from the Roman Church.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geusa, duke of Hungary, greetings and apostolic blessing.

If it is our office to defend everyone’s rights, to establish peace among them, and to strengthen concord, reason requires—and the usefulness of our office demands—even more that we sow charity among great men, whose peace or hatred affects many.

Therefore we take care, and pious concern remains fixed in our hearts, that we may establish peace, if possible, between you and your kinsman, King Solomon. [Col. 0421C] Let justice be preserved on both sides, let each have what belongs to him, let neither cross the boundary of justice nor exceed the limits of good custom. Thus may the most noble kingdom of Hungary, which until now has flourished as a principality in its own right, continue in peace, so that its king may not become a petty ruler.

But when, disregarding the noble dominion of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—for we do not believe that your prudence is unaware that the kingdom belongs to him—the king submitted himself to the king of the Teutons and obtained the name of petty ruler, the Lord, foreseeing the injury inflicted upon his own prince, transferred the power of the kingdom to you by his judgment.

Thus, if he previously possessed any legal right in obtaining the kingdom, he deprived himself of it through sacrilegious usurpation. For Peter is said to derive his name from the firm rock, which shatters the gates of hell and, with adamantine strength, destroys and disperses whatever resists. [Col. 0421D]

Therefore, if you desire anything, if you rightly hope to obtain anything from the Roman Church, we wish you to disclose it to us confidently. Show by your deeds what devotion you have toward the universal mother and how you have resolved to obey her and offer her holy reverence, as is fitting for you.

What we have written less fully here we leave to the bearers of this letter to tell you, since we have sufficient confidence in their fidelity.

May almighty God, who chiefly granted blessed Peter the power of binding and loosing, through his prayers absolve you and your faithful people in Christ from all sins and lead you to eternal life.

[Col. 0422A] Given at Rome, on the eighteenth [fifteenth] day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXI. TO WRATISLAUS, DUKE OF THE BOHEMIANS (1075)

He commends his nephew Frederick and asks him either to grant him the benefice left to him by his father or to provide another. He urges him, after removing disagreements, to ensure that peace is maintained throughout his domain.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wratislaus, duke of the Bohemians, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Frederick, your nephew and a faithful son of the Roman Church, has earnestly petitioned us to ask the prudence of your nobility to allow him to have and possess in complete peace the benefice which his father left him. [Col. 0422B]

Moved by his supplications, we earnestly ask the serenity of your nobility that, if you know he has justice on his side—both because he is your own flesh and blood, being bound to you by the claim of kinship, and because he has fled for refuge to the mercy of the apostolic see—you either restore that benefice to him or grant him an exchange acceptable to him and worthy of the dignity of your lineage.

If he does not appear to have the right, we nevertheless ask you, for the sake of charity and reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose protection he has humbly sought, to grant him some benefice by which he may live honorably.

Do not be reluctant, therefore, to hear our prayers in this matter and to make blessed Peter your debtor, since we are prepared, with justice as our guide, to favor you in whatever we can.

Furthermore, we admonish you to take care to fortify your land and the government of your honor on every side with the strongest bond of peace. [Col. 0422C] Do not permit the scandal of any dispute to arise within your rule, especially between yourself and your brothers, or between the bishops of Prague and Olomouc.

For just as those who devote themselves to discord and litigation are undoubtedly sons of the devil, so those who work for peace are called sons of God, as Truth itself bears witness when it says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5).

May almighty God illuminate your mind and make you pass through temporal goods in such a way that you may deserve to attain eternal ones.

Given at Rome, on the eighteenth [fifteenth] day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction. [Col. 0422D]

## LETTER LXXII. TO THE BOHEMIANS (1075)

He urges them to live well and chastely.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all those established in Bohemia, great and small, greetings and apostolic blessing.

By consideration of the see whose administration we bear, although unworthy, we are, as you know, debtors to the faithful and to the unfaithful: to the faithful, so that they may steadfastly persevere in what they rightly undertake; to the unfaithful, so that by believing in their Creator and punishing their past crimes they may be converted.

Since, therefore, we have learned from the reports of the bishops of your country who were visiting the threshold of the apostles that some of you walk in the way of God’s commandments, while others expose themselves to various dangers through an evil way of life, we have endeavored to admonish you with fatherly charity, so that the good may become better and those who live reprehensibly may show themselves irreproachable. [Col. 0423A]

First of all, love God and your neighbor as yourselves with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; establish peace among yourselves, without which no one will see God; let not only clerics but also laypeople preserve chastity; faithfully give tithes to God, from whom you receive both life and the means of sustaining life; render due honor to your churches; and devote yourselves diligently to almsgiving and hospitality.

Although we do not fail to recognize that your bishops know these things sufficiently and make them known to you, nevertheless, since it is evident that out of reverence for blessed Peter you receive our words more warmly and eagerly, your eagerness to hear what may be given by others compels us to offer instruction, so that we may render you the duty of exhortation with all the greater diligence because you attend to blessed Peter with greater devotion in this exhortation of ours. [Col. 0423B]

Therefore, dearest ones, flee carnal desires and lift your minds toward the heavenly and everlasting joys of the heavenly homeland. Make blessed Peter, to whom God chiefly gave the power of binding and loosing on earth, your debtor through the fidelity of your most devoted service, so that after the dissolution of our earthly dwelling—which, whether willingly or unwillingly, you approach each day, and after which you will shortly be reduced to worms and ashes—you may experience his most powerful patronage before the stern Judge.

Given at Rome, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO BOLESLAUS, DUKE OF THE POLES (1075)

He commends his devotion toward the apostolic see. He sends legates concerning the affairs of the bishops, who were few in number and had no metropolitan. He urges him to assist them, to live well, to conduct himself rightly in governing his realm, and to ensure that the money taken from the king of the Russians is restored.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Boleslaus, duke of the Poles [Note: Concerning the duke of the Poles, Lambert and Berthold, under the year 1077.], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the honor shown to ministers and stewards is recognized as pertaining to the proper reverence of their masters, the labors and services of ministers are undoubtedly received gratefully and with great affection by those who are shown to love the persons and authority of prelates from the heart. In this we recognize that Your Excellency loves blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with sincere affection and is enlarged by an ardent spirit toward reverence for him, since, honoring him with your offerings out of free devotion, you desired to make him your debtor—and, as we trust in the Lord, you have deserved to do so.

[Col. 0424A] Hence we also, who are called and desire to be his servants, are joined to your charity in Christ. The care of the ministry to which, under obedience to the apostolic principate, God’s hidden dispensation has ordained and appointed us, although unworthy, we desire to impart to you all the more diligently in whatever respect we recognize it to be necessary and honorable for you, the more we understand your faith and charity to be prompt in obedience and devoted in deserving favor.

But because the order and provident administration of the Christian religion depend above all, after God, upon those who appear to be shepherds and rulers of the Lord’s flock, we must first consider that the bishops of your land, having no fixed place of a metropolitan see and being subject to no authority, [Col. 0424B] wander here and there, each according to his own ordination, free and unrestrained beyond the rules and decrees of the holy Fathers. We must then consider that among so great a multitude of people there are so few bishops, and the parishes of each are so extensive, that they are entirely unable to carry out or properly administer the care of the episcopal office among the peoples subject to them.

For these and other reasons, which we have omitted to write here, we have sent these legates to you, so that, after discussing with you matters which appear to concern ecclesiastical care and the building up of the body of Christ—which is the congregation of the faithful—they may either themselves determine, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, what ought to be corrected, or refer to us matters requiring determination. Hear them, therefore, as you would hear us, remembering that Truth says in the Gospel concerning the sending of the disciples: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10).

And so that the course of their labor may be fruitful among you, assist them with counsel and benevolent favor, out of reverence for the apostolic legation which they perform. Furthermore, we admonish and exhort you in the Lord always to keep before your eyes the final day of your life, of which you do not know when it will come, and the terror of the future judgment; and to strive to exercise the power entrusted to you with diligent and God-pleasing administration. Prepare riches for yourselves through good works and store up a firm and immovable foundation, so that you may possess eternal life.

For you must know that the heavenly Judge will not leave unexamined what he has entrusted to you; and you will have to answer to him with all the greater strictness the more extensive are the rights and judicial powers that you hold. May almighty God, whose majesty is above all principalities and kingdoms, direct your heart and actions toward every good work, with all prudence and practice of virtue, so that, when the course of this slippery and swiftly perishing life has been completed, you may deserve to attain true and everlasting glory through the merits and intercessions of blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles. May he also grant you, once the pride of your enemies has been overcome through Jesus Christ our Lord, the joys of peace and tranquility, so that from present gifts as well you may recognize with what longing future things ought to be desired.

[Col. 0425A] If these things indeed delight you, then among all things you must preserve charity, which—as we say unwillingly—you appear to have violated in the money that you took from the king of the Russians. Therefore, sympathizing with you, we earnestly beg and admonish you that, for the love of God and of Saint Peter, you cause whatever was taken from him by you or by your people to be restored. You must not be unaware that those who unjustly take away the property of others, unless they make amends when they are able to do so, are in no way to be believed to have a share in the kingdom of Christ and of God. We desire to receive this from you, in the same charity in which we say it, for the salvation of your soul.

Given at Rome, on the seventh [twelfth] day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO DEMETRIUS, KING OF THE RUSSIANS. (Year 1075.)

He writes that he has handed over the kingdom of Russia to their son with their consent, and shows himself ready to comply with their requests. He asks them to receive his legates graciously.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to DEMETRIUS, king of the Russians, and to his wife, the queen, greetings and apostolic blessing. [Note: [Col. 0425D] Lambert mentions King Demetrius in the year 1075.]

Your son, visiting the threshold of the apostles, came to us and, after offering due fidelity to blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles, asked in devout prayers to obtain that kingdom as a gift of Saint Peter through our hands. He confidently affirmed that his request would be ratified and made firm by your consent if it were endowed with the grace and protection of apostolic authority.

Because his wishes and requests appeared just, both on account of your consent and because of the devotion of the one making the request, we finally gave our assent and handed over to him, on behalf of blessed Peter, the governance of your kingdom. We did so with this intention and desire of charity: that blessed Peter might, through his intercession with God, preserve you, your kingdom, and all your goods as his own; that he might enable you to hold that same kingdom in complete peace, honor, and glory until the end of your life; and that, when the course of this service had been completed, he might obtain for you everlasting glory from the heavenly King.

Moreover, let Your Nobility’s Serenity know that we are entirely ready, whenever it may request the authority of this see for any just business required by its needs, and that it will undoubtedly obtain the effect of its requests without delay. Furthermore, so that these and many other matters not contained in the letter may be impressed more deeply upon your hearts, we have sent these messengers of ours. One of them is your known and faithful friend. They will carefully explain to you what is contained in the letter and will complete orally whatever is lacking.

For the sake of reverence for blessed Peter, whose legates they are, show yourselves gentle and approachable toward them; patiently hear whatever they tell you on our behalf and believe it without hesitation. Whatever matters they wish to handle and establish there by the authority of the apostolic see, do not permit anyone’s evil counsel to obstruct, [Col. 0426A] but rather assist them by showing sincere charity and favor.

May almighty God enlighten your minds and make you pass through temporal goods to everlasting glory.

Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXV. TO SUENIO, KING OF THE DANES. (Year 1075.)

He complains of the disobedience of princes toward the Roman Church. He commends him for his proper observance toward the apostolic see. He shows himself ready to favor him and asks him to indicate through legates whether he now desires the same things that he had requested from his predecessor Alexander.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to SUENIO [SUENO], king of the Danes, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Among our predecessors it was a matter of right and custom, through charitable legations, to teach all nations the way of the Lord, to rebuke all kings and princes in those matters deserving reproof, and to invite everyone to eternal blessedness through lawful disciplines. For the law of the Roman pontiffs prevailed over more lands than did that of the emperors. “Their sound has gone out through all the earth” (Psalm 18:5); and those over whom Augustus ruled, Christ ruled.

But now the kings and rulers of the earth have become despisers of ecclesiastical law. Although they ought to have preserved and defended justice more than anyone else, they have united in inflicting so many insults upon the Church and have fallen into such disobedience—which, according to Samuel, is like idolatry—that, since our legations now scarcely continue because they appear almost fruitless, we shall turn our words only in prayer to the Lord of kings and God of vengeance.

But because we know that you and your very strong nation, governed by the bridle of your wisdom, show due reverence toward the mother of all Churches—being all the more humble toward blessed Peter the more exalted you are in your strength—we send you, our most beloved son, this letter and command you with paternal affection: if there is anything you need which the authority of the Roman Church may justly grant you, make it known to us through your messengers and through those whom we are now sending, so that, insofar as is lawful, we may honor you and endow the aforesaid reverence with the dignity deserved by your most noble kingdom.

For we have received a good report about you. May it never depart from you through the prayers of blessed Peter and Paul; rather, as we desire, may it continually be increased and grow, so that you may attain the glory of both lives.

But because you previously requested certain things from our predecessor, Alexander of blessed memory, by which you would make blessed Peter your debtor—or rather acquire his noble patronage for yourself and your kingdom—send word through the same legates whether that desire remains the same, has suffered decline, or, as we much prefer, has increased.

When I was serving in the office of archdeacon, I greatly loved you, and it seemed to me that I was loved by you. But after I received the pastoral office, which rests as upon its foundation in love of God and neighbor, although unworthy, the charity I had toward you became greater. As you advance toward what is better, may it, by God’s favor, always increase to a greater degree.

Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXVI. TO THE BAMBERGERS. (Year 1075.)

He declares that he has deposed the simoniacal bishop of Bamberg. He forbids anyone to dare to plunder or alienate the goods of that Church.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Bamberg, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is known to almost all of you who live in the German regions that the Church of Bamberg, in a certain sense a special daughter, clings to her mother, the Roman Church, which, by God’s authority, we serve, although unworthy. Consequently, we ought to devote ourselves to her care with all the greater vigilance, since she is to be watched over with the more intimate protection of the apostolic see.

Therefore, because a certain ignorant man, overturned by the heretical depravity of simoniacal faithlessness, had invaded that Church, we took prudent measures to free it from the yoke of his sacrilegious invasion. We drew the sword of the prince of the apostles, Peter, and by apostolic authority pronounced sentence against him.

[Col. 0427C] But because Churches often suffer great losses when such men are expelled, and their goods are scattered and destroyed, we considered it right to guard against the impending harm to the Church. Accordingly, by apostolic authority we resist sacrilegious men and tyrants, forbidding them, on the occasion of his expulsion, to presume to take away the Church’s property or alienate it in any manner.

Therefore, in the name of God and of the apostles Peter and Paul, we forbid any person, of whatever dignity, power, or condition, to presume unjustly to seize by plunder the property of the aforesaid Church—especially its treasury and estates—or to alienate it in any way, until almighty God, through the intervention of blessed Peter, provides that Church with a suitable pastor.

If anyone should attempt to act contrary to this written prohibition, let him know that he will lose the grace of Saint Peter and will be punished by the vengeance of apostolic correction.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO GEBOARD, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG. (Year 1075.)

He rebukes him because, after obtaining from the apostolic see that a portion of his diocese should be separated and a bishop established there, he admitted a bishop to share the responsibility but retained all the tithes for himself. He therefore admonishes him to leave the tithes to his churches.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to GEBOARD [GEBEARD], archbishop of Salzburg, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We remember that in previous years Your Charity approached the apostolic see and obtained from our predecessor, Alexander of blessed memory—with my own support and consent—that, because of its great extent, you should divide off a portion of your diocese and establish in it a bishop and a bishopric to supplement the excessive burden of administration.

We heard this intention of your mind and worked to bring it about all the more eagerly because we understood that you were asking it with religious purpose and wished to benefit the salvation of many. For who, especially in these times, when, according to the Apostle, “all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2), if he has spiritual gain at heart, would not most willingly embrace a will that places earthly riches after the salvation of souls?

But in these days word has reached us concerning this same good purpose of yours of something that has greatly saddened us and cast, as it were, clouds of sorrow over our former joy. We have been much astonished at your prudence and religion that you could ever have been persuaded to bend yourself toward such an act.

For we have learned that, after a bishop had been appointed in the portion of your administration, as we have said, you admitted him as a partner in the labor but retained for yourself the fruit of the labor, namely, the tithes. If this is true, we grieve deeply that, in so excellent a work of Your Charity, greed—which is the root of all evils—could steal a place for itself, so that you sent a laborer into the Lord’s vineyard and deprived him of the reward of his work.

Therefore we wish Your Charity to be admonished to fulfill, clearly and sincerely and without any admixture of deceit, what you devoutly offered to God; to avoid the applause of human favor; and to complete in the security of the same recompense what you began in hope of eternal reward. Endow the church with the revenues of its tithes.

Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirteenth indiction.

## THIRD BOOK OF THE REGISTER

In the year 1075 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Rather, the fourteenth indiction, to which the following letters belong, except the first three.]

[Col. 0427]

## LETTER I. TO THE BAMBERGERS. (Year 1075.)

[Col. 0427D]

He confirms the sentence against Bishop Herimann because he had withdrawn from the judgment of the apostolic see, had invaded the Church through simony, and had squandered its goods. He anathematizes him and deprives him of priestly office; likewise, he anathematizes those who received any estates of the Church from him in order to support him, until he presents himself before the apostolic see.

[Col. 0428D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Bamberg, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The letters which Provost Poppo of your Church, together with those who were with him, deceived by the feigned repentance and false religious profession of Herimann, formerly called your bishop, neglected to bring to you, though marked with our seal, when they withdrew from us incautiously and in excessive haste, we have now considered it fitting to send to you, so that you may clearly learn from them what our will concerning the aforesaid pseudo-bishop was and what sentence of condemnation we pronounced against him by the judgment of the holy apostolic see.

You should believe without hesitation that no supplication or fraudulent suggestion could recall our mind from that will or sentence after he withdrew from the judgment of the holy apostolic see; nor, with God’s authority, will anything ever be able to change it. But because, under the pretext of religion and feigned repentance, he attempted tyrannically to corrupt the holy Church of Bamberg, in a certain sense a special daughter of the holy Roman Church, and to squander and destroy its goods, we confirm the earlier sentence and add this to the accumulation of his condemnation: he is to be irrevocably removed from the episcopal office and entirely excluded from the priesthood until he presents himself before the hearing of the apostolic see, ready to give whatever security we determine to be expedient for your Church.

We separate him from the episcopal office because he invaded the Church through simony. We also deprive him of the priesthood because, under the appearance of holiness, he was seen to tear it apart and bring it into confusion. And because he did not fear to carry out such great evils against the Church once entrusted to him, we bind him with the bond of anathema until he presents himself before the apostolic hearing in the manner stated above—unless, brought to his final extremity, he should receive a worthy penance. Even then, if he recovers, he must hasten to present himself before the apostolic see in the same manner, as has been said.

We also strike with the same anathema those who, from the beginning of his promotion, received from him any estates of the Church in order to support him and conceal his wickedness; especially those who, after he withdrew from the judgment of the apostolic see, received from him anything from the Church’s estates or treasury in order to encourage him to persist in his obstinacy—unless they repent, namely, unless they amend through worthy satisfaction the sin they committed by the aforesaid sacrilege and hasten to report their repentance to us.

Given at Laurentum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER II. TO SIGEFRID, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. (Year 1075.)

The subject is almost the same.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to SIGEFRID [Note: [Col. 0429] Sigifrid, and so everywhere], archbishop of Mainz, greetings and apostolic blessing.

How Herimann of Bamberg—now no longer a bishop—conducted himself this year when he came to Rome in repentance [read: seeking; and so in the Mutinensis], how he withdrew from the judgment of the apostolic see, by what fraud he deceived the clergy of the aforesaid Church under the pretext of repentance, how he destroyed the property of that Church entrusted to him, worse than before, and how he rose up like a tyrant against the clergy formerly entrusted to him: your Fraternity, I think, knows, and grieves with certain sorrow.

Therefore, since we could no longer endure such wickedness and newly devised cruelties with impunity, especially against the Church specially entrusted to blessed Peter, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and through the authority of blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles, we have deposed the aforesaid Herimann from the episcopal office [Col. 0430B] and from the priesthood, and decree that he is deposed forever.

And because he joined sacrilege to heresy and open tyranny to sacrilege, we have bound him with the bond of excommunication until he presents himself before the apostolic see, which he attempted not only to deceive but also maliciously to mock. If, however, he should reach the last day of his life, we do not deny him repentance and communion; but we command him absolutely to approach the apostolic see as soon as he is able.

We wish you to make this publicly known, especially to the brother bishops subject to you, and in the name of blessed Peter we command you to take the greatest care, according to the institutions of the holy Fathers, to appoint a pastor in the aforesaid Church of Bamberg, so that you may be shown to correct what you negligently did concerning the aforesaid simoniac.

[Col. 0430C] Given at Laurentum, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER III. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS. (Year 1075.)

Concerning Herimann of Bamberg, the same matters as in the preceding letter. He further admonishes the king to see that the Church of Bamberg is properly ordered.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, king, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Among the other works of good virtues toward which, as we have heard by report, you are rising in your desire for improvement, you have commended yourself to your holy mother, namely the Roman Church, in two particularly notable ways. First, because you resist simoniacs courageously; and second, because you both approve and effectively desire to fulfill the chastity of clerics, as servants of the Lord.

For these reasons you have given us grounds, with God’s help, to hope greater and more excellent things concerning you. Therefore we greatly desire you to hold firmly to these qualities, and we earnestly beseech our Lord God to increase them in you more abundantly.

As for the Church of Bamberg, which by the institution of its founder clings to the holy and apostolic see as a shoulder to the head, as a nearby member, with a particularly special care of solicitude, we grieve deeply over it. The necessity of our office compels us, to the best of our ability, to confront, assist, and provide for its desolation.

For that Herimann, called a bishop, a simoniac, was summoned to Rome this year to the synod but scorned to come. When he had approached Rome more closely, however, he stopped on the way and, sending his messengers ahead with abundant gifts, attempted, through a technique familiar to him, to test and, if possible, corrupt our innocence and the integrity of our confreres by means of a financial bargain.

When this failed contrary to his expectation, now more secure about his condemnation, he hastily turned back. By soothing the souls of the clergy who were with him through flattering and deceptive promises, he said that, if he could return to his homeland, he would withdraw from the episcopate and undertake a profession of monastic life. How he fulfilled this pledge is not hidden from Your Highness, dearest son.

Moreover, advancing still further in reckless audacity, he stripped the clergy of his Church, who were seeking their salvation and honor, of their goods and would have utterly ruined them had your royal power not, as we have heard, restrained him.

After carefully considering these excesses, we cast him out from both the episcopal and priestly offices. Furthermore, because he dared to attack the Church of Bamberg, fortified by the apostolic protection of blessed Peter, more cruelly and grievously than before, we bound him with the bond of anathema until he lays down the ecclesiastical dignity which he has illicitly usurped and nevertheless presents himself before the judgment of the apostolic see.

Now, therefore, most excellent son, [Col. 0431C] we exhort Your Sublimity and, as our solicitude requires, urge you to arrange that this Church be ordered according to God through the counsel of religious men, so that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, to whose name and protection it has been assigned, you may deserve to obtain the assistance of divine protection.

What I have written for this same reason to our brother Sigefrid, bishop of Mainz, and to the clergy and people of Bamberg, you will be able to learn fully from the letters sent to them.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.

## LETTER IV. TO SIGEFRID, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ. (Year 1075.)

[Col. 0431D] He exhorts him to perform the pastoral office faithfully. He orders him to investigate whether the bishop of Strasbourg is guilty of the stain of simony. He rebukes those who thought that the council summoned by him should be postponed, and charges him to eradicate simony and fornication.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to SIGEFRID, archbishop of Mainz, greetings and apostolic blessing.

In your letters, brother, you offered many reasons that are excusable and, so far as human judgment is concerned, valid. Nor would they seem weak to us if such matters could excuse us in the divine judgment.

The disturbance and upheaval of the kingdom, wars and seditions, the invasions of enemies and the loss of your possessions, and even fear of death, which you say threatens our brothers because of the prince’s hatred; or the danger that those who are mutually hostile from different regions might, if they came together, rise up in wars of extermination—all these things certainly appear sufficient to excuse someone.

But if we consider how far divine judgments differ from human judgments, we find almost nothing that we can present as excusable in the heavenly tribunal, so that we may withdraw from the gain of souls without danger: not the loss of property, not the hostility of evil men, not the anger of the powerful, nor even the loss of our own safety and life.

For mercenaries differ from shepherds in this respect: when the wolf comes, while they fear for themselves and not for the sheep, they flee, abandoning the flock and disregarding its seizure and dispersion. Shepherds, however, who love their sheep, do not abandon them when danger threatens; for their sake they do not hesitate to undergo even the destruction of their own lives.

Therefore we too must apply ourselves vigilantly to the duties of the pastoral office, always seeking the salvation of the Lord’s sheep for the glory of the Lord, urging our companions to guard the flock, and salutarily admonishing them to go before the sheep entrusted to them with upright steps.

For if we see our brothers sinning and remain silent, or see them straying and do not try to recall them to the path of uprightness by admonition, are we not ourselves also sinning, and are we not rightly judged to be straying? Indeed, whoever neglects to correct faults commits them.

And why did Eli the priest perish at Shiloh? And what is it that the Lord says through the prophet? “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48), that is, the word of preaching from putting the carnal way of life to death.

But to come to what now weighs upon our mind and is, as it were, the cause of our speech: how can we patiently endure what we have heard about the conduct of our brother, the bishop of Strasbourg, and what we have learned through truthful report to be certain in some respects?

Therefore we wish and command you diligently to investigate one matter which still remains doubtful to us, namely, the contagion of the Simoniacal heresy, and not to delay informing us of whatever you discover to be certain concerning it. If it proves true, Christ’s Church may be cleansed of such defilement and aid may be given to his soul lest it perish; but if it is false—which we much prefer—then, with divine grace assisting us, such a grave disgrace may be driven far from him.

As for those who say that the council we summoned for you ought to be postponed, we ask them to answer this: What would royal soldiers, previously admonished to prepare themselves for war, do if enemies were already raging with weapons and fire in the royal palace? Let them say whether they ought to seize their arms violently in order to disturb and crush those enemies, or merely lie inactive and watch what the enemies were doing.

For what else do evil spirits do except continually strive to devastate Christ’s Church with the fire of vices? And what ought royal soldiers—namely, holy priests—to do except rise up against their fury, armed with the shield of charity and girded with the sword of the divine word, in the strength of authority?

But when you say that certain brothers cannot come to the council because of the prince’s hostility, we say to him that it is sufficient for them to send some of their clergy, who can answer on their behalf [perhaps, “to them,” Harduinus; and so in the Mutinensis].

But because we are not unaware that many carnal and worldly people discourage you from working strongly and faithfully in the Lord’s vineyard for the gain of souls, lest you incur danger to your property or the hatred of the powerful, we ask and admonish you, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of blessed Peter, not to presume to turn aside from the path of uprightness because of anyone’s hatred or favor, or because of any loss of earthly goods. Rather, examine everything carefully, insofar as the Holy Spirit grants you ability, and take the greatest care to communicate to us as quickly as possible whatever is established as certain.

It ought to seem deeply shameful to us that worldly soldiers stand daily in battle for their earthly prince and scarcely fear to endure the dangers of death, while we, who are called the priests of the Lord, do not fight for our King, who made all things from nothing, who did not shrink from undergoing the loss of life for us, and who promises us a reward that will endure without end.

We further charge Your Fraternity to investigate diligently, as you received instruction from the apostolic see, the matter of simoniacal heresy and the fornication of clerics; to punish lawfully whatever you find to have occurred in the past; to cut it out entirely; and to forbid absolutely that anything further occur [perhaps, “that nothing further occur,” Harduinus; and so in the Mutinensis].

[Col. 0433C] Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of September, at the beginning of the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER V. TO BEATRICE AND MATHILDA, HER DAUGHTER. (Year 1075.)

He complains of the inconstancy of King Henry. Although Henry had written that he would send a secret legation because he understood the princes of his kingdom to rejoice more in discord than in peace, he now, having changed his plan, wanted everything to be made public. From this Gregory concludes that Henry does not sincerely desire peace. He explains what he thinks about Gotefrid, who had violated the faith he had promised.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to BEATRICE, duke, and to MATHILDA, her daughter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We are not a little astonished that you have decided to consult us about the matters you communicated through your letters, since it is known to you that the same king sent to us, before the month of August, two noble and religious men as legates. They still remain with us, and through them he sent this message:

“Let Your Holiness know, Father, that, since I perceive almost all the princes of my kingdom to rejoice more in our discord than in mutual peace, I am secretly sending to you these messengers, whom I recognize as sufficiently noble and religious and whom I do not doubt are united in their desire for the good of peace between us. I do not want anyone to know what I am sending except you, my lady and mother, and my aunt Beatrice and her daughter Mathilda.

“When, with the Lord’s help, I return from the Saxon expedition, I will send other legates, whom I shall regard as more intimate and faithful. Through them I shall make known to you all my wishes and the reverence that I owe to blessed Peter and to you.”

Afterward, through the aforesaid legates, he sent word that they should not be surprised or take it badly that he had not yet sent the messengers he had promised; nor should they find it burdensome to wait until he sent them, since he would undoubtedly send them and remained immovably of the same mind.

Now we are utterly astonished at how this plan has been changed and that he wishes what he had arranged to do secretly to be made public—unless this is to be understood as showing that he by no means desires this peace to be established, since he now wants it made public to those from whom he formerly wanted it concealed, and concerning whom he himself testified that they rejoiced more in our discord than in mutual harmony.

Therefore we want you to know that we shall in no way consent to this request, since what has now been devised does not appear honorable to blessed Peter and to us or likely to serve his interests. If he returns to his earlier plan, that appears healthier and should be followed by us.

As for the advice you requested from us concerning what should be answered to Gotefrid, we do not know what to say, since he has openly broken what he promised you under oath, and we cannot place certain trust in any of his promises. But if you are able to enter into some agreement with him that does not depart from the sanction of the holy Fathers, we think it should be commended. If not, we wish you to know with complete certainty that the charity with which God has joined us cannot in any way be dissolved or diminished.

Therefore, if he loves you, we shall love him; but if through his own fault he begins to hate you, then, loving you as our dearest daughters in every way we can, we shall, with God’s favor, resist him.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Ides of September, in the fourteenth indiction.

The deposition of King Henry, son of the emperor Henry, and the absolution of all who had sworn an oath to him.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] All of this is absent in the Mutinensis.]

Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, incline, we beseech you, your merciful ears toward us, etc., as below in the Third Roman Council.

[Col. 0434D]

## LETTER VI. TO ALL CHRISTIANS. (Year 1075.)

Exaggerating the injury done to the apostolic see, he exhorts them to implore divine assistance, so that God may either convert the impious to repentance or restrain their designs; and he sends them an example in the anathematization of the king.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who desire to be numbered among the sheep whom Christ entrusted to blessed Peter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0434D] The whole of this is omitted in the Mutina manuscript; hence the seventh is designated as the sixth.]

You have heard, brothers, a new and unheard-of presumption; [Col. 0435A] you have heard the wicked chatter and audacity of schismatics who blaspheme the name of the Lord in blessed Peter; you have heard the pride raised against the injury and insult of the holy apostolic see, such as your fathers never saw or heard, nor does the sequence of Scripture ever teach to have arisen among pagans or heretics. Even if some example of this evil had ever preceded, after the faith of Christ was founded and spread, nevertheless all the faithful ought to grieve and lament at such contempt and trampling underfoot of apostolic—or rather, divine—authority.

Therefore, if you believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted to blessed Peter by our Lord God Jesus Christ, and if you desire that through his hands the entrance to the joys of eternal life be opened to you, you must consider [Col. 0435B] how greatly you ought now to grieve over the insult inflicted upon him. For unless here, where your faith and hearts are tested through the trials of temptations, you become companions in his sufferings, you are without doubt unworthy to receive a share in the consolation to come and to obtain, as sons of the kingdom, the heavenly crown and glory.

We therefore ask your Charity to strive earnestly to implore the divine mercy, so that it may either turn the hearts of the wicked to repentance or, by restraining their criminal designs, show how foolish and senseless are those who attempt to overthrow the rock founded by Christ and violate divine privileges. You can fully learn in the document enclosed with this letter [Col. 0435C] how and for what reasons blessed Peter bound the king with the bond of anathema.

## LETTER VII. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS (1075)

He rejoices that the king has entrusted to religious men the cause of the disagreement that existed between them; by their counsel, he says, he will receive him into the bosom of the Church. He urges him to treat the defeated Saxons mercifully and to ensure that another person is canonically substituted in the Bamberg Church in place of the deposed Herimann.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, king, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When I received the letters of Your Greatness, we were far from the city—especially [perhaps “for the great,” HARD.] because of illness—and it was necessary to confer with those [perhaps “and with these,” likewise in Mutina] about how I should answer your embassy fully, as was fitting. Your messenger, who was their bearer, also feared remaining with us because of the aforesaid illness.

But because we desire to have peace in Christ not only with you, whom God has placed at the highest summit of affairs, but also with all people, and to observe each person’s rights, we earnestly desire to adhere to this with heart and soul. For I know—and I believe you are not unaware of it—that those who truly love God, and the Roman Church and Roman Empire, do not fear the punishment of their crimes [perhaps “and the punishment,” HARD.], but desire, by action or prayer, to establish peace and concord between us.

Therefore I have conceived a good hope [Col. 0436A] because you have begun to entrust this cause of ours—or rather, of the whole Church—to religious men who love us not for our own sake unjustly, but seek only that Christian religion be restored. I, for my part, to speak briefly, am prepared, with Christ’s favor, on their advice to open to you the bosom of the holy Roman Church, to receive you as lord, brother, and son, and to provide assistance as appropriate. I ask nothing else of you except that you not disdain to incline your ear to the admonitions concerning your salvation and that, as befits you, you offer glory and honor to your Creator without contradiction.

For it is exceedingly unworthy that we should demand from our fellow servants and brothers the honor that we refuse to render to our Creator and Redeemer. Let the divine promise therefore move us, which says: “Those who glorify me I will glorify, and those who despise me will be held of no account” (1 Sam. II). Let us offer him what pleases us in this secular way [life], so that we may enjoy the spiritual gift in heaven.

As for the pride of the Saxons, who unjustly resisted you and have been crushed before your face by divine judgment, there is reason both to rejoice for the peace of the Church and to grieve because so much Christian blood has been shed. In such matters, however, take greater care to defend God’s honor and justice than your own honor. For any prince may more safely punish a thousand wicked men for the sake of justice than strike down any Christian with the sword for the sake of his own glory. He created and rules all things who said: “I do not seek my own glory” (John VIII).

We truly provide for our salvation when in all our actions we set the glory of God before us.

Regarding Herimann, formerly called bishop of Bamberg, let Your Sublimity know that it has long been since, through a certain cleric of that Church, we sent letters to you, to our brother Sigifred, archbishop of Mainz, and to the clergy of the aforesaid Church, stating that by the authority of the apostolic see he had been deposed from every episcopal and priestly dignity and bound by the bond of anathema, because he did not fear to add sacrilege to the Simoniacal heresy and to lay waste, like a tyrant, to the holy Church entrusted to him.

Therefore we have asked—and on the part of blessed Peter we have ordered, and do order—that in the aforesaid Church a pastor be appointed according to God who, with God’s favor, may bring to life what the thief and robber have slaughtered and repair what he destroyed.

May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, in his mercy, through the merits and intercession of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, protect you [us] in this life and lead you [us] with double victory to eternal life.

## LETTER VIII. TO TEDALD, A CLERIC OF MILAN (1075)

He reproves him for having intruded himself into the place of a canonically elected bishop who was still alive. He advises him to attend the synod that was soon to be held and promises him a public guarantee of safety if he comes to him, ordering him meanwhile not to receive holy orders.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Tudald [Col. 0437A], a Milanese cleric, greetings and apostolic blessing—if he obeys.

Some of our [your] faithful and your friends have informed us that you desire and seek our friendship. We freely offer it even when it is not sought; when it is sought, however, we grant it most readily if we discover that in matters belonging to God you are willing to submit to our admonitions—or rather, to the divine will—in the cause of justice.

In the matter that you appear to have undertaken, you have added to our concern the necessity of a heavier burden and have entangled yourself with people with whom you ought not to have become involved. In this matter, just as we would consider it dangerous for us to pursue anything beyond the limits of equity, so also we believe it wrong to deviate from the rules of justice and conceal the matter in silence.

We do not believe that your prudence is unaware that, before you, another person—who is still alive—was assigned to the episcopal see in which you have been placed. Unless that person is first removed for legitimate reasons, neither canonical nor apostolic judgment permits you, or anyone else, to have a lawful place there.

For what are we to say about the man who, while pursuing the honor of that same see with wicked desires, did not hesitate to invade and seize by sacrilegious force and arms what justice had denied him? The guilt of ambition, which he refused to abandon, dragged him to the just destruction of your condemnation. We are speaking of the man who is with us, whom we certainly know was elected in that same Church; but we have so far been unable to discover any reason why he ought to be rejected.

Therefore, with our conscience as witness and with sincere affection, we admonish you: if you love the Church and wish to rescue both yourself and it from the danger of confusion, come to the next synod, which, God willing, we have decided to celebrate in the first week of the coming Lent—or, if you prefer, seek the apostolic threshold and our presence before the synod. Thus, before you plunge yourself more deeply, a fair examination may be conducted with God’s help, and you may follow and maintain without impediment or danger to your soul whatever you yourself recognize to be safe for you.

Nor should you doubt that, if we perceive that justice requires the man who is with us to withdraw, we shall willingly grant our consent and cooperation for your promotion, to the honor of almighty God and blessed [Col. 0437D] Ambrose.

To remove every suspicion of danger, we promise you security through the hands of our daughters Beatrice and her daughter Matilda, and we give it unequivocally: neither you nor those who will be in your company shall suffer any opposition from us or ours. Rather, in your affairs and persons, both on your journey here and on your return, you shall remain completely safe and unharmed, God guarding you, once the decision to be upheld in your case has merely been declared and confirmed.

Meanwhile, on behalf of almighty God and by the apostolic authority of blessed Peter, we order you not to presume to receive any grade of holy orders. Know that if you do not obey us now and do not believe us, you will one day repent, when you see yourself plunged by your own rashness into a place from which, whenever you wish, you will be unable to rescue yourself safely.

If, therefore, some people who do not understand the things of God begin to suggest and persuade you otherwise, displaying how much support you have in the king, how much power in your nobility, and how much aid in your fellow citizens, do not consider it safe to trust them. Remember what Scripture says: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” (Jer. XVII, 7).

And bearing this in mind—that the power of kings and emperors, and all the efforts of mortals, are reckoned as mere ash and straw against apostolic rights and the omnipotence of the supreme God—do not, at anyone’s prompting or through reliance on anyone, allow yourself to become rebellious and obstinate with reckless boldness against divine and apostolic authority [Col. 0438B].

Given at Rome, on the eighth [sixth] day before the Ides of September [December], in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER IX. TO THE SUFFRAGAN BISHOPS OF THE CHURCH OF MILAN (1075)

He states that he has summoned Tedald, who intruded himself into the Church of Milan, to the synod. He orders them not to dare promote him to holy orders.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brothers and fellow bishops: Gregory of Vercelli, Cunibert of Turin, Ingon [Hugo] of Asti, Ogerius of Ivrea, Opizo of Lodi, and the other suffragans of the holy Milanese Church who obey the apostolic see, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We wish you to know concerning Tedald, the Milanese cleric whom the king placed in the Milanese Church contrary to what he had promised us by letter and through the words of his legates, that he appears not to have taken possession in an adequately orderly manner of the episcopal see to which another person, still alive, had previously been assigned.

When, through certain of our faithful, he sought our friendship, we wrote to him that we greatly desired and wished this, and that an agreement could be reached most easily if, after seeking the apostolic threshold and our presence, he wished and was able to demonstrate that the cause of his promotion was pure and credible.

For this purpose we summoned him amicably and, setting before him a fixed date for the next synod of the coming Lent—or, if he preferred, before the synod—we promised him firm security, on our part, for coming to us and returning, and we are prepared to grant it.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we forbade him to receive any grade of holy orders in the meantime. We likewise forbid you, by the obedience that you owe to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by the apostolic authority that we, though unworthy, have received through him, so that none of you may presume to lay a hand upon him for promotion to any order until, after presenting himself to us, we are able, with God’s help, to determine by sincere examination what judgment and decision ought to be made concerning his intrusion.

We greatly desire this to be done with common counsel and the united discretion and judgment of all of you, if either the care of that Church, regard for apostolic reverence, or our affection can summon you to this business.

See, therefore, that none of you, despising this prohibition, extends a hand for the danger both of that man and of himself. For if anyone—though we do not believe it—should rush into such presumption, let him know that he is immediately separated from the grace of blessed Peter and from our affection, and also from communion in the sacred body and blood of the Lord.

Rather, do this—if you love the Lord, strive to accomplish this—that while that brother can and has the opportunity, he may provide for himself and the Church, care for your peace and for the salvation of so great a multitude of people who are nearly in peril, and not, by seeking his own fall through his rashness, drag many with him into a common danger.

In this matter it will now become clear who among you is a shepherd openly resisting iniquity, who is a thief practicing deception, and who is a robber openly contradicting justice. Consider, therefore, how cautiously you walk. For just as it is hard to kick against the goad, so it is harsh to oppose the holy Roman Church, which you must always obey as a mother.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [December], in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER X. TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS (1075)

[Col. 0439C]

He reproves him for associating with excommunicated persons. He advises him, if this is so, to seek absolution from some bishop.
