He expresses wonder that he displays devotion toward the Roman Church in letters and embassies, yet in reality opposes it and does not observe the decrees issued by him in the synod. He urges him to render true obedience to the Roman Church. Finally, he advises him not to impede the freedom of the Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, king, greetings and apostolic blessing [Note: [Col. 0439D] “and apostolic blessing” is absent]; provided that he obeys [or “obey”] the apostolic see, as a Christian king should.

Considering and carefully weighing how strict an account we shall have to render to the Judge concerning the administration of the ministry entrusted to us through blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we sent you the apostolic blessing with hesitation, since you are said knowingly to extend your fellowship to excommunicated persons, contrary to the judgment of the apostolic see and synodal censure.

If this is true, you yourself recognize that you cannot receive the grace of either divine or apostolic blessing unless, after separating yourself from those who are excommunicated and compelling them to repent of their transgression, you first obtain absolution and pardon through suitable repentance and satisfaction for your own offense.

We therefore advise Your Excellency that, if you feel yourself guilty in this matter, you should hasten, by confession, to the counsel of some religious bishop. With our permission, let him impose upon you an appropriate penance [Col. 0440A] for this offense and absolve you, so that with your consent he may dare to inform us truthfully by letter of the manner of your penance.

For the rest, it seems very strange to us that so often you send us letters displaying such devotion and transmit such humility from Your Highness through the words of your legates; that you call yourself a son of the holy mother Church and of us, subject in faith, unique in love, preeminent in devotion, and finally commend yourself to us with every expression of affection and reverence—yet in reality and in your deeds you show yourself most hostile, contrary to canonical and apostolic decrees in matters especially demanded by Christian religion.

To say nothing of the rest, the matter itself shows how you have honored—or with what intention you made—the promise you gave us concerning Milan through your mother, through our brother bishops whom we sent to you. And now, as though inflicting wound upon wound, you have handed over the Churches of Fermo and Spoleto contrary to the statutes of the apostolic see—if, indeed, a Church can be handed over or given by a human being to certain persons unknown even to us, to whom it is not permitted to lay hands canonically except upon persons approved and previously well known.

It would have been fitting for Your Royal Dignity, since you confess yourself a son of the Church, to regard with greater honor the master of the Church, that is, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. If you belong to the Lord’s sheep, you were entrusted to him by the Lord’s voice and authority to be fed, when Christ said to him: “Peter, feed my sheep” (John XVII); and again: “The keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted to you, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

While, in his seat and apostolic administration, we—sinners and unworthy though we are—by divine arrangement exercise the place of his authority, he himself receives whatever is sent to us, whether in writing or through the bare words of messengers; and while we either read the written characters or listen to the voices of speakers, he himself discerns by close examination from what heart the commands have proceeded.

Therefore Your Highness ought to take care that no discrepancy of will be found between your words and embassies to the apostolic see, and that in those matters through which Christian faith and the condition of the Church [Col. 0440D] most advance toward eternal salvation, you not refuse reverence owed not to us but to almighty God, although the Lord deigned to say to the apostles and their successors: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X).

For we know that whoever does not refuse to offer faithful obedience to God does not disdain to observe our admonitions in the matters we declare while following the statutes of the holy Fathers, as though he had received them from the mouth of the apostle himself.

For if, out of reverence for the chair of Moses, the Lord commanded the apostles to observe whatever the scribes and Pharisees sitting upon it said, there is no doubt that the apostolic and evangelical teaching, whose seat and foundation is Christ, must be received and maintained by the faithful with every reverence through those chosen for the ministry of preaching.

For when a synod was assembled this year at the apostolic see, over which heavenly providence willed us to preside, and in which some of your faithful were also present, we saw that the order of Christian religion had already been shaken for many years, and that the principal and proper means of winning souls had long been undermined and, at the devil’s prompting, trampled underfoot. Shaken by the danger and manifest destruction of the Lord’s flock, we returned to the decrees and teaching of the holy Fathers.

We established nothing new and nothing invented by ourselves; rather, we judged that the first and sole rule of ecclesiastical discipline and the well-trodden path of the saints must be recovered and followed after abandoning error.

For we know no other entrance to our salvation and eternal life open to Christ’s sheep and their shepherds than the one shown by him who said: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will find pasture” (John X). We have learned this from the apostles’ preaching and from the observance of the holy Fathers, in the Gospel and throughout every page of the divine Scriptures.

As for this decree, which some people—putting human beings before divine honors—call an unbearable burden and an immense weight, we call it by its proper name: the truth and light necessary for the recovery of salvation. We judge that it ought to be devoutly received and observed not only by you and those who are in your kingdom, but by all the rulers and peoples of the earth who confess and worship Christ.

Although we greatly desire this, and although it would be especially fitting for you that, just as you are more powerful than others in glory, honor, and strength, so also you should be more exalted in devotion to Christ, nevertheless, lest these matters appear excessively burdensome or unjust to you, we instructed you through your faithful not to let the alteration of a wicked custom disturb you. We told you to send us those whom you could find in your kingdom who were wise and religious. If they could demonstrate or establish by any argument how, without compromising the honor of the eternal King and without danger to our souls, we could moderate the sentence promulgated by the holy Fathers, we would accommodate ourselves to their counsel.

Even if you had not been so amicably admonished by us, it would nevertheless have been fair for you first to demand reasonably from us an explanation of what burdened you or obstructed your honors, before violating apostolic decrees.

But how much regard you have shown either for our admonitions or for the observance of justice is made clear by what you later did and arranged. Yet because God’s long patience still invites you to correction, we hope that, as your understanding increases, your heart and mind can be turned toward obedience to God’s commands.

With paternal affection we admonish you: recognize Christ’s sovereignty over you and consider how dangerous it is to place your honor before his. Do not now impede the freedom of the Church, which he deigned to join to himself as a bride in heavenly union. Rather, begin faithfully and devotedly to offer the strength of your assistance to almighty God and blessed Peter, from whom your glory also deserves to be increased.

This is something you must especially recognize as owed to them in return for the victory granted you over your enemies: while they gladden you with memorable prosperity, let them see your devotion in return for the benefits bestowed.

And so that the fear of God—whose hand and power hold every kingdom and empire—may impress this more deeply upon your heart than our admonition, keep in mind what happened to Saul after he had gained the victory in which he acted at the prophet’s command, when he gloried in his triumph and did not carry out the same prophet’s admonitions, and how he was rejected by the Lord. Consider also how great a grace followed King David because of his humility among the marks of his virtues.

Finally, concerning the matters seen and known in your letters that we pass over in silence, we shall give you no definite answer until your legates Rabbodus, Adelprech [Adelpre[c]us], and Vodescal Requos [Vodescalcus, whom] we have included with these matters have returned to us and have more fully disclosed to us your intention concerning what we entrusted to them to discuss with you.

Given at Rome, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XI. TO ARNALD, BISHOP OF ACHERUNTIA (1075)

[Col. 0442C]

He grants him authority to absolve Count Roger, together with his soldiers who will fight against the pagans, provided that they have performed penance. He urges him to encourage them to advance the Christian religion among the pagans. He shows himself ready to absolve Robert from excommunication if Robert demonstrates devotion toward the Roman Church. He orders him, after penance has been completed, to restore the episcopal office to Baldwin, bishop of Melfi.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother and fellow bishop Arnald of Acheruntia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Let Your Fraternity know that Count Roger [Note: [Col. 0441] Regarding Roger, who was count of Sicily: Leo of Ostia, Book III, chapter 15; Otto of Freising, in the book *On the Deeds of Frederick*.], brother of Duke Robert, seeks the blessing and absolution of the apostolic see and desires to be called and to be its son.

Therefore, setting aside all sluggish negligence, we impose this burden of labor upon you in pastoral care—or rather, we command you on behalf of blessed Peter—to visit him. Armed with the authority of this command of ours, if he wishes to obey us as he has promised and has performed penance, as a Christian ought, absolve both him and his soldiers who will fight with him against the pagans—provided, however, that they do penance—from every bond of their sins.

Moreover, admonish him with pious counsel to guard himself against capital crimes and to strive to enlarge the cultivation of the Christian name among the pagans, so that he may deserve to obtain victory over those same enemies.

Further, if he reports anything to you concerning his brother Duke Robert, answer him that the door of mercy of the Roman Church stands open to all who, led by love of penance, abandon the stumbling blocks of offense and desire to return with unhindered step to the path of righteousness.

If, therefore, Duke Robert desires to obey the holy Roman Church as a son, I am ready to receive him with paternal love, preserve justice for him with my counsel, release him completely from the bond of excommunication, and number him among the divine sheep.

But if the same Duke Robert refuses, he will not be able to obtain permission from the apostolic see for anyone to continue in communion with him.

We also impose this upon Your Fraternity: restore the episcopal office to our brother Baldwin, bishop of Melfi, who, as we have received from our brothers, both humbly heard and observed the correction of the universal mother. Armed with the authority of this command of ours and on behalf of blessed Peter, restore it after a penance has been imposed for certain transgressions.

Just as I have heard the requests of our brother Stephen, bishop of Troia, on his behalf, so let him take care to hear from our side the admonition concerning his salvation, and, with God’s help, let him always lead his life toward improvement.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO BISHOPS UDO, THEODORIC, AND HERIMANN (1076)

[Col. 0443C]

He warns them to beware of schismatics and to correct what they have done wrong at their persuasion; and to admonish the bishop of Toul, who had risen up against the apostolic see, to obey the pontiff. If he refuses to obey, they are to declare him excommunicated.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brothers and fellow bishops Udo of Trier, Theodoric of Verdun, and Herimann of Metz, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have judged that letters from the apostolic see ought to be sent to you because we have understood that you did not willingly consent to the schismatics who have risen up against the Lord and the authority of the holy Roman Church.

We have omitted explaining how you ought to repent of this, since you possess the same faith as we do and knowledge from the books of the holy Fathers. We hope that Your Fraternity detests the most foolish presumption of our enemies and faithfully unites itself to the holy apostolic see with the devotion and love that you ought to have and have been accustomed to show.

Therefore we ask and admonish you to correct by suitable amendment what you have done wrong through the persuasion of the schismatics, so that just as your mother grieved over your transgression, she may rejoice over your satisfaction.

We also wish you, in our place, to admonish Pippin, bishop of Toul, so that he does not henceforth fail to do what we have commanded him. For it would have been fitting for him to answer the charges brought against him rather than take up arms against the authority of the prince of the apostles in defense of his wickedness and urge the king to presume against us what was never permitted and, God willing, never will be permitted against any cleric.

If he despises the words of our exhortation, notify him by the authority of blessed Peter that he has been separated from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that he will be punished as deserving vengeance not only in his soul but also in the body of that same prince of the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] In the Mutina manuscript, after “to be punished,” the following is added: “Rather, do this—if you love God, strive to accomplish this—that, while that brother can and has the opportunity, he may provide for himself and the Church, and care equally for your peace and for the salvation of so great a multitude of people who are nearly in peril, lest, seeking his own fall through his rashness, he drag many with him into a common danger. In this matter it will now become clear who among us is a shepherd openly resisting iniquity, who is a thief practicing deception, and who is a robber openly contradicting manifest justice. Consider, therefore, how cautiously you walk, for just as it is hard to kick against the goad, so it is harsh to oppose the holy Roman Church, which we must always obey as a mother.”]

## LETTER XIII. TO THE PEOPLE OF ROSELLA (1076)

[Col. 0444B]

He explains the judgment delivered in the case that was being disputed between the Church of Rosella and the Church of Populonia.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Rosella, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because it is our office to restore those who are at odds to concord, we carefully examined the serious discord that had arisen between the Church of Rosella and the Church of Populonia.

Finally, after various arguments had been presented on both sides, it became clear—not only through the privileges of the apostolic see but also through a certain written judgment confirmed in the presence of Pope Sylvester and by the judgment of the Roman clergy—that whatever had been at issue belonged to the Church of Rosella.

Therefore, with the joint approval of both the bishops and the clergy of the Roman Church, we decided the aforesaid dispute on these terms: the investiture shall henceforth be granted to the bishop of Rosella. If, before the next feast of the Lord’s Ascension, the bishop of Populonia produces any document that, once shown to us, appears capable of justly invalidating the decision of Pope Sylvester, the bishop of Populonia shall be freely admitted to make a claim and offer resistance.

But if, from that same feast onward, this controversy remains in perpetual silence, and the Church of Rosella, supported by the repeated judgment of the apostolic see, rests forever from this dispute [Col. 0444D], then henceforth, fortified by a privilege [perhaps “fortified through a privilege” HARD.] containing our decision more fully, it shall possess without disturbance the estates over which the dispute has been contested for so long.

## LETTER XIV. TO DOMINIC, PATRIARCH OF GRADO (1076)

He gives thanks for his observance toward the Roman Church. He shows that the German and Lombard bishops rise up against him because he opposes their crimes. He postpones answering concerning Giraldus, bishop of Siponto, to another time.

[Col. 0445A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Dominic, patriarch of Grado, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since, as your letters state, you profess to venerate your mother, the holy Roman Church, with a pure heart, and to love us with sincere affection for the love of the prince of the apostles, we give thanks to Your Fraternity. In return for that same affection, and while preserving the balance of equity, we are always prepared to provide for the honor both of your Church and of you.

But because you said that you were astonished and greatly grieved that the Lombards and certain German bishops, raging against us, burn with such vehement hatred, our conscience does not accuse us of any fault in this matter.

We know, however, that they strive with that effort for no other reason than that, in accordance with God’s command and those of our holy predecessors, we oppose their perversities and, if possible, endeavor to restore them to the straight path of justice, as required by the divine dispensation of the pastoral responsibility imposed upon us.

Regarding the letters sent to us by Your Fraternity, we have been unable by any means to discover that they were carried from here to there. As for the matter that Your Fraternity brought to our attention concerning Giraldus, bishop of Siponto, we cannot at present answer you because the bishop is absent. When he comes, God permitting, we shall carefully investigate the case and provide for justice [perhaps “a just decision,” HARD.].

As for the business of the vain prince, we cannot see by any reasoning how he can or ought at present to obtain the result he seeks.

Given at Rome, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO WIFRED, A MILANESE SOLDIER (1076)

He indicates that the Normans are eager to arrange peace and hopes that they will return to the fidelity of Saint Peter, and that he will also have peace with King Henry if Henry changes his ways. He urges him to persevere in defending the Church and to advise others to do the same.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wifred [Col. 0445D], bishop of the Milanese [a Milanese soldier], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because you have indicated in your letter that you are concerned for the honor of the Christian faith, we have considered it appropriate to reply to your prudence. Know, therefore, that the Normans are negotiating peace with us; they would already have made it most willingly and would humbly have satisfied blessed Peter, whom alone, after the Lord, they desire to have as their lord and emperor, if we had yielded to their wishes in certain matters. But, with God’s help, we hope shortly to do this not to the detriment but to the advancement of the Roman Church, and to recall them firmly and steadfastly to the fidelity of blessed Peter.

As for the king of Germany, certain persons have already appealed to us many times concerning the making of peace with him. We replied that we wished to have peace with him if he himself would strive to have peace with God and would correct, as he has often been admonished by us to do, those things that he has committed to the peril of the holy Church and to the accumulation of his own ruin. But because we have placed our faith, hope, and all our thoughts more in the power of divine strength than in any human being, we wish you also—whom we understand to have recovered courage and strength to encourage Christ’s soldiers—to trust firmly in God. Await his help and consolation, which will come to you and to all who love justice and the law of God, while the members of the devil will be able to harm our innocence only insofar as God permits.

Behold, the devil openly rules in the world; behold, he rejoices that all his members have exalted themselves. But may he who said, “Take courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16), grant you the most certain faith that he will hasten to aid his Church and utterly confound the devil and his members. For, considering the changes of ancient times and of our own age, we find with good reason that the devil’s dominion has lasted the less long the more it seemed to be exalted and to have prevailed against the Christian religion.

Therefore, dearest son, “be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might” (Ephesians 6), and strengthen those whom you know to remain in the Christian faith. Admonish those, however, who have denied the Christian faith by their deeds, so that they may repent and be ashamed to live in the devil’s servitude. Whatever we write less fully here, when we have spoken with the faithful of blessed Peter, we shall make known more fully; and, God favoring, we shall see to it that assistance is given you.

May almighty God, through the merits of the most exalted Lady and through the prayers of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of blessed Ambrose, enlighten your minds and establish you always in his law, so that you may deserve to be numbered among those who will judge the devil with his members and reign forever with Christ.

Given at Rome, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO RICHER, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS. (1076)

He complains of the injuries inflicted upon his Church by the bishop of Orléans, of the latter’s disobedience and simony. He wishes him to admonish the bishop to make satisfaction to his Church and, if he does not obey, to excommunicate him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richer, archbishop of Sens: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your Fraternity has understood how great were the injuries suffered by the Church of Orléans through the negligence of its bishop—or rather through his own agency—and how unjustly he abused the patience of the Apostolic See. That See not only delayed investigating the iniquities reported to us, but also gave no assent to the accusations of the king of the Franks, who wished to expel him; indeed, with the most vigilant care it prevented whatever he had contrived to his own danger.

For it did not seem that the charges of this accusation, even if they were true, should be accepted, nor that anything should be pronounced against him except after legal investigation and judgment. But he himself, having forgotten this gentleness and such great charity, is said to have rendered the fruit of disobedience to his mother, the Roman Church, by violating the privilege of our predecessor, Pope Alexander, of shamelessly communicating with Eurard, whom we had excommunicated, and of selling by simony not only the deanery but nearly all the offices of the Church. Having been suspended by God, he seems deservedly to have provoked upon himself the sentence of the Apostolic See through the wickedness of his deeds, as formerly.

Therefore we wish your Religiousness to admonish the aforesaid bishop to make satisfaction to God and to his Church, and to strive to amend his conduct in such a way that the complaint of the clergy may be entirely quieted and that no further report of his disgrace concerning these excesses may reach the ears of the Apostolic See.

But if he should prove disobedient to our letters, which are sent to him through you, and to your admonition, then, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, separate him from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until he has made worthy satisfaction, so that he may recognize, even in this, how greatly he has offended the Lord by his deeds.

Given at Rome [“at Rome” is absent], in the month of April, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVII. TO RAINER, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS. (1076)

He rebukes him for his rashness and orders him to allow the canons to possess the provostship, Joscelin to possess it, and Benedict to possess his canonry; he is also to restore the canonry assigned to the poor, until he comes to Rome to render an account of his crimes.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainer, bishop of Orléans: greetings and apostolic blessing, if he obeys.

We would rightly be gravely moved against you, even to the point of avenging your rash audacity, if we were not restrained by apostolic gentleness. You yourself must and can remember how our predecessor, Pope Alexander, of venerable memory, after seeing the charter of your donation of the deanery [or: “of the deanery”] of Holy Cross from the same provostship, confirmed it for your canons—who had brought it to him—by instruments of apostolic ratification, according to the custom of your donation. By adding the anathema of apostolic authority, he restrained both you and all persons from violence against the aforesaid provostship through the privilege of his confirmation.

You did not fear to incur this anathema by communicating with the excommunicated Eurard [Everard] and, what is even more serious, by accepting payment from him, as is said. Driven by wicked arrogance, you considered it nothing to disturb the whole Church. Therefore, we ought indeed to restrain your presumption by the punishment of apostolic correction; but, in hope of future amendment, we still endure your excesses.

By apostolic authority, therefore, we order you to withdraw your mind from such great rashness and to permit the aforesaid provostship to be possessed in the secure tranquility of peace by the canons and by Joscelin, who holds it from them [the text also reads: “by Loscelin, who likewise has it from them”]. You are not to inflict any further trouble upon them.

For we wish them to possess in full and in complete peace all that belongs to the provostship, so that the privilege of our predecessor, Pope Alexander, of blessed memory, may not seem to be infringed in even the smallest part. Moreover, we order you to present yourself before us by the feast of All Saints, in order to render an account both of these matters and of the many others charged against you.

Meanwhile, the canons and Joscelin, who [perhaps “who,” HARD., thus also in Mutina] holds the provostship from them, are to possess all the things mentioned above in peace. The same Joscelin is likewise to retain his abbey, with all his other movable and immovable property, and possess it in peace, suffering no controversy of any kind to be brought against him by you. Benedict is also to retain his canonry meanwhile in the same tranquility of peace.

We further order you to restore to its former use the canonry assigned for the support of the poor, which you are said to have sold after removing it from that use.

If you obediently comply with these commands and admonitions of ours and patiently carry out everything contained in them, we shall rejoice for the sake of the Church’s peace. Otherwise, know that you are suspended from every episcopal office and separated from communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Given at Rome, in the month of April, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO SIMEON, BISHOP IN SPAIN. (1076)

He commends his observance toward the Roman Church. He exhorts him firmly to embrace the decrees of the Apostolic See and to ensure that the Roman order is observed. He replies that he wishes the decrees of the Apostolic See concerning the celebration of the Church’s offices to be observed by them; therefore he admonishes him to ensure that they are observed in Spain and Galicia.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Simeon, bishop of the Spains: greetings and apostolic blessing.

After learning the contents of your Fraternity’s letter, we were filled with joy, because through it we fully recognized the faith and devotion that you bear toward the Roman Church, and that you desire not to abandon her adulterously, but to embrace her through the succession of legitimate offspring.

Therefore, dearest brother, it is necessary that what has been well begun proceed along the right path; nor should what is established by apostolic tradition be diminished by heretical perversity. For the Apostolic See, over which, although unworthy, we preside by God’s authority, has remained firm from the very beginning under his governance, and, under his protection, will remain forever undefiled. The same Lord bears witness: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 23).

Supported by these safeguards, the Roman Church wishes you to know that she desires the children whom she nourishes for Christ to be fed neither at different breasts nor with different milk, so that, according to the Apostle, “they may be one,” and “there may be no divisions among them” (1 Corinthians 1); otherwise she would be called not a mother but a division.

Therefore let it be known to you and to all Christ’s faithful, concerning the matters on which you consulted us, that we wish the decrees issued or confirmed by us—or rather by the Roman Church—to remain unshaken in the celebration among you of the offices of that same Church. Do not yield to those who desire to infect you with the bites of wolves and the contrivance of poisons.

We do not doubt that, according to the Apostle, “fierce wolves, ravenous wolves that do not spare,” have entered among you (Acts 20); they must be resisted firmly in faith. Therefore, most beloved brother, strive resolutely, even to the shedding of blood if necessary.

For it may be considered unworthy and ridiculous that secular men, for so cheap a price and in so hateful a transaction before God, should voluntarily expose themselves to danger, while every faithful person gives his back to enemies who attack. Those who easily fall wherever they are dragged cannot acquire strength.

As for what the sons of death say—that they have received letters from us—know that this is altogether false. Therefore see to it that the Roman order be observed more correctly throughout Spain and Galicia and wherever else you are able.

Given at Rome, in the month of May, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIX. TO CYRIAC, ARCHBISHOP OF CARTHAGE. (1076)

Since only two bishops were found in Africa, he wishes them to elect another and send him to be consecrated.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Cyriac, archbishop of Carthage: greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has reached our ears that Africa, which is said to be a part of the world and which in ancient times, when Christianity flourished there, was governed by a very large number of bishops, has fallen into such great peril that, when a bishop is to be ordained, it does not possess three bishops.

Considering in this matter the greatest danger to the Christian religion, and compassionating in our hearts the laborers toiling with few workers in so vast a field, we have advised you—namely, you and the man upon whom we recently laid hands—to choose some person according to the constitution of the holy Fathers and send him to us supported by your letters. Thus, with God himself cooperating, after he has been ordained by us and sent back to you, you may be able to assist the needs of the Churches through the ordination of bishops, as the holy canons command; the Christian people may rejoice and advance daily under pastoral governance; and the labor that overwhelms you beyond your strength may be lightened through the necessary administration of companions.

Given at Rome, in the month of June, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO THE PEOPLE OF HIPPO. (1076)

He exhorts them to obedience toward the archbishop and to preserve mutual charity.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people established at Hippo in Mauritania Sitifensis, that is, in Africa: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have consecrated, with the favor of divine clemency, the archbishop whom you elected and sent to us for consecration, according to your request and according to our law. After his consecration, and after diligently instructing him in our lawful customs insofar as opportunity and the time available permitted, we sent him back to you.

We beg you, with all devotion to mutual charity and with every reverence belonging to the Christian religion, and we admonish you with paternal affection, to receive him. We exhort you humbly to render him every obedience required by divine law, so that the peoples of the Saracens who are around you, seeing the sincerity of your faith and also the purity of the divine charity and fraternal love that exists among you, may be stirred by your deeds to emulate rather than despise the Christian faith. For, seeing you, they ought to glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Act, therefore, most beloved sons, according to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said to his disciples: “Love one another, as I have loved you. No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15; 1 John 4).

The Apostle Paul also, the teacher and doctor of the nations, says: “If our Lord Jesus Christ lays down his life for his sheep and has given his blood as redemption for many” (1 Timothy 2; 1 John 3), then we too ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

Thus, most beloved and dearly loved brothers, show yourselves diligent in the worship of the Christian religion, so that after the sea of this life you may happily reach the harbor of perpetual rest and eternal blessedness, granted by the Redeemer himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages [“endless ages”]. Amen.

## LETTER XXI. TO ANZIR, KING OF MAURITANIA. (1076)

He writes that he consecrated Bishop Servandus at his request. He gives thanks for the gifts sent and for the release of Christian captives. He commends to him certain Romans sent by Alberic and Cencius.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anzir [Anazir], king of the Mauritanian province of Sitifensis in Africa: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your Nobility sent us a letter this year asking us to ordain the presbyter Servandus as bishop, according to Christian constitution. Because your request seemed just and most worthy, we undertook to do so.

You also sent gifts to us; out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and out of love for us, you released the Christians who were being held captive among you, and you promised that you would release others as well.

The Creator of all, God, without whom we can do—or indeed even think—nothing good, inspired this goodness in your heart. He who enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1) enlightened your mind in this intention.

For almighty God, who wishes all people to be saved and none to perish (1 Timothy 2), approves nothing more in us than that a person should love another person after loving himself, and should not do to another what he does not wish done to himself (Matthew 7).

Therefore, we owe this charity to one another in a special way, more than to other peoples, because we believe in and confess one God, although in different ways, and daily praise and venerate him as the Creator of the ages and governor of this world. For, as the Apostle says: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2).

Many Roman nobles, learning through us of this grace granted to you by God, greatly admire and praise your goodness and virtues. Among them are two of our familiars, Alberic and Cencius, who have been raised with us in the Roman palace from almost their adolescence. They greatly desire to enter into your friendship and affection and willingly serve you in whatever concerning our fathers may please you. They are sending their men to you so that through them you may understand how prudent and noble they consider you, and how willingly and capably they wish to serve you.

We commend them to your Magnificence and ask that, for love of us and in return for the fidelity of the aforesaid men, you strive to show them the charity that we have always desired to extend to you and to all your people.

God knows that we love you purely for the honor of God and desire your salvation and honor in the present life and in the life to come. With heart and voice we pray that God himself may lead you, after the long course of this life, into the bosom of the blessed patriarch Abraham’s blessedness.

# BOOK FOUR OF THE REGISTER

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, fourteenth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Nevertheless, almost all of them belong to the fifteenth indiction.]

[Col. 0451]

## LETTER I. TO ALL CHRISTIANS. (1076)

[Col. 0451B]

[Col. 0451C] He complains of King Henry’s treachery and of the evils that the Church suffered from him. He admonishes them to lead him toward true repentance; if he refuses to listen, they are to resist him manfully. Those who had adhered to the king, if they wish to repent, are to be admitted to the bosom of the Church. Those who have not withdrawn from communion with the king, however, are shown to be persons whom they must avoid.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all brothers in Christ—namely, bishops, abbots, and priests, and also dukes, princes, and soldiers, and all who truly love the Christian faith and the honor of blessed Peter, dwelling in the Roman Empire: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God, who, because of the excessive love with which he loved us, did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all; who, beyond the merits and even beyond the hope of good people [perhaps “of all people”], protects, governs, and defends his Church.

For you know, dearest brothers, that in this dangerous time, when Antichrist is already at work in his members, scarcely anyone anywhere is usually found who truly loves both God and his honor, and who places his commandments above secular advantage and the favor of earthly princes.

But he who does not reject his people and daily changes sinners from the left hand to the right has looked upon you with a gracious and serene countenance and has raised you up against his enemies for the salvation of many peoples, so that you may prefer to stand firm amid the danger of transitory life rather than place the glory and honor of the eternal King below human favor.

In doing these things, you do not pass by with deaf ears the words of the prince of the apostles, who says: “A chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2); “It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5).

For your Fraternity is certainly not ignorant of how long the holy Church has endured the unheard-of depravity and various iniquities of the king—would that he were a Christian—and of your own people; nor are you ignorant of the ruin and calamity to which she was exposed, with that ancient enemy leading the way and instigating it.

Moved by brotherly love and by affection as of a father and mother toward him, we sent him words of admonition while we were still in the diaconate. After we entered the office of the priesthood, although unworthy, we frequently arranged through religious men that he should look carefully into these matters.

What he himself did in opposition, how he repaid good with evil, and how, raising his heel against blessed Peter, he attempted to tear apart the holy Church that almighty God had entrusted to him—your Charity knows this, and it has already resounded throughout every region of the world.

But because it is our office to love people, not vices; to resist the wicked so that they may repent; and to abhor impieties, not people, we admonish you by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and beg you as dearest brothers: strive from now on to snatch him from the hand of the devil and summon him to true repentance, so that, with God’s favor, we may be able, moved by brotherly charity, to recall him to the bosom of our common mother, whom he has attempted to tear apart. Let this be done, however, in such a way that no relapse through deceit may again confound the Christian religion and trample the holy Church beneath his feet.

But if he does not listen to you, chooses to follow the devil rather than Christ, and prefers to you the counsel of those who have long been excommunicated for the Simoniacal heresy, then, with divine power inspiring us, let us discover and determine together how, placing the Lord before a human being, we may manfully come to the aid of the universal Church, which is now almost collapsing.

Whoever among those who were not ashamed to place the aforesaid king before almighty God and to deny the Christian law, if not in words, nevertheless in deeds, repents—for the Apostle says, “With their mouth they confess God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1)—you, my brothers and fellow priests, receive by the authority of blessed Peter and restore to the bosom of our mother, the holy Church, so that you may deserve to renew joy in heaven before the angels of God.

In all things, however, as befits most beloved sons, keep before your eyes the honor of your devout Father, the prince of the apostles. But whoever of the bishops or laymen, seduced by fear or human favor, has not withdrawn from communion with the king, but, favoring him, has not feared to hand over his own soul and the king’s soul to the devil—if he does not repent and perform worthy penance, have no communion or friendship with him.

These are the people who hate and destroy both their own soul and the king’s soul, and are not ashamed to confound the kingdom, the homeland, and the Christian religion.

For just as the following words spoken through the prophet threaten us: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I shall require his soul from your hand” (Ezekiel 3); and, “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48)—that is, the word of correction from rebuking those who live wickedly—so, if they do not obey, the anger of divine judgment and vengeance threaten them, as Samuel testifies concerning the crime of idolatry [or: “the crime of idolatry”].

God is our witness that no secular advantage or worldly consideration drives us against wicked princes and impious priests, but rather the consideration of our office and the authority of the Apostolic See, by which we are daily burdened.

For it is better for us, if necessary, to suffer the deserved death of the flesh at the hands of tyrants than, through our silence, fear, or advantage, to consent to the destruction of the Christian law.

We know that our holy Fathers said: “Whoever, out of regard for his office, does not oppose wicked people, consents to them; and whoever does not remove what must be cut away, commits it.”

May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, through the merits of our Lady, the heavenly Queen, and through the intercession of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, strengthen and guard your hearts and pour upon you the grace of his Spirit, so that, doing what pleases him, you may deserve to rescue his bride—namely, our mother—from the jaws of wolves and, absolved from all sins, reach her heavenly glory.

Given at Laurentum, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER II. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF METZ. (1076)

He shows that all who have communicated with King Henry, whether bishops or laymen, are excommunicated. He declares that those who assert that kings cannot be excommunicated are mistaken, citing the authority and examples of holy pontiffs; indeed, he demonstrates that pontiffs are far superior to kings. He states that he has granted bishops permission to absolve those who had communicated with the king, but that he himself will not absolve the king unless he has first become certain of his repentance. He further wishes the bishop of Toul to be admonished by the archbishop of Trier not to interfere in the affairs of a certain monastery. He adds certain remarks about Matilda and Godfrey.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Herimann, bishop of Metz: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You ask many questions of me, who am very occupied, and you send a messenger who presses me excessively to grant his request. Therefore, if I do not answer sufficiently, I ask you to bear it patiently.

Let the bearer of this letter tell you how I am in body and how the Romans or Normans are displaying their customs toward me. As for the other matters about which you have questioned me, would that blessed Peter might answer through me, since he is often honored or injured in me, however inadequate a servant of his I may be.

You need not ask me which bishops, priests, or laymen are excommunicated, because without doubt they are those known to communicate with the excommunicated King Henry—if it is lawful to call him king. They do not fear to place human favor or fear before the commandment of the eternal King, nor do they fear to drive that same king by their favor toward the wrath of almighty God.

He himself did not fear to incur excommunication by communicating with his familiar associates who had been excommunicated for the Simoniacal heresy, and he is not ashamed to draw others into excommunication by having them communicate with him.

What remains for us to think about such people except what we have learned in the Psalms: “The fool has said in his heart: There is no God” (Psalm 13), and again: “They have all together become useless in their desires” (Psalm 52)?

To those who say, “A king ought not to be excommunicated”—although, because of their great folly, we ought not even to answer them—we nevertheless refer them to the words and deeds of the holy Fathers, lest we appear impatiently to pass over their stupidity, so that we may recall them to sound doctrine.

Let them read what blessed Peter commanded the Christian people in the ordination of Saint Clement concerning one whom they knew not to have the favor of the pontiff. Let them learn why the Apostle says, “Having at hand the power to avenge every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10), and concerning whom he says, “With such a one, not even to eat” (1 Corinthians 5).

Let them consider why Pope Zacharias deposed the king of the Franks and absolved all the Franks from the bond of the oath that they had sworn to him. In the Register of blessed Gregory, let them learn that, in the privileges that he granted to certain churches, he not only excommunicated kings and dukes who acted against his commands, but also judged that they should be deprived of their dignity.

Nor should they omit that blessed Ambrose excommunicated not only a king but truly the emperor Theodosius, both in conduct and in authority, and also forbade him, lest he presume to do so, to remain in the church among the priests.

But perhaps these men wish to understand that, when God entrusted his Church three times to blessed Peter, saying, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), he excluded kings. Why do they not consider—or rather, why do they not confess with shame—that when God principally gave blessed Peter power to bind and loose in heaven and on earth (Matthew 16), he excepted no one and withdrew nothing from his power?

For whoever denies that he can be bound by the bond of the Church must consequently deny that he can be released from her power. Whoever shamelessly denies this separates himself entirely from Christ.

If the holy Apostolic See, by the principal authority divinely bestowed upon it, makes judgments concerning spiritual matters, why should it not also judge secular matters? Your Charity is not ignorant of whose members kings and princes of this age are when they place their honor and temporal profits before God’s justice and seek their own advantage by neglecting his honor, nor to whom they belong or adhere.

For just as those who place God before all their own desires and obey his command more than human beings are members of Christ, so those of whom we spoke above are members of Antichrist.

If, then, spiritual men are judged when necessary, why should they not all the more bind secular men concerning their wicked acts? But perhaps they think that royal dignity surpasses episcopal dignity. From their own principles they can gather how greatly the two differ.

The one was devised by human pride; the other was instituted by divine mercy. The one continually seeks empty glory; the other always aspires to heavenly life.

Let them also learn what blessed Pope Anastasius wrote to the emperor Anastasius concerning these dignities, and what blessed Ambrose determined in his Pastoral concerning them. “The honor and sublimity of the episcopate,” he says, “if you compare it with the splendor of a kingdom and the diadem of princes, will be as far above it as the brilliance of gold is above the metal of lead.”

Knowing this, the Emperor Constantine the Great chose not the first but the last place among the bishops. For he knew that “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

Meanwhile, let it be known to your Fraternity that, after receiving letters from certain of our brother bishops and dukes, we have granted, by the authority of the Apostolic See, permission for bishops to absolve those excommunicated by us who did not fear to withdraw from communion with the king.

As for the king himself, we have expressly forbidden anyone to presume to absolve him until his certain repentance and sincere satisfaction have been reported to us by suitable witnesses, so that together we may determine how, if divine mercy has looked upon him, we may absolve him for the honor of God and his salvation.

We are not unaware that some among you, under some pretext—as though they had received authority from us—and seduced by fear or human favor, might presume to absolve him if we did not forbid it, and to apply a wound to a wound instead of a remedy. If some bishops truly opposed them, they would judge that those bishops were not defending justice but exercising hostility.

The ordination and consecration of bishops who presume to communicate with an excommunicated king, as blessed Gregory testifies, becomes execration before God. When they proudly despise obedience to the Apostolic See, they incur the crime of idolatry, as Samuel testifies (1 Kings 15).

For if the person who is aroused by zeal for divine love to strike at vices is called God’s own, then certainly the person who refuses, insofar as he is able, to rebuke the lives of carnal people denies that he belongs to God.

And if the one who withholds his sword from blood is accursed (Jeremiah 48)—that is, who withholds the word of preaching from the destruction of carnal life—how much more accursed is the person who, driven by fear or favor, propels his brother’s soul into eternal destruction?

That the accursed and excommunicated can bless, and can bestow upon anyone the divine grace that they themselves do not fear to deny by their deeds, cannot be found in any commandment of the holy Fathers.

Meanwhile, we order you to address the venerable archbishop of Trier, our brother, and have him forbid the bishop of Toul to interfere in the affairs of the abbess of the monastery of Mount Romaric. He is to declare invalid, together with you, whatever the bishop has decreed against her.

As for Matilda, our common daughter and faithful handmaid of blessed Peter, I wish what you wish; but, with God governing, I do not yet know for certain in what condition she will remain.

As for Godfrey, formerly her husband, know without doubt that I frequently remember him before the Lord, although I am a sinner. For neither hostility toward him nor any vanity prevents me; rather, moved by brotherly affection toward you and by Matilda’s entreaty, I desire his salvation.

May almighty God, through the intercession of the heavenly Queen, the ever-virgin Mary, and through the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, granted them by God, absolve you and all our brothers, in whatever order they may be, who defend the Christian religion and the dignity of the Apostolic See, from all sins. May he increase your faith, hope, and charity and strengthen you in the defense of his law, so that you may deserve to attain eternal salvation.

Given at Tivoli, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER III. TO THE GERMANS. (1076)

He instructs them that, if King Henry, excommunicated in the synod and deprived of his royal dignity, has truly repented, they should receive him kindly, removing his wicked advisers and appointing good men in their place; they are also to admonish him not to attack the liberty of the Church. Meanwhile, no bishop is to absolve him until the consent of the Apostolic See has been given. But if he has not truly repented, they are to choose another suitable king, whom he says he will confirm, though only with the advice of the Empress Agnes, to whom they had bound themselves by oath.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all beloved brothers in Christ, and to fellow bishops, dukes, counts, and all who defend the Christian faith, dwelling in the kingdom of the Teutons: greetings and absolution from all sins through the apostolic blessing.

If you carefully weigh the letters in which Henry, called king, was excommunicated in the holy synod by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, you will know beyond doubt what ought to be done about him. From them one understands why he was bound by the bond of anathema, deposed from royal dignity, and why all the people formerly subject to him [Col. 0457A] were released from the bond of the oath they had sworn to him.

But because, God as our witness, it was not secular pride or the empty desire of the world that moved us against him, but concern for and discipline of the holy see and the universal mother Church, we admonish you in the Lord Jesus and beg you, as dearest brothers, to receive him kindly if he should have turned to God with his whole heart, and to show him not only the justice that prevents him from reigning, but also the mercy that erases many crimes.

Be mindful, I beg you, of the human condition and our common frailty; and let the pious and noble memory of his father and mother not escape you—people equal to whom, in our age, cannot be found for the governance of the empire. Yet apply to his wounds the oil of compassion, lest, if the wine of discipline is neglected, his scars grow worse and rot—which God forbid!—and lest the honor of the holy Church and of the Roman Empire, through our negligence, be exposed to great ruin.

Let the wicked counsellors be removed far from him: those who, excommunicated for the Simoniacal heresy, were not ashamed to contaminate their lord with their own leprosy, and, by leading him astray through various crimes, to provoke him to rend the holy Church and drive him into the anger of God and of Saint Peter. Let counsellors be brought to him who love not only their own interests but also him, and who in all things place God before secular profit.

Let him no longer think that the holy Church is subject to him as a maidservant, but let him regard it as his mistress, set over him. Let him not, puffed up by a spirit of arrogance, defend customs of pride devised against the liberty of the holy Church, but [Col. 0457C] observe the teaching of the holy Fathers, which divine power taught them for our salvation.

If he makes us secure concerning these matters and the others that must rightly be required of him, by the means that are proper, we immediately wish to be informed of everything through your suitable legates, so that, with God’s inspiration, it may be possible to determine by common counsel what ought to be done.

Above all else, on behalf of blessed Peter, we forbid that any of you presume to absolve him from excommunication until, after reporting to us the matters we have stated above, you receive the consent and renewed reply of the apostolic see. We have doubts about the differing counsels of different people, and we regard human favour or fear with suspicion.

But if—because of the sins of many, which we do not desire—he has not turned to God from his heart, then, with God’s favour, let someone be found for the governance of the kingdom who promises, by a secret and unquestionable pledge, to observe the matters we have stated above and the other things that appear necessary for the Christian religion and the salvation of the whole empire.

But so that we may confirm your election, if it is altogether necessary that it be made, by apostolic authority, and strengthen the new arrangement in our own times, as we know was done by our holy Fathers, report to us as quickly as you can his affairs, person, and character. Thus, proceeding with a holy and useful intention, you may deserve, as the causes are known to us, to receive through divine grace the favour of the apostolic see and in all things the blessing of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Concerning the oath that was sworn to our dearest daughter Agnes, the empress Augusta, namely, that if her son should depart this life before her, there is no need for you to remain uncertain. For if, moved by excessive affection for her son, she resists justice, or, favouring justice, consents to his being rejected from the kingdom, you yourselves understand what remains to be done.

Nevertheless, this seems praiseworthy: once it has become certain among you—and altogether established—that her son is to be removed from the kingdom, counsel should be sought from her and from us concerning the person found for the governance of the kingdom. Then either she will give her assent to our common counsel, or the authority of the apostolic see will remove all bonds that appear to contradict justice.

As for those who have been excommunicated, I remember that I have already given you permission—since you defend the Christian faith, as is proper for bishops—to absolve them; and I confirm the same permission still, provided that they have truly repented and humbly performed penance.

Given at Laurenti, on the third day before the Nones of September, at the beginning of the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER IV. TO THE PEOPLE OF DOL

*(Year 1076)*

Since the canons opposed his satisfying their request by ordaining as archbishop a certain young man whom they had elected, he says that, at the young man’s request, he ordained the abbot of Saint Melarius [Melanius] as archbishop. He urges them to obey him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Dol in Brittany, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Col. 0458C] You sent to us a certain young man, asking that we ordain him bishop for you. Since the sacred canons oppose this request, we were in no way able to consent to it.

Finally, recognizing that your Church had long been oppressed by the tyranny of a most wicked usurper, we desired, as duty and consideration of our office required, to restore it, supported by apostolic protection and according to our ability in the Lord. Therefore, at the request of that young man and with the consent of his companions, we consecrated for you as father and archbishop Ivo, abbot of Saint Melarius [Melanius]—the man named Ivo whom you sent to us as your envoy—a man, as you know well, prudent, good, adorned with good character, and worthy of every form of religion [Col. 0458D]. We admonish and beseech you: just as you desire the grace of blessed Peter the apostle and of us, his unworthy servant, so render him, as father and ruler, obedience in all things.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, at the beginning of the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER V. TO THE BISHOPS OF ARMORIC BRITTANY

*(Year 1076)*

He writes that he consecrated as archbishop of Dol the abbot of Saint Melarius [Melanius], after the young man elected by the people of Dol had not been approved because of his youthful age, and granted him the pallium, on the condition, however, that the dispute being conducted with the archbishop of Tours concerning subjection and obedience should be examined. Nevertheless, he confirms his use of the pallium. He commands them to render him obedience as archbishop and to provide assistance for recovering the goods of the Church.

[Col. 0459A] **GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Brittany, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that you are not unaware of how the clergy and people of Dol sent to us a certain young man, of sufficiently distinguished birth, as we heard, asking that we ordain him bishop for them. Examining his case—as was proper—we found in him honorable conduct proportionate to his age, but not yet sufficiently mature or instructed to bear the episcopal burden. For this reason we saw that it would be unsafe both for him and for us to load him with so heavy a burden.

But, with God’s inspiration, we found among his companions a person much more suited to this dignity in age, knowledge, and seriousness of character: namely Ivo, abbot of Saint Melarius [Melanius]. Although unwilling and bound by obedience, we ordained him bishop after much urging and at the election of that young man and of the others who had come with him.

Out of affection for you and for the whole province, we also granted him the honour and use of the pallium, on the condition that, at the proper time, he should in no way refuse to appear for the examination of the complaint that our brother Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, has for a long time brought before us and our predecessors concerning the subjection of that see and the obedience denied to him.

If, as reason and justice demonstrate, it should appear that Dol ought to be subject to Tours, then we wish—and by apostolic authority decree—that the right of the holy Church of Tours be preserved and that due subjection be rendered by the Church of Dol. Nevertheless, we grant and confirm the use of the pallium no less to this man and his successors, until their accession and life have proved worthy.

But if it is established by legal defence that Dol is free from the yoke of this subjection, then the apostolic authority will not deny whatever privileges of dignity may thereafter appear to belong to it. Meanwhile, by this present authority, we decree that you render him, as archbishop, subjection and obedience.

Having therefore consecrated and adorned him in this manner, we send him back to the see assigned to him not by human counsel but by divine [Col. 0459D] providence. We wish him to be highly commended to you, so that, just as we have honoured your affection and the primacy of the whole province in him, you too may share with us the concern and loving devotion that we have undertaken for him.

Receive him with every honour and reverence, and assist him so that he may recover the goods of the Church, which for many years have been scattered and seized by sacrilegious usurpers. Thus, with God’s help, that once noble and powerful see may be restored through your efforts to the glory of its former splendour and returned in your times.

For thus, indeed, dearest brothers, God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has called us [Col. 0460A]: if we desire to retain the dignity of the members in the body of his beloved Son, we must also be joined to one another by brotherly affection and the duties of intimate love.

Act, therefore, so that your brotherhood toward this brother and the Church entrusted to him may be such that we may glory before the almighty Lord in the reward of your blessedness, and that amid so many wicked storms of this age, not only we but also your mother, the holy and apostolic Church, may rejoice in the consolation of your cooperation.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER VI. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

*(Year 1076)*

He replies that if the bishop of Utrecht knowingly communicated with the excommunicated king and died without satisfaction, no one can communicate with him even after death; otherwise, he absolves him and desires that sacrifices be offered for him. Finally, he asks that prayers be poured out to God for the tranquillity of the Church.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, bishop of Liège, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Note: [Col. 0459D] See Lambert, under the year 1073.]

Concerning the case of William, bishop of Utrecht, about which you consulted us, your prudence can learn and understand with certainty that the matter has been expressed not so much by us as by the common judgment of the holy Fathers. By preserving or defending their statutes, whenever we have made or make judgments concerning ecclesiastical affairs [Col. 0460C], we do not put forward anything new or our own; rather, we follow and apply what they have pronounced through the Holy Spirit.

See, therefore, and carefully consider what their authority has decreed concerning those who, armed with schismatic and heretical cunning to subvert the sacred regulations and divide the unity of the body of Christ, which is the Church, rise up of their own accord against the Fathers, or knowingly communicate with the excommunicated. Accept from us the answers of those whose footsteps, with God as our guide, we have considered, not only concerning the matter about which your fraternity has inquired, but concerning all who are involved in the same case.

If, without any schism—which ought in no way to have been presumed against the holy and apostolic Church, even against the lowest minister of the Church—he himself, or anyone else who voluntarily subscribed, knowingly communicated with the excommunicated king and departed, or should depart, without penance and satisfaction, we cannot depart from the judgment of the holy Fathers: namely, that we did not communicate with them while they were alive, and dare not communicate with them after death.

But if he subscribed unwillingly and did not communicate with the excommunicated king, in accordance with the prohibition of the holy canons, we absolve him by apostolic authority. We not only consent to, but greatly desire, that prayers, sacrifice, and almsgiving be offered to the Lord for him.

For the rest, we ask your affection [Col. 0461A] to pray to the Lord without ceasing, and to invite and admonish in the same way whatever brothers and subjects you can, so that in his mercy he may look upon the Church, which has long laboured and laboured greatly; and that he may rescue it from being completely submerged, since he sees it miserably afflicted and almost shattered amid the waves of so many and such great storms, and in his goodness lead it back to the shore of tranquillity.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER VII. TO HENRY, ARDERIC, AND WIFRED

*(Year 1076)*

Although the Church suffers frequent persecutions from the Normans and King Henry, he nevertheless hopes to conquer Henry, just as he previously conquered the Normans. He announces that the Germans will elect another king unless the king repents, and encourages and strengthens them in the Lord.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, ARDERIC, and WIFRED, faithful men of the holy apostolic see and legitimate sons of the Church of Milan, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The Apostle’s clear judgment is that all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12). Since this judgment has come to us together with the apostolic see, as though by hereditary right, the Normans repeatedly endeavour from one side to seize the goods of the Church, breaking their oaths; from the other side, the Simoniacs, together with King Henry, strive with every impiety to overturn the decrees of the holy Fathers [Col. 0461C]. But we trust in the Lord, who recently brought down the pride of the Normans beneath our hand, that they will not long prevail against the apostolic see.

Nevertheless, we will never become participants in their sacrilegious invasion by consenting to it. As for the conspiracy of the heretics and the king, and how it is openly opposed by Catholic bishops and dukes and many others in the German regions, we do not believe that you, who are close to them, are unaware.

The faithful of the Roman Church have reached such a great number that, unless the king comes to satisfaction, they openly declare that they will elect another king. We have promised to favour them while preserving justice, and we shall keep our promise firm.

Therefore, take courage in the Lord, for through God’s mercy your redemption is near. Peter’s strength has not yet failed when it comes to overcoming a third opponent: he who cast down those two earlier men, Wido and Gotifred, from the episcopal see because they kicked against the Roman Church [Col. 0461D].

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER VIII TO THE BISHOPS OF TUSCANY

*(Year 1076)*

He orders that the bishop of Siena, who had communicated with King Henry and requested absolution, be summoned by all of them, or by the two bishops who live nearest to him, and that they impose penance upon him. Once he has performed it, he promises to absolve him. Meanwhile, if he should fall into danger of death, he grants him absolution.

[Col. 0462A] **GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops of Tuscany—Constantine of Arezzo, Rainerius of Florence, Leo of Pistoia, Anselm of Lucca, and Lanfranc of Chiusi—greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that your fraternity is not unaware how your fellow-provincial, Rodulf, bishop of Siena, this year approached the excommunicated king without our permission and, by communicating with him contrary to all ecclesiastical authority, incurred the snare of that same excommunication.

Although his own conscience accuses him and judges him guilty in this matter, nevertheless he took care to abstain from no communion, as an excommunicated man ought to have done [Col. 0462B]. Presuming everything, both in the ministry and in his external conduct, he scattered the stains of his sin among many, and, showing nothing in his dress or conduct that pertained to guilt, he now asks through his legates to be received by us for satisfaction concerning his offence and to be absolved.

We judged that this must not be done unless we first knew that, as penance for his guilt, he had for some time been humbled in the form and condition of one who had lost communion.

Therefore we have written to your fraternity, admonishing you to assemble him as quickly as possible, if you can all do so, or otherwise the two of you who live nearest to him, at a suitable place. Impose upon him whatever penance seems proper to you, and admonish him to withdraw to a private place and, as has been established in the sacred canons, abstain from Christian communion [Col. 0462C].

If he does not refuse to present himself with prompt obedience, and if he who failed to avoid the guilt does not spare himself, through human shame, from performing penance, then, when he or his legates request it, with the testimony of your letters, apostolic clemency will not refuse to reply and act concerning his absolution in whatever way, with God’s gift, we judge to be fitting.

Meanwhile, if by divine judgment—which we do not desire—he should come into danger of death, and if he has been humbled in penance as we stated above, then, by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and by that authority which we, although unworthy, have received through them [Col. 0462D], let him, absolved, receive participation in and the grace of the most holy communion.

Given at Rome, on the Kalends of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER IX. TO RICHER, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

*(Year 1076)*

If the bishop of Orléans affirms that he did not see the apostolic letters by which the pontiff ordered him to come to him, he will continue to bear his actions with equanimity; otherwise, he suspends him from every episcopal office and from communion in the Lord’s body. He orders him to come to Rome for the council and admonishs the bishop of Orléans to come with him, together with other clerics claiming various rights.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to RICHER, archbishop of Sens, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We do not believe that it is unknown to your fraternity that, by our letters, we admonished Rainerius, bishop of Orléans, to come to us so that he might answer concerning the many charges brought against him, and especially concerning the disorder of the Church of Orléans.

He so despised our admonition that he neither came himself nor sent any reasonable excuse for his absence. So that you might more fully know the fault of his disobedience, we took care to show your religious authority a copy of the letter that we formerly sent to him.

If he should confirm under oath that he did not see it, and that he did not remain unaware through his own negligence of what he did not see, we will continue to bear his actions with equanimity. But otherwise, according to the terms of this condition, if he does not take the oath, we decree that he is suspended from every episcopal office and separated from communion in the body and blood of the Lord, unless the danger of death should overtake him [Col. 0463B].

Since not only the necessity and tribulation of that Church, but also many other affairs of your kingdom, require your fraternity to attend the Roman council, we admonish you to come to our next synod without any excuse for delay, and to admonish the aforesaid bishop of Orléans to come with you.

We also wish the man who now holds the deanery to come with that bishop. We further order Joscelin, who complains that he was unjustly dispossessed and that he spent much of his property repairing the goods of the Church [Col. 0463C], as well as Everard and some of the clerics who can produce both the bishop’s own decree and the privilege of our predecessor, Pope Alexander, of venerable memory, to come, so that we may investigate each person’s claim with the greatest care and, with God’s help, correct what must be corrected in such a way that everyone may receive his justice and the Church may enjoy complete peace.

Meanwhile, for the firm and inviolable peace of that Church, we decree that the person who now presides over the deanery retain possession of the deanery until our hearing. Joscelin is to be permitted, without opposition, to retain whatever he held before the beginning of this lawsuit. As for Benedict, we order that not only his prebend but also whatever he appears to have lost on account of this discord be restored to him in full.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER X. TO ADELA, COUNTESS OF FLANDERS

*(Year 1076)*

He replies that fornicating clerics ought not to celebrate Mass, but must be driven out of the choir. He orders this to be done, and says that no credence should be given to a certain Hubert, an archdeacon who had fallen into heresy.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ADELA [ADÈLE], countess of Flanders, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It has reached our ears that some of you are uncertain whether priests and Levites, or others who minister at the sacred altars, if they persist in fornication, ought to celebrate the Mass.

To them we reply, on the authority of the holy Fathers, that ministers of the sacred altar who are living in fornication must in no way celebrate the Mass; indeed, they must be driven outside the choirs until they offer fruits worthy of penance.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you to admit none of those who persist in wickedness to celebrate the sacred mystery. Instead, wherever you can, obtain for the celebration of Mass men who serve God chastely. Expel such offenders altogether from all the Church’s benefices, and do not accept the words of the archdeacon Hubert or favour any of his speeches [Col. 0464B], because, as I have heard, he fell into heresy through his wicked disputes and was publicly convicted by Hubert, the legate of this holy Roman see, at Monasteriolum.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XI. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS

*(Year 1076)*

He orders him to persecute Simoniac priests and fornicators. He attacks the bishops who were disobedient to the apostolic see.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROBERT, count of Flanders, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Col. 0464C] It has reached the apostolic see that in the land under your rule those who are called priests, living in fornication, are not ashamed, while singing, to handle the body and blood of Christ in the Mass. They do not consider what madness and what crime it is to handle, at one and the same time, the body of a prostitute and the body of Christ.

Therefore, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we beg you and command you absolutely that, wherever you can, no consideration or favour divert you from resisting this crime and opposing the Simoniacs.

He who said, “Let everyone who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22:17), excluded no one of any order. And whoever wishes to receive the denarius from the master of the household must undertake to labour in the Lord’s vineyard [Col. 0464D] (Matt. 20:1–16).

This universal mother commands those who are called bishops to speak as they ought. But what sort of men they are you can learn from their fruits: they do not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climb in by another way; they are thieves and robbers.

The one who enters through the door—that is, through Christ—is the one who is constituted bishop according to the sacred canons. For what is said in divine Scripture, “Wicked priests are the ruin of the people” (Ezek. 15:8), is proved in our own time more clearly than daylight.

Many of those who are called bishops not only fail to defend justice but also strive in many ways to prevent it from coming to light. Regard such men not as bishops but as enemies of Christ; and just as they do not care to obey the apostolic see, so you must render them no obedience [Col. 0465A].
