For, according to the words of the prophet Samuel, not to obey those set over one is to incur the crime of idolatry (1 Sam. 15:23)—words that blessed Gregory took care to explain in the final book of the *Moralia* (chapter 10), where he speaks about obedience.

Read these words of ours, although rustic, frequently with our common faithful friend Ingelrann, who long remained with us in the sacred palace, or with other lovers of truth. Urge all clergy and laity to know and proclaim the truth, so that, announcing good things to your brothers, you may deserve to receive a portion among the angels and rejoice with the elect in the heavenly homeland.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO THE GERMANS

*(Year 1077)*

[Col. 0465B]

He announces that King Henry performed the humblest penance and that he absolved him, at the supplication of all those present, after receiving an oath of fidelity. He sends a copy of the oath. He promises that he will go to Germany. Meanwhile, he urges them to persevere in faith and in love of justice.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and other princes of the kingdom of the Germans who defend the Christian faith, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Note: [Col. 0465] See Lambert; Berthold, under the year 1077; Leo of Ostia, book 3, chapter 48.]

Because, for love of justice, you have undertaken with us a common cause and danger in the struggle of Christian warfare, we have wished to inform your affection with sincere charity how the humbled king obtained pardon through absolution by penance, and how the whole affair, after his entry into Italy, has proceeded up to the present.

As had been arranged with the legates sent to us from your regions, we came into Lombardy about twenty days before the appointed time at which one of the dukes was to meet us at the Cluses, awaiting their arrival so that we might cross into those regions.

But when the appointed time had already passed, we were informed that, because of many difficulties—which we certainly believe were the cause—it was not possible for an escort to be sent to meet us, and that we had no other means of crossing over to you. We were thus surrounded by no small anxiety as to what course of action we ought especially to take [Col. 0465D].

Meanwhile, we learned for certain that the king was approaching. Even before he had entered Italy, he sent supplicating legates to us, offering to make full satisfaction to God, to Saint Peter, and to us, and promising to observe complete obedience for the amendment of his life, provided that he might deserve to obtain from us the grace of absolution and apostolic blessing.

For a long time we delayed this through many consultations and sharply reproached him for his excesses through all the messengers who passed between us. At last, presenting nothing hostile or reckless, he came with a few men to the town of Canossa, where we were staying. There he remained for three days before the gate, having laid aside all royal attire, miserably—as one barefoot and dressed in woollen clothing—and did not cease imploring, with much weeping, the aid and consolation of apostolic mercy.

He moved all who were there and all to whom the report reached to such pity and compassion that they interceded for him with many prayers and tears. Everyone marvelled at the unusual hardness of our mind; some even declared that in us there was not the gravity of apostolic severity but something like the cruelty of tyrannical savagery [Col. 0466A].

Finally, overcome by the urgency of his remorse and by the great supplication of all who were there, we released him from the bond of anathema and received him into communion and the bosom of holy mother Church, after accepting from him the securities written below. We also received confirmation of these through the hands of the abbot of Cluny, our daughters Matilda and Countess Adelaide, and the other princes, bishops, and laymen whom we judged useful for this purpose.

Since these matters have thus been completed, we wish, once the opportunity is first provided, to cross over to your regions, so that, as we have long desired, we may more fully arrange everything for the peace of the Church and the harmony of the kingdom, with God’s help.

We wish you to know this without doubt: as you can understand from the securities set down in writing, the whole matter remains so suspended that both our arrival and the unanimity of your counsels appear to be supremely necessary [Col. 0466C].

Therefore, strive to remain steadfast in the faith that you have begun and in your love of justice. Know that we have offered ourselves to the king on no other terms than those in which, speaking plainly—as is my custom—we said that he might hope to receive our help for his salvation and honour, either with justice or with mercy, without danger to our soul or his, in whatever matters we can assist him.

### The Oath of Henry, King of the Germans

I, Henry, king, concerning the murmuring and dissension that the archbishops and bishops, dukes, counts, and other princes of the kingdom of the Germans now have against me, and the others who follow them in that same cause of dissension, will, within the period that the lord Pope Gregory shall establish, either do justice according to his judgment or establish concord according to his counsel, unless a definite impediment should obstruct me or him. Once that impediment has been removed, I shall be ready to carry out the same.

Likewise, if the same lord Pope Gregory wishes to go beyond the Alps or to other regions of the earth, he shall be secure, on my part and on the part of those whom I can compel, from every injury to his life or limbs and from capture—both he himself and those who are in his protection and company, those whom he sends, and those who come to him from any regions of the earth, whether while travelling there, remaining there, or returning from there. Nor shall he suffer, with my consent, any other impediment contrary to his honour [Col. 0467A]. And if anyone should inflict such an injury upon him, I shall assist him in good faith according to my ability.

Enacted at Canossa, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIII. TO RODULF, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

*(Year 1077)*

He says that Rodulf ought not to complain about the pallium granted to the bishop of Dol, since he did this while preserving the right of the Church of Tours. He affirms that he will give a more thoroughly examined judgment concerning that right when either he himself has crossed into Germany, as he has planned, or the archbishop himself has come to Rome together with the bishop of Dol, having been summoned. Meanwhile, he explains why he acted as he did.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to RODULF, archbishop of Tours, greeting and apostolic [Col. 0467B] blessing.**

Because you complain against us concerning the consecration of the bishop of Dol and the honour of the pallium granted to him, you appear to be acting more from inclination than from reason. You know that in this matter we have reserved the whole question of justice for the Church over which, God willing, you are recognised as worthy to preside.

When we heard that the princes of that land, contrary to an ancient and most wicked custom, no longer wished, out of reverence for almighty God and apostolic authority, to retain the lordship of investiture in the ordination of bishops or to seek financial gain, and that for this reason they had sent to the apostolic see so that a lawful bishop might be ordained in that place according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, we judged it right to rejoice greatly in their devotion and to grant their requests [Col. 0467C].

How carefully we provided for the Church of Tours and its dignity is set out most suitably in the letters that we sent to the princes and bishops of Brittany—as we think you also know.

Therefore your fraternity will not refuse to await, without any murmuring, the examination and just definition of this case. We acted as we did after consideration, and we wish to investigate and carry out what must be done with diligent inquiry, as so great and ambiguous a matter requires.

Nor, with God’s providence, will this be delayed for long. For if, as we have planned, we cross at this time into the regions of the kingdom of the Germans, we shall either cross over from there to you ourselves or arrange to send men who will examine and determine this case with sincere investigation [Col. 0467D].

But if it should happen that our plan cannot be carried through in this way, at a suitable time we shall summon both you and the bishop of Dol to the presence of the apostolic see. There, after your case has been carefully examined on both sides, we shall, with God’s favour, bring it to an irrevocable conclusion, as sincere truth and justice require.

Given in Lombardy, at a place called Carpineta, on the Kalends of March, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF CHARTRES

*(Year 1077)*

They are not to receive Robert, a perjurer and Simoniac, as bishop in future, but are to elect another legitimate pastor. If anyone has been made bishop non-canonically, he, all his supporters, and those who consented are to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0468A] **GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of the Church of Chartres, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
Although we believe that this very matter has reached your ears, nevertheless, so that no disagreement among you arising from differing reports or opinions may impede the cause of God, we have considered it fitting to notify you by the present letter that Robert the monk, who seized your church through wicked ambition, has bound himself by the terrible guilt of perjury. For, although he had undoubtedly been admonished by our legate—as he had sworn above the body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—he refused to resign that bishopric [Col. 0468B] and violated the other provisions contained in the same oath.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we admonish and command you never again to regard him as bishop or lord, nor to render him any obedience or service. But so that that church may not remain longer without a pastor, or its entrance lie open any further to simoniacal usurpation, by the same authority we command you, after preceding prayers and a three-day fast with almsgiving, not to neglect, out of anyone’s fear or favor, or for any reason whatsoever, to elect for yourselves as bishop such a man as ought to be called and to be a shepherd of the sheep—not one who enters from elsewhere like a thief and robber, but one who enters through the door (John 10). For know this: if anyone should aspire to that see contrary to the rule of the holy [Col. 0468C] Fathers, we shall strike him, all his supporters, and all who consent to him in this matter with apostolic censure and the sword of anathema, and cut them off from the body of the entire Church.

Therefore remember that no one has suffered for you, no one has died for you, except Christ. Holding and defending his freedom as beloved children of God, do not in any way allow the yoke of iniquity or any domination leading to the destruction of your souls to be imposed upon you. Know that in this matter the apostolic authority and defense will never be lacking to you.

Given at Carpineta, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO RICHER, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, ETC. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0468D]

They are to arrange for another man to be canonically elected by the clergy and people of Chartres in Robert’s place and consecrated bishop; and they are to compel that same Robert and his brother Hugh to restore what they had taken from the church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richer, archbishop of Sens, and his suffragan co-bishops, except the one who is under interdict: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your fraternity is not unaware of the reasons for which canonical and apostolic censure deprived Robert the monk, once called bishop of Chartres, of the episcopal see and office, although he has still not ceased to occupy that same see, to his own disgrace, contrary to the oath that he made above the body of blessed [Col. 0469A] Peter, prince of the apostles.

But since we have admonished that church to hold a canonical election of a suitable person, we also admonish you to apply to that election the diligence that is required, either personally or through suitable messengers of your own. Once you have recognized the man who has been canonically elected, do not on any account refuse either to lay hands upon him or to consecrate him bishop. For know that if you omit this through fear or favor toward anyone, we nevertheless shall by no means leave him irregularly appointed; and we shall henceforth judge you unworthy of the honor and dignity that you do not blush ignobly to abandon.

We also command, by divine justice and apostolic authority, that you admonish that same Robert and his brother Hugh [Col. 0469B] to restore completely to the aforesaid church of Chartres and its clergy whatever they have taken, and henceforth not presume to commit any injustice against them. But if, within three weeks after you have seen this letter, he should disdain to fulfill this, expel them from the thresholds of the church as robbers and sacrilegious men, until they have made worthy satisfaction and amends.

Given at Carpineta, on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE CLERGY OF ROMANS (Year 1077)

[Col. 0469C]

He does not send them greeting and blessing, since they are excommunicated. He orders them to appear before the bishop of Die, so that the case being disputed between them and the archbishop of Vienne concerning the jurisdiction of a certain place may be examined; he orders them to show themselves obedient to him and likewise to the bishop of Vienne in all things. Otherwise, he threatens that he will not leave their contumacy unpunished.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy of Romans.

Because we do not send you greeting and apostolic blessing in the customary manner, we omit this on account of the excommunication that, in accordance with sacred authority, you were not afraid to incur through your offenses. Nevertheless, the gentleness of apostolic governance itself [variant: apostolici, “of apostolic governance”] and customary piety require us to write to you and admonish you concerning matters pertaining to your correction. Our confrater Wormundus [Wormandus], venerable archbishop of Vienne, complains against you that you presumed to deny him the ancient authority belonging by right to your locality. You know that this authority belonged from the beginning to the proper jurisdiction of the church of Vienne and has until now been exercised under the administration of his predecessors. He also declares that you irrationally and craftily put forward this occasion for opposing him, on the grounds that the same place ought to belong to the jurisdiction of Saint Peter and to be under his dominion, by I know not what precedents or concessions.

We must therefore attend to this case with much greater caution and provide for its most just examination, so that we may not appear to inflict any prejudice or harm either upon the apostolic see or upon the church of Vienne. For just as we wish the rights and dignities of the holy Roman and apostolic Church to be preserved, so we judge it most fitting that its members—that is, the other churches—should be protected by its foresight and authority.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we admonish and command you to present yourselves, without any delay caused by opposition, to our confrater Hugh, the venerable bishop of Die, to whom we have also entrusted our representative authority in other matters, so that this case may be examined. Whatever he shall determine and judge to be just in this matter, you must not fail to carry out obediently. You are also to show yourselves in all obedience and humility to this representative of ours and to the aforesaid archbishop of Vienne, so as to make satisfaction concerning whatever they may have identified as blameworthy in you and rightly requiring correction.

See, therefore, that you listen to us in all these matters with attentive ears and obedient minds. Know that if the contumacy of your disobedience and rash resistance should again be reported to us, apostolic authority will by no means overlook it unavenged or leave it unpunished with fitting severity. Having by our present authority forbidden all people to enter your church, we also decree that whatever sentence and judgment of punishment the aforesaid confraters of ours exercise against you shall remain valid and firm, enforced with urgent strictness against you.

Given at the castle called Carpum, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVII. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH (Year 1077)

[Col. 0470C]

The case of the bishop of Dol, expelled from the episcopate on account of his crimes, had been handled in such a way that it seemed impossible for it to be handled more carefully. Nevertheless, at his request he has sent legates who are to examine it again in the same church, and he does not doubt that the king will acquiesce in their determination. He shows himself ready to promote the king’s glory; the remaining matters he will entrust to the legate Hubert, whom the king is to trust.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, king of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We thought that the case about which you asked us in your letters had already been brought to its conclusion in such a way [Col. 0470D] that nothing remained in it requiring further reconsideration. For when we ordained a bishop in the church of Dol, we had learned—through not only the clergy and religious persons of that church but also our legate Leuzo the monk—that the man for whom Your Excellence intervened had brought about his own deposition through his own crimes and, finally, through disobedience. We therefore judged that he had more reason to fear and lament the evils committed against the Church and his utterly corrupt life than to plead for or hope for the recovery of his episcopate.

Nevertheless, so that we may not appear to have received your entreaty without the care and kindness that it deserves, and so that, if someone has deceived us through usurpation—which we do not believe—we may not be found insufficiently diligent in investigating and correcting the matter, we have decided to send our legates: namely, our confrater Hugh, the venerable bishop of Die; our beloved son Hubert, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church; and Leuzo the monk himself, if we can send him there after he has recovered from his illness. They are to examine the case through careful inquiry and, if anything in it must be changed or corrected as justice dictates, to endeavor to carry this out with due reason and authority.

For nowhere does this matter seem capable of being handled more properly or carefully than in that same church, where both he and the others can be present, and where your faithful can also attend—men who will be able to report to you, through reliable assertions, what they have fully learned concerning reason and justice. We do not doubt that Your Highness will harmoniously acquiesce in the determination of justice. For although, through God’s mercy, you possess many distinguished virtues, this one is especially celebrated and renowned, and it commends your glory particularly to God and to men: that you love and approve justice when others also administer the justice that you are ready to administer.

For the rest, know that Your Eminence and your often-demonstrated devotion are most pleasing to us. We embrace you yourselves, and whatever, with God as its author, can contribute to the glory of your highness, always in our heart and inmost being, with great desire and the affection of intimate charity. In accordance with your wishes, in all that you seek to obtain from us, we are ready, insofar as we can and according to God’s good pleasure, to be moved and to give our assent.

Since we have decided to send our aforesaid son Hubert all the way to you, we have not thought it necessary to write more to you, since we do not doubt—and do not wish Your Excellence to doubt—that in everything he reports to you on our behalf, he will be as a most certain letter of ours, faithfully containing our words.

May almighty God, through the merits and intercession of the apostles Peter and Paul and of all his saints, grant you, your most serene queen and wife Matilda, and your illustrious sons pardon, remission, and absolution from all your sins; and when he commands you to be removed from worldly affairs [Col. 0471D], may he cause you to pass into his eternal kingdom and true glory.

Given at Bibianello, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE CANONS OF LE PUY (Year 1077)

He confirms the sentence of excommunication imposed by the legate, the bishop of Die, upon Stephen, the invader of the church of Le Puy. He therefore absolves them from every oath they had sworn to him, commands them to render him no further obedience, and orders them to elect another pastor.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of Le Puy.

You know how Stephen, the invader and Simoniac of the church of Le Puy, disregarding the oath that he had made to us over the body of Saint Peter concerning the liberation [Col. 0472A] of that church, does not cease to occupy it and afflict it with tyrannical oppression. We therefore wish you to know that, just as our confrater Hugh, bishop of Die, to whom we entrusted the exercise of our authority in the regions of Gaul, excommunicated him, so we too have excommunicated him and separated him from the bosom of the holy Church.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you to shake your necks free from his yoke, and not to serve him by clinging to the devil, whose member he has become. Rather, avoid him as one who is excommunicated, as is proper. Make satisfaction before the aforesaid bishop of Die concerning the excommunication that you incurred, and, following his counsel, elect for yourselves a pastor according to the Lord.

If you do this, we absolve you, on the part of Saint Peter, from every oath and obligation [Col. 0472B] that you made to the aforesaid Simoniac against the Lord. But if even now you should presume to resist our salutary command, know that you have been condemned by the same anathema.

Given at Bibianello [Biblianello, and so throughout], on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL (Year 1077)

He confirms the sentence imposed upon the bishop of Le Puy, as in the preceding letter. He also excommunicates all who give him counsel to persist in his heresy. He forbids offerings from being made in that church for as long as it remains in his possession.

[Col. 0472C]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Gaul and to all the orders subject to them, to whom greeting and apostolic blessing are due according to their merits.

We wish your charity to know that Stephen, the invader and Simoniac of the church of Le Puy, swore to us over the body of blessed Peter that he would leave that church and faithfully assist in electing and appointing a pastor in it according to the Lord whenever a legate of the apostolic see, bearing our letters, should admonish him by oath to do so.

Afterward, however, when he was admonished by our confrater Hugh, bishop of Die, who had letters from us specifically concerning this matter—even though we had entrusted him with our authority in the regions of Gaul—he did not cease to oppress the Church [Col. 0472D] and to crush its children with a twofold affliction, bodily and spiritual.

Therefore, we confirm the excommunication that our aforesaid legate imposed upon him, and on God’s behalf and that of Saint Peter we anathematize him, together with all who henceforth give him counsel to persist in this heresy, until they repent.

We also forbid anyone to offer any money at the platform of Saint Mary, whether at the altars or into the hands of the priests, until the church is freed from such impious oppression. For the offerings of the faithful cause the aforesaid Stephen to apostatize from God and to grow proud against him.

By apostolic authority we command you, brothers and fellow bishops, to have this excommunication and prohibition read out in your parishes in various places [Col. 0473A] and confirmed on your behalf.

Given at Bibianello, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO JOSFRED, BISHOP OF PARIS (Year 1077)

[Col. 0473B]

He orders a certain Walter, excommunicated by the archbishop of Rheims and conditionally absolved by him, to be absolved by the archbishop if he is free of guilt. If the archbishop refuses to do this, he wishes Josfred himself to absolve Walter; but if Walter is guilty, he is to compel him to make satisfaction. In the same manner he is to absolve a certain canon named Azo; he is to release from excommunication the monks of Saint Lambert who had refused to obey an outside abbot; and he is to excommunicate the men of Cambrai if they burned a man because he maintained that Simoniacs and fornicating priests ought not to celebrate Mass. He is to show himself a faithful minister of the Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Josfred, bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

This man, Walter of Douai, bearer of the present letter, came to us and earnestly implored us, with many supplications, to provide him, through the mercy of apostolic compassion, with counsel and assistance toward absolution through our intervention with our confrater, the archbishop of Rheims, who had excommunicated him. He informed us that, concerning the matter for which he had been excommunicated, he had repeatedly offered himself as ready to argue his case and to do justice, both before and after the excommunication.

But since we judged it insufficiently cautious or reasonable to believe his account without a legitimate examination, we refused to issue a definitive sentence for his absolution. We granted him only this mercy, by the grace and indulgence of the apostles Peter and Paul, to whose thresholds he had come: that on his journey there and back he should have permission to receive holy Communion until the eighth day after his return to his homeland.

However, so that he may not be held any longer in the bonds of excommunication on account of some unworthy pretext, we admonish you by apostolic authority, supported by these letters of ours, to meet with the archbishop. After investigating and learning the simple truth of the matter, if this man should appear to you deserving of absolution either because of his innocence or because he has offered suitable satisfaction, immediately admonish the archbishop on our behalf to absolve him without contradiction. If the archbishop should refuse this under any pretext, you yourself must not fail to absolve him in our place.

But if it should be established that this man is guilty and unwilling to carry out what is just, we decree that he is to be compelled to remain under the bond of excommunication until he has made worthy satisfaction.

Furthermore, it has become known that a certain canon named Azo of the church of Saint-Amatus in the aforesaid place was expelled from the fellowship of the brothers for uttering a certain statement, although it was true, too lightly and irreverently. Since he likewise appeals to the clemency of apostolic mercy for his reconciliation, we entrust him to you. If he is not accused of any other fault more deserving of condemnation, have him corrected in the chapter through monastic discipline and chastened by penance, and then have him received with charity into the fellowship of the brothers and restored to his proper place.

There is also another matter that we wish you to undertake and carry out with the greatest care: namely, the case of two brothers of the monastery of Saint Remigius, Robert and Lambert. They say that they were excommunicated by the archbishop for the following reason, and that, after one of their lay brothers had been blinded, they were surrounded by every misery: they refused to obey a certain outsider abbot, imposed upon them and upon the aforesaid monastery through the intervention of money and entirely contrary to the rule of Saint Benedict and the authority of the holy Fathers, and to remain in the same monastery under his governance. Nor, they say, did it profit them at all in these matters to appeal to the hearing of the apostolic see, seeking to prevent the monastery’s disgrace and to obtain permission for their just defense.

If this is so, you can yourself judge how seriously the archbishop has made himself culpable in this matter, especially through contempt of apostolic authority. Therefore, while awaiting, with God’s help, a more suitable opportunity of meeting with him in a more fitting place and time concerning this and many other matters, we presently entrust this to your fraternity and command by apostolic authority that, setting aside every excuse, you admonish him to release the sentence of excommunication that he pronounced against the aforesaid monks, and thereafter allow them to remain in peace, without any harassment or danger. He should recognize, and fear the judgment of the heavenly Judge, since without a judicial deliberation and despite their appeal to the apostolic see he inflicted such evils upon them.

But if you find him resisting in this matter on account of his rank and personal will, and less obedient, then, supported by our authority, absolve them yourself. As for that abbot who is said to have seized the aforesaid monastery of Saint Remigius through wicked ambition, admonish him to present himself to our confrater Hugh, the venerable bishop of Die, to whom we have entrusted our authority in those regions, or to our other legates, if he learns that they are going to hold a synod in Gaul, so that he may give an account of his entry into office. He must not fail to do this; otherwise, he is to come to us at the next feast of All Saints.

Also admonish the brothers of that monastery who complain against him concerning his unlawful usurpation of the abbacy to present themselves, according to the foregoing determination, for the examination of this matter.

It has also been reported to us that the men of Cambrai handed a certain man over to the flames because he dared to say that Simoniacs and fornicating priests ought not to celebrate Mass, and that their ministry ought by no means to be accepted. Since this appears to us extremely alarming and, if true, to be punished with every severity of canonical strictness, we admonish your fraternity diligently to investigate the truth of this matter. If you discover that they extended their impious hands to such cruelty, do not delay separating from entry into the church and from all ecclesiastical communion both the authors and the accomplices of this crime [Col. 0475A]. Endeavor to inform us as quickly as you can, by your letters, of the certainty of this matter and of whatever result has been achieved in the cases mentioned above.

For the rest, we ask and strongly admonish you to notify all your confraters and fellow bishops throughout France, by apostolic authority, that they are to prohibit entirely from ministering at the sacred altars those priests who refuse to cease from the shame of fornication. You yourself, in every place and assembly, must not cease to preach this.

If in this matter you discover either lukewarm bishops or men who, on account of the aforesaid crimes, presume unworthily to claim the name and office of the sacred orders and are rebellious, forbid the whole people everywhere, on behalf of blessed Peter and by our apostolic authority, to receive their ministry any longer, so that, being confounded even in this way, they may be compelled to return to the correction of their lives and to the chastity of religious continence.

Act, therefore, so that the holy and universal mother Church may, with God’s help, recognize you as a faithful minister and co-worker in our—indeed, apostolic—care. May it come about that we may rejoice, as we greatly desire, in the freedom and fruit of your priestly office in the present, and confidently hope through God’s mercy for the same in the future.

Given at Bibianello, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF METZ (Year 1077)

[Col. 0475C]

He entrusts to him the case between the bishop of Liège and the abbot of Saint-Laurent, who, after being expelled from his monastery by that bishop, had appealed to the apostolic see.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Herimann, bishop of Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Vulpodo, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Laurent at Liège, the bearer of the present letter, came to us and earnestly implored us, with many supplications, to assist him through apostolic intervention with the bishop of Liège, who had expelled him from his monastery, so that the bishop might deal with him more mercifully. He told us only this much about his case: that he had been ready to respond to the charges brought against him, but that he had been entirely unable to obtain the legal time allowed for responding and clearing himself, although he had requested it under invocation of the divine name and out of regard for blessed Peter.

The bishop, however, had previously reported to us in his letter certain unworthy matters concerning the abbot’s conduct. Therefore, so that in this ambiguity we may not appear to deny either party what is just, we ask your fraternity—and admonish you by apostolic authority—to undertake this case. After learning it through careful inquiry, have it handled and determined in the order prescribed by canonical institutions. Take care, moreover, that this man be admitted to a hearing with such moderation, and with justice preserved for him, that he may not appear to have sought apostolic mercy and its support in vain.

[Col. 0476A] Given at Bibianello, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DIE (Year 1077)

He orders a synod of the bishops of France to be assembled, so that the case of the elected bishop of Cambrai may be examined. After his legitimate election, this man had received investiture from King Henry, unaware both that the king was excommunicated and that such investiture had been prohibited by the pope. If he affirms on oath that this was indeed the case, he confirms his election. He also wishes the cases of certain churches to be determined in the council; the abbot of Cluny is to be summoned to the synod on account of the case of the church of Auvergne; and, among other matters, a decree is to be promulgated forbidding the acceptance of investitures from laymen.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, [Col. 0476B] the venerable bishop of Die: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Gerard, the elected bishop of Cambrai, came to us and openly explained how he had been appointed to the position of governance in that same church of Cambrai. He did not deny that, after the election by the clergy and people had taken place, he had received the episcopal gift from King Henry. He offered a defense, however, and repeatedly maintained that he had not learned through any certain disclosure either of our decree prohibiting such acceptance or of the fact that King Henry had been excommunicated by us.

When we demonstrated to him, with suitable arguments, how serious it was—even with ignorance providing him no excuse—to transgress the synodal decree of the holy apostolic see and to defile himself by such participation with an excommunicated man, he immediately renounced into our hands the gift that he appeared to have received, in order to make satisfaction. He entirely left his case to our judgment, subjecting and submitting himself to our every will.

Moved to mercy by his humility, and especially because we heard that a canonical election had preceded his appointment, and relying upon the testimony that some of our confraternal bishops had sent us in their letters, together with many supplications on his behalf—that his earlier life and conduct had been very honorable and praiseworthy—we judged it not unfitting, with discreet moderation, to consent to his advancement [Col. 0476D].

Nevertheless, lest this should later serve others as an example or occasion for seeking mercy, when their cause and conduct had proved entirely different and inferior to his, we established the following: before you, our confrater the archbishop of Rheims, and the other bishops of the province, he must clear himself by oath, affirming that, before he received that gift and, as it is called, the investiture of the bishopric, no one had informed him—neither our legate nor any person who admitted having attended and heard these enactments—that the king was excommunicated and that our decree prohibiting such investiture and the acceptance of churches had been issued and made known to him beyond doubt.

Therefore, we admonish your fraternity to strive to convene and hold a council in those regions, especially with the consent and counsel of the king of France, if this can be done. But if for any reason he should refuse to consent, arrange to hold a council at the church of Langres, and do this with the counsel and prudent direction of our brother, the bishop of Langres. Know that he has promised henceforth to be a faithful helper and co-worker not only to us but also to you [perhaps “to you” rather than “there”; HARD.] and to all our legates in every matter. We place great hope and confidence in him.

Count Theobald also made the same promise to us through his legates: if the king should refuse to receive our legates, he himself would receive them with the greatest devotion and provide them with whatever opportunity, place, counsel, and assistance he could for holding the synod and investigating ecclesiastical affairs.

Therefore, endeavor to meet with our aforesaid confrater, the bishop of Langres, and, by common counsel, establish the synod wherever seems best to you. Summon there the archbishop of Rheims and as many other archbishops and bishops of France as you can. First of all, strive to examine the case of the aforesaid elected bishop of Cambrai, so that he may clear himself before everyone according to the terms of the prescribed oath. Moreover, in the same oath he is to defend himself against having consented to the death of the man who was thrown into the fire.

If this has been done, we decree by apostolic moderation that his earlier election is to be confirmed. We wish you, together with our confrater the archbishop of Rheims, to determine what is proper concerning his consecration, unless some other matter unknown to us should stand in his way. We leave such matters, however, to be examined by your prudence.

That common evil of nearly the whole world—namely, that altars are sold, which this man also does not deny having done in the office of his archdeaconate—forbid henceforth both him and all others to commit.

For the rest, we admonish your affection to handle and bring to completion, in the capacity of our representative entrusted to you, insofar as you are able with God’s help, the remaining cases and affairs: namely, those of the bishop of Châlons, the church of Chartres, Le Puy, Auvergne, the monastery of Saint-Denis, and whatever other matters appear necessary for ecclesiastical religion. Do this so carefully that our anxiety and long weariness concerning them may henceforth be relieved.

We also wish you to arrange, by invitation, entreaty, and persistent insistence, that our brother Hugh, the venerable abbot of Cluny, attend the synod with you on our behalf. This is desirable for many reasons, but especially so that the case of the church of Auvergne may be brought to an end through a suitable and firm determination, with God’s and his assistance.

For we trust, in God’s mercy and in the conduct of his life, that no one’s entreaty, favor, or goodwill, nor any personal consideration whatsoever, will be able to turn him aside from the path of uprightness.

If, therefore, divine clemency grants effect to this arrangement of ours [Col. 0478A], among the other duties that your fraternity has undertaken, consider and carry out this one with the greatest attention: when all have been assembled and are seated in council, proclaim clearly and loudly that, henceforth, in order to preserve canonical and apostolic authority in the promotion of bishops, no metropolitan or any bishop may dare to lay hands upon a man for his consecration if that man has received the episcopal gift from a layperson—unless he himself wishes to lose the honor and office of his dignity.

Likewise, no authority or person whatsoever is henceforth to involve himself in the granting or receiving of such an honor. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he will be bound and held subject to the same sentence and censure of punishment that blessed Pope Adrian established and confirmed in the eighth synod, canon 22, against such presumptuous men and corrupters of sacred authority.

After this chapter has been written down and read in the presence of all, admonish the entire assembly of that session to praise and confirm it. As for those who, after the authority of this decree has been read out by us, have received episcopal investiture through the hands of secular lords and powers, and those who have presumed to lay hands upon them for ordination, admonish and command them by apostolic authority to come to us to render an account concerning this matter.

Given beside the Po, in the place called Ficarolo, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXIII. TO BERNARD THE DEACON AND BERNARD THE ABBOT (Year 1077)

They are to request from Kings Henry and Rudolf a safe route so that he may travel to the regions of the Germans. Whichever of the two refuses to provide this is to be excommunicated and prohibited from governing the kingdom; whoever obeys is to be confirmed in royal dignity.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bernard, deacon of the holy Roman Church, and Bernard, abbot of Marseille: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that it is known to your Fraternity that we left Rome, trusting in God’s mercy and in the help of blessed Peter, for this reason: that we might cross over to the regions of the Germans [Col. 0478D] and establish peace among them, for the honor of God and the welfare of the holy Church. But because those who were supposed to escort us according to the arrangement failed to do so, being prevented by the king’s arrival in Italy, we remained in Lombardy among enemies of the Christian religion, not without great danger, and so far have been unable to proceed beyond the Alps as we desire.

Therefore we admonish you, and command you on behalf of blessed Peter, that, supported by the authority of this our command and girded in our place by that same prince of the apostles, you admonish both kings, namely Henry and Rudolf, to open a safe route for us to travel there and to provide assistance and an escort through persons in whom you have good confidence [Col. 0479A], so that, with Christ protecting us, our journey may be open. For we desire, with the counsel of the clergy and laity of that kingdom who fear and love the Lord, to examine the case between them, God willing, and to demonstrate on which side justice more greatly favors the governance of the kingdom.

For you know that it belongs to our office and to the providence of the apostolic see to examine the greater affairs of the Churches and to determine them as justice dictates. But the matter being conducted between them is of such gravity and such danger that, if it were neglected by us for any reason, it would bring great and lamentable harm not only upon them and us, but also upon the universal Church.

Therefore, if either of the aforesaid kings should refuse to obey this our will and decision and to yield to your admonitions [Col. 0479B], and, kindling the torches of his pride and greed against the honor of almighty God, should attempt to hasten the destruction of the entire Roman Empire, resist him in every way and by every means, even unto death if necessary, in our place—or rather, by the authority of blessed Peter. Oppose both him and all who agree with him in regard to the governance of the entire kingdom, and separate them from participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the thresholds of the holy Church.

Always keep this in mind: whoever disdains to obey the apostolic see incurs the crime of idolatry, and blessed Gregory, that holy and most humble teacher, decreed that kings fall from their dignity if they should presumptuously dare to act against the commands of the apostolic see [Col. 0479C] [Note: Book II, after Letter 58, indiction 11, in the privilege of the monastery of Saint-Médard.].

But to the other king, whoever humbly obeys our command and offers obedience to the universal mother—as a Christian king ought to do—give counsel and assistance in all things, after convening a council of all the clergy and laity whom you are able to summon; and in our place confirm him in royal dignity by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Command all bishops, abbots, clergy, and laity living throughout the kingdom, on behalf of almighty God, to obey and serve him faithfully, as they ought.

Issued at Carpineta, on the second [day], fifteen days before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE GERMANS. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0479D]

The same subject.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and all the faithful of Christ, clergy and laity, both great and small, residing in the kingdom of the Germans.

We wish it to be known to you, dearest brothers, that we have commanded our legates—namely Bernard, a faithful son and deacon of the holy Roman Church, and likewise Bernard, the religious abbot of the monastery of Marseille [Col. 0480A]—to admonish both kings, namely Henry and Rudolf, either personally or through suitable messengers, to provide me with a safe means of coming to you, God willing, in order to examine the matter that has arisen between them through the agency of sin.

For our heart is tossed about in great sadness and grief if, through the pride of one man, so many thousands of Christians are delivered to temporal and eternal death, the Christian religion is brought into confusion, and the Roman Empire is led to destruction. For each king seeks assistance from us—or rather, from the apostolic see over which, although unworthy, we preside. And we, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the help of blessed Peter, are prepared, with your counsel—you who fear God and love the Christian faith—to decide the equity of the case on both sides [Col. 0480B] and to provide assistance to him whom justice is recognized to favor in the governance of the kingdom.

Therefore, if either of them, puffed up with pride, should by any means obstruct our coming to you; and, fearing judgment upon his injustice, should flee from it, becoming disobedient and resisting the holy and universal mother Church, despise him as a member of Antichrist and a destroyer of the Christian religion, and uphold the sentence that our legates pronounce against him in our place. Know that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4).

But to the other, whoever conducts himself humbly and does not despise the judgment—truly, the judgment decreed by the Holy Spirit and pronounced through you [Col. 0480C]—we unhesitatingly believe that wherever two or three are gathered in the Lord’s name, his presence enlightens them (Matthew 18), to that man, I say, offer service and reverence according to what our aforesaid legates decree, striving to assist him and obeying him in every way, so that he may honorably retain his royal dignity and come to the aid of the holy Church, which is already almost collapsing.

For it must not slip from our heart that whoever disdains to obey the apostolic see incurs the crime of idolatry (1 Samuel 15), and that blessed Gregory [Note: At the place cited above.], that holy and most humble teacher, decreed that kings should fall from their dignities and be deprived of participation in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ if they should presume to despise the decrees of the apostolic see. For if the see of blessed Peter releases and judges heavenly and spiritual matters, how much more earthly and secular ones? [Col. 0480D]

You know, dearest brothers, that from the time we left Rome we have remained in great danger among enemies of the Christian faith. Yet neither fear nor affection has moved us to promise either of the aforesaid kings any assistance contrary to justice. For we would rather undergo death, if necessary, than, overcome by our own will, consent to the Church of God’s being brought into confusion.

For we recognize that we were ordained and placed in the apostolic see for this purpose: that in this life we should seek not what is ours but what belongs to Jesus Christ [Col. 0481A] (Philippians 2), and that, following the footsteps of the Fathers through many labors, we may, by God’s mercy, advance toward future and eternal rest.

Issued at Carpineta, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXV. TO NEHEMIAH, ARCHBISHOP OF ESZTERGOM. (Year 1077)

He explains why he kept the bearer of the letter with him for so long and commends him. He does not oppose his promotion to the priesthood. He advises him to admonish the recently elected king to offer the apostolic see its due obedience through legates.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings [Col. 0481B] and apostolic blessing to Nehemiah, archbishop of Esztergom in Hungary.

We do not wish you to wonder for what reason we kept this brother—the bearer of this letter—with us for so long. For when he came to us, we had decided to cross into the kingdom of the Germans so that, with God’s help, we might establish peace and concord between King Henry and the princes of the land. We had also received from that same King Henry, under oath, guarantees which we then thought necessary on his part for our departure. While awaiting the outcome of this matter, we ordered this man to remain with us, so that when he returned we might send you both the definite conclusion of this affair and any other instructions that might prove necessary.

But because the matter, as we believe is known to you, has grown into an extremely serious dispute and almost into the division of the entire country, and because we did not think it opportune for us to cross over at this time, we did not wish to keep him any longer. Through him we wrote to your Fraternity, strongly urging you to let it benefit him in your eyes that, with such fatigue and danger, he sought apostolic mercy and remained with us for so long [Col. 0481C].

We wish you to know this: for as long as he was with us, we recognized in him a peaceful spirit devoted to serving God. Therefore, in view of the misery of these times and by comparison with those persons whom we endure because of infirmity and necessity, we judged that he too was not unworthy to be borne with compassion. Indeed, what he disclosed to us about his conscience, and what he confesses should be blamed in him, does not differ from his confession and account [Col. 0481D].

As for his desire to be promoted to the rank of priest, although we do not determine this by imperial authority, nevertheless, out of consideration for mercy, we do not oppose it; nor have we judged that it should be denied him, provided that no more serious matter unknown to us obstructs his ordination and that thereafter he wishes fittingly to shape his life and conduct according to the dignity of so great a ministry and, by God’s mercy, preserve them steadfastly.

Moreover, we admonish your Fraternity to address, together with your fellow bishops and the princes of the land, the king who has been elected among you. Make known to him and advise him that, through suitable legates, he should declare to us more openly his will and his devotion toward the reverence owed to the apostolic see [Col. 0482A]. Then, for our part, we shall respond to him graciously, for the honor of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and shall strive to offer his Excellency, for his own benefit and that of the entire kingdom, the support of holy and apostolic authority with every charity and goodwill.

The remaining matters, which would have made the letter too long, the bearer will faithfully report by word of mouth, as we have placed them in his mouth.

Issued at Carpineta, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVI. TO DOMINIC, PATRIARCH OF GRADO, AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF VENETIA. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0482B]

Gregory sends a legate to deal with ecclesiastical matters and commands them to obey him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Dominic, patriarch of Grado, and the other bishops of Venetia.

We have heard that many matters have arisen in your Churches. The order of ecclesiastical religion demands that these be examined through sincere investigation and brought to an end by the definition of canonical tradition; both your affection for us and the due concern of our office require this of us. Although, in view of the dispensation entrusted to us, we are debtors to all the Churches, we are bound to you and your affairs by a special concern—both because of the particular connection that you have with the holy Roman and apostolic Church, and because of your proximity, which never permits us either to remain long ignorant of you and of what is happening among you or to deny your Fraternity what we ought and are able to provide [Col. 0482C].

Therefore we have sent to you this beloved son of ours, Gregory, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, so that, working together with you on ecclesiastical matters and on the sacred institutions of the Christian religion that are necessary, he may, in our place, correct what must be corrected and establish what must be established. May he be able effectively, with the help of divine grace, to restore and confirm the interests and efforts of ecclesiastical liberty and justice, long and widely neglected [Col. 0482D], according to the form of canonical and apostolic discipline.

We admonish you to support him with every charity and to give him unanimous assent [the text reads “we,” perhaps “you”], so that through him it may be shown how great a reverence you have for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, from whose household and family he is sent; and also how great is your concern for our affection, since we have sent him from our own side, as one through whom our concern for you and the authority of the power granted to us by the Lord God are represented and administered by delegated authority.

Issued at Carpineta, on the fifth day before the Ides [or: Kalends] of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO DOMENICO SILVIO, DUKE, AND THE PEOPLE OF VENETIA. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0483A]

He reproves them for having associated with excommunicated persons. He sends legates who are to absolve them from excommunication after they have completed their penance.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Domenico Silvio, duke, and the people of Venetia.

You ought to remember how much charity, goodwill, and honor have been shown to you by the holy and apostolic see over many years. And indeed, with our conscience as witness, not only after we came to the pontificate but also for many years before that, we loved you and your land greatly [Col. 0483B], and, not without provoking the indignation and hostility of some, we were eager to provide for your honor. We greatly rejoiced in the love that you showed toward the universal mother of all the faithful, namely the holy Roman Church, and in the liberty that you had received from the ancient stock of Roman nobility and preserved.

But in these times, something that we do not say without great sorrow, you have not only embittered our feelings, but have undoubtedly weakened God’s grace toward you exceedingly. For, through sins whose agency I do not know, you have fallen from the state of uprightness and have placed yourselves outside the fellowship of the members of Christ and of the Church, following and receiving those who have been excommunicated for their crimes [Col. 0483C]. Departing from the faith and from the catholic unity, teaching, and divinely strengthened authority of the holy Fathers, they have fallen through complete disobedience and obstinacy into the devil’s snare and have become ministers—or rather, slaves—of Satan, by whom they are held captive.

Therefore, grieving over the danger to your souls and desiring to call you back to reconciliation with divine grace, we have sent to you this beloved son of ours, Gregory, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, so that, after performing penance, you may be absolved from the bond of excommunication into which you have fallen by associating with the excommunicated, and may be restored to communion with the holy mother Church through apostolic pardon and blessing.

When this has been done, if you receive our admonitions—or rather, the word of God—with the reverence that is fitting, we wish and admonish you by apostolic authority to assist him with all charity and obedience [Col. 0483D], so that, with the counsel of our fellow patriarch and the other bishops of that province, as well as with the assistance of the duke and all of you, he may examine what is necessary concerning the condition of the Churches and the order and administration of the Christian religion according to the form handed down by the holy Fathers, and, with God’s help, arrange it in our place.

Issued at Carpineta, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SPANIARDS. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0484A]

He admonishes them, out of the pastoral care of his office, to live piously and holily. He further reminds them that, by ancient constitutions, the kingdom of Spain belongs by right to blessed Peter; that, through the misfortune of the times and the tyranny of the Saracens, memory of this had begun to fade; and that now, since they have conquered the Saracens, he sends legates to inform them how much they owe to blessed Peter and to recall their obligation to their memory.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the kings, counts, and other princes of Spain.

We believe that your prudence is not unaware that the holy and apostolic see is the chief and universal mother of all the Churches and peoples whom divine clemency has predestined to come to knowledge of his name in the faith of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ through evangelical and apostolic teaching. To these peoples it must offer care and perpetual solicitude, so that, just as it provides instruction for preserving the truth of the catholic faith, so also it may administer instruction and saving admonitions for knowing and maintaining justice [Col. 0484B].

Since, according to God’s will, although unwilling and unworthy, we have been appointed to this office of administration, we greatly fear the ministry entrusted to us. We know that we are debtors both to those who are near and to those who are far away, and that we shall have no place for excuse before the proud Judge if, through our silence, their salvation is neglected or their fault encouraged. On this matter many instructions and examples, accompanied by terrifying threats, have been set before us in both the prophetic and evangelical books. That outstanding preacher and apostle, contemplating them, says: “The necessity of preaching the Gospel is laid upon me; woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel!” (1 Corinthians 9) [Col. 0484C].

Therefore, dearest ones, since we cannot be present with you in person according to our desire, at least while absent we have taken care to admonish you by letter concerning your salvation. We write to you, in accordance with the affection of the charity we owe you, first of all that, giving thanks to God who has regenerated you through Jesus Christ our Lord to the living hope and incorruptible glory of eternal life, you should always fear him and love him with your whole heart. Transfer all your desire to him, above all the riches and honors of this age, above all not only human but also angelic creatures.

Walk before him in all faith and devotion as chosen [Col. 0484D] children, called by his immense grace and goodness to share in the inheritance of the kingdom of God. Do not, according to worldly desire, hold in unrighteousness what God has given you, or will give you, to know of his truth and equity. Rather, show yourselves faithful ministers for doing justice and safeguarding the liberty of the Christian faith and religion in every exercise and administration of your royal power, to the praise and glory of his name, which has raised you to great glory.

For, as Wisdom says through Solomon—a saying that we wish always to be in your hearts—“I love those who love me; those who honor me, I will honor” (Proverbs 8). But to those who despise her she issues this threat: “Those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Samuel 2). And the apostle Paul, declaring the universal judgment of the future, says [Col. 0485A]: “The just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works” (Romans 2).

To those who, through perseverance in good works, seek glory, honor, and incorruption: eternal life; but to those who are contentious and do not submit to the truth, while believing in iniquity: wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress for every human soul that works evil.

Therefore do not be high-minded, nor, because of the eminence of present glory, forget human nature, which is the same for kings and the poor. Rather, as the same apostle urges, humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation (1 Peter 5).

Do not place your hope in the uncertainty of the riches of this age, but in him of whom it is written: “Through me kings reign” [Col. 0485B] (Proverbs 8). And elsewhere: “For power has been given to you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts” (Wisdom 6). In him, too, store up for yourselves the riches of good works, building a firm foundation (1 Timothy 6) and acquiring possession of a better and unfailing substance (Hebrews 10), where you may live eternally.

“For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come, whose architect and builder is God” (Hebrews 13) [Note: This passage, like the one immediately following, has been composed from various sayings of the Apostle. Saint Gregory does not reproduce them either in their original form or in exactly the same words; rather, with their form altered somewhat, he allows them to flow, so to speak, from his memory, filled with the treasures of Scripture, perhaps even unconsciously (Editor).].

You yourselves surely know and see every day how fleeting and fragile the life of mortals is, and how deceptive and misleading is hope in present things. Whether we wish it or not, we are always running toward the end; yet, under such certain danger, we can never foresee how near death is. Nor can anything that is sought or possessed from this present life or age ever be held for long.

Therefore, always considering what your last things will be, how bitterly you will depart from this wicked age and return to the rottenness of the earth and the filth of dust, and how, under strict examination, you will have to render an account of your deeds, fortify yourselves against future dangers.

Turn your arms, wealth, and power not merely toward worldly display, but toward the honor and service of the eternal King. Conduct and administer the governance of the kingdom entrusted to you in such a way that the zeal of your virtue and uprightness may be a sacrifice of justice pleasing to almighty God. Thus you may hope in him who gives salvation to kings and is powerful to rescue them from the hand of death [Col. 0485C], so that he may clothe you with more exalted splendor and the joys of everlasting life, and transfer you from the fleeting honors you now possess into the kingdom of his eternal glory, where blessedness has no end, glory no corruption, and dignity no equal.

Furthermore, we wish it to be made known to you—something that we are not free to conceal, but which is very necessary for you not only for future glory but also for present glory—namely, that by ancient constitutions the kingdom of Spain was handed over to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church as their right and property.

This was concealed until now both by the misfortunes of former times [Col. 0486A] and by a certain hidden negligence on the part of some of our predecessors. After that kingdom was overrun by Saracens and pagans, the service that used to be rendered from there to blessed Peter was withheld because of their unbelief and tyranny. Since it was thus cut off from our practice for so many years, memory of the matter and of the property likewise began to fade.

But because divine clemency has granted you victory over those enemies, and will always continue to grant it, and has delivered the land into your hands, we no longer wish you to remain ignorant of this matter. Otherwise what the heavenly Judge and founder of laws and justice has entrusted to your glory for the recovery and restoration of the justice and honor of Saint Peter and of his holy and apostolic see, might, through our silence, result in the guilt of negligence for us, or, through your ignorance—God forbid!—in the loss of the recompense proposed and divinely offered to you [Col. 0486B].

For we trust in the mercy of God, who gave you strength and victory, that he may also grant you this will: so that, once you know the truth, you may follow the statutes and examples of Christian princes rather than the impiety of those who desire more to persecute the Christian name than to honor it.

We have sent to you our fellow bishop Amatus, the venerable bishop of Oloron, to whom we have also entrusted our authority in those regions. We have associated with him this abbot of Saint-Pons, a venerable man approved for his faith and moral integrity, so that what we have written briefly to your Highness concerning the disclosure of this matter, they may themselves, if necessary, explain to you more fully and clearly; and, insofar as reason demands, demonstrate knowledge of the truth through this present notification and certain assertion.

You may unquestionably trust their counsel in matters pertaining to the Lord and necessary for the salvation of your souls, just as we have found them trustworthy through their zeal for religion and their deeds, and as you will be able to judge from their conduct.

Therefore, as far as concerned us—whether it was necessary to provide for the matter in the exercise of our office or to satisfy the obligation of justice—we have done what we could, by God’s mercy. We have indicated what your salvation requires of you and how much you owe to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that ignorance may not harm you and so that, under a false security concerning the fleeting light and time, a ruinous negligence may not steal upon you—God forbid! [Col. 0486C]

But you must attend to what is yours. With prudent counsel, consider, arrange, and determine what your faith and the Christian devotion of your principality ought to carry out, in imitation of the most pious princes. Show yourselves so ready and generous toward the honor of blessed Peter and of your holy mother, the Roman Church, that your virtue and glory—which, by God’s gift, flourish through illustrious victory—may become brighter and more exalted through apostolic intercession.

May their blessing always protect you, their authority absolve you from sins, and their defense guard you safe and unharmed from every danger—those whose divinely entrusted power binds and looses the whole human race both in heaven and on earth, and opens and closes the gate of the heavenly kingdom for all [Col. 0487A].

Issued at Carpineta, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifteenth indiction.

## BOOK FIVE OF THE REGISTER

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1077, in the fifteenth indiction [Note: Except for two, all the remaining letters belong to the first indiction.].

[Col. 0487]

## LETTER I. TO THE CANONS OF SAINT MARTIN OF LUCCA. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0487A]

He reproves them because, contrary to his admonitions and after promising satisfaction, they bought canonries and prebends. Therefore he utterly forbids all who acquired them in this way to enter the major church or retain them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the Church of Saint Martin of Lucca.

You ought to remember how often, and with how much care, while remaining among you, we admonished you not to value earthly and passing advantages more highly than your souls, but to present yourselves in obedience to justice in such a way that you would no longer remain under the bond of excommunication, which it was clear you had incurred by acquiring prebends contrary to apostolic decrees [Col. 0487B].

But, as the matter itself shows, you make the substance of your possession—although it is an iniquitous possession—more precious than yourselves. Having spurned our admonitions and despised apostolic authority, for the sake of temporal profits and the satisfaction of your desire, you do not fear to lie under the curse of anathema after promising us satisfaction, through a renewed and deliberate crime of transgression.

Therefore, since we dare neither to conceal through silence the contumacy of such great presumption nor, through patience, to foster any longer the guilt of such monstrous avarice—not only to your danger but also to the danger of those with whom you associate—by the present authority, on behalf of almighty God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we forbid all among you who have acquired canonical offices or prebends for money, contrary to the apostolic privileges of Pope Leo, to enter the major church, namely Saint Martin’s, and to retain those canonries or prebends any longer, until they have offered worthy satisfaction [Col. 0487C].

Issued at Florence, on the third day before the Ides of August, in the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER II. TO THE BISHOPS AND CLERGY OF CORSICA. (Year 1077)

On account of his pastoral office, he sends the elected bishop of Pisa as legate to carry out in his place what pertains to religion; he commands them to offer him due obedience.

[Col. 0487D] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to all the bishops, clergy, consuls, and great and small persons residing [variant: existing] on the island of Corsica.

Since, because of our many occupations, we cannot personally visit the Churches of the individual provinces in order to discharge the duty of our pastoral care [Col. 0488A], it is very necessary that, when circumstances or time require, we endeavor to send someone to those regions, through whom the authority entrusted to us may be represented according to God’s will and provision may be made for the salvation of the Lord’s flock and the common welfare.

For we know that it cannot occur without harm and great danger to souls when the diligence of the one to whom the highest necessity of affairs and care principally belongs is absent for a long time from the brothers subject and entrusted to him.

Therefore, considering and greatly fearing that the care of this kind toward you, having been neglected for so long, might be counted as guilt of negligence against us and might prove harmful or contrary to your salvation—God forbid!—as soon as the opportunity arose we sent to you this brother of ours, Landulf, the elected bishop of the Church of Pisa. We have also entrusted him with our authority among you, so that, properly carrying out what pertains to the order of sacred religion, he may, in accordance with the prophet’s saying, “tear down and destroy, build and plant.”

We wish you to obey him and assist him unanimously. We admonish and command by apostolic authority that, receiving him with all charity and honor, you show him such honor and reverence as, according to the constitutions of the holy Fathers, ought to be shown to those whom the holy and apostolic see foresees should be taken into a share of its care and to whom it judges that the authority of the Roman pontiff should be entrusted [Col. 0488C].

Issued at Siena, on the Kalends of September, at the beginning of the first indiction.

## LETTER III. TO BISHOPS RUDOLF AND RAINER. (Year 1077)

He advises them that, since agreement has been reached concerning a suitable person for the Church of Volterra, they should arrange for a general election by everyone and confirm him in his place; they should inform him of whatever has been done and send the elected man to him as soon as possible to receive consecration.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Rudolf, bishop of Siena, and Rainer, [bishop] of Florence.

We believe you are not unaware of how much concern and labor we have had in working to ensure that, according to the Lord and the authority of the canons, a useful and suitable bishop would be elected for the Church of Volterra [Col. 0488D].

And because, according to God’s will, both our counsel and the will of those who belong to that Church have agreed upon the person of Bono, the Mantuan archpriest [Col. 0489A], we admonish you by apostolic authority to go to that Church and take care that a general election be conducted by everyone. Confirm it in our place, as you know has been customary according to the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers.

When this has been done, report to us without delay, by a formal letter from you, how the matter was properly conducted; and send the elected man to us as soon as possible, with the solemn decree of the clergy and people, to receive consecration.

Issued at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER IV. TO THE CORSICANS. (Year 1077)

[Col. 0489B]

He rejoices that they wish to vindicate the island of Corsica, which in ancient times belonged by right to blessed Peter, from its invaders and return it to the rule of the apostolic see; he confirms them in this intention. He promises the readiest assistance for this matter. He admonishes them to obey faithfully his legate, who will undertake the governance of the province.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to all the bishops and noblemen, and to all, both great and small, residing on the island of Corsica.

You know, most beloved brothers and sons in Christ, that it is manifest not only to you but also to many peoples that the island which you inhabit belongs by due obligation [Col. 0489C] or by right of ownership to no mortal and to no power except the holy Roman Church; and that those who have hitherto held it by force, rendering blessed Peter no service, no fidelity, and absolutely no submission or obedience, have bound themselves by the crime of sacrilege and placed their souls in grave peril.

But when we learned through certain faithful friends of ours and yours that you wish, as you rightly recognize you ought, to return to the honor and justice of the apostolic principate, and that the justice long wrested from blessed Peter by invaders should in your time and through your efforts be restored to him, we rejoiced greatly, knowing that this would bring you not only present but also future benefit and glory. You ought not to distrust or doubt anything in this matter, for if your will remains firm and your faith toward blessed Peter unshaken, by God’s mercy we have in Tuscany many forces of counts and noblemen ready, if necessary, to assist and defend you.

Therefore, what seemed to us most opportune in this matter, we have sent to you your brother Landulf, bishop [elected bishop] of the Pisan Church. We have also entrusted him with our authority among you in spiritual matters, so that he may receive the land on behalf of blessed Peter and in our name, govern it with every zeal and diligence, and take charge of all affairs and cases pertaining through him to blessed Peter and to us. We wish you to obey him and faithfully assist him in everything, for the love and reverence owed to that same blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and we admonish you by apostolic authority. Moreover, so that he may be more secure and more ready for every matter among you, if he requests it, do not refuse to swear fidelity to him—subject, however, to the prior fidelity owed to holy Peter, to us, and to our successors—nor refuse to do so for any reason.

Given at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER V. TO THE AQUILEIANS (1077)

He writes that above all he desires this: that in every Church one may be elected who is worthy to bear the name and office of pastor. For this reason he has sent legates to investigate carefully the qualifications of the man whom they have elected bishop. If they find him suitable, they are to confirm him; otherwise, another is to be elected.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Aquileia, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It is an ancient and well-known rule of sacred institution, sanctioned not by human beings but by Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, through the fullest consideration of his wisdom and the definition of truth—he himself saying in the Gospel: “He who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; but he who does not enter through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10).
