Therefore, what through the long neglect caused by sins and through a wicked custom has been corrupted in the Church, we desire to renew and restore, for the honor [Col. 0490C] of God and the salvation of all Christendom: namely, that, whenever the time requires, a bishop be elected in each Church, and elected in such order, that according to the judgment of truth he may not be called a thief and robber, but may be found worthy to bear the name and office of pastor.

This is our will; this is our desire; this, by God’s mercy, will be our tireless labor for as long as we live. As for what pertains to the service and due fidelity owed to the king, we by no means wish to contradict or obstruct it. Therefore we are trying to introduce nothing new and nothing devised by us, but seek only what the salvation of all and necessity alike demand: that in the appointment of bishops, according to the common understanding and approval of the holy Fathers, evangelical and canonical authority be observed before everything else.

As for what you reported to us concerning the election made among you, we received it gladly. If it is established that it was properly conducted, so that in no respect does sacred authority contradict you, then, as my conscience bears witness, we rejoice greatly and give thanks to almighty God.

Yet because, as we said above, in a matter of this kind we wish to proceed not according to our own judgment but by the path and teaching of the orthodox Fathers, we have sent to you these legates of ours, bearers of this letter, so that they may investigate the case carefully from every side. If they find that the man whom you say you have elected is suitable for the summit of such dignity in life, conduct, and knowledge [Col. 0491A], and that he has been assigned in accordance with the rule, let them confirm your election in our name, as is just. But if they find in him anything contrary to this or worthy of censure, such that he ought not to attain episcopal government, then, after removing him, you should take care to elect a person suited to such honor and office, whom our authority, represented through those same legates, may approve and confirm.

Know this: if we learn that you have made a lawful and canonical election, we shall provide you and your Church, with every charity, all the protection that apostolic authority ought and is able to provide. And if anyone should presume to aspire to that see by another path, he will undoubtedly feel the sword of blessed Peter and the missile of apostolic chastisement drawn and hurled with severity, not only against him but also against all his supporters [Col. 0491B].

Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF AQUILEIA (1077)

He urges them to take careful measures so that the election of the bishop of Aquileia, for which he is sending legates, may be conducted canonically. To the schismatics who support the canonical election he promises mercy; but if they oppose it, or if anyone occupies that see, he threatens severe penalties.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops who are suffragans of the Church of Aquileia—to those who have shown [or: show] themselves true brothers—greeting [Col. 0491C] and apostolic blessing; but to those who have departed not only from the charity of brotherhood but also from the unity of the Church through schismatic depravity, an exhortation to the vigilance that is due.**

The clergy and people of the Church of Aquileia, having sent legates and letters to us, reported that, after their bishop Sichard had recently died, they had elected the archdeacon of that same Church to govern in his place, asking us also to give our authority’s assent and confirmation to their election.

But because it was not safe at the first hearing to approve so suddenly a matter requiring such careful examination and still unknown to us, we sent our legates there to investigate the case and the procedure of the election through meticulous inquiry, and to inform us, with diligent care [editorial addition, perhaps: “so that it may be made known to us”], of whatever must thereby be confirmed or rejected.

We therefore admonish you, whose interest in this matter is considerable, to apply the zeal of your concern to it, so that, with God’s help, the man who is to preside at the summit of such dignity may be such that you, who must lay hands upon him, will find him a source not of grief or danger but of joy and honor, and of salvation to the people entrusted to him.

But to you who—I do not know whether led astray by fear or by some other circumstance—have stained your hands and tongues with a new and unheard-of schism, and have thereby fallen into the snare of anathema, we say separately this: if, while you sincerely support the election, someone worthy and suitable is elected bishop of the aforesaid Church of Aquileia [Col. 0492A], then, with the counsel of that man and of those brothers who have stood firm in the bosom of holy Mother Church, we are prepared, under the auspices of divine grace, to show you as much mercy as we can, and, insofar as God’s comfort grants us the courage and ability, to bear the weight of your error.

But if we learn that you oppose this, and seek out and devise objections to impede it, and if you consent to someone’s presuming to occupy that see contrary to divine and canonical authority, then beyond doubt he will find a reward worthy of his wickedness; and the holy and apostolic See, the more gravely provoked by you, will demand an account of your offenses with the greater severity and judge you with the harsher sentence.

[Col. 0492B] Given at Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER VII. TO UDON, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER, AND HIS SUFFRAGANS (1077)

He expresses his concern to quell the disturbance of the Teutonic kingdom. For this reason he has written to all the princes, asking them to bring aid against so great an evil. Since he does not know whether the letters have reached them, he sends copies again, together with the oath of King Henry, who, having disregarded it, allowed his legates to be captured. He exhorts them to defend ecclesiastical liberty and the common welfare.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Udo, archbishop of Trier, and his suffragan bishops, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The one who knows and truly sees all secrets knows above all how great a concern and how much anxiety we have endured for a long time because of the upheaval and disturbance of the Teutonic kingdom. To him, if he deigns to hear such persons, we have made and shall make many supplications. We have urged many brothers and religious communities to devote themselves to the same prayers, asking that he have mercy on that people and not allow them to take up arms against their own entrails and fight in war for the ruin of their domestic strength, but that by his powerful might he restrain the causes of all discord and, through his governance, settle them without a disastrous and mournful end.

More than three months ago we also sent letters there, namely to our legates Bernard, our deacon, and likewise Bernard, the religious abbot of Marseille, whom we have heard was captured, as well as to all the princes of the land, both ecclesiastical and secular. In those letters we earnestly advised them, through counsel and exhortation, to carry out with every effort what seemed to us best for avoiding slaughter, fires, and the other dangers of war, and most just for resolving so great an affair; and we imposed this upon them by apostolic authority, so that they might press forward more vigorously.

But because we do not know for certain whether those letters reached you, or, if they did arrive, lest you have any doubt about their authenticity, we have had the same letters copied from our exemplars and sent to you. We admonish you and, by true obedience, command you in every way to see that the matter is handled according to the judgment of those letters and brought to its conclusion.

We have also sent you the oath which King Henry gave us through certain of his faithful men, written with his own hand and placed in the hand of the abbot of Cluny. When you have read it, you will recognize how properly and honorably he has conducted himself toward us in his own name—although afterward our legates were captured by his men: namely, Gerard [Bernard], bishop of Ostia, in Lombardy, and Bernard, abbot of Marseille, in the Teutonic land. Thus far we have recognized that he has done nothing worthy of approval.

Nevertheless, God providing, we never wish on this account to oppose him in any matter, circumvent justice, or burden him; just as, after the undertaking began, he has never been able, either by prayers or by any display of friendship or enmity, to obtain from us that we should wish to say or decide anything on his behalf beyond what appeared just. In this matter, too, for as long as we live, with God’s help, we shall persist without hesitation, and no danger to life or death will deter us.

Therefore, dearest brothers, act so that it may become clear how much you love the liberty of the Church and the common salvation of all. Know that if the matter is neglected and reaches a more serious—and God forbid, embittered—stage, it will bring forth not only for your people and the Teutonic kingdom but throughout the boundaries of Christendom losses, dangers, confusion, and immeasurable causes of misery [Col. 0493C].

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER VIII. TO RICHER AND RICHARD, AND THEIR SUFFRAGANS (1077)

Reproving the many crimes of the bishop of Orléans, he orders them to assemble to examine his conduct and summon him by letter to answer. If he refuses to come or fails to clear himself of the charges, they are to declare him deposed and deprived, and he orders that this sentence be proclaimed. He commands that a certain Saxo [Sanzon, concerning whom see Letter 14] be substituted in his place.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richer, archbishop of Sens, and Richard of Bourges [Bituricensis, and so throughout], and their suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

As the brotherhood of some among you knows, we have already labored through many appeals and many letters to restore the Church of Orléans to the former state of its nobility. But, because—as we believe—the sins of the people have deserved it, the occupation by false bishops there has prevailed to such an extent that we have still been wholly unable to root out the thorns of its disorder.

Although we do not doubt that you know how greatly their so-called bishop Rainerius has armed himself against the authority of the apostolic See and into what confusion and ruin he has brought that Church, we have nevertheless taken care to state by name to your religious judgment certain of his transgressions.

It is said that, not having reached the legitimate age, he invaded the Church contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers, without a suitable election by clergy and people. It is also said that he added this to his wickedness: in promoting clerics, selling archdeaconries and abbeys through bargaining, he showed no honesty and no fear of God. Moreover, although summoned by us twice and three times in fraternal charity, he not only neglected to come to us but also scorned to send anyone who might lawfully excuse him from the charges. Though forbidden by us—and indeed separated from communion in the body and blood of the Lord—he did not fear to celebrate the episcopal office. He also allowed Benedict, who was carrying our letters, to remain for a long time in captivity among his men, to the contempt of the apostolic See [Col. 0494B].

Therefore, no longer tolerating his wickedness, we command you by apostolic authority to assemble, for examination of his actions, at whatever place you judge most suitable. First summon him there by your letters, and let him answer you there concerning the matters stated above and, if he can, prove himself innocent.

But if, remaining in his pride, he refuses to come within forty days of the admonition, or, when he comes, fails to clear himself canonically of all the matters stated above, then by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority we pronounce against him a sentence of condemnation and deposition, without any hope of restoration.

Following this sentence as you ought, proclaim it in the hearing of the assembled people [Col. 0494C], and, in the place of the deposed man, install in accordance with God’s will Saxo himself, about whom you wrote to me and who sought the counsel of blessed Peter and of us.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER IX. TO RAINERIUS, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS (1077)

He orders him to come within fifty days to the place approved by the Senonese and the other bishops to whom he has entrusted the matter, in order to clear himself of the crimes charged against him. If he neglects to obey or fails to clear himself, he pronounces against him a sentence of condemnation without hope of restoration.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainerius, called bishop of Orléans [Col. 0494D].**

Although your disobedience has long deserved no letters from the apostolic See except letters of condemnation, we have nevertheless attempted to shake something good out of the unfruitful root of your mind, though in vain, and have therefore arranged to send you this summons: namely, that you come to answer the charges in the presence of our brothers Richer, archbishop of Sens, and Richard of Bourges, together with their suffragans and other religious men who fear God.

We have sent them our letters so that they may assemble at whatever place they judge most suitable and convenient, and carefully investigate your case. We set a period of forty days after the receipt of our letters for the examination of this matter.

Because we wish you to be cautious and prepared regarding the charges to be brought against you, we inform you of them before the proceedings. You are said, not having reached the legitimate age, to have thrust yourself upon that Church contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers, without a suitable election by clergy and people. You are also said to have added this to your wickedness: in the promotion of clerics, selling archdeaconries and abbeys through bargaining, you showed no honesty and no fear of God.

Moreover, although, as it seems to us, you were summoned by us twice and three times in fraternal charity, you not only failed to come to us but also scorned to send anyone who might justly excuse you from the charges. Though suspended from episcopal office and from communion in the body and blood of the Lord, you did not fear to celebrate public Masses [Col. 0495B]. You also allowed a cleric carrying our letters to remain for a long time in captivity among your men, to the contempt of the apostolic See.

Therefore, if you know yourself to be innocent of all these matters, do not in any way fail to go to the assembly of our brothers and answer them. But if, remaining in your pride, you either refuse to come there or, when you come, fail to clear yourself canonically of all these matters, then, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the apostolic See, we pronounce against you a sentence of condemnation, without any hope of restoration.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER X. TO THE KING OF DENMARK (1077)

Commending the devotion of his deceased father toward the Roman Church, he urges him to support his father with prayers and almsgiving and to imitate his service to the Roman Church. He wishes him, especially in protecting the Church, to send legates to him regarding the administration of the kingdom.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the king of the Danes, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We do not doubt that you fully know, and that it has not slipped from your memory, with how much diligence in love and affection our holy and universal mother, the Roman Church, watched over the care of your father and concern for your honor—especially since you yourself can recall how pure a reverence of service and due obedience he always displayed in every respect toward the honor of blessed Peter the apostle [Col. 0495D].

In his time, as the apostolic Church bears witness, we know that he was such a devoted, faithful, and singular son in his zeal of love that scarcely any second to him could be found among kings. And if, at the prompting of the devil, he had not loosened the reins of his body by imitating the incitements and allurements of vices, we would have had no doubt that he now inhabited the heavenly dwellings among the kings who pleased God exceedingly.

But because we believe that, through the help of the apostles to whom he was faithful, by the mercy and gratuitous goodness of the Lord he took up, with contrite heart, the tears of repentance before the end of his life, we do not doubt that he can obtain pardon. Indeed, mindful of him, we ask in our prayers, with the affection of charity, that it be granted to him; and we exhort you, as becomes an excellent son, to assist him with generous support in almsgiving and with the prayers of the Churches [Col. 0496A].

For it is fitting that he who, as a good father, left you heir of his bodily and worldly kingdom or honor should not appear to be deprived of spiritual assistance insofar as this can be provided; so that the goods which bring you the distinction of your father’s kingdom, carried by the hands of the poor, may bring your father aid for his rest in heaven.

Now, dearest son, we admonish you by apostolic invitation to look upon, attend to in faith, and consider in your mind the faith and love which your father showed toward the apostolic Church. Thus present yourself as a son of the blessed apostle Peter, so that, seeing you with a serene countenance, he may introduce you, as worthy offspring, into the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and the place of blessed recompense.

If he sees you devoted, he will surely take up the voice of his gracious teacher and say: “I desire that where I am, he also may be with me” (John XXXVII). For we believe that he received this power from the Lord, so that whoever he bound would be bound, and whoever he loosed would be loosed in heaven.

Therefore, again and again we admonish you to strive with every effort, insofar as human frailty permits and the Lord grants, to make yourself worthy and acceptable, so that you may obtain the exaltation of both the present and the future kingdom. If perhaps your father also, persuaded by the devil, incurred some losses to his soul, we urge you to attend to heaven—or rather, to the Lord of heaven—rather than to earth, and daily with a pure heart to set against such things the invincible weapons of your Creator. Thus we may rejoice in your progress as an apostolic son, and you may provide encouragement in virtue to kings equal to you [Col. 0496C].

Moreover, dearest son, we admonish you to guard with every industry, skill, and knowledge the honor of the kingdom entrusted to you by God. Let your life be worthy, filled with wisdom, seasoned with the salt and condiment of justice and mercy, so that true Wisdom, who is God, may say of you: “Through me this king reigns” (Proverbs 8:15).

Be an unfailing helper of the poor, orphans, and widows, knowing for certain that through these works and seasonings God’s love is reconciled to you. We have also heard—and do not doubt—that God’s Church, which is our mother and mistress, is oppressed in your lands, as in many other regions of the world, by wicked men and members of the devil, and is not protected and honored as it ought to be.

We wish and paternal­ly admonish you to watch over her assistance and protection in every way and above all else. For not resisting such men—what else is it than to deny the faith? Therefore we admonish and beseech you, setting aside every human hatred and putting envy behind you, to labor as far as you can, even at the risk of death, to rescue, protect, cherish, and defend her, and to snatch her from the jaws of lurking wolves. Know for certain that you can offer no prayer and no sacrifice more pleasing in the eyes of the supreme Judge.

Moreover, God is witness that this is our desire: we often wish to see your messengers, through whom we might learn more fully of your salvation, both of soul and body, and in turn, as God grants, stir you through apostolic instructions. May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, guard you, dearest son, through the merits of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and strengthen you by his power and goodness, so that you may administer temporal affairs in him in such a way that, after the end of this life, you may deserve to obtain the glory of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0497A].

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XI. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DIE (1077)

He confirms the excommunication and deposition carried out by him against a certain young man intruded into the Church of Chartres. When the abbot of Saint Euphemia was requested by the king of the Franks to govern it, he orders Hugh, after carefully ascertaining everyone’s wishes, to inform him by letter of whatever he finds in favor of or against his canonical election.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, bishop of Die, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We would wish to know from your report, with all ambiguity removed and as was proper, what has been done concerning the affairs of the Church of Chartres. For it has reached our ears that you excommunicated and irrecoverably deposed a certain young man improperly installed there as bishop. If this is so, it greatly pleases us, and by the present authority we confirm it.

We wish your brotherhood to know that King Philip of the Franks has repeatedly sent requests to us on behalf of Robert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Euphemia [Col. 0497C] in Calabria. Earlier this year, when we were in Lombardy, Robert passed through us on his way to France, so that we might approve and ordain him as bishop for the governance of the Church of Chartres.

That same abbot Robert also returned to us, saying that, although the king offered him the episcopate as a gift, he had refused it and had neither wished nor intended to do anything concerning it without our counsel. Two clerics of the aforesaid Church came with him, reporting and strongly affirming to us that the wishes of nearly all the leading and better men of that Church had converged upon him, although no election of him had yet been made.

But because we desire to follow and observe the statutes of the holy Fathers, we judged that nothing concerning him or his promotion should be approved by us without the election of the Church. Nor was what these men reported to us concerning the wishes of those absent sufficiently established. We therefore admonish your prudence to visit that Church either in person or through a faithful and approved person, and by careful inquiry to learn the wishes of all, both great and small, concerning this matter.

If, by divine mercy and providence, you see that the case can be arranged in every respect so that their free will toward the abbot mentioned above, their prudent judgment, and their canonical election are consonant with the rules of the holy Fathers, then take care to inform us as quickly as possible through a clear letter of yours [Col. 0498A], so that, with God as author, we may carry out and fulfill whatever is necessary for bringing this arrangement to effect.

But if you find anything otherwise—something supported by a stronger case and more probable reasoning—do not delay to notify us likewise, so that we may provide appropriately for ourselves and the Church and, with God’s help, may beneficially perform what belongs to our office [Given at Rome, indiction I].

## LETTER XII. TO MICHAEL, KING OF THE SLAVS (1077)

He asks him to send other messengers, through whom, after the case between the bishops of Split and Dubrovnik has been carefully investigated, he may satisfy his request.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Michael, king of the Slavs, greeting and apostolic [Col. 0498B] blessing.**

Let the reverence owed by your devotion toward the apostolic See know that Peter, whom you called our legate among you, has still not come into our presence, although he has sent his letters. These are so inconsistent with your letters that we have been unable to bring your case, or that of the Church of Dubrovnik, to a complete conclusion.

Therefore it is necessary for you to send to us Peter, bishop of Antivari, and the bishop of Dubrovnik, or other suitable messengers, through whom justice may be investigated and canonically defined concerning the dispute between the archbishop of Split and the bishop of Dubrovnik [Ragusanus throughout], and through whom the honor of your kingdom may be recognized by us.

When the matter has been investigated, we shall then be able justly to satisfy your request, as we desire, and, in granting the banner and conferring the pallium, we shall hear you as a most beloved son of blessed Peter, guided by righteousness [Col. 0498C].

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XIII. TO GUIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF RAVENNA, ETC. (1077)

Reproving their rashness in offending the holy Roman Church, he has their salvation at heart and summons them to a synod, promising that they will be safe and that he will temper the rigor of justice.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, and to all his suffragans, and to all bishops and abbots established in the Marches of Fermo and Camerino, in the Pentapolis, and in the regions of Emilia and Lombardy.**

We would gladly send you greeting with apostolic blessing if the authority of the holy Fathers did not stand in the way of your rashness. How gravely, beyond what is fitting for Christians, you have made blessed Peter the apostle and his holy Roman Church—indeed, the mother of all the faithful—offended and angered, God, the rule of the holy Fathers, and your own consciences bear witness.

But since it is human to sin, and God grants pardon to sinners who turn back, that Church itself, founded upon the blood of the same God and Lord, still awaits your return to her bosom as a mother. She by no means desires to rage against you to your death; rather, she wishes to come to your aid for your salvation.

Therefore, moved by concern for your salvation and that of the whole flock of Christ entrusted to us, we admonish and invite you, on behalf of almighty God and of the Roman Church, the universal mother, by apostolic authority, to assemble at the synod which, with God as author, we shall celebrate in the first week of the coming Lent.

Know that you will be safe from every injury to life and limb, from any harm to your property, and from every secular assault by those whom we shall be able to restrain. Know also that among us no hatred, prayers, or shameful boasting of anyone will ever be able to obtain a place from which injustice could be exercised against you in any respect. Rather, tempering the rigor of justice insofar as we can, we are prepared to show you as much indulgence as we can without harm to your souls or danger to ourselves [Col. 0499B].

For, God is witness, we desire rather to provide for your salvation and that of the people entrusted to you than to secure any worldly advantage for ourselves.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF ORLÉANS (1077)

He orders them to show every honor and reverence to Sanzon, who, after refuting before the delegated bishops all the charges brought against him by his rivals, demonstrated that he was worthy of the bishopric of Orléans, to which he had been elected, until he declares the definitive sentence, which is still pending.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy [Col. 0499C] and people of the Church of Orléans, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that you know that the apostolic See received the letters brought by you, in which the episcopal election of Sanzon, a cleric of your Church, was reported. Since we had already long recognized his integrity, we were ready to give it our confidence and assent.

But, by what prompting or through what action we do not know, unexpected letters, containing none of the meaning of the earlier ones and indeed expressing the opposite, were brought into our presence. We therefore judged it appropriate to suspend our definitive sentence in this matter, lest we appear to do anything precipitately or disorderly, until you send us either a messenger or letters through which we may learn more fully all that has occurred in the case [Col. 0499D].

Nevertheless, we wish you to know one thing: we had those clerics who had brought us letters from you, and who held views contrary to Sanzon, carefully examined in the presence of our bishops together with the aforementioned Sanzon, so that, after learning the truth of both sides, we might reject whatever ought to be disapproved and commend whatever ought to be approved.

At length, Sanzon himself refuted nearly all the charges his rivals had brought against him and demonstrated to us, through credible assertions, that justice favored him. But because he wishes to do nothing concerning this matter or his other affairs without our apostolic consent or counsel, and has placed himself and all that belongs to him under the protection of the apostolic See, we do not refuse, with God’s permission, to aid him justly insofar as we can [Col. 0500A].

Meanwhile, with apostolic gentleness, we admonish both you and all others, wherever he holds property, and command by authority that you do not fail to show him every honor and reverence. Permit him and all that belongs to him to remain safely and without any molestation or disturbance. Know that if you act otherwise—which we do not believe—and withdraw honor and reverence from him, and do not allow him and his possessions to remain quietly and securely, then we shall exercise against you, as against our enemies and adversaries of the apostolic See, the vengeance and sword of apostolic retribution.

For our part, with the aforementioned Sanzon, we shall, with God’s help, devise such a plan that the honor of your Church and its usefulness may flourish in every respect more fully than usual.

[Col. 0500B] Given at Rome, on the fifth [or fourth] day before the Kalends of February, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO THE GERMANS (1077)

He says that apostolic legates were appointed at the Roman synod to reconcile peace in the Teutonic kingdom, and excommunicates anyone who presumes to impede them. He explains that the bearer of the present letter has been sent for this purpose: to arrange with the archbishop of Trier the place and time of the assembly, so that the apostolic legates may travel there more safely.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, clerics, dukes, princes, margraves, and all persons both great and small established in the Teutonic kingdom, except those who are held under canonical excommunication, greeting and apostolic blessing [provided they obey the decrees of the Roman Church].**
We wish you to know, dearest brothers, that at the synod which we recently celebrated at Rome, among the many other matters which, with God’s cooperation, we addressed concerning the condition of the holy [Roman] Church, we carefully discussed the ruin and confusion of your most noble kingdom. We judged that the following would be salutary and timely for restoring your peace: that religious legates of the Apostolic See be sent to your regions, to summon archbishops, bishops, and religious clerics, as well as suitable laymen, to assemble at a place convenient and appropriate for both parties, so that they might either, with God’s help, establish peace among you, or truly learn which party justice favors. [Col. 0500D]

For it was determined at that same synod that, against the party which has rejected peace through the arrogance of pride, and which justice does not favor, we should rise up with every effort and by every means, wielding the authority of blessed Peter. And because we have learned that some people in your kingdom love quarrel and discord more than peace, in the name of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we forbid anyone to obstruct, by any device, effort, or violence, the aforesaid men from assembling to restore harmony to your kingdom, or, once assembled, from imposing a just and lawful end upon this discord.

Moreover, to restrain evil designs and unlawful attempts, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of the Apostolic See, we have anathematized—and do anathematize—anyone, whether king, archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, or person of any dignity or order, who presumes in any way to disturb this salutary constitution: namely, anyone who works to prevent the aforesaid assembly from taking place or to prevent harmony from being restored after so great a disturbance.

We have also added this to the same anathema: whoever is guilty of presuming to commit this iniquity shall feel the vengeance of almighty God not only in soul but also in body and in all his possessions. In every encounter of war he shall possess no strength and obtain no triumph throughout his life; rather, struck down by a double crushing, he shall always be held vile and covered with shame, so that at least in this way he may learn to return to repentance.

We are sending the bearer of this letter to you for the following purpose: together with our venerable brother, the archbishop of Trier, who favors Henry, and another bishop who is suitable and religious for this undertaking, he is to determine, on Rudolph’s behalf, the place and time of the aforesaid assembly. Thus our legates, whom we have mentioned, may come to you more securely and with greater certainty and, with God’s help, may accomplish with you whatever is pleasing to almighty God.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO UDON, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER. (1078)

He urges him to work for the establishment of peace in the kingdom of the Teutons; and, after informing him of the pontiff’s plan concerning peace, he orders him to come to him, so that he may not send legates in vain and at risk. He advises him to favor the one whom justice favors and to urge others to do the same.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **UDON**, archbishop of Trier, greetings and apostolic blessing.

How great our concern and sadness have been over the disturbance—indeed, over the discord—of your once most illustrious and powerful kingdom, we think has been sufficiently explained to you in the common letters which we sent to you this year. But because the situation appears to become more dangerously entangled from day to day, our concern has likewise become more deeply fixed in our mind, with exceedingly great anxiety.

Therefore, whatever has presently seemed best to us concerning this matter, and whatever could have been accomplished through our foresight or authority, we have taken care to expedite. Your fraternity will learn this more fully from the letter in which it has been set out separately. We therefore ask and admonish your prudence, in which we have great confidence, that, according to the tenor of that letter, you involve yourself in this matter without any delay, and make known to everyone, both great and small, insofar as you are able, what we have decided and how it has been entrusted to you. Thus, with God’s mercy and with the assistance of those who love the Lord, we may either entirely restrain the fury of this deadly discord and—what we especially desire—restore it to complete peace; or, if sin prevents that from happening, at least avoid the guilt of negligence amid so great a danger to our brothers.

After you have made our plan and decree known, and have requested answers from both sides, so that you may discover such certainty and agreement that we need not hesitate to send legates, and after everything necessary for pursuing this business—place, time, and the other arrangements—has been organized and confirmed, we wish you and that brother who is to be mediator with you in this affair to come to us immediately. Once we have learned what guarantees of safety exist and what hope there should be for peace, we shall then be able to send our legates with you both without danger and without despairing of the fruits of their labor and exertion.

Do not find it burdensome, brother, to undertake what we impose upon you. Since you received the priestly position and office in the Church, you have done nothing more worthy before God or more salutary for your soul than if, with God’s help, you can destroy the wickedness of diabolical deceit in this matter and care for the salvation of so many thousands of people. And if this does not succeed according to your desire despite your exertion, a sure reward nevertheless awaits you with him who will not regard as fruitless any good conceived with a just and persevering will.

We do, however, wish this entirely from your devotion: even if you cannot have as your traveling companion that other man whom we have said above is to be your mediator in this affair, you must nevertheless not fail in any way to come to us.

We also command you, by the authority of blessed Peter, to favor entirely the one whom justice favors, and to admonish on our behalf both clerics and laymen whom you can to do the same. Let the truce which you have arranged also remain unharmed until fifteen days after the dissolution of the assembly. [Col. 0502C]

We wish you diligently to urge the king to ensure that our legates who are in those regions—namely, Bernard, deacon of the holy Roman Church, and Bernard, abbot of Marseille—may, if they wish, return to us freely and safely.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XVII. (1078)

He indicates that, following moderation rather than the strictness of the canons, he examined the cases of the bishops of France and Burgundy and dealt more leniently with each of them; especially with Manasses, archbishop of Reims, whose oath he also appends.

[Col. 0502D] **GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Because it is the custom of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authorization we serve, unworthy though we are, to tolerate some things and to overlook others, we followed the moderation of discretion rather than the strictness of the canons and, not without serious labor, examined the cases of the bishops of France and Burgundy who had been suspended or condemned by our legate Hugh, bishop of Die.

Finally, we restored Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to his proper rank and office. He had been accused on many counts and had withdrawn from the synods to which Hugh, bishop of Die, had invited him, because the sentence passed against him did not appear consistent with the gravity and customary gentleness of the Roman Church. We did so, however, on the condition that he swear upon the body of Saint Peter as follows:

> “I, Manasses, archbishop of Reims, did not fail to attend the synod of Autun, to which the bishop of Die summoned me, out of pride. If I am summoned by a messenger or letter of the Apostolic See, I will not withdraw through any evil device or deception; rather, I will come and faithfully obey the decision and judgment of this Church. If it should please the lord pope Gregory or his successor that I answer before his legate concerning the matters brought against me, I will do the same in every respect. I will faithfully administer the treasures, ornaments, and estates of the Church of Reims entrusted to me, for the honor of that Church, and I will not alienate them in order to resist justice.”

[Col. 0503B] We likewise restored episcopal office to Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, who had been suspended at the same synod, because the letters inviting him to the synod had been withheld by his clerics and not shown to him. This was on the condition that, if our legate should deem it appropriate, he must clear himself of the charges brought against him before our legate, together with his suffragan or neighboring bishops.

To Richer, archbishop of Sens, we restored the office from which he had been forbidden. For he promised into our hands that, whether personally or through his messenger, he would explain before the same legate the reason for which he had not come to the synod of the aforesaid legate, and that in ecclesiastical affairs he would faithfully and humbly provide him, to the best of his ability, with counsel and assistance and would appease his mind.

Gotefred, bishop of Chartres, because he had been judged in his absence without having been summoned, was restored by us to episcopal office, on the condition that his case be reopened and determined before our legate.

Richard, archbishop of Bourges, because he had abandoned his Church in anger and not by synodal judgment, received back his staff and ring, promising to satisfy our legate concerning the charges brought against him.

Rudolph, archbishop of Tours, because he had no lawful accusers, was restored to priestly and episcopal office, especially since the bishops who had accused him had withdrawn from the accusation. And because his case had been reopened and settled by our predecessor, Alexander of blessed memory, it appeared that it should not be reopened without a definite accusation.

Nevertheless, it seemed good to us that our legate should travel to Tours with the legate of the bishop of Die, summon all the suffragan bishops as well as the clergy and people, and admonish them on behalf of blessed Peter to declare truthfully how Rudolph had been elected or ordained. Thus, if it became clear that he was innocent of the charges brought against him, the question of his accusation should thereafter be completely put to rest. But if testimony were given against him with the greatest certainty and in such a way that no doubt could remain, a canonical sentence should be pronounced.

Done at Rome, on the seventh [VI] day before the Ides of March, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF SPEYER. (1078)

[Col. 0504A]

He grants him permission to exercise episcopal office, provided that at a suitable time he satisfies the charges brought against him, expels every form of venality from the Church of God, and appears vigilant and diligent in his office.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **HENRY**, bishop of Speyer, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because, when taking possession of the Church of Speyer, we fear that you knowingly and rashly accepted the staff from the hand of the king contrary to the decree of the Apostolic See, we have not until now permitted you to perform episcopal office. But if, according to the words of your legate, you certainly did not know of our decree before the investiture, we grant you the power and permission to exercise episcopal office, on the condition, however, that you present yourself at a suitable time to satisfy us or our legates concerning the charges brought against you.

And because we have learned that you did not observe, as was proper, the constitutions promulgated in the Roman councils both by us and by our predecessors—namely, that you should expel every form of venality from your church—we can accuse your fraternity of considerable negligence. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we forbid you, after expelling those who were promoted in your Church through money, to permit either the archdeaconate, the archpriesthood, or anything else that appears to pertain to spiritual care to be given for a price. Rather, in accordance with the Lord’s command, which says, “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10), conduct yourself irreproachably and correct clerics who do not live chastely with pastoral severity. Just as formerly you were negligent and idle, so henceforth you must appear vigilant and diligent in administering the office you have undertaken, so that at the end of your life the rectitude of your work may make almighty Lord merciful and compassionate toward you.

Given at Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XIX. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH. (1078)

[Col. 0504D] He says that he is sending a legate to examine carefully and piously whether the bishop of Rouen is able, because of his illness, to preside over the pastoral administration. If his poor health has so overwhelmed him that he is found less suited to such a charge, another man is to be canonically elected without fail.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **WILLIAM**, king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The care of our office requires that we hasten to assist diligently Churches deprived of their pastors. But because, among kings, both by the honorable character in which you shine and by the generous prudence with which you are endowed, we embrace you with special affection, it is fitting that we take particular care of the Churches in the kingdom entrusted to you by divine arrangement.

Accordingly, we have decided to assist the Church of Rouen, which, as we have heard, has long been deprived of its pastor because of illness, in the following manner. We are sending to you, for your generous glory, dearest son, Hubert, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, whom experience has shown to be faithful both to us and to you. Together with religious bishops and abbots, as well as brothers of that Church, he is to visit the aforesaid archbishop and examine carefully and piously whether he is able, as he ought, to preside over the pastoral administration.

But if they judge that he has been so incapacitated by bodily illness that henceforth he is not suited to episcopal governance, they must not cease first trying to persuade him through admonitions, and, if necessary, even by apostolic authority, to consent that the Church be provided with another. But if illness has so overwhelmed him that it has made him senseless and forgetful of his office, so that he does not judge how great a loss his illness is to himself and to the whole realm, we command, by apostolic authority, that a man competent for so great a burden, of good character and wisdom, be canonically elected by the unanimous consent of all and promoted to the archbishopric.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Nones of April, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO RAINERIUS, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS. (1078)

He rebukes him for having abused the patience of the Roman Church and, by adding crime to crime, squandered nearly all the ornaments of his Church. He therefore commands him, after restoring everything, to attend the synod to be held in his region and give the legates an account of everything brought against him.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **RAINERIUS**, bishop of Orléans.

[Col. 0505C] If you wished to show yourself of sound mind, you would not demonstrate that you had entirely forgotten how much you have committed against God and the salvation of your order by perpetrating worse deeds. You ought above all to have reflected on how much patience the Roman Church has shown toward you. While she pitied you beyond what was appropriate, her very mercy has in a sense been turned into guilt through your actions. You abuse this mercy with such excessive shamelessness that you compel us, driven by your provocations, to rise against you with the censure of strict equity.

Among the other things which you formerly did with a perverse mind, adding wound to wound, you have, as has been reported to us, squandered nearly all the ornaments of the Church entrusted to you—namely, pallia, chalices, censers, chasubles, and other things consecrated to God—not for the benefit of God and the aforesaid Church, not to assist the poor and captives, but according to your own pleasure and for empty glory and pride. You can understand how much it grieves us to observe this.

Now therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you, setting aside every excuse, to restore justly whatever you have taken away; and, after restoring everything, to attend the synod which is to be held in your region. There, before our legates—namely, Hugh of Die, Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and also our subdeacon Roger—you are to give a canonical account of these and the other charges brought against you.

But if you do not canonically clear yourself of all the charges brought against you, and do not return what you took away in accordance with our command, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the Apostolic See we shall pronounce against you a sentence of anathema and deposition, without any hope of restoration.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY. (1078)

He asks him to provide assistance to the legate whom he is sending to the king of Spain. He writes that the brothers whom he is sending with the legate will announce his judgment concerning Berengar. He sets out his tribulations and asks that the Lord’s mercy be implored for him.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **HUGH**, abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Wearied by the gathering of people from different nations and by the concentrated burden of many affairs, I write little to one whom I love greatly. Therefore, as the king of Spain requested and as you advised, with God’s authorization we consecrated the abbot as bishop; and we are sending to that same king the cardinal priest Richard, entrusting our place to him, and we ask your fraternity to provide him with assistance and a suitable companion.

Concerning Berengar, about whom you wrote to us, the brothers whom we are sending back to you with our aforesaid cardinal will announce what we think and what we have decided.

But you, with certain faith, indeed with prayer, implore the mercy of almighty God, so that he may direct our minds according to his will, govern us amid this great storm, and bring us to the harbor of his loving-kindness. We are pressed by so many anxieties and wearied by such great labors that those who are with us are not merely unable to endure them, but cannot even bear to witness them.

Although the heavenly trumpet proclaims that each person will receive a reward according to his labor (Luke 6), and the good king declares, “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, have made my soul rejoice” (Psalm 93), nevertheless this life is often wearisome to us, and the death of the flesh is our desire.

But when that poor Jesus, the loving Comforter, true God and true man, stretches out his hand, he makes one who is very sad and afflicted rejoice; when, however, he abandons me, he greatly disturbs me. In myself I am always dying, but in him I sometimes live, and when my strength utterly fails, I cry out groaning to him:

“If you placed such a burden upon Moses and Peter, I believe it would weigh them down. What, then, will become of me, who am worth nothing in comparison with them? It remains, therefore, either that you yourself, together with your Peter, govern the pontificate, or that you watch me succumb and that same pontificate fall into confusion.”

Then I return to this: “Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6). And to this: “I have become like a portent to many; but you are my strong helper” (Psalm 70). Nor do I forget this: “For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3).

May almighty God, who through the holy office that he entrusts to sinners, in wondrous mercy justifies sinners, absolve you and all the brothers entrusted to you from every sin by the authority of blessed Peter entrusted to me, though I am utterly unworthy, and lead you joyfully to the bosom of Abraham our patriarch.

Given at Rome, on the Nones of May, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO HUBERT AND TEUZON. (1078)

He advises them to attend, together with the suffragan bishops, abbots, and clerics of the Church of Dol, along with the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny, to whom the dispute between Evetius and another man concerning the archbishopric has been entrusted. They are to ensure that the king of the English sends his legate there, so that such a case may be settled.

[Col. 0507B] **GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **HUBERT**, subdeacon, and **TEUZON**, monk, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our brother Evetius [Everius], archbishop of Dol, came before us, presenting himself for the examination of the dispute that had arisen concerning his entry into the episcopate. The man who, before Evetius’s ordination, had seized that same see by an allegedly perverse accession and held it through wicked conduct complained that he had been unjustly expelled.

Evetius said that he had been summoned to this appearance by our fellow brother Hugh, bishop of Die; Hugh himself, who was then present, acknowledged this. For that reason Evetius said that he had refused to return with you or turn toward any other place until he learned from our mouth what he ought to do and where he ought to present himself.

But because the bishop of Die, as we have said, was present, we entrusted this business to him, so that at the council where he is to deal with the case of the archbishop of Reims and of the other bishops of France, with the abbot of Cluny associated with him, he may also undertake to determine this matter canonically.

Therefore we admonish you to be present there, either one of you or both if possible, and to urge the bishops and religious abbots of that diocese, as well as the clerics and laymen of the same Church who appear qualified either to accuse or to defend either side, to attend.

Also ensure that the king of the English sends there on his behalf a legate who is both prudent and religious, so that this case, once the parties’ favoritism and every personal consideration have been removed, may, by God’s ordering, reach a just determination. Whatever is established and determined there must be confirmed by all with one harmonious voice and judgment, so that the insolence of the defamatory complaint, and every opportunity and all possibility of reopening the question, may everywhere and completely be cut off.

Given at the Lateran, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XXIII. TO GAUSFRED AND ANOTHER GAUSFRED, COUNTS. (1078)

[Col. 0508A] He asks them to arrange for all the bishops and abbots of Brittany, as well as the knowledgeable clerics and laymen of the Church of Dol, to assemble for the council. Among other matters, the council is to determine the case between Evetius, who had been ordained archbishop, and another man who complained that he had been unjustly expelled by Evetius.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **GAUSFRED** [Gaufred], of Rennes, and likewise to **GAUSFRED**, son of Eudo, noble counts of Brittany, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you are not unaware of how much distress and disturbance the Church of Dol and our fellow brother Evetius [Everius], the archbishop whom we ordained there, are suffering from the man who had previously occupied the see and, abandoning it as though stripped of it by the reproach of his conscience, as is said, now complains that he was unjustly expelled.

When the aforesaid archbishop presented himself before us concerning this matter, we were entirely unable to examine the case in the absence of the man who was making the complaint against him. We therefore deemed it necessary to entrust the whole business to our fellow brother Hugh, bishop of Die, to whom we have given our authority, so that he might examine and determine it through careful inquiry at a time and place where those necessary on both sides in this case could assemble and be present.

For we have decided that our aforesaid brother and vicar should hold a council because many important matters have arisen in the kingdom of France that require examination and judgment by apostolic authority. We wish and decree that this matter too be determined there, with God’s help.

Therefore we earnestly ask and admonish your excellence to devote as much effort as you can to this case, and to attend the aforesaid council, as will be made known to you, together with the bishops and religious abbots of that land, as well as the clerics and laymen of the same Church who appear qualified both in knowledge and in religion.

Thus, with divine mercy assisting, a sincere investigation may make evident in this case whatever justice and the salvation of the people require. Once this dispute and complaint, by which the aforesaid Church of Dol has long and most undeservedly been torn apart, has been completely settled, may that Church, through God’s mercy and with your zeal and your power assisting and providing for it, recover its possessions, as well as peace and tranquility, and return to and remain in a state of well-being.

Given at the Lateran [Laurenti: on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May], on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the first indiction.

## BOOK SIX OF THE REGISTER

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078, the second indiction.

[Col. 0507]

## LETTER I. TO THE TEUTONS. (1078)

[Col. 0507D]

He warns them not to favor or associate with those who, contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See, attempt to prevent the assembly of bishops and laymen to be held before the apostolic legates concerning the rights of Henry and Rudolph in the kingdom of the Teutons. In the meantime, he assures them that he will in no way support the unjust party.

[Col. 0509A] **GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all clerics and laymen established in the kingdom of the Teutons who are not bound by the bond of excommunication, greetings and apostolic blessing.

How great and how serious our concern has been and remains that pestilence, ruin, and desolation be removed from your kingdom and that peace, honor, and its customary dignity be restored to you, we declared at the synod celebrated at Rome during Lent this year.

For by the judgment of the Holy Spirit we decreed and commanded that an assembly of all the bishops in your kingdom, together with those laymen who fear God and desire peace among you, should take place. Before our legates it was to be determined whether justice more strongly favored Henry or Rudolph, who are contending with one another over the governance of the kingdom.

The less just party, defeated by reason and constrained by the authority of blessed Peter, would more readily yield, and, with God’s favor, the destruction of souls and bodies would cease. The more just party, however, would have greater confidence in God and, aided by the power of blessed Peter and by the agreement of all who love justice, would hope confidently for victory, fearing neither form of death.

But because word has reached us that certain enemies of God and sons of the devil among you are attempting, contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See, to render the aforesaid assembly void, and are eager to fulfill their desires not through justice but through pride and the desolation of the whole kingdom, thereby destroying the Christian religion, we admonish you and command you on behalf of blessed Peter to provide such people no assistance and not to associate with them.

For at the aforesaid synod they have all already been bound by the bond of excommunication and anathema. And so that they may be unable to obtain any victory, they have been bound by the power of blessed Peter, so that at least under compulsion they may be confounded and recalled from the death of their souls and the desolation of your homeland.

But you, dearest brothers, must in no way doubt that I would knowingly favor the unjust party in any way. I desire rather to undergo death for your salvation than to seize the glory of the whole world for your destruction.

If some, trusting in falsehood, tell you otherwise by letters or words, do not heed them in any way. For we fear God and are afflicted daily for love of him; therefore we regard the pride and pleasures of the world as of little account, because we firmly believe that we shall soon be consoled by him.

May almighty and merciful God, who in his mercy goes beyond hope and beyond merit and comforts us in all our tribulation (2 Corinthians 1), open your heart to his law and strengthen you in his commandments, so that, absolved from all sins by the authority of blessed Peter, he may lead you to the heavenly kingdom, where you shall reign.

Given at Capua, on the Kalends of June, in the first indiction.

## LETTER II. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. (1078)

[Col. 0510A]

He shows that Roman legates are not only those born or educated at Rome, or promoted there to some dignity, but all to whom the Roman pontiff entrusts his functions. Therefore, when he rebukes Manasses for not obeying his legate, the bishop of Die, he also explains that privileges may be altered as necessity or advantage requires. He advises him to clear himself canonically of the charges before the legates. He writes that he has ordered by letter that the matters of which Manasses complained against certain bishops be investigated and judged canonically.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **MANASSES**, archbishop of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When you demand from the Apostolic See those things which both suit the dignity of your episcopate [Col. 0510B] and in no way disagree with the authority of our predecessors, ask confidently; request with complete assurance of hope, knowing that, with every doubt removed, we are ready to assent to petitions of this kind—both because we embrace you with fraternal affection in Christ and also because we are urged to this by the earnest prayers and interventions of certain of our faithful who love you. Therefore we wish your fraternity to be asked and admonished not to take it badly if, for a time, we endeavor, for the sake of common propriety and advantage, to deny what you request when it is contrary to the good of the Church.

Know, however, that all this has been said because in your letters you request that, contrary to the privilege which you acknowledge yourselves to possess from this Apostolic See, you should not be compelled to answer concerning any matters alleged against you except to me alone or to Roman legates. If by “Roman legates” you seemed to understand anyone of any nation to whom the Roman pontiff entrusts some legation, or—which is more significant—grants his own authority, we should certainly praise your request and readily assent to it. But because, after first saying “Roman,” you immediately add, “not transalpine,” you show that you wish to have as Roman legates only those who were either born at Rome, or educated from childhood in the Roman Church, or promoted to some office in it. We are exceedingly astonished that your prudence has been brought to the point of asking our benevolence to diminish the rights of the Apostolic See, and that you think we ought not, in your case alone, to be permitted to do what our predecessors held, without any contradiction, both lawful and legitimate in the affairs of everyone.

For you know that the bishops Hosius at the Council of Nicaea and Cyril at the Council of Ephesus acted as representatives of the Roman pontiffs, with the latter’s permission. You have also read that Pope Gregory granted his authority to Syagrius, bishop of Autun and suffragan of the bishop of Lyon, so that he might convene a general council in Gaul (Book IV, letter 52, second indiction; letter 112). But why do we speak of bishops, when that same holy pope, supported by the authority of his letters, made a certain monk named Hilary his vicar in Africa to such an extent that a general council was held there through him, and whatever the holy synod decreed was brought to completion through his execution of it? [Col. 0511A]

Therefore, let your fraternity not seek to be raised to so great a height that, in your case alone, you wish to make invalid and unlawful what was accepted and permitted in the cases of everyone by the Roman pontiffs.

Regarding what you say about the privilege, we answer briefly for the present that certain things may be granted in privileges according to the matter, the person, the time, or the place; and that, for the same considerations, if greater necessity or advantage should demand it, they may lawfully be changed. Privileges, after all, ought not to violate the authority of the holy Fathers, but to look to the welfare of the holy Church.

For this reason the Church of Arles, not only by the blessed Gregory, the sweet-speaking teacher (Book IV, letter 52), but also by several of his holy predecessors, when it possessed the authority of the Apostolic See, was empowered to summon all the bishops of the entire kingdom of the Franks—which at that time extended more widely—to a council and to constrain them to appear in judgment. Without its permission, none of the bishops mentioned above was permitted to go far from his own episcopate. After some time, however, for certain reasons, the aforesaid power and authority ceased, and the Apostolic See granted its authority to others whom it chose.

The Church of Rheims, over which you preside, was also for a time subject to a primate and obeyed him as its master after the Roman pontiff. You can find the same concerning many other Churches if you diligently undertake to investigate the statements and deeds of the holy Fathers.

We do not say this because we wish either to violate or to diminish, contrary to reason, the privileges of your Church. If life permits, we shall discuss them more leisurely, face to face, at the proper time. For the present, however, on behalf of the blessed prince of the apostles, Peter, we admonish your affection that, just as we established for you when you were at Rome, you should be prepared on every occasion, with all excuses and obstacles removed, to answer concerning all the charges before the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny, to whom we have entrusted our authority in these matters; you must make legal satisfaction and undergo canonical purification, lest, if something else should be done by you—which God forbid!—many people attribute it to evasion, flight, and consciousness of crimes rather than to the enforcement of justice and equity.

Concerning the archbishop of Vienne, about whom you complain that he both deposed priests in your diocese and restored those same men to their former rank; concerning the bishops of Laon and Soissons, your suffragans, who, without consulting or informing you, even while you were at Rome, consecrated the bishop of Amiens; concerning Manasses, who does not cease to harass you and your Church with curses, since he cannot do so by evil deeds; and concerning all the others about whom you may wish to make complaint—we have sent letters to our fellow bishops mentioned above, namely the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny, instructing them to make every effort to investigate everything diligently, examine it carefully, and, once it has been thoroughly examined and investigated, judge it purely, justly, legally, and canonically. Obeying these admonitions of ours in all things, may you in the present be granted the blessing of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and in the future, freed from the bonds of sins, may you merit through the intercession of those same men to be brought into the fellowship of them all.

Given at [“apud,” ‘at,’ and so in what follows] Saint-Germain, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the first indiction.

## Letter III. To Hugh, Bishop of Die. (Year 1078)

He instructs them to bring the complaints of the archbishop of Rheims to an end and, if he obeys, to assist him; he also sends him a copy of the preceding letters.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, bishop of Die, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since, by divine disposition, we preside over the government of the holy Church of God, we ought to keep vigilant watch over it; therefore, through your continual prayers, we ask that you obtain divine assistance for us. Accordingly, we admonish and command you to apply your utmost diligence, so that you may investigate and, as far as you can, endeavor canonically to bring to an end the matters about which our fellow bishop, the archbishop of Rheims, has complained to us in his letters.

For he complains of our fellow bishop, the archbishop of Vienne, Warmund, who deposed priests in his archbishopric and restored those same men. He also complains that two suffragans of that same archbishop of Rheims—namely, the bishops of Laon and Soissons—disregarding canonical authority, dared to consecrate the bishop of Amiens while he himself was with us at Rome and was humbly awaiting judgment concerning himself. Examine and investigate with every possible care, through a worthy and diligent inquiry, whether the matter is as we have understood from his letters, especially whether the same bishop of Amiens presumptuously accepted investiture from the hand of a layman, through wicked ambition and reckless audacity, contrary to the decree of the Roman synod and the Apostolic See. Strive earnestly to chastise and punish him with such severity of canonical rigor that the others may fear to imitate his example.

As for Manasses, about whom he likewise complains—who does not cease to weary him and the Church by taking refuge in and relying upon Oebalus and his supporters—work to bring him back to peace and make him cease troubling the Church and persecuting the archbishop. But if he should persist in his obstinacy and refuse to obey, unless you discover that he has a just excuse, do whatever seems most just to you.

As for his other needs, assist the same archbishop as is fitting, provided that he obeys you, and defend the Church entrusted to him by the authority of the blessed Peter—which you ought also to do with respect to the other Churches. As we have learned from his letters, which we sent to you, he is seeking delays in order to evade the matter; how we replied to him we also indicate to you by the enclosed copy.

But you, my dearest brothers, act courageously and wisely, and let all your actions be done in charity, so that the oppressed may find you prudent defenders and the oppressors may recognize you as lovers of justice. May almighty God pour the Holy Spirit into your hearts, lead you along the path pleasing to him, and bring you to the fellowship of the holy Fathers.

Given at Saint-Germain, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, first indiction.

## Letter IV. To Henry, Bishop of Liège. (Year 1078)

He reproves him for having rashly uttered words against the authority of the Roman Church and instructs him to settle the case of a certain Werembold, who had complained that he and his wife had been unjustly excommunicated by him, with the assistance of the bishops of Trier and Metz. He says that he absolved Werembold through fear of death, after receiving from him a pledge to satisfy everyone. He calls those men despisers of the synod who hindered the synod summoned by him in the German regions from being held.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, bishop of Liège, greetings and apostolic blessing—provided that he does not associate with the despisers of the Roman synod held during the preceding Lent.

After reading your fraternity’s letter, we were not a little astonished that you did not write to the Apostolic See with the reverence due to it, but reproached us in biting language for absolving that parishioner of yours who formerly came to us, as though the authority of the Apostolic See did not extend to binding and absolving whomever it wishes and wherever it wishes.

Therefore, know that we were greatly provoked against your rashness, had not the gentleness of the Apostolic See restrained us, and had not our mind been in some doubt concerning the letters formerly sent to you about this matter. For we are concerned that those letters may have been altered through someone’s fraud or falsification. We therefore thought that a copy of them should be shown to you so that you might recognize our intention. If it becomes clear that they are the same and have not been altered, understand that you uttered words against the authority of the holy Roman Church either in a spirit of presumption or through ignorance, almost imitating the Easterners who dared to speak against blessed Pope Julius because he had absolved the most holy patriarch Athanasius without their consent. From now on, take care not to write back to us with such rashness; instead, humbly return to the teachings of the holy Fathers, which will instruct you how to speak and write, and strive to bring the case of the aforesaid man to an end according to the tenor of the letter whose copy we are sending you.

This man, named Werembold, complained that he had been unjustly excommunicated by you together with his wife; therefore we can scarcely put faith in him. Nevertheless, we admonish your prudence to have the case brought to the attention of our religious fellow bishops, namely the archbishop of Trier and the bishop of Metz, and to endeavor to settle it according to their counsel and judgment.

As for the monastic habit, the veil imposed, and the money taken away, do not refuse, on the testimony of those same men, either to render justice or to give an account, so that you may remove his opportunity for complaint and protect yourself from every accusation, while preserving the integrity of justice and canonical authority in all things.

In the salutation above, we call those men despisers of the synod who by any device or violence attempted to prevent a council or assembly from being held in the German regions, at which careful investigation would establish whether justice favored Henry or Rudolph more with regard to the governance of the kingdom.

Furthermore, we wish you to know that, because of fear of death, we absolved the bearer of this letter from excommunication after he made a promise in our hand that he would do everything according to your injunction, made with the advice of the aforesaid bishops.

Given at the borough of Aquaependente, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, second indiction.

## Letter V. To Herimann, Bishop of Metz. (Year 1078)

He instructs him to assist the bishop of Toul, to whom he granted permission to clear himself before four bishops if, because of the disturbance in the kingdom, he could not summon six together. He reproves him for having given Church property to certain soldiers for his own defense.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Herimann, bishop of Metz, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your affection knows, dearest brother, how long the bishop of Toul has already been wearied by labor and has struggled amid many hardships to repel the disgrace which, he maintains, has been unjustly alleged against him. But because, on account of the impending disturbance in the kingdom, he cannot summon six bishops together for his purgation, we have granted him, out of our fatherly compassion, that, having been cleared by four bishops who will presently swear with him, he may perform the episcopal office in every respect. From the other two, who ought to be present at the appointed judgment, he has obtained from us a delay until Lent.

Therefore, since you are situated in the same diocese, we admonish and exhort your affection, which is most dear to me, and by apostolic authority command you that, if you know with certainty that the aforesaid bishop of Toul is guilty, you do not delay extending to him a brotherly hand of assistance, as is just. For it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). And again: “If anyone sees his brother in need and closes his heart to him, how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John III).

Furthermore, it has come to us that, because of the imminent attacks of your enemies, you have given your Church’s property to certain soldiers, and that in this way the dignity of your office is daily—something we do not wish—being diminished and reduced. Therefore we wish your prudence to be admonished not to give ecclesiastical estates to anyone, compelled by the magnitude of some tribulation, lest you afterward repent greatly when you are unable in any way to correct what you did while disturbed.

You ought, however, to place all your hope in the Lord, knowing with complete certainty that the Lord does not abandon those who hope in him (Prov. XXIX, 25). For we trust that almighty God, appeased by the prayers of yourself and of the other religious men—of whom we know there are many in your regions—will soon grant peace to his Church.

Given at Sutri [Susa], on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, second indiction.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, on the seventeenth day of the month of November, second indiction, at Rome. I, Marro, son of Gislerius, inhabitant of the duchy of Spoleto, for the redemption of my soul and those of my parents, give, hand over, and offer to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and upon his altar, everything that belongs to me from the estate called Moricicla [Moricida], situated between Murice and Clarignano, which I acquired by exchange from Litald and Hugh, nephews of Hugh, son of Ascarus, in the parish of Luzano, reserving the usufruct for the days of my life, and for my son Brutulus and the sons of Brutulus, if they should be male and born of a legitimate marriage (Pontifical Records under Gregory VII).

## Letter VI. (Year 1078)

He declares that, by his command, an agreement was made between the bishop of Turin and the abbot of Saint Michael’s, and under what conditions. He says that he will punish those who do not acquiesce and defend an unjust cause.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be known to those present and to posterity [Col. 0515C] how we ordered the case of Cumbert [Note: It is Cunipert. HARD.], bishop of Turin, and the abbot of Saint Michael’s to be settled. After they had come into our presence, following many years during which each had complained against the other, they willingly acquiesced and obeyed our command, and, at our order, made peace between themselves.

By apostolic authority we forbade them to give one another any further occasion for discord.
