But the bishop is to make restitution to the abbot and the aforesaid monastery for what he took from it, except insofar as the abbot has remitted it to him. Likewise, the abbot is to do the same for the bishop. This is to be assessed by the bishop of Asti and the bishop of Acqui, as well as by the abbot of Fruttuaria.

If the bishop wishes and is able to prove that the monastery was built on the property and allod of his bishopric, both men are to appear at the next synod and receive there a just and lawful decision. If they are prevented by some obstacle, let them send representatives so that those representatives may report to them how and when we shall bring their case to an end.

But if, having learned the truth, the bishop recognizes that the monastery was not built on the allod of his bishopric, or if the abbot understands that the bishop has a just and true claim in this matter, let him acquiesce without any dispute or controversy to the one who possesses truth and justice. Let them know beyond doubt that we shall punish severely and most strictly anyone who, possessing an unjust cause, attempts to defend it, or who, hoping for some protection or power, dares to pursue an unjust case.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter VII. To Hugh, Bishop of Die. (Year 1078)

He instructs him to absolve Robert, count of Flanders, who was excommunicated by the legate of the Apostolic See and the bishop of Langres, if he finds that this was not done canonically, or if Robert wishes to make satisfaction. If Hugh himself cannot do so, he is to have it accomplished through religious persons.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, bishop of Die, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since, by undertaking the pastoral office, we ought to have great concern for the salvation of all the children of the Church, we must correct as quickly as possible anything we learn to have been done otherwise than ecclesiastical rectitude requires.

Therefore we notify your affection that we have learned from certain persons, especially Ingelrannus, a Flemish cleric, that Robert, count of Flanders, has been excommunicated by our legate Hubert and Hugh, bishop of Langres, through the machinations of his enemies. Since, if this is true, we ought not to tolerate it, we instruct your fraternity by request that, if it is not burdensome to you, you hasten to those regions. If you find that he was not excommunicated canonically, absolve him on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0516C] and on our behalf.

If, however—which we do not wish—he was excommunicated canonically but nevertheless wishes to make satisfaction, do not delay reconciling him again to the Lord’s fold, because the Supreme Shepherd himself desired to carry the lost sheep back to the flock upon his own shoulders.

But if it is not possible for you to do this yourself, send religious persons in your place who, in the manner prescribed above, may bring the matter to its proper conclusion.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter VIII. To Hubert, Wido, and Hugh. (Year 1078)

He orders that a certain estate, with all its appurtenances, be restored to the clerics of Saint Mary and Saint Audomar. If they believe that it rightly belongs to their own Church, they are to approach Hugh, bishop of Die and legate, within forty days; when that period has elapsed, if they are unwilling to obey, he forbids them access to the Church and Christian communion until they repent.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hubert, the clerics, and all the counts of the castle of Saint Paul, and to Wido and Hugh, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The clerics of Saint Mary and Saint Audomar, coming to the Apostolic See, complained about you: for a long time now you have been taking from them and from their Church a certain estate called Reseca, together with everything belonging to it. Although they had often made a complaint about this in provincial synods before your bishop, and finally before Hugh, our fellow bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic Church, at the Council of Poitiers, and although he had commanded by our authority that, before your bishop, you either restore the estate and its property, as claimed by the aforesaid Church and its clerics, or give an account of why you believed they should belong to you by right; and although your bishop had set three deadlines for you, and finally the provincial synod, so that you might do either one of these things—you nevertheless wished to do neither, just as you had never done so before.

Therefore, by the authority of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command you that, if the matter is as stated, you canonically restore without delay the aforesaid property to the aforesaid Church [Col. 0517B] and its clerics. Or, if it is not so, and you know with certainty on sound grounds that the property ought to belong to your Church, then within forty days after you have seen our letters—or, if you avoid seeing them, after you have learned that they have been sent to you—you must approach the aforesaid Hugh, our fellow bishop and brother, on the day previously named and announced to you by Ingelrannus and his brothers, so that, with both parties present before him, he may bring this dispute to a lawful conclusion.

But if you are unwilling to do this within the prescribed days, then, once they have elapsed, we forbid you—Wido, Hugh, and Eustace, counts; Oilard, the subdefender of the aforesaid possession; and all of you who from now on provide assistance and consent to this sacrilege—to enter any church whatsoever, and to receive Christian communion or the grace of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, either in life or in death, unless you should perhaps repent and canonically restore to the aforesaid Church what you have unjustly seized.

But if, after all this, infected with diabolical malice, you should prefer to persist incorrigibly in the prescribed excommunication, which God forbid among all Christians, we command the defenders and patrons of the aforesaid Church to strive by every means to restore the aforesaid property to that Church and its clerics.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter IX. To the Canons of the Church of Tarvenna. (Year 1078)

He orders that the canons of the castle of Saint Paul be denied all access to the Church unless, as he commanded in the preceding letter, they obey the apostolic letters; laymen who do not obey are likewise to be excommunicated. He also wishes Mathilda to be admonished to ensure that the land her husband gave to the Church is handed over, and those who withhold the Church’s tithes are to be admonished to return them; otherwise they are to be subject to condemnation.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ernolf and Hubert, archdeacons of the Church of Tarvenna, and to the canons, if they live canonically, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Summon all the clerics of the castle of Saint Paul, about whom the canons of Saint Mary and Saint Audomar have complained to us through Ingelrannus [Col. 0518A] and his other brothers, to the city of Tarvenna by our authority, and read to them our letters that will be given to you on our behalf.

If they refuse to come, or if, after coming, they refuse to obey our letters, forbid them all access to the Church, and enforce against them what our letters forbid; moreover, deprive them of whatever they possess from the Church of Tarvenna by clerical provision.

Notify the laymen named in our letters, and anyone else who, after seeing or being informed of our letters, gives consent or assistance to the aforesaid clerics so that they may persist in robbery and sacrilege, that they have been placed under the prescribed excommunication.

Admonish Mathilda, widow of Arnulf the advocate, concerning the land which her husband, when dying, gave to the Church of Saint Mary and which he promised, as he lay dying, to set free, to fulfill what he promised. Otherwise, let her remain under the aforesaid condemnation for as long as she fails to do so.

Admonish Renger, Adam, Bereweld, and the others who withhold the tithes of newly cultivated lands belonging to the aforesaid Church to return them and make satisfaction. If they refuse, let them remain subject to the aforesaid condemnation until they repent.

We add this as well: let no one accept any offering from the hand of any of the persons mentioned above, whether in life or in death, until they canonically amend what they have done wrong.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter X. To the People of Ravenna. (Year 1078)

He instructs them to render no further obedience to the bishop of Ravenna, who was deposed in the Roman synod for numerous crimes; whoever dares to resist the apostolic commands is to be condemned with anathema.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the people of Ravenna, great and small, who love blessed Peter and his son, namely Saint Apollinaris, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your fraternity knows very well how faithfully and humbly the Church of Ravenna has always adhered to blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, and how much obedience it has shown in all things to its mother, the holy Roman Church.

But how the man who is now said to be bishop of the Church of Ravenna once devastated it, both exceedingly wealthy and exceedingly devout, through tyrannical plunder, and corrupted it by the example of an irreligious life—you yourselves have perceived by suffering and witnessing it, and we have learned through certain experience.

But because he was entangled and polluted by these and many other crimes, and, so that he might not be accused and convicted, raised up by the arrogance of pride he lifted his heel against the prince of the apostles and persevered in disobedience, which is compared with the crime of idolatry, know with complete certainty from the evidence of this letter that, without hope of restoration, he has been deposed in the holy Roman synod by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command all of you to render him no further obedience of the kind owed to a bishop. But if any, wounded by the contagion of excommunication, dares to resist these salutary commands, we cut them off with the sword of anathema and cast them away like rotten members from the whole body of Christ, which is the Catholic Church.

But to you who love God and obey blessed Peter, by the authority of that same prince of the apostles we grant remission of all sins.

Given at Rome, on the seventh [sixth] day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter XI. To the Clerics of Saint Martin of Lucca. (Year 1078)

He reproves them for disobedience. He orders them, according to the privilege of the pontiffs who preceded him, to live a common and regular life; otherwise, they are to return the Church’s prebend into the hands of the bishop. If they neglect to do either, he forbids them access to all Churches.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics of Saint Martin of the Church of Lucca, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When we were with you, we admonished you very frequently, both through ourselves and through our fellow bishops, to lead a common and regular life according to the privilege of our predecessors, namely the holy popes Leo and Victor, who, at the request of the canons then belonging to your Church, made that privilege for the Church. But you, seeking what is your own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. II, 2), neglected our admonitions.

Although the judgment of justice ought rightly to have struck you for such great negligence and disobedience—which the holy Fathers call a crime comparable to idolatry—the apostolic gentleness, at the prayers of your bishops and of certain of your brothers, with its customary compassion, mercifully endured you as sons until the feast of All Saints, and afterward, through the intervention of the same bishop, until the synod. We ordered you to send some of your number to it who would answer us concerning your obedience. Since this was not done as it should have been, we can no longer delay the judgment of equity.

Therefore, by true obedience, I admonish you to live a common life, as Pope Saint Leo instituted for our Church and as the Roman Church understands it—that is, so that all the goods of the Church are gathered for common use and expended jointly, as was said above—or, if you refuse to do this, return the Church’s prebend into the hands of the bishop for the benefit of the Church.

But if you refuse to do either of these things—which God forbid—by the authority of almighty God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we prohibit you from entering any Church until you make a fitting correction.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter XII. To Landulf, Bishop of Pisa. (Year 1078)

He confirms to him the episcopate of the Church of Pisa with all its rights, granting both what was bestowed in ancient times, what is now bestowed by Matilda, and what others will bestow in the future. He entrusts his authority and that of his successors to him in the island of Corsica and grants him half of all revenues for the labor he will first undertake in restoring it to the dominion of the Roman Church; to two of his successors he grants a quarter of all revenues. He nevertheless reserves the fortresses under the authority of the Roman Church, and wishes their custodians to obey those bishops if necessity should require it.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Landulf of Pisa and to his successors.

In view of the regard of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the concern of apostolic governance so that, with attentive kindness, we may favor the just wishes of those who pray, and, with the balance of equity, assist as far as God grants us the ability all who are placed in need.

Therefore, since you, brother Landulf, requested that we protect, by the defense of our apostolic authority, the Church over which, by God’s will, you are recognized as presiding, together with its goods, from the attacks and assaults of adversaries, we have inclined to your just petitions and, by the grant of this present privilege, confirm to you the episcopate of the aforesaid Church of Pisa with all its rights and appurtenances.

And because the Church of Pisa, which had deviated from the constitutions of the holy Fathers in the appointment of its pastors, at last accepted from its mother, the holy Roman Church, sound counsel for the restoration of its ancient liberty—so that it might rejoice in having you as its pastor, ordained by us, entering not from elsewhere but through the door, which is Christ—we grant, concede, and confirm to it both what was lawfully bestowed in ancient times and what our most serene daughter Matilda has graciously granted through divine compassion, for the remedy of the soul of her mother buried in that same Church: namely, the place called Schannellum, with its castles and appurtenances, as well as whatever other things, with God as their author, are lawfully to be granted in the future by the faithful.

Furthermore, recognizing that the fruit of your faith and religion flourishes abundantly in you, we entrust to you and your successors our authority in the island of Corsica, provided that they enter it canonically by the consent of the Roman pontiff and the election of the people of Pisa, just as it is clear that you entered it. Thus, according to what God has entrusted to you, you are to teach with watchful zeal the bishops, clerics, and people of that island those things which seem to belong to the Christian religion, and to strengthen them in upright conduct, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “To uproot and to tear down, to build and to plant” (Jer. I, 10).

That island, which through the invasion of certain wicked men has been removed from the right and dominion of the holy Roman Church, we grant to you, through whose efforts the Church of Pisa has been restored to its ancient dignity, and who will first labor for the restoration of the aforesaid island, so that, after the invaders have been expelled, it may be brought back to the dominion of the same Roman Church according to ancient custom. You shall receive half of all revenues and half of the entire price acquired from judicial settlements; two of your successors, however, shall receive a quarter of the revenues and of the entire price acquired from judicial settlements.

This is provided, nevertheless, that the fortresses and all fortified places acquired by you remain under our power and that of our successors, on the condition that, if necessity should require it, their custodians obey you and your successors, without prejudice to the right and honor of the Roman Church.

For it is fitting that, if they have received pastoral dignity according to the Lord under the command and with the consent of the holy Roman Church, they should possess, through the generosity of the Apostolic See, support and distinction from temporal goods.

We have also judged that this should be added: our messenger is always to be present when judicial settlements are conducted.

Done at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of December, second indiction.

## Letter XIII. To Olav, King of Norway. (Year 1078)

He confirms him in the faith. Since, because of the distance between the regions and his ignorance of the language, he cannot send men who might instruct him in the law of the Lord, he asks him to send younger men and nobles from his kingdom to the apostolic see. Once instructed in the divine laws, they will then be able to bring the mandates of the apostolic see to him and preach them. Moreover, he must in no way give assistance to the brothers of the king of the Danes, who desire a division of the kingdom; rather, he should ensure that the king receive his brothers with charity. He exhorts him to good and pious works.

[Col. 0521C] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Olav, king of the Norwegians [*Norvecchorum*; Norwegians, MUTIN.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although, by reason of the universal care of the holy and apostolic see, over which by divine mercy we preside, we are debtors to all who profess the faith of Christ, yet we are surrounded by a much greater concern and necessity for you, who are situated, as it were, at the farthest edge of the world, since we know that you have fewer people available to instruct you in the Christian religion and fewer of the necessary sources of comfort. Therefore, when an opportunity presented itself, we wrote to you in order somehow to strengthen your glory in the faith that is in Christ Jesus—who, according to the purpose of the will of the eternal Father God, with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, became human for the salvation of the world; was born of the undefiled Virgin; reconciled the world to God through his death; erased our sins through the redemption that is in his blood; and, having conquered death in himself, brought us to life together with him and raised us up to a living hope, to an imperishable, undefiled, incorruptible inheritance (1 Peter 1).

In him, as we trust in his mercy, eternal salvation and life have been prepared for you, provided that you hold firm hope in him to the end (Hebrews 3), believing—as the apostle Paul says—that “in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2). Therefore serve him with all fear and humility, remembering that the Psalmist says: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21). Let this also always be in your mouth and always in your heart, as follows shortly after that verse: “And my soul shall live for him, and my descendants shall serve him.”

We wish you to know that it is our desire, if in any way we could, to send some of our brothers to you who would be faithful and learned enough to instruct you in every branch of knowledge and teaching in Christ Jesus. Thus, properly instructed according to evangelical and apostolic doctrine, you would not waver in anything, but, rooted and founded upon the firm foundation that is Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 3), would grow more abundantly and perfectly in the power of God and, according to the working of faith, would produce fruit worthy of eternal reward.

[Col. 0522B] Because this is very difficult for us, both on account of the distance of the lands and especially on account of the unknown languages, we ask you—as we have also announced to the king of the Danes—to send from among the younger men and nobles of your land to the apostolic court, so that, carefully instructed under the wings of the apostles Peter and Paul in the sacred and divine laws, they may bring back to you the mandates of the apostolic see, not as unknown men but as people known to us, and may worthily and effectively preach and cultivate among you whatever the order of the Christian religion demands—not as inexperienced or ignorant persons, but as men prudent in language, knowledge, and conduct, with God himself assisting them.

It has also been reported to us that the brothers of the king of the Danes have approached your highness, intending, by relying on your forces and resources, to compel their brother to divide the kingdom with them. How much this matter concerns the kingdom’s ruin, the confusion of the Christian people, the destruction of the churches—which the neighboring pagan cruelty daily longs to attack—and the desolation of the whole land, Truth itself, who is Christ, teaches us in the Gospel when he says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and house will fall upon house” (Luke 11).

Therefore we strongly admonish your eminence to take the greatest care that you never, through anyone’s persuasion, give anyone in this matter either your consent or assistance, lest—as God forbid—this sin be turned back upon you, or divine indignation be stirred against you and your kingdom because of that kingdom’s division.

[Col. 0522D] We gladly wish and advise you to arrange that the aforementioned king of the Danes receive his brothers into the kingdom with charity, and distribute the remaining goods and honors among them wherever he can, so that neither unworthy necessity oppresses them nor the condition or dignity of the kingdom is weakened.

For the rest, always reflect upon the hope of your calling, and, attentive to what the Lord says in the Gospel—“They will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8)—do not delay; run, hasten. You are from the ends of the earth, but if you run and hasten, you will be joined to the first Fathers in the kingdom.

Let your course be faith, love, and longing. Let your journey consist in constantly considering the glory of the world to be fleeting and therefore something to be held with bitterness rather than delight. Let the use and exercise of your power be to aid the oppressed, defend widows, judge orphans, and not merely love justice but defend it with all your strength.

By these footsteps, through this treasure and these resources, one proceeds from the earthly kingdom to the heavenly, from fleeting and fragile things to certain and enduring joy, and from what is transitory and passing to glory that is eternal and ever-lasting.

May almighty God, who is rich and abundant in mercy, through the merits and authority of the apostles Peter and Paul—and through them, through the authority divinely granted to us, though unworthy—absolve you and all your faithful from all your sins and direct you into all his will, so that in this life he may cause you to merit what, in eternal blessedness, he will repay you with a crown increased many times over.

Given at Rome, on the eighteenth [nineteenth] day before the Kalends of January, in the second indiction.

## Letter XIV. To Duke Welfo. (1078)

He shows that Welf will have no cause for murmuring against him if he carefully considers what was established at the synod. If he clings to God with a faithful heart, he will obtain victory.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Welfo, duke, greeting and apostolic blessing.

If you carefully weigh, according to the equity of pontifical office and not according to your own will, what we do and say concerning the common affair—indeed, the greatest disturbance of your kingdom—you will not murmur against us, but, God guiding us, you will recognize that we are proceeding by the path of our Fathers.

Consider what the Holy Spirit, though we are unworthy, deigned to establish through us at the holy synod held at Rome during Lent this year, and you will recognize how much the authority and power of blessed Peter avail and can accomplish. Therefore give continual thanks to almighty God and blessed Peter, and, not murmuring against us but giving thanks to blessed Peter, hope for better things.

Believe me, dearest brothers: those who trust in falsehood and cunning, rather than in justice and simplicity, will utterly fall, and the sword of blessed Peter will confound them by devouring them.

What was done at the Lenten synod, or at the synod we held in November, can be reported to you by your faithful men who were present and by our letters sent to you. But you, trusting in justice and relying upon the help of blessed Peter, take courage in the Lord and in the power of his strength. For if you cling to God with a faithful and steadfast heart, victory and peace will soon smile upon you.

May almighty God, through the merits of blessed Mary, Queen of Heaven, and through the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, entrusted to me, though greatly unworthy, absolve you and all your companions who love justice and cherish the see of blessed Peter from every sin, and lead you to eternal life.

[Col. 0524A] Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the second indiction.

## Letter XV. To the Monks of Marseille. (1079)

He urges them to endure the absence of their abbot with a calm spirit and assures them that he will soon send him back. He desires to unite their monastery to the apostolic see, as he did Cluny. He leaves the remaining matters of these letters to be communicated by the bearer.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brothers residing in the monastery of Marseille, greeting and apostolic blessing.

I have saddened you—or rather, blessed Peter has troubled and disturbed you, and he himself will heal you. For your abbot, his son, came to us and, for love of him, became obedient even to the imprisonment of his body; and because he was prepared, if necessary, to die, he will receive a reward for this.

But, as you know, my brothers, good men who serve God even in peace are rare; rarer still are those who do not fear persecutions for his sake or who do not hesitate to oppose themselves to the enemies of God. Therefore Christian religion has almost perished—alas, woe!—and the pride of the impious has grown exceedingly.

Our aforesaid father, truly loving the prince of the apostles, stood with us in his battle line and, with Christ guiding him, rendered us assistance, not turning a deaf ear to what the Apostle says: “If we are partners in sufferings, we shall also be partners in consolations” (1 Corinthians 1).

But although reason consoles you, charity drives you to grief because you have been deprived, as it were for a long time, of so great a father and such a leader. We therefore ask you, on behalf of almighty God and for love of blessed Peter, to bear with us patiently, since, with God’s help, we shall soon send him back to you rejoicing. For this reason, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, entrusted to us, though greatly unworthy, we promise you forgiveness of all your sins and grant you absolution with a blessing.

For we trust, in the superabundant goodness of the Most High and the ineffable clemency of the Queen of Heaven, that blessed Peter and Paul will guard and protect your place more than usual, since it appears to suffer loss and hardship on account of their service.

For we desire to unite the place of blessed Paul and yours in such a way that, just as Cluny has for a long time been specially attached to the apostolic see and rejoices in the special assistance and blessing of this Church, so may yours be.

May the supreme love of Christ move you, dearest brothers, so that you may love us as you love yourselves and extend a helping hand to us placed amid a great storm, always keeping before your eyes the words: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

Whatever we have written less fully, we have left to be communicated by the bearer of these letters.

May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, through the merits and intercession of the Mother and Virgin of God, and through the authority granted to blessed Peter and Paul, princes of the apostles, look upon you, renew and guard you always, reveal to you what the new song may be, and kindle you in holy rejoicing, so that you may know perfectly how to lament human frailty and to recognize the ineffable goodness of God; and, ever growing in his love, may you deserve, with the heavenly Mother as your guide, to attain certain knowledge of him and wondrous joy.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones [Kalends] of January, in the second indiction.

## Letter XVI. To Berengar, Bishop of Girona. (1079)

He embraces Berengar’s devotion toward the apostolic see and urges him to persevere in it. He instructs him to reconcile peace among Raymond’s sons; if he cannot fully achieve this, he should at least arrange a truce, meanwhile declaring to them that whichever one of them prevents peace will be excommunicated, while the one who obeys the apostolic see will be assisted in obtaining his paternal inheritance. He further instructs him to attend to the salvation of his brother, the bishop of Narbonne.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Berengar, bishop of Girona, greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned through our son, the abbot of Marseille, you say that you are prepared to persevere with the firmest and most steadfast spirit in obedience and fidelity to blessed Peter, and henceforth to order your life and conduct according to our command. You desire and wish, above all others in your regions, to remain familiarly attached to us.

We, for our part, extend the bosom of paternal affection to receive the feeling of such devotion, and in every way favor your pious love toward us, so that you may—as you promise—continue to grow in love of Peter and in concern for ecclesiastical religion and Christian peace, and may render yourself worthy of apostolic fellowship through the sincerest obedience.

Therefore, first of all, we entrust you with a matter about which we are deeply concerned. We have learned that discord has arisen between the sons of Raymond Berengar through vanity and pride, and especially through the counsel of the impious—indeed, through the envy of the devil. I am deeply grieved by this, both because of my love for their father, who has loved me greatly ever since he came to know me, and because I perceive grave danger threatening the Christian people in those regions, who are known to suffer greatly under the hatred of the impious Saracens.

[Col. 0525D] Therefore we command you, joining with you your religious neighboring abbots—namely, those of Tournier, Ripoll, and Sant Cugat—and whatever other clergy and laymen who fear God you can find, to strive to restore and establish peace between them.

If they should perhaps refuse to heed your admonitions, then, after showing them this present letter, compel them by our authority to maintain the firmest truce until the appointed time. Before that time we shall send there legates from our side who will determine their dispute so justly that they will not turn aside toward anyone’s favor, whether by reward or partiality.

You must firmly impress this upon them: if they remain disobedient to us and, at the devil’s instigation, prefer to remain in fraternal hatred, we shall take away the grace of blessed Peter from the one through whose fault or pride this peace has failed. We shall hasten to cut him off, as a member of the devil and a desolator of Christian religion, together with all his supporters, from communion with Christian society, so that thereafter he may have neither victory in war nor prosperity in this world.

But for the other, who humbly consents to peace and renders due obedience to the apostolic see, we shall establish, by the grace of blessed Peter, the unconquerable assistance of apostolic favor. As befits a son of the holy Roman Church, we shall do everything possible to help him obtain his paternal inheritance and dignity, and by apostolic authority we shall command all Christians in those regions to favor him and assist him in obtaining the principate.

Whatever you determine between them in this matter, inform us by letter as quickly as possible; indeed, if it proves appropriate, arrange to present yourself to us.

Moreover, I wish you to be more concerned than you have hitherto been about your brother, the bishop of Narbonne. I grieve deeply over his destruction, and I wonder that you do not strive to lead to salvation one to whom you are joined by a double bond of kinship, when you know that, solely because of someone’s carnal or spiritual relationship, a Christian ought to expose himself [perhaps “oppose himself”; HARD., and likewise in the MUTIN. codex] to such grave danger.

Therefore act, and, inflamed by fraternal charity, approach him with confidence in our admonition. Remind him both of the excesses of his long life already past and of the judgment of divine vengeance that now threatens him. If possible, recall him from the very threshold of eternal death, and by securing your brother’s salvation merit from divine generosity not only the joy of your heart but also the greatest reward of eternal recompense.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones [Kalends] of January, in the second indiction.

## Letter XVII. To the Abbot of Cluny. (1079)

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to N., [Note: [Col. 0525D] He unquestionably means Hugh.] venerable abbot of Cluny and his dearest brother, greeting and apostolic blessing.

If Romans came to your regions as often as your people come to us, we would more frequently inform you by letter or word how earthly and heavenly affairs are being conducted around us. But since, while you are sufficiently intent on nourishing courtiers, you have little concern for peasants, you must further recall to mind that our poor and pious Redeemer fed angels in heaven in such a way that on earth he not only did not despise sinners but even ate with them.

Why, dearest brother, do you not weigh and consider in what danger and in what misery holy Church is found? Where are those who willingly offer themselves for the love of God, resist the impious, and do not fear to undergo death for justice and truth?

Behold, those who appear to fear or love God flee from Christ’s warfare, put the salvation of their brothers second, and, loving only themselves, seek repose. The shepherds flee, and the dogs, the defenders of the flock, flee as well. Wolves and robbers attack Christ’s sheep, with no one resisting.

You have taken—or received—a leader into Cluniac repose and have caused a hundred thousand Christians to be without a guardian. If our exhortation has had little effect with you and the command of the apostolic see has found no obedience in you, why have the sighs of the poor, the tears of widows, the devastation of churches, the cries of orphans, and the grief and murmuring of priests and monks not frightened you, so that you would not set aside what the Apostle says, namely: “Charity does not seek what is its own” (1 Corinthians 13); and so that you would not keep in your heart, as you are accustomed: “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13)?

What will blessed Benedict and Gregory say to you? One commands that a novice be tested for a year; the other forbids a soldier to become a monk before three years have passed.

We say these things because we grieve that scarcely any good prince can be found. Monks, however, through God’s mercy, and priests, soldiers, and not a few poor men who fear God are found in various places; but throughout the whole of the West scarcely any princes who fear and love God can be found.

We shall now refrain from writing further to you about this matter, because I trust that, through God’s mercy, the charity of Christ that habitually dwells in you will pierce your heart by avenging me and will show you how great my grief ought to be over a good prince taken away from his mother. If one no worse than he has succeeded him in government, we may have some consolation.

Moreover, we admonish your fraternity to conduct yourself more cautiously in such matters and to place love of God and neighbor before every virtue. Let these considerations also move you to extend to us the hand of prayer and to urge all the brothers entrusted to you to do the same, so that you may deserve to advance from virtue to virtue and reach the perfection of supreme charity.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the second indiction.

## Letter XVIII. To Evrard, Bishop of Parma. (1079)

He rebukes Evrard for arresting an abbot who was coming to the synod. He orders him to release him. For this reason he suspends Evrard from episcopal office until he comes to Rome. If he does not obey, he forbids him entry into the church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Evrard [Everard], bishop of Parma.

For a long time we have loved you with pure and sincere charity, but by arresting an abbot who was coming to us and hastening to the holy synod, you have not returned an equal measure of love to ours. It was a grave deed, unworthy of your office, and I do not know by whose command or prompting you presumed to act against such a man. Even if he owed you something, nevertheless, since he was coming to us, he did not deserve to be detained.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you that, if you have not yet released him, upon receiving this letter you must immediately have him escorted honorably to Matilda. Meanwhile, because you delayed him, refrain from episcopal office until you yourself come to us. But if—which we do not expect—you are unwilling to obey these commands of ours, namely, to release him, we absolutely forbid you, on behalf of blessed Peter, to enter the church.

Given at the synod, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XIX. To Haremanno, Ulderic, etc. (1079)

He asserts that it was determined at the synod that, unless they return the property of the Church of Bamberg within thirty days, they will be subject to excommunication.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Haremanno, Ulderic, Frederick, Mazelin [Muzolin, and likewise below], and Gotebold [Gotebald], soldiers of the Church of Bamberg.

We have long understood that you, namely Hermann and Ulderic, took the property of that Church in return for the installation of its already deposed bishop, He . . . . . (Hermann), and that you, Frederick, Mazelin, Herold, and Wirint, after his excommunication by this see, likewise received the property of the same Church from him.

We have also learned that you, Gotebold, received the property of the aforementioned Church from the hand of the king while the bishop was being held captive.

Know, therefore, that at the council we recently celebrated it was established that, unless within twenty days after the words of this mission of ours have reached your ears you either return the aforesaid property of the Church, which you unjustly retain, or receive it from the bishop’s hand, you will be subject to the danger of excommunication.

But if, coming to the bishop in repentance, you restore the frequently mentioned property, the bishop may release you from the bond of excommunication.

Given at the synod, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XX. To Count Centullus. (1079)

He asserts that Centullus disgraces the outstanding virtues with which he was endowed by having his kinswoman as his wife. He advises him to abstain from so great a crime and to venerate the bishops and the Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Count Centullus, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard about you from people whom we trust matters that ought to commend a Christian prince in every respect: namely, that you are a lover of justice, a defender of the poor, and a promoter of peace. Therefore we receive you into love and favor as a son of the Roman Church, and we admonish you to strive to advance day by day in the good works you have begun.

Nevertheless, we have learned that there is something reprehensible in you: namely, that you have your kinswoman as your wife. You must be exceedingly careful about this, lest, because of this fault, whatever other good things you do perish.

Act, therefore, and, according to the counsel of Bishop Amatus of Oloron and Bernard, abbot of Marseille—if he is able to reach your regions—strive to amend the aforesaid guilt and do penance for it, lest you lose your soul on this account and bring shame upon the noble woman entrusted to your protection.

Above all, always strive to venerate, honor, and defend the Church of God, and show reverence and obedience to bishops as to your fathers. Know that by this you will merit greater glory both in this world and perpetual life in the next.

If you had the opportunity to come to us, we would wish to see you and instruct you more fully concerning the salvation of your soul.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXI. To the People of Arles. (1079)

He reproves them for being moved by scarcely any concern that their Church is deprived of a pastor. For this reason he sends the bishop of Gap, so that they may either elect a bishop or promise to receive as pastor anyone whom he sends to them. He indicates that he has entrusted the bishop with the rest of what ought to be said.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of the Church of Arles, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we perceive that, once pastoral guardianship has been removed, no small danger threatens the flock, we are greatly troubled by concern for you and pierced with much grief, since we know that your Church has for so long been deprived of the vigilance of a pastor and the governance of a suitable leader.

We have discovered that in this matter you are less concerned than you ought to be—indeed, almost forgetful of your own salvation—and are moved by scarcely any care or affection. This is for us a cause of still greater sadness, since scarcely anything is more destructive than failing by any means to rise against pressing evils and either not knowing how or not wishing to provide for one’s salvation in the supreme danger.

Moved, therefore, by these concerns and by the cause of such great desolation among you, we have sent to you our brother Leodegarius, bishop of Gap, so that, with his counsel, you may either elect according to God such a person as our vicar, Hugh, bishop of Die, recommends to us by letter, or, if—as we believe—no person worthy of so great a government can be found among you, you may, in the hands of our brother Leodegarius, bishop of Gap, firmly promise to receive as pastor the man whom we shall send to you, consecrated and marked with the honor of the pallium, on behalf of blessed Peter.

You must consider that, according to the election of God’s grace, you are numbered among Christ’s sheep, and that you will by no means live securely unless you have one who presides over you in his place and, with God’s help, fortifies you through constant vigilance against the attacks of the cunning plotter.

Act, therefore, so that no one may be able to prevent you from providing for the honor of your Church and the common salvation of your souls. Do not let the visitation of our legation to you appear to have been made in vain, for through it our charity and authority are presented to you. Know that, with God as author, whatever we owe and can provide by virtue of both is accompanied by a ready and tireless will to promote your welfare.

We have entrusted the rest of what must be said to our brother Leodegarius. In this matter of the legation, I wish you to believe him as though these things were being spoken by us in person into your ears.

Given at Rome, on the Kalends of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXII. To Countess Matilda. (1079)

He replies concerning the marriage of Duke Theodoric, concerning his involvement in arranging peace between himself and King Henry, and concerning the duke’s excommunication by the bishop of Metz.

[Col. 0530B] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Matilda, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because you wished to learn our mind concerning these matters, you sent us word that Duke Theodoric desired to take in marriage the former wife of the margrave Petronius. We reply to you: he is not sufficiently known to us, nor has she been entrusted to us in such a way that we wish to undertake anything concerning the matter.

You also reported concerning the same duke that, if it pleased us, he would involve himself in arranging peace between us and King Henry. We therefore reply concerning this. The king’s legate swore in the presence of the universal synod, at his lord’s command, that he would obey our mandates in every respect.

I believe that it is not unknown to your knowledge that for this reason, and in this hope, we have already sent our legates.

As for the aforementioned duke, who has been excommunicated by the bishop of Metz, since you are not unaware that we know of the sentence pronounced against him, you should know that we have consented to it and confirmed it, unless, within twenty days after learning our mandates, he obeys our commands; unless he freely relinquishes the city and property of Saint Stephen, which he unjustly invaded; and unless he makes satisfaction to the Church.

Given at Rome, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXIII. To the People of Orléans. (1079)

Desiring to remedy the afflictions of their Church, he says that he has gladly received Sanzon, whom they had desired as bishop. Yet, lest this prejudice Bishop Rainerius, who was still alive although they asserted him to be useless, he says that he will send legates to investigate the matter, so that he may then confirm the election. Meanwhile, no one is to alienate any of the Church’s property.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Orléans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know without hesitation that we grieve deeply over the afflictions and hardships of your Church, which we have especially loved and which was once one of the noblest Churches of Gaul—and, with God’s favor, will be so again. Since we are concerned to determine how we ought to help it, we are working diligently so that it may return to its former honor and glory.

Concerning our son Sanzon, whom you desire as bishop, know that we gladly received him and treated him with paternal love. But because the aforesaid Bishop Rainerius—who, as is said, has been useless to your Church—has not yet been entirely shown to be separated from it, and lest we appear to prejudice anyone, or lest anyone suspect that, because of friendship with someone, we intend to act against justice, we have decided to send our legates to you. After carefully investigating and establishing the truth, they will be able, by our authority—or rather, that of blessed Peter—to pass judgment concerning him as justice dictates.

Afterward we shall take care to confirm your election according to God and to strengthen it in whatever ways appear necessary, according to canonical institutions.

Meanwhile, on behalf of blessed Peter, we admonish and command all of you and everyone with whom the goods of that Church may be found, wherever they are, that no one presume to alienate or destroy the gifts and ornaments known to belong to it.

If anyone rashly attempts to act contrary to these commands of ours, let him know that he will lose the grace of blessed Peter and, unless he repents, incur the sword of anathema.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXIV. To Amatus, Bishop of Oloron. (1079)

He entrusts to Amatus and the bishop of Die the careful resolution of the dispute between the abbots of Sainte-Croix and Saint-Sever. Meanwhile, he decrees that whatever is under litigation must be restored in full to the abbey of Sainte-Croix.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Amatus, bishop of Oloron (that is, Oleron in the MUTIN. codex; Orolon), in Gascony, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Jozelin, our fellow bishop and archbishop of Bordeaux, came to the threshold of the apostles and brought back to our memory what had formerly been done concerning the disagreement between the monastery of Sainte-Croix and Saint-Sever, and what decision it had received from the Roman Church.

We also found letters formerly sent by us to the abbot of Saint-Sever concerning this matter, and learned that the abbot had been disobedient according to their terms. Therefore, lest either party suspect that it is being prejudiced, we have determined that this case must be carefully reconsidered before you and our brother Hugh, bishop of Die, so that the two of you, as lawful judges, may, with God’s help, bring this matter to an end.

We have also adjudged that whatever is under litigation must be restored in full to the abbey of Sainte-Croix, so that, once possession has been returned to it, whatever you do will be canonical and lawful, and you will appear irreproachable in executing our judgment.

If he proves disobedient and does not restore the investiture of the aforesaid church to the abbey of Sainte-Croix, separate him, as a rebel, deservedly from communion in the body and blood of the Lord.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXV. To Arnald, Abbot of Saint-Sever. (1079)

He indicates that he has entrusted the bishops of Die and Oloron with determining what should be done in the dispute between Arnald and the abbot of Sainte-Croix; therefore he commands Arnald to obey them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Arnald, abbot of Saint-Sever, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know that, after your recent departure, we found certain letters in which we clearly detected your disobedience. Therefore let it be known to you that we have entrusted the case that is known to exist between you and the abbot of Sainte-Croix to our brothers and fellow bishops, Hugh of Die and Amatus of Oloron, our legates, for more careful examination. Whatever they, acting as judges, determine concerning it, you must henceforth regard as settled and firmly binding upon you.

Nevertheless, meanwhile, we command by apostolic authority that you restore in full to the abbey of Sainte-Croix that possession—namely, the church of Sainte-Marie of Soulac—over which a dispute has arisen between you, and we admonish you by command on behalf of blessed Peter to allow it to possess the property peacefully until the case comes to judgment.

For we consider it unworthy and utterly contrary to canonical institutions that a case requiring examination should be brought forward unless the person suffering violence has first been revested with the property under litigation.

Therefore, in accordance with what we have both admonished and commanded, we have taken care to impress upon you again that we must not find you any longer disobedient in this matter, as we have found you until now.

If your disobedience is again reported to our ears, know without doubt that you will have incurred the wrath of blessed Peter and of us, and will have provoked a sentence of due punishment to the peril of your office.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the second indiction.

## Letter XXVI. To Fulcard. (1079)

[Note: Provost and canons of Lille.]

He commands them to receive Lambert, whom they had mistreated contrary to his commands, and to restore what had been taken from him. If they do not obey, he threatens to punish them.

**[Col. 0532D]** Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Fulcard, provost of the Insulan congregation, and to the other canons of that same congregation, both lesser and greater, although otherwise deserving [or: “although you may deserve otherwise”]: greetings and apostolic blessing.

You have gravely offended us by the injury and dispossession of the property inflicted by you upon Lambert, our son—or rather, inflicted upon us in his person—especially since, through our man Ingelrannus, we had commanded you to inflict no injury upon him on account of the obedience which we imposed upon him. Therefore we command you, and by apostolic authority enjoin you, as canons specially protected by the privileges of blessed Peter, that you receive this son of ours, Lambert, your brother and fellow canon, with every kindness and affection, and restore to him everything belonging to him in full. Through his intervention we remit to you whatever offense you have committed against him and against us, on the express condition that henceforth you do not presume to act against our decrees or those of the holy canons.

But if you neglect to do this—which God forbid—and a complaint should again reach us or our vicar, the venerable Hugh, bishop of Die, you will lose the favor of blessed Peter and of us; nor will we in any way thereafter endure to remain unavenged. Rather, as shall be fitting, we shall avenge our contempt with the sword of blessed Peter.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF DOL

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0533B]**

He orders them, after removing Walter, whom they had elected abbot contrary to the excommunication and who had been deposed in a council, to receive the archbishop of Vienne as abbot. Because of their disobedience, however, they are to appear before the bishop of Die and obey him; otherwise, he says that he will confirm the excommunication imposed upon them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the monks of the monastery of Dol.

Know that Walter, whom you appointed abbot over yourselves contrary to the excommunication of the Apostolic See, has been irrevocably deposed by us with the approval of the Roman council; and, if after learning of this letter he should further meddle in the administration **[Col. 0533C]** of your abbey, he is to be entirely excommunicated.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you to receive without any opposition our brother Wormund, archbishop of Vienne, whom, God willing, we have appointed your abbot, and to obey him in everything, with the whole devotion of your hearts, as a father and abbot.

And because by your disobedience you have incurred no slight offense, we command you to present yourselves in the city of Valence on the first Sunday after Pentecost, that is, on the octave, before our vicar Hugh, bishop of Die, in order to make satisfaction, and obediently to observe whatever he commands you. But if, moved by a spirit of pride, you prove disobedient to this letter of ours, know without any doubt that from that day we have confirmed the excommunication imposed upon you by the aforesaid **[Col. 0533D]** vicar of ours.

Given at Rome, on the eighth [thirteenth] day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE NOBLES OF BERRY

**[Note: Princes of the region of Berry.]**

*(Year 1079.)*

The subject is the same.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rodulf, Odo, Eppo, Umbald, Everard, Bozo, Girald, Adelard, and the other princes of the region of Berry: greetings and apostolic blessing, if they obey.

**[Col. 0534A]** We marvel at the audacity and insolence of your presumption: contrary to right and to the apostolic excommunication laid upon you, you have seized the abbey of Dol, which until now you had held under your protection—or rather, invaded it—to the further ruin of both your souls and your bodies, after casting out the man whom, with God’s will, we ourselves consecrated as your abbot with our own hands.

We irrevocably deposed Walter the invader; and under pain of excommunication we forbade him and his supporters the property of the Church. To our brother Wormund, archbishop of Vienne, we granted—or rather restored—the abbey of Dol.

We therefore admonish you, and by apostolic authority command you, that, having rejected the dominion of the aforesaid invader, you obey your abbot, Wormund, archbishop of Vienne, in accordance with canon law, with sincere mind and pure heart.

But if henceforth you prove rebellious against God and blessed Peter in this matter, beginning on the first Sunday after Pentecost, that is, on the octave, you will be subject to excommunication together with the monks of Dol, unless you make satisfaction before our vicar Hugh, bishop of Die, at Valence.

If, however, you offer obedience and assistance to your spiritual father, our brother Wormund, archbishop of Vienne, you will receive the favor of God and of blessed Peter.

But you, Rodulf, because in this matter God has granted you greater power than to the others, we ask and command that you restore him to the abbey without deceit or fraud, and, forgetting every anger and disagreement, cleave to him as a most beloved son, so that you may receive the favor of God and the forgiveness of your sins from him to whom the power of binding and loosing has been given.

Given at Rome, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXIX. TO LADISLAUS, KING OF THE HUNGARIANS

*(Year 1079.)*

He praises the king’s devotion toward the Apostolic See. He commends certain counts and soldiers faithful to blessed Peter who have been unjustly banished. He urges him to defend the churches and orders him to send legates to him.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ladislaus, king of the Hungarians: greetings and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from the frequent reports of your faithful, and confirm as true through the testimony of our own people, your excellence is prepared with all the devotion of your affection and heart to serve blessed Peter, as religious authority ought, and to obey us, as becomes a generous son.

Accordingly, we rightly praise your devotion in this endeavor and sincerely rejoice that, by following the footsteps of the best kings, you are distinguished both by preserving the rule of justice in your conduct and the line of nobility in your blood.

Since, therefore, we have sufficient confidence in the generosity and obedience of your highness, we do not hesitate to invite you to undertake something consistent with our universal pastoral concern and also very much in harmony with your honor. In this way, both those things which have been credited about you on the basis of words alone may be shown true by the evidence of deeds, and a firmer reason may be made clear to us why we ought rightly to love you, above others of royal dignity, with greater and more special affection.

Accordingly, we wish you to regard as commended to you, on our behalf, those counts—or [lacuna], namely D. [lacuna] and C. [lacuna]—and their soldiers, who, as we have learned, because they were faithful to blessed Peter and supporters of justice, were driven into exile by an unjust sentence.

Since your illustriousness has until now taken care on your own initiative to assist them, let them now feel that, because of their fidelity to blessed Peter and our recommendation, a more abundant gift of comfort and aid has come to them.

For the future, we admonish your prudence always to strive to follow the path of justice along an unwavering road; to protect widows, orphans, and strangers with paternal compassion; not merely to refrain from harming churches, but also to defend them from the insolence and presumption of the arrogant and invaders; and diligently to preserve whatever else you rightly understand to be required.

We also wish you to know that some men once came to us as your legates. We likewise charged them to suggest to your affection that you ought to send others, so that we might become more certain. It nevertheless remains uncertain to us whether our commands reached you, or whether you later sent anyone; it is clear, however, that no legate from you has come to us since then.

Therefore we have decided to write to you again, repeating the same request, and likewise to impress upon you again what we have already requested concerning the counts. Thus, if you have not yet sent messengers, you will not neglect to send them any longer, and you will strive to extend the hand of protection to all the aforesaid people more familiarly and readily in every respect.

May almighty and merciful God, from whom all good things proceed, lead your steps along the path of justice through the merits and intercessions of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of the blessed Peter and Paul; may he guide you steadfastly to the end, and grant you to govern the temporal reins of this kingdom in this life in such a way that, by meriting eternal things, you may be able to attain them.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXX. TO LANFRANC, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0535D]**

He reproves him for not having visited him since his accession. Since he knows that the king is the reason for this, he urges him to admonish the king not to presume anything unjust against the Roman Church, and to come to him himself as soon as possible.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Lanfranc, archbishop of the Cantuarians: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the time when, although unworthy, we took upon our neck the priestly yoke of the supreme see, your fraternity has taken little care to come to us. The less we were able to expect this from your affection, the more astonished and amazed we are. Unless apostolic gentleness and the ancient token of affection had held us back until now, you would certainly have learned long ago that we have taken this grievously.

Yet, as we know with complete certainty, either fear of the king—namely, the man whom among all others of that rank we have always loved with particular affection—or, above all, your own fault has prevented your coming to us. If any memory of our former affection remained, or if the love due to the Roman Church, your mother, remained in your mind, no terror of worldly power and no superstitious affection for any person ought to have drawn you away from our presence.

But if a new swelling of arrogance now raises him up against the Apostolic See, or if any desire or insolence impels him against us, we shall bear it all the more grievously in proportion as it becomes clear that he has made himself unworthy of our affection.

Nevertheless, so that this may not happen to him, your religious devotion can prevent it in the following way: by explaining the matter carefully to him and admonishing him steadfastly, give him counsel not to presume anything unjust against the Roman Church, mother of all, nor insolently dare anything alien to religious authority; and do not allow him to attempt any longer to restrain either your devotion or that of anyone else from visiting the Apostolic See.

It is therefore fitting that your fraternity wisely correct the excesses of its negligence and hasten as soon as possible to the Apostolic See, presenting yourself to our sight, as we desire and have often commanded, so that, by discussing these and other matters with you in person, we may, with God’s favor, receive from our conversation an increase of benefit for the Church.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the **[Col. 0536C]** second indiction.

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE INHABITANTS OF THE PROVINCE

*(Year 1079.)*

He orders them, under penalty of excommunication, to restore the property of the monastery of Saint Peter.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, princes, clergy, and laypeople residing in Provence, except those subject to excommunication: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We suppose that you all know that the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the place called Montmajour, is subject by a special right to the holy Roman Church and has long been protected by the privileges of the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, the responsibility of the government we have undertaken obliges us to provide for all churches, we must watch especially over those which in some way adhere more closely to the Roman and Apostolic See and hope above all to be defended by its protection.

Accordingly, since we have heard that some among you have invaded, alienated, and plundered the property of the aforesaid monastery with sacrilegious hands, contrary to right and justice, we admonish you with paternal affection and command by apostolic authority that all who are known to hold by force the property they have invaded hasten to make suitable restitution and satisfaction; and that no one henceforth presume, at the peril of his soul’s salvation, violently to touch the goods of that church.

Whoever, therefore, opposes these salutary commands of ours and attempts, as has been said, to retain the property of the church by sacrilegious audacity contrary to our prohibition, if, after being admonished once, twice, and three times at suitable intervals, he scorns to make amends, will provoke against himself the anger and fury of almighty God through apostolic excommunication.

To those who obey, however, by apostolic authority and through the power of blessed Peter granted to us, although unworthy, we grant forgiveness of their sins.

Given at Rome, on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXII. TO ISEMBERT, BISHOP OF POITIERS

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0537B]** He orders that the property of Rorgon, belonging to his brother Hugh, which has been taken away, be restored under penalty of excommunication.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Is͟e͟mbert, bishop of Poitiers: greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has reached our ears that Hugh of Lezay [*Hugo Delezini*; *de Leziniaco*; in the Mutina manuscript, *Delerzini*] has unjustly presumed to seize the property of Rorgon of Coë, which, after Rorgon’s death, ought by right to pass into the possession of his brother, namely Hugh, our faithful servant and son.

Since, therefore, we have received the aforesaid Hugh, our cleric, and his property under the protection of the Apostolic See, we command your fraternity, acting in our place, to inform Duke William of this matter and urge him to show in this matter also how faithful he is to blessed Peter.

First of all, however, we want your affection to endeavor, on our behalf, to bring the aforesaid man of Lezay [*Leziniacensem*; *Deleziniacensem*] before the said duke, and, rebuking him for his presumption, admonish him to make satisfaction.

If, after being admonished once, twice, and three times at suitable intervals, he remains obstinate and, disobedient to our commands, scorns to obey justice, we command by apostolic authority that you bind him with the bond of anathema until, coming to his senses, he restores what he has taken. You may have no doubt that we shall later confirm this action.

Given at Rome, on the Ides of April, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0537D]**

He orders him either to restore the property which the Church of Mâcon had peacefully possessed and which he had taken away, or to compensate for it by an exchange. Otherwise, the matter is entrusted to the bishop of Die and the abbot of Saint Paul for settlement of the dispute between them.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Landeric, bishop of Mâcon, our brother and fellow bishop, coming to the threshold of the apostles, complained to us that you were taking away from him the rights of his church, which, from the time of his predecessors, even those who were simoniacs, it had appeared to possess peacefully.

We therefore judged it right and proper that the goods which the church held without disturbance in the time of irreligious men should not, under a religious shepherd ordained in the Roman Church, be deprived of them without reason.

Accordingly, we admonish your affection that, if the aforesaid Church of Mâcon possessed the properties about which it complains until the time of our aforementioned brother, you should thereafter either allow it to retain them peacefully or strive to provide a suitable exchange.

But if you yourselves cannot settle this matter between you, we wish our brother, the bishop of Die, and the abbot of Saint Paul to take part in the affair, so that, through their diligent intervention, the dispute may find a proper and suitable conclusion and no further disagreement remain between you.

Without concord, we hold that neither religious devotion [perhaps: “religious conduct”] nor any other work, even if it appears good, has any value.

Given at Rome, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO GEBUIN, ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS

*(Year 1079.)*

He confirms the dignity of primacy granted to the Church of Lyons over four provinces, provided that the archbishop was not elected by simony.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gebuin [*Gebuerius*], archbishop of Lyons.

Desiring, insofar as divine condescension permits, to imitate the ancient footsteps of the holy Fathers, whose successor we are in the administration of this see, although unworthy and far unequal to their merits, it is fitting for us to preserve unharmed and unaltered the right which they themselves conferred upon each church according to its merit and dignity, and to strengthen it for perpetual stability by the protection of our decrees.

Therefore, because you, dearest brother in Christ Gebuin, asked us to confirm the dignity granted by our predecessors to the Church over which, by God’s authority, you are known to preside, and to protect whatever belongs to it from hostile attack through the defense of the Apostolic See, yielding to your prayers we confirm the primacy over four provinces to your Church of Lyons, and through it to you and your successors—provided only that they have not been elected or promoted through any intervening payment, namely, by hand, by service, or by speech.

“By hand”: so that no price whatsoever is given by them or by anyone on their behalf.

“By service”: so that they render no service in return, as certain people customarily offer service to powerful persons with the intention of obtaining ecclesiastical preferment.

“By speech”: so that they do not pour out prayers either personally or through an intermediary.

Nor do we grant this dignity to those who have attained it through secular power, namely, through the gift or confirmation of any person who appears opposed to holy religion and contrary to the pure and authentic authority of the holy Fathers.

Rather, we decree that this dignity is to be granted to those who succeed you through a pure and sincere election and who have entered through the door, just as we know your fraternity to have entered.

But to those who have entered by another way—namely, those who, according to the Lord’s judgment, have not entered through the door but have climbed up elsewhere like thieves and robbers—we not only refuse the primacy of this dignity, but also judge them unworthy and excluded from every honor of ecclesiastical government.

The provinces which we confirm to you are Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens. These provinces are accordingly to show due obedience to the Church of Lyons and humbly and devoutly render the honor which the Roman pontiffs have prescribed in their own writings, with the reverence and authority of the Apostolic See preserved in all things.

Furthermore, in accordance with the tenor of your petition, by this decree of our authority we grant, concede, and confirm to your church privileges of this kind, decreeing that no king, and so forth, **[Col. 0539B]** to the end, as is established in the privilege which stands at the beginning of this booklet.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOPS OF ROUEN, TOURS, AND SENS

*(Year 1079.)*

He orders them to render obedience to the archbishop of Lyons, whose primacy he has confirmed over them on the basis of the ancient authority of the Fathers. He explains the reason and origin of the various ranks in the Church.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the brothers and fellow bishops of Rouen, Tours [*Tutonensis*, *Bituricensis*], and Sens: greetings and apostolic blessing.

As your fraternity knows, the Apostolic See, over which, although unworthy, we preside by God’s authority, under the inspiration of divine grace and instructed by the Holy Spirit, established prelates, archbishops, and primates throughout the various provinces and kingdoms.

By its constitution and authority, the Church of Lyons is known to have held primacy over four provinces—namely, Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens—for a long succession of years.

Desiring, therefore, insofar as with God’s favor we are able, to follow the examples of the holy Fathers, we strive, relying on their authority, to confirm again the primacy of the aforesaid Church, which they established and sanctioned by their decrees.

For this purpose divine providence established grades and distinct orders, so that, while inferiors showed reverence to superiors and superiors extended affection to inferiors, a single bond of concord might arise from diversity and the proper administration of individual duties be generated.

Indeed, the whole could not subsist by any other arrangement unless this great order of distinction preserved it.

Since creation cannot be governed or live in one uniform equality, the example of the heavenly armies instructs us: although there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but differ from one another in power and order, as you know.

If, then, such a distinction exists among those who are without sin, what human being would refuse willingly to submit to this arrangement?

From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn, and firm concord remains in a sincerity of love pleasing to God.

Since every office is then healthfully fulfilled when there is one superior to whom appeal may be made, the provinces were divided for the most part long before Christ’s coming. Later this division was renewed by the apostles and by blessed Clement, our predecessor.

At the head of the provinces, where formerly the primates of secular law and the first judicial authority had been established, the inhabitants of the other cities would seek refuge when necessity required—those who could not or were not permitted to flee to the courts of emperors or kings—on account of their oppressions or injustices. They appealed to these primates whenever necessary, just as their law commanded.

The divine and ecclesiastical laws likewise ordered that patriarchs or primates—holding one form of office, although their names were different—be established in those cities or more celebrated places, so that bishops might flee to them and appeal to them if necessary. Thus they alone, and no others, would enjoy the title of primates.

The remaining metropolitan cities, which had lesser judges, although they belonged to greater counties, nevertheless had their own metropolitans, who were rightly obedient to the aforesaid primates, just as had formerly been arranged in secular law. These did not enjoy the title of primates, but rather that of metropolitan archbishops.

Although each metropolitan city has its own province and ought to have its own metropolitan bishops, just as it formerly had secular metropolitan judges, nevertheless they were ordered, both then and now, to have primates, to whom the most important matters after the Apostolic See should be brought. There, those who required it might be raised up and justly restored, and those who were unjustly oppressed might be rightly reformed and supported; the cases of bishops and the judgments of the most important matters might be most justly concluded, with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you to see that you humbly and devoutly show the oft-mentioned Church of Lyons the honor and reverence prescribed for it over your churches by our predecessors, just as you do not doubt that your suffragans ought to render these things to you.

May almighty and merciful God of peace and justice, the serene observer, graciously inspire your hearts so that you may strive to advance with firm steps along the way of equity and concord in this world, in such a manner that, destined to receive eternal things in exchange for temporal ones, you may deserve to reach the boundaries of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Given at Rome, on the twelfth [XII] day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO THE CANONS OF LYONS

*(Year 1079.)*

He orders that, just as their dean had renounced into his hands the benefices acquired without the consent of his brethren, those who had obtained benefices either contrary to excommunication or by payment should renounce them into the hands of their archbishop.

**[Col. 0541A]** Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the Church of Lyons: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Some of you came to us with your archbishop; after consulting us about the state and welfare of your church, they departed without an apostolic blessing. Although we rightly took this amiss, we conceal it through apostolic gentleness; and, while desiring to care for your salvation, we refrain from pursuing their offenses.

Concerning our son and your church’s dean, B. [lacuna], we inform your affection that, guided by prudent and salutary counsel, he voluntarily renounced into our hands the obediences of the church and the other benefices which he had acquired without the common consent of his brethren, and promised not to meddle in them thereafter.
