Following his example, we command by apostolic authority that both those who withdrew secretly and the abbots and all persons of whatever clerical rank in your church—whoever acquired obediences or ecclesiastical offices through an agreement involving payment, or contrary to the excommunication of Landeric, bishop of Mâcon, which he pronounced in your chapter—arrange without delay to renounce them into the hands of our brother Gebuin, your archbishop.

We wish your affection to guard vigilantly the nobility by which your church has until now shone among all the churches of Gaul in the example of religion, and to begin now to increase in the form of religious conduct the glory which it has hitherto possessed above the others in dignity.

Know, moreover, that if, obeying our salutary commands, you judge it right to relinquish what has hitherto been wrongly held, we shall provide for you in both respects, so that you will neither lack temporal advantages nor be unable, through divine mercy, to obtain forgiveness of your error.

But if anyone, hardened in mind against his own salvation, remains disobedient to these commands for more than twenty days after they have come to his knowledge, we prohibit him, by apostolic authority, from entering any church or receiving the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, until he comes to his senses.

**[Col. 0541D]** Given at Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO JORDAN, PRINCE OF CAPUA

*(Year 1079.)*

He reproves him for not keeping faith with blessed Peter, for forcing his stepmother to marry, for robbing a bishop who was coming to the threshold of the apostles, and for plundering the church of Saint Benedict. He admonishes him to make satisfaction for these offenses.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Jordan [**Note: [Col. 0541]** Jordan is mentioned by Leo of Ostia, Book III, chapter 46, and elsewhere], prince of Capua.

As some people know, we once loved you very greatly, and until now have endeavored both to increase your honor in the present world and to preserve it in the future.

For we believed that, as befitted a noble son, you would keep faith with blessed Peter and increase his honor to the full extent of your ability.

But our opinion was far mistaken, and although previously we could believe nothing of this kind about you, we now realize that many people were not lying about your faithlessness.

For behold, some time ago you presumed most violently to drag your stepmother and lady from the church against right and justice, against her will and while she protested, and to hand her over to a marriage she did not want.

Recently you dared to obstruct a bishop coming to the threshold of the apostles and, in the manner of robbers, to take away what he was carrying.

Finally, you did not fear to enter, plunder, and violate the church of blessed Benedict with sacrilegious audacity. Although you ought to defend the property of the churches—for nearly everything you hold belongs to them—you above all have become their violator and destroyer.

Therefore, on behalf of blessed Peter, we admonish you that, if you do not wish to incur his anger and the indignation of blessed Benedict, you must render us justice concerning all these matters.

If you scorn to do so, we shall appeal to almighty God; and we trust in his mercy that he will grant us counsel concerning what we ought to do against such arrogance and immoderate pride of yours.

At Rome, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0542C]**

In addition to the other solemnities contained in the privilege, he grants him the use of the pallium on two further feast days, for his merits, but only to him and not to his successors.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Henry, dearest brother in Christ and fellow bishop of Aquileia: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your fraternal affection humbly petitioned us through its legate that, in addition to the solemnities contained in the privilege of your church, we should grant you the use of the pallium on the feast of blessed Udalric, confessor of Christ and bishop, and also on the feast of blessed Afra, martyr.

The excellence of this ecclesiastical honor, just as it is rightly denied to the wicked and disobedient, so at times appears, through apostolic moderation, to be something which should be bestowed upon the good and those endowed with upright conduct according to their merits.

Therefore, because we trust that you possess sincere affection toward us; because you are known to have treated our legates—the bishop of Albano and the bishop of Padua—kindly and to have faithfully assisted them as was proper; and finally because you are shown to have labored greatly to establish peace, we have willingly accepted your petition.

By the authority of this decree, therefore, we grant you permission to use the pallium during the solemn celebration of Mass on the feast of blessed Udalric, confessor and bishop, and on that of blessed Afra, martyr.

Know, however, that this has been granted to you for your lifetime, not to your office or see.

Given at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO RAINALD, BISHOP OF COMO

*(Year 1079.)*

He reports that many accusations concerning the elect of the Church of Bergamo have reached him and wishes all of them to be corrected at his exhortation. Otherwise, he orders that the man be carefully examined by the bishop concerning the charges, and either acquitted or condemned by apostolic authority. He also determines what is to be held concerning those who were ordained unknowingly and without payment by simoniacs.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainald, bishop of Como: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your affection took care to inform us by letter, dearest brother, that Arnulf, the elect of the Church of Bergamo, willingly trusts in our counsel and obeys our command.

We, for our part, as you know, have unquestioning confidence in your charitable experience. Nevertheless, many things concerning the aforesaid man have come to our knowledge through the reports of certain people. If these things should prove true—which God forbid—they greatly distress us and deserve to be punished in him by no light vengeance.

For Gorzo, his soldier and standard-bearer, complains, together with his two brothers and coheirs, that the fortress called Rocca di Glizione, which until now they had held and possessed without any opposition as their own rightful property, has now been violently—and, which is shameful to say, fraudulently—taken away from both him and his associates by the aforesaid Arnulf.

Yet Arnulf is said previously to have craftily offered this soldier certain oaths, as though of security and alliance, in order to remove the fear of suspicion; then, setting aside the fear of God, to have incurred the treachery of greed.

Nor, satisfied with such a crime, did he fear to plunder B. [lacuna], a priest and cleric of the aforesaid Gorzo [*Gorzonis*], and, as the priest asserts, to strip him of everything he possessed.

Moreover, he is accused of conducting the pestilential markets of the Simoniac heresy and, among other things, of having sold the archdeaconry of the Church of Bergamo for a price of fifty pounds.

In addition, instead of protecting and assisting the servants of God in every way, as befits a religious man, he attempts to attack and harass them.

Let the concern of your fraternity therefore take care, by correction or exhortation, that the aforesaid elect hasten to amend all these things and strive to possess a good testimony both before God and before human beings.

But if he should wish to deny all or perhaps some of these charges, we wish and command you, at a suitable time and place, by the authority of our office, to examine him carefully concerning the accusations; and, with every opportunity for evasion removed, to carry out in every respect whatever justice dictates.

As for what M. [lacuna], our son the priest, took care to ask: what judgment the merciful discipline of the Apostolic See establishes concerning those who have been ordained by simoniacs without knowing it and without payment—we wish you to observe the following.

Those who, before the time of Pope Nicholas, were promoted by simoniacs to any order without payment may, if their life is shown to be irreproachable, remain and minister in their orders after being confirmed by the laying on of hands.

Given at Rome, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XL. TO BOSO

*(Year 1079.)*

**[Col. 0544B]**

He orders him to leave free the church of the Holy Sepulchre, which he entrusts to Simon. If he thinks that he has any right in it, he is to present himself before the legate at the council to give an account; otherwise, he says that he will confirm the sentence of excommunication pronounced against him by the legate.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Boso [*Brizo*].

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Novo Vico, which is said to belong by right to the Church of Jerusalem and to be subject to its census, we have entrusted to this cleric of ours, Simon, to govern. Wishing it to be free from every disturbance and the calumnious harassment of all men, we decree that it shall remain under our protection. Therefore, [Col. 0544C] since we have heard that you have tyrannically invaded it, by this present document we admonish you that, if you wish to have God and the holy apostles favorable to you, you must henceforth cease entirely from invading the aforesaid church, and must presume to inflict no further annoyance either upon the aforesaid Simon or upon the clerics serving God there. Rather, as has been said, it is to remain free from every disturbance and secure as belonging to the holy Church of Jerusalem, to which the intention of the faithful has devoted it, and, with God’s favor, it is to be preserved forever by our authority.

But if you are confident that you possess some right in the aforesaid church, you must present yourself before our legate, the bishop of Die, at the council which he is about to hold shortly, knowing that in no respect [Col. 0544D] do we wish to weigh against you anything contrary to justice. But if, disregarding our warnings—or rather, the words of God (which God forbid!)—you refuse to hear them and are unwilling to restrain yourself from the unlawful and forbidden invasion of the aforesaid church, we confirm by apostolic authority the excommunication which our legate, Hugh, bishop of Die, pronounced against you on account of that church at the council of Poitiers.

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the second indiction.

## BOOK SEVEN OF THE REGISTER

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1079, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of the lord Gregory, in the second indiction.  
[Note: [Col. 0545D] The following letters belong to the third part.]

[Col. 0545]

## LETTER I. TO HUBERT, SUBDEACON

[Col. 0545A]

He rebukes his delay and orders him to hasten his return. He states that he did not authorize Zeuzon [Teuzon] to speak against the king of England. He wishes the king to be warned to render the Church her due honor. He does not approve the promotion of the son of a priest to the archbishopric of Rouen, nor what Hubert himself had done with the bishop of Langres; he entrusts the matter to the bishop of Die for settlement. He instructs him to arrange for two bishops from the provinces of England and Normandy to come to the synod.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Hubert, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly astonished, and you should know that it displeases us exceedingly, that you have hitherto made such lengthy delays and [Col. 0545B] have postponed your return to the apostolic see for so long. No excuse for any matter can sufficiently clear you, unless you have been detained either by illness or because access for returning was unavailable. For you yourself were long ago able to judge very well how highly I regard money paid without honor. Therefore, knowing that we desire your presence for many reasons, strive to hasten your return as much as you can.

You have informed us that Zeuzon [Teuzon], as though acting as our legate, spoke against the English king; you should know that he had received no such instructions from us. There are, however, many grounds on which the holy Roman Church can bring complaints against him. None of all the kings, even among the pagans, has presumed against the apostolic see to attempt what he did not blush to do—namely, to prevent bishops and archbishops from approaching the thresholds of the apostles with so irreverent and shameless a spirit. Therefore we wish your prudence, acting in our place, to admonish him that he should not strive so greatly to diminish the honor of the holy Roman Church which he would take very badly if he were not shown it by his subjects. By giving due thanks, he should endeavor to obtain the favor of blessed Peter.

For our part, mindful of our former friendship with him and imitating, insofar as God permits, apostolic gentleness, we have thus far spared his fault. But if he does not impose a limit upon this and upon similar matters known to you, let him know with certainty that he will gravely provoke the wrath of blessed Peter against himself. [Col. 0545D]

We have also heard that the archbishop of Rouen is the son of a priest. If this is found to be true, you should know that we in no way give our assent to his promotion. As for what we understand you did in Flanders with the bishop of Langres, without instructions from us, know that it was presumed both contrary to reason and unjustly, since in those regions we entrusted the bishop of Die in particular with acting on our behalf in every matter requiring our concern. Therefore [Col. 0546A] we instruct you to arrange to approach him as soon as possible and to explain the matter to him, so that in this affair he may correct whatever requires correction and strengthen whatever ought to be confirmed.

Moreover, we instruct you, in the name of blessed Peter, to order and invite both the English and the Normans to send two bishops from each archbishopric to the Roman synod which, with God’s approval, we shall hold during Lent. If they should perhaps protest and say that they cannot attend at that time, let them endeavor to present themselves to the apostolic see after Easter.

Given at Rome, on the ninth day before the Kalends of October, in the third indiction.

## LETTER II. TO THE PEOPLE OF LUCCA  
*(Year 1079)*

[Col. 0546B]

Against clerics hostile to their bishops, he confirms the decrees of the supreme pontiffs, removing them forever from orders and prebends, and warning clergy and people neither to associate with them nor to offer them assistance.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Lucca, except those who associate and agree with the excommunicated, greeting and apostolic blessing.

After carefully examining the case of the clerics of your church and laboring over it for a long time, we found in them none of the reason and truth proper to Christians. Although, according to the synodal judgment which they had brought upon themselves, we ought to have punished their astonishing and unheard-of arrogance without granting them a hearing, nevertheless, in a spirit of gentleness, we deemed it proper to hear their case, so that at least, once confounded and convicted, we might recall them to sound counsel and a sense of humility. For if our mind had discerned in them any sign of humility, they would not have departed from us without some mercy.

Since they persisted in their arrogance, the authority of the blessed martyrs and pontiffs Fabian and Stephen was cited before us. Seeing that it applied in every respect to this matter, we condemned them as rebels and disobedient persons by the judgment of that same authority, which we thought ought to be inserted into our letter, so that it might be made plainly evident by what crimes they are ensnared [Col. 0546D] and by what insults they deserve condemnation.

Fabian: “We decree that if any cleric is hostile or treacherous toward his bishop, whether because he has attempted to accuse him or has been a conspirator, he shall immediately, before the case has been examined judicially, be removed from the clergy and handed over to the civil authority, which he shall serve for the rest of his life; and he shall remain infamous, without any hope of restoration.”

Pope Stephen: “A cleric who has accused his bishop or has been treacherous toward him is not to be received, because he has become infamous; he must withdraw from his rank and be handed over to the civil authority for service.”

Having therefore promulgated this sentence against them, we thought that perhaps the terror of so great an authority would turn them to humility. But they, given over to a depraved mind and plunged into the pit of diabolical blindness, withdrew separated from the communion of the holy Church and excommunicated.

Therefore, confirming the statutes of the aforesaid saints, by the authority of blessed Peter we remove them forever from the orders and prebends of the church of Saint Martin. We decree that henceforth they shall hold no place among the canons of that church and shall have neither any support from its prebends nor any hope of receiving one in the future.

Therefore, beloved sons, we admonish you—or rather, by apostolic authority we forbid you—to associate with their criminal acts of contumacy, or to offer counsel or assistance against the Lord. Rather, so that you yourselves may remain unharmed and free from their condemnation, and so that they may be brought to shame and repentance, do not permit them to live within the bounds of your city; and strive to cleanse the whole province of their presence and contagion. If you do not do this, and love them more than justice and the salvation of your souls, you will bring upon yourselves the danger of their entire excommunication and will undoubtedly feel the wrath of God in the present life and in the life to come. But those who have resisted them, lest they remain in their arrogance and be brought to shame, we judge and promise shall be rewarded by the grace of blessed Peter.

[Col. 0547C] Given at Rome on the Kalends of October, in the third indiction.

## LETTER III. TO THE GERMANS  
*(Year 1079)*

He excuses himself concerning certain charges brought against him, placing the blame upon the legates if they acted by force or deceit against apostolic instructions, and exhorts them to persevere.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Saint Peter residing in the German kingdom, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to our attention that some of you doubt me, as though at the present moment, under pressure of necessity, I had resorted to worldly fickleness. In this matter, certainly, none of you except those pressed by the battles suffers greater anxieties or endures greater injuries than I do. For almost all the Latins praise and defend Henry’s cause, and reproach me for excessive harshness and impiety toward him.

By God’s grace we have resisted all of them so far, without inclining in either direction except according to justice and equity, as we understand them. For if our legates did anything contrary to what we had charged them to do, we are grieved; yet, as we have learned, they acted partly under violent compulsion and partly because they were deceived by fraud. We had instructed them to establish jointly a suitable place and date to which we might send wise and capable legates to examine your case, and to restore the bishops to their sees and teach them to abstain from association with excommunicated persons. If, deceived or compelled, they did anything contrary to these instructions, I do not approve it.

Know with certainty that, with God as our guide, no human being—whether through love, fear, or any desire—has ever been able, or will ever be able, to lead me away from the straight path of justice. Therefore, if you are truly faithful to God and blessed Peter in sincere charity, do not fail in your tribulations; rather, as good imitators, remain steadfast in the fidelity you have begun. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10).

For the present we can send you no other instruction concerning the matter mentioned above, because our messengers have not yet returned. Once they arrive, we shall truthfully inform you as soon as we can of what we learn from them.

Given at Rome on the Kalends of October, in the third indiction.

## LETTER IV. TO WEZELIN  
*(Year 1079)*

He orders him to cease harassing the king of Dalmatia, who was established by apostolic authority. He advises him that, if he has any claim against the king, he should seek judgment from the apostolic see; otherwise he will incur a sentence of excommunication together with all his supporters.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wezelin, noble soldier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know that we greatly wonder at your prudence: although you once promised that you were faithful to blessed Peter and to us, you now attempt to rise against the man whom apostolic authority established as king in Dalmatia. Therefore we admonish your nobility and, in the name of blessed Peter, command you not to presume henceforth to take up arms against the aforesaid king. Know that whatever you dare against him you will undoubtedly be doing against the apostolic see.

But if you say that you have some claim against him, you ought to seek judgment from us and await justice rather than arm your hands against him to the injury of the apostolic see. If you do not repent of your rashness, but stubbornly attempt to proceed against our command, know with certainty that we shall draw the sword of blessed Peter against your audacity and, unless you repent, shall punish by it your obstinacy and that of all who support you in this matter.

But if you prudently prove obedient, as befits a Christian, you shall obtain the grace of blessed Peter and the blessing of the apostolic see as an obedient son.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the third indiction.

## LETTER V. TO ACON, KING OF THE DANES  
*(Year 1079)*

He congratulates him on his faith and observance of the Christian religion, and on his recognition of the holy Roman Church as his mother and his request for her instruction. He exhorts him to make daily progress, so that by his example he may call his subjects to sounder counsels. He wishes him to send a prudent cleric, who may explain the customs of that people to him and, on returning, convey the commands of the apostolic see to the king.

[Col. 0549A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Acon [Canute], king of the Danes, greeting and apostolic blessing.

With sincere affection of charity we congratulate your devotion, because, although you are situated at the farthest ends of the earth, you diligently strive to inquire into those things known to pertain to the observance of the Christian religion. Recognizing the holy Roman Church as your mother and that of all peoples, you desire and request her instruction for yourself.

We also wish and admonish you [f., “that,” HARD.] that, while your devotion persists in these studies and desires and increases as divine piety grants, it should in no way fall away from its right purpose, but should grow daily toward better things, as befits a prudent man and the constancy of a king.

Your excellence must indeed observe that the more widely you surpass and rule others, the more your subjects can, by your example, either be bent toward worse things—which God forbid—or even be summoned, though sluggish, to sound counsel. Your prudence must also consider how fleeting and transitory are the joys of temporal life. Even if life were believed likely to last long, it cannot remain secure when many adversities suddenly arise.

Therefore you must take the greatest care to direct your steps and apply your mind steadily toward those things that do not pass away and cannot abandon the one who possesses them. We would certainly desire that some prudent cleric from your people come to us, one who could fully make known to us the customs and practices of your nation and, better instructed in the teachings and commands of the apostolic see, could convey them to you.

Given at Rome on the Ides of October.

## LETTER VI. TO ALPHONSE, KING OF CASTILE  
*(Year 1079)*

He congratulates him on his faith and obedience toward the apostolic see. He exhorts him to persevere in good works. He sends him a golden key containing a blessing from the chains of blessed Peter and commends his legate, who will report many matters to him in his name.

[Col. 0549D] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, Alphonse [“Alphonso” absent], glorious king of the Spaniards, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We offer praise and thanks to almighty God, who, illuminating your glory by the grace of his visitation, joined you to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in faith and devotion. Subjecting to him all the principalities and powers of the world, he granted him the authority to bind and loose in heaven and on earth.

For this reason you also rightly ought to rejoice, since greater rewards are prepared for you because divine favor reserved for your times the correction of your kingdom, which had long remained in error, so that your sublime humility and faithful obedience might merit to receive the truth of God and the justice from which those who preceded you as rulers and princes, and the whole people, had been deprived for so many years, partly through the blindness of ignorance and partly through obstinate rashness.

But because every good work looks for its due reward not so much from its beginning as from its end, we admonish your excellence with paternal charity to hold firmly what you have received from our legates concerning the religion of the faith and ecclesiastical order, and what, with God’s help, you will yet receive. For just as those who remain in observance of the faith and teaching of this holy apostolic see possess a sure hope of salvation, so those who stray from its concord and unity face the unquestionable terror of condemnation.

Indeed, we have good hopes concerning you, because we have learned from the report of our beloved son Richard, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, whom we are now sending to you for the second time, that you possess good will. Yet because devoted hearts always rejoice in admonition, and virtues also require exercise, we exhort your eminence to lift your mind from this earthly and fleeting dignity to that which is heavenly and eternal. Use this dignity as something passing and soon to perish; seek that which possesses both eternity and the fullness of glory.

You must attend and carefully consider that, whether you wish it or not, you hasten daily toward the end of life. Whatever wealth, honor, or power now smiles upon you, nearby death, when least expected, will snatch away and close everything in darkness and bitterness. What hope, glory, pleasure, or desire, then, ought there to be in those things which deceive those who love them, flee from those who pursue them, and abandon those who possess them? The less anyone delights in these things and the less he is carried away by exaltation over himself, the more securely he is led toward the true goods.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself clearly displayed an example of this when, in pious humility, he rejected the kingdom offered to him by men and did not even wish to display the appearance of earthly greatness in the eyes of men—he who came into this world to lead us to the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, as a most beloved son, we admonish you to think carefully about these matters and present yourself humbly before him who has made you exceedingly exalted. Strive to please God in everything and above all things, and with God’s help endeavor to administer the reins of the kingdom entrusted to you in such a way [Col. 0550D] that your eminence may experience no future fall or misfortune, but may pass to the crown of the incorruptible kingdom and the throne of eternal glory.

So that our exhortation may be impressed more deeply upon your heart, according to the custom of the saints we have sent you a little golden key containing a blessing from the chains of blessed Peter. Through its presence and patronage, may you experience greater benefits, and may you burn ever more ardently in love for him, obtaining that almighty God, who by wondrous power freed him from iron bonds, may, by his merits and intercessions, release you from the bonds of all your sins and lead you to eternal joys.

Furthermore, we commend to you this beloved son of ours, whom, as we said above, we are now sending to you for the second time. Hear him as you would hear us and show him favor in all things, so that his journey and labor among you may not be fruitless, but that, concerning the ecclesiastical matters entrusted to him which he finds requiring attention, he may effectively carry them out and, with God’s help, bring them to a sound condition.

As for the other matters not sufficiently included here, we have placed them in his mouth. You should have no hesitation in believing him, since you know that through him our authority is being represented to you.

Given at Rome, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the third indiction.

## LETTER VII. TO RICHARD, CARDINAL  
*(Year 1079)*

He appoints him abbot of Marseille at the request of the brothers. He exhorts him to undertake the burden faithfully. He says that he desires to unite the monastery of Saint Paul with the monastery of Marseille, and orders him, after properly arranging his monasteries, to continue his legation to Spain.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richard, cardinal appointed to the legation of Spain, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The unanimity of the brothers of Marseille, who in their letter recalled the death of your brother of holy memory, wounded me with fresh grief. They further asked, out of love for your holy brother and hoping that you would become, as it were, his second self, that I grant you to them as abbot; and I have done so.

Therefore I wish you in no way to grieve your brothers by stubborn resistance, but to acquiesce readily in the will of God and of the holy brothers. We also wish and admonish you that, insofar as you can, the hopes of so many brothers in you should not prove vain. Rather, put on the spirit of your brother with manly courage; flee secular and youthful desires as you would death; bind yourself inwardly to the holy rule, lest, because of your youth, the holy monastery—God forbid—suffer any loss of religious discipline.

Know also that it is my desire to bind the monastery of the blessed apostle Paul and the monastery of Marseille together in such a union of charity that the latter may continually increase, by apostolic authority, out of love for the most blessed Paul, and that the monastery of the most blessed Paul may advance toward holy religious observance through the religious discipline of that monastery.

After, with God’s approval, you have properly arranged your monasteries, do not delay in fulfilling the legation entrusted to you in Spain.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the third indiction.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE MONKS OF MARSEILLE  
*(Year 1079)*

He grieves over the death of their abbot, and unites their monastery to the apostolic see just as he has united the monastery of Cluny. He confirms the election they made of Cardinal Richard as abbot.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ, the congregation of Marseille, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0552A] We do not doubt that your brotherly affection, filled with mourning and sadness over the death of its venerable father, is constrained by profound grief. At his departure, indeed, I remember and believe that a greater—or at least an equal—loss has befallen us, since we feel that such a great and powerful helper has been taken from our side.

We have understood that, if life had remained his companion for some time longer, through his prudence and counsel a great deal of benefit, with God’s favor, would have come to the holy Roman Church, not only in the regions beyond the Alps but also in the parts of Italy, together with the salvation of many. Thus you yourselves can clearly judge how great is the anguish of mind that holds us, since we too bear the burden of so great an office, beyond our strength, and, deprived of such assistance, find no supporters of his kind—or scarcely a few.

But because the immeasurable providence of almighty God disposes all things justly and wisely, we, brothers, must endure his judgments—truly, his righteous counsels, full of equity and mercy—with equanimity. And since your aforesaid father, having merited in life what he received in death, was unquestionably received into Abraham’s bosom, we, bound to you by the sweet memory of him and especially moved by divine love, have resolved to love and assist your place in a special way and to defend it from every act of violence, since it is specially attached to the Roman Church.

Just as the monastery of Cluny has long been established as united to the apostolic see, so we wish and decree that yours also henceforth be similarly attached to that see forever.

We have heard that your charity wishes to choose our son and cardinal priest Richard as abbot in place of his brother. We approve this election and confirm it by apostolic authority. In this too you become bound to us and attached, as though by doubled bonds, because you desire a son of the holy Roman Church as your ruler.

We therefore think it right to entreat the dispenser of all good things to make him so vigilant a guardian of your salvation that, for his salutary care and multiplied talents, he may receive the gifts of the eternal inheritance and, bringing back blessed rewards, gladden his mother.

Given at Rome on the fifth [III] day before the Nones of November, in the third indiction.  
[Col. 0552D]

## LETTER IX. TO THE BISHOPS OF ASTI, TURIN, AND ACQUI  
*(Year 1079)*

He orders them to prevent a certain Boniface from marrying a woman who had previously been betrothed to his deceased brother.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brothers and fellow bishops, the bishop of Asti, the bishop of Turin, and the elected bishop of Acqui, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to us that the margrave Boniface, brother of the recently slain Mainfred and Anselm, is attempting to take the betrothed of that same Anselm as his wife. No one who knows the sacred canons can doubt how full of wickedness this is and how alien it is from the laws of the Christian religion.

Therefore we command your charity to approach him in our place and admonish him to cease henceforth, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers, from undertaking such a criminal marriage. If he thinks himself bound to carry this out by an oath, we judge that the foolish pact of a destructive obligation must not be observed but must be annulled; and we command you to treat it accordingly.

But if, hardened in mind and against his own salvation, he persists in so wicked an agreement and, as befits a Christian, scorns to obey salutary admonitions, promulgate the first canonical sentence against him. With God’s approval, we shall thereafter confirm and strengthen it by apostolic power, so that others, led by his example, may neither fall into worse things nor perhaps suppose that similar conduct is permitted to them.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Nones of November, in the third indiction.

## LETTER X. TO ALL THE BRITONS  
*(Year 1079)*

He complains about the practice of false repentance, which at that time had grown up in the Church among other vices. To provide a remedy for this evil, he sends there as his legate the bishop of Oloron, so that under his presidency the matter may be carefully discussed in a synod to be convened. Meanwhile, he explains what true repentance is.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops, priests, princes, and all others residing in Britain, greeting and apostolic blessing, if they obey.

The dignity of the priestly office, through both the ignorance and the negligence of priests, as your charity knows, has for a long time, because of the demands of sins, fallen into decline. From this, as from a poisonous root, countless evils have arisen, so that even down to our own times, among the other vices that grow up wrongly, the practice of false repentance has likewise taken root.

Therefore, since by reason of our office and the greatness of our responsibility it falls upon us, insofar as we can and as God grants, to correct this and similar things, we wish and command by apostolic authority that your fraternity reverently summon our legate, namely Amatus, bishop of Oloron, to whom we have entrusted our place in your regions, and that, through his agency, a synodal council be convened. There, along with other matters pertaining to the salvation of souls, the question of repentance is to be examined with particular care.

In this matter you must take the greatest care, and you must admonish others, that if anyone has fallen into murder, adultery, perjury, or anything similar, and remains in any such crime; or if he devotes himself to commerce, which can scarcely be practiced without sin; or if he bears military arms—except for defending his own justice, or that of his lord, or of a friend, or of the poor, and also for defending churches, though he must not take them up without the counsel of religious men who wisely know how to give advice concerning eternal salvation—or if he unjustly possesses another’s goods, or burns with hatred toward his neighbor, he cannot in any way produce the fruit of true repentance.

We call repentance fruitless when it is accepted in such a way that one remains in the same fault, or in a similar fault that is worse or only slightly less serious. Therefore whoever wishes to repent worthily must return to the origin of faith and take care vigilantly to preserve what he promised in baptism: to renounce the devil and his pomp, to believe in God—that is, to form right thoughts about him—and to obey his commands.

Whoever repents in this manner—for anything else may be called pretense, not repentance—we, relying upon apostolic authority, grant remission of his sins and, trusting in the mercy of almighty God, promise him the joys of eternal blessedness.

Given at Rome on the eighth [VII] day before the Kalends of December, in the third indiction.  
[Col. 0554B]

## LETTER XI. TO URATISLAUS, KING OF THE BOHEMIANS  
*(Year 1079)*

He advises him to defend the churches from invaders. He forbids the Divine Office to be translated into the Slavonic language. He promises to send the legates whom he had requested.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Uratislaus, duke of the Bohemians, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have now maintained, though not without hesitation, our customary form of greeting to you, namely the apostolic blessing, because you appear to associate with excommunicated persons. For all who invade the goods of churches—that is, seize them without the definite permission of bishops [Col. 0554C] or abbots, or receive them from some other person—are not only by the apostolic see at this time, but also by many holy Fathers, as we find in their writings, [lacuna].

However the matter may stand, we are moved to provide for your inner salvation not only by our longstanding affection for you, but also compelled by consideration of the honor you have undertaken and of your labor, especially because your eminence can serve as an example for the advancement of many. You cannot be permitted either to say or to think: “It is not my concern to investigate or discipline the life and conduct of another in spiritual matters.” For undoubtedly you are guilty of as many people as you could voluntarily turn back from the path of destruction.

You must also consider with vigilant mind that you should not place your own honor before divine honor, or money before justice, nor calmly endure toward your Creator and the Creator of all what you would not tolerate without severe punishment being done to you by a subject like yourself. Those who pursue their own injuries even to bloodshed but neglect insults against God even to the point of oblivion are unquestionably shown to be members not of God but of the devil and false Christians.

Your power must regard the riches it possesses as entrusted to it, not given on account of merit but for the sake of responsibility. Indeed, poverty does not appear to burden secular men as much as riches, and power spread widely, burden spiritual men. They should consider that if a man to whom one sheep is entrusted on pain of death would not only refuse to accept a hundred under the same condition but would also watch anxiously, not without fear, that the single sheep should not perish by any accident, then the more people over whom he has received care or authority, the more relentlessly he must keep watch and the more he must fear.

Having considered these things [or: “having completed these matters,”], the fleetingness of the present age invites you to greater vigilance of mind. Since that which is most loved in this life—namely, the present life itself—hastens secretly [f., “stealthily,” HARD.; likewise in the Mutina manuscript] toward its setting, sound reason sends you, as you draw nearer to the day of strict judgment, to meditate upon and attain eternal things with ever greater care.

Therefore we wish—or rather, we command—that your excellence frequently place these admonitions or commands before the eyes of your mind and meditate upon them by reading and hearing them often. This is not because you could not find more elegantly written words in the pages of the saints, but because these have been sent to you personally from us—or rather, from blessed Peter—and by recalling them frequently you may, with God’s favor, rise toward the knowledge of better things.

Since your nobility requested that we permit the Divine Office to be celebrated among you according to the Slavonic language, know that we cannot in any way favor this petition. For it is clear, when we often reflect upon the matter, that not without reason sacred Scripture pleased almighty God by being hidden in certain places, lest, if it were completely clear to everyone, it should perhaps become cheap and subject to contempt, or, being wrongly understood by ordinary people, lead them into error.

Nor does it help as an excuse that certain religious men patiently tolerated what the simple people seek, or left it uncorrected, since the primitive Church tolerated many things which, after Christianity had been strengthened and religion had grown, were later corrected by the holy Fathers through careful examination.

Therefore, lest what your people imprudently request should occur, we forbid it by the authority of blessed Peter, and we command you, for the honor of almighty God, to resist this vain rashness with all your strength.

As for our legate, whom your devotion requested to be sent to you, know that for the present we have been unable conveniently to fulfill your requests. Nevertheless, during this year, with divine clemency assisting, we shall endeavor to find persons who can be usefully assigned to your affairs and who, knowing your needs more fully, can bring them to our attention.

Therefore, so that we may be able to send our legates safely to you, we think and wish it necessary that you make every effort to send our son Frederick and this Felix—or one of them—to us again, so that they may safely come to the place to which we shall direct them.

Given at Rome, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS (1080)

Refusing entirely to accept his excuse, he orders him to come—having previously been summoned—to the Council of Lyons, where he is to answer before the apostolic legates for the charges brought against him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to MANASSES, archbishop of Reims: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

We marvel that your Fraternity finds so many opportunities for remaining for so long in disgrace, both personally and with regard to your Church, and that you appear—at least in the judgment of public opinion—to be attempting to evade judgment, when you ought rather to have labored earnestly to remove the suspicion of so great a crime from yourself and your Church.

Indeed, last year, as an argument for your defense, you presented us with a certain authority, namely, that you ought to submit to judgment only in our presence. Hence, as now also appears, you have been deservedly reproved in copies of our letters. But now, forgetful of your promise—which you made binding upon yourself at Rome over the body of blessed Peter—you put forward another excuse: namely, that because of the fear inspired by a kingdom torn by dissension, you cannot come to the Council of Lyons, to which you have been summoned.

How unstable your excuse is in this matter can readily be assessed. For neither was the legate of the Roman Church to be despised in your case; as your Fraternity knows, he presided over the greatest and most important councils, namely Nicaea and Chalcedon, as well as many others, and gave a firm and definitive resolution to questions of this kind. Nor ought you now to claim that you cannot come to Lyons, since you could cross all the dangers of that journey, if any exist, under the safest and most secure guides—namely, the archbishop of Lyons and the bishop of Langres. They would treat you with fraternal charity and bring you without any fear to the aforesaid place.

You ought certainly to have gone there voluntarily and without any invitation, so that, if you are free of that fault, a synodal commendation might silence the disgrace attached to you, and so that your case might be examined more carefully not only by the bishop of Die but also by our confrere, the bishop of Albano, and by the abbot of Cluny, whom we hope will attend that synod. If [but if, HARD.] any sentence against you should perhaps prove excessively severe, they would act with the restraint demanded by justice: not only would they refrain from proceeding against you, but would even correct, on your behalf, anything said or done too hastily.

But if you do not go to the aforesaid council, and do not [read: and, added by HARD.; likewise in the Mutina manuscript] incline your ear to the obedience owed to your mother, the Roman Church, which has supported you for so long; if the bishop of Die, with the agreement of our religious brothers, takes any action against you, we shall not merely leave unchanged the sentence pronounced against you, but shall confirm it by apostolic authority.

If, however, it should seem to your Fraternity that the sentence pronounced can reasonably be opposed, we wish you rather to set forth your arguments before our vicar, namely the bishop of Die, and before other religious men, in that region where a greater number of accusers and defenders can be found, than to seek in vain the hope of judgment by coming to Rome through so many toils and difficulties, where both are lacking.

Meanwhile, in the name of almighty God and by the authority of blessed Peter, we admonish your Fraternity that, if you recognize yourself to be guilty in this matter, rather than suppose that you should excuse yourself by some secular artifice, you should strive to free your soul through worthy fruits of repentance.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XIII. TO THEODORE, BISHOP OF VERDUN (1080)

He orders him to compel Count Arnulf—who plundered the bishop of Liège when he was coming to the apostolic see and forced him to swear that he would never seek the return of the things taken—to undergo penance and make satisfaction after an assembly has been held. Otherwise, he is to forbid him entry into the church and participation in the communion of the Lord’s body and blood; and, unless he rejects his conduct within fifteen days, he is to strike him, together with his supporters, with the sword of anathema. He promises forgiveness of sins to those who avenge the bishop’s injuries, while absolving the bishop from the oath forced upon him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to THEODORE, bishop of Verdun: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

The grave misfortune of our brother and fellow bishop Henry of Liège has reached us. As he was coming to the threshold of the apostles, Count Arnulf stripped him of all the possessions he was carrying and, to increase his wickedness, after the seizure of his property, compelled him at sword-point to swear that he would never seek the return of what had been taken and that he would obtain from us forgiveness for so great and serious a crime.

When we learned of this monstrous outrage, we grieved exceedingly: both because our brother’s devotion had been obstructed and because of that man’s detestable audacity. Unless it is punished with fitting correction, an opportunity will remain for him and those like him to commit still worse acts, if worse acts exist and are possible. Nevertheless, lest we be judged to be consulting anger rather than obeying justice, we wish and, by apostolic authority, command your Fraternity to endeavor to assemble whatever bishops, abbots, priests, and clerics you can, and, after an assembly has been held concerning this matter, to invite that wicked man to penance and satisfaction.

If, persisting in his wickedness, he refuses either to do penance or to restore what was taken with worthy satisfaction, your Fraternity shall forbid him entry into the church and participation in the Lord’s body and blood. Grant him fifteen days’ delay; and if within that period he does not repent and does not come to amend his crime, strike him with the sword of anathema, supported by the command of apostolic authority. We shall certainly confirm this in every way thereafter.

Moreover, we wish and command that your devotion rise up against him by whatever means it can. Whoever gives aid or consent to his wicked presumption should know that he will undoubtedly lose the grace of God and of blessed Peter.

But whoever strives with all his strength to avenge the injuries done to our aforesaid confrere—and indeed to blessed Peter—we grant our apostolic blessing and, trusting in the gift of divine mercy, promise him forgiveness of his sins.

We also do not wish your Prudence to be unaware that we have absolved the aforementioned fellow bishop from the terms of the oath maliciously forced upon him and have granted him permission to avenge the insult done to Holy Church. We admonish and beg you again and again to assist him as far as you are able in all things.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XIV. TO HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE (1080)

He grieves over the insult inflicted upon him by Arnulf, absolves him from the oath violently imposed upon him, and orders him to rise against Arnulf and exact punishment for his crime. He states that he has ordered the bishop of Verdun to assist him in this matter.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HENRY, bishop of Liège: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

Having learned of the adversity and insult inflicted upon your Fraternity—and indeed upon blessed Peter—we have been compelled to grieve very deeply [read: exceedingly, nimium].

Concerning the most unjust obligation of the oath, we respond to your devotion as follows: you should not be considered capable of being bound by any bonds of an oath when you have been compelled to swear in so wicked a manner. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we absolve you, so that you may not appear, on this account, to be bound or indebted in conscience, either to yourself or to anyone else.

Moreover, relying upon that same authority, we grant your Fraternity permission—or rather, we exhort you—to rise with all the strength you possess against the injuries inflicted upon blessed Peter, unless that presumptuous man repents and makes worthy satisfaction; attack him in every way, and, with God’s help, seek and exact from him punishment for so great a crime.

For it seems unworthy to us, and would become an example encouraging other wicked men to attempt worse things, if this man were to undertake such an outrage with impunity. Therefore we also earnestly command our brother the bishop of Verdun and the other faithful of blessed Peter, assisting your devotion with one accord, to attack that tyrant and trampler upon the Christian religion, and, pursuing and constraining him everywhere and on every side with both carnal and spiritual weapons as far as they can, to hem him in.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO THE BRETONS AND THE PEOPLE OF TOURS (1080)

He wishes the dispute between the Church of Tours and the Church of Dol to be settled by legates of the apostolic see, after the rights of both parties have been heard. Synodal decision concerning the pallium between the archbishop of Tours and the bishop of Dol.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Brittany and to the clergy and people established in the province of Tours.**

We wish it to be known that the pestilential dispute which arose between your Church and the Church of Dol has imposed much labor upon us in the Roman synod. Nevertheless, by God’s mercy, after a lengthy examination, we have found the following decision, as justly as we could.

Your archbishop, complaining that the Church of Tours had lost its right in Brittany, brought forward the authority of the Roman pontiffs. This clearly proves that Brittany owes submission and reverence to the Church of Tours as to its spiritual mother and metropolitan church.

The bishop of Dol, however, not only failed to acknowledge the authority of our hearing, but even the words he put forward in his defense appeared to be supported by no certainty deserving of belief. Nevertheless, because he asserted that he had retained some authority in his own country, it seemed to us that time should be granted for reconsidering the matter and that legates of the apostolic see should be sent for this and other reasons.

Thus, after hearing the arguments of both parties, if they discover that the Bretons possess authentic authority from the apostolic see—namely, from those pontiffs whose ordination and life were worthy and canonical—by which they can withdraw themselves from subjection to the aforesaid Church of Tours, let them henceforth remain undisturbed in their liberty.

But if it should happen that they cannot produce a defense based upon the authority just mentioned, then, with every dispute thereafter quieted and ended forever, let them recognize the Church of Tours as their mother and metropolitan church, and render to your archbishop the submission and obedience owed to a metropolitan. The bishop of Dol is to retain the use of the pallium, but only on this condition: none of his successors may at any time lay claim to this dignity [the text is materially corrupt here]. Rather, as we have said above, both those appointed to the Church of Dol and all the other bishops of Brittany shall remain perpetually subject to the teaching authority of the archbishop of Tours.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO HUBERT, BISHOP OF TEROUANNE (1080)

Accusing him of contumacy, he orders him, whenever summoned, to appear without fail before the bishop of Die, legate of the apostolic see, in order to clear himself of the many charges brought against him. He forbids the canons who had usurped a certain estate to perform the divine Office there, and wishes it to be forbidden by him as well.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUBERT, bishop of Terouanne.**

The principal reason why we do not send you greetings and apostolic blessing is that our register records that you were publicly convicted of heresy by Hugh, legate of this holy see, at Monasteriolum; and afterward, before you had been cleared of this disgrace, we heard that you had become a bishop through simony.

Furthermore, you utterly disregarded the commands of the apostolic see issued against you and your canons of the castle of Saint Paul concerning an estate called Kesseca [Reseca; and in the Mutina manuscript, Resena]. The canons of Saint Mary and Saint Audomarus have often complained in our presence that this estate, with its appurtenances, was being taken from them and from their Church; and they complain of the same thing again.

Consequently, by incurring with them the excommunication recorded in our register, you presumed, as we have heard, to celebrate the divine Office without regard for God or apostolic reverence.

For these and many other reasons, you were summoned once and again to a council by our brother Hugh, bishop of Die, and afterward invited by us to the Roman synod so that you might clear yourself. Since you did not come and did not offer a canonical excuse, the sentence of just deposition would long ago have overtaken you on account of your disobedience—which is truly idolatry—had not the gentleness of apostolic mercy, acting as a steward, supported us for a time.

Nevertheless, still sparing you with paternal affection, and because we can no longer honorably endure all the many and serious things that have been said about you, by apostolic authority we command that, wherever and whenever our aforesaid brother Hugh, bishop of Die, summons you to answer for these or other matters, setting aside excuses, you come so prepared and watchful that, if you know yourself to be innocent and falsely accused, you may, with God’s help and a clear conscience, canonically clear yourself of all charges already brought or yet to be brought.

Furthermore, we forbid all the canons of the castle of Saint Paul to perform the entire divine Office, with you alone temporarily excepted until the matter is heard. This prohibition is to remain in force for them and their places until the canons of the Church of Saint Mary and Saint Audomarus have restored the aforesaid estate, with its church and other appurtenances, and have made satisfaction before Hugh, bishop of Die, for their disobedience and excommunication.

Unless, upon seeing our command, you immediately forbid your aforesaid canons and all their places—and especially the place where the named canons are established—to perform the entire divine Office, know that your entire official ministry has been forbidden by apostolic authority.

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE MONKS OF DOL (1080)

He orders them to restore to the bishop of Limoges, until the arrival of the legate of the apostolic see, two monasteries which the bishop had complained they had taken away from his Church. If they believe that they possess any legal right in the matter, they are to demonstrate it before the legate.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the monks of Dol: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

Our brother and fellow bishop of Limoges complained to us at the synod which, with God’s help, we recently held at Rome, that your Fraternity was taking two monasteries away from his Church.

That brother and fellow bishop, and our legate Hugh, bishop of Die, also testified that he had summoned you twice concerning this matter, namely so that a judicial resolution might be reached between you and the aforesaid bishop. But, as he asserts, you were unwilling to show any justice or obedience.

Therefore the synodal assembly decreed that the aforesaid monasteries must return to the authority of the Church of Limoges and, without opposition from you or your people, be peacefully possessed by that Church until the arrival of our legate.

Accordingly, confirming the decision reached above with the agreement and advice of our brothers, we command and order you to permit the aforesaid Church of Limoges to retain those monasteries until the appointed time.

If, however, you are confident that you possess some legal right in them, await the arrival of our legate and present your case to him at a suitable place and time, where the bishop of Limoges can be present. Before his hearing, let your case be examined more carefully and fully understood, so that it may reach a just conclusion; and, with every dispute between you quieted, let each of you, content with his own right, cease to inflict injury.

Given at Rome on the Kalends of April [the eighth day before the Kalends of April], in the third indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO WILLIAM, ARCHBISHOP OF AUCH (1080)

Reproving him for disobedience, he orders him to compel the abbot of Pessan to restore to the abbot of Aurillac a certain church granted to that monastery by the apostolic see, forbidding entry into the church to the contumacious church.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, archbishop of Auch [bishop]: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

We marvel that your Prudence has shown itself so disobedient to the apostolic see that, neglecting to obey and carry out the business entrusted to you by our vicars, you have refused to bring it to completion.

They entrusted you with the task of administering justice to Peter, abbot of the monastery of Aurillac [Aurelian; and likewise thereafter], concerning the rights of this holy Roman Church, against Abbot Dodon of Pessan. For a long time he has held by invasion a church belonging likewise to blessed Peter, but granted to the aforesaid monastery of Aurillac, called Saint Mary of Dalmairac.

The extent of your reverence for blessed Peter in this matter is clearly shown by the fact that the invader still does not cease to occupy the church under a fraudulent claim, while the aforesaid abbot of Aurillac is compelled on that account to appeal to the apostolic ears—especially since the aforementioned abbot of Pessan was convicted and adjudged by our legates, Cardinal Stephen and our fellow bishop Gerard of Ostia, to be obliged to return that church, and, because he did not do so, incurred excommunication.

Therefore we admonish your devotion and, by apostolic authority, command you to compel the aforesaid abbot of Pessan to restore to the abbot of Aurillac the church at issue, and to make himself acceptable to him through fitting satisfaction.

But if, hardened by a spirit of pride, he refuses to comply, forbid the monastery that has been invaded to perform the divine Office, and, by our authority, forbid the invader entry into every church. For a man who is not afraid to commit sacrilege ought not to be counted among religious monks—or even among laymen.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Ides of April [the day before the Ides of October], in the third indiction.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE PEOPLE OF BOURGES, NARBONNE, AND BORDEAUX (1080)

He orders that the benefices taken from the monastery of Aurillac be restored and that the viscount render service and fidelity to the abbot, whom he states he has bound by an obligation not to give any soldier more than one mansus from the property of the Church. He confirms the renunciation of the monastery of Viac, made by the prince into the hands of the abbot with the consent of the bishop and clergy.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all established in the provinces of Bourges, Narbonne, and Bordeaux, except those held under apostolic excommunication: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

The cry of the abbot of the monastery of Aurillac has reached our ears. This monastery is known, by the grant of its founder, namely blessed Gerald, to belong to the proper right of blessed Peter. The abbot complains about certain persons who unjustly retain benefices of the aforesaid monastery, formerly granted to them and their predecessors under fidelity and lordship, for the defense of the Church.

He complains especially about Bérenger, viscount of Carlat, who, driven by personal greed, refuses to render the abbot the service and fidelity owed to him unless the benefice he unjustly retains is further increased from the property of the Church.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command that everyone known to have once received a benefice of the aforesaid Church for this purpose render submission and fidelity to the abbot, not refuse to provide service in return for the benefice, and cease demanding an unlawful increase. Otherwise, he is proved to be an invader and sacrilegious person.

Recognizing the loss suffered by the aforesaid monastery, we bound the abbot by a pledge of faith made into our hands: no soldier may be given more than one mansus from the property of the Church under this or any other pretext, nor may anything be given to any other person unless the common benefit of the brothers living according to the rule should require it and he should dare to disregard apostolic equity.

We command by apostolic authority that the monastery of Maurzice [Maunziac], with all its appurtenances, and the churches of Dalmairac [Dealmairac] and Montsalvy, as well as the others, and the lands and possessions in any of the provinces written above that have been taken away or oppressed by evil customs, but were formerly justly granted to the monastery of Aurillac by written documents or witnesses, be restored and allowed to remain without disturbance.

As for the monastery of Viac, renounced into the hands of the abbot by the princes of that land with the consent of the bishop and clergy, we grant and confirm it to him and his successors, and we bestow apostolic blessing upon those who supported the renunciation. We order that those who unjustly retain the churches or estates of the aforesaid monastery restore them without any delay.

Therefore, whoever refuses in a spirit of pride to obey these commands of ours—and especially Bérenger, if he scorns obedience—will lose the grace of blessed Peter and incur the anger of almighty God.

To those who obey, we grant, trusting in divine mercy, the grace of God and apostolic blessing.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Ides of April, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XX. TO MANASSES, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS (1080)

He states that he has confirmed the sentence of deposition pronounced against him by the legate at the Council of Lyons. Nevertheless, he still grants him permission to clear himself before certain bishops, provided that meanwhile the property of his accusers is restored in full, that he leave the Church of Reims, withdraw to another place, and allow the clergy there to serve God in safety.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to MANASSES, archbishop of Reims.**

Your Fraternity should know that we have confirmed by apostolic authority, as justice dictated, the sentence of deposition pronounced by our legate, the bishop of Die, in the Council of Lyons, an assembly of religious men.

Nevertheless, moved—if I may put it so—by excessive mercy, contrary to the custom of the Roman Church, we grant you permission to clear yourself, provided that the bishops of Soissons, Laon, Cambrai, and Châlons—or their equals—are associated with you, together with two others whose testimony we can equally trust, if you are confident in the justice of your case and can obtain them. This permission lasts until the feast of Saint Michael.

The condition is that, after Manasses, Bruno, and the others who appear to have spoken against you in defense of justice have been fully restored to their property, you leave the Church of Reims entirely free from your occupation by the next Ascension of the Lord, and withdraw to Cluny or to the House of God, living religiously at your own expense with one cleric and two laymen.

If you wish to do this, arrange to notify the aforesaid bishop of Die, so that in his presence you may confirm by oath that meanwhile you will alienate nothing belonging to the aforesaid Church except what is reasonably sufficient for you and the companions mentioned above.

Permit the clerics who have suffered exile for so long in defense of justice to serve God safely in the Church.

And since it would be burdensome for you to come all the way to us, we grant that you may clear yourself of the disgrace before the bishop of Die and the abbot of Cluny—or, if the abbot should be absent, before Amatus—in the manner stated above and with the witnesses mentioned above.

But if you scorn to obey this command of our dispensation, know that we can no longer bear your iniquity. The sentence of deposition will not only remain unaltered, but no further hearing will be left to you in the future.

Given at Rome on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO ACON, KING OF THE DANES (1080)

He exhorts him to persevere in obedience to the apostolic see and to imitate the virtues of his father the king, whom he greatly commends. He warns him to ensure that his subjects do not attribute the calamities of the times to the faults of priests, to whom, he teaches, honor must be shown, nor attack women for the same reason.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ACON, king of the Danes, and to the bishops, princes, clergy, and people: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

Since, as far as we have been able to understand, the love of your devotion has hitherto striven to show God and blessed Peter a willing obedience and the reverence owed to them, we have no doubt that divine grace has therefore bestowed upon you triumph and glory above others.

If, by persevering in the same devotion, your loyal affection takes care to remain constant to the end, you will certainly be able both to retain the glory you now possess and, with the Lord’s help, to attain still greater glory hereafter.

Therefore, dearest son, to whom divine providence has entrusted the care of the kingdom, we admonish you with paternal affection to strive to imitate the royal probity and outstanding virtues of your most excellent parent.

His exceptional character so far surpassed that of the other kings that, setting all others aside—and with the sole exception of the emperor Henry, who adhered more closely to the holy Roman Church—we judged that he should be embraced by us with singular affection. We grieve exceedingly, indeed beyond measure, over his death, and wish, exhort, and again admonish you to set him before yourself as an example, so that you may draw forth the adornments of virtue from the source of the noble blood from which you visibly descend.

Finally, you must think and carefully consider how fleeting and worthless these earthly things are, how everything hastens unceasingly toward decline, so that no stability can persuade anyone to trust in them and so that terrible fear lies hidden in possessing them.

When you have clearly recognized and wisely despised these fugitive things, you will be able to extend the sharpness of your mind toward those things that are stable and eternal—things that invite your spirit to obtain them and toward which the examples of the good kindle your desire.

Among the other virtues that you judge worthy of imitation, we wish the defense of the Churches to stand foremost in your mind; reverence for the priestly order should hold the next place; and thereafter you should preserve justice and mercy with discretion in all your judgments.

Meanwhile, this matter must not be passed over but must be strongly prohibited by apostolic interdiction: it has come to our attention concerning your people that you attribute the harshness of the seasons, corruptions of the air, and whatever bodily afflictions occur to the faults of priests.

How grave a sin this is you can clearly perceive from the fact that our Savior himself showed honor even to the Jewish priests by sending lepers cleansed [puratos; for purgatos; HARD. reads curatos, “healed”] to them, and commanded the others to observe whatever they instructed, although your priests, whatever their condition may be, are nevertheless far better than those men.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you to eradicate this destructive custom completely from your kingdom. Do not presume any longer to inflict such an insult, contrary to your salvation, upon priests and clerics worthy of honor and reverence, by assigning to them causes hidden within the divine judgment.

Furthermore, do not suppose that you are permitted to do anything impious to women condemned with similar barbarity by a barbarous custom for the same reason. Rather, learn to avert the sentence of divine vengeance through worthy repentance, instead of provoking the Lord’s anger still further by savagely attacking those who are innocent.

For if you persist in these crimes, your prosperity will undoubtedly be turned into calamity, and you will be compelled to bear, overcome and unable to resist, the yoke of those whom, after conquering them, you have hitherto been accustomed to rule [perhaps nimium, “excessively,” rather than nimirum].

But if you obey us—or rather, blessed Peter—in these matters, then, as we trust in divine clemency, you will be able to obtain both forgiveness of your sins and apostolic blessing.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO ARNOLD, BISHOP OF LE MANS (1080)

He restores the episcopal ministry that had been forbidden by the apostolic legate. He absolves Abbot Joel. He deposes Rainald, the invader and perjurer, and orders that the aforesaid Joel be restored in his place.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ARNOLD, bishop of Le Mans: greetings and apostolic blessing.**

The episcopal ministry which our legate had forbidden you, as justice dictates, we restore.

We absolve Abbot Joel.

We depose Rainald the invader, because he committed perjury through ambition, so that he may no longer be abbot either in the place he desired or in any other monastery.

Therefore we wish you to compel the aforesaid Rainald to withdraw and to restore Joel as abbot in his place.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXIII. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH (1080)

Having testified to his love for him, he exhorts him to render the obedience owed to the apostolic see.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to WILLIAM, king of the English: greetings and apostolic blessing.**
I believe it is known to you, most excellent son, how, even before I ascended to the pontifical dignity, I always loved you with the affection of sincere devotion, and how I showed myself toward your affairs, and how effective I was; moreover, with what zeal I labored so that you might rise to the royal summit. For this reason I endured almost great disgrace from certain brothers, who murmured that I had devoted my efforts with such favor to the perpetration of so many murders. But God was witness in my conscience of how rightly I had acted, hoping by the grace of God—and not vainly trusting in the good virtues that were in you—that [Col. 0566A] the more you advanced toward higher things, the better you would show yourself before God and the holy Church (as is indeed now the case, thanks be to God).

Therefore, now, as to a most beloved son and a faithful servant of Saint Peter and of us, I disclose to you briefly our counsel, and what it is fitting for you thereafter to do, just as I would do in a private conversation. For when it pleased Him who exalts the humble that our holy mother, the Church, should—God as my witness—snatch me, quite unwilling and resisting, to govern the apostolic see, immediately I could not, compelled by the necessity of my office (which has been enjoined upon me to cry out and never cease), and overcome also by love and fear, conceal the abominable evils that she suffers from the worst of men.

By love, indeed, because Saint Peter had sweetly nourished me from childhood in his house, and because the charity of the Lord our God, regarding me as something, had chosen me as the vicar of so great a shepherd to govern our holy mother. By fear, however, because the divine law thunders terribly, saying: “Cursed is the man who spares his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII), that is, who withholds teaching from the slaying of carnal life.

Now, therefore, dearest son, whom I shall always embrace in Christ, since you see your mother excessively afflicted and the unavoidable necessity of coming to her aid presses us, I want you—and I admonish you with great concern for your honor and salvation, in true and not feigned charity—to render every obedience. Just as, with God’s cooperation, you have deserved to be a jewel among princes, so may you deserve to be a model of the rule of justice and obedience to all the princes of the earth; [Col. 0566C] without doubt, in the future glory you will be the foremost prince of as many princes as will be saved until the end of the age through the example of your obedience. And if some of them do not wish to be saved, your reward will nevertheless in no way be diminished.

Not only this: in this world also, victory, honor, power, and exaltation will be bestowed upon you and your heirs more abundantly from heaven. Set yourself as an example to yourself. For just as you would rightly wish to be honored by one whom you had made from a wretched and poorest servant into a most powerful king, so hasten always zealously to honor Jesus, your almighty honorer, protector, and helper, who made you from a wretched and impoverished servant of sin—for thus, indeed, we are all born—a most powerful king, freely.

Nor should the crowd of the worst princes impede you in this. The wickedness of many is one thing, but the virtue of a few another. It is more glorious for a proven soldier to stand in battle while many are fleeing. That jewel is more precious which is found more rarely. Indeed, the more the powerful of this age, blinded by their pride and impious acts, fall into the abyss, the more it befits you, who have been found far dearer to God than they, to be raised up through pious humility and exalted through obedience, so that it may be as it is written: “Let the wicked still do wickedly, and let him who is filthy still be filthy, and let the righteous still practice righteousness” (Rev. XXIII).

I would write more to you in exhortation, but because you sent men who, together with our son Hubert, greatly rejoiced me concerning your prudence, integrity, and justice, I judged that enough had been said for a wise man.
