I hope that almighty God will deign to work in you and through you for his honor beyond what we can say. What is less suited to a letter we have entrusted to your legates to tell you orally.

May almighty God himself, our Father, mercifully deign to inspire and plant these things so deeply in your heart, dearest son, that in this age he may deservedly increase your kingdom and power through your virtues, and in the age to come may happily lead you with the holy kings into the heavenly kingdoms, immeasurably better than anything conceivable. Amen.

At your request, and with justice dictating it, we have favored the bishop of Le Mans and restored his episcopal office. We have also absolved the abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, which is at Le Mans.

[Col. 0567B] Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXIV. TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF HIRSAU  
*(Year 1080.)*

He approves that he has undertaken the care of the monastery of Saint Saviour, and appoints him his vicar to see that an abbot is canonically ordained there. He prohibits secular princes from having any rights in that place. He annuls the privilege granted by Alexander II, formerly induced by deception, to Everard. Since the bishop of the Church of Constance is at variance with the Roman Church, he grants that the abbot may receive from any religious bishop whatsoever the ordinations and consecrations belonging to episcopal office, or may have recourse to the apostolic see.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **WILLIAM**, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since it has come to our attention that your religious devotion undertook the care of the monastery of Saint Saviour, belonging to the jurisdiction of the apostolic see, to which twelve gold pieces—of which twenty make an ounce—are to be paid annually from that same monastery, situated in the village of Scaphusa [Satfusa], in the diocese of Constance, at the entreaty of Count Burcard and the urging of religious men, on this sole condition: that the aforesaid count, who claimed for himself in the said monastery certain conditions as though they were his own, should, after abandoning and renouncing all secular power, permit that place to remain free—we approve your devotion’s action and confirm what has been done by apostolic authority.

And because through you that place, as we have heard, has begun, by the Lord’s mercy, to rise toward a religious state, we, desiring insofar as we can to provide perpetual stability of holiness there, entrust to your fraternity responsibility for that coenobium in our place, namely, that you instruct the brothers there in the regular disciplines, diligently provide through suitable instruction for their morals and way of life and for matters pertaining to the salvation of souls, and, above all, take care that an abbot be appointed there according to God.

Moreover, so that the brothers of the aforesaid monastery may be able to pursue their purpose more securely and earnestly, without disturbance, and may eagerly and gladly render the service of due devotion to almighty God, we will and command by apostolic authority that no priest, [Col. 0568A] king, duke, or count, nor any powerful or wicked person, presume to claim for himself in that place any conditions of ownership—not hereditary right, advocacy, investiture, or any authority whatsoever—that might harm the freedom of the monastery; nor may anyone invade, diminish, or alienate the church’s ornaments or possessions.

Rather, let it be secure from every secular power and peaceful in the freedom of the Roman see, just as the monasteries of Cluny and Marseille are known to remain. Let the abbot choose whatever advocate he wishes. If that man later proves of no use to the monastery, let him be removed and another appointed.

The privilege that our predecessor of blessed memory, Alexander, induced by some surreptition or deception contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, granted to this place—by which he conceded to Count Everard and his descendants the advocacy, the power to appoint the abbot, and the administration of the entire property—we, exercising apostolic authority by a sentence of canonical correction, weaken, invalidate, and cancel; and, lest anyone’s rash greed burst forth through this into the audacity of his own destruction, we revoke it as null by apostolic authority.

Therefore, if anyone stubbornly attempts to act against this salutary command of ours, let him not doubt that he will lose the grace of blessed Peter. After he has been admonished once, twice, and three times, with suitable intervals, if he does not repent and disdains to correct his offense, let him know that he is bound by divine anathema and excluded from communion in the body and blood of the Lord.

Also, adding this in confirmation of the freedom of the Roman Church, we decree that if at any time the bishop presiding over the Church of Constance should dissent from the apostolic see and disobey it—which, as Samuel confirms, is “the sin of divination and the crime of idolatry” (I Reg. XXXV), and as blessed Ambrose says, “It is clear that he is a heretic who does not agree with the Roman Church”—the abbot and his people may seek and receive from any religious bishop they choose ordinations, consecrations, and whatever pertains to episcopal office, or may have recourse to the apostolic see.

May those who observe this command of ours obtain from the Lord remission of all their sins and good favor.

[Col. 0568D] Done at the Lateran, on the eighth [seventh] day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXV. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH  
*(Year 1080.)*

He urges him to place the honor of God before his own honor and to love God with all his strength and with an undivided heart.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **WILLIAM**, king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your prudence is not unaware that, above all other dignities, God almighty has distributed the apostolic and royal dignities in this world for its governance. For just as, to display the beauty of the world to carnal eyes at different times, he arranged the sun and moon as lights more eminent than all others, so, lest the creature whom his goodness had created in this world in his own image be drawn into perilous error, he provided that it should be governed through different offices by the apostolic and royal dignity.

Yet, despite this distinction between greater and lesser, Christian devotion conducts itself in such a way that the royal power is governed, after God, by the care and administration of the apostolic dignity. Although your vigilance, dearest son, does not ignore this, nevertheless, so that it may be indissolubly bound to your mind for your salvation, divine Scripture testifies that apostolic and pontifical dignity will present Christian kings and all others before the divine tribunal and render an account to God for their offenses.

If, then, you are to be presented by me before the just Judge, who cannot lie, and before the terrible judgment of the Creator of all creatures, let your diligent wisdom judge whether I ought or can fail to take the greatest care for your salvation, and whether you ought or can, without delay, disobey me when I seek your salvation, so that you may possess the land of the living.

Therefore, take care—if you love yourself—to strive incessantly to place God and the honor of God before yourself and your own honor, and to love God with a pure mind, with all your strength, and with an undivided heart. Believe me: if you love God with a pure mind, as you hear and as Scripture commands, and if in all things you place the honor of God before your own, he who does not know how to love falsely, and who is powerful enough even to place you first, will embrace you both in this life and in the future, and will enlarge your kingdom with his almighty arm.

[Col. 0569C] Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXVI. TO MATHILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH  
*(Year 1080.)*

He commends her faith. He says that he desires no gifts from her other than a chaste life, the distribution of her possessions among the poor, and love of neighbor.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **MATHILDA**, queen of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Having read your letters, we understood with what faithful mind you obey God and with what great love you cling to your faithful subjects. We also perceive from your magnificent promises how your mind keeps us present in its memory, since you indicated that whatever we might wish from your possessions, once you knew of it, you would provide without delay.

Understand, dearest daughter, with what affection we have received this and what gifts we desire from you. For what gold, what jewels, what precious things of this world should I expect from you more than a chaste life, the distribution of your possessions among the poor, and love of God and neighbor? These and similar gifts we desire from you. We ask that you love your nobility with integrity and simplicity, obtain what you love, and never abandon what you possess. Do not cease to arm your husband with these and similar weapons whenever God gives you the opportunity.

[Col. 0570A] We entrust the rest, which we have omitted, to be conveyed through our son and common faithful servant Hubert.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ROBERT, SON OF THE KING OF THE ENGLISH  
*(Year 1080.)*

He advises him to heed his father’s counsels and to obey him in all things, showing him honor.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **ROBERT**, son of the king of the English, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Reliable reports of your character, prudence, and generosity, which have reached us, have made us rejoice, partly because of your parents and partly because of you. But the reports of certain others, which troubled our ears with the counsel of wicked men, have made us sorrowful instead of joyful.

Now, however, because through our son Hubert we have heard that you heed your father’s counsels and have entirely dismissed the wicked, we rejoice. Moreover, we admonish and fatherly entreat you always to keep fixed in your mind how, with what strong hand and widespread glory, your father drew whatever he possesses from the mouths of his enemies, while knowing that he would not live forever, but striving so manfully for this purpose that he might leave it to some heir of his.

Therefore, dearest son, we admonish you to beware lest henceforth you heed the counsels of the wicked, by which you offend your father and grieve your mother. Let these divine commands and admonitions be indissolubly fixed in you: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth” [Col. 0570C] (Exod. XX; Deut. V). And this also: “Whoever curses his father or mother shall be put to death” (Exod. XXI).

If longer life is granted to you because of honoring your father and mother, consider what, conversely, is granted if you dishonor them. If divine Scripture thunders that curses bring death to a son, much more certainly it indicates that evil deeds bring a more certain death.

What, then, remains, if you wish to live as a member of Christ and conduct yourself honorably in this world? By virtue of our office, we command you to dismiss entirely the counsels of the wicked and to heed your father’s will in all things.

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE BISHOP OF BENEVENTO  
*(Year 1080.)*

He wishes him to seek out and examine a certain convicted heretic; if he finds him repentant, he is to dismiss him unharmed in every respect; otherwise, he is to take care to restore him to sound doctrine through penance. If he is obstinate, he is to expel him from the archbishopric and settle his case together with the abbot of Monte Cassino and certain bishops.

[Col. 0570D]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother and fellow bishop, the Beneventan R . . . . . . ., greetings and apostolic blessing.

We inform your fraternity that John the priest, bearer of this letter, a man orthodox, as we have learned from his own profession, has complained to us on behalf of the Armenian archbishop of Synnada [Col. 0571A] concerning a certain wicked man whom we judged a convicted heretic from his own mouth: because, having been expelled from Armenia on account of this impiety, he is giving rise in the Latin, apostolic, and catholic Church to grave suspicion—indeed, to a judgment—against Armenia of that same heresy.

Therefore, approving the faith of that Armenian Church, as we have learned from this man’s words, we instruct your affection by admonition to seek out diligently and examine carefully the aforesaid heretic, who, fearing our judgment of his perfidy, has fled from our hands.

If it becomes clear to your understanding that he has repented and returned to the catholic faith, then, properly instructed and confirmed, you shall dismiss him safe and unharmed in every respect. But if he has not yet been converted from the gravity of his error to the bosom of mother Church and the right faith, procure by admonishing him to bring him back to the counsel of sound doctrine by the path of penance.

But if, hardened by a diabolical spirit, he refuses to heed your most salutary admonitions supported by true reasons and to consent to the sincere understanding of the faith, lest his madness remain hidden from the ignorant and thereby harm the unwary, we order you to have him openly marked with the stigma of perfidy. Then, having expelled him from your entire archbishopric and exposing his heresy everywhere to all as far as you can, do not cease to pursue him as an apostate and enemy of Christian unity.

So that you may find him and more quickly recognize him when found, we add his name, Macharus [Macharion], and the name of the place where he resides, Frigentium. We also command you to join with the religious abbot of Monte Cassino and all your fellow bishops in examining the case of the aforesaid heretic and, once examined, to determine it.

Moreover, forbid him to carry any longer the iron which we prohibited him from carrying, lest by this hypocrisy he further deceive unwary minds. As for the money he acquired through such great fraud, take it from him by our command and distribute it to the poor.

# BOOK EIGHT OF THE REGISTER

In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1080, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Gregory, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0571]

## LETTER I. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF SYNNADA

[Col. 0571B]

[Col. 0571C] He grieves to have heard that the Church of the Armenians has deviated in certain matters from the rectitude of the catholic faith. He wishes to know from him whether this is so, and wants him to indicate by letter and messengers what he himself thinks about these matters and about everything pertaining to the faith, and whether he accepts the four general councils. He advises him to believe what the catholic Church believes and not to cease offering unleavened bread in his Church. He reports the calumnies of the Greeks, who persecute the Roman Church in this matter with an even graver insult, though doing nothing to it; nevertheless, he neither rejects nor condemns their leavened bread. He exhorts him to keep the day of the final judgment before his eyes and prays God to preserve him in the concordant unity of the faithful.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to G . . . . ., beloved brother in Christ, the archbishop of Synnada, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The watchtower of the highest see, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, unworthy though we are, and the care of the universal Church, which by his providence we administer, compel us, just as to grieve intensely over the destruction of those who separate themselves from the body of Christ, so also to rejoice with ineffable gladness over the salutary agreement of those who think rightly and are known to preserve the unity of the faith.

Therefore, since it has been reported to us that your Church—that is, the Church of the Armenians—has deviated into certain perverse opinions from the rectitude of the faith which the universal Church holds as handed down by the apostles and holy Fathers, we have certainly grieved exceedingly out of fatherly compassion.

From the report of certain persons we have learned that, in celebrating the saving sacraments of the sacrifices, water is not mixed with wine among you at all, although no Christian who knows the holy Gospels doubts that water flowed from the Lord’s side together with blood. We have also heard that, contrary to the custom of the holy Church, your Church makes holy chrism not from balsam but from butter, and that it venerates and approves Dioscorus of Alexandria, the arch-heresiarch who, because of the hardness of his perfidy, was deposed and condemned at the Council of Chalcedon.

Although your legate, the bearer of this letter, denied before us that these things are so, nevertheless, wishing to know more firmly from your fraternity, we want you, through this same John the priest, to arrange to write back to us with your seal, explaining what you think about these matters and about anything else concerning which you may be uncertain; and thereafter to direct your letters frequently to the apostolic see.

We also want your charity to indicate by letter whether your Church accepts what the universal Church embraces, namely, the faith of the four councils which, approved by the holy Fathers and confirmed with apostolic authority by the Roman pontiffs Sylvester, Leo, and others, are accepted.

Among these, blessed Pope Gregory, an outstanding teacher, testified in his letter that he held this faith, writing to the greater Churches [possibly “churches”; Hardouin: likewise in the Codex of Modena] of Alexandria, Antioch, and others (Book I, Letter 24), in these words:

“Because one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Rom. X), I confess that I receive and venerate four councils, just as I receive and venerate the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, at which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, at which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; the First Council of Ephesus, at which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, at which the perversity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with utterly complete approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of holy faith rises, and the rule of every life and action is established. Whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he is seen to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

I likewise venerate the Fifth Council, at which the letter called that of Ibas, full of error, was rejected; at which Theodore, separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two substances, was convicted of having fallen into the impiety of perfidy; and at which the writings of Theodoret, by which the faith of blessed Cyril was criticized, were refuted as produced with deranged audacity.

I reject all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and embrace those whom they venerate. Since they were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to loosen what they bind or to bind what they loosen destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Having carefully explained these words of that most holy and distinguished teacher, we have judged that your prudence should be admonished with affection concerning the clause that you add to that hymn of praise: “Holy God, holy mighty, holy immortal”—namely, “Who were crucified for us” [perhaps: “es”; Hardouin]. Since no Eastern Church except yours has this, nor does the holy Roman Church, avoid henceforth adding it, so as to avoid giving occasion for every scandal and suspicion of a perverse interpretation.

For if the vessel of election, blessed Paul, declared that it was better for him not to eat or drink than to scandalize a brother (I Cor. VIII), you should consider how grave and dangerous it is to cause scandal among brothers concerning the faith where it can be avoided through a sounder understanding.

Therefore, let your fraternity consider that the Church entrusted to your care must hold, and believe that it is sufficient, what the catholic Church spread throughout the world is known to think and is declared to hold, having been instructed by the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, because we have learned that your Church offers unleavened bread and is for this reason criticized by ignorant Greeks as though for heresy, we want you to marvel greatly at their reckless chatter, but not to desist from your established practice. Know that their insolence not only brings this charge against you as a calumny, but also, for a similar reason and with a graver insult, has until now risen against the holy Roman Church, which through blessed Peter is established, as if by a certain privilege, from the very beginnings of the faith by the holy Fathers as the mother of all Churches, and will always be held so until the end.

No heretic, as far as is known, has ever presided over it, nor, especially because of the Lord’s promise, do we trust that one will ever be placed over it. For the Lord Jesus says: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII).

They, commending their leavened bread, do not cease stubbornly to jest with the lightest words of criticism against us. We, however, defending our unleavened bread with an unassailable argument according to the Lord, neither condemn nor reject their leavened bread, following the Apostle who says that “to the pure all things are pure” (Tit. I).

But let these things suffice for now to expose and despise the Greeks’ recklessness. We once again impress upon your affection that you should strive to send us through the aforesaid priest, or through another suitable messenger, your letters explaining how you hold the matters written above and the other matters that are seen to pertain to the faith.

Moreover, although we believe your diligence to be well instructed, nevertheless, out of due affection, we briefly admonish it as though you always had the day of strict judgment before your eyes. Consider the burden of the care entrusted to you; and the more quickly you see that day approaching without delay, the more earnestly do not neglect to watch over the account you will render of the money, lest the severe Lender, who is also the strict Judge, find you deserving of punishment not because of a talent badly buried, but, smiling upon multiplied profit, invite you to receive the fruit of blessed recompense.

May almighty God, to whom belongs whatever we rightly understand, think, and believe, illuminate your fraternity’s mind more abundantly, guide it along the path of sound understanding, and, preserving you in the concordant unity of the faithful, govern and guard you so that you may effectively instruct the peoples subject to you in divine knowledge, enter eternal glory with them, and receive the highest rewards on their behalf.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

[Note: Pagius argues that this oath belongs to the year 1077, in the year of Christ 1080, no. 5.]

## Oath of Duke Robert

I, Robert, by the grace of God and of Saint Peter duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, from this hour and henceforth shall be faithful to the holy Roman Church, to the apostolic see, and to you, my lord Gregory, universal pope.

In counsel or deed by which you might lose life or limb, or by which you might be captured in an evil captivity, I shall not participate. The counsel that you entrust to me and forbid me to reveal, I shall not reveal to your detriment, knowingly.

I shall be a helper to the holy Roman Church and to you in holding, acquiring, and defending the royal rights of Saint Peter and his possessions, to the best of my ability, against all men, except in the matter of the March of Fermo and Salerno and Amalfi, concerning which no determination has yet been made. I shall help you to hold the Roman papacy securely and honorably.

I shall neither invade nor seek to acquire nor presume to plunder the land of Saint Peter that you now hold or will hold, once I know it to be under your power, without the definite permission of you and your successors who will have been ordained for the honor of Saint Peter, apart from whatever you grant me or your successors may grant.

Regarding the tribute from the land of Saint Peter that I hold or shall hold, I shall faithfully strive to ensure that the holy Roman Church receives it annually, as has been established.

I shall also leave all the churches that remain under my rule, together with their possessions, in your power, and I shall be their defender in fidelity to the holy Roman Church.

And if you or your successors depart this life before me, I shall, according to what I am instructed by the better cardinals and by the Roman clergy and laity, help to ensure that a pope is elected [Col. 0575A] and ordained for the honor of Saint Peter.

I shall observe all the matters written above toward the holy Roman Church and toward you with right faith. I shall observe this fidelity toward your successors ordained for the honor of Saint Peter, who, provided that no fault of mine has intervened, will confirm for me the investiture granted to me by you.

Done at Ciprani, on the third day before the Kalends of July.

## Investiture of Pope Gregory, by which he invested Duke Robert

I, Pope Gregory, invest you, Duke Robert, with the land that my predecessors of blessed memory, Nicholas and Alexander, granted to you.

As for the land that you unjustly hold—namely Salerno, Amalfi, and part of the March of Fermo—I now patiently tolerate you in the confidence of almighty God and of your goodness, so that afterward you may conduct yourself in regard to it for the honor of God and Saint Peter as it is fitting for you to act and for me to receive, without danger to your soul or mine.

Done as above.

## Establishment of the payment of tribute on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection

Namely, twelve denarii of Pavia currency from all Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.

I, Robert, by the grace of God and of Saint Peter duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, in confirmation of the transfer and acknowledgment of fidelity, promise that, from all the land that I possess in my own dominion and that I have not yet granted to any man from beyond the Alps in such a way that he holds it, I shall annually pay to blessed Peter, to you, my lord Pope Gregory, and to all your successors or to the messengers of your successors, a tribute of twelve denarii of Pavia currency for each yoke of oxen.

The term for this payment of tribute shall always be the Sunday of the holy Resurrection, once each year has been completed. Under this condition of paying the tribute, I bind myself and my heirs or successors to you, my lord Pope Gregory, and to your successors.

## LETTER II. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF CLUNY  
*(Year 1080.)*

He censures the crime of the simoniacal monk Robert, whom he orders to be corrected by his abbot and separated from entry into the church and from every ecclesiastical ministry. He also wishes the king, deceived by Robert’s fraud, to be admonished that, unless he repents, he will have to be excommunicated, and that all the faithful in the regions of Spain will have to be summoned against him. He further advises the abbot to take care that his monks, dispersed throughout the regions of Spain, return to their own monastery; and he indicates that no ordination there will have force unless it has been strengthened by the authority of the apostolic legate.

[Col. 0575D]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **HUGH**, venerable abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You can learn from the letters of our legate Richard, the abbot of Marseille, how great an impiety has gone forth from your monastery through the presumption of your monk Robert.

That Robert, having become an imitator of Simon Magus, did not fear to rise against the authority of blessed Peter with all the cunning of wickedness he could muster, and by his persuasion to lead back into their former error one hundred thousand people who, through the diligence of our labor, had begun to return to the way of truth.

We do not believe that you consented to his wickedness; rather, we understand that because of the enormity of the crime you grieve with us and have resolved to exercise the punishment that is due—especially since you have given us an ancient demonstration of your faith by sharing our view concerning the honor of the holy Roman Church and by preserving the freedom of rectitude for carrying out justice, which, as charity grows cold, has almost departed from the earth.

No report and no suggestion will be able to tear us away from this certainty formed in our mind. Nor will those who murmur against you concerning many matters be able, before a fraternal conversation takes place, to generate in us any scandal that would make us suspect otherwise.

For, to say nothing of other matters, nearly all the brothers who are with us, unless they were restrained by the bridle of our reason, would have turned the love they showed toward you in our place into serious hostility.

Therefore, since we love your salvation as our own, we admonish you, while correcting your subjects, not to give those who love your religious community an occasion for such murmuring.

In particular, we admonish you to separate that Robert, who proved to be the author of the aforesaid wickedness and who, through a diabolical suggestion, brought such great danger upon the Church of Spain, from entry into the church and from every ministry of your affairs [Col. 0576C] until he returns to you and receives a punishment worthy of his presumption.

Make the king, who was deceived by Robert’s fraud, understand carefully through your letters that he has provoked the anger and indignation of blessed Peter against himself and his kingdom, unless he repents; for he treated the legate of the Roman Church indecently and believed falsehood rather than truth.

In order to make worthy satisfaction to God and blessed Peter concerning these matters, let him commend himself and make himself devoted through due humility and fitting reverence, just as he dishonored our legate.

We also consider it appropriate that you inform him that, if he does not correct his fault, we shall excommunicate him and summon all the faithful of Saint Peter who are in the regions of Spain against him, to his confusion.

If they were less obedient to our command, we would not consider it a great hardship to travel to Spain and undertake harsh and difficult measures against him as an enemy of the Christian religion.

Let it also be your concern that the monks unjustly dispersed throughout those same regions return to their own monastery, and that no ordination there have force unless it has been approved by the authority of our legate.

We also wish you to order that another letter of ours be delivered to the aforesaid king.

Given at Ciprani [Carpetani; Codex of Modena: Coperani], on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in the third indiction.

## LETTER III. TO ALPHONSUS, KING OF CASTILE  
*(Year 1080.)*

[Col. 0577A]

He warns him that, once evil counselors have been removed, he should heed the salutary admonitions of the apostolic legate and bring joy to himself and the Church of God by correcting his conduct; that he should reject the unlawful marriage contracted with a kinswoman of his wife and not allow himself to be carried away by love for the incestuous woman. He declares that the monk Robert, a seducer and disturber of the kingdom, will pay the penalties deserved for his rashness and crime.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, King ALFONSO, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It cannot be expressed, dearest son, how greatly your distinguished obedience, as reported to us by our son Richard, legate of the Apostolic See, had gladdened us. For you were always before God in the deepest places of our heart; among men you were for us the greatest example of outstanding virtue. We gloried in you before other kings, and rejoiced that, in the Lord’s portion, we possessed in you a truly Christian king, and therefore a true king, against the members of the devil. Hence the fragrance of your good works had already spread through many regions, and, like a sun born in the west, you were sending the rays of heavenly light toward the east.

But now, having learned that the devil, as is his custom envying your salvation and that of all who were to be saved through you, has through one of his members, a certain false monk named Robert, and through his ancient accomplice, a ruined woman, driven your manly spirit from the right path, just as greatly as we had first rejoiced over you, so greatly now are we confounded, ashamed, and saddened.

Therefore, so that you may know how piously concerned we are for you, in the name of Christ’s goodness and glory we admonish and charge you in a father’s voice: remove from yourself as quickly as possible the counselors of falsehood; for evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15). Moreover, heed our legate, Brother Richard, in all things. If I had not known him to be prudent and religious, I would never have entrusted our place to him.

May love for the incestuous woman not carry you away from our salutary admonitions and instructions, for women make the wise apostatize (Ecclus. 19). Indeed, the shameful love of women brought down that most wise king Solomon himself, and by God’s judgment almost snatched the flourishing kingdom of Israel entirely from the hand of his descendants.

Therefore, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the power of his coming, and also by the authority of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we again admonish and command you: do not despise yourself; do not place a stain upon your glory; do not make the posterity of your flesh useless and rejected. Recover your strength; utterly reject the unlawful marriage which you contracted with a kinswoman of your wife. Quickly gladden us and the entire Church of God by correcting your conduct, lest, if you should prefer to be disobedient—which God avert!—you incur the anger of almighty God, and we—which we say with great reluctance and grief—be compelled to unsheathe blessed Peter’s sword against you.

As for the aforementioned most wicked monk Robert, your seducer and disturber of the kingdom, we decree that, having been separated from entry into the church, he is to be shut away for penance within the cloister of the monastery of Cluny. The abbot of Cluny, however, will do this in imitation of us; for we walk by the same path, with the same mind and the same spirit. May almighty God deign quickly to gladden us, dearest son, by your correction.

## LETTER IV. TO RICHARD. (Year 1080.)

He consoles him concerning the persecutions of his enemies. He urges him to patience, promising that meanwhile he will see to it that the false monk Robert suffers the penalties for his crime.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richard, his most beloved son, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Because, in letters you sent, you informed us that the ancient enemy had, through his members—as is not unusual—hindered your work, which was directed in part toward Christian benefit, and that because of this your brotherly heart had incurred excessive sadness, we too, rightly sympathizing with you, are affected by the same grief.

But when we recall how much and how greatly the apostles, and their successors as well, suffered in laying the foundation of the Church, partly from pagans and partly from false Christians, we take courage, trusting in the Lord’s mercy and awaiting with complete confidence the triumph of victory over that same enemy, without doubt as did our predecessors.

For the present, patience and perseverance are altogether necessary to your religious purpose, since the Apostle’s saying has been rightly brought forward: no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. 2). Nevertheless, we shall not fail your zeal in anything. We will send the abbot of Cluny letters concerning your complaint together with our own, so that he may compel the false monk Robert to return to the monastery as quickly as possible, restrain him from entering the church, and subject him to the prolonged squalor of so severe a penance that, for the wicked deed he committed against you—or rather against God—he may feel the punishment of penance.

## LETTER V. TO THE BISHOPS OF APULIA AND CALABRIA. (Year 1080.)

He complains of the presumption of certain bishops against the Roman Church. Nevertheless, he says that, like others of the same kind, they remained confounded both in the time of Pope Alexander and in his own time; but afterward, with hardened hearts, those who ought to have returned to their senses conspired again against that same Church and appointed the bishop of Ravenna as a heresiarch. Therefore, hoping that their pride will soon collapse and that the peace of the holy Church will be extended after its enemies have been confounded, he urges them to aid the suffering Church with their prayers.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops established throughout the principalities, Apulia, and Calabria, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that it is not unknown to your brotherhood that many disciples of Satan, who are called bishops in name only throughout various regions, inflamed by diabolical pride, have attempted to confound the holy Roman Church. But, through the help of almighty God and the authority of blessed Peter, their wicked presumption brought shame and confusion upon them, just as it brought glory and exaltation to the Apostolic See.

Indeed, from the least to the greatest—that is, H . . . [namely, King Henry], who is shown to have been the head of kings [perhaps “of the kings”; HARD.] and the originator of the baneful plot—he has learned through very many dangers to body and soul how much strength the authority of blessed Peter possesses for avenging their iniquity.

For you know that, in the time of our lord Pope A . . . [Alexander], the same H . . . [Henry] devised an injury against the Church of blessed Peter through Cadulus [elsewhere “Cadalous”; [Col. 0579B] HARD. reads “cedula”], and how great and how shameful a pit of confusion he deserved to fall into with that same Cadulus, with the whole world as witness; and how much honor and how many triumphs our R. P. [“reverend fatherhood,” that is, the commonwealth; HARD.] gained in the conduct of that struggle.

You also know with what detestable conspiracies, three years ago, especially the Lombard bishops armed themselves against us, with the same H . . . ruling; and that, through the protection of blessed Peter, we remained unharmed and safe, not without great exaltation of our honor and that of our faithful.

But since they thought that the former confusion was not enough for them, the wound itself still gives evidence of how greatly the sword of apostolic vengeance struck them from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head [alternative reading: “how greatly it burned”; HARD.].

Yet in all these matters, bearing foreheads hardened like those of prostitutes and storing up for themselves, through their shamelessness, the anger of just judgment, they—who, in view of their disgrace, ought to have returned to their senses—followed their father, who said, “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). They attempted to renew their former conspiracy against the Lord and the holy universal Church, and to appoint as their Antichrist and heresiarch a sacrilegious and perjured man, marked throughout the Roman [R . . ., that is, “Roman”; HARD.] world by the most abominable crimes: W . . . [that is, Wibert; HARD.; Gibert]—we mean the devastator of the holy Church of Ravenna.

In that assembly of Satan were present those whose life is detestable and whose ordination is heretical through the enormity of their manifold crimes. Indeed, desperation finally dragged them into this madness because they preferred not to seek forgiveness for their crimes from us either by prayers or by promises of services and gifts—unless, perhaps, they were willing to submit themselves, through mercy, to ecclesiastical judgment and to our censure, as our office requires.

We therefore despise them all the more, unsupported by any consideration and utterly ruined by the consciousness of every crime, the more they themselves imagine that they have climbed to higher places.

Through God’s mercy and the prayer of blessed Peter—which wonderfully cast down Simon Magus, their master, when he was striving toward higher things—we hope that their downfall will not be long delayed and that, once their enemies have been defeated and confounded, the peace of the holy Church will, as usual, be extended most gloriously.

Therefore, dearest brothers, considering the innocence of your common mother, the holy Roman Church, and observing how greatly the devil exercises his members to bring disturbance upon the aforementioned Roman Church, devote your efforts and zeal, as is fitting and as the duty of your office demands, to prayers and to the other means by which a suffering mother ought to be aided. Thus it may become clear that you are her legitimate sons and that you feel her disgrace from the heart, sharing the diligence of our labor.

If you become partners in compassion, then, with God’s help, you will be participants in joy and consolation. The other matters which we have not included we have entrusted to our legates to report, just as you may trust them as you trust us.

Given at Cicani, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August.

## LETTER VI. TO THE SAME. (Year 1080.)

He instructs them to assist Michael, emperor of Constantinople, who was unjustly expelled from imperial dignity and was imploring the aid of the Apostolic See and of Duke Robert. He commands the soldiers who wish to serve with him to serve him faithfully; and he directs the bishops to admonish those soldiers to preserve right faith toward him, to keep the fear and love of God before their eyes, and to persevere in good works, and thus to absolve them from their sins.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brothers and fellow bishops residing in Apulia and Calabria, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We do not doubt that your prudence knows that the most glorious emperor of Constantinople, namely Michael [Note: He understands Ducas, who was called Parapinaces and had laid aside the purple on 7 April 1078], was removed from the height of imperial majesty more disgracefully and maliciously than justly or reasonably. He came to Italy to seek the aid of blessed Peter and also of our son, the most glorious Duke Robert.

Therefore, although unworthy, since we exercise the care of that See, moved by compassion, we judged that we ought to consent to his prayers and also to those of the same duke, and that he ought to be assisted by the faithful of blessed Peter.

Since, among the many kinds of assistance, the aforesaid princes judge this one to be no less useful—namely, that the soldiers who are to provide aid should go constantly to the assistance and defense of the aforementioned emperor with right faith and with undivided purpose—we command by apostolic authority that those who decide to enter his service must not dare to turn treacherously to the opposite side. Rather, as the honor and duty of the Christian religion require, they are to provide him faithful support.

We likewise command your devotion that you diligently admonish those who are to cross over with the same duke and the aforesaid emperor, as your office requires, to perform fitting penance, to preserve right faith toward them as Christians should, to keep the fear and love of God before their eyes in all their actions, and to persevere in good works. Thus, supported by our authority—or rather by the power of blessed Peter—absolve them from their sins.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

## LETTER VII. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL. (Year 1080.)

He declares that the promised aid of many princes is at hand and says that he will come to Ravenna with an armed force in order to rescue that Church from the hands of the wicked. Therefore he urges them, together with him, to despise the pride and efforts of those wicked men; from this they may hope that divine clemency will establish peace for the holy Church.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brothers and fellow bishops defending the Christian religion, and to the other faithful of Saint Peter of clerical and lay rank, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Let it be known to your devotion that, both personally and through our legates, we have spoken with Duke R . . . [Robert], Jordan, and the other more powerful princes of the Normans. They unanimously promise that, as they have sworn, they will provide aid for the defense of the holy Roman Church and our honor against all mortals.

The princes who are near and far around the City, and in Tuscany and the other regions, firmly promise us the same. Therefore, after the Kalends of September, when the season has begun to grow cold, desiring to rescue the holy Church of Ravenna (S. R.) from the hands of the wicked and restore it to its father, blessed Peter, we shall go to those regions with an armed force, as we hope from the Lord; and through his help we undoubtedly believe that we shall liberate it.

Therefore, since we regard as nothing the audacity of the wicked and the plots of those who have risen against us—or rather against blessed Peter—we want and urge you, together with us, likewise to despise their pride and efforts. You may be all the more certain of their ruin when you see them striving to climb higher and higher.

For the Prophet, invoking such things against them, says: “The pride of those who hate you has always ascended” (Ps. 73), openly declaring that bold impiety is nearer to its fall the more it thinks that it has ascended.

You, therefore, who fear God and preserve fidelity to blessed Peter, without any hesitation place your complete hope in the Lord’s mercy. Hope that the disturbance caused by the wicked will soon be quieted by the ruin they deserve, and that the peace and security of the holy Church will shortly be established—as we confidently promise, trusting in divine clemency.

## LETTER VIII. TO ALPHANUS, BISHOP OF SALERNO. (Year 1080.)

He rejoices over the discovery of the body of the blessed apostle Matthew. He urges the bishop to honor the relics with due veneration and to admonish Duke R . . . and his wife to show fitting reverence and honor to so distinguished a patron and strive to merit his aid.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother and fellow bishop, ALPHANUS of Salerno, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We offer immense thanks to the gracious regard of divine mercy, whose favor has mercifully revealed in our times a great treasure destined to benefit the whole world. We rightly congratulate your devotion as well, which carefully sought to make us participants in so great a joy, truly manifested from heaven.

We believe and confidently affirm that, at the discovery of so great a body, not only the blessed apostle Matthew himself but also the other fellow apostles, together with all the saints, the heavenly spirits, and the glorious mother of God, Mary, rejoice with mortals, and that the efforts of all of them on behalf of the human race at this time are much more eager and much more abundant than at other times [variant: “more overflowing,” likewise in the Mutina manuscript].

For if the pious patronage of the saints does not abandon us at other times, we must most certainly hope for their aid especially when their most holy bodies are manifested to us, as though brought back to life, by the divine will. And just as, through the sight of their bodily appearance, faith is, as it were, seen and hope is already held, so we must believe that their benefits toward the devoted are then renewed more abundantly and flow forth more richly.

Therefore, let the holy universal Church no longer doubt that her cry has been heard by the Lord, though formerly driven by great storms and various blasts of tempests. Let her eagerly direct her eyes nearby toward the safety of a tranquil shore, and contemplate beside herself the protection of the blessed apostle Matthew, since the ancient helmsman now shows his presence to the one who is struggling in the harbor.

Therefore let your brotherhood exult in the Lord over the revelation of so great a treasure. Embracing the most blessed relics with the services of due veneration, urge and admonish the glorious Duke R . . . and his most noble wife to show fitting reverence and honor to so distinguished a patron, who has deigned to reveal himself to them, and to strive with the utmost devotion to merit his grace and aid for themselves and their people.

Given at Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.

## LETTER IX. TO THE GERMANS. (Year 1080.)

He attributes the Church’s calamities to sins but shows that patience and hope are necessary. He therefore urges the priests first to correct the actions of their subjects, and then all the others to place their trust in the Lord. Nevertheless, he hopes that some will be converted to the embrace of Mother Church.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, and clerics and laypeople of every rank and authority residing in the Teutonic kingdom, but only to those who faithfully obey the holy Roman Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Since nothing happens on earth without a cause, as the words of the wise testify (Job 5), it must be believed that the fact that the holy Church has long been shaken by the weight of waves and storms, and that until now has suffered the fury of tyrannical blows, occurs only because our sins demand it.

For all the judgments of God are truly just. Yet amid all these things, illustrious brothers, the virtue of patience in the divine disposition must be maintained, and the certainty of hope must be firmly extended toward the regard of heavenly mercy. Its hand is found neither weak in raising up the humility of the faithful nor powerless in casting down the pride of hostile arrogance.

If we apply the medicine of penance to the diseases of our faults, and, by strictly correcting our excesses and negligences, shape our conduct according to the form of justice, then surely, with heavenly strength assisting us, the fury of our enemies will quickly perish, and the holy Church will recover the peace and security long desired.

Therefore we now speak especially to you who preside at the summit of priestly governance, since the life of your subjects is known to belong to your care, and at the coming judgment you must render an account for the flock entrusted to you. Examine carefully the actions and conduct of your subjects, without allowing favor or fear to hinder you; do not neglect to cut away, with the edge of discerning correction, what must be removed, according to what you have received from your mother, the holy Roman Church. Always keep in mind the prophetic saying: “Offer the sacrifice of justice, and hope in the Lord” (Ps. 4).

For the rest, we admonish and urge all of you: place your trust in the Lord and in the power of his might, because the wickedness of your adversaries has drawn near to its end. Thus those who, despairing of the Lord and of the holy Roman Church, the mother of all, have exalted themselves will pay the penalties of their presumption, with the ruin they deserve not greatly delaying.

Nevertheless, some—something we would wish of all—are, through God’s mercy, repenting of their error and the path of iniquity and returning to the embrace of Mother Church.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of October.

## LETTER X. TO ORZOCCO, JUDGE OF CAGLIARI.

Recognizing his devotion toward blessed Peter in the honor shown to the apostolic legate, he urges him to retain in memory what he heard from that legate and not to take it amiss that he compelled a certain archbishop to shave his beard. Rather, receiving him as his shepherd, he should, on his advice, compel all the clergy under his authority to shave their beards. He says that he refused to give consent to those who asked that they be granted the opportunity to invade his land, and that he will not give it if he wishes to keep faith; indeed, if anyone attempts this, he will be prohibited by him, and he will have the aid of blessed Peter if he remains faithful to him.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the glorious judge of Cagliari, ORZOCCO [perhaps more correctly ORZOCCOR, as in Book I, Letter 41; HARD.], greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We give thanks to almighty God that your highness, recognizing blessed Peter, showed due honor and reverence to our legate, the bishop of Populonia, Vu. . . . . Therefore we receive the devotion you displayed in him as though you had shown it to us—or rather to blessed Peter—for the Lord says: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10).

We therefore admonish your devotion always to retain deeply in memory what you heard from the aforementioned legate of ours and from Azo, a prudent man, if you wish us to remember you continually before the Lord. Since the aforesaid bishop testifies that he was reverently received and honorably treated by you, we wish henceforth to keep you especially in mind before him whose place, although unworthy, we occupy.

We do not want your prudence to take it amiss that we compelled your archbishop James to obey the custom of the holy Roman Church, mother of all Churches, and especially of your own Church—namely, that just as the clergy of the entire Western Church has maintained the custom of shaving the beard from the very beginnings of the Christian faith, so our brother, your archbishop, should shave his.

Therefore we command your eminence, receiving and obeying him as your shepherd and spiritual father, to make and compel all the clergy under your authority to shave their beards with his counsel. You should also publish the property of those who altogether refuse, unless they finally consent—that is, hand it over to the jurisdiction of the Church of Cagliari—and restrain them from exercising any further control over it. You should also most promptly assist him in defending the honor of the Churches.

Moreover, we do not want your knowledge to be unaware that your land has been sought by many peoples, and that great services were promised if we allowed it to be invaded, so that they wished to leave half of the entire land for our use and to hold the other part themselves in fealty to us.

Although this had repeatedly been requested of us not only by Normans, Tuscans, and Lombards, but also by certain men from beyond the Alps, we resolved never to give anyone consent in this matter until, by sending our legate to you, we had discovered your disposition.

Therefore, since you have shown in his person that you are devoted to blessed Peter, if you wish to preserve that devotion as you ought, not only shall we grant no one permission to enter your land by force, but, if anyone attempts it, we shall prohibit and repel him both temporally and spiritually.

Finally, if you persevere in fidelity to blessed Peter, we promise without doubt that you will have his aid, which will not be lacking to you, both now and in the future.

Given on the third day before the Nones of October.

## LETTER XI. TO THE KING OF SWEDEN. (Year 1080.)

He rejoices that certain ministers of the sacred word have entered his land and declares that he has great hope for his salvation, since the Gallican Church received from the treasures of the holy mother, the Roman Church. And so that he may attain a more abundant grace of religion, he wishes him to send someone who can report to him the customs of that people and convey the apostolic commands to him. Meanwhile, he should govern the kingdom entrusted to him in justice.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to I . . . ., glorious king of the Swedes [Suetones], greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Since we have heard that certain ministers of the sacred word have entered the land of your kingdom, let your excellence know that we rejoice greatly in the Lord. Henceforth we also have unwaveringly great hope for the restoration of your salvation.

For the Gallican Church did not instruct you with foreign teachings; rather, what it received from the treasures of its mother, the holy Roman Church, it has passed on to you as salutary instruction.

Therefore, so that you may obtain a more abundant grace of Christian religion and doctrine, we wish your highness to send a bishop or a suitable cleric to the Apostolic See, who can both report to us the conditions of your land and the customs of your people and, fully instructed in all matters, more reliably convey the apostolic commands to you.

Meanwhile, we admonish your prudence to govern and order the kingdom entrusted to you in the guardianship of concord and justice, and, among your other pursuit of virtues, to strive to preserve toward your subjects the laws of peace and the strictness of equity. Thus, through the care of temporal governance, you may deserve to receive eternal security and, with the righteous, worthily hear at the final judgment the voice full of every joy: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 22).

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of October.

## LETTER XII. TO THE PEOPLE OF FIRMA, RAVENNA, AND TUSCANY. (Year 1080.)

He complains that the Church of Ravenna has been devastated by its sacrilegious archbishop. Since he has been excommunicated and deposed in a Roman synod, he wishes to restore that Church to its former condition and provide it with a suitable person; he commands them to give him unanimous assistance in this matter.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, abbots, clerics, and laypeople established in the march of Firma, Tuscany, and the exarchate of Ravenna who obey the holy Roman Church as Christians ought, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We do not doubt that your prudence knows with what religious devotion the holy Church of Ravenna has flourished, with what abundance of necessary goods it was accustomed to overflow in past years, and—what matters more—that from the very beginning of the Christian faith it has always clung to its mother, the holy Roman Church, with particular affection.

When we recall its ancient dignity in spiritual and temporal matters, we now see it suffering in such devastation, not without profound grief. So that you may understand more clearly: we endure the fact that the archbishop called Vu. . . . . ., its instigator and destroyer, has so ruined its religion and squandered its goods with nearly no less pain than if he had done the same against the holy Roman Church because of his own audacity.

Yet when his other deeds are considered, this does not seem so surprising. For he did not fear to commit perjury through disobedience and infidelity; he considered it a small matter to conspire against the Apostolic See itself, to which he had sworn falsely; and, while planning to invade it, he most vehemently desired to ravage it in the same manner. He was an exceedingly proud man, conscious of his abominable crimes. It ought therefore to seem no wonder if, having obtained power, he behaved in this way wherever he was permitted.

But I pass over the recollection of his crimes, which have become known throughout almost the entire Roman world. For these, in the holy synod held at Rome, he was struck three years ago by the sword of anathema, without hope of restoration, through the unanimous sentence of all the bishops who were present. These matters have not escaped your knowledge.

Therefore, desiring to rescue the aforementioned Church of Ravenna from violent hands and restore it to its former condition, in accordance with the office which, although unworthy, we hold, we have judged that a person should be chosen and placed over it whose religious character and prudence, with God’s favor, will know and strive both to restore within it the light of holiness and to repair the losses of its external goods.

Accordingly, since we greatly need your help for the accomplishment of this necessary arrangement, we invite, ask, and command you by apostolic authority that, in restoring that Church, holy from ancient times, you all unanimously give your consent and assistance to the extent of your ability. Work with us to rescue it from servile oppression—or rather tyrannical slavery—and restore it to its former liberty. Labor and watch with the greatest care to find a suitable person for its governance.

For we confidently believe that all who devote the zeal of their devotion to this matter will merit apostolic grace and, if they persevere in good works, will most certainly acquire blessed Apollinaris as a patron for themselves before the divine clemency.

Given on the Ides of October.

## LETTER XIII. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAVENNA. (Year 1080.)

The same subject.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all clerics and laypeople residing at Ravenna who love the apostle blessed Peter [blessed Apollinaris] and obey the holy Roman Church as Christians ought, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that you know that the Church of Ravenna was accustomed to cling more closely than others to the Apostolic See, and that it was especially loved by that See. Whatever dignity and honor it possessed from ancient times through blessed A . . . . [Apollinaris; HARD., likewise in the Mutina manuscript], it held by gift granted by the aforementioned See.

But after the devil, the author of pride and sower of discord, through his members and with obstinacy intervening, separated that Church from Rome, you yourselves know well what losses and detriments it suffered—not only in religion but also in its goods—and especially how great a destruction it endured in both respects through the tyranny of the aforementioned archbishop, Vu . . . . [Wibert; HARD., likewise in the Mutina manuscript].

It endured the bite of this dismemberment all the more savagely because his more impure conscience compelled him, in his despair, to withdraw backward. Finally, after the criminal, sacrilegious, and perjured man had been punished on account of [ob] such wickedness in a universal synod [below, “in the Roman synod”], with all the bishops who were present agreeing and approving, by a condemnation worthy of his conduct, he did not immediately recover his senses and return to sound counsel. Instead, imitating his father the devil and storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath (Rom. 2), he undertook whatever he could imagine that was more grievous and dared whatever was most proud.

And because he considered it too little that he had largely destroyed your Church, one of the noblest, he planned—as everyone plainly knows—to invade the holy Roman See itself and drag it down with him into ruin and destruction.

Therefore, since by reason of the eminence of the place over which, by God’s authority, we preside, although unworthy, we are both admonished to extend our concern to all and compelled to watch more carefully over those who are in a certain sense closer to us, we do not regard the devastation of your Church as foreign to us. Rather, since it is a special daughter of ours, we grieve for it as for our own. With the counsel and assistance of all of you who fear God, we wish and desire to restore it, insofar as the Lord grants us the ability, to its ancient dignity and religious condition.

Therefore, once that rotten member has been cut off by the sword of excommunication and deposed in such a way that he must not be counted among priests even forever, we admonish your devotion and ask for your salvation that, with all the affection and intention of your mind, you strive, together with our brother bishops, the archdeacon, and the other deacons whom for this reason we have sent to you in our place, to choose a person who, in God’s sight, appears suitable for so great an honor—namely, the governance of your archbishopric.

Do not allow your Church any longer to be oppressed by servile bondage under impious hands. Rather, like good sons, strive with us to reclaim it into the maternal liberty of the Roman Church, so that, by loving the liberty of God’s bride, the holy Church, you may show yourselves to love God, and, as free sons, may rightly and deservedly hope for the inheritance of eternal blessedness.

Given on the Ides of October.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAVENNA, FIRMA, AND SPOLETO. (Year 1080.)

He commends to them the man elected archbishop of the Church of Ravenna. He urges them to show him due reverence and especially to assist him against the condemned devastator of that Church.

**GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, abbots, counts, and soldiers residing in the diocese of Ravenna and in the Pentapolis, as well as in the march of Firma and the duchy of Spoleto—namely, to those who love blessed Peter and are not held by the bonds of excommunication—greeting and apostolic blessing.**
We believe it known to you, dearest brothers, that throughout the world religious men, clerics and laymen, love us by the grace of God, and willingly approve and obediently receive what we say or command—namely, those who discern justice and understand our intention. But the enemies of the cross of Christ, indeed the enemies of their own souls, rise up against us and, struck down by the blindness of madness, endeavor against their own salvation to trample upon the holy Church. [Col. 0588B] We greatly rejoice at this, observing that those who love God favor our cause, and that it is not these but only those who hate their own soul (Ps. X) who are our enemies. We have incurred their hatred chiefly for this reason, as you know: because we have endeavored to tear them from the snares of the devil and restore them to the bosom of Mother Church.

We therefore believe that you, whom we consider removed and alien from their treachery, ought to demonstrate what sort of disposition you harbor toward us—or rather toward blessed Peter, whose office, though unworthy, we hold—and, if you conduct yourselves faithfully as we suppose, to declare this by evident signs when the time comes and circumstances demand it. There is, moreover, an opportunity in which you can conspicuously display your devotion: if you earnestly strive, to the best of your ability, to support the decrees and statutes [Col. 0588C] of the apostolic see.

Accordingly, you should endeavor to confirm by your counsel and assistance our brother R . . . ., archbishop of Ravenna, whom, after long and countless occupations by usurpers, Ravenna has most recently deserved to receive from the Roman Church—just as Apollinaris was formerly received from blessed Peter—both out of love for the most holy martyr whose church is adorned by his see and relics, and out of due reverence for the apostolic see. You should also assist him in every way against Vu . . . ., the sacrilegious and condemned devastator of that holy place.

For we command you, in accordance with the advice of our legate who bears this letter, to promise our aforesaid fellow-bishop and archbishop your counsel and assistance so firmly that, when his enemies hear of it, they will be compelled and entitled to fear for their possessions; while, when our friends and faithful supporters learn of it, they may confidently hope, together with us, for the fulfillment of your promises.

Given on the third day before the Ides of December.

## LETTER XV. TO THE VALVENSES (Year 1080)

He attacks a certain Transmundus, who, after being rebuked by him for abandoning the bishopric and warned not to intrude himself into it any longer, dared to invade that very Church. He orders that no obedience be shown to him, but that the Church’s goods be wrested from his hands and assistance be given to the legate of the apostolic see in this matter.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who dwell [Col. 0589A] in the bishopric of Valva [Valvanensi], both great and small, and to those who exercise authority there, who desire the grace of blessed Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your so-called bishop Transmundus came to us. We rebuked him severely, because he had abandoned the bishopric without justification. We also ordered him, on account of this folly, to have no further involvement with the bishopric, but to go to Monte Cassino and remain there until, together with the abbot of that place and other religious and prudent men, we could deliberate what should be done concerning him and your Church.

But, despising our command—as we have heard—and incurring through disobedience the crime of idolatry, he has dared, to increase his wickedness, to invade the church placed under interdict [Col. 0589B], and now does not fear stubbornly to occupy it. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you that, if you love the grace of God and of blessed Peter and fear for the peril of your souls, none of you should show him episcopal reverence. Rather, wresting the Church’s goods from his hands, regard him as an invader, and defend the Church’s property from his power, so that he may not be able to alienate it.

Furthermore, we order you to provide assistance to our legate, John the subdeacon, whom we have sent to you for this purpose, in whatever matters prove necessary, so that he may be able, together with you, to carry out more effectively what must be done in this affair.

Given on the second day before the Ides of December.

## LETTER XVI. TO N. N. (Year 1080)

He praises them for imitating the example of their parents in maintaining a devoted attitude toward the Roman Church, and exhorts them to advance in this more and more each day. He commends to them Dalmatius, canonically elected archbishop of the Church of Narbonne, so that they may assist him as the true shepherd and resist the invader.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R . . . . and B . . . ., noble counts: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How greatly your house has long loved blessed Peter, and how faithful it has been to him, is known not only among you but also widely throughout many regions of different peoples. Hence it is recognized far and wide that it has hitherto gained victory over its enemies and honor and glory above its other peers.

But because we have learned that you imitate your parents not only in the line of your nobility but also in your pursuit of virtue, we rejoice greatly and sincerely. We salutarily exhort and admonish you always to maintain a devoted spirit toward blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, mother of all. You can undoubtedly demonstrate your love for her in no better way than by ensuring, among the other good works you ought to perform, that you assist and defend the holy Church.

Therefore, with particular concern for your salvation, we ask you and command you on behalf of blessed Peter promptly to come to the aid of the Church of Narbonne, which for a long time has been occupied by members of the devil, and to assist in every way our brother Dalmatius, archbishop, whom that Church has at last deserved to receive as one canonically and according to the Lord elected and ordained. Resist in every way you can that invader who, entering not through the door like a shepherd but from elsewhere like a thief and robber, slaughters and destroys Christ’s sheep (John X)—indeed, hands them over to the devil—if you desire to obtain the grace of almighty God.

Act, then, and take every care to make blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, your helper—or rather your debtor. He can grant or take away from you the salvation and honor of this life and the next; he does not abandon his faithful, but knows how to resist the proud and put them to shame, while giving grace to the humble (James IV) and exalting them.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

## LETTER XVII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF RHEIMS (Year 1080)

He censures Manasses, formerly archbishop of Rheims, who, condemned by the judgment of an apostolic legate, presumed to invade that Church. He therefore warns them to resist him in every way and, with the consent of the bishop of Die, the legate, to elect another shepherd capable of assisting their suffering Church.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of the Church of Rheims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0590C] We do not doubt that it has come to your attention that Manasses, formerly called your archbishop, underwent the synodal sentence of condemnation which his crimes deserved, adjudicated by our fellow-bishop of Die, the legate of the holy Roman Church. We carefully examined that sentence and, recognizing it as most just in view of the magnitude of his wickedness, confirmed it in the Roman synod, at the request of many brothers, in such a form that, after being granted a period of grace, he would, if possible, have permission to come and purge himself of the charges and free opportunity to plead his case; yet on the condition that meanwhile he would relinquish the governance of that Church and reside at Cluny or in some other religious monastery, so that his obedience and humility might be tested.

But he—as you yourselves know—not only failed to obey this decision; in contempt of our prohibition, he also presumed to invade your Church and defile it by shameless devastation, since he entered it not through the door like a shepherd but from elsewhere like a thief and most savage predator, clearly in order to slaughter and destroy the Lord’s flock, not to protect and defend it with a shepherd’s vigilance (John X).

Indeed, the wickedness of his deeds has grown to such enormity that he is most deservedly subject to condemnation and excommunication, and ought never to entertain any hope of restoration. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish you to have no share whatsoever in his perverse acts. Rather, resist him in every way, so that he may be removed from your midst and handed over to Satan for the destruction of his flesh, so that his spirit may be saved (1 Cor. V). Also take care, by common counsel and unanimous vote, with the agreement of our aforesaid fellow-bishop of Die, to elect for yourselves a Father according to the Lord, who may assist your Church, long afflicted by the wickedness of false shepherds, and, with Christ’s help, restore its ancient freedom together with you.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

## LETTER XVIII. TO COUNT HEBOLUS (Year 1080)

He declares that Manasses, archbishop of Rheims, was deposed by the judgment of Hugh, bishop of Die and apostolic legate, at the Council of Lyon. He warns Hebolus to withdraw both himself and others from Manasses’s friendship, resist him to the best of his ability, and assist the other archbishop whom the greater part of the clergy, with the consent of the legate, has elected.

[Col. 0591B] **GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **HEBOLO [EBULOI]**, noble and glorious count: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your prudence may remember, for a long time we tolerated Manasses, the so-called archbishop of Rheims, against your wishes and those of the religious men who knew him. Believing that he was concerned with his own correction, we bore with him for a very long time. But he abused our patience and—as is plainly evident—having fallen through a guilty conscience into the pit of despair, he showed himself not only ungrateful for our supposed gentleness but also henceforth unworthy of the mercy of blessed Peter.

Accordingly, although we had deferred for a time the sentence pronounced and approved at the Council of Lyon by our vicar Hugh, bishop of Die, concerning his deposition, we now adjudge that it shall henceforth remain permanently firm and ratified, and that he is deposed without hope of recovery. Therefore, announcing to your highness that he has been deprived by irrevocable judgment of the governance of the episcopal see, we admonish you—and command you on behalf of blessed Peter—to withdraw yourself from his pestilential friendship from now on and to make it known that you will protect from him others whom you can.

That you may [deserve] more abundantly the grace of God and blessed Peter, which you may rightly hope for, let the zeal of your diligence not be lacking [the text reads *merito quas sperare studium*; read *merito queas sperare, studium*, HARD., and likewise Mut.]: both personally and through all whom you can [endeavour, *studeas*], resist the aforesaid deposed man as your rank permits, and assist in every way the archbishop whom the sounder judgment of the better part of the clergy, with the consent of our aforesaid legate, Hugh, bishop of Die, shall have elected to that see [Note: [Col. 0591D] The passage is obscure].

In this matter, therefore, openly show yourself so devoted and obedient to apostolic commands as you would wish your own faithful subjects to be in your needs. Just as you would not tolerate your faithful subjects’ evading you with impunity in matters of the highest importance, so take care, out of regard for blessed Peter—to whom the cause of the whole Church belongs—to undertake this affair wholeheartedly, so that you may deservedly have him as your protector here and your patron in the future.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE SUFFRAGANS OF THE CHURCH OF RHEIMS (Year 1080)

The subject is almost the same.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops, namely the suffragans of the holy Church of Rheims—yet only to those who guard themselves from the excommunicated: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe it known to your fraternity that for a long time we tolerated the iniquities of Manasses, the so-called archbishop of Rheims, and, hoping that he would turn from his wickedness, we refrained from acting far too long. But because blessed Mary, whose see that lost man occupied, did not wish her Church to be polluted any longer by his crimes, the more serious offenses that had long remained hidden concerning him burst forth into public knowledge.

For these offenses he deserved, at the Council of Lyon, over which our brother and vicar Hugh, bishop of Die, presided, to receive the sentence of deposition, pronounced by Hugh and accepted by all the religious brothers who were present.
