We therefore confirm by apostolic authority that the judgment of the aforesaid assembly—which we, employing apostolic gentleness, had tempered by appending a qualification—now stands firm, since he, in the despair of his conscience, chose to remain in his hardness and contempt of disobedience rather than bend his mind toward the counsel of sound judgment. We adjudge him henceforth irrecoverably deposed.

Therefore we release your fraternity from any further obligation to show him episcopal reverence. Rather, by apostolic authority, we command that no one obey him as a shepherd, but that each of you, according to his office and strength, resist him as an invader. Let your charity take care to announce this judgment of ours—or rather, of the Holy Spirit—to your subjects and to all peoples whom you can reach; and do not neglect to admonish them to beware of sharing in his acts and to restrain him by every means available.

Furthermore, we wish, and command on behalf of blessed Peter, that, after summoning the clergy of that Church, you arrange for a person to be elected, with the consent of our aforesaid legate, the bishop of Die, who appears worthy to govern so great a charge. For, with God’s favor, we confirm and strengthen by apostolic authority the election made by the better and more religious part of the clergy and people, with the consent of our aforesaid vicar.

Let your diligence therefore show itself in this matter so ready and obedient to us—or rather to blessed Peter—that, when your zeal and vigilance are recognized, if you have previously failed through negligence or disobedience, we may rightly be obliged to bear with you on that account.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

## LETTER XX. TO PHILIP, KING OF THE FRANKS (Year 1080)

He asks him not to offer any further favor to Manasses, the deposed archbishop of Rheims, but to reject him from his friendship. He also warns him not to obstruct the election that the clergy and people of the Church of Rheims were about to conduct, but to provide assistance to the man elected by the greater part.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to **PHILIP**, glorious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have often heard through messengers of your highness that you desire the grace of blessed Peter and our friendship. You should know that we willingly accepted this then and that it still pleases us greatly, if you retain that disposition. For you show yourself a friend and zealous guardian of your salvation if, as befits a Christian king, you desire to obtain and preserve apostolic goodwill.

You will attain this much more easily and worthily if you reverently demonstrate diligence and devotion in ecclesiastical affairs. In this matter, you will doubtless recognize that formerly you acted much less watchfully and far more negligently than would have been proper. But, bearing with hope for your correction the past offenses of your youth, we admonish you, as our duty requires, henceforth to be attentive, with your conduct amended, to what is necessary.

Therefore, among the other pursuits of virtue appropriate to royal excellence which we desire to see in you, since it is necessary that you be a lover of justice, a guardian of mercy, a defender of churches, and a protector of orphans and widows, we believe and affirm that, for the safeguarding of your inward salvation, you must also reject the counsels of the wicked and, above all, detest association with the excommunicated.

Accordingly, on behalf of blessed Peter we command your highness, and on our own behalf we ask, that you offer no further support of your favor to Manasses, the so-called archbishop of Rheims, but irrecoverably deposed for his iniquities—which your knowledge does not overlook. Cut him off from your friendship and reject him, despised, from your presence, so that it may be evident that, by spurning the enemies of the holy Church, namely those hardened by excommunication, you love God and, obeying apostolic commands, truly desire the grace of blessed Peter.

Furthermore, we wish, and command on behalf of the apostolic see, that you obstruct by no device or effort the election which the clergy and people of the aforesaid Church of Rheims are, with God’s assent, about to conduct. If anyone attempts to impede it by any secular influence, oppose him in every way, and give your assistance to the man whom the more faithful and religious party shall have elected.

Act, then, and now that you have become a man in age, take care in this matter that we may not seem to have spared the faults of your youth in vain, or to have awaited your correction without purpose. Above all, strive to make blessed Peter, in whose power are your kingdom and your soul, who can bind and loose you in heaven and on earth, your debtor; and may you deservedly merit his eternal assistance—not judgment for negligence or concealment of the truth, but grace for diligence and the execution of justice.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

## LETTER XXI. TO HERIMANN, BISHOP OF METZ (Year 1080)

He encourages him to be prepared for toil and danger in defense of the truth. He replies to his questions concerning the authority of the apostolic see to excommunicate King Henry and absolve his subjects from the oath of fidelity.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, **HERIMANN**, bishop of Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0594B] We do not doubt that it is a divine gift that we understand you to be prepared to endure labors and dangers in defense of the truth. Its ineffable grace and divine mercy consist in this: that it never permits its elect to go wholly astray, never allows them to be utterly shaken or cast down, but, having tested them through a useful trial in the time of persecution, makes them stronger than themselves even after some trembling.

Moreover, just as among cowards fear paralyzes one man so that he flees more shamefully than another, so among the brave a manly heart is inflamed to act more vigorously and break forth more ardently than another. We have taken care to commend this to your charity in words of exhortation, so that you may take greater pleasure in standing among the foremost in the battle of the Christian religion, the nearer and more worthy of the victorious God you know them to be.

You requested that you be assisted and fortified, as it were, by our letters against the madness of those who babble with sacrilegious mouths that the authority of the holy and apostolic see could not excommunicate King Henry—a man who despises Christian law, a destroyer of churches and the empire, and an author of and accomplice in heresy—nor absolve anyone from his oath of fidelity. This does not seem particularly necessary to us, since the sacred Scriptures contain so many and such certain proofs of this matter.

Nor do we believe that those who, to heap up their own condemnation, shamelessly detract from and oppose the truth have fashioned these arguments for the audacity of their defense out of both ignorance and the madness of miserable despair. Nor is this surprising: it is the custom of the reprobate, to protect their own wickedness, to strive to defend those like themselves, since they regard incurring the ruin of falsehood as nothing.

For, to say a little about many matters, who does not know the voice of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI)?

Are kings excluded here? Or are they not among the sheep whom the Son of God entrusted to blessed Peter? Who, I ask, in this universal grant of the power to bind and loose considers himself excluded from Peter’s authority, unless perhaps it is that wretched man who, unwilling to bear the Lord’s yoke, subjects himself to the burden of the devil and refuses to be numbered among Christ’s sheep? Yet it does not help him toward a miserable freedom that he shakes from his proud neck the power of Peter, divinely granted to him. For the more arrogantly a person refuses to bear it, the more harshly he will carry it at the judgment to his own condemnation.

Thus, receiving and preserving with great reverence this institution of the divine will, this foundation of the Church’s administration, this privilege principally delivered and confirmed by heavenly decree to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the holy Fathers called the holy Roman Church the universal mother both in general councils and in their other writings and deeds. Just as they accepted her teachings for the confirmation of faith and instruction in sacred religion, so they accepted her judgments, agreeing on this and concurring as though with one spirit and one voice: that all greater matters and principal affairs, as well as the judgments of all Churches, ought to be referred to her as to a mother and head; that there is nowhere any appeal from her; and that her judgments neither ought nor can be reconsidered or refuted by anyone.

Hence blessed Pope Gelasius, writing to the emperor Anastasius (Epistle), supported by divine authority, instructed him in this way concerning what he ought to think, and how, about the primacy of the holy and apostolic see:

“Although it is right that the necks of the faithful be submitted generally to all priests who rightly administer divine things, how much more ought consent to be given to the prelate of that see whom the supreme divinity wished to place above all priests and whom the continuing devotion of the universal Church has celebrated thereafter!”

Here your prudence clearly perceives that no one can ever, by any purely human counsel, make himself equal to the privilege or confession of him whom the voice of Christ placed above all, whom the venerable Church has always confessed and continues devotedly to hold as primate.

Again, Pope Julius, writing to the Eastern bishops, says of the power of that same holy and apostolic see:

“It was fitting for you, brothers, to speak about the holy Roman and apostolic Church with refinement and not ironically, since our Lord Jesus Christ himself, addressing it suitably, says: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. XVI). For it possesses, by a singular privilege granted to it, the power to open and close the gates of the heavenly kingdom for whomever it wishes. To him, therefore, to whom the power of opening and closing heaven has been given, is it not permitted to judge the earth? Far be it that this should be denied! Do you not remember what the blessed apostle Paul says: ‘Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, matters of this life?’ (1 Cor. VI.)”

The blessed Pope Gregory also declares that kings fall from their dignity if they presume to violate the decrees of the apostolic see. In the privilege of the monastery of Saint-Médard (Book II of the Letters), writing to a certain Senator and abbot, he says:

“If any king, priest, judge, or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly taken, or mourns what he has illicitly done through worthy repentance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected eternally to the examination of strict retribution.”

If blessed Gregory, certainly a most gentle teacher, decreed that kings who violated his statutes concerning a single hospice were not only to be deposed but also excommunicated and condemned at the eternal judgment, who could criticize us for deposing and excommunicating Henry, not merely a despiser of apostolic judgments but also, insofar as he is able, a trampler upon Mother Church herself, and the most wicked plunderer and most savage destroyer of the entire kingdom and of the Churches—unless perhaps it were someone like him?

As we have learned from blessed P . . . . . (that is, blessed Peter; HARD.) teaching in the letter concerning the ordination of Clement, in which he says:

“If anyone is a friend to those [*de*] concerning whom he himself, speaking of that same Clement, does not speak, he too is one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. And although he may appear to be with us in body, in mind and spirit he is against us; he is a much worse enemy than those who are outside and openly hostile. For under the appearance of friendship he does what is hostile, and he scatters and devastates the Church.”

Note, therefore, dearest brother: if he judges so severely him whom [perhaps, him who, HARD.] through friendship or conversation associates with those whom the pope opposes on account of their deeds, with what severity does he condemn the man whom he himself opposes on account of his deeds?

But to return to the matter: shall a dignity invented even by secular men who do not know God fail to be subject to the dignity which the providence of almighty God devised for his honor and mercifully granted to the world—whose Son, just as he is unquestionably believed to be God and man, is also held to be the supreme Priest, the head of all priests, seated at the right hand of the Father and always interceding for us (Rom. VIII)? He despised the secular kingdom in which the sons of the world swell with pride and willingly came to the priesthood of the cross.

Who does not know that kings and leaders originated among those who, ignorant of God and driven by the prince of this world, the devil, sought in blind desire and intolerable presumption to dominate their equals—that is, human beings—through pride, plunder, treachery, murder, and finally almost every crime? While they strive to make the priests of the Lord bow at their feet, to whom can they more fittingly be compared than to him who is the head over all the sons of pride (Job XLI), who, tempting the supreme pontiff, head of priests, the Son of the Most High, and promising him all the kingdoms of the world, said: “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me”? (Matt. IV.)

Who could doubt that Christ’s priests are regarded as the fathers and teachers of kings, leaders, and all the faithful? Is it not recognized as pitiable madness if a son attempts to subjugate his father, a disciple his teacher, and to subject him through wicked obligations to his own power—one from whom he believes that he can be bound and loosed not only on earth but also in heaven?

As the blessed Gregory recalls in a letter addressed to the emperor Maurice (Book IV, Epistle 31), the great emperor Constantine, lord of almost all the kings and leaders of the entire world, clearly understood this. At the holy Council of Nicaea, he sat last, after all the bishops, and did not presume to pronounce any judgment over them. Rather, calling them gods and declaring that they ought not to be subject to his judgment, he judged that he himself depended upon their decision.

The aforementioned Pope Gelasius, persuading the emperor Anastasius not to regard the truth communicated to his understanding as an insult, added:

“There are, indeed, two powers, O august emperor, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of priests and royal power. The burden of the priests is so much the heavier because they must render an account in the divine judgment even for the kings themselves.”

And a little later he says:

“You know, then, that amid these matters you depend upon their judgment, and that they do not wish to be reduced to your will.”

Strengthened, therefore, by such institutions and supported by such authorities, many pontiffs have excommunicated some kings and others emperors. If a particular example concerning the persons of rulers is required, blessed Pope Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius, who consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from his see.

Another Roman pontiff, namely Zacharias, deposed the king of the Franks—not so much for his own iniquities as because he was unfit for so great a power—and substituted Pippin, the father of the emperor Charlemagne, in his place. He also absolved all the Franks from the oath of fidelity that they had sworn to that king.

The holy Church often does the same, by frequent precedent, when she absolves soldiers from the bond of the oath sworn to bishops who, by apostolic authority, are deposed from episcopal rank.

And blessed Ambrose, although a saint but not the bishop of the universal Church, excluded the great emperor Theodosius from the Church by excommunicating him for a fault that did not seem so serious to certain other priests. In his writings he also shows that gold is not more precious than lead by as much as the priestly dignity is higher than royal power. At the beginning of his *Pastoral* he writes:

“Honor and the sublimity of the episcopate, brothers, cannot be equaled by any comparison. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, it will be found far inferior, just as lead is inferior to the brilliance of gold. For you see kings’ necks and those of princes submitted to the knees of priests, and, having kissed their right hands, they believe themselves fortified by their prayers.”

And shortly afterward:

“You should understand, brothers, that we have said all this in order to show that in this world nothing is more excellent than priests, and nothing more sublime than bishops.”

Your fraternity should also remember that greater power is granted to an exorcist, when he is appointed as a spiritual commander to cast out demons, than can be granted to any layman on account of secular domination.

For demons—alas, woe!—rule over all the kings and princes of the earth who do not live religiously and who, in their deeds, do not fear God as they ought; they bring them to ruin through miserable servitude. Such men, not led by love of God, as religious priests are, to preside for God’s honor and the benefit of souls, desire to dominate others in order to display their intolerable pride and satisfy the lust of their minds.

Concerning such men, blessed Augustine says in Book I of *On Christian Doctrine*:

“But when anyone desires to dominate even those who are naturally his equals—that is, human beings—it is altogether intolerable pride.”

Moreover, as we said, exorcists receive from God authority over demons. How much more, then, over those who are subject to demons and are members of demons? If exorcists therefore hold such preeminence over them, how much greater is that of priests?

Furthermore, every Christian king, when approaching death, humbly and pitiably seeks the aid of a priest in order to escape the prison of hell, proceed from darkness into light, and appear absolved from the bonds of sins at God’s judgment.

But who, whether priest or layman, when placed in his final extremity, has implored the aid of an earthly king for the salvation of his soul? Which king or emperor can, by the office imposed upon him, rescue a Christian through holy baptism from the power of the devil, number him among the children of God, and fortify him with holy chrism? And, what is greatest in the Christian religion, which of them can consecrate the Lord’s body and blood with his own mouth? Or to which of them has the power been given to bind and loose in heaven and on earth?

From these considerations it is plainly gathered how greatly the dignity of priests surpasses all others in power. Or which of them can ordain a cleric in the holy Church—how much less depose him for some fault? For in ecclesiastical orders, deposing is a greater exercise of power than ordaining. Bishops can ordain other bishops, but in no way can they depose them without the authority of the apostolic see.

Who, then, even with slight learning, could doubt that priests are to be placed before kings? And if kings are to be judged by priests for their sins, by whom should they more properly be judged than by the Roman pontiff?

Ultimately, it is much more fitting to understand any good Christians rather than wicked rulers as kings. For these men, in seeking the glory of God, rule themselves vigorously; but those men, seeking not what is God’s but what is their own (Phil. II), become their own enemies and tyrannically oppress others. The former are the body of Christ the King, the latter the body of the devil. The power of the former is directed toward this end: that they may reign eternally with the supreme Emperor; the power of the latter brings it about that they perish in eternal damnation with the prince of darkness, who is king over all the sons of pride (Job XLI).

Nor is it at all surprising that wicked prelates consent to an unjust king, whom they love and fear because of the honors they have wrongly acquired through him—men who, by ordaining people through simony, sell God even for a paltry price. For just as the elect are indissolubly united to their one Head, so also the reprobate, especially against the good, stubbornly form an alliance with him who is the head of wickedness. Against such men, indeed, one ought not so much to argue as to lament for them with tearful mourning, so that almighty God may rescue them from the snares of Satan, by which they are held captive, and may at last, even after their dangers, lead them to knowledge of the truth.

This has been said about kings and emperors who, excessively swollen with worldly glory, reign not for God but for themselves. But since it is our duty to distribute exhortation to each person according to the rank or dignity in which he appears to flourish, we take care, with God as our author, to provide emperors, kings, and the other princes with the weapons of humility, so that they may be able to restrain the swellings of the sea (Ps. XCII) and the waves of pride.

For we know that worldly glory and secular responsibility very often draw those who rule toward pride, so that, always neglecting humility and seeking their own glory, they desire to surpass their brothers. Therefore it seems especially useful for emperors and kings that, when their minds wish to raise themselves to lofty things and to delight in singular glory, they should find ways by which to humble themselves, and should recognize that the source of their joy is something more to be feared.

Let them therefore carefully consider how dangerous and fearful imperial or royal dignity is: in it very few are saved, and those who, by God’s mercy, attain salvation are not thereby equally honored in the holy Church, according to the judgment of the Holy Spirit, as are many of the poor. For from the beginning of the world down to our own times, throughout the whole of authoritative Scripture, we do not find emperors or kings whose lives were so distinguished by religion and adorned by the virtue of miracles as those of the innumerable multitude who despised the world, although we believe that many of the former found salvation through the mercy of almighty God.

For—to say nothing of the apostles and martyrs—which emperors or kings shone with miracles as greatly as blessed Martin, Anthony, or Benedict? Which emperor or king raised the dead, cleansed lepers, or gave sight to the blind? Behold Constantine, the emperor of pious memory; Theodosius and Honorius; Charles and Louis, lovers of justice, propagators of the Christian religion, and defenders of the Churches: the holy Church praises and venerates them, certainly, but it does not thereby indicate that they possessed such glory of miracles.

Moreover, for how many royal or imperial names does the holy Church dedicate basilicas or altars, or decree that Masses be celebrated in their honor? Let kings and the other princes fear lest, to the extent that they rejoice in being preferred to other people in this life, they may be subjected all the more to eternal fires. Hence it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI). For they will have to render an account to God for as many people as they had subject to their rule. If it is no small labor for a religious private person to guard his one soul, how great a labor threatens princes who are responsible for many thousands of souls?

Furthermore, if the judgment of the holy Church severely binds a sinner for the killing of one person, what will become of those who hand over many thousands to death for the honor of this world? Although they sometimes say with their lips, “My fault,” for the killing of many, nevertheless in their hearts they rejoice in the apparent extension of their honor; they do not wish that they had failed to do what they did, nor do they grieve that they drove their brothers into Tartarus. Since they do not repent of them with all their heart, and do not wish to relinquish what they acquired or retained through human blood, their repentance remains before God without the worthy fruit of repentance.

Therefore it is greatly to be feared, and frequently recalled to their memory, that—as we have already said—from the beginning of the world only very few holy kings are found among the innumerable multitude of kings throughout the various kingdoms of the earth, whereas in one single see of prelates succeeding one another in order, namely the Roman see, nearly a hundred have been counted among the saints from the time of blessed Peter the Apostle.

Why is this, except because the kings and princes of the earth, enticed by vain glory, prefer what is theirs—as was stated above—to spiritual things? Religious prelates, however, despising vain glory, prefer what belongs to God to carnal things. The former are easily punished when they offend against themselves, but bear with equanimity offenses against God; the latter quickly forgive those who sin against themselves, but do not lightly spare those who offend God. The former, excessively devoted to earthly affairs, regard spiritual things as insignificant; the latter, diligently meditating on heavenly things, despise what is earthly.

All Christians who desire to reign with Christ must therefore be admonished not to seek to reign through ambition for secular power, but rather to keep before their eyes what the most holy Pope Gregory advises in the *Pastoral Book*, saying:

> “In this matter, then, what ought to be followed and held to, except that a man strong in virtues should come to rule when compelled, while one lacking in virtues should not approach even when compelled? But if those who fear God come under compulsion and with great fear to the apostolic see, in which those who are rightly ordained are made better through the merits of the blessed Apostle Peter, with how much fear and trembling must one approach the throne of a kingdom, in which even the good and humble become worse, as is recognized in Saul and David? For what we mentioned earlier about the apostolic see is contained in the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus, although we know it by experience: that blessed P . . . . . . [Peter], namely, sent an everlasting endowment of merits, together with the inheritance of innocence, to his descendants.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For who would doubt that he is holy whom the summit of so great a dignity elevates? If good qualities acquired through merit are lacking in him, those bestowed by the predecessor of the place are sufficient. For either he raises distinguished men to these heights, or he ennobles those who are raised.”

Therefore, those whom the holy Church of her own accord and by deliberate judgment calls to rule or to imperial power should obey humbly—not for passing glory, but for the salvation of many—and they should always beware of what blessed Gregory testifies in the same *Pastoral Book*:

> “For a man becomes like the apostate angel when he disdains to be a man like other men [manuscript: *simul*; read perhaps *similis*, ‘like’].”

Thus Saul, after earning merit through humility, grew through the summit of power into the swelling of pride. Through humility he was preferred; through pride he was rejected, as the Lord bears witness, saying: “When you were little in your own eyes, did I not make you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Kings XV). And a little farther on:

> “In a wondrous manner, when he was little in his own eyes, he was great in the Lord’s eyes; but when he appeared great in his own eyes, he was little in the Lord’s eyes.”

Let them also retain vigilantly what the Lord says in the Gospel: “I do not seek my own glory” (John VIII); and: “Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be the servant of all” (Mark X).

Let them always place the honor of God before their own. By preserving each person’s right, let them embrace and guard justice. Let them not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, but, always yielding to religious people, let them cleave to them in heart. Let them not seek to subject or subjugate the holy Church to themselves as a handmaid, but, recognizing those eyes of the Lord—namely, the priests, teachers, and fathers—let them take the greatest care to honor them fittingly.

For if we are commanded to honor our carnal fathers and mothers, how much more our spiritual ones? And if the person who curses a carnal father or mother is condemned to death, what does the one who curses a spiritual father or mother deserve?

Let them not, enticed by carnal affection, endeavor to set their son over the flock for which Christ shed his blood, if they are able to find someone better and more useful than he. Otherwise, by loving their son more than God, they will inflict the greatest injury upon the holy Church. For the person who neglects, as far as he is able, to provide for so great and necessary a benefit to holy Mother Church is plainly shown not to love God and neighbor—as a Christian ought.

When this virtue, namely charity, is neglected, whatever good anyone may do will lack every fruit of salvation. Therefore, by acting humbly in these matters and preserving the love of God and neighbor as one ought, let them trust in the mercy of him who said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). If they imitate him humbly, they will pass from a servile and transitory kingdom to the kingdom of true freedom and eternity.

Given on the Ides of March.

## LETTER XXII. TO A . . . , DAUGHTER (1081)

[Col. 0602A]

He urges her to despise earthly things and seek heavenly things. He exhorts her to draw the heart of her royal husband toward divine love, to benefit the holy Church as much as she can, and to pursue every work of charity.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in Christ, A . . . ., greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because, out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you asked us to send your Excellency a letter written by our own hand, we have granted your devotion’s request. In it we also admonish you to take the greatest care always to despise earthly and transitory things, and always to seek heavenly and eternal things.

Write in your heart that the supreme Queen of Heaven, who is believed to have been exalted above all the choirs of angels, who is the adornment and glory of all women—indeed, the salvation and nobility of all the elect—because she alone was worthy, as both virgin and mother, naturally to give birth to God and man, the head and life of all good things, did not disdain to lead a poor life on earth and to preserve herself in all holy humility. For the more the glory of this life is sought, the less the future life is desired.

That woman is truly called a queen before God who orders her conduct in the fear and love of Christ. Hence it comes about that holy women, although they may have been poor in this life, are glorified in heaven and on earth; while many worldly women, even queens or empresses, do not deserve to have a good reputation before God or human beings.

We therefore ask and command you always to strive to draw the mind of your most beloved lord the king, our son, toward the fear and love of God; to benefit the holy Church as far as you can; to defend the poor, orphans, widows, and all who are unjustly oppressed; to show reverence especially to all clerics and monks who are deeply religious; and always to keep the death of the flesh before your eyes, so that you may deserve to escape the fear [Note: Col. 0601D. I think “swelling” (*tumorem*) should be written instead: everything points toward humility.] of the soul [Note: Col. 0602D. Perhaps “death” (*mortem*). HARD.].

Devote yourself diligently to almsgiving and prayers, and willingly accept admonition. Always turn this over in your heart: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. III); and: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

May almighty and merciful God, from whom all good things proceed, through the merits of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and by the authority he gave to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, absolve you from all your sins; may he always guard your mind, fill it with true charity, and lead you to eternal life.

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE BISHOP OF ALBANO AND THE PRINCE OF SALERNO (1081)

He orders them to instruct the Gauls that each household should pay one denarius annually to blessed Peter as a census payment; and he displays the generosity of the Emperor Charles toward the Roman Church.

[Col. 0603A] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved sons P . . . ., bishop of Albano, and G . . . ., prince of Salerno, legates of our apostolic see in Gaul, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The affairs entrusted to you are not hidden from you, as though they were ours—indeed, because our presence is there in you, since they are ours, conduct everything worthily. You must tell all the Gauls, and command them under true obedience, that each household pay at least one denarius annually to blessed Peter, if they acknowledge him as their father and shepherd according to ancient custom.

For Emperor Charles, as is read in the volume of his records preserved in the archive of the church of Saint Peter, collected annually twelve hundred pounds in three places for the service of the apostolic see: at Aachen, at Le Puy of Saint Mary, and at Saint-Gilles; in addition to what each person offered from personal devotion. That same great emperor offered Saxony to blessed Peter, with whose assistance he conquered it, and established a sign of devotion and freedom, as the Saxons themselves have written and their prudent men know well.

## BOOK NINE OF THE REGISTER

[Note: Col. 0603. Since the indictions and days of the months are lacking, the year can scarcely be determined with certainty.]

[Col. 0603]

## LETTER I. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN (1081)

[Col. 0603B]

He reproves him because neither he nor his suffragans have come to the thresholds of the apostles, nor visited the apostolic legates, and because he has not requested the pallium from the apostolic see. Therefore he forbids him henceforth to ordain a bishop or priest, or to consecrate churches, until he has obtained the pallium.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, archbishop of Rouen, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The letter you sent us displays sufficient devotion, but the facts themselves entirely lack testimony to its truth. For if matters were really as you say, you yourself would not, like your suffragans, have treated visiting the thresholds of the apostles as so unimportant for so long. Since divine condescension, although I am unworthy, raised me to the care of this see, I do not remember seeing any of you. This seems less surprising, however, because you take little care to visit our legates, who are closer to you.

What labor, or what difficulty, dissuaded you more than others from neglecting blessed Peter for so long, when even peoples newly converted to the faith from the very ends of the world strive to come to him annually, women as well as men?

There is another matter in which, unless apostolic gentleness restrained us, you would certainly already have felt more severe discipline: to this point you have postponed acquiring from the apostolic see, according to custom, the most distinguished insignia of your dignity, namely the pallium. We think you yourself are not unaware how strictly the judgment of the holy Fathers has decreed that those who, after their consecration, have been sluggish for three continuous months in obtaining the pallium proper to their office are to be judged.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command you that, because you have treated the statutes of the holy Fathers as unimportant, you presume henceforth neither to ordain any bishop or priest nor to consecrate churches, until you have obtained from this see the completion of your honor, namely the use of the pallium.

For the rest, we admonish both you and your suffragans to take the greatest care to correct the aforesaid fault, lest, if you remain negligent in this matter as before, you experience the power of blessed Peter through us—delayed all the more, and therefore all the more severe—because of your contempt.

## LETTER II. TO ALPHONSUS, KING OF CASTILE (1081)

He explains that he has incurred the hatred of many on account of truth and justice, and that for this reason those same people slander him. He praises the king for ensuring that divine offices are celebrated in the churches of his kingdom according to the custom of the Roman Church. He says that he will answer through his legates concerning the king’s wife and the abbey of Saint Secundus. He rejects a man lacking learning who had been chosen for the archbishopric, and orders another to be elected on the advice of the legate. He warns the king not to permit Jews to rule over Christians in his kingdom. He gives thanks for the gift sent to him by the king and grants him and his faithful people absolution from all sins.

[Col. 0604C] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Alphonsus, glorious king of Spain, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence knows that lying is a sin, since an account must be rendered in the strict judgment even for an idle word. But even a lie told with a pious intention for the sake of peace cannot be shown to be entirely free from guilt. We have mentioned this beforehand so that, while you have no doubt that this is a sin in other cases, you may regard it as almost sacrilege when it occurs among priests; and so that you may recognize, with truth as witness, that what we are directing to you is truly so.

It is not hidden from us that much about our deeds and words is brought to your ears with sinister interpretation. Therefore we have thought it appropriate to answer, for your information, those who slander us. I am not at all reluctant to confess that I am a sinner, as is true. Yet, if the cause of the hatred or detraction of those who rage against us is carefully investigated, it will plainly appear that they have flared up against us not so much because of any consideration of my iniquity as because of our assertion of truth and opposition to injustice.

We could certainly have had their services and very generous gifts in even greater abundance than many of our predecessors, if, to the danger of them and of ourselves, we had preferred to keep silent about the truth and conceal their wickedness. But, weighing the end of this life and the character of temporal advantages, we have decided that no one can be more rightly called a bishop than when he suffers persecution for justice (Matt. V). We have therefore resolved to obey the divine commands and incur the enmity of the wicked rather than provoke God’s anger by pleasing them wrongly.

Now we turn our speech to your diligence, dearest son. Let your Excellency know, dearest one, that one thing pleases us greatly—or rather, pleases divine mercy: that you have caused the order of our mother, the holy Roman Church, to be received in the churches of your kingdom and celebrated according to ancient custom. For, as we have learned from religious men, in the rite which you appear to have maintained until now certain things are plainly shown to have been inserted contrary to the Catholic faith.

When you resolved to abandon these and return to the ancient custom, namely that of this Church, you clearly showed that, inspired by heavenly grace, you desire blessed Peter as your patron and care for the salvation of your subjects, as befits a king. We report this joy over your wisdom all the more fully when we occasionally recall the illustrious reputation of your humility, and consider that the virtue which, together with royal power, is accustomed to dwell under one roof only rarely or scarcely ever, resides in your heart.

As for what you requested concerning your wife and the abbey of Saint Secundus, we have judged that it would be more suitably answered through our son Richard, cardinal and legate of the holy Roman Church, and through Brother Simeon, bishop.

Concerning the person who had been chosen for the archbishopric, we say this: although he appears sufficiently prudent and generous, nevertheless—as we know, and as your letter does not deny—he lacks the foundation of discipline, namely knowledge of letters. You yourself understand well how necessary this virtue is not only for bishops but also for priests, since without it no one can teach others or defend himself.

Therefore your serenity ought to take care that, with the advice of our aforesaid legate Richard, abbot of Marseille, and of the other religious men, such a person be chosen from there, if one can be found; but if not, that one be sought elsewhere whose religion and learning will bring honor and salvation to your Church and kingdom.

Nor should it annoy or shame you to appoint to the governance of your Church an outsider, perhaps even a man of humble birth, provided that he is suitable. For the Roman commonwealth, both in pagan times and under the titles of Christianity, has grown above all, with God’s favor, because it judged that not the nobility of lineage or homeland but the virtues of mind and body should be considered.

But just as we are obliged to rejoice with you, according to the merit of your glory, over the good things you do, so we are compelled to grieve over what does not befit you and to prohibit it as deserved. We therefore admonish your affection never again to permit Jews in your land to rule over Christians or exercise authority over them.

For what is it to place Christians under Jews and subject them to Jewish judgment except to oppress the Church of God and exalt the synagogue of Satan? And what is it but, while wishing to please the enemies of Christ, to despise Christ himself? Therefore beware, son, of doing to the Lord and your Creator what you would not endure to be done to you with impunity by your servant.

Remember the honor and glory that the mercy of Christ has granted you above all the kings of Spain. By applying his will to your actions as a model, strive to repay him with a corresponding return in everything; indeed, so that you may deserve to be exalted both here and in the future, always remember to submit yourself to him in all things.

For it is very unworthy not to subject one man—namely, yourself—perfectly to him who has subjected to you more than a thousand thousands of men and entrusted them to your judgment.

For the rest, we rejoice in your royal generosity. We recognize clearly enough, and in recognizing it embrace, the devotion of your spirit in the fact that you wished plainly to show by your gift how highly you esteemed blessed Peter. Certainly, while that gift itself sufficiently displays the love of your heart, the gift itself also, in reciprocal fashion, commends the merit of your faith far more truly and makes it clearly known to the many peoples coming from every part of the world into the embrace of their mother, the holy Roman Church, to your honor.

Although the gift was so ample and magnificent that it was fitting for you as king to give it and for blessed Peter to receive it, nevertheless we embrace much more the devotion of your spirit, which the gift plainly reveals by showing how highly you esteemed blessed Peter. Having therefore received it fittingly and honorably, the apostolic see sends back to your sincere devotion the gift which, by the Lord’s generosity, it possesses.

May almighty God, creator and ruler of all things and ineffable disposer of all dignities, who grants salvation to kings, through the merits of the most exalted Lady Mary, Mother of God, and of all the saints, and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, entrusted to us, unworthy though we are, through them in whatever manner, absolve you and your faithful people in Christ from all sins, and grant you victory over visible and invisible enemies.

May he always enlighten your mind so that, carefully discerning his goodness and human frailty, you may despise the glory of the world and, with blessed Peter as your guide, attain eternity.

## LETTER III. TO THE BISHOP OF PASSAU AND THE ABBOT OF HIRSAU (1081)

He reports that, after the death of King Rudolf, everyone is persuading him to receive Henry back into favor. He advises them to inform Matilda whether she should expect support from them against Henry; and to admonish Duke Welf and others to remain faithful to blessed Peter. He urges everyone not to elect a king rashly, but to beseech God that the enemies may come to their senses and that he may grant his Church a defender. He says that during wartime canonical rigor must be moderated with regard to priests. At the synod he excommunicated all the excommunicated again.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop in Christ, A . . . . . ., bishop of Passau, and to the venerable abbot of Hirsau, W . . . . ., greetings and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice sufficiently in your prudence because, as was fitting, you have taken the greatest care to report the truth to us, especially since many different reports from your regions reach us.

We inform your devotion that nearly all our faithful, upon hearing of the death of King Rudolf of blessed memory [Note: Col. 0607. Marianus Scotus and Bertoldus give “by violent death” (*nece, morte*) in the year 1080.], are striving through frequent exhortations to persuade us to receive Henry back into our favor—Henry who, as you know, was formerly prepared to do many things for us and whom nearly all the Italians support. They add that if he comes into Italy against the holy Church, unable to make peace with us according to his will and undertaking, it will be useless to expect assistance from you.

If that assistance should fail us, who have treated his pride as insignificant, it does not seem especially serious. But if our daughter Matilda, whose soldiers’ disposition you yourselves understand, receives no support from you, what remains except that, when her own people refuse to resist—regarding her, in this matter, as insane—she should either yield, even under compulsion, to his peace, or lose whatever she appears to possess?

Therefore you must strive with the greatest care to make her certain whether she should firmly expect support from you.

If Henry should perhaps enter Lombardy, we also wish you, dearest brother, to admonish Duke Welf to show loyalty to blessed Peter, as he arranged with me in the presence of the Empress Agnes and Bishop Cumanus, after the benefice of his father had been granted to him upon his father’s death. We desire to place him wholly in the embrace of blessed Peter and to call him especially to his service.

If you discover this intention in him, or even in other powerful men who, out of love for blessed Peter and for the absolution of their sins, are moved to it, work to bring it to completion and take diligent care to inform us. With this confidence, we believe that, with God’s help, the Italians will remain separated from Henry and faithfully cling to us—or rather, to blessed Peter.

Moreover, all those in your regions who fear the Lord and love the freedom of Christ’s bride must be admonished not to hurry, persuaded by any favor or compelled by any fear, to choose rashly a person whose conduct and other qualities that ought to be present in a king are at odds with undertaking the defense and care of the Christian religion.

We judge it better that, after some delay and according to the Lord’s will, a suitable person be provided for the honor of the holy Church than that, through excessive haste, an unworthy person be appointed king.

We know that our brothers are weary from a long struggle and various disturbances. Nevertheless, it is recognized as far nobler to fight for the freedom of the holy Church for a long time than to be subject to wretched and diabolical slavery. The wretched—namely, the members of the devil—fight so that they may be oppressed by that same wretched servitude. Conversely, the members of Christ fight to restore those wretched people to Christian freedom.

Therefore the most frequent prayers must be offered, the most generous alms given, and our Redeemer entreated in every way: may our enemies, whom we love at his command, come to their senses and return to the embrace of the holy Church; and may he mercifully grant his bride, for whom he deigned to die, a defender and ruler such as befits her.

For unless the person is obedient, humbly devoted to the holy Church, and useful, as a Christian king ought to be—and as we hoped Rudolf would be—then without doubt the holy Church will not merely fail to favor him; it will also oppose him.

You yourself, dearest brother, know well what the holy Roman Church hoped for from the aforesaid King Rudolf, and what he promised. Care must therefore be taken that we do not have to hope for less from the one who is to be chosen king amid so many dangers and labors. Accordingly, in what follows we indicate what the holy Roman Church requires from him by an oath of promise.

### The King’s Oath

> “From this hour and henceforth I shall be faithful, in upright faith, to blessed Peter the apostle and to his vicar, Pope Gregory, who now lives in the flesh; and whatever that pope himself commands me, specifically in these words, ‘By true obedience,’ I shall faithfully observe, as a Christian ought.
>
> “Concerning the ordering of churches, and concerning the lands or revenues which Emperor Constantine or Charles gave to blessed Peter, and concerning all churches or estates that at any time have been offered or granted to the apostolic see by any men or women, and that are or shall be in my power, I shall come to an agreement with the pope so that I do not incur the danger of sacrilege and the loss of my soul; and, with Christ’s help, I shall render to God and blessed Peter the honor and service due to them. And on the day when I first see him, I shall faithfully become, by my own hands, a knight of Saint Peter and of that pope.”

Since we hold your devotion faithful to the apostolic see both by your promises and, without doubt, by your actions, if you judge that anything should be reduced or added to these matters, while nevertheless preserving the complete manner of fidelity and the promise of obedience, we commit the matter to your authority and to the faith you owe to blessed Peter.

As for what you asked about the priests, we approve that for the present you should tolerate them by moderating canonical rigor according to the circumstances—both because of the disturbances among the peoples and because of the scarcity of good men, since there are very few who perform the offices of religion for faithful Christians. These matters can be considered more appropriately and more fully, and the canonical order can be observed, in a time of peace and tranquility, which, by the Lord’s mercy, we believe will come soon.

As for Bugo, whose wickedness you reported, we do not yet remember having entrusted to him so great a power—namely, the power of absolving—so rashly; nor do we remember ever having known him either by conversation or by sight.

At the holy synod which, with God as our author, we recently celebrated, we excommunicated all the excommunicated again until they should offer worthy satisfaction. We asked the multitude of brothers who were present to beseech God’s mercy daily, so that he might bring them back through true repentance to the embrace of holy Mother Church and grant them perseverance in goodness. For we seek the destruction of no human being, but desire the salvation of all in Christ.

## LETTER IV. TO THE ABBOT OF CASSINO (1081)

He asks him to find out whether Duke Robert will come to the assistance of the apostolic see, and whether, during Lent, when he used to refrain from military service, he would be willing to keep one of the towns of the apostolic see in its allegiance. He wishes the duke to be warned to restrain his nephew from invading the lands of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0609B] Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable abbot of Cassino, D . . . . . [Desiderius; so also in the Mutina manuscript], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your devotion knows well how much benefit the holy Roman Church hoped to gain from Duke Robert’s reconciliation, and how greatly his enemies feared this; nor do we think it is hidden from you what advantage accrued to this apostolic see from his side.

Therefore, since the hope of many of the faithful concerning him, as is plainly evident, has not advanced to this point, we wish you henceforth to strive to learn truthfully what his attitude is toward the Roman Church.

Above all, we want you diligently to ascertain his intention in these matters: if an expedition should be necessary for us after Easter, whether he confidently promises that he will suitably come to our aid either in person or through his son; or, if he cannot do this, how many soldiers he will unquestionably promise to send after the Easter festival, so that they may serve in the household military service of blessed Peter.

Take care also to observe skillfully whether the aforesaid duke agrees to offer to God those Lenten days on which the Normans customarily abstain from fighting, on these terms: that, properly equipped, he should come either with us or with our legate to whatever lands of blessed Peter he may be invited to visit. Thus, through this zeal for service, he may both strengthen the good in their fidelity to the apostolic see and recall rebels and contumacious persons, either by fear or by force, to the reverence and service owed to the holy Roman Church; and in this way offer God a free gift of military service.

Moreover, recall to the memory of Duke Robert what he promised us concerning his nephew Robert of Loritello: namely, that the count swore that he would not thereafter invade the lands of the apostolic see beyond those he already held. Nevertheless, as we have heard, he still does not cease to invade them as far as he can.

Therefore, advising him, admonish him to restrain the sacrilegious boldness of his aforesaid nephew, and exhort him, by correcting the past and abstaining in the future, to make blessed Peter favorable to him. By provoking Peter he may obtain ruin; by his favor he may obtain perpetual life and happiness.

We have no certain news from beyond the Alps, except that nearly everyone arriving from there asserts that Henry has never been in a more wretched position.

## LETTER V. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DIE

When the legate had deposed the Norman bishops because they had not appeared at the synod to which they had been summoned, he orders Hugh to restore them, lest he provoke the king of England, who was more obedient than the other kings to the apostolic see; and he commands him to act more gently toward all the king’s subjects. He wishes the same treatment to be observed toward certain soldiers who had brought assistance to the legate for restraining simoniacal and fornicator clerics.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ, HUGO, bishop of Die, and A . . . , greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that your religious devotion suspended all the Norman bishops, except the bishop of Rouen, and the abbot of Coutances himself, whom we restored, after they had been summoned to the council. Yet, as has been brought to our attention, it was not disobedience so much as fear of the king of the Franks—that is, because they could not come safely—that kept them away. In this matter, let your prudence take note of what seems right to us.

Although the king of the English does not conduct himself in certain matters as religiously as we wish [Note: [Col. 0609] William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, Book I, chapter 1], nevertheless, in that he neither destroys nor sells the churches of God, and strives to administer peace and justice among his subjects; and because, when asked by certain enemies of the cross of Christ [Col. 0610C] to enter into a pact against the apostolic see, he refused to consent; and because he compelled married priests to dismiss their wives, and laymen to relinquish—even under oath—the tithes which they were withholding, he has shown himself sufficiently more worthy of approval and honor than the other kings. Therefore it ought not to be considered improper that his authority be treated more gently, and that, out of regard for his integrity, some negligence on the part of his subjects and of those whom he loves be borne.

Finally, your affection may remember how blessed Pope Leo endured the neophytes, and how blessed Gregory endured Venantius the expatriate, whom his own bishop had unjustly punished; and how the clemency of the Lord forgave Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, who had incurred divine anger by giving assistance to the impious Ahab. Therefore we wish [Col. 0610D] your fraternity to send, by the bearer of this letter, letters of restoration to the bishops and abbots mentioned above whom you suspended—not omitting the abbot of Coutances—and not to exasperate the aforesaid king further in such matters without our consent.

For it seems much better and easier to win him for God, and to draw him toward perpetual love of blessed Peter, by the sweetness of gentleness and the demonstration of reason than by austerity or the severity of justice.

Moreover, it has come to our attention that you have disturbed by excommunicating many soldiers who had previously offered you support and assistance for restraining fornicating and simoniacal priests, because they were unwilling to relinquish the tithes. We, by synodal judgment and discretion, have so far delayed binding such men with the bonds of anathema. Concerning these matters, therefore, we advise and exhort you that, for the present, your wisdom temper canonical strictness, and during this storm of disturbance moderate your conduct by sparing some and overlooking others, so that they may not take from the severity of justice an opportunity for becoming worse; rather, with judgment suspended for now and having time to recognize what is equitable, they may later submit more readily. Then, in a time of tranquillity—which, with God’s permission, we hope will come soon—let justice, by resolving the matter, restore them to their proper state, in accordance with what the discernment of the apostolic see now patiently postpones.

## LETTER VI. TO THE ABBOT OF MARSEILLES. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0611B]

He entrusts to him the care of certain monasteries established under the protection of the Roman Church. He grants permission to recover whatever belonging to those monasteries is unjustly withheld by others.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, RICHARD, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and abbot of Marseilles, and to his successors who shall lawfully be advanced to that office, forever, etc.

Although the care of the apostolic office admonishes us to watch generally over all the Churches and to be concerned for the condition and restoration of them all, we nevertheless judge that we ought to extend our care especially to those places which, established under the protection of the Roman see, we know expect from this Church, whose jurisdiction they are, chiefly the confirmation, advancement, or restoration of their condition.

Since, therefore, we have learned that certain monasteries—one in the province of Saint Peter, namely the one called at Montmajour, and another in the archbishopric of Narbonne, Saint Mary of Grasse—which are known to belong to the defense of this see and to be its proper jurisdiction, had long ago strayed from the path of religion through the fault of secular monks, we have judged it highly necessary to reform them and restore their fallen dignity. For you know that it is considered more fitting and more appropriate to rebuild what has been destroyed and to restore what has fallen to its proper rank than to labor in enlarging or newly building other things.

Therefore, judging your religious prudence highly useful for the restoration of the aforesaid places, although you, urged by the petitions of certain worthy men, were unwilling to take charge of them without our permission, we have nevertheless decided, through the diligence of you and your successors, to provide perpetual observance of the regular life for the brothers who shall henceforth remain in those monasteries.

Accordingly, entrusting to your affection the exercise of our care concerning the aforesaid monasteries, we wish and command you to cut away whatever must be cut away, correct whatever must be corrected, and supply by your vigilance and labor whatever they have lacked according to the requirements of discipline [Col. 0612A].

Furthermore, whenever their superiors die, it shall be your responsibility to choose and install others, with the consent of the more reputable brothers of the same congregation, if this can be done; but if not, to choose and install abbots from elsewhere, according to God and the rule of Saint Benedict. We have decreed that they are to be ordained by the bishop in whose diocese they are located, provided that he has not been excommunicated by this see or branded with the disgrace of simoniacal heresy.

If either of these conditions prevents this, let the abbot await his consecration from the Roman pontiff, or let him have permission to go for his ordination to whatever bishop the pope orders him to approach. Nevertheless, it will especially belong to your care to examine the conduct and life of that abbot, as well as those of his subjects, and to correct their offenses [Col. 0612B]. But if he should happen to fall into some crime deserving deposition, it will be your responsibility to bring the matter before the apostolic tribunal, so that either he may receive the sentence of his condemnation here from the Roman pontiff, or, through an apostolic legate solemnly sent to carry out the matter, he may undergo a judgment worthy of his merits.

We also establish that, whatever is known to belong to those monasteries, if it is irrationally withheld by anyone, you shall have, by the authority of this decree of ours and with God’s help, full permission to reclaim, demand, and vindicate it. For it is fitting that you should in no way be defrauded of the goods of those whose care you undertake.

Therefore, granting to you and to your successors, as we have said, who shall lawfully be advanced to that office, the exercise of our care and disposition concerning the aforesaid monasteries in the manner specified above, we prohibit any of our successors, or any archbishops or bishops, and no one of clerical or lay rank, from daring to take away from you or disturb this authority, confirmed by the force of the present decree. Rather, as has been established, let it remain forever undisturbed in your wholesome ordering and disposition.

## LETTER VII. TO ALL CHRISTIANS. (Year 1081)

He commands that no one molest the church of Saint Peter, situated in the village of Mascharans and entrusted to the protection of the apostolic see.

[Col. 0612D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who are faithful to God and blessed Peter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Let it be known to you that we have received the church of Saint Peter, situated in the village called Mascharans, under the jurisdiction and protection of the apostolic see, having been voluntarily entrusted to it by its founders. In perpetual remembrance of that donation, they established and vowed that those who build for themselves houses around the same place, out of love for and in protection of blessed Peter, would pay an annual census of eight Poitevin coins for each house.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command that no one henceforth presume to molest the aforesaid place, fortified by apostolic protection; rather, under the protection of blessed Peter, whose property it is, let it remain quiet and secure from every disturbance [Col. 0613A].

If anyone, therefore, should harass the aforesaid place contrary to these commands of ours, let him know that, after being warned once, twice, and even a third time, at suitable intervals, if he does not repent, he has been separated from the grace of blessed Peter and, unless he makes satisfaction, is to be bound by the bonds of anathema.

But whoever, out of apostolic reverence, restrains himself—as befits a Christian—from molesting or injuring that place, and strives to help it, should have no doubt that, if he perseveres in good works, he will merit the forgiveness of his sins and the grace of blessed Peter.

## LETTER VIII. TO THE VENETIANS. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0613B] He exhorts them to beware of excommunicated persons. He excuses himself for not presently granting their request, while promising that at a suitable time he will assent to their petition.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the glorious doge and people of the Venetians—provided, however, that they do not associate with the excommunicated—greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not think that it is hidden from your knowledge how greatly we have loved you and your homeland for a long time. Yet, after the favor of almighty God raised us to this office, we did not recognize from you the affection that was proper.

But although matters have previously stood thus, since, recognizing your mother—the apostolic see—you have begun, with sound-minded counsel, to seek and venerate her, we, who, though unworthy, bear responsibility for this see, desire no less to love and preserve your honor, both now and in the future, according to God.

Therefore, exhorting you with paternal affection, we warn and command you on behalf of blessed Peter to take the greatest care and precaution to guard yourselves from the excommunicated, and above all to beware lest, by seeking perhaps their friendship or favor, you entangle yourselves in the same snares of damnation [Col. 0613C].

As for the fact that at present we do not appear to grant your request by fulfilling it, please attribute this not so much to what might seem our negligence as to the difficulty of the times. Finally, when the suitable time arrives—which, with the Lord’s favor, we hope will be soon—we shall not hesitate, with divine clemency assisting us, properly to fulfill your petition and preserve your honor without compromising justice [Col. 0613D].

For just as charity is recognized as something to be maintained generally toward everyone in the holy Church, so we judge that each person’s proper honor, as justice dictates, should not be specially denied but preserved.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

## LETTER IX. TO A CERTAIN COUNT. (Year 1081)

He congratulates him on his observance toward the Roman Church and exhorts him to persevere in it and to separate himself from association with the excommunicated.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to T . . . . . , most noble count [Col. 0614A], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because we know—many reputable men bearing witness, and especially our most beloved brother Hugh, bishop of Die, reporting it—that your devotion toward our common mother, the Roman Church, is utterly faithful in all things, we rejoice greatly and give thanks to the supreme clemency of almighty God.

We also pray that, with divine clemency going before you, you may bring the good you have begun to its completion, so that he to whose judgment the Church of Christ of the faithful has been entrusted may enroll you, freed from the bonds of sins, among the company of the elect.

Therefore, dearest son, we exhort you to fix the eyes of your mind continually on the love and hope of the eternal King, lest your nobility, exalted above others by his divinity, softened by earthly cares and pleasures, lose the force of spiritual desire [Col. 0614B].

For it is fitting that, since he has subjected so great a multitude of people to your command, you should repay him in kind by preserving one man—namely yourself—always for him with a pure mind and heart.

Regarding the matter of the excommunicated, about which you consulted us, we can answer you nothing beyond what the sacred canons command: namely, that you abstain from communion with them, as God grants and as your prudence is able.

You should not think that you accomplish little by abstaining from such persons. Rather, believe with complete certainty that in the future blessedness you will receive from the Lord a double crown: that of obedience and that of holy preaching [Col. 0614C]. The voice of preaching accompanied by action is good, but good action without a voice is by no means insignificant.

Nor can or ought we give anyone permission to sin, since we ourselves do not possess such permission. Yet we do not refuse to assist sinners by apostolic authority, and we desire to extend the hand of salutary counsel.

We also wish your prudence to observe that, if one of those excommunicated persons were to offend you gravely, you would withdraw yourself from his friendship until he made satisfaction. If you would do this for your own honor, consider what you ought to do for God.

Therefore, dearest son, we admonish you not to neglect, for love of him who created you in his image and redeemed you with his precious blood, to do for those subject to you what you wish to be done for yourself [Col. 0614D].

Given at the Lateran, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May.

## LETTER X. TO THE BISHOP OF PASSAU. (Year 1081)

He advises him to receive kindly those who had adhered to Henry if they repent, and especially the bishop of Burgos.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, A . . . . . . , bishop of Passau, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because we have entrusted our place in the German lands to your prudence, we earnestly admonish your discernment—as we did in letters already sent to you, if they have reached you—that, with the counsel of our brother the archbishop of Salzburg and our other fellow-bishops, you diligently recall those whom you know to have strayed from the purpose of truth by adhering to H . . . . [Henry, thus also in the manuscript of Modena].

Receive fraternally those who wish to return, and especially receive kindly the bishop of Osnabrück, whom we have heard wishes to adhere faithfully to us. Do not hesitate, where appropriate, to meet with fraternal assistance any injury that might be inflicted upon him. As for the dispute he has with the abbot of Corvey concerning the tithes of his church, either settle it justly before you, or, without injury to his church, establish a definite period within which it is to be settled before us by both parties.

Farewell.

## LETTER XI. TO DESIDERIUS, ABBOT OF CASSINO. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0615B]

He announces that King Henry will come to Rome with a small force; if he wished to favor Henry’s will, he would have him obedient to himself, but he asserts that he is prepared rather to die than to give his assent to Henry’s impiety. He advises Desiderius to adhere to him in defense of the Church. He reports that from Countess Matilda’s letter he has learned that the king has entered into an agreement with Duke Robert, and he wishes Desiderius to investigate what has been arranged. He shows that the Romans are prepared to obey the apostolic see.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to DESIDERIUS, venerable cardinal of Saint Peter and abbot of Cassino, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We wish you to know, dearest one, that—as we have learned with certainty—the man called King Henry is staying in the suburbs of Ravenna, intending, if he can, to come to Rome around Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0615D] Marianus Scotus and Berthold, under the year 1081. [Col. 0616D] Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 49]. We know with complete certainty that he has a small band of men from beyond the Alps and from Lombardy.

We have heard, however, that he thinks he can gather an army from those staying around Ravenna or in the March. We consider this most unlikely, since he cannot even obtain a fire from those through whose territory he passes [Col. 0615D].

But you yourself, beloved brother, know that if love of justice and the honor of the holy Church did not hold us back, and if we wished to favor the king’s and his followers’ depraved will and wickedness, none of our predecessors ever received from earlier kings or even archbishops as great and devoted a service as we have received from this king and from the archbishop.

But because we regard their threats and savagery as nothing, we shall be more ready, if necessary, to accept death than to give our assent to their wickedness or abandon justice.

Therefore we ask and admonish you to adhere to us as befits you, so that the honor of your holy mother, the Roman Church, which has great confidence in you, may now and always obtain strength.

We also wish you to know that Countess Matilda sent us a letter stating [Col. 0616A] that, as she had learned with certainty from her close associates, the aforesaid king has reached an agreement with Duke Robert: namely, that the king’s son should take the duke’s daughter in marriage, and that the king should grant the March to the duke.

The Romans will readily believe this if they see the duke withdraw his assistance, as he promised us by oath of fidelity. But let your prudence keep careful watch and learn, through diligent inquiry, what has been arranged in this matter.

You yourself should also hasten to us as soon as possible. Moreover, know that the Romans and those who are with us are entirely ready, in faith and with willing spirit, for the service of God and of us.

## LETTER XII. TO THE VALVENSIANS. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0616B] The same matters as in Letter Fifteen of Book VIII. The oath of Bertrannus, count of Provence.

“I, Bertrannus, by the grace of God count of Provence, from this hour and henceforth shall be faithful to you, my lord Pope Gregory, and to all your successors who have been elected by the better cardinals of the holy Roman Church; and whatever you may believe, I shall not knowingly reveal to your detriment. So may God help me, and these holy Gospels.”

Another oath of the same man:

“I, Bertrannus, by the grace of God count of Provence, for the remission of my sins and those of my parents, offer, concede, and give all my honor—that is, whatever lawfully belongs to me by right of my parents—to almighty [Col. 0616C] God, and to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and to my lord Gregory, seventh pope, and to all his successors, so that henceforth my lord Pope Gregory may do whatever he wishes with me and with all my honor, without any contradiction.

“As for all the churches that are in my power, I entirely relinquish them to my aforesaid lord Pope Gregory and to all his successors; and I shall faithfully assist, to the best of my ability, in ordering them justly and according to God.”

## LETTER XIII [Note: [Col. 0616D] This letter was placed here through a copyist’s error; it ought to have been placed below.] TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS. (Year 1081)

He commands him to ratify whatever has been established by the archbishop of Lyon concerning the election of the bishop of Thérouanne, and not to permit any injury to be done to the clerics who had come to Rome for this reason.

[Col. 0616D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROBERT, noble count of the Flemings, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that the archdeacon of Thérouanne, who had previously elected R . . . . . together with a certain part of the clergy against Lambert the intruder, has now contradicted himself and, having changed his mind, has put forward another man.

We entrusted this matter by our letters to our brother H . . . . . . . , archbishop of Lyon [Humbert], to handle carefully, so that, unless the earlier election were canonically rejected, he should not substitute another man for that see [Col. 0617A].

Whatever he carries out concerning this matter, therefore, since we are certain that he will not depart from justice, we command your nobility in no way to refuse to hold it ratified and firm. Rather, observe what he establishes as though it were ours, and, on account of your greatness, threaten the others so that they do not dare to contradict it.

Moreover, we wish and admonish you not to inflict, or permit to be inflicted, any injury thereafter upon the clerics who have sought the apostolic see because of this matter.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE KINGS OF THE VISIGOTHS. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0617B] He rejoices in the conversion of their people and kingdom to the Christian faith. He exhorts them to good works. He wishes them frequently to send clerics to him who, after being instructed in the institutions of the Roman Church, can later instruct them.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the glorious kings of the Visigoths, L . . . . . and A . . . . . . , and to their peoples, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, your bishop [bishop R.], coming to the threshold of the apostles, brought us word concerning the recent conversion of your people—namely, how, abandoning the error of paganism, it reached the truth of the Christian faith.

Accordingly, rejoicing greatly in the Lord, we give heartfelt thanks to the merciful one over all, who in his eternal goodness has deigned to visit your minds with his light and to lead you from darkness into light and from death into life.

At the same time, we have entreated his ineffable mercy, and we desire to ask continually that he make you flourish in this life both through the grace of faith and through the fruits of good works, and in the future cause you to be counted among the assemblies of the saints [Col. 0617C].
