Therefore, dearest sons, by the authority of the holy Roman Church granted to us, though unworthy, in the place of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we admonish you, considering the uncertainty of this fleeting life and the instability of temporal things and joys, to despise them, and to remember always to extend the gaze of your mind toward those things that will endure without end and that, by their greatness, surpass the narrow limits of human sense and desire.

Strive unfailingly to maintain concord and love among yourselves; take care to offer honor to churches, compassion to the poor and afflicted, and reverence and obedience to priests, especially bishops, as to fathers [Col. 0617D]. Also give tithes, which may benefit both them and the churches and the poor, and impose them throughout the whole kingdom.

This ought not to seem burdensome to anyone for the sake of the better part—namely, the soul, which will live forever—when each person offers a tenth to God, since, for the sake of a body destined to die, many peoples are compelled by their laws to pay a third of their possessions to their wives.

Moreover, strive with all the strength of your souls so that, having entered to labor in the Lord’s vineyard as though at the end of the world and of the ages, you may receive the same denarius among the first to be rewarded, like the laborers of the eleventh hour (Matthew 20).

Act also so that, just as we have greatly rejoiced at the praiseworthy reputation of your predecessor [Col. 0618A], the report of your endeavors and virtues may likewise bring us the joy we desire.

But because we think that, having recently been converted to Christ, you have not yet sufficiently acquired the teaching of the Christian faith and religion, we wish you frequently to send your clerics to this see, and to take care to send us such persons as can be more fully instructed in the customs of the holy Roman Church and, once instructed, can report to you knowledgeably and beneficially what ought to be done.

## LETTER XV. TO HUGH, BISHOP OF DIE. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0618B] He reports that the bishops of Paris and Chartres have complained to him that he deposed the bishop of Chartres without a canonical accusation and excommunicated him without admitting his defense; and because Hugh had not informed him sufficiently about the matter, he orders him, while requiring them meanwhile to await him in Rome, either to come himself or to send a messenger.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, HUGH, bishop of Die, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our brother and fellow bishop of Paris came to the apostolic see with the bishop of Chartres, not, as they themselves reported, without great fatigue and loss of property, having even been captured in certain places and released only after paying a ransom.

They therefore brought before our hearing the complaint that your fraternity had prejudiced one of them—namely, the bishop of Chartres—and had subjected him to a sentence of excommunication and deposition without a canonical accusation [Col. 0618C].

They also complained that the greatest burden had been imposed by the fact that, although the accusation was of such a kind, and although the aforesaid bishop of Paris, who knew and had carried out the whole matter of his constitution, and the bishop of Beauvais without qualification, while two archbishops and two other bishops who had not been present wished to swear conditionally—that is, according to their knowledge—in his defense, you nevertheless refused to accept the oath of defense solely because those four added a condition.

Yet we do not think that anything unsuitable should rashly be presumed concerning your prudence, especially since we remember having admonished you about this matter both orally and by letter, so that you should send us a careful written account of whatever you did in synods.

Although they said that they had notified you of their arrival, we nevertheless, awaiting your messenger or letters, detained them for several days so that they might receive a determination of their case. After entering the City, they remained there for more than twenty days in that hope [Col. 0618D].

But when, after they had been worn out by the labor of the journey, the loss of their property, and great expenses, we received neither messenger nor letters from you, and when our brothers also felt great compassion for them and judged it exceedingly unworthy of apostolic gentleness that they should depart without consolation, we ordered them to wait still longer, until we received a response from you [Col. 0619A].

Therefore we command your fraternity either to come yourself—which we prefer—to discuss this matter and other more important affairs with us, or to send a suitable messenger with letters composed concerning this matter, who, if necessary, can confirm them by oath.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of December.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF CHARTRES. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0619B] He commands them to receive their bishop, cleared of the false charge of simony, with the honor due to him, and to obey him as their proper shepherd.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Chartres, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You should know that we detained your bishop with us for so long because we wished, after fully examining his case, to conclude it with an irrevocable judgment.

For this reason we also instructed, by our letters addressed to our legate, the bishop of Die, either to come to us himself or to send us his messenger with letters containing the course of this matter.

But when we received his written communication, we found that he differed somewhat from the statements of the uncle of this man, namely the bishop of Paris.

After examining the difference most carefully, however, we learned that the aforesaid case could, without violating justice, suitably be handled with mercy.

Therefore, trusting in divine assistance, we judged that this man should no longer be torn apart by the disgrace of so serious a false charge, and that he should clear himself in person and through his uncle by giving an oath over the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0619C].

For we did not believe that either favor toward any person or the ardor for temporal gain could have such force that any sane man—especially a bishop—would willingly commit so serious a perjury, scorning the dread of divine judgment.

Accordingly, admonishing your affection, we command you on behalf of blessed Peter to receive your aforesaid bishop with paternal reverence and, rendering him the honor due to him, obey him as your shepherd.

Moreover, by apostolic prohibition we forbid you to harass him thereafter concerning that accusation of simony from which he has cleared himself, or concerning any other false charges; nor are you to permit him to be unjustly troubled further, as some are accustomed to do, by smearing prelates with criminal suspicions [Col. 0619D].

Rather, venerating him as a spiritual father, as we have indicated, show that you both render obedience to apostolic commands and, as Christians ought, care for your souls.

## LETTER XVII. TO ROBERT, DUKE. (Year 1081)

When Robert had announced to the pontiff and the Romans that he had achieved victory, Gregory exhorts him, remembering that he obtained it through the help of blessed Peter, to repay the due favor and, fulfilling his promises, to assist the Roman Church, which is being harassed by Henry.

[Col. 0620A] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROBERT, glorious duke, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You acted as prudence required when you informed us and the Romans of the outcome of the war and the palm of the victory you had gained, so that the success you had gloriously obtained in accordance with the wish of your friends might be made more glorious and more pleasing to you by their congratulations.

Meanwhile, you ought to fix deeply in your memory him by whose favor and assistance you do not doubt that your affairs have long advanced. For just as ingratitude provokes indignation, so devotion unquestionably increases grace.

Therefore remember always to keep blessed Peter before your eyes, whose patronage your great deeds testify to be present with you [Col. 0620B]. When necessary, repay his benefits with grateful reciprocity, and strive henceforth to make him, as it were, your debtor; indeed, you will be able to presume upon him all the more as you bind him to yourself more firmly by your services, as though he were obligated to you.

Remember, then, your holy mother, the Roman Church, which has special confidence in you among the other princes and loves you in a particular way. Remember what you promised her; and what you pledged—something which, even without promising it, you owe by the law of Christianity—do not delay fulfilling once you have promised it.

For you are not unaware how great a disturbance has arisen against her through the man called King Henry, or how greatly she needs the assistance of you, who are her son.

Act, therefore, so that, to the extent that the son of iniquity strives to oppose her [Col. 0620C], the mother Church may have no less reason to rejoice in the help of your devotion.

We hesitated to place a lead seal on this letter, lest, if the enemies captured it, they might use it to fabricate some forgery.

## LETTER XVIII. (Year 1081)

He instructs him to arrange for a suitable archbishop to be ordained in the Church of Lyon; if one cannot quickly be found, he himself is to assume the governance of that Church.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to V . . . . [Note: [Col. 0619] Perhaps to Hugh, who succeeded Gebuin for many years? Thus also in the manuscript of Modena], beloved brother and fellow bishop in Christ, greetings and apostolic blessing.

You must take the greatest care that the great see of Lyon not long remain without an archbishop being ordained—one who is truly a soldier of Christ and a defender of justice, for which he desires not only to labor but also to undergo the death of the flesh.

But if such a man cannot quickly be found, by apostolic authority we command you, when asked by your brothers and elected by the sons of that Church, to approach without hesitation the governance of the aforesaid holy Church of Lyon, trusting fully in heavenly assistance and imitating our lord and father, blessed Peter the apostle, who was transferred from the lesser Church of Antioch to the Roman Church.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

## LETTER XIX. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LYON. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0621A]

He entrusts to him the settlement of the case of an abbot whose office he had interdicted because of contumacy, although the contumacy was excusable; he wishes the office meanwhile to be restored to him. He commands that, if it is so, the privilege said to have been obtained surreptitiously from Pope Alexander by his opposing monks be annulled, and that, after the case has been examined, he pronounce judgment concerning it according to the truth.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, H . . . . [HUGH, thus also in the manuscript of Modena], archbishop of Lyon, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The bearer of this letter, the abbot, reported to us that your Fraternity had placed an interdict upon him and his church, [Col. 0621B] because, when summoned to the place appointed for judging the matter of justice between himself and the abbot of Casa Dei, he was not present. He says that he did not refuse to come there, but that, because of the discord which existed among the counts of that region, he did not dare to do so. Therefore, since we neither know his case fully nor ought to judge in the absence of one party, we entrust it to your Fraternity, so that, after appointing a suitable place and time for both parties, you may bring their case to the conclusion dictated by justice.

Nevertheless, for love of blessed Peter, from whom no one ought to return without mercy, we wish you, insofar as you can do so consistently with justice, to treat this man mercifully, so that in your gentleness he may perceive that he did not undertake so great a journey to the apostolic see in vain. Meanwhile, it also seems proper—and we wish it—that, unless you know with certainty that this would impede the execution of justice, you restore to him and to his church their office, [Col. 0621C] so that in this matter also he may not regret having sought the assistance of the apostolic see.

Furthermore, this same brother reported to us that he had brought before your hearing a case which he had against certain monks; but because the aforesaid monks claimed a privilege of our predecessor, Alexander, of revered memory, you were unwilling to examine the matter. Therefore, since—as you yourself know—that predecessor of ours was sometimes deceived by the malice of certain people, we command your religious prudence nevertheless to investigate the case itself. If you discover that the privilege [Col. 0621D] was made contrary to justice, cancel it, and, supported by our authority, do not hesitate to carry out whatever equity requires. Whatever you decide concerning these matters, take care to report to our understanding.

## LETTER XX. TO THE BISHOP OF CANTERBURY (1081)

To the bishop of Canterbury, who, although frequently summoned to Rome, had neither come nor had a canonical excuse, he orders that he come to Rome within four months; otherwise he suspends him from episcopal office.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to L . . . . . [LANFRANC, so in the Mutina manuscript], archbishop of Canterbury, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have often invited your Fraternity by apostolic summons to come to Rome, also for the confirmation of the faith and Christian religion, [Col. 0622A] but until now, as is evident, you have delayed, either arrogantly or negligently abusing our patience, since you have not even offered a canonical excuse. The labor or difficulty of the journey does not sufficiently excuse you, for it is well known that many who live far away, although physically weak and ill and scarcely able to rise from their beds, nevertheless, burning with love for blessed Peter, hasten by carriage to his threshold.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you, setting aside every excuse or empty fear, that, after a period of four months from the time when these commands of ours reach your knowledge, you ensure and strive to be present at Rome for the feast of All Saints in the present year, and that you no longer neglect to amend the guilt of your disobedience, which has been endured for so long. [Col. 0622B] But if even now the apostolic commands do not move you, and, disregarding them, you prefer to persist in contempt and are not ashamed to incur the danger of disobedience—which, as blessed Samuel testifies, is like the sin of idolatry (1 Samuel 15)—know that you will unquestionably be removed far from the grace of blessed Peter and struck down entirely by his authority, namely, that if you do not come to us within the aforesaid period, you will be suspended from all episcopal office.

## LETTER XXI. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL (1081)

He exhorts them to endure persecutions patiently.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, abbots, clerics, and laypeople faithful to the apostolic see, [Col. 0622C] greetings and apostolic blessing.

We know, dearest brothers, that you sympathize with our tribulations and distresses and remember us before the Lord in your prayers. You should not doubt that we do the same for you, and rightly so; for the Apostle says: “If one member suffers, all the other members suffer with it” (1 Corinthians 12). We also believe that the love of God has been poured into our hearts because we all will one thing, desire one thing, and strive toward one thing.

We will one thing: that all the ungodly may come to their senses and return to their Creator. We desire one thing: that the holy Church, trampled and disgraced throughout the world and torn apart in various regions, may return to [Col. 0622D] its former beauty and solidity. We strive toward one thing: that God may be glorified in us and that we may deserve to attain eternal life with our brothers, even with those who persecute us.

“Do not be surprised, dearest brothers, if the world hates you” (1 John 3), for we ourselves provoke it against us by strongly opposing its desires and condemning its works. What wonder is it, then, if the princes of the world and the powerful of this age hate us, the poor of Christ, who oppose their wickedness, and rage against us in anger, when some of their subjects, even slaves, ordered to abandon their iniquities, attempt to take the lives of their superiors? And yet, until now, few among us have resisted the impious even unto bloodshed, and—something that was altogether to be desired—very few of us have suffered death for Christ. Consider, dearest ones, consider how many worldly soldiers each day, induced by meager pay, surrender themselves to death for their lords. And what do we suffer or do for the supreme King and eternal glory? What disgrace, what reproach, and what mockery are placed before our eyes: that they do not fear to suffer death as if for a worthless seaweed, while we avoid even enduring persecution for the sake of the heavenly treasure and eternal blessedness!

Therefore, raise your spirits to strength, conceive a living hope, keeping before your eyes the standard of our leader, namely, the eternal King, who says: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21). If we wish, with divine grace supporting us, to crush the ancient enemy quickly and bravely and to treat all his schemes as nothing, let us strive not only not to avoid the persecutions sent by him and death for justice, but even to desire them for the love of God and the defense of the Christian religion.

In this way we shall trample underfoot all the surges of the sea and the pride of the world (Psalm 92), count them as nothing, and, by his gift, be joined to him who is our head, seated at the right hand of God the Father, and reign with him. For our Teacher cries out: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Timothy 2).

Meanwhile, my brothers, to you who are weaker with me, we announce stronger battles of the contest, because our merciful Redeemer will soon bring about an outcome together with our temptations, so that, overcome by excessive weakness, we may not be able to endure, but [Col. 0623C] that, placed among whatever kinds of his faithful people there may be, we may learn to serve him even in prosperity.

[Note: [Col. 0623D] In the original there follows another letter, which is identical, in the same words, with Letter Sixteen of Book Eight.]

## LETTER XXII. TO COUNT OF ANJOU (1081)

He laments that the count has deprived himself, on account of a certain woman, of the reputation and distinguished virtues with which he had formerly been adorned, and that he has persecuted the bishop who had excommunicated him for this reason. He advises him to come to his senses; and, if he trusts that his innocence can be proved, he wishes a council to be convened at which a judgment concerning this matter may be given. He does not accept the gifts sent to him by the count. He orders him to restore what he took from the bishop.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to G . . . . [GAUFRID], glorious count of Anjou [Note: [Col. 0624D] This letter ought to have been written above; original manuscript].

We are deeply grieved that the devil’s cunning could prevail against your glorious reputation, spread throughout the regions of Gaul and brought even to the knowledge of the apostolic see. For just as we rejoiced in you and, in a certain sense, relied uniquely upon your good endeavors in our speeches, asserting that you surpassed not only princes but even kings in justice and moral integrity, so now it seems to us a matter for lament that your prudence has fallen from such grace and from so great a summit of virtues.

In this affair we recognize the ancient fraud of the enemy of the human race working with utter wickedness: he who expelled Adam from paradise through a woman deprived you, through the same sex, of the same glory and of the praiseworthy reputation of this life, and confused many of your good qualities through this form of his deception. For this reason, after being corrected and excommunicated by your bishop, so that you might rescue yourself and the woman joined to you from so great a danger and free your household from perpetual disgrace, you not only failed to make satisfaction to God and justice for the crime committed, but also tyrannically persecuted the bishop himself, even though you ought to have obeyed him had he pronounced an unjust sentence against you, contrary to your usual equity. For it is clear that no one can possess any love of God who is shown to have lost the favor and affection of his spiritual father through the fault of his disobedience.

When we heard this, overcome by our love for you and mindful also of your virtues, which religious men had commended to us, we have borne with you until now, hoping that, touched by divine mercy, you would return to sound counsel and strive to present yourself purified to the eternal King, whose judgment you approach each day. Since in this matter you have valued love of the world more than the salvation of your soul, we fear that divine indignation may severely punish a crime prolonged and left uncorrected.

Therefore, with paternal affection we admonish you to rise from this iniquity—which utterly dissipates the fruits of your good qualities—using wise counsel, and to free both yourself and the woman joined to you from the devil’s chain. If you trust that your innocence in this matter can be proved, it seems to us highly useful that a synod be established, at which our legates Hugh, bishop of Die, and Richard, or one of them, may be present, so that in the hearing of religious men it may be investigated what in you, or in the sentence pronounced against you, ought to be corrected.

God knows, and our conscience bears witness, that our mind would greatly rejoice over you—we who formerly loved you with sincere and complete affection—if you could free yourself in any way from this disgrace and close off from the ancient enemy every avenue by which he might harm you, through the fruit of your correction.

We have judged that your gifts ought not to be accepted because your offering is shown not to be acceptable in the eyes of God so long as you have not made yourself free from this sin and returned to the grace of almighty God, as befits a Catholic prince. Although we have not accepted your gifts because of that sin, nevertheless we will not cease to implore God’s mercy for you. For the rest, we admonish your nobility, and command you, by restoring to your aforesaid bishop the things you took from him, to strive to appease him by making worthy satisfaction, and thereafter not to presume to trouble him in any way.

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE TOURAINE AND ANJOU PEOPLE (1081)

He orders them not to associate with the count of Anjou, who has been excommunicated by the archbishop of Tours. Moreover, they are to assist the archbishop, who had been expelled from his see and deprived of the Church’s goods by the count.

[Col. 0625A] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbots, clerics, and laypeople of the archbishopric of Tours and the bishopric of Anjou who obey God, blessed Peter, and the legates of the apostolic see, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that you know the count of Anjou has been excommunicated because of his wickedness; it is also clear to all who know Holy Scripture that this excommunication extends to those who adhere to and support him. Though he was long awaited, he has not only failed to turn from his most evil path toward God, as a Christian ought, but, adding to his wickedness, he joined himself to other excommunicated persons, expelled our brother, the archbishop of Tours, [Col. 0625B] from his see, and completely stripped him of the Church’s possessions.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you to beware most carefully both of the aforesaid count and of all his followers and accomplices, entirely abstaining from familiarity and participation with them. Concerning our aforesaid brother the archbishop, who was driven out and suffered persecution for the sake of justice (Matthew 5), we nevertheless command and instruct you to obey him faithfully and devotedly as your father, and willingly to assist his needs, like good sons.

For just as those who support the aforesaid count undoubtedly provoke God’s hatred against themselves, so those who assist this brother of ours wherever necessary undoubtedly merit the grace of blessed Peter and the absolution of their sins. Furthermore, we expressly command B . . . . . . . ., the venerable abbot of Saint Mary, to carry our letters, which we are sending to the canons of Saint Martin.

## LETTER XXIV. TO COUNT ROBERT (1081)

His request concerning the elected bishop of Melitene cannot be fulfilled, since it is said that the consecration belongs to the Church of Reggio. Therefore, he wishes the matter to be examined together with legates to determine whether such a consecration pertains to that Church. He grants that the elected bishop of Trajanus, though elected without the authority of the apostolic see, be consecrated, while nevertheless ordering that such an election not take place in the future.

[Col. 0625D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ROBERT, noble count, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence should not doubt that we willingly support your request insofar as it can be done with God’s approval and without scandalizing our brothers. For there is no person of secular rank to whom, while preserving justice, we would more readily wish to give our assent.

Concerning what you requested regarding the elected bishop of Melitene, let your nobility know that we have been informed that the matter belongs to the right of the Church of Reggio. Therefore, we do not judge that your request can be granted in any other way unless, after careful examination, it is established that the Church of Melitene does not pertain to the consecration of the aforesaid diocese of Reggio.

For investigating this matter, because we love you, [Col. 0626A] we have arranged an opportunity for you without an irksome delay of time: namely, that, after summoning our brothers, the archbishop of Bari, V . . . . . . . . and W. [“and W.” is absent] . . . . . . . bishop of Fermo and our legate, if possible the case be examined jointly in the presence of all three, or otherwise of two of them. If, then, after the case has been carefully investigated, it is found to be free from that authority, we will not delay giving effect to your requests as shall be proper.

But if otherwise, it is fitting and necessary that your devotion, especially in matters belonging to God, should conduct itself with equal regard, so that it may beware of breaking the bond of fraternal charity and concord and of severing the unity of affection among people, keeping in mind what is written: “If you offer rightly but do not judge [or divide] rightly, you have sinned.”

For the rest, since you request that the elected bishop of Trajanus be consecrated by us, although his election lacked this—that the legate of the apostolic see and our consent were not present—we nevertheless, while warning that this must not happen in the future, grant your devotion and the man himself, on the strength of his commendable reputation, this present request, so that, when he comes, he may, God willing, be consecrated by us.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF CAPUA AND OTHERS (1081)

They are to abstain from participation with excommunicated persons and forbid it to others. Those who cannot endure persecution are given permission to flee either to the apostolic see or to the duke.

[Col. 0626C] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ H . . . . . . . . , archbishop of Capua, and to the other bishops of the principalities who, obeying blessed Peter, steadfastly defend the Christian religion, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We congratulate your devotion, dearest brothers, because you have been found worthy to suffer hostility, hatred, and insults for the Christian religion with undivided courage and strong steadfastness. We wish you henceforth to persevere with immovable strength, not only abstaining from unlawful and wicked participation with excommunicated persons, but also forbidding the other priests to share in their communion.

If there are any who, contrary to your prohibition and ours, stubbornly presume thereafter to celebrate Mass and divine offices for them, let them know for certain that, with God’s consent, such persons will be permanently deprived of the sacred ministries which they are not afraid unworthily to usurp and will be removed without hope of restoration.

For the rest, if any of you, unable to endure the oppression of the impious, wishes to withdraw, we do not object. Such a person may go either under the authority of the glorious duke or of his brother; or, if he prefers to come to us, we will gladly receive him with the charity we owe. But whoever, becoming an example to others, perseveres bravely among the impious will undoubtedly, by the Lord’s gift, receive a greater crown of virtue and triumph of glory.

## LETTER XXVI. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF NAPLES (1081)

He orders him, under penalty of excommunication, to forbid the master of the soldiers to provide further assistance to Jordan, a perjurer and an excommunicated man.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to L . . . . , archbishop of Naples, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence does not fail to know that it is incumbent upon us to provide salutary counsels for everyone and everywhere and to offer admonitions or prohibitions to all, as circumstances seem to require. We also wish you to know that, since our dearest prince of Salerno recently returned, we have begun in a special way to love both the most noble master of the soldiers and the greater and lesser people of your city.

For this reason we now grieve all the more, because we have heard that they are giving assistance to wicked men separated from the Church and from God. It has been reported to us that they are assisting Jordan, who knowingly committed perjury against blessed Peter and us and is therefore bound by the bonds of anathema. This unquestionably makes them alien to the grace of blessed Peter and unworthy of our affection; and, unless they come to their senses and desist, it will make them liable to eternal punishments.

Therefore, we command your Fraternity to admonish the aforesaid master of the soldiers and all those entrusted to you, and by episcopal censure to prohibit and forbid them from associating with the aforesaid Jordan or with any of his accomplices. [Col. 0627C] They must provide him absolutely no assistance until he has made satisfaction to blessed Peter, whom he denied by his perjury.

If anyone, obeying neither your counsels nor our commands nor the authority of blessed Peter, should die while remaining in his allegiance or providing him assistance, it is certain that we are not to pray for him; and we also order that he not be committed to burial in Christian fashion. It must also be feared that, if they do not withdraw their hearts from him, your own region may experience the anger of divine vengeance.

## LETTER XXVII. TO CARDINAL HERIMANN (1081)

He exhorts him to conduct himself patiently for Christ’s name and to defend justice. Concerning the elected Corsican, he wishes him to send his testimonial before the man is consecrated.

[Col. 0627D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HERIMANN, beloved brother in Christ and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God, the giver of all good things, who has judged you worthy to be counted among those of whom it is written: “They were considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). This is what, dearest brother, you had often read: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels” (Ecclesiasticus 27); and this also: “He cannot possess the innocence of Abel whom the wickedness of Cain does not exercise.”

Your prudence clearly understands that these and similar things are now being carried out openly. It also considers what is demanded of it [Col. 0628A] and does not ignore what is owed to it at the end for such things. Therefore, to speak briefly to your diligence is to say much: we admonish you to set as a seal beneath your heart the saying of Truth, which we think is always present to your memory: “In your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21). For this is the consolidation of justice, the foundation of faith, the security of hope, the indissoluble bond of charity, and, in short, the perfection of virtues.

For the rest, since the elected Corsican has recently arrived to be consecrated, we need your testimonial concerning him, since we believe that you know his situation more clearly. Since his election and character are unknown to us, it is certainly necessary that hands not be laid upon him rashly. Therefore, brother, so that we may know what should be done concerning him, we wish and command you to take care to send us a truthful judgment concerning him. Be mindful of one who is mindful. Pray for us.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL (1081)

He says that he wishes to convene a general synod in a safe place, in order to draw the author of such great evils—and especially the disturber of peace between the pontificate and the kingdom—from his hidden lairs and to confirm that peace. He offers himself ready to defend the innocence of the apostolic see. He threatens to depose King Rudolf, who was elected without his command, and the electors who ordained him, unless they rightly defend what they did: the electors from their dignities and Rudolf from the kingdom.

[Col. 0628C] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics and laypeople who are not bound by excommunication, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We make known to you, dearest brothers and sons, that we greatly desire and wish to decree by apostolic authority that a general synod be convened in a safe and secure place, and one so conveniently situated that friends and enemies of both the clerical and lay orders may come to it without fear from every part of the world.

For we intend to investigate and, after careful examination, to drag into the sight of the whole world from the hidden lairs of his evasions whoever he may be who is the cause and author of such great evils, which have long been raging and doing violence against the Christian religion. His impiety and unheard-of audacity [Col. 0628D] have until now obstructed and disturbed the establishment of divine peace and proper concord between the pontificate and the kingdom. With God’s assistance, we wish to restore and confirm that peace in the same council, as Christian devotion desires and requires.

Moreover, in that synod, with God as our guide and for the honor of blessed Peter, we will be prepared, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, to do what is just. By revealing the wickedness of the impious in matters brought against the apostolic see, and concerning which some of the brothers murmur, we will clearly demonstrate its innocence, provided above all that the possessions of the holy Roman Church, of which it is known to have been stripped, are restored if this is right.

Yet we do not disdain to make this especially known to your affection: with God as witness, Rudolf, who was ordained king by people from beyond the Alps, did not then assume the kingdom at our command or on our advice. Moreover, in the synod we decreed and confirmed that, unless the archbishops and bishops who had ordained him could rightly defend their action, we would depose both them from their dignities and the aforesaid Rudolf from the kingdom.

Meanwhile, many of you know who has disrupted this arrangement of ours, and it cannot escape our knowledge. If King Henry and his party had kept the obedience they had promised to us—or rather, to blessed Peter—I say confidently that, with God’s help, so many evils would not have occurred: murders, perjuries, sacrileges, the pestilence of the heresy of simony, and betrayals.

Therefore, you who are moved either by such great calamities or by reverence for divine fear and are encouraged toward peace and concord worthy of God, strive and labor with all your strength so that the synod we have mentioned above may take place, so that the head of the holy Church and the entire body—which plainly surges and trembles amid the stormy deceptions and machinations of the impious—may henceforth, through the common agreement and strength of all good people, rest and be firmly consolidated.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE ABBOT OF MARSEILLES (1081)

He orders him to warn certain people who were harassing the canonry of Saint Saturninus, entrusted to the protection of the apostolic see, to desist and correct what they had done against it. If they do not obey, he wishes him to restrain their audacity and take charge of the said canonry.

[Col. 0629C] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R . . . . (RICHARD, so in the Mutina manuscript), cardinal of the holy Roman Church and abbot of Marseilles, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence knows that the canonry of Saint Saturninus, situated near the city of Toulouse, has been entrusted to the apostolic see. Although, through the general care of all the Churches, it is fitting that we provide it with the assistance of our protection, we must nevertheless extend the defense of our protection to that place all the more specially because it is increasingly clear that its injuries and affairs pertain to the Roman see, whose jurisdiction it is.

The aforesaid Church, although recently established, nevertheless established canonical life properly, and until now, as your diligence knows, it is recognized to have lived according to the rule. But since it is the custom of the ancient enemy to grieve and employ the torches of envy all the more when he sees the Christian religion growing and his profits—or rather, his plunder—diminishing through the advancement of good people, secular agitation has now begun against this place, and, what is more surprising and grievous, hatred from ecclesiastical persons has arisen.

Therefore, the canons sent us a complaint concerning the clerics of Saint Stephen, at whose instigation, through a fugitive cleric, the privilege which we had granted to the canons was fraudulently obtained. They are attempting to take away the cemetery which that place had peacefully possessed for a long period before its regular organization, and to reduce the churches belonging to it [Col. 0630A] to their own power under unlawful conditions.

They also complain about the monks of Moissac, who are trying to retain a certain church which, after the dispute between them had been settled according to the judgment of our legate A . . . . . . . , bishop of Elne [Amatus, bishop of Oloron], with the approval of the other bishops who were present and with the holy Gospels interposed, was occupied through a renewed and more serious injury by force of Count W . . . . . , with gifts allegedly having been given.

Therefore, we command your experience to take care to warn, by letter and by whatever means you can, both the aforesaid clerics and monks and the count himself, so that they may correct, by making satisfaction to God and justice as they ought, whatever they are known to have done unjustly or maliciously against the oft-mentioned church. Henceforth, showing the reverence due to apostolic privileges, they must beware of provoking God’s anger and bringing a curse upon themselves through their presumptuous acts.

You should also admonish the bishop of that diocese both not to trouble the same canonry himself and not to allow others whom he can restrain to trouble it. Concerning the monks, however, since they belong to the abbey of Cluny, we think that the venerable abbot himself must first be informed, so that he may restrain the insolence of his subjects and compel them to submit to justice if they should be unwilling to do so.

Finally, if any of them should disdain to obey your admonitions—or rather, those of blessed Peter—know that whatever sentence you pronounce against their audacity will be confirmed by our authority. We wish and command [Col. 0630C] that your vigilant care remain attentive to the aforementioned canonry and that you show yourself readily and willingly available for its affairs and needs, so that, strengthened by the security of Roman liberty, it may, like the other Churches adhering to the apostolic see, make ever greater progress, with the Lord’s favor, in the practice of holy conduct and the love of religion.

## LETTER XXX. TO THE SOLDIERS OF THÉROUANNE (1081)

He rebukes the crime of those who, after breaking open the church doors and plundering sacred vessels, ornaments, crosses, and other objects, cut out the tongue and severed the fingers of the right hand of the bishop while he was praying before the altar. He advises them to present themselves before the legates to make satisfaction and declares that, unless they make satisfaction, they are to be excommunicated.

[Col. 0630D] GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the soldiers of Thérouanne [Tarvanne], O . . . . . . . . and E . . . . . . .

A report of intolerable audacity and a horrible crime has reached us concerning you. Since this deed is said or heard to be unprecedented in our age, and not attempted even since the time of the pagan persecutors, it all the more moves and provokes the zeal of apostolic gentleness to execute justice against it.

Lambert, the aforementioned bishop of Thérouanne, complained to us that, after committing so many and such great sacrileges by plundering that same church, breaking down its doors, and carrying off silks, silver and gold objects of various kinds, and countless ornaments, and after smashing the sacred crosses and removing both them and two chapels [Col. 0631A] and relics, you dragged that same bishop away from the altar where he lay prostrate in prayer, and, adding this to your heap of crimes, cut out his tongue and severed the joints of his right hand.

In this matter you should not attempt to offer any excuse, as though it concerned his reprehensible life, an unlawful ordination, or an imposed deposition. For, as we noted above, no one is known to have presumed such a thing up to now, except perhaps someone who, fearing neither God nor Christian reverence, thought nothing of laying a hand upon sacred orders.

Therefore, we admonish you, and command you on behalf of blessed Peter, recognizing your great wickedness, either to come before our legates, the archbishop of Lyons and the abbot of Cluny, in order to make satisfaction, or in no way to refuse to make satisfaction to God and the holy Church according to their counsel or command. We wish, and decree that it is just, that you humbly correct what you wickedly committed.

But if, hardened by a devilish spirit and disobedient to our salutary commands, you are unwilling to perform worthy penance, know for certain that you are to be excommunicated, and that whatever judgment our legate pronounces against you will be confirmed by our authority.

### Preliminary Notice to the Following Letter

After Letter 30 of Book Nine of the Register, the Mutina manuscript records the following letter, which does not appear in the printed editions; I therefore judge that it should be appended here.

[Col. 0631C] B., count of Arles, to Pope Gregory VII.—Concerning Bernard, abbot of Saints Peter and Romain of Montmajour, expelled, and William appointed in his place, whom the count commends to the pontiff and who had been lawfully elected.

To the supreme pontiff and universal pope, Gregory VII: B., count of Arles, wishes prosperity in all things and the gift of enjoying eternal blessedness with the citizens of heaven.

Most exalted lord and prince of the whole world, if you are well, I rejoice greatly. If, however, which God forbid, it is otherwise, I am exceedingly troubled. For I am your servant, and I have been so afflicted by the injustice which you have endured until now from an unjust judge that I seem to have been beaten in body and mind by the greatest whips.

For the rest, most holy Father, I inform you how Bernard, abbot of Saints Peter and Romain of Montmajour, was justly expelled from the abbey, and how this man whom I am sending to you, named William, took possession of it. For Bernard was guilty of so great a crime and such great immodesty that I am ashamed to say anything fitting for an honorable man. But I cannot be silent about one of many matters. For a Sodomitic lust ruled him beyond measure, and afterward he could not be corrected by any living person.

When I and the monks of the aforesaid place recognized this detestable matter, we could not endure it for long. After taking counsel together, we consulted the archbishop of Lyons, who had given him the abbatial blessing. By his counsel and judgment, Bernard lost the abbey which he had received from the archbishop of Arles, who had been struck with anathema by you through simony. This man who now presides was regularly appointed in his place shortly before by the decree of the aforesaid pontiff and received the blessing from him.

Now I humbly implore your clemency: let him receive the abbey from you in person, strengthen with your own hand the privileges once granted by the Fathers to that place, which is under your jurisdiction, and grant him a new privilege on your behalf. For you know how, for love of God, Saint Peter, the Roman Church, and you, I have abandoned all bishoprics and abbeys, and I do not wish this place—which has always remained free from every living person except Saint Peter, the Roman Church, and you—to be subject to anyone else.

[Note: [Col. 0631] In the Mutina Register the preceding letter is numbered XXXI; the letter that follows here in the same Register is XXXII, and so thereafter.]

## LETTER XXXI (1081)

[Col. 0632B]

When the clerics of Autun were disputing with the monks of Fleury over a certain monastery, and it was said that a privilege had been fraudulently obtained from the pontiff contrary to equity, he wishes the bishop, if this is so, to cancel it and issue a sentence according to justice. To him, who was casting accusations against himself by saying that he had absolved the bishop of Chartres, he shows that he had done so for a reason.

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brother and fellow bishop H . . . . [HUGH], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Certain clerics of Augustodunum have recently come to us against the monks of Fleury, having a case concerning a certain monastery—namely, that of Saint Symphorianus. They said that you had previously heard and decided this case, but that we had reopened it and written to your fraternity otherwise than they thought and than reason required. We have no recollection whatsoever of having done this, nor have we been able to find letters concerning this case in our register. Let your prudence therefore know that many things are brought forward and represented as written or spoken by us without our knowledge. Many things can also be slipped past those who are too closely occupied with individual matters, since we are divided among many concerns and focused upon the greatest ones, by which we are severely constrained. Therefore, in this case—which we certainly do not remember—if anything was perhaps slipped past us, we much prefer to correct it, as we desire, rather than depart from the path of equity and reason or leave its correction to others.

To whatever conclusion of a just decision this matter has reached after your fraternity’s consideration of the case—or, if it has not yet been sufficiently settled, may reach—we not only do not alter it, but, with God as author, approve and commend it. For it appears more consistent with reason that clerics, if they wish to live canonically and persist in what they have vowed, should not be deprived of their ancient possession, the monastery, which the monks themselves are accused of having obtained through the intervention of money. Concerning this, know without doubt that we condemn what was wrongly conducted or slipped past us; we confirm what was justly conducted and decided; and we command that you confirm and establish it.

As for the bishop of Chartres, concerning whom your fraternity seems to murmur, you know that, out of regard for your affection, we kept him in Rome for a long time together with the bishop of Paris, either so that you might come in person or so that you might delegate suitable legates and witnesses to substantiate the charges brought against him. Since you did not do this, compelled by the necessity of justice, we acquiesced in his restoration according to the judgment of the holy Roman Church. If divine mercy ever grants your blessedness a respite, you will clearly understand that she acted in this matter far more irreproachably than you have extended the hand of reproach against the judicial censure of your mother.

Indeed, it would have been fitting for you, and more worthy in this time of adversity, amid the straits she suffers, to offer her—as your mother, through zeal for God and a good conscience, and as her sons—sweet ministrations of consolation, rather than, by issuing such commands and entangling her in such lamentations, to add sorrow to sorrow, multiply burdens, and refuse to share them.

Farewell.

## LETTER XXXII. TO THE ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS. (Year 1081)

He signifies that, before receiving the archbishop’s letter, he had absolved the bishop of Thérouanne after receiving an oath that he would submit to the judgment of the apostolic see or its legate. He therefore orders him, after convening a council and associating with him the abbot of Cluny, to confirm the sentence if his deposition is proved just; otherwise, he is to restore him completely and excommunicate those who had treated him improperly, unless they make satisfaction.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable H. . . . [HUGH], archbishop of Lyons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0633C] Since the case of Lambert, called bishop of Thérouanne, is partly known and partly unknown to us—especially since Count Robert of Flanders sent us words in his letters very different from those which Ingelrannus had previously reported to us in person—we send it to your fraternity for fuller investigation. The aforesaid bishop denies that he knew that a synodal sentence had condemned or excommunicated him through you, or that you had summoned him to any synod. Therefore, before we had learned the tenor of your letter, moved by compassion for his many hardships, we absolved him; but first we received from him an oath that, concerning the episcopate of the see of Thérouanne, he would submit to the judgment of the apostolic see or of our legates.

Since the matter is important and requires more diligent investigation, we order you to assemble a council of bishops, abbots, and other religious men. And because, on account of the king of France, who is at odds with you, the aforesaid bishop suspects you, associate with yourself the venerable abbot of Cluny, so that you may handle the same case more fully and carefully.

Accordingly, this is our present judgment: if the cause of his deposition is proved with complete certainty to have been just, and it is established that a definitive sentence was issued against him, then, ceasing to exercise the episcopate, he is to submit to the judgment of the holy Church. But if he can establish that he was unjustly deposed or that he did not know of the synodal summons, he is to be restored in full to his property and dignity, and thereafter answer canonically to any charges brought against him.

Whatever the judgment concerning his dignity may be, we absolutely command this: that, concerning those who treated him so badly, through your insistence justice must be done to him as it requires. That is, if they refuse to make satisfaction, the sword of excommunication is to be drawn against them and against the supporters of their treachery.

We especially wish you to observe this in the present case, both because of the labor which the aforesaid bishop undertook in coming to the apostolic see and out of regard for the noble Count Robert, who sent us petitions concerning him, asking that he be treated with mercy and that, so far as justice permits, the rigor of the canons be tempered out of compassion.

Finally, let the sagacity of your fraternity proceed in such a way that it does not incline either to the right or to the left, but, making one thing out of both, holds safely to a single middle course.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO COUNT ROBERT OF FLANDERS. (Year 1081)

He pardons the words he had uttered against the apostolic see and then repeats what he had said in the preceding letter.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Robert, glorious count of Flanders, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence said certain things in its letter to the apostolic see that were not fitting. Since we earnestly desire to preserve you within the holy Church, we continue to bear with them and willingly forgive them, hoping in divine mercy that at some time we shall demonstrate to you, through words spoken directly, both the ignorance of those who persuaded you of such things and the authority and discernment of the holy Roman Church.

Therefore, concerning the case of Lambert, called bishop of Thérouanne, although the words of the clerics of Thérouanne were very different from those contained in your noble letter, nevertheless, since it is beyond doubt that things can sometimes be slipped past us, we entrust the matter to a renewed examination according to your wish. To comply with your desire as decently as we can, we have arranged that it proceed as follows.

Since the archbishop of Lyons—although I have sufficient confidence in him—is suspect to you, we have decided to associate with him the grave and illustrious abbot of Cluny, so that suspicion may not impede the useful conduct of the proceedings. Accordingly, we order them, after convening a council, to undertake a more careful investigation of the case of that bishop. If he is proved to have been justly deposed, he is to submit and withdraw in accordance with sounder counsel. But if it becomes clear that he was condemned either wholly unjustly or prematurely, then, after recovering his property and honor, he is to be restored, and thereafter answer canonically to any charges brought against him.

Whatever judgment the synod may reach concerning his dignity, we have ordered that those who, inflamed by diabolical fury, committed so grave and wicked an act against him be immediately admonished to make satisfaction. If, to increase the sum of their iniquities, they refuse, we command that both they and their supporters be punished with the sword of anathema for their obstinacy.

When this has been carried out with the care that is fitting, it will then be incumbent upon your excellence to assist the Church and, as befits a Christian prince, defend the injury done to her.

Just as we wish your diligence in this matter to possess a love of justice, so also, in the case of the other clerics and laymen who are members of the same Church, we admonish and ask you to preserve equity. After their property has been restored to them, let whatever must subsequently be decided concerning them be determined according to justice.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO THE FLANDRIANS. (Year 1081)

[Col. 0635B] Since the count of Flanders, favoring Lambert, the aforesaid bishop of Thérouanne, who had been excommunicated and deposed, had burst into the church of Thérouanne with him through a broken door, and since Lambert had plundered everything from it, wounded some clerics, driven others out half-dead, and caused others who refused to communicate with him to be deprived of their property by the count and expelled from his territory, he orders them to approach the count, reprimand him, and admonish him to come to his senses, drive Lambert away from him, and restore the expelled clerics. If he does not obey, he declares him and everyone who adheres to him excommunicated.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to G. . . . . , bishop of Cambrai; R. . . . [RATBOD], bishop of Noyon; R. . . . [RORIC], bishop of Amiens; and to all the rulers of Churches and princes serving under Robert, the most noble count, in Flanders—greeting and apostolic blessing, if they obey.

Let all of you, dearest brothers and sons, know that, although we are sinners and unequal to bearing so great a burden, nevertheless the care and concern of all the Churches has been entrusted by God to our lowliness. For the Lord Jesus Christ made blessed Peter prince of the apostles, giving him the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth; upon him he also built his Church (Matthew 16), entrusting his sheep to him to feed (John 17). From that time, by divine privilege and hereditary right, that principate and power passed through blessed Peter to all who have received, or will receive until the end of the world, his chair.

Because of the succession of this see, an unavoidable necessity lies upon us: we must bring aid to all the oppressed and, in defense of justice, fight against the enemies of God with the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6), until they are converted—even unto death, if necessary.

Therefore we wish all of you to know that A. . . ., archdeacon of Thérouanne; M. . . ., abbot; and L. . . ., deacon—and through them many clerics of that Church—have made a tearful complaint to us about Count Robert. Formerly, because of the good reputation we had often heard concerning him, we loved him as our dearest son, and, if he does not reject the admonitions that would bring him salvation, we wish to continue loving him.

They said that he had stripped them of all their possessions and expelled them from their land because, in obedience to apostolic commands, they refused to obey a certain Lambert, a pseudo-bishop excommunicated by us and by our legates, H. . . . [Hugh], archbishop of Lyons, and A. . . . [Amatus], bishop, at the council of Meaux—both for other abominable acts and because he had subjected five clerics, who wished to go to the Roman synod and lodge a complaint about his wickedness, to the worst imprisonment, and because, avoiding canonical discipline, he had fled from his own Church without permission and become a fugitive.

While under this excommunication, through heretical depravity he had himself consecrated—or rather accursed—as deacon, priest, and bishop by bishops suspended from their office.

Then, proceeding hostilely and with armed force toward the city itself, with Count Robert accompanying him with an army, he attacked and broke through the church doors, which the clergy and people had barred against him, using axes, hatchets, and other acts of violence. He also tore away from the doors the cross and the image of the Savior, which, with his right hand, seemed to be extending a written protest toward him before the closed doors and, as though with his own mouth, forbidding him entry into the church. He did this so diabolically that he tore off the image’s right hand—a deed which we have never before read or heard of.

Thus, bursting in like a thief and robber with lances and drawn swords, he wounded some of the clerics, drove others away half-dead, and plundered and ransacked the houses of all who refused to communicate with him. He so misled the count himself that the count expelled from his entire land all clerics who refused to obey him, after depriving them of all their possessions. He also rejected two of our letters with such arrogance that he addressed to their bearers insulting words, wholly unworthy of so great a prince.

How intolerable all these things are to the reverence owed to the apostolic see and how contrary they are to the Christian religion, your diligence understands well enough—if you fear God and do not place a human being above him.

For all these reasons we have now written to the aforesaid count for the third time, with exhortations and entreaties, asking him no longer to support or shelter a member of Antichrist, but rather to expel him promptly from the oppressed Church and restore in full everything taken from the clerics exiled for justice. We also required him, by correcting all these evils, to produce worthy fruits of repentance within forty days after our letter had been shown or delivered to him.

But if he should refuse—which God forbid, and may God keep it far from him!—then, according to the Apostle, who says, “Being ready to punish every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10), and elsewhere, “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of him and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed” (2 Thessalonians 3), and in another place, “Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (1 Corinthians 5), because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (Galatians 5)—if, I say, he should refuse to obey, then, by God’s authority and the judgment of the Holy Spirit, whom he in a certain sense blasphemes by knowingly supporting his enemy against him, he would be separated and excommunicated from the body and communion of the holy Church. That man, repeatedly excommunicated, does not fear daily to profane the Holy Spirit’s spiritual gifts and gifts of grace; this will continue until he repents by making satisfaction.

May almighty God reveal to all your hearts and to his heart from how great a sorrow of heart I say these things. I love all who love God, and I loved him with a certain special affection, as I have already said, because I had often heard good things about him. But I could not conceal these matters, nor could I do so without great danger to my soul, because of the prophet’s words: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezekiel 3), and the Apostle’s: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to them, are worthy of death” (Romans 1).

Blessed Gregory says:

> “We dare not conceal the evils that have come to our knowledge, because whoever can correct them and neglects to do so unquestionably makes himself a participant in the offense.”

And elsewhere:

> “Whoever, in consideration of his office, does not burn intensely against neophytes and Simoniacs must not doubt that he shares in the guilt of the one from whom this sacrilegious crime took its beginning.”

Therefore, dearest brothers and sons, we ask all of you, and in the name of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, command you through true obedience: approach him individually at a suitable time, respectfully and persuasively entreat and reprimand him, as is fitting for so great and noble a man, always placing God before him. Do this so that he does not destroy himself and that entire people by defending that apostate, but may rescue him from destruction as quickly as possible by driving him far from himself.

You also, brothers G. . . . . . , Ra. . . . . . , and Ro. . . . . . . , I separately and above all ask and command: the three of you, either together or separately, with our letters and their bearers, approach the aforesaid prince, read our letters to him, and firmly reprimand him, because he so strongly defends one who, when he implores the Lord on behalf of himself and his people, rather offends him and provokes him to anger.

Does Isaiah not speak of such people?

> “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me. When you stretch out your hands toward me, I will turn my eyes away from you, and when you multiply your prayers, I will not hear” (Isaiah 1).

And Malachi says:

> “And now this command is for you, O priests, says the Lord: If you will not listen and take it to heart, to give glory to my name, I will curse your blessings. You have departed from me and scandalized many in the law, offering polluted bread upon my altar” (Malachi 2).

Blessed Gregory says:

> “One must greatly fear that calamity will exist in those places where such intercessors are brought to positions of governance—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to appease it on their own behalf. We all clearly know that, when one who displeases God is sent to intercede for the people, the angered mind is more quickly provoked to worse things.”

And elsewhere:

> “To be subject to wicked shepherds—what else is this than for the people, destined to be ravaged by robbers, to remain so, and to suffer destruction from the very source from which it ought to have received protection? Wicked priests are the cause of the people’s ruin.”

Again, elsewhere:

> “Whoever improperly hastens to seize a place of holiness for empty glory is, by the very fact that he seeks the honor, unworthy of it. For just as the one who is invited but refuses, and the one sought but withdraws, should be brought near the sacred altars, so without doubt the one who seeks the position voluntarily or thrusts himself upon it unbidden must be rejected. For whoever strives in this way to climb higher, what does he accomplish except that, while increasing, he diminishes, and while ascending outwardly, descends inwardly to the depths?”

(Saint Gregory, Homily 39 on Luke, and Book 9, Letter 64 of the Letters.)

A little later he says:

> “When the Lord and our Savior entered the temple, he began to drive out all those selling and buying in it, and he overturned the seats of those selling doves. Who are these sellers and buyers whose seats were overturned, except those who sell and buy the priesthood and the Holy Spirit? Their priesthood’s fall before God’s eyes was plainly signified by the overturning of the seats. And since it is clear that this heresy, with its poisonous root, has crept into the Church before all others and has been condemned in the very harbor by the weapon of apostolic malediction, why is it not guarded against? Why is it not understood that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted so as to become a heretic?”

Tell him all these things and others like them, since we have heard that he is a learned man. Carefully and fearfully consider that the disobedient, as the prophet Samuel testifies (1 Samuel 15), incur the crime of idolatry. Without this obedience, as blessed Gregory explains in the last book of the *Moralia*, everyone is proved unbelieving, even if he appears to be faithful.

I have said very much to him in letters, just as I have now said much to you, because I loved him greatly. For if I had not loved him greatly, I would not have said so much to him or about him. It is not our custom to write so lengthy a letter to anyone unless the matter is extremely important.

I did this because we desire to restore him to the embrace of the universal mother, the holy Roman Church, and to cherish him beneath the wings of blessed Peter as our dearest son.

But if, through any fraud or arrogance, he refuses to receive or hear the letters of the apostolic see within the prescribed period, know with certainty that this will not merely fail to benefit him; rather, because of the guilt of his still greater disobedience, he will unquestionably be bound more tightly by the bonds of anathema under divine judgment. The same applies not only to him but also to everyone who thereafter knowingly communicates with him in ecclesiastical offices or serves him in secular warfare.

Therefore I ask you again, and in the name of God and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, command you: beware of him, and do not allow any divine office to be celebrated within your provinces wherever he himself or anyone knowingly communicating with him is present, until, by God’s mercy, he has made satisfaction.

Again we admonish you—and we know that your prudence must vigilantly observe this—not to neglect obedience to apostolic commands through any dissimulation. Rather, carefully considering the matter and retaining in constant memory blessed Gregory’s words concerning disobedience in his sermons on Samuel, take care that, by obeying as you ought, you may appear both to safeguard your own salvation and to provide prudently for his.

## Observation concerning the following letters

I have judged that the three following letters should be added here, since I recognized that they pertain to the affairs of Lambert, bishop of Thérouanne, which the preceding letters contained in the *Register* discuss. I have drawn them from volume 10 of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 393, in the Appendix.

## I. TO R., COUNT OF THE FLANDRIANS, CONCERNING LAMBERT, INVADER OF THE SEE OF MORINI. (Year 1081)

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., glorious count of the Flandrians, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that you know how much we have hitherto loved your nobility, whose ability was commended among the other princes of France by a sufficiently honorable reputation. Therefore, because we rejoice in your good endeavors, we are certainly very grieved when contrary reports about you reach us.

Recently we heard that you had assented to a certain sacrilegious cleric, Lambert, who had publicly purchased the episcopate of Thérouanne, after he had been imposed upon that Church against the will of its clerics—or rather, after he had long since been wholly rejected by them—and that you had provided him with assistance and power to invade the Church. Of such men Truth itself says:

> “He who does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1).

And blessed Pope Leo says:

> “Let no one be counted among the bishops who has not been elected by the clergy and sought by the people.”

Your prudence must therefore keep before its eyes continually the omnipotence and strictness of the divine Majesty, and must prefer no mortal’s favor or fear to him, to whom you do not doubt that you owe your life, salvation, and honor.

Since we have heard that, at the prompting of the fidelity you had pledged to King Philip, you were dangerously led into this matter, we command you in the name of almighty God: if the aforesaid Lambert forced his way into the episcopate by such wicked means, do not in any way offer him priestly obedience or reverence. Rather, assist the aforesaid clerics in making him an outsider and exile from the see he wrongly purchased and invaded.

You must not think that the oath by which you swore binds you to so grave a crime. It is more harmful to offend the one by whom an oath is sworn than the one to whom it is sworn, and to offend God than a human being; at the same time, you clearly understand that more is owed to the soul than to the body.

Fidelity is plainly better preserved toward the one who gives an order when the salvation of his soul is given precedence over bodily advantages and unjust commands. Therefore, act nobly, so that you may await punishment not on behalf of a human being but reward for fear of God. Assist and defend the aforesaid clerics, who freely opposed his promotion in God’s name, so that, the more highly divine grace has exalted you, the more you may offer confidence to the good and terror to the wicked, and make yourself an example for the other princes.

For this reason we did not wish these letters to be sealed with a leaden seal, lest, if they should fall into the hands of wicked men, that same seal might be used to fabricate some falsehood.

## II. TO THE PEOPLE OF THÉROUANNE. (Year 1082)

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Thérouanne, and especially to the noble Count R., greeting and apostolic blessing, if they obey.

As we wrote in another letter, your sagacity does not fail to know that we have long loved you greatly, because, as report has told us, you excel among the other princes of France in good endeavors. The principal reason why we should cherish a stronger affection for you has been that we have recognized you in certain matters as a lover of the Christian religion and a supporter and defender of ecclesiastical discipline and honor.

Therefore, when we heard something contrary to your accustomed uprightness, your prudence can judge how greatly we grieved. Recently something became known about you which, just as it was foreign to your ancient customs, also seemed wholly unworthy of belief: namely, that, while the clerics of the Church of Thérouanne contradicted and resisted him, a certain Lambert had invaded the see of that Church, relying upon your protection and assistance. Since he is publicly a Simoniac, a buyer of divine office, the more shameful and impudent he showed himself in such an affair, the more he ought to have encountered from you not favor but zeal, not assistance but expulsion.

But because you are said to have been led into this evil, with the king opposing, under the pretext of fear of perjury, we have therefore judged it necessary, both formerly and now, to admonish you by letter to cast aside empty fear and attend to what must rightly be feared.

Let your prudence know, then, that fidelity is not rightly preserved toward an earthly lord when through it one is proved to offend the grace of the heavenly Lord and Creator. Faith and devotion are owed more to the soul than to the body, and much more to the eternal God than to a mortal human being.

Therefore, in the name of blessed Peter, we command both your nobility and the aforesaid Church, clergy, and people: offer no episcopal reverence to the aforesaid Lambert. Regard him as a thief and robber, and take care to drive him from the see he has invaded and restrain his supporters until they come to their senses.

But if the aforesaid invader says that he has suffered prejudice, and thinks that he can prove that his case is as he claims, let him seek a hearing before our legate of Die—or rather, the archbishop of Lyons—so that, through an appropriate investigation and just judgment by him, he may obtain what equity requires.

## III. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS. (Year 1082)

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., glorious count of the Flandrians and beloved son in Christ, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have often written to your excellence concerning the case of the clerics of the Church of Thérouanne: E., the provost; S., the dean; J., the deacon; and the others whom, through the deadly suggestions of wicked men, you deprived of their property and drove into exile for their obedience to the apostolic see. We asked you to restore them completely, as is just, and no longer support that heretic L., who had been deposed and excommunicated, but rather free the captive Church from his tyranny and oppression.

Since, as they still tearfully complain, you have not yet fully done this, worn down by their repeated complaints we continue to command your nobility, and in the name of God and of the prince of the apostles we order you: rescue the Church from the aforesaid member of Antichrist; mercifully restore all their property to the aforesaid clerics; and permit them to enjoy your former favor toward them. Thus may almighty God grant you his grace in this world and in the world to come, and may blessed Peter, to whose presence they have fled for refuge, open the gates of heaven to you after the blessed end of this life.
