# BOOK ELEVEN OF THE REGISTER

## LETTER I. TO ROBERT, COUNT OF FLANDERS. (Year 1082)

[Col. 0641A]

[Col. 0641B] He warns him not to provide further assistance to Lambert, who has been excommunicated in Thérouanne, but, after expelling him, to receive the bishop canonically elected and give him assistance.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Robert, glorious count, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has reached our ears that Lambert, the enemy of God and invader of the Church of Thérouanne, is still, through your aid and support, storing up God’s anger for himself. Since he has been handed over to Satan, we are not surprised that he is led by Satan’s counsels and persists in wickedness.

But concerning you we are not merely surprised; we grieve from the heart that a man whom a good reputation had commended everywhere should now, through an evil purpose, turn that country toward common danger.

Therefore, greatly fearing for your soul, we admonish you to return to your senses from this transgression. Do not offend the Lord by supporting the aforesaid man; guard yourself from him as from a very wicked and excommunicated person. He avoided the hearing granted to him by us out of regard for you and has thereby stained himself with anathema from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

For this crime and his preceding offenses, the holy universal Church has irrecoverably deposed, cursed, and anathematized him, and has judged him wholly exiled from communion with the entire Church.

Therefore we admonish your nobility not only not to offer him assistance, but also to ensure through your efforts that he, who pollutes the multitude of the Lord’s flock with his foulness, be torn from your midst as a rotten and useless member.

We also enjoin upon your nobility that you receive G. . . . Gerard, canonically elected and entering the Church of Thérouanne through the door—that is, through Christ—with honor and as is fitting; and, offering him pastoral reverence, provide him counsel and assistance. Thus, having offended the Lord in the one, you may through this man commend your justice to God himself and to blessed Peter.

## II. TO WILLIAM, KING OF THE ENGLISH. (Year 1083)

He recalls the mutual affection between them and grieves that the king has thrown his own brother, a bishop, into prison.

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The common love and sincere devotion that we bear toward the apostle blessed Peter have joined us in friendship for a long time, and this friendship has grown stronger between us because I have observed that, above others of your rank, you are devoted to the apostolic see, while your illustriousness has believed that, among some of your predecessors, I labored more earnestly for the honor of the apostolic see.

In short, since in evil conduct the same willing and refusing often produces a pernicious faction, it follows that, in good matters, the same zeal and desire of mind should bind together in one bond of affection people separated by whatever distance of land.

Yet, although certain men of royal power grieve greatly and frequently murmur against us, complaining that they are in some way despised—complaining that they are not loved by the apostolic see in the same way, nor honored by us in deeds or words—we are not at all sorry, nor, with God’s favor, shall we be sorry hereafter.

For we hope that your majesty’s diligence will always remain devoted to the same holy Church and committed to justice, and that, with the Lord’s help, it will henceforth expand still further for the better. It is therefore right for us to persevere in the constancy of this same affection, or rather, as time passes and merits increase, to grow in it more and more.

Meanwhile, however, one matter touches and troubles us, and violently darkens the joy among the memorials of your royal virtues in a friendly heart: namely, that, when you seized your brother, the bishop, you did not look to your own honor as was fitting, but, placing secular caution and calculation above divine law, paid insufficiently vigilant attention to priestly reverence.

We believe that your prudence is not unaware that it is written—words that must especially be understood of priests:

> “He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2).

And elsewhere:

> “Do not touch my anointed ones” (2 Chronicles 16).

Nor has the Lord himself disdained to show honor to priests, even when they were wicked and wholly unworthy.

Understanding this matter, the emperor Constantine, of pious memory and especially distinguished among emperors, refused at the Council of Nicaea to accept any accusation against bishops, even from bishops themselves, and presumed to pass no judgment against them. He said:

> “You are gods, appointed by the true God; therefore we human beings ought not presume to judge gods” (Rufinus, Book I, chapter 2, *Ecclesiastical History*).

Let blessed Ambrose, that outstanding teacher, instruct your greatness and teach your prudence how great is the dignity of the priesthood and how great the sublimity of the episcopate. In his *On the Dignity of the Priesthood* he writes:

> “The honor, therefore, brothers, and the sublimity of the episcopate cannot be equaled by any comparisons. If you compare it with the splendor of kings and the diadem of princes, those will be far beneath it, as the metal of lead is beneath the radiance of gold.”

# THE SECOND PART OF THE WORKS OF SAINT GREGORY VII, ROMAN PONTIFF

## LETTERS WANDERING OUTSIDE THE REGISTER

### [GENUINE]

### I. Letter of Gregory VII to Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury: On the difficulties of apostolic governance. (Year 1073)

[*Mansi*, *Councils*, vol. XX, p. 274.]

[Col. 0643B]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother in Christ, Lanfranc, venerable archbishop of the people of Canterbury, greeting and apostolic blessing.

How the honor and burden of apostolic governance have been imposed upon us, and by how many difficulties we are beset on every side, the bearer of this letter will explain to you. Out of regard for your affection, we have also disclosed to him certain matters that remain concealed even from some of our intimates. For the rest, we first ask your fraternity not to be reluctant to pray continually to God for us, and to remind those subject or attached to you to assist us before God through their fraternal prayers. For the greater the danger in which we are placed, the more greatly we need your support and that of all good people.

For if we wish to escape the judgment of divine vengeance, we are compelled to rise up against many and provoke them against our own souls. For while almost everyone, as the Apostle says, seeks what is his own and not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), the rulers of kingdoms and the powerful of this world, in order to satisfy their desires, no longer merely neglect the law and justice of God but attack them with all their might. Thus we now see fulfilled before our eyes the words of the prophet: “The kings of the earth rose up, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

But bishops, and those who ought to be shepherds of souls, pursuing the glory of the world and the pleasures of the flesh with insatiable desire, not only confuse within themselves what is holy and religious, but also drag their subjects into every kind of wickedness by the example of their deeds. Your prudence knows how dangerous it is for us not to oppose them, and how difficult it is to resist them and restrain their wickedness. But since, as we said above, we have entrusted to this common son of ours an account to be reported to you of the sorrows we suffer amid these difficulties, we shall refrain from saying more about them.

Although your fraternity has no need of an admonisher, nevertheless, driven by our concern, we exhort you to strive everywhere to cut away the more serious vices. Above all and before everything else, endeavor by every means to prohibit the crime we have heard about the Scots: namely, that many of them not only abandon their own wives but even sell them. We wish you to be supported by apostolic authority for this purpose, so that you may punish with severe correction not only this crime among the Scots, but also among others—if you discover any such men in the island of the English—and may not delay completely uprooting the root of so great an evil with the prudent hoe of correction.

## II. Letter of Gregory VII to the monks of Vallombrosa

He urges the disciples of John Gualbert, abbot of Vallombrosa, to imitate their master. (Year 1073.)

[MANSI, Councils, XX, 374.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clerics and monks who imitate the discipline of John Gualbert, abbot of holy memory: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although we have not seen John, your father, with bodily eyes, nevertheless, because the purity of his faith shone forth wondrously in the regions of Tuscany, we loved him greatly. Although we do not doubt that you are imitators of his holy way of life, we offer you these words of fatherly exhortation so that your zeal for his holy manner of living may cause the vigor of your righteousness to watch more diligently and burn more ardently for the uprooting of the weeds from the field of the Lord.

Therefore, beloved, following his life insofar as human ability permits, and proving yourselves truly his sons and heirs by a similar way of life, act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord and in the patience [power] of his strength. Let your mind meditate daily upon the testimonies of the holy Scriptures by which the arguments of heretics are destroyed and the faith of the holy Church is defended against the members of the devil, who by various machinations strive to overthrow the Christian religion; and let your mind rise with the freedom it habitually displays when confronting evil.

Receive, according to the custom of the aforesaid Father, those who place their trust in you and intend to follow the counsel of your religious life, and instruct them through holy exhortations in whatever seems conducive to their salvation, so that the surrounding peoples, seeing the holy works not only of you but also of those who follow you, may glorify your Father who is in heaven.

For our part, we desire to show you the same love that we formerly showed your Father and you, for as long as our spirits govern our limbs. Indeed, we shall cherish you with all the greater affection hereafter in proportion as we find you more fervent in divine affairs; and, with God’s help, we shall provide you not only spiritual but also secular assistance, if necessary.

Pray, therefore, to almighty God that he may grant us the strength and resources by which we may endure the unbearable burden of the governance we have undertaken and restore the holy Church to the condition of its ancient religion. Farewell.

## III. Letter of Gregory VII to Sancho, king of Aragon and Pamplona

Gregory, recently made pope, following the example of his predecessor Alexander II, grants to him and his successors free disposition of all the churches that he or his successors shall wrest from the hands of the Saracens, or that they themselves shall build in their kingdom, except only for episcopal dues. The illustrious archbishop of Toulouse and Paris, Peter de Marca, a man whom I can never commend enough, freely and willingly promised me a copy from the royal archive of Barcelona. See the public and solemn charters of that donation in the historical synopsis of the Councils of Mansi, p. 379. (Year 1073.)

[MANSI, Councils, XX, 622.]

## IV. Letter of Saint Gregory

To Otto, bishop of Constance. On Simoniac bishops. (Year 1074.)

[BALUZE, Miscellany, Lucerne edition, II, 232.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, **OTTO**, bishop of Constance: greetings and apostolic blessing.

The urgency of your messengers, who wished to return quickly, did not permit us to communicate to your fraternity in detail what was established in the Roman synod. Nevertheless, we judged it necessary to write you the following: in accordance with the authority of the holy Fathers, we gave sentence in that synod that those who, through the Simoniac heresy—that is, through the intervention of payment—have been promoted to any rank or office of the sacred orders shall have no further place of ministry in the holy Church.

Those who obtain churches by the payment of money shall likewise lose them entirely; and henceforth no one shall be permitted to sell or buy them. Nor should those who lie in the crime of fornication celebrate Mass or minister at the altar according to the lesser orders.

We also decree that, if these contemptuaries of our constitutions—or rather, of those of the holy Fathers—should refuse to reform, the people shall in no way receive their services, so that those who are not corrected by love of God and the dignity of their office may repent through worldly shame and the rebuke of the people.

Let your fraternity therefore strive to show itself our collaborator in these matters, and to uproot these crimes completely from your churches, so that you may obtain before God the merit of a good shepherd and the Roman Church may rejoice in you as in a good brother and zealous fellow worker.

## V. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII for the hermitage of Camaldoli

(Year 1074, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, vol. II, appendix, p. 247, from the old authentic document in the archive of Saint Blaise of Fabriano.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rusticus, prior, and his entire congregation at the place called Campus Amabilis, in perpetuity.

No believer doubts that the apostolic see, because it is the prince and mother of all churches, ought by right and with due concern to preside over all churches, so that it may not only unite them in the unity of the Catholic religion but also, by its authority, generally protect and defend them from whatever is promoted externally. Among these, however, many are found that have placed themselves under the protection of the same apostolic see through a special and particular commendation, so that, embraced with the special love and care of their mother, they might remain safer and freer from every attack.

As was fitting, the Roman Church received them into her bosom and protected them everywhere with such great diligence that she provided all with adornments and granted some the grace of enlargement. Our most holy predecessors left us many examples of this. Before us, shining in the apostolic see we have mentioned, they were more concerned for the honor and exaltation of the churches of God than for their own life or safety.

For we know that many monasteries and other ecclesiastical goods, brought by religious men under the patronage and protection of the apostolic see, were received by them with the greatest charity and fortified by the privilege of apostolic protection as by a most secure wall. Their glory shows us how piously and holily they acted in this matter, as does the fruitful grace of the matter itself. For when places of prayer remain in peace and tranquility, and ecclesiastical benefices nourish the poor of Christ, praise worthy of God is proclaimed, and remedies for sins are piously bestowed upon both the living and the dead.

Therefore we, placed in the same apostolic see not through our own merits but by divine grace, have received into the protection of apostolic authority, and into our own protection and that of our successors, the oratory of Saint Saviour constructed at Campus Amabilis, together with its attached and surrounding cells and everything belonging to it, at the common request of the brothers, while preserving the due and canonical reverence owed to its mother church, the Church of Arezzo.

We desire that so pious a contribution of faithful souls, by whom that oratory was begun and brought to its present state, may increase before God and benefit them, their descendants, and their successors for the salvation of body and soul.

Accordingly, we receive that oratory and the aforesaid place, with all its cells and hospices and all things belonging to it, under our protection, so that both what it now seems to possess and hold and whatever, by God’s gift, it may justly acquire in the future, wherever located, may remain under apostolic custody and protection.

First, therefore, we list the hermitage and oratory situated at the place called Campus Amabilis. Second, its hospice, called Fons Bonus. Third, the monastery constructed at the place called Cerritum, which lies within the county of Volterra, together with the abbey of Saint Mary the Virgin adjoining the aforesaid place, situated at the place called Puliciano. Fourth, the place called Agna. Fifth, the place called Monte and Soci. Sixth, the place called Caliano and Punina. Eighth, the place called Chio, and the church of Saint Sabinus. Ninth, the place called Fogiano.

We decree by this privilege of ours that no king, emperor, duke, count, bishop, or any other person shall presume to invade, molest, or disturb in any way that oratory, the brothers serving God there, its territories, or anything justly belonging to it now or in the future. We confirm in this document the freedom and license of ecclesiastical law that it has appeared to possess up to now, or that it may justly possess hereafter, and we decree that they shall be perpetual.

To prevent anyone from introducing evil customs by which the same oratory might be disturbed in its religious observance, we prohibit this by apostolic authority. We nevertheless desire and establish that the aforesaid oratory, with its cells, shall always remain in the same strength and stability, in the manner and under the conditions in which it was first begun and brought down to our times: namely, that it shall always persevere in the eremitical path and in the loftiness of the contemplative life.

No one shall be permitted to place an abbot there or establish a monastery. The place shall always be devoted to solitary life and dedicated to continual stability.

At your loving request, we also attach the following to the privilege of the apostolic see. If at any time it should be appropriate for someone from your congregation to be ordained to ecclesiastical orders, and if the bishop to whose diocese the aforesaid oratory of Saint Saviour belongs—or any of your churches or cells that may later belong to it—should be corrupted by the Simoniac heresy, so that he cannot properly and canonically fulfill the episcopal office, then you shall have free power and permission to approach a Catholic and well-living bishop wherever one may be found in your province or a neighboring province, so that he may ordain and consecrate from your congregation whoever is worthy in the ecclesiastical ranks and offices.

For the sacred canons and good morals entirely agree that, just as those who are to be ordained must be of good life and upright knowledge, so those who lay hands upon the ordinands must, according to the Apostle’s teaching, be found blameless and without crime.

If anyone should attempt, with rash audacity and incorrigible obstinacy—which we do not believe will happen—to act against this document of our apostolic authority and confirmation, let him know that, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, he will undergo the sentence of strict punishment. But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege may deserve to obtain from the Lord God the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and chief librarian, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory VII, that is, in the year 1074 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction.

## VI. Gregory VII confirms the possessions of the Church of Bologna at the request of Bishop Lambert

(Year 1074.)

[UGHELLI, *Sacred Italy*, II, 16.]

**GREGORY**, servant of the servants of God.

We wish it to be known to all that the most reverend Lambert, bishop of the city of Bologna, came to Rome to visit the thresholds of the apostles and showed us the documents and investitures made by our predecessors, namely Agapitus, Pelagius, Gregory the Dialogist, and Formosus, apostolic men, concerning the goods of his church.

Accordingly, yielding to his prayers, we grant and confirm to his church, saving in all things the rights and privilege of the Roman Church, the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel situated on the paternal estate, with all its goods and appurtenances. We also grant the estate of Brento, with its male and female servants and all its appurtenances.

We likewise grant the monastery of Saint Mary situated in the estate called Monte Pulense, which Emperor John handed over to the Church of Bologna, together with the estate held there called Aurelia, with the mountains situated around the aforesaid monastery; another estate called Bombiania, with its cottages and appurtenances; and the mountain called Cavallorum.

We grant the port called Galliona, with its river dues, tolls, marshes, fisheries, woods, and all things recognized as belonging to it. We also grant two estates, one called the Greater Estate and the other the Lesser, situated within the parish called Boida.

In addition, we give the monastery of Saint Anastasius founded on the estate of Petriculo, with its port, tolls, and river dues, its woods and hunting rights, its marshes, and everything that appears to belong to the estate called Petriculo and to the aforesaid monastery.

We also grant the estate called Cellula beside the river called Savena, with its olive groves, vineyards, fields, woods, servants, tenant farmers, and everything belonging to it; and nearby, the entire estate of Venetiae, called that of the Associates, belonging to the same estate.

We grant the estate at Panigale, which contains within it three estates of land and vineyards called Candidatis, Pulosia, and Grisintilli; the monastery of Saint Prosper situated in the aforesaid place called Panigale; and the estate called Cumo with all its appurtenances.

We also grant the monastery of Saint Martin at Pojo, with its estate and everything belonging to it; the monastery of Saint Peter at Strata; the monastery of Saint Mary at Strata with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Peter with the estate called Nurisatico and all its goods; and the monastery of Saint Martin at Casalichio with all its appurtenances.

We give your fraternity the gate in the city of Bologna commonly called Saint Peter, and the road called Salaria, with its road dues and all the revenue that the people who customarily travel along that road, going or returning, used to pay from ancient times.

We also remind them that, at the appointed time, they should diligently pay the aforesaid revenue without negligence. We grant the monastery of Saint Mary called the Greater, with all its appurtenances and with the rent-paying house within the city of Bologna belonging by right to that monastery; the monastery of Saint Columbanus the Confessor with all its goods; the monastery of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius with all its goods; the monastery of Saint Thomas the Apostle situated before the gate of Saint Peter with all its goods; and the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist founded on the mountain called Olivet, with all its appurtenances.

Likewise, we grant the monastery of Saint Stephen called Jerusalem, which the blessed Petronius built for the use of the same church, together with the market of Saint John the Baptist held there.

We confirm and establish the estate called Milonis, with its port, river dues, tolls, market, woods, hunting rights, marshes, fisheries, male and female servants, and everything belonging to it.

Likewise, we grant all the estates and possessions—namely, monasteries, parishes, baptismal churches, castles, villages, abbots, monks, priests, deacons, clerics, the learned and unlearned, male and female servants of God, deaconesses, servants of both sexes, and all the people residing on the land of the aforesaid Bolognese Church—so that they may be under the authority and protection of you and your successors within the boundaries and limits of the bishopric of Bologna, namely from the river called Gaibana [the wording here is uncertain], and the stream called Sablosolus, and the road called Ungarista as far as Stalogalam, and the place called Culce, and the river called Leo, and another called Mazza.

Likewise, we grant to the aforesaid church the estate called Maxamaticum, with its goods, possessions, and all its appurtenances.

All these things read above, which the aforesaid church now justly holds or will acquire hereafter, we decree shall be preserved perpetually both for you and for all who succeed you in the office and place you hold, and for those whose interest it may concern.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of a cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory VII, in the year 1073, in the eleventh indiction.

## VII. Gregory urges all abbots and prelates established throughout Gaul to pay to Hugh, bishop of Die, the censuses owed by churches tributary to Saint Peter; he announces that he has entrusted his duties to Hugh

(Year 1074.)

[Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny, in PERTZ, *Monuments of German History*, Historical Writers, VIII, 412.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all abbots and prelates, both of monks and of canons, established throughout Gaul: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not at all believe that your fraternity, beloved brothers, is unaware that, according to the institutions of our preceding Fathers, certain churches of yours ought to pay annual censuses to blessed Peter and to us. But because some of you, partly through negligence and partly through stubborn obstinacy, have so far carried this out less fully than you ought, we admonish those men to reform and strive to pay what is owed, and all of you to obey the apostolic command: “To whom tax is due, tax; to whom tribute, tribute.”

For each person should seek not what is his own but what belongs to another. If one who does not give his own as he ought is rightly rebuked, what sentence is deserved by someone who neither fears seizing what belongs to another nor fears retaining what is owed? The Lord says: “Whatever you wish others to do to you, do also to them”; and: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.”

Now, because we are sending our beloved son Hugh, bishop of Die, into Gaul to carry out our duties in various matters concerning ecclesiastical advantage, and because we should trust no one more than a man whom we have found to have faithfully carried out everything entrusted to him by us, we order you to pay to him, for transmission to us, whatever you specifically owe us from your churches, and to make satisfaction for what has been withheld.

## VIII. Letter of Gregory to the clergy and people of Mâcon

That they may show reverence and assistance to Landric, bishop of Mâcon, ordained by him. (Year 1074.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Collection of Historians*, XIV, 575.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Mâcon: greetings and apostolic blessing.

How great the benevolence of the apostolic see toward you and your place is may be recognized from the love we have for your bishop, Landric. By the imposition of our hands, with God as author, he is known to have received the blessing and dignity of the episcopal office.

Moreover, so that he might demonstrate clear signs of his ordination, we sent him back to you, as we judged proper, with our letters and the apostolic seal. We admonish you and command by apostolic authority that, receiving him with every expression of love and joy, you honor him unanimously and show him, through faithful obedience and devoted submission, the reverence owed to a father and bishop, attending to the Lord’s words: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

You ought to receive, venerate, fear, and love him with spirits all the more joyful insofar as it is clear that he is pure and undefiled by every Simoniac ambition, that he entered the Church for the guardianship of your souls by no other way than through the door, and that he has ascended the watchtower of episcopal vigilance.

Therefore, sharing greatly in your joy, we ask and admonish your affection to provide him with as much counsel and assistance as you can in governing the Church entrusted to him, preserving its rights, and recovering them wherever necessary. In all matters pertaining to the Christian religion, obey his admonitions, knowing that apostolic support for him, for you, and for the Church whose spiritual children you are in Christ will be, insofar as God permits us, everywhere ready and prepared for the freedom of your faith and of ours, and the progress of salvation.

## IX. Letter of Gregory VII to the canons of Saint Hilary of Poitiers

Privilege for the church of Saint Hilary of Poitiers. (Year 1074.)

[MANSI, Councils, XX, 623.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Saint Hilary of Poitiers: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Therefore, out of reverence for blessed Hilary the Confessor, whose body rests in that church and whose teaching’s splendor not only drove away the darkness of error from the regions of Gaul but also, shining forth universally, brought light to the Church, we have yielded to your prayers and specially received the aforesaid church of blessed Hilary, built by the kings of the Franks and the princes of Aquitaine and enriched by their estates and gifts, under the protection and defense of the apostolic see. We grant this privilege by decree of our authority.

We further establish that whatever goods the aforesaid church of blessed Hilary justly possesses through the donations of the aforementioned kings and princes, or may in the future acquire by lawful means, shall remain yours perpetually and without disturbance. We add that henceforth no archbishop or bishop shall presume to excommunicate or place under interdict the church of blessed Hilary, its canons, or its clerics; rather, every more serious matter concerning them shall depend upon the judgment of the apostolic see.

You may receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or basilicas, and the ordination of canons and clerics from whichever Catholic bishop you prefer.

We further add that the same church of blessed Hilary shall remain subject only to the Roman Church and shall always enjoy so great a freedom and authority. As a sign of the freedom received from the Roman Church, however, it shall pay one ounce of gold each year to the Lateran palace.

If any archbishop, bishop, or any other person, recognizing the text of this privilege, should rashly presume to act against it and fail to correct whatever has been wrongly done, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the eternal rewards of peace.

Given at the Lateran on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the eleventh indiction.

## X. Privilege of Gregory VII for the monastery of Saints Peter and Hubert of Andage

(Year 1074.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, IV, 947.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Hubert of Andage, situated in the Ardennes, and to his successors who canonically enter there in regular succession, in perpetuity.

No believer doubts that the apostolic see, because it is the universal mother and prince of all churches, ought by right and with due concern to preside over all these things, so that it may not only unite them in the unity of the Catholic religion but also, through general vigilance, protect and defend them by its authority from whatever is promoted externally.

Among these, however, many are found that have placed themselves under the protection of the same apostolic see through a special and particular commendation, so that, embraced with the special love and care of their mother, they might remain everywhere safer and freer from every attack. The Roman Church received them as was fitting and protected them everywhere with such great diligence that she supplied all with safeguards of defense and granted some the grace of enlargement.

Our most holy predecessors left us many examples of this. Before us, shining in the apostolic see we have mentioned, they were more concerned for the honor and exaltation of the churches of God than for their own life or safety. They received monasteries and venerable places into the patronage of apostolic protection and confirmed them by their own privileges, so that through daily tranquility they might advance more fervently in devotion to divine service and in every good work.

Their glory shows us how piously and holily they acted in this matter, as does the fruitful grace of the matter itself. For when places of prayer remain in peace and tranquility, and ecclesiastical benefices nourish the poor of Christ, praise worthy of God is duly proclaimed and remedies for sins are bestowed upon both the living and the dead.

Therefore we, placed in the same apostolic see not through our own merits but by divine grace, considering the duty of the office we have undertaken, have received the aforesaid monastery, over which you, beloved son and aforementioned abbot, are known to preside, at your request into the protection of the apostolic see and into our protection and that of our successors.

By this present document of privilege, we confirm and strengthen for it the church of Saint Mary situated on the Aisne, the church of Saint Sulpicius on the Meuse, and all its other possessions, whether in villages or castles, in other churches, and in cultivated or uncultivated lands, or in all movable and immovable goods that it now lawfully possesses or may hereafter acquire by God’s mercy. Thus everything may remain undisturbed and unimpaired for the common use of the brothers serving God there, under your governance and that of your successors and through suitable administration.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this text of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and—unless he restores what he has wrongly taken from that place or mourns with worthy repentance what he has unlawfully done—be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer and subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

The lord pope also signed with his own hand: “Your mercies, Lord, are over all your works.” Farewell.

Given at the Lateran on the Kalends of May, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the eleventh indiction.

## XI. Letter of Gregory VII to the viscount Tierneus

He grants “the authority to inaugurate the monastic order undertaken according to the rule of blessed Benedict.” (Year 1074.)

[MABILLON, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, sixth century, part II, preface, p. L.]

**GREGORY**, servant of the servants of God, for perpetual remembrance of the matter, to his beloved son Stephen, viscount of Tierneus, and to his brothers who are to profess the regular life: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since those instituting a religious life ought to use apostolic judgment and counsel, lest some, following only their own opinion, rashly and with untested strength undertake the path of penance that they cannot complete and then fail along the way, so that they are forced to withdraw from their purpose, to the disgrace and injury of the ecclesiastical order, we have learned that you undertook a novitiate of virtue without the habit with our venerable brother Milo, archbishop of Benevento, in the company of our sons and brothers, the Benedictines of Calabria.

Having gained, over four years in the papal court of the most holy Father of blessed memory, Pope Alexander II, our predecessor by divine providence, proof of the steadfast fervor of your desire—for while we were acting before that most blessed pontiff as cardinal archdeacon, we distrusted your naturally delicate strength—we did not lay hands upon you so quickly (1 Tim. 5:22), as the Apostle taught us with Timothy, at whose tomb we stand.

But since you have constantly and without ceasing requested from the holy see in which we sit, though unworthy and unwilling, the authority to inaugurate the monastic order you have undertaken according to the rule of blessed Benedict, which you have long experienced among the brothers of Calabria, we, unwilling to extinguish the Spirit, now more readily and kindly yield and consent to you, since we desire, kindled by a greater flame of the Holy Spirit, that the field of the Lord be enriched with such holy seeds of virtue.

Therefore may the Lord, the crown of righteousness, the holy mountain, bless you. May the eternal Father adopt you and your future companions in the good life as sons. May the eternal Son receive you as brothers and extend to you his open side, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. May the eternal Holy Spirit kindle in you and yours the fire of his love and the flame of eternal charity.

May you and yours be blessed by the God of hosts from above, at your entrance through profession and at your departure through death. May he who began the good work in you complete it, establish, confirm, and strengthen it now and forever. May he grant you his holy angel from heaven; you propose to imitate the lives of those saints, and may he strengthen you by their patronage.

May innumerable companions be brought to you, like the stars of heaven, which cannot be counted because of their multitude. May they be taught by God for the consolation of your mortal pilgrimage.

Therefore, from the fullness of our authority, we decree that no human being shall be permitted rashly to disturb the places you will later choose for your penance, or to burden or harass you or yours with any kind of vexation.

If any secular or ecclesiastical person should attempt to act against this present document of our ordinance, let that person know that he or she is guilty of the iniquity committed—for we wish you to belong without intermediary to the holy see—and that, by the very attempt, will deservedly be deprived of every dignity of honor and subjected to divine malediction.

May the fields you cultivate be fields of first fruits. May blessed Father Benedict obtain blessings for you in spiritual and temporal matters.

Be strong and courageous in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Given at Rome in the presence of our dearest daughter Agnes, empress, and six of our cardinal brothers, on the Kalends of May, in the first year of our pontificate.

## XII. Letter of Gregory to Otto, bishop of Constance (Year 1074)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 626.]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to Otto, bishop of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us concerning your fraternity—a report I heard with great reluctance and grief—that, even if it had been brought to our hearing concerning the least member of the Christian people, it would unquestionably have deserved correction by the severest and strictest disciplinary censure.

For when, stirred by apostolic authority and by the truthful judgments of the holy Fathers, we burned with zeal, as our office required, to eradicate the Simoniac heresy and to command clerical chastity, we imposed upon our venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz, who has many suffragans scattered over a wide region, this duty of obedience: that both personally and through his coadjutors he should diligently impress this decree of the Roman Church upon the entire clergy and present it as something inviolably to be observed.

For the same reason, we were also pleased to compose special letters to you, whose clergy and people of the bishopric of Constance are very numerous and widely dispersed. These letters, impressed with our seal, were intended to support you with authority, so that you might obey our commands more safely and boldly and drive from the Lord’s sanctuary both the Simoniac heresy and the foul pollution of lustful contagion.

For the apostolic authority of blessed Paul prevails, in which, counting fornicators and adulterers among the other criminals, he adds this definitive sentence of his command: “with such a one, not even to eat” [1 Cor. 5:11]. Moreover, the entire assembly of the Catholic Church consists either of virgins, or of continent persons, or of married people. Therefore whoever is found outside these three orders is not counted among the children of the Church or within the boundaries of the Christian religion.

Consequently, if we should clearly discover even the lowest layman clinging to a concubine, we exclude him, as a severed member from the Lord’s body, from the sacraments of the altar until he repents. How, then, should one be a distributor or minister of the holy sacraments who in no way can even be a partaker of them?

But the authority of blessed Pope Leo moved us to this course: he entirely removed from subdeacons the permission to enter marriage. The decree of Saint Leo was subsequently established as law by the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church, especially by the outstanding teacher Gregory, so that thereafter the bonds of marriage were wholly prohibited to these ecclesiastical orders—to priests, deacons, and subdeacons.

When, therefore, we transmitted all these matters to you for observance with pastoral care, you, placing your heart not above but below, upon the earth, loosened—as we have learned—the reins of lust for the aforesaid orders, so that those who had joined themselves to women might persist in their crime, while those who had not yet taken wives would not fear your prohibitions.

O shamelessness! O singular audacity! Namely, that a bishop should despise the decrees of the apostolic see, tear down the commands of the holy Fathers, and indeed thrust upon his subjects, from a more sacred place and from the pontifical chair, commands contrary to those precepts and opposed to the Christian faith.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command you to present yourself at our next synod, during the first week of the coming Lent, prepared to answer canonically both for this disobedience and contempt of the apostolic see and for everything that is charged against you.

## XIII. Letter of Gregory VII to the clergy and laity of the bishopric of Constance—He announces that Bishop Otto has been summoned to the synod (Year 1064)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 627.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the greater and lesser clergy and laity residing in the bishopric of Constance and devoted to the Christian law: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We sent letters of exhortation to our brother, your bishop Otto, in which, as required by our office, we commanded him by apostolic authority to exclude the Simoniac heresy entirely from his Church, to undertake diligently the preaching of clerical chastity, and to impress upon the clergy, with episcopal vigilance, that it must be firmly observed.

For the evangelical and apostolic writings, the decrees of authoritative synods, and the commands of eminent teachers present this matter to us in such a way that we cannot disregard or neglect it without great harm to our soul and to the Christian people.

But your bishop, as has been reported to us, did not take care to carry out what we had advised him in a fatherly manner. And, so that he might incur not only the offense of disobedience but also that of rebellion, he openly permitted his clergy, as we have learned, to act in a manner wholly contrary to our command and indeed to that of blessed Peter: those who had kept women retained them, while those who did not have them introduced them with unlawful presumption.

When we heard this and were deeply displeased, we wrote him a second letter, showing him the movement of our indignation and impressing the same command upon him again with greater severity. We also summoned him to the Roman synod, which is to be held during the first week of the coming Lent, so that he might give an account of himself and set forth before the entire assembly, if he has reasonable grounds, the causes of his disobedience.

We make this known to you, dearest brothers, so that we may provide for the salvation of your souls. For if he wishes to resist blessed Peter and the holy apostolic see with open hostility and obstinacy, it is plainly evident that one who dishonors father or mother ought neither to demand nor to seek from the faithful the obedience due by the right of father and mother. It is unworthy that one who refuses to submit to his teacher should demand to preside as teacher over his hearers.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we command all, both greater and lesser, who cling to God and blessed Peter: if he wishes to persist in his hardness, show him no reverence of obedience, and do not think that this will endanger your souls.

For if, as we have already said so many times, he wishes to oppose the apostolic commands, we absolve all of you, by the authority of blessed Peter, from every yoke of subjection to him, so that, although anyone may be bound to him by an oath, no one shall remain obligated to him by any display of loyalty so long as he persists in rebellion against almighty God and the apostolic see.

No one ought to obey any person against his Creator, who must be placed before all others. Rather, we ought to resist one who grows proud against God, so that, compelled at least by this necessity, he may learn to return to the way of justice.

From the words of blessed Samuel the prophet you can recognize how great a danger it is, and how alien it is from the Christian law, not to render obedience, especially to the apostolic see. The most holy Pope Gregory arranged to explain these words in the last book of the *Moralia*. So that they may be readily available to you, we have sent the written text, in order that you may know without doubt that we are not proclaiming something new to you, but revealing the ancient teaching of the holy Fathers.

Thus Samuel says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams” (1 Sam. 15:22); “for rebellion is as the sin of divination, and refusal to obey is as the crime of idolatry.” Obedience is rightly placed before sacrifices, because through sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, whereas through obedience one’s own will is put to death.

Therefore each person pleases God more quickly when, having restrained the pride of his own will before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the commandment.

For this reason disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the virtue of obedience may be demonstrated. Its excellence is shown even more clearly by contrast: if rebellion is the sin of divination and refusal to obey is like the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it, everyone is proved faithless, even if he appears faithful.

## XIV. Letter of Gregory VII to the Germans (Year 1074)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 625.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all clergy and laity established in the kingdom of the Germans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that certain bishops residing among you, or priests, deacons, and subdeacons, associate with women, consent to such conduct, or neglect it. We command you in no way to obey these men or consent to their commands, just as they do not obey the commands of the apostolic see or consent to the authority of the holy Fathers.

Divine Scripture bears witness that “the same punishment embraces both those who do these things and those who consent to them” (Rom. 1:32).

The archbishops and bishops of your land know—and this ought to be known to all the faithful—that the sacred canons prohibit those who have been promoted to any rank or office of the sacred orders through the Simoniac heresy, that is, through the intervention of payment, from having any further place of ministry in the holy Church. Nor should those who lie in the crime of fornication celebrate Mass or minister at the altar according to a lower order.

And below:

Therefore we now turn to all whose faith and devotion we trust, asking and admonishing you by apostolic authority that, whatever the bishops may henceforth say or remain silent about, you should in no way receive the ministry of those whom you know to have been promoted and ordained through simony or to be lying in the crime of fornication.

## XV. To the canons of the Church of Beauvais (Year 1074)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 624.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church of God of Beauvais: the blessing of the apostolic see.

Because we have heard that you have been fully reconciled with our dearest son and fellow bishop, your father, Guido, we rejoice; and, so that no further division may occur, we ask and forbid it.

You should also know that whatever was done concerning Lanzelin was done by our will (see Gregory VII, Book II, Letter 5), despite the strong resistance and protest of our lord son and fellow bishop Guido, who even dared to speak against us in terms still more serious and bitter.

But, looking to the advantage of your Church entrusted to us, and breaking the excommunication imposed by him, which had been undertaken without sufficient prudence, we absolved that same fellow bishop of ours and restored him to the soldier toward whom he had been less faithful for your sake, and for the sake of your Church and your father.

Therefore we earnestly ask and command you not to be less favorably disposed toward our fellow bishop, your father, on this account. For I speak the truth to you: he neither wished nor consented to it.

Farewell, my sons.

## XVI. Declaration by Pope Gregory VII of the canonization of Heribert, archbishop of the Church of Cologne (Year 1074)

[LACOMBLET, *Urkundenbuch für die Geschichte des Niederrheins*, vol. I, p. 145.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, but especially to those among the Alpine peoples: most heartfelt greeting with apostolic blessing.

Whatever is strengthened by divine testimonies needs no human support to strengthen it. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, by the merits of his most holy life deserved to be counted among the hosts of the saints in the heavenly court.

This was asserted both by the virtues he performed while he lived in this world and by the signs that followed after he had been transferred there. We have seen his life committed to writing, and from it we have learned of his great holiness.

Therefore, with the Lord’s approval and by the apostolic authority divinely entrusted to us, we command that from this time he be numbered among the saints, be inscribed in the catalogue of confessors, and be celebrated by all as most holy on his natal day.

For it seems fitting that he whom God the Father honored in heaven should also be honored on earth by us, his servants.

## XVII. Gregory VII confirms the possessions and privileges of the “monastery of Saint Mary the Virgin, constructed in the place called Banza” (Year 1075)

[In the register of the Roman Church, from the papers of Pertz, according to Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 417. Begins: “In view of heavenly mercy.”]

## XVIII. Bull of Gregory VII for the monastery of Passau (Year 1075)

[*Monumenta Boica*, vol. IV, p. 290.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Alamannus, bishop of Passau, and through him to the church which he constructed in the territory of that city, at the port of the river Inn, and consecrated in honor of the Holy Trinity, the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Saints Andrew the Apostle, Pantaleon the Martyr, and Nicholas the Confessor, in perpetuity.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to yield to religious desires and petitions with such kindness and devotion of spirit, and to grant them effect, that while spiritual authority fulfills the duty of its office, and while, by strengthening the statutes of the faithful, it provides venerable places with the protection of defense, it may gain an increase of heavenly reward—since in granting a benefit charity was no less present than piety.

This gives encouragement to the efforts of the good through the hope of progress and renders the work itself acceptable to God through the fruit of perfection.

Therefore, beloved brother, since our dearest daughter Agnes, ever august empress and daughter of Saint Peter, has informed us that you constructed a church in the suburb of your city beside the port of the aforesaid river Inn, and that, in accordance with the intention of your devotion, you asked us to confirm it with the privileges of an apostolic constitution—and since she herself, at the request of Saint Desiderius, petitioned on your behalf—we judged that we ought all the more readily to assent to the wishes of both, the more certainly we understand your requests to be just and the more we desire that her desires, kindled by the Holy Spirit, prosper everywhere.

Therefore, by the authority of this apostolic decree, we grant to you and to the aforesaid church that those who are now ordained in that church, or who may at any later time be ordained there, shall always remain under a common life and cloistered observance.

For their common use we confirm and establish as unalterably to be held the following properties—namely, those which the aforesaid empress Agnes, ever august, donated for the remedy of her soul: a ninth part of everything cultivated and rendered at Persenburg into her hands; and those which you yourself delivered there through the hand of your advocate Rembert, namely the aforesaid port of the river Inn, with all its revenues, on condition that those travelling for prayer be ferried across free of charge.

In addition, two estates at Senftling and Neunhoven with all their appurtenances; one *h ofsacha* which Egeno gave for the bishop’s use; one and a half hides at Stainfelde; three *h ofsachas* in the place called Alburch, together with the tithe of that village and one hide; one estate at Enzenwis with Genezeo and every appurtenance; and three *h ofsachas* at Euchendorf with every appurtenance.

At Richestorf, one hide and one mill; one church called Aitenbach with all the utility belonging to it; one tithe in the parish of Huttarn; and one *h ofsacha* at Ousta with the other goods belonging there.

At Alnkoven, one hide with the tithe of the same church; at Rustam, a tithe; at Leuben, one vineyard; at Mautarn, one hide; at Wachawe, two vineyards; at Schenenbohel, two; at Aschach, two and three *sagenae*, one at Passau, another at Sebach, and the third at Mathsee.

For clothing: twenty-four pounds; ten from the ships; six from Golderbert; four from Evirding; three from the revenue of Mathsee; one from Aufhoven; and a mill in the same place.

One *hofsacha* at Richestorf; one at Peringen; [one at] Aunchirchen and Altheim, with all their appurtenances; one at Gerichwis; one at Heiming; one tithe at Ruebrechtshoven; two vineyards at Liumating; one church with its tithe at Grieschirchen; one *h ofsacha* at Kaltenpach; a tithe in the countryside of Beugen; and also the tithe of Gumtis.

All these things, I say, and whatever other unnamed goods have already been justly conferred upon the same church or may hereafter, by God’s arrangement, be conferred, we decree and strengthen by this authority, for the common use of the brothers serving God there, on the condition that, while leading a common and regular life, they claim nothing from the church’s goods as their own individually.

If, however, any emperor, king, priest, cleric, judge, or religious person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly taken away or laments his unlawful acts with fitting repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Rome through the hand of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Gregory VII, in the thirteenth indiction.

## XIX. Letter of Gregory VII to the priest Liprand (Year 1075)

[Note: Gregory VII gave this letter to Liprand immediately after he had suffered the shameful mutilation of his ears and nose in defense of the chastity of priests in the year 1075. The most holy pontiff wrote it not only to congratulate him on having attained the glory of martyrdom, but also to declare by apostolic authority that he was in no way bound by the ecclesiastical impediments that might, because of the disfigurement of his body, prevent him from serving at the altars.]

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* V, 477.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the priest Liprand: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If we venerate the memory of the saints whose death and cutting off of limbs we read about, and if we praise the endurance of those whom neither the sword nor any punishment separated from the faith of Christ, then you too, whose nose and ears were cut off for Christ’s name, are worthy of greater praise, since you have deserved to attain that grace which all ought to desire, by which, if you persevere to the end, you do not differ from the saints.

The integrity of your body has indeed been diminished, but the inner person, who is renewed day by day, has received a great increase of holiness. Your visible appearance has become more shameful, but the image of God—which is the form of righteousness—has become, through this diminishment, more pleasing and, through this disfigurement, more beautiful.

Therefore in the *Song of Songs* the Church glorifies itself, saying: “I am black, O daughters of Jerusalem.”

But if the inner form has suffered no loss, your priestly office has not been cut away from you by these amputations. That office is proper to holiness and is considered not so much in the integrity of the limbs as in the integrity of virtues.

For this reason the emperor Constantine often kissed the eye of a certain bishop of Jerusalem that had been torn out for Christ’s name; and from the example of the Fathers and the teaching of our predecessors we have learned that sacred office is not taken away from martyrs because of such mutilation of their limbs.

Therefore, martyr of Christ, take courage in the Lord. Believe all the more that the office of the presbyterate is now in you: previously it was entrusted to you through the anointing of oil, but now through the staining of blood. And the less you have that can be taken away, the less you should fear to preach what is right and sow what will be returned a hundredfold.

We know that you have always been hated and afflicted by the enemies of the holy Church. But do not fear or be terrified by them, because we hold both you and all that belongs to you under our protection and that of the apostolic see, with great affection. If anything should be necessary for you, we grant you permission to appeal to the apostolic see; and if you come to us and to our see, we are ready to receive you with joy and great honor.

## XX. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII confirming for the monastery of Cluny all the places and monasteries it had already acquired, which he also names individually; likewise confirming its right to elect its own abbot and to summon whichever bishop it prefers for his consecration, as well as for all other consecrations and ordinations, etc. (Year 1075)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 18.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Hugh, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, constructed in the place called Cluny, and to his successors who shall regularly be advanced there, in perpetuity.

In view of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance, so that with attentive kindness we may favor the just requests of those who pray and, with the balance of equity, assist all who are in need as far as, by God’s gift, we are able. Above all, however, we recognize that, for the honor due to the supreme and apostolic see, to which venerable places adhere by a special right, we must consider and labor for their stability as far as divine assistance makes possible.

Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we grant, concede, and confirm by the present decree of our authority to the aforesaid monastery, over which you are known to preside, together with the neighboring chapels—namely, those of Saint Mary, Saint Maiolus, and Saint Odilo—the following privileges.

We decree that no king or emperor, bishop, person endowed with any dignity, or anyone else shall dare, under any pretext or occasion, to diminish or take away anything that has already been donated to that venerable place by anyone from his own rightful property, or that may hereafter, by the Lord’s mercy, be conferred upon it; nor shall anyone apply such property to his own uses or grant it to others, as though for private reasons, to excuse his own avarice.

Rather, we wish everything that has been offered there or may happen to be offered there to be possessed perpetually, without impairment or disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place. These goods are to be useful in every way for the needs of those for whose support and administration they have been granted.

We also confirm by name to the same monastery of Cluny, in the county of Mâcon, a cell in honor of Saint Martin and the neighboring church in honor of Saint John, with all their appurtenances; the village of Cavinias with its church; the village of Solestriacum with its church; Sactiola with its church; Galliniacum with its church; Rufiacum with its church; Masilia; the village of Bargiserena with its church; Clarmanum with its church; the village of Curtirias; Parona with its church; Arpogiacum with its church; Darboniacum with its church; Betorniacum with its church; the church of Saint Columba; the villages of Verreriam and Berguliensem; the church of Saint Lawrence; the castle of Lordonum; Blanuscum; Costa with its church; Laisiacu[m] with its church; the monastery of Charum Locum with everything belonging to it; the cell of Regniacum with everything belonging to it; the church of Saint Victor with everything belonging to it; also the cell of Saint Victor on Mount Algidus with all its appurtenances; and the churches and lands beside it for which the church of Saint Gengulf was formerly given; the estate of Equiranda with the church of Saint Andrew and its other churches and appurtenances; the new village in the castle of Petrogoicum with its church; and all the churches and lands, or whatever the aforesaid place possesses in the said county.

In the county of Chalon, the cell of Bellomonte with the church of Saint Mary and everything belonging there; the church of Campilocus with its appurtenances; the estate called Juliacum with the churches and lands formerly granted to that place by Bishop Manasses; the church of Saint Gengulf with its appurtenances; the cell of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian; and the monastery of Saint Marcellus with all its appurtenances. Also all the churches and lands and whatever the aforesaid place is shown to possess in the said county.

In the bishopric of Autun, the monastery in Aurea Vallis called Paredum, with all its appurtenances; also the monastery of Marciniacum with all that belongs to it; the cell of Oiadella with its appurtenances; and the lands and churches that the cleric Theodardus transferred to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the agreement that Lord Walter, bishop of the Church of Autun, made concerning the monastery of Magatro, which belonged to his church, with everything belonging to it.

The monastery of Bourbon with its appurtenances; the church in the village called Melai; the church in the village called Simullai; the church of Saint Christopher beside Castrum Caninum; and the abbey of Vézelay. Also all the churches and lands, and whatever the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the same bishopric.

In the territory of Dijon, the estate of Giuracum with everything belonging to it.

In the county of Auxerre, the monastery called Saint Mary at Charity with its appurtenances; Bonaiacum; and the monastery of the holy Mother of God in the castle of Donzy, with everything Cluny appears to possess in that bishopric.

In the county of Auvergne, the monastery of Silviniacum, where Saints Maiolus and Odilo rest, with everything belonging there; the cell called Firmitas; the cell called Scuriolas; the church of Saint Sulpicius in the village called Langiacum; the little cell called at the Wood; the estate called at Fridomons; the monastery called Rivis with the estate of Lipsiacum and its appurtenances; the church called at the Mountains; the monastery of Celsinianum with its cells, churches, villages, and lands; and the monastery where Saint Florus rests, which the cleric Eustorgius gave to the aforesaid place, with everything belonging to it; houses in the town of Brioude; the monastery called Volta with its appurtenances; Rocca Fortis; the cell of Reiliacum with its estate and everything belonging to it; the cell of Saint Mary called at the Bridge; and all the churches and lands and whatever Cluny appears to possess in the said county.

In the bishopric of Nevers, the monastery of the Savior within the walls; the monastery of Saint Stephen in the suburb of that city; the cell of Saint Reverian with its appurtenances; the church called Lupertiacum, which Fraemundus gave, with its appurtenances; the place called Baiard; and the obedience called Villa.

In the county of Poitiers, the village called Molgon.

In the bishopric of Saintes, the monastery on the island called Aias; the monastery of Saint George beside the castle of Didonius; the monastery of Saint Mary beside the castle of Berbeziacum; the abbey of Saint John called Ingeriacum; and the abbey of Malliacum.

In the abbey of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers, we grant you what your predecessors held there.

In the bishopric of Limoges, the monastery of Saint Martial.

In the bishopric of Angoulême, the monastery of Saint Maurice beside the castle of Mount Beroltus.

In the bishopric of Paris, the monastery of Longpont.

In the bishopric of Troyes, the monastery of Saint Margaret with the possessions belonging to it.

In the bishopric of Soissons, the village of Conciacum, which Count Theobald and his wife gave to the Cluniac monastery.

In the bishopric of Périgueux, the church of Saint Mary called Anessa.

In the bishopric of Cahors, the abbey of Saint Peter of Moissac with all its appurtenances; the monastery called Fiacus; and the monastery of Carennac.

At Toulouse, the monastery of Saint Mary of the Aurade; and in the same bishopric the monastery called Lajad; the castle called Lordag; and the lands that Count Roger gave to Cluny in the valley of Javart.

In the county of Agen, the monastery called Lairacum; another called Muiracum; another called Saint Genevieve; and the monastery called Meediziacum.

In the county of Lectoure, the monastery of Saint Genu.

In the territory of Auch, the monastery of Saint Orientius; the church called at the High Mountain; the monastery called Monasterium; and the monastery of Saint John called at the Holy Mountain, with its appurtenances.

In the territory of Bigorre, the monastery of Saint Licerius.

In the territory of Labourd, in the village called Fureas, the church of Saint Faith.

Also all the churches, villages, and lands that Cluny is proved to possess in Gascony.

In the bishopric of Seville, the monastery of Saint Isidore the Martyr with its appurtenances.

In the bishopric of Viviers, Misoscum; the cell of Mount Rompon; the cell at the Fountains; and the cell of Rion.

In the bishopric of Uzès, the monastery of Saint Saturninus with the castle of Columcellas, the estate of Tueleta, and everything belonging to it on both sides of the river Rhône.

In the bishopric of Nîmes, the monastery of Saint Giles.

In the city of Troyes, the monastery of Saint Amand.

In the bishopric of Orange, the cell called Podiolenus and the monastery of Saint Pantaleon.

In the bishopric of Agde, the cell of Saint Andrew, granted to Cluny by the cleric Ricaud; the monastery of Ganagobie; and the estate of Valentiola.

In the bishopric of Valence, the village called Ales and Montel; and the monastery of Saint Marcellus called Salicetum.

In the bishopric of Vienne, the monastery of Taherniacum; the cell called Causella; the village of Bracost; the village called Island; and the cell in the castle of Candiac.

In the bishopric of Lyon, the monastery called Amberta; the cell of Talusiacum; the cell of Poliacum; the cell of Artedunum; the cell of Saviniacum; the estate of Ambariacum; the church of Saint Andeol; the church called at the Oratory; the estate of Romans; the cell of Cavariacum; and the church in the castle of Gosan.

Also all the villages and lands that Wichard, when dying, transferred to Cluny.

In the bishopric of Grenoble, the cell called Borget and the monastery called Domena.

In the bishopric of Besançon, the cell called Portus.

In the bishopric of Toul, the cell called Ramengas.

In the bishopric of Lausanne, the monastery called Paterniacum, and the possessions in Alsace that the emperors gave to the same place; the cell called Mount Richeri; and the monastery called Romanum.

In the bishopric of Geneva, the monastery of Saint Victor the Martyr.

In the bishopric of Strasbourg, the monastery of Salsum.

In the bishopric of Constance, the cell called Romisino.

In the bishopric of Pavia, the monastery of Saint Maiolus.

In the bishopric of Laus, the monastery of Saint Mark.

In the city of Piacenza, the church of Saint Gregory.

Beside the city of Cremona, the monastery in honor of Saint Gabriel and Saints Barnabas and Luke.

In addition to these, as we said above, whatever it now possesses or may hereafter, with the Lord’s consent, happen to possess, whether movable or immovable.

We also establish that, when an abbot dies, no other person shall be appointed there through any deceitful maneuver, except one whom the brothers of that monastery elect by common consent in the fear of God.

For his consecration, those same brothers may summon whichever bishop they wish. Nor shall any bishop or archbishop in any way dare to excommunicate or judge that place itself, the aforesaid chapels—namely, those of Saint Mary, Saint Maiolus, and Saint Odilo—or the priests appointed there by the abbot, or the monks of that monastery. Rather, always remaining under the protection and immunity of Rome and subject only to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, they shall serve almighty God in peace and security.

From whichever bishop they wish, they may also receive chrism, holy oil, and oil for the sick for the consecrations to be carried out in that place, as well as for the consecration of altars and chapels and for the ordinations of monks.

We grant and confirm to you and to that venerable place, by apostolic authority, that whenever and for as long as you wish you may strike your own coinage or currency, just as we have learned that the privileges of our venerable predecessors granted and confirmed this to you; and we grant and confirm it.

All these things contained in the page of this command and decree of ours we decree must be observed in perpetuity both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the order and place you hold, and by those whose concern it may be.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly offered and laments his unlawful acts with fitting repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and at the eternal judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just for that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of peace.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, in the fourteenth indiction. Fare well.

## XXI. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII by which he entrusts the newly founded monastery in the suburb of Poitiers, built by Count William of Poitou, at the count’s request, to Saint Hugh and his successors, the abbots of Cluny, to govern in perpetuity. (Year 1075.)

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 20.]*

[Col. 0666B]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, HUGH, abbot of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, built in the place called Cluny.

In consideration of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance, so that with attentive kindness we may favor the rightful requests of those who pray, and, with the scales of equity, may assist all who are in need as far as, with God’s gift, we are able. Above all, however, we recognize that we must carefully consider and labor, insofar as divine assistance grants the possibility, for the stability of venerable places, out of due regard for the supreme and apostolic See, to which they are attached by a special right.

Therefore, in accordance with the petition of yourself and of our son William, count of Poitou, who built a monastery in the suburb of that same city in honor of the blessed apostles John the Evangelist, Simon, and Jude, and who entreated us to entrust it to you and your successors to govern perpetually according to the Lord, we grant, concede, and confirm this privilege by the present decree of our authority.

We decree that no king or emperor, bishop or count, no person possessing whatever dignity, nor anyone else, shall dare to diminish or take away, under any pretext or guise of cause, those things which have already been donated from their own rightful property to that venerable place by the aforesaid count or by any other persons, or which in the future, with the Lord’s gift, may be bestowed upon it; nor shall anyone apply them to personal use or grant them to others under the pretense of pious reasons as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, we wish that everything which has been offered there, or may happen to be offered, be possessed perpetually and without disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place. In every respect, these things are to benefit those for whose support and administration they have been granted.

[Col. 0666C]

Likewise, we establish that, when the abbot dies, no other person shall be appointed there through any stratagem of deception, except one whom you and your successors shall have elected according to the fear of God. We also add to the present decree that the monastery itself, its abbots, and its monks shall be secure from every intrusion of secular servitude and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, diligent and peaceful in the observance of holy religion. They shall be subject to no one else on any pretext except the abbot of Cluny.

The consecration of abbots and churches, and the ordination of monks or clerics belonging to the aforesaid monastery, shall be received from the bishop in whose diocese they are situated, provided that the bishop has been canonically ordained and performs the ordination freely. But if either of these conditions is lacking, they shall have permission, by the authority of the apostolic See, to go freely to whatever Catholic bishop they may choose for the consecration and ordination both of places and of persons.

[Col. 0666D]

All these provisions contained in the page of this decree and command of ours, we decree must be observed perpetually both by you and by all who succeed you in the office and place which you hold, or by those whose concern it may be. If, however, any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away and mourns his unlawful conduct with worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subject to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and librarian, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, in the fourteenth indiction.

Fare well.
