## XXII. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII by which he entrusts the monastery of Gigny to Saint Hugh and his successors, the abbots of Cluny, to govern in perpetuity. (Year 1075.)

*[Bullarium Cluniacense, 21.]*

[Col. 0667D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son HUGH, abbot of Cluny.

We ought to lend a favorable ear to those who request what will benefit just and holy religion, so that those who ask may find the remedies they hope for, and so that proper solicitude and pastoral compassion may not be lacking toward churches and monasteries deprived of support. Accordingly, the monks of the monastery of Gigny—which is recognized as the property of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—hoping for the help of our mercy, have lamentably complained to us that the monastery itself and the religious observance which was once held there in the highest esteem have now, because of the more negligent care of its abbots and superiors, entirely lost their vigor, and that it has also been completely deprived of temporal resources.

[Col. 0668A]

To drive away these miseries, the monks themselves, suggesting what remedy might be applied, pressed us with many supplications to commend the aforesaid monastery to your vigilance, so that through your provident care the religious life which has perished through the drowsiness of others might revive, and that its material resources might likewise, with the Lord’s help, be renewed and increased.

Therefore, entrusting the aforesaid monastery of Gigny to you, most beloved Hugh, son of the Holy Roman Church and most reverend abbot of the monastery of Cluny, we command, assent, and grant by the authority of this decree that, from the present day for as long as you live, you shall have free power to organize, govern, correct, and alter it, with all its appurtenances, as you wish under the Lord’s mercy.

[Col. 0668B]

But after you, when summoned by the Lord, have departed from this world to receive from Christ the desired reward of your long labor, we wish all your successors to have such power in the aforesaid monastery of Gigny, and we strengthen this by our authority: namely, that no abbot shall be elected or appointed there unless either the abbot of Cluny himself is present and approves him, or, through his legate, gives his assent according to the fear of God.

If any king, emperor, duke, count, or any person whatsoever, great or small, violates the sanction of this command of ours or dares to infringe it, we remove him, as a sacrilegious person, from the sacred body of the Lord until he has made satisfaction to you or your successors and has performed worthy penance; and by apostolic authority we prohibit him from communion.

[Col. 0668C]

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, in the fourteenth indiction.

Fare well.

## XXIII. Gregory VII confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Peter of Condom. (Year 1076.)

*[In Acherius, Spicilegii, vol. II, p. 584.]*

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, RAYMOND, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter situated in the place called Condom, and to his successors in perpetuity.

[Col. 0668D]

In consideration of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance, so that with attentive kindness we may favor the rightful requests of those who pray, and, with the scales of equity, may assist all who are in need as far as, with God’s gift, we are able. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we grant, concede, and confirm to the aforesaid monastery, which you are known to govern, privileges of this kind by the present decree of our authority.

We decree that no king or emperor, bishop, person possessing whatever dignity, or anyone else shall dare to diminish or take away, under any pretext or guise of cause, those things which have already been donated from their own rightful property to that venerable place by any persons, or which in the future, with God’s mercy, may be justly bestowed upon it; nor shall anyone apply them to personal use or grant them to others under the pretense of pious reasons as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, we wish that everything which has been justly offered there, or may happen to be offered, be possessed perpetually and without disturbance both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place. In every respect, these things are to benefit those for whose support and administration they have been granted.

[Col. 0669A]

And because Bishop Hugh enriched this monastery from the goods of his inheritance and transferred it under the jurisdiction of the Roman Church, it has been established, for the future security of its protection, that an annual payment of five solidi in the coinage of that land be rendered to the apostolic See.

Accordingly, we expressly confirm to the same monastery those possessions which the aforesaid Bishop Hugh, founder of that monastery, conferred upon the aforesaid place from his patrimonial right in the district of Leumania: namely, the church of Saint Peter and the place called Condom, which is interpreted as “lofty house,” together with all its appurtenances.

Likewise, we establish that, when the abbot dies, no other person shall be appointed there through any stratagem of deception, except one whom the brothers of that place shall elect by common consent according to the fear of God.

[Col. 0669B]

We also add to the present decree that the monastery itself, its abbots, and its monks shall be secure from every intrusion of secular service and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, diligent and peaceful in the observance of holy religion, and shall not be subject on any pretext whatsoever.

[Col. 0669C]

All these provisions contained in the page of this decree and command of ours, we decree must be observed perpetually both by you and by all who succeed them in their offices and places. If, however, any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his possession and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away and mourns his unlawful conduct with worthy repentance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0669D]

But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good work and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII, in the fourteenth indiction.

## XXIV. Gregory VII takes the monastery of Fonte Avellana under his protection. (Year 1076, tenth day before the Kalends of April.)

*[Mittarelli, Annales Camaldulenses, vol. II, p. 258.]*

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, marquises, counts, nobles, valvassors, and all believers in Christ: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0670A]

Let it be known to all of you that we have taken under our protection, solely through fear of God and out of love for our most beloved son Peter Damian, cardinal of this Roman Church, the church of the Holy Cross of Fonte Avellana and everything belonging to that hermitage: namely, the monasteries, hermitages, and all the churches or chapels subject to it, castles, villages and estates, landed properties together with those who hold them, herds as well, and so forth. Therefore, we command all people, and by the authority of blessed Peter and by our own authority we order, that everything belonging to the aforesaid church, wherever it may be found, be guarded without injury; by no one, whether by us or by any authority, etc.

[Col. 0670B]

Given at the Lateran on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory VII.

## XXV. Letter of Gregory VII to Henry, bishop of Trent.—He explains that he rightly excommunicated Emperor Henry and asks him to assist the pope by sending troops. (Year 1076.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 375.]*

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother and fellow bishop Henry of Trent: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0670C]

We are astonished that the prudence of your brotherhood has disregarded our words and, in accordance with them, has decided to give no reply, especially since, after the synodal sentence pronounced against King Henry, your affection ought by no means to have delayed. We do not think that your diligence can be unaware, nor that any sound-minded person can doubt, that in publishing that sentence we acted under the impulse of zeal for justice and were not provoked by any desire to inflict injury. Yet if this should come into anyone’s doubt, it is clear that the reason for the matter must first be sought from us before it can rashly be believed that prejudice was created against him.

[Col. 0670D]

However the opinion may stand, and however the deed may be interpreted, we confidently promise, hoping in divine mercy, that the feast of blessed Peter shall not pass before it is made absolutely clear to everyone that he has been excommunicated with complete justice.

Therefore, we wish and admonish your brotherhood to make us certain whether you have chosen to obey God or human beings, and whether you have judged it preferable, by obeying justice, to preserve faith toward God and the holy Roman Church, rather than, by clinging to the sons of iniquity, to trample it underfoot.

We therefore ask and invite you to endeavor, as far as you can, to send soldiers into the service of blessed Peter. If you decide to send them, arrange to notify our daughter Matilda, through whose assistance they may safely reach us and, with the Lord’s favor, arrive without hindrance.

## XXVI. Letter of Gregory VII to the Germans.—He explains the reasons for the excommunication of Emperor Henry. (Year 1076.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 377.]*

[Col. 0671A]

GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops, dukes, counts, and the others in the kingdom of the Teutons who defend the Christian faith: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have heard that some among you doubt the excommunication which we imposed upon the king and ask whether he has been justly excommunicated, and whether our sentence proceeded from the authority of lawful discipline with the deliberation it required.

[Col. 0671B]

Therefore, we shall endeavor, as truthfully as we can and with our conscience as witness, to make clear to the eyes and understanding of everyone how we were led to excommunicate him—not so much to cast the individual causes, alas, which are too well known, into public view by our own outcry, as to satisfy the opinions of those who think that we rashly seized the spiritual sword, more from the impulse of our own mind than from fear of God and zeal for justice.

When we were still serving in the office of deacon, an evil and highly dishonorable reputation concerning the king’s conduct reached us. Out of respect for his imperial dignity and for his father and mother, and also because we hoped and desired his correction, we often admonished him by letter to abandon his depravity and, mindful of his illustrious lineage and dignity, to shape his life according to the conduct befitting a king and, with God’s gift, a future emperor.

[Col. 0671C]

After we had ascended, though unworthy, to the summit of the pontificate, and as both his age and his iniquity began to increase, we understood that almighty God would require his soul from our hand with all the greater strictness because greater freedom and authority had been granted to us than to others to rebuke him. We therefore urged him much more earnestly, by every means, admonishing, entreating, and reproving him to amend his life.

Although he often sent us greetings and letters, excusing himself both on the grounds that age was fleeting and fragile and because those into whose hands his care had been entrusted had repeatedly given him bad advice and counsel, he promised in words that he would readily accept our admonitions day by day. In deed, however, and by aggravating his faults, he utterly trampled them underfoot.

[Col. 0671D]

During this period, we summoned to repentance certain of his familiars, whose counsels and machinations had polluted bishoprics and many monasteries with the Simoniac heresy by introducing wolves for payment in place of shepherds. We required them both to restore to the venerable places to which they belonged the goods of the churches which they had received with sacrilegious hands through the intervention of so wicked a transaction, while there was still an opportunity for correction, and to make satisfaction to God for the iniquity committed through the lamentation of repentance.

When we learned that they despised the time granted for carrying this out and obstinately persisted in their customary [Col. 0672A] wickedness, we separated those sacrilegious ministers and members of the devil from communion and from the body of the whole Church, as was fitting, and admonished the king to expel them from his household, his counsels, and all his association, as excommunicated persons.

Meanwhile, as the conflict against the Saxons grew more serious, and as he saw that the strength and resources of the kingdom were for the most part beginning to fail him, he sent us a supplicatory letter, full of every humility. In it he declared himself very guilty before almighty God, blessed Peter, and us, and also offered prayers that, whatever had been done through his fault in ecclesiastical matters against canonical justice and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we should strive to correct by our apostolic prudence and authority.

[Col. 0672B]

He promised us his obedience, counsel, and faithful assistance in this matter. Later, too, after he had been received into penance by our brothers and legates, Humbert, bishop of Praeneste, and Gerald, bishop of Ostia, whom we had sent to him, he confirmed the same promise into their hands, swearing by the sacred stoles which they wore around their necks.

Then, after some time, when he had fought a battle against the Saxons, the king offered God such thanks and sacrifices for the victory he had gained that he immediately broke the vows he had made concerning his correction. Paying no attention to any of the promises he had made to us, he received the excommunicated into his familiarity and communion and dragged the churches back into the confusion to which they had been accustomed.

[Col. 0672C]

Struck by deep sorrow at this, although the king’s contempt for the benefit of the heavenly King had nearly removed all hope of his correction from us, we nevertheless decided that our spirit ought still to be restrained, preferring that he should hear apostolic gentleness rather than experience severity.

Accordingly, we sent him letters of admonition, urging him to remember what he had promised and to whom he had promised it; not to think that he could deceive God, whose anger, though his patience is longer, is all the more severe when he begins to punish; not to dishonor the God who honors him; and not to attempt to extend his power to the contempt of God and the insult of the apostolic See, knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.

[Col. 0672D]

Moreover, we sent him three religious men, certainly loyal to him, through whom we admonished him privately to do penance for his crimes—which, although horrible to recount, are nevertheless known to many and have been spread through many regions of the earth. On account of these crimes, the authority of divine and human laws both testifies and commands that he should not only be excommunicated until he has made worthy satisfaction, but also deprived of every honor of the kingdom without any hope of recovery.

Finally, unless he separated the excommunicated from his association, we could neither exact nor decree anything else concerning him except that, separated from the Church, he should remain in the company of the excommunicated, with whom he had chosen to share rather than with Christ.

[Col. 0673A]

Indeed, if he were willing to accept our admonitions and correct his life, we called and still call God as witness to how greatly we would rejoice in his salvation and honor, and with how much charity we would embrace him in the bosom of holy Church—as one who, appointed prince of the people and holding the reins of a very great kingdom, ought to be a defender of Catholic peace and justice.

But how highly he has valued our words, whether sent in writing or through legates, his deeds make clear. Indignant that anyone should rebuke or correct him, he could not be recalled from his crimes to amendment; rather, seized by a greater fury of conscience, he did not cease until he had caused nearly all the bishops in Italy, and as many as he could in the Teutonic lands, to suffer shipwreck with regard to the faith of Christ, forcing them to deny the obedience due to blessed Peter and the apostolic See, and the honor granted by our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0673B]

When, therefore, we saw that his iniquity had reached its height, we excommunicated him by synodal judgment for these reasons: first, because he refused to abstain from the communion of those who had been excommunicated for the sacrilegious crime of Simoniac heresy; next, because, on account of the criminal acts of his life, he was unwilling not only to undertake penance but even to promise it, having altered the faith which he had promised into the hands of our legates; and likewise because he did not fear to divide the body of Christ and the unity of holy Church.

For these faults, I say, we excommunicated him, so that we might be able, with God’s help, to recall to the way of salvation by severity the man whom we could not recall by gentleness; or, if—God forbid!—he should not even fear the strictness of discipline, at least our soul might not succumb to the danger of negligence or fear.

[Col. 0673C]

If, therefore, anyone should think that this sentence was pronounced unjustly or irrationally, let him, if he is willing to bring the understanding of sacred rules to bear, reason with us also, and patiently hear and accept not what we teach, but what divine authority teaches and decrees and what the harmonious voice of the holy Fathers indicates.

We nevertheless do not suppose that any believer who knows the ecclesiastical statutes is held by this error, so that, even if he does not dare to affirm publicly that the sentence was rightly imposed, he does not at least acknowledge it as right in his heart. Yet even if, God forbid, we bound him with such a chain without a sufficiently serious cause or in an insufficiently orderly manner, as our holy Fathers assert, the sentence is not for that reason to be despised; rather, absolution must be sought with complete humility.

[Col. 0673D]

But you, beloved [the Saxon Annalist reads: “most beloved”], who have refused to abandon God’s justice either because of royal indignation or because of any danger, disregarding the foolish claims that will be proclaimed at the end concerning execration and falsehood, stand firm like men and be strengthened in the Lord, knowing that you defend the cause of him who is the unconquerable King and glorious Victor, who will judge the living and the dead and render to each according to his work.

You too can be certain of his manifold recompense if you remain faithful and unshaken in his truth to the end. Therefore we also pray to God for you without ceasing, that he may grant you strength through the Holy Spirit in his name, and turn the king’s heart toward repentance, so that he may at last recognize that we love him much more truly than those who now serve and favor his iniquities.

[Col. 0674A]

If, however, inspired by God, he wishes to repent, whatever he may plot against us, he will nevertheless always find us prepared to receive him into holy communion, insofar as your charity shall advise us.

## XXVII. Letter of Gregory VII to all bishops, abbots, and the other faithful. (Year 1076.)

*[Hugh of Flavigny, Chronicle, in Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores VIII, 442.]*

[Col. 0674B]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the brothers in Christ—bishops, abbots, priests, dukes, princes, and soldiers—and to all who truly love the Christian faith and the honor of blessed Peter and live in the Roman Empire: greetings and apostolic blessing.

After we sent your brotherhood a letter beginning, “We give thanks to almighty God,” we learned from faithful members of the holy Church that the king is making every effort to separate us from one another and deceive us by his fraud, sometimes through spiritual persons and sometimes through secular persons.

[Col. 0674C]

Therefore, we fear that some of our brothers, being less cautious because of the permission we granted, may be deceived. For this reason, on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command that no one presume to release him from the bond of anathema until his satisfaction and repentance have been reported to us by suitable representatives of your own, so that, after jointly deciding through our legates what is equitable and pleasing to God, with every fraud removed, we may act by apostolic authority.

You, for your part, diligently strive to obtain from him such a promise and such security that we may not seem, through the simplicity of the dove, to neglect the prudence of the serpent.

If, meanwhile—which we do not desire—he should be overtaken by death, let your brotherhood not doubt that you must extend to him the medicine of absolution which true repentance and true satisfaction merit.

Given at Tribur, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

## XXVIII. Letter of Gregory VII to William, king of the English.—Concerning simony, sexual immorality, and the deposition of John, bishop of Dol, and the appointment of Owen in his place. (Year 1076.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 383.]*

[Col. 0674D]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most excellent son W., the glorious king of the English: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not doubt that it has become known to your Highness that the aforesaid bishop of the Church of Dol, which is the principal see of the province of Brittany, forgetful of his salvation and trampling upon the decrees of the holy canons, shamelessly invaded that same Church through Simoniac heresy [Col. 0675A] and has violently oppressed it for a long time.

For, having given Count Alan rich gifts, which to this day remain openly displayed as proof of his former wickedness, he entered not through the door into Christ’s sheepfold but came in from elsewhere like a thief and robber. Not content even with this crime, he added iniquity to iniquity and, considering it too little and of no account merely to be a Simoniac, hastened also to become a Nicolaitan.

For, after publicly celebrating a wedding in the bishopric which he had acquired so disastrously, he was not ashamed to take a prostitute rather than a bride, and fathered children by her. Thus, having already prostituted his spirit to the corrupter of souls through Simoniac dealings, he consecrated his body through the incest of vile lust as an insult to the devil, [Col. 0675B] so that no place might remain in him for the Creator, whom the adversary had wholly claimed for himself, bound inwardly and outwardly.

Nor did his effort toward wickedness stop there. He compounded the most atrocious crime and most shameful disgrace with horrifying sacrilege as well. For he married off his daughters, grown to adulthood from that illicit union, after assigning and alienating church estates and revenues to them as dowries, in an act of monstrous crime.

Covered with these iniquities, he nevertheless attempts, if permitted, to remain over that same Church, torn apart and scattered. For these reasons, let your Highness know that he has already been pierced by the dart of the blessed apostle Peter and, unless he repents of his crime, has been condemned by a deadly anathema.

[Col. 0675C]

Therefore, with paternal charity, we have endeavored to admonish you and briefly explain the matter, lest through ignorance you continue to offer assistance to so wicked a man lying so long in his darkness, or make yourself a participant in his crimes. Rather, by obediently submitting in a moderate manner to the apostolic See and to our admonitions, drive him away from you; or, at least, gently persuade and induce him, if you can, to look after himself at last and flee to the remedy of repentance.

For to support and assist those who persist in evil is nothing other than to provoke the Lord’s anger against oneself.

We, however, no longer able to endure the affliction of the aforesaid Church, have, with God’s inspiration, ordained and consecrated there a man of proven life and recognized piety: namely, the abbot of Saint Melanius, who, although he had come to us for other reasons which it would be lengthy to explain, was unexpectedly compelled to undertake the burden of the episcopate.

[Col. 0675D]

We trust in the Lord concerning him that, if—as we desire and have earnestly requested in many letters—he should merit the favor and support of the rulers of the earth and of good men, then, with the Lord’s cooperation, he will restore the Church to a better condition under the protection of blessed Peter.

## XXIX. Bull of Gregory VII for the church of Saint Autbert of Cambrai. (Year 1076.)

*[Balderic, Chronicle of Arras and Cambrai, edited by Leglay, p. 545, in the notes.]*

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LIBERTUS, beloved son in Christ, bishop of the Church of Cambrai, and to his successors: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0676A]

In consideration of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance, so that we may favor the rightful requests of those who pray and, with our scales of equity, assist all our beloved who are in need as far as, with God’s gift, we are able.

Therefore, in accordance with your person, we grant, concede, and confirm to the church of Saint Autbert a privilege of this kind and a decree of our authority, establishing that none of your successors, nor anyone possessing any dignity, nor anyone else, shall dare, under any pretext or guise of cause, to diminish, take away, apply to personal use, or grant to others those things which have already been donated from their own rightful property to that venerable monastery by you or by any other persons, or which in the future, with God’s mercy, may be brought to it.

[Col. 0676B]

Rather, we wish that everything which has been offered or may happen to be offered there be possessed intact and without disturbance by the clerics of that place in perpetuity. In every respect, these things are to benefit those for whose support and administration they have been granted.

All these provisions contained in the page of this aforesaid decree and command of ours, we decree must be observed perpetually both by you and by all who succeed you.

[Col. 0676C]

If, however, any bishop, cleric, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away, let him be separated from the most holy body and blood of the Lord God, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subject to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But for all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran on the Kalends of November, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory.

## XXX. Letter of Gregory VII to the Germans.—He announces that he has decided to hasten his journey to them so that he may be at Mantua on 8 January 1077. He instructs them to see that he is well received. (Year 1076.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 379.]*

[Col. 0676D]

GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and also the greater and lesser persons established in the kingdom of the Teutons: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We, unworthy and useless servants of the prince of the apostles, have resolved, with the divine assistance of mercy, to come to you. Setting aside the counsel of all our faithful, we shall hasten our departure so that we intend to be at . . . . . . . on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in accordance with your will and desire, so that, trusting in your proven faith, we may not hesitate, with pure and sincere intention, to undergo every hardship and, if necessary, the shedding of blood itself for the freedom of holy Church and the salvation of the empire.

[Col. 0677A]

It is therefore your responsibility to give advance notice concerning our reception and service to those whom your prudence recognizes as able and obliged to do so. It is also your responsibility to establish peace throughout your regions, so that nothing may impede the purpose of our intention.

The bearers of this letter will explain more fully how many and how great struggles we have had with the king’s messengers, and by what arguments we have answered their words, whatever may seem to be lacking from the letter. Just as we confidently believe you concerning what you promised to blessed Peter and to us, so we emphatically wish you to believe us concerning what they will report on our behalf.

## XXXI. Letter of Gregory VII to the Germans.—He announces that he is traveling to them against the will and advice of the Romans. He urges them to make every effort so that he can reach them. (Year 1076.)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 383.]*

[Col. 0677B]

GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, marquises, counts, and all who defend and observe the Christian faith and the faith and teaching of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, throughout the entire kingdom of the Teutons: greetings, and the blessing of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the absolution of all sins.

[Col. 0677C] I, an altogether unworthy priest, servant of the prince of the apostles, am coming to you against the will and counsel of the Romans, trusting in the mercy of God and in the true Catholic faith, prepared to undergo death for the honor of God and the salvation of your souls, so that through many tribulations we may press onward and reach rest. But you, my most beloved and most eagerly desired brothers, take the greatest care that, with God’s help, I may be able to visit you and be of benefit to you in all things. May he bless you by whose grace it was said to me at the body of blessed Peter on the day of my ordination: “Whatever you bless shall be blessed, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” Amen.

### XXXII. Gregory VII undertakes the protection of the cathedral church of Florence and confirms its property, at the request of Bishop Rainerius. (Year 1076.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 79.]

[Col. 0677D]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Martin, provost of the Church of Florence, and to the other fellow canons, and to your successors forever.

If we satisfy the just petitions of God’s servants, without doubt we observe the apostolic commands. Therefore, at the intervention of our fellow Bishop Raynerius, your bishop, we confirm and strengthen for you and your successors whatever is recorded in the charter of concession and confirmation which your Gerard—then bishop and afterward pontiff of the Roman see—made for you, as well as whatever belongs to your canonical body. This canonry, which the same bishop entrusted and subjected to the protection and defense of the authority of my most holy predecessor Pope Leo and his successors by that same charter, we likewise command to be protected and defended, so that you may remain peaceful and secure from every injury.

Thus, moved—as we have said—by your desire and petition, we receive the provost and his successors, who shall lead the canonical life, under the protection of our apostolic defense. We confirm and establish forever all the property which your canonry possesses, or shall possess, or which belongs to it: namely, estates, lands, the King’s Meadow beside the city of Florence, and the King’s Field in its entirety, with all its holdings and territories, whatever it possesses and retains in the Florentine estate, or which belongs to your aforesaid canonry; the estate of Saint Andrew with everything belonging to it; the estate of Quinto; the estate of Cintoria with all its appurtenances; and that part which Peter the primicerius appears to have usurped contrary to the canonical statutes; the parish of Exinea with its estate, holdings, all its territories, and tithes, whatever appears to belong to that parish or estate.

Furthermore, everything which Theuzo son of Lepizi contributed, for the salvation of his soul, to the church of Saint John or to the same canonry; the land of Saint Proculus in the aforesaid parish; the estate of the Lake, situated within the parish of Saint Peter at Valia, with all its adjacent and appurtenant properties; likewise the field of Randi; and also the church of Saint Peter called Cantuari, with its appurtenances, which Gerard, the venerable bishop of the aforesaid Church of Florence, bestowed upon the canonry.

Also, wherever your canonry appears to possess or hold anything, or anything appears to belong to it; and whatever Gerard the archpriest held as a benefice, and the Church of Florence itself held, both in tithes and in holdings and estates; and whatever Abbot Stephen held as a benefice. Likewise, whatever benefices belonged to the primicerii; the parish of Saint Hippolytus situated at Elsa; also the field and garden beside the church of Saint Reparata; and the estates, churches, and castle in the territory of the parishes of Saint John Major, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Cassian, from the boundaries of the ridge of the Mucelline Alps as far as the river Sieve, which Jeremiah son of Ildeprand, for the salvation of his own soul and that of his son, bestowed upon the canonry by a charter of offering.

Also the estates, houses, allotments, demesne lands, and the church of Saint Martin with everything belonging to it in the village of Bagnolo, which is known to lie within the parish of Saint Mary of Pinita, and which the men of Rufina gave to the aforesaid canonry; the church of Saint Ambrose with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary the New with its property; the castle of Scharaboni; one holding at Conciano; and whatever Imelda gave to the aforesaid canonry within the city of Fiesole, both inside and outside.

Also the estate of Petramala with everything belonging to it; the land given by Thetberga, wife of Rodulfus; and, as we said above, whatever your canonry now justly possesses, or whatever, with the Lord’s favor, it may happen to possess in the future, in any movable or immovable property, whether given by the bishop of that city or by other public or private persons, to you and your successors: all this we confirm and establish forever.

We therefore decree, by apostolic authority, that all the things contained in the charter of this command and decree of ours shall be preserved forever, both for you and for all who shall succeed you in the order and place which you occupy, and for those whose interest it may be.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this charter of our constitution, should attempt to act against it with rash audacity, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away or mourns his unlawful act through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the rights of this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

**Sign of Pope Gregory VII:** “Your mercies, O Lord, are over all his works.”

Given at Florence on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and librarian, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, namely in the year 1076 of the Lord’s incarnation, indiction XIV.

### XXXIII. Letter of Gregory VII to the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and other princes, together with all the people of the kingdom of the Teutons. (Year 1077.)

[Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicon*, in PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Scriptores, vol. VIII, p. 445.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brothers and sons in Christ, the archbishops, bishops, dukes, counts, and other princes, together with all the people of the kingdom of the Teutons who defend the Christian faith and religion: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0679D] As we informed you in our earlier letters and through the words of our legates, understanding that you had shown yourselves, as was worthy before God, defenders of justice in true obedience and reverence for the apostolic principate, and placing confident hope in your faith and counsels, we undertook a journey to you—against the will of almost all our faithful, with the exception of the most beloved and most faithful daughter of blessed Peter, namely Matilda—not only amid many hardships but also dangers. Indeed, we could have reached you if we had had a guide from your side at the time and place appointed.

But when the suspension of our departure gave the king, who was hastening into Italy, an opportunity to come to us, overcome by his humility and by his many demonstrations of repentance, we released him from the bond of anathema and received him back into the grace of communion. For the rest, we made no arrangement with him except what we judged would serve the caution and honor of all of you.

When the Lombard bishops understood that the whole matter had been reserved for a common assembly and for your deliberation, and that they could not obtain absolution for their crimes with the impunity they had hoped for, they launched against us such pride and such efforts of malice that it is sad to speak of them and abominable to hear of them. Those who ought to have been pillars in the Church of God not only occupy no place in the structure of Christ’s body but persist as its opponents and, so far as lies with them, its destroyers.

As for the king, we cannot greatly rejoice as to whether he has acted simply and obediently in the matters he promised us, especially since, because of his presence, the worst men have more boldness than fear in perpetrating iniquity against us and the apostolic see.

Meanwhile, while awaiting your counsels, we finally learned through our son Rapoto, whom we sent to you, that you wished and requested us, if it could in some way be done, to cross over to your region, and that we should strive to arrange this more cautiously with the king’s counsel and assistance. Therefore, as we instructed you, desiring to satisfy your will and counsels in all things according to God’s good pleasure, we are working through our messengers to establish and arrange this very matter with the king.

But with what intention he ought to agree with us and with you in this matter, we could not know before the dispatch of this embassy, since the king was far from us. As soon as we learn it, however, we shall not delay informing you.

Know, therefore, that this is our will and desire: either with the king’s consent, or, if it can be done despite his unwillingness, to cross over to you for the common advantage and salvation of you all. If, however, because of our sins and the efforts of evil men, this cannot be done, even while absent I shall always pray to almighty God with earnest prayers that he may strengthen your hearts and faith in every grace and virtue, and direct your counsels and actions in all things so that you may be able, with tireless courage, to defend the freedom of the Christian religion and to foresee and accomplish whatever is most pleasing to God and most useful to you for the stability and glory of your most noble kingdom.

But remain steadfast in the purpose of defending justice which you have begun for the name of Christ and for eternal reward, so that, by God’s gift, you may reach the crown of so holy and God-pleasing a struggle. We would have sent you more by letter, had we not sent such messengers to you as you may trust without hesitation. Whatever is less fully contained in this letter, and whatever our heart holds for you or toward you, we have placed in their mouths. Amen.

### XXXIV. Letter of Gregory VII to all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, kings, princes, clerics, and laypeople established in Narbonese Gaul, Gascony, and Spain, when he sent Amatus, bishop of Oloron and legate of the Holy Roman Church, into Gaul and Spain. (Year 1077.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 622.]

[Col. 0681A]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, kings, princes, clerics, and laypeople in the regions of Narbonese Gaul, Gascony, and Spain: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Most beloved brothers and sons, it is manifestly known to your prudence that from the very beginnings of its foundation the Roman Church has had this custom: to send its legates to all regions marked with the title of the Christian religion, so that through them, in its place, it might announce to all the Churches established throughout the world the admonitions of salvation and moral uprightness which the governor and ruler of that Church cannot accomplish through his personal presence, and might diligently instruct them by apostolic teaching in all things suitable to sacred religion.

Therefore we are sending to your regions the bearer of these presents, our venerable fellow Bishop Amatus, so that he may strive, with diligent vigilance and with God as author, to uproot from their foundations the vices which must be eradicated there and to plant saplings of virtue.

By apostolic authority we command you to receive him as you would receive our presence—or rather that of blessed Peter—and, out of reverence for the apostolic see, whose messenger he is, we order you in all things to obey him and listen to him as to our own face or the oracles of our living voice. For it is written: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16).

Act, therefore, prudently and religiously, and show yourselves obedient to God and to Saint Peter in all things, so that, through the intercession of the prince of the apostles, you may be found worthy to attain the glory and happiness of both lives.

### XXXV. Gregory VII undertakes the protection of the monastery of Saint Michael at Pisa and confirms its property and rights. (Year 1077.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 361.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel situated at Pisa, and to his successors who shall regularly be appointed there forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to aid with benevolent compassion those who abound in pious religion and to grant the minds of petitioners their assent with eager devotion. From this, above all, we shall undoubtedly receive a reward from God, the creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have unquestionably been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you, beloved son, have requested that we strengthen with apostolic privileges the monastery over which, with God as author, you are recognized as presiding, out of reverence for blessed Michael the Archangel, in whose honor that venerable place was founded, we have decided to grant your prayers with benevolent concession.

Accordingly, receiving the aforesaid place and everything belonging to it, as well as the community of brothers serving God there, into the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church, we grant by apostolic authority the privilege of apostolic protection which, through blessed Peter and by God’s arrangement, we have assumed from that time onward. We confirm and strengthen for the same venerable monastery whatever it now justly possesses in cultivated or uncultivated lands, or in any movable or immovable property, and whatever, with God’s help, it may acquire in the future, so that these things may remain undisturbed and inviolate for the common use of the brothers, under your administration and that of your successors, with suitable distribution.

By the same authority of this document we also decree that those who, renouncing the world through pious devotion and love of the heavenly homeland, wish to enter there regularly for the monastic life may be received and retained by the abbot who shall be in office at the time and by the other brothers, without any person’s opposition.

Furthermore, we establish and, in accordance with what blessed Pope Agapitus prescribed for the City, decree by firm command that no one oppose faithful Christians who wish to be buried in the same monastery, or forbid Mass to be sung there in any way, or presume to remove or in any manner take away alms which anyone, living or dead, has assigned there or may assign there for the love of God.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away or mourns his unlawful act through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the rights of this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Florence on the fourth day before the Ides of August, through the hands of Cono, cardinal priest, in the year 1077 from the Lord’s incarnation, and in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, indiction XV.

### XXXVI. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Savior of Septimianus. (Year 1078.)

(UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 83.)

[Col. 0682D]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Azo, abbot of Saint Savior, founded in the place called Septimo, and to his successors who shall regularly be appointed there forever.

Mindful of divine grace toward us, we clearly recognize how benevolently we ought to yield to upright desires and just petitions, and how we ought to extend the administration of the dispensation entrusted to us for the benefit of many, just as we desire to receive a reward from him for the profit bestowed from above, from whom, by the free goodness of his gifts, we receive the talents entrusted to us.

Therefore, most beloved son, as your devotion and that of your brothers requested, we receive—as did our predecessors—the aforesaid monastery over which, with God as author, you are recognized as presiding, into the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church. Through this charter of our decree, to strengthen its condition with God as author, we grant you the privilege of apostolic protection.

We confirm everything that has already been given to this venerable place by any persons from their own rights, or that shall in the future, by God’s mercy, be bestowed upon it, whatever kind of possessions or property they may be, whether movable or immovable. Finally, we confirm all that it now legally possesses and all that, with God’s help, it may acquire in the future.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we decree and establish that no king or emperor, duke, marquis, count, castaldus, prelate, person endowed with any dignity, or any secular or ecclesiastical person, great or small, dare tear the aforesaid monastery away from the stability of its order and security, or invade, plunder, or remove its property through greed, violence, or the oppression of unjust domination, whether by impiously applying it to his own uses or by granting it to others under the appearance of pious causes as an excuse for his avarice.

Rather, we will and decree that everything which has been offered there or may happen to be offered there shall be possessed forever, inviolate and without any disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, and shall in every way benefit those for whose support and administration it was granted.

We further establish that, when an abbot dies, no one shall be appointed there through any trickery or intrigue except one whom the brothers of that monastery have chosen in accordance with the fear of God, preferably from the same community, if a suitable person is found. If no one suitable for this administration can be found among them, let them seek a father and master from elsewhere; he shall be consecrated according to the custom of the former abbots by no one other than the Roman pontiff, and shall be subject to the judgment of no one other than that same Roman pontiff.

The consecrations of churches and the ordinations of clerics belonging to the aforesaid monastery shall be received from the bishop in whose diocese it lies, provided that the bishop himself has been canonically ordained, has not at that time been excommunicated by the Roman Church, and performs the ordination freely. But if any of these conditions should prevent it, the abbot may freely go to whichever Catholic bishop he prefers for the consecration and ordination both of places and of persons; and that bishop shall be permitted canonically to perform whatever the abbot requests of him.

We decree that all the things contained in the charter of this command and decree of ours shall be observed forever, both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the order and place which you occupy.

If any king, emperor, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it with rash audacity, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away or mourns his unlawful act through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the rights of this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran on the fourth day before the Ides of January, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and librarian, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, and in the year 1078 from the Lord’s incarnation, indiction I.

### XXXVII. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII for the monastery of Holy Cross of Kimperlegium. (Year 1078.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, old edition, vol. IV, p. 553.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Holy Cross situated in Brittany, in the village called Avantot, and to his successors living there regularly, and to the monks forever.

Brittany, as some of our people testify, was entrusted to the protection and defense of the holy Roman Church not only by emperors but also by the inhabitants themselves. But our predecessors in this matter, as in many others, were so negligent that the love and promise of apostolic protection, and the former intention of our devotion, came on both sides to injury and almost, so to speak, to “washing away” [*ablutionem*]—[sic].

Therefore, with God as author, we are striving to bring back to memory those things which have hitherto been neglected, and we are applying ourselves all the more diligently to the salvation and honor of your homeland because, as we have already said, we recognize that your people, out of devotion, have bowed their necks to the patronage of blessed Peter. Although, beloved son, we owe Brittany universally whatever you request from us, we nevertheless extend more particularly our protection and assistance for the liberation and defense of your monastery.

Accordingly, in keeping with the tenor of your petition, we receive under the protection and defense of the apostolic see the monastery over which, with God as author, you are recognized as presiding, together with the whole island called Guedel, or by another name Bella Insula, and with its other possessions which appear justly to belong to it. By the decree of our present authority we grant, concede, and confirm privileges of the following kind:

No king, emperor, prelate, person endowed with any dignity, or anyone else shall dare, under any pretext or occasion, diminish or remove anything that has already been given to this venerable place by any persons from their own rights, or that shall in the future, by God’s mercy, be bestowed upon it, or apply such property to his own uses, or grant it to others under the appearance of pious causes as an excuse for his avarice.

Rather, we will that everything which has been offered there or may happen to be offered there shall be possessed forever, inviolate and without any disturbance, by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, and shall in every way benefit those for whose support and administration it was granted.

We decree that all the things contained in the charter of this command and decree of ours shall be observed forever, both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the order and place which you occupy.

If any emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it with rash audacity, and, having been admonished once and again, and for a third time after suitable intervals, does not come to his senses and satisfy the aforesaid monastery, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken away or mourns his unlawful act through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and let him be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the rights of this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of Peter, cardinal priest and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, indiction I.

### XXXVIII. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII for the monastery of Saint Benignus of Dijon. (Year 1078.)

[PERARD, *Collection of Pieces Serving the History of Burgundy*, p. 192.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son Gerento, abbot of the monastery of Dijon, and to his successors who shall regularly be appointed forever.

In view of divine mercy, we have undertaken the care of the venerable Church and bear the concern of apostolic governance, so that we may favor the just petitions of suppliants with attentive kindness. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Abbot Gerento, meeting your petitions with grateful assent, we have decided, with the Lord as author, to provide for the liberty and peace of your monastery.

Accordingly, we receive the monastery itself under the protection of the apostolic see. When you, now abbot of that place, die, or when any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery or violence except one whom the brothers have chosen by common consent, according to the fear of God and the rule of Saint Benedict, preferably from the same community, if a suitable person is found.

If no one suitable for this administration can be found among them, let them seek a father and master from elsewhere, and provide for him to be consecrated and ordained by the bishop of Langres, provided that this bishop enjoys the grace of the apostolic see and is willing to perform the ordination canonically. If anything prevents this, the elected abbot of the same monastery may either have recourse to the apostolic see or receive consecration, the ordination of clerics, and the other matters belonging to a bishop from any religious bishop he chooses.

We also establish that divine offices shall not be forbidden in your monastery by the bishop or ministers of the Church of Langres, but shall be celebrated continually, unless the brothers ought to cease for the same reasons which were defined by the determination of Benedict, prelate of the apostolic see. The peace and liberty among your monks which that same prelate confirmed by his decree we decree, by the authority of blessed Peter and our own, shall remain inviolate forever.

If any clerics or laypeople wish to enter your monastery, you shall be permitted to receive them without any opposition, provided that they have not been personally excommunicated or specifically interdicted.

We also confirm to you all your churches, whatever you now possess or whatever, with God’s favor, you may canonically possess in the future. We establish that no cleric shall dare to minister in them without your consent. Whenever a minister must be appointed in any of them, you shall choose a suitable person, in the presence of the bishop; the bishop shall entrust him with the care of souls, and thus he shall be accountable to you for temporal matters and to the bishop for spiritual matters.

If anyone should presume to minister in those churches contrary to this arrangement, we suspend him from the exercise of his office.

To the cloister in which your monastery is situated we also grant the liberty and immunity which the illustrious King Robert is known to have bestowed, so that it shall remain forever free and secure from every invasion and act of violence by the duke and his men. No one shall presume to take away or receive anything at all from the stream which divides the estate of the castle and of the saint (*castri sanctique causam*; the construction is uncertain).

We also confirm to you forever the church of Saint Germanus of Laré, where the nuns reside, and we prohibit under anathema that those nuns should ever remove themselves from subjection to the Church of Dijon. Rather, they shall always be governed through your care.

We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions and retain what has been taken, diminish them, or trouble them through presumptuous harassment. Rather, they shall be preserved wholly intact and shall in every way benefit those for whose support and administration they were granted.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, recognizing this charter of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it and, after being admonished once and again, fail to amend the matter by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor and acknowledge himself or herself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed. Let that person be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the rights of this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Gregory, bishop of the holy Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1078 from the Lord’s incarnation, indiction I, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Gregory, Pope VII.

### XXXIX. Letter of Gregory VII to the Gauls. — He summons them to a synod to be held for settling the disputes between the kingdom and the priesthood. (Year 1078.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, vol. XX, col. 381.]

[Col. 0687B]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the archbishops, bishops, and abbots established in Gaul who appear to remain within the bosom of the holy Roman Church: greetings and apostolic blessing.

How many oppressive tribulations, storms of persecution, and burdens of danger the universal mother, the holy Roman Church, has suffered in these times is for the most part hidden from your knowledge, though it can scarcely be believed. You yourselves recognize what counsel and assistance she has received from you, her sons, with the compassion that was owed.

What we can scarcely remember without grief has become such that the charity of many toward her grows cold, so that the very things foretold in the Gospel appear in a certain way to have been specially fulfilled: “When iniquity has abounded, the heart of many will grow cold” (Matthew 29 [as printed]).

What else, then, should I say except that you, who either sluggishly neglected or fearfully refused to bring comfort to your mother in such distress, have shown yourselves unworthy of the name of sons and alien from the bowels of charity?

What sane person would not feel shame—or rather, how great a grief—when considering that the persecutors of the Christian religion, through such a conspiracy of faction and with every effort, have labored to fulfill the cruelty of their spirit, not only by pouring out their possessions but even by handing themselves over to death, while no one, or scarcely a very few, among the supporters of justice has cared either to undertake bodily labor, endure the loss of possessions, or bring aid from his goods to his mother the Church?

However your fraternity may have conducted itself, blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, protecting us from the hands of adversaries and the violence of persecutors, has until now defended justice in our hands according to the testimony of our conscience. Strengthening our human weakness by the power of his might, he has permitted neither the allurements of promises nor the terrors of those who harass us to turn us toward iniquity.

To him, therefore, we offer immense thanks: preserving us unbroken until now amid the storm of distress, he has led us by free paths toward a certain hope of tranquility, so that neither our own conscience nor the examination of religious persons who know us may reproach us for having acted against the principal intention of justice.

For the future, brothers, so that the cause of the quarrels and discord which has long been carried on between the kingdom and the apostolic see may, with the Lord’s favor, obtain a suitable conclusion, we invite and summon you, by these letters and on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to the synod which we intend to celebrate in mid-November.

We also wish your fraternity to know that, so that you may come to us safely and, with God’s protection, return to your homeland, our faithful have received security by oath from the leading men who are at the court of the said King Henry.

We desire, therefore, with you and strengthened by divine assistance, to discuss how we may confirm peace and, with God’s help, recall the schismatics to the bosom of holy mother Church.

### XL. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII for the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Year 1078.)

[GATTULA, *History of Cassino*, p. 254.]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, and to his successors.

It seems necessary and useful that matters which come before us and reach the conclusion of their determination [Col. 0688C] should be made known in writing for the memory of future generations, and should also be secured by the authority of the apostolic see. For when we were at Capua, the clergy of that city complained, saying that the church of Saint Angelus, which had formerly belonged by right to the church of Capua, had passed by an unjust exchange into the ownership of the monastery of Saint Benedict. Not allowing this complaint to remain unexamined, we carefully investigated through discerning and truthful men whether what had been given in exchange for that church seemed sufficient. These men, diligently investigating what we had charged them to examine, proved that what had been given in exchange—namely, the church of Saint John situated within the city of Capua—had possessed more property [Col. 0688D] and ornamentation. Erbeus, then archbishop of that same city, also testified that he had unquestionably recognized this fact. Accordingly, once appropriate testimony had been brought forward and every uncertainty in the dispute removed, we judged that both the archbishop and the clergy of Capua should rest from this matter forever and should thereafter bring no lawsuit concerning the exchange already mentioned.

Therefore, at the request of your fraternity, judging by this present privilege that this arrangement is firm and permanently stable, we decree that in the aforesaid place of Saint Angelus the religious community of monks shall serve almighty God under the care and governance of the abbot of Monte Cassino. To this church we grant, concede, and confirm a privilege of this kind, establishing [Col. 0689A] that no emperor, king, prince, bishop, anyone endowed with any dignity, or anyone else shall dare, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, to diminish, remove, or appropriate for his own use the things already donated to that venerable place by any persons from their own lawful possessions, or those which, by God’s mercy, may hereafter be granted; nor shall anyone grant them to others, as though for pious causes, to excuse his own avarice. Rather, we wish everything that has been offered there, or that may be offered by anyone, to be possessed for all time, unimpaired and without any disturbance, by those who succeed you in your office and place, so that it may in every way benefit the uses for which it has been granted, namely, their support and administration.

We decree, therefore, that all the provisions contained in the page of this our precept and decree shall be preserved forever. But if any emperor, king, prince, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt with rash presumption to act against it, then, after having been admonished once, twice, and three times at suitable intervals, if he does not repent and does not make satisfaction to the aforesaid church, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity he has committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken from it, or mourns his unlawful deed through worthy penance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ [Col. 0689C] and, at the final judgment, be subjected to a more severe punishment.

But for all who justly observe these provisions toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

“Your mercies, O Lord, are over all your works” (Psalm 144).

Given at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of December, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian; in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the second indiction.

## XLI. Letter of Gregory VII commending Berengar, given after the Roman Council. (Year 1079.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 621.]

[Col. 0689D]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of blessed Peter: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We make known to you all that, by the authority of God almighty, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we have anathematized all who have presumed to inflict any injury upon Berengar, son of the Roman Church, whether against his person or against any of his possessions, or who have called him a heretic. After he had remained with us for as long as we wished, we are sending him back to his home, together with our faithful man named Fulco.

## XLII. Letter of Gregory VII to the Germans. (Year 1079.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 383.]

[Col. 0690A]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all the archbishops residing in the Teutonic and Saxon kingdoms, and to all the princes and all the great and small who are not excommunicated and are willing to obey: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since we recognize daily what a great danger to the holy Church is arising from your dispute and dissension, it has seemed good to us—and it has seemed good to our brothers assembled in council—to labor with all our strength, so that suitable envoys, distinguished both for religious commitment and for knowledge, might be sent from the side of the apostolic see to your regions. They would gather together in your lands religious bishops and laymen who love peace and justice and are suitable for this work. With the grace of the Lord going before them, on the day and at the place appointed by those men, they themselves and those whom we must still associate with them would either establish peace or, having first learned the truth, exercise canonical censure against those who are the cause of such great dissension.

But because we know that some, fashioned by diabolical instigation, inflamed by the torches of their iniquity and led by greed, desire discord rather than peace, both to create it and to witness it, we have established in this synod, as in the previous one, that no person of any power or dignity, whether small or great, prince or subject, [Col. 0690C] may presume to resist our legates or, when they have reached you, oppose the making of peace. Nor, afterward, against their prohibition, may one party dare to rise up against the other. Rather, until the day appointed by them, all shall observe a firm peace without any pretext or fraud.

Whoever attempts with any presumption to violate these arrangements of yours, we bind with the bond of anathema; and by apostolic authority we bind him not only in spirit but also in body and in every prosperity of this life, and we take victory from him in arms, so that at least in this way they may be put to shame and crushed by a double affliction.

## XLIII. Letter of Gregory VII to King Rodulf. (Year 1079.)

[Bruno, *On the Saxon War*, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores V, 378.]

[Col. 0690D]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to King Rodulf and to all who together with him defend the Christian religion: greetings and apostolic blessing.

That the kingdom of the Germans, hitherto the noblest among all the kingdoms of the world, is now being devastated, thrown into confusion, and destroyed by fires, slaughter, and plunder—how great a sorrow this has planted in my heart, how constant a groaning it causes within me—is known to that one alone who searches and tests the hearts of all human beings.

For embassies from Henry are now repeatedly brought to me, both through his own envoys and through relatives, princes of other lands, and kinsmen. Sometimes they promise every obedience; sometimes they seek to influence me by various devices, striving with all their might to bring this about: that they may bend me to their side according to their desire. But because, on both sides, Roman gravity and apostolic gentleness compel me to walk along the middle path of justice, I must devote every possible effort to discerning, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, true justice from false justice and perfect obedience from feigned obedience, and to bringing the matter to its end in an established order.

These matters, and others besides, my envoys will testify and explain more effectively in person than these letters, if, with God’s favor, they reach you safely.

## XLIV. Letter of Gregory VII to King Rodulf and the Saxons—He reports that he has arranged for his legates to inform them of what he decreed in two synods; then he urges patience and instructs them to make the best provision for the archbishopric of Magdeburg. (Year 1079.)

[Col. 0691B]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to King R. and to all residing with him in the kingdom of Saxony, bishops as well as dukes, counts, and both great and small: absolution from sins and apostolic blessing.

Since Truth itself says that the kingdom of heaven belongs to all who suffer persecution for the sake of justice (Matthew 5), and the Apostle cries out that no one can be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Timothy 2), do not, my sons, grow faint in the warlike fury that has now harassed you for so long. Do not, through the lies of any deceitful person, doubt our faithful assistance. Rather, labor more and more quickly to bring the struggle to an end: to defend ecclesiastical truth and to preserve the freedom of your nobility. On the other side, strive to ascend and set yourselves and your bodies like a wall before the house of God.

Whatever has now been established in the two assemblies of our synod concerning King R. and H., whatever has there been defined concerning peace and harmony in the kingdom, including the oaths, you can learn most clearly from our letters and from our legates, unless they have been taken captive. If anything still remains, you have it, so to speak, ready to hear from the bishops of Metz and Pavia and the abbot of Augsburg, who remain with us awaiting the conclusion of the matter; when they themselves come to you, they will explain it.

Finally, we do not want you to be unaware that, with all the urgency required—both through the constancy of our prayer and through the gravity of our office—we do not hesitate to provide for true necessity and to foresee what must be provided.

We have heard that a dispute has arisen concerning your archbishopric of Magdeburg over the correction of certain sons of that Church, who seek to acquire secular dress and honor. By every means, in obedience to almighty God, Saint Peter, and us, forbid them to seize the summit of governance for themselves as a place of condemnation. Appoint, as justice and order require, a dispenser worthy of God, with our consent and apostolic blessing and through the common election of all good men, both clerics and laymen. You yourselves know that, in the appointment of bishops, the neglect of the institutions of the holy Fathers has produced the blood that is now being shed and, unless remedies are provided, is still giving birth to worse errors by nourishing those that preceded it.

## XLV. Letter of Gregory to all the faithful throughout the Teutonic and Italian kingdoms. (Year 1079.)

[Marianus Scotus, *Chronicle*, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores V, 561.]

Gregory the pope, servant of the servants of God, to all throughout the Italian [Col. 0692B] and German kingdoms who render due obedience to blessed Peter: apostolic blessing.

If there are priests, deacons, or subdeacons who lie under the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of Saint Peter, access to the church until they repent and amend their conduct. But if any prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you dare to listen to their ministry, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will curse your blessings.”

## XLVI. Letter of Pope Gregory VII to the monks of Monte Cassino. (Year 1079.)

[Gattula, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, II, 149.]

[Col. 0692C]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons in Christ, the monks of Saint Benedict: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have heard something that we cannot mention without the deepest sorrow: certain men, sent by Prince Jordan at the devil’s prompting, entered your treasury and, with unheard-of audacity, carried away certain things entrusted to you. In this deed we can accuse you and your abbot of excessive negligence and a cowardice that must be sharply punished, and we ought to be moved more gravely against you, were we not restrained by the charity with which we have always loved you. Indeed, it would seem more tolerable to us for the villages and castles of Saint Benedict [Col. 0692D] to be handed over to plunder and pillage than for a holy place, famous and venerable throughout all Christendom, as we believe, to be subjected to the danger of such disgrace.

Therefore, since we cannot tolerate the offense of this audacity to remain unpunished, especially since we perceive that your place has been violated and that, following the example of this crime, worse things could happen to you, we admonish you not to celebrate the divine office in the church of blessed Benedict. Rather, uncover all the altars that are inside, and cause everyone to recognize the danger of such a violation. For if, in the church of Saint Peter, sprinkled with human blood, the divine office is not celebrated without careful reconciliation, much more does this deed, [Col. 0693A] committed—[the manuscript reads *pernicio* (sic)]—in the church of blessed Benedict, require appropriate expiation.

You, therefore, earnestly beseech almighty God to deign to grant us consolation in our sorrow of mind over this matter and to instruct us by the means that are fitting for restoring your dignity in every respect.

## XLVII. Letter of Pope Gregory VII to the monks of Monte Cassino. (Year 1079.)

[Gattula, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, II, 149.]

[Col. 0693B]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of the monastery of Monte Cassino: greetings and apostolic blessing.
