Recently, compelled by the violence of the sacrilege inflicted upon this most reverent place, we imposed an interdict upon the services of your church because of the outrage committed. But since the solemnity of the Lord’s Ascension, venerable throughout the whole world, is now approaching, and since we do not wish such a religious place to be deprived of the office of worship on so great a feast because of anyone’s crime, we have decided to absolve both you and that place from the interdict. Therefore, led by apostolic gentleness, we restore to your devotion both the ministry of the church and permission to celebrate the rites of religion.

We also wish and ask your charity to remember us and pour out prayers to the Lord for us; to supplicate daily the Ruler of all things for the state of the holy Roman Church; and diligently to remember and strive to pray to almighty God with an affection of love both for enemies and for friends. Also pour out prayers for the man who violated so holy a place, famous throughout the world, so that God may give him a penitent heart and convert him to himself in such a way that he may deserve to obtain God’s grace in this life and in the life to come.

The following additional words immediately follow in the manuscript:

This, however, happened through … the bishop of Rosella; for that same bishop had entrusted a considerable sum of money to this place. Prince Jordan then sent soldiers and ordered them to bring that money to him. But the brothers replied: “The money entrusted to Saint Benedict we do not give to any living person, but we place it upon his body; let whoever dares take it away do so.” The soldiers, however, removed the treasure from the altar and carried it to the prince. As soon as he had received it, that same prince, the author of so great a crime, lost his sight and remained so until death.

## XLVIII. Letter of Gregory VII to Peter of Albano and Odelric of Padua. (Year 1079.)

[Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle*, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores VIII, 450.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ and fellow bishops, Peter of Albano [Col. 0694A] and Odelric of Padua: greetings and apostolic blessing.

There are many—although we do not believe them—who have begun to complain about your legation, suspecting that you wish to proceed otherwise than we have commanded. They allege that one of you will act too simply, while the other will not act with sufficient simplicity. You must therefore take the greatest care to extinguish both suspicions. This will easily come about with God’s help if you always keep our instructions before the eyes of your mind and presume to accomplish nothing other than what we are known to have impressed upon you and commanded, not only in bare words but also in writing.

We wish you to presume to exercise no judgment concerning the cause of the kings or of the kingdom, nor concerning the elected bishops of Trier, Cologne, or Augsburg, nor concerning any of those who have received investiture through a lay hand. Let your greatest concern be this: if the king agrees with you concerning the arranging of a conference, the establishment of peace in the kingdom, and the restoration of the bishops to their sees, announce these matters quickly to us, either through yourselves or through reliable envoys, so that we may be able to send there, at the appointed time, as many and such persons as will be sufficient, with God’s help, to determine so great a matter together with you.

Meanwhile, present yourselves to both parties as common to both and, insofar as lies within you, free from every stain of suspicion, with the assistance of divine grace; always uphold justice and in no way favor either side, as you have our example. For after the judgment of this great matter was entrusted to the hand of blessed Peter, we have intended nothing else, as you can testify, than to walk along the path of justice. We have bent the sincerity of apostolic discernment toward no party, yielded to no promises or threats, and, with God protecting us, we trust that we shall never act otherwise.

Furthermore, we specifically charge you concerning the abbot of Reichenau (Augia), who, when he recently came to the threshold of the apostles, was not only captured but also had someone tyrannically substituted in his place. See to it that, after that usurper has been expelled, the goods of which he was deprived are restored to him. Once he has been fully reinstated in what he lost, if anyone has a charge against him, he will be ready to answer before our judgment. For he ought not to be judged by anyone else, since it is known that he was consecrated by me at the apostolic see. Certainly, it was a grave presumption to lay hands upon one protected by so great a privilege.

But if that usurper, contrary to our prohibition, refuses to restore his property to the aforesaid brother, immediately pronounce against him, as against a rebel and usurper, a sentence of excommunication by apostolic authority.

Whatever you do, and whatever happens to you, always take care to commit it to writing and send reports to us frequently. May almighty and merciful God, from whom all good things proceed, through the merits of blessed Mary, Mother of God and our Lady, and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, deign to defend you from every evil and lead you into all truth, so that whatever you do may be accomplished happily according to the fear of God and the benefit of the holy Church.

Above all, remember most diligently the bishop of Worms. Although he had long been expelled from his Church and had therefore come to Rome to obtain the assistance of the apostolic see, he not only gained nothing for himself but has now fallen into a worse situation.

Meanwhile we greet you and ask you to remember us, who remember you, before God.

## XLIX. Letter of Gregory VII to Hugh, bishop of Die—He congratulates him on the restoration of peace to his Church. (Year 1079.)

[Hugh of Flavigny, *Chronicle*, in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores VIII, 421.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Hugh, bishop of Die: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your fraternity should know that, because divine clemency has restored peace to your Church, we rejoice no otherwise than over the tranquility and progress of our own Church or of the holy Roman Church. Let this also remain firmly fixed in your mind: almighty God, whom you strive to serve faithfully with your whole heart, will suitably establish temporal peace for you and, as a good rewarder, repay you with eternal peace in accordance with your merits.

Concerning the disagreement that you have reported between the archbishop of Lyon [Col. 0695C] and the abbot of Cluny, let your affection know that it weighs heavily upon us; but because the quarrel is between religious men, we grieve greatly. Their harmony could and should have benefited many; there is no doubt that from their dissension great destruction has arisen and will arise for very many. Therefore, you must remain vigilant and must take care to bring religious men to them, and in our name to confer with the aforesaid parties concerning harmony. Finally, whoever among them does not accept justice according to your counsels, let no one doubt that we shall be gravely moved against him, setting aside all partiality toward persons.

But since you were unable to hold a council usefully in the regions previously designated, we think it appropriate that you diligently find a suitable place where, once a synod has been assembled, the case of the archbishop of Reims may be carefully examined. If suitable accusers and witnesses are found who canonically prove what is charged against him, we want you to deliver without hesitation whatever sentence justice dictates. Otherwise, if the persons brought forward are such that they cannot reasonably be accepted, then, since a shameful reputation concerning him has filled not only Gaul but also almost all Italy, let him, if possible, take six bishops whose lives are not marked by infamy and defend himself before them; thus, once cleared, let him remain in peace in his Church and in his proper dignity.

Furthermore, concerning the man whom you reported to have entered the Church of Chalon through secular power—that is, through royal investiture—we decree by apostolic authority that he is excluded from all governance of that Church and from all hope of it. If, after this sentence of our prohibition, he should aspire to the dignity of its governance, he will certainly experience what the sword of blessed Peter can do, and no confidence in ecclesiastical governance will be left to him forever.

To restrain also the unlawful attempts of many who, with obstinate minds, do not fear to set God aside and display their pride, imitating the devil, who, not content with what was granted him, unlawfully strove for higher things and justly lost what he had, we want you, in all your councils, acting in our place, to excommunicate all who presume to oppose the synodal decree of the apostolic see concerning this matter and who have received investiture of Churches from the hand of any layman. Thus, at least through these threats, brought back from their ambitious hopes, they may not climb from elsewhere like thieves and robbers into the Lord’s sheepfold, but, invited from the dwelling-place of religious men, may enter through the door as good and suitable shepherds.

We also admonish you to let the sorrow and calamity of the Church of Langres penetrate your compassionate heart and, together with our brother the archbishop of Lyon, assist it in its great dangers by whatever means you can. Above all, accomplish this: pass a just sentence against the dean, who has seized nearly all the offices of that Church through the worst ambitions, and ensure that those offices are thereafter administered purely by religious and suitable men.

## L. Letter of Pope Gregory VII to Anselm, abbot of the monastery of Bec—On Anselm’s very celebrated reputation. (Year 1079.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 619.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable abbot of Bec: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since the good fragrance of your fruits has wafted even to us, how worthy a thanksgiving do we offer to God, and how wholeheartedly we embrace you in the love of Christ! For we firmly believe that, through the examples of your labors, the Church of God is being advanced toward what is better, and that through your prayers and those of men like you she can, with the mercy of Christ assisting, be rescued even from present dangers.

You know, brother: if the prayer of a righteous person has prevailed before God (James 5), how much more that of the righteous? Indeed, it has prevailed—or rather, without doubt it will obtain what it asks (1 Kings 17). We are also compelled by the authority of Truth itself to confess this: “Knock, and it will be opened to you; ask, and you will receive” (Matthew 7:7). Knock simply; ask simply for those things also that please him. The door is simple; the giver wishes simple things, things that accord with him, to be requested. In this way it will be opened; in this way you will receive; in this way the prayer of the righteous will be heard.

Therefore, we wish you and your community to pray to God continually, asking him to rescue his Church and us, who, though unworthy, preside over it, from the present oppressions of heretics, and to lead them, having abandoned their error, back to the way of truth.

A certain pilgrim did indeed bring a complaint before us concerning one of your converts: “The Lord is just; he has loved justice; his countenance has seen equity” (Psalm 10:8). Imitate your Lord; imitate your teacher, from whom you have the teaching of life. We also command you to do justice for him in the presence of our beloved son Hubert—and, as we understand, your friend.

## LI. Letter of Gregory VII to Henry, bishop of Liège. (Year 1080.)

[Note: [Col. 0697D] See Book VII, letters 13 and 14 of the *Register*.]

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 625.]

It has reached us that you, our brother and fellow bishop Henry, bishop of Liège, while coming to the threshold of the apostles, were stripped of your possessions by Count Arnulf and, to increase his wickedness, were compelled at sword-point to swear that you would never reclaim what had been taken from you and that you would obtain from us pardon for him for so great a crime.

Having learned of the insult inflicted upon you—or rather upon blessed Peter—we grieved greatly, declaring that your fraternity cannot be bound by any bonds of an oath, since you swore under such atrocious compulsion. Therefore, by apostolic authority we absolve you, so that you may not appear bound by this oath before your own conscience or anyone else’s. Moreover, relying upon that same authority, lest this become an example encouraging other wicked men to dare worse things, we earnestly command our brother the bishop of Verdun and the other faithful of blessed Peter in that region to oppose him as a tyrant and trampler of the Christian religion, and to pursue him everywhere and by every means, both with carnal and spiritual weapons, as far as they can, unless he makes worthy satisfaction.

We therefore wish the aforesaid bishop first to associate with him as many bishops and other priests as he can and summon that enemy of God to make worthy satisfaction. But if he is unwilling to repent worthily and restore what he took, then, after granting him an interval of fifteen days, let him be deprived of entry into the church, and let the injury to blessed Peter be avenged in the manner stated until satisfaction is made.

## LII. Letter of Gregory VII to Aymeric, viscount, and the people of Narbonne. (Year 1080.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 621.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, the viscount Aymeric [Col. 0697D], and all the people of Narbonne: we would gladly send you an apostolic blessing if we did not know that you had incurred guilt against the apostolic see. But once we learn that you have withdrawn from that excommunication and have rendered obedience to your father, the archbishop Dalmatius, we shall send you the blessing of blessed Peter.

As your prudence knows, the enemy of the human race possessed your Church for a long time as though it were his own property, after it had been invaded by evil and simoniacal pastors. But, grieving over your need and danger, we judged that a good and lawful pastor should be placed over you—not from elsewhere, but entering through the door, that is, through Christ (John 10:2). For those who enter by another way, that is, without Christ, are thieves and robbers, appointed for this purpose: to slaughter and destroy the Lord’s flock (ibid., 10). Thus, confirmed by the blessing and authority of the apostolic see, through the example of his praiseworthy conduct and the instruction of his preaching, he will be able, with the Lord’s help, to correct whatever has been committed among you through the fault and injury of evil bishops, and, as a good shepherd, commend you most devotedly to the supreme Shepherd.

We therefore admonish your prudence to receive honorably and with goodwill the man whom the Roman Church has lawfully appointed for you, and to offer him obedience and reverence as your spiritual father and archbishop, remembering the Lord’s saying when he commends his faithful: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

Nor do we want you to be unaware that if any one of you—which we do not expect—should refuse him obedience, he will, at his own peril, provoke the anger of God and the vengeance of blessed Peter, and we shall confirm by apostolic authority the sentence of excommunication promulgated by our legates at the synod of Toulouse. But whoever is obedient will rejoice in the grace and blessing of that same apostolic see.

## LIII. Letter of Gregory VII to Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, and Eusebius, bishop of Angers—He orders them to defend the priest Berengar against the injuries of Count Fulco of Anjou and others. (Year 1080.)

[Francis de Rove, *Life, Heresy, and Penance of Berengar*, 75.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, and Eusebius, bishop of Angers: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have heard, brothers, that the count of Anjou, instigated by certain people who are hostile to our dearest son Berengar, has been inflamed with hatred against him. Therefore we command your fraternity to order that count, in our name, not to presume to disturb the aforesaid man any further. Not only this: against all his enemies and those who trouble his possessions, assume our role in bringing him assistance. We command this by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Farewell, and do not in any way disregard what I command.

## LIV. Privilege of Gregory VII for the monastery of Saint Zeno at Pisa. (Year 1080.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, III, 364.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Leo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Zeno in the city of Pisa, and to his successors.

In view of the mercy from above, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the concern of apostolic governance so that, with attentive kindness, we may favor the just wishes of those who petition us, and especially so that we may provide the protection of our authority for establishing the tranquility of venerable places.

Therefore, in accordance with your request, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the monastery over which you are recognized as presiding. By the decree of this present privilege, we grant and confirm everything that it has hitherto appeared to possess lawfully or that, with the Lord’s generosity, it may justly acquire hereafter. Moreover, with the consent of the bishop of Pisa, we grant the tithes of all the lands that you cause to be cultivated for your demesne. We add that it shall be lawful for you, without anyone’s opposition, to accept the offerings of the faithful, to bury in your cemetery those who have bound themselves to be buried there, and also to admit anyone who, renouncing the world, wishes to come to your way of life.

Confirming all these provisions as they are written, so that your aforesaid monastery may securely, peacefully, firmly, and without disturbance possess them throughout the succession of ages, we establish by apostolic authority that no king, emperor, bishop, person endowed with any authority, or anyone else shall dare, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, to diminish, remove, or appropriate for his own use the things already donated to that venerable place by any persons from their own lawful possessions, or those which, by God’s mercy, may be granted in the future; nor may anyone grant them to others, even for supposedly pious causes, to excuse his own avarice.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts with rash presumption to act against it, then, after having been admonished once, twice, and three times by suitable witnesses, if he does not repent and does not make satisfaction to the aforesaid Church, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity he has committed. But unless he restores what he has unjustly taken from it or mourns his unlawful deed through worthy penance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ and, at the final judgment, be subjected to strict punishment.

But for all who justly observe these provisions toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran on the fourth day before the Nones of March, by the hand of Peter, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and librarian, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the fourth indiction, 1081.

## LV. Letter of Gregory VII to Landric, bishop of Mâcon, concerning the confirmation by him of the privileges of the Church of Cluny. (Year 1081.)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 21.]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Landric, bishop of Mâcon: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We are compelled to wonder greatly how your fraternity, persuaded by clerics, as we have heard, proved disobedient when the privileges of the Church of Cluny were being confirmed by the bishop of Albano, who was carrying our legation—especially since, even if he had wished to impose something upon you somewhat inconsiderately, which we do not believe, whatever it might have been, you ought to have endured it out of reverence for the Apostolic See.

Therefore, bearing with this fault on account of the good life and pastoral vigilance with which you labor on behalf of the Church entrusted to you, we command you that, having summoned some of the better monks of the Church of Cluny, you come to a common place between Mâcon and Cluny, so that in their presence you may confirm the aforesaid privilege and, thus restored to your episcopal office, may be able, with the Lord’s help, to console your people.

For the rest, we admonish your fraternity with the paternal affection with which we embrace you: do not henceforth remain credulous toward the wickedness or frivolity of your clerics, but yield rather to the counsels of myself, who love you—not what belongs to you—than to theirs. If you do this, know for certain that we will in no way permit the Church entrusted to you to suffer prejudice.

Meanwhile, may you and the abbot of Cluny remain in peace, without any disturbance or discord, until such a dispute among religious persons can be settled before the bishop of Die, our vicar, with the counsel of religious men; or, if that cannot be done, until we, after summoning both parties and carefully examining the case, are able, with God’s grace assisting us, to impose a suitable conclusion.

But the clerics who, driven by the spirit of pride, stirred up a disturbance against our legate, the bishop of Albano, and insultingly attacked the archbishop of Vienne as he was returning from Cluny, after taking away his belongings, are to make satisfaction at Cluny, barefoot before the altar of Saint Peter, and, their conduct thus amended, are to be absolved.

No date.

## LVI. Letter of Gregory VII to the canons of Saint Martin of Tours. (1081)

[MABILLON, *Annals of Saint Benedict* V, 176.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of Saint Martin of Tours.

Because we have heard that you not only disobeyed our legates and your archbishop, but even expelled him, and because we have learned that you were excommunicated by them on account of your fault, we have not dared to send you greetings and the apostolic blessing; and we ourselves grieve more than you do that you have proved unworthy of this.

For if you cared for the salvation of your souls, you would have had no intention at all of presuming such an act, nor of remaining so long in impenitence after the crime.

Therefore, admonishing you with paternal address, we command you on behalf of blessed Peter, after making worthy satisfaction for so great a crime, to arrange that our aforementioned brother, the archbishop, be restored with honor to his Church; and thereafter, showing him the paternal obedience and reverence that are fitting, do not in any way refuse to obey him.

We also command you to restore in full both the property of that archbishop and that of the canons of Saint Maurice; and, henceforth showing due obedience to our legates, to take vigilant care to keep yourselves apart from Count Fulk, who is excommunicated, and from all excommunicated persons.

But if you are unwilling to obey even these salutary commands, we confirm against you the sentence of anathema and decree that you are subject to apostolic vengeance.

## LVII. [Note: See Gregory VII, Book IX, chapter 29. See also Castellus, in the *Historical Memoirs of the West*, pp. 871, 874, and in the *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 126.] Letter of Gregory VII to Richard, cardinal of the Roman Church and abbot of Marseille.—He orders him to absolve the excommunicated monks of Saint Saturninus. (1082)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 656.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., venerable cardinal of the holy Roman Church and abbot of Marseille, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

It has come to our attention that those monks who had taken possession of the church of Saint Saturninus without the permission of their own abbot, and had afterward abandoned it because they were compelled to do so by the command of the abbot of Cluny, were excommunicated by your fraternity after they had departed in order to make satisfaction.

If this is so, we are not a little astonished at your prudence. Therefore we wish and command you to release them from the bond of excommunication and, for the future, to take the greatest care not to pronounce such a sentence so lightly against religious men.

For what else is it than to disparage authority by using the license of authority indiscriminately or rashly against any honorable persons? We admonish you again and again to attend to this vigilantly and provide for it carefully in the future.

## LVIII. Letter of Gregory VII to Hugh, bishop of the Church of Die, and Richard of Marseille, cardinals. (1082?)

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 186.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to U., bishop of Die, and R., cardinal and abbot, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

The archdeacon of Aix, A. (Arnald), complains that Archbishop W. (William), A. (Amatus), our legate, and also the bishop of Bazas have risen against his church and have seized and violently invaded certain churches of that bishopric. The archbishop of Auch and Bishop Amatus have likewise informed us by letter that, according to the people of Aix, those same churches have belonged from ancient times to the property of the Church of Oloron.

Therefore we charge your fraternity that, if both of you can do so, or otherwise one of you, hear their case in a suitable place; and, after carefully investigating the canonical arguments on both sides, impose a conclusion pleasing to God and consistent with justice.

## LIX. Letter of Gregory VII to the clergy, the viscount Aymericus, and the entire people of Narbonne. (1082)

[CATEL, *Memoirs of the History of Languedoc*, p. 782.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, to Viscount **AYMERICUS**, and also to the entire people of Narbonne.

We would gladly send you the apostolic blessing if we did not know that you had incurred guilt against the Apostolic See. But once we have learned that you have recovered from that excommunication and are showing archiepiscopal obedience to your father Dalmatius, we will send you the blessing of blessed Peter.

As your prudence knows, the enemy of the human race possessed your Church for a long time as though it were his own property, after it had been invaded by evil and simoniacal pastors. But, grieving over your need and danger, we judged that a good and lawful pastor ought to be placed over you, one who entered not from elsewhere but through the door—that is, through Christ. For those who enter by another way, that is, without Christ, are thieves and robbers, appointed for this purpose: to slaughter and destroy the Lord’s flock.

This man, therefore, confirmed by the blessing and authority of the Apostolic See, will be able, through the example of his praiseworthy conduct and the instruction of his preaching, with God’s help, to correct whatever has been committed among you through the fault and injury of wicked pontiffs, and, as a good shepherd, to commend you most devotedly to the supreme Shepherd.

We therefore admonish your prudence to receive with honorable goodwill the man whom the Roman Church has lawfully appointed for you, and to show him obedience and reverence as your spiritual father and archbishop, remembering the Lord’s saying in which he commends his faithful: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me.”

For we do not wish you to be unaware that if any one of you—which we do not expect—should refuse him obedience, he will call down upon himself the wrath of God and the vengeance of blessed Peter to his own peril; and we will confirm by apostolic authority the sentence of excommunication promulgated by our legates at the Council of Toulouse. Whoever, however, is obedient will rejoice in the grace and blessing of that same Apostolic See.

## LX. Gregory VII confirms all the privileges of the Church of Palermo. (1083)

[COCQUELINES, *Collection of Roman Pontifical Bulls*, vol. II, p. 58, from Rocco Pirro, *Sacred Sicily*, vol. I, col. 70.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ **ALCHERIUS**, archbishop of Palermo, greetings.

Contemplation of the supreme Apostolic See, whose care we bear, although unworthy, admonishes us willingly to grant, insofar as justice permits, the requests of all holy Churches that seek to be defended or strengthened by privileges of our authority; and, when the rulers of those Churches seek the marks of their honors, which they are known to have possessed from ancient times, we should, by the Lord’s generosity, more readily grant our assent.

Above all, however, we judge it necessary that Churches still inexperienced—namely, those newly coming to the faith or returning to it—receive the assurance of our favor and of apostolic protection [lacuna]. Through the Lord’s mercy they have escaped the darkness of unbelief and the snares of error and, with his help, may be able to grow more and more in the strength of Christian faith and the greatness of religion. [Note: Something appears to be missing.]

Therefore, dearest brother Alcherius, because you are recognized as presiding, by the Lord’s appointment, over the Church of Palermo—which was once noble and famous but afterward, on account of the demands of sin, was reduced to the power and unbelief of the Saracens, and which has now truly been converted to the Christian faith through the labor and perseverance of our son, the glorious Duke Robert, at the Lord’s prompting—we gladly grant, bestow, and confer upon you the support of a privilege of apostolic liberality, both in consideration of so just a request and out of love for the aforementioned duke, whom we know to desire and seek this.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we confirm to that Church, and through it to you, whatever dignity it is proved to have held in ancient times: that is, all its suffragan bishoprics, or, if any have been destroyed and others established in their place, or are to be established with the Lord’s assistance, so that they may return to the former authority of your aforementioned church. In addition, we confirm whatever property it is known to have possessed from ancient times through royal generosity and lawful grant, and whatever it is known to have added to those possessions—provided that this does not contradict justice.

Accordingly, by the decree of our present authority, restraining the presumption of all present and future persons, we forbid and decree that no king, emperor, bishop, person endowed with any dignity, or anyone else dare take away or diminish anything that has already been given to that Church by anyone from his own lawful property, or that may be granted to it in the future.

Moreover, we grant your fraternity the use of the pallium according to the ancient custom of your Church, so that you may use it during the solemn celebration of Mass only on these festivals: the Nativity of the Lord; the feast of Saint Stephen; the Epiphany; the Lord’s Supper, on Easter Day; the Ascension; Pentecost; the four feasts of Saint Mary; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feasts of the Apostles; Saint Lawrence; the feast of All Saints, celebrated on the Kalends of November; the day of your ordination; the feasts of the saints whose relics adorn your Church; and at the ordination of bishops or other clerics, and at the consecration of a church.

We therefore exhort your fraternity to make the honor of so great a dignity—which is truly an adornment of the entire priestly order—accord with your conduct; and to provide both outward and inward beauty and grace to your person. For these are the signs of the pallium and of such a garment: that you love the Lord with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.

Although the adornment of all virtues is necessary for the use of the pallium, charity, which surpasses them all, must inseparably accompany one who is distinguished by dignity.

Therefore, so that you may imitate every instrument of goodness, let your life and knowledge be a model and rule for your subjects, so that if anything blameworthy is found in them through human weakness, it may be corrected toward uprightness and sincerity by regard for your holy conduct. Strive to regulate the rights of administration in correcting faults in such a way that you burn with zeal for uprightness but do not exceed the measure of moderation.

In short, to express much in few words, whatever you find in the sayings of the holy Fathers, judge it suitable for your own edification and for that of those subject to you, so that, instructed by your teaching, they may be able with you to reach the seat of the Good Shepherd and receive the happiness of eternal life.

Given at Rome, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Benjamin, acting in the place of Peter, priest, cardinal, and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the year 1083 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, indiction V.

## LXI. Privilege of Gregory VII for the Church of Saint Quintinus. (1083)

[The Works of Guibert, edited by D’ACHERY, p. 600.]

**GREGORY** to his beloved son in Christ **YVO**, provost of the Church of Saint Quintinus, situated in the diocese of Beauvais, and to his successors who are to be regularly appointed.

In view of the mercy from above, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance so that, with attentive kindness, we may favor the just desires of those who pray, and, with the balance of equity, may assist all who are in need as far as we are able, with the Lord’s gift.

Therefore, at the intervention and request of our brother Guido, bishop of Beauvais, founder of the aforementioned church, granting your petition, we receive under the protection and defense of the holy Apostolic See the place over which you are recognized as presiding—namely, the Church of Saint Quintinus the martyr.

To it, by this decree of our present authority, we grant, concede, and confirm privileges of the following kind: we decree that no king or emperor, bishop, person endowed with any dignity, or anyone else dare, under any pretext or appearance of a cause, diminish or take away, apply to his own uses, or grant to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his avarice, anything that has already been given to this venerable place by the aforementioned bishop or by any other persons from their own lawful property, or that may in the future, by God’s mercy, be bestowed upon it.

Rather, we wish all that has been offered there, or may happen to be offered, whether by you or by those who succeed you in your office and place, to be possessed perpetually, undiminished and without disturbance, and to serve in every way the needs of those for whose support and governance it has been granted.

Namely, etc., followed by an enumeration of all the possessions.

Given at the Lateran on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, by the hand of Peter, priest, cardinal, and librarian of the holy Roman Church, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, that is, in the year 1083 from the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction VI.

## LXII. Bull of Gregory VII for the monastery of Saint Mary of Pinerolo. (1083)

[GUICHENON, *Genealogical History of the House of Savoy*, Proofs, vol. III, p. 16.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son **ARNULPH**, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary established at Pinerolo, and to his successors who regularly enter upon the office, forever.

Religious desires and just petitions ought to receive fulfillment through the zeal of kindness and the gift of benevolence, so that, while the effect of the administration undertaken through spiritual authority is carried out, and while the affection of protection is extended to venerable places, the merit of divine recompense may thereby increase, since in conferring a benefit charity has been no less present than power.

For this both grants authority to the endeavors of good men as they advance in time and makes the work itself, the fruit of perfection, acceptable to God.

Therefore, considering the equity of your petition, we receive under the protection of the holy Roman and Apostolic See the aforementioned monastery of Saint Mary, over which you appear to preside, dearest son and aforementioned abbot, together with everything belonging to it. This is done at the intervention of the most beloved daughter of Saint Peter, the countess Adelaida, with her sons, who founded and established this venerable place from her own resources for the redemption of her soul and those of her parents.

By this present privilege of apostolic authority we fortify it and decree that it remain perpetually strengthened. We grant and confirm to that monastery and to its Catholic abbots forever, both in churches and in villages, fields, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and in everything that it now lawfully possesses or may in the future possess by any just means [possess], that all these things, under apostolic protection, in the right and property of the aforementioned monastery and under abbatial governance, remain always undiminished for the common use of the brothers serving God there.

We decree that no one prohibit the burial of the dead there, according to what blessed Pope Gregory promulgated to Agapitus, bishop of the Old City, without prejudice to the lawful custom of its bishop and of holy Mother Church.

Likewise, in this same decretal document we decree and establish that, when the abbot of the aforementioned monastery dies, the abbots of the monasteries of Fruttuaria, Bremen, Saint Savior of Turin, Saint Michael of Chiusi, and any other religious men who may be in those regions shall assemble. In their presence the brothers shall, by common consent, elect as abbot someone from the congregation of that same monastery, if they are able to find a suitable person.

But if they cannot find among their own members someone suitable for this governance, let them elect from elsewhere a person whom the sacred canons and monastic rule do not oppose. If the election is good, let it be approved by the aforementioned abbots; but if their prudent judgment rejects it, let the brothers proceed to another suitable person.

Finally, an abbot elected according to this procedure and with this precaution, after receiving, according to custom, the rule and responsibility of governance, shall be approved without contradiction by whatever secular authority is then present there. Nor shall permission to oppose him be protected by the power of any lord, unless perhaps the election of some person is rejected by a number of religious men.

Concerning the abbot’s consecration and the brothers’ common life, we decree as follows: if the bishop in whose diocese the monastery lies is religious in ordination and life, let him perform the ordination without charge. Otherwise, the abbot shall seek the bishop of Asti, observing the same religious discipline, for the ordination of himself and his monks. If that bishop too is found lacking such religious discipline, the abbot shall have permission to approach the bishop of Albenga.

But if, through the working of sins, he too should appear to have been appointed contrary to religion, the aforementioned abbot shall have free permission to approach the Apostolic See, so that he may receive from the Roman pontiff the honor and commands concerning his own ordination and that of his brothers.

All these things contained within the boundaries of the same parish: the church of Adreio; the Church of Saint Saturninus, which is above the Loire; the Church of Saint Peter of Monte Foleti; whatever Robert of Monte-Contorio gave to the monastery of Vendôme and his son Bertrannus granted; and the Church of Saint John, which is above the Loire.

Nor shall anyone be permitted to excommunicate or place under interdict the churches subject to the aforementioned place, wherever they may be, except openly for faults, and only when the abbot and brothers of Vendôme, canonically admonished by the bishops concerned, have refused to correct them.

If anyone wishes to bring a legal case against that place of blessed Peter concerning any property, let neither the abbot nor the brothers answer him before he has consulted the Roman pontiff, because whatever is decided or alienated without our judgment or that of our successors shall be invalid.

Moreover, we wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, and to be attached to this confirmation of ours, that Theodoric, bishop of Chartres, in whose diocese the aforementioned monastery of Vendôme is known to be situated, sent his letter to Pope Clement, asking him to strengthen that monastery by his authority in such a way that none of his successors after him would be permitted to take away or diminish the property of that place, excommunicate it, place it under interdict, exercise any authority in that place, or dare to trouble or disturb its ruler or brothers in any way. Pope Clement graciously granted this request, and we have judged it worthy to grant it by our authority as well.

But if anyone should violate this command of ours, unless he repents and makes satisfaction to the Roman Church, let him know that by apostolic authority he has been struck with perpetual anathema, separated from the body of the holy Church, and handed over to the devil with the impious.

Whoever, however, is a preserver of and obedient to this confirmation of ours and to apostolic authority, may he enjoy the blessing and grace of almighty God; may he remain humble amid prosperity and secure amid adversity; and, fortified by divine mercy, may he be able through blessed Peter to enter the heavenly kingdoms and rejoice with Christ forever.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace, in the month of April, indiction XIV.

## LXIII. Letter of Gregory VII to the monks of Conques and Figeac.—He unites the abbey of Figeac with that of Conques in such a way that thereafter one father would be over both monasteries. (7 January 1084)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Collection*, XIV, 664.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers in Christ dwelling in the monasteries of Conques and Figeac, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

After laboring long and greatly in the examination of your dispute, we understood that the place of Figeac ought to be subject to the monastery of Conques and joined to it as a limb to its head, according to the arrangement of those who built those places.

But because each abbot had received his appointment by the authority and command of the Apostolic See, providing for peace and concord on both sides, we adjudicated that both places should be governed by duly appointed abbots, on this condition: if Stephen, abbot of Conques, should die first, Ayrald, abbot of Figeac, should succeed him, and both he and the monks of Figeac should thereafter recognize the monastery of Conques as their head; and, just as they are to be subject to one abbot, so they are to make their profession to one monastery, namely Conques.

But if the abbot of Figeac should die first, we nevertheless adjudicated that the Church of Figeac be united forever to the monastery of Conques, and that, every dispute and controversy having been quieted, it be entirely subject to one abbot alone, namely the abbot of Conques. Let this be firm and unshaken with perpetual stability, so that, when the present abbot of Figeac dies, the abbot of Conques shall be elected by the common congregation and shall preside over both places according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

We therefore admonish and forbid by apostolic authority that anyone act contrary to the tenor of this decision or presume to oppose it in any respect; and, since provision has been made beneficially and prudently, we order that it remain in force. [Note: At the Council of Narbonne, held in 1096, this controversy was debated again and settled in such a way that each place was to have a cardinal—that is, its own abbot. See below the letters of Urban II on this matter.]

But if anyone—which we do not expect—should attempt to oppose our decision, then, if he is an abbot or bishop, he shall be subject to the peril of his own order; if he is a monk or layman, he shall without doubt be excommunicated.

[Note: The anonymous author who wrote the history of the monastery of Figeac, edited by Baluze, recounts the cause of the dispute in vol. II of the *Miscellany*, p. 298. At the end he says: “After Lautard, William succeeded at Figeac; he long proved victorious in overcoming his enemies. Accused of simony—a plague that had already been condemned by the last Pope Leo and was vigorously pursued by Gregory VII, his successor—he reluctantly abandoned the abbey, leaving the place vacant for the introduction of a legitimate shepherd. But the monks of Figeac, choosing as their legitimate abbot Lord Hugh of Cluny, warned the men of Conques that, having cast aside their simoniacal abbot, they should in the customary manner submit to their legitimate abbot. But those men, indignant, not only failed to reform but, doing many things and devising more lies, attempting to raise the head to the tail and the tail to the head, became so much worse that, in the manner of Judas, they caused the men of Figeac to be handed over with a kiss and expelled from their own monastery, and they cast out from themselves, contrary to the custom of all Christendom, Ayrald, abbot of Figeac, to whom they had been subjected by apostolic authority.”]

Given at Rome, on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, that is, in the year 1084 from the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction VII.

## LXIV. Letter of Gregory VII to all the faithful.—He explains that he is involved in these evils because he refuses to allow the Church to be reduced to servitude. (1084)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 628.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful in Christ who truly love the Apostolic See, greetings and the apostolic blessing.

It has come to your knowledge, dearest brothers—it has, as we believe—that in our time what is said in the Psalmist’s question has been renewed: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise empty things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm IV, 1).

For the princes of the nations and the chief priests, together with a great multitude, gathered against Christ, the Son of almighty God, and against his apostle Peter, in order to extinguish the Christian religion and spread heretical depravity.

But, through God’s mercy, they were unable to bend those who trust in the Lord toward their impiety by any terror, credulity, or promise of worldly glory. For they raised their hands against us, conspiring wickedly for no other action than this: we did not wish to pass over in silence the danger threatening the holy Church, and we resisted those who are not ashamed to reduce that same bride of God to servitude.

Throughout all lands, even poor women are permitted to take a husband lawfully according to the law of their homeland and their own will. But the holy Church, which is the bride of God and our mother, is not permitted, according to the desire and detestable custom of the impious, to cleave lawfully on earth to her bridegroom according to divine law and her own will.

For we must not allow the sons of the holy Church to be subjected to heretics, adulterers, and invaders as though to fathers, and to be branded by them as though with adulterous disgrace.

From our legates you can learn, with the clearest light and truthful report, how many and varied dangers and unheard-of crimes of cruelty have arisen from this. And if you truly grieve and are saddened by the ruin of the Christian religion and its disgrace, and wish to extend a helping hand to it, you can receive sufficient instruction from those men, once your hearts have been inwardly touched by genuine sorrow.

They are most faithful to blessed Peter, and each of them, in his own order, is numbered among the foremost members of his household. No terror or promise of temporal goods has been able to separate them in any way from fidelity to him and from defending him, or to remove them from the embrace of holy Mother Church.

But because, as your fraternity knows, although unworthy and a sinner, I am divinely told through the prophet: “Upon a high mountain” (Isaiah 57:7), and the rest; and again: “Cry out, do not cease” (Isaiah 58:1), whether I wish it or not, setting aside all shame and also fear or earthly affection for anyone, I evangelize, I cry out, I cry out and cry out again, and I announce to you that the Christian religion and the true faith, which the Son of God, coming from heaven, taught us through our fathers, having been turned into a perverse secular custom, has, alas, in deep sorrow, almost come to nothing. Having lost its ancient color, it has fallen into derision not only by the devil but also by Jews, Saracens, and pagans.

They observe their own laws, although at this time those laws are useful for no one’s salvation of soul and, unlike our law of the eternal King, are not attested and strengthened by frequent miracles—as they believe. We, however, drunk with love of the world and deceived by vain ambition, putting every religion and honesty behind greed and pride, appear lawless and almost foolish, because we do not possess, nor even hope for as we ought, the salvation and honor of the present and future life as our fathers did.

And if there are any who fear God, although they are exceedingly rare, they fight in some fashion for themselves, not with ready will for the common salvation of their brothers. Who are there, or how many are there, who for fear or love of almighty God, “in whom we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28), labor so earnestly or struggle even to the point of death as secular soldiers do for their lords, or even for their friends and subjects?

Behold, many thousands of secular men run daily into death for their lords. But for the heavenly God and our Redeemer they not only do not run into death; they even disdain to endure the hostility of certain men.

And if there are any—indeed, by God’s mercy there are, although very few—who strive, for love of Christian law, to resist the impious face-to-face even unto death, they are not only not helped by their brothers as is fitting, but are even regarded by the imprudent and less discerning as madmen.

But because these matters and others like them specially threaten us, we tell you of them so that, with God’s gift, we may be able both to uproot vices from the hearts of our brothers and to plant virtues in them. We ask and beseech you in the Lord Jesus, who redeemed us by his death, to investigate carefully and understand why and how we suffer the tribulations and distresses inflicted by the enemies of the Christian religion.

For from the time when, by divine arrangement, Mother Church placed me—very unworthy and, God as my witness, unwilling—on the apostolic throne, I have labored with the utmost care so that the holy Church, the bride of God, our Lady and mother, might return to her proper dignity and remain free, chaste, and catholic.

But because this displeases the ancient enemy entirely, he armed its members against us so that he might turn everything in the opposite direction. Therefore he has done against us—indeed, against the Apostolic See—as much as he was unable to do from the time of the emperor Constantine the Great. This is not very surprising, for the nearer the end approaches, the more vigorously he strives to extinguish the Christian religion.

Now, dearest brothers, listen carefully to what I tell you. All who are reckoned by the Christian name throughout the entire Christian world, and who truly know the Christian faith, know and believe that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is the father of all Christians and the first shepherd after Christ, and that the holy Roman Church is the mother and teacher of all Churches.

If you believe and hold this without doubt, then I, whatever sort of brother and unworthy teacher of yours I may be, ask and command you by almighty God: help and succor your aforementioned father and mother, if you desire through them to have the forgiveness of all your sins and blessing and grace in this world and in the future.

May almighty God, from whom all good things proceed, always enlighten your minds and make them fruitful through love of him and of your neighbor, so that you may deserve, through certain devotion, to make your aforementioned Father and Mother your debtors, and to reach their fellowship without shame. Amen.

## LXV. Privilege of Gregory VII for the Church of Saint Sophia of Benevento. (1084)

[*Anecdota Ughelliana*, 491.]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of the Lord, to our beloved son in Christ, **MADELMO**, venerable abbot of the monastery of Holy Wisdom, coeternal with the Lord Father, built within Benevento in the place called the Old City, and to his successors who are to be regularly appointed in the same monastery, forever.

Since it is an apostolic duty to provide, insofar as our ability permits, salutary care for the interests of all the Churches of the Lord, we ought nevertheless, with unremitting vigilance and devout solicitude, to devote more attentive care to the worship of venerable places and to those who devotedly serve the Lord. Therefore, most excellent son, since in the fervor of holy devotion you asked us [Col. 0710D] to admit and receive your aforesaid monastery under the protection of the Apostolic See, and to confirm by the charter of our privilege whatever it now appears justly to possess in that church, or may hereafter be able to acquire, we most willingly grant your petitions, since a ready assent is owed to just requests and, insofar as possible, a prompt disposition to pious desires.

Accordingly, by the decree of this constitution of ours and by the edict of apostolic liberality, in accordance with the privileges of our predecessors, we grant, confirm, and perpetually [Col. 0711A] strengthen to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Sophia the Virgin, and to you, our aforesaid beloved son, and to your successors who shall be regularly and justly appointed, everything that the aforesaid church of your venerable monastery presently possesses, or shall thereafter justly acquire under divine and human law in perpetuity: whether churches, houses, lands, vineyards, gardens, olive groves, meadows, fields, woods, estates, or castles; likewise male and female servants; and all its movable, immovable, and self-moving goods and possessions; whatever it has acquired, or shall be able to acquire, through the generosity, donation, or grant of religious persons by lawful and praiseworthy endeavor; and, in short, whatever has been granted and confirmed to it by the decrees of pious emperors or princes.

Although there are also the chapel in Pantano called Saint Benedict; another, Saint Vitalis, with all its appurtenances; another [Col. 0711B], Saint Michael the Archangel, called “at Olivola,” together with all its appurtenances; in Paletria, one chapel of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle and Martyr; an estate on the hill; the estate of Muriano; houses at Petra Strumina; woods; the estate of Lapillo; the inheritance of Bato; in Curtiano, a chapel in honor of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles; in Cereto, the chapel of Saint Martin the Bishop, with all its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Sylvester the Confessor at Corneto, in the county of Capua; in the place called Biniano, the chapel of Saint Mary, Virgin and Mother of the Lord our God; in Bibino, the church of Saint Marcianus; at the Beletro River, below the city of Ascoli, the church of Saint Desiderius, together with the entire inheritance outside it; in the territory of Cannae, the church of Saint Julian; [Col. 0711C] in the county of Trani, the estate of Pazano with all its olive groves; in the county of Siponto, a fishery; in the county of Lesina, a fishery; at Cajazzo, an estate at the mill; one estate at Lania; Saint Rose of Sessa with all its estates; in the territory of Capua, Saint Reinerus and Saint Robertus with their territories; in the Campo Marini, in the territory of Tremons, Saint Adiutor beside the Volturnus River with its lands; in the territory of Capua, Saint Stephen of Strada with its territories; also, at Castello Magno, the church of Saint Magnus with all its territories; and the church of Saint Angelus at Altissimo, above the Biferno River, in the territory of Campo Morano, with the inheritance of that church, [Col. 0711D] which is two miles in length; likewise the church of Saint John with all its appurtenances at Casa Pollucis; the church of Saint Peter in the territory of Loreto, together with all its appurtenances; the castle called Becclo, with the church of Saint Marcianus and of Saint Nicholas the Bishop; Saint Maurus; in Curfiano, the village called Leo Cubante; in the city of Alife, the church of Saint Mercury with the other churches belonging to it; at Ripa Longe, in the city of Arole, the church of Saint Mercury; Saint Peter at Mortita, with all its appurtenances; Saint Stephen of Lucore; Saint Stephen of Fromari; Saint Angelus at Plesco; Saint Angelus of Atriano; Saint Angelus at Palumbara; Saint Gregory of Lescle; Saint Martin of Ventecano; Saint Peter; Saint Mary [Col. 0712A] of Aliperga; Saint Nicholas of Pazano; Saint Marcellus at Tommano; Saint Mary at Calisi; Saint Mary of Regina, with all their appurtenances; at Eliceto, Saint Ephrem with its territories; Saint Marcianus of Parituli; and Saint Mary of Sableta; Saint Mary in the village of Geldoni, with all their appurtenances.

Furthermore, by the authority of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors, in their entirety, all offerings of men and of the deceased that have lawfully come to the monastery itself by testament or even without a testament. Let that same monastery remain perpetually under the protection, dominion, or jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, free and immune from subjection to every other Church and undisturbed by every other jurisdiction. We also decree that your monks shall be secure from every interference by secular office and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, quiet in the observance of the holy Rule, and bound on no occasion to be subject to anyone except the Roman and Apostolic See, to which the place belongs by right. They shall choose from among themselves, according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, whatever abbot they wish. If a suitable man is lacking among them, they shall receive another useful and religious man, with the counsel of the Roman Pontiff, to be blessed and consecrated by him.

They shall also receive the consecrations of their churches and the ordinations of the monks or clergy belonging to the aforesaid monastery from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated, provided that those bishops have been canonically ordained and perform the ordinations without payment. If either of these conditions is lacking, the abbot, with the permission and authority of the Roman Pontiff, may freely go to whichever Catholic bishop he wishes for the consecration and ordination of both places and persons. [Col. 0712C]

We have therefore decreed that all these things contained in the charter of this precept and decree of ours are to be preserved in every respect and forever. If any emperor, duke, marquis, count, prince, or judge, or anyone invested with any dignity, of whatever rank or condition, whether great or small, knowingly attempts to act against this constitution of ours, or consents to such an attempt, or becomes its supporter, and, after being admonished once, twice, and a third time at suitable intervals, does not humbly satisfy the Church by restoring what he has unjustly taken from it, let him fall from the dignity of his power and honor; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; and let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ until he repents.

But for all who observe the matters written above, let there be absolution and remission of all their sins, joy and exultation, gladness and peace on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; and in this world let them receive the fruit of good action, so that in the future they may find the rewards of eternal peace before the strict Judge. Farewell.

Given at Salerno on the third day before the Ides of December, by the hand of Gregory, [Col. 0713A] deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the Lord Pope Gregory VII, but from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1084, in the eighth indiction—successfully, successfully.

### LXVI. Letter of Gregory VII to Altmann, Bishop of Passau

*(Fragment—1073–1085.)*

*[Life of Altmann, Acts of the Saints for August, vol. II, p. 374.]*

Because I believe that with a sincere heart you love, for God’s sake, the honor and freedom of the holy Church, I wish and command you to take the greatest care, together with your clerics and with those laymen who appear suited to this purpose, that the Bride of Christ may no longer be treated as a slave.

### LXVII. Letter of Gregory VII to Altmann, Bishop of Passau

*(Fragment—1085.)*

*[Life of Altmann, Acts of the Saints of August, vol. II, p. 374.]*

[Col. 0713B]

…that he restore priests who have fallen into fornication to their former rank, if they have truly repented; but if they are negligent and useless, that he reject them entirely.

### LXVIII. Letter of Gregory VII to the Bishop of Rouen  
*Concerning those who sell churches or ecclesiastical benefices*

*(Fragment—1073–1085.)*

*[Decretum of Gratian, Cause I, Question 3, chapter 2.]*

If anyone, whether giver or receiver, has obtained the churches of God or ecclesiastical benefices—which are indeed called prebends—through the intervention of money, whether he has bought them by giving or sold them by receiving, he is not excluded from the perdition of Simon. But if he persists, let him be punished with perpetual damnation. For whoever wishes to serve God under the guise of religion, if he receives anything, loses his merit and is deprived of the benefice he has received. Therefore, by the force of reason, he is compelled to restore what he unjustly received and not to retain whatever he accepted for the sake of shameful profit.

### LXIX. Letter of Gregory VII to Wimund, Bishop of Aversa  
*Whatever the custom may be, it must yield to the truth*

*(Fragment—1073–1085. [Note: [Col. 0713] Whether this fragment should rightly be attributed to Gregory VII is doubtful. Jaffé.])*

*[Decretum of Gratian I, distinction 8, chapter 5.]*

If perhaps you oppose custom, you must heed what the Lord says: “I am the truth and the life.” He did not say, “I am custom,” but “the truth.” And certainly—as we may use the words of blessed Cyprian—every custom, however ancient and however widespread, must yield entirely to the truth; and a practice that is contrary to the truth must be abolished.

### LXX. Letter of Gregory VII to the Spanish Bishops  
*Concerning those who confer holy orders in exchange for gifts*

*(Fragment—1073–1085.)*

*[Decretum of Gratian, Cause I, Question 3, chapter 1.]*

We have heard what we ought to have heard, beloved ones, but what we certainly did not wish to hear: namely, that there are some professed holders of holy orders who, in exchange for the giving or receiving of gifts, seize for themselves the churches of God or their benefices. We are greatly astonished that you have not already corrected this crime severely. For both parties must rightly be rebuked and removed from the thresholds of the holy Church: both the one who bestows gifts in order to obtain the Church and the one who presumes to accept something in order to enter the Church. The former presumes to buy the house of God; the latter to sell it. I would say that this crime is no different from sacrilege, since what ought to have been done freely, voluntarily, and through sacred deliberation is made conditional upon a monetary agreement. Therefore, dearest brothers, carefully reject acts of this kind, forbid them as invalid, and do not hesitate to strike those who resist your commands with the appropriate bond of anathema. [Col. 0714B]

### LXXI. Privilege confirming the possessions and immunities of the monastery of Hirsau, which is received under the protection of the Apostolic See, with the obligation of an annual census

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Cocquelines, Complete Collection of the Summaries of the Pontifical Bulls, II, 59.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son William, abbot of the monastery of Saint Aurelius at Hirsau, situated in the diocese of Speyer, and to his successors forever.

Since the Apostolic See ought, through the general providence of pastoral governance, to guard and provide for the salvation and security of all the children of the Church, it must receive with greater eagerness and diligence the vows of pious intention [Col. 0714C] and religious devotion, and commit them to salutary effect, so that it may graciously respond to the petitions of good endeavors and firmly establish, by the solidity of its authority, those institutions founded for the praise and glory of the divine name.

Therefore, rejoicing in the praiseworthy desire of our beloved son Adalbert of Calw, we have decided to heed the prayers humbly directed by him to the Apostolic See and have effectively granted what he religiously requested. Inflamed by love of eternal reward, he recently restored what had been lost and handsomely repaired the monastery anciently built by his ancestors on his estate called Hirsau; then, adding many possessions and revenues for the use of the brothers serving God there, he enlarged it more generously. Lest anyone’s audacity thereafter presume to diminish or violate this institution of his liberty [liberality], he asked that it be fortified by the privilege of apostolic authority and strengthened by the protection of the holy Roman Church, upon payment of an annual pension of one Byzantine gold coin. He rightly considered that, while honor, fear, and obedience are offered by the faithful of holy Mother Church to the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, whatever has been strengthened and confirmed by their decree and in their name cannot be shaken by any unlawful attempt at overthrow.

For this reason, we embrace the aforesaid monastery, with everything that now justly belongs to it, [Col. 0715A] what has been lawfully granted to it, and whatever shall hereafter be conferred through the authentic donation of any persons, under the general guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See. Under the wings of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, with every disturbance by those who cause trouble removed and prohibited, we confirm by the testimony of this present document that you, son William, and your successors may possess it freely and absolutely and order it regularly and usefully.

We also decree that the forms of constitution, immunity, and liberty which the aforesaid illustrious Count Adalbert inserted in the written instrument of his donation and caused to be impressed with the royal seal shall be carefully observed, for the security of posterity and the prevention of attacks by those who cause trouble—namely, insofar as they do not conflict with canonical enactments—so that nothing permitted is neglected and nothing forbidden is imposed. [Col. 0715B]

We have therefore decreed that all these things contained in the charter of this precept and decree of ours are to be observed forever by you and by all who succeed you in the rank and place you hold. If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge before the divine judgment that he is guilty of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken or mourns with worthy repentance what he has unlawfully done, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ and be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment.

But for all who observe what is just toward that place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal recompense. Given at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0715D] Thus far the author of the chronicle. As for the charter itself, at whose end the chronological characters may have been worn away by age and which he did not read, we believe that it should be dated to the year [Col. 0716D] 1083, as may be inferred from the history of that same monastery.]

### LXXII. Privilege of Gregory VII to Almodo, Abbot of Roton  
*He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Roton*

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Dom Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, I, 204, from a manuscript of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Almodo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Savior, built in the place called Roton, situated in Brittany, and to his successors regularly appointed there forever.

In view of the mercy above, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance so that, with attentive kindness, we may favor the just petitions of those who pray and, with the balance of equity, assist all who are in need as far as, by God’s gift, we are able. Above all, however, we judge that we must consider and labor, as far as divine assistance makes possible, for the stability of venerable places, in due honor of the supreme and Apostolic See, whose members they are.

Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we grant, concede, and confirm by this decree of our authority the following privileges to the aforesaid monastery, which you are recognized as governing and which is recognized as belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church, from which it receives an annual census of three gold denarii: no king or emperor, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, may diminish or take away, under any pretext or occasion, anything that has already been donated to that venerable place from its own property or that, by God’s mercy, may be granted in the future; nor may anyone apply such things to his own uses or grant them to others under the pretense of pious motives as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, we wish that everything offered there, or that may happen to be offered, be possessed by you and by those who succeed you in your office forever, undiminished and without disturbance, and that it serve in every way the needs of those for whose sustenance and governance it was granted. [Col. 0716B]

We also decree that when the abbot dies, no one shall be installed there through any cunning act of usurpation except one whom the brothers of that monastery, by common consent and in the fear of God, shall have chosen—preferably from the same community, if a suitable man is found. If no one suitable for this governance can be found among them, let them seek another father and master for themselves with the counsel of the Roman Pontiff.

We add this to the present chapter: the monastery itself, its abbots, and its monks shall be secure from all interference by secular service and removed from every burden of worldly oppression, diligent and peaceful in the observance of holy religion, and bound on no occasion to be subject to anyone except the Roman and Apostolic See, to which the place belongs by right. The consecrations of the churches and the ordinations of the monks or clergy belonging to the aforesaid monastery shall likewise be received from the bishops in whose dioceses they are situated, provided that the bishops have been canonically ordained and perform the ordinations without payment. If any obstacle arises, the abbot, with the permission and authority of the Roman Pontiff, may freely go to whichever Catholic bishop he wishes for the consecration and ordination of both places and persons. [Col. 0716D]

We have therefore decreed that all these things contained in the charter of this precept and decree of ours are to be preserved forever by you, by all who succeed you in the rank and place you hold, and by those whose interest it may be. If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, knowing this charter of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him recognize before the divine judgment that he is guilty of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what has been unjustly taken or mourns with worthy repentance what has been unlawfully done, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ and be subjected to strict punishment at the eternal judgment. But for all who observe what is just toward that place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal light. Amen.

### LXXIII. Bull of Gregory VII for the monastery of Saint Peter of Juncel

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Gallia Christiana, Instruments, vol. VI, p. 12, from the archives of Juncel.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, …, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Juncel, situated in the place called Lunate, and to his successors regularly appointed there forever.

In view of the mercy above, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the solicitude of apostolic governance so that, with our accustomed kindness, we may favor the just petitions of those who pray and, with the balance of equity, assist all who are in need as far as, with God’s help, we can. Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we receive the aforesaid monastery of Juncel, which you are recognized as governing, into the protection and defense of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, and decree that it shall always be free from every secular domination. By this privilege and by the present decree of our authority, we grant and confirm the following: no king or emperor, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, may presume, under any pretext or occasion, to diminish or take away anything that has already been donated to that venerable place by any persons from their own property or that, by God’s mercy, may be granted in the future; nor may anyone apply it to his own uses or grant it to others under the pretense of pious motives as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, we wish that everything offered there, or that may happen to be offered, be possessed by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place forever, undiminished and without disturbance, and that it serve in every way the needs of those for whose sustenance and governance it was granted. [Col. 0717D]

We also decree that when you die, no one shall be installed there through any cunning act of usurpation, whether by investiture or through secular power, except one whom the religious brothers of that monastery shall choose by common consent, in the fear of God, from the same community, if a suitable man is found. If no one suitable for this governance can be found among them, let them seek another father and master for themselves elsewhere, with the counsel of religious men. He is to be appointed by the bishop in whose diocese your monastery is situated, unless it should be clear that the bishop himself has been prohibited by the Apostolic See; and as long as he remains under that prohibition or in rebellion, let no obedience be rendered to him by you. [Col. 0718A]

If any bishop, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, … your monastery, its abbots, and its monks shall be secure from all interference by secular service and, removed from every burden of worldly oppression, shall remain diligent and peaceful in the observance of religion.

We have therefore decreed that all these things contained in the charter of this precept or decree of ours are to be observed forever. If any king, emperor, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, in ignorance of this charter of our constitution, attempts with reckless audacity to act against it, then, after being admonished once, twice, and a third time at suitable intervals, if he does not repent and satisfy your aforesaid Church, let him lose the dignity of his power [Col. 0718B] and honor, and let him acknowledge before the divine judgment that he is guilty of the iniquity committed. Unless he restores what he has unjustly taken or mourns with worthy repentance what he has unlawfully done, let him be excluded from the most holy body and blood of our Redeemer Jesus Christ. But for all who observe what is just toward your place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace.

### LXXIV. Privilege of Pope Gregory concerning the monastery of Saint Benedict

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Mabillon, Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict, V, 640.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, [Col. 0718C] venerable abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors forever.

The care of the office we have undertaken compels us to apply such diligence of administration to venerable places, especially those belonging by right to the holy Roman Church, that in them the matters most beneficial to the study of sacred learning, to the purpose of religious life, and to the lasting edification of spiritual grace may be especially strengthened by apostolic privileges and memorable authority.
