Therefore, concerning the spiritual governance and condition of the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated between the banks of the rivers Po and Lario, we have judged it right to enact and confirm the following institutions, so that the concern we have once bestowed may, with God’s help, always remain vigilant. Just as the devotion, faith, and piety of its founders—by whom it was built and offered to God—live there at all times, so, by God’s ordering, may our authority there live and act, for the common merit of their devotion and ours.

That monastery was established by Thedaldus, an illustrious man and father of the Marquis Boniface. It was then given and transferred as property to blessed Peter and to his Apostolic See, as were certain other monasteries during our pontificate, by Matilda, daughter of that same Marquis Boniface, through a constitution formerly decreed and confirmed. This is also contained in the privileges we have issued concerning the communion and confirmation of that place: namely, that every year, in the presence of the Roman Pontiff or his archlegate, at Rome or wherever he orders, eight days before or after the Kalends of May, that is, on the Roman reckoning, one ounce of gold be paid to blessed Peter and to his Apostolic See.

But because you, dearest brother and venerable abbot, gave us, from the congregation of the monastery of Cluny over which, by God’s authority, you are recognized as presiding, Brother Wido, a religious and prudently instructed man, to teach and establish there, with God’s help, the form and discipline of sacred religion according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the customs of your manner of life, lest the traces of this edification thereafter be erased, or the fruit of your spiritual offspring, brother, fail or perish at some future time through the substitution of an alien and barren way of life, we entrust the care of that place to you and to your successors forever in our stead. In its governance and guardianship, you and all your successors shall have both the authority and the duty to devote yourselves to its administration.

We also decree that, when the abbot there dies, your diligence shall always ensure that a suitable person worthy of this office is substituted in the place of governance according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Whatever ought to be instituted or corrected in the monastery for the increase and observance of monastic religion shall always be administered under your direction and governance, [Col. 0719C] while the authority of the Apostolic See remains intact in all things, since that place is recognized as belonging to it by right, together with the other matters that we have decreed and established concerning the consecration of the abbot and the brothers of the monastery, as well as others pertaining to it, the payment of the census, and finally its entire condition, in the privileges granted to it for its stability and particular protection.

### LXXV. Gregory VII confirms the privileges of the Church of Saint Audomarus in Artois, at the request of Robert, Count of Flanders

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Miraeus, Diplomatic Works, vol. IV, p. 5, from the suit of the chapter of Saint Audomarus against the monks of Saint Bertin.]*

Gregory … to his beloved … son Robert, Count of the Flemings … [Col. 0719D]

To the church founded by blessed Audomarus, third bishop of the Morini, in honor of blessed Mary, Mother of God, and which to this day is honored as possessing the body of that same bishop, we grant and confirm, by the decree of our authority, privileges of the following kind … We also renew the privileges which blessed Nicholas, the forty-second from blessed Gregory, granted to that church, in the presence of Baldwin, formerly your ancestor. Baldwin, having come to that same pope at the threshold of the Apostles, earned, by their authority, reconciliation with his father-in-law, the Emperor Charles, whose daughter he had married without his knowledge.

We decree that no king, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, may diminish or take away anything that was donated to that church by blessed Audomarus, Adroaldus, and the others. Rather, we wish that everything offered there be possessed forever, undiminished and without any disturbance, and that it serve in every way the needs of those for whose sustenance and governance it was granted.

We also decree that, when the provost or dean of that church dies, no one shall be substituted there through any cunning act of usurpation except one whom the canonical consent of the canons shall have provided and appointed in accordance with the fear of God, or whom it shall have elected to be installed, and so forth.

### LXXVI. Bull of Pope Gregory VII by which he grants and confirms certain monasteries to the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Cava

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Muratori, Italian Antiquities, V, 479.]*

[Col. 0720B]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ, clergy and laity, health and apostolic blessing.

We wish it to be known to all clergy and laymen who worship God in pious and Catholic faith that we have received under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Cava, which is recognized as having been built near Salerno in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. To this monastery we formerly donated, for perpetual possession, governance, and ordering according to God, certain monasteries situated on Mount Cilento—namely, the monastery of Saint Mary of Gulia; the monastery of Saint Nicholas; Saint Archangel; Saint Magnus; Saint Fabianus; Saint George; Saint Matthew at the Two Rivers; and the church of Saint Angelus of Mount Corace; Saint Blaise of Butrano; Saint John of Turesino; Saint Savior of Nuce; Saint Zachariah of Lauris, together with their cells—when Gisulf, our dearest son, the prince, granted them to the venerable Peter, abbot of that monastery. Now we entrust them to the same abbot and to his successors for governance, correction, and administration, and confirm them by apostolic authority. [Col. 0720D]

Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, in whose place we preside over the holy Roman Church, we forbid and absolutely prohibit any archbishop or bishop, any king, duke, prince, or count, any cleric or layman, or any person whatsoever, great or small, from presuming, under any circumstances or on any pretext, to diminish anything belonging to the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Trinity in the aforesaid monasteries or churches, or in anything pertaining to them; to impose fraud, trouble, or any violence; or to disturb the servants of God. Thus the same monastery, together with the aforesaid churches, shall be subject in full right to the Roman Church alone.

For the religious monks serving God there will be able to perform the divine work with that much greater sincerity and devotion, the more carefully we strive to provide in every respect for their peace by our authority—or rather by that of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles. [Col. 0721A]

If anyone believes that he has a just complaint against the aforesaid monastery, but does not wish to have his dispute settled and decided before the abbot or monks of the monastery, we wish and establish by perpetual decree that the complaint be brought before us or our legates, so that, with God as author, justice may be rendered to each person by an equitable judgment without respect of persons. But if anyone attempts to act against the authority of this decree of ours, let him know that he will lose the grace of blessed Peter the Apostle and be struck by the vengeance of apostolic indignation. Those who obey and observe the precepts of this charter, however, shall receive worthy recompense from God and obtain the apostolic blessing.

### LXXVII. Letter of Gregory VII to Laetus, Abbot of Saint Michael at Passignano

*(1073–1085.)*

*[Lami, Deliciae Eruditorum, vols. III–IV, p. 198.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Laetus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel at Passignano, and to his successors regularly appointed there forever.

With supreme mercy in view, we have undertaken the care of the universal Church and bear the responsibility of apostolic governance so that, with attentive kindness, we may favor the just petitions of those who pray, and, with the scales of equity, assist as far as God grants us the ability all who are in need. Above all, however, we judge that we must carefully consider and labor, in keeping with the honor owed to venerable places and to the supreme Apostolic See, of which they are members, insofar as divine help grants us the possibility.

Therefore, in accordance with your petition, by this present decree of our authority, with the consent and request of our brother Guillelmus, bishop of Fiesole, we grant, concede, and confirm the following privileges to the aforesaid monastery, or to your church, over which you are known to preside. We decree that no king or emperor, no prelate of whatever dignity, nor anyone else, may dare to diminish, remove, or appropriate for his own use any of the things that have already been lawfully given to that venerable place by any persons from the beginning, or that, by God’s mercy, may hereafter be granted to it, under any pretext or appearance of a case, or to grant them, as though for pious reasons, as an excuse for his own greed.

Rather, we wish everything that has been offered there, or that may happen to be offered, to be possessed perpetually and without disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, and to be wholly useful for the needs of those for whose support and governance it has been granted. We also specifically grant to that church or monastery the tithes of its possessions, for the use of the poor and of those who arrive; and, as we said above, we confirm whatever it now justly possesses, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s consent, happen to possess, whether movable or immovable, while preserving the canonical subjection owed to its own bishop.

We therefore decree that all the things contained in this page of our command and decree are to be preserved forever. If any king, emperor, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished once, twice, and even a third time, with suitable intervals, if he does not repent and make satisfaction to the aforesaid Church, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has committed. And unless he restores what he has wrongly taken from it, or mourns his unlawful acts with fitting penance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him be subjected to strict punishment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is justly due to that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

## LXXVIII. Privilege of Pope Gregory VII for the Church of Saint Paul at Rome  
*(In the year of Christ 1074, March 13.)*

*[Margarini, Bullarium Casinense, vol. II, p. 106, from the archives of the sacred monastery of Saint Paul in the City, chest T, nos. 1–2.]*

[Col. 0722C]

To the holy, most blessed, and great preacher, the teacher of the nations in faith and truth, the apostle Paul, Gregory, an unworthy servant.

Whenever we seem to give you something, holy apostle Paul, chosen vessel, we do not grant what is ours, but rather return or confirm what is yours. For what is ever ours without you? Therefore I, Gregory, bishop, servant of him and of all the servants of God, for the remedy of my soul, cede, deliver, and inviolably bestow upon you all offerings that faithful Christians have offered upon your altar, beneath which your most sacred body is believed to be buried; likewise, the offerings of the confession and of all the altars of your church, and the provisions for the brothers serving God there in perpetuity, just as it is known to have been granted by our holy predecessors who served you.

I also grant the whole estate called Lapigio, with the church of Saint Proculus—or by whatever other name it is called—cultivated or uncultivated, together with everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid estate; half of the castle of Ardea, with its fortress and the Greater Tower, together with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary in Cannella, with its appurtenances; the estate of Fulana, with all its appurtenances; half of Lake Caprulacus; the castle of Velletri, with all its appurtenances, as it was granted by the holy pontiffs; at Albano, the cell of Saint Nicholas and the cell of Saint Mary called Minor, situated in the palace, together with everything belonging to the aforesaid cells; and in the palace, the church of the Holy Trinity, together with the entire palace.

I also grant the estate called Floriana, or by whatever other name it may be called, with lands, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, and everything generally and wholly belonging to the aforesaid estate of Floriana; likewise the farm called Castellione, together with the neighboring farm called Filioli, with lands, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, and everything belonging to them; the farm called Ulmetum, with its vineyards, woods, and meadows; the farm called Squezanellum, with its appurtenances, houses, farms, and vineyards; the wine-cellar of the Antoniones; the estates of Pertusa, Bifurcum, Priminianum, Cassianum, Silo, Cornelius, Tesolata, and Cornelianum, with all their rights and instruments, and with everything generally belonging to them.

[Col. 0723B]

We further add to this cession two gardens situated between the Tiber and the portico of that church, to the right as one goes from the city gate, separated by the river Almo, between the boundaries of the garden of the monastery of Saint Stephen—which is the monastery of the handmaids of God situated at Saint Peter the Apostle—and the estate of Piscinianus, with its vineyards and gardens.

Likewise, the little plots called the Fossae Latronis, also situated beside the same portico, to the left as one goes from the gate, where vineyards have now been planted; these little plots adjoin on one side the property once belonging to Eugenius the scholasticus, and on the other the property of the monastery of Saint Eristus.

Likewise, the monastery of Saint Cosmas, situated in the Tiber valley, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Paul the Apostle, situated within the city of Tibur; the city of Antedonia, with its appurtenances and harbor; the mountain called Argentarius, with Lake Catamarus, where the church of Saint Michael is located; half of the castle of Orbitello, with its appurtenances; the castle called Elsa, with all its appurtenances; and likewise the lake near Mount Argentarius, with its fisheries, so that half of the fish caught there is to be delivered to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Paul the Apostle.

Moreover, Casamaria, with its lands and dependents, in the entirety in which it was accustomed to render payment at the royal court; all these things in full, just as they were granted and perpetually confirmed by emperors and most holy pontiffs. Also, a portion of the lake called Dulia; Cesina, situated at Pireto; the vineyards situated at Semproniano; the land beside Piscaria, or the vineyards situated at Cerbarola; and other vineyards situated at Querquetum.

Likewise, the farm called Visilianum, with the oratory of Saints John and Paul, houses, vineyards, tenant holdings, and dependents, together with everything belonging to it; also the saltworks in the Old City, and two other pairs of saltworks situated at Abinea; likewise a house and tenant holding with its dependents, together with everything wholly belonging to it; and two other pairs of saltworks situated in the aforesaid territory.

Moreover, the church of Saint Michael at Semproniano, with the oratory of Saint John situated at the port of Hercules, all belonging by right and ownership to the same monastery. I further deliver to you four mills at Albano and one in the valley of Aricia, with its watercourse, together with everything that appears to be held there by your right.

Likewise, we confirm to you, teacher of the nations, the monastery of Saint Sergius, situated in the Subura, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Prisca, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Focas the martyr, formerly belonging by right to Saint Anastasius; the church of Saint Leo the pope, situated beside the monastery of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri; the church of Saint Nicholas, situated beside the aqueduct of Claudius; and likewise the fishery in the Tiber at Marmorata; in short, everything within the city of Rome that religious men or any other persons have granted to you.

[Col. 0724B]

We further confirm the estate of Saint Cecilia, called de Mega, situated outside the gate of Saint Lawrence and bounded as follows: on one side by the Tiber, on the other by the stream of Mega; along that stream it ascends as far as the land of Saint Lucia de Renati, and from there as far as the public road called Saint Valentine; then it descends as far as the public well, and from there descends through the channels as far as the aforesaid Tiber.

We also confirm the estate of Paternus, likewise situated outside the gate of Saint Lawrence, with lands, plantations, gardens, watermills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, all its appurtenances, and all its boundaries, as it was granted to your monastery by Pope Paschal, our predecessor, except for the small parcel of land there held by Saint Sabas.

We confirm the entire estate of Caesana, with its male and female tenants, as Benedict Campaninus gave it to your monastery when he became a monk; and the entire estate of Luliana with its castle; and Julianellum with its male and female tenants.

Likewise, we confirm to you the farm of Solone with its castle called Ponte de Nona; and also the farm called Casa Arsicia. Moreover, we grant you the castle called Longezza, with all its appurtenances: woods, fields, meadows, pastures, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees of every kind, springs, streams of perpetual water, buildings, ruined walls, caves, sandpits, and its watermills.

We also grant half of the New Castle with its appurtenances; likewise the estate and holding of Saint Julian with its marshes, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, as it was bounded in ancient times, together with half of Lake Borranus, namely: on the first side, the Tiber; on the second, the stream of the Osa, along that stream as far as the bridge of Saints Digna and Merita; on the third side, from that bridge along the Silix as far as the Broken Pillar, and from there along the same Silix to the stream of Spineto; on the fourth side, bounded by that same stream of Spineto as far as the stream of Silicinum, and along that stream as far as the river.

[Col. 0725A]

Furthermore, we confirm and strengthen for your venerable monastery the castle of Passarano, with its fortress and everything belonging to it. We likewise grant you the fortress called de Guerro, with all its appurtenances; half of the castle called Colonna, with all its appurtenances inside and outside; the entire church of Saint Saviour; and another church of Holy Mary, Mother of God, situated in Oliveto.

We also grant the church of Saint Lawrence called Marmorio, with all its appurtenances; the castle of Saint Victorinus, with everything belonging to it; and in the city of Tibur, the monastery of Saint Michael called Placiule. Also, the fortress of Saint John called Camporacius, with all its appurtenances; the hill of Nomentana with all its churches and appurtenances; the Round Castle with the church of Saint Reparata and the wood called Saint Reparata; and, at Albano, the estate of Tribunus.

Moreover, we give you, eminent teacher of the nations, the castle of Flaianus with its appurtenances inside and outside; the castle of Vaccaricia with all its appurtenances; the castle of Morilupo with all its appurtenances; the castle of Lepronianus with all its appurtenances; a third part of the city of Scapranata with all its appurtenances; the city of Collinis with all its appurtenances; the castle of Formello with all its appurtenances; and the estate of Maceranus, situated beside the church of Saint Cornelius.

[Col. 0725C]

We also grant the monastery of Saint Benedict of Nepi, situated at Pentoma; the estate called Ulmetum, situated in the territory of Nepi; likewise the estate called Meiana, situated near the city of Nepi; and the lake called Jamela.

We further grant you, eminent teacher of the nations, the church of Saint Stephen with its castle and borough, situated near the city of Sutri, with lands or gardens, mills, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, and fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees. We also confirm to you the estate called Lubre, with vineyards and meadows, sowable lands, plantations, and its marshes.

Likewise, we confirm the inheritance that once belonged to Guido of Sergi and was later purchased by your monastery—namely, a fourth part of Castellione; six pedes of sowable land, with vineyards, plantations, and meadows; a fourth part of the stream of Octavius; and the church of Saint John, situated on the estate called Maliano, together with that estate, as it was granted to you by the holy pontiffs.

Likewise, in the city of Ostia, the church of Holy Mary, our Lady and Mother, with its appurtenances; beside the sea, half of the church of Saint Lawrence, situated in the territory of Ardea; the church of the Saviour, situated at Decimum; the castle called Saint Paul at Jona; the land of Canneto, situated outside the gate of Saint Paul beside the portico, now held by the monks of Saint Boniface; the city gate called Saint Paul, with its revenues; and two mills on the river Almo beneath the bridge, with the church of Saint Andrew.

We also confirm the entire castle of Saint Paul called Joannipolis, with the mill beside it; the entire castle called Curcurlum, with the estate of Saint Primus; the castle called Polis; the castle called Fustinianum; and the castle called Gallicani, as Theodore of Rufino formerly gave it to you.

We confirm the city of Patrica, with all its appendages and the entire church of Saint Lawrence, as Pope Marinus, of blessed memory, granted it to your monastery; Mount Porculus; and the monastery of Saint Peter of Massa, situated in the territory of Palestrina.

Likewise, we grant you Saint Mary, surnamed Domine-Quo-Vadis, and the entire plain before the doors of that church, where fullers whiten cloth, with the three mills located there; half of the circus, with all the caves where earthen vessels are baked; the bathhouse now held by Gregory of Tusculum; the church of Saint Saviour at the head of the bridge of Saint Mary, with its house; and, within the city and the portico of Saint Peter, fifty dwellings.

We further grant eighteen rows of saltworks in the field of Salinae; the entire farm called Fulco’s, as far as the bridge of Mellius and as far as Saint Leucius; the entirety of Fascanorum; the entirety of Quintus; and the entire estate of Gallera, with its male and female tenants.

We grant half of the city of Manturana and its entire territory, with its male and female tenants, as Pope Agapitus gave it to your monastery while retaining the other half in his own dominion; half of the Bridge of Venom; and two churches on the hill near Vaccaricia, with all their villages, namely Saint Christina and Saint Lucianus.

We grant four estates at Nazzano, extending to the gate of the castle called Nazzanum and to the murmuring house; their names are Monumentum, Priscianum, Paramentum, Cascanum, and Casaretuli, near Mount Soracte, with their male and female tenants. Farulfus, the count, gave these to you; he is buried in your monastery.

Likewise, we grant the entire field of Veranus, where the church of Saint Lawrence the martyr is situated, which the emperor Constantine gave to you, teacher of the nations, on the condition that each year you render three hundred and fifty solidi; and the two castles held by Count Raynerius, son of Veilla, namely Mount Pado and Campum Lacum, together with Grossetum. All these were given to you by Pope Marinus of blessed memory, along with Greater Elsa, which is called Crassa.

In conclusion, since it would be lengthy to go through each item, we confirm and strengthen for you and your monastery in perpetuity whatever is known to have been confirmed and strengthened for you by the privileges of our predecessors, and whatever has been justly granted to you, or shall thereafter be granted, by the written instruments of any persons.

By this privilege of our authority we also absolve the aforesaid monastery from every yoke or jurisdiction of any person whatsoever. We further decree that all urban or rural places—that is, estates, holdings, farms, vineyards, lands, and various cultivated or uncultivated properties, with male and female tenants, male and female slaves—which have been granted to the same monastery by any faithful Christians, and those which have been granted and confirmed to the aforesaid monastery by pages of command from our predecessors of blessed memory, namely the eight pontiffs: Gregory, once the honeyed teacher; Leo IV; Sylvester; Marinus; Leo IX; Agapitus; Paschal; and Alexander; and also those which, through any safeguards or commands of our predecessors, appear to belong to the same pious place, may be possessed forever in complete security by the servants of your place.

Nothing whatsoever that has been granted there by our predecessors or by any God-fearing persons is to be diminished in any way, on any pretext, through any device of greed, or under the guise of any distinction, especially from the inheritances of that place. We forbid this by the authority of the holy Roman See, which, by God’s agency, you founded.

We further decree that this aforesaid monastery is to be subject in jurisdiction to no other church except the Roman pontiff. Therefore, apart from our Apostolic See, we forbid any priest of any church to exercise authority over the aforementioned monastery or over any of the churches belonging to it, under any pretext; and we prohibit this solemnly under the invocation of the divine judgment and by our authority—namely, the authority of both your fellow apostle Peter and of you, which has been entrusted to me, though unworthy.

Unless he has been invited by the head of your aforesaid monastery, no one is to presume in any way to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there. Wherever and by whichever bishop your servants wish to be ordained to the various ecclesiastical orders, or to build altars, or to receive chrism, let them have free permission.

We also grant your holy congregation that no bishop may dare to excommunicate any of the monks or clerics belonging to your most sacred place, in whatever locations its churches are subject to it, or summon them to a synod without the permission of their superior.

Moreover, we grant to the congregation of your aforesaid most sacred place, and to all the monks serving you there spiritually according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, the power to choose for themselves a special superior, by equal measure and common counsel, for the praise of God and the salvation of their souls, from that same congregation, if among them there should be found someone able to govern the aforesaid monastery according to God’s will.

But if no one suitable for such governance should be found in the monastery—which, with you and all the saints assisting, we hope will never happen—then our successor, together with special clerics and laymen of various orders, from whatever place he can, is to take the greatest care to choose a worthy minister to govern those who serve you, holy Paul, leader of good men and most powerful preacher.

Furthermore, in accordance with this privilege of our authority, and because of the devotion of that monastery, which we especially cherish in you, preacher of truth, and because of the usefulness of that monastery, which we have entirely recognized and continue daily to recognize, we remit and permanently release your monastery from every service or gift that was customarily paid to our predecessors and to us according to the practice followed by the other monasteries of the city of Rome.

Thus it is not to be compelled to pay wine, a boar, a cow, or anything at all, whether within or outside Lent, nor to perform any service at the Lateran palace, unless voluntarily. By this decretal page, therefore, let your monastery be absolved and completely free from every condition, burden, and payment, in accordance with what you yourself protest when those who compel you to diminish your glory equate your freedom with that of the first apostles, saying: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? For I have labored more than all.”

If any rash person, disregarding the fearful judgment of God, should diminish or dare to alter this privilege of our authority, affection, and devotion toward you, or the decrees of our ancient predecessors, to the detriment of your monastery, then in every respect what he has done against it shall be void. Unless he repents, he shall be punished by an anathema and, at the final judgment, shall share the portion of Judas, the betrayer of Christ.

By the authority that God granted to blessed Peter, your fellow apostle, and to you, in heaven and on earth, to bind and loose, let him be forever excluded from the fellowship of all the faithful. Moreover, he shall be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of precious gold to our palace and to your monastery, so that the honor owed to you by the whole Church may, with divine grace assisting, be shown in every respect, and so that the praise of God may at all times be worthily celebrated in your most sacred monastery.

Written by Benjamin, notary of the sacred palace, in the month of March, on the thirteenth day, in the first indiction.

[Note: The closing clause is corrupt. Jaffé.]

## LXXIX. Privilege for the Church of Saint Audomarus  
*(1077–85.)*

*[Miraeus, Opera diplomatica, IV, 5.]*

[Col. 0728D]

Although this holy see . . . Therefore we strengthen the church of blessed Audomarus, fortified and greatly strengthened by the privileges of our predecessors, also by the presence of our authority and the judgment of apostolic dignity; and, in strengthening it, we decree that the brothers and canons of that church shall possess free lordship over their properties . . . .

Moreover, in the presence of the bishops Gaulfridus of Paris, Rabodo of Noyon, Gerard of Cambrai, as well as Arnulf, provost of that church, and John, abbot of Saint Bertinus, we decree that no cleric or layman, whether of great or small rank, shall dare to inflict any trouble upon the canons of the aforesaid church, or introduce a new custom into their monasteries against their will . . . .

## LXXX. Gregory VII sends a letter to Altmann, bishop of Passau, “in which he permits him, for the time being, to bend the strictness of the canons”  
*(1073–85.)*

*[Life of Altmann, Acta Sanctorum of the Bollandists, August, vol. II, p. 374.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Altmann, bishop of Passau: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you departed from us, dearest brother, we remember that a legate has come to us several times in your name . . .

## DOUBTFUL

[Col. 0729]

## LXXXI. Privilege of Gregory VII for the Monastery of Vendôme  
*(1073–85.)*

*[Launoi, Opera, vol. III, part I, p. 367.]*

[Col. 0729B]

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Oderic, religious man and abbot of the venerable monastery of Vendôme, and to all his successors who shall regularly be promoted there in perpetuity.

A fitting and readily granted assent is owed to just petitions and to those that provide for the peace of God’s servants. Therefore, concerning the monastery of the holy and undivided Trinity, situated near the castle of Vendôme, which we know was offered as an allod and patrimony to blessed Peter and the Roman Church by its founders, namely Gaufredus, the most noble count of Anjou, and Agnes, his most noble countess-wife, we decree, both in accordance with the founders’ wish for that place and for all the abbots of this place, with the judgment of the Holy Spirit, that the church of Saint Prisca, together with its cardinal dignity, may not henceforth be taken from them by any ecclesiastical or secular person under any pretext.

We also decree that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, his successor shall be elected from the same congregation, provided that someone worthy of such holy governance is found. But if no worthy person should be found among them—which God forbid!—the monks shall arrange to choose for themselves, according to God’s will, a father from Cluny, or from the Greater Monastery, or from wherever they can find someone better, though not without the counsel of three abbots whom they can obtain from the neighboring places as the more religious men.

The elected man, so that he may not immediately be wearied by having to come to Rome, shall receive consecration from whichever Catholic bishop he wishes. The monks, however, shall take care to report to the pope by letter how the election or ordination was conducted, so that he may either correct what requires correction, or, if the election or consecration was carried out according to God’s will and our decree, may rejoice with appropriate goodwill and confirm it himself.

We also command that the abbot himself, who is known to be an allodial holder of the Roman Church, not be summoned to a council by a bishop or by any representative of the Apostolic See, nor be compelled to come; rather, he should endeavor to visit the Roman Church personally or through his legate.

We wish the annual census of twelve solidi, in the currency of that region, to be paid to blessed Peter, as established by the founders of the place, for perpetual remembrance and knowledge.

If a legate of the Roman Church should wish to visit the aforesaid place of blessed Peter, let him be received there with charity, and let the brothers carefully provide him, according to the resources of the place, with whatever is necessary for the body. He himself, however, shall not presume to correct anything there on his own or to trouble the rector of the place or the brothers on the pretext of his legation; but if he should see anything requiring correction, he may report it by letter to the pope.

We also confirm that the place of Saint Saviour, built near the walls of Angers, shall always remain under the monastery of Vendôme, and that no rector or provost shall ever be appointed there except by the will of the abbot of Vendôme.

Strengthened by divine confidence, we also prohibit by apostolic authority that, in the monastery of Vendôme or in the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, any person except the pope alone should ever exercise any authority or lordship, excommunicate, or impose an interdict—even if the region of Chartres or of Angers should have been excommunicated or placed under interdict. The monks, however, are not to receive excommunicated persons.

We confirm and strengthen by our authority in perpetuity whatever has been offered to that place by the founders themselves or by other persons up to this day, so that it may remain in the right of that place without diminution or any deprivation.

Among these things, the following have appeared to require expression by their proper names: the church of Saint George of Oléron on the island, with a large part of that island; the church of Blessed Mary of the Castle of Oléron; the church of Saint Nicholas of Oléron; the church of Blessed Mary of Surgères; the church of the Holy Sepulchre of Beaugency; and the parish church of Saint Clement of Credon.

All the churches contained in this page of our decree, both for you and for all who shall succeed you in the order in which you now stand, we decree are to be preserved forever.

If any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the impiety he has committed. Unless he restores what he has wrongly taken or mourns his acts with fitting penance, let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment let him be subjected to strict punishment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is justly due to that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the merciful Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Peter, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church.

## LXXXII. Confirmation of the Primacy of the Church of Vienne and Granting of Privileges, Confirming Those Granted to It by Earlier Pontiffs  
*(1073–85.)*

*[Cocquelines, Bullarium Romanum pontificum collectum, vol. II, p. 41.]*

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Waramundus, venerable brother and archbishop of Vienne, and through him to his successors and to the Church of Vienne, in perpetuity.

Since, by the governance of the Apostolic See, over which by God’s authority we preside, we are charged with caring for all the Churches that exist anywhere, and nevertheless must watch over them so that whatever may now have been diminished in their rights may henceforth be preserved inviolate, we ought to devote all our concern to those Churches that are both called and are the principal and special daughters of the holy Apostolic See, and that contain the primacies of other Churches.

For it is certain that the Church of Vienne, by concession of this see, holds primacy over seven provinces: Vienne itself, Bourges, Bordeaux, Auch, which is called Novempopulania, Narbonne, Aix, and Embrun. In these provinces it has been granted to the archbishop of Vienne, in accordance with the decree of Nicholas, to exercise the place of the Roman pontiff, namely, to convoke synodal assemblies and to define ecclesiastical rights justly and canonically by apostolic authority.

This is found in the privileges granted to that Church by our most holy predecessors; it is also contained in the privilege of Pope Leo of blessed memory. From this privilege, and from many others that are authentic, it is clear that the aforesaid seven provinces justly and reasonably belong to the privilege of the Church of Vienne, since they were founded by the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

According to the ancient authority of the catalogues, ten and eight [the wording is uncertain], it has likewise been determined that seven towns or cities—namely Grenoble, Valence, Die, Alba-Viviers, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Maurienne—shall meanwhile remain subject to the Church of Vienne, until the remaining [cities] have been examined more certainly and fully investigated and are brought under the authority of the Church of Vienne.

Furthermore, we decree that Tarentaise shall always remain under the primacy of the Church of Vienne, as it is known to have been confirmed by the holy Fathers Leo and Nicholas.

You also reported one matter to us concerning the archdeaconry of Salmaria. The consecrations and ordinations, and whatever belongs to the pontifical office, just as your predecessor Leodegarius and other predecessors held them more firmly, we grant that you and your successors may hold without any disturbance or diminution.

It is likewise beyond doubt that the abbey of Saint Peter situated outside the gate of Vienne, the abbeys of Saint Andrew within the same city—one for monks and the other for holy women—and the abbey of Saint Theuderius, which that venerable confessor built, are wholly subject by right to the Church of Vienne.

As for the Church of Romans, although it supports itself by our freedom, nevertheless, having examined the imperial commands, both in secular matters and in the canonical regular matters ordered there through the counsel of our vicar Hugh, bishop of Die, we decree by apostolic authority that you and your successors are to possess all authority over it in every respect.

Since, therefore, dearest brother, you who by divine arrangement preside over the governance of that Church, your venerable religious devotion humbly asked the Apostolic See to confirm the ancient privileges delivered to the sacred see of Vienne by our holy predecessors, and since a worthy matter was requested, we gladly assent out of love for you and with the charity owed to that Church.

We therefore confirm and strengthen by this present privilege and by apostolic authority the privileges, estates, and goods that were given or restored to your Church by blessed Sylvester, Leo, and Nicholas and by their successors, or by the Roman emperors, or by the kings of the Franks or of Burgundy.

In the name of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we command that henceforth they remain firm and unshaken and endure unaltered.

But if anyone violates the sanction of this privilege, unless he repents and corrects his offense through fitting satisfaction, let him be an exile from the kingdom of God, let him rightly be condemned by excommunication and become an outsider to the Church of God, and let him be subject to perpetual curse.

Given by the hand of Peter the chancellor, on the second day before the Nones of March, in the year 1077 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fifteenth indiction, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Gregory VII.

### LXXXIII. Letter of Gregory VII to the clergy and people of the Church of Vienne

Concerning the election of Warmund as their archbishop: he congratulates them and urges them to assist him in recovering the possessions taken from the Church of Vienne. (1073–1085.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 609.]

[Col. 0732D]

**GREGORY**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of the Church of Vienne, to whom, by reason of their merits and devotion, greeting and apostolic blessing are due.

[Note: In C. Charvet’s *History of the Church of Vienne*, this letter, rendered into French, bears the name of Alexander II [Col. 0731D], but incorrectly, as we shall presently demonstrate from authentic documents [Col. 0732D].]

It is most clearly known not only to you but also to nearly the whole world that for a long time now the Simoniacal heresy has disturbed the Church of God by its crafty machinations. It has violently gained such strength within her that, like a savage beast—which indeed it is [Col. 0733A]—it has nearly crushed her by tearing her apart with the bites of its cruel ministers. Therefore we, who, at the nod of the divine ordering and by the providence of divine mercy, though not by our own merits, nevertheless stand as guardians at the summit of the universal Church for the defense of the liberty of our mother, the holy Church, neither ought nor are able to restrain our spirit or our tongue.

For it is written: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48), that is, he who withholds his tongue from rebuking the carnal. We shall indeed strive, by speaking the truth, to scatter seeds upon the soil of the hearts of God’s servants; but he who is the Truth himself will nourish the harvest toward fruitful maturity as he pleases.

In your own time he has granted you so ripe and praiseworthy a fruit [Col. 0733B] that not only we but the whole Church rejoices, nourished by the pasture of such [lacuna] (abundance) [Col. 0734A]. Who would not rejoice that a religious and prudent man has been canonically and in every respect, according to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, ordained bishop in the Church of God?

You have, by the gift of divine favor, Warmund [Note: Warmund, or Guarmund, abbot of the monastery of Dol, was ordained archbishop of Vienne in 1077, according to the *Chronicle of Dol*, vol. XII of our collection, p. 455. In the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Vienne*, ibid., p. 346, it is stated: “Warmund was canonically elected to the see of Vienne around the year 1071, after those who had been attempting to administer it simoniacally had been expelled; and he was confirmed by Pope Gregory, who knew him to be faithful and prudent, etc.” [Col. 0733D]], a good and righteous bishop, ordained for you.

Therefore strive to show him obedience in all things, both out of fear of the divine name and out of reverence for the apostolic see, by whose authority this has been done [Note: Namely, Herimann having been deposed. Concerning him, at the Roman council of 1076, in Labbe, vol. X of the Councils, col. 356: “We excommunicate Herimann, bishop of Vienne, justly deposed for simony, perjuries, sacrileges, and apostasy, because he does not cease to trouble the Church of Vienne.” Hence one can see how greatly mistaken are those who imagine Herimann and Warmund to have been one and the same person! [Col. 0734D]]—to retain all that belongs by right to your Church, just as the Church itself possessed it in ancient times, and to help him recover what has been violently taken from it, especially the abbey of Saint Bernard. In this way you may obtain God’s favor through him and make blessed Peter your debtor, so that he may deign to grant you his aid in the present and future life [Col. 0734B].

## LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO GREGORY VII

### I. Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, to Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church

After speaking of his goodwill toward him, he explains that the dispute concerning York had been settled and that a report of what had occurred had been sent to the apostolic see, which he wishes Hildebrand to read.

[*Works of Lanfranc*, p. 304.]

[Col. 0733B]

To Lord **HILDEBRAND**, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, **LANFRANC**, his servant, joins a holy conclusion to holy beginnings.

My mind cannot express in writing with what affection it is bound to your sincerity, nor with what sweetness it continually recalls the favors that your kindness has always shown me, both when present and when absent [Col. 0733C]. Therefore, if by God’s gift I accomplish anything good in any sphere of life, I cannot consign your temporal and eternal salvation to oblivion.

And this I pray of almighty God: that he may prolong your life in this world for the honor and strengthening of his holy Church; preserve you undefiled by every contagion of sin; and in the future, as an abundant rewarder, repay you with enduring life multiplied according to your works.

Moreover, the accusation that the bishop of the Church of York brought against me concerning primacy and the subjection of certain bishops was heard and decided according to the command of the apostolic see. I have sent our lord the Pope a brief written account, in due order, of the conduct of this affair [Col. 0733D]. I wish and ask that your Charity read it with appropriate diligence [Col. 0734B], so that you may know with complete certainty what the apostolic see ought to grant to me and to my Church by confirming through a privilege, and to confirm by granting it.

### II. Hildebrand to Lanfranc

He explains that the pallium requested by Lanfranc’s envoys was not sent because such things are not ordinarily sent to an absent recipient. It is therefore necessary that Lanfranc come to Rome.

[Ibid.]

To **LANFRANC**, venerable archbishop of the people of Canterbury, **HILDEBRAND**, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, greeting in the Lord.

We received the words of your envoys with great seriousness [or: gratefully] [Col. 0734C]. But we deeply regretted that we could not properly satisfy your wish by sending, as they requested, the privilege belonging to your person while you were absent. Your prudence should not take this amiss, for if we had seen this granted in your time to any absent archbishop, we would certainly, with the readiest affection, have bestowed this honor upon your religious devotion without subjecting you to the trouble of coming.

It therefore seems necessary to us that you visit the thresholds of the apostles, so that concerning this and other matters we may consult together more effectively about what ought to be done and establish it accordingly.

For the rest, if it should happen that our envoys come to you, receive them with your customary affection. Whatever they say to you secretly [or: whatever they say and whatever they do] [Col. 0734D], strive to arrange in the manner suitable to one who is a most beloved son of the holy Roman Church and a religious priest.

### III. Lanfranc to Gregory VII

He clears himself of the charge brought by the pontiff that, after attaining the episcopate, he loved Gregory and the Roman Church less than he had formerly done; he says that, on the contrary, the pontiff’s love appears to have grown weaker toward him. He states that he had advised the king, as Gregory had suggested through his legate, but had not persuaded him.

[*Works of Lanfranc*, p. 304.]

[Col. 0735A]

To the revered supreme shepherd of the holy universal Church, **GREGORY**, **LANFRANC**, a sinner and unworthy bishop, offers service with due submission.

I received the letters of Your Excellency, delivered through Hubert, subdeacon of your sacred palace, with the humility that was fitting. In nearly the whole of their composition you endeavored, with paternal sweetness, to rebuke me because, having been placed in episcopal dignity, I love the holy Roman [Col. 0735B] Church and you, on account of its reverence, less than I once used to love you before receiving that dignity—especially since I do not doubt, nor do I think anyone else doubts, that I reached the summit of this honor by the authority of the apostolic see.

Indeed, venerable Father, I neither wish nor ought to cast an accusation upon your words. Yet, with my conscience as witness, I cannot understand in myself what either bodily absence, or so great a distance between places, or the very elevation of whatever kind of honors could claim any power in this matter, so that my mind would not remain subject in all things and through all things to your commands, according to the prescriptions of the canons.

If, by God’s favor, I could one day speak with you face to face, I would show—not so much in words as in the facts themselves—that I have grown in my love, while you, if I may say so with your permission, have in some measure declined from your former love.

I conveyed the words of your embassy, together with your aforementioned legate, to my lord the king as well as I could [Col. 0735C]. I advised him, but I did not persuade him. But since [or: why] he did not agree in every respect with your wishes, he himself makes this known to you both by word and by letter.

### IV. Letter of Sigefrid, bishop of Mainz, to Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 53.]

**SIGEFRID**, by the grace of God what he is, bishop of Mainz, to **HILDEBRAND**, archdeacon of the holy apostolic see and archchancellor, greeting and the complete sincerity of fraternal affection.

We give the greatest thanks to Your Charity because you have always stood favorably by all our embassies and petitions that we have directed to the apostolic see, and in every dispute and affair you have always defended our side with the shield of your wisdom and good will [Col. 0736A].

Therefore, first, we offer you many thanks; then we ardently desire that an opportunity may at some time arise in which we may repay you in kind for your affection. Although, amid the many affairs of the Church that you bear daily, you seek nothing except the grace of God, and do not wish to touch earthly things except for the purpose of ordering them rather than possessing them, nevertheless, since a cheerful giver, in order to give much for God, must justly possess much, we inform Your Love that, if anything belonging to us should be pleasing to you, let us merely be told, and it will immediately become yours from what is ours [Col. 0736B].

For who could fail to love so great a man? Who would dare deny him anything?

We ask, however, that the sweetness of your affection open access for our embassy, which we are now sending to the sacred apostolic see, and that through your assistance you obtain the fulfillment of what we request: namely, that for the synod we have decreed to hold concerning the rebellious Thuringians over tithes, the apostolic lord may deign to send one of his own assistants who may preside over the synod and, by his authority, determine whatever matters arise for determination.

If this cannot be done, at least let our synod be strengthened by written authorization from His Blessedness [Col. 0736C], and let the boldness of the rebels be restrained by such an authority. Therefore let your affection strive to obtain the fulfillment of our petition.

### V. Letter of Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz, to Gregory VII

[Note: Jaromir, also called Gebehard, bishop of Prague, unable to endure the separation from Prague of the bishopric of Moravia, entrusted to Bishop John, together with the assignment of certain revenues of the bishopric of Prague, left nothing undone in his efforts to harass his rival. He did not even refrain from inflicting wounds and committing other disgraceful acts.

When Pope Alexander II learned of this, he sent his legates Bernard and Gregory, who publicly declared the bishop of Prague suspended from office. These events occurred shortly before Alexander’s death. Gregory, succeeding him, took up the entire case again. He first wrote to Wratislaus, duke of Bohemia and brother of Jaromir, though favorable to Jaromir’s rival, complaining of the injury inflicted by Jaromir upon the apostolic legates; he then added that he would aggravate the sentence unless Jaromir returned to his duty.

Meanwhile Jaromir fled to his metropolitan, the archbishop of Mainz, asserting that, though unheard and not condemned by his metropolitan in a synod, he was being unjustly forbidden to exercise his episcopal office. Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz, conveyed both the complaints of the bishop of Prague and his own complaints by letter to Pope Gregory. I reproduce his letter here because it sheds light on Gregory’s letters to Wratislaus, published in *Register*, book I, letter 17. [Col. 0735D]]

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 390.]

To the most reverend Father, newly invested with the mitre of the first apostolic see, **S.**, administrator of the Church of Mainz by the grace of God, offers devoted service of goodwill and due submission of obedience.

We had always ardently desired that the bishop of the apostolic see might be one who, by his life and conduct, words and example, would preside over and benefit the holy Church of God for its salvation. But now, as though the heavens have become honeyed [Col. 0736D] and distill the dew of God’s grace more sweetly than usual, divine mercy has fulfilled our prayers with more than customary abundance and has placed over that holy Roman Church the one whom we most desired—the man who has always stood favorably by us in all affairs and has never failed us in our own.

Therefore, with all the inmost marrow of our hearts, we give thanks to almighty God, who has illumined and adorned the chair of Peter, the head of the churches, with your priesthood, reverend Father. We humbly and earnestly beg that he who has poured upon the first fruits of your apostolate the oil of gladness beyond that of your companions may multiply grace and peace for his Church throughout all your days.

We also desire to deserve a special favor with you and to receive from your fatherhood a particular expression of mercy—not only the affection that you owe to the universal Church, but also that privilege of favor which your holy see has always extended to the Church of Mainz, like a devoted mother to a special daughter [Col. 0737A].

Relying, therefore, upon this favor, in all matters that confront us we have recourse to you, and whatever opposes us we report to you as members to their head.

We humbly inform Your Holiness of one matter: under your predecessor, Pope A., of pious memory, we suffered, if we may say so without compromising reverence, an unjust prejudice and were harshly deprived of that right which the sacred canons and the decrees of the Fathers command to be preserved for metropolitans.

In the first place, a sinister report was brought before that most holy Father concerning our brother and suffragan, the bishop of Prague, and he was accused before him by his enemies without my knowledge. From him there then came an unprecedented edict: that this same brother and fellow bishop—who had neither first been canonically heard among his brothers, nor canonically summoned before him, nor charged with the fault of disobedience [Col. 0737C]—should not only be suspended from his office, but also wholly stripped of the possessions and revenues of his Church and expelled.

He even sent messengers and caused public notice to be given among clergy and people that they were to regard him as excommunicated and were neither to seek nor receive from him anything belonging to a bishop.

Whether such an act is consistent with apostolic gentleness and preserves the authority of the decrees does not escape Your Holiness. For, according to the decrees of the canons, the case ought first to have been referred to us; he ought to have been summoned to a council within the province and heard among his brothers. I and my brothers ought then to have referred the matter to the apostolic see, as to our head, if it were so serious that it could not and ought not be settled by us.

But now our brother and fellow bishop, wandering and exiled from his see and, as we have said, unjustly stripped of the possessions and revenues of his Church and expelled, suffers an unworthy judgment. From this a great scandal has arisen among all our brothers and fellow bishops, and the episcopal name and office, which are sacred before God and human beings, suffer intolerable disgrace [Col. 0737D].

Moreover, that Church has now been without pastoral administration for many days, and, widowed of its only shepherd, remains deprived of episcopal blessing. The bishop who caused this expulsion and disturbance is usurping its office for himself and, contrary to what all councils and decrees have taken the greatest care to prevent, is going about that bishopric performing consecrations and confirmations.

This is especially dangerous because that people is a recent planting in the Catholic faith and has not yet been rooted and established in Christianity [Col. 0738A]. If it sees such great dissension continue among its pastors, it will easily relapse into the ancient error of paganism.

Therefore I and all my brothers, prostrate at the feet of Your Holiness, pray and beseech you first to take up the cause of the Church and likewise to denounce the oppressive circumstances of this evil age. I also had certain matters to discuss with you in person, which I can neither insert into a letter nor disclose even to any most faithful messenger.

For this reason I am sending to you these brothers with a letter explaining my absence. They will inform you that my failure to come to you is not due to presumption but to unavoidable and extreme necessity.

Let your holy fatherhood know, however, that there is no man on earth more faithful to you than I, or more devoted to fulfilling every command of yours. No affair could delay my coming to you if only my bodily health gave me the strength.

Concerning the long-standing obstinacy of the Thuringians, I make a new complaint to you. As always, so still now, they resist the Holy Spirit and his most just laws by refusing to pay the tithes of their revenues. When I admonished them to obey almighty God, they instead besieged me and my people with armed force, using a mixed multitude of commoners. If the Lord had not rescued us with his almighty hand, their cruelty might perhaps have raged against us even to the point of destruction [Col. 0738B].

I ask one thing of your sacred fatherhood: out of regard for ecclesiastical discipline, come to our aid in compassion against so wicked and unprecedented a crime, and take up the sword against the enemies of God, so that rebellious and defiant Thuringia may feel that Rome, the empress, still lives and reigns in Peter’s key-bearing hand.

### VI. Letter of Sigefrid, archbishop of Mainz, to Pope Gregory

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 433.]

To the venerable Lord and Father beloved in Christ, **GREGORY**, bishop of the first see, **S.**, bishop of Mainz, by the grace of God what he is, offers the submission of due obedience and devoted dedication of service.

What cause intervenes, and what impediment prevents me from attending this sacred council of the holy apostolic see, I already explained in my previous embassy, and now I declare to Your Holy Fatherhood from the truth itself: namely, that I am suffering from the same disease of paralysis from which I was then suffering—not less severely, but with increasing and worsening force each day.

I do not mention this out of the pride of arrogance or the contempt of disobedience; may divine mercy keep such a disease of the soul far from me. No impediment arising from any affair, however great, could hold me back, since it is not mere willingness that leads me to you but burning desire that draws me.

It was my duty, and the rule of obedience and order of charity required it, to attend this fellowship of the saints, and, rejoicing in the presence, conversation, and salutary discourse of my divine Father Gregory and of Christ’s priests, to advance toward better things. The long journey and great labor would not have been regrettable, since from them would have come the fruit of great salvation.

With profound gratitude and humble bowing I thank Your Holiness because you so kindly inclined your ear to our embassy, received the envoys themselves so well, and dismissed them even more favorably. I also thank you because it pleased Your Holiness to remember so kindly our ancient love and brotherly affection, and, at the summit of your watchfulness and amid your concern for all the churches, not to overlook the fact that, long ago, while we were still living together in private, the charity of Christ had joined us to one another [Col. 0739A].

The many expressions of your kindness toward me cannot be erased by any length of time or obliterated by any variation of circumstances or events. Our diligent care will instead watch over this matter, so that you may deign to persevere in your goodwill toward us.

As for what you wrote in your memorandum—that I had entrusted to your fatherhood the counsel of my secrets, indeed of my salvation—and that you added certain matters requiring the file of correction for the discipline of my life and conduct: this I have always done and will always do, and I shall never desist from it as long as life remains. Whatever was guarded there I shall guard most carefully, and whatever was commanded there I shall fulfill completely, insofar as God grants me strength [Col. 0739B].

If anyone hostile to you should report otherwise about me, let Your Holiness know that by his falsehood he is attempting to divide unity and corrupt charity—unless, perhaps, he should accuse me of occasionally being compelled, for the sake of healing, by the counsel of my brothers to loosen somewhat the disciplinary rein by which I correct myself [Col. 0739C].

As for your command concerning the examination of the bishops whom you named to me—that I should investigate their entrance into office and their conduct most carefully and make the results known to you through our messengers—let that watchful eye of your wisdom consider that, from the return of our envoys until this renewed embassy, there was not enough time either to gather the brothers or to conduct an examination.

Concerning this matter I can still tell you nothing beyond what you already know or what common report conveys. Nevertheless, I sent your letters to them as soon as possible and diligently admonished them by my own letters to fulfill your command.

Regarding the penance of the bishop of Strasbourg, we can give you no certain answer. I did not previously know whether any penance had been imposed upon him, and, because of the shortness of time, I have been unable to inquire whether he is observing it [Col. 0739D].

Concerning the chastity of the clergy and the Simoniacal heresy, in short, in everything that you have commanded me, I shall always obey God and you, insofar as he himself assists me.

It will be an act of apostolic gentleness and paternal affection if, when directing ecclesiastical commands to the brothers, you deign to consider both the opportunities presented by the times and the capacity of each individual. Thus discipline may be applied to the wayward and disorderly as they deserve, while compassion of charity may not be denied to the weak and to those who need a physician. After the causes of affairs have often been examined, let the rigor of judgment be applied so that the measure of justice does not exceed the bounds of apostolic discretion and paternal piety [Col. 0740A].

May that Samaritan guard your sacred apostolate, praying for us—the one who, in guarding his Israel, neither sleeps nor slumbers. May he who entrusted the key to you preserve in you united and whole the divisions of grace that he has united in Peter’s key.

### VII. The same to the same

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, p. 433.]

To the father of special reverence, **GREGORY**, bishop of the first see, **S.**, bishop of Mainz, by the grace of God what he is, as a son to his father and a subject to his prelate.

The vigilance of your pastoral office, my reverend Father, has aroused us as though from sleep by applying the stimulus of sacred exhortation and admonition to the idleness of pastors and their negligence. It urges us with great zeal and invites us with religious seriousness to take unceasing care to fulfill the work of the Gospel, to which we have been appointed as servants of the head of the household [Col. 0740B].

The pious concern of a prudent shepherd is sacred; the execution of this divine work is blessed and worthy of reward. But, alas, the upheaval of events and the wickedness of the times cry out loudly against it.

Even if the days are evil, your vigilant caution has nevertheless admonished us that the time must be redeemed, lest, if someone ceases to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard because of inclement weather, every useless laborer be condemned for negligence; and if a storm descends today and drives us from our work, then, when fair weather is restored from heaven tomorrow, our zeal should hasten back to that same task.

Accordingly, the authority of your holy fatherhood has ordered that on the appointed day, after gathering the brothers in accordance with the command of the apostolic legation [Col. 0740C], we must celebrate a council and not delay cutting away with the sickle of justice whatever in our province or kingdom may be found to have been wrongly done, unlawfully appropriated, or rashly presumed, whether through the Simoniacal heresy or in any other way contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical rectitude.

What you command me, Father, is fair and just, and the decrees of the sacred canons command that this be done twice each year throughout the provinces. But from what the authority of the decrees and your fatherhood urge us, the disorder of circumstances and the oppressive conditions of this evil age drive us far away.

We believe that Your Fatherhood has heard how great is the upheaval in our kingdom, how great the disturbance, and how dangerously wars and seditions rage, as we have heard in the Gospel [Col. 0740D].

We believe, I say, that you have heard about the war waged by our lord the king against the Saxons and Thuringians, and how the right hand of the Lord has struck down and put to flight the rebellious and impious. Yet, even though defeated, they persist in the same obstinacy; they raise again the head of treachery and, sharpening the swords of the whole kingdom against themselves, prepare renewed wars.

We fear one thing: that, on account of the people’s sin, the sword of the Lord has been drawn from its sheath. Unless he is appeased by the intercession of ourselves and other holy men, it may perhaps rage even to destruction.

For the bond of peace has been loosened and the bridle of discipline broken; nation rises against nation within the borders of the kingdom. The hostile sword has destroyed harmony and peace. Thus, while the trumpets of the Gospel are silenced, neither does the herald possess a voice for shouting nor the people an ear for hearing.

Through hostile plunder and invasion, the property and revenues of our bishop have largely perished, and many of our brothers are suffering the same fate. This distress prevents them from coming to the council [Col. 0741A].

Moreover, many of our fellow bishops who have been summoned to the council are not in the prince’s favor and dare not go anywhere without risking their lives. If we consider both the bishops who are accused and those who dare not attend, scarcely any judges will be found if the council is convened.

This also adds to the sum of our fear and increases the force of our grief: if those who are enemies of one another, summoned from different, indeed hostile, regions, are gathered for the council, then, while we think we are collecting brothers for a council, we may have battle lines prepared for war. While we strive to come together in one communion of ecclesiastical peace to correct errors and settle disputes, our assembly may perhaps, unless God watches over it, be thrown into confusion even to the point of destruction [Col. 0741B].

Let Your Holiness remember what once occurred at Goslar on account of the abbot of Wulten: how many good soldiers were killed by the sword within the church precincts on the very eve of Pentecost; how the altars were drenched with the blood of the slain; and how, at the devil’s instigation, the entire sanctuary was profaned.

At that time, certainly, they had all gathered at the court under the appearance of peace, except that a certain hostility lay hidden among them, like a fire placed beneath treacherous ashes. What do we think will happen if those who are openly hostile are gathered together [Col. 0741C]?

For these reasons and others like them, our brothers who hold the sounder view say that it seems good to them for the council to be postponed for now, until we see whether, once peace has been restored, the Lord may be appeased.

We, however, place your judgment above all counsels and councils, and, out of regard for you, we will in no way omit what you command us. Therefore, immediately after the royal expedition, we shall send you an embassy with great haste. We do not even take into consideration the inclement season of the year, so that you may perceive how much the authority of your command means to us.

Let your wisdom, which measures all things within itself, reconsider what outcome might arise from this disturbance. Anticipating by counsel and prayer the dangers we fear, arrange matters for the better [Col. 0741D], and whatever, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, you decide should be done concerning such matters, deign to announce to us from the oracle of your sacred heart.

If you approve, let the council now convened be postponed on account of the dangers we fear, and let it be celebrated for the same purpose whenever it pleases you and a suitable opportunity arises.

### VII bis. Letter of Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to Gregory VII

Written after the Council of Autun, or Augustodunum, but before the Council of Poitiers. (*Gregory VII*, book VI, letters 2 and 3.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX.]

To **GREGORY**, supreme pontiff, his father and lord, **MANASSES**, archbishop of Reims by the grace of God, offers the faithful submission of service and obedience and the devotion of prayer.

Through your intervention and entreaty, lord, I restored to Lady M., the marchioness, everything that her predecessor had held from me; and I faithfully promise—and have promised—my counsel, assistance, and protection for defending these possessions. Whatever she had requested concerning rejecting G. and receiving Count A., I am prepared to carry out. To confirm all this, during the holy days of Pentecost I was present in his city with our brother and your faithful servant, Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, having left behind, because of the necessity of his situation, all my own essential affairs at that sacred time.

But I, your faithful servant, prepared in every respect to obey you in the rights of the Church, earnestly seek your counsel and wish to carry out your judgment concerning Guarmond, archbishop of Vienne, [Col. 0742B] who degraded priests in my archbishopric and then restored them to their rank. Although he was not one, he pretended to be a Roman legate; he filled his purse—not under the pretext of truth, but imitating those who, as the Apostle says, regard piety as a source of gain—and, once he had finally filled it, returned from my diocese to his own. Therefore, for the honor of God and of the Roman Church, correct this kind of presumption and pretense as is fitting, lest anyone henceforth presume to do anything of the sort in another’s jurisdiction.

I also inform you that two of my suffragan bishops, those of Laon and Soissons, consecrated a third, the bishop of Amiens, in my archbishopric while I was unaware of it, since I was in Rome. First, this was contrary to your decree, by which you had ruled that no one—not even an archbishop—should consecrate as bishop one who had received the gift of a bishopric from a layperson; all the more so since these very men had been present at the council at Autun, where Lord Hugh, bishop of Die, proclaimed and established this ecclesiastical decree of yours before everyone.

Let this action, therefore—apart from what we have already said, contrary to authority and the canons, and also unheard-of, astonishing to all who think soundly, and more than can be expressed, astounding—if it pleases you, be declared invalid. Indeed, since the consecration of a bishop cannot rightly be completed by fellow bishops without the metropolitan, as you know, I wish you to be entreated and earnestly implored to correct, for the honor of God and of yourself and of us, so rash a [Col. 0742D] confusion of ecclesiastical order through zeal for justice, so that each person may know how to remain in his own rank and proper sphere, and not rashly arrogate to himself what belongs to another.

I also beseech the benevolence of your dignity to deem worthy of preserving for me the honor which your predecessors maintained for my predecessors, the archbishops, and which they left recorded for the memory of posterity in privileges and other documents. May the privilege which you yourself granted me not be annulled or violated: namely, that when summoned by you or not summoned, I should answer you and your Roman legates—not transalpine ones, who, joined to the Romans, seek what is theirs rather than what is Jesus Christ’s, and under honorable names advance their own greed rather than the Church of God.

Therefore, because of the shameful accusations and summonses of such men, may I, who am obliged to summon the bishops of all Gaul, be permitted to rely on you without a summons from legates, until I come to you at Easter, God willing.

Moreover, I earnestly wish to petition and forewarn you that, since, in my absence—although I had recently been staying with you—many things were done improperly and disorderly in the regions of my diocese, I shall not be able to refrain from using your ministry to correct these matters ecclesiastically. If any accusation against me concerning this should be brought before you, do not readily believe it or receive it with displeasure against me; instead, defer that matter until our presence before you, because I have no desire at all to exceed the limits of my authority.

For since those who make themselves out to be your legates are involved, I have a much more just claim through you to correct what belongs to our administration [Col. 0743B] than anyone has to meddle in what belongs to another.

Concerning Count Oebalus, who attempted to accuse me in your presence and, with deceptive words, commended himself and his loyalty to you, you can readily determine whose sincerity of loyalty toward you appears the greater: mine, who am prepared to obey God and you in everything, or his, who both attacks the Church of blessed Peter personally in your presence and, among us, through Manasses and his followers whom he harbors in his castle, persecutes blessed Mary.

For Manasses, of whom we have spoken, to whom, at your command, we had granted pardon for what he had done against us, provided that he returned to the Church his mother, crushed by the consciousness of his crime, neither wishes to return to us nor to reconcile himself with the peace of the Church; rather, together with those followers of his, since he cannot wound the Church and me by deeds, he does not cease to tear us apart by words and curses. Therefore, to say nothing of Oebalus, against whom I believe you are exercising a just and apostolic judgment, I earnestly implore your holiness concerning Manasses: either command him to return to his own possessions and cease henceforth to attack the Church, or direct against him and his supporters and accomplices a punishment worthy of apostolic vigor.

Deign also to write an appropriate letter to those who harbor them, so that they either may not retain them contrary to the rights of the Church, or may acknowledge themselves punished by the same sentence.

It remains for me to tell you that Lord Hugh, bishop of Die, placed our bishop Drogo of the see of Thérouanne under interdict, [Col. 0743D] although he is of such advanced age that, having long remained in the priestly order before his episcopate, he has now held the episcopal rank for more than sixty years and approaches his end almost from moment to moment. Therefore we wish to implore you most earnestly to deign, by your command, to restore him to his ministry, lest—as we greatly fear—he die under this interdict.

As for the matter concerning which you summoned me to send you some soldiers as an escort for the bishop of Paris, I inform you that I intended to send them. But Count Fulk of Arlon, returning from the city of Rome, reported to me on your behalf that you were urgently requesting that deployment of soldiers, so that I might carry out more vigorously and diligently in our region the business of Lady M., the marchioness. Therefore, because this message came from you, the dispatch of the aforementioned expedition was suspended on our part.

May your holiness prosper, most reverend father.

## VIII. Letter of Hugh, bishop of Die, to the pope

[MANSI, Councils, vol. XX.]
