To the most reverend father and lord Pope Gregory, his holiness, his most useless servant, Hugh, humble priest of Die, sends greetings.

Since we have learned that your Parisian R. has returned—we had instructed him, as your son, faithfully to report to you the proceedings of the council of Autun, which he attended—but that he neither returned by way of us nor wrote anything to us concerning your situation, we ask your fatherly care to deign to write us your judgment concerning the ordering of the Churches of Reims, Bourges, and Chartres. [Col. 0744B]

Your fatherly care should also know that the man called the bishop of Noyon, whom we had privately pressed under threat of a public examination, confessed his simony to us in the presence of the bishops of Laon and Langres, together with certain others. He also confirmed to us by an oath over the holy Gospels that, when he saw your letters or your legation, he would willingly relinquish the Church which he had wrongly occupied and would assist, according to his ability and knowledge, in having it properly ordered according to God.

The bishop of Senlis, after receiving investiture from the hand of the king, was ordained by that heresiarch of Reims, whom by your letters you had forbidden to receive men of this sort as bishops. The bishop of Auxerre, ordained before the proper years of age, [Col. 0744C] did not receive investiture from the hand of the king, although he obtained the king’s favor through the king’s household.

As for the archbishop of Sens, how great an insult and injury he inflicted upon your authority during our legation, you have, I hope, heard sufficiently from the aforementioned R. In saying this, God is my witness, I am not seeking my own glory.

The bishop of Bordeaux, moreover, because he was summoned last year to the council of Auvergne but neither came nor canonically excused himself, was suspended from episcopal office at that council. Disregarding this, he usurped the office from which he had been forbidden. Summoned again to the council of Autun, because he sent us no explanation, we also suspended him from the priesthood. [Col. 0744D]

Therefore, concerning all these matters—what your greatness has judged and what you have decided should be done—please write back to our lowliness.

Furthermore, we earnestly ask you to send us the pallium through Bishop Valentine, in order to confirm the ordination of the most devout archbishop of the Church of Lyons, against the barking of heretics and those who carnally rejoice in the king’s indignation against God’s ordination. He himself would have presented himself most devoutly before your holiness, setting aside every hardship and danger of poverty and travel, if the Church entrusted to him—so long languishing and deprived of the comfort of its shepherd—could in any way have endured his absence without great harm.

Give orders to Bishop Valentine, and receive security from him at your hands, so that around the feast of Saint John the Baptist, as we have agreed with him, his Church may receive him to celebrate the liturgy. He seems very well suited to oppose the arrogance of the provincials.

We commend to the grace of your holiness our friend in Christ, Manasses, who at the council of Clermont relinquished into our hands the unlawfully acquired prelacy of the Church of Reims, as a sincere defender of the Catholic faith; and also Lord Bruno, a teacher of the Church of Reims in every form of uprightness [Note: He means the man who later became the founder of the Carthusians.]. Both are worthy to have you confirm them by your authority in the things of God, since they have been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus. Therefore admit them as useful advisers and fellow workers for God’s cause in the regions of France.

The deposition of the heretic of Reims con[lacuna]; revealed iniquity, the blood of heaven, and [lacuna] cry out. Strengthen [lacuna] by a written act of your authority [lacuna]; we ask that you send these [lacuna] to the Church of Reims [lacuna] his satisfaction, or, if it pleases you, command that he himself [lacuna], or that we receive it [lacuna]. Because [lacuna] they made an episcopal election without consulting us, despite your excommunication.

Your son Tiezo would already have returned to you, if he had not been detained to summon the council which, with God’s consent, is to be held at Poitiers on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. At that council we humbly beseech you to grant us the protection of your merits.

Pray for us, most holy Father.

(I believe that what Pope Gregory has above, in letter 17 of book V, first indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of [Col. 0745C] March, pertains to this matter.)

## IX. Letter of the Saxons to Gregory VII

—What they did to obey his decrees; they complain that he favors them less and their adversaries more.

[MANSI, Councils XX, 385.]

Your holiness knows, and it is known to everyone around us, with what difficulty and at what risk to our bearers we send legations to you, because the road which at all times was open to all peoples, tribes, and languages is now closed particularly to those who have labored greatly for the honor of the one whose body that same road leads to.

And afterward:

After a long wait, when our messenger returned, the only consolation he brought us was that you had not given credence to the reports which we had conveyed. From this, dearest lord, it has seemed incredible to you that our brothers and fellow bishops, the bishops of Würzburg and Passau, together with other religious men, reported the truth to you, and that they testified to having seen and heard it. Certainly, we do not trust in words of falsehood to be delivered; rather, we believe that the Truth will deliver us. God has not abandoned those who hope in him.

For our king Rudolf, strong in him who grants salvation to kings, has triumphantly conquered the Lord’s enemies. Henry, however, together with his accomplices—apart from those who fell by the sword—has been put to flight, along with that count whose wickedness you tried in vain to overcome with goodness: Robert of Bamberg, who is the author and instigator of all these things. [Col. 0746A] If only you had been sufficiently instructed concerning his deceit and that of his associates! Do not, dearest lord, any longer flatter such men to the mockery of your holy name, nor, after so many repeated rejections, again seek guidance from them.

Your coming to us would be as desirable to us as it is necessary; but we truly know that you will never come of your own will to our regions unless they are certain that you favor their party.

And afterward:

Therefore, if not for our sake, at least for the honor of the apostolic see, confirm what the legate of that see has done, so that you may announce without ambiguity what must be held and followed in this division of the Church. If this had been done long ago, perhaps the unjust party would by now have lost so much strength that it could harm neither us nor you.

We also ask that you not allow these canonical statutes to fail: do not permit the bodies of the excommunicated who were killed while persecuting the Church to be buried in churchyards; and wherever they have been buried, prohibit the celebration of divine offices. Many of them have been buried in the city of Augsburg. You can easily send your letters to the communities of that place through passing pilgrims.

## X. Letter of the Saxons who favor Rudolf to Gregory

[In MANSI, same work.]

Your excellence and your letters, which we possess as testimony, bear witness that you deprived our king of his royal dignity—not for our counsel or our cause, but for the injuries inflicted upon the apostolic see. You also forbade us, with a terrible threat, to serve him as king; you released all Christians from the bond of the oath which they had sworn or would swear to him, and bound him with the chain of anathema.

In all these matters we obeyed your fatherhood at great risk to ourselves, as is now evident. And because we did not wish to agree with the one who had been deposed concerning your deposition of him, together with the others, he exercised such cruelty against us that many of our people, having lost all their possessions, gave their lives in this struggle and left their children disinherited and the rich poor. Those who remain, daily anxious for their lives, have lost almost all the means of sustaining life. [Col. 0746D]

But when he could not overcome us by any persecution, he himself was overcome, so that, though unwillingly, he appeared before us and, to his own disgrace, rendered honor to the one whom he had dishonored. For this labor we received the following reward: that the man who had been compelled, at the peril of our souls, to adore your footsteps was absolved without our counsel and without correction, and regained the freedom to harm us.

And after a short interval:

Since, therefore, we had already been without a ruler for more than a year, another of our princes was substituted, by selection, in the place from which he had defected. And when hope of an elected king, rather than of kings, began to arise for the restoration of the empire, behold, unexpectedly, your letters proclaimed two kings in one kingdom and assigned a legation to each. The plurality of the royal name and the division of the kingdom were followed also by the division of the people and the parties’ allegiances, since they saw in your letters that the person of the transgressor was always placed first and that he was required, as though he were powerful, to provide you with a dukedom into these regions for investigating the case.

And afterward:

This also troubles our weakness: just as we are urged to remain firmly in what we have begun, so hope is suggested in words and deeds to the opposing party. For the household members of the aforementioned Henry—men branded with infamy throughout the kingdom, openly disobedient to the synodal commands by serving him as king, and separated from the Church, together with their head, by the apostolic legate—come to this see and are received kindly. They return not only unpunished but crowned with glory and honor, and, returning proudly to their former disobedience, insult our misery.

We are treated as though ridiculous and foolish because we abstain from the company of those whom our very head receives so charitably into communion.

This also adds to the accumulation of our misfortune: besides the faults which we ourselves commit, the guilt of our adversaries is forged against us, since it is attributed to our negligence that we do not send suitable and frequent legates here. For it is clearer than daylight that those men prevent this, although they promised you under oath that they would not prevent it. [Col. 0747C] And now the obstruction of the dangerous journey and their manifest perjury are passed over in silence, while the failure to send messengers is charged against us.

We know and hope, from consideration of your piety, that you are doing all these things with good intention and some subtle deliberation. But we, inexperienced men, unable to penetrate that hidden dispensation, report to you that what we have plainly heard and seen concerning the strengthening of both parties and the uncertain postponement of definite measures has arisen and continues daily to arise—namely, civil wars, innumerable murders, devastation and burning of houses and churches indiscriminately, oppression of the poor, plundering of ecclesiastical goods such as we have never heard of, and the collapse of divine and secular laws without hope of restoration. Finally, in the struggle of the two kings, each of whom receives from you hope of obtaining the kingdom, there has been such destruction of royal resources that thereafter the kings of our regions will have to be sustained by plunder.

These evils would either already not exist or would be much smaller if your judgment had turned neither to the right nor to the left.

And after an interval:

For if what was defined in the Roman synod and afterward confirmed by the legate of the apostolic see must be concealed in silence, we have absolutely no idea what we should henceforth believe or regard as settled.

## XI. Letter of William, king of the English, to Gregory VII

—Warned by the legate to render fidelity to the pontiff and to send money to Rome, the king agreed concerning the money but refused concerning the fidelity because it was unprecedented.

[LANFRANC, Works, p. 304.]

[Col. 0748A]

To the most excellent shepherd of the holy Church, Gregory, the glorious William, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of the Northmen, sends greetings with friendship.

Hubert, your legate, reverend Father, came to me on your behalf and admonished me to render fidelity to you and your successors and to reconsider more favorably the money which my predecessors were accustomed to send to the Roman Church. I accepted one request and did not accept the other.

I did not wish, and do not wish, to render fidelity, because I find neither that I promised it nor that my predecessors did so to your predecessors. The money was collected negligently for nearly three years while I was in Gaul. Now, by divine mercy, since I have returned to my kingdom, what has been collected is being sent through the aforementioned legate; and what remains will be sent through the legates of Lanfranc, our faithful archbishop, when the opportunity arises.

Pray for us and for the condition of our kingdom, because we have loved your predecessors and desire sincerely to love you above all and to hear you obediently.

## XII. Oath of Robert, called bishop of Chartres, whom Gregory VII mentions in Book IV, letter 14 of his Register

[MANSI, Councils XX, 461.]

[Col. 0748C]

I, Robert, promise to almighty God and to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose body rests here, that whenever a legate of the apostolic see sent by our lord Gregory, who is now Roman pontiff, or by any of his successors, likewise Roman pontiffs, comes to me, within the period which that legate [variant: “the same legate”] shall establish for me, I shall relinquish the bishopric of Chartres, with every pretext and fraud removed. I shall faithfully endeavor that that Church be ordered according to God, doing nothing knowingly, either personally or through any person sent by me, whereby that Church or its clergy might suffer injury or loss through my efforts or malice.

I, Cono, humble priest of the title of Christ the Martyr and of Saint Anastasia the Virgin, wrote this oath at the command of our lord Pope Gregory VII, and I was present in the Church of blessed Peter, at the confession, beside his body, where it was made. Also present were John, bishop of Porto; Theodinus, archdeacon; Gregory and Bernard, deacons [deacon] of the holy Roman Church; and two others, namely Ingelrannus [Engelramus], dean of the Church of Chartres, and Ivo, then master of the schools in that same Church.

Done at Rome in the month of April, fourteenth indiction.

[Col. 0749]

## Decree of Pope Gregory VII

(MANSI, Councils XX, 385.)

[Col. 0749A]

Pope Gregory VII and Pope Urban II established that the feasts of the Roman pontiffs should be celebrated: those of martyrs with nine lessons, and those of confessors with at least three lessons, except for certain men who were regarded as especially renowned because of their excellence, such as Saint Sylvester, Gregory, and others. For if every Church solemnly observes the feast of its own patron—and, if he was a confessor, observes it as such—how much more should it honor those who have been not so much patrons as Fathers of the whole Church, and who did not cease to instruct it by word and example even unto martyrdom? [Col. 0750A]

For these holy martyrs, the invitatory, hymn, responsories, psalms, and verses are sung as for martyrs. Note also that Saint Gregory I, the pope, established in the gradual book offices for these martyrs, just as for confessors administering pontifical offices: for Saint Marcellus, pope and martyr, *The Lord established him*; and for Saint Felix, pope and martyr, *Priests*. This is certainly quite appropriate because of the excellence of apostolic dignity.

# Part Three of the Works of Saint Gregory VII, Roman Pontiff

## Roman Councils

[Roman Councils.]

## First Roman Council for Reforming the State of the Church

Held in the year of the Lord 1074.

(From MANSI, Collection of Councils, vol. XX, col. 401.)

[Col. 0749B]

Gregory, following in the footsteps of his predecessors, announced through a letter sent to the bishops of Lombardy that a synod was to be held in the first week of Lent. On the appointed day, the bishops who had been summoned attended in great number.

At the outset, to cleanse the Church of priests living with concubines, they established, as Lambert says, that “according to the provisions of the ancient canons, priests are not to have wives; those who have them must either dismiss them or be deposed. No one at all is to be admitted to the priesthood who does not profess perpetual continence and a celibate life.”

When the bishops had promulgated this constitution in Germany at the pope’s command, the events which Lambert describes for the year 1074 occurred in these words:

“Against this decree [Col. 0749C] the whole faction of the clergy immediately roared with fierce indignation, loudly declaring that the man was plainly a heretic and of insane doctrine. He had forgotten the Lord’s saying, ‘Not everyone can receive this word; let the one who can receive it receive it’ (Matthew 19:11–12), and the Apostle’s: ‘If he cannot remain continent, let him marry; for it is better to marry than to burn’ (1 Corinthians 7:5). By violent compulsion he was forcing men to live according to the way of angels, and, while denying nature its customary course, was loosening the reins on fornication and impurity. If he persisted in confirming his judgment, they would prefer to abandon the priesthood rather than marriage; and then he would see, since human beings were displeasing to him, where he would obtain angels to govern the peoples through the Church of God.”

Nevertheless, he persisted, and through repeated legations accused all the bishops of sluggishness and negligence. He threatened that, unless they quickly carried out the task imposed upon them, he would take action against them by apostolic censure.

The archbishop of Mainz, knowing that it was no small undertaking to tear out a custom rooted over so long a period and to reform an already aging world according to the beginnings of the nascent Church, dealt with them more moderately. First, he granted them a delay of six months and an opportunity for deliberation, urging them voluntarily to do what necessarily had to be done and thereby to remove from himself and the Roman pontiff the necessity of decreeing something otherwise against them.

Finally, when a synod had been convened at Erfurt in October, he pressed them more closely, [Col. 0751A] demanding that, with every evasion set aside, they should immediately either renounce marriage or withdraw from the ministry of the sacred altar.

They, on the other hand, brought forward many arguments by which they tried to elude the pressing and urgent harshness [perhaps, “importunity”] and to invalidate the judgment. Since neither arguments nor supplications and prayers achieved anything against the authority of the apostolic see—which he claimed compelled him to this demand against his own will—they went out as though to deliberate and resolved not to return to the synod, but all to depart to their homes without permission.

Some even shouted in confused voices that it seemed better to them to return to the synod, drive the bishop from his episcopal chair before he promulgated his execrable judgment against them, and, after punishing him with deserved death, transmit a notable memorial to posterity, so that none of his successors would thereafter attempt to bring such a calumny against the priestly name.

When it was reported to the bishop that they were plotting this, his people warned him to forestall the rising tumult with timely moderation. He sent outside to them and asked them, with their minds calmed, to return to the synod. He said that, as soon as an opportunity arose, he would send to Rome and, if possible, persuade the apostolic lord to withdraw from the severity of this judgment.

The next day, after laymen and clergy had been admitted together into the audience chamber, he renewed the old complaint concerning the restoration of tithes, and so forth.

At this same synod Robert Guiscard, prince of the Northmen, was excommunicated. Concerning him, the following is reported toward the end of the first book of Gregory’s letters:

“He held a synod at Rome in which, among the other matters conducted there, he excommunicated and anathematized Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, together with all his supporters, until he should repent.”

After this, the cases of various abbots and bishops were heard and judged.

The canons of Poitiers were granted the privilege that their bishop, dean, or some other prelate should retain the right, on certain days, to sing Mass in another and exempt church, as was customarily observed at Rome and elsewhere in the station churches.

By decree of this synod, the Churches of Spain were ordered to receive the Roman order and rite, as the Spanish bishops who were present had promised to do. [Col. 0751D]

Moreover, a letter from Géza, king of Hungary, was read. In it the king expressed his incomparable devotion and reverence toward the apostolic see, asking that no credence be given to the complaints and slanderous accusations of his hostile enemies.

At the same synod, William, bishop of Beauvais, offered a worthy example of Christian charity and episcopal modesty. Although he had suffered very serious injuries from his own people, both clerics and laymen, he interceded with the pontiff for those who had been excommunicated for that reason and asked and obtained their absolution from excommunication.

The canons of Lucca were summoned to this same synod to give an account [Col. 0752A] of why they had conspired against their bishop, Anselm of Lucca. Convicted of conspiracy and of the plots prepared against their bishop, they too, in accordance with the canons and the chapter of Saint Fabian, martyr and pontiff—which decrees that conspirators and plotters against their bishops are to be handed over to the curia—were, by the judgment of the entire holy synod, handed over to the curia.

This is drawn from Gregory’s letter 51 and the following ten letters, and from Baronius, year 1074, no. 36 and following.

See Gregory’s letter to Otto, bishop of Constance, below in chapter 1 of the following apologetic work. There he briefly and summarily informs him about the matters conducted at this synod and orders him to promulgate the salutary decrees issued there against simoniacs and priests living in concubinage.

A certain author of this period wrote an apologetic discourse for this synod. It survives in a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Weingarten, from which we reproduce it here.

## Table of Chapters

I. The decretal letter of the venerable Pope Gregory, etc.

II. On the authority of the four principal ecumenical councils.

III. On the authority of the apostolic constitutions.

IV. On the authority of the remaining councils.

V. A brief enumeration of the decrees of the preceding letter.

VI. On the first statute, that is, on the simoniacs.

VII. On the second statute, that is, on the buyers of churches.

VIII. That sacred Scripture also condemns sellers of spiritual offices.

IX–X. Likewise, that it condemns the buyers of such offices, and that it condemns the intermediaries in this transaction.

XI. On the third statute of the said decretal letter: that incontinent men may in no way minister at the altar.

XII. On the anathema of those who defend the incontinence of priests, drawn from chapter [lacuna] of Sozomen from the *Tripartite History*.

XIII. That permission to have a wife has been granted not to ministers of sacred things but to laymen, so that each person may have his own wife.

XIV. What the Apostle establishes concerning the sacred orders.

XV. A useful consideration of the same institution.

XVI. An exposition by blessed Jerome on the same institution.

XVII. On the fourth statute of the aforementioned decretal letter: that the people should not receive the offices of clerics whom they see despising the apostolic statutes.

XVIII. Why their offices have been forbidden to the people.

XIX. An explanation of a certain chapter which seemed to oppose the present statute.

XX. What compelled the apostolic lord to issue these statutes.

XXI. That indignation should be directed not against those men but against the holy Fathers for statutes of this kind.

XXII. Why no delays were attached to these same statutes.

XXIII. That the apostolic lord can condemn not only bishops but also their subjects.

XXIV. That the parishioner of any bishop owes obedience to the apostolic lord even more than to his own bishop.

# Apologetic Work on the Decrees Which the Venerable Pope Gregory VII Promulgated in the Roman Synod against Simoniacs and Incontinent Ministers of the Altar

## Prologue

In the preceding letters I endeavored to satisfy that man who was our rival—God forbid that I should henceforth call him so—but our very dear friend. I clearly demonstrated that the chapter contrary to the statutes of our apostolic lord was in no way to be heeded, since it was expressly forbidden under anathema. Thus our friend wrote back to me that he would devote himself no longer to contention but to friendship.

Yet many still remain who stubbornly resist those same statutes, with great danger—indeed, with great ruin. They also mislead other simpler people, who are not very diligent in examining the canons, to such an extent that these too disregard the authoritative sanctions mentioned above and insist on retaining their own custom, extremely pleasant indeed but extremely pernicious.

In my view, more of them would not have done this if they had properly understood how little—and rather, how not at all—our apostolic lord departs in the aforementioned statutes from the holy Fathers. Therefore I judged that it would be useful for me and others like me to compare those statutes with the canonical writings, briefly and faithfully to commend their mutual agreement, however limited my literary ability may be, and to do so with this intention: that if perhaps one of the unlearned should deign to examine this work, he might more vigorously recover his senses and obey the apostolic decrees, the more clearly he saw that these decrees in no way depart from the most sacred canons but proceeded from those same canons through sacred Scripture itself.

## Chapters

### I

First, therefore, it is useful to set down the decretal letter of our apostolic lord, so that what follows may shine forth all the more clearly.

“Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Otto, bishop of Constance, greetings and apostolic blessing.

‘The persistence of your messengers,’ etc. It appears above among the letters.

### II

But before we consider the statutes individually, I think it useful to offer a preliminary word about the authority of the canons themselves, so that whatever is announced to us from them for observance may be held all the more firmly.

Most holy Pope Gregory, whom our apostolic lord has represented in our own times both in name and in conduct, confirms the four most holy councils in his synodical—that is, synodal—letter as follows:

“Just as I confess that there are four holy Gospels, so I confess that there are four councils which I receive and venerate: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius is destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius is refuted; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius is judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus is condemned. I embrace them with complete devotion and guard them with unimpaired approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises, and the norm of every life and action stands firm. Whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

“But I reject all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject, and I embrace those whom they venerate; for since they were established by universal consent, whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Thus far Gregory.

This same apostolic man composed this synodal letter immediately after his ordination and sent it to the other patriarchs—namely, those of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem. For at that time it was customary for anyone newly ordained to one of the patriarchal sees to declare, in a letter sent to the other sees, that he observed the aforesaid four synods, before he could deserve to have his name entered in the diptychs at the other sees. The name of his predecessor, even though he was dead, was counted by the other sees among the living until they received the synodal letter of the newly enthroned bishop. Since that letter indicated that the same bishop accepted the four synods, it seems not inappropriate that they borrowed from those synods the name “synodical” for it.

That this was the custom of that time is attested by the same most holy pope in his letter to Secundinus, servant of God and recluse. John, deacon of the Roman Church, asserts that the custom continued until the time of blessed Pope Hadrian, specifically until the time of King Charles; on the order of Pope John, he faithfully composed the Life of Saint Gregory. Whether the same custom still continues, however, I do not know, although I have no doubt that it existed in the times mentioned.

It is therefore most clearly evident how great is the authority of those four councils, which Saint Gregory—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit—not merely once, as stated above, but repeatedly compares with the Gospels, and anathematizes all who dissent from them. Every newly appointed patriarch was also required, in a letter of his own, to profess to the other sees that he would observe them, if he wished to have himself entered among the Catholic patriarchs in the diptychs.

### III.

As for the decrees of the most holy Roman pontiffs, we ought, if possible, to venerate and observe them even more diligently than those four councils, since the councils themselves would lack all firmness if the pontiffs of the apostolic see had not decided to convene and confirm them by apostolic authority.

Thus blessed Pope Marcellus, who consecrated his decrees to martyrdom before the Council of Nicaea, that apostolic man himself testifies in the eleventh chapter of his decrees:

“The apostles themselves and their successors, under the inspiration of the Lord, established that no synod should be held without the authority of the Roman see.”

Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, who was no small part of the Council of Nicaea, likewise says in chapter 2 of his letter to Pope Felix:

“We know that at the great Council of Nicaea, consisting of three hundred and eighteen bishops, it was unanimously confirmed by all that councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff.”

Blessed Pope Julius also professes the same thing in chapter 5, saying:

“The rights and judgments of convening general councils have been granted, by a singular privilege, to the Church of the first see through evangelical, apostolic, and canonical institutions.”

Blessed Pope Damasus likewise inserted this judgment in chapter 9 of his decrees:

“No councils are ever read as having been ratified that were not supported by apostolic authority.”

Blessed Isidore, the most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, faithfully agrees with these judgments, saying:

“The authority to convene synods has been entrusted by private power to the apostolic see; nor do we read that any synod is valid which was not convened and supported by its authority.”

Canonical authority testifies to this. Ecclesiastical history confirms it. The holy Fathers establish it.

If, then, those four councils would lack all authority unless they principally received their firmness from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, who could deny how much more deserving of veneration the decrees promulgated by those apostolic men are rightly considered than the councils themselves, which deserved to become authoritative not through the presence of those apostolic men but only through their legates?

For in this way the legates of the apostolic see, by their primary subscription, canonized the decrees of those principal councils in the place of the apostolic see. Under the most devout emperor Constantine, the great Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the Roman Church, presided at the Council of Nicaea on behalf of holy Pope Sylvester, and confirmed it by their primary subscription.

Likewise, in the time of the younger Theodosius Augustus, Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, and Arcadius, bishop from Italy, presided at the Council of Ephesus in the place of blessed Pope Celestine, and strengthened it in the apostolic capacity.

Likewise, in the time of Emperor Marcian, the bishops Paschasius and Lucentius and the presbyter Boniface, in the place of Saint Pope Leo, were the first at the Council of Chalcedon, which was held over twelve days. They generously opposed Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, when he usurped a certain privilege in the council, and subscribed to the remaining decrees in the apostolic capacity, as the book of Liberatus, deacon of Carthage, testifies concerning that council.

Anyone who carefully examines the subscriptions of those councils will see all this still more clearly.

Therefore, the reverence or obedience which, following Saint Gregory, we rightly show to the four most sacred councils, we must in no way withhold from the decrees of the apostolic see. Rather, if possible, we ought to show it even more diligently, since without the authority of those decrees it would not have been lawful to receive the councils themselves.

### IV. [Col. 0756A]

Nor ought we to disregard the remaining councils, in which we find many things found nowhere else but nevertheless necessary for the Church’s administration. These do not in any way disagree with the higher authoritative decrees, since they agree most openly with the Christian religion.

Such chapters, I say, wherever they are found in councils, must not be despised by any Catholic, especially since there can be no doubt that the other councils themselves proceeded from the authority of those most sacred decrees, which most firmly order that two councils of bishops be held every year in each province.

Blessed Anacletus, ordained presbyter by the prince of the apostles himself, most certainly decrees this in chapter 17 of his decrees:

“A gathering of the highest-ranking men is accustomed to take place, and ought to take place, every year.”

The excellent Council of Nicaea established this in chapter 5:

“It has seemed very good that councils be held twice a year in each province, so that such questions may be examined when all the bishops have been gathered together in common.”

The Council of Constantinople, after listing the privileges of various Churches, establishes in chapter 2:

“While the rule written concerning administrations is preserved, it is clear that matters belonging to each province should be administered by the synod of that province, just as it is established to have been decreed by the Council of Nicaea.”

The Council of Chalcedon says in chapter 19:

“The holy synod has decreed, according to the canons of the Fathers, that the bishops of each province come together twice a year, wherever the metropolitan bishop has approved, in order to correct whatever may perhaps have arisen.”

It is therefore clear that the authoritative decrees also command that provincial councils be held. They would command this in vain unless they also determined that we should observe the sound judgments of those councils.

Accordingly, the Third Council of Toledo universally decreed:

“Whoever does not accept the councils of orthodox bishops that agree with the four most holy councils, let him be anathema.”

Therefore, whoever attempts to oppose the reasonable statutes of these councils is also shown, at his own peril, to dissent from the higher authoritative decrees.

Blessed Isidore also agrees with these arguments in the eleventh chapter of one of his prefaces concerning the canons, as follows:

“It must also be known that, although the others are not invalidated, there are four principal councils.”

After listing these, he adds in the same chapter:

“But if there are councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established, then, after the authority of these four, they remain established with complete force.”

It is therefore fitting that the statutes of councils of this kind also be obeyed. For if it is acknowledged to be no small folly when someone refuses to yield to the sound counsel of any single person, how much more blameworthy does it appear when someone shamelessly resists statutes of this kind, issued and approved not by the authority and judgment of one wise man but of many?

Indeed, many Catholic and distinguished teachers are read as having taken part in such councils. In the African councils there were the legates of the apostolic see, the bishops Faustinus, Honoratus, and Urbanus; also Saint Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage; and Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, a man endowed with every virtue.

Celestine, an apostolic man, commends Augustine to us in his decrees as follows:

“Augustine, a man of holy memory, we have always held in our communion on account of his life and merits, and never has even a rumor of sinister suspicion touched him. We remember that he was once a man of such great learning that even by my predecessors he was counted among the teachers. Therefore all rightly formed the same judgment about him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.”

As the book of Liberatus testifies, Emperor Theodosius also instructed Augustine by his sacred command to present himself at the Council of Ephesus. But alas, so outstanding a teacher had already been taken from the world before the letter of invitation from the Roman emperor could reach him.

Those whom I have mentioned, therefore, together with innumerable other holy Fathers, attended the African councils—or rather, presided over them.

Likewise Saint Marianus [Marinus] attended the Council of Arles, approved by Saint Pope Sylvester; Saint Caesarius, the Council of Agde; Saint Hilary, the Council of Orange; Saint Albinus, the Council of Orléans; and Saint Boniface, the Council of Mainz.

[Note: [Col. 0757] No one has yet explained what that council was or who that Albinus was.]

Other saints are likewise read as having taken part in other councils, not alone but together with many other holy Fathers. They are believed to have been so distinguished in Christian religion and doctrine that it would have been excessively rash to oppose the individual judgment of even one of them.

Therefore, it is much more intolerable not to yield to the judgment of many wise men—at least in those chapters that do not conflict with the authoritative statutes mentioned above but unquestionably support Christian discipline.

For, according to the judgment of blessed Augustine, nothing that is found opposed to canonical truth in any council or anywhere else is to be accepted out of reverence for any person.

Moreover, it is beyond doubt that the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon also canonized provincial councils held before it, decreeing in chapter 1:

“We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council up to the present time retain their proper force.”

The councils that are read to have preceded Chalcedon were the Councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which are reported to be older even than the Council of Nicaea; also the Councils of Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, and Laodicea. Therefore, there is no doubt that the same councils were also confirmed at the Council of Chalcedon. It is likewise read that Pope Hadrian gave these councils, together with the African canons, to Emperor Charles at Rome for the regulation of the Churches in his kingdom.

Accordingly, the statutes of provincial councils must not rashly be rejected by anyone, since the apostolic see has judged that they should be received.

Let what has been said about the authority of the sacred canons suffice. Let us now return to our subject and arrange in order the statutes which our apostolic lord most carefully described and sent in the preceding letter to Otto, bishop of Constance.

### V. [Col. 0758A]

The first of these was that clerics who had obtained any grade or office of sacred orders by payment should thereafter in no way minister in the Church; the second, that no one should retain a Church acquired by payment, and that no one thereafter should be permitted to sell or buy the rights of a Church; the third, that all who make themselves blameworthy through incontinence should cease from clerical office; the fourth, that the people should in no way accept the services of clerics whom they see despising apostolic institutions.

Let us therefore proceed through these points individually and briefly demonstrate, not from our own conjectures but from the statutes of the holy Fathers, how authoritative, how deserving of attention, and indeed how unavoidable they are.

### VI. [Col. 0758B]

The first statute is found most fully and clearly in the Council of Chalcedon. This council is one of the four mentioned above; in time it was the last, though not in dignity. The holy Fathers ordered Leo Augustus to vindicate it even to the shedding of blood, as Liberatus testifies in his book.

In that council it is written in chapter 2:

“If any bishop performs an ordination for money, and reduces to a price the grace that cannot be sold; if he ordains for money a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or anyone at all numbered among the clergy; or if he promotes for money a steward, defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the advantage of his own most shameful profit, then the person proven to have attempted this shall be subject to the loss of his own rank. The person ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or promotion, which was carried out by trafficking, but shall be excluded from the dignity or office which he acquired with money.

“If anyone has acted as a mediator in such shameful and impious payments or receipts, he too, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized.”

It should be noted how carefully this chapter excludes every stratagem of the Simonians, since it deposes, without any hope of recovery, everyone promoted by money in whatever manner.

For Simonians customarily purchase sacred dignities in various ways but with one and the same guilt. Sometimes they themselves, sometimes their friends on their behalf, have given the price for a sacred dignity before their ordination, or give it at the time of ordination, or promise to give it afterward—sometimes to their electors, sometimes to those who ordain them, and finally to any of their supporters.

Therefore, whoever promotes anyone by one of these methods, or recognizes that he himself has been promoted in this way, is unquestionably ordered by the foregoing chapter to be degraded, since there can be no doubt that either he has promoted another by money or has himself been promoted by it.

Nor should it be passed over without consideration that this same chapter condemned two kinds of traffickers: first, those who are ordained by money to the diaconate, presbyterate, or some similar grade; and second, those who are promoted by money to the ministry of administration or to some similar clerical office, such as the office of vicedominus, provost, dean, archpresbyter, and the like.

Thus our apostolic lord also included two kinds of traffickers, and all the tricks of those who traffic, in his first statute. In it he deposes clerics who have acquired, in any manner whatsoever by money, any grade or office of sacred orders. Yet this statute is plainly milder than the preceding chapter, since it does not punish with the due penalty the sellers of spiritual offices or the mediators of such wicked commerce, whom the aforementioned chapter decreed should be degraded and anathematized together with the buyers.

And consider: if the mediator is rightly ordered to be degraded or anathematized, what do you think of the man who is unworthily promoted through the same commerce?

This is precisely what most holy Pope Gregory—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit—unquestionably decreed concerning such traffickers. He was accustomed to dictate to the ear of that apostolic man, under the form of a dove, whatever had to be decreed.

For it is written in chapter 131 of his decrees:

“Whoever therefore strives to purchase ecclesiastical office by giving a price, since he pays attention not to the office but to the name, desires not to be a priest but merely to be called one without substance.”

A little later in the same chapter—book IX of the Letters, letter 34—he says:

“Since it is clear that this heresy first crept in with a pestilential root and was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation, why is it not guarded against? Why is it not understood that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic?”

What wonder, then, if our apostolic lord separated from ecclesiastical ministries only those whom his most holy namesake declared to be separated from the Church together with the other heretics?

### VII. [Col. 0759C]

The second statute of our apostolic lord, which orders that Churches be taken away from their buyers, also appears to be contained, although obscurely, in the aforementioned chapter of the Council of Chalcedon. That chapter likewise orders the ministry of administering Church property to be removed from an administrator promoted by money.

Every presbyter ought to be an administrator, not only of preaching but also of the Church’s property entrusted to him; and the holy Fathers judged that such property should be administered not merely for the needs of the presbyter but for the needs of all who are in want.

Moreover, in the same chapter every ecclesiastical office acquired by money is ordered to be taken away from any cleric. To care for the Church itself with priestly diligence is, if I am not mistaken, a clerical and ecclesiastical responsibility. Therefore, in the same chapter, care of a Church usurped by money is ordered to be removed.

Accordingly, blessed Pope Gregory, writing to Clement of Byzantium [perhaps Byzacena] concerning a certain presbyter, decrees as follows:

“If that presbyter had obtained a certain Church by money, he should be deprived not only of that Church but also of the honor of the presbyterate.”

Likewise, in the ancient councils of our provinces—the Councils of Mainz, Reims, and Tours—it is read that a presbyter who acquired a Church by payment is to be deprived both of the presbyterate and of the Church.

Blessed Pope Leo, ninth of that name and almost contemporary with our own time, also utterly condemned the Simoniac heresy in his first Roman synod and prohibited, under anathema, the buying and selling of altars. Those who afterward presumed to engage in such wicked commerce did not escape that anathema.

It is therefore worth considering how mercifully our apostolic lord has merely taken purchased Churches away from their buyers, when he knew that, according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, they ought to be deprived of both Church and presbyterate—or rather, of the Christian name and communion as well.

### VIII. [Col. 0760B]

But why do we labor so greatly to demonstrate that the statutes of our apostolic lord proceeded from the synodal judgments of the holy Fathers, when I think no learned person can doubt that they flowed from the treasury of sacred Scripture itself?

For in that Scripture all the persons involved in such wicked commerce are found condemned: sellers, buyers of spiritual offices, and mediators of this transaction.

The Lord himself expelled both buyers and sellers from his temple, and already then overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matthew 21:12). Our Saint Gregory the Theologian explains this in his twenty-second homily as follows:

“The seat of those selling doves is overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood both before human eyes and before the eyes of God. And rightly so, for Truth itself commands in the Gospel: ‘You received freely; give freely’ (Matthew 10:8). Since such men do not heed this, they alienate themselves from God, who says in the same Gospel: ‘He who is of God hears the words of God. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God’ (John 8:47).”

Moreover, the prince of the apostles, Peter—or rather, Christ himself through him—commands all prelates in the Church:

“Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight not under compulsion but willingly, according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly” (1 Peter 5:2).

Those act against this command who shamefully provide this spiritual office to their subjects for worldly profit. Concerning them the same apostle testifies in his second letter:

“They followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the reward of iniquity; but he received a rebuke for his madness: a mute beast, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly” (2 Peter 2:15–16).

The venerable presbyter Bede clarifies this in his commentary on the same letter:

“Some Catholics love the reward of iniquity so greatly that, although learned, they are rightly torn apart by the unlearned, and clerics by laymen. They are rightly compared to the prophet who is rebuked by the words of a she-ass speaking contrary to nature, yet is not restrained from his intended evil path.”

This Balaam is said to be the same man who is read to have taught blessed Job excessively and arrogantly, and who was called Elihu—that is, “divine”—from the office of divination. Thus Saint Jerome testifies in his book *On Hebrew Questions*.

When this man was a prophet hired by Balak, king of the Moabites, to curse the children of Israel, he indeed attempted, for payment, to curse them by the word of the Lord; but because the Lord forbade it, he did not bring his wickedness to completion, nor did he receive the reward of iniquity. Nevertheless, he is marked as so rejected by God that his she-ass is read to have rebuked his wisdom—or rather, his madness and folly—and to have rescued him from the sword of the resisting angel. The angel himself testified that she would not have died, even if he had struck down that rejected prophet with the death he deserved.

If, then, Balaam is read to have been so rejected merely because he loved the reward of iniquity, how much more must that man be counted among the rejected who, together with Balaam, eagerly demands payment for the most wicked sale of a spiritual office and does not desist until he brings his ambition to completion?

Moreover, blessed Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, testifies that the scribe who said to Jesus, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go” (Matthew 8:19), was rejected by the Lord because he wished to follow him in the manner of Simon Magus, in order to obtain profit from the miracles of his works. Hence the Lord answered him:

“Foxes have dens” (ibid.), and so forth.

It was as though he said: “Why do you wish to follow me for the sake of profits and riches, when I am so poor that I do not even have a lodging of my own, although even foxes and birds have their own habitations?”

If, then, the man who wished to exercise a spiritual office solely for profit is rightly rejected by the Lord himself, how much more is the man to be rejected who is discovered to have sold such an office outright to others?

### IX. [Col. 0761C]

Buyers of spiritual offices are read as condemned in the Acts of the Apostles together with their prince, Simon Magus. There our Simon, the prince of the apostles, imposed eternal condemnation upon the other Simon, prince of the apostates, decreeing as follows:

“May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money. You have neither part nor share in this matter. Your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.”

Simon answered:

“Pray for me to the Lord, so that none of the things you have said may come upon me” (Acts 8:20–24).

Observe that the heresiarch Simon Magus was condemned by his namesake for a wicked thought alone. We do not read that he actually carried out such wicked commerce; we read only that he thought of purchasing a spiritual office. Do you see how reasonably those are condemned who not only eagerly desire, like Simon Magus, to purchase spiritual offices, but also complete the transaction they desire, and who do not fear to use—or rather, abuse—what they have acquired wickedly?

They therefore appear to surpass Simon Magus considerably in guilt. He never brought to completion the purchase that he wrongly desired. Condemned for his wicked desire alone, he sought through the apostles to avoid the sentence of condemnation before the Lord, not to obtain more criminally the office that he had criminally desired.

But why would that heresiarch have desired to purchase a spiritual office unless he intended afterward to sell it still more wickedly? For it does not seem to have been written without reason that he foolishly admired signs and virtues and wished, by means of his money, to acquire the ability to perform them himself—namely, as Saint Jerome asserts, in order to obtain temporal profit from miracles.

Therefore, not only buyers but also sellers of spiritual offices are marked as followers of the aforesaid heresiarch. There can be no doubt that they are bound together with him by the bond of eternal condemnation, as blessed Gelasius attests in chapter 24 of his decrees:

“Those who are clearly found to have purchased sacred dignity without deserving it must be expelled once convicted. Those who commit such a crime do so at their peril, because the condemnation of Simon, which sacred Scripture attests, embraces both the giver and the receiver.”

Blessed Pope Gelasius, treating this general judgment in connection with the ordinations of the individual grades, included among them doorkeepers, notaries, and defenders. These are not ordained through the imposition of hands, nor are they themselves permitted to impose hands upon anyone. For this reason there is no doubt that Saint Alexander calls that man a Simonian who, for payment, assists a penitent before a bishop in obtaining reconciliation.

From this it follows that not only those are reckoned among the Simonians who attain the imposition of hands through payment, but also those who acquire other clerical offices by money.

The same Spirit works all things in such offices (1 Corinthians 12:11); to give and receive his gift not freely but for payment is not Catholic but unquestionably Simoniac.

### X. [Col. 0762C]

The mediators of this most wicked commerce are likewise condemned by the chosen vessel, who denounces them as follows:

“They deserve death not only who do such wicked things but also those who consent to those who do them” (Romans 1:32).

Likewise our harpist David says:

“If you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Psalm 49:18).

And:

“Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue contrived deceit” (ibid.).

Then, in the same psalm, a terrifying judgment is pronounced against such an accomplice: he is to be reproved by the Lord and thereafter not to be rescued from the hand of the Lord by anyone.

Nor should you be surprised that the seller of a spiritual office is designated under the name of a thief, since Truth itself names him so in the Gospel:

“For whoever enters by another way, unless he enters through the door, is not the shepherd of the sheep but is called by the Lord a thief and a robber” (John 10:1).

Certainly, no prelate in the Church entered through the door—that is, through the Lord himself—into pastoral care if he reached this office through avarice, which is service of idols.

It is therefore not unfitting that such a trafficker or hireling should be disgraced under the name of a thief, since he did not shrink from imitating the thief’s stealthy intrusion.

Let the mediators of this most criminal commerce also pay close attention to Gehazi, the servant of Elisha. Acting on behalf of his master, though Elisha knew nothing of it, Gehazi willingly accepted gifts from Naaman the Syrian, who had already been cleansed of leprosy by the prophet Elisha.

Although Gehazi wickedly sought profit while acting as an intermediary between Elisha and Naaman, he did not make either of them liable with himself for the same crime. Elisha had nobly refused the voluntary offering, whereas Naaman offered it generously, not as a debt owed by a buyer but from the kindness of his mind.

Yet although Gehazi did not draw either of these men into guilt with him, but alone bound himself by a simple crime as an intermediary between them, he himself and all his descendants are nevertheless read to have been punished most severely for the same fault. They also inherited the leprosy from which Naaman had been cleansed, as though it were hereditary, forever.

Therefore, let the mediators of Simoniac commerce consider how strictly—or rather, how most strictly—they must be condemned, since they have placed not only themselves but also those whose mediators they are under eternal condemnation.

It has therefore been sufficiently demonstrated, as I think, how exceedingly we ought to venerate and observe the aforesaid sanctions of our apostolic lord. It has been established most clearly that they proceeded not only from the synodal and authoritative judgments of the holy Fathers but also from the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures.

The Truth itself unquestionably promulgated them, both through itself and through its faithful servants. Under faithful testimony it says to us:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death forever” (John 8:51).

And elsewhere:

“If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23).

Therefore, whoever does not observe his commandments does not love Truth itself. “Whoever does not love,” as Saint John testifies, “remains in death” (1 John 3:14). Whoever despises the divine commandments will in no way be able to escape death.

### XI. [Col. 0763C]

The third statute of our apostolic lord, which prohibits incontinent clerics from the ministry of the altar, was likewise defined by the holy Fathers. For it is written in the Council of Nicaea, which is the greatest among the four councils likened to the Gospels, in chapter 3:

“The great synod absolutely forbids a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who is among the clergy to have a woman who has been introduced into his household, unless she is perhaps his mother, sister, or aunt, or one of those persons who escape suspicion.”

So that the intention of this chapter may shine forth more clearly, I do not hesitate to append a clearer translation of it:

“The holy synod has altogether forbidden a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever to have a strange woman living with him, unless she is his mother, sister, or aunt. For in these persons and those similar to them every suspicion is avoided. Anyone who acts otherwise, beyond these exceptions, will endanger his clerical rank.”

Do you see, therefore, that conjugal relations are wholly forbidden to clerics, since even for the cohabitation of women they are rightly judged to endanger not only their ministry at the altar but also their clerical rank?

This is decreed clearly not only concerning priests but concerning all sacred orders.

The Council of Neocaesarea, which is read to have preceded the Council of Nicaea, decreed in chapter 1:

“If a presbyter marries a wife, let him be deposed from his order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be expelled still further and reduced to penance.”

The Council of Chalcedon, which, as stated above, confirms the sanctions of the Neocaesarean and Nicene councils themselves—or rather, all the sanctions of the holy Fathers enacted before it—also condemns in general terms those who violate them, decreeing in chapter 10:

“The holy synod has decreed that those who dare, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to intrude into any of the things that are forbidden shall withdraw from their own rank.”

Blessed Pope Sylvester, who convened the Council of Nicaea and confirmed it by apostolic authority, likewise decrees in chapter 6 of his synodal decrees:

“No presbyter shall take a wife from the day he receives the honor of the presbyterate. If anyone acts otherwise in disregard of this, we order him to be deprived of his honor for twelve years. But if anyone acts against this present written and publicly proclaimed instrument, he shall be condemned forever.”

Also blessed Pope Siricius, in his decrees, chapter 7:

“Let every bishop, presbyter, and deacon—something we do not wish to happen—understand that, if henceforth he is found incontinent, every avenue of indulgence has now been closed to him by us.”

Again, in the same work, chapter 12:

“We likewise do not allow any women to be in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely on account of necessary family relationships.”

Likewise the most holy Pope Gregory, writing to the Roman defensor, decrees in chapter 10:

“If any of the bishops within the bounds of the patrimony entrusted to you live with women, we command you to restrain them completely and henceforth to permit those women to live there in no way, except for those whom the judgment of the sacred canons allows: namely, a mother, aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no improper suspicion can arise. Nevertheless, they do better if they also abstain from cohabiting with such women. For it is recorded that blessed Augustine did not even agree to live with his sister, saying: ‘Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.’ The caution of learned men ought therefore to be a great instruction for us.”

And shortly afterward:

“Moreover, let it be your concern to exhort these same brothers of ours to admonish those placed under them in the sacred orders to preserve in every way, in imitation of themselves, what they themselves observe.”

Again, Pope Zacharias, in his decrees, chapter 1:

“We decree that bishops must not live with women at all, lest they be deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy.”

Again, in the same work, chapter 11:

“Presbyters and deacons must in no way dare to keep with them women introduced into their households, unless perhaps such a woman is their comother, or is related to them by blood in a degree that excludes suspicion, as is stated in the Council of Nicaea: ‘If anyone presumes to act contrary to these statutes, let him be deprived of the honor of his priesthood.’”

Blessed Jerome also, writing to Oceanus, proved by authoritative arguments that clerics may not associate with women. He subsequently added:

“If, after our admonitions, any cleric should seek to love agapetae more than Christ, let him be summoned according to the synodal rule, and let the precepts defined at Nicaea be read to him. But if, once summoned, he flees from and abandons the aforesaid gatherings, we have achieved the greatest gain. Otherwise, such a man must be anathematized by the Church. For women living with men cause thorns to grow, and with a sharp blade they strike the secret places of the mind.”

But what more can I say? I lack the time to recount individually all the holy Fathers who subscribed to the statutes mentioned above of our apostolic ruler. For all Catholics judged that these things must be observed, and they did not wish to dissent from the four most holy councils, from which our apostolic ruler produced the decrees mentioned above. Therefore, I do not think even the ignorant can fail to see how dangerously—or rather, how destructively—those who do not fear to attribute incontinence to priests through the passage in Sozomen concerning priests behave toward themselves and their followers. Although the assertion of the preceding letters ought to suffice for them, let us nevertheless not shrink from warning them again to beware of the anathema.

## XII

The Old Testament consists partly in mysteries and partly in moral precepts. But when Christ came, it ceased with respect to mysteries and carnal observances, because he is the end, or completion, of the law. It remains with respect to moral precepts, because these must always be observed: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XII), and so forth.

Whoever, therefore, dogmatizes that some carnal observance from the Law which is contrary to the New Testament must still be observed is undoubtedly judaizing with the Galatians, or rather with the Ebionites.

The conjugal act of priests is counted among the observances of the carnal Law. It is recorded that this was once permitted to priests only for the sake of hereditary succession, because at that time no one from another tribe could attain the priesthood. In our time, however, priests may be chosen from any lineage, and the conjugal act is rightly forbidden them, since they no longer need to have successors.

Therefore, whoever in our time dogmatizes, with Sozomen—or rather with Ebion—that this Judaic marriage is permitted to priests does not heed carefully [perhaps: “should not heed carefully,” HARD.] the unavoidable anathema by which the Apostle himself specifically anathematizes preachers of Judaic observances. He thus deters the judaizing Galatians:

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians I).

Again, insisting on the point, he adds:

“Now I say again: if anyone preaches to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed” (ibid.).

Paul likewise freely rebuked Peter, the prince of the apostles, at Antioch, although Peter was bishop of that same see. Peter was compelling others to judaize, not by preaching but by his example, when, out of fear of the Jews, he withdrew from their table while pretending otherwise.

Moreover, the heresiarch Ebion himself, together with all his followers, was anathematized among the other heretics by the most holy Council of Constantinople and by blessed Pope Gelasius in the apostolic see. No one will be able to escape this anathema who dares to follow that heresiarch through Sozomen’s account.

## XIII

Some also seem to themselves exceedingly learned—or rather, little scholars [*scioli*]—when they assert that incontinence is permitted to priests in the Apostle’s saying:

“Let each man have his own wife” (1 Corinthians VII).

They do not understand either what they are saying or concerning what they are making assertions (1 Timothy I); or, if they do understand, they are attacking their own conscience.

For, as blessed Jerome attests, among other questions the Corinthians had asked the Apostle whether carnal intercourse was lawful for those recently reborn in Christ. The Apostle therefore wrote back to them:

“Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But, because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians VII, 1).

Blessed Jerome explains this in his book *Against Jovinianus*:

“The Apostle did not say, ‘Because of fornication, let each man take a wife’; otherwise, under this excuse, he would have loosened the reins of lust, so that whenever a wife died another would have to be taken lest we fornicate. Rather, he said: ‘Let each man have his own wife.’ ‘His own,’ he says: let him have his own and use the one he had before he believed. It was good not to touch her and, after faith in Christ, to know her only as a sister and not as a wife—unless fornication alone made this excusable.

“‘Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.’ I ask you: what sort of good is that which prevents one from praying, which does not permit one to receive the body of Christ? For as long as I fulfill the duty of a husband, I do not fulfill that of one who practices continence. The same Apostle commands elsewhere that we should pray always (1 Thessalonians V). If we are always to pray, then we must never serve marriage, since whenever I render the marital debt to my wife, I cannot pray.

“Peter the Apostle likewise teaches Christians to honor the weaker female vessel, abstaining from the conjugal act, so that their prayers may not be hindered.”

Who, then, being of sound mind, would apply the Apostle’s statements above concerning the exercise of the conjugal act to priests, whose daily office is not only to pray but also to handle the divine sacraments—especially since in the same passage continence is enjoined even upon every Christian during the time of prayer?

For if the Apostle granted carnal intercourse even to these priests, he would certainly be contradicting himself when, writing to Titus, he commands that priests be sober, just, and continent (Titus VI).

And here the same Apostle provides not priests but laymen—and not solid food but milk, as it were, for neophytes who were not yet sufficiently instructed either for themselves or for others . . . . [lacuna] The same Apostle entirely bars them from priestly office.

By the same reasoning it is proved that whatever the same Apostle writes about the exercise of the conjugal act applies to laymen, not priests, such as:

“If they cannot practice continence, let them marry. It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians VII);

that is, it is better to unite with a legitimate husband than to fornicate.

And this:

“Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (ibid.).

This, therefore, is in no way said of priests or of others dedicated to continence, but only of those who may legitimately marry.

Thus blessed Jerome says in the book mentioned above:

“‘If a virgin marries, she will not sin.’ He does not mean that virgin who has once been dedicated to the worship of God. For if any of these should marry, she will incur condemnation, because she has made her first pledge void. If someone objects that this was said about widows, how much more does it prevail concerning virgins, since even those may not do what was once permitted to them? Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous.”

If, therefore, the Apostle’s statements cited above do not grant carnal intercourse to persons of this kind who practice continence, how much less do they grant it to priests—especially since the former are simply consecrated to continence, while the latter are placed above those who practice continence, both through the venerable laying on of hands and through the anointing of the most sacred chrism?

Furthermore, the same Apostle permits those to whom he allows the conjugal act also to enter into a second marriage. He permits a man released from his wife to take another and grants a widow permission to marry. He therefore does not at all include priests under the permissive statement concerning carnal intercourse, since in his letters to Timothy and Titus he absolutely forbids them to marry twice, commanding that only a man of one wife be chosen for the priesthood.

For, as blessed Jerome asserts against Jovinianus, even among the pagans bigamy was not permitted to priests:

“Let our countrymen read that, before our religion shone in the world, it was always considered an honor among married women to have had only one husband; through them the rites of Fortuna Muliebris were customarily performed; that there was no priest who was a bigamist, no flamen who had married twice. Let them also read that the hierophants of the Athenians are to this day castrated by drinking hemlock and, after they have been elected to the pontificate, cease to be men.”

Those who so distort the Apostle’s words that under their perverse interpretation they certify that even priests may be incontinent undoubtedly follow the heresiarch Nicolas. Clement of Alexandria reports in the third book of the *Stromata* that Nicolas prostituted his wife to anyone who wished her and by this example taught that promiscuous and common relations with women were permitted to all. He did this because of the saying handed down from the apostles . . . . [lacuna] “And everything was held in common among them” (Acts II), among which Nicolas also counted marriages.

Therefore, just as he is reported to have changed the apostolic example into heresy by taking it in an excessively general and perverse sense, so these men are observed to have turned the Apostle’s statement, “Let each man have his own wife” (1 Corinthians VII), into error by interpreting it in an excessively general and utterly perverse manner. With deceitful obstinacy, they contend on the basis of the same example that the conjugal act is granted to priests, against that same Apostle.

Although promiscuous relations with women are more detestable in the sacred orders than individual marriages, nevertheless the corruption of apostolic teaching seems less imputable to the heresiarch Nicolas than to these men. He misinterpreted apostolic doctrine at a time when the name of Christianity had scarcely begun, when evangelical and apostolic teaching had not yet been spread throughout the whole world and had not yet been confirmed by so many virtues, so many signs, and so many most holy triumphs of the martyrs.

These men, however, attempt with the most obstinate recklessness to corrupt that same doctrine, now known everywhere and long since not unknown even to the rustic population [perhaps: “now known everywhere and no longer long unknown even to rustics,” HARD.], indeed consecrated from ancient times by the blood of the holy Fathers and irrefragably confirmed.

They will therefore be unable to escape the destruction that the prince of the apostles himself assigns to corrupters of Scripture, when he commends to us the letters of his fellow apostle Paul:

“In these letters,” he says, “there are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (1 Peter III).

“Therefore, beloved brothers, since you know these things beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, led astray by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness.”

But so that it may shine more clearly that in the statements above the Apostle granted carnal intercourse not to priests but to laymen, let us carefully examine what the same Apostle decrees concerning the conduct of ministers of holy things, and to whom he establishes that the sacred orders may be granted or denied.

For in that same apostolic institution, perpetual silence is evidently imposed upon the defenders of priestly incontinence, and the aforesaid statutes of our apostolic ruler are irrefragably confirmed, since they deny sacred office to no one except one whom the apostolic precepts themselves entirely exclude from the sacred order.

## XIV

Blessed Paul the Apostle, therefore, writing to Timothy concerning the sacred orders, testifies as follows:

“Faithful is the saying: if anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. Therefore a bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, chaste, well adorned, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, not violent but moderate, not quarrelsome, not covetous, but ruling his own household well, having children subject to him with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? He must not be a neophyte, lest, lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. He must also have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.

“Likewise, deacons must be chaste, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not pursuing disgraceful gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. Let these also first be tested, and then let them minister, being without accusation. Likewise, women must be chaste, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own households well. For those who have ministered well acquire for themselves a good standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy III).

Again, to Titus:

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in each city, as I directed you. If anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of dissipation or disobedient. For a bishop must be without accusation, as God’s steward: not proud, not irascible, not given to wine, not violent, not covetous of disgraceful gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, continent, holding fast the faithful word that accords with the doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict it.

“There are many disobedient, vain talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision. They must be refuted, for they subvert entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of disgraceful gain.”

And shortly afterward:

“Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith and not attend to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn away from the truth” (Titus I).

## XV

First, then, it should be noted that in these apostolic institutions presbyters are also included under the name “bishop.” For it would be inappropriate for the Apostle, after describing the bishop, immediately to introduce the deacons, unless he also included presbyters under the episcopal description—presbyters who are next after the bishop and are unquestionably placed above the deacons.
