Either he said nothing anywhere about the ordination of presbyters, or he described them under the name “bishops.” But it would be incongruous to describe the minister while omitting the master, since the master would nevertheless be more necessary to ecclesiastical arrangements.

Moreover, when the Apostle commands Titus to appoint presbyters throughout the cities, immediately instructing him concerning their ordination, he adds:

“A bishop must be without accusation” (Titus I).

He writes the same to Timothy:

“Do not neglect the grace that was given you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate” (1 Timothy IV).

Immediately afterward he says to him:

“Lay hands hastily on no one” (ibid.),

which properly belongs to bishops. Therefore, he calls the same person both bishop and presbyter.

Thus blessed Jerome and holy Ambrose, faithfully explaining the Apostle’s statements cited above, testify that among the ancients bishop and presbyter were the same, one name referring to the office and the other to age.

Later, as Jerome asserts, when each person began to think that those whom he had baptized belonged to him rather than to Christ, it was decreed throughout the world, in order to remove schisms, that one of the presbyters should be placed over the others, with responsibility for the entire care of the Church.

After describing the bishop and presbyter, the Apostle carefully adds his decree concerning deacons:

“Likewise, deacons”—that is, they must be chaste, and so forth (1 Timothy III);

as though he were saying: “Know that what I decreed concerning bishops and presbyters I have likewise decreed concerning deacons.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear, as I judge, that in the definitions above the Apostle included presbyters together with bishops and deacons. Hence any one of them who is proved to have corrupted the apostolic instruction in himself is rightly removed from the sacred offices.

For the Apostle testifies that bishops, presbyters, and deacons must not be covetous of disgraceful gain. Every simoniac, however, is unquestionably covetous of the most disgraceful and wicked gain. Therefore he must in no way be counted among the sacred orders, having long since been completely separated from them by apostolic judgment.

It should also be noted that if a neophyte is not admitted among the sacred orders, although he is believed capable of being saved among the laity, how much more must the covetous or greedy be excluded, since they are servants of idols and, according to the Apostle, have no inheritance at all in Christ and in the kingdom of God (Ephesians V).

Again, above the Apostle commands that bishops, presbyters, and deacons be chaste and continent. Nor is this surprising, since he also exhorts laymen to continence, saying:

“I wish all people to be as I am”—that is, continent (1 Corinthians VII).

Again:

“It remains that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them” (ibid.).

Again:

“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Ephesians V).

Hence Jerome says:

“If Christ loves the Church in holiness and chastity, without any blemish, husbands too should love their wives in chastity, and each should know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire like the nations that do not know God” (1 Thessalonians IV).

Blessed Jerome interprets this honor as follows:

“If we abstain from intercourse, we show honor to the female vessel; if we do not abstain, it is clear that insult is contrary to honor.”

Moreover, when the entire people of the children of Israel was about to approach the mountain and hear God’s word only from a distance, they were commanded to sanctify themselves for three days and abstain from their wives (Exodus XIX).

The Apostle therefore rightly forbade incontinence to ministers of sacred things, who ought also to surpass secular people in chastity and, having become the mouth of the Holy Spirit, ought daily to intercede with the Lord for the people.

Therefore, anyone among them who is discovered to be incontinent is forbidden by the Apostle himself to participate in the sacred orders, since through incontinence he appears to have withdrawn himself from the apostolic institution.

For when the Apostle says, “the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy III), this must be understood, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, as referring only to the period before ordination, not after it.

Thus Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Twelve Abuses*, says that a bishop ought to be such that before his episcopate he had had only one wife, not several.

Hence holy Jerome also says in his *Apology to Pammachius*:

“Let bishops, presbyters, and deacons be chosen either as virgins or widowers, or certainly let them remain perpetually chaste after the priesthood.”

Likewise blessed Zacharias, an apostolic man, writing to Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, decreed as follows:

“When your fraternity sits in council at Mainz with the most excellent man Carloman, if you find any bishops, presbyters, or deacons to have transgressed the canons or the statutes of the Fathers—that is, to have committed adultery, or to have had several wives, or to have transgressed in any other matters in which you find the canons opposed—your holiness must in no way permit them, by apostolic authority, to exercise the priesthood.

“For such men are called false priests by their own mouth, and they are known to be worse than secular people because they abstain neither from fornications nor from wicked marriages.

“As for what they understand from the Lord’s saying, ‘My priests shall marry only once,’ and from the Apostle’s saying, ‘the husband of one wife’: this was permitted before they undertook the priesthood. From the day on which they receive the priesthood, however, they must be forbidden even their own marriage.”

Hence Jerome, writing to Vigilantius, likewise testifies:

“The Church of the East and of Egypt, and the apostolic see, accept as clerics either virgins or continent men; or, if they have had wives, they cease to be husbands. For how, according to the same Apostle, as was said above, could they practice continence if they were required to exercise incontinence with their wives? Since these things are contrary, they cannot exist together in any way.”

This too must be carefully considered: whom did the Apostle command to be chosen for the priesthood? Not one who had already generated children through incontinence, but one who had previously had adult and well-raised children.

Note also that the Apostle in no way counted the disobedient and vain talkers among the sacred orders. Rather, he commanded that skilled priests be appointed to refute precisely those who subvert entire households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of disgraceful gain. He also commands that they be rebuked sharply, so that they may not attend to Jewish fables and the commandments of people who turn away from the truth—such as those who, following the command of Paul of Samosata or Ebion, dogmatize that Judaic incontinence is permitted to Christian priests.

What wonder, then, if our apostolic ruler also removed such disobedient men from sacred office, whom the Apostle decreed should be rebuked sharply and not counted among the sacred orders?

Do you see, then, how unavoidably the statutes of our Gregory must be observed, since we see them derived from the most sacred fountain of Scripture?

It should be understood, however, that the Apostle established that those to be ordained, or those already ordained, should be without accusation, not without sin. For in this world no one, according to Augustine, lives without sin except baptized infants, as the beloved John himself testifies:

“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John VIII).

Again, James, the brother of the Lord:

“For we all offend in many things” (James II).

Yet many are found without accusation. Hence blessed Augustine testifies in his forty-first tractate on the Gospel of John:

“Certainly many just people are called without complaint, which is understood as without accusation. For no just complaint can be made in human affairs against those who have no crime. A crime, however, is a serious sin deserving accusation and condemnation. Therefore, whoever has committed so serious a sin ought not, according to the Apostle, to hold a sacred order.”

## XVI

But so that this apostolic institution concerning the sacred orders may become clearer to us, let us not hesitate to consider the exposition of blessed Jerome, who explains it in his book *Against Jovinianus* as follows:

“The episcopal election itself also supports my position. For it is not said, ‘Let a bishop be chosen who takes one wife and begets children,’ but rather, ‘who has had one wife and has children subject to him in all discipline.’ Certainly you admit that a man cannot be a bishop while begetting children during his episcopate. Otherwise, if he were discovered doing so, he would not be treated as a husband but condemned as an adulterer.

“Either permit priests to perform the works of marriage, so that virgins and husbands are the same, or, if priests may not touch their wives, they are holy in this respect because they imitate virginal chastity.

“Let this also be added: if a layman and any faithful person cannot pray unless he is free from the duty of marriage, then a priest, who must always offer sacrifices for the people, must always pray. If he must always pray, then he must always be free from marriage.

“For under the old Law also, those who offered sacrifices for the people were not only absent from their houses, but were purified by being separated from their wives for a time and by not drinking wine or strong drink (Leviticus X), things that are accustomed to provoke lust.

“Married men are chosen for the priesthood. I do not deny it, because virgins are not as numerous as the priests who are needed. But because the strongest person must be chosen for the army, are the weaker therefore not also enlisted, since all cannot be strong? If an army consisted only in strength and not also in the number of soldiers, the weaker would be added; now men of second and third degrees of strength are also admitted, so that the army may be filled out by its multitude and numbers.

“And how is it, you ask, that in priestly ordination a virgin priest is frequently passed over and a married man chosen? Perhaps he does not possess the other works compatible with virginity; or he is thought to be a virgin when he is not; or his virginity is disgraced; or certainly virginity itself produces pride in him. While he congratulates himself on bodily chastity alone, he neglects the other virtues: he does not support the poor, or he is more desirous of money.

“Sometimes a gloomy face, a drawn brow, and a gait resembling one carrying the trappings of pomp offend the people, so that one who has nothing in his life deserving reproach comes to hate only his appearance and manner of walking.

“Many are chosen not out of love for themselves but out of hatred for another. In many cases simplicity alone wins support, being set against another’s prudence and cleverness as though these were malice.

“Sometimes it was the judgment of the common people and the crowd; and when priests were being approved, each person favored someone according to his own character, seeking not so much a good superior as one like himself.

“Sometimes married men, who form the larger part of the people, applaud married men as though they were applauding themselves, and believe that they are not virgins if a married man is preferred to a virgin.

“I shall say something that perhaps I am about to say to the offense of many, but good men will not be angry with me, because the consciousness of sin does not sting them. Sometimes this also occurs through the fault of bishops, because they choose not the better men but the cleverer ones for the clergy, and consider simple and innocent men unsuitable.

“They distribute offices as though they were offices of earthly warfare to their relatives and kinsmen, or obey the commands of the rich. Worse still, they bestow the clerical rank on those whose services have won their favor.

“Otherwise, if according to the Apostle’s statement only married men may be bishops, the Apostle himself ought not to be a bishop, since he says: ‘I wish all to be as I am’ (1 Corinthians VII). John too would be judged unworthy of this rank, as would all virgins and continent people, with whom the Church’s necklace is adorned as with the most beautiful gems.

“Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not names of merit but of offices. Nor is it said, ‘If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good honor [or: rank],’ but ‘he desires a good work’ (1 Timothy III), which one established in the higher order may, if he wishes, have the opportunity to practice.

“Therefore, a bishop must be irreproachable, so that he is enslaved to no vice; ‘the husband of one wife,’ that is, one who has had one wife, not one who has one now; sober—or, as it is better said in Greek, watchful, *nēphaliōn* [νηφάλιων]; chaste, for this is what *sōphrōn* [σώφρων] means [the manuscript gives *sōphrōna* (σώφρωνα)]; adorned both in chastity and in conduct; hospitable, so that we may imitate Abraham and receive Christ with strangers, indeed in strangers; a teacher, for it does him no good to enjoy the consciousness of virtues unless he can also instruct the people entrusted to him and is able to exhort in doctrine and refute those who contradict it.

“Let him not be given to wine, because one who is always in the Holy of Holies and offers sacrifices does not drink wine or strong drink. Let a bishop drink in such a way that it is not known whether he has drunk [because there is lust in wine]. Let him not be violent—that is, one who does not strike the consciences of individuals. The apostolic statement does not describe a boxer but establishes a pontiff; it teaches what he ought not to do and now, in turn, what he ought to do.

“But what? ‘Moderate, not quarrelsome, not covetous, ruling his household, having children subject to him with all chastity’ (1 Timothy III).

“See how much chastity is required of a bishop: if his children are unchaste, he himself cannot be a bishop, and by the same office by which Heli the priest offended, he too offends the Lord. He had indeed rebuked his sons, but because he had not expelled the offenders, he fell backward and died, the lamp of God before it was extinguished.

“‘Likewise, women must be chaste,’ and the rest (ibid.). Chastity holds the primacy in every rank and sex.

“You see, therefore, that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon is not blessed simply because he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, but if he possesses the virtues appropriate to his name and office. Otherwise, if a deacon is holier than his bishop, will he be worse in Christ’s presence merely because he is in the lower rank? Far be it from us to say that the deacon Stephen, who was the first to be crowned with martyrdom, will be lesser in the kingdom of heaven than many bishops, or than Timothy and Titus. I would not dare place him below them, nor can I place him above them.”

Thus far Saint Jerome. How great his authority was, even among bishops, is sufficiently indicated by the decrees of blessed Pope Gelasius, which determine that his works are to be received among authoritative and canonical sanctions, just as the works of Saints Cyprian, Ambrose, and Augustine, or the treatises of the other holy Fathers who did not deviate from the holy Roman Church either in faith or in preaching, but remained in communion with it to the end of their lives.

Indeed, in the decrees mentioned above blessed Gelasius commends the authority of Saint Jerome to us so highly that he likewise decrees there, according to Jerome’s judgment, that the works of others are to be seized upon or rejected.

Therefore, whoever wishes to render due obedience to the apostolic see will in no way oppose the individual statements of these holy Fathers.

Let it suffice to have said this far concerning what the Apostle requires of priests. Whoever examines it faithfully will certainly not judge that the statutes of our apostolic ruler should be erased—statutes that no one can despise unless he also wishes to oppose the statements of the apostles themselves, to whom Truth itself most faithfully promises in the Gospel:

“Amen, I say to you: it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for those who did not receive your words” (Matthew XI).

### XVII

The fourth decree of our apostolic ruler commands that the people not receive the services of clerics whom they perceive to be opposed to the sacred canons—indeed, to evangelical and apostolic institutions—namely, those whom they see, in accordance with the judgment of the holy Fathers, condemned and ministering at the altar to their own destruction. For the Council of Antioch, unquestionably confirmed by the most sacred Council of Chalcedon, as we have said, most strictly forbids the people to receive the services of condemned clerics, to such an extent that it even judges those who have communicated with clerics whom they knew to have usurped a ministry forbidden to them should be expelled from the Church.

Thus the fourth canon of that same council testifies:

> If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by a bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop, in accordance with the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—let it in no way be permitted to him to have hope of restoration or a place for satisfaction in another synod. Let all who communicate with him also be expelled from the Church, and especially after they [perhaps: “those who, after”] have learned that a sentence has been pronounced against the aforesaid persons and have attempted to communicate with them.

In accordance with the tenor of this canon, the holy Fathers who promulgated the most sacred canons at Chalcedon judged all those who communicated with a certain condemned bishop, Timothy of Alexandria, to be excommunicated. To the Emperor Leo, who consulted them on Timothy’s behalf, they replied as follows:

> We also judge those who, knowing that Timothy had been condemned, believed that they could communicate with him without danger to be strangers to the Church of God; according to the regular rule, no pardon or hope of restoration in any way remains for them, just as the eighty-third canon clearly decrees concerning such persons. Its beginning is: “If any bishop has been condemned by a synod,” and so forth.

Therefore our apostolic ruler rightly prohibited the people from receiving the services of such clerics—of those, I say, whom he did not so much condemn himself as demonstrate to have long since been condemned by the holy Fathers.

Moreover, the most holy Pope Alexander, fifth after Blessed Peter, who chose to be burned in a furnace of fire rather than to lie, as a most courageous athlete, himself testifies that one must not even speak with those against whom a bishop is judged to be acting because of their crimes. He confirms this by the authority of the prince of the apostles, saying in chapter 6:

> Blessed Peter, instructing the clergy and people at the ordination of our holy predecessor Clement, said: If Clement should be an enemy to anyone because of his deeds, do not wait for him to say to you, “Do not be friends with that man.” Rather, you must prudently observe his will without admonition, and turn away from the one toward whom you perceive him to be hostile. Do not even speak with those with whom he does not speak, so that each person who is at fault, while desiring to retain the friendship of all of you, may hasten to be reconciled with him who presides over all and thereby return to salvation, once he has begun to obey the commands of the one who presides.
>
> But whoever is a friend to those with whom he himself does not speak is also one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. Although he may appear to be with you bodily, in mind and spirit he is against you. This enemy is much worse than those who are outside and are openly enemies; for under the appearance of friendship he practices what is hostile, and he scatters and devastates the Church.

Therefore, where the prince of the apostles so strictly forbids anyone even to speak with those who are found not to obey apostolic institutions, there he also most clearly forbids the people to receive Masses or other services of this kind from them. For, according to Augustine, the custom of the people of God is to be held as law and proves to us, together with the canons, that [perhaps: not] the people should hear the Masses of any priest and respond to each of his greetings during the Mass. Therefore, if the people wish to observe the judgment of the prince of the apostles, they must in no way receive the Masses of such transgressors.

### XVIII

The most holy Pope Gregory, writing to the kings of the Franks concerning such priests who despise the canons, testifies in chapter 135 that a kingdom is weighed down by the guilt of such priests. Shortly afterward he adds:

> Greater calamity must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought to positions of governance—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to appease him on behalf of the people.

Therefore, rightly, the Gregory of our time prohibited the people from receiving the services of such presumptuous men, whom that most holy namesake of his asserted both to burden the kingdom by their guilt and to provoke God’s anger against themselves more greatly. For it is written:

> He who turns his ear away from hearing the law—his prayer will be accursed. (Prov. XXVIII)

All who stubbornly resist canonical decrees are bound by this crime. Hence the services of those whose prayers Almighty God—not merely fails to receive, but curses—are rightly forbidden to the people.

But let us now come to the very Vessel of Election, who is found to agree with the present statute of our apostolic ruler. He says:

> If the one who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even eat with such a one. (I Cor. III)

That is, do not eat with those who refuse to be corrected according to ecclesiastical decrees, although they are bound by certain and public crimes.

Likewise, to the Thessalonians:

> We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us. (II Thess. III)

And shortly afterward:

> If anyone does not obey our word expressed in this letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame. (Ibid.)

With those, therefore, with whom the Apostle does not even permit the faithful to take bodily nourishment, and from whose fellowship he commands the faithful to withdraw, our apostolic ruler commands the people not even to communicate at the Lord’s table; at least, he commands them to withdraw from their company at the time when those men usurp the sacred mysteries unlawfully and to their own destruction.

For according to the Apostle:

> Whoever eats the Lord’s bread and drinks the cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eats and drinks judgment upon himself. (I Cor. XI)

All who not only practice fornication and greed but also presume stubbornly to defend them do this. Concerning such persons the Apostle says:

> Those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God. (Gal. V)

This also applies to those who, having been condemned for the same crimes according to the canonical decrees, persist in the forbidden ministry through reckless usurpation.

Indeed, those whom we properly call penitents, although they submit their necks to canonical discipline for such crimes, nevertheless do not approach the divine sacraments with such recklessness. Hence, according to the judgment of blessed Pope Innocent, even sick penitents and other ill persons may not be anointed with sacred chrism. For, he says, the remaining sacraments are denied to such penitents, lest they acquire condemnation rather than remission for themselves if, still unworthy and not yet fully purified through penance, they receive those sacraments.

If, therefore, penitents who are satisfying for their crimes even canonically are judged unworthy of the divine sacraments, how much more are those unworthy who try not to repent but stubbornly to defend their long-publicized faults, and who, resisting with obstinate mind, are also proved to blaspheme the Holy Spirit?

Thus blessed Pope Damasus testifies in a letter to Saint Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage:

> Voluntary violators of the canons are judged severely by the holy Fathers and are condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift the holy Fathers have been endowed. For those who act or presume to speak against the holy canons—not compelled by necessity but willingly, as has been stated—or who voluntarily consent to those wishing to do so, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.
>
> Such presumption is clearly one form of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, since, as has already been mentioned, it acts against him by whose effort and grace those same holy canons were issued.

Accordingly, those priests who are bound by such grave crimes—or rather, who have already been condemned for them according to canonical institutions—can sacrifice only to their own destruction. Therefore those who knowingly presume to cooperate by the customary responses at Mass with such men usurping sacrifice to their own death would not [perhaps: have] commit a small offense. It would not be considered a minor crime if someone knowingly cooperated with another who was cruelly killing himself.

Most wisely, therefore, the apostolic man prohibited the people from taking part in the usurpations of such presumptuous men. He knew that these practices were destructive not only to their leaders but also to those who received them.

Thus the Lord himself commanded the other children of Israel to withdraw from Korah and his followers when they usurped the ministry of sacrifice, lest they become entangled in their sins and thereby deserve to be condemned with them by a most cruel death. For those heresiarchs—namely Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—descended alive and unexpectedly into hell with all their possessions; while their followers deserved to be utterly consumed by fire from the Lord. (Num. XVI)

Let those who, against apostolic commands, usurp the priestly ministry forbidden to them with obstinate recklessness carefully consider their sudden and most cruel punishment. Nor should they carelessly overlook the death of Uzzah, who, when David was bringing back the ark of the Lord from Philistia on a new cart, was struck down by the Lord and died because he had presumed to support the ark with his hand, although it was already falling.

If, therefore, the man deservedly perished who rashly yet kindly touched only the ark of the Lord, how much more does the unworthy man deserve to perish who presumes, against law and right, to handle the very body of the Lord and incorporate it into himself?

### XIX

Some, however, quite ineptly object to our apostolic ruler the fourth canon of the Council of Gangra:

> Whoever distinguishes himself from a presbyter who has had a wife, on the ground that one ought not to receive an offering from him while he is ministering, let him be anathema.

They corrupt this canon, according to the testimony of the Apostle Peter, to their own destruction, and proclaim it in this fashion:

> Whoever refuses the Mass of a married presbyter, let him be anathema.

They say this in order to show that those who obey apostolic institutions and refuse to receive the Masses of incontinent priests are themselves anathematized.

But in vain. For the aforesaid canon anathematizes only those who reject the offering of a presbyter who not merely now has a wife, but once had a wife. At that time, as the prologue of the Council of Gangra testifies, there were heretics who followed a certain Eustathius. They condemned lawful marriage as though it were a mortal crime, asserting that no one placed in the married state had hope before the Lord. Accordingly, they are said to have rejected even the offerings of presbyters who had lawfully married before ordination, since they regarded lawful marriage as a mortal crime.

If anyone is discovered to have committed such a deed even in the present time, he is likewise not permitted, according to the canons, to minister at the altar. Those heretics are therefore rightly anathematized, since they dogmatized against the Apostle’s statement:

> If you take a wife, you have not sinned. (I Cor. VII)

And against this statement:

> A bishop must be the husband of one wife. (I Tim. III)

The frequently mentioned institution of our apostolic ruler, however, forbids no one to hear the Mass of a presbyter who, in accordance with apostolic permission, had only one wife before sacred ordination, at a time when he could marry without sin. It forbids the Mass of that presbyter who, against the Apostle, is discovered to be persisting in the crime of fornication—the presbyter whom the Apostle himself, the other holy Fathers, and their successor, our apostolic ruler, excluded from the sacred ministry.

Therefore, whoever rejects the Masses of such presbyters will in no way be subject to the foregoing anathema of the Eustathians, since he agrees perfectly with the Apostle, who both enjoins continence upon priests and does not permit the faithful to associate with transgressors of his words.

It should be noted, however, that our Gregory, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers, first deprived incontinent presbyters of their ministry and afterward prohibited the people from receiving their services. Thus he prohibited the hearing not so much of the Masses of the incontinent as of those who had been condemned for incontinence, lest the people, if they presumed to receive their services, place themselves under excommunication according to the Council of Antioch.

The Holy Spirit himself, through the prophet Samuel, teaches the people to obey the institutions of our apostolic ruler rather than receive the sacrifices of such presumptuous men to their own danger. For he says:

> Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit is like the crime of idolatry. (I Reg. XV)

Therefore the people who obey apostolic institutions reject the services and sacraments of disobedient priests, lest through disobedience they incur the crime of idolatry.

The Lord also declares elsewhere:

> I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. (Matt. IX)

By these words, that is, he teaches that the person who is pleasing to God should, through obedience, have mercy rather on his own soul—as it is written—than offer sacrifice to the Lord, either personally or through another, in disobedience. (Eccli. XXX)

It is worth considering how mercifully our apostolic ruler treated even the despisers of the canons in his earlier statutes. He merely removed them from such a ministry, although they could celebrate only to their own destruction if, while resisting canonical decrees, they did not cease blaspheming the Holy Spirit.

Their long-standing obstinacy certainly deserved to be punished more severely long ago; yet he did not punish it with the severity it deserved. Instead, with paternal affection, he waited for them to return at least then to their senses, so that they might wish to recognize their own condemnation when they could not deny that the people had been most justly forbidden to receive their services.

### XX

Perhaps someone will say: Why did our Gregory command statutes so contrary to our custom to be observed? Why did he not rather tolerate our custom through a merciful act of dissimulation?

Let such a person hear what Pope Leo, who presided over the most sacred Council of Chalcedon, decreed. Restraining the presumption of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, he pronounced as follows: it is to be charged as guilt against the Roman pontiff if, where the institution of the canons does not prohibit it—and where he has, as it were, connived at it—something is violated.

Likewise, the most holy namesake of our apostolic ruler, writing to Bishop Victor, delivered this terrible and universal judgment:

> Whoever, in consideration of his office, does not burn with zeal to correct this crime—namely, the heresy of simony or of the neophytes—must not doubt that he shares a portion with the one from whom this abominable wickedness and crime first took its beginning.

Therefore, whoever does not strive, in accordance with the duty of his office, to prohibit that heresy of the heresiarch Ebion—namely, Jewish incontinence—in the priests of the present day is likewise revealed to be a participant in Ebion’s heresy.

The most sacred councils themselves, from which the statutes of our apostolic ruler proceeded, were embraced by the holy Fathers to such an extent that, as their writings testify, they preferred to be afflicted by various torments—even to permit themselves to be cruelly killed—rather than consent to violators of those same decrees.

For this reason the great Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, was sent into exile after various calamities. For this reason also Felix, pope of Rome, is read to have been deposed from the episcopate and crowned with martyrdom; and many of his presbyters, deacons, and the rest of the clergy are likewise read to have been most cruelly killed, even within the Church, because they refused to assent to the followers of Arius in violation of the Council of Nicaea.

You can readily gather innumerable examples of this kind from ecclesiastical histories.

Let anyone, therefore, say how our apostolic ruler could, without danger to himself—or rather, without his own destruction—have neglected to oppose, in fulfillment of his office, not merely the violators but even the assailants of decrees so unavoidable, when he knew that the holy Fathers themselves had resisted them to the shedding of blood.

Although some people today do not attack the faith of the holy Fathers as openly as Arius and the other heresiarchs did, nevertheless they stubbornly resist their moral statutes, which were strengthened by those same holy Fathers at the same time and by the same subscription as the faith itself, and which proceeded, together with that same faith, from the most sacred fountain of Scripture.

In this their most wicked rebellion, they are also shown to nullify the faith itself, since in authentic decrees they treat as worthless the authority of those who confirmed the faith by their authority. Certainly, the faith of the holy Fathers will benefit no one who strives not to obey their canonical and moral precepts but stubbornly to resist them.

For, as James, the brother of the Lord, testifies:

> Faith without works is dead. (James II)

He admits that the demons also possess such faith.

Therefore stubborn assailants of authentic institutions must be resisted no less than violators of the sacred faith, since all who pursue the institution of the holy Fathers with all their strength only in faith and not also in conduct are likened to demons. They do not fear stubbornly to defend, by diabolical inspiration, a fault whose commission was human.

Moreover, the very Vessel of Election says in his own person to all ecclesiastical pastors:

> If I preach the Gospel, that is no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me; woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel. (I Cor. IX)

How, then, could our apostolic ruler escape this “woe” if he neglected to instruct the flock entrusted to him according to the Apostle’s commands?

The Holy Spirit also, through the prophet Ezekiel, sets before every shepherd a terrible condition:

> If you do not say to the sinner, “You shall surely die,” and show him how to turn away from his iniquities, he will indeed die in his sins, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you do say this, and he despises it and does not obey, he will die in his crimes, but you will save your soul. (Ezek. XXXIII)

Saint Augustine uses this translation in his sermon on Psalm XLIX and immediately adds to his hearers:

> I tell you: I am freeing my soul. For I am placed in great danger—not merely danger, but destruction—if I remain silent.

It is therefore sufficiently clear how unjustly some are angry with our apostolic ruler over the foregoing statutes, since he is shown to have instituted them under the compulsion of such unavoidable necessity—namely, lest he incur the guilt of his own death if he neglected to instruct us as required by his office.

### XXI

Furthermore, if they strive to be angry with our apostolic ruler for this reason, why are they not rather angry with the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, [perhaps: or] with the 630 Fathers assembled and gathered at Chalcedon, who, as has been said, issued much more severe judgments against Simoniacs and incontinent ministers of the altar than our apostolic ruler?

Let them indeed be angry with the most holy Pope Clement, who confirmed his decrees by martyrdom, and whom the prince of the apostles himself appointed as his successor. For it is read in his decrees, chapter 46, that he completely removed incontinent men from the ministry of the altar, prohibited clerics from cohabiting with foreign women, and utterly anathematized violators of this kind of institution.

Let them also be angry with the blessed Pope Sylvester, who, established in the apostolic see, prohibited incontinence among the presbyters of the whole world, as has been stated, and decreed that all who resisted this decree should be condemned forever.

Let them also be angry with blessed Pope Damasus the martyr, by whose authority the Second Universal Council, that of Constantinople, is said to have been confirmed.

Likewise, let them be angry with the most holy Pope Leo, author of the canons of Chalcedon. Both of these men, each by apostolic authority, decreed the following generally in their statutes—Leo in chapter 4, and Damasus in chapter 5:

> We command that all the decretal constitutions of all our predecessor pontiffs, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, be so observed by all bishops and by all priests generally that anyone who violates them must know that pardon will thereafter be denied him.

Let them also be angry with the most holy namesake of our apostolic ruler, who condemned under a general anathema all who dissented from the four most sacred councils.

But since no sane person is angry at the judgments of such holy Fathers, it is perfectly evident how irrationally some are angry at the institutions of our apostolic ruler. In promulgating them he in no way differed from the holy Fathers, except in this one respect: he opposed the despisers of the canons less severely than they did.

He merely deprived those clerics of their ministry whom the holy Fathers deprived not only of their ministry but also of pardon and ecclesiastical communion.

Finally, our apostolic ruler imposed upon us no new observance which, even if he had done so, could be despised without danger. For, by divine confession [perhaps: “concession”; HARD.], the apostolic see has always possessed and will always possess this primacy: to govern the Churches of the whole world not only by ancient institutions but also by new ones, as the need of changing times requires.

For, Saint Augustine says to Boniface, the experience of many illnesses compels one to discover many medicines. The various decrees of the Roman pontiffs certainly testify to this, for in them they are read to have provided for the needs of different times.

### XXII

In vain do public despisers of apostolic institution seek from our apostolic ruler a delay of their condemnation. As has been stated, the holy Fathers condemned them without granting any delay.

In doubtful matters, even when they are true but have not yet been made public, a delay must necessarily be granted so that, according to the decrees of the apostolic men Felix, Julius, and the others, the accused person may fully prepare himself against his accusers to cleanse himself of the crimes. Hence blessed Eleutherius, twelfth after blessed Peter, testifies in his decrees, chapter 1:

> A substantial delay must be granted for investigation, lest anything appear to be done hastily by either party, since many things arise through surreptitious action.

Those, therefore, are rightly condemned without delay who try not to deny their guilt—already definitively condemned long ago by the holy Fathers—but publicly to defend it against apostolic statutes.

Indeed, blessed Gregory, rightly to be imitated by every Catholic pastor, used to excommunicate despisers of the apostolic see even before the guilt had been committed.

Thus he excommunicated Maximus, who had been enthroned in the bishopric of Salona through ambition, together with all those who ordained him. The same excommunication bound them before the offense for which they were excommunicated had been committed. For before Maximus was ordained, Saint Gregory prohibited under excommunication that this should be attempted.

The bishops who despised that command and ordained Maximus were excommunicated before the ordination had taken place, according to Saint Gregory’s testimony. For, writing to that same presumptuous Maximus and condemning his consecration, he says:

> We can in no way call this a consecration, because it was celebrated by excommunicated men.

He did not say that they were to be excommunicated after the ordination, but that they were excommunicated in the very act of ordaining.

Similarly, through his subdeacon Natalis, he judged that the bishop of Salona should be deprived of the pallium and communion without delay if he did not obey his command.

Thus, I say, he and the other bishops of that same see condemned without delay anyone who rashly usurped something forbidden under excommunication or suspension from office.

Let modern presumptuous men carefully consider these and similar arguments, and let them no longer imagine unjustly that they have been condemned without delay.

Perhaps, however, someone is so delirious as to say that the subjects of any bishop can be condemned only by that bishop and not by the Roman pontiff.

### XXIII

But the Truth itself contradicts such a person in the Gospel. Among the other apostles it granted this privilege principally to blessed Peter:

> Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven. (Matt. XVI)

Since he subjected all people generally to apostolic power, he in no way excepted the subject of any bishop.

Hence the same Apostle demanded obedience generally both from the elders of his time—that is, presbyters or bishops—and from their subjects, since in his Epistles he gave particular rules of life both to subjects and prelates, and to women and men alike. He would have done this in vain if everyone were not generally required to obey his instruction.

Blessed Anacletus, ordained presbyter by the prince of the apostles himself, also testifies in his decrees, chapter 3:

> The holy Roman and apostolic Church obtained its primacy not from the apostles but from our Lord himself, just as he said to blessed Peter: “You are Peter,” and so forth. (Ibid.)

Therefore this apostolic see was established by the Lord, not by another, as the hinge and head of all the Churches. Just as a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the authority of this holy see and by the Lord’s arrangement, all the Churches are governed.

Likewise blessed Gelasius, an apostolic teacher, says in chapter 11:

> The whole Church throughout the world knows that the holy Roman Church has the right to judge concerning every Church, and that no one is permitted to judge its judgment. For an appeal must be made to it from every part of the world, but from it no one is permitted to appeal.

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see has possessed the power, without a preceding synod, both to release those whom an unjust synod had condemned and to condemn, when no synod existed, those whom it was appropriate to condemn. This is certainly because of its primacy, which the Apostle Peter both held by the Lord’s word and will always retain.

The most holy Fathers Callistus, Fabianus, Sixtus, Sylvester, Julius, and innumerable others support this, for they embraced the truth so fully that they preferred to die rather than to lie.

By the authority of this privilege, blessed Pope Simplicius, forty-ninth in succession, completely freed Gregory, bishop of Mutina and suffragan of the archbishop of Ravenna, from the jurisdiction of that archbishop, because the archbishop had enthroned him against his will in the see of Mutina.

Likewise, Saint Gregory restored Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona, who had advanced from the archdeaconate to the presbyterate, to his former rank, even against the will of the bishop. He deposed the man whom that bishop of Salona had ordained in Honoratus’s place.

Therefore those who rashly prejudice the authority of the apostolic see are plainly insane and make themselves guilty before it, when they pretend that the subjects of any bishop can be bound or released not by the Roman pontiff but only by their own bishop.

Moreover, blessed Pope Leo, who convened the Fourth Universal Council at Chalcedon; Pope Vigilius, under whom the Fifth Universal Council met at Constantinople; and blessed Father Gregory—each of these men, preeminent by the same authority, testify with almost the same words in their decrees:

> The holy Roman Church has so imparted its functions to the other Churches that they have been called to share in its solicitude, not in the fullness of its power.

It is therefore clearly demonstrated that no bishop possesses as much power [for *quantam*] over the flock entrusted to him as the apostolic prelate possesses. Although he has divided his care among individual bishops, he has in no way deprived himself of his universal and principal power, just as a king does not diminish his royal power by dividing his kingdom among different dukes, counts, or judges.

Since, therefore, the apostolic lord possesses such principal power in every Church that, even against the will of the bishop of any Church, he may arrange matters within it according to canonical decrees, who can deny that throughout the world he can condemn both the subjects of bishops and the bishops themselves who despise apostolic institution?

### XXIV

These arguments also make clear that the parishioner of any bishop ought to obey the apostolic lord rather than his own bishop, since the authority of his own bishop cannot in any way free him from apostolic condemnation if he has been disobedient to apostolic commands.

Conversely, if he obeys the apostolic lord, the apostolic lord can very easily defend him against every act of violence by his own bishop—by completely emancipating that parishioner from the bishop’s jurisdiction and restraining the bishop from injury through apostolic correction and condemnation.

Let the subject of any bishop take care not to obey his own bishop in anything contrary to apostolic commands. Saint Gregory deposed the archdeacon of Salona who had been substituted in the place of the already deposed Honoratus, because that man had obeyed his own bishop and accepted ordination in Honoratus’s place after the apostolic prohibition.

From this it is also perfectly clear how insane are those who say that the subjects of any bishop ought in no way to obey the apostolic see if they obey their own bishop. Saint Gregory rightly degraded the man who was found, through obedience to his bishop, to have acted against the apostolic see.

No one can therefore render due obedience to his own bishop unless he strives first of all to obey the apostolic see. Everyone who wishes to be a bishop particularly impresses upon his subjects that they must obey the institutions of the holy Fathers without any contradiction. Those institutions, as has been said, declare that all must obey the apostolic see above all.

Therefore whoever renders due obedience to his legitimate pastor will also strive to obey the apostolic lord principally. For, according to the decree of the Truth itself:

> A disciple is not to be honored above his teacher. (Matt. X)

If the apostolic lord is rightly placed above one’s own legitimate pastor, how much more is he placed above one who does not even strive to be what he is called?

Whoever, even among the uneducated, takes care faithfully to examine these and similar arguments will in no way attempt to proscribe the foregoing statutes of our apostolic ruler, especially when he sees clearly that they proceeded from the judgments of the holy Fathers—or rather, from the divine Scriptures.

I have moreover omitted, for this consideration, attaching many other arguments to those already presented and assigning innumerable examples of the holy Fathers to the aforesaid statutes, lest I become burdensome to the uneducated, whom I have specifically undertaken to satisfy here. A few examples drawn from many, of such incontrovertible truth, can be sufficient for them if they wish to devote themselves to seeking the truth rather than to unprofitable contention.

## Observation of Philip Labbe, S.J.

Concerning the same Roman synod, on the occasion of the consecration of Hugh of Die as bishop, as stated above, Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, has the following in the *Chronicle of Verdun*, p. 196, volume I of our new library of manuscript books.

When, therefore, they were staying in Rome—namely, Anselm of Lucca and Hugh of Die—awaiting the day of their consecration, messengers of King Henry came to Rome, asking that the lord pope not wish to consecrate, contrary to the custom of his predecessors, those who had received only the election to the episcopate, but not investiture by royal gift. The pope himself, however, having summoned the cardinals, disclosed the king’s embassy and explained what answer should be given and what ought to be done. When they replied that this was the Church’s custom, that it was treated as law, although no authority supported them in this matter, he nevertheless yielded to them in the case of the elected bishop of Lucca, agreeing to defer his consecration until he had received investiture of the episcopate from the royal gift. In the case of the bishop of Die, however, he refused to yield, and consecrated him first as a priest on the Saturday of the first week of Lent, and as a bishop on Sunday.

And because he saw that it was contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers for the king’s gift to prevail over the canonical election of a bishop, indeed repeatedly to alter the election itself, or rather to make it invalid, in that same year [Note: Indeed, Pagius says that it was 1075, in which he maintains that the first decree against investitures was issued in the Roman council; see under A.D. 1075, no. 1 ff.], at a Roman synod of fifty bishops, with a multitude of priests and abbots in attendance, he prohibited anyone from presuming to do this any longer, under threat of anathema, issuing the following decree:

> If anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or an abbacy from the hand of any layperson, let him in no way be regarded among the bishops or abbots, nor let any hearing be granted him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we forbid him the grace of blessed Peter and entry into the church until he has abandoned the position which he acquired under the charge both of ambition and of disobedience, which is the crime of idolatry. We likewise decree concerning the lower ecclesiastical dignities.

> Likewise, if any emperor, duke, margrave, count, or any other secular power or person should presume to give investiture of a bishopric or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the same sentence.

In this he followed the examples of the Fathers, although this condemnable custom had already become established over the course of many years and had been converted into ordinary practice. For it is said in the Seventh Ecumenical Council, held under Pope Hadrian by five patriarchs and 350 Fathers, chapter 111:

> Every election of a bishop, priest, or deacon made by princes is to remain invalid, according to the rule which says: If any bishop, by making use of secular powers, has obtained a church through them, let him be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.

Likewise, in the Eighth Ecumenical Council, held by five patriarchs under Pope Nicholas I, chapter [lacuna], this holy and universal synod, agreeing with the earlier councils concerning the appointment or consecration of bishops, established that these things were to be carried out by the election and decree of the bishops. It decreed and promulgated that no lay prince or powerful layman should insert himself into the election or advancement of a patriarch, metropolitan, or any bishop, lest disorderly and inappropriate confusion or contention arise from this—especially since no layperson possessing secular power ought to have authority in such matters, but should rather remain silent and attend to his own affairs until the election of the future pontiff has regularly received its conclusion from the assembly of the Church.

> If, however, any layperson is invited by the Church to deliberate and cooperate, he may respectfully obey those who summon him. But whoever among secular princes or powerful persons, or any layman of another rank, attempts to act against the common, harmonious, and canonical election of the ecclesiastical order, let him be anathema until he obeys and consents.

Likewise, from the Council of Nicaea, chapter 6:

> It is entirely clear that if anyone has been ordained contrary to the will and knowledge of the metropolitan, this holy and great council decrees that he ought not to be a bishop.

Likewise, from the Council of Antioch, chapter [lacuna]:

> If any priest or deacon has obtained the Church of God through secular rank, let him be removed, and both he and the one who ordained him be cut off from communion in every way; and let them be under anathema like Simon Magus by Peter.

In the election and consecration of the lord bishop of Die, therefore, divine action is clearly shown to have been at work, because through this occasion the truth of ecclesiastical election, obscured for many years under the papacy of the lord Gregory, shone forth in the holy Church of God. Let thoughtful men, then, consider what right is reserved to emperors, kings, and princes in the election of a pontiff.

He entrusted the exercise of his authority to him in Gaul, where the wicked plague of simony was spreading most widely, since there were very few there who were not either simoniacs, ordained by simoniacs, or invested by a lay hand. He repeatedly impressed upon him that he must not abuse the power granted to him, but must correct what had been corrupted, cut away what deserved condemnation, teach what was holy and honorable, and ensure that what ought to be taught was taught.

## Addition to the First Roman Council, held by Pope Gregory VII in the first week of Lent of the year 1074, against simoniacal and incontinent clerics

*(Supplement to Mansi, volume II, p. 2.)*

[Col. 0785]

[Col. 0785D] Labbe presents only a synopsis of the acts of this council, volume XII, p. 547, Venetian edition. The acts themselves have perished. I was able to investigate a fragment of those acts in the exposition of Gerhoh of Reichersberg on the Psalms, on Psalm X, p. 157. This fragment contains the third and fourth canons of the council itself, as we understand from comparing the synopsis of those same canons.

[Col. 0786D] Gregory VII says:

> If there are any priests, deacons, or subdeacons who lie in the crime of fornication, we forbid them, on behalf of Almighty God and by the authority of holy Peter, entry into the Church until they repent and amend their lives. But if any prefer to persist in their sin, let none of you presume to hear their office, because their blessing is turned into a curse and their prayer into sin, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “I will curse your blessings.” Those who refuse to obey this most salutary command incur the sin of idolatry, as Samuel testifies and blessed Gregory teaches: “Not to obey is the sin of divination, and to refuse acquiescence is the crime of idolatry.” Whoever, therefore, while claiming to be a Christian, scorns obedience to the apostolic see incurs the sin of paganism.

## Second Roman Council

*[Note: Pagius, under the year 1075, nos. 1 ff., teaches that the first decree against investitures was issued at this council.]*

Held for the reform of the Church in the year of the Lord 1075.

*(In Mansi, Councils, volume XX, p. 443.)*

[Col. 0787]

[Col. 0787B] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1074 [Note: The years are counted not from the Nativity of the Lord, but from the day of the Annunciation of the Virgin and of the Incarnation of the Word, as noted above], in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Gregory [Note: The third year, however, begins in this year, on 22 April], in the thirteenth indiction, the lord Pope Gregory himself held a synod at Rome, from the sixth day before the Kalends of March until the day before the Kalends of the preceding (or “following”) month. A multitude of archbishops, bishops, and abbots was present, together with a considerable number of clerics and laypeople of various orders.

Among the other decrees enacted there, he separated five members of the household of the king of the Teutons, by whose counsel churches are sold (or “were being sold”), from the thresholds of the holy Church, so that, if they did not come to Rome and make satisfaction between then and the Kalends of June, they would be regarded as excommunicated. If Philip, king of the Franks, did not provide security to the pope’s messengers travelling to Gaul concerning his satisfaction and amendment, he was to be regarded as excommunicated.

He suspended Liemar, archbishop of Bremen, from episcopal office because of the disobedience arising from his pride, and barred him from the body and blood of the Lord. He suspended Werner of Strasbourg from episcopal and priestly office. He suspended Henry of Speyer. He likewise suspended Herimann of Bamberg if he did not come before Easter to make satisfaction. In Lombardy he suspended William of Pavia and Cunibert of Turin. He deposed Dionysius of Piacenza. He excommunicated Robert, duke of Apulia, who had already been anathematized, and Robert of Loritello, invaders of the possessions of Saint Peter.

## Notes of Severinus Binius

[Col. 0787D] Council. To reform the Church’s discipline, Gregory convoked a synod in 1074, to be held at the beginning of Lent in the year 1075. To it he summoned especially bishops and abbots from more distant Britain, as well as the bishop of Toul, who had been publicly accused of simony and of cohabiting with a woman whom he treated as his wife.

Isambert, bishop of Poitiers, who had attacked with soldiers the bishops investigating the case of the incestuous count, and had treated some of them with blows and others with insults, was suspended from office and ordered to come to Rome, as were Benno, bishop of Osnabrück, and the abbot of Corvey, who were quarrelling with one another. He also summoned Liemar, archbishop of Bremen, for the reason described above. He ordered Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, to attend the same synod in person with all his suffragan bishops.

By letter he asked King Henry to send legates to the synod and not to listen to those who sow discord among them. He also ordered Cunibert, bishop of Turin, who was accused of having seized the monastery of Saint Angelus, to come, as he likewise ordered William of Pavia to come because of the divorce between Azo and Matilda. He summoned Hugh the knight, who had invaded the property of the Church of Turin, to give an account.

The matters mentioned above concerning the suspension of Herimann, bishop of Bamberg, and the deposition of Dionysius, bishop of Piacenza, are also found in Gregory’s Book II, letters 54 and 76, and Book III, letter 3. Gregory’s Book II, letter 93, declares that disputes between the bishops of Prague and Moravia were settled at the same synod.

He ordered the synodal decrees to be promulgated throughout the world, and, in letters written to Saint Anno, bishop of Cologne, and to Siegfried, bishop of Mainz, he instructed them to have the councils assembled in their dioceses promulgate especially those decrees and enactments that had been established concerning clerical continence and the correction of simoniacal depravity. Baronius, under the year 1075, no. 10 and following.

## Third Roman Council

At which Henry, king of Germany, Siegfried of Mainz, William of Utrecht, and Robert, bishop of Bamberg, were excommunicated, in the year of the Lord 1077.

*(Mansi, Councils, volume XX, p. 467.)*

[Col. 0789]

[Col. 0789A] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1075, in the fourteenth indiction, the lord Pope Gregory himself [Note: The word “lord” is absent in the Modena manuscript] held a synod at Rome in the Church of the Lord Savior, which is called the Constantinian Church. A considerable number of bishops and abbots was present, together with clerics and laypeople of various orders.

Among the other decrees enacted there, he excommunicated Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, in the following manner:

> Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, who has attempted to separate the bishops and abbots of the Teutonic kingdom from the holy Roman Church, namely, their spiritual mother, we suspend from all episcopal office by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and we separate him from communion in the body and blood of the Lord, unless the danger of death should intervene, provided that, moved to repentance, he come to his senses. As for the others who voluntarily subscribed to his schism by consenting to it and wish to persist in that iniquity, we likewise suspend them from all episcopal office. But those who did not consent voluntarily we spare until the feast of Saint Peter, with this condition: if within that period they do not offer suitable satisfaction to our presence, either in person or through their messengers, they are thereafter to be deprived of episcopal office.

### Excommunication of the bishops of Lombardy

> The bishops of Lombardy, who, despising canonical and apostolic authority, conspired by oath against blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we suspend from all episcopal office by the authority of that same blessed Peter, and we separate them from communion with the holy Church.

### Excommunication of the bishops beyond the Alps

> We excommunicate Berengar, bishop of Agde, because he communicated with the excommunicated bishop of Narbonne and exercised episcopal functions on his behalf. We excommunicate Herimann, bishop of Vienne, lawfully deposed for simony, perjuries, sacrileges, and apostasy, because he does not cease to trouble the Church of Vienne; and we prohibit divine worship in the Churches of Romans and of Saint Irenaeus at Lyons for as long as he occupies them. We excommunicate Desiderius and the clerics of the Church of Romans, who expelled our regular clergy from it and communicated with excommunicated persons, until they make satisfaction. Likewise, we excommunicate the abbot of Saint-Gilles and the count of Saint-Gilles, on account of a female relative, and the count of Forez, and Humbert of Beaujeu [Imbert of Bellojoco], on account of their attacks upon the Church of Lyons. We excommunicate the simoniacal man of Le Puy, Stephen the murderer—namely, one excommunicated by our legates—and Pontius of Grenoble, until he comes to his senses. We also confirm what the bishop of Die did in the bishopric of Die concerning tithes, first fruits, and churches, as well as the other matters that he established during our legation.

### Excommunication of Henry, king of the Teutons

> Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, incline, I beg you, your gracious ears toward us, and hear me, your servant, whom you nourished from infancy and whom until this day you have freed from the hand of the wicked, who hate and have hated me because of my fidelity to you. You are my witness, as are my lady, the Mother of God, blessed Paul, your brother, and all the saints, that your holy Roman Church compelled me, against my will, to take up its governance, and that I did not regard it as an act of robbery to ascend your see. Rather, I wished to end my life in pilgrimage than to seize your place through worldly and secular ingenuity. Therefore, by your grace and not by my own works, I believe that it pleased and pleases you that the Christian people specially entrusted to you should obey me, especially in place of your life entrusted to me; and by your grace I have received from God the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth.
>
> Relying, therefore, upon this confidence, for the honor and defense of your Church, in the name of Almighty God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, through your power and authority, I forbid Henry, king, son of the emperor Henry, who has risen against your Church with unheard-of arrogance, to exercise the governance of the entire kingdom of the Teutons and of Italy. I absolve all Christians from the bond of the oath which they have sworn or may swear to him, and I forbid anyone to serve him as king. For it is right that he who strives to diminish the honor of your Church should himself lose the honor which he appears to possess.
>
> And because, as a Christian, he has scorned to obey and has not returned to the Lord whom he abandoned, by communicating with excommunicated persons and, as you bear witness, by scorning the admonitions which I sent him for his salvation, and because he has attempted to separate himself from your Church by trying to rend it, I bind him with the bond of anathema in your place. I bind him with such confidence in you that the nations may know and acknowledge that you are Peter, and that upon your rock the Son of the living God built his Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matthew 16).

## Notes of Severinus Binius

[Col. 0791A]

Council. What was done at this synod in Rome is summarized by Lambert in the following words:

> “The legates, hastening their journey with the greatest effort, entered Rome on the day before the synod appointed by the pope was to be held there—according to custom, it was the first week of Lent—and delivered the letters. Then they carried out the rest of their embassy, as they had been instructed, in words no less insulting than those of the written document. The pope, unmoved by the atrocity of the message, caused the letters to be read aloud the following day, when clergy and people had gathered in great numbers for the synod. Thus, with all the bishops who had assembled decreeing that this should be done, he excommunicated the king, and with him Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, William, bishop of Utrecht, and Robert, bishop of Bamberg. He set a day for the others who had taken part in this conspiracy, so that, unless they appeared in Rome and pleaded their case concerning this new and unprecedented rebellion against the apostolic see, they would receive a sentence of excommunication like the others. He had already excommunicated Otto, bishop of Regensburg, Otto, bishop of Constance, Burchard, bishop of Lausanne, Count Eberhard, Ulrich, and several others whom the king chiefly used as counselors.”

At this same synod, as the priest Donizo testifies in his *Life of Matilda*, Pope Gregory used the following symbol to represent and express the substance of the whole tragedy which he was undergoing with the king:

> “A certain serpent, struck, gathered itself into coils. When, with a savage bite, it sought to attack a stone egg placed beside it in order to injure it, it was itself wounded by the stone it intended to harm and fled.”

He undoubtedly spoke this symbol with the intention of signifying that the rock, which is the Church, cannot be harmed by the fury of the persecuting king; rather, the king himself is harmed, since he attempted to tear the Church apart through persecution. The words of the priest Donizo, composed in verse, are as follows:

> Gregory the shepherd, beginning the synod, carried an egg  
> Sculpted like a hen’s, with a shield upon its shell,  
> And a black serpent, which stretched out its head;  
> For, struck by a certain blow in return,  
> It could not reach upward, and, bending its tail,  
> It formed a winding shape. It was not flat,  
> But was a raised sculpture.  
> Never before, they say, had an equal object been brought to the synod.
>
> While he was marveling at it, behold, the aforesaid Roland  
> Came into the midst and immediately began to say to the pope:
>
> “The king of the earth has ordered it, and the pontiffs have ordered it also:  
> Leave the see which you are not worthy to hold.”
>
> The same messenger then said to the Roman clerics:
>
> “‘Costes in pente’ [meaning uncertain]: I attest that the king will come to Rome;  
> He will send away the pope—for this man is not a pope.”

The same things concerning Roland are contained in the acts of Gregory himself, from which the life of that pontiff is composed, and the other passages agreeing with them are appended there. Donizo now continues:

> It is fitting to bear these virtues, not merely in truth,  
> And let us strive to carry Christ’s cross ourselves.  
> Let tribulation not separate us from Christ  
> At this time; rather, let us submit our necks  
> And our limbs to martyrdom.  
> Let the serpent displayed here be struck by the word of faith—  
> The serpent which carries a shield and sword  
> Against the Roman and Catholic mother,  
> The Church of Christ, reddened with the blood  
> Of the gracious one.
>
> While the pope was saying more, the holy synod said to him:
>
> “You are the father of fathers; crush the blasphemous and the wicked.  
> It is our task to obey your commands,  
> And for Christ we all eagerly endure death.  
> Pronounce judgment, draw the sword, strike the strong.”
>
> With everyone loudly declaring that it was right  
> To deprive the king of his kingdom  
> And to curse him as well,  
> The sorrowful pope immediately bound the aforesaid king  
> With the chains of anathema,  
> And forbade him that very kingdom.
>
> Let this synod, held in Lent, be celebrated.  
> Whoever loves holy Peter, whoever loves the gracious pope,  
> Approves this anathema.

The same events are found in the *Deeds of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca*, in these words:

> “Then, possessed by unheard-of audacity and astonishing pride in his crime, he gathered into the city of Worms bishops who ought not to be called bishops and, having held a little council, proscribed the bishop of the first see—something never heard of throughout the ages. Next he sent an embassy into Italy, affirming the same presumption through bishops who were his accomplices in schism.
>
> “The bearer of this embassy was a certain man (Roland), named Eberard, a Teuton by nationality, a son of the world, a hook of the devil, and the inventor of almost every falsehood. He traveled around and traversed the land in order to infect everyone with the contagion of schism. Indeed, with unheard-of audacity and pride, although himself under interdict and bound by the bond of perdition, he reconciled many who, because of the lord pope’s interdict, had ceased from divine office, and, on behalf of his lord the king, ordered them to celebrate the office according to the former custom.

> “Since, therefore, the apostolic could no longer conceal the wickedness of so great a crime, he excommunicated both him and all his supporters, forbade him every royal dignity, and absolved from every obligation of fidelity those bound to him by oaths. For—something shameful even to say—in addition to the heretical guilt which we have mentioned, messengers of that man dared to bark in the holy council:

> “‘Our lord the king commands that you relinquish the apostolic see, namely, his papacy, and no longer obstruct this holy place.’

> “Shame upon such wickedness! O execrable audacity of a most wretched man! He said that what the Lord Christ had entrusted solely to Peter, prince of the apostles, belonged to him; and Christ did not entrust it suddenly, but questioned him three times before entrusting it: ‘Simon, do you love me? Feed my sheep’ (John 21). He excepted neither king nor emperor nor any rank within the Christian profession, except one who should deny that he was his sheep. Yet this man dares not only to judge him whom the Lord reserved to himself alone, but also to call him his own and, insofar as he can, to condemn him. For this reason the entire holy synod, rightly indignant, pronounced and confirmed anathema against him.”

Thus far concerning these matters.

In the *Life* of the same pontiff it is added that on the following day, after the speech delivered by that Roland in the synod, letters arrived from the repentant bishops. They are written there as follows:

> “On the following day letters from the bishops beyond the Alps were brought to the pontiff. In them they confessed that they had erred and sinned greatly; they also asked pardon and firmly promised that henceforth they would observe complete obedience toward him. When the uproar had scarcely been calmed, the synodal proceedings continued peacefully. But when the time had come to conclude the synod, the pontiff, having taken more useful counsel with 110 bishops, pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the same king, who had attempted to divide ecclesiastical unity, and ordered that this sentence be firmly observed until suitable satisfaction had been made.”

The author teaches that this was done piously, holily, justly, and properly, on the basis of numerous examples of his predecessors. Therefore, when Gregory had struck King Henry with the sentence of anathema at the synod, together with all who had been responsible for the crime committed, he sent the following letter to all the faithful of Christ, adding to it the sentence of excommunication pronounced against them:

> “GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all who desire to be numbered among the sheep whom Christ entrusted to blessed Peter: greetings and apostolic blessing.
>
> “You have heard, brothers, something new and unheard-of,” and so forth, as above, letter 6 of Book III.

The shorter sentences known by the title *Dictatus papae*, found among Gregory’s letters in Book II after letter 55, also appear to belong to this synod. Without doubt the pontiff promulgated them with the intention that the king might learn from them the audacity of the schismatic bishops and princes who at that time were rising up against the Roman Church. See Baronius, under the year 1076, no. 16 and following.

## Addition to the Third Roman Council

*(Mansi, Supplement, volume II, p. 16.)*

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793A] It is well known that the cause of holding this Roman council was the impudence of Henry, king of Germany. Under his leadership, the assembly at Worms had been convened and had advanced so far in audacity as to depose Gregory from the papal see. Relying on the authority of this decision, Henry sent a letter full of insults to Hildebrand, or Pope Gregory; he inserted it in full into another letter sent for that reason to the Roman clergy.

These letters—both the one written to Henry and the one written to the Romans—were sent by a messenger and, by Gregory’s order, read aloud in the full Roman synod of the year 1076, as the Saxon annalist Eckhard testifies under the year 1076; from him we possess the letters in full. Since these writings likewise belong among the acts of the synod, readers devoted to ecclesiastical history will judge it reasonable that they be transferred here. I nevertheless wish to warn them beforehand that the disgraceful things asserted against Gregory should be understood as the words of an unrestrained man who follows the insanities of an agitated mind rather than counsels of truth.

### Henry, by the grace of God king, to the entire clergy and people of the holy Roman Church: grace, health, and every good thing

This is believed to be firm and unshaken faith: that it is always preserved unchanged both toward the absent and toward the present, and is altered neither by the prolonged absence of the one to whom it is owed nor by the weariness of a long period. We know that you preserve such faith toward us, and we give thanks; and we ask that it continue, namely, that, as you do, you remain continually friends to our friends and enemies to our enemies.

Among these, of course, we point out the monk Hildebrand, and we stir you up against him. We have discovered him to be an invader and oppressor of this Church and a plotter against the Roman commonwealth, or our kingdom, as is plainly shown in the following letter addressed to him by us.

> “HENRY, by the grace of God king, to HILDEBRAND.
>
> “Since until now I expected from you the things that belong to a father and obeyed you in all matters, to the great indignation of our faithful, I have received from you a return such as ought to come from one who would be the most destructive enemy of our life and kingdom. For when, at the beginning, you had seized by proud audacity every hereditary dignity owed to me by that see, you proceeded farther and attempted by the worst methods to alienate the kingdom of Italy.
>
> “Not content with this, you did not fear to lay hands upon the most venerable bishops, who are united to us like our sweetest limbs, and, against divine and human law, as they themselves say, you embittered them with the most arrogant injuries and the harshest insults.
>
> “While I concealed all these things with a certain patience, you, judging this not patience but cowardice, dared to rise up against my very head, issuing the commands you know—namely, to use your own words, that either you would die or you would take away my life and kingdom.
>
> “Judging that this unheard-of insolence ought to be refuted not with words but in deed, I held a general assembly of all the leading men of the kingdom, at their own request. There, when the matters that had until then been kept silent through fear and reverence were brought into the open, their truthful assertions—which you will hear from their letters—made it clear that you could in no way remain in the apostolic see.
>
> “Because their judgment appeared just and reasonable before God and human beings, I too agreed with it. I renounce every right of the papacy which you appear to possess, and I order you to descend from the see of the city whose patriciate is owed to me by God’s gift and by the sworn assent of the Romans.”
