This is the sequence of our letter to the monk Hildebrand. We have written it to you so that our will may be known to you and so that your devotion may satisfy both us—and, indeed, God and us. Rise up against him, therefore, most faithful men, and let each of you be foremost in faith, foremost in condemning him.

We do not say that you should shed his blood, since after his deposition life would be a greater punishment for him than death. Rather, compel him, if he is unwilling to descend, and receive into the apostolic see another man chosen by us in the common council of all the bishops and of yourselves—one who both wishes and is able to heal what this man has wounded in the Church.

### Henry, not by usurpation but by the pious ordination of God king, to Hildebrand, no longer apostolic but a false monk

You have earned this kind of greeting as a confession of your character, since you have passed over no order in the Church without making it share in confusion rather than honor, in cursing rather than blessing. To speak briefly and notably of many things: you did not merely dare to touch the rulers of the holy Church—archbishops, bishops, and priests—as the anointed of the Lord; you trampled them beneath your feet as though they were servants who did not know what their lord was doing.

By trampling upon them, you obtained favor from the mouths of the common people. You judged that all of them knew nothing, while you knew everything, and you strove to use this judgment not for building up but for destroying. Accordingly, we rightly believe that blessed Gregory, whose name you have claimed for yourself, prophesied about you when he said: “Through the abundance of those subject to him, the mind of the prelate is often lifted up, and he thinks he knows more than everyone when he sees that he can do more than everyone.”

We endured all these things while striving to preserve the honor of the apostolic see. But you understood our humility as fear, and therefore you did not fear to rise up even against the royal power granted to us by God, which you dared to threaten to take away from us—as though we had received the kingdom from you, as though the kingdom or empire were in your hand and not in God’s, when our Lord Jesus called us to kingship but did not call you to the priesthood.

You ascended through these steps: cunning, which the monastic profession abhors; money for money; favor for favor; iron for iron. You approached the seat of peace and from the seat of peace disturbed peace, when you armed subjects against prelates, when you, though not called, taught that our bishops, called by God, should be despised, when you made laypeople usurp their ministry over priests, so that they might depose or despise those whom they themselves had received from the hand of God through the laying on of episcopal hands.

You also touched me, although unworthy, anointed among the anointed for kingship, whom the tradition of the holy Fathers entrusted to God alone to judge and depose. Blessed Peter himself, the true pope, cries out: “Fear God; honor the king” (1 Peter 2). But because you do not fear God, you dishonor me, established by him. Thus, when blessed Paul did not spare an angel from heaven if he preached something else, neither did he exempt you, teaching something else on earth.

Therefore, condemned by this anathema, by the judgment of all our bishops, and by our own judgment, descend. Leave the apostolic see which you have claimed; let another ascend the see of blessed Peter, one who does not cloak any violence with religion but teaches the sound doctrine of blessed Peter. I, Henry, by the grace of God, together with all our bishops, say to you: Descend, descend.

When these letters, the Saxon annalist Eckhard adds, had been brought to the lord pope as he presided over the holy synod in the Lateran basilica and had been read aloud before the synod, such commotion arose in the Church that the legate of Henry would have perished, torn limb from limb, had he not found protection at the feet of the apostolic.

On the following day the lord pope declared before the synod with what gentleness he had rebuked the king for his great crimes, how graciously he had begged and ordered that the bishops be freed from captivity, and how bitter an arrogance he had received in return. Then, when everyone cried out that such an insult must not remain unpunished, by the counsel and consent of all he condemned Henry by synodal judgment, deprived him of the king’s name and honor, and struck him with the sword of anathema. Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and so forth. See above among the letters.

## Fourth Roman Council

At which Gilbert of Ravenna, Theobald of Milan, and several other bishops were excommunicated, in the year of the Lord 1078.

*(Mansi, Councils, volume XX, p. 503.)*

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795C] [Note: [Col. 0795D] Variant readings are supplied from the Mutina manuscript.]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1078, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, that same Lord Pope Gregory held a synod, at which nearly one hundred archbishops and bishops from various cities were present, together with an innumerable multitude of abbots and clerics and laymen of various orders. At it he confirmed the apostolic constitutions, corrected many things that required correction, and firmly established those that required confirmation. Among other matters, at the end of the synodal absolution he appended the following and ordered it to be written down for perpetual remembrance by posterity, saying:

“We entirely suspend from the episcopal and priestly office Theobald—called Tebaldus—archbishop of Milan, and Gilbert of Ravenna, who, exalting themselves against this holy Catholic Church with unheard-of heresy and pride; and we renew against them the anathema already pronounced.

“Arnulf of Cremona, publicly convicted and confessing in our presence that he is a Simoniac, we depose from every episcopal office without hope of restoration, and strike him with anathema until he has made worthy satisfaction.

“But Roland of Treviso, who, having become a deceitful legate in order to obtain the honor of the episcopate, did not shrink from causing schism between the kingdom and the [Col. 0796C] priesthood, we decree by apostolic censure shall henceforth and forever lack episcopal dignity. We prohibit by every means that any of our successors should in any way consent to his consecration, and we bind him perpetually with anathema, unless he comes to his senses and makes worthy satisfaction to God.

“Hugh, cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, condemned for the third time by the Apostolic See because, having become an aspirant and associate in the heresy of Cadalus, bishop of Parma, and having again been appointed legate of the Apostolic See, he joined himself to heretics and Simoniacs condemned by the Apostolic See; and because, having become an apostate and heresiarch for the third time, he attempted schisms, divisions, and rifts in the Church of God and caused it to be torn apart—we deprive him of every priestly office, and remove him, under a perpetual and irrevocable sentence, both from entry into and honor in the aforesaid Church and in all Churches; and we strike him with anathema until he makes satisfaction.

“We also renew the excommunication imposed by our predecessors upon Gaufred, archbishop of Narbonne, and remove him from episcopal office without any hope of restoration.”

[Col. 0797A] Concerning the case of King Henry [“of Henry and the others” is missing], and of the others.

“And since we see that the dispute and disturbance (*lis et perturbatio*; variant *litem et perturbationem*) of the kingdom daily overflow [read: “are seen”] into the greatest danger and injury of the holy Church, it pleases us to labor with all our strength so that suitable envoys, distinguished both by religious commitment and by learning, may be sent from the side of the Apostolic See to those regions. They shall summon all religious men and lovers of justice residing in the lands of the Teutonic kingdom, men of both clerical and lay status who are suitable for this undertaking. With them, God’s grace going before them, they shall either justly arrange an end and peace, or, having first learned the truth and discovered which side justice favors more, be able to ascertain the matter fully; so that the unjust party may desist and the party supported by apostolic authority may obtain the strength and power of justice.

“Yet we are not unaware that certain men, gathered together at the devil’s prompting, inflamed by the torches of their tyranny, and enslaved to the avarice of shameful profit, desire discord rather than peace to be made and witnessed. Therefore we decree that no person of any power whatsoever—whether king, archbishop, bishop, duke, count, margrave, or knight—may attempt, through presumption or rash daring, fraud, deceit, or any disturbance, to resist or oppose our legates, lest they establish justice and an end to the conflict.

“Whoever, however, with rash daring—which God forbid—becomes a violator of this our constitution, and attempts to oppose fraud to our aforesaid legates as they go to arrange this peace, we bind him with the bond of anathema. By apostolic power we fetter him not only in spirit but also in body and in every prosperity of this life, and we take victory from him in arms, so that at least in this way they may be put to shame and be crushed by a twofold shame and contrition.

“We likewise grant Rainerius, son of Ugizzo [variant: Rainerius, son of Vidicio], a three-week truce. If during this period he is unwilling, either in person or through his legates, to do justice in our presence, because he killed his brother with his own hand, did not shrink, as a criminal, from incurring many perjuries, and does not cease, at the peril of his soul, to harass his female relative and the orphans—that is, his brother’s children—by plundering their castles [Col. 0797D] and estates, we shall strike and bind him with anathema when the aforesaid term has elapsed.

“And the count’s son …, after a truce has been granted until Palm Sunday, we likewise bind with excommunication, because he does not permit the Church of Lucca to remain in peace, plundering its possessions.

“We excommunicate”—says Leo, bishop of Ostia, Book III—“all the Normans who strive to invade the land of Saint Peter, namely, the March of Fermo and the Duchy of Spoleto; those who besiege Benevento; those who attempt to invade and plunder Campania and the maritime region; the Sabines; and those who attempt to throw the city of Rome into confusion.”

[Col. 0798A] “As for the bishops who, after receiving or learning of our letters, have come neither in person nor by canonical excuse to the present synod, we suspend them from episcopal office. And whoever among them—whether bishop or priest—performs the divine office for the aforesaid Normans before they have been excommunicated, we remove forever from the priestly office.

“We likewise grant the abbot of Farfa a truce of eight days. After that term, unless he comes for correction, we excommunicate him, forbid him the body and blood of the Lord, and decree that he shall forever lack the rank of abbot.”

And since we know that some perish by shipwreck through God’s judgment, and see that they are plundered by those from whom they ought mercifully to be rescued and comforted, as though by a kind of already legalized, indeed diabolically prompted, right, we establish and command under the bond of anathema, as was established by our predecessors, that whoever finds any shipwrecked person and his possessions shall safely release both him and all that is his [variant: his possessions].

As for the ordinations of those who have been ordained by excommunicated persons, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers, we decree that they are to be invalidated. Again, holding to the statutes of our holy predecessors, we absolve by apostolic authority those who are bound to excommunicated persons by fidelity or oath, and in every way prohibit them from observing such fidelity.

Likewise: Since, on account of our sins, we see many daily perishing because of excommunication—some overcome by ignorance, some by excessive simplicity, some by fear, and some by necessity—we temper the sentence of anathema for a time, as far as we can, suitably and opportunely, moved by mercy. By apostolic authority we withdraw from the bond of anathema wives, children, male slaves, female slaves or bondservants, as well as peasants and servants, and all others who are not so close to the court that crimes are perpetrated on their advice; also those who unknowingly associate with excommunicated persons, and those who associate with people who associate with excommunicated persons.

“Whoever—whether a petitioner, pilgrim, or traveler—comes into the land of excommunicated persons where he cannot buy, or has no means with which to buy, we grant permission to receive what he needs from the excommunicated. And if anyone wishes to give something to excommunicated persons for their support—not out of pride but for the sake of humanity—we do not prohibit it.”

Done at Rome, in the Church of the Lord Savior, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the first indiction.

## Notes of Severinus Binius

### Council

By these synodal acts Marianus Scotus is refuted in his Chronicle, where he writes that Gregory deprived King Henry of the kingdom and transferred it to Rudolf, duke of Swabia. For Rudolf was not elected by the Saxons and the princes of the Empire, and confirmed by Gregory’s authority, until two years later, as we shall say below in the Seventh Roman Council, in the synodal letter concerning the events conducted at this synod, above, Book V, Letter 15.

## FIFTH ROMAN COUNCIL

Celebrated in the year of the Lord 1078, for the restoration of the holy Church.

(Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 507.)

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799A] [Note: [Col. 0799C] Variant readings are supplied from the Mutina manuscript.]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1078, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, on the third day before the Kalends of December [variant: the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December], in the second indiction, a synod was held at Rome in the Church of Saint Savior for the restoration of the holy Church. Among other matters, the emperor of Constantinople and others listed below were excommunicated there. The envoys of Henry and Rudolf also swore, each on behalf of his own lord, that they would not obstruct by any deceit the conference to be held in the Teutonic kingdom by the envoys of the Apostolic See. Certain chapters were likewise established there for the benefit of the holy Church, which are set out below:

Concerning opposition to the Teutons, so that they may not retain ecclesiastical estates granted by kings or held from unwilling bishops. That those through whose fault the conference failed should be excommunicated again. That the archbishop of Narbonne should be excommunicated again. And those who have been excommunicated by Bishop Amatus. That the count of Saint-Gilles should be excommunicated on account of his wife. And likewise the monastery, if it should be in the count’s power. That the monastery of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino should be defended against all Normans. That opposition should be made so that no one receives the investiture of Churches from the hands of laymen. And that prebends or ecclesiastical offices should not be sold. Concerning consanguinity. Concerning Simoniacs. Concerning the chastity of clerics. Concerning false ordinations. Concerning false penances. How true penance is to be given. [Col. 0799C] Concerning tithes unjustly held by laymen. Concerning the patriarch of Aquileia. Concerning the patriarch of Grado. Concerning the emperor of Constantinople. Concerning the celebration of the feasts of the Roman pontiffs. Concerning abstinence on Saturday. Concerning Jews not being placed over Christians. Concerning the concealment of Saint Peter’s inheritance.

That no penitent be received without letters from his bishop, unless perhaps the bishop is dead or excommunicated. That no abbot retain tithes and firstfruits without the authority of the Roman pontiff or the consent of the bishop in whose diocese he lives. That no bishop impose any burden or servile service upon abbots by custom. That priests not be received without the permission of their bishop, nor monks from recognized monasteries without the permission of their abbots. [Col. 0800A] That bishops who have consented to fornication or incest in their parishes be suspended from their office. That all bishops give an undertaking not to sell ecclesiastical estates. That no bishop grant the estates of the Church as a benefice without the pope’s consent if they belong to his own consecration. The others likewise shall not presume to do this without the consent of their archbishop and their brethren; but if they presume to do so, they shall be suspended from office, and whatever has been sold or granted as a benefice shall be restored to the Church, every sale or grant as a benefice being entirely annulled. That all bishops arrange for the arts of letters to be taught in their Churches, and in no way or by any means remove the ornaments of the Church from Churches without definite usefulness or grave necessity, lest they incur the danger of sacrilege, which God forbid. That it be announced to laymen with how great a danger to their souls they retain tithes and possess Churches. [Col. 0800B] That those who wish to have a fixed part in the solemn Mass should arrange to offer something.

Certain decrees made at this synod; for many are lacking, of which only the titles are preserved.

### I

Whoever among the military, or any person of whatever order or profession, has received, receives, invaded, or holds ecclesiastical estates from any king or secular prince, or from unwilling bishops or abbots, or from any governors of Churches, or has held them with the corrupt or vicious consent of their governors, unless he restores those same estates to the Churches, shall be subject to excommunication.

If any Norman or any other person [Note: [Col. 0799C] These words are absent from the Chronicle of Verdun by Hugh of Flavigny] has invaded the estates of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, or has unjustly taken away any possessions of that monastery, and, after being admonished twice or three times, has not made amends, he shall be subject to excommunication until he repents and makes satisfaction to the Church.

### II

Since we know that the investiture of Churches is being carried out in many regions by lay persons contrary to the statutes of the holy Fathers, and that from this very many disturbances arise in the Church [Note: [Col. 0799C] “Indeed, the ruin of holy religion arises in the Church” [Col. 0800C]], by which the Christian religion is trampled underfoot, we decree that no cleric shall receive the investiture of a bishopric, abbey, or church from the hand of an emperor, king, or any lay person, whether male or female.

If anyone presumes to do so [Note: [Col. 0800C] These words too are absent from the same Chronicle], let him acknowledge that this investiture is invalid by apostolic authority, and that he is subject to excommunication until he makes worthy satisfaction.

[Col. 0801A] ### III

If anyone has sold prebends, archdeaconries, provostships, or any ecclesiastical offices, or has otherwise appointed them contrary to the commands of the statutes of the holy Fathers, he shall be suspended from office. For it is fitting that, just as he received the episcopate freely, so he should distribute the members of that episcopate freely.

### IV

We judge that ordinations carried out with the intervention of money, prayers, or service rendered to any person with that intention [variant: to a person], or ordinations not carried out by the common consent of clergy and people according to canonical decrees and not approved by those to whom the consecration belongs, are invalid and void. For those who are ordained in this way do not enter through the door—that is, through Christ—but, as the Truth itself testifies, they are thieves and robbers (John X).

[Col. 0801B] ### V

We call those penances false that are imposed not according to the authority of the holy Fathers and the quality of the crimes. Therefore, if any soldier, merchant, or person committed to an office that cannot be exercised without sin, entangled in serious offenses, comes to penance; or if anyone unjustly retains another’s goods, or harbors hatred in his heart, and recognizes that he cannot perform true penance by which he may attain eternal life unless he lays down his arms and no longer bears them except at the counsel of religious bishops for the defense of justice, or unless he abandons his business, or relinquishes his office, and dismisses hatred from his heart and restores the goods that he unjustly took away—let him not, however, despair. In the meantime we exhort him to do whatever good he is able to do, [Col. 0801C] so that almighty God may enlighten his heart toward penance.

### VI

We prohibit by apostolic authority that tithes, which canonical authority shows to have been granted for the use of piety, be possessed by laymen. For whether they have received them from bishops, kings, or any other persons, unless they return them to the Church, they should know that they commit [variant: incur] the crime of sacrilege and incur the danger of eternal damnation [variant: suffer punishment].

### VII

Since the day of Saturday has been held in honor among our holy Fathers as a day of abstinence, following their authority we give the salutary admonition that whoever desires to be a participant in the Christian religion should abstain from eating meat on that day, unless a greater feast intervenes or illness prevents it.

### VIII

By apostolic sanction we confirm [variant: decree by authority] that no abbot retain tithes, firstfruits, or the other things that, according to the statutes of the canons, belong to bishops, without the authority of the Roman pontiff or the consent of the bishop in whose diocese he lives.

### IX

No bishop shall impose a burden or servile service upon his abbots or clergy by custom contrary to ecclesiastical norm. Nor shall he restore a priestly office that has been interdicted [variant: *interdictum*] in return for payment. If he does so, let him incur the danger of his office.

[Col. 0802A] ### X

If anyone has usurped into his own property the estates of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, wherever they are located, or, knowing that they have been concealed, has not disclosed them [or, [Note: [Col. 0801D] Absent from the Chronicle of Verdun] has not rendered the due service from them to blessed Peter], let him acknowledge that, as a sacrilegious person, he incurs the wrath of God and of the holy apostles. Whoever is discovered in this crime shall lawfully restore the same inheritance of blessed Peter and pay a fourfold penalty from his own goods.

### XI

If any bishop has consented, through prayers or payment, to the fornication of priests, deacons, or subdeacons, or to the crime of incest in his parish, or, once the offense has come to his knowledge, has not opposed it by the authority of his office, he shall be suspended from office.

[Col. 0802B] ### XII

Let every Christian arrange to offer something to God at the solemn celebration of Mass, and let him be reminded [variant: let it be brought to remembrance] of what God said through Moses: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Exodus XXIII). For it is clearly evident from the collections of the holy Fathers that all Christians ought, according to the custom of the holy Fathers, to offer something to God.

## Addition of Philip Labbe, S.J.

The often-mentioned Hugh of Flavigny, abbot, prefaces these canons of the Roman council with the following: “Consecrated, etc.” It has already been printed elsewhere.

## Notes of Severinus Binius

### Council

After the matters contained in the acts reviewed above, the letter of Gregory, Book VI, Letter 10, which he wrote to all the people of Ravenna concerning Gilbert’s crimes and deposition, indicates that the most infamous Gilbert, archbishop of Ravenna, was frequently summoned to the synod, abused the patience and kindness of the Apostolic See, and was deposed on account of the immense crimes he had committed.

### The emperor of Constantinople was excommunicated

Namely Nicephorus, surnamed Botaniates, who, tyrannically claiming the empire for himself, imprisoned Michael, together with Maria Augusta, his wife, and their son Constantine Porphyrogenitus, at Blachernae and banished them to a monastery. Nicephorus was crowned by the patriarch Cosmas, who, in that same year, after John Xiphilinus had died, had been appointed by the emperor Michael to replace him. Cosmas had come from Jerusalem and was held in high esteem by the emperor. John Curopalates.

### “If any of the Normans”

Leo, bishop of Ostia, who was present, recounts the occasion for enacting this canon in Book III, chapters 45 and 46, as follows:

“At that time the bishop of the Church of Rosella, coming to this monastery, deposited a considerable sum of money in this place. When this was reported to Jordan, prince of Capua, he sent soldiers and ordered them to take it from the church treasury and bring it to him. To this the brothers replied: ‘The money entrusted to Father Benedict we give to no living person at all; but let anyone who presumes to do so take it from the treasury where it has been stored.’

“The soldiers, drunk with diabolical fury, took the money from the treasury and carried what they had taken to the prince. When so great, so monstrous, and unheard-of a crime came to the ears of Pope Gregory, he could not tolerate leaving the offense of this rash act unpunished. Fearing that by this example our church might again be violated, he interdicted the divine office in the church of Father Benedict and ordered all the altars to be stripped. He declared that, in the face of so great a crime, Desiderius, the abbot, and the brothers could rightly be accused of excessive negligence and blameworthy fear; and that he would be moved more severely against our community unless he were restrained by the charity with which he had always loved this place. For it was more tolerable that the villages and castles belonging to us be given over to plunder and devastation than that a holy place, famous throughout the world, should be subjected to such disgrace.

“But divine vengeance was not long delayed. For the prince, the author of so great a crime, lost his sight after taking the church’s money. Then Gregory, presiding at the council, decreed that if any Norman or any other person invaded the estates, monasteries, villages, or possessions of our monastery of Cassino, and, after being admonished a second and a third time, did not make amends, he should be subject to excommunication until he made satisfaction.”

### “Since the investiture of Churches”

Concerning this canon, Leo of Ostia writes in chapter 41:

“At that same time, while the aforesaid Pope Gregory was holding a synod, Leo, the librarian of this monastery, who later became [Col. 0803B] bishop of Ostia, brought forward a dispute concerning the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento, which the Beneventans had recently and violently removed from the jurisdiction of our monastery. When the matter had been brought to judgment, all the privileges of our monastery were read out in the hearing of everyone. From these it was proved that princes, Roman pontiffs, emperors, kings, and dukes had given the aforesaid cell to this monastery. The supreme pontiff decreed that the cell had nothing to do with the Beneventans but was to remain perpetually under our jurisdiction.

“At the same synod it was also established that whoever received the investiture of a Church from a layman should be punished by anathema—both the one who gave it and the one who received it.” Thus Leo.

## Addition of Philip Labbe, S.J.

Concerning Gregory VII’s zeal against Simoniacs, clerics living with concubines, and others, the same Hugh of Flavigny says the following on page 207 of the *Chronicle of Verdun*.

[Col. 0803C] Therefore, consecrated in justice and holiness, keeping watch in an extraordinary manner through constant prayers for himself and for the flock entrusted to him, compelled by the necessity of pastoral office, striving with all his strength to correct the distorted hearts of the wicked toward the line of uprightness, he made God’s truth known to all without respect of persons. He gained the love of all good people through the fervor of his zeal for God and the execution of justice.

But since there is no fellowship between light and darkness, he incurred the hatred and slander—indeed the fiercest persecution—of lost men. Nevertheless, steadfast and immovable, he advanced vigorously by the weapons of justice on the right and on the left along the royal road that he had once entered.

First, animated by apostolic authority and by the truthful judgments of the holy Fathers, he burned with great zeal, as his office required, to eliminate the Simoniac heresy and to command the chastity of clerics. Let those who wish to hear hear, so that they may be strengthened; and let those who do not wish to hear hear, so that they may be put to shame: let them hear with what freedom and with what Catholic voice this defender of the Church thundered against the mad barking of the impious, their impious schemes, and their wicked attempts.

For when almost everyone sought his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and preferred to adhere to the discipleship of Simon rather than preserve Christ’s poverty in the unity of faith; and when the ministers of the divine sanctuary were unwilling to cast off the foul pollution of lustful contagion, unlawfully assumed and secretly introduced; and when the investiture of Churches was also being wrongfully usurped by laymen, he, for the common usefulness and necessity of the Church, gathered a synod in the Lateran palace. With archbishops, bishops, abbots, religious clerics, and God-fearing monks sitting around him, and while he was treating of the matters written above and of other concerns beneficial to the Church, he promulgated the following decretal chapters.

[Col. 0804A] I. Whoever among the military, etc.

These are the synodal decrees of the most blessed pope (page 208 of the same Chronicle), suitable for correcting morals, consonant with the decrees of the holy Fathers, distilled as dew from heaven, to be impressed upon, embraced, and maintained by all the faithful; issued at the command of justice, strengthened by courage, promulgated by prudence, and endowed with the virtue of temperance.

But while the perverse encounter their own perversity in the rule of these decrees, they call them serious, difficult, and, because they refuse to be corrected, impossible in every respect. O foolish mind! O filthy wickedness and most wicked filth! If the morals of lost men, who refuse correction, become foolish, will justice be silenced, piety trampled underfoot, and the sword of ecclesiastical discipline be forbidden blood? Woe to the ruler whom the sentence of this curse shall mark! “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood.” To withhold the sword from blood is to restrain the word of preaching from killing carnal life.

For this reason, because he wished the holy Church of God to be chaste, free, and Catholic; because he wished to drive from God’s sanctuary the Simoniac heresy and the heresy of neophytes, as well as the foul pollution of lustful contagion, the members of the devil began to rise against him. They presumed to lay hands upon him even to the point of bloodshed, and attempted by many means to overthrow him so as to bring him down through death or exile.

Thus strife arose between the kingdom and the priesthood, and the tribulation of the holy Church of God grew more severe than usual. For Henry, son of the Emperor Henry, proudly swollen against God and against the Roman Church, the mother of all Catholics, because his wicked life opposed the decrees of the holy Fathers and canonical institutions, rose up against God and against his Christ (Acts IV), impiously becoming rebellious against ecclesiastical sanctions. He stirred up the members of the devil against him and armed against him, by threats, flatteries, terrors, and gifts, all whom he could, having reached an agreement with many bishops of Lotharingia and of the lands beyond the Rhine.

While that most holy pope was still in the diaconate, sinister and dishonorable reports about Henry were spread everywhere. Because of his imperial dignity, the respect due to his father and mother, and the hope that he might be corrected, the pope repeatedly admonished him by letters and messengers to remember his illustrious lineage and imperial dignity, to order his life according to conduct fitting for an emperor, to show himself a king and emperor in character and to demonstrate it in his deeds.

But as his iniquity grew together with his age, once the pope had been elevated to the pontificate, he urged him day by day, with much greater concern and by the authority of the office entrusted to him, to improve his life. Henry, however, using the excuse of his fleeting and fragile age, promised in words from day to day that he would accept the pope’s admonitions, but in reality, through the worsening of his offenses, utterly trampled them underfoot, following the evil counsel of those into whose hands the court had fallen.

From this point, becoming more inclined to crimes and rushing headlong according to rash counsel, he was carried along by crooked paths. The most blessed pope decided to call Henry’s associates to penance—those whose schemes, by introducing Simoniac wolves in place of shepherds into bishoprics and monasteries, had polluted the innocence of the Church with a wicked heresy. He resolved to receive those who came, but to separate from communion in the body of Christ and from the fellowship of the faithful those who refused, in order thereby to remove Henry from their deception and evil counsel. He admonished him to drive those excommunicated persons from his house, his table, all his familiarity, and his fellowship.

Meanwhile, as the cause of the Saxons against him grew stronger and he saw that the forces of the kingdom and its defenses were about to fail him, he sent the pope a letter full of supplication and humility, expressing repentance for the crimes he had committed, promising amendment, and promising him obedience and faithful assistance against the rebels. Later he confirmed this before his legates, Humbert, bishop of Praeneste, and Gerald, bishop of Ostia, swearing it into their hands upon their sacred stoles, which they wore around their necks. The text of the letter is as follows:

### “Letter of Emperor Henry to the pope”

[Col. 0805C] “To the most vigilant and most desired lord Pope Gregory, marked by heavenly dignity through apostolic office, Henry, by the grace of God king of the Romans, offers the faithful performance of due service.

“Since kingdom and priesthood, if they are to subsist rightly administered in Christ, always need one another’s assistance, it is certainly necessary, my lord and most beloved Father, that they should in no way disagree with one another, but rather cleave inseparably to each other, joined most closely by Christ’s bond. For only in this way is the concord of Christian unity and the state of ecclesiastical religion preserved in the bond of perfect charity and peace.

“But we, who by God’s favor now bear the administration of the kingdom, have not rendered to the priesthood in every respect the lawful right and honor that we ought to have rendered. Indeed, we did not carry without cause the avenging sword of the power given to us by God, yet we did not unsheathe it against the guilty through judicial judgment, as was just.

“Now, however, somewhat moved by divine mercy and having returned to ourselves, we accuse and confess our sins to your most indulgent fatherhood, hoping from you in the Lord that, absolved by your apostolic authority, we may deserve to be justified. Alas, we are criminal and unhappy! Partly through the prompting of flattering youth, partly through the imperious freedom of our authority, and partly through the deceptive seduction of those whose misleading counsels we followed too closely, we have sinned against heaven and before you, and are now unworthy to be called your sons.

“For we not only invaded the property of the Churches, but also sold the Churches themselves to any unworthy persons—persons embittered with Simoniac gall and entering not through the door but from elsewhere—and did not defend them as we ought to have done.

“But now, because we cannot correct the Churches by ourselves without your authority, we earnestly seek your counsel and help concerning these matters and all our affairs together. Your command shall be most diligently observed in everything. And now, first of all, we ask that your apostolic strictness correct canonically the Church of Milan, which through our fault is in error, and that from there your authoritative judgment proceed to the correction of the Churches.

“Therefore, God willing, we shall not fail you in anything. We humbly ask your fatherhood to be graciously and readily present to us in all things. After no long time we shall send you our letters with our most faithful men, from whom, God granting it, you shall hear more fully what still remains to be said.”

But after he had engaged in battle and obtained victory, he quickly returned to his vomit, broke his promises, received excommunicated persons into communion and favor, and did not shrink from bringing confusion upon the Churches. The pious pope, still believing that Henry’s disposition should be tested, sent him admonitory letters, telling him to remember the Lord his God and remember his promise; not to dishonor the one who honored him, nor believe that he could deceive God; and adding that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Peter V). He spared him and preserved toward him the restraint of apostolic discipline, although he could justly have punished him for this one crime alone.

## Second Addition of Philip Labbe, S.J.

### Concerning the Fifth Roman Council

From the *Chronicle of Verdun*, page 214, volume I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1078, in the first indiction, in the fifth year of his pontificate, in the month of March, Pope Gregory VII, presiding over a Roman synod of one hundred bishops, said, after certain preliminary matters:

“We judged that the ordinations of those who have been ordained by excommunicated persons should be invalidated, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers. Holding to the statutes of our holy predecessors, we absolve those who have sworn fidelity or taken an oath to excommunicated persons, [Col. 0806D] and in every way prohibit them from observing such fidelity.

“And since, on account of our sins, we see many daily perishing because of excommunication—some through ignorance, some through excessive simplicity, some through fear, and some through excessive necessity—we temper the sentence of anathema for a time, as far as we can, suitably and opportunely, moved by mercy.

“Therefore, by apostolic authority, we withdraw from the bond of anathema wives, children, male slaves, female slaves or bondservants, as well as peasants and servants, and all others who are not so close to the court that crimes are perpetrated on their counsel; also those who unknowingly associate with excommunicated persons, and those who associate with people who associate with excommunicated persons.

“Whoever, whether a petitioner, pilgrim, or traveler, comes into the land of excommunicated persons where he cannot buy, or has no means with which to buy, we grant permission to receive what he needs from the excommunicated. And if anyone wishes to give something to excommunicated persons, not for the support of pride [read: ‘for support, not out of pride,’ as above in the Fourth Roman Council, HARD.], but for the sake of humanity, we do not prohibit it.”

Done in the Church of the Lord Savior, which is called Constantiana [perhaps “Constantiniana,” HARD.], on the fifth day before the Nones of March.

## Observation of P. Antonio Pagi on the year of Christ 1078, nos. 4 and 5
Bertold adds the following concerning the Fifth Roman Synod in his *Chronicle*: “At this synod, Berengar, a canon of Angers, was summoned synodally so that he might recover from his heresy, and a postponement was granted to him until the next synod.” To this should be referred what the anonymous Chiffletian writes in his little work *On the Multiple Condemnation of the Arch-Heresiarch Berengar*: “The most reverend Pope Gregory VII, successor of Alexander, again granted the same Berengar a hearing at two general synods in Rome. But since he could not renounce his sect, which was contrary to the Catholic faith, he chose again to abjure it under oath and to profess the Catholic faith, just as he had done at the preceding councils. Thus we learn that the Berengarian heresy was condemned at so many councils, both from the report of faithful men who took part in those same councils, and from the registers of the Roman pontiffs, and from the writings of religious men who wrote about these matters with complete fidelity. For those same councils are found to have been held in our own times, within forty years—that is, the number of years reckoned from the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Saint Leo to the present year, which is 1088 from the Incarnation of the Lord (the year in which the author wrote his little work). Hence many still live who took part in those councils; and they have testified to us with complete fidelity concerning those same councils.”

Berengar, who had made his first profession of faith before Pope Nicholas in 1059, made a second one at this synod. Mabillon presents it here, previously unpublished, from an old manuscript in volume II of the *Analecta*, in his observations on the multiple condemnation of Berengar:

“I profess that, after its consecration, the altar bread is the true body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, which suffered on the cross, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and that, after it has been consecrated, the altar wine is the true blood that flowed from Christ’s side. And just as I proclaim this with my mouth, so I affirm that I hold it in my heart. So may God and these holy things help me.”

“It is probable,” Mabillon says, “that after Berengar had torn apart his earlier confession with such violence in his writing—confuted by Lanfranc—as though it were the personal product of Cardinal Humbert, so that every avenue for complaint and evasion might thereby be closed to him, he was granted permission to explain in his own words his personal view concerning the Eucharist. This he did by issuing this second confession, in which he appeared to profess the Catholic faith by means of the artful expressions ‘true body’ and ‘true blood,’ although under such attractive disguises he concealed his heresy. It therefore happened that this confession did not satisfy very many bishops of that synod, and consequently the fuller examination of the matter was referred and postponed to the synod of the following year, for which a larger number of bishops was to assemble in Rome; meanwhile Berengar was ordered to remain in Rome until that time.” This conjecture of the most learned man is, in my view, highly convincing.

## Addition to the Fifth Roman Council

[Col. 0807]

[Col. 0807C] Since the affairs of the monastery of Cassino were defended at this Roman council against the invasions of the Normans, I have no doubt that the sentence issued against those same Normans also belongs to this Roman council. By it they were punished for a similar invasion of the property of the monastery of Casauria, or Pescara, an island in the Adriatic Sea in Further Abruzzo. [Col. 0807D] We therefore give it here from the *Chronicle* of that same monastery, published in *Rerum Italicarum*, volume II, part II, page 365.

Moreover, since two complete decrees concerning the non-reception by laymen of the investiture of ecclesiastical dignities are not found in the synopsis of the acts of this council—the only document which Labbe offers here in place of the lost acts—we supply them from the little work of Saint Anselm of Lucca against the antipope Wibert, book II, page 384, in the Canisian-Basnage edition. But before presenting these, it is useful to investigate somewhat the matter of the heretic Berengar, whose case was treated not only at the Roman council of the following year, a fact which did not escape Labbe, but also—something he did not know—at the present council he was likewise ordered to present a confession of his faith. If he related the truth in a certain writing of his published by Martène in the *Anecdota*, volume IV, page 103, some of the Fathers of that council then recognized it as Catholic; but others, suspecting that some heretical poison lay hidden within it, persuaded the pontiff to detain him in Rome until the council of the following year. [Col. 0808D] There he was compelled to express a clearer confession of his faith.

Furthermore, from Berengar’s account of his own affairs we understand that this Roman council began on the feast of All Saints; and the fact that it continued throughout that entire month is demonstrated by the heading of the same council in Labbe’s edition, which assigns it to the third day before the Kalends of December. At last, then, let us produce the confession of faith of that same Berengar from the same little work.

### Oath of Berengar of Tours

I profess that, after its consecration, the altar bread is the true body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, which suffered on the cross, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and that, after it has been consecrated, the altar wine is the true blood that flowed from Christ’s side. And just as I proclaim this with my mouth, so I affirm that I hold it in my heart. So may God and these holy things help me.

[Note: [Col. 0809D] Berengar relates this in a writing published by Martène.]

When I was staying in Rome with the pope at the assembly of bishops which he held on the feast of All Saints, he had this writing proclaimed publicly to everyone amid much shouting, saying that it ought to be sufficient for the faith and ought to suffice for those to whom milk, not solid food, should be given, in accordance with what Blessed Augustine writes concerning the sacrifice of the Church: “What you see on the altar is bread and wine, as your eyes also report to you; but what faith, which must be instructed, demands is that the bread is the body of Christ and the wine the blood.”

He loudly proclaimed to the people that I was not a heretic, asserting before everyone in his hearing that I held this view from the Scriptures, not from my own heart. He also testified that Peter Damian—no inferior to Lanfranc in the refinement of learning and no inferior to him in the dignity of Christian religion—had not agreed in Rome with Lanfranc’s statements concerning the sacrifice of the Church, and that he gave his judgment in favor of disregarding what Lanfranc said rather than what Peter Damian said, Peter being a son of the Roman Church and, if I remember correctly, bishop of Saint Rufina; no inferior, to repeat the words, to Lanfranc in the refinement of learning or in the dignity of Christian religion, and much more diligent than Lanfranc in the study of divine reading, in accordance with the Lord’s own command: “Search the Scriptures” (John 5).

Thus that pope, with whom I had spent almost a year, seemed to think that the madness of the agitated crowd had been restrained and quieted—as Blessed Augustine says, “of stirred-up mud”—the crowd which had accused me, as far as it could, of being a heretic. This was especially so because the pope had caused books to be brought from everywhere for the bishops and abbots, clergy and monks, and had proposed for reading the inviolable sacrifices of Christ and the opinions and writings of Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and others. Those who were with the pope agreed with me: the bishop of Porto, the bishop of Sutri [read: Sutrinensis], the bishop of Terracina, the cardinals Atto of Milan, the monk of Tui, the cardinal of the Roman Church named Deusdedit, Peter the chancellor, the brother Fulco from beyond the mountains, of kindly and humble heart, and the cleric Tethbald, likewise a companion of that lord pope, who at that time was regarded at Saint Peter’s as a cleric of exceptional literary diligence; and a certain brother who was called by the surname Bonadies, [Col. 0810A] together with several others whose names and dignities I do not retain.

Nevertheless, since those pestilential men and perverters of the Scriptures pressed that pope as strongly as possible to require me to remain in Rome until the assembly of bishops that was to be held with him during Lent, etc.

Gregory VII, while a synod of fifty bishops was in session, with a multitude of priests and abbots present, decreed as follows:

**I.** If anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or an abbacy from the hand of any lay person, he is in no way to be regarded among the bishops, nor is any hearing to be granted to him as bishop or abbot. Moreover, we prohibit him from the grace of Blessed Peter and from entry into the church until, by repenting, he abandons the position which he acquired under the crime both of ambition and of disobedience, which is the sin of idolatry. [Col. 0810B] [Note: [Col. 0809D] From the little work of Saint Anselm of Lucca against Wibert, book II, *Canones Veteres Lecti*, volume III, page 384, Basnage edition.] We likewise decree concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.

**II.** If any emperor, king, duke, marquis, or any secular power or person should presume to grant the investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the same sentence.

### Sentence promulgated by Pope Gregory VII against those who seized the possessions of the monastery of Saint Clement

[Note: [Col. 0810D] *Rerum Italicarum*, volume II, part II, column 865.]

If any Norman or any other person invades the estates of the monastery of Blessed Clement, or unjustly takes away any of the property of that monastery, and, after being warned twice or three times, does not make amends, let him be subject to excommunication until he repents and satisfies the Church.

If anyone appropriates to his own ownership the estates of Blessed Clement, wherever they may be situated, or knowingly conceals them and does not disclose them, or does not render the due service arising from them to Blessed Clement, let him recognize that he incurs the wrath of God and of Saint Clement as a sacrilegious person.

Whoever is discovered in this crime shall restore that inheritance to Blessed Clement and pay a fourfold penalty from his own goods.

Any soldier, or person of whatever rank or profession, who has received or receives, or has invaded, ecclesiastical estates—whether granted by any king or secular prince or by certain bishops—against the will of the abbots or rectors of the churches, or who has retained them with the corrupted and malicious consent of those same rectors, shall be subject to excommunication unless he restores those estates to the churches.

This was promulgated at Rome in a universal synod, with Blessed Pope Gregory presiding, and was approved by the universal council.

# Sixth Roman Council

At this council Berengar, often summoned to repentance and more often relapsing, again abjured his heresy and professed the Catholic faith, in the year of the Lord 1079.

*(Mansi, Councils, volume XX, page 523.)*

[Col. 0809]

[Col. 0809D] [Note: [Col. 0809D] From Thomas Waldensis, volume II, chapter 43, who says that he found the formal acts of this council in an old book of pontifical decrees, under the decree of Pope Gregory. Hardouin. Variants are supplied from the Mutina manuscript.]

In the year 1079 from the Incarnation of the eternal Prince [read: “Principle”], in the month of February, in the eleventh indiction, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Gregory [Note: [Col. 0811D] Waldensis: “Pope Gregory the Seventh.” Hardouin.], the universal pontiff, for the honor of God and the edification of holy Church, as well as for the salvation of bodies and souls, neighboring archbishops, bishops of various regions and provinces, and religious persons assembled at the command of the Apostolic See to celebrate a holy synod.

When all had gathered in the church of the Savior, a sermon was delivered concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Some had previously held one view and some another. [Note: [Col. 0811D] The same appears on page 214 of volume I of the new manuscript library, in the *Chronicle of Verdun* by Hugh, abbot of Flavigny.] The greater part asserted and defended in every way, by the authoritative testimonies and arguments of the orthodox holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin, that the bread and wine were substantially converted, through the words of the sacred prayer and the consecration of the priest, with the Holy Spirit invisibly effecting this, into the Lord’s body born of the Virgin—which also hung upon the cross—and into the blood which flowed from his side when pierced by the soldier’s lance.

Certain others, struck by extreme and long-standing blindness, tried through various quibbles to maintain that that substantial body, seated at the right hand of the Father, was merely a figure, deceiving both themselves and others [variant: “deceiving themselves and others only figuratively”].

But when the matter began to be treated, even before the third day had arrived in the synod, the other party ceased to resist the truth. The fire of the Holy Spirit consumed the benefits of the chaff [Note: [Col. 0812D] Waldensis reads “the benefits of the straw.” Hardouin.], and, obscuring the false light by striking it with its radiance, turned the darkness of night into light.

Finally, Berengar, the teacher of this error, after having taught his impiety for a long time, confessed before the assembled council that he had erred. He asked and prayed for pardon, obtained it through apostolic clemency, and swore an oath, as is contained below. [Note: [Col. 0812D] Waldensis reads: “as now follows.” Hardouin.]

### Oath of Berengar, priest of Tours

[Note: [Col. 0812D] The words enclosed in brackets are absent.]

I, Berengar, believe in my heart and confess with my mouth that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, through the mystery of the sacred prayer and the words of our Redeemer, substantially converted into the true, proper, and life-giving flesh and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord; and that after consecration they are the true body of Christ, which was born of the Virgin, which was offered for the salvation of the world and hung upon the cross, and which sits at the right hand of the Father; and the true blood of Christ, which was poured from his side—not merely through the sign and power of the sacrament, but in the properness of its nature and the truth of its substance—as is contained in this brief statement, which I have read and which you understand.

Thus I believe, and against this faith I will teach nothing further. So may God and these holy Gospels of God help me.

Then the lord pope, by the authority of almighty God and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, ordered Berengar never again to presume to dispute with anyone or to teach anyone concerning the body and blood of the Lord, except for the purpose of bringing back to this faith those who had departed from it through his teaching [variant: “who departed”].

These matters having been conducted piously and successfully, amid many proclamations the envoys of King Rodulf complained about Henry: sparing neither place nor person, he was crushing and trampling upon religion beyond the Alps; no one was protected by due honor, reverence, or dignity; and priests, as well as bishops and archbishops, were being seized like worthless slaves and bound in chains, while some were being slaughtered.

Therefore many members of the council decreed that the apostolic sword ought to be drawn against his tyranny; but apostolic gentleness postponed the act.

The envoys of King Henry therefore swore the oath written below.

### Oath of the envoys of King Henry

The envoys of my lord the king will come to you within the period extending to the Ascension of the Lord, except in cases of lawful excuses [Note: [Col. 0812D] Or *exonia*, that is, lawful excuses, which are called serious causes. The Mutina manuscript gives: “causes of death, serious illness, or captivity”]—that is, death, serious illness, or captivity—without deceit. They will safely escort and bring back the envoys of the Roman See, and my lord the king will obey them in all things according to their justice and judgment. He will observe all these things without deceit, except insofar as he may be prevented by your command. I swear this at the command of my lord King Henry.

[Col. 0812C] The oath of the envoys of King Rodulf, and likewise of Rodulf himself, follows.

If, at your command, a conference is arranged in the German lands, at the place and time determined by you, our lord King Rodulf will either come in person before you or your envoys, or he will send his bishops and faithful men. He will be ready to submit to the judgment decreed by the holy Roman Church concerning the matter of the kingdom, and he will not obstruct by any deceitful scheme the assembly arranged by you or your envoys.

After he has received a definite message from you concerning the establishment and confirmation of peace in the kingdom, he will endeavor to ensure that your embassy can bring about peace and concord in the kingdom.

All these things will be observed except insofar as they may be prevented by your explicit permission or by a lawful impediment, namely death, serious illness, or captivity, without deceit.

### Oath of the archbishop of Aquileia

At the same time Henry, archbishop of Aquileia, swore according to these words:

From this hour and henceforth I will be faithful to Blessed Peter and to Pope Gregory, and to his successors who enter through the better cardinals. [Variant: “I will not be…”; Hardouin, and likewise the Mutina manuscript.]

I will neither give counsel nor take action so that they may lose life, limb, or the papacy, or be captured by an evil captivity.

I will come to the synod to which they summon me, whether in person, through their envoys, or by their letters, and I will obey canonically; or, if I cannot come, I will send my envoys.

I will assist in retaining and defending the Roman papacy and the regalia of Saint Peter, saving my own order.

I will disclose to no one, knowingly, the counsel which they entrust to me in person, through their envoys, or by letter, to their detriment.

I will treat the Roman legate honorably on his journey there and back and will assist him in his necessities.

I will knowingly have no fellowship with those whom they have expressly excommunicated.

I will faithfully assist the Roman Church with secular forces when I am invited.

I will observe all these things except insofar as they may have been set aside by their explicit permission [variant: “except insofar as you may have released me”; Hardouin].

At the same synod, the archbishop of Narbonne, Theobald, called the archbishop of Milan, Siegfried, called the bishop of Bologna, Roland of Treviso, and likewise the bishops of Fermo and Camerino, were excommunicated without hope of recovery. All of them were excommunicated together with their followers, both clerical and lay.

### Oath of the bishop of Reggio

I, Gandulf, will not hold the bishopric of Reggio against your prohibition or that of your legate for eight days, nor will I seek by any means to resist your embassy. So may God and these holy Gospels of God help me.

# Notes of Severinus Binius

[Col. 0814A]

**Council.** Since Berengar’s heresy was condemned at this synod, who does not see that the charge is a most mendacious calumny by which Gregory is said to have been condemned at the assembly of Mainz on the ground that he had once been Berengar’s disciple?

Among Gregory’s other letters there is one written to Matilda in the first year of his pontificate, in which he clearly professes that the very body and blood of the Lord are truly contained under the species of bread and wine. If no other document existed, this one letter would be sufficient to demonstrate Pope Gregory’s unimpaired faith and to close the shameless mouth of the schismatics who slander him.

The acts of the life of Saint Bruno attest that at this council Saint Bruno—who shortly afterward was made bishop of Segni—disputed against Berengar.

Peter Igneus, bishop of Albano, was sent as legate to Germany, and Udalric, bishop of Padua, was assigned to him, as Berthold relates in his *Chronicle* for this year.

In addition to these matters, the letters numbered 18 and 19 of book VI indicate that certain other matters were discussed at this synod. These letters were written from this synod to the Church of Parma and to the Church of Bamberg.

# Addition by Philip Labbe, S.J.

In the same sixth year of Pope Gregory VII, another Roman council was held on the fourth day before the Nones of May. Its question was whether the property of the churches could be pledged in order to raise money for resisting Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, who was attempting to invade the Roman See.

Two very old manuscript codices formerly possessed by the illustrious lord Peter de Marca, archbishop of Toulouse, attest that four bishops took part, together with several cardinals, abbots, and archpriests, as we noted on page 379 of the synopsis of our history.

# Seventh Roman Council

At this council the kingdom of Germany was taken away from Henry and conferred upon Rodulf, with the additional provision that henceforth investitures of benefices were neither to be granted nor received from laymen, in the year of the Lord 1080.

*(Mansi, Councils, volume XX, page 531.)*

[Col. 0813]

[Col. 0813C] In the year 1080 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, in the third indiction, that same lord pope held a synod at Rome. Archbishops, bishops [variant: “and bishops”] of various cities were present, together with an innumerable multitude of abbots and clergy and laity of various orders.

At this synod, reinforcing what had been established by apostolic authority, he corrected many matters that needed correction and confirmed those that needed confirmation. Among other things, at the end of the synodal absolution he appended the following and ordered it to be written down for perpetual memory among posterity, saying:

**I.** Following the statutes of the holy Fathers, as in the earlier councils which, by God’s mercy, we have celebrated, we establish concerning the ordination of ecclesiastical dignities; and now, by apostolic authority, we decree and confirm that if anyone henceforth receives a bishopric or an abbacy from the hand of any lay person, he is in no way to be regarded among the bishops or abbots, nor is any hearing to be granted to him as bishop or abbot.

Moreover, we prohibit him from the grace of Saint Peter and from entry into the church until, by repenting, he abandons the position which he acquired under the crime both of ambition and of disobedience (1 Kings 15), which is the sin of idolatry. We likewise decree concerning lower ecclesiastical dignities.

**II.** Likewise, if any emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, or any secular power or person should presume to grant the investiture of bishoprics or of any ecclesiastical dignity, let him know that he is bound by the same sentence.

Moreover, unless he repents and leaves to the Church her own liberty, let him experience in this present life the vengeance of divine punishment, both in his own body and in his other possessions, so that at the coming of the Lord (1 Corinthians 15) the spirit may be saved.

**III.** Likewise, we confirm and reinforce the sentence of deposition and excommunication already pronounced many times against Theobald [variant: Tebald] called archbishop of Milan, and Wibert [variant: Gibert] of Ravenna, and Roland of Treviso. We likewise condemn Peter, formerly bishop of Rodez [variants: Ruthenensis; the Mutina manuscript: Redonensis], now an invader of the Church of Narbonne, under the same sentence.

**IV.** Likewise, if any Norman should presume to invade or plunder the lands of Saint Peter—namely, that part of the March of Fermo which has not yet been invaded, the duchy of Spoleto, Campania, the Maritime territories, the Sabina, the county of Tivoli, the monastery of Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, and the lands belonging to it—and, in addition, Benevento, we prohibit him from the grace of Saint Peter and from entry into the church until satisfaction has been made.

Nevertheless, if any one of them has a just cause against the inhabitants of these lands, let him first seek justice from us or from the rulers or ministers established there. If justice is denied him, we grant him permission to take from that land what is necessary for recovering his property—but not beyond measure and not in the manner of robbers. Let him act as befits a Christian, as one who seeks to recover his own rather than plunder what belongs to another, and who fears losing the grace of God and incurring the curse of Blessed Peter.

**V.** Moreover, we admonish all who desire to escape the punishments of eternal damnation and to enter the glory of true blessedness to beware of false penances.

For just as a false baptism does not wash away original sin, so after baptism a false penance does not erase the offense committed. It is therefore extremely necessary that anyone who recognizes that he has committed some serious crime entrust his soul to prudent and religious men, so that through true penance he may obtain certain forgiveness of his sins.

This is true penance: after committing some serious crime—for example, a premeditated and voluntary homicide, or perjury committed out of a desire for honor or money, or other similar offenses—each person must turn to the Lord in such a way that, having abandoned all his iniquities, he thereafter perseveres in the fruits of good works.

For the Lord teaches through the prophet: “If the wicked man turns away from all his iniquities and keeps all my commandments, he shall live by life and shall not die” (Ezekiel 18).

These words clearly show that anyone who has plundered another’s goods and, when able, has refused to return or make restitution for them; or who has borne arms against justice [variant: “who has borne arms”]; or who retains hatred in his heart; or who has become involved in such businesses or offices that he cannot carry them out without fraud, falsity, envy, or deception of his brothers, is neither to be considered converted to the Lord nor believed to have performed true penance for his crimes.

Therefore, among all our exhortations and warnings, we urge you not to seek penance from those who possess neither a religious life nor the knowledge necessary for giving counsel, and who lead human souls more toward destruction than salvation, as the Truth testifies, saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit” (Matthew 15). Rather, go to those who, instructed in religion and in the teaching of the Scriptures, are able to show you the way of truth and salvation.

**VI. On the election of pontiffs**

Whenever, after the death of the pastor of any church, another is to be canonically appointed in his place, the clergy and people, with the visiting bishop who has been sent to them by the apostolic or metropolitan See taking the lead, shall choose for themselves a pastor according to God, with every secular ambition, fear, and favor removed, and with the consent of the Apostolic See or of their metropolitan.

If anyone, corrupted by some vice, should presume to act otherwise, he shall lose all benefit from an improperly made election and shall henceforth have no power of election. The entire power of election shall rest with the deliberation of the Apostolic See or of the metropolitan.

For if the person to whom consecration belongs, by not consecrating properly, loses the grace of blessing, as Blessed Leo testifies, then consequently the person who turns toward an improper election is deprived of the power to elect.

**VII. Excommunication of King Henry**

Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and you, blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, deign, I ask, to incline your ears to me and mercifully hear me.

Because you are disciples and lovers of truth, help me to speak the truth to you, with every falsehood removed, which you utterly detest, so that my brothers may more readily listen to me and may know and understand that, trusting in you after the Lord and his ever-virgin mother Mary, I resist the wicked and unjust, while I provide assistance to those faithful to you.

For you know that I did not willingly enter the sacred order, and that against my will I went beyond the mountains with Lord Pope Gregory; but even more unwillingly I returned with my lord Pope Leo to your special church, in which I served you as best I could. Then, very unwillingly, with great sorrow, groaning, and lamentation, I was placed upon your throne, wholly unworthy.

Nor do I say this because it was not I who chose you, but you who chose me and placed upon me the heaviest burden of your Church; and because you commanded me to climb a lofty mountain and cry out and announce to the people of God their crimes and to the children of the Church their sins (Isaiah 58), the members of the devil began to rise up against me and dared to lay violent hands upon me, even to the shedding of blood.

For the kings of the earth and secular and ecclesiastical princes stood together, and courtiers and common people assembled as one against the Lord and against you, his anointed ones, saying: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm 2). They tried in many ways to rise up against me, so as to overwhelm me completely either by death or by exile.

Among them, Henry in particular—the man whom they call king, son of the Emperor Henry—raised his heel against your Church. He formed a conspiracy with many bishops from beyond the Alps and from Italy and sought, by overthrowing me, to subject the Church to himself. Your authority resists his pride [variant: “resisted”; Hardouin], and our power destroyed it.

Confounded and humbled, he came to me in Lombardy and sought absolution from the excommunication which I had pronounced against him. Seeing him humbled, and having received many promises from him concerning the correction of his life, I restored communion to him alone. I did not, however, restore him to the kingdom, from which I had deposed him at the Roman synod; nor did I command that the fidelity of all those who had sworn or were about to swear allegiance to him be maintained, since I had absolved them all from their oaths at that same synod.

I retained these matters in order to administer justice or establish peace between him and the bishops and princes beyond the Alps who had resisted him because of the command of your Church, just as Henry himself had promised me under oath through two bishops.

But those bishops and princes from beyond the Alps, hearing that he was not keeping what he had promised me, and as though despairing of him, without my counsel and with you as witnesses, chose for themselves Duke Rodulf as king.

King Rodulf then hastily sent a messenger to me and declared that he had been compelled to take up the reins of the kingdom; nevertheless, he was ready to obey me in every way. To make this more credible, from that time onward he continually sent me the same message, adding that he would confirm his promise through his son as hostage and through the son of his faithful duke Berthold.

Meanwhile Henry began to beg me to assist him against the aforementioned Rodulf. I replied that I would gladly do so after hearing the case of both parties, so that I might know which was more favored by justice.

But he, thinking that he could defeat Rodulf by his own strength, disregarded my reply. After he realized that he could not act as he had hoped, two bishops—namely, the bishop of Verdun and the bishop of Osnabrück [variant: Osnebrugensis; the Mutina manuscript: Osneburgensis]—came to Rome from among his supporters. At the synod they asked me on Henry’s behalf to administer justice to him, and Rodulf’s envoys also approved this request.

Finally, with God’s help, as I believe, I decided at that same synod that a conference should be held in the lands beyond the Alps, so that peace might either be established there or it might be determined which side justice favored more.

For, as you, Fathers and lords, are my witnesses, up to this day I have decided to assist no party except the one more favored by justice. And because I thought that the more unjust party would not want a conference to be held where justice would maintain its place, I excommunicated and bound by anathema all persons—whether king, duke, bishop, or any other human being—who by any means might obstruct the conference so that it would not take place.

But the aforementioned Henry, together with his supporters, fearing no danger of disobedience, which is the sin of idolatry (1 Kings 15), incurred excommunication by obstructing the conference and bound himself by the chain of anathema. He also delivered a great multitude of Christians over to death, caused churches to be destroyed, and gave almost the entire kingdom of the Germans over to desolation [variant: “desolated”].

Therefore, trusting in the judgment and mercy of God and of his most merciful mother, the ever-virgin Mary, and supported by your authority, I subject the often-mentioned Henry, whom they call king, and all his supporters to excommunication and bind them with the bonds of anathema.

Again, in the name of almighty God and of you, I forbid him the kingdom of the Germans and of Italy; I remove from him all royal power and dignity; and I forbid every Christian to obey him as king. I absolve all who have sworn or will swear allegiance to him concerning the rule of the kingdom from their oath and its obligation.

May Henry himself, together with his supporters, obtain no strength in any battle and no victory at any time in his life.

But so that Rodulf may rule and defend the kingdom of the Germans, whom the Germans chose for themselves as king, I give, bestow, and grant him to your faithfulness and in your name. To all who faithfully adhere to him, trusting in you, I grant an absolution from all sins and your blessing in this life and in the life to come.

For just as Henry is rightly cast down from the dignity of the kingdom because of his pride, disobedience, and falsehood, so power and the dignity of the kingdom are granted to Rodulf because of his humility, obedience, and truth.

Act now, I beg you, most holy Fathers and princes, so that the whole world may understand and know that, if you can bind and loose in heaven, you can on earth take away and grant, according to each person’s merits, empires, kingdoms, principalities, duchies, marches, counties [Col. 0818C], and the possessions of all human beings. For you have frequently removed patriarchates, primacies, archbishoprics, and bishoprics from wicked and unworthy men, and given them to religious men [but to religious men]. If, then, you judge spiritual matters, what should we believe that you are able to do concerning secular matters? And if you will judge the angels who rule over all proud princes, what can you do to their servants? Let kings and all the princes of this age now learn how great you are and what you can do; let them fear to disregard the command of your Church, and exercise your judgment against the aforesaid Henry so promptly that all may know that he will fall not by chance but by your power. Would that he might be brought to shame and repentance, [Col. 0818D] so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Done at Rome on the Nones of March [May], in the third indiction.

## Statement of Rudolph, King of the Romans, and of the Princes of the Empire, in the Roman Synod against Henry IV, Emperor

1. We, acting as envoys of our lord King Rudolph and of his princes, complain to God, to Saint Peter, to your fatherhood, and to this entire most holy council that Henry—the man whom you, by apostolic authority, deposed from the kingdom—has tyrannically invaded that same kingdom in defiance of your prohibition, devastating everything around him with sword, plunder, and fire. With impious cruelty he expelled archbishops and bishops from their bishoprics and distributed their episcopal offices as benefices to his supporters; through his tyranny Werinharius, Archbishop of Magdeburg, of pious memory, was killed; Adelbert, Bishop of Worms, is still being tortured by him in captivity, contrary to the command of the Apostolic See; many thousands of people have been killed by his faction; and very many churches, together with the relics of their abbots [sic], have been burned and utterly destroyed [Col. 0819A].

2. There are indeed countless crimes that this same Henry has perpetrated against our princes because they refused to obey him as king, contrary to the decree of the Apostolic See. The meeting that you ordered to be held for investigating justice and arranging peace remained unfulfilled through the fault of Henry and his supporters.

3. Therefore we humbly implore your clemency to administer justice to us—or rather, to the holy Church of God—which has been decreed against the sacrilegious invader of the Churches [Col. 0819B].

[Col. 0820A] Done at Rome in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1080, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory, in the third indiction.

## Notes of Severinus Binius

On the crown that Pope Gregory sent to Rudolph from this council, this verse was inscribed:

> The Rock gave [it] to Peter; Peter [gave] the diadem to Rudolph.

The letters of this same Pope Gregory to the bishops of Britain indicate that the ancient controversy between the Church of Tours and the Church of Dol in Brittany was also debated at this synod. Nothing certain was decided in it, but deliberation took place about sending a legation to Britain to investigate the case; and the same letters testify that proceedings were also held concerning the rights of the Church of Limoges over monasteries usurped by the monks of Dol, as well as over others occupied by the Archbishop of Reims [Col. 0820B]. Baronius, under the year 1080, number 16.

## Addition to the Seventh Roman Council, in the Year 1080

In which Henry is stripped of the kingdom and Rudolph is invested.

*(Supplement to Mansi, II, 46.)*

[Col. 0819]
