[Col. 0819C] The Saxon Annalist reports that letters were written from this synod by Eccard; I reproduce them here as received from him. Nevertheless, these letters may have preceded the sentence pronounced against King Henry in the council. I believe that this sentence was pronounced in the year 1080, when Henry, inflated by his victory over the Saxons, cast off all respect for the Apostolic See. The Saxon Annalist records that battle as having taken place on the sixth day before the Kalends of February. From this it would follow that this council met in the month of January. Once these matters have been established, this Roman council is clearly distinguished from the one in which the sentence of deposition against Henry was pronounced, which is recorded as having taken place in the month of March.

In that same year the Lord Apostolic sent the following letter from the synod to the German regions.

> “GREGORY, servant of the servants of God, to all the archbishops [Col. 0819D] and bishops residing in the German and Saxon kingdoms, and to all the princes and all the greater and lesser persons who are not excommunicated and have been willing to obey: greeting and apostolic blessing.”

Since we recognize daily how great a danger to the holy Church arises from your quarrel and dissension, it has seemed to us—and it has seemed so also to our brothers gathered in council—that we should labor with all our strength and ability so that suitable envoys, distinguished both by religious commitment and by learning, might be sent from the side of the Apostolic See to your regions. They would gather in your lands religious bishops and also laymen who love peace and justice, and who are suitable for this work. With the Lord’s grace going before them, on the day and at the place appointed by those men, they themselves and those whom we must still associate with them should either establish peace or, after the truth has been learned, exercise canonical censure against those who are the cause of dissension among the holy.

But since we do not fail to recognize that certain men, overcome by diabolical inspiration, inflamed by the torches of their wickedness, and led by greed, desire rather to create and witness discord than peace, we have decreed in this synod, as in the preceding one, that no person of any power or dignity, whether small or great, whether prince or subject, may dare, through any presumption, to oppose our legates. When they reach you to arrange peace, no one afterward may dare to rise against another in defiance of their prohibition; rather, until the day appointed by them, all shall observe a firm peace without any pretext or fraud. Whoever attempts to violate these regulations through any presumption, we bind with the bond of anathema and, by apostolic authority, fetter him not only in spirit but also in body and in every prosperity of this life; and we take victory from him in arms, so that at least in this way they may be confounded and crushed by a twofold affliction.

## Eighth Roman Council

Concerning the Case of King Henry and Certain Bishops, Held in the Year of the Lord 1081

*(Mansi, Councils, XX, 577.)*

[Col. 0819]

[Col. 0819D] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1081, while the eighth year of the pontificate of Gregory VII had not yet ended, a synod was held at Rome, with the same Apostolic presiding, in the basilica of the same Savior [Col. 0820D] and our Redeemer Jesus Christ. Among other matters, the sentence of deposition of the Archbishops of Arles and Narbonne and of excommunication, promulgated by the legates of the Apostolic See, was confirmed by the Lord Pope, with those present expressing their approval [Col. 0821A].

He also excommunicated again the man called King Henry and all his supporters, who had hardened their hearts in the previous excommunication.

He likewise anathematized Ildimundus and Lando, Campanian tyrants, and all their associates.

Moreover, he suspended from office certain bishops who, although invited to the council, came neither themselves nor through representatives on their behalf.

## Roman Council Held in the Year 1081

[Col. 0821B] In the ninth year of Pope Gregory VII, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, bishops, cardinals, abbots, and archpriests assembled to determine whether the goods of the Churches could be pledged for money to be collected for resistance against Guibert, Archbishop of Ravenna, who was attempting to invade the Roman See. Having examined the authorities and examples of the saints, they unanimously [Col. 0822A] declared that the sacred possessions of the Churches must in no way be exposed for secular warfare, except for the nourishment of the poor, the holy use of divine things, and the redemption of captives. Thus, under Joseph’s administration, the estates of the priests had been exempt from tribute; nor was the price of blood deposited or placed in the treasury [corban] (Matthew 27), nor did Heliodorus, the plunderer of sacred things under the high priest Onias, go unpunished (2 Maccabees 3).

Those present at these proceedings were John, Bishop of Porto; John, Bishop of Tusculum; Umbertus, Bishop of Palestrina; Bruno, Bishop of Segni; Cardinal Beno of San Martino; Ber . . . . . , Cardinal of San Crisogono; Benedict, Cardinal of Santa Pudenziana; Cono, Cardinal of Sant’Anastasia; Azo, Cardinal of San Marco [Col. 0822B]; Romanus, Cardinal of Santa Susanna; Bonus the Elder, Cardinal of Santa Maria; Maurus, Abbot of San Saba; Laurentius the cantor; Peter, archpriest of the Latin Gate; John, archpriest of San Sebastiano; John, archpriest of Santa Cecilia; . . . . . . , archpriest of the Savior; and many others.

## Ninth Roman Council, Held in the Year of the Lord 1083

*(In Mansi, Councils, volume XX, column 587.)*

[Col. 0821]

[Col. 0821C] [Note: [Col. 0821D] Variants are given from the Mutina manuscript.] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord one thousand [Note: [Col. 0821D] It should read 1083, as the fact that the eleventh year of Gregory’s pontificate began in this year clearly demonstrates. Moreover, Gregory VII was not at Rome in November of 1084. Pagius, under the year 1083, no. 5.] eighty-four, but in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Gregory VII, on the twelfth [fourteenth] day before the Kalends of December, with the same Apostolic presiding, a synod was held for three days in the Lateran basilica. Present were archbishops, bishops, and [the word “and” is lacking] abbots from Campania and from the principalities and Apulia, together with a few also from Gaul; for Henry’s treachery forced very many to turn back on the way, since he ordered or permitted the Bishop of Ostia, returning from an apostolic mission, to be captured contrary to law and to the faith of his oath. Henry’s persecution also impeded [praepedivit: “hindered”] three Lenten synods.

He who had once attacked Saint Paul and twice attacked Saint Peter eventually, after much blood had been shed, seized the portico’s walls [porticu; porticae: “of the portico”]—not so much through the courage of his own men as through the negligence of the citizens. The Roman populace, namely the larger part of the city [Col. 0822C], exhausted by two years of war, was suffering from severe famine: they were not permitted to go out to the neighboring towns or fortresses, and Henry’s sworn men were unwilling to come into the City to conduct business; many, driven out by hunger, had also abandoned the City. Consequently, the others applied themselves less energetically to the war, carried on the matter with less commitment, and, as each person found possible, withdrew from the guard posts more carelessly and without fear. Since the occasion has presented itself, it is enough to have briefly touched on these matters concerning Henry’s tyranny.

For the rest, in the same synod the Apostolic Lord openly expounded the form of the faith and the conduct of Christian religion, as well as the strength and steadfastness of spirit necessary for the present oppression—not with a human voice but with an angelic one. On the third day he compelled almost the entire assembly to sighs and tears, and then dismissed the council, made joyful by the apostolic blessing, in peace [Col. 0822D].

## Tenth Roman Council

In which Guibert, the Antipope and Heresiarch, and Henry, the Pseudo-Emperor, together with all their supporters, are excommunicated, in the Year of the Lord 1084

*(Mansi, Councils, XX, 589.)*

[Col. 0821]

[Col. 0821D] Berthold writes the following about this council: “The Lord Pope, having assembled the synod, again promulgated the sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch, against Henry, and against all their supporters; he had already done this at Rome on the preceding feast of Saint John the Baptist, when Henry was still staying there. The legates of the Apostolic See—namely Peter, Bishop of Albano, in France, and Otto, Bishop of Ostia, throughout the German lands—spread this sentence everywhere.” Thus far Berthold.

What Hugh of Flavigny writes in his Chronicle under the year 1084 should also be referred to this year:

“Henry came to Rome, captured the City, destroyed its walls, shut Pope Gregory up behind the wall in the Tower of Crescentius, and established his own pope in the church of Saint Peter, so that what is written might be fulfilled: ‘When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to stand, let the reader understand [Col. 0824A]’ (Matthew 24), and so forth. Nor did the leopard change its spots (Jeremiah 13)—that is, Henry did not change his wickedness. Rather, he won over, by threats, terrors, flatteries, and promises, as many as he could of those who were in Rome; he carried on wars, slaughters, and murders through himself and his men; he supported wickedness with all the strength he could and resisted the truth; and, in addition, he sent letters to his own people in which he falsely claimed that he had gained possession of Rome, deposed the pope, and prevailed over absolutely everyone. But Mathilda, and so forth. Gregory, therefore, shut up behind the wall in the Tower of Crescentius, sent envoys to Robert, Duke of Apulia, asking him to come and lift the siege, and so forth.”

# Appendices to the Works of Saint Gregory

## First Appendix: Works Attributed by Some to Saint Gregory

[Col. 0823]

### I. Commentary on the Seven Penitential Psalms

*(See Saint Gregory I, Pope, his Works, volume V, column 549, Patrologia, volume LXXIX.)*

[Col. 0823]

### II. Fragment of an Exposition on Matthew

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimi aevi, III, 92.)*

The exposition on the seven penitential psalms, which I listed above among the writings of Gregory I, is attributed by some, on rather uncertain conjecture, to Hildebrand; likewise, the following fragment was produced by Peter Allix from a manuscript in the Lambeth Library, in the preface to the *Determination of John, the Parisian Preacher, concerning the Mode of the Existence of Christ’s Body in the Sacrament of the Altar*, London, 1686, octavo. It comes from a more extensive Commentary on Matthew.

“For since bread and wine,” he says, “are said by all the saints, and are believed by the faithful, to pass into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, it is commonly asked how that conversion takes place: whether formally or substantially. That it is not formal is clear, because the form of bread and wine remains. Whether it is substantial, however, is not evident. Some say that the substance passes over and is converted here, so that this becomes that, yet they do not say that the latter is thereby increased, nor do they concede that this can truly be called that. Others say that this passes over into and is converted into that, so that under those accidents under which the substance of bread and wine previously existed, after consecration there is the substance of the body and blood, though it is not brought about by those accidents. But we, leaving uncertain matters aside, profess what is certain from the authorities: namely, that the substance of Christ’s body and blood is converted, while we do not blush to confess that we do not know the manner of the conversion.”

The distinguished Allixius adds after this:

> “That this work belongs to Hildebrand, who afterward became Gregory VII, is demonstrated by the words with which it closes: ‘THE EXPOSITION OF HILDEBRAND, SERVANT OF JESUS CHRIST, ON MATTHEW, THROUGH THE WORDS AND MEANING OF THESE EXPOSITORS AND THE SUBTLETY OF THE GLOSSES OF THE VENERABLE MASTERS, IS COMPLETED. I ADJURE YOU TO CORRECT THIS BOOK BY THE PRESENT COPY.’”

But Henry Warthon must be heard without qualification. Having used the same Lambeth manuscript, he attributes this Commentary not to Gregory VII but to a certain younger Hildebrand, around the year 1150. I shall reproduce his words [Col. 0825], so that the reader may more accurately understand the still unpublished commentary:

> “The younger Hildebrand, in an exposition on the Gospel of Saint Matthew preserved in manuscript in the Lambeth Library, repeatedly praises the richness and fullness of Holy Scripture, which is equally available to all Christians. Hence he compares it with leaven, by whose admixture the whole mass of flour is enlivened; with the pearl, for whose acquisition everything must be sold; with the vineyard into which the Lord sent all his servants together to work; with the talent that the master, about to depart abroad, entrusted to all his servants for investment; and finally with the banquet to which the Lord wished all kinds of people to be invited.

> “Thus he writes in Book VIII, Homily 64, on Matthew 22: ‘Tell those who have been invited that I have prepared my banquet’: ‘The banquet is the doctrine of righteousness and the words of the heavenly mysteries concerning the Son of God. Therefore, from the whole Law, and from all the prophets and Scriptures, he arranged the table of Holy Scripture; and on that table there is every doctrine of righteousness and of diverse mysteries, because there are diverse foods. Thus the greatness and abundance of the divine mysteries, indeed the food of souls, are found on the table of Holy Scripture.’

> “The learned P. Allixius believed that this exposition belonged to Cardinal Hildebrand, who afterward became Gregory VII, and he published from it the Eucharistic fragment in the preface to John of Paris. Yet the author of this book is very far removed from the character and opinions of Gregory VII. Gregory called for heretics and adversaries of the Roman Church to be cut down by sword and flame, and led the way by his example; he exalted the power of the keys given by Christ to Peter above every distinction of right and wrong; he consistently taught that the Church was founded upon Peter; and he held the monastic order, which he greatly favored, devoted to himself with the utmost zeal.

> “This author, by contrast, maintains that heretics should by no means be punished with death; he thought no less soberly about the power of the keys than any Protestant and teaches that it was given equally to all the apostles; he asserts that the Church was built not upon Peter but solely upon Christ himself; and, comparing the order of monks with the Pharisees more than once, he criticizes their tonsure, religious garments, and vigils (Book VI, Homilies 42 and 50; Book VI, Homily 69).

> “Add to this that Gregory VII strongly approved prayers made in a language unknown to the people. Our Hildebrand, however, clearly disapproves of such prayer, in commenting on Matthew 23, ‘Straining out the gnat but swallowing the camel’: ‘Woe to us, to whom the vices of the Pharisees have come down! For in tonsure, religious clothing, the prayer of the lips, fasts, and certain vigils we display ourselves as though we were good. And why do we do such things? What else is this than tithing petty herbs while abandoning love of God and neighbor, justice, faith, simplicity, humanity, pure prayer in the Holy Spirit, and the other shoots of virtue?’

> “Finally, what places the matter beyond all doubt is that our author cites Bernard, who was later than Gregory VII. Having attacked the vices of ecclesiastics, he adds: ‘Read the book of Lord Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, *On Consideration*, a very good work, which he wrote to Pope Eugenius; there you will find more fully described the errors of bad prelates.’

> “Thus a certain younger Hildebrand was the author of this exposition. We place him around the middle of the twelfth century, both because a more certain calculation is lacking and because the age of the manuscript and the manner in which Bernard is discussed suit that period very well.”

Thus writes the most distinguished Henry Warthon.

## Second Appendix: Wibert, the Antipope (Clement III)

[Col. 0825]

### Historical Notice

*(Ciacconius, On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 340.)*

[Col. 0825A] Clement III, a native of Parma, previously called Guibert of Corrigia, was made Archbishop of Ravenna by Alexander II. Formerly chancellor of the Emperor Henry IV, and, with Henry’s support, created Roman antipope during the schism, he sat in opposition to Gregory VII and his successors, Victor III, Urban II, and Paschal II, for twenty-one years, and some months and days. He was created at Brixen in Noricum by thirty schismatic bishops, through the agency of the Emperor Henry IV, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, Monday, in the third indiction; he was crowned at Rome [Col. 0826A], at Saint Peter’s, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, Palm Sunday, in the year 1084. He created twenty-nine cardinals, four bishops, ten priests, and four deacons. He died at Rome in the fortress of Sant’Angelo after the Kalends of September in the year 1101; he was buried at Ravenna in the cathedral church, and not long afterward his body, exhumed by order of Paschal II, was burned.

The twenty-third and worst schism in the Roman Church.

[Col. 0825]

### Diplomatic Notice

*(Jaffé, Registers of the Roman Pontiffs, p. 443.)*

[Col. 0825B] In Wibert’s bulls we find these sentences:

> “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness”;  
> “Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us” (7);

and:

> “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established; confirm, O God, and so forth” (8).

[Col. 0827A] They were issued *per manum* (“by the hand”) of:

Robert, cardinal priest (1); Bernerius, vice-chancellor (7); Bernerius, vice-chancellor in place of Peter (8); Robert, Bishop of Sanentini [read: Faventini/Faenza], vice-chancellor in place of Peter (9); Theodoric, Bishop of Albano (11).

In Bull 2 it reads: “By the hand of John, our scrivener and notary of our palace,” who appears to have written it.

[Col. 0827]

# Letters and Privileges of Wibert, the Antipope

## I. He Confirms the Possessions and Privileges of the Canons of Verona

*(Year 1084.)*

*[Ughelli, Italia Sacra, V, 769.]*

[Col. 0827B]

**CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ, PAUL, archpriest, and TOTON, archdeacon, and TOTON, provost, and to all the canons of the holy Church of Verona, both present and future, perpetual salvation in the Lord.**

It befits apostolic governance to come with kindly compassion to the aid of those who flourish in pious devotion, and to grant fitting assistance to petitioners’ desires. Therefore, in the name of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of blessed Mary ever-virgin, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the other saints whose names are written in the book of life, and also by the authority of the sacred canons, we command all patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, dukes, marquises, counts, and all persons, great and small, that no one may harm, strip, disturb, or take away your persons, or your estates and benefices, or any of your rightful possessions and investitures of the benefices of the aforesaid chapter, which you have held until now. Likewise we command that none of you, by any device, seek from your bishop the benefices that you have been accustomed to invest, or receive their investiture from his hands.

Likewise we command concerning all the possessions of your chapter—both courts and castles, villages, hospices, factitia, incensita, libellaria, tithes, male and female slaves, lands, vineyards, meadows, willow groves, mountains, and plains, both within the city and outside the city—which have been or shall be granted to you by the faithful—that no person, great or small, interfere with them. Rather, let it be permitted to you to hold them peacefully in the manner in which, through the favor of my pontifical predecessors, or of emperors and kings, you have held them until now, namely according to the order contained in the pages of your cartularies. Nor shall an archpriest or archdeacon from any other church be preferred over you. I say this because I hope that your church will never lack clerics suitable for these honors [Col. 0828B].

If, however, the archpriest and archdeacon should die at the same time, let the provost be permitted to exercise their office concerning the investitures until an archpriest or archdeacon has been ordained. If any written fabrication should be found by anyone for the destruction of the lawful order, your inheritance, or the matters mentioned above, we command that it be destroyed in every way and never appear again.

But if—God forbid!—anyone should attempt to act against this written authority of ours, or should offend you in the matters mentioned above and fail to make amends within a year, let his attempt be invalid, and let the earth swallow him alive, as it swallowed Dathan and Abiron in the rebellion of Korah. Let the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian come upon him [Col. 0828C], and the curse that was pronounced on Mount Ebal, and the anathema *maranatha*, and all those plagues and curses with which God struck Pharaoh and Egypt, which are written in the five books of Moses. Let him, associated with Judas the traitor and with Ananias and Sapphira, suffer eternal punishment, and let him be subject to our judgment and that of our successors. All these provisions, in accordance with the privilege of the most holy Pope Leo IX, we have decreed should be confirmed and strengthened.

Done at Ravenna, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084, in the seventh indiction. Given by the hand of Robert, cardinal priest, in the third year of the ordination of Lord Clement III, Supreme Pontiff, on the sixth day before the Nones of March. May it prosper.

## II. Letter of Clement III, the Antipope, to All the Faithful, Establishing the Order of Seating among the Bishops Attending the Council

*(Year 1085.)*

*[Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores, I, II, 583.]*

[Col. 0828D]

**CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church, perpetual salvation in Christ.**

That those who did not enter through the door into the most holy sheepfold entrusted by Christ the Lord to the chief of the apostles, Peter, but crept in from elsewhere like thieves and robbers, seeking their own advantage rather than the welfare of the flock, have been driven from the Apostolic See is not to be attributed to our merits but to divine goodness, which chose things that are not as though they were, so that the things that are might be brought to nothing [Col. 0829A].

Among the many matters conducted at the very beginning of our pontificate in the synod that we hastened to convene for the common good, holding it around the Nones of January, the Lord, in his favor, granted us the opportunity to settle one matter that had often been debated by the pontiffs who preceded us and had scarcely, or not at all, been brought to an end: namely, the dispute that had arisen in the sitting synod between the Archbishops of Ravenna and Milan. The Patriarch of Aquileia also muttered about it at our synod. Each claimed the place on our right side, and we were uncertain to whom it belonged by right.

It happened that on the first day of the synod the Archbishop of Milan was not present from the beginning, but, when the day was already declining, the patriarch was seated at our right, with the seat of our most beloved son, the Emperor Henry, interposed—he was already expected to arrive—because the Archbishop of Milan had been elevated to that position, as though he were to sit to our left of the Church of Ravenna. When the Archbishop of Milan came into the midst and requested the place on the right, the elected Archbishop of Ravenna acclaimed that place as belonging to him. Thereupon the Patriarch of Aquileia claimed it in a similar manner, and thus a dispute over one matter arose among three men.

The entire synod decided that the disagreement of the three parties should be brought forward publicly. Immediately a certain catalogue was produced containing the names of those archbishops and of those who had attended the synod of Pope Symmachus; in it the Archbishop of Milan was listed. In opposition, the privilege of the Church of Ravenna was displayed [Col. 0829C], containing a written list of names. It stated that it had happened not by any right or legal entitlement but rather for the sake of humility—namely, that the Archbishop of Ravenna had allowed the Archbishop of Milan to be listed before him by chance; and, so that no [lacuna], of whatever kind it might be, might arise thereafter, Pope John, Symmachus’s successor, had decided that this privilege should be established.

When this had been presented, so that one of them might appear to be the greater, although the right-hand place of the Roman pope had always by right belonged to the Archbishop of Ravenna, it was nevertheless to be yielded to the emperor alone if he were present, so that the archbishop would then have to move to the left. Once the privileges of the two disputants had been displayed, the privilege made by Pope John XIX concerning the seat on the right side was also displayed for the third disputant, the patriarch [Col. 0829D].

After these matters had been heard, we questioned the entire synod: first of all, the clergy of the Roman bishop and the Roman people, whose authority was greater and to whom the matter itself was better known; then all the others. When, in due order, John, Bishop of Porto, and Peter, deacon and chancellor of our Apostolic See, praised the privilege of the Church of Ravenna on behalf of the whole assembly, Poppo, Bishop of Brescia, did the same, and the entire synod followed his voice. Since, therefore, everyone’s voice had converged in a single judgment, our assent was likewise given in the same manner [Col. 0830A].

But so that what was done might become known to everyone, it pleased us to have it recorded in our apostolic letters and communicated to those present and to those who would come later, so that it might be believed all the more firmly because it is established that it was heard from our own mouth. To prevent either the Archbishop of Milan or the Patriarch of Aquileia from hereafter raising any dispute concerning the seat on our right side, we prohibit them, by our apostolic authority, from doing so. If anyone should rashly violate our prohibition, he will incur not only the indignation of Saint Peter and of our See but also the snares of our excommunication and anathema.

We command that the seat of the Archbishop of Ravenna always be on our right and on that of our successors, according to the authority of the ancient constitution, unless the emperor should be present; and then the Archbishop of Ravenna is to occupy our left. This is established by the firmness of our authority, appended to this account by the hand of John, scrivener and notary of our sacred palace.

Farewell in good health.

I, Ubaldo, notary of Ravenna and notary of the holy Church of Ravenna, have written this just as I saw and read it in the original.

I, Artufinus, and Bartelinus, and Canulius of the Artusini, saw the authentic privilege of the bulls with the bull of Lord Pope Clement.

And I, Paul Scordili of Candia, doctor of decrees, provost and cardinal canon of the holy Church of Ravenna, saw that privilege in the original and read it sealed with an apostolic leaden bull, though not in the manner of the other apostolic bulls, in the year of the Lord Jesus Christ 1413, in the sixth indiction, on the first day of May. Amen.

## III. The Privileges of the Church of Ravenna Confirmed by Wibert the Antipope, Who Wished to Be Called Clement

*(Year 1086.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, XX, 615.]*

**CLEMENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the holy Church of Ravenna and to all future archbishops in it, forever.**

Since the care of the Churches concerns us, and it is fitting to think about each one, and since, by the duty of the governance we have undertaken, we ought to provide for all, we must nevertheless look especially and above all to the Church of Ravenna over which, by God’s favor, we preside, as to a bride and daughter.

Therefore, grieving deeply over her misfortunes and wishing, insofar as it lies within our power, to cut them off, we have at last taken care to aid her with this remedy and this antidote of counsel: having examined the privileges of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, and the commands of emperors preserved in the archive of our Church of Ravenna, we confirm by the support of our privilege whatever is read in them, so that, once the seeds of litigation have been removed, neither the Roman Church may wrong the Church of Ravenna, her daughter, nor the daughter contradict the mother, but each may possess her own dignity.

And what is better, what is more pleasing to God, than to remove scandals, restrain disputes, establish peace, and see concord among the Churches? God rejoices and delights in these things, and by such gifts he is appeased above every sacrifice.

With the consent and approval first of our cardinals—Robert of San Marco and Anastasius of Sant’Anastasia—and of our brothers and fellow bishops—Roland of Treviso, Milo of Padua, Hecelinus of Vicenza, Fulco of Fossombrone, Theobald of Castel—and of many others who were present, we confirm by the authority of this privilege whatever is read in the privileges of the Roman pontiffs: Paul, Sergius, Anastasius, Leo, Hadrian, Eugenius, Theodosius, Valentinian, Louis, Charles, Otto, Conrad, Henry, and others. All their donations [Col. 0831B] and grants, which they are said to have made to the Church of Ravenna, whether concerning bishoprics, abbeys, counties, the exarchate, or other similar matters, which are more fully contained in the privileges and commands, we protect with the assertion of this document.

We decree and establish by apostolic authority that if anyone attempts to act against this privilege of ours, or if anyone becomes its opponent, let him be anathema *maranatha*, and let his portion be with Pilate, Herod, and Judas the traitor. So that this may be believed more certainly and observed more diligently by all, we have ordered these present letters to be strengthened by our seal.

These acts were performed at Ravenna, in a plenary synod, in the mother church called *Agiae Anastaseos* (“Holy Resurrection”), in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1086, while Henry III was reigning as Augustus of the Romans, in the second year of his reign, in the ninth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of March.

## IV. Letter of Clement III, the Antipope, to Wratislaus I, Duke and Later King of Bohemia

He urges him to pay the offering to the Roman See and to promote a certain man to the episcopate.

*(Petz, Thesaurus anecdotorum, VI, I, 286, from the Library of Saint Emmeram, Regensburg.)*

**C. bishop, servant of the servants of God, to W., glorious prince of the Bohemians and most beloved son, greeting and apostolic blessing.**
We believe, dearest son, that your prudence knows [Col. 0831D] with how many deceits and frauds our adversary the devil assails the human race, and with how many wiles he works daily to sow among Christians the discord which he planted between the angels, between God, and the first man. For, to tell you the truth, many reports have repeatedly been brought to us about you which would have stirred our mind against your affection—God forbid! But he who searches hearts is himself our witness that we do not wish either to believe or to hear anything concerning your dignity beyond what is fitting, and that in all things we have desired and continue to desire your prosperity.

Only your own disposition, and this grieves and saddens us, does not appear to show toward us that affection, that devotion which it ought, since—for we do not know by what fault of ours, or by what offense of ours against your affection—you have withheld for so long the offering owed to blessed Peter, contrary to the most devout institution and practice of all our predecessors; and although we have often admonished you about this with paternal affection, you have entirely disregarded either us or our commands, treating them as of little account. Perhaps such things have been reported to you. For today the earth is full of perverse informers who, as it seems, have cast a sinister suspicion of us into your mind; and, credulous toward falsehood, you have obtained some sort of opportunity for unlawfully retaining what is unlawful.

But God knows that, however you may have conducted yourself toward us, we have always loved you with a pure heart and desired your prosperity in every way. Therefore, dearest son, remove from your mind any rust of hostility, if any is there, and let there be in you toward us the same sincerity of affection that we have toward you. Since, however, we cannot remain silent about the injury done to the holy Roman Church without endangering our soul, we again admonish you as a father; we also ask and beseech you, and lovingly counsel you, not to retain any longer the offering owed to blessed Peter. By retaining it, you would surely provoke his anger against yourself, and without him opening the way no one can enter the kingdom of heaven. Rather, send it with the reverence that is due, so that you may be able to find him reconciled to you.

Moreover, we do not believe that you have forgotten that we made very earnest requests to your affection both by letter and through your messenger. We urgently asked you concerning a certain dearest son of ours, [Felix], [Col. 0832C] a man indeed most faithful and well known to you, appealing to your highness that in the matter we had requested you would assent to our will. But afterward you sent us no reply at all about this matter, at which we are greatly surprised. The man himself would already have been magnificently placed, as he deserves, had he not been held back by this expectation; and, God knows, you will not be able to find a more faithful man for yourself.

Let this also be known to your dignity: we have not yet discussed this matter with the lord emperor, our dearest son, because until now we have awaited certainty concerning your will. But be entirely certain of this: if, for our sake and at our request, you do this one thing, whatever you may thereafter ask of us that is worthy of both you and me, you will obtain. Whatever, therefore, your mind decides about this matter—whether you will assent, as we do not doubt you will, to our petitions, so worthy [of assent] [Col. 0832D]—make us certain of it as soon as possible. For we do not wish so great a man, so useful to ecclesiastical government, to be kept any longer in such suspension.

For this reason we order these letters to be marked with a new seal, as being more conspicuous, so that your dignity may also deign to send us the clearest sign of your concession—some new token of admiration, as it were, in electing and appointing the new bishop [of Meissen] whom we request.

## V. Synodical Letter of Clement the Antipope and the Roman Council to the Whole Clergy

*(Year 1089.)*

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all orthodox brothers, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the orders of the holy Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We believe that your fraternity is not unaware how many and how pestilential the inventions of the schismatics have been in our times, disturbing the holy Church, and how many peoples—because our sins have demanded it—they have infected with their errors. Their poison, spread indiscriminately from the head of the holy Church to its furthest members, has plainly generated no small struggle for you and your subjects, and the pain of such presumption has entered into the very marrow of your body.

Compelled, therefore, by this necessity, lest the boat of blessed Peter, bent nearly to the point of shipwreck by so many waves of disturbance, should plunge headlong into destruction, [Col. 0833B] we turned to the weapons which the Fathers used in defense of the Christian faith. We summoned bishops, abbots, and many honorable men from different regions to a synod to be held in the church of blessed Peter. When they had assembled through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, among the other matters which the synodal gathering had undertaken to consider, certain impious doctrines concerning questions newly arisen to the ruin of many were brought forward for common hearing by some persons. We considered it appropriate to make these known to your fraternity, so that we might make you more ready and watchful to avoid them—or rather, with God’s help, to destroy them.

There, indeed, a considerable outcry arose concerning the perjuries which they themselves encourage to the peril of imperial dignity. Since that matter appeared to be the root and origin of the other crimes, it pleased us that it should first be examined and that the extreme wickedness and danger of such an exhortation should be demonstrated. Accordingly, by necessary proofs we disproved the excommunication pronounced against the emperor, since it appeared to have derived its force from the occasion of the perjuries and all their assertions.

To refute their temerity, although many examples presented themselves both from the sacred canons and from secular laws, the following proofs seemed sufficient for our purpose: namely, that, with the Council of Nicaea approving, no sentence of condemnation may be issued against those who have not been lawfully summoned and reasonably convicted, and who have been stripped of their goods:

> “Let no pontiff presume to judge uncertain matters; for, even if they are true, those things are not to be believed unless they are established by clear indications, unless they are proved by manifest judgment, unless they are published according to judicial procedure.”

In the same council:

> “Let the judges of the Church beware lest they pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being discussed; for such a sentence will be void.”

In the same place [Note: [Col. 0833D] The Fathers of the Perestad synod of the year 1085 also used this testimony, as taken from Gelasius and the synods of Nicaea and Sardica; it may be read in the *Collection of Councils*]:

> “There is no privilege from which one already stripped bare can be stripped.”

Likewise blessed Augustine, treating the matter more fully in his book *On Penance*, says among other things:

> “We cannot exclude anyone from communion unless that person has either voluntarily confessed or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical court.”

[Col. 0834A] And so that it might be entirely clear to everyone that those very men had incurred the same sentence of excommunication, it seemed useful to recite the following words from blessed Augustine (*Augustine, Sermon 351, On Penance, vol. V, p. 948, new Antwerp edition*):

> “Certain people, looking to the commands of severity by which we are ordered not to give what is holy to dogs, to regard a despiser of the Church as a pagan, and to tear out from the body’s structure the member that causes scandal, so disturb the peace of the Church that they attempt to uproot the weeds before the proper time; and, blinded at this time, they themselves are rather separated from the unity of Christ.”

After these passages had been brought forward, with the whole synod adjudicating, we decreed that henceforth no one should presume, to the injury of the lord emperor, to dispute this question or to withdraw his subjects from the emperor’s service and communion.

To show also what kind of punishment those deserve who, at the urging of the schismatics, do not fear to violate oaths sworn to the king and princes, we cited the authority of Augustine:

> “If anyone, by violating a lay oath, profanes the oath which he swore to his king and lord, and afterward wickedly and deceitfully plots against his kingdom and lays some kind of ambush for his death, because he commits sacrilege by laying his hand upon the Lord’s Anointed, let him be anathema unless he makes amends through a worthy satisfaction of penance, as has been established by the holy synod; let him abandon the world, lay down his arms, enter a monastery, and do penance all the days of his life. Nevertheless, let him receive communion with the Eucharist at his death. But if a bishop, priest, or deacon has committed this crime, let him be degraded.”

After these matters had been carefully expounded, the greatest necessity compelled us to set measured authorities against the things which the enemies of the Christian religion blaspheme against the Catholic faith concerning the ecclesiastical sacraments, and to refute with persuasive arguments what it is impious to say and hear.

They nevertheless say that the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the consecrations of chrism, and indeed whatever belongs to episcopal and priestly office, when celebrated by those who do not share their sect, are in no way sacraments and confer nothing upon those who receive them except condemnation. For they assert, blaspheming with impious mouth, that the bread which descended from heaven, in which our entire salvation and life consists, is polluted rather than consecrated by them. They likewise say that the water of baptism, receiving no sanctification through the prayers and blessings of priests and the admixture of chrism, gives those who are to be regenerated stains of filth rather than spiritual cleansing. They hold equally wicked opinions concerning the repetition of ecclesiastical orders, the reconsecration of churches, and the reconfirmation of children; finally, they make the same claim about everything conferred upon Christians through priestly office.

As they labour at length over these matters [sic], we judged that each of their errors should be met with passages demonstrating clearly that all these things are valid not only among us, the Catholics who possess God’s grace, but also among schismatics and heretics, and that they must never be repeated for any reason.

Augustine, *On John*:

> “Whether a good servant baptizes or a bad servant baptizes, let the one who is baptized know that he is baptized by no one except him who holds the power to baptize.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let the dove not shrink from the ministry of the wicked; let it look to the Lord’s power. What can a wicked minister do to you when the Lord is good? And let seducers not deceive you. Recognize what the dove taught: ‘This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

And in what follows he says:

> “Seducer, you do not have baptism; a wicked man gave it to you, some traitor gave it to you. I do not argue about the minister; I await the judge. I have been baptized by Christ himself. ‘No,’ he says, ‘that bishop baptized you, and that bishop was in communion with those others.’ I have been baptized by Christ himself; I know it. The dove whom John saw taught me. O kite, do not tear me apart with evil intent.”

> “They say that the ministers of so great a judge ought to be righteous. Let the ministers be righteous, if they wish; but if the minister is proud, he is counted with the Devil. Yet through him the gift of Christ is not polluted. What flows through him is pure; what passes through him is clear. Suppose that the minister himself is made of stone, unable to produce fruit from water: in a stone channel water produces nothing, but it brings forth fruit in gardens. The spiritual power of the sacrament is like light, which is received pure by those who are illuminated and is not defiled if it passes through the unclean. Those whom a drunkard baptizes, those whom a murderer baptizes, those whom an adulterer baptizes—Christ himself baptizes.”

The same, *To Vincentia the Donatist*:

> “It is not the Christian sacraments that make you a heretic, but perverse disagreement. Because of the evil that has proceeded from you, the good that remains in you must not be denied. You possess it to your harm if you do not possess there that from which comes the good that you possess. Therefore all the Lord’s sacraments are from the Catholic Church, and you possess and give them as they were possessed and given before you departed from it. Yet you do not therefore fail to possess them because you are not in that place from which the things you possess originated. We do not change those things in which you are with us. For it has also been said of such people that they were with me in many things. But we correct those things in which you are not with us, and here we wish you to receive those things which you do not possess there, where you are. You are with us in baptism, in the Creed, and in the other sacraments of the Lord. But in the spirit of unity, in the bond of peace, and finally in the Catholic Church itself, you are not with us.”

Likewise, in the fourth book *Against the Donatists*:

> “I seem to be pressed when I am told: ‘Then does a heretic forgive sins when, according to your view, he baptizes?’ So too am I pressed when I say: ‘Then does a greedy pretender to religion forgive sins?’ If by the power of the sacrament, the one does so and so does the other; if by his own merit, neither does so. Thus that sacrament is recognized as Christ’s even in wicked men.”

Likewise, in the fifth book *Against the Donatists*:

> “How does a murderer cleanse and sanctify water? How do darknesses bless God? But if God is present with his sacraments and words, whoever administers them, then God’s sacraments are everywhere sound, while wicked people, from whom they receive no benefit, are everywhere overthrown.”

In the same book:

> “How will God hear a murdering man praying over the baptismal water, over oil, over the Eucharist, or over the heads of those upon whom hands are laid? Yet all these things are both performed and effective even through murderers—that is, through those who hate their brothers even within the Church itself.”

In the same book:

> “Just as those who have falsely pretended are truly received when converted, yet their baptism is not rejected, so too that baptism which schismatics or heretics possess in another manner, and in which they act no differently from the true Church, is not corrected when they come to us; rather, it is approved. Thus no one who belongs to the Devil’s party, either outside or inside, can defile in himself or in anyone else the sacrament which belongs to Christ.”

Jerome, *To the Luciferian*:

> “Just as it is Christ who baptizes here, so it is Christ who sanctifies here.”

The same:

> “I beg you either to grant him the power to offer sacrifice whose baptism you approve, or to reject the baptism of the man whom you do not regard as a priest. Therefore it cannot be that one who is holy in the baptistery is a sinner at the altar.”

Pope Anastasius also, writing to the emperor Anastasius, asserts that all whom Acacius ordained—although Acacius had been excommunicated by blessed Pope Felix and infected with heretical depravity—ought to remain in their orders without any reordination. He says among other things:

> “Acacius harmed himself by administering what was good badly; nevertheless, the inviolable sacrament which was given to others through him obtained the perfection of its power.”

After these and many other judgments of various Fathers had been recited, we summoned that synagogue of Satan to the synod by letters and messengers, to give an account of its impiety—not, however, so that they might deserve a hearing, which had already been entirely denied them in earlier councils, but so that we might restore to unity the peace of the holy Church, which they had completely divided. The text of the letter was as follows.

## VI. Letter of Wibert to O., Bishop of Ostia

—Concerning the matters he decreed in the Roman synod, and rebuking him for not having come when summoned to the synod. *(Year 1089.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 599.]

[Col. 0836D]

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to O., formerly called bishop of Ostia, and to his followers, what they deserve.**

Although you had made yourselves unworthy of a synodal hearing because, having been summoned repeatedly to the synod of the holy Roman Church, you refused to come, and for this reason were excommunicated, nevertheless, so that the murmur of the people infected by your errors may be removed, we command by apostolic authority that you come entirely without fear to the synod which, with God’s help, we are celebrating in the church of blessed Peter, so that you may render a proper account of the matter by which you have disturbed the holy Church.

But they, fearing neither God nor reverencing man, refused either to hear or to see our legates and letters. Therefore, persisting in their errors, from the hiding places which they inhabit like serpents they emit dreadful hisses to deceive the unwary and the simple, sharpening their tongues like serpents, with the venom of asps beneath their lips, and so forth.

[Col. 0837A] How many therefore were the outpourings of human blood in the Italian and German kingdom caused by their preaching; how many the destructions of churches; how many the groans of widows and orphans; finally, how great the depopulations of the entire Roman kingdom—the matter is proved more clearly by the groans of those who are oppressed than by our report.

Moreover, it pleased the holy assembly that we should proceed with due severity against the Simoniacs, who have made the Church of God a den of thieves, and that we should cut off with the sword of blessed Peter the revived head of that heresy, so often severed by the holy Fathers. Therefore, following the decrees of those same holy Fathers, we command by apostolic authority that henceforth no one presume to lay hands upon anyone by an agreement of the most shameful commerce. If, however, which God forbid, this crime is thereafter found in anyone, let the ordainer be deprived forever of his dignity, while the ordained person shall complete the ordination made through commerce.

Moreover, since this ought not to have been passed over in silence, because the people’s murmur against the incontinence of clerics is everywhere growing and spreading, it seemed useful that you should admonish the ministers of the altar, with the diligence you owe, to live according to the statutes of the canons and to preserve irreproachably the purity of chastity, without which, as the Apostle testifies, they cannot please God. Thus, once those outside have a good testimony concerning their correction, you may bring the insolence of the murmuring people to rest.

Those, however, who reject the Masses of sinful priests, and who, before our judgment has censured them, impose the prejudice of their own opinion upon those priests, shall be deprived of communion with the holy Church until they make amends.

Forbid the unions of blood relatives, since both divine and secular laws prohibit them.

Let your excellent prudence, dearest brothers, consider how good it is to persist in the administration entrusted to you and in the true faith, to oppose heretics and Christ’s adversaries, and never to depart from the path of truth. The Lord and Savior of all, whose faith we hold, who did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood, promised that the faith of blessed Peter would not fail and commanded him to strengthen his brothers. It is known to all that the apostolic pontiffs who preceded my insignificance always did this confidently; and my own smallness, though unequal and least in the ministry undertaken, nevertheless desires, by divine condescension, to be their attendant.

Woe, therefore, to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to preach the truth of the faith for the destruction of this error. Woe to us if we suppress in silence the truth which we are commanded to distribute to the money-changers. Therefore, brothers, I exhort, implore, and admonish your affection to watch with the diligence you ought and can exercise, to investigate heretics and enemies of the holy Church of God, and to uproot this plague with all the severity within your power, lest it spread more widely among sound minds. For just as the one who diligently carries out whatever may benefit the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God a worthy reward, so whoever refuses to guard his people against the authors of so sacrilegious a persuasion will be unable to excuse himself before the tribunal of the Lord for the guilt of negligence.

## VII. Privilege of Clement III for the Convent of Saint Peter of Padua

*(Year 1091.)*

[ORSATO, *History of Padua*, p. 262.]

[Col. 0838B]

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved daughter in Christ, Theophila, abbess of the monastery of Saint Peter situated in the city of Padua, and to the handmaids of God serving there, and to all who shall regularly succeed them there, forever.**

In consideration of the pastoral care which we exercise through the administration of the apostolic see, over which we preside not by any merit of our own but by the dispensation of divine providence, it is fitting that we vigilantly attend to the advancement of all the Churches everywhere, grant the just petitions of the faithful the assent of equity, and bestow the support of our favor and authority upon good and religious undertakings, so that they may increase from day to day and be brought to perfection. In this way, persons dedicated to God and perpetually bound by right to divine worship may be removed from every disturbance of secular persons and freed from all worldly impediments, so that they may devote themselves with pure and attentive minds to the praises of their Creator.

Therefore, reverend daughter Theophila, since your most holy devotion, supported by religious conduct, humbly requested that we strengthen the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter by the authority of our privilege, so that for all future times it might remain a monastery of the handmaids of God, and that the nuns might live there under the rule of an abbess without contradiction from anyone, we gladly receive your devout petitions through the intervention of our honorable confreres Milo, bishop of that same city, and Robert, bishop of Faenza, as well as our dearest son Peter, archdeacon of Padua, and we willingly assent to your religious desires.

Therefore, by apostolic authority and by the constitution of this our privilege, we grant and confirm that henceforth, for all future times, that aforesaid monastery shall be regarded as a monastery of nuns, and that no person, great or small, shall thereafter dare in any way to alter this.

We also confirm to that monastery, and to you and all who regularly succeed you, for the use of the nuns serving God there, everything contained in the charter of donation [Col. 0839A] which Bishop Milo made to you, and everything which you now possess or have acquired, and whatever you and those who succeed you shall thereafter justly acquire.

Moreover, we command and prohibit by apostolic authority that no duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any other person, great or small, ecclesiastical or secular, dare henceforth disturb or molest the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter or the handmaids of God serving there concerning anything which we confirm by the authority of this privilege.

If anyone should violate the sanction of this privilege, unless he repent and make amends with worthy satisfaction, let him be an exile from the kingdom of God, as a sacrilegious despiser of apostolic authority; and, condemned by worthy excommunication, let him become wholly estranged from the Church of God and subject to perpetual malediction. But whoever proves a pious observer, we decree, shall be filled with the abundance of perpetual blessing.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, indiction XIV, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Given by the hand of Bernerius, vice-chancellor, in the city of Padua; successfully executed.

## VIII. Bull of Clement III, or Wibert, the Pseudo-Pope, Confirming All Their Goods and Rights to the Canons of the Church of Reggio

*(Year 1092.)*

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, II, 185.]

[Col. 0839C]

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the canons of the church of Reggio and to their successors forever.**

It is fitting that we who have been placed as watchmen over the apostolic see should vigilantly devote ourselves to the defense and strengthening of the Churches of God, so that, with God’s help, they may advance from good to better; so that, when the disturbance of all wicked people has been removed, those who minister in divine offices may be able to serve more readily and attentively in peace; and so that we may deserve to receive the rewards of the good shepherd.

Therefore, by this present document, we confirm by apostolic authority, to remain forever, that the canons of the holy church of Reggio shall inviolably retain as their canonical estate one curia called Villa, three manses at Gova, one manse at Noniano, one curia at Campilia and two manses, together with one given by Sigefridus, called Galliulo; the curia called Massa, with its appurtenances; Prenniano with its appurtenances; and the land situated at Castro Holeriano; at Mucleto one manse, at Dinazano one, at Valle Birli one, at Mount Babuli one, at Casalicio one, at Braciano three, at Veterivola one, and at Mount Todioni one.

Also everything belonging to the aforesaid canons’ church of Saint Mary and Saint Michael at Tabiano, Caterniano, Mellocio, Grazano, and Verniano, with their appurtenances; in Civita Nova and Curlo; those properties with the forest at Bajarola; one parish at Rivalta with its castle and appurtenances; a manse at Corniano and at Runcho, Folliano, and Alliano; properties at Gavassa with tithes and forest; and at Corrigia, or at Butrio, Rio, Fazano, Campogalliano, Fontana, Prato, Canule, Mandrie, and Gurgo.

Also two allotments near Curtenova; two manses at Cetlole; the parish of Nuvalara with all its appurtenances; three manses at Canole, Corviatico, and Mandriole; at Fabrica one manse; and at Seso, Rodano, Silvarano, Carbognano, Caldariola, Campaniola, Bedullo, the village of Martinus, Querciola, and Mount Gamoni.

Also the chapel of Saint Vitus at Offiano, and the chapel of Saint Abundius with its appurtenances; the meadow of Boceto; Ariole, Gaziata, Motelena, Campigene, and Marmoriolo; the properties lying beside the little bridge of Rodano; the forest of Groseto; Purciliole and Runcise; at Casale Fossedunde; Razolum with its fisheries; and all its appurtenances at Saint Stephen, at Saint Possidonius, in the district of Modena, at Buyda, on Mount Passararius, at Puliagnello, Serra, and Appollina at Saint Mary, with its olive grove.

Also the tithe in the city called Reggio, in its entirety, and at Marsia; and all the properties situated around the city called Emilia.

Also one curia in the territory of Tortona, called Nova; all the properties at Aqueductio; and the curia of Saint Stephen with the parish situated below the castle, with all its appurtenances, just as they were entirely and properly bestowed upon the same canonical church by the bishop Sigefridus, of blessed memory, or by other bishops, for the souls of themselves and their successors, by written charter or investiture.

And all the properties which are known to have been offered from the gifts of bishops or by the devotion of the faithful to the aforesaid canonical church or to its canons, we have entered in this privilege, by the authority of the holy canons and by our apostolic immunity, to be preserved inviolably forever with all their adjacent lands and appurtenances, without contradiction from any person, great or small.

If anyone should presume, with rash audacity, to act against this our apostolic privilege, or to arrange the canonical properties otherwise, or to put them to any use other than that established by the bishops Teuzo, Sigefridus, Adhelberius, Wolmarus, [Col. 0840D] and Gandulfus, let him know that by the power of almighty God, of the apostle blessed Peter, and of all the saints, as well as by our authority, he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and to be burned with all the impious in eternal fire.

But whoever proves an observer may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful Lord.

Given at Cesena by the hand of Bernerius, deputy for Peter the chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, indiction XV, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Clement III, on the Ides of June.

## IX. Letter of Clement III the Antipope to Ruithard, Archbishop of Mainz

—He appoints a day for him to attend the synod to be held at Vercelli. *(Year 1097.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 601.]

[Col. 0841A]

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., our brother and fellow bishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Very recently, through our brother the bishop of Faenza, we instructed your fraternity and commanded you under the strictest obedience to come, setting aside every excuse, to the synod which we are going to celebrate at the aforesaid place and time for the necessary affairs of the whole Church. At first you promised well; but afterward, when you had carried out your will in some measure, and the aforesaid messenger, returning, was about to impose true obedience upon you as upon the others, you said that you had been released from our command through your messenger.

When we heard this, it is impossible to express how gravely we took it. For this statement seemed greatly to disturb the synod, since nearly all your suffragans look to you, and the voice of all is: “What my master has done, I shall do.”

Therefore, to the same N., who uttered so wicked, so execrable, and so harmful a lie against the holy and universal Church, we prohibit every divine office by apostolic authority until he comes to us and makes satisfaction for the iniquity of so great and detestable a lie. If he does not come to us by the feast of Saint Michael to make satisfaction concerning this matter, he shall be subject to an excommunication more severe than he perhaps supposes.

[Col. 0841C] To you, however, we command again and again by apostolic authority and under true obedience that you come to the synod to be celebrated at Vercelli on the feast of Saint Dionysius, and that you admonish all your suffragans under the same obedience.

## X. Letter of Clement III the Pseudo-Pope to Rotbert, Bishop of Bamberg

—He urges that the accuser of Ruithard, Archbishop of Mainz, should come to the synod. *(Year 1097–98.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 600.]

**Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., our brother and fellow bishop of Bamberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

[Col. 0841D] We have heard and rejoiced that you stood firmly by disputing justly against the destroyers of the Church and our adversaries, and therefore we give you thanks. But as for the things which you owe to the Roman Church from your own church and which we have patiently awaited for a long time, we did not do so through ignorance, but because we awaited the voluntary goodwill of your obedience.

We warn you how little we have advanced in this matter and firmly command you to pay what you owe, and not delay restoring what you rashly took away. If you do not do this, we shall publicly and through our legates bring a complaint against you before our advocate, the emperor, and all our brothers.

We have granted the bishop of Mainz, whom you accused and denounced to us with the worst crimes, a postponement for answering us until the feast of Saint Michael. We wish you to be present at this matter with our other brothers, so that, just as you accused him in his absence, you may convict him in his presence by true testimony under our authority.

It has been reported to us by certain persons that baptized Jews have, for some reason unknown to me, been permitted to apostatize and practice the rite of Judaism. Since this is unheard-of and utterly wicked, we bind you and all our brothers by the word of God to hasten to correct it according to canonical sanction and in accordance with the examples of the Fathers, lest the sacrament of baptism and the saving invocation of the Lord’s name appear to be annulled.

## XI. Clement III the Antipope Writes to Godebold, Provost, and to the Whole Clergy of Mainz Concerning the Crimes of Archbishop Ruithard

He says that, because of the infamy of simony, Ruithard was summoned three times—first “by the cardinals of the Roman Church, Warinus, Anastasius, and Adalmarius; afterward by the bishops Tidericus of Albano and Ruopperthus of Faenza; and finally by Hugo, deacon of the sacred palace”—but did not come. Rather, having violated his loyalty to the emperor, he went over to the enemies of the kingdom and the priesthood, incited them, and plotted against the emperor’s life and crown. After adding other accusations, he releases them from obedience to Ruithard and forbids anyone to communicate with him under penalty of anathema.

“Given by the hand of Tidericus, bishop of Albano, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August; Urban having died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August without the viaticum of the body and blood of the Lord.”

(It should doubtless be read: “Given on the second day before the Kalends of August, Urban having died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August,” etc.)

*(Year 1099.)*

[In SCHUNCK, *Contributions to the History of Mainz*, II, 115, according to JAFFÉ, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, 447. It begins: “How great in these times …”]

[Col. 0842C]

[Col. 0842D]

# APPENDIX III

**Ancient Documents against the Schismatics, Once Written on Behalf of Gregory VII and Several Other Roman Pontiffs, and Now for the First Time Brought to Light through the Diligence of the Most Illustrious and Most Learned Lord Sebastian Tengnagel, Doctor of Both Laws and Imperial Librarian at Vienna**

(*Works of Gretser, VI, 429.*)

[Col. 0843]

## To the Noble and Most Illustrious Man and Lord, Lord Sebastian Tengnagel

While you draw ancient charters, buried in dense darkness,  
Out into the light, taking care that they not perish,  
The company of scholars rightly applauds you and asks  
That you continue always to bring forth such treasures.

Let others be *condi* (“keepers”), let others be *clusii* (“closers”), and let them close everything;  
for us be both a *promus* (“steward”) and an *aperta* (“opener”).

[Col. 0843]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the most reverend and most illustrious prelate and lord, Lord Melchior Klesl, nominated bishop of Vienna, confirmed administrator of the bishopric of Wiener Neustadt, provost of the cathedral church of Vienna, and chancellor of the celebrated archgymnasium there, counsellor to His Sacred Imperial and Royal Majesty, his most gracious lord, etc.

How greatly those on the opposing side, most illustrious and reverend prelate, fight with open engines, weapons, and mines in order to violate, shake, and finally uproot altogether that most sacred majesty and authority of the Roman pontiffs is made evident—clearer than midday light—by their indefatigable zeal, with which they investigate, unearth, and heap into the broad daylight the obsolete chatter, trifles, and refuse of the schismatics, long deservedly condemned to dreadful darkness, as though with a canine nose. It is as if, whenever some insolent intellect, enslaved to love, hatred, or profit, has smeared something upon unsound documents against that venerable head of the sacred hierarchy—which Indians, Ethiopians, Arabs, Persians, Tartars, and even those not consecrated to our religion, to say nothing of Europeans, acknowledge to possess supreme authority among Christians—those thorn-gatherers (*akanthologoi*) and reed-cutters (*kalamosphaktai*) seize upon it as though it had been dropped from heaven, as some rare windfall (*hermaion*); they forge it, refashion it, and deem it almost worthy of cedar and immortality. Hence have emerged those tortuous *Centuries* and *Memorable and Recondite Readings*, and other badly sewn patchworks of the same sort, like abscesses and cancers upon pure truth, although the very authors whom they so love, publish, and prostitute themselves to promote differ for the most part from the profane doctrines and variously divided sects of these men—and thus the axe which they labor so strenuously to bring down upon us rebounds upon their own legs.

[Col. 0845] Stirred, therefore, by their zeal and industry, I too—whom, as I borrow Blessed Augustine’s expression [Epistle 165], a succession of priests holds in the Church from the very see of the Apostle Peter, to whom Christ entrusted the feeding of his sheep, down to the present episcopate—might contribute some small offering to this august Catholic Church, enclosed within the same boundaries as the sun. I shook out and transcribed certain little works on parchment which otherwise would have perished through neglect and decay, and through moths and cockroaches, and I gave them to the outstanding champion of our side, the reverend Father Jacob Gretser of the Society of Jesus, to be printed with his types. Of what quality their style may be, I refrain from explaining in a long-winded discourse, lest I hear that line of Lucilius from the street:

> “The scrutineer praises a scraper,  
> merely to sell it; the rogue splits a broken shoe in half.”

Let this meanwhile serve as their encomium: that the blessed storekeeper and dispenser of ecclesiastical annals, the illustrious Cardinal Baronius, ardently desired to see these materials of ours and insert them into his commentaries. Had he obtained them, he would have added a not-to-be-regretted supplement to volumes XI and XII, and would have scattered, more brightly than by this illustrious sun of truth, those clouds of calumny which they pour forth, as though from a wagon, against Gregory VII, Alexander III, and Adrian IV—“with a tongue of evil” (*kēkadi syn glōssē*), to use Callimachus’ words. Let this little work of ours, then, be like a slender ear of grain left behind after Baronian’s great harvest.

I now publish it under your illustrious name, most illustrious prelate, as beneath the aegis of Pallas, shielded against the uncouth snouts of quibblers and faultfinders; and I dedicate it to you, with the highest justification, as you repeatedly undergo the same hazard of labors and dangers as our pontiffs, whom this writing defends, preserving the source’s dedication-formula initials, L. M. For you, great and unconquered athlete, frequently engaging your adversaries hand to hand, have severed their stratagems, stitchings, and variously woven devices, like a spider’s web, with a single blow. So thoroughly have they been bound, stunned, and overthrown by your grandiloquence, as though by some Mercurial chain, that they have yielded to the truth and, having cast off the profane mysteries with which they had hitherto been imbued, enrolled themselves in the ranks of our orthodox faith. For its sake they have been willing to be burned, bound, flogged, and killed by iron, gladly and readily binding themselves by oaths.

While you work vigorously to strengthen their minds, you have often exposed your head, devoted to the propagation of religion, to immediate danger for Christ and his Church. Disregarding the ambushes threatening from every side by the enemy, and scorning concern for the present life, you have steadfastly and firmly taught your neophytes, guided by grace and accompanied by faith, to enter upon the royal road to eternal life—a road worn smooth by the tracks of all venerable antiquity—while passing over the byways, deviations, and twisting precipices of error.

So much so that the Catholic religion, which at that time seemed here gradually to be collapsing and being carried backward into worse conditions, openly declares that it owes all the worship, adornment, and growth with which it now shines and flourishes to you alone, its incomparable champion, who more than a thousand times set yourself as a bronze wall and rampart before the house of the Lord against the weapons of the assembled enemies, and it declares this with the deepest gratitude. Although now once again, through the injury of the times, something seems here to be taken from it, and the opposing force to raise its neck and press upon our foot, there is nevertheless hope that this new and ignoble offspring of the Titans, wickedly attacking heaven and the heavenly ones, will, under the direction and auspices of the supreme Ruler, who establishes and repeals his decrees, be cast down from above and finally lie buried and crushed beneath the mass of the mountains it has piled up.

Let them therefore give ground, though they rush upon and attack, like blindfolded fighters, this formidable Roman Church—truly happy in its condition, and ordered like a well-arrayed line of a camp—as Tertullian the African says [*On the Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 36]. To it the apostles poured out the whole of their doctrine together with their blood; there Peter is made equal to the Lord’s Passion; there Paul is crowned with the death of John; there the Apostle John, after being plunged into boiling oil and suffering no harm, is banished to an island. Nevertheless it will stand, an adamant-footed pillar (*ad﻿amantopēdilos kiōn*), as the pillar and foundation of truth, against which not even the gates of hell will prevail.

Under this auspice I conclude. I ask, most illustrious Maecenas, that you receive with willing hand and serene face this slight paper gift, a memorial of your merits toward me; that you, who almost alone

> “look back upon the sorrowful Camenae  
in this troubled age …,”

embrace and cherish its editor with your authority and favor; and that you spur him on to publish greater works. From my heart I pray and vow that the supreme God may by his assent confirm and prosper your endeavors beneficial to the Christian commonwealth.

Given at Vienna in Austria, from the Imperial Museum, on the thirteenth day before the feast of Saint Hippolytus, patron of Austria, in the year of salvation restored by Christ 1611.

**Sebastian Tengnagel, Doctor of Both Laws, Imperial and Royal Librarian**

[Col. 0845]

# Letter of Saint Gebhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, to Hermann, Bishop of Metz, for Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiff

Against the Schismatics of the Same Period. Now First Brought Forth from Darkness into Light.

[Col. 0847]

## To the Reader

Friend reader, if you wish to know who and how great the author of this letter was, read his Life published by G. V. D. Henry Canisius in volume II of the *Ancient Readings*, and in volume VI, where you will find his deeds explained at much greater length. Consult also Bruno, published by Freher in volume I of the *German Writers*, at the end of the commentary on the *Saxon War*, where he records that at a certain assembly of bishops and princes from both parties the task of delivering the case was entrusted to our Gebhard. “Our men,” says Bruno, “breaking the silence, sought Gebhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, that he might speak for them all. He rose; and, being in every respect a prudent and honorable man, conferring no small honor upon the office he held, he poured forth, with modest countenance and moderate voice, the thought of a wise and devout heart.”

Since the speech of Saint Gebhard greatly assists both in seeing more clearly the calamities of those times and in understanding more clearly this letter which we are publishing, I shall not hesitate to reproduce it here for readers, since Bruno’s history of the *Saxon War* is known to few. Thus Saint Gebhard addressed the bishops and princes who stood on the side of the schismatics:

“Venerable bishops, and the rest …” The remainder may be found in the *Patrologia*, volume CXLVII, column 489, under **Bruno**.

Saint Gebhard delivered this speech in the year 1081. Bertold of Constance placed the following memorial to him in his *Chronicle* under the year 1088:

“Gebhard, of venerable memory, Archbishop of Juvavia, foremost in the cause of Saint Peter, who was accustomed publicly to refute the schismatics in speech and writing, was taken from this light on the seventeenth day before the Kalends [lacuna] and left the Catholics in great sorrow.”

In the Life in volume VI of the *Ancient Readings* he is said to have died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, in his own castle, which is called Werfen.

Moreover, Hermann, Bishop of Metz, to whom Saint Gebhard sent this letter, is honored by the same Bertold with the following encomium under the year 1090:

“Hermann, Bishop of Metz, of pious memory, and Bertold, Duke of Alemannia, son of King Rudolf, closed their final day in the fidelity of Saint Peter in the month of May, and left the Catholics in great sorrow and the schismatics in exultation.”

But now let us hear Saint Gebhard himself speaking. A schismatic apologist, in an apology for Henry IV which our heretics have printed more than once, gnashes his teeth fiercely at him because, through the authority and auspices of so great a man, many were kept away from and recalled from the camp of the schismatics. But this anonymous writer broke his own teeth sooner than he could diminish Saint Gebhard’s fame and reputation. Gebhard will grow through extended ages, and a pen afraid to be silenced will carry forward his surviving renown.

[Col. 0847]

# Letter of Saint Gebhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, to Hermann, Bishop of Metz

[Col. 0847A] To the venerable Father and Lord in Christ, Hermann, Bishop of the holy Church of Metz, Gebhard, brother and fellow bishop: whatever is best in Christ.

[Col. 0848A] Your charity has now for the second time instructed me and my companions in persecution to inform your fatherhood what we think must be held and believed in this dissension of the Church, so that you may be able to answer those who think and speak otherwise. We, however, aware of our own limited measure, do not presume to instruct your prudence, since that would be no less ridiculous than if someone wished to assist the sun with torches. Besides, just as ability does not provide the means, neither does inclination prompt us to do so. It seems tiresome and superfluous to prepare replies for men whom no one considers worthy of hearing.

We suffer a rare kind of misfortune: we are accused on many counts, yet are allowed no opportunity at all for defense.
