For our elders—that is, the bishops of the opposing party—disdain to show us, in conducting cases, the humanity which no one ought to deny even to his own slaves, not following the example of blessed Job, who says: “If I have rejected the judgment of my male servant or my female servant” (Job 31).

Ever since these scandals of dissension began to arise among us, have we not been able, even by frequent and devout prayers, to entreat them to permit both us to hear them and them to be heard by us, in order to restore the Church’s order? We promised that, if it became clear that justice favored their party, we would unquestionably follow their judgment.

But perhaps what we say seems incredible to those who do not know the facts: that men of such dignity and reverence should not only show no compassion to afflicted brothers, but should even deny them justice. To establish the credibility of our words, because certain embassies were privately sent to some of them, we name the persons themselves with whom these matters were discussed in public conversation and in living speech: the Archbishop of Cologne; the bishops of Bamberg and Speyer; the elected bishops of Trier (*electos*; read *electum*) and of Utrecht (*electos*; read *electum*). Nearly all these men were met by the leading men of Saxony and Thuringia wherever the meeting had been arranged. Agreeing with the position we have described, they voluntarily offered themselves for examination, on the condition that, if they could not defend their case according to ecclesiastical laws and customs, they would submit to the sounder counsels of their opponents, not regarding it as disgraceful if, learning from them what was better and nearer to salvation, they abandoned their error.

We presented these things humbly, not contentiously, in the hearing of all who were present, but accomplished nothing. And now, over and above all this, our brothers and lords, moved neither by brotherly accusations nor by supplications, persist in the hardness toward us with which they began. They deny us a hearing, while to others, with whatever influence and to whatever extent they can, they insinuate evil things about us. They declare that we have been seduced and are seducers, that we are treacherous, and that we are the source and cause of the evils threatening us. They teach this incessantly, though not effectively.

For royal munificence assists priestly teaching, making both eloquent teachers and teachable, receptive hearers attentive through one and the same kind of encouragement. Such zeal in persuading has been followed by such credulity among many that even our sheep no longer hear our voice but follow strangers. In the places from which the bishops of our party have been expelled, they claim the right to teach; and there, in churches that are not theirs, they have so shaped sheep who do not belong to them with the fodder of an arrogated preaching that they think it proper not only to despise pious shepherds but even to persecute them.

Therefore, if our wickedness has been exposed to such a degree that no doubt about our error remains, and we deserve punishment rather than a hearing, nevertheless men who share our name and office ought to devote themselves to converting brothers rather than destroying them, to showing the way of truth to those who wander, and by salutary admonitions to winning divided members back to unity. This would be good and acceptable before our Savior, so that those who have received more abundantly from his fullness might minister to one another the grace received in greater measure than by others (1 Peter 4), as it is written: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come.’”

It would also be good, and fitting for those who love brotherhood, to hold back those placed on such a precipice, as they say, even against their will—how much more those who desire this with the greatest longing and are ready to obey those teaching what is more correct. They should not regard it as burdensome or dishonorable to be overcome by others in such a way that they themselves also overcome their error.

Finally, if we were so obstinate that the word of truth could find no place in us (John 8), they could nevertheless free their own souls by announcing to the impious their wickedness. They would heap coals of fire upon us, because then a greater accumulation of shame would fall upon us, when, having recognized the truth, we could have no excuse for ignorance before them.

Come now, dearest Father and lord: since we are judged unworthy to be instructed by the word of truth, because we are a “rebellious house” (Ezekiel 2), you nevertheless, because of your neighboring residence, have easier access to converse with them; and because of the integrity both of your life and of your dignity, you ought not to suffer rejection. You, I say, speak on our behalf; assume for yourself the role of mediator between us. Hear from them what we may hear; learn from them what you may teach. Inquire by what ecclesiastical sanctions they prove their case and disprove ours, so that through you we may hear those whom we have no opportunity to hear in person, and what we could not obtain by the service of our own mouths we may obtain through the reverence due to an advocate.

If, yielding to your charity, they demand from you this exchange—that just as you make their judgment known to us, so you should make ours known to them—say what you know. Say that we are devising nothing new or unusual, nothing from ourselves as though from ourselves, but only what we have heard and seen, what our fathers have told us (Psalm 77); that we presume nothing on our own authority, but are content to stand by and hold the traditions which we have learned (2 Thessalonians 2); that we do nothing through contention or through the cunning of arguments, which is hostile to faith.

This is neither our purpose nor appropriate to our age. Rather, we leave such things more suitably to frivolous persons, to those who have trained their faculties for this—not, in the Apostle’s phrase, for discerning good and evil (Hebrews 5), but so that by the subtlety of their intellect and the agility of their tongue they may perversely make what is just appear to be rightly perverted. It is neither our office nor ought it to be our concern to call good evil and evil good; rather, as imitators of our Lord, let us strive, insofar as he grants it, to reject evil and choose good (Isaiah 7).

Content with this purity, concerning the matter now before us we hold only what the Catholic Church has always held, what has remained firm and unshaken from the beginning of Christianity down to these monstrous times: namely, that one must not associate with the excommunicated. This is the cause of the dissensions and rebellions: they do not abstain from the excommunicated and teach that abstention is unnecessary. We, however, both abstain and persuade others to abstain, especially from those excommunicated by the foremost and primary see.

This divergence among priests teaching contrary things has truly become the ruin of the people, truly the root of many evils. From it, many banefully fruitful branches have sprung throughout the Church, producing and continuing to produce various fruits. The bitterness—indeed, the extreme bitterness—of these fruits must be attributed not so much to the branches as to the root. Whatever the partisan zealots rave, whatever is perversely done by subjects amid this turmoil of affairs, justly returns upon the heads of those who perversely teach. [The text appears to lack a word, perhaps “falls back,” “returns,” or something similar.]

Truly now is fulfilled what is written: “Wickedness has gone forth from the elders who seemed to govern the people” (Daniel 13). For if those who are called heralds of truth, to whom the utterances of God have been entrusted for proclaiming to God’s people, all said the same thing and there were no schisms among them; if, in the manner of watchmen, they saw to it that contention did not arise among them, or that, once arisen, it was settled through fraternal deliberation according to custom; there is no doubt that the unity of the people would follow the unity of those who affirm the truth, and the Church, still remaining in its proper state, would possess its ancient peace. Now, however, exposed to the feet of its enemies, it is crushed with unheard-of devastation and drenched in blood through an incomparable slaughter both of bodies and of souls. Its blood is rightly required from the hands of those who, having undertaken its care, made God’s people transgress against it by teaching doctrines contrary to it.

We, therefore, and those who belong to our party, to whom the discipline of the Church has also been entrusted, satisfy the Church in this matter because we have taught and teach nothing beyond what we have learned. If we are asked from where and from whom we learned it, certainly we have many supporters of our teaching, and they are by no means obscure in name. The apostles taught us; the successors of the apostles, the pontiffs of the apostolic see, taught us; besides them—or rather, in accordance with them—a great multitude of other Fathers, renowned for holiness and authority, whose teaching makes the Church shine, who reign with the Lord in heaven and sparkle with miracles on earth.

To resist their sanctions not through ignorance or negligence but deliberately—what else is that than to blaspheme the Spirit who spoke through them? Without doubt, all who do not abstain from the excommunicated before canonical examination, and who teach that abstention is unnecessary, oppose those Fathers, not us. For that the aforementioned Fathers forbade such conduct by unanimous and continual prohibition is known not only to those who have learned it from their writings but also to the uneducated and illiterate, who, even if they do not know the law, have nevertheless learned what belongs to the law (Romans 2) through an ancient custom that has never been altered.

Since these things, established by the unanimity of such lawgivers and maintained to this day by the most ancient usage, cannot be shaken by open and direct attacks, schemes are prepared from the side, as it were, to deceive the opinions [perhaps: souls] of those who are considered less intelligent.

And because among such people serious efforts are being made to lead them astray from the course of so familiar and widely open a road, “a stumbling block is placed beside the path” (Psalm 139), when certain vices are presented to them as though they served truth, for the subversion of truth. We have heard that certain clerics of the opposing party, boasting of their learning, make it their business to collect from sacred books everywhere those statements which the holy Fathers composed to restrain the intemperance of priests who are rash in pronouncing judgments, binding or loosing indiscriminately.

In this matter, as in all others, the Fathers’ judgments are truly praiseworthy and deserving of acceptance. They cared for everyone in such a way that they both restrained prelates from rashness and provided the necessary defense of the innocence of their subjects.

But those who introduce these statements in support of what they have undertaken to persuade others of make use of a good thing, but not well. What the holy teachers established for the common benefit both of those who rule and of those who are subject, these men undoubtedly employ to the contempt of episcopal ministry and to stir up discord between shepherds and sheep.

This is plainly evident from the fact that they impress upon their hearers only those judgments which they consider convenient to their own persuasion, while suppressing in complete silence the others which the Catholic Fathers nevertheless established concerning the same matter, and which are so necessary for settling this dispute that it cannot possibly be decided justly without them.

We need not teach them what those judgments are. They themselves know better than we do that many teachers of the Church established, in many ways and with many words, that whenever a dispute arose concerning a sentence of excommunication, a careful examination of both parties should be conducted through canonical proceedings, and that in this way the sentence of the excommunicator should either be confirmed or corrected.

These and similar matters the aforementioned brothers conceal, as though they were unknown and irrelevant, while instructing their followers to despise, rashly and without any legitimate proof, the sentence pronounced against them, and so to shake off the yoke of discipline entirely.

Although they are by no means ignorant that it was known even in antiquity that a shepherd’s sentence, whether just or unjust, must nevertheless be feared, these men make those placed under anathema feel secure and not at all concerned about that sentence which must be feared; the printed reading is *a nostra diversione* (“from our divergence/separation”), with the variant *nobis diversa* (“different from us”). They repeatedly cite those testimonies of Scripture which establish that one who curses the innocent harms himself more than the one whom he seeks to harm, and others of this kind.

We do not dissent at all from these words of the saints. Rather, we receive them with love and reverence, striving, insofar as we can with the help of divine generosity, both to guard ourselves against abuse of the pastoral office and to persuade others to guard against it.

But to those who twist these things beyond measure to support their own party, we give our assent only with such moderation that we do not follow their footsteps beyond the boundaries established. We do not add what they have caused their hearers to infer from their teachings: namely, that if an excommunicated person merely asserts in bare words that he has been unjustly excommunicated, the sentence of the excommunicator must immediately be judged void.

If this consequence is accepted, then no one abstains from any excommunicated person, because none of them admits that he has been justly judged. But it is not an equal division of justice for subjects to be heard in such a way that prelates suffer prejudice by being unheard, as the saying goes: “He is not a just mediator who hears one party in such a way that he leaves nothing for the other.”

If this newly arising doctrine begins to bear fruit in the Church, the ancient Fathers labored in vain (Psalm 126). They strove by every means and exerted themselves to ensure that, in the one body of Christ, which is the Church, neither the lesser members should be oppressed by the more excellent nor the lower members rebel against the higher.

Many of their constitutions, applicable to the case being debated among us, are frustrated and annulled by this new dogma. If we inserted here their synodal and decretal judgments, we might perhaps weary our readers, since these are familiar and exceedingly well known both through usage and through authority.

Since, however, those who act contrary to them attempt to cast darkness over so clear a light, we consider it necessary, against the advancing obscurities of this novelty, to place the Church’s ancient and well-known lamp upon its stand (Luke 11), so that we may recall to memory what they are trying with such effort to consign to oblivion. We judge it sufficient for our defense to repeat what is known rather than seem to introduce something new.

The holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea, when decreeing, in accordance with the institution of the apostles and of those apostolic men who preceded the Council of Nicaea, concerning those deprived of communion—whether from the clergy or from the laity—by bishops, so that those who expel and those who are expelled [a word such as “should be made known” appears to be missing], added:

“Let inquiry also be made, lest it appear that he has been excluded from the assembly through the bishop’s pusillanimity, contentiousness, or any other fault” (Council of Nicaea, canon 5).

As to how and by what means the inquiry should be conducted, they added these words:

“Therefore, in order that the inquiry may be conducted more properly, it has seemed good that councils be held twice each year in every province” (Council of Nicaea, cited passage), and the rest that follows.

Thus those who decreed that councils should be held for the proper investigation of this matter certainly did not think, as is now customary, that it could suffice to prove the innocence of those who had been expelled if they indiscriminately and vaguely spewed insults and slanders against their absent excommunicators.

Therefore, let those who, contrary to the sacred canons of Nicaea, receive into communion persons deprived of canonical communion without any synod having been convened and without any prior investigation hear whether the statutes of that same council are to be so lightly violated and despised. Let them hear what Saint Gregory thinks of the authority of the four principal councils, of which this one is the chief.

In a letter addressed to the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem, he says as follows (book I, letter 24):

“As I receive and venerate the four books of the holy Gospel, so I confess that I receive and venerate the four councils, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises and the rule of every life and action stands firm. Whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.”

A little later, concerning the same councils:

“Since they were established by universal consent, whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Whoever therefore thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Let those also hear who strive so vigorously to nullify the statutes of the holy and great Council of Nicaea, and let them hear Blessed Leo’s special judgment concerning it (letter 53):

“Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop. Let no one,” he says, “dare either to compare himself with the three hundred and eighteen bishops, however much greater the number of priests may be, or to prefer himself to them. The Council of Nicaea has been consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are celebrated by fewer or by more, whatever differs from their constitution is utterly devoid of authority.”

Again, concerning the same matter:

“The holy and venerable Fathers in the city of Nicaea, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would remain until the end of the world. Among us, throughout the whole world, they live in their constitutions; and if anything is presumed anywhere otherwise than they decreed, it is immediately annulled. Behold, we are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Corinthians 10)—in whose times those laws are being utterly destroyed which the holy teachers declared would remain until the end of the world.

Since, therefore, all authentic councils, and those which the Church receives, grant primacy to the council whose testimonies have been inserted here, it is less necessary than tedious to append the individual judgments of the others. Nevertheless, we think it not irrelevant to extract one passage from the Council of Sardica.

In the preface to this council, when various regulations of various councils were being discussed, the following was finally added:

“But in all these matters we must follow whatever we see does not differ from the Council of Nicaea and from the holy and apostolic Roman [Church].”

[Col. 0855B] Let those attend to what is found in canon 17 of the same council who so readily rescind even the sentence of any bishop—let alone that of the Roman pontiff—without legal examination, as though whatever they assert in their words, whether just or unjust, required no investigation.

The prescribed canon reads as follows:

“If some bishop happens to be angry—which ought not to happen—and is quickly and harshly provoked against his priest or deacon, and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion.”

After a short interruption, it concludes:

“Nevertheless, before all things have been carefully and faithfully examined, no one may presume, before the inquiry, to join to communion the one who had been separated from communion.”

Behold, this passage deals specifically with that kind of excommunication which is committed when anger prevails and which is hastened by a quick and harsh impulse; nevertheless, the greatest care is taken that no one receive even such an excommunicated person before a diligent examination.

These and similar provisions are impressed upon us almost to weariness in the councils and in the decrees of the Roman prelates. Nor is it omitted to specify what punishment follows each side: those who knowingly communicate with excommunicated persons before a just examination of both parties, and who offer excuses and hiding places to prevent them from being brought to satisfaction; and the excommunicated, if they presume to communicate before being heard, if they neglect to attend to their own case, if they do not pursue their case before their excommunicators within the prescribed period, or if they usurp a ministry forbidden to them.

Since these matters are unknown to no one, necessity does not require us to enumerate them more fully here, and the brevity proper to a letter does not allow it.

But since no excuse is available against these provisions, perhaps someone objects to us from the very words established in the aforementioned canon—words which, like certain other matters, we omitted for the sake of brevity—namely, where it says:

“For one who has been expelled must not be denied a hearing when he asks for it; and the bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, must patiently accept that the case be examined.”

From this, we suppose, they take grounds “for making excuses upon excuses” (Psalm 140), as though, because of this, an examination properly conducted had not taken place [Note: [Col. 0855] The passage appears corrupt; read: “As it ought to have been conducted, it had not been conducted”], because the excommunicator did not show them patience for proving or disproving the sentence.

To refute this, let not the testimonies of Scripture or the authority of the canons respond, but the very sequence of events. For it is known to everyone throughout the surrounding regions that the anathema under discussion was pronounced at the Roman synod which, as usual, was held in the first week of Lent in 1080. [Col. 0856B] When this had resounded in the German regions, at the following Easter the bishops who celebrated that feast in the city of Bamberg, on the holy day and during the solemn celebration of Mass, hurling many shameful and dishonorable reproaches against the lord pope Gregory VII, announced to all who had assembled that from that time onward he was in no way to be regarded as apostolic. Beginning there, they passed through the entire kingdom preaching the same things, with other ministers of the same message joining them.

But if they claim that they undertook such actions because they had been denied a hearing, let all who are of sound judgment decide whether this could in any way have happened within so short an interval: after learning of the sentence pronounced against them, they would have appealed to the Apostolic See for an examination of their case, and, only after it had refused this, would have stirred up this rebellion in the place and at the time mentioned. It is perfectly clear that, even if their will had suggested this to them—as in fact it did not—the shortness of the time would not have allowed it. Thus the whole matter is equally confirmed: neither was an examination held, nor was one requested or denied. It is therefore evident that the excommunicated were received into communion through the impulse of rashness rather than necessity, before any legitimate examination.

Just as this is found to be contrary to the councils and decrees mentioned above, so too, not by our judgment but by the judgment of the apostolic men Gregory and Leo, it is devoid of all authority and must without hesitation be annulled. And because it conflicts no less with ecclesiastical customs than with laws, let us join a third witness, blessed Augustine, to the two witnesses already mentioned, and thus make a threefold cord. Writing to the presbyter Casulanus, he says among other things:

> Just as violators of the divine laws, so also despisers of ecclesiastical customs must be restrained.

Likewise, to Januarius:

> All such things as are contained neither in the authority of the sacred Scriptures, nor found established in the councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, I consider ought to be cut away.

But, for the moment passing over the Lord’s soldiers, let us come to the words of their own Lord, who says [Col. 0857A] in the Gospel: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10). Truly they must have judged evangelical and apostolic doctrine to have preceded its proper time, who judged in so disorderly a fashion, condemning not only the sentence of the supreme pontiff but the very man who issued it: without examining the sentence, they condemned its author—unheard, unconvicted, and not confessing, indeed not even summoned or admonished!

They rejected the sentence promulgated at that time by the Roman synod, when there had been no objection whatsoever to its president; they rejected the president himself, to whom at that time not only the Church existing in these regions but also the Church spread throughout the whole world rendered due submission. I repeat: they rejected him by their own judgment and not by a synodal judgment, and they designated as pontiff of that same see another man who shortly before had been condemned by the Apostolic See, without the knowledge or consent of the Roman Church.

What need, then, have we of testimonies from the canons to disprove these judgments, which do not even preserve the appearance of considered judgments but, at first sight, appear to be filled with blasphemy? For, to speak truthfully, we do not remember having found anything specifically decreed in the writings of the holy Fathers against presumptions of this kind, because no law needed to be made for madness.

Out of abundant caution, however, the ancient teachers established rules against those assaults of ignorant bishops which, although they proceed from the plots of adversaries, nevertheless pretend to bear some appearance of equity—namely, through adjournments, summonses, examinations, and other procedures in accordance with the form of judicial proceedings. If authority is required from us to distinguish the caution appropriate to these matters, we produce not excerpts from Scripture but entire volumes, such as the book of pontifical decrees, which is devoted almost wholly to the examination of such cases.

But lest we appear to have introduced none of this for the present purpose, let us at least insert the statement of blessed Gregory, which he wrote to John the Defender, who was going to Spain, concerning Bishop Stephen, who complained that he had been unjustly deposed. “First,” he says, “it must be carefully investigated whether the judgment was conducted in an orderly manner; whether some were accusers and others witnesses; then the nature of the charges—whether, with the accused present, testimony was given against him under oath; whether he had an opportunity to respond; whether the examination of the persons accusing and giving testimony was regularly conducted. If perhaps these things were not formally carried out, let him be restored in every way to his own Church. But those who condemned him contrary to the fear of God and the provisions of the canons are to be sent to perform penance for six months, with this qualification: if any of them should happen to face the danger of death, the blessing of viaticum is not to be denied him.”

Let the mediators of the judgments mentioned above see whether, in rejecting the Roman prelate, they observed even one of those precepts of the holy man which he decreed ought to be observed in the examination of any bishop whatsoever.

To this must be added the fact that it has been defined in many statutes of the saints [Col. 0858A] that no bishop may be judged or condemned except in a legitimate synod, at the proper time, convened by apostolic authority; and that councils cannot be ratified without the authority of the First See. Whoever seeks these provisions will be able to find them in the writings of the apostolic men Julius, Damasus, Marcellus, Gelasius, and others, with blessed Isidore bearing witness to the same thing.

It is therefore astonishing that prudent men have consigned to oblivion matters so well known: in the absence of any synod, they rejected that bishop by judging him, although without his authority it is lawful neither to condemn any bishop nor to convene a general council. Behold a new judicial order; behold the mature judgments of the Lord’s priests!

If these judges were judged by the judgment with which they judged, so that they received from their own subjects the same condemnation which they inflicted upon their prelate, they would certainly call this not an ecclesiastical judgment but genuine tyrannical madness. Nor is this surprising. For, to say nothing of bishops, no human being, whatever his profession or condition, is legally entitled to exercise against anyone a judgment of the kind that was brought against one who is to be judged by no human being. As Nicodemus said—still ignorant of apostolic teaching and unaware of the canons—“Does our law judge anyone unless it first hears him and learns what he does?” (John 7).

But what shall we say about that man, Guibert, who was so carefully raised up by the deliberation of the diligent to fill the place of this deposed man? We say of him, and affirm through truthful witnesses, that even if he had not already been condemned—or were not destined to be condemned—for his errors, and even if he had found that see vacant, to which he has now been assigned as an adulterous usurper while its pontiff is still alive, nevertheless, as blessed Leo bears witness, no consideration would permit him to be counted among the bishops, since neither the clergy elected him nor the people desired him.

And since the judgments of that same Leo and of Celestine have established that no bishop is to be given to those who do not wish him, how much less ought a bishop from elsewhere to have been imposed upon that unwilling Church, which had attained security through the preservation of its pontiff and concord.

Therefore, because we have not consented to take part with such a faction, “we are cursed and suffer persecution” (John 3), and we and what belongs to us have been handed over for plunder to all who surround us, as though we were the authors of so great a discord. Truly, as they say, we disagree with those who do these things—but not from love of disagreement; rather, from fear of eternal damnation, certain that we would be under an endless anathema if we happened to end our lives amid such actions.

Behold, most beloved prelate, as you commanded, we have laid before your charity what appears to our mediocrity to be the case in this matter. If, however, we hear better judgments from wiser men, we are ready to obey—provided that the proper reciprocity is maintained between us and those who think differently from us, so that the matter is not handled through evasions or externally distorted plausibilities.

Nor is it a mark of sound judgment to rely upon arguments sought from every direction when, concerning the matter itself, so many specific and [Col. 0859A] definitive judgments have been promulgated by the holy Fathers that cannot be shaken by any reasoning and have left no room for doubt. Behold, with every evasion removed, we have set forth the grounds of our position: we do not communicate with the excommunicated with whom they communicate; we do not presume to renounce the pontiff of the Apostolic See, the vicar of blessed Peter; and, while he is alive and acting in concord with the Roman Church, we do not consent either to elect another to that same see or to agree with those who elect one.

Therefore, if those who act contrary to us prove by more truthful and superior documents that what we have shown to be unlawful is permissible, it is only fair that we should give hearing and assent to those who teach what is more correct.

[Col. 0859B] But leaving aside what concerns the matter itself, they loudly proclaim insults and reproaches—so it is said—against the apostolic lord. What does that have to do with us? If his life is at issue, we do not obey him because of our assessment of his personal life, but because of the ministry of the dignity conferred upon him. For the quality of his merits does not prejudice his priestly office. Therefore, however learnedly or skillfully they may attack him in their criticisms, their insults must not be accepted as an accusation.

For they themselves, being wise, know very well that this would be a truly confused and inverted order: to condemn him without accusation or examination, and only afterward, once judgment had been passed, to accuse and examine him.

But in this matter too, as we hear, they display their zeal, collecting many passages from Scripture to show their followers how grave a crime it is to commit perjury and to take the name of the Lord in vain (Exod. 20). And concerning bishops, as we stated shortly before, because by condemning the innocent they harm themselves more than those whom they wish to harm, they say things that do indeed possess the substance of truth when they are put forward in their proper place and time. Yet they are thought to suggest something other than what they say, in order to strike the weak conscience of simpler brothers, so that they may cast a snare over them under the appearance of piety and deceive them by speaking what is, in itself, true.

But to those who look more carefully, these matters appear to have nothing to do with the controversy before us. For how could this pertain to the dispute being carried on between us, when we disagree about absolutely nothing here, but both sides confess one and the same thing? Who of sound mind would doubt that perjury is a grave sin? Likewise, what they say about the rash issuing of sentences, we also say; but we do not pursue the conclusion toward which they aim by saying it. Their words have one sound but another meaning.

What the ancient Fathers generally argue against disorderly episcopal pronouncements, we praise to such an extent that we in no way, as they now wish, rashly and without proof reject the specific sentence of any bishop. Likewise concerning perjury, we say the same thing as they do—indeed, the same thing as everyone says: it is a grave danger to the soul and must be avoided in every way.

But although those precepts of divine law upon which they rely are worthy of all veneration, we do not understand them as they wish to be understood: namely, that whatever anyone swears must invariably and without reconsideration be kept. Rather, we believe that the following words are to be observed by all with caution: “You shall not profane the name of your God in vain” (Lev. 18); “You shall not swear falsely by my name” (Lev. 19). This means that they should either swear nothing that ought not to be sworn, or that oaths which ought neither to be kept nor can be kept—or which, if kept, lead to some greater or equally grave danger—must not be observed.

If some teachers do not instruct their subjects either not to swear at all or, when oaths are made under some necessity, to exercise care concerning them, but instead preach that oaths must be fulfilled, however and under whatever circumstances they were made, such teaching has never at any time been sound—least of all in the present age, in which almost everything the people say is a conspiracy.

Let us explain plainly, setting aside evasions, where these assertions are heading, as though touching the matter to the quick. Without doubt, by their schemes they are striving to bring their followers to the point where they consider what is the height of wickedness to be lawful, so that those burdened by their own sins do not fear to share in the sins of others by communicating with the excommunicated; so that, without any rational persuasion but merely at the whim of secular power, they cast off the yoke of that authority in which our Lord and Savior has established the primacy of the whole Church; and so that they offer consent and assistance to those who violently invade the see established with such particular distinction. [Col. 0860C]

Since they cannot find suitable testimonies to persuade people of such blasphemies, they resort to oaths, being deficient in reason and authority, as though the necessity of their oaths made it necessary to perpetrate those things which openly contradict prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic institutions.

They contradict the prophetic institutions, as we know the lawgiver and prophet said in Deuteronomy: “The man who is proud and refuses to obey the command of the priest who ministers to the Lord your God at that time shall die by the decree of the judge, and you shall purge the evil from Israel” (Deut. 17). The evangelical trumpet resounds: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matt. 10). As for the apostles and apostolic men [lacuna; Note: [Col. 0859D] Something appears to be missing here.], and how severe are the punishments directed against those who rise up against the see of blessed Peter and his successors, we forbear to set these out individually, because the matter is familiar and lengthy.

Nevertheless, we do not think we should leave unmentioned the statement of Saint Gregory IV [Note: Gregory IV, in his letter to all the bishops, vol. III of the Councils, fol. 539], in which priests opposing the Apostolic See are expressly identified:

> Let whoever wishes to oppose the apostolic decrees be struck down by the grief of his own ruin, and let him no longer have a place among the priests; rather, let him be excluded from the sacred ministry.

And shortly afterward:

> He to whom the discipline of the holy Church has been entrusted must be subjected to a more severe excommunication and deposition, since he ought not only to have obeyed the commands of the aforesaid holy Church but also to have instructed others not to disregard them.

But all must fear what the first of the apostles himself says concerning his first successor:

> If anyone, he says, should now grieve Christ, who entrusted the chair to him, he will not receive him; and therefore he himself will not be received into the kingdom of heaven.

Let those who take up the words of the law in order to destroy the law say whether, because of certain oaths, one ought to fall back into those transgressions which in the Old Testament are punished by death, but which in the New, as the Disciple of Truth teaches, separate one from Christ and from the kingdom of heaven.

All who have sworn that they would transgress these matters are providing too late for the observance of their oaths. For it is absolutely certain that at the very hour when they swore what they did not know ought not to be sworn, they profaned the name of their God and took the name of their God in vain (Exod. 20).

Since, therefore, the Lord said to the apostles, “Do not swear at all” (Matt. 5), was it not contrary to the Lord for bishops, acting in the place of the apostles, to renounce by oath and proscribe that bishop who occupies the place of the prince of the apostles?

Let us therefore hear, between two opposing positions—one of which must necessarily be weakened—which the Church ought nevertheless to choose: whether it should choose what the prophets, the apostles, and finally the teacher of the prophets and apostles himself established; or what, contrary to all these, the modern pontiffs—or rather, men from among the pontiffs who have become palace conspirators—have newly fabricated.

But, to say nothing of the Church’s more exalted authorities, is greater reverence owed to those 318 who assembled in the city of Nicaea in the name of the Lord, or to those who [Note: [Col. 0861] This letter was therefore written by St. Gebhard in 1081, because the pseudo-synod of Brixen was held in 1080; see Baronius, under this year, vol. XI.] gathered last year at Brixen against the Lord and against his Christ? (Ps. 2.) For what the former established at that holy and most renowned synod under the direction, as we must believe, of the Holy Spirit, the latter repudiated without a synodal assembly in the tribunals of the court.

Indeed, the canons of Nicaea teach that those deprived of communion are in no way to be received without a legitimate examination. These men, however, not only received those excommunicated by the holy and Apostolic See without examination, but, to the disgrace and confusion of the entire ecclesiastical region, chose one of the very anathematized men as their apostolic, or, to speak more truly, by naming that apostate an apostolic, likened him to the apostate angel. They also promised under oath that they would install him in the very see by which he had been condemned; and now, in order cruelly to fulfill what they wickedly promised, they rage with the edge of the sword, with no small shedding of blood, and with the sacrilegious devastation of the property of blessed Peter.

Nor are the devastation of the kingdom or the destruction of churches spared, so long as their conspiracy is not without effect. Those whom they employ in the bloody execution of these crimes—men indeed without learning, and therefore credulous when they are deceived—have been so infected with those new doctrines about avoiding perjury that they think it lighter and more pardonable to complete the measure of any crime than to break the vows of their foolish and treacherous promise.

They do not consider that even those oaths which are made according to custom and called legitimate are sometimes rescinded through fear of greater guilt, because of various intervening events. Thus soldiers often exact and receive the customary oaths from their servants or from those who profess themselves their retainers.

But if, in return, those who have promised fidelity are invited to carry out acts of brigandage, to arrange the murder of a prince or of ecclesiastical men, to violate and plunder churches, or to abduct virgins consecrated to God, would it not then be foolish for those who are invited to offer the desired aid toward the destruction of both parties and, under the name of loyalty, to perform works of treachery and cruelty?

In the same way, oaths are customarily given to bishops, dukes, and others placed in high positions, whether by the Church or by men of the treasury. If, as sometimes happens in accordance with the provisions of the laws, they are deprived of their honors, their swearers, when they acquire other lords, withdraw from the sworn allegiance and subjection owed to the former ones.

Since these men make their sworn promise void not voluntarily but under compulsion, what is surprising if they obtain pardon for that fault from some who possess the power of binding and loosing, a fault into which they fell through unforeseen necessity rather than through evil intention?

But the new dogmatists, judging very differently, call ministers of such absolutions subverters and persuaders of perjury. For this reason they assert that such ministers no longer sit upon the chair of Moses, because Moses said, “You shall not swear falsely” (Lev. 19).

If the antiquity of the written law must be held immutably without the new discernment of the Spirit, they may indeed say that Moses himself descended from the chair of Moses. For he who said, “You shall not swear falsely,” also said, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20); and yet afterward he frequently ordered, “Whoever does this or that shall be put to death.”

Because of these variations in sentences, neither are those who remit the aforesaid faults opposed to Moses, nor is Moses himself inconsistent with himself. Rather, the dispensatory edicts of the sacred institutions, referred to different circumstances, are in both cases consonant with truth and justice and appropriate to the order of events.

Behold, the lawgiver changes the legal sentence for this reason: to restrain people from transgressing the law. The new legislators, by contrast, have become transgressors of the laws for this reason: so that the sentence of their conspiracy will not be changed.

There are some among the bishops who acknowledge that they were not bound by oath together with the others, and yet do not deny that they vowed their support for the same cause. We know that by this action they make light of nothing other than the guilt of conspiracy. [Note: The passage is corrupt; the meaning is: “Whom we know by their action to make light of nothing other than the guilt of conspiracy.”]

But if anyone makes light of the guilt of conspiracy, let him reread the statutes of the Council of Chalcedon (canon 18), where, without distinction between swearers and conspirators, both are punished by an equal judgment.

Since, then, they guard this promise of theirs, whatever its name may be, with such caution, we ask them—peacefully, despite their opposition—by what order and for what reason they prefer that new vow to the earlier one which they made on the day of their ordination, when, as they were being promoted to the supreme priesthood, they were questioned about their faith and obedience.

For we believe that they have not forgotten that, in that sacred assembly of bishops and clergy [Note: In the Brixen council, held in 1080], they promised, in order to obtain their promotion, that they would preserve faith and submission toward blessed Peter and his vicars and successors. Yet recently, to the injury of that same prince of the apostles, they publicly denied the faith and submission promised to his successor.

They did the former after being instructed by the authority of the ancient holy Fathers; in the latter they carried out only the will of worldly power. How, then, do they value more highly what they conspired to do in a chamber or in the royal hall amid the tumult of courtiers than what they professed before the sacred altar and the holy relics of the saints, in the presence of Christ and the Church?

But perhaps, for their defense and our reproach, they will invoke the necessity of the oath which they share with us, saying that they feared violating their sworn fidelity unless they complied with the royal will.

In replying to this, we do not presume to say anything dishonorable about them. Concerning ourselves, however, all of us who swore fidelity to the prince bear this true and incontrovertible testimony: if, encouraged by our counsel and relying upon our assistance, he had undertaken that by which he would have incurred so great a danger to his soul and so great a loss to the kingdom and royal honor, we would undoubtedly be judged violators both of our oath and of our fidelity, and declared public enemies not only of the ecclesiastical realm but also of the state.

Although he was senior in dignity, the person to whom this faithful pledge was made was nevertheless young in age. Therefore it was more faithful for the age of those more advanced to restrain the irrational impulses of a youthful mind than to incite them through harmful flattery.

This, I say, would have been fidelity and duty. But, under the appearance of fidelity, to perform acts that would cause harm is contrary to fidelity and duty, as Saint Ambrose testifies in Book III of *On Duties* (chapter 12), where he discusses the wicked fulfillment of Herod’s oath:

> What was considered an act of fidelity was madness.

Likewise, in the same book (chapter 50), concerning the discernment required in performing one’s duty:

> It is a duty, he says, to preserve and return what has been entrusted. But sometimes an alteration is required by time or necessity, so that it is not a duty to return what one has received. For example, if someone who is bringing aid to barbarians against his fatherland openly demands the money he entrusted, or if you return a sword deposited with you to a madman, with which he may kill himself—is it not contrary to duty to return it?

Likewise (chapter 12):

> Sometimes it is contrary to duty to fulfill a promise and to keep an oath, as with Herod, who swore an oath and brought about John’s death lest he fail to fulfill his promise.

And elsewhere:

> Let everyone speak plainly and not lead his brother astray by verbal deception; let no one promise anything dishonorable. If he has made such a promise, it is more tolerable not to fulfill it than to do what is shameful. Often, he says, many bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and, although they themselves recognize that they ought not to have made the promise, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they pledged.

And shortly afterward:

> It is better not to fulfill a vow which the person to whom it was made would not wish to have fulfilled. Not every promise must always be fulfilled. Indeed, the Lord himself, as Scripture indicates, frequently changes his decision.

Saint Isidore says in the book of the *Sentences*:

> An oath that is made wrongly and carelessly ought not to be kept—for example, if someone promises an adulterous woman that he will remain with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfill the oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.

Likewise, in the book of the *Soliloquies*:

> In evil promises, withdraw your pledge; in a shameful vow, change your decision. Do not do what you have rashly vowed. A promise that is fulfilled through crime is foolish.

The Venerable Bede also says in his *Exposition of the Gospel*, which is publicly pronounced each year in the Church on the beheading of Saint John the Baptist:

> If it should happen that we have sworn something carelessly, which, if observed, would lead to a worse outcome, let us recognize that it must be changed by more salutary counsel.

And shortly afterward:

> This moderation must be observed with particular care not only in swearing but in everything we do: if, perhaps, through the snares of the crafty enemy, we fall into a pit from which we cannot rise without contamination, let us seek instead that means of escape through which we see that we shall suffer the least danger. [Note: This homily exists in volume VII of the works of the Venerable Bede.]

It is therefore not surprising that the elders learned in Scripture, when they spoke about oaths, said nothing about the caution in swearing mentioned above, but undertook only to establish the point concerning which no question had ever been raised. No one denies, but all equally confess, that perjury is evil.

Therefore, if it is evil—or rather, because it is evil—let the prudent beware of swearing in such a way that they are compelled to commit perjury, knowing for certain that by swearing wrongly and carelessly they can destroy themselves, but that, by the grace of God, they cannot destroy the law of the Lord and the law of our Fathers by swearing.

Behold, the statements of the Catholic Fathers cited above have sufficiently demonstrated that we are compelled to alter oaths unjustly promised and tending toward greater danger, although we have sworn nothing unlawful.

But we are told: “You swore fidelity to a faithful prince. If you wish to remain faithful to him, renounce your fidelity and obedience to the apostolic lord, confirm that renunciation by oath or writing, and do not abstain from those excommunicated by the Apostolic See, nor teach others to abstain. If you do not do this, you will be subjected, as faithless men, to the royal sentence.”

A harsh proposition, and in some way like that ancient one which says: “If you wish to be Caesar’s friend, sacrifice to the gods; if you do not, you will be punished.”

If we render to the king the fidelity we are commanded to render, we incur the guilt of treachery not only before this king but before the King of all kings, for, as Scripture teaches, all who willingly violate the divine laws become apostates.

How, then, are we compelled to apostasy and treachery as though this were required by the sanctity of an oath, when we are said to have sworn nothing except fidelity? What an astonishing thing! We swore fidelity, and unless we commit treachery we are called perjurers and faithless. We never swore anything except what could be done without violating our proper order.

Let us therefore see whether it belongs to the priestly order or office to provide counsel or assistance so that a Christian prince may compel people to depart from Christian law and persecute those unwilling to depart through public punishment; so that, after driving out the priests, he may possess the sanctuaries of God as though by hereditary right (Ps. 82); so that he may seize the offerings of the faithful and the patrimonies of the poor for the incomparable—or, as some read, irrecoverable—use of himself and his own; so that, following Nero’s example, he may make Peter and Paul suffer again in their members; so that he may once more rouse Simon Magus against Simon Peter; so that he may enter the sanctuary with pride, where until now the faithful have been accustomed to enter the church barefoot, with contrite and humbled hearts, for the remission of their sins; so that he may pollute places consecrated by the blood of the saints with the bloody slaughter of the servants of Saint Peter.

Is it the pastoral office to participate in such things by action or counsel? Does fidelity require persuading kings that, by tearing Christ’s tunic and the vestments of his priests, they should deserve to have the kingdom torn away from them?

But the new teachers attribute all these actions to fidelity, saying that they are devoted to blessed Peter and to the Apostolic See, but that unusual injuries are deservedly inflicted upon the man sitting upon that see, since he pronounced so unusual a sentence of condemnation against undeserving men—namely, the king and the bishops.

They must be answered that, even if severity in those synodal judgments had exceeded gentleness, so that the apostolic lord had laid his hand upon them more heavily than usual and beyond what the matter warranted, orthodox bishops ought nevertheless to have advised the Catholic prince to avenge his injury in such a way that he would not provoke divine vengeance upon himself, would not utterly confound the rules of the Church, and would not accomplish through killings, fires, and devastations what ought to have been accomplished through ecclesiastical examinations.

Let both those men and those who have been taught by them to believe that all these things may lawfully and with impunity be committed because of the urgent necessity created by the earlier injury attend to another point.

Even if it belonged to Christian or ecclesiastical religion to repay such injuries with such retaliation, they could certainly not have become inexcusable in this way. For they themselves were the cause of the apostolic punishment of which they complain as an injury, and they themselves had first kindled what they now complain had inflamed them. Therefore they did not so much return injuries as inflict them.

When they had first gathered at Worms to initiate this affair [Note: This council was held in 1076. See Baronius, vol. XI], where all the calamity we suffer began, the lord pope had not yet sent any sentence of excommunication or anathema. They themselves—the first fruits of the discord—without his knowledge and while he suspected nothing of the kind, renounced their obedience to his pre-eminence with proud and sudden rashness.

“These are the beginnings of sorrows” (Mark 13). “This leaven corrupted the whole mass of the Church” (1 Cor. 5).

If anyone denies this, it can easily be proved by reviewing the sequence of events and the passage of time. The assembly of which we speak was arranged between the Nativity of the Lord and the following Lent, with intervals sufficiently long that whatever actions were undertaken could have been postponed until the time of the synod at Rome.

Before that same feast of the Nativity of the Lord, however, when the king had celebrated the birthday of the Apostle Andrew at Bamberg, such concord still prevailed between the kingdom and the supreme priesthood that everything done there concerning the bishop of that place who had been deposed and the man substituted in his place [Note: [Col. 0856D; Col. 0866D] He speaks of Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, deposed for simony, and of Rupert substituted in his place.] was attributed entirely to the command and obedience of the Roman pontiff.

The prince himself testified, both by his words and by letters sent to him with charity from the Apostolic See, that this had been enjoined upon him. Behold clear indications that concord still endured.

What, then, could have intervened so quickly that the man who, shortly before the Nativity of the Lord, had possessed such magnificence in the Church that changes of dignities were made at his command, should, only a few days after the Nativity, be proscribed without being summoned or heard, and while entirely unaware even of the disagreement?

For from that day—one held in such high regard by them, indeed by everyone—he received no embassy from them until the embassy arrived which said: “Descend, descend; we forbid you every right of the papacy,” and other things of this kind.

[Col. 0866D] Let the composers of this embassy, who were present at the assembly held at Worms—where they freely cast off the yoke of discipline, where they composed a writ of repudiation against holy obedience, where they established this new law for the world, that a prince’s servant should have the right to forbid the supreme pontiff an episcopal see—let them speak, then, let them speak; and, if not to us, at least let them answer the Church, which rightly cries out against them, by what preceding causes they repaid such things as a matter of duty. But if they cannot give a fitting account—indeed, because they cannot—[Note: Here, in order that the discourse may have greater force, clarity [Col. 0867B], and what they call συμμετρία (“proportion”), we have altered the order of the words somewhat, namely by placing “indeed, because they cannot” before “they must confess.” We judge, moreover, that the author himself wrote it as we print it, and that it was only later corrupted by copyists’ negligence. EDITORS, PATROLOGY.]—they must confess that they are the authors of a new confusion, [Col. 0867A] but the disturbers of ancient peace and tranquillity, the destroyers of divine and human laws. Would that they preferred to confess rather than defend what was wrongly undertaken, and by confession to correct it rather than multiply it by defending it! May God bring this about, and add this as well: since they see that everything answers their undertakings in confusion, may they at last return to their senses and not bring it about that they make their end like their beginning!

**End of the letter of Saint Gebhard.**

## Note on the preceding letter

Formerly the schismatics, especially the Guibertines under Henry IV, greatly insulted the orthodox, as though they were perjurers, because they withdrew and separated themselves from obedience to King Henry, who by the Apostolic See had been not only excommunicated but also deposed from the kingdom and from every royal power. This can be seen both in other schismatic writers and in a certain decree of Guibert, the false pope, sent to the whole gathering of schismatics from a certain disgraceful council assembled at Rome in the church of Saint Peter—when Guibert was profaning and defiling everything in the city of Rome by his sacrileges—where the three-times, indeed four-times, perjured Guibert writes as we found it in a manuscript codex:

“For there a considerable outcry arises concerning the perjuries which they urge others to commit, to the peril of imperial dignity. And because that matter seemed to be the root and origin of the other crimes, it was decided that it should first be discussed, and that it should be shown how wicked and dangerous such an exhortation is. Therefore, by necessary proofs we disproved the excommunication pronounced against the emperor, because it seemed to have drawn its force from the occasion of his perjuries and of all his assertions.”

These and many other things of this kind the execrable Guibert set forth in that decree of his.

Saint Gebhard refutes and demolishes this accusation in his letter all the more fully and precisely because it was more frequently brought forward and inculcated by the schismatics. It has also today been revived in the minds of the modern Guibertines—that is, the Lutherans and Calvinists—who call the most widely received doctrine in the Catholic Church concerning the supreme pontiff’s power over pernicious kings and princes the origin of all perjuries, although they themselves are plunged in oath-breaking perjuries—from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, as may be said especially of the Calvinists. Gebhard therefore refutes them no less than those ancient, perjured Guibertines.

[Col. 0867]

# The Life and Deeds of Saint Altmann, Bishop of Passau, in Which the Reader Will Find Glorious Things Concerning Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiff

Now copied and published for the first time from a manuscript codex.

## To the Reader

It seemed appropriate to append the Life of Saint Altmann, bishop of Passau, to the letters of Saint Gebhard, both so that the monuments of writers would not separate those whom, while living on earth, love of piety from their earliest years and the defense of the Apostolic See had joined in the closest bond, and because an honorable mention of Gregory VII, the pontiff, occurs in this history. Under his banner Altmann preferred to serve rather than draw pay in the camp of the schismatics. To him Berthold of Constance, in his Chronicle under the year 1091, addressed this eulogy:

“Altmann, bishop of Passau, of holy memory, most devoted to the cause of Saint Peter and to ecclesiastical religion, after many dangers, tribulations, and exiles which he endured for Christ, departed to the Lord in a good old age on the sixth day before the Ides of August. In his episcopate he founded three monasteries of clerics living in common according to the rule of Saint Augustine, and built and established a third in the bishopric of Freising, on the allod of Duke Welf, through his clerics and according to regular discipline. He was of such holiness, continence, and religious devotion that he was revered and loved by the most reverend Pope Gregory, by the holy bishop of Lucca, Anselm, and indeed by all religious people, but was hated and feared by schismatics and criminals. Thus, at his death, he left great sorrow to the good, but great rejoicing to the wicked.”

The name of the author who composed this Life is not given. His period can be inferred from these words of his: “The holy prelate, with the pious prince, Margrave Luipold, consenting—the grandfather of this Luipold who rules today,” and so forth. The earlier Luipold, or Leopold, of this name was the fourth, who died in 1096, or, as Berthold has it, in 1095. The other Luipold, under whom the author lived, was Luipold VI, son of Saint Luipold V and grandson of the fourth; he assumed the margraviate in 1136, as stated in the *Chronicle of Austria* published by Freher. Lazius, however, gives a different account.

## The Prologue to the Life of Saint Altmann, Bishop

[Col. 0867]

[Col. 0867C] The Founder and Governor of all things, of whom Scripture testifies that he commands the sun, and it does not rise, and that he shuts up the stars as though under a seal, in order to temper the darkness of this night, which has grown more deeply dreadful in our times, sometimes causes those lights which he placed in the firmament to shine more brightly over the earth, and mercifully makes known to human beings those which previously shone only for himself.

Among these I may rightly number the blessed Altmann, venerable bishop of the Church of Passau. After the setting of this mortal life, he was placed among the stars of heaven, and so frequently flashes upon us from above with a new radiance—namely, through the virtues and signs which God, wondrous in his saints, works through him—that one may appropriately judge that the blessed Job said to him: “When you think yourself consumed, you will rise like the morning star” (Job 11). For the manifestation of his merits, demons flee, paralytics are healed, the blind are given sight, the crippled are restored, and the harms of various illnesses are driven away. Will the present age, then, be so blind that the brightness of so great a light, by which God illumines and glorifies his saint, will not strike your ungrateful eyes? Will it not terrify them? Has it not until now said: “O crooked and provoking generation!” (Psalm 77), “We have not seen our signs; there is now no prophet” (Psalm 74)? Behold, he who “makes a sign for us for good” (Psalm 85) and consoles us through the merits of his servant renews signs and changes wonders even to this day (Ecclesiasticus 36). Will you, unbeliever, then doubt concerning this man that he has entered into the powers of the Lord (Psalm 70), when he does not delay to be so powerfully present to those who beseech him? You do not hear his voice, nor see his shadow, nor feel his hand, as once the sick among the apostles heard, saw, and felt; yet you do experience his benefits, and at his invocation rejoice in your former health.

Believe, therefore, that he lives with God and has great power with him, since your own health proves that he was invisibly present also. Therefore believe him holy, proclaim him approved: he now commends not himself, but is one whom God commends (2 Corinthians 10); he now bears no testimony concerning himself (John 8), but the Three who are in heaven—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—bear testimony to him (1 John 5). Thus, if the lepers who lived at the gate of Samaria reproach themselves for keeping silent to the city about the day of good news (2 Kings 7), we shall be much more liable to reproach and marked with the sin of unbelief and ingratitude if we envy or conceal from the Church of God such great praises of God, such great proclamations of this saint, such a great treasure stored up among us.

For this reason, overcome and assisted by your prayers, reverend lords and brothers, I shall endeavor to write something about the life and miracles of so great a pontiff. I shall not do so in persuasive words of human wisdom (1 Corinthians 2), which I do not possess and which, with the Apostle, I know to be foolishness before God; rather, in simple and pious speech I shall present to the reader whatever you, sons of truth, have indicated and established from certain older writings and from recent memory. You neither ask, nor do I promise, to write things irrelevant to the subject or to digress farther from the narrative for the sake of embellishment. I do promise that, if you judge anything in these writings should be corrected, changed, or removed, I shall not allow this to disturb my mind. I do not deny that these things may be criticized even by friends whose eyes are not those of doves but of eagles. For them I seek no glory, but only to show you the obedience I owe and to obtain from God the intercession and mercy of the one about whom we write.

**The prologue ends.**

# The Life of Saint Altmann, Bishop of Passau, Begins

[Col. 0869]

[Col. 0869D] Blessed Altmann was therefore descended from the Saxon people. Yet he had learned nothing savage or stony from that nation; rather, like a most precious gem that shines more brightly than gold, so he, born of illustrious parents, shone more illustriously in every goodness and virtue. Given over to liberal studies, with the one who teaches human beings knowledge (Psalm 93) inspiring and instructing him inwardly, he was most elegantly trained in both divine and philosophical disciplines. Although this knowledge inflates some people (1 Corinthians 8), it did not inflate this man but adorned and commended him. He was far removed from those who “know more than they ought to know” (Romans 12), who, through the pride of their knowledge, despise the simple and trample the humble. Otherwise, if he had not agreed with the humble and had not thought lofty thoughts (ibid.), how would the Holy Spirit have entered him—the Spirit who is Lord of sacred knowledge, since he rests only upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at his words? (Isaiah 66.) Thus, according to the judgment of the one who said that glory follows—perhaps, “receives”—a humble spirit, he was considered worthy of exaltation because he had wisely learned to humble himself before God.

In the Church called Paderborn he was not only a canon but was also chosen to direct the schools and bound to this work for many years. As the reputation of so great a man grew, so too did his honor. Therefore, in that noble Church of Aachen, already long adorned by antiquity as the seat of the Teutonic kingdom, he deserved to be elevated as provost of the canons. At that time also, in the palace of Emperor Henry III, he was found faithful and prudent in the conduct of affairs. I think that God was then testing his servant to see whether he would be worthy to receive the greater trust, if he proved faithful in what was least. When the emperor died, his proven fidelity did not die with him; rather, he preserved it tirelessly for the Empress Agnes amid the whirlwinds of various disasters by which kingdom and priesthood were then being miserably thrown into confusion.

At that time certain nobles, moved by love and longing for the heavenly Jerusalem which is above and free (Galatians 4) and is our mother, undertook to visit this earthly Jerusalem in which the Redeemer of the human race mercifully completed the work of our salvation that the Father had given him to accomplish (John 4; Matthew 28). Following the example of the holy women who once came with spices, they too went with the fragrant offerings of their vows and prayers to approach and see the place where the Lord had been laid (Luke 24).

[Note: This pilgrimage was undertaken in the year 1064, under the leadership of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz.]

Who would dare suppose that bishops of various cities, men distinguished for prudence and nobility, had despised the highest honors, their homeland, relatives, and riches because of some common superstition—as though the day of the final judgment were imminent—because Easter happened to fall in that year on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, the day on which Christ’s resurrection was said to be inscribed? I would rather think that they were moved by pious devotion, or disturbed by evils multiplying everywhere, and undertook the labor of this pilgrimage because, as wise and religious men, they preferred to spend evil days in fulfilling their vows to the Lord their God rather than pass them fruitlessly amid the dangers of such times.

Among this multitude were distinguished men: Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and Gunther, bishop of Bamberg, together with other notable men, both clerics and laymen.

[Note: See Baronius, volume 11, under the year 1064.]

Saint Altmann also joined them, accompanied by several honored men from the palace.

When they had begun the journey they had undertaken, they encountered robbers. For the enemies of the cross of Christ, their accomplices and allies—of whom David complains, “On the road by which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me” (Psalm 139)—surrounded them with ambushes and stripped, wounded, and killed many of them.

[Note: It is said that barely two thousand returned out of seven thousand.]

Here we are taught that not only those descending from Jerusalem to Jericho suffer the dangers of robbers, but likewise those ascending from Jericho (Luke 10)—that is, from this world to Jerusalem—endure the ambushes of enemies, both invisible and visible. Considering the ambushes and snares of both kinds, the saint confesses and says: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Psalm 24). Again he says of the Lord: “He himself delivered me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm 90).

But the men of virtue, whose confidence in the fear of the Lord was the source of their strength, became stronger through adversity. After suffering losses, insults, and blows, with which the savage barbarians cruelly and repeatedly afflicted them, they finally reached Jerusalem. There they fulfilled the vows which their lips had declared to God (Psalm 65), and visited with due reverence the places where our Lord and Savior had appeared on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), especially the places of his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. Since they had no lasting city there but sought the one to come, they sought to revisit the homeland they had left (Hebrews 13), and from there, by common vows, desired to migrate to their heavenly homeland.

When they reached Pannonia and were staying in the fortress which in our language is called Wizzeburch (Albaregalis), the venerable Bishop Gunther departed from this world to the Lord. We hope that he heard: “Well done, good servant” (Luke 19), for he had brought and multiplied the talent and was called within to the joy of his lord (ibid.). At the same time Egelbert, bishop of Passau, also died and was added to those in heaven whose dignity he had borne on earth.

After his death, they took counsel together, and with the support of Empress Agnes, as well as of the nobles of the kingdom, Saint Altmann was unanimously appointed bishop in the place of the deceased in the see of Passau. The clergy applauded, the people rejoiced, and, with no one dissenting, they approved as most worthy of the episcopal insignia the man whom the nobility of his birth, the holiness of his life, the soundness of his doctrine, and the testimony of an unblemished reputation commended. Accordingly, honored men were sent to meet him, carrying the pastoral staff and episcopal ring to the elect in Pannonia, and faithfully bearing witness through these insignia to what the heavenly disposition had ordained concerning him.

[Col. 0872C] Called by God like Aaron, not taking the honor upon himself (Hebrews 5), neither pursuing it as many do when it flees nor winning over one who resists by flattering him with services, he was received with the greatest rejoicing by the sheep entrusted to him. Shortly afterward he was consecrated by the reverend Archbishop Gebhard of Salzburg with the due blessing, and received from the Spirit—who bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8)—the testimony that he truly was the son for whom the holy patriarch had effectively prayed, saying: “Let whoever curses you be cursed, and let whoever blesses you be filled with blessings” (Genesis 27).

From that day onward the Spirit of the Lord was directed in him. From then on he was wholly inflamed with love of God; refreshed by the vision of God, he paid less attention to vanities and false insanities (Psalm 39). Constant in fasting and persevering in vigils, he labored frequently in prayer, watering his bed every night with his groaning and tears (Psalm 6). He hid alms in the bosoms of the poor, so that they might pray for him when he himself was less able to pray. He did these things in secret, so that his Father, who sees in secret, might repay him (Matthew 5).

But because he had learned from the Apostle that he must provide what is good not only before God but also before all human beings (Romans 12), what had been established for him from his earliest age was adorned outwardly by the finest conduct, such as the same Apostle seems to teach when he instructs Timothy or Titus, saying: “A bishop must be irreproachable, sober, prudent, chaste, hospitable, kind, modest, and holding fast to the faithful word that accords with sound doctrine” (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).

Yet in all these things, following the example of blessed Job, he did not see the sun when it shone above, nor the moon proceeding brightly (Job 31). For, to use the words of blessed Gregory, although his work gave the light of example to others, the holy man did not attend to it for the sake of the glory of presumption; rather, fearing that he might be exalted because of it, he turned the eyes of his mind away from contemplating it. For just as the moon receives illumination from the sun’s ray, so reputation draws strength and the favor of approval from a good work, scattering a kind of brightness of light. Thus the holy man, whom neither manifest work nor praiseworthy reputation exalted, did not see the sun shining above or the moon proceeding brightly.

Moreover, since no one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand so that it may shine for everyone in the house (Matthew 5), it pleased the invisible God alone, who dwells in inaccessible light, to make this lamp—which the Father of lights himself had kindled—shine before human beings, so that they might see his good works and glorify God (ibid.), and to make it known and manifest more fully to those who see only the face and cannot look into the heart. He manifested it in this way:

In the city of Passau there was a certain woman whose only daughter had been struck by the affliction of leprosy. As she prayed frequently and earnestly begged the Lord for her daughter’s health, it was revealed to her in a dream that, if she anointed her daughter with the water used to wash the hands of Saint Altmann after the sacraments of the Mass, she would be restored to her former health. When she faithfully did this, her daughter was healed from that hour.

In what respect does this saint seem inferior to the great prophet Elisha, who taught Naaman the Syrian to cure his leprosy in the Jordan? (2 Kings 5.) Elisha ordered him to wash seven times to be healed; this girl, washed once, had no need to be washed a second time, because she immediately felt the health she had sought.

Nor did the Lord declare by this miracle alone what merit his beloved servant possessed before him; he had also foreshadowed long beforehand, through preceding prophecies, what he would become after many years. When he was in the years of adolescence, and he, Gebhard—whom we mentioned above [Note: See the Life of Saint Gebhard, volumes II and VI of *Antiq. Lect.*]—and Albero, later bishop of Würzburg, were together, it happened that they sat down beside the bank of a spring to eat bread. While they furnished their poor table with mutual conversation, they began to hope for greater things concerning themselves and, with a certain hidden and prophetic spirit, to predict them.

Gebhard said: “I shall become bishop in the Church of Salzburg.”

Albero replied: “And I shall preside in the see of Würzburg.”

Altmann said: “And I shall govern the see of Passau as bishop.”
