The outcome of events proved this prophecy true. Each was elevated in the Church he had chosen, and, lest they be found fruitless trees by the one who had planted them in his house, they produced fruit in their proper seasons. For each bishop established a monastery in his diocese and ennobled it by his burial. Gebhard rests in the monastery of Admont, Albero in that of Lambach, and Altmann in the monastery of Göttweig.

Their bodies were buried there in peace, but their names will live forever (Ecclesiasticus 44). How could those names not live, since they are recorded in the book of life, when they truly belonged to those to whom the Lord promises: “I will not erase their names from the book of life” (Revelation 3)?

There are people who call upon their own names in their lands (Psalm 48), yet are not known by name (Exodus 33), because they have been erased from the book of the living and are not enrolled with the just. Hence the stern Judge will say to them in that dreadful separation of the good and the wicked: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25), because I do not know you. According to blessed David, the memory of such people perishes with a sound (Psalm 9); or, if any memory of them remains, it is not in blessing but in cursing. Was it not enough for them to be troublesome to human beings, since they were also troublesome to God, as Isaiah testified concerning people like them? (Isaiah 7.) Therefore far from them is what is said of one beloved by God and human beings, whose memory is in blessing (Ecclesiasticus 45).

Consider, I beg you, bishops of our age, what kind of memory will follow you—not because of the construction of churches but of castles, which you restore on lofty and precipitous mountains with the sweat of the poor and the pennies of widows. But for what purpose, except to drive people away from them? Not so that demons bound there may groan in prisons and waste away in punishments; not so that sinners may be converted there, but so that they may be punished—not for the forgiveness of sins, but in revenge for the injury done to you.

You, holy servants of the Lord, ministers of our God, of whom we are speaking, instructed monasteries with sounder counsel from the offerings of the faithful and the possessions of the churches. From them demons are driven away; in them the poor are received, sinners are converted, and the religion of holy simplicity and blessed poverty is preserved. There, day and night, those whom God has gathered from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea, from every people and language, every age and condition, sex and nation, will not cease praising the name of the Lord, to glorify him who makes all who serve him “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4).

Although you rest in your sleep, as you have always desired, and rest from your labors (Revelation 14), I nevertheless do not believe that your spirits are absent from the places which, while alive, you built and loved with such devotion. I believe that you are present to all who dwell there: standing beside those who pray, assisting those who labor, raising up those who have fallen, and advancing the prayers of each person before the presence of the divine majesty. I would suppose that from heaven you look down with the Lord to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God (Psalm 52). If you find someone acting sluggishly, lying to God in his vows, and limping along the paths of the Lord, I think that you immediately weep with the angels of peace and pour out from the depths of your hearts before the face of the Lord a lamentation of groaning for him—or against him—who is such.

Therefore, brothers and lords, you must consider with what discipline and reverence you should conduct yourselves among those holy Fathers and patrons of yours who, together with the holy angels, are present, move about among you, and ceaselessly watch over your salvation, lest anything irreligious, indecent, or uncorrected be found that might grieve them or drive them away.

But now we must return to the narrative. I am not acting as your teacher, but as the narrator of those things alone which you had taught me in writing or by the living voice.

Thus the blessed servant of God, daily adding with the Prophet the works of God to the praise of the Lord, attributed them not to his own merits but to divine mercy, saying with the Psalmist: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm 113). And with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15).

So that he might truthfully add, “and his grace in me was not in vain,” the holy man built, in the suburb of Passau, a church in honor of Saint Nicholas on the bank of the river Inn, enriching it with many possessions and properties. He placed Hartmann, a man commended for wisdom and eloquence, in charge there as provost. Hartmann was very dear to King Rudolf and was also well known to Pope Urban and his successors. As he himself was religious, so he carefully gathered religious clerics and laymen from every place and trained them to live a common life according to the rule of Saint Augustine, by its words and examples.

When these things had been accomplished, Christ’s tireless minister turned his hand to stronger things—truly stronger things, because it brings far more difficulty and labor to uproot entrenched and long-standing depravity than to implant good disciplines from the beginning. Since the very name of bishop reminded him that he was to oversee the Church of God, he considered the field and vineyard which the Lord had leased to him, and behold, nettles had completely filled it, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed (Proverbs 24).

But what do you think I mean by nettles and thorns? Surely, the earthly desires that prick the hearts of the negligent and the goads of vices. And what wall? Certainly, the discipline of the Fathers, which lay fallen in the hearts of the wicked. How had all this come about? Because people were sleeping, and the enemy came and sowed weeds over the grain in the field (Matthew 13), which the most excellent master of the household had sown with the best seed.

Understand by “people” the prelates of the churches, whose torpor and sleepiness give the enemy—that is, the devil—confidence and an opportunity to sow his seed in the Lord’s field. The universal field is the world; but we are not speaking of it here. By a field or vineyard I understand any monastery; by many fields or vineyards, many monasteries.

At that time, growing vices were choking the fruitful crop in these places, namely, holy religion. In them the true vine had been turned into bitterness. “I am,” says Christ, “the true vine” (John 15). Is not this sweet and upright Lord turned into bitterness for the one who abhors what is upright, holy, chaste, of good repute, virtuous, and strict? (Philippians 4.) Does he not judge Christ bitter who refuses to taste and see how sweet he is? (Psalm 33.)

With the Lord’s field or vineyard in such a state, do you not believe that the man of God groaned to the Lord from the depths of his heart and said:

“Why does the farmer labor? You have destroyed its wall, and all who pass along the road pluck its grapes. The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it. God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven, come, and visit this vineyard” (Psalm 79).

Your enemy says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matthew 15). Behold how many things have grown up that you did not plant, O Father! Is it because you appointed me to uproot, tear down, scatter, and destroy them? (Jeremiah 1.) I shall attack these thorns, which cling to one another. One adheres to another, so that no opening remains among them (Job 41).

Or, because you tell us your servants to allow both to grow until the harvest (Matthew 13), shall I disregard so arduous and difficult a task? I certainly know, as Ecclesiastes teaches, that whoever moves stones—that is, the weighty and hard ways of the wicked—will be hurt by them; and that whoever splits wood—that is, the hearts of the stubborn—will be wounded by it (Ecclesiastes 10).

Therefore, if you permit it, let both grow. But what shall we do, when we see the thorns growing and the wheat being choked? You are concerned lest, while gathering the weeds, we should uproot the wheat together with them (Matthew 13). But there is no difficulty in discerning whether something is wheat or weeds; these scandals are manifest. They do not need an accuser; they stand even without a witness. Public reputation—indeed, infamy—cries out.

Has this cry not already risen to you? I, your inadequate representative, descended to them and see that they have completed everything in this way. I do not find there even the Decalogue of your commandments, out of regard for which I ought to spare them, though I would prefer to spare them. Trusting, therefore, in your help and in the counsel of your Apostle, I shall remove the evil from your houses, which holiness should characterize (1 Corinthians 5; Psalm 93). And if anything more grievous follows from this, I shall console myself with the words of your teacher, who says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Corinthians 7).

Thus he drove out from the holy places everywhere all who were pestilential, corrupt, and made abominable by their practices (Psalm 13), providing religious men in their place, both superiors and disciples. From this came the renewed flowering of religion; from this the return of the sweet fragrance of a reputation for holiness; from this reverence shown to the servants of Christ.

[Col. 0877A] Through this fortunate undertaking of the diligent cultivator, the newly cleared fields of the monasteries were renewed, and a more fertile harvest arose, since it would have been fruitless to sow upon thorns. Hence the house of Saint Florian the martyr bore fruit in the sweetness of fragrance, and its flowers became fruits of honor and honesty (Ecclesiasticus 24). So too the monastery of Saint Hippolytus became distinguished to this day for the study of the schools; and likewise the monastery of Saint Agapitus the martyr at Kremsmünster, because the Lord gave graciousness and they themselves gave their fruit (Psalm 84).

Just as it is written of Abraham that he was journeying and advancing farther toward the south (Genesis 12), so too this could be seen in this holy man, because he also was a son of Abraham. It was not enough for him to establish a new monastery and correct institutions already established. He advanced still farther toward an exalted work: namely, to build upon a high mountain a magnificent basilica for the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary.

For when he was staying one day in a village called Mautern, he noticed at a distance a mountain not joined to the neighboring mountains, which the common people called Göttweig. The mountain appeared pleasant and quite suitable for habitation. After learning its character from the inhabitants, he immediately ordered his mule to be saddled and, accompanied by a large crowd, climbed the mountain by a certain steep and precipitous path, demonstrating by his ascent that from earth one travels to the stars only by the arduous and narrow paths of God’s commandments.

After surveying the entire mountain, when he saw that it was spacious and highly suitable for building a monastery, he immediately pitched his tent, ordered the dense forest that had grown there to be cut down, and commanded that an oratory be begun. While he was still uncertain to which saint it should principally be dedicated, with different people giving different advice according to their various vows and affections, a messenger sent by the dukes of Bohemia happened to arrive. He brought the bishop a panel, suitably offered as a gift to so great a man, on which the image of the blessed Virgin Mary was wonderfully represented in Greek workmanship. It deservedly remains preserved in that same church and is to be preserved forever.

The pontiff, beloved of God, reverently kissed it; as though instructed by a divine oracle, he immediately assigned the place to that most glorious Mother of God, Mary. When he had successfully completed and solemnly dedicated the work of the basilica, he provided, with generous benevolence, possessions for those who would dwell there. He also provided ornaments appropriate to the divine offices. When these things had been properly completed, he gathered religious men together and placed over them a prudent man named Otto, commanding them to lead a spiritual life according to the rule of blessed Augustine.

Now there comes to mind what is sung in the psalm: “The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away” (Psalm 111). What had this sinner seen, that he should become angry, gnash his teeth, and waste away? There is no doubt that he had seen that the one who distributed his possessions among the poor would have his justice endure forever, and that his horn would be exalted in glory (ibid.).

Thus, in this servant of God, the malicious enemy saw what he envied. He saw his merits accumulating before God; he saw his leisure occupied in advancing the salvation and way of life of many. Therefore he devised ambushes and set up obstacles by which he might force him to abandon those works whose benefit to the progress of so many caused him grief. He therefore used his customary instruments and did not hesitate to accomplish through his members what he had little hope of accomplishing by himself. The order in which this happened remains to be explained.

At that time, throughout almost the whole Teutonic kingdom there was a serious scandal and a general complaint concerning the incontinence of priests. For it was not hidden in secret; rather, “their forehead had become that of a prostitute, and they were unwilling to feel shame” (Jer. 3). The matter was brought to the ears of the Roman pontiff, and it seemed appropriate that he should rebuke and prohibit so great an enormity by decretal letters. The bishops agreed and rejoiced, and, as far as they were able, cooperated with the salutary commands [Col. 0878B].

Therefore Blessed Altmann, having assembled a council of the brethren at the see of Passau, ordered the letters addressed to him concerning this matter to be read aloud. He entreated and exhorted them not to regard chastity as burdensome, since it is rewarded by God with a special crown. Although it is an adornment of every faithful soul, it ought especially to adorn those who must offer the holy and immaculate sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood to the divine Majesty on behalf of us all.

What more need be said? In many words the good Father and prudent teacher urged love of so great a virtue and of such a purity, so worthy of embrace; but he did not persuade them. They defended themselves by the antiquity of the times and the authority of their predecessors, none of whom, they said, had they ever seen act severely and violently in such a matter. The servant of Christ replied that he too would willingly refrain from these measures if the lord pope’s command permitted it; but for now he feared for himself and feared for them, because it is written that not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death (Rom. 1). Since he accomplished nothing, he dismissed the assembly [Col. 0878C].

After consulting wiser men and entrusting the matter to their confidence, when the feast of Saint Stephen the protomartyr arrived—the church revered him as its patron—and many of the nobles had gathered for the solemn day, because “the righteous man is confident as a lion” (Prov. 28), he mounted the ambo before the entire gathering of clergy and people and fearlessly proclaimed what the apostolic letters directed. Then he added a threat backed by authority, so that those who had refused to yield to entreaties might be broken by severity [Col. 0878D].

Immediately a clamour and fury resounded from every side. And perhaps at that moment they would have torn the servant of God apart with their frenzied hands, had not divine power and the integrity of the nobles present restrained the enraged crowd.

In those days Henry IV, son of the Emperor Henry, who had been surnamed “the Pious,” was reigning; he was still very young and had been raised in pleasures, without the restraints of discipline. In him was fulfilled the saying of the wise man, who prophesies: “Woe to you, land, whose king is a child” (Ecclesiasticus 4). What the Church and the kingdom suffered in his time, how many shepherds were driven from their sheep, how much human blood was shed, what acts of lust, fires, and robberies were committed—the world knows, and the historians of the times have not kept silent [Col. 0879A].

Those who detested chastity fled to this enemy of religion and adversary of continence, excommunicated for his tyranny by Pope GREGORY IV. Such accusers and such witnesses deserved a hearing before such a judge; and against the man of God, who detested crimes, they fixed crimes by which they believed they could strip him of his episcopal honour.

If he had been allowed to stand before them, this man could have answered on his own behalf in a brief statement, just as his teacher Christ answered on his own behalf: “The works that I do bear witness about me” (John 10). But “in his humiliation judgment was denied him” (Acts 8); his adversaries making the same assertion that the Jews once made about the Saviour: “If this man were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you” (John 18) [Col. 0879B].

And if he had answered what Christ answered those who stoned him—“I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?” (John 10)—he would indeed have given a true and evident reply; but before such men it would not have sufficed.

Henry, therefore, having been won over, entered Passau as an enemy and, like Herod, confusing right and wrong and doing everything according to his will, restored to their property and dignities all the criminals who had been expelled from the episcopal residence. When he had departed, the brethren of Saint Nicholas, who lived a religious life in the suburb of the city, jointly detested his cruel deeds. Henry’s supporters therefore violently dragged them from the monastery, beat them publicly, and expelled them from that territory; their property fell to the robbers [Col. 0879C].

With iniquity thus prevailing, Blessed Altmann was expelled from his see for the sake of justice and returned to his homeland in Saxony. After this he visited the threshold of the apostles and explained the reason for his journey and the sequence of the wrong done to him to Pope Gregory in detail. Because all the saints fear concerning all their works, he resigned the episcopate to the lord pope, troubled by the scruple that he had received his investiture from a lay hand.

While the pope was resting for a little after becoming weary, one day, when he was seated in the church and discussing the restoration of Saint Altmann with the cardinals, Altmann humbly refusing the honour of so great a burden, a certain dove flew around all the parts of the basilica and at last came to Altmann, poor and humble in spirit. It was as though it were saying: “This is my rest for ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen it” (Ps. 131); and what follows: “I will surely bless her widow”—that is, the church of Passau, widowed of her lawful spouse—“and I will satisfy her poor with bread” (ibid.). It settled upon the bishop’s head [Col. 0879D].

Everyone saw and understood the sign. Without hesitation the pope removed the mitre from his own head, placed it on Altmann’s head, appointed him bishop and legate of the Roman see, and sent him back to his own country increased with blessing, as though saying to him at his departure: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10); “abide in my love” (John 15).

[Col. 0880A] Meanwhile Henry IV’s supporters assembled a council at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0879D] In the year 1080, see Baronius, under this year, no. 17.]. Let them themselves see who presided over it.

There the schismatics, cut off from the Church, denied Pope Gregory, a Catholic man and universal Father, the title of Father; and, themselves condemned, they condemned his followers. In these circumstances the shepherd of the Church considered yielding the city and the arms, I think remembering the Saviour’s permission when he said to his disciples: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 5).

This being done, a certain Wichpert—Guibert, the false pope—who has no praise in the catalogue of pontiffs, was intruded into the apostolic see. Why do I say “intruded”? By his own ambition he invaded it, grasped at it, and seized it. From then on true shepherds were driven from their sees throughout the world, while schismatics or [Col. 0880B] Simoniacs were substituted in their place.

By the faction of these men Altmann too was driven from his flock, and a certain Hermann, brother of Duke Luipold, was substituted. In him the curse pronounced against Judas—“Let another take his bishopric” (Ps. 108)—was quickly fulfilled. For scarcely two years did he shear and milk another’s sheep, and he ended his life together with the title of shepherd that he falsely bore. It is nevertheless said that at the end he repented, restored everything belonging to the episcopate to Bishop Altmann, and humbly sought absolution from the anathema.

He was succeeded by Timo, a canon of Würzburg, although money secured the appointment; and he violently held the bishopric as a robber as far as the river Anesis [Anasus] [Note: [Col. 0879] See Hundius, *Metropolis*, in the catalogue of the bishops of Passau.].

But the holy prelate, with the support of the foremost prince, Margrave Luipold—the grandfather of this Luipold who now rules, whose nobility, piety, and faithfulness remain to this day as a most abundant inheritance—vigorously governed clergy and people in the eastern province. He devotedly watched over the work he had begun on Mount Kotwikc [Gotwic], from which the enemy’s deceit had attempted to hinder him through the obstacles mentioned above [Col. 0880C].

On one occasion, while celebrating the solemn Masses in that place, a certain newly arrived deacon of dubious reputation was about to read the Gospel and asked for a blessing. The bishop gazed at him for a long time as he was to be blessed, then removed the stole from his neck and ordered another man to read. From this it is clear that he had learned something about the man through revelation which the others did not know.

The wretched man was confounded with the confusion that brings sin, not with the confusion that brings glory. Trusting in Henry, the refuge of the wicked, he fled to him; and, wishing to accuse the bishop and the brethren, although he was judged unworthy of a hearing, he was punished by God’s vengeance with the worst death of sinners [Col. 0880D].

Because dangerous times were pressing upon them and the grave schism had grown—one which the leading men of the empire had originated and daily fostered for its increase—it pleased God, who never ceases to provide for all, to honour his servant with an appropriate sign in order to strengthen wavering faith, and to commend his Catholic minister to all the faithful.

He had ordered his cupbearer, because of his stricter and more secret abstinence, to place water on his table and to cover it with beer foam so that it would not be known. The cupbearer did what he had been commanded. When the holy man brought it to his mouth, he tasted wine—and excellent wine at that. Thinking that the cupbearer had mocked him, he angrily rebuked him as a serious transgressor. But the cupbearer confirmed with dreadful oaths that he had placed before him exactly what he had been ordered to place.

The bishop wished to conceal the matter, but the cupbearer removed the cup from the table and determined with greater certainty by tasting it what the bishop had drunk. Later, having become a monk at the monastery of Kotwikc [Gotwic], he related the matter in due order, so that he may be blessed in all things who alone works great wonders for the glory of his saints and for the strengthening and consolation of the fainthearted (Ps. 71) [Col. 0881A].

Receive, without growing weary, something further to the praise of God concerning the servant of God. For who could grow weary of such remarkable signs, which establish faith in invisible things and prove that God’s power has not failed?

Withdraw, O foolish man, who say in your heart, “There is no God” (Ps. 13), and who insult him with such great impiety, saying, “Where is your God?” (Ps. 113). Behold, “in his holy one dwells the praise of Israel” (Ps. 21). In his holy one God performs the things you see. If he is not present, what can a human being do? What can dust accomplish when it knows that the Lord has said to it: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15)?

Know, therefore, that God exists and is present, performing what a human being cannot perform. But if you think that a human being performs this, go and do likewise; command the demons, and test their obedience. What if they resist? Revere and devoutly embrace the one in whom and through whom God performs such things. Why are you worse than the Jews? They said of Christ: “If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John 9).

But listen nevertheless, and turn from your unbelief. Once the venerable bishop was standing at the holy altar, about to celebrate Mass. He heard behind him a demoniac crying out horribly in the church. He asked what this might be. Those standing nearby explained that a man was being tormented by a cruel demon and could scarcely be restrained, though many were holding him bound. The bishop ordered that the poor man be brought to the hospice for the poor and that food be set before him in the name of the Lord. Immediately the evil spirit departed from him, and the man returned home healthy [Col. 0881C].

I wish to recount further, O unbeliever, something that may convince you that the servant of God was not lacking even the spirit of prophecy, although you dislike hearing it. A certain cleric, full of a demon, was brought to him. The bishop, persisting more intensely in continuous prayer, drove out the demon and forbade the sin on account of which that unclean spirit had been permitted to afflict the man.

He foretold that, if the man repeated the sin, the punishment of the sin would immediately be repeated in him, and he ordered him to devote himself to a better life in the cloister with the brethren. After this the brethren asked the bishop to promote him to the priesthood. The prelate said that this would not be advantageous for him. Yet, overcome by the brethren’s compassion, he granted their request, but with the warning that he would not escape God’s terrible judgment if he did not guard against the sin forbidden to him.

For several years the man avoided the sin and honourably fulfilled the office he had received. At last, disregarding the bishop’s threat, the wretched man returned to his vomit, and at that very moment suffered the most violent attack by the demon [Col. 0882A]. Again the holy man, pitying the miserable man, attacked the enemy with his customary weapons and triumphed. He removed him from the ministry of the altar, repeatedly warning and exhorting him, now healed of the abominable deed.

Terrified by the recent scourging, the man abstained from sin for some time. But, alas, overcome again by long habit, after the bishop’s death he fell back into sin. Therefore, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, the evil spirit took seven other spirits more wicked than itself (Matt. 12), and they entered the sinner. Cruelly tormenting him night and day, they compelled him to confess with his own mouth every disgraceful and abominable thing he had done.

He was bound, lamenting, in harsher chains and cast into the custody of men—he who had deserved the custody of angels [Col. 0882B]. At last, on the feast of the Annunciation, he was scarcely rescued from the evil spirit by the prayers of the brethren. After three days he was anointed with sacred oil and strengthened with the body of Christ; then, terribly scourged, he died. We believe that, having been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5).

Another cleric, likewise handed over to a most evil demon, so that scarcely any healthy person could escape the madman’s hands, was blessed by the bishop, freed from the demon, and restored to his former health.

One of the brethren, devoted with persistent zeal to lengthy prayers and very many genuflections, contracted a flow of blood that continued until he was near despair. Sent to the bishop, he received his blessing, and with the blessing immediately recovered.

Another brother, similarly intent beyond his strength on prayers and genuflections, suffered a rupture of the vital organs. He too was cured by the bishop’s blessing and returned joyfully to his own people.

How dangerous it is to lie to the Holy Spirit was sufficiently demonstrated by the first shepherd of the Church when he punished this sin with sudden death in Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5). Since this holy man had shown himself to be a true dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, the Lord rightly took vengeance on those who lied to him; to him the Prophet also says: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5).

A certain count belonging to King Henry’s party came to the bishop and promised fidelity and service under oath. The bishop happened to see a flock of crows and prayed to himself that, if the man did not keep the faith he had promised, as many demons would possess his soul as there were crows he had seen [Col. 0882D].

Not long afterward, repenting of his promise, the man returned to Henry, the enemy of the Church—himself now an enemy. The bishop branded him with an anathema, marked him with the disgrace of his faithlessness, and left him to divine vengeance.

It was not delayed. That vengeance struck the guilty man. Unexpectedly surrounded by enemies, he was wounded by many blows and almost severed at the thigh. Because he had limped away from his promise, from that day forward and thereafter he limped in one foot as a sign of his transgression.

Someone may wonder whether the curse that the wretched man had called down upon himself was fulfilled in him. I certainly would not deny it, since I know that in many people demons have remained mute for a long time, and that many are tormented inwardly by demons more grievously than if they were torn apart outwardly [Col. 0883A].

How steadfastly the energetic shepherd restrained the wolves of this age from plundering ecclesiastical property, although he received no assistance from relatives either by aid or counsel, is shown by the following example. Yet he was not alone, for God was always with him. Thus he truly said: “He who sent me is with me, and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John 8). And in the psalm: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes” (Ps. 117).

There was a certain very wealthy and noble man who usurped, as though by hereditary right, the benefice that his deceased brother had received from the bishop. The bishop opposed him according to the law of the province. But the man attempted by violence to take what he could not obtain by justice.

For a time the servant of God endured the madman, giving and wishing him an opportunity for repentance. When he persisted in wickedness, the bishop took vengeance with the dart of anathema. Since all religious people avoided his communion, and the leading men of the eastern province likewise avoided him, shame and the reproach of everyone compelled him to approach the bishop at the village of Saint Hippolytus. There he prostrated himself before the bishop’s feet in deep snow and, humbly pleading for a very long time, made satisfaction.

Yet he did not deserve reconciliation until he handed over the village called Ratoldesdorf to the jurisdiction of the episcopal see. Only then, after the prayers of many nobles had scarcely intervened, was he released from the bond of excommunication [Col. 0883C]. The bishop assigned the village he had received to the altar of Blessed Mary in the monastery of Kotwigc [Gotwic].

Meanwhile Margrave Luipold, assembled with his leading men at the village called Tulna, detesting the tyranny of King Henry and the schism of which Henry had made himself the author, rejected his rule under oath. He expelled all his supporters from the province, while with all his strength he encouraged and protected those who obeyed the apostolic see and its legate Altmann.

Therefore the king, inflamed with anger, handed Luipold’s margraviate over to the Duke of Bohemia. The duke did not delay, but gathered a very great army both from his own province and from neighbouring provinces and arrived at the borders of the margraviate. Luipold was no slower; with all his people he met the enemy at the place called Meurberch.

But, alas, having been surrounded through the inspiration of his adversaries, and being unable to form his troops into battle because the army had been thrown into confusion, he was overcome by the enemy after much blood had first been shed on both sides [Col. 0883D].

These are your judgments, Lord. Thus, Lord, you are silent while the impious tramples upon one more righteous than himself. Did the victorious cause please you? If it pleased you, it pleased you not for the salvation of the victors but for their condemnation. For thus you allow the destruction of the lost to be completed; thus you make them fall into your most severe judgment.

The cause of the defeated, however, undoubtedly pleased you, because they did not fear to provoke so grave an enemy for the sake of their better devotion toward your Church and the Roman pontiff. And because they thought that they were rendering you service if they restrained your enemies, they did not spare their own lives; devoted and stronger in faith than the victors, they fell in your camp [Col. 0884A].

After this slaughter came a very great famine, so that the Lord might test his faithful in works of mercy, having already sufficiently proved them in steadfast courage. Father Altmann kept nothing for himself in this necessity. He sold all the furnishings of the episcopal residence, down to the very linen cloth, and distributed them to the needy. For this reason he was also called the Father of the Poor. Especially on Mount Kotwikc [Gotwic] he preserved many thousands of poor people from the danger of famine.

How active he was in the cause of the Church, which in his time was thrown into such great turmoil, is shown by the letters sent to him so frequently by the lord pope. In them, among other matters, the pope seems both to advise and to indicate that, during so grave a disturbance of the holy Church, those matters which could to some extent be overlooked and tolerated should be allowed to rest—not abolished entirely, but moderated in their strictness. When, however, by God’s mercy, victory and peace had been restored to the Church, they should carefully consider and labour with all their strength for the restoration of justice, insofar as this might be possible with God’s help [Col. 0884B].

For this reason the chapter concerning the incontinence of priests remained unaddressed, not approved, by so invincible a defender of chastity.

Moreover, I would describe how greatly the Church of Passau advanced during his episcopate in the construction and correction of monasteries, in the building and adornment of churches, and in the uprightness of its ministers, if the condition—indeed, the ruin—of present circumstances did not in large part contradict me [Col. 0884C]. Yet I, a little worm, judge no one in this matter. For who am I to judge another’s servant? “He stands or falls before his own master” (Rom. 14).

The holy bishop himself, during the time of Reginar, who succeeded him as the third bishop after him, deigned to reveal to a certain religious brother that the disruption of this better state would soon be avenged upon that same prelate. The brother seemed to himself to be in Rome at a council, where Blessed Altmann sat among several bishops, wearing episcopal vestments of exceptional splendour.

Altmann rose, stood in the midst, and asked the lord pope for an advocate in his case. Having received one, he brought a complaint against Bishop Reginar, asserting that Reginar had found the bishopric of Passau excellently ordered in monasteries and parishes, but that through his negligence almost the whole of religious life in it had perished [Col. 0884D].

Reginar stood far behind, terrified. The apostolic judge asked the bishops for their decision in the matter and received from all no other than a sentence of condemnation. In that same year Reginar fell ill, and remained ill until his death.

Let us now explain what end of life—or rather, what beginning of life—the blessed man received. For, as it is written, “when a man has finished, then he begins” (Ecclesiasticus 18).

After spending twenty-six years in the episcopate, following many labours and battles against the beasts at Ephesus, when it already pleased the Lord to reward the sweat of his veteran soldier, he was seized by a fever at the village called Zarzimuor. As it grew stronger, he understood that the message of death had arrived.

Although he shuddered at it because of human frailty, he nevertheless rejoiced because of his good conscience, knowing that through this gate he would enter into the joy of his Lord. Since he had not said to himself, “Peace and security” (2 Thess. 5), destruction did not overtake him suddenly. He had always remembered his last things and had continually desired them, saying every day in his heart: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41) [Col. 0885A].

Therefore, feeling that the dissolution of his body was approaching—a body in which he had long been a pilgrim away from the Lord—he prayed joyfully, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141).

Because he knew and had often taught that, at the departure of even the most righteous, the adversarial spirits gather, he also fought against them, saying: “Save me from the mouth of the lion and from the horns of the wild oxen my humility” (Ps. 21). And as he anxiously fixed his attention upon the strict judgment of the heavenly Judge, worshipping and pleading with whatever groaning he could and with inward sighs, he said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, Lord, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142).

He summoned each of the saints whom he had loved and revered, and above all that blessed and glorious Mother of God, Mary, for whom he had established so worthy a dwelling, so that she might lead him into the tabernacle prepared for him by God; and also that most holy confessor and pontiff of God, Nicholas, whose church he too had founded with supreme devotion. He commended himself entirely to them and prepared them as companions and guides for his journey [Col. 0885C].

He likewise surrounded himself entirely with those ministering spirits whose power and authority keep hostile powers at bay, so that the enemy demons might rightly be compelled to say: “Behold, the strong ones, the strongest of Israel, surround this bishop’s bed; all hold swords and are most skilled in war” (Song 3). “Why do we stand here? These surpass us in power and number. Is he not the one who drove us from the bodies of others with such power? Especially since there are more with him than with us.”

Thus the holy prelate placed his hope at that time not in military camps, not in weapons, nor in the splendour of those serving him, but in the Lord his God, in a good conscience, and in sincere faith (1 Tim. 1). Hence he said: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72).

In our own age the noble and very wealthy man Otto of Lengenbach felt and confessed the same thing. When he was at the point of death, he was caught up—how, I do not know; God knows—and, returning to himself, he related many things that had been shown and understood. At the time, many who heard his account were astonished and moved to compunction.

At last, naming one by one the many castles that had belonged to him, he said: “What help can my castles now provide, my most powerful lords, my dearest friends?” Despairing of the help of them all, he commended himself to various religious people with great contrition. For then he truly understood how difficult it is for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19) [Col. 0886A]. Therefore, groaning, he cried out: “Alas for me, miserable man, who ever possessed more wealth than the simple food and clothing I needed!”

As the venerable prelate passed through the final stage of this mortal life, there was no need for anyone to remind him to provide for his departure. He had provided for himself throughout the whole time of his life, and because he had lived well, he was dying happily.

Otherwise, if he had first needed to be warned then, he would rightly have answered what the venerable Chuono, bishop of the Church of Regensburg and formerly abbot of Sigberg, is said to have answered when those standing around him at last advised him, as he was dying. He said:

“You advise me well, O sons, to look to my salvation at this dreaded hour. But were you offering this counsel of salvation when it pleased you that I should gladly accept gifts, sell spiritual things by simony, pervert judgments, and overlook the sins of my subjects? I would be providing for myself too late if I had made no provision until now.”

Thus the blessed servant of God had wisely provided for himself in due season, and therefore he departed all the more readily [Col. 0886B].

Accordingly, after being anointed with sacred oil by religious men and refreshed with the Lord’s sacraments, he blessed his sons and earnestly commended them to the heavenly Father. Then, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1091, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, he joyfully entered upon the way of all flesh. Everyone wept and mourned with pitiable lamentation, grieving that they had been deprived of so great a Father and left without so great a pontiff [Col. 0886C].

They did not, indeed, envy his glory; they grieved over their own great misery. They rejoiced that he was received by the angels and led into the blessed dwellings of the elect. For themselves they groaned that they were miserably left in this valley of tears without a comforter and tossed about in this great sea without a helmsman.

Where, in those days, were men who would bear a father’s affection toward their sons and fulfil a father’s duty? Like ostriches, they harden themselves toward their children, as though the children were not their own; and, following the custom of hired servants, they stand by the prosperous for the sake of temporal profit, while in adversity they are the first to flee.

This was far from the character of this holy Father, in whom both a father’s love and a shepherd’s care abounded, together with vigilance in prosperity and steadfastness in adversity.

Meanwhile an innumerable crowd came from every direction to the bishop’s funeral. The whole province mourned: people of high rank, every age, and both sexes. At last the venerable body was lifted by Christ’s priests, and, accompanied by a great crowd of nobles and an infinite multitude of people, was brought to Mount Kotwitgc [Gotwicensem] with great glory to God but with heavy sorrow for those carrying it [Col. 0886D].

Who could now recount the groaning and wailing of the brethren who lived there, which caused the whole mountain to resound? Everyone mourned the dearest, most compassionate, and holiest Father. Every day a great multitude of rich and poor came, commending him humbly to God and themselves to him.

Among them came Tiemo, archbishop of Salzburg, of reverend memory, who had been consecrated by Bishop Altmann as his suffragan. Later, while travelling to Jerusalem, he was crowned by the pagans with a glorious martyrdom. He hastened to meet the funeral procession, bathed the deceased in abundant tears, offered the saving sacrifice for him, and committed the venerable body with due honour to burial in the church of the Holy Mother of God [Col. 0887A].

There, to prove the merits of so great a man, signs of various kinds of power frequently occur, to the praise of God the almighty Father, who with his only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through immortal ages of ages. Amen.

A certain cleric, seized by a savage demon, was scarcely brought to his tomb by many people who bound and dragged him. He filled everything with a horrible cry and dreadful stench. When the brethren prayed more earnestly for him, he suddenly collapsed and, while everyone watched, vomited out an extremely black beetle, which immediately disappeared and could nowhere be found [Col. 0887B]. Everyone praised God. The man who had arrived bound and insane departed healthy and freed from the bonds of mind and body.

Likewise, a girl possessed by an unclean spirit was brought by her parents to the tomb of the man of God and was immediately freed and healed.

Another girl, who had been deprived of her sight for many years, recovered the light she had lost through the merits of the same servant of God.

A woman whose little son had been mute and lame from birth placed him pitifully at the bishop’s tomb. She herself, pitiable, left the church with great weeping. Shortly afterward, when the boy had recovered speech and the ability to walk, he followed his mother, walking and speaking properly [Col. 0887C].

A certain soldier, who had been mentally deranged for six years, approached his tomb without his reason and departed healthy, having recovered his mind.

Another man, entirely contracted and supporting himself on small stools, came crawling to the body of the holy bishop. But he became whole, sprang up, walked, and praised the Lord.

Likewise, a certain man weak throughout his body, scarcely supported by a staff, approached the prelate’s tomb. But after his infirmity had been driven away through the blessed man, he no longer needed the staff, because he felt himself joyful and well.

Once, when a sudden and violent storm was crushing the mountains and tearing down the roofs of houses, churches, and towers, a brother who was mentally deranged climbed into the oratory of Saint Michael, which is situated very high, while everyone was unaware of it and was singing the nocturnal praises in the meantime [Col. 0887D].

He fell from the height onto the pavement, but was lifted up alive, although he was not destined to live much longer. On that very day, after being anointed with sacred oil and receiving communion of the life-giving body of Christ, he was released from the flesh.

No one should doubt that this must be attributed to the merits of the blessed man, whose intercession caught the falling man, so that his blood would not sprinkle the basilica which he himself, devoted to God and to the blessed ever-Virgin Mary, had consecrated as a royal hall.

By these and many other signs of miracles, which we do not believe have all come to our knowledge, the Lord magnified his priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous (Ecclesiasticus 44) [Col. 0888A].

Yet even if he had performed no sign at all, nothing would thereby have been taken away from his holiness, either before God or before human beings. Signs do not create holiness; they display it. For the Gospel testifies concerning John the Baptist—among those born of women no one greater arose (Matt. 11)—that he performed no sign.

It is also written concerning the Lord and Saviour himself that he did not perform many signs because of the unbelief of certain people (Mark 6). What wonder, then, if this holy man, hindered by the unbelief of the present times, had performed no works of power and no healings?

But divine grace, which promises that it will glorify those who glorify it, made this beloved servant, so that he might nevertheless become beloved among human beings and so that his memory might remain in blessing, like the saints in glory through the greatness of his signs (Ecclesiasticus 44) [Col. 0888B].

Yet, when I contemplate this man—or anyone else who performs such wonders—with greater attention, the man who performs them seems to me far more wonderful than the things he performs.

For if, in the case of insensible things, the causal principle that produces an effect has more to astonish the person who considers inwardly than the effect itself, then that holiness is much more worthy and religiously deserving of admiration which so pleases and is accepted in the sight of the divine Majesty that, through its regard and intervention, human afflictions are driven away and the desired health of souls and bodies is restored.

I say that the holiness within is far more to be admired than any wonders it performs outwardly. Let others marvel at seeing the blind, at the lame walking; let them marvel at the healing of paralytics and the flight of demons. I will rather marvel at the merits of so great a bishop, which perform such things with as much power as the things themselves [Col. 0888C].

You, then, proclaim to the praise of God what the holy man of God performs in others through his merits and the faith of those who plead. I will always marvel at the wonders he performed in his life: his humility, chastity, piety, charity, devotion, diligence in carrying out affairs, prudence in arranging them, discernment in imposing duties, patience in enduring them, and courage in adversity.

These are the wonders of his life that I judge worthy of wonder—especially because in our times we see these virtues rarer than those signs which, nevertheless, the Lord promises will follow all who believe, saying: “These signs will follow those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons” (Matt. 28), and so forth.

Do you perhaps still not agree that the life of a holy man is to be admired more than his miracles? Miracles are sometimes performed, by God’s hidden permission, even by men who are not holy. For you know that certain rejected and reprobate persons will say to the Lord: “Did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and perform many miracles?” (Matt. VII). But let that be; I leave you to your own judgment. For my part, however, I shall always regard it as more marvelous to have driven avarice, pride, and lust from one’s heart than blindness from another’s eyes, sickness from his limbs, or a demon from his body. Yet because we do not always know—since we see what is on the surface and not what is in the heart—what the inner condition of the saints is, what virtue and freedom they possess, [Col. 0889A] the Lord in his great mercy acts so that, through outward miracles, it may be recognized how worthy of admiration inwardly are those through whom he himself performs such wonders outwardly.

Let us therefore consider, dearest brothers, with what veneration this servant of God should be embraced, whose merits the Lord deigned to prove and commend through so many miracles. Let this be an invincible argument against our lack of faith, if indeed there is any—though may it be far from us that there should be any—that the man who is ready and powerful to cure the diseases and infirmities of our souls is no less ready to relieve, and so often and so piously relieves, the infirmities of our bodies. For there should be no doubt that he wishes to benefit souls more than bodies, since the salvation of the former is eternal, whereas that of the latter, together with the bodies themselves, will shortly pass away [Col. 0889B].

Up to this point we have related the deeds of Saint Altmann from the writings of devout men. Who would think that they transmitted anything uncertain to posterity, or—what would be sacrilegious—anything false, when they knew perfectly well that God has no need of anyone’s lie? Moreover, the miracles that occur daily before the eyes of those now living bear witness to the earlier ones, confirm them, and add to them. Before proceeding to describe these, we may perhaps usefully explain for what reason and in what manner the monastery of Kotwigc (Gotwic), which we stated above had been founded by him and made illustrious by his sacred bones, was changed from its original institution as a community of regular canons into the monastic profession, as it may be seen at the present time [Col. 0889C].

During the time of the venerable bishop, a certain priest came to Mount Kotwich: a Scotsman by nationality, a monk by profession, and religious in his way of life. The name he bore suited him, for he was called John, which means “the grace of God.” Bishop Altmann loved this grace in him; and, so that he might live with him more freely, he confined him, at his own request and desire, in a small dwelling beside the church of blessed Mary. People saw his good works and glorified their Father who is in heaven (Matt. V). They also gladly listened to his words, because they themselves breathed grace and edification.

After the death of blessed Altmann, during whose days the lambs of that monastery grazed in their proper order, certain men who, under the appearance of lambs, carried wolves’ hearts (Matt. VII), driven from various places and living as fugitives, gathered there. Before long they appeared as genuine wolves, turned savage, and, with wolfish teeth, pouring the poisons of their wickedness into the simplicity of others, they did not hesitate to corrupt and infect the innocence and good reputation that had flourished there in the greatest holiness and had spread its good fragrance far and wide. Thus it came about that the place itself became an object of contempt, horror, and detestation [Col. 0889D].

Blessed Altmann, whose eyes we believe to watch over that place day and night, appeared in a vision to the aforesaid John and admonished him to cleanse the mountain itself of filth and wipe away the stench of the dung [Col. 0890A]. The man of God understood the vision and, reporting it to the superior of the brothers, advised that all the disgraceful persons should be expelled and those whom they had led astray cleansed by penance. Yet, since this did little to suppress the disgrace, whose stench had spread farther, they were overcome by prolonged weariness and all resolved to leave the place.

Therefore the aforementioned John, again inspired by divine counsel, advised that they should change both their profession and their habit together. He asserted and promised that, if they changed and increased their vow, they would then entirely strip off the reproach of their former disgrace. The advice was approved; it was also approved that the religious rule of monks should be chosen. Accordingly, it seemed advisable that the matter itself be referred to the lord pope. He too approved “the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

Thus Chuonrad, the superior who had succeeded Outto and had shown himself a pious supporter and promoter of this change, promptly announced the consent of the Roman pontiff to Oudalric, bishop of Patavium, who had succeeded blessed Altmann, and requested his counsel and discretion in so important a matter [Col. 0890B]. Accordingly, with Bishop Oudalric giving counsel and support, Hartmann—who held the office of prior in the monastery of Saint Blaise—was elected abbot. And deservedly so. He was a religious man, thoroughly instructed in sacred letters, agreeable in speech, and suitably disposed to shape or encourage people of every kind. As he himself later related to the brothers, Saint Altmann appeared to him in a dream while he was still established in the aforementioned monastery of Saint Blaise [Col. 0890C]; he handed him a pastoral staff and entrusted the monastery of Kotwigc to his governance.

After the religious man had been elected abbot, he set out, all weeping, even though they had previously rejoiced in his companionship. When he reached the sheep entrusted to him by God, he was received favorably and, by the unanimous wishes of all, confirmed by the bishop of Patavium with the appropriate blessing. From then on, the inhabitants of that place changed their former habit without delay or resistance; they changed their minds and their zeal as well. The earth rejoiced at this, but heaven even more—where joy is celebrated over one sinner who repents (Luke XV); how much greater, then, over the salvation and correction of so many?

From that time many nobles from the world began to turn to God, submit themselves to the discipline of so great a man, and contribute all their possessions for the use of the monastery [Col. 0890D]. Through him the fame and reverence of the place grew thereafter; buildings arose, the supply of books increased, and so did all the adornment of the divine mysteries.

Yet none of this would have mattered if the walls had prospered while morals remained in ruins. The discerning man devoted himself rather to instructing the latter, knowing that God does not dwell in things made with hands (Acts XVII), but in the rational temples of holy souls, which are raised by devout vows, advance through religion, and are completed by perseverance.

And because glory, as a certain wise man says, follows even one who does not seek it, this great man began to be esteemed by those whose name was great, in keeping with the name of the great men who are on earth [Col. 0891A]. For this reason, offices of dignity and the governance of many monasteries were offered to him everywhere. It came about that King Henry V appointed him over the abbey of Campidona; the bishop of the city of Augsburg likewise placed him over the monastery of Saint Oudalric; and the duke of Carinthia entrusted to him the governance of the monastery of Saint Lambert.

During his days, since he was welcome and well regarded at the Roman court, privileges were obtained by which the place itself was protected and strengthened. After he had been removed from this light, prudent men and lovers of religion succeeded him; through their diligence and vigilance the monastery advanced so far that it is plainly evident to all who live that the Lord truly is in that place, and that it is nothing other than “the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. XXVIII). Blessed in all things is he who does everything he wills in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses (Ps. CXXXIV). To him be honor, praise, glory, and thanksgiving forever and ever. Amen [Col. 0891B].

With these matters thus concluded, I think we should return to the miracles that deserve to be entrusted to human memory, by which, even to the present day, the Lord bears witness before our eyes to the merits of his servant and raises up and invites the prelates of our own time to imitate his way of life. For if the deceptive glory of this world delights them, they ought to seek that glory far more which the Lord of glory would share with their desire—not a glory that ends with the shadow of this mortal life, but one that remains both here and in the kingdom of future blessedness, with blessed and unshaken permanence forever [Col. 0891C].

At a certain time, on the feast of the dedication of the church, a girl seized by a most savage demon stood beside the tomb of Saint Altmann in the presence of the brothers who were singing divine praises, and was miserably tormented. Suddenly she cried out in horrifying voices, asking for help. But who among men would dare approach such a horror? Nevertheless, the blessed bishop was invisibly present and, in the presence of all, saved the wretched girl from both the torment and the demon. When she came to herself, she asked that the sacred communion of the Lord’s body be given to her, by which she did not doubt that she would thereafter be protected from the evil spirit.

One of the monastery’s servants had been deprived of the light of his eyes for a long time. After visiting holy places where he hoped, through the merits of the saints, to receive the grace of healing, and finding none, he returned to the monastery and remained sadly in his darkness as before. At some point it occurred to him that he should earnestly implore his chief patron, through unremitting prayer, to restore his sight. One day, as he prayed more frequently and devoutly, when he had reached the doors of the basilica and was about to go out, with a boy guiding his steps, he suddenly said to the boy: “Leave me, so that I may walk by myself; for I see.” From that hour he went out to his work, seeing and rejoicing and praising God [Col. 0891D].

A certain boy’s foot had swollen enormously, so that it could scarcely be discerned whether that limb was a foot at all. He was brought to the tomb of the blessed man, and after his parents had faithfully prayed for him [Col. 0892A], he was carried home and immediately restored to health when the harmful fluid broke out.

There was a certain member of the community of brothers in that same monastery who had long been weighed down by a very serious illness and was deeply saddened by the hopelessness of recovering his health. It was revealed to one of the sisters of that place that he would be restored to his former health if offerings were made for him at the memorial of blessed Altmann and a Mass for the faithful departed were celebrated there in the sick man’s presence.

He was brought in a litter carried by four men, while two others supported him as he staggered from side to side. During the sacred mysteries his strength gradually increased, and he declared that he no longer needed another’s support. When the Mass was completed, he returned to the house of the sick [Col. 0892B], already using his own feet, with only one brother assisting him. After recovering full health a few days later, he rose energetically to his duties, going out and returning at the command of his abbot.

A certain girl from a neighboring village called Murlingen, the daughter of an honorable and well-known soldier named Wolckerus, was suddenly struck with paralysis in half of her body. Her name was Pertha. The skill of physicians attended her, but was of no benefit. The physician himself advised that divine help should rather be sought through the merits of Saint Altmann. She was brought to the tomb of the man of God. She prayed, and her parents prayed as well. The prayer of the faithful petitioners was heard, and the restoration of health became the sign that their prayer had been heard [Col. 0892C]. Yet, to arouse greater Sabbath devotion and make the manifestation of divine grace more evident, some infirmity remained in the girl’s hand. On the anniversary of the bishop’s burial, however, she returned to the compassionate and proven physician and, while praying, received the remedy she desired.

A woman from a village called Hunteheim, brought almost to death by a prolonged and serious illness and deprived of all strength, was carried to the tomb of the servant of God with great labor by those bearing her, and was restored to her former health.

Likewise, a little girl from a village called Panse, who had long been deprived of sight, received her sight there.

Another boy from a village called Marquartesdorff, weak and lame in both feet, was brought there that evening. Many people saw what affliction he suffered. After he had kept vigil through the night with the man who had brought him, he was cured at first light, when his sound condition was restored [Col. 0892D].

From the same village a certain woman who had been blind recovered her sight.

A certain noble and devout matron came from her castle, called Hosstein, bringing with her a blind girl. When they prayed more fervently at the tomb of the holy man, the girl recovered the sight of which she had long been deprived and rejoiced. In celebration and testimony of this miracle, the matron took the aforementioned girl as her own daughter [Col. 0893A] and kept her constantly with her. The girl’s name was Truta.

At the same time, another woman from a village called Beheimkirchen, who had been blind, received her sight through the intervention of Saint Altmann and rejoiced.

Another woman from a village called Indernich, named Heilka, who—as she confirmed under oath—had not seen light for nine weeks, was restored to sight at the tomb of the holy man of God.

A certain man named Henry, himself a citizen of the market village called Heinvelde, a mature man who had the testimony of all in support of his truthfulness, suffered intolerable pain after his eye had been struck by a small branch and was entirely deprived of sight in it. When he faithfully and humbly prayed at the sacred bones of this bishop [Col. 0893B], the pain was driven away and he recovered both health and sight.

A poor woman from the region of Bavaria had come with her recently born child and, because of necessity, entered the service of a certain matron in the city of Krems. After remaining in her service for some time, she was afflicted by pain in her eyes and suffered loss of sight. Alas, how many troubles beset the wretched woman! With what pain, do you suppose, was she now tormented, when blindness oppressed her and the heavy burden of poverty weighed upon her? She could be of no use either to herself or to her recently born child, for whom she was even more anxious.

When the loss of her sight forced her to cease serving the aforementioned matron, the matron also stopped providing her with food. One night, dissolved in tears over so great a deprivation [Col. 0893C], she implored from the depths of her heart the grace of divine light through the merits of the blessed bishop. He who hears the desire of the poor also heard her prayers and saw her tears. For when she rose in the morning to perform all the duties of her limbs, she was fully able to do so, her sight guiding her.

But I omit describing individually all the occurrences involving those who deserved to receive the benefit of sight at the memorial of the holy bishop, lest I weary the reader. For apart from those who suffered other misfortunes, scarcely any person afflicted in the eyes failed to obtain a remedy.

There was a certain woman who had a demon of such importunity and fury that scarcely anyone could live with her [Col. 0894A]. Wherever she was, there were shouting and rage, for all her limbs were shaken by the spirit of fury. At times the same demon—because it is interpreted as knowing—used the possessed person’s organs as an instrument for uttering learned speech, as though the woman herself had acquired knowledge of letters and the manner of polished pronunciation through formal studies. Indeed, what seemed marvelous to some, she recited the Creed in its entirety, just as the Catholic faith has it. Yet this is not surprising, since the authority of [Scripture] says that demons have faith, but not works.

When this woman had been brought to the memorial of the blessed man in a solemn procession of the people of the parish called Tuln, she was freed, as the merits of the holy bishop drove away the most evil invader. When the crowds saw the manifest signs of her deliverance [Col. 0894B], they glorified God and the praises of his beloved Altmann all the more, because they had previously brought her to various shrines of the saints without obtaining any manifestation of power.

But because variety is pleasing, accept another miracle solemnly celebrated by the testimony of the Church standing by, so that you may recognize more fully how great is the preeminence of this holy bishop’s merits.

A certain weak man suffered such a bodily affliction that, with his vital blood diminished by the contraction of his veins, he could not walk upright on his feet; instead, he dragged himself along by crawling on his hands in place of his feet. Living far away in a village called Lo, he learned of the wondrous works of this grace and, in the hope of being healed, chose the saving tomb of the blessed man as something to be sought, as though by a divine oracle. When he had persisted there in vows and prayers over his bodily defect and suffering, as it were with his innermost strength, behold—wondrous to say—the nerves that had long been contracted began to stretch out with a cracking sound, and the dried channels of his veins were filled with vital blood [Col. 0894C]. Thus, receiving strength, the contracted man stood upon his feet and blessed his healer in a loud voice.

Glory to you, Christ, who to this day work through the merits of your saints and thus raise up the crushed, making known to mortals the glory of those who have pleased you.

**End of the Life of Saint Altmann, Bishop of Patavium.**

[Col. 0893]

# THE LIFE OF BLESSED TIEMO, ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG

Who suffered greatly at the hands of schismatics under the Roman pontiffs Gregory VII and Urban II, and was finally crowned with martyrdom. Now brought into public view from ancient manuscripts.

## To the Reader

The life of Tiemo was published by D. Henricus Canisius in the fourth volume of *Ancient Readings*. But because we found it written somewhat differently in another manuscript, and indeed in a very ancient codex, we thought it worthwhile to insert it into this volume. For Gebhard, Altmann, and Tiemo were most closely connected, inseparable companions both in prosperity [Col. 0895] and adversity, and unconquered defenders of the Roman pontiffs against the factions of the schismatics. Let the written page therefore join those whom charity and holy concord once bound together most closely.

Concerning Tiemo, Berthold writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 1091: “Dimo, bishop of Salzburg, came into Bavaria and ordained as bishop of the Church of Patavium, which had long been widowed, a man named Udalric,” and so forth.

D. Henricus Canisius, in the prefaces to the *Life and Martyrdom of Tiemo* in volume I of *Ancient Readings*, untangled certain knots that arise in this history, especially the matter concerning idols and idolaters.

## The Passion of Saint Tiemo the Bishop Begins

[Col. 0895A] We commit to the memory of writing the distinguished triumph of the excellent bishop and renowned martyr Tiemo, with his merits lending assistance, so that every generation of Catholics may learn of a previously unknown manner of suffering, and may know that, if the singular victory of this outstanding champion is worthily recalled, it can provide richer grace with God.

Truly, the Lord’s mercy kindled in him a great and conspicuous light in the latter days, amid the dangerous darkness of the times (II Tim. III), from which true light may shine more brightly, as though from a living and transparent image of itself. Therefore, lest so brilliant a lamp be hidden beneath the bushel of oblivion (Luke XI), let a candlestick of eloquence be fashioned for it, even if poor and bronze, so that it may be set forth publicly for viewing in the house of the Lord.

Let the Church’s beautiful face be seen in his light, although she is black (Song I); let him be seen walking among the seven golden lampstands, clothed in a long robe and girded around the chest with a golden belt (Rev. I). And let Christ, as he promised, be perceived as remaining with his people and their rulers until the end of the age—white with innocence and radiant with wisdom [Col. 0895B].

Our blessed Redeemer has fulfilled, and does not cease eternally to fulfill, for this man the declaration of that joyful promise: “Whoever conquers, I will make him a pillar in my temple” (Rev. III). For he conquered the suggestions of the ancient serpent in himself; therefore he became a strong pillar in the building of God’s endangered house. He conquered terrors and the assaults of persecutors, and thus established before all an example and spectacle of greatness of spirit [Col. 0895C] and a glory of perseverance.

Like a silver column, he supported the litter of the true peacemaker with the sonorous confession of truth; by his immovable strength he became a golden resting place on which the Church confidently leaned. Thereafter he provided her with a purple ascent, spreading before her a path to heaven reddened with his own blood.

He gained eternal remembrance through a composition made with the finest fragrance, the work of the heavenly perfumer (Eccles. XLIX). For he directed his heart toward God, and in the days of sinners strengthened his devotion.

This man, therefore, most worthy by God’s choice, was born of high-ranking Bavarian stock. From his earliest age he lived in the monastery called Altaha, loving the delight of the monastic life, and there advancing daily—*diatim* or *dietim*—he climbed from virtue to virtue.

In the diocese of Juvavum, the abbot of a certain monastery had become so weak that he was wholly incapable, in the words of the Apostle, of reproving, entreating, and rebuking with patience and instruction (II Tim. IV) [Col. 0895D–0896A]. When he heard that the venerable man Gebhard, of holy memory, had been ordained bishop there, he disclosed the extent of his weakness and began to beg insistently, and ever more insistently, to be relieved of such a burden. He obtained his request.

After he had been canonically and mercifully released, the venerable Tiemo, an alumnus of the aforementioned monastery, was elected in his place. He was stern in character, austere in life, yet instructed in every aspect of monastic discipline. He immediately corrected offenders with fitting severity and full authority; while the gentle and obedient he piously admonished through entreaty, so that they might advance toward better things. He did not cease cultivating the Lord’s vineyard there with the richest fertility of evangelical sowing [Col. 0896B].

At that time, therefore, the ship of the Church began for a while to be battered on every side amid the waves of persecution. Gebhard, the most faithful and powerful physician and guardian of the Lord’s flock, was expelled by the supporters of Henry, who had already been excommunicated by the apostolic see more than once [Note: [Col. 0895] Bertholdus. See Hundius’s *Metropolis*, in the catalogue of the bishops of Salzburg, title 3.]. Another, truly a disciple of Simon, was introduced by the aforesaid king, ordained, consecrated—or rather execrated—and enthroned as quickly as possible.

Then the venerable abbot Tiemo, fleeing the new invader and heretic and truly wishing to follow the apostolic command, “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and condemned by his own judgment,” went to the spiritual training grounds of the monks of Schaffhausen [Col. 0896C] and Hirsau. At that time both places abounded in perfect monks, like a fragrant meadow filled everywhere with beds of spices. All who came there, loving the contemplative life and desiring to bear the Lord’s yoke, which is sweet, and his burden, which is light (Luke XI), found in both places an impregnable refuge.

Then, instructed by evangelical teachings, he left everything behind. Choosing the better part in the cloister at Hirsau, he sat with Mary at the Lord’s feet, listening to his word (Luke X), and at some future time hoping to reach Rachel’s embraces (Gen. XXIX). With those who were of one heart and one soul (Acts III), who possessed nothing yet owned everything, he spent several years in the common life. Thus, having finally grown in spiritual discipline, he returned honorably to his homeland.

The invader of the Church of Juvavum received him most kindly [Col. 0896D–0897A], hoping that he would accept his abbey and assist him in every respect in his error. But the man of God, mindful of the counsel of the Apostle Peter—“It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (II Pet. II)—and knowing that one should not even eat with such people, refused to yoke himself with heretics. He preferred to be rejected in the house of the Lord rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. LXXXIII), and withdrew into a neighboring wilderness, to the servants of God, the poor of Christ.

There he was received by the brothers dwelling there with every charity. Together with the Apostle John they began individually to say these words: “We ought to receive such men” (III John), so that we might be fellow workers of our Lord Jesus Christ. He himself very often began to sing psalms to Christ in the voice of the Psalmist: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV) [Col. 0897B].

Not long afterward the venerable physician Gebhard, most worthy father of Christ’s sheep, brought his life to an end and, with his talent well doubled, entered honorably into the joy of his Lord (Matt. XXV), on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, as we believe. Alas, he left his sheep not to a shepherd but to a hireling placed over them, to be torn apart.

When the Catholics saw this, they grieved greatly over the death of their devout teacher and master. After taking counsel, they strove to associate with the bride of Christ a worthy teacher and worthy shepherd, lest the wolf be able to scatter or disturb the Lord’s flock any longer with such power and sorrow.

The good and just came together not in doubt but in unity; others, however, came together not in unity but in doubt. Those who were spiritual and pursued spiritual things elected a spiritual man, namely Lord Tiemo [Col. 0897C]. At that time the oracle that God used in ancient days to speak to one of his friends could rightly be applied to him: “I know you by name” (Exod. XXXIII).

The secular men, occupied with the things of this world, praised someone who was not spiritual but very distinguished and powerful by birth and worldly rank. To him the Psalmist’s saying about the reprobate could rightly be fitted: “You cast them down when they were exalted” (Ps. LXXII). To the agreement of these men, as though it represented the greater power, everyone gave assent—not in heart, but in voice.

But God, the disposer of all things, showed to all who looked that such an election was not pleasing in his sight [Col. 0897D]. When Altmann, bishop of Patavium and legate of the apostolic see, together with the clergy, Duke Welf, the counts, and a large crowd of both sexes, had gathered at the place of assembly, the man who had been elected by the judgment not of the Lord or of spiritual persons but of a few men distinguished by secular rank wished to cross the river by boat. The expectation of both parties was suspended.

What more need be said? God, knower of hidden things and guardian of the future, who wished those offering strange fire to perish by a death not miraculous but pitiable (Num. III), cut down this fruitless tree (Jude, XII), this branch that bore no fruit (John XV). Before the eyes of all and to the astonishment of all, he submerged him in midstream with Pharaoh [Col. 0898A]. Thus, by God’s judgment, their election came to an end.

When everyone saw this, they were stirred to praise the true shepherd of Christ, saying with the Psalmist: “God is a just judge” (Ps. VII), and with the Apostle: “How inscrutable are his judgments!” (Rom. XI).
