The one whom God had chosen, as became clear to all, was immediately raised to the episcopal chair and received by the Catholics with the greatest honor. He was praised and honored by everyone.

Later, at the appropriate time, the priest of God—chosen according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX), anointed with the oil that descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps. CXXXII), and with the oil of gladness (Ps. XLIV)—was consecrated and enthroned in the archiepiscopal see amid hymns and songs [Col. 0898B].

From that time onward, as a true soldier of Christ, chosen from among the sixty mighty men of Israel who surround the bed of the true Solomon (Song III), he held the chosen sword of the Holy Spirit. Armed day and night, in peace and in war, wearing the breastplate of justice, the helmet of faith, and the armor of salvation, he extinguished the fiery darts of the wicked one in his body (Eph. VI). Daily he strove to rescue the flock entrusted to him from the jaws of the enemy.

But the ancient enemy, who through himself had expelled the human race from the delights of paradise in our first parent, tried through his members to drive this fellow minister of God from the episcopal seat, indeed from those territories altogether.

The man of God, instructed by the evangelical saying, “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X), attempted to withdraw from there. He came to Alamannia and stayed there for some time with the venerable Gebhard, bishop of Constance [Col. 0898C], and humbly and charitably visited the venerable places in the surrounding region.

At that time many attempted to go to Jerusalem and, with God’s aid, rescue the holy places from the rule of the gentiles. Just as formerly the Israelite people entered the promised land by the royal road in a warlike manner (Num. XXI), so these men, strengthened by that example, chose war for the sake of peace. Many, stained red in the blood of the Lamb, lost their lives for Christ so that they might preserve them in eternal life, and fell in battle against the heathen. At last a few who had been delivered reached the places they desired.

The venerable man of whom we are speaking, the archbishop of Juvavum, wishing to follow evangelical perfection and wanting to say with Peter, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. XVI), had long since been expelled and now undertook the pilgrimage to Jerusalem with Duke Welf.

But all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution (II Tim. III). The man of God endured various persecutions courageously and patiently, and on that day joyfully sang with the voice of the Psalmist: “The pains of death surrounded me; the dangers of hell found me. I found trouble and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXIV). And he also uttered the apostolic words: “If God is for us, who is against us? Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger?” and so forth, up to “who loved us” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0899A].

In the city of Corozain, cursed by the Lord and the seat of Satan, which is the most famous of the gentile cities in those regions, three extremely powerful brothers lived. Gathering an innumerable multitude against the Christian pilgrims, they crushed some by killing them and others by wounding them. Just as the Israelite people were once led captive into Babylon, so this Christian people was for the most part led into captivity by those kings.

In Babylonian captivity, the Israelite people sat by the rivers of Babylon, remembering Zion, and wept, saying: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI). But this Christian people sang in heart and mouth a song worthy of the Lord, in these words: “Praise befits you, God, in Zion, and to you shall the vow be fulfilled in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXIV) [Col. 0899B]. And elsewhere: “You have given us like sheep for food, and among the nations you have scattered us, for on your account we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII; Rom. VIII).

Thus, chosen from so great a multitude—he whom God knew by name, namely the venerable hero to whom our pen renders service—he was captured and dragged away, and at last became, through martyrdom, a worthy sacrifice reserved especially for God.

When they were dividing among themselves the spoils of goods and men, the most powerful of the three kings took the venerable archbishop as his portion. Like a sacrificial victim destined for sale, he handed him over with the others as a purchased slave, hoping to increase his treasury with the price.

Since all the condemned Christians revered him particularly, above the others, as a father and with devoted affection, the pagans carefully inquired who he was and where he came from. When they learned that he had been a bishop, they did not delay reporting it to their king.

The king quickly had the blessed man brought before him. When asked who he was and what skill he possessed, the man of God reflected on the poetic saying:

“You have character, conduct, speech, and faith:

If you act rightly, let this be a bronze wall.” (Horace, *Epistles* I.)

With this reply he said: “I know various arts, but above all, like a wise architect, I know how to lay a firm foundation. Upon it, if anyone builds gold, silver, or precious stones (I Cor. III), neither storm nor wind nor any human being will be able to destroy it, because I lay it upon the firm rock, which is Christ” [Col. 0899D].

“I am not asking you,” said the king, “about the construction of such a foundation; rather, I ask you about the goldsmith’s art or some other skill necessary for our benefit.”

To this the venerable bishop replied: “If you wish to know whether I am an artisan, I know very well how to renew ancient things.”

But the angry king, not understanding the words of God’s bridegroom-attendant, employed these words of Horace:

“Everything superfluous pours forth from a full breast.” (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*)

The holy bishop said: “Indeed, as I said, I know how to renew what is ancient, because, with Christ my Lord as its author, I know how to transfer the old law into the new; and, moreover, I fully understand the material arts you seek—namely, goldworking and painting.”

Then the king, delighted and full of joy, said: “I give thanks to my god, because he has delivered into our hands a servant trained in such crafts. Do not delay any longer, good craftsman. Restore with your hands my god, who has been mutilated; or, if you can, put his limbs back in their proper places, so that he may be gracious to all of us throughout the days of our lives. Bring him to me,” he said.

And behold, the devil’s monster was brought forth, mutilated in the hands, as has been said; the entire pagan people venerated it as the greatest god. A great hammer was brought, as he had ordered. Holding it in his hand, the bishop attacked the shrine in which the devil lay hidden—that is, the grievous hammer of the whole earth. “I adjure you,” he said, “devil, poisonous serpent and ancient deceiver of souls, who lie hidden in this shrine to deceive human souls; I adjure you by the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to give me an answer to whatever I ask.”

The demon immediately answered the questioner. After they had conversed together for a long time, the wicked demon uttered some blasphemy against Christ. Against this blasphemy the bishop was powerfully consumed by zeal for the house of the Lord (Ps. 68; John 2); and at once he threw that shrine down with his feet and, with the hammer he held in his hand, smashed and reduced it piece by piece, like a clay vessel—for he was mighty in strength—in the presence of all who stood by and watched, as though in an instant. The pagans rushed together and attempted to kill the man of God as a sacrilegious criminal, wishing to avenge their god with his blood.

Then the king arrived in a fury, full of anger and bitterness, in accordance with the poetic line:

“Words full of threats befit an angry countenance.” (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*)

“I do not wish,” he said, “I do not wish him to end in such a slight and easy death. Instead, flog him, bind him in chains, and guard him most carefully for the time being.”

But the athlete of God, led away to prison, sang that Davidic verse, saying:

“Deliver me from my enemies, my God, and free me from those who rise up against me. Save me from men of blood, for behold, they have seized my life; the mighty have rushed upon me” (Ps. 58).

When the king saw that his god had now been completely destroyed, he sent to another nearby idol, seeking counsel from it about what he should do. But, as Scripture says: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21).

By what means, and through what sort of martyrdom, the supreme Judge wished to unite his chosen one with the citizens of heaven, even the evil spirit could not conceal in silence. Rather, as we believe, by divine command the evil angel had to provide its answers, inciting wicked men to bring this matter to the outcome pleasing to God.

For the demon from that shrine gave its answer to the king’s servants with great trembling: “Alas for me! What shall I do? I have lost my companion, and, terrified with fear, I have scarcely recovered the strength to speak. Go quickly, report my words to your lord, and without delay let him strive to carry out my counsel. Lead the destroyer of your god into a great field; make him a spectacle for Christians, for natives, and for foreigners; and there, before all who look on, kill him with various and most dreadful punishments, if he refuses to worship your greatest gods. For this spectacle bring all the Christians—whether captives or inhabitants—so that they may openly learn to honor the immortal gods and to obey their masters in everything.”

The king, then, made joyful by the demon’s counsel—or rather, its command—carried out everything in order, as the account that follows demonstrates.

The venerable bishop was brought into the middle of the field, bound with iron. In these words he addressed his God:

“O Christ, God from God, Light from Light, King of kings and Lord of lords, who suffered and was crucified for the salvation of the whole world: I praise you, I adore you, and I glorify you. You who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Pet. 2), strengthen me by your protection, so that I may praise you with a free voice, following in your footsteps and offering my sins to you.”

When Christ’s champion reached the place of combat, the most impious and God-detested king ordered all the Christian captives, bound, to attend the spectacle. He made them stand around the man of God in a circle, so that they might more fully watch him being cruelly tortured and might learn by sight and hearing to honor the gods, obey and serve their masters; otherwise, they would know that they too would be brought to an end by a similar punishment.

A tribunal was prepared for the king in the midst of the entire multitude that had gathered for the spectacle from that city and from the neighboring fortresses. Sitting in judgment, he ordered God’s servant to be brought before him. When he saw the true soldier of Christ approaching boldly and without any trembling, he said: “Are you that profane man who smashed my god, who refused either to worship the immortal gods or to keep the king’s decrees?”

The bishop replied: “How can one be called a god who could not even help himself? As for keeping the decrees of my king, I desire to do so with his help. Therefore I shall daily sing that truthful saying of the Psalmist:

‘I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments. The cords of sinners have entangled me, but I have not forgotten your law’” (Ps. 118).

The most wicked king said: “Where did you get this great boldness?”

Unwillingly, the soldier of Christ replied: “From a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1). Boldness is necessary. For boldness serves as a wall. In battle, those who fear most are in the greatest danger. The Lord says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. 10).

The most impious king said: “Lay aside your boldness now and worship the most powerful gods; restore also my god, whom you smashed. For your Lord, whom you worship, cannot free you from the torments prepared for you.”

But Christ’s martyr gave him no answer, turning over in his mind the Gospel saying: “Do not throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

Then the king ordered the soldiers: “Cut off,” he said, “the tips of the fingers of both his hands, one by one.”

They immediately carried out the order and cut off the tips of each of his fingers. But the wicked king addressed the soldier of Christ in this way:

“There are words and utterances by which you may soothe this pain and remove a great part of the disease.” (Horace, *Epistles* 1)

“Sacrifice only to the gods, who continually display their divinity to us.”

But he replied:

“Everyone takes care not to commit what he will strive to undo.” (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*)

Then the king said to the soldiers: “Again, cut off the successive parts of his fingers one by one. For I want him to suffer through prolonged torture.”

At these words they cut off his several limbs—his hands and his arms—and thus mutilated, they set him before the king.

Then all the Christians who had been brought to the spectacle, weeping and wailing, were able to utter the lamentations of Jeremiah:

“Our eyes have failed because of tears; our inward parts are troubled” (Lam. 2).

The unconquered martyr turned toward them and spoke in their native language:

“Do not weep for me, my sons; do not be sad, but rather rejoice, giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the portion of the saints, who has transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1). Rejoice, I say, and give thanks to God that in your time he has deigned to choose such a sacrifice for himself; and pray to the divine mercy that he may deign to complete the work begun in me.

“For he himself says: ‘Stand firm in the faith; act manfully’ (1 Cor. 16); ‘Let everything you do be done in charity’ (1 Cor. 14), which is Christ Jesus. When I look upon you as soldiers of Christ, and consider your deeds, great hope of victory possesses me. Your courage, your age, and your strength encourage me.”

After he had said this, the wicked king ordered his feet and legs to be cut off piece by piece, just as his hands and arms had been.

What madness, citizens—what such insanity could ever have been endured? Who could look with clear eyes upon so great a crime committed against a human being? What horror to relate; what dread to hear! Who could have looked upon or heard with dry eyes such a fatal deed, such a cruel crime?

But the undaunted soldier of Christ still awaited greater torments, destined for him alone and reserved by the Lord—torments which this most wicked man devised beyond those of all the persecutors of Rome and the other provinces. For he ordered the martyr, already mutilated, to have his navel cut open and his intestines gradually drawn out and gathered around a piece of wood prepared for that purpose.

While they were being drawn out for a long time, the true soldier of Christ raised his eyes to heaven, gave thanks to God, and commended his spirit and his final breath to him in these words:

“Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23).

After these words, he was immediately released from the prison of the flesh and, visibly received into the hands of the angels, as those who were present testified. In heaven he was welcomed with fitting praises by the holy martyrs.

Thus the unconquered martyr of Christ, his countenance somewhat changed, paid the debt of bitter death on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, to live forever as an heir indeed of God and co-heir of Christ (Rom. 8). He worthily carried back with the profit of his passion the talent entrusted to him.

He was therefore worthy of this sweet, joyful, and truthful summons:

“Because my soul has been pleased in you, enter the place of exultation and joy, that you may see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life” (Ps. 127).

Who could ever adequately describe in writing so marvelous a work of martyrdom in such a martyr of Christ? Truly, he would have entered the joys of paradise gladly and without public martyrdom, because he strove to fulfill in himself what he had heard from the Apostle:

“Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, and so forth” (Eph. 5).

For the Gospel counsel to despise the world was pleasing and joyful to him, because he offered to God not only what he possessed, but also what was greatest and most precious to God—himself. He took up the strongest weapons of obedience, with which he served for a long time, perfectly and honorably, in the monastery.

This holy pontiff was indeed like Jehoiada, who strengthened the temple during his life and, appearing like a flower in the days of spring, was finally adorned with the redness of his passion (Ecclus. 50). His lips guarded knowledge, and many sought the law from his mouth, because he was an angel of the Lord of hosts (Mal. 2), announcing the word of life and striving, through daily instruction, to lead the sheep entrusted to him through the narrow gate.

He was also an animal with eyes before and behind (Ezek. 1), watching on every side for the snares of the most wicked enemy; striving to attain an ethical life full of every virtue; holding the Lord’s plow firmly, he did not make a crooked furrow. Rather, by living chastely and offering his subjects a good example, he joyfully ascended Jacob’s ladder (Gen. 28), constructed from the various steps of spiritual progress.

Why should we delay any longer? The Creator of the world, whom this blessed man served worthily, openly showed his own people—that is, the Christians—as well as the hostile and condemned pagans, with what glory and praise his spirit had been joined to the holy martyrs and placed in the heavenly dwelling.

For the gentiles placed the severed limbs of Christ’s martyr in a most filthy place, to be trampled under horses’ feet, in accordance with the saying: “Let his memory perish from the earth” (Job 18), lest the Christians be able to claim him as their martyr.

But the Lord of all, for whom nothing is impossible, subjected all his enemies to him, so that a church might be founded in his name, in which he himself might become a living victim in perpetual sacrifice of praise.

When they attempted to lift the holy martyr’s limbs from the ground, God made them as heavy as the foundations of the highest mountains; and the pagan crowd could not raise even the smallest finger-joint by any device.

Nor is it surprising that God allowed him, while still alive, to be purified through their hands by various torments and permitted his body to be killed, but afterward willed that the Lord of lords himself should reign over his soul and body. For he says in the Gospel:

“Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do” (Matt. 10; Luke 12).

And elsewhere he promised his faithful:

“Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21).

When the king heard of this miracle, he and his companions were terrified that they had committed such an unheard-of murder. After taking counsel, he sent again to his adviser, the most wicked idol named Machmit. He reported what had happened and asked what still had to be done.

The idol is said to have immediately given him this answer:

“Great and powerful is the God of the Christians. For he grants his witnesses life after death in the kingdom of heaven. It is clear that the man you killed was his closest associate, and therefore you cannot exercise power over his limbs. Since you cannot do so, grant the Christians permission to bury him honorably, as their greatest Father, so that they may rejoice to have as a worthy patron after death the one whom they deserved to have as their bishop while he lived.”

The messengers returned and reported to their king the answer they had heard.

He immediately ordered the Christians to assemble in one place and prepare fitting funeral rites, with the highest veneration, for their archimandrite.

What joy, what happiness then possessed the hearts of the Christians? Who could record it with a pen? Who could express it with a human tongue? The earth resounded with their joy; the heights of heaven could answer their exultation. What abundance of tears, filled with gladness, flooded the cheeks of the Christians? What wealth of words could recount it?

After the Red Sea had been crossed on dry feet, after the enemies had been drowned, the people of the Hebrews sang praises to the Lord with great joy; and, after the Babylonian captivity, their children, when they saw Jerusalem, exulted with great rejoicing. Yet scarcely could their joy be compared with the joy of these people singing and chanting to the Lord as they performed the rites of Christ’s holy martyr and their patron.

What praise or jubilation could have been greater among the ancient people than that which belonged to this modern people in honor of such a martyr? Perhaps you might have seen another Jacob being buried by his sons, embalmed with spices (Gen. 50), by everyone together, as Christ himself was buried by Joseph and Nicodemus (John 19).

When the Christian people had assembled, they lifted the limbs of Christ’s martyr Tiemo with the greatest veneration and carried them into the church. After celebrating vigils for three days and three nights, they finally buried him with fitting honor, hymns, and praises.

On the day of his burial, and thereafter, frequent miracles occurred at his tomb—not only among Christians but also among the pagans themselves, who from that time forward venerated him daily.

[Note: Tiemo undertook his pilgrimage in the year 1100, according to Otto of Freising, Book VII. The *Chronicle of Reichersberg*, recently published by G. V. D. Christoph Gewold, Bavarian counsellor, attests that he was captured and killed in the following year.]

The blessed martyr of Christ Tiemo suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, during the reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

*End of the Life of Blessed Tiemo.*

# Life of Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca

Who was a close associate, disciple, and energetic champion of Gregory VII, the supreme pontiff. Now published for the first time. In this history the reader has a notable testimony to Gregorian sanctity against the slanderous mouths of its detractors.

## The Observations of D. Costantino Gaetano on the Life of Saint Anselm of Lucca

The author of this history was an eyewitness and witness to the deeds of Saint Anselm. He was endowed with no small learning and piety, as he often acknowledges: he was Saint Anselm’s priest in penance and his son, and the holy man promoted him to that same order amid many tears.

It is known that his name began with the letter B. We have it from an ancient parchment manuscript in our museum and from another belonging to the monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone, as Dom Arnold, a Cassinese monk, reports in Book III of *The Tree of Life*. We have not yet been able to determine whether the name represented by the letter B was Benedict, Bernard, Bartholomew, or someone else.

The author mentioned above recorded, besides the history of the Life, twenty-nine miracles of the holy man. Thirty others were subsequently described by different people, according as they themselves saw or heard them. This is how the Benedictine manuscript reads. But our manuscript contains, in addition to these, many more miracles of the holy pontiff, although at the end several others seem to be missing; neither the Church of Mantua nor that of Lucca was able to remedy this deficiency.

This annotation by the most learned D. Costantino Gaetano, who was deeply devoted to the study of antiquity, was found at the end of the copy that came from Rome to Jacob Gretser through the kindness of the most reverend Father in Christ and lord, Don Pietro Consolini, most worthy provost of the Congregation of the Oratory.

From this Life the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius transcribed not a few passages in his eleventh *Annals*. We now publish it so that those who burden Gregory VII with so many calumnies and assail him with insults may consider whether they can produce, on behalf of the schismatics, anyone comparable in holiness of life and performance of miracles to Anselm, Altmann, Gebhard, and others of that kind.

Berthold of Constance placed the following enduring encomium of Anselm in his *Chronicle* under the year 1086:

“Blessed Anselm, formerly bishop of Lucca, began to shine with innumerable miracles in that very year of his deposition. While he was still living in the flesh, after the death of the venerable Pope Gregory VII, he greatly encouraged the faithful of Saint Peter against the tyranny of Henry; but after his death, shining with miracles, he encouraged them still more to persevere against that same man. Thus Henry’s party began day by day to decline, while the Catholics did not cease to advance in fidelity to Saint Peter.”

See D. Henri Canisius, volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*, in the preface to the two books of Saint Anselm against Guibert the antipope, which he inserted, previously unpublished, in that sixth volume.

Rangerius, third bishop of Lucca after Saint Anselm, also wrote the Life and miracles of Saint Anselm of Lucca in connected verse, as Domnizo testifies in Book II, chapter 3, of *The Life of Countess Matilda*, in these lines:

“Being the third bishop of Lucca after him, that Rangerius, the rector, composed in verse for Countess Matilda the Life of Anselm.”

Domnizo adds that the same Rangerius wrote an excellent book on the controversy over investitures:

“He recently composed a beautiful second book,

Which settles the dispute over the staff.”

But these monuments have either perished or are still struggling somewhere against dust, decay, moths, and worms. Domnizo inserted the beginning of the first book into his own work.

# Life of Blessed Anselm, Bishop of Lucca

Briefly written by A. B. (for so he calls himself), a priest and the spiritual son of that same holy pastor. Several other miracles of the same holy man are appended to it.

We are urgently compelled by the persistent prayers of certain devout persons to set forth, in a concise work, the Life of our most holy Father Anselm, bishop of Lucca, which we saw with our own eyes and faithfully received from those who lived alongside him. It shone with so many and such great virtues that we are scarcely adequate to undertake a task of this kind. Yet when we consider their venerable desire, although we are unequal to it, we nevertheless begin, as best we can, what they request.

For to all the faithful he provides the foundation of faith and the horn of salvation; but to the excommunicated, confusion, shame, loss, and destruction.

We pass over how he lived in childhood, partly because we do not know it fully and partly because we judge it better to remain silent about it for the present. Yet we learned from his frequent reports that even then he was diligent in reading scholarly books; and the result itself clearly proved this, because he was skilled in grammar and dialectic. [Note: Baronius, vol. XI, under the year 1073, no. 2, quotes this passage.]

When he appeared suitable—worthy in merits, conduct, and knowledge—to be elevated to the honor of the episcopate, the most reverend Pope Alexander sent him to the king, assigning him as companion the religious bishop of Santa Rufina, named Meginard. [Note: Pope Alexander II had himself formerly been bishop of Lucca and had borne the name Anselm.] But because he had already begun perfectly to hate the practice of ecclesiastical orders being conferred by secular powers, he withdrew, by whatever opportunity or means he could find, without receiving the investiture of the dignity, although the lord pope had sent him with that intention.

Nor is this surprising. For God, who later worked many things through him, reserved him for a canonical election. The king, however, grieved as though he had been despised and lamented it as a great loss to the royal empire.

After the death of the aforesaid Pope Alexander [Note: Baronius, vol. X, under the year 1073, nos. 60–61, quotes this passage], when the most holy Gregory VII had been elected Roman pontiff—after long resistance, through the prompting of the Holy Spirit and by the common vote of clergy and laity—this man too was elected bishop of the Church of Lucca, so that he might follow Gregory in all things, and was afterward religiously consecrated by him.

Thus, while he stayed for some time—not once or twice, but often—with this most religious consecrator of his, he observed a life ineffably marvelous and marvelously ineffable. For, when people came to him from every region and boundary of the world, he properly satisfied them all. Truth and justice were never absent from his mouth. Indeed, what is more astonishing, even amid secular affairs he frequently rose above himself in spirit, his soul gladdened by heavenly contemplation. If he was sometimes in private, he was also delighted and strengthened by divine revelations.

While he fervently desired to follow in Gregory’s footsteps, he began to forget the world and to sigh toward God with all the powers of mind and body, day and night, committing himself not only to constant reading but also to continual affliction. [Note: Baronius here continues: “For the blandishments of the world and bodily delights in which other men rejoiced, he had already turned into torment for himself, abhorring all such things as the bitterest poisons of death. Since he loathed even the most delicate foods, when those seated around him compelled him to partake, he plausibly feigned illness, a vow, or some other pretext, so as to preserve his desired chastity and not bring sadness upon his fellow diners.” Nevertheless, all these things appear below in our copy.]

He searched through books of various authorities and began to regard his own life as deserving the most complete condemnation. He considered the dignity of the ministry he had received as a grave danger of responsibility, not as a joy of honor.

Above all, he feared that after his canonical election he had accepted from the king a ring and pastoral staff. He therefore judged everything he had done under the authority of that detestable investiture to be entirely invalid. The lord pope, however, censured him only for that particular matter.

He therefore decided, for the sake of prayer, to visit some shrines of the saints. Without the knowledge of his parents and of the faithful who were with him, he suddenly became a monk subject to the rule of Saint Benedict [Note: Baronius adds: “and subject to the custom of Cluny”].

Before long, blessed Pope Gregory recalled him against his will. Anselm returned and renounced everything he had received from the king; every royal grant to him was annulled. He himself was restored to the fullness of his dignity, scarcely being allowed to retain his monastic habit [Note: Baronius reads “with his habit merely changed,” but our manuscript is more correct]. Indeed, the lord pope threatened to take even that away from him.

What his religious discipline was thereafter, neither tongue can relate nor hand express in writing. He strove to fulfill both the life and order of monks and of canons. In every way he also endeavored to be a prudent and faithful servant (Matt. 25), so that he would not be found idle in the Lord’s harvest or hide his master’s money, but might confidently meet the returning Lord and say:

“Lord, behold, your mina has earned ten minas” (Luke 19).

He became an outstanding preacher of the word of God and a principal instructor in religious life. He reverently loved the clergy and taught them wisely; he instructed the entire people with propriety. To conclude briefly, he became all things to all people, so that he might win all (1 Cor. 9).

He carefully traveled throughout his diocese and earnestly sought to discern the life of everyone, especially the clergy. He openly warned and greatly desired that every cleric should be worthy of his name. For the most learned teacher Jerome, describing the life of clerics, says that a cleric is so called from the lot of God—that is, having cast aside the impediment of this world, he should possess nothing except God as his portion.

Accordingly, he first approached the canons of the principal church in the city of Lucca, which was dedicated in honor of Saint Martin, the most holy bishop and confessor. He addressed, admonished, encouraged, and persuaded them most gently to practice by their deeds what they were called by name. For “canon” is so called as if from “regular”; and he earnestly preached and urged them to live a regular life.

When he continued to press them for a long time and repeatedly urged them, they finally became indignant and answered with extreme rashness. But he, like a kind and gentle father, received everything graciously. Nevertheless, he did not wish to be overcome by evil, but strove to conquer evil with good (Rom. 12).

Finally, like another most religious bishop Augustine, he promised to share a common life with them. He wanted nothing to be his own apart from them, but wished to hold everything in common with them. He wanted to become poor in order to make them rich in Christ (1 Cor. 1), and with every possible effort, both spiritual and worldly, he strove to attract them.

At last he invited the marchioness Matilda, the helper of his undertaking, most noble in character and lineage. In secret she was living a spiritual and deeply religious life, while publicly she was living a secular—or, more accurately, a military—life. Yet she possessed both the spiritual and the secular life in such a way that she made the former belong to Christ and the latter serve Christ.

The secular life was more difficult and burdensome for her, but, I hope, also much richer in reward. The former arose from her own will; the latter from obedience. Whatever intelligence, wisdom, or counsel she possessed, she gladly poured into this undertaking.

He therefore addressed the aforementioned canons, both collectively and individually. He stirred them up, urged them on, encouraged them, and promised an increase in the Church’s prosperity and honor, as well as benefit for themselves, both in the future and in the present. He also promised wealth and honors to their parents, hoping by this means to draw their wills toward him.

But blinded by the wicked world, they rejected everything. They preferred the water of distress leading to damnation to the wine of joy leading to salvation. They chose to be poor men of the devil rather than rich men of Christ.

The bishop and most diligent pastor, unwilling for the sheep entrusted to him to perish, approached them with both threats and entreaties. When they resisted him and contradicted him as much as they could, he would, I believe, have ceased, already excessively—but fruitlessly—weary, had not blessed Pope Leo IX decreed under threat of anathema that the canons of that church should live a common life and observe a regular way of life. Whenever he saw or remembered the command of that decree, he was terrified and did not dare to remain silent.

It happened, then [Note: Baronius, under the year 1074, nos. 46–47, quotes this passage], that the most holy Pope Gregory VII came to that same city, and the matter was brought before him. He immediately began by admonishing them with fatherly affection, saying:

“Since it is not permissible to disregard the decrees of the Roman pontiff,” he gently asked and urged them to obey the most salutary decrees and fulfill the will of the most reverend Father. He addressed them not once or twice but often and at length—sometimes with the holy bishop, sometimes without him—at times harshly and at times gently, presenting to them the sacred Scriptures and authoritative texts.

Although they occasionally pretended to listen humbly to the blessed admonitions, they nevertheless distorted everything in his absence.

Finally they were summoned to the apostolic see, where they were exposed as conspirators against their own bishop and as plotters. The canons were produced, and the chapter of Saint Fabian, martyr and bishop, was read; it decreed that conspirators and plotters against their bishops should be handed over to the curia. By the judgment of the entire holy synod, they too were handed over to the curia.

Then the faithful and prudent marchioness Matilda, calling them servants, summoned them into the service of the curia. For this reason, they were exceedingly sorrowful and caused as many as they could to conspire even against her. [Note: Baronius, in the passage cited, no. 48, quotes this.]

Accordingly, many bishops again assembled at San Genesio, which is not far from the city of Lucca (Baronius reads “the castle”). Among them was the most reverend bishop of Albano, named Peter, surnamed Igneus, acting in the place of the lord pope. Together with Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and all the others, he excommunicated those conspirators.

They, grieving and enraged beyond consolation, maliciously stirred up the entire city. Relying on the aid of that utterly depraved man formerly called King Henry, they drove the most religious bishop from the city and became completely rebellious against the aforementioned lady.

The head and leader of this conspiracy was a certain man named Peter, a canon only by false profession; in the order of his damnation he was a subdeacon, proud in mind, incontinent in conduct, shameless in speech, disorderly in body, a man of blood and a source of every impurity. Because of the enormity of his wickedness, he suddenly became an insolent herald of Henry’s tyranny. After some time he also became a familiar of the court of iniquity—a court which, by a just interpretation, I call a court of blood, or rather the sewer of every disgrace.

Not long afterward, when Henry came into Tuscany with the heresiarch Wibert, whom we shall discuss more fully later, this Peter—who seemed ready to rage at the first opportunity, since he possessed neither fear of God nor respect for man—was imposed as the bishop of that same city of Lucca, the bishop of error.

Joining to himself the most wicked men throughout the land—perjurers, robbers, fornicators, and adulterers—he invaded the Church’s territory and acquired castles and men for himself by force, fraud, or payment.

Only one fortress remained to the venerable bishop. But that tyrant, because it was near the city and he attacked it almost daily, devastated it with plunder, fires, and murders. The gentlest of all men endured everything gladly and chose poverty for Christ. Content with two chaplains and a few servants, he remained humble with the most reverend lady whom we mentioned above.

Yet, so that his adversary might finally put on the garment of universal cursing, Peter was at last not consecrated but rather execrated by the heresiarch Wibert, so that like might imitate like in every respect.

For just as Wibert polluted the Roman Church by invading it while the most holy Pope Gregory VII was still alive, so this man polluted the Church of Lucca while its most religious bishop was still living.

Thus, to use the words of the most blessed martyr Cyprian: “Neither this man nor that one is anything; for neither is either a successor or a predecessor of anyone. Both are parricides; both are most wicked violators of their mother, the Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0911] Baron, vol. II, year 1074, no. 14, cites this passage; he reads: “since he had been utterly expelled.”]

While that man, expelled, desired to sit securely with Mary, nearly all the bishops and princes became not merely, I say, disobedient, but altogether rebels against the holy Roman See. Only one person was found—and alone—remaining steadfast in the faith: the duchess and marchioness Matilda, who possessed zeal for God and obeyed the lord pope Gregory. For when she had come to know his most holy life and ardor for religion, she surrendered herself entirely to his direction, hoping by such obedience to be released from the burdens of this world. Conversely, this was assigned to her for the remission of sins, so that, like a second Deborah (Judges 4), she might judge the people, conduct military affairs, and resist heretics and schismatics.

And lest she should fail as though left alone, she was entrusted for safekeeping to the aforementioned Lucan bishop, Saint Anselm. I say, she was entrusted with every care and with an affection of charity: the most blessed master entrusted his most faithful disciple with her, just as Christ, upon the cross, entrusted the Virgin Mother to the virgin disciple, saying, “Mother, behold your son”; and to the disciple, “Behold your mother” (John 19). Thus, while each sought to escape the abysses of the world and devote himself to contemplation, he became involved in the world’s greatest affairs.

That most holy disciple [Baronius: “therefore our most holy lord and Father Anselm”], then, undertook and labored diligently for her protection, and with every effort grew increasingly ardent in holiness day by day. We may state with complete certainty concerning him that “the Lord filled him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Ecclesiasticus 15). He was indeed “an angel of great counsel.” For although the aforesaid lady Matilda, a devoted handmaid of Saint Peter [Baronius: “Lady Matilda, the only daughter of Blessed Peter”], had many secular judgments and affairs, he enabled her to conduct everything through his counsel in such a way that she observed both the precepts of the Gospel, the ordinances of the canons, and the rights of the laws—something rarely, or perhaps never, found in human minds and talents. But he had learned this from his own master, the blessed Pope Gregory; and the Holy Spirit had filled them both.

At that time, therefore, the Roman world, now in an extraordinary fashion, raged and went mad against itself. For Henry, son of the Emperor Henry III, waged great hostility against all Catholics. Since, after his father’s death, he had assumed the governance of the kingdom from early childhood, what was spoken through Solomon was fulfilled: “Woe to the land whose king is a child” (Ecclesiastes 10). Entrusting himself to childish counsels, instructed in every kind of filth, he soon did not blush to throw all religion and every law into confusion, and he devoted himself to his lust in every form of depravity [the manuscript reads *instuduit*; perhaps *studuit* should be read].

At that time, no one could be a bishop, abbot, or provost unless he possessed more money, or had become an accomplice and supporter of the emperor’s filth. Certainly no one’s life or conduct was considered good; rather, the whole of religion, as well as truth and justice, was held in contempt. That priest was considered the more praiseworthy whose garment was more elegant, whose table was more plentiful, and whose concubine was more splendid. Nor was any soldier called glorious unless he had been perjured three or four times. When the most blessed Pope Gregory considered this with grief and sorrow, desiring to restore the holy Church to ecclesiastical use and canonical laws, he frequently sent him gracious legations, at times admonishing him as a father, at times rebuking him more harshly.

[Col. 0912D] But when he perceived that even by this means he was making no progress, he finally sent to him his deeply religious mother, the Empress Agnes, together with two most reverend bishops, the bishop of Praeneste and the bishop of Como. In their presence, after carefully hearing their counsel, Henry feigned repentance, vowed obedience, and promised reform in all things. But when they had returned, he reverted to himself and became worse than before.

Then, with unheard-of audacity and astonishing arrogance, he gathered in the city of Worms bishops who had become partners in his crimes and who should not be called bishops at all. Holding a little council, they proscribed the bishop of the First See—a thing unheard of for centuries.

Afterward he sent a legation into Italy, asserting the same presumption through bishops who were his accomplices in schism. The bearer of this legation was a certain man named Eberhard [a count; see Baronius, year 1076, no. 16], German by birth, a son of the world, a hook of the devil, and the inventor of nearly every kind of lie.

He went around and traversed the land in order to kill [variant: infect] everyone with schismatic contagion. Many who, because of the lord pope’s interdict, had ceased from divine office, he—himself under interdict and bound by the chain of perdition—reconciled with unheard-of recklessness and arrogance, and in the name of his lord king ordered them to celebrate the office as before.

[Col. 0913B] Since the apostolic bishop could no longer conceal the wickedness of so great a crime, he excommunicated both Henry himself and all his supporters. He also interdicted him from every royal dignity and absolved from every obligation of loyalty those bound to him by oaths. For, shameful even to say, besides the heretical guilt mentioned above, the envoys of that man were present at the holy council and dared to bark as follows:

“Our lord the king commands you to relinquish the apostolic see and the papacy, since it is his own, and not to obstruct this holy place any longer.”

Shame upon such wickedness! Oh, the execrable presumption of that most wretched man! Behold, he says that what the Lord Christ entrusted to the sole prince of the apostles, Peter, belongs to him. And Christ did not entrust it suddenly; rather, before entrusting it, he asked three times: “Simon, do you love me?” (John 21). He did not ask because he himself was ignorant, but to foreshadow providence for future times, so that the care of souls might not be entrusted quickly and rashly to just anyone.

After that man had finally given a sure pledge of his love on the third occasion, Christ said: “Feed my sheep” (ibid.). He excluded neither king nor emperor, nor any rank within the Christian profession, except the one who had denied his own sheep and himself. Therefore, the man whom the Lord reserved for his own judgment alone dares not only to judge him, but also to call him his own and, insofar as he can, to condemn him. For this reason, that entire holy synod, rightly indignant, proclaims and confirms an anathema against him.

[Col. 0913D] Not long afterward, therefore, the same most reverend pope—through whom all canonical rights, almost entirely abolished up to that time, began to be restored—was earnestly requested by many of the kingdom’s princes, especially with the support of Countess Matilda, who then ruled a large part of Italy, to come into the German lands for the common need of Mother Church.

Because of his arrogance and anathema, they had deposed King Henry from his royal lordship. Meeting together, they also compelled him to remain privately in a certain castle after rejecting his wicked counselors, lest he infect many with the leprosy of his anathema. For they had resolved among themselves that, after humbly summoning the holy Pope Gregory to the city of Augsburg, they would together adore him before the judge of all Christendom in the common council of the entire kingdom. They desired that, by apostolic authority, they might either recover Henry reformed and absolved, or, if he were rightly rejected, elect another in Christ.

But Henry, accused by his own conscience, did not await the holy assembly. He went to meet the lord pope at the town of Canossa, humbled to his feet. Having secured the lord pope’s safety by oaths, as the pope himself had graciously commanded, and in the presence of bishops and abbots, Countess Matilda, and Adelaia [Adelaide, or Adelheid, who was a countess], together with many others, he was finally absolved on the third day. Nevertheless, he was not restored to the kingdom.

[Col. 0914B] Thus he returned again to his former counsels and to the perverse gatherings of the excommunicated, and for a short time observed what he had promised under oath. For within fifteen days, as I believe, when the blessed Bishop Anselm was carrying the lord pope’s legation to Milan together with the deeply religious Bishop Gerard of Ostia, they were hindered by Henry’s soldiers, and the bishop of Ostia was captured.

They did not dare to touch Saint Anselm at all, because he was a native and of noble lineage. He himself, however, voluntarily offered to be captured, saying that he would not abandon his companion in the legation: either they should release him, he said, or keep him captive together with Anselm. Since they did not dare to do this, he departed sadly, wishing, if possible, to lay down his own life for his brother.

“For this is the perfection of charity, this is the height of love: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). In such great necessity others commonly pretend and conceal many things; some lie, and very many commit perjury. But Anselm would not, by even a single deceptive word, practise pretence toward anyone [variant: anything]. He could indeed have done so, as we later learned from those who had been captured. Thus, by these and many similar events, the oaths once sworn by King Henry were rendered void.

Meanwhile, in the German lands Duke Rudolf was chosen as king to defend the unity of the Catholic Church. For this reason Henry, becoming increasingly indignant, disregarded the counsel and aid of the lord pope and wickedly raged against all Catholics.

[Col. 0914D] After King Rudolf died in the Catholic faith, Henry dared to do what the most powerful emperors of old had never dared, whether they were heretics, apostates, or even pagans. I repeat: having summoned several heretical bishops, while Pope Gregory was still alive and while Henry had even become obedient to him by oath, without any universal council and without judgment, he dared to elect as pope Wibert, formerly bishop of Ravenna, who had then already been excommunicated for many years and whom we mentioned above, though only briefly.

But who was as suitable for this as Wibert, who, filled with the spirit of pride from his very cradle, meditated on nothing except arrogance and pride? While we were watching, he had displayed every obedience and submission to our lord Pope Gregory. Gregory himself received him honorably and lovingly as a guest in the sacred Lateran palace, kept him near his right hand in the holy council, and placed him first in everything in which it was fitting to place him, hoping that what the utterly depraved man pretended was true.

But not long afterward, through pride, Wibert fell into disobedience, became perjured, and finally became an unjust parricide, because he persecuted the holy Father even unto death. Such a man—so just, so holy—Henry raised to the papacy together with his supporters.

Rome was not consulted; neither the Roman clergy nor the people. Only one man was present, named Hugo—named Candidus, but blackest in mind—formerly a cardinal, though long since justly excommunicated and cast out for his crimes. This condemned man praised a condemned man; the perjured man, a perjurer; the parricide, a parricide.

This took place in a dreadful and extremely rugged place, amid the snowy Alps, where hunger is constant and the cold almost perpetual. The place itself, called Brixen, is a village in place of a city, surrounded by the highest cliffs, where scarcely even the name of Christianity is maintained.

There the privileges of the principal church, there the rights of the supreme priest, there the ordinances of the holy Fathers, there all canonical decrees were emptied of force. Indeed, if someone had asked him to set another god over the heavens, he would, I think, insofar as it lay within his power, have done and confirmed it. For the trick he is practicing is not entirely new; he learned it in this way from his youth.

Indeed, when the venerable Pope Alexander had once been canonically elected, Henry himself elected Cadolus [Cadalous], bishop of Parma, as his pope in the German lands and sent him to Rome. Cadolous caused prolonged discord and waged many wars.

His mother, the Empress Agnes, was involved in this wicked presumption. Later, touched by the illumination of the Holy Spirit, she made confession before Pope Alexander himself and received penance. Among other things, she was ordered to remain in Rome, and there to make satisfaction to Saint Peter through vigils, prayers, and fasts, and to benefit the Church by her counsels and aid as far as she was able.

But while Henry persisted in his detestable obstinacy, worshiping the demon Wibert, he was again admonished by the apostolic father through bishops sent to him, the bishop of Albano and the bishop of Padua. Since he did not reform, he was once again excommunicated with the utmost severity.

He then, as though beginning a new seizure of tyranny, started to distribute among his soldiers both the estates and nearly all the treasures of every church. He attached these soldiers, and nearly everyone, to his party, except for the very few whom the Lord reserved for himself, so that they would not bend their knees before Baal.

Having gathered an army, he advanced toward Rome. At his first entry he immediately turned all his fury against the aforesaid lady Matilda: he burned villages and destroyed castles. Nevertheless, because divine mercy protected her, she suffered no very great loss.

Then, I say, one could have praised the genius and wisdom of the man—that is, of the holy Bishop Anselm. For although a ship is strong and well built, and its sailors prudent, it is easily endangered unless its helmsman is wise and powerful.

She was solicitous out of filial devotion; he contemplated the art of governing. She exercised authority; he directed it. She gave the command; he gave counsel. Yet he surpassed her in everything, because she and all her people obeyed his holiness—she above all. Nor is this surprising. He advised each person on each matter with such foresight and wisdom that, almost alone, that household resisted the aforesaid king and all the great and small throughout nearly the whole of Italy; it avenged God’s injury and its own, secured honor, and did not lose God’s favor.

This was plainly obtained through his merits, so that that praiseworthy and glorious woman was proclaimed even in foreign lands. Why should this be surprising? She acted nobly and magnificently, in a manner unusual for women—indeed, I say, more than manfully. She feared scarcely any danger. Which powerful person ever led his own army as she did?

Nevertheless, many of her own withdrew from her and went backward. They were separated from us, I say, because they were not of us. For some angels too fell from heaven, while others were so strengthened that they could no longer fall. Those who remained were likewise strengthened, both by the sweetness of pastoral wisdom and by the goodwill and cheerfulness of so desirable a matron.

[Col. 0916C] That outstanding shepherd and teacher was with them day and night, instructing and admonishing them spiritually. Above all else he repeatedly urged them to keep away from the excommunicated, since if anyone participated with excommunicated persons, unless he was first absolved after receiving penance, he could have no communion with the others.

He hated the excommunicated with perfect hatred. Thus he made many attentive through his teaching and prevented very many from participating in such tyranny; some he even converted completely. Finally, he composed a warning for the aforesaid king, and admonished in salutary writings Wibert himself, the heresiarch and invader of the holy Roman See.

What more is there to say? That tyrant invaded Rome as he had begun, and attacked it for three years. In the end he conquered it by perjury and by money more than by strength or wisdom. Thus the holy Church of Saint Peter became “a den of impious thieves” (Matthew 21).

Yet he had not conquered all Rome. For the most reverend Pope Gregory remained in the castle called Crescentius. Some of the more noble Romans also remained, neither corrupted, deceived, nor defeated, desiring to obey God rather than man (Acts 5), especially one who was a heretic.

As the impious persecution of the heretics increased, Duke Robert of Apulia and Calabria, invited by the apostolic man, hastened to Rome. Before his arrival, Henry abandoned the city and fled. In a single day the duke confidently conquered it by force of arms and led the lord pope from the confinement of the tower into the spaciousness of the sacred Lateran palace with great triumph and glory.

After spending several days there, they proceeded together to Salerno, where the most holy pope departed to Christ. The miracles that the Lord worked through him we saw some ourselves and heard others from reliable witnesses; this is not the place to recount them.

After Henry had been driven from the city, he immediately returned to the German lands, having first stirred up nearly all the Lombards against the aforementioned lady, against her holy protector, and against the entire Catholic unity.

[Col. 0917A] Not long afterward, bishops and marquises were assembled, together with many others, and suddenly invaded the land of that same countess with great force and fury, thinking that they would immediately subject the whole territory to their rule.

Then our own men were gathered, though they were few, since they had learned of the danger scarcely one day beforehand. Nevertheless, they were greatly strengthened because our lord, Saint Anselm the bishop, sent them his blessing through our humble agency. He especially instructed us to absolve first anyone who had participated with excommunicated persons, and then to bless all of them together by apostolic authority and by his own blessing. We were to instruct them how and with what intention they ought to fight, and so entrust them to the danger of the impending battle for the remission of all their sins.

When the engagement took place, the enemies very quickly turned their backs. The bishop of Parma was soon captured, together with many nobles and countless lesser men; nor was any number found for the dead. Of our own men, three were killed and a few wounded. In this matter all the faithful may recognize the glory of God and the power of the most reverend bishop’s blessing.

From that point the councils of the heretics were thrown into confusion and their excessively arrogant insolence was greatly diminished. All the Catholics rejoiced and were strengthened, especially that household which our holy Father, Bishop Anselm, afterward guarded undefeated and preserved in the Catholic faith.

And the man who had once been bishop of a single city, expelled though innocent, became magnificently the prelate of many cities. For the lord pope entrusted him with his authority and office throughout Lombardy wherever Catholic bishops could not be found; and at that time such bishops were certainly exceedingly rare.

[Col. 0917D] Therefore, from every part of Lombardy, all who possessed zeal for the Catholic faith flocked to him. There the Catholics received blessing; the excommunicated, when converted, received absolution. There they sought chrism and the sacred orders; there the desolate found consolation, the uninstructed counsel, and the instructed joy.

Whatever was uncertain anywhere was wisely resolved by him. He was always found with the same gravity and reverence, and he could not be corrupted either by money or by prayers.

Many often came to him—sometimes nobles, sometimes commoners, poor and rich—wishing either to obtain something from the aforesaid countess or to secure more safely what they had obtained. Some promised him great gifts, others still greater ones. Although he himself was poor and all his dependents were needy, he responded angrily, rejected their gifts, and refused his assistance. Had they asked freely, they would certainly have obtained their requests more quickly.

For he said:

“If what they seek is unjust, I shall be a participant, indeed the author, of their injustice. But if it is just, I shall be guilty if I sell justice.”

If some, perhaps blinded by God because of their perverse minds, or perniciously entangled in worldly greed, resisted the Catholic and apostolic judgment, they began to reason among themselves but suddenly fell completely silent, because they could not resist his wisdom. Rather, they marveled at the man’s eloquence, so great and so rational.

He knew almost all sacred Scripture by heart, so that as soon as one asked him what each individual holy interpreter, or all of them together, thought about any matter, he would answer immediately. We learned that many things had been divinely explained to him from the sacred Scriptures; some of these we possess in his written works, while others we retain in memory.

He wrote many little books with his own hands.

[Note: [Col. 0917] The lord Doctor Henricus Canisius published this apologetic book in volume VI of *Antiquae Lectiones*.]

He compiled one *Apology* from various works of the holy Fathers, by which he defended the judgment of the lord pope, together with all his deeds and commands, by canonical arguments and confirmed them by orthodox authorities. He produced a very clear exposition of the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

At the request of the most blessed handmaid of God, Matilda, he also expounded the Psalter most brilliantly—briefly indeed, but usefully—up to the passage where it says: “We have blessed you in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 128). There he ended both the life and the exposition, and blessed all of us like another patriarch Jacob, whose blessing, as everyone knows, descended throughout Italy.

In him and through him, some heretics and schismatics are converted, while others are confounded; their teeth are immediately broken when the Lord’s words are spoken to them: “The blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, the mute speak” (Matthew 11).

What shall I say about his abstinence? He regarded almost all foods as though he hated them, even the most delicate. What the aforesaid daughter of his in Christ often had specially prepared for him, I will not say that he ate—he scarcely even tasted it.

He turned all the enticements of the world and all bodily pleasures in which people delight into torment for himself, despising each of them as though they were every kind of poison. When he was sometimes compelled by those sitting around him to take the foods placed before him, he honorably pretended illness, a vow, or some other excuse, so that he might both preserve the chastity he desired and not cause sadness to his table companions.

He fled wine almost as though it were poison, as the blessed Jerome says. I saw—and silently took note of this—that when he had taken a morsel into his mouth, he did not chew it with his teeth, as is customary among people, lest he experience any sweetness. Instead, after touching it softly and turning it over briefly, he swallowed it.

Often he did not drink throughout the entire meal. If thirst sometimes pressed more urgently upon him, perhaps toward evening he privately drank a little water. For even in water, as he often said to me, he regarded the gluttony of the throat and feared a snare; therefore he tasted it sparingly.

If the necessity of nature had not compelled him, he would, I think, have remained awake at all times. Throughout the night he either read, wrote, or prayed. If sleep pressed more strongly upon him, he dozed standing; if occasionally he slept more comfortably, he fell forward onto his knees.

He lay in bed only very rarely, unless extreme modesty or necessity compelled him, and even then not for extended hours but, as it were, for moments. He had almost overcome nature itself, so that he no longer seemed a body but almost entirely spirit.

In him we were truly able to recognize the Gospel saying, as it were bodily [the text has “and,” for “as it were”], that “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matthew 4). For although he removed nearly all nourishment from himself, he nevertheless labored more than everyone else.

He kept many [vigils?] at night; if he withdrew privately, he performed very many [devotions?] during the day. He very frequently remained standing until the third hour. When consecrating churches or altars, he trembled throughout as though filled with the Spirit, because he performed everything ecclesiastical with the fervent love of devotion.

We all marveled at the unsurpassable strength of his endurance, because when we were completely exhausted, he alone continued to work.

[Col. 0919C] When the solemn celebration of Mass was reached, he immediately poured forth entirely in tears. Wherever (*ubivis*; variant *ubicunque*) he found a book, he at once devoted himself to examining it most diligently, so that whatever he snatched up during the day as if merely passing over it, he might chew over fully during the night.

Whenever he was on campaign, as often happened, or traveling, although greatly fatigued he neither took more sumptuous food on that account nor rested in bed. His greatest delicacies were fruit or herbs.

He concealed his entire life and conduct as much as he could. Whether he was with the enemy in the field or privately at home, a small curtain surrounded his bed, and there (*ibique*; variant *ut ibi*) he would be alone, either reading or writing.

Every night, from midnight onward, as the Prophet says (Psalm 118), he rose for the morning office, unless, on rare occasions, he spared the weakness of the daughter entrusted to him, namely the glorious lady Matilda; for discretion, the mother of all virtues, reigned in him.

O how fortunate she was to have such a wise and provident tutor always at her side—not merely as a prudent man, but as an angel of provident counsel! Never, as I believe, while he stood beside her, was she defrauded or deceived.

It is wonderfully astonishing that, although at times he spent the whole day with secular men in many and varied counsels, he was not distracted in mind, but always inwardly occupied himself with something divine and contemplated heavenly things.

All the soldiers of that household, though exceedingly worldly, nevertheless looked to him. They feared him more than their natural lady. On campaigns and in chambers, amid every conversation or council, he either preached or spoke some good word.

They faithfully followed his counsel, and whatever he foretold them frequently came to pass. If he did not convert absolutely everyone, he nevertheless preserved many as more faithful to God and to their lady. He restrained all of them from many crimes and made them stand against the heretics, except for a very few sons of darkness.

He honored all religious men as fathers and rebuked those who sinned. After correcting a heretical man a second or third time, if he had not reformed, he avoided him.

Throughout the various churches in all the land of the aforesaid lady, he frequently established the regular life of clerics or monks. He used to say that he would prefer there to be neither cleric nor monk in a church rather than one who was irregular, so to speak, and irreligious.

I am not capable of adequately testifying to [variant: explaining] the devotion and contrition with which he performed the divine offices.

He permitted nothing to be read in church except the writings of orthodox Fathers, as sacred authority commands. He strove to observe order and harmony both in singing and in the readings, according to what the holy Fathers had established.

He did not admit any apocryphal writings into the Church’s office, as the most blessed Pope Leo had decreed. Nevertheless, he did not entirely reject them for private reading at table or during a conference.

He instructed us to sing the Psalms carefully and meditatively; otherwise he rebuked us harshly. God knows that at times, merely from looking at him, I seemed to myself to be filled with the Spirit. As though forgetting myself, he appeared to me almost like an angel.

During the divine mysteries he never, or scarcely ever, sat. As far as we could tell, he never completed the solemn celebration of Mass without tears. Above all, he always devoted himself to imitating his first master, Pope Gregory, in everything, to such a degree that he absolutely refused to differ from him in anything. Whatever existed in him, he always attributed to Gregory’s merits.

When he recalled the monastic and solitary life, which he often lamented having lost, he found consolation in that same master because he had become obedient to him even to that point. Gregory was the fountain; Anselm flowed from him like a good stream and irrigated the dry land.

Gregory was the head who governed the entire body; Anselm was like an industrious hand carrying out what had been commanded. Gregory illuminated everything like the sun; Anselm declared each thing like a ray of light. At his death, Gregory transmitted the mitre from his head to Anselm as a sign of his power to bind and loose—and, I believe, also of his power to perform miracles.

Not long afterward, as we all came to know, through Anselm’s counsel and great faith, God performed certain splendid miracles through that same mitre.

Among them was the following. The most reverend lord Ubaldus, bishop of Mantua, had suffered for many years from an extremely severe disease of the spleen. His entire body was covered with ulcers, especially his legs, so that he could scarcely stand in any manner, and scarcely even lie down or sit. He had also spent much money on physicians without receiving any benefit.

When the same mitre was placed upon the spot where the pain had become most severe, he was restored to his former health.

Thus that most blessed and so great a master performed many miracles both while alive and after death. The good disciple also performed miracles. The master, I say, was in God, and the disciple was in God; and, as it is said, the disciple performs more through the blessed master.

Nor is this surprising. Peter performed more than Christ—not by his own power, certainly, but because, denying himself, he followed Christ, just as this venerable Father of ours did. Because he piously imitated his master in all things, he performed many miracles.

There are many whose most holy lives we know, who truly possess everlasting rest, but who did not display the power of miracles. This man, however, not merely because he lived a religious life, but because he fulfilled faithful obedience, hated the party of the excommunicated with perfect hatred, and loved and defended the unity of Catholics, proves by miracles what he taught in words.

Therefore, all of you who have thus far obeyed the commands of the lord Pope Gregory within Catholic unity, rejoice and exult. Tell those who have gone backward and abandoned the footsteps of truth to believe now through deeds what they formerly refused to believe through words.

**I.** We saw, while he was alive, his subdeacon named Tenton, who always had diseased eyes. If he occasionally kept watch beyond his usual time or perhaps drank wine, for a long while on the following day he could scarcely see anything, and for some time he could not read at all.

He therefore took the water with which the lord bishop washed his hands after the sacrifice, washed his eyes with it, and thereafter had healthy eyes. He was no less able than the rest of us to keep vigil and read.

**II.** Similarly, his priest Wido, suffering from fevers, took the water used to wash the bishop’s hands, drank it, and recovered.

**III.** Likewise, his deacon John, when he fell ill at Milan, hastened to send him a message. He added in his message that, as soon as Anselm heard of his suffering, he wished him to experience the power of his blessing. It happened as he believed: he felt it immediately, and shortly afterward recovered completely. The same lord bishop later ordained him a priest.

**IV.** He often healed the aforesaid daughter entrusted to him—namely, the most noble lady Matilda—from various illnesses by his blessing alone. As she herself was accustomed to report to us, she frequently felt power going out from him, so that at his touch every illness then afflicting her fled.

**V.** At times he clearly knew the thoughts of people, saying to them while they were thinking: “You thought this and that at such an hour and in such a place.”

**VI.** God is my witness that I am not lying. Once, when I was speaking with him about my sins, as I was often accustomed to do, I confessed a certain temptation with which the evil spirit was then striving to attack me especially fiercely. He said to me: “You are telling the truth, because it sometimes comes upon you even during the ministry of the altar.”

When I heard this, I was immediately terrified, and thereafter I strove to restrain myself from every evil thought, especially in his presence. During the sacred celebration of Mass he was accustomed above all to perceive such things. He also always made it his practice to celebrate Mass every day.

If on any day he did not celebrate—which nevertheless happened only very rarely because of some impediment—he was sadder throughout that entire day and seemed exceedingly burdened. He likewise lamented that night as heavy and restless when, compelled by excessive vigils, he was forced to sleep for a little while.

**VII.** He also very often saw revelations worthy of remembrance, some of which I wish briefly to touch upon.

At one time, while he was consecrating an altar in the church of Saint Paul, in the Mantuan territory near the episcopal residence, in honor of Saint Mary, he saw her with his bodily eyes upon that same altar during the very solemnities of the consecration.

**VIII.** At another time, on the Feast of the Purification of the same glorious Virgin Mary, when he was coming late to the church and the clerics were already singing the invitatory, at the words “coming to meet his God,” he saw Christ coming to meet him as he entered.

**IX.** On another occasion, while singing Psalm 81 in great contrition of heart and with tears—namely, “Incline your ear, O Lord”—he sensed the Lord inclined toward him and, as it were, applying his ear to listen.

He did and saw many other things besides these, but for the moment, because we are in haste, we pass them over.

[Col. 0922C] Finally, many bishops, clerics, and distinguished laymen who were present saw how happily he brought his life to its end. He made no will, because he had nothing from which to make one, imitating in this also the master whom we know to have died poor and in exile. In his final moments, as we learned from his chaplains, he likewise said to the religious: “After all things, I loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore I die in exile.” Indeed, what master and disciple taught during their lives, this they also confirmed in their conduct, as though by a will. The master, whom while still alive he had blessed as obedient to him, commended to the Lord with his prayers even at his death; but the followers of Henry he utterly and completely rejected, unless after a great conversion and penance. Here, in our presence, he commanded us in the word of the Lord to remain steadfast in the faith and teaching of the most blessed Pope Gregory. He imposed this upon us with his blessing and commended us to the remission of our sins.

### X

A certain matron named Berta was present at this blessing. Noble by birth, nobler in disposition of mind and devotion of spirit, she was the wife of the most illustrious Count Bernard and suffered from an unusual disorder of the head. For she was troubled by such intense coldness at the crown of her head that at times she could imagine that ice had been placed upon it. She often tried to drive it away with skins or cushions warmed at the fire, but, despite consulting many highly regarded physicians, she obtained no relief. If cold or wind touched that spot, especially when she had imprudently fallen asleep without carefully covering her head, she was tormented by such violent pain that she feared her eyes might turn or leap from their sockets, and, as though the nerves of her neck had contracted, she could not bend her head.

She had come, then, during that Lenten season to the city of Mantua, to Countess Matilda, so that she might hear the holy and daily office of so venerable a bishop. It therefore happened that, at his final blessing—the one we have mentioned—she arrived more quickly than many others. When she most devoutly asked his blessing, he placed his hand upon her head. The incurable cold immediately departed, and she received a most salutary warmth. As sweat and a little pus issued through her ears, every cause of the illness was removed before the octave of Easter. How many further and most splendid signs God worked through him, what need is there for me to say, when it is certain that very many people saw everything with their own eyes?

### XI

As long as he lived, therefore, he asked that he be committed for burial in the chapter-house of the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated on the bank of the river Eridanus and subject to the sacred monastery of Cluny, from which he himself had been a brother and monk. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Baronius cites what follows under the year 1086, no. 10.] When, with the consent of the bishop, the countess, and everyone else, his body was already being carried to the monastery, the bishop of Sutri, named Bonizo [Baronius: Bishop Domnizo of Sabina], suddenly arrived. The Holy Spirit had stirred him up to declare that it was fitting for a bishop to be buried in the episcopal church. “Such a lamp,” he said, “ought not to be hidden. He humbled himself while still alive as though unworthy; but we ought to exalt as truly worthy the man whom we know to have been most holy.”

Everyone immediately acclaimed this, and the body was taken away from the monks’ attendance and carried to the episcopal church, where it was buried with due honor. At first we wondered at this as a great miracle, not knowing that what was to follow would be much more marvelous.

For we also noted at that time that many bishops and cardinals, and a great multitude of soldiers as well, had come to the same city on the day of his death. The bishop of Maguelonne, named Godefridus, was present, as were Benedict, bishop of Modena, Aribert, bishop of Reggio, and the bishop of that same city, namely Mantua, named Ubaldus. There was also Damian, cardinal of the Roman Church and abbot of the monastery of Nonantola.

All these had come to hear his wisdom and receive his counsel, as they and the other Catholics often used to do. The bishop of Sutri had also departed only the day before, but immediately after the saint’s passing he was opportunely present again on that same day.
