These men, I say, and very many others, both great and small, were present; they saw his passing and, after his death, witnessed and learned of his clear miracles.

[Col. 0924A] [Note: [Col. 0923D] Baronius cites this under the year 1086, no. 9.] In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1086, in the thirteenth year of his episcopate, in the ninth indiction, after seven full years had already passed since the excommunication of Henry, formerly king, and nine months and twenty-three days after the passing of the most blessed Pope Gregory VII, the venerable lord and our Father Anselm, bishop of Lucca, fell asleep in the Lord on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the city of Mantua, while the most reverend Bishop Ubaldus presided and the most noble duchess and marchioness Matilda ruled there.

### XII

On the third night after the venerable death of the most holy Father, a certain crippled woman—who always crawled along the ground on one hand and her hindquarters rather than walking—had remained for a year, two months, and half a month in the house of the bishop’s nephew, near the tomb of the aforesaid Father. During the first watch of the night she was restored upright and healed by his merits. [Note: [Col. 0924D] Baronius cites this under the year 1086, no. 11.]

### XIII

On the following day, about the third hour, as it appeared, a certain woman who had been blind from birth is said to have received her sight there. We heard at that time that she was an inhabitant of the county of Brescia.

### XIV

On that same day, at about the sixth hour, a certain poor man in the hospice for the poor belonging to the aforesaid Bishop of Mantua—who had been supported there for some time by alms and was bent forward from the waist—prayed at the tomb of the same holy Father and suddenly rose upright, healed.

### XV

When such miracles had been spread far and wide, behold, a certain woman from the castle called Capitellum, who had completely lost her sight, began to insist that her husband take her to the body of the holy man. When he refused, her brother, moved by compassion, yoked oxen to a cart and began to carry her. But when he had traveled about two miles, she began to see the trees, the cart, the oxen, and everything else. Giving thanks to God and to his holy confessor, and making a vow from her poverty, she returned home.

### XVI

On the ninth day, another woman in the same castle, crippled in her legs and lower back, was unable, from sheer necessity, to get out of her bed by herself. She obtained from a certain citizen of Mantua who had come there that she be placed on his cart. He carried her to the city and bore her on his shoulders to the tomb of the holy bishop. After she had prayed for some time, she rose shortly afterward healed.

### XVII

On the eleventh day, a certain woman from the castle called Goudium, who had been deprived of her sight for twenty months, remained fasting for two days beside the holy body and recovered the former clarity of her eyes.

### XVIII

On the fifteenth day, another woman from the castle called, as they say, Lazese, crippled in hand and foot, with her mouth twisted and suffering severely from epilepsy, endured her affliction there for some time and recovered complete health.

### XIX

On the sixteenth day thereafter, while the most glorious Lady Matilda was present with us and we were singing psalms on Good Friday, a certain woman from a place called Coloniole arrived. She had lost her sight and came weeping and wailing, making the most devout prostrations. After rising some time later, she wiped her eyes on the tomb’s cloth and recovered her sight.

### XX

On the eighteenth day, a woman of the same city, not unknown there, was tormented by toothache and pain in her entrails. Fleeing to the tomb of the aforesaid confessor, she was immediately healed.

### XXI

Another woman from the town called Castellucule had become so ill that she could not rise from her bed in any way. After hearing of all these miracles, she made a vow and shortly afterward escaped her illness. On the eighth day she came on foot to the holy man’s tomb and fulfilled the vow herself.

### XXII

On the twenty-first day, there was also a citizen of Mantua who, when a film had formed over one eye, had lost the sight of it. After spending much money on physicians and accomplishing nothing, he fled to the true physician of salvation through the merits of the aforesaid most holy bishop, and recovered his sight.

### XXIII

On the twenty-third day, a boy from a village called Vadumferratum, whom arthritis [or: an arthritic disease; the manuscript reads *arthetica*, perhaps for *artritica*] had deprived of the use of his arms, was carried to the same oratory and recovered his health.

### XXIV

On the twenty-fourth day, another boy from Burbassic, deprived of the light of his eyes and suffering as though from dropsy, was repeatedly admonished in dreams and at last fled to the protection of the most holy Father, escaping his illness.

### XXV

On the thirty-first day, there was a priest from the bishopric of Brescia, from a castle named Gorelengo. A disease which, by an antiphrasis, people call “good” had taken away the sight of one of his eyes. Having heard the report of so many signs, he hurried to the holy tomb. After praying there, he set out on his return. When some itching on the road provoked him to rub his eye with his finger, he opened his eyelids and immediately saw clearly. Returning, therefore, to the city, he gave thanks before everyone for such a merciful protection.

### XXVI

On the night following the thirty-first day, a certain woman from a castle named Maratica, near the port of Lignacum in the county of Verona, had her left hand closed and that entire side of her body deprived of movement by a paralytic stroke. On the thirtieth day after the death of the same holy bishop, she prayed at his tomb and rose healed.

### XXVII

A certain cripple from the county of Milan, from the parish of Rosade, had also come. In that contracted condition he had already gone about visiting many saints’ thresholds, seeking health. Throwing himself down before the holy tomb and praying, he was immediately made well.

### XXVIII

On the thirty-ninth day, something occurred that was joyful and marvelous in the eyes of many. During the litanies called Gregorian, when an innumerable multitude of people was hastening to the aforementioned city of Mantua, certain men came from a village named Fornicata and another called Blittolo, with banners and sacred relics, as is customary. Along the road they saw a large hind. At the prompting of one of their priests, they began to invoke the omnipotence of God, asking that, through the merits of his most holy priest, to whom they were devoutly traveling, he might grant the animal to them unharmed. And so it happened. It stood still, as though fixed to the spot. They placed a cord around its neck and led it most gently all the way to the tomb of the venerable confessor.

An immeasurable crowd then gathered. Some tore out its hairs as a sign of the truth. Others desired only to see it. All marveled at it with composure. But because it was pregnant, it could not endure such pressure. It reached the tomb, however, and there collapsed. Shortly afterward, since it could not live, it was killed; its flesh was divided into various portions as a blessing, and it certainly restored health to many sick people. But what follows is no less praiseworthy and glorious.

When these same people were returning after completing their prayer, they came to a body of water which they could not cross except by boat. To make the works of God manifest, one boat had been taken across to the other side. They waited a long time, somewhat saddened because they were fasting and tired. Recalling the earlier miracle, they again invoked God, asking that through the merits of his holy confessor Anselm he might provide a means of crossing. Scarcely had they finished praying when, behold, the boat, released and without any oarsman, came to them. Giving thanks to God and to his most holy confessor, they all crossed safely. Many people suffering from various pains were healed by pieces of wood from that boat.

### XXIX

We also wish you to know of your holy desire—not because we learned it from elsewhere, but because we ourselves saw and did it. The venerable countess whom we mentioned was at the siege of a certain castle. There a certain German was struck in the head by a stone. Three days later he was brought to our hospice, so that he might have greater peace there than among laymen.

Then a stroke, which physicians call paralysis, attacked him so cruelly that he became completely deranged: he felt nothing properly and recognized no one. At last we were summoned so that, after imposing a penance upon him, we might give him Communion. But we could not make him understand even what penance was. Finally, we could not make him acknowledge what God was, nor invoke God or any saint. We were entirely convinced that he was possessed by a demon.

For he shouted, as madmen do, many inappropriate things in a loud voice; and unless he was held by force, he would have torn apart not only his clothing but also his limbs. A cry was heard everywhere; many people hurried there, some lamenting, others marveling. We too heard in the lady’s chamber his pitiable voice. Moved by divine inspiration, she told me to wash in water a ring that had belonged to Saint Anselm, which the blessed Pope Gregory had also possessed for some time, and to give the water to the sick man to drink, hoping that he might be freed through their merits.

I rose, took the ring, and went to him. I found him shouting and tearing himself apart in a marvelous fashion. Although five strong men held him—two by the legs, two by the arms, and one by the head—he struggled with his chest and stomach more violently than I could have believed had I not seen it myself.

We therefore placed the ring inside the water in the name of the Lord. With great force we opened his mouth and, using a spoon, scarcely managed at first to give him a little drink. Not long afterward he called me by name and began to recognize my voice. Immediately prompted, he invoked Saint Anselm. To put it briefly, after about an hour, I think, through the merits of the holy confessors who had used that same ring in the divine office, he became completely peaceful and spoke rationally.

Many people were present at this miracle. They saw and heard what happened and glorified the mercy of God in his holy confessors.

These very few accounts concerning the most blessed Father and our patron, Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca—few indeed in comparison with his merits, but, I hope, beneficial to your pious desires—I, B., his sinful priest in penance, not his son, I say, but his servant, promoted by him with many tears to that same order, have devoutly explained to you at your venerable request. I ask you: pray for me.

What follows was written by more recent authors, either because they themselves saw these things or because they learned of them from faithful people.

### XXX

On the forty-ninth day after the holy man’s passing, with the sun already setting, the Lord deigned to show this miracle through his servant. A certain woman from the bishopric of Cremona, from the district called Cancer, came to the tomb of our most holy Father. A film had completely taken away the sight of one of her eyes; in the other she could scarcely see during the day. After persisting in prayer for some time, she recovered the clarity of the blinded eye through the merits of the holy bishop. As for the other eye, for which previously even noon had scarcely provided enough light to see, now the twilight of night is sufficient.

### XXXI

A great multitude from the city and bishopric of Brescia had gathered in the city of Mantua for the veneration of the holy man. Among them were certain people who came under the pretext of religion—or rather, from a motive of hypocrisy. To refute their unbelief and strengthen the faith of those who were present there, the almighty Lord displayed his mercy.

An old man from the household of Manfredus, from a place called Pigognata, had been deprived of the use of his legs for three months because of an incision in one knee, which was followed by a stroke affecting the other as well. Through the merits of the blessed Anselm, he was restored to his former health on the fiftieth day after the saint’s death.

### XXXII

**Bishop Ubaldus of Mantua to Lady Matilda: joy and gladness.** [Note: [Col. 0927D] Baronius cites this letter under the year 1086, no. 12.]

We write to you of the joy desired by your immense longing. There was a certain woman from Capriana who went on her hands and feet like an animal. Almighty God, through the merits of our most holy Father, raised her upright and granted her the use of her legs for walking, as human nature requires.

### XXXIII

He likewise deigned to grant similar relief to a certain person from the island of Parma, which lies near the head of the Parmula, who was similarly bent over.

### XXXIV

Moreover, a certain boy from Monte Claro had a contracted hand and foot. God restored the use of both to him through the prayers of the most blessed bishop.

### XXXV

A certain woman from a place called Insula Ogeru [Baronius: Egeni], who had a withered hand, also received the desired healing through the intercession of the same patron of ours.

### XXXVI

He also restored the sight of a certain boy from Ripalta [Baronius: Rivalta].

### XXXVII

Similarly, a certain woman from the bishopric of Verona recovered the clarity of her eyes when she was already approaching our city.

### XXXVIII

A certain man from Plevazano [Baronius: Plovizano], whose heels were immovably attached to his buttocks, was restored to his former health. We showed him to the lord and religious man, the archbishop of Lyon, and pointed out the place where his heels had been joined.

Many people from the bishoprics of Brescia and Verona and from various other regions had gathered for the veneration of the man on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension. Seeing these things take place, they were converted to the Lord, renouncing the devil and his followers, and promising that, if they should come into such danger, they would sooner endure the shedding of their blood than fall away from this faith.

All these things happened on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension and during the following night, along with many others which, because of the multitude, we were unable to discover. If we find them, we shall write to you. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Thus far the letter of Ubaldus.]

### XXXIX

There was also a certain woman from a castle called Gudiciole. Because her foot could not reach the ground owing to the contraction of her knee, she walked bent over and could scarcely support her weak limbs with two staffs. After asking for the mercy of the holy bishop for several days, she obtained a healing remedy for her affliction.

### XL

There was likewise a certain man noble by birth, named Adecherius. For two days blood had burst from his nostrils as though from a vein struck by iron, and he was already thinking only of awaiting death. When no medical treatment could restrain the blood that continued to break forth, he called upon the holy bishop and vowed that he would go to his body. Through the merits and prayers of the most holy man, he escaped the danger of impending death.

### XLI

[Note: [Col. 0929D] A second letter of Ubaldus, bishop of Mantua, to the same most illustrious Lady Matilda.]

I wish to present to your knowledge certain miracles that had either been consigned to oblivion or were previously unknown but have now been discovered. The people of Brescia of whom I recently wrote to you were returning joyfully. When they had reached the ford somewhat above Godium, they found no boat, yet they felt no distress in their hearts, placing all their confidence in God and Saint Anselm.

While they were waiting, they saw on the opposite bank a certain horse which, dying and gasping, had lain there for three days without food or drink. One of them confidently asked God and Saint Anselm that it might rise and carry them all across. It immediately rose and offered itself for transporting them.

Behold how magnificent are the merits of our Father! Behold how commanding his power! The law of death is broken; it complains that its rights are altered; the one subject to death is snatched away, life is granted, life is restored, so that he may serve the servants of God. He who could not carry himself was prepared to carry a burden, and offers himself so obediently for service as though he possessed reason. He seems to wish to say: “If nature allowed it, why do you not mount me? Why do you not employ me in your service? I was restored to life and snatched from the jaws of death for no other reason.”

Meanwhile, certain sailors saw them waiting on the bank and came in a boat to carry them across, hoping to receive payment from them. They entered the boat and crossed safely.

Behold how much the horse labored to show itself obedient and how it strove to make its willingness to serve manifest! What it cannot say with its mouth, it professes through the movement of its body. When the boat crossed, it crossed; when the boat returned, it returned. Finally, after carrying them all across, it went back to the place from which it had come, and shortly afterward ended its life there.

### XLII

A certain boy from Cremona was carried by several of his neighbors to the holy man’s tomb. He had a withered hand. They reverently and confidently—and, because of their great confidence, almost threateningly—asked for his healing, saying:

“Most merciful bishop, holy Anselm, confessor of God, hear us as we pray for your servant. If we have deserved anything from you in life, if we faithfully received your preaching, if we preserved an uncorrupted faith, if we steadfastly resisted those who opposed you, hear us, help him, and set him free. You have healed many unbelievers; grant at least one to the faithful, lest our enemies perhaps mock us, saying: ‘Now it is clear how grateful and faithful you were to him in life. If he had loved you in life, he would also have honored you in death; but because he judged you unworthy, detestable, and contemptible, he made you strangers to so great a grace.’ Drive this reproach from us, most merciful Father, and quickly bring forth our joy. Show yourself favorable to us, for we have always looked to you alone, whom we set before ourselves as a mirror to behold, from whom we ask assistance.”

While they prayed so devoutly, the boy obtained the healing for which they asked through their prayers. A certain Hermannus of Scorzariolo, who likewise had a contracted hand, obtained the same healing.

[Note: [Col. 0930D] After this, no further numbers are marked in our copy.]

Moreover, a certain woman who always looked down at the ground with her head bowed and could not walk unless supported by a staff was raised upright at the tomb of the aforesaid Father, in the sight of many people. I did not record her place of origin, because it could not be discovered amid the multitude.

On the third day before the Lord’s Ascension, two miracles occurred. A certain woman from the bishopric of Cremona, from a place called Casa Anserii, recovered through the intercession of the most holy patron the sight which she had lost for eight years.

[Col. 0930B] On that same day, a certain woman from the abbey of Leon, who had a withered right hand, which she always held near her shoulder because the arm’s nerves were contracted, and whose knee on that same side was so contracted that she could scarcely touch the ground with the tips of her toes, found healing from both afflictions at the tomb of our holy Father.

Among the works which God magnificently performed through his servant at the Ascension of his Son, I eagerly report to your desire a marvelous manifestation of his power, later related to me by the very man to whom the Author of our salvation granted his healing.

There was a certain man from your village near Rosina, named Ciliano, who complained less that the straightness of his loins [read: knees] had been denied him than that the strength of his hands had been entirely taken away. For, when a terrible stroke pressed upon him, they trembled so violently that he could do and hold nothing. The Lord therefore revealed to him in a vision that, if he reverently vowed to go to the tomb of the most holy Anselm, he would immediately rejoice in receiving healing from both infirmities.

When he awoke, he considered the vision, uncertain what to do and doubtful what to believe, disbelieving the revelation but desiring health. He summoned certain good men from his neighborhood, related the vision, and received their advice to make the vow. Once he had made it, he immediately recovered.

Likewise, a certain woman from Fossa Capraria, bent at the loins [read: knees], deprived of the use of her legs and for a long time using staffs in their place, had already reached the tomb of our Father. With the sun already setting, she suddenly recovered from her severe and varied infirmity.

A certain honorable matron, the mother of John of Persico, reported this to me, and I thought it should also be reported to you. Full of faith, perfected in the love of God, and instructed in the discipline of the most holy Anselm, she rejected the ministry of her priests because of the excommunication. One day, while asking those around her where she could find someone worthy and suitable to celebrate Mass, a certain man from Casale Maggiore who was standing there said:

“Why do you despise the ministry of your priests?”

“Because of love for and the preaching of Saint Anselm,” she replied, “for whose merits the almighty Lord performs miracles every day.”

The man said: “Now I beg you, pray to him with all your heart that, if he has raised anyone upright, he may cripple me; or, if he has given sight to anyone, he may take away my sight.”

Scarcely had he finished speaking when he felt God’s vengeance upon him. He immediately bent over to one side and began to limp badly. When the matron saw this, she began to pray to God more fervently, asking him still to increase the punishment of this son of unbelief. At once the pain grew so severe that he could scarcely reach the hospice and was left there as though dead.

As this matron was coming to give thanks to God and Saint Anselm, a certain well-known man from the hills of Guibertus met her. He was already returning from the city and told her the great miracle that had happened to him.

One night he had gone to the river Oleum to draw water. Because the bank was high, he extended a hook, but the current carried away his bucket. Since the night was dark, it also carried off his torch. When he saw the bucket being swept away by the river’s whirlpool, he asked Saint Anselm to return it to him. After praying, he lowered the hook; when he had come scarcely two cubits from the water, the handle of the bucket immediately rose and caught upon the hook.

Through the merits of the same most holy Father, a certain nun from the regions beyond the Alps, from a village called Gamudium situated near the castle of Cisne, recovered the sight of one eye. By the grace of God she now sees more clearly with the other, with which she had previously seen only a little.

A certain woman from the bishopric of Cremona, from a castle named Benengo situated near Jovisalta, had a twelve-year-old boy who, from the days of his birth, had never known how to walk because his nerves were contracted. His mother, eager for his healing, full of devotion and perfect in faith, vowed to carry him to venerate the saint. As she brought him along, already exhausted by the burden, she set him down when she came to the royal road. Through the faith and devotion of which he had always been deprived, he immediately found healing.

Moreover, a certain woman from Wartalda, warned beforehand in a dream and trusting the revelation, came to implore the healing assistance of our holy Father. She suffered so severely from dropsy that she could not carry herself. Her body had swollen so greatly that she could scarcely contain it without bursting. It could no longer be called a body, but rather a trunk; no human form appeared in her, but she was entirely misshapen, a kind of image of death. The joints of her hands and feet had become solid and immovable. Her form and the sockets of her eyes had been destroyed; death seemed nearer than life, yet she did not despair of healing. It was therefore fitting that the most holy Anselm grant her the grace of healing from whom she expected so great a remedy, and on the following night she rejoiced that she had obtained it.

As I have just learned from Count Guifred and Sigefred of Beredo, his soldier, I write this to you. While you and the abbess of Saint Paul of Parma were staying at Mantua, his soldiers, having heard of many signs performed by the holy man, wished to go to his venerable tomb for prayer. They asked a certain man named Alberic, son of Alberic of Palmia, to go with them to seek pardon for his sins.

“As I would go to a donkey,” he said, “with foolish and envious speech, so I shall go to him—unless, perhaps, it is merely for the sake of mockery—to obtain his help.”

They rebuked him and insulted him, and finally compelled him to come with them. On the last day, a certain cripple had been brought there, whom they wished to see lying prostrate at the tomb. They approached, prayed reverently, kissed the stone of the tomb, and returned joyfully.

The man, wishing also to approach in order to see the one who had been healed, was prevented from coming within about two paces of the tomb, as though he were unworthy and a blasphemer. His feet clung heavily and sluggishly to the ground. Believing that his legs had been bound with bandages, he went outside. Discovering that nothing had actually obstructed him, he entered again, but was unable to go beyond the same limit.

Grieved that he had been rejected so many times, he went out in shame, wondering and astonished why this had happened to him. Meanwhile, a certain blind man was given sight. He recognized his own folly and, repenting of his curse, wept bitterly. Finally, when he was returning from Saint Andrew’s with the canons after singing praises, he poured out many tears before the door of Saint Peter. Like the others, he was granted access to the tomb of our Father.

For fear that his companions might reproach him, he kept silent. But now, to the glory of God and of the most holy Anselm, he proclaims everywhere what happened to him.

When several people from Brescia had come to venerate our Father’s tomb, they met a certain poor man who was likewise coming to seek healing from the bishopric of Como, from Valtellina. He was bent forward and could not walk unless supported by staffs. They took him with them and, out of charity in honor of the most holy Anselm, gave him the means to travel.

To confirm their faith and increase their devotion, the Lord, through the intercession of the aforesaid Father, raised him upright on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, when night was already approaching, and allowed him to walk without the support of staffs.

[Col. 0932D] Moreover, he restored hearing to a certain boy who had been deaf and mute from the days of his birth. This happened through the merits of the most holy Anselm shortly after his passing, without our knowing of it. On the second day of the month of June, about the ninth hour, he also released the bond of the boy’s tongue, in accordance with what is read in the Gospel: “He has done all things well; he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark 7).

[Note: [Col. 0931] From a letter of a certain Hugh to the bishop of Mantua.]

I was not reluctant, venerable Father, Bishop of Mantua, to write to your paternal reverence, as you commanded, of another miracle which I learned from Vitalis, a fellow priest of the Church of Brescia, a man of religious life, and from several others who reported it.

In a village called Murana, seven miles from the city of Brescia, there was a certain woman who had a daughter so deprived of the use of her tongue and feet that she could not rise in any way unless someone else carried her. One day, as she customarily carried the crippled girl outside the house, sighing from weariness at her daily labor, she said:

“Most merciful God, through the merits of your most holy confessor Anselm, have mercy on my affliction: either restore this wretched girl, already half-dead, to health, or take her from this present life and free me from such great labor. Otherwise, I leave her here to you. Do what pleases you, because from now on I shall endure no labor for her.”

Having said this, she went away, leaving her daughter behind, as she had said. After a short interval of time, she returned home and found the girl whom she had left to the most holy Anselm healed. She heard her, who shortly before had possessed a tongue bound fast, clearly and readily uttering words. Astonished and rejoicing at what had happened, the woman gave praise to the Lord and to the holy bishop for her daughter’s restored health.

From the account of the priest Otto, a man of praiseworthy life, corroborated by certain citizens of Cremona, I also learned another miracle which must not be passed over in silence.

One day, as several men from Cremona were riding outside the city, they began speaking among themselves in various ways about certain miracles which the Lord performs through the merits of the most holy confessor Anselm. As they discussed these things with one another, one of them, being of a faithless mind, asked them mockingly whether they believed such vanities or that God displayed miracles through Anselm.

When they replied that he was undoubtedly a holy servant of God, glorified by many signs of miracles, that faithless man said:

“If he is a saint, as you say, or if he has restored anyone’s ability to walk, let him now cripple the horse on which I am sitting.”

And so it happened. For after proceeding a short distance, the horse immediately stood still, its limbs contracted, and the aforesaid man suffered from the affliction for a long time, until he resolved to go humbly to the holy body.

I also learned from my mother, who related it concerning herself, something that must not be handed over to oblivion. One day a stroke suddenly came upon her, covering the sight of one eye with blood so completely that she could not even look straight at the ground. As pain in the eye pressed upon her, she fled to the tomb of the holy confessor and humbly asked relief for her pain in these words:

“Most holy confessor, bring me healing medicine. For I shall seek no physician except you. You are able to bring salutary help to my infirmity.”

After rubbing her eye against the stone covering the chest in which the saint’s body lay, she returned home. I myself bear witness that the harmful stroke immediately withdrew.

From the report of Vitalis, a presbyter of the Church of Lodi, given in the hearing of many, as were the other accounts, I learned of an event worthy of remembrance; he had himself been present at it. His faith and life, long since proven in the service of God, unmistakably show that credence ought to be given to his testimony.

Arialdus, the brother of the most holy confessor Anselm, had a five-year-old daughter who was worn out by the violence of fevers. Moreover, from the opening of her little ear, a drop—said to produce a fistula—continually dripped a certain putrefaction, drop by drop, which also caused disgust to those approaching her. The girl’s parents gave her to drink some of the water in which they had washed a fragment of wood from the ship [whose miracle was recorded above], invoking the most holy confessor to assist their niece. When she had drunk it, the girl was immediately freed from both illnesses.

The event I am now relating I learned from the account and testimony of the Lady Countess Matilda [Col. 0934B]. We know that her attestation must be believed without hesitation, because of her proven faith and religious character. It also became known to me personally through the assertion of the same girl to whom this happened:

One night a sudden pain, as often before, cruelly tormented a girl named Athelasi(a), the daughter of Marquis Azzo, who was staying in the chamber of the aforesaid lady, in the region of her abdomen, and compelled her to utter loud cries. When the aforementioned lady asked what was wrong, she was told that the girl was repeatedly invoking Saint Anselm’s aid. At the lady’s command, a cushion on which the holy bishop, while alive, had been accustomed to sit was placed against that part of the girl’s body where the pain was afflicting her. Immediately the girl cried out [Col. 0934C] that she had been freed from all pain.

From the testimony of a certain man named Constantius I learned of another event that ought to be committed to memory. An illness had come upon a boy, the squire of a certain soldier, and had so choked his voice that he could scarcely be heard even by those a little way off. Since, because his voice was obstructed, he could not call his master by shouting, he had a horn, by whose sound he indicated where he was. Thus, when he came with the aforementioned Constantius to the tomb of the holy confessor, devoutly asking relief for his strangled voice, he obtained such restoration of his voice that he can now be heard even by people at a considerable distance.

After completing his prayer devoutly, the aforesaid Constantius reverently scraped away some dust from the stone of the holy confessor’s tomb. The custodian reverently received it, and Constantius carried it away with him. Having mixed it with water, he gave it to drink, invoking the aid of the most holy bishop, to a certain woman suffering greatly from the violence of a fever. As soon as the woman had drunk the water, the fever’s entire affliction was driven away, and she immediately recovered.

A certain citizen of the city of Mantua, named Oddo Martini Canevarius, was compelled by such an agony of pain that his entire body was frequently covered with watery sweat because of it. Since he was tormented by the persistent force of an excessive pain, he said that he could be cured only by this remedy: if he were allowed, after tearing his clothes, to split open his chest with a knife. When he was already thinking only of awaiting death, the cushion on which the holy bishop had sat while living was brought. When it had been placed upon his chest [Col. 0935A], and the name of the holy bishop had been invoked, all the pain immediately departed.

From the report of Guido and Vitalis, presbyters of the Lucchese diocese and men of honorable life, and likewise under the testimony of Allucio, a nobleman of the city of Lucca, I learned the event I am relating; they had been present at this miracle.

A certain man had one hand contracted beside the arm. The brother of the aforementioned Allucio, out of compassion, had long provided him with what he needed in his own house. The aforesaid presbyters, together with the aforementioned Allucio, placing the greatest confidence in the mercy of the most holy bishop, led the man with the contracted hand to a certain church, in which the priest Guido had deposited some garments of the holy bishop out of reverence and honor. [Col. 0935B]

As they prayed together and made their request with great devotion, asking that God, to confound and overcome the wickedness of Peter, the heretic and usurper of the Church of Lucca, should reveal in this man the wondrous glory of the most holy pontiff, the man whose hand had been contracted was healed.

The aforesaid priests, beholding the joy of so illustrious a deed, ordered the healed man, under obedience, to hurry to the city of Lucca with a raised cross, so that the crowds of the people, seeing this man—whom shortly before they had known to be crippled—miraculously healed by the Lord’s mercy, might at least repent because they had without cause driven the holy bishop from his own see, where he had proclaimed a life of holiness, and so that those who had refused to believe his words might believe such evident works. But the heretic Peter, who, even laying hands upon the Lord’s anointed, did not fear to presume to expel the holy pontiff from his own see and wickedly seize it for himself, hardened in heart by the signs and wonders he had seen, still persisted in the unbelief of his wickedness.

Finally, that impious man, considering that this had occurred to his own confusion and harm, attempted to thrust the healed man into custody, wishing by such treachery to conceal the sign of this event. But, because the word of God is never bound (2 Tim. 2), and because he feared that the people would on this account be stirred against him, he shamefully allowed the man whom he had imprisoned to depart.

Under the testimony of the same men I also learned of another remarkably wondrous miracle. The people of a place called Castellonium had long been digging a deep well, but by no art or ingenuity could they find a vein of water. When, exhausted by their long labor and despairing of finding water, they were ready to give up in vain effort, they began to encourage one another, saying:

“Let us unanimously beseech the Lord, through the persistence of our prayers and the generosity of our almsgiving, that by the merits of the most holy bishop Anselm he may grant us to find the water for which we have long labored in vain.”

As they practiced charity by giving alms to the poor, a boy suddenly arrived announcing that an abundant supply of water had been found in the well.

This event became known to me and to many others through a letter addressed by the archdeacon of the Church of Treviso to the Lady Matilda and through the report of the messenger who brought it. [Col. 0936A]

There was a certain man named Lanzo the Judge, by origin a Milanese and by residence a man of Treviso. He had been severely afflicted by a violently advancing illness—[the manuscript’s reading is uncertain: “ficus”]—and by the disease of gout, which grievously affected his feet; he had been deprived of the use of his legs, and no rest of sleep was granted him at all. Since his strength was already failing and he could scarcely turn himself in bed, a rope had been fastened above the bed, with whose assistance he shifted himself from one side to another.

One day, therefore, after sighing and shedding abundant tears, he began to pray in these words:

“God, through the merits of Saint Anselm, whose wondrous glory I hear of, show in me also the clemency of your power. Holy confessor, remember the friendship that joined us as companions in our studies. Most merciful bishop, may the words of friendship that I so often exchanged with you benefit me. I shall come to venerate your tomb, if you grant me the joy of health.”

Thus, after being overcome by the sleep of slumber, he rested through the whole of the following night until the next day. When morning came, he felt that he was already recovering, and immediately began to walk confidently. Thus freed through the mercy of the holy bishop, he now rejoices that he has been restored to excellent health. [Col. 0936B]

Moreover, there was a young man who had been deprived from birth of hearing and of the use of his tongue. He had stayed with us for more than two months and had made known his illness to us and to many others with certainty. Four times in dreams he saw the holy pontiff opening his ears, at his request, beside the holy tomb, and likewise loosening the bond of his tongue.

Accordingly, coming to the holy body as he had been instructed, moaning and beating his breast, he devoutly asked for the aid of the most holy bishop to the extent of his strength. After persevering in prayer for several days, he obtained the joy of hearing and the full ability to speak distinctly. We who were present saw this, as did almost the entire population of our city. [Col. 0936C]

Furthermore, a certain woman had long been deprived of sight. When gout attacked her, she was afflicted for a time by such a severe headache that, driven mad by her anguish, she gnawed her own limbs. With the encouragement and assistance of Opizo of Gonzaga, she was brought to the tomb of the holy confessor; there she was freed from the torment of gout and likewise recovered the joy of light. The aforementioned Opizo, who had long provided her with bodily sustenance out of compassion in his own house, is a witness to her former illness. [Col. 0936D]

In the estate of the canons of blessed Peter, in a place called the village of Saint Laurence, there was a certain woman whose nose had swollen horribly, while a burning internal heat discharged pus. Devoutly beseeching the holy bishop, she obtained the salvation she desired.

Likewise, a boy from Sacciula had been deprived of the joy of light. Returning from Cremona, he was hastening to the tomb of the holy bishop, from which he had departed only a few days before. Eagerly hurrying back to the holy body, he struck his feet very frequently against stones, since he was utterly unable to see what lay before him. Thus grieving and groaning, he humbly begged the holy confessor to deign to look upon so great a calamity. As he prayed in this manner along the road, the remedy of the light he desired met him while he was coming. [Col. 0937A]

Likewise, a certain man from the diocese of Treviso could not open his eyes for his own use. He too came to venerate the tomb and received the joy of the light he desired.

There was likewise a girl in a village to which common usage had given the name Mairana, not far from the city of Brescia. She had been deprived of the use of her tongue and was unable to use any of her limbs properly except her right hand. Her wretched mother, seeing her half-dead, solemnly vowed in devotion that she would carry her to the mercy of the most holy confessor, like another Canaanite woman interceding for her daughter (Matt. 15). [Col. 0937B]

In accordance with the promise of her vow, while her parents were carrying her, the girl recovered on the road both the use of her tongue and the use of all her limbs. We saw her giving thanks to God beside the holy tomb, and her father giving testimony to this event.

When many people were coming to the holy body to obtain healing for their illnesses, a certain man from a place called Carpum, situated beyond the Adige and near the port of Lignano, also arrived. He had a contracted hand and an arm weakened by wasting; he received the benefit of healing during the journey itself.

We also learned of an event worthy of remembrance, related by the Lady Matilda, the venerable countess, concerning herself. Her testimony is confirmed by her most proven faith and by her life, which was likewise filled with religious devotion. The aforesaid lady had suffered excessively from fevers for many days, and a severe headache had exhausted her. One day, as usual, she was present at the solemn Mass. While the Gospel was being read, she strove to rise to her feet but, worn down by her illness, immediately fell.

Beside her, out of reverence, there lay in the bishop’s chapel a wooden board on which the holy body had been washed for the funeral rites after the bishop had breathed his last. Humbly asking for the holy man’s aid and drawing her forehead across the aforesaid board, she was immediately freed from her headache. [Col. 0937C]

Not many days later, the hands and almost her entire body had been horribly covered with no small number of breaks or eruptions of scabies. Since she had in her hands the episcopal ring which the bishop of God had used in the celebration of Mass, she began to consider that the merits of so great a bishop might come to her aid, even through contact with the ring with which he had offered many sacrifices to God. Thus, placing the ring upon the eruptions, she was healed of her illness from that day onward. [Col. 0937D]

A few days later, the sight of the aforementioned most Christian lady had become so disturbed that at night she was afraid to devote herself to reading as usual. During the solemn celebration of Mass, she held in her hands a prayer which the holy pontiff had written for that lady in his own hand, a sheet intended for her use in prayer and containing the written prayer. She placed it upon her eyes and wiped them with it. Thereafter, having recovered the brightness of light, she was no longer afraid, as before, to continue reading by night and by day.

A certain Everardus, a Frank by origin and a presbyter by rank, was staying with us. A sudden attack of gout had made the two little fingers of one hand rigid, as well as part of the palm and the joint by which the hand is joined to the arm, so severely that he could not bend the hand for any use. Since the strength of his entire arm had also failed, a strap tied around his neck supported the suspended arm.

While he was dining with his companions, a poor woman came, asking for alms out of charity for Saint Anselm. He held out a piece of broken bread to her with his hand, and immediately he was healed of the illness described above. [Col. 0938B]

Let no one with a perverse mind presume to claim that the event I am now attempting to relate is fabricated or fabulous. The man himself, to whom this happened, is present as a witness: after breaking no small number of chains, he was miraculously freed from the distress of imprisonment through the aid of the most holy confessor Anselm. The broken chains bear witness before the bishops present; in the hearing of the people he proclaimed, and continues to proclaim, the pitiable misery of his captivity and the joy of his liberation, which ought to be proclaimed.

As the storm of a powerful persecution against Saint Gregory VII, the worthy apostolic bishop of the Roman Church, was increasing—as is known throughout the world—because of his preaching of truth and justice, and against the Catholics of the entire Roman Empire, while the most Christian Countess Matilda was likewise exerting all her strength in defense of the Church, Ubertus, son of Ardicio and one of the aforementioned lady’s captains, wished the lady to have unquestioning confidence in his loyalty and service during this disturbance.

Among many other pledges of loyalty, he compelled all those to whom he had entrusted the custody of his fortresses to swear that, if Ubertus should act disloyally against the lady or maliciously plot anything against her, they would freely hand over to the power of the aforementioned lady the strongholds they guarded and thereafter remain faithful to her.

After Ubertus was captured because of the wickedness of his disloyalty, his men, contrary to the pledges of their oath, did not hesitate to do whatever harm they could against the same lady.

From their number was a certain Lanfrancus, called “of Piola,” a knight by office. Because he refused to join in their perversities, he was captured by their ambushes and treacheries, and from the month of August until the eighth day before the Kalends of April he was subjected to a harsh imprisonment and bound with no small number of chains. Those same malicious men were also considering how they could take his life, though they did not want it to be known that this had been done by their design.

While he was bound by so many hardships and awaited only death, on the vigil of the holy bishop Anselm he fell asleep. In his sleep he seemed to see the most holy bishop walking before him in the clothing in which he had been accustomed to walk while still alive.

Immediately he cried out to him, saying:

“Saint Anselm, how aptly and usefully I served you many times! You often promised me that you would reward me well for my service. Behold my sufferings and, since you are able, bring me help. And since you were in no way deceived, now fulfill your promises. Never could you repay the service I rendered you more suitably than now. At least restore me to the church, which they prevent me from entering.”

The most merciful bishop of God said to him:

“Do not fear. I shall restore you to the church.”

Immediately it seemed to him that the bishop led him into a certain church, marked him with the sign of the cross, and blessed him. Then he said to him:

“Behold, you have been restored to the church.”

The man replied:

“I rejoice greatly that I have been returned to the church; but I still implore your help, lord.”

The holy bishop consoled him kindly and said:

“From today, on the eighth day, I shall send you my knife and provide you with the necessary aid.” [Col. 0939B]

When the eighth day arrived, a certain man from the city of Reggio, previously unknown to him, came to him, carrying an extremely sharp file. Once it had been given to him, and while everyone watched and the guards who were present offered no resistance, he quickly cut through the fetters and chains.

When Lanfrancus hesitated to leave because of the guards, the most holy confessor suddenly arrived, and the Lady Matilda appeared to have arrived as well, followed by a crowd of people. She said to him:

“What are you waiting for before leaving? Do not delay. Rise confidently.”

He rose in the sight of the guards and departed unharmed.

The miracle of this account became known to us in the hearing of many, related and attested by the same woman to whom it happened.

In the summer of the past year, a certain woman from Ripalta had gone out into the fields, as was customary, to perform the work of beggars, taking her little daughter with her. At that time the plague of wolves had increased so greatly that they did not even fear snatching children from the sight of their parents.

While she was, as I have said, in the fields, a wolf suddenly seized her daughter. When the wretched mother saw her daughter being carried away, torn apart by the beast, she called upon the most holy Anselm with all the strength of her voice [Col. 0940A], asking him to bring aid both to herself and to her miserable daughter. Immediately, when the name of the most merciful bishop had been invoked, the rabid beast threw the girl from its mouth; it did not dare touch her and watched her from a distance.

The anxious mother, nevertheless trusting in the aid of the most holy confessor, hurried to help her daughter. As she led her away, the wolf followed them both. She repeatedly cried out for the aid of the holy bishop, and at last that beast’s hunger was restrained; both women were freed from its bites.

We saw the following event ourselves and decided that it must not be passed over in silence. A certain woman, crippled with her legs twisted beneath her, carried her entire body on her hands and buttocks. After long asking for the aid of the holy pontiff, she rose to venerate the tomb. We and many of our fellow citizens had known that she had previously been supported by alms. [Col. 0940B]

The son of the archpriest, Ubaldus by name, from Colurnius, is still present with us. He related this account and, often questioned, continues to relate it in the same way.

While he was studying the art of grammar in our city, he showed no devotion or reverence toward the holy confessor and disparaged his holy powers. One day, however, he was seized by a violent headache and, believing that because of the pain he was already near death, invoked the aid of the holy bishop. He promised that, once freed, he would thereafter believe and proclaim the glory of his powers, just as he had previously spoken perversely about him.

Exhausted throughout the night, around the hours of matins he was overcome by a gentle sleep. In dreams he saw the holy servant of God place his hand upon his head and bless him with the sign of the holy cross. When the vision had passed and he awoke, he realized that he had been freed from the torment of the pain. [Col. 0940C]

On the recently past feast of the Ascension, a certain woman from Godi, named Richilda and known to many, had for an entire year and more—beginning from Epiphany . . . . the remainder is lacking in the manuscript.

End of the Life of Saint Anselm, Bishop of Lucca.

THE LIFE OF COUNTESS MATILDA, IN TWO BOOKS, WRITTEN BY DOMNIZO THE PRESBYTER. A truly outstanding monument of antiquity, in which the reader will find much concerning the eminent holiness and moral innocence of Pope Gregory VII, and concerning Urban II and Paschal II. Now, for the first time, it is brought from darkness into light for the benefit of the orthodox Church.

[Col. 0939]

TO THE READER

The illustrious Cardinal Baronius frequently cites and reproduces in volumes XI and XII of his Annals verses by Domnizo the presbyter from the Life of Countess Matilda. Burning with the desire to obtain and publish the work of this author, Jacob Gretser wrote from Rome to the Reverend Father Ferdinand Alber, assistant of the Society of Jesus. Because of his singular courtesy and his ready willingness to serve the history of the Church well, Alber immediately arranged for a copy to be made from the Vatican manuscript and carried to Gretser in Germany. For this reason, all lovers of Catholic unity and haters of schisms owe many thanks to that excellent Father.

[Col. 0941]

If anyone thinks Domnizo’s verses too rough and uncultivated, let him remember that here it is not the wording but the subject or matter that is being sought. Let him also recall that the verses of the anonymous author On the Life of Charlemagne, published by Reineccius, are not even one hair more elegant; nor are the verses of Roswitha On the Deeds of the Othos, nor those of the unnamed versifier On the War of Henry IV against the Saxons. Yet Justus Reuber did not consider them unworthy of assigning them a place among the historical works he published.

Indeed, the Calvinist Guldinastus also seemed sufficiently polished to the man who, in his Miscellany, set him against Gregory VII and his defenders together with other schismatic authors. I pass over others brought to light by the innovators themselves, in whose company our Domnizo has no reason to blush—not to mention the books of Abbo On the Siege of the City of Paris and the books of the Philippid written by William of Nangis, which the illustrious Petrus Pithoeus brought out from the hiding places of libraries; sectarians read these without disgust.

They will immediately grow nauseated at Domnizo—not because of his unworked verses, but because he stood for Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II, the supreme pontiffs, against the schismatics. In this work he paints their deceptions, impostures, and wickedness in vivid colors, so that it is hardly surprising if he displeases a heretical and schismatic palate. But now let us faithfully render everything that we found in the Roman copy.

(As we have already noted, we follow Muratori, [Script. Ital., V]. EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGY.)

[Col. 0941]

PREFACE OF LUDOVICO ANTONIO MURATORI TO DONIZO’S POEM ON THE LIFE OF COUNTESS MATILDA

[Col. 0941A]

In the year of Christ 1046, the illustrious princess Countess Matilda was born from Boniface, duke and marquis of Tuscany, and Beatrice of Lorraine; in the year 1115 she was taken from the living. She was a woman most renowned both for the virtues of her mind and for her deeds and the extent of her territories, and the noblest glory of Italy and of her age.

Benedictus Luchinus, Dominicus Mellinus, Felix Contelorius, and Julius de Puteo have expressly committed her life to writing. But two men especially adorned this portion of history, men distinguished no less for learning than for refined judgment: namely, Francesco Maria Fiorentini, in his Italian-written Monuments of Countess Matilda, and Benedictus Bacchinius, abbot of Saint Peter of Modena of the Cassinese Order, in his Italian History of the Monastery of Polirone.

[Col. 0941B]

Yet one author surpassed all these writers and indeed supplied much of the material concerning the deeds of Countess Matilda: Donizo, who both saw the distinguished deeds of that most courageous woman himself and expressed them in verse.

Certainly, unless time had snatched this writer from us, as it has so many others, we would possess a less mutilated and less heavily obscured history of Matilda and her ancestors. I say “of her ancestors,” for he begins his account with them and includes much about them that would be sought in vain elsewhere.

He carried out his task in a truly rough and disordered style, devoid of every poetic color, so that without doubt one would continually call him a barbarous and iron-age writer. But what he lacked in elegance of style was sufficiently supplied by his love of truth and a certain appearance of sincerity. [Col. 0941C]

Moreover, he himself was a witness of the events he relates that took place during Matilda’s lifetime. I will set aside the common belief that he served as chaplain to the same countess—for I do not see by what documents this is affirmed, and indeed I think it false. Certainly, he wrote these things while she was alive and could have been knowledgeable about events, since he was close and dear to Matilda.

He mentions Canusium, or Canossa—that most powerful and famous fortress of the Reggio region, which both the countess herself and her ancestors held dear above all others—everywhere, everywhere praises it, and indeed presents it to us as though it were speaking. For Donizo had already lived there for five lustra [twenty-five years] when he undertook to compose this work. [Col. 0942A]

Donizo had composed his poem while Matilda herself was alive and had decided to dedicate it to her. But then death carried off the most pious princess. For this reason the poet added to his work a final chapter on the distinguished death of the memorable Countess Matilda, after he had concluded the book with the preceding chapter, whose title is: “How she behaved toward the worship of God,” and so forth.

In this penultimate chapter—which perhaps few people have noticed up to now—Donizo expressed by an acrostic, that is, by the initial letters of the verses, his name and office. He also warned the reader of this very fact in these words:

> These verses, by their name and meter, declare our office.

The acrostic is as follows:

> A presbyter finishes this book, and the monk Donizo.

Here *fincit* is the same as *finxit* (“made” or “composed”), since he had written the name of Christ by the abbreviation XPI. From this you may also understand why I prefer to call him Donizo rather than Domnizo, as the others do.

[Col. 0942C]

This writer left us another acrostic in the prologue, from whose initial letters these two verses are formed:

> Daughter of Matilda, of Boniface and Beatrice,  
> Now a handmaid of God, a daughter worthy of Peter.

[Col. 0943A]

In the final verse he wished to remind us of this play, writing:

> These verses give her name, and give the names of her parents.

But to return to the earlier acrostic: through it we learn that Donizo was not only a priest but also a monk. Without doubt he lived in the monastery of Canossa, as is sufficiently clear from his dedicatory letter.

Indeed, on his testimony, in Book I, chapter 17, we know that the monastery of Frassinoro in the Modenese mountains was built by Matilda herself and by her mother Beatrice. We also know that the monastery of Canossa was established when a church formerly administered by one provost with twelve clerics or canons was given to monks:

> They also changed the name of the holy  
> Church of Canossa, and its honor,  
> Which long ago one provost alone  
> With no more than twelve clerics  
> Had been accustomed to serve. Now an abbot serves there  
> With many monks serving Christ in that place.

Therefore it must certainly be concluded that Donizo served in that very monastery under the rule of Saint Benedict.

The illustrious Mabillon entirely failed to notice this in his Benedictine Annals, under the year 1115. Indeed, he confused the church of Saint Caesarius, situated in the Modenese territory and administered in Matilda’s time by regular canons, with the Benedictine monastery of Canossa in the Reggio region. He wrote that, during the final days of her life, when Matilda was ill, many benefits had been conferred by her upon the church of Saint Caesarius of the regular canons at Canossa. [Col. 0943C]

Donizo’s book was first published by Sebastian Tengnagel, imperial librarian, or by Jacob Gretser of the Society of Jesus, at Ingolstadt in the year of Christ 1612, among the Ancient Monuments Against the Schismatics collected by him. For that edition Tengnagel used a copy sent to him from Rome.

Then the distinguished Godefridus Guilielmus Leibniz gave us another edition of the same poem in 1707, in volume I, page 629, of his notable work Illustrations of the Brunswick Writers. This edition was certainly more accurate than the earlier one: the oldest Roman manuscript, formerly belonging to Cardinal Sirleto, had been collated with the published text and supplied assistance, and Zaccagni, custodian of the Vatican Library, had also helped him with a new collation. [Col. 0943D]

Now, through my own efforts, that same poem of Donizo will appear once again. I have taken every care to make it emerge more polished and elegant, and perhaps not without useful study and labor. For the most learned Father Bacchinius—taken from us by the great loss of learning in the year 1721—lent me a copy of Donizo taken from an ancient manuscript in the library of Polirone.

Moreover, and more importantly, the Marquis Gaetano de Canossa, a man conspicuous among the foremost in the city of Reggio for the nobility of his lineage, gave me another extremely old manuscript to use with the greatest courtesy. His ancestors had received Canossa itself in fief from the emperors a few years after Countess Matilda’s death and had retained it for several centuries, as certain monuments still attest. [Col. 0944A]

I collated both manuscripts with the printed editions. The readers must now be informed of what I found especially worthy of notice in the Reggio manuscript.

From the form of the letters, that manuscript seemed to me to have been written four hundred years ago. First appeared figures of Matilda and Donizo, the latter offering her the book, with this verse:

> Shining Matilda, dear one, I beg you to accept this volume.

Dominicus Mellinus had a similar portrait, painted in miniature and taken from Donizo’s manuscript work, engraved on copper; Mabillon reproduced it again in his Benedictine Annals under the year 1115.

But, if I understand anything, these images should be considered worthless, since they were invented later through the individual skill of scribes or painters and express nothing of the true likeness of Matilda. This opinion was impressed upon me even more strongly by the portrait of Donizo himself, which presents him as perhaps a layman, certainly never a monk, although that is what he was.

In the Reggio manuscript, chapter 2, there are figures of a standing king offering a small box to a presbyter, on which is written: “The Body of the Holy Corona.” Two clerics hold another box, on which is written: “The Body of Saint Victor.” At the king’s side stands Atto in the garb of a soldier, with sword and hood. Above is written:

> The king gave Atto the bodies of these saints.

Other figures follow, with this verse:

> Godefridus cuts the saint’s limbs, giving them to the father.

[Col. 0944C]

Before chapter 8 appears a portrait of Boniface, accompanied by this verse:

> May the Savior redeem you, Boniface, marquis and duke.

Before chapter 10 there is a portrait of Beatrice, with this verse beneath it:

> May God grant you, Beatrice, to stand in splendid chambers.

At the beginning of Book II, chapter 1, there are portraits of Matilda, Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and King Henry kneeling before Matilda, with this inscription:

> The king asks the abbot and humbly entreats Matilda.

Finally, at the end of the book, the following was added by the scribe:

[Col. 0944D]

> Reader, for God’s love, often remember me.  
> When the book is finished, let thanks be rendered to Christ.  
> May Christ’s grace be granted to the writer of the book,  
> Whose name is said to be and is called Zanelinus,  
> By all his acquaintances, parents, and friends,  
> Whom he truly loves and wishes to obey in all things;  
> According to his ability, he ardently loves his friend,  
> Whom he knows to be faithful and openly loyal to him.

From these manuscripts I therefore learned that not a few of Donizo’s verses are missing from the printed books, especially in Book I, at the end of chapter 7 and the beginning of chapter 8, where there is a dispute between Canossa and Mantua concerning the body of the duke and marquis Boniface.

In this edition, therefore, sixty-eight verses have been restored that had not previously been printed. I also extracted from the manuscripts several variant readings that may shed some light on this obscure writer. [Col. 0945A]

Leibniz appended to his edition another Life of Matilda, composed in prose from a Lucchese manuscript formerly belonging to the distinguished Francesco Maria Fiorentini. I too decided to retain it in this edition, since it seemed useful for grasping Donizo’s meaning more easily in certain places. For this Life is nothing other than Donizo’s poem itself, expressed concisely in prose.

The aforementioned Reggio manuscript contains a similar Life, composed by another writer in different words and likewise formed by abbreviating Donizo’s poem. I had this copied for myself, but I did not intend to publish it, lest I burden the page and the readers with unnecessary material. [Col. 0945B]

Nevertheless, this manuscript Life taught me that the dispute between Canossa and Mantua—which I shall now print with the addition of several verses, as I indicated above—should not be placed in Book I, chapter 7 or 8, as it is in the printed editions, but rather before chapter 17 of the same book. The sequence of events itself also indicated this, since the discussion there concerns Duke Boniface after his death.

Perhaps some verse of Donizo’s also fell out at that point from the manuscripts, since the same Life contains the following:

> “When Boniface wished to go overseas and had prepared ships according to the command of the said lord abbot, he died and was buried in the city of Mantua, between Saint Peter and Saint Paul. A church was built there in his honor, so that sacred mysteries might be celebrated for him. And a great dispute arose between Mantua and Canossa. For Canossa said that it ought to have the body of the said Boniface, since it possessed his ancestors; but Mantua defended itself because it was the greater.”

In Donizo’s poem there is now nothing concerning that church in which Matilda’s father, Duke Boniface, was buried. I shall therefore restore that dispute to its proper place in the present edition.

At the end of this *Life* there is an account of the death of the same Boniface, which begins:

> “As for the true history, it is said of the death of Boniface, the father of the countess, that when he had offended a certain man from Campitello, named Scarpeta de Canevariis, Scarpeta took a bow and poisoned arrows. When the margrave Boniface had gone hunting in a certain wood beyond the Oglio, in the region of San Martino of Arzino, in the bishopric of Cremona, the said Scarpeta struck the lord margrave from behind an oak—or holm oak—which is still said to have stood there at that time, as Boniface was ascending by what was almost a little hill. He struck him with bow and arrow while standing with one knee bent to the ground, and took several steps. Even now traces and footprints are visible in that place, and it is said that grass never grows there. If those footprints or traces are destroyed, they are said to appear again the next day just as they appeared before. Nor was the place ever cultivated afterward; but that oak still stands, and afterward it continued to stand.”

This monument gave Pigna and Sigonius occasion to write that the prince, while hunting in the region of San Martino of Arzino in the bishopric of Cremona, was treacherously killed by a certain Scarpeta de Canevariis. The illustrious Bacchinius rejects this account as a little fable in his *History of the Monastery of Padolirone*, p. 48. I, however, relying on the testimony of Hermannus Contractus and Arnulf of Milan, do not think that such an account should be wholly disbelieved; for it is established that Boniface was killed in an ambush by treacherous men in a forest.

Another monument, concerning the foundation of the church and monastery of Saint Andrew in the city of Mantua, is also appended in the same manuscript *Life*. Since I decided that it should be inserted here as by no means contemptible, I leave it to the judgment of the readers. It runs as follows:

> “Concerning Beatrice, the true history says that she had a little servant named Adelbert. This little servant, as it pleased the Lord, became blind, lost his sight, and led a fitting life by fasting, keeping vigils, and practicing great penance. Where the church of Saint Andrew now stands in the city of Mantua, there was then a new and small hospice, built in the name of Blessed Andrew the Apostle. In the time of the said Beatrice, Saint Andrew appeared to Adelbert by night in a dream and said: ‘O Adelbert, go to the countess and tell her that I have commanded you to say that she should have the ground dug at a certain place near the church, where the body of Blessed Longinus the martyr was located—he who had pierced the Lord’s side with a lance and drawn out blood and water from it. There, in two vessels, are hidden the aforesaid things, namely the blood and water that flowed from the body of Jesus Christ.’ And he did so.
>
> “The said duchess or countess said: ‘Adelbert, if this is not true, I shall have you beaten with whips.’ And the said Adelbert was flogged. A second time Blessed Andrew appeared to Adelbert and told him what he had previously said. Adelbert reported this to the countess, but nothing was found, and he was flogged. A third time Blessed Andrew appeared, comforting him and telling him again to urge the countess to have the place dug. He did so on the aforesaid condition.
>
> “At last, in the presence of several bishops, the blood and water that had flowed from Christ’s body were found, together with the body of Blessed Longinus. The body was placed in a beautiful chest in the said church. The blood and water, together with their vessels, were deposited in the confessio of the church, and are still there.
>
> “For this reason the church, which had previously been a small hospice, became a great and noble monastery. An abbot and monks remain there, singing divine praises by day and by night. The church was made as it now is—large, beautiful, broad, and richly endowed—by the said Beatrice and by her daughter Matilda, with almost everything they possessed between the Po and the Lake, and with the whole court of Fornicata.
>
> “Because of their reverence, countless peoples, both from beyond the mountains and from Germany, as well as Lombards, Tuscans, and people of various nations, used to come to the city of Mantua out of devotion at the time of the Lord’s Ascension, and there they made many offerings. In the city of Mantua people fasted during that week until Thursday, although the Roman Church holds no vigil or fast between the two Easters.”

> “This is the record of Margrave Theobald: when he died, the year was 1017, in the fifth indiction.
>
> “Likewise, Margrave Boniface lived forty-five years after the death of his father Theobald; when he died, the year was 1052, in the fifth indiction.
>
> “Likewise, Countess Matilda lived sixty-three years after the death of her father, Margrave Boniface. When she died, the year was 1115, in the thirteenth indiction.”

Besides these works, two other *Lives of Matilda* are found in two manuscripts of the Este Library, likewise derived from an abridgment of Donizo. The first is entitled *History of All the Nobles and Ancestors from Whose Lineage Countess Matilda Descended*, and so forth. Its first chapter begins:

> “Count Sigefred came from the county of Lucca into the bishopric of Reggio with three sons…”

In the other manuscript one reads:

> “Here begins the History of the blessed duchess and countess Matilda, and of all her predecessors.”

Then the following note is written in red:

> “Note that a certain monk of Canossa wrote this legend in verse. I therefore examined the verses and took from it, in brief, the sequence of its History, cutting away much unnecessary material.”

In its prologue he proceeds as follows. First he says that the deeds and exploits of the Indians, and so forth. At the end there are two prayers composed by the venerable bishop Saint Anselm for the consolation of Lady Countess Matilda.

Nor should it be passed over that, already two centuries ago, a history of the deeds of Countess Matilda and her ancestors was composed in Latin, and in an elegant style, by Baptista Panetius of Ferrara, a Carmelite who flourished around the year 1490 and also promised posterity a history of Ferrara. I myself copied this *Life* from a manuscript preserved by the Jesuit Fathers of the College of Modena and intended to publish it. I nevertheless abstained, fearing that, after Matilda’s history had been worked out by more recent writers with considerably greater diligence, this one might appear either superfluous or defective.

Panetius, however, who is called on the title page of his book “a most polished historian” and “a lucid writer,” had himself consulted Donizo’s poem and transferred it whole into his own book, but without naming the writer through whom he had made such progress. No one, I think, will praise or tolerate this silence, any more than that of those who, having plundered the archives of some ancient writer, hoped that, once he had been deprived of them—or rather, once he had been removed from the world through the height of their dishonesty—their own works alone would thereafter be read and sought out.

These, then, are the matters I had to discuss concerning Donizo and his poem. The reader may ask whether he left us anything else composed from his own invention. I shall mention one item. The celebrated manuscript of Reggio also contains an exposition of Genesis in hexameter and pentameter verse, composed by Donizo himself. This is attested by the following verse placed at its beginning:

> “[The text prints *fictio*; read *finxit*:] Donizo gladly fashioned this Genesis in verse.”

It begins as follows:

> The Wisdom fashioned the beginning of all things, heaven.  
> At first he created all the earth and the firmament.  
> For six days he adorned all these things most magnificently, saying:  
> “Let many stars shine; let the moon be one that drives away the stars,” and so forth.

The whole work is completed in 368 verses. I had no intention of copying them, for they displayed nothing that could ever attract the eyes of readers. At the end of the exposition are these verses:

> Ubertus, the painter of Lucca, certainly painted these things.  
> Behold the great God, who protects the wretched lambs.  
> May the sacred right hand of God bless us within and without.  
> I, Peter, open the gates, and so forth.  
> Let the writer of the book be given the thanks of Christ.

In the margin of the manuscript, where the death of Duchess Beatrice is narrated, the following is written concerning her tomb:

> Verses on the tomb at Pisa:
>
> Although I am a sinner, I am called Lady Beatrice.  
> I was placed in the tomb, although I had been a countess.  
> Therefore let every priest say the Lord’s Prayer three times for my soul.

See Florentinius, *Life of Matilda*, book II, p. 161.

From the notes of Leibniz appended below, which I have retained, the reader will sometimes receive a torch amid the darkness spread by the poet. For this purpose I too have added brief notes. Whoever desires more should consult the aforementioned *Lives of Matilda* and the ecclesiastical history, where he will find many matters recounted more fully that I have thought it unnecessary to repeat here.

## Leibniz’s Notice

Matilda, daughter of Boniface, duke and margrave of Tuscany, and of Beatrice, daughter of Frederick, duke of Mosellan Lorraine, was heiress to extensive territories in Italy. Together with her mother she supported Pope Gregory VII against the emperor Henry IV. Since our Guelph, Azzo’s son, duke of Bavaria, had withdrawn from the emperor, she was joined to him by treaty and also married his eldest son, Guelph; from him, however, she later separated again.

The marriage settlement contained a clause that, if the husband survived, he should possess his wife’s territories. On this ground the descendants of Duke Guelph, Henry and Guelph, later under Lothair the Saxon emperor, claimed these territories and, with imperial authority, enlarged their inheritance—an inheritance that Henry V, Lothair’s predecessor, had previously usurped for himself.

Guelph, who in charters called himself duke of Spoleto and Tuscany and lord of the house of Matilda, held these regions into old age. At last, disregarding Henry the Lion, his brother’s son, he surrendered them for money to the emperor Frederick I, his enemy. Frederick gave them to his son Philip, duke of Swabia and later king of the Romans.

After Philip was killed, Pope Innocent III crowned Otto IV and claimed Matilda’s lands for the Roman Church on the basis of her testament. Otto opposed both the rights of the empire and those of his ancestors, denying that Matilda could have taken anything from them by her testament. As a result he experienced the pope as an enemy, to his great misfortune. The pope set against him Frederick II, king of Naples and Sicily, the young son of the emperor Henry IV. From that time a considerable part of Matilda’s inheritance remained under the authority of the Roman Church.

Matilda earned fame and the praise of writers by her great generosity toward churches no less than by her manly deeds. Her chaplain Domnizo, or Donizo, the ecclesiastic of the fortress church of Canossa, wrote her life in verse while she was still living, in the style suited to the age, and had resolved to dedicate it to his sovereign. Thus, in an ancient Vatican manuscript, he is painted in the dress of one presenting the work, while Matilda appears seated on a throne as one receiving it. But before the work could be brought to completion, the illustrious princess died.

Among later writers, Lord Mellinus wrote her life; Felix Contelorius, prefect of the archives at Rome under Urban VIII, subsequently recorded certain matters with greater care. But the diligence and learning of all were surpassed by the eminent Francesco Maria Florentinius, a physician at Lucca, who, in asserting the origin of this princess as belonging to his native city, transmitted the history of her and her ancestors on the basis of charters and authors close to the events in time.

After him came Julius de Puteo, not contemptible in talent and eloquence, but inferior in the firmness of his historical narrative.
