Most recently, the learned Benedictine Benedictus Bacchinius, in his book on the celebrated monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone—which had been founded by Matilda’s ancestors and enriched by Matilda herself—illustrated Matilda’s history with new evidence from documents.

Since Matilda had been buried in that monastery, many centuries later, by order of Urban VIII, her body was secretly removed and transferred to Rome, where it received an imposing monument in the basilica of Saint Peter. This occurred despite the vehement protest of the duke of Mantua, who complained that his territory had been violated.

The *Life of Matilda* by the priest Domnizo was first published from a copy sent from Rome by Sebastian Tengnagel, imperial librarian—or by Jacob Gretser, who assisted him in the undertaking—at Ingolstadt in 1612, in the work entitled *Ancient Monuments Written Long Ago against Schismatics, Especially on Behalf of Gregory VII and Several Other Roman Pontiffs*. The work was directed chiefly against Goldastus.

When I later investigated the matter at Rome, however, I discovered that the copy had been taken from a more recent manuscript, not from the most ancient one, which at that time was not yet in the Vatican but in the library of Cardinal Sirleto. I therefore collated the latter with the printed edition and restored many passages with its help. The illustrious Laurentius de Zaccagnis, first custodian of the Vatican Library, recently assisted me with a new collation.

I corrected several passages from the sense of the matters themselves, so that now scarcely anything in this half-barbarous and extremely obscure writer should escape the reader, whereas previously many passages made no sense. I had the illustrations from the same manuscript reproduced by a painter according to the model of the original. I have not appended them here; they will be presented elsewhere at a suitable time. From time to time I have scattered notes through the work to clarify its meaning.

I have also added the charter of Countess Matilda concerning the grant of her possessions to the Roman Church, which is found copied into the same manuscript. I do not know whether its authentic exemplar exists elsewhere.

Moreover, just as we supplied an account of the work of William of Apulia, so that we might do the same for Domnizo—that is, provide an outline of the work—it was less necessary here, because its place will be taken by the prose *Life of Matilda* appended to the same volume. It was written by an anonymous author, though not a very recent one, and was supplied to us by Maria Florentinius, son of Francesco Maria Florentinius, a most learned and obliging man and heir to his father’s praises. For this *Life* is largely taken from Donizo.

# Life of Matilda, Most Celebrated Princess of Italy, Written in Verse by Donizo the Priest, Who Lived with Her in the Fortress of Canossa

Appended are the charter of Countess Matilda concerning the grant of her possessions to the Roman Church, and also an account of the treasure of the church of Canossa sent to Rome and of the compensation made in return.

## The Epistle Begins

To the most munificent Matilda, and by the grace of God most invincible, to be associated with the chorus of orthodox women [Note: This epistle is not found in the manuscript codices I used. Here I would restore “of orthodox women,” or something similar. MURATORIUS], the lowest of all priests, Donizo, offers whatever humanly he is worth through pious merit, and whatever he possesses divinely.

Since my humility had already been residing for five lustrums [Note: At Canossa, clearly, where the bodies of the countess Matilda’s ancestors had been placed in the church of Saint Apollonius. Here observe that Donizo had already served for five lustrums in the monastery of Canossa when he undertook this writing, in the year 1114 or even earlier. MURATORIUS] beside the mausoleum of illustrious princes [Note: Write: “my humility was residing.” MURATORIUS], and saw no memorial of them that the permanence of written letters might preserve, it happened that recently the exalted greatness of your honor [Note: Canossa. LEIBNIZ] ordered marble coffins to be brought to Canossa for the more worthy burial of their bodies. Thus our humble ability attempted, with fervent zeal, to engrave [*caraxare*, from Greek *χαράσσω*, “to scratch, engrave,” hence “to write down, compose”; the ancient Vatican manuscript has *caracare*. LEIBNIZ] in heroic verse what we had heard from old men and more truthful men of our own time, so that the brave and most illustrious deeds of such great heroes might not remain hidden. With Christ’s gracious help, we brought this to completion.

And since, through the generosity of the heavenly Maker, the report has reached the knowledge of the entire kingdom that you are inferior to them in no virtue, although the wise king says, “Do not praise anyone during his lifetime,” nevertheless we do not think that your golden dignity or wisdom will be diminished by this. We also find that the chief ancient poets offered poems worthy of the highest praise to eminent rulers. Thus the poet Horace writes to Octavian Augustus:

> “To you, while you are present, we bestow mature honors”—that is, “while you live, we write poems about you.”

And just as the most learned of poets offered Augustus poems most pleasing to him, having received liberty from him, so he again, rejoicing in the praise of that Caesar, produced verses such as these:

> Before the light deer graze in the sky,  
> and the seas abandon their fish naked upon the shore;  
> before, having wandered through the boundaries of both lands,  
> the Parthian exile drinks from the Saône, or Germany from the Tigris,  
> than his likeness slips from my heart.

The same may likewise be conjectured about you, most gracious lady. And, as the Book of Esther relates concerning King Ahasuerus, he spent the whole night sleeplessly listening with attention to the histories written about him, until he heard the readers tell how Mordecai had reported the plot against his life; and immediately he rewarded Mordecai for this with royal recompense.

We too have written a useful history about you for generations to come, which will be a most approved example for those who love God and his holy Church. Your life and health are our security and joy; your sickness is our weakness and sorrow. May the mercy of the Savior of all grant you continual life and health. Amen.

## The Chapters of the First Book Begin

1. Canossa recounts who built her, by which kings she was besieged, and how she escaped with a great victory.
2. Canossa recounts Acto’s love for her, and how Acto acquired the bodies of Victor and Corona, as well as Saint Apollonius, bishop and confessor.
3. What kind of woman Acto’s wife was, how many children she had, how her son Theobald became ruler after him, and how that same Theobald built the monastery situated between the Po and the Larione.
4. Concerning Theobald’s three sons and his wife.
5. Concerning the bishop of the city of Arezzo, who was Boniface’s brother.
6. How certain margraves of Lombardy tried to separate Conrad from Boniface; how Boniface married Countess Richilda; and concerning the great war that all Lombardy waged with Boniface and Conrad at Curaliolus [Note: The more recent Vatican manuscript has *Curtiliolum*; the ancient one has *Cuviliolum*, which is more correct, since the summary of the chapter below has the same form. LEIBNIZ], near the city of Reggio.
7. How the margraves were buried at Canossa.
8. What Boniface’s stature and character were, and what the Sibyl prophesied about him.
9. With how much glory and honor Duke and Margrave Boniface married the illustrious Duchess Beatrice.
10. How King Conrad conquered Parma with Boniface’s help, and how the same king and the same margrave were joined by oath.
11. What Boniface did in going to Burgundy and returning.
12. Concerning the vinegar that Margrave Boniface sent to King Henry II, and the great gift that one of his servants gave to that same king.
13. How King Henry II at one time in his council, and at another time on the occasion of a night vigil, attempted to capture Boniface.
14. How Boniface was devoted to divine matters.
15. How the custom of selling churches came from the Teutonic kings, and how Boniface accepted penance for this from Saint Guido the abbot.
16. The urban dispute between Canossa and Mantua over the body of Duke and Margrave Boniface.
17. How many years Beatrice lived after Boniface, and how prudently she governed everything.
18. How Henry II died during Beatrice’s lifetime, and how Henry III became greatly embroiled in discord with Pope Alexander II.
19. How, after Alexander, Gregory VII became pope, and how that king remained in such prolonged disagreement with him that he was condemned by the pope.
20. Concerning the death of Lady Beatrice, how Canossa mourned her, and concerning her body.

*The chapters of the first book end.*

## The Second Book Begins

1. Concerning the first arrival of King Henry III and Pope Gregory VII in Lombardy; how they were received by Duchess Matilda at Canossa; how Archbishop Guibert overthrew that same king; and how he came with him to Rome on another occasion against the pope.
2. How Lady Matilda rose up against the king and Guibert, and how she assisted all Catholics.
3. Concerning the death of Pope Gregory; the election of Popes Desiderius and Urban; how she assisted all Catholics; how Lady Matilda fought for the Roman Church; and concerning the death of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca.
4. Concerning King Henry III’s third arrival in Italy and the siege of the city of Mantua.
5. A rebuke and denunciation, or fitting exhortation, against Mantua.
6. Likewise concerning the same king and the same lady, and concerning the battle of the countess’s soldiers with the king at the Three Counties.
7. Concerning the siege of Montebello and the king’s banner captured at Canossa.
8. Concerning Queen Praxedis’s separation from King Henry and Pope Urban’s arrival in Lombardy.
9. Concerning the siege of Nogara.
10. What Pope Urban gained in Gaul and concerning his return to Italy.
11. Concerning Conrad’s withdrawal from his father Henry and the death of Pope Urban.
12. Concerning the election of Pope Paschal and Guibert’s evil death.
13. Concerning the death of King Conrad and the siege of Ferrara.
14. How, out of pious concern for Lady Matilda, Pope Paschal sent the venerable Cardinal Bernard to Lombardy.
15. Concerning the death of King Henry III.
16. A fitting exhortation of Pope Paschal.
17. Concerning Pope Paschal’s arrival in Lombardy and Gaul.
18. Concerning the legates and the first arrival of King Henry IV in Italy.
19. How the people of Mantua, out of fear, returned to loyalty to Lady Matilda.
20. How intensely devoted Matilda was to the worship of God.

## This Prologue Explains in Whose Name the Book Is Written

> The wars of the Franks have been published in resonant prose;  
> we know the style that depicts Italy’s battles;  
> the hunting deeds of the ancient Lombards;  
> the impious or worthless sayings of many men  
> have been added to books, lest they fall from memory.  
> I prefer, under so great an example, to unfold in verse  
> the difficult deeds of our dukes. Although it is my custom  
> only to follow what is plain and report in unadorned speech,  
> I shall nevertheless fashion this history with songs:
>
> We see subtle things stored in coarse sacks.  
> Often the dull farmer gives generous seeds to the earth;  
> with God granting time, they grow more richly.  
> The inner field is coarse, my sack is coarse everywhere;  
> yet if it contains any seeds, they are subtle,  
> if it has received any.
>
> For the arms of the supreme Creator have been given to us.  
> While this excellent sower sows his own fields,  
> they do not produce thistles but return the grain that was entrusted.  
> The grain is better than the field, yet the grain truly belongs to the field;  
> the digger places in the field seed that is equally fitting.
>
> One man has many tongues; another pursues Wisdom;  
> one discerns the sick [the printed *fessum*, “weary,” may perhaps be *aegrum*, “sick”], and another is endowed differently [Note: We may suspect that the word intended was *aegrum*, “sick,” in place of *fessum*, “weary.” Here the poet alludes to the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 12:8: “To one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, to another the gift of healing, to another kinds of tongues,” and so forth. MURATORIUS].
>
> Divine fire gives its gifts and desires them,  
> just as shining Wisdom illuminates learned minds.  
> It makes stammering mouths speak correctly and teaches them modesty;  
> Wisdom shows how to dictate remarkable things.  
> It treats the heights of heaven, which this gracious one loves completely;  
> no one can touch the highest things who has not wholly clung to her.
>
> But it is better that one to whom it is not granted to utter lofty things  
> should nevertheless bring forth what he contains and labors over.  
> When he grows hot through labor, great things plainly follow.  
> Therefore my animated mind, wishing to improve,  
> dares at least to write earthly things in verse.
>
> Nor do I doubt that the truths which the poet has fashioned are true [Note: Correct this, with our manuscripts lighting the way: *nec titubo vera*, “nor do I doubt the truths.” That is, “I do not doubt that what the poet composes is true.” MURATORIUS].
>
> Labor conquers all, if persistent, fierce ardor remains [Note: Or perhaps Donizo wrote *improbus ardor*, “fierce ardor.” MURATORIUS].
>
> I shall not cease to write what my foolish learning, unhappy as it is,  
> has judged that I know [Note: The ancient Vatican manuscript has *quae quivi*, correctly, as it almost always does. LEIBNIZ. The Reggio manuscript likewise has *quae quivi*. MURATORIUS],  
> in meters, once the deeds are completed;  
> I shall give them to no one except the wise—  
> namely, to our nectarean Matilda,  
> whose immense renown fills the world because of her honor;  
> she flourishes more broadly, preserving the manner of her ancestors.
>
> Four virtues flourish in her:  
> for those generous virtues dwell with her at all times.  
> Prudence, governing lofty things, rules all the just in her;  
> the duchess proceeds discreetly and tempers her deeds [Note: It should be written *temperat*. LEIBNIZ. Our manuscript codices likewise have this form. MURATORIUS].
>
> She practices piety and justice with great devotion;  
> she observes the fearful laws of the heavenly Judge;  
> strong in adversity, she is not elated in prosperity;  
> and trusting in the true faith of the Godhead, she hopes.
>
> As she excels in pleasing deeds, so also in the light of faith;  
> therefore she shall gather the hundredfold fruit of her works [Note: The Padolirone manuscript has *colligit*, “she gathers.” MURATORIUS].
>
> One holds the thirtyfold crown, another the sixtyfold;  
> the greater one possesses the hundredfold.  
> She rightly receives all the crowns of goodness.
>
> Let these things be suitably recited at the table of the school,  
> so that it may be known that great prudence  
> plainly accompanies winged simplicity in her.
>
> I wish our descendants to know so great a lady.  
> Behold, I shall dictate as I can, and afterward ask  
> the venerable and beloved Matilda to look more safely  
> upon any indecent word that may have slipped in here and to pardon it.
>
> These verses give her name and give that of her ancestors.

*The prologue ends.*

# Beginning of the Book Concerning the Canossan Princes

Many verses will be written concerning them, so that they may be remembered.

> If Plato were still alive, and Maro himself,  
> they would devote countless hours to composing verses  
> about our dukes, whom the whole world here  
> declares to be thoroughly wise [Note: I congratulate Donizo, who ordinarily follows only what is plain and uses a very rough and common style, for bringing forth a word employed almost exclusively by authors of deeper Latin. *Catus*, from which the name Cato derives, signifies in Ennius, Plautus, and other Latin authors a wise, prudent, or keen-minded man. MURATORIUS],  
> and indeed bears witness to such men and mourns  
> that no misfortune ever overwhelmed such distinguished figures.
>
> In ancient times no one was better than these;  
> for the offspring of Priam would not be nobler than they,  
> nor will anyone equal to them be born in a later age.
>
> They shine like stars with the light of Wisdom,  
> just as Phoebus illuminates all the earth,  
> warms and nourishes the plants, makes them ripen, and burns them.  
> Thus the cultivated court of these men shone even more brightly [Note: Especially after the year 1000 from Christ’s birth, writers commonly used *curia* to mean the palace or household and servants of kings and princes; hence the French *la cour* and our *la corte*, and those who are now called *cortigiani* in the vernacular were called *curiales*. I omit the examples. Hence Donizo says above that the court of Matilda and her ancestors shone above the halls of the dukes. MURATORIUS].
>
> It surpassed the customary halls of dukes and counts;  
> it gave royal gifts, taught men to wage war, and destroyed  
> those whom it saw wickedly committing crimes,  
> while sparing the good—just in judgment, wealthy and capable, beautiful.
>
> If any quarrels arose, this court alone brought them to an end.  
> These men never knew how to turn their backs on enemies;  
> skilled in war, the standard-bearers of the kingdom conquered battles [Note: Perhaps *regum*, “of kings.” They were standard-bearers, like masters of cavalry, possessing in the army the authority immediately below that of the prince himself. Conrad, later king, held the standards of the kingdom under Lothair the Saxon. Godefridus of Viterbo. LEIBNIZ].
>
> Their spears often cut down harmful men;  
> they always bore the palm of justice and the weapons of war.  
> As violent hail devastates crops in the field,  
> so they condemned traitors [Note: A word familiar to Italians and Gauls, formed from a Germanic word, meaning a treacherous person who violates a given pledge and fulfilled oath, such as vassals plotting against their lord or taking up arms. Here it is used more broadly for wicked and criminal men. MURATORIUS]  
> and tortured thieves on the gallows.
>
> In their time peace and order of morals flourished;  
> strong Catholics begot Catholics.  
> They always loved, honored, and feared  
> the rule of key-bearing Peter and of the holy clergy.  
> From their own possessions they gave many things to the holy;  
> they willingly supplied food and clothing to the poor.
>
> These worshipers of Christ were buried together.  
> Now, strengthened by firm defenses, they are dearer to all.  
> Let white Canossa [Note: Canossa is situated on a lofty and steep rock, whose sides, being bare stone—or, as Donizo himself says, bare flint—display a certain whiteness. To me, when I sometimes observe it from the windows of the Este Library, especially with the aid of a telescope, it has appeared so. It lies in the mountains of Reggio Emilia toward the south and west, more than thirteen thousand paces from the city. MURATORIUS] mourn and also report their true names;  
> let it rightly sing their names, lest these verses become vain.

## Chapter One

Canossa recounts who built her, by which kings she was besieged, and how she escaped with a great victory.

> Atto was the first prince, cunning as a serpent.  
> He was nobly born from Sigefred,  
> an illustrious prince [Note: Atto the prince—that is, the count—for in those times, and long afterward, counts too were included under the name of princes. He was born from Sigefred, a prince—that is, a powerful dynast—who possessed an allod, or personal territory, even if he perhaps held no royal fief or bore the title of any defined dignity, which some people disdained as diminishing nobility or freedom, as is clear from the history of the Guelphs. LEIBNIZ.
>
> Counts once had a place among princes, and it is established that Atto, or Azzone, son of Sigefred, was regarded under that title. But it is not easy to show why Sigefred himself should also be called a prince; for neither in those times nor in ours did an abundance of allods ordinarily make a prince. I have wondered whether Donizo perhaps intended by those words, “from the Lucchese county,” to indicate that Sigefred was count of the city of Lucca. But I shall speak of this elsewhere. Meanwhile, if *princeps* is taken here merely as “powerful,” Donizo will have used the word somewhat imprecisely. MURATORIUS.]
>
> From the Lucchese county,  
> and he begot two other sons, both very illustrious.  
> The first was called Sigefred, the second Atto,  
> and the youngest son was named Gerard.  
> Wishing to enlarge his own honor, Sigefred  
> came with his sons into this Lombardy [Note: Tuscany too was Lombard territory, whose ancient capital was Lucca. But Lombardy, not only in our time but also in Donizo’s, was used in a narrower sense for the region on this side of the Apennines embracing the Insubres and part of Emilia as far as the river Secchia. Thus you see the county of Reggio, in which Canossa lies, assigned to Lombardy. MURATORIUS].
>
> Just as a vine spreads widely and high,  
> so he spread himself greatly, far and wide.  
> For he properly governed lands and peoples beneath him,  
> and retained many under his own protection [Note: That is, he acquired various castles, either as allods or as fiefs, from the kings of Italy or from bishops, and ruled their inhabitants. He also kept many people under his protection: he was the advocate of many churches, or he had an abundance of vassals whom it was his duty to protect on behalf of their lords. MURATORIUS].
>
> The terror of his sons, chiefly through the sword [Note: The ancient Vatican manuscript reads *terror*. LEIBNIZ],  
> had struck down diverse peoples and multitudes.  
> But since Sigefred was exceedingly great and wealthy,  
> he left this bitter age in the manner of his fathers.  
> His sons, enriched and adorned,  
> began to stand apart, completely divided.
>
> The two brothers both became powerful men of Parma.

The youngest gave Guibertina; the eldest, Baratina [Note: There are those who write, and with whose opinion I would readily concur, that from this line descended Guibert of Parma, archbishop of Ravenna and subsequently the notorious antipope in the time of Pope Gregory VII, together with the family of the lords of Correggio, which entirely died out a few years ago, with women alone surviving. MUR.].

Both offspring were great, and radiant with honor.

As the fir surpasses the oaks among the great Alps,

So Atto had far outstripped all his brothers,

Growing, rejoicing, and abounding in many things:

Seeing me, Canossa, standing as a bare rock,

Count Atto received me as his own fortress;

He strengthened these towers and fortified me above the cities,

So that I should fear neither kings nor any powerful men.

The king of the Latins [Note: I would not dare to call Berengar II “king of the Latins” (Berengherius is read in the Reggio manuscript), for he was never granted the imperial title and never ruled the Romans. Therefore only Henry IV seems to be intended here, who was at once, whether by his own people or in their estimation, emperor of the Romans and king of Germany. MUR.] knows this, and the king of the Teutons;

King Berengar proves this, and his son.

[Col. 0958B] These Lombards are known to have been strong in arms,

But by me they were destroyed and made exiles [Note: Made exiles from the kingdom, that is, outcasts. The meaning of the entire passage is as follows: Berengar, king of the Latins, and Henry IV, king of the Teutons, perceived how strongly fortified I was (Canossa is speaking). Berengar proves this, and his son Adalbert, who were indeed known to have been strong Lombards in arms, but were overthrown by me (while attempting to overthrow me) and expelled from the kingdom by Otto the Great. For these two kings, Berengar and Adalbert (colleagues in the kingdom, as the charters show), were both Franks, deriving their origin from the Franks or holding the Frankish kingdom in Italy; they thought they could surround me or fight by besieging me. This undertaking turned bitterly against them—that is, it went badly for them—while Atto the prince, that is, Count Atto, was still alive. LEIB.]

Expelled from the kingdom: for, being Franks [Note: The Reggio manuscript has *me quia frangi*, that is, “because they thought me to have been demolished and cast down.” Donizo has recently counted Berengar II and his son Adalbert among the Lombards; therefore he would not have called them Franks, and certainly no meaning results from reading *Franci*. MUR.],

These two kings, while Atto the prince was alive,

Believed they could surround me [Note: The old manuscript has *circumdar*, that is, “they surrounded.” LEIB.

The Padolirone manuscript has: “They surrounded me, an undertaking which turned bitter for them.” That is, the siege became their great ruin, since, driven from the throne, they never recovered it. MUR.],

An undertaking which turned bitter for them.

Let events be recounted as they happened; let trifles cease.

From the brutish people [Note: In Italian he would call it *brutale*, “brutish” or “beastlike.” [Col. 0959C] But why does Donizo call the people of the province brutish? See Liutprand, *History*, book III, chapter 12, vol. II, p. 450 of the *Rerum Italicarum*, where the provincials, whom he calls Burgundians and Allobroges, are accused of arrogance and greed. MUR.] the excellent King Hugh arose;

He himself was descended from Allobrogian fathers,

And the Lombard people properly made him king,

And he ruled the Italian kingdom piously and justly:

He forbade a public assembly to be held without command

And authority from the illustrious King Hugh;

While he lived, no one, however lowly, dared to plunder the common people by force [Note: The old manuscript has *minimis*, that is, “no one”; while he lived, no one dared to plunder the common people. The manuscript from antiquity likewise has this reading. LEIB.].

After his death his son reigned,

Lothair, prudent, wise, and lord of Atto.

He also had as wife the splendid Adelaide.

After lofty Lothair was removed from life,

Without the assent of his wife, the one

Who was praised as king of the Lombards, Berengar, a bitter man [Note: This king is called “a bitter man” because, after Lothair’s death, he was praised or elected without the consent or assent of Adelaide. Although he had already wielded power while Lothair, and even Hugh, were alive, he did not count the years of his reign until after Lothair’s death, as the charters show. LEIB.],

Seized the aforesaid queen, impelled by anger [Note: The Padolirone manuscript has *praedictam*, “the aforesaid.” Nor is it surprising that Adelaide detested Berengar, since by his schemes, authority, and perhaps even through his life, he had deprived Lothair, her husband, of kingship. MUR.];

He never wished that this man should become king.

Therefore, after capturing her, he finally sent her

To the fortress of Garda [Note: Namely, on the shore of Lake Benacus. Therefore not in the territory of Como, as stated by the inscription to the Empress Adelaide cited by Broverus, book IX of the *Annals of Trier*. MUR.],

[Col. 0959B] And provided her with only one female servant

And a good priest named Martin.

For a long time they lay at the bottom of a tower.

Secretly the old man broke through the wall with iron;

At last, fleeing, he brought the mistress and the servant

Together out through one opening, and gave them men’s clothing,

So that the two women might not be recognized and captured again;

They came as far as the lake guarded by Mantua;

They found a boat and a kindly fisherman.

The priest invited him to sail with them

As companions, saying what he could give him.

The fisherman said; the priest replied: “If you knew,”

“Who we are, you would immediately be very glad

To carry the three of us across without payment.”

“Tell me who you are, if you now wish to cross.”

“If you swear to us that you will keep us completely hidden,

We shall reveal a secret to you,

One that will be very dear to you.”

There was no book [Note: That is, a Gospel book, upon which Christians customarily pledged their faith by taking an oath. MUR.]; immediately, in the manner of a cross,

The rustic placed two sticks on the ground, making no mistake;

He swore upon the sticks, as though a beautiful cross were there.

Then Lord Martin the priest said to him:

“Dear man, now I am compelled to tell you everything for your safety:

This is the queen whom King Berengar seized in anger;

We have fled—be a faithful friend.”

Praising God, the fisherman quickly carried them across with him.

That rustic also offered a fish, not a small one,

And said to the queen: “Remember me; you shall have it

If the mighty Lord God should perhaps add honor to you.”

Then the boatman set the queen down near a forest

Adjoining the aforesaid lake. There she remained,

Worshiping Christ faithfully for a whole week;

The priest sought bread as a guest for the woman kept in hiding.

At last the experienced queen sighed and said:

“I always think myself captured; what good is it for me to remain here?”

The bishop of Reggio, our faithful friend,

Adalardus [Note: Bishop of Reggio. Ughelli, vol. II of *Italia Sacra*, p. 301, states that he was raised to the see in 945. But it happened earlier. His charter is preserved in the chapter archive of the canons of Reggio, in which he is styled: “Servant of the servants of God, given in the city of Reggio in the eighteenth year of our lord Hugh, most serene king; and in the fourteenth year of Lothair, his son, likewise king, on the Kalends of January, in the second indiction”—that is, in the year 943. Here one also finds evidence for establishing the chronology of Kings Hugh and Lothair. Those who listed this Adalard among the bishops of Verona were profoundly mistaken. MUR.],

Would perhaps draw us from here, Lord Geronta, if you tell him

How great my sorrow is [Note: That is: “My dear lord priest, or elder Martin.” LEIB.].”

At once, although weary, the exiled priest went.

[Col. 0960B] When the bishop recognized him, he asked about the queen:

“Oh, what has happened? Please tell me; I hope to learn.”

The priest replied to the lord that she had died in a dreadful prison.

Uttering lamentations, the bishop mourned her in these words:

“Great danger—indeed, it is clear that there has been a great crime” [Note: The passage requires emendation. Either write “Gods, a great crime!” or read “speak of a great crime.” MUR.].

The priest, recognizing from this that the bishop abhorred

The queen’s death, and that he would be very glad for her life,

Privately disclosed to him that the queen was alive,

And wished him to provide her with protection.

“I rejoice exceedingly that she lives,” said the bishop.

“But I know of no secure fortress under my control.

My soldier Atto [Note: “Soldier,” that is, vassal. LEIB.] has one, if he is willing,

In which the queen can remain for a long time

Against the king’s anger. It is called Canossa” [Note: The Padolirone manuscript has *fit dicta Canossa*, “it becomes called Canossa.” Canossa is indeed its ancient name; it still survives and gave its surname to the noble family of Canossa, which ruled there after Countess Matilda. MUR.].

[Col. 0960C] “Tomorrow take our little horses and ride, as I urge you;

Perhaps you will ask Atto and obtain what you desire.”

When day had dawned, the same priest rode away.

Prince Atto questioned him at length:

“What has happened to the queen? Tell me.”

He reported that the woman had died in a terrible prison.

Atto, grieving greatly, poured forth bitter tears;

And when he plainly saw that Atto was weeping, he said secretly to him:

“She lives, and through you she wishes to be rescued and received.”

The prince asked for horses and immediately hurried there.

It was then the third hour, and the heat of day was shining;

Yet this energetic man did not stop;

By the sixth hour of the day he finally arrived,

And lofty Canossa held the illustrious queen,

Together with her servant Abra [Note: *Abra* is Greek for “female servant” or “maidservant.” LEIB.].

Or he boasted that he possessed them.

She secretly sent this news to Rome, and soon to the pope,

Praying and asking him to give her suitable counsel

Concerning this affair, since she wished to give the queen

To King Otto, whom the Alemannic people [Note: Thus already at that time, though more rarely, the Alemanni were used for the Germans, as also in William of Apulia. LEIB.] obeyed.

Pope John, a man of great integrity [Note: John XII. But at that time Agapetus II was seated on the papal throne; he was still alive after Otto’s and Adelaide’s marriage and was succeeded by John XIII. LEIB.],

Wrote to him, praising what he had done, and told him to do

What he wished and intended.

After this, Atto’s messenger led the king to the region

Of Verona, with only a small company.

King Otto came there, and Atto accompanied him [Note: A fable worthy of Roman history: that Otto the Great secretly came to free Adelaide. LEIB.

The Padolirone manuscript has *contulit*. Donizo is speaking here of Adelaide’s marriage with Otto the Great, king of Germany, carried out without Berengar II’s knowledge, the king of Italy; after it was completed, Otto is said to have returned to his own land. But the Saxon chronicler edited by Leibniz, the continuator of Regino, and other distinguished historians report that in 952 Otto drove out Berengar and captured the royal city of Pavia, where the marriage was also celebrated with royal magnificence. Here, therefore, one must depart from Donizo, who gives the substance of the event but was ignorant of several circumstances. Only Ditmar, book II of his *Chronicle*, contains something not far removed from this account. MUR.],

And brought away the queen, who then also married the king.

[Col. 0961B] Having taken a wife, he quickly returned to his own land,

Promising Atto that he would do the greatest things for him.

The Lombard king had not yet learned of these deeds

Of the queen, nor had he discovered where she had fled,

Until he heard that King Otto was at Verona,

And finally heard that Atto had carried out this affair.

Angry and gnashing his teeth, he immediately gathered his people;

He came to Canossa, thinking to break it all apart.

“I am a stone, not wood; Atto remains above inside,

With prudent and wise men beside him.

King Berengar, strike our fortress with as many weapons as you wish.

You can perish before you break through our mass;

Neither a battering ram, a fox [Note: A siege machine beneath which soldiers sheltered, as it were, cautiously. LEIB.],

Nor any engine can prevail with its lofty blows

To reach our roofs.”

[Col. 0961C] Encouraging his enemies, the king surrounded me on every side,

Often attacking me in battle; the king remained at Lavadello [Note: The old manuscript has *Lavaclello*. LEIB.],

Hoping that he would not withdraw until he had taken me.

Nearby was the mountain called Branciana.

From the summit of a tower Atto often began

To descend, speaking to those who were better men.

When the king learned this, he had him set hanging [the reading is uncertain].

One of his acquaintances reported this from a distance

To Atto, shouting that he himself should speak to him

From the tower through a narrow little window.

At once Atto thrust out his head and heard the welcome words.

A bear, carrying hunger in its belly, hung suspended for food.

Because it was suffering from weakness, it pretended to love the deer [Note: It pretends to be ill out of love for obtaining the deer. LEIB.];

It sent word that the deer should visit the sick creature.

The deer went to it, and while he was speaking,

The bear clung to the deer’s ear, tearing it with its claws;

Then, releasing him, it sent him away again,

Ordering him to come, saying: “If you come, I shall give you great gifts.”

The deer had forgotten what the savage beast had done.

He approached again, and the savage creature drew out its claw,

Tore away the ear, leaving the deer only one;

Disfigured, the wretched and foolish animal returned.

The bear, professing love for the deer, sent him another message,

Telling him to come safely, because it wished to reveal many things to him.

Mad and foolish, the deer went to the bear.

[Col. 0962B] The bear looked at him, smiled at his approach, and spoke to him;

Suddenly, raging, it cut the captive apart with tooth and claw.

After depriving him of life, it gave him to the fox to burn.

The fox roasted him and then brought the whole carcass to the bear,

Keeping only the heart. Let the bear learn the animal’s cunning [Note: The Reggio manuscript has: “so that the bear might know its cunning.” MUR.].

The bear, having the flesh, first sought the deer’s heart.

The fox replied: “He had no heart, nor did I take one.”

He said to it again: “I want the heart at once.”

The fox said to the bear:

“When he was sought three times, he proved to be without a heart.”

“Let this plain story be dear to you, my Atto.”

Atto, recognizing why he was telling this,

For that reason drew himself upward and did not descend again,

Until the king remained at the siege.

The king, fixing his position, and likewise his army,

Thought: “I shall go nowhere, unless I capture him” [Note: “Unless he captures me.” LEIB.].

[Col. 0962C] After three and a half years spent around me [Note: Since King Lothair, Adelaide’s husband, died in November 950, and Otto the Great came into Italy with an army in 951 or 952 and freed Adelaide, who was besieged in the fortress of Canossa, and then sought her hand in marriage, the siege of Canossa could not have lasted three and a half years. Even though the Chronicle of Novalese also says that the queen remained in the castle for almost three years. LEIB.

Although Leo of Ostia and the author of the Chronicle of Novalese write that Queen Adelaide, later empress and holy woman, was besieged at Canossa for three years, Donizo certainly does not relate this. But after Adelaide’s liberation and marriage he reports the siege of Canossa, and there is nothing to prevent us from believing that it continued for more than three years. MUR.],

Atto grew weary of enduring such a long inactivity.

For he stood above and did nothing except amuse himself.

At night he drove out a messenger, sending a brief letter

To King Otto, asking him not to approach slowly,

But to try confidently to come to his aid from nearby,

Reminding him of what he had promised him long before.

When Otto saw the messenger, he rejoiced greatly at him.

[Col. 0963A] He gathered armed men and came to the fields

Of Verona, considering giving battle to Berengar.

He crossed the Po, wishing to find the reported

King of Canossa, together with all his men.

The report of Otto suddenly reached the Ligurian king,

Who therefore withdrew from the siege.

Surrounded everywhere by arms and many troops,

The king met him in the meadow of Fontana.

A great uproar suddenly arose; they were torn by spears and lances,

They struck one another with swords; the blows resounded far away.

The Alemannic people captured Berengar,

After the Lombards had been defeated.

Otto surveyed the field and immediately pulled back his reins,

Rejoicing that the king had been taken.

As quickly as he could, he returned to his own borders

And bound the unarmed king with heavy fetters.

[Col. 0963B] For as long as Berengar lived, he remained there [Note: The poet confuses Otto’s first expedition, in which he accepted Berengar’s submission, satisfied with the queen Adelaide, with the second, in which he captured him, deprived him of the kingdom, and transferred him to Germany. LEIB.].

Afterward his son Albert is praised,

And as king of the Lombards: he was strong in arms.

When mounted on a horse he struck anyone with his right hand,

That man immediately fell far away, his bone often shattered [Note: The old manuscript has *conciso*, “shattered.” LEIB.].

He bitterly despised Atto’s peace.

With expenditure, the shrewd Atto thoroughly armed his own fortress.

The fierce king, riding, surrounded his fortress

For two periods of three months, in anger.

“You strive in vain, father; O king, you are mistaken:

I shall not be captured unless you remain here as long as you live.”

When Atto saw that the king would never depart,

He again sought Otto’s aid with swift movement:

If Otto himself could not come, let his son come,

Litulphus by name, and let him be sent.

Without tumult, Otto sent a thousand ready men

[Col. 0963C] With his son; they came cautiously into familiar Italy and reached Verona [Note: Ludolph undertook an expedition into Italy against Berengar in 957 and died there before Berengar was captured by Otto, which happened only in 964. After his father was captured, Adalbert did not have sufficient forces for Canossa to be besieged; nor did he reign after his father, but he reigned with his father. Thus our author is wrong to write that he was praised by the Lombards as king “after this,” that is, after his father’s capture. LEIB.].

The king staying at Canossa heard that he was present.

When the horn sounded, he went to Bagisium.

Then Litulphus left Verona and arrived at the meadow

Of Bottonis at evening; before

The dreadful night came, Atto spoke into

King Litulphus’s ear [Note: He was not king but the king’s son, Ludolphus, appointed duke of Alemannia by his father Otto in 950. MUR.]:

“May you be safe,” he said, and joined him.

“A mouse in a sack fares badly with a cat in the same confined space.”

“King,” he said, “I ask you to explain this riddle to me.”

Atto said: “It is not fitting for two kings to be together

In one retinue. Therefore first take counsel” [Note: The Reggio manuscript has: “Take counsel first.” MUR.].

“Whatever you tell me to do for me,

I promise that I shall do.”

Litulphus answered him:

“Atto the warrior, let us eat here in this field,” he said,

“Let us rest briefly through the night; afterward let us go.

Immediately let a messenger from our people go to see

How Albert is situated, and how his army.”

The king approved everything Atto had said and did it.

At the beginning of daylight, in the meadow of Palude [Note: In the ancient Estense parchment manuscript, from which I drew the Reggio history published in this work, there is a history entitled *The Deeds of Countess Matilda*. It is an epitome of the metrical history composed by Donizo, rendered in prose; the following is read there: “And the aforesaid Litulphus came with the aforesaid soldiers on a certain day in the month of May of that same year from the city of Verona to the fortress of Canossa in one day. And on the following day he went to Parma and received the crown of Lombardy.” Other writers are entirely silent about this coronation; Donizo himself is silent, if indeed these are his verses. [Col. 0964C] The same writer continues: “And he returned with the said soldiers and with Count Atto; and on that same day he went with armed force in the meadow of Antognano against King Albert, son of the late King Berengar. And a battle was fought there between the two sides in the said meadow of Antognano near Carpinetum,” and so forth. Below, Donizo states that Litulphus was buried at the place of Antonianum. MUR.],

A messenger returning from Albert, having found Atto,

Said to him: “Certainly, if these were cooked beasts,

They could, I think, suddenly be eaten by them, my lord.”

[Col. 0964B] “They are so numerous.” Atto ordered him to say nothing of this.

Atto, speaking to the king, changed the messenger’s words:

“Oh, if the enemies were roasted rams,

We could surely gnaw their flesh.

Put on your cuirass, fasten a helmet to your head,

Throw the shield around your neck, take the spear in your hands,

Rush immediately upon him, for he now stands unarmed.”

The king took his cuirass, shield, helmet, and spear.

All the strong Teutons took up their arms;

They advanced in compact groups as far as they could.

The scattered phalanx of Albert perceived them across the open ground.

Many ran [Note: The old manuscript has *currerunt*, “they ran.” LEIB.], and reported this to the king.

At matins the king had already risen.

Completely unperturbed, he said: “I wish you to see how many they are;

Call our men, and let the trumpet scatter its voice everywhere.

Meanwhile, I wish the priest to sing Mass first.”

While the sacred office was being sung, they returned [Note: The Padolirone manuscript has *remearunt*, “they returned.” MUR.],

Already near, saying: “There are a thousand; they appear to be so.”

The king, scarcely armed and helmeted, with a few men,

Went out to battle. King Litulphus at once

Offered him his iron; the Lombard king extended his spear

Against him, pierced Litulphus’s cuirass and limbs,

And he immediately lost his life [Note: A fabrication. Ludolphus died of illness. Hepidanus says that he was seized by fever in 957 from grief, that is, sorrow. Ditmar, book II. Sigonius asserts that Berengar was suspected of having hastened his death. Only Widukind seems able to support Donizo’s account, in book III, in these words: “While he [Ludolphus] was acting in Italy, after nearly an entire year he died on the final day, leaving a grievous wound from his own wound upon the whole Frankish empire”; but “wound” may here mean loss or injury, unless one should perhaps read “from his own funeral.” Hermannus Contractus says that in this year a battle was fought at Canossa, Ludolphus won, and after all had been subjected to him together with the kingdom of Italy, he died prematurely at Plumbium in the same year. LEIB.].

[Col. 0965A] The Alemannic people, grieving, trembled with great fear,

But Atto raised his voice and encouraged the Teutons.

At his voice they all scorned their fear.

Then both sides suffered heavy loss.

Although with loss, Atto nevertheless held the field.

King Albert resolved to depart far away,

Certain that he would no longer find rest in the kingdom;

Exiled from the kingdom [Note: Ludolphus was taken from the living in 957. Nor did Adalbert immediately leave Italy, but only in 962, when Otto the Great descended into Italy. The continuator of Regino, under the year 963, writes that he then withdrew to Corsica. His father, King Berengar, was at the same time being besieged in the fortress of San Leo by the German army. MUR.],

He crossed the great sea.

This enemy came no farther into our territories.

“If he had loved me, he would not have departed from here in such misery” [Note: Our manuscripts have: “He would not have departed from here.” MUR.].

The Lombard people no longer sought or established

A king from their own nation, nor did it seek one again.

Then too the month of May was flowering in the grass,

In the nine-hundredth and fifty-seventh year [Note: *Quindeni*, that is, five times ten; but seven must be added. LEIB.] of the Word.

Atto, having Litulphus’s corpse, extracted

The entrails completely from his body.

His people mourned him and then placed them suitably

In a single tomb.

It is said that the church of Saint Prosper [Note: To learn what kind of church this was, see the manuscript epitome of Donizo mentioned above, preserved in the Estense library. “And Count Atto honorably buried the aforesaid Litulphus at the Church of Saint Prosper of Antognano, which is near the meadow of Carpinetum, in the place called Zianum.” The ancient German annals under the year 957 report that Liudolphus’s body was carried to Germany by his venerable archbishop brother, William, and honorably buried at Saint Alban’s in Mainz. Indeed, Donizo himself testifies that only the entrails were committed to a tomb in the church of Saint Prosper, while the body was sent by Atto to his father. MUR.] contains those remains,

And the place of Antonianum as well.

The body, embalmed with spices within,

He sent to his father, comforting and encouraging him:

“Do not mourn too much, for you will be able to conquer great things.

If you come immediately, you will overcome the Lombards,

For their king has fled; if only you hasten,

You will rule this kingdom of the Lombards.”

Otto grieved greatly over his son, when he had buried him.

The king himself immediately led many men back into Italy;

All the Lombards peacefully sought him,

Giving him their towns freely.

[Col. 0965C] With them he also sought Rome and received

The crown of the kingdom from the pope; from there he prospered.

He enriched Atto with great and lofty gifts,

And freely granted him several counties [Note: The Reggio manuscript has: “He granted him several.” Which counties were bestowed upon Atto (also called Adalbert) by Otto the Great will be shown by a charter published by Bacchinius in the appendix to the history of the monastery of Padolirone, p. 3, where in the year 967 we read of Adalbert, also called Atto, count of Modena by the grace of God. Indeed, he was also count of the city of Reggio, as is attested by a diploma of the same Otto in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 1582. There, under the year 964, mention is made of “Adalbert, illustrious count of Reggio, or of Modena, our faithful man.” Add that Atto himself is granted the title of marquis in the charters of his son Theudaldus, in the same Bacchinius, p. 16 of the cited appendix. Since in no charters written during his lifetime is Atto called anything other than count, there is reason to suspect that after his death the notaries gave him greater titles, so that greater honor might accrue to Theudaldus, his son. MUR.],

Through which he ruled; no wonder that he loved him deeply.

## CHAPTER II. Canossa recounts Atto’s love for her and how he acquired the bodies of the martyrs Victor and Corona and Saint Apollonius, bishop and confessor

[Col. 0966A]

As Atto grew wealthy, he raised my walls high.

Through me he was rich; through me he possessed all his things.

And therefore he sent me everything beautiful that came to him:

Cuirasses, spears, shields, and swords.

He adorned me with sacred limbs as with weapons;

A certain king gave him Victor and Corona [Note: See the Roman Martyrology, 14 May. LEIB.].

Victor, that most holy soldier, endured the punishment of the neck

Instead of heaven’s diadem;

Saint Corona was washed together with him in blood.

Atto brought these and many other saints here.

[Col. 0966B] Great Brescia gave him other relics as well.

For it freely offered him the head, right shoulder,

And arm of this highly honored Apollonius [Note: See the Roman Martyrology, 7 July. LEIB.].

Bishop Gotefredus accomplished this,

Because he was descended from the loins of this prince.

This bishop opened the sacred chest of the body,

And cut off the limbs; blood immediately came forth.

Therefore the good prince, greatly amazed,

At once vowed to him his own land

And a tenth of his coinage;

And happily brought the sacred relics here with him.

After this he endeavored to construct for himself a lofty church.

Within it the excellent man established divine schools [Note: A college of men engaged in sacred service. LEIB.],

Which would sweetly sing the hours to Christ

By night and day.

[Col. 0966C] He fashioned organs for the singers through their voices,

With which they might rejoice in the holy rites with high voices.

Good ornaments and shining crowns,

Of bright gold and tested silver,

He offered; these number twice twelve [Note: This may refer to the treasury of the Church of Canossa. LEIB.].

[Col. 0967A] Great censers, chalices, carved panels,

Palls, chasubles, and twelve copes

He presented to the church with sincere and upright heart.

Near the entrance he ordered his own tomb to be made,

In which, according to the custom of his fathers,

The prince now rests buried.

## CHAPTER III. What sort of wife Atto had, how many sons he had, that Prince Tedaldus succeeded him, and that Tedaldus built the monastery situated between the Po and the Lario

Let us not forget Atto’s wife.

Ildegarda was indeed the name of this beloved woman,

Learned, governing, prudent, upright, and a counselor.

[Col. 0967B] She often urged her husband toward better things.

With him she built Birsellum [Note: The monastery of Saint Genesius, founded by Atto at Brixellum, or Brescello, on the Po, flourished for a long time. I searched in vain for its foundation, or even a mention of it, in the Benedictine Annals of the celebrated Mabillon. It is now worn away and has for several centuries been without monks; its revenues are commended to ecclesiastical princes. Fulvius Azzarius in the manuscript histories of Reggio, and Bacchinius, p. 76 of the appendix to the history of Padolirone, present a charter of Countess Matilda in which she grants many estates to the monastery “which my parents built in the fortress of Brixellum, in a place belonging to them, where Lord Thebaldus now appears to preside as abbot; it was built in honor of the Holy Trinity, Saint Michael the Archangel, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and Saint Genesius.” MUR.] for the monks to possess.

From these two were born three whom the world admires:

Rodulphus, very young and exceedingly handsome,

Who died before his father;

After him came the good and great bishop Gotefredus [Note: Of Parma. LEIB.],

And Tedaldus,

Who after Atto preserved all his honor [Note: That is, he alone succeeded to his possessions and honors. [Col. 0968D] Sigebertus is therefore rightly rejected, whom Sigonius assigns as Atto’s son and Thedaldus’s brother, or Albert Azo, or Albertatius, whom Pigna assigns. LEIB.],

Enlarging his own lands, being exceedingly rich,

Dear to kings and well known to them.

The Roman pope sincerely loved him

And granted him Ferraria [Note: Namely Ferrara, where Thedaldus’s fortress, built by him, long remained. MUR.] in his service.

He cared for the Canossan fortress no less than his father.

Near the Po and beside the waters of the Lario

[Col. 0967C] He built a worthy monastery [Note: The history of this monastery was published at Modena in 1696 by the celebrated Benedictine abbot of the Modenese Benedictines, Benedict Bacchinius, who died a few years ago. MUR.] for the Lord, dedicated to Saint Benedict.

Certainly he preferred that monks should be there.

Blessed is this place, for it is exceedingly religious.

Yet Prince Theudaldus was not permitted

To bury his own limbs there;

He rests buried with his father.

He fought many battles; Thedaldus’s deeds are very great.

## CHAPTER IV. On Thedaldus’s wife and his three sons

Thedaldus’s wife was named Guillia the duchess.

She pleased the lowly through her piety, and also pleased the great.

She bore three splendid persons to the world:

Tedaldus, bishop of Arezzo,

And the lofty and wise duke Boniface,

And the learned Conrad, strong as a lion.

O good offspring, which he who sits above the stars,

Through whom all things were created, bestowed upon the earth!

Whatever can be found as a beautiful example,

This offspring found, whether in arms or in religion.

For their father, when dying, blessed their persons

And ordered that the elder should be

His beloved and modest son Boniface.

While their father was still alive, the faithful servants,

Prudent nobles and counts alike, swore allegiance to him [Note: If counts were subject to Theudaldus, he must have been a marquis. Indeed, he is given this title in charters of those times, some of which I shall produce, if God grants it. But which march he ruled is entirely uncertain. Certainly not Tuscany, as I shall eventually reveal. Thedaldus was count of Reggio, as a charter now in my possession attests. MUR.].

After their father’s death he gave them very many gifts.

Their father had left twelve deerskin sacks filled with money,

In his own chamber at Canossa.

He gave all of them away at one time as a gift.

His goodness and his resounding deeds are celebrated everywhere.

## CHAPTER V. On the bishop of the city of Arezzo, who was Boniface’s brother

Thedaldus, bishop of Arezzo and friend of Christ,

Was devoted to religion [Note: The manuscript of Reggio has: “He was religious.” MUR.],

And undertook the devoted care of the Lord’s flock,

Showing noble examples.

He was so chaste that once certain wicked men,

Foolishly, on account of a certain weakness,

Urged him to commit fornication.

After considering the matter, the bishop ordered

A certain prostitute (*lupa*) to be brought in,

First commanding that a fire be placed before his bed.

He saw the fire blazing with flames.

As he approached it and felt the flames, overflowing with tears,

He cried: “Woe, woe is me! If I cannot endure

A slight and worthless little flame,

If it should happen that I perish, wretched man,

How shall I endure that flame of the abyss?

This crime will lead me to the pit of Etna.

This sin—I reject it and utterly refuse it,

Lest I be completely burned in the hidden fire.”

Bishop Thedaldus gives such an example of what must be done.

He began to speak against the Simoniacs,

Detesting them, and said with a temperate mind:

“I would certainly give a thousand pounds for the papacy

If, by what I am striving to do, I could drive

All the accursed Simoniacs from the whole world at last.”

Music or song began to praise this Thedaldus.

They never cease, but are continually renewed by him,

[Col. 0969A] the book *Micrologus* [Note: [Col. 0969C] Its author was Guido, a Benedictine monk. Vossius, *De scientia mathematica*, chapter 22, p. 95, commits more than one error, following Trithemius when he writes that Guido flourished in the year 1070. He also makes him a monk of the monastery of Saint Leufredus near Évreux, then a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and identifies him with the Guitmund who wrote against the arch-heresiarch Berengar. This Guido was indeed a monk, [Col. 0969D] but in the year 1022 he was committing the art of music to writing; he was an Aretine by birth and had been educated in the monastery of Pomposa. His book, written by hand—so it seemed to me—more than four hundred years ago, is still preserved in the celebrated Ambrosian Library under this title: *Micrologus*, that is, “A Short Treatise on Music.” It is preceded by these verses:

The hearts of men, softened by my Muses, yearn;

A single virtue has given me measured strokes;

At the summit of heaven I pour forth most welcome songs,

Giving the court of Christ a gift with the minister’s voice.

I painted myself in order, I who first fashioned songs.

It pleased me to recall the Muses, released, to the school,

So that they might be open to the young, until now confined to lofty paths.

May love with me destroy the weapon of envy.

A dreadful plague has carried all blessings from the earth.

I painted myself in order, I who first fashioned songs.

[Col. 0970C] Observe an acrostic in the initial letters of these verses—indeed a double one: Guido, Guido. The book’s prologue begins: “Since both natural disposition and the imitation of honor made me diligent in the common good, I began, among other things, to teach music to boys,” etc. The same codex contains other writers on musical matters. MUR.]

Guido, the skilled musician,

A monk, and also a blessed hermit, dictates this for himself, etc.

## CHAPTER VI. How certain Lombard margraves sought to separate Conrad from Boniface; how Boniface married the countess Richilda; and concerning the great war waged by almost all Lombardy against Boniface and Conrad at Cuviliolo, near the city of Reggio

Let this style now return plainly to the lay brothers.

Their chief concern centers on Canossa:

As father or grandfather, so they have always loved it;

They are lovers of peace, yet strong as lions.

These men maintained true peace together with prosperity;

But fierce envy, because of them, possessed the greater part

Of the Lombard counts, after the manner of wicked men.

[Col. 0969B] For they took great pains [Note: [Col. 0970C] The ancient codex reads: “For they took excessive pains.” LEIB.

[Col. 0970D] The Regiensian manuscript likewise has: “For they took excessive pains.” MUR.]

to injure the brothers’ fraternal peace.

But since they could not destroy the fraternal bond,

They promised to give Conrad, who was then very young

And believed them, a bride born from among themselves.

At last, taking certain servants privately,

Without the elder brother’s approval, he went empty-handed

To those counts; when he saw them, he rejected them.

He soon appeased his brother’s mind; the brothers were quickly reconciled, and their enemies were thereby confounded.

Those who had gone with Conrad and the servants mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0970D] That is, the servants who had gone with the aforesaid Conrad. The same applies below to *praetaxatus*, meaning “previously mentioned.” MUR.],

Were thrown out altogether by the learned prince Boniface;

He gave them all to other masters.

The aforesaid margrave married Richilda,

The countess who was of the blood of the princely Giselbert [Note: [Col. 0970D] The ancient codex has *ex*, that is, *exit*, “comes forth.” LEIB.

The Padoliron codex also plainly has *exit*, “comes forth.” In chapter 8, p. 55 of the *Antiquities of Este*, I showed that this countess Richilda was not the daughter of Giselbert, count of Luxembourg, but of Giselbert, count of the Palace in Italy, and that she was of Lombard origin. MUR.]

[Col. 0969C] because she was rich in honor.

She gave abundant alms to the poor and paid tribute;

Now dead, she lies at Nogara without descendants [Note: [Col. 0970D] In a town of the Veronese territory. MUR.].

Since these two leaders were strong against all their enemies,

And great, as though they were giants,

A great multitude, with the tumult of their enemies,

Hastened from the whole kingdom to Cuviliolo [Note: [Col. 0970D] The Estense manuscript, containing the *Epitome of Donizo*, supplies this: “And this took place in the village of Cuvilio, near the city of Reggio, a mile and a half away. It is now called Coviolo.” MUR.],

Attacking them in battle and attempting to defeat them.

[Col. 0970A] These men overcame them by fighting fiercely.

At the front Boniface struck the enemy.

A certain soldier was seeking him with a savage cry;

The renowned leader struck off his head. Great fear of death

And of the sword seized all those whom Boniface

Cut down with his powerful sword [Note: [Col. 0970D] The ancient codex reads *dense*, “thickly,” rather than *dente*. LEIB.].

When he had become exceedingly tired, though not defeated,

He turned his horse, while all the crowds rejoiced around him,

And, growling, abandoned the battle. Then, like a stag,

The well-equipped Conrad—no one was stronger than he—

Came out of the groves with nearly five hundred shields.

“Why are you leaving, prudent brother Boniface?” he said.

“Gather your strength; let it please you to return with me.

The field must not be surrendered to these enemies; let us return.”

Strengthened at once by this exhortation,

[Col. 0970B] Boniface returned with his renewed brother, banners flying.

They renewed the former battle and brought woe upon their enemies.

They kill and cut down, and the field is filled with blood;

The rumps of the war-horses become red there with blood,

As they overthrow them; the fugitives turn their backs and flee.

Then there was a great slaughter of men and horses.

The long spear, bold as a thousand arms,

And Boniface’s strength seemed to all the enemies

As great as a hundred cubits, while Conrad’s sword

Seemed a hundred cubits broad.

Driven far away, they scarcely returned to shelter,

Often turning their eyes behind them in fear.

Conrad the leader and Boniface, renowned avenger,

Sheathed their sword-points stained with blood.

As Conrad lowered his own weapon, he wept bitterly for you;

He saw that his white cuirass was dripping with blood.

[Col. 0970C] Recognizing the wound, he comforted his foster-brother.

Their phalanx gathered the field and the weapons.

The city of Reggio also gave Conrad medical treatment.

Once this famous soldier was almost healed,

He rose in play, failing to take care of himself while eating.

As a result, the wound became greatly inflamed again

And brought deep grief to his brother for many years.

For the handsome young man departed from the body in the city.

[Col. 0971A] At his funeral, the Three-in-One was entreated,

That he might forgive his sins and grant him blessed rest.

For his obsequies, holy bands were summoned [Note: [Col. 0971C] The Regiensian codex has “For whose obsequies.” LEIB.],

So that they might obtain for him that he be joined to heaven.

A gathering of bishops and clergy from every order

Was present to bury so great an athlete.

His illustrious brother took up his brother’s body

And carried it to the secure tomb of fathers and mothers,

Namely, to the revered church of Canossa.

Countless peoples, grieving with him for his brother,

Gathered and raised their voices over such a nobleman.

But when this skilled soldier had been buried,

So that his spirit might be free from the punishments of gloomy pains,

Germanicus, at that time, gave to Saint Apollonius

The productive estate called Cagnaula,

[Col. 0971B] In the thirty-third year of the peaceful Word.

## CHAPTER VII. How many margraves were buried at Canossa

I praise God at Canossa, who granted me the pleasant

Time of living with noble princes,

Whom, while alive, I had as sweet lords and friends,

And whom, when dead, I was worthy to bury in the tomb.

From this my lament, grief, and tears are revealed [Note: [Col. 0971C] In the Regiensian manuscript, *relevantur*, “are raised.” MUR.],

Especially when I commemorate the anniversary of bitter death.

Both bishops [Note: [Col. 0971C] That is, Gotefridus, bishop of Brescia, and Thedaldus, bishop of Arezzo, each buried in his own [Col. 0971D] church. MUR.] are far from the fathers’ cave.

Death carried off Hildegard on the third Ides of “Sabat” [Note: [Col. 0971D] This appears to have been written for *Sabbato*, “Saturday.” But how can this be the place for “Saturday,” when a month must be mentioned? MUR.].

The Ides of February once took away Atto’s soul.

On the eighth Ides of May [Note: [Col. 0971D]

May. LEIB.

The manuscript *Epitome* reads: “On the third Ides of January.” MUR.],

I mourn and bury Thedaldus.

On the third Ides of July, you punish Conrad.

Rudolph left the earth, and before the Kalends

[Col. 0971C] Of August, with twelve days joined together.

Two days before August finally came to an end,

The earth received the virtuous Guilia [Note: [Col. 0971D]

The same manuscript *Epitome*: “And Countess Guilia, on the penultimate day”—it should be written “the antepenultimate day”—“of August, lies with boys and girls in a single monument. There is still, in the hills of the Modenese territory, a fortress called Guilia, which perhaps received its name from this illustrious woman.

In all editions to this point, and even in Leibniz himself, although he used the Vatican codex, the bones of Donizo’s poem were dislocated here. After this verse there followed:

“Never did his provost and his clergy seek

Any divine offices,” etc. …

[Col. 0972C] But since these verses make no sense with what precedes, they had to be transferred below to chapter 16. Other verses were missing here, which I now supply from two manuscripts, the Regiensian and the Padolironian. The dialogue between Canossa and Mantua, therefore, since it does not belong here, will be read below, after the death of the margrave Boniface has been related. MUR.]

I covered these with stone, together with their sons and girls.

May God lead them to the folds and halls of paradise.

May they not be mingled with the goats, but be pure members of the flock,

Where they may pasture forever in the kindly pastures of Christ. Amen.

## CHAPTER VIII. What was Boniface’s stature and character, and what the Sibyl prophesied about him

I beg all the people to hear the deeds of Boniface.

[Col. 0972A] I know that the deeds of Boniface were illustrious.

Whoever loves to retain radiant honors worthily,

Let him love his deeds and know them to be radiant.

In intellect he flourished, like Daniel in understanding;

While he was still a boy, he flourished in intellect.

He was handsome, excellent, beautiful, and comely,

Prudent like Joseph, handsome and excellent.

When he became a young man, he attained the stature of Saul;

As a young man, he governed all things prosperously.

As Saul stood out among the ranks while riding,

So he too was greater than the ranks while riding.

He was vigorous in strength like that slayer of Goliath,

Who was vigorous in lips, hands, and strength.

He possessed the countless wealth of the wise Solomon,

For he possessed the countless splendors of the world.

Nothing was lacking to him on land, sea, or in the heavens;

Conducting himself wisely, nothing was lacking to him.

This nobleman learned to be more generous than all others;

This nobleman learned to give lavishly.

The ancient Sibyl sings of him—believe her now, all of you;

I write what the ancient Sibyl sings about him.

That the beginning of this leader’s name is B [Note: [Col. 0972D] Perhaps *infit*, “she declares.” MUR.],

It is not without reason that B is its beginning.

Boniface appears clear and good in face,

Clear and good in arts [Note: [Col. 0972D] The Regiensian manuscript has *actibus*, “in deeds.” MUR.] and in speech.

She prophesies that he will be wealthy and peaceful,

She prophesies that he will always be victorious.

Whatever the woman sang about you, good leader, you possessed;

I believe that what the woman sang was true.

She spoke many things about Christ and judgment,

And many things about the end of the world.

God gave you a noble and worthy marriage;

Great Beatrice is a noble marriage.

Beautiful Beatrice was born from royal stock [Note: [Col. 0972D] See the brief genealogical table of Duchess Beatrice on p. 64 of the *Antiquities of Este*. MUR.]. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Hadwigu, daughter of Henry the Fowler and sister of Otto the Great, bore Hugh—commonly called Hugh Capet, king—and Beatrice. Beatrice, married to Frederick the Elder, duke of the Mosellans, bore him Duke Theodoric, father of Duke Frederick, whose daughter this Beatrice was. This was well observed from an ancient genealogy of Saint Arnulf by Francesco Maria Florentinus, who illuminated the affairs of the great Matilda and her ancestors in a distinguished volume. LEIB.]

She was born from the stock of the world’s ancestors.

She shone far away with the honor of Leah and Rachel,

As wise Sarah shone far away.

A single figure gives the name Beatrice to Boniface;

A single figure gives the letter B to both their names.

They are equal in goodness and resemble one another in nobility [Note: [Col. 0972D] Correct from the Regiensian manuscript: *similantur*, “they resemble.” MUR.];

Those who are equal in goodness fit together well.

[Col. 0973A] Italy produced the noble Boniface,

And Gaul brings Beatrice to the Italians.

Thus both are blessed for this world and for Olympus;

May both shine in heaven as they do in this world.

## CHAPTER IX. With how much glory and honor the duke and margrave Boniface married the illustrious duchess Beatrice

May God grant you, Beatrice, to stand in shining chambers [Note: [Col. 0973C] The Regiensian codex has “to stand for you.” MUR.].

I now wish the heroic poem joyfully to adorn

The memorable deeds of the great duke Boniface.

First, brave Gaul recognizes how great he is,

When he sought the daughter of the radiant Duke Frederick [Note: [Col. 0973C] Duke of Upper Lorraine, or of the Mosellans. LEIB.],

Whom Matilda, his lawful wife, finally bore [Note: [Col. 0973D] Namely, that Matilda, daughter of Herman, duke of Swabia, who married Frederick, duke of Upper Lorraine. Hence the name of the maternal grandmother was renewed in the great countess Matilda, according to an ancient custom that still survives. MUR.].

Frederick gave this Beatrice

[Col. 0973B] To Boniface; and when the duke went there,

He brought great ornaments and horses with him.

Under their feet he ordered not merely steel

To be placed, but silver, as though it were iron.

He also wished no nail to be struck from this,

So that the people could discover who he was.

The war-horses ran, while the silver sprang back;

It was gathered everywhere and found throughout the fields

By the people of the land, testifying that this man was rich.

Then the excellent prince did many things worthy of record,

But the pen, carried by affection, hastens

To our lady [Note: [Col. 0973D] Namely, the great countess Matilda, whom Donizo had decided to treat above all others. MUR.],

Whom the poem greatly embraces.

The bridegroom enriches her, and through her is enriched himself;

From her he receives servants, maidservants, towns [Note: [Col. 0973D] Alberic of the Three Fountains, a monk, says in the chronicle published by Leibniz under the year 1076: “The marchioness Matilda ruled her land manfully and founded an abbey of canons of Saint Peter at the mountains near Brescia, in the diocese of Metz.” It therefore seems likely to me that the towns Beatrice brought to the margrave Boniface as her dowry, and which passed by inheritance to their daughter Matilda, were situated in that region. MUR.], and villages.

[Col. 0973C] Through her, Gaul fears this lord together with us.

What Gallic prince, richer and greater than this man,

Rules Italy? Gaul provides him with much,

Bringing this countess to Lombardy.

The Ligurians and the Romans come to meet her;

The poor rejoice, and the very rich rejoice with them.

For three months banquets are held. There spices [Note: [Col. 0973D] Aromatic substances. LEIB.]

Are ground like spelt at the course of running water.

From one well they draw the drink of Bacchus;

From another well the true beverage flowed.

A bucket hung from a silver chain,

[Col. 0974A] With which the sweetest drink, wine, was drawn.

Bowls and platters were carried to the table by a horse;

The table vessels gleamed with silver and gold.

Drums, citharas, pipes, and lyres sounded there,

And the renowned duke gave exceedingly great gifts.

At Marego [Note: [Col. 0973D] Here the ancient author of the manuscript *Epitome* in the Estense Library must be heard: “And he led her”—namely Beatrice—“with great honor to the bishopric of Mantua, and there held the wedding in the place called Marago, near the river Mincio.” MUR.] these great banquets were held.

The noble wife bore a son, Frederick,

Then Beatrice, and afterward Matilda,

Who resembled her mother, while her color was especially that of her father.

While I desire at least to speak of the other children,

A great groan increases, and grief grows young again.

She will preserve these memorials of her fathers, as the best of mothers;

Her father’s honor and her mother’s love are her glory.

God granted her to these Lombards in those years.

[Col. 0974B] Let us now dismiss this and speak only of her father.

In her own time she will have a happy poem.

## CHAPTER X. How King Conrad conquered Parma with Boniface’s help, and how the same king and the same margrave were joined by an oath of alliance

Let the swift-handed pen return to adding to the pages

How the illustrious avenger Boniface aided Augustus

And made with him a memorable treaty.

Chrysopolis [Note: [Col. 0974D] When Jerome Albertutius said in his book *On the Cities of Italy* that he had seen an ancient inscription in which Parma seemed to be called “Julia Chrysopolis,” Leander Alberti denied that the name Julia or Chrysopolis of Parma was found among the ancients and declared the inscription spurious. Had he read our Donizo, he would have judged more fairly. An anonymous geographer of Ravenna, recently published, now places the matter beyond dispute; in book IV he has: “Julia Chrysopolis, which is Parma,” as the editor Porcheron properly noted. That anonymous author supports Donizo, and Donizo supports him. LEIB.

Gruter, p. 492, no. V, cites an inscription reading: “Colonia Julia Augusta Parmensis.” But it contains no name Chrysopolis. See nevertheless what Leibniz notes.

In the very ancient Acts of Saint Domninus the Martyr, in Surius under 9 October, it is said that blessed Domninus had come to the fifteenth milestone from the city of Julia Chrysopolis, that is, Parma, from which the village of San Donnino is fifteen Roman miles distant. Perhaps this name was given to the place when the Greek emperors ruled all Italy. The manuscript epitomator mentioned above therefore says that it was called “Golden,” because the seven liberal arts were diligently studied there. Hence, instead of *quae grammatica*, he appears to have read *quia grammatica*, “because it is grammatical.” MUR.]

has long been called by the usage of the Greeks.

Under the golden tongue this Latin city sounds;

Namely, the city of Parma, which remains exalted in grammar.

The seven arts have been diligently studied there.

This city is enclosed by Conrad’s narrow Caesar’s rampart.

[Col. 0974C] To capture it, he orders it to be pierced with the people’s arrows;

Then a slaughter of Alemannic soldiers follows.

A certain Pacificus, in anger, killed twice four men;

Whereupon Caesar’s fury grew greater. At once he applies

Armed and helmeted guards to the walls,

And orders our well-taught hero Boniface

To hasten and help break the foolish city.

Immediately gathering troops of horsemen and foot soldiers,

The king’s friend hastened to the city’s destruction.

At this sight the citizens tremble and consider themselves doomed.

Without maintaining their ranks, they go at once to the king’s feet and house,

And all together open the city’s gates for him.

[Col. 0975A] At that time two wicked men were confined with the king [Note: [Col. 0975C] Should this be distinguished from what precedes, so that the meaning is that the citizens attacked two Germans, whom they held captive, because they were hostile to the king? For why did Conrad weep when they were killed? Certainly there is ambiguity here, and interpreters are needed. In any case, these events took place in 1037, on the holy birthday of our Redeemer, as Wipo testifies in his *Life of Conrad*, in the chapter “On the Sedition that Occurred at Parma.” In the Fulda Necrology, published by Leibniz, vol. III, p. 767, the Brunswick writer under the same year records: “Diethelm, Cuono, Sviggerus, and Hartwinus, and many others, were killed at Parma.” MUR.],

Very fat and strong men, beyond all others.

Breaking the bonds on their right and left hands,

They rush forward, tear, and also kill the citizens.

The young men of the city, eager to cut them down with knives,

Stand before them and slash their shoulders with swords.

When they had been killed in this way, the king and his friends wept,

And immediately he ordered the entire place to be burned.

Let the poem now tell with certainty

How Augustus was joined by oath to our prince.

Conrad, preserving and governing the empire,

Truly recognized that none was more powerful than all others

Than the marvelous, illustrious, generous, often-praised

And venerable great athlete Boniface.

He asked him, as a faithful man, to swear allegiance to him.
