[Col. 0975B] And therefore he said that the march [Note: [Col. 0975D]

The king therefore gave Boniface the march as a fief. LEIB.

But what march was this? Certainly not Tuscany, as I shall show, God willing, in the diplomatic volume. It must therefore have been another march subject to Boniface and his father. Perhaps it consisted of Mantua, Parma, Reggio, Modena, and other towns in these regions. But we easily stumble when the monuments of antiquity fail us. MUR.]

would serve him,

And that the king would repay the oath to him in turn.

Boniface agreed to this with the king and carried it out,

And the king then swore aloud [Note: [Col. 0975D]

That the king in turn swore to Boniface seems scarcely credible, nor was it customary in those times. LEIB.

Leibniz considered this quite incredible. I do not. Donizo reports it precisely because it was remarkable: it was not customary for emperors to swear to their vassals. From this, however, Boniface’s power as margrave should be judged. Donizo himself states that the oath was written in a charter; indeed, we may reasonably conjecture that he had discovered and seen such a charter. Finally, Conrad is not said to have sworn anything that diminished his dignity. See p. 275 of the *Antiquities of Este*, where Margrave Fulco of Este, in 1097, is recorded as having been granted the privilege that no royal collector of the ban might exact it from the margrave. Boniface, being far more powerful, could obtain greater concessions, especially since around the year 1037 he was enlarged by the march of Tuscany. MUR.]

To preserve for him his life,

His limbs, and the honor proper to a prince,

Without deceit and uprightly in all things,

As long as life remained to them—this they confirmed.

No duke ever deserved such carefully honored treaties.

This oath was written in a charter.

## CHAPTER XI. What Boniface did when going to Burgundy and returning

[Col. 0976A]

When King Conrad died, and his son Henry succeeded him,

A prudent and skilled king,

He maintained peace with our prince.

It happened that he surrounded Miroaltum with a rampart [Note: [Col. 0976C]

In Burgundy. The distinguished Florentinus denies that he had found anything concerning Henry’s expedition against the Burgundians. Nevertheless, Hermannus Contractus of Canossa mentions it under the year 1042. King Conrad had already captured the castle of Murat, according to Wipo; therefore, if Donizo reports correctly, it must have revolted again. It lies not far from Neufchâteau. LEIB.

The Regiensian codex has *Muroaltam*, which agrees better with the castle of Murat. But, as I already noted in the *Antiquities of Este*, p. 262, Donizo is mistaken here. It was not Henry III, king of Germany and the second of the emperors, who invaded the kingdom of Burgundy. This happened under his father, Conrad I Augustus, as Wipo in his *Life* and Heppidanus in his *Chronicle* attest. Arnulf of Milan, the historian, also mentions the same expedition in vol. IV of the *History of Italy*; according to him, Bishop Heribert and the excellent Margrave Boniface, the two lights of the kingdom, brought aid to Conrad. MUR.]

which yielded to neither warfare nor missiles.

When the king and his army had become exhausted around it,

He sent for a well-equipped man, one accustomed to such things,

Namely, for the prudent and sufficiently courageous Boniface [Note: [Col. 0976D] “The bold.” LEIB.],

So that he would not fail to come to his aid or abandon him.

He granted the emperor’s request, and then

Led with him a trained army, exhorting them

To act wisely and prudently and to seize their weapons together

[Col. 0976B] Promptly, since the strong would be able to conquer.

Proceeding with great expense and power, [Note: [Col. 0976D] Perhaps: “With many soldiers.” LEIB.]

He approached the fortress and sent a suitable messenger

To the king, so that the latter would not batter the exhausted army [Note: [Col. 0976D] “The army.” LEIB.],

But should withdraw, since Boniface wished the fortress to yield to him [Note: [Col. 0976D] Boniface wanted the fortress to yield to him, not to surrender itself to the king. LEIB.].

Once the fortress had been captured by him alone,

He preferred to return immediately to his native borders.

The king [Note: [Col. 0976D] Perhaps: “Let him depart.” The duke means that he desired the honor of the conquest and therefore wanted the king and his men to withdraw three days before the duke’s arrival. Otherwise, if the fortress were captured through the king, he would never afterward come to his aid beyond the mountains, but would immediately return to Italy. LEIB.] went far away, and all his attendants with him,

Before the duke set foot there on the third day.

[Col. 0977A] He gave this order: if the fortress were captured through him,

He would not proceed beyond the mountains,

But would plainly return immediately.

The aforesaid fortress, planted in hostile Burgundy,

When the king carried away its armed clients [Note: [Col. 0977D]

When the king withdrew with his soldiers or vassals. LEIB.

Correct this from the Regiensian codex: “The clients of this fortress.” Those called clients in this verse are armed retainers or soldiers; the ancient authors of the Genoese Annals, whose work is to be published, used this word especially in that sense. MUR.],

Exalted themselves greatly, roaming through the fields [Note: [Col. 0977D] They carried off booty through the countryside. LEIB.].

It happened that they heard Duke Boniface was approaching,

With his own Lombards, properly armed.

They rejoiced because they believed they could take away all

Their property [Note: [Col. 0977D] *Causas*, that is, plunder their possessions; *cosa* means “thing” or “property” in Italian. LEIB.]. But the outcome prevented this.

On the third day the prince arrived there,

With his cohort skillfully arranged in divisions.

The barbarous and savage people quickly fortified themselves,

Then came out from afar in a shielded and helmeted column,

And thought to break the hard shield in battle.

[Col. 0977B] No phalanx ever prevailed completely

To break Boniface’s shield, nor can any ever do so.

When battle arose, the savage people began to cut with steel;

The duke struck more fiercely everywhere,

And urged his men to stand firm with hardened hearts.

Many horns and trumpets echoed over the heights,

Until the enemies turned their backs and retreated inside.

When he had spoken these words, he filled the people with terror.

The Lombard people held their weapons manfully,

And trumpets and many great horns sounded.

The terrified people [Note: [Col. 0977D] Both manuscripts I have used read: “And the people, fearing the dreadful thing, returned, heavily cut down.” MUR.]

returned, gravely wounded and driven back,

And sought the fortress, wishing only to shut themselves inside.

Swift Boniface did not permit this,

But entered at the same time and pierced them with bitter javelins.

Immediately he sent word to the king concerning the fortress,

[Col. 0977C] That he should come unarmed and take it,

Since he himself and his people desired and intended to return

To their native land without delay.

When the king, the dukes, and the counts learned this news,

They praised and marveled that the fortress had been so quickly captured.

The king had sent renowned athletes to capture and hold it,

With the aforesaid leader giving it to them [Note: [Col. 0977D] “With the aforesaid leader giving it,” that is, delivering or handing it over to them. LEIB.].

Then the Lombards, honored together with their prince,

Returned refreshed to their own homes,

After taking great wealth by valor and arms.

When the same remarkable victor returned,

It happened that he stopped to pasture his army

In the camps of a certain fortress [Note: [Col. 0977D] The Regiensian codex has “in the camp.” MUR.] [Note: [Col. 0977D] The ancient codex reads: “In the fields of a certain camp, a camp,” that is, to obtain provisions and fodder for Boniface’s forces. LEIB.],

In deserted fields. As servants commonly do,

Many of the boys began secretly to run

[Col. 0978A] To the yellow crops and eagerly carry them off for their horses.

Then the men of the place were greatly angered,

And, seizing weapons and war-horses with armed retainers,

They beat the boys on the necks [Note: [Col. 0978D] Perhaps: “They beat the boys on the necks and take their horses for themselves”—that is, take them from the boys. LEIB.] and took their horses for themselves.

The brutish Burgundians did this like fools.

But the duke, greatly angered, as a great man is accustomed to be,

Ordered thirty lances [Note: [Col. 0978D] “Thirty spearmen.” LEIB.] to advance toward the fortress.

He had the entire people rise again,

And ordered them to flee far away and return to the battle in the field,

Once they had come near the concealed band [Note: [Col. 0978D] He placed his entire people, or all his soldiers, in ambush. He ordered the thirty men to flee from the field of battle as far as the place of ambush. LEIB.].

You should know that this was according to the duke’s command.

For, driven far from the fortress’s protection,

An ambushing phalanx, spreading from many directions [Note: [Col. 0978D] *Alans*; *spirans*, “breathing” or “spreading.” LEIB.],

Held all the Allobroges exposed in its grasp.

The terrifying margrave ordered that their ears and noses be cut off.

[Col. 0978B] A certain noble matron pleaded for her son,

Asking him to deign to spare him, so that she herself might finally

Offer him the young man placed on the scales,

Together with as much white silver as he weighed.

“Never!” he said, shaking his beard and threatening:

“I want your posterity to know that these things were done thus

As long as the world shall exist: that this Boniface remained firm.

I may not retreat at all” [Note: [Col. 0978D] “I may not retreat and change what I have said.” LEIB.].

Their noses were cut and their ears likewise severed.

Three shields were filled with these parts all around.

With the whole sound company and a great triumph,

The duke thus returned to his own home.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the vinegar that Margrave Boniface sent to King Henry II, and the great gift that one of his servants gave to the same king

[Col. 0978C]

The king Henry II of magnificent appearance came to Italy [Note: [Col. 0978D] The third Henry of Germany, the second of Italy. LEIB.],

Wise, agreeable, and wealthy.

He sent Boniface many new commands [Note: [Col. 0978D] “His own commands.” LEIB.].

And since he wished to have with him the celebrated vinegar

Which the fortress called Canossa contained,

He ordered a silver cask to be made at once.

The margrave sent these to the king with two living oxen, a cart, and a yoke.

The king regarded the gift as dear, great, and splendid.

The king’s lodging at that time happened to be the city of Piacenza.

No prudent person should be surprised at such a gift

Once he learns that this duke’s servant shone

[Col. 0979A] With so great a gift and gave it to the king,

While Mantua was entertaining both the king and the duke.

Then Count Albert, wealthy in rank as a vice-count [Note: [Col. 0979D] Count Albert, vice— that is, vice-count. LEIB.],

A servant of the aforesaid duke and an inhabitant of that city,

Freely offered the king a hundred shining bay horses [Note: [Col. 0979D] Perhaps *balios* or *badios*? It is the color the French call *bai*, bay. LEIB.],

With rough saddles and rough bridles or reins;

A hundred dappled horses [Note: [Col. 0979D] *Mutatos*, that is, varied; the French call such variety of color *muance*. LEIB.],

And another hundred undappled, beautiful Asturian horses.

“What sort of man is he who gives you such gifts?” the queen cried.

The king replied to her as though in wonder:

“He who has servants such as Boniface has

Has no equal in the whole kingdom, as far as I can see.

Let this little servant tell me what he now wants for himself.”

“I seek nothing else, desire nothing, and hope for nothing from you,

[Col. 0979B] Except that my master may be loved.”

So Albert said to the king, who invited him

To dine with him at his own well-supplied table.

Albert feared this word, because he was Boniface’s servant.

He had never dared to eat with the king at the same table.

When the king was about to dine, he suddenly insisted

On the matter mentioned above; at last the duke granted the request.

With the king and duke together, the man just mentioned entered the dining room,

Almost alive [Note: [Col. 0979D] That is, scarcely alive from fear, half-dead. MUR.],

And accepted only a small portion of food.

After the meal the king gave him especially beautiful *mastrucae* [Note: [Col. 0979D] A kind of garment made from the skins of wild animals, worn by northern peoples and formerly by the Sardinians, according to Cicero, Prudentius, and Isidore. The manuscript epitomator thought *bursas* belonged to Donizo. The *pelliciones* mentioned below may have been a more splendid type of the same garments; the word still survives among Italians and French. MUR.],

And likewise flourishing fur garments.

[Col. 0979C] He carried this royal gift to the duke’s chamber, together with a stag’s hide,

Which he himself had filled with coins.

He fell at the prince’s feet, seeking pardon

For having shared the royal table with him.

Recognizing that he possessed the authority to retain it, the duke

Kindly pardoned the servant, while nevertheless forbidding the deed.

## CHAPTER XIII. How King Henry once attempted to capture Boniface, first in his council chamber and later on the occasion of a night watch

Each day this prince, Boniface, grew in power.

Holy faith protected him as a just and kindly man.

Moved by excessive envy, the king already mentioned

With cruel ingenuity planned to seize secretly

The man whom no one beneath the sky could capture.

[Col. 0979D] The king stood in his chamber, wishing to deliberate,

[Col. 0980A] And ordered that this shrewd duke come quickly to him.

He commanded that, by this ruse, the duke might be forcibly detained:

He ordered the doorkeeper to keep the doors tightly closed,

And not to let Boniface enter unless he himself came fifth [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Quintusmet*: “himself the fifth,” *selb funfte*, “he himself with four others”; *lui cinquième*, “he, the fifth.” LEIB.].

When the duke received the king’s order, he immediately sent word

That he would go to him.

“Against the aforesaid command,” I remember,

“Nothing clever can prevail,” [Note: [Col. 0980D] The Regiensian codex reads: “Against the learned man.” Perhaps the sense is: “Against a clever and prudent man, no cunning can prevail.” MUR.]

For the duke, having quickly gathered his own personal retainers [Note: [Col. 0980D] His household members, or his servants. MUR.] and many others carrying swords concealed beneath their clothing, ordered them to follow promptly behind him. The lofty margrave, surrounded by nobles, hastened forward. He ordered the chamberlains to open the first royal door [Note: [Col. 0980D] In an ancient manuscript it reads: “The chamberlains reopened it,” that is, after the doorkeepers had opened the first door, they immediately closed it once Boniface had been admitted. But his followers broke it open again. LEIB. The manuscripts I use likewise read “they opened.” MUR.]. They hastened to close it, but, pressed by anger, he advanced farther and burst through the second door as well. A third remained, beneath which the king was then staying; this too was broken, and the duke entered surrounded by his men [Note: [Col. 0980D] Perhaps: “which the duke, surrounded by his men, entered.” MUR.].

[Col. 0980B] At this the shrewd and cunning king was exceedingly disturbed.

“What do I see? What is this?” he said. “I am astonished at you, Boniface.”

“This has always been the custom of my household, O king: my men have always been accustomed to be with me and have always been so,” the duke replied.

At once the king offered peace. This time the king saw that he could not retain him; therefore he pretended peace with smooth words.

Again considering the matter and seeking to capture him, he cleverly devised that this should be done by a blind stroke of war. During the night he asked the duke himself to keep watch for a while [Note: [Col. 0980D] In the Regiensis manuscript, “asked voluntarily.” MUR.], saying that this would please him. The prudent fox knows the Getulian custom in speech.

The margrave in no way rejected the king’s request. He had many beautiful little candles arranged. [Col. 0980C] Altogether they contained a pound of wax, and he ordered all his men to carry them lit. He commanded that spears be fixed above them [Note: [Col. 0980D] The Padoliron manuscript reads: “and stretched spears.” MUR.] and ordered a column of wax, shining with a great light, to go before his numerous retinue.

Dense with soldiers and surrounded by wondrous light, he hastened toward the king’s lodging. At last the king’s servants saw him approaching from a distance: it looked as though the whole earth itself were burning with torches. The king also perceived this. Recognizing that he could do nothing against him, he sent him back with thanks and great expressions of gratitude.

## CHAPTER XIV. That Boniface was devoted to divine matters

[Col. 0980D] Just as this Boniface shone in the deeds of the world [Note: [Col. 0980D] After this, the following is added in an ancient manuscript epitome of the Estense codex: “Duke and margrave Boniface was wise, kind, prudent, generous, a lover of the poor, merciful, beloved by all, provident and discerning in counsel, eloquent in speech and steadfast in spirit, a defender of churches; he gladly listened to divine offices and gave gifts to churches,” and so forth. These words were undoubtedly drawn from Donizo’s poem, although none of these things appears in the printed editions. Either, therefore, some verses must be thought to have perished, or the author of the epitome rendered in these words chapter 8 of Book II, where Boniface is praised. MUR.], so he was renowned in divine and venerable deeds. He held holy bishops especially dear and gave them what he judged would be pleasing to them. His chaplains always reverently sang the nocturnal hours and the daily hours for him. No bishop possessed a chapel more splendid than his [Note: [Col. 0981D] More richly adorned than his own chapel. LEIB.].

He loved the clergy, but he loved a true monk even more. This nobleman openly confessed his own sins and offenses with great devotion every year to the brethren who served Christ in splendid attire, speaking with his own mouth, grieving in his heart, and asking forgiveness. The brethren and their abbot washed away his transgressions. To their church he habitually gave the finest gifts; no king ever gave better ones there.

Once he happened to go there and to observe the custom that he had long been accustomed to maintain, namely, to assist in the divine service as a good man. [Col. 0981B] He stood on a lofty throne, though not with a proud heart, and, looking at the choir, saw the faces of the boys bowed toward the ground as they sweetly sang the hours. Wondering at them, he asked why they stood in this way and conducted themselves so.

He learned from the monks that they always stood fixed in this manner. The cheerful and excellent duke did not forget this. He secretly had a certain man climb onto the roof of the church with money, because he himself wished to see something astonishing. The man threw ten pounds from the roof, and a clatter sounded in the middle of the choir; yet the boys’ eyelids did not open at all. [Col. 0981C] He looked at the money, but no one touched even a single coin.

The illustrious duke therefore rejoiced still more and said: “Within a few years these boys will be like alders. Let such a jest be praised, recounted, and cherished.”

## CHAPTER XV. That the custom of selling churches came from the Theutonic kings, and that Boniface received penance for this from Abbot Guido [Note: [Col. 0981D] Thus also in the Regiensis manuscript. The Padoliron manuscript adds: “from Saint Guido.” This was the abbot of the monastery of Pomposa, situated in the Ferrara region near the Adriatic. Having attained a reputation for proven holiness, he was called to heaven in 1046, according to Hermannus Contractus; Bollandus published his Life. MUR.]

The Theutonic kings, following a perverse doctrine, very often gave the temples of the supreme Lord to all the bishops for money; and every bishop of a city sold the parishes which each governed under himself.

[Col. 0982A] Following their example, churches of Christ were sold into the hands of laymen and of accursed priests and clerics—a thing that brought confusion upon the people. For this reason the holy abbot Guido rebuked Boniface; indeed, so that Boniface should sell no more [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript copies read “Bonifacium.” MUR.], he flogged him severely, naked before the altar of the Mother of God, although he had been accustomed to luxuries [Note: [Col. 0981D] The manuscript reads: “with bitter blows.” MUR.]. Boniface then vowed to Abbot Guido of Pomposa that he would never again sell any church [Note: [Col. 0981D] The same manuscript reads: “that he would sell none on his own.” MUR.].

For this sin, and for many others committed besides, he made yet another vow, one known to some at last: namely, that he would go to worship Christ and to the holy Sepulchre, if life and health should permit him, even if only for one full year. The duke immediately ordered a new ship to be built, [Col. 0982B] and arranged the expense by which he might fulfill this vow.

But he could not fulfill it, because death did not allow this. He himself left the earth on the sixth day after the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0982C] I possess a charter of agreement between our Boniface and Otta, abbess of the monastery of Saint Julia in Brescia, written only a few days earlier—namely, in the year 1052, in the eighth year of Emperor Henry’s reign, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth indiction. It was executed in the city of Mantua, in the palace of the same Margrave Boniface. Thus you see that this agrees correctly with what Donizo records. Arnulf of Milan, in his History, presents Boniface as an extremely old man. Indeed, since he began acting as margrave around the year 1004, he must have been old in 1052. MUR.] and may Christ lead him to heaven [Note: [Col. 0982D] Hermannus Contractus says that he was killed in an ambush in 1052, a fact the poet conceals. LEIB.].

When he died, was given to the earth, and was buried, then there stood one thousand and fifty-two years of God’s era. Mantua, you possess his body; this is a great honor to you, and you ought very often to give thanks to God. Remember always to beseech God with an upright heart, that he may guard the soul of this ancestor from punishments [Note: [Col. 0982D] Perhaps: “God of the age,” that is, Lord of the ages. LEIB. In the manuscripts I use, it reads “God of the age.” Nor was there any need to consult the manuscripts. MUR.].

On account of Christ crucified, let every person pray: “O God, remove from him the punishments and chains of Tartarus; when you come as judge with the saints, give him light. May the Virgin Mary stand at his head, blessed Michael at his right hand, and Peter, Andrew, and Apollonius at his left; may they lift him up and place him above the stars. Amen.”

## CHAPTER XVI. The urban dispute between Canossa and Mantua concerning the body of Duke and Margrave Boniface [Note: [Col. 0982D] In the editions published thus far, chapter 17 followed here with the title: “How many years Beatrix lived,” and so forth. But the urban dispute between Mantua and Canossa belongs here, although until now it had been placed elsewhere. Canossa complains that Mantua appropriated the body of the illustrious Duke Boniface, whereas his other ancestors had been buried at Canossa. It is also something for which the present new edition should be congratulated that I drew from the Regiensis and Padoliron manuscripts many verses lacking in the earlier editions, and now restore them all to their proper place. MUR.]

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

My lord Boniface wished his own body to be placed in the tomb of his fathers. You, Mantua, presuming this to be true, carried it away. Why did you disturb me by stripping me of so great a body?

### MANTUA REPLIES

I am called a city; you are called the Canusine fortress.

[Col. 0983A] I have men with me—look and consider what I possess [Note: [Col. 0983C] Perhaps one should read: “how many, look and consider with yourself,” that is, “I abound in citizens; you, consider how few you have with you.” Or: “tell what you yourself see.” MUR.].

I have abundant wealth, while you are a foolish little pauper. I am surrounded by a river and strengthened everywhere by ships. Nowhere else would it rightly be fitting for this body to be except in a city.

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

You possess the name of a city, but you are not great in honor. Even if you have many people, we know that you live without triumph unless another friend helps you.

If wars rise against you, what will you do, poor creature? You are not surrounded by a strong wall. When you rebel, you are struck from the waters and from the land. Your hope lies behind a palisade; a stake demands a shield [Note: [Col. 0983D] If I understand correctly, at that time Mantua was not yet surrounded by built walls, but defended itself with stakes placed around it and fixed into the ground—what is now called a palisade. Such a wall required many men for its defense. Canossa, by contrast, needed only a few to repel an enemy attack. My interpretation therefore seems to be this: each stake requires an armed man, and even in this way you would scarcely prevent the enemy from defeating you. MUR.] and a sword.

For you will scarcely be able to escape in this way if battles press you for even three periods of time. All your wealth will be exhausted.

From the foul waters, and from the fever that lingers in them, the cold is sent forth, as well as heat that burns too fiercely [Note: [Col. 0983D] Thus Mantua was situated six hundred years ago as it is in our own age, exposed to the same inconveniences from the surrounding marsh, of which Livy also makes mention. Catullus, who was born in the neighboring countryside, likewise called it a “foul marsh.” MUR.]. Yet I live unharmed through a thousand ages. Moreover, far from me lies a muddy and watery ditch.

If a war should come upon me, a true duel [Note: [Col. 0983D] A manuscript reads “duel.” Writers on etymology maintain that this was formed from *bellum* and in antiquity actually signified the same thing. The possible meaning here is: “If a war should ever arise in which there must be fierce fighting.” MUR.], I, strong, defeat my battles with few soldiers.

Even if—which I do not believe—there should ever occur a siege lasting around me for two lustrums, I would not be overcome in war, nor through lack of food, since I am made of stone and a wall stands above me.

My lofty strongholds are filled, beyond all fortresses, with grain, meat, and wine.

[Col. 0983C] I live securely with few people and sit at ease in play. No siege engine, no arrow shot against me, does me harm; I reduce and count a missile as nothing. I fear no king; but you fear every rebel. Know that the bones of the aforesaid lord rightly belong to me.

[Col. 0984A] ### MANTUA REPLIES

Truly you are strong, and savage pride is with you. Yet this is not surprising: you yourself understand no danger. I have often been beneath the waters and have frequently been exhausted in warfare.

Although you are at last close to the long-lived heaven, from which you remain proud, you nevertheless pleasantly seek the belly [Note: [Col. 0984C] At the end of this invented contest Donizo again uses the same word, saying: “I wish you to hold the belly of our lord.” Thus I think *alvum* is used for “body,” though with rather inelegant license. MUR.].

Behold, I possess a truly wondrous sanctuary of the saints, through which I defeat you. But if you wish, I shall leave words aside.

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

Whatever you can and know, immediately pour into our ears.

### MANTUA REPLIES

I have a church richly endowed with a proper bishop, and priestly chants resound there clearly. Many relics are venerated there, carefully preserved.

### CANOSSA, PROVOKED, SPEAKS

I am subordinate to you in nothing, because what is nobler stands with me. Mine is subject to the pope, whereas yours is subject to the patriarch [Note: [Col. 0984C] Ughellus records that under Pope Leo III, in 804, the bishopric of Mantua was first established and placed under the patriarch of Aquileia. In 1453 it began to obey the apostolic see immediately, as they say. Donizo therefore found an opportunity here to exalt the Canusine church, which even then depended directly upon the Roman pontiff. MUR.].

Mine is Roman; yours is Aquileian. Your bishop, whether he wishes it or not, attends the synod of the patriarch. If you renew him, the father-patriarch consecrates him [Note: [Col. 0984D] Although it is superfluous to point this out, the poet uses the word “father” for “patriarch.” MUR.]. For all your clergy remain servants forever.

My clergy’s song remains free through the pope [Note: [Col. 0984D] The manuscripts read *mea lirrica*. I have written *lyrica*. But what does this unusual word mean here? If Donizo truly wrote it, he used intolerable license to signify the choir of clerics of the Canusine church. MUR.].

Those ancient lords of mine—the noble men who built me—once wished this to be so. For this reason Father Atto sent Tedald to Rome, who with proper prayers petitioned Benedict, pontiff of the city of Rome. He freely granted this to it, releasing it so that no pontiffs there might establish any law, and so that it might never be subject to them but remain faithfully subject to the Roman see [Note: [Col. 0984D] Namely Benedict VII. The Estense archive has supplied me with a very old parchment containing a fragment of the same bull of Benedict, written by the hand of Stephen, notary of the sacred scrinium of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth indiction; issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of January through the hands of Guido, bishop and librarian of the holy apostolic see—whom Ciampini overlooked in his catalogue of the librarians of the Holy Roman Church—in the second year of the pontificate of Benedict VII, the most holy pope, and in the third year of the reign of Otto. This is the year 976, or rather 975; there is no time here to resolve the difficulty. The document reads: “How Count Teudaldus, son of the already deceased Count Adelbert, visiting the threshold of the apostles with worthy devotion, asked from our apostolic authority, on behalf of his father, as follows: that the church consecrated in honor of the holy confessors of God—namely Apollonius, Ursicinus, and Rusticianus—and of the martyrs Mauritius, Alexander, and Victor, which Adelbert himself had built from its foundations on his own property, namely on the rock called Canusia, should be so established.” It then adds that a tithe was assigned for the use of twelve canons, and so forth. Donizo says that Tedald was sent to Rome for this purpose by his father Atto. The same thing is inferred from the bull’s words “on behalf of his father.” What, then, do the other words of the bull mean: “of the already deceased Count Adelbert”? They seem to indicate that the man had already died. Either Atto, who was also Adelbert, died during Tedald’s journey, or, advancing into old age, he had already withdrawn from governing the people and had placed his son in charge of public affairs; this may also be suggested by the count’s title assumed by the son. This document will have its proper place elsewhere. MUR.].

He does not permit our provost to seek any synod, and his clergy never request one. If they wish to obtain divine offices, they may go wherever they please, provided only that the Catholic bishop there properly, holily, and reverently perform the sacred office.

May the Canusine vestibule be adorned with the dust of the saints and with the singing of priests.

### MANTUA REPLIES

I did not know these things about you, believe me, blessed one; but I am not surprised that you are not so under your bishop Regino [Note: [Col. 0985D] “Not to be,” that is, “not to exist.” LEIB.].

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

If I fear Regino, it is customary for me to regard him as a friend. My private law [Note: [Col. 0985D] The privilege of Pope Benedict VI or VII. LEIB.], which Pope Benedict granted me in a document written on papyrus [Note: [Col. 0985D] An ancient manuscript reads *fortiter*. I think *charta carecti* means a document made from papyrus or reed. LEIB. The ancients called certain sharp, dense, rush-like grasses *carices*, as Isidore testifies; places covered with sedge were called *carecta*. For this reason the word seems suspicious to me, although I do not deny that Egyptian papyrus remained in use down to that period. Did Donizo write *characti formiter ampla*, that is, “broad in the form of its letters”? Or *carecta*, or *characta*, meaning “written,” from *charaxo*, “I write”? MUR.], broad in its lettering,

separates him from Christ if he should in any way harm me. All my rights are far removed from his oversight. It likewise afflicts all pontiffs with a similar penalty.

### MANTUA REPLIES

Spare me, I beg you; I see that you touch the heavens.

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

I spare you greatly; at least sing songs with me, as I wish, about our lord Boniface.

### MANTUA REPLIES

What excellent thing have you said? I have composed many verses without you. Perhaps you forget that I am a gate of poetry [Note: [Col. 0986C] “To be.” LEIB.].

My sweet friend, I gave birth to the poet Virgil [Note: [Col. 0986C] The Regiensis manuscript reads “Virgil, Virgil,” certainly. MUR.], who surpassed all others in producing verses.

### CANOSSA SPEAKS

With your own mouth, deceitful one, you condemn yourself too much. Do I not know how much Virgil belongs to you? Certainly he was born from you, but he cannot endure the harsh reproach that you suffered long ago at the hands of a king.

He sings a verse about you that you know well with me:

“Alas, Mantua, too near to wretched Cremona.”

So that you may recognize yourself, I shall immediately recall the causes to you. A certain Antonius aroused Caesar’s anger; because of him, highland Cremona lost its fields. Caesar indeed gave your lands to his soldiers, while Tityrus, leaving you trampled underfoot, sought our breezes and woods, and likewise the mountains and farms [Note: [Col. 0986C] If Donizo is to be believed, Virgil, driven from his homeland by the disturbances in the Mantuan countryside, withdrew into the Regiensian region, where he composed his pastoral poems. But where did our Donizo obtain reliable records of such a thing? MUR.].

He ate good chestnuts and tender fruit. Let this be known to you: it is called the court of Maro, and the forest through which he pastured his little sheep.

Mount Balista rises beside this forest [Note: [Col. 0986C] Read: “And Balista rises.” The Regiensis manuscript follows this with: “and is born near the forest.” It is now called Monte di Valestra; anyone who looks upon its position takes pleasure in it. Nature, competing with art, has made a kind of square at its summit. Beneath it, in the rock, are various caves, where, according to the credulous populace, treasures lie hidden, guarded by an evil spirit. Donizo took these verses from an ancient Life of Virgil attributed to the grammarian Donatus. Yet the name of Mount Balista existed long before Virgil. MUR.].

On it Virgil made an inscription written in this manner:

“Beneath this stone lies buried Balista.

By night and by day, traveler, take your safe path.”

Here Balista was a great robber; Maro too [Note: [Col. 0986D] Our manuscripts read “here also.” MUR.] wrote here, because he—your beloved (*amor tuus*) [Note: [Col. 0986D] An ancient manuscript reads *quia*. LEIB. See how many errors an inattentive eye creates for us! Here there is nothing else than “because he died there.” Thus read our manuscripts. MUR.]—died there.

From this, which we know, you too can learn by sight. If you doubt anything, read the poems of the first book of his work, and immediately you will not deny my words.

When he fled you, wretched Mantua, he ran near me [Note: [Col. 0986D] The ancient manuscript reads *meque*. LEIB.]; what he fashioned in meditation he first told to me, not to you.

With what face, then, can you claim him? Did he not proceed to Rome to seek the crown of kingship [Note: [Col. 0986D] He means the king, that is, Augustus Caesar. MUR.], so that he might be free? Caesar immediately granted it to him after he recognized the learned poems of the wise man.

I do not want you to deny this; I suddenly recall the verses to you:

“The rain falls all night; the spectacles return in the morning.

Caesar, you share divided rule with Jove” [Note: [Col. 0987B] I would more readily read *habet*, “you have.” Thus it appears in the ancient Life of Virgil by Tib. Claudius Donatus, which our Donizo plundered here so that, in his dispute with Mantua about Virgil, he might show that Virgil settled in the mountains of Canossa, or of royal Reggio. MUR.].

Nor did Maro throw small verses [Note: [Col. 0987C] Perhaps: “threw out.” LEIB. The Padoliron manuscript reads: “few verses.” MUR.] into the king’s court. When they had been found, the king honored a certain man who claimed that he had composed these beloved verses. Tityrus, grieving at this, wrote the same verses again, beautifully exposing the fraud:

“I composed these little verses; another received the honor.

Thus, sheep, you carry fleeces not for yourselves” [Note: [Col. 0987C] In both of our manuscript copies, two verses are added:

“Thus, oxen, you bear plows not for yourselves.

Thus, birds, you build nests not for yourselves.”

They should indeed be added, for they also appear in the recently mentioned Life of Virgil.].

“Thus, bees, you make honey not for yourselves.”

Having put forward some of these verses in the same court of Caesar [Note: [Col. 0987C] The Regiensis manuscript more correctly reads: “Putting forward these equally.” MUR.], he did not remain unknown to the king as the author of such great poems. He ordered Maro to be brought before him and granted him whatever he asked; he asked for freedom, and Caesar gave it to him.

To you he returned by the order of this Caesar, but you were unable to give him what he requested of you, our [Note: [Col. 0987C] That is, “our own.” LEIB. Perhaps: “you knew.” Donizo thought that Virgil had once actually lived a servile life and had been granted freedom by Augustus. But this cannot in any way be extracted from his first eclogue, which Donizo had before his eyes here. Indeed, the testimony of the ancients contradicts it. MUR.] one.

[Col. 0987B] When he was reclaiming the fields, as the emperor had ordered, a certain centurion named Arius [Note: [Col. 0987D] In the Life of Virgil he is called Atius. MUR.] was stirred by anger. Because he held Virgil’s fields, he sought to kill him savagely. But the river Mincius concealed Virgil; by throwing himself into it, he escaped death there and also his enemy.

He soon turned back toward Caesar’s face [Note: [Col. 0987D] Perhaps: “he returned.” LEIB. The Regiensis manuscript does indeed read *repedavit*. Perhaps it should also be *replicavit*. MUR.] and restored his course. The king sent three distinguished men with him to restore the fields to Virgil, and they did so at once.

You preserved neither his life nor the fields themselves. Stop now boasting, Mantua, of these empty praises; they are empty for you, as I have told you. Lower your brows and cease contending with me.

[Col. 0988A] ### MANTUA REPLIES

Tell me whatever pleases you; I deeply regret what I have done [Note: [Col. 0987D] The Regiensis manuscript reads: “I deeply regret the deed.” MUR.].

### CANOSSA SPEAKS [Note: [Col. 0987D] These words are not found in our manuscripts, as though Mantua continued speaking. But what follows presents Canossa as the speaker. MUR.]

I desire and command only that you hold something else belonging to our lord [Note: [Col. 0987D] The ancient manuscript reads *alvum*, “the belly.” LEIB.], but I no longer wish to sing any verse with you. I have learned better by speaking [Note: [Col. 0987D] That is, if I understand correctly: “since, remaining alone, I have learned to compose better things.” MUR.]. Remaining alone, let the true verse depart [Note: [Col. 0987D] The ancient manuscript reads *desedere*, that is, “to depart.” LEIB. Our manuscripts are preferable, where they read *Deus edere*. If the copyist of the Vatican manuscript had examined it more carefully, he would have understood that *Deus edere*, not *desedere*, was written there. MUR.], which, once recited, pleases the whole world exceedingly.

## CHAPTER XVII. How many years Beatrix lived after Boniface, and how prudently she governed everything

Who can relate how prudently, after his death, his wife, while living, held his honors—after twice ten years and five had been completed? [Col. 0988B] She properly governed the towns, castles, her own march [Note: [Col. 0987D] Namely, that of Tuscany. In the records of those times this Beatrix is called a duchess, for the Tuscan margraves also enjoyed the ducal title. MUR.] and territory. Beatrix held them as countess [Note: [Col. 0988C] The poet conceals her second marriage to Duke Godfrey and the captivity in which Emperor Henry held her because she had married his enemy. Godfrey died in 1069, the same year in which Florentinus believes that Beatrix’s daughter Matilda was betrothed to Godfrey, the son of Godfrey. LEIB.].

She raised from infancy, in fine conduct, the lofty and modest-minded Matilda, with whom she herself founded two monasteries, so that the one who guides heaven’s reins might protect them.

The first was the monastery of Fraxinorum [Note: [Col. 0988C] The ancient manuscript reads “the monastery of Fraxinorum.” LEIB. It should be written *Fraxinorense*, now Frassinoro, a village in the mountains of the Modenese territory, on the route from Sassuolo toward Carpineta and Tuscany. See the Casinense bull, constitution 107, where the donation made by Beatrix to the same monastery is recorded. I possess a diploma of Frederick I, issued in 1164, by which he receives the monastery of Saint Claudius of Fraxinorum and its venerable abbot William under his protection and confirms its rights. When I once investigated the traces of the ancient monastery, apart from the church, which is notable for its antiquity, I found scarcely anything else worth seeing. The revenues of the place, once considerable, were assigned to the Roman college of the Maronites. MUR.].

Great Beatrix gave them many estates [Note: [Col. 0988D] The Regiensis manuscript reads “gave there.” The monastery of Fraxinorum was endowed not only with a vast accumulation of estates, which now yield an emphyteutic rent, but also once ruled various castles that for many centuries have passed into the jurisdiction of the Modenese republic. MUR.], because both women believed monks to be more worthy of reverence than clerics [Note: [Col. 0988D] Thus the author himself was a monk. LEIB.].

They changed the name and honor of the holy Canusine church for the better. Formerly, a single provost used to serve it together with not merely twelve clerics [Note: [Col. 0989B] “Only.” LEIB.]. Now an abbot serves there with many monks serving Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That Henry II died during Beatrix’s lifetime, and that Henry III was excessively at odds with Pope Alexander II

We know that Emperor Henry lived during the time of the countess, because he was her kinsman [Note: [Col. 0989C] *Herus* is from the Greek *hérsis*—a bond, namely of kinship—“bound by relationship”; ἕρσις or ἔρσις means a bond. Florentinus reads *quam haenus* instead of *quod herus*, but does not explain it. The degree of kinship between Emperor Henry III—whom the poet calls the second, in Italy—and Beatrix is not sufficiently established. Henry IV certainly calls her his aunt in a letter included in Gregory VII’s register. Uspergensis, under the year 1054, calls Matilda a niece of Henry III; Donizo calls Matilda (Beatrix’s daughter) a cousin of Henry IV below in Book II, chapter 1. Henry V likewise claimed by right of kinship the inheritance of Matilda, Beatrix’s daughter. But since the lineage of Beatrix’s mother, who was also named Matilda, is unknown, it is not surprising that the degree of relationship is uncertain, since among such writers the terms “aunt” and “niece” are used broadly. What if Beatrix’s mother was the sister of Gisela, who was married to Emperor Conrad? That would satisfy both the precise wording and the circumstances. LEIB.], and a relative of the great Beatrix and of her daughter Matilda.

Augustus died and was buried in peace. [Note: [Col. 0989C] I read: “After whom.” MUR.] After him arose the one who came forth as a child from his loins, through whom the kingdom would be badly governed—namely the cruel serpent Henry III.

His mother was Queen Agnes. While carrying him in her womb, she saw in a dream that the infant was truly a dragon, and she reported this to many.

Pope Victor had recently praised this king [Note: [Col. 0989D] Namely Pope Victor II; in 1056, when Henry, second among the emperors, had died, his son Henry, still a child, took control of the German and Italian kingdoms. Paul of Bernried writes in the Life of Gregory VII, volume III of the *Rerum Italicarum*, that this occurred with the permission of the Roman pontiff Victor. Our poet says that Victor praised the king. The pope’s consent is mentioned because the king was not appointed without his authority, since from the kingdom he received the right to the Roman empire. MUR.].

This young king, exercising excessive cruelty, like a spirited mule, without any understanding, was repeatedly admonished by the holy popes with gentle words; yet his mind produced thorns from within itself. His evil mind despised Pope Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0989D] Namely Nicholas II. But Donizo should be forgiven. Henry, fourth among the kings of Germany, if the author of the Hildesheim Annals is to be trusted, was born in 1048. According to Hermannus Contractus, his birth falls in 1050; according to Lambert of Hersfeld, Empress Agnes gave birth to him in 1051. Yet Pope Nicholas II was elected in 1058 and died in 1061. How, then, can Henry be said, as a little boy only ten or eleven years old, to have despised Nicholas II? There are, indeed, other certain vices and crimes of this prince which may rightly be condemned. MUR.].

He rejected Alexander, the truly venerable pope, and attempted to remove him from the Roman pontificate. He ordered a certain Cadalus of Parma to be pope. Cadalus was a very wealthy bishop of Parma, and without delay prepared to march against Rome.

[Col. 0990A] This son of evil was despised by the learned Beatrix. She then ordered a small pit to be made in the road of Modena [Note: [Col. 0990C] In the less refined centuries it was customary to call this city *Motinensis* rather than *Mutinensis*. The Modenese road is the same as the Via Aemilia passing through Modena, though we call it the Claudia—not a recent name, but a very ancient one, as the city’s old charters show. The Acts of Saint Domninus the martyr, in Surius under 9 October, state: “Blessed Domninus proceeded along the Claudia road; some Christians fled along the Flaminia, others along the Aurelia, and others likewise along the Claudia.” Usuard’s Martyrology and the Roman Martyrology also call it the Claudia on 9 October. I would have scholars take note of this, for it seems to show that the Via Aemilia was restored by a certain Claudius and thereby lost its ancient name. Emperor Tiberius Claudius, in Reinesius, class 3, no. 80, ordered the Via Valeria restored by him to be called Claudia. Why should the same not have happened to the Via Aemilia? MUR.], in the darkness of night.

But gloomy Cadalus came, leading many men, and reached the city, the head of the world. The perverse party, straying from the words of Cephas, received him at a higher price [Note: [Col. 0990D] The ancient manuscript reads *pretio suscepit*, that is, “received him simoniacally.” LEIB.]. But the righteous party immediately came to meet him for battle. Cadalus and his troop resisted; they overcame the righteous party and stained the Tiber with blood.

The bishop gained the chair, filled three times with blood [Note: [Col. 0990D] The Padoliron manuscript reads: “then with blood.” These events took place in 1062. Donizo says that victory initially fell to Cadalus’s soldiers. In fact, matters first went badly for the Romans fighting on behalf of the true Pope Alexander. MUR.], because of the fevers of the land. Soon the Parmese returned, leaving the pontiff Cadalus alone.

At last the righteous party, exhausted by them, seized him and carried him up onto the open tower of Crescentius [Note: [Col. 0990D] He means the Mausoleum of Hadrian, which we now call the fortress or castle of Saint Angelo. Other writers call it the Tower of Crescentius rather than “of Crescent.” In the Life of Alexander II, volume III of the *Rerum Italicarum*, Cadalus is said to have been received into the castle of Saint Angelo by Cencio, the prefect’s son, and besieged there for two years. What Donizo says here about the strong chains with which he was bound should be understood liberally as referring to that siege. MUR.], where he was bound all around with strong chains.

[Col. 0990B] Bishop Alexander reverently recovered the chair. The other, having fled, returned everywhere exhausted to Parma. He bore the name of pope, a name he had taken in vain, and died in Parma, greatly mocked and under accusation.

Pastor Alexander ruled joyfully as before and endeavored, like a father, to recall the erring king.

The perfidious man despised the words of the holy Father, but this man wishes to believe only the perverse and insolent; moreover, as a vagabond, he sold the pontificate amid these evils—he who, for the pope’s sake, did not abandon such great evils.

Thereupon Mathildis and Beatrix were very sorrowful, for they stood with Pope Alexander in reverence.

When these matters had thus been arranged, the aforesaid pope departed

[Col. 0991A] nine suns before * [Note: Leibniz placed an asterisk here, as though something were missing. Yet the sense is quite clear and requires nothing else. It means: “The aforesaid pope departed,” that is, he was taken away by his final fate, nine suns before Madius would bring forth fragrances—that is, nine days before the Kalends of May, the month that brings flowers and scents. Indeed, Alexander II died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May in the year 1073. MUR.]

before Madius brought forth his fragrances [Note: That is, in April of the year 1073. LEIB.].

From this world, may he rest in the heavenly garden.

A thousand years of God, three, and then also seventy.

CAPUT XIX. How, after Alexander, Gregory VII was consecrated pope, and how the aforesaid king remained so long in disagreement with him that he was condemned by him.

After Alexander, Hildebrand, beloved,

was made bishop; previously he had nobly served

as archdeacon of that revered see in the city.

While he was being consecrated, he himself was called Gregory;

God rightly gave him such a name, or such an honor,

so that he might watch diligently lest a wolf break into the sheepfolds.

He knew how to be compassionate toward the wretched, but harsh toward the powerful [Note: More correctly, our manuscripts read “harsh” (durus) also. MUR.];

in various ways he maintained the height of his honor.

[Col. 0991B] He was filled with wondrous wisdom beyond all others;

this Gregory became the seventh bishop.

Seeking the profits of the flock, he strove to admonish the king gently,

so that he might repent of such great evil deeds [Note: In the Padolirone manuscript, “curses” (maledictis). MUR.],

and wrote to him that he should not sell churches for money.

To his letter the king sent back a favorable reply;

when the pope read his lines, he rejoiced and said that

all the just in heaven rejoiced at such a thing.

The king lived beyond the mountains, while the shepherd was in Rome;

a swift messenger repeatedly carried news between them.

Between the two stood Mathildis, a renowned mother,

so that peace might come about throughout the kingdom without war.

She urged the king to love peace with the pontiff

and pleaded with the pious pope on the king’s behalf.

[Col. 0991C] [Note: Baronius, vol. XI, under 1074, cites the following nineteen verses. LEIB.

Agnes Augusta, who in the year 1074 supported Gregory VII and tried to heal the wounds inflicted upon the Church by her son. MUR.]

The king’s mother was then at Rome, subject to the pope.

The man who loved peace arranged for her to be sent for her son’s peace,

and with her sent the true bishop of Christ of Praeneste,

joining to him the bishop of sorrowful Ostia [Note: Ostia. LEIB.],

the great pontiff whom I name Giraldus.

The pope sent these two beyond the mountains,

and the king graciously received them together with his mother Agnes [Note: Coming to him with his mother. Lambert says that bishops came with the empress as legates: the bishops of Ostia, Praeneste, Curi, and Como, in 1074. LEIB.].

Through their hands he promised to follow, as far as he could,

the commands of the pious pope and of holy Peter,

and not to sell the Church of the supreme Lord for money [Note: The Regian manuscript reads, more correctly, “churches.” MUR.].

The mother rejoiced greatly at her son’s answer;

returning to Rome, she reported the good news to the pope.

The pope gave immense praise to God for this matter.

[Col. 0992A] But after a short while the king returned again to his crimes.

To him he sent his mother once more, as to a liar;

from nearby he sent her his own letter.

At last the pope grieved and promised the mother as before.

The mother immediately believed what the king was feigning.

She returned to Rome, reverently honoring the pope.

After this the pope wrote twice to the king in fitting fashion.

The king held these sacred letters especially dear.

At that time the fierce Saxons rejected the king,

and finally determined to engage in battle with him.

[Note: Baronius cites the following thirteen verses, 1075, no. 25. LEIB.]

The king immediately informed the pope of this, worshipfully,

and asked him to pray on his behalf, as one crucified.

The shepherd promptly took care to send word to the Saxon people,

plainly wishing to restore peace;

and he ordered the king, until his messenger should return,

[Col. 0992B] not to advance against them in any way. But the king

did not wait; instead, armed, he rode out

against the Saxons, who are strong and fierce.

Although a sinner, this man was nevertheless prudent in warfare.

When battle was joined, the king emerged victorious.

Thus he came back proud and, like a madman, despised the pope.

He broke everything that he had previously promised

to the pope and to his mother, invaded, and restored the Simonians.

The apostolic man was deeply affected by this.

Having summoned many messengers, he immediately wrote about it,

and also wrote to Lady Beatrix and to her daughter Mathildis,

who always loved the lord pope with burning devotion [Note: The older manuscript has flagranter. LEIB. Our manuscripts likewise read flagranter. MUR.].

They detested the perfidy of the swelling king.

[Note: Baronius cites the following twenty-eight verses, 1076, no. 15. LEIB.]

The holy shepherd wrote to the king with still greater severity,

and declared that he could no longer endure such great evils.

The king soon began to run here and there, gathering

many perverse men at a fixed time,

with whom he spoke against the revered Father.

The archbishop of Mainz was there; to him

the wicked king entrusted the entire judgment.

At this point the false Hugh arrived, who was called White.

[Note: The older manuscript has offuit, that is, “was harmful.” LEIB. Our manuscripts also have offuit. Concerning Hugh the White—or White, or Blanc—whom I believe the Italians called Ugo Bianco, the history of those times has much to say. See especially the third volume of the Rerum Italicarum on the Life of Gregory VII. MUR.]

He was harmful to many; a presbyter of the Roman city [Note: A cardinal presbyter, whom Lambert says was deposed because of his incompetence and uncultivated manners. MUR.]

had been condemned three times because for money he reinstated

the purchasers of Christ’s churches; joining himself to them,

he invented accusations against the pope and delighted

the hearts of the malicious—the king’s and his associates’.

[Col. 0993A] That archbishop of Mainz was exceedingly bold.

He did not fear Christ when he cursed the pope.

All subscribed; in doing so, they cursed themselves even more.

O blasphemy that must be abolished neither now nor hereafter!

The same man immediately sent this anathema [Note: The Regian manuscript reads mandarunt, “they sent”: that is, the schismatic bishops sent this same anathema from the conventicle at Worms in 1076. MUR.]

far away to the exceedingly powerful Simoniac Lombards [Note: Baronius reads “the Allobroges,” but the older manuscript has the reading printed here. LEIB.],

who, made joyful, hastily

all assembled at Pavia against the pope [Note: The older manuscript reads Papiam, “Pavia,” where, that is, the synod was held against Gregory. LEIB. Our manuscripts likewise read Papiam. MUR.].

They also carried out the king’s command,

swore and subscribed that letters should be sent to Rome

against the lord and master.

The king himself issued them, saying that the pope

should be removed from the sacred see,

because he stood there unjustly and was plundering the papacy;

they resolved to send these charges to Rome before the synod.

A certain Roland, a cleric from Parma, suitable for the task,

[Col. 0993B] was chosen as the bearer of these little letters.

[Note: Baronius cites the following fifteen verses, 1076, no. 17. LEIB.]

When shepherd Gregory began the synod, he was carrying

a shield carved upon the shell of a hen’s egg [Note: The poet relates that a hen’s egg was brought into the synod as a portent. Upon it a serpent had been carved—whether by nature or by art—and, when struck, it vainly tried to raise its head. This was seen as a symbol of the matter then being dealt with and, I suppose, represented the Simoniac heresy. LEIB.],

and a black serpent that was stretching its head upward—though,

struck back by a certain blow,

it could not reach upward; rather, it had twisted its head

along its belly and, by tripling it, made its tail winding.

This was not a flat image but raised relief-carving.

It was brought to the synod, where no equal marvel had ever before been found.

While everyone was admiring it, behold, the aforesaid Roland

came into the midst and immediately began to say to the pope:

“The king of the land has ordered it, and the bishops have ordered it,

that you leave the see which you are not worthy to possess.”

The same bearer then said to the Roman clergy [Note: This verse had dropped out of all editions published until now. I add it on the authority of the manuscript copies I use. The passage therefore follows after this verse:

‘The same bearer then said to the Roman clergy:

Costes in pente, etc.’

That is, “at Pentecost.” MUR.]:

“Costes in pente: I testify that the king will come to Rome

to send a pope, for this wolf is not pope.”

While he was thus blaspheming, the prefect, moved by anger,

wanted him to be deprived of life by the sword [Note: In a letter preserved by Reuber, the king complains that his legates had been thrown into prison and treated disgracefully. See also Berthold under the year 1076. LEIB.].

He would indeed have done so, but the kindly Father stood beside him.

The assembly, scarcely holding its peace, was filled with heavenly inspiration.

The blessed pope said: “Cease to be troubled, my sons,

for times are coming upon the holy Church that are very

full of deceit and filled with great dangers [Note: I would write nimiis, “with excessive dangers.” MUR.].

It is necessary that the things written as scandals should come to pass.

But woe, I declare, to that wicked man through whom scandals come!

‘Behold,’ says God, ‘I am sending you like sheep

[Col. 0994A] into the midst of wolves.’

You must therefore be prudent like serpents;

you should live simply, as doves also live.

You ought to bear these virtues not only in truth [Note: The Regian manuscript reads, “not us only.” MUR.],

but let us strive to carry Christ’s cross ourselves.

Let tribulation not separate us from Christ

at this time; rather, let us submit our necks

and our limbs to martyrdom.

Let the serpent displayed here, bearing shield and sword,

be struck by the word of faith:

the serpent that stands against the Roman,

catholic Church, reddened by the blood

of gracious Christ.

“After the pope had spoken further, the holy synod said to him:

‘You are the Father of Fathers; crush the wicked blasphemer.

It is our duty to obey your commands.

For Christ we all eagerly desire death.

[Col. 0994B] Pronounce judgment, draw the sword, strike the strong man!’

All cried out that he was supremely worthy

of being deprived of his kingdom and cursed as well.”

The grieving pope immediately bound the aforesaid king

with the chains of anathema and forbade him his kingdom.

This synod was celebrated during Lent [Note: In the year 1076. LEIB.].

Whoever loves holy Peter and the gracious pope

approves this anathema, by which the king is thus dishonored.

Whoever in those times departed from Peter—or from the pope [Note: I read “departed” (discrepat) in the sense of “was at variance.” Many turned away from Gregory VII; Beatrix and Mathildis, however, remained firm in his obedience and protection. Thus reads the Padolirone manuscript, though not “they remained.” MUR.]—

the great countesses remained steadfast:

Mathildis like a rock, and lofty Beatrix.

They acted as mediators and were friends of the king.

When they saw the king continually turning toward crooked paths,

since he was their close kinsman and their king,

they openly declared themselves very sorrowful on his account;

[Col. 0994C] nevertheless, they proclaimed that they would not depart from the pope.

CAPUT XX. On the death of Lady Beatrix, and how Canossa speaks through her and concerning her body.

Beatrix, full of good deeds and rich in good words,

exceedingly dear to all, great and small alike,

remained ill at Pisa and departed well from the present life.

On the eighteenth day of April [Note: In the Pisan Chronicles published by Ughellus in volume III of the Italia Sacra—and which I shall again publish in a corrected and enlarged form in some places—it is written: “In the year 1077” (according to the Pisan reckoning, that is, 1076), “the countess Beatrix died on the fourth day before the Kalends of May and was buried in a magnificent tomb at the principal church in Pisa. Out of reverence for her, the countess Mathildis, her daughter, who died in 1116 (that is, according to our era, 1115), endowed the Pisan Church in Tuscany and Lombardy with very numerous possessions and ample royal privileges.” But this date of the duchess Beatrix’s death must be corrected from Donizo: it should be written not the fourth but the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, that is, 18 April. MUR.], after Christ’s birth from the true Virgin,

in the year one thousand, three, and seventy,

her body was buried at Pisa. May all the just fathers

lead her into the light of paradise above the heavens.

[Col. 0995A] I think that Pisa would now consider me exceedingly base

if I did not lament and complain aloud over this.

I wished the radiant lady to live a long life,

so that I might lead a joyful age.

I hoped to return her dead body

to worthy earth; this grief burns me utterly,

since the city holds her, though it is not so worthy.

Whoever goes to Pisa sees marine monsters there.

This city, filthy with pagans, Turks, Libyans, and Parthians,

is visited along its shores by the foul Chaldean.

I, Canossa, am clean from all filth, and beautiful with me is the place

of the tomb. It is not fitting to seek cities

[Col. 0996A] that are perjured and commit many crimes [Note: The Padolirone manuscript reads “many crimes” (crimina multa). Donizo attacks the Pisans severely here, presenting them as guilty both of perjury and of many crimes. The history does not say what these were; indeed, he recounts their brave deeds against the Saracens, enemies of the Christians. But Donizo was angered that the Pisans allowed the Saracens free access to their ports and city, together with commercial dealings, and perhaps also that they practiced piracy, as was customary in those times. MUR.].

In such streets they scorned to be buried,

our distinguished and great lords worthy of remembrance.

But after death they wished to be laid to rest at Canossa.

Let Pisa now possess the limbs of the aforesaid lady;

let it keep them carefully and honor them reverently.

But from this time onward I remain exceedingly sorrowful in spirit.

Nevertheless, I hope that he who consoles the needy

will make me joyful by preserving for me

Mathildis, the illustrious lady marked by every virtue,

whose life I seek through the ages.

[Col. 0995] The first book ends.

[BOOK TWO.]

THE PROLOGUE OF THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0995B] A small subject is made great by the master [Note: Perhaps from Greek κοσμέω, “I adorn,” as though “a master of adornment.” LEIB.];

he knows how skillfully to expand his words.

A clever little man may describe a great subject joyfully,

so that what sharp expertise forbids him to know—

namely, how to extend a small matter into joyful speech—

he may accomplish with a familiar or very abundant subject.

But I, a poor little writer, shall make

a subject known to almost the whole world exceedingly long.

Although the things we have written may flourish and shine,

concerning the illustrious leaders whom the first book loved,

the deeds of the duchess Mathildis that must be written

will flourish and shine much more abundantly [Note: The older manuscript reads: “They will flourish much more abundantly and shine.” LEIB. Hear also our manuscript copies: “They will flourish more abundantly and shine.” MUR.].

Describe Canossa’s long history in verse.

[Col. 0995] The prologue ends.

THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 0995C] Whatever I can say about so great a woman

is less than the people know with me;

she deserves more, and you should know that it is wiser simply to admire her.

She is so radiant, like Diana’s shining star [Note: In the Regian manuscript, “Diana’s star.” MUR.];

she is radiant with faith and wondrously surrounded by hope.

A sincere and greater love continually remains in her.

She greatly loves the exalted Word through whom all things exist.

She loves, praises, reverently obeys, and honors

his servants whenever she finds them modest.

She herself hates vices and approves virtues [Note: In the same manuscript, “she approves these.” MUR.].

Toward the proud she is lofty, but she stands gently beside the gentle.

She knows how to soothe the pious, yet she knows how to terrify the wicked.

Prosperity does not change her, nor do troubles disturb her.

In all things, discernment walks with her.

Throughout all kingdoms her enduring fame runs,

[Col. 0995D] and Mathildis’s fame is carried in a little boat across the sea.

The camps of the Turks speak of her by name.

The Greek king is rich in much knowledge of her.

The Greek king Alexius gives her robes with jewels [Note: The older manuscript reads Alexius. LEIB.].

The German king loves and hates her at various times;

the German people everywhere serve her willingly.

Russians, Saxons, Gascons, and Frisians,

[Col. 0996C] Auvergnats, Franks, Lotharingians, and even Britons

know her only in this respect: that they ask much from her.

These peoples often send swords to her;

the lofty Mathildis has horsemen from all of them.

She gives an answer to all these peoples without complaint,

always cheerful in countenance and peaceful in mind.

She dictates letters and knows the German language well;

she also speaks happily in the French tongue.

She nourishes the Lombards, governs them, and makes them great.

You who number the stars, I beg you: preserve her life,

if I should depart from this world before I desire it.

Grant what I thirst for: I ask that my body be buried

where it is truly fitting to have a tomb with the just fathers.

The ancient fathers Isaac, Abraham, and Jacob,

together with their holy wives, were all buried in one ark.

[Col. 0996D] After many years, in that same tomb,

the body of the great Joseph was found buried.

I love her fathers, but I love her much more.

She has greatly exalted me and has also loved me.

This woman gave me the bones of the holy martyr Quirinus.

She continually renews me by building fresh towers

and often caused my name to grow in Rome.

CAPUT PRIMUM. On the first arrival of King Henry III and Pope Gregory VII in Lombardy; how they were received by the duchess Mathildis at Canossa; how Archbishop Guibert subverted that same king; and how on another occasion he went with him to Rome against the pope.

[Col. 0997A]

The king begs the abbot [Note: Leibniz inserted this verse into Donizo’s text. But, as I noted in the preface, it belonged to a depiction of King Henry kneeling before Mathildis, in which Hugh, abbot of Cluny, was also seen painted. Therefore this chapter begins with “After the mother’s death,” and so forth. MUR.], and entreats Mathildis,

after news of his mother’s death had spread throughout the world,

recalling the king condemned by the pope.

The strong and powerful were certainly disturbed,

throughout the whole kingdom, saying that he was proud,

that he did not piously, sincerely, and kindly obey

the Roman see, which holds the keys of the world.

Therefore they rightly determined that the king should be despised

unless he returned and strove to restore peace with the pope.

[Col. 0997B] Since the king knew that he could not otherwise continue to reign,

[Note: Baronius cites the following eight verses, 1077, no. 21. LEIB.]

he sent to his cousin Mathildis, asking her to obtain

that the pope should come from Rome to Lombardy

and seek a fitting pardon for him.

He himself would certainly obey his command willingly.

When the pope saw Lady Mathildis’s prayers,

he granted what she asked and finally departed for Rome.

The worthy shepherd came into Canossa,

and there she fittingly received him in Saint Peter’s stead:

she received saving dew from the pope’s mouth.

King Henry, accompanied by Lady Mathildis,

was present nearby, with a large crowd.

Because of such events, Rome became new in my eyes.

Behold your honor, city: king and pope together,

the Italian nobles, and also the French nobles

[Col. 0997C] and the nobles from beyond the mountains, Romans,

many wise men shining with pontifical distinction,

among whom stood Hugh, abbot of Cluny,

who had been Henry’s father at the sacred baptismal font [Note: Henry had been received at the sacred font by Hugh of Cluny in the year 1051; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, also relates this in his Life of that same holy Hugh. Among these nobles should also be counted Azzo, margrave of Este, and Adalheis, margravine of Susa, Henry’s mother-in-law, together with her son Count Amadeus. Along with Countess Mathildis, they were mediators of the most celebrated peace, as I have noted in the history of Este. MUR.].

These elders discussed the terms of peace.

[Note: Baronius cites the following ten verses in the place mentioned above. LEIB.]

When they had spent three days speaking about peace,

and there was still no peace, and the king wished to depart,

that same king sought the chapel of Saint Nicholas.

There he tearfully prayed to the shepherd Hugh

to become his guarantor for the sake of peace.

“This is not permitted,” the abbot replied to the king.

Mathildis, who was standing there, also entreated him,

and she too pleaded with him.

[Col. 0998A] “No one will do this,” he replied, “unless you, I believe.”

With bent knees the king said to Mathildis:

“Unless you greatly help me now, I shall not break

my shield any further; the pope has punished me severely.

Mighty cousin, make me be blessed; go.”

She rose and promised the king, then departed.

She went upward and stood above, while the king himself remained below.

She addressed the pope, pleading concerning the king’s fate.

Because of these sincere words of the venerable lady,

the bishop believed him, provided that the king himself should swear

that he would be faithful to him and to the Roman see,

and that whatever Gregory the bishop wished, he would do for him [Note: An oath. LEIB.].

The king previously mentioned [Note: The older manuscript reads: “And January gave more cold and snow than usual,” meaning that January had brought snow and cold beyond the ordinary. LEIB.]; that January in this year gave cold far greater than usual,

for Janus was giving excessively severe weather that year,

[Col. 0998B] seven days before January came to an end,

the pope allowed the king to come before him,

with bare feet, seized by the cold.

In penance [Note: In penance. LEIB.] he threw himself before the pope, crying out repeatedly:

“Spare me, blessed Father; kindly spare me, I plainly beg.”

When the pope saw him weeping, he had great pity on him.

For he blessed him, finally granted him peace,

celebrated Mass, and gave him the body of the Godhead [Note: Lambert relates that, after the king had been absolved, the pope celebrated the solemn rites of Mass. To clear himself of the charge of Simony brought against him, the pope received one part of the Lord’s body and offered another to the king as a testimony of innocence; but the king declined this. LEIB.],

sharing a meal with him above the Canossan fortress [Note: The older manuscript reads quin, “and indeed.” LEIB.].

After the king had sworn, he dismissed him, and he went

to the royal city, where a malicious crowd of bishops stood,

greatly afraid that this peace would endure.

The greatest among them was Guibert, bishop of Ravenna,

learned, wise, and of noble birth.

[Col. 0998C] He had previously been a citizen or cleric of Parma.

When this Gregory was elected, Guibert swore allegiance to him,

but now he wickedly acts against him [Note: The Regian manuscript reads “now he acts wickedly.” MUR.].

For he teaches the king’s mind to stand against the pope.

The king returned on the sixth day to Bibianello [Note: Now Bianello, one of four castles not far from Canossa. MUR.],

with a heart full of deceit and a mind full of poison.

The shepherd, free from gall, came down to him from the fortress

mentioned above, and the countess soon followed.

But the crafty king said many things to the pope and then

desired a common conference beyond the river Eridanus.

The pope praised this, and Mathildis desired it also.

These two distinguished persons did not know why the king wanted it.

In truth, he feared that Mantua would be subjected to an agreement.

[Col. 0999A] Indeed, the king had first crossed the waters

of the Eridanus in vain, planning with a few men to hand over the pope,

and, if he could, to hand over the countess as well.

By arranging this agreement he thought to complete an unspeakable crime.

Seeing everything, Christ forbade that crime to occur.

The bishop and excellent Mathildis crossed the Eridanus with him,

hoping to establish a genuine peace.

A messenger arrived for Lady Clara, widely known and much-observed,

and disclosed Henry’s secret: he said that the king intended to hand over the pope.

When the prudent lady learned this, she quickly moved herself and her people

and sought the strong mountains with the bishop.

The king’s ambush was broken and exposed.

After this the king saw neither the pope nor Mathildis again.

The false bishops were thereby greatly delighted.

[Col. 0999B] Above all, the aforesaid Guibert, who had given this counsel to the king,

because he wished to invade Peter’s worthy see,

imitating what the Devil did [Note: Thus, in a corrupted form, they formerly called the Devil—not only the common people but also Christian writers. I remember seeing an ancient inscription set up for a Christian deacon in which he was called Zaconus. MUR.].

He who, hateful one, desired to seize the heavenly seat.

That slippery and deceitful Guibert was a wanderer,

an accomplice and supporter of murderers as well.

No one loved worldly pomp more than he did.

He lacked religion, so that he did not even know how to love it.

The king praised him in place of the pope and exalted him [Note: Or perhaps: “he exalted this man.” MUR.].

He returned beyond the mountains, readily committing evil deeds.

Whatever wickedness he wished, he safely and unjustly did.

For as his exactor, judge, and false shepherd,

he did not rebuke the cruel acts that the king committed.

He assiduously sold churches to many for money.

Often one city held two false bishops in a single year,

as they competed in giving rewards and standing firm.

The common people assigned chapels to clerics for a price.

All the perverse lived according to Guibert’s law.

[Note: Baronius cites the following seven verses under the year 1077, no. 23. LEIB.]

But Lady Mathildis despised the wicked man’s deeds.

In her heart she greatly loved true faith, full of grace.

She put the king second and for three months maintained

Pope Gregory, serving him like another Martha.

With attentive ears she diligently received in her mind

all the Father’s words, as Mary received Christ’s words.

She submitted all her possessions to Peter the key-bearer [Note: In that century, and especially in the time of Pope Gregory VII, the custom became widespread of offering to the apostolic see not only castles but entire kingdoms, and then receiving them back from it as fiefs. Demetrius, king of the Russians, did this two years before the peace of Canossa, in 1075; so did another Demetrius, duke or king of Croatia and Dalmatia. Bertrand, count of Provence, likewise offered everything he possessed to the same see in 1081, to omit other examples. Indeed, Gregory VII himself seems to have suggested in Letter III of Book IX that other powerful men should do this out of love for blessed Peter, for the absolution of their sins. MUR.];

his heir is the gatekeeper of heaven, and she herself is Peter’s.

The gracious pope, receiving the document concerning everything,

then freed the church of Canossa,

dictating for himself a broad charter of freedom

[Col. 0999D] and commanding that no one should violently touch his property;

because of this, let every such man be punished by anathema.

[Col. 1000A] At the urging of the great countess, the pope granted this matter.

The year was 1077.

Recognizing that a cruel time was coming upon the world,

the pope likewise strengthened the duchess with his words,

so that she might be exceedingly brave in adversity and not defenseless,
