and might freely assist all Christians as far as she could.

Let her crush, uproot, and kindly recall the blasphemers,

who are also offspring of Satan.

The wise countess stored up the commands of her pious lord,

as the queen of Sheba stored up Solomon’s blessed words.

[Note: Baronius cites the following six verses, 1077, no. 43. LEIB.]

When Pope Gregory had taken leave of Countess Mathildis,

he visited the Roman city while April was flowering across the fields.

The people themselves came out to meet his arrival,

rejoiced, and together received their shepherd.

He himself commended what Mathildis had nobly done

[Col. 1000B] for him and for holy Peter.

“May Mathildis live forever!” cried all the clergy

and the entire populace.

Together with them he rightly cursed the king again,

and absolved the men who had sworn to him, the small men [Note: That is, the lesser people, or commoners. I have added this explanation for the benefit of the unlearned populace, when good Donizo decided here to play the Greek. MUR.],

and also the great nobles, if they preferred to abandon him.

When the king realized this, he again gathered the strong men

[Note: Baronius cites these eight verses, 1081, no. 25. LEIB.]

and after some time once more entered Italy.

Wandering, he stained the whole land.

Mathildis, daughter of Peter, alone resisted him.

The enraged king stirred up swords against her,

battles, terrors, and sieges of fortresses.

He fought to no purpose; she could never be overcome.

Many impregnable places stood fixed in her possession.

She was greatly loved and defended villages and castles.

When the king saw that this quarrel was growing only in vain,

[Col. 1000C] he considered how to trouble the head alone and went to the Roman city.

Guibert seemed to have gone with him.

It had been customary for the king’s arrival to be a festival for the people [Note: “Was to be,” that is, “ought to be.” LEIB.];

but this man’s arrival was a lamentation, for his crimes disturbed heaven.

The city was not opened to him because of the pope.

Fighting around it, he shattered the lofty walls,

devastating the city and installing there a shameful pope.

[Note: Baronius cites these four verses, 1083, no. 2. LEIB.]

He placed him in the chair; this man was falsely called Clement.

This is Guibert the deceiver, the manifest devastator

of Christ’s Church, whom the Beast of the abyss,

seen by the beloved disciple in the Apocalypse, rightly signifies.

That phalanx of the king also stained all Rome.

[Note: Baronius cites these six verses, 1084, no. 6.]

The ever-watchful rector Gregory, from his weary flock,

greatly and equally grieved over the polluted see,

hoping in Peter, begged Robert to fight,

[Col. 1001A] a certain Hermann [Note: The older manuscript reads “Normannus.” LEIB. Our manuscripts likewise have “Normannus.” The error was obvious to everyone. But, good Donizo, do you mention a certain Robert the Norman as though he were some petty nobleman unknown to you? MUR.],

who drove the king out of the city.

The king fled like a little doe along the road [Note: The older manuscript has dammula. LEIB.],

a bad guest returning beyond the mountains to the French.

His pope Clement, offering rewards to the Romans,

the plunderer himself seized Peter’s earthly chair.

Although he displayed himself as though he were shepherd in the city,

no portion of heaven’s citadel remained for him.

This boundary of heresy wickedly deceived the world.

He despised God’s commands and neglected the words of the saints.

He violated the laws and destroyed the divine buildings.

He persecuted the worthy lord pope and master,

who, full of sacred admonitions, remained in the Lateran.

[Col. 1001B] Standing there, this excellent spermologus [Note: Donizo again leads us into Greek territory, though here the navigation is uncertain. Although spermologus may mean “one who gathers seeds,” the Greeks customarily took the word in a worse sense. The Apostle himself was called σπερμολόγος in Athens as an insult, as we read in Acts 17:18—that is, “little fellow,” “babbling man,” or “seed-scatterer,” as the Vulgate translator has it. Donizo may determine for himself which authors he followed here, if indeed this passage is entirely free from error. MUR.],

by his deeds and words denounces Guibert’s schism,

condemning such great schisms with perpetual anathema.

From this there arises immense tribulation for all the just.

The pious party feels the king’s sword most severely.

Many bishops were expelled from their sees,

afflicted with blows and confined in prison bonds.

The king and Guibert make the age of ancient Nero

live again—Nero, who ordered Peter to be crucified,

struck Paul’s neck with the sword,

and, so that he might see his own mother’s belly,

made it be ripped open by the sword, where the wicked man himself rested.

Thus Guibert, the wicked emissary of Satan,

pierced the palms of his own mother with sharp spurs.

[Col. 1001C] Guibert feared no man except Nero, his master.

Nero, with his veins cut open, took his own life in water.

These two men described above, having almost forgotten the name of faith,

strive finally to destroy the supreme teacher.

Simon the Magician stands forth as their teacher

and their shaggy author.

Perhaps they do not know that, when fortune turns,

the unjust will fall from high places down below.

God therefore sometimes allows them to prosper [Note: Punctuate as follows: “the unjust will fall down below; therefore God sometimes allows them to prosper.” LEIB.].

CAPUT II. How Lady Mathildis rose up against the king and Guibert, and how she assisted all Catholics.

[Col. 1002A]

Burning with pious zeal, Mathildis, a radiant lamp,

raises, spends, and urges against these two enemies

of the Lord’s cross her weapons, her will, her servants,

and her own treasure, and wages battles.

If I were to recount everything that this noble woman did,

the poems would grow as countless as the stars.

But I shall omit much; learn the marvels from a little.

From this quarter, relying on the four regions of the world,

the Guibertine leprosy had grown horrible and black.

Because of this leprosy, no place in the world remained clean.

Only the spacious house of Mathildis was clean [Note: The Padolirone manuscript reads speciosa, “beautiful.” Yet it cannot be said that Mathildis’s house alone was immune from this infection. For neither the other regions of the Christian world, nor even Italy itself, lacked pious men who approved Gregory VII’s zeal and hated Henry, his followers, and their vices. It is unnecessary to produce examples. Rather, what should be understood is that no Italian princely family except Mathildis’s consistently favored and assisted the true Roman pontiff amid that upheaval of affairs. Hugh of Flavigny writes in the Chronicle of Verdun: “At that time Countess Mathildis alone among women was found to despise the king’s power and to resist his cunning and power even in armed conflict, so that she deserved to be called a woman-warrior, who surpassed even men in strength of spirit.” Add also the contemporary author of the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca: “Mathilda was found to be the sole and unique duchess and marchioness who remained in the faith, possessed the zeal of God, and obeyed Lord Pope Gregory.” MUR.]

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Baronius, 1081, no. 25. LEIB.]

For Catholics she was altogether a safe haven:

For those whom the king condemned, drove out, or despoiled—

[Col. 1002B] Pontiffs, monks, clerics, Italians as well as Gauls—

All ran utterly to the living fountain:

That is, to the aforesaid lady, now kind in heart.

Whatever they sought, they found with her;

She failed no one, but, most excellent, benefited everyone.

No honest man who came to her in sorrow

Ever departed from her without consolation.

I remember that this renowned leader clothed many

Catholic fathers in sacred garments.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Baronius, 1074, no. 17. LEIB.]

Among them shone the revered bishop of the city

Of Lucca, the luminous Anselm, [Note: [Col. 1002D] You will find the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca, in Bollandus, *Acta sanctorum*, vol. II, March, p. 649. It was written by Anselm’s chaplain, or penitentiary. MUR.] supremely prudent,

Learned in God’s law, a thoroughly religious monk.

The Roman prelate Gregory, as Jesus did,

Who, dying on the cross, gave his Mother to the disciple,

[Col. 1002C] Thus entrusted the lady Countess to Anselm;

He taught her by his words and guided her kindly by his example,

And always warned her to resist the perverse sect.

This angel was a great counselor to her in those years,

And the countess followed his gracious counsel.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Baronius, 1081, no. 26. LEIB.]

For the mother could convert those whom she was able to reform,

And by whatever means she could, she acted at every hour:

Many by granting them fiefs, many by bestowing gifts,

More by fighting, and often by burning castles,

[Col. 1003A] She continually separated them from the wicked king’s allegiance.

To the transalpine nobles dear to her

She wrote that they should shun the king’s errors and rebel against him.

Thus, believing in God, she produced abundant fruit,

Urging the nobles to serve Pope Gregory.

To him she frequently used to send gifts in the Lateran,

Many gifts indeed, which the pope piously blessed.

The Canossan household then sent the pope

Two hundred pounds of silver, which the pope ought to bless.

## CHAPTER III. On the death of Pope Gregory, the election of Popes Desiderius and Urban, the way in which Lady Mathilda fought for the Roman Church, and the death of Saint Anselm, bishop of Lucca

Meanwhile [Note: [Col. 1003C] Baronius cites the following, section 6, in the year 1085, no. 15. LEIB.] a loud lament arose

For the prelate Gregory, whom the Lord Christ carries to heaven,

Seven days before the end of May was to come.

The monks mourned him, since he was known to be a monk;

The clerics mourned him, and the laity too grieved deeply,

Whose pure faith is far removed from that of schismatics.

When his holy body was reverently buried,

It was the year of God one thousand and eighty-six.

After him Pope Desiderius was made pope, a worthy abbot

Of Monte Cassino, who lived only a short time.

In the year after that, Urban was consecrated shepherd there,

An eloquent man, formerly a monk and now ruler

Of the Church of the supreme and everlasting Father.

As Solomon says, the righteous man trusts like a lion.

He boldly condemns the king and the deeds of Guibert,

Who, falsely desiring to retain Peter’s seat,

[Col. 1003C] Guibert summons the prudent Odo of Bayeux [Note: [Col. 1003C] This is Odo, bishop of Bayeux, brother of William the Conqueror, king of England, who aspired to the papacy by sacrilegious designs. See Orderic Vitalis, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, [Col. 1003D] under the year 1085. MUR.] 

Against the pope, whom he often constrains by war.

Yet that just man, although often beaten back,

Endures unmoved, believing that peace will come.

To Peter’s little daughter, Christ’s faithful servant,

He then sent his pious writings, encouraging her,

Especially recalling Gregory’s rule,

So that she might observe it and not attempt to abandon it.

Hence he grants her forgiveness for her sins.

Gregory’s messengers [Note: [Col. 1003D] That is, Gregory VII often sent letters and messengers to Mathilda; Urban II did so even more frequently. She, in turn, never ceased to assail these fathers, that is, the Roman pontiffs, with letters. MUR.] often sought Mathilda;

[Col. 1004A] Couriers more frequently ran to her from this man.

Nor did she cease, in return, to press these fathers

With letters and messengers in those very days,

For whose sake nearly the whole Italian kingdom

Had risen against her, but especially all Liguria.

She herself holds the road along the Po, whence she is driven from the cities. [Note: [Col. 1003D]

“Mathilda is driven from the cities along the Po.” LEIB.

In the Este manuscript, where Donizo’s epitome is written, the following is read: “And the lady herself crossed the road of the Po and went to the cities, from which the high road is made.” From this you see that another meaning emerges. MUR.]

While her champions fought, they lost nothing

Except through their own fault, but won the war most splendidly.

From many cities, at that time, many citizens,

Armed with shields and equipped with harnessed horses,

Under the lofty and thoroughly prudent prince Obertus [Note: [Col. 1003D] I have said something about this Marquis Obertus in *Antiquities of Este*, chapter XXV, p. 248. MUR.],

Lead the Parmese [Note: [Col. 1003D] Namely Eberhard, and the Reggian, namely Gandulf. MUR.] and the bishop of Reggio.

They say that they are strong enough to march to Rome.

These wrestlers went forth for the king’s honor,

Roaming about and laying waste the surrounding lands.

[Col. 1004B] At last, bold men who loved Mathilda’s land [Note: [Col. 1003D] Perhaps Donizo wrote *amentes*, “madmen,” rather than *amantes*, “lovers.” By “Mathilda’s land” her allodial estates, castles, villages, and so forth are to be understood. MUR.]

Enter it, believing that they will suddenly ravage her territory.

Sorbaria [Note: [Col. 1003D] A village in the Modenese district on the river Scultenna, below the city. MUR.] receives this army of men into its fortress;

In its own fields it grants them places to encamp.

They rest by night, taking sleep with their eyes,

And when July had assumed its second light [Note: [Col. 1004C] Perhaps one should read *jam venit*, “had now come.” MUR.],

Behold, suddenly Mathilda’s phalanx appears, crying, “Peter,

Help your own.” The enemies [Note: [Col. 1004C] Ancient manuscript, *inimici*, “the enemies.” LEIB.] begin

To rise secure, while the fields are stunned by such a din.

Many turn their backs; others fight with savage bite [Note: [Col. 1004C] Ancient manuscript, “others without”; *alii sine*. Our manuscripts also have *alii sine*. MUR.];

Many are thrown down there, and the wicked are captured.

The aforesaid marquis pierces one of them with a blow;

And, as though speaking aloud, he says: “Does he not flee without honor,

Carrying such a grunt? Nor, I think, will this enemy

Ever again lead a throng against this lady.” [Note: [Col. 1004D] The Padoliron manuscript gives the verse thus:

“Now this enemy carries such a grunt.”

These words indicate that Obertus did not in fact fall, but fled in such disgrace—and with an additional wound, perhaps in the face—that, in Donizo’s judgment, he was never again expected to lead forces against Mathilda. “He flees without honor.” These events took place rather in 1085 than in 1084. Donizo’s chronology is nevertheless confused. He first records Urban II’s election, which occurred in 1088; then he records the death of Anselm, bishop of Lucca, which must be assigned to 1086. MUR.]

[Col. 1004C] Eberhard, bishop of Parma, was captured;

They hid the bishop of Reggio, Gandulf, naked,

For three days in a thorny thicket.

Some nobles were captured, while others nearly escaped.

Peter’s host rejoices; the king’s army is thrown into confusion.

The illustrious Mathilda was a terror to them all.

When the month arrived that begins the year’s order,

On its eighteenth day the Lord reigning in heaven

Carried Anselm [Note: [Col. 1004D] Bishop of Lucca, 1086. LEIB.] to the heavens. [Note: [Col. 1004D] Good Donizo wrote *ad aethram*, “to heaven,” as the manuscript codices remind us. MUR.]

[Col. 1005A] I believe that no one like him existed at that time:

By night and day he fulfilled the twofold office

Of monk and bishop; he mortified his body as an enemy.

He was equally Catholic, celibate, pious, and sober.

At his death the faithful were truly saddened;

The schismatics rejoiced, for he was opposed to them.

The countess, entrusted to him by Gregory [Note: [Col. 1005D] The Padoliron manuscript reads *sibi commissa*, that is, the countess Mathilda entrusted to him. MUR.],

Buried him in mourning and kindness, as was fitting.

Mantua received Anselm’s remains into its earth.

Through him, Christ, you showed Mathilda what was growing.

For by your power he performed many miracles.

This humble servant of yours became one of the saints;

He was a sign of uprightness to the Catholic party,

And to the schismatic party almost a sign of weakness.

[Col. 1005B] From this the countess rejoices in triumph while praying,

For she believes that she is aided by the prayers of this father.

When the saint’s tomb performed many miracles,

So that it might reveal them to many in future ages,

She, the protectress of justice, ordered some of them to be composed [Note: [Col. 1005D] Baronius, 1080, no. 13. LEIB.]

And at the same time dictated a Life to her chaplain.

Rangerius, rector and the third Lucchese after him,

Composed it for her in verse. [Note: [Col. 1005D] This is Rangerius, who succeeded Gothifred in the bishopric of Lucca and is therefore called “the third Luccan after him.” The Life of Saint Anselm, committed to writing by Rangerius himself, is lost. MUR.]

He also composed a beautiful second book,

Which defines the dispute over the staff [Note: [Col. 1005D] That is, the dispute over the investiture of bishops and abbots, which the emperors and kings of those times claimed for themselves by the handing over of the staff. MUR.] and sent it to her.

Let this be its beginning, and let no reader hesitate,

But know that the rest consists of learned verse:

[Note: [Col. 1005D] The verses of Rangerius. LEIB.]

“Let Peter’s little daughter receive violets after lilies [Note: [Col. 1005D] Is Mathilda the countess here being praised first for her virginity, then for her widowhood? Certainly she lived most piously in both conditions. MUR.];

Let dew from God’s fountain be given her, by which she may be watered.

There was a struggle as long as Guibert was able to rage,

The leader of treachery, the manifest devastator of the Church.

But what could he attempt against God’s strongest camp?

When God reigned, did he reach the stars?

He died and was delivered into perdition,

And so did everyone who defended him against reason.

Whoever denied Gregory, that excellent vessel,

Now let him see, if he can, how falsely he judged.

And Urban, who shattered the two statues [Note: [Col. 1005D] Namely, as I suppose, King Henry, deprived of his kingdom through the apostolic see, and Guibert the false pontiff, whom he calls idols and who were defeated and reduced to no small straits. MUR.], flows from that

Fountain and washes him far more vigorously than that one. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Ancient manuscript, *cluit*, “washes.” LEIB.]

Whoever does not confess him before God, whether early or late,

Is rejected and astray, and deserves punishment.”

With these wonderful leaders our collection

Did not remain silent as long as it held barking mouths.

[Col. 1006A] Now let those who sprang forward return, if they can,

Those whom I see, when God touches them, mostly grieving.

But let them return and gladly have us and what is ours;

Only let them take care not to return secretly behind our backs.

Now, therefore, no one demands whatever he wished to remedy [Note: [Col. 1006D] The ancient manuscript has *quicunque*, “whoever.” LEIB. Our manuscripts also have *quicumque*. MUR.]

While he wished to be regarded as divided [Note: [Col. 1006D] “Was able.” LEIB.] concerning

The price, the crime, and the sedition.

They understand these things and say that we possess knowledge.

For neither the price nor the crime pleases them;

Those who desire and plunder are condemned by them.

The same reasoning and the same tradition appear to prevail on both sides;

May God’s judgment supply what seems to be lacking.

A dispute over the staff arose among the people and the fathers.

This was the gate that did not lack obscurity;

This was what plundered both Paul and Peter;

[Col. 1006B] This was what treated king and God as equals.

This madness is not heresy; it is not a labyrinth;

There is no inward toil through darkness and concealment.

All of us who belong to Christ’s teaching desire this:

Let these men flee from it and reject it together.

Therefore I wish us, lest we be deceived by trickery,

To speak briefly, but not lightly, of matters worthy of consideration.

Christ, you are wise; because you seize hearts [Note: [Col. 1006D] The Padoliron manuscript reads *quo corda*, “by which you [seize] hearts.” MUR.],

Set them, inflamed with heat, to do what you know must be done,

For the love of peace.

Rangerius knows Mathilda to be more devoted than all layfolk

To the law of the Lord and to eternal life.

Because this was clear to him, he himself published this volume,

Now let the first [order] return; let this order remain as it is. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Consult the Reggio manuscript: “but let this first one be here.” MUR.]

## CHAPTER IV. On King Henry’s third arrival in Italy and the siege of the city of Mantua

[Col. 1006C]

When King Henry had become a grave enemy

Of the holy Church and of the beloved lady Mathilda,

Wherever he could take something from her, with all

His strength he took the lands wherever he found them,

Especially the villages and fortified towns that the countess

Had possessed beyond the mountains from her mother [Note: [Col. 1006D] Donizo had already noted above, while discussing the marriage of Beatrice and Boniface in chapter 9, that she had brought these fortified towns and villages as her dowry, and that they were situated in Gaul. MUR.],

He took them all away, except the fortress of Brigerinum [Note: [Col. 1006D] The name seems to correspond to Brieg, or Brigense Castle, now La Brie in France. Yet Henry’s arms could not have reached so far. It therefore seems more likely that the fortress mentioned here lay at the borders of the German kingdom, or even within those borders. MUR.],

Perhaps because it was large, wealthy on every side, and richly endowed [Note: [Col. 1006D] Our manuscripts read: *Forte quod et magnum*. MUR.].

The king attacked it but could not set foot within it.

[Col. 1007A] When nearly twice five years had now passed

Since the king had departed from Italy, [Note: [Col. 1007D] The emperor had departed from Italy in 1084 and returned in 1090. LEIB.]

He armed the backs of horses with men,

Swearing to remain for seven years and more

Upon Mathilda’s land, with peace disregarded.

He summoned dense armies and descended into the Italian kingdoms.

The third month was blooming with leaves and grasses.

A city belonging to the aforesaid lady had long remained

A noble city; it was truly called Mantua,

Very rich in many things and in treasures.

The king desired it and fixed his tents around it,

Which the noble and powerful Mathilda, greatest of leaders [Note: [Col. 1007D] “Leader.” LEIB.],

Soon filled with champions and supplies [Note: [Col. 1007D] That is, she filled it with champions and provisions, namely soldiers, grain, and food. MUR.],

Holding the mountains and looking down upon all her enemies.

The king’s dark battle line repeatedly attacked the city.

The citizens and the countess’s champions sallied forth,

[Col. 1007B] Killed and broke them, and drove away the Alemannic force.

The city was well defended, while the king remained outside;

The siege clung to the citizens for eleven months.

Then Ripalta [Note: [Col. 1007D] There is indeed a village of this name between Canossa and Reggio, now Rivalta. But here the reference is to a fortress in the county of Mantua, as will be clear below, in chapter 19 of this book. MUR.] is said to have been surrendered during those months;

And the tower of Governolo [Note: [Col. 1007D] At the mouths of the Mincio, where it flows into the Po; now Governolo. MUR.] was also surrendered to the king’s followers.

Dangers do not change Peter’s handmaid or her see [Note: [Col. 1007D] More correctly, in our manuscripts, “the dangers of the age.” MUR.];

Yet she very often ordered many expenses for the citizens

And urged them especially to preserve their loyalty.

The citizens truly declared themselves faithful to her.

The powerful Mathilda, trusting in those citizens,

Was deceived by their words, since secretly they

Were arranging to hand the city over to the king,

And to surrender part of her army [Note: [Col. 1008D] The ancient manuscript reads: “and likewise they were arranging to hand over the phalanx, or garrison, of Mathilda to the king.” LEIB. The same manuscripts also have *pariterque*. Mantua was given to King Henry through treachery in 1091. MUR.],

Before Easter. For that day was near

Which, in the second month, the world was then celebrating.

[Col. 1007C] They confirmed the plan, carrying it out in imitation of Judas [Note: [Col. 1008D] The ancient manuscript reads *peragunt*, “they carry out.” LEIB. Our manuscripts have the same. MUR.].

For on the night when Judas the merchant

Betrayed Jesus, that very same night this city,

Called Mantua, was betrayed.

But when the cruel king entered the city,

The countess’s nobles escaped,

Drawn out in their own ships with their possessions and weapons.

Like adamant stone, the steadfast leader remained firm

Through the great losses that came in those years.

Only a stone, they say, is split by the blood of a kid;

She does not yield to losses, nor does shed blood bend her,

For she remained founded upon the firm Rock.

Therefore she cannot be bent by rivers [Note: [Col. 1008D] *Flaminibus*, “by flames.” LEIB.] or by winds.

[Note: [Col. 1008D] Baronius, 1091, no. 3. LEIB.]

“In the year one thousand ninety-one,

You, Mantua, are defiled and blackened by treachery.”

## CHAPTER V. Rebuke and denunciation, or a fitting exhortation, against Mantua

[Col. 1007D]

How great your glory would have been, Mantua, anyone would know

[Col. 1008A] If only you had wisely kept your gates closed [Note: [Col. 1008D] The ancient manuscript reads *tenuisses*, “if you had held.” LEIB. Our manuscripts have: “if you had wisely kept your gates closed.” MUR.]

To the king. By then your name and honor had begun

To be spoken throughout almost the whole world.

They truly called you strong and wealthy,

And praised you as though you would endure like Troy.

When you bore that siege according to custom,

And your citizens, shed from strong blood,

Were said throughout all Italy to be the cities’ defenders,

Just as once the Greeks slaughtered the Phrygians’ camps,

So your citizens were accustomed to slaughter the Alemannic camps.

For Troy itself, though surrounded for ten years,

Would never have yielded to the Argives

Had it not been surrendered and burned by night.

O evil treachery, which plunges the lofty into the depths,

Corrupts the secure, and suppresses the victorious city [Note: [Col. 1008D] I would read *orbis*, “of the world.” LEIB.],

Disturbs kings, counts, nobles, and commanders,

[Col. 1008B] And, wicked and shameful, wrongs every order too greatly.

If you had wished to preserve faith with the countess,

Mantua, since Mathilda had already given you

Aid, you could have held out not merely ten,

But twelve years, fearing nothing from your enemies.

If you had done this, great peace would have returned to you;

The king would have withdrawn far from you,

And you would have remained fortunate, exceedingly dear to the countess,

By whom you were enriched and wonderfully endowed.

You would now be flourishing above the cities that came before you.

You could stand in your toga-bearing citizen assembly like the Roman people.

And even if the king’s battles had overcome you,

Do you not know how much honor that would have been,

And that it would have involved no disgrace?

For no one would have known to call you treacherous.

Would that you had never truly borne this name!

Unhappy, mournful, you now stand because of that name.

Why have you cast away every good name

For shameful treachery, surrendering yourself to the wicked?

Once full of Catholics, you used to celebrate

Christ’s Easter with splendid Mathilda,

Whose court was filled with banquets and gifts;

And, as a dutiful court, it remained truly like a king’s court.

Now you celebrate Easter with false Alemannic men,

Who passionately love Bacchus and burn with lust.

You do not know their tongues; and when they are drunk,

They are also quick to quarrel.

For bitter words, it is said, they draw their swords

And cut down the entrails of their companions.

They bite like wolves when they all seize their food [Note: [Col. 1008D] The Reggio manuscript reads *consumunt*, “consume.” MUR.];

They know how violently to break into the courts of the saints.

[Col. 1008D] Mantua, I show you that such companions are not [Note: [Col. 1008D] The ancient manuscript has *nc*, that is, *nunc*, “now.” LEIB. Our manuscripts also have *nunc*. MUR.] to be recognized as yours.

Flee them; despise them. It is death to be with such men.

The king’s friendship itself will not last long;

He will not do for you what he himself promised.

[Col. 1009A] He will truly deceive you, or he himself will withdraw far away.

Therefore beware lest his great peace become your ruin.

Take worthy counsel; mourn this crime, O Mantua [Note: [Col. 1009C] The ancient manuscript reads *lungeto*, “you will join.” LEIB. Our manuscripts plainly give *luget*, “mourn.” MUR.].

Although you have corrupted ancient laws and new writings,

Mourn nevertheless with a pure heart, and let every citizen mourn in the city.

With a common vote, strive to recall

Christ’s protectress and your lady, Mathilda.

Then you will restore the laws and shine with honor.

Neighboring cities praised you abundantly;

Yet you can never again be secure in any other way.

## CHAPTER VI. Further concerning the same king and the same lady Mathilda, and concerning the battle of the countess’s soldiers with the king at Tres-Comitatus

Therefore the king, rejoicing after the city had been captured,

[Col. 1009B] Ordered the false pontiff Conon [Note: [Col. 1009C] That is, Conrad. I have also learned that he was intruded into the see of Mantua from a diploma granted to him by Henry himself; a copy is preserved in the manuscript *Annales Peregrini Prisciani* in the Este library, though without a date. It reads: “Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, third emperor Augustus of the Romans, etc. Let everyone know that Cono, bishop of the holy see of Mantua, approached our clemency, etc.” This diploma may perhaps have been issued in 1091. MUR.] to remain there with the Lemannic people.

Bishop Ubaldus had already fled from the city

To the great and Catholic countess.

The king held nearly all the lands beyond the Po,

Except the notable towns of Platena and Nogara [Note: [Col. 1009D] Two distinguished towns, one of them Platina, now Pladena, in the Cremonese district; it gave us Bartholomeo Platina, the celebrated man whom many called Battista, but incorrectly, misled by the initial letter by which his name is sometimes written alone, as the distinguished historian of learned Cremona, Francesco Arisius, has now demonstrated. The other, Nogaria, now Nogara, belongs to the city of Verona. In a charter of the cathedral of Cremona, which I shall someday publish, Marquis Boniface in 1022 subjected the court of Pladena to the bishop of Cremona. MUR.],

Which alone preserved their loyalty to the countess [Note: [Col. 1009D] “They preserved.” LEIB.],

And despised the king’s terror and fury.

There the king could neither thrust his spear nor set foot.

That summer Minervia [Note: [Col. 1009D] A town in the Brescian district, now Manerbio above Ostiano. There is also a village near Leniaco [Col. 1010C] in the Veronese district called Menerbe. Let others determine which Donizo means. I would prefer the first. MUR.] was captured,

Or, according to report, seized by hunger [Note: [Col. 1010C] Correct this, following our manuscripts: “or seized by hunger.” MUR.] and finally by some weapons.

The king possessed it, but for that reason the countess did not withdraw

From Peter’s cause, for which she had suffered such great evils.

She went joyfully through the Reggian or Modenese county,

And strengthened her own fortresses [Note: [Col. 1010C] Indeed, the Modenese and Reggian district, or county, provided Mathilda with her principal strength and protection. More castles and fortresses belonged to her rights there than anywhere else, whether by title of allodial possession or by feudal title from various churches. MUR.],

In no way despairing of defeating the king.

[Col. 1009C] She herself often discovered his habits and routes,

So that wherever the wicked man went,

She always knew how many champions he himself possessed [Note: [Col. 1010D] “He himself.” LEIB. Our manuscripts likewise have *ipse*. MUR.].

For after the great fortress of Minervia had been captured,

In winter the king crossed the river Adige,

Then without nobles and unsupported by soldiers.

The prudent countess learned this at once

[Col. 1010A] And ordered more than a thousand brave men

To march against the enemy and fight only in the field.

When they had crossed the waters of the Po

And likewise the fords of the Adige,

The king, full of ambushes, avoided them for eight days,

Delaying while recalling his own phalanxes.

Their betrayer told them that the king

Did not dare to join battle with swords, because he lacked the power;

He was recalling his forces in order to join them.

Believing such things, they stood secure and unarmed.

Suddenly the king’s banners gleamed before them.

His men rushed upon them; much was cut down on both sides.

A soldier was captured by the king’s host, but he was unarmed.

More escaped and fled through the pathless forest slopes.

This village is called Tres-Comitatus [Note: [Col. 1010D] Now Tricontai, a village said to be situated in the county of Padua, according to the records I have collected in *Antiquities of Este*. MUR.].

The betrayer was the noble Hugo, son of Manso [Note: [Col. 1010D] The Reggio manuscript clearly has *e Manso*, “of Manso”; this is therefore how the passage should be restored. I had already noted the matter in the aforementioned *Antiquities of Este*, chapter 27, p. 271, where I freely acknowledged that Hugo of Manso, an Este prince, is indicated here; forgetting the nobility of his blood, he played this trick on Mathilda, if Donizo is to be wholly trusted here. He was the son of Marquis Azzo of Este and the uncle of Duke Welf, whom Mathilda had made her husband. MUR.],

Who committed this treachery against her contrary to custom.

For true nobility never commits a shameful crime.

[Col. 1010B] At last, having assembled, they returned sadly,

Mourning the companions captured, both small and great.

Among them was the good and distinguished Manfred,

Son of Albertus, who had been captured.

The king’s army rejoiced greatly over him;

The countess’s army mourned.

She came, weary, and disclosed to her own lady

The adverse, harsh, and exceedingly grievous events.

With sweet and gentle words the leader comforted them,

So that they would not fear the enemy.

“The time for winning the war and the time for losing

Are thus exchanged,” she said; “as arduous valor decrees.”

## CHAPTER VII. On the siege of Montebello and the capture of the king’s banner at Canossa

[Col. 1010C]

When winter had passed—the winter in which the king fought

With the countess’s soldiers—the third summer came [Note: [Col. 1010D] The year 1092. LEIB.].

The king had already spent two Italian summers there.

When June burns the waters of the river Eridanus,

He crossed escorted by Lombards and Alemannic troops

And seized the nobler locations of the plains.

He climbed toward the Modenese mountains, which he greatly coveted.

[Col. 1011A] Soon Mount Maurellus [Note: [Col. 1011C] Adjacent to Montebello, or Bellio, now Monte Morello. It once belonged to the Modenese county and now lies within the Bolognese territory, on the borders of Savignano. MUR.] was captured without a battle of the sword.

Mount Alfredus [Note: [Col. 1011C] I believe that this too was then situated in the Modenese district. Since the fortress has been completely destroyed, it is now useless to search for the name. What Donizo means by writing that this mountain—that is, the fortress situated there—was captured in a contest of the bridle, I cannot determine. Did he use “bridle” for cavalry? But what place would cavalry have had in storming the fortress? In the manuscript register of the commonwealth of Modena, under the year 1188, one reads: “The oath of citizenship,” as it was once called, “made to the people of Modena by Lothair of Monte Alfredo.” MUR.] too was captured in a contest of the bridle.

In it the eloquent Gerard, the lofty standard-bearer,

Fell into the chains of the aforesaid wicked king.

Mathilda herself grieved greatly over his chains.

The God who tested Job and Tobias also tested this lady,

The sole guardian of Saint Peter,

Who, burning with love for him, endured the thickest scourges,

So that one day he might open for her a chamber of paradise.

This time the king proved plainly more fierce than usual.

He besieged the fortress of Montebello [Note: [Col. 1011D] Now Monteveglio, or Montevio. It was then enclosed within the Modenese district and now belongs to the Bolognese. Its name became famous through the wars fought in later centuries between Bologna and Modena. MUR.],

Which he thought could be subdued either by weapons

Or by siege; but he could neither take its entrance

Nor prevent its exit.

A brave force supplied a garrison to the mountain,

And with its spear used to goad the sluggish king.

At that time the false Pope Clement came to see him.

Speaking much with him, he strengthened the siege,

And lost the whole summer around the mountain.

When he had remained there for a long time,

The pious party began to tremble,

And the nobles and servants began frequently

To ask the magnificent lady for peace.

This pleased the king only if they praised Guibert’s deeds

And prostrated themselves at his feet as though before a pope.

Then he would immediately make this peace.

The countess’s ears certainly did not wish to hear this.

“But I want you to know,” she said, “if you love the king’s peace,

I shall negotiate with him; this is not considered just.”

Soon the mediators tested the king

About his love of peace and asked him not to postpone it.

At last the king deceitfully assented.

The leaders of the peace negotiations strove

For the leader herself to complete the peace,

Which the king claimed to love.

She delayed believing the words of those laymen.

After many abbots and hermits had been summoned [Note: [Col. 1011D] By this name Donizo designates monks. If one prefers to understand here only those monks who chose a stricter way of life in solitude—and there were many such men—I do not object. But below the hermit John is called abbot of the Canossan monastery. MUR.],

[Col. 1012A] And sacred bishops, the woman of peace said to them:

“If it can be done, peace asks to be discussed justly.”

The bishop of Reggio, Heribertus, like a mirror and a light, [Note: [Col. 1011D] Ughellus did not know this Reggian bishop sufficiently well in *Italia sacra*. He was obedient to the Roman see and therefore dear to the countess Mathilda. He flourished at the very time when Henry Augustus and Guibert, or the false pope Clement, had elevated Gandulf and later Ludovicus to the bishopric of Reggio. MUR.]

With the others declared that peace must plainly be made,

Adding that the distress of the time was pressing them.

The lady’s mind seemed to begin yielding to these words.

At last the hermit John replied [Note: [Col. 1012C] The illustrious Mabillon suspects that he was abbot of the Canossan monastery, in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 1092, and not without reason, as I shall say below. MUR.]:

“Far be it from this to happen! For this peace is hostile

To the Holy Spirit, to the Father, and to his own Son.

Therefore you will lose the sweats and labors

That you have endured in Christ’s name.

Do not waver; fight, for abundant victory

Will come to you almost from heaven,

With serene Christ granting it because of Peter’s prayers,

And you will enjoy it joyfully.”

When faith bears fruit, this hermit’s words bear fruit.

[Col. 1012B] Thus he proved a true prophet.

For the countess left the king’s pact unfulfilled

And promised to preserve the highest loyalty,

Peter’s foster daughter, until God granted her the life of eternity.

The company of Catholic priests was strengthened.

They preferred death to the king’s covenant.

That worthy conference took place at Carpineti [Note: [Col. 1012C] In the Reggian district, namely in its mountains, where the name remains in Castello delle Carpinete. MUR.].

The king, never ceasing to batter Montebello with wars,

Had his war machine catch fire.

While battle was being waged near Cucherl[a],

One of his sons fell [Note: [Col. 1012C] The other historians, remarkably, are silent about his name and death. Sigonius wrote that he fell in the assault on Carpineti. But his death occurred during the siege of Montebello, as Donizo’s words clearly show. MUR.].

The king grieved over him at length

And sent the body to Verona, where he built a beautiful tomb for him.

Seeing that the fortress had become impregnable,

The king ordered the sound of trumpets

To resound densely across the broad field,

[Col. 1012C] And, departing from there, rested.

Immediately thereafter, leaving the memorable fortress of Montebello,

The king himself reached Aemilia [Note: [Col. 1012D] That is, the city of Reggio Lepidi, which was called Aemilia, at least in those times. Yet consider the bull of Guibert, or the antipope Clement III, addressed to the canons of Reggio and preserved in their archive. It was issued at Cesena by the hand of Bernerius, vice-chancellor in Peter’s place, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, indiction XV, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Clement III, pope, on the Ides of June. There Clement confirms the tithe “in the city called Reggio, and in Martia, and all the possessions that are around the city called Aemilia.” Do you see here both the city of Reggio and the city of Aemilia? Let others decide whether they were one and the same or two different, though neighboring, places. I myself think that just as Reggio Lepidi took its name from Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, its restorer, so Aemilia also received its name from the same man. Yet I find no trace of such a designation among the ancients. As for the ancient abridgers of Donizo, the Este manuscript explains these words, “he reached Aemilia,” as follows: “And he came to the city of Reggio and stayed in the city of Reggio for several days.” Hear also the Reggian manuscript: “And thus the emperor, having gathered his tents, came to Reggio,” and so forth. Thus they explain Aemilia. MUR.]

And stayed there for a few days, deceitful in speech.

From there he moved his camp, pretending to go to Parma.

[Col. 1013A] The weather was clear. He returned toward Cavilianum [Note: [Col. 1013D] Fulvius Azzarius, in the Reggian Chronicle, writes that it is now called the fortress of Saint Paul, San Paolo, beside the river Enza. Ancient charters indeed confirm this. MUR.],

And remembered what evil Canossa had suffered,

When he had stood there naked, lamenting, and cold,

While snow likewise scorched his feet.

From this he thought that the time for vengeance had now come.

But the countess had come to Canossa with her own force.

When she learned that the king was at Cavilianum,

She left part of her troops in the stronghold

And took part with her.

She soon went to Bibianello,

Entrusting herself to Apollonius,

Hoping that through his merits she could be saved from the enemy.

While she was at Mount Jumigna [Note: [Col. 1013D] Write *Vimignae*. Thus have our manuscripts. MUR.],

The enemies came in denser numbers on foot

Over Mount Lintregnanus, slowly advancing.

These two are neighboring mountains.

Each side, horrified, perceived the uproar.

The lady’s party entered Bibianello,

[Col. 1013B] Hurrying in, while the king’s phalanx,

With its banner widely unfurled, hastened toward Canossa.

Several nobles, the king’s men, then returned from the lady

To the rear; the king sought [Note: [Col. 1013D]

“Seek.” LEIB.

The same manuscripts have *quaerunt*. MUR.] to lead them

Into battle, but they refused the fight and quickly made their way

To the others in the fortress.

At the same time he urged them, weapons in hand,

Boldly to return the battle to the king.

When the great trumpet resounded, and Abbot John [Note: [Col. 1013D] He seems to be the same as the hermit John mentioned above. If this is correct, we have here a hermit used in the sense of “monk.” Mabillon suspected that he had presided as abbot over the Canossan monastery of Saint Apollonius. For the battle was fought not far from Canossa; inside, the abbot and monks were commending the better cause to God. I establish the matter as certain from a charter now in my possession, written in 1105 by Cardinal Bernard and Lord Paschal’s vicar, in which he entrusts to the venerable John, abbot of Canossa, the governance and arrangement of the monastic church of Saint Michael on the mountain, situated in the diocese of Luni. MUR.],

was singing psalms with the monks, and with his heart was entreating all the saints that the place might be protected from the enemy,

a very dense darkness suddenly arose.

The abbot prayed; the people mentioned above fought.

The king’s host was struck by iron missiles;

[Col. 1013C] from the country people only one certainly hurled missiles,

one who had struck many arms with his spear.

The king’s standard was carried by the son of Obertus [Note: [Col. 1014C] Namely, the son of that same Marquis Obertus whom above, Book II, chapter 3, we saw driven to flight by Matilda’s soldiers [Col. 1014D] in the battle of Sorbara. Below this same son of Obertus is called marquis. MUR.].

When he saw a straight spear being directed against him,

he avoided the blow, but his coat of mail drew the spear in too far;

for he fell to the ground. Then a foot soldier ran up,

took the spear, and raised the standard to the stars.

The aforementioned marquis had scarcely been lifted back onto his horse when he returned

to the king, who had taken his stand on a little hill;

with all his companions he came back at once. When they had joined him there,

because of the great fog no one could see the fortress,

[Col. 1014A] the king turned his reins. He made for Bajanum [Note: [Col. 1014D] Azzarius says that the fortress of Bebianum is indicated here. The following verses certainly show that Henry had already descended to the plain, since at dawn he hurried beside the Po. MUR.].

His heart was exceedingly sorrowful, because he saw that the circumstances against him had changed.

For four thousand pounds he would not have wanted to travel that beaten road,

nor even to know it.

From that point the loss of the standard signified his defeat; moreover, his name grew into the term *officiperdi* [Note: [Col. 1014D] The word is taken from the distichs commonly attributed to Cato. It denotes a man who wastes time and oil. MUR.].

Matilda’s party, rejoicing, reverently worshiped Christ

and respectfully carried to the church of Saint Apollonius

the king’s standard, which is still kept there.

While these things were happening, October was cultivating the fields.

The sorrowful king, resting for one night at Bajanum,

hurried in the morning beside the Po; and from there, at the following

daylight, he crossed the Po, which diminishes every year.

Matilda’s army made for the nearby level ground,

and she too afterward crossed the waters of the Eridanus.

[Col. 1014B] Little by little the peoples restored the lands which the renowned duchess had long before lost, by the shields of that man, striking down each of the rebels.

The tower of Gubernula was also restored to its mistress,

loaded with many of the king’s possessions [Note: [Col. 1014D] Restore *onerata* (“loaded”). The manuscript codices likewise read this. MUR.] and sufficiently honored with treasures.

Not long afterward Ripalta was restored to her [Note: [Col. 1014D] It should be written *non longe*, in accordance with the same codices. MUR.].

The pious party gained a great increase in that year.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the separation of Queen Praxedis from King Henry [Note: [Col. 1014D] Read Baronius, years 1093, 1094, and 1095. LEIB.] and on the arrival of Pope Urban in Lombardy

An evil omen also befell the king:

his wife began utterly to despise his disgrace,

though the meter keeps silent on this, lest it degenerate too greatly.

[Col. 1014C] Yet let the verses speak of Queen Praxedis:

she herself fears her husband as a ewe fears the wolf’s tooth.

Trembling with fear, she secretly seeks protection from Matilda,

asking her to separate her from the enemy.

Seeing that the time had come, or the hour,

she, a new Deborah, sends a troop secretly to Verona

to strike down this Sisera; the queen remained there.

She came privately [Note: [Col. 1014D] It should be restored as *privatim*. The sense requires it, and the ancient codices agree. MUR.]; she was carried away and departed rejoicing.

The king’s servants lost her without the tumult of battle.

She was properly, reverently, and nobly received

by the lady Matilda, who, like Jael [Note: [Col. 1014D] Write *Jahel*. Donizo also wrote this, as the manuscripts testify, and the story requires it. MUR.],

[Col. 1015A] had now driven a great peg into Sisera.

Because of this, the fortunate victory of Christ grew among the people

and for the leader of the Church, namely the shepherd of the city.

The queen’s messengers reported this matter to the countess.

Whoever knew that this crime had truly occurred

despised the king’s party, and likewise Guibert’s.

In every region Peter’s party rose to greatest prominence.

The good Urban, illustrious in deeds and in name,

recognizing that the time had come to triumph over King Jabin [Note: [Col. 1015D] *Rasin*. LEIB. This is certainly an error; nevertheless, it should be restored not as *Rasin* but as *Jabin*, as our manuscripts have it—the king defeated by Joshua, Joshua chapter 11. MUR.],

left Rome and came to the shores of Lombardy

with the countess’s counsel.

She received him as though he were wholly the holy Peter.

This power was blessed by the pontiff’s right hand.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Baronius, year 1095. LEIB.] Then the holy shepherd held a synod [Note: [Col. 1015D] Namely, at Piacenza in 1095, whose canons are reported by Labbe, volume X, page 503 of the Councils. MUR.], and the year

[Col. 1015B] was the thousandth, ninety-fifth of Christ.

It was the first month, when moisture is born in the grasses.

By the mouths of priests the deeds of evil men were condemned,

and the heresy of Pope Guibert, the arch-heretic, and of Lord King Henry, because they were enemies of the Lord.

Praxedis and Matilda herself were present for these declarations.

The pope fully blessed the faithful Catholics.

Spacious Piacenza contains this holy synod.

When the synod of the lady whom I often recall was completed,

the pope said farewell and departed, accompanied by clerics,

passing through many cities and striving to convert many.

Gaul received him as a father with the greatest affection.

## CHAPTER IX. On the siege of Nogara

[Col. 1015C] The king, reduced to a state more contemptible than usual, like an exile,

did not know what to do and found no rest by night or day.

At last, lacking courage, he thought of recovering as before.

He summoned the Veronese citizens to join him and went

to besiege the fortress of Nogara, strong and spacious.

Matilda’s ears learned this. She immediately summoned

the Motinenses, men strong in body [Note: [Col. 1015D] Matilda is believed to have been countess of Modena, as her ancestors also had been. There are also considerations that impel me to this opinion. I likewise think that she held authority over other cities by the same right. Since counts of many cities could not reside in each of them, they left a viscount in their place. MUR.].

She crossed the Eridanus, and Gubernula then received her gladly

by night. But this did not escape the king;

now drained of blood [Note: [Col. 1015D] Read with our codices: *nunc exsanguis*, “now drained of blood.” MUR.] and utterly stunned,

he moved away from there that same night, in fear,

by which God once stupefied the wicked Assyrians

when they had surrounded Samaria and did not hesitate to believe that it would be overcome by dreadful and overpowering famine [Note: [Col. 1015D] The manuscripts read *praevalidaque fame*, “and overpowering famine,” and *fore victam nec titubarent*, “and they did not hesitate that it would be conquered.” MUR.].

[Col. 1015D] Terrified, they rose in the black night; vessels and bridles,

various garments—they forgot their swords as well.

[Col. 1016A] They withdrew far away, and the city was filled with wealth.

God himself suddenly made this king tremble.

Fleeing from Matilda, he abandoned the camp by night,

leaving there vessels, bridles, and sound halters [Note: [Col. 1016D] The Regian codex has *capistria sane*. MUR.].

The countess eagerly desired the fortress of Nogara [Note: [Col. 1016D] The same codex has *comitissam*, “the countess.” MUR.].

In the morning she received it, for she was extremely eager,

and, like Judith herself, she was blessed with her own company.

More than once she killed this king as Judith killed Holofernes;

but more often she drove him onward and also laid traps for him,

into which he fell whenever he thought he was taking precautions.

## CHAPTER X. What Pope Urban gained in Gaul, and on his return to Italy

The Gauls received Urban’s [Note: [Col. 1016D] Baronius, year 1095, no. 49. LEIB.] words

as though they were those of Peter, the holy pope,

and gave him many good things.

[Col. 1016B] This shepherd gave them words of salvation in Peter’s place,

for the supreme Father taught them to go to the tomb

of our Lord, so that the place might be cleansed

and the bitter pagan people driven away from it.

O seed of faith, how many good shoots you now produce,

when shining flowers flow again from the shepherd’s mouth

and worthily bring forth fruits for the Lord’s service!

For a father began to leave his dear son for Christ,

and the son clearly began to leave his father;

a husband likewise began to leave his wife, contrary to custom.

Both sexes eagerly hastened to obey God in serenity.

They ran in rivalry to cleanse Christ’s tomb.

The entire Frankish people, from whom the shepherd Urban had arisen,

advanced above all others in triumph.

After the shepherd had spent nearly two years there,

[Col. 1016C] he returned again to Italy and spoke

with gentle Matilda. She received the words of the lordly master,

the highest bishop, with sweetness of heart.

The father absolved her and blessed her above all others,

then, saying farewell, attempted to go to Rome

to cleanse Peter’s chair, which Guibert’s evil

occupation had polluted and, for a long time,

had kept the law of the canons corrupt, as well as the king.

Urban had aspired to this as an orator [Note: [Col. 1016D] I would more willingly read *rector*, “ruler.” These events took place in 1096 and 1097. MUR.].

First, therefore, he cleansed the Roman see of the enemy.

His famous name was growing, especially at Rome.

The people received him and drove Guibert from Rome.

Thrown outside the city, Guibert began constantly

to remain at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1016D] Write *Ravennae*, as our manuscripts have it. MUR.].

His own Oddo [Note: [Col. 1016D] Namely, that same bishop of Bayeux whom he mentioned above, Book II, chapter 3. MUR.] received death.

Because of the papacy, he had not abandoned his lordship

of Ravenna, believing that he might one day relinquish the see [Note: [Col. 1016D] Both the meter requires this, and our manuscripts read *hic quandoque relinquere*, “to leave it one day.” Before he usurped Peter’s see, Guibert presided over the Church of Ravenna; afterward he appointed no archbishop there, so that, if fortune should turn against him, he might still reclaim the vacant chair. Rubeus reports and confirms the same in his *History of Ravenna* [Col. 1017D]. Indeed, in documents relating to the see of Ravenna he styled himself Archbishop Wibertus, whereas in papal documents he used the name Clement. MUR.] the see.

## CHAPTER XI. On Conrad’s departure from his father Henry and on the death of Pope Urban

[Col. 1017A]

Peter the Father, be present to the prayers of the one dictating [Note: [Col. 1017D]

“Of the one dictating.” LEIB.

Our codices likewise display *dictantis*. MUR.];

be present, so that you may teach us to compose our thought into verse [Note: [Col. 1017D] The Regian codex has *rursum*, “again.” MUR.],

and let us tell of one blow by which the king might be overcome.

While Urban was traveling through the Frankish regions,

that king remained until then in Lombardy.

Fortune forbids him to carry the diadem any farther.

The plague that at last struck the king of Egypt struck this king also:

his firstborn deserted him.

The firstborn of the Egyptian king died;

this man’s son did not die, but while alive became a grievous enemy to him,

because of his deed, which was exceedingly wicked.

This man was called Conrad, baptized with chrism [Note: [Col. 1017D] In 1093 Conrad defected from his father Henry, and was hailed as king of Italy. MUR.].

[Col. 1017B] Powerful in intellect, he utterly detested his father

and submitted himself beneath the broad wings of Lady Matilda.

She received him at once as a very worthy and dear relative,

praising him so that he might be called king.

She treated his father as Esther treated Haman:

first she took his wife from him, and now his offspring [Note: [Col. 1017D] The Regian codex has *ut modo*. MUR.].

Troubled by these losses, after remaining seven years

in Italy [Note: [Col. 1017D] Henry had descended into Italy in 1090 and, leaving in 1097, returned to Germany. MUR.],

the exile visits the land of the Gauls,

his son Conrad likewise driven far away.

He now remained with the lady mentioned above.

At her counsel the handsome, ruddy, and truly prudent young man

took a Sicilian woman [Note: [Col. 1017D] Namely, Matilda, whose father was Roger, duke or count of Sicily and Calabria. The abbot of Usperg also mentions this marriage, but the highly learned Rocchus Pirrus seems to have been unaware of it in his chronology of the kings of Sicily. MUR.],

the daughter of Duke Roger.

The pope also tells this young man that, if he wishes to trust him,

he does not forbid him to be king.

[Col. 1017C] He was not a trembling ruler, like a reed in the wind,

but like iron he cut away harmful things with his word.

As a serpent fears a stag, so the crowd fears him because of heresies;

all perverse and false doctrines submit to him.

The freedom of the Roman see never declined [Note: [Col. 1018D] From *decresco*: that is, the liberty of the Roman see suffered no diminution while Urban II sat in it. MUR.] through him,

for he loved holy Peter exceedingly.

That golden bishop, of the finest character, was Urban,

rightly associated with the saints.

Alas for Rome when it lost such a shepherd!

He died at Rome and was buried with fitting honor,

when July itself was near its end by two days,

in the thousandth year, the ninety-ninth,

from the Word born of the exalted Virgin.

## CHAPTER XII. On the election of Pope Paschal and the evil death of Guibert

[Col. 1017D]

After him the good and very religious pope Paschal

was praised and immediately consecrated.

Plain in speech, he was wholly loved throughout Rome,

giving a great love-feast and nourishing the poor and afflicted.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Baronius, volume XII, year 1100, no. 7. LEIB.] To Matilda, who was also fighting for Christ’s doctrine,

he sent letters bearing his blessing,

admonishing her to preserve the earlier customs

taught by the Fathers, who loved her greatly,

in the simplicity of the Father of the holy patriarch Jacob.

Paschal is governed by these, and deceitful practices do not live with him.

Guibert, that little man, learned his plainness

and soon began eagerly to raise up for himself the seat of Antichrist.

He came to Sutri and began to seduce

the Roman citizens, both the poor and the prominent, with excessive payment [Note: [Col. 1018D] The Regian manuscript has *pretioque, minis*, namely, “both with money and with threats.” MUR.].

This enemy made the road of Lord Peter [Note: [Col. 1018D] The same codex has *dompni Petri*, that is, *domni*, “Lord.” MUR.]

guarded, ordering men to rob travelers.

[Col. 1018B] For twenty-three years this wicked man

had disturbed Christ’s Church with all his strength,

while he was able to seduce many foolish minds.

The unhappy man never ceased, nor does he now harm [Note: [Col. 1018D]

The ancient codex has *nunc*, “now.” LEIB.

Our codices also have *nunc*, namely because he had been taken from the living. MUR.]

bodies;

the great world now despises his deeds.

Peter, key-bearer, now provide protection for the whole Church [Note: [Col. 1018D] That is, “key-bearer.” LEIB.]

so that this dull old man may allow people to remain faithful.

Two years after Urban had been carried from this world

and joined to the choir of heaven,

this empty Guibert, struck by grievous pain,

died carrying an anathema with him forever.

Therefore let the people of heaven and the faithful alike,

and let the good rejoice, because the son of perdition has perished.

May God never permit one like him to arise.

A certain author composed these verses about him:

[Col. 1018C]

You would deserve to be mourned with weeping and tears, Guibert,

if perhaps you could be redeemed by weeping and tears.

But no groans can atone for your deeds,

since death could not recall you from your treachery.

There is no counsel that can restore life,

or recall to himself at the end one whom God rejected.

Living and dying, you gave us examples:

that a member of Satan is not part of Christ’s body;

while alive, you possessed not the Lord but the devil;

while dying, you possessed not the Lord but the devil.

Therefore it is abundantly clear that those who follow your deeds

will be struck by a similar sword for a similar crime.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the death of King Conrad and the siege of Ferrara

[Col. 1018D] Since writing of deeds is not a dishonorable undertaking,

be present to my poem, so that you may utter nothing except what is true.

[Col. 1019A] Thereafter Conrad, accompanied by the Lombards,

While he was at that time in disagreement with Matilda [Note: [Col. 1019C] It seems likely that the cause of the disagreement proceeded from Matilda herself, as I have already noted in the *Antiquities of Este*, chapter 4. As long as she believed Conrad useful to her, she honored and respected him as well. But once his father Henry had been almost overthrown, Conrad’s favor and influence declined in Matilda’s eyes. See the contemporary Landulf of Saint Paul in the *History of Milan*, volume IV of the *Italian Matters*. MUR.],

such discord lasted only a short while.

For the king sought the Tuscan regions. There, at last,

when certain nobles acted, he expelled his anger

and returned peacefully to firm peace with the countess.

After this peace he was struck by fever.

It was the month of July, and Conrad died,

in the third year after the aforementioned Urban had passed away [Note: [Col. 1019D] In 1101; the abbot of Usperg notes that suspicion of poison was not absent. LEIB.].

Florence, flourishing in every way, possesses his body.

After this summer, it is pleasant to recall the autumn.

When it came, it found the hard walls of Ferrara besieged,

for Ferrara itself had rebelled against the duchess

and did not wish to serve her.

Against it she led peoples and swords without number:

[Col. 1019B] armored Tuscans, Romans, and Lombards,

and Ravennates—Ravennates whose ships are especially numerous,

for many sea-going vessels and keels surrounded it,

sent by the illustrious Venetian commander [Note: [Col. 1019D] That is, Vitalis Michael, to whom Matilda granted certain immunities and privileges in the city of Ferrara, as Venetian historians relate. MUR.].

At last, considering how it might avoid defeat,

Ferrara desired to cherish peace with great Matilda,

whose custom it always is to overcome living enemies.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Pope Paschal, out of pious concern for Lady Matilda, sent the venerable Cardinal Bernard [Note: [Col. 1019D] The Regian codex has *direxit*, “sent.” MUR.] to Lombardy

With Peter’s help I have already composed many verses.

Paul, teach our mind, and do not recount verses [Note: [Col. 1019D] Read with our codices: *nunc metra*. MUR.]

that would teach minds to endure punishments calmly.

[Col. 1019C] Paschal, carefully feeding the Lord’s sheep with constant love,

often remembered the countess, mentioned above so many times,

before Christ’s altar.

He strove to send to that beloved woman someone

more praiseworthy than all the clerics of Rome [Note: [Col. 1019D] For this Bernard was a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. [Col. 1020C] Our codices also have “abbot of the Valley of Ambrosia,” although *Umbrosae* should be written. One ancient Regian epitomator has: “who had been abbot of the Valley of Umbrosa.” MUR.],

namely Bernard, distinguished by the priesthood,

and plainly a monk, as well as abbot of holy

Ambrose’s Valley [Note: [Col. 1020D] “Valley of Umbrosa.” LEIB.].

He was completely filled with holy deeds.

Matilda reverently loved him and received him cautiously,

as though he were the pope himself, with a faithful mind.

This heavenly man, showing heavenly things in word and deed,

gave good examples openly before everyone

and then produced worthy fruit for the Lord.

His name was carried far and wide on the lips

of many, and a large part of the people of Parma,

strengthened by his name,

[Col. 1020A] devoutly sought this holy elder with an earnest vow,

asking him to go to Parma, blackened by many errors,

which this Father might drive far away by his words.

He agreed to these requests, with Matilda’s counsel as well,

and, shining with hope and faith, accompanied by clerics,

he proceeded to the city.

The Dormition of the holy Virgin was then being celebrated,

in the middle of the month known as the sixth.

Parma rejoices in that feast.

There is said to be a great temple there named for Mary,

in which the entire people of Parma worship Christ.

The agreeable and patient man, Bernard, beloved of Christ,

entered it, prepared to sing Mass,

wishing to proclaim to the people the words of the heavenly kingdom.

He began the Mass devoutly in honor of the feast.

After the Gospel he delivered his message to the people,

[Col. 1020B] and some were displeased because of the king.

While the gentle man was placing the chalice upon the holy altar,

entreating the kindly Christ on behalf of all the people,

a great cry and tumult of the crowd arose.

For they began to utter dreadful blasphemies

against Christ, as though against the crucified Jew.

Many said: “Let the false prophet die!”

Many shouted: “Let the city’s deceiver fall!” [Note: [Col. 1020D] In the Regian codex, *orbis*, “of the world.” MUR.]

“He is standing inside,” they said, “as an enemy of the king!”

They unsheathed their swords. The women’s voice rang out as one:

“If you allow him to live, you will lose your friend the king.

If you wish to live, let him not depart alive!”—they shouted.

Glass vessels fell and were shattered high above the upright spears.

All the Father’s companions fled far away together.

[Col. 1020C] But Abbot Theobald [Note: [Col. 1020D] It has so far been uncertain over which monastery he was abbot. It seems almost certain to me that he was Theobald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Genes in Brescello; above, Book I, chapter 18, I suggested that a charter of Countess Matilda had been granted to him. The age and proximity of the place agree. Bacchinius calls him Thedaldus, while Azzarius calls him Theobaldus. MUR.] stood there with the Father alone.

He exposed his neck and said:

“Strike my neck; here I gladly desire death.”

At once someone drew a sword across his neck in anger,

inflicting on him a small and narrow wound.

Undaunted, Bernard the patient, wise, and venerable man

stood with a joyful face before Christ’s altar.

When he saw the crowd laughing as though at his face,

he cried out:

“This man has the appearance of the Devil!

Let him be removed at once, beaten, imprisoned, and scourged!”

Then a greedy citizen laid hands upon him [Note: [Col. 1020D]

The ancient codex has *civis*, “citizen.” LEIB.

Our codices also have *civis avarus*, “a greedy citizen.” The Regian codex then has *et foris asportat*, “and carries him outside.” The ancient abridger of the Estense Library has: “Then one of the greedy citizens laid hands upon the cardinal mentioned above and carried him outside the said church.” MUR.],

and they carried him outside.

Alas! The Mass that had begun was abandoned.

Neither the solemn Dormition of the great Lady, the blessed Virgin,

nor God’s altar, nor even reverence for Peter,

terrified this people that followed Pharisaic deeds.

The entire precious chapel, which Countess Matilda had provided

[Col. 1021A] for this worthy lord in the very temple,

the worst of the people immediately seized and broke apart.

On the following morning, a messenger from a nearby place

came to the great countess and informed her of this matter.

She sighed and wept,

then ordered all her strong champions

to bring their weapons together against Parma.

At that time the Motinenses were holding its territory.

Swift as a flying bird, she hastened there;

on the third day Parma nearly felt her presence and feared her.

Then Parma immediately strove, through her noble vassals [Note: [Col. 1021D] Correct according to our codices: *nobilibus vassis*. Noble vassals, to whom a fief was entrusted, were accustomed to join their lord when war threatened and were obliged to provide assistance as their duty required; this custom still endures. MUR.], to restore the aforesaid man, unjustly captured,

and restored the entire chapel to the lady,

retaining nothing further and seeking to avoid dangers

which she would not have avoided unless she had loved the patient man.

[Col. 1021B] Countess Matilda pardoned the citizens and the city,

at Bernard’s command, through whose piety the matter was settled,

in the year one thousand one hundred and four of the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XV. On the death of King Henry III [Note: [Col. 1021D] Our codices have only “King Henry.” Certainly, in calling him king, the author would more correctly have called him the fourth rather than the third, since he is numbered third only among the Augusti. MUR.]

I wish the friend of the world to learn by what end

the king already mentioned, Henry, was released,

so that, when he knows it, he may recognize what he must do for himself.

The aforementioned king lived entangled

in wicked deeds. Once he pretended to convert,

but he did so with a heart full of poison.

He always honored and willingly upheld the schismatics.

Because of this, his younger son [Note: [Col. 1021D] Namely, Henry, the fifth among the kings of Germany, whose crimes are extremely well known. MUR.]

burned with anger and raised his swords against his father.

He sought to take the kingdom from him;

he did not shrink from engaging him in harsh battle,

and defeated him in the field by fighting.

Over the entire period he was filled with great sorrow,

pierced and battered on every side and tortured everywhere.

At last, without expecting death, he was nevertheless seized

by death’s own chain; it snatched him from his wretched body.

He died on the fourth Ides of August

in the year of Christ one thousand one hundred and six [Note: [Col. 1021D] The Regian codex has *denique quinto*, “one thousand one hundred and five.” Donizo may perhaps have written this, since both the Estense and Leibnitian epitomes, following Donizo himself, place the death of Henry IV in 1105. But it is beyond all doubt that Henry died in 1106; and in a matter whose report filled everyone’s ears while Donizo was alive, he can scarcely be believed to have erred. Therefore *seno* should be retained, and it is more reasonable to think that this is how he transmitted it in writing. [Col. 1022C–D] MUR.],

and he sleeps in the church at Speyer,

which he himself had built [Note: [Col. 1022D] Read with our codices: *quod struxerat*, “which he had built.” MUR.].

## CHAPTER XVI. A fitting exhortation to Pope Paschal

Peter [Note: [Col. 1022D] More correctly in our manuscripts: “O Peter.” MUR.] and Paul, rulers of the world, head of all things in the City,

your persecutors are already traversing foreign places

with a crow’s feather.

With this white feather, send these words to the pope:

“O shepherd, supreme priest and ruler, Paschal,

meditating on these things [Note: [Col. 1022D] The same codices have *nunc meditans*, “now meditating.” MUR.], consider and wisely guide your actions.

Rejoice that Christ’s Church has been snatched

from the kingdom of the deathly abyss;

see that it remains free and protect it cautiously.

Let no one dare any longer to violate its peace.

Let this be your fatherly care.

Let your firm will stand fixed upon him

who submitted himself to death, the enemy, for his bride.

You are the one to whom Christ entrusted and left the bride.

See to it that you hasten always to return her,

perfectly entrusted to you [Note: [Col. 1022D] The Regian codex has *perfecte*, “perfectly.” MUR.],

as a bride worthy of her bridegroom.

Suffer death before she is violated by the enemy.

Let no robber snatch her from you;

let no false lover seduce her gently by any power.

The Lord Christ knows that, if you stand firm and well,

the freedom of the bride will never be diminished by the enemy.

All Rome is also under you [Note: [Col. 1022D]

*Romam*. LEIB.

Our codices have *nunc Roma*, “now Rome.” Nothing else should be changed, since the sense is complete and clear. Namely: now all Rome is subject to you, and no one may carry or place upon himself the crown of the kingdom unless you grant it. Here you see the prerogative of the Roman pontiff in the election and confirmation of the emperors. MUR.],

and no one can bear the crown of the kingdom

unless you grant it to him.

Whoever wears it without you—for you, as teacher,

guide and hold the reins of the king—will be able to remain empty-handed [Note: [Col. 1022D] The Regian codex has *poterit remeare*, “will be able to return.” MUR.].

When a certain false man did not fear to tear apart the gracious bride,

may many strive to keep watch with you [Note: [Col. 1022D]

*Studebunt*. LEIB.

The same codex has *studerunt*. MUR.].

Among them, ready at hand, is Matilda, daughter of the bride,

ever-watchful and strong, often biting back at the perverse.

She entered into fierce wars with the king,

for a full thirty periods she remained steadfast,

fighting night and day while treading down the storms of the kingdom.

The end of the war is at hand. She asks you to grant her rest.

[Col. 1022C] If your task grows, you will never lack strength

or power, and you will recognize [Note: [Col. 1022D]

The ancient codex has: “His, and you will recognize that he does not love Peter’s enemies.” LEIB.

The Vatican codex and our own agree; in *quies* I read: “His, and you will recognize that he does not love Peter’s enemies,” and so forth. MUR.]

that he does not love Peter’s enemies.”

## CHAPTER XVII. On the arrival of Pope Paschal in Lombardy and Gaul

After the death of the king and of the aforementioned Guibert,

the peace of the holy Church began greatly to increase.

Errors ceased, and neglected truths returned.

No one dared to rise up against the pope

or against the blessed see; instead, they kept silent.

Everyone desired that he should travel through the world,

correcting, absolving, and healing contagions and filth.

[Col. 1023A] Seeing such a time, the venerable Pope Paschal

left Rome, where the entire people greatly honored him.

He came to this countess in Lombardy,

whose custom it had always been deeply to honor the pope as father.

This was Matilda, who joyfully went out to meet him.

She received the pope with abundant joy.

She herself was all goodness, the glory and honor of the kingdom.

The aforementioned pope then held a synod beside the Po [Note: [Col. 1023C] Baronius, year 1106. LEIB.].

The son of the dead king sent his messenger to him,

asking that he grant him the right to the kingdom.

He himself wished to be faithful to the holy see,

as to a mother, and desired to submit to it as to a father.

The gracious Father blessed the king’s messenger’s words.

The noble Matilda was present with many others for these declarations.

She praised the pious words of the king’s messenger,

[Col. 1023B] and with everyone magnified the Father’s response.

Then the citizens of Parma came.

They devoutly sought and revered the love of the supreme pontiff,

begging him from the heart to grant Parma a shepherd.

Parma asked the pontiff for the man whom it had once despoiled:

Bernard, a highly venerable monk.

The same city asked the Father to consecrate him

to the church of Parma, of the blessed Virgin [Note: [Col. 1023D]

The ancient codex has *nunc*, “now.” LEIB.

Our codices likewise read *ut nunc*. MUR.].

The pope rejoiced that the wicked daughter Parma,

given over to certain errors and steeped in frivolity,

was herself asking to return to the embrace of her worthy mother.

It was then the month that splits the fields for the young oxen.

The year was the thousandth, one hundred and sixth [Note: [Col. 1023D] Baronius, year 1106, no. 41. LEIB.].

Guastalla [Note: [Col. 1023D] As everyone knows, now Guastalla. It was called Guarstalla because the word is contracted from Guardastalla, or Wardistalla, as it was called in antiquity. Azzarius, in the Estense manuscript history, attributes the construction of this town to Beatrice, the mother of Countess Matilda. It is in fact much older. In 865 the Emperor Louis II granted, among other properties, the estate of Wardistalla, then belonging to the county of Reggio, to the monastery of Saint Sixtus at Piacenza, as is clear from a privilege preserved by Campi in his *History of Piacenza*, volume I, page 459. In 877 the Empress Angilberga likewise left in her testament to the same sacred monastery an estate called Guardastalla. It is mentioned in other records as well. It is a Lombard word—or, which is the same thing, Germanic—composed of *Warda*, meaning “guard,” and *stallum*, meaning “seat” or “station.” In Italian we might say Guarda-Sito. I infer that there was a military station and guard there to protect the route of the Po River. I possess a settlement made in 1102 between Countess Matilda and Imelda, abbess of the monastery of Saint Sixtus at Piacenza, concerning the fortress and estate of Wardestalla; from this it is clear that Matilda held authority there. MUR.] had been the site of the synod.

[Col. 1023C] From there the pious pope departed and came to the Parma

mentioned above, doing there everything they had requested.
