For there he consecrated the temple of Christ’s Mother [Note: [Col. 1024D] He also consecrated the temple at Modena in this same year, 1106, with Matilda herself present and with great solemnity—something Donizo ought also to have mentioned. I shall add elsewhere in this collection the account of the dedication of the greater temple at Modena, committed to writing by a contemporary author. MUR.],

giving a decree that it should be subject to no one

except Peter, the key-bearer of heaven, and his see as well.

Matilda came to this temple to see it.

She gave such a gift, which greatly pleased the people.

Then the pope consecrated Bernard as bishop

and ordered him to remain at Parma as the pope’s representative.

From there, saying farewell to the lady so often mentioned,

the same venerable man sought the lands of the Franks.

He produced abundant fruit there for a considerable period.

One year later he returned from there,

the beloved shepherd coming back again.

[Col. 1024A] Matilda was soon found at his service.

Speaking readily, the bishop quickly returned with her to Rome.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the legates and the first arrival of King Henry IV in Italy

The new king, exalting himself and spreading his wings far abroad,

conquered lands and famous kingdoms by warfare.

This Henry IV was prudent and fond of cunning [Note: [Col. 1024D] Redundant. LEIB.].

To prevent him from seeming to be against holy Peter,

when the years of Christ had increased to eleven hundred and ten [Note: [Col. 1024D] Baronius, year 1110. LEIB.],

he sent great pontiffs, counts, and high-ranking men

to splendid Rome, seeking the crown of the kingdom.

“If the king wishes to be Peter’s son and faithful,

I will give him Rome,” the pope replied, “and the crown with it.”

[Col. 1024B] As they returned, or as they proceeded onward, Matilda

received them and gave them many things.

They returned joyfully at last to the young king.

He himself soon gathered a strong force.

In that same year, armed with many men, at the beginning

of autumn he came and slaughtered the Lombards,

burning and devastating their greatest camps.

His anger terrified their fortified cities.

The city of Novara rejoiced in becoming rebellious against him;

he set it on fire and afterward broke down its walls.

The entire city finally sent him many golden

and silver vessels, together with much money.

The noble and populous city of Milan alone

did not serve him, nor did it contribute a copper coin.

[Col. 1024C] No house of a count or duke in Italy

could be found over which the aforementioned king

cared greatly, because he was able to overcome them.

Matilda alone always held the king

in great hatred [Note: [Col. 1024D] *Exosum*, “hated.” LEIB.]

and repeatedly drove him back in battle.

The duchess herself then stood in famous fortresses.

Many distinguished nobles from beyond the mountains

came to her, amazed at the woman.

The king was burning for peace, on whose behalf she labored.

The king came as far as the bank of the Taro, seeking peace.

Then the countess, having been thoroughly instructed,

left Canossa.

Perhaps he reached the lofty Bibianellum [Note: [Col. 1024D] Write *Bibianellum*, now Bianello. The manuscript copies likewise read it. MUR.].

There he said many things to the king’s great envoys,

[Col. 1025A] Speaking of peace, of the king’s honor and his own;

At last both sides praised that same peace,

But he did not promise that he would be with Peter.

After peace had been concluded, the king took the Frankish road [Note: [Col. 1025C] Namely, the Aemilian Way, which we call the Claudian. They gave it this name because it led directly to France, or Gaul. MUR.],

And crossed over, December then beginning.

He passed through Mount Burdon [Note: [Col. 1025C] The manuscript copies likewise read this. But the older ones customarily call it Mount Bardon, over which there is a passage from Berceto into Tuscany by way of Pontremoli. MUR.] into Tuscan territory [Note: [Col. 1025C] *Oris* (“shores,” “regions”). LEIB.],

The whole people trembled and gave him money as tribute;

As the Lombards had done, so the Tuscans were terrified,

And with the Florentines [Note: [Col. 1025D] Join this with what follows. The Este abridger’s manuscript reads: “And the aforesaid king celebrated the Nativity of Christ in the city of Florence.” The Regio and Leibnitian epitomes have the same, not to mention the Hildesheim Annals and other histories. MUR.] he finally celebrated Christ’s

Nativity; the people brought him abundant provisions.

He stormed the walls of Arezzo and burned them with fire.

On the fourth day before the Ides of February he was at Rome, graciously

Sending word to Pope Paschal that he wished to honor

His command, and did not wish to sell any bishopric

Or grant one, unless the pious duke himself should order it.

[Col. 1025B] All Rome rejoiced, gathering from every quarter:

The pope, priests, levites, and the people, out of love

For the king; nobles, young men, and likewise the lesser folk,

Women, monks, and also a hundred nuns,

Carrying many lamps with bright light.

Following ancient custom, an extended procession was made

In the king’s honor, covered with coins thrown over it [Note: [Col. 1025D] “What,” you may ask, “does this obscure passage of Donizo mean?” If I understand it correctly, he means that the people’s procession was extended and that coins, by order of the Augustus, were thrown over the people, so that they seemed to be covered as if by a rainstorm. Otto of Freising testifies to this: “Henry V won over the Roman citizens by gifts.” It is also established that gold was customarily scattered among the people by other Augusti at their coronations. I omit the examples. MUR.].

They entered the venerable church of Saint Peter.

The king, humbly and very graciously seeking the altar,

Went slowly up the steps, bending his knees.

At the top of the stairs he extended his kisses to the pope;

He established one investiture [Note: [Col. 1025D] What Donizo relates here should be compared with what is reported in the *Life of Paschal II*, vol. III of *Rerum Italicarum*, and by Dodechin in the appendix to Marianus, and by Baronius in the *Annals* under the fourth year. For this account does not seem sufficiently to agree with those, and the principal cause of that impious deed is left unmentioned. MUR.] over the altar,

That he would never sell any church for money,

Nor invest anyone, unless the pope kindly ordered it.

[Col. 1025C] At this the people, the clergy, and especially the pope triumphed;

And when the pope prepared to give the king everything he had asked,

He sent word that the king should come; but the king delayed, handling secret matters.

For the Devil, the ancient and wicked seducer of humankind,

Burning with envy at the kingdom’s peace, suddenly

Sowing the seed of treachery, loves passionately

To disturb the faithful. Whatever has been properly established

Is immediately shattered; thus the king also said:

[Col. 1026A] “I desire the custom and dignity of the ancient kings.

“I do not want my lord the pope to give me only the crown;

“I want a ring and staff to be given by me to all

“The prelates of our kingdom, as was once the custom.”

The pope was unwilling in any way to grant this to him,

And the king had him led away and received him into custody.

Night was approaching when the king did these things.

Many pontiffs and citizens were captured there,

And the German people seized the holy crosses.

That drunken people does not know Christ’s pious teachings.

The joys of peace were turned into broad tears [Note: [Col. 1026C] Our copies read “into broad tears.” MUR.].

That night the entire Roman cohort consulted together.

In the morning they rose with swords and shields, horses caparisoned.

They attacked the Germans, strong in body;

They struck them down and killed them, and almost completely defeated them.

[Col. 1026B] But they were exceedingly eager for these chests [Note: [Col. 1026C] The Regio manuscript has *Zabernas*. I think Donizo wrote it in this form. According to Papias, *zaberna* is a chest or small cupboard in which clothes are kept, or any other such object. See Du Cange in the *Glossary* and Vossius, *De vitiis sermonis*, book II, chapter 21, under the word *Zabyra*, where Hariulf and Abdias of Babylon are cited as using the same word. I therefore interpret *Zabernas* as chests, coffers, boxes, trunks, bags, and similar containers in which the German people stored money and household goods. MUR.],

Loaded with weapons and money alike.

They valued money more than the effort of winning the battle.

The king of the Lombards was very secure here in arms.

They surrounded him and cut the Romans to pieces.

The king, an outstanding horseman, swift beyond compare [Note: [Col. 1026D] The Regio manuscript reads *celerís quo nemo repertus*, “swift, than whom none was found”; in place of *celerior*. MUR.],

Stood among his own men and crushed the citizens of the City.

After an immense slaughter of the people,

The Romans abandoned the miserable battle they had begun.

But the king seized the pope, peace having been violently denied.

Among the others captured was the venerable Parmesan

Bishop Bernard, filled with the teaching of Christ,

And that good elder [Note: [Col. 1026D] It should be written *Bonus-Senior*, the bishop of Reggio. That was indeed the name of the Regio bishop, namely Bonsignore. In the Regio epitome of Donizo he is called Bonsegnorius; Ughellus has some information about him in volume II of *Italia Sacra*, and Fulvius Azzarius has more in his manuscript *History of Reggio*. MUR.], the bishop of Reggio,

[Col. 1026C] I believe no simpler priest can be found.

On behalf of these men, the eloquent and bold man,

The noble Arduin [Note: [Col. 1026D] Clearly, as can rightly be conjectured, Arduin of Palude, son of Guido. From him the noble and ancient family of the counts of Palude, long prominent in Reggio, descended and still survives. He is frequently mentioned in the records of Countess Matilda preserved by Florentius and Bacchinius. MUR.],

A Lombard skilled in speech,

And the faithful envoy of Lady Matilda,

Addressed the king, reminding him of the countess’s agreement.

Immediately, in honor of Matilda, the king allowed them to go.

A report spread throughout the world concerning the captured supreme pontiff,

Who, because of the citizens whom he had captured with him,

[Col. 1027A] Fearing that they would all suffer death together,

When the feast of Easter arrived, granted him peace;

He subjected the Romulean City to him, placed the diadem

Upon his head, anointed him, and blessed him.

The last day of the first month [Note: [Col. 1027B] The manuscript copies and the ancient Este epitome likewise read this. The distinguished Pagius, in his critical notes on Baronius for year four, no. 3, has a long discussion of the date of Henry V’s Roman coronation [Col. 1027C] and argues that it took place on the fifth day before the Ides of April, Sunday in White Week. To defend that view, he had to correct Malmesbury himself, on whose authority he relies, as well as other writers. Baronius assigns the event to the Ides of April, as do the Hildesheim Annals and the Saxon chronicler cited by Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals*. Since Pagius may not have known the latter’s words, it is useful to quote them: “King Henry celebrated Easter in his camp not far from the city, and during the octave of Easter, namely on the Ides of April, he was consecrated emperor in the church of Saint Peter.” It is remarkable that, concerning an event of such importance and not separated from us by any great span of centuries, the date should still remain uncertain. Even more astonishing is that our Donizo writes in clear letters that Henry V was crowned, anointed, and blessed when the feast of Easter arrived, and then adds:

“The last day of the first month brought Easter back,

“In the eleven-hundred-and-eleventh year of the Lord.”

The last day of the first month is the final day of March. You can see how far Donizo differs from the opinion of the others, although he was committing these events to writing at those very days. There is another cause for astonishment. According to chronologists and the canons of the cycles, Easter in year four fell on the second day of April; yet Donizo, occupied at that very time in writing this history, says that it occurred on the last day of March. Unless our author stumbled very seriously here, I would certainly prefer his view that the coronation took place on Easter Sunday to the others’, since, given his proximity in time and place, he can scarcely be believed to have been mistaken. Moreover, hear Roger of Hoveden, part I of the *Annals*, who says this about Henry: “He captured Pope Paschal and placed him in custody, but afterward, at the Ponte Salaria, where they celebrated the Easter festival in the field, he made peace with him.” Roger flourished in the same century. Add Robert of Mont, praised by Hagio—or, as it seems to me, Sigebert of Gembloux—who writes in his *Chronicle*: “On Easter Day, after Henry had been crowned emperor, etc.” Labbe and Pagius are forced to emend these words because they conflict with their opinion. Sigebert was then alive and writing his *Chronicle*, and he died not long afterward. Thus he plainly agrees with Donizo concerning the day of the coronation. As for the day of Easter, however, Donizo seems to me to have been shamefully mistaken in a matter so celebrated, whose date he could not have failed to know. I therefore leave the matter for others to weigh. MUR.] then brought Easter back,

In the eleven-hundred-and-eleventh year of the Lord.

The Augustus plainly gave the pope illustrious gifts.

Rejoicing but weary, and with his army as well,

He left Rome and crossed the Tuscan regions.

Guiding the reins properly and riding without drawing his swords,

He sought the spacious Lombard kingdom.

The illustrious dukes, going before the king himself,

Well supplied, greeted Matilda in return.

The wise Caesar did not wish to go anywhere

Unless he first looked upon the face of the aforesaid countess.

[Col. 1027B] When six days of May had already begun to pass,

He himself approached, knowing that she was at Bibianellum.

In the German language he likewise conveyed his words;

He had no need of any interpreter.

He promised her [Note: [Col. 1028C]

The ancient manuscript has *promsit*. LEIB.

Our manuscripts also read *promsit*, that is, “he confessed” or “declared.” From what Donizo, an eyewitness, relates here, the account of Orderic Vitalis, book X, p. 763 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, collapses—namely, that at this time Henry V devastated the extensive territory of Matilda, the powerful lady, which possessed Pavia, Piacenza, and a large part of Italy now called Lombardy. Nor is there any truth in the claim that Matilda ruled Pavia. MUR.]

That he would never find anyone like her.

He gave her the government of the Ligurian kingdom in place of the king [Note: [Col. 1028D] Thus Countess Matilda was appointed by Henry V as something like viceroy of the Italian kingdom. Even before this time the illustrious woman had ruled extensively, as, among other historians, the contemporary Landulf of Saint Paul sufficiently demonstrates, whose Milanese Chronicle we published in volume IV of *Rerum Italicarum*. MUR.],

And in clear words he would call her “mother” [Note: [Col. 1028D] Write *vocitavit*, “he called,” with our manuscripts. MUR.].

Spending three days with her, he also established a firm treaty.

Completely joyful, growing continually like a cedar,

He went with the great Germans beyond the mountains.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the people of Mantua returned, through fear, to loyalty to Lady Matilda

[Col. 1028A]

Glory to you, Christ, by whose power Matilda

Remains victorious over all her enemies,

For she overcame many nobles, counts, and cities.

She despised the king [Note: [Col. 1028D] Henry IV. MUR.] when she fought battles against him.

The March [Note: [Col. 1028D] In my interpretation, the March of Tuscany, as Florentius previously understood it in his records of the same countess. It should nevertheless be remembered that some include the March of Ancona among the territories formerly belonging to Matilda. In the following age this region was called simply “the March,” as though by antonomasia. But I have not yet learned from any firm documents that Matilda ruled there. Indeed, as Pompeius Compagnonus noted in the *Regia Picena*, in those very times Warner, duke and marquis, seems to have ruled that region. MUR.] obeyed her, unwillingly as well as willingly.

Cruel Mantua forbade itself to be faithful to her,

And abandoned her for twenty-four years,

Refusing to serve her and taking pride in treachery.

Therefore the aforesaid king issued an especially harsh edict,

Which hard Mantua rejected.

Although it stood with a strong German people [Note: [Col. 1028D] *Alemanna*. LEIB.],

The illustrious Matilda nevertheless did not cease to send it

Distinguished envoys with worthy gifts.

The Caesar glorified her with gifts, and she him in return.

Meanwhile a very great tribulation occurred,

Troubling the earth, revealing the hearts of the wicked,

And exposing their intentions and impieties.

Disperse, Christ, such ways; erase the ruins.

Hear the wretched, our God; hear the needy.

Grant life to the duchess Matilda.

For when she dies, the needy will be stripped bare,

And the churches will certainly be grievously despoiled.

This is what these nobles now believe they will do.

[Col. 1029A] Thief will give thief aid, as though to his offspring;

The plunderer will attack the plunderer, as a lion gnaws a lion with its jaws.

Flowers are now seen; what will the robbers do hereafter?

Thus far the prudent Countess Matilda still lives,

But Mount Baranzone [Note: [Col. 1029C] Now Mount Baranzone, in the territory and mountains of Modena beyond Mount Zibinio. Some charters of donations made there by Matilda still survive in Silingardus and Bacchinius. MUR.] holds her exceedingly weak.

From this point tares spring up and choke the wicked crop.

From every side the sinister and insolent gather.

They report that the aforementioned countess has died.

The citizens whom Mantua is accustomed always to have with it

Believe this report and immediately begin to plan

How to renew their former treachery.

They investigate and seek out Ripalta [Note: [Col. 1029D] The ancient author of the manuscript Este epitome calls it the territory of Ripalta in the bishopric of Mantua. The Leibnitian epitomator calls Ripalta a castle of the countess, three miles from the city of Mantua. See above, chapter 4 of this book. MUR.].

Its guards, struck down by fear,

Doubting greatly whether their own lady was alive,

Submit the entire castle, themselves and their children,

To the people’s will, though not without stipulation.

[Col. 1029B] Such was the agreement: if Matilda were alive,

They did not wish to retain the castle against her.

But the citizens acted with far too little good faith.

After they saw the castle brought under their control,

They secretly plotted to burn it all.

Meanwhile the prudent Bishop Manfred [Note: [Col. 1029D] Namely, the bishop of Mantua. MUR.] came to the city

And said that the countess had been left alive.

At his statement the people were angered against him.

Had he not been distinguished and born of a great family,

I believe they would have laid hands upon him; but they were afraid.

It was not fear of the king that restrained them, nor the treaty with the people.

They burned the castle to the ground, as they had long desired.

They broke down the towers, and the stones were carried into the city.

For a month [Note: [Col. 1029D] The Regio manuscript has “for the Parmesan month.” But the earlier reading should be retained. MUR.] this damage and crime was not made public,

So that it would not become the cause of the weak lady’s ruin.

[Col. 1029C] It was the sixth month, when the heat was growing exceedingly.

The protectress of widows was scarcely recovering. That widows might live chastely, they prayed that the countess might live [Note: [Col. 1029D] The Regio manuscript reads, “who live chastely.” What follows is very obscure, namely, that they seek the countess’s life. I think *captent* has been used for *optent*, “wish.” Thus below *vivens haec* occurs, against Priscian’s rule, in place of *vivente hac*. MUR.].

The peasant should take the plow in his hand and furrow the earth,

Tame and feed the bulls, work safely,

Travel a secure road, while she lives, and the traveler likewise.

Let the sailor cease fearing the pirate of the Eridanus

As long as the countess enjoys the present life.

But when she learned how much harm Mantua had done her,

She said: “A certain time will come when Mantua must perish;

The unjust city will atone for its dire offenses.”

She arranges shield-bearing troops and bowmen,

High ships armed above this city.

When these new events were suddenly made known throughout the city,

The city rich in birds [Note: [Col. 1029D] He alludes to verses of Virgil, *Aeneid* X, which must be quoted:

“Mantua, rich in birds, but not one race for all,

Threefold is the people there,” etc. [Col. 1030C] Mantua is therefore called “rich in birds,” that is, very illustrious in the glory of its ancestors. But one may immediately laugh at Donizo for writing *avibus* rather than *avis*. Yet he did this deliberately, to mock Mantua, which he calls no longer “rich in ancestral glory” but “rich in birds.” Perhaps, moreover, he understood the words “the people there are threefold” in another sense. MUR.],

Lived there as a threefold people.

They quickly investigated what they should do, and labored together.

“Let us wage war,” one faction unjustly said.

Another said that we had used the night sufficiently to defend the walls [Note: [Col. 1030D] Our copies prefer *hostis*, “the enemy.” MUR.].

A poorer faction said that it would go outside.

While they uttered such words and entertained foolish thoughts,

The better faction rose and addressed the young men and the city [Note: [Col. 1030D] Correct to *et urbis*, “and of the city,” as the sense requires and our copies likewise attest. MUR.]:

[Col. 1030A] “Does it please you, young men, to live as though by plunder?

“But shame on us, young men, to be held under siege [Note: [Col. 1030D] This is how the passage appears in the Regio manuscript, with one additional verse:

“Does it please you, boys, to be held under siege?

“Does it please you, boys, to live by what we seize or by plunder?

“But shame on us, boys, to be held under siege.” MUR.].

“An invading soldier wishes to cut down our vines.

“O brave young men, let discord flee far away!

“Let one faction go to seek forgiveness from our lady;

“Let it plead with her, to whom it is altogether more fitting

“For us to be faithful with joy.”

[Col. 1030B] At this exhortation of the better faction, the strongest hearts

Of the young men softened; at last concord prevailed.

They approached timidly and asked the countess’s forgiveness.

She kept her eyes fixed on the ground, turning away,

And did not wish at all to hear such pleas.

The envoys softened her anger as best they could:

“Noble power, we beg you, forgive our offenses against you.

“We lay our city before you.

“Let all the people who live in the city swear allegiance to you.”

At the words of these men and of their nobles,

She scarcely gave her assent.

Yet the city brought her its tribute,

And the lowest and proudest people alike

Swore an oath to her in the city.

They became her friends, and, whether willingly or unwillingly,

They were as they had formerly been.

For this agreement is known to have been made at Bondeno [Note: [Col. 1030D] This place will be mentioned below, when Countess Matilda has departed from human affairs. MUR.].

[Col. 1030C] It was then October, which had nearly reached its end.

The reckoning of the years of Christ was written down [Note: [Col. 1030D] Rather, in our copies, *taxatur*, “is reckoned.” MUR.],

And one thousand, one hundred, and fourteen years had passed away.

## CHAPTER XX. How intensely Lady Matilda devoted herself to the worship of God

Like a flowering palm, Matilda flourishes in honor,

With branches and leaves, as the palm does through every season.

She preserves them all exceedingly green, within and without.

So may her honor flourish without failing, O God, I pray.

She carries the little ones, sustains the poor and the great.

She conquers priests by the love of Christ [Note: [Col. 1030D] That is, she overcomes them through the love of Christ. MUR.].

[Col. 1031A] By night, and even more diligently by day,

She is devoted to the sacred psalms and venerable offices,

With pious religion, sufficiently attentive and skilled.

The wisest of the clergy always cling to her.

No prelate will be found more diligent than she

In properly consecrated garments and precious vessels.

An abundance of books and good things did not fail her [Note: [Col. 1031C] More correctly, our manuscripts read *defuit*, “was lacking.” MUR.].

She possessed books from every art and in every form.

She never forgot to preserve good ordinances.

She waged God’s wars; therefore she stands victorious though unarmed.

O King of Paradise, she strives to give her possessions

To the saints for you [Note: [Col. 1031C] The ancient manuscript has *Res*. LEIB. Our copies also have *Res*. What follows, “to give to the saints,” means to bestow upon churches dedicated to God under the names of saints. MUR.].

Fulfill the vows of her heart, O heavenly husbandman.

Most especially you, Prince Peter, to whom she has left all that is hers [Note: [Col. 1031D]

The ancient manuscript has *relinquet*, “will leave.” For the author wrote this while she was still alive, although he completed the book after her death. LEIB.

Our copies also read *relinquet*. It refers to her intention, since earlier she had already donated all her possessions to the Apostolic See. MUR.].

May that blessed man and levite, Caesarius [Note: [Col. 1031D] The acts of Saint Caesarius can be found in Surius under 1 November. He is invoked here because Countess Matilda had richly endowed the church of Saint Caesarius in the Modenese territory and had granted it to regular canons. In a privilege of Emperor Lothair III that I have seen, mention is also made of the property that Lady Countess Matilda donated to the church of Saint Caesarius for the salvation of her soul and those of her parents. The diploma was issued in 1138 at Vignola. Pagius argues that Lothair died in the preceding year, 1137. If this diploma is genuine, his death is more correctly dated by Baronius. MUR.], tossed by the waves of the sea and released from a sack,

[Col. 1031B] be in no way slow, but a most prompt and gracious

Intercessor with merciful Christ, so that she may live

In the heavenly dwellings and not experience the wrath of the abyss.

She adorns the churches, priests, and levites

Of this martyr, whose church she is known to have founded most excellently.

Long ago she fully caused the church to shine,

For it glitters with gold and shines with splendid silver.

She gave it broad lands [Note: [Col. 1032C]

The ancient manuscript has *cui*, “to which.” LEIB.

Our copies also read *cui*. MUR.],

Books, vestments, and gems.

She knows how to surpass the foremost churches.

Thus the Canossan Muse has spoken of her work:

“As long as the world exists, may this provident lady

Continue to seek these things.

May Saints Apollonius, Victor, Corona, and Quirinus

Ask before God that Matilda may be blessed,

Fed with heavenly life and everlasting bread.

Toward them may she show righteous love, in the manner of parents.”

[Col. 1031C] At the beginning we spoke of the composition of the book.

If we seemed to have written anything improper

With mouth or hand, we would ask the Lady herself

At the end of the book, that she herself might patiently chastise us.

Burning zeal compelled us to bring forth so much.

Our duty dictates these verses, our name, and this [Note: [Col. 1032C] As I noted in the preface, Donizo expressed his name and office through an acrostic formed from the initial letters of the verses of this chapter. MUR.].

The end of the book is here; let us praise the Lord, friends.

## Concerning the distinguished death of the memorable Countess Matilda

A man thinks and plans, but God orders what is fitting.

[Col. 1032A] Recently I composed two books in verse,

Which I said I would send to Countess Matilda.

The first speaks of her fathers,

And the second remains published in praise of her.

I avoided trifles and approved what I wrote as true.

While I was weaving the books onto tablets with joyful mind,

A messenger arrived and greatly stunned me,

Saying that the aforementioned countess had died.

My strength broke apart, and suddenly my marrow failed.

The sweet sleep of my eyelids fled.

My entrails grew cold, and at once my bones and flesh melted.

Whatever I was working on fell empty from my hands.

Her death does not harm me alone; it is well known

That it harms, indeed, all who live rightly.

For wherever good people are, they had been especially well known to her.

[Col. 1032B] Those who dwell beyond the sea or remain in Galicia

Often took care to offer prayers to Christ on her behalf

And kindly sent envoys to her.

The patriarch of Jerusalem knew of her,

As did the Roman and Constantinopolitan patriarchs.

They rejoiced so greatly in her that they diligently

And properly strove to send her their own writings.

Then all honor and glory of Italy fell,

When you died, Matilda, illustrious duchess.

You conquered kings and all rebels for yourself.

Peoples throughout the earth desired to know your council [Note: [Col. 1032D] That is, your court. The Regio manuscript, however, reads *consilium*, “counsel.” MUR.] and also your radiant face.

To them you gave answers and honored them all.

Oh, how many cruel tyrants stood there

Under the appearance of justice, knowing that you were just.

Once unrestrained, they now break the treaties of peace.

They despoil the churches, and now no one defends them.

If someone perhaps presents himself as their protector [Note: [Col. 1032D] He attacks the advocates of the churches, who often pursued not their interests but their own, plundering them. MUR.],

He first takes away a large part of the churches’ land.

With your death, Matilda, sound custom perishes.

For the soldier [Note: [Col. 1032D] That is, the noble vassals who, after receiving fiefs from bishops and abbots, later behaved arrogantly before those lords and against them. MUR.] strives more boldly to rise above his lord.

The cleric now strays from the right path [Note: [Col. 1032D] A typographical error: *Deviat a recto*, “he strays from the right path.” The manuscript copies read this. They also have *ergo*, not *ordo*. Donizo needed that word to close the verse with the rhyme. MUR.] [Note: [Col. 1032D] *Ordo*, “order.” LEIB.],

And the rich man spends for himself what the poor had for their necessities.

Different sects of the world arise throughout its regions,

Which, O Matilda, you rightly restrained as evils.

[Col. 1033A] Let the cause of your death be written, so that the world may hear it.

As your life shone, so your death gleamed with praise.

When the eighth indiction continued, and the year

Of the Virgin’s birth, which had begun to run [Note: [Col. 1033C] [Col. 1033] Attribute this leap in the numbers of the notes to the small works already prepared for the press and transferred from one place to another.] Baron., 1115. LEIB.]

Was the one-thousand-one-hundred-and-fifteenth,

Matilda wished to celebrate Christ’s Nativity

In a certain village called Bondeno [Note: [Col. 1033C] In the charters cited by Bacchinius it is called *Bundenum de Ronchoris*. It is not the place now situated in the territory of Ferrara on the Scultenna [Col. 1033D] River, but another nearer the monastery of Polirone. In a bull of Pope Lucius II preserved by Ughellus, volume V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 1607, the parish of Bondeno de Roncolis is confirmed to the bishop of Reggio. Therefore Matilda died in the diocese of Reggio, and for that reason Bonsignore, the bishop of that city, attended her at her death. In the ancient manuscript Annals of Modena, to be published in their proper place, the following is read: “In the year of the Lord 1115, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, the most noble Countess Matilda died in the Modenese county, in a place called Bondenum de Diacono, where, while lying ill, she built a church in honor of Saint James the Apostle; beside its walls she departed from this world.” MUR.].

On the eighth day, that father came from Rome,

Who shines most brightly among all in religious devotion,

Namely, Ponzo, priest and visitor of Cluny [Note: [Col. 1033D] Read *Cluniaci* with our copies. Ponzo was abbot of Cluny and therefore head of all monasteries subject or attached to the Cluniac congregation [Col. 1034C], including Polirone. Yet Ponzo abounded more in vices than virtues, to such an extent that he died under an anathema, as reported in the Benedictine Annals edited under the direction of the distinguished Mabillon. MUR.],

Received by such a great lady that the renowned abbot,

According to his custom, rose to sing the nocturnal office

To the saints, although a severe cold gripped his limbs.

Even so, Matilda herself, frail though she was, rose devoutly,

Listening attentively as he sang his words.

[Col. 1033B] Struck by the cold, she did not abandon

The extended chants that pleased her,

But immediately suffered a severe attack of illness.

She barely remained one day for the Mass of the venerable Father.

When the day dawned on which Christ was baptized in the waters,

Revealed himself to the pagans by the star,

And changed liquid water into the fragrance of Falernian wine,

The duchess, scarcely led by the hands of the aforesaid Father,

Heard Mass, although she remained ill throughout it.

Weak, she returned to her bed after the service had been celebrated.

When the abbot plainly asked her leave to depart

(The meter requires this wording),

She, trusting in his prayers, gave him

Vestments, sacred garments, silver vessels,

And a holy cross beautifully covered with gems.

O worshiper of Christ, how devoted you were!

[Col. 1033C] No little man ever left you empty-handed,

If he could be recognized as a true servant of the Lord.

When the time came in which Jesus also fasts,

She, though weak, wished to fast out of love for him.

The bishops arrived and forbade the fasts.

Instead, they ordered her to give abundant and generous banquets.

Matilda obeyed the bishops’ words,

To whom she had confessed [Note: [Col. 1034C]

The ancient manuscript has *Quis confessa fuit*. LEIB.

Our copies likewise have *confessa*. MUR.]

her debts with pure tears,

[Col. 1034A] In accordance with the law by which she deserved

To be absolved by those venerable elders.

Meanwhile, since the illness in her belly did not cease,

She, fearing what might follow, while still alive gave her possessions to the churches.

Seeking to enlarge many churches,

She did not forget the church of Canossa,

Which had always been dear to her and to her relatives.

Therefore she granted it, under legal title, Felina [Note: [Col. 1034C] A castle in the Reggio territory, among the mountains above Bismantua [Col. 1034D]. It was formerly called Felina and is still called so. MUR.],

An excellent estate yielding abundant crops.

This lady ordered all her countless servants

To be free after her life had ended.

Lying ill, for seven months she remained in the same place,

Resting before the house of the bed where she constantly

Ordered a small church to be built in honor of God

And of pious James, the son of Zebedee; it was quickly built.

[Col. 1034B] She offered it, freely, liturgical vestments

And fields for the sustenance of its table.

When the bishop consecrated it,

She heard Mass there while reclining, according to her custom.

Learn from this woman’s life and death, all you who live,

How she served Christ, living and dying.

For sixty-nine years she lived in honor,

And eight days before the end of July [Note: [Col. 1034D] Baronius, year 1115. LEIB.],

That is, before the celebrated feast day of James the son of Zebedee,

She gave up her life.

The bishop of Reggio, serene in heart,

Gave her the body of Christ and likewise the cross of the Crucified,

He who was called “Bonus Senior” by his proper name [Note: [Col. 1034D] The ancient manuscript has *Bonus-Senior*. LEIB.].

In whose hands Countess Matilda departed

From the misery of this world, forever to be remembered.

For fixing her kisses upon the cross of Christ, she said:

“I have always worshiped you; now I beg you, wipe away my sins.”

[Col. 1034C] Receiving the venerable body of Christ, she said:

“God, you know that as long as I lived I placed my hope in you.

“Now, at my end, receive me and save me, I beg you.”

Thus praying, the wise countess soon departed,

Although we believe that God also had mercy on her [Note: [Col. 1034D] Our copies read *huic quod*, “that to her.” MUR.].

Yet there is no one who does not earnestly pray [Note: [Col. 1034D]

The ancient manuscript has *sit*. LEIB.

The same manuscripts have *sit*; this is indeed how it should be written. MUR.]

That God may grant her the true joys of Paradise.

[Col. 1035A] As she was dying, she took care to love you,

Blessed Father Benedict,

And your monastery, whose body now enriches it [Note: [Col. 1035D] Namely, the Benedictine monastery of Polirone, where her body was first buried and from which it was later transferred to Rome under Pope Urban VIII. While her tomb beside the Po still remained intact, in 1613, on 22 June, as I find recorded at the time, the duke of Mantua, moved by curiosity, ordered the coffin to be broken open. The body of the noble and celebrated woman was seen there intact, with open mouth and exceedingly white teeth, none of which had fallen out. The small veil placed over her face turned to dust as soon as it was touched by hand. The ornament of her head, however, remained uncorrupted, as it can be seen in her portraits, especially above the Polirone tomb and among the patrician marquises of Canossa in Reggio. MUR.].

By your prayer, show her how to know the gates of heaven.

You, Peter, shepherd greater in number than the Twelve,

To whom he subjected the whole allotment of his own earth,

Open promptly for her the gates of the heavenly kingdom.

She built this church for you, James,

And although we hope that for this reason you will bless her,

Especially since she suffered death near your feast [Note: [Col. 1036D] Correct from our copies: “since she suffered death near your feast.” MUR.],

We ask that you hasten to her before the tribunal.

Shepherd Apollonius, do not disdain Matilda,

Although it may be unjust that she looks toward [Note: [Col. 1036D] The ancient manuscript has *respuit*, “rejects.” The author was displeased that Matilda did not order herself to be buried in the Canossan fortress. LEIB.] the tomb

That your church contains, where her fathers lie.

[Col. 1035B] Nevertheless, she greatly honored your altar,

So ask the pious king to grant her forgiveness.

Virgin Mary, Mother of God, day and night

She never ceased to hear your office.

Now make it possible for her to see you and serve you,

And, above the ether, for all of you who retain

Your dwellings in heaven,

[Source ends here.]

[Col. 1036A] She obeyed excessively on earth, moving about in this body:

“Now grant all of you a share in rest for her.

Amen.”

Here ends the poem on the death of Countess Matilda.

## CANOSSA EXHORTATION ON THE ARRIVAL OF THE EMPEROR AND EMPRESS

“Drive away fears, but not honors, white Canossa [Note: [Col. 1036D] That is, Canossa, or Canusium, a fortress founded upon gleaming white rock. Donizo writes this because, in the year 1116, Henry V descended into Italy, claimed for himself the entire inheritance of Countess Matilda, and among other possessions claimed Canossa itself. MUR.].

Until now you bore very prosperous and joyful times,

because great Matilda fashioned you over a long period,

and her nobler parents willingly

loved you greatly, and finally built you high;

but her offspring, now resting, has ceased to exist.

Cease your mourning; look to your joys. You will stand honorably;

the Caesar honors and adorns you; may you always be his.

[Col. 1036B] Do not mourn: you shall retain the summit of honor.

High-born Matilda, though dead, lives on, splendid and blessed:

she, the new mother, will bless the blessed realms and you;

such a woman is commemorated above under that name.

May all the emperor’s enemies be far away; may he himself be blessed,

and may his radiant wife live completely throughout eternity.”

[Col. 1035]

## CHARTER OF COUNTESS MATILDA CONCERNING THE GRANT OF HER POSSESSIONS TO THE ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 1035C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1102, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the tenth indiction. In the time of Lord Gregory VII, pope, in the Lateran palace, in the chapel of the Holy Cross, in the presence of Cencius Frangipane, Gratianus, Cencius Franculinus, Albericus de Petro Leone, and Benincasa, brother of Ubertus of Tuscany, and many others.

I, Matilda, by the grace of God countess, for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents, gave and offered to the Church of Saint Peter, through the intervention of Lord Pope Gregory VII, all my possessions by right of ownership—both those which I then possessed and those which I was thereafter to acquire, whether by right of succession or by any other right pertaining to me—and both those which I held on this side of the mountains [Col. 1035D] and those which seemed to pertain to me in transalpine regions. All these, as stated, I gave and handed over to the Roman Church through the hand of Lord Pope Gregory VII, and I asked that a charter concerning this be drawn up.

[Col. 1036C] But because the charter nowhere appears, and I fear that my gift and offering may be called into question, therefore I, the aforesaid Countess Matilda, again, from the present day, give and offer to that same Roman Church, through the hand of Bernard, cardinal and legate of that same Roman Church, everything that I gave at that time through the hand of Lord Gregory: all my possessions, both those which I now have and those which in the future, with God’s favor, I shall acquire; both those which I possess on this side of the mountains and those which I possess in transalpine regions; and whatever else in the future, with God’s favor, I shall acquire by any other right, for the reward and remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents.

As for these possessions of mine, which are stated above to be my right, together with their appurtenances, or with their upper and lower parts, [Col. 1036D] in their entirety, as I have bequeathed above [Note: [Col. 1036D] The customary formula of those times is *qualiter supra legitur*; thus it should be written here. MUR.], from that day I give and offer them to the same church, and by this present charter of offering, to be kept there [Note: [Col. 1036D] In such charters *habendum* is the customary formula of notaries. MUR.], I confirm them.

Moreover, by means of a knife, a knotted staff, [Col. 1037A] a *ganton* [Note: [Col. 1037C] *Guantonem*, that is, a glove. LEIB.], a *vascio* [Note: [Col. 1037C] I read *gwascionem*, *gwasionem*, that is, a sod of earth. LEIB.], and a branch of a tree [Note: [Col. 1037C] Supply: “I handed over,” or something similar. LEIB.], I expelled myself from it, *guarpivi* [Note: [Col. 1037D] *Guarpivi*, that is, “I expelled.” LEIB.], and made myself absent, and left it to be held by the part of that Church [Note: [Col. 1037D] *Habenda*, “to be held.” LEIB.], so that from the present day the part of that Church may do with it whatever it wishes [Note: [Col. 1037D] *Ad faciendum exinde pars ipsius Ecclesiae* is barbarous, meaning: “so that the part of that Church may do with it whatever it wishes.” The word *dederit* appears to be redundant. LEIB.], without any contradiction from me or from my heirs or successors.

But if—which I do not believe will happen—I, Countess Matilda, God forbid, or any of my heirs or successors, or any opposing person, should at any time attempt to proceed or bring an action against this present charter of offering, or should seek to violate it by any device whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1037D] Also. LEIB.] [Note: [Col. 1037D] Write *aut eam*; thus it appears in other charters of this kind. MUR.], then we shall pay to that party against which we have brought the lawsuit a fine consisting of one thousand pounds of the finest gold [Col. 1038A] and four thousand weights of silver; and in whatever we have sought to reclaim, we shall not be able to vindicate our claim. But this present charter of offering shall remain and persist firm for all time.

And I lifted the parchment and inkwell from the ground, handed them to the page of Guido the notary [Note: [Col. 1038C] “The page to Guido the notary.” LEIB.], and asked him to write. Having confirmed it below, I offered it to be strengthened by witnesses. Done successfully at Canossa, Matilda, by the grace of God—[the text is corrupt: “what is this in this charter made by me,” etc.].

+ I, Arderic, judge, was present, etc.

+ I, Ubaldus, judge, was present, etc.

The sign by the hand of Atto of Monte Barranzone and Bonvicinus of Canossa, witnesses summoned for the purpose.

I, Guido, notary of the palace, having written this charter of offering, completed it after its delivery and gave it, etc.

[Col. 1037]

## ON THE TREASURE SENT FROM THE CHURCH OF CANOSSA TO ROME, AND ON THE COMPENSATION MADE TO THE CHURCH OF CANOSSA

[Col. 1037B] In the year of the Lord 1082, Countess Matilda, together with Bishop Anselm, who was also the vicar of Pope Gregory VII in Lombardy in those days, requested from Abbot Gerard, who then presided over the aforementioned Church, the treasure of the Church of Canossa, to send it to the pope for the defense of the Roman Church, which at that time was undergoing a great persecution from Guibert the heresiarch.

Accordingly, the aforementioned abbot, together with the community of brothers, having faithful love and devotion toward blessed Peter and the Roman Church, gladly offered the treasure in response to the request of the vicar and the countess. It consisted of twenty-four crowns [Note: [Col. 1038C] Perhaps *coronarum*, “crowns.” LEIB.], one of them gold and likewise bearing a small gold cross; two silver altar panels; a silver covering for the altar chest of Saint [Col. 1037C] Apollonius; and a large silver censer. When melted down at Canossa, this amounted to seven hundred pounds of silver and nine pounds of gold.

Finally, after the treasure had been sent to Rome with the pope’s consent and authorization—for he had received from the aforesaid countess a charter of offering [Note: [Col. 1038C] Perhaps *oblationis*, “of offering.” LEIB.] concerning all her estates—the aforementioned vicar, who at that time also governed this bishopric by the pope’s command, at the request of the noble countess, in partial restoration of the treasure that had been taken away, placed two other chapels at Filma [Note: [Col. 1038C] The Codex Regiensis has *in Filina*. MUR.] and one at Casula under the Church of Canossa.

Later, Bishop Heribert, who devotedly loved the Roman Church in a Catholic manner, praised Bishop Anselm’s action; in praising it, he confirmed it, and consecrated the Church of Canossa. Whatever the Church possessed by its own right, he assigned to it as its endowment. At the request of the same noble countess, he also placed under that Church two other chapels, one situated in the village of Placiola and the other at Jano [Note: [Col. 1038D] The same codex has *in Fano*. MUR.], as well as the chapel situated at Gurgo, through the will and nod [Note: [Col. 1038D] The same codex has *ac nutu*, “by the nod.” MUR.] of this bishop, from the patrons of that Church.

The Church of Canossa then acquired [Note: [Col. 1038D] The same codex has *acquisivit Ecclesia*. Then follows: “in the year 1090 of this bishop,” etc.] in the year 1090. During the time of this bishop, we cleared that church at Gurgo, inside and out, of thorns and brambles.

After this, Bishop Heribert, wishing to go to Sicily for the advantage and honor of the queen’s Church—for he loved the Church of Canossa with genuine affection—borrowed a precious chasuble of blood-red purple with a beautiful gold fringe [Note: [Col. 1038D] *Aurifrigio*, “with a gold fringe.” LEIB.] and a suitable linen garment. He said that the chasuble together with the garment was worth thirty pounds. While once more strongly confirming, in his episcopal words, everything that the Church of Canossa possessed by its own right, he pledged in true faith and with a firm promise that, if he returned alive from Sicily, he would place under the Church of Canossa some of the better chapels of his bishopric; and if he should fail to return, or if he lost the chasuble and garment, he himself would arrange for one of the good [Note: [Col. 1038D] The Codex Regiensis has: “from the queen’s Church, so that the Church of Canossa might receive restoration for the garment lent to him.” Then follows another matter. MUR.] [Col. 1039A] possessions of the queen’s Church to be given, so that the Church of Canossa might receive restoration for the garment lent to him.

Finally, after the agreement between Pope Paschal and the emperor, and after the death of Countess Matilda, the Church of Canossa sent the pope five years’ census, requesting security for its churches [Note: [Col. 1039C] The same codex has “security for all its churches.” MUR.] and that liberty which the Roman Church had set down for it from the time of the first Emperor Otto—namely, that none of the bishops should ever exercise lordship over it in any matter—and asking that Gregory VII, who had received its ownership [Note: [Col. 1039C] The same codex has: “who had received it into the ownership.” MUR.] [Col. 1040A] of Saint Peter from the countess, with an annual census of twenty solidi being paid, should strengthen and protect it with his apostolic privilege.

And the most holy pope did so, subjecting by perpetual anathema and excluding from the body and blood of Christ anyone who knowingly took away by force what belonged by right to Saint Apollonius, or anyone found to have violated that privilege. The witnesses to this matter were Lord Peter, Vincentius, Pertus, John, [Note: [Col. 1040C] The same codex has: “Peter, John, and Donatus, clerics of this monastery,” etc.] and Donatus, clerics of that monastery, etc.

[Col. 1039]

## LIFE OF COUNTESS MATILDA

Written in prose by an anonymous author and first published from the manuscript of Francesco Maria Florentini by Wilhelm Gottfried Leibniz.

## HISTORY OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS COUNTESS MATILDA, AND OF THE DEEDS OF HER MOST POWERFUL ANCESTORS

Her body rests in the most worthy monastery of Saint Benedict at Padolirone, in the diocese and territory of Mantua. She died in the year 1105 of the Incarnation, on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Col. 1039B] The illustrious Countess Matilda, a woman exceedingly skilled in war, is considered distinguished among women by her outstanding deeds and by virtues surpassing those of men, while Henry IV was emperor. The history that follows, containing in summary both the origin and deeds of her ancestors and of herself, was collected from various chronicles and proceeds as follows.

## CHAPTER ONE

### On the Siege of the Fortress of Canossa and the Liberation of Queen Adelaide, Whom Berengar, King of Italy, Was Detaining

Sigifredus, a certain illustrious prince born in the region of Tuscany, in the county of Lucca, eager to enlarge the glory of his name, entered the territory of the Lombards with his sons Sigifredus, Atto, and Gerard, [Col. 1039C] conquered many cities, peoples, and fortified towns, and subjected them to himself.

When he finally died, his aforementioned sons divided their father’s property among themselves. Two of them, namely Sigifredus and Gerard, inhabited the city of Parma. But Atto, who far surpassed his brothers in strength and possessions, took the fortress of Canossa as his residence, fortified it with towers, and adorned it with walls. For by the nature of the place it was fortified on every side, truly an impregnable stronghold, situated in the diocese of Reggio.

When Berengar, king of Italy, came with his son and the Lombard army to besiege this fortress, intending to subject Atto and the castle to himself, the king and his son were killed. The Lombards then established as their king Hugh, an illustrious man of Burgundian nationality.

After Hugh’s death, his son Lothair, a prudent man, reigned. He had a wife named Adelaide, a splendid queen. When Lothair was taken from this life, a certain Berengar, a Lombard—the fourth of that name—was made king of Italy without the consent of the widowed queen Adelaide, and despite her vigorous opposition.

For this reason he was inflamed against her with such savagery and anger that he shut her, an opponent of his elevation, in prison behind the tower of Garda, allowing her only a single maidservant. After the queen had remained confined for a long time, she finally escaped from prison through the resourcefulness of her chaplain.

This man, named Martin, a faithful and shrewd person, secretly broke through the tower wall and, taking the lady away from there unnoticed with her maidservant, dressed them in men’s clothing [Col. 1040C] and led them as far as Lake Mantua. There they found a fisherman with a little boat and asked to be ferried across.

When he demanded payment for the passage, the queen’s chaplain said to him: “If you knew who we are, you would gladly carry us across without payment.”

He replied: “Then reveal to me who you are.”

When they asked him to swear that he would reveal the secret to no one, he placed two staffs on the ground in the shape of a cross and swore that he would keep the matter hidden. Then the chaplain disclosed it to him, explaining that she was the queen.

The fisherman therefore became joyful, raised his hands toward heaven, immediately took them aboard his boat, and ferried them to the opposite shore of the lake, near a forest adjoining the lake. He also offered the queen a fish, asking her that, if fortune should ever smile upon her, she remember the very poor fisherman.

They reached the island itself and hid there anxiously for a week. The chaplain secretly went around the places adjoining the forest and obtained food for the queen. After the week had passed, the queen, sighing and lamenting her condition, said to the chaplain:

“Alas! I see that I am forever a captive. What benefit is there for me in remaining here? Go, I beg you, to Adalard, bishop of Reggio. Since he has always been faithful to me, I hope that, if you tell him how great my weeping is, he may perhaps take pity on us.”

As she said this, the chaplain immediately hurried to the bishop. Privately revealing to him the queen’s misery, he begged that assistance be provided for her.

The bishop sympathized with them, but was nevertheless glad that the queen was alive. He replied to the chaplain that he possessed no town in which the queen could safely remain. He did, however, have a certain soldier named Atto, whom we mentioned above, the son of Sigifredus and his very close friend. His castle, called Canossa, was truly the safest refuge for the queen.

Accordingly, he immediately sent the chaplain to Atto. When Atto saw him and asked about the queen, he deliberately replied that she had died in prison. Then Atto, who loved the queen faithfully, was deeply grieved and shed bitter tears.

When the queen’s chaplain saw this, he immediately disclosed the truth to him. Atto therefore mounted a swift horse and went with the chaplain and servants to the queen. Finding her in the forest with her maidservant, he brought her to Canossa.

Afterward he sent a messenger concerning this affair to Pope John XII in Rome, asking that suitable advice be given him concerning it. Atto had decided to join the queen in marriage to the emperor Otto, then king of Germany.

The pope approved what Atto had done and instructed him to carry out wisely what he had proposed concerning the queen. Once Atto had learned the pontiff’s will, he gave the queen in marriage to Otto, who was coming to Verona. King Otto promised Atto great rewards for these services.

## CHAPTER TWO

### The Emperor Otto Comes to Atto’s Aid While He Is Besieged at Canossa, and Berengar Is Captured

[Col. 1041D]

While these things were happening, they remained entirely unknown to King Berengar. He certainly knew that the queen had escaped, but he did not know where she had fled or what she had done.

When he heard of King Otto’s arrival at Verona and of everything Atto had arranged with him concerning the queen, he became angry and, gnashing his teeth, gathered an army, came to Canossa, and surrounded it with a siege.

But the prudent and energetic Atto had fortified the town, already made very strong by the nature of the place, with every necessity. He therefore fearlessly encouraged his men solely to defend it.

When King Berengar attacked the besieged fortress with many weapons and engines, its lofty walls nevertheless could not be reached. Meanwhile, Atto was accustomed occasionally to descend from the high tower and speak with the more distinguished men there.

When the king learned this, he devised a plan to capture him. But a certain friend of Atto, who knew of this, secretly called him down from the tower and asked him, with his head put out through a small tower window, to listen to his words. When Atto had done so, the man told him this little tale:

“A bear,” he said, “with an empty stomach, hanging suspended in search of food, pretended to be languishing for friendship with a certain stag and sent word that the stag should come quickly to visit him.

“When the stag came, the bear clung to his ear, tore it apart, and wounded it with his claws. At last the stag escaped.

“Afterward the bear again sent for the stag, promising him great gifts if he came. The stag, unaware and having forgotten the offense, returned once more. When he approached the bear, the bear deprived him of the remaining ear, and so the deceived stag returned disfigured.

“Finally, when the bear sent for the stag a third time, saying that he wished to speak with him about important matters, the unwary stag came. The bear smiled at him, suddenly tore him apart with tooth and claw, killed him, and gave him to the fox to roast.

“When the fox had presented the roasted stag to the bear, the bear asked the fox to give him the stag’s heart. The fox replied that the stag had had no heart.

“But when the bear insisted that the stag had possessed a heart and demanded that it immediately be given to him, the fox said: ‘Since he so foolishly granted your requests for the third time, it is immediately proved that he had no heart.’”

When Atto understood why the man had told this tale, he no longer descended from the tower during the siege, preserving the useful example for himself.

When the cruel siege had continued at Canossa for three years and six months, Atto, overcome with weariness, wrote to the emperor Otto, asking him, mindful of the promise once made to him when Atto had joined him to Queen Adelaide, not to delay coming to his aid.

Otto therefore arrived with a gathered army in the territory of Verona. Crossing the Po, he prepared to fight Berengar in open battle. When Berengar heard this, he immediately withdrew from the siege.

The emperor met him at Prato Fontano. Suddenly, at the outbreak of a great clamor, battle was joined between Berengar and Otto. The fighting was fierce on both sides; nevertheless, many were slain and many died. Berengar’s army turned its back, and while the Germans pursued the fleeing Lombards, [Col. 1042D] Berengar was captured and presented to Otto. Otto kept him bound in chains and captive for the rest of his life.

## CHAPTER THREE

### On the Battle between Adalbert, King of Italy, and Lithulf, Son of the Emperor Otto

After this, Adalbert, the son of Berengar, was raised by the Lombards as king. Energetic in arms, he never wished for peace with Otto.

Atto, however, shrewd in judgment and confident in spirit, fortified the town of Canossa with all necessary supplies. King Adalbert also besieged the town.

When he had remained in the siege for thirty months, Atto, seeing King Adalbert’s mind stubbornly opposed to him, again sent to Otto, asking that, without failing to provide the aid he hoped for, either Otto himself or his son Lithulf come to the assistance of the besieged.

Otto therefore sent his son Lithulf to help him with one thousand armed men. Coming into Italy, Lithulf entered Verona. When King Adalbert heard this, he abandoned the siege and went to Bafigium.

Lithulf, leaving Verona in the evening, arrived at Batto’s field, where Atto was present. Atto received him cheerfully and said:

“A cat and a mouse are said to fare badly together in a narrow sack.”

Lithulf replied, asking him to explain the riddle.

“It is not fitting,” Atto said, “for two retinues to be together in one man.”

“Let us therefore,” said Lithulf, “take counsel about what we should do.”

Atto replied: “It is good to rest here in the countryside tonight; and, while attending to the care of our bodies, let us send someone to reconnoiter Adalbert’s army.”

This was done. When the messenger returned, he first found Atto and said:

“The enemies are so numerous that, if our men were sheep, they could be eaten by them.”

Atto then silenced the messenger, approached Lithulf, and reversed the meaning of the messenger’s words:

“The enemies are so few,” he said, “that if they were roasted two-year-old sheep, their flesh would not be enough for us.”

He therefore encouraged Lithulf to take up arms and attack Adalbert’s army.

At daybreak Lithulf, with his armed men, approached Adalbert’s army. The sentries noticed him and immediately reported to Adalbert. Astonished at this, Adalbert ordered them to investigate what was happening and to summon his men by a signal.

Meanwhile, after Mass had been heard, he was informed that the enemy numbered one thousand. King Adalbert therefore went out to battle with a few armed men. When Lithulf attacked him with the sword in the terrible clash of battle, Adalbert hurled a spear at him, pierced his breastplate, and drove it through his chest, killing him.

The Germans, deprived of their commander, were plunged into grief, trembling, and fear alike. But Atto, a man of extraordinary courage, immediately arrived. Encouraging them to renew the battle with restored strength and spirit, he fought with the utmost ferocity as their leader.

At last, although at the cost of heavy slaughter among his own men, Atto emerged victorious with them, and deprived the defeated Adalbert of his kingdom. Unable to endure the disgrace of the lost kingdom, Adalbert crossed the Ocean, or Adriatic Sea, never to return.

From that time onward the Lombards established no further king for themselves. These events took place in the year 815 of the Incarnation of the Word of God.

Atto, who had possession of Lithulf’s body, removed its entrails and buried them in the church of Saint Prosper. Then, embalming the body suitably with spices, he sent it to his father Otto. Through solemn messengers he urged Otto not to grieve over the death of his son, who had fallen while fighting bravely, but to hasten to Italy and enter the kingdom deprived of its king.

Although Otto was deeply shaken by his son’s death, after giving him an honorable burial he came to Italy with a powerful army. He was received peacefully by everyone; after the kingdom, together with all its cities and fortified towns, had been handed over to him, he went to Rome and received the imperial diadem from Pope John XII.

Afterward he enriched Atto with great gifts and honored him with the dignity of a count. Atto eventually died, leaving by a good woman named Hildegard two sons: Gotfred, bishop of Brescia, and Thedald.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### On Thedald, Son of Atto, and His Sons—Thedald, Boniface, and Conrad—and on the Death of Thedald and Conrad

After the death of his father Atto, Thedald preserved all his father’s dignity, imitated his virtues, enlarged his own lands and fortified towns, and became known and dear to princes.

Pope John, who was closely attached to him in affection, granted him the city of Ferrara [Note: [Col. 1043D] *Ferrariam*.]. He guarded the fortress of Canossa with great care.

He also built a worthy monastery beside the waters of the Po, ten miles from Mantua, which is now called Saint Benedict of Padolirone. There he established monks living under the Rule of Benedict.

He had a wife named Voilia [Note: [Col. 1044D] Guillia.], pleasing to everyone by her goodness. By her he fathered three sons: namely Thedald, who became bishop of the city of Arezzo; Boniface, an energetic soldier; and Conrad, a prudent man.

When their father Thedald was dying, he established Boniface in the honor of primacy and gave him twelve sacks filled with coins, which he kept in his chamber. He also wished his subjects, while his son Boniface was present, to swear oaths of loyalty to him.

Thedald, the brother of Boniface and bishop of Arezzo, a great devotee of holy religion, faithfully governed the bishopric entrusted to him. An example concerning him must not be omitted.

When he was once suffering from a serious bodily illness, and the physicians, despairing entirely of his recovery, said that he would not survive unless he committed adultery, his friends persuaded him to perpetrate this crime and sent for a woman.

When she arrived, he immediately ordered a fire to be lit before his bed. As it approached the bed and he already felt the heat of the flames, he suddenly burst into tears and cried out:

“Woe, woe is me! If I cannot endure this small flame, how, if I should happen to die, shall I overcome the fires of the abyss? This crime will lead me to that pit, where I shall suffer torments utterly beneath the foul fire. Therefore, far be it from me that, for the sake of temporal health, I should be deprived of eternal salvation!”

By such an example the prudent bishop warned the flock subject to him, and, with God’s approval, he deserved to regain his health. He also detested simoniacal depravity in a remarkable manner.

After Thedald died, his sons Boniface and Conrad lived together in brotherly harmony. Although many rivals tried to divide them, nevertheless the affection between them continually grew stronger.

Boniface took Richilda, daughter of Gisbert, a prince, as his wife; she lies dead without children at Nogara.

When these brothers flourished in wealth and strength, to such an extent that they inspired fear in their enemies, many men, including neighboring rulers, gathered at Caviliolo and attempted to attack and defeat them.

When Boniface and Conrad heard this, they bravely took up arms and attacked them. After a remarkable battle had been fought, the enemies were at last beaten and put to flight, and the field was filled with horrific slaughter and much blood. Thus the brothers remained victorious.

Conrad, however, was wounded in that battle. After several years, because the wound had been badly cared for, he ended his life.

His brother Thedald, the bishop of Arezzo mentioned above, carried his body to the town of Canossa and buried him with great funeral rites in the year 1030 of the Incarnation.

There too, beneath a single stone, lie together the two aforementioned bishops, Gotfred, bishop of Brescia, and Thedald, bishop of Arezzo; Hildegard, the wife of Atto; Rodulf and Conrad, the sons of Boniface; and Voilia, the wife of Thedald, the son of Atto.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### On Boniface, Father of Matilda, and How He Took Beatrice as His Wife

After his brother Conrad had died, Boniface became renowned for great virtues. Even while still a boy, he possessed great intelligence and displayed extraordinary understanding. He was tall in stature, handsome in body, prudent in conduct, vigorous in strength, and generous to all. Concerning him the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied magnificently:

[Col. 1045C] “For there shall arise a future leader whose name shall begin with B., clear in words and deeds, wealthy in possessions, peaceful in his works, and victorious in battles.”

This Boniface also had another illustrious wife, namely Beatrice from Gaul, descended from royal stock and endowed with great beauty of form and the splendor of wisdom. Her father was Federic, and her mother was Matilda.

When Boniface hurried to Gaul to be betrothed to her, he clearly displayed the honor in which he was held and the great glory in which he excelled. For, accompanied by a most solemn company of princes and nobles, among the other marks of his magnificence he ordered silver horseshoes to be attached to the feet of the horses.

If any of these happened to spring off, none of his men considered it worthwhile to pick them up; instead, they were collected throughout the fields and paths by passersby.

She gave him, as a dowry, towns and villages and male and female servants in the regions of Gaul. When he brought her back from Gaul to Lombardy, he was received by all with great applause and honor.

The wedding banquets continued for three months, at enormous expense and amid great universal rejoicing. During them, every vessel shone with silver and glittered with gold.

By Beatrice he fathered children, namely Federic and Matilda, the noble countess about whom this present history is written. But after Federic and Beatrice had been taken from this life, Matilda alone survived as the daughter and heir of her father Boniface.

Nevertheless, some hold the opinion that Henry IV, the emperor of that name, was the father of the mother of this Countess Matilda, in the following manner:

They say that Matilda’s mother, while still a maiden, fell passionately in love with a noble young man of Lucchese birth who served in the emperor’s court. When he finally learned that she was the emperor’s daughter, fearing the consequences, he went away with her and lived in hiding for a long time.

At last, when the emperor came to a certain city in whose bishopric the young man and the emperor’s daughter were hiding, the young man revealed the matter to the bishop of the city. The bishop reported it to the emperor. When pardon had been promised at the emperor’s request, he received both of them back into his favor.

The young man’s name was Boniface. By the emperor’s daughter he fathered this countess, and the emperor increased their power from the resources of the empire, granting them many possessions.

## CHAPTER SIX

### On Boniface’s Alliance with the Emperor Conrad and His Death

When Emperor Conrad II was besieging rebellious Parma, he summoned this Boniface to his assistance. Supported by his aid—for he was a man vigorous in strength and trained in arms—the emperor captured the city itself. Later the emperor bound Boniface to himself by an oath of alliance and advanced him with great honor.

Afterward, when Henry III was emperor and had gone to war against the Burgundians, the aforementioned Boniface performed memorable and magnificent deeds against the enemy in the emperor’s aid.

Among these, I must not pass over the following in silence. When Boniface had captured many Burgundians by the sword during the siege of a certain castle, he threatened to mutilate their noses and ears.

A certain noble and wealthy matron was present. She promised to give as much silver for the ransom of her son as her body weighed when placed on a balance.

Boniface shook his head and said:

“Far be it from me that enemies captured by the sword should be ransomed with silver! I want this kind of punishment to be an everlasting disgrace to your descendants.”

He therefore ordered their noses cut off and their ears severed, and had three shields loaded with them.

When the emperor Henry saw that this same Boniface was energetic in magnificent deeds, he repeatedly attempted to kill him by treachery, driven solely by envy. But with God protecting him and Boniface continually evading the ambushes, the emperor’s effort was frustrated.

Boniface was also often diligent in divine matters. He honored wise bishops [Note: [Col. 1045] That is, “wise men.” Or should one rather read *sanctos*, “holy men”? Write *sacros*, “sacred.” MUR.] and greatly loved the clergy, especially monks.

For the love of God he opened his hand to them in generosity; and, confessing his own sins to them, he undertook suitable penance.

Finally, after he had vowed to visit Christ’s tomb and had completed everything for arranging his pilgrimage, he entered the way of all flesh in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, which was the twelfth year of Henry III. He was buried at Mantua.

After him his illustrious wife, Countess Beatrice, lived fifteen years, properly governing the entire march and carefully raising her daughter Matilda, instructing her in good morals and virtues.

She founded two monasteries, namely Frassinoro and Canossa, and gave them extensive estates. At last, stricken by illness, she happily departed this life on 18 April in the year of grace 1076, while Henry IV was emperor. Her body was buried at Pisa.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### On the Fame of Countess Matilda and on the Fame and Reputation of Her Husband
Therefore Countess Matilda, after the deaths of her father Boniface [Col. 1047B] and her mother Beatrice, became widely known and renowned in many kingdoms, both for the uprightness of her character and for the illustrious lineage of her ancestors. For the princes of the Greeks, the Alemanni, the Rus’, the Saxons, the Frisians, the Auvergnats, the Basques, the Franks, the Lotharingians, and the Britons praised her highly and sent her many gifts. Among them, Alexius of the Greeks and the kings of the Alemanni sought her in marriage, as did many other distinguished dukes and princes, to whom she responded courteously, though without effect. For she was always cheerful in countenance, tranquil in mind, and beautiful in body. She knew the Teutonic, French, and Lombard languages extremely well. Among all the other nations, she cherished the Lombards with particular affection.

There is uncertainty, however, concerning the husband of this Countess Matilda. For by these words the author of this history seems to imply that the countess had no husband, since in what follows he makes no mention either of her having had one or of her having borne children. Nevertheless, it is written in the book called *The Copy of Landulf of Saint Paul* that, when a certain duke named Gottfried, son of Gottfried, had withdrawn into seclusion, he was stabbed to death with a sword, leaving behind his wife Matilda, the very illustrious daughter of Boniface and Beatrice. From this it follows that this countess married a man—namely, this Gottfried.

Some also hold that this Gottfried was Duke of Spoleto, although in the same *Copy* his duchy is not named. Martin of Opava writes in his *Chronicle* [Col. 1047D] that Gottfried, Duke of Spoleto, and Countess Matilda, the devoted daughter of Saint Peter, drove out the Normans, who, while Pope Alexander II—a Milanese by nationality—was presiding, had invaded the kingdom of Apulia to the detriment of the Church and were ravaging the borders of Campania.

James of Varagine, of the Order of Preachers and archbishop of Genoa, likewise states in his *Chronicle* that this Matilda, having been given in marriage and having borne a son by her husband, refused thereafter to be joined to her husband because of the pains she had suffered in childbirth. Thus, after her son died while she herself survived, she ultimately died childless.

It is also said that, maddened by the pains of childbirth against her husband, she pursued him and perhaps—as some assert—arranged for him to be killed by their son in the manner described above [sic]. [Col. 1048A] Consequently, by a hidden divine vengeance, she was later widowed of her husband and deprived of her son, while she herself survived. After first being harassed by many battles and the goads of adversity, as will be shown below, she died at last among her own people and, for the remedy of her soul, left what she possessed to the key-bearer of the apostles.

It is written, however, in the book called *Darius* that, after her two brothers had died—men whom she believed to have been killed through the treachery of the Emperor Henry—and seeing herself alone as the survivor, Countess Matilda, more cunning than the serpent that once deceived our first parents in the paradise of God, sought by the sharpest stratagems, rather than by arms, to deprive the emperor himself of his kingdom. She attached herself to Gregory VII, who had previously been called Hildebrand.

Although she was still a virgin, she took as her husband Gigon, a most prudent man and duke of Normandy. After living with him for a few years, she repented of having anyone exercise authority over her. Having formed a plan with a servant girl who was utterly faithful to her, she had him killed by thrusting a sword through the privy while he was seated over a latrine beside a lake.

When she was exercising almost alone the power of her retinue from Tuscany to Rome, she made a most secret pact with that same Hildebrand, then a deacon of the Roman Church, and with very many religious men scattered from the borders of Albino and Ruffino, so that they might elect him Roman pontiff without the emperor’s consent; and she worked to have him consecrated. But lest the present account seem to accuse the dead, let us proceed to what follows.

## CHAPTER VIII. The peace made by the countess between the emperor and the pope.

[Col. 1048C]

After the death of Countess Matilda’s mother, fame spread throughout the world that King Henry IV, with the consent of Hildebrand—also called Gregory VII—and in the twenty-first year of Henry’s reign, which was the year of the Lord 1077, had been separated from the bosom of holy Mother Church. The Alemannic dukes—namely Berthold, Rudolf, and Unelpho—together with many counts and bishops, had withdrawn from his association, marking him with great infamy.

When the emperor acknowledged this, he sent messengers to his illustrious cousin, Countess Matilda, asking her to seek advice about how the pope might hasten to Lombardy, and promising to make satisfaction for his offenses. Through the countess’s efforts, he was received honorably; the Emperor Henry was also present. In the presence of bishops and princes, among whom was the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny and Henry’s godfather at the baptismal font, negotiations concerning peace were undertaken.

When three days had already passed without the peace negotiations producing any result, the emperor humbly begged Abbot Hugh to stand surety for him in the cause of peace. Hugh replied that this was not permitted to him, while the countess, standing nearby, repeatedly pleaded on the emperor’s behalf.
