The abbot himself then replied to her: “You alone can accomplish this.”

The emperor therefore humbly begged his kinswoman that, through her intercession, he might deserve to receive the blessing of the Roman pontiff. She promised that she would do so and immediately went to the supreme pontiff. After addressing him humbly, she finally obtained his agreement. He trusted her words and requested that the emperor swear an oath of fidelity to him and to the Roman Church.

The emperor therefore came into the pope’s presence, walking barefoot over snow and ice. Throwing himself on the ground before the pontiff’s feet in the form of a cross, he said: “Spare me, most blessed Father, spare me.” Moved by compassion at his presence, the pope blessed him and admitted him to the kiss of peace. After Mass had been solemnly sung, he made him participate in the communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ as a sign of peace and concord, and led him to the fortress of Canossa amid extraordinary rejoicing.

Thus, through Matilda’s great prudence, the bonds of peace between the emperor and the pope were strengthened, although certain bishops opposed them and remained involved in the dispute, as what follows will make clear.

## CHAPTER IX. How the pope and the countess escaped the emperor’s ambush after his change of allegiance, and how he opposed them and their supporters.

After this, the emperor, leaving the pope in the town of Canossa, went to Reggio, which certain bishops—namely, those of Modena, Cremona, and Bologna—were ravaging because they were extremely fearful of the peace between the pope and the emperor. Their leader was Guibert, archbishop of Ravenna, a noble and shrewd man by birth a Parmese. He so thoroughly turned the emperor’s mind against the pope that, repenting of the peace settlement, the emperor conceived the plan of taking the pope captive.

On the sixth day [Col. 1049C] after he had departed from the pope, the emperor returned to Bibianello. The pope and the countess came toward him. [Note: [Col. 1049D] Perhaps *veniunt* or *properant* has been omitted.] The emperor asked to meet with them beyond the Po. They agreed; and, while the emperor had crossed, they too hastened to cross, unaware of the deception he had planned.

After they had crossed, he came to the countess and revealed what had been concealed. When the ambush had thus been exposed, the pope and the countess returned to the town, unwilling to meet the emperor again.

When the bishops mentioned above heard this, they rejoiced, and Guibert most of all. He, the author of this sedition, was striving to seize the apostolic see against Gregory. The emperor eventually praised him as pope. The rebellious bishops assembled at Brescia and elected Guibert pope, calling him Clement. Later, the emperor took him with him to Rome, had him blessed as pope, and on Holy Easter Day received from him the imperial diadem.

Countess Matilda, however, abhorring these and similar actions, always adhered to Pope Gregory. She honorably sheltered him for three months in the town of Canossa. He also consecrated the church of Canossa and made it immune by endowing it with a privilege of liberty in the year 1077 of the Incarnation of the Son of God.

After instructing the countess with salutary counsels and forming her in the divine commandments, he took leave of her and went to Rome. The Roman people went out to meet him with great rejoicing and received him as their shepherd. He absolved all who opposed the emperor from disloyalty and perjury.

When the emperor recognized this, he entered Italy with a powerful army. He traversed it, breaking castles and towns; only Countess Matilda resisted him. The emperor, burning with great anger against her, stirred up battles against her, sent terrors upon her, and threatened sieges. But since the countess had innumerable forces, she always defended herself vigorously against the emperor’s oppression.

When the emperor perceived this, he hastened to Rome. Since the city did not obey him according to his wishes, he surrounded it with a siege, ravaged it, and destroyed many of its walls. After gaining possession of the city, he installed in it, as has been said, Guibert, the antipope called Clement.

Pope Gregory, gravely offended by these events, summoned Robert Guiscard, lord of Apulia, to his aid. When the emperor heard that Robert was coming from Apulia, he withdrew from the city. But Guibert, the antipope, enticing the emperor with rewards and gifts, retained possession of the usurped apostolic throne. Having become a boundary-marker of heretical depravity, he corrupted many both in the city and throughout the world.

For, setting aside the divine commandments, he violated the sacred laws and destroyed the churches of God. He also persecuted Pope Gregory severely, afflicted many bishops and Catholic men with scourges, and tormented them in the squalor of prisons, supported by imperial favor.

## CHAPTER X. The treasure sent by the pope for the Church of Canossa at the request of Countess Matilda.

[Col. 1050C]

Meanwhile, Countess Matilda, burning with a devout heart against the emperor and Guibert the antipope and abhorring their actions, fought many battles and did all she could to support those who opposed them. For she was a faithful protector of the bishops, clerics, monks, and all Catholics.

Those whom the emperor condemned, stripped of their possessions, and sent into exile amid the turmoil of the schisms returned to her; she sustained them with kind consolation and beneficial assistance. Among them was that venerable man Anselm, bishop by birth a Milanese, who later became pope and was called Alexander II. Gregory VII, with paternal affection, commended him to instruct the countess through salutary admonitions and kindly examples.

Countess Matilda, together with this Bishop Anselm, who was then Gregory’s vicar in the regions of Lombardy, requested from Abbot Gerard of the Church of Canossa the treasure of that church, so that it might be sent to the pope for the defense of the Roman Church against the persecution of the aforementioned heretic Guibert.

The abbot readily agreed to this request, together with the flock entrusted to him, out of reverence for the apostolic see, and gladly offered the treasure: namely, twenty-four crowns, one of them gold, together with one small gold cross; two silver altar panels; a silver covering for the altar chest of Saint Apollonius; and a large silver censer. The entire treasure of Canossa amounted to seven hundred pounds of silver and nine of gold.

[Col. 1051A] After it had been sent to Rome at the countess’s request, Bishop Anselm, the pope’s vicar, provided two chapels in [lacuna] and one in the cope of the Church of Canossa, as a partial restoration of the treasure that had been taken away. These events took place in the year of the Lord 1085.

Afterward, in the year of Christ 1086, the same Pope Gregory died on the fourteenth day of May. His death was an occasion of the greatest sorrow to many. After his death, a certain Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, was elected pope; he was also called Victor and lived only a short time. He was succeeded by Odo, a Cluniac monk and bishop of Ostia, called Urban II.

Urban condemned all the actions of the emperor and of Guibert. Addressing his exhortatory letters to Countess Matilda, daughter of Saint Peter, he granted her forgiveness for her sins. [Col. 1051B]

## CHAPTER XI. The persecution directed against the countess for her support of the Church, and the siege of Mantua.

When the pope’s and the countess’s messengers were frequently traveling back and forth, the same countess stirred almost the whole Italian kingdom against itself. Many battles followed. In them, the countess’s side became famous for many victories.

At that time, many men from the cities of Italy, under a certain Oberto, took up arms and hastened to Rome; Reginus, bishop of Parma, was among them. They traversed the countess’s lands and ravaged them with great destruction.

While they were encamped in the fields of Sorbara, sleeping fearlessly one night, suddenly the countess’s soldiers fell upon them, shouting: “Blessed Peter, come to the aid of your own!” Awakened by such terror and clamor, and stunned by the sudden uproar, they scattered in every direction and turned their backs. Many of them were struck down and killed, while many others remained prisoners; among them was Eberard, bishop of Parma.

At that time Anselm, bishop of Lucca, died and was buried at Mantua. But in his *Acts* I read that, after becoming pope and being called Alexander, he rests in the Lateran church.

The Emperor Henry, now openly directing his hostility against Matilda’s supporters in his persecution of her, also took from her whatever she possessed in Gaul by maternal and paternal right, except only the castle of Brigerino, which was in truth an impregnable fortress.

After this [Col. 1051D] the emperor invaded Mantua and surrounded it with a terrible siege for eleven months. The countess repeatedly encouraged the Mantuans through her intermediaries to remain steadfast and supplied them with provisions. But when their loyalty changed, they surrendered to the emperor without the countess’s knowledge. Certain nobles of the countess who had been staying in the city to aid the Mantuans happened by chance to escape.

After conquering the city, the emperor appointed as its bishop a man named Conon, an Alemann by birth, while Bishop Ubald was driven out. The emperor also obtained nearly all the cities and towns beyond the Po, except Placentia and Nogara, which remained faithful to Countess Matilda. He also captured Minervia, which had been weakened by famine.

The countess was not therefore dismayed or cooled in her zeal for the Church. Riding through the counties of Reggio and Modena, she repaired her own fortifications.

In winter, after the town of Minervia had been captured, the emperor crossed the river Adige with only a few soldiers in his company. When the countess learned this, she immediately sent a thousand armed horsemen against him. After they had crossed the Po and the Adige, the emperor avoided them by his cunning for eight days.

He pretended that he did not wish to engage in battle. While they therefore remained fearless and suspected no ambush, the emperor’s soldiers secretly fell upon them at a place called Tres Comitatus. Many were killed, many were captured, and others finally escaped by fleeing through the byways. The author of this treachery was a certain Hugh, who had degenerated from the nobility of his own lineage.

## CHAPTER XII. The seizure of the emperor’s standard by the countess and the victory won against him.

[Col. 1052B]

When winter had passed, the emperor hastened with Alemanni and Lombards to the mountains of Modena. He captured Mount Maurellus and Mount Alfred, where Gerard, the countess’s standard-bearer, was taken prisoner; she grieved deeply over his capture.

Afterward he besieged the castle of Montebello. Since the town was supported by the countess’s aid, he could not conquer it. Then the antipope Guibert came to the emperor and promised that, if those who were besieged and exhausted in the castle recognized Guibert as Roman pope, the emperor would grant them permission to depart.

The countess did not agree to this, although certain nobles and prelates acted as intermediaries. Among them, Heribert, bishop of Reggio, seemed inclined toward a bond of peace. But a certain abbot named John, acting on the countess’s behalf, dissuaded them from making peace, asserting that such peace would be contrary to Catholic unity.

The countess was therefore encouraged to take courage and strength, trusting in the Lord. These events took place at a place called Carpinetum.

The castle of Montebello was attacked with many engines and other instruments of war. There the emperor’s son fell, not without the most grievous sorrow of his father. The emperor ordered his body to be carried to Verona and buried in a worthy tomb.

At last, seeing that the castle was impregnable, he withdrew from the siege. He came into Emilia and pretended to be heading for Parma. But, returning through Camisiano, he decided to attack the castle of Canossa, recalling what he had suffered when he had walked barefoot over snow and ice into the pope’s presence.

When he came to attack the castle of Canossa, the countess’s soldiers girded themselves for battle. In the ensuing engagement, the emperor’s standard was captured; it had been carried by the son of Marquis Adalbert. Many of the emperor’s soldiers were wounded.

The victorious men of Canossa carried the emperor’s standard into the castle, where it remains to this day. Afterward the emperor crossed the Po and withdrew. Many who had abandoned the countess out of fear of him returned to her and restored the castles.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the emperor’s son joined the countess, abandoning his father, and how she recovered Ferrara.

[Col. 1053A]

Meanwhile an ill omen befell the unhappy emperor. For his wife, Queen Praxedis, abhorring his crimes, secretly negotiated a divorce with the countess. The countess gladly embraced the proposal and sent solemn messengers to her at Verona. They brought the queen to the town of Canossa.

At the same time, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, Pope Urban came to Lombardy with the countess’s advice. After holding a council at Piacenza, in that same year on the first day of March, he condemned the emperor and the antipope Guibert by Catholic judgment. Taking leave of the countess, he then crossed into Gaul.

The emperor, dismayed by these events, summoned the citizens of Verona and besieged the castle of Nogara. When the countess heard this, she immediately summoned the men of Modena and crossed the Po. When the emperor perceived her arrival, deprived of both strength and courage, he immediately fled, leaving all his baggage in the camp. The countess abandoned it to her soldiers as plunder. Thus the castle of Nogara was freed from the siege.

The emperor was also afflicted by another hostile circumstance: domestic hostility attacked him. For his son Conrad, abhorring his crimes, withdrew from him and joined the countess. On her advice, he married the daughter of Roger, prince of Apulia.

At that time Pope Urban died, in the year of Christ 1099, and Paschal was elected in his place. When the antipope Guibert tried to attract the people to oppose him, Guibert was removed from the midst of the living, carrying his anathema away with him. For twenty-four years he had troubled the Church of God with a destructive schism. Concerning him, someone composed these verses:

> If you could perhaps be redeemed by weeping and tears,  
> You would, Guibert, be mourned with weeping and tears;  
> But no lamentations can atone for your deeds,  
> Since death could not recall you from your treachery.

At the same time, the aforementioned Conrad, the emperor, died in the month of July, in the third year after Urban’s death, and was buried at Florence.

Afterward the city of Ferrara rebelled against the countess. She besieged it with a united army drawn from the Tuscans, Lombards, and also the people of Ravenna, together with a fleet assembled from the Venetians. But when peace was interposed, it returned to her allegiance.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the countess freed Abbot Bernard from prison, and concerning Henry, the emperor’s son, who, with the countess’s support, obtained his father’s kingdom.

Meanwhile Pope Paschal sent Bernard, abbot of Vallis Ambrosia and cardinal of the Roman Church, a man worthy of the greatest veneration, into Lombardy to protect Matilda.

When she had received him honorably and the fame of his good reputation had increased among the Lombards, many of the people of Parma asked him to come to their city and root out the heretical thorns there with the sickle of God’s word. On the countess’s advice, and with a fitting company of clerics, he went to that city.

As the solemnity of the most glorious Virgin, Mother of God, approached, he entered the major church, which bears her name, to celebrate Mass. While he was there, with the entire people standing by, he preached to them after the reading of the Gospel. Some of his words seemed harsh to those who adhered to the emperor.

When he had placed wine and water in the chalice to offer sacrifice to God, a great tumult resounded in the church. Men and women alike wickedly shouted dreadful blasphemies and terrible threats against the man of God, the aforesaid abbot, condemning him to death as an enemy and rebel of the emperor.

In the midst of the tumult, the glass vessels on the altar were smashed and scattered, and the precious vestment that the devout countess had given the abbot was plundered. All the abbot’s companions [Col. 1054B] and clerics fled. He himself remained fearless, but was seized and committed to prison.

When the countess heard this, she hastened to Parma with her soldiers on the third day. She arranged for the venerable man to be freed and for everything that had been taken to be restored. She did not proceed further with vengeance for the crime, at the abbot’s request, since after the restoration of peace he had shown affection toward many.

These events took place in the year 1104 after the rising of the Son of God.

At the same time the emperor’s younger son, enraged against his father and heaping the greatest insults upon him, attempted to seize the kingdom. In a single battle against his father, he became the victor. The emperor escaped, but spent the rest of his life in sorrow; not long afterward he died, in the year of Christ 1105, and was buried at Speyer.

After his death, Pope Paschal came to Lombardy and was joyfully received by the countess. He summoned a synod beside the Po at a place called Guastalla. To Henry, the son of the deceased Emperor Henry—the fifth of that name—he sent legates, asking him to grant the pope the right to reign and promising that he would be devoted to the holy apostolic see.

The pope gladly accepted this embassy. The countess, however, praised these pious words of the father and king and extolled the pope’s reply.

At that time the people of Parma came to the pope and requested that Bernard, the abbot who had been treated disgracefully in their city, as stated above, be given to them as bishop. The pope rejoiced at their request, came to Parma with the abbot, and consecrated him bishop of that city. He also decreed that the Church of Parma belonged to the Roman see, in the year of Christ 1106. Thereafter the pope returned to Rome.

## CHAPTER XV. The peace confirmed between the emperor and the countess, and how the emperor received the imperial diadem from the pope.

After this, when Emperor Henry V was prospering in the kingdom by conquering cities and towns, he wished to make public the signs of his devotion to the Church. In the year of Christ 1110 he sent venerable bishops to the city of Rome. Through these legates, pledging himself to be a son of Saint Peter, he requested the diadem of his empire.

The pope replied that he would give him the crown if he came to Rome to receive it. The legates therefore returned and, stopping at the residence of Countess Matilda, were received by her cheerfully. After being honored with great gifts, they finally returned to the emperor.

At once the emperor gathered an army and entered Lombardy. Ravaging cities and castles, he terrified all the Lombards with his anger. When Novara persisted in rebellion, he set it on fire, destroyed its walls, and carried away a great quantity of gold and silver goods. Only the city of Milan did not obey the emperor according to his wishes.

Although the countess hated the emperor because of these invasions, he was eager to make peace with her. Nevertheless, the emperor came as far as the bank of the Taro, while the countess proceeded from Canossa to Bibianello.

At last, after much negotiation between her and the emperor, their legates confirmed a mutual peace. The countess promised to observe it, provided that fidelity to the Roman Church was maintained.

After these matters had been settled, the emperor crossed Mount Bardonis [Note: [Col. 1055D] *Bardonis*.] into Tuscany. The Tuscans, terrified by his arrival, paid him tribute. He celebrated Christmas at Florence. At Arezzo he destroyed the walls and consumed the city with fire.

Finally, arriving at Rome on the fourth day before the Ides of February, he was received by the pope, clergy, and people in a solemn procession. Entering the basilica of Saint Peter and kneeling at every step of the stairs, he was received by the pope before the altar with the kiss of peace. He promised not to sell the churches of God and not to grant investitures except with the pope’s permission.

When the pope was preparing to crown him, an enemy of peace sowed the seed of treachery and changed the emperor’s purpose and promise. For the emperor requested that the pope grant him the right to confer bishoprics and abbeys by rod and ring, just as his predecessors had until then conferred them.

When the pope refused, the emperor took him captive together with the prelates and the entire court. Among them were Bernard, bishop of Parma, and Senior, bishop of Reggio.

For these bishops and the other Lombards who were held captive, a noble and eloquent man, Arduin, the countess’s legate, addressed the emperor. Recalling the pact of peace, he secured their release.

At last the emperor came to his senses and, fearing future dangers, released the pope and the prelates. After making peace with him, he received from him the imperial blessing and the diadem of the empire. He also obtained from him the investiture by rod and ring, in the year of Christ 1111.

The emperor then returned to Lombardy and came to Bibianello, where the countess was residing. After remaining with her for three days, he finally reached Alemannia.

## CHAPTER XVI. The rebellion of Mantua and how its people surrendered to the countess.

When the same Countess Matilda had overcome dukes, princes, and counts and had subjected cities and towns that had rebelled against her, Mantua alone remained in rebellion for twenty-three years, completely despising the emperor’s edicts sent to them in the countess’s favor.

While this rebellion continued, an event arose for the countess from the city’s disorder. When the countess was staying on Mount Baruntius, seriously ill, a false report of her death spread abroad.

The Mantuans rejoiced and, spreading this report, attacked the countess’s castle of Ripalta, three miles from the city of Mantua. The castle’s guards, struck by great fear both because of the sudden attack and because of the false report that had been spread concerning the countess, surrendered the castle to the Mantuans on the condition that, if the countess were alive, it should in no way be held against her.

But the Mantuans, filled with the vice of treachery after gaining possession of the castle, decided to destroy it by fire. Meanwhile the venerable Bishop Manfred came to Mantua reporting that the countess was alive.

When the people of Mantua heard this, they gnashed their teeth in anger and scarcely restrained their hands from him; but the nobility of his lineage checked their audacity. The castle of Ripalta was nevertheless handed over to flames and ruin, and for a month afterward plunder was carried from it to Mantua.

All these events were concealed from the countess. For her loyal servants did not want to distress her, already afflicted by illness, with this damnable report.

When she had finally recovered her health and learned what harm the Mantuans had inflicted upon her, she said that the time had come for Mantua to be overthrown for its demerits. She therefore urged her people to war and hastened with an armed fleet to besiege Mantua.

While a severe siege pressed hard upon the Mantuans, they were thrown into great fear, and their defenders divided into opposing opinions. Some decided that resistance was necessary; the weaker party tried to leave the walls.

Finally, terrified and wavering amid this uncertainty, both groups humbly asked the countess for pardon. When the countess gave an unreceptive ear to their legates and looked upon them with stern eyes, her heart was nevertheless appeased by their most gentle supplications and by the most urgent prayers of her nobles.

They therefore surrendered the city to her. All swore oaths of fidelity and promised an annual tribute. These events took place at Bondeno [Note: [Col. 1056D] *Bondeni*.] in the month of October, in the year 1014 from the incarnation of the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XVII. How devoted she was to the worship of God, and concerning her glorious death.

The illustrious countess, therefore, wondrous and flourishing in virtues, was always intent upon divine worship [Col. 1056D], supporting the needy, raising up the oppressed, and honoring the servants of God with the greatest distinction.

She was also constantly devoted to holy religion, psalmody, and prayer. She enriched the churches and ministers of God magnificently with vestments and sacred vessels. She was likewise devoted to the study of the sciences, and she possessed a considerable library of the liberal arts.

For the Church of Christ she also fought many battles.

While she was staying in the district of Bondeno, wishing to celebrate Christmas there, the great father of religion, Ponzo, abbot of Cluny, came to her on the eighth day after departing from Rome. Received by her according to her custom, he sang the office on Christmas Day.

Out of reverence for God, the countess went to the office and listened devoutly. But the immense frost of the night so stiffened her limbs and afflicted her body that afterward she lay sick in bed.

When the day of the Epiphany arrived, she heard Mass again while still ill and again took to her bed. When the abbot was departing from her, the devout worshiper of God, trusting in his prayers, gave him vestments and sacred clothing, silver vessels, and also a holy cross adorned with jewels.

When the Lenten fast arrived, she, weakened by illness, attempted to fast. The bishops present objected, deciding that she should instead discharge the fast by generous almsgiving.

As her illness increased, she endeavored to enlarge the churches of God, especially that of Canossa, with landed properties, and gave it many possessions. She ordered that her innumerable servants [Col. 1057B] be free after her death.

Before the house in which she lay sick in bed, she also ordered a church to be built in honor of God under the title of the apostle James, son of Zebedee. She enriched it with vestments and lands. Bishop Reginus dedicated it while she was still alive.

When she was laboring at the point of death, the same Bishop Reginus gave her the Lord’s body and placed the cross of Christ in her hands. As she carried it and repeatedly pressed kisses upon it, she said:

“I beg you, Christ, whom I have always worshiped and always loved, to deem me worthy of cleansing the offenses of my filth.”

After this, having received the holy sacrament, namely the most reverend body of Christ, she said:

“You are my one and only hope and my singular refuge. I beg you to receive me in salvation.”

And saying this, she departed to the Lord [Col. 1057C] in the year 1115 of the Incarnation of the Divinity, on the twenty-fourth day of July, at the age of sixty-nine. This was the eighth year of the reign of Henry V, with Paschal II presiding in the apostolic see and Philip I reigning as king of the Franks.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the presumed place of her burial.

I have found no history that explicitly records the burial place of this Countess Matilda. It nevertheless seems clear that she was not buried at Canossa.

For the compiler of the aforementioned history, from whom this account is taken, in the poem in which he mourns her death asks Saint Apollonius, patron of the town of Canossa, to intercede for her before the pious king. He says that, although it would be unjust for the countess herself to have refused to possess a tomb in the church of that saint, where her ancestors also rest, she had nevertheless always worshiped him devotedly. He does not, however, state where she was buried.

Nevertheless, a mausoleum is displayed in the monastery of Saint Benedict of Padolirone in the diocese of Mantua. This monastery was founded beside the Po by a certain Tedaldus, father of Boniface and grandfather of the countess, and lies ten miles from Mantua. It is said and believed that she was buried there.

There is a large stone sarcophagus of the purest and clearest alabaster, which is preserved in great reverence because of her memory. The countess endowed the monastery itself, which her grandfather had built, with exceedingly extensive possessions and likewise enriched and adorned it with golden and silver vessels, coverings, and very costly vestments.

A little book is also kept there in the treasury, bound in silver and gold, in which this history is written in verse.

It is also recorded in the chronicles that this countess, although she possessed exceedingly extensive lands and had no son as heir, offered her entire patrimony upon the altar of Saint Peter and made the Church of God and Saint Peter her heir.

That patrimony is today called the Patrimony of Saint Peter; it extends from Radicofani to Ceprano [Note: [Col. 1057D] *Ceperanum*.].

Here ends the history of the memorable Countess Matilda.

In the year of the Lord 1445, on 9 August, which is the eve of Saint Lawrence after vespers, the body of the great and most noble Countess Matilda, of imperial lineage, was transferred. She had been the principal and singular benefactress of this monastery of Saint Benedict at Polirone, after her father, Boniface the margrave, and after her grandfather, Tedald the margrave and founder of this monastery. The body had previously stood upon eight columns at the entrance of the church, between the first and second columns, on the left side of the church, because by reason of the great [mass] those eight columns had already been broken. It was then placed farther on the left, beside the church wall, next to the tomb of Saint Simeon. The tomb was first opened to establish the truth, in the presence of the reverend lord Guido of Gonzaga, rebuild­er of the monastery, and of Lord Eusebius, abbot of the monastery, together with the convent of that monastery and many others. The body was found intact, single, and female, and was closed again in their presence. It is beside the altar of Saint Justina.

# [Works of Bernald of Constance]

[Col. 1057]

## On the Author of the Following Minor Works

(Grets­er, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 23.)

A manuscript codex of the cathedral church of Regensburg calls the author Bernalaus. I suspect that he is the man about whom Trithemius writes the following in his book *On the Illustrious Men of Germany* and in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Bernoldus, priest of the Church of Constance in Swabia, a German by birth, a devout man, diligent and learned in the Holy Scriptures, and adequately trained in the discipline of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and polished in expression, left behind some minor works of his study, which nevertheless have not come down to the notice of our reading,” and so forth. He flourished in the time of Henry IV, in 1060. Thus Trithemius.

[Col. 1059] It is of no consequence that Trithemius reads *Bernoldus*, whereas our manuscripts have *Bernaldus*, since a difference of one letter should not be considered to constitute a difference of persons—especially when the remaining features agree, as certainly they do here. Moreover, our Bernaldus or Bernoldus seems to have been Bertoldus, a priest of Constance, who composed a chronicle of events after the death of Hermann the Lame, while Henry IV governed the Roman Empire, from the year of the Lord 1054 through the end of that century, for forty-six continuous years. The editor of that chronicle himself calls him Bertoldus, though relying only on Cuspinian’s authority; and what Trithemius writes about Bernoldus, this author attributes to Bertoldus. How slight, indeed, is the difference among these three names: *Bernaldus*, *Bernoldus*, *Bertoldus*. For the form which some appear to have altered into *Bernardus* is somewhat farther removed from the true orthography, although the variation is not so great that it could not have arisen in a name composed of letters so closely related.

That this Bernaldus, or Bernoldus, was exceedingly devoted to the cause of Gregory VII—that is, to a cause consistent with the laws of divine and human justice—is clear both from the works that we are now publishing and from his chronicle, in which he always praises Gregory VII as a holy man, as he truly was, and attacks his opponents with deserved denunciations, to such an extent that it nearly stirred the bile of the heretical editor on this account.

That Bernard to whom Bernald’s first treatise is addressed—and especially two other letters of the same Bernaldus to the same Bernard, together with one letter from Bernard to Bernaldus—was no other than the man about whom Trithemius writes the following in his *Book on Illustrious Men* and in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Bernard, monk of the monastery of Saint Vitus at Corvey in Saxony, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man diligent and learned in the divine Scriptures and adequately instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in expression, skilled in verse and prose. He wrote several minor works of his intellect, by which he made his name known to posterity. To Hartwic—called Hartungus in Bertold’s *Chronicle*—archbishop of Magdeburg, he published a volume, indeed in brilliant but bitter language, against King Henry IV, but the third emperor of that name. In it, how harsh and hateful that same Henry was to the Saxons is plainly evident. He also wrote many different letters,” and so forth. He flourished in the time of the same Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1070, and composed various works. Thus Trithemius.

Before professing the monastic life, he had been master of the schools at Constance, as Bernaldus, or Bernoldus, himself testifies in his chronicle:

“In the year 1088, Bernard, master of the schools of Constance, a most learned man and exceedingly zealous in the cause of Saint Peter, entered into the Lord under the monastic profession in Saxony”—that is, in the monastery of Corvey.

Of this same Bernard Bernoldus writes in the year 1091:

“Bernard of Constance, also master of the schools, whose death we recorded above, left us many monuments of his intellect and wrote many elegant works on behalf of the Catholics against the schismatics of his time.”

And after many other passages, which we quoted above in the *Apology for Gregory VII* as the nineteenth testimony, concerning this Bernard’s excessive zeal—which advanced so far that he denied the validity of the sacraments of excommunicated persons—Bernaldus adds:

“Moreover, if anyone wishes to know these matters more fully, let him read with the greatest care the writing of a certain person addressed to this same Bernard on the same question; in it he will be taught most clearly, by testimonies of the holy Fathers, what the holy Fathers judged should be held concerning that question.”

Who is that “certain person” whose writing Bertoldus or Bernoldus cites as an antidote, if not the very author and writer of that chronicle? What is this writing, if not the first treatise *On the Sacraments of the Excommunicated*, addressed to Bernard, whom he also calls his teacher? Add to this the *Apologetic Treatise for the Decrees of Gregory VII* and the letter to Bernard, which you will find below, in which he refutes Bernard’s letter insofar as it departed from the truth. Thus no doubt remains concerning Bernaldus, who writes, or Bernard, to whom he writes.

Eisengrinius, in his *Catalogue of the Witnesses of the Truth*, brings forward another Bernard, a monk of Saint Blaise, who was engaged in the same controversy against the schismatics. He writes as follows:

“Bernard, a monk of Saint Blaise, German by birth, a man learned and especially well educated in the study of sacred letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquent in speech, a most ardent defender of the faith, the leading philosopher of his age and the most subtle teacher of sacred letters, wrote apologetic speeches against the objections of the schismatics to Adalbert, provost of Speyer. In these he principally defended the position that he and the other monks of Saint Blaise rightly abstain from excommunicated persons. A letter of the same man concerning the law of excommunication to Adalbert, provost of Strasbourg, is also in circulation. Two letters on the same matter were likewise written to a certain Recho, together with several other writings of his that will benefit the Church of God.” Thus he.

The epitome of Gesner’s *Library* adds:

“A letter to Paulina concerning the purchase of churches. A letter to a certain priest concerning the rejection of Otho, bishop of Constance, and the substitution of another in his place. *On the Office of Priests*, to the brothers at Rettenbach. A treatise to Walter the priest concerning the dissolution of oaths. To the most reverend bishop Gebhard, concerning the ordination of excommunicated persons, the salvation of little children baptized by excommunicated persons, and certain other matters pertaining to the council soon to be held. He flourished around the year of the Lord 1066.”

The same epitome testifies that this Bernard is called Bernaldus in *V. C.* And when it discusses Bernoldus, it says:

“Bernoldus, priest of the Church of Constance, wrote one book on the Roman order, and other works. He lived in the year 1060.”

Perhaps this is the Bernaldus of Saint Blaise. But it is more probable that he was not. For Eisengrinius distinguishes Bernoldus of Constance from Bernard of Saint Blaise. Nor is there anywhere any trace that Bernoldus or Bernaldus, whose writings we are now publishing, professed the monastic life. What if these men fashioned for us a monk of Saint Blaise out of our Bernard, the monk of Corvey, formerly master of the schools at Constance? For, if such a man existed, what caused him to escape Trithemius, who recognizes no Bernard of Saint Blaise, but only Bernaldus the priest and Bernard of Corvey? And why does no Bernard of Corvey appear in Eisengrinius, but only Bernard of Saint Blaise and Bernoldus the priest of Constance, even though Bernard of Corvey appears in Gesner’s epitome? But it makes little difference: one may hold that there were three different men, provided that Bernard or Bernaldus of Saint Blaise is not confused with our Bernoldus or Bernaldus.

Moreover, Adalbert, who sent two letters with Bernaldus to Bernard, master of the schools at Constance and later a monk of Corvey, seems to have been none other than the man about whom Bernaldus himself writes in his chronicle:

“Doctor Adalbert, eloquent in deed and word, crucified to the world for thirty years, and at last brought to evangelical perfection, departed to the Lord on the third day before the Nones of December”—namely, in the year of the Lord 1079.

Alboin, to whom Bernaldus writes several letters, pleased Illyricus so greatly that he placed him among the witnesses of Lutheran truth in his catalogue. Illyricus writes:

“In fragments of Aventinus I find a certain Alboin, a very learned man who lived four hundred years ago, defending the marriage of priests.”

Thus anyone who opposes chastity—or continence—and the decrees of the apostolic see suddenly becomes, in Illyricus’s school, a learned and pious man, even without learning or piety, and fit to bear witness to the truth—though Lutheran and [Col. 1061] Calvinist truth. For that Alboin was not very learned is sufficiently demonstrated by his badly written letters, which Bernaldus rightly calls poorly composed. Enough of the preface. Let us now append the list of the minor works, and afterward hear Bernaldus himself.

[Col. 1061]

## List of the Minor Works of Bernaldus, Priest of Constance

[Col. 1061A]

I. Treatise *On the Sacraments of the Excommunicated*, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers.  
II. *Apology concerning the Excommunication Pronounced by Gregory VII*.  
III. The Roman Synod under Gregory VII.  
IV. Bernaldus’s first letter to Alboin concerning the celibacy of priests.  
V. Alboin’s response to the preceding letter.  
VI. Bernaldus’s response to Alboin.  
VII. Bernaldus’s second response to Alboin.  
VIII. Alboin’s second response to Bernaldus.  
IX. Bernaldus’s third response to Alboin.  
X. Alboin’s reconciliatory letter to Bernaldus.  
XI. Bernaldus’s *Apology for the Decrees of Gregory VII Made in the Roman Synod*.  
XII. The letter of Adalbert and Bernaldus to Bernard, master of the schools at Constance, concerning the sacraments of the excommunicated.  
XIII. Bernard’s response to the preceding letter.  
XIV. Another letter of Adalbert and Bernaldus to Bernard.

[Col. 1061]

# Treatise of Bernaldus, Priest of Constance, on the Sacraments of the Excommunicated According to the Testimony of the Holy Fathers

Now published for the first time from the library of the very reverend and noble chapter of the cathedral church of Regensburg.

[Col. 1061B]

To the most religious priest and most prudent teacher Bernard, who has now entered the king’s chamber [Note: [Col. 1061C] Because he had embraced the monastic order at Corvey], Bernaldus, a priest in name alone, not in conduct, offers the assurance of the most devoted prayer and service.

Concerning the sacraments of the excommunicated, about which we wrote many things to one another long ago, over many years, although at that time we were unable to find any certainty, it pleases us at last to make known to you what our smallness has discovered through God’s mercy, and to submit it to your judgment. For we no longer fear, as once we did, undergoing the scrutiny of your examination, but desire it—we who formerly, many times, submitted our hand to your schoolmaster’s rod [Note: [Col. 1061C] Bernaldus was a pupil of Bernard, master of the schools at Constance, later a monk of Corvey; [Col. 1062C].].

The opinions of the holy Fathers concerning sacraments performed outside the Catholic Church according to Catholic custom are found to differ. Some appear entirely to annul them, whereas others, although they forbid their reception, do not altogether deny that they are performed.

For blessed Pope Leo I, writing to the Emperor Leo concerning the excommunicated Timothy of Alexandria, says:

“It is evident that through the most cruel and insane madness [severity]”—in the Alexandrian see—“all the light of the heavenly sacraments there has been extinguished. The offering of the sacrifice has been interrupted, the sanctification of the chrism has failed, and all the mysteries have withdrawn themselves from the murderous hands [of the impious].”

[Col. 1062B]

Likewise, blessed Pope Innocent, writing to all the bishops concerning ordinations outside the Church, asserts and says:

“He who has lost the honor cannot give honor; nor can he receive anything, since nothing remained in the giver that the other could receive.”

We agree, and it is true: he could not give what he did not possess. Therefore he gave the condemnation that he possessed through the laying on of hands performed perversely.

Likewise, blessed Pope Pelagius, writing to the patrician John, says:

“In schism, a bishop is not consecrated but execrated.”

Likewise, Saint Gregory I, writing concerning the ordination of Maximus, presumptuous bishop of Salona, says:

“We can in no way call that consecration which was celebrated by excommunicated persons.” [Note: [Col. 1062C] Saint Gregory the Great, Book III, Letter 20, where the words are presented as follows: “We can in no way call that consecration which was celebrated by excommunicated men.” [Col. 1063D].]

These opinions plainly seem to proscribe the sacraments of the excommunicated, since they declare that through their hands not consecration but condemnation and execration are administered.

There are, however, other statements which affirm that sacraments can be performed outside the Church. Thus blessed Pope Anastasius, writing to the Emperor Anastasius concerning the sacraments of Acacius, says at the end of his only letter:

“Therefore he”—Acacius, whose name, we say, should be left unmentioned—“harmed only himself by administering good things badly. For the inviolable sacrament that was given through him obtained in others the perfection of its power, but harmed him.” [Note: [Col. 1064D] The words “but harmed him” were supplied by the Roman edition.]

[Since this is so. Roman edition.]

Some people’s inquisitive suspicion extends so far that, after the judgment pronounced by Pope Felix, they imagine that Acacius thereafter acted ineffectively in the sacraments that he usurped; consequently [likewise, Roman edition], they fear for those who received the mysteries transmitted either in consecrations or in baptism, lest the divine gifts should appear void. They should remember that the preceding argument prevails in this respect too [in this respect also, Roman edition], because, after being condemned, he did this not without usurpation of the priesthood. Since the mysteries retain their power, the guilty person did not harm the others in this matter either.

For to him pertains [pertained, Roman edition] the saying of David’s trumpet:

“Nevertheless God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk about in their delights” (Psalm 67). [Roman edition: “in their crimes.”]

For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, as the entire authority of Scripture testifies. Likewise, through the Holy Spirit it is said in the prophet:

“He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100).

Therefore, when the condemned man claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head. The people who thirsted for his gift in the ministries [mysteries; Roman edition] were not excluded; only that soul which had sinned was, by a just judgment, liable to its own guilt.

Likewise, blessed Augustine, writing to Vincentius the Donatist, says:

“All the sacraments of the Lord belong to the Church. You possess and administer them in the same way in which they were possessed and administered even before you departed from us. Yet it is not for that reason that you do not possess them, because you are not there whence come the things that you possess.”

And shortly afterward:

“You are with us in the creed, in baptism, and in the other sacraments; but in the spirit of unity and the bond of peace, and finally in the Catholic Church itself, you are not with us.”

But although these statements differ, they are nowhere proved to depart from the truth if they are properly understood—namely, if the preceding statements are referred to the effect of baptism, which is truly asserted to be impossible outside the Church, while the latter statements are referred to the truth of the sacraments, which are believed to be present in the same integrity among the good and the wicked. It is as though the holy Fathers, with one voice, were saying to us together:

“Outside the Church, sacraments neither exist nor are performed effectively—that is, with the salvation of the soul. Nevertheless, we do not deny that they both exist and are performed uselessly, indeed perniciously.”

For if they wholly denied that these sacraments exist or are performed outside the Church, they would in no way regard the same sacraments as valid in those who had been reconciled.

For the aforementioned Pope Leo permitted the clergy of heretics to be received with their rank, although above he had asserted that all the sacraments had withdrawn themselves from the hands of the condemned.

Likewise, blessed Innocent, who had declared that the ordination of heretics was nothing but condemnation, proved that the ordinations of the Novatians were valid in accordance with the Fathers of Nicaea, since he judged that a person was not to be ordained again, but permitted him to exercise the order he had received.

Likewise, the Council of Nicaea received the clergy of the Novatians with their rank. The African Council did the same with the clergy of the Donatists, namely, that after reconciliation they might usefully exercise the rank which they had received outside the Church without effect—that is, without the salvation of the soul—and indeed perniciously.

Hence blessed Augustine, writing to Boniface concerning converted Donatist clergy, says:

“Let those be clergy in the Church; let those be usefully bishops who had been hostile against it.”

All such statements, then, which condemn consecration performed outside the Church so completely that they call it nothing but condemnation, execration, or curse, we appropriately refer not to the sacraments themselves but to their effect. Otherwise we would appear to blow away the very sacraments which the holy Fathers taught to remain intact in those who had not converted, since they did not reordain the converts but permitted them to exercise outside the Church the order they had received.

There is also the statement [Note: [Col. 1064D] Not found in the Roman edition] in which blessed Pope Pelagius, writing to the distinguished men Viator and Pancratius, says that what a schismatic confers is not the Lord’s body. This is appropriately understood to mean that for the schismatic himself it is not the Lord’s body effectively, just as, conversely, at Mass the priest prays that it may become the Lord’s body for us—namely, for the salvation of the soul.

Hence Saint Gregory also says in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 59:

“Then the victim will truly be a sacrifice to God for us, when we have made ourselves a sacrifice.”

There is indeed true flesh of Christ and true blood even for sinners and for those who receive unworthily, but in essence, not in saving efficacy.

I say that we appropriately interpret this statement as referring to the effect of the sacrament, not to the sacrament itself, lest we appear to contradict blessed Augustine. Writing to Eleusius and the grammarian Felix, he testifies that the Donatists also sacrifice both in dissension and in schism.

The same author writes to Boniface:

“Heretics seek the Holy Spirit only in the body of Christ, whose sacrament they possess outside; but they do not possess within the reality itself of which it is the sacrament, and therefore they eat and drink judgment upon themselves. For the one bread is the sacrament of unity.”

Because some of the ancient Fathers paid insufficient attention to this distinction between the sacrament and its effect, they went so far as to believe that baptism received in heresy was nothing. Blessed Augustine bears witness to this in Book VI *Against the Donatists*, chapter 1:

“For no other reason did it seem to certain distinguished bishops of Christ—among whom blessed Cyprian especially stood out—that the baptism of Christ could not exist among heretics or schismatics, except that the sacrament was not distinguished from the effect or use of the sacrament. Since its effect and use—in liberation from sins and rectitude of heart—were not found among heretics, the sacrament itself was thought not to exist there. But when it was considered that the reprobate also possess the sacraments in the Church without their effect, and nevertheless possess them, ecclesiastical pastors likewise judged that those who are outside the Church possess the same sacraments perniciously, and nevertheless possess them.”

Hence the same teacher says in Book III *Against the Donatists*, chapter 19:

“Heretics possess [hold] the sacraments and the Scriptures for appearance, not for salvation.”

Likewise, in Book IV, chapter 12:

“Neither outside nor inside can anyone who belongs to the devil’s side stain, either in himself or in another, a sacrament which belongs to Christ.”

Likewise, in Book V, chapter 19:

“God is present with his sacraments and words, by whomever they are administered; and God’s sacraments are everywhere rightly constituted, whereas wicked people, to whom they are of no benefit, are everywhere perverse—that is, both inside and outside.”

Likewise, in his letter to a certain Festus—Letter 167 to Festus—he says:

“Nor are their sacraments”—those of the heretics—“hostile to us, since they are shared by them and us, because they are not human but divine. Their own error, which they have wrongly imbibed, must be taken away—not the sacraments, which they received in the same way as we did. They carry and possess these for their punishment; the more unworthily they possess them, the more severely they are punished, but nevertheless they possess them.”

Likewise, in the exposition on the Letter of Saint John—*Tractate VII on the First Letter of John—he says:

“A wicked person can possess baptism; a wicked person can possess prophecy. We find that King Saul possessed prophecy, although he persecuted holy David; he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and began to prophesy. A wicked person can receive the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord. For concerning such persons it is said: ‘He who eats and drinks unworthily’” (1 Corinthians 11). “A wicked person can possess the name of Christ—that is, he can be called a Christian and yet be wicked. Concerning such persons it is said: ‘They profaned the name of their God’” (Ezekiel 36). “Therefore a wicked person can possess all these sacraments; but he cannot possess charity and remain wicked.”

Likewise, in his letter to the heretic Emeritus [the Donatist]—Letter 164, near the end—he says:

“You must be changed in that aspect in which you dissented, although the sacraments that you possessed, since they are the same in everyone, are holy. Therefore we wish you to be changed from your perversity, so that your schism may be rooted up anew. For the sacraments, which you have not changed but possess as before, are approved by us, lest, when we wish to correct your wickedness, we should sacrilegiously wrong the mysteries of Christ which have not been corrupted by your wickedness.”

The same author says in Book I *Against the Donatists*, chapter 13:

“Thus, when schismatics and heretics possess and administer those sacraments in no other way than the true Church, when they come to us we do not correct them but approve them.”

From these statements, then, it is most clearly declared that God’s sacraments exist even outside the Church, since they are not repeated in those who have converted but are rather judged valid. The same principle must be maintained concerning ordination and baptism received outside the Church.

For, according to Augustine, no sacrament is to be wronged. If a person departs from the wicked, both depart; if he remains among the wicked, both remain. Either the convert exercises what he previously exercised, if the usefulness of the Church requires it, or, if he does not exercise it, a hand is nevertheless not placed upon him among the laity, since he retains the sacrament of ordination.

Since, therefore, we too ought without hesitation to agree with the assertion of so distinguished a teacher—whom the Roman pontiffs, according to the testimony of Pope Caelestine, counted among the teachers while he was still alive, and whose minor works they decreed by synodal judgment should be received as authoritative after his death—we should not give such weight to the writing of the musician Wido [Note: [Col. 1065D] Wido, or Guido of Arezzo, who wrote books on music. See Baronius, vol. II, year 1022.] which you honored under the name of Pope Paschal, that we rashly blow away the sacraments usurped by heretics contrary to the assertion of the aforesaid teacher.

For he writes rather imprudently concerning the annulment of the sacraments of the Simonians, whereas Peter Damian, cardinal and bishop of Ostia, of pious memory, a man most renowned for religion and learning and exceptionally perceptive in such matters, proved in his book, which he called *Gratissimus*, that the sacraments are administered by Simonians no less than by other heretics.

The holy Roman Church likewise demonstrated that they possess at least some sacraments, since in the time of Pope Nicholas it permitted those ordained freely by Simonians to remain in the orders they had received.

When Simonians are said to possess the sacraments, this must not be understood to their honor but to their disgrace, since they are judged all the more sacrilegious the holier the thing is which they do not fear to usurp contrary to right and law.

We must pursue human wickedness only so far as not, in accordance with Augustine, to inflict a sacrilegious injury upon the divine mysteries, which human wickedness could in no way corrupt.

Nor do we dare to proscribe the sacraments of neophytes, whose ordinations the holy Fathers judged valid when they permitted them to exercise the order they had received.

Hence blessed Pope Leo I, writing to the bishops of Mauretania in Letter 87, permitted those who had been ordained from among the laity to remain in their order.

Likewise, Saint Ambrose, in the order which he received as a neophyte—perhaps, if the reading is sound, on the eighth day after baptism—worthily administered the divine sacraments to God until the end of his life (*Paulinus, Life of Saint Ambrose*).

Saint Ambrose himself would not have done this, nor would the holy Fathers elsewhere have permitted it, if they had believed that the sacrament of ordination was wholly lacking in neophytes.

Nor can we place before the authority of these men those examples concerning the annulment of such sacraments which you borrowed not from ancient but from more recent times. In those times, I say, many things are found to have been usurped contrary to right and law; they seem more fit to be rejected than taken as examples.

The Roman *Pontifical* itself [Note: [Col. 1066D] A historical book], from which you produced those examples, often records in the simple manner of a historian not what ought to be done but what was done; and it is accustomed to report not only legitimate institutions but also the inconsiderate usurpations of certain persons.

Therefore we ought not to accept everything that is read in it as ecclesiastical regulations—especially those matters which we see to depart entirely from the carefully considered opinions of the ancient Fathers. From these you produced two examples which so profane the sacraments of neophytes that they judge those ordained by them to require reordination. There is no doubt that this contradicts the apostles themselves, their Roman successors the pontiffs, and other holy Fathers.

For the apostles themselves are read to have condemned in their canons anyone discovered to have received a second laying on of hands.

Likewise, Saint Gregory I, Pope, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, in Book II, Letter 32, and his predecessors Pope Zosimus and Pope Boniface, together with the 217 holy Fathers of the Council of Carthage, condemned reordination just as they condemned rebaptism.

That those who were ordained as neophytes possess the sacrament of ordination no less than heretics was taught to us most clearly above by the most holy Fathers Pope Leo and Ambrose, the one by decree and the other by example.

Whoever, therefore, judges that neophytes who have been ordained must be ordained again undoubtedly acts against the holy Fathers.

In the same way, the reordination performed by Alfred, bishop of Hildesheim, is rejected—he reordained those whom Ebo, bishop of Reims, although condemned, had ordained.

For, according to Augustine (*On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 24), if a bishop is removed from office because of some fault, he will not lack the sacrament once imposed, although, while it remains for judgment, he can nonetheless damnably give it rather than possess it.

Thus Acacius, who had been deposed and whom we mentioned above, ordained many persons. Yet blessed Pope Anastasius, in his only letter, judged that they had received from him the complete sacrament of ordination and therefore were not to be ordained again.

Let no condemned or excommunicated person congratulate himself on the administration of the sacraments. Rather, let him recognize in this the accumulation of his condemnation, since he is so much more criminal—and therefore so much more harmful to himself—the holier he considers the thing which he does not fear to usurp by sacrilegious audacity.

Indeed, he would sin more tolerably if he refreshed his body from the altar with ordinary bread than if he killed his soul with a condemnatory communion. For, according to the Apostle:

“He who receives the Eucharist unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

A person receives unworthily if he has not yet cleansed himself from his crimes through repentance, and if canonical severity has not been able to rouse him to repent.

In ordinations, too, any condemned person would sin less if he gave nothing than if, through the sacrament of ordination, he inflicted his own condemnation upon the person ordained. And, astonishingly, while inflicting it upon another, he does not diminish it in himself at all but multiplies it.

Therefore the condemned should by no means congratulate themselves on their pernicious usurpation of the sacraments, since they condemn themselves all the more irreparably the holier are the things which they sacrilegiously presume to give or receive contrary to right and law.

Hence Saint Gregory I, Pope, in his *Register*—Book IV, Letter 5, to Gregory Venantianus, bishop of Luni [Note: [Col. 1067] See also Distinction 50, chapter 10, “Accedins”]—condemns a condemned priest who usurps his former office to perpetual excommunication, scarcely granting him viaticum at the end of his life.

Hence the holy Fathers at the Council of Antioch, chapter or canon 4, entirely denied to any condemned person who touched anything belonging to the sacred ministry every hope of restoration or any opportunity for satisfaction; and they condemned under excommunication all who communicated with him while he remained under condemnation.

If, then, those who are deprived only of office are condemned so severely for usurping the sacred ministry, how much more severely are those to be condemned who, deprived both of office and of communion, have presumed such things, being unworthy?

Let Catholics themselves also beware lest they ever receive sacraments from the condemned, lest they place themselves under the excommunication of the holy Fathers.

Above all, let them beware of the sacraments of the excommunicated, because through these, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, anyone who participates receives not salvation but condemnation and execration. Such persons will be unable to evade canonical excommunication—not merely if they participate in the sacraments, but even if they communicate with them in a kiss.

[Col. 1067]

# Apology of the Same Bernaldus, Priest of Constance, Concerning the Excommunication of Gregory VII

[Col. 1067D]

The sentence of excommunication which our lord Pope Gregory VII promulgated by apostolic authority, some presume, with sacrilegious recklessness, to judge invalid, and by doing so, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, they most dangerously make themselves guilty of opposition to apostolic authority.

But in this presumption of theirs they would neither sin themselves nor cause others to sin if they paid attention to the privilege of any prelate in the Church—not to mention the primacy of the Roman pontiff. For, according to the institution of the holy Fathers, the general privilege of such prelates is that they judge their subjects, while their subjects must not rashly resist their judgments; rather, they must obey them without contradiction, in accordance with the canons.

For it is written:

“The disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 10);

and:

“He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Romans 2).

And if the apostles said this concerning secular authority, what ought we to do who live under ecclesiastical authority, where disobedience is counted as divination [the reading is uncertain] and idolatry (1 Samuel 15)?

If, then, someone disobedient to ecclesiastical authority—that is, to divine ordinance—is rightly considered an idolater, what must be thought of one who attempts wholly to abolish that same authority?

Let every prelate consider what reverence he demands from his subjects, and let him not wish to deny it to the Roman pontiff, from whom all ecclesiastical authority proceeds.

For will he immediately judge his own authority invalid if even a few of his subjects should judge it so? Will he immediately deny his own prelacy if some of his sheep should refuse to regard him as their prelate? Will he consider his canonical excommunication of his subjects invalid if only some of those same subjects attempt to assert this, although they have obeyed him as their legitimate shepherd to that extent and have regarded his sentences against others as valid?

Will he ever permit his sentence to be retracted, much less wholly annulled, by the judgment of his subjects? Certainly not.

Therefore let him render to his own prelate, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers—and especially to the bishop of the apostolic see—the reverence which he himself demands from his subjects.

This judgment, certainly, the holy Fathers have nowhere permitted anyone to retract, much less annul. Hence blessed Pope Nicholas I, writing to all the bishops [Note: [Col. 1069D] See C. 17, q. 4, c. 30, *Nemini*, where this scholion is appended. The letter from which this chapter was taken is no longer extant; something similar, however, is found in Letter I to the emperor Michael.], says: “No one is permitted to judge the decision of the Apostolic See, nor is anyone allowed to retract its sentence,” evidently on account of the primacy of the Roman Church.

Likewise blessed Gelasius, writing to the bishops of Dardania [Note: [Col. 1069D] Blessed Gelasius I. On this, see 9, q. 3, cc. 107 and 108, *Cuncta*. It is otherwise Letter X of the Roman edition.], says: “The whole Church throughout the world knows that the holy Roman Church can release those whom the judgments of any bishops have bound, and that it has the right to judge concerning the whole Church, while no one is permitted to judge its judgment.” [Note: [Col. 1070D] “Since the See of blessed Peter the Apostle has the right to release those bound by the sentences of any bishops, inasmuch as it has the authority to judge concerning the whole Church; and so forth.” Thus the Roman edition.]

Likewise holy Pope Sylvester, by the judgment of the universal synod (chapter 20), decreed: “No one shall judge the First See. For it shall be judged neither by the emperor, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people.”

Now our blessed Pope Gregory, canonically ordained—as the holy Roman Church most faithfully testifies—was always regarded by all Catholics as the universal judge of the Church and as the Roman pontiff; and even those whom he had excommunicated judged this concerning him, since they repeatedly sought reconciliation with him, although afterward they did not fear returning to their vomit. Certainly no crime was ever discovered or proved in him, even by his enemies, that would have made the office he had undertaken unlawful. But if he had committed such a crime, could he nevertheless have been condemned unheard, without confession, and without canonical conviction, even if he had occupied the lowest rank of the ecclesiastical order? Would he [or, with the variant Nonne, “Would he not”] have lawfully exercised his office until, after canonical judgment, he was ordered to cease from it? Indeed, our lord Pope Gregory did not deny that he ought to be heard canonically, in the manner of any other cleric. This would seem unfitting for the privilege of the Roman pontiff; yet his adversaries were never willing to concede even this. For they did not doubt that in such an examination he would be cleared while they themselves would be liable for making an insulting accusation (contumeliose, “insultingly”; variant contumeliosae, “insulting”). Therefore no Christian who refuses to contradict the canonical decrees of the holy Fathers will judge invalid the sentence of apostolic authority which he pronounced against manifestly contumacious persons. For the Fathers themselves held that even the excommunication of any merely inferior Catholic bishop remained valid until canonical examination, as is read in canon 17 of the Council of Sardica.

Nor did our apostolic pontiff pronounce that excommunication privately. Rather, while presiding over a general synod, he exercised the right of binding and loosing, received in the person of Peter and perpetually possessed by the universal judgment of the Church—a right whose validity no faithful person doubts, as our most holy and faithful Fathers Cyprian, Augustine, and Leo the Great taught in their writings. Whoever, therefore, have been bound on earth by his judgment are nevertheless undoubtedly believed to have been bound in heaven also. Consequently, setting aside every objection, we too believe those whom our lord Pope Gregory excommunicated by the judgment of a universal synod to be excommunicated, lest we rightly be judged more damnable than those excommunicated persons, who, although they may be subject to excommunication for whatever reason, nevertheless do not rashly deny the Church’s bonds. For without doubt it is considered more wicked not to believe that the Church possesses the power of binding and loosing than, while preserving the faith, not to obey ecclesiastical statutes. [Col. 1071A] Hence holy Pope Gregory I, writing to the patrician Theoctista (Book IX, Letter 39), testifies: “They themselves are witnesses that they are not Christians, because they imagine that by empty [or, in the Roman edition, various] efforts they can loose the bonds of the holy Church.”

It must also be understood that the holy Fathers regarded as excommunicated not only those who, after openly displaying their contumacy, were specifically excommunicated, but also those who did not fear to incur an excommunication already imposed—namely, either by joining themselves to the party of the excommunicated or by accepting something specifically forbidden to them under excommunication. Hence, as blessed Pope Gelasius testifies, the holy Council of Nicaea condemned all the Arians, or anyone who had fallen into that plague either by agreement or by communion; and holy Mother Church has been accustomed to observe the same practice in her other excommunications. Blessed Pope Gregory I also (Book III, Letter 20) declared the consecrators of the usurper of Salonica to be excommunicated, because they had attempted to perform the very consecration specifically forbidden to them under excommunication. “For this reason,” he says, “we can in no way call it a consecration, since it was performed by excommunicated persons.”

Thus all the Roman pontiffs have regarded as excommunicated those who have presumptuously undertaken anything prohibited under a special excommunication. Therefore all such persons are rightly avoided by us as excommunicated until they have been reconciled according to ecclesiastical custom. There are four matters in which we must specifically avoid them: greeting, the kiss, prayer, and table fellowship. As Pope Callistus testifies (Letter 2), whoever communicates with excommunicated persons in these matters or in other prohibited matters will likewise be subject to excommunication, according to the institution of the apostles.

But many, “to make excuses in sins” (Ps. 140), offer various excuses for why they ought not to avoid the excommunicated. Some invoke that saying of blessed Augustine that association with the wicked does not defile anyone except those who consent; others say that they are not subject to ecclesiastical pastors or to their sanctions because they have wholly renounced the world; still others think that their obedience to their own prelate is sufficient, so that they need not obey canonical regulations (St. Augustine, passim in his books against the Donatists). Although the apostles themselves, as was stated above, have unquestionably annulled all these excuses by forbidding everyone in general, under excommunication, to associate with the excommunicated, we nevertheless shall not hesitate to demonstrate individually how frivolous they are. Those experienced in ecclesiastical regulations easily recognize this for themselves; but we wish to satisfy our simpler brothers in this matter, so that they may abstain from the excommunicated with all the greater diligence as they recognize that they are all the less able to excuse themselves if they share their communion.

Those, therefore, who invoke blessed Augustine’s statement that association with the wicked does not defile anyone except those who consent commonly add, to heighten their excuse, that they strongly disapprove of the crimes of the excommunicated and in no way agree with their crimes; consequently, they say, their external association with them does them no harm. But blessed Augustine’s statement is demonstrably taken only concerning association with wicked persons who are still within unity and have not yet been excommunicated for their wickedness, as Augustine’s own words clearly prove. Writing to the Donatists, he says:

“Whoever lives well in the Church is not prejudiced by the sins of others, because each person will bear his own burden” (Gal. 6). Likewise the Apostle says: “Whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily in it, eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11). When he says, “eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” he sufficiently shows that the judgment is not upon another but upon himself. We have done this, demonstrated it, and established it: association with the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through agreement in their deeds. For if someone does not consent to wicked deeds, the wicked person bears his own case and his own person, and does not prejudice another who has no share in the guilt through agreement in the evil deed.

Behold, blessed Augustine most clearly shows that he did not say this concerning the excommunicated, since he speaks of one who unworthily receives the Lord’s body. For earlier, speaking to the same Donatists about the excommunicated, he had said:

“Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however commendably he may think he is living, will not have life because of this one crime alone—that he is separated from Christianity—but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3).

Then he added, concerning those who remain within the Church: “But whoever is in the Church,” and the rest, as we have said above.

Likewise, in Letter 162 to Eleusius and Grammatianus [Felix Grammaticus], he says:

“Those to whom wicked persons are pleasing within unity associate with the wicked; but those to whom they are displeasing, and who cannot correct them, lest they dare to uproot the weeds before the harvest, lest they uproot the wheat along with them” (Matt. 13:29), associate not with their deeds but with Christ’s altar. Thus they are not only undefiled by them, but even deserve to be praised and proclaimed by the divine words, because, so that the name of Christ may not be blasphemed through dreadful schisms, they tolerate for the sake of the good of unity what they hate for the sake of the good of equity.

This plainly concerns wicked persons who remain within unity, not the excommunicated.

Likewise, writing to Emeritus, he says:

“This also must not be left unsaid: known wicked persons do not harm the good within the Church if either the power to exclude them from communion is lacking or some consideration for preserving peace prevents it.”

And shortly afterward:

“It is clear that a person is not made evil by the fact that someone evil approaches the Lord’s altar with him, even if that person is not unknown, provided that he is not approved and is separated from the good conscience by its disapproval.”

Likewise, in Sermon 17 on the Gospel according to Matthew, concerning the two blind men, he says:

“In many passages of the holy books it is stated most clearly that both good and wicked persons are within the Church; we often call them wheat and chaff.”

And concerning these same wicked persons—that is, those who remain within unity—he subsequently explains in the same sermon how the good are not defiled:

“In two ways the wicked person does not defile you: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him; that is, if you do not associate with him and do not consent. Association occurs when a partnership of will or approval is attached to his deed. Therefore the Apostle warns us, saying: ‘Do not associate with the unfruitful works of darkness’” (Eph. 5:11).

And below:

“Do not consent to wicked persons, so as to approve them; do not be negligent, so as not to rebuke them; do not be proud, so as to rebuke them insultingly. But whoever abandons unity violates charity; and whoever violates charity, whatever great thing he may possess, is himself nothing, according to the Apostle” (1 Cor. 13).

[Col. 1073B] Hence, in the book *On Faith and Works*:

“When, through the negligence of those set over us, or through some excusable necessity, or through secret infiltrations, we find wicked persons in the Church whom we cannot correct or restrain by ecclesiastical discipline, then—lest an impious and destructive presumption arise in our hearts, by which we think that we ought to separate ourselves from them so as not to be defiled by their sins, and thus attempt to drag behind us disciples as though they were clean and holy, separated from the structure—we should call to mind those figures from the descriptions and the divine oracles by which it has been demonstrated and declared that the wicked will remain mixed with the good in the Church until the end of the age and the time of judgment, and that they will harm nothing in the good who remain in unity and participation in the sacraments, provided that the good have not consented to their deeds.”

[Col. 1073C] Behold the wicked persons whose association blessed Augustine says does not harm us: those who remain within the Church and have not yet been separated by ecclesiastical judgment. Even if that holy teacher himself did not express this distinction so clearly everywhere, we nevertheless ought never to understand him as speaking of the excommunicated, lest we assert that he contradicted the apostles and the holy Fathers, as well as himself. For the apostles and their successors taught that association with the excommunicated is so harmful that, as we noted above, they condemned under excommunication anyone who presumed to associate with them even externally. Nor was this teaching unknown to blessed Augustine, who confirmed it by his subscription at the Council of 217 bishops. Therefore let no one uselessly invoke blessed Augustine as a witness in defense of association with the excommunicated.
