Rather, let him obey Augustine by refusing to associate with them in any way, lest he too, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, become subject to the same excommunication.

Those who think that they are excused from avoiding excommunication because, having renounced the world, they are not subject to ecclesiastical pastors or to their sanctions—monks, that is, or other religious persons—should carefully consider what the holy Council of Chalcedon decided concerning this matter. For it decreed generally that all monks in every city or region should be subject to the bishops, and it anathematized those who disobeyed ecclesiastical statutes. This is one of the four councils which St. Gregory (Book I, Letter 24) declares must be venerated like the holy four Gospels. Writing to the patriarchs concerning them, he testifies:

“For every kind of life and conduct, the rule is [or, ‘consists in’] this: whoever does not hold fast to the solidity of these councils, even if he may appear to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.”

And shortly afterward:

“Whoever presumes either to loose those whom they bind or to bind those whom they loose destroys himself, not them. Whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

Do you see how no religious status can excuse anyone from obeying ecclesiastical statutes, since every disobedient person is considered to lie outside the building, even if he is so religious that he appears to be a stone? Indeed, the very privilege of religious status subjects to greater condemnation the person who is not more obedient to his most holy mother, the Church, in proportion as he wishes to be regarded as more religious. Religious persons ought certainly to do something beyond what ecclesiastical statutes require, not rashly abolish the statutes themselves. Otherwise they will undergo a greater judgment, since they have been placed in a higher degree of holiness and nevertheless do not fear to transgress even the common commandments. It is an apostolic and universal commandment of the whole holy Church that the excommunicated be avoided. Therefore religious persons too must observe this; otherwise they will rightly be subject to a greater condemnation than even laypeople.

Nor will obedience to a prelate excuse us from the necessity of obeying apostolic statutes, if we wish to be children of the Church. Hence the attendants of Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, were anathematized with Eutyches himself at the Council of Chalcedon, because they had chosen to obey him rather than the apostolic ordinances. But the subjects of Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, were praised by the most holy Synod of Ephesus because, obeying the apostolic ordinances, they resisted their own bishop; for this reason they later deserved to be wholly emancipated from his authority.

Hence blessed Pope Eutychianus, the seventeenth martyr after blessed Peter, most truly declares in his decrees, which he consecrated by martyrdom, that a subject ought to obey neither his bishop nor his abbot if they order him to celebrate Mass for an excommunicated person.

Likewise, blessed Pope Gregory I restored Honoratus, archdeacon of the bishop of Salonica, who had been deposed by that bishop, to his position against the bishop’s wishes; and he deposed the man who had already been substituted for Honoratus, because that man had obeyed his bishop in making such a substitution, contrary to the prohibition of the Apostolic See. The same apostolic pontiff, writing to John, bishop of Corinth, deposed the clerics Paul, Eufemius [Euphemius], Thomas, and Clematius from their order because they had refused to obey by accusing their own bishop; yet he later restored Paul and Clematius to their former rank. Likewise, writing to all the bishops of the Council of Nichacium [Byzacium] [Note: [Col. 1073D] See St. Gregory, Book X, Letter 35.], he firmly commanded them to investigate their primate Clementius concerning the charges brought against him with the utmost care, so that, if the charges proved true after a hearing, he might be punished by canonical penalty. He added this terrifying warning: whoever among them neglected to investigate those charges carefully would stand before God as a participant in the same crimes.

You can find these and many other similar provisions sufficiently in the ecclesiastical statutes of the holy Fathers. They demonstrate most clearly what obedience the subjects of any prelate owe to a higher authority, and that this higher authority can condemn them if they obey their own prelate against it. Therefore let no one uselessly invoke obedience to his prelate as an excuse for not obeying the highest authority—namely, apostolic and ecclesiastical authority—in avoiding the excommunicated. Rather, both subject and prelate should strive to avoid them, lest, according to the apostles’ institution, they likewise become subject to the same excommunication.

There is also the excuse advanced in our time by certain simple people: the excommunicated have now become so numerous that they can scarcely, or not at all, be avoided. The easy answer is that the difficulty of avoiding them ought not to nourish negligence but should arouse greater caution in avoiding the excommunicated. Although they are difficult to avoid, we must not therefore regard it as no sin if we associate with them contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, which, as we know from the holy Fathers, must be defended even to the shedding of blood. We likewise regard daily sins as sins, even though we cannot avoid them entirely in this life. Remedies have therefore been provided for them—namely, prayers and almsgiving—so that what seems daily to sprout up evilly may be cut away each day. In the same way, whenever we are defiled by association with the excommunicated, we must immediately hasten to repentance and reconciliation. The difficulty of avoiding them will help us little or not at all as an excuse if it makes us more negligent in taking precautions beforehand and in making satisfaction afterward; instead, that difficulty ought to have stirred us to greater diligence in such a necessity.

Some also most foolishly excuse themselves by the death of Lord Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1075D] Bernaldus therefore wrote this apology after Gregory VII had already died.], as though they need not observe the Roman pontiff’s excommunication after his death. But let them hear that the binding of the Roman pontiff is considered no less valid than his loosing, since the Lord granted blessed Peter and his successors the authority to bind with the same force and firmness as the authority to loose. The loosing performed by any apostolic pontiff—whether in reconciling the excommunicated or restoring those who have fallen—is unquestionably valid even after the death of the one who loosed them. For will anyone who has been reconciled or restored immediately regard himself as excommunicated or deposed once his reconciler or restorer has died? I do not think so. If, then, the loosing of any Catholic pastor remains valid and must be observed after his death, the same must necessarily be judged concerning his binding: namely, that even after the death of the one who bound him, the person who has not been reconciled according to ecclesiastical custom remains equally bound.

It is worthwhile to append the opinion of blessed Cyprian, martyr and distinguished teacher, concerning those who associate with the excommunicated, so that they may recognize how dangerously they fail to guard themselves from their company. Writing to the presbyter Magnus, he says:

“We find that in such a crime not only the leaders and authors but also the participants are consigned to punishment unless they separate themselves from association with the wicked. The Lord commanded through Moses, saying: ‘Separate yourselves from the tents of these most wicked men, and do not touch anything that belongs to them, lest you perish together in their sins’” (Num. 16). And what the Lord had threatened through Moses he fulfilled, so that whoever had not separated himself from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram immediately paid the penalty for his impious association. This example demonstrates and proves that all who mix themselves with schismatics against their prelates and priests with irreligious presumption will become liable both to guilt and to punishment (Letter 76).

Let everyone, therefore—subject and prelate, secular and religious—beware of association with the excommunicated. Absolutely no one is excepted, since the apostles themselves forbid everyone to associate with such persons under penalty of excommunication. At the very least, let us fear perishing with the excommunicated if we do not take care to avoid them out of reverence for the apostolic prohibition.

Those who associate with the excommunicated must themselves also be avoided, even though their association is not so evidently prescribed for us under excommunication as is association with the excommunicated themselves. For the sacred canons repeatedly state that whoever associates with an excommunicated person is to be excommunicated. Nor is it always expressly added there that the associate of the associate is likewise to be condemned under excommunication. Indeed, many—indeed, most—things are nowhere read as forbidden to us either under a special prohibition or, still less, under excommunication, such as eating meat on Good Friday and other matters of this kind. Nevertheless, we necessarily avoid them solely because of ecclesiastical custom, lest, as Augustine says to the presbyter Casulanus, we be judged transgressors of the divine law. If, then, we avoid many things solely because of ecclesiastical custom, how much more must we avoid that which we know has been most firmly proscribed by the holy Fathers, even if not under excommunication—namely, associating with those who associate with the excommunicated.

For blessed Pope Gelasius, who also canonized the writings of other holy Fathers by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1076D] That is, he declared them authentic and distinguished them from the apocryphal.], promulgated this judgment in a letter to the bishops of Dardania:

“Let us have nothing in common with persons of external communion, especially in those matters which we know the holy Fathers forbade us.”

Likewise, later in the same letter (Letter 11):

“What benefit is it if someone does not associate with a more conspicuous heretic, yet is joined in communion with those who are not different from that heretic’s communion?”

Lest anyone despise this judgment as less binding because the penalty of excommunication is not specifically attached to it, let him carefully consider what blessed Pope Nicholas I, presiding over a general synod, decreed by the general judgment of that synod (26, q. 1, c. 18):

“But if anyone despises the teachings, commands, prohibitions, sanctions, or decrees promulgated by the prelate of the Apostolic See, let him be anathema.”

The holy Fathers did not consider it necessary to prohibit each individual forbidden matter by a separate excommunication, since they very often punished violators of all ecclesiastical institutions under a general condemnation. Ecclesiastical custom itself also strives to observe the judgment of blessed Pope Gelasius, since it ordinarily does not receive the associate of an excommunicated person unless he has been reconciled. Nothing, as St. Augustine testifies, is to be held more firmly than that in which truth supports custom.

The holy Fathers wished such associates to be avoided because they regarded them as condemned by themselves. Thus the apostolic pontiff mentioned above testifies that Acacius condemned himself when he received Peter’s communion. Hence blessed Pope Felix, in the very sentence by which he anathematized Acacius, significantly added:

“Have your portion, then, with those whom you willingly embrace”—that is, with the excommunicated.

As though he were saying: “We have not imposed a new excommunication upon you so much as confirmed the old one, since by associating with the excommunicated you have bound yourself to them.”

Nor should we carelessly overlook the reason blessed Gelasius gave so explicitly for why the Apostolic See rejected Acacius, who associated with Peter’s excommunicate:

“The See of blessed Peter removed him from its communion so that, through Acacius, it would not be led into fellowship with Peter.”

Likewise, writing to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 10), he says:

“After Acacius became one of external communion, he could not but immediately be cut off from Catholic and apostolic fellowship, lest, if we delayed even briefly because of him, we too might seem to have undergone the contagion of the faithless.”

And somewhat earlier:

“No one can receive an associate of perversity without likewise being proved perverse; nor can perversity be rejected when an accomplice of perversity has been admitted.”

Do you see how necessarily we must avoid such associates, lest we too be judged to have undergone the contagion of the faithless through their fellowship? If anyone wishes to consider all this at greater length, let him read without haste the writings of that same apostolic pontiff to various persons concerning the anathema of Acacius. If he reads them faithfully, no doubt will remain concerning the avoidance of those who associate with the excommunicated.

Let the aforementioned associates, therefore, accept sound counsel and hasten to ecclesiastical reconciliation. Let them not defile Catholic sincerity through external association, according to blessed Gelasius. But if they neglect their own salvation, let us nevertheless, since we are Catholics, guard ourselves against being defiled by them.

[Col. 1078B] **Concerning the cases of the Simoniacs.**

[Note: [Col. 1077D] The following material occurred in a manuscript codex. Since it pertains neither to what precedes nor to what follows, it has nevertheless not been omitted, so that we might faithfully reproduce all the contents of the codex.]

We do not accept the judgment of cold water, nor the testimony of those who approve the same disease, but that of religious brothers who resist the same crime with zeal and resolve. These witnesses, however, are to be obtained not through cold water but [read: or, Ed. P.] through red-hot iron or boiling water [Note: [Col. 1078D] All these ordeals are prohibited by the sacred canons, as is evident in the decretals, title “Concerning Vulgar Purgation.”].

Simoniacs are not admitted to trial if credible persons—even laypeople or women—testify that they have received payment from them. To come to trial when the facts are manifest is nothing other than tempting the Lord. Hence we are often deceived in such matters, because God is far from those who tempt him (Wis. 1).

[Col. 1078C] For many years now the extent of the Teutonic kingdom has been divided from union with the Apostolic See. In this schism so much danger has arisen that—as we say with grief—scarcely a few Catholic priests or clerics can be found across so vast an expanse of land. Since so many sons are lying in this slaughter, the necessity of Christian peace demands that the maternal compassion of the Church be opened toward them. Therefore, instructed by the examples and writings of our Fathers, who at various times received Novatians, Donatists, and other heretics into their orders, we receive into the episcopal office the bishops of that kingdom who were ordained in the schism, unless they are proved to be usurpers, Simoniacs, or criminals. We establish the same concerning clerics of whatever order whose life and learning commend them.

[Col. 1079]

**THE ROMAN SYNOD CELEBRATED UNDER GREGORY VII.**

(We gave it above among the councils held at Rome in the time of St. Gregory VII. It is fifth in order.)

[Col. 1079]

**HERE BEGINS A USEFUL DISPUTATION BETWEEN TWO PERSONS CONCERNING A CERTAIN CHAPTER, ON THE INCONTINENCE OF PRIESTS.**

**[LETTER]**

[Col. 1079A] To ALBOIN, lord and venerable priest, adorned with learning and character: BERNALDUS sends the unfailing good which is Christ.

When we were recently together and were discussing the sanctions of the canons with one another, we disagreed somewhat about a chapter of the Council of Nicaea. For, as you remember, when discourse was being held [perhaps, “being discussed”] between us concerning the prohibition of priestly incontinence—which is prohibited in the third chapter of that council to such an extent that even clerics are not to live with women unrelated to them by blood—you produced a certain other chapter from the ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite History* (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 14). It states that a certain Paphnutius rose up at [Col. 1079B] that council and obtained permission from the entire synod for priests to sleep with their wives. In addition, you rather carelessly counted this very passage among the chapters of the Council of Nicaea.

Therefore I am deeply grieved that you, a man of such promise and so learned in sacred letters, did not hesitate to attribute to this most excellent council—venerated, according to St. Gregory, as equally as the Gospel—a statement that has no place among the canonical chapters, indeed no place at all, since it contradicts apostolic and evangelical teaching. For the prince of the apostles himself, in his Epistle (1 Pet. 3), even commands laypeople to show consideration for their wives, so that their prayers may not be hindered. The chosen vessel, Paul, agrees with him, saying: “Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7).

If, then, laypeople are forbidden marital relations on the day when they wish to pray, it plainly follows that priests, whose daily duty is to pray, offer sacrifice, or baptize, ought never, from the day of their ordination onward, to have intercourse with their wives.

Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage, testifies that this continence was imposed by the apostles upon priests and Levites in the general council of 217 Fathers, which the distinguished teacher Augustine attended—the very treasury of sacred Scripture. For the aforesaid archbishop deliberates as follows [Note: [Col. 1079C] See the African Council under Pope Boniface I and Pope Celestine I, canon 37, Distinction 32, chapter 13, *Placuit*. See also Distinction 83, chapter 4, *Cum de quorundam*. There the words of this canon differ slightly, as they also do in recently published councils; the sense, however, is otherwise in agreement.]:

“It is our decision that priests and Levites, and those who serve the divine sacraments, should be continent in all things, so that they may simply obtain from God what they ask, and so that we too may observe what the apostles taught and antiquity itself preserved.”

This decree was confirmed by the legate of the Apostolic See, the venerable bishop Faustinus, and unanimously by all the bishops with their subscriptions.

Likewise, Truth itself affirms in the Gospel:

“Amen, I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

The righteousness of the ancients was that priests, during the year of their service, while they were still celebrating not true sacrifices but only shadowy ones, entirely avoided returning not only to their wives but even to their houses. Whoever among modern priests strives not merely to surpass but at least to imitate this righteousness of the ancients will never return to marital relations after his ordination, since no day passes on which he ought not to devote himself to priestly service.

Furthermore, the holy and venerable Synod of Nicaea, to which you assigned the aforesaid chapter, entirely forbids clerics in its third chapter even to cohabit with women, except those closely related to them by blood. Your chapter, however, does not even prohibit intercourse. Therefore whoever agrees with your chapter disagrees with the aforesaid council. For this reason he has also been condemned by the anathema with which St. Gregory, in his synodal letter, condemned all who disagreed with the Synod of Nicaea.

But if you perhaps deny that the same synod prohibited clerics from living with women, investigate the ancient and authentic copies, which contain the council there confirmed in twenty chapters by the subscriptions of 318 Fathers. You will also read that the same number of chapters was transmitted by the most holy bishops Cyril, [Col. 1081A] Alexander [Alexandrian], and Atticus of Constantinople to the aforesaid bishop Aurelius and the other bishops of Africa. The *Tripartite History* itself, which you seem excessively to venerate, testifies that twenty chapters were established at the aforesaid synod. In these copies, I say, if you will deign to read them, you will find that the aforesaid council, in its third chapter, forbids clerics not only intercourse but also, in every respect, cohabitation with women.

Moreover, Pope Siricius in his decretals (Decretals 3 and 4 at the Council of Arles), Blessed Jerome in his letter to Oceanus, Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History* [Note: [Col. 1081D] Ruffinus understands this as an appendix to Eusebius.], and also Saint Gregory, writing to the defender of Rome (Book VII, Letter 39), together with many others, approve that the aforesaid chapter was enacted at the Council of Nicaea. Therefore your chapter, since it is utterly contrary to these authorities, will in no way escape the Gregorian anathema. For that apostolic teacher himself (Book VII, Letter 112) caused everything contrary to the canons to be condemned under anathema at a general synod, writing thus to Syagrius, bishop of Autun:

> “Everything,” he says, “that is contrary to the holy canons, as we have said, must be strictly condemned with the imposition of anathema; that is, no one should presume to give any advantage in order to obtain ecclesiastical orders, or to receive one for advantages given; nor should anyone suddenly proceed from lay dress to attain a place of sacred governance. Nor should other women live with priests, except those whom the sacred canons permit.”

But perhaps, in defending your position, you assert that the Council of Nicaea, according to the testimony of the great Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, and of Pope Mark, also consisted of seventy chapters. Of these, since we have only twenty in use, you try to number your chapter among the others customarily used by you—but in vain. I neither wish nor am able to deny the testimony of the holy Fathers concerning the seventy chapters; nevertheless, by God’s mercy, I shall never be so foolish as to suspect that those venerable 318 Fathers established anything contrary either to themselves or to apostolic teaching. Rather, I do not doubt that they condemned everything opposed to their own judgments or to those of the apostles.

For who of sound mind would establish that two things should be observed simultaneously when observance of one would prohibit observance of the other? If, according to your chapter, priests may licitly sleep every night with their wives, how will the rule that they must not live in the same house be observed? Clearly, if they lie in one bed, how will they not remain in one house?

Nor will I pass over what you think especially supports your position: namely, what is read in Saint Gregory’s letter, that he did not compel the deacons of Sicily to continence—those, I mean, whom a new prohibition found married to wives three years earlier.

[Note: In the margin of the manuscript these words have been added: “Note that in more corrected copies it is read not ‘deacons’ but ‘subdeacons’ [Col. 1082D], and this is the reading that should be adopted. For the same is found in Book I, Letter 42, to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily.”]

Did Saint Gregory nevertheless grant anywhere in that same letter that the aforesaid deacons might exercise their office if they refused to remain continent according to your chapter? Certainly not. For he knew that even laymen are not permitted to receive the divine sacraments unless they have first practiced continence for three days. David himself, whom the Lord chose according to his heart, would not have received the showbread until, questioned by the priest, he had replied that he had kept himself continent for three days (Leviticus 21). How, then, could incontinent deacons have been permitted to exercise their ministry, when, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, they ought, together with the priests, to be continually—and indeed daily—ready to celebrate, receive, or at least handle the divine sacraments?

Moreover, the same apostolic teacher, writing to Leo, bishop of Catania (Book III, Letter 34), also testifies that his predecessor had established this concerning subdeacons: those who were married at that time were to choose one of two alternatives—either to abstain from their wives or certainly not to presume to minister at all. Pay close attention also to the fact that Saint Gregory required continence from the deacons of Sicily only for a time. For in that very letter he decreed that thereafter no bishop should presume to ordain a deacon unless he had promised to live chastely, and that none of the aforesaid deacons should advance to sacred orders if, after the prohibition made three years earlier, he had not remained continent from his wife.

Therefore it is clear that this same apostolic teacher did not compel only the subdeacons of that time and place to continence, although he established that thereafter continence was to be required by profession from all who wished to become deacons. Let your charity consider with me how greatly this opposes your position. Your chapter permits everyone, even bishops, to engage frequently in marital relations, whereas Saint Gregory tolerated this only temporarily in certain deacons, and not without penalty, for he entirely removed from them the hope of promotion.

You grant priests, indeed bishops, the very incontinence on account of which that teacher shut off from deacons the hope of a higher rank. Thus, according to your chapter, bishops sleeping with their wives will renounce the chastity that he commanded to be required by profession from all who thereafter wished to become deacons! Since, therefore, Saint Gregory is so opposed to your chapter even in this matter—where he relaxed the rigor of the canons to no small degree, and where he merely connived at certain things as tolerable at that time—it is evident even to fools how greatly your position is attacked, indeed condemned, by the general statutes of that same Father. Those statutes he promulgated, in accordance with the strictness of the canons, as rules to be observed not merely for a time but forever thereafter; among them, as I said, he prohibited priests, under imposition of anathema, from living with women.

[Col. 1083A] But perhaps, so that your position may seem to receive at least some support, you also contend that in our own time the incontinence of deacons, as in the case mentioned above, should be tolerated. But this is in vain. It would follow that marriage within the fourth degree should also now be tolerated—a concession that the same apostolic teacher (Book XII, Response to Augustine’s sixth question) declares he made temporarily to the newly converted English.

If either of these things were tolerable at the present time, then the marriage in question—which is at least once read as having been licitly permitted—would more properly be endured now than the incontinence of deacons, which is nowhere said to have been permitted, but is recorded as having scarcely been tolerated in a few cases and for a time, and not without subsequent punishment, as I have said. Therefore, since such a marriage is now in no way to be tolerated in anyone, however weak in continence, much less is the incontinence of deacons anywhere to be endured at this time.

From these arguments, then, you yourself may gather what judgment you ought to form concerning the priestly dignity. But I shall not linger any longer in seeking arguments, since any one of those mentioned above is sufficiently certain to destroy your chapter. That chapter was not taken from any book canonized by the holy Fathers, but from the Tripartite History. Although this work is quite useful to us for learning about past events, it will never make me believe anything in it that I find opposed to sacred Scripture, to the statutes of the holy Fathers, or indeed to the Holy Spirit, their author.

Blessed Pope Gelasius—an exceptionally diligent investigator of the Scriptures—examined in his decrees, together with seventy highly learned bishops, the books of various Greek and Latin authors, and carefully deliberated which of them should be received and which rejected. Yet he nowhere counted that History, composed long ago by three Greeks, among the Scriptures to be received. Rather, he showed that it should be rejected in this matter of your chapter, since it is wholly contrary, as we have said, to the decrees of the holy Fathers, which must be received with reverence.

[Note: Decree on the Apocryphal Scriptures; *Decretal Letters*, Roman edition, vol. I, pp. 416 ff., and in Gratian.]

But perhaps you argue that the aforesaid History must be believed in every respect because Cassiodorus, formerly a senator and later a monk, a man exceedingly learned in both divine and human letters, arranged it. Yet the person of this man, however venerable, cannot invalidate the canonical institutions of the holy Fathers. As I have said, we cannot observe those institutions if, out of reverence for him, we fulfill your chapter.

Nor should you be surprised that his History must be rejected in certain matters, since the History of Eusebius—which Saint Jerome, or rather Rufinus, translated from Greek into Latin—barely obtains from the decrees of Pope Gelasius the privilege of not being wholly rejected, although much useful material is found in it. Holy men have not only translated many things useful for our instruction but have also written works from their own knowledge; and later they themselves judged some of those things worthy of rejection.

Saint Augustine gives us a sufficiently clear testimony to this in his book of *Retractions*, where he himself judged that not a few passages from nearly every book he had composed should be rejected. This gift is so particularly characteristic of the wise that they do not wish to defend in their own books, much less in those of others, anything they find contrary to Catholic truth.

Augustine likewise, writing to Saint Jerome (Letter 9), testifies that he reads Jerome’s writings, and those of any saints, in such a way that he nevertheless refuses to accept anything he finds contrary to manifest truth.

With this consideration, therefore, Cassiodorus’ History should be read.

[Note: See Cassiodorus’ preface to the *Tripartite History*.]

He did not compose it wholly from his own person, but arranged a work composed long ago by three relatively obscure Greeks, assigning to each of the three his own contribution. Hence what is objectionable in that History should be attributed not so much to Cassiodorus as to its authors. Or perhaps Epiphanius, some sort of scholar, when translating it from Greek into Latin, did not faithfully commit to Latin letters what he had found written in Greek, though it had appeared probable.

[Note: Epiphanius translated it faithfully. The authors of the story of Paphnutius are Sozomen, Book I, chapter 22, and Socrates, Book I, chapter 8—two of the three authors from whose accounts the *Tripartite History* was compiled.]

Whether, however, the same History is found to oppose canonical truth to a considerable degree for this reason or for any other, I think must be left to your judgment.

Since, then, your aforesaid chapter—deprived of every authority—has been proved with absolute certainty to oppose the decrees of the holy Fathers, the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures, and indeed the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration all these things were undoubtedly brought forth, what else remains except that anyone who thereafter attempts to defend it against the canonical decrees should be struck with the Gregorian anathema?

Therefore let your fraternity cease henceforth to number it among the most sacred chapters of the Council of Nicaea, or even to regard it as having any importance. Otherwise, if you receive it as authentic, you will be judged, as has been said, to oppose the Holy Spirit—a sin which, it is certain, will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12).

## An Insulting Reply to the Preceding Chapter

[Note: Concerning what sort of man Alboin was, we have spoken above, in the preface to these little works. He was evidently inflamed by the same spirit as the sectarians of our own day, although he seems to have changed his mind, as appears from the final letter and from the beginning of Bernald’s *Apology* for the decrees of Gregory VII. On this entire controversy, see Bellarmine, *On Clerics*, especially chapter 20, where he methodically refutes the story of Paphnutius.]

[Col. 1083]

[Col. 1083D] Alboin to Bernald—against the preceding book—who lends at interest an upper millstone without a lower one [perhaps: who turns an upper millstone without a lower one].

[Col. 1084D] It is not possible for the ambidextrous Aod (Judges 3) to be unexpectedly struck down among the yawning, while I can scarcely make my way between the thorny diverging paths of you, a novice charging with your horn—indeed, among the thousandfold shapes of Proteus, when one must snatch him with a swift hand. The pressure of various affairs, alas, grants you neither place nor time to answer even briefly at your pleasure.

On one side, a certain long-established obligation of our fellow brothers presses upon me, requiring prayer; on the other, the preparations of our senior for setting out on campaign demand attention. In his company, like a donkey of perverse disposition, although driven by a thousand goads, I have barely escaped—an admission I whisper in your ear at no great risk to myself. Amid all this, lest I seem to disdainfully pass over your words, I wish to make the effort to answer you at least in part.

As I understand from your letters that you have alleged, I do not at all admit that I have rebelled in any respect against canonical institutions or decrees. But I am not ashamed to confess—and I do not now refuse to confess, wishing to have it confirmed and strengthened by every assent—that what has not yet been prohibited by law should not at the first approach be prohibited or punished with the severity of law, but should rather be nourished as a little child with milk rather than solid food.

This is undoubtedly what Gregory the Theologian intends. The same is also proved by Paphnutius himself—though one-eyed, seeing God—who, whether you wish it or not, both accommodate themselves to our weaknesses. For regarding practices assumed before consecration, which, as I think, your canon 3 does not yet prohibit so severely—your canon to which you cling beyond measure with an urbane face and obstinate mind, as though it had been canonized—the matter may be understood either as acting more cautiously on account of certain weak men who had been bound by marriage before the synod, since that matter was then considered not so great a crime as it is now, or on account of certain heretics who anathematized lawful marriages.

The former acted more mercifully concerning what had been canonically handed down but not canonically prohibited; the latter acted more cautiously concerning those already bound by marriage. Each approach, like a paired double—seeing inward and outward, before and behind—is not without reason.

Are you not also ashamed, my brother, to have defended your controversy on the ground that Saint Gregory’s suspension of the Sicilian deacons from office was a kind of punishment, when it is clear that he credited those same men with a worthy reward for living chastely with their wives after the prohibition made three years earlier? Once you have properly proved this point of yours, you will be a great Apollo to me.

What connection or reason is there for us, after so many centuries, to reject the *Tripartite History*, which, because of Eusebius’ writings, was scarcely approved as authentic by Gelasius, yet was not rejected either by Gelasius himself or by any learned man, and was affirmed by the probable testimony of three witnesses, both secular and ecclesiastical? Nonsense! Either you think you have told a story to a deaf man, or you are seeking a knot in a reed.

What more? If you continue to address us and our fellow brothers—many of whom are far better than either you or I—in such perplexing terms, I shall place my finger over my mouth, lest I be accused of going further than is fitting for a priest.

For the rest, compelled by your own provocation, I shall attack you with plain words, so that you may see what it means not to fear exposing the nakedness of Father Noah. Since it is certain that, according to your own sect, you yourself were begotten from that same sin, by what reason or in what manner do you yourself wish to condemn sin in another?

Take care that I address you according to Solomon:

> Youth, exalted too high before its time,  
> should be drawn back lest it fall disastrously,  
> its foot being withdrawn from above.

## Irrefutable Rejection of the Preceding Controversies and Proscription of the Aforesaid Chapter

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085C] Bernald to Lord Alboin the priest—not fraudulently attacked like Ishbosheth (2 Samuel 4), but faithfully warned against the treachery of Hushai the Archite (2 Samuel 17)—also ready to offer charity even to one who reproaches him, and to be blessed by him who not only wished to curse but also wished to become sin for us.

I am greatly astonished at your fraternity, that you replied to me with so disturbed a mind, since you had found nothing in my letter that, if there was anything in yours worthy of offense for any reason, I would not have shown myself willing and unashamed—especially toward so learned and friendly a man—to yield, if you had demonstrated that I had deviated from the truth even to some degree rationally.

But God is witness to my conscience that my arguments have in no way departed from the footsteps of the holy Fathers; indeed, they should be judged to belong not so much to me as to them. Therefore you seem to have been moved against me without cause, since my letter merely set before you, in a spirit of charity, the judgments of the holy Fathers—judgments that condemned not your chapter, but rather, I know not whose, Sozomen’s.

You ought, I think, to have offered thanks rather than become indignant, because I warned you as a friend to beware of anathema, lest, if you received Sozomen’s chapter (*Tripartite History*, Book II, chapter 14), you should place yourself under the Gregorian anathema. For that apostolic teacher—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit—caused all who dissented from the Council of Nicaea, and everything contrary to the sacred canons, to be condemned under anathema at a general synod.

The aforesaid chapter of Sozomen, and all who receive it, are opposed to the most sacred canon that Blessed Pope Siricius, Saint Gregory, Blessed Jerome, and countless other saints prove to have been established at that most eminent council, which is to be venerated equally with the Gospel. Let your charity therefore consider under what dangerous anathema all who attempt to support Sozomen’s chapter are punished. I took care to warn your fraternity diligently of this danger, intending not to offend you but rather to appease you if you had been offended.

But alas! The matter, as I think, has turned out otherwise. For your letter—if indeed it was yours—so badly shaped indicates that you rejected a friendly warning and replied with insults; yet it does not in any way prove that I wrote anything to you worthy of insult.

For this reason I have not yet thought it credible that you, my friend, so learned in sacred Scripture, ever wrote me such a letter—one that blasphemed me, although it had convicted me by no argument, and yet did not even assist your own position in any way. I would show clearly how deserving it was of attack if I had not received it as having been sent by such a friend.

For who cannot see how negligently it serves your will, with its obscure circumlocutions, since it not only does nothing to assist your intention but entirely attacks it? It indicates that you in no way rejected the decrees of the holy Fathers. Therefore, since Truth says, “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12; Luke 11), it has proved that you accepted those decrees and, through them, condemned Sozomen’s chapter.

Moreover, it confirms at length that a matter not yet prohibited by law should be punished with the severity of law, whereas it would have suited your position better if it had said that, in matters not yet prohibited by law, not the severity of law but leniency should be exercised. Even this would not have attacked your position so greatly, although it could contribute nothing to it, since the matter in which the aforesaid chapter attempts not merely to mitigate the law but wholly to annul it is recorded as having been prohibited under anathema by lawful authority in a general synod more than two hundred years ago.

[Col. 1087D] The same letter also praises Saint Paphnutius to me, as though, under the authority of so great a man, it could persuade me of something contrary to truth—but in vain. I too gladly praise him, and readily believe that he bore the marks of Jesus in his body. Yet I shall never be so foolish as, out of reverence for his person, to accept something contrary to sacred Scripture, indeed to the Holy Spirit, as has been irrefutably proved concerning Sozomen’s chapter.

Regarding Blessed Paphnutius, long since dead, I would rather believe that Sozomen invented the story than presume to suspect that he uttered such blasphemy to the detriment of the confessor’s holiness. For it is quite common in books that have never been canonized that, when their authors wish to make their fables—unbelievable to everyone—at least seem plausible, they attribute them to persons of unquestioned holiness, so that their fables may be accepted under the authority of those persons’ sanctity. But in vain. The less we doubt the holiness of such persons, the more we believe that the fables attributed to them, when contrary to canonical institutions, are false.

I pass over the conjectures of the same letter, in which it cautiously asks on what occasion the aforesaid chapter was fabricated. It makes no difference to me to discover why it was written, since it has been proved with certainty that it is contrary to sacred Scripture.

You will be able to gather from the writings of Blessed Gregory how far that letter departs from the truth concerning the deacons of Sicily. Anyone who carefully considers both those writings and the writings of Blessed Gregory will judge that I have in no way departed from them in my arguments. Such a person will not say that I claimed Saint Gregory punished the incontinence of the Sicilian deacons by suspending them from office, rather than by withholding advancement to a higher rank. Nor will he say that Saint Gregory granted those same deacons permission to minister at the altar if they did not remain continent.

He will also be able to see that Saint Gregory declared the continent deacons of Sicily worthy of praise for their continence, not for living with women.

As for what your later letter invents concerning the *Tripartite History*, it too seems not to have explained itself. I considered nothing in that History worthy of rejection except that I did not presume to receive what had been anathematized by the holy Fathers. The letter does not subsequently prove by any argument that I said something objectionable against the order of priests; it merely asserts this verbally. Nor does it even prove, against you, to whom I wrote specifically, that I said anything deserving rejection or your offense.

Did it really offend you or them with good reason if I faithfully gathered not my own arguments but those of the Fathers, which destroyed and condemned Sozomen’s chapter under anathema, and warned you as a friend to beware of that anathema? What did I do against you that was worthy of blasphemy if I asserted that the testimony of the holy Fathers—Jerome, Gregory, Siricius, and the others—concerning the chapters of the Council of Nicaea ought to be believed rather than the History of some Sozomen or other?

But why should I continue further with the circumlocutions of that letter, which has now tried to defend Sozomen’s chapter by insults, since it could not defend it by argument? I would have shown easily that those insults harmed not me but rebounded upon the head of the author himself, if I had not omitted them out of reverence for such a friend.

I always desire to have Father Noah before me. Since his shame has long since been abolished through repentance, I neither wish nor am able to expose it. For whoever testifies that it remained after repentance is judged not a Christian but a Novatian, since the Lord himself says through the prophet Ezekiel: “The wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness” (Ezekiel 33).

I have exposed, not the shame of Noah, but that of Nicolaus, Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, and other such fathers, all of whom unanimously agreed with the anathematized chapter of Sozomen. Nicolaus, designated in the Apocalypse as a heresiarch, even granted his fellow deacons wives held in common (Revelation 2). Paul of Samosata, lest he himself be accused by his clergy of intimacy with women, is said in the ecclesiastical History to have granted them cohabitation with women (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 25, translated by Rufinus).

For this reason they were condemned, among their other heresies, to eternal anathema for this very usurpation. Their shame, I say, must be exposed by you and by all who possess zeal for God, lest you incur the guilt of fraternal death if the ignorant perish through their most pernicious deception—men who, through their obstinate defense, have made the shame of others their own.

Furthermore, that letter blasphemes by calling Catholic truth a sect. In favor of the Pelagian heresy, it imputes to a baptized son the sin of his father, although that sin had long since been destroyed in the father himself through repentance. How impious, heretical, and detestable this is, I could easily demonstrate if I did not judge that, out of regard for your charity, it should rather be passed over than aired publicly.

For the Holy Spirit himself testifies through the prophet Ezekiel: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18). Under a dreadful warning he also forbids anyone to teach that the teeth of sons should be set on edge by the bitter grape eaten by their fathers (ibid.).

I, too, do not disdain to say with him whom the Lord chose according to his heart: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50). Yet, by God’s mercy, I shall never attack myself so far as to doubt, with Pelagius and against the Catholic faith, the full remission of sins in baptism. Certainly, whoever attempts to blaspheme another excessively is proved, by that very blasphemy, to attack the Catholic faith.

That letter also assisted your position very little when, against the Lord’s command, it blasphemously called me “sin.” It proved—not you alone but everyone who receives Sozomen’s chapter—to be truly a slave of sin, not indeed voluntarily but compelled by the divine will. According to the Gospel, whoever sins is a slave of sin (2 Peter 2; Romans 6).

Since that letter, by agreeing with the statutes of the holy Fathers, anathematizes those who receive Sozomen’s chapter, it teaches that they are bound by mortal sin; therefore it also confirms that they are truly slaves of sin.

Do you see, then, how little that letter honored those men, since it called me “sin,” though falsely, and showed that they were truly slaves of sin, while wishing to treat me as their master?

Moreover, if I did not pass over the matter out of charity toward you, I would know how to utter against those who embrace Sozomen’s chapter not names that I invented, but names imposed upon them in antiquity. In uttering those names, I would not, because of a lie, kill my own soul and earn a place in the lake of burning fire; rather, I would clearly prove that those men—already anathematized under those names and later destined for eternal fire unless they repent—deserve to be handed over to it.

I do not, however, wish to become excessively angry with that letter. I understand that, to the dishonor of its own author rather than of me, it falsely called me “sin” on behalf of Truth itself, which, according to the Apostle, was made sin even for the ungodly (Galatians 3).

For Truth itself says to us in the Gospel: “Blessed are you when men curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely for my sake,” and so forth (Matthew 5). Therefore I too do not wish to blaspheme that letter, as it deserves, by speaking what is true.

I know how terribly the Apostle Jude imposes silence on blasphemers, asserting that even the archangel Michael did not dare to blaspheme when disputing with the devil. The chosen vessel also testifies that the abusive shall not possess the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6). David likewise, speaking in his own person, presents a sufficiently terrifying condition to all:

> “If I have repaid those who returned evil to me,” he says, “may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Psalm 7),

and other things of this kind.

If such punishment is owed even to one who repays evil with evil after having received good, what judgment will be rendered against one who is convicted of returning evil to his brother when that brother deserved nothing but good?

The same letter therefore confronts me in vain with Solomon’s saying that a young man seeking things too lofty should be restrained. This should be said not to me but to those who, trampling upon the commands of the Holy Spirit himself, consider themselves lofty while following the empty—or rather fabricated—traditions of men.

Let your fraternity therefore see how little, or rather how completely not at all, that letter provided for your honor. It attacked your position, as has been proved, and, what is worse, indicated that you had falsely blasphemed your friends—men who had deserved nothing from you but good—in opposition to the priestly office. Yet according to the Lord’s command, one must not curse even an enemy (Matthew 5).

Therefore I charitably admonish you never again, to the detriment of your religious standing and learning, to send anyone such a cursing and unrestrained letter. Otherwise, if someone who gladly wishes to quarrel and cares little for your honor should examine it, he will turn all its blasphemies back upon you yourself.

## Another Insulting Reply to the Preceding Chapter

[Col. 1091]

[Col. 1091A] Alboin to Bernald, alas, swelling into so many heads of a Hydra, declaring that he is in no way endangered by the blind, horned venom of the cerastes.

If I had not long ago submitted my neck to Christ’s gentle yoke and desired to breathe again under the testament of peace, I would not have failed to return a fitting retaliation for your abusive reply. But at the present time, reason herself acting as guide, this is plainly forbidden me—reason, I say, lest I return evil for evil (Romans 12).

As is perfectly clear from your letter, I could more easily have cleared myself in a few words from the charge that I, having torn Pallas’ robe, was the first to stir up injuries, if any concern had been shown. Yet it is clearer than daylight to anyone reading the letter, even though badly composed, that nothing abusive was said.

What have I done wrong, or what have I deserved, if, after you had supposedly warned me faithfully, I in turn took care to warn you about something? But, to make myself safer from this accusation before others—not before you—and to safeguard my honor, I shall draw back for a moment and bring the beginnings of our dispute into the middle.

When, in your more careful—or perhaps more exact—writings, and with testimonies of the saints heaped up, you indirectly indicated, as though faithfully warning me, that I had deviated from the canonical rule, I could not easily discover what thanks or good deed you had deserved. For what is it to warn a friend without cause except to scatter upon him still more the stain of infamy?

For where neither a matter nor an action requiring warning is present, where the who, what, when, and to whom—in short, every circumstance—is absent, what can warning someone without these things accomplish except what the poet says:

> “Everything superfluous flows from a full breast”?

It is clear to anyone who wishes to know that, in accepting Sozomen’s chapter, a matter still under judgment, I have never deviated from sound doctrine, for two reasons.

First, I see nothing recited, written, or translated in that chapter—though it is presented in a definite place and time and by approved persons—that is not authentic and probable.

Second, if one applies an interpretation better than the merely probable one, I do not, under its pretext, dogmatize anything perverse. I therefore have no need of your warning, nor do I fall under the Gregorian anathema.

For neither you nor anyone of sound countenance can, with truth preserved, confess openly that anyone ever heard me, under pretext of this chapter, grant priests their own wives together with the Nicolaitans or the Paulianists. I admit without shame only that, because of the great compassion of the great Paphnutius, I have accepted something as Gregorian.

For this reason I do not fear being reproached either by you or by anyone else: just as Saint Gregory was displeased that the Sicilian deacons should be violently and disorderly separated from wives whom they had not been forbidden to have at that time, fearing a worse outcome, so Paphnutius, abhorring the occasion of fornication, opposed priests’ intercourse with wives lawfully taken before consecration.

In the same way, I, a little man, consenting in this respect with such holy men, could find the prohibition of our own time altogether too severe and not blessed in every respect. For example, what has never been acquired is much more easily denied than what, once accepted, can be taken away, if you please.

If for this reason I must fall under anathema, I am very glad that Gregory and Paphnutius will share the case with me. But I fear that the man who, lacking discernment, resists such great men may be the one more deserving of anathema; and that an even worse anathema may overtake the man who, against the decrees of the same Gregory, Pope Eleutherus, Anacletus, Pontianus, and Eusebius, approves of priests being harassed, accused, restrained, despised, scorned, and expelled from churches by laymen without synodal judgment.

Whoever diligently strives to heal a sick person should first carefully touch the surrounding members before touching the wound itself. If he handles the wound incautiously at the first approach, the sick man protests in every way. [Col. 1092C] With this intention Moses himself, Christ’s secretary [perhaps *secretarius*], in order to restrain worse things, commands that a bill of divorce be brought. For this reason also righteous Lot, so to speak, wishing to avoid a worse evil, was willing to surrender his own daughters to the Sodomites for abuse (Gen. XVIII). Did not the supreme Pontiff himself, who penetrated the heavens, declare that not everyone can receive this word of chastity (Matt. XIX), that new wine should not be poured into old wineskins (Matt. IX), and, moreover, that inexperienced disciples should not fast while the Bridegroom was with them (Mark II; Matt. IX)? Does he not mercifully condescend to sympathize with our weaknesses? Does not Paul, the vessel of election, who was caught up to paradise as far as the third heaven (II Cor. XII), seek to urge us toward compassion, reminding us that we are human beings, [Col. 1092D] just as he himself was? Indeed, like Paphnutius, he permitted each person to have his own wife, not only for the begetting of children but also to avoid fornication (I Cor. VII). Therefore the passage from Sozomenus, so often discussed by us, does not at all seem so rashly to deserve anathema; for, as Saint Augustine says in his *Speculum*, whatever in the divine Scriptures appears in any way probable must not readily be prejudged by anyone. Thus far.

But if I possess good sense not for every day, but for alternate days, must I be subject to anathema? Far from it! The supreme Physician himself neither deprived sinners of his table (Matt. IX), nor kept the sinful woman from touching his feet (Luke VII). When he saw that the chief of the publicans desired to behold his face, he did not at all deprive him of his presence, indeed not even of his companionship (Luke XIX). But, I believe, you object that they repented. Yet I ask: whence do you believe that the impulse of repentance fell into their minds? Certainly the Son of Man, who descended from heaven, persuaded Zacchaeus by a hidden inspiration to climb the tree. So even now, unless he who draws all things to himself draws us, miserable as we are, by the hidden prompting of his grace, there is no doubt that the authority of our pope falters, while the right hand of the Most High confesses that the Lamb feeds with the wolf (Isa. XI). Therefore it would be more fitting for every pious person to pray for the weak than, in these evil days, to lay upon them the yoke of so many persecutors. Since the nations began, none of those who came before us has seen so grievous a time. Setting aside all divine laws, they devour us at will, like a morsel of bread (Ps. XIII). Pope Siricius did not impose the penalty of expulsion on account of incontinence, nor did he withdraw the people’s communion; he merely postponed advancement to the higher order. [Col. 1093C] Let your curiosity recall without delay how discreetly and mercifully, mediating between present and future matters, Pope Leo—most learned in both Greek and Latin letters—deals with this affair. What need is there for words? No sorrow is like ours.

I should like you, my brother, to notice that Gregory and Siricius seem to me to disagree with one another somewhat in this matter. Gregory does not deny advancement to deacons on account of the stain of a former fault if they wished thereafter to remain continent, whereas Siricius, since he did not approve of compelling deacons to chastity after a period except by a determination of mind, nevertheless, as you agree with me, compelled them before ordination to make that same determination at the proper time, and prohibited bishops from promoting them unless they remained continent. Thus there is almost no difference between his opinion and that of Paphnutius, so that they converge into one. The former deals with practices unlawfully undertaken after ordination; the latter with those undertaken before consecration. The former concerns sexual relations; the latter, so to speak, sleeping together. Yet for this reason neither of them, as it seems to me, appears in any respect to resist the canonical decrees: where knowledge of sin has not yet been inculcated by law, persuasive admonition rather than legal severity should be employed; either an unjust practice should be prohibited at the proper time, or, if this is culpably neglected, the prophet is drawn out of the pit with cords wrapped in cloths (Jer. XXXVIII).

[Col. 1094A] What more is there to say? Truly, if Paphnutius, as you judge with foreign understanding or argue of your own accord, were generally granting all priests permission to marry, he would not have taken such particular and evident pains to discuss practices undertaken before consecration. Moreover, if he had perceived that the matter opposed sound doctrine in any respect, Cassiodorus, a man of blessed memory and of great conduct and prudence, would never have labored so dutifully to translate that very passage from Greek into Latin. Do you think that, if someone dared, as you say, to conceal his heresy under the persona of Paphnutius by means of theatrical art, Cassiodorus, so outstanding a man, would have taken care to favor him by translating it? Surely not, because all his work everywhere throughout the churches bears the mark of authenticity and praise. Since we accept many writings lacking an author in the Old Testament, such as Tobit, and in the New Testament, such as the Apocalypse, lacking a translator, why should we not value this one all the more, approved by both?

Furthermore, since I know that Jerome, our own panegyrist [perhaps *panegyricum*], after so much has been cut away in accordance with the law—namely, the hair and nails of the foreign woman (Deut. XXI), that is, the superfluous passages of Scripture opposed to sound faith—nevertheless at times refuses to renounce the apocryphal books, with what face would I dare to regard the aforesaid passage, so authentic, more precious than gold and topaz (Ps. CXVIII), and so pleasing in these times, as worthless? Not at all; for that would be contrary to right and justice. In that passage, moreover, the same matter is treated concerning bishops as concerning the other orders; hence you seem to mutter so summarily, as though you were surprised that in this respect they are placed on an equal footing. For the bishop consecrates chrism with the presbyters, the presbyter consecrates the Lord’s body with the bishops, the deacon arranges the ministries upon the altar, and first offers the chalice to them, communicating equally. What distinction can I find Paphnutius making among them?

All these things ought to be impressed upon not you but some foolish salt-cellar with such elaboration. Enough of this. O sea of Neptune! O sacred things! What a crime! That I should be rebuked to my face so mercilessly; that I should moreover be thrust into the mill, although I faithfully warned you not to carry a rope for yourself to the cross. Although with God there is no partiality, and although there is complete remission of original sin in baptism, and although it is impious for me to murmur, I nevertheless bury it in a pit: procreation does not proceed in every respect legitimately without legitimate marriages. But as to how this is so, test it upon yourself; for I desire that such a matter be concealed on account of my fellow priests. Yet, lest I seem to defraud you entirely, take care that you are not at least caught in one thing. For whatever applies to the part applies also to the whole.

I would have kept silent about your having written back to me that my letters were badly turned, had I not been distressed that, for some reason, you so disgracefully dishonored me in the presence of my fellow countrymen. Therefore, although in those letters, as in these, I was more intent upon the intention of the meaning itself than upon the propriety of its pompous arrangement, nevertheless, if they had returned to my hands not universally condemned but marked point by point, I would have returned them to you, as far as possible, defended or corrected. Otherwise, by giving you my right hand, I would be accommodating your caviling. O charming intellect! How elegantly you hesitated, as though concerned for my honor, asking whether they were mine—thereby adding to my disgrace. Bah! What a clever plan: to draw your friend back into the precipice in this way! If I had confronted you on equal terms, I would have compelled you in large measure to agree with me that your letters deserved to be marked with charcoal, if I perceived them to lack, God forbid, a thesis, distinction, subdistinction, middle clause or period, colon and comma, unless, faced with such enormous disgrace over their poor construction, I had been too stunned to speak, my brow wrinkled in astonishment. For if you had avoided the *macrologia*—the prolixity that you so often [Note: The passage appears corrupt.] [that you so often practice]—in your letters, you would not have struck me in the face like a corpse. Enough.

# REVISION OF THE PRECEDING LETTER, AND THE IRREFUTABLE ANATHEMATIZATION OF THE OFT-DISCUSSED PASSAGE

[Col. 1095]

[Col. 1095B] To Lord Alboin, who plants a grove unsuitably in the temple of the Lord, Bernard: not fabulous leaves of words, but statements founded upon unquestionable truth.

After receiving the letter sent to me by your fraternity, I wished to find in it something that might soften my spirit, rightly stirred by the insult of your earlier letter, and might at least somehow cleanse you, under some appearance of defense, from such pernicious blasphemy. But alas! I could find nothing of the sort in that same letter. On the contrary, it says, adding to the heap of the earlier insult, that my letters are accursed, without offering any argument, and merely declares that I provoked the earlier insults and that you said nothing insulting to me, without proving this by even the slightest reasoning. How far this declaration of theirs deviates from the truth will be evident even to an uneducated person who carefully examines both our letters.

For my first letter, which I sent to you concerning this dispute of ours, faithfully and amicably warned you only, through the testimonies of the holy Fathers, to beware of anathema. You yourself could not find in it anything that your letter could prove worthy of giving me any offense. I am ashamed to recount how many blasphemies—how dishonorable and pernicious—you wrote back to me in response to this goodwill, since they stink so badly that it would be improper to inflict such things even upon an enemy.

My second letter, directed to you against those same blasphemies, did not repay you like for like by cursing you. It merely attempted, as a friend, to restrain you from blasphemies that were most destructive not to me but to yourself. For I certainly know that Paul himself, the vessel of election through whom Christ himself speaks, handed blasphemers over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I). It is therefore sufficiently clear who was the origin, indeed the summit, of this insult, and how unjustly your letters call mine accursed, when mine wished to recall you from the abyss of abuse through a charitable admonition.

It is not now necessary for me to refute individually—not, I say, the arguments but the assertions of this letter, which I have already unquestionably annulled in my earlier letters. In those letters I proved by the clearest arguments that my admonition was reasonable and friendly, while your reply was pernicious to you and insulting to me; and in this letter you have not destroyed even the last of those arguments.

Since these matters have thus been irrefutably proved, I would rightly refuse to answer you for a final time, were I not resolved on this occasion also to accommodate your charity, so that in this letter too I may not shrink from faithfully pointing out to you what disgraces your learning and your religion.

[Col. 1096C] First, then, I want you to know that the circumstances of rhetoricians do not apply to our affair. From these circumstances orators construct their conjectures, caring not so much for truth as for probability. Our case, however, is judged to belong rather to a thesis than to a hypothesis; it must not be handled by the plausible persuasion of orators but by the irrefutable demonstration of philosophers. You therefore say in your letter that Sozomenus’s passage seems authentic to you because it was recited, written down, and translated in a definite place and time by approved persons. But you are mistaken in this inference. Are the *Categories* of the principal doctor Augustine, or his work *On the Election of Jacob and the Reprobation of Esau* [Col. 1096D] with Paul’s examples [Note: Something appears to be missing.], received by any sound-minded person as authentic? Yet they are undoubtedly recorded in a definite place and time, from a most approved person. No one in his right mind would number the *Categories* among authentic works, while the same doctor did not blush to repudiate the other work in his book *Retractions*. These and similar examples, I say, destroy the inference mentioned above. Therefore, since you had not proved Sozomenus’s passage authentic, you could not thereby prove that, by accepting it, you had deviated from sound doctrine in nothing.

It seems most absurd that you deny having taught anything perverse under that same passage, since my earlier letter already proved that very passage to be perverse with irrefutable force, as it is opposed to the evangelical and apostolic writings and to the decrees of the holy Fathers. You therefore protest in vain that no one has ever heard you grant wives to priests. Both I and many others have often heard you grant this, since even now you do not fear to proclaim the same passage not only true but also authentic. For the passage itself asserts that Saint Paphnutius rose in the Council of Nicaea and obtained permission for priests to sleep with their wives. [Col. 1097B] Whoever therefore proclaims that this passage must be received and observed not only as true but also as authentic cannot possibly deny that he grants wives to priests.

You also add in vain on what occasion you received it as authentic, since you have in no way proved it authentic after leaving it under inevitable anathema. For it makes no difference on what occasion you receive it as authentic, when it is still unquestionably forbidden under anathema that it be received in that way. Whoever receives it in any manner as authentic will always remain under the same anathema. Blessed Paphnutius, moreover, must not be dishonored by this blasphemy; rather, the blame belongs to Sozomenus, to whom Cassiodorus assigned that passage. However many words you use to reconcile things that contradict one another, I shall never become so foolish as to think that Sozomenus agreed with blessed Gregory in the passage mentioned above. Sozomenus invents the claim that at the Council of Nicaea conjugal intercourse was not forbidden to priests but instead counted as chastity—a practice that Saint Gregory did not grant even to the deacons of Sicily in his letter. Rather, he is read as having tolerated the incontinence of some of them for a time only, by overlooking it, not by asserting it to be lawful, and not together with the administration of the diaconate, but under the prohibition of a higher order.

Finally, nothing is found so unlike another thing that it does not bear some appearance of likeness to it, since even the devil himself habitually transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. II). What wonder, then, if you have somehow compared Gregory’s writings with Sozomenus’s fabrications, when in fact they differ so greatly that those fabrications cannot in any way escape Gregory’s anathema? With complete justice, however, we are now commanded to observe generally not this temporary and dispensatory tolerance of Saint Gregory, but his general decrees and those of the other Fathers, since blessed Pope Leo, whom you judge to be a flatterer of your party, pronounces this general sentence to the bishops of Mauretania. Therefore what is contained in general statutes must not be set aside in anyone’s case. Yet in the general statutes promulgated by the authority of Saint Gregory at a general synod, not only sleeping together but also priests’ cohabitation with women, and everything opposed to the sacred canons, are condemned under terrible anathema.

If you had faithfully attended to these matters, you would never have rashly called the sentence of the apostolic lord rash, thereby endangering yourself. That sentence had mercifully separated only Simoniacs and incontinent priests from an office pernicious to themselves—men whom Saint Gregory, together with the other adversaries of the canons, had condemned at the same time under the severest anathema. Gregory did not bind himself by this condemnation, although he tolerated the incontinence of the Sicilian deacons by overlooking it, not as though it were lawful. The Nicene Fathers themselves in no way remove primacy or privilege from the apostolic see, since they command the bishops of all provinces also to observe their own privileges according to the custom of the Roman pontiff. The privilege of the Roman pontiff, according to the assertion of Saint Sylvester, Gelasius, and the other Fathers, is that he may judge concerning all the churches and be subject to the judgment of none; and that, as the need of the times requires, he may indeed—and ought to—mitigate the severity of the canons and decrees themselves (as above). By the authority of this privilege, he spared the Sicilian deacons for a time, not by attacking the canons but by observing them; he did not grant them, with Sozomenus, permission to sin. Thus he did not bind himself by his own anathema together with the adversaries. Rather, according to your own assertion, he left only you—not merely with Paphnutius but also with all the followers of Sozomenus—under the same anathema. For they themselves presume to annul the statutes of the holy Fathers, although the canons have granted them no privilege by which they might mitigate even one of the apostolic statutes.

The anathema that you add applies especially to the followers of Sozomenus—or, to put it more briefly, to the Sozomenists—who not only approve but are in fact the cause and origin of the incitement of secular persons against priests. By their most wicked persuasion they so embolden simpler presbyters to despise the canons that the rulers of the churches are necessarily compelled to bring Gregorian sentences before secular authorities. For the apostolic doctor himself writes to the patrician Jennasius: “Know, most excellent son, that if you seek victories, if you are concerned for the security of the province entrusted to you, nothing will contribute more to this than zeal for the life of priests and, as far as possible, the suppression of the intestine wars of the churches.” He likewise stirred the kings of the Franks to assist him in correcting priests with this terrible sentence, declaring: “There is no doubt that the person who neglects to correct what he can correct is guilty of the fault of the one who does it.” Yet by this the same apostolic man committed nothing against the statutes of the holy Fathers that defend priests from secular persons. For he knew with complete certainty that these statutes did not defend from secular authorities any priest who obstinately resisted the sacred canons, indeed any priest who, having long since been condemned by them, had fallen from the priesthood before God.

[Col. 1099A] Do you see, then, how justly the Sozomenists mentioned above are subject to anathema? They teach any priests to despise the canons and to disregard their own condemnation to such a degree that their prelates are necessarily compelled to appeal to secular authorities for assistance in recalling them from condemnation.

What you gain for your position by enumerating so many examples of compassion is little—indeed, nothing—since it is evident to every learned person that no one may separate himself from Christ on account of another’s weakness. This is what all those do who attempt, with such obstinate resolve, to support others against the most sacred canons that they deserve, by right, to be punished with them under one anathema. For, according to the Apostle, those are worthy of death not only who do such things but also those who approve of those who do them (Rom. I). If we wish to give things their proper names, this will not be called merciful compassion but rather pitiable condemnation, when someone does not hesitate to defend not only his own sin but also another’s to such an extent that he is not afraid to alienate himself from the source of all good. It is not now necessary for me to examine individually the examples of compassion that you multiply in vain, since I have already shown generally that none of them benefits your side; and I judge it too lengthy to treat them individually even within the brevity of a letter.

Nevertheless, I wish faithfully to make this clear to your fraternity: the example that says righteous Lot offered his daughters to be violated for the sake of his guests [Col. 1099C] (Gen. XVIII) is counted by blessed Augustine among the examples of sacred Scripture to be avoided rather than imitated, just as Rahab’s lie is judged. Augustine also proves by the clearest arguments that no one may commit a sin on account of another’s weakness, and that, in order to avoid such a sin, he ought not spare even his own weakness.

As for the Apostle’s statement, “Let each man have his own wife” (I Cor. VII): since it does not in any way condescend to the weakness of monks or the frailty of any veiled women, it condescends much less to priests. They have been dedicated to continence not merely by a simple blessing but, through the venerable imposition of hands and the anointing of the most sacred chrism, have been placed above the other continent persons, indeed above virgins; and they must be ready daily to perform the office that may lawfully be performed only by the continent. Finally, the same Apostle, instructing Titus concerning the ordination or conduct of priests, unequivocally affirms that a priest must be continent.

Know also for certain that blessed Augustine made no mention of your passage when he was treating the ways in which divine Scripture could be understood. Who in his right mind would count as divine something that was known to have been irrecoverably anathematized by the divine sanctions themselves from ancient times? No Sozomenist can be compared with the supreme Physician, because he cannot favor his adherents without bringing ruin upon himself, whereas Christ himself did so. Nor will the authority of the apostolic lord be diminished even if anyone tries to perish rather than obey the apostolic institutions; indeed, the Lord’s beloved himself forbids prayer for such a person: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (I John I). Such people, returning to their senses, should rather pray for themselves and for others, saying: “All the things that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we sinned against you and did not obey your commandments” (Dan. III).

I also want you carefully to observe that people are to be avoided not so much on account of human incontinence as on account of diabolical disobedience, as the Holy Spirit testifies through Samuel: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams; for rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to acquiesce is like the crime of idolatry” (I Sam. XV).
