Hence the prince of the apostles himself, as blessed Pope Alexander testifies in chapter 6, firmly decided, in the ordination of blessed Clement, that the people should not even dare to speak to anyone whom they perceived to be disobedient to the commands of the apostolic see. Because of disobedience, Paul of Samosata, whose error Sozomenus restored in the oft-discussed passage, was disgracefully expelled from the episcopate by public authority, as the very History that you venerate excessively admits. Pope Siricius likewise not only deprived those who defended priestly incontinence of promotion, but at that time completely closed every avenue of indulgence to them. The decrees of Pope Leo, which you thought favored your side, wholly condemn the Sozomenists; they show that pardon is denied to all who despise the apostolic commands.

You greatly detract from your learning by wondering that Saint Gregory’s dispensatory tolerance, being local and temporary, differs from the general statutes of blessed Siricius. No apostolic successor deprives his predecessor of the privilege of the apostolic see, by which, as the need of his own time requires, he may mitigate not only the canons but also the sanctions of his predecessor; yet in doing so he does not resist his predecessor, whom he knows also to have occasionally mitigated his own statutes.

I do not wish again to empty out that deceptive resemblance of yours between Sozomenus and Gregory, nor do I consider it necessary to break your prophetic cord, since I know that Jeremiah, who desired to be drawn out of the muddy pit and was not obstinately resisting his own salvation, was in fact drawn out (Jer. XXXVIII).

Let your fraternity also know that it was not Cassiodorus but some schoolmaster Epiphanius who translated the Tripartite History. Cassiodorus’s reputation cannot in any way canonize Sozomenus’s anathematized passage, since even the unquestioned holiness of Jerome did not make authentic the history of Eusebius translated by him [Note: Rufinus translated it], a history that Jerome himself, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, calls deceptive.

The same outstanding doctor also taught you to cut away that same passage, as contrary to sound doctrine, within the hair of the foreign woman. Since it is pernicious to the one who receives it, as has already been emphasized so often, it must not at all be loved among the divine commandments as something more precious than gold and topaz.

You have indeed carefully frightened everyone away from receiving Sozomenus’s passage by teaching that the administration of such venerable sacraments is imposed upon bishops, presbyters, and deacons on equal terms. But which of us would carry a rope for himself to the cross? Or who, once already hanging on the cross, would fail to break the strangling knot, instead striving to fasten it more tightly around his own throat? You yourself clearly demonstrated this above, where you left yourself hanging on the gallows of Gregory’s anathema.

I do commend you, however, for professing that you believe in the full remission of sins in baptism. By this profession you rejected the blasphemies of your letter, in which, I say, you are noted to have imputed the father’s sin to a son already baptized. I could also very easily demonstrate the error of your proposition—“Whatever applies to the part applies also to the whole”—and of other examples of this kind, if I did not judge it unsuitable to speak of technique in such a matter. I believe that what should be judged concerning the composition of your letters or mine ought to be left to the judgment of others, not to ours.

Having therefore once more irrefutably repelled your objections, I am pleased, despite your ingratitude, to address you charitably through the arguments written below, so that, admonished now at least for the third time, you may return to your senses and not perish eternally, anathematized together with the followers of Sozomenus. No passage contrary to canonical truth is to be received as authentic; yet your topaz is contrary to the most sacred canons. For it asserts that the Council of Nicaea did not forbid incontinence to priests, whereas Saint Jerome, Siricius, and Gregory testify that at that same council not only sexual intercourse but also cohabitation with women was wholly prohibited. Therefore your topaz is not to be proclaimed even as true, much less as authentic, by anyone learned in sacred letters, since it is written: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I). Likewise the blessed Apostle John says: “For the timid … and liars, their place is in the pool of burning fire” (Rev. XXI). Likewise the Psalmist: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. V).

Furthermore, the most holy Pope Leo sent this sentence, among others, through the bishops assembled at the First Council of Toledo to Balconius, bishop of Galicia [Note: In the confession of faith found after the canons of the First Council of Toledo.]: “If anyone says or believes that other writings besides those which the Catholic Church receives are to be held or venerated as authoritative, let him be anathema.” By this anathema, therefore, without doubt those are punished who venerate your passage as authentic, since the Catholic Church does not receive it and it is not doubted that it is opposed to the sacred Scriptures.

Furthermore, blessed Pope Damasus, writing to Aurelian, archbishop of Carthage, most truthfully testifies that those manifestly blaspheme the Holy Spirit who, not compelled by necessity but willingly, either do or presume to say anything against the sacred canons, or freely consent to those who wish to do so. Whoever receives your topaz as canonical not only violates those same canons but also, as has already been proved so often, opposes them with an obstinate mind. Therefore, since they blaspheme the Holy Spirit, they will not escape his condemnation, according to the testimony of the aforesaid apostolic authority—especially since Truth itself testifies in the Gospel that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Luke XII). The Council of Constantinople itself, which is one of the four councils to be venerated equally with the Gospel, anathematizes in its first chapter, together with all heresies, those who obstinately resist the Holy Spirit; it also calls them, according to one translation, by the special name *pneumatomachi* (‘fighters against the Spirit’).

Furthermore, the Holy Spirit promulgated this sentence through the Apostle: “If anyone does not love Christ, let him be anathema: *maran atha* (‘Our Lord, come’)” (I Cor. XVI). The followers of Sozomenus do not love Christ, since they undoubtedly blaspheme the Holy Spirit, through whom Christ himself inspired the canonical sanctions in the holy Fathers. Therefore they are subject to the apostolic anathema.

Furthermore, Pope blessed Gelasius, sitting in the apostolic see with seventy bishops, declared that Nicholas, the fellow deacon of blessed Stephen the protomartyr; Paul of Samosata, patriarch of Antioch; all heretics or schismatics; and all their followers had been irremediably anathematized, together with everything they had taught or written. But whoever teaches that Sozomenus’s passage ought to be received as authentic follows Paul and Nicholas, the heresiarchs, since in that same passage they ascribe conjugal intercourse to priests. How, then, unless they repent, will they be able to escape the anathema of those whose wicked doctrine they have not feared to confirm and disseminate?

Furthermore, the heresiarch Jovinian, specially anathematized by blessed Gelasius among the other heretics, although he heretically equated incontinence with continence, nevertheless never became so foolish as to teach that the episcopal office—the singular and principal dignity of the continent—could be assigned to the incontinent. For he thought it better to oppose his own heresy by condemning this than to equate incontinence with continence so completely that he would assert, contrary to right and justice, that even the incontinent could be admitted to the divine mysteries. Therefore the Sozomenists, who by their shameless assertion advance beyond that same heresiarch in error, how will they be able to escape his unavoidable anathema? Examine carefully, then, these irrefutable sentences of the holy Fathers, and do not thereafter dare, against your own salvation, to receive Sozomenus’s passage as authentic.

But perhaps you still say that you receive it as authentic for no other reason than out of compassion for certain weak people. Although I sufficiently and reasonably answered this objection above, I shall nevertheless, for the sake of your charity, not shrink from confronting it again. Blessed Father Augustine—or rather, the Holy Spirit through him—testifies in his book *Against Lying* (ch. 7), saying: “Things that are clearly sins must not be done under any pretext of a good cause, under any supposed good end, or under any apparently good intention.” But it is proved that receiving Sozomenus’s passage not merely as true but also as authentic or canonical is a damnable sin, since it is both contrary to canonical truth and forbidden under anathema by the holy Fathers. Therefore it must not be received under any pretext of a good cause, any supposed good end, or any supposed good intention. Consequently, not even out of compassion for certain people.

If you faithfully attend to this book of Augustine, you will never judge that we ought to commit any sin, even for someone’s eternal salvation.

For this reason I do not cease to implore your fraternity carefully and earnestly that, now at least, after having been so often and so reasonably [Col. 1103C] admonished, you may provide for the salvation of your soul, withdraw yourself from such a pernicious anathema, and not lead simpler people to destruction—both yours and theirs—by receiving the anathematized passage. Watch carefully, indeed, the words of the Lord, who terrifies with threats the one who causes any of his little ones to stumble (Matt. XVIII). I also beg you to accept my admonition in this matter and, following Saint Gregory, not make yourself any longer guilty of opposing apostolic authority. You have already been proved to have done so, since you did not hesitate to despise the command of the apostolic lord and to disparage him in word and writing. You are also accused of having strengthened others, by listing the anathematized passage among authentic works, so that they might resist the apostolic statutes. I want you to know with complete certainty that you will not escape the anathema of the present Gregory either [Note: Gregory VII was therefore still alive when Bernard wrote this letter], if this infamy about you—already spread abroad among the people—reaches him. It claims that you are the chief teacher, defender, indeed the voice, of all who obstinately resist the canonical and apostolic institutions.

I therefore faithfully admonish you to suppress this disgrace, and henceforth not dare in any way to oppose the apostolic statutes, to your own peril. But so that you may not doubt that the condemnatory judgments of our apostolic lord and of that prince of the apostles himself concerning Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V) possess equal force, carefully consider the condemnation and death of the bishop of Speyer. In the past year—namely, the year 1075 from the Lord’s Incarnation—in the first week of Lent, on the very same day, that is, 6 Kalends of March, [Note: [Col. 1103D] Bernaldus therefore wrote this letter in the year 1076. Concerning this bishop of Speyer, our Bernaldus writes in his chronicle under the year 1075. This bishop’s name was Henry. See concerning this Roman Council, volume III of the Councils, and Baronius, volume XI, under the year of Christ 1075.] indeed at the very same hour at which our apostolic lord began to examine his case at the Roman synod, he suddenly began to fall ill at Speyer, as though struck by some invisible weapon. On the third day, likewise—that is, 4 Kalends of March—alas, he expired miserably, at the very time when the defined judgment of our Gregory condemned him at Rome with unquestionable force. For this is attested by the unanimous report of faithful men: some of them had been present at the Roman synod when that transgressor was condemned; others were at Speyer and, being present, shuddered that the same bishop had died so suddenly and so miserably. Therefore, you too must beware. *Das dir jeth alsamo beschehe* [“May the same happen to you now in this way.”] [Note: [Col. 1104D] These German words close the letter in the manuscript codex.]

## LETTER OF RECONCILIATION

For the injuries of the preceding letters.

[Col. 1103]

[Col. 1103C] To his son of the right hand, BERNHALDUS, ALBONIUS: equal in willing and likewise in refusing.

“Let there be no jealousy and contention between us,” says the prophetic word together with the Apostle (1 Cor. III). Therefore let us strive to be good rivals, so that we may most easily escape whatever may cause harm. If any tares of disagreement or rivalry appear to have sprung up between us, let them be torn out by the roots with the sickle of pure affection and of the faith closely joined to it. Let our whole business, according to the principles of Tully and Quintilian, turn upon what is useful and honorable. If until now we have acted contentiously and fruitlessly through long night-watchings, let us now, with few words, accomplish much through judgment and charity. If I were not obliged to be subject to every creature for God’s sake (1 Pet. II), I would nevertheless refuse in no way to yield to contention for the sake of restoring your friendship. As for me, if I have said anything that may seem offensive to you or to anyone, I do not refuse to be handed over to the destruction of the flesh so that the spirit may be saved (1 Cor. V). From now on, whatever the circumstances may be, let the fervent power of charity, which knows not how to diminish, remain forever and beyond: hotter than the sun, more enduring than adamant. Let us now stand firm and strive to appear to be generating anew between us a pair of friends.

**End of the Disputation Concerning the Continence of Clerics**

[Col. 1105]

# BERNALDUS THE PRIEST’S APOLOGETIC

For the decrees of Gregory VII, supreme pontiff, issued in the Roman synod against the Simoniacs and incontinent ministers of the altar. Now published for the first time, from two manuscript codices, one of Regensburg and the other of Weingarten.

## CONTENTS OF THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 1105A]

**Chapter I.** The decretal letter of the venerable Pope Gregory.  
**II.** On the authority of the four principal councils.  
**III.** On the authority of apostolic institutions.  
**IV.** On the authority of the remaining councils.  
**V.** A brief enumeration of the decrees of the preceding letter.  
**VI.** On the first statute, namely, concerning the Simoniacs.  
**VII.** On the second statute, namely, concerning buyers of churches.  
**VIII.** That Holy Scripture also condemns sellers of spiritual offices.  
**IX.** Likewise, that it condemns their buyers.  
**X.** Likewise, the mediators of such a Simoniacal transaction.

[Col. 1105B]

**XI.** Explanation of the statute of the aforesaid decretal letter: namely, that the incontinent may in no way minister at the altar.  
**XII.** Concerning the anathema of those who defend the incontinence of priests, through a chapter of Sozomen drawn from the *Tripartite History*.  
**XIII.** That it has been permitted not to ministers of the sacraments but to laymen that each man should have his own wife.  
[Col. 1106A]  
**XIV.** What the Apostle establishes concerning sacred orders.  
**XV.** A useful consideration of the same institution.  
**XVI.** An exposition by Blessed Jerome of the same institution.  
**XVII.** On the fourth statute of the aforesaid decretal letter: that the people should not receive the offices of clerics whom they see disregarding the apostolic statutes.  
**XVIII.** Why their offices have been forbidden to the people.  
**XIX.** An explanation of a certain chapter that appears to conflict with the present statute.  
**XX.** What compelled the apostolic lord to issue these statutes.  
**XXI.** That indignation concerning such statutes ought to be directed not against him but against the holy Fathers.

[Col. 1106B]

**XXII.** Why no delay was attached to these statutes.  
**XXIII.** That the apostolic lord can condemn not only bishops but also their subjects.  
**XXIV.** That the parishioner of any bishop owes obedience even more to the apostolic lord than to his own bishop.

## Bertoldus, or more correctly Bernaldus, our author, in his *Chronicle*, under the year of the Lord 1075

[Col. 1105]

Pope Gregory convened a synod at Rome in the first week of Lent, at which he examined the case of the bishop of Speyer, who was a Simoniac. On the very day when his case was being examined at Rome—that is, 6 Kalends of March—he fell ill at Speyer; then, on 4 Kalends of March, he expired miserably, at the time when he also received from Pope Gregory at the Roman synod the judgment of his condemnation as it had been defined.

At that same synod Pope Gregory decreed that clerics who had obtained any grade or office of sacred orders for a price should henceforth not minister in the Church; that no one should retain a church acquired for a price; that henceforth no one should be permitted to sell or buy a church; and then that all who made themselves blameworthy through incontinence should cease from clerical office. Likewise, that the people should in no way receive the offices of clerics whom they perceived to disregard the aforesaid apostolic institutions.

# HERE BEGINS BERNALDUS’S APOLOGETIC ON THE DECREES

Which the venerable Pope Gregory VII, of that name, promulgated at the Roman synod against the Simoniacs and incontinent ministers of the altar.

[Col. 1107]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1107A] In the preceding letters I strove to satisfy our friend—God forbid that I should henceforth call him a rival—Alboin, and I clearly demonstrated that a chapter contrary to the statutes of our apostolic lord was in no way to be heeded, since it had plainly been prohibited under anathema. Thus our friend wrote back to me that he would no longer devote himself to contention but to friendship.

Yet many still remain who obstinately, and indeed dangerously—rather, disastrously—resist those same statutes. They also mislead simpler people, who are not very diligent in examining the canons, to such an extent that these too despise the aforesaid authoritative decrees and insist on retaining their own custom, very pleasant indeed but most harmful. In my view, more of them would not have done this [Col. 1107B] if they had understood clearly how little—or rather, how not at all [Regensburg codex: *nothing*]—our apostolic lord deviates in those statutes from the holy Fathers.

Therefore I judged that it would be useful for me and for those like me to compare those same statutes with the canonical Scriptures and briefly and faithfully commend their mutual agreement, whatever the limitations of my style. I have done this with the intention that, if perhaps one of the unlearned should deign to examine these matters, he may recover his senses and obey the apostolic institutions all the more eagerly, the more clearly he sees that these statutes in no way deviate from the most sacred canons but have proceeded with them from Holy Scripture itself.

## CHAPTER I

First, therefore, it is useful to transcribe the decretal letter of our apostolic lord, so that what follows may shine forth more clearly.

“GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, OTHON, bishop of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Your messengers’ insistence,” etc. The remainder is extant in the First Roman Council above.

## CHAPTER II

Before we consider these statutes individually, I think it useful to say something in advance concerning the authority of the canons themselves, so that whatever is announced to us from them for observance may be held all the more firmly.

The most holy Pope Gregory (Book I, Letter 24), whom our apostolic lord represents in name and in action in our own times [C. R.: “represented”], confirms the four most holy councils in his synodical—that is, synodal—letter as follows:

“Just as I confess that I receive and venerate the four holy Gospels, so also do I receive and venerate four councils: namely, Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches [Roman edition: Eutychius] and Dioscorus was rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with unimpaired approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises and the standard of every life and action is established. Whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone [Roman edition: ‘is seen to be a stone’], nevertheless lies outside the building, etc.

[Col. 1108B] “I reject all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable councils reject; I embrace those whom they venerate. Since they have been established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to dissolve what they bind or to bind what they dissolve destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.” Thus far Gregory.

This same apostolic lord composed this synodal letter immediately after his ordination and sent it to the other patriarchs—namely, to the patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and Jerusalem. For at that time it was customary that anyone newly ordained to one of the patriarchal sees should profess in a letter sent to the other sees that he would preserve the aforesaid four synods, before he could deserve to have his name entered in the diptychs of the other sees.

The other sees counted the name of his predecessor, although he was dead, among the living until they received the synodical letter of the newly enthroned prelate; and because that letter indicated that the same bishop had received the four synods, it seems not inappropriately to have borrowed the name *synodical* from those same synods.

The same most holy pope testifies that this was the custom of that time in his letter to Secundinus, a servant of God confined in seclusion (Book VII, Letter 54). John, a deacon of the Roman Church, who faithfully wrote the life of Saint Gregory at the command of Pope Saint John, asserts that the custom continued even until the time of Blessed Pope Adrian—namely, in a letter to King Charles.

[Col. 1109A] But whether the same custom still continues, I do not know. I have no doubt, however, that it existed in the times mentioned above. It is therefore completely evident how great is the authority of those four councils, which Saint Gregory—or rather, through him, the Holy Spirit—not only once, as has been stated, but repeatedly compares with the Gospels and anathematizes all who dissent from them. Every newly appointed patriarch was also required to profess by letter to the other sees that he would observe them, if he wished to be entered among the Catholic patriarchs in the diptychs.

## CHAPTER III

We ought, if possible, to venerate and observe the decrees of the most holy Roman pontiffs even more diligently than those four councils, since the councils themselves would lack all firmness if the pontiffs of the apostolic see had not resolved, by apostolic authority, both to convene and to strengthen them.

Thus Blessed Pope Marcellus (Letter I, Roman edition), who consecrated his decrees to martyrdom even before the Council of Nicaea, that same apostolic man, testifies in his decrees, chapter 11:

“The Apostles themselves and their successors, under the inspiration of the Lord, established that no synod should be held without the authority of the Roman see.”

Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, who was no small part of the Council of Nicaea, also says in his letter to Pope Felix, chapter 11:

“We know that at the great Council of Nicaea, consisting of 318 bishops, it was confirmed by the unanimous agreement of all that councils ought not to be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff.”

Blessed Pope Julius likewise professes the same thing in chapter 5, saying:

“To the Church of the first see, by a singular privilege granted through evangelical, apostolic, and canonical institutions, belong the rights and judgments concerning the convocation of general synods.”

Pope Damasus, of blessed memory, also inserted this judgment in his decrees, chapter 9 [C. R.: “inserts the general judgment”]:

“No councils are ever read as ratified which have not been supported by apostolic authority.”

Blessed Isidore, the most discerning investigator of the Scriptures, faithfully agrees with these judgments, saying:

“The authority to convene synods has been entrusted privately to the Apostolic See, by whose authority [C. R.: ‘power’] they are assembled or supported. The canonical authority bears witness to this; ecclesiastical history confirms it; the holy Fathers affirm it.” [Note: [Col. 1110D] Nor do we read that any synod is ratified which was not ratified by it.]

If, then, those four councils would lack all authority unless they principally received their firmness from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, who could deny that the decrees promulgated by those apostolic men are rightly judged worthy of greater veneration than the councils themselves, which deserved to become authoritative not through the presence of those apostolic men but only through their legation?

For the legates of the apostolic see, by apostolic representation, canonically confirmed the decrees of those principal councils with the primary subscription. Under the most pious Emperor Constantine, Hosius, the great bishop of Córdoba, together with Victor and Vincentius, priests of the Roman Church, presided over the Council of Nicaea on behalf of Saint Pope Sylvester and confirmed it with the principal subscription.

Likewise, in the time of Theodosius the Younger Augustus, Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, and Arcadius, a bishop from Italy, presided over the Council of Ephesus in the place of Blessed Pope Celestine and strengthened it in apostolic representation.

Likewise, in the time of Emperor Marcian, the bishops Paschasinus and Vincentius, and Boniface the priest, acting in the place of Saint Pope Leo, were first at the Council of Chalcedon, which was held for twelve days. They generously opposed Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, when he arrogated a certain privilege to himself at the council, and they subscribed to the remaining decrees in apostolic representation, as the book of Saint Liberatus, archdeacon of Carthage, testifies concerning that council.

All these matters will be seen more clearly by anyone who carefully examines the subscriptions of those councils. Therefore, the reverence or obedience that, in accordance with Saint Gregory, we rightly offer to the four most sacred councils, we must in no way deny to the decrees of the apostolic see; indeed, if possible, we ought to offer it even more diligently, since without their authority it would not be lawful to receive the councils themselves.

## CHAPTER IV

Nor ought we to think little of the remaining councils, in which we find many things—nowhere else found—which are nevertheless necessary for ecclesiastical administration [C. R.: “disposition”]. These do not differ in any way from the higher authoritative decrees, since they most clearly agree with the Christian religion.

Such chapters, I say, wherever they are found in councils, are in no way to be despised by any Catholic, especially since there can be no doubt that the remaining councils themselves descended from the authority of the most sacred decrees, which most firmly determine that two councils of bishops should be held annually in each province.

Blessed Anacletus, ordained a priest by the prince of the apostles himself, most certainly decrees this in his decrees, chapter 17:

“The assembly of the highest [bishops],” he says, “is customarily and necessarily held each year.”

The most excellent Council of Nicaea established this in chapter 5:

“It was well agreed that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that such questions might be examined jointly when all the bishops are gathered together.”

Likewise, the Council of Constantinople, after listing the privileges of various Churches, establishes in chapter 11 [C. R.: “thus”]:

“While the rule written concerning administrations is preserved, it is clear that matters belonging to each province should be administered by the synod of that province, as is established by the decree of the Council of Nicaea.”

Likewise, the Council of Chalcedon says in chapter 19:

[Col. 1111A] “The holy synod decreed, according to the canons of the Fathers, that bishops should gather twice each year in each province, at the place approved by the metropolitan bishop, so that they may correct whatever may perhaps have arisen.”

It is therefore clear that the authoritative decrees also command that provincial councils be held; they would command this in vain unless they also decided that we should observe the sound judgments of those councils.

Hence, at the Third Universal Council of Toledo it was decreed:

“Whoever does not receive the councils of orthodox bishops, in agreement with the four most holy councils, let him be anathema.”

Therefore, whoever attempts to oppose the reasonable statutes of any of these councils is shown to dissent, to his own peril, even from the higher authoritative decrees.

Blessed Isidore also agrees with the aforesaid arguments in a certain preface on the canons, chapter 11, as follows:

“It must also be understood that, although the others are not invalidated, there are four principal councils.”

After listing these, he adds in the same chapter:

“But if there are any councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have established, after the authority of these four they all remain established with full force.” (*Isidore, Origins*, Book VI, chapter 15.)

It is therefore proper to obey the statutes of councils of this kind as well. If it is evidently no small folly for anyone to refuse to yield to the sound advice of a single person, how much more blameworthy does it appear if anyone impudently resists statutes of this kind, issued and approved by the authority and judgment not of one wise man but of many?

Indeed, many Catholic and eminent teachers are recorded as having taken part in such councils. Thus, in the African councils there were the legates of the apostolic see—Faustinus, Honoratus, and Urbanus, bishops—and also Saint Aurelius [Note: [Col. 1111] Missing in C. R.], archbishop of Carthage.

Likewise, there was Augustine himself, that man of every virtue, bishop of Hippo Regius, whom Saint Celestine, an apostolic man, commends to us in his decrees (Letter 8) as follows:

“We have always held Augustine, a man of holy memory, in our communion because of his life and merits; nor did even a rumor of sinister suspicion ever stain him—him whom we remember to have once possessed such great learning that even before my predecessors he was counted among the best teachers. Therefore all rightly held a common opinion of him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.”

As the book of Liberatus testifies, the Emperor Theodosius also sent Augustine a command in a “sacred” letter that he should present himself at the Council of Ephesus. But alas! So distinguished a teacher had already been taken from the world before the letter of invitation from the Roman emperor could reach him.

These men whom I have mentioned, then, and countless other holy Fathers took part in, indeed presided over, the African councils. Likewise, Saint Marinus took part in the Council of Arles approved by Saint Sylvester [C. R.: “the pope”]; Saint Caesarius in the Council of Agde; Saint Hilary in the Council of Orange; Saint Albinus in the Council of Orléans; Saint Boniface in the Council of Mainz. Other saints likewise are recorded as having taken part in other councils, not alone but together with many other holy Fathers, who are believed to have been so distinguished in Christian religion and doctrine that it would be exceedingly rash to oppose the individual judgment of even one of them.

Therefore, not to yield to the judgment of many wise men is much more intolerable, at least in those chapters that do not oppose the aforesaid authoritative statutes but undoubtedly support the institution of the Christian religion. For, according to the judgment of Blessed Augustine, “no matter contrary to canonical truth, wherever it is found—in any council or elsewhere—is to be accepted out of reverence for any person.”

Moreover, the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon is also held to have canonized provincial councils held before it, decreeing in chapter 1:

“We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in the several councils down to the present possess their proper force.”

The councils held before Chalcedon are said to have been these: Ancyra and Neocaesarea, which are also transmitted as older than the Council of Nicaea; likewise Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, and Laodicea.

Therefore, these too are understood to have been strengthened at the Council of Chalcedon. Blessed Pope Adrian is also said to have delivered them, together with the African canons, at Rome to the Emperor Charles for the ordering of the Churches in his kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1111] This epitome of the canons, compiled by Adrian and delivered to Charlemagne, is extant.]

Consequently, the statutes of provincial councils are not to be rashly rejected by anyone, since the apostolic see itself judged that they should be received. Let what has been said concerning the authority of the sacred canons suffice. Let us now return to our subject and arrange in order the statutes that our apostolic lord carefully described and sent in the preceding letter to Otho, bishop of Constance.

## CHAPTER V

The first of these was:

“That clerics who have obtained any grade or office of sacred orders for a price should henceforth in no way minister in the Church.”

The second:

“That no one should retain a church acquired for a price; nor should anyone henceforth be permitted to sell or buy a church.”

The third:

“That all who make themselves blameworthy through incontinence should cease from clerical office.”

The fourth:

“That the people should in no way receive the offices of clerics whom they see disregarding the apostolic institutions.”

Let us therefore proceed through them individually and demonstrate briefly, not from our own conjectures but from the statutes of the holy Fathers, how authoritative, how worthy of attention, and indeed how unavoidable they are.

## CHAPTER VI

The first statute is found most fully and clearly in the Council of Chalcedon. This was the last in time, though not in dignity, of the four councils mentioned above; the holy Fathers commanded Leo Augustus to vindicate it even unto blood, as Liberatus testifies in his book.

In that council, I say, it is written in chapter 3 [Note: [Col. 1113D] See C. 1, Q. 1, C. 8]:

“If any bishop performs an ordination for money, reducing to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and for money ordains a bishop, chorepiscopus, priest, or deacon, or anyone at all among those numbered in the clergy; or promotes for money a steward, defender, doorkeeper, or anyone whatsoever who is subject to the rule, for the sake of his own most shameful profit, the person proved to have attempted this shall be subject to the peril of his own rank, and the person ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or promotion made through trafficking but shall be excluded from the dignity or responsibility that he purchased with money.

“If anyone has acted as mediator in such shameful and wicked gifts or acceptances, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized.”

It should be noted how carefully this chapter excludes all the tricks of the Simoniacs, since it deposes, without any hope of recovery, all who have been promoted through money, however that may have occurred.

For Simoniacs customarily purchase sacred dignities in various ways but under one guilt. Sometimes they themselves, sometimes their friends on their behalf, have given the price for a sacred dignity before their ordination, or give it at the time of ordination, or promise that they will give it afterward. They give it sometimes to their electors, sometimes to those who ordain them, and finally to any of their supporters.

Therefore, whoever promotes anyone by one of these methods, or recognizes that he himself was promoted in this way, is unquestionably ordered by the preceding chapter to be degraded, since it is beyond doubt that he either promoted another through money or was himself promoted through it.

Nor should this be passed over without consideration: the same chapter condemned two classes of traffickers. One consists of those who are ordained through money to the diaconate, priesthood, or any similar rank; the other consists of those who are promoted through money to the ministry of administration or to some similar clerical office, such as vice-dominus, provost, dean, archpriest, and the like.

Thus our apostolic lord also included two classes of traffickers and all the tricks of those who traffic in his first statute, in which he deposes clerics who have obtained any grade or office of sacred orders by money, in whatever manner.

This statute is plainly proved to be milder than the preceding chapter, since it does not condemn with the due punishment the sellers of spiritual offices and the mediators of such a wicked transaction. The preceding chapter, however, decreed that they should be degraded or anathematized together with the buyers. [Col. 1114A]

And note: if a mediator is rightly ordered to be degraded or anathematized, what do you think about the person who is unworthily promoted through the same transaction? Surely this: what the most holy Pope Gregory (Book VII, Letter 112), or rather the Holy Spirit through him, unquestionably decreed concerning such traffickers, dictating to the ear of that apostolic lord, under the appearance of a dove, whatever needed to be decreed.

For it is written in his decrees, chapter 131 (in Gratian, C. 1, Q. 1, C. 13):

“Whoever therefore strives to purchase this—that is, an ecclesiastical office—by giving a price, since he gives attention not to the office but to the name, desires vainly not to be a priest but merely to be called one.”

And shortly afterward in the same chapter:

“Since it is clear that this heresy first crept into the Church with a poisonous root and was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation, why is it not guarded against? Why is it not considered that the blessing is turned into a curse for the one who is promoted in order to become a heretic?”

What wonder, then, if our apostolic lord separated from ecclesiastical ministries those whom his most holy namesake counted as separated from the Church along with the other heretics?

## CHAPTER VII

The second statute of our apostolic lord commands that churches be taken away from their buyers. Likewise, in the aforesaid chapter of the Council of Chalcedon, it appears to be included, though obscurely, that the office of administration should also be taken away from a steward of ecclesiastical goods who has been promoted through money.

Every priest ought to be a steward, not only of preaching but also of the Church’s property entrusted to him, which the holy Fathers judged should be distributed not merely for the needs of the priest but for the needs of all who are in want.

Moreover, in the same chapter every ecclesiastical responsibility acquired for a price is ordered to be taken away from any cleric. To care for the Church itself with priestly diligence, unless I am mistaken, is a clerical and ecclesiastical responsibility. Therefore, in the same chapter, responsibility for a Church usurped through money is ordered to be taken away.

Thus Blessed Pope Gregory, writing to Clement of Byzantium, makes the following ruling concerning a certain priest:

“If that priest had obtained a certain church through money, he should be deprived not only of that church but also stripped of the honor of the priesthood.”

Likewise, in the ancient councils of our provinces—namely, those of Mainz, Rheims, and Tours—it is recorded that a priest who acquired a church for a price should be deprived both of the priesthood and of the church.

Likewise, Pope Leo, of blessed memory, the ninth of that name and almost adjacent to our own times, utterly condemned the Simoniacal heresy in his first Roman synod and prohibited the buying and selling of altars under anathema. [Col. 1115A] Those who afterward presumed to practice such a wicked transaction did not escape that anathema.

It is therefore worth considering how mercifully our apostolic lord merely took purchased churches away from their buyers, although he knew that, according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, they ought to be deprived of both Church and priesthood, indeed of the Christian name and communion itself.

## CHAPTER VIII

But why do we labor so much to demonstrate that the aforesaid statutes of our apostolic lord proceeded from the synodal judgments of the holy Fathers, when we may suppose that no learned person doubts that they flowed from the treasury of Holy Scripture itself?

For in that Scripture all the persons involved in such a wicked commerce are found to be condemned: sellers of spiritual offices, buyers, and mediators of the transaction.

For the Lord himself “drove the sellers and buyers alike out of his temple, and overturned the seats of those selling doves”; he had already overturned them then (Matt. XXI; Mark XI).

Our Saint Gregory, the theologian, explains this in Homily XXII [C. R.: XVII, correctly], as follows:

“The seat of those selling doves is overturned when those who sell spiritual grace are deprived of the priesthood either in the eyes of human beings or in the sight of God.”

And rightly so. For Truth itself commands in the Gospel:

“You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. X).

Since such people do not heed this, they also estrange themselves from God, who says in the same Gospel:

“He who is of God hears God’s words; therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God” (John VIII).

Moreover, the prince of the apostles, Peter—or rather Christ himself through him—gives the following command to all prelates in the Church:

“Feed the flock of God that is among you, overseeing it not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for the sake of shameful gain but willingly” (1 Pet. V).

All who shamefully provide spiritual office to their subjects for secular profit act against this command.

Concerning such people the same Apostle testifies in his Second Letter:

“They followed the way of Balaam of Bosor, who loved the reward of iniquity; but he received a rebuke for his madness when the mute beast, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly” (2 Pet. II).

The Venerable Priest Bede clarifies this in his commentary on the same letter as follows:

“For many Catholics love the reward of iniquity to such an extent that learned men are rightly assailed by the unlearned, and clerics by laymen; they are compared to the prophet who was rebuked by the words of a she-ass speaking contrary to nature, yet was not restrained from his purpose of following the wicked road.” [Col. 1115D]

This Balaam is asserted to be the same person who is said to have taught Blessed Job excessively and arrogantly in the book bearing Job’s name; he was also called Elihu—that is, “divine”—from the office of divining. Thus Saint Jerome testifies in his book *On Hebrew Questions*.

When this man was a prophet hired by Balak, king of the Moabites, to curse the children of Israel, he did indeed strive to curse them for a price, in accordance with the word of the Lord; but, because the Lord forbade it, he did not bring his wickedness to effect, nor did he receive the reward of iniquity.

Nevertheless, he is marked as rejected by God, since his she-ass is said to have been wiser than he: she rebuked his madness and folly and rescued him from the sword of the resisting angel. The angel himself testified that the she-ass would not die, even though he would strike down the rejected prophet with the death he deserved (Num. XXII).

If, then, Balaam is read as rejected by God merely because he loved the reward of iniquity so greatly, how much more must that man be counted among the rejected who most eagerly demands from Balaam the price of the most wicked sale of spiritual office and does not stop until he brings his ambition to fulfillment?

Moreover, Blessed Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, testifies that the scribe who said to Jesus, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. VIII), was rejected by the Lord because, in the manner of Simon Magus, he wished to follow him in order to obtain profit from the miracles of his works.

Therefore the Lord answers him:

“Foxes have dens,”

and the rest; as if he were saying:

“You wish to follow me for the sake of profits and riches, although I am so poor that I do not even possess a lodging of my own, while even foxes and birds have dwellings of their own.”

If, then, the person who wished to exercise spiritual office solely for profit is rightly rejected by the Lord himself, how much more is the person exposed as having sold such an office outright to others?

## CHAPTER IX

Buyers of spiritual things are likewise read as condemned in the Acts of the Apostles together with their prince, Simon Magus. There our Simon, the prince of the apostles, inflicted eternal condemnation upon that other Simon, the prince of apostates, decreeing as follows [Col. 1116C]:

“May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You have neither part nor lot in this matter. Your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.”

But Simon answered and said: “Pray also for me to God, that none of these things which you have said may come upon me” (Acts VIII).

And note that Simon Magus, that heresiarch, was condemned by his namesake for a single wicked thought [Col. 1116D], although we read that he merely thought of purchasing a spiritual office and in no way that he actually completed so wicked a transaction. Do you see how reasonably those are condemned who, with an eagerness no less than that of Simon Magus, desire to purchase spiritual offices and, moreover, complete the transaction they have desired—those who, having acquired them by crime, do not hesitate to use, indeed to misuse, them even more criminally? Hence they appear to surpass Simon Magus himself by no small degree in guilt. For he never brought to completion the purchase which he wickedly desired; condemned for his wicked appetite alone, he sought through the apostles to bring it about with God that he might evade their condemnatory sentence [Col. 1117A], not that he might obtain, in an even more criminal manner, the office which he had criminally desired.

But why would that heresiarch have desired to purchase a spiritual office unless he subsequently wished to sell what he had bought in an even more wicked manner? For it does not seem that the following was written about him without reason: that he, being foolish, marveled at signs and powers, and wished to bring it about through his money that he himself might perform them—namely, “so that,” according to Jerome’s assertion, “he might obtain temporal profit from miracles.”

Therefore not only buyers but also sellers of spiritual offices are marked as followers of the aforementioned heresiarch. Accordingly, there is no doubt that they are bound together with him by the chain of eternal condemnation, as the blessed Gelasius attests in his decrees, chapter 24 (Epistle 6, 1, q. 1, [Col. 1117B] c. 6):

“Those whom it is established to be unworthy by their merits, yet who have purchased the sacred dignity for a price, ought, once convicted, to be excluded. They do not commit such a crime without danger, because the condemnation of Simon, which sacred Scripture attests, encompasses both the giver and the receiver.”

The blessed Pope Gelasius applied this general judgment to the ordinations of the individual grades; among them he also counted doorkeepers, notaries, and defenders, who are neither ordained by the laying on of hands nor permitted themselves to lay hands upon anyone [Note: [Col. 1117] This period is lacking in C. R. in the text, but is nevertheless found in the margin.]. Hence there is no doubt that the man called a Simoniac in the decrees of Saint Alexander is one who, for a price, assists a penitent before a bishop in obtaining reconciliation. From this [C. R. *ratione*, “on this basis”] it is inferred that not only those are reckoned among the Simoniacs who reach the laying on of hands by means of a price, but also those who acquire other clerical offices through money. In such offices, however, one and the same spirit performs everything (I Corinthians XII); to give or receive his gift not freely but for a price is not Catholic but unquestionably Simoniacal.

## CHAPTER X

The mediators of this most wicked transaction are also condemned by the very Vessel of Election, who detests them in these words: “They are worthy of death not only who do wicked things but also those who consent to the doers” (Romans I). Likewise our harpist David says: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him” (Psalm XLIX), and: “Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceits” (ibid.). Then, in the same psalm, a terrifying sentence is pronounced concerning such an accomplice: namely, that he is to be reproved by the Lord and thereafter rescued by no one from the hand of the Lord (ibid.).

Nor should you be surprised if the merchant of a spiritual office is designated under the name of a thief, since he is also named thus by Truth itself in the Gospel: “He who enters by another way, rather than through the door, is not the shepherd of the sheep but is called by the Lord a thief and a robber” (John X). Certainly no prelate in the Church entered through the door—that is, through the Lord himself—for pastoral care if he attained that office through avarice, which is the service of idols. It is therefore not undeserved that such a merchant or hireling should be disgraced under the name of a thief, since he was not afraid to imitate his own furtive intrusion.

Let the mediators of this most criminal commerce carefully consider Gehazi, the servant of Elisha, who, on behalf of his master though without his knowledge, freely accepted gifts offered by Naaman the Syrian, who had already been cleansed of leprosy by the prophet Elisha. Although Gehazi wickedly profited as an intermediary between Elisha and Naaman, he nevertheless did not make either of them liable with himself for the same crime. For the one generously rejected the voluntary offering, while the other offered it freely, not as something owed by a purchaser but out of kindly disposition.

Yet although Gehazi did not draw either of these two into guilt with him, but alone bound himself by a simple crime as the intermediary between them [Col. 1118B], he and all his descendants are nevertheless read to have been punished most severely for the same offense, having, as it were, received as an everlasting inheritance the leprosy from which Naaman had been cleansed (IV Kings V). Therefore let the mediators of the Simoniacal transaction consider how strictly—indeed, how most strictly—they must be condemned, since they have placed not only themselves but also those whose mediators they are under eternal condemnation.

It has therefore, as I think, been sufficiently demonstrated how greatly we ought to venerate and observe the aforesaid decrees of our apostolic authority. It has been proved most clearly that they derive not only from the synodal and authoritative judgments of the holy Fathers, but also from prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic [Col. 1118C] writings [C. R. *Scripturis*, “Scriptures”]. Truth itself undoubtedly promulgated them both through itself and through its faithful servants, because [C. R. *quae*, “which”] it also says to us under faithful attestation: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will not see death forever” (John VIII); and elsewhere: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John XIV). Therefore whoever does not observe his commandments does not love Truth itself. “But whoever does not love,” as the blessed John attests, “remains in death” (I John III). Whoever, then, despises the divine commands will in no way be able to escape death.

## CHAPTER XI

The third statute of our apostolic authority, which forbids incontinent clerics the ministry of the altar [Col. 1118D], was likewise established by the holy Fathers. For it is written in the [C. R. “most sacred”] Council of Nicaea—which is the greatest among the four councils, equal to the Gospels—chapter 3:

“The great synod absolutely forbids that a bishop, a presbyter, a deacon, or anyone at all belonging to the clergy may have a woman introduced into his household, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, or aunt, or one of those persons who escape suspicion.”

To make the intention of this chapter clearer, it is not burdensome to append a more explicit translation of it. The holy synod has altogether forbidden and does not permit a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or any cleric to keep with him an unrelated woman, unless she is his mother, sister, or aunt. In these persons and their equivalents, every suspicion is avoided. Whoever acts otherwise, beyond these exceptions, will endanger his clerical status [Col. 1119A].

Do you see, then, that conjugal intercourse is altogether forbidden to clerics [C. R. *istic*, “here”]? For on account of their cohabitation with women they are rightly judged to endanger not only the ministry of the altar but also their clerical status. Nor is this decreed only concerning priests; it is clearly decreed concerning all the sacred orders.

Likewise the Council of Neocaesarea, which is read to have preceded the Council of Nicaea, decreed in chapter 1:

“If a presbyter takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order. But if he has fornicated or committed adultery, he must be expelled altogether and brought to penance” [Col. 1119B].

The Council of Chalcedon also, which—as has been stated—confirmed the Nicene and Neocaesarean sanctions, indeed all the sanctions of the holy Fathers enacted before it, generally condemns those who violate these sanctions, saying in chapter 10:

“As for those who have dared, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything forbidden by these provisions, the holy synod has decreed that they must withdraw from their own rank.”

Likewise the most blessed Pope Sylvester, who convened the Nicene synod and strengthened it with apostolic authority, decrees in his synodal decrees, chapter 6 [Col. 1119C]:

“No presbyter, from the day of his presbyteral dignity, shall take a wife. If anyone, disregarding this, acts otherwise, we order him to be deprived of his dignity for twelve years. If anyone acts against this written and publicly promulgated decree, he shall be condemned forever.”

Likewise the blessed Pope Siricius says in his decrees, chapter 7:

“Any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who, contrary to our wishes, is henceforth found to be incontinent must understand that every avenue of indulgence has been closed to him by us.”

And in the same decrees, chapter 12 [Col. 1119D]:

“We permit no women to be in the houses of clerics except those whom the Nicene synod permitted to live with them solely on account of relationship.”

Likewise the most holy Pope Gregory, writing to the Roman defensor (Book VII, Letter 39), decrees in chapter 10:

“If any of the bishops whose dioceses are enclosed within the boundaries of the patrimony entrusted to you live with women, restrain them [Latin *hos*, “them”; C. R. *hoc*, “this”] altogether, and henceforth in no way allow those women to live there, except those whom the judgment of the sacred canons permits—that is, a mother, aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no evil suspicion can arise. It is better, however, if they abstain even from cohabitation with such women. For it is read that the blessed Augustine did not agree even to live with his sister, saying: ‘Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.’ The great caution of learned men ought therefore to be an instruction to us.”

And shortly afterward [Col. 1120A]:

“Furthermore, let it be your care to exhort these same brother bishops of ours to admonish those subject to them who have been established in the sacred orders to observe in every way, after their own example, what they themselves observe.”

Likewise Pope Zacharias says in his decrees, chapter 1:

“We decree that bishops must not live with women at all, lest they be deceived by the fraud of the ancient enemy.”

In the same decrees, chapter 2:

“Presbyters and deacons must in no way dare to keep introduced women with them, unless perhaps they are their godmothers or have a degree of blood relationship that escapes suspicion, as is contained in the Nicene synod. If anyone presumes to act contrary to these statutes, let him be deprived of the honor of his priesthood.”

[Col. 1120B] Likewise the blessed Jerome, writing to Oceanus, proved by authoritative arguments that clerics may not associate with women. Later he added:

“If, after our admonitions, any cleric should continue to desire to love his *agapetae* [ms. *sagapetas*, quite erroneously] more than Christ, let him be summoned according to the synodal rule, and let the commands of the Fathers defined at Nicaea be read to him. Then, if he is summoned and abandons and leaves the women mentioned above, we shall have gained the greatest profit. Otherwise such a man must be anathematized by the Church. For women who live with men produce thorns, and with a sharp blade they strike the secret places of the mind.”

But why should I say more? Time will fail me [Col. 1120C] if I relate individually [C. R. *viritim*, “one by one”] the virtues of the holy Fathers mentioned above, who subscribe to our apostolic statutes. For all Catholics judged that these things must be observed, and they did not wish to dissent from the four most sacred councils. From these sources our apostolic authority produced the aforesaid decrees.

Therefore I do not think it remains hidden even from the ignorant how dangerously—or rather, how ruinously—all those foolishly err for themselves and their followers who, through Sozomen’s chapter, do not fear to attribute incontinence to priests. Although the preceding assertion from the letters ought to be sufficient for them, it is nevertheless not wearisome to warn them once [C. R. *iterum*, “again”] about avoiding anathema.

## CHAPTER XII

The Old Testament consists partly in mysteries and partly in moral commandments. But when Christ came, it ceased with respect to mysteries and carnal observances, because he is the end, or completion, of the law. In moral commandments [C. R. *autem*, “however”], it still remains, because it must always be observed: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [C. R. “and so forth”] (Matthew V; Deuteronomy VI).

Whoever, then, teaches that some carnal observance from the law which is contrary to the New Testament must still be observed is undoubtedly Judaizing with the Galatians, indeed with the Ebionites [*Hebionitis*, “Ebionites”]. Conjugal intercourse among priests is counted among the carnal observances of the law. For to what priests was this alone ever [C. R. *inquam*, “I say”] permitted in the law for the sake of succession? It was because at that time no one from another tribe could attain the priesthood. In our time, however, priests may be chosen from any lineage, and conjugal intercourse is rightly forbidden to them, since they no longer have necessary successors [Col. 1121A].

Therefore whoever, even in this time, teaches with Sozomen—or rather with Ebion [*Ebione*, “Ebion”]—that this Jewish marriage is permitted to priests should not carelessly overlook the unavoidable anathema by which the Apostle himself specifically anathematizes preachers of Jewish observances. He thus deters the Judaizing Galatians:

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be anathema” (Galatians I).

The same Apostle, repeating the warning, adds: “Now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Galatians II).

The same Paul freely rebuked the prince of the apostles himself at Antioch [Col. 1121B], although he was bishop of that see, because by his example—not by preaching—he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, when he withdrew from their table while pretending to do so out of fear of the Jews.

Moreover, the heresiarch Ebion himself, together with all his followers, was anathematized among the other heretics by the most sacred synod of Constantinople and by the blessed Pope Gelasius in the apostolic see. No one who presumes to follow that heresiarch through Sozomen’s chapter will be able to evade this anathema.

## CHAPTER XIII

Some people also seem excessively learned in their own eyes, asserting that incontinence is permitted to priests in the Apostle’s statement: “Let each man have his own wife” (I Corinthians VII) [Col. 1121C]. Such men either do not understand what they say or about what they make assertions (I Timothy I), or, if they do understand, they attack their own consciences.

For, as the blessed Jerome attests, among other matters the Corinthians had asked the Apostle whether carnal intercourse was lawful for those recently reborn in Christ. He replied to them as follows:

“Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (ibid.) [Col. 1121D].

Saint Jerome explains this in Book *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 4:

“The Apostle did not say, ‘Because of fornication, let each man take a wife.’ Otherwise, by this excuse he would have loosened the reins for lust, so that whenever a wife died another should be taken lest we fornicate. Rather, he says, ‘Let each man have his own wife.’ Let him have his own, he says; let him use the wife whom he had before he believed—the wife whom it was good not to touch—and after faith in Christ let him know only a sister, not a wife, unless fornication made his touching her excusable, and so forth. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.

“I ask you, what kind of good is that which forbids prayer, which does not permit the reception of Christ’s body? For as long as I fulfill the duty of a husband, I do not fulfill that of one who practices continence. The same Apostle commands elsewhere that we should pray always (I Thessalonians V). [C. R. *Ergo*, “Therefore”] If we must always pray, we must never be subject to marriage, since whenever I render the debt to my wife I cannot pray.”

Thus the Apostle Peter also teaches Christians to honor the weaker feminine vessel, abstaining from conjugal intercourse lest their prayers be hindered (I Peter III).

Who, then, in sound mind would apply the Apostle’s foregoing statements about the exercise of conjugal intercourse to priests, whose daily duty is not only to pray but also to handle the divine sacraments—especially since in the same passage continence is enjoined even upon every Christian during the time of prayer [Col. 1122B]? For if the Apostle were here granting carnal intercourse even to priests, he would plainly contradict himself, since, writing to Titus, he commands that priests be sober, just, and continent (Titus I).

Therefore here he ministers not to priests but to laymen—and to these not solid food but milk (Hebrews V), that is, to neophytes who were not yet sufficiently instructed either for themselves or for others. To such persons the same Apostle entirely denies priestly office.

By the same reasoning it is proved that whatever the same Apostle writes about exercising conjugal intercourse concerns laymen, not priests, such as the statement: “But if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn” (I Corinthians VII). It is better to unite with a lawful husband than to fornicate. And also: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. If you take a wife, you have not sinned. If a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (ibid.) [Col. 1122C].

This, then, is in no way said about priests or others devoted to continence, but only about those who may lawfully marry. Hence Jerome says in the book mentioned above:

“If, I say, a virgin marries, she has not sinned—but not that virgin who has once dedicated herself to the worship of God. For if any of these marries, she will have condemnation, because she has nullified her first faith” (I Timothy V).

But if someone should object that this was said about widows, how much more will it prevail concerning virgins, since even those may not do what was once permitted to them? Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women [Col. 1122D].

If, therefore, the Apostle’s foregoing statements do not grant carnal intercourse to such persons devoted to continence, how much less do they grant it to priests—especially since the former are simply consecrated to continence, whereas the latter have been placed above those who practice continence, both through the venerable laying on of hands and through the anointing of the most holy chrism.

Moreover, the same Apostle permits those to whom he grants conjugal intercourse also to enter lawfully into second marriages. He allows a man released from his wife to take another and grants widows permission to marry (I Corinthians VII). Therefore he in no way includes priests under the permissive statement concerning carnal intercourse; to them, in the Letters to Timothy and Titus [Col. 1123A], he entirely forbade bigamy, commanding that only a husband of one wife be chosen for the priesthood (I Timothy III; Titus I).

For even among the pagans bigamy was not permitted to priests, as the blessed Jerome asserts against Jovinianus:

“Let our people read that, even before our religion shone in the world, it was always considered honorable among matrons to have had only one husband. Through them sacrifices were customarily offered to Fortuna; there was no priest who was a bigamist, no *flamen* who had married twice. Even to this day the hierophants of the Athenians are castrated by drinking hemlock; those men who have been admitted to the pontificate cease to be men.”

But whoever so corrupts the Apostle’s words that, under their perverse interpretation, he invents that incontinence is permitted even to priests is undoubtedly following the heresiarch Nicolas. Clement of Alexandria reports in Book III of the *Stromata*, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 9, that Nicolas prostituted his wife to anyone who wished and taught by this example that promiscuous and common relations with women were permitted to all. This was so, as handed down by the elders, because it is written: “And all things were common to them” (Acts II); among these Nicolas also counted marriages [Col. 1123B].

Therefore, just as that man is reported to have changed the apostolic example into heresy by understanding it too generally and perversely, so these men are noted to have turned the Apostle’s statement, “Let each man have his own wife,” into error by interpreting it too generally and most perversely. Under the same example [Col. 1123C] they obstinately contend, against the same Apostle, that conjugal intercourse is permitted to priests.

Although promiscuous relations with women are more detestable in the sacred orders than relations with a single woman, the corruption of apostolic teaching nevertheless seems less imputable to the heresiarch Nicolas than to these men. He misinterpreted apostolic doctrine at a time when the name of Christianity had scarcely begun, when evangelical and apostolic doctrine had not yet been spread throughout the world and had not yet been confirmed by so many signs and powers and by so many most sacred triumphs of the holy martyrs.

These men, however, strive with the utmost obstinacy to corrupt that same doctrine, already known even to the rustic, already long ago—or rather from ancient times—consecrated by the blood of the holy Fathers and strengthened beyond refutation [Col. 1123D]. Therefore they will not be able to evade the destruction which the prince of the apostles assigns to corrupters of Scripture. He commends to us the letters of his fellow apostle Paul in these words:

“In them,” he says, “are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction. Therefore, brothers, since you know this beforehand, guard yourselves, lest, being led astray by the error of the foolish, you fall from your own steadfastness.”

To make it clearer that in the foregoing statements the Apostle granted carnal intercourse not to priests but to laymen, let us carefully examine what the same Apostle decrees that ministers of holy things [C. R. “sacred ministers”] [Col. 1124A] must observe, and to whom he determines that the sacred orders may be granted or denied. For in the same apostolic institution, perpetual silence is plainly imposed upon the defenders of priestly incontinence, and the aforesaid statutes of our apostolic authority are irrefutably strengthened. They deny sacred office to no one except those whom the apostolic commands themselves entirely exclude from the sacred order.

## CHAPTER XIV

The blessed Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, bears witness concerning the sacred orders as follows:

“Faithful is the saying: if anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work. Therefore a bishop must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, chaste, well adorned, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, not violent but moderate; not quarrelsome, not greedy, ruling his own household well, having children subject to him with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how will he care for the Church of God? He must not be a recent convert, lest, puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from those outside, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.

“Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not pursuing shameful profit, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. Let these also first be tested, and then let them serve, being without any crime. Women likewise must be chaste, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own households well. For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ the Lord” (I Timothy III) [Col. 1124C].

Likewise, to Titus:

“For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains and appoint presbyters in every city, as I instructed you: if anyone is without crime, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For a bishop must be without crime, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not irritable, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful profit, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, continent, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it [Col. 1124D].

“For there are many disobedient people, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision. They must be rebuked, because they overturn whole households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful profit” (Titus I).

And shortly afterward:

“Rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in the faith and pay no attention to Jewish myths and the commandments of men who turn others away from the truth [Latin *aversantium*; C. R. *avertentium se*, ‘turning themselves away’]” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XV

First, therefore, it must be noted that in these apostolic institutions presbyters are also included under the name of bishop. For the Apostle would introduce the subject of deacons immediately after describing the bishop incongruously if he did not also include presbyters under the description of the bishop; they are next after the bishop and are unquestionably placed above the deacons [Col. 1125A].

Either, then, he said nothing anywhere about the ordination of presbyters, or he described them under the name of bishops. It would plainly be incongruous to describe the minister while passing over the teacher, since the teacher was more necessary to ecclesiastical arrangements. Moreover, when the Apostle commands Titus to appoint presbyters throughout the cities, immediately informing him about their ordination, he adds: “A bishop must be without crime” (ibid.).

He writes similarly to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (I Timothy I). Immediately afterward he says to him: “Do not lay hands upon anyone hastily” (I Timothy V), which properly belongs to bishops [Col. 1125B]. Therefore he calls the same man a bishop whom he also called a presbyter.

Thus the blessed Jerome [Note: [Col. 1125D] On this saying of Saint Jerome, see Bellarmine, *On the Clergy*, chapter 15.] and the holy Father Ambrose, faithfully explaining the Apostle’s foregoing statements, testify that among the ancients a bishop and a presbyter were the same, so that one name referred to the office and the other to age. Later, as Jerome asserts, when each man considered those whom he had baptized to belong to himself rather than to Christ, it was decreed throughout the whole world, in order to remove schisms, that one of the presbyters should be placed over the others, with responsibility for the whole Church.

After describing the bishop and presbyter, the Apostle carefully adds a decree concerning deacons:

“A deacon likewise”—that is, he must be chaste, and so forth (I Timothy III).

It is as though he were saying: “Know that what I decreed concerning bishops and presbyters I have likewise decreed concerning deacons.” It is therefore sufficiently clear, as I judge, that in his foregoing definitions the Apostle included presbyters together with bishops and deacons.

Accordingly, any one of them is rightly removed from the sacred offices if he is proved to have corrupted in himself the apostolic instruction. For the Apostle testifies that bishops, presbyters, and deacons must not be greedy for shameful profit (Titus I). Every Simoniac, however, is unquestionably greedy for the most shameful and wicked profit. Therefore he is in no way to be counted among the sacred orders, having long ago been entirely separated from them by apostolic judgment [Col. 1125D].

It must also be noted that if a neophyte is not admitted among the sacred orders, although he is believed able to be saved among the laity, how much more must the greedy or avaricious be excluded from them—those who are servants of idols and who, according to the Apostle, have no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (Ephesians V)?

Likewise the Apostle commands above that bishops, presbyters, and deacons be chaste, that is, continent. Nor is this surprising, since he also exhorts laymen to continence, saying: “I wish that all men were as I myself am” (I Corinthians VII)—that is, continent. Likewise: “It remains that those who have wives should live as though they had none” (ibid.). And: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Ephesians V) [Col. 1126A].

Hence Jerome says:

“If Christ,” he says, “loves the Church holily, chastely, and without any stain, husbands too should love their wives in chastity.”

And:

“Let each one know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God” (I Thessalonians IV).

Jerome interprets this honor as follows:

“If we abstain from intercourse,” he says, “we grant honor to the feminine vessel; if we do not abstain, it is clear that insult is contrary to honor.”

Moreover, when the whole people of the children of Israel was about to approach the mountain [C. R. “Sinai”] and hear God’s utterance only from a distance, it was commanded to sanctify itself for three days and abstain from its wives (Exodus XIX). Rightly, therefore, the Apostle forbids incontinence to ministers of sacred things [C. R. “enjoins continence”], who ought also to excel secular people in chastity and who, having become the mouth of the Holy Spirit himself, must daily intercede with the Lord for the people [Col. 1126B].

Whoever among them, then, is found to be incontinent is forbidden by the Apostle himself to participate in the sacred orders, since through incontinence he appears to have removed himself from the apostolic institution. For what the Apostle says—“the husband of one wife”—is to be understood, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, as referring only to the period before ordination, not after it.

Thus Saint Cyprian says in the book *On the Twelve Abuses* [Note: [Col. 1126D] This book is not considered to be by Saint Cyprian]:

“Such should a bishop be that before his episcopate he had had only one wife, not several.”

Hence Saint Jerome also says in his *Apology to Pammachius* [Col. 1126C]:

“Bishops, presbyters, and deacons are either chosen as virgins or as widowers; or certainly, after the priesthood, they remain chaste forever.”

Likewise the blessed Zacharias, an apostolic man, writing to Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz (Letter 1), decreed as follows:
