“When your Fraternity sits in council at Mainz with the illustrious man Carloman, if you find any bishops, presbyters, or deacons to have transgressed against the canons or the statutes of the Fathers—that is, to have committed adultery, or to have had several wives, or to have shed the blood of Christians or pagans, or to have violated the canons in any other matters—your holiness must by no means permit them, by apostolic authority, to exercise the priesthood. Such men are falsely called priests by their own mouths and are known to be worse and more depraved than secular people, who neither abstain from fornication nor from wicked marriages nor keep their hands innocent from the shedding of human blood.

“What sort of priests do they think themselves to be, or what do they think of the matter, when God says, ‘My priests shall marry only once,’ and the Apostle says, ‘the husband of one wife,’ and so forth? This was permitted before the priesthood was received. From the day on which they receive the priesthood, however, they must be forbidden even their own marriage” [Col. 1126D].

Hence Jerome, writing to Vigilantius, testifies:

“The Churches of the East and of Egypt, and the apostolic see, accept as clerics either virgins or continent men; or, if they have had wives, they cease to be husbands” [Col. 1127A].

For how, according to the same Apostle, could they practice continence, as has been stated, if they were to practice incontinence with their wives? Since these things are contrary, they cannot exist together in any way.

Here too we must carefully examine that the Apostle ordered men to be chosen for the priesthood not those who had already fathered children through incontinence, but those who had long before had adult and well-raised children.

Note also that the Apostle did not count the disobedient and empty talkers among the sacred orders. Rather, he commanded that skilled priests be appointed to rebuke those who overturn whole households, teaching what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful profit. He also commands that they be rebuked sharply, lest they attend to Jewish myths and the commandments of men who turn others away from the truth [Latin *aversantium*; C. R. *avertentium se*, ‘turning themselves away’]. Such are those who, according to the command of Paul of Samosata or Ebion, teach that Jewish incontinence is permitted to Christian priests [Col. 1127B].

What wonder, then, if our apostolic authority likewise removed such disobedient men from the sacred office, whom the Apostle decreed should be rebuked sharply and not counted among the sacred orders? Do you see, then, how unavoidably the statutes of our Gregory must be observed, since we see that they have been derived from the most sacred fountain of Scripture?

It must be understood that the Apostle established that those to be ordained, or those already ordained, should be without crime, not without sin. For in this world no one, according to Augustine, except baptized infants, lives without sin, as the Lord’s beloved John himself attests: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Likewise James, the Lord’s brother: “For we all offend in many things” (James 3). Yet many are found to be without crime. Hence blessed Augustine, in Tractate 61 on the Gospel of John, testifies:

“Clearly, many have been called righteous and blameless, which is understood as ‘without crime.’ No just complaint can be made in human affairs against those who have no crime. Crime, however, is a serious sin, worthy of accusation and condemnation.”

Therefore, whoever has committed so grave a sin ought not, according to the Apostle, to retain sacred orders. But so that this apostolic institution concerning sacred orders may become clearer to us, let us not hesitate to consider the exposition of blessed Jerome on the same subject. In his book Against Jovinianus (chapters 19 and 20), he elucidates it as follows:

## CHAPTER XVI

“But the very episcopal election also supports my position. For he does not say, ‘Let a bishop be chosen who takes one wife and begets children,’ but rather, ‘one who has had one wife and has children subject to him in complete discipline.’ Surely you admit that a man who begets children while in the episcopate cannot be a bishop. Otherwise, if he is discovered, he will not be treated as a husband but condemned as an adulterer. Either allow priests to engage in marital relations, so that virgins and husbands are alike; or, if priests may not touch their wives, then they are holy in this respect because they imitate virginal chastity. But this too must be added: If a layman, and any believer, cannot pray unless he abstains from marital relations, then a priest, who must always offer sacrifices for the people and must always pray, must also abstain continually. If he must always pray, therefore he must always abstain from marriage. For under the old law those who offered sacrifices for the people were not only absent from their own homes, but were also purified, separated from their wives, and did not drink wine or strong drink (Leviticus 10), things that commonly provoke lust. Husbands are chosen for the priesthood. I do not deny that there are not as many virgins as there are priests needed. But just because the strongest men must be chosen for an army, are the weaker not also admitted, since everyone cannot be strong? If an army consisted only in strength and not also in the number of its soldiers, the weaker would be rejected. Now men of second- and third-rank strength are also admitted, so that the army may be completed in multitude and numbers.

“‘How then,’ you ask, ‘does it frequently happen in priestly ordination that a virgin priest is overlooked and a married man is chosen?’ Perhaps the former lacks other works appropriate to virginity; or he is thought to be a virgin but is not; or his virginity is disreputable; or, certainly, his virginity produces pride in him. While he congratulates himself on bodily chastity alone, he neglects the other virtues: he does not care for the poor, or he is more desirous of money. Sometimes a gloomy face, a knitted brow, and a gait resembling a ceremonial processional litter offend the people. And because they have nothing to criticize in his life, they hate only his clothing and his manner of walking. Many are chosen not out of love for themselves but out of hatred for another. In many cases simplicity alone earns support, and it is set against another’s prudence and cleverness as though these were wickedness. Sometimes the judgment of the common people and the crowd is mistaken; and in approving priests, each person favors his own ways, seeking not so much a good superior as one like himself. It sometimes happens that husbands, who form the larger part of the people, applaud husbands as though they were applauding themselves; and they think that they are no lesser than virgins if they prefer a married man to a virgin.

“I shall say something that I may perhaps utter to the offense of many, but good men will not be angry with me, because their conscience of sin will not trouble them. Sometimes this too happens through the fault of bishops, because they choose not the better but the more clever for the clergy, and consider the simple and innocent incapable; or because they distribute ecclesiastical offices to relatives and kinsmen as though these were offices in an earthly army; or because they obey the commands of the wealthy. What is worse, they grant clerical rank to those whose attentions have captivated them. Otherwise, if, according to the Apostle’s judgment, only husbands may be bishops, the Apostle himself ought not to have been a bishop, since he said: ‘I wish that all were as I myself am’ (1 Corinthians 7). John too would be considered unworthy of this rank, as would all virgins and continent persons with whom, like beautiful jewels, the Church’s necklace is adorned. Bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not names of merits but of offices. Nor does he say, ‘If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good rank,’ but ‘he desires a good work’ (1 Timothy 3), so that, established in the higher order, he may, if he wishes, have the opportunity to practice the virtues.

“Therefore a bishop must be blameless (1 Timothy 3), so that he is enslaved to no vice; the husband of one wife, who has had one wife and does not have one now; sober—or, as it is better expressed in Greek, watchful, that is, νηφάλεον (*nēphaleon*). Chaste—for this is what σώφρονα means [C. R., Σώφρων (*sōphrōn*)]. Decorated both by chastity and by conduct. Hospitable, so that he may imitate Abraham and receive Christ with strangers, indeed in strangers (Genesis 18). A teacher, for it is of no benefit to enjoy the consciousness of virtues unless he can also instruct the people entrusted to him, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it. Not addicted to wine, because he who is always in the Holy of Holies and offers sacrifices does not drink wine or strong drink (Leviticus 10), since there is debauchery in wine. Let a bishop drink in such a way that no one knows whether he has drunk. Not a striker—that is, one who does not strike the consciences of individuals; for the apostolic passage is not describing a boxer but instructing a bishop concerning what he must not do. It now teaches, by contrast, what he should do: to be modest, not quarrelsome, not greedy, managing his household well, having children subject to him with complete chastity. See how much chastity is required of a bishop: if his children are unchaste, he himself cannot be a bishop; and by the same office he would offend God by which the priest Eli offended him. Eli had indeed rebuked his sons, but because he had not expelled the offenders, he fell backward and died (1 Samuel 4), the lamp of God before it was extinguished. ‘Women likewise chaste,’ and so forth. In every rank and sex, chastity holds the chief place. You therefore see that a bishop, presbyter, and deacon are not blessed merely because they are bishops, presbyters, or deacons, but if they possess the virtues appropriate to their names and offices. Otherwise, if a deacon is holier than his bishop, he will not be worse before Christ because he is lower in rank. Far be it that Stephen the deacon, who was crowned with the first martyrdom, should be lesser in the heavenly kingdom than many bishops and than Timothy and Titus—whom, just as I would not dare to subordinate, so I would not dare to place above them.”

Thus far Jerome.

How great Jerome’s authority was, even among the bishops of the apostolic see, is sufficiently indicated by the decrees of blessed Pope Gelasius (On Apocryphal Scriptures), because they decree that his writings are to be received among authentic and canonical authorities, just as the writings or treatises of Saint Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and the other holy Fathers are to be received—those who deviated neither in faith nor in preaching from the holy Roman Church, but remained in communion with it until the end of their lives. Indeed, in the aforesaid decrees blessed Gelasius commends the authority of Saint Jerome to us so highly that he there decrees that the writings of others are to be received or rejected according to Jerome’s judgment.

Therefore, whoever wishes to render due obedience to the apostolic see will in no way resist the individual judgments of such holy Fathers. Let what has been said about what the Apostle requires of priests suffice for now. Whoever considers it faithfully will by no means judge that the statutes of our apostolic ruler should be erased. Nor can anyone despise them unless he wishes to resist the judgments of the apostles themselves, to whom Truth itself most faithfully promises in the Gospel:

“Nevertheless I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment” than for those who did not receive your words (Matthew 11; Luke 10).

## CHAPTER XVII

The fourth decree of our apostolic ruler commands that the people not accept the services of clerics whom they recognize as opposed to the sacred canons, indeed to evangelical and apostolic institutions—namely, those whom, according to the judgment of the holy Fathers, they see ministering at the altar to their own destruction, although they have already been condemned. For the Council of Antioch, unquestionably confirmed by the most sacred Council of Chalcedon, as we stated above, most strictly forbids peoples to accept the services of condemned clerics. It judges that even those who have merely communicated with clerics whom they know to have usurped a ministry forbidden to them should be expelled from the church.

Thus the fourth canon of that same council testifies (in Gratian, 11, question 3, chapter 6):

“If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop, according to the earlier custom, or a presbyter or deacon—in no way may he have either the hope of restoration in another synod or any place for making satisfaction. Moreover, all who communicate with him must be expelled from the church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the aforesaid men, they have attempted to communicate with them.”

According to the tenor of this canon, the holy Fathers who had promulgated the most sacred canons at Chalcedon judged that all those who communicated with a certain condemned Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, were excommunicated. When the emperor Leo consulted them on behalf of Timothy, they replied as follows:

“We judge that even those who, knowing Timothy to have been condemned, believed that they could communicate with him without danger are strangers to the Church of God. According to the regular rule, no pardon or hope of restoration in any way remains for them, just as the eighty-third canon clearly decrees concerning such persons. Its beginning is: ‘If any bishop has been condemned by a synod,’ and so forth.”

[Note: Concerning Timothy Aelurus, see Baronius, volume 6, in the year of Christ 457, numbers 12 and following, and in the years 460 and 475–477. What Bernald cites here does not come from the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon, but from certain bishops in a letter to the emperor Leo. Together with other letters written by distinguished persons on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon, it is found at the end of the Council of Chalcedon, volume 2 of the new edition of the Councils, Cologne, folio 161, column 2.]

Therefore our apostolic ruler rightly forbade the people to accept the services of such clerics—of those, I mean, whom he himself did not so much condemn as demonstrate to have been condemned long ago by the holy Fathers.

Moreover, the most holy Pope Alexander, fifth after blessed Peter, who chose to be burned in a fiery furnace rather than lie, that most courageous athlete, testifies that one must not even speak with those against whom a bishop is judged to be opposed on account of their crimes. He confirms this from the authority of the chief of the apostles himself, saying in chapter 6 (Letter 1):

“Blessed Peter [C. R., ‘chief of the apostles’], while instructing the clergy and people at the ordination of our holy predecessor Clement, said: ‘If Clement is an enemy to anyone on account of his deeds, do not wait for him himself to tell you, “Do not be friends with that man.” Rather, you must observe carefully, obey his will without alteration [*commonitione*, ‘admonition’; thus the Roman edition], and turn away from the one toward whom you perceive him to be opposed. Nor should you speak with those with whom he does not speak, so that each person who is guilty, while desiring to retain the friendship of all of you, may hasten to be reconciled to him who presides over all; and by this may return to salvation once he begins to obey the warnings of the ruler. But if anyone is friendly with those with whom he himself does not speak [‘with whom he himself is not a friend, and speaks with them,’ Roman edition], he is himself one of those who wish to destroy the Church of God. Although he may seem to be with you in body, in mind and spirit he is against you. Such an enemy is much worse than those who are outside and are openly hostile. For under the appearance of friendship he does what is hostile, and he scatters and devastates the Church.’”

Where, then, the chief of the apostles himself so strictly forbids anyone even to speak with those who are found not to obey apostolic institutions, there he also most clearly forbids the people to receive Masses and other services of this kind from them. For, according to Augustine (Letter 86 to Casulanus), “the custom of the people of God must be held as law.” This confirms, together with the canons, that the people should hear the Mass of any priest and respond to each of his greetings during Mass. Therefore the people will in no way receive the Masses of such transgressors if they wish to observe the judgment of the chief of the apostles himself.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The most holy Pope Gregory, writing to the kings of the Franks concerning such priests, contemptuous of the canons, testifies in chapter 135 [C. R., 75] (Book 7, Letter 116) “that the kingdom is burdened by the guilt of such priests.” Shortly afterward he added:

“Greater calamity must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought into positions of government—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to have appeased it on behalf of the people.”

Therefore the Gregory of our own time rightly prohibited the people from accepting the services of such presumptuous men. His most holy namesake asserted that they burdened the kingdom by their guilt and provoked God’s anger against themselves all the more. For it is written:

“Whoever turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be accursed” (Proverbs 28).

All who stubbornly resist the canons and decrees are bound by this crime. Hence the services of those whose prayers almighty God—I do not say merely does not receive, but curses—are rightly forbidden to the people.

But let us now come to the Vessel of Election himself, who is undoubtedly in harmony with the present statute of our apostolic ruler:

“If the man who is called a brother among you is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a person you must not even eat” (1 Corinthians 5).

This refers, plainly, to those who refuse to be corrected according to ecclesiastical decrees, although they are bound by certain and public crimes.

Likewise, to the Thessalonians:

“We command you, brothers, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition that they received from us” (2 Thessalonians 3).

And shortly afterward:

“If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark him, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed” (ibid.).

With those, therefore, with whom the Apostle does not permit the faithful even to eat bodily food, and from whose companionship he commands the faithful to withdraw, our apostolic ruler also commands the people not to communicate with these same despisers of apostolic institution even at the Lord’s table, and to withdraw from their society at least at the time when they usurp the sacred mysteries unlawfully and unjustly, to their own destruction.

For, according to the Apostle:

“Whoever eats the Lord’s bread and drinks the cup unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

All who presume not only to practice fornication or greed but also to defend them stubbornly do this. Concerning such persons the Apostle says:

“Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (Galatians 5).

These men, although condemned for the same crimes according to canonical decrees, nevertheless persist in their forbidden office through reckless usurpation. Indeed, those whom we properly call penitents, although they submit their necks to canonical discipline for such crimes, do not therefore approach the divine sacraments so rashly. Hence, according to the judgment of blessed Pope Innocent (Letter 29, Roman edition), not even sick penitents may be anointed with sacred chrism like other sick persons:

“For to those,” he says [also in On Consecration, distinction 3, ‘But concerning penitents’], “to whom the other sacraments are denied, how can it be thought that one kind of sacrament may be granted?”

They might otherwise acquire condemnation rather than remission if, being so unworthy and not yet fully cleansed through penance, they received the same sacraments.

If, therefore, even penitents who are making canonical satisfaction for their crimes are judged unworthy of the divine sacraments, how much more are those unworthy who do not repent but stubbornly attempt to defend their faults, already made public long ago? By stubbornly resisting the canons [C. R., “the canons”], they are also shown to blaspheme the Holy Spirit.

Thus blessed Pope Damasus testifies in his letter to Saint Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage (25, question 1, chapter 5, “Violators”):

“Voluntary violators of the canons are judged severely by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were composed. For those who, not compelled by necessity but willingly, as stated above, act insolently against the sacred canons, presume to speak against them, or willingly consent to those who wish to act against them, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption is plainly one kind of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, because, as has already been indicated, it acts against him by whose command and grace the holy canons were issued.”

Therefore those priests who are bound by such grave crimes, indeed those who have already been condemned for them according to canonical institutions, can in no way offer sacrifice except to their own destruction. Accordingly, those too have committed no small offense who knowingly presume to cooperate, through the customary responses at Mass, with men who usurp the right to sacrifice to their own death. It would not be considered a minor crime if someone knowingly cooperated with another who was cruelly killing himself.

Our apostolic ruler therefore acted most wisely in prohibiting the people from taking part in the usurpations of such presumptuous men. He understood that these practices were harmful not only to those who conducted them but also to those who received them. Thus the Lord himself commanded the rest of the children of Israel to withdraw from Korah and his followers when they usurped the office of sacrifice (Numbers 16), lest they become entangled in their sins and thereby deserve to be condemned with them by a most cruel death. For the heresiarchs themselves—Korah, Dathan, and Abiram—descended alive and suddenly into hell with all their possessions. Their followers, however, deserved to be utterly consumed by the fire that went forth from the Lord (ibid.). Those who stubbornly usurp, contrary to right and law, the priestly office forbidden to them should carefully attend to the sudden and most severe punishment of these men.

Nor should they thoughtlessly overlook the death of Uzzah. When David was bringing the ark of the Lord back from Philistia on a new cart, Uzzah was struck down by the Lord and died because, although the ark was already falling, he presumed to support it with his hand (2 Samuel 6). If the man deserved to perish who rashly, though with good intention, merely touched the ark of the Lord, how much more does one deserve to perish who, unworthy, presumes contrary to right and law to handle the very body of the Lord and incorporate it into himself?

## CHAPTER XIX

Some, however, quite ineptly bring against our apostolic ruler the fourth canon of the Council of Gangra:

“Whoever distinguishes himself from a presbyter who has had a wife, on the ground that one ought not to receive from the offering while he is ministering, let him be anathema.”

They corrupt this canon, to their own destruction, according to the testimony of the apostle Peter (2 Peter 3), and pronounce it in this form:

“Whoever refuses the Mass of a married presbyter, let him be anathema.”

That is, they seek to demonstrate that those who, obeying apostolic institutions, decline to receive the Masses of incontinent presbyters are themselves anathematized.

But in vain. For the aforesaid canon anathematizes only those who reject the offering of a presbyter who does not now have a wife but once had one. At that time, as the prologue to the Council of Gangra testifies, there were heretics who followed a certain Eustasius [Eustathius]. They condemned lawful marriage as though it were a mortal crime, asserting that no one placed in the married state could have hope before God. Consequently, they are said to have rejected the offerings of presbyters who had been lawfully married even before ordination. They regarded lawful marriage as a mortal crime, just as anyone discovered to have committed such a crime at the present time is not permitted by the canons to minister at the altar.

These same heretics were therefore rightly anathematized, since they taught against the Apostle’s statement:

“If you take a wife, you have not sinned” (1 Corinthians 7),

and against this:

“A bishop must be the husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3; Titus 1).

The frequently mentioned statute of our apostolic ruler, however, forbids no one to hear the Mass of a presbyter who, in accordance with apostolic permission, had only one wife before sacred ordination, at a time when he could take a wife without crime. Rather, it forbids the Mass of that presbyter who is found, contrary to the Apostle, to lie in the crime of fornication—one whom the apostles themselves, the other holy Fathers, and their successor, our apostolic ruler, separated from the most sacred office.

Therefore, whoever rejects the Masses of such presbyters will in no way be subject to the earlier anathema of the Eustasians [Eustathians], since he agrees perfectly with the Apostle, who both enjoins continence upon priests and does not permit the faithful to associate with transgressors against his words.

It should also be noted that our Gregory, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers, first deprived incontinent presbyters of their office and afterward forbade the people to receive their services. Hence he prohibited the hearing not so much of the Masses of incontinent men as of those condemned for incontinence, lest the people too should be placed under excommunication if they presumed to receive their services according to the Council of Antioch.

The Holy Spirit himself, through the prophet Samuel, teaches the people to obey the canonical institutions of our apostolic ruler rather than receive the sacrifices of such presumptuous men to their own danger. Scripture says:

“Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen than to offer the fat of rams; for to resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to acquiesce is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15).

Therefore the people, obeying apostolic institutions, rightly refuse the services—or [C. R., “sacrifices”—] and sacred rites of disobedient priests [Col. 1135A], lest through disobedience they too incur the crime of idolatry. The Lord likewise declares elsewhere:

“I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9),

that is, so that anyone who pleases God may, through obedience, have mercy on his own soul (Ecclesiasticus 30)—on the soul that most deserves mercy—rather than offer sacrifice to the Lord either personally or through another in disobedience.

It is worth considering how mercifully our apostolic ruler treated even the despisers of the canons in the statutes discussed above. He merely removed them from an office in which they could celebrate only to their own destruction if, while resisting canonical decrees, they continued to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. He has not yet punished their long-standing obstinacy with the severity it deserved, but waited for them with paternal affection, so that they might at least then return to their senses and recognize their own condemnation when they could not deny that the people had been rightly forbidden to receive their services.

## CHAPTER XX

Perhaps someone will say: Why did our Gregory command that statutes so contrary to our custom be observed? Why did he not rather tolerate our custom through a merciful act of concealment?

Let such a person hear what blessed Pope Leo, who presided [through legates] over the most sacred Council of Chalcedon, decreed (Letter 54, to the emperor Marcian). Restraining the presumption of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, he pronounced:

“that it should be counted as a charge against the Roman pontiff if the institution of the canons were violated anywhere while he did not prohibit it and, as it were, connived at it.”

[Note: The passage of Saint Leo in the same letter reads: “It would be charged to me if, with my connivance—which God forbid!—the rules of the Fathers’ decrees, which were established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God, were violated; and if, in my estimation, the will of one brother were more important than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord.”]

Likewise, the most holy namesake of our apostolic ruler, writing to Bishop Victor (Register, Book 10, Letter 32), delivered this terrible and general judgment:

“Whoever, in consideration of his office, does not burn intensely to correct this crime—namely, the heresy of Simony or of the Neophytes—should not doubt that he shares in the portion of the one from whom this abominable wickedness first took its origin.”

Therefore anyone who, in fulfillment of his office, does not strive to prohibit that heresy of the heresiarch Ebion—that is, Jewish incontinence—from modern priests is likewise shown to be a participant in Ebion’s heresy.

The most sacred councils themselves, from which the statutes of our apostolic ruler had flowed, were embraced by the holy Fathers to such a degree that, as their writings testify, they preferred to permit themselves to be afflicted by various tortures, indeed to be cruelly killed, rather than consent to violators of those decrees. For this reason the great Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, was deported into exile after various calamities. For this reason too Felix, Roman pope, is read to have been removed from the episcopate [C. R., “expelled”] and crowned with martyrdom. Many of his presbyters, deacons, and other members of the clergy are also read to have been most cruelly killed, alas, even inside the Church, for the same reason: they did not wish to assent to the followers of Arius in violating the Council of Nicaea. You can readily gather innumerable examples of this kind from ecclesiastical histories.

Let someone therefore explain how our apostolic ruler could, without his own danger—or rather destruction—neglect to oppose, as his office required, not merely the violators but the attackers of decrees that could not be evaded, when he knew that the holy Fathers themselves had resisted them even to the shedding of blood.

Although some now do not attack the faith of the holy Fathers as openly as Arius and the other heresiarchs did, nevertheless they obstinately resist their moral statutes, which were confirmed by those same holy Fathers at the same time and by the same subscription as the faith itself. These statutes too proceeded from the most sacred source of Scripture together with that same faith. In this most wicked rebellion of theirs, they are shown to nullify even the faith of the holy Fathers, since in authentic decrees they regard as worthless the authority of those who had confirmed the faith by their authority.

The faith of the holy Fathers will certainly benefit no one who strives not to obey their canonical and moral commandments but stubbornly to resist them. For, as James, the Lord’s brother, testifies:

“Faith without works is dead” (James 2),

and he acknowledges that the demons possess such faith.

Therefore one must resist stubborn attackers of authentic institutions no less than violators of the sacred faith, since all who follow the institution of the holy Fathers only in faith and not, to the extent of their strength, in conduct are made like the demons. They do not fear, through diabolical instigation, stubbornly to defend the fault that it was human to commit.

Furthermore, the Vessel of Election himself says in his own person to all ecclesiastical pastors:

“If I preach the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9).

How, then, could our apostolic ruler escape this woe if he neglected to instruct the flock entrusted to him according to the Apostle’s commands?

The Holy Spirit also, through the prophet Ezekiel, sets before every pastor a terrifying condition:

“If,” he says, “you do not say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die,’ and show him how to turn away from his iniquities, he himself will die in his sins, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you do say it, and he despises it and does not obey, he will die in his crimes; but you will save your soul” (Ezekiel 33).

Saint Augustine uses this translation in his sermon on Psalm 49, and immediately adds to his listeners:

“I say to you, I free my soul. For I am placed in great danger—not merely danger, but destruction—if I remain silent.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear how unjustly certain people are indignant against our apostolic ruler for the statutes discussed above. He is shown to have established them under the compulsion of such unavoidable necessity, namely, so that he would not incur the crime of his own death by neglecting to instruct us as his office required.

## CHAPTER XXI

Moreover, if they strive to be indignant against our apostolic ruler for this reason, why are they not rather indignant against the 318 holy Fathers assembled at Nicaea and the 630 Fathers assembled or gathered at Chalcedon? As stated above, they pronounced much more severe judgments against Simonians and incontinent ministers of the altar than our apostolic ruler did.

Let them be indignant, then, against the most holy Pope Clement, who confirmed his decrees by his martyrdom and whom the chief of the apostles himself appointed as his successor. For it is read in his decrees, chapter 46, that he entirely removed the incontinent from the office of the altar, prohibited clerics from cohabiting with foreign women, and utterly anathematized violators of this institution.

Let them also be indignant against the most blessed Pope Sylvester, who, established in the apostolic see, prohibited incontinence among the presbyters of the whole world, as stated above, and decreed that all who resisted this decree were to be condemned forever.

Let them also be indignant against Pope Damasus, of blessed memory, by whose authority the Second Ecumenical Council, that of Constantinople, is read to have been confirmed; and likewise against the most holy Pope Leo, guide of the Chalcedonian canons. Both of them, with the same apostolic authority, decreed the following generally in their statutes—Damasus in chapter 4 and Leo in chapter 5:

“We command that all the decretal constitutions of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons, must be observed by all bishops and by all priests generally, so that whoever commits an offense against them may know that pardon will thereafter be denied him.”

Let them also be indignant against the most holy namesake of our apostolic ruler, who condemned under a general anathema all who dissented from the four most sacred councils.

But since no person of sound mind is indignant at the judgments of such holy Fathers, it is entirely evident how irrationally certain people are indignant at the institutions of our apostolic ruler. In promulgating them he differed in no way from the holy Fathers, except only in this: he did not confront the despisers of the canons with as much severity as they did. He merely deprived those clerics of their office whom the holy Fathers denied not only office but also pardon and ecclesiastical communion.

Finally, our apostolic ruler imposed nothing new upon us for observance. Even if he had done so, his command could not have been despised without danger. For, by divine acknowledgment, the apostolic see has always possessed and will always possess this primacy: to govern the churches of the whole world not only by ancient institutions but also by new ones, as the needs of different times require.

“For,” Augustine says to Boniface, “the experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.”

The various decrees of the Roman pontiffs certainly testify to this, for in them they are read to have provided for the differing needs of different times.

## Chapter XXII

But in vain do public contemners of the apostolic institution seek from our apostolic lord a postponement of their condemnation: those whom, as has been said, the holy Fathers condemned without any postponement. For in doubtful matters, although they may be true, but have not yet been made public, postponements are necessarily granted so that, in accordance with the decrees of the apostolic men Felix, Julius, and the others, the accused himself may fully prepare to defend himself against his accusers and clear himself of the charges. Hence also the blessed Eleutherus, the twelfth after the blessed Peter, testifies in his decretals, chapter 1:

> “A considerable postponement must be granted for investigation, lest anything appear to be done rashly by either party, because many things come about through surreptitious deception.””

Rightly, therefore, those are condemned without postponement who do not deny that their guilt was long ago definitively condemned by the holy Fathers, but publicly attempt to defend it against the apostolic statutes.

Indeed, the blessed Gregory, rightly to be imitated by every Catholic pastor, used to excommunicate contemners of the apostolic see even before the offense had been completed. Thus he excommunicated Maximus, who had been enthroned in the bishopric of Salona through ambition, and all those who ordained him; that same excommunication bound them before the offense for which they were excommunicated had been completed. For before Maximus was ordained, Saint Gregory prohibited the act under threat of excommunication, lest they presume to do this [C. R.: “lest this be presumed”]. The bishops who despised that command, when they ordained Maximus, were excommunicated before the ordination had been completed, according to Saint Gregory’s testimony. For in his letter to Maximus himself (Book III, Letter 20), he writes to that presumer [C. R.: “to Maximus”], detesting his consecration:

> “We can in no way call that a consecration which was celebrated by excommunicated men.”

For he did not say that they were to be excommunicated after the ordination, but that they were excommunicated during the ordination itself.

In the same way, through his subdeacon Natalis, he judged that the bishop of Salona was to be deprived of the pallium and of communion without postponement if he did not obey his command (Book II, Letters 14, 15, 16). Thus, I say, he and the other bishops of that same see condemned, without postponement, anyone who rashly usurped something prohibited under excommunication or suspension from office. Let modern presumers therefore carefully consider these and similar arguments, and henceforth not suppose that they have been unjustly condemned without postponement.

## Chapter XXIII

Perhaps someone is so delirious as to say that the subjects of any bishop can be condemned by that bishop alone, and not by the Roman pontiff. But Truth itself in the Gospel contradicts him, for it principally granted this privilege to the blessed Peter among the other apostles:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

Since he subjected all people generally to apostolic authority, he excluded the subject of no bishop whatsoever. Hence that same apostle generally required obedience both from the elders of his time—that is, presbyters or bishops—and from their subjects, since in his letters he gave particular rules of life to subjects and prelates alike, to women as well as men. He would have done this in vain if all were not generally required to obey his instruction.

The blessed Anacletus, ordained presbyter by the prince of the apostles himself, also testifies in his decretals, chapter 111:

> “The most holy Roman and apostolic Church obtained its primacy not from the apostles but from our Lord himself, just as he said to the blessed apostle Peter: ‘You are Peter,’”

and so forth. Therefore this apostolic see was established by the Lord, not by anyone else, as the hinge and head of all the Churches. And just as a door is governed by its hinge, so all the Churches, by the Lord’s arrangement, are governed by the authority of this holy see.

Likewise the blessed Gelasius, an apostolic teacher, says in chapter 11:

> “The whole Church throughout the world knows that the most holy Roman Church has the right to judge concerning every Church, and that no one is permitted to judge its judgment. For an appeal must be made to it from every part of the world, but from it no one is permitted to appeal” [C. R.: “no one is permitted to appeal”].

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see has had the power to release those whom it ought to release without any preceding synod [Note: [Col. 1139] C. R.: “those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and to condemn when no synod existed.”]. This was certainly on account of its primacy, which the apostle Peter both received through the Lord’s own voice [Col. 1139C] and will always retain. The most holy Fathers Callistus, Fabianus, Sixtus, Sylvester, Julius, and countless others support this. They so embraced unity [C. R.: “truth”] that they resolved to die rather than lie.

By the authority of this privilege, therefore, Pope Simplicius [XLIX] completely freed Gregory, bishop of Modena, a suffragan of the archbishop of Ravenna, from the jurisdiction of that archbishop. He did so because the same archbishop had enthroned him unwillingly in the see of Modena.

Likewise Saint Gregory (Book II, Letters 14, 15, 16) restored Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona, who had advanced from the archdeaconate to the presbyterate, to his former rank against the will of his bishop; and he deposed the man whom that bishop of Salona had ordained in his place. Therefore those who rashly prejudice the authority of the apostolic see are plainly deranged and make themselves guilty before it, when they pretend that the subjects of any bishop can be bound or released not by the Roman pontiff but only by their own bishop.

Moreover, Pope Leo, who convened the fourth universal synod at Chalcedon, Pope Vigilius, under whom the fifth universal synod assembled at Constantinople, and the blessed Father Gregory—each of these men, pre-eminent by the same authority, testify with almost one voice in their decrees, most truthfully, as follows:

> “The holy Roman Church has so shared its responsibilities with the other Churches that they have been called to participate in its care, not in the fullness of its power.”

Hence it is clearly demonstrated that no bishop has over the flock entrusted to him as much power as the apostolic prelate. Although he has divided his care among individual bishops, he has in no way deprived himself of his universal and principal power—just as a king does not diminish his royal power although he has divided his kingdom among various dukes, counts, or judges.

Since, therefore, the apostolic lord possesses such principal authority in every Church that, even against the will of the bishop of any Church, he can regulate everything in it according to the canonical decrees, who can deny that throughout the world he can condemn both the subjects of bishops and the bishops themselves when they contemn the apostolic institution?

## Chapter XXIV

These arguments also make clear that the parishioner of any bishop ought to obey the apostolic lord rather than his own bishop, since the authority of his own bishop cannot in any way free him from apostolic condemnation if he has been disobedient to apostolic commands. Conversely, if he obeys the apostolic lord, the apostolic lord can very easily defend him against every violence of his own bishop, either by completely emancipating the parishioner from that bishop’s jurisdiction or by restraining the bishop from injury through correction or condemnation by apostolic authority.

Let the subject of any bishop take care that he does not obey his own bishop in anything contrary to apostolic commands. Saint Gregory (Book II, Letters 15, 16) deposed the archdeacon of Salona who had been substituted in the place of the already deposed Honoratus, because that man had obeyed his own bishop by allowing himself to be ordained in Honoratus’s place after the apostolic prohibition.

From this it is also perfectly clear how deranged are those who say that the subjects of any bishop ought in no way to obey the apostolic see if they obey their own bishop, since Saint Gregory rightly degraded even the man who was discovered, through obedience to his bishop, to have opposed the apostolic see. Indeed, no one can offer due obedience to his own bishop unless he has first endeavored to obey the apostolic see. For everyone who wishes to be a bishop especially impresses this upon his subjects: that they obey the institutions of the holy Fathers without any contradiction. Those institutions, as has been said, declare that all must obey the apostolic see principally.

Whoever, therefore, gives due obedience to his legitimate pastor will also endeavor to obey the apostolic lord above all. For, according to the decree of Truth itself:

> “The disciple is not above the teacher” (Matthew 10).

But if the apostolic lord is rightly placed above one’s own legitimate pastor, how much more above one who does not even strive to be what he is called?

Whoever, therefore, even among the uneducated, faithfully considers these and similar arguments will in no way attempt to proscribe the statutes of our apostolic lord, especially when he sees most clearly that they have proceeded from the judgments of the holy Fathers, indeed from the divine Scriptures. I could append many other arguments to those already given and assign countless examples of the holy Fathers to the aforesaid statutes, but I have omitted them here out of consideration [Col. 1142A], lest I burden the simple, whom I have especially undertaken to satisfy here. A few things drawn from many, of such unquestionable truth, can suffice for them if they wish to devote themselves to seeking the truth rather than to fruitless contention.

**The end.**

## [III. Letters]

### Preface to the Three Following Letters

These three letters seem to have been written before the treatise *On the Sacraments of the Excommunicated*, to which we have assigned the first place among these little works concerning Gregory VII. For here Adalbert and Bernald seem still to be wavering in uncertainty about what ought to be thought concerning the controversies that had arisen in that age. In the aforementioned work, however, Bernald expresses his judgment without any hesitation, although he indicates that much had been debated between himself and Bernard concerning this controversy. That Bernard is none other than the master of the schools at Constance, mentioned above in the preface to these little treatises and in the testimonies for Gregory VII; he later became master of the schools at Hildesheim and finally a monk of Corvey in Saxony. As appears from the second letter, he defended the cause of Saint Peter with the greatest fervor; but because he did not temper his ardor with ecclesiastical learning, he stumbled somewhat, as Bernald himself teaches in his *Chronicle*.

That Adalbert is the man whom Bertold, or Bernald, honors in his *Chronicle* with this eulogy under the year 1079:

> “Doctor Adalbert, eloquent in word and deed, crucified to the world for thirty years and brought at the end to evangelical perfection, migrated to the Lord on the third day before the Nones of December.”

Bernald calls him “Father and lord” as a mark of honor in the second letter.

### On the Condemnation of Those Who Attempted to Discredit the Pope and the Entire Roman Synod, and on the Sacraments of the Condemned

#### First Letter: Adalbert to Bernald

To the lord and venerable priest Bernard, adorned with learning and character, Adalbert, an unworthy presbyter, and his unfailing good [Note: [Col. 1141C] There is a lacuna in the manuscript; read “and his Bernald,” as below in the third letter.]—which is Christ.

We rejoiced greatly over your greeting, but we would rejoice much more if we had any opportunity of meeting one another and carrying on a sweet conversation. Since the necessity of various affairs prevents this, let us at least not hesitate to commend mutual conversation through the service of letters.

[Note: [Col. 1141C] The manuscript codex contains this gloss not in the margin but within the continuous body of the text. This judgment is treated most fully in the letter that follows this one in third place, namely, how impiously these men sinned against the apostolic see, and how canonically the Roman synod condemned them.]

We ask you, therefore, to write back to us something concerning the judgment of the apostolic lord against public and contumacious proscribers of the apostolic see, if anywhere you have found anything authentic opposed to that judgment. For we have not yet found anything contrary to it, although we have examined with exceptional diligence the statutes of various Fathers.

In those statutes we have found two judicial procedures: one concerning public crimes, the other concerning doubtful matters which, although true, have not yet been made public. For the examination of doubtful matters, postponements are recorded as having been granted, so that the accused may prepare himself against his accusers. In such a judgment the presence of both accused and accuser is necessary. But nowhere do we read that postponements must be granted as a matter of obligation in cases of public contumacy. Such a case does not require an accuser or the production of witnesses, since the defendant himself is not ashamed to disclose his crime, nor ought he to delay his condemnation through his absence.

We do not think it necessary to point out these two judicial procedures by examples, since it is judged a great impertinence to offer anything to one more learned.

In accordance with this procedure, the apostolic lord quite canonically condemned, even in their absence, public and contumacious proscribers of the apostolic see. We ask your charity to write back to us what you think about this. We most willingly receive your judgment on the matter, since we have no doubt that you are more diligent and discerning than others in sacred letters.

We would also like to know what you think concerning the confection of sacraments usurped by Simoniacs or by any excommunicated persons—if, that is, such sacraments lack reality. For the most holy Father Augustine testifies:

> “There is no place for a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.”

Therefore there is no place for a true sacrifice among heretics or excommunicated persons.

The most blessed Pope Leo, by whose authority the Council of Chalcedon was convened and confirmed, and whom Saint Gregory compared with the Gospel—Leo, I say, writes to the Emperor Leo concerning a certain condemned bishop Timothy [Note: [Col. 1143D] The intruder in Alexandria, surnamed Aelurus], who was guilty of killing the Alexandrian prelate [Proterius] and had invaded his see through simony. Concerning the sacraments of this Simoniac, Pope Leo writes to the Emperor as follows (Letter 75):

> “It is manifest,” he says, “that through the most cruel and insane savagery every light of the heavenly sacraments was extinguished there [in the Alexandrian see]. The offering of the sacrifice was cut off; the sanctification of the chrism failed; and all the mysteries withdrew from the murderous hands of the impious,”

and so forth.

Saint Gregory also, writing about the rash ordination of Maximus, bishop of Salona (Book III, Letter 20), detests it as follows:

> “Even after our prohibition—which was made under threat of excommunication against you and those who ordained you—you are said, after presbyters, deacons, and the rest of the clergy had been beaten, to have been brought forward by military force. We can in no way call that a consecration which was celebrated by excommunicated men.”

For the bishops who consecrated him were excommunicated.

We therefore await your judgment concerning what we ought to judge about such sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 1143D] Thus the manuscript codex.] After this question the substantial answer begins, though it must be read cautiously in its later portion.

#### Second Letter: Bernald to Adalbert

To Adalbert, a man of delights, the fragrant garden whose lily feeds the stag of Lebanon and in whose shade he lies at midday: Bernard, cauterized like an Ethiopian in the tents of Kedar, condemned to the millhouse in Ur of the Chaldeans, no longer enduring misery—not of the body, but of a soul already exposed to death—offers whatever the devotion of a groaning sinner offers to angelic holiness.

To God, the fountain of mercies and Father of all consolation, I repeat thanks with heart and voice, because he deemed me worthy of your greeting at that time—the sound of whose name restores me—and of the sweetest conversation. Hail, cedar of paradise that knows no corruption; hail, charioteer of Israel; hail, breathing immortality, O healing of souls; hail, rock which the crafty serpent does not rejoice to mark with his tracks, indeed which he shuns because it has been wholly cleansed from every stain of the body. Hail, golden recliner of Solomon’s table, not signifying but signified. Hail, heavenly luminary, shining unquenchably in the midst of a wicked and perverse nation (2 Peter 1).

Although conscience, because of the holiness of the matter, forbids me to carry out your command, and although folly strikes me in the face for presuming to do so, I nevertheless begin, certain that even if I do not know what ought to be said, I do know this: that I obey you, my lord. You therefore command me to set down your own words, written by me to you, concerning the judgment of the apostolic lord against public and contumacious proscribers of the apostolic see, if anywhere I have found anything authentic opposed to that judgment.

It belongs to the apostolic see, as conscious of the divine mystery, to turn the keys of the kingdom of heaven. For, as Pope Anacletus writes:

> “It was established by the Lord, not by anyone else, as the head and hinge of the Churches.”

And just as a door is governed by its hinge, so all the Churches, by the Lord’s arrangement, are governed by the authority of this holy see.

Hence the blessed Gelasius, in a general decree to all bishops concerning ecclesiastical institutions, says:

> “Since we desire to presume that we may do nothing contrary to the reverence due to salutary rules, and since the apostolic see, with the Lord’s favor, diligently strives to preserve with pious and devoted purpose all that has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is most unworthy for anyone, whether among the bishops or among the subordinate orders, to reject this observance, which he sees the see of blessed Peter both following and teaching. It is entirely fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree in this observance of itself, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord has established the primacy of the whole Church.”

Leo likewise writes to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica (Letter 84):

> “Although there is a common dignity among these priests, there is not a general order, since even among the most blessed apostles, despite the similarity of their honor, there was a certain distinction of power. And although the election of all was equal, nevertheless one was given precedence over the others.”

Since the unworthiness of the president does not diminish the excellence of the highest see, that same Leo testifies:

> “Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain; rivals may perhaps bring some disturbance against them, but they cannot diminish their dignity. Yet the prelates of this holy see often tolerated being admonished by their subjects. They did not wish to extinguish the spirit in them. Finally, with ecclesiastical law as guide and teacher, they preferred themselves to live according to the institutions of the canons rather than to oppress their subjects through canonical institutions. When the prince of the apostles, in his dissimulation, compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, his judgment was changed by Paul’s correction, which suggested that Jews should not be prohibited from such practices as though they were abominable, nor Gentiles compelled to them as though they were necessary” [Note: [Col. 1144D] The passage appears mutilated.]

The blessed Gregory says:

> “I am prepared to imitate in good even my inferiors, whom I prohibit from unlawful things. For I would be foolish [the manuscript has “he would be foolish”] if I considered it my first duty to refuse to learn the good things I saw. Even he who had not learned from a human being yielded to the authority of the Corinthians, saying: ‘If you have forgiven anyone anything, I also forgive’ (2 Corinthians 2).”

From this we gather that, although the right and dominion of this see, founded upon the rock which is Christ, cannot be abolished, reason nevertheless permits its prelates sometimes to be admonished.

Concerning the judgment made by the apostolic lord against those whom you call public and contumacious proscribers, I answer according to my foolishness. The pope did what is apostolic when he condemned those whom you said were public and contumacious, provided only that the following letter sufficiently clarifies this doubt, declaring that they were condemned after a written confession, just as Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, is recorded as having been anathematized by Saint Felix the pope, since he had confessed in writing but had not been summoned beforehand by a synod; or after they had truly confessed, or had been regularly convicted; or if, having been canonically summoned to the judgment at which they were to give an account, they refused to come.

Hear, Father, what Saint Augustine, who took part in the Council of Carthage, confirmed by apostolic authority and by 217 Fathers, says about the judgment of that council to the clergy and people of Hippo, among other things (Letter 137):

> “Recently it was established in the council of bishops that no cleric who has not yet been convicted ought to be suspended from communion, unless he has failed to present himself for the examination of his case.”

The council itself demonstrates what that presentation means: either the accused himself, summoned by letter to speak on the appointed day in his own case, must appear; or he must prove some genuine necessity by which it is evident that he was unable to appear. Notice that it says “unable,” not “unwilling.” The same applies to the accuser if he should be unwilling to appear at the annual universal council. Certainly, whether accuser or accused, if someone wished to appear but was unable to do so, he will be absolved by the decrees of the Council of Carthage.

The African synod also agrees, saying:

> “If within a year he has neglected to clear his case.”

Observe the words: it does not say “if he was unwilling,” but “if he neglected.” Hence Augustine says in his book *On Penance*:

> “We cannot exclude anyone from communion, although this exclusion is not yet deadly but medicinal, unless he has either voluntarily confessed, or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. For who would dare assume both roles for himself, so as to be someone’s accuser and judge?”

“For this reason,” says Saint Gelasius, “a particular person is summoned to judgment so that he may either admit the charges or be convicted by the charges.” And the canons of Antioch say:

> “Let all who think themselves injured be present at the councils, and let them undergo the examination of the synod.”

But you say that there are two judicial procedures: one concerning doubtful matters, although they may be true, which requires postponement so that the accused may take counsel and arrange how he can suitably answer the charges; the other concerning manifest matters, for which postponement must not be granted because it is unnecessary. You say that the pope used this latter procedure, by apostolic power, against contumacious bishops.

We accept what you assert, lord, provided that you do not add the conjunction “only.” There are indeed two judicial procedures, just as there are two commands, two kinds of sin—one against God, the other against human beings—and two advents of the Lord, one hidden and the other manifest. Of the first it is written:

> “He will descend like rain upon a fleece” (Psalm 71);

of the second:

> “God will come openly” (Psalm 49).

Concerning the first judicial procedure, the Apostle says:

> “If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator,”

and so forth (1 Corinthians 5). Augustine, in his book *On Penance*, explains that he wished “that designation to be understood which is made against someone together with a sentence in judicial order.” For he did not wish a person to be judged by another according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion, or even according to an extraordinary judgment usurped outside the proper procedure, but rather according to God’s law and the order of the Church—whether the person had confessed voluntarily, or had been accused and convicted.

The blessed Gregory describes how this procedure ought to proceed and be handled in his commentary to John the Defender, who was going to Spain (Book XI, Letter 56). He decrees and establishes as Catholic that, after the nature of the cases has been considered, some should be accusers and others witnesses; that, in the presence of the accused, testimony should be given under oath and committed to writing; that the accused should have an opportunity to answer and defend himself; and that the examination of the persons accusing and testifying should take place according to the rules.

The Lord also indicates this judicial procedure when, in raising the girl who lay dead in the house, as though in the disclosure of a case not known to everyone, he took with him certain of his disciples as witnesses, as well as the girl’s father and mother (Matthew 9; Luke 8).

Leo describes how such a conjectural dispute is to be determined in his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne:

> “Because we wish the judgments of the priests of the Lord to be mature, we can determine nothing in matters unknown to the prejudice of either party until we have truthfully heard everything that was done.”

Elsewhere it is also excellently said:

> “He is not a just mediator who hears one party in uncertain matters in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other party.”

But what is to be done if the accused, after the canonical postponements, neither comes nor proves the necessities that prevented him? Saint Gregory prescribes this in the aforementioned commentary (Book XI, Letter 56), saying:

> “Since some enter before the defenders of places, or before the distinguished judges of the provinces, or even, as commonly happens”—here, before the distinguished “master of the census”—“and complain as though they had suffered something contrary to the laws at another’s hands, or had otherwise been injured, or wish to produce witnesses of damage inflicted, lest it later be objected to them” that the proceedings were conducted by one party alone, “the person against whom the case is brought, being present in that city where the testimony is given, must be summoned by the judge or defender to come and hear the testimony. If he refuses to come but neglects to do so, so that on this account the testimony against him may be useless because it was given by one party alone, we decree that such testimony shall have the same force as if it had not been given by one party alone but had also been given in his presence. For if he refuses, declines to come, and refuses to hear what is being stated, although the matter is public and he cannot claim that he was unable to come because of some unavoidable necessity, he shall be treated like one who did come. His contempt shall bring him no advantage; rather, the proofs shall be regarded as having been made in the presence of both parties. Behold,” says Saint Gregory, “the adversary must always be admonished to come and hear the witnesses; otherwise what was done contrary to the laws cannot have validity.”

Pope Boniface also demonstrates this, writing to the seven provinces about Maximus, who, although regularly summoned, refused to appear for judgment after being notorious for many crimes (Letter 2):

> “No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment in the same way in which the innocent person seeks acquittal; but the cunning quibbling of those who think matters must be handled by crafty devices will never receive the name of innocence. For whoever thinks that he can evade judgment by delays confesses everything.”

After some intervening material he says:

> “We have decreed that your judgment must take place within the province, and that a synod must be assembled before the day of the Kalends of November, so that, if he wishes to be present, he may answer the charges in person if he has confidence. But if he neglects to appear, he shall not gain a postponement of the sentence through his absence. For it is manifest that he confesses the crime who does not use the opportunity granted by the repeatedly assigned judgment to clear himself. It makes no difference whether all that has been said is proved in the present examination, since his repeated absence itself is evidently contrived as a confession. We shall send letters throughout all the provinces so that he may not plead ignorance as an excuse, and so that he may be compelled to come to the province and, once there, present himself for judgment.”

The blessed Gregory summoned and awaited Maximus, bishop of Salona, in a similar manner, since he was plainly guilty and contumacious (Book V, Letter 3):

> “We urge you to hasten to come to us, setting aside every excuse, so that, justice having been preserved, we may, with Christ revealing the truth, examine and resolve these matters”—the matters “of which you are accused”—“according to the canonical institutions. Act in such a way that you do not now impose further delays upon your coming, lest your very absence assign you more fully to the things alleged against you. This matter will compel us to pass a more severe judgment from the council against you as a contumacious person, not only because of the crimes alleged, which you evade clearing, but also because of the guilt of disobedience.”

You see, lord, that the blessed Gregory did not wish to condemn Maximus of Salona—both a presumer and a contumacious man, who had illegally assumed the order and insolently tore up the pope’s letter forbidding the celebration of the mass for him—unless he had been canonically summoned and regularly awaited. Hence he himself also wrote to Martianus (Book II, Letter 27):

> “No one is to be condemned without an examination.”

There is another form of judicial procedure, the one you also mentioned, in which the crime is not denied, when the guilty person is already carried out, as it were, beyond the city gate, for the execution of his crimes [or: “for the execution of his crime”]. Unless your prudence judges otherwise, we divide this procedure into two further forms, and we wish each form to be summoned before a synod and determined by judgment.

[Note: These and the following annotations to this letter stood in the margin of the manuscript codex, as a caution, whether added by Adalbert and Bernald themselves or by someone else. Here, most cautiously, the word “always” was not added, nor any other term denoting universality, lest its addition prejudice the apostolic see; for that see certainly is not compelled by contumacy to await a synodal summons.]

One form of manifest judicial procedure occurs when the defendant defends neither himself nor the act alleged against him—that is, when he admits both that he did it and that he sinned by doing it. In this case, when the accusers do nothing, the defendant alone is summoned to judgment, to undergo the penalties that nearly every page of the canons prescribes medicinally for one who has confessed or been convicted.

The Apostle seems to have spoken according to this procedure to the Corinthians:

> “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit, and I have already judged him who has done this as though I were present. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled, and my spirit is present with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Corinthians 5).

Note that he said, “When you are assembled in the name of Jesus,” as though he were saying: “After you have assembled in council, after you have gathered together in the Lord’s name—that is, canonically—let the defendant be judged there, with me spiritually present among you; let him there be removed from the fellowship of the Church. Let it then be shown openly to him that by sinning he has subjected himself to the yoke of the one whose yoke, I mean, he rejected.” This is not done out of regard for a private injury, nor with any other intention than that his carnality, tending toward death, may perish in him, and that his spirituality, seeking eternal things, may recover. Let him perish in the flesh so that he may be saved in the spirit.

A little earlier the Apostle also says:

> “That he who has done this deed may be removed from among you” (ibid.).

Explaining this, Ambrose says in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 5:

> “Once this deed had become known, he had to be expelled from the fellowship of the brethren. For everyone knew his crime, yet they did not rebuke him. He publicly kept his stepmother as his wife. In this matter there was no need of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

The second form of manifest judicial procedure occurs when the crime is admitted in a manner seeking purification, but the guilt is removed—that is, when someone admits that he did what is alleged but asserts that in doing so he did not at all deviate from ecclesiastical law. We strongly advise that such an accused person be granted a synod, so that he may either be convicted or, by proving his case, be acquitted.

The proscribed men before the apostolic prelate now loudly demand that they be treated according to this procedure. Many accused persons who defended justice, and many who had experienced the tyranny of prelates, supplied us with examples of this judicial procedure. After they had been heard in an assembly, the accused themselves were often acquitted by establishing their integrity, while their oppressors, once the charge had been brought against them, were condemned.

Thus Constantia, when Bishop Carlomannus [Note: [Col. 1149D] Carlomannus, also called Charles, was the intruded and Simoniacal bishop of Constance, appointed by Emperor Henry IV in 1069. See the recently published catalogue of the bishops of Constance by D. Pistorius, and Lambert, for 1069 and 1071; Council of Sardica, canon 17.] accused her of disobedience, pleaded the dignity of disobedience and blew him away like an infernal fury.

The Council of Sardica prescribes the rule and procedure for this controversy:

> “If some bishop, perhaps in anger—for that ought not to happen—is quickly and harshly moved against his presbyter or deacon and wishes to expel him from the Church, care must be taken lest an innocent man be condemned or lose communion. Therefore the one who has been expelled must have the power to appeal to neighboring bishops, and his case must be heard and examined with the greatest care, because a person who asks must not be denied a hearing. And let the bishop who expelled him, whether justly or unjustly, patiently accept that the matter be examined, so that his judgment may either be approved by many or corrected. Yet before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one should presume to restore to communion the one who had been separated from communion before the inquiry.”

Note the words that are spoken: “so that his sentence may be approved or amended”—namely, so that, after the matter has been examined, the sentence of the one who had condemned him may be approved if he has acted justly toward him, and amended if it lacks justification. Since, therefore, ecclesiastical law does not permit anyone to be condemned hastily or improperly, we reasonably say that if any bishops, summoned regularly by the pope to a synod, failed to come or did not prove definite necessities preventing them, they deserved suspension from office [Note: [Col. 1149D] Here the phrase “that the pope cannot condemn anyone without a synod” is very cautiously not added. For this adjective might appear prejudicial to apostolic authority.]—yet they should nevertheless be heard, following the humane counsel of Augustine (Letter 50, near the end) in his letter to Boniface:

> “In such cases, where, through grave fissures of dissension, it is not the danger of this or that individual but the slaughter of peoples that lies before us, something must be withdrawn from severity, so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils.”

And Leo, writing to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne (Letter 92, near the end), says:

> “Just as there are certain things that cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so there are some things [many things] that ought to be tempered either out of consideration for age or because of the necessities of circumstances, always preserving this condition: that, in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we know that what must be followed is that which is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical precepts nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.” [Col. 1149D]

[Note: [Col. 1150D] These methods of examining anathemas are indeed to be discussed by bishops; they do not, however, appear to have been established for those publicly declared contumacious, as may be gathered from a reading of the same council. Nor can these methods prejudice apostolic authority.]

Moreover, the decrees of the synod of Tribur, at which the Catholic King Arnulf was present, prescribe for us only three things that deserve an episcopal anathema: first, “if anyone canonically summoned to a synod has disdained to come”; second, “if, when presented, he has not obeyed priestly commands”; third, “if, before the examination of his case has been completed, he has presumed to flee away from the synod.”

But lest this synod lose authority because of the lowliness of the place, let Gelasius be heard in his letter to the bishops established throughout Dardania:

> “We are confident,” he says, “that no one who is truly a Christian now remains ignorant that the constitution of every synod which the assent of the universal Church has approved ought to be carried out by no other see more than by the first. For that see both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it through continuous moderation, by virtue of that primacy which the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord’s own voice (Matthew XVI), while the Church nevertheless followed it, and has always both held and retains it.” [Col. 1150B]

And blessed Isidore (Book VI, chapter 15), after describing the authentic Scriptures and the synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, added:

> “If there are any councils instituted by the holy Fathers, after the authority of these four, we decree that they are both to be observed and received.”

Hence Augustine also says in *On True Religion* (volume I of his works):

> “The eternal law may rightly be known by pure minds; it may not rightly be judged.”

In the case of these temporal laws, however, although people judge concerning them when they establish them, once they have been established and confirmed, it is not permitted for a judge to judge the laws themselves, but to judge according to them. And the Carthaginian canons say:

> “We ought to observe whatever has been included above, whether done or said, or whatever has been written down by other councils and is found to accord with the law. But if anyone transgresses and violates the statutes, or thinks that they should be regarded as nothing: if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if a cleric, of his honor.”

With these answers concerning the pope’s judgment, may I, in my foolishness, be permitted, Father, to obey your command and, before answering concerning the Simoniacs and the excommunicated, take some delight in discussing with you certain matters that we ignorant men bring together on both sides. The person of the apostolic ruler therefore requires of him that, if the Church which has entrusted itself to his protection wishes to be helped, if he has decided to do what is said, he unsheathe the sword [Col. 1150D] of the Spirit against bishops who had not entered through the door, who had not listened to him when he commanded what apostolic authority proclaims. They impose this necessity upon him: that, for the correction of ecclesiastical persons, he should use the services of secular men, so that those whose office was to consult concerning the conduct of clerics, as though they were a mirror of clerical life, should now arrogate to themselves the right to rule clerics.

Examine, therefore, what they call the subject matter lying behind ecclesiastical law: those who had not entered through the door [Note: [Col. 1151D] The manuscript has a lacuna here.] into the sees they now occupy—those who were not elected before they were received, but, alas, were received before they were elected; very often ordained before [Note: [Col. 1151D] There is a lacuna here as well, and the sense is not established.] all hands, tongues, or bodily service had intervened, rather than merely spiritual conduct and commendation, promoted them. From their contagion the Church has now contracted such a stain that she has almost lost her sacraments—that is, the ordinations of clerics, the consecrations of churches, and certain other distinctions of hers—since, consecrated by such men, she has rather been accursed by these accursed persons, the Lord saying to them through the prophet: “I will curse your blessings” (Malachi II).
