[Note: [Col. 1151D] From this point the slanderous objections of the conspirators against the pope follow; some of them are refuted in the following letter—those, I mean, which seemed in some way to harm the apostolic ruler. For the decrees of the holy Fathers, which they distort for themselves, appear, if properly understood, to attack them more than him.]

These things are said—indeed, lamented—concerning certain of these men, because of the miseries of the present ecclesiastical condition. The apostolic ruler is called upon to come to the aid of the suffering Church. These men, on the other hand, cry out on their own behalf and against the apostolic ruler, claiming that he has proscribed them, to use your word, tyrannically rather than ecclesiastically, out of regard for a private injury to himself rather than for public equity. And especially because, in doing this, he has acted in a matter that was not examined in proportion to its importance, but was dangerous to the Roman situation and would be harmful to the whole Church.

They say, indeed, that Pope Stephen [Note: [Col. 1151D] Pope Stephen X, called IX. Concerning him, see Baronius, volume XI, under the year 1058.], formerly Frederick, brother of Duke Gotefrid, decreed in a public synod, with the consent of the man who now holds the papacy and of all who were present, that, while Henry—whom we now have as king—was reigning, his consent should be awaited in the election of the Roman pontiff. They also testify [Col. 1151C] that this same pope twice swore to the very same words, wearing the *orarium* around his neck. From this they add that, by ascending the papacy on the basis of this agreement, he denied his decretal consent, his profession, and his subscription, and made himself perjured—which it is impious to say—not only then, by accepting it, but continues to do so daily by holding it.

Let him hear the decrees of the Council of Carthage:

> “If anyone in any respect acts against his profession [Note: [Col. 1151D] That is, a profession made deliberately, not rashly.] or subscription, he has deprived himself of his own honor.”

And lest he think that, because of the eminence of his position, everything is permitted him, let him hear Gregory, whose name he is pleased to bear:

> “We who preside ought to become known not by the dignity of place or lineage, but by nobility of character; not by the splendor of cities, but by purity of faith.” [Note: [Col. 1151D] Those who have behaved with such unheard-of arrogance—not, I say, toward subjects, but toward their own prelate—ought above all to restrain their pride by these arguments.]

That is: the first man, Adam, was cast out of paradise because of sin. Thus, whoever has cast away from himself the nobility of God should be deprived of the nobility of his position; that is, guilt is greatly extended as an example when a sinner is honored out of respect for his rank. Let him also hear Pope Simplicius:

> “He deserves to lose the privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.”

Let him also hear Jerome (11 q. 3, c. 63):

> “It is not easy to stand in the place of Peter and Paul and hold the chair of those who reign with Christ, because it is said: Those who hold the places of the saints are not the children of the saints, but those who perform their works.”

Hence Augustine also says in *On the Sermon on the Mount*:

> “Those judge most recklessly who love to blame and condemn more than to amend and correct.”

This vice is pride or envy.

Finally, so that canonical defenses may be set before canonical weapons by canonical men, they say: When the lord pope condemned us, although we had not been canonically summoned and had been forbidden to come [Col. 1152B], it was necessary for him to hear his predecessor, Gregory, whose name he is pleased to bear, writing to Bishop John, who was excommunicating unjustly [Note: [Col. 1152D] “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the pit that he made” (Psalm VII). For if Saint Gregory excommunicated John, who had rashly excommunicated his inferior without synodal summons, why do they lament being excommunicated without summons, when they attempted to test the authority not merely of an inferior but of Christ, who is superior to all, indeed of the entire Roman synod, as the following letter most truthfully attests.]:

> “First annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of your aforesaid sentence, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that you are deprived of holy communion for a period of thirty days and that you should implore from our almighty God, with the greatest penitence and tears, pardon for so great an excess. But if we learn that you have fulfilled this sentence of ours too lightly, know that, with the Lord’s help, not such great injustice but the contumacy of your brotherhood will be punished more severely.

And elsewhere:

> “But if at any time, on any occasion or through any underhanded means, you attempt to act against what we have decreed, we decree that you are deprived of holy communion and that you may not receive it—except at the final moment of your life—unless by a command granted by the Roman pontiff. For we establish this in harmony with the definition of the holy Fathers: whoever does not know how to obey the sacred canons is not worthy either to administer at sacred altars or to receive communion.” [Col. 1152C]

It is astonishing that he does not hear Leo writing to Anatolius [Note: [Col. 1152D] If you had heard this properly, you would not have so rashly desired to depose your superior. Or did Saint Gregory exempt you when he anathematized all adversaries of the canons? You, I mean, who attempted to depose the father of the first see without convicting him and without being able to convict him by your own judgment.]:

> “A Catholic man and an outstanding priest of the Lord, just as he ought not to be entangled in any error, so he ought not to be corrupted by any desire, since Scripture says: ‘Do not follow your desires’ (Ecclesiasticus XVIII).”

He does not consider the judgment of the Catholic Emperor Justinian, which the Church approves and observes, saying (1 q. 6, c. 11):

> “Let no bishop, let no presbyter excommunicate anyone before the cause for which the ecclesiastical canons command this to be done has been proved. But if anyone excommunicates someone contrary to this rule, let the person who has been excommunicated return to the grace of holy communion by the authority of a greater priest. Let the one who has excommunicated unlawfully abstain from holy communion for as long as the greater priest thinks appropriate, so that he may justly suffer what he unjustly did.”

Therefore, in the case of this excommunicating man, whom we ought to approach with an ear inclined toward private vengeance rather than just examination, we should listen to the Apostle saying:

> “Do not defend yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath” (Romans XII).

We should also hear him whose seat the prince of the apostles occupies:

> “Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a slanderer” (1 Peter IV).

Catholic teachers say that a person suffers as a slanderer when, having been insulted, he pursues his own injuries with unrestrained fervor of tongue and mind.

They ought also to have heard Gregory writing to Januarius (Book II, Letter 34):

> “Amid many complaints, Isidore, a most distinguished man, complained that he had been unjustly excommunicated and anathematized by your brotherhood. When we wished to learn from your cleric, who was present, for what reason this had been done, it became clear that it had been done for no other reason than that he had insulted you. This matter deeply afflicts us. If this is so, you show that you think of nothing heavenly, but indicate that your conduct is earthly, since, in revenge for a personal injury [Note: [Col. 1153D] Why do you wish to count this as a private injury to the Roman pontiff, when you wished to annul the entire Roman synod along with him?], you have brought upon him the curse of an anathema, something forbidden by the sacred rules. Therefore, from now on be wholly watchful and careful, and do not again presume to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your own injury. For if you do anything of this kind, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.” [Col. 1153C]

The same writer also says to Euphronius (read “Eusebius the abbot,” Book II, Letter 24):

> “The humility of the servants of God ought to appear in a time of affliction, and so forth. For it is not a great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored, since any secular person also does this. But we ought to be especially humble toward those from whom we suffer something. For the Psalmist says: ‘See my humility before my enemies’ (Psalm IX).”

Likewise, in Homily VI:

> “Those who follow either their hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot rightly judge their subjects. [Note: [Col. 1154D] This sentence precedes the one before it in Saint Gregory’s homily.] Hence it comes about that the very person who exercises the power of binding and loosing for his own desires, and not according to the character of his subjects, deprives himself of that power. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: ‘They were killing souls that do not die, and making alive souls that do not live’ (Ezekiel XIII).”

It is permitted for prelates to be moved by zeal for their see or rank; nevertheless, they must not forget that where authority is greatest, license is least. [Note: [Col. 1154D] The passage is mutilated.]

Hence Gregory, in his letter to the deacon and legate Sabinianus (Book VII, Letter 1):

> “I am more ready,” he says, “to die than to see the Church of blessed Peter degenerate during my days.” [Col. 1154A]

Likewise, to the Empress Constantina (Book IV, Letter 34):

> “And if Gregory’s sins are so great that he ought to suffer such things, the sins of the apostle Peter are nevertheless not such that he should deserve to suffer these things in your times.”

Likewise:

> “He whom the dignity of his see and rank has raised up has restrained himself by consideration of his own condition.”

Again, writing to the bishops Eulogius and Anastasius of Antioch, he says (Book IV, Letter 36):

> “When the excellent preacher says, ‘Since I am indeed the apostle of the Gentiles, I will glorify my ministry’ (Romans XI),” and again elsewhere says, “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians II), “he undoubtedly shows us who follow him that we should hold humility in our minds and nevertheless preserve the dignity of our rank in honor, so that in us there may be neither timid humility nor proud self-exaltation.” [Col. 1154B]

As for the arguments themselves, since they themselves sully his elevation, I think he would answer that he was elected by the Romans, compelled to ascend to that eminence, and unworthy; and that it is unreasonable for the Roman see, the mother of the churches, to be deprived of the freedom of its election, through which the other sees obtain the right that there should not be bishops who were not elected by the clergy and people of their own see—not because of nobility of lineage, but because of holiness of life; not rich in possessions, but holy in conduct.

He may perhaps also defend himself by the decrees of his predecessors, Nicholas, Stephen, and others, who established under anathema that no one should deny the Roman see the privileges of election. On the other hand, they affirm that an election may not carry the person elected into that which he himself had made unlawful.

And here, as the Church of the Shunammite—crushed, as though between the collision of two stones—we who groan in this valley of tears in hope of children must beseech the fountain of mercies “that the leaven which,” as Gregory says, “mixed the whole mass of the human race into unity with three measures of flour, may now restore the whole body of the Church to the form of that bread which descended from heaven, so that Christ’s vineyard, cleansed of the little foxes that destroy it (Song of Songs II), and purged of the branches destined for the fire, may put forth new growth and flower through the harmony of unity, adhering to the true vine in the fragrance of sweetness [perhaps this should be added].”

[Col. 1154D] Hear, bishops who now oppose the apostolic ruler, that statement of Gregory (Book VI, Letter 10) to Bishop Felix:

> “You yourself do not doubt, from your own subjects, how obedience or reverence ought to be shown to superiors. In this matter it is very useful if humility, without compulsion from anyone, preserves with praise what the rigor of discipline imposes.”

And hear Leo:

> “Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over certain people should not resent that someone has been placed over him, but should himself render the obedience that he demands.”

On the other hand, let the lord apostolic ruler, who bears the heart of a teacher toward those subject to him, hear the words of one who says:

> “As a nurse cherishes her children, so, in our yearning for you, we were eager to impart to you not only the gospel of God but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians II). [Col. 1155A]

In this matter of the apostolic ruler—whether, as he thinks, it is a reproach, or, as they think, a necessary consideration [Note: [Col. 1155D] This is the Catholic profession in which the writer is shown to have presented the matters he wrote against the apostolic ruler not in his own person but in the person of the schismatics.]—I, your servant, although I lack an inner rational faculty, nevertheless desire to follow the apostolic rope rather than pull it. I venerate the Roman see as the tribunal of Christ, its pontiff as the sanctuary of the gracious Spirit, and I embrace its decrees as the edicts of the heavenly court.

Moreover, you ask me, to repeat your words, what I think about the confecting of the sacraments by Simoniacs or by any excommunicated persons who usurp them, especially if they lack truth. I am foolish, therefore, but not foolishly obedient. I shall say what I think.

A Simoniac is one who, for the sake of temporal profit, in any manner buys or sells ecclesiastical honors. Some of these, although ordained, nevertheless lack the ecclesiastical honor, since they received it from no one. Others, regularly ordained, although afterward made Simoniacs, still possess the orders that they had not yet lost when their heresy was publicly declared. We call those unordained who were ordained by a Simoniac who could give them nothing, or who were ordained through money or the intervention of secular favor by someone who was not a Simoniac, from whom they could receive nothing by purchase. We call those ordained and yet Simoniacs who, after receiving orders from those by whom they ought to have received them, bought or sold churches or other things that their Simoniacal heresy persuaded them to buy or sell.

But the former, whom we said were ordained, will in no way confect the sacraments unless, after making satisfaction, they are admitted by episcopal authority. The latter—that is, those who are ordained and Simoniacal—will not confect them [Note: [Col. 1155D] There is a small lacuna here in the manuscript.] if they are manifest, unless they are converted.

Since, however, Mother Church, united with Christ her head into one body, belongs to her children only through the sacraments of Christ and the Church, I propose to distinguish and establish by Catholic authority what is to be held concerning Simoniacs and excommunicated persons who claim these same sacraments for themselves.

[Col. 1155D] [Note: [Col. 1155D] Concerning the sacraments of heretics or excommunicated persons, let Augustine be heard. From his book *On Baptism against the Donatists* it is gathered that both ordinations and baptism can exist and be administered outside the Church, although this is destructive both to the one who possesses them and to the one who administers them.]

We therefore divide Simoniacs and excommunicated persons into two groups. Some of them are those whose zeal has become known; others are those who, although accused and although stained by the mark of suspicion, have not yet been exposed. Among those whose wickedness is manifest, some have not yet been presented for judgment, while others have been condemned by the public judgment of the Church.

We therefore believe that those whose crime is still hidden from human eyes can confect the sacraments of the Church. But although these sacraments help us through faith, they condemn those men because of their presumption: “He eats judgment,” says the Apostle [Col. 1156A] (1 Corinthians XI). “To himself,” Augustine says in the letter of the council to the Donatists, “not to you.” Communion with evil persons does not defile anyone through participation in the sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. For if someone does not consent to them in evil deeds, the evil person bears his own cause and his own person. He does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the consent to an evil work.

And so that you may know that Simoniacs and excommunicated persons who have not yet undergone the winnowing fan remain hidden in the Church, like chaff among the grain in the harvest, all those whom the Simoniacal heresy has polluted have been condemned by the sentence of the prince of the apostles. Blessed Gelasius says:

> “The very error which has once been condemned together with its author carries with it its own execration and punishment in anyone who becomes a participant through perverse communion.” [Col. 1156B]

Likewise:

> “There is no doubt that, just as in every heresy—which must be repeated without cease, since no Christian doubts that it is firm—all accomplices, followers, and communicants of a perversity once condemned are judged to share the same lot.”

I know that all presumptuous persons and transgressors of the canons have been anathematized, as Saint Gregory writes to the Gallican bishops:

> “Let everything contrary to the sacred canons be strictly condemned with the imposition of an anathema.”

But these men, I say, although accused, have nevertheless not yet been manifestly exposed in this transgression. They possess, as we believe, something of the grace and holiness of Mother Church, against which the gates of hell will not prevail (Matthew XVI). Under her wings they still lie hidden in hope of pardon, so that they may confect the sacraments of that same mother [Col. 1156C], whose children they had not yet publicly ceased to be.

But you say: How will those who, through heresy or by the sentence of anathema, have torn themselves away from the body of Christ confect the body of Christ?

The answer is: Judas was one of the twelve and possessed the same power as they did to perform miracles. Although he was a thief, carrying the money box (John XII), he appeared equal to them in signs and equal in merits. Before human eyes, in the splendor of miracles, he was the companion of Peter, Andrew, James, and John. But before the eyes of the one who did not need anyone to testify to him concerning a person, because “he himself knew what was in a person” (John II), he was the devil. [Col. 1156D]

For it was said of him:

> “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John VI.)

He was therefore the devil because he breathed a divided hope: namely, that he might be both the seller of the Lord and the Lord’s disciple. But when he was already promising the price of his wickedness for the Lord whom he had sold, when he was already seeking an opportunity to betray him (Matthew XXVI; Luke XXII), in this abyss of crime he nevertheless continued to use his apostolic power—and did so until, after hearing “What you are doing, do quickly,” he went out. “And it was night” (John XIII). [Col. 1157A]

In the same way, we believe that these men too can confect ecclesiastical sacraments, so long as their unrestrained contumacy has not yet publicly exposed them and, in a certain sense, prejudicially expelled them from the Church before episcopal ecclesiastical excommunication.

[Note: [Col. 1157D] Do not suppose that this must be believed as a definitive conclusion until you have read through Saint Augustine’s book *On Baptism against the Donatists*.]

But concerning those who are demonstrably guilty of Simoniacal heresy, although they have not yet been publicly judged, we firmly deny that the sacraments of the Church can be confected by them. For public, shameless presumption is greater than the crime itself once committed. While it is evident, it becomes an obvious example of sinning, as though saying, “Imitate me, imitate me!” For example, one who does not lay aside honors acquired through Simony proposes nothing other than that Simon, who lives in him, should be imitated. But one who sins shamefacedly and only before God will at some point fear being what he is ashamed to be seen as.

But, I know, you will object to me: Since daily experience presents us with one and the same Simoniac—unknown to one Christian, but completely manifest to another—how will he confect for the one who does not know what he cannot confect for the one who knows?

The answer is: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans I). The effect of faith is believed more beneficially than it is investigated by reasoning. I say indeed [Note: [Col. 1157D] This is not confected, and indeed not by anyone who knows the matter through the Simoniac.] that what is believed not to be confected through a Simoniac nevertheless becomes, for someone who simply and faithfully believes without knowing, a sacrament through faith. [Note: [Col. 1157D] These things are erroneous.] The one who confects it, however, is condemned by the very fact that he confects it.

Do not be surprised, because the recipient is spiritually nourished through faith in the sacrament. Hear also that the grace of the sacrament [Col. 1157C] is shared even by one who does not receive it. Augustine says in his sermon to the infants at the altar concerning the sacrament (*On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter 131, “No one”):

> “No one ought in any way to doubt that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the body and blood of the Lord when, in baptism, he becomes a member of Christ; nor is he alienated from participation in that bread and cup, even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body. For he is not deprived of participation in and benefit from that sacrament when he finds in himself what that sacrament is.”

Therefore, lest you doubt that one who simply believes receives it profitably from someone whom he does not know to be a heretic, hear also that the simplicity of faith [Note: [Col. 1157D] Perhaps: *simplicitas* (“simplicity”).] receives it effectively from someone whom he knows to be a heretic. Augustine, in the same sermon (24 q. 2, c. 40, “If necessity should”):

> “If extreme necessity should compel someone, and he should find no Catholic through whom he might receive it, and, while preserving Catholic peace in his heart, he should receive through someone placed outside Catholic unity what he would have received within that Catholic unity, if he should immediately depart from this life, we count him as Catholic. But if he is delivered from bodily death, when he presents himself bodily to the Catholic congregation, from which he had never departed in heart, we not only do not disapprove what he did, but also praise it most securely and truly. For he believed that the Lord [God] was present to his heart, where he preserved unity.” [Col. 1157D]

Let us therefore learn that, if I deal with a Simoniac who is still merely among those whose condition is manifest but who have not yet been publicly condemned—if, I say, such persons cannot confect certain sacraments of the Church, and if the spiritually perfect believe that neither can they confect them nor can they receive from them what they have confected, nevertheless the faith of the simple and wise person, and of the simple-minded person who is wise, fully receives what lacks the wickedness of the giver, with the grace of Jesus fulfilling everything, as in the case of that fortunate thief, for whom, as Augustine says, “the goodness of God spiritually supplied what was lacking from the sacrament of baptism.”

There appears to be this difference between those manifestly guilty and those publicly excommunicated: we are forbidden to communicate with the excommunicated unless they are converted. With those whose guilt is manifest but who have not yet been judged, we ought to associate so that they may be converted. It is impious for us even to say “hail” to the former; it is impious even to eat with them. With the latter the Apostle permits association, saying:

> “Not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world” (1 Corinthians V).

The tax collectors and sinners with whom the Savior had eaten (Matthew IX) therefore represented those whose guilt is manifest. The excommunicated are signified by those whom the Apostle had handed over to Satan (1 Corinthians V).

When I associate with such manifest sinners, who have not yet been publicly judged, I do not excommunicate myself, since I love the person as a Christian while condemning his deed as un-Christian, Augustine prescribing:

> “A wicked person does not defile you in two ways: if you do not consent and if you rebuke him”—

that is, do not share in the deed and do not consent to it. One communicates with him when one joins oneself to his deed through will or approval.

But concerning these men—that is, Simoniacs, even if they have not yet been publicly excommunicated—you should believe the apostolic pontiffs Innocent and Paschal when they say that clerics cannot be ordained by them and that the Lord’s body cannot be confected.

Pope Innocent says concerning Simoniacs [Note: [Col. 1158D] If we interpret this sentence to mean that heretics can give nothing beneficial and no honor, while nevertheless possessing the sacrament of ordination, which becomes condemnation both to themselves and to the one who receives it from them, then, I say, if we understand it in this way, we differ from blessed Augustine.]:

> “It is asserted that one who has lost his honor cannot give honor. Nor do we accept that anyone has received anything from him, because there was nothing in the giver that another could receive from him. And this is certainly true: what he did not possess, he could not give.”

Hear Pope Paschal in his letter to the Church of Milan [Note: [Col. 1158D] This letter was not written by Pope Paschal but by a certain Guido, who also composed music. So assert very devout men who investigated the matter most carefully among his disciples. Moreover, the same letter is nowhere found written among the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. It therefore cannot in any way prejudice blessed Augustine.]:

[Col. 1159A]

> “Whoever bestows sacred orders for a price will perish with Judas, that most wicked merchant, who sold the eternal Son of the Father for thirty pieces of silver. Let the heretic hear this; let the Christian hear it also. Let the one who wishes to authorize this heresy with rabid mouth hear it. To these I say: Where is what you received? To those I say: Where is what you gave? Miserable men, unhappily, bargained with one another: the one to provide for his greed, the other to satisfy his own wickedness. Therefore the one does not have the price, nor do the others possess Christ. Rejoice, Christian, because what Judas sold and the Jew bought, you have acquired. The two of them have brought us a great good through their own evil.”

Likewise, in the same letter:

> “If the one who sold Christ was handed over to such destruction, what will become of his associates who buy or sell the Paraclete? Are those who are equal in crime not equal in punishment? He sold the Son; these, insofar as they can, attempt to sell the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 1159B]

But since certain persons, especially among you, flatter themselves by asserting that they are not Simoniacs because they have neither bought nor sold churches or altars, but only the property and revenues attached to churches, let them hear the same Paschal in the same letter:

> “If anyone objects that it is not consecrations but the actual things that proceed from consecration that are sold, he appears to say something, but in fact understands nothing at all. For since a physical church—or a bishop, abbot, or anyone else—can accomplish nothing without physical and external possessions, just as a soul does not live temporarily without a body, whoever sells one of the two without which the other cannot be possessed leaves neither of them unsold.” [Col. 1159C]

Moreover, that Mass cannot be celebrated by such men is indeed declared in the same letter:

> “Can a cursed man, by his blessing, change bread into the flesh of Christ [Note: [Col. 1159D] Let us read the opinion of this modern dogmatist cautiously, until we investigate more carefully the decisions of the holy Fathers concerning the sacraments.], especially when the Lord asserts that whatever he blesses he will curse?”

And shortly afterward:

> “If heretical priests cannot utter the words of exhortation, how can they turn wine into Christ’s blood? And if the Lord commanded that his body and blood should by no means be given to murderers, adulterers, rapacious persons, and others entangled in criminal sins until they have made satisfaction, how will he himself [Col. 1159D] give the priesthood to one who usurps it through Simoniacal heresy, condemned everywhere?”

Hear the same writer concerning how greatly hearing their Mass harms one:

> “Therefore, when we do not avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics, if we hear their Masses or pray with them, we undergo excommunication together with them. It is altogether erroneous even to believe that they are priests, since Peter says to Simon: ‘May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money’ (Acts VIII).” [Col. 1160A]

When it says “you thought,” it is clear that he is condemned not for what he had done, but because he had believed that he could do it. It is therefore clear from the authority cited above that clerics cannot be ordained by them and that the Lord’s body cannot be confected; rather, by Peter’s word, they are lost clerics. And if they do not confect these two sacraments, certainly they can confect none—unless perhaps baptism alone.

And so that you may know that ecclesiastical sacraments can in no way be made by a Simoniac, hear that, by an apostolic decree, everything that appeared to have been done by a neophyte was annulled.

After Paul, the ninety-fourth bishop of the Roman see under that name, had died [Note: [Col. 1160D] This pseudopope was made in the year of Christ 767. See Panvinus, *Book on the Pontiffs and Caesars*; Baronius, volume IX.], a certain Constantine, consecrated pope by a layman, occupied the apostolic see for a year and a month. During this period he ordained bishops, presbyters, and others of various ranks; he did everything that belonged to an apostolic ruler.

Meanwhile, certain Romans, abhorring the fact that the head of the Church—the Roman see—had been invaded by a neophyte, obtained the consent of the clergy and people, deposed Constantine, and elevated Stephen, a Sicilian by nationality and learned in ecclesiastical traditions, as Pope Stephen III [Baronius: Stephen IV], the ninety-fifth pope, by consecration to the apostolic dignity.

Here immediately he sent legates to the kings of the Franks, Charles and Carloman, who had recently succeeded their deceased father Pippin. With their consent he chose twelve bishops from Francia, men of more credible life and distinguished learning. [Note: [Col. 1160D] Read Baronius under the years 768 and 769.] [Col. 1160C] He also summoned the bishops of Apulia, Campania, and Italy, and held a synod at Rome in the church of the Savior. There all Constantine’s enactments were torn up by common judgment, and his writings were burned in public.

Pope Stephen himself, prostrate with the clergy, repented that he had ever obeyed the neophyte pope and received communion from his hands. It was therefore decreed in that council, under the bond of anathema, that henceforth no neophyte should aspire to the episcopal dignity. Concerning the bishops, priests, and others whom the wretched Constantine had ordained by consecrating them, it was decreed that all, stripped of the ecclesiastical honors which they had claimed through him, should descend to only those orders in which they had stood before they had been advanced by him to higher ones. If, however, any of them, hidden under the bushel, should ask that the lampstand of the Church be set above him, [Note: [Col. 1160D] I fear to praise this example, if indeed it is true, lest, by affirming it, I should also regard all those consecrated by St. Ambrose as likewise to be blown away; for he too was a neophyte, having been consecrated to the episcopate at the deposition of the white garments—that is, on the eighth day after baptism.] then, after being elected again by clergy and people, he would again be consecrated, as though he had not previously been consecrated by Pope Constantine, but would deserve only the rank from which he had been deposed and never a higher honor.

Concerning those whom he had promoted from the laity to the priesthood or diaconate, it was decreed that, once admitted to the order, they should remain wherever they wished, but only in religious dress. None of them would be promoted to the height of the pontificate; none at all would hope for a higher order, lest this error of novelty take root in the Church of God.

Finally, it was decreed that whatever Constantine the invader had done in the ecclesiastical sacraments should all be repeated, as is read in the Acts of the Pontiffs, [Note: [Col. 1161D] Read Baronius, vol. IX, under the year 769, and you will see that this author did not sufficiently understand what is reported concerning this matter in the History of the Pontiffs.] except for holy baptism and the mystical chrism. When the holy synod had ended, all the people fell at the pope’s feet and asked pardon for ever having shared communion with Constantine the invader. He imposed penance on each of them for this offense. As for the bishops who were judged worthy, he had them elected again by their subjects and consecrated them anew himself. [Note: [Col. 1161D] “Reconciled.” Thus the word “consecrated” must be understood in the account of this event.] As for the rest of the clergy, he judged that no one who had lost his order should be restored to it.

It is clear, then, my lord, from the ordinations of clerics—those who had been ordained and those whose ordinations had been annulled—and from the altered consecrations of churches, that the chrism consecrated by a neophyte consecrator was also annulled, except that Pope Stephen did not wish to annul baptism celebrated with that chrism. For one may not rebaptize even someone baptized by a heretic, provided that he baptizes only in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

For this same reason, when the king was celebrating Easter at Bamberg in the previous year—that is, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1075—[Note: [Col. 1161D] Thus this letter was written in the year 1076.] Archbishop Liemar of Bremen refused to use in baptism the chrism that appeared to have been prepared by Herimann, who was then bishop there, [Note: [Col. 1161D–1162D] Concerning this Herimann, Bernald says in his Chronicle under the year 1075: “Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, accused by his clerics of the Simoniacal heresy, is deposed by the pope.”] knowing him to be a Simoniac, although he had not yet been convicted, and acting in this matter according to ecclesiastical practice. For although baptism is not annulled after it has been performed by a heretic, a heretic must not nevertheless be permitted to perform it; for it is one thing to tolerate a deed after it has been done, without approving it, and another to anticipate it lest he fear that it may be disapproved.

It must also be understood that not only those are neophytes who are suddenly promoted from the laity to ecclesiastical dignities, such as the man whom your Herimann advanced from a tanner to the priesthood in one and the same day. He suddenly transferred him from the vat in which he had pounded bark to the altar of Christ: O hasty promotion! He becomes a deacon, although previously he had not read a lesson during the celebration of Mass; a priest, although then for the first time he became a Levite; he received all the ecclesiastical orders at once, having come on that same day with a lavish payment compelling consecration [perhaps: had bought it], and without even being marked with the tonsure.

I say that not only such men are called and are neophytes, but even more so those who are shapeless in morals, untrained in religion, and rustic in knowledge. Many heads of the reborn Hydra are now emerging, and through this they destroy themselves with perpetual anathema. Hear Gregory in his *Register*, in a letter sent to Virgil, bishop of Arles:

“Since the Apostle Paul forbids a neophyte to come to the sacred orders (1 Tim. III), we must understand that just as at that time a neophyte was called one who had only recently been planted in the faith, so now we count among neophytes one who is still new in holy conduct.”

I shall write still further about the deeds of the Pontiffs, concerning the council of the pope and the sacraments annulled which Leo the neophyte had usurped.

[Note: [Col. 1162D] There is an error in the date. See Baronius, vol. X, under the years of Christ 963 and 964.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 944, in the third year after Otto, emperor and son of King Henry, had subdued Italy by suppressing the tyranny of Berengar and his son, Pope John, having proved faithless to the emperor—whom, together with his wife Adelaide, he had elevated by imperial anointing in the previous year—admitted Adalbert, an enemy of the state, into the city. [Note: [Col. 1162D] That is, in the year 962.] The emperor, unwilling to tolerate this, invaded Rome hostilely. Fearing the emperor on one side and distrusting the Romans on the other, the pope fled with his accomplice Adalbert, after seizing for himself a considerable treasure of the Church.

The Romans, whether seized by fear or attracted by respect for the law, received their lord with congratulations. Since the emperor needed the pope in order to settle the affairs then threatening, he recalled Pope John to his abandoned see. When John refused to return, Leo, still a layman, [Note: [Col. 1162D] This Leo was not a legitimate pope but an antipope, or pseudopope. See Baronius, under the year 963.] though by secular standards quite energetic, was elected and ordained pope. A synod was held in the presence of the emperor and many Teutonic and Italian bishops. Many things were decreed that either ecclesiastical necessity or the emperor’s will demanded.

Thus, while presiding over the apostolic see, Lord Leo meanwhile performed ordinations and did everything that belonged to the apostolic office. Before long, [Note: [Col. 1162D] In the year of Christ 964; read Baronius.] the Romans, having changed their allegiance toward the emperor, received Pope John back. He assembled a council at Rome in the church of St. Peter and condemned Leo, who had succeeded him while he was alive and was a neophyte, stripping him of every ecclesiastical order. He condemned him according to the canonical statutes in such a way that, if he later aspired to any clerical order, he would lie under perpetual anathema, together with all who helped him in this.

The two bishops who had promoted him were summoned to the synod and presented during the third session. By apostolic authority he deprived them of their priestly honor in such a way that afterward they would not dare even to attempt access to restoration in any synod. A third of them, named Sicon, who had been canonically summoned and awaited but finally refused to come, he deprived of ecclesiastical communion.

It was also established by the public judgment of all that the synod gathered by Leo should not be called a synod at all, but a brothel favoring adulterers. Thus all the decrees of the aforesaid Leo were annulled. All who had been consecrated by him were ordered to put on chasubles and to present their own proscription in writing on a document containing these words: “My father had nothing for himself; he gave nothing to me.” Thus deposed, they remained in those orders which they had held before they had been promoted by Leo, by the same reasoning and authority as those whom we mentioned above as having been promoted by Constantine the neophyte.

To show you also that the sacraments of the Church cannot be performed not only by Simoniacs, and not only—what is less serious—by neophytes, but even by others promoted irregularly, I shall report what happened at the most holy Church of Hildesheim, [Note: [Col. 1163D–1164D] Note. Bernard came from Constance to Hildesheim, where he seems to have acted as master of the schools of that Church, as earlier at Constance. From there he came to Corvey and embraced the monastic life. Krantzius, *Metropolis*, book V, chapter 26, on Benno, bishop of Osnabrück: “When he had been in charge of the schools at the Church of Hildesheim (for in that age schoolmasters taught sacred literature and had assistants who taught the trivium), he was winning for himself a distinguished name through learning and religious life with Emperor Henry, etc.”] to which I, most unworthy as I am, now serve—if not fruitfully, nevertheless devotedly; if not usefully, nevertheless faithfully; if not as I ought, nevertheless as I can.

[Col. 1163B] [Note: [Col. 1164D] Concerning this Ebbo, see Baronius, vols. IX and X, especially under the years 853 and 866, where Baronius shows that the acts which this author praises as legitimate were not legitimately performed.]

Ebbo, bishop of Reims, gave his assent to Lothair when he deprived his father Louis, son of Charles the Great, of the kingdom. When Louis was restored to the kingdom with the help of his sons, namely Pippin and Louis—the former duke of Aquitaine and the latter duke of Bavaria—a synod was convened. Ebbo was deposed and exiled to Hildesheim.

When Reginbert, the second bishop of the Church of Hildesheim, died, the emperor, out of regard for humanity rather than justice, placed Ebbo, then the third bishop, over that see. That wretched former bishop stupidly usurped for twelve years the sacraments of the Church granted to episcopal dignity. After he had been stripped of his office, his successor Alfrid, by apostolic authority, stripped the clerics of the orders they had received from his predecessor and rededicated the churches. He annulled everything Ebbo had done concerning the sacraments of the Church, except baptism alone, in accordance with the decrees of the aforementioned Pope Stephen.

See how dangerously those who nevertheless do not perform the Church’s sacraments usurp them for themselves—those presumptuous robbers of ecclesiastical dignity whom the apostolic anathema both condemns by binding them and binds by condemning them.

It would remain for me to prove the case concerning those who have been publicly excommunicated. But since the sacraments of the Church are not performed by presumptuous men who have not yet been brought before a tribunal, who would ask, who would doubt, whether such men are alienated from the assembly of the Church? Therefore, cut off from the body of Christ—that is, separated from the Church—they will be able to perform nothing within the Church. You have proved this most convincingly both by reason and by authority, when Augustine says against the Donatists:

“Whoever has been separated from the Catholic Church, however much he may think that he lives laudably, through this one crime alone—that he has departed from the unity of Christ—does not possess life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (Col. III).

But let no excommunicated person, because of the testimony of his conscience to his innocence, promise himself that he has been absolved. Let him hear the decree of the Council of Carthage:

“Whoever has been excommunicated for his own negligence, whether bishop or any cleric, and during the time of his excommunication presumes to receive communion before a hearing, is judged to have pronounced upon himself the sentence of condemnation.”

And that of the Council of Sardica:

“Before everything has been carefully and faithfully examined, no one ought to presume, before the inquiry, to join to communion the person who had been separated from communion” (Council of Sardica, XVII).

As I deal with synods, and as I read that the synod of Leo [Note: [Col. 1164D] The pseudopope mentioned above.] was called not a synod but a brothel favoring adulterers, I cannot help remembering your synod, which in the past year [Note: [Col. 1164D] He is speaking of the synod held at Rome under Gregory VII in the year 1075.] was assembled, as I hear, from three thousand six hundred among priests and the other ecclesiastical orders. How little it considered its own profession when, with what countenance I do not know, it contradicted the decrees of the Nicene Synod!

If, looking around them, they were encouraged merely by the number surrounding them, let them read in the decrees of the apostolic see what the Roman clergy had sent to John, a priest but a schismatic, at the time [Note: [Col. 1164D] See Bellarmine, book IV, *On the Pontiff*, chapter 10, and Baronius, vol. VII, under the year of Christ 538.] when Vigilius, having fallen from the apostolic office into heresy, was being held at Constantinople. In those decrees, now held by the Roman Church among the Catholic rules, they would read:

“Even if all the priests and the whole world should assent, condemnation involves those who consent; assent does not absolve them from transgression. For the crime is not diminished but increased; what was private becomes public. This is what the Lord judged concerning the whole world when he destroyed the sinful world by a universal flood” (Gen. VIII).

They would also hear Leo addressing Anatolius (Epistle 53):

“That condition of the Nicene canons, established through the truly holy Spirit, is in no respect dissoluble. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the increased number of their assembly. Nor may a larger number of priests dare to compare itself with or prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen, since the Synod of Nicaea was consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more, anything differing from their constitution is utterly devoid of authority.”

Of this privilege blessed Ambrose also says:

“Not through human industry or by any arrangement did three hundred and eighteen bishops come together for the council; rather, through the sign of his passion and name, the Lord Jesus proved himself present in their number and in the council. The cross is in the three hundred, the name of Jesus in the eighteen priests.”

“And for me,” says Hilary, “that very number is holy, in which Abraham, conqueror of impious kings, is blessed by him who is the form of the eternal priesthood” (Gen. XIV).

And the same blessed Pope Leo says (Epistle 53):

“Those holy and venerable Fathers who, in the city of Nicaea, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would endure until the end of the world, live among us throughout the whole world in their constitutions. And if anything is presumed anywhere otherwise than they established, it is canceled without hesitation.”

Hence St. Leo says to Pulcheria Augusta (Epistle 55):

“Against the statutes of the paternal canons, which many ages ago were founded in the city of Nicaea upon spiritual decrees, no one is permitted to dare anything. Thus, if anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting them.”

Let them also hear blessed Gregory affirming the decrees of the Nicene Synod in many letters of his, not of his *Register* but of his *Regest*. Let them also place inwardly in their minds that statement of Gregory which I cited earlier:

“With a definition consonant with the holy Fathers, we decree that one who does not know how to obey the sacred canons is not worthy either to minister at the sacred altars or to receive communion.”

If they say that these things have newly emerged, as though a third Cato had now fallen from heaven, let them hear Pope Celestine (Epistle 2):

“No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his own canons, nor to do anything that could oppose the laws [or rules] of the Fathers. Let them not pass over or erase the pronoun ‘their.’ For the canons belong to the priests, just as the law of Moses belongs to the Jews. Hence the Lord says to them: ‘In your law, it is written’ (John VIII). And concerning them: ‘In their law, it is written’ (John XV).”

From this it is clear that if, as Celestine asserts, those are priests whose canons they are, then those whose canons they are not will not be priests either. But enough of this.

Whenever I remember you, venerable Father, I am compelled to cry out: “O unhappy me—rather, more unhappy than the most unhappy—that formerly I did not obey your fingers when, distilling the finest myrrh, they prescribed for me what I ought to do; that, like a deaf asp, I stopped my ears against your admonitions!” (Ps. 57.)

For now that saying of Solomon accuses me: “As a thorn enters the hand of a drunkard, so is a parable in the mouth of fools” (Prov. XXVI). Just as a drunkard holding a thorn in his hand first wounds himself, so my own opinion strangles me with its noose; so my own sword cuts my throat.

By teaching me his law, God wished to soothe me during the days of evil (Ps. XCIII). But I confess to you, holy Father, that toward you I became, in the midst of the furnace, brass by murmuring; tin, like a whitened wall, by lying about better things; iron, by harming my neighbors; lead (Ezek. XXII), by always sinking toward the lowest things.

“We healed Babylon,” says the Lord, “but she was not healed” (Jer. LI). “It cracked,” Scripture says, in the furnace (Ezek. XXII), namely, the one who was not without the wind of pride. Hence I grow pale at that word of the Lord in Ezekiel:

“Woe to the city of blood, for I shall make a great pyre” (Ezek. XXIV),

although God has made in me the way of the path of his anger (Ps. LXXVII). Yet I desire that anger of which Jerome says:

“Great is the offense, after we have sinned, not to deserve the wrath of God, so that I may avoid that anger of which the Psalmist says: ‘The sinner provoked the Lord according to [his mercy / the multitude of] his wrath’ (Ps. X); not because the same sinner sins freely, but because it is a sign of God’s excessive anger that prosperity smiles upon the sinner, that his wickedness is not blunted, and that his crime is not answered according to its deserts.”

And lest I continue too long to detain the majesty of your spirit by lingering over these matters, kissing your feet, embracing your knees, I cry out to you, Father and Lord—one in piety, the other in dignity—asking for the grace of pardon which you had often given to my most holy elder Rumold when he bade you farewell, now a member of the heavenly court. [Note: [Col. 1165D] Is this the same Rumold who was first provost of Goslar and afterward bishop of Constance? Concerning him, see the *Life of St. Benno*, chapter 12, and Lambert, under the year 1069. [Col. 1166D]]

I ask to be worthy of the blessing of your raised hand, for whom no place is distant. I ask that, in that unspeakable joy in which you enter heaven and proclaim matters to the divine ear, you not forget me—who at least then remember you, when I devotedly desire your way of life and the well-trodden path of your conduct.

With my pen scarcely restrained, I shall say with unwilling lips: Farewell, glory of Israel; farewell, senator enrolled in the heavenly court. “I have become foolish by speaking,” you will say to me. I answer: “You compelled me.” In urging moderation upon love, you will waste your effort.

[Col. 1166C] Farewell also, Bernald, little flower of desirable character blooming in spring. I ask you, together with the Apostle’s words to the Philippians:

“If there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort from love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any affection and mercy” (Phil. II),

that I may soon deserve letters dictated to you by your lord, letters more flavorful to me than every nectar, and bearing me only news of your welfare and that of your lord.

Take care, I admonish you, not to fail yourself, so that you may present yourself to us such as I do not know whether I desire or hope you will be. I desire it because of the affection I have for you. I hope it because of regard for the kinship owed to your virtue.

## LETTER III: ADALBERT TO BERNALD

To the lord and most reverend priest Bernald, who now embraces not the frivolous lyre of Horace but David’s mystical harp, more fruitfully for himself and for his hearers, Adalbert, a priest in age but not in conduct, and his Bernald, bound in each of them by the most assured affection of service.

We are not sufficient to render you thanks worthy of you for your sweetest reply. But we entrust this matter, with humble supplication, to the Retributor of all good things, asking that he himself repay you—whom we do not doubt that you have honored in us by such a charitable response and such laborious correspondence.

But because several things in that reply disturb us, secure in our experience of your prudent goodwill, we presume once again to trouble you, and once again eagerly await your diligent judgment concerning certain obscure matters.

Concerning the primacy of the most holy apostolic see, your charity wrote to us with sufficient elegance. You proved most clearly from the decrees of the holy Fathers that, although it has at times been possessed by unworthy men, it must nevertheless always be preferred to all Churches. You taught, in a most Christian pronouncement, that the pontiffs of this see are to be admonished by their subjects in due time, but not rashly proscribed—just as the first possessor of that see was admonished with charitable generosity by his fellow apostle Paul, not deposed by the heretical usurpation of the Arians like St. Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria.

[Col. 1167B] We received with the greatest gratitude your treatise *On the Orders of Judgments*, which we afterward found expressed in the same way and strengthened by the testimonies of the holy Fathers in a certain little book. You agree with us that there are two judicial orders: one concerning doubtful matters, the other concerning manifest ones.

But you subdivide the order concerning manifest matters into two kinds. One occurs when the accused admits both that he did what is alleged and that he sinned by doing it. The other occurs when the accused admits that he did what is alleged but denies that he sinned in doing it. We, however, include this latter kind of your subdivision in our division below the category of doubtful crimes.

For we say that among judicial orders one is concerned with doubtful crimes and the other with manifest crimes. [Col. 1167C] Let no one think that I have said this as though we were prejudicing your division; I have said it chiefly so that we may point out the agreement between the two divisions. For, as it seems to us, both divisions can stand, if your prudence does not judge otherwise.

That category of your division in which the deed is admitted but the guilt is denied is proved to be partly manifest and partly doubtful. The deed, since it is admitted, is manifest; but whether that same deed is to be regarded as a crime is greatly doubted. It is therefore not surprising that the same category, from different points of view, is now assigned to doubtful matters and now to manifest ones.

We have placed it among the doubtful matters chiefly because we divided judicial orders not generally according to deeds but according to crimes. Some concern doubtful crimes; others, manifest ones.

Therefore, the aforementioned category of your division, in which the deed is admitted but whether it is a crime is doubted, could appropriately be counted among the doubtful matters in our division. You, however, divided judicial orders not among crimes but absolutely between hidden and manifest matters. Thus you could, without contradiction, count the aforementioned category—in which guilt is denied but the deed admitted—among manifest matters.

We also praise the fact that you wish a synodical summons to precede the examination of individual cases. The decrees of the holy Fathers likewise command this: those defamed concerning doubtful matters are to be summoned to a gathering of priests and awaited through canonical delays; then, if they come, they are to be heard in the assembly. If they refuse to come, they are to be suspended from communion for contempt.

This is rightly granted to those who either confess that they have done nothing of what is alleged or deny that what they have done is a crime.

Nor do we deny that those bound by public crimes should also be summoned to synodal judgment for contempt, so that they may be judged with greater caution, greater irrefragability, and finally with greater benefit to the Church, in proportion as they have been heard by more people.

But we do not dare to make this synodical summons so universal that we attempt to infringe the privilege of the apostolic see, granted to it not by the apostles but by the Lord himself. For it is the privilege of the apostolic see that, even without a synod being held, it can condemn whomever ought to be condemned and reconcile whomever ought to be reconciled, as blessed Gelasius shows in the decrees sent to the eastern bishops (Epistle 11). There he proves beyond dispute that Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, was canonically condemned by the apostolic see without any synod.

Among other things, he writes:

“The whole Church throughout the world knows that the most holy Roman Church has the right to judge concerning every Church; nor is anyone permitted to judge its judgment, since appeal must be made to it from every part of the world, while no one is permitted to appeal from it.”

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see has had the power, without any preceding synod, to absolve those whom an unjust synod had condemned and to condemn, without any synod existing, those whom it was necessary to condemn. This is surely because of its primacy, which blessed Peter the apostle both held and will always retain by the word of the Lord (Matt. XVI; John XXI).

By the authority of this privilege, therefore, the most holy bishops of the Roman see have been accustomed to condemn, without any synod, those whose contumacy they learned from an incontrovertible report of any kind. This will not escape anyone who carefully reads through the *Register* of St. Gregory and the other decrees of the holy Fathers.

Thus, I say, Maximus, who had presumptuously been enthroned in the episcopate of Salona, was deprived by blessed Gregory of the celebration of Mass, without any synod, because of this presumption. St. Gregory (Book V, Letters 3 and 25) summoned him not so much for manifest crimes as for doubtful ones: Gregory did not know for certain that he had been involved with the Simoniac schism or with women, but had heard that he was so defamed.

Concerning these same crimes Maximus afterward cleared himself by oath (also Book VII, Letter 83). For if Gregory had known him to be so certainly a Simoniac or fornicator that he was presumptuous, he could have condemned him without any summons or examination, in accordance with the aforementioned privilege of the apostolic see.

Furthermore, if we judge that no one, however notorious his crime, should be judged except after a synodical summons, we greatly undermine ecclesiastical correction. We shall defer an excessive multitude of cases [perhaps read: *causarum*, “cases”] to a synod; indeed, on this pretext we shall undoubtedly neglect many of them.

But the custom of the Churches has established that not only a bishop but even a single priest may subject his subordinate, when bound by a manifest crime, to canonical judgment. He does not compel him to come to a synod unless the man has proved disobedient to his judgment.

Nor should it be passed over without consideration that the holy Fathers were accustomed to judge doubtful crimes even without any synod—not definitively, indeed, but under a certain judicial condition. Thus St. Gregory judged Andrew, bishop of Tarentum, who had been defamed because of a concubine after his ordination, in such a way that he was to lay down the priestly office entirely if his conscience declared him guilty of the crime alleged.

[Col. 1169B] But now let us come to our case. Since it will make the matter clearer, let us not hesitate to set it down briefly and faithfully in writing, as we learned it from the most certain report of faithful men. We know that some of them were physically, though not in spirit, present at the conspiracy of Worms, while others were unquestionably present at the Roman synod that condemned the same conspiracy. [Note: [Col. 1169] Read Berthold, or our own Bernald, in the *Chronicle*, under the year 1076.]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, when Pope Gregory VII occupied the apostolic see, King Henry, having already for three years repeatedly been summoned by the apostolic see to do penance for his offenses, refused to come to his senses. Since he foresaw that he would be excommunicated at the approaching Roman synod, he received this counsel from Simoniacs or excommunicated men: he should separate all his subjects from the apostolic bishop, so that he might discredit the holy Roman synod, which was to be held in the first week of Lent and would excommunicate him together with his accomplices.

Having accepted this advice, before that synod, during Septuagesima, he announced a general assembly at Worms. Besides the princes of his kingdom, he gathered a great many bishops and his other faithful—or rather, faithless—men.

Almost all of them, whether Simoniacs, excommunicated persons, or their inseparable accomplices, did not doubt that they would undergo the censure of the Roman pontiff if the king came to his senses, obeyed the apostolic see, and wished to offer it its due assistance in ecclesiastical affairs.

Therefore, taking advantage of the king’s insolence, they not so much agreed with him as persuaded him to send to the apostolic see letters of proscription, strengthened by the subscriptions of all their hands. In those letters, the bishop of the Roman see was treated as proscribed; the Roman synod, which was going to excommunicate the king, would nevertheless be halted, and thus they themselves, together with the king, would be freed from the censure of the apostolic see.

In those letters, after many blasphemies against the Roman pontiff, each had confirmed by his own subscription that he would no longer submit to such a criminal or render him any obedience.

When these letters had been brought to the Roman synod, they did everything in their power through their legates to disrupt it. Blaspheming the apostolic bishop shamefully at the Roman synod, they ordered him to descend from the apostolic see like a most worthless slave, though he had not confessed and had not been convicted of any crime.

Moreover, at the command of the aforementioned Henry, king of the Franks—but certainly not Roman emperor—they insolently forbade the entire Roman synod to obey their lord, the apostolic shepherd, in any way: the shepherd, I say, whom they had hitherto obeyed; whom they had hitherto regarded as their legitimate pastor, canonically ordained and canonically conducting himself in his order; to whom the aforementioned king had also sworn due obedience by a special promise; and whom the bishops and princes of various kingdoms had honored as the vicar of St. Peter.

This man, then, who had not confessed and had not been convicted—or, even if he were guilty, had not been convicted in such a manner or for such a matter—the conspirators wanted through their legates to degrade. With what rashness, or rather with what insane madness! No one would permit even a tavern keeper to be dispossessed in such a way.

For, as blessed Pope Marcellinus testifies in writing to all the orthodox, chapter 11:

“Bishops can bring no prejudice against the pontiff by whom they are proved to have been consecrated.”

Likewise blessed Pope Anacletus, ordained a priest by blessed Peter, says (Epistle 3):

“The sentence by which the sons of Ham are condemned also condemns those who expose the fault of their teachers or superiors, like Ham, who did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for mockery” (Gen. IX).

“But if a teacher or pastor of the Church should depart from the faith, he is to be corrected by the faithful; yet for blameworthy conduct he is more to be tolerated than disciplined.”

Likewise St. Pope Alexander and St. Sixtus, the apostolic bishop—men who all preferred to die rather than lie. These men, each preeminent by the same authority, established nearly the same rule in almost the same words:

“If anyone has a case against bishops, let him first have recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished through familiar conversation, they may heal what needs to be healed. But if anyone presumes to tear them apart, accuse them, or attack them before doing these things, let him be excommunicated.”

If those conspirators of ours had faithfully examined these and countless similar sentences of the holy Fathers, they would never have blown away their own bishop, so to speak, the bishop of the first see, with such sudden abuse, without summoning him and without his confession. Nor would they have killed themselves by so rash an act under a pernicious excommunication.

Indeed, even if he were guilty, he ought not, according to the canons, to be examined by the judgment of foreign bishops, much less rashly deposed. Rather, he should be heard in the Roman synod—if, in doubtful matters, he could be examined anywhere or by anyone according to the canons without his consent.

For it is written: “The disciple is not above the teacher” (Matt. X).

Therefore St. Sylvester, author of the Nicene canons and presiding over the general synod with the consent of 277 bishops, established in chapter 7, saying:

“No one shall judge the first see when it desires to temper justice. For it shall be judged neither by the emperor, nor by all the clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people.”

Likewise Pope Symmachus, writing to all the bishops, decreed in chapter 7:

“God has willed that the cases of other men be resolved by men, but he has reserved the sacred judgment of the bishops of the holy Roman see to himself, without question.”

Likewise St. Pope Alexander, who consecrated his decrees by martyrdom, testifies in chapter 1:

“He cannot be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment.”

But we would consume time before examples if we attempted to enumerate individually all the statutes of the holy Fathers of this kind. For the aforementioned Pope Symmachus, that tireless defender of the Catholic faith, when he was being branded with numerous crimes, was not so rashly proscribed by the Arian king Theoderic, who at that time ruled the Romans; rather, he awaited examination in a Roman synod, and by no one other than one lawfully convened for that purpose. Accordingly, the synod assembled at Rome by his own authority nevertheless did not presume to examine him, although he permitted it, contrary to the decrees of the holy Fathers; instead, as the acts of that synod testify, it entrusted his entire case to divine judgment. Nor do we say this as though we believed that anything wicked whatsoever were permitted to the Roman pontiff with impunity—as though he himself could not be accused if he were publicly exposed as belonging to some heresy—but we are acting against those who, in a matter of doubt, rashly judged that the bishop of the apostolic see ought to be expelled.

Indeed, our own apostolic bishop repeatedly requested from his plotters that they assemble at Rome or elsewhere, wherever he might be able to come, in a synod; and since he willingly granted this, they were to examine his ordination or conduct canonically, in whatever manner they wished. He promised that he would withdraw from the apostolic see without any opposition if they found anything in him deserving deposition. This could easily be believed of one who, having been seized and driven to that eminence, ascended it with great lamentation; for in the Roman pontificate he had no need to seek either riches or secular honors, since before his pontificate he had possessed both in abundance with less anxiety.

But his plotters have thus far refused to meet him in person—not so much in order by any means to escape from an accusation of this kind as to avoid receiving from him the sentence they deserved for their crimes. For, as Pope Boniface of blessed memory testifies (*Epistle* 2): “No one doubts that the guilty person evades judgment in the same way that the innocent person seeks acquittal.”

[Note: [Col. 1171] For the year of Christ 1076, read Baronius, volume eleven, under the year 1076.]

Accordingly, when an assembly had been held at Worms, they had forged a schismatic conspiracy against the Lord and against his Christ, which, as has been stated, they had made public through their legates in that same synod in order to invalidate the holy Roman synod. Therefore the Roman citizens, rightly angered at the dishonoring of the holy Roman Church, seized the legates of the aforementioned men, deeming them worthy of every punishment, and wished at least in some measure to avenge their monstrous crime. But the Roman pontiff, although he was specially attacked by the aforesaid legates, nevertheless at last scarcely rescued them from the hands of the Romans, who were treating them cruelly; after the crowd had been calmed and silence had been made, he had them sit at his feet. He did this so that they themselves might hear what the holy synod would decree in that same synod concerning such a schismatic conspiracy, which had been made public there to his injury.

The holy synod therefore decreed that all who had deliberately and willingly forged that wicked conspiracy and that most contumacious embassy should be deprived of office and communion. But to all the remaining participants in the same conspiracy it granted a period of grace, so that before the next feast of Saint Peter they might prove, by sending legates, either that they had committed the offense under compulsion or that they would submit, as bound by the same crime, to the excommunication of the aforementioned men.

But the king, who after many admonitions refused to repent—indeed, who was the author of this schismatic conspiracy—the apostolic lord bound, deprived of his kingdom, under the bond of anathema, just as he had promised him before the excommunication. We confidently believe that no one will doubt the canonical promulgation of this anathema against him who carefully considers that letter of the apostolic lord, in which he most clearly proved that he had repeatedly warned the king, awaited him for a long time, and only then anathematized him canonically. Therefore, setting aside the king’s particular case, let us see what the holy Fathers generally defined concerning conspirators of this kind.

The most holy Pope Fabian, an indefatigable soldier of truth, writing to all the bishops, decreed as follows:

“If any cleric is hostile or treacherous toward his bishop, and attempts to accuse him, or is a conspirator, let him immediately, before judgment has been examined, be removed from the clergy and handed over to the civil court, which he shall serve throughout the days of his life; and let him remain infamous, without any hope of restoration.”

Likewise Saint Callistus, pope and most vigorous champion of truth, writing to the Gallican bishops, says:

“We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies are flourishing in your regions, and we have been informed that the peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The cunning of this crime is execrable not only among Christians but also among pagans, and it is prohibited by the law of outsiders. For this reason the laws condemn those guilty of this crime not only ecclesiastically but also civilly—and not only those who conspire but also those who consent to them. Our predecessors, together with a very large assembly of bishops, ordered that all who had been constituted in the priestly order or who were clerics should be deprived of the honor they enjoyed. They ordered all the others to be deprived of communion and expelled from the Church. And this applies not only to those who commit the act but also to those who consent to them.”

Likewise the most sacred Council of Chalcedon, which should be held in the same reverence as the Gospel, decreed irrevocably in chapter 18:

“If any clerics or monks are found to be swearing together, conspiring, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, let them be utterly removed from their own rank.”

Therefore, those whom the holy Fathers most strictly judged should be degraded even before judgment had been examined, or utterly expelled from the Church, the apostolic lord, by synodal judgment, treated with sufficient mercy by depriving them of office and communion until they should give satisfaction. Yet he did not fail to recognize that, before they had been cleansed of that crime, it would be dangerous—indeed destructive—for them to usurp these things.

Perhaps one of them says: “What was done against a man whom we did not wish to regard as a bishop should not be considered a conspiracy.” But let him hear this, if he is nevertheless a bishop: Does he also decree that he should not be regarded as a bishop if one of his subjects refuses to regard him as bishop, although he has not been publicly exposed as a heretic or condemned for any crime? We certainly do not believe this, so long as the episcopate is so pleasing to them. Therefore let them not deny their pastor what they would not wish to have denied to themselves by their subjects; but, in accordance with that decree of Saint Leo:

“Let them themselves render to their own prelate the obedience which they demand from their subjects. Indeed, they themselves now demonstrate that even at the time when they were conspiring, they ought to have regarded him as bishop, since for that very conspiracy they do not cease to come to him to give satisfaction.”

Certainly, even if they were not held liable for the guilt of any conspiracy, they would nevertheless rightly be condemned without precedent, since without precedent they presumed to make their contumacy public in the Roman synod and, in addition, to disturb that same synod. They complain in vain that they were condemned without a synodal summons, since even in provincial synods this is observed as canonical: that the contumacy of anyone publicly exposed in a synod is in no way to go unpunished, even if it is not disclosed that it was perpetrated there in order to invalidate the synod itself.

Moreover, the bishop of the Roman see, by virtue of his privilege, as we have already mentioned, can condemn or reconcile anyone who ought to be condemned or reconciled without any synod. Thus Saint Gregory, writing to Januarius, bishop of Caralis (*Book VII, Epistle 67*), deprived the counselors of that bishop of communion until they gave satisfaction, although they had not been summoned by any synod; through their counsel that bishop, in a mad frame of mind, had devastated the harvest of certain people on the Lord’s days. Likewise the Gregory of our own time was able to condemn those who had not been summoned to any synod but were nevertheless bound by a manifest crime. Through their counsel King Henry attempted, in a new act of presumption, to devastate not an earthly harvest but an ecclesiastical one.

Likewise Saint Gregory (*Book II, Epistles 6 and 7*) excommunicated John, bishop of Justiniana Prima, although he had not been summoned by any synod, because he had presumed unjustly to depose Adrian, bishop of the city of Thebes. In the same way our own apostolic bishop could excommunicate bishops of unmistakable contumacy without summoning them, since they had attempted to invalidate not merely one bishop but the entire Roman synod. Our conspirators thought that they could apply that example to themselves; in accordance with its judgment, they will have no doubt that they were reasonably excommunicated, if they are willing to be readers rather than violators of the sacred canons.

They also proclaim in vain that the procedure of judgment ought to be followed in their case where it is doubtful whether a manifest deed is a crime. For, as it seems to us, there can be no doubt concerning any deed whether it is a crime when it is shown to have been generally condemned as a crime by the defined judgments of the holy Fathers. For if we doubt whether those things which they generally and synodally prohibited are faults, we will likewise appear to doubt whether their statutes are just. Blessed Pope Leo, writing to Leo Augustus (*Epistle 78*), altogether prohibited this:

“To inquire into things that have been disclosed, to reconsider things that have been completed, and to overturn things that have been defined—what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what has been obtained and to extend the wicked desires of deadly greed toward the food of the forbidden tree?”

He says further:

“Concerning matters defined both at Nicaea and at Chalcedon, as God willed, we dare not undertake any discussion, as though they were doubtful or weak, since such authority has fixed them through the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, to Emperor Marcian:

“If anything anywhere is presumed contrary to what the holy Fathers decreed, it shall be annulled without hesitation.”

Therefore our conspirators wished in vain to examine whether their manifest deed was a crime, although they themselves knew without doubt that it had been condemned as a crime by the defined judgments of the holy Fathers. Accordingly, they were not to be awaited during a period of grace as people bound by doubtful crimes; rather, as contumacious persons and most open despisers of the canons, they were to be condemned without delay. Concerning such persons divine Scripture has decreed most plainly, as the Council of Carthage established in chapter 5: the sentence is not to be delayed but rather carried out. Hence Saint Gregory, writing to the abbot Mariniano and others (*Epistle 27*), testifies:

“If we delay pursuing or avenging those things by which God is grievously offended, we provoke the patience of the Divinity to anger.”
