Likewise Pope Damasus of pious memory, writing to Stephen, archbishop of Mauretania, and the remaining bishops of Africa, says:

“Whoever is able to oppose and restrain the perverse but does not do so does nothing other than favor their impiety.”

We do not presume to affirm the three forms of anathema prescribed for us by the Council of Tribur as so general that we assert, contrary to the privilege of the apostolic see, that no one may be condemned without a synodal summons. It would be better for us—and, if it seems so to you, for you as well—to say that the same council omitted some form of anathema rather than that it prejudiced the privilege of the apostolic see.

We do not consider it necessary to answer each individual objection—or, more accurately, each criticism—of the conspirators. They had in no way purged themselves of their guilt; instead, by a perverse interpretation of Scripture and by disparaging the Roman pontiff, they had doubled their crime. As for the perjury which they pretend that he committed, even if he had been their subject, they ought nevertheless first to have proved that he had committed it, though he did not confess it, before they so tyrannically punished it in him. But if, as they pretend, he had sworn that the Roman pontiff was to be elected with the consent of King Henry, nevertheless—as you prudently foresaw—he ought never to have anathematized himself by opposing the privilege of the Roman election, especially since the canons say: “An incautious definition is commendably revoked.” This is not treachery but the correction of rashness.

Furthermore, if some anchorite or enclosed monk, who had most firmly promised God a solitary life, is sought for the episcopal rank, should he give more consideration to his promise, however cautiously made, than to the Church’s cause? Certainly not. Our conspirators themselves willingly concede this, some of whom rushed into the episcopate after completely casting aside even the monastic habit. Therefore, if even the most carefully made promise is commendably revoked for the sake of the Church, how much more so in a matter which is prohibited from being fulfilled under anathema. We do not say this as though we believed that the apostolic lord had ever sworn such a thing, but chiefly so that, even if he had done what he did not do, we would nevertheless not on that account prove that he should be proscribed in this way.

The judgments of the holy Fathers which they cite concerning the restraint of the pride of prelates, or concerning rash condemnation, strike them most severely. For they had shown unprecedented pride not only toward their subjects but toward their own prelate, whom with singular contumacy they had ordered to descend from the apostolic see as though he were their servant. But enough of this.

We cannot repay Almighty God with fitting thanks, whose grace has granted us that in this perilous time, when everyone seeks what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ (Philippians 2), adulterating the word of the Lord (2 Corinthians 2), we at least have you—one whose nose does not wrinkle at hearing the truth, but to whom the proclamation of truth tastes all the sweeter the more freely it is spoken. We would not presume to speak so freely and sincerely to anyone else, since we would think that he would interpret each matter according to some private interest rather than according to the truth itself. It would be wicked even to suspect this of you, who have judged that the very herald of truth ought to be venerated as a shrine of the Holy Spirit. Having therefore experienced your zeal and prudence in investigating and proclaiming the truth of matters, we especially await your judgment concerning those things about which we still have doubts.

Concerning the Simoniacs, then, we ask that your prudence explain more clearly to us whether those also are to be counted among heretics who buy or sell, for the sake of sacred orders, certain ecclesiastical offices, such as a deanery or a provostship. We do not deny that they can reasonably be called Simoniacs, since they seek secular profit from a spiritual office; and we judge that they should be expelled from those offices in accordance with the canons. But we should like to be taught more clearly, from the testimonies of the holy Fathers, why they are to be counted as heretics.

Saint Gregory, namely, in his decrees (*Epistle 55*), seems specifically to call that Simoniacal heresy which occurs when the laying on of hands is bought or sold for money. Kindly also write to us whether those are counted as heretics who have bought or sold sacred offices through a payment other than one made by hand.

[Note: [Col. 1175D] That is, not with money; for they called this a *munus a manu*, “a gift from the hand,” as is clear from Book I of Saint Anselm *Against Guibert*, where he lists three kinds of gifts by which ecclesiastical benefices were bought: *munus a manu*, a gift from the hand; *munus a lingua*, a gift from the tongue; and *munus ab obsequio*, a gift from service.]

We would rather have such people considered ambitious than liable to the heresy of Simony, lest the ecclesiastical sacraments be utterly proscribed, since we are aware that until now they have been almost entirely usurped by people of this kind, driven by ambition.

But concerning what you write—that the sacraments usurped by a Simoniac who has not yet been publicly exposed are not sacraments to one who knows, but are sacraments to one who does not know—we have not yet been able to understand it faithfully. For opposition between the opinions of disputants does not ordinarily alter the essence of things. Therefore, if sacraments are truly effected in any manner by a Simoniac, how can they truly be proved not to have been effected for someone who knows of his heresy? It does indeed seem credible that bodily things placed upon the altar can, through priestly blessing and by the consent of the Church, be converted into divine sacraments even in the hands of heretics who have not yet been publicly exposed within the Church. We fear, I say, to proscribe such sacraments. Or, in the judgment of one who alone, or together with another, has recognized the madness of the celebrating heretic, it would seem better to us to believe that they are sacraments both for the heretic who effects them and for another who knows his heresy than to declare that they both are and are not sacraments—namely, that the same offering might result in condemnation for the heretic who offers it or for his associate, but in salvation for the Catholic who is unaware.

For when Saint Augustine testifies that neophytes who were overtaken by death before communion were nevertheless not deprived of the sacrament, he seems to have been speaking not of the thing itself but of the power of the sacrament: that a person is not deprived of the sacrament’s power when extreme necessity prevents him from real communion. And indeed, if we all continue to cooperate with the Catholic faith, we are never deprived of the power of that sacrament, although we may partake of the sacrament itself less frequently. Thus we could more easily understand you if you said that any Catholic who receives from someone whom he does not know to be a heretic receives not the thing of the sacrament—which the heretic himself cannot effect—but the power of the sacrament, not from that reception but from his own faith. This would seem more intelligible to us than to say that the same bread was both made and not made into a divine sacrament. Therefore explain to us more plainly what we ought to judge concerning sacraments of this kind.

Your opinion concerning those ordained by a heretic and to be ordained again by a Catholic also seems to conflict with the fact that we read of many clerics of heretics who, after converting to the Catholic faith, were accepted in their orders—not reconsecrated. Thus the Council of Nicaea decreed in chapter 8 that the Novatians were to be received in their orders, and the African Council in chapter 35 made the same decision concerning the Donatists, without reconsecrating them. Indeed, the Council of Nicaea established that only the clerics of the Paulianists were to be reordained by Catholics, and it also decreed that those whom they had baptized were to be baptized by Catholics. For that heresy did not make an invocation of the Holy Trinity.

Pope Damasus, however, writing to Prosper, bishop of the first see of Numidia, and to the other bishops (*Epistle 5*), seems to support your opinion concerning reordination, if we are not mistaken in the copy:

“Through that illicit laying on of hands, as we mentioned a little earlier, the head of the one who seemed to have received something was wounded. And where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied by which the stain may be healed once it has been inflicted—that is, what was neither lawfully performed nor lawfully conferred must be repeated, if it is to be considered complete. For I cannot discover how one who received honor from someone who did not lawfully possess the power to confer it could retain that honor.”

[Note: [Col. 1177D] This statement of Damasus, and similar statements, should be understood either of the reconciliation of those ordained with the Church or of true reordination, if someone was not validly ordained by a heretic or schismatic—namely, when the person who ordained the ordained had neither the right nor the power to ordain.]

We do not know how to reconcile the contradiction between these opinions unless we perhaps say that, by the authority of the apostolic see and with the consent of the holy mother Church, it is permitted, in a particular temporal necessity, to receive into their order those ordained by heretics through invocation of the Holy Trinity without reconsecrating them; yet that at some time it may order them to be reconsecrated, in order to proscribe more clearly the heretical ordination. For some appear to have received no consecration at all from heretics, since the latter had long been deprived of every spiritual grace, as blessed Jude the Apostle testifies concerning them:

“These are the ones who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit.”

Hence blessed Innocent says:

“When heretics departed from the Catholic faith, they lost the perfection of the Spirit which they had received.”

From this it is inferred that those ordained by a heretic received not some consecration, but only the form of consecration without the power of sanctification. Whether that form is retained by converts, once they have received the power of sanctification through the consent of the holy Church, or is utterly proscribed through repetition, there is presently no reasonable objection that occurs to us.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Adalbert and Bernaldus discuss these matters not by way of assertion but for the sake of inquiry.]

For the objection which says that an invocation of the Holy Trinity, even if performed by a heretic, ought not to be annulled is easily refuted, since we are likewise commanded to reconsecrate churches consecrated by heretics through invocation of the Holy Trinity. Thus Saint John, the first apostolic bishop of that name, is read to have decreed, writing to various bishops (*Epistle 2*):

“Wherever you find churches of the Arians, consecrate them as Catholic churches without delay through divine prayers and works, because we also did so when we were at Constantinople on account of King Theoderic.”

Certainly, although the form of sacred baptism in the name of the Holy Trinity has been received from a heretic, we do not repeat it, lest we appear to violate the Apostle’s commandment prescribing one baptism. Moreover, as Pope Felix, presiding over a general synod, most truthfully declared:

“No one can come to a second baptism unless, after first professing paganism, he has denied that he is a Christian.”

This denial seems rightly to occur through the repetition of baptism, so that the person may be punished most severely in accordance with the Council of Nicaea.

[Note: [Col. 1177D] Felix III does not wish those who have denied Christ to be baptized again, or admitted to a second baptism, as the author of this letter seems to have understood. Rather, while exaggerating the crime of the bishops, priests, and deacons who had allowed themselves to be rebaptized, he says that they could not proceed to a second baptism—that is, to repeated baptism—unless they utterly denied Christ and professed themselves pagans. For this reason he subjects them to perpetual penance.]

This much, however, we know without doubt: in accordance with the apostolic sanctions, no one ordained by a heretic is either to be received by Catholics in his order or to be reordained, unless some temporal necessity is being accommodated in this matter. For, as the aforementioned Pope Innocent asserts:

“By an evil laying on of hands, the heretic inflicted condemnation upon the ordained person; and because the remedy of penance is necessary for him, he cannot possess the honor of a lawful ordination.”

Likewise the African Council, in chapter 35, decreed that those ordained in the party of Donatus, if they wished, after correction, to pass over to the Catholic faith, were not to be received in their honors, in accordance with the Transmarine Council, except those whose reception served the unity of the Catholic Church.

It should also be noted that the African Council, in chapter 75, decrees that rebaptisms, reordinations, or transfers of bishops may not be carried out.

Likewise the most holy Pope Gregory, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna (*Book II, Epistle 32*), says:

“Just as one who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has once been consecrated ought not to be consecrated again in the same order. But if someone perhaps came to the priesthood with a minor fault, penance should be imposed for the fault, while the order nevertheless remains.”

But in these statements, as it seems to us, it is not so much the usurpations of heretics as the ordinations of Catholics that are prohibited from being repeated. For a consecration which cannot be given to anyone by a heretic, as has been proved, if it is bestowed by a Catholic upon converts is more properly called not a repeated consecration but one bestowed for the first time.

If we regard the consecrations of the excommunicated, as of heretics, as worthless, we fear that we would contradict the judgments of blessed Pope Anastasius, addressed to Emperor Anastasius. He contends that the sacraments which Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, usurped were not invalid, although Acacius had long before been anathematized by Pope Felix. Thus the aforementioned Pope Anastasius writes to the emperor in chapter 8:

“Therefore Acacius—whose name, we say, ought to be passed over in silence—harmed only himself by administering good things wickedly; for the inviolate sacrament which was given through him obtained the perfection of its power for others, but was harmful to him.”

If someone’s overly curious suspicion extends so far that, imagining that after Pope Felix’s judgment had been issued Acacius thereafter acted ineffectively in the sacraments which he usurped, he fears on the same account for those who received the mysteries imparted either in consecrations or in baptism, lest the divine gifts appear invalid, let him remember that the foregoing argument applies equally here. For Acacius did this after he had been judged, not without usurpation of the priesthood. Since the mysteries retained their power, the guilty person did not harm others in this matter either.

For to him applied what is sung in David’s trumpet:

“Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 67).

For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, as the entire authority of the heavenly Scriptures testifies; so too it is said through the Holy Spirit in the Prophet:

“He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100).

Therefore, since he claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own head in condemnation; the people, who thirsted for his gift in the mysteries, were not excluded.

This judgment of Pope Anastasius seems therefore to forbid us to consider even the sacraments of excommunicated persons invalid. It is clearly opposed to your assertion concerning the annulment of sacraments of this kind, unless perhaps we say that blessed Pope Anastasius did not say this about those publicly exposed under anathema, but specifically about Acacius, whose condemnation is believed not to have been made public while he was alive. For he refused to receive Pope Felix’s letter of excommunication, as Liberatus testifies in his book. In that letter Acacius was commanded not to doubt that he was excommunicated after he had received the same letter through the deacon Toleratus. But the legate of the apostolic see did not presume to deliver or publish it to Acacius, because the emperor was supporting his error.

For if his condemnation had been published to his subjects, then, according to the assertion of blessed Pope Innocent, he would have inflicted condemnation rather than consecration upon those whom he ordained. That his condemnation was concealed in this way seems sufficiently proved by the fact that Bishop Euphemius, Acacius’s successor, asks blessed Pope Gelasius when Acacius would be condemned, as is contained in the same pope’s letter to Euphemius (*Pope Gelasius I, Epistle 9*). We also believe that those who have been condemned, but whose condemnation we do not yet know, can effect divine sacraments through the consent of the Church; yet we do not dare to attribute their effecting of the sacraments to those who have been publicly condemned.

Your charity should not hesitate to write back to us concerning what you think of all these matters. Likewise, if we regard as worthless the consecrations of those who were once ordained as Catholics but have now been removed for some fault, we seem to contradict the statements of Saint Augustine, who testifies in *On the Good of Marriage* (chapter 24) that the sacrament of ordination remains even in the condemned:

“If the clergy are ordained in order to gather the people, even if the gathering of the people does not follow, the sacrament of ordination nevertheless remains in those who have been ordained. And if someone is removed from office because of some fault, he will not be without the sacrament of the Lord once it has been imposed, although he remains subject to judgment.”

According to this man’s judgment, those who have been removed from office, since they retain the sacrament of ordination, can celebrate the divine sacraments, although to their own condemnation—unless you think it should be understood otherwise.

We therefore await your deliberative judgment concerning all these matters: both those which we ourselves have resolved, in whatever manner our understanding has been able to manage, and those which we have not yet been able to resolve or understand:

“May the God of peace sanctify you completely, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5).

[Col. 1181]

A BOOK OF BERNALDUS THE PRIEST: ON AVOIDING COMMUNION WITH THE EXCOMMUNICATED, ON THE RECONCILIATION OF THE FALLEN, AND ON THE AUTHORITY OF COUNCILS, CANONS, DECREES, DECRETALS, AND OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS THEMSELVES. NOW FIRST RECOVERED FROM DARKNESS INTO THE LIGHT.

TO THE READER

Who Bernaldus of Constance was, and what he wrote, Gretserus explained in his *Apologia for Gregory VII*. He also inserted there various previously unseen works of Bernaldus in support of that same pontiff Gregory against the schismatics. Meanwhile, by a kindly providence, this little treatise, now being published, has also emerged from darkness. As a defender of the Gregorian name and honor, we have not delayed sharing it with the orthodox reader.

Gebhardus, whom he addresses in a brief preface, may perhaps be the man whom Bernaldus mentions in his *Chronicle* under the year 1098. Gebhardus—for that is how it should be read, not Gerhardus as in the Urstisian edition—the venerable abbot of Schaffhausen, out of humility resigned his position with the consent of the lord pope, and obtained from him permission for another abbot to be placed over that house. Likewise, under the year 1100: “Gebhardus, the venerable abbot, who had previously resigned the abbey of Schaffhausen for God, and with the authority of the lord Pope Urban undertook the journey to Jerusalem with the army of Christians; after many labors they captured the city, and entrusted the keeping of the Lord’s Sepulchre to the aforementioned abbot.”

Moreover, whatever Bernaldus argues in this little work is directed toward showing that the decrees of Gregory VII and of other recent pontiffs deserve no less reverence, observance, and obedience than the statutes of the ancient pontiffs and councils; and consequently that those excommunicated by the apostolic see were rightly to be avoided, but that those who returned, or desired to return, to a better mind were rightly to be received and granted pardon. For there were people who showed themselves harsher toward those fallen into schism than was proper.

[Col. 1181A]

TO THE LORD AND VENERABLE GEBHARDUS, A MAN OF EVANGELICAL PERFECTION, BERNALDUS, A PRIEST IN NAME ONLY, NOT IN CONDUCT: AFTER THE TRANSITORY PILGRIMAGE OF THIS LIFE, THE ETERNAL POSSESSION OF THE HEAVENLY HOMELAND.

“We have endeavored, by writing, to satisfy as far as we could your request concerning the need to avoid the dangerous communion of the excommunicated. But we have also not been reluctant to add other matters which we thought would please you no less—namely, what is to be understood concerning the rigor of the canons with regard to the condemnation or deposition of those who have fallen. Likewise, concerning their reconciliation, or that of heretics. Concerning all these matters we have faithfully collected not our own opinions but those of the holy Fathers. Consideration of these matters is especially necessary in our time, in which the holy Church is suffering beyond measure among the excommunicated and condemned, whether in receiving some of them into her bosom or at least in keeping herself immune from their contagion. May the mercy of Almighty God always protect you in safety and mindful of us, dearest lord brother.”

As far as we have been able to gather from the judgments of apostolic men, there are three classes of persons whom our holy Fathers have marked out for punishment under excommunication. First and foremost is the excommunicated person himself, who has been separated from ecclesiastical communion by a formal judicial process. Next is his supporter, who does not hesitate to favor him by agreeing and cooperating with him both inwardly and outwardly. Likewise there is his communicant, who, even if he does not reveal that he agrees with his error, nevertheless does not separate himself from his communion.

But let all these also hear what blessed Pope Gelasius says in writing to the Eastern bishops:

“All accomplices, followers, and communicants of a wickedness once condemned are judged to share the same fate.”

And a little later:

“Acacius, who communicated with Peter, became a participant in the crime and thus also in the punishment.”

Likewise, to all the bishops of Dardania:

“Our fathers judged that, once the author of any madness had been condemned, together with the error itself, it was sufficient that whoever at any time became a communicant of this error should be condemned by its principal sentence [Roman edition: ‘should be bound by the sentence of his condemnation’], since anyone can plainly be recognized either by his possession or by his communion.”

And a little later:

“The form of Catholic faith and communion, once the Council of Nicaea had been promulgated, excludes without reconsideration all Arians, or anyone who has fallen into this plague either by consent or by communion” [Roman edition: “concluded”].

Likewise, he says further:

“The same error, once condemned together with its author, bears both execration and punishment in anyone who becomes a participant in its wicked communion.”

How, moreover, we ought to avoid excommunicated persons has been prescribed for us with the utmost clarity by the holy Fathers. Among them Callistus I, pope and martyr, enumerates four matters in which we must avoid an excommunicated person: namely, in greeting, in kissing, in prayer, and at table. “For whoever,” he says, “knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or in other prohibited matters shall, according to the institution of the apostles, himself likewise be subjected to excommunication.”

We must likewise avoid their supporters and those who communicate with them, as is attested by Blessed Pope Gelasius, who, writing to the eastern bishops concerning Acacius, who communicated with excommunicated persons, testifies as follows: “We have nothing in common with men of external communion.” Again, in what follows: “What does it avail if someone does not communicate with a more evident heretic, yet is joined in communion with those who have not separated themselves from that person’s communion?” Hence many religious men among the Romans also withdrew from communion with Pope Anastasius, because he had communicated with a certain deacon of Thessalonica who had already communicated with Acacius. For so the Roman *Pontifical* testifies.

[Note: [Col. 1183B] This letter is extant in vol. I of the new edition of the Councils.]

[Note: [Col. 1183C] See Anastasius the Librarian, *Lives of the Pontiffs*, under Anastasius II.]

Therefore the holy Fathers wished those who communicate with the excommunicated to be avoided just as the excommunicated themselves are, [Col. 1183D] because they regarded them as having, so to speak, condemned themselves. Hence Blessed Pope Gelasius, writing to the aforementioned persons concerning that same Acacius, says: “Why do they complain that Acacius was condemned by us, when he is shown to have condemned himself by accepting communion with Peter?” Since every excommunicated person is outside the Church, and no one can be simultaneously within and outside it, whoever does not separate himself from the communion of the excommunicated unquestionably separates himself from Catholic unity. Therefore Catholics rightly avoid, as excommunicated persons, those who have not separated themselves from the communion of the excommunicated.

It must be understood, however, that as long as the wicked remain within [Col. 1184A] Catholic unity, they do not defile the good by their communion, unless the good consent to them, as Blessed Augustine proves very frequently and irrefutably against the Donatists. Once, however, they are separated from the Church, they undoubtedly defile those who communicate with them not only by consent, but also by external communion.

Accordingly, Blessed Augustine, at the Council of Carthage held by 217 bishops, confirmed by his signature the sentence of excommunication against anyone who thereafter should communicate with an excommunicated person, even in prayer. By this sentence the apostles themselves also condemned such a person, according to the testimony of Pope Callistus.

Up to this point we have in some measure satisfied your request concerning the law of excommunication. But because we ought not to repay so dear a brother and lord what we owe without interest, and because we wish to contribute to you other matters no less pleasing—namely, what is to be understood concerning the rigor of the canons regarding the condemnation or deposition of those who have fallen, as well as their reconciliation—for in such cases we need great discernment, lest we seem either excessively rigid, despairing with the Novatians of the salvation of the fallen, or excessively lax and be judged not to possess zeal for God. Let us begin with the rigor of the canons.

In ancient times the Church is said to have granted a place for penance only once, and it was not to be granted to anyone who fell again after penance. Thus Blessed Pope Siricius, in his decrees, states concerning such fallen persons [Col. 1184C] that they no longer have a refuge in which to do penance. We must not, however, understand this as though the holy Fathers despaired of the salvation of such fallen persons, even if they refused to receive them among those doing penance. We must believe that they instituted this not to deter people from penance, but from sin; nor to make them do penance less earnestly, but more humbly after their fall, when they saw themselves regarded as inferior even to those who were doing penance. The same is observed almost as a law in the case of others who have fallen criminally: they are removed from the order which they are discovered to have held before their fall and in which they sinned. In the same way, those established in the order of penitents, if they fall again, are rightly judged unworthy of their former order.

Nevertheless, the holy Fathers are not believed to have decreed these things so harshly out of despair of forgiveness, [Col. 1184D] especially since the Lord wishes all human beings to be saved, as he says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner [the wicked]” (Ezek. 33). And: “On whatever day the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (ibid.). No, I say: we believe that these rules were established not out of despair of forgiveness, but as a precaution for discipline. This too we can approve from the words of Blessed Augustine to the presbyter Macedonius (Letter 54):

“Sometimes,” he says, “the iniquity of human beings advances so far that even after penance has been performed, after reconciliation with the altar, they commit either similar or more serious offenses. Yet God causes his sun to rise even over such persons, [Col. 1185A] and grants them no less generously than before the gifts of life and salvation. And although that place of penance is not granted to them in the Church, God nevertheless does not forget his patience toward them.”

And shortly afterward:

“Although, therefore, it has prudently and beneficially been provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted only once, lest a remedy become less useful to the sick because it is cheap—for a remedy is more health-giving insofar as it is less contemptible—who, nevertheless, would dare to say to God: ‘Why do you still spare this person who, after his first penance, again binds himself in the snares of iniquity?’ Who would dare to say that what the Apostle says is not being done in the case of these people: ‘Do you not know that the patience [kindness] of God leads you to repentance?’ (Rom. 2). Or that, with these people excepted, what is written has been defined: ‘Blessed are all who trust in him’ (Ps. 2), as though he were saying: ‘Who can bar divine mercy even from persons who have fallen in this manner, so that they too may be blessed if they trust in the Lord?’”

Among people of the present time, however, a place of penance is not denied to them, because human depravity has grown so strong and has cast off the yoke of the ancient discipline to such an extent that the holy Church would now rejoice greatly if they were even willing to repent in this way. For she knows that God’s mercy is most ready to pardon, and that with God it makes little difference with what severity or leniency, according to the diversity of times, sins are punished, provided only that the sinner turns back with his whole heart.

Some are also moved by the fact that Blessed Pope Innocent, writing to Victoricius, bishop of Rouen, asserts that a virgin consecrated to God is not to be admitted to perform penance if she marries while the man who corrupted her is alive. “For,” he says, “the same rule is observed in marriages: a woman who, while her husband is alive, marries another is not admitted to perform penance as long as the adulterer lives.” This too must certainly be understood as instituted rather from the rigor of discipline than from despair of forgiveness—namely, so that people might cease from such a sin, knowing that it could bar them even from the place of penance. Such a woman is quite appropriately regarded as unworthy of performing penance, especially while she and those with whom she sinned [Col. 1185D] are still alive. For at that time also the holy Church is accustomed to be scandalized by them, since their sin is made public every day not only through the women themselves but through the presence of the fornicators.

Not only in the matters mentioned above, but also in other judgments of the canons, the advancement of ecclesiastical discipline is especially considered: both that those who have sinned may be corrected and that others may be deterred from sinning. Hence some are separated from ecclesiastical communion for seven years, others for ten, and sometimes even until the end of their lives, on account of their crimes. Under this strictness they ought willingly to labor, not only to wash away their sins, but also to make satisfaction to the holy Church of God and reconcile her to themselves by doing penance—the Church whom they scandalized by their wrongdoing.

[Col. 1186A] Nevertheless, that number of years does not prevent God from being able, and accustomed, to forgive them before the period has been completed, if they have done worthy penance, according to the statement of Blessed Pope Leo: “Because,” he says, “we can neither impose measures upon God’s mercy nor define times for it; with him the turning of the sinner suffers no delay in receiving forgiveness.” Therefore the holy Fathers often judged that this number of years should be anticipated in reconciliation, provided that ecclesiastical discipline was not thereby harmed, at least in the case of those who had done worthy penance. For, as Blessed Augustine testifies in his *Enchiridion*, in such an act of penance the measure of sorrow is to be considered more than the measure of time.

Likewise Blessed Pope Innocent says: “It belongs to the priest to judge the weight of sins, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the sighs and tears of the one who is correcting himself; and then order forgiveness to be granted when he sees that satisfaction is adequate.”

Hence the Council of Nicaea, which had prescribed that the fallen should suffer for three years among the catechumens and afterward for ten years among the penitents, permitted bishops to treat them more humanely if they had repented not deceptively but truly, with fear and tears. Those who were lukewarm and did penance carelessly, however, it ordered by every means to fulfill the appointed period. Blessed Jerome most evidently agrees with this judgment:

“With God,” he says, “the measure of time is not as valuable as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices. For this reason the canons command that the periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of the penitents, and lengthened because of negligence.”

[Col. 1186C] The circumstances of the times sometimes also compel the rigor of the canons to be relaxed. Thus Blessed Pope Innocent decreed that this should be done in certain cases (in his letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse), involving those who, after spending this life in pleasures, finally seek both penance and reconciliation at the point of death.

“Toward such persons,” he says, “the earlier practice was harsher; the later, when mercy intervenes, is more inclined to leniency.” For the earlier custom maintained that penance should be granted but communion denied.

“For since persecutions were frequent in those times, lest the general permission of reconciliation should make people secure and fail to recall them from [Col. 1186D] falling, communion was rightly denied while penance was granted, so that nothing might be refused altogether; and the reckoning of time made forgiveness more severe. But after our Lord restored peace to his Churches, when terror had been driven away, it was judged fitting that communion be given to those departing this life. Because of the Lord’s mercy, it was granted as viaticum to those about to depart, lest we seem to follow the harshness and severity of the heretic Novatian, who denied forgiveness. Therefore communion is granted [will be granted] together with final penance, so that such people, even at their last hour, may, with the permission of our Savior, be rescued from everlasting destruction.”

Behold to what extent this apostolic man considered it proper to relax the ancient rigor: he allowed communion, which had been denied to certain persons even at the end, to be restored. He then carefully attached rational explanations both for the ancient rigor and for the later remission.

Sometimes even the multitude of offenders does not permit the rigor of discipline, so that what is committed by many can be punished canonically. In such a case, according to the testimony of that same apostolic man, the earlier matters are to be committed to God’s judgment, while great care must be taken concerning what follows. Consideration of human frailty also sometimes compels the rigor of the canons to be softened. Hence Blessed Pope Nicholas first decreed that communion at the altar should be restored to parricides and fratricides after two years, lest they despair; the Council of Ancyra, however, [prescribed] that it should not be restored even to homicides except at the end of life.

In the same way, voluntary confession has customarily mitigated canonical severity, according to the Council of Chalcedon, which decreed that mercy should be shown to monks and consecrated virgins who had fallen from their profession but confessed their fault. Such remissions would in no way be admitted among authentic sanctions if people were believed capable of being saved only when they completed penance according to the rigor of the canons. That would plainly appear not Catholic but Pelagian. For Pelagius taught as a dogma that forgiveness was granted to those who asked for it not according to God’s grace, but according to their merits and labors.

But with God, as we have already said, conversion suffers no delay in receiving forgiveness. Therefore the holy Fathers are believed, in the canonical rigor, to have prescribed not a limit to indulgence but a pattern of discipline, so that they might restrain people from sins and deny forgiveness to no one who truly turned back. Such forgiveness is received more humbly and fruitfully the less it is recognized as owed according to the rigor of the canons. Accordingly, when the holy Fathers are read to have denied certain persons the place of penance or communion—sometimes entirely, sometimes for a period—we must understand this not as despair concerning the fallen, but as discipline for the correction of those who had sinned, lest we judge that the holy Fathers despaired of the fallen together with the Novatians.

The sacred canons also depose clerics who have fallen into crime in many places, and prescribe no hope of restoration for them. Yet we must not attend to this rigor of the canons so excessively that, together with the Novatians, we rashly prejudice the ecclesiastical authority to bind and to loose. For, as Blessed Augustine testifies in a letter to Boniface:

“Such irreparable deposition of clerics was instituted not so much out of despair of forgiveness as from the rigor of discipline. Otherwise one would be arguing against the keys of the Church, concerning which it was said: ‘Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’” (Matt. 16).

The canons themselves sometimes grant such condemned persons their former order, as at the Council of Nicaea in the case of the Novatians and in Africa in the case of the Donatists. The holy Fathers would not have done this if, together with the Novatians, they had despaired entirely of indulgence for the fallen.

Blessed Pope Callistus, martyr, also writes to all the bishops: “They are mistaken who think that priests cannot be restored after a fall if they have performed worthy penance.”

Likewise Blessed Pope Gregory, writing to Secundinus, a servant of God living in enclosure, asserted that the fallen could be restored to their order; yet elsewhere in his *Register* he prohibited their restoration in accordance with the rigor of the canons. For in a letter to Constantius, bishop of Milan, he says:

“If permission is granted to the fallen to return to their former order, the rigor of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore strive above all else to ensure that no supplication whatsoever persuade you to restore the fallen to the sacred order.”

Do you therefore see the singular diligence of the holy Fathers? They declared both that the restoration of the fallen belonged to the ecclesiastical authority and that it should not be granted to the fallen, so that the rigor of discipline might everywhere generally be feared, yet it might not be judged unlawful if, in some place, ecclesiastical usefulness were served by restoring a particular fallen person. We should not consider them self-contradictory in this, if they sometimes restored to the order those whom elsewhere they prohibited from being restored. For there is no doubt that in both cases they had one and the same intention: to provide with the greatest care for ecclesiastical welfare, whether they observed the rigor of the canons or tempered it for a time according to the circumstances. They always strove above all to prohibit evils and establish good things; and they clearly could not have accomplished this if they had not sought, according to the diversity of times, to proceed now more gently and now more severely.

Thus the Fathers of Nicaea judged that the Novatians, and the African Fathers that the Donatists, should be treated more gently, as has been stated, in order that they might recall them from error even by this means. Likewise Blessed Pope Gelasius mitigated the rigor of the canons in the case of certain laymen, whom, because of ecclesiastical necessity, he permitted to reach the priesthood within a year; and he asserted that, in the necessary discharge of his office, he had thereby properly yielded to the circumstances of the time. Similarly, his predecessor Blessed Pope Leo the Great is said to have tolerated in the episcopate even neophytes—that is, men advanced from the laity to the episcopate. In the ordination of Ambrose also, no small concession was made to the rigor of the canons: because of ecclesiastical necessity he was ordained bishop on the eighth day after his baptism. Yet the holy Fathers are nowhere read to have accommodated themselves to circumstances in this manner except where dispensatory leniency appeared likely to benefit the Church more than canonical severity.

Those, therefore, are not to be considered self-contradictory who are believed to have had everywhere the same intention of prohibiting evils and establishing good things. If this consideration is faithfully applied to ecclesiastical institutions, they will not appear contradictory to themselves, even if they sometimes seem to have decreed different things. For if we carefully investigate the original causes of each statute, we shall find that each is most fittingly adapted to its own cause according to the diversity of times and that it chiefly aims at ecclesiastical welfare. This will not escape anyone who reads with vigilant attention not merely excerpts from ecclesiastical sanctions but their complete traditions.

It must be understood, according to apostolic tradition, that priests and deacons who have fallen into crime ought not to obtain the remedy of penance among the laity through the imposition of hands, as Saint Pope Leo testifies in his decrees, chapter 25. He also says that such fallen persons should seek a private place in order to obtain God’s mercy, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

Likewise the Council of Carthage, chapter 27:

“If a presbyter or deacon is ever convicted of a serious offense for which it is necessary to remove him from the ministry, hands are not to be laid upon him as upon a penitent or as upon a faithful layman. Those who have fallen into heresy and afterward returned, however, are reconciled through the imposition of hands, even if they are sometimes received with their order for ecclesiastical necessity, as was established concerning the Novatians at the Council of Nicaea. Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, ‘the pure,’ it pleased the holy and great council that, if they should ever come to the Catholic Church, they should receive the imposition of hands and thus remain in the clergy.”

This must be understood to mean that, once reconciled through the imposition of hands, they were also permitted to retain their order. For here we must not understand the ordaining imposition of hands, by which sacred orders are conferred, but rather the reconciling imposition of hands, by which we are accustomed to receive penitents. The imposition of hands is not always understood in one way, but is found with different meanings according to the diversity of contexts.

Sometimes it is taken for the confirmation of neophytes, as is repeatedly and explicitly found in the decrees of the apostolic men Clement, Urban, and Melchiades. At other times it signifies the ordination of priests or deacons, according to the Apostle’s statement to Timothy: “Lay hands quickly on no one” (1 Tim. 5); the canons also prescribe this most clearly. There is also the reconciling imposition of hands, through which heretical or excommunicated penitents are reconciled to the holy Church. The canons likewise say much about this, and Blessed Augustine, in Book III of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, testifies that it is nothing other than a prayer over a person, which may also be repeated.

Hands are also laid upon the sick, according to the statement of the Gospel: “They will lay hands on the sick” (Mark 16). They are also laid upon catechumens and those possessed by evil spirits for the expulsion of the devil; this is specially granted to exorcists in their ordinations, so that they may have the power to lay hands upon catechumens or those possessed by evil spirits. Likewise, when we simply bless someone, we lay a hand upon that person according to ancient custom. Thus the patriarch Jacob laid his hands upon the sons of Joseph when he blessed them (Gen. 49), and the Lord is said in the Gospel to have blessed the little children brought to him by laying on his hands (Mark 10).

Whether the imposition of hands is administered for the reconciliation of penitents, for the expulsion of illness or the devil, or for a simple blessing of people, it is quite appropriately understood, according to Augustine, as nothing other than a prayer over a person; hence it is not prohibited from being repeated whenever necessary. When, however, it is administered for confirmation or ordination, it must be regarded not merely as a prayer but also as a sacrament. The holy Fathers prohibited its repetition in these cases. For it is no less sinful to lay hands upon someone a second time for confirmation or ordination than to baptize that person a second time. Hence the holy Fathers are read to have imposed the same penance upon those reconfirmed and reordained as upon those rebaptized.

Saint Gregory also, writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, says: “Just as someone once baptized ought not to be baptized again, so someone once consecrated cannot be consecrated again in the same order.”

Likewise the African Council, chapter 75, prohibits rebaptisms and reordinations. The apostolic canons likewise say:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon receives a second imposition of hands, let him himself and the person who ordained him be deposed.”

If anyone gives insufficient credence to this chapter because he does not find it among the apostolic canons preserved among us, he should know that many chapters of those canons are missing from our collection. For Blessed Pope Zephyrinus testifies in his sixteenth order that the apostles established seventy canons; Isidore admits in his preface to the canons that he found only fifty of them, and these are the ones we use. Nevertheless, Peter Damian, of pious memory, cardinal bishop of the holy Roman Church and a second Jerome in our time, assigned the aforesaid chapter to the apostolic canons in his book entitled *Gratissimus*.

Therefore, when the Council of Nicaea orders that hands be laid upon clerics converted from the Novatians, this must in no way be understood as the ordaining imposition of hands, as certain less cautious translators of that council appear to have understood it when they interpreted the decree as requiring that these men be ordained again.

We should instead believe Blessed Pope Innocent, who, discussing those same Novatians, asserts that the Fathers of Nicaea decreed that they should not be reordained but received with their order. We must necessarily understand it in this way also, lest we appear to oppose the holy Fathers, who entirely proscribed reordinations, as we have stated.

[Col. 1190D] Certainly the holy Fathers nowhere permitted clerics converted from heresy to be ordained again, except in the case of the Paulianists and others of this kind, who do not perform the invocation of the holy Trinity according to Catholic practice; these they also ordered to be baptized. We cannot properly call such persons reordained or rebaptized, since what they are shown to have received without invoking the holy Trinity is not counted in the Catholic Church either as baptism or as ordination.

It must be understood, moreover, that among those who are converted from heresy, some had already been ordained in the Church and afterward fell into heresy, while others were ordained within heresy itself. Those who fell after receiving ordination can, upon returning, be received with their order, but without hope of promotion, according to the statute of the most holy [Col. 1191A] Pope Leo:

“Any cleric of whatever order who, abandoning the Catholic Church, has joined himself to heretical communion, if he returns to the Church and unequivocally confesses both his former errors and the very authors of those errors as condemned, shall remain without promotion in the rank which he held.

“Likewise, one ordained in a heresy which nevertheless has not erred concerning faith in the holy Trinity may, if necessary, be received with his order, as in the case of the Novatians and Donatists.”

Someone ordained among heretics who err concerning faith in the holy Trinity, even if they somehow perform its invocation, as the Arians do, is in no way to be received with his order or ordained thereafter, according to the assertion of Saint Pope Innocent, who discusses these matters at very great length.

[Col. 1191B] We also think it will not be displeasing to your fraternity if we append the judgment of Saint Pope Gregory I concerning the manifold reconciliation of heretics. Writing to the bishops Quirinus of Ireland and the others, he testifies as follows (Book IX, indiction 4, Letter 61):

“We have learned from the ancient institution of the Fathers that those who are baptized in the name of the Trinity among heretics, when they return to the holy Church, are recalled to the bosom of Mother Church either by anointing with chrism, by the imposition of hands, or by the mere profession of faith. Hence the West restores the Arians to entry into the Catholic Church through the imposition of hands, while the East does so through anointing with holy chrism.

“The Monophysites, however, and others, the Church receives on the basis of a true confession alone, because the holy baptism which they received from heretics then receives in them the power of correction when either they themselves have received the Holy Spirit through the imposition of hands, or those others have been united to the bosom of the holy and universal Church through their profession of faith.

“Those heretics, however, who are not baptized in the name of the Trinity, such as the Bonosians and Cataphrygians—for the former do not believe in Christ the Lord, while the latter, in their perverse understanding, believe the Holy Spirit to be some evil man named Montanus, and there are many like them—when they come to the holy Church are baptized, because it was not baptism which they received while in error, since they did not receive it in the name of the holy Trinity.

“And those whose understanding of the only-begotten Son is obscured by a heretical error similar to Jewish unbelief, when they come to the holy Church, must be instructed in the firmness and confession of the true faith.”

The Eastern Fathers, moreover, decreed that not only Arians but also Novatians, Quartodecimans, and Photinians should be received through anointing with chrism, as is read in the Council of Laodicea. The Westerners, however, more appropriately receive such heretics without anointing with chrism, lest they appear to repeat the sacrament of confirmation which those persons received many times from heretics together with their baptism. This sacrament, I say, must be avoided from being repeated just as baptism must.

If, however, they have not yet been confirmed by heretics, when they come to the Church they must certainly be confirmed through anointing with chrism, like the other Christians, because no one ought to neglect this sacrament. It must be understood that those who were baptized among heretics are not received through the same imposition of hands as those who were baptized in the Catholic Church and afterward fell into heresy. Hence Blessed Pope Vigilius, writing to Bishop Eleutherius, says:

“The reconciliation of those baptized persons who were baptized again among the Arians takes place not through that imposition of hands which operates through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, but through that by which the fruit of penance is obtained and restoration to holy communion is accomplished.”

Thus different prayers for these impositions of hands are assigned in the ancient orders. For the prayers said over those who were baptized by heretics ask that the Holy Spirit come upon them; whereas those administered to apostates returning to the Church appear to seek for them only the grace of reconciliation under penance.

Whoever is converted from any heresy whatsoever is not to be received unless he has abjured and anathematized the heresy. Hence the most holy Council of Ephesus, one of the four principal councils, decreed the following concerning Nestorius, a bishop but a heretic:

“It follows that, if you wish to repent, you must confess under oath and anathematize your polluted and profane doctrines; but you must think and teach what all of us—bishops, teachers, and leaders of the peoples throughout East and West—believe and teach.”

Hence, in the proceedings of that same council, chapter 15, the same form of oath is expressed as follows:

“I, Hesychius, son of Curialis, a Thessarescaedecatite, recognizing the true faith of orthodoxy and approaching the most holy and Catholic Church, anathematize every heresy, and especially that of the Thessarescaedecatites, in which I previously erred. I assent to the aforesaid exposition of the Catholic faith, anathematizing those who do not celebrate the holy day of Easter according to the custom of the Catholic and apostolic Church, and I swear by the holy ὁμοούσιον [consubstantial] Trinity. And if I should undermine any of these commitments, I shall be subject to the severity of the laws. I have subscribed with my own hand to the exposition read to me.”

The holy Roman Church has been accustomed to require this form of oath from heretics who are converted. It accepted this oath from Berengarius when the venerable Pope Nicholas received him in the universal council assembled at Rome, after he had renounced his heresy, if not in his heart, then at least with his lips.

The holy Church has likewise not been accustomed to receive schismatics without the satisfaction of an oath. Blessed Gregory left the form of that oath in his *Register* in these words (Letter 10, chapter 3):

[Note: [Col. 1191D] Thus the manuscript; Roman edition, Letter of St Gregory.]

“I, N., bishop of that city, having recognized the snare of division by which I was held and having deliberated on it for a long time within myself, have returned, with a willing and spontaneous resolve, to the unity of the apostolic see, by the guidance of divine grace. And lest I be thought to have returned not with a pure mind but deceptively, I promise and undertake to you, N., and through you to Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicar, the most blessed Gregory, and to his successors—under penalty of forfeiting my rank and under obligation of anathema—that I shall never, through anyone’s persuasion or in any other way, return to the schism from which the grace of the Redeemer has delivered me [Roman edition: from which the mercy of our Redeemer has rescued me], but shall always remain in the unity of the holy Catholic Church and in communion with the Roman pontiff in all things.

“Therefore I swear by almighty God and by these four holy Gospels, which I hold in my hands, that I shall remain in the unity of the Church, as I have said, to which, by God’s favor, I have returned, and shall always and without doubt remain in communion with the Roman pontiff. But if—God forbid—I should separate myself from this unity by any excuse or argument, I shall incur the guilt of perjury, be found bound to eternal punishment, and in the future age have my portion with the author of the schism.

“I have subscribed with my own hand to this written statement of my confession and promise. Done in that place, on that day, under that consul.”

Subscription [Roman edition: the subscription of that bishop]:

“I, that bishop of that city, have subscribed to this promise and profession of mine [confession and promise of mine], having given an oath concerning the preservation of all the matters written above.”

It must be understood, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers Augustine and Pope Pelagius, that those are unquestionably schismatics “whoever are divided from the apostolic see.” But Saint Jerome sufficiently explains how they differ from heretics in his treatise on the Epistle to Titus:

“We judge that this is the difference between heresy and schism: heresy possesses a perverse doctrine, whereas schism separates itself from the Church because of episcopal disagreement.”

This can indeed be understood to some extent at the beginning. But in the end, no schism fails to invent some heresy for itself, so that it may appear to have departed rightly from the Church. Hence Blessed Augustine, writing to Emeritus, asserts concerning the Donatists that by persisting wickedly they turned their schism into heresy.

The fact that the holy Council of Nicaea, as we stated above, asserted that clerics of the Novatians were to be received through the imposition of hands must in no way be considered contrary to the judgments of the other holy Fathers, who prohibited priests or deacons who had fallen from receiving, through the imposition of hands, the remedy of penance among the laity.

For it is one thing for someone converted from heresy or schism to be restored to the holy Church through the imposition of hands; it is another thing for someone who has fallen criminally while in the priesthood or diaconate not to receive, as a layman, the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands. Blessed Leo I, in his decrees, chapter 25, unquestionably testifies that this observance concerning fallen priests or deacons descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?”

The apostolic canons also contain the following in chapter 25:

“A bishop, presbyter, or deacon discovered in murder, perjury, or fornication shall be deposed, but not excommunicated. For God does not judge twice for the same matter.”

Indeed, according to ecclesiastical custom, a cleric is ordered to be deposed for the crime for which a layman, if he committed it, would be excommunicated, as is very frequently decreed in the statutes of the holy Fathers.

Thus laymen are accustomed to do penance without ecclesiastical communion, just as clerics do so without the administration of their office. It is therefore not surprising if clerics do not obtain the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands for crimes they have committed, as laymen do, since they are not ordered to be excommunicated for their crimes in the same way as laymen.

If, however, they have remained disobedient up to the sentence of anathema, it follows that, upon their return, they are restored to the holy Church through the imposition of hands, just as the holy Council of Nicaea established concerning the Novatians. Yet they will never obtain, like laymen, the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands, even if they are received entirely without the order they had received.

Hence Blessed Augustine, in Book I of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, testifies concerning any heretic received from heresy without the administration of office that hands are not to be laid upon him among the laity, because the sacrament of ordination remains even in one who has been deposed.

We have received the institutions of ecclesiastical rules partly from the apostles themselves, partly from the Roman pontiffs, and partly from other holy Fathers, whose judgments the Roman pontiffs nevertheless confirmed.

[Col. 1194C] We have learned from the Book of Acts and from the tradition of our forebears that the apostles established only five synods for the instruction of the nascent Church. They celebrated the first of these immediately after the Lord’s Ascension, concerning the election of the apostle Matthias in place of the traitor Judas. The second was held when they chose seven deacons for the ministry of administration. The third concerned converts from the Gentiles, so that they would not be compelled to Judaize, but only to abstain from fornication, from sacrificial offerings to idols, and from blood. Blessed Augustine considers the last of these to have been established as a matter of pastoral dispensation, if it is understood to mean that they were to abstain from the flesh of animals whose blood had not been shed. For he writes about this in Book II Against Faustus:

“They seem to me,” he says, “to have chosen for the time being an easy rule, and one by no means burdensome to those observing it, under which the Gentiles and Israel, because of that cornerstone which joined the two [perhaps ‘walls’] in itself, might observe something in common. But when the Church of the Gentiles had become such that no carnal Israelite could be found in it, what Christian observes that he should not touch thrushes or smaller birds unless their blood has been shed? Or that he should not eat a hare if it has been killed by a blow to the neck, without a bloody wound? And those few who perhaps still fear to touch such things are mocked by the others. Thus that saying of the Truth has taken possession of everyone’s mind in this matter: ‘It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out’ (Matthew 15)—condemning not any kind of food that human fellowship permits, but the sins that wickedness commits.”

It should therefore not be surprising [Col. 1195A] if the successors of the apostles established certain things as a matter of dispensation, which their successors, when a change of circumstances required it, were accustomed reasonably to alter at times or completely abolish.

We read that the apostles held a fourth synod concerning those who believed from among the Jews, when they prohibited them from the legal ceremonies; and this was done to abolish the suspicion of certain people who thought that the apostles rejected the legal ceremonies as though they were idolatry. These four synods were held by the apostles at Jerusalem, as the Book of Acts itself seems to indicate.

We have received the fifth apostolic synod from the tradition of our forebears: when the apostles, each putting forward his own statement, composed the creed that the universal Church holds, as they were about to depart from one another, “so that their sound might go forth into all the earth” (Psalm 18). For Blessed Pope Clement, a disciple and successor of the apostles, testifies to this in his decrees. Likewise Saint Pope Leo I, writing to the Empress Pulcheria, says:

“The brief and perfect confession of the Catholic creed is marked by twelve statements, corresponding to the twelve apostles.”

Likewise, the most blessed Father Ambrose, declaring the apostles’ faith to be the key of the kingdom of heaven, says:

“I judge that this key was forged by the work of twelve craftsmen. For faith was conceived in the creed of the twelve apostles, and they, like skilled craftsmen, coming together as one, forged the key by their council.”

This, then, is the Catholic creed, or the faith of the apostles, without whose profession [Col. 1195C] we are neither baptized nor canonically received into penance. In accordance with the tradition of the holy Fathers, we ought also to recall it every day when we rise. Hence Blessed Augustine says in Homily 43:

“Surely, when you rise, do you not clothe yourself? So also, by recalling your creed, clothe your soul, lest forgetfulness perhaps strip it, and you remain naked, and what the Apostle says come to pass—far be it from you!—‘provided that we are found clothed and not naked or stripped’ (2 Corinthians 5).”

Thus we shall be clothed in our faith. Faith itself is both a tunic and a breastplate: a tunic against shame, and a breastplate against adversity.

Besides these things, there are found fifty chapters entitled the Canons of the Apostles. Those who find nothing concerning them mentioned in the aforementioned apostolic synods have difficulty believing that they are apostolic. Yet there are also many matters that we have received from apostolic institution but that we do not find at all in those synods. It was not in any case necessary for the apostles to establish everything jointly, since they could also establish such matters individually, just as the Roman pontiffs, on the basis of their authority, still customarily do.

Therefore, setting aside the thoughtless opinion of certain people, let us place greater trust in the testimony of apostolic men—namely, the Roman pontiffs—who testify in their decrees, scattered throughout them, that the apostles established almost every one of these canons. Indeed, Pope Zephyrinus testifies that the apostles, sixteen after Blessed Peter, established seventy canons; of these, Blessed Isidore asserts in his prologue On the Canons that he found only fifty [Col. 1196A], and these are the ones we use.

Saint Pope and martyr Anacletus, the fifth after Blessed Peter and ordained presbyter by Peter himself, declares that the apostles established the ninth chapter of these canons, namely, “that the ministers of the altar, after making the oblation, should communicate.” Saint Pope and martyr Callistus likewise bears witness concerning the eleventh, namely, “that one who communicates with an excommunicated person should be subject to the same excommunication.”

Other holy Fathers likewise are found to testify concerning other chapters of these canons. They chose to die for the truth rather than to lie even for the sake of life. We too, therefore, necessarily believe their testimonies, lest we be judged to believe the Holy Spirit himself less, by whose prompting we do not doubt that they gave such testimony [manuscript: “were to give such testimony”].

[Col. 1196B] It must be understood, however, that Blessed Pope Gelasius classified the book entitled among the Greeks On the Canons of the Apostles as apocryphal. We ought not contradict him in this, because we do not believe that he did so without cause. Perhaps that book says nothing about the chapters that the Fathers also received; or, if it does say something, it appends a number of corruptions. Yet the diligence of a Catholic translator prudently removed this from us in Latin, just as Blessed Jerome is often shown to have done when translating Origen.

But whatever may be conjectured about that book, we can nevertheless receive without hesitation those fifty chapters that we read were translated from Greek by Saint Clement, Roman pontiff. The holy Roman Church also preserves them and has commanded us to preserve them through Blessed Pope Adrian.

Thus the holy Fathers received many things drawn from apocryphal writings, just as the apostle Jude in his Epistle accepted testimony drawn from the prophecy of Enoch; yet the holy Church rejected that prophecy as apocryphal. Ecclesiastical teachers explain that writings are called apocryphal not because they all tell lies, but because they appear to possess doubtful and suspect authority. For they very often insert many canonical matters into their worthless tales, and Catholics ought by no means to reject these matters together with the same tales.

Hence the aforementioned Pope Gelasius says:

“Are not many things pertaining to the truth found written in the books of those very heretics? Is the truth therefore to be rejected because their books are rejected where perversity is involved? Or are their corrupt books to be accepted for that reason, because the truth inserted there is not denied? The Apostle says: ‘Test everything; hold fast to what is good’ (1 Thessalonians 5). Therefore, in accordance with that same apostolic teaching, we ought to do both: reject the book On the Canons of the Apostles as apocryphal, and not reject any chapters found in it that pertain to the truth—those, I mean, that the holy Fathers received as authentic, indeed whose authority they very often used to confirm their own decrees.”

We do not doubt that the apostles established many other things, although we do not find them promulgated in any particular writing of theirs. Hence Blessed Augustine says in Book I Against the Donatists:

“That which the universal Church holds, and which was not established by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by no authority other than that of the apostles.”

Therefore those who despise traditions of this kind must be restrained no less than transgressors of divine laws, as the same teacher testifies in a letter to the presbyter Casulanus.

After the apostles, the Roman pontiffs, their successors both in authority and in preaching, are found to have shaped ecclesiastical discipline most diligently by their institutions and to have propagated it once shaped, though in different ways. For just as they are read to have presided over the holy Church in different periods, so they are found to have provided for it differently in their respective times.

From Blessed Peter to Saint Sylvester there were varied and extremely frequent persecutions, in which bishops, as the heads of others, were especially endangered. Accordingly, the Roman pontiffs of that period consoled them in many ways through their writings, according to the character of the persons, the necessity of the circumstances, and the suitability of the times. In those writings they established many or nearly all of the relevant judgments, so that they might restrain the presumption of wicked people from attacking the bishops in whatever way they could.

For, as Saint Pope and martyr Fabian testifies, the apostles themselves and their successors established that bishops should either never be accused or should be permitted to be accused only with the greatest difficulty. For, as Blessed Pope and martyr Eutychian testifies, if accusations against bishops had then been easily and indiscriminately [Col. 1197C] admitted, scarcely any would have been found who did not flee the episcopate at that time, since they feared daily death from persecution and yet could not avoid the accusations of wicked people.

Saint Pope and martyr Anacletus, writing to all the bishops of Italy, also testifies that the Lord reserved the deposition or condemnation of bishops to himself, as though they should not appear subject to human judgment. Nor is it surprising that they judged the matter in this way at that time, when the fierce persecution permitted only the most perfect men to enter the episcopate—men who already had no fear of suffering every extremity for Christ.

In a time of peace, however, something of that difficulty concerning the accusation or condemnation of bishops is not incongruously relaxed. The episcopate is no longer religiously feared by a few as though it were death, but is eagerly sought by many as though it were glory, and the desire for it is administered criminally. For now such persecution no longer deters anyone from the episcopate or from sin; rather, the tranquility of peace and the eminence of honor invite people more strongly to sin.

Hence at the Council of Nicaea no more leniency is shown to bishops than to any other clerics in matters of condemnation, since all who do not fear to set themselves against the sacred rules are condemned there generally. Before that council, persecutions had raged everywhere with such force that the Roman pontiffs could scarcely console the afflicted by their writings or defend them against the wicked in any way, much less establish ecclesiastical discipline everywhere fully and regularly.

[Col. 1198A] From the time of this council onward, once the persecutions had been somewhat quieted, the same pontiffs began to promulgate ecclesiastical rules much more fully and suitably, both personally in their decrees and through others in councils, or to confirm rules already promulgated. Ecclesiastical teachers later became accustomed to making greater use of these rules.

Blessed Pope Adrian also sent these rules, together with the Canons of the Apostles, for the instruction of the Churches of the West—namely, the Council of Nicaea itself and other councils of this kind, some of which, although older than the Council of Nicaea, were nevertheless received as authoritative after Nicaea; and likewise those decrees of the Roman pontiffs that are read to have been established after that council.

He should certainly not be thought to have done this as though he had in any way prejudiced the older statutes; rather, he did it so that he might provide whatever was more suitable for the regular instruction of the Churches.

Nor should you be surprised that we attribute the authority of these councils to the Roman pontiff. For, as Blessed Pope Damasus asserts in his decrees, chapter 9, “no councils are read to have been ratified unless they were supported by apostolic authority.” Saint Athanasius, Pope Julius, the Council of Nicaea, and the other holy Fathers agree with him.

Saint Pope and martyr Marcellus likewise says in his decrees, chapter 5:

“The apostles themselves, and their successors also, under the inspiration of the Lord, established that no synod should be held apart from the authority of the Roman See.”

For the bishop of that See is the judge of the whole Church. No judgment is valid without a legitimate judge.

There are four councils to which the Roman pontiffs are read to have shown great reverence: namely, the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Constantinople, the Council of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon. Blessed Gregory repeatedly declares these to be worthy of veneration like the four books of the Gospels, and prohibits their contempt under a dreadful anathema.

The first of these was held at Nicaea in Bithynia by 318 Fathers, on the authority of Saint Pope Sylvester, against Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, who asserted three ranks within the Holy Trinity: the Father as greater, the Son as lesser, and the Holy Spirit as a creature. This occurred during the reign of the emperor Constantine and the episcopates of Atticus of Constantinople, Macarius of Jerusalem, and Alexander, patriarch of Alexandria.

At this council, after the Arian heresy had been condemned, they promulgated the Creed, second after that of the apostles, and twenty canons. The legates of the apostolic See presided over this council: the great Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the Roman Church, acting in place of Pope Sylvester. They confirmed the council’s statutes with the primary subscription.

Pope Sylvester himself, presiding over a general synod at Rome, strengthened the aforesaid synod with the subscription of 275 bishops.

It must be understood that the Roman pontiffs never customarily went out from Rome to councils, but presided over such councils through their legates. Hence Saint Pope Leo, when he had been most devotedly invited by the most Christian emperor Marcian to the Council of Chalcedon, excused himself on the grounds that he had received no such precedent from his predecessors.

Writing about the Council of Nicaea, Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, says:

“The 318 bishops did not come to the council through human effort or by any arrangement, but so that the Lord Jesus might prove his presence at the council through the sign of his passion and name in their number: the cross in the 300, the name in the 18, and the priests.”

Likewise Leo, mentioned above, writing to Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, says:

“That rule of the Nicene canons, truly established through the Holy Spirit, can never be dissolved in any respect. Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the increase in their assemblies. Nor should any number of priests, however much greater, dare to compare itself or give precedence to those 318 bishops, since the Nicene synod has been consecrated by so great a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are conducted by fewer or by more, whatever differs from the constitution of those bishops is entirely void of authority.”

The same Leo says elsewhere:

“Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after sacrilegious Arius and his impiety had been condemned in the city of Nicaea, established laws of the ecclesiastical canons that would endure to the end of the world live among us throughout the world in their constitutions. If anything is presumed anywhere to be done otherwise than they decreed, it is annulled without hesitation.”

[Col. 1199C] From these statements, therefore, we can gather how unwavering a reverence we ought constantly to show the Nicene canons.

Among us, twenty chapters are attributed to the Council of Nicaea, although many more chapters of that council are found. For the Council of Antioch asserts that the matter of Easter was established there, namely, that it should not be celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon, as the Tessarescaedecaditae, that is, the Quartodecimans (Fourteenth-day observers), do. They took the name of their heresy from this matter.
