Likewise Saint Athanasius, patriarch of Alexandria, who attended the Council of Nicaea not yet as a bishop but already as one eminently worthy of the episcopate, asserts in a letter to Pope Felix that the Nicene Fathers established, as we reported above, that councils should not be held without the judgment of the Roman pontiff.

Pope Zosimus likewise affirmed a statute concerning appeals of bishops in the memorandum that he sent to his legates at the African council. The African Fathers, however, protested that they did not find this in their copies. Those copies had no more than twenty chapters, as did the copies that they later borrowed from the Eastern bishops as an authoritative version.

Pope Julius also attributes more than twenty chapters to that council, although these are found in the ancient decretals of the Roman bishops; hence they are believed to have been transferred from them to the Council of Nicaea.

The aforementioned patriarch Athanasius, as well as Pope Mark, also assert that the council had seventy chapters, although only twenty are now everywhere attributed to it. From the writings of our forebears we have learned that this happened because the Nicene Fathers are read to have established only those twenty as matters especially instituted by themselves. The rest, up to seventy, are found to have been not so much instituted principally by them as already established by others and confirmed by them.

For Hosius, bishop of Corduba, is read to have borrowed those other matters from elsewhere and recited them in the synod. It was the custom of the holy Fathers in such councils not only to establish their own statutes but also to confirm the statutes of others. They were accustomed to discuss many matters there and to deliberate upon matters discussed; yet ecclesiastical custom does not appear to have counted all such matters among the statutes specifically established by that council.

Thus the Council of Chalcedon is read to have deliberated and confirmed many matters over twenty days, but only the statutes of a single day appear to have been attributed to it. In the same way, therefore, we appropriately attribute its special statutes to the Council of Nicaea, but we ought not contradict the testimony of the holy Fathers concerning its seventy chapters.

The aforementioned Hosius and Januarius, bishop of Beneventum, acting as legates of the apostolic See, are later read to have confirmed these same chapters at the Council of Sardica.

Blessed Isidore, in his prologue On the Canons, excuses the question of the seventy chapters by appealing to the size of the book of that council, which he asserts to be as large among the Greeks as the books of the four Gospels.

It must also be understood that the Latin copies do not contain the names of all 318 Fathers who nevertheless subscribed at the Council of Nicaea. For, as we read, diligent servants of God devoted themselves to recording the names not so much of the Western Fathers as of the Eastern Fathers, because the Westerners had not been similarly troubled by the question of the heresies.

The second of those four councils, the Council of Constantinople, was held by 150 Fathers against Macedonius, bishop of that see, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God. It took place in the year 418, during the reigns of the emperors Gratian and Theodosius and the episcopates of Pope Damasus, Cyril of Jerusalem, Nectarius of Constantinople, and Timothy of Alexandria.

At this council, after all heresies had been condemned, the creed was handed down that the whole confession of the Greeks and Latins now uses in the Churches, and three canons were established there.

The Easterners first began to recite this creed, and afterward the Westerners. Hence the holy Fathers are read to have established at the Fourth Council of Toledo, during the time of Pope Pelagius, that it should be recited in the churches every Sunday according to the custom of the Eastern Churches.

The Gauls and Germans are believed to have borrowed it from the tradition of that same council, since they still appear to follow almost the same translation. For, after the condemnation of the heretic Felix, they are read to have begun finally to use it under the emperor Charles, on account of the heretics of that time who denied that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son. They wished to refute those heretics by means of the creed itself, since it says so openly that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

But because the name “Son” was not found at all in the authentic copies, the venerable Pope Leo of that time prohibited the creed from being recited with such an addition, since the holy Fathers had altogether prohibited such additions to the creeds.

The Romans also refused to use that creed until the time of the emperor Henry I, of blessed memory. That emperor then obtained from the Roman pontiff that the Romans too should chant it, according to the custom of the others, as the venerable abbot Berno testifies in his book On the Institution of the Masses.

Although the Nicene Creed appears to possess greater authority than the Constantinopolitan Creed, we nevertheless rightly recite the Constantinopolitan Creed more frequently in the Church. For we find in it more matters necessary against heretics than in the Nicene Creed [Col. 1201B], since the latter deals especially with the Arians. Nor did the Nicene Creed confront as many heresies with its statements as the Constantinopolitan Creed did.

In the Constantinopolitan Creed there is teaching concerning the unity of the Church and of baptism, the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come—matters not found in the Nicene Creed. It also speaks more fully about the Holy Spirit than the Nicene Creed. Hence it is said to have come especially into use among our people.

It must be understood, however, that we customarily add to this creed not only the name “Son,” of which we spoke above, but also many other expressions, especially from the Nicene Creed, such as “God from God, light from light.” Yet in this we have not sinned very greatly, since the Roman Church no longer objects; indeed, it does not refuse to admit such additions itself.

The third universal council was held at Ephesus by 200 Fathers against Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who said that Saint Mary was not the mother of God but only the mother of a man, thus making one person for the flesh and another for the deity. It took place in the year 468, during the time of the younger Theodosius, Saint Pope Celestine, Cyril of Alexandria, and Juvenal of Constantinople [Jerusalem].

At this council twelve chapters were established against Nestorius, which are very often attributed to Blessed Cyril. The same Cyril, together with Arcadius, a bishop from Italy, acting in place of Saint Celestine, presided over this synod as legates of the apostolic See and strengthened it with apostolic authority.

Blessed Augustine is read to have been invited to this council by a sacred letter of the emperor Theodosius, but he departed to the Lord before the letter of the Roman ruler reached him.

The fourth universal council was held at Chalcedon by 630 Fathers against Eutyches, an abbot of Constantinople, who asserted that Christ, after assuming humanity, did not consist of two natures, but that only the divine nature remained in him. It took place in the year 489, [during the time of] the emperor Marcian, Saint Pope Leo, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Anatolius of Constantinople.

At this council twenty-seven canons were established. The legates of the apostolic See presided over the synod: Paschasinus and Lucentius, bishops, and Boniface, a presbyter, acting in place of Saint Pope Leo. They confirmed the statutes of that synod and freely opposed the aforementioned Anatolius when he rashly presumed something.

Many later doubted this council and strove by every means to have it reconsidered. But because Blessed Pope Leo did not permit this at all, they finally obtained from the emperor that he send letters throughout the provinces to all the bishops who had assembled at Chalcedon, asking them to state their opinion concerning that council. They all replied unanimously that the Council of Chalcedon had to be defended even to the shedding of blood.

[Col. 1202B] Besides these, a fifth universal council is read to have been assembled at Constantinople against all heretics, and especially against Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said that the Word of God was one person and Christ another, and denied that the holy Virgin was the mother of God. It took place during the reign of the emperor Justinian and the pontificate of Pope Vigilius, with Domnus of Antioch and Eutychius of Constantinople. At this council fourteen chapters are read to have been established under anathema.

Likewise, the sixth council was held at Constantinople by 150 [Note: [Col. 1201D] 289, see Bellarmine, Book I On Councils, chapter 5; but Bernaldus follows Bede, Ado, and others. See Anastasius Bibliothecarius on Agatho.] Fathers against Macarius of Antioch and his associates, who falsely asserted that Christ had one will and one operation. It took place during the reign of the emperor Constantine and the pontificate of Pope Agatho, with George of Constantinople.

At this council, while the aforementioned Macarius was being condemned, an oratory [orarium, a prayer-cloth] was taken away by a certain bishop at the command of the synod, and he himself, together with his followers, was disgracefully expelled from the synod with his throne, as is recorded in the Roman Pontifical.

After their condemnation, many spiderwebs fell into the midst of the assembly, signifying that the empty deceit of the heretics had been cast down. Then nine chapters are read to have been established there.

Legates of the apostolic See presided over this council. Among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church, but not long afterward its apostolic bishop.

Concerning the four councils mentioned above, Saint Pope Gregory, writing to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion, testifies that it was customary for every newly appointed patriarch, before deserving to be counted among the patriarchs by the others, to profess by sending a synodal letter that he would observe those councils.

Accordingly, at the beginning of his own ordination, that same apostolic bishop sent a synodal letter to the patriarchs and professed the following concerning those councils:

“Just as I confess that I accept and venerate the four books of the holy Gospel, so I confess that I accept and venerate four councils: namely, the Council of Nicaea, the First Council of Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and the Council of Chalcedon, because in these, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises.

“Whatever a person’s life and conduct may be, whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

“I likewise venerate the fifth council, at which the letter called the Letter of Ibas, [Col. 1203A] full of error, was rejected; and Theodore was shown to have fallen into the treachery of impiety by separating the person of the Mediator between God and human beings into two substances. The writings of Theodoric [Theodoret], by which Blessed Cyril’s faith is criticized, are also refuted as produced through an envious act of presumption.

“I reject all the persons whom those venerable councils mentioned above reject, and I embrace those whom they venerate. For since they were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to dissolve what they bind or to bind what they dissolve destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

We must not, however, praise the excellence of those four councils in such a way that we in any respect prescribe against the authority of the others—those councils, I mean, that we do not doubt were established in the same manner and universally, and confirmed by apostolic authority.

Since in ancient times the patriarchs professed in their synodal letters that they venerated only those four councils, they should not at all be thought to have done this in contempt of the other councils of this kind, but rather because they did not yet have others. For if they had already possessed them, beyond doubt they would not have despised those four any more than these others, since they would have recognized the latter as no less authentic, universal, and necessary to the Catholic confession.

Hence Blessed Pope Gregory added the fifth council, which was assembled after the four, to his synodal letter. He could not do the same with the sixth, because that council had not yet been established; it was instituted later, long afterward, under his sixteenth successor.

[Col. 1203C] There are also provincial councils, which we must necessarily receive after those universal councils, because we find in them many matters necessary for ecclesiastical affairs. The decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the statutes of the universal synods themselves also prescribe their observance to us. They very often command that such councils be held annually in each province. They would certainly command this to no purpose unless they also determined that we should receive and observe the reasonable judgments of those same councils.

Moreover, Pope Gelasius, in his Decretals, when treating most carefully which Scriptures should or should not be received, after the reception of the four universal councils adds this conclusion:

“But whatever things have been established by the holy Fathers in councils, we have decreed that, after the authority of these four, they too are both to be received and observed.”

Likewise the holy Council of Chalcedon says:

“We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council up to the present are to retain their proper force.”

The Eastern councils and many of the Western councils had already been established when this was to be constituted by synodal confirmation. Therefore, there is no doubt that we ought also to observe the statutes of councils of this kind, since we see that the apostolic decrees and universal councils support them.

Some of these councils are Eastern and others Western. The Eastern councils are those established by Eastern Fathers: namely, the Council of Ancyra, the Council of Neocaesarea, the Council of Gangra, the Council of Antioch, the Council of Laodicea, and the Council of Sardica.

The Council of Ancyra is read to have taken place before Nicaea, but because it had lesser authority it is placed below it in order. At it, eighteen Fathers established twenty-four canons, whose principal author is said to have been Vitalis, bishop of Antioch.

The Council of Neocaesarea is traditionally said to have taken place after Ancyra but before Nicaea. At it, eighteen Fathers established fourteen canons, whose principal author was Vitalis of Salamis.

The Council of Gangra is read to have taken place after Nicaea. At it, fifteen Fathers established twenty canons because of certain ecclesiastical necessities, especially against Eustasius [Eustathius], who said that no married person, or anyone who did not renounce all his possessions, could have hope before God, along with other blasphemous teachings of this kind.

The Council of Antioch was held at the dedication of the church at Antioch. At it, thirty Fathers established twenty-five canons, whose author was Eusebius, bishop of Palestine.

At the Council of Laodicea, twenty-two Fathers established fifty-nine canons, whose author was Bishop Theodosius.

At the Council of Sardica, sixty Fathers established twenty-one canons. Its principal author was Hosius, bishop of Corduba and legate of the holy Roman Church.

This is that Hosius who presided over the Council of Nicaea in place of Saint Pope Sylvester, and who continued in Spain until the time of the emperor Constantius. Yet at the end of his life he is said to have acted quite foolishly, as Severus Sulpicius testifies in his Chronicles.

For when legates of that same Arian emperor, or of the Council of Ariminum, asked him to give testimony concerning the faith—whether the Nicene synod asserted that the Son was ὁμοούσιος to the Father, that is, “consubstantial,” which is the Catholic position, or ὁμοιούσιος, that is, “similar in substance,” which is the Arian position—he is said to have given this answer:

“Both are correctly said.”

From that point onward, therefore, he was acceptable neither to Catholics nor to Arians.

The rules of the Council of Sardica, although they are associated with the Eastern councils, are nevertheless found more among the Latins than among the Greeks. Concerning this council, Blessed Augustine, writing to Eleusius and Glorius, testifies that it seemed to him more likely to have belonged to the Arians than to the Catholics, because the Catholic bishops Athanasius and Julius are found to have been criticized in the book of that council.

We, however, ought by no means to reject the aforesaid canons on account of that council. The holy Roman Church venerates them, and the Council of Nicaea is reported to have heard and confirmed them when they were recited by the aforementioned Hosius.

These, then, are the Eastern councils that are read to have been held before the Council of Chalcedon, and therefore they are not doubted to have been confirmed by that council.

It must be understood that many editions or translations of the Eastern councils from Greek into Latin are found. For Philo and Evaristus are read to have translated the Constantinopolitan synod from Greek into Latin.

Likewise, a certain Dionysius is said to have translated many editions of the canons and Eastern councils for Bishop Stephen.

Likewise, the abbot Eugepius [Eugipius] translated those same canons from Greek into Latin, as the most learned man Cassiodorus—formerly a senator and later a monk—testifies in his book On Illustrious Men, chapter 23:

“Eugepius [Eugipius],” he says, “formerly my colleague in dialectic, at the request of Stephen, bishop of Salona, composed from Greek copies ecclesiastical canons suited to his own character, with great brilliance of eloquence, as he was simple and articulate. The Roman Church embraces them with the most celebrated use. You monks ought also to read them constantly, lest you culpably appear to be ignorant of rules of the Church so beneficial.”

Blessed Isidore likewise, in his Collection on the Canons, assembled four editions of the Council of Nicaea, and assigned two or three editions to the remaining Eastern councils.

We chiefly follow that edition which appears more correct than the others and more acceptable to the Apostolic See [Col. 1205B], namely, the one which Blessed Pope Adrian sent through the hand of the Emperor Charlemagne to the Churches of the West. It should also be noted, not without purpose, that many obscure passages are repeatedly clarified by comparing the various editions. Thus, regarding the Council of Nicaea, what is meant by “a woman introduced into the household”? Another edition states this more clearly: “an unrelated woman.” It is as though it said: “Let a cleric have no unrelated woman with him, but only his mother, sister, or aunt”—which another edition again calls more explicitly an aunt. For the Tuscans use *zia* for “aunt.” Likewise, in the same council, we learn from the various translations that the statement “deaconesses are denied the laying-on of hands” must be understood only of the deaconesses of the Paulianists. For the deaconesses of the Catholics do receive the laying-on of hands, according to the Council of Chalcedon. Likewise, at the Council of Laodicea we read, “Let ordinations not take place in the presence of hearers”; another edition states this more explicitly as “catechumens.” For catechumens are forbidden to attend the administration of any sacraments. In this way, you will be able to investigate many things expressed obscurely there by your own efforts, if you take care to examine the various editions diligently. Perhaps more learned men regard these matters as not requiring notation; nevertheless, those like us ought to attend to them, since we do not doubt that such people sometimes become entangled in matters of this kind, just as we ourselves have very often done.

The Western councils are those which are shown to have been held in the western part of the world, such as the African and Gallican councils, or those celebrated in Spain. Almost all those held at Carthage are called African. The first of these established fourteen chapters through eleven bishops under the Emperor Constantius; its author was Gratus, bishop of Carthage. The second Council of Carthage, held under Valentinian Augustus in the year 418 of the era, established thirteen chapters; its author was Genelius [Genedius], bishop of Carthage. The third Council of Carthage, held by forty-seven bishops in the year 435 of the era, established fifty canons; its author was Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, together with Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo. The fourth Council of Carthage, held under Honorius Augustus by 214 bishops in the year 437 of the era, established 103 canons; its author was the same Aurelius together with Saint Augustine. The fifth Council of Carthage, held by seventy-three bishops in the year 439 of the era, established fifteen canons; its author was the same Aurelius. The sixth Council of Carthage, held in the time of the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the seventh of Theodosius Augustus by 217 bishops, in the year 455 of the era, established thirteen chapters. There it was arranged that the Council of Nicaea should be requested from the eastern bishops. At this synod, the legates of the holy Roman Church—Bishop Faustinus and the presbyters Philip and Asellus—presided on behalf of Pope Zosimus, together with the aforesaid Aurelius and Saint Augustine. The seventh Council of Carthage, held in the time of the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the seventh of Theodosius Augustus [Note: [Col. 1205D] The word “consuls” appears to be missing.], [Col. 1206B] by eighteen bishops in the same year of the era, established five canons. The aforesaid legates of the Apostolic See presided at this synod together with Aurelius and Saint Augustine. The eighth council of Africa, held in the city of Milevis under Honorius Augustus by 214 bishops in the year CCCCXLX of the era [numeral uncertain], anathematized the Pelagian heresy with its eight chapters and then established twenty-eight canons; Aurelius and Saint Augustine, bishops, likewise presided at this synod.

The statutes of these councils are said to have been sent by the African Fathers to the Roman pontiff for confirmation. They are still found in Roman exemplars, collected in two Breviaries. One of them includes the subscription of 216 bishops; both, however, were confirmed by Apostolic authority. Blessed Adrian is likewise said to have delivered these Breviaries, together with the aforesaid Eastern councils, to the Emperor Charlemagne at Rome for the ordering of the Churches of the West. Therefore, we too must necessarily accept and observe as authentic the same materials which we have received, unmistakably confirmed by Apostolic authority and sent to the Churches for observance.

The era prefixed to councils of this kind is understood as referring to the year of the Lord’s Incarnation. According to Isidore, it is called *aera* from *aes* (“bronze”), because among the ancients years were marked on bronze, at the time when indictions were also instituted. But since *aes* lacks aspiration, it appears to be derived from ἥρᾳ, that is, from the name of Juno, that is, of the air, beneath which periods of time are chiefly varied [the wording is uncertain]. It should also be noted that the Chronicles assign fewer years from the Lord’s Incarnation to the councils than are found in their titles. I mean those Chronicles which Dom Heremannus, an eminent calculator and exceptionally careful investigator of times, compiled most diligently from various chronicles and histories, carrying them faithfully up to the year 1054 of the Lord’s Incarnation. For in those Chronicles the second universal council, namely the First Council of Constantinople, is assigned the year 380, whereas its title assigns it 418. Likewise, in those Chronicles the third universal council, that is, the Council of Ephesus, is assigned the year 430, whereas its title associates it with 488. Likewise, the Council of Chalcedon is placed in those Chronicles under the year 450, whereas its title assigns it 489. [Col. 1207A] Thus, in these titles the era contains thirty-seven more years than are found in the Chronicles.

This same diversity is often found in the African and other Western councils, to which an era is likewise prefixed. Whatever the occasion on which such a difference arose, it ought in no way to hinder our confidence in the facts, since even in the sacred Scriptures different datings of time have in no way impeded the truth of the events. For the authority of the Seventy Translators differs so greatly from the Hebrew text in its number of years that, reckoning from the beginning of the world, it places more than a thousand additional years before the Lord’s birth. Such diversity is familiar to chroniclers, and readers do not concern themselves greatly with it, provided only that they know the things they have read to be of unquestionable truth.

[Col. 1207B] It should nevertheless be understood that our predecessors were accustomed to confirm writings by recording the dates, just as the Roman laws received by the Church prescribe. For they say: “If any edicts or constitutions issued after these are found without a date and consul, they shall lack authority.” Hence the holy Fathers also customarily assign a date and consul to ecclesiastical statutes or writings, and expressly record the year of that consul or those consuls. Thus, in the statement that the sixth Council of Carthage was held under “the twelfth consulship of Honorius and the seventh of Theodosius,” the annual consulship is understood. The African canons also prescribe that the letters which bishops receive from those who ordain them must bear a date and consul, so that they may always attend to the time of their ordination [Col. 1207C] and not rashly place themselves before those who were ordained earlier. Nevertheless, ecclesiastical institutions received their firmness not so much from the recording of the date or consul as from Apostolic and universal agreement, so that their authority is in no way to be doubted. Therefore, we too ought not to prejudice their authority, even if we do not know the exact time of their institution. It should also be noted that *era* is sometimes used improperly for “chapter,” as in that writing of the Council of Toledo where the order for conducting a synod is discussed.

There are also many Gallican councils, assembled in many places; the Council of Arles is placed first among them. The first Council of Arles, therefore, held in the time of the Emperor Constantine and the Council of Nicaea by 600 bishops and sent to Pope Saint Sylvester for confirmation, established twenty-two canons; its author was Saint Marinus, bishop of Arles. The second Council of Arles, held by thirty-two bishops from various provinces, established twenty-five canons. At this synod, Bishop Theodore from Dalmatia and Agathon, deacon and legate of Pope Saint Sylvester, presided together with Saint Marinus, bishop of Arles; Caecilianus, bishop of Carthage, was also present. The third Council of Arles, held under Marcian Augustus by fourteen bishops in the year 461 of the era, established four canons; its author was Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles [Col. 1208A]. The Council of Valence, held in the time of the emperors Gratian and Valentinian by twenty bishops in the year 413 of the era, established four canons; Bishop Fegadius presided at this synod. The Council of Turin established seven canons. It was held in the time of Felix the heretic, whom the Council of Riez mentions. The Council of Riez, held by thirteen bishops under the Emperor Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian in the year 477 of the era, established seven canons; Saint Hilary, bishop, presided at this synod. The Council of Orange, held by seventeen bishops in the time of Theodosius the Younger in the year 479 of the era, established twenty-nine canons; its author was Saint Hilary, bishop. The Council of Vaison, held under Bishop Auspicius and Theodosius the Younger in the year 480 of the era, established ten canons [Note: [Col. 1207D] Volume I of the Councils, according to Urbicus.]. [Col. 1208B] The Council of Agde, held by twenty-four bishops in the twenty-second year of King Alaric, in the year 514 of the era, established seventy-one canons; its author was Bishop Gozarius. The Council of Orléans, held by twenty-eight bishops, established twenty-seven canons; Bishop Defrodius presided at that council. Thus far concerning the Gallican councils; let us now consider the Spanish councils.

The Council of Elvira, held in the time of the Emperor Constantine by eighteen bishops, established eighty-one canons; Bishop Hosius of Córdoba was present. The Council of Tarragona, held in the sixth year of King Theodoric by ten bishops, in the year 516 of the era, established thirteen canons; Bishop John presided. The Council of Girona, held in the seventh year of King Theodoric by seven bishops, in the year 517 of the era, established ten canons. The Council of Zaragoza [Col. 1208C], held by twelve bishops, established eight canons; Bishop Fetadius [Fitadius or Siradius] presided. The Council of Lleida, held in the fifteenth year of King Theodoric by eight bishops, in the year 524 of the era, established sixteen canons; Bishop Sergius presided. The Council of Valencia, held in the fifteenth year of King Theodoric by six bishops, in the same year of the era, established six canons; Bishop Celsinus presided.

The first Council of Toledo, held under the emperors Arcadius and Honorius by eighteen bishops, established twenty-one canons; Patroinus presided. The second Council of Toledo, held in the fifth year of King Amalaric at the residence of Bishop Montanus by eight bishops, in the year 566 of the era, established five canons. The third Council of Toledo, held in the fourth year of King Reccared by seventy-two bishops [Col. 1208D], in the year 627 of the era, anathematized the Arian heresy and all who had not accepted the councils of all orthodox bishops, consonant with the four principal synods; it then established thirteen chapters. The fourth Council of Toledo, held in the third year of King Sisenand by sixty bishops, in the year 681 of the era, established seventy-five canons. The fifth Council of Toledo, held in the time of King Suintila by twenty-four bishops, in the year 684 of the era, established nine canons. The sixth Council of Toledo, held in the second year of King Suintila by six bishops, in the year 685 of the era, established nineteen canons; Bishop Solva [Silva, Selva] of Narbonne presided [Col. 1209A]. The seventh Council of Toledo, held in the fifth year of King Chindaswinth [Cindasiundus] by thirty bishops, established six canons. The eighth Council of Toledo established thirty-two canons. The ninth Council of Toledo, held in the seventh year of King Recceswinth by sixteen bishops, in the year 614 of the era, established seventeen canons. The tenth, held in the ninth year of King Recceswinth by eighteen bishops, in the year 696 of the era, established ten canons; Bishop Eugenius of Toledo presided. The eleventh, held in the fourth year of King Wamba by seventeen bishops, in the year 714 of the era, established sixteen canons; Bishop Quiricus of Toledo presided. The twelfth, held in the first year of King Erwig by fifty-two bishops, in the year 719 of the era, from the Ides of January until the eighth day before the Kalends of February, established fourteen canons; Bishop Julian of Seville presided.

[Col. 1209B] The first Council of Braga, held in the third year of King Ariamir [Arimarius] by seven bishops, in the year 569 of the era, promulgated seventeen chapters against the Priscillianists; it then established twenty-two canons. The second Council of Braga, held in the second year of King Miro [Mirus or Ariamirus] by twelve bishops, in the year 610 of the era, established ten canons; Bishop Martin of Braga presided. The third Council of Braga, composed of eleven bishops, excerpted and corrected, together with the same Martin, the following seventy-three chapters of the Eastern Fathers. The fourth Council of Braga, held in the fourth year of King Wamba by nine bishops, in the year 614 of the era, established eight canons; Bishop Isidore of Seville was present.

[Col. 1209C] The first Council of Seville, held in the fifth year of King Reccared by six bishops, in the year 628 of the era, established three canons; Bishop Leander of Seville presided. Saint Gregory wrote the *Moralia* to him. The second Council of Seville, held in the time of King Sisebut by eight bishops, in the year 657 of the era, established twelve canons, with forty-seven chapters on the faith appended; Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, who compiled the body of the canons, presided at this council. Thus far concerning the councils of Spain.

These, then, are the councils of the various provinces which the aforesaid Isidore most diligently described in his *Collection on the Canons*. Whoever reads that Collection attentively will rejoice to find there, in full, the matters which we have touched upon above only in summary [Col. 1209D].

Besides these, many other councils are found, such as those of Mainz, Nantes, and six hundred others of this kind. We ought nevertheless not to despise them, since in them we find many things necessary for ecclesiastical administration, especially since the Roman pontiffs also ordered such councils to be held throughout the provinces and were accustomed to authorize them through their legations. The following, however, must generally be observed in every provincial council: we should always accept those chapters which we see to accord with Apostolic and universal institutions and to serve ecclesiastical usefulness. For the holy Fathers are said to have condemned under strict anathema anyone who failed to accept the statutes of the orthodox Fathers which he perceived to accord with the universal councils [Col. 1210A]. Conversely, we must nowhere accept anything which we perceive to be opposed to Apostolic and universal institutions, lest we likewise perish under unavoidable anathema. Blessed Pope Gregory I anathematized in his synodical letter all who dissented from the principal councils. Elsewhere also he condemned under anathema everything contrary to the sacred canons. By these judgments, unquestionably, those are punished who presume to admit into canonical authority anything that they discover to be opposed to authentic enactments. We have also learned from Blessed Augustine that councils held in individual regions or provinces yield without any ambiguity to the authority of plenary councils, which are held from the entire Christian world.

[Col. 1210B] As for the authority of the pontifical decrees themselves, no doubt is left to us, since the universal councils themselves received their authority from them and could not have obtained synodal firmness from any other source. We too must therefore observe these decrees irrevocably, just as the Apostolic Fathers commanded us on the basis of Apostolic authority. Through that authority, they are also said to have canonized the statutes of others for our observance—namely, our most blessed Fathers Damasus and Leo the Great, one of whom confirmed the second universal council and the other the fourth, that is, the Council of Chalcedon, by Apostolic authority. By that same authority and in the same voice they decreed generally as follows: “We command that all the decretal letters of our predecessors, which were promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders [Col. 1210C] and the disciplines of the canons, be observed by all bishops and generally by all priests, so that anyone who violates them may know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.” The same Damasus, writing elsewhere to all the bishops, says: “Let all observe that those things which have been established by Apostolic institution and the tradition of the Fathers must always be held under the fear of irrefragable authority.” Likewise, Blessed Pope Agatho, who established the Fourth Universal Synod through his legates and confirmed what had been established by Apostolic authority, says: “All the sanctions of the Apostolic See must be received as though they had been confirmed by Peter himself with a divine voice.” Likewise, their successor, Blessed Pope Nicholas I, presiding over a general synod, decreed by the judgment of that synod [Col. 1210D] “that anyone who had despised decrees promulgated by the Roman pontiff should also be anathema.” Saint Pope Adrian likewise anathematizes even kings who do not fear violating the decrees of the Apostolic See.

By these testimonies, therefore, we are sufficiently instructed how unquestionably we ought to obey Apostolic institutions.

These, then, are the ecclesiastical statutes, both in the councils and in the pontifical decrees, by which ecclesiastical discipline, instituted from the times of the Apostles and propagated down to the present, is without doubt established.

These are the ecclesiastical canons, which are properly called “the canons of priests,” just as the law of Moses is called “the law of the Jews.” Hence Pope Saint Celestine says: “No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, nor to do anything that could conflict with the laws of the saints.” They are properly called the canons of priests, not inappropriately, since it is their special duty to provide for themselves and for others according to the canons and, if anything is committed wrongly, to strive to correct it according to those same canons. Hence Pope Saint Celestine also forbids them to be ignorant of them. For they could in no way form either themselves or others according to the canons if they were ignorant of the canons’ instructions. Consequently, knowledge of the canons is necessary for priests. We can acquire it above all in this way: by reading them frequently and, in reading, striving to seek the appropriateness of their meaning. For although the sacred canons appear to present a clear literal sense, many obscure matters are nevertheless found in them. Negligent readers sometimes regard these as less suitable, though they are entirely apt when understood properly.

Consider, for example, the provision of the Council of Nicaea concerning the transfer of bishops. In chapter eleven of that council it is expressly forbidden “that a bishop should move from one city to another.” Likewise, Blessed Pope Damasus, writing to all the bishops after the Council of Nicaea, prohibited the transfer of bishops so strictly that he recalled a bishop who had transferred himself to his own place under threat of excommunication. He also forbade him the priestly office for as long as the other lived, if he had happened to receive a successor during his transfer.

But before the Council of Nicaea, the most holy martyrs and Apostolic pontiffs Evaristus, Callistus, and Antherus, each writing to all the bishops in his own time, taught that the transfer of bishops was lawful. Among them, Saint Antherus enumerated many holy Fathers who had been transferred from one place to another, such as Peter from Antioch to Rome and Eusebius from a certain small city to Alexandria. We could understand this difference in a simple way by attributing one case to the necessity of persecution and the other to the freedom of peace, if such a transfer were found to have occurred nowhere during peacetime. But since it often happens even now, let us seek another appropriate explanation, especially one by which we can show that the holy Fathers agreed with one another both in peace and in persecution.

Let Saint Antherus, then, state what he thinks about the transfer of bishops:

“He does not pass from one city to another, nor is he transferred from a smaller to a larger one, if he does not do this through ambition or of his own will, but has been driven by force from his own see, compelled by necessity, or transferred and enthroned by others, not proudly but humbly, for the usefulness of the place or people. For just as bishops have the power regularly to ordain bishops and the other priests, so, whenever usefulness or necessity demands it, they have the power, in the manner stated above, both to transfer and to enthrone them; yet not without the authority and permission of the holy Roman See. For the cause of usefulness and necessity is one thing, and the cause of greed, presumption, or one’s own will is another.”

See how openly this Apostolic man indicates what we ought to understand concerning the transfer of bishops [Col. 1212A]: namely, that we should condemn presumptuous and ambitious transfer with the Council of Nicaea, but accept necessary and useful transfer with Apostolic authority.

Likewise, Pope Saint Callistus says: “A bishop who is to be transferred must not do this on his own, but must act at the invitation of his brothers and with the authority of this holy See—not, however, for the sake of ambition, but either from necessity or for usefulness.” Saint Evaristus likewise says: “A bishop must not leave the Church without unavoidable necessity or Apostolic or canonical transfer and join himself to another for the sake of ambition.” These Apostolic men, therefore, together with the Council of Nicaea, condemned ambition in the transfer of bishops but taught that necessity and usefulness were to be admitted.

[Col. 1212B] It is not surprising that the Council of Nicaea did not expressly make an exception for necessity and usefulness, as the ancient Fathers did, since it prohibited the transfer of bishops so simply. Before the Council of Nicaea, frequent persecutions very often compelled bishops to be moved from place to place. Ambition could have no place where the man who appeared to be preeminent over others was precisely the one being led to martyrdom. The holy Roman pontiffs themselves attest that this was true, since nearly all of them before the Council of Nicaea are said to have been crowned with martyrdom. From the time of the Council of Nicaea, however, after persecution had been somewhat quieted, the transfer of bishops did not seem so necessary, since it was already possible for anyone to preside over his own sheep [Col. 1212C], or, where a bishop was lacking, to ordain another according to the canon. It is therefore not surprising that the Nicene Fathers, unlike the earlier Fathers, made no exception in their prohibition, since they no longer had so reasonable a cause for exception—especially since those who appeared to seek another’s see without necessity were now rightly suspected of ambition.

But the Council of Sardica, which is said to have been presided over by Hosius the Great, as was the Council of Nicaea, appears to have interpreted that council’s judgment concerning the transfer of bishops in this way. For in its first chapter it forbids anyone “to transfer a bishopric through ambition,” and deprives one who has transferred himself in this way even of lay communion. Hence Blessed Pope Leo I, writing to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, declares that “he should lose his own place and not retain another’s who, scorning his own, desires through ambition to obtain another’s” [Col. 1212D]. If, therefore, we understand the judgment of the Council of Nicaea in this way, we shall in no respect oppose any reasonable transfer of bishops, should such a necessity arise even in our own time and Apostolic authority consent to it.

Likewise, the holy Fathers very frequently prohibit sheep from accusing their shepherd unless he has erred in the faith; they have judged that subjects who accuse their prelates should be excommunicated and branded with infamy. Yet Blessed Gregory, writing to John, bishop of the Corinthians, condemned the clerics Paul, Euphemius, Thomas, and Clematius because they had refused to obey in accusing their own bishop of a certain crime. The same Apostolic man also confirmed the deposition of the bishop of the city of Dodavena, who had been accused and convicted by his clerics of a bodily crime, to such an extent that he judged him likewise to be deprived of communion if thereafter he presumed to say anything concerning the episcopate.

But we shall not judge these statements to be contradictory if we take care to understand the earlier judgment appropriately: namely, that sheep must not presume in any way to accuse their shepherd out of their own rashness, yet they must not proudly resist a superior authority that canonically commands them to do so—least of all an authority capable of condemning them if they refuse to obey it against their own bishop. Thus it is understood: “Subjects shall neither rashly accuse their prelates nor stubbornly resist superior authority” [Col. 1213B].

We sometimes necessarily require this kind of opening-up of the meaning even in sacred Scripture, as in the command: “You shall not kill” (Exodus 20). For if you understand that too simply, the law itself will contradict itself, since elsewhere it very often decrees that the guilty are to be punished by death. God himself, who established the law, frequently commanded many people to be killed. Therefore, lest you blaspheme by saying that God ever commanded contradictory things, we must understand the foregoing statement more carefully: namely, with the qualification that no one should kill out of his own presumption, but that he should not refuse to obey God if God commands this either directly or through the law of God. For Blessed Augustine explains in Book I of *The City of God* that whoever obeys one who commands this ministry is not himself the killer. Thus, in the matter of accusation also, we properly understand that what is proscribed is not the obedience of subjects but their presumption. We do not doubt that many ecclesiastical corrections are safeguarded by allowing such accusations. For prelates necessarily take greater care both of themselves and of their subjects the more they know that they may be struck by accusations from their subjects. Ecclesiastical discipline would also be seriously weakened if such an accusation were nowhere permitted. Few prelates of such perfection would be found that they would not neglect both themselves and their subjects in discipline all the more if they despaired of being restrained by some judgment through their accusations. Subjects, however, must in no way presume to do this without the authority of a higher power [Col. 1213D], lest, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, they incur a sentence deserving their condemnation.

It should be understood, however, that subjects are not forbidden to accuse their prelate for their own injury or for heresy, according to the statement of Pope Symmachus to Bishop Caesarius: “Sheep cannot accuse their shepherd except for heresy or their own injury.” Hence the African canons, promulgated and confirmed by Apostolic authority, after listing all those to whom permission to accuse is denied, immediately add: “Nevertheless, in their own cases permission to accuse is not denied to any of these.”

Likewise, the holy Fathers very often decree that no one should be judged in his absence, as Pope Blessed Zephyrinus says: “Because both divine and human laws forbid this.” Pope Felix likewise, writing to all the bishops, says: “In the absence of the adversary, let the accuser not be heard, nor shall a sentence pronounced by a judge when the other party is absent possess any validity.” Pope Saint Cornelius likewise says: “Everything that is done or judged against absent persons in any matter or place shall be entirely annulled, because no one condemns an absent person and no law condemns him.” Pope Zosimus, in his forty-third letter, together with the 217 bishops of the African council, deprived of communion every accuser or accused person, even if absent, who had refused to come after canonical summons. Pope Boniface, his successor, decreed concerning one who was contumaciously absent that he should not profit by delay of judgment on account of his absence. Blessed Gregory also judged Maximus, a presumptuous man from Salona, worthy of condemnation not only for the crimes brought against him but also for his absence, because, having been canonically summoned, he had delayed coming. Likewise, Pope Theodore, writing to Paul of Constantinople, ordered him to condemn in his absence Pyrrhus, formerly bishop of that see: “Because his presence is not necessary, since his offense is present.” Pope Felix likewise condemned Acacius of Constantinople in his absence; Blessed Gelasius, his successor, demonstrated by irrefragable approval that his sentence was canonical. I would certainly not doubt that more people are found who have received a sentence of condemnation in their absence than those who, while present, have awaited canonical examination and condemnation.

We can readily reconcile the diversity of these judgments if we refer the earlier statement—that an absent person is not to be judged—only to one whose case still appears to require investigation, and who did not have an opportunity to answer rather than having refused a canonically offered opportunity. For if someone who had been canonically summoned refused to come and did not offer a canonical excuse, he could be canonically condemned in his absence, both among the ancients and among the moderns. If, then, we explain both judgments concerning an absent person in this way, we shall see that it is reasonable both that an absent person be judged when he is discovered to have disregarded a canonical summons or admonition, and that an absent person not be judged when his contumacy is still uncertain.

[Col. 1214D] Thus, in other apparent divergences among the canons also, we must seek an appropriate meaning, lest we rashly reject as contradictory things of this kind which we nevertheless know to have been promulgated or confirmed by Apostolic authority. Let us strive, then, to investigate the coherence of their meaning, lest we interpret such statutes anywhere as contradictory to one another. For we appear to inflict a great injury upon the Holy Spirit if we are not afraid to interpret as contradictory, and therefore contemptible, the things which he is said to have established through the holy Fathers.

Nor should we be reluctant to consider carefully and compare with one another not only the exceptions to canonical institutions but also their complete statements, if we wish to arrive at a full knowledge of them. For individual chapters, considered in their proper places, will sometimes become sufficiently clear; but examined by themselves, they could scarcely or not at all be properly understood. The context of a reading itself often prescribes many things for us which a single isolated chapter does not contain, yet without which it cannot be fully understood. Comparison of different statutes with one another also helps us greatly, because one often clarifies another. Consideration of the times, places, or persons likewise often supplies us with an appropriate meaning, so that the diversity of statutes does not appear absurd or contradictory, since it is found to correspond most clearly to the diversity of times, places, or persons. This will provide the reader with much understanding if he does not fail to investigate with exceptional diligence the original causes of such statutes [Col. 1215B]. From such investigation, many measures will appear to have been instituted reasonably, though, when their causes are unknown, they might have seemed less suitable.

This above all must be investigated with the greatest diligence and, once investigated, firmly entrusted to memory: what the holy Fathers established dispensationally, as something to be observed for a time; and what they judged to be held generally at all times. For one principle applies to things that appear to have been established dispensationally, and another to general provisions. Hence Blessed Pope Innocent, writing to the bishops of Macedonia, says: “What necessity discovered as a remedy must, when the necessity has ceased, likewise cease together with what necessity had required; for one order is legitimate [Col. 1215C], and another is an usurpation which the present time compels to be done. And observe that what necessity, as you say, commanded cannot now be presumed in Churches already established in peace.”

For this reason Blessed Innocent asserted that the provision of the Council of Nicaea concerning the reception of heretics with their clerical orders was no longer to be observed, because the necessity of that time had already passed which had compelled the Nicene Fathers to receive the Novatians in this way. Hence the African Fathers also decreed, in chapter 32, that the Donatists should not be received with their orders, except those through whose reception ecclesiastical usefulness would be served.

Regarding those things that were established not dispensationally but generally, Pope Saint Leo I, writing to all the bishops, testifies: “What is contained in general statutes must not be omitted in the case of any person.” Pope Gelasius also judges that these provisions must always be observed according to the rule, unless some pressing hardship of circumstances or times intervenes. For the holy Fathers are sometimes said to have relaxed something in these matters because of the needs of the times, as in the ordination of Saint Ambrose, whom they ordained although he was a neophyte; yet the general institutions of the canons prohibited this. Likewise, the same Leo mentioned above confirmed certain men who had been ordained from among the laity in the episcopate, although the holy Fathers had by then generally prohibited this as well.

When some reasonable cause arises that requires the sacred canons to be tempered to a certain degree, the following judgment of that same Leo, addressed to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne [Col. 1216A], must always be faithfully observed:

“Just as there are certain things which cannot be overturned by any reasoning, so there are some which ought to be tempered either out of consideration for age or because of the necessity of circumstances; provided always that, in matters which are doubtful or obscure, we know that we must follow what is found to be contrary neither to the precepts of the Gospel nor to the decrees of the holy Fathers.”

We do not doubt that this authority to temper or alter the canons belongs above all to the Roman pontiff, as the holy Fathers taught. For blessed Pope Gelasius and Pope Nicholas I, in their decrees, and Symmachus, in a general synod, though at different times, protested with one and the same voice concerning the authority of the Roman pontiff:

> “We are constrained by the necessary ordering of affairs, and are bound by the guidance of the Apostolic See to weigh the decrees of the Fathers’ canons and to measure the commands of our predecessors and those who formerly presided, so that, with careful consideration, we may temper, insofar as it can be done, whatever the necessity of the present times demands for the restoration of the Churches.”

Nor should you be surprised that the Roman pontiffs have always possessed this particular power, to dispense from the canons according to circumstances. For they themselves are the authors of the canons, and that See has always possessed the privilege that whatever it binds or looses is bound or loosed. Hence, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, it stands above all the Churches and can judge concerning them all. [Col. 1216C] No unworthiness of those presiding can diminish this privilege, as the most blessed Pope Leo testifies:

> “Although,” he says, “the merits of those who preside are sometimes different, nevertheless the rights of the sees remain. Rivals may perhaps inflict some disturbance upon them, but they cannot diminish their dignity.”

Nor did Saint Peter himself—much less any bishop of the Roman See—by any prejudice deprive any of his successors of that power, so that, by the same authority, he could not, and indeed should not, provide for the whole Church, both by ancient and by new ordinances, now more leniently and now more strictly, according as he judged it suitable for his own time. The singular decrees of the Roman pontiffs plainly attest this, [Col. 1216D] for in them they are read to have provided in different ways for the needs of their own times. The canons of Nicaea likewise wished the privilege of the Roman pontiff to remain valid, since, following his example, they judged that the privileges of all the provinces should also be observed.

The Roman pontiff therefore does nothing at all against the canons when, in consideration of circumstances, he now tightens and now relaxes them, since the canons themselves undoubtedly granted him such a privilege. Other bishops, too, although they are in no way able, as an apostolic prelate can, either to establish canons or to judge those already established, nevertheless sometimes temper certain regulations within the limits of their own authority, especially in the laws governing penitents; and the canons themselves grant this to them. For the Council of Nicaea is read to have granted bishops permission to treat penitents worthily with greater humanity and to mitigate canonical severity toward them to some extent. According to Pope Innocent, they ought to consider the penitent’s confession, and the sighs and tears of the one who is correcting his life, and then order him to be released when they have seen that he has made adequate satisfaction. For, according to Augustine, in this kind of penance it is not so much the measure of time as of sorrow that must be considered.

Ecclesiastical discipline could in no way continue to exist if the apostolic prelate did not possess concerning the canons the authority we have mentioned above. For the regulations of earlier Fathers would not so much establish ecclesiastical discipline as throw it into confusion if their successors could in no way alter them, since the necessity of the times nevertheless persuades us to proceed now more gently and now more severely. Anyone who has taken care to investigate carefully the regulations of the earlier and later Fathers will not be unaware of this. Indeed, if blessed Gelasius had been unable to reduce the number of years that his predecessors had assigned to the individual grades, he could in no way have come to the aid of the poverty of the clergy of his own time by ordaining men from the laity who had reached maturity in less than a year. Likewise, if modern pontiffs had been unable to relax the ancient rigor of the canons regarding priests who had fallen, the Christian religion itself could not continue to exist, entirely deprived of the priestly office, since now scarcely any priests are found who have not fallen into serious crime—men whom the ancient canons are read to have deposed.

It must certainly be understood that the Roman pontiffs have always been accustomed to carry out and observe ancient provisions rather than establish new ones, unless some reasonable cause pressed urgently. Hence blessed Pope Gelasius wrote to the bishops of Dardania:

> “No one who is truly a Christian is now ignorant that the constitution of every synod—which the universal consent of the Church has approved—ought to be carried out by no See more than by the first See, which both confirms every synod by its authority and preserves it by continuous moderation.”

Hence Saint Pope Leo says:

> “The guilt will fall upon me if, God forbid, the rules of the Fathers’ sanctions, which were established for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God, are violated with my connivance.”

Likewise Pope Julius, writing to the Eastern bishops [*Letter to the Easterners, near the end*]:

> “Do not despise the ordinances of the apostles and apostolic men. You have the canons; make use of them. For it is exceedingly unworthy that any pontiff or any of the later orders should reject the rule that the See of blessed Peter is seen both to follow and to teach. It is highly fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which derives its authority from the place where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church, as Scripture says: ‘He has ordained love in me’ (Song of Songs II).”

And again:

> “Let all things be done in an orderly manner” (1 Corinthians XIV).

Blessed Gelasius expressed the same judgment in a general decree on ecclesiastical institutions, writing to all the bishops:

> “Since, in our desire to show reverence toward salutary rules, we wish nothing rash to be permitted to us, and since the Apostolic See, with the Lord’s favor, diligently strives to maintain with pious and devoted purpose all that has been established by the canons of the Fathers, it is exceedingly unworthy that any pontiff or any of the later orders should reject the observance that the See of blessed Peter is seen both to follow and to teach. It is likewise most fitting that the whole body of the Church should agree with itself in this observance, which it sees flourishing there where the Lord established the primacy of the whole Church. In this respect, certainly, the holy Roman pontiffs wished to be equal to the others: they strove to be not so much authors of new institutions as executors of the ancient ones”—a statement by which Gelasius testifies that this is permitted not only to the Roman bishop but to any bishop.

Thus far the ancient manuscript. I am uncertain whether it presents the whole of Bernaldus’s work, because it ends so abruptly and concludes with no address either to the reader or to Gebehard. Whoever has obtained a fuller and more complete copy should publish a more complete Bernaldus.

# Apologetic Arguments against the Objections of the Schismatics

## Editor’s Notice in the *Patrologia*

To the little works of Bernaldus already published from Gretser we add others that the most learned editor of *Germania sacra* first brought to light. Then we shall append Bernaldus’s *Chronicle*, in which much is related concerning the deeds of Gregory VII. The little works listed last in the index prefixed to the Collection will close Tengnagel’s *Sylloge* thus enlarged.

## Editor’s Notice in *Germania sacra* (II, 356)

Thus far Bernaldus’s little works have been published; we now append those that have not yet seen the light of publication, drawn from a parchment manuscript of the twelfth century preserved in our library. This is the same ancient codex in which Simler, in his *Bibliotheca*, p. 96, lists the following works of Bernard or Bernaldus. Among them the first to appear is *Apologetic Arguments against the Objections of the Schismatics*, addressed to Adalbert, provost of Speyer, in which he chiefly defends the position that he and the other monks of Saint Blaise rightly abstain from excommunicated persons.

[Col. 1219] Here he plainly declares himself a monk of Saint Blaise, though he suppresses the title of priest, even if he had already held it at that time. For he writes after the death of Gregory VII in 1085, but still before 1088, the year in which Bernard of Corbie died, to whom Bernaldus’s letter is addressed above; in that letter he accepts the sacraments of excommunicated persons, whereas here, still wavering, he rejects them. The style shows that the same author wrote the preceding little works, as will be evident to an attentive reader; the arguments also, both here and throughout the following works, sufficiently establish the same conclusion.

# Bernaldus’s Apologetic Arguments against the Objections of the Schismatics

To the lord and venerable Adalbert, provost of Speyer:

[Note: This Adalbert is missing from the list of provosts of Speyer in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 740. In the old Speyer Necrology, on 3 January, Albert, provost and brother, and Gebehard, provost and brother, are recorded; the others listed there as provosts do not have the designation “brother.” Hence one may reasonably conjecture that these two were monks. Whoever this Adalbert may have been, the correspondence between him and our Bernaldus shows that he was familiar with him, although the letter of his mentioned here has been lost. Adalbert of Saint Blaise, likewise a monk, may have brought it to Bernaldus, perhaps to arrange the domestic affairs of this monastery, which had several properties in the region of Speyer and to which he had been sent.]

Bernaldus, the last of the brothers of Saint Blaise.

### I

Your letter, which you sent to Saint Blaise through our brother Adalbert, seems to criticize us rather severely, as though we had strayed from the right path, and it admonishes us quite faithfully not to be ashamed to correct our error. But we do not at all presume to correct as an error what we have learned from evangelical and apostolic sanctions ought to be observed. For this would not be correcting an error but falling into an error far more dangerous and detestable. Nor could we extricate ourselves from the Gregorian anathema, since in such a correction we would be found opposed to the sacred canons. Therefore, in matters of this kind, we necessarily follow the ecclesiastical sanctions, which we wish briefly to recall to you—even though you do not need an admonisher—so that we may be cleared of error in your judgment all the more easily, the less we are shown to have departed from the footsteps of the holy Fathers in the matters you have criticized.

### II

First of all, you criticize us as leaning too far to the right in neglecting fraternal compassion; yet we are not conscious of this. It is our custom, in accordance with evangelical teaching, to strive to apply no less oil than wine to the wounds of our brothers. Nor will anyone rightly criticize us in this matter as having strayed from the right path through excessive inhumanity, if we endeavor, within the limits of our ability, to follow the footsteps of the one who rebukes and chastises those whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives (Hebrews XII, 6). Yet, by God’s mercy, we shall never reach that inhumanity in which we present ourselves as fierce and rigid toward every sin of our brothers, as you seem to criticize us under the name of Saint Jerome.

### III

We are astonished at your prudence that you pretend not to know why our people strive to abstain from excommunicated persons. Can it be hidden from anyone instructed in the sacred canons that the apostles themselves, and the Roman pontiffs who succeeded them in their See and authority, established that communion with excommunicated persons must be avoided? Among them, blessed Pope and martyr Callistus, seventeenth from blessed Peter, enumerates in his decrees the ways in which we ought to avoid excommunicated persons [Note: In Gratian, chapter *Excommunicatos*, 17, Cause 11, question 3], namely in greeting, in the kiss, in prayer, and at table. Then, drawing the conclusion, he says:

> “Whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or any other prohibited matters shall himself, according to the institution of the apostles, be subject to a similar excommunication.”

Blessed Pope and martyr Fabian judged that this sentence must be observed without resistance in his decrees [Note: Ibid., chapter *Sicut*, 16]. The most sacred Council of Nicaea wished it to be confirmed [Note: Canon 5]. Blessed Pope Gregory, in his synodical letter, approves it as he would the Gospels and anathematizes all who dissent from it [Note: Ibid., chapter *Rogo*, 25]. Blessed Augustine embraced it so fully that he is read to have confirmed it by his subscription in a council of 217 bishops [Note: That is, at the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 73, at which 214 bishops were present. Among them the first to subscribe was the bishop of Carthage, the presiding officer of the council, while Saint Augustine subscribed third]. Therefore we too must necessarily avoid excommunicated persons, lest, in accordance with the institution of the apostles, we become subject to a similar excommunication.

### IV

Guibert of Ravenna is unquestionably excommunicated [Note: King Henry, after renouncing Gregory, made him antipope under the name Clement III at the assembly of Brixen in 1080. See Bernoldus, *Chronicle*, under that year], together with all his supporters: he is an invader of the Apostolic See and a supplanter of his own lord—namely, Pope Gregory—to whom he had sworn obedience. Gregory repeatedly anathematized him for specific crimes in a general synod [Note: The Roman synod, evidently that of 1078], even before he had invaded the Apostolic See, while the princes of your party, like those of ours, were still jointly rendering the obedience owed to that apostolic authority.

He never took care to emerge from that anathema. Although anathematized and perjured, he presumed to invade the See of his lord and to become the head of all the excommunicated. Therefore, according to the regulations of the holy Fathers, we necessarily avoid him and all his accomplices, because, according to blessed Gelasius (*Letter* 13, Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1200), all accomplices, followers, and communicants of once-condemned depravity are judged to share the same lot, and wickedness cannot be rejected when partnership in wickedness has been admitted.

### V

But the fact that you write that Isaac communicated with the Palestinians and that our Lord communicated with publicans can in no way prove that we too ought to communicate with excommunicated persons, since we nowhere read that those Palestinians or publicans, although guilty, had been anathematized. Evil people, so long as they have not been excommunicated, do not defile anyone through external communion; but they will undoubtedly do so after they have judicially received the sentence of excommunication for their crimes.

Nor, as you criticize us, do we utterly shrink from them. For the sake of their conversion, if necessary, we would not refuse even to suffer hardship, provided only that we did not depart from the regulations of the holy Fathers. Nor do we approve the fact that certain people among us sin; rather, insofar as we can, we strive to invite them to repentance. We are not commanded to avoid them as excommunicated persons so long as they remain within Catholic unity. We do not say that their sins are Christian; nevertheless, we have greater hope for their salvation than if we knew that they had been completely separated from the body of Christ. For even members who are as weak as possible are hoped to be healed more easily so long as they remain in the body than if, while completely sound, they are entirely cut away from it.

### VI

We certainly know that the holy Fathers prohibited many things under excommunication; among these, Pope Gregory also prohibited everything contrary to the sacred canons. Nevertheless, if someone has now done something against the canons, we shall not immediately avoid him as excommunicated before we hear that a sentence of excommunication has been pronounced against him in due judicial order.

Hence blessed Augustine says in his book *On Penance* (*Sermon* 351, no. 10, vol. V of the works):

> “We cannot exclude anyone from communion unless he has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment.”

Regarding this naming, the Apostle says: “If anyone is named as a fornicator among the brothers” (1 Corinthians V), and so forth, “with such a one do not even eat.” Blessed Augustine explains this as follows:

> “The Apostle wished that ‘naming’ to be understood as that which is pronounced against someone together with a sentence issued in due judicial order.”

### VII

Criminals must first of all be admonished so that they may come to their senses. Then, if they refuse to come to their senses, they must be excommunicated according to the canonical sanctions; and only then must they be avoided by everyone as excommunicated persons.

Thus we avoid any sacrilegious persons after we have heard that they have been canonically excommunicated by their prelates. In the same way, after the sentence of the venerable Pope Gregory I [Note: *Book VI, Letter* 27], we necessarily avoid Guibert the heresiarch and all his supporters. Yet we would in no way avoid them as excommunicated persons if we did not know that some specific excommunication had already been pronounced against them.

We may lawfully communicate with criminals who have not yet been excommunicated. We do not do this, as you write, in order to take precautions for our position [Note: That is, the monastery of Saint Blaise, which obtained from the same Henry IV, before the anathema, in 1065, a charter confirming the boundaries granted to its monastery by Emperor Otto and other possessions transferred to it. Later, nothing further is found concerning communion maintained with him or with the antipope; indeed, the contrary is evident from this very letter. This nevertheless does not display ingratitude toward that emperor, whom the men of Saint Blaise still gratefully acknowledge as their benefactor in publicly displayed paintings, but rather demonstrates the necessity of observing the canons thereafter. Thus they were enemies in the matter, but friends in person], or, as you put it, for the sake of religion. Rather, we do so because we recognize that in this matter we are doing nothing contrary to canonical authority. Without doubt, however, anyone who presumes to communicate, according to ecclesiastical custom, with wicked persons who have been excommunicated does act contrary to it.

### VIII

We are also greatly astonished at your prudence, since you strive so vigorously to remove kings from ecclesiastical authority. Did our Lord Jesus Christ make any exception when he granted blessed Peter—or, as blessed Augustine explains, granted the holy Church in the person of Peter—that whatever it bound or loosed on earth would be bound or loosed in heaven? (Matthew XVI, 19.)

Who, I ask, could emancipate himself from such universal authority, except perhaps one who chose to perish under the tyranny of the devil rather than reign beneath the Lord’s gentle yoke? Yet even for him this would not lead to a wretched freedom, since under ecclesiastical authority he would always remain, if not for salvation, then for condemnation.

Therefore emperors too cannot emancipate themselves from this authority. Blessed Pope Gelasius made this declaration to the Emperor Anastasius (*Letter* 8, Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1182):

> “There are two powers, O Emperor Augustus, by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Among them the burden of the priests is all the heavier, since they will render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves. For you know, most merciful son, that although in dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless you devoutly bow your neck to those who preside over divine matters and await from them the causes of your salvation. Hence you recognize that, in the order of religion, you ought to be subject to them rather than preside over them; and in these matters you depend upon their judgment, rather than wishing to reduce them to your will.”

### IX

By this authority, blessed Pope Innocent is read to have excommunicated the Emperor Arcadius [Note: This is said to have occurred in letters of that pontiff to Arcadius and of Arcadius to Innocent, which Glycas and Nicephorus report. Natalis Alexander, however, against Baronius, demonstrates that these letters are spurious (*Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, chapter 2, article 1). See Pagi, *Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 137], because he consented to the expulsion of Saint John Chrysostom from his See.

Likewise blessed Pope Nicholas I excommunicated King Lothair, after whom Lorraine is named, because he repudiated his lawful wife for a certain concubine [Note: See the letter of Nicholas I to King Charles, Labbe, vol. VIII, p. 502, where the pontiff states that he regards Lothair as excommunicated by him. Bernoldus himself gives nearly the same examples for this purpose, in an expanded form, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1077].

Bishops of lower rank are also read to have excommunicated emperors and kings. Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, is read to have excommunicated the elder Emperor Theodosius and, after his satisfaction, to have reconciled him. Likewise Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, excommunicated Heribert [Note: Or Charibert, in Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 26], king of the Franks, who died while still excommunicated.

In general, blessed Pope Adrian also excommunicated all kings who presumed to violate the statutes of the Apostolic See [Note: *Capitularies*, 80; Labbe, vol. VI, p. 1838; Gratian, Cause 25, question 1, canon 11]. Saint Pope Gregory likewise decreed that kings should fall from their dignities and be deprived of participation in the body and blood of the Lord if they presumed to despise the decrees of the Apostolic See [Note: This is indeed found in Saint Gregory, *Letter* 33 of Book XII, in the privilege allegedly granted to the abbot of Saint Medard. Labbe, however, notes concerning it, vol. V, p. 1582: “This privilege was rejected by orthodox scholars Cardinal Perronius, Sirmundus, Launoius, and other highly learned men, and by heterodox scholars Blondel and others.” Hence in the new edition it is relegated to the appendix, *Works*, vol. II, p. 1284].

[Col. 1223B] We know that Gregory VII and his defenders used these and similar arguments and examples, although at that time other opponents loudly proclaimed that the action and deed he had undertaken, and the unheard-of deposition of a king, were entirely alien to the Spirit of the Gospel and to the holy Fathers to whom appeal is made here. This matter has already been discussed in the preliminary observations, § 24 and following.

If we had no other evidence of this prerogative of ecclesiastical authority, this should be sufficient for us: we read that such holy men exercised it over kings and emperors. They would not have done so in any way if they had not known that they were canonically able to do it.

But what is surprising about the fact that the holy Church can judge secular princes, who are her members, when, according to the Apostle, she will unquestionably judge even angels? “Do you not know,” he says, “that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life?” (1 Corinthians VI.) We shall therefore by no means deny that kings or emperors are subject to ecclesiastical judgment, if we are willing to believe and assent to evangelical and apostolic sanctions.

### X

You seem to go far beyond what is proper in your words when you try to compare our religious brothers with the Jews.
