They are not crying out with the Jews for Christ to be killed; rather, they desire that faith in him be strengthened in the hearts of the faithful and defended from the contagion of anathema.

We too venerate the holy Council of Chalcedon. Nevertheless, it in no way prescribes against the dignity or authority of the Apostolic See, so as to prevent it from claiming any monasteries as subject to its own authority, so that they may be subject not to the bishop of the city but specifically to the Apostolic See [Note: Already at the Council of Arles in 455 (Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1024), concerning the monastery of Lérins, it was decreed that, apart from ordinations, the whole lay community of that monastery should belong to the care of the abbot, and that the bishop should claim nothing from it or presume to make anyone from it a cleric unless at the abbot’s request. The Fathers add that this is full of both reason and religion: clerics should look to the bishop for ordination in due submission, while the entire lay congregation of the monastery should belong solely and freely to the ordering and administration of its own abbot, whom it has itself chosen. Thus the exemptions of monasteries were by no means wares of Isidore Mercator; they were acknowledged and established by these bishops themselves and confined within their proper limits].

Nor should you be surprised that the office of preaching is not entirely forbidden to monks of our own time, as it was to the ancient monks about whom the Council of Chalcedon and Pope Leo wrote. For those ancient monks did not possess ecclesiastical orders, as we may infer from the regulations of that council. In this respect they are equal to laymen: when they violate the canons, they are not degraded as clerics but excommunicated as laymen. This would certainly not happen if they possessed ecclesiastical orders, for the canons command that those who have been ordained be degraded for their offenses, not excommunicated.

But since modern monks possess ecclesiastical orders, who can deny that, when commanded, they may exercise the offices of those same grades, especially since in receiving consecration they differ in no respect from clerics? Either, then, you must remove ecclesiastical orders from them entirely, or you cannot prevent them from administering those same grades [Note: See the preliminary observations, § 60, on this argument].

You are also excessively zealous on behalf of your bishop [Note: Huzmannus, the schismatic bishop of Speyer, excluded from sacred functions in 1085], if you think that he must be obeyed more than the Apostolic See. You yourselves must obey the Apostolic See more than your own bishop, if, according to Saint Gregory, you do not wish to be considered enemies of apostolic authority.

### XI

The statement in which the Apostle predicts that some will depart from the faith in the last times (1 Timothy IV, 1) would more appropriately be applied by you not to certain Catholics but to all excommunicated persons. By attending to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, they have departed from Catholic unity into the hands of Satan.

Their cruelty has long since increased to such a degree that the holy Church has very often needed military assistance against their attacks and could not be freed from their tyranny without the shedding of blood. Soldiers, therefore, who, compelled by that necessity, have killed an excommunicated person did so not so much for their own sake as for the defense of the Church, and they do not appear in any way to have incurred the condemnation of the first fratricide, Cain, who, according to John, “was of the evil one and killed his brother. And why did he kill him? Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were righteous” (1 John III)—for he killed him out of envy.

These men, however, would not wish to kill even their enemies if they could defend the holy mother Church against the wicked by another means. In this very undertaking they lay down their own lives for their brothers, whom they see endangered in soul and body through the violence of excommunicated persons. Therefore, if we wish to judge rightly, we shall not compare them with Cain, that most wicked fratricide.

We know that homicide is prohibited in Holy Scripture. But we must not understand this in such a way that we judge Phinehas, Elijah, and the zealots, together with the other holy Fathers who killed many out of zeal for God, to be liable to the condemnation of murderers. For one never commits an offense where one specially obeys God, whether God commands directly or through the law.

Blessed Augustine likewise says in the first book of *The City of God* (chapter 26):

> “When a soldier, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, kills a man, he is not guilty of homicide under any law of his state.”

Nor do we completely absolve all who have killed excommunicated persons; but neither do we judge them as harshly as you would wish. We judge them so, first, because such an act can scarcely, or never, be carried out without guilt; and second, because we recognize that they undertake it, driven by zeal for God, for the sake of the Church’s necessity [Note: The entire context makes clear that Bernaldus is speaking only of killings carried out in war and in legitimate defense; otherwise this assertion of his would be entirely false].

As for the preaching of monks, which you criticize again: we too approve that only those who have been ordained should preach and that they should obey a Catholic prelate, unless they have been emancipated from him by the Apostolic See.

### XII

Why are you surprised that the sacraments of the Church are denied among excommunicated persons [Note: Bernaldus later retracted this opinion, as we saw in the preliminary observations, § 21. This letter, therefore, was written before 1088, the year in which Bernard died; Bernaldus’s letter to him, related above as little work II, defends the opposite position], when blessed Augustine declares that there is no place for the true sacrifice outside the Church (*Sermon* 181, *On Time*, chapter 21)?

Likewise Saint Gregory, writing about the consecration of Maximus the usurper (*Book III, Letter* 20), says:

> “We can in no way call this a consecration, because it was celebrated by excommunicated persons.”

His predecessor, Pope Pelagius, says likewise:

> “Outside the Church a bishop is not consecrated but desecrated” (Gratian, Cause 24, question 1, chapter 33).

Blessed Pope Innocent likewise says (*Letter* 22, no. 3):

> “He who has lost honor cannot give honor.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore he gave the condemnation that he had received through a wrongful laying-on of hands.”

Saint Pope Leo, writing to Leo Augustus about a certain condemned Timothy [Note: Namely, Timothy Aelurus, the intruded bishop of Alexandria, who sacrilegiously caused his predecessor Proterius to be killed. See Saint Leo’s *Letter* 25, Labbe, vol. IV, p. 904] and his followers, testifies that he withdrew all the sacraments from their sacrilegious hands.

If we also wish to believe blessed Augustine, we do not doubt that all heretics and excommunicated persons are outside the Church, although even now within the threshing floor we tolerate much chaff together with the grain [Note: These are nearly the same arguments used above by Bernard of Hildesheim in Letter 2, col. 1143].

### XIII

You compare our lord, Pope Gregory of blessed memory [Note: It is clear from this that the letter was written after the death of Gregory VII, in 1085, by which time Bernaldus was already a priest], in vain to a staff of reed, because you greatly regretted that he remained firm and unbending in his judgment to the end of his life. He did not anathematize all the provinces that you list in their entirety, but Guibert and all his accomplices, wherever they might be.

Nor should you say that only a few remained outside this excommunication, since so many remained in the Teutonic kingdom alone that they very often resisted the multitude of the excommunicated courageously, and are still able to resist them.

### XIV

Our lord Pope Gregory did not drive us into perjury, as you criticize us, but by the same authority absolved us from the oath of submission [Note: This concerns Otto, bishop of Constance, whom Gregory VII excluded from communion in 1075 because he resisted the decrees of the Roman synod, and to whom he ordered the clergy and people of Constance no longer to render obedience. The letters sent to them, omitted from the *Register*, are preserved by Hugh of Flavigny in his *Chronicle* and by Paul of Bernried in his *Life of Gregory VII*, in Gretser, *Works*, vol. VI, p. 135. Among other things, it says: “If your bishop wishes to oppose the apostolic commands, by the authority of blessed Peter we absolve all of you from every yoke of submission to him, so that although each of you may be bound to him by an oath, as long as he remains rebellious against almighty God and the Apostolic See, no one is to be made subject to him by any display of loyalty.” He first gives the reason: “For it is unworthy that one who refuses to submit to his master should demand to preside over his disciples”]. By that authority he could also depose and excommunicate their prelates.

Thus the most sacred Council of Ephesus, convened and confirmed by the authority of Pope Celestine, is read to have absolved the subjects of Nestorius from his power. [Col. 1226C] Thus the Council of Chalcedon emancipated the Alexandrians from subjection to the patriarch Dioscorus. Thus the holy mother Church has always been accustomed to emancipate her sons from the hands of deposed and excommunicated persons without any stain of perjury, even when they had promised them submission by oath.

Blessed Augustine, writing to Boniface, judged that something should be taken away from the strictness of the canons in this matter, so that the clergy of the Donatists might be received into the Catholic Church together with their orders—not, certainly, so that the sentence of anathema might be treated as worthless in the case of those who had been anathematized. We read that Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, was excommunicated by the blessed pontiffs Boniface and Celestine [Col. 1227A] [Note: Where Bernaldus read this is unknown to us; for neither in Augustine nor in the letters of these pontiffs or of the Carthaginians can any trace of this event be found. I would believe that Bernaldus was deceived by the homonymy of another Aurelius, concerning whom Baronius, from the booklet of the schismatics Marcellinus and Faustinus, reports the following under the year 371: “A certain bishop Aurelius suffered punishment at Rome because he had communicated with Gregory of Eliberitanum”—an event that had already occurred before the time of Aurelius of Carthage.], not Saint Aurelius [Note: Le Quien (Christian East, vol. I, p. 452) and the Bollandists [Col. 1228D], under 25 May (vol. VI, p. 41), in the preliminary commentary to the Life of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Milan, who was sent into exile there and died, relate much about this Saint Aurelius, bishop of Ariarathia in Lesser Armenia, or Cappadocia. At the request of Saint Ambrose, Aurelius himself later brought Dionysius’s body to Milan, where, according to Trithemius (Annals of Hirsau, vol. I, p. 7), he also died around the year 383. His relics were later brought by Notingus, bishop of Vercelli, to the monastery of Hirsau under the emperor Louis the Pious. We regret that Saint Ambrose’s sermon delivered at his funeral, whose opening Trithemius records, is missing from his works.]—whose body we preserve at Hirsau. For this saint, insofar as we have been able to gather from the chronicles, departed to the Lord before the time of these pontiffs. Nor, with God’s help, shall we ever stray so far from the truth as to call someone both a saint and excommunicated. For, according to blessed Augustine, those separated from the Church are by no means considered saints, but are believed to be consigned to eternal fire.

XV. If we wish to believe the eminent teacher and most faithful martyr, the blessed Cyprian, I say that we shall believe that there is no Church whatsoever among Guibert and his accomplices. For, writing *On the Church’s [or: the Unity of the Church]* to the priest Magnus [Note: In the Oxford edition it is Epistle 69, without a title, addressed “To Magnus, son.”], he says:

“The Church is one, and it cannot be both inside and outside. For if it was with Novatian or Novatus, it was not with Cornelius. But if it was with Cornelius, who legitimately succeeded Bishop Fabian, Novatian is not in the Church.”

And it is as though he were saying: If the Church was with Pope Gregory—and this was also acknowledged by Guibert—it is not with Guibert, nor with his accomplices. For Guibert intruded upon Gregory through adulterous usurpation in the same way, except that not without perjury, as Novatus intruded upon Cornelius. For we do not read that Novatus ever swore obedience to Saint Cornelius, whereas Guibert did so to Pope Gregory.

And, to speak of our lord Gregory what blessed Cyprian wrote of Saint Cornelius (Epistle 55):

“He became bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of all the clergy, by the assent of the people who were then present, and by the college of the ancient priests and good men; no one had been made before him, since the place of Peter and the rank of the priestly chair were vacant. Once it had been occupied, and he had been ordained by the will of God and the consent of all, whoever thereafter wished to become bishop necessarily became one outside; nor does he possess ecclesiastical ordination who does not maintain the unity of the Church. He is profane, alien, outside. And since there cannot be a second after the first, whoever was made after the first, who alone ought to exist, is no longer a second, but nothing.”

XVI. We must not, however, understand statements about the universality of the Church in such a way that we say that all nations are in the Church. For would any Christian maintain that pagans or Jews are in the Church, although the Lord himself promised Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis XXII)? Nor shall we doubt, in accordance with the testimony of the holy Fathers, that all heretics and excommunicated persons are outside; for unquestionably it would have been better for them never to have entered the Church than, according to the Gospel, to have become twice as much sons of Gehenna (Matthew XXIII).

Saint Augustine himself also repeatedly asserted that schismatics are outside the Church, although he never doubted the Church’s universality. The holy Church is therefore to be understood as spread throughout all nations in its members—not, certainly, in those who were never incorporated into it, or who, after their incorporation, were severed from it by ecclesiastical judgment.

XVII. It does not seem to us a perverse but a sound policy that monks should obey not so much secular persons, whose way of life they have renounced, as their abbots, to whom they have promised obedience. Let everyone generally, spiritual and secular alike, observe this most firmly: that no one should ever obey anyone against God and apostolic authority. “It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts V). Therefore, however exalted imperial majesty may appear, it is nevertheless not right to obey it against God.

XVIII. Nor should you be indignant if the holy Church does not accept the alms of those whom it has recognized as belonging to an external communion. For the holy canons also command that the offerings of dissenting brothers be received neither in the sacristy nor in the treasury; rather, those very alms are to be repaid through ecclesiastical prayers. Therefore the holy Church necessarily avoids the alms of those with whom it does not share in ecclesiastical prayers.

We could establish all these points more fully by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, but we fear that we would be too burdensome to your prudence, since we have no doubt that you yourselves can investigate all these matters more abundantly and carefully.

XIX. In these and other similar judgments of the holy Fathers, therefore, we wish to persevere, according to our ability, to the end. With God’s help we shall never be ashamed of their faith—or rather, of the faith of Christ himself, who declared in the Gospel that he would be ashamed of whoever was ashamed of him and of his words before men. We also wish you to agree with these judgments, and we continually ask the God of peace and consolation to grant you to think the same with us, or rather with the holy Fathers [Col. 1229A].

But amid all these things, charity—which is not provoked, does not seek its own, and never fails—makes us deeply concerned for your salvation. For we know, as blessed James declares, that “friendship with this world is enmity with God, and whoever wishes to be a friend of this age is made an enemy of God” (James IV). Hence that disciple whom Jesus loved, drawing counsel from the secret of the Lord’s breast, instructs us as follows:

“Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the charity of the Father is not in him; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever. Little children, it is the final hour, and the whole world lies in the evil one” (1 John II).

You know all these things very well and have no need of our report to impress them upon you. We ask you in the Lord to strive to exercise your learning for the salvation of your soul, lest you value this life—which is temptation and vapor, existing for a brief time (James IV)—so highly that you unhappily lose the future life, which is one of eternal happiness.

[Col. 1229]

## BERNALDUS’S LETTER TO ADELBERT, PROVOST OF STRASBOURG, ON THE LAW OF EXCOMMUNICATION

That obedience must be rendered to the pope rather than to one’s own pastor.

### Notice

Bernaldus already treated this same subject above, in chapter 24 of the *Apologeticus*, col. 1140; here he briefly reviews it again for Adelbert, his intimate associate, in order to strengthen him in obedience to the pope against Otho, bishop of Strasbourg, elected in 1085 but a schismatic, as Bernoldus calls him in his *Chronicle* under the year 1100.

This Adelbert, moreover, is not listed among the provosts of that church in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 822, though he is correctly listed in a twelfth-century necrology, as the distinguished Grandidier testifies; Grandidier searched for him in vain in the charters of that period. In *History of Alsace*, vol. II, title 501, under the year 1089, Burchard is presented as provost. Whether Adelbert preceded or followed him is uncertain. He must have preceded him, however, if Burchard held the provostship from 1089 to 1104, as the authors of *Gallia Christiana* maintain.

Bernaldus wrote this letter when he was already a priest, and therefore after the year 1084; moreover, Gregory VII had already died, as we shall note at the end of this letter.

[Col. 1229B]

To the lord Adelbert, provost of Strasbourg, a careful supporter of apostolic authority, placed upon the flesh-pots of Egypt not so much in mind as in body; Bernaldus, a priest in name only—would that he were infirm in body alone.

When you were recently with us, you showed that you approved all the statutes of the holy Roman pontiffs and councils. Therefore we cannot give God thanks worthy of him, who inspired you, in so dangerous a time, with love for his law; who strengthened Daniel and his companions amid the Babylonian persecution, so that they would not adore the statue of Nebuchadnezzar.

There was, however, something that troubled you: namely, whether a subject could in any way excuse himself from obedience to a superior power if he obeyed an inferior power. We could provide you with many reasons and examples from the holy Fathers, if we did not fear exceeding the brevity proper to a letter. We shall nevertheless speak briefly, lest we appear excessively talkative to those who already know these matters.

Natalis, bishop of Salona [Note: On this event, see Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXXXV, § 26.], deposed his deacon Honoratus from the archdeaconate contrary to the command of the Apostolic See, and substituted another in his place. Therefore Saint Gregory restored Honoratus to the archdeaconate against the will of that same bishop [Col. 1230B] and deposed the man who had been substituted for him, because that man had obeyed his own bishop in making the substitution contrary to the command of the lord pope.

We have therefore touched upon this only briefly, and we leave it to you to examine more carefully in Gregory’s *Register* (book II, letter 18). There it will be most clearly evident that no subject can excuse himself by obedience to his prelate; rather, he must obey the Apostolic See—which can canonically condemn him even against the will of his own bishop or dean—more than his own bishop or dean.

Furthermore, the Third Council of Carthage, at which Saint Augustine participated and presided together with Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, testifies in its seventh canon that a condemned and excommunicated bishop is not to be communicated even by his own church [Col. 1230C]. If, therefore, the judgment of a provincial council must be obeyed more than one’s own bishop, how much more must one obey the most holy Apostolic See’s universal synod?

Moreover, did not the most holy Fathers of the Churches—namely, the apostles—devoutly obey the priests of their own time, especially when the Lord commanded:

“The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ chair; observe and do everything that they tell you” (Matthew XXIII)?

But when they departed from the truth and wished to lead the apostles astray with themselves, the apostles are not said to have waited for the Lord specifically to absolve them from obedience to the Pharisees. Rather, they immediately refused to obey them, saying:

“It is necessary to obey God rather than men” (Acts V).

Thus blessed Peter the Apostle is said, at the ordination of Saint Clement, to have decreed most firmly that the person whom the ecclesiastical pastor is perceived to oppose should be avoided by men. Nor should one await some special command from a prelate for carrying this out; rather, they should immediately turn away from the man whom they perceive to be opposed to the ecclesiastical pastor.

No one, I say, is to be obeyed against God and the statutes of the holy Fathers. Indeed, one must resist in every way a prelate who has been condemned by a superior power for disobedience [Col. 1232A]. Hence, at the most holy universal synod of Ephesus, those who bravely resisted their own bishop, namely Nestorius, were greatly praised.

At the end of the *Apologeticus* [Note: I believe that the *Apologeticus* cited here is the same work that Gretserus published among Bernaldus’s minor works (*Works*, vol. VI, p. 29), though it does not bear his name and treats nearly the same subject as the work above, col. 1105, which certainly belongs to Bernaldus. Since it is said to have been brought from Hirsau, we reasonably conjectured (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII), in connection with the *Chronicon Petershusanum*, book III, no. 2, that it may have been composed by Bernardus, a monk and scholar who had gone from that monastery to Hirsau, and thence brought around the year 1085 by Herold either to the monastery of Schaffhausen or to that of Petershausen. Colonies from Hirsau had arrived at both places at nearly the same time, as is narrated in the cited passage and in Trithemius (*Annals of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 266). Among them is also listed the writer Henry, who is said here to have copied this apologetic treatise for Bernaldus in these regions after Gregory VII had already died.], which the lord Herold formerly brought from Hirsau, and which, as I think, the lord Henry copied here—in the end, I say, of that *Apologeticus* it is demonstrated by authoritative arguments that we must not obey our own bishop, even if he is Catholic and devout, against the lord pope.

May the God of peace and consolation grant you to think the same with us (Romans XV), so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit (ibid., XIII).

[Col. 1231]

## BERNALDUS’S LETTER TO RECCHO ON AVOIDING THE EXCOMMUNICATED AND THOSE WHO COMMUNICATE WITH THEM

### Notice

It is unknown whether this Reccho, to whom these letters were addressed, was a cleric or a layman. This alone is established: he stood with the party of the schismatics, from which Bernaldus strives to turn him away by his customary arguments. See above, col. 1181. Thus the same author again appears in both places.

### FIRST LETTER TO RECCHO

[Col. 1231B]

To the lord and venerable man Reccho: Bernaldus, a priest in name only, not in conduct.

I. When we were recently together, we discussed among ourselves several matters concerning the avoidance of those who communicate with the excommunicated. But since we were then unable to satisfy your wishes, it seemed best to satisfy you in writing, since conversation had not permitted it.

Blessed Callistus, pope and martyr, an apostolic man, lists in his decretal letters four matters in which we must avoid an excommunicated person: greeting, kissing, prayer, and table fellowship (Letter 2, chapter 2; Labbé, vol. I, p. 614). Then, adding his judgment concerning one who communicates with an excommunicated person [Col. 1231C], he says:

“Whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters, according to the institution of the apostles, is himself also subject to a similar excommunication; for one who communicates with an excommunicated person is to be avoided just as the excommunicated person is.”

Hence blessed Pope Gelasius, writing to the Eastern bishops concerning Acacius, who communicated with excommunicated persons (Letter 15; Labbé, vol. IV, p. 1218), distinguishes as follows:

“All accomplices, followers, and communicants of a condemned depravity are judged to share the same lot. For although outside the Church one person sins more tolerably than another, in this they are considered equal: none of them is to be received into Catholic fellowship unless he is reconciled in the Catholic manner.”

II. The same Gelasius, later in the same letter, concerning avoiding those who communicate with the excommunicated, says:

“We have nothing in common with people of external communion.”

And again:

“What does it help if someone does not communicate with a more evident heretic, yet joins himself in communion to those who are no different from that man in their communion?”

Hence many devout Romans are said to have withdrawn from communion with Pope Anastasius, because he had communicated with a certain Thessalonian deacon [Col. 1232C] who had already communicated with Acacius. Thus the *Roman Pontifical* testifies [Note: Pagius demonstrates that this is false, in his Life of Anastasius II.].

III. You should not be surprised that one who communicates with an excommunicated person is avoided just as the excommunicated person is, since he is bound by the same sentence, as was said above. Hence the same Gelasius, writing to the emperor Anastasius (Gelasius, Letter 8; Labbé, cited volume, p. 1184), says:

“No one who has accepted a communicator of depravity can fail to be proved likewise depraved; nor can depravity be rejected when an accomplice of depravity is admitted. By your laws, those conscious of crimes and those who receive robbers are constrained by an equal judicial penalty; nor is he considered free of the crime who, although he did not commit it himself, nevertheless accepted the friendship and alliance of the one who committed it. Therefore, just as the communicator of a thief is punished with the same condemnation as the thief, so the communicator of an excommunicated person is condemned with him by the same measure.”

The condemnation of an excommunicated person is that he is separated from God and from his members. You yourself should connect what follows: namely, that the holy Fathers wished those who communicated with the excommunicated to be avoided just as the excommunicated, because they regarded them as persons who had condemned themselves.

[Col. 1233B] IV. Hence blessed Gelasius, writing to the aforesaid bishops concerning the same Acacius (cited passage, p. 1223), says:

“Why do they complain that Acacius was condemned by us, when he is shown to have condemned himself by receiving Peter’s communion?”

And blessed Pope Felix, who anathematized Acacius, expressly placed the following in the same sentence (Letter 6, cited work, p. 1704):

“Have a share with those whom you gladly embrace”—that is, with the excommunicated.

It is as though he were saying: We are not imposing a new excommunication upon you so much as confirming the old one, by which you bound yourself through communicating with the excommunicated. For since every excommunicated person is outside the Church, and no one can be both inside and outside at once, whoever does not separate himself from the communion of the excommunicated unquestionably separates himself from Catholic unity.

Catholics therefore rightly avoid as excommunicated those who have not separated themselves from the communion of the excommunicated. You should attend most carefully to what blessed Gelasius prescribes for us concerning why the Apostolic See rejected Acacius, who communicated with Peter:

“The See of blessed Peter, lest through Acacius it be led into fellowship with Peter, also removed Acacius himself from its communion.”

The same point is made to the emperor Anastasius (cited Letter 8):

“After Acacius became part of an external communion, he could not but be immediately cut off from Catholic and apostolic fellowship, lest, if we delayed even slightly on his account, we too should appear to have submitted to the contagion of the faithless.”

V. Do you see how necessarily we must avoid such communicants, lest we be judged to have submitted to the contagion of the faithless through their fellowship [Col. 1233D]? For, according to blessed Gelasius, as I stated above, no one who has accepted a communicator of depravity can fail to be proved likewise depraved, nor can depravity be rejected when an accomplice of depravity is admitted.

Let such communicants therefore cease imprudently to thrust themselves into ecclesiastical communion, lest, according to the same Gelasius, they stain Catholic purity by their communion. For unquestionably it is judged less severely before God if someone falls into excommunication under some necessity than if, after his fall, he does not seek reconciliation.

Let them also consider, not without profound sorrow of heart, how greatly they offend God—those who either stain others by their communion or teach by their example that they need not fear falling into excommunication. Let them therefore accept sound counsel and hasten to reconciliation, lest at some point, together with Acacius, they be compelled unwillingly to suffer the excommunication to which they long ago did not fear voluntarily to bind themselves.

I could write more to you about this matter, if I did not fear exceeding the brevity of a letter. But it seems that enough has been said for the wise.

## SECOND LETTER TO THE SAME PERSON

On avoiding the kiss of the excommunicated, and on Guibert and those who communicate with him.

[Col. 1234B]

To the lord and venerable man Reccho: Bernaldus, an unworthy priest.

I. I am greatly surprised that you have taken so much trouble in replying, since you did not at all approve your own assertion concerning communion with the excommunicated. For you did not prove that those who communicate with the excommunicated ought to be received; rather, you left them bound under apostolic excommunication. Therefore I did not think it necessary to respond in every respect to your writings.

II. You think that we are easily excused concerning avoidance of the kiss of the excommunicated because you testify that you did not find it in certain decretals—as though apostolic statutes could not retain their integrity even when some defective book contains them less completely. If you search more accurate and complete copies, you will be able to find the kiss itself in the decretals of Saint Callistus, pope, as I wrote (Gratian, “On the Excommunicated,” 17, cause 11, distinction 3; see the preceding letter).

Moreover, even laypeople know that they ought not to kiss the excommunicated. If they have done so, they hasten to be absolved through reconciliation without any dispute, and they judge that they may be received only through reconciliation.

III. This has certainly been confirmed by the agreement of the universal Church; therefore, following Augustine, we can assert it confidently and truthfully. He also most truthfully testifies that nothing should be held more firmly than that in which truth is supported by custom.

But Pope John X [Note: Bernoldus’s autograph codex itself records this same event in Hermannus (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII), under the year 916, at the Council of Altheim; it is not found elsewhere. Hence this provides a new argument for the identity of Bernoldus and Bernaldus.], an apostolic man, decreed by the judgment of a universal synod that whoever thereafter violated the ban imposed by bishops, especially through communion with the excommunicated, should do penance for forty days on bread and water, as murderers do.

IV. From the judgment of blessed Pope Gelasius, which says, “We have nothing in common with people of external communion” (see the preceding letter), it necessarily follows that we must avoid both Guibert’s communicator and Guibert himself—and this especially in those matters which we know the holy Fathers prohibited.

Nor do I arrogate to myself the power to judge the canons for the present circumstances, since that belongs particularly by privilege to the Roman pontiff. He excommunicated the heresiarch Guibert and all his accomplices by the judgment of a universal synod, and declared that they were to be avoided in greeting, kissing, prayer, and table fellowship, under penalty of excommunication, according to the institution of the apostles.

Therefore either you will purge Guibert of excommunication, or you will not be able to clear his communicants of the obligation of excommunication; they necessarily require reconciliation in order to return to Catholic unity. Nor should I raise any difficulty about my obligation to obey apostolic authority. If anywhere I fail to observe it, I do not delay at once to come to reconciliation.

Nor should you be angry with me if I believe blessed Gelasius more than I believe you. He says:

“It does not help if you avoid a heretic while communicating with his communicator.”

It is as though he were saying: What does it help if you avoid Guibert while communicating with his communicator, who, according to the institution of the apostles, is judged subject to a similar excommunication?

V. Accept, therefore, sound counsel, be reconciled to Catholic communion, and cease from your stubborn defense, which, as blessed Augustine testifies, commonly turns schism into heresy. I ask you in the Lord to recover your senses quickly and restore yourself to communion with us, lest, if you resist the Church’s authority too stubbornly, you should—God forbid—deserve to hear something more severe from the same mother Church.

[Col. 1235]

## BERNALDUS’S LETTER TO PAULINUS, A CLERIC OF METZ, ON THE PURCHASE OF CHURCHES

### Notice

Bernaldus treats another kind of simony—the purchase and sale of churches—in an informed and concise manner, prompted by Paulinus, a canon of the Church of Metz, as appears from the end of this letter. The people of Metz were especially devoted to the Catholic Fathers, so much so that in 1088 they expelled an intruded bishop from their city and received Hermannus when he returned from exile.

Hermannus, bishop of Metz, was most steadfast in the cause of the Church. Together with Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, he resisted courageously but unsuccessfully in the assembly at Worms in 1076 the deposition of Gregory VII (German Councils, vol. III, p. 178), as Lambert of Hersfeld reports under that year. Gregory VII’s Letter 21, book VIII, addressed to him around the year 1081, is extant (Labbé, *Councils*, vol. X, p. 267); in it Gregory urges him to be ready for labors and dangers in defense of the truth.

Driven from his see by King Henry in 1080, Hermannus was still being held captive in Tuscany in 1088, as our Bernoldus writes in his *Chronicle*. Bernoldus also narrates his return to his see under the year 1089, and his death under the year 1090, in May. Therefore this letter could have been written only in one of those two years, when this bishop was again at Metz.

Gretserus first published a letter of Saint Gebhard, archbishop of Salzburg, to the same Hermannus, concerning Gregory VII and the schismatics of that period (*Works*, vol. VI, p. 434).

### THIRD LETTER: TO PAULINUS

[Col. 1235B]

To his dearest brother Paulinus: Bernaldus, a priest in name only, not in conduct; the unfailing good that is Christ.

I. Dearest brother, the question that you ask me to resolve greatly exceeds our powers. Even if I knew how to explain it adequately, I would still need leisure for books in order to carry it out. Nor would I wish to write anything hastily on this matter that I could not irrefragably prove from the authority of the holy Fathers.

But you, impatient of all delay, do not cease pressing your demand; hence, out of affection for you, you force me to hurry excessively. I shall nevertheless say what I can for the present, reserving a more careful investigation for another time [Col. 1235C], and on this condition: that you meanwhile investigate as well, and do not hesitate to communicate to me anything you may discover.

II. First, therefore, I want you to know that blessed Augustine, in the book of his *Retractations* (book II, chapter 38), asserts that he composed not five books *On Faith and Works* but only one [Col. 1236B], which, he says, begins as follows: “To some it seems.” Therefore your testimony concerning the Simoniacs will not be able to satisfy us if it has been excerpted from another book of blessed Augustine entitled *On Faith and Works* [Note: I do not find what testimony from Augustine Paulinus cited. For the holy doctor wrote nothing against the Simoniacs; hence Bernaldus himself was perplexed, since he found nothing of the sort in his copy.].

For it seems unbelievable that Augustine composed another book *On Faith and Works*, apart from the one he mentions in the *Retractations*. Moreover, the testimony itself, if I remember correctly, says that the sale or purchase of ecclesiastical goods is simoniacal. This seems too broad, since it appears to include legitimate sales and purchases of such goods as well. Therefore I do not presume to attribute this statement to blessed Augustine. Nor should you take this as though I were prejudging your opinion; rather, I wish to be taught more certainly by you concerning it.

[Col. 1236C] III. Your question, then, is whether selling or purchasing churches is simoniacal. I can answer you as follows: among the ancients, priests did not, as they do now, customarily acquire churches after they had long since been ordained, but received them at the very time of their ordination.

For the holy Fathers at the Council of Chalcedon (act 15, canon 6 [Col. 1237A]) judged the ordination of anyone invalid if he were not found assigned to a particular place. That is, the place to which the minister was to be consecrated was announced first. Thus the ordination of the minister was solemnly celebrated for the designated place, just as is still observed everywhere in the ordination of bishops and abbots.

At the ordination itself the minister was incardinated into the Church. One person did not confer the church and another the consecration; the same person conferred both, and at the same time. Nor was the ordination considered complete unless the designation of the place had preceded it.

Therefore among the ancient Fathers there is not so much a specific prohibition of the purchase of churches, since they knew that churches were included in the ordinations themselves and that both were prohibited from being obtained for money. And since they considered ordinations purchased for money to be simoniacal, they unquestionably did not exempt the purchase of churches; indeed, they could not have exempted it.

IV. But after the appointment to a church began to be separated so far from consecration itself that men long since consecrated acquired churches only after a considerable interval, it became necessary for the purchase of churches to be prohibited by a special statute, just as the purchase of consecrations was; neither was to be condemned as simoniacal any less than the other.

You acknowledge that consecrations received for a price are simoniacal. To me it seems no less so with appointment—that is, with the care of souls—if it is obtained for money. For Simon Magus, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, wished to obtain by money not that the apostles should lay hands upon him, but that he himself might lay hands upon others [Col. 1237C] (Acts VIII).

To the person entrusted with a church or the care of souls is also granted the power to lay hands upon the catechumens, the possessed, or the sick entrusted to him. Who, then, will deny that it is simoniacal if someone obtains such an office for money?

Moreover, if the office of doorkeeper, notary, or defender is acquired for money, blessed Gelasius judges it simoniacal in his decretals [Note: In the canon of Gelasius, cause 1, question 1, chapter 6, there is no mention of a doorkeeper or the other offices.], chapter 24. Yet none of these offices is conferred through the laying on of hands, nor are those who hold them granted the power to lay hands upon others.

If, then, the purchaser of an ecclesiastical office that is neither acquired nor exercised through the laying on of hands is judged simoniacal, how much more the purchaser of pastoral care, in which the laying on of hands occurs so frequently?

V. Blessed Pope Alexander I likewise judged in his decretals (Labbé, vol. I, p. 553) that the person who, corrupted by a bribe, obstructs or assists a penitent’s reconciliation with the bishop is simoniacal.

If, then, the person who, corrupted by money, causes another to receive the laying on of hands from a bishop is rightly called simoniacal, how much more the person who purchases such an office for himself by money, so that he may lay hands upon his subjects [Col. 1238B]?

Peter, bishop of Albano [Note: This is that Peter surnamed “the Fire-Bearer,” then a monk of Vallombrosa, concerning whom Mabillon writes in the Life of Saint John Gualbert (*Acta Sanctorum*, sixth century, part II, p. 283, and *Benedictine Annals*, vol. V, p. 1). Bertholdus also relates this event in his *Chronicle* under the year 1067 [Col. 1238C], on the authority of our manuscripts. He later became bishop of Faenza. Concerning him, see the same work under the year 1079.], a man of extraordinary holiness and faith, proved Peter of Pavia to be simoniacal by the judgment of fire, because he had received from a layman, for money, merely the investiture of the episcopate.

Our ancestors are said to have designated as heresy simoniacal, by synodal judgment [Note: Namely, the Council of Tribur, which Hermannus Contractus in his *Chronicle* and Pagius under the year 1035 report, although its decrees have perished.], anyone who gave or demanded money for chrism, baptism, or communion (cause 1, question 1, chapter 105).

If we do not deny that all these things are simoniacal, why do we hesitate to judge the purchase of churches in the same way?

VI. Dearest brother, I have gathered these points for you for the present, as I was able, and with considerable haste. Write back to me with your view of all these matters. And if you should happen to discover anything more certain concerning the question mentioned above, do not hesitate to share it with me.

Give my humble greetings to your bishop of Metz [Note: Hermannus, namely. See the notice.], or rather ours, and invite him, if these answers are insufficient, to consider your question himself.

May the mercy of almighty God always preserve you unharmed, and mindful of us, in his holy service, most beloved lords and Fathers in Christ.

[Col. 1237]

## BERNALDUS’S APOLOGETIC LETTER FOR GEBHARD, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE, APPOINTED OVER THE CHURCH OF CONSTANCE IN PLACE OF THE DEPOSED OTTO

*(After the year 1088.)*

### Notice

We have already presented above Gregory VII’s decretal letter to Otto, bishop of Constance, concerning acceptance of the decrees of the Roman synod. Since Otto resisted them, he was first sharply rebuked and then suspended from office, and his diocesan subjects were forbidden to render him obedience, as we saw above in booklet VI.

Finally, when he had openly become a schismatic, Gregory struck him with anathema and appointed Gebhard bishop in his place after Otto’s deposition [Col. 1239], as Bernoldus relates in his *Chronicle* at the end of the year 1084.

Many people were displeased by this appointment. Bernaldus therefore undertook in this letter to defend it against their criticisms; consequently, the affairs of the Church of Constance are illuminated at considerable length.

[Col. 1239A] To the most reverend priest and most beloved Father R., [Note: [Col. 1239C] I would not presume to determine whether the initial letter R. indicates Reccho, to whom Bernaldus’s letters presented above are addressed, although this seems very probable.] B., a priest in name alone, not in conduct, sends the assurance of his prayer, whatever its worth.

I. It has been a long time, most beloved Father, since you reported to me, with a complaint, the criticism of certain persons concerning the ordination of our lord, the bishop of Constance, and asked me to furnish you, by letter, with an answer to their objection. But because at that time I replied too briefly for the matter, [Note: [Col. 1239C] This brief reply has perished.] I am not reluctant to satisfy you again—or, through you, them—more fully concerning the same issue.

II. First, therefore, I wish those critics of ours to investigate the matter carefully and, once they understand it, to examine it faithfully according to the statutes of the holy Fathers; only then, if they perceive anything contrary to the sacred [Col. 1239B] canons, should they censure it canonically, if they can. The substance of their criticism, as you reported it, is that our lord Gebhard cannot be [bishop], because he was appointed in place of his predecessor Otto while Otto was still alive. But the sacred canons very often prescribe this kind of appointment to us—namely, that someone else be substituted for any person who has been deposed—and establish it as legitimate and authoritative, without any contradiction.

Thus the holy Council of Constantinople, which according to Blessed Gregory is to be venerated as much as the Gospel, substituted Blessed Nectarius for Maximus, the deposed patriarch of Constantinople. Likewise the holy Council of Chalcedon, likewise comparable to the Gospel, decreed that Saint Proterius be substituted for Dioscorus, the condemned patriarch of Alexandria. [Col. 1239C] [Note: Evagrius likewise says this, whereas Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XXVIII, §35, attributes Proterius’s appointment to only four bishops, not to the entire council.] Thus Blessed Gregory, in his *Register*, ordered that others be substituted for many deposed persons. Thus Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, was substituted for the deposed Ebbo. Thus also in our own time Rupert, bishop of Bamberg, was substituted for the condemned Hermann. [Note: [Col. 1239C] Hermann was indeed deposed by Gregory VII in 1075 for simony, and Rupert was substituted for him—not by the pope, however, but imposed by King Henry. He was displeasing to almost all the clergy and people, as Bernoldus records under that year in the fuller *Chronicle*.]

[Col. 1240A] III. Therefore our bishop was substituted for Otto, once Otto had been deposed, even though he was still alive—not contrary to the canons, but in accordance with canonical ordinances. I wish to set out more fully and in order how canonically, and for what reasons, Otto suffered perpetual condemnation, so that our critics may henceforth have no doubt either about his irreversible condemnation or about the canonical appointment of the other.

IV. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1076, [Note: [Col. 1239D] Bernoldus the fuller describes at length the proceedings of this Roman council, held during Lent, as well as those of the preceding council held at Worms on January 23 by King Henry and the schismatic bishops, where they rashly attempted to depose Gregory from the papacy and even to deny him obedience in writing. Otto was among them, angered at the pope because of his deprivation of episcopal office. Lambertus seems to have understood this as referring to the excommunication, since, when discussing this very Roman synod, he includes Otto among those who had already been excommunicated by the pope. Nevertheless, we give greater credence to Bernoldus, a writer close to the events, who carefully distinguishes between the disobedience shown the previous year by their denial of the pope’s decrees, for which Otto had been deprived, and the conspiracy of this year, for which he was additionally subjected to anathema.] in the fifteenth indiction, during the first week of Lent, Pope Gregory VII, presiding over a general synod at Rome in the church of the Savior, deprived Otto, bishop of Constance, of office and communion by synodal judgment, because he had openly demonstrated, by letters sent and by his own subscription, that he had conspired with the other schismatics against [Col. 1240B] the apostolic see.

In this conspiracy he raged against the Roman pontiff far more audaciously than the other conspirators, and dared insolently to attack him before a secular ruler with a specific accusation—namely, accusing him of having deprived him of episcopal honor because he had forbidden laymen to accept the offices of condemned priests or to obey them. [Note: [Col. 1240C] Something is missing here. For from Gregory’s cited letters, both to Otto and to his subjects, it is sufficiently clear that he was removed from his office because he had despised the decrees of the Roman synod concerning incontinent priests and the refusal to accept their offices, [Col. 1240D] not because Otto himself had issued such prohibitions. This material must therefore be supplied here.]

V. Nevertheless, the lord pope treated him much more mercifully than he deserved. For, having sent the venerable Altmann, bishop of Passau, to him at Ulm in the following autumn, [Note: [Col. 1240D] This agrees with what the same Bernaldus, in the fuller version under the year 1076 above, p. 37, reports concerning the bishops reconciled by apostolic legates at the assembly of Tribur. There he likewise writes that Otto of Constance was reconciled at Ulm; for him, Hansizius (*Germania Sacra*, vol. I, p. 264) incorrectly reads “last.” In reality, the assembly of princes at Ulm preceded the council of Tribur, as the Schaffhausen chronicler states for that year (*Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 180). Otto, being nearer, could easily have attended at Ulm and been absolved there before the others by the legates of the apostolic see.] in the presence of many people, he restored communion alone, without office. Otto, however, contrary to the command of the lord pope, [Col. 1240C] did not cease to usurp the office until the end of his life. For the lord pope never afterward restored his office, as the pope himself repeatedly reported later to many who inquired about the matter.

Moreover, Otto did not cease to favor simoniacal and incontinent priests, contrary to the synodal decree of the apostolic lord, indeed contrary to [Col. 1241A] the decrees of all the holy Fathers. Therefore the lord pope, by letters sent, absolved all his subjects from obedience to him by apostolic authority. [Note: [Col. 1241C] See what was said immediately before and above, in the same place. From this account it further follows that, after the reconciliation mentioned, he soon returned to his former conduct; at least, he afterward usurped the episcopal office from which he had been forbidden. Bernoldus the fuller testifies to this in his *Chronicle*, writing that Otto fled when the emperor Rudolf came to Constance after Easter.] Above all these things, he did not hesitate to desert of his own accord entirely to the party of the schismatics, abandoning the Catholic Church.

VI. Each of these acts, therefore, could have sufficed for his irrecoverable condemnation according to the ordinances of the canons: the crime of conspiracy, the usurpation of a forbidden office, support for simoniacal or incontinent priests, and—what appears greater than these—the departure from the Catholics to the party of the schismatics.

For the most blessed Pope Fabian, martyr, in his decrees, chapter 2 (*Labbé*, vol. I, p. 644, letter 11), orders that a cleric who has conspired, after formal examination, be permanently removed from the clergy and branded with infamy. Likewise Saint Callistus, pope and martyr, and afterward the thirty holy Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon (*acts* 15, canon 8; Gratian, *Decretum*, cause 11, canon 21), together with countless others, completely depose clerics who conspire.

The Council of Antioch, in chapter 4, [*Labbé*, vol. II, p. 563] condemns a usurper of forbidden office so terribly that it grants him thereafter neither hope of restoration nor opportunity for satisfaction. Saint Gregory likewise, in his *Register*, chapter 240 of the second part (book V, letter 7), condemns such a usurper to perpetual excommunication, so that he scarcely grants him Viaticum at the end of life.

The same Gregory also declares that any bishop who does not burn fiercely against that heresy has a portion with Simon Magus; how much more does the person who is not afraid to nourish that same heresy by his consent? The same Gregory also says, without doubt: “Whoever neglects to correct what he can correct shares in the guilt of the one who does it.” Pope Damasus likewise writes to the bishops of Mauritania (letter 4; *Labbé*, vol. II, p. [Col. 1242A] 875): “Whoever can oppose and restrain the wicked, but does not do so, does nothing other than favor their impiety.” According to the Apostle, those who do and those who consent are embraced by an equal punishment (Romans 1).

VII. By voluntarily departing to the party of the schismatics, Otto therefore condemned himself by his own judgment, according to the ordinance of the holy Fathers. For this reason the lord pope Gregory, at a Roman synod, by synodal judgment, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1080, in the third indiction, during the first week of Lent, condemned and anathematized the aforesaid Otto—who had already been admonished and awaited for three years in vain to repent—without hope of recovery. [Note: [Col. 1241C] This three-year period must be reckoned from Otto’s reconciliation at Ulm in the autumn of 1076. Afterward he again adhered to the schismatics and did not abstain from the office forbidden to him; finally, in 1080, he was completely deposed and bound by a new anathema.]

He entrusted his authority to the venerable bishop of Passau, so that he might go to the Church of Constance [Col. 1242B] and arrange for a legitimate pastor to be ordained there. [Note: [Col. 1241D] It is clear from this that another bishop of Constance had then been elected, but was not ordained because of illness. He may have been the man of whom the schismatic author of the Augsburg Chronicle (*Freher, German Writers*, vol. I, p. 503) writes under the year 1084: “While Otto, bishop of Constance, was still alive, Berchtold was compelled to assume the bishopric; from then on he became completely mute until his death.” Bucelinus writes in his catalogue: “Rupert, imposed by the emperor, his chaplain; Berchtold, likewise chaplain of Henry IV, removed from his see and omitted by most, together with his predecessor Rupert, from the list of bishops.” He claims that Berchtold was a canon at Buochau. We rightly doubt that he was a chaplain, for Altmann of Passau would not have chosen a man beholden to the emperor.]

The same bishop made every effort to accomplish this. But after the election had taken place, illness prevented the elected man from ever being fully consecrated. Since that Church consequently remained without pastoral provision for several years, Pope Gregory finally sent there, from his own side, the venerable Otto, bishop of Ostia, who soon afterward became pope. [Note: [Col. 1242C] A letter exists under the name of Urban II addressed to Guiehardus—that is, Gebhard, bishop of Constance—in which this is confirmed most explicitly at the beginning: “Because we recognize that, after God, you are a special work of our hands,” and so forth.] Otto canonically ordained the legitimate pastor Gebhard for that Church in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084, in the seventh indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January. [Note: [Col. 1242C] Bernoldus describes this ordination in the same way in his *Chronicle*. At the end of 1084, Bernoldus was made a priest together with Gebhard on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle. For this reason others assign the ordination to the year 1085. The *Gallia Christiana* (vol. V, p. 910) wrongly attributes to Bishop Gebhard what Bernoldus writes happened to the man ordained for himself, both there and in the immediately following treatise: namely, that the legate, when anointing him as priest, simultaneously granted him, by authority of the pontiff, the power to receive penitents. The *Chronicle of Petershausen* (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII), edited by us, discusses this election more fully in book II, no. 44, p. 342.]

He confirmed Gebhard’s ordination during the following Easter week by synodal judgment in a general council of Saxony, [Note: [Col. 1242D] Namely, the council held at Quedlinburg in 1085 by the same legate (*Councils of Germany*, vol. III, p. 200). There Gebhard’s ordination was confirmed, and a new anathema was pronounced against Otto, who, as the same *Chronicle* records in the same place, driven from possession of that church, went to a place called Colmbra and remained there for almost a year before ending his life.] convened with apostolic authority.

This bishop did not enter, as others have done, through secular power and against the canons. Rather, he entered canonically: he had been lawfully elected and requested by all the clergy and people, and, by apostolic authority, was solemnly enthroned and consecrated by the legate of the apostolic see for the vacant see, with the most reverend bishops and [Col. 1243A] abbots supporting him with the greatest eagerness and assent, and with the Catholic dukes [Note: [Col. 1243A] Namely, Berthold II, duke of Zähringen or Alemannia, who was this Gebhard’s brother, and Welf, duke of Bavaria.] and counts, together with the other faithful of Christ, likewise consenting.

He was, I say, elected and ordained so canonically that no one who does not wish to oppose apostolic and canonical institutions could in any way contradict his election or ordination. Moreover, the venerable Pope Gregory himself, by whose authority our bishop was ordained, and likewise Pope Victor, his successor, regarded our bishop as the legitimate pastor for as long as they lived. The most reverend Pope Urban, who now presides over the highest affairs, [Note: [Col. 1244A] Urban II presided from 1088 to 1099; Bernaldus’s letter must therefore have been written during this interval.] likewise always regarded and still regards him as the canonical pastor, [Col. 1244A] recognizing him as one canonically ordained by himself under apostolic legation.

If we knew no other arguments concerning his ordination, it would be enough for us to know that so many Roman pontiffs supported it.

VIII. Therefore I ask you to admonish those critics of ours to beware of disparaging an ecclesiastical ruler, contrary to the Lord’s command, lest wise people rightly judge that by this they harm him less than they gratify their own fault. May Almighty God preserve your fraternity, praying for me, here and forever, most reverend lord and Father.

[Col. 1243]

BERNALDUS’S TREATISE ON THE OFFICE OF PRIESTS

EDITORIAL NOTICE

The anonymous author of Melk, chapter 101, attributes this treatise, under the title *The Book on the Power of Priests*, to the same Bernaldus who disputed with Alboin, whom we presented above, column 1079 and following. There, as in his other writings, the author calls himself Bernaldus, although here he is indicated only by the initial B. More will be said about its subject in the preliminary observations and below, especially concerning certain aspects of the rites and discipline of that period that differ from modern practice.

What the author argues here is, for the most part, of such a kind that it might seem to have been taken from the condemned teaching of Arius, who, according to Epiphanius, heresy 75, recognized no distinction between bishops and priests. Yet Bernaldus’s profound difference from Arius is demonstrated by the fact that throughout the work he maintains that several functions are lawful for priests only by permission of bishops.

Nor does he anywhere include among the duties that he says were once common to bishops and priests the power of ordaining. This is decisive for proving the eminence of episcopal dignity and order above that of priests. Saint Jerome, whom Blondellus thought entirely to be on his own side, expresses this sense in his letter to Evangelus (letter 101, *Works*, vol. IV, part II, p. 802): “What does a bishop do, except ordination, that a priest does not do?” Saint John Chrysostom likewise says in homily 11 on 1 Timothy 3 that bishops are superior to priests by ordination alone, and that this is the only thing they possess beyond priests.

The increasingly influential followers of Arius will certainly never prove the contrary, even if, by gathering arguments from everywhere, they contend that the dignity of bishops was not greater than the power of priests from the Church’s earliest beginnings.

That this distinction exists by divine ordinance is testified by Saint Ignatius, a disciple of the apostles, in his letter to the Philadelphians, no. 7 (Cotelerius, vol. II, p. 32):

“I cried out, and when I was present I spoke with a loud voice, the voice of God: Pay attention to the bishop, the presbyterate, and the deacons. Some suspected that I said these things because I foresaw the division of certain persons. But he in whom I am bound is my witness that I did not know anything from human flesh; rather, the Spirit announced it, saying these things: Do nothing without the bishop.”

Let many bishops, however, blame themselves if the hierarchical order established by the canons is not observed by the priests subject to them, since they themselves are also attempting to cast off the obedience owed to their superior pastor, paying no attention to Saint Jerome’s letter 58 to Damasus: “The Church, divided into three parts, hastens to draw me to itself. Meanwhile I cry out: If anyone is joined to the chair of Peter, he is mine.”

[ON THE OFFICE OF PRIESTS]

OCCASION AND ARGUMENT OF THIS TREATISE

[Col. 1243B]

To the lords and beloved brothers in Christ at Reitenbuch, [Note: [Col. 1243B] Raitenbuch, commonly called Rotenbuch, is a famous community of regular canons on the Ammer River in Upper Bavaria. Around the year 1080, Welf I, duke of Bavaria, and his wife gave the canons the cell that had long before been built at this place. See *Raitenbuch Monuments*, vol. VII of the *Monuments of Bavaria*.] faithfully observing the form of apostolic life, B., a priest in name alone, not in conduct, sends the promise of eternal fellowship in apostolic blessedness after the legitimate struggle of this life.

I. Your letter of affection recently reached us. It reported that a certain question concerning the power of priests had arisen among you, and that you had submitted it to our weakness for resolution. You indicated that you were seeking from us—or rather, through us, from the judgment of the holy Fathers—a response to it.

Although weakness of mind and body impedes the execution of this task, charity nevertheless obtains that we do not fail to comply with fraternal requests, even beyond our strength. With that charity, which is God, assisting us, we shall try to obey your fraternity—not only addressing what you ask, namely, from where priests derive the ability to receive penitents, but also adding other matters that you did not ask about: what priests were in ancient times, and by what kind of privilege they later deserved to be restricted.

May God, who is charity and almighty, [Col. 1245A] always protect and preserve you unharmed and mindful of us, most beloved lords, brothers, and Fathers.

HERE BEGINS A USEFUL DESCRIPTION OF THE OFFICE OF PRIESTS

II. Blessed Paul the Apostle most clearly prescribes for us in his letters that among the ancients priest and bishop were the same. For when writing to Titus about the ordination of bishops, he commands him to appoint priests in every city, and immediately adds what sort of men should be ordained, saying: “For a bishop must be blameless” (Titus 1).

Likewise he writes to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate” (1 Timothy 4). Immediately afterward he says to him: “Lay hands quickly on no one” (1 Timothy 5), which properly belongs to a bishop.

In these words the Apostle sufficiently and plainly indicated that in ancient times priest and bishop were the same, in accordance with the way Blessed Ambrose and Jerome interpreted the same Apostle in these passages.

Likewise, in the Letter to the Philippians, he addresses priests under the name of bishops, saying: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons” (Philippians 1). For, according to Jerome, Philippi is a single city of Macedonia and could not have had several bishops.

In the Acts of the Apostles, too, we read that the apostles summoned the priests of Ephesus and did not fail to say that they had been placed as bishops by the Holy Spirit (Acts 20)—that is, calling the priests of one city bishops.

Likewise Peter himself, the chief of the apostles, says in his letter: “I appeal to the priests among you, as a fellow priest and witness of the sufferings of Christ” (1 Peter 5).

The apostle and evangelist John, writing in his own person, says: “The priest to the chosen lady and her children” (2 John 1). Likewise in another letter: “The priest to the most beloved Gaius” (3 John 1).

III. These statements, therefore, with Blessed Jerome and Ambrose bearing witness, prove most clearly that priest and bishop were the same. Why they later began to differ from one another both in name and in office, so that one among the priests came specially to possess the name of bishop, Jerome explains quite plainly in his commentary on the Letter to Titus:

“After each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than as Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one chosen from among the priests should be placed over the others, to whom the entire care of the Church should belong, and that the seeds of schisms should be removed” (*Commentary on chapter 1*, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 413).

And below:

“Gradually, so that the plantings of dissensions might be uprooted, all solicitude was transferred to one person. Therefore, just as priests know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than priests more by custom than by an arrangement of the Lord’s truth, and that they ought to govern the Church jointly, imitating Moses, who, although he alone possessed the power to preside over the people of Israel, chose seventy with whom he might judge the people.”

[Col. 1246A] IV. Since, therefore, priests and bishops are read to have been the same in ancient times, there is no doubt that they also possessed the same power of binding and loosing, as well as other powers now particular to bishops.

But after priests were restrained by episcopal eminence, they began not to be permitted to do what had once been permitted—namely, what ecclesiastical authority delegated for the bishops alone to perform: the making of chrism, the consecration of virgins, the reconciliation of penitents, and other such acts, which the statutes of the Fathers prohibit them from undertaking.

For the Council of Carthage, at which Blessed Augustine was present, in chapter 6 (*Labbé*, vol. II, p. 1052), forbids priests the making of chrism, the reconciliation of penitents, and the consecration of virgins.

Saint Eusebius likewise, in his decrees 22 [Col. 1246B] (letter 3; *Labbé*, vol. I, p. 1392), asserts that the confirmation of neophytes can and must be performed only by bishops, and that it is not to be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments when it has been presumed upon by others.

V. But concerning each of these acts that priests came to be forbidden after they had been separated from episcopal eminence, Pope Damasus explains the matter more fully in his decrees, where he restrains the vain superstition of chorepiscopi by authoritative arguments.

For, writing to all the bishops (letter 5; *Labbé*, vol. II, p. 876), he first proves that chorepiscopi are nothing other than priests. Then he separates both groups from the episcopal dignity in these words:

“Chorepiscopi may not consecrate priests, deacons, or subdeacons, or virgins; nor erect an altar, anoint or consecrate it; nor dedicate churches; nor make chrism; nor mark the baptismal fonts with chrism; nor publicly reconcile any penitent at Mass; nor send letters of communion; nor bless the people; nor enter the baptistery or sacristy before the bishop; nor, in the bishop’s presence, baptize or sign a child; nor reconcile a penitent without the command of their bishop; nor, while he is present, celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood unless he orders it; nor teach or greet the people when he is present; nor exhort the congregation. You have been taught that all these things belong exclusively to bishops, both from what has been said above and from other statutes of the Fathers and sacred canons. . . . The same rule is to be held concerning priests: they are to do nothing proper to their office without the bishop’s command.”

Likewise Saint Leo I, writing to all the bishops (letter 88; *Labbé*, vol. III, p. 1394), maintained the same judgment concerning chorepiscopi and priests, so that they should likewise recognize their proper limits and not presume to usurp episcopal privilege.

Blessed Pope Gelasius, too, in his decrees, chapter 6 (*Labbé*, vol. IV, p. 1189), after listing the matters belonging to the office of priests, adds this general sentence:

“Nor should a priest in any way doubt that, if he thinks of performing on his own initiative anything specially belonging to episcopal ministry, he must immediately be deprived of the dignity of the presbyterate and of sacred communion.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear how far episcopal authority stands above priests, and what they are entirely forbidden to usurp.

[Col. 1247A] VI. Nevertheless, there are still certain things that may be granted to priests at the bishop’s discretion, such as the private reconciliation of penitents, since they are read to be entirely prohibited from public reconciliation, just as from the making of chrism.

They may indeed privately reconcile penitents who have confessed and are ill, provided that the bishop has ordered it, in accordance with what Pope Evaristus, martyr, asserts in his decrees (cause 26, question 6, canon 4), decreeing that priests are to reconcile penitents concerning hidden sins at the bishop’s command, and absolve and communicate the sick.

Likewise the Council of Carthage (*Labbé*, vol. II, p. 1160), chapter 7 [read: 4], says that persons placed in danger may be reconciled by a priest when the bishop is absent, but only at his command.

VII. It should be noted that priests are not even permitted to perform this private reconciliation unless specifically commanded by the bishop. The priests of the holy Roman Church themselves do not customarily perform it except by permission. Nor does the Roman pontiff grant this to all whom he ordains, but only to those whom he judges suitable for carrying out this task.

Blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, likewise granted only a few priests in his diocese permission to receive penitents, although he had ordained very many priests everywhere. [Note: [Col. 1247D] This Anselm was a vigorous assistant of Gregory VII. His life is preserved in Tengnagel’s collection, *Monuments against the Schismatics*, p. 83. Our Bernoldus frequently discusses him in his *Chronicle*, especially under the year 1066, when he records his death.]

Other bishops up to the present have likewise been accustomed to act in this way in their dioceses, namely, those who wished to be more careful observers of the canons.

VIII. It therefore seems sufficiently clear that priests ordinarily reconcile penitents not so much by the office of their own consecration as by the discretion of an episcopal grant.

For if they possessed this power by their own consecration, as bishops do, then, since they had received the same consecration of the presbyterate, all of them would likewise possess the same power of reconciliation. Nor would they need an episcopal command for this any more than for the exercise of the office of the Mass, if they had long ago received this power in the consecration itself, just as they received the power to perform the office of the Mass. [Note: [Col. 1247D] In fact, they received both powers in ordination; the latter, however, is to be exercised only with the bishop’s permission or approval. Bernaldus must be understood here in this sense.]

How they did not receive this power in their consecration can easily be determined by anyone who wishes to consider carefully the manner of their consecration. In it they nowhere receive, as bishops do, the power of binding and loosing, [Col. 1248A] but rather the power of offering sacrifice both for the living and for the dead. [Note: [Col. 1247D] Bernaldus is not speaking here of the modern rite of ordination, in which the newly ordained priest is explicitly given by the bishop the power to remit sins; rather, he is speaking of the custom of his own time, when the words “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you remit,” together with a third laying on of hands, had not yet been introduced. Drouven, among others, observes this in *On Sacramental Matters*, vol. II, p. 362: “The third laying on of hands, joined with a prayer, was not formerly solemn in the Church, since the ancient rituals of the Latin Church written before the twelfth century are entirely silent about it; nor is it observed even now by everyone, since it is omitted in Greece and the East. Bernaldus wrote this while the eleventh century was still in progress.”]

IX. Parish priests, to whom the bishop entrusts pastoral care of the people, are certainly understood to have received in that very commission the right to receive penitents as well, since this appears to belong especially to that care.

Those who have been ordained but are not entrusted with such care should not presume to usurp the aforesaid power before the bishops grant it to them. For if they presume to do so, they bind themselves by their presumption rather than absolve penitents through their reconciliation—unless, when penitents simply receive the absolution, ignorance excuses them from the charge of presumption. [Note: [Col. 1248D] Here *excusat* (“excuses”) should plainly be read, so that the meaning is that one who knowingly confesses to a priest not yet approved by the bishop, in the sense described here, is not absolved from sins; but that he is absolved if he does so in good faith, believing the priest to have been approved. Many theologians teach that in this case the Church supplies the defect of jurisdiction.]

Bishops very often grant the right of reconciliation to priests who lack pastoral care, as the venerable Pope Gregory VII and Saint Anselm of Lucca did for many, and as many others still do.

We ourselves received this grant from our ordination onward. [Note: [Col. 1248D] It is quite clear from this that the author of this treatise is that same Berthold of Constance who records the same fact about himself in the *Chronicle* under the year 1084.] We know that many others received it from their ordainers as well.

X. It should nevertheless be known that Blessed Jerome ascribes the power of binding and loosing indiscriminately to priests and bishops in his commentary on Matthew, where he explains the words “Whatever you bind” (Matthew 16) and what follows.

“Bishops and priests,” he says (*Works*, vol. IV, p. 75), “not understanding this passage, assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance, so that they either condemn the innocent or presume to absolve the guilty, when before God it is not the judgment of priests but their life that is sought.

“We read in Leviticus concerning lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests, and, if they have leprosy, then to be declared unclean by the priest (Leviticus 14)—not because priests make them lepers and unclean, but because they have knowledge of the leper and the non-leper and can discern who is clean and who is unclean.

“Just as there the priest makes the leper unclean, so here the bishop and priest bind and loose—not those who are innocent or harmless, but, in keeping with their office, when they have heard the varieties of sins, they know who is to be bound and who is to be loosed.”

Jerome likewise writes to Heliodorus (letter 5, *Works*, vol. IV, part II, p. 10):

“I am not permitted to sit before a priest; but he is permitted, if I sin, to hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

These statements do not contradict the foregoing in any respect. They likewise attribute such power concerning penitents to priests, but not as bishops possess it by virtue of their consecration; rather, priests possess it by command of the bishops, as the canons prescribe.

In the statements cited above, Blessed Jerome did not expressly indicate the source from which they possess this right; he merely noted without qualification that they possess it. Moreover, if he had said that they possessed it by consecration, even in the manner of bishops, we still would not presume, out of reverence for him, to contradict the canonical ordinances on this point.
