XI. Blessed Pope Gregory, too, writing to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari (book IV, letter 26), permitted certain priests to confirm neophytes—an act that he certainly knew was not wholly foreign to the office of priests.

“It has come to our attention,” he says, “that some have been scandalized because we prohibited priests from touching with chrism those who have been baptized. We acted according to the ancient custom of our Church. But if some are greatly troubled about this matter, where bishops are absent, we grant that priests should also touch the baptized on the forehead with chrism.”

We have no doubt that these confirmations were valid, since those priests performed them by apostolic grant, not by their own presumption. Had they been performed presumptuously, those confirmations would have been entirely invalid according to the aforesaid decree of Pope Eusebius.

Therefore, just as those priests possessed the right to confirm not by consecration but from the apostolic lord, so every priest possesses the ability to reconcile penitents not so much from consecration [Note: [Col. 1249C] It is also evident from this that our author did not altogether deny that the power of absolving is conferred on priests in ordination; he denied only that its exercise, or jurisdiction, is conferred in the same way. Modern theologians distinguish jurisdiction from the power of orders, differing from the ancients in terminology alone, not in doctrine.] as from episcopal grant.

We do not presume to attribute to their office anything that we read to have been entirely forbidden to them in the apostolic statutes.

## XII.

We likewise do not presume to attribute to presbyters as their proper office the blessing over the people which St. Jerome assigns to presbyters in his letter to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne [Note: This is St. Jerome’s Letter 95 (*Works*, vol. IV, part II, p. 769), written to Rusticus while he was still a monk, though he later became bishop of Narbonne; he is discussed in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, p. 7], lest we be judged to oppose Pope St. Damasus and the sacred canons, which prohibit this same practice [Col. 1250A]. For it seems safer to say that they possess this authority by some episcopal concession rather than by the inherent right of their office. Likewise, subdeacons are believed to have been granted permission to read the Epistle at Mass, although they do not appear to possess this by virtue of their consecration [Note: Amalarius Fortunatus writes similarly about subdeacons in the ninth century, *On the Divine Offices*, book I, chapter 11, as does the contemporary Micrologus Bernaldus, *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, chapter 8: “Among the lower orders, Roman authority grants only to subdeacons that, clothed in sacred vestments, they may read the Epistle at Mass; yet they have obtained this not from their own consecration, but rather from ecclesiastical consent. Hence at that time the handing over of the Book of the Epistles was not yet customary in their ordination; indeed, it is absent from all Latin rituals written before four hundred years ago.”]

This custom of presbyters blessing the people in church has become so widespread that it is rightly believed not to have been propagated without episcopal concession; nor would a small scandal arise if presbyters were now to discontinue it.

## XIII.

Blessed Damasus likewise, in order to restrain the insolence of chorepiscopi, most strictly circumscribed the office of both presbyter and chorepiscopus [Col. 1250B], judging them to be the same. Nevertheless, he did not prescribe for himself or his successors that they could not grant presbyters certain powers which he had declared not to belong properly to their office.

We must not arrogate to their authority anything contrary to canonical authority and ecclesiastical custom, even if we read in certain less authoritative opinions that various powers have been granted to them beyond measure—for example, in canon 4 of the Council of Riez [Note: The Council of Riez in Provence was celebrated on 29 November 439, under St. Hilary of Arles. See Labbe, vol. III, p. 1287, and the Maurist *New Collection of the Councils of Gaul*, vol. I, p. 444] presbyters are granted permission to consecrate virgins and to consecrate neophytes, although apostolic authority and ecclesiastical custom entirely prohibit this for them.

The chorepiscopi and presbyters themselves must also beware lest they rashly presume illicit acts, so that it may truly be said of their presumption what Pope Blessed Damasus most truthfully declares concerning such presumptuous men (Letter 5; Labbe, vol. II, p. 876):

> “Chorepiscopi or presbyters who presumed to do illicit things: what they were doing was not regarded as done; and therefore many, having fallen into a false security, were deprived of and frustrated in ecclesiastical ministry.”

Accordingly, presbyters must still beware of usurping illicit and unauthorized acts in ecclesiastical offices, lest they justly be punished by canonical retribution, since by their rash usurpation they are judged also to defraud the faithful of ecclesiastical ministry.

[Col. 1249]

# BERNALDUS, TREATISE ON THE RELEASE OF OATHS

## Notice

This little work deals with nearly the same subject as the work presented above at col. 1219—namely, the action of Gregory VII, who in 1076, after deposing King Henry, released his subjects from their oath of fidelity, and specifically forbade the people of Constance to obey Otto, their excommunicated bishop.

It is not complete, however, but is mutilated at the end, eight pages having been cut out of the manuscript. Immediately after it there followed another work, of which a fragment is preserved there, dealing with the same subject as the preceding treatise XI, *On the Office of Presbyters*. Hence one may conjecture that this was the book *On Confession* which the Anonymous of Melk attributes to Bernaldus, and which we regret to have perished in this manner. The same may be said of another work, *On the Harmony of Offices*, which the same Anonymous places after the book *On the Power of Presbyters*; perhaps it was contained in these very eight excised leaves.

[Col. 1251A] To the most reverend priest and beloved brother WALTHER, a man of evangelical perfection and canonical profession [Note: From these words it seems that this Walther was a regular canon, perhaps likewise at Raitenbuch. I think that both this treatise and the preceding one were written for the canons of that college], B., an unworthy presbyter—would that he were infirm in body alone—wishes him, after the course of this life, the prize of eternal blessedness.

### I.

What your fraternity asks us to write greatly exceeds the weakness of our powers. But charity, which “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. XIII), compels us to comply with your wishes, judging it better to expose itself in some way to danger beyond its capacity than not to obey the request of your affection.

For you ask us to answer on your behalf a certain friend of yours who imprudently declares our countrymen [Note: By “our countrymen” I think he means either the people of Blasien or all the subjects of the diocese of Constance, whom Gregory VII released from the oath they had sworn. See above, cols. 1219 and 1238] to be perjurers because, after their superiors have been deposed and excommunicated, they do not presume to keep their oath of subjection [Col. 1251B].

But we do not know this friend of yours well enough to determine whether he assents in any way to canonical authority, or whether, in heretical fashion, he stubbornly resists it by every argument. Therefore we have decided to write not to him, but to your fraternity, and to suggest arguments with which you may address him, as seems more suitable to his character and correction.

With God’s favor, we shall attempt to write in such a way that it may suffice for his correction, provided he has not yet stubbornly hardened himself in heretical perversity, which the Apostle Paul judged more deserving of avoidance than of repeated admonition.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the charity of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with all of you (2 Cor. XIII), most beloved lords and brothers [Col. 1251C].

### II.

Many of the adversaries of the holy Church habitually accuse the Catholics of our time of perjury because they refuse to keep their oath of subjection to those who have been deposed and excommunicated, although the Roman pontiff released them from that oath by synodal judgment [Note: It is uncertain whether he means the Roman synod of 1076, or Pope Urban II, whose decree Gregory IX invokes in a letter sent to the bishops of Apulia. According to that decree, subjects are not bound to keep the faith sworn to a Christian ruler who opposes God and his saints and violates their precepts; yet Fleury testifies that he has seen this nowhere else, *Ecclesiastical History*, book LXXIX, § 40. It is more likely, however, that Bernaldus here is speaking of Otto, his bishop, rather than of King Henry].

But none of those who carefully consider ecclesiastical and apostolic authority will charge them with perjury, since that authority has always been accustomed to release subjects just as effectively as it deposes their prelates.

To make this clearer, let us not shrink from faithfully considering this same authority somewhat more deeply [Col. 1252A]. Properly considered, it will both unquestionably clear our countrymen of perjury and decisively refute the slander of our adversaries.

### III.

Our Lord Jesus Christ gave blessed Peter in the Gospel this universal and unquestionably effective power: that whatever he bound would be bound, and whatever he loosed would be loosed (Matt. XVI).

Nor did this power remain with Peter alone; it also passed to the other apostles, indeed to all the rulers of the churches, as Blessed Leo I testifies, saying (Sermon 3, *On the Anniversary of His Assumption*):

> “What is said to blessed Peter, ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (ibid.), and what follows, certainly passed also to the other apostles as the right of that power, and the constitution of this decree passed to all the rulers of the Church. Yet it is not without reason that what is entrusted to all is entrusted to one alone. For this is singularly committed to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the rulers of the Church.”

By this authority, therefore, the apostolic prelates—namely, the successors of St. Peter, exalted especially and principally—have been accustomed to depose any prelates in the Church for particular crimes, and they can still do so.

This is found to be so customary in canonical and apostolic decrees that no learned person seems able to doubt it. Thus Pope St. Celestine, at the holy Synod of Ephesus (Labbe, vol. III, p. 533), the third of the four principal councils, condemned Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, by apostolic authority. Likewise Leo the Great, at the holy Council of Chalcedon [Col. 1252C] (ibid., vol. IV, p. 417), the last of the four principal councils, condemned Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, through his legates.

Pope Felix likewise deposed and anathematized Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, while he was absent, at a Roman synod (ibid., p. 1095), because Acacius refused to avoid communion with excommunicated persons.

In our own time, too, the venerable Pope Alexander deposed Peter of Florence [Note: If Ughelli is to be trusted (*Italia Sacra*, vol. III, p. 77), Raynerius succeeded Peter in 1071—not the simoniacal and deposed Peter, but another man of the same name who was truly Catholic; Alexander II’s letter to him from 1067 is preserved there (ibid., p. 76)—and replaced him with the venerable man Reginherius.

But we would labor in vain if we attempted to enumerate all such depositions, for we shall undoubtedly run out of days before we run out of examples.

### IV.

Just as Roman pontiffs can depose the highest patriarchs, so also can they depose inferior rulers, including secular princes [Note: The novelty of this fallacious argument is already exposed in the observations preceding this passage], whose dignity appears to have arisen more from human invention than from divine institution [Note: The Apostle says, “There is no power except from God, and those powers that exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. XIII); therefore they do not arise simply from human invention].

For what is surprising if apostolic authority is believed able to judge kings, when according to the Apostle it will also judge angels? “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters belonging to this life?” (1 Cor. VI.)

It is certain that kings are subject to priestly authority, as Pope Blessed Gelasius declares to the emperor Anastasius (Letter 8; Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1182):

> “There are two powers, O Emperor Augustus, by which this world is principally ruled: the sacred authority of pontiffs and royal power. Among these, the burden of the priests is so much heavier, as they will render an account for the kings themselves before the divine tribunal. For you know, most merciful son, that although by your dignity you preside over the human race, nevertheless you devoutly bow your neck to the rulers of divine things and await from them the causes of your salvation [Col. 1253B], and hence you recognize that in matters of religion you must submit to them rather than preside over them. In these matters, you depend upon their judgment; you do not wish them to be reduced to your will.”

[Note: Gelasius’s genuine meaning is clear from the complete passage cited here, though it has been abbreviated. He says: “You devoutly bow your neck to the rulers of divine things and await from them the causes of your salvation; and in receiving the heavenly sacraments and in arranging them as is fitting, you recognize that you ought to be subject to them, by the order of religion, rather than to preside over them.” Thus, as he explains immediately afterward, this concerns matters pertaining to religion, or ecclesiastical matters. Although the bishops recognize that imperial power has been conferred upon him by heavenly disposition, they too obey his laws.]

Thus Pope St. Gregory I is often read to have decreed in the privileges he issued that kings as well as priests, or any secular persons, should fall from their dignities if they attempted to act against the decrees of the apostolic see [Note: See what was said above on this subject at col. 1219].

By the same authority, Pope Blessed Stephen II of that name deposed Hilderic, king of the Franks, for his slothfulness, sent him—deposed and tonsured—to a monastery, and substituted Pippin in his kingdom [Note: Bernaldus follows the accounts of Frankish writers. On this matter Pagius rightly observes in the *Life of Pope Zacharias*, drawing on Peter de Marca, *Marca Hispanica*, book III, chapter 4, that this should be understood only as having occurred on the pope’s advice and recommendation. Eginhard, in the *Annals*, added the authority of the apostolic see to the petition and consent of the nobles of France so that people would not think that changes of kings had been permitted to the king’s subjects by their own arbitrary decision [Col. 1254C]. Hence no argument can be extracted from this for pontifical power to depose kings, since all these things were done with the pope merely consenting to the nobles of France, not commanding or acting by his authority. See note 1132 below. Nor do the examples of the other pontiffs cited here apply, since they prove only that kings too can be excluded from the communion of the faithful if they are rebellious and obstinate against the decrees of the Church, not that they are thereby deprived of their dignity. Certainly the pontiffs mentioned here never intended this even through their anathemas.]

Nor is it surprising if Roman pontiffs can take secular dignities away from secular persons, so that they may not rule Christians, when they can cut them off entirely from the body, so that they may not even appear to hold the lowest place among Christians.

Thus Pope St. Innocent is said to have excommunicated the emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of St. John Chrysostom from his see.

Likewise Pope Blessed Nicholas I excommunicated King Lothair on account of a certain concubine.

And Pope Blessed Adrian anathematized all kings generally who presumed to violate the decrees of the apostolic see.

### V.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that apostolic prelates are able to depose both ecclesiastical and secular rulers. It necessarily follows that they can also emancipate subjects from the hands of their prelates; for the deposition of prelates could not be valid if no subtraction of their subjects could occur [Note: This is certainly valid concerning the deposition of ecclesiastical prelates, since in respect of their office they too depend upon the Church. Yet it is not at all permissible to conclude from this to kings, who, although equally subject to the Church in spiritual matters, will render an account for the exercise of their power to God alone, as the testimonies of Sts. Ambrose and Gregory cited above in the observations prove. Such things must be excused in Bernaldus, who wrote in the spirit of his age].

It is also certain to all Catholics and learned persons that Blessed Peter received from the Lord, equally universally and effectively, the power both to loose and to bind (Matt. XVI). Therefore his vicars, who by apostolic authority can bind prelates so that they may not rule over their subjects, can by the same authority also release the subjects so that they may not remain subject to those prelates.

Thus Pope St. Celestine, at the Synod of Ephesus, emancipated the people of Constantinople from the authority of Nestorius, once their bishop [Note: Bernaldus already used these arguments and examples above against refractory bishops, at col. 1237].

Likewise Pope St. Leo, at the Council of Chalcedon, freed the people of Alexandria from Dioscorus, once their bishop, by synodal judgment and apostolic authority, and granted them permission to choose St. Proterius as their bishop.

These most sacred councils, in which such emancipations or releases are recorded as having taken place, deserved such reverence from apostolic authority that Pope Blessed Gregory compares them even with the Gospels and anathematizes all who dissent from them. In his synodal letter to the patriarchs he declares concerning them:

> “Whoever presumes to loose those whom they bind, or to bind those whom they loose, destroys himself, not them.”

Likewise Pope Blessed Stephen, whom we mentioned earlier, is said to have entirely released all the Franks from the dominion and oath of subjection to King Hilderic [Col. 1255A] [Note: See note 1229 below. I know that this is commonly reported by others as well. But what need would there have been for Stephen to make such a release if Childeric had been deposed by the authority of his predecessor Zacharias? Greater credence therefore seems due to Theophanes, although he was a foreigner, who candidly testifies in his *Chronography* (Paris edition, p. 338) to what native writers did not dare to say: that Pippin was absolved by the pope from the perjury committed in accepting the kingship from Childeric (Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. V, p. 187)].

Likewise Pope St. John released Emperor Louis from the oath by which he had been reconciled with the tyrant Adalgisus, because it could not in any way be observed without endangering the welfare of the state [Note: Hermannus and the Annals of Metz assign this to the year 871; Pagius, however, maintains that it was done not by John VIII but by Adrian II].

### VI.

In our own time, too, the apostolic see released the people of Bamberg from Heremannus and the Florentines from Peter, once their bishops, and did not permit anyone to remain subject to them as bishops, even though they had sworn oaths of subjection to them.

Thus apostolic authority has always been accustomed to absolve any Christians specially entrusted to it from the hands of deposed and excommunicated persons without any accusation of perjury, even when they had promised their prelates subjection by oath.

St. Boniface too, martyr and bishop, who is said to have sworn complete obedience to the younger Pope Gregory, urgently requested to be released from that oath—but by that same apostolic authority [Col. 1255B] [Note: Gregory II, or the younger Gregory, ordained St. Boniface of Mainz bishop in 723 and required from him an oath of fidelity, as Othlonus relates in his *Life* (Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints*, Benedictine century III, part II, p. 36). Nothing is noted there, however, concerning a requested release; indeed, Boniface seems rather to have renewed it later to Gregory III and Zacharias].

Why would so holy and wise a man have requested this if he thought that such a release was invalid and that it could not therefore excuse perjury?

### VII.

Moreover, if we consider the matter carefully, an oath of subjection is not ordinarily offered to prelates except out of regard for their prelacy. Although this is not specifically expressed in the words of the oath, it is undoubtedly understood in the swearing: namely, that the one person is to remain faithfully subject to the other for as long as the latter presides over him in the office of prelate.

But once the prelate has been deprived of his prelacy [Col. 1255C], the person who was his subject is by no means required to continue keeping an oath of subjection to him, since he swore it to him only in relation to the office of prelacy.

Those who refuse to keep an oath of subjection to persons deprived of their prelacy therefore do not appear to deserve condemnation as perjurers, since they once swore that oath to them, while they were prelates, for the sake of the office of prelacy.

Nor would it have been especially necessary for the Church to release subjects from such an oath, since it had already canonically deposed their prelates, except on account of the doubts of certain weak persons who think that nothing has been done in such cases unless it has been specifically stated beforehand.

For it is sufficiently evident to every learned person that we ought not at all to remain subject to someone whom we unquestionably know to have been deposed so that he may no longer rule over us [Col. 1256A]. In the canonical deposition of prelates, the absolution of their subjects is likewise contained; it is always understood there, even when it is not expressly listed in the sentence of deposition.

Thus Pope Blessed Felix deposed Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, at a Roman synod (Labbe, vol. IV, p. 1095), without specifically mentioning there any absolution of his subjects. Nor was this necessary, for thereafter they were in no way bound to remain subject to him as bishop, since they were no longer subjects of one who had been deprived of the episcopate, and so forth.

Here the manuscript is truncated: an entire gathering of eight pages was cut out, containing both the end of this treatise [Col. 1256B] and the beginning of another. What follows from this point is only a fragment or conclusion of a work different from this one, dealing with the subject that Bernaldus treated above at col. 1243, *On the Office of Presbyters*. We regret the loss of this little work, which has thus perished; because of the deficiency of the other manuscript, we cannot restore it. Perhaps my other colleagues will be more fortunate if they search their chests more carefully.

They unquestionably prescribed that it must be observed. The venerable Pope Gregory VII of this name did precisely this in his own time. Blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was accustomed to imitate him in his bishopric. Our most reverend lord Pope Urban likewise granted this permission—not, I say, to Roman presbyters alone, but also to presbyters of other nations [Col. 1256C], and likewise to monks. He is even said to have granted such a concession generally to a certain congregation of presbyters.

Therefore, other unattached presbyters should likewise not neglect to receive this concession from their bishops before they presume to exercise such an office toward penitents.

Nothing harmful to religion will result if, with the authority of the bishop, we humbly strive to do even those things which we do not doubt that we possess absolutely by virtue of our office—how much more, then, that which the canons do not permit us to exercise without the bishop’s command?

Nor shall we be able to excuse ourselves for presumption if thereafter we knowingly and disobediently attempt to usurp what has been prohibited.

[Col. 1255]

# BERNALDUS’S TREATISE ON AVOIDING REORDINATION AND ON THE SALVATION OF CHILDREN BAPTIZED BY EXCOMMUNICATED PERSONS

## To Gebhard, Bishop of Constance

## Notice

We have not found that Gebhard ever came to Italy before the year 1100, in which Bernaldus died; Bernaldus wrote this letter to him, in which he again confirms, partly with the same arguments and partly with new ones, the opinion concerning the sacraments of excommunicated persons that he had established in work II [Col. 1257].

This matter was eventually treated and decided at the Council of Guastalla in 1106, with Gebhard also present; the previous year Henry V had sent him to Rome to the pontiff.

I think, however, that Gebhard had already been designated to attend some Roman council and had consulted Bernaldus about it, although he was prevented from carrying this out while Henry IV was alive because Henry’s faction blocked the Alps. Hence nothing definite can be established concerning the time when this letter was written, although it must certainly be assigned before the year 1100, since the author died in that same year.

[Col. 1257A] To the lord and most reverend bishop GEBHARD, exalted by the authority of an apostolic legation [Note: Gebhard III of this name, mentioned above at col. 1237, was elevated by Urban II to the dignity of apostolic legate, as Bernoldus relates in his *Chronicle* under the year 1089. Urban’s letter concerning this matter is found in Labbe, vol. X, p. 444], BERNALDUS, a presbyter in name alone and not in conduct, sends the assurance of his whatever kind of prayer and service.

### I.

Your paternal excellence recently deigned, through a legation, to instruct my littleness to hasten to write you briefly whatever I thought would be necessary for you at the forthcoming council of the lord apostolic [Note: It is not known which Roman council this was, which Gebhard wished to attend. Bernaldus nowhere indicates in his *Chronicle* that Gebhard came to Rome before the year 1100. Perhaps he had intended to attend the council of 1099, but was prevented by the supporters of Henry. Only after Henry’s death and the restoration of peace in 1105 was he sent to Rome by Henry V, and in the following year he is said to have attended the Synod of Guastalla celebrated by Paschal II, according to *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 911. There the question concerning the reception of schismatically ordained persons into the communion of the Church was treated and decided in the manner that Bernoldus had already recommended in this letter].

Although I do not doubt that this injunction exceeds my powers, I nevertheless judge it better to expose myself to danger than not to obey your request—indeed, your command.

### II.

I do not doubt that at that synod it will be debated how those who have hitherto been ordained by excommunicated persons are to be received into the Church [Col. 1257B].

Therefore, as your servant, searching for authoritative decrees concerning this matter with singular diligence, I have found abundantly and everywhere that, according to the strictness of the canons, none of those who received ordination while in excommunication ought to administer the office of his order in the Church.

But since the present urgent necessity compels that strictness to be softened to some extent, let us take the greatest care to temper this mitigation not contrary to the canons but according to the canons: namely, if ecclesiastical necessity compels the Church to receive one of them, converted from excommunication, together with his office, we should by no means reordain him contrary to the canons, but rather receive him with his order according to the canons [Col. 1257C].

Thus the most sacred Council of Nicaea, which the holy Fathers compared with the Gospel, decreed that the clerics of the Novatians should be received with their order and not ordained again. In canon 8 it commands as follows (Labbe, vol. II, p. 41):

> “Concerning those who call themselves Cathari, that is, the Pure, whenever they come to the Catholic Church, it has pleased the holy and great council that, after receiving the imposition of hands, they should remain in the clergy.”

And shortly afterward in the same canon:

> “Those of them who are found in the clergy shall remain in the same rank.”

And again:

> “The bishop shall provide that they appear to be entirely members of the clergy” [Col. 1258A].

These Cathari, or Novatians, were followers of a certain heresiarch Novatus [Note: This was not the African Novatus, but the Roman presbyter Novatianus. Petavius observes in his notes on St. Epiphanius, heresy 59, that they must be distinguished from one another (*Works of Epiphanius*, vol. II, p. 226)]. He is said to have been ordained in opposition to Pope Blessed Cornelius, just as the heresiarch Wibertus (Guibertus) was ordained in opposition to the venerable Pope Gregory.

They withdrew from the Church, condemned not only by ecclesiastical judgment but also by their own judgment, and, to their perpetual confusion, established a heresy under their own name. Yet when they were converted, the holy Fathers received them with their order and did not ordain them again.

It is therefore entirely reasonable that we too should adopt this manner of receiving the Wibertists [Note: Catholics called those who adhered to Guibert, the antipope under the name Clement III, “Wibertists.” Their case nevertheless differed from that of the Novatians: the former were merely schismatics, whereas the latter were also heretics], which we read that the holy Fathers observed toward their like and prescribed as the rule to be followed [Col. 1258B].

### III.

Likewise, the African council, attended by a delegation from the apostolic see and by Blessed Augustine, prescribes that the clerics of the Donatists be received with their order and not ordained again. In canon 35 (Labbe, vol. II, p. 1651) it decrees as follows:

> “It has pleased us that any clerics from among the Donatists who, having corrected their judgment, wish to pass over to Catholic unity should, according to the will and counsel of each Catholic bishop who governs the Church in that place, be received in their honors, if this seems beneficial to Catholic peace, just as it is evident that it was done in the earlier periods of this division. The examples of many, indeed almost all, the African churches testify to this.”

Writing about the same Donatists to Boniface, St. Augustine says:

> “Let there be useful clerics in the Church; let there be bishops who were once hostile against it.”

Pope Blessed Innocent I, although he judged the ordination of heretics to be condemnation rather than consecration (Letter 22, chapter 3; Labbe, vol. II, p. 1273), nevertheless reverently accepted in his decrees the judgment of the Council of Nicaea concerning the reception of the Novatians [Col. 1259A] (Labbe, ibid., p. 1274); he did not reordain them [Note: Something must have been omitted in our manuscript. What follows here pertains neither to Novatian nor to Innocent, but to the time of Gregory the Great and to the ordination of Maximus, bishop of Salona, concerning which Gregory writes (book IV, Letter 20): “We can in no way call this consecration, because it was performed by excommunicated men.” Nevertheless, he later received this same Maximus with his order (book IX, Letter 81). The decretal *Sicut*, Distinction 68, chapter 1, is taken from his letter (book II, Letter 46) to John of Ravenna].

Yet Gregory himself declared that Maximus had been ordained by excommunicated persons while he was under excommunication, and asserted that his ordination ought not to be called a consecration, protesting as follows:

> “This matter we can in no way call a consecration, because it was celebrated by excommunicated persons.”

Nevertheless, when Maximus was converted and cleansed through penance, Gregory received him with his order and did not reordain him, lest he in any way contradict his own judgment. In this matter Gregory appears to have entirely proscribed reordination as he did rebaptization, writing to John, archbishop of Ravenna (Gregory, book II, Letter 46):

> “Just as one who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once in the same order cannot be consecrated again” [Col. 1259B].

There is no doubt that Pope St. Innocent held the same judgment concerning the avoidance of reconsecration when writing to the bishop of Naissus (Letter 16; Labbe, vol. II, p. 1271). He earnestly endeavored to reconcile to that bishop his clerics, whom he knew to have been reasonably grieved, out of zeal for justice, because a certain reconsecrated person had been retained in the Church.

Likewise, the African council, assembled and confirmed by apostolic authority, attended and subscribed by Blessed Augustine, firmly decreed in canon 15 that reordinations, just like rebaptisms, were entirely forbidden (Labbe, vol. II, p. 1644).

Likewise, the Apostolic Canons (canon 67; Labbe, vol. I, p. 39):

> “If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon receives a second imposition of hands from anyone, let both him and the one who ordained him be deposed” [Note: Bernaldus did not cite the canon in full. It continues: “Unless it is established that he received ordination from heretics; for those baptized and ordained by them cannot be made faithful or clerics.” See Drouven, *On the Sacraments*, vol. II, p. 275].

Nor would I say this rashly: nowhere in the authoritative decrees do we read that persons converted from heresy are to be ordained, except the Paulianists and others of this kind, who do not invoke the holy Trinity in the Catholic manner and who must also be baptized again when they come over to us.

## IV.

Nevertheless, there are certain people who are overly simple and excessively zealous. They think that anyone ordained while under excommunication, if he comes to his senses, should not be received with his clerical rank but must be entirely reordained. They hold this because they do not hesitate utterly to invalidate the sacraments administered under excommunication.

But we ought rather to believe Blessed Anastasius, the apostolic bishop, who, writing to the emperor Anastasius, demonstrated that the Church’s sacraments remained valid both in those who administered them and in those who received them—sacraments that Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, administered while under excommunication, although he had been condemned by Pope Felix. He writes to that same emperor as follows (LABB., vol. IV, p. 1280):

> “In accordance,” he says, “with the custom of the Catholic Church, let the most sacred heart of Your Serenity recognize that none of those whom Acacius either baptized or ordained as priests or deacons according to the canons is touched by any share of injury on Acacius’s account—an injury by which the grace of the sacrament, perhaps unlawfully conferred, might seem less firm. For even baptism, whether administered far from the Church by an adulterer or by a thief, reaches the recipient as an unimpaired gift, because that voice which sounded through the dove excludes every stain of human pollution. By it this is declared and said: ‘This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire’ (Luke III).

> “And a little later:

> “Acacius, whose name we say ought to be suppressed, harmed only himself by administering good things wickedly. For the inviolable sacrament given through him obtained for others the perfection of its power. But if some people’s excessively inquisitive suspicion extends so far that, after the judgment pronounced by Pope Felix (LABB., vol. IV, p. 1095), they imagine that Acacius subsequently acted ineffectively in the sacraments he usurped, and consequently fear for those who received the mysteries conferred either in consecrations or in baptism, lest the divine benefits should appear void, let them remember that the preceding treatment applies equally here. He performed this deed not without usurping the name of the priesthood; yet, while the mysteries retained their power, the guilty person was harmed by it, not others.

> “For what was said in the Davidic trumpet applies to him: ‘Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, and the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins’ (Psalm LXVII). For pride always brings ruin upon itself, not upon others, as the authority of all the heavenly Scriptures testifies. Thus it is said through the Holy Spirit in prophecy: ‘He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house’ (Psalm C). Since, then, although condemned, he claimed for himself the name of priest, the swelling of pride was inflicted upon his own crown; the people of God, who thirsted for his gift in the mysteries, were not excluded.”

Blessed Augustine likewise clearly held the same view. Writing to Vincent, a Donatist (Epistle 93, Works, vol. II, p. 249), he declares:

> “All the Lord’s sacraments belong to the Church. You possess and administer them in the same way in which they were possessed and administered before you went out from us. Yet you do not possess them for that reason outside the place from which the things you possess come.”

And a little later:

> “You are with us in the Creed, in baptism, and in the other sacraments; but in the spirit of unity and in the bond of peace, and finally in the Catholic Church itself, you are not with us.”

Likewise, in his letter to Festus (Epistle 89, no. 7, cited above, p. 222):

> “The sacraments of heretics are not hostile to us—those which we share with them—because they are not human but divine. Their peculiar error, which they have wrongly absorbed, must be removed, not the sacraments that they received in the same way as we did. They carry and possess those sacraments to their own condemnation; and the more unworthily they possess them, the more they have them nonetheless.”

Likewise, in his letter to the heretic Emeritus (Epistle 87, no. 9, cited above, p. 212):

> “Change yourselves in that respect in which you were dissenting, although the sacraments that you possess are holy, since they are the same in everyone. Therefore we want you to be changed from your perversity, so that your schism may again be cut out at its root. For the sacraments that you have not changed are approved by us as you possess them, lest, while we wish to correct your depravity, we sacrilegiously wrong the mysteries of Christ that have not been corrupted in your depravity.”

Likewise, in his book to Constantine, *On the One Baptism* (Works, vol. IX, chapter 2, p. 528):

> “It is just that, while we reject the evil found in human beings, we should approve whatever good of God we find in them. It is just, I say, that even in a sacrilegious person I should not violate the true sacrament that I discover, nor correct the sacrilegious person in such a way that I commit sacrilege in him.”

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 3):

> “When a schismatic or heretic comes to us in order to become Catholic, we cut away his schism and heresy by persuading him and destroying them. But if we find the Christian sacraments in him, and whatever else he holds that is true, far be it from us to violate them; far be it from us, if we know that they were once given, to repeat them. Otherwise, while treating human vices, we might condemn divine remedies; or, by seeking to heal what is not wounded, we might wound the injured man where he is sound.”

Likewise, in Book I against the Donatists, *On Baptism* (chapter 1, cited above, p. 80), declaring that both ordination and baptism can exist outside the Church:

> “No sacrament is to be wronged. If a person departs from evil, both depart; if he remains in evil, both remain.”

Likewise, in the same work (chapter 13):

> “When schismatics and heretics possess and administer the sacraments in no other way than the true Church does, we do not correct the sacraments when they come to us; rather, we approve them.”

Likewise, in Book III (chapter 10):

> “They do not cease to be the sacraments of Christ and of the Church because heretics use them unlawfully, nor because wicked and impious persons administer them. Nevertheless, those people must be corrected or punished, while the sacraments must be recognized and venerated.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 19:

> “Heretics possess the sacraments and Scriptures outwardly, not for salvation.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 15:

> “If the sacraments are the same, they are everywhere complete, even if they are wrongly understood and administered discordantly; just as the text of the Gospel itself, if it is the same everywhere, is everywhere complete.”

Likewise, in Book IV, chapter 11:

> “The perversity of human beings must be corrected both within and outside; but divine sacraments and utterances must not be attributed to human beings.”

Likewise, in Book V, chapter 19:

> “God is present with his sacraments and words, whoever administers them; the sacraments of God are everywhere correct, while wicked people, to whom they bring no benefit, are everywhere perverse”—that is, both within and outside.

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 27:

> “The gifts granted by God are partly proper to the good, such as tireless charity in the present age and eternal life in the age to come; partly they are shared with the wicked and perverse, such as all the other things among which are the most holy mysteries.”

I could not preserve the brevity of a letter if I wished to collect all testimonies of this kind. But if anyone wishes to investigate these matters more fully, let him diligently examine Blessed Augustine’s writings against the Donatists. Thereafter he will not be permitted to doubt that the Church’s sacraments can be given and possessed both outside and within the Church, although outside it both are altogether harmful.

Thus far concerning clerics ordained while under excommunication.

## V.

I also think that in the future synod some mention should be made of infants baptized while under excommunication: namely, whether they are saved even if they die before reconciliation. Here too the authority of Saint Augustine can satisfy us, if we faithfully read what he judged.

Concerning adults who die immediately after such baptism, he writes in Book I of *On Baptism* (chapter 2, cited above, p. 81):

> “If extreme necessity should compel someone, when he has found no Catholic through whom he might receive baptism, and, while preserving Catholic peace in his heart, he receives through someone situated outside Catholic unity what he would have received within that very Catholic unity, then, if he immediately departs this life, we count him as nothing other than Catholic. If, however, he is delivered from bodily death and, when he has restored himself bodily to the Catholic congregation, to which he had never departed in heart, then not only do we not disapprove what he did, but we praise it most securely and truly. He believed in his heart in the present God, where he preserved unity; and, recognizing that the sacrament of holy baptism, wherever he found it, belonged not to human beings but to God, he did not wish to depart this life without it.

> “But if someone, although he could receive baptism within the Catholic Church itself, through some perversity of mind chooses to be baptized in schism, even though he later intends to come to the Catholic Church—because he is certain that the sacrament is beneficial there, although it may indeed be received elsewhere but cannot be beneficial there—he is unquestionably perverse and wicked, and all the more harmful because he acts knowingly.”

Likewise, in Book VI of *On Baptism* (chapter 5, cited above, p. 163):

> “All wicked people are spiritually separated from the good; but if they also separate themselves bodily through open dissent, they become worse. Yet, as has been said, it makes no difference to the holiness of baptism when a worse person possesses it or to whom a worse person administers it. A person who is separated can administer it, just as a person who is separated can possess it; but he possesses it as harmfully as he administers it. The person to whom he administers it, however, can receive it beneficially if he himself receives it without being separated, as happens to many through some necessity of death.”

## VI.

If this is therefore true of adults who possess knowledge, how much more must it be believed concerning infants, who know nothing at all of heresy and do not receive baptism from one who is separated? The turning away of the heart normally prevents the gift of remission wherever it occurs. Since such a turning away is not found in a baptized child, is it surprising if one believes that the child can be saved through the power of the sacrament—the same power that, in adults, when a turning away of the heart is absent, was not doubted to work salvation?

Indeed, the baptism of heretics usually brings greater disadvantage to adults than to children: according to the canons, it prevents adults from ecclesiastical ordinations, whereas it does not refuse children canonical ordination once they have grown up. Thus the African Council testifies in chapter 24.

Moreover, Blessed Augustine made no exception for any child baptized according to ecclesiastical usage in Book XXI of *The City of God* (chapter 16, Works, vol. VII, p. 636), where he treats the salvation of children generally as follows:

> “So great is God’s mercy toward the vessels of mercy that he has prepared for glory that even the first age of human life, namely infancy, which is subject to the flesh without any resistance, and the second, which is called childhood—when reason has not yet undertaken this struggle and the child is almost subject to no vicious pleasures [Note: This variant reading of our manuscript seems better suited to the whole context than that in the printed editions, where “all” (*omnibus*) is read instead of “no” (*nullis*), with a plainly contrary sense.], because, although he can now speak and therefore seems to have passed beyond infancy, the weakness of his mind is not yet capable of receiving a command—if he receives the sacraments of the Mediator, even if he ends his life during those years, having been transferred, that is, from the power of darkness into the kingdom of Christ, is not only not prepared for eternal punishments but does not even suffer those purgatorial torments after death. Spiritual regeneration alone is sufficient, so that after death the fact that carnal generation contracted death does not bring harm.”

In this statement Blessed Augustine seems to have excluded no one baptized in infancy. Therefore it is not safe for us to exclude any child whom, having been initiated with the complete sacrament of the Mediator and without any turning away of the heart, we cannot at all deny to be saved.

## VII.

Furthermore, if an adult who, knowing nothing at all of heresy and with an undeceitful heart, were baptized by a heretic according to Catholic usage and then immediately died, would he not rightly be considered Catholic and fit for Christian salvation? For plainly, according to Augustine, the sins of others do not stain, much less condemn, those who have been entirely unaware of them. Thus, writing to Vincent the Donatist (Epistle 93, Works, vol. II, p. 236), he says:

> “No one’s crime stains a person who is unaware of it.”

Likewise, to Emeritus (ibid., no. 2, p. 209):

> “Let the vigilance of your mind now attend to this: no one can be contaminated by an unknown person or by unknown crimes.”

In his book *On Faith and Works* (chapter 7, no. 10, Works, vol. VI, p. 170), he even excuses a virgin from adultery if she unknowingly marries another man’s husband, and does so for as long as she remains unaware of the fact.

If, then, this is rightly believed concerning adults, how much more concerning infants who know nothing of any evil whatever? They are not condemned for the sins of those who baptize them, through whom they unknowingly receive the divine sacraments without any deception of the heart.

## VIII.

But it is objected that heretics cannot give the Holy Spirit or the remission of sins. We too say the same concerning heretics that we read Blessed Augustine asserted even concerning any members of the devil who baptize within the Church. It would be excessively long, and not especially necessary for this question, to discuss fully from where the baptized receive remission of sins, even when the faithless baptize them.

Nevertheless, we can respond sufficiently to the objections by saying that infants are believed to receive remission of sins from the same source as adults baptized by heretics with an undeceitful heart or in ignorance. If anyone wishes to know fully concerning the grace of the Holy Spirit, or concerning the remission of sins and from where it is received, he will find sufficient treatment in Blessed Augustine’s books against the Donatists. In them it is also asserted clearly enough that divine sacraments administered by any reprobate person can be salutary for those who receive them without a false or turned-away heart.

## IX.

Perhaps it is still objected that the holy Fathers would not have said that children baptized in heresy should be received into the Catholic Church by the laying on of hands if they judged them to be entirely blameless.

Thus Pope Gregory I ordered that children baptized by Arians be reconciled (Book I, Epistle 17), just as the African Council noted that those baptized by Donatists ought to be reconciled.

[Note: Canon 14, LABB., vol. II, p. 1644, and canon 47, ibid., p. 1072.]

We certainly do not contradict these authorities; indeed, we gladly accept them. Children baptized among heretics should be received through the laying on of hands if they live long enough to reach reconciliation.

But if death overtakes them in infancy, it is astonishing if the necessity of death cannot excuse them from the guilt of ignorance—a necessity that customarily excuses adults from the guilt of deliberate action, as Blessed Augustine demonstrated above. Thus many people are very often excused from numerous observances because of the necessity of death, although, if they survive, they are rightly ordered to fulfill them according to ecclesiastical usage.

In the same way, penitents are frequently admitted to communion before completing their penance because of the danger of death; nevertheless, according to the Council of Nicaea (canon 13; LABB., vol. II, p. 35), if they survive, they are ordered to complete their penance according to the proper rule.

Nor should we think that the holy Fathers ordered this as though they entirely despaired of the penitents’ salvation, even if those who had been admitted to communion before completing their penance should die. For according to Saint Leo the pope (Epistle 91, LABB., vol. III, p. 1402):

> “We neither can nor ought to set a limit to divine mercy, since the thief repented on the cross and passed immediately from the cross into paradise.”

It is also written:

> “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

Therefore, we too must not despair of children baptized in heresy if death overtakes them before they reach legitimate reconciliation through the laying on of hands. Nevertheless, no one baptized in heresy ought to neglect that reconciliation if the necessity of death does not prevent it.

## X.

I, therefore, your servant, have hastened to set down briefly and faithfully, in the most willing obedience to Your Paternity, these matters which I did not doubt would be necessary for you in the future synod. May the God of peace and consolation direct your journey in prosperity, and may he deign soon to restore your blessedness to us, always safe and sound, most beloved lord and father.

[Col. 1265]

# BERNALD’S TREATISE ON THE PRUDENT DISPENSATION OF ECCLESIASTICAL SANCTIONS

## Prefatory Notice

Bernald has already dealt in part with this same subject above, in the short work *On the Authority of the Canons*. The certainty that Bernald received and held the office of apostolic penitentiary is provided by the distinguished excellence of his learning and the ardor of his religion evident throughout all his other writings.

How cautiously, prudently, and intelligently one must proceed in this matter, which is exposed to such great dangers for souls, and in which excessive inclination in either direction is dangerous, he explains in the short work addressed, apparently, to the venerable Gebehard, later abbot of Saint Saviour at Schaffhausen, rather than to the bishop of Constance, although no one would have been more appropriate as its dedicatee.

Thus, after first saying a few things about the law of excommunication in order to satisfy Gebehard’s request, he undertakes the other subject:

> “But,” he says, “because we ought not to repay what we owe to so dear a brother and lord without interest, and because we wish to offer you other things that will be no less pleasing—namely, what is to be understood from the rigor of the canons concerning the condemnation or deposition of those who have fallen, as well as concerning their reconciliation—for in such cases we need great discernment, lest we either appear, through excessive strictness, to despair with the Novatians of the salvation of those who have fallen, or be judged, through excessive leniency, not to possess zeal for God.”

Beginning first with the rigor of the canons, he places this at the forefront: that “a place for penance was granted only once in ancient times” in the Church, “and was not to be granted to anyone who fell again after penance.” He repeatedly emphasizes that these provisions were established “not from despair of pardon, but for the sake of disciplinary precaution.” He does the same in a treatment of a similar subject that is now published for the first time from the Blasian manuscript (no. XIV), *On the Prudent Dispensation of Pontifical Sanctions and Penitential Canons*.

In the earlier work cited, he treats the matter point by point and brings forward ancient examples of dispensations:

> “Namely,” he says, “so that the rigor of discipline would everywhere generally be feared, yet it would not be judged unlawful if, in some place, the welfare of the Church were served by restoring someone who had fallen.”

Both of the aforementioned works cite further examples of stricter discipline, with the same explanation:

> “Therefore, just as we read that a place for penance was completely denied by the holy Fathers to those who fell after penance—not from despair of pardon but from the rigor of discipline—so we properly understand that penance was for a time denied to fallen consecrated virgins, indeed postponed for a period.”

There is also another reason for which the holy Fathers judged that certain people should be suspended from such penance: namely, youthful age and the weakness of the flesh.

The distinction between ancient and later penance should be carefully placed before our eyes. The former was like an external restraint, whereas the latter was internal and involved secret confession, together with secret or private satisfaction and absolution, after the practice of public penance had gradually fallen into disuse, when absolution was granted after satisfaction had been completed.

Just as this practice of penance was once denied in some places to all who relapsed, so, because of the enormity of the crime, it was denied to consecrated virgins who had fallen, and, because of the instability of youthful age, it was denied without despair of pardon. Holy Mother Church therefore left the obtaining of pardon to God, the giver of pardon, and to the private act of penance arising from a contrite heart. She was concerned lest the guilt be increased through profanation and the bond of condemnation made heavier:

> “Not to deter people from penance,” as I say with Bernald, “but from sin; and not so that they would repent less after falling, but more humbly, when they saw themselves regarded as inferior even to those who were doing penance.”

And later:

> “Among modern people, however, a place for penance is not denied to anyone who has fallen, because human perversity has become so universally prevalent and has cast off the yoke of ancient discipline that Holy Church would now rejoice greatly if they were willing to come to their senses in any way. For she knows that God’s mercy is most ready to forgive, and that in God it makes little difference with what severity or leniency sins are punished according to the diversity of times, provided only that the sinner turns with his whole heart.”

The Church binds what is to be loosed and looses what is bound, according as the Holy Spirit, assisting her until the end of the age, judges it more useful for the welfare of the faithful. The examples cited by Bernald, and the variety of earlier and later discipline that he explains, demonstrate above all the breadth of the power of the keys. This breadth became still more evident after his time, until, in the chapter *Omnis utriusque sexus*, Pope Innocent III established at the Fourth Lateran Council, chapter 21 (LABB., *Councils*, vol. XI, part I, p. 172), the arrangement and practice that now obtain in the sacred tribunal of penance, so that it would be continually open to the faithful not only at the point of necessity but also for the exercise of devotion.

I had once intended to explain its salutary character, as well as the variety of public and private discipline, through several examples, but time has not permitted me to do so. I have at least touched on it briefly in the little book *On What Belongs to Divine and Ecclesiastical Law or Institution Concerning the Sacraments*.

The multiple laying on of hands distinguished by our Bernald is relevant to this subject. He distinguishes three forms, corresponding to three sacraments: confirmation, penance, and ordination.

Bernald also has much relevant to the present subject concerning clerics who have fallen or who have been received into the Church from heresy, schism, or excommunication, in his more extensive work addressed to the monk Gebehard. These matters are missing from the following treatise, published from the Blasian manuscript, *On the Prudent Dispensation of Ecclesiastical Sanctions*.

## I.

All decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs must be received with complete reverence. Their authority has itself been canonized by general councils. Blessed Gregory compares them in his synodical letter with the Gospels and anathematizes all who dissent from them (Book I, Epistle 25). Saint Pope Adrian likewise anathematizes kings who do not fear violating the decrees of the Apostolic See (Cause 25, question 1, chapter 11).

The decrees themselves, however, require a sober reader and a most careful interpreter, one who knows how to bear patiently the fact that he may not fully understand everything at first approach. For many things are found in them that are different, but they should not be judged contrary to the truth if they are understood appropriately.

## II.

To discern this, however, excerpts from the decrees alone cannot suffice. Indeed, even complete consideration of them scarcely suffices for diligent students, so that, after their original circumstances have been considered, anyone may fully discern what appears generally to be intended as a dispensation.

For example, general statutes most explicitly prohibit marriages between blood relatives. Yet Pope Saint Gregory is read to have granted such marriages by way of dispensation to the newly converted Anglo-Saxons.

[Note: The sixth and following responses of Saint Gregory to the inquiries of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, concerning marriages between blood relatives belong here (Book XI, Epistle 64), specifically concerning those who had contracted marriages within prohibited degrees before receiving the faith. Gregory did not wish such people to be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord on this account. He added the following—if his successors had observed it after nearly a thousand years, England might perhaps still be persevering in the faith received through his efforts:

“In the present age, Holy Church corrects some things through fervor, tolerates some through gentleness, and overlooks and bears some through consideration, so that often, by bearing and overlooking the evil she detests, she may restrain it.”]

Gregory himself confirms this in his letter to Felix, bishop of Messana [read: Messanensis] (Book XIV, Epistle 17): he did not establish this generally, but only for the newly converted Anglo-Saxons, until they grew strong in the faith.

It is indeed a privilege of the Apostolic See to judge the canons and decrees, and, according to the circumstances, either to apply them strictly or to relax them, as it sees to be more suitable to ecclesiastical welfare at the time.

## III.

Many things, however, are falsely attributed to the statutes of the holy Fathers. One example is the writing of Wido the musician on the Simoniacs; another is the text placed under the name of Saint Gregory that appears to prohibit the marriage of two sisters to two brothers. Gregory himself, writing to Augustine (Book XI, Epistle 64), testifies that this was permitted.

Likewise, certain people falsely attribute to the same Gregory the chapter that appears to permit another woman to be brought in when a wife is unable, because of illness, to endure intercourse. They wish this to be understood as follows: the woman was first joined to a husband, but later, when she could not have intercourse because of illness, the husband might lawfully bring in another woman.

But this interpretation contradicts the Gospel, in which such an act is unambiguously judged and condemned as adultery. It is therefore improperly attributed to Blessed Gregory and is rightly rejected by ecclesiastical men.

[Note: This canon, which Bernald complains was falsely attributed to Saint Gregory the Great, was taken from a decretal of Gregory III addressed to Boniface, which is found in *Councils of Germany*, vol. I, p. 33. Fleury also mentions it, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XLI, §47, and adds:

“This opinion of the pope, taken strictly, is contrary to the Gospel and Saint Paul, as Gratian noted” (Cause 32, question 7, chapter 18). “Hence even today this canon is regarded as a singular indulgence granted to these German converts.”

Since, however, an indulgence of some sort is vainly thrust forward against the laws of the Gospel, the other interpretation of the same canon assigned by Bernald, and adopted by several modern writers, appears altogether preferable. Certainly, in keeping with the character of that age, when words are not always used in their natural sense, the words “if a woman, overcome by illness,” and so forth, can be understood of a woman whose marriage was indeed valid but had not been consummated because impotence had either preceded it or arisen afterward.]

Nevertheless, some wish to understand that woman differently: namely, as one with whom the husband had never been able to have intercourse because of her illness, after which he brought another woman into the marriage. If the context of the reading permits this interpretation, it ought also to please us, since it neither conflicts with the Gospel nor dishonorably attributes anything to an apostolic writer.

The same chapter is found to have been transmitted by the Apostolic See to Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, who is said to have preceded Saint Gregory by more than a hundred years. Therefore the chapter should not readily be trusted—least of all on the ground that it is contrary to the Gospel.

## IV.

The statement of Blessed Pope Innocent (Epistle 2, chapter 12; LABB., vol. II, p. 1252), which says that a fallen nun is not to be admitted to penance for as long as her seducer lives, should certainly not be understood to mean that her virginity is considered impossible to recover.

If Blessed Innocent had intended it to be understood in that way, he would not have granted her penance after the seducer’s death, since it would be clear that she could recover the status of virginity no more afterward than before.

This statement should instead be understood in the same way as other statements of this kind, which appear to threaten sinners with terror.

[Note: The true reason was the danger of relapse: once that had occurred, she could no longer be admitted to penance, since she had already completed it once, as the author correctly explains below in section 6.]

There are even much stricter statements that seem to prohibit penance not merely for a time but entirely. Thus Blessed Pope Siricius, concerning those who sinned criminally again after completing penance, writes to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona (Epistle 1, chapter 5; LABB., vol. II, p. 1019), and unambiguously affirms that they thereafter have no refuge in penance.

Likewise, Blessed Ambrose testifies in his book against the Novatians (Works, vol. II, p. 436) that there ought to be only one penance, the public penance, just as there is one baptism.

Similarly, Blessed Augustine, writing to Macedonius (Epistle 153, no. 7), says that a place for penance is granted in the Church only once.

## V.

The holy Fathers are therefore understood to have instituted these provisions not from despair of pardon but from the rigor of discipline—not to deter people from penance but from sin, and so that after falling they would repent not less, but more humbly, when they saw themselves regarded as inferior even to those who were doing penance.

The same is observed almost as a law with respect to others who have fallen criminally: they are removed from the order that they possessed before their fall and in which they are found to have sinned. Thus, if those enrolled among the penitents fall again, they are rightly judged unworthy of their former order.

Yet the holy Fathers do not appear to have established this harshly out of despair of pardon, especially since the Lord wills all people to be saved, and “on whatever day the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel XXXIII).

Not, I repeat, from despair of pardon, but as a disciplinary precaution, we understand this to have been established. We can confirm it from Blessed Augustine’s words to Macedonius (cited above). He says that it was prudently and beneficially arranged that a place for penance should not be granted to those who fall after penance, lest the medicine become cheap and less useful to the sick—medicine that is more salutary in proportion as it is less despised.

This was certainly for the rigor of discipline, but not so far as to entail despair of pardon. For Augustine continues in the same letter:

> “Who would dare deny to those who have fallen after penance that God’s patience may lead them to penance, or even that they are blessed if they trust in the Lord?”

Therefore, just as we read that the holy Fathers entirely denied a place for penance to those who fell after penance—not from despair of pardon but from the rigor of discipline—so we appropriately understand that penance was for a time denied, indeed postponed, to consecrated virgins who had fallen.

## VI.

There is also another reason for which the holy Fathers judged that certain people should be suspended from such penance: namely, youthful age and the weakness of the flesh.

For this reason Pope Saint Sylvester established (Roman Council, chapter 12, LABB., vol. I, p. 1553) that no one should impose penance on a person unless he was forty years old.

Likewise, Saint Ambrose writes more fully in his book against the Novatians (cited above, p. 438):

> “If the flesh resists the mind and is not subject to the governance of the spirit, one should not seek the works of penance, lest during the very penance something occur for which penance will afterward be necessary. If penance is once undertaken but not properly completed, it neither obtains the fruit of the former penance nor leaves room for a later one.”

Likewise, the holy Fathers at the Council of Agde state in chapter 17 [read: chapter 15; LABB., vol. IV, p. 1586]:

> “Penance should not readily be entrusted to the young.”

What wonder, then, if Blessed Innocent also took this reason into account when he said that a virgin who had fallen from her religious purpose ought not to be admitted to penance—especially since he adds: “For as long as her seducer lives”?

At that time, while the man with whom she had sinned was still alive, particular care had to be taken for her weakness. It is extremely common for people to return readily to those with whom they previously sinned, and human weakness is much more inclined to return to a familiar mire than to undertake a new crime for the first time.

It is therefore not surprising if Saint Innocent suspended such a fallen woman from penance until the death of her seducer, lest she commit something during the very penance by which, according to Ambrose, she would both lose the fruit of penance and thereafter, according to the ancient custom, fail to obtain a place for penance.

## VII.

Among modern people, however, a place for penance is not denied to anyone who has fallen, because human perversity has become so universally prevalent and has cast off the yoke of ancient discipline that Holy Church would now rejoice greatly if they were willing to come to their senses in any way.

For she knows that God’s mercy is most ready to forgive, and that in God it makes little difference with what severity or leniency sins are punished according to the diversity of times, provided only that the sinner turns with his whole heart.

## VIII. Concerning the consecrated virgin who has fallen from her resolution

Concerning the consecrated virgin who has fallen from her resolution and is not thought capable of being restored to the rank of virginity, we must not contend too vehemently, lest we appear by this very contention to oppose Blessed Jerome, who says:

> “I shall speak boldly: although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her fall. He can indeed free her from punishment, but He cannot crown one who has been corrupted.”  
> —St. Jerome, Letter 18, to Eustochium, *Works*, vol. IV, part II, p. 29.

For the writings of St. Jerome were so authoritatively canonized by Blessed Gelasius in the Roman synod (Labbé, vol. IV, p. 1263), that anyone who stubbornly attempts to contradict them is considered not to hesitate to oppose apostolic authority itself. We must therefore receive his venerable writings with reverence, and no one should rashly pass judgment upon them.

But when he himself said that God cannot restore a virgin after her fall, this is no more astonishing than many other things which God is freely read and believed to be unable to do—for example, the statement in the Epistle of John: “God is faithful; He cannot deny Himself” (2 Tim. 2). Hence the Apostle says: “In God there is no ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but in Him there is ‘Yes’” (2 Cor. 1). It is also freely said that He cannot do evil, cannot be changed, cannot be deceived, cannot deceive, and cannot die.

Thus Augustine, in Book V of *The City of God* (chapter 10, *Works*, vol. VIII, p. 125), says:

> “For this ‘cannot’ is said in such a way that, if He could, He would actually be of less power. He is rightly called omnipotent, although He cannot die or be deceived; for He is called omnipotent because He does what He wills, not because He suffers what He does not will. If that happened to Him, He would in no way be omnipotent. Therefore He cannot do certain things precisely because He is omnipotent.”

Likewise, the power of a rational creature is not diminished but increased in eternal life, although there it will be wholly unable to do many things which, while living in this life, it was plainly able to do. For in this life it could hunger, thirst, be corrupted, deceive, be deceived, and do six hundred other things of this kind; yet in eternal life it will not be able to do them, and for that very reason it will unquestionably be more powerful there. For the ability to do such things is not an increase of power but the clearest indication of weakness.

St. Jerome himself explained those words—that God cannot raise up a virgin after her fall—when he added: “He can indeed free her from punishment, but he cannot crown one who has been corrupted,” because He is a just judge, whose disposition cannot be changed.

The holy martyrs Nereus and Achilleus are likewise said to have received this teaching concerning lost virginity from Blessed Peter, and to have encouraged Domitilla, the granddaughter of the emperor Domitian, to preserve her virginity. For they said to her:

> “A virgin, if she loses her virginity, can escape the guilt of this through repentance, but she cannot in any way regain virginity itself. For every holiness lost in whatever manner can be recovered through repentance; virginity alone, once it has perished, cannot reach again the stability of its former integrity.”

These words are found in their *Life* under 12 May, vol. III of the Bollandists, p. 7.

Thus it is safer for us also to interpret St. Jerome’s statement in this way, lest, if we attempt to interpret something unworthy of him, we be judged to disgrace not so much his authority as our own slowness of understanding.

## IX.

We must take the greatest care, however, to argue about the restoration of virginity with such moderation that we do not appear, according to the heresy of Jovinian, to place widows and married women—or any other corrupted women—on an equal footing with virgins. For the Catholic faith does not admit this. In accordance with evangelical authority, it knows these ranks to be so distributed that the thirtieth fruit is assigned to married women, the sixtieth to those who practice continence, and the hundredfold to virgins themselves.

We do not doubt that this was divinely predestined in this way from the beginning. Hence we must obey Blessed Jerome in this matter also, for he said that God cannot act against His own predestination, since He cannot deny Himself, and in Him, according to the Apostle, there is no “Yes” and “No,” but He is always “Yes” (2 Cor. 1).

## X.

It is sufficiently astonishing that we should contend so vehemently that sacrilegious virgins who have fallen cannot be restored to their own rank, while we patiently allow true widows and lawfully married women to remain in their respective ranks—even though, according to the Apostle, these have not sinned in the loss of virginity as greatly as those who, because of the magnitude of their sin, were not deemed worthy to be admitted to repentance.

Most holy Pope Leo, in his decrees, chapter 49 (Letter 87, no. 5; Labbé, vol. III, p. 1394), declares that not even those virgins who endured barbarian violence physically but not willingly are in any way to be counted among virgins who have persevered, in accordance with the prophetic saying: “The virgin of Israel has fallen; there is none to raise her up” (Amos 5).

**Note.** Leo’s words do not appear to exhibit the same severity attributed to them by the author. They read: “But those handmaids of God who lost the integrity of their chastity through barbarian violence will be more praiseworthy in humility and modesty if they do not dare compare themselves with uncontaminated virgins,” etc.

The holy Fathers plainly wished this to suffice for fallen virgins, who on account of their sin were assigned a status below that of married women: if, through repentance, they sometimes deserved to be preferred even to those lawfully married and to be associated with true widows or with those practicing continence. Let this therefore suffice for us also, and let us not desire to proceed so far in disputation that we may in some way be marked as exceeding the limits of the holy Fathers.

# On the Sacraments of Dying Infants. Another Author (G)*

## Notice

The word “another,” prefixed here, seems to indicate an author different from Bernold, although this short treatise agrees sufficiently with his manner of expression; at least, the passages which he admits below, in section 4, to have collected for the use of his friends may be attributed to the same compiler. That word may, however, also designate another treatise.

## I.

If someone wishes to anoint a newly baptized child who has been stricken by illness with holy oil, it will not be necessary for him to recite the entire office of anointing, and least of all those prayers which seem to concern the remission of sins. For the Catholic faith holds that a newly baptized child is to be believed to have received the remission of sins.

We would unquestionably act against this faith if we prayed for the child as though he had not yet been absolved and needed to be absolved—although Blessed Augustine testifies that such a child is without sin in Book XX of *The City of God* (chapter 26, *Works*, vol. VIII, p. 610):

> “Except for the one mediator, no one is clean from uncleanness, even after the bath of regeneration—not even infants who are still so young.”

If, therefore, someone wishes to administer the ministry of anointing to such sick children, he may appropriately use those prayers which seek health or eternal life for the sick, but not those which ask pardon for penitents. We may say that the customary psalms are sufficiently appropriate for such anointing, since in them the voice of the Church seems to pray generally for all her members.

**Note.** It is nowhere reported that this anointing of infants was once in use, nor have we read that it was formerly prohibited, although it was certainly superfluous, since the form of the sacrament cannot be realized in those who were not yet able to sin through the senses that are to be anointed. Theodulf of Orléans, however, when he says in his capitulary that anointing is necessary even for children, is speaking of those who are already capable of deceit or sin, as is clear from what follows. If some people formerly anointed infants before the use of reason, they should be considered to have done so for the sake of obtaining bodily health, which is a secondary effect of this sacrament. The theologians nevertheless deny that it can be given to those who are not capable of its primary effect, namely the remission of sins.

## II.

It must also be known that some do not consider viaticum necessary for dying children, since the Lord says generally to all who belong to Him: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Hence Blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Baptism of Infants*:
