> “Will anyone even dare to say that this sentence does not apply to infants, and that they can have eternal life in themselves without sharing in this body and blood?”

And shortly afterward:

> “If they do not eat the flesh of the Son of Man, they too shall not have life.”

**Note.** This statement of St. Augustine has caused difficulty for many theologians. Yet he explains it sufficiently both in the passage cited and especially in Book III, chapter 5, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*. He clearly demonstrates that infants eat the body and blood of the Lord when, through baptism, they are inserted into Him as living members. He says:

> “What could be clearer than the many and great testimonies of the divine Scriptures, by which it most plainly appears that no human being can attain eternal life and salvation apart from fellowship with Christ? … It follows that, since nothing else is done when infants are baptized except that they are incorporated into the Church—that is, joined to the body and members of Christ—it is clear that, unless this has been conferred upon them, they belong to damnation … And therefore, if the Apostle’s words, ‘through one man,’ and so forth, contain any ambiguity, what shall we say of this statement also: ‘Unless human beings eat His flesh,’ that is, become participants in His body, ‘they shall not have life’? In the light of these and other testimonies, which I now pass over, so clear by divine light and so certain by divine authority, does not the truth proclaim without any ambiguity that unbaptized infants not only cannot enter the kingdom of God, but cannot possess eternal life apart from the body of Christ, into which they are incorporated through the sacrament of baptism?”

Hence the Roman order immediately commands that communion be given to them after baptism—how much more in extreme necessity, when they begin to depart from this world? For, according to canonical authority, extreme communion seems not to be denied to anyone, however lost he may be.

We shall certainly not deny ecclesiastical communion to infants more than to other Christians, whether during life or at the point of death, if we wish to follow the institution of the holy Fathers. Nor did they ever exclude infants wherever they prescribed the general custom of giving communion to all Christians. They even used to kiss infants while communicating, as St. Cyprian not only testifies in his writings but also most earnestly urges should be done.

**Note.** St. Cyprian does indeed discuss this kiss of infants in Letter 64 to Fidus, but there he refers it only to baptism. From his book *On the Lapsed* we infer that, after baptism, infants were at that time at least given the sacred chalice.

Moreover, the very words with which holy communion is distributed seem to apply especially well to infants. They do not say that holy communion is to contribute to the remission of sins, which would apply only to adults, but to eternal life—a benefit which no one doubts is appropriate to the innocence of infants.

**Note.** The Roman orders show that in the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries infants were accustomed to receive baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist on the same day. They add at the same time:

> “Provision must be made for infants that, after they have been baptized, they are not suckled without the greatest necessity before they communicate in the sacrament of Christ’s body.”

Gregory the Great was somewhat more indulgent at the beginning of the seventh century. In his *Sacramentary*, under Holy Saturday, he notes:

> “Infants are not to be forbidden milk before holy communion if necessity requires it.”

Communion for infants at the point of death was not so common in practice as communion for the newly baptized. Bernold’s conclusion on this subject should therefore be attributed to his pious wishes. The ancients believed it sufficient for infants to receive the Eucharist at least once after baptism, before they reached the use of reason. Nor does the comparison adduced hold: even notorious sinners, provided that they were penitents, had to be supplied with this remedy at the point of death, whereas innocent infants do not yet need it.

## III.

How long infants remain in that innocence, we do not know, except insofar as we may infer it from Augustine’s words in Book XXI of *The City of God* (chapter 16, *Works*, vol. VII, p. 636). There he writes concerning a baptized child that, if he dies in the first age—that is, infancy—or in the second, that is, childhood, he will not suffer any purgatorial torments after death.

From these words it may reasonably be inferred that infants are believed to preserve their innocence after baptism until childhood, since they are said not to undergo any punishment, even purgatorial punishment, after death. Therefore, if we wish to anoint such sick infants, we would need to pray not for their sins but for the sins of their elders, believing that the children themselves had lived innocently until that hour.

## IV.

Yet we seem to labor unnecessarily over their anointing, since nowadays not even adults, except for very few, appear to care about it. We have not arranged these matters so carefully because we thought that they had already been restored—or ought to be restored—to the general practice of the Church. Rather, we have done so to satisfy our friends, who, although they themselves are not accustomed to perform such rites, are nevertheless very glad to know what should be done in such cases, should the persistent request of some member of the faithful ever require them to anoint his sick child with holy oil.

Nor should it be regarded as hopeless that the anointing of infants might somewhere come into use, just as the anointing of adults did, although the latter too seemed to have been entirely abolished down to our own times. If, however, that anointing of infants never comes into use, we shall nevertheless not regret having satisfied in this writing the inquiry of our simple brethren.

**Note.** The author gained only this fruit from his labor on this matter. His proposal was never put into practice; rather, just like extreme unction, the Eucharist had been forbidden to infants for at least four hundred years. In some places even today, however, certain drops from the washing of the priest’s chalice during the sacrifice of the Mass are given to these infants in memory of the ancient rite when the mother is presented for her purification.

## V.

If illness should ever force such a child to depart from this life, it does not seem necessary that everything ordinarily said for the commendation of adult corpses should be said at his burial, and least of all those prayers which specifically concern the remission of sins, as we noted above concerning anointing.

For we believe that God has absolved them from sins, so that, if they die at that age, we may be completely certain that they will not experience purgatorial punishment. Accordingly, when such children are carried for burial, some people, with sufficient prudence, do not recite the customary office in full, but only the psalms, to which they append those three prayers which precede the years of temerity—prayers which, as it seems, say nothing about such absolution. In this way we bury them honorably without appearing to ask anything contrary to our faith.

The canons generally prescribe that the bodies of the dead be carried to burial with psalms. This is entirely appropriate, since there is no doubt that in them the voice of the Church prays for all her members.

# Bernold’s Chronicle

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. V, p. 385.)*

## Preliminary Observations

Among the other dioceses of Upper Germany, Constance, especially agitated by the schism that tore apart the Empire and the Church at the end of the eleventh century, produced a writer who undertook to announce to the faithful, for the praise and glory of God, the events of his own time which he had learned by sight or hearing.

Bernold, still young—the son, apparently, of a married cleric, educated in the schools of Constance under Bernhard as his teacher, a man distinguished for religion and prudence, and professed as a monk in the then-famous monastery of St. Blaise—began his *Chronicle* in the year after the simoniacal bishop Charles had been deposed at the synod of Mainz, that is, toward the end of 1072 or in the first months of 1073.

**Notes.**

- *Chronicle*, year 1086.
- In 1076: “Bernold, a young man of promising character, a flourishing little flower, then a novice, is heard as a young man.” See Ussermann, *Prodromus*, II, pp. 214, 247–248.
- Ibid., p. 248.
- Ibid., p. 230.
- *Chronicle*, year 1088, and the *Necrology*.
- The year in which this occurred is unknown. Neugart, *Episcopatus Constantiensis*, p. 504, considers that in 1085 Bernold accompanied Gebhard, who had fled from Constance, to St. Blaise.
- The autograph codex shows that the *Chronicle* from the year 1073—“By whose prudence,” etc.—and certainly from 1074—“Margrave Hermann,” etc.—was written at different times. When the *Necrology* prefixed to the *Chronicle* is compared with it, the days of death of men who died before Peter Damian, except for a few inserted later, are seen to have been written by the same hand and at the same time as the *Necrology*. From 1075 onward, however, the days of death were added in another ink, the same as is regularly found in the continuation of the text of the *Chronicle*. I therefore infer that Bernold began his work at the end of 1072 or the beginning of 1073, before receiving news of the deaths of Widerold and Alexander II and of the election of Gregory VII, and that in the same year, 1073, he continued it down to his own time. In the *Chronicle*, the deaths of Widerold and Alexander II, as well as Gregory VII’s election, are due to the first style. The list of pontiffs, added after the completion of the *Chronicle*, likewise presents Gregory VII’s election written in the first ink, while the text of the *Chronicle* under the years 1056 and 1061 already recognizes Gregory as pope.

For twenty-eight years, amid the gravest changes in affairs in which he was involved, he brought it down to the beginning of the twelfth century. Bernhard, his teacher, fervently devoted to the cause of St. Peter, had nurtured a pupil no less fervent as a champion of ecclesiastical liberty.

Since the questions agitated between the Empire and the Church, between Gregory and Wibert, and between Henry and Rudolf and their followers had to be judged according to public and canon law, Bernold, after carefully examining the sources of ecclesiastical history and the sacred canons, transferred his complete allegiance to the party of Gregory VII. Thereafter he became an exceedingly vigorous defender and champion of Gregory’s decrees against simony, incontinent clerics, and lay investiture.

We see him as such throughout the entire course of the *Chronicle*, and he displayed himself as such in many other writings, as well as in word and deed. In 1076, at the dictation of Adalbert, a priest and monk, he wrote to his teacher Bernhard, Adalbert’s pupil, concerning the condemnation of the schismatics. He disputed in person and by letter with Alboin, a priest of Constance, concerning clerical incontinence. In 1077 he wrote an apology for the decrees of Gregory VII against simoniacs and incontinent clerics.

Two years later he took part in the Roman synod held against Berengar of Tours, and saw Berengar standing in the midst of the synod and renouncing the heresy concerning the Lord’s body by the sacrament of his own hand. Since he had already become closely associated with Hermann, the son of Duke Berthold, through his admiration for the household of Duke Berthold, in 1084, on the feast of St. Thomas, he was ordained priest with Gebhard, Berthold’s son, who had been elected bishop of Constance, by the authority of the bishop of Ostia, sent by Gregory VII. He received from apostolic authority the power to receive penitents.

At that time he also dedicated to Gebhard, later abbot of Schaffhausen, a book on the authority of the canons. But shortly afterward, when Bishop Gebhard was driven into exile by the pressure of his adversaries, Bernold took part in the battle at Bleichfeld and in the siege of the city of Würzburg in 1086.

At that same time he wrote to the monk Bernhard concerning the sacraments of the excommunicated, to Albert, provost of Strasbourg, concerning the law of excommunication, and to Albert, provost of Speyer, an apology against the schismatics. He had already obtained permission to be enrolled in the catalogue of the brothers of St. Blaise, following the example of many noble and prudent men who, to avoid the dangers of the wars raging throughout Alamannia, withdrew especially into the monasteries of St. Blaise, Hirsau, and Schaffhausen.

**Notes.**

- Ussermann II, pp. 213–214.
- Page 213.
- Ussermann II, pp. 187 ff.
- Ibid., p. 231 ff.
- Page 271 ff.
- Page 435, concerning Berengar’s multiple condemnations.
- *Chronicle*, year 1074.
- *Chronicle*, year 1084.
- Ussermann II, p. 312.
- *Chronicle*, year 1086.
- Ussermann II, p. 230 ff.
- Ibid., p. 368 ff.
- Ibid., p. 357 ff.
- Page 357: he calls himself the last brother of St. Blaise.
- *Chronicle*, year 1083.

Nor did he later cease writing against the enemies of the Church. In 1088 he wrote concerning Berengar’s multiple condemnation and concerning the avoidance of excommunicated persons, to Recho. In 1089 or 1090 he wrote to Paulinus, a cleric of Metz, concerning the purchase of churches, and, on behalf of Bishop Gebhard, to the brothers of Raitenbuch concerning the office of priests. He also appealed to Bishop Gebhard concerning the avoidance of reordination and the salvation of children baptized by excommunicated persons.

In 1091, when the number of monks at St. Blaise had grown so greatly that it was clear new buildings had to be added to the old, and shortly before several colonies were sent from there to the monasteries of Wiblingen, Muri, Göttweig, Engelberg, and others, Bernold seems to have moved to Schaffhausen, to the monastery of St. Salvator, and to have spent the remainder of his life there.

**Note.** From 1091 onward he touches Schaffhausen affairs more frequently, as Gerbert had already noted in the *Prodromus Germaniae Sacrae*, II, p. XVII. Moreover, a sentence in the *Chronicle* deleted by the author himself in the autograph but surviving in the Muri transcript of the St. Blaise copy shows that this copy was written in 1091.

At St. Blaise, however, he left behind a copy of the *Chronicle* that ended in the middle of 1091. He subsequently continued working on the authentic book that he had taken with him, altering and correcting what he had written earlier, and he did not lay down his pen until the very year in which he died.

He outlived Adalbert, Bernhard, and William, abbot of Hirsau, by many years. In the year of the Lord 1100, after extending his book to 3 August, he died in the monastery of Schaffhausen, which he had entrusted with it, on 16 September, and was buried in the same tomb as Adalbert.

**Notes.**

- Adalbert had died in 1079.
- Bernhard died in 1088.
- William died in 1091.
- Ussermann, cited work, p. 178; *Schaffhausen Chronicle*, Prologue, no. 3.

His principal work, namely the *Chronicle*, is arranged as follows. After prefacing it with a *Necrology*, and appending to the completed work a list of the Roman pontiffs, he first copied Bede’s *Chronicle* concerning the six ages of the world. He then continued the thread of history from the birth of Christ to the year 1054 by excerpting from Hermann’s *Chronicle*. From 1054 onward he added the events of his own time by his own effort.

**Note.** *Chronicle*, year 1086.

He himself identifies the authors of the earlier part:

> “These are the authors of the chronicles: Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Dionysius, Jordanes, Bede, and Hermann of our own time, and thereafter whatever writers have recorded their own times.”

He reproduced Bede word for word, from the creation of the world down to the reign of Domitian, by dictation, so that we can dispense entirely with that portion of the book. He then excerpted Jordanes’ account of the principal kingdoms from his book *On the Succession of Kingdoms*, and Bede’s chapter 16, *On Times*, concerning the six ages of the world.

**Note.** See below the passage where it is written (folio 18), “If, however, the parenthesis itself is thus,” etc.; there the word *parenthesis* ought not to have been written at all, but expressed by some sign.

Beginning again with the birth of Christ, he transcribed Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, translated by Jerome into Latin as it is read in Hermann, and Hermann’s *Chronicle* down to the year 1054. He added, however, several items from Eusebius’ own *Chronicle* and a few from his *Ecclesiastical History*, Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men*, Cassiodorus’ *Chronicle*, Orosius, the *Miscellaneous History*, and Bede’s *On the Six Ages*. Throughout the work he also inserted information from the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* and various catalogues, from Dionysius’ collection of the councils transmitted by Pope Hadrian I to Charlemagne, from Ansegisus, and from the councils of Mainz in 847, Altheim in 916, Aachen in 992—which is now lost—and Seligenstadt in 1023. He also excerpted from Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* and Regino’s *Chronicle*.

**Notes.**

- In the year 69 he prefers this material from Eusebius, whom he had previously followed, for example, in the case of Anacletus; under the year 605 he corrects Hermann’s corrupt reading.
- He regards the letters of Pseudo-Clement as spurious under the year 94.

Thus, in the whole earlier part of the work, Bernold acts independently only where, under the years 1044 and following, he defends the cause of the Roman pontiffs. From the year 1055 onward he proceeds in an entirely different manner.

In the second part of the book he follows the footsteps of no leader. Nevertheless, aided by public documents of the Church and the Empire and by the letters of Gregory VII, he wrote continuously the events of the years 1054–1072. Later he completed these by adding the texts for the years 1054, 1055, 1056, and 1060. He committed the entire remaining history, namely that of the years 1072–1100, to writing at the very time when the events occurred or became known to him.

Nor did he refrain from correcting, explaining, and adding to this material as he had done in the earlier part, as the autograph codex demonstrates, whether the additions were made by the author himself or after his death.

**Note.** Compare, for example, the words added under 1061 and what I shall propose below concerning corrections made by the author himself after the year 1091.

He wrote with a spirit hostile to the emperor and to his lay and clerical supporters alike, intending to announce to the faithful of the Church, for the praise and glory of God, the disasters inflicted upon him. He used a simple and lucid style, generally retaining the earlier words of his sources and preserving the connection of their sentences. Only rarely did he depart from the reckoning of time which he had found in Jerome and Hermann.

Where he reports events known to him personally, one may praise his fair and concise narrative, undisturbed by embellishment. He departs two or three times from the rules of Latin usage, using the genitive and accusative of *Saxonia* and *Longobardia* where one would expect *in Saxonia*, *in Saxoniam*, and *in Longobardia*; he also uses *adjuvare* with the dative and joins *a* with *Heinrico*.

In writing individual words he often departs from Hermann. Thus one looks in vain for *Alemannia*, *Longobardia*, *Lotharius*, *Ludowicus*, *Luitoldus*, and the spellings *litera* (“letter”) and *aeclesia* (“church”), which occur consistently in our text. In other cases he is inconsistent even with himself—for example, *Bertaldus* and *Berthaldus*, *Gundharius* and *Guntharius*.

**Notes.**

- *Chronicle*, years 1080, 1083, and 1087, and 1093.
- For Duke Welf, year 1093.
- Year 1090: *Luitoldus*.
- Year 1074.
- Year 1084.
- Year 1065.
- In the additions under the same year.

Since Bernold’s book had been brought down only to the year 1091, it was excerpted in that year at the monastery of St. Blaise. It was copied in full, while Bernold was still alive or not long after his death, in the monasteries of Gengenbach and St. George at Villingen. At nearly the same time it was copied by Ekkehard of Aura, apparently the author of the *Chronicle of Würzburg*, which was derived from the *Hildesheim Annals* and the *Chronicle of Würzburg*, recently obtained from the distinguished Molter.

It was also copied by the scribes of the Annals of St. Blaise, or Engelberg, and of the *Chronicle of St. George in the Black Forest*, as well as by the author of the six books *On the Course of Time*, which I examined in the Strasbourg library and which were written at Ensdorf in 1135. It was further copied by the writers of Ekkehard’s codex at Zwiefalten and of the *Annals of Zwiefalten* and the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, transcribed in the middle of the twelfth century. (*Archiv*, VII, p. 504.)

Urstisius prepared its first edition in 1585 from the Villingen and Basel codices, under the name of Hermann the Lame and the priest Bertold, with the codex of Hermann of St. Gall set out beside it. See above, p. 73. Excerpts from this edition may be read in the Bouquet collection, vol. XI, pp. 23 and XIV, pp. 548–564 and 674–688.

In the middle of the eighteenth century, Oefelius inserted several readings from the autograph, together with Bernold’s *Necrology* and the *Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs*, in *Scriptores rerum Boicarum*, vol. I, pp. 644–653. Aemilian Ussermann also used these materials in his edition, corrected several passages, recorded readings from the Göttweig, Muri, and Engelberg codices, placed the text beneath Hermann and Berthold, and added his own observations.

He rendered an especially valuable service to our author by printing the rest of his works, which he had for the most part collected from manuscript books. But since he neglected the autograph codex, he fell far short of restoring the text as the author wrote it. This has finally been permitted in our edition, for which the following materials were collected and used:

### 1. The autograph codex

This codex was formerly handed over by the author to St. Salvator at Schaffhausen and was supplemented there around the year 1118 by the following marginal notes under the years 1009, 1052, and 1064:

## Annals of Schaffhausen

### 1009

At this time Count Ebbo of Nellenburg took Hedwig, the cousin of King Henry, from the royal court and married her.

**Note.** *Nellenbucr* in the manuscript.

### 1052

In this year the blessed Count Eberhard of Nellenburg began to build the place at Schaffhausen, where St. Pope Leo IX consecrated an altar in honor of the Lord’s resurrection on 22 November and inaugurated and confirmed the place with his holy blessings.

### 1064

In this year also, the church of St. Salvator was dedicated by Ruomuld, bishop of Constance, in the monastery at Schaffhausen, which the noble Count Eberhard of Nellenburg had built and endowed with his estates.

**Note.** *Scafhensi* in the manuscript.

In the fourteenth century, at the beginning of which it was being kept at Schaffhausen—

**Note.** See the inscriptions of the fourteenth century, folio 49: “This chronicle belongs to the monastery of Schaffhausen.” On folio 24, the following words were written in an empty space by a hand from the beginning of the fourteenth century:

[Col. 1281D: thus in c.] In the year one thousand two hundred and seven [Col. 1281D: thus in c.], F. likewise undertook the journey. In the year one thousand two hundred and twelve, the journey to Jerusalem by sea of foolish boys took place [Col. 1281D: thus in c.]. In the year one thousand, thirty, and thrice three [the numeration is corrupt or uncertain], under King Henry, Jerusalem is sought by a great multitude; the cross marks the earth and overshadows the seas. In the year one thousand one hundred and eighty-two, under the emperor Alexius, Jerusalem was captured by the Constantinopolitan [force?; the reading is incomplete] [Col. 1281D: thus in c.], and its entire kingdom was subjected to the Christian faith. On fols. 82, 83, and at the beginning of the codex, a census inscribed in the year 1325, payable to Ulrich of Valendaus, is found: “First, the freemen from beyond the forest, forty marks,” etc.], it passed into the monastery of Pfäfers [Note: [Col. 1280D] We read the following inscription, written by a contemporary hand on fol. 81: “Note that Lord Burkhard of Wolfurt, a monk of the monastery of Pfäfers, celebrated his first Mass on the Sunday immediately following the feast of Christ’s Ascension in the year of the Lord 1375. Afterwards, when the venerable father in Christ, Lord John of Mendelbüren, abbot of the said monastery, departed this life, the same Burkhard was elected abbot of the aforesaid monastery by unanimous decision of his Pfäfers brethren in the year of the Lord 1386, on the second day after the feast of the apostle Thomas. After the aforesaid election he was confirmed on the feast of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, in the city of Chur, by the honorable father in Christ, Lord John, of blessed memory, bishop of Chur. After this confirmation, on the Sunday immediately following Epiphany, the aforesaid Lord Abbot Burkhard was ordained abbot by the said bishop in the monastery of Saint Luzius the King, situated outside the walls of Chur, in the presence of the venerable father in Christ, Lord John, abbot of the monastery of Disentis [Col. 1281D: thus in c.], the lord provost of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1282C] of Saint Luzius, and the lord prior of the house of the Preachers of Chur. Amen.”], and was subsequently brought into the Bavarian library, where it is numbered among the Latin manuscripts as 432. Even today it has no rival save Liudprand’s autograph, and at the command of the most serene King of Bavaria it was sent to me at my request.

It contains eighty-one pages of old parchment, arranged in gatherings of eight pages, except for the first, penultimate, and last gatherings, which consist respectively of eleven, ten, and four pages. The script belongs to the end of the eleventh century [Note: [Col. 1282C] It may be useful to record certain peculiarities of this manuscript. The spelling *ae* is very frequent, as in *aecclesia*, *persae*, *prae*, *praeter* (881, 1083, 1084); *q* is used for *quae*, *quaerimonia*; *v* sometimes occurs, as in *vt*, *vsque*, *vnanimiter*, *wluelingin*, *wlgariter*, *videlicet*, *venerabilis*, *vita*, *veniret*, *lvitoldus*, *excommvnicatorum*, *div*, *cuivs*, *associatvs*; the sign 7 and 7 [for *et*] occurs as conjunction and ending, for example in *videlicet*, *sederet*, *consentiret*, *proveniret*, *usurparet*, *immineret*, *incoronaret*, *veniret*; *id* for *id est* (729); *tm* for *tamen* (fols. 75, 76); *c* for *con*; [abbreviations] for *est*, *H* for *enim*, [abbreviation] for *hoc*, *h-* for *haec*, *s.* and *S.* for *sanctus*, etc.; *qq* for *quoque*; *RP* for *res publica*, etc., occur. *Nunquam*, *unquam*, *quendam*, *eundem*, *heresim*, *nichil*, *epdomada*, and once *caelum* are written in these forms. *Natalis* and *nativitas*, *s* [for *set*] and *sed*; *CI* for 900, *CI.I* for 901, etc. *marhbach* and *marchbach*.]—a slender script, though in many places it has faded and has been revived by a fairly recent hand of about the seventeenth century, or has been completely obscured.

The different color of the ink [Note: [Col. 1282D] The ink of the year 1088, brown in color, may be observed both in the Necrology and in the Catalogue of the Pontiffs, as, for example, in these passages: “1060. He anathematized Rome”; “1065. The chaplain of Passau succeeded”; in the same year, “He succeeded simoniacally”; “1066. Hugo is substituted”; “1067. Einhardus—Henry succeeded”; “1080. He chose the once-Ravennate”; The word *gratis* at 1058 shows the dark color of the year 1092.] and the script [Note: [Col. 1282D] In a small script, the following are written in an erased place, for example: “1054. To this man the subdeacon [gave] poison,” etc.; “1055. The emperor [entered] Italy,” etc.; “1056. Victor,” etc.; at the end of 1084: “Whom on the preceding day—he granted.”] show that the author corrected and enlarged the work in various places, for example around the years 1088 and 1091, and later. But the notes for the years 674 and 1096 concerning Dagobert and the Jews were added by another hand at the beginning of the twelfth century; the notes concerning the counts of Nellenburg and the monastery of Schaffhausen were added around 1119 by a Schaffhausen scribe [Col. 1281B], to whom the final lines added to the Catalogue of Pontiffs—namely, those concerning the years of Paschal II and Popes Gelasius II and Calixtus II—are also owed.

Since these additions are absent from the other codices derived from ours, those manuscripts must have been copied from it during the first years of the twelfth century, certainly before 1119; and indeed their—

2) C., formerly a parchment codex of the monastery of Gengenbach, very well written in folio, displays a script of the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century so clearly that no doubt on this point is possible. I examined it in 1833 in the Royal University Library of Würzburg and, with the most generous permission of the distinguished Ludewig, its librarian and public professor at Würzburg [Col. 1282A], put it to use for our purpose.

The scribe, whom we saw accurately following the authentic manuscript in the first part, omits quite a few things in the second part of the work and adds others. Attached to Henry IV, he tries at least to preserve the imperial dignity in the narrative hostile to him, and he frequently refrains both from the insults which Bernold hurled at Henry and his adherents and from the praises bestowed upon Gregory, Matilda, and their followers [Note: [Col. 1282D] Compare, for example, the year 1085.]. He presents the annals of his own monastery, first placed in the margin and later incorporated into the text itself; here we have decided to set them out in continuous sequence:

## ANNALS OF GENGENBACH

**1027.** Reginald, abbot, died.

**1034.** Rousteinus, abbot, died.

**1052.** Berthold, abbot, died.

[Col. 1282B] **1071.** Poppo, abbot, died.

**1074.** Acelinus, abbot, died.

**1075.** Roupertus [Note: [Col. 1282D] These words occur only very briefly in the Gottweig, Muri, and Engelberg codices, at the end of the year 1073.] the venerable abbot of the monastery of Gengenbach, seeing that all who possessed newly cleared lands were claiming the unlawful rights of that place for themselves, and grieving over the loss suffered by the monastery, compelled everyone to pay the due. When all were indignant at this action, it also happened that one of his knights, H., and his son C., built a mill in the district called Antersbach against his will, and made a road across the public field beside the monastery bridge. But the mill was demolished by the authority of the advocate, at the abbot’s own insistence. He ordered the field to be enclosed by a ditch on his own authority. When the workers were digging, they were driven away by the knights.

Seeing this, the abbot, moved by zeal, came there with his chaplain. But those men, inflamed with anger, rose up [Col. 1283A] against him and wounded him severely. His chaplain, named Otto, grieving over his death, rebuked a certain knight named Eggehard for not coming to his lord’s aid; Eggehard struck him down with his sword, and thus Otto rested in peace on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January. The abbot, carried back to the monastery half-dead, put everything properly in order and, having arranged all things, departed to the Lord on the second day before the Ides of December. Willo succeeded him.

**1085.** When Willo had presided over the monastery of Gengenbach for a short time, he was expelled on the charge of excommunication, though it later became clear that the true cause was envy. A certain cleric and provost named B., appointed by him and likewise defamed on account of his expulsion, held the same position for several years. The abbot himself was released from the flesh at Mainz, in the monastery of Saint James, on the third day before the Nones of July of this year, where he had also served as abbot.

**1096.** [Between *habuit* and *Sigifredus*.] Hugo, a devout abbot of the monastery of Gengenbach, elected in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1089, was deprived not only of his office but also expelled from the cloister through the fraud of the provost and canon Bertholf, by whose authority he had also been promoted. After suffering many hardships for seven years, he finally, with the consent of Duke Bertolf—who at that time was violently occupying the same position—recovered his office this year and was honorably received by all on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.

The spelling practices of the codex itself depart slightly from those of the autograph, so that it consistently has *sollempniter*, *assumpto*, *inposuit*, *inproviso*, *inmittere*, but also *immitti* and, at 1083, *suueuia* [Note: [Col. 1283D] *qdo* for *quando*.].

3) The codex formerly belonging to Saint George of Villingen, extending as far as the year 1052, and another belonging to Francis Rechburger, tribune of the people of Basel, covering the years 1053–1100, which Urstisius published in his edition, were not [Col. 1283C] copied from the Gengenbach manuscript [Note: [Col. 1283D] For they contain no passages peculiar to that manuscript and preserve passages omitted by it.], but, like it, were copied from the autograph before the Schaffhausen additions were made to it.

The text which we read in Urstisius from the Saint George codex, destroyed in the fire of the monastery of Saint Blasien in 1768 [Note: [Col. 1283D] P. Hohenbaum van der Meer writes in the previously mentioned unpublished preface that he saw the codex before the fire of Saint Blasien.], departs from the autograph quite often through omitted, added, or altered words. For the year 1054, where one might rightly expect a eulogy of Herman, in whose place the autograph now has something else on the scraped parchment, it is read in manuscript 3; and at 1088 traces of the earlier reading still appear in the autograph [Note: [Col. 1284D] Compare also the year 1091.].

The edition therefore deserved to have me reproduce its readings in full wherever they depended upon Bernold’s earlier text. I omitted material only where an obvious error of the scribe or editor was apparent—for example, *in primis* in place of *imperatoris* [Note: [Col. 1284D] At 1095.]—or where a word appeared to have been omitted through the scribe’s negligence [Col. 1283D] [Note: [Col. 1284D] For example, at 916; at 924, where *Vindelicae* is absent; and at 937, where *Galliam* is absent in 3.]. In some places the scribe also inserted material peculiar to himself [Note: [Col. 1284D] For example, at 1005 and 1007.].

[Col. 1284A] In addition to the complete codices, an apograph of the book left at Saint Blasien in 1091 must be taken into account. Its traces survive only in codices derived from it, especially the Muri manuscript. When I compared it with the autograph, I discovered that certain words and sentences which Bernold had deleted or altered in the autograph after 1091 had been preserved in it; in their place the parchment is still visibly scraped. Such passages include the following: at 1054, the passage beginning “so that Gebehard might be freed”; the entire narratives of 1055 and 1056; at 1058, the word *gratis*, added around 1092; at 1059, the sentence “and afterwards they come to him for surrender,” followed by the events of 1060; at 1090, the words *jam dudum* [“long ago”], subsequently corrected in that year; at 1091, in August, later corrected to “the sixth day before the Ides of August”; at 1088, “And these things were indeed being done among the faithful of Saint Peter already” [Col. 1284B], followed by “But he departed to the Lord on the eighth day before the Ides of April”; at 1088, *Welfo*, later *Welf*; at the end of 1088, the words “to whom Oudalricus succeeded,” formerly absent; and at 1091, the final sentence beginning “Therefore—lest they perish,” which made room for other material.

These passages therefore appear to have been altered by the author himself, but only after the apograph of Saint Blasien had already been made—that is, after the year 1092.

4) The Gottweig manuscript; 4b) the Muri manuscript; 4b*) the Engelberg manuscript; and 5) the Saint Gall manuscript, listed above on pp. 73, 74, 264, and 265, followed Bernold and transcribed very many of his sentences. The Saint Gall manuscript ends in the middle of the sentence for the year 1066; the Gottweig manuscript ends at 1081; and the Muri and Engelberg manuscripts end in 1091. We have decided to indicate the material peculiar to codices 4, 4b, and 4b*.

[Col. 1284C] I organized the new edition as follows: Bernold’s text was reproduced as faithfully as possible according to the autograph, while the supplements and principal readings of the other codices were indicated at the foot of the page. I retained Ussermann’s annotations, or such part of them as might be useful, and added my own.

In the autograph codex Bernold prefixed to his chronicle a Necrology, enlarged in various places with different ink, and chronological notes, some of which it seemed appropriate to insert here. He also prefixed a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, carried down to Gregory VII and, in the course of time, extended as far as Paschal II; a certain Schaffhausen monk later continued it to Calixtus II. These materials, first published by Oefelius in *Scriptores rerum Bavaricarum* I, pp. 640 ff., we present here, indicated by numbers according to the authority of the autograph codex and the sequence of the notices added by Bernold to the primary text, followed by the additions of the Gengenbach codex.

## On the Lunar Regulars

The Egyptians and Romans, from whom we have acquired the art of calculation, decided that the lunar ages which they established for the Kalends of the first year of the nineteen-year cycle should be maintained as regulars throughout the whole cycle. Whichever Kalends they chose as the beginning of the year, they first completed the leap of the moon. For example, the Romans began from January, whereas the Egyptians began from September, that is, beginning four months higher. The former, namely the Romans, completed that leap on the thirtieth of November; the latter, namely the Egyptians, on the thirtieth of July. Thus each established the lunar ages of the Kalends of its first year as regulars and arranged them as prescribed.

## On the Regulars of the Fathers

It is now known, however, as Hermann, the most subtle of computists, has clarified, that the ancient fathers began the first year of the nineteen-year cycle with the paschal new moon on the second day before the Nones of April, five months higher even than the Egyptians. They began in the year in which they announce the twenty-seventh moon on the Kalends of January, and in that year they complete the leap of the moon on the third day before the Kalends of August; popular usage also counts this as the nineteenth [year].

Although, therefore, in that same year, according to the ancient fathers, the lunar age appropriate to the Kalends of each month is always supplied by the epacts—or even exceeds it by one in May—namely, twenty-eight in April, twenty-nine in May, thirty in June, one in July, [Col. 1289C] three in August, five in September, and so on up to the Kalends of April, nevertheless anyone who decides to maintain those lunar ages of the Kalends as regulars should add one unit to the lunar ages of the first four months, because in those months the leap of the moon has not yet occurred, and therefore the ages which follow it always become greater.

Thus, following the order of the embolisms, he should arrange the lunar ages of the Kalends of that same year as regulars, especially as their principal character becomes clear through the order of the embolisms, beginning with April in the first order of the regulars prescribed above. This is what concerns the regulars of the fathers.

They insert the first embolismic month in the third year on the fourth day before the Nones of December; the second, in the sixth year on the fourth day before the Nones of September; the third, in the eighth year on the second day before the Nones of March; [Col. 1289D] the fourth, in the eleventh year on the second day before the Nones of December or the third day before the Nones of January; the fifth, in the fourteenth year on the fourth day before the Nones of November; the sixth, in the seventeenth year on the fourth day before the Nones of August; and the seventh, ending in the nineteenth year, on the third day before the Nones of March.

## On the Controversy concerning the Embolisms

From this, as we think will be sufficiently clear to an experienced and careful calculator, it is apparent that the more ancient fathers began the lunar years more correctly from the paschal new moons and arranged them so that, according to the Egyptians and Romans, the embolisms occur one year earlier than they ought—that is, when they should be inserted in the third, sixth, and eleventh years, and likewise in the others, they appear, contrary to the rule, in the second, fifth, and tenth years, and similarly thereafter [Col. 1290A].

The fact that two embolisms—those of the eight-year cycle (*ogdoadis*) and the eleven-year cycle (*endecadis*)—retain a fixed order of their sequence both according to the Egyptians and Romans and according to the ancient fathers results from their being joined to the end of the years of the ancient fathers. For according to the ancient fathers the end of any year is almost the beginning according to the Romans. Those who begin the lunar year from the paschal new moons and bring it back to the same point discover that January, February, and March are the final months of those years.

There are some who, when questioned about the foregoing controversy concerning the embolisms, try to resolve it in this way: after they have begun, from September, the epacts of the following year, which according to popular usage begins in January, although in some martyrologies they are assigned to the preceding year, they may reasonably be regarded as belonging to the subsequent year.

I would gladly agree with this defense if I saw that it helped in the case of all the embolisms. Let it be so, if it can in some way be done. But to which year do they wish to assign the sixth embolism, inserted on the fourth day before the Nones of August? To which year is it attributed—namely, the sixteenth or the seventeenth? If to the sixteenth, they should know that it never receives an embolism in the regular order. If to the seventeenth, they should remember that they have not yet begun the epacts of that year.

But since they are in no way able to unravel this question, they must confess that their proposed remedy for the difficulty is ineffective, that they have gone wrong, and that until now they have not understood the truth of the matter. Henceforth, in calculations of this kind, they must follow the ancient fathers rather than the Romans [Col. 1290C].

The confusion of this question is therefore easily resolved if one turns one’s attention more carefully back to the earlier part of our argument. For in this way the nineteenth year of the Romans is recognized as the first, the first as the second, and the second as the third; and, when the same regular path is followed, the sixteenth is necessarily found to be the seventeenth.

## On the Usefulness of the Lunar Regulars

If it should also be asked what all the lunar regulars mentioned above are individually capable of indicating, one should know that they specifically show what the lunar age is on the Kalends in the year in which there are no epacts, except for the four first regulars of the ancient fathers. These are always reduced in that same year because of the aforementioned fact that the leap of the moon has not yet occurred. In all other years, the epacts of the current year are added to the same regulars; and whatever number remains below thirty, or exceeds thirty, after the number thirty has been removed, that is the lunar age on the Kalends.

## On the Leap of the Moon

The leap of the moon increases each year by one hour, one point, and one nineteenth of a point. The moon’s illumination therefore does not occur at one and the same temporal moment or under the same celestial climates; rather, it always occurs somewhat earlier than it did in the preceding month, so that there is a basis for skipping one day.

The years from the creation of the world change on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April; the years of the Lord’s incarnation change on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. The beginning of the nineteen-year cycle begins on the second day before the Nones of April, in the year in which the twenty-seventh moon is announced on the Kalends of January. The year of the nineteen-year cycle is renewed always at the paschal new moon; the common and embolismic years, the civil or ordinary and lunar years, on the Kalends of January; and the year of the solar cycle on the Kalends of March. [Col. 1292A] The leap year changes on the fifth day before the Kalends of March. The concurrent days change on the Kalends of March. According to the Romans, the epacts change on the Kalends of January; according to the Egyptians, on the Kalends of September; according to the ancient fathers, on the Kalends of April—which is also the truth. The indiction changes on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. The solar cycle is arranged from the first natural concurrent number in this order: first, second, third, fifth, with the leap year.

[Col. 1291B] **Note** [Note: [Col. 1291] The word is partly cut off.] that the Roman pontiffs have been arranged here according to the *Pontifical Book*, in which Linus and Cletus are said to have been not so much successors as assistants of Saint Peter. For Linus is also said to have departed before Saint Peter’s death, and Cletus is said to have existed not only during Saint Peter’s time but also during Clement’s. Saint Peter granted no portion of apostolic authority to Linus or Cletus, but did grant it to his successor Clement, as the decrees of the pontiffs testify. These, as well as the aforementioned *Pontifical Book*, seem more deserving of belief than Eusebius.

162. Paschal II, also called Reginherius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, was ordained in the same year as above. [Note: [Col. 1299] The following words were added in another ink.] [Note: [Col. 1299] In another hand, not Bernold’s, the following is added: “He held office for 19 years and 6 months, up to the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119.”]

163. Gelasius II, also called John, archdeacon of the Roman Church, ordained in the same year as above, held office for approximately one year.

164. Calixtus II, also called Guido, archbishop of Vienne, was ordained in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1120.

[Note: [Col. 1299] Thus in manuscript 1.]

These are the chronicles of Bernold, which he handed over to the monastery of the Lord Savior.

[Col. 1299]

# THE CHRONICLES OF THE VENERABLE PRESBYTER BEDE BEGIN, ACCORDING TO THE HEBREW TRUTH

[Col. 1299B]

The first [Note: [Col. 1209] From Bede, *On the Six Ages of the World*.] age of this world extends from Adam to Noah and contains, according to the Hebrew truth, 1,656 years, but according to the Seventy interpreters, 2,240 years; the generations number 10 according to both editions. This age was wiped out by the universal Flood, just as forgetfulness customarily submerges the first age of every human being. For who is there, after all, who remembers his own infancy?

The second age extends from Noah to Abraham and encompasses 10 generations according to the Hebrew truth, but 292 years; according to the Seventy interpreters, however, it contains 1,072 years and 11 generations. This was, as it were, the childhood of the people of God, and therefore the language was discovered in [Col. 1299C] it, that is, Hebrew. For it is in childhood that a human being begins to know how to speak, after infancy, which is so called because it cannot speak.

The third [Note: [Col. 1299] These are the authors of the chronicles: Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Dionysius, Jordanes, Bede, Hermann of our own time, and thereafter any writers of their own time.] age extends from Abraham to David and encompasses 14 generations according to both authorities, but 842 years. [Note: [Col. 1299] “DCCCCXLII,” corrected to “DCCCXLII,” in manuscript 1.] This was in a certain sense the adolescence of the people of God, the age at which a human being begins to be able to beget children. For this reason the evangelist Matthew took the beginning of his genealogy from Abraham, who was also established as the father of the nations when he received a changed name.

The fourth age extends from David to the Babylonian captivity and contains, according to the Hebrew truth, [Col. 1299D] 460 years [Note: [Col. 1299] “CCCCLXXIII,” corrected to “CCCCLX,” in manuscript 1.], but according to the translation of the Seventy, more than 12 additional years; according to both books, the generations number 17, although [Col. 1300B] the evangelist Matthew gives 14 for the sake of a certain mystery. During this age, as though in the youthful period, the time of kings began among the people of God. For this age [Note: [Col. 1299] The word was added above the line.] is ordinarily suitable among human beings for governing a kingdom.

The fifth age, as though an old age, extends from the Babylonian captivity to the coming and incarnation of the Lord Savior. It too extends over 14 generations, but over 570 years [Note: [Col. 1299] “DLXXXVIIII,” corrected to “DLXX,” in manuscript 1.], during which, wearied as though by burdensome old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly numerous evils.

The sixth age, which is now taking place, has no definite sequence of generations or times, but, like an age of decrepitude, is to be consumed by the death of the whole world. All the saints have overcome these wretched and labor-filled ages of the world through a blessed death.

Having already entered the seventh age, the age of perpetual Sabbath, they await the eighth age, [Col. 1300C] that of the blessed resurrection, in which they will reign forever with the Lord.

## The Course of the Ages Mentioned Above

Therefore, in the first age of the newly born world, on the first day of this age, God made light, which he called day. On the second day he balanced the firmament of heaven in the midst of the waters; the waters and the earth, together with the heaven above and the powers that were to praise their creator in it, had been created before the beginning of these six days, and so forth. [lacuna] as in Bede’s account of the six ages of the world.

Jehoshaphat, son of Asa, for 25 years. Elijah the Tishbite withheld rain for three and a half years because of the sins of Ahab and the people of Israel. Among his other great deeds, he anointed Elisha, [Col. 1300D] son of Shaphat, who was from Abel-meholah, as prophet in his place. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1299] These words are in the margin, but in the same hand in manuscript 1; they are absent in manuscript 3.], in his Book of Hebrew [Col. 1301A] Questions, asserts that Elijah was Phinehas, who, inflamed by zeal for the Lord, pierced Zimri while he was fornicating with the Moabite woman. Properly he is called Phinehas, for he is called Elijah from the event. When this same Phinehas was sent by the Israelite people to the tribe of Reuben and Gad, who had built an altar of enormous size, he received this answer of defense from them: “The strongest God, the Lord himself, knows.” From this answer Phinehas himself was called Elijah, which is interpreted as “God the Lord,” and so forth. [lacuna]

Rome was founded on the Palatine Hill on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May by the twins Remus and Romulus, sons of Rhea Silvia, who was the daughter of Numitor, the brother of King Amulius, and a Vestal virgin, but who was violated during the Salian games. [Note: [Col. 1301] Manuscripts 1 and 2 distinguish the phrase in this way: “violated”; manuscript 3 has “during the Consualian games,” as in Bede.] In the third year after the rape of the Sabine women, Remus was killed by Fabius, Romulus’s commander, [Col. 1301B] with a pastoral mattock. [Note: [Col. 1301] Manuscripts 1 and 2 read this way, that is, *rutro*; manuscript 3 and Bede have *rastro*, “with a hoe.”]

Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, for 29 years. In his sixth year, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured Samaria and transferred Israel to Assyria. Its kingdom had stood for 360 years from the first Jeroboam, and so forth. [lacuna]

Those Jews who remained fled to Egypt. After five years, when Egypt had been struck by the Chaldeans, they too were carried into captivity to Babylon.

## On the Fifth Age of the World

The fifth age of the world began with the destruction of the Jewish kingdom, which, according to the prophecy of Jeremiah, lasted 70 years, and so forth. [lacuna]

Josephus agrees with this. In the tenth book of the *Antiquities*, he writes that the Temple, Jerusalem, and all Judea [Col. 1301C] remained desolate for 70 years. Then, when he again enumerates the kings of Babylon—if indeed he himself wrote it in this way, and the faulty manuscript is not at fault [Note: [Col. 1301] “Si tamen” is a parenthesis in this form in manuscripts 1 and 2.]—he makes it possible to reckon one hundred years [Note: [Col. 1301] Manuscript 3 reads “almost.”] from the destruction of Jerusalem to the destruction of the Chaldean kingdom, and so forth. [lacuna]

In the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, the Lord redeemed the world through his Passion. The apostles, about to preach throughout the regions of Judea, appointed James, the Lord’s brother, bishop at Jerusalem. They also appointed seven deacons; and after Stephen had been stoned, the Church was scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria. [Note: [Col. 1301] At this point especially we stop; the following words are written in manuscript 1, folio 20, beside the history of Ptolemy Philadelphus, though in another ink: “Five synods are reported to have been held by the apostles: the first concerning the election of Matthias; the second concerning the election of the seven deacons; the third, that circumcision should not be imposed on the Gentiles; the fourth, that the Jews should not be prohibited from the Law; the fifth, when the apostles were about to depart from one another.”] Agrippa, surnamed Herod, son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, went to Rome as the accuser of Herod the tetrarch and was thrown into chains. [Note: [Col. 1301] Manuscript 3 reads “was cast into chains.”] There he won many people to his friendship, [Col. 1301D] especially Gaius, the son of Germanicus, and so forth. [lacuna]

Domitian, younger brother of Titus, for 15 years and 5 months. He was the second after Nero to persecute Christians. Under him the apostle John was exiled to the island of Patmos, and Flavia Domitilla, niece through her sister of Flavius Clemens [Col. 1302A] the consul, was exiled to the island of Pontia on account of her testimony to the faith.

## On the Principal Kingdoms

[Note: [Col. 1301] Everything before this was copied from Bede; for what follows, compare Jordanes, *On the Succession of Kingdoms*.]

The first Assyrian kingdom began with Ninus, son of Belus, and his wife Semiramis, and continued up to the king Thonosconcoleros, who in Greek is called Sardanapalus. Abarces, prefect of the Medes, defeated him and transferred that kingdom to the Medes. Thirty-six kings ruled in it for 1,240 years. From the beginning of the world until the rise of this kingdom, according to the chronicle of Eusebius, 3,142 years had passed. Babylon was the capital of this kingdom. After its destruction, the kingdom of the Medes began. It had stood from King Abarces to Astyages, whom Cyrus defeated, for 259 years under 8 kings, while the Chaldeans meanwhile ruled Babylon with considerable power.

[Col. 1302B] Next came the Persian kingdom. Cyrus greatly enlarged it by adding the kingdoms of the Medes and Chaldeans. From Cyrus himself to King Darius, son of Arsames, it stood for 231 years under 14 kings. Alexander the Great, king of the Macedonians, destroyed it after killing Darius, subjected the entire East to himself, and founded Alexandria in Egypt.

Then came the kingdom of the Greeks, or Alexandrians, lasting from Alexander the Great himself to Ptolemy Dionysius and his sister Cleopatra and the monarchy of Julius Caesar. It lasted 281 years under 11 kings, although Cleopatra herself later reigned for 20 years with Julius’s permission, up to the fifteenth year of Octavian Augustus.

[Col. 1302C] After this came the most excellent Roman kingdom. It had already grown under kings and consuls; rising with Julius Caesar himself and Octavian Augustus, it ruled almost the whole world and continued up to the present time, gradually declining.

These are the principal kingdoms succeeding one another in the course of time, together with the other kingdoms shaken by the storms of war.

Among these there were many other kingdoms, indeed smaller than those mentioned above but nevertheless very famous in the writings of historians. The more prominent among them are these: those of the Sicyonians, Egyptians, Argives, Hebrews, Athenians, Mycenaeans, Lacedaemonians, Corinthians, Macedonians, Lydians, Syrians, Asians, and Latins, who were later called Romans. But how the Latins rose to Roman greatness, let us say briefly.

Before the famous Trojan War and the destruction of Troy, the following ruled in Italy: Janus, Saturn, Picus, Faunus, and Latinus, for 150 years. Then, [Col. 1303A] three years after the destruction of Troy—which occurred in the 877th year of the Assyrian kingdom [Note: [Col. 1303] From “De” to “morte ferienda” below in this same column is lacking in manuscript 3.]—Aeneas, an exile who came from there to Italy, took Lavinia, the daughter of Latinus, as his wife. Succeeding to the kingdom, he and his fifteen descendants, all surnamed Silvii, ruled in the city of Alba, which Ascanius, son of Aeneas, had founded, down to Amulius Silvius, brother of Numitor, for 426 years. Meanwhile, while Amulius was reigning, Rhea Silvia, also called Ilia [Note: [Col. 1303] Correct to “Ilia.”], daughter of Numitor and a Vestal virgin, falsely claimed that she had been violated by Mars and bore the twins Remus and Romulus from the union. A certain Lupa, the wife of Faustulus, the royal shepherd, nursed them. When they had grown into young men, they founded Rome; after Remus had been killed, Romulus succeeded Amulius Silvius. He and his six successors reigned down to Tarquinius Superbus for [Col. 1303B] 243 years.

Then, after Tarquin had been expelled and the royal title renounced, consuls began to hold office under Brutus. After these, tribunes of the plebs and dictators, and again consuls, governed the republic for 464 years, up to the dictatorship and monarchy of Julius Caesar. During these various wars the Roman kingdom grew. Then, enlarged by Julius Caesar and Octavian Augustus, it subjected nearly the whole world to its laws and held a unique empire throughout the world for a long time, until, through the negligence of succeeding rulers and the savagery of wars rising from every side—[Note: [Col. 1303] Manuscript 1 reads “whence”]—it reached the decline that we see today.

## On the Six Ages of the World

*(Bede, On the Times, chapter 16.)*

[Col. 1303C] The periods are divided into six ages of the world. The first age extends from Adam to Noah and contains 10 generations and 1,656 years; it perished entirely in the Flood, just as forgetfulness ordinarily submerges infancy. The second extends from Noah to Abraham and likewise encompasses 10 generations, but 296 years; it was discovered in the language, that is, in Hebrew. For it is in childhood that a human being begins to learn to speak, after infancy, which cannot speak. The third extends from Abraham to David and contains 14 generations and 940 years; and because a human being begins to be capable of begetting children from adolescence, Matthew took the beginning of the genealogy from Abraham, who was also established as the father of the nations. The fourth extends from David to the Babylonian captivity and contains, according to Matthew, likewise 14 generations and 483 years; from this age the time of kings began. [Col. 1303D] For youthful dignity is suited to kingship. The fifth then extends to the coming of the Savior in the flesh and likewise comprises 14 generations, but extends over 589 years. In it, as though wearied by burdensome old age, the Hebrew people are shaken by increasingly numerous evils. The sixth age, which is now taking place, has no definite sequence of generations or times, but, like an age of decrepitude, is itself to be struck by the death of the whole world.

In the forty-second year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, and in the twenty-eighth year after Egypt had been reduced to a province and Cleopatra had been defeated with Antony; in the [Col. 1304A] 752nd year from the founding of the City; in the third year of the 193rd Olympiad; our Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea. From the beginning of the world, 3,952 years had elapsed according to the Hebrew truth, but 5,199 according to the Seventy interpreters.

44. *(Jerome.)* The infants are slaughtered by Herod for the Lord’s sake.

46. The orator Asinius Pollio dies.

47. Herod, king of Judea, dies in great agony; Archelaus reigns in his place for 9 years.

48. A great famine occurs at Rome (A.D. 9).

50. Tiberius Caesar subdues the Dalmatians and Sarmatians. [Note: [Col. 1303] Manuscript 1 reads “Salmatians.”]

53. The gates of Janus, which had been closed by Augustus for 12 years, are opened.

[Col. 1304B] 54. The orator Messala Corvinus dies.

55. A solar eclipse occurs.

56. Archelaus is exiled by Augustus to Vienna, a city of Gaul; Augustus dies at the age of 76, and Judea is entrusted to tetrarchs (A.D. 15).

## Tiberius II

Tiberius II, Augustus’s stepson, reigned for 23 years.

1. Herod the tetrarch held the kingdom of the Jews for 24 years.

2. The mathematicians are expelled from the City.

3. The historian Livy dies. The poet Ovid dies in exile.

4. Germanicus, sent by Tiberius, defeats the Germans.

5. *(Cassiodorus.)* Thirteen cities collapse in an earthquake. Germanicus Caesar dies.

[Col. 1304C] 6. The historian and poet Fenestella dies.

7. Tiberius, after summoning many kings to him, never sent them back because of his treachery.

8. The theater of Pompey burns.

9. Tiberius makes Drusus his partner in the kingdom; Drusus dies by poison in that same year.

12. Pilate is sent by Tiberius as governor of Judea.

15. [Note: [Col. 1303] This had previously been written under year 14; “John … is beheaded in year 16” was added in manuscript 1.] Our Lord Jesus Christ is baptized by John, beginning the thirtieth year of his life, and begins to preach (A.D. 30).

17. John the Baptist is beheaded by Herod the tetrarch.

18. The Lord suffers and rises again at Jerusalem. A solar eclipse and a very great earthquake occur.

[Col. 1304D] 19. *(Jerome.)* James, the Lord’s brother, appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles, presides for 30 years. Stephen is stoned. Paul is converted. [Note: [Col. 1303] Added in the margin in another ink in manuscript 1.]

20. Pilate, placing an image of Caesar in the Temple, provokes a revolt (A.D. 35).

21. Pilate comes to Rome and reports to Caesar concerning the Lord’s miracles.

22. Tiberius reports to the Senate what he had heard from Pilate, but the Senate rejects it.

23. Tiberius severely afflicts the Roman people, and himself dies by poison.

[Col. 1305A]

## Gaius Caligula III

Gaius Caligula III, for 4 years [Note: [Col. 1305] “III” corrected to “IIII” in manuscript 1], 6 months, and 8 days, a most wicked man.

1. Herod Agrippa is appointed king of Judea by Gaius and reigns for 7 years.

2. The Jews are defeated at Alexandria (A.D. 40); Philo, the most renowned writer, pleads with Gaius on their behalf, but accomplishes nothing.

3. Pilate kills himself, oppressed by great calamities inflicted by Gaius.

4. Matthew writes the Gospel in Hebrew. Gaius is killed by his protectors.

## Claudius IV

Claudius IV, for 13 years, 8 months, and 28 days.

2. The apostle Peter comes to Rome and, preaching there for 25 years, holds the episcopate.

3. Herod Agrippa is struck by an angel and dies; [Col. 1305B] his son Agrippa reigns in his place for 26 years. Mark preaches in Egypt (A.D. 45).

4. A great famine occurs; Claudius subdues Britain.

5. A new island of 30 stadia appears in the sea.

6. The Roman citizens are counted under Claudius and found to number 6,944,000. [Note: [Col. 1305] Manuscript 1 writes the number as “LXes VIIII es C et XLIIII.”]

7. Thirty thousand Jews are killed during the days of Unleavened Bread in a revolt (A.D. 49).

9. Claudius expels the Jews from the City.

10. A great famine occurs at Rome.

11. Claudius appoints Felix procurator of Judea.

12. During these times Simon Magus, the founder of the Simoniac heresy, appears (A.D. 55).

[Col. 1305C] 13. A certain Egyptian false prophet, leading many Jews astray, is suppressed by Felix.

14. Claudius dies by poison at the age of 64.

## Nero V

Nero V, for 13 years, 7 months, and 28 days. This man, infamous in every respect, carried out the first persecution of Christians.

1. A revolt arises at Caesarea and destroys many Jews.

2. The apostle Paul is sent to Rome by Festus, the governor.

3 [Note: [Col. 1305] For this year, by some error, the number LX (60) was entered in manuscript 1; likewise below LXX (70), and others.]. Up to this point, the Acts of the Apostles, covering 27 years from the Lord’s Passion.

4. The poet Statius is held in renown (A.D. 60).

[Col. 1305D] 5. Nero killed his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister.

6. Nero raged in boundless luxury, debauchery, and indolence.

7. (Jerome.) James, the brother of the Lord, is stoned by the Jews.

8. Mark the Evangelist suffered at Alexandria.

9. Nero built the Neronian Baths.

10. So that he might see a likeness of burning Troy, Nero burned a large part of Rome [Col. 1306A] (A.D. 65).

11. Nero killed his teacher Seneca [Note: [Col. 1305] This is written in the margin in another ink.]. Jerome, in his *Book of Illustrious Men*: “Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Cordoba, a disciple of the Stoic philosopher Photinus, uncle of the poet Lucan, wrote many letters to the apostle Paul, and Paul to him. He wished to be among his own people what Paul was held to be among the Christians.”

12. Vespasian, commander of the army, was sent by Nero against the rebellious Jews.

13. Peter and Paul were slaughtered by Nero on account of Simon Magus on the third day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1305] “Third day before the Kalends of July,” in another ink.]; a plague also occurred at Rome, and Nero killed himself (A.D. 69).

[Codex marginal note: This chronicle, in the succession of the Roman pontiffs, follows Eusebius, not the pontifical book, which nevertheless, I think, ought to have been trusted more for this account; for Pope Damasus, at the request of Saint Jerome [Note: [Col. 1305] “Jerome” in manuscript 1.], copied it with the greatest care.]

Linus, the first pope after blessed Peter, held office for 12 years and suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 1305] “P., sixth day before the Kalends of December,” in another ink, manuscript 1.].

Ignatius was ordained the second bishop of Antioch.

GALBA, the sixth, seven months. OTHO, three months. VITELLIUS, eight months.

VESPASIAN, the seventh, while fighting in Judea, was appointed emperor by the army and reigned 9 years, 11 months, and 22 days. He was a man outstanding in military valor.

1. Titus [Note: [Col. 1305] “Eight” has been added in error, and is also found below in its proper place, manuscript 1.] besieged the Jews, who were tormented by an indescribable famine.

[Col. 1306C] 2. Jerusalem was conquered and destroyed by Titus, 42 years after the Passion [Note: [Col. 1305] “Two” and “one” added in another ink, manuscript 1.], and 1,089 years after the original construction of the Temple under Solomon [Note: [Col. 1305] “Two” and “one” added in another ink, manuscript 1.].

5. At this time Josephus the historian was held in renown.

7. The Colossus was erected, with a height of 107 feet.

9. A plague occurred at Rome, and an earthquake overthrew three cities in Cyprus.

10. Vespasian died at a villa near the Sabines from a discharge of the bowels.

TITUS, the eighth, son of Vespasian, reigned 2 years and 2 months. He was remarkable for every kind of virtue, so that he was called “the delight” [Note: [Col. 1305] “wealth” in manuscripts 1 and 2.] and love of the human race.

[Col. 1306D] 1. Titus built the amphitheater at Rome; at its dedication he killed 5,000 wild beasts.

2. Anacletus, the second pope, held office for 12 years and suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1305] “Sixth day before the Kalends of May,” in another ink; this should not be assigned to Anacletus but to Cletus.]. After Pope Linus, certain books list Cletus, and after Clement, Anacletus; but Eusebius’ history entirely omits Pope Cletus.

Titus died in the same villa as his father, in the forty-second year of his life.

DOMITIAN, the ninth, brother of Titus, reigned 15 years and [Col. 1307A] 5 months. Polluted by every crime, he carried out the second persecution of the Christians.

1. Domitian prohibited the making of eunuchs.

2. By decree of the Senate, Titus was enrolled among the gods.

3. Three Vestal virgins were condemned for sexual misconduct (A.D. 85).

4. Anianus, the first bishop of Alexandria after Mark the Evangelist, died after 22 years; Abilius, the second, succeeded him and held office for 13 years.

6. Domitian ordered himself to be called “God” and “Lord.”

8. Quintilian the rhetorician was held in renown at Rome (A.D. 90).

9. At this time the heresy of Menander the magician, the Ebionites, the Cerinthians, and the Nicolaitans arose.

[Col. 1307B] 10. At this time the Romans suffered many evils from Caesar and from their enemies.

11. Domitian celebrated triumphs over the Dacians and Germans.

12. Clement, the third pope, held office for 9 years. Cornelia, a Vestal virgin, was buried alive for sexual misconduct.

[Marginal note in the codex: Note [Note: [Col. 1307] In another ink in the margin, manuscript 1.] the apparent contradiction: Clement is said to have been enthroned in the apostolic see in the thirty-second year after the death of James, the brother of the Lord, and to have issued certain decretal decisions to the same person.]

13. Domitian killed many nobles.

14. The apostle John was sent by Domitian into exile on the island of Patmos, where he wrote the Apocalypse.

15. Domitian banished Flavia Domitilla, together with many others, into exile for the faith of Christ.

16. After committing many evils, Domitian was cruelly [Col. 1307C] killed by his own men.

NERVA, the tenth, an old man, reigned 1 year, 4 months, and 8 days. In his first edict he recalled all exiles.

1. Saint John the Apostle, returning from exile, wrote the Gospel. Nerva died, worn out by illness.

TRAJAN, the eleventh, a Spaniard by birth, reigned 19 years, 6 months, and 15 days. He was useful to the state but deceived by error, and carried out the third persecution of the Christians.

1. Cerdo, the third bishop of Alexandria, held office for 12 years.

2. The apostle John “fell asleep in peace” at Ephesus, 68 years after the Lord’s Passion.

3 [Note: [Col. 1307] These words were inserted in somewhat different ink, manuscript 1.]. Jerome’s *Book of Illustrious Men* asserts that Pope Clement died here on the ninth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 1307] “Ninth day before the Kalends of December,” in another ink, manuscript 1.] and was the fourth after blessed Peter.

[Col. 1307D] 4. Evarestus, the fourth pope, held office for 8 years and suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 1307] “Suffered on the sixth day before the Kalends of November,” in another ink, manuscript 1.]. Trajan celebrated triumphs over the Dacians and Scythians.

5. Trajan subjected many peoples to Roman rule.

6. At this time Symeon, son of Clopas, was crucified as bishop of Jerusalem. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was held in renown as a learned teacher (A.D. 105).

8. (Jerome.) There was a great earthquake [Note: [Col. 1307] Added in another ink.]. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostles, was still flourishing [Col. 1308A] at that time.

9. At this time Pliny Secundus, a renowned philosopher, softened Trajan’s attitude toward the Christians.

10. An earthquake overthrew many cities; Nero’s Golden House was destroyed by fire, and the Pantheon was burned by lightning (A.D. 109).

12. Alexander, the fifth pope, held office for 10 years [Note: [Col. 1307] The following words are in another ink, manuscript 1.]; he was crowned with martyrdom on the fifth day before the Nones of March.

13. Primus, the fourth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 12 years.

14. After Justus, bishop of Jerusalem, Zacheus held office.

15. An earthquake almost destroyed all of Antioch.

[Col. 1308B] 16. Trajan made Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia provinces (A.D. 115).

17. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was martyred.

18. The Jews, having risen in revolt, carried out great massacres; but in Alexandria they were defeated and slaughtered everywhere by all.

19. Trajan died at Seleucia from a discharge of the bowels, in the sixty-fourth year of his life.

HELIUS HADRIAN, the twelfth, reigned 21 years. Having been instructed through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides, a wise man, by apologetic writings, he became mild toward the Christians.

1. Hadrian restored Alexandria at public expense.

[Col. 1308C] 2. Hadrian again crushed the Jews (A.D. 120).

[Col. 1308C] 3. Sixtus, the sixth pope, held office for 12 years. Hadrian remitted many taxes.

4. An earthquake occurred. War was waged against the Sarmatians.

5. Hadrian led colonies into Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews.

6. Justinus, the fifth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 11 years. Hadrian gave a law to the Athenians.

7. After Philip, Seneca became the tenth bishop of Jerusalem (A.D. 125).

8. At this time Aquila was regarded as an interpreter.

9. Having received the apologetic writings of our people, Hadrian sent letters on behalf of the Christians.

11. At this time Saturninus, Basilides, and Carpocrates [Col. 1308D] founded a heresy.

12. Hadrian was first called “father of his country” (A.D. 130).

13. Cornelius was appointed bishop of Antioch. Nicopolis and Caesarea collapsed in an earthquake.

14. Pope Sixtus [Note: [Col. 1307] This is in another ink, manuscript 1.] suffered under the emperor Hadrian on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

15. Thelesphorus, the seventh pope, held office for 7 years; according to [Note: [Col. 1307] “i. h. E. a. XI.” in another ink.] the history [Col. 1309A] of Eusebius [Note: [Col. 1309D] Namely, Jerome’s *Chronicle* and the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*.], 11 years. He suffered on the fourth day before the Nones of January [Note: [Col. 1309] “P., fourth day before the Nones of January,” in another ink.].

16. The Jews took up arms and devastated Palestine.

17. Eumenes, the sixth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 13 years (A.D. 135).

18. The Jews, having again risen in revolt, were slain everywhere in great massacres.

19. Jerusalem was restored by Hadrian [Note: [Col. 1309] A red “h,” manuscript 1.] and, from his name, called Aelia; entry was forbidden to the Jews.

20. Mark was ordained the first bishop of Jerusalem from among the gentiles, after fifteen bishops from the Jewish people had died.

21. Hadrian died of dropsy, more than sixty [Col. 1309B] years old.

ANTONINUS, surnamed PIUS, the thirteenth, reigned 23 years [Note: [Col. 1309] “Twenty-two” corrected to “twenty-three,” manuscript 1.] and 3 months. Instructed by the apology of Justin, the Christian philosopher [Note: [Col. 1309] In a scraped-out place, manuscript 1.] and later martyr, he became merciful toward our people.

1. Hyginus, the eighth pope, held office for 4 years [Note: [Col. 1309] The remainder is in another ink.]. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of January (A.D. 140).

2. Antoninus was called “father of his country.”

3. Valentinus and Cerdo, and after them Marcion and Marcus, attacked the Church with heresy.

4. Justin the philosopher wrote an apology for the Christians to Antoninus [Note: [Col. 1309] “Justus,” manuscript 1.].

5. Pius, the ninth pope, held office for 15 years [Note: [Col. 1309] The remainder is in another ink, manuscript 1.]. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of July.

6. Heros was appointed bishop of Antioch (A.D. [Col. 1309C] 145).

9. Marcus, the seventh bishop of Alexandria, held office for 10 years.

10 [Note: [Col. 1309] This is in another ink, manuscript 1; it is absent from the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*.]. Pope Pius consecrated, beside the baptistery of Saint Praxedis, the titular church of Saint Hermas, concerning whom the Apostle says to the Romans: “Greet Phlegon, Hermas.” The book called *The Shepherd* is believed to be his, although apocryphal; it is much used among the Greeks.

13. Apollonius and Basilides were held in renown as philosophers (A.D. 152).

17. Crescens the Cynic philosopher stirred up persecution against our philosopher Justin, in which the latter died for Christ.

18. Celadion, the eighth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 14 years.

[Col. 1309D] 19. Anicetus, the tenth pope, held office for 11 years. He was crowned with martyrdom on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1309] “M. C., sixteenth day before the Kalends of May,” in another ink, manuscript 1.]. In his time, Hegesippus records that he came to Rome and remained there until Pope Eleutherus [Note: [Col. 1309] “From ‘whose’ through ‘remained’ in another ink,” manuscript 1.].

[Col. 1310A] 21. After Mark, Cassianus became the seventeenth bishop of Jerusalem (A.D. 160).

22. Antoninus Pius died at Lorium, in the seventy-seventh year of his life [Note: [Col. 1309] The year “fourteen” has been added in another ink to “twenty-three.”].

MARCUS ANTONINUS VERUS, the fourteenth, together with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus, reigned 19 years and 1 month.

1. They first administered the empire with equal authority.

2. When Caesar Lucius was sacrificing at Athens, a fire was seen in the sky being carried from east to west.

3. Fronto was held in renown as an eminent orator (A.D. 165).

4. The Caesars celebrated triumphs over the Parthians.
