5. Under these emperors the fourth persecution arose; at that time Polycarp and many others in Asia, and many saints in Gaul, received the crown.

[Col. 1310B] 7 [Note: [Col. 1309] This is in a scraped-out place, manuscript 1.]. At this time a very great plague devastated many cities and almost destroyed the Roman army.

8. Soter, the eleventh pope, held office for 9 years [Note: [Col. 1309] “Eight,” corrected to “nine,” manuscript 1.]. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1309] “H., eleventh day before the Kalends of May,” in another ink.]. Theophilus, a wise man, was ordained bishop of Antioch (A.D. 170).

10. Agrippinus, the ninth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 10 years. Caesar Lucius died of apoplexy.

11. (Jerome.) At this time Hegesippus, Dionysius bishop of Corinth, Pinytus bishop of Crete, Theophilus bishop of Antioch, Modestus [Note: [Col. 1309D] Absent from Jerome.], Melito, Apollinaris, and many other renowned teachers were held in renown.

13. The heresy of the Cataphrygians arose.

14. At this time Tatianus [Note: [Col. 1309] Read “Tatianus.”] founded the heresy of the Encratites.

15. Antoninus made his son Commodus his associate in the kingdom.

16. The emperors celebrated triumphs over their enemies and remitted debts owed by the common people.

17. Eleutherus, the twelfth pope, held office for 13 years [Note: [Col. 1309] “E. P., twelve years, then thirteen; initially written at the beginning of year 15, then placed under year 16, and in another ink assigned to year 17.”]. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1309] “H., eighth day before the Kalends of June,” in another ink.]. Lucius, king of Britain, obtained from Pope Eleutherus that he might become a Christian.

18. Antoninus died in Pannonia (A.D. 180).

LUCIUS ANTONINUS COMMODUS, the fifteenth, reigned 13 years after his father’s death. He successfully defeated the Germans; otherwise he was obscene and depraved.

1. Julianus, the tenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 10 years.

2. The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned.

3. At this time Pantaenus and Clement were held in renown at Alexandria [Col. 1310D] (A.D. 185).

4. Maximus was ordained the twenty-seventh bishop of Jerusalem.

5. The Commodian Baths were built at Rome.

6. Origen was born at Alexandria.

[Col. 1311A] 7. At this time a certain Montanus founded the Cataphrygian heresy.

8. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, and other teachers became renowned.

9. The Capitol and the library at Rome were burned by lightning (A.D. 190).

10. Victor, the thirteenth pope, held office for 11 years [Note: [Col. 1311] “Victor—forty-three” had first been assigned to the following year in manuscript 1. In Jerome’s *Chronicle*, the name Demetrius precedes the discussion of Easter.]. Demetrius, the eleventh bishop of Alexandria, held office for 43 years. After removing the head of the Colossus, Commodus ordered that the head of his own image be installed.

12. A great dispute about Easter arose, and it was ordered that it be celebrated on Sunday.

13. Commodus, a burden to everyone, was strangled in the Vestal residence.

HELIUS PERTINAX, the sixteenth, reigned 7 months. JULIANUS, an expert in law, killed him and reigned [Col. 1311B] for 7 months.

SEVERUS, the seventeenth, an African by birth, reigned 17 years. He defeated Julianus in civil war and called himself Pertinax.

3. [Note: [Col. 1311] In manuscript 1, the year of the world 4150 and the year of Christ 200 are assigned to this year.] At this time Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, Theophilus of Caesarea, and also Polycarp and Bacchylus of Asia, together with other distinguished bishops, were held in renown.

5. A Jewish and Samaritan war broke out.

6. Severus defeated the Parthians, Adiabenians, and Arabs (A.D. 200).

8. The Severan Baths were built at Antioch. [Note: [Col. 1311] This is in another ink.] Pope Victor was martyred on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

9. Pope Zephyrinus, the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 1311] “Who—September” in another ink.], who died on the seventh day before the Kalends of [Col. 1311C] September, held office for 17 years [Note: [Col. 1311] “Eighteen,” corrected to “seventeen,” manuscript 1.].

10. In the fifth persecution Severus crowned very many saints with martyrdom. Among them was Origen’s father, Leonides, who was martyred with many others.

12. During this persecution Perpetua and Felicity were condemned to the beasts at Carthage.

13. At this time Symmachus and Theodotion were regarded as interpreters.

14. Severus built a wall among the Britons for 132 miles, from sea to sea.

16. Tertullian the African was held in the highest renown (A.D. 210).

17. Severus died in Britain.

ANTONINUS CARACALLA, the eighteenth, reigned 7 years.

1. Asclepiades was ordained the ninth bishop of Antioch [Col. 1311D].

2. At this time Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, was appointed by Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem.

3. Antoninus Caracalla received his surname from the type of garment he distributed at Rome.

5. Antoninus built at Rome baths bearing his name.

6. Antoninus, driven by the impatience of lust, married his stepmother Julia.

[Col. 1312A] 7. Antoninus was killed in the forty-third year of his life.

OPIINUS [Note: [Col. 1311] Thus in manuscripts 1 and 2; “Opilius” in manuscript 3.] MACRINUS, the nineteenth, reigned 1 year.

1. Macrinus was killed together with his son Diadumenianus. At Antioch, Philetus, the tenth bishop, was appointed [Note: [Col. 1311] “At Antioch—was appointed” in another ink.].

MARCUS AURELIUS ANTONINUS, the twentieth, reigned 4 years.

1. Pope Callistus, the fifteenth, held office for 5 years; he suffered under the emperor Alexander on the second day before the Ides of October (A.D. 220) [Note: [Col. 1311] “Who—October” in another ink.].

2. Hippolytus was held in renown as a bishop.

3. In Palestine, Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, was founded.

4. Aurelius was killed at Rome in a military uprising.

AURELIUS ALEXANDER, the twenty-first, reigned 13 years. He was exceptionally devoted to his mother and beloved by all.

[Col. 1312B] 1. Alexander defeated Xerxes, king of the Persians.

2. Urbanus, the sixteenth pope, held office for 8 years. He converted many nobles to the faith of Christ and departed this life on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 1311] “Who—departed” in another ink.] (A.D. 225).

4. Ulpian, a distinguished legal expert, was held in renown.

5. The Neronian Baths were called Alexandrian.

6. Geminus the presbyter, Hippolytus and Berillus the bishops, and Bostrenus were held in renown.

7. Zebennus was the eleventh bishop of Antioch.

8. Mammea, the mother of Alexander, summoned Origen, the most celebrated teacher, to her and had him heard (A.D. 230).

10. Pontianus, the seventeenth pope, held office for 6 years; he suffered under the emperor Maximinus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 1311] “Who—December” in another ink.].

[Col. 1312C] 11. Heraclas, the twelfth bishop of Alexandria, a wise man, held office for 14 years.

13. Alexander was killed in a military uprising (A.D. 235).

MAXIMINUS, the twenty-second, reigned 3 years. He persecuted Christians, especially the leaders of the Church, in the sixth persecution after Nero.

1. (Jerome, year 213.) Alexander, the thirty-fifth bishop of Jerusalem.

2. Pope Pontianus and his successor, Pope Antherus, the eighteenth, were martyred after the first month of his pontificate, on the third day before the Nones of January [Note: [Col. 1311] “Third day before the Nones of January,” in another ink.].

3. Fabianus, the nineteenth pope, held office for 14 years. Maximinus was killed at Aquileia.

GORDIAN, the twenty-third, reigned 6 years.

[Col. 1312D] 2. Pupienus and Albinus, who had seized the empire, were killed in the palace (A.D. 240).

3. At this time Julius Africanus the chronicler was held in renown.

4. At this time Origen instructed Theodore [Note: [Col. 1311] Adds “surnamed Gregory.” 5. (See year 266.)] and Athenodorus, brothers who later became distinguished bishops, in divine philosophy.

6. Gordian, while returning victorious from the Parthians, was killed not far [Note: [Col. 1311] Written above the line, manuscript 1.] from Roman territory.

[Col. 1313A] PHILIP, the twenty-fourth, together with his son Philip, reigned 7 years. He was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian. [Note: [Col. 1313] What follows is written in the margin.] Concerning this Philip it is read in ecclesiastical history that, when he wished to receive communion on Easter Day itself, he was not permitted to do so by the local bishop until, after making a prior confession of his sins, he had made satisfaction among the penitents.

1. Philip made his son Philip his associate in the kingdom (A.D. 245).

3. (Jerome, year 249.) Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of Alexandria, a renowned teacher, held office for 19 years. [Note: [Col. 1313] What follows is in another ink.] In his time he asserted that the Sabellian heresy had arisen at Ptolemais [Note: [Col. 1313D] Eusebius reports that this was done by Saint Babylas, bishop of Antioch, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.27; despite this testimony, however, Pagius, in his critique of Baronius at year 244, no. 4, denies, together with other scholars, that Philip was a Christian. Uss.].

4. The thousandth year from the founding of the City was celebrated with festivities.

5. In these times Origen the presbyter wrote so much [Col. 1313B] that Jerome says in one place that he had read five thousand of his books [Note: [Col. 1314D] Perhaps in the letter to Paula, in which he testifies that he had compiled a catalogue of Origen’s works, chapter 54 of *On Illustrious Men*; that work, however, has perished. Uss.].

7. Philip the elder was killed at Verona, and the younger at Rome.

DECIUS, the twenty-fifth, reigned 1 year and 3 months. He launched the seventh persecution against the Christians.

1. Fabianus was martyred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1313] “Thirteenth day before the Kalends of February,” in another ink.], and Pope Cornelius, the twentieth, succeeded him and held office for 3 years. Decius was killed with his son in Thrace [Note: [Col. 1313] “In Thrace by the Goths,” in another ink.] by the Goths.

GALLUS, the twenty-sixth, together with his son Volusianus, reigned 2 years and 4 months.

1. Origen died in the seventieth year of his life. [Note: [Col. 1313] “And was buried at Tyre,” Mur.] Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 1313] “Of the Roman Church” written above the line.], became the founder of the heresy of the Novatians, who called themselves Cathars, that is, “the pure” [Note: [Col. 1313] “That is, the pure” written above the line.]. The Novatians [Note: [Col. 1313] This is written in the margin.] deny pardon to those who have fallen into sin [Col. 1313C], even if they repent worthily.

2. (Jerome, year 256.) Gallus and Volusianus were killed at Terni.

VALERIAN, the twenty-seventh, together with Gallienus, reigned 15 years. He carried out the eighth persecution against the Christians.

1. Pope Cornelius was made a martyr on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 1313] “Eighteenth day before the Kalends of October,” in another ink.]. Pope Lucius, the twenty-first, held office for 8 months and suffered on the fourth day before the Nones of March [Note: [Col. 1313] “Suffered on the fourth day before the Nones of March,” in another ink.] (A.D. 255).

2. Pope Stephen, the twenty-second, held office for 2 years and was crowned with martyrdom on the fourth day before the Nones of August [Note: [Col. 1313] “Who was crowned with martyrdom on the fourth day before the Nones of August,” in another ink.].

3. Cyprian, an outstanding teacher and bishop of Carthage, was crowned with martyrdom.

4. (Jerome, years 260–262; HERM., year 259.) Pope Sixtus, the twenty-third, held office for 11 years [Note: [Col. 1313] This is in another ink.]; he was beheaded for Christ on the eighth day before the Ides of August. Valerian, after initiating a persecution, was captured by Shapur, king of the Persians, and deprived of his eyes; he grew old in miserable slavery. Terrified, Gallienus restored peace to the Christians.

8. The Germans ravaged Italy; the Alemanni ravaged Gaul and Italy.

[Col. 1314A] 9. (Cf. Jerome, year 266.) Greece, Macedonia, Pontus, and Asia were devastated by the Goths.

11. (Jerome, year 267.) Maximus, the fourteenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 18 years.

12. At this time Theodore, also called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, became renowned for his miracles.

13. Hymenaeus was appointed the thirty-seventh bishop of Jerusalem.

14. Dionysius, the twenty-fourth pope, held office for 9 years. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 1313] “He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January,” in another ink.].

15. Gallienus was killed at Milan.

CLAUDIUS, the twenty-eighth, reigned 1 year and 9 months. He defeated the Goths, who had already been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for 15 years.

1. Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, [Col. 1314B] was proved to be a heretic. [Note: [Col. 1313] This is in the upper margin of the page, manuscript 1.] As bishop of Antioch, he took pleasure in the company of women and permitted the same to his clergy, so that they could not accuse him of this crime, since they were bound by the same crime. He also asserted that Christ was a human being of common nature. When he refused to leave the Church after being condemned, he was expelled from the Church by public authority, to add to his disgrace, as the ecclesiastical history relates (*Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History* VII, chapters 23–24) [A.D. 270].

2. Claudius died at Sirmium; his brother QUINTILLUS reigned for 17 days and was killed at Aquileia.

AURELIAN, the twenty-ninth, reigned 5 years and 6 months. Useful to the state, he was at first merciful toward the Christians, but later became their persecutor.

[Col. 1314C] 2. Zenobia [Note: [Col. 1313] “Zenobia,” with the letter C in red; compare the following year.] queen of the East was defeated.

3. When Aurelian celebrated a triumph at Rome, Tetricus and Zenobia preceded him as captives.

4. Aurelian built a temple to the Sun and launched the ninth persecution against the Christians (A.D. 275).

5. (Jerome, year 278.) Aurelian, terrified by a divine thunderbolt, was killed by soldiers between Byzantium and Heraclea.

(Ibid., year 279.) TACITUS, the thirtieth, reigned 6 months. After he was killed in Pontus, FLORIAN reigned for 88 days and was killed at Tarsus.

1. Felix, the twenty-fifth pope, held office for 5 years [Note: [Col. 1313] “Six,” corrected to “five”; the remainder is in another ink, manuscript 1.] and was crowned with martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of June.

PROBUS, the thirty-first, reigned 6 years and 4 months.

1. Gaul, devastated by the barbarians, was restored to the Roman Empire by Probus [Col. 1314D].

2. Anatolius was held in renown as bishop of Laodicea.

3. A certain Manes, a Persian by birth, founded the deranged heresy of the Manichaeans (A.D. 280).

4. Quirillus was appointed the eighteenth bishop of Antioch.

[Col. 1315A] 5. Eutychianus, the twenty-sixth pope, held office for 10 months [Note: [Col. 1315] The remainder is in another ink.] and suffered for Christ on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

6. Gaius, the twenty-seventh pope, held office for 15 years. Theonas, the fifteenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 18 years. Probus was killed at Sirmium in a military uprising.

CARUS, the thirty-second, together with his sons Carinus and Numerianus, reigned 2 years.

1. Carus, victorious over the Parthians, died after being struck by lightning over the Tigris.

2. Numerianus was killed. Carinus was killed by Diocletian at Margus. Up to this point, according to Dionysius, 284 years have been reckoned from the Lord’s incarnation (A.D. 285).

DIOCLETIAN, the thirty-third, reigned 20 years.

1. From this year the Greeks began their paschal cycles.

[Col. 1315B] 2. Diocletian took Herculius Maximian into partnership in the empire.

3. Maximian defeated Amandus and the peasants in Gaul.

4. At this time Carausius ravaged Britain, Narses, king of the Persians, the East, Achilleus Egypt, and the Quinquegentiani Africa (A.D. 290).

6. Diocletian made Constantius, the father of Constantine, Caesar; he reigned 16 years.

7. Diocletian made Galerius Maximian Caesar.

8. At this time the presbyter Pierius, Achillas, and Melitius became renowned at Alexandria.

9. At this time, in many different battles, various enemies were defeated [Col. 1315C].

11. Diocletian ordered himself to be worshiped as God.

13. After Pope Gaius was martyred on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1315] “Tenth day before the Kalends of May,” in another ink.], Marcellinus, the twenty-eighth, succeeded him and held office for 9 years [Note: [Col. 1315] “Who—May” in another ink.]. He likewise suffered for Christ, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. Up to this point, Eusebius’ ecclesiastical history clearly describes the successions of the Roman and Alexandrian bishops, as they are also set out here.

14. After defeating Achilleus, Diocletian recovered Alexandria and Egypt.

15. Constantius killed 60,000 Alemanni (A.D. 300; Jerome, year 304).

16. Peter, the sixteenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for 12 years.

17. Galerius [Note: [Col. 1315] “Valerius,” with the letter V in red, manuscript 1.] Maximian defeated Narses [Col. 1315D] and captured his wife and children.

18. Diocletian and Herculius Maximian celebrated a magnificent triumph over their enemies.

19. Diocletian in the East, and Herculius Maximian in the West, overthrew the churches, burned the divine books, and afflicted the Christians in the tenth persecution after Nero.

20. (Orosius VII.25.) Diocletian at Nicomedia and [Col. 1316A] Maximian at Milan voluntarily laid aside the purple and imperial power because of the weakness of old age.

GALERIUS [Note: [Col. 1315] “Valerius,” with the letter V in red, with a black G added.] and CONSTANTIUS, Augusti. Maximinus, a persecutor of Christians, and Severus were chosen as Caesars.

1. (The same; Jerome, year 309.) Constantius Augustus, a gentle man, died at Eboracum in Britain.

CONSTANTINE, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, reigned 30 years, 10 months. He was the first Christian emperor, apart from Philip; from him onward Christian emperors began.

1. Maxentius, son of Herculius Maximian, was called Augustus. Marcellus, the twenty-ninth pope, held office for 5 years and suffered on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1315] “Suffered on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February,” in another ink.].

2. Herculius Maximian was disgracefully killed near Massilia [Col. 1316B].

3. After Severus was killed, Licinius was made Caesar.

4. (Orosius VII.28.) Galerius [Note: [Col. 1315] “Valerius,” with the letter V in red, manuscript 1.], the persecutor of Christians, struck by divine vengeance, ordered that the Christians be spared.

5. Caesar Maximinus renewed the persecution (A.D. 310).

6. (Jerome, year 316; *Miscellaneous History*.) Peter, bishop of Alexandria, was crowned with martyrdom; Achillas succeeded him. Pope Eusebius, the thirtieth, held office for 6 years [Note: [Col. 1315] “Sixth day before the Nones of October,” in another ink.]; he died on the sixth day before the Nones of October. A great famine and plague occurred among the persecutors.

7. At last the persecution ended after 10 years.

8. (Cf. Jerome, year 315.) With God’s help, Constantine defeated Maxentius in civil war at the Milvian Bridge [Note: [Col. 1315] “Vulius,” manuscripts 1 and 2.] [Col. 1316C].

9. Caesar Maximinus died miserably and deservedly, amid great suffering.

10. Very many persecutors and magicians were slaughtered.

12. (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.10; Orosius VII.28.) Licinius Caesar, at first a good avenger of the Christians, plotting evil against Constantine and persecuting the Christians, was vic[lacuna]s and died in war. Pope Melchiades, the thirty-first, held office for 4 years and died on the fourth day before the Ides of January [Note: [Col. 1315] “Fourth day before the Ides of January,” in another ink.].

14. At this time the presbyter Arius of Alexandria founded the detestable heresy of the Arians, under Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, who had succeeded Achillas.

16. Pope Silvester, the thirty-second [Note: [Col. 1315] “Thirty-second,” corrected to “twenty-third,” manuscript 1.], held office for 23 years and 10 months. He died on the second day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 1315] “Who died on the second day before the Kalends of January,” in another ink.].

[Col. 1316D] 17. A council of 318 bishops was convened at Nicaea under Pope Silvester [Note: [Col. 1315] Above a scraped-out place, where, for example, “July” or something similar had been written, manuscript 1.]. Arius was condemned [Note: [Col. 1315] “Condemned,” and the remainder of the year, in another ink.] and 70 chapters were established, as Athanasius says, who took part in that synod.

“There are seventy statutes from Nicaea,

As Athanasius writes, together with Pope Mark.”

19. At this time the Lord’s cross was discovered at Jerusalem by Helena, the mother of Constantine [Col. 1317A], under Macarius, bishop of that city.

20. Constantine’s twentieth anniversary was celebrated at Rome (A.D. 325).

22. (Orosius VII.28.) Constantine subjected the Sarmatians, Goths, and many nations to Roman rule.

24. Constantine restored the city of Byzantium, called it Constantinople after himself, and wished it to be the seat of the Roman Empire.

25. Athanasius was ordained bishop of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1317] In another ink.].

26. At this time the Indians and Iberians became Christians (A.D. 330).

27. At this time Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, the poet Juvencus, and very many teachers became renowned.

[Col. 1317B] 28. (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IX.11; Jerome, year 340.) Antony the monk was held in renown.

29. Constantia, the sister of Constantine and wife of Licinius, died.

30. Constantine fell into the Arian doctrine.

31. While preparing for war against the Persians, Constantine died at Nicomedia in the sixty-sixth year of his life (A.D. 335).

CONSTANTIUS, son of Constantine, together with his brothers Constantine and Constans, reigned 24 years, 5 months, and 13 days.

1. Constantius became an Arian through the presbyter Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia, and persecuted the Catholics.

2. (Jerome, year 341.) James, bishop of Nisibis, became renowned for his miracles.

3. Constantine, waging war against his brother Constantius, was killed near Aquileia.

4. An earthquake destroyed many cities.

5. The Franks were subdued by Constans and received into peace (A.D. 340).

6. After the Arians expelled the bishop Paul from Constantinople, Macedonius, an arch-heretic, was substituted in his place.

7. (Jerome.) At this time Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was held in renown; Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, a fugitive from Constantius, was honorably received by him.

8. [Note: [Col. 1317] This is in another ink.] Pope Mark, the thirty-third, held office for 2 years [Note: [Col. 1317] That is, died.] and died on the Nones [Note: [Col. 1317] “On the Nones,” in yet another ink.] [Col. 1317D] of October.

9. Bishop Athanasius returned to Alexandria in response to letters from Constans.

10. An eclipse of the sun occurred, and an earthquake overthrew many [Note: [Col. 1317] This is in another ink.]. Pope Julius, the thirty-fourth, held office for 15 years and died on the second day before the Ides of April [Note: [Col. 1317] “Second day before the Ides of April,” in yet another ink; that is, “died.”] (A.D. 345).

11. War was waged against the Persians, with great loss to the Romans.

[Col. 1318A] 12. Constans was killed not far from Spain (Jerome), in the thirtieth year of his life.

14. At this time the bones of the apostles Timothy and Saint Andrew, and of Luke the Evangelist, were brought to Constantinople.

16. Antony the monk died in the wilderness in the 105th year of his life; at that time many hermits became renowned for their miracles (A.D. 351).

17. Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian were held in renown at Rome.

18. Julian was made Caesar by Constantius.

19. Great forces of the Alemanni were destroyed at Argentarium [Note: [Col. 1317] “Argentariam,” corrected to “Argentarium,” manuscript 1.].

20. Julian defeated the Germans on the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1317] Hermann and Bernold appear to have transcribed this from Orosius VII.29: “He subdued the Germans on the Rhine.”] (A.D. 355).

[Col. 1318B] 21. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, Athanasius of Alexandria, and all the Catholic bishops suffered many evils from the Arians.

22. At Rimini a synod of 400 Arian bishops was held against the faith [Note: [Col. 1317] “400 bishops” written above the line.].

23. (Orosius VII.29; cf. Jerome, year 352.) Julian, elated by the success of his wars, usurped the title of Augustus. Constantius prepared for war against the Parthians [Note: [Col. 1317] What follows is in another ink.]. Pope Liberius, the thirty-fifth, held office for 6 years. After he was expelled, Pope Felix, the thirty-sixth, occupied his place for one year; Liberius was then restored to his own see [Note: [Col. 1317] “Restored,” and the remainder, in another ink.]. Saint Felix, however, declaring the emperor Constantius to be a heretic, was martyred on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

24. Constantius, abandoning the Parthian war and taking up arms against Julian, died.

[Col. 1318C] JULIAN THE APOSTATE reigned 1 year and 8 months. Having changed from a Christian reader into a pagan, he persecuted the Christians.

1. Pagans invaded the tomb of Saint John the Baptist at Sebaste (A.D. 360).

2. Julian set out for the Parthian war and, vowing the blood of the Christians to his gods, died after being killed by a certain enemy through God’s judgment, in the thirty-second year of his life.

JOVIAN reigned 8 months. He returned again to Christianity together with his entire army.

1. A heretical synod was held at Antioch. Jovian, reclining in a new house, died by suffocation from the odor of burning coals and lime.

[Col. 1318D] **VALENTINIAN**, 11 years. Because of the faith of Christ, he had been deprived by Julian of his military tribunate.

1. Valentinian gave the rule of the East to his brother Valens.

2. (OROSIUS VII, 32.) Valens, led astray and baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted the orthodox after his brother’s death.

3. (JEROME, year 370.) Gratian, the son of Valentinian, [Col. 1319A] was made emperor at Amiens. True wool, mixed with rain, flowed from the clouds.

4. Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted the Christians among his people [Note: [Col. 1319] The following words are in different ink.]. Pope Damasus, the thirty-seventh, sat for 18 years. —3. [Note: [Col. 1319] “The third day before the Ides of December” is in different ink.] The Ides of December.

5. At this time Bishop Apollinaris wrote many works, but later founded a heresy.

6. A great famine occurred in Phrygia.

7. In these days, after the death of Auxentius the Arian, Ambrose was ordained bishop of Milan.

8. (JEROME, year 377.) Valentinian subdued the Saxons in the region of the Franks by slaughter.

9. (The same.) Nearly 80,000 Burgundians settled beside the Rhine.

10. After Auxentius the Arian, when Ambrose had been ordained, Italy returned to the true faith.

11. (OROSIUS VII, 32.) Valentinian, preparing war against the Sarmatians, died of apoplexy.

**VALENS**, after his brother’s death, ruled with Gratian and Valentinian for 4 years.

1. Gratian destroyed 30,000 Alemanni.

2. Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army; when they refused, he ordered them to be killed with clubs. When the Goths were given Arian teachers by Valens, they became Arians (A.D. 375).

3. (JEROME, year 381.) Driven by famine, the Goths rebelled.

4. Valens, fleeing after his army had been killed by the Goths, was burned alive in a certain house. Up to this point Jerome brought the chronicle of Eusebius. From here onward, to the year 1054 from the Lord’s incarnation, Lord Hermann brought down his chronicle.

378. After the death of Valens, the Arian emperor, Gratian ruled with his brother Valentinian for 6 years [Note: [Col. 1319] The word “one” was added in different ink.].

379. The emperor Gratian appointed Theodosius emperor of the East. At this time Priscillian, a bishop from Gaul, founded the heresy named after himself.

380. From this year Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, began the paschal cycles.

381. The second universal synod of 150 bishops was held at Constantinople against Macedonius, the heresiarch and bishop of that city, under the emperor Theodosius and [Note: [Col. 1319] In an erased place, formerly “a?”] Pope Damasus; and [Note: [Col. 1319] “and three canons are established after the condemnation of the aforesaid heretic” is written in an erased place in different ink.] after the condemnation of the aforesaid heretic, three canons were established.

[Col. 1319D] 383. Arcadius, the son of the emperor Theodosius, was taken by his father into partnership in the kingdom and ruled for 26 years.

384. Maximus, usurping the kingdom for himself, killed Gratian at Lyons. At Rome, after Pope Damasus, Siricius—called Ursinus in the chronicles of Prosper—the fortieth pope, sat for 14 years. If you count Saint Peter and Pope Cletus among the aforesaid pontiffs, whom we omitted from the numbering, you will certainly find Pope Siricius to be fortieth in order. [Col. 1320A] Note also that the succession of the Roman prelates and their years are found recorded very differently in certain books. Jerome the presbyter, now living at Bethlehem, was held in renown. Priscillian the heretic, about to be condemned at the synod of Bordeaux, fled, but was killed at Trier by the prefect Evodius.

386. At this time Pope Siricius wrote 15 decretal chapters to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona [Note: [Col. 1319] These same words were written by the same hand but in different ink.].

388. The emperor Theodosius killed the tyrant Maximus at Aquileia.

389. The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius were deprived of communion with the Church because of the killing of Priscillian, whom they had accused.

390. At this time Saint Martin and Ambrose, bishops, Jerome the presbyter, John Chrysostom, [Col. 1320B] Augustine, Severus, and many other teachers flourished.

392. Valentinian ended his life by a noose through the treachery of Arbogast. Jerome brought down to this point the book he wrote about the illustrious men of the Church.

393. The emperor Theodosius ruled for three years with his sons Arcadius and Honorius.

394. John the anchorite, whose life Jerome described, foretold that the emperor Theodosius would be victorious against the tyrant Eugenius.

395. The emperor Theodosius defeated the tyrant Eugenius and himself rested in peace at Milan in the same year. In his place, his sons Arcadius and Honorius ruled for 13 years [Note: [Col. 1319] “In his place … 13” is in the margin.]. Augustine was ordained bishop at Hippo. The hermit John migrated to the Lord. Up to this point Eusebius Rufinus [Note: [Col. 1319] The initials “R. S. I. P. T. E.” are in an erased place, written by the same hand.] or Jerome brought down the ecclesiastical history, translating it.

396. Count Gildo tyrannically usurped Africa for himself.

397. Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, migrated to the Lord at the age of 81 and after 26 years in the episcopate; Sulpicius Severus excellently composed his life and miracles.

398. Saint Ambrose, archbishop of Milan and outstanding teacher, migrated to the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. At Rome Anastasius, the forty-first pope, sat for 4 years. Count Gildo was defeated in battle and died.

399. The temples of the idols were destroyed, and the gladiatorial games were abolished.

400. (BEDE.) The Goths devastated Italy. At this time [Col. 1320D] Pope Anastasius issued his decrees and condemned the Manichaeans found in the City. The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by the Lord.

401. John of Constantinople and Theophilus were held in the highest esteem, but were so opposed that through Theophilus’s efforts John was exiled to Pontus.

402. The Goths put the commander Stilicho to flight together with the Roman army. Innocent, the forty-second pope, sat for 14 years, and [Note: [Col. 1321] “who … wrote” was added in different ink.] wrote 57 decretal chapters.

403. A council was held at Carthage against the Donatists.

404. (BEDE.) At this time Pope Innocent issued many decrees. The presbyter Orosius was held in renown.

405. At this time Radagaisus, with 200,000 Goths, was defeated by God’s gift.

406. The Vandals, Suebi, and Alans, having crossed the Rhine, entered Gaul as enemies on the third day before the Kalends of January.

407. Pope Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius because he consented to the expulsion of John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 1321] All these words are in an erased place, in different ink; compare Hermann.] [Note: [Col. 1321D] Learned men judge the letter of Innocent to Eudoxia and the two letters of Arcadius to Innocent—from which Bernold derived this account—to be spurious; compare Pagius, in the life of this pontiff, *Brev. Rom. pontif.*, vol. I, no. 28. Ussher.].

408. The emperor Arcadius died at Constantinople, [Col. 1321B] leaving his son Theodosius as his successor. From then on his uncle Honorius ruled with him for 15 years. The brave commander Stilicho was killed by the emperor Honorius.

409. The Vandals, Alans, and Suebi occupied Spain on a day in October [Note: [Col. 1321] Thus in the first and second copies.].

410. Alaric, king of the Goths, besieged and entered Rome, 1164 years after the founding of the City; and because he was a Christian, he spared only the sacred places and those who fled to them.

411. Pestilence, famine, wild beasts, and the barbarian sword devastated the wretched world far and wide.

412. Most of the Goths entered Gaul. Heros, the holy and innocent bishop of Arles and disciple of Saint Martin, was driven from his see, and Patroclus was ordained in his place.

[Col. 1321C] 413. At this time Pelagius the Briton, with the support of Celestius and Julian, disturbed the faith of the Church by exalting free will beyond what was proper and asserting that a human being could become perfect by his own effort, without the help of the Lord’s grace. Blessed Augustine attacked his heresy more singularly than all others, and Pope Innocent condemned it together with the other heretics. The Burgundians acquired the part of Gaul adjoining the Rhine.

414. At the instigation of the Goths, Attalus seized tyrannical power in Gaul.

415. The Goths marched toward Spain; deprived of their protection, Attalus was captured by the Romans. At Jerusalem, the bodies of the holy protomartyr Stephen, Gamaliel, and Nicodemus, divinely revealed to the presbyter Lucian, were found.

416. At Rome Zosimus, the forty-third pope, sat for three years. He also promulgated decrees concerning the condition of the Church to Bishop Hesychius [Note: [Col. 1321] “Y. E. S. Q. C.” was added in different ink.] in four chapters.

417. The emperor Honorius entered Rome in triumph, [Col. 1322A] with Attalus preceding his chariot and later being sent into exile. A question and dispute concerning the Easter of this year arose [Note: [Col. 1321] The word was added.] under Pope Zosimus.

418. A council of 217 bishops was assembled at Carthage and confirmed by Pope Zosimus; Pelagius and the other heretics were condemned. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

419. The emperor Honorius made the commander Constantius his partner in the imperial power. At Rome Boniface, the forty-fourth pope, who issued four decrees [Note: [Col. 1321] “who made four decrees” was written above the line by the same hand.], sat for four years. During his pontificate Eulalius was ordained pope by others, but was nevertheless deposed by the emperor.

420. At Bethlehem the presbyter Jerome, an outstanding interpreter, died at the age of 91 [Note: [Col. 1321] The copy has *obiut*.].

421. The emperor Constantius died at Ravenna.

[Col. 1322B] 423. The empress Placidia, driven out by her brother Honorius, went eastward to the emperor Theodosius. At Rome Celestine, the forty-fifth pope, sat for 9 years; he wrote 22 decretal chapters to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 1321] “22 chapters of decrees written to the bishops of Gaul” is in different ink.]. The emperor Honorius of the West died at Ravenna, and the tyrant John seized his kingdom.

424. Theodosius made Valentinian, the son of his maternal aunt Placidia, Caesar and sent him back with his mother to possess the kingdom of the West.

425. Valentinian, together with his mother, overthrew the tyrant John at Ravenna.

426. Patroclus, bishop of Arles, was innocently murdered by a certain barbarian tribune.

427. Boniface, powerful in Africa, killed certain commanders who were fighting against him. When barbarians were summoned against him, the sea, previously unknown, was made passable.

428. Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who preached two persons in Christ and affirmed that a mere human being was born from the Virgin and later received divinity, was accused of heresy by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and Pope Celestine.

429. Agricola, a Pelagian heretic, infected Britain with his error.

430. Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, was besieged by barbarians in his own city. While, amid the hardships of the siege, he was concerned for the Church and, fighting for God’s grace, had answered the arguments of Julian, he was taken away by God’s grace itself, so that he would not see the ruin of his people. He migrated to the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, at the age of 76 and after 40 years as bishop or presbyter.

431. The third universal synod of 200 bishops was assembled at Ephesus under Pope Celestine. There, among other heresies, Nestorius and his sect were condemned, and [Note: [Col. 1321] “and 12 chapters were written against him” is in different ink.] 12 chapters were written against him.

[Col. 1323A] 432. At Rome Xystus, the forty-sixth pope, sat for 8 years.

433. The emperor Valentinian gave many gifts to the churches.

434. The Vandals, now ravaging Africa for their ninth year, requested a treaty from the Romans.

435. Peace was made with the Vandals.

436. The Goths pressed Narbonne, which they had besieged, by famine.

437. The Romans waged war against the Goths.

438. At this time Saint Prosper, bishop of Riez, wrote against Cassianus’s book *On the Protection of God*, in which he proved that Cassianus had exalted free will too greatly [Note: [Col. 1323] These words were written in somewhat different ink.] [Note: [Col. 1323D] Here Saint Prosper of Riez, a bishop in Lombardy, is confused with Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, who was never a bishop and whose book against Cassianus survives among his works, published at Venice in 1744. See the preface there, p. XXI. Ussher.].

439. Julian, bishop of Eclanum, a most boastful Pelagian, attempting stealthily to gain communion with the Church, was again condemned by Pope Xystus.

[Col. 1323B] 440. After Xystus died at Rome, Leo, a man distinguished for learning and character, became the forty-seventh pope and sat for 22 years [Note: [Col. 1323] The following words are in an erased place.]. He condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies, and [Note: [Col. 1323] “and 49 decrees” is in different ink.] composed 49 decrees.

441. The emperor Theodosius undertook war against the Vandals through his commanders.

443. Saint Brictius, bishop of Tours, died, and Saint Eustochius succeeded him. Pope Leo exposed many Manichaeans in the City and burned their books. [Note: [Col. 1323] What follows was added in the margin.] He established [Note: [Col. 1324D] From the *Deeds of the Pontiffs of Rome*.] that a nun should in no way receive a head-covering blessed by a bishop unless her virginity had first been proved. Hence Augustine also asserts that she should not be consecrated among the holy virgins if she had been violated even before baptism.

[Col. 1323C] 444. Attila, king of the Huns, killed his brother Bleda, his partner in the kingdom. Concerning the Easter of this year, Proterius and Paschasinus wrote to Pope Leo.

445. At this time Pope Leo, among his other good works, restored the basilicas of the apostles Peter and Paul.

446. At Ephesus the Seven Sleepers, who under Decius had suffered many torments for Christ and fallen asleep in a certain cave, awoke after 196 years; once faith in the resurrection had been confirmed, they fell asleep again.

447. Eutyches, a Constantinopolitan presbyter and abbot, confusing the substance of divinity and humanity in Christ and teaching that there was one nature in him, together with the younger emperor Theodosius Augustus and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, persecuted Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, who resisted them, after expelling him, even unto death. Against this heresy Pope Leo sent legates.

448. The emperor Theodosius summoned Pope Leo to himself in defense of Eutyches. Prevented by the Roman people from coming, he sent legates in his place.

[Col. 1324A] 449. The Catholics were again summoned by the emperor Theodosius to a hearing.

450. Pope Leo arranged to send legates to refute the heresy. The emperor Theodosius died. In his place Marcian acquired the empire of the East and, ruling for 7 years, condemned Eutyches and his followers. The empress Placidia died. The Romans, under the commander Aetius and with the Goths as allies, defeated Attila, king of the Huns.

451. Attila, having gathered his forces again, captured Aquileia with great violence. The emperor Valentinian sent Pope Leo to him, and Leo made peace with him.

452. Attila, king of the Huns, died in his own territory. At this time the fourth universal synod of 630 bishops was assembled at Chalcedon against Eutyches and all the [Col. 1324B] heretics; there, after the heretics had been condemned, they established 27 canons [Note: [Col. 1323] What follows is in different ink.].

453. The emperor Valentinian treacherously killed the patrician Aetius with his own hand in the palace.

454. The emperor Valentinian was killed on the Field of Mars by Aetius’s friends. In his place Maximus seized the empire but was killed by the soldiers within two months; after him Avitus assumed the empire. In the same year Geiseric, king of the Vandals, stripped Rome of all its wealth. Up to this point Prosper brought down his chronicle; he is also believed to have composed Pope Leo’s letter on the true incarnation of the Lord against Eutyches.

455. Avitus laid down the empire at Piacenza. In his place Majorian ruled for 4 years.

[Col. 1324C] 456. The emperor Marcian of the East died; in his place the emperor Leo ruled for 17 years [Note: [Col. 1323] “one” is absent.]. From this year Victorius began the paschal cycles, though full of errors, at the command of Pope Hilary.

457. Majorian, emperor of the West, set out with an army against the Vandals in Africa.

460. The emperor Majorian was treacherously killed by the patrician Ricimer.

461. Severus was made emperor at Ravenna by Ricimer and ruled for 4 years. At Tours blessed Perpetuus became bishop and transferred the body of Saint Martin.

462. At Rome Hilary, the forty-eighth pope, sat for 6 years and 3 months. He condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies [Col. 1324D] and, among his other good works, founded two libraries in the City [Note: [Col. 1323] The copy has *biblitnecas*.], [Note: [Col. 1323] The following words are in different ink.] and established six synodical chapters.

463. The king of the Alans, marching toward Italy, was defeated in battle by the patrician Ricimer near Pergamum and died.

464. The emperor Severus perished by fraud, as they say, through Ricimer’s poison.

[Col. 1325A] 466. The emperor Leo sent Anthemius from Constantinople to Rome to govern the empire of the West; he ruled for 5 years.

467. At Toulouse, where the seat of the Gothic kingdom was, blood burst forth from the earth in the middle of the city and flowed for an entire day.

468. Arvandus, attempting to seize the empire, was transported into exile by order of the emperor Anthemius. At Rome Simplicius, the forty-ninth pope, sat for 15 years and 3 months [Note: [Col. 1325] “who … two decrees” is in different ink.]; he promulgated two decrees.

469. The patrician Romanus, aspiring to the empire, was beheaded.

470. In Gaul Saint Remigius, foretold from heaven before his birth, was forcibly taken from the cell into which, as a young man serving God, he had shut himself, [Col. 1325B] and became archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 1325] “At the age of 22,” added by Muratori.].

471. Ricimer killed the emperor Anthemius with great slaughter in the city of Rome, appointed Olybrius emperor, and himself died.

472. At Ravenna Glycerius assumed the empire. At Constantinople Leo made Leo, his nephew, his partner in the kingdom.

473. The elder emperor Leo died. After him the younger Leo ruled for a few months and then also died. After him the emperor Zeno ruled for 17 years. At Rome Nepos succeeded Glycerius in the empire.

474. The patrician Orestes drove out the emperor Nepos and gave the empire to his own son Augustulus.

475. Odoacer, king of the Torcilingi and Rugians, having overrun Italy, seized Rome; in the 1230th year from its foundation [Col. 1325C] he killed the patricians Orestes and Paulus and condemned the emperor Augustulus to exile.

476. Odoacer ruled at Rome against Zeno’s will.

478. In the time of the emperor Zeno, the body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of the evangelist Matthew, written in Matthew’s own hand, were found when the matter was revealed by him.

479. Pope Simplicius condemned Peter, the Alexandrian bishop and Eutychian heretic, accused by Acacius of Constantinople.

480. After Hilderic, king of the Franks, died, his son Ludovic succeeded him, whom they call Clovis; he ruled for 30 years.

482. Theoderic, son of Theodemir, king of the Ostrogoths—that is [Note: [Col. 1325] “id” in copy 1; “id est” in copy 2.], of those Goths who had formerly remained in Italy—became a friend of the emperor Zeno [Note: [Col. 1325] Added above the line.] and served him with his Goths.

483. The emperor Zeno made Theoderic consul and master of the soldiers for this year. At Rome Felix III, the fiftieth pope, sat for nearly 9 years [Note: [Col. 1325] What follows is in different ink.] and established one chapter of canons [Note: [Col. 1325] The first hand corrected this to “27 chapters,” or perhaps “one chapter.”].

485. At this time Acacius of Constantinople, favoring the heresy, recalled Peter of Alexandria, whom [Note: [Col. 1325] Added above the line.] he had formerly [Note: [Col. 1325] Added above the line.] accused [Note: [Col. 1325] Added above the line.]. When Pope Felix heard this, he condemned both men and their followers in error.

488. Theoderic, king of the Ostrogoths, with the permission of the emperor Zeno, marched toward Italy. Odoacer met him and engaged him in battle, but, defeated, fled.

489. Theoderic defeated Odoacer for the third time, drove him into flight, and besieged him at Ravenna.

490. Odoacer engaged Theoderic for the fourth time, but was defeated and captured. At Constantinople the emperor Zeno died. After him Anastasius ruled the empire of the East for 28 years.

491. After Pope Felix died at Rome, a council was held by the presbyters and deacons.

492. Theoderic killed Odoacer, who was plotting against him, at Ravenna, and himself held the empire of the West for 30 years. At Rome Gelasius, the fifty-first pope, sat for 4 years and 7 months, a learned and devout man; he condemned all [Note: [Col. 1325] Added above the line.] heretics, increased the Roman clergy, [Col. 1326B] and issued many decrees, namely [Note: [Col. 1325] “28 chapters” is in different ink.] 28 chapters.

493. At this time blessed Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe in Africa, flourished in learning and works.

494. King Ludovic of the Franks defeated the Alemanni in battle, with God’s help; when he was in danger in that same battle, he promised that he would become a believer.

495. Ludovic, also called Clovis, king of the Franks, urged by his Christian wife Rodhilde, was instructed in the faith of Christ by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, and was baptized with his people.

496. Trasamund, king of the Vandals in Africa and hostile to the Catholics, closed the churches and afflicted 240 bishops with exile in Sardinia.

497. The patrician and consul Boethius at this time published many excellent monuments of his intellect in secular philosophy [Col. 1326C]. At Rome Anastasius, the fifty-second pope, sat for nearly two years and [Note: [Col. 1325] “and made eight decretal chapters” is in different ink.] issued eight decretal chapters.

498. The Isaurians, after killing their own commander Liling, were slaughtered by the emperor Anastasius.

499. King Theoderic built many remarkable buildings at Rome and elsewhere during this period. At Rome Symmachus, the fifty-third pope, sat for nearly 15 years and 8 months. During his pontificate Laurentius was also ordained through excessive dissension; great discord arose at Rome between the clergy and the people, until Symmachus was confirmed in the see by the judgment of King Theoderic. He [Note: [Col. 1325] “13 synodical chapters” is in different ink.] established 13 synodical chapters.

500. After a synod had been held at Rome, Pope Symmachus ordained his rival Laurentius bishop of Nocera.

501. King Theoderic built an aqueduct at Ravenna. At this time Saint Mamertus, archbishop of Vienne, flourished through his miracles. Because of the ferocity of wolves and bears and other afflictions, he was the first to institute three-day litanies before the Lord’s Ascension, and thereby obtained the Lord’s mercy and the cessation of the afflictions.

503. Certain Romans falsely accused Pope Symmachus and denounced him to the king; recalling Laurentius, they caused a great schism at Rome, and [Col. 1327A] Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum, with Theoderic’s permission, invaded the apostolic see.

504. A synod of 115 bishops was assembled. Blessed Pope Symmachus was cleared of the charges brought against him and restored with glory to his see; the invaders of his see, Laurentius of Nocera and Peter of Altinum, were condemned.

505. King Ludovic of the Franks built the basilica of blessed Peter at Paris.

506. King Theoderic led an army from Italy against the Franks in Gaul.

507. Dissension again arose between Pope Symmachus and the Church.

508. In this year at Rome Boethius, a most learned man, held the consulship. At this time also Avitus, abbot of Orléans, shone forth in miracles and in the spirit of prophecy.

509. Ludovic, also called Clovis, king of the Franks, died at Paris, where he established the seat of his kingdom.

510. At this time Pope Symmachus, among his other good works, condemned the Manichaeans found in the City. He paved the basilica of Saint Peter and its portico with marble, and did other such things.

513. Cassiodorus was consul in this year. Later he converted and became a monk, built a monastery, and flourished in secular and divine learning; he expounded the Psalms, composed books of instruction and a chronicle, and arranged a tripartite history. Finally, at Rome, when the dissension had ceased, Pope Symmachus died in peace.

514. At Rome Hormisdas, the fifty-fourth pope, sat for 8 years. [Col. 1327C] Among other things, he condemned the Eutychians and Manichaeans, instructed the clergy, adorned the basilicas, [Note: [Col. 1327D] “and made four decrees” is in different ink.] and issued four decrees.

515. Vitalianus, a certain servant, rebelled against the emperor Anastasius together with the Scythians.

516. Pope Hormisdas sent legates to the emperor Anastasius at Constantinople on behalf of the Catholic faith. Among other things the emperor replied to him as follows: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.”

518. The emperor Anastasius, favoring the heresy of Eutyches and persecuting the Catholics, was struck by lightning and died, being more than eighty years old. In his place Justin, a Catholic emperor, ruled at Constantinople for 8 years and made peace with the tyrant Vitalianus, whom he nevertheless later killed.

[Col. 1327D] 519. The emperor Justin Augustus honorably received the legates sent by Pope Hormisdas on behalf of the faith; agreeing with them in condemning the heresy, he sent many gifts through them to Rome.

521. The emperor Justin, hostile to the heretics, also persecuted the Arians at Constantinople. Angered by this, Theoderic, the Arian king of Italy, threatened destruction to the Catholics in Italy.

522. After Trasamund, the Arian king of the Vandals, died in Africa, Hilderic ruled in his place for 8 years [Col. 1328A]. He immediately opened the churches that had long been closed and recalled all the Catholics from exile.

523. At Rome John, the fifty-fifth pope, sat for 2 years and 9 months. Sent by Theoderic to Constantinople, and honorably received by the emperor Justin Augustus and all the citizens, he restored sight to a blind man at the gate called Golden. After crowning the emperor Justin, he returned with many gifts.

524. Theoderic, king of the Goths and tyrant of the Romans, killed the patrician and philosopher Boethius, who had long been imprisoned; not long afterward he likewise killed his father-in-law, the patrician Symmachus. He also killed the blessed Pope John by the suffering of imprisonment, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

525. Three months after the death of Pope John, the tyrant Theoderic suddenly died at Ravenna; as was revealed to a certain solitary, he was cast by Pope John and the patrician Symmachus into the cauldron of Vulcan. After him his grandson Athalaric ruled with his mother for 8 years. At Rome Felix IV, the fifty-sixth pope, sat for 4 years and 2 months.

526. The emperor Justin died at Constantinople; in his place his nephew Justinian ruled for 38 years.

527. The emperor Justinian made his friend Belisarius commander-in-chief. The people of the Winili, or Lombards, under their king Audoin, invaded Pannonia and settled there.

528. At this time blessed Benedict, the abbot, flourished with immense glory for his miracles. The grammarian Priscian also lived at this time.

[Col. 1328C] 530. After Hilderic, the Catholic king of the Vandals, was killed in Africa, Gelimer seized the kingdom and raged against the Catholics and everyone else. At Rome Boniface II, the fifty-seventh pope, sat for 2 years and nearly 1 month.

531. Pope Boniface decreed in writing that the deacon Vigilius should be elected pope after him at a synod. Because this was contrary to the canons, he later burned the document.

532. From this year, namely the sixth year of the emperor Justinian, Dionysius, a Roman abbot, began the great paschal cycle, which, since 532 years had already been completed once from the Lord’s incarnation, contains the same number of years within itself. At Rome John II, also called Mercury, the fifty-eighth pope, sat for 2 years and 4 months. The emperor Justinian sent him a letter concerning his faith.

[Col. 1328D] 533. After Athalaric, king of the Goths, died at Rome, his mother Amalasuntha took Theodahad into partnership in the kingdom; he nevertheless later ordered her death and ruled alone.

534. The patrician Belisarius, sent by the emperor Justinian, defeated and destroyed the nation of the Vandals in Africa, captured their king Gelimer, and restored Carthage to the Roman state.

535. At Rome Agapetus, the fifty-ninth pope, sat for nearly one year. Sent by the tyrant Theodahad to Constantinople on behalf of the emperor Justinian’s favor, [Col. 1329A] he condemned Anthimus, the heretical bishop of that city; after appointing another bishop, namely [Note: [Col. 1329] “namely Menas the Catholic” is in different ink.] Menas the Catholic, he himself died there, being exceedingly learned in ecclesiastical rules [Note: [Col. 1329] “Exceedingly learned in ecclesiastical rules” is in different ink. —Hermann has: “He steadfastly contended with the emperor for the faith of Christ.”].

536. At Rome Silverius, formerly the son of Pope Hormisdas, was violently promoted as the sixtieth pope against the will of the clergy by the tyrant Theodahad, who had been bribed with money; he sat for 1 year and 5 months.

537. When Pope Silverius refused to obey the emperors concerning the restoration of Anthimus and communion with the heretics, he was falsely accused by the patrician Belisarius at their command, afflicted by the deacon Vigilius, and died in exile on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July; afterward he became renowned for miracles. Vigilius himself was ordained pope, the sixty-first, and sat for 17 years and 7 months.

[Col. 1329B] 538. The patrician Belisarius and Pope Vigilius brought Vitiges, king of the Goths, defeated in battle, to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople.

539. The patrician Belisarius forced the Persians, who were devastating Antioch and Syria, to withdraw.

541. Totila, king of the Goths, devastated Rome and Campania.

542. In the time of this Justinian, the body of Saint Antony the monk, divinely revealed, was transferred to Alexandria. At this time the fifth universal synod was assembled at Constantinople against Theodore and all the heretics under Pope Vigilius; it established 14 chapters [Note: [Col. 1329] The first hand corrected “sixth” to “fifth.”] [Note: [Col. 1329] “14 chapters” is in different ink.].

543. At this time Abbot Benedict, after sending his disciple Maurus to Gaul, himself [Col. 1329C] migrated to the Lord after many miracles.

544. Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims and apostle of the Frankish people, full of miracles, migrated to the Lord in the 74th year of his episcopate, on the Ides of January. Arator, a Roman subdeacon, publicly recited before Pope Vigilius his book on the deeds of the apostles, composed in heroic meter.

545. Totila, king of the Goths, again invaded Rome.

546. At this time there was Saint Liberatus, archdeacon of Carthage, who wrote many useful works on the authority of the Council of Chalcedon and showed that Pope Vigilius had at one time favored the heretics [Note: [Col. 1329] All these words were added by the same hand.].

547. Since Pope Vigilius could in no way be brought to agree to the heresy or to the restoration of Bishop Anthimus, he was forcibly taken to Constantinople and severely afflicted by exile.

548. The emperor Justinian constructed at Constantinople, with incomparable workmanship, the basilica of the Savior called Hagia Sophia [Note: [Col. 1329] The copy has *constantinopili*.]. He himself composed the laws called Justinian’s.

550. Victor, bishop of Capua, writing about the Easter of this year, criticized the erroneous cycles of Victorius.

[Col. 1330A] 551. Up to this point Bishop Jordanes brought down his abridged chronicle of Roman affairs.

552. At this time the emperor Justinian made the eunuch Narses commander-in-chief [Note: [Col. 1329] The word was added.] and sent him to Italy.

554. Pope Vigilius, finally released from exile at the entreaty of the Romans and Narses, had begun to return to Rome when he died in Sicily from stone disease. In his place Pelagius, the sixty-second pope, sat for 11 years and 10 months. Accused by the Roman people of a faction against Vigilius, he ascended the pulpit at Saint Peter’s, placed the Gospel upon his head, and cleared himself by oath [Note: [Col. 1329] What follows is in different ink and is written in place of the years 555 and 556.] of the charge brought against him. (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, at Saint Mark’s.) He was ordained by the bishops of Perugia and Ferentino and by Andrew, archpresbyter of Ostia [Col. 1330B]. For this is the privilege of the Church of Ostia: its bishop, and [Note: [Col. 1329] A half-erased word is missing in the first copy; the second has “and.”] its archpresbyter, if the bishop is absent, must by perpetual right take part in the ordination of the Roman pontiff. If the bishop is present, he thereafter has the privilege of wearing the pallium, which no other cardinal bishop is permitted to wear.

557. Hildibert, king of the Franks, died and was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Vincent; his brother Lothar assumed his kingdom and obtained the entire monarchy of their father’s realm.

558. At this time at Tours the basilica of Saint Martin was burned by fire when rebels fled into it.

559. King Lothar, doing penance for his sins and diligently repairing the basilica of Saint Martin, covered it with tin. Saint Medard, a bishop full of miracles, migrated to the Lord and was buried by King Lothar of the Franks at Soissons with great honor.

560. King Lothar, son of the great Clovis, died at Compiègne in the 51st year of his reign.

563. King Charibert, devoted to lust, was excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and died.

564. At Constantinople the emperor Justinian died in the 38th year of his reign. In his place Justin the Younger ruled for 11 years, an unjust and avaricious man. At this time an immense pestilence and mortality devastated all Italy, especially Liguria.

[Col. 1330D] 565. Saint Columba, presbyter [Note: [Col. 1329] “and abbot” is in different ink.] and abbot, coming from Ireland, preached the word of God to the Britons. The patrician Narses, enriched with wealth and therefore envied by the Romans and accused before the emperor, departed from Rome for Campania. His successor Longinus was sent to Italy.

566. At Rome John III, the sixty-third pope, sat for nearly 14 years. He completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun.

567. The patrician Narses, who had labored greatly for the Roman state, provoked by injuries from the emperor Justin, invited the Lombards, living in Pannonia, to devastate and occupy Italy. Many portents, especially fiery armies, were seen in the sky.

568. In April the Lombards, under King Alboin, entered Venetia and subjected it to themselves, except for a few cities.

569. King Alboin invaded Liguria with the Lombards, captured Milan and most of the other cities, and besieged Pavia for more than three years.

570. Alboin captured most of the cities in Tuscany. Saint Vedastus, bishop, died.

[Col. 1331B] **571.** The people of Pavia came to King Alboin to surrender. The patrician Narses died.

**574.** King Alboin of the Lombards was killed by his own armed retainer through the treachery of his wife at Verona.

**575.** At Constantinople, the emperor Justin, after his many misfortunes, became insane and died. In his place Tiberius Constantine, who had governed the palace while Justin himself was mentally incapacitated, reigned for seven years; he was a man devoted to God.

**576.** Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, departed to the Lord.

**578.** At Rome, Benedict, the sixty-fourth pope, held office for four years and two months. He removed blessed Gregory from his monastery, ordained him deacon, and sent him to Constantinople as *apocrisiarius* [papal representative]. There, in the presence of the emperor Tiberius, Gregory convicted Eutychius, bishop of that city, of error concerning the faith in the resurrection. There too, at the bishops’ urging, when his own monks came to him, he was compelled to write the *Moralia on Job*.

**579.** A great inundation and overflow of waters, lightning, and earthquakes terrified the people.

**580.** A comet was seen on Easter Day. At Soissons the sky appeared to burn. A great pestilence arose.

**581.** At this time the army of the emperor Tiberius powerfully defeated the Persians.

**582.** At Constantinople Tiberius, worthy of every praise, died. In his place Maurice reigned for twenty-one years. At Rome Pelagius II, the sixty-fifth pope, held office for ten years and two months. He covered the church of Saint Peter with gilded silver panels and did many other good works.

[Col. 1331D] **583.** King Childebert of the Franks, after receiving 50,000 gold solidi from the emperor Maurice so that he might drive the Lombards from Italy, made a treaty with them and gave no answer to the emperor when he demanded his money.

**584.** King Guntram built the monastery of Saint Marcellus in the suburb of Chalon.

**585.** King Chilperic of the Franks was killed by treachery and buried at Paris.

**586.** The Lombards chose Authari as their king.

**587.** A fiery, sparkling globe, as though roaring, fell from the sky to the earth. In Spain, Reccared, son of Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths, became king after his father’s death and was converted to the Catholic faith by Leander, bishop of Seville, together with the entire Gothic people.

**588.** In Spain the Arian heresy was destroyed, and a synod was convened at Toledo through the efforts of Bishop Leander and King Reccared. Queen Cesara, wife of Aunulf, king of the Persians, was secretly baptized; afterward she persuaded her husband and his entire people to be baptized at Antioch.

**589.** King Childebert gave his sister, who had been promised to Authari, king of the Lombards, in marriage to the king of the Goths, who had recently become Catholic.

[Col. 1332B] **590.** The tunic of the Lord and Savior, pointed out by a certain Jew named Simon under torture, was found in a marble chest at the town of Zaphad after a three-day fast had been solemnly observed by Gregory of Antioch, John of Constantinople, Thomas of Jerusalem, and several other bishops. It was brought to Jerusalem with the highest honor.

**591.** The king of the Lombards married Theodelinda, the beautiful and devout daughter of the king of the Bavarians.

**592.** A great mortality occurred, in which Pope Pelagius first died, followed by countless others. Blessed Gregory, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, established litanies; when the plague had ceased, he was ordained the sixty-sixth pope. In doctrine and conduct he deservedly surpassed all, and he held office for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. Immediately, among many other works, he published the *Pastoral Book* in an excellent style. He also made a canopy over the body of blessed Peter and instituted the celebration of Masses there, and likewise at Saint Paul’s; he also wrote six synodal chapters [Note: “and six synodal chapters,” written in another ink.].

**593.** A severe drought and famine occurred, together with an extraordinary multitude of large locusts.

**594.** Again, a multitude of locusts damaged the crops.

**595.** Pope Gregory convened a synod of twenty-four bishops at Saint Peter’s, in the fourteenth indiction.

**596.** Saint Columba, priest and abbot, after many miracles on the island of Iona near Ireland, departed to the Lord at the age of seventy. At this time blessed Pope Gregory, sending the teachers Augustine, Mellitus, John, and others, converted the people of the Angles in Britain to the faith of Christ.

**597.** King Childebert of the Franks died.

**598.** At this time, when the patrician Romanus had recovered by surrender several cities formerly captured by the Lombards, and King Agilulf of Italy and his army were consequently threatening Rome with hostile intent, peace was made between both sides through the efforts of holy Pope Gregory and the support of the devout Queen Theodelinda.

**599.** At this time the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated in the fortress of Cassino, was completely destroyed and left desolate by the Lombards after the monks had fled from it.

[Col. 1333A] **600.** Pope Gregory, sending a pallium, decreed that the bishops of London [Note: “Lugdunae” was written above, with “Lundoniae” substituted in one copy.] and York in Britain should be metropolitans, in the fourth indiction. A plague of glandular swellings afflicted many cities.

**602.** The emperor Maurice made Phocas, useful to the state, commander of the army. Fiery globes were seen in the sky.

**603.** At Constantinople Phocas shamefully killed the emperor Maurice and reigned in his place for eight years. The body of Saint Victor the martyr, who suffered together with blessed Ursus at Solothurn, was discovered by divine revelation in a silver casket near the city of Geneva and was made known through miracles.

**604.** Etherius, archbishop of Lyon, died, and Secundinus succeeded him.

[Col. 1333B] **605.** Blessed Pope Gregory, the most holy teacher, departed to the Lord in the eighth indiction. After him, the episcopal office remained vacant for more than five months; then Sabinian [Note: “S. P.” stands in an erased place; thus our copy, following the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*, emended the name to Herimannus.] the sixty-seventh pope held office for one year and five months. After him the episcopal office was again vacant for nearly a year because an imperial embassy from Constantinople was awaited. In this year the wicked synod of Chalon was convened, and blessed Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, was unjustly deposed and condemned to exile.

**606.** Famine occurred at Rome, and peace with the Lombards was made for one year. A comet was seen in April and May.

**608.** At Rome Boniface III, the sixty-eighth pope, held office for about nine months. After him the episcopal office was again vacant for ten months. Because the church of Constantinople was claiming in writing that it was the first, he obtained from the emperor Phocas a decree that the Roman Church should be regarded as the head of all churches. He also convened a synod of seventy-two bishops at Rome.

**609.** At Rome Boniface IV, the sixty-ninth pope, held office for six years and eight months. After him the episcopal office was vacant for about seven months. From the emperor Phocas he obtained the temple of all the idols, called the Pantheon, and dedicated it in honor of holy Mary and all the saints on 13 May. He called it Saint Mary at the Martyrs and established that the feast of all the saints should be celebrated on the Kalends of November. In the time of this pope [Note: “This pope … defended,” added in another ink in the margin.], a certain blind man at Rome is said to have disputed with the Jews concerning the virginity of Saint Mary. When the Jews objected to him, asking why he defended the mother of Christ so vigorously although he could not restore his own sight, he said: “Wait three days, and you will see the great works of Christ in me.”

The Purification of Saint Mary occurred after those three days. At that time the feast was celebrated at Rome not, as now, at Saint Mary Major, but at Saint Mary of the Martyrs. When the lord pope had summoned both Jews and Christians to the same solemnity, the blind man was present as well. He himself sang, at the eighth lesson of the night office, the responsory he had composed, namely, “Rejoice, Mary” [Note: “M.” in one copy.]. When it had been sung, he both refuted the error of the Jews and received his sight, through the intervention of her whose virginity he had defended in that responsory.

Blessed Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, was recalled from exile, but was stoned through the faction of Brunhild and Theuderic. After his death he became renowned for miracles.

**610.** At this time the Persians, taking many provinces from the Romans, stripped Jerusalem of the Lord’s cross.

**611.** Heraclianus deprived Phocas of the imperial throne and granted it to his son Heraclius, who reigned for twenty-six years. Blessed Abbot Columbanus, teacher of Saint Gall, was expelled from the monastery of Luxeuil, which he himself had founded, through Brunhild’s plotting; he left Saint Eustasius there as abbot in his place.

**612.** Blessed Augustine, archbishop of the Angles, departed to the Lord. Saint Columbanus, expelled from Luxeuil, came with the permission of King Theudebert to Brigantium and remained there for three years.

**613.** In Spain, after the death of Witteric, Sisebut became king of the Goths.

**614.** The emperor Heraclius made his son Constantine co-emperor. Blessed Columbanus, expelled from the Burgundian territory, left Gallus there suffering from fever; he himself came to Italy and was kindly received by King Agilulf, and built the monastery of Bobbio. Saint Gall also began to inhabit the solitude of his cell.

**616.** At this time Isidore, bishop of Seville, was held in high renown in Spain. The most wicked Brunhild, tied to untamed horses, suffered a fitting death by order of Sigibert, king of the Franks. The aforesaid Isidore brought his abridgment of the ages down to this point.

**617.** At Rome Deusdedit, the seventieth pope, held office for three years and about one month.

**618.** At this time Jerusalem, among the other cities of Palestine, was captured by Chosroes, king of the Persians, and the Lord’s cross was carried away to Persia [Note: “This” was written in another ink in an erased place. Perhaps the author had first written the statement of Herimannus concerning the earthquake and related events, then remembered that the seizure of the holy cross had already been assigned to 610.].

**620.** At Rome Boniface V, the seventy-first pope, held office for five years; he was a very gentle and devout man. In Britain, after the death of Archbishop Laurence, Mellitus succeeded him. Magundat the magician, a Persian by birth, converted to the faith of Christ and called Anastasius, became a monk of extraordinary holiness at Jerusalem.

[Col. 1334D] **622.** Queen Bertrude [Note: The initial G of “Gertrudis” was written in red in one copy.], the most devout wife of Lothar, king of the Franks, of blessed memory, died.

**623.** At this time blessed Attala, and after him Bertolf, abbots of Bobbio, and Saint Gall became renowned [Note: The word stands in a damaged place.].

**624.** In Britain, after the death of Mellitus, archbishop, Justus succeeded him. In the following year he ordained blessed Paulinus bishop and sent him as preacher and teacher to those Angles who were still pagans.

**625.** At Rome Honorius, the seventy-second pope, held office for thirteen years, abounding in many good works.

[Col. 1335A] **627.** In Britain King Edwin of the Angles was converted by Bishop Paulinus and baptized with his people, nearly 180 years after the arrival of the Angles in Britain.

**628.** Blessed Anastasius the monk, after suffering many tortures for Christ, was finally strangled in Persia by King Chosroes together with seventy others and became a martyr. In that same year the emperor Heraclius invaded Persia, defeated and killed Chosroes, and brought the Lord’s cross back to Jerusalem.

**630.** Lothar, a strong, devout, and religious king of the Franks, died in the forty-fifth year of his reign.

**631.** King Dagobert of the Franks, employing as counselors Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and Pippin, mayor of the palace, burned with an excessive love of justice [Note: Some editions read “love of Justina.”].

[Col. 1335B] **632.** Perpetual peace was arranged between the emperor Heraclius and Dagobert through the mediation of ambassadors.

**633.** In Britain Edwin, the peaceful and devout king of the Angles, was killed by pagan kings.

**634.** Oswald, son of Æthelfrith, a most Christian man, gathered a small force, adored the cross he had erected, and defeated Edwin’s killers. He then reigned for eight years.

**635.** At this time, when Sergius of Constantinople, supported by Cyrus of Alexandria, was reviving the heresy of the Acephalites [Note: One copy reads “Acephali”], and had proclaimed as doctrine one will and one operation of divinity and humanity in Christ, he was condemned by the Apostolic See after having seduced the emperor himself.

**637.** At Constantinople the emperor Heraclius died, having been led into heresy, as they say, by Sergius, bishop of Constantinople. In his place Heraclonas reigned with his mother Martina for two years.

**638.** At Rome, after Pope Honorius died, the Apostolic See remained vacant for one year, seven months, and fourteen days because imperial authority at Constantinople was wavering after the deaths of the rulers. During this time the Lateran treasury was dispersed.

**639.** At Constantinople, after the emperor Heraclonas died, his brother Constantine reigned for six months.

**640.** At Constantinople, after Constantine’s death, his son Constantine, also called Constans, reigned for twenty-eight years. At Rome Severinus, the seventy-third pope, held office for two months and four days; after him the episcopal office was vacant for five months.

[Col. 1335D] **641.** At Rome John IV, the seventy-fourth pope, held office for one year and about ten months. By sending money, he redeemed many captives in Istria and Dalmatia from the barbarians.

**642.** At Rome Theodore, the seventy-fifth pope, held office for six years and about six months. He elevated the bodies of Saints Primus and Felician and condemned the heretics. In Britain Oswald, the most devout king of the Angles, fell while fighting the pagan king Penda and became renowned after death through many miracles. His brother Oswi succeeded him and reigned for twenty-eight years.

**644.** Saint Paulinus, bishop of York and teacher of the Angles, departed to the Lord in the twentieth year of his episcopate, on 10 October.

[Col. 1336A] **645.** At this time Pyrrhus of Constantinople, successor of Sergius both in the see and in heresy, had long been condemned by Theodore the pope. When he came from Africa to Rome and pretended to perform a false penance and make satisfaction, he was kindly received and reconciled. Later, however, after returning home and repeating his error, he was again deposed, condemned, and anathematized by the same pope.

**646.** At this time the blessed virgin Gertrude, daughter of Pippin and sister of Grimoald, mayor of the palace, and mother of the monastery of Nivelles, became renowned for her virtues. Her sister Begga, herself a religious woman, married Ansegisel, son of Saint Arnulf, and bore him Pippin the Younger.

[Col. 1336B] **647.** At this time, when Paul of Constantinople, successor of Pyrrhus, not only refused to abandon the heresy but increased it, and seduced the emperor and others, he did not amend his ways even after being admonished and rebuked by the lord pope, and was himself repeatedly condemned.

**648.** During the reign of the emperor Constans, the extremely savage people of the Saracens ravaged many provinces.

**649.** At Rome Martin, the seventy-sixth pope, held office for six years and about two months. At that time Paul of Constantinople, after seducing the emperor Constans himself, afflicted legates of the Apostolic See who were accusing him of heresy with imprisonment and exile, and wherever he could he stirred up persecution against Catholics.

[Col. 1336C] **650.** In the ninth indiction Pope Martin convened a synod of 105 bishops at Rome, at which he condemned Cyrus, Sergius, and Paul with their followers in error.
