**651.** Blessed Aidan, a Scottish-born [Note: One copy reads “Scottish-born” with a different spelling.] bishop and teacher of the Angles, died on 31 August.

**652.** At this time Olympius the exarch, sent to Italy by the emperor Constans, was unable to corrupt or harm the lord pope and the others who were united in the Catholic faith; finally he was reconciled with the pope.

**653.** In Britain Honorius, archbishop of the Angles, died; Deusdedit governed in his place for ten years.

**654.** Blessed Pope Martin, by order of Constans, the heretical emperor, was arrested in the basilica of the Savior called Constantiniana and taken to Constantinople. Since he could not in any way be bent, he was condemned to exile in Cherson.

[Col. 1336D] **655.** Pope Martin departed to the Lord in exile and was buried there; afterward he became renowned through miracles. In his place at Rome Eugenius, the seventy-seventh pope, held office for two years and about ten months; he was a kindly and gentle man. In Britain Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, was defeated and killed by Oswi, brother of Saint Oswald, and the people of the Mercians accepted the faith of Christ.

**656.** Peter of Constantinople, as though offering satisfaction for his faith, sent to Rome a very obscure and ambiguous synodal letter, but it was not accepted by the lord pope and the Roman Church.

**657.** After Pope Eugenius died at Rome, the episcopal office was vacant for two months.

**658.** At Rome Vitalian, the seventy-eighth pope, held office for fourteen years and six months [Note: “VII” corrected to “VI” in one copy.]. Having been confirmed in his see through letters customarily sent to Constantinople, he governed the Roman Church with distinction.

**659.** Constantine, also called Constans, the emperor, sent precious gifts to Rome, to Saint Peter.

**660.** In Italy, after Haribert, king of the Lombards, died, his two sons Godabert and Pertharic divided the kingdom between them. When one of them, Godabert, had been killed and the other had fled to the Huns, Grimoald, duke of Benevento, obtained their kingdom.

[Col. 1337B] **661.** At this time Pertharic, having returned from exile, was compelled to go into exile again.

**662.** Constantine, also called Constans, came to Italy against the Lombards, but accomplished nothing.

**663.** The emperor Constantine came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Vitalian. He offered Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold, but removed nearly all the ornaments of the city [Note: The passage stands in an erased place.] [Note: The word “removed” stands in an erased place.].

**664.** An eclipse of the sun occurred on 3 May. In Britain a dispute concerning Easter was debated by the Scots and the Angles, and the Scots were reasonably defeated by the priest Wilfrid, who was later ordained bishop (see under 678).

[Col. 1337C] **665.** The Angles sent an embassy to Pope Vitalian to request a bishop and teacher.

**668.** In Sicily the emperor Constantine, also called Constans, after carrying out many depredations throughout the provinces, was finally killed by his own men in a bath. His son Constantine reigned in his place for seventeen years; he was a truly Catholic and devout emperor. In this year Archbishop Theodore was ordained by Pope Vitalian and sent with Abbot Hadrian to the Angles; he benefited many both by word and by example.

**669.** The Saracens ravaged Sicily.

**670.** In Italy, after Grimoald, king of the Lombards, died, Pertharic held his hereditary kingdom for seventeen years.

**672.** After Pope Vitalian died in the fifteenth indiction, Adeodatus, the seventy-ninth pope, succeeded him after two months and held office for four years and two months. He was a very gentle and devout man and built many structures at Rome.

[Col. 1337D] **673.** In this year Theodore, archbishop of the Angles, convened a useful synod.

**674.** [Dagobert [Note: Inserted in this manuscript by a different hand and in different ink. It conflicts with the histories both of Dagobert I and Dagobert II; in manuscript 2 the same words are read in the same hand as the rest, and they are also present in manuscript 3.], king of the Franks, a distinguished venerator of God’s churches, died. He reigned for forty-four years. He was buried at Paris.]

**676.** After Pope Adeodatus died at Rome, Donus, the eightieth pope, succeeded him after four and a half months and held office for one year and five months. He paved the portico of Saint Peter with marble. A comet was seen for three months.

**677.** The church of Ravenna, which had separated from Rome by usurping autocephaly, submitted again to Pope Donus.

**678.** After Donus died at Rome, Agatho, the eighty-first pope, succeeded him after two months and held office for two years and six months. [Note: This material, written in another ink in the margin, assigns the event to the year 677.] (*Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.*) This pope obtained from the emperor a reduction of the payment customarily made for the ordination of a pontiff, but only on condition that a general decree concerning the election of the pope should first be sent to the emperor before the pope was consecrated. Wilfrid, bishop of the Angles, was driven from his see by King Egbert and converted many people to the Lord during his exile.

**679.** The emperor Constantine sent an embassy to Rome and requested that a synod be held at Constantinople by apostolic authority for the refutation of the heretics. Pope Agatho convened a synod of 120 bishops at Rome and condemned the heretics who taught one operation in Christ.

[Col. 1338B] **680.** An eclipse of the moon and a great mortality occurred at Rome. Pope Agatho sent legates to Constantinople in the ninth indiction. The emperor received them honorably; they presided over the Sixth Ecumenical Synod of 150 bishops, and they condemned the heretics who, once convicted, asserted one will and one operation in Christ [Note: “and nine chapters,” written in another ink.]. They also composed nine chapters. Theodore, archbishop of the Angles, convened a synod.

**681.** At Constantinople the Sixth Ecumenical Synod of 150 bishops was held in the ninth indiction, in the month of February; Macarius of Antioch and his followers in error were condemned. After their condemnation, suddenly a great many spiders’ webs fell in the basilica before everyone, signifying that the heretical trifles had been cast down. Pope Agatho died.

**682.** After Pope Agatho died at Rome, the episcopal office was vacant for one year and seven months.

**683.** At Rome Leo II, the eighty-second pope, held office for about eleven months. He was in every respect highly learned and most devout; he issued his own decrees, wrote, taught, and established many things with great distinction. Saint Cuthbert, bishop of the church of Lindisfarne, adorned Britain with many virtues.

[Col. 1338D] **684.** After Leo died at Rome, the episcopal office was vacant for nearly a year. Benedict II, the eighty-third pope, then held office for ten months; he was a sufficiently praiseworthy man. Comets appeared.

**685.** After Benedict died at Rome following Easter, and more than two months had elapsed, John V, the eighty-fourth pope, held office for one year. He had previously been archdeacon and had served as a legate of the Apostolic See at the Sixth Synod. At Constantinople, after the emperor Constantine died, his son Justinian reigned for ten years; polluted by heresy, he was hostile to the orthodox.

[Col. 1339A] **686.** After John died at Rome, Conon, the eighty-fifth pope, was ordained after three months and held office for eleven months; he too was a praiseworthy man. In Britain Saint John of Hexham was held in high renown as a bishop.

**687.** After Conon died at Rome and nearly three months had elapsed, Sergius, the eighty-sixth pope, held office for thirteen years and about nine months. Strong in the Catholic faith, he suffered persecution from the emperor Justinian. He was indeed a holy man, devoted to every good work.

**688.** King Cædwalla of the West Saxons, converted to the faith of Christ [Note: Added above the line.] and coming to Rome [Note: Added above the line.], was baptized by Pope Sergius on Holy Saturday and called Peter. He died there in the white baptismal garments; the pope himself buried him with the highest honor and adorned his tomb with an epitaph.

[Col. 1339B] **689.** In Italy the duke Alachis seized power as a tyrant and persecuted the clergy above all.

**690.** Theodore, the venerable archbishop of the Angles, died in the twenty-third year after his arrival in Britain and in the eighty-eighth year of his life. He composed a quite useful penitential book.

**694.** In these days two English priests, while preaching to the Saxons, were crowned with martyrdom and made known through miracles; Pippin buried them at Cologne.

**695.** At Constantinople the heretical emperor Justinian was expelled from the imperial throne by Leo and Tiberius after his nostrils had been cut off, and Leo himself held the throne for three years. The holy man Willibrord, ordained archbishop by Pope Sergius and called Clement, became renowned for his virtues while preaching to the Frisian people.

[Col. 1339C] **696.** Pope Sergius, by revelation from the Lord, found a reliquary containing a portion of the Lord’s cross.

**697.** In Britain Saint Cuthbert, a bishop who had formerly been a hermit, departed to the Lord after many virtues; the priest Bede wrote his life.

**698.** At Constantinople Tiberius seized the empire and kept the emperor Leo in prison for the seven years during which he himself reigned after him.

**699.** At this time the Synod of Aquileia was held, and certain persons who refused to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council were corrected by Pope Sergius.

**701.** After Sergius died at Rome, John VI, the eighty-seventh pope, held office for three years and two months.

**703.** The English priest Bede, a learned man, brought the chronicle in his shorter book *On Times* down to this point. At this time, when Gisulf, duke of Benevento, was ravaging Campania and carrying away captives, he received gifts from Pope John, who requested peace, and returned the captives.

[Col. 1339D] **704.** In Britain Æthelred, king of the Mercians, abandoned [Note: The word stands in an erased place.] the kingdom [Note: The word stands in an erased place.] and became a monk.

**705.** At Constantinople the emperor Justinian, recovering the empire with the help of Terbel, king of the Bulgars, killed Leo and Tiberius, the usurpers of the empire. He sent the blinded patriarch Callinicus to Rome and promoted in his place Abbot Cyrus, who had supported himself in exile in Pontus. It is said of this emperor that whenever he wiped the discharge from his mutilated nostrils, he ordered one of his enemies to be killed. At Rome John VII, the eighty-eighth pope, held office for two years and about eight months; he was eloquent and learned. Saint Heddi, bishop, departed to the Lord [Note: This sentence was added by the same hand.].

**706.** Pope John built an oratory of Saint Mary at Saint Peter’s and adorned many churches.

**707.** At this time Haribert, king of the Lombards, returned to Saint Peter and Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, which had long before been captured and held by the Lombards, by means of a privilege written in gold letters.

**708.** At Rome Sisinnius was ordained the eighty-ninth pope. As his gout worsened, he survived only twenty days. After him Constantine became pope, the ninetieth, and held office for seven years and fifteen days.

**709.** King Cœnred of the Mercians, together with Offa, a royal youth and son of King Sighere, abandoned their kingdoms and came to Rome. There they became monks and died not long afterward. Wilfrid, bishop of the Angles, died, and Acca succeeded him.

**710.** The venerable Abbot Hadrian died in the forty-first year after Pope Vitalian had sent him to Britain with Archbishop Theodore. King Childebert of the Franks died; Dagobert succeeded him for five years.

[Col. 1340C] **711.** At Constantinople Philippicus became emperor, killed the emperor Justinian, and himself reigned for one year and six months, persecuting Catholics and favoring heretics. (*Cf. Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.*) Therefore [Note: Added in another ink.] he was anathematized by Pope Constantine [Note: The following words stand in an erased place.]. Because the leaders of the kingdom shunned him as excommunicated, he was compelled to lay down the imperial diadem.

**712.** King Heribert of the Lombards died; Liutprand succeeded him.

**713.** At Constantinople Anastasius deprived Philippicus of his eyes and kingdom and himself reigned for three years.

**714.** The emperor Anastasius, having sent a letter to Pope Constantine, declared himself Catholic. Pippin, son of Ansegisel and grandson of Saint Arnulf, mayor of the palace and duke of the Franks, died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign; his son Charles succeeded him and reigned for twenty-seven years.

[Col. 1340D] **715.** After Pope Constantine died at Rome [Note: In Herimannus, the nine months belonging to Rome were first assigned to the year 714.], Gregory II, the ninety-first pope [Note: “Popes 91 and the one who wrote seventeen chapters,” in another ink.], held office for fifteen years and nine months. He wrote seventeen chapters [Note: “Popes 91 and the one who wrote seventeen chapters,” in another ink.] [Note: “714 according to Herimannus.”]. Dagobert the Younger, son of Childebert, king of the Franks, died; Helperic, also called Daniel, succeeded him.

**716.** Egbert, a holy man of English birth, taught the Scots to celebrate Easter correctly. At Constantinople Theodosius became emperor and reigned for one year. He had the emperor Anastasius, defeated in battle, ordained a priest.

**717.** At Rome the Tiber rose beyond measure and overturned many buildings. At this time Winfrid, also called Boniface, an Englishman by birth, preached the word of salvation to the peoples of Germany by the authority of Pope Gregory.

**718.** At Constantinople the emperor Leo reigned for nine years. During his reign the Saracens besieged Constantinople for three years but were finally driven back, by divine aid, hunger, pestilence, and the sword.

**719.** Saint Boniface was ordained archbishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory and benefited many peoples by his words and example.

**720.** After Helperic died, Theuderic, son of Dagobert, was appointed king by Charles. Saint Othmar was appointed the first abbot of the cell of Saint Gall and governed it for forty years.

**721.** Charles defeated Ragenfred and captured the city of Angers by force. Saint John of Hexham, bishop, died.

**722.** Charles subdued Alemannia and Bavaria.

**723.** (*Chronicle of Bede.*) At this time the body of Saint Augustine was transferred by Liutprand from Sardinia to Pavia.

**724.** After crossing the Loire, Charles ravaged Aquitaine. Saint Pirmin, abbot and chorepiscopus, was appointed by Charles to govern the island of Reichenau. He drove the snakes from it and established monastic life there for three years. [Note: This was added in another ink in the margin.] In Greek, *choros* means “region”; in Latin, *regio*. Hence *chorepiscopus*, that is, “regional bishop,” one who travels through the regions.

**725.** The Saracens ravaged Gaul with plunder and fire.

**726.** (*Cf. Einhard, *Life of Charles*, chapter 1.*) Charles defeated the Saracens together with their king. Up to this point the venerable priest Bede brought his chronicle in his larger book on the ages. Up to this point is the history of the Romans; from here onward the reckoning is of the Franks. Charles, son of Pippin, after having held the office of mayor of the palace for twelve years, thereafter held that same office for fifteen years, although kings continued to reign in Francia, but with little authority.

[Col. 1341D] **727.** Charles marched into Burgundy and subdued it. Saint Pirmin, expelled from Reichenau, appointed Eto abbot in his place; he himself went to Alsace to establish other monasteries.

**728.** Charles recovered Aquitaine without a battle.

**729.** Saint Egbert, an English priest, died at the age of ninety on Easter Day, that is, 24 April.

**730.** The Saracens captured the city of Avignon and devastated the surrounding regions.

**731.** Charles, having slaughtered the Saracens, recovered Avignon by storm. The English priest and monk Bede, an outstanding teacher, died on 26 May. At Rome Gregory III, the ninety-second pope [Note: Here and in the following entries up to 872, the papal number was added in another ink.], held office for ten years and nine months. Three monasteries—Altaha, Murbach, and Pfäfers—were established with brothers from Reichenau.

**732.** Charles invaded Gothia.

**733.** Charles destroyed the army of the Saracens coming from Spain.

**734.** Eto, abbot of Reichenau, leaving Keba as his successor, was promoted to be bishop of Strasbourg. Not long afterward he built the monastery of Ettenheim, named after him [Note: Or “of Argentoratum”; a gloss in one copy.].

**735.** Charles returned victorious once again after destroying the Saracens.

**736.** Charles marched against the Goths and returned victorious. Bishop Audoin died. After Keba died at Reichenau two years later, Ernfred became abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Constance and governed for ten years.

**737.** Charles defeated the Saxons and made them tributaries.

[Col. 1342B] **739.** Charles subjected the whole of Provence to his authority.

**740.** After the enemies everywhere had been defeated, peace and quiet were established in the Frankish kingdom through Charles.

**741.** At Rome Zacharias, the ninety-third pope, held office for ten years and four months. Charles died at Quierzy and was buried at Saint-Denis. His sons, having divided the Frankish kingdom between them, governed as mayors of the palace: Carloman for six years and Pippin for ten.

**742.** Carloman and Pippin quickly suppressed the rebellious dukes of Aquitaine and Swabia [Note: A line has been erased from this point onward in one copy.].

**744.** The monastery of Fulda was founded in the Bochonia forest by Saint Boniface, archbishop.

**745.** Carloman ravaged rebellious Saxony together with his brother.

[Col. 1342C] **746.** With Carloman’s approval and by the authority of Pope Zacharias, Saint Boniface established two bishoprics in his province: Würzburg, for which he ordained his fellow countryman Saint Burchard as first bishop, and Eichstätt, for which he ordained Saint Willibald, also his fellow countryman, as first bishop. Sidonius, a monk of Reichenau, became its fifth abbot and bishop of Constance and governed for thirteen years. While also seeking the cell of Saint Gall, he consented with wicked rulers to the condemnation of Saint Othmar, abbot.

**747.** Carloman, renouncing the world for the love of God, became a monk in the fortress of Cassino.

**750.** Pippin gave Grifo twelve counties in the region of Neustria.

[Col. 1342D] **751.** Pippin sent ambassadors to Rome and consulted Pope Zacharias about the kingdom of the Franks and its incompetent kings.

**752.** By the authority of Pope Zacharias, and not long afterward of Stephen, the ninety-fourth pope, who succeeded him in the pontificate for six years, King Childeric was deposed and tonsured; Pippin was elected king of the Franks and anointed at Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop, and reigned for seventeen years. Audogar, the first founder and abbot of the monastery of Kempten, began to inhabit that place.

**753.** King Pippin ravaged Saxony, where Hildigarius, archbishop of Cologne, was killed. Pope Stephen came to Pippin, king of the Franks, seeking aid against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, and anointed his sons Charles and Carloman as kings at Paris.

[Col. 1343A] **754.** Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was preaching among the Frisians when they martyred him, in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate. He was buried at the monastery of Fulda. Lullus succeeded him as archbishop and governed for thirty-two years. Carloman, Pippin’s brother, died at Lyon when he wished to come to him to dissuade him from the Italian expedition. Pippin marched into Italy with an army and compelled King Aistulf, besieged at Pavia, to give hostages and to return Saint Peter’s property under oath. Pope Stephen returned to Rome with Jerome, Pippin’s brother.

**755.** Aistulf, despising his oath, besieged Rome and devastated everything around it with sword and fire. For this reason the pope sent envoys by sea to Pippin to request aid.

**756.** King Pippin marched into Italy again, besieged Aistulf at Pavia, and compelled him, through an envoy, to return Ravenna and the other cities he had seized to Saint Peter and the lord pope.

**757.** Among other gifts, the emperor Constantine also sent an organ to King Pippin.

**758.** At Rome Paul succeeded Pope Stephen as the ninety-fifth pope and held office for ten years.

759. Waifarius exercised tyranny in Aquitania. [Col. 1343C] Saint Othmar, abbot, unjustly condemned by Warinus and Roudhard with the agreement of Sidonius, bishop, and banished to the Rhine island of Stein, departed to the Lord. When Sidonius, bishop and abbot, had rashly invaded his abbey, he died before the altar of Saint Gall from a flux of the bowels. In his place John, a monk of the Reichenau, received the bishopric and both abbeys and presided for 21 years. He was the first to obtain from Pope Hadrian a privilege of the Roman See for the Reichenau.

760. Pepin invaded Aquitania, or Wasconia, and compelled Waifarius to restore under oath what he had unjustly usurped.

761. Waifarius again exercised tyranny.

762. King Pepin, advancing into Aquitania with his son Charles, captured many cities there.

[Col. 1343D] 764. Pepin held a great assembly at Carisiacum.

765. Roudgang, archbishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 1343] “metentis”], obtained from Pope Paul the bodies of Saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius.

766. The body of Saint Gorgonius was buried in the monastery of Gorze, that of Saint Nabor at Nova Cella, and that of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch.

767. Pope Paul died at Rome; Stephen, the 96th pope, succeeded him and held office for four years.

768. Having subdued Aquitania, Pepin died at Paris on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [September 24], in the 54th year of his age. His sons divided the kingdom between them: Charles the Great reigned for 46 years, and Karlomann for four.

769. After ten years, the body of Saint Othmar, abbot, was found incorrupt on the island where he had died and was transferred to the monastery of Saint Gall.

770. Charles married the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, but later repudiated her.

771. Karlomann died and was buried at Reims. Charles convened a great synod.

772. Charles advanced against the Saxons and returned after receiving hostages from them. At Rome, after Stephen, Hadrian I, the 97th pope, held office for 24 years.

773. At the request of Pope Hadrian, who appealed to him for the defense of the possessions of Saint Peter, Charles went to Italy. While Desiderius was besieged at Pavia, he himself went to Rome to pray and celebrated Easter there.

774. The Lombards, with their king Desiderius, surrendered themselves to Charles, in the 205th year since they had entered Italy with King Alboin. The bodies of Saints Gordian and Epimachus were transferred from Rome to Alemannia.

775. Charles ravaged Saxony, which had rebelled again.

776. Charles killed Roudgaud, who was aspiring to the kingdom of Italy.

777. The Saxons, finally subdued after much slaughter, submitted to Charles and became Christians.

778. Charles went into Spain; after subduing it, he returned. The Saxons rebelled again.

[Col. 1344C] 779. Charles again defeated the Saxons.

780. Having arranged affairs among the Saxons and Slavs, Charles himself went to Rome to pray.

781. At Rome, Pepin, the son of Charles, was baptized by Pope Hadrian, [Note: [Col. 1343] “and—was received,” written by another hand and in another ink], and was received from the baptismal font by the same pope; together with his brother Louis, he was anointed king. John, bishop of Constance and abbot, died; Bishop Egino then presided for 32 years, Peter as abbot of the Reichenau for five years, and Roudpert as abbot at Saint Gall for one year. At this time crosses appeared on the garments of many people. Blood is said to have flowed from the earth and from the air. [Note: [Col. 1343] The following items are written in the upper margin. I judged that they should be placed chiefly here; cf. Legg. I, 44. Codex 2 assigns them to the year 789; they are absent from 3.] It should be known that Hadrian gave Charles a book at Rome containing the Canons of the Apostles, together with those of the Councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, and Sardica, and containing also a certain excerpt from the African councils, together with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs: Siricius, the 40th; Innocent, the 42nd; Zosimus, the 43rd; Boniface, the 44th; Celestine, the 45th; Leo, the 47th; Hilary, the 48th; Simplicius, the 49th; Felix, the 50th; Gelasius, the 51st; Anastasius, the 52nd; Symmachus, the 53rd; Hormisdas, the 54th; and Gregory, the 71st. [Note: [Col. 1343] “Henceforth in another ink.”] Some people call this book the “Hadrian.” The same Charles, because he did not want any apocryphal writings to be read in the church, had two books compiled by his deacon Paul from the treatises or sermons of the holy Fathers. For the two books mentioned above, together with the library, can almost suffice for the nocturnal readings on each feast or fast throughout the cycle of the year. Those two books were completed in the year of the Lord 808.

782. Charles ordered 4,500 Saxons to be beheaded. At Saint Gall, Waldo presided as abbot for one year.

783. Queen Hildegard, wife of Charles, died on the second day before the Kalends of May [April 30], and Bertrada, his mother, on the fourth day before the Ides of July [July 12].

784. The younger Charles, sent by his father into Saxony, subdued the Westphalians in war.

785. The Saxon Widukind came to Charles to surrender and was baptized.

786. Charles again went to Rome to pray. At the Reichenau, after Peter, Waldo, the eighth abbot, presided for 20 years.

[Col. 1345B] 787. Roudtrud, daughter of Charles, was betrothed to the Emperor Constantine.

789. [Note: [Col. 1345] “The following items are in another ink.”] In this year Charles sent 83 chapters, almost all of the canons of his entire kingdom, to his bishops, so that with their help they might correct what needed correction.

790. Charles spent this year quietly at Worms.

791. Charles devastated the land of the Huns.

792. At a synod held at Regensburg, the Felician heresy was condemned.

793. The Saxons again rebelled, according to their custom.

794. At a great synod held at Frankfurt, the Felician heresy was again condemned. A false synod of the Greeks, held in support of the veneration of images, was condemned by the bishops. At this time Alcuin, also called Albinus, was held in high regard by the king and the others for his life and teaching.

795. The Huns, having sent ambassadors, surrendered themselves and their land to Charles and promised Christianity.

796. After Pope Hadrian died at Rome, Leo III, the 98th pope, held office for 20 years.

797. At Constantinople, Emperor Constantine was blinded by the Greeks.

798. Helena, mother of the blinded Emperor Constantine, sent ambassadors to Charles seeking peace.

799. As the report has it, Pope Leo was blinded by the Romans in the greater litany, his tongue having been cut out; after being rescued by certain men, he was brought to Charles in Saxony. Gerold, prefect of Bavaria, standard-bearer and counselor of Charles, pious and devout, fell while fighting against the Huns. He was buried at the Reichenau, which he had enriched with many gifts and estates. The patriarch of Jerusalem sent relics from the Lord’s sepulchre to King Charles.

800. Charles sent distinguished gifts to Jerusalem. Going to Rome, he restored Pope Leo to his see after the pope had purged himself by oath of the accusations brought against him and not proven.

801. On Christmas Day, Pope Leo placed a crown on Charles, and, while the Romans shouted acclamations, he was proclaimed Caesar Augustus and emperor, the first of the kings of the Franks to be so called. Later, according to Roman law, he condemned to death the men who had attacked Pope Leo; but at the prayers of that same pope he spared their lives and banished them into exile. An earthquake occurred on the second day before the Kalends of May [April 30].

802. Aaron, king of the Persians, sent an elephant to Emperor Charles among other gifts.

803. The Blood of the Lord was found at Mantua, and this was reported to Emperor Charles. The emperor entrusted Pope Leo with investigating the truth of the matter. Taking this as an opportunity, the pope set out and came to the emperor; with him he celebrated Christmas at Carisiacum.

804. The lord pope, presented with great gifts by the emperor, returned to Rome.

805. The younger Charles, sent by his father, subjugated Bohemia.

[Col. 1346B] 806. Emperor Charles divided the kingdom among his three sons.

807. Aaron, king of the Persians, sent Emperor Charles, together with other gifts, an ingenious clock.

808. King Eardwulf of the Northumbrians, driven from his kingdom, came to Emperor Charles to seek justice.

809. The question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit was debated at a synod.

810. The Spaniards and Greeks, through ambassadors, made peace with him. He learned that his son Pepin, king of Italy, had died.

811. Heito, abbot of the Reichenau and bishop of Basel, sent to Constantinople, wrote his “odoporic,” that is, his itinerary [Note: [Col. 1345] “i. i.” in another ink; absent from 3].

[Col. 1346C] 812. After Emperor Michael had sent back Charles’s ambassadors, he also sent his own to confirm the peace. The people of Benevento paid Charles a tribute of 25,000 gold solidi.

813. Emperor Charles sent Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of Nonantola, to Constantinople; their “odoporic,” that is, their book of travel [Note: [Col. 1345] “i. l. i.” in another ink], is likewise said to have been written. He made his son Louis his associate in the kingdom. After the death of his son Pepin, king of Italy, he made Pepin’s son Bernard, his grandson, king of Italy. He ordered five very large councils to be held for the condition of the churches, at Mainz, Reims, Tours, Chalon, and Arles.

814. The great Emperor Charles, after he had first distributed his treasures among the 21 archbishoprics of his kingdom and among the other bishoprics and churches, was struck by fever and pleurisy. He died at Aachen on the fifth day before the Kalends of February [January 28] and was buried there with honor, in the 71st year of his age, the 47th of his reign, the 44th since the subjugation of Italy, and the 14th of his empire, in the seventh indiction. His son Louis, called the Pious, succeeded him and reigned for 27 years. [Note: [Col. 1345] “In another ink.”] He immediately held a general assembly at Aachen and corrected many wrongful acts committed throughout the kingdom.

815. Certain leading Romans conspired for the death of Pope Leo and were punished.

816. Pope Leo died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [May 25]. Stephen, the 99th pope, held office for seven months. Coming to King Louis in Francia, he crowned him emperor at Reims and then returned to Rome. The emperor, after convening a synod, made many good arrangements concerning the condition and religious life of the monasteries.

817. Pope Stephen died on the ninth day before the Kalends of February [January 24]; Paschal, the 100th pope, held office for seven years. Ambassadors of Emperor Leo came from Constantinople to Emperor Louis seeking peace.

818. Emperor Louis subdued the Britons on this side of the sea.

819. At a synod held at Aachen, many matters concerning the condition of the churches were arranged.

820. As a result of floods caused by the rains, a great pestilence occurred. [Note: [Col. 1347] “Henceforth in another ink, but the same hand.”]

821. Emperor Louis divided the kingdom among his sons, released exiles, and remitted the debts of all.

822. Emperor Louis performed public penance for his public sins and corrected whatever in his kingdom needed correction. Lothair was sent to Italy, and Pepin, having taken a wife, to Aquitania, as kings. At Fulda, Abbot Eigil died; Rabanus, a learned man and an excellent interpreter of the divine books, succeeded him. At the Reichenau, when Heito, abbot and bishop, adopted a private life, Erlebald succeeded him as the tenth abbot.

823. At the request of Pope Paschal, Lothair, king of Italy, was crowned emperor by him at Rome. Many fields were devastated by hail beyond the usual measure; in spring also [Note: [Col. 1347] “v. e. i. i.” and absent from 3], between it and [the following season?], great stones fell in some places.

824. At Rome, after Paschal, Eugenius, the 101st pope, held office for three years. At the Reichenau, the monk Wettinus was taken out of his body and brought back [Note: [Col. 1347] “and brought back,” absent from 3]; after three days he died. Bishop Heito wrote down his visions in prose, and Walahfrid in heroic verse.

826. King Harald of the Danes, with his wife and sons and a great multitude of his people, was baptized at Mainz. Hildwin, abbot of Saint-Denis, obtained from Pope Eugenius the bones of the blessed martyr Sebastian and placed them at Soissons in the basilica of Saint Medard.

827. The bodies of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter were transferred to Francia. In this year Abbot Ansegis compiled in four little books both secular and ecclesiastical laws promulgated by Emperors Charles the Great, Louis, and Lothair.

[Col. 1347D] 828. At Rome, after Eugenius, Valentinus, the 102nd pope, held office for 40 days [Note: [Col. 1347] “At Rome … 16 years” was first written under 827 and then under 828 in 1]. After him Gregory IV, the 103rd pope, held office for 16 years. The relics of Saint Marcellinus were brought to Aachen and were glorified by very many miracles.

829. An earthquake occurred at Aachen on Holy Saturday of Easter.

830. Ratolf, bishop of Verona, obtained from the duke of Venice the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist, under the name of the martyr Valens, and brought it with the body of the martyr Genesius to the island of the Reichenau.

831. The emperor, depriving all his opponents of their honors, provoked the hostility of both his sons and the others against him.

832. The emperor took up arms against his sons; out of fear of his sons he repudiated his wife.

833. The emperor again came into Alsace against his sons. When Pope Gregory arrived there with the sons, the emperor was abandoned by his own men and fell into his sons’ power.

834. By the judgment of the bishops, the emperor, having laid down his arms, was confined to perform penance.

835. The emperor held a great assembly at Lyon with his sons Pepin and Louis.

[Col. 1348B] 837. It is said that Ticinum trembled eight times during the night on the third day before the Kalends of January [December 30].

838. After holding an assembly at Nijmegen, the emperor forbade his son Louis the kingdom of the Franks. Puoto, a palace deacon, fell into Judaism.

839. The emperor was reconciled with his son Lothair. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims [Note: [Col. 1347] “E. R. a. d.”; these items are in another ink, belonging to the year 1088 in 1], was degraded.

840. The emperor, having designated his son Lothair for the empire, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [June 20] and was buried at Metz.

841. Louis the Younger, having joined his forces with those of his brother Charles, was unable to reach an agreement with Lothair, who sought sole rule, concerning the division of the kingdom. They fought a battle near the estate of Fontenay on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [June 25]. Louis and Charles gained possession of the camp after Lothair had been put to flight.

[Col. 1348C] 842. At last, since all desired peace, they decided to divide the kingdom into three parts. At the Reichenau, Walahfrid Strabo, a learned man and the twelfth abbot, presided; he wrote many works in verse and prose.

843. Lothair received Italy with the imperial title, and Belgic Gaul, which to this day is called the kingdom of Lothair after him [Note: [Col. 1347] “after him,” in another ink]. Louis obtained Germany, and Charles received Gaul.

844. [Note: [Col. 1347] These items were first assigned to 843 and then to 844 in 1.] After Pope Gregory died, Sergius II, the 104th pope, held office for three years.

845. [Note: [Col. 1347] These items were first assigned to 844 and then to 845 in 1.] Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, sent to Pope Sergius a book that he had composed about the holy cross in various figures and in verse.

846. [Note: [Col. 1347] These too appear to have first been assigned to the preceding year.] Emperor Lothair compelled the Burgundians, who were preparing to rebel, to surrender.

847. *(Deeds of the Roman pontiffs.)* [Note: [Col. 1347] The words “At Rome … confirmed” were likewise first assigned to the preceding year in 1.] At Rome, Leo IV, the 105th pope, held office for nine years and three months. He built the fortification at Rome called the Leonine City, dedicated it with apostolic blessing, and confirmed it in perpetuity under anathema. [Note: [Col. 1347] This number has been erased.] At Mainz, Rabanus, the most learned abbot of Fulda, was ordained archbishop. Soon afterward, at Louis’s command, he convened a great synod at Mainz. During the time of Pope Leo IV and Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, at the assembly of the bishops at Mainz (the Council of Mainz), the heresy of the Predestinarians was refuted; its chief tenets had been shattered and crushed by Saint Augustine in *On Rebuke and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance* [Note: [Col. 1349] “and the gift of perseverance,” in somewhat different ink in 1; absent from 3].

848. A certain priest, Gottschalk, teaching as a doctrine that some people were inevitably predestined by God to life and others to death, was convicted at the assembly of the bishops at Mainz and expelled from the kingdom.

849. At the Reichenau, Abbot Walahfrid Strabo died; Folcuin, the thirteenth abbot, succeeded him and presided for nine years.

850. There was a great famine around the Rhine, during which Archbishop Rabanus fed many poor people.

852. A great synod and general assembly was held at Mainz by Archbishop Rabanus and King Louis.

853. The Northmen burned the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours.

855. Emperor Lothair, having abandoned the world and divided his kingdom among his sons, became a monk at Prüm; not long afterward, on the third day before the Kalends of October [September 29], he departed to the heavenly kingdom. After him, his sons Louis the Emperor held Italy, and Lothair the Cisalpine parts of the kingdom.

856. At Mainz, after Archbishop Rabanus died, Charles, son of King Pepin of Aquitania, succeeded him. At Rome, after Leo died, Benedict III, the 106th pope, held office for two years and six months.

857. A synod was convened at Mainz by Archbishop Charles.

858. A certain village near Mainz and the Rhine, called Cammunt, was devastated when an evil spirit afflicted its inhabitants in many ways. At Rome, after Benedict, Pope Nicholas, the 107th pope, held office for nine years.

859. Frequent earthquakes shook Mainz. There, the devout and holy priest Probus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [June 25].

860. A very severe winter made even the Ionian Sea as far as Venice passable for horses across the ice.

861. Meginrad, a monk of the Reichenau and the first inhabitant of the wilderness adjoining Lake Zurich, was killed there by certain robbers on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [January 21]. After his death he became renowned for miracles and was buried at the Reichenau. From him, that wilderness itself, cultivated to this day by holy and devout men, has grown into a noble monastery.

862. King Lothair, with the support of the archbishops Gunthar of Cologne and Theutgaud of Trier, repudiated Tiutberga, his lawful wife, after a synod had been convened to contrive this.

863. At a synod convened at Rome, the archbishops Gunthar and Theutgaud, who had been sent there, were deposed by Pope Nicholas and anathematized together with their synod; King Lothair was excommunicated unless he repented.

[Col. 1350A] 864. Gunthar of Cologne, usurping the episcopal office after the prohibition, later moved by penance came to Rome, but did not deserve to be reconciled.

865. Bishop Arsenius, legate of Pope Nicholas, restored Tiutberga as wife to Lothair after Lothair had pledged by the oaths of twelve of his nobles that he would honor the marriage bond.

866. The Bulgarians, with preachers sent by Pope Nicholas and King Louis, received the faith of Christ.

867. King Lothair, disregarding the oaths of his nobles, again repudiated Tiutberga and united himself with his former concubine. For this reason Pope Nicholas excommunicated him and his accomplices, sending letters to various persons.

[Col. 1350B] 868. A great synod was convened at Worms in the presence of King Louis. At Rome, after Pope Nicholas died, Hadrian II, the 108th pope, held office for five years. When King Lothair came to him and, with the futile assistance of his brother, Emperor Louis, pleaded at length for a marriage with his concubine Waldrada, it accomplished nothing. *(Regino, Chronicle, year 869.)* [Note: [Col. 1349] These words were written in the margin in another ink in 1; assigned to the year 869 in 2.] The condition imposed on him was that, if he were innocent, he should receive the Lord’s body confidently; but if he were guilty, he should in no way presume to receive it. But he, rash man, approached, and with his accomplices received an unavoidable judgment upon himself and his kingdom—alas, in his great madness. For such a great disaster followed this presumption by divine judgment that in the kingdom of that same Lothair the entire strength and nobility seemed to have been destroyed, not by plague but as if by an enemy’s sword.

[Col. 1350C] 869. King Lothair, excusing himself before Pope Hadrian with his accomplices for the crimes laid against him and rashly receiving the Lord’s body from him, perished at Piacenza while returning home; nearly all the perpetrators of the crime also perished one after another. His uncle Charles invaded his kingdom.

870. A great synod was convened at Cologne, and many measures were decreed for the condition of the church.

871. *(Regino, Chronicle.)* [Note: [Col. 1349] Added in the same hand in 1.] Emperor Louis was reconciled by oath with the tyrant Adalgis. Nevertheless, Pope John later released him from that oath and incited him to fight against the same tyrant.

872. Emperor Basil of the Greeks sent a portion of the Lord’s cross to King Louis.

[Col. 1350D] 873. After Hadrian died at Rome, John VIII, the 109th pope, held office for ten years [Note: [Col. 1349] The remainder was added in another ink]. At his command, John the deacon of the Roman church authentically wrote the life of Saint Gregory.

874. Ratolf, bishop of Verona, died. He had built a cell bearing his name near the Reichenau.

875. After Emperor Louis of Italy died, he was buried at Milan, in the twentieth year of his reign. His uncle, King Charles of Gaul, invaded his kingdom and had himself crowned emperor by Pope John.

876. The devout King Louis died at Frankfurt on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [August 28], in the 36th year of his reign. His three sons received his kingdom: Karlomann Bavaria, Louis Germany, and Charles Alemannia, each with the adjoining provinces.

877. King Charles of Gaul died in the 37th year of his reign. His son Louis the Stammerer succeeded him in the kingdom of Gaul.

878. King Louis of Germany divided the kingdom of Lothair with his brother Charles.

879. Louis the Stammerer, son of Charles and king of Gaul, died at Compiègne on the third day before the Ides of April [April 11].

880. Karlomann, king of Bavaria, died at the estate of Oettingen on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April [March 22].

881. The Northmen ravaged many provinces in Gaul. King Charles, brother of Louis, came to Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope John together with Queen Richgard, through imperial anointing. All the bishops of Italy, except the pope, were subjected to the emperor by oath. [Note: [Col. 1351] The remainder is in a scraped-away place in 1.]

882. King Louis of Germany died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February [January 20]. Emperor Charles compelled the Northmen, who were ravaging everything all around, thereafter to confirm peace with his kingdom by oath, and received their king, who had professed Christianity, from the baptismal font. Thus, with the friendship confirmed, they departed.

883. At Rome, Pope John died after being poisoned by one man and struck with a hammer by another; immediately his attacker died, unharmed by anyone. Marinus, archdeacon and the 110th pope, presided for one year and six months. King Louis of Gaul died.

884. Karlomann, son of Louis the Stammerer and king of Gaul, died, and Emperor Charles obtained the kingdom of Gaul.

885. Pope Marinus died; Hadrian III, the 111th pope, succeeded him and held office for one year and four months.

886. Invited by the pope, the emperor came to Italy. At Rome, Stephen V, the 112th pope, held office after Hadrian for six years.

887. Empress Richgard, accused of adultery with Liutward, bishop of Vercelli, proved by divine judgment that she was untouched by sexual relations with any man and remained a virgin, although she had already appeared in the emperor’s marriage for twelve years. Soon separated from the king, she withdrew to the convent of virgins at Andlau, which she herself had built, and there, serving God, remained a virgin queen. The emperor, meanwhile, was abandoned by everyone, and Arnulf, son of his brother Karlomann, was chosen king.

888. Emperor Charles, now deprived of power and devoutly serving God, died on the Ides of January [January 13], as some say strangled by his own men, and was buried at the Reichenau. [Note: [Col. 1351] “imp.” in 1; “imperio” in Hermann.]

890. King Arnulf was requested by the apostolic see to come to Rome and defend Italy for himself against the tyrants.

891. King Arnulf destroyed the Northmen utterly.

[Col. 1352A] 892. At Rome, after Stephen, Formosus, formerly bishop of Porto, the 113th pope, held office for four years and seven months.

893. Pope Formosus invited King Arnulf to receive Italy and rescue it from the tyrants.

895. [Note: [Col. 1351] Absent from 3.] A great synod was convened at Tribur. Likewise, at the pope’s request, the king went to Italy.

896. King Arnulf finally came to Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope Formosus. Pope Formosus died on Easter Day. In his place Boniface VI, the 114th pope, was ordained; he died of gout on the fifteenth day.

897. [Note: [Col. 1351] These items were first assigned to 896 in 1, as in Herimann.] Stephen VI, the 115th pope, was substituted for him and held office for one year. He favored the tyrants.

898. [Note: [Col. 1351] These items were first assigned to 897 in 1, as in Herimann.] At Rome, after Stephen’s death, Pope Romanus, the 116th pope, held office for a little more than four months. After him, Theodore II, the 117th pope, held office for 20 days. After him, John IX, the 118th pope, was ordained and held office for two years.

899. Queen Ota, accused of adultery, was acquitted by the oath of 72 nobles.

900. [Note: [Col. 1351] “At Rome for five months,” first assigned to 899, as in Herimann, in 1.] At Rome, Benedict IV, the 119th pope, held office for three years and five months. Emperor Arnulf died at Regensburg, where he most often resided, on the sixth day before the Ides of December [December 8] [Note: [Col. 1351] “December 8,” in another ink], in the twelfth year of his reign; his son Louis, still a boy, succeeded him.

902. Beringer, Reginolf, and Gerhard, noble brothers, sons of Count Ato and Adellinda, were killed and buried at the convent of virgins at Buchau, founded by the aforementioned Adellinda; their mother herself was later buried there.

904. At Rome, after Benedict, Leo V, formerly a foreign priest, the 120th pope, held office for about two months. After him, as I have found in some sources, Christopher, formerly a cardinal, the 121st pope, held office for four months; he was deposed and became a monk.

905. At Rome, Sergius III, the 122nd pope, held office for seven years and four months.

906. Adalbert, a noble and warlike man of Babenberg, killed his rival Conrad, whom he had defeated in battle, along with many others.

907. Adalbert was brought to King Louis through the treachery of Archbishop Hatto and Liutpald, on the expectation of an agreement, and was ordered to be beheaded.

[Col. 1352D] 908. The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia. Liutpald was killed.

909. The Hungarians ravaged Alemannia.

910. The Hungarians defeated the Franks.

911. King Louis, still a young man, died and was buried at Regensburg. After him, since the royal line had died out in our regions, Conrad, son of Conrad, was elected and anointed king and reigned for seven years. Duke Burchard of Alemannia was killed at his own assembly.

912. The Hungarians were killed by Bavarians and Alemanni near the river Inn. Comets were seen. Rudolf, king of Burgundy, died; his son Rudolf succeeded him and reigned for 25 years. At Rome, Anastasius II, the 123rd pope, held office for two years and two months. At Saint Gall, the learned master Notker died.

913. The Hungarians ravaged Alemannia.

914. Solomon, bishop of Constance, was captured.

915. At Rome, Pope Lando, the 124th pope, held office for five months. After him Leo VI, the 125th pope, held office for about two months; after him John X, the 126th pope, held office for 14 years and two months.

916. The Hungarians ravaged all Alemannia with fire and sword. A synod was held at Altheim before the papal legate, that is, Peter, bishop of Ostia. [Note: [Col. 1353] “that is, P. O.,” added in 1; absent from 3.] At this general synod it was decreed by general ordinance that whoever thereafter violated a ban imposed by bishops should expiate his offense by a 40-day fast consisting only of bread, water, and salt. [Note: [Col. 1353] “At which … should expiate,” added in 1.] At Saint Gall, the blessed virgin Wilborada was enclosed more strictly.

917. Basel was destroyed by the Hungarians. Duke Erchanger and his brother were beheaded.

918. Burchard, appointed duke of Alemannia, seized tyrannical power. King Conrad died.

919. Henry, a count and by nationality a Saxon, was elected king and reigned for 18 years without royal anointing. Duke Burchard of Alemannia defeated Rudolf, king of Burgundy.

920. King Charles of Gaul came into Francia. [Col. 1353C] At [Note: [Col. 1353] “A. s. G. R. v. i. e.” in another ink] Saint Gall, the virgin Rachildis was enclosed.

923. The Blood of the Lord was brought to the island of the Reichenau by a certain matron, as is made clear by writings preserved there.

924. Saint Oudalric, bishop of Augsburg, presided for 50 years.

925. While the Hungarians were again ravaging Alemannia and coming to the monastery of Saint Gall, the enclosed virgin Wilborada was killed by one of them and crowned with martyrdom; Rachildis, her companion in enclosure, was divinely preserved unharmed.

926. After ravaging Alemannia, the Hungarians raged with fire and sword throughout Francia, Alsace, and Gaul. Duke Burchard was killed; in his place Herimann was made duke of Alemannia.

927. Heriger, archbishop of Mainz [Note: [Col. 1353] “For according to the ancients it is called not Mainz but Mogonciacum,” written in the margin in 1 and 2], died; Hildibert succeeded him.

929. At Rome, Stephen VII, the 127th pope, held office for two years and one month.

930. King Henry advanced against Bohemia.

931. At Rome, John XI, the 128th pope, held office for four years. King Henry caused the kings of the Abodrites and Northmen to become Christians, and then himself went into Gaul.

932. Henry killed the Hungarians at Siurbia.

[Col. 1354A] 934. At Constance, Conrad, a prelate distinguished by birth and life, was ordained and presided for 41 years.

935. At Rome, Leo VII, the 129th pope, held office for three years and six months.

936. King Henry died and was buried in Saxony at Quedlinburg. His son Otto succeeded him and reigned for nearly 38 years.

937. The Hungarians, ravaging Francia, Alemannia, Gaul, and Burgundy, finally returned through Italy to Pannonia. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. Rudolf, king of Burgundy, died; his son Conrad succeeded to the kingdom. Arnulf, duke of Bavaria, died, and Berthold received his duchy. The Bavarians, together with many others, rebelled against King Otto.

[Col. 1354B] 938. King Otto took the field against the Bavarians and subjugated almost all of them. At Rome, Stephen VIII, the 130th pope, held office for three years and four months.

939. King Otto subjugated all his rebels except the bishop of Metz.

940. King Otto advanced into Gaul against King Louis. There was a severe winter and a mortality among animals.

942. Kings Otto and Louis were reconciled. At Rome, Marinus II, the 131st pope, held office for three years and six months.

943. The Hungarians, invading Bavaria, were defeated.

944. An earthquake occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May [April 16].

945. At Rome, Agapetus II, the 132nd pope, held office for nearly ten years. King Otto entered Gaul.

[Col. 1354C] 946. At Saint Gall, the enclosed virgin Rachildis departed to the Lord.

947. Berthold, duke of Bavaria, died; Henry, brother of King Otto, succeeded him in the duchy.

948. Herimann, duke of Alemannia, died; Liudolf, son of King Otto, received his duchy. A great synod of bishops was held before Kings Otto and Louis at Ingelheim.

949. After Lothair, king of Italy, died, Berengar invaded his kingdom and inflicted many injuries upon his widow Adelheid, daughter of King Rudolf of Burgundy.

950. King Otto went to Italy and subjected it to himself. After expelling Berengar, he freed Lady Adelheid.

[Col. 1354D] 951. A synod of 25 bishops and a great assembly of the entire kingdom were convened at Augsburg. There Berengar came to King Otto to surrender. A fiery stone, like a mass of glowing iron, came through the air from the west, and a dragon was seen walking.

952. King Otto entered Italy with his son Liudolf, and a royal wedding was celebrated at Pavia.

953. Duke Liudolf rebelled against his father Otto, but they were reconciled by holy bishops.

[Col. 1355A] 954. The Hungarians again came forth and ravaged Francia, Bavaria, and Italy.

955. The Hungarians, laying waste all Bavaria, were defeated in battle near Augsburg, a city of Alemannia, by King Otto with God’s help, and were slaughtered in immense numbers on the fourth day before the Ides of August [August 10]. On our side also Duke Conrad fell with many others. The Hungarians who were then able to escape were likewise butchered throughout Bavaria. Their kings were hanged on gallows at Regensburg. At Rome, John XII, also called Octavian, the 133rd pope, held office for eight years and four months; alas, forgetting the dignity of so great an office, he was devoted to vanity and impurity.

956. Duke Liudolf invaded Italy in a hostile manner and put Berengar and his son to flight.

[Col. 1355B] 957. Duke Liudolf defeated Adalbert in battle; in that same year he died, and Burchard received his duchy.

958. Crosses appeared on certain garments.

961. King Otto had his son Otto, by Queen Adelheid, elected king, and he himself went to Italy with an army. A sign appeared in the sun.

962. King Otto came to Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope John, or Octavian. He rebuked the pope for his crimes but was quite unable to correct him.

963. After spending Christmas at Pavia, the emperor again came to Rome to investigate and judge Pope John’s crimes. But John fled before the emperor into Campania; in his place, Leo VIII, a venerable man, the 134th pope, was ordained by the Romans and the emperor.

964. The Romans expelled Pope Leo. After the earlier Pope John died, Benedict, a deacon, was ordained by the Romans against the emperor’s wishes; the fifth of that name and the 135th pope, he held office for two months. The city was besieged by the emperor and oppressed by such great famine that a bushel of bran sold for 30 denarii. Not long afterward, when the city had surrendered and Benedict had been handed over, the emperor restored Pope Leo and compelled the Romans to promise allegiance to him by oath.

965. The emperor returned from Italy, and Duke Burchard of Swabia defeated the rebels against the emperor in Italy.

966. After Leo died at Rome, John XIII, formerly bishop of Narni [Note: [Col. 1355] “was ordained”; the remainder is absent], the 136th pope, held office for a little more or less than seven years.

968. A solar eclipse occurred on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December [November 21].

969. At this time Pope John, severely afflicted by certain men and driven into exile, was scarcely restored to his see by a certain John.

970. Emperor Otto came to Rome and severely avenged the wrongs inflicted upon the lord pope on the perpetrators of the crimes.

971. Saint Ulrich, bishop, while ill, obtained from the emperor his episcopate for Adalbero, his sister’s son.

[Col. 1356A] 972. When a synod had been convened by the bishops at Ingelheim, Blessed Bishop Ulrich and Adalbero were accused of violating the canons; but after stating and defending their case, they departed acquitted. At Rome Benedict VI, the 137th pope, sat for one year and ten months.

973. Adalbero the cleric, who was expected to become bishop, died. Emperor Otto died suddenly on the Nones of May at Parthenopolis—that is, Magdeburg—where he himself had established an archbishopric [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *archiepm*.], and was buried there; his son Otto succeeded him as ruler. Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, migrated to the Lord in the eighty-third year of his age and the fiftieth of his episcopate, on the fourth day before the Nones of July. Burchard, duke of Alemannia, died, and Otto, son of Liutolf, assumed his paternal duchy.

974. At Rome Pope Benedict was accused by the Romans [Col. 1356B] and strangled, and while he was still alive Boniface was ordained pope; but after being expelled one month later, he made for Constantinople. Benedict VII, previously bishop of Sutri, the 138th pope, sat for nine years. At Constance Bishop Conrad, of blessed memory, departed this life on the sixth day before the Kalends of December; Ganenolf [Note: Thus manuscript 1.] succeeded him.

976. Dissension arose between King Otto and Henry, duke of Bavaria.

977. Discord arose between Otto, duke of Swabia, and Henry, duke of Bavaria. [Note: “Arose” is repeated in manuscript 3.]

978. King Otto led an army against King Lothair into Gaul.

979. At Constance Bishop Gamenolf died; Gebhard, a noble prelate, succeeded him and governed the church for sixteen years. He built the basilica of Saint Gregory on the bank of the Rhine, as well as an abbey, from his own estates.

981. King Otto, having traversed Italy, entered Calabria with an army.

982. King Otto, after his army had been destroyed by the Greeks and Saracens in Calabria, escaped by leaping from the ship in which he had been captured. [Compare Alpertus.] Otto, duke of Swabia, died, and Conrad succeeded him.

983. King Otto fell ill at Rome, died on the sixth day before the Ides of December, and was buried in the portico of Saint Peter.

984. Otto III, son of Otto II by a Greek wife, still a boy, reigned in place of his father. At Rome John XIV, also called Peter, previously bishop of Pavia, the 139th pope, sat for eight months. Boniface, who had first exiled Benedict and had been improperly ordained, returned from Constantinople, whither he had fled, seized him, and, as they report, poisoned him; he then usurped his see as the 140th pope.

985. At Rome Boniface VII, after occupying the usurped see for eleven months, perished by a sudden death. After his death, his own men beat him, pierced him, and dragged him through the streets by his feet; only after a long while, when the clergy took pity on him, was he buried.

986. At Rome John XV, the 141st pope, sat for ten years and seven months. Since he held his clergy in contempt, he was hated by them.

987. A great famine occurred.

[Col. 1357A] 991. Theophanu, the Greek empress and mother of King Otto, died.

992. [Note: Inserted in another ink.] At Aachen, in a general synod held in the presence of the envoys of Pope John, it was decreed that no one should presume to conduct secular legal proceedings or contract a marriage during the four weeks before Christmas, from Septuagesima until Easter, or during the fourteen days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist. [Note: The acts of this synod have perished; this is therefore all that is known about it.]

994. When Conrad, king of Burgundy, died, his son Rudolf succeeded him in the kingdom. [Note: Manuscript 3 lacks “son of him succeeded in the kingdom.”]

995. Henry, duke of Bavaria, died, and his son, of the same name, obtained the duchy. At Constance the venerable Bishop Gebhard died and rests buried in the basilica of Saint Gregory the pope, which he himself had built. Lambert the monk succeeded him in the episcopate and ruled for twenty-three years.

996. King Otto went to Italy with an army and subdued those who were rebelling against him.

997. King Otto, having subdued the rebels, gained possession of Italy and Rome. Gregory V, also called Bruno, son of Otto the duke, was ordained the 142nd pope, and Otto was crowned emperor by him. This venerable pope, striving to restore canonical discipline there, sat for three years and nine months. At Reichenau Alawicus was promoted as its twenty-sixth abbot; he was consecrated at Rome by the pope himself and was granted a privilege. Conrad, duke of the Alemanni, died, and Hermann received the duchy in his place.

999. Emperor Otto again invaded Italy with an army. [Note: “Army” is miswritten as *exercertitu* in manuscript c.]

[Col. 1357C] 1000. When Pope Gregory died at Rome, Silvester II, also called Gerbert, first archbishop of Rheims and later of Ravenna, excessively devoted to secular learning and therefore greatly loved by the inquisitive emperor, sat as the 143rd pope for five years.

1001. Emperor Otto surveyed Italy, which was everywhere subject to him.

1002. Emperor Otto died in Italy on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighteenth year of his reign. His intestines were buried at Augsburg, but the rest of his body was buried at Aachen. In his place Henry, duke of Bavaria, became king and reigned for twenty-three years.

1003. King Henry went with an army against Henry the margrave and others who resisted him. Strasbourg was plundered by Hermann, duke of Alemannia, who had rebelled against the king; divine vengeance severely punished the perpetrators of the crime, and the duke himself made satisfaction in a holy place.

1004. As King Henry advanced into Italy, he subdued it. On the very day on which he was crowned, he stormed Pavia and brought it under control by sword and fire. Returning from there to Saxony, he subdued Bohemia and Boleslaus, duke of the Slavs, together with his entire people.

[Col. 1358A] 1005. [Note: “A great famine occurred.” John XVI, pope 3: an error of the printer.] At Rome, after Gerbert, John XVI, the 144th pope, sat for one year.

1006. At Rome John XVII, also called Phasanus, was ordained the 145th pope and sat for six years. [Note: “Six” was added in another ink in manuscript 1.]

1007. With the greatest zeal, King Henry built a noble and wealthy bishopric at his castle called Babenberg. [Note: Manuscript 3 adds: “in honor of Saint George the martyr.”] Eberhard was promoted as its first bishop in this year.

1008. At Reichenau, after the cruel abbot Immo had been removed, Bern, a learned and pious man and a monk of Prüm, was appointed abbot. He was gladly received and consecrated by Lambert, bishop of Constance, as the twenty-ninth abbot of that place. Distinguished for piety and learning, he ruled for forty years.

1009. [Note: Written in another ink and assigned to the year 1010. A line in the same ink assigns it to 1009 in manuscript 1; manuscript 2 assigns it to 1009, manuscript 3 to 1010.] At Rome Sergius IV was ordained the 146th pope.

[Col. 1358B] 1011. Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Erchenbald succeeded him.

1012. When Conrad, duke of Carinthia, died, he left the duchy to Adalbero. Hermann, duke of Alemannia, died, and Ernest received his duchy.

1013. When Pope Sergius died at Rome, Benedict VIII, the 147th pope, sat for nearly twelve years.

1014. King Henry was crowned emperor at Rome by Pope Benedict with the imperial blessing.

1015. Ernest, duke of Alemannia, was wounded by an arrow and died while Count Adalbero was pursuing a wild animal during a hunt. His duchy was received by his son, who bore the same name, while his widow Gisela was taken by Conrad, son of Henry and later to become emperor. Megingaud, archbishop of Trier, died; Poppo succeeded him.

1017. Gotefrid, duke of part of Lotharingia, defeated Count Gerhard in battle.

1018. When Lambert, bishop of Constance, died, Roudhard governed for nearly five years.

1019. Conrad, son of the late Conrad, duke of Carinthia, defeated Duke Adalbero in battle at Ulm and drove him into flight.

1020. Invited by the emperor, Pope Benedict came to Babenberg and there dedicated the church of Saint Stephen.

1021. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, a man of great holiness, departed this life and became renowned for many miracles; Piligrin succeeded him. When Erchenbald, archbishop of Mainz, also died, Aribo succeeded him. Emperor Henry set out on an expedition to Italy.

1022. Emperor Henry, advancing into Campania, received Troia, Naples, Capua, and the other cities into submission. To certain Normans who had gathered there during his reign he granted, as they report, a certain territory in those regions. Thus he returned victoriously through Rome to Germany. Roudhard, bishop of Constance, died; Heimo governed in his place for nearly [Note: The duration is missing in manuscripts 1 and 2.] years. Notker, the master of Saint Gall, also died.

1023. At Regensburg, after Bishop Gebhard, a man most worthy of praise, another Gebhard was enthroned.

In this year a synod was held at Mainz. [Note: “In—be admitted” was added later in the margin, by the same hand in manuscript 1.] [Note: More probably at Seligenstadt, not far from Mainz and Frankfurt; compare the *Life of Meinwerk*, chapter 178.] It decreed that the Christian people should abstain from meat and animal fat for fourteen days before the feast of Saint John, except when illness required otherwise or on account of a feast celebrated with particular solemnity in that bishopric. Likewise, they were to abstain for fourteen days before Christmas. It was also decreed there that fasts should be observed on the vigils of Epiphany, All Saints, the Assumption of Saint Mary, and Saint Lawrence, so that one hour for eating might be allowed.

1024. When Benedict died at Rome, his brother John XVIII, a layman who became the 148th pope, sat for nearly nine years. Emperor Henry also died without sons on the third day before the Ides of July and was buried at the bishopric of Babenberg, which he himself had built and to which he had left all his estates and treasures as heir. After an assembly had been held at the village of Kamba, Conrad the Elder, son of Henry, was raised to the kingship and anointed by Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, on the sixth day before the Ides of September. Not long afterward his wife Gisela was blessed as queen by Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.

[Col. 1359C] 1025. A rebellion against King Conrad was undertaken by Conrad, his paternal cousin, Ernest, duke of Alemannia, and many others.

1026. King Conrad advanced into Italy and subdued almost the whole of it on this side of Rome. At Constance, after Heimo, Warmannus governed as bishop for nearly eight years.

1027. King Conrad reached Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope John on Holy Easter Day. Returning from there to Alemannia, he consigned Ernest, duke of Alemannia, and Conrad—who surrendered themselves to him—into exile at Ulm.

1028. Henry, son of the emperor, was elected king at Aachen and anointed on Holy Easter Day by Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne.

[Col. 1359D] 1029. Brun, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Eberhard succeeded him.

1030. Duke Ernest, released from exile and again rebelling against the emperor, was killed with many others on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

1031. Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, died. Bardo, a monk venerable in life and habit, succeeded him.

[Col. 1360A] 1032. Rudolf, the feeble king of Burgundy, died and sent his crown to Emperor Conrad. Odo, son of his sister and prince of the French Champagne, invaded his kingdom. Bern, abbot of Reichenau, sent the privileges of his monastery to Rome and received from Pope John, in turn, a privilege with sandals, permitting him to celebrate Mass in episcopal vestments. For this reason he was accused before the emperor by Warmannus, bishop of Constance, as an invader of the bishop’s office. He was so pressed by both sides that at last he handed the same privilege with the sandals to the bishop himself, to be burned publicly in his synod—that is, on the Lord’s Supper of the following year. In that same year the monastery of Bouchain was consumed by fire on the second day before the Ides of June. [Note: “January” was corrected to “June” in manuscript 1; manuscript 3 has “July.”]

1033. Invading Odo’s French province, the emperor devastated Champagne for so long [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “Gaul”; but see below under 1037.] that Odo himself eventually came humbly and promised satisfaction, although falsely. When John died at Rome, Benedict IX, also called Theophylact, the 149th pope, though unworthy of so great an office, sat for more than twelve years.

1034. The emperor advanced into Burgundy and subjected it to himself. When Warmannus, bishop of Constance, died, Eberhard succeeded him. Brun, son of Mathilda, succeeded Meginhard as bishop of Würzburg.

1035. A great synod was convened at Tribur by the emperor.

1036. Hermann succeeded Piligrin as archbishop of Cologne. After Gebhard II, bishop of Regensburg, died, a third Gebhard succeeded him. King Henry, son of the emperor, took Chunihild, daughter of Knut, king of the Danes [Col. 1360C] and English, as his wife at Nijmegen in a royal marriage. The Slavic Lutici became tributary to the emperor. The emperor advanced into Italy in winter.

1037. When the emperor came to Pavia, he placed Heribert, archbishop of Milan, accused of disloyalty, in custody. Escaping by flight, Heribert strove with all his strength to rebel against the emperor. The emperor besieged Milan and devastated everywhere whatever belonged to the rebels. Odo, prince of French Champagne, was defeated in battle by Gotzelo, duke of Lotharingia; as he fled, he was killed by a certain soldier.

1038. While the emperor was celebrating Christmas at Parma, a tumult arose between the people of Parma and the army. Many fell on both sides, but more among the Parmans, and the city itself was consumed by fire. The pope excommunicated the archbishop of Milan, who was rebelling against the emperor. Queen Chunihild, wife of King Henry, died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, and Hermann, duke of Alemannia, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, together with many others in Italy. Stephen, king of the Hungarians, of good memory, died; he had converted himself and his entire people to the faith of Christ. Peter succeeded him.

[Col. 1361A] 1039. Emperor Conrad died on the third day before the Nones of June. His son, King Henry, succeeded him.

1040. King Henry went to war against the duke of Bohemia, but after many nobles and soldiers had been killed or captured in the forest fortifications on both sides, he could accomplish nothing worthy of note. [Note: The text is the same in manuscripts 4, 4b, and 5.] When Eberhard, the first bishop of Babenberg, died, Suideger succeeded him.

1041. The Hungarians established a certain Ovo as their king [Note: “Choosing” appears in manuscripts 4 and 4b.] and expelled their king Peter. As a fugitive and exile, Peter sought and obtained the favor of King Henry, against whom he had rebelled the previous year. King Henry entered Bohemia with an army, devastating everything with fire and plunder. He compelled the rebellious duke to give hostages, to come humbly after him to Regensburg and surrender, and to confirm his loyalty and service to him by oath. [Note: The text is the same in manuscripts 4, 4b, and 5.]

1042. When Ovo, the tyrant of the Hungarians, was devastating the borders of Bavaria, the greater part of his army perished after being defeated in battle by Margrave Adalbert. Advancing into Pannonia, King Henry destroyed the fortified cities and subjected many others by surrender. Since they refused to receive their king Peter, he appointed a certain duke over them; immediately after Henry’s departure, Ovo drove this duke into Bohemia.

1043. King Henry again advanced into Pannonia. Ovo, scarcely obtaining an agreement, offered satisfaction and gifts, and Henry withdrew. From there he came into Alemannia and, at the synod of Constance, remitted every debt to all who had offended against him. Urging others to do the same to their debtors, he established a peace such as many ages had not seen. Afterward he took Agnes, daughter of William of Poitiers, and had her anointed queen at Mainz; he celebrated a royal wedding at Ingelheim. There Liutpald, son of Margrave Adalbert, died.

1044. When Gotzelo, duke of Lotharingia, died, he left his duchy, promised by King Henry, to his son Gotzelo, although the latter was incompetent. But his other son, Godfrey, already a duke, since he could not obtain from the king the duchy owed to his brother, dared to rebel against the pious king. King Henry fought bravely with a small army against the very powerful Hungarian nation [Note: Missing in manuscripts 1 and 2.] and defeated it. He put the tyrant Ovo to flight and restored the expelled Peter to his former dignity. Later, when Peter had been strengthened in the kingdom, he seized Ovo together with his wife and sons and beheaded him. A great force of famine compelled people to eat unclean animals. [Note: The sentence beginning “A great force” is also found in manuscripts 4 and 5.]

The Romans expelled Pope Benedict for his crimes [Note: “The Romans … 1046” was added later in the margin in manuscript 1.] and rashly appointed a certain Sylvester as the 150th pope. [Note: Added in another ink.] Pope Benedict nevertheless later expelled him with the help of certain persons. Restored to his see, Benedict voluntarily withdrew from the papacy [Note: “Voluntarily … 1046” was added later in another ink.] and allowed Gratian, called Gregory VI, to be ordained pope in his place, in the year of the Lord 1046.

1045. Otto, count palatine, was made duke of Alemannia. Peter, king of the Hungarians, after inviting King Henry to come to him, handed over the kingdom of Pannonia to him; nevertheless, he received it back from Henry to possess for himself during his lifetime. Brun, bishop of Würzburg, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. [Note: “Würzburg” is written thus in manuscripts 1 and 3.] Godfrey, coming to surrender to the king, was sent into custody. The Lutici surrendered to the king and promised their customary tribute. Gunther the hermit migrated to Christ and rests buried at Prague, a city of Bohemia. [Note: “A city of Bohemia” is missing in manuscript 3.]

1046. At Aachen, on Pentecost, the king restored the duchy to Duke Godfrey, releasing him from custody. He also removed the episcopate from Widger, prelate of Ravenna, who was excessively credulous and had not yet been consecrated. The Hungarians blinded their king Peter and set up a certain Andrew as king in his place. When King Henry came with an expedition to Italy, Pope Gratian, called Gregory VI [Note: Added in manuscript 1; absent in manuscript 3.], whom the Romans had appointed after expelling his predecessors, met him at Piacenza and was received honorably. Nevertheless, afterward at a synod at Sutri he resigned the pastoral office, not unwillingly. [Note: “Not … resigned” was written over an erased passage in manuscript 1; compare the different account in Hermann’s text.] In his place Suideger, bishop of Babenberg, was elected by common consent, though he resisted greatly. During the time of this apostolic bishop innumerable and very great earthquakes occurred in Italy. This was perhaps because the same apostolic bishop had not been canonically substituted for his predecessor, who had not been canonically deposed—namely, the one whom no fault had deposed, but simple humility had persuaded to withdraw from office. [Note: The sentence beginning “During the time” was added in the margin in manuscript 1.] Eberhard, bishop of Constance, died at Rome; Theoderic succeeded him.

1047. On Christmas Day itself Suideger was consecrated as usual and was called Clement II, the 152nd pope. [Note: “151st” was corrected to “152nd” in manuscript 1.] He sat for nine months. Immediately, on that same day, he raised King Henry, together with his wife Agnes, by the imperial blessing. Hunfrid was made archbishop of Ravenna. The citizens of Benevento, mistreating the emperor’s mother-in-law after she had returned from Mount Gargano, rebelled against the emperor. The emperor transferred the body of Blessed Guido, abbot of Pomposa, from the city of Parma to Speyer with him. Poppo, archbishop of Trier, died; Eberhard succeeded him. Godfrey, duke, and Baldwin of Flanders rebelled against the emperor. [Col. 1362D] The margrave Theoderic of Flanders also rebelled against the emperor. [Note: The name is in an erased passage in manuscript 1.] The emperor led an army against him but accomplished little. Clement, also called Suideger, pope, died on the seventh day before the Ides of October. [Note: “Seventh,” “before the Ides,” and “October” were added in manuscript 1.] Among other things that Godfrey did against the king, he burned the city of Verdun; the emperor gave his duchy to a certain Adalbert.

[Col. 1363A] 1048. The emperor appointed Otto of Schweinfurt duke of the Swabians. The blood of the Lord was discovered near the city of Mantua, as is believed, through a divine revelation given to a certain blind man. Bern, abbot of Reichenau, a man distinguished in learning and conduct, died; Ulrich succeeded him.
