Poppo, bishop-elect of Brescia, was sent to Rome by the emperor, received honorably, and ordained the 153rd pope, called Damasus II. [Note: “The 152nd” was corrected to “the 153rd” in manuscript 1.] [Note: “And he sat for thirty days” was added in manuscript 1.] He sat for thirty days. Emperor Henry and Henry, king of Gaul, met in the territory of Metz and confirmed peace between them by oath. Godfrey killed Duke Adalbert; the emperor gave his duchy to Gerhard. [Note: Some material has been erased here in manuscript 1.]

1049. The emperor appointed Conrad duke of Bavaria and promoted Gotebald as patriarch of Aquileia, after the recently deceased Eberhard. Several princes and bishops entered Flanders, killed Theoderic after defeating him in battle, and subjected that province to the emperor. Brun, bishop of the Leuci—that is, of Toul—was elected by the emperor and sent to Rome. [Note: “Of Toul” is written above the line in manuscript 1 and is absent in manuscript 3.] He was called Pope Leo IX, the 154th pope, [Note: “The 153rd” was corrected to “the 154th” in manuscript 1.] and sat for five years. At the next Easter he consecrated Ulrich of Reichenau as abbot at Rome and confirmed and renewed the privileges of his monastery, granted by the apostolic see. The same pope held a synod at Rome, chiefly against the heresy of simony. At a plenary synod he decreed that from then on the concubines of Roman priests should be assigned as servants to the Lateran palace. [Note: The sentence beginning “At a plenary synod” was added in the margin in manuscript 1.] He prohibited, under anathema, the buying and selling of altars.

Imma died in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1049, on the second day before the Nones of April. [Note: “The second day before the Nones of April” was added later in the margin.] The venerable Odilo, abbot of Cluny, migrated to the Lord on the Kalends of January. [Note: “The fourth day before the Nones” was later corrected to “the Kalends” in manuscript 1; manuscripts 2 and 3 have “the fourth day before the Kalends.”] Godfrey and Baldwin were reconciled with the emperor.

1050. The lord pope convened a synod at Rome after Easter, at which he condemned the Berengarian heresy, recently brought before the apostolic see. He also convened a synod at Vercelli in the autumn, at which he anathematized the same heresy. [Note: The wording beginning “at which” was written over an erased passage.] [Note: Almost the same words occur in Bernold’s work on the several condemnations of Berengar. See Ussermann, *Prodromus*, II, 432.] At this time Empress Agnes gave birth to a son by the emperor.

1051. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Goslar and compelled many of the princes to promise allegiance by oath to his son. Hunfrid, archbishop of Ravenna, was reconciled with the lord pope at Augsburg. [Note: Manuscripts 1 and 2 read “to the lady pope.”] After Easter Pope Leo convened a synod at Rome, where he excommunicated Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, for a certain adultery and perjuries he had committed, although Gregory was absent and unaware. When Gregory later came to Rome and promised satisfaction [Note: Written in an erased passage in manuscript 1.], Leo restored him to his former office. In the same summer Bardo, venerable archbishop of Mainz, died on the third day before the Ides of June and became renowned for many miracles; Liutpald succeeded him. At Constance, when Bishop Theoderic died, Rumald succeeded him. In the autumn the emperor devastated the kingdom of Hungary. At this time Touta, a noble and religious widow, was placed by the emperor as abbess over the monasteries of Bouchain and Lindau.

1052. While the emperor was celebrating Christmas at Goslar, certain Manichaean heretics there, who condemned the eating of every kind of animal, were hanged by his order, with the consent of all, lest the heretical infection spread to others. In these days Boniface [Note: Manuscript 2 spells the name *Bonefacius*.], the richest margrave of Italy and husband of the most noble Countess Beatrice, was wounded by two soldiers with poisoned arrows, died, and was honorably buried at Mantua. The relics of Blessed Zeno the Confessor, brought to Alemannia and the village of Ulm by Walter, bishop of Verona, shone forth through many miracles. [Note: After this there is an erased passage in manuscript 1, perhaps once containing an account of the collapse of the basilica of Saint Mary at Constance, which had been copied from Hermann’s chronicle. Today the material transcribed above at Col. 1280, lines 34–40, is found there and in the margin.]

1053. The emperor celebrated Christmas with the lord pope at Worms. There, since the pope, as he had begun earlier, had demanded from the emperor the abbey of Fulda and several other places and monasteries said to have been given to Saint Peter in ancient times, the emperor finally handed over to him, in exchange for the territories on this side of Rome, most of the properties in the regions beyond Rome that belonged to his jurisdiction. He also assigned him assistance to repel the violence of the Normans.

That people had flowed into the regions of Calabria, Samnium, and Campania from the time of the former Emperor Henry. Since they boldly aided the natives in fighting against the incursions of the Greeks and Saracens, they were at first gladly received. Later, however, when more of them flocked to the fertile land and grew in strength, they violently took possession of the natives and their property. Therefore the lord pope, returning to Rome with many Germans, led an army against the Normans after Easter. But after part of his army had been put to flight and part killed by the Normans, the pope himself was besieged by them in a certain fortress. When the fortification was on the point of being stormed, necessity compelled him to restore to them the communion previously forbidden them. They then received him and escorted him honorably to Benevento, where they detained him for some time so that he would not return.

The emperor Henry held an assembly at Tribur and had his son, of the same name, elected king by everyone. He made them promise submission to him after his death, provided that he should be a just ruler. Hazelinus, bishop of Babenberg, also died in disgrace.

1054. The emperor appointed his cousin Adalbero over the church of Babenberg at the village of Ötting, where he had celebrated Christmas. At last the lord pope returned to Rome as Easter approached. Falling ill, he died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May after a glorious end, blessing everyone beforehand, bidding farewell to those whom he had admonished, confessing his sins to Saint Peter, and devoutly commending himself to him. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter beside the tomb of Saint Gregory and is said to have become renowned for miracles.

In his place Gebhard, called Victor II, the 155th pope, sat for three years. [Note: “The 154th” was corrected to “the 155th” in another ink in manuscript 1.] [Note: The words “sat for three years” were written in an erased passage. From here to the beginning of 1057, the text was written in small letters in an erased space by the same hand and inserted around the year 1092. What was erased is uncertain. Perhaps something had been written in praise of Hermann of Reichenau. At least, in the necrology, in nearly the same ink, the following appears under the eighth day before the Kalends of October: “Hermann, an outstanding teacher, died.” And in the little book on the authority of the canons he writes: “The chronicle which the lord Hermann, an outstanding calculator and most diligent investigator of times, composed with the greatest care from various chronicles and histories, which he faithfully brought down to the year 1054 of the Lord’s incarnation.” See Ussermann, *Prodromus*, II, p. 340. The notice which Urstisius prints in this year after “was freed from the demon”—“Hermann, son of Count Wolferad,” etc., through “was buried”—is taken from the St. Gall Berthold; see above. [*Patrologia Latina*, vol. CXLVI, under the year 1080.] Traces of the earlier text seem to survive in the Reichenau and Muri Berthold under the years 1055–1057.]

[Note: The same account, in the same words, occurs in Lambert under the year 1054 (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. CXLVI).]

A subdeacon put poison into his chalice. When he himself wished to lift it after the consecration but could not, he prostrated himself with the people in prayer, seeking from the Lord the cause of what had happened. Immediately his poisoner was seized by a demon. Thus, when the cause had been revealed, the lord pope ordered the chalice containing the Lord’s blood to be enclosed within a certain altar and preserved there forever as a relic. Then he again prostrated himself with the people in prayer and remained there until the subdeacon was freed from the demon. Baldwin rebelled against the emperor. Godfrey, the duke, secretly entering Italy, took Lady Beatrice, widow of Margrave Boniface, as his wife.

## Genuine Second Part (Years 1055–1100)

[Col. 1365]

### 1055

[Col. 1365B]

The emperor visited Italy and carried away the aforementioned Beatrice as a captive, since he was greatly displeased that she had been joined to Duke Godfrey. Welf, duke of Carinthia, died.

### 1056

[Note: This section was written in small letters by the same hand.]

Pope Victor, sending Hildebrand, then archdeacon and later pope, convened a general synod at Tours. There Berengar, a canon of the church of Angers, from whom the Berengarian heresy takes its name, was examined synodally and in person on account of that heresy. Since he could not defend himself, he anathematized and abjured his heresy before everyone, according to the form prescribed by the holy and universal synod of Ephesus. [Note: “Victor … Berengar, and the material concerning him … prescribed” is found in Bernold, final treatise, sections 3 and 5.]

### 1057

[Note: The numeral may originally have been 1056 and was later altered to 1057.]

[Col. 1365C]

Emperor Henry, commending his son, who had already become king, to the princes of the kingdom, died on the third day before the Nones of October. His son Henry, still very young, began to reign in his place with his mother Agnes. At Rome, after Victor, Frederick, brother of Duke Godfrey, formerly archchaplain of Pope Leo of blessed memory, who had become a monk from being a cleric and had later been promoted abbot on Monte Cassino, took the name Stephen IX and governed as the 156th pope for nine months. [Note: The following material was added later by the same hand.]

He separated from ecclesiastical fellowship all Roman clerics who, after the prohibition of Blessed Pope Leo, had remained incontinent. Thus Peter Damian, bishop-cardinal, of pious memory, testifies in his letters. [Note: See Peter Damian, *Epistle* IV.3 to Cunibert.] [Note: “Letters” is written *ltis* in manuscript 1.] [Note: Peter Damian died in 1072.]

### 1058

At Rome, after Stephen, a certain Benedict was ordained contrary to the canons through the private favor of certain persons. He governed the church without consecration for seven months. [Note: “Seven months” was inserted shortly afterward in manuscript 1.] He was expelled by Duke Godfrey, and Gerhard, bishop of Florence, called Nicholas II, the 157th pope, governed for nearly three years. [Note: “The 157th” was corrected to “the 158th” in another ink in manuscript 1.]

He decreed that those who at that time had been promoted by simoniacs without payment [Note: “Without payment” was added about 1092 in manuscript 1 and is absent in manuscripts 4 and 4b.] should be permitted to exercise their ministry. Thereafter, however, whoever was ordained by simoniacs was to gain nothing from such promotion. Peter Damian, the bishop of pious memory, also urged this pope to correct the incontinence of the clergy in accordance with the canons. [Note: Similar statements are found in Bernold, Col. 1066.]

### 1059

Frederick and his brothers [Note: “Brother” appears in manuscript 3.] of Gleiberg [Note: In manuscript 1 the letter *l* has already become visibly an *i*.] rebelled against King Henry. [Note: Gleiberg is near Giessen.]

### 1060

[Note: The entire year 1060 was erased from the earlier text and inserted in smaller letters around the year 1092. Compare the text of manuscript 4b above in Berthold, p. 271.]

[Col. 1367A]

At Rome Pope Nicholas, presiding over a general synod, again examined Berengar [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *beringaerium*, with the *e* added.] in person and synodally on account of his heresy. At last, as though converted, Berengar burned the books of his heresy before the synod and, as before, anathematized that heresy by oath. [Note: Almost the same account occurs in the final treatise, section 1; *Acta Conciliorum*, in Mansi XIX, 897.]

### 1061
At Rome, after Pope Nicholas died on 27 July, the Romans sent a crown and other gifts to King Henry, the fourth of that name, and appealed to the king concerning the election of the supreme pontiff. He held a general council at Basel; after the crown sent by the Romans had been placed upon him, he was called patrician of the Romans. Then, by common agreement of all and with the Roman legates conducting the election, Chadelo, bishop of Parma, was elected pope on 26 October and called Honorius, though he was never to possess the papacy. But twenty-seven days before his promotion, Anselm, bishop of Lucca, was ordained pope by the Normans and certain Romans, and was called Alexander, having been ordained as the 158th pope. He held the see for twelve years. He vigorously destroyed the simoniacal heresy and, in accordance with the canonical statutes, forbade ministers of the altar to have intercourse with their wives, under penalty of excommunication; he also openly prohibited laypeople, under ban, from attending the offices of clerics notoriously living in incontinence. Thus he restrained clerical incontinence with considerable prudence. The chief author of this constitution, however, was Hildebrand, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, who was especially hostile to heretics.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Above the line, “the supreme pontiff” was added in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1367] In the margin, in another ink in manuscript 1, “p. n. p.” was added after the death, as it seems, of Kadalaus, concerning whom nothing certain is known; nevertheless, after the year 1073. Compare Affò, *History of Parma*, vol. II. This is also found in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 4b.]

[Note: [Col. 1367] “157th” was changed to “158th” by the addition of I in another ink in manuscript 1.]

## 1062

[Col. 1367C]

At this time there was a great famine. A great dissension arose between Empress Agnes and Gundhar, bishop of Babenberg.

## 1063

King Henry moved an army into Pannonia and restored Solomon, son of King Andrew, to his father’s kingdom. Henry, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Imbrico succeeded him. A great slaughter occurred at Goslar in the church, with the king present.

## 1064

[Note: [Col. 1367] The account of this year is absent from manuscript 3.]

A great rebellion arose between Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, and the princes of the kingdom.

## 1065

[Note: [Col. 1367] Manuscript 3 has “1064.”]

The royal palace at Goslar was burned.

[Note: [Col. 1367] So read manuscripts 1, 2, 4, and 4b; manuscript 3 has *Goslar*.]

In that same year, 1065 from the incarnation of the Lord, when Easter was celebrated on 27 March, on which day Christ also rose, on the third day of Easter week, 29 March, in the third indiction, King Henry, in the ninth year of his reign and the fourteenth of his age, was girded with the sword in the name of the Lord. The bishop of Passau died, and Altmann, the empress’s chaplain, succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 1367] In the margin, in another ink in manuscript 1: “P. e. o. c. A. i. c. s.”; these letters are also present in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 4b.]

At this time Sigifred, archbishop of Mainz; Gundhar, bishop of Babenberg; Otto, bishop of Regensburg; and William, bishop of Utrecht, set out for Jerusalem with a great multitude and suffered many hardships on that journey. For they were even compelled to engage in battle with the pagans.

[Note: [Col. 1367] The remainder of the year was added in another ink in manuscript 1.]

Gundhar died on the same journey. Ricimann succeeded him through simony.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Manuscript 2 has *Rizimannus*.]

[Note: [Col. 1367D] The author does not intend to say that Christ rose on Easter, but that Easter occurred in this year on 27 March, the day on which the ancients believed the Lord’s resurrection had taken place. Hence, in ancient calendars, the Resurrection of the Lord is commonly noted on that same day, just as the Incarnation and Passion of the Lord are noted on 25 March. Medieval writers therefore distinguished the Easter day, which varied from year to year, from the day of the resurrection fixed in calendars on 27 March. — Uss.]

[Note: [Col. 1367] The letters “P. e. o. c. A. i. c. s.” were written in the margin in another ink in manuscript 1; they are also present in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 4b.]

## 1066

[Note: [Col. 1367] Manuscript 3 has “1065.”]

[Col. 1368B]

Many nobles perished in the civil war. Comets were seen during the octave of Easter, on 23 April, and appeared for thirty days. Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, on 15 April, Holy Saturday of Easter, after completing the offices of that day, rested in peace clothed in the priestly vestments. Conrad, provost of Cologne, ought to have succeeded him, but he was not elected by the citizens. Therefore a certain count named Theoderic seized Conrad while he was making his way to the city of Trier and, after keeping him long in custody, handed him over to four soldiers to be killed. When they had thrown him three times over a certain precipice and had been able to break nothing but his arm, one of them, moved by repentance, obtained his forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Manuscript 1 has *pcipium*.] Another, wishing to behead him, cut off only his jaw. Thus he, a martyr worthy of God, departed to the Lord.

He suffered on 1 June, in the year 1066 from the incarnation of the Lord and the tenth year of Henry’s reign, and was buried at an abbey called Dole. Later, fitting vengeance overtook the three soldiers responsible for the death of this servant of God. For one of them was unable to swallow the food he had taken, while the other two tore their own hands; and they descended into the prison of hell.

[Note: [Col. 1367] Manuscript 3 inserts the year “1056” here.]

After Conrad was killed, Udo was appointed bishop of Trier. The marriage of King Henry took place.

A comet was also seen.

In these times the venerable Peter Damian, a cardinal-bishop formerly a hermit, wrote many works and refuted the incontinence of priests quite reasonably in his writings; but, they say, he treated those ordained by simoniacs with excessive clemency.

[Note: [Col. 1367] The remainder of the year was added later in another ink in manuscript 1, but is also present in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 4b.]

Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, died.

[Note: [Col. 1369D] He died on 27 July; compare Dunod, *History of the Church, City, and Diocese of Besançon*, I, pp. 104 ff.]

A canon of that same church, elected by the brethren, was appointed in his place by the king.

[Note: [Col. 1369D] Hugh II.]

## 1067

Saxony was afflicted by civil discord. The Normans wished to march hostilely against Rome. Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, ravaged the people of the Lutici with courage.

[Note: [Col. 1369] The remainder of the year was added in another ink in the margin of manuscript 1, but is also found in manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 4b.]

Heinhard, bishop of Speyer, died on the Roman journey. Henry succeeded him.

## 1068

[Note: [Col. 1369] The first line is in an erased place in manuscript 1, but is present in the others.]

King Henry, led astray by the error of his youth, so completely forgot his lawful wife and was reported to be involved in such unspeakable crimes that even his princes began plotting to deprive him of the kingdom. That entire year was rainy.

## 1069

[Col. 1369B]

Peace and reconciliation among the people were confirmed at Christmas in Goslar by royal decree under oath. King Henry ravaged the people of the Lutici. Dedo, margrave of Saxony, rebelled against King Henry, but afterward, compelled to do so, came to surrender. Oudalric, abbot of Reichenau, died, and Meginhard succeeded him. Rumald, bishop of Constance, died; Karolus succeeded him in the bishopric through simoniacal heresy. Gotefrid, the most distinguished of secular men, exceptionally ready to be moved to penitential tears by remembrance of his sins, and most generous in distributing alms, rested in peace at a most praiseworthy end on the vigil of Christmas.

[Note: [Col. 1369] “In peace” was added slightly later in manuscript 1; it is absent from manuscript 3.]

## 1070

France was afflicted by civil discord. Otto, duke of Bavaria, rebelled against King Henry, as did Magnus, son of Otto, duke of northern Saxony. But when the aforementioned Otto refused to come after being lawfully summoned to make satisfaction, the king deprived him of the duchy. Meginhard voluntarily abandoned the abbey of Reichenau; after him, a certain Roudpert was appointed over that abbey unworthily and was later expelled deservedly.

[Note: [Col. 1370D] Compare Gregory, *Register*, I, 82.]

The winter was windy and rainy.

## 1071

Welf became duke of Bavaria. King Henry endured many ambushes and passed through them all courageously. At Pentecost, Otto, formerly duke of Bavaria, voluntarily came with his associates to surrender to King Henry, in the year 1071 from the incarnation of the Lord, the fifteenth year of Henry’s reign, the thirtieth of his age, in the ninth indiction, on the third day of that same week, 14 June.

[Note: [Col. 1370D] 12 June.]

Karolus, who had acquired the bishopric of Constance by simony and, like a sacrilegious thief, had scattered the treasures of that church for his own uses, was deposed at a council held at Mainz by command of Pope Alexander. This disciple of Simon had not yet been consecrated, since, when accused there by the clergy of Constance, he could not deny the charges brought against him. Otto succeeded him in the bishopric.

[Note: [Col. 1369] “Simoniacal” was corrected to “by simony” in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1370D] Mansi, vol. XX, p. 10.]

## 1072

King Henry overcame those resisting him with scarcely any difficulty in war. Peter Damian, cardinal-bishop of blessed memory, long since crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on 22 February.

[Note: [Col. 1369] “VII Kalends of March” was added above the line in manuscript 1; it is also present in the other manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1370D] In the necrology, Bernold assigns his death to 21 February.]

Lord Gerold, truly a monk, distinguished in knowledge of the Scriptures and not inferior in character to his predecessor, succeeded him in the bishopric. Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg or Bremen, died. Leobmar succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 1369] Manuscript 2 has *Leothmarus*; manuscript 3 has *Leomarus*.]

The king built many very strongly fortified castles for himself in the regions of Saxony and Thuringia, and unjustly seized many fortifications for himself; consequently, he stirred up the minds of many against him.

## 1073

Rudolf, duke of Alemannia; Bertholf, duke of Carinthia; and Welf, duke of Bavaria, withdrew from King Henry because, after other counselors had entered the king’s service, they saw that their advice no longer carried weight with him.

Count Theoderic, moved by repentance for the crime he had committed against blessed Conrad, appointed bishop of Trier, although many dangers stood in the way, nevertheless began to go to Jerusalem with many others, in ardent faith. When they entered the sea in ships, they were overtaken by a sudden storm, and, when daylight was immediately darkened so that they were uncertain where they were going, they were repeatedly cheered by heavenly light. Then, no longer fearing death amid the dangers but contemplating eternal life, cleansed by the waves of the sea from the filth of their sins, they departed to the Lord on 17 February: namely, Count Theoderic, Widerolt, Marcuart, and 113 others.

Pope Alexander died at Rome. In his place the venerable Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Roman Church, was sought by the common agreement of all to be appointed pope. When he heard this, the archdeacon himself, judging that he was unequal to so great an honor—or rather burden—asked for time to reply. Thus, escaping by flight, he remained hidden for several days at Saint Peter in Chains. But at last, scarcely found and forcibly brought to the apostolic see, he was ordained as the 159th pope on 25 April and called Gregory VII.

[Note: [Col. 1369] “158th” was changed to “159th” by the addition of I in another ink in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1369] “25 April” was added in another ink by Bernold’s hand in manuscript 1; it is present in manuscript 3 but absent from manuscripts 2, 4, and 4b.]

[Note: [Col. 1369] Up to this point Bernold seems to have written first and then to have added what follows in the year 1074.]

[Col. 1371A]

Through his prudence, the incontinence of priests was restrained not only in Italy but also in the German regions. What his predecessor had prohibited in Italy, he endeavored to prohibit throughout the Catholic Church.

All Thuringia and Saxony rebelled against King Henry because of the aforementioned fortifications and many other things that the king had imprudently done in their region against the will of that people. Eggehard at last became abbot of Reichenau and was consecrated at Rome by the aforementioned pope.

## 1074

King Henry was reconciled with the Saxons, while the princes of his kingdom were absent, on the condition that the aforementioned fortifications, on account of which the rebellion had arisen, be destroyed; and they were subsequently destroyed. Duke Rudolf and the others were reconciled with the king.

At this time legates of the apostolic see came to the king in Alemannia to correct the king’s conduct.

[Note: [Col. 1371] In an erased place, in the same hand in manuscript 1: “p. i. r. m. c.”; the words are also present in the other manuscripts.]

The king placed himself in their hands under a pledge of correction and firmly promised his assistance to the apostolic lord in deposing the simoniacs. All the king’s counselors also promised under oath before the same legates that they would restore all the property of the churches that they had unjustly acquired, since they had purchased those possessions from simoniacs and, by their advice, had assisted men unworthy of ecclesiastical honor.

After these arrangements had been made, the legates of the apostolic see returned.

[Note: [Col. 1371] Additions in another ink occur here and there in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Gregory VII, *Register*, I, 85; II, 30.]

Heremann, margrave and son of Duke Bertald, while still a young man, took up the angelic life at Cluny with the utmost perfection. He abandoned his wife, his only son, and everything he possessed; truly a monk, he departed to the Lord on 25 April.

[Note: [Col. 1371] “Son of Bertald the duke, and after abandoning his wife and all that he possessed” is in an erased place in manuscript 1, in the same hand, and is present in the others.]

[Note: [Col. 1371] “Having abandoned” is in an erased place in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Bernold’s necrology gives 26 April.]

## 1075

King Henry celebrated Christmas at Strasbourg. He organized an expedition into Saxony. Heremann, bishop of Babenberg, accused by his clergy of simoniacal heresy, was deposed by the pope, and Roubert was substituted for him.

Pope Gregory convened a council at Rome in the first week of Lent, at which he examined the case of Henry, bishop of Speyer, though a simoniac.

[Note: [Col. 1371] This entry is absent from manuscript 3.] On the very day when his case was being examined at Rome, 24 February, he fell ill at Speyer; then, on 26 February, he miserably expired, when he also received from Pope Gregory the sentence of his condemnation, determined at the Roman synod.

[Note: [Col. 1371] “By his clergy” is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Mansi XX, p. 443.]

[Note: [Col. 1371D] Compare nearly the same words in the letter on the condemnation of the schismatics in Ussermann, *Prodr.*, II, p. 268, and in the defense of Gebhard, bishop of Constance, ibid., pp. 379–382: “But so that you may not doubt that the condemnatory sentences of our apostolic lord and of the prince of the apostles himself against Ananias and Sapphira possess equal force, consider carefully the condemnation of the bishop of Speyer and his death,” etc. The remainder may be found above in this volume, col. 1170.]

At the same synod Pope Gregory decreed that clerics who had obtained any rank or office of sacred orders by payment were henceforth not to minister in the Church; that no one was to retain a church acquired by payment; and that no one henceforth might sell or buy a church. He further decreed that all who made themselves reprehensible through incontinence should cease from clerical office. Likewise, the people were not to receive the offices of clerics whom they perceived to be disregarding the apostolic institutions mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 1372D] *Defense of the Decrees of Gregory*, col. 1107.]

The king celebrated Easter at Worms and, after Pentecost, advanced with an army into Saxony. In that expedition an innumerable multitude on both sides fell near the river called the Unstrut on 9 June, and many of the Saxons came to surrender to the king. Detwin, bishop of Liège, died; Henry succeeded him. Anno, archbishop of Cologne, of extraordinary holiness, rested in peace on 4 December; Hiltolf, inferior in birth and character, succeeded him.

## 1076

The king celebrated Christmas at Goslar, where he compelled certain men to swear that after him they would elect his son to the kingship. At this time King Henry did not cease to defile the holy Church through simoniacal heresy—investing bishoprics, abbeys, and other such offices for payment—and, among his other crimes, communicating with excommunicated persons.

A certain Roman citizen named Cintius seized Pope Gregory while he was celebrating the solemn Masses on Christmas Day. One of Cintius’s soldiers intended to kill him after he had been seized. But when he brandished his sword over the pope’s head, he collapsed, overcome by excessive terror, and could not complete the blow.

Cintius led the captured pope to his own tower, which the Romans immediately razed completely. The pope was prudently rescued and scarcely obtained life for his captor from the Romans.

Since the king, though repeatedly warned by the pope long before, refused to correct himself, and since the pope accomplished nothing by admonishing him, he finally sent him word that he would excommunicate him at the next Roman synod unless he repented. This message reached the king during the octave of Christmas.

[Note: [Col. 1371] “Cintius—while he was celebrating” is in an erased place, in the same hand, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1372D] Compare the letter on the condemnation of the schismatics, col. 1169, where, for example, these words occur: “In the year, therefore, of the Lord’s incarnation 1076, with Gregory VII established in the apostolic see.” See the remainder of this volume, col. 1169.]

Therefore, after holding an assembly at Worms on Septuagesima and another in Lombardy at Piacenza, the king made all whom he could swear off obedience to the aforementioned pope. He sent a delegation to the Roman synod, which was held in the following Lent, and insolently ordered the apostolic lord to descend from the apostolic see.

[Note: [Col. 1371] Manuscript 1 has “Septuagesima.”]

[Note: [Col. 1373D] Mansi XX, 467.]

[Note: [Col. 1373D] See col. 1169.]

But his messengers were treated most shamefully at the synod and escaped from the Romans only with the pope’s help. As for the king himself, the synod deprived him of the loyalty of his subjects, the kingdom, and communion; and it absolved from their oaths all who had sworn allegiance to him as king. It also deprived all the bishops who had voluntarily supported the king against the pope of office and communion; but it granted a delay until the feast of Saint Peter to the others who had taken part in the same conspiracy unwillingly.

[Note: [Col. 1373D] “From office … it granted a delay.” Ibid., p. 220.]

Gotefrid, duke and son of Duke Gotefrid, a participant, indeed an author, of the conspiracy mentioned above, was shamefully wounded from behind by a certain cook while he was sitting on the toilet and died before the middle of Lent.

[Note: [Col. 1373] “Before” was added above the line in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1373] “The middle” was added above the line in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1373] Manuscript 3 has “of the night.”]

Likewise, William, bishop of Utrecht, who had heaped many insults upon the apostolic lord, was struck down by a sudden death after Easter without ecclesiastical communion; Conrad was substituted for him.

[Note: [Col. 1373] “After” was added above the line in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1373] “Easter” was added above the line in manuscript 1.]

By now almost all the princes of the kingdom had separated themselves from communion with Henry. In October, therefore, the princes of the kingdom convened an assembly at Oppenheim, which was attended by a delegation of the apostolic see. There Henry firmly promised that he would appear before the lord pope at Augsburg on the approaching feast of the Purification of Saint Mary. He himself also invited the apostolic lord to come there with the princes of the kingdom.

Brother Kadalaus, converted from secular military service, brought the pope’s delegation to the assembly at Oppenheim. The pope, who was very ill, imposed this mission upon him for the remission of all his sins. After completing the mission, Brother Kadalaus received the monastic habit and rested in peace under evangelical perfection.

## 1077

The duke of the Poles crowned himself king.

[Note: [Col. 1374D] Boleslaus II.]

A very great snowfall covered the entire kingdom from 31 October of the previous year until 26 March of the present year.

King Henry, called so but distrustful of his own case and therefore evading a general hearing, secretly entered Italy against the pope’s command and the resolutions of the princes. Before the Purification of Saint Mary, at Canossa, he met the apostolic lord, who was traveling to Augsburg on the appointed day (28 January). There, through a pretense of unprecedented humiliation, he finally extorted from him, as best he could, a concession not of the kingdom but only of communion. Beforehand, however, he had given an oath that he would make satisfaction before the pope concerning the crimes charged against him and would never consent to any harm being inflicted upon the pope or any of his faithful, whether going or returning.

He did not observe this oath even for fifteen days, for he captured the venerable bishops Gerald of Ostia and Anselm of Lucca.

[Note: [Col. 1373] “Venerable” is misspelled *venerabibus* in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1373] “Ostian” was corrected to “of Ostia” in manuscript 1.]

Therefore the pope sent legates to the princes of the kingdom and declared that he had achieved little by receiving Henry into communion, since Henry was then favoring simoniacs and excommunicated persons no less than before.

[Note: [Col. 1373] The word “all” is absent from manuscript 3.]

After hearing this, the princes of the kingdom, at a general assembly held at Forchheim on 13 March, raised the excellent Duke Rudolf to the kingship. They crowned him at Mainz on 26 March, when the middle of Lent fell in that year.

The very great snowfall that had covered the whole land for so long finally began to melt at the election of the new king. On the day of his consecration, however, at the instigation of simoniacal clerics, a great rebellion arose at Mainz, so that they even attempted to break into the palace and kill the most religious clerics and monks. But the right hand of God protected the soldiers of the new ruler, although they were unarmed, so that they lost no one except one of their own men, while more than a hundred of their adversaries were killed, some by the sword and some by water.

For such killings, the legates of the apostolic see imposed this penance upon them: each man was either to fast for forty days or feed forty poor people once, yet they were not to avoid ecclesiastical communion as murderers.

After his consecration, King Rudolf withdrew into Swabia and subjected the kingdom to himself. Meanwhile Henry remained in Lombardy. Cintius, a Roman citizen, brought to Pavia with him the captured venerable bishop of Como, Reginald, wishing to receive a reward from Henry because he had captured this bishop in Henry’s service and the apostolic lord in the preceding year. But he was overtaken there by a sudden death and received the reward he deserved, which he had not feared to earn by so many sacrileges.

[Note: [Col. 1373] Manuscript 2 has “King Henry.”]

When Henry heard of Rudolf’s elevation, he implored the pope’s assistance against him, although he allowed the aforementioned bishop of Ostia still to be held captive. The pope therefore replied that he could not satisfy Henry’s appeal so long as Saint Peter remained bound in his legate, held captive by Henry.

His supplication thus frustrated, Henry turned his mind toward tyranny and decided to obtain the kingdom no longer through justice but through violence.

King Rudolf celebrated a most glorious Easter at Augsburg (16 April) with the legates of the apostolic see. One of them, the highly religious Abbot Bernard, was sent to Rome, but Count Oudalric, an accomplice of Henry, captured and robbed him. He spent almost half a year in captivity, from which the abbot of Cluny finally scarcely rescued him from Henry’s hands.

[Note: [Col. 1373] Manuscript 2 has “King.”]

[Note: [Col. 1374D] “Of Lenzburg” is added in manuscript 3.]

After Easter, the king convened a general assembly at Esslingen with the princes of the kingdom. When it had ended, he himself went with very few men to besiege a certain castle. But suddenly his rival Henry arrived with a very great multitude of Bohemians and Bavarians, whom he had suddenly been able to acquire for himself with church property. The king would most gladly have met them with the few men he then had, if his princes had not judged more prudently that this should be postponed to another time.

Henry, therefore, taking the opportunity, did not cease to devastate everything around him with plunder, sword, and fire, and to capture people like animals.

[Note: [Col. 1375] “And to capture people like animals” is absent from manuscript 3.]

For his supporters from Bohemia plundered human beings more readily than beasts, so that they might prostitute them to their inhuman lust until they were satisfied, and afterward sell them to the Cynocephali to be devoured even more inhumanly.

King Rudolf, after celebrating Pentecost at the cell of Saint Aurelius (4 June), sent a legate to the apostolic lord and hurried into Saxony.

[Note: [Col. 1375D] Hirschau.]

At that time Henry, having placed a crown upon himself at Ulm, usurped the forbidden kingdom. There he also rewarded the aforementioned Count Oudalric with a benefice, as though he had deserved extremely well, because he was still tormenting the venerable Abbot Bernard, the legate of the apostolic lord, in captivity.

[Note: [Col. 1375] The phrase “as having deserved extremely well” is in an erased place in manuscript 1; the same hand added it later, but the reading is uncertain.]

The bishop of Vercelli, chancellor of the deposed king, together with all his followers, summoned a general assembly at Runcalia around 1 May, so that, if possible, he might depose Pope Gregory. But at that very time he miserably laid down both life and bishopric without ecclesiastical communion, when he had presumed wickedly to depose the pope.

[Col. 1375C]

Not long after his death, the prefect of the Roman city, an indefatigable soldier of Saint Peter against the schismatics, was cruelly killed by a certain supporter of Henry. At his body, in a short time, more than twenty miracles occurred, as we learned from the report of faithful men.

Imbrico, bishop of Augsburg, who had sworn fidelity to King Rudolf at the preceding Easter, caring nothing for his perjury, joined Henry when he arrived. One day, while celebrating Mass before him, the wretched man imposed this condition upon himself: that his reception of the sacred offering should become a judgment against him if his lord Henry unjustly usurped the kingdom for himself. After this rash reception, during the short time he survived before his death, he never rose healthy from his bed. For he died around 1 July without ecclesiastical communion.

Likewise, Sigehard, patriarch of Aquileia, came armed to assist Henry against the apostolic ban. At Regensburg he was driven mad and, on that very journey, was struck down by a sudden death. Thus he was carried home dead in body and soul, not without the funerals of some of his own men.

When August was already nearly over, Henry decided to advance into Saxony with a schismatic army (August).

[Note: [Col. 1375] Manuscript 2 reads: “he moved the expedition into Saxony, to whom …”]

King Rudolf proceeded to meet him with the Saxons as far as Würzburg

[Note: [Col. 1375] “King Rudolf” is absent from manuscript 2.] and besieged that city, which had rebelled against him. While his faithful men from Swabia were hurrying there, they encountered Henry, his rival. Henry withdrew before them, burned more than a hundred men who resisted him in a single church, namely at Wizinloch, and then fled beyond the Rhine; thus he could not turn the king’s faithful men aside from the journey they had begun.

[Note: [Col. 1375] Manuscript 1 has “at Wizinloch” written above the line; it is absent from manuscript 3.]

[Note: [Col. 1375D] Wisloch.]

At that time the pope commanded both kings, in the name of Saint Peter, to make a truce with one another and not to obstruct his coming to the German regions to settle the dispute, but to provide him with the necessary counsel and assistance for this journey. He commanded his legates who were still staying in the German regions to excommunicate whichever of the two kings did not obey the aforementioned delegation, and to confirm the obedient one in the kingdom in the name of Saint Peter.

This was done not long afterward, in November: on the day after the feast of Saint Martin, at Goslar, Henry was again excommunicated for disobedience, while Rudolf was raised to the kingship for obedience. For Henry did not deign even to receive the pope’s delegation, nor did he turn his mind toward arranging a truce, but toward the cruelty of tyranny.

[Note: [Col. 1375] What follows was added in smaller letters in the margin in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

Gerald, the venerable bishop of Ostia, whom we mentioned above,

[Note: [Col. 1375] “Whom we mentioned above” is absent from manuscript 2.]

long alive to God and crucified to the world, was freed from the prison of this life on 6 December.

[Note: [Col. 1375] Manuscript 1 has “8 Ides”; manuscript 3 has “9 Ides.”]

[Note: [Col. 1375] The correction from “to the world” to “to God” is in manuscript 1; manuscript 2 has “to God,” and manuscript 3 has “to the world.”]

Agnes, the most religious empress, who had served God with the greatest devotion for twenty years in widowhood and had in no way consented with her son Henry against the apostolic see, rested in peace at Rome on 14 December. She was buried at Rome in the church of Saint Petronilla.

[Note: [Col. 1375] “Already for twenty years” is found in manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1375] “In widowhood” is misspelled in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1375] “14 December” is absent from manuscript 3.]

## 1078

Henry again complained to the apostolic see about his supposedly unjust condemnation. Therefore Pope Gregory, having held a council in March, again sent suitable legates who, after convening a general assembly, were to determine the case of the kingdom justly. He condemned by synodal sentence all who might prevent the assembly from taking place.

[Note: [Col. 1376D] Mansi XX, 503.]

[Note: [Col. 1376D] In this council an exception was made concerning certain persons affected by Henry’s excommunication, temporarily that is: wives, children, servants, and others who associated with excommunicated persons neither knowingly nor at least willingly. This was added in the margin of manuscript 1 and is absent from manuscript 2; it is found in manuscript 3 after “March.”]

Rudolf very much wished this to happen, but Henry did not cease to prevent it by every means he could. For, contrary to the apostolic lord’s command, he gathered a very large multitude of wicked men and prepared an army for Saxony.

King Rudolf met him at Strowe with an army; after putting him to flight, he won the field of victory on 7 August. Nevertheless, Wecel, the venerable bishop of Magdeburg, fell there on Rudolf’s side, and the bishop of Worms was captured. An infinite multitude fell on both sides, though more and more distinguished men fell on Henry’s side.

At the same time, while the Alemanni were hastening with an army to their lord, King Rudolf, nearly twelve thousand of the conspirators who barred their passage across the Neckar River were partly killed, while very many others were more mercifully punished by being castrated. Then, having made an assault, they seized a certain fortification belonging to the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 1377] Manuscript 2 omits “to their lord, King Rudolf.”]

[Note: [Col. 1377] Manuscript 3 has *Neccari*.]

After Rudolf returned to Saxony, Henry suddenly gathered his forces again and devastated Alemannia with plunder, sword, and fire around the feast of All Saints. He undertook to destroy completely the land of the Catholic dukes Bertholf and Welf and of the other faithful of Saint Peter.

[Note: [Col. 1377] The phrase “he attacked the land” is in an erased place in manuscript 1.]

Nearly a hundred churches were also violated in that expedition. At the same time Bertholf, duke of Carinthia, of blessed memory, and Henry, margrave, died in peace.

At another council held at Rome on 19 November, the legates of both kings swore in the synod, though not with the same truthfulness, that their lords had not prevented the assembly from being established to settle the case of the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1377D] Mansi XX, 507.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “Had not prevented” was corrected from “were not preventing” in manuscript 1.]

Therefore the pope could not judge between them on that occasion, although he knew very well which side justice favored more.

At this synod Beringarius, a canon of Angers, was summoned synodally so that he might repent of his heresy, and a postponement was granted to him until the next synod to come.

[Note: [Col. 1377] The name “Beringarius” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “A canon” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “From” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “Heresy” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “His” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “Might repent” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “Synodally” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] “Was summoned” is in an erased place, written in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1377D] Compare Bernold’s book *On the Condemnation of Beringarius*, p. 435.]

## 1079
Gregory the pope convened a synod at Rome in the month of February [Note: [Col. 1377D] Mansi XX, 525.], at which Berengar, already convicted for the third time [Note: [Col. 1377] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.], abjured and anathematized his heresy [Note: [Col. 1377] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.], which asserts that the bodily substances placed upon the altar pass into the body and blood of the Lord not truly, but only figuratively [Note: [Col. 1377] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.; [Col. 1377D] Bern., *De Bereng. damn.*, p. 435.].

At the same synod, Henry, patriarch of Aquileia, swore to the pope that henceforth he would communicate with no one whom he knew to have been excommunicated by the pope [Note: [Col. 1377D] “In … deposuit” is written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.]. At this synod the pope deposed priests who thereafter fell into fornication, without hope of restoration [Col. 1378A] [Note: [Col. 1377] “In … deposuit” is written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.], and condemned the writing said to be by Saint Ulrich to Pope Nicholas concerning the marriages of priests, as well as Paphnutius’s chapter on the same matter—indeed, everything opposed to the sacred canons.

At this synod the legates of King Rudolf lodged a complaint against Henry, because he did not cease to throw the whole kingdom into confusion and trample upon the holy Church. Therefore the pope once again sent his legates to the German lands to settle the matter of the kingdom: namely, the venerable Peter, bishop of Albano—yes, that Peter who some time before proved a certain Florentine bishop named Peter to be a simoniac: for, passing unharmed through the midst of fire, he consequently earned the cognomen “the Fiery” and was judged worthy to obtain the bishopric of Albano. With him Bishop Ulrich of Padua was also sent on the legation.

Before they departed from the same synod, Henry’s legate made the pope’s legates secure by oath concerning their safe conduct and his lord’s obedience [Note: [Col. 1377] “l. p. p. a. in e.” is written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.]. Likewise, Rudolf’s legate swore at the synod concerning his lord’s obedience. When, therefore, the legates of the apostolic see reached the German land, they established beyond doubt Rudolf’s obedience and Henry’s disobedience; and when they later returned, they reported this to the pope in person [Note: [Col. 1377] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.].

That summer the venerable abbot Bernard of Marseille, a man full of charity, rested in peace, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 1377] “XIII K. Aug.” added above the line 1.]. Doctor Adalbert, eloquent in speech and deed, crucified to the world for thirty years and at the end brought to evangelical perfection, departed to the Lord on the third day before the Nones of December.

## MLXXX.

[Col. 1378C]

Again, as Henry was planning to come into Saxony with an army after Epiphany, he was put to flight by Rudolf on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 1377] “VI. K. Febr.” added above the line 1.], yet he was not restrained from the tyranny he had begun. Concerning this expedition Rudolf immediately sent a legate to Rome for the synod [Note: [Col. 1377] “ad s.” written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.].

Pope Gregory convened a synod at Rome in the month of March. To it the aforementioned legates of the apostolic see returned from the German lands and reported to the apostolic lord Rudolf’s complete obedience and Henry’s disobedience. Therefore, at the end of the synod, he deposed Henry [Note: [Col. 1377] “H. … anathematizavit” written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.], anathematized him together with all his supporters, and confirmed Rudolf in royal dignity by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1378D] Concerning the condemnation of Otto, bishop of Constance, made at this same council, see Bernold’s *Apology for Bishop Gebhard* in Uss., II, 381; cf. the acts of the council, Mansi XX, p. 531.].

Consequently his rival [Note: [Col. 1377] Added above the line 1.] [Note: [Col. 1377] Added above the line 1.], having assembled a multitude of all the schismatics and excommunicated persons, at Brixen [Note: [Col. 1378D] See *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Leges* II, 51.] renounced the legitimate pope [Col. 1379A] (June 25), and chose Guibert, formerly bishop of Ravenna [Note: [Col. 1379] From “ravennatem” through “depo” written in a space erased; from “situm” through “elegit” written in the margin in smaller letters 1.], but already for three years irrecoverably deposed and anathematized by Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1379] From “ravennatem” through “depo” written in a space erased; from “situm” through “elegit” written in the margin in smaller letters 1.], not as pope for himself, but as a heresiarch [Note: [Col. 1379] From “ravennatem” through “depo” written in a space erased; from “situm” through “elegit” written in the margin in smaller letters 1.]. Then, after an assembly had been held at Mainz, he caused that same election to be confirmed by everyone he could.

By the middle of October, however, as Henry was again preparing an expedition into Saxony, he was put to flight by Rudolf’s soldiers over the course of a day’s march, although in that same engagement King Rudolf of blessed memory fell (October 15). He—the other Maccabee, as I say—while pressing the enemy among the foremost, was found worthy to fall in the service of Saint Peter; and, surviving for one day thereafter, having properly arranged all his affairs, he is believed to have departed to the Lord on the Ides of October. He reigned three and a half years [Col. 1379B].

All the religious of both sexes, and especially the poor, mourned his death. In commendation of his soul the Saxons gave innumerable alms [Note: [Col. 1379] “anmae” for “animae” 1.]. For without doubt he was the father of his country, an exceptionally devoted guardian of justice, and an indefatigable champion of the holy Church. He was buried with the greatest honor at Merseburg.

On the same day as his death, in Lombardy the soldiers of the most prudent duchess Matilda [Note: [Col. 1379] “entissimae ducis” in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.] were put to flight by the army of nearly all Lombardy at Vulta, near Mantua. On that very day Gilbert, a most devout priest and monk and King Rudolf’s legate to the pope, also rested in peace in Lombardy [Note: [Col. 1379] “ita” for “ipsa” 1.].

At this time Henry so disturbed all Italy that no one could safely go to the threshold of the Apostles without first swearing that he would not go to Pope Gregory [Col. 1379C].

## MLXXXI.

After the death of King Rudolf, Henry came to Verona at Easter, and from there set out to invade Rome [Note: [Col. 1379D] Cf. Gregory’s letter to the bishop of Padua, *Register* IX, 3, and to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, *Register* IX, 11.], with his non-apostolic but apostate Guibert—who had repeatedly perjured himself before the apostolic lord and had been anathematized [Note: [Col. 1379] Added above the line 1.] [Note: [Col. 1379] Added above the line 1.]—but returned unsuccessful [Note: [Col. 1379] “macte” for “inacte” 3.].

At the same time the princes of the German kingdom—that is, the archbishops, bishops, dukes, margraves, and counts—held an assembly and elected the nobleman Heremann as king. He immediately led an army from that same assembly against Henry’s supporters. For those men, wishing to obstruct his election, had at the same time gathered a very large multitude. But when the new king unexpectedly attacked, all of them were either utterly struck down in slaughter or irretrievably put to flight, although they outnumbered the royal soldiers who pursued them by no small margin [Col. 1380A].

Therefore, assured by such a triumph of divine assistance, the king pitched his camp that same night on the field of victory, and afterward departed to bring the kingdom under his authority. He was elected before the feast of Saint Lawrence, and on the day following that saint’s feast he triumphed over his enemies on the Bavarian frontier, at a place called Hostete [Note: [Col. 1380D] Hochstedt, by the Danube.]. Afterward he departed for Saxony to be consecrated.

## MLXXXII.

King Heremann celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously at Goslar. There also, on the feast of Saint Stephen, since that saint was his patron, he solemnly received from the bishops the anointing and crown of royal dignity, with the princes of the kingdom supporting him.

Henry, however, set out from Italy with his apostate Guibert, having assembled a multitude of schismatics, intending once again to invade Rome. Having remained there that summer, he labored almost in vain, except that he installed his soldiers in certain fortresses so that they might wage war against the Romans, since they did not allow him to enter Rome on this occasion either.

He also attempted to set fire to the house of Saint Peter through a certain traitor, but, protected by God’s mercy, he could not do so. For he had planned to break through the gates unexpectedly if the Romans, abandoning the fortifications to hurry to extinguish the fire, should all assemble there; and for this reason he had fire set to certain houses adjoining Saint Peter’s.

But the apostolic lord thwarted this trickery. For as soon as he saw the fire, he sent all the Roman soldiers to defend the fortifications [Col. 1380C] [Note: [Col. 1379] “romonas,” corrected from “romonos” 1.], while he himself, relying upon the protection of Saint Peter, made the sign of the cross against the fire [Note: [Col. 1379] Added above the line 1.] [Note: [Col. 1379] Added above the line 1.] [Note: [Col. 1379] Added above the line 1.] and did not allow the flames to advance any farther.

Thus Henry, after capturing the venerable bishop of Sutri [Note: [Col. 1380D] This was Bonizo. Uss.], along with several others, and leaving his apostate Guibert in the city of Tivoli to harass the Romans, himself returned to Lombardy. King Heremann, however, grieving deeply over the adversity of the apostolic see and wishing to free it from Henry’s hands, prepared an expedition into Italy [Note: [Col. 1379] “ita” 1; “praeparavit” 2.], and therefore came from Saxony into Swabia.

## MLXXXIII.

King Heremann celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Swabia with the princes of the kingdom, in considerable honor. From there, when he wished to advance his army into Lombardy, an unwelcome embassy came to him from Saxony: namely, that Otto, the most prudent duke and soldier, had died—the man whom he had left in Saxony as the head [Note: [Col. 1379] “capitaneo” 2.] of all his people—and he had no doubt that a great schism would arise at his death [Col. 1381A] [Note: [Col. 1381] Here the letter is somewhat smaller, but soon grows again 1.], unless he hastened to forestall such a schism. Therefore, compelled by this necessity to postpone the expedition, he hurried back to Saxony.

Again, before Pentecost, Henry advanced with a multitude of schismatics and excommunicated persons to attack Rome [Note: [Col. 1381] “pugnaturus” 2.], and on the Saturday within Pentecost week he attacked the church of Saint Peter with armed force. Thus he enthroned Guibert of Ravenna—perjured, deposed, and anathematized [Note: [Col. 1381] From “Sicque” through “anathematizatos” added in the margin in smaller letters 1.]—at Saint Peter’s, not through the bishops of Ostia, Albano, and Porto, who possess the privilege of consecrating a pope, but through the former bishops of Modena and Arezzo [Note: [Col. 1381] “aritinensem” 2; “ariminensem” 3.], who had already been deposed and anathematized for many years.

Immediately, beside Saint Peter’s, he fortified a certain hillock called the Palaceolum [Note: [Col. 1381D] By the Tiber, near the fortress of Sant’Angelo.], and stationed many soldiers there to attack the Romans. They prevented him from entering the Transtiberine regions of the city by any means [Note: [Col. 1381] From “qui” through “jam” added in smaller letters; “jam” in a space erased 1.].

Nevertheless, many Romans had already agreed with Henry, some induced by money [Note: [Col. 1381] “conducti” 2.], others led astray by many promises, while all alike had been excessively wearied by the three-year-long [Note: [Col. 1381] “triennii” 2.] attack.

What more need be said? Nearly all the Romans, except the prince of Salerno, agreed with Henry on this point: that Pope Gregory should convene a synod at Rome in the middle of November, and that no one at all—neither Henry nor the Romans—would be permitted to violate the synod’s decrees concerning the matter of the kingdom. Henry also secured by oath the safety of those going to and returning from that synod.

Therefore the pope summoned all religious bishops and abbots to the synod by his letters. When Henry had returned to Lombardy, a sudden death attacked nearly all the soldiers he had left in that fortress near Saint Peter’s. Among them Ulrich of Goscezheim [Note: [Col. 1381] “gozcezheim” 4b.] perished miserably, alas, without ecclesiastical communion [Note: [Col. 1381] Added above the line 1.], the author and instigator of this schismatic conspiracy. Of the three hundred soldiers who had been left in that fortress for its defense, scarcely thirty escaped, as they say, with their lives granted by the sword of Saint Peter. The fortress itself was utterly leveled to the ground by the Romans.

Henry, meanwhile, having sent his Ravennate to Ravenna, set out for the aforesaid synod [Note: [Col. 1381] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.] [Note: [Col. 1381] Written in a space erased, in smaller letters 1.]. The legates of the German princes were also supposed to go there, but Henry captured and plundered them on the way at Forum Cassii [Note: [Col. 1381D] Today Santa Maria di Forcassi, south of Viterbo near Vetralla.] around the feast of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 1381] From “hunc” through “fecit cruciari” three lines were written in a space erased; what follows was written in different ink 1.], although he had promised by oath security to all who were traveling to that synod [Col. 1382A].

Consequently the Romans began to murmur loudly against Henry. They were exceedingly devout monks and clerics whom he had tortured while they were in captivity; with them he also captured the venerable Otto, bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 1382D] Cf. Mansi XX, 587.], who had been sent to him from the apostolic see.

Many bishops and abbots from Francia nevertheless reached that synod. But the better bishops and those more necessary to the apostolic lord—namely Hugh of Lyon, Anselm of Lucca [Note: [Col. 1381] “anshelmus” 2.], and Reginald of Como [Note: [Col. 1381] “reginaldus” 2, and so below.]—were specifically prevented by Henry from reaching the synod [Note: [Col. 1381] “pervenire” corrected from “venire” 2.].

The lord pope nevertheless solemnly celebrated the synod for three days. Although he was scarcely persuaded by the synod not to anathematize Henry once again in particular, he nevertheless excommunicated everyone who in any way hindered anyone coming to Saint Peter’s or to the pope.

But now the appointed time arrived by which the Romans, without the pope’s knowledge, had sworn that they would bring it about for Henry either that Pope Gregory would crown him or that, after expelling Gregory, they would choose another whom they themselves selected. Although that oath had been made during the preceding summer, it nevertheless remained hidden from nearly all the pope’s closest associates until the appointed time.

When the time arrived, the Romans disclosed the oath to the pope, saying that they had sworn to Henry not that the pope would solemnly crown him with royal anointing, but merely that he would give him a crown. The pope therefore consented to their wishes in order to release them from the oath: namely, that he would give Henry the crown, if he wished, with justice; otherwise, with a curse [Col. 1382C].

The Romans therefore sent word to Henry that he should come to receive the crown with justice, if he wished; otherwise, he could receive it from the fortress of Saint Angelo by means of a staff left there for him by the pope. But when Henry refused both alternatives, they sent another legate to him, who would defend them in war if necessary: they had carefully considered what they had sworn [Note: [Col. 1381] “q.” 1; “qd” 2; “quid” 3.], and they were no longer bound by that oath.

Therefore they adhered to the lord pope much more firmly than before, in counsel [Note: [Col. 1381] A sixteenth- or seventeenth-century hand corrected this to “plio.”.] and assistance [Note: [Col. 1381] “papa” 2; “apostolico” 3, 4b.]. Henry, however, worked all the more insistently to bring them over to his side, now by threats, now by promises; and, remaining for a long time around Rome, he devoted himself to this business.

At this time Stephen, formerly king of Hungary and of blessed memory, who converted himself and his people to the faith of Christ, became renowned for miracles after the fortieth year following his death [Note: [Col. 1382D] Hermann places his death in the year 1038. Uss.].

Solomon, king of Hungary, but utterly unworthy of royal dignity, a kinsman of the aforementioned Henry [Note: [Col. 1383D] Namely, the husband of his sister. Uss.], was deprived of his kingdom and imprisoned by a countryman of his named Ladislaus [Note: [Col. 1383] “Talislao” 4b.], and that man was elevated to royal dignity in his place.

Berengar, the author of the new heresy concerning the body of the Lord, departed this life at that time and went to his own place. Although he had very often abjured the same heresy in a synod [Note: [Col. 1383] “in s.” is absent in 2.], nevertheless, like a dog, he did not shrink from returning to his vomit. For, after being canonically convicted in a Roman synod, he burned the book in which he himself had written out his heresy, and anathematized what he had abjured; yet afterward he did not abandon it [Note: [Col. 1383] The word is almost erased 1.].

But for seven years now the entire Roman Empire had been suffering from civil war, indeed from the division of schism, with some favoring the apostolic lord and others Henry; and for this reason both sides were miserably devastating the whole kingdom with plunder, sword, and fire [Col. 1383B] [Note: [Col. 1383] “plerumque” written by a sixteenth- or seventeenth-century hand in 1.]. Very few Catholic bishops remained on the apostolic side; and, driven from their own sees, they were not allowed to provide for their flocks.

Therefore nearly all religious persons, whether clerics or laymen, withdrew into the hiding places of certain monasteries to escape such evils, lest they should behold the devastation of the holy Church, which they could in no way assist. For they thought it better at least to save themselves by hiding than to perish with the others while laboring in vain on their behalf.

At that time three monasteries in the German kingdom, together with their cells, flourished outstandingly, established according to regular disciplines: namely, the monastery of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest; that of Saint Aurelius, which is called Hirsau; and that of the Holy Savior, which is called Schaffhausen [Col. 1383C], that is, “house of ships.”

In this troubled period a remarkable multitude of noble and prudent men took refuge in these monasteries within a short time, laid down their arms, and resolved to pursue evangelical perfection under regular discipline—so great was their number, I say, that the buildings of the monasteries necessarily had to be enlarged, since otherwise they would not have had room to live there together.

In these monasteries even the external duties themselves are administered not by secular persons but by religious brothers; and the nobler they had been in the world, the more they desire to occupy themselves with contemptible duties, so that those who were once counts or margraves [Note: [Col. 1383] “marchio” 2.] in the world now count it the greatest delight to serve their brothers in the kitchen or bakery, or to pasture their pigs in the fields. There, indeed, the swineherds and oxherds, apart from their clothing, are the same as the monks [Col. 1383D] [Note: [Col. 1383D] Cf. Gerbert’s *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, pp. 239, 325; Burchard, *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 7, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores II, p. 159.].

All alike burn with such ardor of charity that each desires not his own benefit so much as that of another; and in practicing hospitality they labor so astonishingly that they seem to regard themselves as having lost whatever they have not distributed to Christ’s poor or to guests.

## MLXXXIV.

King Heremann celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Saxony. His rival, however, wintered in Roman territory and there awaited his Ravennate Guibert’s arrival in Rome, so that he might be crowned by him at Saint Peter’s, since he could not bend Pope Gregory to crown him unless he had been lawfully reconciled.

Reginald, bishop of Como [Note: [Col. 1383D] Of Como.], illustrious in learning and religion, and for that reason a most zealous helper of Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1383] “greg” 1; “gregorio” 2.], departed to the Lord on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

Duke Welf of Bavaria courageously recovered the city of Augsburg, which had been invaded with the Bavarians by a certain Siegfried, an unnamed bishop, and subjected it to its legitimate shepherd, named Wigold.

Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, an indefatigable helper of Pope Gregory through many tribulations, rested in peace [Note: [Col. 1384D] He died in exile in Thuringia on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March. Uss.].

The queen of the English died [Note: [Col. 1384D] Matilda, daughter of Baldwin V, count of Flanders; others record that she died on November 2, 1083. Uss.], the wife of King William [Note: [Col. 1383] “Willihalmi” 2.], who made the whole land of the English tributary to the Roman pontiff and permitted no one under his authority to buy or sell anything if he discovered that person to be disobedient to the apostolic see.

Ladislaus, king of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 1383] “Tatislaus” 4b.], who favored the Catholic party, released his rival Solomon from prison and allowed him to go to his wife at Regensburg, although she was ungrateful. For neither she nor he had until then maintained the marital bond with each other; indeed, contrary to the Apostle, they did not fear to defraud one another [Note: [Col. 1383] “faudare” 1.].

She was the sister of the often-mentioned Henry, and had long been supported by him at Regensburg, even before her husband was captured.

Henry, former patriarch of Aquileia, repeatedly perjured toward the apostolic lord and excommunicated, died in body and soul [Note: [Col. 1384D] See above, under the year 1079.].

At this time the king of Constantinople sent a very large sum of money to the former King Henry, so that he might attack in war Robert Guiscard, duke of Calabria and Apulia and the sworn soldier of the lord pope, in vengeance for that same king. For Robert had already invaded the borders of the Constantinopolitans some time before and was again planning to launch an expedition there.

But Henry spent the money he had received not on a campaign against Robert, as he had promised by oath, but on winning over the Roman populace. With their assistance he entered the Lateran palace on the Thursday before Palm Sunday (March 21), together with his Ravennate Guibert [Col. 1385A].

The Roman nobles, except for a very few, remained with Pope Gregory, and they gave him forty hostages. The pope withdrew into the fortress of Saint Angelo and kept all the bridges across the Tiber and the stronger Roman fortifications under his authority.

On the day of the Lord’s Resurrection (March 31), Henry received from his heresiarch Ravennate a crown not of glory but of confusion. For such a coronator, according to the testimony of the holy fathers, imposed upon the one he crowned not the blessing he had lost, but the damnation he possessed.

He himself had once been archbishop of Ravenna and had sworn complete obedience to the Roman pontiff, which he faithfully carried out for some time [Col. 1385B]. But not long afterward, despising his oath, he rose up with singular obstinacy against the apostolic see. Consequently, after canonical periods of grace, he was irrecoverably deposed and anathematized by the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1385D] From “Ab apostolica sede” through “sedi praesidente,” the words correspond exactly with the letter of Gebhard of Salzburg in Hugh of Flavigny, Mansi XX, 542.] and by the bishops of the whole Church in a Roman synod [Note: [Col. 1385D] Held in Rome during Lent in 1078, and likewise in another in the year 1080. Uss.]; and this happened not once, nor in a single synod, but in every synod held at Rome during the past six years [Note: [Col. 1385] Gebhard of Salzburg has “seven years.”].

This man, therefore, so hardened in perjury, and repeatedly irreversibly deposed and anathematized for it, invaded the see of the Roman pontiff to whom he had sworn obedience, through the hands of anathematized persons like himself, in the preceding year [Note: [Col. 1385] “praet. anno” is absent in Gebhard.], while its legitimate shepherd was still presiding over that see.

The former bishops of Modena and Arezzo, together with the other excommunicated persons, ordained him; but even if they had been Catholics, and even if the apostolic see had had no shepherd, they nevertheless could not ordain a pontiff for that see [Col. 1385C]. For the privilege of this ordination was granted by the holy fathers solely to the cardinal bishops—the bishops of Ostia, Albano, and Porto [Note: [Col. 1385] Written in a space erased 1.]—and is granted to no others, even when those bishops are able to fulfill it.

But these men would more willingly endure every extreme hardship than take part in so sacrilegious an ordination of so proud a usurper; and they themselves, together with the apostolic lord, had canonically condemned him by synodal judgment.

Therefore the bishops of Modena and Arezzo, together with the other heretics, promoted that Ravennate not as Roman patriarch—which they could in no way do—but as a most condemned heresiarch, so that the higher he stood among them [Col. 1385D] [Note: [Col. 1385] Written in a space erased 1.], the greater the privilege of damnation he might possess [Note: [Col. 1386D] “Ergo … promoverunt.” Ibid.].

Consequently, Henry, crowned by him, is believed to have inherited his damnation; and likewise all who usurped anything as though received from the aforesaid heresiarch that ought to have been received from the lord pope.

Henry was staying in the Lateran palace with his Ravennate, and the pope’s faithful would not allow him to cross the city to Saint Peter’s [Note: [Col. 1385] “p. populis,” according to Uss., against the authority of the manuscripts.]. But during that very Easter week (April), he attacked the apostolic faithful in battle. In that engagement he lost nearly forty of his own among the dead and wounded, while the rest fled; but on the side of the lord pope not a single man fell.

King Heremann celebrated Easter in Saxony [Note: [Col. 1386D] At Goslar.], where very substantial truces were made among the faithful of the lord pope; not long afterward these were confirmed throughout nearly the whole German kingdom [Note: [Col. 1385] “trewae” 1; “treugae” 3; “treuve” 4b.].

After the Kalends of May, Robert Guiscard, duke of the Normans [Col. 1386B] [Note: [Col. 1386C] Invited by the pope. See his letter 17, book IX. Uss.], invaded Rome with armed force in the service of Saint Peter. After putting Henry to flight, he utterly stripped the whole city, which had rebelled against Pope Gregory, and consumed most of it with fire, because the Romans had wounded one of his soldiers [Note: [Col. 1385] “wlneraverint” 1.].

Then, after taking hostages from the Romans and placing them in the fortress of Saint Angelo, which they call the House of Theoderic, he himself advanced from Rome with Pope Gregory and an army to recover the land of Saint Peter, intending to return to Rome on the feast of Saint Peter. Within a short time he recovered many fortresses and cities for the lord pope.

Unable to resist Robert, Henry returned rather hastily to the German lands (June).

At the same time the soldiers of the most prudent duchess Matilda fought bravely in Lombardy against Henry’s supporters and the enemies of Saint Peter. From among the latter they captured the bishop of Parma and six [Note: [Col. 1385] Written in a space erased 1.] commanders, together with nearly one hundred other good soldiers. They also obtained more than five hundred horses, very many coats of mail, and all the tents of the enemy, having achieved a complete victory [Col. 1386C].

Around the Kalends of August, Henry prepared an expedition into Swabia (August). But when the Swabians came out to meet him, he did not wish to fight, although for several days they challenged him to battle with many standards raised, and had killed or captured more than one hundred of his men.

For he pitched his camp near the River Lech, protected by its bank, and could not easily be attacked by the enemy. The Swabians pitched their camp on the opposite side of the river, in his sight, sufficiently far from the bank so that they would not seem to have deprived the enemy of the opportunity to ford it [Col. 1386D].

But it was in vain. Henry refused to cross—or rather, he did not dare to do so—and even after the Swabians departed, fearing an ambush by them, he was afraid to leave the riverbank for almost an entire day [Col. 1387A].

At last Henry returned to Regensburg and from there proceeded beyond the Rhine to Mainz. The Swabians likewise advanced beyond the Rhine into Burgundy with an army and bravely rescued a certain fortress belonging to Duke Bertald, son of King Rudolf, which had been besieged by Henry’s supporters.

For, having forded—or rather swum across—certain extremely swift rivers, they so terrified the besiegers of the fortress, although still far away, that they abandoned their tents, horses, and coats of mail and fled in all directions from the siege. Thereafter they did not dare resist the Swabians as they ravaged their land with sword, plunder, and fire.

After rescuing the fortress, provisioning it with suitable supplies for the coming year [Note: [Col. 1387] Uss. reads “praesidiis” against the authority of the manuscripts.], and destroying certain enemy fortifications, the Swabians returned peacefully to their own land (October) [Col. 1387B].

Meanwhile Henry, having assembled a multitude of schismatics, rewarded Wecilo, a fugitive cleric of the bishop of Halberstadt, with the bishopric of Mainz, because he had been his indefatigable fellow worker in every obstinacy against God and Saint Peter.

This man had long before been anathematized [Note: [Col. 1387C] Namely, from the time when, even before his intrusion, he had long served King Henry, who was under anathema, as Urban II says in letter 19.
