Uss.], and, elected by the anathematized, was nevertheless not consecrated but cursed by the anathematized, according to Pope Pelagius. For, according to the most blessed fathers Innocent, Leo, and Gregory, he could receive from the condemned nothing but damnation and a curse.

The lord pope, having convened a synod at Salerno, again promulgated a sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch, Henry, and all their supporters [Col. 1387C] [Note: [Col. 1387C] “We necessarily avoid Guibert the heresiarch and all his supporters after the sentence of the venerable Pope Gregory.” Bernold, *Opusculum* VI, 7, above.]. He had already done this at Rome on the feast of Saint John the Baptist in the preceding year, while Henry was still staying there.

The legates of the apostolic see—that is, Peter, bishop of Albano, in Francia, and Otto, bishop of Ostia, in the German lands—proclaimed this sentence everywhere [Note: [Col. 1387] “deest” in 4b.].

While the bishop of Ostia was staying in Alemannia, he also ordained a Catholic shepherd for the holy Church of Constance, which had long been widowed [Col. 1387C] [Note: [Col. 1387C] Cf. Bernold’s *Apology for Gebhard*, above.]: namely, Gebhard, son of Duke Bertald, noble by birth but nobler in monastic conduct.

Although Gebhard was unwilling—indeed, he lamented and protested vehemently—the bishop of Ostia consecrated him on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January, at the request and acclamation of the clergy and laity of Constance. On the preceding day, that is, on the feast of Saint Thomas, he had made him a priest together with other clerics [Col. 1388A]. Among these he also promoted the writer of this chronicle to the priesthood at the same solemnity [Note: [Col. 1387] “ad presbyteratum” 4b; “in presbyterum” 3.], and granted him, by apostolic authority, the power to receive penitents [Note: [Col. 1387] From “quem” through “concessit” added in small letters 1; absent in 2.] [Note: [Col. 1387C] Bernold discusses this power, granted to him at his ordination, in his *Opusculum on the Office of Priests*, no. XI. Uss.].

## MLXXXV.

Heremannus the king celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Goslar, to [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] which [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] the aforementioned [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] bishop [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] of Ostia [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] arrived in Saxony after [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] Epiphany [Note: [Col. 1387] In an erased place, in smaller script, manuscript 1.]. He attended a conference [Note: [Col. 1388C] At Perestad (today Bechstedt) in Thuringia, on 20 January; the Saxon Annalist gives an extensive account of its proceedings for this year. Uss.] at which the Saxons agreed with the supporters of Heinricus (21 January) that they would prove to them that, by right, they avoided Heinricus as an excommunicated man. After the conference had taken place, they proved this most firmly on the fifteenth day after Epiphany, namely because the Roman pontiff had announced to them by letter that he had anathematized him in a Roman synod [Note: [Col. 1388C] These words are absent from Gregory’s register.].

Their adversaries, however, objected that the pope could not excommunicate him, since a man stripped of his possessions could not be summoned, judged, or condemned [Note: [Col. 1388C] “A man stripped of his possessions cannot be summoned, judged, or condemned” are the words of the archbishop of Mainz, as the proceedings of the council reported by the Saxon Annalist testify.]. To this the Saxons replied that they neither ought nor could evade the judgment of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 1388C] The words of Gebehard of Salzburg; ibid.]; that this matter ought rather to be discussed with the one who had condemned him, not with the Saxons, who had not taken part in his condemnation and who owed no reconsideration, but obedience, to the judgment of the Apostolic See. Thus, when the conference had been concluded, they departed from one another.

At that time the bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 1388C] Named Uto. Uss.] scarcely escaped the hands of the Saxons with his followers [Col. 1388C], because he had joined the Heinricians against the common resolve of all Saxony. For the same fault, Count Theoderic was also killed at that time by supporters of our party. The aforesaid legate of the Apostolic See likewise imposed a complete suspension from office upon the aforesaid bishop, since he was unwilling to repent.

King Heremann celebrated Easter at Quedlinburg (20 April). There, as the legate of the apostolic lord, he solemnly held a general synod during that same Easter week [Note: [Col. 1388C] Cf. Bernold, col. 1138.] with archbishops, bishops, and abbots faithful to Saint Peter. The most reverend Gebehard, archbishop of Juvavum, took part in this synod. Likewise the venerable Hartwic, archbishop of Magdeburg, with his suffragans. Likewise the suffragans of the see of Mainz from Saxony. For the bishops of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1388C] Adalbero, Adelbertus, Gewoldus, and Gebehard; they subscribed to the synod through their legates. Uss.] and Worms, and also those of Augsburg and Constance from Alemannia, since they could not come because they were prevented by canonical necessity, represented themselves before the holy council through their legation and ordered that they would assent in every respect to the statutes of that synod.

King Heremann also attended the same synod with his princes. When, therefore, all had taken their seats according to their rank, the decrees of the holy Fathers concerning the primacy of the Apostolic See were brought forward: that no one might ever reconsider its judgment or judge its judgment. This was praised and confirmed by the public profession of the entire synod. It was directed against the Heinricians, who had wished to compel the faithful of Saint Peter to presume to reconsider with them the excommunication that Pope Gregory had imposed upon Heinricus.

A certain cleric of Bamberg, named Gumpertus [Note: [Col. 1389] The initial letter is written above the line.], who wished to diminish the primacy of the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 1389D] Others call him Cunibertus. Uss.], came forward into the midst of the synod, asserting that the Roman pontiffs had claimed this primacy for themselves and had inherited it as something granted from no other source—namely, that no one ought to judge their judgment and that they should be subject to the judgment of no one.

When he was openly refuted by the entire synod, he was nevertheless especially convicted by a certain layman through the Gospel: “A disciple is not above his teacher” (Matthew 10:21). Since this is generally held to be observed in all ecclesiastical orders, so that the greater is not judged by the lesser, who could deny this to the vicar of Saint Peter, whom all Catholics venerate as lord and teacher?

In the same synod, the ordination of Wecilo, the intruder into the see of Mainz, and of Sigefrid of Augsburg and Norpert of Chur—indeed, all ordinations and consecrations of excommunicated persons—were judged completely invalid, in accordance with the decrees of the holy Fathers Innocent [Note: [Col. 1389] Absent in manuscript 2.], Leo I, Pelagius, and his successor Gregory I.

Likewise, the sect of the aforesaid Wecilo and his associates was condemned under anathema. It asserts that laymen stripped of their possessions are not subject to ecclesiastical judgment and cannot be excommunicated for their offenses; it also maintains that excommunicated persons may be received without reconciliation.

It was established there that anyone excommunicated by his bishop—although deprived of neither office nor communion, and even if unjustly—should in no way be received into communion unless absolved according to ecclesiastical custom. Likewise, the holy synod decreed that those excommunicated for sacrilege were not to be received without the customary reconciliation, even if they had already returned what they had sacrilegiously claimed.

In the same synod, perpetual continence was imposed upon priests, deacons, and subdeacons, in accordance with the decrees of the holy Fathers.

Likewise, it was decreed that laymen should not touch altar cloths or sacred vessels.

Likewise, that laymen should not claim tithes as their property or even as a benefice, unless by concession of the rightful possessors.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 1389] This sentence is in an erased place in manuscript 1.], that the spring fast should always be celebrated in the first week of Lent and the summer fast at Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1389] “At Pentecost” in manuscript 4b.].

Likewise, that no one should eat cheese or eggs during Lent.

Likewise, the ordination of the lord Gebehard, bishop of Constance, was confirmed and praised by synodal judgment—indeed, everything that the aforesaid legate of the Apostolic See had ordained when he was at Constance.

There, too, a question was raised concerning the consanguinity of the king himself and his wife [Note: [Col. 1389D] Venericus discusses this matter; others wish him to have been Walramus or Waltramus, bishop of Naumburg. Some say that King Heremann’s wife was Adelheid, daughter of Otto of Orlamünde, margrave of Meissen, by Adela. Her father was Lambert II, count of Leuven, and her mother Oda, daughter of Gothelin, the great duke of Lorraine. From this perhaps arose the consanguinity or affinity which, according to the custom of that period, impeded the marriage up to the seventh degree. Uss.]. The king therefore rose in the midst of the synod [Note: [Col. 1389] Thus in manuscript 1.] and declared that he would observe in every respect the judgment of the holy synod on this matter [Note: [Col. 1389] Thus in manuscript 1.].

The holy synod, however, judged that this case could not at that time be examined canonically [Note: [Col. 1389] “Judged” abbreviated as “dijud.” in manuscript 2.], because legitimate accusers were not present.

At the end of the synod, a sentence of anathema was promulgated with burning candles against Gibertus, the heresiarch and intruder into the Apostolic See, and against the apostates from Saint Peter: Hugh the White; John, former bishop of Porto [Note: [Col. 1389] “Bishop” in manuscript 2.]; and Peter, the former chancellor.

Likewise against Leomar of Bremen [Note: [Col. 1389] Teomar in manuscript 4b.], Uto of Hildesheim, Otto of Constance, Burchard of Basel, and Houzemann, former bishop of Speyer [Note: [Col. 1389] “Bishops” in manuscript 2.].

Likewise against Wecilo, the intruder into Mainz, Sigefrid of Augsburg, and Norpert of Chur. Against these men, I say, and against all their accomplices, an inescapable sentence of anathema was promulgated [Note: [Col. 1390D] The names of those who subscribed to the synod either personally or through legates are found in Mansi XX, 609.].

But all these adversaries of the Church of God, in the third week after the synod had ended [Note: [Col. 1390D] Waltramus and several others hold that this council was held on 29 April, in the second week after Easter. Its Acts, collected from various writers, are found in Mansi XX, 613. Uss.], assembled their own gathering at Mainz—not a synod, but a council of pretence. In it they brought forth a shadowy sentence of excommunication against the faithful of Saint Peter: since they were entirely unable to excommunicate them, they most openly separated themselves from the communion of Catholics, so that they would be separated from the Catholics not only by the judgment of the holy Church but also, like all heretics, by their own judgment.

In their rash and blinded greed they did not fear to claim for themselves the sees of the Catholic bishops who were still living.

But almighty God did not cease to aid his faithful by himself, and he wondrously exercised his judgment upon the enemies of the holy Church. For almost all Italy, where the excommunicated were especially raging, was seized by so great a famine that people ate not only every kind of unclean thing but even human flesh. That famine was followed by such an unheard-of mortality that not even a third of the people remained; when the cultivator disappeared, the greater part of the land was reduced to wilderness.

The river Po [Note: [Col. 1391] “Phadus” in manuscript 2.], overflowing its banks in Lombardy, completely submerged and rendered uninhabitable many castles, villages, and even the surrounding regions.

At that time the very leaders of the schismatics also, alas, miserably went to their appointed place: namely, the former bishops of Parma and Reggio [Note: [Col. 1391] Eberardus and Gandulphus. See Donizo, Life of Matilda, book II, chapter 3. Uss.]; Theodaldus of Milan, not an archbishop [Note: [Col. 1391] Absent in manuscript 2.] but an Antichrist [Note: [Col. 1391] The words “and so forth” are absent in manuscript 2.]; the margraves Adelbertus and Reginherius; Count Boso; and countless others, through whose faction almost all Italy rose against the lord pope and Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1391] The words “and Saint Peter” are absent in manuscript 2.].

These men had also inflicted many injuries in Italy upon Matilda, the most prudent duchess [Note: [Col. 1391] The words “most prudent and faithful soldier of Saint Peter” are absent in manuscript 2.] and most faithful soldier of Saint Peter.

But when they had been removed from the midst by divine punishment [Note: [Col. 1391] “Punishment” appears as “aniadversione” in manuscript 1.], she recovered her authority and did not cease to support the holy Church of God in every way. Thus, through her prudence, Catholic pastors were appointed for the churches of Modena, Reggio, and Pistoia.

But now almighty God, not wishing his servant Pope Gregory to labor any longer, or rather wishing worthily to reward him for his labors [Note: [Col. 1391] The phrase occurs in an erased place in manuscript 1.], summoned him from the prison of this life [Note: [Col. 1391] The words occur in an erased place in manuscript 1.] (25 May).

For after he had been gravely weakened in body for some time [Note: [Col. 1391] Absent in manuscript 2.], yet remained most steadfast in the defense of justice until death [Note: [Col. 1391] The words from “but” through “until death” are absent in manuscript 2.], he closed his final day at Salerno. At his death, all religious persons of both sexes, and especially the poor, mourned.

For he was an exceedingly fervent founder of Catholic religion and a most vigorous defender of ecclesiastical liberty. He did not wish the ecclesiastical order to be subject to the hands of laymen, but wanted it to surpass them both in holiness of conduct and in the dignity of its order. This cannot have been hidden from anyone who carefully reads through his apostolic register [Note: [Col. 1391] The passage from “He was” through “carefully reads through” is absent in manuscript 2.].

After he had lawfully struggled for twelve years and one month in the governance of the Apostolic See—or rather, of the whole Church—he was finally taken from this light in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, on 25 May [Note: [Col. 1391] Absent in manuscript 2.], and there is no doubt that he received the prize of the heavenly calling. He was buried at Salerno in the church of Saint Matthew, which he himself dedicated in that same year.

But Guibertus the heresiarch rejoiced greatly at his death, although his party gained little prosperity from it [Note: [Col. 1391] The passage from “But” through “forced him” is absent in manuscript 2.]. For all Catholics resisted that heresiarch after the death of the apostolic lord no less than before, and forced him to retreat from Rome to Ravenna.

At that time certain Saxons, apostatizing from fidelity to Saint Peter and shamefully abandoning their king Heremannus, received the king Ἡυνρυκυμ [Note: [Col. 1391] “Heinricum” is written in Greek as IHyNPyky in manuscript 1 and IHyNyky in manuscript 4b.] Heinricus (Greek: Ἡυνρυκυμ), whom they had so often renounced. They supposed that they would thereafter suffer no evil from him and that, with him reigning, they would enjoy the peace they desired. Events turned out otherwise. For as soon as he had recovered power, he did not cease to exercise his former tyranny over them.

Therefore, in turn, they shamefully drove him away and expelled him from their territories with great disgrace. But the bishops of Saxony and certain of the princes remained with their king Heremannus in fidelity to Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1391] Manuscript 2 has a different account in place of what follows; see above, col. 1280.], and chose rather to abandon their honors than to associate with excommunicated persons.

Nevertheless, they were later recalled by the Saxons to their own sees, after the Saxons had expelled Heinricus (Greek: Ἡυνρυκυμ) [Note: [Col. 1391] HyNPky in manuscript 1; H. in manuscript 4b.] from there, as we have said.

## 1086

King Heremann celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Saxony. At this time many killings, plunderings, and burnings took place between the supporters of Heinricus and the faithful of Saint Peter. Because of the same discord, the Apostolic See was still unable to have a legitimate pastor.

Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1391] “King H.” in manuscript 2.] advanced an army against the Saxons on 27 January. But the Saxons came against him with a great multitude and forced him to retreat without accomplishing anything.

At that time Count Palatine Heremannus and Otto, former bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 1391] “Bishop” in manuscript 2.], miserably perished on Heinricus’s side, outside ecclesiastical communion. On the Catholic side, the most reverend Anselm, bishop of the Church of Lucca, who had long been crucified to the world, departed to the Lord on 19 March [Note: [Col. 1391] “The sixteenth” corrected to “the fifteenth” in manuscript 1.].

The princes of Bavaria were reconciled to their duke Welf at Easter (5 April), withdrew from Heinricus, and with that duke and the other princes of Alemannia attacked him at Regensburg with armed force. They detained him there for a long time so that he could not depart.

Robert, duke of the Normans, after invading many lands and oppressing many poor and rich people—and since neither Calabria nor Sicily sufficed for his greed, while he longed, against divine and human law, to subject overseas kingdoms to himself—undertook the way of all flesh.

At this time the princes of Swabia who were faithful to Saint Peter arranged, together with the Saxons and Bavarians, a general conference near Würzburg after the feast of the Apostles (July). Heinricus wished to disrupt it by gathering a multitude of schismatics, but, unable to resist the advancing Swabians, he gave way to them for a time.

They proceeded to besiege Würzburg in order to attack the supporters of Heinricus, and, joining with the Saxons, surrounded the same place with a siege enclosure.

Meanwhile Heinricus gathered an army of nearly twenty thousand infantry and cavalry and directed his battle line toward the liberation of the city, which had already been besieged for five weeks.

When the faithful of Saint Peter heard this, they raised the siege and advanced to meet him two miles away. They trusted not so much in their own numbers as in the mercy of God and the justice of Saint Peter, and not so much in arms as in the power of the holy cross. Therefore, they had a very tall cross erected on a certain wagon, adorned with a red banner, and carried with them to the place of battle.

Duke Welf with his legion, and the Magdeburg legion, leaving their horses behind, advanced on foot (11 August). When they were just about to engage, they all prostrated themselves on the ground and pierced heaven with prayer. The most reverend archbishop of Magdeburg [Note: [Col. 1393D] Hartwic.] poured out that prayer there for them with many tears and groans.

Then, having engaged in the name of the Lord, they inflicted an unbelievable slaughter upon the enemy, so that nine very high heaps of corpses could be seen there, apart from those who fell while fleeing through the fields and woods.

At the first onset of the engagement, Heinricus, concealing his identity, was the first among the foremost to turn his back, abandoning all his banners to us, and reached the Rhine in very great haste.

But our men pursued him over a long distance and finally carried away great booty from the enemy. They took his chests with the royal garments, as well as I know not how many episcopal chapels [Note: [Col. 1393D] Chapels are vestments and sacred vessels, relics of the saints, and other things necessary for the solemn divine service. Uss.], together with countless other things [Note: [Col. 1393] The passage from “His” through “took” is absent in manuscript 2.].

How many thousands of the adversaries fell in that engagement, we have not yet been able to ascertain. On the side of the faithful of Saint Peter, however, we could find no more than fifteen dead, although we searched most diligently; and of those fifteen, only three died at the place of battle, for the others lived for several days afterward. Among the dead and wounded we were able to find no more than thirty of our own men. This must certainly be attributed not to any human strength but rather to divine power, since the faithful of Saint Peter numbered scarcely ten thousand, whereas the adversaries are reported to have exceeded even twenty thousand [Note: [Col. 1393D] The passage from “and this” through “twenty thousand” is absent in manuscript 2.].

Thus, having gained victory through God’s mercy, our men spent that night encamped on the field of battle. On the following day they returned to the siege of the city and captured it without bloodshed.

Then, after the bishop of Würzburg had been restored to his see amid the great praises of the citizens, clergy, and laity, and a suitable military garrison had been placed in the city, they returned individually to their own homes with great glory and joy.

This battle took place on the day after the feast of Saint Lawrence, namely on the anniversary of the day on which King Heremann had also defeated the Bavarians with the Swabians.

I myself, who brought this chronicle from the year 1054 of the Lord’s incarnation to this point [Note: [Col. 1393] The words “from the year 1054 of the Lord’s incarnation” occur in an erased place, in smaller letters, in manuscript 1.], took care to announce this battle to the faithful for the praise and glory of God—not so much on the report of others as on what I myself saw and heard [Note: [Col. 1393] From here, manuscript 1 continues at another time.].

The most reverend abbot of the cell of Saint Blaise, named Gisilbertus, departed to the Lord on 10 October. The venerable Uto, prior of that same monastery, succeeded him in the abbacy [Note: [Col. 1393] From here, manuscript 1 continues at another time.].

Count Chonradus [Note: [Col. 1393D] Of Luxembourg. Uss.], brother of King Heremannus but an indefatigable supporter of Heinricus, was finally, as they say, reconciled to the Church and died on the journey to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1393] The word “died” is followed in manuscript 2 by “Heinricus nearby”; the intervening section is missing.].

Blessed Anselm, formerly bishop of Lucca, began to shine with innumerable miracles in that very year of his deposition [Note: [Col. 1393D] See his Life in Mabillon, *Saeculum VI*, part II, p. 483. Uss.]. After the death of the venerable Pope Gregory VII, while he was still alive in the flesh, he greatly encouraged the faithful of Saint Peter against the tyranny of Heinricus; but after his death, shining with miracles, he encouraged them still more to persevere against the same tyrant.

Therefore, Heinricus’s party began to decline from day to day, while the Catholics did not cease to advance in fidelity to Saint Peter.

Nevertheless, near the Nativity of the Lord, Heinricus besieged a certain castle in Bavaria (December) and, as they say, wished to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord during that siege. When Duke Welf and Duke Berthaldus heard this, they suddenly arrived without a great multitude of Swabians and Bavarians and did not allow him to withdraw from the siege until they had first obtained security from his princes [Note: [Col. 1393] “Having obtained security,” expanded in manuscript 4b* as “having received a most certain guarantee” in the year 1089 below, p. 449, line 34; the relevant folio is cut away.], namely that he would permit a conference to take place at which the kingdom’s long-standing discord might somehow finally receive a suitable conclusion.

After they had obtained this security, they granted him a peaceful opportunity to depart. Thus, on the very vigil of the Nativity, he was compelled to celebrate his feast elsewhere.

The dukes, however, returned peacefully and joyfully to their own territories and immediately arranged, together with the other princes of the kingdom, the previously planned conference at Oppenheim in the third week of Lent.

## 1087

King Heremann celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Saxony.

Count Berthaldus [Note: [Col. 1394D] Perhaps the count of the Turgau, fighting against Ulrich III, abbot of Saint Gall, an especially fierce defender of King Heinricus; at that time, out of hatred for Margrave Berthold, Ulrich ravaged the entire district of Turgau. Uss.], a most faithful soldier of Saint Peter, fell while fighting most bravely against the schismatics.

Meanwhile Heinricus tried by every artifice and deceit—since he could not do so by force—to prevent the aforesaid conference from taking place [Note: [Col. 1395] The words “because he could not prevail by force” are absent in manuscript 2.]. But the faithful of Saint Peter, despite his opposition and even his threats of war, arrived at the appointed time (late February).

He himself, as usual evading justice and refusing to follow even the reasonable counsel of his own men, scorned to attend. Consequently, he caused almost all his own people to murmur against him and some of them to depart from him, while our men returned peacefully to their homes.

The Apostolic See was still unable to have a legitimate pastor, because Guibertus of Ravenna, the perjured and anathematized heresiarch, had already for eight years afflicted that see through the faction of Heinricus.

Although he himself could not obtain it peacefully, he nevertheless prevailed so greatly through the instruments of the devil that the Apostolic See had now been without pastoral governance for two years [Note: [Col. 1395] From here, manuscript 1 continues at another time.].

Since all Catholics were therefore rightly grieving, at last the cardinal bishops of the holy Roman Church and the other Catholics of the clergy and people, with the assistance of the Normans, ordained Desiderius, cardinal of that same Church and abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, as the 160th pope, and gave him the name Victor III. Immediately after his election, he announced everywhere by letters that he would proceed according to the decrees of the holy Fathers.

He also confirmed the judgment of his predecessor, Pope Gregory, of pious memory, against Heinricus and all his supporters.

He was consecrated near the end of May [Note: [Col. 1395D] Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* III, chapter 6, writes that this happened on 9 May, which was then a Sunday. Uss.] at Saint Peter’s by the cardinal bishops Otto of Ostia [Col. 1395C] and Peter of Albano, together with the other cardinals.

Guibertus the heresiarch, however, did not desist from his wicked undertaking; rather, he fortified himself at Saint Mary’s at the Martyrs, which they call the Pantheon.

The lord pope withdrew to the island situated between the two bridges.

The princes of the Teutonic kingdom—namely, those faithful to Saint Peter—held a general conference with Heinricus and his supporters on 1 August near the city of Speyer. They faithfully promised him their assistance in obtaining the kingdom if he wished to emerge from excommunication.

But he persisted in his customary obstinacy and did not deign to acknowledge that he was excommunicated, although our men repeatedly proved this to his face. Therefore, our men decided to have neither peace nor concord with him [Note: [Col. 1395] The words “with him” are absent in manuscript 2.].

For this reason he announced an expedition against them for the approaching octave of Saint Michael.

Our men, however, agreed that they would anticipate that expedition by eight days and would go out to meet him at the place of assembly with as many men as they could muster.

At the aforesaid conference, the letters of the lord pope were read. In them he announced his elevation to the princes of the kingdom and most openly confirmed the judgment of his predecessor, Pope Gregory, of pious memory [Note: [Col. 1395] The words “of pious memory, Pope Gregory” are absent in manuscript 2.], against Heinricus and his supporters.

Ladislaus, king of Hungary, sent a legation to the same conference and declared that he would persevere in fidelity to Saint Peter. He promised that, if necessary, he would come to the aid of the faithful of Saint Peter with twenty thousand horsemen [Note: [Col. 1395] The words “of Saint Peter” are absent in manuscript 2.].

Nevertheless, the aforesaid expedition was postponed by both sides until that date [Note: [Col. 1395] From here, manuscript 1 continues at another time.].

Solomon, formerly king of Hungary—that is, long since deprived of the kingdom and driven into exile by Ladislaus [Note: [Col. 1395] “Namely” in manuscript 1.]—while attempting some bold undertaking against the king of the Greeks, fell manfully after an incredible slaughter of the enemy.

At the same time, a certain schismatic who had long before invaded the bishopric of Passau while its legitimate pastor was still alive [Note: [Col. 1395D] Hermannus, brother of Luitold, duke of Carinthia; he was intruded against Altmannus at the council of Mainz in 1085. Therefore, “long before” can extend only over a period of two years. Uss.], departed from this life [Note: [Col. 1395] The word “departed” is followed in manuscript 2 by “Pope Victor at Rome”; the intervening section is missing.] and left the other schismatics a most certain example of his own damnation.

For when he lay at the point of death and did not doubt that he was about to depart immediately to eternal damnation, the bishop of that same Church appeared to him, so that he might know all the more clearly the guilt that he would have to expiate in hell.

Nevertheless, he asked him to forgive his guilt and release him from excommunication. He also asked those standing around to remove him from the bishopric and not to bury him in the episcopal see.

But these words seemed to those standing by to be mere ravings. He himself, however, protesting that he was of sound mind, did not cease to make the same request. But in vain, for death overtook him before ecclesiastical absolution.

Nevertheless, some of those who were present at the schismatic’s perilous death were moved to repentance. They later returned to the legitimate pastor and obtained pardon and absolution [Note: [Col. 1395] From here, manuscript 1 continues at another time.].

At Rome, Pope Victor, who had been ill for several years and had been ordained during that same illness, closed his final day after the fourth month of his pontificate (16 September). The heresiarch Guibertus and his followers rejoiced greatly at this.

At that time Heinricus, although ill, advanced with the Bohemians on an expedition into Saxony. But with Saint Peter protecting his faithful, he returned from there in great haste and without glory.

For King Heremann followed him with such a multitude of Saxons that he could very easily have captured him with all his men, had he not escaped through the treachery of Count Eggibertus [Note: [Col. 1396D] Margrave of Meissen. Uss.].

This count, greatly envying the glory of his lord King Heremannus [Note: [Col. 1395] Absent in manuscript 2.], preferred by his treachery to free the enemies of the holy Church from his hands rather than, together with his lord, triumph over them for the honor of God and Saint Peter, almost without danger.

This was certainly because he had already conceived in his mind the intention of depriving his lord of the kingdom.

## 1088
Heremannus, King, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Saxony, where Count Eggibert also openly revealed that he aspired to the kingship; but in vain, for the princes of the kingdom refused to support him. Rather, they began thereafter to adhere all the more firmly to the lord king [Note: [Col. 1397] “At another time” continues in manuscript 1.].

Berthaldus, an outstanding teacher, exceptionally learned in sacred literature, full of days, departed to the Lord in a good old age on the fourth Ides of March.

In these times the Pisans and Genoese [Note: [Col. 1397D] Concerning this victory, compare Leo of Ostia, book 3, chapter 10, and the poem preserved in the Royal Brussels manuscript; see our *Annales*, vol. VII, p. 539.] and many others from Italy hostilely invaded the pagan African king; after ravaging his land, they forced him into a certain stronghold and subsequently made him tributary to the Apostolic See.

Duke Welf recovered the city of Augsburg, capturing Sigifred, the invader of its bishopric [Note: [Col. 1397] “Welfo,” with the *o* erased, manuscript 1; “welfo,” manuscript 4b.].

Count Ugo of Egenesheim invaded Alsace, which had long been occupied by enemies, and attempted to recover it [Note: [Col. 1397] In a place erased, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1397] In a place erased, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1397] In a place erased, in smaller script, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1397] In a place erased, in smaller script, manuscript 1.].

The people of Metz completely expelled Bruno, the usurper of that see, and confirmed by oath that henceforth they would receive no one except a legitimate shepherd; at that time he was being detained in Tuscany in captivity.

In Saxony, the bishop Burchardus of Halberstadt, of pious memory and exceedingly steadfast in the cause of Saint Peter—alas!—was killed. But it makes no difference whether fever or the sword sends us to the Lord. He departed to the Lord on the eighth Ides of April [Note: [Col. 1397] “He departed … April” is missing in manuscript 4b; in manuscript 1 it occurs in an erased passage in smaller script. In its place manuscript 4b has: “And these things were being done among the faithful of Saint Peter.” Traces in manuscript 1 show that this was Bernoldus’s original wording before he adopted the present reading.].

Guibert, the heresiarch, had not yet ceased his invasion of the Apostolic See, nor did Emperor Heinricus wish to lay aside his long-standing tyranny [Note: [Col. 1397] “against … was unable” occurs in an erased passage in smaller script in manuscript 1.] against the faithful of Saint Peter, whom nevertheless he was unable to conquer.

At Rome the cardinal bishops and the other Catholics of the clergy and people ordained Otto, bishop of Ostia, a man distinguished for religion and learning, as the 161st pope, and gave him the name Urban II, on the fourth Ides of March. On the following day he immediately sent letters [Note: [Col. 1397D] They are extant in Martène’s collection, *Thesaurus novus anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 520. Ussher.], declaring his ordination to all Catholics and announcing that in all things he would observe the footsteps of his predecessor, Pope Gregory, of pious memory [Note: [Col. 1397] “of pious memory” and “Pope Gregory” are absent from manuscript 2.].

Wigoldus, bishop of Augsburg, after recovering his city and capturing Sigifred, the pseudo-bishop who had supplanted him [Note: [Col. 1397] “his supplanter” is absent from manuscript 2.], also closed his final day.

Hezel, the most faithful soldier of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1397] “of Saint Peter” is absent from manuscript 2.] and advocate of the monastery of Saint Mary of Reichenau, built a monastery on his own allod in honor of Saint Gregory [Note: [Col. 1397] “in honor of” is absent from manuscript 2.] [Note: [Col. 1397D] In the *Chronicle of Saint George*, which existed in the now-lost Villingen manuscript, the following was read under the year 1084: “In this year the cell of Saint George was first begun to be built”; and under the year 1088: “Hezil, founder of the cell of Saint George, died.” This agrees with Bernoldus. Ussher.]. There he eventually became a monk and departed to the Lord on the Kalends of June.

At that time a certain disciple of the heresiarch Guibert—namely, the pseudo-bishop of Worms—who had invaded that see through schismatics, not consecrated but accursed, finally came to his senses and, returning to the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 1397] Absent from manuscript 1 and manuscript 4b.], resigned the bishopric and surrendered himself to penance in the monastery of Hirsau [Note: [Col. 1397] “Hirsau” is written above the line in manuscript 1.].

Thus, already three years earlier, another disciple of the same Guibert—the pseudo-bishop of Metz, that is [Note: [Col. 1398D] Walo, abbot of Saint Arnulf, according to Hugo of Flavigny. Ussher.]—moved by penitence, had resigned the bishopric. Bruno, whom we mentioned above, immediately invaded it no less sacrilegiously. For he entered through schismatics, while the legitimate shepherd of that see, Heremannus, was still alive; Heremannus chose [Note: [Col. 1397] This passage occurs in an erased place in smaller script in manuscript 1.], in Catholic fashion, to be detained in captivity rather than to be honored as bishop in schism [Note: [Col. 1397] “At another time” continues in manuscript 1.].

Gebehardus, archbishop of Salzburg, of revered memory and pre-eminent in the cause of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1397] “Pre-eminent in the cause of Saint Peter” is absent from manuscript 2.], who was accustomed publicly to refute the schismatics in speech and writing, was taken from this light on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 1397] “On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July” is absent from manuscript 4b.], leaving the Catholics in great sorrow [Note: [Col. 1397] Here one leaf has been cut out in manuscript 2; the text continues, “to consider [him] mad” (*matizatum censere*; the reading is uncertain).].

Bernhardus, master of the schools at Constance, a most learned man and exceedingly zealous in the cause of Saint Peter, departed to the Lord in Saxony under monastic profession [Note: [Col. 1397] Continues in manuscript 1.].

Wecilo, pseudo-bishop of Mainz, and Meginhardus, pseudo-bishop of Würzburg, pre-eminent among the schismatics in learning and error, went miserably—but not pitiably—without ecclesiastical communion to their own place.

The Saxons, abandoning the fidelity of Saint Peter, received Heinricus, whom they had repeatedly renounced. Therefore the Catholic King Heremannus withdrew from them into Lorraine, and there, not long afterward, took the road of all the earth, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, in the seventh year of his reign and the thirteenth indiction. He was honorably buried in his native city of Metz [Note: [Col. 1398D] Compare the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, book II, no. 39.].

Again, through the faction of Margrave Eggibert, the Saxons rebelled against Heinricus. After stripping him of his royal insignia, they shamefully drove him from the siege of a certain stronghold [Note: [Col. 1399D] Gleichen in Thuringia.] onto a mountain (December 24), and there, after a two-day siege, compelled him to confess the anathema and seek reconciliation. Having thus received peace, he withdrew, but did not abandon his customary tyranny.

Eggehardus, abbot of Reichenau, although not especially religious, was nevertheless laudably converted at the end, as they say [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.], and closed his final day [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.]. Oddalricus succeeded him [Note: [Col. 1399] “O. succeeded him” was added at another time, but shortly afterward and by the same hand; it is absent from manuscript 4b.].

## MLXXXIX.

On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, Margrave Eggebertus, strengthened by a few soldiers and encouraged by certain religious men [Note: [Col. 1399] “Heinricus … strengthened” occurs in an erased passage in manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399D] Waltramus counts Archbishop Hartwig of Magdeburg among them above all. Ussher.], attacked Heinricus and his entire army with great courage, and most shamefully drove him from the siege of one of his castles [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399] In a place erased, manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 1399D] Waltramus counts Archbishop Hartwig of Magdeburg among them above all. Ussher.], where he had planned to celebrate the Nativity.

In this attack, on Heinricus’s side, Leomarus [Note: [Col. 1399] “Teomarus,” manuscript 4b.], archbishop of Bremen, and Count Berthaldus were captured. The bishop of Lausanne [Note: [Col. 1399D] Burchardus.], not so much a bishop as an Antichrist, was killed while attempting to act valiantly.

Heinricus himself, having lost the royal insignia, barely escaped from the hands of his pursuers. Fleeing in this way from Thuringia, he finally reached Bamberg, where he was compelled to celebrate without honor.

Margrave Eggebertus, having gained possession of his castle and of the enemy’s camps with scarcely any bloodshed, and having captured and killed many men, did not cease giving thanks to God and Saint Peter, to whom he resolved thereafter to adhere with purer fidelity [Note: [Col. 1399] “To whom … he resolved” is in a place erased, manuscript 1.].

Heremannus, bishop of Metz and a Catholic, returned to his bishopric after a long captivity [Col. 1399C] and was gladly received by many. Bruno, however, the rash invader of that same bishopric, was despised by everyone. Indeed, he had become highly displeasing even to Heinricus because of his most shameful conduct [Note: [Col. 1399D] Waltramus depicts his conduct as extremely bad, although he was devoted to Heinricus, in *On the Unity of the Church*, book II, chapter 30. He makes him the son of Count Adalbertus from the province of Alemannia—specifically, from Calw—and formerly a monk of Saint Trond. Ussher.], although Heinricus had once sold that same bishopric to him [Note: [Col. 1399] “At another time” continues in manuscript 1.].

Thus compelled by this necessity, Bruno was forced to resign the bishopric and return to his father, Count Adalbertus, among the Catholics.

At this time the lord Pope Urbanus was staying at Rome on the island situated between the two bridges. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May he sent a decretal letter [Note: [Col. 1400D] See Mansi XX, 666; the epitome of the letter ends here. Ussher.] to the venerable Gebehardus, bishop of Constance. In it he granted him episcopal authority over the clergy and people of the island of Reichenau, except for the monks, and also gave him authority to ordain an abbot there in his place, and likewise to arrange for the appointment of bishops at Augsburg or Chur.

Indeed, throughout all Alemannia, Bavaria, Saxony, and the neighboring regions, he entrusted his authority to the aforementioned bishop and to the venerable Almanno, bishop of Passau, so that they might reject ordinations that ought to be rejected and strengthen those that ought to be strengthened [Note: [Col. 1399] “Gebehardus” is added in manuscript 3.].

He also confirmed the sentence of anathema promulgated by his predecessor, Pope Gregory, with this distinction: in the first degree he regarded the heresiarch of Ravenna and King Heinricus as anathematized [Note: [Col. 1399] Continues in manuscript 2.]; in the second degree, their supporters—those who assisted them with the same weapons, money, counsel, or obedience, and those who received ecclesiastical orders or honors from them or from their supporters; in the third degree, he placed their communicants. Although he did not excommunicate these, he nevertheless declared them so polluted by external communion that they ought not to be received into the Catholic fellowship without absolution and penance: namely, those who had communicated with the excommunicated through greeting, a kiss, prayer, shared meals, or even unknowingly [Note: [Col. 1399] “Who” is “which” in manuscript 2.].

Those who had been ordained while under excommunication, but not through simony, by bishops who had once been canonically ordained, he permitted to remain in the order they had attained, without promotion, if their integrity and the needs of the Church appeared to demand this. He also permitted some to be promoted to higher orders, but very rarely and only in the greatest necessity.

Guibert, the heresiarch, and his accomplices on the side of their king Heinricus did not cease performing anathematized ordinations, and bestowed them on their followers only after selling them at the highest price. [Col. 1400C] Consequently, the evil of excommunication spread so widely at that time that the Catholics could scarcely keep themselves unharmed from its contagion.

In the German regions four bishops remained in Catholic communion: namely, the bishops of Würzburg, Passau, Worms, and Constance, as well as the bishop of Metz. With their encouragement, the other Catholics resisted the schismatics from the beginning.

Count Ugo of Eginisheim, an indefatigable soldier of Saint Peter, but excessively trusting of the pseudo-bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1399] “An indefatigable soldier of Saint Peter, but excessively trusting of the pseudo-bishop of Strasbourg” is absent from manuscript 2.], was killed by servants of that bishop in the bishop’s bedroom, having lain down with him to sleep, on the second day before the Nones of September.

Bonizo, bishop of Sutri, of pious memory, who had long before been expelled from there for his fidelity to Saint Peter [Col. 1400D], was finally received as bishop by the Catholic people of Piacenza after many captivities, tribulations, and exiles. But he was crowned with martyrdom by the schismatics of that place, who gouged out his eyes and cut off nearly all his limbs. [Col. 1401A]

In Alemannia, Count Otto, an utterly shameless adulterer, excommunicated by the bishop of Constance for his adultery, was most shamefully beheaded by the soldiers of Count Ludwig, whose wife he had infamously joined to himself in a public marriage while her husband was still alive.

His own people buried him near the monastery he had built on his estate, but at the command of the bishop of Constance he was cast out and, as it is written, assigned to the burial of an ass. His soldiers also plundered his possessions, and both his allod and his fief were held not by his heirs but by outsiders, according to what is prophesied in the curses against Judah: “Let strangers plunder his labors” (Psalm 108, 11).

Thus, even after his death, through his burial and the plundering of his property, he most clearly showed how effectively he had incurred the sentence of excommunication. [Col. 1401B]

In Italy, the most noble Duchess Mathildis, daughter of Margrave Bonifacius and widow of Duke Gotefridus, was joined in marriage to Duke Welfo, son of Duke Welfo. This was done not so much because of incontinence as out of obedience to the Roman pontiff, namely so that she might be able to assist the holy Roman Church with greater manliness against the excommunicated.

Those who immediately wished to attack her husband, since they could not resist him, obtained from him a truce lasting until Easter through the intervention of his wife.

King Heinricus was greatly saddened by the aforesaid marriage [Note: [Col. 1401] Absent from manuscript 2.]. He again set out on campaign into Saxony and was compelled to return without honor.

Petrus, bishop of Albano, of pious memory and exceedingly zealous in the cause of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1401] “In the cause of Saint Peter” is absent from manuscript 2.], departed to the Lord.

This is that Petrus who proved by the judgment of fire that Petrus of Pavia, the invader of the bishopric of Florence, was a simoniac. Consequently, the holy Church thereafter called this Petrus “the Fiery.” For he entered a great pyre with confidence and passed through it without any injury, so that the flames blew his garments upward, yet did not harm them—or him—in any way [Note: [Col. 1401D] See above, under the year 1080.].

Therefore the aforesaid Petrus of Pavia was deposed by Pope Alexander, while the other Petrus, at that time a monk of a very poor monastery [Note: [Col. 1401] “Of a very poor monastery” is in a place erased, manuscript 1.], was elevated to the bishopric of Albano. He was of such great holiness, steadfastness, and faith that scarcely anyone of his time could be compared with him. Departing this life, he therefore left the Catholics in great sorrow. [Col. 1401D]

The lord Pope Urbanus assembled a general synod of 115 bishops and confirmed the ecclesiastical statutes of his predecessors by apostolic authority.

Guibert, the heresiarch, was shamefully expelled by the Romans [Col. 1402A] and compelled by oath to promise that he would not again presume to invade the Apostolic See.

But the long-standing discord of the kingdom between Catholics and schismatics had already begun to grow somewhat weaker, so that they now judged it wiser to establish peace between them than to wage war.

Therefore the dukes and counts faithful to Saint Peter held a conference with Heinricus and firmly promised him their counsel and aid for obtaining the kingdom, if he were willing to abandon Guibert, the heresiarch, and return to ecclesiastical communion through a Catholic shepherd.

He himself would not have strongly rejected this condition [Note: [Col. 1401] In a place erased, manuscript 1.], if his own princes had been willing to agree with him in it—namely, the bishops who did not doubt that they themselves would be deposed along with Guibert, because in his faction they had received ordination, or rather execration [Col. 1402B]. These men therefore completely dissuaded him on this occasion from being reconciled to the holy mother Church.

The lord pope absolved the emperor of Constantinople from excommunication through his legates [Note: [Col. 1401] “The king,” manuscript 2.]. He likewise received letters from Philip, king of the Franks, promising him due submission.

## MCX.

In Bavaria the faithful of Saint Peter had by now gained such strength against the schismatics that they appointed a Catholic archbishop in the archbishopric of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 1401D] Thiemo, abbot of Saint Peter, consecrated on the seventh day before the Ides of April. Ussher.]. The exceedingly religious bishop of Passau, legate of Pope Urbanus, immediately consecrated him solemnly together with the bishops of Würzburg and Freising.

Heremannus, bishop of Metz, of pious memory, and Berthaldus, duke of Alemannia and son of King Roudolfus, ended their final day in the fidelity of Saint Peter in the month of May, leaving great sorrow to the Catholics and rejoicing to the schismatics.

The sister of the aforementioned duke, the queen of the Hungarians [Note: [Col. 1401D] That she was Adelheid, daughter of the anti-emperor Rudolf and married to Saint Ladislaus, king of Hungary, is proved at length against those who assert this king’s celibacy by Gerbertus, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 233, and in the treatise *On Rudolf and the Rheinfelden Family*. Ussher.], also died in the same month.

On the side of the excommunicated [Note: [Col. 1401] “Of the king,” manuscript 2.], Duke Luitoldus of Carinthia was carried off by an unexpected death, after most recently repudiating his own wife contrary to law and justice and taking another in her place, with the heresiarch Guibert granting him permission to do so [Note: [Col. 1401] “With Guibert …” is absent from manuscript 2: [lacuna].].

Margrave Eggebertus of Saxony, also sufficiently vigorous in the cause of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1401] “In the cause of Saint Peter” and the following words are absent from manuscript 2: [lacuna].], was treacherously killed through the plot of a certain abbess of Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 1402D] Adelheid.], the sister, as they say, of King Heinricus.

The lord Pope Urbanus [Note: [Col. 1401] Absent from manuscript 2.] assembled through his legates a general synod of bishops from various provinces at the city of Toulouse around Pentecost [Note: [Col. 1402D] See Mansi XX, 733.]. There he corrected many matters in ecclesiastical affairs that required correction.

At that synod the bishop of Toulouse [Note: [Col. 1402D] Isarnus.] was canonically cleared of the accusations brought against him [Col. 1403A], and a legation was sent to restore Christianity in the city of Toledo, at the request of the king of the Spaniards [Note: [Col. 1403] Continues in manuscript 1.].

This year, as King Heinricus entered Lombardy, Duke Welfo of Italy suffered many burnings and plunderings at his hands [Note: [Col. 1403] “This year” is in a place erased in manuscript 1; where “for a long time” had previously been written, manuscript 4b has “for a long time.” Both are correct, since Heinricus was already present at Verona in April.]. But, at the urging of his dearest wife, the lady Mathildis [Note: [Col. 1403] Manuscript 2 reads “Mathildis, his wife, to the same [Heinricus].”], he vigorously strove to resist that same Heinricus and to remain in the fidelity of Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1403] “And to remain in the fidelity of Saint Peter” is absent from manuscript 2.].

This year a great famine suddenly afflicted many regions, although no great barrenness of the earth had preceded it [Note: [Col. 1403] Continues in manuscript 1.].

Adelbero, bishop of Würzburg, of revered memory and one of the more senior bishops, exceedingly steadfast in the cause of Saint Peter against Guibert and his accomplices [Note: [Col. 1403] “Against Guibert and his accomplices” is absent from manuscript 2: [lacuna.]], after many dangers, persecutions, and exiles—which he endured most willingly for Christ—closed his final day in a good confession (October 6), on his estate called Lambach [Note: [Col. 1403C] Lambach in Upper Austria, where he had founded a monastery.] [Col. 1403B].

## MCXI.

The lord pope was at that time residing in the region of Campania, and was honored with the reverence owed him by all Catholics—namely, by the emperor of Constantinople, by Philip, king of the Franks, and by other princes of various kingdoms, both ecclesiastical and secular—except in the kingdom of the Germans, where many Catholics, deceived by greed, voluntarily transferred themselves to the party of the excommunicated. The Romans also tried to demolish the tower of Crescentius, which until then had obeyed the lord pope, after capturing it by treachery. The lord pope could easily have entered Rome with an army and subdued the rebels’ arrogance [Col. 1403C], had he not preferred to conduct his cause with greater gentleness.

At that time the Mantuan people, having already been kept under siege by King Heinricus for a year, abandoned their lord, Duke Welfo, and surrendered themselves and their city to their devastator. The Romans likewise permitted Guibert, the heresiarch whom they had expelled some time before, to enter Rome again and to harass the holy Church with his maledictions rather than with his blessings. The Capuans expelled the Normans from Capua, to whom they had long been subject under several popes and kings. Consequently, the Normans ravaged them on every side, as far as the city wall, with plunder and fire.

[Col. 1404A] The lord pope Urban convened a general synod at Benevento (March 28), and by synodal judgment confirmed the sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch and all his accomplices.

[Note: [Col. 1403C] The synod was held on March 28, the fifth day before the Kalends of April. Mansi XX, 738.]

[Note: [Col. 1403] The text continues in manuscript 1.]

Count and margrave Fridericus rested in the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of July.

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place, where manuscript 1 states that the earlier reading of manuscript 3 was “in peace.”]

Willihelmus, abbot of Hirsau, of blessed memory, most fervent in the cause of Saint Peter and most devoted to monastic discipline—

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place in manuscript 1.]

being, as it were, the father of many monasteries—departed to the Lord on the third day before the Nones of July.

[Note: [Col. 1403] The words “Fridericus … as far as ‘in the Lord’” are absent from manuscript 4b.]

[Note: [Col. 1403] The date is in an erased place.]

He first raised the monastery of Hirsau to remarkable eminence both in its buildings and in its regular discipline, and permanently freed it by a privilege of the Apostolic See under Pope Gregory. He also constructed many other monasteries everywhere, entirely from the ground up:

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

two indeed in the Black Forest [Col. 1404B]: one dedicated to Saint George and the other to Saint Gregory;

[Note: [Col. 1403C] At Reichenbach. See Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 282; concerning Saint George, p. 283; concerning Zwiefalten, p. 288; concerning Schaffhausen, p. 262. Compare Mabillon’s preliminary observations to his *Life*, in the same work, p. 717, and Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 267. Uss.]

also another at the Two Waters, near the Danube;

[Note: [Col. 1403] That is, Zwiefalten, according to a fourteenth-century gloss in manuscript 2.]

and another in the diocese of Würzburg, at a place called Chamberg. He also established the monastery of Schaffhausen and that of Petershausen, which had long before been built on the bank of the Rhine, in regular discipline.

[Note: [Col. 1403] “Schaffhausen monastery” is absent from manuscript 2.]

He likewise established many other monasteries in different regions, some through himself and others through his subordinates, either building them anew or instituting regular discipline in those already built.

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place.]

He also left us many memorials of his natural ingenuity.

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place.]

For he devised a natural clock modeled on the celestial hemisphere; he showed, by definite experiments, how to discover the natural solstices and equinoxes and the condition of the world; and one of his familiars took care to commit all these matters to writing.

[Col. 1404C]

[Note: [Col. 1404D] He seems to allude to Heymo, his disciple and the author of his *Life*. A catalogue of his works was supplied by the Anonymous of Melk and by Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in the *Chronicle* under the year 1070. Uss.]

He also solved many questions concerning the computation of time by the most firmly established arguments. He was highly skilled in music and clarified many subtle points of that art unknown to the ancient teachers.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] Gerbert published Saint William’s musical works in volume II of the *Musical Writers*. Uss.]

He also corrected, with sufficient reason, many errors detected in chants according to the principles of the art. In the quadrivium—

[Note: [Col. 1404D] By this word the ancients designated the four mathematical disciplines: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. Uss.]

—he seemed to surpass nearly all the ancients. Yet above all these accomplishments, devotion to strict monastic discipline prevailed in him. In this he burned so completely that he seemed never to have possessed any other kind of intellectual pursuit. For he was a man of wondrous holiness,

[Note: [Col. 1403] In an erased place in manuscript 1.]

holy simplicity, and most fervent charity, alive to God and truly crucified to the world. The Lord called him, in a good old age, back to the eternal homeland, the one whom he had served from youth onward in this pilgrimage with tireless labor.

[Col. 1405A]

Bernhardus, too, master of the schools at Constance, whose death we mentioned above,

[Note: [Col. 01405] “Bernhardus … exceeded the bounds of doctrine” is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1405C] That is, in the year 1088.]

left us many great memorials

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

and wrote many elegant works on behalf of the Catholics against the schismatics of his time. First,

[Note: [Col. 1405] The word is written above the line in manuscript 1.]

he wrote to certain friends concerning the judgment of Pope Gregory VII against the schismatics and concerning sacraments usurped outside the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1405C] Published in Ussermann, *Prodr.* II, pp. 185ff.]

Afterward he composed, with great brilliance, a substantial book for the venerable Hartvic, bishop of Magdeburg, on the same subject, writing in the person of the holy Church. In it, by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, he seems prudently to have annihilated all the deceitful quibbles of those same schismatics.

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

But in these writings he is said in one place to have exceeded proper measure, carried away by excessive zeal—namely, where he deals with the sacraments of schismatics. For he categorically denies that sacraments can be confected by them or by those who communicate with them, to such an extent that he holds that those ordained by them, if they repent, must be ordained again.

But this contradicts the most sacred Council of Nicaea, to be venerated equally with the Gospel, which ordered that clerics converted from the Novatians be received with their order and not ordained again.

[Note: [Col. 1405] “Nicene” corrected from “necene” in manuscript 1; manuscript 3 has “niceno” and manuscript 4b likewise.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] “Gospel” appears as *euglmo*, with the *o* erased, in manuscript 1.]

It is also read that the African Fathers decreed the same concerning clerics converted from the Donatists.

[Note: [Col. 1405C] Similar statements occur above in Bernhardus’s *Opusculum* II, 4.]

Likewise, Pope Gregory I received Maximus of Salona, an excommunicated usurper who had been ordained by excommunicated men, with his order; he certainly did not ordain him again.

[Note: [Col. 1405C] *Opusculum* I, 9, above.]

They would plainly not have done this if they had believed that those men had received no sacrament of ordination outside the Church. Likewise, blessed Pope Anastasius, writing to the emperor Anastasius, asserts that those ordained by Acacius, although he had been anathematized, suffered no impairment whatever regarding the integrity of the sacraments. Blessed Augustine, too, in many of his writings, and especially in his book *On Baptism against the Donatists*, proves with irresistible force that ecclesiastical sacraments can both be possessed and administered outside the Church, but to the detriment of both the giver and the recipient.

[Note: [Col. 1405C] *Opusculum* II, in the same place.]

We have touched on these matters only in summary, so as to make the reader cautious concerning the writings mentioned above, lest he too hastily assent to some opinion that he discovers to be opposed to the equally authoritative judgments of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 1406A]

But if anyone desires to know these matters more fully, let him carefully read a writing sent to the same Bernhardus by a certain person on this same question. In it, by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, he will be taught most clearly what the holy Fathers judged should be thought concerning that question.

[Note: [Col. 1405C] He means Bernoldus’s own little work, *On the Sacraments of the Excommunicated according to the Assertion of the Holy Fathers*, dedicated to the same Bernhardus around the year 1085. *Prodr.* II, pp. 187–188. Uss.]

Yet the same venerable Bernhardus, in this matter, just as blessed Cyprian did in the question of rebaptism, did not act stubbornly against the Church. Rather, both, zealous beyond measure against the schismatics, exceeded the rule of ecclesiastical doctrine to some extent.

[Note: [Col. 1405] The text continues in manuscript 2.]

Altmannus, bishop of Passau, of holy memory, most devoted to the cause of Saint Peter and to ecclesiastical religion,

[Note: [Col. 1405] The words “in the cause of Saint Peter and” are absent from manuscript 2.]

after many dangers, tribulations, and exiles which he endured for Christ [Col. 1406B], departed to the Lord in a good old age, on the sixth day before the Ides of August.

[Note: [Col. 1406C] These were Saint Nicholas near Passau, Saint Florian in Upper Austria, and Saint Hippolytus in Lower Austria, now the seat of a bishop. Uss.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] “Sixth,” formerly “seventh,” day before the Ides of August, in an erased place; “in the month of August” in manuscript 4b.]

In his episcopate he established three communities of clerics living together according to the rule of Saint Augustine, and built a third in the diocese of Freising, on the allod of Duke Welfo, through his clerics, and instituted it in regular discipline.

[Note: [Col. 1406C] Read “the fourth,” namely the Raitenbuch community, to whose brothers the same Bernoldus wrote a treatise on the office of priests. See the *Life of Saint Altmann*, vol. II of the Bollandists’ *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 357, under August 8, where there is also further information about the monastery of Göttweig. Uss.]

[Note: [Col. 1405] Manuscript 2 has “instituted.”]

[Note: [Col. 1405] Manuscript 2 has “increased.”]

He was a man of such holiness, continence, and religious devotion that he was revered and loved by the most reverend Pope Gregory, by the holy bishop of Lucca, and indeed by all religious people,

[Note: [Col. 1405] In an erased place.]

but was hated and feared by schismatics and criminals. Thus, at his death, he left great sorrow to the good, but great exultation to the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 1405] The words “Thus … exultation” are absent from manuscript 2.]

Duke Welfo of Bavaria came into Lombardy in the month of August, in order to be reconciled with King Heinricus, if the king were willing to permit the Apostolic See, which had been seized by Guibert the heresiarch, to be canonically restored, and if he were also willing to return to the same duke, to his son Welfo, and to their other supporters the goods which had been unjustly taken from them.

[Note: [Col. 1405] “He entered” in manuscript 3.]

He refused to fulfill this condition. Consequently, the duke did not delay returning to Alemannia. Nevertheless, many of the Alemannians were reconciled with King Heinricus and made the excommunication of the Apostolic See common to themselves with Heinricus.

[Note: [Col. 1405] Manuscript 4b adds: “Thus excommunication prevailed so greatly in Alemannia that many religious men and women chose permanent exile rather than perish under communion with the excommunicated. These words, first written by Bernoldus and in manuscript 1, were erased while the text continued; in their place were written the words beginning ‘The duke … should decide.’”]

The duke, however, again stirred up many against Heinricus and his supporters, so that they might even decide to elect a new king, if the laziness or malice of certain people did not prevent them. [Col. 1407A]

[Note: [Col. 1406C] Everything that follows from here to the end of the book was written by Bernoldus in the monastery of Schaffhausen.]

In those times, common life flourished in many places throughout the kingdom of the Germans—not only among clerics and monks living together with the greatest religious devotion, but also among laypeople, who most devoutly offered themselves and their possessions to the same common life. Although they did not appear by their dress to be either clerics or monks, they were nevertheless believed to be in no way inferior to them in merit.

[Note: [Col. 1407] The passage beginning “They made themselves …” and ending “we confirm by authority” is absent from manuscript 2.]

They made themselves servants of those men for the Lord’s sake, imitating him who came not to be served but to serve, and who taught his followers to attain greatness through the performance of service. Indeed, renouncing the world, they devotedly transferred themselves and their possessions to communities of both clerics and monks living according to a rule, so that they might merit living together under their obedience and serving them.

[Col. 1407B]

Therefore the devil’s envy stirred up certain rivals against the tested way of life of these brothers, so that they might gnaw away at their life with malicious teeth, although they saw them living together according to the pattern of the primitive Church.

Accordingly, the lord pope Urban, judging that their way of life—planted by the apostles themselves but propagated most widely by their successors—was praiseworthy and all the more worthy of perpetual preservation because it had been impressed with the form of the primitive Church, approved it, called it holy and catholic, and confirmed it by apostolic authority.

He also arranged for his decree to be announced in these words to the prelates of those brothers:

“Some people, we understand, are attacking the custom of your monasteries, by which you receive laypeople who renounce the world and transfer themselves and their possessions to the common life, accepting them to be governed under obedience.

“But we, having observed this same way of life and custom with our own eyes, [Col. 1407C] judge it praiseworthy and worthy of perpetual preservation, because it has been modeled on the form of the primitive Church. We approve it, call it holy and catholic, and by these present letters confirm it by apostolic authority.”

[Note: [Col. 1407] The text continues in manuscript 1 with “Not only … to obey,” in an erased place.]

Not only an innumerable multitude of men but also of women devoted themselves in those times to this kind of life, so that they might live together under the obedience of clerics or monks and most devoutly discharge to them, like maidservants, the daily duty of service. In the villages themselves, countless daughters of peasants strove to renounce marriage and the world and to live under the obedience of some priest.

[Note: [Col. 1407] The words beginning “In those …” and ending “ceased to grieve” are absent from manuscript 2.]

Married people too continued nevertheless to live religiously and to obey religious persons with the greatest devotion. This kind of devotion flourished everywhere especially in Alemannia. In that province many villages wholly devoted themselves to religion and tirelessly strove to surpass one another in holiness of conduct.

Thus God deigned wonderfully to console his holy Church in a most perilous time, so that it might rejoice over the conversion of many, though it had long since not ceased to grieve over the turning away of the excommunicated.

[Col. 1408A]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

In the German regions, flesh rained together with blood, and toads fell from the sky along with fish, as many reputable men testified that they had seen. In Alemannia, at the Two Waters near the Danube, blood seemed to flow out of loaves of bread. Many religious men believed that each of these events portended something new in the kingdom.

Juditha, marchioness of blessed memory, noble by birth but nobler in holiness, formerly the wife of Heremannus, a most religious margrave,

[Note: [Col. 1407C] Of Baden; see the year 1074.]

departed to the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of October. She had lived religiously with her husband and, after his death, remained for nineteen years in widowhood and holy conduct. [Col. 1408B] Finally she reached the lord pope at Salerno and died there under his obedience.

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

Adelheida, countess of Turin,

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407C] The mother-in-law of Heinricus IV. Concerning her, see Gerbert, *Treatise on Rudolf the Antiking*, p. 118ff. Uss.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January.

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

MXCII.

The lord pope celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the territory of Saint Peter outside Rome. For Guibert the heresiarch had fortified himself so strongly near the house of Saint Peter that he could not easily be expelled without the shedding of human blood. Heinricus, his emperor,

[Note: [Col. 1407] “His impious emperor” is absent from manuscripts 2 and 3; manuscript 3 has “impious emperor.”]

had already been residing in Lombardy for two years,

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

and there he did not cease ravaging the surrounding territory of Welfo, the Italian duke, with plunder, sword, and fire,

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

in order to compel that duke and his most prudent wife to abandon the fidelity of Saint Peter and adhere to himself.

[Note: [Col. 1408C] “Most prudent” is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] The words beginning “and abandon the fidelity of Saint Peter” are absent from manuscript 2.]

But in vain: the duke remained firm in his judgment and resisted him with considerable courage.

The father of this duke, Welfo, duke of Bavaria, also wonderfully confounded the same Heinricus before the preceding Nativity of the Lord. He prevented him from reaching a meeting which that same Heinricus and the king of Hungary had arranged and to which they had almost already come together.

[Note: [Col. 1407] “The same King Heinricus” in manuscript 2.]

In Alemannia there was a certain layman who professed the common life in the manner of the apostles and had surrendered himself and his possessions to the monastery of Saint Saviour.

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] The passage beginning “In Alemannia …” and ending “if he repented” is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1407C] The monastery of Schaffhausen; compare the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, book III, no. 24.]

He long rendered the obedience that was owed there, but suddenly began to apostatize and did not fear sacrilegiously to drag himself and his possessions away from the aforesaid monastery.

Therefore the lord pope Urban, sending letters, commanded the venerable Gebehardus, bishop of Constance, by apostolic authority to summon that apostate canonically and, with the sword of anathema, cut him off entirely from the members of Christ, unless he quickly repented of that apostasy [Col. 1409A] and sacrilege.

[Note: [Col. 1408C] Urban’s letter was before the editor’s eyes and was published from the *Codex Udalrici* by Mansi XX, 707–708. The bishop of Constance is incorrectly called Gaufredus there.]

[Note: [Col. 1407] “Unless … he repented” was added shortly afterward in manuscript 1.]

Again, the princes of Alemannia unanimously assembled for the defense of holy mother Church against the schismatics and appointed Berthaldus, the brother of the bishop of Constance, duke of all Swabia to carry out this undertaking. He had not yet held any duchy, although he had long been accustomed to bear the title of duke.

[Note: [Col. 1409] “Named Berthaldus” in manuscript 2.]

A great famine seized all Saxony and compelled the princes of that province to withdraw temporarily to other regions that year. Consequently, the general assembly which the princes of Alemannia wished to hold with the Saxons could not take place.

In Lombardy, Chounradus, the son of King Heinricus, seized the goods of Adelheida, countess of Turin,

[Note: [Col. 1409C] Among the goods that had fallen to Adelheida through her paternal inheritance, Guichenon (*Genealogical History of the House of Savoy*, vol. IV, p. 200) counts the margraviate of Susa, the duchy of Turin, the Aosta valley, and other lands around Geneva. On the death of her mother, all these devolved upon her eldest son Peter, and from the father upon his daughter Agnes of Savoy, married to Fridericus of Montbéliard, or Bar, and to the count of Luxembourg. Uss.—The genealogy of Agnes from Adelheida follows: [Col. 1409]]

which belonged by right to the son of Fridericus, the countess’s grandson.

[Col. 1409B]

[Note: [Col. 1409] Everything that follows up to “The clerics” is in an erased place in manuscript 1.]

This count, although he wore secular dress, was a most courageous soldier of Christ in the manner of Saint Sebastian: namely, a most fervent lover of ecclesiastical religion and an indefatigable defender of Catholic peace. Venerable Pope Gregory loved him as an only son, as did blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca. Clerics and monks, indeed all religious people, loved him most fervently.

This man fought with the greatest devotion in fidelity to Saint Peter against the schismatics until death. [Col. 1409C] On the very feast of Saint Peter, he was released from the prison of this life and is believed to have been united with him in the heavenly homeland.

[Note: [Col. 1409] The passage beginning “This man …” and ending “was united” is absent from manuscript 2.]

He was the son of Lady Sophia and Count Ludowicus; Sophia was the maternal aunt of Countess Mathildis, who labored greatly with her lord, Duke Welfo, in Italy against the schismatics.

[Note: [Col. 1409] The passage beginning “who” and ending “labored” is absent from manuscript 2.]

The aforesaid count died in the preceding year, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, indiction 14, on the third day before the Kalends of July,

[Note: [Col. 1409] “Fourteenth.”]

[Note: [Col. 1409] The passage beginning “namely …” and ending “brought evil” is absent from manuscript 2.]

namely on the feast of Saint Peter, and was buried the next day, that is, on the solemnity of Saint Paul.

Heinricus the king therefore planned to disinherit his son, born from the granddaughter of Lady Adelheida, and by invading his territory as an enemy and devastating the surrounding region, he also inflicted much harm on the monastery of Fruttuaria.

[Note: [Col. 1409] In an erased place.]
