[Note: [Col. 1409] The text continues in manuscript 1.]

In Bavaria, the venerable Diemo, bishop of Salzburg,

[Note: [Col. 1409] In an erased place.]

ordained as bishop of the church of Passau, long left widowed, a man named Oudalricus, provost of the church of Augsburg. Together with the bishops of Constance and Worms, he solemnly consecrated him on the very day of Pentecost. This gave great confidence to the Catholics, so that they might persist in fidelity to Saint Peter and resist the madness of the schismatics with still greater steadfastness.

[Col. 1410A]

[Note: [Col. 1409] The text continues in manuscript 1.]

In Hungary many prodigies occurred in those times, as we have heard. For a certain mountain hurled itself into the Danube, and that river was thereby forced to change its channel and devastated the neighboring lands far and wide. Likewise, a great lake emerged elsewhere on dry land, and in another lake a certain mountain suddenly appeared. A river called the Tisza—

[Note: [Col. 1409C] The Theiss.]

—flowed blood-red for three days. There was also an unheard-of earthquake there [Col. 1410B], so violent that people could not withstand its force while standing. A great thunderclap, unheard by men for centuries, also terrified the inhabitants. It passed above the earth and was felt returning underground by the same route.

In Alemannia, Count Chono of Wülflingen, a most courageous soldier of Saint Peter, died on the Ides of October. He was honorably buried in the monastery which he and his brother, Count Luitolfus, had founded on their own allod. His brother Luitolfus inherited his possessions by hereditary right, although he had long since renounced secular military service.

[Note: [Col. 1409] Manuscript 1 reads “He certainly did this.”]

He did not do this with the intention of returning to the world, but rather in order to enrich the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1410C] with those possessions.

[Note: [Col. 1409] The text continues in manuscript 1.]

In this year four priests from Swabia, men of no small reputation among their own people and of considerable religious devotion,

[Note: [Col. 1409] Manuscript 1 continues.]

[Note: [Col. 1409] Thus punctuation is given in manuscript 1.]

set out for Jerusalem on pilgrimage and prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1409] “The holy men, traveling to Jerusalem, set out on pilgrimage.” Manuscript 3.]

After many tribulations and hardships on the journey, they died quite happily, in a good confession, while returning. One of them, who had been accustomed to venerate holy Mary every day with singular devotion, deserved, when he was dying at sea, by God’s providence to be carried by ship to the church of Saint Mary. There he was honorably buried by his fourth fellow priest, who alone of those four was still alive. The man who buried him also died not long afterward.

[Col. 1411A]

[Note: [Col. 1411] After “not long afterward,” the next leaf is missing in manuscript 2.]

[Note: [Col. 1411] In an erased place.]

[Note: [Col. 1411] In an erased place.]

Beatrix, sister of Margrave Fridericus

[Note: [Col. 1411D] This is the same Fridericus discussed shortly above, count of Moncionis and Montbéliard, called margrave because of the inheritance mentioned earlier. Schoepflinus gives the genealogy of him and his sister Beatrix, *History of Zähringen and Baden*, vol. I, p. 58ff. Uss.]

and formerly wife of Duke Berthaldus,

[Note: [Col. 1411D] The first Zähringen duke of that name. Uss.]

at last, after being mercifully chastised and tested by the Lord through a prolonged illness, most happily

[Note: [Col. 1411] In an erased place.]

died on the seventh day before the Kalends of November. She was honorably buried in the city of Toul by the bishop of that place.

The lord Oudalricus, who had obtained the abbey of Saint Gall and the bishopric of Aquileia without entering through the door, attempted through a certain monk of his monastery to overthrow Gebehardus, bishop of Constance. He obtained from Heinricus the investiture of that bishopric for the monk.

[Note: [Col. 1411D] Burkhardus calls him Arnoldus, *On the Misfortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 7; compare the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, book III, no. 26. Uss.]

But when he wished to enthrone that usurper before the Nativity of the Lord, he was not received by the people of Constance. Indeed, he was compelled to retreat, not without insult.

A great earthquake also occurred at that time by night in the same diocese, at the monastery of the Saviour. Consequently it became known to only a few, apart from certain religious men and women who had not yet fallen asleep that night.

[Col. 1411B]

[Note: [Col. 1411D] Was one of them Bernoldus?]

The Catholics did not doubt that, in accordance with the Gospel, this earthquake portended divine anger on account of the presumption mentioned above.

MXCIII.

Dom Pope Urban celebrated the Nativity of the Lord outside Rome, in the territory of Saint Peter, because he had not yet been able to enter Rome without an armed force. For the Guibertists and excommunicates still held great power there and would not readily allow themselves to be expelled without violence [Col. 1411C]. Guibert himself at that time was staying with his emperor, Henry, in Lombardy, and was plotting with him whatever he could against Duke Welf and his wife Matilda, the daughter of Saint Peter.

The venerable Wernher, bishop of the church of Merseburg, after many struggles against the evasions of the schismatics, at last ended his life in fidelity to Saint Peter; he alone then remained in Saxony as a bishop of the Catholic communion. Thus, at his death, he left great sorrow to the Catholics and great joy to the excommunicates. He died rather happily on 11 January.

In Alemannia, in various places, many fires seemed to be carried simultaneously through the air very early in the morning on the eighth day after Epiphany [Col. 1411D]. These fires were generally understood to signify the many conflagrations that not long afterward would spread widely through that land [Col. 1412A]. For Duke Welf, Count Odalric of Bregenz [Note: So in one witness. [Col. 1411] See *Disquisitio ad Chronicon Petershusanum*, pp. 292 ff. (*Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII, in Herman the Lame), and *Chronicon*, book III, no. 16. Uss.] and many others began to devastate one another with every kind of fire.

Sigifred, abbot of Schaffhausen, obtained from Richard, abbot of Marseilles, a place in Alemannia called Nobiliacum [Note: Urstisius conjectures in his note that this was the place of Saint Faith at Grafenhausen, now belonging to Saint Blaise. See Gerbert, *Historia Silvae Nigrae*, vol. I, p. 264. Uss.], and prepared the place for himself and his brothers, so that he might withdraw there for a time if, because of the excommunication, he should be unable to remain in his own monastery. For that long-standing excommunication which Pope Gregory of blessed memory had pronounced against Guibert and his accomplices had by then contaminated high and low alike in Alemannia to such an extent that all religious people despaired of remaining among them without endangering their Catholic communion [Col. 1412B].

The most noble Countess Sophia, widow of Count Louis and mother of Duke Beatrice, of blessed memory, and of Margrave Frederick, ended her life in a good old age, when she had already seen many of her sons’ sons [Note: The following words are missing in witness 3. [Col. 1411]].

In Lombardy, the most prudent soldiers of Saint Peter, Duke Welf and his wife Matilda, who had now fought manfully against the schismatics for three years, were at last, with God’s help, greatly strengthened against them. For Conrad, son of King Henry, withdrew from his father and aided Duke Welf and the other faithful of Saint Peter against his father and his supporters. The cities of Lombardy—Milan, Cremona, Lodi, and Piacenza—also swore a twenty-year league against Henry, and all faithfully adhered to the aforesaid duke. Certain people also secured the Alpine passage into Lombardy, so that Henry’s supporters could not travel to him [Col. 1412C].

The people of Augsburg expelled the bishop whom Henry had given them [Note: Siegfried. [Col. 1412D]], and canonically elected for themselves a Catholic shepherd [Note: Eberhard; see the *Annals of Augsburg* under the year 1094, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. III, p. 124. [Col. 1412D]]. He captured the bishop of Ivrea in the fortress guarding the Alpine passage [Note: Bard. [Col. 1412D]], which that bishop had decided to do to him.

The church of Metz, and those of Toul and Verdun, withdrew from obedience to Eigilbert, the excommunicated archbishop of Trier, and openly declared that they would obey him no longer [Note: Witness 2 continues with *dientia*. [Col. 1411]]. The church of Metz, having rejected the bishop whom Henry wished to give it [Note: Adalbero. [Col. 1412D]], canonically elected for itself a Catholic shepherd [Note: *Canonice* is absent in witness 2; Poppo. [Col. 1412D]], and had him consecrated both canonically and in Catholic fashion by Gebehard, bishop of Constance and legate of the Apostolic See, on 27 March, in the middle of Lent [Note: Witness 1 continues again with *iam*. [Col. 1411] [Col. 1413A]].

Pope Urban convened a general synod of nearly one hundred bishops from various provinces during Lent in Apulia, and competently provided by synodal action for the various needs of the churches [Note: Witness 1 continues. Namely, the synod was held at Troia in Apulia on 11 March, with seventy-five bishops present. Mansi XX, 789. [Col. 1413] [Col. 1413D]].

In Lombardy, Conrad, son of King Henry, was deceitfully ambushed and captured by his father. But by God’s mercy he was rescued from there and crowned king by the archbishop of Milan [Note: Anselm. [Col. 1413D]] and the other faithful of Saint Peter, with the support of Duke Welf of Italy and his most beloved wife Matilda [Note: Two words are missing. [Col. 1413]]. His father, Duke Welf of Bavaria, also came not long afterward into Lombardy to the newly crowned king and endeavored to adhere faithfully to him together with his son.

Henry, the king’s father, withdrew into a certain stronghold [Note: *Monitionem* corrected to *munitionem*, “fortification.” [Col. 1413]], where he remained for a long time without royal dignity and, overcome by no little grief, wished—as they say—to surrender himself to death; but his men forestalled him, and he could not carry this out.

In Alemannia, Duke Berthold built from the foundations a new monastery in honor of Saint Peter on his estate in the Black Forest, and endowed it with many possessions. He also transferred to it all the goods of another monastery which his father had built elsewhere [Note: Weilheim below Teck Castle; see Gerbert, *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, vol. I, p. 290. Uss. [Col. 1413D]]. His brother Gebehard, bishop of Constance and legate of the Apostolic See, inaugurated this monastery by its consecration, while another Gebehard, abbot of Hirsau, established there the regular discipline of the monks.

This consecration took place on the Kalends of August, when the station of the Chains of Saint Peter is observed. The venerable abbot Sigifred of the cell of the Savior also gave that place a large part of those chains [Note: The passage from *quorum* (“of which”) through *committitur* (“is committed”) is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1413]], together with many relics of other saints. At the same consecration an abbot was elected for the place, and the monks, the construction of the site, and everything belonging to it were freely entrusted to his administration. The place itself was designated as being specially subject to the Apostolic See [Note: The text continues. [Col. 1413]].

Likewise in Alemannia, Count Hartmann and his brother Otto built a new monastery in honor of Saint Martin on their own allod, at the place where the Danube and the Iller River meet [Note: Wiblingen, a dependency of Saint Blaise, with Abbot Werner sent there with his brothers. See Gerbert, *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, p. 250. Uss. [Col. 1413D]]. The aforesaid bishop of Constance likewise inaugurated it by his consecration in the month of September; but the venerable Abbot Uto of Saint Blaise established the regular discipline there [Col. 1414A].

At the same time that bishop consecrated another monastery [Note: Ochsenhausen, then a cell of Saint Blaise; see Gerbert, *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, p. 294. Uss. [Col. 1414D]] not far from that place [Note: That is, from the monastery of Wiblingen. [Col. 1414D]], in honor of Saint George. A certain nobleman, Conrad [Note: So in one witness. [Col. 1413]], and his brothers handed over that place and everything belonging to it to Saint Blaise without any condition, and asked the aforesaid abbot to establish the service of God there. The abbot did not cease to comply with their wishes.

At this time the wife of the distinguished Count Adalbert [Note: This was the second Count of Calw, who restored the monastery of Hirsau. See the work cited above, p. 260. Uss. [Col. 1414D]], named Weliga [Note: Wilga, according to Uss., against the authority of the manuscripts. [Col. 1413]] [Note: Or Wiltrud. [Col. 1414D]], daughter of the great Duke Godfrey [Note: “The Bearded.” [Col. 1414D]], having lived with her husband in the world in a sufficiently praiseworthy manner, ended her life and was buried with considerable honor at the monastery of Hirsau, which she herself had chiefly founded and loved [Note: The text continues. [Col. 1413] [Col. 1414B]].

A sign appeared in the sun on 23 September before noon [Note: The words from “before” through “it might shine” are in a partially erased passage. [Col. 1413]], so that a kind of circle appeared in it and it itself shone very darkly in a clear sky [Note: Two words are missing. [Col. 1413]] [Note: The abbreviated words *Nam e. c. d. H.* occur in an erased passage in witness 1. [Col. 1413]]. Some, however, thought that this had been an eclipse rather than a sign, especially since the moon was twenty-eight days old on that day. For the distinguished calculator Lord Heremannus [Note: Herman the Lame. [Col. 1413]] also writes that an eclipse occurred on the twenty-seventh lunar day in the year of the Lord 1033 [Note: At this point in witness 2 nearly an entire folio has been cut away. [Col. 1413]] [Note: The text continues. [Col. 1413]].

Gebehard, bishop of Constance and legate of the Apostolic See, received Duke Welf of Bavaria by the laying on of hands into knighthood, just as he had long before done for his own brother, Duke Berthold of Alemannia. With them and the other princes of Alemannia he held a great assembly at Ulm. At this assembly it was most firmly decreed that the bishop of Constance should be obeyed in every respect according to the statutes of the canons, and that Duke Berthold and the counts should be obeyed according to Alemannian law.

Then both dukes and counts, both great and small, swore that they would observe a firm peace from 25 November until Easter, and from Easter for two years: namely, for all monks, whether converts or clerics, subject to the Catholic bishop; for churches, their atria, and their endowments; for merchants; and for all persons bound by the same oath, except Arnold, the invader of the church of Constance, and all his supporters. Each of the princes who had assembled caused the peace to be sworn, person by person, throughout his own authority [Note: The manuscripts read variously *usquequisque* and *vfq; qfq;*. [Col. 1413]] [Col. 1414D].

At this time Adefonsus, king of Spain, Catholic in faith and obedient in his manner of life to the abbot of Cluny, fought very frequently and manfully on behalf of the Christians against the pagans, and restored many churches that had long been utterly devastated to their former condition. He also built the greater church at Cluny from its foundations, sending an immense amount of money to Cluny for the construction of that church. He would also long before have made himself a monk there, if the lord abbot [Note: Hugh, who died in 1108. [Col. 1415D]] had not judged it preferable to retain him for a time in secular dress.

In Lombardy, the venerable Anselm, archbishop of Milan, most devoted to the cause of Saint Peter, who had recently crowned Conrad king, made a very praiseworthy end and left great sorrow to the faithful of Saint Peter. The venerable Arnolf of the Silver Gate succeeded him in the episcopate [Col. 1415B].

MXCIV.

Pope Urban solemnly celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Rome, although several Wibertists were still hiding in the city, whom the pope could not easily expel without a military force. He therefore preferred to endure their injury for a time rather than disturb the Roman citizens with an armed force.

Guibert the heresiarch was then with his emperor at Verona, and pretended willingly to abandon the papacy if peace could not otherwise be restored in the church. The emperor’s wife, long harassed by many injuries and kept under guard for many years lest she flee, at last fled to Duke Welf of Italy. Among her own people she complained of having suffered so many, such great, and such unheard-of evils that she did not doubt she would find mercy even among her enemies; nor was she deceived in this hope. For the duke and his wife Matilda received her gladly and treated her honorably.

Judith, wife of Duke Welf of Bavaria, long afflicted by illness and considerably improved by that chastisement, ended her life on 4 March and was honorably buried by Gebehard, bishop of Constance, at the monastery which her husband had built in his own allod in honor of Saint Martin [Note: Weingarten. [Col. 1415D]]. To that monastery her husband, the duke, gave her chapel [Note: This refers to the reliquary of the Lord’s holy blood. See P. Hess, *Prodromus Monumentorum Guelphorum*, p. 47. In the *Necrology of Weingarten* it is recorded under 5 March, which may perhaps have been the day of deposition. Compare *Origines Guelphicae*, vol. II, p. 277. Uss. [Col. 1415D]], which was worth nearly one thousand pounds in gold, silver, and the most precious vestments. He also enriched the monastery with possessions amounting to nearly one hundred hides, and, thus enriched and emancipated from his authority, transferred it to Saint Peter under tributary tenure, so that henceforth it might be principally subject to the Apostolic See and might enjoy perpetual legal standing under its protection, like the other free monasteries.

The pope was staying at Rome near Saint Mary the New [Note: The word is worn away and restored in recent ink. [Col. 1415]], in a very strong fortification [Col. 1416A]. But the Wibertists, who held the tower of Crescentius, still did not permit travelers free passage over the bridge of the Tiber to the pope [Note: The text continues. [Col. 1415]]. For, while a certain abbot from the cell of Saint Peter in Alemannia [Note: He appears to have been Adalbero. Uss. [Col. 1416D]], sent to the pope by Gebehard, bishop of Constance, and by his brother Duke Berthold, was attempting to cross that bridge, they detained him in captivity.

Duke Welf of Bavaria extended the very firm peace which he had earlier established with the Alemannian duke Berthold and the other princes of Alemannia as far as Bavaria, indeed as far as Hungary [Note: The words abbreviated *q. d.* are absent in witness 3. [Col. 1415]]. German Francia and Alsace likewise decreed by oath that they would observe the same peace in their territories. This peace, however, took greatest effect in Alemannia, because each of its princes did not cease to administer justice within his own authority; the other provinces had not yet resolved to do so.

And especially Duke Berthold burned with such zeal to administer justice in the duchy of Alemannia that in observing justice he almost surpassed all his predecessors, and filled everyone’s mouth with favorable praise [Note: The passage from “And” through “filled” is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1415]].

Yet in those regions the holy mother Church still suffered great difficulty in avoiding the excommunicated. She could scarcely have avoided them if the pope, with apostolic authority, had not already tempered the sentence of excommunication in some way. For, following the custom of his predecessor, the venerable Pope Gregory, he excluded many people from excommunication—travelers, peasants, male and female servants, wives, and children—although their perverse will did not bind them by the same chain of excommunication [Col. 1416C].

Gebehard, bishop of the church of Constance, canonically celebrated a great synod at Constance in Holy Week before Easter with abbots and innumerable clerics, and with the aforesaid dukes and the other princes of Alemannia (April beginning). There he corrected many things that needed correction. He also prohibited the incontinence of priests [Note: Witness 1 reads *inenentia*. [Col. 1415]] and the violence of the simoniacs so rigorously that he would have prohibited the people entirely, under ban, from receiving their ministry if those engaged in such crimes had presumed to minister contrary to right and law.

There he also decreed, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, that the March fast should always be observed in the first week of Lent, and the June fast in the week of Pentecost. He further decreed that only three days should be celebrated as festivals both in the week of Pentecost and in the Easter week. Until that time, the bishopric of Constance had not followed the custom of the neighboring dioceses: namely, celebrating the entire week at Easter [Note: This ancient rite is inferred from Sermon 259 of Saint Augustine and is prescribed in canon 66 of the Council in Trullo. Even in 948, canon 6 of the Council of Ingelheim decreed that the entire Easter week should be celebrated festively, adding: “And at Pentecost, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday should be solemnly honored no less than Sunday.” From Bernold it is nevertheless inferred here that this had fallen into disuse. Uss. Compare the *Annals of Augsburg* for this year. [Col. 1416D]], while observing only one day at Pentecost. Yet both weeks ought to have been observed in the same manner, and nearly all the other dioceses had long maintained the aforesaid regulation [Col. 1417A].

These things, I say, he was canonically able to establish in his own bishopric both by episcopal authority and by his apostolic legation, for he was legate of the Apostolic See throughout the whole of the Teutonic land [Note: The phrase *per totam Teutonicam terram usquequaque* (“throughout the whole Teutonic land”) is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1417]].

The complaint of Queen Praxedis, who had earlier left her husband and gone to Duke Welf of Italy, reached the synod of Constance. She complained that she had suffered such great and unheard-of filthinesses of fornication, and from such men, that she could easily excuse her flight even before her enemies, and win all Catholics to compassion for such injuries. In this synod [Note: The passage from “In this synod” through “judged” is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1417]] the venerable Abbot Sigefrid of the cell of Saint Salvator brought a complaint against Touto, his obedientiary [Note: Bernold had already dealt with this under the year 1092, though the *Chronicon Petershusanum* recounts the matter differently. [Col. 1417C]]. Touto had freely transferred himself and his property to that monastery, but not long afterward sacrilegiously attempted to alienate himself and his possessions from it completely.

Therefore the holy synod, according to the statutes of the canons, judged that this man should return without any opposition to the obedience of his abbot, humbly remain perpetually subject to him together with his possessions, and strive to perform a fitting penance for his past disobedience according to the abbot’s command. Thus it was done as the synod had judged it should be [Col. 1418A].

A great mortality was raging in Bavaria, so that in the city of Regensburg alone 8,500 people were counted as having been carried off by that mortality within twelve weeks [Note: “Weeks.” [Col. 1417]]. The same mortality afflicted other provinces, though not as severely as Bavaria.

Many prodigies occurred in the Teutonic regions. People hanged themselves, and wolves devoured many. It was not doubted that this had happened through divine vengeance, because they had neglected the divine law and had not feared to be stained by excommunication. Lightning also greatly terrified the people. For at the monastery at Utenburron [Note: Utenbourron in another witness. [Col. 1417]], the large crucifix and the monks’ seats—since they were not living according to the rule—were shattered by lightning [Col. 1418B]. Likewise, in the major church of Basel, lightning crushed the beam supporting the crucifix, precisely when many excommunicated people had gathered there.

At this time Master Manegold of Liutenbach began to establish a monastery of clerics at Marbach [Note: This phrase is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1417]] [Note: In Alsace, near Colmar. Since this Manegold was, like Bernold, an apostolic penitentiary, and Bernold praises him in this and the following years, it seems appropriate to add some notes about him. He appears to have taken his surname, de Lutenbach, from the town of Lautenbach or Luterbach in Upper Alsace, where he was born. Richard of Poitiers says the following about him in his twelfth-century chronicle (*Martène, Collectio amplissima*, vol. V, p. 1169): “At this time”—during the reign of Henry I, king of France, and therefore before 1056—“Manegold the philosopher began to flourish in the Teutonic land, learned in divine and secular letters beyond his contemporaries. His wife and daughters, also distinguished for their religious devotion, possessed much knowledge of Scripture, and his aforesaid daughters taught their own pupils.” Bulaeus likewise praises him (*Historia Universitatis Parisiensis*, vol. I, p. 347): “Manigaud of Lutenbach, a German instructed in every discipline at Paris, returned to his homeland and explained what he had learned to his countrymen.” Trithemius gives a fuller account (*Annales Hirsaugienses*, vol. I, p. 282), writing under the year 1087 about Theoger, formerly abbot of Saint George and later bishop of Metz: “He was devoted to letters and, under the instruction of a certain Manegold, head of the schools in the province of Alsace, a man not only most learned but also wholly upright in character—rightly called and truly a Christian philosopher—was excellently trained. In a short time he became learned in every kind of science.” This appears to have happened around 1060, judging from Theoger’s age. After his wife’s death he entered the clergy; thus the anonymous Mellicensis writes in *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, chapter 105: “Manegold the priest, master of the modern masters, was a vigorous defender of the truth, from which neither promises nor threats from the schismatic king Henry IV could bend him. Indeed, during the dispute that arose between Gregory VII and Henry IV, he labored to defend justice even to the point of imprisonment,” as Bernold reports under 1098. The following is found in the short twelfth-century Annals of Strasbourg (Grandidier, *Preuves du volume II de l’histoire d’Alsace*, title 433): “In the year of the Lord 1090 the church of Saint Augustine at Marbach was founded by the military and illustrious man Burchard of Gebelsweiler, whose most faithful helper and collaborator was Master Manegold of Lutenbach.” The same is read in a historical fragment in Urstisius, part II, p. 83. Thus, when Bernold refers this to 1094, he must be understood as speaking of the period when the monastery had been completed, canonical life was established there, and he himself joined its canons, soon becoming their first provost. He is already recorded in that capacity in Urban’s bull to them, issued at Tours on 24 March 1096 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, instruments, p. 474). At that time Manegold himself was with the pope at Tours, doubtless intending to seek confirmation of his monastery, and perhaps then was first appointed provost by him. This is gathered from a letter of Urban II to Gebehard, bishop of Constance, in 1096 (Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. VI, part I, p. 297), in which Urban states that, while at Tours, he attempted through Master Manegold, head of the schools, to settle a dispute that had arisen between the communities of Schaffhausen and Raitenbuch. He was therefore still head of the schools when he went to Tours, and was afterward named provost of Marbach by the pope. See *Gallia Christiana* (vol. V, p. 384), although that monastery should perhaps more properly be assigned to the diocese of Basel than to that of Strasbourg. Pez also preserves another letter of Urban II (same work, p. 298), in which, reproving the provost and M., dean at Raitenbuch, for disobedience and deceit, Urban commands under penalty of interdict that they satisfy the men of Schaffhausen. Mauriani (*Histoire littéraire de France*, vol. IX, p. 285) identify this Manegold—if the initial M. denotes him—as the dean of Raitenbuch, the same person as the provost of Marbach. Although there was at that time a certain Manegold who was dean at Raitenbuch and who composed a book against the slanderers of Gregory VII, as Gerhohus, formerly a canon of Raitenbuch and provost of Reichersberg, testifies (Pez, same work, part II, p. 491), it does not seem at all credible to us that he acted as provost of Marbach. For according to Berthold, the latter established the Marbach collegiate foundation in 1094; appointed provost at Tours in 1096, he returned home and devoted himself exclusively to reconciling the schismatics in Alsace. For this reason he was also held captive for a long time by King Henry, as is recorded there under 1098. How could one and the same Manegold have carried out monastic offices in such distant places—provost in Alsace and dean in Bavaria? Nor is it credible that a man so devoted to the pope that he even endured imprisonment from the schismatics would nevertheless have resisted his repeated commands until compelled by censures to carry them out; yet this is what the Raitenbuch dean did, as we have just seen from another letter of Urban II. Pez likewise distinguishes the two Manegolds (*Preface to vol. II of the Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 30) on the basis of Manegold’s book against Wolfhelm of Cologne, edited by Muratori (*Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 163). In chapter 24 he mentions Wirricus, master of Trier, who, in the person of the bishop of Verdun, composed a letter overflowing with insults against the holy Church, to which he intends to reply promptly. This Wirricus is none other than Wenericus, a cleric of Trier and later bishop of Vercelli, who, according to Trithemius (*Annales Hirsaugienses*, vol. I, p. 253), wrote under the name of Theodoric, bishop of Verdun, a volume to Gregory VII entitled *On the Discord between the Priesthood and the Empire*. It is preserved in Martène (*Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, p. 214); Mauriani also discuss him (*Histoire littéraire de France*, vol. VIII, pp. 252 ff.). Manegold’s promised reply against this Wenericus, which Pez and others had thought either never to have been written or at least to have been lost, was recently found in a manuscript of the library of the Serene Margrave of Baden at Karlsruhe. A copy reached the monastery of Polling, where it comprises seventy-eight chapters; Grandidier presents the titles together with part of the preface (same work, title 495). The author addressed the work to Gebehard—whether to the bishop of Constance or to the archbishop of Salzburg, who had already died in 1088 is uncertain—and there mentions his once-destroyed little monastery, whose former provost was Hartmann. I believe this can be none other than Lautenbach or Lutembach, built by Manegold in his native town in Upper Alsace perhaps around 1070, or at least endowed by him, and perhaps destroyed by the schismatics out of hatred for Manegold, later being converted into a collegiate foundation of secular canons, still distinguished today. At any rate, Manegold himself testifies that he met Wolfhelm in the gardens at Lutenbach, near the beginning of the work cited above against him. Uss. See Bernold below, at the end of the year. [Col. 1417C–1419D]].

He wished to be one of those clerics living together according to a common rule [Col. 1419A]. In the Black Forest, at the place called Saint Blaise, a monastery in honor of that same saint began to be built from its foundations on 11 September [Note: The passage from “In the Black Forest” through “sent” is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1419]]. For God so exalted that place and caused so many people to come there for conversion that they necessarily had to undertake more spacious buildings.

On the very day when this construction began, Lord Uto, the venerable abbot of that place, sent his prior, Lord Hartmann [Note: Concerning this new foundation and Hartmann its leader, see Gerbert, *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, vol. I, p. 253, and the *Life of Saint Altmann, Bishop of Passau and Founder of Göttweig*, in Pez, *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*, vol. I, p. 115. Uss. Hartmann, appointed prior of Saint Nicholas at Passau by Bishop Altmann, was driven out by the soldiers of Henry IV in 1076 and migrated to Saint Blaise. See Ussermann’s note 9 on this passage. [Col. 1420D]], into the Eastern kingdom [Note: Austria, *Osterriche*, *Oesterreich. [Col. 1420D]], that is, into the march bordering Hungary, with other brothers of his, to establish a new abbey in the bishopric of Passau, at the place called Göttweig.

There was at that place a community of clerics living according to a rule; they nevertheless obtained from the lord pope, and through the pope from their own bishop, permission to lay aside their clerical habit and become monks [Col. 1419B]. Therefore the lord abbot of Saint Blaise, at the command of the lord pope and at the request of the bishop, resolved to establish an abbey in that place and sent his brothers there to carry this out.

Heremannus, a young man of good character and advocate of the island monastery of Reichenau, was cruelly cut to pieces—alas!—by the servants of the church of Reichenau while he was going to the church to pray, on 25 September. He was honorably buried in the monastery of Saint George, which his father had built on his own allod [Col. 1420A].

The venerable priest Perhicherus, a most religious guardian of many holy women, departed to the Lord on 30 September and left great sorrow to both men and women [Note: The phrase abbreviated *m. m. r. t. v. q. f.* is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1419]] [Note: The text continues. [Col. 1419]].

Many other innumerable priests also died in the Teutonic regions, leaving their parishioners amid the great danger of the same mortality. For such a very great mortality was raging everywhere that in one village more than 1,050 people were counted as having died within six weeks. In another place, more than forty died in a single day in a single village [Note: The reading “somewhere” is in a partially erased passage; Uss. reads “elsewhere,” against the authority of the manuscripts. [Col. 1419]]. The cemeteries of the churches themselves became so filled with burials that people could no longer bury their dead there. Therefore, in many places, after digging a very large pit outside the cemetery, they threw all their dead into it [Col. 1420B].

This mortality afflicted not only the Teutonic regions but also France, Burgundy, and Italy everywhere. Yet to wise people it did not seem wholly detestable. For a very great multitude departed with repentance, confession, and an honorable end, which those confined by illness [Note: Witnesses 1 and 2 read *detentis*. [Col. 1419]] knew would come to them after a few days. Almost all the sick prepared themselves for the certainty of their death, something that at another time scarcely any holy people [Note: Uss. reads “scarcely any healthy people,” against the authority of the manuscripts; “some” is absent in three witnesses. [Col. 1419]] would have been able to do. The survivors also strove to abstain from worldly vanities—that is, from games, taverns, and other such excesses—and did not cease to hasten to confession and penance and to commend themselves to priests [Col. 1421A]. Thus a very great multitude died in that mortality with a sufficiently commendable end.

In the Gallic city commonly called Oston [Note: Autun. [Col. 1421D]], a general council was assembled by the venerable Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the Apostolic See [Note: Compare the letter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, concerning the convocation of that council, Mansi XX, 799. [Col. 1421D]], with archbishops, bishops, and abbots from various provinces, on 16 October. At that council the excommunication of King Henry, Wibert the invader of the Apostolic See, and all their accomplices was renewed. King Philip of the Franks was also excommunicated because, while his wife was still alive, he had taken another woman in marriage. The heresy of simony and the incontinence of priests were likewise condemned under excommunication. The monks were also forbidden by that council to usurp in parishes the offices belonging to parish priests [Col. 1421B]. All these things, I say, were established there and confirmed by apostolic legation.

Count Adelbert of Calw [Note: The manuscript has *caleuua* in two witnesses. [Col. 1421]], a young man of good character, died on 3 December [Note: The remainder of the year is absent in witness 2. [Col. 1421]].

In Alsace, Master Manegold of Liutenbach, by God’s mercy, wonderfully rekindled ecclesiastical religion, which had long been entirely extinguished in those regions. For, when the prolonged mortality grew severe among them [Note: *Immortalitate* corrected to *mortalitate*, “mortality.” [Col. 1421]], nearly all the leading men and knights of that province came to him in crowds. Having been absolved by him from excommunication through the authority granted to him by the lord pope, they also did not cease to be absolved by him from their other sins after receiving penance.

All these men thereafter resolved to obey Pope Urban faithfully. Consequently, they refused entirely to receive the services of simoniacal and incontinent priests. Lord Manegold was the principal cause of this obedience, and therefore he aroused great hatred against himself among the treacherous. He nevertheless considered this of little account, because he did not doubt that to be despised for God’s sake is also most glorious.

MXCV.

The lord Pope Urban, having long since departed from Rome, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously in Tuscany. In that province the Pisan bishop, named Dagobert, served him with the greatest zeal; the pope had long before raised him to the archiepiscopal pallium and authority, which until then the bishop of the Pisan see had not customarily possessed [Note: [Col. 1421] “have” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1421] “not” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1421] “been accustomed” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.]. King Heinricus, however, was at that time staying in Lombardy, deprived of nearly all royal dignity [Note: [Col. 1421] “King” is lacking, 2.]. For his son Chonradus, already crowned king some time before, completely separated himself from him and, firmly joined to the lady Mathildis [Note: [Col. 1421] “lady” is lacking, 2.], and to the other faithful of Saint Peter, held the entire strength of his father’s army in Lombardy.

Welfo, son of Welfo, duke of Bavaria, completely withdrew from marriage with the lady Mathildis, asserting that she had remained entirely free of him; she herself would most gladly have kept this silent forever, if he had not first published it quite thoughtlessly [Note: [Col. 1421] “Mathildis” written “mathidis,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1421] “too” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1421] “carelessly” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1421] “published” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.]. Therefore his father came into Lombardy in an exceedingly angry spirit and labored long and fruitlessly for this reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1421] “exceedingly” is lacking in a damaged place, 1.]. He also summoned Heinricus to his aid against the lady Mathildis, so that he might compel her to give her possessions to his son, although he had not yet known her in marital intercourse [Note: [Col. 1421] “known” written “onosceret,” 1.]; consequently, the effort continued for a long time without result.

With God and Saint Peter granting success, the lord pope had now prevailed almost everywhere. In the middle of Lombardy, in the city of Piacenza, among the schismatics themselves and against them, he announced a general synod [Note: [Col. 1421D] Mansi XX, 804] (1 March); by letters sent with canonical and apostolic authority he summoned to it the bishops of Italy, Burgundy, France, Alemannia, Bavaria, and the other provinces.

This synod was held at Piacenza around the middle of Lent. Such an innumerable multitude flowed together for the synod that it could in no way be contained in any church of that place. Therefore the lord pope was compelled to celebrate it outside the city, in a field; yet this too was not without the authority of a credible precedent. For Moses himself, the first legislator, established the people of God in the fields, instructing them in legal precepts at God’s command; and the Lord himself instructed his disciples in evangelical ordinances not in houses but on a mountain and in the fields [Note: [Col. 1422D] These examples are taken from the preface to the Acts.]. We also sometimes celebrate Mass outside a church quite reasonably, when necessity compels us, although we know that churches are specially assigned for such celebrations.

At this synod Queen Praxedis, long since separated from Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1421] “King Heinricus,” 2.], complained before the apostolic lord and the holy synod against her husband concerning unheard-of filthinesses of fornication [Note: [Col. 1421] “filthinesses,” written “spurciis,” 1.] that she had suffered at her husband’s hands. The lord pope, together with the holy synod, received her complaint with great mercy, because he knew with certainty that she had not so much committed such great filthinesses as endured them unwillingly. Therefore he mercifully released her from the penance to be imposed for such crimes [Col. 1422D]; she was not ashamed voluntarily and publicly to confess her sin.

King Philippus of the Franks sent his embassy to this synod and reported that he had begun the journey to it [Note: [Col. 1421] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] but had been hindered by lawful delays [Note: [Col. 1422D] That is, delay. Lex Salica, title 1.] [Col. 1423A] [Note: [Col. 1423D] See Ivo of Chartres, letter 46 to the pope, in Baronius under this year, manuscripts.]. Therefore, with the synod interceding, he obtained from the lord pope a postponement for himself until Pentecost.

The lord Hugo, archbishop of Lyon [Note: [Col. 1423] “Hugo,” written “ugo,” 1.], was also summoned to the same synod and was suspended from office because he had neither come himself nor sent a legate there in his place with a canonical excuse.

Likewise, the embassy of the emperor of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1423D] Emperor Alexius.] arrived at this synod. He humbly implored the lord pope and all the faithful of Christ to provide him with some aid for the defense of the holy Church against the pagans, who had by then nearly destroyed it in those regions and had occupied the land as far as the walls of the city of Constantinople. For this reason the lord pope stirred many people to provide assistance, so that they even promised on oath, if God permitted, to go there and to offer the emperor their most faithful aid against the pagans to the best of their ability.

Among other things, these provisions were made at that synod: that those who refused to abandon concubines, hatred from the heart [Note: [Col. 1423D] Mansi XX, 814.], or any mortal sin should in no way be admitted to penance. Likewise, no priest was to receive anyone for penance unless his own bishop had entrusted him with this responsibility. Likewise, we are not to deny the Eucharist to anyone who properly comes to confession, when we know that such persons remain among the excommunicated in body only, not in mind, and nevertheless do not share in their sacraments.

At this synod the heresy of the Simoniacs was utterly condemned: whatever had been acquired or promised with money, whether in sacred orders or in ecclesiastical matters, and therefore appeared to have been acquired by simony, was to be considered void, and judged to have had or to have no force [Col. 1423C] [Note: [Col. 1423D] “Whatever ... force” are words taken from chapter 2; what follows is from chapters 3 and 4.]. Nevertheless, mercy was granted in the preservation of their order to those who had been ordained by Simoniacs without simony and unknowingly; but those who had knowingly been ordained by such men were condemned irrecoverably together with their ordainers [Note: [Col. 1423D] In conformity with what Bernoldus wrote at his request to Gebehardus, bishop of Constance, who was going to this synod. See tract XIII, manuscripts.].

Likewise, the heresy of the Nicolaitans—that is, of incontinent subdeacons, deacons, and especially priests—was condemned irrevocably. Henceforth, those who were not afraid to remain in that heresy were not to take part in the ministry; nor was the people in any way to receive their services if the Nicolaitans presumed to minister contrary to these prohibitions.

Likewise, the Beringarian heresy, which had long before been anathematized very frequently, was condemned again, and the judgment of the Catholic faith against it was confirmed: namely, that bread and wine, when consecrated on the altar, are converted into the body and blood of the Lord not only figuratively but also truly and essentially.

Likewise, a sentence of anathema against Guibertus, the heresiarch and invader of the apostolic see, and against all his accomplices, was again promulgated by synodal judgment with burning candles.

It is reported that nearly four thousand clerics and more than thirty thousand laypeople were present at this synod.

At this synod it was decreed that nothing whatsoever should ever be demanded for chrism, baptism, or burial [Note: [Col. 1424D] Chapter 13.]. Likewise, that the fasts of the four seasons should be celebrated in this order: the first in the first week of Lent, the second in the week of Pentecost, and the third and fourth in September and December, as usual [Note: [Col. 1424D] Words of chapter 14.].

Most reverend bishops attended this synod: from Bavaria, Diemo, archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 1423] “salbburgensis,” corrected to “salcburgensis,” 1.], and Oudalricus, bishop of Passau [Col. 1424B], his suffragan; from Alemannia, Gebehardus, bishop of Constance. At that time they also consecrated Arnoldus, archbishop of Milan, who had long been elected [Note: [Col. 1424D] See at the end of the year 1093.] but had not yet been consecrated, with the permission of the lord pope, at Milan.

The lord pope himself also consecrated Oudalricus, abbot of Reichenau, at that time; he likewise attended the aforesaid synod. In the presence of the bishop of Constance, the pope forbade him to exercise all episcopal authority over the clergy and people of the island of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 1423] “over them” is lacking, 2.], an authority that he had formerly granted to the bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 1424D] See above under the year 1089.]. Nevertheless, not long afterward that abbot took it upon himself to exercise this authority. When the bishop consequently lodged a complaint, the lord pope again restrained him from such presumption by sending letters.

King Chonradus, son of Heinricus, went out to meet the lord pope as he came to Cremona and performed for him the office of strator on 10 April. Then he swore fidelity to him concerning his life, his limbs, and the Roman papacy [Note: [Col. 1423] “Again,” 1.]. The lord pope received him as a son of the holy Roman Church and firmly promised him in the presence of the people counsel and aid for obtaining the kingdom and acquiring the imperial crown, while preserving the justice of that Church and the apostolic statutes, especially those concerning investitures in spiritual offices, which are not to be usurped by a layman [Note: [Col. 1423] “in spiritual” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “offices” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “spalibus” for “spiritualibus,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “offices” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “by” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “a layman” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “not” added by the same hand, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1423] “to be usurped” added by the same hand, 1.].

Duke Welfo of Bavaria, together with his son Welfo, finally returned from Lombardy to Alemannia and labored in vain with the princes of the kingdom for the restoration of Heinricus to the kingdom, although Heinricus had not yet been absolved from the anathema [Note: [Col. 1423] “so,” 1.]. For even Heinricus’s supporters did not readily believe his persuasion; while the Catholics feared incurring excommunication and perjury if they received Heinricus, whom they had jointly renounced under excommunication.

King Chonradus went with royal pomp into Tuscany, to Pisa, and there accepted his bride, the daughter of Roger, duke of Sicily, who was still a very young girl, together with an unheard-of sum of money offered to him.

The lord pope, having arranged matters successfully in Lombardy, began to turn toward Gaul by sea and reached Saint Mary at Le Puy on her Assumption (15 August). He announced that a synod would be held at Clermont on the octave of Saint Martin, by apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 1425] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1425] The word is in a damaged place, 1.], and invited bishops of various provinces to it by letters of canonical summons.

Liutolfus, son of the most holy Pope Leo IX [Note: [Col. 1425D] Spiritual son: while Leo was still bishop of Toul, Liutolfus was educated under his care in the cloister of that Church. Concerning this celebrated abbey of Saint Leo, see Gallia Christiana, vol. XIII, p. 1104; among the instruments, col. 472, it also contains Liutolfus’s foundation charter, dated 10 October 1091. Manuscripts.], and dean of the holy Church of Toul, built near that city a monastery of clerics which they call Roman Canonical. In it he gathered clerics who professed to live according to the Rule of Saint Augustine; he also placed over them a provost of the same profession, whom the bishop of the place solemnly consecrated abbot of that congregation. For it is the custom in those regions for the provosts of such congregations to be called abbots and consecrated as abbots, with this one exception: they do not carry staffs.

The lord pope Urban also granted that place a privilege in which he firmly decreed that the clerics of that place should observe the Rule of Saint Augustine forever and henceforth always possess the freedom to elect an abbot. That monastery was specially built in honor of Pope Saint Leo, and its church was solemnly dedicated in honor of the same apostolic man.

This privilege was granted in Lombardy by the lord pope to the venerable Liutolfus in the year of the Lord’s [Note: [Col. 1425] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1425] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] 1095.

Liutolfus, the very wealthy margrave from the eastern kingdom, most faithful in Saint Peter’s cause against the schismatics [Note: [Col. 1425] The remainder of the phrase is lacking, 2.], ended his life. As much as the Catholics grieved at his death, so much did the adversaries of the holy Church rejoice [Note: [Col. 1425] From “at whose death” through “rejoiced” is lacking, 2.].

Heinricus, count palatine, also very wealthy, but not so obedient to the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1425] The remainder is lacking: “but not so obedient to the apostolic see,” 2.], set out upon the way of all the earth and left behind many riches to be uselessly seized by many [Note: [Col. 1425] The remainder is lacking: “and left many riches to be uselessly seized by many,” 2.].

In Gaul a general synod was convened by the lord pope at Clermont on the octave of Saint Martin (18 November) [Note: [Col. 1425D] See the Acts of this council, Mansi, vol. XX, p. 815. Manuscripts.]. Thirteen archbishops with their suffragans were present, and 205 pastoral staffs were counted. At this synod the lord pope confirmed the same statutes as at the preceding synod of Piacenza; moreover, he excommunicated King Philippus of the Franks because, having dismissed his own wife, he had taken the wife of one of his knights in marriage.

There he also announced that another synod was to be held at Tours in the third week of the following Lent.

## MXCVI

The lord pope celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously at Arles with bishops from various provinces [Note: [Col. 1426D] The Acts of the Council of Limoges testify that the pope celebrated the solemnities of Christ at Limoges. Mansi XX, 921.]. In those regions, a bishop of the schismatic party, the bishop of Würzburg [Note: [Col. 1426D] Einhardus.], came to the apostolic lord and obtained his mercy; yet in such a way that this same mercy was to be completed for him by the pope’s legates in the German lands.

In the third week of Lent (17 March), the lord pope held a synod [Note: [Col. 1426D] 21 March. Mansi, vol. XX, p. 927.] with bishops of various provinces [Col. 1426B] in the city of Tours. There he again strengthened the statutes of his earlier councils by the agreement of a general synod. Not long afterward he received the bishop of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1426D] Otto.] into communion, since he had repented of his excommunication, but on condition that he clear himself of the charges brought against him.

At this time a very great multitude from Italy and all Gaul and Germany began to go toward Jerusalem against the pagans, in order to liberate the Christians. The lord pope was the principal author of this expedition. At the preceding synods he had earnestly warned everyone about this expedition [Note: [Col. 1425] “preceding,” written “ptitis,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1425] “promoted,” 3.] and had very firmly commended it to them as something to be undertaken for the remission of sins.

He also caused all who had devoted themselves to this journey to mark themselves with the sign of the cross on their garments [Col. 1426C]; this sign even appeared marked upon the flesh of some. Therefore many believed that the journey had been begun by God’s ordinance and inspiration.

Nevertheless, an innumerable multitude of common people undertook the journey with excessive simplicity; they neither knew nor were able to prepare themselves in any way for such a danger. Consequently, a considerable part of them perished in Hungary, having rashly presumed to devastate the land of the Hungarians. The king of Hungary did not allow the remaining multitude that followed to enter that land; a considerable part of them also perished at the entrance to Hungary.

It was not surprising that they could not complete their intended journey to Jerusalem, since they had undertaken it without the humility and devotion that they ought to have shown. They also had many apostates in their company, who, having cast aside the religious habit, intended to fight alongside them. Nor were they afraid to bring innumerable women with them; these women wickedly changed their natural dress into men’s clothing, and the men fornicated with them. In this they grievously offended God, just as the Israelite people once did.

Therefore, after many labors, dangers, and deaths, when they were finally not permitted to enter Hungary, they began to turn back home in a wretched manner [Note: [Col. 1427] “at last” corrected to “home” by the same hand, 1; “at last,” 2.] with great sadness [Note: [Col. 1427] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1427] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1427] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1427] The word is in a damaged place, 1.].

King Philippus of the Franks, long since excommunicated for adultery, finally came to the lord pope while he was still in Gaul to make satisfaction, with considerable humility. Having renounced the adulterous woman, he was received back into favor, and showed himself very ready to serve the lord pope.

The lord pope, having arranged matters well in Gaul, after the reconciliation of the king of the Franks and after many councils, finally returned to Lombardy [Note: [Col. 1427] “Lombardy,” written “logobardiam,” 1.] with great triumph and glory, and solemnly celebrated the Exaltation of the Holy Cross at Mortara near Pavia [Note: [Col. 1427D] Mortara, west of Pavia. Manuscripts.]. He had many bishops and princes in his company.

Sigifredus, abbot of Schaffhausen, of pious memory, a man [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking: “a man of great prudence and admirable benevolence,” 2.] of great prudence and admirable benevolence, departed to the Lord on 28 October, leaving at his death great grief to all the faithful, both lay and spiritual [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking from “to all” through “November,” 2.]. The venerable Gerhardus succeeded him in office on 2 November [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking from “to all” through “November,” 2.].

Count Werinharius died on 11 November [Note: [Col. 1427D] Werner II, count of Habsburg, who summoned Liutfridus from Saint Blaise to the monastery at Muri. See Gerbert, History of the Black Forest, vol. I, p. 246.].

Luitfredus, abbot of Saint Martin’s monastery, of holy memory, who had been crucified to the world for nearly thirty years and lived for God alone, ended his life in a good old age, that is, full of days [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking from “already” through “full of days,” 2.], on 31 December [Col. 1427C].

In this year Jews were slaughtered in a great massacre in certain cities by those who were going to Jerusalem. I mean that at Speyer the Jews fled into the palace of the king and the bishop and could scarcely defend themselves even by resistance; Bishop John himself aided them. Later, angered on this account and hired with Jewish money, he caused certain Christians to be beheaded.

Likewise, at Worms the Jews, fleeing Christians who were pursuing them, hurried to the bishop. When he promised them safety only if they were baptized, they asked for a delay in order to confer. Entering the bishop’s chamber at that very hour, while our people waited outside to hear what answer they would give, persuaded by the devil and their own hardness, they killed themselves.

## MXCVII

The lord pope finally returned to the apostolic see with great glory and rejoicing and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously in Rome with his cardinals, since nearly the whole city of Rome had been subjected to him, except for the tower of Crescentius, in which the Wibertines were still hiding.

Azzo, margrave of Lombardy, father of Welfo, duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1427] The words “of Bavaria” are lacking, 2.], having already reached, as they say, more than a hundred years of age, set out upon the way of all the earth and left a great war among his sons over his possessions. For Duke Welfo wished to obtain all his father’s goods, since they had been given to his mother; but his brothers, born of another mother, refused to allow themselves to be completely disinherited. Therefore they barred his entry into Lombardy when he went to take possession.

The outstanding lady Mathildis, duchess and marchioness, a most devoted daughter of Saint Peter, acquired a great name for herself everywhere at that time [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking: “the distinguished and most devoted daughter of Saint Peter,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1427] The phrase is in a damaged place; it seems that “before that time” had previously been written, 1.] [Note: [Col. 1427] The phrase is in a damaged place; it seems that “before that time” had previously been written, 1.]. For almost alone, together with her followers, she had fought most prudently for seven years against Heinricus, the heresiarch Wibertus [Note: [Col. 1427] “Heinricus” is lacking, 2.], and their accomplices [Col. 1428B]; at last she drove Heinricus from Lombardy with great courage [Note: [Col. 1427] “Heinricus” is lacking, 2.]. Having recovered her possessions, she did not cease to give thanks to God and Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1427] “she” is written in a damaged place, 2.].

Heinricus came with a few men to Regensburg at Pentecost (24 May) and stayed there throughout the summer, living quite privately near the fortress of Nuremberg [Note: [Col. 1427] The word “fortress” is inserted, 1.]. At last he moved to Speyer, where he likewise intended to remain for a long time in considerable privacy [Note: [Col. 1427] “having stayed,” 2.].

Meanwhile Duke Welfo of Bavaria went to Lombardy to take possession of the inheritance of his father, the margrave Azzo, who had recently died. But the sons of that margrave by another wife [Note: [Col. 1427D] Garsende.] resisted the aforesaid duke with all their strength. Therefore the duke was compelled to summon the aid of Heinricus, duke of Carinthia, and of his brother, the patriarch of Aquileia. He attacked his brothers with armed force and thus claimed for himself a large part of his father’s inheritance from their hands [Note: [Col. 1427] “continues,” 1.] [Note: [Col. 1427D] See Origins of the Guelfs, vol. II, pp. 280 and 298.].

Count Oudalricus [Note: [Col. 1428D] This count of Bregenz and Chur was already discussed above under the year 1093. He founded the greater Reichenau, where he and his wife Bertha, daughter of the anti-emperor Rudolf, also obtained their burial place. See Gerbert on Rudolf the anti-emperor. The Petershausen Chronicle relates the circumstances of his death. Manuscripts.], most illustrious [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking from “most illustrious” through “confession,” 2.], a most ardent champion of Saint Peter’s cause against the schismatics, alas, ended his life by a sufficiently premature death, but with a good confession [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking from “most illustrious” through “confession,” 2.]. He was honorably buried at Bregenz, where he had established the monastic life, on 27 October [Note: [Col. 1427] The remainder is lacking: “27 October,” 2.] [Note: [Col. 1427] “continues,” 1.].

## MXCVIII

The lord pope celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Rome and established the greatest peace most firmly in the city itself and its territories. There too he celebrated the Paschal solemnity (28 March) with great glory.

But his rival Guibertus, who was at that time staying in the region of Ravenna, lost a certain fortification in which he had placed his greatest hope: a castle named Argenta [Note: [Col. 1429D] Argenta, a village on the Po di Primaro, north of Imola and Faenza.], which overlooks the Po and can harass all who travel along it.

The venerable Gerhardus, abbot of Schaffhausen [Note: [Col. 1429] “Gerhardus ... grieved” is lacking here; in its place, at the end of the year, “Gerhardus ... obtained” and “Manegoldus ... detained” are added, 2.], resigned his position out of humility, with the consent of the lord pope, and obtained from him permission for another to be placed as abbot over that house [Note: [Col. 1429] “He, who succeeded Sigifredus,” 2.]. But a great calamity immediately followed upon that place being deprived of its shepherd, so that many of the brothers abandoned it and laymen sacrilegiously claimed its possessions for themselves. Consequently, an abbot could not be appointed there for a long time, contrary to what the lord pope had arranged.

The advocate of that place, Count Adelbertus, also fortified a certain stronghold nearby and sacrilegiously claimed the abbey’s possessions for himself. Therefore the monks proceeded supplicantly to that fortification with crosses, relics, and litanies [Col. 1429B]. But the count’s soldiers partly killed them and partly wounded them; all were badly treated and forced to return or be carried home, while the crosses and relics were broken into pieces and, alas, miserably scattered across the field. For this reason that count was greatly detested by both clergy and laity.

Yet many also judged that the monks had deserved this by God’s judgment, because they had not treated their abbot well and had not merely left him without proper reason but had driven him away.

Manegoldus [Note: [Col. 1429] Manegoldus, canon of Marchbach, captured by King Heinricus and detained by him in captivity for a long time, 2.], the venerable provost of the canons living at Marchbach, was long detained in captivity by King Heinricus [Note: [Col. 1429] The words from “was ... detained” through “grieved” are lacking, 2.], because he refused to obey the schismatics contrary to ecclesiastical authority. Therefore the whole Church far and wide grieved for him [Col. 1429C] [Note: [Col. 1429] Manegoldus, canon of Marchbach, captured by King Heinricus and detained by him in captivity for a long time, 2.].

Gotefretus, duke and nephew of the great Duke Gotefredus; Roubertus, son of Count Baldowinus; Behemundus [Note: [Col. 1429] “Boimundus,” 2.], son of Roubertus, duke of Calabria and Sicily; Count Rimundus of Saint-Gilles; Otto, bishop of Strasbourg; and Count Hartmannus of Alemannia [Note: [Col. 1429D] Count of Kirchberg, founder of Wiblingen monastery in Swabia. See History of the Black Forest, vol. I, pp. 251 ff. Manuscripts.]—all these, I say, and many others began some time before to go toward Jerusalem with an innumerable multitude. After the city of Nicaea, Antioch, and other cities had been wrested from pagan power, and especially after the patriarch of Jerusalem had been restored to his own place, they reached a point near Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1429] The word is in a damaged place, 1.] through many battles and victories.

Therefore the lord pope sent his embassy to that multitude, namely the venerable Theobertus, archbishop of the Church of Pisa [Col. 1429D] [Note: [Col. 1430D] Above, in column 1421, he is called Dagobertus.], so that he might assist them in all things in the apostolic capacity and restore the churches in the places from which the pagans had been expelled [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.].

But the king of Constantinople impeded this arrangement; he withdrew himself in every way from aiding our people. He did not hesitate to devastate by fire or return to the pagans the cities that our men had wrested from their hands [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.], and through his authority he completely prohibited all pilgrims from making the journey to Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1429] The remainder is lacking, 2.].

In this year a miraculous sign occurred in the sky on 27 September: for nearly the entire night a large part of the sky appeared blood-red. That redness did not remain in one place only but spread through every part of the sky except the south, and many rays resembling rays of the sun seemed to proceed from that redness.

## MXCIX

The lord pope celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Rome with great peace. He retained the castle of Sant’Angelo and other fortifications under his authority, and, with God’s help, either pacified or subdued by force all his rivals in the city with considerable courage [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.]. He also announced everywhere by letters that his synod was to be held in Rome after Easter, in the third week [Note: [Col. 1429] The remainder of “week” is cut away, 2.].

Rapoto, count palatine of Bavaria, the most stubborn supporter—indeed, the head—of those who had until then opposed the apostolic see and Catholic unity, ended his life.

Likewise Chonradus of Utrecht, not a bishop but a schismatic, died disgracefully, killed by a certain man whom he had ordered to plunder [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.].

In Rome the lord pope assembled a general synod of 150 bishops and abbots [Col. 1430C], together with an innumerable number of clerics, in the third week after Easter (30 April) [Note: [Col. 1430D] Mansi, vol. XX, 961, 30 April.]. At this synod, after confirming the statutes of his predecessors, he also repeated the sentence of anathema against Guibertus the heresiarch and all his accomplices.

He also decreed there that those who had concubines should not presume to receive communion unless they first dismissed them altogether.

Concerning the journey to Jerusalem, he earnestly urged them to go and come to the aid of their suffering brothers [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.].

In Alemannia, after many dangers, an abbot was finally appointed in the monastery of Schaffhausen, named Adelbertus. He had been slandered as though he had expelled the previous abbot; therefore he cleared himself so fully before the judgment of the Church that, when the bishop questioned him under obedience concerning what he owed to the Rule, he declared himself innocent of that crime.

He was ordained by the venerable Gebehardus, bishop of Constance and legate of the apostolic see, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist [Note: [Col. 1429] “continues,” 1.].

Count Liutoldus, of good memory [Col. 1431A], long afflicted in his feet but an indefatigable champion of Saint Peter’s cause against the wickedness of the schismatics, was finally transferred from secular dignity to monastic religion [Note: [Col. 1431] “monachiam,” 1.] and happily departed to the Lord on 18 August. He was honorably buried in the monastery [Note: [Col. 1431C] Zwiefalten.] that he founded on his own hereditary land from his own possessions and in which he himself became a monk.

In Rome the venerable Pope Urban II, after governing the Roman see for eleven years and five months, finally departed from this light on 29 July, after many tribulations. After his death, the lord Paschalis, also called Reginherius, was ordained the 163rd pope; everywhere it was proclaimed that this had occurred through divine revelation. He was solemnly ordained by clergy and people on the sixteenth day after the departure of his predecessor [Col. 1431B].

Count Adelbertus, of pious memory, long devoted in the faith of Saint Peter against the schismatics and finally made a monk after being a count, happily ended his life on 22 September. He was honorably buried in the monastery that he built from his own possessions and in which he assumed the monastic habit, namely at Hirsau, under the presidency of the lord abbot Gebehardus [Note: [Col. 1431] Everything from “In Rome” through “Abbot Gebehardus” has been written over in fresh ink, 1.].

## MC

Pope Paschalis celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in Rome in great peace. By his letters he entrusted the venerable Gebehardus, bishop of Constance, with the apostolic legation in the German lands [Col. 1432A], which Gebehardus had already held for many years under his predecessor.

In Alemannia the venerable abbot Manegoldus, from the monastery of Saint George [Note: [Col. 1431C] At the monastery of Isny; compare the Isny Chronicle in Hess, *Prodr. Monum. Guelph.*, p. 275. Manuscripts.], was, alas, miserably killed in that place by one of his monks—a deed bringing perpetual salvation to the abbot but most certain damnation to the monk. He was killed on 15 February, which that year was the beginning of the fast [Note: [Col. 1431] “The fast began,” 3.]. Nevertheless, he survived until Saturday, embracing his martyrdom with great devotion; for he ended his life on 18 February.

The sentence of excommunication had now begun to grow lukewarm almost everywhere, so that even certain religious men, who until then had been most fervent in that cause, withdrew from the Catholics and were not afraid to be promoted among the excommunicated.

Yet the holy Church remained none the less steadfast in obedience to the apostolic see concerning the excommunicated. It knew that after Judas’s apostasy the remaining apostles had stood even more firmly with the Lord [Col. 1432B].

The venerable abbot Gerhardus, who had formerly resigned the abbacy of Schaffhausen for God and with the authority of Pope Urban, went to Jerusalem with the Christian army. After many labors they captured the city and entrusted the keeping of the Lord’s Sepulchre to the aforesaid abbot [Note: [Col. 1431] The words from “who ... undertook” are in a damaged place, 1.].

Otto, the schismatic bishop of Strasbourg, returned from the journey to Jerusalem, but was thought not to have been reformed from the schism; he ended his life [Note: [Col. 1431C] Others write that he died repentant on 3 August. He was the brother of Frederick, duke of Alemannia of the Hohenstaufen family. Bernoldus ended his writing here in the month of August; according to our calendars, he lived only a short time thereafter, dying on 16 September. Manuscripts.].

## [WORKS OF SIGEFRIDUS OF MAINZ

(We reproduce what follows from the collection of Tengnagel, in Gretzer, *Works*, vol. VI.)]

[Col. 1431]

### THE SYNOD OF MAINZ IN THE CASE OF CAROLUS, SIMONIAC BISHOP OF CONSTANCE, UNDER SIGEFRIDUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

Together with six letters of that same Sigefridus, four of them to Alexander II, supreme pontiff, and two to Gregory VII. Also added are letters of the clergy and people of Mainz to Sigefridus, by which they recall him from Cluny to his own see. All these materials are now published for the first time from ancient parchments.

### TO THE READER
## On Sigefrid—or Sigifrid or Sifrid—and His Deeds

Read Serarius, *Moguntiacarum rerum*, book V, concerning Sigefrid, or Sigifrid, or Sifrid, and his deeds. Concerning the synod that we publish, Bertold—or Bernald—in his *Chronicle* under the year 1071 [Col. 1433] writes as follows:

“Charles, who acquired the bishopric of Constance by simony, and who, like a sacrilegious thief, scattered the treasures of that Church for his own uses, was deposed at a council held at Mainz by order of Pope Alexander. The aforesaid disciple of Simon had not yet been consecrated, since, when accused there by the clergy of Constance, he could not deny the charges brought against him. Otto succeeded him in the episcopate.”

Marianus and Lambert also speak of this same synod.

At that time Hildebrand was living at the Roman court and in the Roman Church as archdeacon and archchancellor; he was later called Gregory VII in the papacy. He was an exceedingly fierce enemy and persecutor of schismatics and incontinent clerics. At his prompting Pope Alexander—although he himself was already sufficiently inflamed of his own accord against sacrilegious and disgraceful men—undertook many measures and tried to tear out by the roots the fibers of this long-established evil. He too was harassed by schismatics, who set up Cadalus as antipope, just as Gregory VII was later troubled by the Guibertine faction.

## The Mainz Synod in the Case of Charles, Bishop of Constance

[Col. 1433A] While the King of kings, our Lord Jesus Christ, eternally reigns over all things, and beneath him the most serene King Henry, fourth of that name, ruled temporally; while the venerable Sigefrid, primate of the Church of Mainz and legate of the Apostolic See, guided the chariot of God in the twelfth year then current—that is, in the year 1071 of the Incarnation of the Word and the eighth indiction of the Roman census—a holy synod was celebrated at Mainz, the metropolis of Eastern Francia and the principal seat of the episcopate of all Germany and Cisalpine Gaul.

The same memorable Sigefrid presided, with the venerable archbishops Gebhard of Salzburg and Uto of Trier sitting and cooperating with him; and with the reverend bishops Adelbero of Würzburg, Gundechar of Eichstätt, Embricho of Augsburg, Hermann of Bamberg, Werenher of Strasbourg, Henry of Speyer, Benno of Osnabrück, Ermenfrid of Sion, and Heribert of Modena sitting and laboring alongside them. Most holy abbots also sat and assisted, together with very many men of the lower orders, possessing great authority and wisdom.

There were also present envoys of the remaining brethren, namely, men bearing letters and instructions from the suffragans of that metropolitan bishop. These letters excused the suffragans for being unable to attend the council because certain definite impediments prevented them: some were hindered by the distress of bodily illness, others by the power of royal command, which detained them in various affairs of the kingdom. Since they were canonically excused, the envoys themselves, each in his proper place and order, fulfilled the office of his own bishop.

This holy synod was summoned and held partly because of many matters belonging to pastoral care and many cases in which the discipline of ecclesiastical correction was justly required, but chiefly on account of a certain Charles, who had been designated bishop of the Church of Constance, though, as the outcome of the matter later showed, he had not been canonically elected or advanced.

[Note: [Col. 1433D] Bertold, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1069: “Romald, bishop of Constance, died; Charles succeeded him in the episcopate through the heresy of simony.”]

As is customary, Charles had received from the king the investiture of the episcopal ring and pastoral staff, had been received into the episcopal seat, and, at the command of the royal authority, requested the primate of Mainz to consecrate him bishop of the Church of Constance. But the venerable Sigefrid, with the dove’s eye of serpent-like prudence guarding against every impiety, said that this sacrament of apostolic blessing ought not, and canonically could not, be celebrated upon him without examination. He had learned from the reports of serious and trustworthy persons—and indeed public rumor had spread everywhere—that Charles did not wish to enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep (John 10), but was striving to climb up by another way, by the furtive ladder of simoniacal impiety. Sigefrid also declared that he did not wish to become the doorkeeper of such an entrance, which Christ himself, who is the door, appeared to oppose.

He said that he wished to crush that very ladder of impiety upon the stone of stumbling and rock of offense (1 Peter 2), and to drive Charles far, far away from the mercenary occupation of the Lord’s flock.

Charles, on the other hand, tried by many arguments to assert that he was free from this crime and from heretical impiety. He declared that, if time and opportunity were granted him, he wished to remove this stain of infamy from himself. Accordingly, he requested a hearing before the synodal council, where he might prove his innocence in this matter, and where the consecration he sought might either be canonically granted or canonically denied him.

In the meantime frequent embassies were sent from the palace to the venerable metropolitan: prayers were mingled with threats and imperious commands concerning this consecration. Letters were also sent by the prelate of the Apostolic See, ordering that Charles should in no way be consecrated without the scrutiny of canonical purgation.
