What the king commanded by his power, the Roman pontiff prohibited by his authority.

The canons of the Church of Constance also arrived as an embassy from the entire clergy and people. [Col. 1434C] They unanimously asserted that Charles ought under no circumstances to be consecrated. Ever since they had elected and received him unwillingly and under condition, he had shown them no care of pastoral office; rather, he had never ceased to impose the pressure of tyrannical domination upon them. He had not restrained his hand from sacred things, nor spared the treasures of the Church from plunder. Whatever he could scrape together by rapacious violence, he had distributed entirely to the ministers—indeed, to the magicians—of that Simon, that is, to his own supporters. Thus those whose efforts had secured for him an adulterous election might, through their venal commerce, obtain for him a mercenary curse in place of consecration and a malediction in place of blessing.

But the metropolitan prelate, amid the shifting variety of these embassies, as though amid harsh storms and whirlwinds, remained fixed immovably within himself with praiseworthy constancy. [Col. 1434D–1435A] Nowhere was he bent from the state of canonical rectitude by favor or affection, by terror or bribery.

Many messengers were therefore sent back and forth, and many days were assigned to this hearing. Yet the examinations of the case, which the prince’s command had occupied and prevented from being completed, were still not fulfilled. Meanwhile the Church of Constance, deprived of its shepherd, had now been without priestly blessing for almost two years. At last, by divine mercy, authority outweighed power, and the divine will breathed upon Christ’s priests.

Therefore, with their common consent, a definite and lawful day for the synodal council was announced, and the brother bishops were invited to the council. Some attended without delay, as was proper; others, who could not attend for a definite reason, were canonically excused and supplied an equivalent presence through a delegated embassy.

On the first day of the council, which the Dormition of Saint Mary made especially solemn, the senators of the spiritual court assembled together, with the Holy Spirit as their patron, within the royal church of the Greater Church, before the chancel of the altar of the protomartyr Stephen, which had been constructed in the eastern apse.

First, as was fitting, they offered due thanksgiving to the holy and undivided Trinity and presented humble prayers to God for the undisturbed condition of the whole Church. Then, after the solemn greeting of the brethren and the proper recognition of their seats, following the authentic synod of the tradition of the fathers, they conferred with one another concerning the truth of the Catholic faith, condemning Simon and all heresiarchs together with their doctrines and followers. For the time being they discussed briefly the nature of the matter at hand. Finally, in order to celebrate the offices of so great a solemnity, they dissolved the council, intending to return early the following day to the same place.

On the next day, at the appointed hour of the council, when the apostolic priests had again assembled, and after the praises and prayers offered to God and their salutary seating according to rank, they brought forward for rational discipline whatever had come into doubt for any priest in his own diocese.

[Note: [Col. 1435D] See the corrupt passage.]

As the circumstances required, each matter was either discussed or settled by synodal judgment.

The matter that was chiefly at issue—the case of the designated bishop of Constance—was carefully debated among the brethren. But, because of an intervention by the prince’s command, it was postponed until the following day. Intermediaries worked to bend the priests from the firmness of their resolve toward the royal will; others pressed for the designated man voluntarily to relinquish the honor he had wrongly usurped.

On the third day, Christ’s priests, suspended in expectation by the long delay of this matter and inflamed by a certain free indignation—or rather by zeal for justice—approached their prince with priestly constancy. They admonished him concerning the salvation of his soul, the peace of the Churches, and the spiritual condition of the kingdom. They presented him with suitable examples of salutary teaching from the Scriptures and the deeds of the Old and New Testaments, by which his mind, still waxlike and untaught, might be formed for similar things. They said and taught that the throne of his kingdom could in no way be established unless it were strengthened by justice and observance of God’s commandments.

But that supreme Lord of lords, who rules over every power, so tempered the prince’s mind and so softened him toward the words of holy exhortation that he was moved by no youthful harshness and—something difficult for those in power—did not injure the priests with any insolent response.

He did, however, make many excuses. He said that, in this exercise of his power, he had practiced no venality and had made no agreement concerning this matter with Charles himself. If he had made some agreement with his household members or close associates, without his own knowledge, in exchange for the help of their intercession, it was not his place either to accuse or to excuse them. They themselves must see to that.

As for his right hand, which he had extended to Charles as a gift of his favor because of their former goodwill when Charles held the provostship, he said that he cast away every stain of avarice. If Charles had corrupted what he himself had done simply by means of someone’s poison and malice, he did not wish on that account to oppose divine justice.

After this salutary conversation with the priests, the prince came with them to the council. The designated bishop of Constance was admitted to hear the proceedings. Clerics of Constance were also present outside the doors, asking through envoys that they too might be granted admission.

Then one would have seen the most joyful celebrations of holy Church and the true lights of the world gathered together, when a noble crown of the sacred orders shone around them, jeweled with the living stones of Christ’s priests, like the gleams of glittering stars. Then the heavens declared the glory of God, and day poured forth speech to day (Psalm 18), when priest explained a judgment of justice to priest and their salutary teaching instructed holy Church.

Then the vessels of election overflowed with the fragrant liquor of the Holy Spirit, and the righteous shone like the brightness of the firmament (Daniel 12), when the priests of the Lord rained down words of wisdom like clouds and poured them into the hearts of their hearers like fruitful soil, so that they might bring forth growth.

When these matters had thus been arranged and distinguished by the ordering finger of God, both parties were admitted: namely, the aforesaid Charles and those who brought accusations against him.

In the first proceeding, the regular prelate of the Church of Constance produced a written accusation. It contained the grounds on which Charles was to be considered unworthy and judged unfit for the sacrament of apostolic blessing. The first and greatest charge was that, following the example of his pestilential master Simon, he had invaded the episcopal seat by means of money. All the other matters read there proclaimed the violent devastation of that same Church.

The prelate himself and the brethren who were present likewise offered written statements of their testimony. In these, each identifying his name and office, they asserted that they would canonically prove whatever they had brought forward in accusation or testimony.

Charles, on the other hand, attempted to discredit the persons, saying that they were covered with the stain of his infamy and could canonically accuse neither him nor anyone else. He added that he would purge himself of all the charges by synodal judgment and was innocent of everything with which they attacked him.

A long dispute therefore took place on both sides, and, while many throughout the day struggled against one another, the council continued until deep into the night. There was uncertainty concerning the number of accusers and witnesses, and after long deliberation they sought to determine whether Charles should be permitted to defend himself against their accusation. While the matter was debated among the brethren for a very long time, the council, still without a decision because of the untimely hour, was dissolved [the printed reading *pretio* is uncertain].

What Charles himself did that night, and with what blows of remorse he scourged his guilty conscience, the following day certainly revealed. For, as the outcome of the matter itself can prove, we truly believe that God, the judge and witness of conscience, sat as judge in his heart and exercised the scrutiny of his judgment with him. There the consciousness of sin, through the testimony of accusing thoughts rather than excusing ones, was condemned and constrained, lest he resist truth and equity.

On the following day, when we expected him, according to his promise, to purge himself of the charges and to prove himself worthy of consecration by demonstrating his innocence, he was already confused in mind. He could no longer endure the sight of the council, and, judged within himself, could not bear outside himself the weight of the judgment hanging over him. He himself therefore pronounced sentence against himself. Resigning the ring and pastoral staff to the man from whom he had unjustly received them, he released the priests from the toil of a longer inquiry and from the hope and fear they had borne on his behalf. He concealed his guilt beneath a single cloak of excuse: that, according to the decretals of Pope Celestine, he did not wish a bishop to be given to unwilling people.

When the most holy priests saw the great things the Lord had done, and recalled with faithful wonder how incomprehensible are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways (Romans 11), they blessed God Most High with heart and mouth and every form of devotion. They prayed and entreated that he remove from his kingdom every apostasy and every scandal and no longer allow Satan and his apostles to reign in his holy Church. They also prayed that God would deign to console his servants in all their counsels and works and mercifully fulfill what he had promised: that he would be present with his Church all the days, until the consummation of the age (Matthew 28).

By common decree they ordered that the acts of this synod be inserted into the ecclesiastical records and preserved in the archives of the holy Church of Mainz, for perpetual remembrance and instruction of future generations. Thus, instructed by the example of their elders, their juniors would not fear to resist if they found themselves oppressed in a similar matter, knowing with complete certainty that the grace of the Holy Spirit would in no way be lacking to the faithful if, in holiness and justice, they resisted injustice unto the crown of perseverance.

They further decreed, in accordance with the ancient tradition of the Fathers and the authentic rectitude of the early councils, that all these matters be reported in sequence to the Roman pontiff in a written letter. Thus, what had been begun and completed by his command and encouragement might be confirmed and strengthened by his apostolic authority; and to almighty God, the author of every good thing, due thanksgivings might be rendered with faithful devotion at Rome and Mainz, and wherever on earth these things should be read or heard.

These proceedings took place at Mainz, the metropolis of Eastern Francia, in the year 1071 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth indiction, on 18 September, while the most serene King Henry IV of that name was reigning, in the thirteenth year of his reign and the seventeenth year of his ordination at Mainz; while the most reverend primate Sifrid was presiding, in the twelfth year of his ordination; and, above all, while our Lord Jesus Christ was reigning, to whom tomorrow does not approach as future, nor yesterday depart as past, but with whom today remains eternal, for ever and ever. Amen.

## Letters of Sigefrid, Bishop of Mainz, to Alexander II and Gregory VII, Supreme Pontiffs

(See *Patrologia*, volume 146, under Alexander I, and above, column 735 of this volume.)

## Letter of the Clergy and People of Mainz to Sigefrid, Archbishop

[Col. 1437C] To their father and shepherd, as venerable as he is desired, Sifrid, archbishop, his pasture’s sheep—that is, all the clergy and people of the see of Mainz, old and young, rich and poor—offer, with unanimous devotion, diligent prayers, and prayers more fervent than usual because accompanied by tears.

We beseech you, venerable Father, and adjure you by him by whose precious blood we have been redeemed, by the pastoral care through which we have been entrusted to you [Note: [Col. 1439D] In 1072 Sigefrid had withdrawn to the monastery of Cluny, intending to spend the rest of his life there. But, recalled by the clergy and people of Mainz, he recovered his see. On this, see Lambert and Marianus in their *Chronicles*.], by the dread judgment of the heavenly King, and by that terrible tribunal before which you must stand on the day of judgment and render an account of us to the Prince of Shepherds: remember the day on which, anointed with the oil of divine consecration, you undertook the care of our souls, and, promoted to apostolic blessing, became in Christ’s place the shepherd of the sheep.

On that day the ring of the Church’s betrothal and the staff of pastoral care were given to you; you also received the keys of the kingdom of heaven and a judicial seat in the choir of the apostles. Remember, I beg you, that most sweet word spoken to you on that same day, so that you might always remember God and that day.

O father, why do you abandon us? To whom do you leave us desolate? Did you not receive the ring so that you might love your Church like a bride? Did you not receive the staff so that you might defend her from the attacks of wolves? Where is that love by which Christ laid down his life for his sheep and by which he entrusted them to you to govern?

Why do you cast the keys of the kingdom of heaven from your hands? Why do you thrust yourself down from your seat, indeed from the choir of the apostles? We would certainly wish your fatherhood to ascend to whatever higher things there might be, rather than thrust yourself down from the heights to lower things.

We confess, Father, that those who leave the world do well—those who deny themselves, carry their cross, and follow Christ; those who have received no responsibility for cultivating the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts; those who are content if they can save only themselves, since they must render an account to no one except themselves.

But you, Father, rule the world better than you abandon it. You follow and love Christ more devotedly if you feed his sheep, because he established the proof of his love in feeding his sheep, saying: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21).

Therefore, if we may say so without diminishing your reverence, you are convicted of loving Christ less to the extent that you withdraw yourself from the shepherding of his sheep entrusted to you. Will the one who returns alone and empty from the harvest to the threshing floor be more pleasing to him, or the one who brings many sheaves of souls and wheat cleansed of tares to the granary of his Lord?

Why do you not remember that evangelical steward who, when he faithfully and wisely distributed the measure of wheat to his lord’s household and brought back the profitable increase of the talent entrusted to him, was set over much because he had been faithful in little, and, hearing the blessed “Well done,” was commanded to enter into the joy of his Lord (Luke 12)?

Did Peter and Paul and the other apostles, whose office you exercise, follow the Lord while carrying their cross in such a way that, by leaving the world, they also abandoned the care of souls? Did Peter not undergo the cross for the winning of souls, following the example of his Master? Did Paul not offer his neck to the sword?

Was not Christ himself, our life and salvation, coeternal and co-omnipotent in the bosom of his Father, made mortal man through love for the salvation of humanity in the bosom of the Virgin Mother? Every order, every dignity, every apostolic profession is subject to episcopal dignity. Nothing in the world is more eminent or nearer to God than the episcopal life, to which every monk yields—whether lesser brother or recluse, cenobite or hermit.

O most holy Father, we beg you by God and by the salvation of your soul to remember what we have said and to keep the tribunal of Christ watchfully before your eyes. Do not abandon us, his sheep, whom you undertook to guard, so that you may receive from him not the punishment of negligence but the reward of obedience.

Hasten to return to your seat as quickly as possible and console with fatherly affection those who are in mourning and grief. For already the possessions of your bishopric are being plundered here and there, and many other things are being seized by the king’s officials. Great disturbance is taking place throughout your various territories, and there is contention among many concerning the seizure of your see. Father, your single presence will calm all these things. Your presence alone will restore all these disturbances and contentions to peace.

Finally, even if the statutes of the Church and the laws of the canons permitted you to abandon your see and adopt a life of another profession, you could never serve God better than by putting aside that intention and defending your see and episcopate against those who wish to seize them.

Now, therefore, we sons beg you, our father, and we sheep of your flock beg you, our shepherd: return to us as quickly as possible and wipe away the sorrow and grief of our hearts with the serenity of your countenance.

Otherwise, first we shall invoke God, the Father of all; we shall bow before Christ, the Prince of Shepherds; we shall approach the Apostolic See against you; we shall call every order and dignity to our aid; and we shall leave no one throughout the entire kingdom whom we do not ask. While you live, we shall never accept a mercenary in place of a shepherd.

## Two Letters of Stephen, Bishop of Halberstadt, and Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, against the Schismatics, under the Roman Pontiffs Gregory VII and Urban II

## To the Reader

These are indeed two letters: one, written under the name of Louis, count of Thuringia, by Stephen, bishop of Halberstadt, and addressed to Walram, bishop of Naumburg or Numburg; the other, by Blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, addressed to William, abbot of Hirsau.

They were previously published in print, but since Dodechin, the continuator of Marianus Scotus, in whose work Stephen’s letter is found, is not readily available everywhere, and since the works of Saint Anselm are not in everyone’s hands, it seemed appropriate to publish them here separately, together with other monuments of the same class and character.

Would that Stephen’s letter might someday be brought to light in its entirety, for Dodechin did not insert it whole into his *Chronicle*! It is certainly most worthy of being read attentively by lovers of Catholic unity and concord and of being set before and opposed to the schismatics and heretics even of our own age as an unconquerable shield. Walram’s letter also appears to be mutilated at the end.

This Louis was the second of that name, count of Thuringia, surnamed the Leaper because he escaped from prison by leaping into a flowing river. He died in the year 1123 at the age of seventy-three and was buried in the monastery of Reinhardsbrunn, which he had built, together with many other towns and castles, in Thuringia. See the *History of the Landgraves of Thuringia*, chapter 13, volume I of the *Illustrious Writers of Germany* published by D. Pistorius.

Concerning Stephen of Halberstadt, the epitome of Gesner’s *Library* says:

“Stephen, also called Herrand, bishop of the Church of Halberstadt, wrote, in the person of Count Louis, a letter to Waltram, bishop of the Church of Naumburg, defending Henry, a rebel against the Roman Church; a defense of the pope, book I; and several letters to various persons, book I; together with some other works. Would that they still existed!”

The letter of Saint Anselm deals for the most part with the topics treated in Bernald’s little book, which you have above.

## Dodechin the Abbot in His Additions to the Chronicle of Marianus Scotus

[Col. 1441A] In the year 1090 Waltram, bishop of the Church of Magdeburg [read: Naumburg or Numburg], being especially favorable to King Henry, sent a letter to Count Louis, urging him to protect the king’s cause by submitting himself to that often-mentioned king. In this letter, while laboring as though in defense of God’s ordinance but in reality favoring the king, he had spoken disparagingly against Pope Gregory of blessed memory, King Rudolph of pious memory, and other princes who had already fallen asleep in the sleep of peace. He said that they had perished as though they had never existed, and asserted that those whose end had been most evil must have had an evil beginning. The form of his letter is as follows.

## Letter of Waltram or Walram

[Col. 1441B] Waltram, by the grace of God whatever he is, to Louis, most serene prince: with the earnestness of prayers, offering himself most devoted to every duty.

Concord is useful to every kingdom; justice is desirable. For this virtue is the mother of uprightness and the preservation of all honor. But whoever, by fomenting internal dissension, incites others to the shedding of human blood is surely a man of blood and a participant with him who, thirsting for our blood, is always prowling about, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5).

You, therefore, most glorious prince, considering that God is the God of peace and not of dissension (1 Corinthians 14), should, so far as depends on you, have peace with all (Romans 12). God is love (1 John 4); the devil is hatred. The whole law and the prophets depend upon love (Matthew 22). Whoever hates his brother is a murderer and has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God (1 John 3).

This is proclaimed by Truth itself; this is proclaimed by that disciple of Truth who, having drunk more deeply of the truth from the Lord’s breast, makes the city of God rejoice more abundantly with the force of a river (Psalm 45).

But that Vessel of Election, who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12) and learned his gospel not according to man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1), says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power except from God. Whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God” (Romans 13).

Our friends dream among little women and the simple crowd that one ought not to be subject to royal power; therefore, they say, it is false that every soul ought to be subject to power. But must Truth itself be accused of falsehood? Or should we seek proof concerning him who spoke in the Apostle—Christ? (2 Corinthians 13.) Should we rival the Lord? Are we stronger than he?

He who resists the ordinance of God confidently considers himself stronger, since there is no power except from God. But what does the prophet say? “Let all who fight against you, O Lord, be confounded, and the men who resist you shall perish” (Isaiah 41).

Rudolph, Hildebrand, Eggebert, and countless princes resisted God’s ordinance in the emperor Henry. And behold, they perished as though they had never existed, because it was plainly necessary that their beginning should have been evil, since their end was most evil.

Now, since those on the opposite side fight against us from a distance with their arguments, let us contend before your judgment, where the right is—or even before your own judgment—and use the testimony not of a usurer in a dwelling almost not his own [the printed wording is uncertain], but of Christ and the ancient Fathers. And lest it perhaps be rejected, let this be the law of the contest: either let me pass over to the judgment of the peoples, or let us win you for our Lord the emperor through our triumph.

Let this also be heeded: “If anyone preaches another gospel to you than the one that was preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1). This anathema was thundered not by a trafficker in profane novelty but from the third heaven.

Concerning those who, ignorant of God’s justice and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted themselves to God’s justice (Romans 10), I would say confidently: “Let them be cursed” [perhaps, “They will be cursed”], “and you will bless; let those who rise against me be confounded, but your servant shall rejoice” (Psalm 108). For, as you say, Lord, “without me you can do nothing” (John 15), and you do not condemn the just man when he is judged” (Psalm 36).

“Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master” (Romans 14).

*End of Waltram’s Letter.*

When the aforesaid Count Louis received this letter, he summoned the venerable Stephen, also called Herrand, bishop of Halberstadt, and gave it to him to read. He asked him, after examining it carefully, to counter it with a suitable response according to the rule of truth, and, by the authority of the Holy Spirit and the testimony of the Scriptures, to close the mouth of the blasphemer and the lips of the man uttering iniquity against justice, so that he might no longer bark madly against the Church of God or rage against it.

The venerable bishop, having accepted the letter at the count’s request and examined it carefully, summoned a notary and dictated a letter. In it he first rebuked the aforesaid Bishop Waltram as a heretic and simoniac. He also proved that King Henry was a heretic and excommunicated and therefore ought not to be called king. He declared that Henry sold bishoprics for money, for the sword, for adultery, and for Sodomitic impurity.

But let the text of that letter itself now be set forth, so that the fervor of that venerable man in maintaining justice may be recognized.

## Letter of Count Louis, or of Stephen, Bishop of Halberstadt

[Col. 1443D] Count Louis to Waltram: whatever is worthy of such a title.

“Just as a good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart, so an evil man brings forth evil from an evil treasure” (Matthew 12; Luke 6). Whence comes such arrogance in you that you provoked me to indignation with insults so injurious?

You obliquely call my lords and fathers, who strengthen me on the way of justice, men of blood, like Satan; and you say that the admonitions of salvation which they offer are dreams of little women and the simple crowd.

Does God need your judgment in order for you to speak deceitfully on his behalf? Iniquity has taught your mouth, and you imitate the tongue of blasphemers, so that the Prophet rightly says of you: “He refused to understand, so as to do good; he meditated iniquity in his bed” (Psalm 35).

Although you have spoken perversely in proportion to your perversity, we nevertheless resolved to set a guard over our mouth and kept silent when the sinner stood against us (Psalm 38).

But the divine word stirs us, saying: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Proverbs 26). Shall folly resound while wisdom is silent? Shall falsehood speak while truth is silent? Shall darkness cover the earth and the Lord not rise?

No indeed: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it” (John 1). Through this reflection our heart grew hot, and in our meditation the fire burned” (Psalm 38).

Therefore we speak out and cry aloud, and, as far as we can, ward off the little foxes that demolish the Lord’s vineyards (Song of Songs II), fearing that prophecy which reproaches us: “You have not gone up to oppose them, nor set up a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezek. XIII). Let all who have ears to hear listen—not you, who have ears and do not hear, who have eyes and do not see (Ps. CXIII), who have made the light within you into darkness (Luke XI)—let all, I say, who are whole-hearted and have ears for hearing listen to how either you fail to understand, or pretend not to understand, what you say and what you affirm (I Tim. I). You invite us to submit to Lord Henry, whom they call emperor, and, insofar as one can understand you, you impose upon us the necessity of being subject to him in every respect, as though by an apostolic argument, saying: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers; for there is no power except from God. Therefore whoever resists the power resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII). We say that you understand this sentence of the Apostle badly and interpret it worse.

For if every power is from God, as you understand it, what does the Lord mean when he says through the prophet concerning certain men: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not acknowledge them” (Hos. VIII)? If every power is from God, as you understand it, what does the Lord mean when he says: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you” (Matt. V)? For what is power if not an eye? Certainly Augustine, in his exposition of the Apostle’s sentence, “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. XIII), says: “If the power commands something that is against God, then despise the power, fearing the power.”

Is there injustice with the Lord? Is Christ a minister of sin? Far be it! What, then, shall we say? Is a prophetic declaration issued that differs from the Apostle’s? Augustine says: “The one Spirit does not blow discordant pipes.” Let us therefore listen to the Apostle agreeing with himself, explaining himself, and destroying his own enemy and avenger: “There is no power except from God.” What follows? “Whoever,” you say, “resists the power,” and so forth. Far be it! That does not follow. What does follow? “But the things that are from God have been ordained”—this, precisely, is what we are asking.

[Col. 1445D] O deceitful tongue, O heart contriving evil! “A spirit passing away and not returning” (Ps. LXXVI). Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit? (Acts III.) Let your own conscience accuse you. “Behold, the wicked flees when no one pursues” (Prov. XXVIII). Why, in order to deceive, did you wish to suppress the truth? Why did you steal the marrow, why the soul, of this sentence? For if these words are removed from the middle of the apostolic sentence, it will lie there, inconsistent with itself and lifeless.

The divine saying is fulfilled: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it” (Prov. XXVI). Certainly you will be able to escape neither the guilt of theft nor its punishment. What will you answer, wretched man, to the Judge who is to come, when he demands profit from his merchant-servants, while you are brought forward as a defrauder of the Lord’s money? (Matt. XXV.) Why did you not fear the judgment and the noose of the traitor, lest a similar offense be followed by a similar vengeance?

Foreseeing through the Holy Spirit that you and heretics like you would arise in the Church—men who would call good evil and evil good, who would make darkness light and light darkness (Isa. V), who would seize upon sentences of truth as opportunities for introducing error—the Apostle, after saying, “There is no power except from God,” cut off the conjecture of a depraved interpretation by adding: “But the things that are from God have been ordained.” Give us, then, an ordained power, and we will not resist it; indeed, we shall immediately submit our hands.

I wonder whether there is even a drop of blood in you, since you are not ashamed to say that Lord Henry is a king, or even that he possesses rank. Does rank, in your view, give the right to crime, to confuse what is permitted and what is forbidden, divine and human? Does it seem to you an office to sin against one’s own body—namely (shameful to say, unspeakable!), by an unheard-of crime throughout all the ages of the world, to turn one’s own wife into a brothel? Does it seem to you an office, when the Lord says, “Defend the widow” (Isa. I), to prostitute widows who plead for the equity of judgment through unspeakable defilement? Whoever calls such things ordered and sound—let mad Orestes himself, in his madness, swear that such a man has an insane head. Until these most wretched times, nature loved secrecy; but your king, delivered over to a depraved mind, has exposed nature’s covering, putting every form of shame on public display.

[Col. 1446C] But let us pass over the countless other matters—namely, the burning of churches, plundering, murders, arsons, mutilations, and similar deeds, which he is capable of committing but which we cannot enumerate—and speak of those things that weigh most heavily upon the Church of God. Listen, then, to what is true, not embellished; listen to what is strong, not witty.

Everyone who sells spiritual dignities is a heretic. Lord Henry, whom they call king, sells bishoprics and abbeys: the Constance, Bamberg, Mainz, and several other bishoprics, for money; Regensburg, Augsburg, and Strasbourg, for the sword; the abbey of Fulda, for adultery; and the bishopric of Münster—what it is impious to say or hear—for Sodomitic impurity. If you should shamelessly wish to deny these things, heaven and earth being witnesses, even all the little scholars returning from the bakehouse will conclude: “Therefore Lord Henry is a heretic.”

For these unspeakable evils he has been excommunicated by the apostolic see; and because we are Catholics, he will be able to obtain neither the kingdom nor any authority over us. Indeed, since you weary us with the hatred of our brothers, understand that we direct hatred toward no one out of lack of affection, but out of piety. Far be it from us to say that Henry should be counted among brothers or Christians: since he does not listen to the Church correcting him so many times, he is regarded “as a heathen and a publican” (Matt. XVIII).

We offer our hatred of him to God as a great sacrifice, saying with the Psalmist: “Have I not hated those who hate you, O Lord, and wasted away because of your enemies? I have hated them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII). The truth, commending the dignity of this hatred, says: “If anyone does not hate father and mother, brothers and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV).

Those, therefore, are not rightly reproached for hatred who are commanded, when we stray from the way of God, to hate our own life, father and mother, and every affection that obstructs us on the way of God. Hence it is that, with every zeal and every effort, we labor so that we may also beware of the enemies of the Church as adversaries, and hate them not because they are ours, but because they are enemies of God.

Moreover, when you persuade us that peace must be maintained with all human beings, you must remember that the Apostle prefaced this with: “If it is possible” (Rom. XII). It is not possible, however, for us to have peace with those who are opposed to God. Who does not know that the Lord and Savior not only commends peace when he says, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV), but that he himself is peace, as the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II)?

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Our peace,” while commending peace? “Do not think,” he says, “that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). What is this? Why peace, and a sword? Why does peace declare war? Clearly, so that the devil’s peace may be destroyed. For the devil has his own peace, of which the Lord says: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his courtyard, his possessions are in peace” (Luke XI).

O how powerfully the devil now guards this courtyard through you, his satellites! Protected by the shield of falsehood and the helmet of faithlessness, you admit no darts of truth and no arrows of faith. Yet our Lord, coming as the stronger armed man, can overcome your strong man and take away the weapons in which he trusts (ibid.). We are therefore not rightly blamed if we detest that peace, more cruel than every war, which Truth itself rejects with tears over Jerusalem, saying: “If only you had known, even on this your day, the things that are for your peace” (Luke XIX); and which the Psalm also rejects: “I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII).

[Col. 1448A] But since you condemn Pope Gregory, King Rudolf, and Margrave Egbert to the most wretched death, while you praise your lord because he survives them, it is plainly evident that you are devoid of all spiritual reflection. Is it not better to die well than to live badly? “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness” (Matt. V). By your reasoning, you would also consider Nero blessed because he survived the Apostles Peter and Paul, Herod because he survived the Apostle James, and Pilate because he survived the Lord Jesus Christ. What could be said more insane or more wretched than such an opinion?

Therefore restrain your grandiloquent tongue from this blasphemy as well—unless perhaps you count yourself among those who, seeing the glory of the righteous at the end and performing repentance too late and without fruit, groaning in anguish of spirit, will say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We senseless people considered their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they have been counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness did not shine upon us. What did pride profit us? What did the boasting of riches bring us? All things passed away like a shadow” (Wis. V).

Writing these words upon an adamantine memory, we despise every likeness that exalts itself against the truth of God. We may glory in tribulations; we may be slandered, proscribed, driven out, and finally killed; but we cannot be bent or conquered. And with great rejoicing we exult over what you, as a boy, an adolescent, and a much-frequented young man, not yet old in heart, conceived concerning our fathers, who, by despising the commands of princes, earned eternal rewards.

Moreover, weighing your statements with careful scrutiny, we wish, as it were, to compare spiritual things with spiritual things. But just as . . .

And many other things follow. The rest is lacking; that it was extensive is attested by this closing statement of Dodechin: “And many other things follow.”

[Col. 1447]

[Col. 1449]

# Bernaldus’s Treatise on the Multiple Condemnation of Berengar, Arch-Heresiarch

(*Germania sacra*, vol. II, p. 427, from the edition of P. F. Chifflet.)

## Notice

It is regrettable that this treatise—or rather, its preface—to another treatise on the body and blood of the Lord, bearing Bernaldus’s name, perished in the last fire of our monastery, in 1768, together with its copy. I have as an unimpeachable witness our most illustrious abbot and prince, Martin Gerbert, who before that disastrous fire had manuscripts of this kind copied by scribes. This little work would therefore have been lost, had not both Bernaldus’s name and the treatise itself been preserved by such weighty testimony and by Chifflet’s *Writers on the Catholic Faith* (Dijon, 1656, quarto). From this, too, Chifflet’s conjecture that Blasius was the author of this treatise is placed beyond doubt; the similarity of style and subject also reveals that he was this same Bernaldus of ours. This very treatise is also found in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. IX, p. 1050, taken from the cited collection of Chifflet; it seemed appropriate to place here beforehand his preface, furnished with notes.

## Chifflet’s Preface

[Col. 1449A] It is certain that Berengar, the deceitful arch-heresiarch, died in advanced age, in the year of Christ 1088 [Note: [Col. 1449B] Bernoldus records his death in the *Chronicle* under the year 1083.], on the sixth day of January. Concerning him William of Malmesbury says in Book III of his *History of England*: “He also died on the very day of the Epiphany, and, recalling with a prolonged groan that [Note: [Col. 1449B] In the printed editions it reads: ‘How many wretched young men, once, in the first heat of youth, his sect infected,’ etc.] his sect had infected certain wretched youths in the first flower of their age, he said: ‘Today, on the day of his manifestation, my Lord Jesus Christ will appear to me, as I hope, for glory on account of my repentance, or, as I fear, for punishment on account of the others.’”

Nor did he lack a panegyrist, though at that time one whose praise was itself unpraiseworthy—namely Hildebert [Note: [Col. 1449B] P. Anton. Beaugendre Maurianus published at Paris in 1708, folio, the works of Hildebert of Le Mans, first bishop and later archbishop of Tours, together with a preliminary account of his life. There he ably defends him against the twofold accusation brought against him here, as does Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, eleventh century, chapter 6, article 7.] [who composed an epitaph for him full of many praises]—a shameful young man, also disgraced in his clerical life because of incontinence; this is what Ivo, bishop of Chartres, reproaches him with in Letter 277, after his recent election as bishop of Le Mans.

Our present author conducted his funeral more prudently in that same year, 1088, as he himself testifies, in the fortieth year from the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Saint Leo IX [Col. 1450A]. Fearing that Berengar might perhaps have hidden followers even in monasteries, he first recalls that the Berengarian heresy had been condemned by the Catholic Church in so many councils as no heresy had previously been condemned; then, from the Fathers, he teaches that all accomplices, followers, and communicants of a depravity once condemned are regarded as sharing the same fate [Note: [Col. 1449B] He treats the same argument repeatedly in the preceding little works as well.].

He reveals himself to be a monk when, near the end of the work, he numbers himself among the simpler brethren. That he was a Benedictine from the monastery of Saint Blasius in Swabia is made probable by the fact that in the Jura manuscript this note on Berengar’s multiple condemnation is appended to a catalogue of the Roman apostles, apparently written by the same author and ending with Gregory VII. Under Gregory he collects, incidentally (*παρέργως*, “by the way”), information about the flourishing religious life of the cell of Saint Blasius and its early fathers.

[Note: [Col. 1450B] Bernoldus mentions the flourishing condition of this monastery in several places in the *Chronicle*, under the years 1083, 1094, and others, although he says nothing there about its earliest fathers.]

If you ask how this codex came to the monastery of Saint Eugendus, or Saint Claudius of the Jura, so far removed from the monastery of Saint Blasius, consider the following. Around the year 1090, Cuno of Hasenburg, bishop of Lausanne, founded the monastery of Herilac, or Erlach, on the island of Saint John, adjacent to Lake Biel, in the Raurican region of Burgundian Switzerland, now in the Bernese territory. [Col. 1450B] Its foundation was completed by Burchard of Hasenburg, Cuno’s brother and, from the year 1072, bishop of Basel. He sent there, from the monastery of Saint Blasius—whose advocacy he then held—the first colony of monks with Abbot Ekkehard (*History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 248). These men, like the colonists sent elsewhere to the monasteries of Muri and Göttweig, as we have already said, brought with them codices written at Saint Blasius, especially recently composed ones. Among them, without doubt, were the works of the author Bernaldus, above all the present work, written for the purpose of preserving monks from Berengar’s heresy. This could easily have been the reason why a copy of it was sent from the monastery of Erlach to the not very distant monastery of Saint Claudius.]

Of the six councils [Note: [Col. 1450B] Bernaldus lists only those councils held by the supreme pontiffs against Berengar. Natalis Alexander enumerates the other particular councils, especially those held in France, *Ecclesiastical History*, eleventh century, dissertation 1, where all these matters are examined more carefully.] in which he says that Berengar’s heresy was attacked, the first was the Roman council presided over by Pope Leo IX, after Easter in the year of Christ 1050. The second was the Vercelli council in September of that same year, under the same pontiff [Note: [Col. 1451C] Here Mabillon must be consulted in his observations *On Berengar’s Multiple Condemnation* (*Old Analecta*, new edition, p. 513). There, not without hesitation, he assigns both councils to the year 1050, relying chiefly on the authority of Hermann the Lame, a contemporary, who likewise assigns the same year to both in his chronicle. Yet Mabillon himself is not sufficiently consistent: in *Benedictine Centuries*, V, p. 895, he places the same Roman synod, at which Gerard, bishop of Toul, was simultaneously enrolled among the saints, in the year 1049, because that synod must have preceded the solemn elevation of the saint’s body at Toul by the pope, carried out around the end of October. P. Bouquet likewise holds this view in his collection, vol. XI, p. 474. But that both events took place in 1050 is clear from the letters of canonization, in which this synod is said to have been held around the Nones of May, whereas the synod of 1049 was held on April 11. See Natalis Alexander, cited work.].

The third was the Council of Tours in 1055, presided over by Hildebrand, legate of Pope Victor, later Pope Gregory VII. The fourth was the Roman council of 113 bishops under Pope Nicholas II, in April 1059. The fifth was a Roman council under Gregory VII. The sixth was likewise a Roman council under the same pope, of 150 bishops, in February 1079; the present author testifies that he attended it. Lanfranc and Guitmund, in their books against Berengar, mention the first four synods. The council volumes contain the sixth. But, so far as I know, no one except this author has committed that fifth council under Gregory VII—the earlier of the two—to writing [Note: [Col. 1451D] Therefore, if no one else mentions this synod, Bernaldus is none other than Berthold of Constance, who records the same matter in his *Chronicle* under the year 1078: “At this Roman autumnal synod Berengar of Angers, a canon, was summoned synodally so that he might recover from his heresy, and a postponement was granted to him until the next synod. See Mabillon, cited work, p. 515, and Natalis Alexander, cited work.]. Yet it must have been one of the five held at Rome under the same Gregory before the year 1079; and certainly, as we think, it was the one convened in November 1078 [Col. 1451B]. For this author writes that Berengar was granted a hearing by Pope Gregory VII at two general synods in Rome, and reports that only at the later one was he compelled to abjure his heresy and profess the Catholic faith.

Hence, no doubt, the pseudo-cardinal Benno [Note: [Col. 1451D] Flacius Illyricus counts this Benno, a pseudo-cardinal—if he ever existed, since he is unknown to other writers until the thirteenth century—among the witnesses to the truth of his Church. He also inserted his book *On the Life and Deeds of Hildebrand* into his own work at p. 220, and others later eagerly adopted this excellent witness [Col. 1452C]. Yet Baronius, both Pagius and Natalis Alexander, and even Fleury proved him false in most matters and manifestly nothing but an impudent slanderer.] seized the opportunity to slander and to invent the following lies about the most holy pontiff:

“‘That same presumptuous man,’ he says, ‘ordered the cardinals to fast, so that God might show who held the more correct opinion concerning the body of the Lord: the Roman Church or Berengar. By this he was plainly proved an unbeliever, since it is written in the Council of Nicaea that “one who is doubtful in faith is an unbeliever.”’”

Accordingly, nineteen schismatic bishops who gathered against Gregory at Mainz in 1080, on Pentecost itself, judged him unworthy of the pontificate [concerning this pseudo-synod, see the Abbot of Ursperg under the year 1080 [Note: [Col. 1452C] See also Baronius under this year, no. 18 and following]], both for other utterly false reasons and also because he called into question the Catholic and apostolic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and because he had formerly been a disciple of the heretic Berengar.

We therefore suppose that Berengar was granted his first hearing by Gregory at the Roman council held in November of the year of Christ 1078. There, when the crafty old man had brought forward many arguments in defense of his error, especially arguments drawn from a mistaken understanding of Augustine, the pontiff pronounced further judgment and postponed the decision of the whole matter to the next synod, to be held three months later, that is, in February of the year 1079. In the meantime he ordered fasts and prayers to obtain divine assistance, lest he appear to have decided precipitately on so grave a matter.

For the issue was not merely Berengar’s condemnation, which was already known to have been carried out by four previous synods; the pious shepherd also had to take care that the many sheep that had strayed after Berengar should be brought back to the folds of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1452B] Berengar’s objections therefore had to be weighed, and the fathers of the synod had to be shown how he, by misusing the words of divine Scripture, Saint Augustine, and other ancient teachers, spoke contrary to their meaning. There was nothing here for the schismatics to criticize in a most prudent and pious pontiff. But by their monstrous slanders they achieved this much: driven by hatred against a most holy man, they were thought by everyone of sound judgment to be raving and insane.

Concerning Christinus, as this author calls him, already a bishop in the year 1088, who shortly before his episcopate had refuted the Berengarian heresy in writing together with Lanfranc, I would have some hesitation, unless it were evident that this very man was Guitmund [Note: [Col. 1452C]

That Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, had two names is clearly inferred from Paul of Bernried in his *Life of Gregory VII*. When describing the pope’s legates sent to the assembly at Forchheim in 1077, he lists them as follows:

“Among these were Bernard, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and another Bernard, a religious abbot from Marseille . . . He also brought with him a certain outstanding teacher named Christian, later bishop of the city of Aversa, whose excellent work against Berengar of Tours survives.”

D. Rivet, author of the *Literary History of France* (vol. VIII, p. 556), holds that Guitmund first changed his name at Rome, where he had taken refuge from his monastery of Saint Leutfred in Normandy, so that he might in this way remain hidden from William, king of England, who was planning to promote him to ecclesiastical dignities. The anonymous author of Melk likewise calls him Christian in chapter 90, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, though he is far from consistent. For, after reporting in the cited chapter that a Christian, bishop of Apulia—and therefore of Aversa—had argued invincibly against Berengar, which certainly refers to our Guitmund, he immediately introduces in chapter 102 another Guidmund, also called Christian. This man had first been a monk at Stavelot; when he was about to be made abbot and sent to govern another place, he fled, and, seeking an unknown province so that he could not be recognized, changed his name to something better, taking for himself the name Christian, common to all the faithful. Eventually, after being sought and found, he was made bishop of Aversa under Gregory VII.

But this Christian or Guitmund of Aversa is wrongly confused with another Christian, surnamed Druthmar, a writer of the ninth century. Druthmar, from Old Corbie, where he was a monk, was summoned to the monastery of Stavelot, where he taught the younger monks sacred letters for a long time; he also dedicated his commentary on Matthew to them (vol. XV of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, p. 86). Since the Melk author says that this was done by Guitmund, he was entirely mistaken, confusing Druthmar with Guitmund. See the *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 84.

Scholars disagree about when Guitmund or Christian became bishop of Aversa. Some report that it happened as early as 1061, under Alexander II; others, under Gregory VII; and others, under Urban II. The first group is shown to be mistaken by the testimony of Paul of Bernried cited above, according to which he was not yet a bishop in 1077. Pagius, in his critical notes under the year 1105 [Col. 1453D], maintains that this was done by Gregory VII, on the basis of Ivo of Chartres’s *Decree* (part IV, chapter 213). There Gregory heads the chapter “If custom” in a letter to Wimund, bishop of Aversa, whom we believe to be the same person as Christinus or Christian—namely, the second bishop of that see with this name (Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol., p. 487). His works are found in vol. XVIII of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, where he is called archbishop because of the honor of the pallium granted him by the pope. Chifflet’s conjecture is therefore sound.]

the bishop of Aversa. For since Peter of Cluny, in his book against the Petrobrusian heretics, section “After the denial of baptism,” not far from the beginning (vol. XXII of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, p. 1057), mentions only three men who wrote against Berengar [Col. 1453A]—namely, Lanfranc, Guitmund, and Algerus—and since it is certain that Algerus [Note: [Col. 1453D] While he was still alive, Nicholas, a canon of Liège, wrote a eulogy of Algerus, first a scholastic of Liège and later a monk of Cluny; Mabillon published it in his *Analecta*, p. 129. Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, also makes honorable mention of him after his death in Book III, Letter 2 (Cluniac Library, p. 798). In the cited letter against the Petrobrusians, he gives the following judgment concerning these three opponents of Berengar:

“Of these, the first, Lanfranc, argued well, fully, and perfectly concerning the truth of the body and blood, which is veiled beneath the sacraments; the next, Guitmund, better, more fully, and more perfectly; the last, Algerus, best, most fully, and most perfectly, leaving nothing even for the most scrupulous reader to seek.”

Erasmus judges the last two in the preface to the works he published at Antwerp in 1536: “Guitmund is sharper and more ardent, and possesses more rhetorical spirit; Algerus is calmer and more religious. Both are well versed in dialectic and in the rest of philosophy, although without obstinacy. The three books of Algerus, *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which alone among nearly all his other works have survived to our time, are also found in vol. XXI of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*.] was neither a bishop nor perhaps even born in 1088—for he became a monk at Cluny after the death of Frederick, bishop of Liège, who was killed by poison on May 27, 1121, and lived for a long time under the discipline of Peter the Venerable, as Peter the abbot himself testifies in Book III, Letter 2, and as the ancient Cluniac chronicle records in Wion, Book II, *Tree of Life*, chapter 62.

Therefore, since before the year 1088 no bishop other than Lanfranc and Guitmund is found to have written against Berengar, and since this author says that Lanfranc and Bishop Christinus did so, we either suppose that Guitmund had two names and was also called Christinus—or rather Christian—or else that this writer, suffering a lapse of memory, put Christinus in place of Guitmund.

Finally, what is said here about the form of professing the Catholic faith, or of abjuring the error prescribed for heretics by the Council of Ephesus, is indeed found in the letter of Cyril, or of the Council of Ephesus, to Nestorius, which begins “Our Savior” and is entitled in the canon book of the ancient Roman Church “The Canon of the Holy First Council of Ephesus.” It appears in the Greek-Latin acts, part I, chapter 26; nevertheless, as it seems, in the codex used by this author it was chapter fifteen.

# On the Multiple Condemnation of Berengar, Arch-Heresiarch

[Col. 1453]

[Col. 1453B] **1.** Berenger of Angers [Note: [Col. 1454D] In this work he is addressed in this form, “Beringerius,” apparently through a copyist’s error, although elsewhere both names are commonly used indiscriminately.] founded the heresy named after him and dared to deny the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, contrary to evangelical truth. Specifically, he asserted that the bread and wine in the Lord’s sacrifice are changed into the Lord’s body and blood not truly or essentially, but only figuratively. This is manifestly contrary to the Catholic faith and evangelical truth, as the holy Fathers have taught.

**II.** Therefore Pope Saint Leo IX, in his own time, investigated this same heresy, which had been brought before the apostolic see by Berengar’s own letters, through the judgment of a general synod, and condemned it after investigation by synodal judgment. He also deprived Berengar himself of communion with the Church, which Berengar, by his assertions, had sought to deprive of communion with the body and blood of the Lord.

Then he summoned him to be heard at the next synod, which he was to hold at Vercelli in the following September [Col. 1454B]. Berengar himself did not come to this synod; certain supporters of his arrived instead. Claiming to be his legates and wishing to defend him, they failed at the very first entrance.

The apostolic lord, however, once again condemned Berengar’s doctrine by synodal judgment, as well as John Scotus’s book *On the Body of the Lord*, under anathema [Note: [Col. 1454D] This is John Scotus, called Eriugena, a professor at Oxford in the ninth century, whom Berengar regarded as his predecessor. See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, ninth century, dissertation XIV]. He confirmed the faith that all Catholics had hitherto held, and still hold, concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood.

At both synods Lord Lanfranc, later archbishop of the English, confesses in writing that he was present. He testifies that at the former he was accused and cleared of Berengar’s heresy, and that at both he assented, together with all Catholics, to the condemnation of that heresy [Col. 1454C] [Note: [Col. 1454D] In the fourth chapter of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, among his works published at Paris in 1648, p. 234, where he discusses the Council of Vercelli; and likewise Guitmund, Book III.].

**III.** Pope Victor, too, successor of Pope Saint Leo both in office and in authority, sent a legate into Gaul—namely, the venerable Hildebrand, then archdeacon and the apostolic pontiff of our own time [Note: [Col. 1455D] He had already died by the year 1088, when this was written. Concerning this Council of Tours, see Labbe, vol. IX, p. 108, from Guitmund and Lanfranc, as well as other writers throughout; also Bernoldus in his chronicle under the year 1055]—and convened a general synod at Tours.

There Berengar himself, after being given the choice of defending himself, since he was entirely unable to defend himself, anathematized his own heresy under oath and promised under the same oath that from then on he would preserve the common faith of the holy Church concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, although afterward he returned to the same heresy.

**IV.** Pope Nicholas, however, granted this same Berengar a hearing at a general synod in Rome [Note: [Col. 1455D] Namely, in 1059, although Bernoldus in his *Chronicle* first reports this in the year 1060 in nearly the same words] and investigated his case by synodal judgment with 113 bishops.

But once again, since he was unable to defend his sect, he finally, as though corrected, burned with his own hand the books of his heresy in the presence of the apostolic lord and the entire synod. Having renounced his error, he renewed under oath the Catholic profession he had made at the Council of Tours, declaring as follows:

V. “I, Berengarius, an unworthy deacon of the church of Saint Maurice of Angers, acknowledging the true Catholic and apostolic faith, anathematize every heresy, especially that of which I have hitherto been accused: the heresy that attempts to assert that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, after consecration, merely a sacrament and not the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they cannot be handled or broken sensibly except in the sacrament alone by the hands of priests, or be ground by the teeth of the faithful.

[Col. 1455C] “But I consent to the holy Roman Church and to the apostolic see; and with mouth and heart I profess that, concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table, I hold the faith which the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas, and this holy synod by evangelical and apostolic authority, handed down as binding and confirmed for me: namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, after consecration, not merely a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they are handled, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful sensibly not merely in the sacrament but in truth. I swear this by the holy consubstantial Trinity (ὁμοούσιον), and by these most holy Gospels of Christ.

[Col. 1455D] “Those who come against this faith, together with their doctrines and followers, I declare worthy of eternal anathema. [Col. 1456A] But if I myself should at any time presume to think or preach contrary to these things, let me be subject to the severity of the canons. Having read and reread this, I willingly subscribed.”

[Note: [Col. 1455D] This oath is also reported in the acts of this council in Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 1112, and in Lanfranc, where Cardinal Humbert, by the pope’s command, offered Berengarius the oath which he himself had composed for Berengarius to confirm. That this is to be done in the abjuration of heresy is prescribed in Saint Cyril of Alexandria’s letter to Nestorius, in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, Labbe, *Councils*, vol. III, p. 397, no. 2.]

The holy Synod of Ephesus prescribed this form of oath and anathema for those renouncing any heresies in chapter 15, and decreed that those disgraced by accusation of heresy should be purged from heresy only through an abjuration of this kind. Accordingly, they received such a satisfaction from Berengarius.

VI. The lord Pope Nicholas immediately sent this sworn profession of Berengarius throughout various kingdoms, so that everyone might give thanks to God for his conversion, since they had previously been greatly scandalized by his defection. But Berengarius, in his customary manner, did not fear to return to his own vomit, and, more than all other heretics, presumed in words and writings to blaspheme the Roman pontiffs and the holy Roman Church. Indeed, he did not fear to call Pope Saint Leo not a pontiff but a “pompous pontiff” (*pompificem*) and a “fleshy pontiff” (*pulpificem*); the holy Roman Church a council of vanity and the church of the wicked; and the Roman see, in speech and writing, not the apostolic see but the seat of Satan.

[Note: [Col. 1455D] All these things are abundantly established from Lanfranc; [Col. 1456D] for only a few of Berengarius’s writings have come down to us. On this subject, see Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, eleventh century, dissertation I; Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 405 onward; and Rivetus Maurianus, *Literary History of France*, vol. VIII.]

Nevertheless, after so many synodal condemnations and abjurations, he did not cease secretly to disseminate his heresy everywhere through his disciples and to infect every unwary person with the poison of his heresy.

VII. Therefore the venerable Pope Alexander, Nicholas’s successor, warned him in a sufficiently friendly letter to abandon his sect and no longer scandalize the holy Church. But he did not wish to desist from what he had begun, and did not fear to send him this very reply in a letter of his own. [Col. 1456C]

[Note: [Col. 1456D] Apart from Bernold, no one makes mention of this matter, nor is anything recorded as having been done against this heretic under this pontificate, except that Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, held a council against his errors in 1063, as Mabillon writes in *Analecta*, p. 514; though others place it as early as 1055.]

VIII. For this reason the most reverend Pope Gregory, Alexander’s successor, again granted Berengarius a hearing at two general synods in Rome.

[Note: [Col. 1456D] Namely, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December in 1078, where, according to Bernold in his *Chronicle*, a postponement was granted to Berengarius until the next synod, which was held in February of the following year, 1079.]

But since he could not deny that his sect was contrary to the Catholic faith, he once again chose under oath to renounce it and to profess the Catholic faith, as he had done at the earlier councils.

IX. We have learned of Berengarius’s heresy being condemned at so many councils both from the reports of faithful men who took part in those councils and from the writings of religious men who wrote about them with complete fidelity. [Col. 1456D] For these same councils are found to have been held in our own times, [Col. 1457A] within fewer than forty years, counting the years from the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Saint Leo IX to the present year.

[Note: [Col. 1457D] That is, the year in which this work was written.]

The present year is 1088 from the Incarnation of the Lord. Thus many who took part in those councils are still alive, and they have given us wholly faithful testimony concerning them. We ourselves also attended the last general synod under Pope Gregory VII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089.

[Note: From this it is clear why Bernold, in the expanded *Chronicle*, reported concerning the synod of 1079 things that are found nowhere else and that plainly reveal an eyewitness and present informant. I would suppose that Bernold, as a most skilled expert in the canons, reached Rome in the company either of Altmann, bishop of Passau and apostolic legate, or of the abbot of Reichenau, whom he likewise says in the expanded *Chronicle* to have gone to that synod in the same year. On this occasion Bernold appears to have become known to Pope Gregory; later, in 1084, by Gregory’s command, he was ordained by the legate Otto as a priest and apostolic penitentiary, as he himself acknowledges concerning himself in the *Chronicle*.]

We saw Berengarius stand in the midst of the synod and, as we said above, renounce with the sacrament of his own hand the heresy concerning the body of the Lord before everyone—namely, in the presence of Pope Gregory; Henry, patriarch of Aquileia; and the most reverend bishops Peter of Albano, Blessed Anselm of Lucca, [Col. 1457B] Landulf of Pisa, Reginher of Florence, Hugh of Die, Altmann of Passau, and the remaining one hundred and fifty bishops and abbots, as well as innumerable clerics.

X. The decrees of these councils, therefore—so many general councils, and so authoritatively established by apostolic authority—ought to suffice for us against the Berengarian heresy, since the holy Fathers also judged that the authority of a single general council was sufficient against any heresy, even though the Roman pontiff had confirmed that council not in person but through his legates.

Thus they judged the Council of Nicaea sufficient against the Arians, the Council of Constantinople against the Macedonians, the Council of Ephesus against the Nestorians, and the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians. [Col. 1457C] None of these did the Roman pontiffs sanction in person, but through their legates. Much more, then, ought several general synods against one single heresy to suffice for us when the Roman pontiffs themselves attended them and personally confirmed them by apostolic authority—especially since they did not differ from one another in these many synods, but unanimously condemned the Berengarian heresy under anathema at different councils.

Certainly, for any Catholic who does not seek to comprehend by reasoning everything that he believes, so that faith may have merit where human reason provides no demonstration, those many general councils of apostolic authority against this heresy ought unquestionably to suffice. [Col. 1458A] For, according to Saint Augustine’s assertion, every Catholic safely detests what he knows not to be in communion with the universal Church, established in the apostolic sees.

Augustine likewise says (*On Baptism*, book VII, chapter 53): “It is safe to assert with the confidence of a secure voice that which has been strengthened by the universal Church’s consensus in the governance of our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ.”

When any Catholic who is simply wise and wisely simple faithfully attends to this, he refuses even to listen to the quibbles of heretics, whose speech spreads like cancer, provided that he is secure about what he ought to believe according to the testimony of the holy Fathers and the universal consensus of the Church.

XI. [Col. 1458B] We too have resolved to satisfy such simple people in this brief document by simply presenting the testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and faithfully appending the synodal condemnations of the Berengarian heresy.

[Note: [Col. 1457D] Another little work by Bernold, *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body*, [Col. 1458D] arranged according to his customary practice from testimonies of the holy Fathers, evidently preceded this one; this short treatise on Berengarius’s condemnation was merely an appendix or preface to it. We lamented the loss of that work in the preliminary notice. I believe I have discovered it in the same Weingarten manuscript that contains the other works of Bernold published above. There I found two treatises on the same subject. The first, without a title, begins: “Thus it seems appropriate to treat concerning the body of the Lord,” and so forth; it also contains the same abjuration of Berengarius. The other, namely the *Questions on the Lord’s Body*, is nothing more than a continuation of the first. Since neither bears the author’s name and, moreover, their style is unlike Bernold’s, we have not thought it appropriate to insert them here, although they deserve publication.]

Nor did it seem necessary to us to enumerate Berengarius’s individual ravings and separately annul those once enumerated—especially since the most learned doctors, namely Lanfranc and Christianus, both most Christian in religion and learning and not long afterward bishops, wrote about these matters with the greatest clarity and decisively refuted each one with authoritative arguments.

[Note: More about these men was noted above, note 1474.]

Their books can indeed suffice even for the most inquisitive investigators, so that they may detect each of Berengarius’s evasions and consequently [Col. 1458C] recognize the arguments by which they were annulled. It was therefore unnecessary for us to awaken by enumeration those errors, already somewhat dormant and destined to sleep forever, and after the synodal condemnations once again offend Catholic ears with them.

XII. In this statement of faith, then, we offer these things by fraternal admonition to our simpler brethren—that is, to those like ourselves.

[Note: Bernold uses a similar expression frequently in his other little works.]

They should take the greatest care to ensure that nowhere do they assent to heretical persuasion against the Catholic and apostolic faith. For, according to the Apostle, “the doers and the consenters are encompassed by equal punishment”; according to Blessed Gelasius, all accomplices, followers, and communicants of an evil once condemned are judged to share the same lot; and according to Saint Ambrose [Col. 1459A] and the other holy Fathers, anyone who disagrees with the holy Roman Church in the doctrine of faith is plainly a heretic.

The oath set forth above, which apostolic and synodal authority confirmed and proposed to Berengarius for his satisfaction, contains in a sufficiently brief and clear form either the error in which he himself had fallen or what the holy Roman and universal [Col. 1460A] Church established must be believed. We must therefore observe this carefully and faithfully carry out what we have observed, so that we may condemn what the Church herself has condemned and receive what she herself receives; lest we ourselves rightly be condemned if we are found either to assent to heresy or in any way to dissent from the holy Roman Church.

# PART THREE OF THE WORKS OF SAINT GREGORY VII.—ROMAN COUNCILS

**First Roman Council**, for the reform of the condition of the Church. In the year of the Lord 1074. 750  

**Second Roman Council**, for the reform of the Church. 787  

**Third Roman Council**, at which Henry, king of Germany; Sigefredus, archbishop of Mainz; William, bishop of Utrecht; and Robert, bishop of Bamberg, are excommunicated, in the year of the Lord 1077. 789  

**Fourth Roman Council**, at which Gilbert of Ravenna, Theobald of Milan, and several other bishops are excommunicated, in the year of the Lord 1078. 796  

**Fifth Roman Council**, for the restoration of the Holy Church, in the year of the Lord 1078. 800  

**Sixth Roman Council**, at which Berengar, repeatedly summoned to penance and repeatedly relapsing, again abjured his heresy and professed the Catholic faith, in the year of the Lord 1079. 809  

**Seventh Roman Council**, at which the kingdom of Germany was taken from Henry and bestowed upon Rudolf, with the additional provision that thereafter investitures of benefices might neither be conferred nor received from laymen, in the year of the Lord 1080. 814  

**Eighth Roman Council**, concerning King Henry and certain bishops, in the year of the Lord 1081. 820  

**Ninth Roman Council**, in the year of the Lord 1083. 821  

**Tenth Roman Council**, at which Guibert, the antipope and heresiarch, and Henry, the false emperor, together with all their supporters, are excommunicated, in the year of the Lord 1084. 821
